Initially created: 2025-12-05T12:35:10.406+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial decree.
Later Study Heaven Tái
Táng,
an ancient state name.
Lù Démíng said: Zhōu Chéngwáng's younger maternal brother, Shū Yú, was enfeoffed in Táng.
Its land was the site of Emperor Yáo and Xià Yǔ's capital.
During the Hàn dynasty, it was called Tàiyuán Commandery,
located west of Mount Tàiháng and Mount Héng in ancient Jìzhōu,
in the plains of Tàiyuán and Tàiyuè.
The ancestors of the Lǐ Táng,
Lǐ Hǔ, along with Lǐ Bì and eight others, assisted Zhōu in conquering Wèi and achieved merit.
They were all made Pillar States,
and known as the Eight Pillar Families.
When Zhōu Mǐndì received the abdication from Wèi,
Hǔ had already passed away.
His merits were then posthumously recognized,
and he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Táng State.
His son, Bǐng, was born,
and succeeded to the title.
Bǐng fathered Yuān,
who succeeded to the title,
raised an army and captured Cháng'ān,
and was promoted to King of Táng.
He then received the abdication from Suí,
and the state was consequently named Táng.
Gāozǔ Shényáo Dàshèng Guāngxiào Huángdì, Superior, First Class
His personal name was Yuān,
courtesy name Shúdē,
originally from Lǒngxī Chéngjì.
His seventh-generation ancestor, Gǎo, ruled Xīliáng,
known as Liáng Wǔzhāo Wáng.
His great-grandson Xī settled in Wǔchuān;
Xī's grandson Hǔ,
followed Zhōu Wéndì,
and first settled in Cháng'ān.
Wǔdé First Year
(wùyín, 618)
In the fifth month of this year, he received the abdication from Suí,
and first changed the reign title.
1 Spring,
first month,
dìngwèi *shuò*.
Suí Gōngdì issued an edict allowing the King of Táng to wear his sword and shoes into the palace hall,
and be addressed without his personal name during ceremonies.
*Suí Zhì* says: According to Hàn custom, from the Son of Heaven to the myriad officials, none did not wear a sword.
Cài Mó's deliberation states: High officials granted special courtesy all wore swords and shoes into the hall.
They were not removed by attendant officials,
presumably to guard against blades.
In recent times, wooden ones have been used,
the origin of which is unclear;
Eastern Qí issued a decree,
calling them "xiangjian" (image swords),
meaning they resembled swords.
During Zhōu Wǔdì's time,
officials at banquets
all ascended their seats wearing swords.
At the beginning of Kāihuáng,
the old custom was followed,
and when ascending the hall in court attire,
they also did not remove them.
In the twelfth year,
following Cài Zhēng's memorial,
it was first decreed that all those who attended court and were to sit in the hall
should remove both swords and shoes.
For those not sitting,
who were summoned by imperial decree for memorials,
or needed to ascend the hall,
they should also remove their swords at their seats before ascending.
Ministers of Nàyán, Huángmén, Nèishǐ Lìng, Shìláng, and Shèrén, as officials who stood by and attended, did not remove them.
Their swords were all real blades, not fakes.
Also,
according to the decree set in Jìn Xiánkāng First Year,
the old custom was that from the Son of Heaven downwards, all wore hats, robes, and swords.
Today, the Son of Heaven uses a jade-ornamented, fire-pearl-tipped sword,
and only attendant officials wear swords into the hall;
from kings and dukes downwards,
unless granted special courtesy,
when led to ascend the hall,
all sit at their seats,
remove them, and then ascend.
Shoes with double soles are called *xì*,
single-soled ones are called *lǚ*.
All non-attendant officials
removed their *lǚ* before ascending the hall.
*Xì* were only worn with ceremonial robes and full dress;
*Lǚ* were used with all other attire.
During all court assemblies, when announcing or bowing,
one would say "So-and-so official";
not using the personal name
was also a special courtesy.
The character shàng
is pronounced *pān*.
The character biāo
is pronounced *pīzhāo*.
After the King of Táng captured Cháng'ān,
he sent letters to all commanderies and counties.
Consequently, from Shāngluò in the east,
*Suí Zhì* says: Shāngluò County belongs to Shàngluò Commandery,
named after Mount Shāng and the Luò River.
The chief officials of commanderies and counties, as well as bandit leaders and Dí and Qiāng chieftains,
competed to send their sons and younger brothers to meet him and offer surrender.
The relevant authorities received hundreds of such letters daily.
2 Wáng Shìchōng 既得東都兵，
進擊 Lǐ Mì 於洛北，
敗之，
遂屯鞏北。
鞏縣之北。
On the Xīnyǒu day,
Shìchōng ordered all his armies to build pontoon bridges to cross the Luò River and attack Mì.
Those whose bridges were completed first advanced first,
resulting in a disorganized front.
The Hǔbēn Lángjiàng, Wáng Biàn, broke Mì's outer stockade.
Mì's camp was thrown into a panic
and on the verge of collapse.
Shìchōng, unaware of this,
sounded horns to recall his troops.
Mì thereupon led his dare-to-die soldiers to counterattack.
Shìchōng was utterly defeated,
and over ten thousand men drowned while scrambling for the bridges.
Wáng Biàn died.
Shìchōng barely escaped with his life,
and all the armies north of the Luò River scattered.
Shìchōng dared not enter Dōngdū.
He fled north to Héyáng.
That night,
there was a strong wind and cold rain.
The soldiers, having waded through water and gotten soaked,
died by the tens of thousands from the cold along the way.
Shìchōng arrived at Héyáng with only a few thousand men.
The Kǎoyì states: The biographies of Lǐ Mì in the Suí Shū and Běi Shǐ say:
"Shìchōng moved his camp again to the north of the Luò River,
facing Gǒng County to the south.
Afterward, he built pontoon bridges across the Luò River
and attacked Mì with his entire army.
Mì sallied forth to attack them.
The government troops gradually retreated,
and tens of thousands drowned themselves.
Shìchōng barely escaped with his life
and dared not return to Dōngdū,
so he fled to Héyáng.
That night,
there was over a foot of snow and rain,
and nearly all those who followed him died."
The biography of Wáng Shìchōng says:
"Chōng was defeated,
and over ten thousand men drowned themselves in the water.
At that time, the weather was cold with heavy snow.
The soldiers, having crossed the water,
had their clothes all soaked.
Tens of thousands more died of cold along the way."
The biography of Púshān Gōng says:
"Shìchōng moved his camp to the north of the Luò River,
facing Mì across the Luò River.
Mì then built a long wall
and dug deep moats,
seventy lǐ in circumference, to fortify himself.
On the fifteenth day,
Shìchōng fought Mì east of Shíkū Sì.
Mì's army retreated in defeat.
Shìchōng crossed the Luò River to pursue them,
approaching Cāngchéng to establish a camp and moats.
Mì unleashed his troops in a fierce battle.
Shìchōng's cavalry abandoned their weapons and fled.
Innumerable men drowned.
Mì also issued a proclamation to his headquarters, saying: 'On the eleventh day of this month, Shìchōng deployed troops north of the Luò River at dawn
and secretly entered Yuèchéng.
On the fifteenth day of the same month,
Shìchōng and Wáng Biàncái and others again secretly crossed the water south of Cāngchéng,
daring to approach the city walls.'"
The Hélùo Jì says: On the sixteenth day,
"Chōng fought Mì east of Shíkū Sì."
It also says:
"That night,
they encountered strong wind and cold, rapid rain.
The soldiers froze to death,
fewer than one in ten survived.
Chōng escaped alone and fled by night,
straight to Héyáng."
The rest is as in the biography of Púshān Gōng.
The Lüè Jì says:
"On the Xīnyǒu day,
Wáng Shìchōng and others moved their troops north of the Luò River,
and ordered all armies to deploy troops along the bank.
Each army built pontoon bridges.
Those whose bridges were completed first immediately crossed.
As they did not cross in a unified manner,
Lǐ Mì launched an ambush.
Our army was utterly defeated.
Fifteen or sixteen out of ten drowned while scrambling for the bridges."
The Zá Jì says:
"In the twelfth month,
the Yuè King sent Tàicháng Shǎoqīng Wéi Jì and others to lead thirty thousand garrison troops and be under Shìchōng's command."
It also says:
"Wáng Biàn Zòng and others were defeated,
and the mass of troops also scattered.
More than half died scrambling for the bridges and plunging into the water.
Wáng Biàn Zòng and others were all lost.
Only Shìchōng was defeated but escaped,
fleeing with a few hundred cavalry to Dàtōngchéng.
Those defeated soldiers who managed to return
encountered heavy rain on the way,
and six or seven thousand froze to death.
Shìchōng remained at Dàtōng for over ten days,
fearing punishment and not returning.
In the fourteenth year,
first month,
the Yuè King sent Shìchōng's elder brother, Shìyùn, to Dàtōng to console him,
pardoning Shìchōng for the crime of losing his army."
According to Lǐ Dàoxuán's memorial to Lǐ Mì urging him to ascend the throne, it says:
"At that time, the pitch-pipe had just reached tài cù,
it was not yet time for light rain,
yet a downpour suddenly came,
and nearly all who were frozen died."
Now, consulting various books,
the date follows the biography of Púshān Gōng,
and the rain follows the Hélùo Jì.
Yuè Wáng Dòng sent an envoy to pardon him
and summoned him back to Dōngdū,
bestowing upon him gold, silk, and beautiful women to appease his mind.
Shìchōng gathered his scattered and lost troops,
obtaining over ten thousand men.
He garrisoned them at Hánjiāchéng.
Hánjiāchéng
was probably located north of the capital city.
According to the biography of Wáng Shìchōng in the Old History,
Hánjiā
was Cāngchéng.
Mì, capitalizing on his victory, advanced to occupy Jīnyōngchéng.
He repaired its gates, walls, and barracks and resided there.
The sound of gongs and drums
could be heard in Dōngdū.
Soon after,
he commanded an army of three hundred thousand,
deployed on Běimáng,
pressing south against Shàngchūnmén.
On the Yǐchǒu day,
Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū Duàn Dá and Mínbù Shàngshū Wéi Jīn led troops out to resist him.
Dá, seeing the strength of Mì's forces,
was afraid and returned first.
Mì unleashed his troops in pursuit,
and the army then disintegrated.
Wéi Jīn died.
The Kǎoyì states: The biographies in the Suí Shū do not mention the date of the battle.
The biography of Púshān Gōng places this battle on the ninth day of the fourth month.
The Lüè Jì also says:
"In the fourth month,
on the Yǐwèi day,
Lǐ Mì led his troops to occupy Mángshān to the north,
connecting to Shàngchūnmén to the south.
Duàn Dá, Wéi Jīn and others led troops out to resist him.
Before the armies engaged, Dá was afraid
and returned to the city first,
and the army then disintegrated in chaos."
The Yǐwèi day
was the twenty-first.
Now, according to the Hélùo Jì,
"On the nineteenth day of the first month,
Shìchōng again fought Mì outside Shàngchūnmén,
and Wéi Jīn perished there."
Also,
in the second month,
Fáng Yànzǎo's letter to Dòu Jiàndé also states:
"On the nineteenth day of last month,
the staff personally led brave troops
to take Luòyì to the west."
The dates in the biography of Púshān Gōng after the fourth month
often differ and do not match the events.
Today, the date follows the Hélùo Jì,
and the events follow the Lüè Jì and the biography of Duàn Dá in the Suí Shǐ.
Under the Suí system: the Zhífāng Láng
was subordinate to the Bīngbù Shàngshū.
Dòu Jiàndé, Zhū Càn, Mèng Hǎigōng, Xú Yuánlǎng, and others all sent envoys to present memorials urging him to ascend the throne.
Mì's officials such as Péi Rénjī and others also submitted memorials requesting him to formally assume the imperial title.
Mì said:
"Dōngdū has not yet been pacified;
this cannot be discussed now."
3 On the Wùchén day,
the Táng King made his heir apparent, Jiànchéng, the Zǔ Yuánshuài,
and Qín Gōng Shìmín the Yòu Yuánshuài,
to command over one hundred thousand troops to relieve Dōngdū.
4 Dōngdū lacked food.
Tàifù Qīng Yuán Wéndū and others recruited those who would guard the city without consuming public rations, offering them a second-rank scattered official position.
Thereupon, merchants who offered ivory tablets as tribute
were innumerable.
Xiàng (象) refers to
an ivory tablet (象笏).
Since the Western Wèi dynasty,
officials of the fifth rank and above generally used ivory.
Jiǎ (賈),
pronounced gǔ.
Cháo (朝),
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
Shèng (勝),
pronounced shēng.
5 In the second month,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
the King of Táng dispatched Tài Cháng Qīng Zhèng Yuánshú with troops to march out of Shāng and Luò,
to pacify Nányáng.
Emperor Yáng changed Dèngzhōu to Nányáng Jùn.
Shú,
pronounced like "shū yù" when inverted.
Jiāng,
pronounced like "jí liàng" when inverted.
The twelve guard headquarters of the Suí dynasty each had a Zhǎngshǐ and a Sīmǎ.
Emperor Yáng changed Ānzhōu to Ānlù Jùn;
Jīngzhōu to
Nán Jùn;
Xiāngzhōu to
Xiāngyáng Jùn.
6 Lǐ Mì dispatched Fáng Yànzǎo and Zhèng Tǐng and others
eastward out of Líyáng,
to recruit and comfort the prefectures and counties by different routes.
He appointed Yáng Wāng, the Grand Administrator of Liáng Jùn, as Shàng Zhùguó and Sòngzhōu Zǒngguǎn.
Emperor Yáng had changed Sòngzhōu to Liáng Jùn.
Shǒu,
pronounced like "shì yòu" when inverted.
"Formerly in Yōngqiū,
I was once pursued and captured by you.
The details are in volume one hundred eighty-three, Dàyè twelfth year.
I dare not hope for such a thing."
Guǎn Zhòng shot Duke Huán of Qí, hitting his belt hook,
and Duke Huán employed him as prime minister.
In Jìn, the eunuch Pī attacked Gongzi Chóng'ěr,
cutting off his sleeve,
but Duke Wén did not resent it.
Nowadays, qū (袖) refers to mèi (袂, sleeve).
Shè,
pronounced like "ér yì" when inverted.
Jī,
pronounced like "jū xī" when inverted.
Mì also kept him in a loose rein.
Yànzǎo wrote a letter to Dòu Jiàndé,
inviting him to meet Mì.
Jiàndé replied with a letter,
using humble words and generous gifts,
using the pretext of Luó Yì's southern invasion
to request to defend the northern border.
Yànzǎo returned,
and upon reaching Wèizhōu,
the bandit leader Wáng Dérén ambushed and killed him.
Dérén had tens of thousands of followers,
occupying Línlǜ Shān.
Wèizhōu was
Jí Jùn during the Suí dynasty.
Línlǜ Shān is
in Línlǜ Xiàn, Wèijùn.
Lǜ,
pronounced "lú".
He became a menace to several prefectures.
7 In the third month,
on the day Jǐyǒu,
Qí Guó Yuánjí was appointed Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn.
Kǎoyì states: The note on Chuàngyè says,
"The Táiyuán Liúshǒu was changed to Zhèn Běi Fǔ
in the twelfth month of last year, on the day Jǐsì."
This was probably said because Yuánjí was promoted and enfeoffed as Qí Gōng.
We now follow the Shílù.
He was allowed to act according to his discretion.
8 Emperor Yáng of Suí reached Jiāngdū.
In Dàyè twelve,
Emperor Yáng reached Jiāngdū.
There were over a hundred rooms in the palace,
each lavishly decorated and furnished,
filled with beautiful women.
Each day, one room was made the host.
Zhào Yuánkǎi, the Jiāngdū Jùnchéng, was in charge of supplying wine and food.
The emperor, Empress Xiāo, and his favored concubines successively attended banquets,
never letting the wine cup leave their mouths.
The more than a thousand attending concubines were also constantly drunk.
However, seeing the world in chaos,
the emperor's mind was also restless and uneasy.
After court, he would wear a turban and short clothes,
leaning on a staff and walking about,
visiting all the palaces and pavilions,
not stopping until night.
He eagerly watched the changing scene,
only fearing it would not last long enough.
The emperor understood divination and physiognomy,
and was fond of speaking in the Wú dialect.
He often held night banquets,
looked up at the stars,
and said to Empress Xiāo:
"There are many people outside who are plotting against me."
Wú people often referred to themselves as "nóng".
"You will not fail to become Empress Shěn."
Chángchéng Gōng was
Chén Shúbǎo.
Shúbǎo's empress was from the Shěn clan.
Then he would fill his cup and drink deeply until drunk.
He also once looked at himself in a mirror,
and turning to Empress Xiāo, said:
"What a beautiful head and neck!
Who will chop it off?"
The empress was startled and asked why.
The emperor laughed and said:
"Nobility and lowliness, suffering and joy,
alternate with each other.
What harm is there in that?"
Seeing that the Central Plains were already in chaos,
the emperor had no intention of returning north,
wishing to establish his capital in Dānyáng.
The emperor changed Jiǎngzhōu to Dānyáng Jùn,
probably intending to make Jiànkāng his capital.
Kǎoyì states: Dàyè Jì says:
"The emperor wished to tour south to Kuàijī."
We now follow the Suí Shū.
He ordered his close ministers to discuss it in court,
and Nèishǐ Shìláng Yú Shìjī and others all thought it was good.
Yòu Hòuwèi Dàjiāngjūn Lǐ Cái strongly argued against it,
requesting the imperial carriage to return to Cháng'ān,
and left in anger after a quarrel with Shìjī.
Ménxià Lùshì Lǐ Tóngkè of Héngshuǐ said:
According to Suí regulations,
the Ménxià Shěng had six Lùshì, six Tōngshì, and six Lìshǐ.
Héngshuǐ Xiàn belonged to Xìndū Jùn,
established in the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng by dividing the northern border of Xìndū, the western border of Wǔyì, and the southern border of Xiàbó.
Sòng Bái said: Héngshuǐ Xiàn was
originally Táo Xiàn of Hàn.
"The Jiangdong region is low and humid,
and the land is dangerous and narrow.
Internally it must support the emperor,
and externally supply the armies.
The people cannot endure this burden,
and I fear it will eventually lead to chaos and dispersal."
The censor impeached Tóngkè for slandering the court.
Thereupon, all the high officials flattered the emperor, saying:
"The people of Jiangdong have long awaited your visit.
Your Majesty crosses the Jiāng,
to comfort and oversee them.
This is the achievement of Dà Yǔ."
Yǔ made a southern tour,
assembling the feudal lords in Kuàijī.
He was about to move his capital there.
At that time, Jiāngdū’s糧 (provisions) ran out.
The Xiāoguǒ who accompanied the Emperor
were mostly people from Guānzhōng,
and having been away from home for a long time, they longed for their hometowns.
Seeing that the Emperor had no intention of heading west,
many plotted to rebel and return.
The Commander Dòu Xián then led his unit west,
and the Emperor sent cavalry to pursue and execute him.
However, the number of those absconding did not cease,
and the Emperor was troubled by this.
The Hǔbēn Lángjiàng, Sīmǎ Dékān of Fúfēng, had always been favored by the Emperor.
The Emperor made him lead the Xiāoguǒ to garrison in the eastern city.
Dékān conspired with his close associates, Hǔbēn Lángjiàng Yuán Lǐ and Zhíhé Péi Qiántōng, saying:
[Suí] Yángdì established the Left and Right Jiānmén Fǔ, each with six Zhíhé,
ranking fifth grade.
“Now, every Xiāoguǒ wants to desert.
If I speak of this,
I fear I will be punished before the event.
If I don’t speak,
and the matter is discovered later,
I will also not escape extermination of my clan.
What should be done?
Furthermore, I heard that Guānnèi has fallen,
and Lǐ Xiàocháng has rebelled with Huáyīn.”
[Details are in the previous volume, previous year.]
[Huá, pronunciation Hù-huà fān.]
“They want to kill him.
Our families are all in the west.
How can we not have this concern? ”
Both men were frightened,
and said:
“If so, what plan should we come up with? ”
Dékān said:
“If the Xiāoguǒ desert,
it would be better to leave with them. ”
Both men said:
“Excellent! ”
Thus, they went about recruiting others.
The Nèishǐ Shèrén Yuán Mǐn, Hǔyá Lángjiàng Zhào Xíngshū, Yīngyáng Lángjiàng Mèng Bǐng, Fúxǐ Láng Niú
Fāngyù, Zhícháng Xǔ Hóngrén, Xuē Shìliáng, Chéngmén Láng Táng Fèngyì, Yīzhèng Zhāng Kǎi, Xūnshì Yáng Shìlǎn and others
[In early Suí,
the Ménxià Shěng administered six bureaus: Chéngmén, Shàngshí, Shàngyào, Fúxǐ, Yùfǔ, and Diànnèi,
each with a Zhícháng.
Yángdì placed the Chéngmén, Shàngshí, Shàngyào, Yùfǔ, and other five bureaus under the Diànnèi Shěng;
changed the Fúxǐ Jiān to Láng;
established a Xiàowèi for Chéngmén,
later changing Xiàowèi to Chéngmén Láng;
and also established officials such as Sīyī and Yīzuǒ.
It is likely that Yīzhèng was the Sīyī.
Xūnshì was one of the Sānshì.]
[Xūnshì, one of the three attendants.]
[Xǐ, pronunciation Sī-shì fān.]
[Zhǎng, pronunciation Zhī-liǎng fān.]
day and night formed alliances,
openly discussing plans for rebellion in large gatherings,
without any fear or avoidance.
A palace woman reported to Empress Xiāo, saying:
“Everyone outside wants to rebel. ”
The Empress said:
“Let me report it.”
The palace woman told the Emperor.
The Emperor was furious,
believing it was inappropriate to speak of such things,
and executed her.
Afterwards, another palace woman reported to the Empress again.
The Empress said:
“The affairs of the world have reached this point in a single morning;
there is nothing that can save it.
What is the use of speaking of it?
It will only cause the Emperor more worry! ”
From then on, no one spoke of it again.
Zhào Xíngshū and the Jiàngzuò Shàojiān Yǔwén Zhìjí were long-time friends.
Yáng Shìlǎn was Zhìjí’s nephew.
The two informed Zhìjí of their plan.
Zhìjí was greatly pleased.
Dékān and others planned to gather their party and flee west on the full moon day of the third month.
Zhìjí said:
“Although the Emperor is without principle,
his authority still holds sway.
If you gentlemen flee,
it will be just like Dòu Xián inviting death.
Now, Heaven is truly destroying Suí,
and heroes are rising everywhere.
Tens of thousands of people have already joined forces in rebellion.
Seize this opportunity to accomplish a great deed;
this is the work of an emperor. ”
Dékān and the others agreed.
Xíngshū and Xuē Shìliáng requested that Zhìjí’s elder brother, the Yòutúnwèi Jiàngjūn Xǔgōng Huàjí, be made their leader.
After the alliance was settled,
they informed Huàjí.
Huàjí was naturally timid and cowardly.
Hearing of it,
his color changed and he sweated.
Soon after, he complied.
[The Kaoyì states: The Biography of Púshān Gōng says:
“Zhào Xíngshū and Yáng Shìlǎn informed Huàjí of Sīmǎ Dékān’s plot.
Huàjí’s brothers were greatly pleased upon hearing this,
and then introduced Dékān and the others to meet.
Shìjí advised Dékān and the others, saying: ‘You gentlemen are relying on the hearts of the people
to plan an extraordinary affair.
Merely wishing to flee
is not a long-term strategy.’
Dékān asked: ‘What should we do?’
Shìjí said: ‘Although the Emperor is said to be without principle,
his subordinates still fear and obey him.
If he hears of your rebellion and flight,
he will surely pursue and arrest you urgently.
Dòu Xián’s incident
is a recent warning.
It is better to strictly command your troops and horses,
attack his palace,
and, appealing to the people’s desires,
declare the deposition of the dark and wicked ruler.
The deed will surely succeed.
Afterwards, carefully establish a wise and enlightened ruler,
and the world can be at peace,
and we will have no worries.
Once merits are accumulated,
you gentlemen will receive glorious emoluments.
Even if the matter does not succeed,
your prestige will greatly increase,
enough to make the Emperor tremble with fear,
not daring to lightly pursue and suppress you.
In the interim of hesitation,
you will gain several days.
By the time they finalize their decision,
you gentlemen will already be far away.
In this way,
whether to stay or to leave,
both plans are entirely safe.
Is this not good?’
Dékān and the others were greatly pleased, saying: ‘The hope for a wise and enlightened ruler
is not only for the Yáng family;
the hearts of the multitude are truly with Xǔgōng.
This is truly a concord between man and Heaven.’
Shìjí feigned surprise and said: ‘This was not what I intended;
I was merely thinking with you gentlemen how to save our lives.’ ”
The Gémìng Jì says:
“The Emperor knew his reign was nearing its end,
and intended to cross the Jiāngshuǐ to the south.
Everyone said it was not possible.
The Emperor knew the court officials did not want to cross,
so he prepared twenty shi of poisoned wine,
intending to hold a banquet on the sixteenth day of the third month and poison all the officials.
Princess Nányáng feared her husband would die,
so she secretly informed them,
and the plot was exposed.
Because of this,
they began to plot against the Emperor to avoid disaster.”
These are all false narratives concocted by the rebellious and malicious group.
At that time, superiors and subordinates were estranged,
and everyone harbored different intentions.
The Emperor was deeply suspicious,
and did not confide in anyone.
If the wine was not a false rumor,
the poison would need to be distributed.
Where would it be sent, and by whom?
And twenty shi of poisoned wine?
If the wine was truly poisoned,
one shi would be enough to kill a thousand people.
If he genuinely intended to kill all his officials,
the plotters would surely be three to five people,
and the plot would naturally leak early.
How could it be known only by Nányáng?
It is simply that Qiántōng and others were ashamed to bear the name of regicide,
and shifted the blame onto the ruler!
The Biography of Huàjí in the Suí Shū states:
“When Huàjí committed regicide,
Shìjí was in the Princess’s residence
and did not know of it.
Zhìjí sent his household servant Zhuāng Táoshù to the residence to kill him.
Táoshù could not bear to,
and seized him and brought him to Zhìjí.
After a long time,
he was released.”
The Biography of Princess Nányáng reproaches Shìjí, saying:
“But on the day of the rebellion,
it was observed that you were not privy to it.”
The Biography of Shìjí in the Jiù Táng Shū states:
“When Huàjí plotted rebellion,
because Shìjí was the Princess’s husband,
he deeply feared him and did not inform him.”
We note that Shìjí served as chancellor in the Táng dynasty,
and the Suí Shū was also compiled in the early Táng.
Perhaps the historians concealed Shìjí’s wrongdoing.
The words in the two books by Jiǎ and Dù also seem credible,
but since Dù Rútóng knew that the poisoned wine was false,
then the matter of Nányáng secretly informing them is also not true.
According to Jiǎ Rùnfǔ’s account,
then the plot to assassinate the ruler all came from Shìjí,
and Zhìjí was a good person.
For now, we shall follow the Suí Shū and delete the accounts of Zhuāng Táoshù and Nányáng’s words,
so as to pass on doubts as doubts.
Dúgū Déhān sent Xǔ Hóngrén and Zhāng Kǎi to enter the Bèishēnfǔ.
The Emperor changed the Zuǒlǐngzuǒyòufǔ and Yòulǐngzuǒyòufǔ to Zuǒbèishēnfǔ and Yòubèishēnfǔ.
"Your Majesty has heard that the Xiāoguǒ intend to rebel,

Someone said:
“What has been practiced throughout the dynasties,

he would certainly not consent to this.
If he has no awareness,
and I exalt myself and feign humility,
it goes against my lifelong principles.”
He merely changed the Chancellery to the Chancellor’s Office,

On jǐmǎo,
Wǔdū, Dàngqú, Wǔyuán, and other commanderies all surrendered.
(Wǔdū,

Dàngqú,

宕 (Dàng),

Chángxùn also forged an imperial edict for Mòhèduō Shè,

Mòhèduō Shè then rejected Jǔ, Shīdū, and others,

17 On wùxū,
Crown Prince Jiànchéng and others returned to Cháng'ān.
(Kǎoyì says: The Chuàngyè records it in the third month.
We follow the Tàizōng Shílù here.)

people lacked firm resolve.
Cháoyìláng Duàn Shìhóng and others plotted to respond to the Xīshī.
However, the Xīshī had already returned,
(Xīshī,

They planned to let them in on the night of jǐhài.
The plot was discovered,

Mì, hearing that the city was already pacified,

19Yǔwénhuàjí 擁衆十餘萬,
据有六宮,
自奉養一如煬帝.
每於帳中南面坐,
人有白事者,
嘿然不對;
下牙,
方取啟狀與唐奉義, Níufāngyù, Xuēshìliáng, Zhāngkǎi 等參決之.
Liúféng 事始曰: 兵書曰: 牙旗者,
將軍之精,
凡始建牙,
必以制日.
制者,
其辰在五行以上剋下之日也.
又尚書
色紅,
八幅.
大將牙門之旗,
出引將軍前列.
又黃帝出軍決曰: 牙旗者,
將軍之精;
金鼓者,
將軍之氣.
周禮司常職云: 軍旅會同置旌門.
夫以旌為門,
即旗門也,
後世軍中遂置牙門將,
又有牙兵,
典總此名者以押牙為名.
至於官府,
早晚軍吏兩謁,
亦名為衙.
呼謂既熟,
雖天子正殿受朝謁,
亦名正衙.
以少主 hào 付尚書省,
令衞士十餘人守之,
遣令史取其畫敕,
隋門下省,
有錄事, 通事, 令史各六人.
至 Péngchéng,
水路不通,
復奪民車牛得二千兩,
並載宮人珍寶;
其戈甲戎器,
悉令軍士負之,
道遠疲劇,
軍士始怨.
Sīmǎdéyí 竊謂 Zhàoxíngshū 曰:
「君大謬誤我!
行樞建言以化及為主.
必藉英賢;
化及庸暗,
㣥小在側,
事將必敗,
若之何? 」
行樞曰:
「在我等耳,
廢之何難! 」
初,
化及既得政,
賜司馬德戡爵溫國公,
加光祿大夫;
以其專統驍果,
心忌之.
後數日,
化及署諸將分部士卒,
以德戡為禮部尚書,
外示美遷,
實奪其兵柄.
德戡由是憤怨,
所獲賞賜,
皆以賂智及;
智及為之言,
乃使之將後軍萬餘人以從.
於是德戡, 行樞與諸將 Lǐběn, Yǐnzhèngqīng, Yǔwéndǎoshī 等謀,
以後軍襲殺化及,
更立德戡為主;
遣人詣 Mènghǎigōng,
結為外助,
孟海公據 Cáozhōu.
待海公報.
Xǔhóngrén, Zhāngkǎi 知之,
以告化及,
化及遣 Yǔwénshìjí 陽為遊獵,
至後軍,
德戡不知事露,
出營迎謁,
因執之.
化及讓之曰:
「與公戮力共定海內,
出於萬死.
今始事成,
方願共守富貴,
公又何反也? 」
德戡曰:
「本殺昏主,
苦其淫虐;
推立足下,
而又甚之;
逼於物情,
不得已也. 」
化及縊殺之,
幷殺其支黨十餘人.
Mènghǎigōng 畏化及之強,
帥衆具牛酒迎之.
Lǐmì 據 Gǒnglào 以拒化及,
洛水至鞏入河,
故曰鞏洛.
引兵向東郡,
東郡通守 Wángguǐ 以城降之.
20辛丑,
Lǐmì 將 Jǐngxíng Wángjūnkuò 帥衆來降.
隋志,
井陘縣屬恆山郡.
將,
即亮翻;
下同.
陘,
音刑.
帥,
讀曰率.

從君廓傳.

漢解縣地,
後魏分置虞鄉縣,
隋志屬河東郡.
帥,
所類翻.
寶, 豹欲從唐王,

In the `xīnwèi` year, 27th
day, Shǐbì Kèhán of the Tujue dispatched Gǔduōlù Tèlès to come.
He was entertained in the Tàijí Hall,
and the Nine-Part Music was performed.
Dù Yòu said: In the early Wǔdé reign,
following the old Súi system,
the Nine-Part Music consisted of: one, `Yàn Yuè` (Banquet Music);
two, `Qīngshāng` (Clear Music);
three, `Xīliáng` (Western Liang);
four, `Fúnán` (Funan);
five, `Gāolí` (Goguryeo);
six, `Guīcí` (Kucha);
seven, `Ānguó` (An Kingdom);
eight, `Shūlè` (Kashgar);
nine, `Kāngguó` (Samarkand).
The note by Dù Yòu in the previous 180 `juàn`, cited from the 4th year of Dàyè of Súi,
states that the Nine-Part Music was different from this.
Furthermore, upon examining Sòng Qí’s `Xīn Táng Zhì`, it says: Táng had Ten-Part Music
and skills from fourteen countries,
with eight countries included in the Ten Parts;
but it does not explicitly state which eight countries these were.
This is also a discrepancy that is difficult to investigate.
The Tujue were powerful and prosperous.
From the Qìdān and Shìwéi in the east,
to the Tǔyùhùn and Gāochāng kingdoms in the west,
all submitted to them.
They controlled over a million archers.
The Emperor, having relied on their troops and horses in the initial uprising,
had sent countless provisions
and gifts to them.
The Tujue, relying on their achievements, became arrogant and haughty.
Each time they sent envoys to Cháng’ān,
they were often violent and unrestrained.
The Emperor tolerated them with generosity.
On the `rénshēn` day, 28th
day, an order was given to Péi Jì, Líu Wénjìng, and others to revise the `lǜlìng` (statutes and ordinances).
Students were established in the Guózǐ, Tàixué, and Sì mén institutions,
totaling over three hundred members.
The `Táng Lìu Diǎn` states: Guózǐ students were
sons and grandsons of civil and military officials of the third rank and above, and great-grandsons of those of the second rank and above.
Tàixué students were
sons and grandsons of civil and military officials of the fifth rank and above, and of county and district lords, and great-grandsons of those of the third rank and above.
Sì mén students were
sons of civil and military officials of the seventh rank and above, and of marquises, counts, viscounts, and barons, or commoners who were talented scholars.
Líu Fāng of the Later Wèi stated in his memorial:
"In the 20th year of Tàihé,
Four Gates Academicians were appointed,
and schools were established at the Four Gates.
According to the `Lǐjì`, the Son of Heaven established four schools.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states that these were
the schools in the four suburbs of Zhōu.
Now, considering their remoteness,
they were placed at the Four Gates.
I request that they be moved to the same location as the Tàixué."
This was adopted.
In the sixth month, on the `jiǎxū` day, the first day of the month,
Zhào Gōng Lǐ Shìmín was appointed as Shàngshū Lìng,
Huángtái Gōng Yuàn as Xíngbù Shìláng.
He was the Duke of Huángtái County.
The Eastern Wèi established Huángtái County in Yǐngchuān.
It was abolished in the early Dàyè period.
Yuàn
is pronounced `yuàn` (`yú juàn fān`).
Sīmǎ Líu Wénjìng was appointed Nàyán;
Sīlù Dòu Wēi as Nèishǐ Lìng;
Lǐ Gāng as Lǐbù Shàngshū,
also overseeing selection matters;
Yuàn Yīn Kāishān as Lìbù Shìláng;
Shǔ Zhào Cíjǐng as Bīngbù Shìláng;
Wéi Yìjié as Lǐbù Shìláng;
Zhǔbù Chén Shúdá and Bólíng Cuī Míngàn were both made Huángmén Shìláng.
Emperor Yáng renamed Dìngzhōu to Bólíng Jùn.
Lùshì Cānjūn Péi Xī was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒchéng;
the Súi Mínbù Shàngshū Xiāo Yǔ was appointed Nèishǐ Lìng;
Lǐbù Shàngshū Dòu Jìn was appointed Hùbù Shàngshū.
According to the `Lìu Diǎn`,
in the 23rd year of Zhēngguān, to avoid the taboo name of Tàizōng,
Mínbù Shàngshū was first changed to Hùbù Shàngshū.
Historians later used the contemporary official title.
Yǔ
is pronounced `yǔ`.
Jìn
is pronounced `jìn` (`zé lín fān`).
Cháng’ān Lìng Dúgū Huái’ēn was appointed Gōngbù Shàngshū.
Yuàn was
the Emperor's nephew (son of his younger brother);
Huái’ēn was
his maternal cousin.
The Emperor treated Péi Jì with exceptional kindness,
such that no other minister could compare.
The rewards of clothes and trinkets
were innumerable.
He ordered the Shàngshū Fèngyù to daily bestow imperial meals upon Jì.
"Shàngshū"
should be
"Shàngshí."
The `Lìu Diǎn` states: There are two Shàngshí Fèngyù,
subordinate to the Diànzhōng Shěng.
When Jì entered the palace, he was invited to the Emperor's sleeping quarters;
his words were always heeded.
He was referred to as Péi Jiān, and not by his given name.
Jì had served Súi as Jìnyáng Gōngjiān.
Out of familiarity,
he was addressed by his old official title.
Cháo is pronounced `zhí yáo fān`.
Regardless of the matter, great or small,
he was involved and in charge.
Yǔ also worked diligently,
correcting wrongs and pointing out faults.
Everyone feared him,
and there were many who slandered him,
but he never defended himself.
Once, the Emperor issued an edict, but the Nèishǐ did not proclaim it in a timely manner.
According to the Súi and Táng system,
all imperial edicts that reached the Nèishǐ Shěng
were proclaimed, signed, reviewed, and then put into effect.
Yǔ replied:
"In the era of Dàyè,
the edicts proclaimed by the Nèishǐ
sometimes contradicted each other,
and the responsible officials did not know which to follow.
The easy part came first,
the difficult part followed.
Your minister has been in the department for a long time,"
Yǔ was Nèishǐ Shìláng during the Súi dynasty,
hence he said this.
Yi is pronounced `yǐ shì fān`.
Now that the imperial enterprise has just begun,
matters are linked to stability and danger.
If there are doubts in distant regions,
I fear opportunities might be lost.
Therefore, each time I receive an edict, I must carefully examine it
to ensure it does not contradict previous edicts.
Only then do I dare proclaim it.
The fault of tardiness
is indeed due to this."
The Emperor said:
"Since you use your heart in this way,
what more do I have to worry about!"
Initially,
the Emperor had sent Mǎ Yuánguī to pacify and comfort the Shānnán region.
Lǚ Zǐzàng of Hédōng, the Nányáng Jùnchéng, unilaterally held the commandery and refused to comply.
Mǎ Yuánguī was dispatched in the second month of this year.
All were killed by Zǐzàng.
When Emperor Yáng was assassinated,
Zǐzàng held a mourning ceremony and performed the rites,
and only then requested to surrender.
He was appointed as Dèngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Nányáng Commandery was restored as Dèngzhōu.
Jiàng is pronounced `hù jiāng fān`;
the same below.
The Dàyè `lǜlìng` were abolished,
and new regulations were promulgated.
Each time the Emperor attended to state affairs,
he referred to himself by name,
and invited esteemed ministers to sit with him on the same mat.
Líu Wénjìng admonished him, saying:
"Wáng Dǎo once said: 'If the sun were to stoop to be one with all things,
how would all living beings look up to its radiance!'
This event is found in `juàn` 90, 1st year of Tàixīng of Emperor Yuán of Jìn.
This is not a long-lasting way."
The Emperor said:
"In the past, Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn slept with Yán Zǐlíng,
and Zǐlíng placed his foot on the Emperor's belly.
This event is found in the biography of Yán Guāng in the `Hòuhànshū`.
How can I forget
the intimate friendships and joy of old times
with my lifelong friends?
You should not find it objectionable!"
On the `wùyín` day, 33rd
day, Lǚ Mín, the Súi Ānyáng Lìng, surrendered with Xiāngzhōu.
Súi Ānyáng County belonged to Xiāngzhōu.
Xiāng
is pronounced `xī liàng fān`.
On the 34th day, *jǐmǎo*,
the ancestral tablets of the four progenitors were enshrined in the ancestral temple.
Emperor Gāozǔ Yíngzhōu Fǔjūn was posthumously honored as Xuānjiǎgōng;
Emperor Zēngzǔ Sīkōng as Yìwáng;
Emperor Zǔ Jǐngwáng as Jǐng Huángdì,
with the temple name Tàizǔ,
and his ancestral consort as Jǐngliè Huánghòu;
Emperor Kǎo Yuánwáng as Yuán Huángdì,
with the temple name Shìzǔ,
and his consort, Dúgū Shì, as Yuánzhēn Huánghòu;
Dòu Shì was posthumously honored as Mù Huánghòu.
Yíngzhōu Fǔjūn was Xī,
Sīkōng was Tiāncì,
Jǐngwáng was Hǔ,
Yuánwáng was Bǐng.
Jǐngdì was paired with
the Earth Deity of Shénzhōu,
the deities of Shénzhōu, Yíngzhōu, Jìzhōu, Róngzhōu, Shízhōu, Zhùzhōu, Yíngzhōu, Xiánzhōu, and Yángzhōu.
*Qí*,
pronounced *qiáo yí fān*.
Yuándì was paired with
the ancient custom that when emperors and kings rose,
they were always born from sensing the qi of the five essences.
As the Suí ruled by the virtue of fire,
they sacrificed to Chìbiāonù as Gǎndì.
As the Táng ruled by the virtue of earth,
they sacrificed to Hánshūniǔ as Gǎndì.
On the day *gēngchén*,
the heir apparent Jiànchéng was established as Huáng Tàizǐ,
Zhàogōng Shìmín as Qínwáng,
Qígōng Yuánjí as Qíwáng,
the imperial relative Huángguā Gōng Báijū as Píngyuánwáng.
According to records, Báijū was previously enfeoffed as Huángguā Xiàn Gōng.
Huángguā Xiàn was established by the Tuòbá Wèi,
located on the border of Shàngguī.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: Huángguā Shuǐ originates from the west of Huángguā Gǔ,
flows eastward past the north of Huángguā Xiàn,
and then northeastward merges with Jí Shuǐ.
After Jí Shuǐ joins Huángguā Shuǐ,
it flows eastward past the south of Shàngguī chéng.
Zhùguó Dàoxuán as Huáiyángwáng,
Chángpíng Gōng Shúliáng as Chángpíngwáng,
Zhènggōng Shéntōng as Yǒngkāngwáng,
Ānjí Gōng Shénfú as Xiāngyìwáng,
Zhùguó Déliáng as Xīnxīngwáng,
Shàng Zhùguó Bóyì as Lǒngxīwáng,
Shàng Zhùguó Fèngcí as Bóhǎiwáng.
Xiàojī, Shúliáng, Shénfú, and Déliáng
were the Emperor's cousins (father's younger brothers' sons);
Bóyì and Fèngcí
were his nephews (brothers' sons);
Dàoxuán
was his cousin (father's elder brother's son).
On the 35th day, *guǐwèi*,
Xuē Jǔ attacked Jìngzhōu,
and Āndìng Jùn was again made Jìngzhōu.
The Later Wèi established Jìngzhōu,
with its seat at Gāopíng,
named after Jìng Shuǐ.
Eight Chief Commanders were dispatched with troops to resist him.
On the 36th day, an envoy, Tàipú Qīng Yǔwén Míngdá, was sent to pacify Shāndōng,
and Yǒng'ānwáng Xiàojī was appointed Shǎnzhōu Zǒngguǎn.
In the early Yìníng period,
Shǎnxian in Hénán was made Hóngnóng Jùn,
now it is Shǎnzhōu.
*Shǎn*,
pronounced *shī rǎn fān*.
All strategically important border prefectures
were established with Zǒngguǎnfǔ
to govern the armies of several prefectures.
On the 37th day, *yǐyǒu*,
the Suí emperor was granted the title of Xīguógōng.
An imperial edict stated:
"In recent generations,
as the times have changed and revolved,
the relatives of previous dynasties
have all been exterminated.
How could the success and failure
be merely due to human effort!
The descendants of the Suí Càiwáng Zhìjī and others
shall all be handed over to the relevant authorities
and selected for service according to their talents."
On the 38th day, when the Eastern Capital heard that Yǔwén Huàjí was approaching from the west,
everyone was terrified.
A man named Gài Cóng
submitted a memorial requesting to persuade Lǐ Mì to join forces with them to resist Huàjí.
Yuán Wéndū said to Lú Chǔ and others:
"Now our shame is not yet avenged, and our military strength is insufficient.
If we pardon Mì's crimes and have him attack Huàjí,
the two bandits will fight each other,
and we can then exploit their exhaustion.
Once Huàjí is defeated,
Mì's army will also be weary;
moreover, his generals and soldiers will covet our official rewards,
making them easy to sow discord among,
and Mì himself can also be captured."
Chǔ and the others all agreed,
so Cóng was immediately appointed Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì.
*Sàn*,
pronounced *xī dàn fān*.
*Qí*,
pronounced *qí jì fān*.
On the 39th day, *bǐngshēn*,
Qū Léng of Dōnglái, the Suí Xìndū Jùnchéng, surrendered,
and was appointed Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
Suí Xìndū Jùn,
in the Táng dynasty, became Jìzhōu.
Dōnglái Jùn became Láizhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Láizhōu,
was the ancient land of Lái Yí,
and the state of Lái Zǐ in the Spring and Autumn period.
Qí destroyed Lái,
and because it was east of the state,
it was called Dōnglái.
*Jiàng*,
pronounced *hù jiāng fān*.
On the 40th day, Sūn Fújiā of Wǔchéng, Fǎcáo of Wànnián Xiàn, submitted a memorial.
In the second year of Zhōu Míngdì,
Cháng'ān was divided into Wànnián Xiàn,
coexisting with Cháng'ān in the imperial capital.
The Suí renamed it Dàxīng Xiàn.
When Táng received the abdication,
it was restored to Wànnián,
and, along with Cháng'ān, became a Chìxiàn.
Wànnián Xiàn was administered from Xuānyáng Fāng,
governing fifty-four wards east of Zhūquè Jiē.
Cháng'ān Xiàn was administered from Chángshòu Fāng,
governing fifty-four wards west of the street.
Suí Yángdì changed Xiànwèi to Xiànzhèng,
and soon after changed it to Hùcáo and Fǎcáo, dividing their responsibilities,
to assist the six divisions of the prefecture.
The Táng restored the position of Xiànwèi,
and each of the six divisions had assistant officials.
Sūn Fújiā,
Wànnián Fǎcáo,
was likely a Suí official.
Wǔchéng Xiàn,
was the Dōngwǔchéng of the Hàn dynasty,
according to Táng records, it belonged to Bèizhōu.
*Gā*,
pronounced *qiú jiā fān*.
"The Suí perished because they were unwilling to hear of their faults.
Your Majesty ascended the throne in Jìnyáng,
with distant and near responding,
and in less than a year ascended to the imperial seat;
you only know how easy it was to gain it,
but do not know how not difficult it was for the Suí to lose it.
Your servant believes it is appropriate to change their disastrous course,
and diligently seek to understand the sentiments of the people below.
All the words and actions of a ruler

Qí (Qí) Prince Yuánjí (元jí) sent Chējì Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍) Zhāng Dá (Zhāng Dá) with infantry to
probe the enemy.
*Cháng* (嘗)
means "to test."
*Jì* (騎)
is pronounced *qí* or *jì*.
Yuánjí (元jí) compelled him to go,
but upon arrival, they were all annihilated.
Dá (Dá), filled with resentment,
on the *gēngzǐ* day,
led Wǔzhōu (Wǔzhōu) to attack Yúcì (榆次),
capturing it.
Yúcì (榆次) county belonged to Bīngzhōu (幷zhōu) and
was an ancient county from the Hàn (Hàn) dynasty.
41. Sǎnjì Chángshì (散騎常侍) Duàn Què (段Què),
who was fond of alcohol, was sent by imperial decree to comfort Zhū Càn (Zhū Càn) at Jútán (菊tán).
In the second month of this year,
Duàn Què (Duàn Què) had served as Qíqián Yùshǐ Dàfū (以前御史大夫) on an embassy.
Now he is referred to as Sǎnjì Chángshì (散騎常侍),
probably a continuous appointment.
*Sàn* (散)
is pronounced *sàn*.
*Jì* (騎)
is pronounced *qí* or *jì*.
*Láo* (勞)
is pronounced *láo*.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
in his drunken state, he insulted Càn (Càn) saying:
"I hear you like to eat people.
What do people taste like?"
*Hǎo* (好)
is pronounced *hào*.
*Dàn* (噉)
is pronounced *dàn* or *dǎn*;
similarly below.
"Eating a drunkard is just like storing pork in fermented grains."
Què (Què) became enraged

42. Wáng Shìchōng (Wáng Shìchōng) ordered Chángshǐ (長史) Wéi Jié (韋Jié), Yáng Xù (楊Xù), and others, along with Tàicháng Bóshì (太常博士) Kǒng Yǐngdá (Kǒng Yǐngdá) from Héngshuǐ (衡shuǐ),
to devise the ceremony for abdication.
He dispatched Duàn Dá (段Dá), Yún Dìngxīng (雲Dìngxīng), and over ten others to present a memorial to the Huángtài (皇tài) Emperor, saying:
"The Mandate of Heaven is not constant.
The achievements and virtues of the Zhèng (Zhèng) Prince are immense.
We wish Your Majesty to follow the path of Táng (Táng) and Yú (Yú)!"
The Huángtài (皇tài) Emperor, drawing his knees to the table,
angrily said:
"The empire
is the empire of Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ).
If the Suí (Suí) dynasty's fortune has not ended,
such words should not be uttered.
If the Mandate of Heaven has indeed changed,
why bother with abdication!
You gentlemen, some are old ministers of my ancestors,
some hold high positions in the imperial court.
Since you have spoken thus,
what hope do I have left!"
His expression was severe and cold.
After dismissing the court,
he wept before the Empress Dowager.
Shìchōng (Shìchōng) again sent someone to tell him:
"Now the empire is not yet settled.
A mature ruler is needed.
When the four directions are peaceful and stable,
we shall restore you to your rule,
surely fulfilling our previous oath."
This refers to the oath made last July when he cut his hair in the forbidden palace.
On the *guǐmǎo* day,
Shìchōng (Shìchōng) declared the Huángtài (皇tài) Emperor's command,

He sent his elder brother Shìyùn (Shìyùn) to imprison the Huángtài (皇tài) Emperor in the Hánliáng Diàn (含涼殿).
Although there were three memorials offering the throne and imperial edicts urging him,
the Huángtài (皇tài) Emperor knew none of it.
He sent his generals to lead troops to cleanse the imperial city,
and also dispatched sorcerers to perform exorcisms with peach-wood water and reed-fire in the forbidden palace.
43. Suí (Suí) generals, administrators of commanderies and counties, and bandit leaders successively surrendered.
An imperial edict appointed Wáng Bó (Wáng Bó) as Qízhōu Zǒngguǎn (Qízhōu Zǒngguǎn).
Qízhōu (Qízhōu) was governed from Lìchéng (Lìchéng) county,

In the Hàn (Hàn) dynasty, it was Lìchéng (Lìchéng) county.

The Táng (Táng) restored its old name from the early Suí (Suí) period.

Qí Gōngshùn (Qí Gōngshùn) was appointed Huáizhōu Zǒngguǎn (Huáizhōu Zǒngguǎn).

44. On the *jiǎchén* day,
Dàlǐ Qīng (大理卿) Láng Chǔzhī (Láng Chǔzhī) from Xīnlè (Xīnlè) was sent to pacify Shāndōng (Shāndōng).
The *Jiùzhì* (舊志) states: Xīnlè (Xīnlè) was the ancient subordinate state of Xiānyú (Xiānyú).
In the Hàn (Hàn) dynasty, it was Xīnshì (Xīnshì) county,

Xīnlè (Xīnlè) refers to when Fēng Zhāoyí (Fēng Zhāoyí), the mother of Xiàowáng (孝wáng) of Zhōngshān (Zhōngshān) during Emperor Chéng's (Chéng) reign of the Hàn (Hàn) dynasty,

*Lè* (樂)

45. On the *yǐsì* day,

46. On the *dīngwèi* day,

Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu) was the land of Guǎnglíng (Guǎnglíng) and Jiāngdū (Jiāngdū) in the Hàn (Hàn) dynasty.
Since the Hàn (Hàn) dynasty, the seat of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu) was not fixed in one city.
It was not until Guǎnglíng (Guǎnglíng) in the Táng (Táng) dynasty
that it exclusively held the name Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu).

Wáng Shìchōng (王世充) set up couches at the palace gate and at Xuánwǔmén (玄武門), and in several other places.

49. On the *bǐngchén* day,

Fourth was the *Yì Zhàng* (翊仗),
formed by the Flank Guards;
all wore *hè* (鶡) hats and scarlet lined gowns.

Whenever Wáng Shìchōng (王世充) held court,

repeating his words,

The attendants were utterly exhausted,

51. Wáng Shìchōng (王世充) repeatedly attacked Yīzhōu (伊州).

52. In the fifth month,

Fù,

According to the Suí (隋) records,
Jiāngdū Jùn (江都郡) included Jiāngyáng Xiàn (江陽縣),
and had Jiāngdū Gōng (江都宮) and Yángzǐ Gōng (揚子宮).
In the first year of Yǒngchún (永淳) of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
Yángzǐ Xiàn (揚子縣) was first established by dividing Jiāngdū Xiàn (江都縣).
Today, Zhēn Zhōu (真州) is located in that territory.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Qīngliú Xiàn (清流縣) was named after the clear flowing water east of the county.
Emperor Wén (文) of Suí (隋) changed Liáng's (梁) Xīnchāng Xiàn (新昌縣) to Qīngliú Xiàn (清流縣).
(Lǐ Zǐtōng) recruited people from Jiāngnán (江南) to pretend to be Lún's (綸) soldiers,
and attacked Fúwēi's (伏威) camp by night.
Fúwēi (伏威) was enraged,
and in turn sent troops to attack Lún (綸).
Consequently, the two suspected each other,
and neither dared to advance first.
Zǐtōng (子通) was thus able to throw his full force into attacking Jiāngdū (江都),
conquering it.
Líng (稜) fled to Fúwēi (伏威).
Zǐtōng (子通) entered Jiāngdū (江都),
and then launched a general assault on Lún (綸),
thoroughly defeating him.
Fúwēi (伏威) also withdrew.
Zǐtōng (子通) then ascended the throne as emperor,
naming his state Wú (吳),
and changing the era name to Míngzhèng (明政).
The bandit chief Lè Bótōng (樂伯通) from Dānyáng (丹陽) led over ten thousand men to surrender to him.
Dānyáng Jùn (丹陽郡) was
Jiǎng Zhōu (蔣州) in early Suí (隋).
Zéishuài (賊帥),
*suǒ lèi fān* (所類翻).
Tōng shuài (通帥),
read as *shuài* (率).
Jiàng (降),
*hù jiāng fān* (戶江翻).
78 Dù Fúwēi (杜伏威) requested to surrender.
On the *dīngchǒu* (丁丑) day,
Fúwēi (伏威) was appointed Pacification Commissioner of Huáinán (淮南) and Administrator of Hé Zhōu (和州).
Hé Zhōu (和州)
was the territory of Lìyáng Xiàn (歷陽縣) during the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
the administrative seat of the Jiǔjiāng Dūwèi (九江都尉).
When the Jìn (晉) clan moved south,
a garrison was established there to defend the Jiāng (江).
During Hóu Jǐng's (侯景) rebellion,
all of Jiāngxī (江西) fell to Gāo Qí (高齊).
Hé Zhōu (和州) was established in Lìyáng (歷陽),
signifying the harmony between north and south,
and an important ford for traffic.
During the Dàyè (大業) era, the prefecture was abolished and became Lìyáng Jùn (歷陽郡).
Now, Lìyáng Jùn (歷陽郡) is again Hé Zhōu (和州).
Shǐ (使),
*shū lì fān* (疏吏翻).
79 Péi Jì (裴寂) arrived at Jièxiū (介休).
Jièxiū (介休)
was Gǔ Xiàn (古縣) during the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
named after Jiè Zǐtuī (介子推) and Jiè Shān (介山).
At that time, it was Jiè Zhōu (介州).
Jì's (寂) army encamped at Duósuǒ Yuán (度索原).
They drank stream water in the camp.
Sòng Jīngāng (宋金剛) cut off their water supply,
causing the soldiers to suffer from thirst and exhaustion.
Jì (寂) wanted to move the camp closer to water.
Jīngāng (金剛) unleashed his troops to attack them.
Jì's (寂) army subsequently collapsed,
almost completely annihilated.
Jì (寂) galloped to Jìn Zhōu (晉州) in one day and one night.
Previously,
Liú Wǔzhōu (劉武周) had repeatedly sent troops to attack Xīhé (西河).
Liú Shàn (劉贍), the Prefect of Hào Zhōu (浩州), resisted them.
Hào Zhōu (浩州)
was Xīhé Jùn (西河郡) during the Suí (隋) dynasty.
Xiān (先),
*xī jiàn fān* (悉薦翻).
Shàn (贍),
*ér yàn fān* (而豔翻).
And jointly defended Xīhé (西河).
After Péi Jì's (裴寂) defeat,
all cities and towns north of Jìn Zhōu (晉州) were lost,
with only Xīhé (西河) remaining.
Jiāng Bǎoyì (姜寶誼) was again captured by Jīngāng (金剛).
He plotted to escape and return,
but Jīngāng (金剛) killed him.
Péi Jì (裴寂) submitted a memorial expressing his apologies.
The emperor comforted and reassured him,
and again appointed him to garrison and pacify Hédōng (河東).
Liú Wénjìng's (劉文靜) defeat at Qiǎnshuǐ Yuán (淺水原) led to his demotion, misfortune, and eventually his execution.
Péi Jì's (裴寂) defeat at Duósuǒ Yuán (度索原),
his position and responsibilities remained unchanged.
Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖) of Táng (唐) certainly manipulated rewards and punishments in controlling his officials.
Liú Wǔzhōu (劉武周) advanced and pressed upon Bìng Zhōu (幷州).
Qí Wáng Yuánjí (齊王元吉) deceived his *Sīmǎ* (司馬), Liú Déwēi (劉德威), saying:
"You defend the city with the old and weak,
I will go out to battle with strong soldiers."
On the *xīnsì* (辛巳) day,
Yuánjí (元吉) led his troops out at night,
taking his wives and concubines, abandoned the prefecture, and fled back to Cháng'ān (長安).
As soon as Yuánjí (元吉) left,
Wǔzhōu's (武周) troops arrived at the city gates.
Xuē Shēn (薛深), a local notable of Jìnyáng (晉陽), surrendered the city to Wǔzhōu (武周).
The emperor heard of this,
and was greatly enraged.
He said to Lǐ Gāng (李綱), the Minister of Rites:
"Yuánjí (元吉) is young and weak,
not yet experienced in current affairs,
so I sent Dòu Dàn (竇誕) and Yǔwén Xīn (宇文歆) to assist him.
Jìnyáng (晉陽) has tens of thousands of strong soldiers,
enough provisions for ten years.
The foundation of our rising dynasty
was abandoned in one day.
I heard Yǔwén Xīn (宇文歆) was the first to propose this plan,
I shall execute him!"
Gāng (綱) replied:
"The Prince is young and unrestrained,
Dòu Dàn (竇誕) offered no remonstrance,
and moreover concealed his faults,
causing the soldiers and common people to be angry and resentful.
The defeat today
is Dàn's (誕) crime.
Xīn (歆) remonstrated,
but the Prince did not repent.
All these matters were reported in due course,
see the second month above.
Quān (悛),
*chǒu yuán fān* (丑緣翻).
How can he be killed!"
The next day,
the emperor summoned Gāng (綱) and,
ascending the throne, said:
"Having you, sir,
I shall avoid wrongful punishments.
Yuánjí (元吉) brought this misfortune upon himself,
it is not something the two of them could have prevented."
And he pardoned Dàn (誕).
Liú Zhèngkuài (劉政會), the Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Insignia, was in Tàiyuán (太原)
and was captured by Wǔzhōu (武周).
Zhèngkuài (政會) secretly
reported on Wǔzhōu's (武周) situation.
Wǔzhōu (武周) occupied Tàiyuán (太原)
and sent Sòng Jīngāng (宋金剛) to attack Jìn Zhōu (晉州),
taking it.
He captured Liú Hóngjī (劉弘基), the Grand General of the Right Valiant Guard.
Hóngjī (弘基) later escaped and returned.
Jīngāng (金剛) advanced and pressed upon Jiàng Zhōu (絳州),
capturing Lóngmén (龍門).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Jiàng Zhōu (絳州)
was the capital of Jìn (晉),
what the *Zuǒzhuàn* (左傳) called Xīntián (新田).
In the second year of Wǔchéng (武成) of the Later Zhōu (後周),
Jiàng Zhōu (絳州) was established.
Lóngmén (龍門)
was Píshì Xiàn (皮氏縣) during the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
The Later Wèi (後魏) renamed it Lóngmén Xiàn (龍門縣).
During the Suí (隋) and Táng (唐) dynasties, it belonged to Pú Zhōu (蒲州).
80 The Western Tūjué (突厥) Kěhàn (可汗) Hésuōnà (曷娑那) had a grudge against the Northern Tūjué (突厥).
Hésuōnà (曷娑那) was in Cháng'ān (長安).
The Northern Tūjué (突厥) sent envoys requesting his execution,
but the emperor refused.
All the imperial officials said:
"To protect one person and lose a nation
will certainly cause trouble later!"
Qín Wáng Shìmín (秦王世民) said:
"A man in distress comes to us for refuge;
to kill him would be unrighteous."
The emperor hesitated for a long time,
and having no other choice,
on the *bǐngxū* (丙戌) day,
he invited Hésuōnà (曷娑那) to an inner palace banquet.
Afterwards, he sent him to the Central Secretariat,
and released the Northern Tūjué (突厥) envoys to kill him.
81 Lǐ Gāng, Minister of Rites, concurrently served as太子 Tàizǐ Zhānshì (Grand Master of the Crown Prince’s Household).
The “Hundred Officials Table” in the Hànshū states: The Zhānshì,
a Qin official,
was in charge of the Empress’s and Crown Prince’s households.
Yīng Shào said: Zhān
means “to inspect” [shěng],
and “to provide” [jǐ],
meaning to provide service to the Crown Prince’s household.
During the Jìn, Sòng, and later Northern Wèi dynasties, important people were increasingly appointed to this position.
In Northern Qí, the Zhānshì oversaw all internal and external affairs of the Eastern Palace,
managing everything regardless of size.
The Later Zhōu established the太子 Tàizǐ Gōngzhèng and Gōngyǐn;
the Suí re-established the Zhānshì;
and the Táng oversaw the administration of the three directorates and ten commanderies of the Eastern Palace.
After a long time,
the Crown Prince grew close to petty men,
and resented Qínwáng Shìmín’s great achievements,
often suspecting and fearing him.
Gāng repeatedly remonstrated but was not heeded,
so he requested to retire due to old age and illness.
The Emperor scolded him, saying:
"Why do you act like Pān Rén’s chief secretary,
yet are ashamed to be My Minister?
Moreover, I am just about to use you to assist and guide Jiànchéng,
yet you are determined to leave.
Why is that?"
Gāng bowed his head and said:
"Pān Rén
was a villain;
whenever he wanted to kill innocent people,
I would remonstrate with him and he would stop.
As his chief secretary,
I could feel no shame.
The account of being a chief secretary can be found in Volume 184, Yìníng first year.
Your servant is untalented;
my words are like water thrown onto a stone.
To say ‘water thrown onto a stone’
means although it dampens, the stone cannot absorb the water.
How dare your servant continue to disgrace Tiāntái and dishonor Dōngcháo!"
Tiāntái
refers to the Ministry of Rites.
Dōngcháo
refers to the Eastern Palace.
Wū,
pronounced Wū gù.
Cháo,
pronounced Zhí yáo.
"I know you are an upright official.
Please stay and assist My son."
On the day Wùzǐ,
Gāng was made太子 Tàizǐ Shàobǎo (Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince),
and his positions as Minister and Zhānshì remained as before.
Gāng again submitted a memorial, remonstrating with the Crown Prince about his intemperate drinking,
believing slanderers,
and estranging his relatives.
The Crown Prince was displeased,
but continued his behavior as before.
Gāng was frustrated and discontented.
That year,
he insisted on resigning due to old age and illness.
An imperial edict relieved him of his position as Minister,
but he remained Shàobǎo.
82 Huái’ān Wáng Shéntōng sent the comfort and pacification commissioner Zhāng Dàoyuán to garrison Zhàozhōu.
On the day Gēngyín,
Dòu Jiàndé captured Zhàozhōu,
seizing Commander Zhāng Zhì’áng and Dàoyuán.
Jiàndé wanted to kill the two men and Xíngzhōu Prefect Chén Jūnbīn for not surrendering early,
but Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Líng Jìng remonstrated, saying:
"Every minister serves his own lord;
their firm defense and refusal to surrender demonstrate their loyalty.
If Your Majesty kills them now,
how will you encourage your subordinates?"
Jiàndé angrily said:
"When I arrived at the city walls,
they still did not surrender, but were captured by force.
How can I spare them?"
Jìng replied:
"Now Your Majesty has sent General Gāo Shìxīng to resist Luó Yì at Yìshuǐ.
As soon as Yì arrived,
Shìxīng immediately surrendered.
What does Your Majesty think of that?"
Jiàndé then understood,
and immediately ordered their release.
83 On the day Yǐwèi,
Liáng Shīdū again invaded Yánzhōu.
Duàn Décāo attacked and defeated him,
beheading over two thousand.
Shīdū fled with about a hundred cavalry.
Décāo was appointed Zhùguó for his achievements
and granted the title Píngyuán Jùn Gōng.
Fūzhōu Prefect Fūchéng Zhuàng Gōng Liáng Lǐ died in battle.
The Suízhì states: In Shàngjùn,
the Later Wèi established Dōngqínzhōu,
later renamed Běihuázhōu.
The Western Wèi made it Fūzhōu.
In the second year of Dàyè, it was renamed Fūchéngjùn,
and later Shàngjùn.
The Táng made it Fūzhōu.
Fū,
pronounced Fū.
84 Winter,
Tenth month,
On the day Jǐhài,
Yáng Gōngrén, Grand Administrator of Liángzhōu, was appointed Nàyán (Grand Councilor);
Luó Yì, Grand Administrator of Yōuzhōu and Yàn Gōng, was granted the imperial surname Lǐ
and enfeoffed as Yànjùn Wáng.
He was promoted from Duke of a State to Prince of a Commandery.
According to Táng regulations,
a Duke of a State had an actual emolument of three thousand households,
and a Prince of a Commandery had five thousand households.
Both were of the first rank.
Yàn,
pronounced Yīn jiān.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
Lǐ Yì defeated Dòu Jiàndé at Héngshuǐ.
Héngshuǐ County
belonged to Jìzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Héngshuǐ County was originally Hán Táoxiàn.
In the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng of the Suí dynasty,
Héngshuǐ County was established.
85 On the day Guǐmǎo,
Páng Yù, Grand General of the Left Wǔhóu, was appointed Grand Administrator of Liángzhōu.
At that time, the Láo of Jízhōu rebelled.
The Xīnzhì states: In the first year of Wǔdé,
Nánjiāng from Liángzhōu, and Fúyáng, Chángchí, and Báishí from Bāzhōu were separated to establish Jízhōu.
According to the Jiùzhì,
Hán Dàngqú
was the land of Fúyáng.
Sòng Bái said: The Later Wèi Emperor Gōng changed Liáng’s Dōngbāzhōu to Jízhōu,
naming it after the Jíchuān River to its northeast.
Láo,
pronounced Lǔ hào.
The Láo held strategic positions and defended themselves,
so the army could not advance,
and provisions were almost exhausted.
The domesticated Láo and the rebels were all neighbors and relatives.
Those near the border were called domesticated Láo,
and those further away were called wild Láo.
They requested Yù to return.
Yù publicly declared:
"The autumn grain is about to ripen.
The people are not allowed to harvest it;
everything will be supplied to the army.
I will not return until the rebels are pacified."
Those who heard this were greatly terrified and said:
"If the army does not leave,
we will all starve to death."
Thereupon, strong men among them entered the rebel camp,
secretly conspired with their relatives,
beheaded their leader and surrendered.
The remaining factions dispersed,
and Yù pursued and completely pacified them.
86 Liú Wǔzhōu's general, Sòng Jīngāng, attacked Huìzhōu,
and captured it.
Xīnzhì (New Gazetteer) states: In the first year of Yìníng, Huìzhōu was established from Yìchéng and Jiàngxiàn of Jiàngjùn,
named after the Huìshuǐ River.
將 (jiàng),
read as liàng;
same below.
澮 (huì),
read as gǔwài.
Péi Jì was timid
and lacked the strategies of a commander.
He only dispatched envoys in quick succession,
urging the residents of the two prefectures of Yú and Tài to enter fortresses,
and burn their accumulated supplies.
駱驛 (luòyì),
means continuously without interruption.
Xīnzhì states: In the first year of Yìníng,
Ānyìjùn was established from Ānyì, Yúxiāng, and Xià of Púzhōu.
In the first year of Wǔdé, it was renamed Yúzhōu.
Also, in the first year of Yìníng,
Fényīnjùn was established from Fényīn and Lóngmén of Púzhōu.
In the first year of Wǔdé, it was renamed Tài zhōu.
使 (shǐ),
read as shūlì.
趣 (qù),
read as cù.
積聚 (jī jù),
the first character read as zǐcì,
the second as cíyù;
modern people mostly read them as written,
which is incorrect.
All desired to become bandits.
Lǚ Chóngmào, a commoner from Xiàxiàn, gathered followers, proclaimed himself King of Wèi,
and responded to Wǔzhōu.
Xiàxiàn was
the land of ancient Yúgōng.
Jìshān and Yúbǎn were both within the county's borders.
During the Suí dynasty, it belonged to Hédōngjùn,
and at that time, it belonged to Yúzhōu.
Dù Yòu said: Xiàxiàn
was the territory of Hàn's Ānyìxiàn.
The Xià capital was Ānyì,
and the city was fifteen lǐ north of the county.
It was probably named after this.
夏 (xià),
read as hùyǎ.
[He] was defeated by them.
An imperial edict commanded Prince Yǒng'ān Xiàojī,
Dúgū Huái'ēn, the General Administrator of Shǎnzōu Yú Yún, and the Internal Secretary Shìláng Táng Jiǎn and others to lead troops to suppress them.
At this time, Wáng Xíngběn still held Pú and rebelled,
not yet subdued.
He also corresponded with Wǔzhōu.
In the twelfth month of last year,
the Suí general Yáo Jūnsù died.
Wáng Xíngběn held Pú and rebelled.
This matter is found in the previous volume.
The emperor personally issued an imperial edict, saying:
"The bandit's momentum is such that
it is difficult to contend with them.
It is advisable to abandon the land east of the Great River
and carefully guard only west of the pass."
What is called Pújīn is west of the pass.
"Tàiyuán
is the foundation of the imperial enterprise,
the root of the state.
Hédōng is rich and substantial,
a resource for the capital.
If we abandon it,
I am secretly indignant.
I request to be granted thirty thousand elite soldiers,
and I am certain to pacify and exterminate Wǔzhōu,
and recover Fén and Jìn."
The emperor then mobilized all the troops from Guānzhōng to augment those under Shìmín's command,
and sent them to attack Wǔzhōu.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
he journeyed to Huáyīn,
and reached Chángchūngōng to see him off.
87 Dòu Jiàndé led his troops towards Wèizhōu.
Wèizhōu was
the territory of Hàn's Jíxiàn.
The Eastern Wèi established Yìzhōu,
and the Later Zhōu changed it to Wèizhōu,
with its seat in Jí.
Sòng Bái said: Its prefectural city,
before the Suí, was called Zhènchéng.
The Jùnguó Xiàndàojì states: King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
lined up his forces here,
and it was named after that.
[Jiàndé's army] usually formed three columns,
with baggage and the vulnerable in the center,
and infantry and cavalry flanking them,
about three lǐ apart.
Jiàndé went ahead with a thousand cavalry.
After passing Líyáng by thirty lǐ,
Líyángxiàn
was 120 lǐ northeast of Wèizhōu.
Xiàogāng was fierce and brave,
skilled with the horse spear.
He encountered Jiàndé
and attacked him.
Jiàndé fled in defeat.
The right flank of his army came to his rescue.
右方 (yòufāng) [right flank],
using a term from the Hànshū.
This refers to the part of Jiàndé's army that was on the right.
Jiàndé was enraged,
returned to attack Líyáng,
and captured it.
Kǎoyì (Critical Examination) states: The Shílù (Veritable Records) states that
Líyáng fell on the day Bǐngzǐ in the eleventh month.
This was probably the day the report arrived.
We now follow the Gémìngjì (Record of the Revolution).
Lǐ Shìjì's father Gài, Wèi Zhēng, and the imperial sister, Princess Tóng'ān, [were captured].
Only Lǐ Shìjì, with a few hundred cavalry, crossed the river and fled.
A few days later,
because of his father,
he returned to Jiàndé and surrendered.
Wèizhōu, hearing that Líyáng had fallen,
also surrendered.
Jiàndé appointed Lǐ Shìjì as Zuǒ Xiāowèi Jiàngjūn (General of the Left Valiant Guard),
and made him defend Líyáng,
always keeping his father Gài with him as a hostage.
He appointed Wèi Zhēng as Qǐjū Shèrén (Official of the Imperial Diary).
Wáng Guǐ, the Cìshǐ of Huázhōu, was murdered by his servant,
who took his head to Jiàndé and surrendered.
Jiàndé said:
"A servant murdering his master is a great transgression!
Why should I accept him?"
He immediately ordered the servant to be executed
and returned Wáng Guǐ's head to Huázhōu.
The officials and people were moved and pleased,
and on that very day requested to surrender.
Thereupon, the surrounding prefectures and counties, and Xú Yuánlǎng and others, all flocked to him.
On the day Jǐwèi,
Jiàndé returned to Míngzhōu,
built Wànchūngōng,
and moved his capital there.
He placed Huái'ān Wáng Shéntōng in Xiàbó.
Xiàbóxiàn at that time belonged to Jìzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Xiàbó
was an old county from the Hàn dynasty.
Yīng Shào said: Tàishān has a Bóxiàn,
hence this is called Xià (Lower).
The old county was twenty lǐ south of the present county.
The present county was moved by the Later Wèi to the north of the Héngshuǐ.
It is popularly called Gùxiànchéng (Old County City)
because in the sixth year of Zhōu Jiàndé,
the county seat was again moved to its present location.
The present location
is the old fort of Jì Zūn from the Later Hàn,
with the Héngshuǐ to its north.
88 Luó Shìxìn, the Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn (General Administrator of the Expeditionary Army), led brave warriors to enter the outer city of Luòyáng by night,
set fire to Qīnghuàlǐ, and then returned.
On the day Rénxū,
Shìxìn captured Qīngchéngbǎo.
This fortress was likely built upon the Qīngchénggōng.
89 Wáng Shìchōng personally led troops to campaign for territory as far as Huátái,
and approached Líyáng.
Shí Déruì, the lord of Wèishìchéng, Wáng Yàohàn, the Cìshǐ of Biànzhōu, and Dīng Shūzé, the Cìshǐ of Bózhōu, sent envoys to surrender to him.
Biànzhōu was
the land of ancient Dàliáng.
During the Warring States period, it was the capital of Wèi.
In the Hàn dynasty, it was Chénliújùn.
The Eastern Wèi made it Liángzhōu.
The Later Zhōu changed it to Biànzhōu,
because the city was on the Biànshuǐ,
and was named after it.
Sòng Bái said: Bózhōu
was Jiāoyì of the Eastern State during the Spring and Autumn period.
In the Hàn dynasty, it was Qiáoxiàn.
The Wèi dynasty made it Qiáojùn.
Emperor Wǔ of the Later Zhōu established Bózhōu,
taking the name of ancient Nánbó remotely to name the prefecture.
將 (jiàng),
read as liàng.
使 (shǐ),
read as shūlì.
Yàohàn was the elder brother of Bódāng.
Xiàhóu Duān (夏侯端) arrived at Líyáng (黎陽).
In the fourth month of that year,
Xiàhóu Duān (夏侯端) was sent to pacify Huáizuǒ (淮左).
In the summer,
Hùyǎ (戶雅) is pronounced fān (翻).
From Chányuān (澶淵), he crossed the river.
In the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng (開皇) of the Suí (隋) dynasty,
Chányuān (澶淵) County was established;
at that time, it belonged to Lízhōu (黎州).
Chán (澶),
Shìlián (市連) is pronounced fān (翻).
East to the sea,
south to the Huái (淮) River,
over twenty prefectures,
all sent envoys to surrender.
When he reached Qiáozhōu (譙州),
the old gazetteer says: Bózhōu (亳州) was near Yúxiàn (漁縣),
Suí (隋) established Qiáozhōu (譙州).
His return route was then cut off.
Duān (端) had always enjoyed popular support;
the two thousand men who followed him,
though their provisions were exhausted, could not bear to abandon him and leave.
Duān (端) sat in the marsh,
killed his horses to feed his soldiers,
and then sighed, saying to them:
"Your hometowns have all gone over to the bandits.
It is solely out of the sentiment of having served together
that you have not yet been able to abandon me.
Wěi (委),
means to abandon.
I cannot follow you;
you have wives and children,
you should not imitate me.
You may cut off my head and return to the bandits,
and you will surely obtain wealth and honor."
All the men wept and said:
"My lord, you are not related to the Táng (唐) house,
but purely out of loyalty and righteousness,
you are determined not to seek survival.
Although we are lowly,
our hearts are also human;
how could we harm you to seek profit?"
Duān (端) said:
"If you cannot bear to kill me,
I will commit suicide."
The men held him,
and so they continued to advance together.
They travelled secretly for five days;
more than half died of starvation or were routed and lost to the bandits' attacks.
Only fifty-two men remained, fleeing together,
gathering and eating wild beans raw.
Duān (端) carried his official staff and never let it leave his side.
He repeatedly sent his followers to disperse
and seek their own lives,
but the men would not.
At that time, all the land south of the Huánghé (黃河) had fallen into Shìchōng's (世充) hands,
except for Yōngzhōu (雍州), whose prefect, Lǐ Gōngyì (李公逸), held firm for Táng (唐).
He sent troops to welcome Duān (端)
and provide him with lodging and supplies.
Shìchōng (世充) sent an envoy to summon Duān (端),
sent him clothes,
and also sent an official appointment document,
appointing Duān (端) as Duke of Huáinán (淮南) Commandery and Junior Minister of Personnel in the Department of State Affairs.
Duān (端), facing the envoy, burned the document and destroyed the clothes,
saying:
"Xiàhóu Duān (夏侯端) is an envoy of the Son of Heaven;
how can he accept an office from Wáng Shìchōng (王世充)?
If you want me to go,
you can only take my head!"
Thereupon, he untied the ornamental yak tail from his staff and put it in his bosom,
placed a blade on the staff,
and fled west through the mountains.
There were no more paths;
he bravely trampled through thorns,
traveling day and night.
He managed to reach Yíyáng (宜陽).
Yíyáng (宜陽) was
Táng's (唐) Xióngzhōu (熊州).
Tigers and wolves ate him,
and he lost half again;
those who survived had bald temples and hair,
no longer resembling humans.
Duān (端) went to the imperial court and met the emperor,
only apologizing for his lack of achievements,
never once mentioning his hardships.
The emperor reinstated him as Mìshūjiān (祕書監).
Láng Chǔzhī (郎楚之) went to Shāndōng (山東),
and was also captured by Dòu Jiàndé (竇建德).
Chǔzhī (楚之) did not yield
and eventually returned.
Láng Chǔzhī (郎楚之) and Xiàhóu Duān (夏侯端) were sent on their missions at the same time.
History records that when Táng (唐) rose,
those who were sent as envoys to the four directions
were all able to uphold their lord's command without disgrace.
Huán (還),
Cóngxuān (從宣) is pronounced fān (翻).
Wáng Shìchōng (王世充) sent his younger cousin, Shìbiàn (世辯), with troops from Xú (徐) and Bó (亳) to attack Yōngqiū (雍丘).
Lǐ Gōngyì (李公逸) sent an envoy to ask for help,
but the emperor, due to being separated by enemy territory,
could not send aid.
Gōngyì (公逸) then left his subordinate Lǐ Shànháng (李善行) to defend Yōngqiū (雍丘),
and personally led light cavalry to the court.
Upon reaching Xiāngchéng (襄城),
he was captured by Shìchōng's (世充) Yīzhōu (伊州) prefect, Zhāng Yīn (張殷).
Shìchōng (世充) said to him:
"You crossed Zhèng (鄭) to serve Táng (唐);
what is the reason for this?"
Gōngyì (公逸) said:
"In this world,
I only know of Táng (唐);
I do not know of Zhèng (鄭)."
Shìchōng (世充) was enraged
and executed him.
Shànháng (善行) also perished.
The emperor enfeoffed Gōngyì's (公逸) son as Duke of Xiāngyì (襄邑).
In the *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) year,
the emperor offered sacrifices at Huàshān (華山).
The New Gazetteer says: Huàshān (華山) is in Huáyīn (華陰) County of Huàzhōu (華州);
there is a temple for the sacred mountain.
Huà (華),
Hùhuà (戶化) is pronounced fān (翻).
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ (王崇武), revised by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖) and Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
