Later, Xué (學) Tiāntái (天台)
The second year of Wǔdé (武德)
(*jǐmǎo* (己卯), 619 CE)
1. In the eleventh month,
on the *jǐmǎo* (己卯) day,
Liú Wǔzhōu (劉武周) attacked Hào Zhōu (浩州).
Wǔzhōu (武周) again attacked Xīhé (西河).
2. Qín (秦) King Shìmín (世民) led troops from Lóngmén (龍門), crossed the river on the solid ice,
and encamped at Bǎibì (柏壁).
Bǎibì (柏壁) is northeast of Lóngmén (龍門) Pass.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Bǎibì (柏壁) is twenty *lǐ* (里) southwest of Zhèngpíng (正平) County.
Zhèngpíng (正平)
was the administrative seat of Jiàngzhōu (絳州).
At that time, the prefectures and counties of Hédōng (河東) —
here Hédōng (河東)
generally refers to east of the great river,
not specifically the Hédōng (河東) Commandery —
had no granaries.
The people were frightened and unsettled,
gathering in castles.
No provisions could be levied,
and the army lacked food.
Shìmín (世民) issued a proclamation to instruct the people.
When the people heard that Shìmín (世民) was their commander and had come,
none did not rally to him.
From near to far,
those who arrived increased daily.
Only then did he gradually collect their grain and food,
and the army's provisions were filled.
Confucius said:
"Sufficient food, sufficient weapons,
and the people's trust."
Since the people already trusted him,
sufficient food and sufficient weapons,
one should know the order of priorities.
He only allowed his subordinate generals to seize opportunities for raids;
the main army fortified its positions and did not fight.
Consequently, the strength of the bandits declined daily.
Shìmín (世民) once personally led light cavalry to scout the enemy.
His cavalry all scattered,
and Shìmín (世民), alone with one armored soldier, climbed a hill and slept.
Suddenly, enemy troops converged from all four sides.
At first, they were unaware,
but a snake chasing a mouse
touched the armored soldier's face.
The soldier awoke in surprise
and immediately alerted Shìmín (世民) to both mount their horses.
History says Shìmín (世民) had a heavenly mandate.
Shàng (上),
Shízhǎng (時掌) is pronounced fān (翻).
They were overtaken by the bandits.
Shìmín (世民) shot and killed their valiant general with a large feathered arrow.
History says Shìmín (世民) not only had a heavenly mandate,
but also possessed extraordinary martial skill.
Shè (射),
Éryì (而亦) is pronounced fān (翻).
Yì (殪),
Yījì (一計) is pronounced fān (翻).
Xiāo (驍),
Jiānyáo (堅堯) is pronounced fān (翻);
the same below.
Jiàng (將),
Jíliàng (即亮) is pronounced fān (翻);
the same below.
Cáo Dàn
was the elder brother of Jiàndé's wife.
While in Hénán,
he engaged in much raiding and harassment,
and all the bandit subordinates resented him.
The bandit leader Lǐ Wénxiāng from Wèijùn,
known as Lǐ Shānghú,
gathered over five thousand men
and occupied Zhōngtàn in Mèngjīn;
this was the Zhōngtàn Fort of Héyáng.
Sòng Bái said: Zhōngtàn Fort
was built by the Eastern Wèi
and the Héyáng Pass was also established there.
"Tàn"
is pronounced like "tú hàn."
He was also skilled in horsemanship and archery,
and called himself Huò Zǒngguǎn.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Gémìngjì* states
that Shānghú's mother, Lady Zhāng,
was known
as "Nǚ Jiāngjūn."
We now follow the *Héluòjì*.
(Lǐ Shìjì) entered and bowed to Shānghú's mother.
The mother wept and said to Shìjì:
"The Dòu clan is without principle,
how can we serve them!"
Shìjì said:
"Mother, do not worry.
In no more than a month,
we will kill him [Cáo Dàn],
and together return to Táng!"
Shìjì took his leave.
The mother said to Shānghú:
"The Duke of Dōnghǎi has promised me to plan against this bandit.
If the matter drags on, changes will arise.
Why must we wait for his arrival?
It is better to make a swift decision."
That night,
Shānghú summoned twenty-three of Cáo Dàn's subordinate officers
and gave them wine,
then killed them all.
Dàn's separate generals Gāo Yǎxián and Ruǎn Jūnmíng were still north of the Hé (Yellow River) and had not yet crossed.
Shānghú used four large boats to ferry three hundred soldiers from north of the Hé,
and when they reached mid-stream,
he killed them all.
A veterinarian swam and escaped.
The veterinarian
followed the army because he could treat oxen and horses.
"Jiāng"
is pronounced like "liàng."
"Sōu"
is pronounced like "sū zāo."
He reported to Cáo Dàn,
who then became strictly vigilant and prepared for defense.
After Shānghú initiated the action,
he first sent someone to inform Lǐ Shìjì.
Shìjì and Cáo Dàn had continuous camps.
Guō Xiàokè urged Shìjì to attack Dàn,
but Shìjì was undecided.
Hearing that Dàn was already prepared,
he and Xiàokè led dozens of cavalry to defect.
Shānghú then led two thousand elite soldiers
to attack Ruǎn Jūnmíng in the north
and defeated him.
Gāo Yǎxián gathered his men and left.
Shānghú pursued him
but failed to catch him and returned.
Jiàndé's [Dòu Jiàndé's] favored ministers requested to execute Lǐ Gài.
Jiàndé said:
"Shìjì,
a Táng official,
was captured by me,
yet he does not forget his original court.
He is a loyal subject.
What crime has his father committed!"
So he pardoned him.
On *Jiǎwǔ*,
Shìjì and Xiàokè arrived in Cháng'ān.
Cáo Dàn then took Jìzhōu.
At the beginning of Wǔdé,
Zhāng Qīngtè occupied Jìběi.
Jìběijùn was Jìzhōu.
After this, Jiàndé and Táng were in a standoff at Hǔláo.
Zhāng Qīngtè's grain transports were captured by Táng,
presumably because Jìzhōu had previously surrendered to Cáo Dàn.
"Jì"
is pronounced like "zǐ lǐ."
3 In the second month,
on *Gēngzǐ*,
the Emperor visited Huáyīn.
4 Liú Wǔzhōu sent troops to invade Lùzhōu,
capturing Chángzǐ and Húguān.
Both counties belonged to Lùzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Lùzhōu
was the state of Lùzǐ in the Spring and Autumn period,
and Shàngdǎngjùn in Qín and Hàn;
the Northern Zhōu established Lùzhōu,
named for its proximity to the Fén and Lù rivers.
The Emperor sent General Wáng Xíngmǐn of Hédōng to assist them.
Hédōng county was part of Púzhōu,
which is the Púfǎn mentioned.
In the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng of the Suí dynasty,
a county was established by separating it from Púfǎn.
In the early years of Dàyè,
Púfǎn was merged into it.
Someone said that Zǐwǔ was about to rebel,
so Xíngmǐn beheaded Zǐwǔ for public display.
On *Yǐsì*,
Wǔzhōu again sent troops to invade Lùzhōu,
and Xíngmǐn attacked and defeated them.
5 On *Rénzǐ*,
the Mán rebel Rǎn Zhàozé from Kāizhōu captured Tōngzhōu.
Old records state: Kāizhōu
was Shèngshān county of Bādōngjùn during the Suí dynasty;
Shèngshān
was Qúnín county of Bājùn in the Hàn dynasty.
In the first year of Yìníng,
Wànzhōu was established by separating Shèngshān and Xīnpǔ from Bādōng,
and Wànshì and Xīliú from Tōngchuān.
In the first year of Wǔdé,
it was renamed Kāizhōu.
Tōngzhōu
was the land of Dàngqú county in the Hàn dynasty.
The Liáng dynasty established Wànzhōu,
which the Northern Wèi renamed Tōngzhōu.
The Suí dynasty called it Tōngchuānjùn,
and in the first year of Wǔdé,
it was again Tōngzhōu.
Sūn Miǎn said: Tōngzhōu was originally Dàngqú county in the Hàn dynasty.
There were over ten thousand *qǐng* of land within it,
hence it was named Wànzhōu;
later the Northern Wèi, considering Wànzhōu to be at a crossroads,
changed its name to Tōngzhōu;
the Sòng dynasty called it Dázhōu.
6 On *Jiǎyín*,
generals Sāng Xiǎnhé and others were sent to attack Lǚ Chóngmào in Xiàxiàn.
7 Initially,
the Minister of Works, Dúgū Huái'ēn, attacked Púfǎn.
It did not fall for a long time,
and there were many losses.
The Emperor repeatedly sent imperial edicts to reproach him,
causing Huái'ēn to resent and grumble.
The Emperor once playfully said to Huái'ēn:
"All your aunts' sons have become emperors"
(referring to Emperor Yáng of Suí and the current Emperor).
Huái'ēn was quite proud of this
and sometimes clenched his fists, saying:
"How can only women in my family be noble?"
(Empress of Zhōu Míngdì, Empress of Suí Wéndì, and the current Emperor's mother were all of the Dúgū clan.)
"Wàn"
is pronounced like "wū guàn."
It so happened that Huái'ēn, Jūnbǎo, and Táng Jiǎn were all captured by Yùchí Jìngdé.
Jūnbǎo said to Jiǎn:
"Minister Dúgū recently plotted a great affair.
If he had decided early,
how could we have suffered this humiliation!"
When Qínwáng Shìmín defeated Jìngdé at Měiliángchuān,
Huái'ēn escaped and returned.
The Emperor again ordered him to lead troops to attack Púfǎn.
Jūnbǎo again said to Jiǎn:
"Minister Dúgū successfully escaped the danger and returned,
and is again at Púfǎn.
This can be called 'a king does not die'!"
Jiǎn feared that Huái'ēn would realize his plot,
so he persuaded Yùchí Jìngdé
to allow Liú Shìràng to return and establish peace with Táng.
Jìngdé agreed,
and thus reported Huái'ēn's rebellion.
At that time, Wáng Xíngběn had already surrendered,
and Huái'ēn entered and occupied his city.
The Emperor was about to cross the river to visit Huái'ēn's camp,
and had already boarded the boat,
when Shìràng arrived.
The Emperor was greatly surprised and said:
"My escape,
is it not Heaven's will!"
He then sent for Huái'ēn.
Huái'ēn, unaware that the matter was exposed,
came in a light boat.
He was immediately seized and handed over to officials,
and his confederates were arrested separately.
On *Jiǎyín*,
Huái'ēn and his party were executed.
8 Dòu Jiàndé attacked Lǐ Shānghú
and killed him.
Jiàndé
encouraged agriculture and sericulture in Míngzhōu.
There were no bandits within the territory,
and merchants could sleep in the open.
9 The Eastern Göktürk Chùluó Kèhán welcomed Yáng Zhèngdào
and established him as the King of Suí.
Yáng Zhèngdào
was the posthumous son of Qí Wáng Yǎn.
Jue,
pronounced jiǔ wù fān.
Chù,
pronounced chāng lǚ fān.
Kè,
from kān, entering tone.
Hán,
pronounced hán.
Chùluó allocated all of his possessions to him
and gave him an army of ten thousand men.
He established a hundred officials,
all according to the Suí system,
and resided in Dìngxiāng.
This was presumably the Dìngxiāng Commandery of Suí,
with its seat at Dàlìchéng.
10 In the third month,
on the Yǐchǒu day,
Liú Wǔzhōu sent his general Zhāng Wànsuì to raid Hàozhōu.
Lǐ Zhòngwén attacked and routed him,
capturing and beheading several thousand men.
11 The position of Nàyán was changed to Shìzhōng,
Nèishǐlìng to Zhōngshūlìng,
and Gěishìláng to Gěishìzhōng.
These were restorations of old official titles.
Dù Yòu said: According to the Hàn system,
a Gěishìzhōng
attended court daily, reviewed memorials from the Shàngshū,
and was involved in matters within the palace,
hence the name Gěishìzhōng.
It was abolished in the Eastern Hàn,
restored in Wèi,
and continued through the Northern and Southern Dynasties.
In the Later Zhōu, among the officials of the Tiānguān, there was a Gěishìzhōng
who was in charge of studying the Six Classics
and serving the emperor directly;
later, a separate Gěishìzhōng was established,
outside the Six Ministries.
In the early Suí,
a Gěishìláng was established in the Lìbù (Ministry of Personnel).
During Yángdì's reign,
it was moved to the Ménxià (Chancellery)
with four members
to review memorials.
By this time,
it was changed to Gěishìzhōng.
In the second year of Lóngshuò,
it was changed to Dōngtái Shèrén;
in the first year of Xiánhéng,
it reverted to its old name.
Its duties included attending the emperor, reading and signing memorials,
checking for errors,
and assisting in managing provincial affairs.
The Gěishìzhōng name was derived from the Hàn,
but its functions followed the Zhōu and Suí.
12 On the Jiǎxū day,
Fēng Déyí, Nèishǐ Shìláng, was appointed Zhōngshūlìng.
13 Commanders and officials from prefectures and counties under Wáng Shìchōng who surrendered
continued to arrive monthly.
Shìchōng then made his laws more severe:
if one person absconded,
the entire family, regardless of age, was executed.
Fathers and sons, brothers, and husbands and wives were allowed to inform on each other to be spared.
He also organized five families into a mutual surveillance group.
If an entire family absconded,
and the four neighboring families did not notice,
they were all executed.
The more people he killed, the more people absconded,
to the point that woodcutters and gatherers
had limited numbers for their comings and goings.
Both public and private life were distressed,
and people found life unbearable.
He also turned the palace into a large prison.
Those he distrusted,
along with their families, were arrested and confined in the palace.
When generals went on campaigns,
their families were also held hostage in the palace.
Those forbidden to leave numbered no less than ten thousand,
and dozens died of starvation daily.

Shìchōng also appointed officials from the Tái and Shěng (central government) as commanders for agricultural garrisons in twelve prefectures: Sī, Zhèng, Guǎn, Yuán, Yī, Yīn, Liáng, Còu, Sōng, Gǔ, Huái, and Dé.
Shìchōng renamed Luòzhōu to Sīzhōu,
Sìshuǐ to Zhèngzhōu,
Guǎnchéng to Guǎnzhōu,
Qìnshuǐ to Yuánzhōu,
Xiāngchéng to Yīzhōu,
Huòjiā to Yīnzhōu,
and Suīyáng to Liángzhōu.
Còuzhōu
is missing;
the Jiǔyùzhì states that there was Còushuǐ as an ancient site in Zhèngzhōu,
so Còuzhōu should have been established there.
Sōngyáng to Sōngzhōu,
Dàgǔ to Gǔzhōu,
Hénèi to Huáizhōu,
and Wǔdé to Dézhōu.
He was as happy as if ascending to heaven.
Chéng and Láng
refer to the Shàngshū Zuǒyòuchéng and various Cáoláng.
The historian states that Wáng Shìchōng was about to fail.
14 On the Jiǎshēn day,
the Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Army, Zhāng Lún, defeated Liú Wǔzhōu at Hàozhōu,
capturing and beheading over a thousand men.
15 The Duke of Xīhé, Zhāng Lún—
this Zhāng Lún is the same Zhāng Lún mentioned above;
above, his official title was recorded,
here, his noble rank.
Shízhōu
was the Líshí Commandery of Suí.
On the Yǐyǒu day,
Jìzhēn was appointed Shízhōu Zǒngguǎn,
granted the imperial surname Lǐ,
and enfeoffed as King of Péngshān Commandery.
16 The Man chieftain Rǎn Zhàozé raided Xìnzhōu.
According to the Xīnzhì: Xìnzhōu
was the Bādōng Commandery of Suí,
renamed Kuízhōu in the second year of Wǔdé.
The historian uses its old prefectural name.
Dù Yòu said: Kuízhōu
was the State of Yú in the Spring and Autumn period,
and Liáng established Xìnzhōu there.
In the second year of Wǔdé in Táng,
to avoid the taboo name of the emperor's maternal grandfather Dúgū Xìn,
it was renamed Kuízhōu,
with its seat in Fèngjié County.
Qiú,
pronounced cí yóu fān.
They were unsuccessful.
Lǐ Jìng led eight hundred soldiers,
launched a surprise attack,
beheaded him,
and captured over five thousand men.
On the Jǐchǒu day,
Kāi and Tōng prefectures were recovered.
Xiàogōng also attacked Xiāo Xiǎn's King Dōngpíng, Shétí,
and beheaded him.
17 Summer,
fourth month,
on the Bǐngshēn day,
the Emperor offered sacrifices at Huàshān;
on the Rénxín day,
he returned to Cháng'ān.
18 The Yìzhōu Dào Xíngtái was established,
with the six Zǒngguǎn of Yì, Lì, Huì, Fū,
Jīng, and Suì subordinate to it.
Yìzhōu was the Shǔ Commandery of Suí.
Lìzhōu was the Yìchéng Commandery of Suí,
the Lízhōu of Liáng,
the Jìnshòu of Jìn,
the Hànshòu of Shǔ,
and the Jiāměng of Hàn.
Huìzhōu was the Huìníng Garrison of Liángchuān County of Suí,
and the Huìzhōu of Western Wèi.
Fūzhōu was the Shàng Commandery of Suí,
the Fūzhōu of Western Wèi,
and the Běihuázhōu Zhōngbù Fūchéng Commandery of Later Wèi;
in the middle of Tàihé, it was Dōngqínzhōu.

his spear was less than a foot from Hǎilíng (海陵).
Jì (勣) cried out in alarm repeatedly, saying: 'Ah xiōng (阿兄),
this is Jìwáng (勣王)!'
Xióngxìn (雄信) then reined in his horse and stopped.
He looked back and smiled, saying: 'Hú'ér (胡兒)! If it weren't for you,
I would have finished him!' "
The Jiùshū (舊書) probably made a mistake based on this.
If Xióngxìn (雄信) had known it was Qínwáng (秦王),
he would have been even more eager to capture him;
how could he have been frightened and retreated!
Even if it were as stated in the Xiǎoshuō (小說),
Xióngxìn (雄信), having received Shìchōng's (世充) order
to target Yuánjí (元吉),
would he have let him go because of Jì (勣)?
Moreover, when Yuánjí (元吉) besieged Dōngdū (東都),
Jì (勣) was with Tàizōng (太宗) at Wǔláo (武牢).
This account is not adopted now.
He captured their Zǒujiànwēi Jiāngjūn (左建威將軍) Yān Qí (燕琪),
and Shìchōng (世充) then retreated.
Shìmín (世民) returned to the camp,
his face covered in dust,
the army did not recognize him,
and wanted to bar him;
Shìmín (世民) removed his helmet and identified himself,
only then was he able to enter.
The next day,
he led fifty thousand infantry and cavalry to advance towards Cíjiàn (慈澗);
Shìchōng (世充) withdrew the garrison from Cíjiàn (慈澗)
and returned to Luòyáng (洛陽).
Shìmín (世民) dispatched Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn (行軍總管) Shǐ Wànbǎo (史萬寶) from Yíyáng (宜陽) to occupy Lóngmén (龍門) to the south.
This is the Lóngmén (龍門) of Yīquè (伊闕).
Lì Dàoyuán (酈道元) said: The Yī (伊) river flows north into Yīquè (伊闕).
In ancient times, Dà Yǔ (大禹) dredged it to let the water pass,
the two mountains face each other,
looking like a watchtower,
hence it is called Yīquè (伊闕).
In the Chūnqiū (春秋),
in the twenty-sixth year of Zhāogōng (昭公),
Zhào Yāng (趙鞅) sent Nǚ Kuān (女寬) to guard Quèsāi (闕塞),
which is this place.
Fù Yì's (傅毅) Dōngdū Fù (東都賦) says: "By Lóngmén (龍門) to spread civilization,
opening Yīquè (伊闕) to reach understanding."
After this, Wǔhòu (武后) resided in Dōngdū (東都),
often visited Lóngmén (龍門),
which is exactly this place.
Shànggǔgōng Wáng Jūnkuò (上谷公王君廓) cut off their supply route from Luòkǒu (洛口),
Huáizhōu Zǒngguǎn (懷州總管) Huáng Jūnhàn (黃君漢) attacked Huíluòchéng (迴洛城) from Héyīn (河陰);
the main army was encamped at Běimáng (北邙),
with連營 (liányíng) to press upon it.
Shìchōng's (世充) Wěizhōu Chángshǐ (洧州長史) Fánshuǐ (繁水) Zhāng Gōngjǐn (張公謹) and Cìshǐ (刺史) Cuī Shū (崔樞) surrendered with their prefecture city.
Shìchōng (世充) probably established Wěizhōu (洧州) at Fúgōu (扶溝) and Yānlíng (鄢陵).
The Suí Zhì (隋志) says:
Fánshuǐ (繁水) county belonged to Wǔyáng Jùn (武陽郡).
In the eighteenth year of Zhēnguān (貞觀) of Táng (唐),
it was merged into Chānglè Xiàn (昌樂縣),
belonging to Wèizhōu (魏州).
Wěi (洧),
pronounced Yú Guǐ (于軌) fan.
Jiàng (降),
Hù Jiāng (戶江) fan;
same below.
41 In the eighth month,
on the day Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
the Nánníng Xīcuàn Mán (南寧西爨蠻) sent envoys to offer tribute.
Originally,
at the end of the Suí (隋), the barbarian chief Cuàn Wán (爨翫) rebelled,
was executed,
his sons were enslaved by the government,
and their territory abandoned.
For Cuàn Wán (爨翫), see volume 178, Suíwéndì Kāihuáng (隋文帝開皇) seventeenth and eighteenth years.
Shǐ (使),
Shū Lì (疏吏) fan.
Qiú (酋),
Cí Yóu (慈由) fan.
His son Hóngdá (弘達) was made Kūnzhōu Cìshǐ (昆州刺史).
The Xīn Zhì (新志) says: Kūnzhōu (昆州) was originally established by the Suí (隋),
and abandoned during the chaos of the Suí (隋).
In the first year of Wǔdé (武德),
it was re-established after opening Nánzhōng (南中),
administering Jìnníng (晉寧), Qínzàng (秦臧) and other counties.
Yìzhōu Cìshǐ (益州刺史) Duàn Lún (段綸) then sent envoys to invite and pacify their tribes,
and they all surrendered.
42 On the day Jǐhài (己亥),
Dòu Jiàndé's (竇建德) Gòngzhōu (共州) county magistrate Táng Gāng (唐綱) killed the Cìshǐ (刺史)
and surrendered with the prefecture.
The Xīn Zhì (新志) says: Gòngchéng Xiàn (共城縣) of Wèizhōu (衞州).
In the first year of Wǔdé (武德), Gòngzhōu (共州) was established.
Last year, Dòu Jiàndé (竇建德) defeated and assimilated Lǐ Shìjì (李世勣),
taking Wèizhōu (衞州),
so Gòngzhōu (共州) also attached itself to Jiàndé (建德).
Táng Gāng (唐綱) should be the Gòngchéng Xiànlìng (共城縣令).
Gòng (共),
read as Gōng (恭).
Jiàng (降),
Hù Jiāng (戶江) fan.
43 The local gentry of Dèngzhōu (鄧州) captured the Cìshǐ (刺史) appointed by Wáng Shìchōng (王世充) and surrendered.
In the fifth month of this year,
Wáng Shìchōng (王世充) captured Dèngzhōu (鄧州).
44 On the day Guǐmǎo (癸卯),
Liáng Shīduō's (梁師都) Shíbǎo Liúshǒu (石堡留守) Zhāng Jǔ (張舉) led over a thousand men to surrender.
This Shíbǎo (石堡) was probably east of Xiàzhōu (夏州),
not the Shíbǎochéng (石堡城) that was contested with the Tǔbō (吐蕃) during the Kāiyuán (開元) and Tiānbǎo (天寶) eras.
Shǒu (守),
Shì Yòu (式又) fan.
Shuài (帥),
read as Shuài (率);
same below.
45 On the day Jiǎchén (甲辰),
Huáng Jūnhàn (黃君漢) sent Xiàowèi (校尉) Zhāng Yèchā (張夜叉) with a naval force to attack Huíluòchéng (迴洛城),
capturing it.
With a naval force, he crossed the river from Huáizhōu (懷州), attacked and captured Huíluò (迴洛).
He cut off the southern bridge of Héyáng (河陽) and returned,
capturing over twenty forts and settlements.
Shìchōng (世充) sent Prince Xuányìng (玄應) leading Yáng Gōngqīng (楊公卿) and others to attack Huíluò (迴洛),
but could not capture it,
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Gémìngjì (革命記) writes "Gōngxiāng (公鄉)".
The Hélùojì (河洛記) and Tángshū (唐書) write "Gōngqīng (公卿)",
which is followed here.
He left troops to garrison it.
Yuán Shìchōng arranged his army at Qīngchéng Gōng.
Qín Wáng Lǐ Shìmín also deployed his army to confront him.
Nowadays, people refer to the grand lodging place for fasting and offering sacrifices to Heaven in the suburbs as Qīngchéng Gōng,
so its location should be south of the capital city.
This Qīngchéng Gōng, however, seems to be northwest of Luòchéng.
According to the Liùdiǎn,
the western forbidden garden of Luòchéng
faced Běimáng to the north,
reached Xiàoshuǐ to the west,
and bordered Luòshuǐ to the south.
Tributaries of Gǔshuǐ and Luòshuǐ converged within it,
and it contained eleven palaces, including Héhépì, Cuìwēi, Sùyǔ, and Qīngchéng.
Chén [陣],
is pronounced as zhèn.
"The Suí dynasty is overthrown,
the Táng emperor is in Guānzhōng,
and the Zhèng emperor is in Hénán.
Shìchōng has never invaded the west,
so why has the King suddenly brought his army to the east?"
Lǐ Shìmín sent Yǔwén Shìjí to respond:
"All within the four seas look up to the imperial prestige,
but only you obstruct the sounds of moral instruction;
it is for this reason we have come!"
Shìchōng said:
"How good it would be if we ceased hostilities and made peace!"
The reply again was:
"We are commanded by imperial decree to take Dōngdū,
not to make peace."
By dusk,
each withdrew their troops.
The Emperor sent an envoy to make an alliance with Dòu Jiàndé.
Jiàndé sent Tóng'ān Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ back with the envoy.
Tóng'ān Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ was
the Emperor's paternal cousin (daughter of his mother's sister).
When Líyáng was defeated,
she fell captive to Dòu Jiàndé.
Shǐ [使],
is pronounced as shū lì.
Zhǎng [長],
is pronounced as zhī liǎng.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
Liú Déwēi attacked Huáizhōu,
entered its outer wall,
and subdued its strongholds.
In the ninth month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
Liáng Shīdu's general, Liú Mín, surrendered with Huáchí,
and was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Línzhōu.
Huáchí Xiàn of Qìngzhōu
was Wèizhōu of the Western Wèi.
After the Zhōu prefecture was abolished by the Later Zhōu,
in the early Rénshòu era of the Suí dynasty,
Huáchí Xiàn was established,
and now Línzhōu is established there.
Jiàng [將],
is pronounced as jí liàng.
Jiàng [降],
is pronounced as hù jiāng.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
Wáng Shìchōng's Grand Administrator of Xiǎnzhōu, Tián Zàn, surrendered with his twenty-five prefectures;
in the sixth month of that year,
Tián Zàn had surrendered to Shìchōng.
Zàn [瓚],
is pronounced as cáng hàn.
Shìchōng sent Wáng Hóngliè to garrison Xiāngyáng.
From Xiāngyáng to Luòyáng,
the route passed through Nányáng.
As Dèngzhōu now belonged to Táng,
the Nányáng route could not be used.
Thus, one would go from Xiǎnzhōu, through Cài and Rǔ, to Luòyáng.
Xiǎnzhōu has now also surrendered to Táng,
so communication with Xiāngyáng is cut off.
Shǐ Wànbǎo advanced his army to Gānquán Gōng.
The Hàn Gānquán Gōng was in Lǐquán Xiàn of Jīngzhào.
Shǐ Wànbǎo advanced from Xīn'ān, pressing towards Luòyáng,
and should not have reached the Hàn Gānquán Gōng.
The Suí Zhì states: Shòu'ān Xiàn in Hénán
was Gāntáng Xiàn of the Later Wèi,
and had Xiǎnrén Gōng.
Perhaps Xiǎnrén Gōng was mistaken for Gāntáng Gōng.
"Quán" [泉],
should perhaps be
"Táng" [棠].
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Qín Wáng Lǐ Shìmín sent Yòu Wǔwèi Jiàngjūn Wáng Jūnkuò to attack Huányuán,
and captured it.
The Xīn Zhì states: Southeast of Gōushì Xiàn in Luòzhōu is the old pass of Huányuán.
Huán [轘],
is pronounced as huán.
Wáng Jūnkuò feigned retreat,
set an ambush,
and decisively defeated them,
then advanced eastward to take territory,
reaching Guǎnchéng before returning.
The Suí Zhì states: Guǎnchéng Xiàn in Xíngyáng Jùn,
formerly called Zhōngmóu,
was established as Guǎnchéng Xiàn in the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng by separation,
and in the eighteenth year, Nèimóu was abolished and incorporated into it.
The Suí changed Zhōngmóu to Nèimóu,
which at that time was the seat of Guǎnzhōu.
Jiàng [將],
is pronounced as jí liàng;
the same below.
Huán [還],
is pronounced as cóng xuān.
Wáng Shìchōng's generals Guō Shìhéng and Xǔ Luóhàn plundered Táng territory.
Wáng Jūnkuò repelled them with strategy.
An imperial edict commended him, saying:
"You, with thirteen men, defeated ten thousand bandits.
From ancient times, to control the many with the few,
this has never happened."
Shìchōng's Prefect of Wèizhōu, Shí Déruì, led his forces from seven prefectures—Xià, Chén, Suí, Xǔ, Yǐng, and Wèi—to surrender.
Wáng Shìchōng likely established Wèizhōu in Yōngqiū,
Xiàzhōu in Yángxià,
Chénzhōu in Wǎnqiū;
Suízhōu has no verifiable location,
possibly a mistake for Wèizhōu;
Xǔzhōu in Chángshè,
Yǐngzhōu in Rǔyīn,
and Wèizhōu in Wèishì.
Shuài [帥],
is pronounced as shuài.
Jiàng [降],
is pronounced as hù jiāng;
the same below.
With no alterations,
Wèizhōu was renamed Nánbiànzhōu.
Thereupon, the commanderies and counties of Hénán successively surrendered.
Liú Wǔzhōu's surrendered generals, Xún Xiāng and others, defected.
The generals suspected Yùchí Jìngdé,
and imprisoned him in the army camp.
Xíngtái Zuǒ Púshè Qūtú Tōng and Shàngshū Yīn Kāishān said to Lǐ Shìmín:
"Jìngdé is extraordinarily brave and fierce.
Now that he is imprisoned, his heart must be resentful.
Keeping him might lead to future trouble;
it would be better to kill him."
Lǐ Shìmín said:
"Not so.
If Jìngdé were to rebel,
would it be after Xún Xiāng and the others?"
He immediately ordered his release,
brought him into his sleeping quarters,
bestowed gold upon him,
and said:
"A man's aspirations are understood between us;
do not let small resentments trouble your mind.
I will never believe slanderous words to harm loyal and good men;
you should understand this.
If you must leave,
take this gold as a resource,
representing the sentiment of our shared work for a time."
On the day Xīnsì,
Lǐ Shìmín, with five hundred cavalry, went to the battlefield,
and ascended the Wèi Xuānwǔ Líng.
Wèi Xuānwǔ Líng was called Jǐnglíng,
and was located on Běimáng Shān.
Emperor Shìzōng of Wèi was posthumously honored as Emperor Xuānwǔ.
He was surrounded.
Shàn Xióngxìn, wielding his spear, charged directly at Lǐ Shìmín.
Yùchí Jìngdé galloped forward with a great shout,
thrust his spear sideways, unseating Shàn Xióngxìn,
and Shìchōng's troops somewhat retreated.
Yùchí Jìngdé protected Lǐ Shìmín as they broke out of the encirclement.
Lǐ Shìmín and Yùchí Jìngdé then led the cavalry back to battle,
entering and exiting Shìchōng's formations,
moving back and forth without obstruction.
Qūtú Tōng arrived later with a large army.
Shìchōng's army was greatly defeated,
barely escaping with his life;
his Grand General of Champions, Chén Zhìlüè, was captured,
over a thousand heads were taken,
and six thousand shield and spear soldiers were captured.
Páishuò [排矟],
refers to those who wield shields and spears.
Shuò [矟],
is the same as suò [槊].
"How quickly you have repaid me!"
Yùchí Jìngdé was given a casket of gold and silver,
and from then on, his favor and treatment increased daily.
Jìngdé (敬德) was skilled at dodging spears.
Each time he rode alone into the enemy formation,
the enemy would thrust many spears at him,
but in the end, none could wound him.
He could also snatch the enemy's spears and use them to counter-stab.
Qí Wáng Yuánjí (齊王元吉) prided himself on his skill with horses and spears.
Hearing of Jìngdé's (敬德) ability,
he requested that they both remove the blades from their spears and compete to determine superiority.
Jìngdé (敬德) said:
"Jìngdé (敬德) will duly remove his,
but Your Highness need not remove yours."
Afterwards, Yuánjí (元吉) thrust at him,
but was unable to hit him.
Qín Wáng Shìmín (秦王世民) asked Jìngdé (敬德):
"Snatching a spear or dodging a spear,
which is more difficult?"
Jìngdé (敬德) replied:
"Snatching a spear is more difficult."
So, Shìmín (世民) ordered Jìngdé (敬德) to snatch Yuánjí's (元吉) spear.
Yuánjí (元吉) wielded his spear, leaped on his horse,
intent on stabbing him,
but Jìngdé (敬德) snatched his spear three times in a short while.
Although Yuánjí (元吉) praised and marvelled at him to his face,
he was deeply ashamed internally.
51 The rebellious Hú (胡) troops captured Lánzhōu (嵐州).
52 Originally,
Wáng Shìchōng (王世充) appointed Bǐng Yuánzhēn (邴元真) as the Púshè (僕射) of Huázhōu (滑州) Xíngtái (行臺).
Dù Cáigàn (杜才幹), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Púzhōu (濮州),
(According to Suí Zhì (隋志): The county of Juànchéng (鄄城) was in Dōngpíng Jùn (東平郡).
Previously, Púyáng Jùn (濮陽郡) was established.
In the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng (開皇), Púzhōu (濮州) was established.
In the early years of Dàyè (大業), the prefecture was abolished,
and Juànchéng (鄄城) county belonged to Dōngpíng (東平).
It was probably Lǐ Mì (李密) who re-established the prefecture.)
(Pú (濮),
pronounced bómù.) resented Yuánzhēn (元真) for betraying Mì (密).
(The matter of the betrayal of Mì (密) can be found in Volume 186, first year, ninth month.)
Yuánzhēn (元真), relying on his official position and power,
went himself to recruit and pacify Cáigàn (才幹).
Cáigàn (才幹) came out to meet him,
invited him in to sit down,
seized him, and enumerated his faults, saying:
"You were originally a mediocre talent.
Wèi Gōng (魏公) appointed you a principal aide,
referring to Lǐ Mì (李密) as his Zhǎngshǐ (長史).
Yet you stirred up a monstrous calamity.
Now you come to your death,
this is your due!"
Thereupon, he beheaded him,
and sent someone to carry his head to Líyáng (黎陽) to offer sacrifice at Mì's (密) tomb.
On the day Rénwǔ (壬午),
Púzhōu (濮州) surrendered.
53 The Tujue (突厥) Mòhèduō Shè (莫賀咄設) plundered Liángzhōu (涼州).
The Zǒngguǎn (總管) Yáng Gōngrén (楊恭仁) attacked them,
but was defeated by them,
and they left after plundering several thousand men and women.
54 On the day Bǐngxū (丙戌),
Tián Zàn (田瓚) was appointed Xiǎnzhōu (顯州) Zǒngguǎn (總管),
and was granted the noble title Càiguó Gōng (蔡國公).
55 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Jiǎwǔ (甲午),
Wáng Shìchōng's (王世充) Dàjiāngjūn (大將軍) Zhāng Zhènzhōu (張鎮周) surrendered.
56 On the day Jiǎchén (甲辰),
the Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn (行軍總管) Luó Shìxìn (羅士信) raided Wáng Shìchōng's (王世充) Xiáshíbǎo (硤石堡)
and captured it.
(According to Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註): The Gǔshuǐ (穀水) flows east from Xīn'ān Xiàn (新安縣), passing through Qiānqiūtíng (千秋亭),
then flows east through Yōnggǔxī (雍谷溪).
Its winding cliffs and rugged stone paths
give it the name Xiáshí (峽石).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Hélùojì (河洛記) records it as
"Xiáshānbǎo" (峽山堡).
We now follow the Shílù (實錄).
This fortress was built near the ancient Qiānjīn'è (千金堨).
Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) states: The Gǔshuǐ (穀水) passes north of Zhōu Gàn Jìmén (周乾祭門),
and flows east to Qiānjīn'è (千金堨).
The Hénán Jìngbù (河南境簿) states: Fifteen *lǐ* (里) east of the city of Hénán Xiàn (河南縣) is Qiānjīn'è (千金堨).
The Luòyángjì (洛陽記) states: Qiānjīn'è (千金堨) was formerly used to dam the Gǔshuǐ (穀水);
in the Wèi (魏) period, this dam was repaired
and called Qiānjīn'è (千金堨).)
Shìxìn (士信) sent over a hundred men at night, carrying several tens of infants, to the foot of the fortress,
making the children cry out,
pretending to say:
"We have come from Dōngdū (東都) to surrender to Zǒngguǎn (總管) Luó (羅)."
Soon after, they said to each other:
"This is Qiānjīnbǎo (千金堡).
We have made a mistake."
Then they left.
The people in the fortress thought that Shìxìn (士信) had already left
and that these were refugees from Luòyáng (洛陽).
They sent troops to pursue them.
Shìxìn (士信) had ambushed troops on the road.
When he saw the gate open,
he burst in
and slaughtered them.
57 When Dòu Jiàndé (竇建德) besieged Yōuzhōu (幽州)—
in the fifth month of this year,
Jiàndé's (建德) troops attacked Yōuzhōu (幽州).
Kāidào (開道) led two thousand cavalry to rescue it.
Jiàndé's (建德) troops withdrew,
and Kāidào (開道) then sent an envoy to surrender.
On the day Wùshēn (戊申),
Kāidào (開道) was appointed Wèizhōu (蔚州) Zǒngguǎn (總管).
(Wèizhōu (蔚州) was formerly the territory of Língqiū (靈丘) county in Suí (隋) Yànmén Jùn (鴈門郡) and Fēihú (飛狐) county in Shànggǔ Jùn (上谷郡).)
(Wèi (蔚),
pronounced yūwù.)
and enfeoffed as Běipíng Jùnwáng (北平郡王).
Kāidào (開道) had an arrowhead in his cheek.
He summoned a doctor to remove it.
The doctor said:
"The arrowhead is deep;
it cannot be removed."
Kāidào (開道) became angry
and beheaded him.
He summoned another doctor,
who said:
"Removing it may be painful."
He also beheaded him.
He summoned yet another doctor,
who said:
"It can be removed."
Thereupon, he chiseled the bone,
inserted a wedge in between,
splitting the bone by more than an inch,
