with an increased stipend of 20,000 households.
Táng peerage had nine ranks;
a king's stipend was 10,000 households;
this was double.
*Shǎn*,
read *shīrǎn*.
Official positions were established for his staff.
The Tiāncè Fǔ had one Zhǎngshǐ and one Sīmǎ,
and two Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
all responsible for general administration of the mansion's affairs.
Two Jūnzī Jìjiǔ
advised on military matters, assisted in ceremonies,
and received guests.
Four Diǎnqiān
were responsible for conveying messages and guidance.
Two Zhǔbù
were responsible for reviewing edicts and orders.
Two Lùshì,
and two Jìshì Cānjūnshì
were responsible for writing memorials and reports,
and disseminating orders and edicts.
Two Cānjūn for each of the six bureaus: Gōng, Cāng, Bīng, Qí, Kǎi, Shì,
and six Cānjūnshì.
As peace gradually settled throughout the realm, Shìmín
established a college west of the palace,
inviting scholars from all directions.
He issued an order

appointing the following as officials of the princely mansion: Dù Rúhuì as Fǔshǔ, Fáng Xuánlíng as Jìshì, Yú Shìnán, Chǔ Liàng, Yáo Sīlián as Wénxué, Lǐ Xuándào as Zhǔbù, Cài Yǔngōng, Xuē Yuánjìng, Yán Xiàngshí as Cānjūn, Sū Xù as Zīyì Diǎnqiān, Yú Zhìníng as Tiāncè Fǔ Cóngshì Zhōngláng, Sū Shìcháng as Jūnzī Jìjiǔ, Xuē Shōu as Jìshì, Lǐ Shǒusù as Cāngcáo, Lù Démíng as Guózǐ Zhùjiào,
Kǒng Yǐngdá,
Gài Wéndá of Xìndū, Xǔ Jìngzōng as Hùcáo of the Sòngzhōu Zǒngguǎnfǔ.
Orders issued by princes were called *jiào*.
*Xiàng*,
read *xīliàng*.
*Gài*,
read *gǔhé*.
The *Kǎoyì* says: In the old book,
Cānjūn Xuē Yuánjìng is placed after Xǔ Jìngzōng.
Now it follows the *Tàizōng Shílù*.
Zīyì Diǎnqiān Sū Miǎn,
the old book has Jūnzī Diǎnqiān.
Now it follows the *Shílù*.
Sòngzhōu Zǒngguǎnfǔ Hùcáo Xǔ Jìngzōng,
the old book's biography of Chǔ Liàng states *Zhùzuò Zuǒláng shè Jìshì*.
Jìngzōng's biography says
"intended as Liánzhōu Biéjià."
Now it follows the *Shílù*.
They took turns on daily duty and overnight watch,
provided with precious meals,
treated with exceptional grace and courtesy.
In his leisure from court audiences and official duties, Shìmín
would often go to the college,
inviting the scholars to discuss literature and classics,
sometimes not resting until midnight.
He also ordered Yán Lìběn, a Kùzhí, to paint their portraits.
Kùzhí
was attached to the Qīnshì Fǔ.
They were known as the Eighteen Scholars.
Those gentry who were selected
were at the time referred to as
"ascending to Yíngzhōu."
It has been traditionally held that there are three divine mountains in the sea:
Pénglái, Fāngzhàng, and Yíngzhōu,
which people cannot reach.
Those who reach them become immortals,
hence this analogy was used.
This refers to Dàbǎo's disciple.
Cài Dàbǎo assisted Xiāo Chá, the ruler of Later Liáng.
This refers to Shōu's cousin.
Xiàngshí
was the younger brother of Shīgǔ.
Yán Shīgǔ was famous for his profound scholarship.
This refers to Pí's son.
Yán Pí served Suí Yángdì with his ingenious craftsmanship.
At first,
Dù Rúhuì was a Staff Officer of the Military Bureau in Qínwáng's Prince's Establishment.
Soon after, he was promoted to Governor of Shǎnzhōu.
At that time, many officials from the Prince's Establishment were assigned to external posts,
which Shìmín found troubling.
Fáng Xuánlíng said,
"Other people are not worth regretting,
but as for Dù Rúhuì,
he possesses the talent of a King's assistant.
If Your Highness wishes to manage affairs in all four directions,
it cannot be done without Rúhuì."
Shìmín exclaimed in surprise,
"If it weren't for your words,
I would have nearly lost him."
He immediately memorialized to have him appointed as a subordinate in the Establishment.
He and Xuánlíng often followed Shìmín on campaigns,
participating in strategy discussions in the tent.
When there were many matters in the army,
Rúhuì would resolve them like flowing water.
Whenever Shìmín defeated an army or captured a city,
the generals and staff officers would scramble for treasures and goods,
but Xuánlíng alone collected talented individuals
and brought them to the headquarters.
Moreover, if there were generals or staff officers with courage and strategy,
Xuánlíng would certainly form a deep bond with them,
making them exert their utmost strength for Shìmín.
Whenever Shìmín ordered Xuánlíng to report on affairs,
the Emperor sighed and said,
"When Xuánlíng presents matters for my son,
even though a thousand *lǐ* separate us,
it is as if we are speaking face-to-face."
Lǐ Xuándào once served Lǐ Mì as a Records Officer.
When Mì was defeated,
his officials and subordinates were captured by Wáng Shìchōng.
Fearing death,
they all stayed awake until dawn.
Only Xuándào remained calm in his demeanor,
saying,
"Life and death are fated;
worry cannot avert them!"
The multitude admired his discernment and composure.
In the 60th *gēngyín* year,
Liú Hēitā occupied Yíngzhōu,
killing its governor, Lú Shìruì.
The people of Guānzhōu seized their governor, Léi Débèi,
and surrendered the city to him.
The Suí dynasty established Guānzhōu from Dōngguāng county.
In the early part of the Dàyè reign,
it was abolished.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé,
Gōnggāo, Húsū, and Dōngguāng from Dézhōu,
and Fùlíng, Tiáo, Ānlíng, and Guānzhēn from Jìzhōu,
were used to establish Guānzhōu.
Guān,
pronounced like *guǎn* (ancient).
Jiàng,
pronounced like *hùjiāng* (ancient);
same below.
In the 61st *xīnmǎo* year,
Xiāo Xǐn's governor of Èzhōu, Léi Chángyǐng, surrendered Lǔshān.
When the Suí pacified Chén,
they established Èzhōu from Jiāngxià Commandery,
governing Jiāngxià south of the river.
In the early part of the Dàyè reign,
it was restored as a commandery.
Xiāo Xǐn likely established the prefecture at Lǔshān.
Zhào Jùnwáng Xiàogōng led over two thousand warships downriver to the east.
Xiāo Xǐn, seeing the river in flood,
made no preparations whatsoever.
Xiàogōng and others captured his two garrisons of Jīngmén and Yídū,
advancing to Yílíng.
Xiāo Xǐn established the Yídū garrison in Yídào county of Xiázhōu.
Yílíng county was part of Xiázhōu.
On *guǐsì* day,
Xiàogōng defeated and drove him away,
capturing over three hundred warships
and killing tens of thousands who drowned.
He pursued the fleeing enemy to Bǎilǐzhōu.
From Qīngjiāng eastward,
passing Guīzhōu and Xiázhōu,
and then reaching Bǎilǐzhōu.
He defeated them again
and entered the North River.
Bǎilǐzhōu is in the middle of the river in Zhījiāng county.
The river divides here;
the stream that flows north of Bǎilǐzhōu and eastward
is therefore called the North River.
Bài,
pronounced like *bǔmài* (ancient).
The Liáng dynasty established Yídū Commandery and Yíchāng county from Hàn's Yídào county.
The Later Zhōu established Jiāngzhōu.
The Suí abolished it and made it Bāshān county,
belonging to Qīngjiāng Commandery.
Xiāo Xǐn likely re-established Jiāngzhōu here.
Gài,
pronounced like *gǔhé* (ancient).
The governor of Máozhōu, Zhào Yuánkǎi—
Máozhōu was formerly established in Guǎntáo county of Wèizhōu.
In the early Dàyè reign of the Suí,
the prefecture was abolished.
Dòu Jiàndé re-established it,
and the Táng followed suit,
administering Guǎntáo and Guànshì from Wèizhōu,
Tángyì from Bózhōu,
and Línqīng and Qīngshuǐ from Bèizhōu.
The people below could not endure his rule.
On *dīngmǎo* day,
the prefectural people, including Dǒng Dēngmíng, revolted,
killing Yuánkǎi in response to Liú Hēitā.
Shèng Yànshī escaped from Xú Yuánlǎng's control and returned.
Wáng Bó then persuaded the prefectures of Qīng, Lái, and Mì,
all of which submitted to him.
Láizhōu was the Dōnglái Commandery,
which was the Guāngzhōu of the Later Wèi.
Mìzhōu was the Gāomì Commandery,
which was the Jiāozhōu of the Later Wèi.
Shuō,
pronounced like *shūrùi* (ancient).
When Xiāo Xǐn disbanded his troops to engage in agriculture,
see scroll three above.
Hearing that Táng troops had arrived
and that Wén Shìhóng had been defeated,
he was greatly alarmed and hastily conscripted soldiers.
They were all beyond the Jiāng and Lǐng regions,
and the roads were distant and obstructed,
making it impossible for them to gather quickly.
So he led all his available troops to resist and fight.
Xiàogōng was about to attack them,
but Lǐ Jìng stopped him, saying,
"Their army is coming to rescue a defeat;
their strategy is not well-established,
and they cannot last long.
It would be better to anchor on the south bank for now.
The south bank of Jiānglíng is Mǎtóu bank.
They will certainly divide their forces,
either remaining to resist us
or returning to defend themselves.
With their forces divided and their strength weakened,
if we attack when they are relaxed,
there is nothing we cannot overcome.
If we press them now,
they will join forces and fight to the death.
The Chǔ troops are swift and fierce,
not easily matched."
Xiàogōng did not listen.
He left Jìng to guard the camp
and personally led the elite troops to battle,
but indeed he was defeated and fled,
heading for the south bank.
Xiāo Xǐn's troops abandoned their boats and plundered military supplies,
each carrying heavy loads.
Jìng saw their forces in disarray,
let loose his troops, and attacked fiercely,
greatly defeating them.
He pressed on with the victory directly to Jiānglíng,
entering its outer wall.
He then attacked the water city,
captured it,
and obtained many boats and ships.
Lǐ Jìng had Xiàogōng scatter them all into the river.
All the generals said,
"What we gain from defeating the enemy
should be used.
Why abandon them and provide resources to the enemy?"
Jìng said,
"Xiāo Xǐn's territory
extends south of the Lǐng range
and east to Dòngtíng.
Dòngtíng Lake is in Bālíng county of Yuèzhōu.
If we attack the city but fail to take it,
and reinforcements gather from all four directions,
we will be attacked from both inside and out,
unable to advance or retreat.
Even with boats and oars,
what use would they be then?
Now, by abandoning the boats and ships,
causing them to block the river downstream,
the reinforcing troops, seeing this,
will certainly think Jiānglíng has already fallen
and will not dare to advance lightly.
As they go back and forth scouting,
they will be delayed for a month or more.
We are certain to take it."
Xiāo Xǐn's reinforcements, seeing the boats and ships,
indeed hesitated and did not advance.
His governor of Jiāozhōu,
Qiū Hé, his Chief Clerk Gāo Shìlián, and his Sīmǎ Dù Zhīsōng were about to proceed to Jiānglíng,
Jiāozhōu was
the Suí's Jiāozhǐ Commandery.
Zhǎng,
pronounced like *zhīliǎng* (ancient).
Cháo,
pronounced like *zhíyáo* (ancient).
All submitted to Xiàogōng.
Xiào Gōng (孝恭) led his troops to besiege Jiānglíng (江陵).
Xiāo Xiǎn (蕭銑) was cut off both internally and externally.
He asked the Minister of the Secretariat, Cén Wénběn (岑文本), for advice.
Wénběn (文本) persuaded Xiǎn (銑) to surrender.
Xiǎn (銑) then said to his subordinates:
"Heaven does not bless Liáng (梁),
and it cannot be sustained any longer.
If we must wait until our strength is exhausted,
then the common people will suffer.
How can I, for my own sake, plunge the people into misery?"
On the Yǐsì (乙巳) day,
Xiǎn (銑) offered a grand sacrifice (tàiláo) at the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
then issued an order to open the city gates and surrender.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The *Gāozǔ Shílù* (高祖實錄) states:
"On the Guǐsì (癸巳) day,
Zhào Jùnwáng (趙郡王) Xiào Gōng (孝恭) encountered Xiāo Xiǎn's (蕭銑) general Wén Shìhóng (文士弘) at Qīngjiāng Hékǒu (清江合口).
He attacked him,
capturing over a thousand of his warships.
He then took the four counties of Yíchāng (宜昌), Dāngyáng (當陽), Zhījiāng (枝江), and Sōngzī (松滋)."
The *Jiù Shū Xiào Gōng Chuán* (舊書孝恭傳) says:
"They attacked his water city
and captured it,
scattering the captured ships in the river.
All the generals said: 'When we capture enemy ships,
we should utilize them.
Why abandon them?
Are we not aiding the enemy?'
Xiào Gōng (孝恭) said: 'Not so.
Xiāo Xiǎn's (蕭銑) false realm
extends south to the Ling (嶺) mountains and
east to Dòngtíng (洞庭) Lake.
If we attack the city but fail to take it,
and their reinforcements arrive,
we will be caught between enemies,
unable to advance or retreat.
Even if we had boats,
what use would they be?
Now, Xiǎn's (銑) garrisons along the river,
upon suddenly seeing boats and ships floating downstream in disarray,
will surely know that Xiǎn (銑) has been defeated,
and will not dare to advance.
They will come and go, observing the situation,
delaying for a month or so.
This will slow down their rescue efforts,
and we will surely conquer the city.'
Xiǎn's (銑) relief force arrived at Bālíng (巴陵),
and seeing the ships floating down the river,
they indeed became suspicious and dared not advance rashly."
The *Tàizōng Shílù Xiào Gōng Chuán* (太宗實錄孝恭傳) says:
"The army advanced to Qīngjiāng (清江).
Xiǎn (銑) sent his general Wén Shìhóng (文士弘) with troops to resist.
They attacked and routed him,
pursuing the fleeing enemy to Bǎilǐzhōu (百里洲).
Shìhóng (士弘) regrouped his forces and fought again,
but was again defeated.
They pursued him into the North River (Běijiāng),
where Xiǎn (銑) brought out all his troops to resist.
Xiào Gōng (孝恭) was about to engage in battle,
but Lǐ Jìng (李靖) stopped him, saying: 'The Chu (楚) people are light and sharp,
difficult to contend with directly.
Having just lost Jīngmén (荊門),
they have brought out all their troops to fight.
This is a force attempting to salvage a defeat,
not their original strategy,
and they cannot sustain it for long.
If we do not fight for one day,
the enemy will surely split into two:
keeping light troops to confront us,
and withdrawing their weak forces to defend themselves.
At that point, their position will be fragmented and their strength weakened,
and we will surely win if we attack.'
Xiào Gōng (孝恭) did not listen.
He sent Jìng (靖) to guard the camp
and personally led his elite troops into a naval battle.
Xiào Gōng (孝恭) was indeed defeated,
fleeing to the south bank.
The rebels abandoned their boats and plundered extensively,
everyone heavily laden.
Jìng (靖) saw their army in disarray,
advanced with his troops and attacked them.
The rebels were greatly defeated.
Taking advantage of the victory, he advanced,
entering their outer city.
He attacked their water city
and captured it,
taking all their boats and ships
and scattering them in the river.
The rebel relief force saw this,
thought the city had already fallen,
and dared not advance rashly.
Xiǎn (銑) was cut off both internally and externally,
and dissent arose within the city.
Because of this, he feared and surrendered."
The *Táng Lì* (唐曆) says:
"Xiào Gōng (孝恭) and Jìng (靖) advanced, capitalizing on their victory,
attacked their water city
and captured it,
taking all their boats and ships and scattering them in the river.
The generals said: 'Abandoning them will surely aid the enemy?'
Jìng (靖) said: 'Not so,'
and so on.
As recorded in the *Jiù Shū* (舊書) as Xiào Gōng's (孝恭) words.
'Soon after, Xiǎn's (銑) relief force saw this,
thought the city had already fallen,
and dared not advance rashly.
Xiǎn (銑) consequently feared and surrendered.'"
According to the *Shídào Zhì* (十道志): Jīngmén (荊門) is within the borders of Yídū (宜都) County, Xiá Zhōu (峽州).
Yílíng (夷陵) is a county name in Xiá Zhōu (峽州).
Qīngjiāng (清江) is within the borders of Bāshān (巴山) County, Xiá Zhōu (峽州).
Bǎilǐzhōu (百里州) is within the borders of Zhījiāng (枝江) County, Jīng Zhōu (荊州).
The river divides from this island,
and it is already close to Jiānglíng (江陵).
Therefore, Xiǎn (銑) committed all his troops to fight to the death.
The *Tàizōng Shílù* (太宗實錄) is closer to the truth,
and we follow it now.
For the rest, we consult the words from the four books.
Xiào Gōng (孝恭) made Lǐ Jìng (李靖) his chief strategist;
it was Jìng (靖) who devised the plans and Xiào Gōng (孝恭) who spoke them to the generals.
We now follow the *Táng Lì* (唐曆).
Xiǎn (銑), leading his officials, came to the army gate dressed in sackcloth and a simple headband,
saying:
"Only Xiǎn (銑) deserves to die;
the common people are innocent.
I beg that you do not kill or plunder them."
Xiào Gōng (孝恭) entered and occupied his city.
The generals wanted to plunder heavily.
Cén Wénběn (岑文本) persuaded Xiào Gōng (孝恭), saying:
"The people south of the Yangtze,
since the end of the Suí (隋) dynasty,
have suffered under tyrannical rule.
Furthermore, with all the heroes contending like tigers,
those who survive today
are the remnants of war,
craning their necks and standing on tiptoes, looking for a true lord.
This is why Xiāo (蕭) clan officials and the elders of Jiānglíng (江陵) decided to surrender their lives,
hoping to finally rest their shoulders.
If we now unleash our soldiers to capture and plunder,
I fear that from this point southward,
there will be no more hearts inclined to submit!"
Xiào Gōng (孝恭) praised his words
and immediately forbade the plundering.
The generals again said:
"The generals and commanders of Liáng (梁) who fought against the government army and died,
their crimes are already grave.
We request that their families be confiscated
to reward the officers and soldiers."
Lǐ Jìng (李靖) said:
"The army of a true king
should make its righteous reputation precede it.
Those who died fighting for their lord are loyal subjects.
How can their families be confiscated like those of rebels and traitors?"
Thereupon, the city was settled peacefully,
with not a single hair harmed.
When the southern prefectures and counties heard of this,
they all submitted at the mere mention of it.
Several days after Xiǎn's (銑) surrender,
more than a hundred thousand relief troops arrived.
Hearing that Jiānglíng (江陵) was lost,
they all cast off their armor and surrendered.
Xiào Gōng (孝恭) sent Xiǎn (銑) to Cháng'ān (長安).
The Emperor rebuked him.
Xiǎn (銑) said:
"The Suí (隋) lost its deer,
and the whole world chased it.
Xiǎn (銑) had no mandate from Heaven,
and therefore came to this;
if this is considered a crime,
there is no escape from death!"
He was eventually executed in the marketplace.
An edict appointed Xiào Gōng (孝恭) as the Grand Governor (Zǒngguǎn) of Jīng Zhōu (荊州);
Lǐ Jìng (李靖) was appointed Grand Pillar of State (Shàng Zhùguó)
and bestowed the title Duke of Yǒngkāng (永康) County.
Yǒngkāng (永康) County belongs to Wù Zhōu (婺州).
He was permitted to make appointments and bestow offices by imperial authority (chéngzhì).
Earlier,
Xiǎn (銑) had sent the Palace Gentleman (Huángmén Shìláng) Liú Jì (劉洎) of Jiānglíng (江陵) to seize territory south of the Ling (嶺) mountains.
He obtained over fifty cities.
He had not yet returned when Xiǎn (銑) was defeated.
Jì (洎) came to surrender with the cities he had obtained,
and was appointed Administrator (Chángshǐ) of Nánkāng Zhōu Dūdū Fǔ (南康州都督府).
In this year, Nánkāng Zhōu (南康州) was established from Duānxī (端溪) in Duān Zhōu (端州),
and a Grand Commandery (Dūdū Fǔ) was also established,
overseeing Duān (端), Kāng (康), Fēng (封), Xīn (新), Sòng (宋), Lóng (瀧), and other prefectures.
At that time, Grand Governorates (Zǒngguǎn Fǔ) were renamed Grand Commanderies (Dūdū Fǔ).
In the early years of Zhēnguān (貞觀) era,
prefectures were first divided into upper, middle, and lower ranks.
Jì (洎),
pronounced like "Jì" (冀) or "Fān" (翻).
Cháng (長),
pronounced like "Zhī Liǎng" (知兩) or "Fān" (翻).
66On the Wùshēn (戊申) day,
Xú Yuánlǎng's (徐圓朗) Governor (Zhìzhōng) of Chāng Zhōu (昌州), Liú Shànháng (劉善行), surrendered with Xūchāng (須昌).
Yuánlǎng (圓朗) had probably established Chāng Zhōu (昌州) from Xūchāng (須昌) in Yùn Zhōu (鄆州).
Jiàng (降),
pronounced like "Hù Jiāng" (戶江) or "Fān" (翻).
67th year, Gēngxū (year of the metal dog),
an edict was issued to Shǎndōng Dào Grand Secretariat's Department of State Affairs, from the Secretariat Director and Vice Director down to the department heads and clerks.
The "Six Canons" state: Han officials' records say: the Grand Minister of the Household had southern and northern residence clerks and three department clerks.
Among the various lang officials,
those of outstanding talent and high achievement were chosen for these positions,
with a salary of four hundred shí.
Next, they were appointed as Secretariat lang officials,
and then sent out to govern districts.
Xiè Chéng's *Hòu Hàn Shū* (History of the Later Han) records: Hú Bófān, Fàn Pāng, and Gōngshā Mù were all nominated as Filial and Incorrupt for their outstanding talent,
and appointed as lang officials and clerks under the Grand Minister of the Household.
In the Later Wèi dynasty, the Secretariat's Departments of Personnel, Ceremonies, Three Dukes, Parks and Game, Justice, Two Thousand Shí Officials, and Audit,
each assigned the appropriate number of archivists and clerks according to their duties.
The Department of the Palace Gate appointed clerks and document scribes,
all holding the rank of from-the-eighth-rank, upper grade.
In the early Suí dynasty,
the Grand Secretariat and the Department of State Affairs both appointed clerks and document scribes.
In the third year of Emperor Yáng's reign,
the title "document scribe" was removed.
The number of clerks was determined by the workload of each department.
One clerk was appointed for every ten document scribes.
If there were fewer than ten, one person was still appointed.
Talented and skilled individuals from various backgrounds were used.
By the Táng dynasty, these positions were filled by those from outside the regular bureaucracy who had entered it.
Shǎn,
pronounced with the sound of "rán" when combined with "shī".
The number of officials was slightly smaller,
and the Shāndōng Grand Secretariat, the commander-in-chief's offices, and all the prefectures were subordinate to it.
For the Secretariat Directors and Vice Directors and below in the provinces such as Yìzhōu, Xiāngzhōu, Shāndōng, Huáinán, and Héběi,
their ranks were one grade lower than those in the capital,
and the number of officials was also reduced.
The Grand Secretariat's Director of State Affairs had the authority to appoint and assign officials.
Besides the officials of the Qín Wáng and Qí Wáng's princely establishments,
each established left and right six protectorate armies,
and left and right personal attendant (zhàngnèi) guard units.
The protectorate armies,
were only present in the two establishments of Qín and Qí;
other princely states were not allowed to establish them.
The personal attendant (qīnshì) guard units and the attendant (zhàngnèi) guard units of the imperial princes each appointed two military supervisors (diǎnjūn),
holding the rank of principal-fifth-rank, upper grade;
and two deputy military supervisors,
holding the rank of from-the-fifth-rank, upper grade.
68th year, intercalary month,
Yǐmǎo (year of the wood rabbit),
the Emperor visited Jìzhōu.
In the third year of Wǔdé, Jìzhōu was established from Wǔgōng, Hǎozhì, and Zhōuzhì counties of Jīngzhào.
Xúnzhōu was also abolished,
and Méi and Fèngquán counties were attached to Jìzhōu.
Jǐwèi (earth goat),
the Emperor visited the old villa in Wǔgōng.
Rénxū (water dog),
the Emperor hunted in Hǎozhì.
In the second year of Wǔdé, Hǎozhì county was established by splitting from Lǐquán,
subordinate to Yōngzhōu,
named after the old Hàn name.
Yǐchǒu (wood ox),
the Emperor hunted in Jiǔzōng.
Jiǔzōng Shān,
is in Lǐquán county, Yōngzhōu.
Zōng,
pronounced with the sound of "hóng" when combined with "zǐ".
Dīngmǎo (fire rabbit),
the Emperor hunted in Zhòngshān.
Wùchén (earth dragon),
the Emperor hunted in Qīngshuǐ Gǔ.
The Suí records state: Jīngzhào's Yíjūn county has Qīngshuǐ.
Sānyuán originally belonged to the territory of Hàn Chíyáng county.
The Later Zhōu dynasty established Jiànzhōng Commandery,
the Suí dynasty established Sānyuán county,
and the Táng dynasty made it subordinate to Yōngzhōu.
Xīnwèi (metal goat),
the Emperor visited Zhōu Shì Pí.
Rénshēn (water monkey),
the Emperor returned to Cháng'ān.
69th year, eleventh month,
Jiǎshēn (wood monkey),
the Emperor performed the sacrifice at the Yuánqiū.
The Zhēnguān rituals state: On the winter solstice, sacrifice to Hào Tiān Shàngdì at the Yuánqiū.
70th year, Dù Fúwēi sent his general Wáng Xióngdàn to attack Lǐ Zǐtōng.
Zǐtōng defended Dúsōng Lǐng with elite troops.
From the southeast of Xuānzhōu's Guǎngdé county, passing over Dúsōng Lǐng to Húzhōu,
the mountain path was treacherous and narrow.
Jiàng,
pronounced with the sound of "liàng" when combined with "jí".
The same applies below.
Under Chén Dāng, there should have been the character
"shì".
This is probably because the Táng history avoided the taboo name of Tàizōng,
removing the character
"shì".
Xióngdàn seized the high ground and strongholds to press them,
displaying many banners and flags.
At night, he tied torches to trees,
scattering them across the mountains and marshes.
Zǐtōng was frightened,
burned his camp, and fled to protect Hángzhōu.
Xióngdàn pursued and attacked him,
defeating him again outside the city.
Gēngyín (metal tiger),
Zǐtōng, in dire straits, requested surrender.
Fúwēi captured Zǐtōng and his Left Vice Director, Yuè Bótōng, and sent them to Cháng'ān.
The Emperor pardoned them.
Earlier,
Wāng Huá had occupied Yī and Shè,
proclaiming himself king for more than ten years.
Xióngdàn returned with his army to attack him.
Huá resisted him at Xīn'ān Dòngkǒu.
Táng's Shèzhōu,
was Suí's Xīn'ān Commandery.
Xīn'ān Dòngkǒu was the narrow pass of Shèzhōu.
Xiān,
pronounced with the sound of "jiàn" when combined with "xī".
Yī,
pronounced "yī".
Shè,
pronounced "shè".
Xióngdàn ambushed elite troops in the mountain valleys,
and led a few thousand weak soldiers to assault their formation.
As soon as the battle began,
he feigned defeat,
and retreated to his camp.
Huá advanced to attack him,
but could not overcome him.
As night fell,
he withdrew.
The ambushed troops had already seized the Dòngkǒu.
Huá could not enter,
and, in desperation, requested surrender.
Wénrén Suí'ān had occupied Kūnshān,
without any allegiance.
Fúwēi sent Xióngdàn to attack him.
Xióngdàn, seeing Kūnshān's treacherous narrowness,
knew it would be difficult to win by force.
So, he rode alone to the city walls,
proclaiming the might and prestige of the Chén state.
The might and prestige of the Táng state.
Suí'ān was moved and pleased,
and led his generals out to surrender.
Thereupon, Fúwēi gained control of all the land south of the Huái River and east of the Yangtze River,
reaching south to the mountains and
east to the sea.
Xióngdàn, for his merits, was appointed Commander-in-chief of Shèzhōu,
and granted the title of Duke of Yíchūn Commandery.
Yíchūn Commandery of Yuánzhōu.
71st year, Rénchén (water dragon),
Lízhōu Commander-in-chief Liú Mín attacked Liú Xiānchéng,
thoroughly defeating him.
Old records state: Qìngzhōu's Huáchí county was established by Suí.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé, the Lízhōu Commander-in-chief's office was established.
All the tribes surrendered.
72nd year, Lǐ Jìng crossed the mountains,
sending envoys along different routes to appease and recruit the various prefectures.
Wherever they went, all surrendered.
Xiāo Xiǎn's Guìzhōu Commander-in-chief, Lǐ Xízhì, led his department
to surrender.
Guìzhōu,
was Suí's Shǐ'ān Commandery.
The following year, he paid respects at court.
Lǐ Jìng was appointed Grand Commissioner for Pacification of Língnán,
acting Commander-in-chief of Guìzhōu.
He led his army to subdue ninety-six prefectures,
gaining over six hundred thousand households.
73rd year, Rén Yín (water tiger),
Liú Hēità captured Dìngzhōu,
seizing Commander-in-chief Lǐ Xuántōng.
Hēità admired his talent
and wanted to make him a grand general,
but Xuántōng refused.
Some former subordinates brought him wine and meat.
Xuántōng said:
"Gentlemen, you pity my humiliation
and kindly bring wine and meat to comfort me.
I shall get drunk for you all."
When he was tipsy,
he said to his guards:
"I can perform a sword dance.
Please lend me a sword."
The guards gave it to him.
After the dance, Xuántōng sighed and said:
"A true man, having received great kindness from the state
and having been entrusted with governing a region,
yet unable to protect what he was charged with,
what face do I have to continue living in this world!"
He then drew the sword and stabbed himself,
disemboweling himself and dying.
When the Emperor heard,
he shed tears for him,
and appointed his son, Fúhù, as a grand general.
74th year, Gēngxū (metal dog),
Zhōu Wénjǔ, a local of the prefecture, killed the Prefect Wáng Wénjǔ,
and offered the city to Xú Yuánlǎng.
75 Yōuzhōu was struck by a severe famine.
Gāo Kāidào promised to relieve it with grain.
Lǐ Yì sent the old and weak to Gāo Kāidào for food,
and Kāidào treated them all generously.
Yì was pleased,
and so he dispatched three thousand commoners,
several hundred carts,
and over a thousand donkeys and horses to receive grain.
Kāidào detained them all,
broke off relations with Yì,
and again proclaimed himself Yān Wáng.
Zhèn,
pronunciation 'jìn' or 'rěn'.
Chéng,
pronunciation 'shèng' or 'zhèng'.
Fù,
pronunciation 'fú yòu',
also pronounced as 'rú zì' (as written).
Yān,
pronunciation 'yīn jiān'.
To the south, he allied with Liú Hēità,
led his troops to attack Yìzhōu but failed,
then plundered extensively and departed.
He also sent his general Xiè Léng to feign surrender to Yì,
requesting troops for support.
Yì dispatched troops to assist him.
When they were about to reach Huáiróng,
the old gazetteer states: Huáiróng County of Běi Yānzhōu
was Pān County of Shànggǔ during the Later Hàn,
renamed Huáiróng by Běi Qí.
The Guīshuǐ River flowed through it,
and it was where the prefecture seat was located.
In the eighth year of Zhēngguān,
Běi Yānzhōu was renamed Guīzhōu.
Gāo Kāidào, in league with the Tūjué, repeatedly invaded and raided,
and Héng, Dìng, Yōu, and Yì Prefectures all suffered from their depredations.
76 In the twelfth month,
on the day Yǐmǎo,
Liú Hēità captured Jìzhōu,
and killed the Cìshǐ Qū Léng.
After Hēità defeated Huái'ān Wáng Shéntōng,
he sent letters to Zhào and Wèi,
referring to the great boundaries of Zhào and Wèi during the Warring States period.
On the day Gēngshēn,
(the emperor) dispatched Yòutúnwèi Dàjiàngjūn Yì'ān Wáng Xiàocháng to lead troops to subjugate Hēità.
Hēità led tens of thousands of troops to press upon Zōngchéng.
Lízhou Zǒngguǎn Lǐ Shìjì, who was previously stationed in Zōngchéng,
abandoned the city and fled to Míngzhōu.
The new gazetteer states: In the second year of Wǔdé,
Lízhou was established from Líyáng County.
Zōngchéng was originally Guǎngzōng County.
In the early Rénshòu era of Suí,
it was renamed Zōngchéng County
to avoid the name of Emperor Yáng.
It belonged to Qīnghé Prefecture.
At that time, Zōngzhōu was established.
Míng,
pronunciation 'mí bīng'.
The "Kǎoyì" (Textual Research) says: The "Shílù" (Veritable Records) states:
"Shìjì and Hēità fought in Sòngzhōu,
and our army was defeated."
The "Gémìng Jì" (Record of Revolution) states:
"Lǐ Jì was the Grand Commander,
Zhāng Shìguì was his deputy,
and they led twenty thousand troops into Sòngzhōu.
Jì, with five hundred cavalry, scouted ahead himself.
Hearing that Hēità had arrived at Nángōng,
he galloped to Sòngzhōu,
did not enter the city but passed west to Míngzhōu.
On horseback outside the south gate,
he called for Chén Jūnbīn, Dǎng Rénhóng, Qín Wǔtōng, and others to abandon the city and retreat westward.
Chéng Míngzhèn, the County Magistrate of Yǒngnián, seeing Wǔtōng escaping in disarray,
rode towards the county to retrieve his family,
but upon entering the city,
the townspeople, fearing mutual looting,
immediately closed the city gates and defended themselves.
Míngzhèn then tied a rope from the north gate of the city and lowered himself,
leading his mother, wife, and children to walk westward.
After traveling less than four or five *lǐ*,
his mother, wife, and others were robbed and scattered.
Míngzhèn himself escaped.
Hēità attacked Sòngchéng
and captured it.
Shìguì broke through the encirclement with light cavalry and fled,
seeking refuge in Xiāngzhōu.
A few days later,
Hēità's main army arrived at Míngzhōu."
According to the old geographical gazetteer,
in the fourth year of Wǔdé, Zōngzhōu was established in Zōngchéng County.
The character "Sòng"
should all be written as "Zōng".
Shìjì was a famous general,
and would not have acted as described in the "Gémìng Jì";
he merely abandoned the city because he lacked the strength to resist.
Now we follow the biography of Hēità in the old history books.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Hēità pursued and attacked Shìjì and others,
defeated them,
killed five thousand foot soldiers,
and Shìjì barely escaped with his life.
On the day Bǐngyín,
the local strongmen of Míngzhōu rebelled within the city and sided with Hēità.
Hēità,
to the southeast of the city, made an announcement to Heaven and offered sacrifices to Dòu Jiàndé before entering.
Ten days later,
he led his troops to attack and capture Xiāngzhōu,
seized the Cìshǐ Fáng Huàng,
and the Yòuwǔwèi Jiàngjūn Zhāng Shìguì broke through the encirclement and fled.
Hēità then took Lízhou and Wèizhou to the south.
Within half a year,
he had completely recovered Dòu Jiàndé's former territory.
He also sent envoys to the north to ally with the Tūjué,
and Jiélì Kèhán dispatched the Sijīn Sòngyé Nà
to lead Khitan cavalry to follow him.
Yòuwǔwèi Jiàngjūn Qín Wǔtōng,
Míngzhōu Cìshǐ Chén Jūnbīn, Yǒngníng Lìng Chéng Míngzhèn.
"Yǒngníng"
should be "Yǒngnián".
77 On the day Dīngmǎo,
Qín Wáng Shìmín and Qí Wáng Yuánjí were ordered to subjugate Hēità.
78 Kūnmí sent envoys to offer allegiance.
Kūnmí
is the Kūnmíng of the Hàn dynasty.
The Kūnmíng barbarians were west of the Cuàn barbarians,
with the Xī'ěrhé River as their boundary.
The Xī'ěrhé River
is the Yèyúhé River.
Cuīzhōu was the land of Hàn Yuècuī Commandery.
The Later Zhōu established Yánzhōu.
In the sixth year of Kāihuáng, it was renamed Xīníngzhōu.
In the eighteenth year,
it was renamed Cuīzhōu.
Nánníng
was the land of the ancient Nánzhōng Wèi and Shēngmá counties.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé, Nánníngzhōu was established.
Cuī,
pronunciation 'suǐ'.
They then came and surrendered.
79 On the day Jǐsì,
Liú Hēità captured Xíngzhōu and Zhàozhōu.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
he captured Wèizhou,
and killed the Zǒngguǎn Pān Dàoyì.
On the day Xīnwèi,
he captured Xīnzhōu.
In the sixteenth year of Suí Kāihuáng,
Xīnzhōu was established from Xīn County of Wèizhou.
It was abolished in the early Dàyè era.
In that year,
Xīnzhōu was re-established from Xīn, Línhuáng, Wǔyáng counties of Wèizhou,
and Wǔshuǐ County of Bózhōu.
The "Kǎoyì" (Textual Research) says: The "Shílù" states "Huázhōu",
and the "Xīn Shū" (New History) states "Yèzhōu".
According to the "Dìlǐ Zhì" (Treatise on Geography), there is no Yèzhōu,
so it must be Xīnzhōu.
The "Shídào Zhì" (Treatise on Ten Circuits) states: In the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng, Xīnzhōu was established in Xīn County.
The old gazetteer states
it was established in the fifth year of Wǔdé.
80 On the day Rénshēn,
Sòng Wáng Yuánjiā was transferred to become Xú Wáng.
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ, collated by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by Imperial Command.
Hòu Xué Tiāntái
Fifth Year of Wǔdé
(Rénwǔ, 622 CE)
1 Spring,
First month.
Liú Hēità proclaimed himself Hàn Dōng Wáng,
changed the era name to Tiānzào,
and established his capital at Míngzhōu.
He appointed Fàn Yuàn as Zuǒ Púyè,
Dǒng Kāngmǎi as Bīngbù Shàngshū, Gāo Yáxián as Yòulǐngjūn;
he summoned Wáng Cóng as Zhōngshū Lìng,
Liú Bīn as Zhōngshū Shìláng;
all civil and military officials from Dòu Jiàndé's time were restored to their original positions.
His establishment of laws and administration
entirely emulated Dòu Jiàndé,
but his courage and decisiveness in battle surpassed him.
2 On the day of Bǐngxū,
Yīn Gōngsuì (殷恭邃), a rebel leader from Tóng'ān (同安), surrendered with Shūzhōu (舒州).
Shūzhōu
was Tóng'ān Jùn (同安郡) during the Suí (隋) dynasty.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Shūzhōu
was Wǎn Xiàn (皖縣) in the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
subordinate to Lújiāng Jùn (廬江郡);
Jìn (晉) established Jìnxī Jùn (晉熙郡);
Liáng (梁) established Nányù Zhōu (南豫州),
which was later restored as Jìn Zhōu (晉州);
Běiqí (北齊) renamed it Jiāngzhōu (江州);
early Suí renamed it Xīzhōu (熙州);
during Dàyè (大業), it was renamed Tóng'ān Jùn (同安郡);
Táng (唐) renamed it Shūzhōu,
because the area was formerly the state of Shū Zǐ (舒子).
帥 (shuài) is read suǒ lèi fān.
降 (jiàng) is read hù jiāng fān.
3 On the day of Dīnghài,
Liú Bótōng (劉伯通), the Biejia (別駕) of Jìzhōu (濟州), seized the Prefect Dòu Wùběn (竇務本)
and offered the prefecture to Xú Yuánlǎng (徐圓朗).
4 On the day of Gēngyín,
Wáng Cáiyì (王才藝), the Zhizhong (治中) of Dōngyán Zhōu (東鹽州), killed the Prefect Tián Huá (田華)
and offered the city to Liú Hēitá (劉黑闥).
Yánshān Xiàn (鹽山縣) of Cāngzhōu (滄州)
was originally the land of Gāochéng Xiàn (高成縣) in the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
Last year,
Dōngyán Zhōu (東鹽州) was established,
with Qīngchí Xiàn (清池縣) subordinated to it.
5 Qín Wáng (秦王) Shìmín (世民)'s army arrived at Huòjiā (獲嘉).
According to Sòng Bái (宋白)'s Xù Tōngdiǎn (續通典): In the fourth year of Kāihuáng (開皇) of the Suí (隋) dynasty,
Huòjiā Xiàn (獲嘉縣) was moved to the old city of Xiūwǔ (脩武).
They retreated to secure Míngzhōu (洺州).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Míngzhōu (洺州) city
was the land of Qǔliáng (曲梁) in Jìn (晉) during the Spring and Autumn period.
相 (xiàng) is read xī liàng fān.
On the day of Bǐngshēn,
Shìmín (世民) retook Xiāngzhōu (相州).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Shílù (實錄) states:
"People of Lùzhōu (祿州) killed Prefect Dúgū Chè (獨孤徹) and offered the city to Hēitá (黑闥)."
According to the Dìlǐ Zhì (地理志), there is no Lùzhōu (祿州);
perhaps the character is mistaken.
The Xīn Shū (新書) writes Xiāngzhōu (相州),
which is an even greater error.
According to the records, Liú Hēitá (劉黑闥) attacked and captured Xiāngzhōu (相州),
seizing Prefect Fáng Huàng (房晃).
When Qín Wáng (秦王)'s troops arrived,
he abandoned Xiāngzhōu (相州),
hence Qín Wáng (秦王) retook it.
The Xīn Shū (新書) Dìjì (帝紀) states that capturing Xiāngzhōu (相州)
and killing Fáng Huàng (房晃) occurred on the Yǐyǒu (乙酉) day of the first month,
and that the people of Xiāngzhōu (相州) killed Dúgū Chè (獨孤徹) and rebelled to join Hēitá (黑闥) on the Bǐngshēn (丙申) day;
the error is clear.
Since the location of Lùzhōu (祿州) cannot be verified,
however, Hēitá (黑闥)'s capture of Xiāngzhōu (相州)
and Qín Wáng (秦王)'s recapture of Xiāngzhōu (相州)
are very clear in their sequence,
and entirely unrelated to Lùzhōu (祿州).
And the Xīn Shū (新書)'s account of killing Fáng Huàng (房晃)
and capturing Xiāngzhōu (相州)
also has incorrect dates.
復 (fù) is read fú yòu fān,
and also pronounced as it is written.
Féixiāng Xiàn (肥鄉縣)
was the land of Hángōu Xiàn (邯溝縣) in Wèijùn (魏郡) during the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
Cáo Wèi (曹魏) established Féixiāng Xiàn (肥鄉縣),
subordinate to Guǎngpíng Jùn (廣平郡).
Early Wǔdé (武德), it belonged to Zǐzhōu (紫州).
Last year, Zǐzhōu (紫州) was abolished,
and Féixiāng (肥鄉) was subordinated to Cízhōu (磁州).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: Féixiāng (肥鄉) is thirty-five li southeast of Míngzhōu (洺州).
The Shuǐ Jīng (水經) states: The Míngshuǐ (洺水) flows east past Qǔliáng (曲梁) city.
Qǔliáng (曲梁) is Yǒngnián (永年),
where Míngzhōu (洺州) was governed.
6 After Xiāo Xiǎn (蕭銑) was defeated,
many of his scattered troops returned to Lín Shìhóng (林士弘),
and his military power was restored.
Lín Shìhóng (林士弘) was defeated by Zhāng Shàn'ān (張善安),
and his military power declined from then on,
as seen in Volume 184, Yìníng (義寧) first year of Suí (隋).
7 On the day of Jǐyǒu,
Yáng Shìlüè (楊世略), a Lí (俚) leader from Língnán (嶺南), surrendered with Xún (循) and Cháo (潮) prefectures.
Xúnzhōu (循州)
was Lóngchuān Jùn (龍川郡),
the land of Lóngchuān (龍川) and Bólúo Xiàn (博羅縣) during Qín (秦) and Hàn (漢);
the Southern Dynasties established a commandery,
and Suí (隋) established a prefecture.
Cháozhōu (潮州)
was Yì'ān Jùn (義安郡),
the land of Jiēyáng Xiàn (揭陽縣) in Nánhǎi Jùn (南海郡) during Hàn (漢);
Liáng (梁) established Dōngyáng Zhōu (東揚州),
soon renamed Yíngzhōu (瀛州).
When Suí (隋) pacified Chén (陳),
it was renamed Cháozhōu (潮州).
俚 (lí) is pronounced lǐ.
帥 (shuài) is read suǒ lèi fān.
降 (jiàng) is read hù jiāng fān;
same below.
8 The Táng (唐) envoy Wáng Yìtóng (王義童) took Quán (泉), Mù (睦), and Jiàn (建) three prefectures.
Mùzhōu (睦州)
was Suí'ān Jùn (遂安郡),
the land of Fùchūn (富春) and Shè Xiàn (歙縣) in the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: In the fourth year of Wǔdé (武德),
Jiànzhōu (建州) was established from Jiàn'ān Xiàn (建安縣) of Jiàn'ān Jùn (建安郡).
It means Suí (隋) established Quánzhōu (泉州) (Jiàn'ān Jùn (建安郡)) governing Mǐn Xiàn (閩縣).
In the first year of Jǐngyún (景雲),
it was renamed Mǐnzhōu (閩州),
and in the thirteenth year of Kāiyuán (開元), it was renamed Fúzhōu (福州).
In the second year of Shènglì (聖曆),
Wǔróng Zhōu (武榮州) was established by dividing Nán'ān (南安), Lóngxī (龍溪), and Pútián (莆田) three counties from Quánzhōu (泉州).
In the second year of Jǐngyún (景雲),
Wǔróng Zhōu (武榮州) was changed to Quánzhōu (泉州).
Therefore, the Fúzhōu (福州) of today was the Quánzhōu (泉州) of early Táng (唐),
and the Quánzhōu (泉州) of today was the Quánzhōu (泉州) of Jǐngyún (景雲) second year.
使 (shǐ) is read shū lì fān.
9 Lǐ Yì (李藝), the Grand Administrator of Yōuzhōu (幽州), led his troops, several tens of thousands strong, to join Qín Wáng (秦王) Shìmín (世民) in attacking Liú Hēitá (劉黑闥).
Hēitá (黑闥), hearing this,
left ten thousand soldiers
and ordered Fàn Yuàn (范願) to guard Míngzhōu (洺州).
He personally led troops to resist Yì (藝).
At night,
they encamped at Shāhé (沙河).
Suí (隋) made Xiāngguó Xiàn (襄國縣) of Hàn (漢) into Lónggāng Xiàn (龍岡縣),
and further divided Lónggāng (龍岡) to establish Shāhé Xiàn (沙河縣).
At that time, it belonged to Xíngzhōu (邢州).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Shāhé (沙河) is the Yùshuǐ (湡水).
The Shuǐ Jīng (水經) says: The Yùshuǐ (湡水) flows out from the western mountains of Xiāngguó Xiàn (襄國縣) in Zàojùn (趙郡),
east past Shāhé Xiàn (沙河縣).
The Shāhé (沙河) is five li south of the county.
Fàn Chéngdà (范成大) said: From Línmíng Zhèn (臨洺鎮), it is thirty-five li east to Míngzhōu (洺州),
thirty li across the Mínghé (洺河) to Shāhé Xiàn (沙河縣),
and twenty-five li to Xíngzhōu (邢州).
將 (jiàng) is read jí liàng fān;
same below.
He launched a swift attack on the embankment two li west of the city,
and the ground inside the city trembled.
Fàn Yuàn (范願) was shocked and frightened,
and quickly reported to Hēitá (黑闥);
Hēitá (黑闥) immediately returned,
dispatching his younger brother Shíshàn (十善) and Xíngtái (行臺) Zhāng Jūnlì (張君立) with ten thousand soldiers to attack Yì (藝) at Gǔchéng (鼓城).
On the day of Rénzǐ,
they fought at Xúhé (徐河).
Gǔchéng Xiàn (鼓城縣)
was formerly called Qǔyáng (曲陽),
later abolished by Hòuqí (後齊);
in the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng (開皇) of Suí (隋), Jìnyáng Xiàn (晉陽縣) was established by division,
and in the eighteenth year,
it was renamed Gǔchéng (鼓城).
According to the Shuǐ Jīng Zhù (水經註),
there is Gǔ Jù (鼓聚) in Xiàqǔyáng Xiàn (下曲陽縣).
This county was named after the state of Gǔ Zǐ (鼓子) from the Spring and Autumn period.
In the Táng (唐) dynasty, it belonged to Zhàozhōu (趙州).
The Shuǐ Jīng (水經) says: The Xúshuǐ (徐水) flows out from below the Dàlǐng (大嶺) southeast of Guǎngchāng Xiàn (廣昌縣),
northeast past Wǔhuí Xiàn (五回縣),
then past the border of Běipíng Xiàn (北平縣),
southeast out of the mountains,
then east to the north of Qīngyuàn (清苑) city,
and then east to Gāoyáng (高陽) where it enters the river.
Fàn Chéngdà (范成大) said: Xúhé (徐河) is ten li north of Qīngyuàn (清苑).
Eight thousand men were lost.
10 Míngshuǐ person Lǐ Qùhuò.
The Suí Zhì states: Míngshuǐ County,
formerly called Chìzhāng,
was merged into Píng'ēn by the Later Qí.
In the sixth year of Kāihuáng,
Qǔzhōu was established by division.
In the early years of Dàyè,
Qǔzhōu was abolished and merged into Míngshuǐ;
at the end of Táng,
Míngshuǐ was abolished and merged into Qǔzhōu.
Qù
is pronounced Qī Lǚ.
Qínwáng Shìmín sent Péng Gōng Wáng Jūnkuò with 1,500 cavalry to go to them,
and they entered the city to defend it together.
In the second month,
Liú Hēitǎ led his troops back to attack Míngshuǐ.
On the guǐhài day,
they arrived at Lièrén.
Lièrén County,
during Hàn, belonged to Guǎngpíng Commandery;
during Later Hàn, it belonged to Wèijùn;
during Jìn, it again belonged to Guǎngpíng;
during Later Wèi, it again belonged to Wèijùn;
it was abolished during Suí.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Míngzhōu has Lièrén City,
northeast of Hàn's Chìqiū County
and southwest of Wǔ'ān County.
Dù Yòu said: The ancient city of Hàn's Lièrén County
is northeast of Féixiāng County.
Qí
is pronounced Qí Jì.
They defeated him.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù records:
"On the guǐhài day,
Qínwáng attacked Liú Hēitǎ at Lièrén
and greatly defeated him."
The Gémìng Jì records:
"In the eleventh month,
Tàizōng crossed the river and entered Xiāngzhōu.
Liú Hēitǎ, from Míngzhōu, mobilized his troops to resist the royal army,
setting up camp thirty *lǐ* east of Yèxiàn.
Every day, both armies challenged each other,
but the main army did not sally forth.
After more than ten days,
Lǐ Qùhuò, Lǐ Pānmǎi, Lǐ Kāibì, and others from Míngshuǐ County served as Chējì and Piàojì generals,
leading troops in Liú Hēitǎ's camp.
Qùhuò and the others defected from the bandit camp and entered Míngzhōu City,
deceiving people by saying: 'Liú Hēitǎ has already been defeated
and has fled back first.'
Then they summoned more than two hundred members of the imperial clan's children and younger brothers,
secured the city,
and sent an envoy through secret paths to inform Tàizōng.
Tàizōng sent Péngguó Gōng Wáng Jūnkuò with 1,500 cavalry into Míngzhōu.
After about ten days,
Hēitǎ led his troops to attack Míngzhōu.
When they arrived west of the old Lièrén City,
Qín Shúbǎo and others attacked them with 5,000 cavalry.
Shúbǎo and the others were defeated by Tǎ,
but then a hidden force rose from the river,
attacking Hēitǎ from the flank and
defeating him.
As dusk fell,
the troops were recalled.
That night, at the third watch,
the bandit troops all arrived at the camp east of Míngzhōu City,
immediately digging trenches and erecting palisades at the two city gates
to prevent Wáng Jūnkuò from escaping.
Míngzhōu City was surrounded by water on all four sides,
more than fifty *bù* wide,
and all three or four *chǐ* deep.
Hēitǎ, at two places in the northeast corner,
filled it with firewood and transported earth,
making a covered passage
to attack the city with battering rams.
Tàizōng led troops to attack him three times.
The bandits set up formations to resist the government army,
and attacked the city even more fiercely."
According to the Gāozǔ and Tàizōng Shílù, it was in the twelfth month of the previous year that Tàizōng was ordered to subjugate Hēitǎ,
and he only arrived in Héběi in the first month of this year,
so there was no crossing of the river in the eleventh month.
The Tàizōng Shílù also has no record of the Lièrén battle.
Presumably, Shúbǎo defeated the bandits,
and Qínwáng reported it.
Also, regarding Míngshuǐ,
it was a county subordinate to Míngzhōu.
What Qùhuò and Jūnkuò occupied was Míngshuǐ County City,
and the character "水" (shuǐ)
was mistakenly written as
"州" (zhōu).
11 Yùzhāng bandit chief Zhāng Shàn'ān surrendered with five prefectures including Qián and Jí,
and was appointed Hóngzhōu General Superintendent.
Hóngzhōu was Yùzhāng Commandery;
Qiánzhōu was Nánkāng Commandery;
Jízhōu was Lúlíng Commandery;
all were prefectures established by Suí after its conquest of Chén.
Shuài
is pronounced Suǒ Lèi.
12 On the wùchén day,
Yáng Xiàochéng of Jīnxiāng rebelled against Xú Yuánlǎng
and surrendered with the city.
Jīnxiāng County,
during Hàn, belonged to Shānyáng Commandery;
during Jìn, it belonged to Gāopíng Commandery;
during Suí, it belonged to Cáozhōu;
in the fourth year of Wǔdé,
Jīnzhōu was established.
In the same year, the prefecture was abolished,
and the county was made subordinate to Dàizhōu.
13 On the jǐsì day,
Qínwáng Shìmín recaptured Xíngzhōu.
On the xīnwèi day,
Féng Bóràng of Jǐngzhōu surrendered with the city.
In the sixteenth year of Suí Kāihuáng,
Jǐngzhōu was established from Jǐngxíng County of Héngzhōu.
It was abolished in the early years of Dàyè,
and re-established in the first year of Wǔdé.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù writes it as
"Bìngzhōu."
However, Bìngzhōu was never lost.
Perhaps at that time, Jǐngzhōu was established at Jǐngxíng County,
and it was a mistaken character.
14 On the bǐngzǐ day,
Lǐ Yì captured Dìng, Luán, Lián, and Zhào, the four prefectures of Liú Hēitǎ.
In the sixteenth year of Suí Kāihuáng,
Luánzhōu was established by dividing Guǎng'ā County from Zhàozhōu.
In the early years of Dàyè,
the prefecture was abolished
and merged into Zhàozhōu.
The Xīnzhì states: In the fifth year of Wǔdé,
Zhàozhōu was renamed Luánzhōu.
According to this, Zhàozhōu was governed from Píngjí,
and Luánzhōu was governed from Guǎng'ā.
Dòu Jiàndé and Liú Hēitǎ successively occupied Shāndōng,
presumably establishing Luánzhōu themselves.
It was after Hēitǎ was defeated and fled in this year
that Zhàozhōu was first merged into Luánzhōu.
In the first year of Wǔdé,
Liánzhōu was established by dividing Gǎochéng County from Héngzhōu.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù writes it as
"Dìng, Shuài, Lián, and Suí, four prefectures."
However, there were no Shuài and Suí prefectures in Héběi.
This translation follows the Táng Tǒngjì.
He led his troops to meet Qínwáng Shìmín at Míngzhōu.
Míng
is pronounced Mí Bìng.
15 Liú Hēità attacked Míngshuǐ very urgently.
On all four sides of the city there was water,
more than fifty bù wide.
Hēità built two covered approaches (yǒngdào) on the northeast of the city to attack it.
Shìmín led his troops to relieve it three times,
but Hēità repelled them,
and they could not advance.
Shìmín feared that Wáng Jūnkuò would not be able to hold out,
so he summoned his generals to deliberate.
Lǐ Shìjì said:
"If the covered approaches reach the city wall,
the city will surely not be held."
The Grand Commander (xíngjūn zǒngguǎn) Tán Yǒng Gōng Luó Shìxìn requested to replace Jūnkuò in defending it.
Shìmín then ascended a high mound south of the city,
and waved a flag to signal Jūnkuò.
Jūnkuò, leading his followers, fought vigorously
and broke through the encirclement.
Shìxìn, leading two hundred men of his immediate retinue, took advantage of this to enter the city
and replaced Jūnkuò in holding it firmly.
Hēità attacked fiercely day and night.
Heavy snow fell,
and relief troops could not reach them.
After eight days,
on the dìngchǒu day,
the city fell.
Hēità had long heard of his bravery
and wanted to spare his life,
but Shìxìn's words and demeanor showed no submission,
so he killed him.
He was twenty years old at the time.
The Kǎoyì says: The Gāozǔ Shílù states:
"Wáng Jūnkuò knew it could not be held,
and broke through the encirclement and left.
Qín Wáng asked his generals: 'Who can replace him?'
Shìxìn said: 'I am willing to defend it to the death.'
So he sent him."
However, if Jūnkuò had already broken through the encirclement and left,
then Hēità's siege would have been even stronger.
How could Shìxìn have entered the city again?
The Gémìng Jì says:
"Tàizōng knew the enemy's strength was great,
and feared Wáng Jūnkuò could not hold it,
so he asked his generals.
Shìxìn thought it was nothing to worry about.
Tàizōng made Shìxìn enter and defend it.
Tàizōng ascended Duàn Wáng's tomb
and waved a flag to signal Wáng Jūnkuò to break through the siege from the south gate,
but he failed.
He then turned to the north gate,
combined his troops and attacked to capture it.
The gatekeepers retreated slightly,
and he was able to get out.
Shìxìn also entered the city with two hundred men of his immediate retinue.
After eight days,
being attacked day and night,
all wood and stones were exhausted.
Shìxìn was seized by his subordinates and surrendered to the bandits.
In the first month of the fifth year,
the city fell.
Lǐ Qùhuò, with dozens of men, broke through the encirclement
and returned to Tàizōng.
Qùhuò was later appointed Dūdu of Qínzhōu.
Lǐ Pānmǎi was appointed Cìshǐ of Tánzhōu.
Lǐ Kāibì perished when the city fell.
He was posthumously granted Shàng Zhùguó
and buried with the rites of a duke."
We follow this account now.
The Gāozǔ Shílù says
Shìxìn was twenty-eight when he died,
while the old tradition says he was twenty.
However, Shìxìn first followed Zhāng Xūtú to attack Wáng Bó and others
when he was fourteen.
If he died at twenty-eight,
that would be in Dàyè Year 4,
at which time Wáng Bó had not yet become a bandit.
If he was twenty,
that would be in Dàyè Year 12,
the year Xūtú died.
We follow this now.
16 On the wùyín day,
the Zǒngguǎn of Biànzhōu, Wáng Yàohàn, attacked Xú Yuánlǎng's prefecture,
captured it,
and apprehended his general Zhōu Wénjǔ.
17 On the gēngchén day,
the Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn of Yánzhōu Dao, Duàn Décāo,
(Yánzhōu, the land of Fūshī in Hànshàng Jùn.
At the end of the Yuán Wèi,
Dōngxiàzhōu was established.
The Xī Wèi changed it to Yánzhōu.
The Suí called it Yán'ān Jùn.)
Shī Dū personally led troops to relieve it.
Décāo engaged him in battle
and thoroughly defeated him.
Shī Dū escaped with sixteen horsemen.
The Emperor increased his troops
and ordered him to press the advantage and attack Xiàzhōu.
He captured its east city.
Shī Dū, with several hundred men, held the west city.
Just then, Turkic relief forces arrived.
An imperial edict ordered Décāo to withdraw.
18 On the xīnsì day,
Qín Wáng Shìmín captured Míngshuǐ.
(Míng,
pronounced like míng in míngbìng.)
Shìmín and Lǐ Yì encamped south of Míngshuǐ,
and divided their forces to garrison the north of the river.
Hēità frequently challenged them to battle,
but Shìmín held his strong defenses without responding.
He secretly dispatched a detachment (qíbīng) to cut off Hēità's supply route.
On the rénchén day,
Hēità appointed Gāo Yǎxián as Zuǒ Púshè,
and there was a grand banquet in the army.
Lǐ Shìjì led his troops to press towards Hēità's camp.
Yǎxián, in his drunkenness,
chased them alone on horseback.
Shìjì's subordinate Pān Máo stabbed him, causing him to fall from his horse.
His retinue arrived immediately after,
helped him return,
but he died before reaching the camp.
On the jiǎwǔ day,
the generals again went to press towards Hēità's camp.
Pān Máo was captured by Wáng Xiǎohú.
Hēità transported provisions from Jì, Bèi, Cāng, and Yíng Prefectures,
advancing by both water and land.
Chéng Míngzhèn, with over a thousand men, intercepted them,
sank their boats,
and burned their carts.
19 The Zǒngguǎn of Sòngzhōu, Shèng Yànshī, led the Zǒngguǎn of Qízhōu, Wáng Bó, to attack Xūchāng.
He requisitioned military provisions from Tánzhōu.
The Cìshǐ, Lǐ Yìmǎn, had a feud with Bó,
and closed the granaries, refusing to supply them.
When Xūchāng surrendered,
Yànshī arrested Yìmǎn
and imprisoned him in Qízhōu.
An imperial edict ordered his release.
Before the messenger arrived,
Yìmǎn, overcome by anxiety and indignation,
died in prison.
When Bó returned,
passing through Tánzhōu,
on the night of the wùxū day,
Yìmǎn's nephew, Wǔyì, seized Bó
and killed him.
( "潭州" (Tánzhōu)
should be "譚州" (Tánzhōu).
In Wǔdé Year 2,
Lǐ Yìmǎn surrendered with Zhāngqiū County of Qízhōu.
Tánzhōu was established at Pínglíng,
and Pínglíng County was also established.
This was probably named after the state of Tán Zǐ from the Spring and Autumn period.)
Those implicated and put to death,
the court considered Yìmǎn's death Yànshī's crime and killed him.
20 The Emperor sent an envoy to bribe the Turkic Xiélì Kèhán
and also promised a marriage alliance.
Xiélì then sent Hányáng Gōng Wáng Huái, Zhèng Yuánshú, Chángsūn Shùndé, and others back.
(Wáng Huái and others had been detained;
the incident is described in the previous volume, Year 4.)
(Huái, pronounced like huí in gōnghuí.)
(Shú, pronounced like yù in shūyù.)
(Cháng, pronounced like liǎng in zhīliǎng.)
On the gēngzǐ day,
he again sent envoys to restore good relations.
The Emperor also sent his envoys, Tèlè Rèhán and Āshǐnà Dé, back.
The Zǒngguǎn of Bìngzhōu, Liú Shìràng, was stationed at Yànmén.
Xiélì, together with Gāo Kāidào and Yuàn Jūnzhāng, gathered their forces to attack him.
After more than a month,
they withdrew.
The Kǎoyì says: The old biography of Shìràng says:
"At that time, Hónglú Qīng Zhèng Yuánshú was already an envoy in the barbarian lands.
The Kèhán ordered Yuánshú to persuade Shìràng.
Shìràng sternly said: 'How can a true man act as a persuader for barbarians!'
After more than a month,
the barbarians withdrew.
When Yuánshú returned,
he reported Shìràng's loyalty, steadfastness, and courage.
Gāozǔ issued a decree praising him."
However, Gāozǔ praised Yuánshú, saying that Sū Wǔ himself was no better than him.
How could he have possibly acted as a persuader for the Kèhán?
If it truly happened,
then Yuánshú would only fear the Emperor knowing about it.
How could he have praised Shìràng's loyalty and steadfastness,
saying that he could not be persuaded?
According to the Shílù biography of Shìràng, there is no such incident.
We do not adopt this account now.
On the *jiǎchén* day of the 21st year,
Qíu Hé (丘和), the Grand Administrator of Jiāozhǐ (交趾) under the Suí, was appointed Governor-General of Jiāozhōu (交州),
and Jiāozhǐ Commandery (交趾郡) was made Jiāozhōu.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Jiāozhōu,
in the Zhōu (周) dynasty, was the land of the Yuèsháng (越裳) with repeated interpreters,
bordering the Hàn (漢) commanderies of Jiāozhǐ and Rìnán (日南).
Regarding the name Jiāozhǐ,
among the southern barbarians of today,
their big toes are wide apart;
if they stand with their feet together,
their toes cross over each other,
hence the name Jiāozhǐ (交趾, lit. "crossed toes").
During the Huángwǔ (黃武) reign of Wú (吳),
because Jiāozhǐ county was distant,
it was divided into two *zhōu*:
the four commanderies north of Hépǔ (合浦) and east of the sea were allotted to establish Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
and the area south of Jiāozhǐ established Jiāozhōu.
Shǒu (守)
is also pronounced *shì*.
The emperor granted permission,
and sent his son Shīlì (師利) to welcome him.
As the righteous army approached Cháng'ān (長安),
Qíu Shīlì came to join them with his troops.
Qín Wáng Shì Mín (秦王世民) and Liú Hēitá (劉黑闥) were locked in a standoff for over sixty days.
Hēitá secretly led his troops to attack Lǐ Shìjì's (李世勣) camp.
Shì Mín led his army to flank his rear to rescue him,
but was surrounded by Hēitá.
Yùchí Jìngdé (尉遲敬德) led brave warriors to break through the encirclement and enter.
Shì Mín and Lüèyáng Gōng Dàozōng (略陽公道宗) seized the opportunity and escaped.
Dàozōng
was the emperor's cousin.
Shì Mín, estimating that Hēitá's provisions were exhausted,
knew he would eventually come for a decisive battle.
So, he had people dam the upstream of the Míngshǔi (洺水).
Míng (洺)
is pronounced *mí-bìng*.
"Wait until I am battling the bandit," he said,
"then release the water."
On the *dīngwèi* day,
Hēitá led twenty thousand infantry and cavalry south across the Míngshǔi,
forming ranks to press the Táng (唐) camp.
Shì Mín personally led elite cavalry to attack his cavalry,
defeating them,
and riding the momentum to overrun his infantry.
Hēitá led his troops in a desperate fight.
From noon until dusk,
they fought several engagements,
but Hēitá's forces could no longer hold.
Wáng Xiǎohú (王小胡) said to Hēitá:
"Our wisdom and strength are exhausted;
we should flee early."
Thereupon, he fled first with Hēitá.
The remaining troops, unaware,
continued to fight.
The officers guarding the dam released the water.
The Míngshǔi rose greatly,
over a *zhàng* (丈) deep.
Míng (洺)
is pronounced *mí-bìng*.
Shēn (深)
is pronounced *shì-jìn*.
Over ten thousand heads were cut off,
and several thousand people drowned.
Hēitá, with Fàn Yuàn (范願) and two hundred cavalry, fled to the Tūjué (突厥).
Shāndōng (山東) was completely pacified.
Gāo Kāidào (高開道) raided Yìzhōu (易州),
killing the Inspector Mùróng Xiàogàn (慕容孝幹).
Summer,
fourth month,
on the *jǐwèi* day,
Níng Chángzhēn (甯長真), the Suí Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials, offered to surrender Níngyuè (寧越) and Yùlín (鬱林) to Lǐ Jìng (李靖),
thus opening the route between Jiāo (交) and Ài (愛).
Chángzhēn was made Governor-General of Qīnzhōu (欽州).
Níngyuè Commandery (寧越郡) is Qīnzhōu,
land of Hàn Hépǔ County (漢合浦縣),
in Sòng (宋) was Sòngshòu (宋壽) and Sòngguǎng (宋廣) Commandery.
Yùlín Commandery (鬱林郡) is Yùzhōu (鬱州),
an ancient Hàn commandery,
where the Suí established a *zhōu*.
Àizhōu (愛州) is Jiǔzhēn Commandery (九真郡),
an ancient Hàn commandery,
where the Liáng (梁) established a *zhōu*.
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: Jiāozhōu is seven thousand five hundred twenty-three *lǐ* (里) from the capital;
Àizhōu is eight thousand eight hundred *lǐ* from the capital.
Zhào Jùnwáng Xiàogōng (趙郡王孝恭), Governor-General of Kuízhōu (夔州), was appointed Governor-General of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Xú Yuánlǎng (徐圓朗), upon hearing of Liú Hēitá's defeat,
was greatly alarmed,
not knowing what to do.
Liú Fùlǐ (劉復禮) of Héjiān (河間) persuaded Yuánlǎng, saying:
"There is a man named Liú Shìchè (劉世徹), whose talent is exceptional,
whose fame is high in the East and Xia (夏),
and who possesses an extraordinary countenance,
truly a vessel for an emperor.
If the general tries to establish himself,
I fear he will ultimately achieve nothing;
but if he welcomes and serves Shìchè,
the world can be settled with a wave of the hand."
Yuánlǎng agreed,
and sent Fùlǐ to welcome Shìchè at Jùnyí (浚儀).
Jùnyí County (浚儀縣),
in the Hàn, Jìn (晉), and Hòu Wèi (後魏) dynasties belonged to Chénliú Commandery (陳留郡),
in Zhōu, Suí, and Táng was the seat of Biànzhōu (汴州).
"The general has been misled by others,
wishing to welcome and serve Liú Shìchè.
If Shìchè achieves his ambition,
how could the general keep his territory intact?
I dare not draw on ancient history from afar,
but has the general not seen Zhái Ràng (翟讓) and Lǐ Mì (李密)?"
The affairs of Lǐ Mì and Zhái Ràng began in Volume 183, Suí Dàyè (大業) 12th year,
and ended in Volume 184, Yìníng (義寧) 1st year.
Zhái (翟)
is pronounced *cháng-bó*.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Gémìngjì* (革命記) says:
"Shèng Yànshī (盛彥師), fearing that Shìchè had an undeserved reputation in Xú (徐) and Yǎn (兗),
and that if the two became allies,
the trouble would deepen,
persuaded Yuánlǎng not to accept him."
According to the *Shílù* (實錄), Yànshī fled to Wáng Bó (王薄)
and together with Bó killed Lǐ Yìmǎn (李義滿).
In the third month,
on the *wùxū* day,
Wáng Bó died.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
Hēitá was defeated.
When Yànshī was with Yuánlǎng,
Hēitá had not yet been defeated.
The current text says "or said" to indicate uncertainty.
When Shìchè arrived,
he already had several thousand followers and
encamped outside the city,
awaiting Yuánlǎng to come out and welcome him.
Yuánlǎng did not come out,
but sent someone to summon him.
Shìchè knew the situation had changed
and wanted to flee,
but feared he would not escape,
so he entered to pay his respects.
Yuánlǎng completely stripped him of his troops
and made him a *sīmǎ* (司馬),
sending him to campaign in Qiáo (譙) and Èr (二) *zhōu*.
People in the east had long heard of his name,
and all places he went submitted.
Yuánlǎng then killed him.
Qín Wáng Shì Mín led his troops from Hébĕi (河北), intending to attack Yuánlǎng.
But the emperor summoned him,
ordering him to travel by express messenger to the court.
He then handed over his troops to Qí Wáng Yuánjí (齊王元吉).
On the *gēngshēn* day,
Shì Mín arrived in Cháng'ān.
The emperor welcomed him at Chánglè (長樂).
Chánglè Bǎn (長樂坂) is east of Cháng'ān city.
Lè (樂)
is pronounced *luò*.
The emperor again sent him to Líyáng (黎陽),
to join the main army heading towards Jìyīn (濟陰).
Cáozhōu (曹州) was governed from Jìyīn County.
Qū (趨)
is pronounced *qī-yù*.
Jì (濟)
is pronounced *zǐ-lǐ*.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
the Shāndōng (山東) Provisional Government was abolished.
This was because Liú Hēitá had been defeated and fled.
28th day, *rénshēn* (壬申).
Lǐ Dà'ēn (李大恩), Prince Dìngxiāng (定襄王) and Grand Administrator (總管) of Dàizhōu (代州), was killed by the Tujue (突厥).
Previously,
Dà'ēn (大恩) had reported that the Tujue (突厥) were suffering from famine,
and Màiyì (馬邑) could be taken.
An imperial edict ordered Dúgū Shèng (獨孤晟), Junior Supervisor (少監) of the Palace Interior (殿內), to lead troops with Dà'ēn (大恩) to jointly attack Yuàn Jūnzhāng (苑君璋),
planning to meet at Màiyì (馬邑) in the second month.
Shèng (晟) failed to arrive on time,
and Dà'ēn (大恩) could not advance alone,
so he encamped his troops at Xīnchéng (新城).
Xīnchéng (新城)
should be south of Shuòzhōu (朔州).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: The Northern Wei (魏) capital Píngchéng (平城)
established Huáishuò Town (懷朔鎮) over three hundred *lǐ* north of Màiyì Commandery (馬邑郡).
After moving to Luòyáng (洛陽),
Shuòzhōu (朔州) was established over three hundred *lǐ* north of the commandery.
In the early Northern Wei (魏), Yúnzhōng Commandery (雲中郡)
was north of Dìngxiāng (定襄) old city, over three hundred *lǐ* north of the present commandery.
Northern Qi (北齊) established Shuòzhōu (朔州) southwest of the old capital.
Xīnchéng (新城)
was also called Píngchéng (平城),
later moved to Màiyì (馬邑),
which is the present commandery city.
The seat of Màiyì Commandery (馬邑郡) was Shànyáng County (善陽縣),
also the territory of Dìngxiāng County (定襄縣) in the Han (漢) dynasty.
Xīnchéng (新城) was the Xīnpíngchéng (新平城) of the Wei (魏).
Shèng (晟),
*chéngzhèng* (承正) pronunciation.
Jiàng (將),
*jìliàng* (即亮) pronunciation.
The Emperor dispatched Lǐ Gāoqiān (李高遷), Grand General (大將軍) of the Right Guard of Valiant Cavalry (右驍衞), to rescue him.
Before he arrived,
Dà'ēn (大恩) ran out of provisions.
He fled by night,
but the Tujue (突厥) ambushed him,
his forces collapsed, and he died.
The Emperor regretted his loss.
Dúgū Shèng (獨孤晟) was sentenced to a reduced death penalty and exiled to the frontier.
29th day, *bǐngzǐ* (丙子).
Shǐ Wànbǎo (史萬寶), Minister (尚書) of the Ministry of Revenue (民部) in the Traveling Secretariat (行臺), attacked Chénzhōu (陳州),
and captured it.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Chénzhōu (陳州),
King Xiāng of Chu (楚襄王) moved here from Yǐng (郢),
calling it Xīchǔ (西楚).
In the Han (漢) dynasty, it was the territory of Huáiyáng Kingdom (淮陽國).
Later Wei (魏) established Chén Commandery (陳郡).
In the second year of Tiānpíng (天平, 535 AD),
Běiyángzhōu (北揚州) was established.
The Sui (隋) dynasty renamed it Chénzhōu (陳州),
with its seat at Wǎnqiū (宛丘).
It was the capital of the State of Chén (陳國) during the Spring and Autumn period.
30th day, *wùyín* (戊寅).
Dèng Wénjìn (鄧文進), a rebel leader in Guǎngzhōu (廣州), and Níng Xuān (甯宣), Sui (隋) Grand Administrator (太守) of Hépǔ (合浦), and Lǐ Jùn (李晙), Grand Administrator (太守) of Rìnán (日南), all came to surrender.
Hépǔ Commandery (合浦郡),
was Yuèzhōu (越州),
renamed Liánzhōu (廉州) during the Zhēngguān (貞觀) era.
Rìnán Commandery (日南郡),
was Dézhōu (德州),
renamed Huānzhōu (驩州) during the Zhēngguān (貞觀) era.
Shuài (帥),
*suǒlèi* (所類) pronunciation.
Shǒu (守),
*shìyòu* (式又) pronunciation.
Jùn (晙),
*zǐjùn* (子峻) pronunciation.
31st day, fifth month,
*gēngyín* (庚寅).
Wáng Gàn (王幹), a local strongman in Guāzhōu (瓜州), beheaded Hèbá Xíngwēi (賀拔行威) and surrendered.
Guāzhōu (瓜州)
was Jìnchāng Commandery (晉昌郡).
In this year, Guāzhōu (瓜州) was established from Chánglè County (常樂縣) of Guāzhōu (瓜州);
the old Guāzhōu (瓜州) became Xīshāzhōu (西沙州).
Hèbá Xíngwēi's (賀拔行威) rebellion was first mentioned in Volume 188, third year.
32nd day. The Tujue (突厥) raided Xīnzhōu (忻州).
Xīnzhōu (忻州)
was Xīnxīng Commandery (新興郡),
established in the first year of Yìníng (義寧, 617 AD) from Xiùróng County (秀容縣) of Lóufán Commandery (樓煩郡).
This Xiùróng (秀容)
was the territory of Fényáng County (汾陽縣) in the Han (漢) dynasty,
not the Běixiùróng (北秀容) of the Later Wei (後魏).
33rd day, sixth month,
*xīnhài* (辛亥).
Liú Hēitǎ (劉黑闥) led the Tujue (突厥) to raid Shāndōng (山東).
An imperial edict ordered Lǐ Yì (李藝), Prince of Yànjùn (燕郡王), to attack him.
34th day, *guǐchǒu* (癸丑).
The Tuyuhun (吐谷渾) raided Táo (洮), Xù (旭), and Dié (疊) three prefectures.
Lǐ Chángqīng (李長卿), Grand Administrator (總管) of Mínzhōu (岷州), attacked and defeated them.
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) of the Later Zhou (後周) expelled the Tuyuhun (吐谷渾),
establishing Diézhōu (疊州) in Diéchuan (疊川),
Xùzhōu (旭州) at Táoyuán (洮源),
and Mínzhōu (岷州) at Líntáo (臨洮).
In the first year of Yìníng (義寧, 617 AD),
Líntáo (臨洮) was changed to Yìlè (溢樂).
The *History of the Later Zhou* (後周書) states: Xùzhōu (旭州) was established at Jīmíngfáng (鷄鳴防) in Hézhōu (河州),
and Mínzhōu (岷州) was established at Qúzhūchuān (渠株川) in Dàngzhōu (宕州).
Tǔ (吐),
from *tūn* (暾) entering tone.
Gǔ (谷),
*yù* (浴) pronunciation.
Táo (洮),
*tǔdāo* (土刀) pronunciation.
Xù (旭),
*xūyù* (吁玉) pronunciation.
Cháng (長),
*zhīliǎng* (知兩) pronunciation.
35th day, *yǐmǎo* (乙卯).
The Emperor dispatched Shéntōng (神通), Prince of Huái'ān (淮安王), to attack Xú Yuánlǎng (徐圓朗).
36th day, *dīngmǎo* (丁卯).
Liú Hēitǎ (劉黑闥) led the Tujue (突厥) to raid Dìngzhōu (定州).
37th day, autumn,
seventh month,
*jiǎshēn* (甲申).
The Emperor had the Hóngyì Palace (弘義宮) built for Qínwáng (秦王) Shìmín (世民).
Hóngyì Palace (弘義宮)
was later renamed Dà'ān Palace (大安宮),
located on the western side outside the palace city.
Wèi (為),
*yúwèi* (于偽) pronunciation.
Shìmín (世民) attacked Xú Yuánlǎng (徐圓朗),
capturing over ten cities.
His fame shook the Huái (淮) and Sì (泗) rivers,
and Dù Fúwēi (杜伏威) feared him,
requesting to enter the court.
As the region between the Huái (淮) and Jì (濟) rivers was mostly pacified, Shìmín (世民)
ordered Shéntōng (神通), Prince of Huái'ān (淮安王), and Rèn Huái (任⿰王褱) and Lǐ Shìjì (李世勣), both Traveling Army Grand Administrators (行軍總管), to attack Yuánlǎng (圓朗).
On the *yǐyǒu* (乙酉) day,
he returned with his army.
38th day, *dīnghài* (丁亥).
Dù Fúwēi (杜伏威) entered the court.
He was granted a seat on the Emperor's couch,
appointed Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (太子太保),
and concurrently held the position of Director of the Department of State Affairs (尚書令) in the Traveling Secretariat (行臺).
He was kept in Cháng'ān (長安),
his rank above Qíwáng (齊王) Yuánjí (元吉),
to show special favor.
Kàn Léng (闞稜) was appointed General of the Left Leader Guard (左領軍將軍).
During the Jiàn'ān (建安) era of the Han (漢) dynasty,
Wèi Wǔ (魏武) as Chancellor (丞相)
first established the Central Leader Guard (中領軍).
Northern Qi (北齊) established the Leader Guard Bureau (領軍府).
Emperor Yáng (煬帝) renamed it Imperial Guard (禦衞).
The Tang (唐) dynasty renamed it Leader Guard (領軍衞).
Lǐ Zǐtōng (李子通) said to Yuè Bótōng (樂伯通):
"Now that Fúwēi (伏威) has come,
and Jiāngdōng (江東) is not yet pacified,
if I go and gather my old troops,
I can achieve great merit."
So they fled together to Lántián Pass (藍田關).
Lántián County (藍田縣) in Yōngzhōu (雍州) has Lántián Pass (藍田關).
Both were executed.
39th day. Liú Hēitǎ (劉黑闥) reached Dìngzhōu (定州).
His former generals Cáo Zhàn (曹湛) and Dǒng Kāngmǎi (董康買), who had fled, were in Xiānyú (鮮虞).
Xiānyú County (鮮虞縣)
was formerly called Lúnú (盧奴).
It was renamed in the early Kāihuáng (開皇) era
because its territory was the State of Xiānyú (鮮虞子) in the Spring and Autumn period.
It was the administrative seat of Dìngzhōu (定州).
On the *jiǎwǔ* (甲午) day,
Dàoxuán (道玄), Prince of Huáiyáng (淮陽王), was appointed Grand Administrator (行軍總管) of the Traveling Army of Héběidào (河北道) to suppress them.
40th day, *bǐngshēn* (丙申).
Dèng Shìzhèng (鄧士政) of Qiānzhōu (遷州) seized Lǐ Jìng'áng (李敬昂), the Prefect (刺史), and rebelled.
The Western Wei (西魏) established Qiānzhōu (遷州) in Fánglíng (房陵).
In the early Dàyè (大業) era,
it was renamed Fángzhōu (房州).
In the early Wǔdé (武德) era,
it was again called Qiānzhōu (遷州),
Fánglíng Commandery (房陵郡).
41. On the *dīngyǒu* day,
Féng Àng (馮盎), the Grand Administrator of Hányáng (漢陽) under the Suí (隋) dynasty, acceded to Lǐ Jìng’s (李靖) summons,
and led his troops to surrender.
His territory was designated as the eight prefectures of Gāo (高), Luó (羅), Chūn (春), Bái (白), Yá (崖), Dān (儋), Lín (林), and Zhèn (振).
Gāozhōu (高州) was
the Gāoliáng (高涼) Commandery.
Luózhōu (羅州) was
the Shíchéng (石城) Commandery.
Chūnzhōu (春州) was
the Yángchūn (陽春) Commandery.
Báizhōu (白州) was
the Nánchāng (南昌) Commandery.
Yázhōu (崖州) was
the Zhūyá (珠崖) Commandery.
Línzhōu (林州) was
the Guìlín (桂林) Commandery.
Zhènzhōu (振州) was
the Línzhèn (臨振) Commandery.
Luózhōu (羅州) is
present-day Huàzhōu (化州).
Báizhōu (白州) is
present-day Bóbái (博白) County in Yùlínzhōu (鬱林州).
Yá (崖), Dān (儋), and Zhèn (振) are all overseas.
Zhènzhōu (振州) is
present-day Jíyáng Jūn (吉陽軍) territory.
Línzhōu (林州) was
later renamed Xiùzhōu (繡州).
The *Tóu Huāng Lù* (投荒錄) states: Gāozhōu (高州), Gāoliáng Jùn (高涼郡),
has thick soil and is surrounded by mountains.
It is high but slightly sunken,
hence its name.
Luózhōu (羅州) was where
Sòng (宋) general Tán Dàojì (檀道濟) built a city at the mouth of the Língluó (陵羅) River.
Consequently, Luózhōu (羅州) was established,
but it is now abolished.
Língluó (陵羅) County is 120 *lǐ* north of Huàzhōu (化州).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: The prefecture is between the Líng (陵) and Luó (羅) rivers.
Chūnzhōu (春州) governed Yángchūn (陽春) County,
hence its name.
Báizhōu (白州) was named after the Bóbái (博白) River.
Yázhōu (崖州) was named after Zhūyá (珠崖).
Dānzhōu (儋州) was named after Dān'ěr (儋耳).
Línzhōu (林州) was named to reflect the pacification and embrace of Lín Yì (林邑).
Zhènzhōu (振州) was named after the ancient Hàn (漢) county of Línzhèn (臨振).
Dān (儋),
read as *dīnggān* (丁甘) in fanqie.
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Gěng (耿).
Previously,
someone persuaded Àng (盎), saying:
"Táng (唐) has just pacified the Central Plains
and has not yet reached distant regions.
The twenty prefectures under your command are already larger than Zhào Tuó’s (趙佗) territory."
Zhào Tuó (趙佗)
is mentioned in *Hàn Jì* (漢紀).
“Xiān” (先),
read as *xījiàn* (悉薦) in fanqie.
“Shuō” (說),
read as *shūruì* (輸芮) in fanqie.
“Tuó” (佗),
read as *túhé* (徒何) in fanqie.
Àng (盎) said:
"My family has resided here for five generations.
The Féng (馮) family's residence in Gāoliáng (高涼) first appeared in Volume 163, during the first year of Emperor Jiǎnwén's (簡文帝) Dàbǎo (大寶) reign in Liáng (梁).
Our wealth and status are extreme.
I have always feared being unable to bear the burden
and bringing shame upon my ancestors.
How could I emulate Zhào Tuó (趙佗) and declare myself king of a region?!"
Thus, he came to surrender.
Thereupon, the entire Língnán (嶺南) region was pacified.
42. In the eighth month,
on the *xīnhài* day,
the five prefectures of Míng (洺), Jīng (荊), Jiāo (交), Bìng (幷), and Yōu (幽) were established as Grand Commanderies.
Míng (洺),
read as *míbìng* (彌幷) in fanqie.
Bìng (幷),
read as *bēimíng* (卑名) in fanqie.
43. The Suí (隋) Emperor Yáng (煬帝) was reburied at Léitáng (雷塘) in Yángzhōu (揚州).
Léitáng (雷塘) was
what the Hàn (漢) dynasty called Léibēi (雷陂),
located on the Pínggāng (平岡) hill north of present-day Yángzhōu (揚州) city.
The *Kǎo Yì* (考異) states: The *Shílù* (實錄) says,
"On the *guǐsì* day of the sixth month of the second year of Wǔdé (武德),
an edict was issued to bury the Suí (隋) emperor and his descendants."
This account also states that Emperor Yáng (煬帝) was buried.
Perhaps Lǐ Zǐtōng (李子通) still occupied Jiāngdū (江都) in the third year
and, although there was such an edict,
the burial did not actually take place.
44. On the *jiǎxū* day,
the Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) raided Mínzhōu (岷州)
and defeated Grand Commander Lǐ Chángqīng (李長卿).
Tǔ (吐),
read with entering tone from *tūn* (暾).
Gǔ (谷),
rhymes with *yù* (浴).
Bài (敗),
read as *bǔmài* (補邁) in fanqie.
Cháng (長),
read as *zhīliǎng* (知兩) in fanqie.
Wèizhōu (渭州) was
the Lǒngxī (隴西) Commandery.
Qiě (且)
is a surname, read as *zǐyú* (子余) in fanqie.
45. On the *yǐmǎo* day,
the Eastern Turkic (突厥) Khagan Jiélì (頡利) raided the border.
Duàn Décāo (段德操), Left Wǔwèi (武衞) General, and Lǐ Zǐhé (李子和), Grand Commander of Yúnzhōu (雲州), were dispatched with troops to resist them.
Zǐhé’s (子和) original surname was Guō (郭).
Guō Zǐhé (郭子和) surrendered with Yúlíng (榆林) Commandery in the third year of Wǔdé (武德).
The territory of Yúlíng (榆林)
originally belonged to Yúnzhōu (雲州).
The Suí (隋) dynasty separated it and established Shèngzhōu (勝州) Yúlíng (榆林) Commandery.
When Zǐhé (子和) surrendered with Yúlíng (榆林),
he was appointed Grand Commander of Yúnzhōu (雲州).
He was granted the imperial surname.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
Jiélì (頡利) with 150,000 cavalry entered Yànmén (鴈門).
On the *jǐwèi* day,
he raided Bìngzhōu (幷州),
and separately dispatched troops to raid Yuánzhōu (原州).
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
the Crown Prince was ordered to proceed via the Yōuzhōu (幽州) route.
"Yōuzhōu (幽州)"
should be
"Bīnzhōu (豳州)."
"Qínzhōu (秦州)"
should be
"Tàizhōu (泰州)."
He was to proceed from Bīnzhōu (豳州) to resist the raiders in Yuánzhōu (原州),
and from Tàizhōu (泰州) to resist the raiders in Bìngzhōu (幷州).
Tàizhōu (泰州) at that time was governed from Lóngmén (龍門).
They were to ambush the Khagan,
at what the Hàn (漢) called the ancient city of Yúnzhōng (雲中),
forty *lǐ* northeast of Yúlíng (榆林) Commandery.
Qū (趨),
read as *qīyù* (七喻) in fanqie.
And intercept his return path.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
the Emperor addressed his officials, saying:
"The Turks (突厥) have invaded
and now again seek peace.
Which is more advantageous, peace or war?"
Zhèng Yuánshú (鄭元璹), Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, said:
"War will deepen animosity;
peace is more advantageous."
Fēng Déyí (封德彞), Chief Minister of the Central Secretariat, said:
"The Turks (突厥) rely on their multitude of 'dogs and sheep' (barbarian troops)
and have an attitude of looking down upon China.
If we make peace without fighting,
showing them weakness,
they will return next year.

At this time,
many local heroes in Shāndōng killed local officials to respond to Hēità,
with mutual suspicion between superiors and subordinates,
and people becoming increasingly estranged and resentful.
Liú'ān alone treated his officials and commoners with openness and no suspicion.
Those who came to report matters, regardless of their closeness or distance,
were all allowed to enter directly into his sleeping quarters.
He often told his officials and commoners:
"I and you all are defending the country against bandits;
we should naturally be united and work together.
If anyone is determined to abandon loyalty and follow rebellion,
just cut off my head and take it."
The officials and commoners all cautioned each other, saying:
"Duke Tián treats people with utmost sincerity;
we should collectively exert our utmost effort to repay him,
and must not let him down."
There was a man named Yuàn Zhúlín,
originally a member of Hēità's faction,
who secretly harbored dissenting intentions.
Liú'ān knew of this,
but did not expose his plot.
He brought him to his side
and entrusted him with keys and management.
Zhúlín was deeply moved,
and consequently changed his allegiance,
ultimately proving useful.
For his merits, he was promoted and enfeoffed as the Duke of Dào.

Hēità (黑闥) ran out of food,

Sòng Bái (宋白) said: "Guǎntáo (館陶),

On *rénshēn* (壬申),

The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: "According to the *Gāozǔ Shílù* (高祖實錄):
'On *rénshēn* (壬申),
