On *jiǎxū* (甲戌),
Tà (闥) was pursued to Máozhōu (毛州).
The bandits arrayed their forces with their backs to the Yǒngjì Qú (永濟渠).
They engaged in battle,
and he was again defeated.'
The *Jiù Chuán* (舊傳) states:
'In the second month of the sixth year,
the Crown Prince defeated Hēità (黑闥) at Guǎntáo (館陶).'
The *Gémìng Jì* (革命記) states:
'Tà (闥) fled to Guǎntáo (館陶).
On the twenty-fifth day,
the imperial army arrived,
and Tà (闥) was defeated and fled.'
We hold that Guǎntáo (館陶) is Máozhōu (毛州).
According to the *Chánglì* (長曆),
*rénshēn* (壬申) in the twelfth month
is the twenty-fifth day.
*Jiǎxū* (甲戌)
is the twenty-seventh day.
Presumably, the *Shílù* (實錄) recorded the date of the report's arrival.
The *Jiù Chuán* (舊傳) is particularly sparse.
We now follow the *Gémìng Jì* (革命記)."
The *Tàizōng Shílù* (太宗實錄) states:
"When Hēità (黑闥) rebelled again,
Gāozǔ (高祖) said to Tàizōng (太宗): 'When Hēità (黑闥) was defeated before,
I wanted to have all his followers killed,
to make Shāndōng (山東) empty.
You did not heed my words,
which led to today's situation.'
When the Hidden Crown Prince went to conquer Tà (闥)
and pacified him,
he was about to send Táng Jiǎn (唐儉)
to have all men aged fifteen and above buried alive,
and the young, weak, and women were to be driven into the passes
to populate the capital region.
Tàizōng (太宗) admonished him, saying: 'Your subject has heard that only virtue moves Heaven,
and only benevolence accommodates the masses.
Shāndōng (山東) is a region of talented people,
and Héběi (河北) is a land of silk and cotton,
providing tribute to the imperial treasury,
and relied upon for its produce.
Now, if we see them repeatedly rebel and suddenly slaughter all the innocent,
and scatter the weak and vulnerable,
I fear that killing will not stop the unrest;
this is not the way of a punitive expedition to bring comfort.'
The matter was then dropped."
The *Xīnshū Yǐn Tàizǐ Chuán* (新書隱太子傳) states:
"When Hēità (黑闥) was defeated at Míngshuǐ (洺水),
Crown Prince Jiànchéng (建成) asked the attendant Wèi Zhēng (魏徵): 'Will Shāndōng (山東) be pacified now?'
He replied: 'Although Hēità (黑闥) is defeated,
the casualties are too severe.
His principal followers are all marked for execution,
and their wives and children are enslaved.
There is no way for them to surrender.
Although there is an amnesty,
those captured will certainly be executed.
If there is no great pardon and amnesty,
I fear that the remaining bandits will gather and incite,
and the people will not be able to live in peace.'
Soon after, Hēità (黑闥) revived,
Lújiāng Wáng (廬江王) Yuàn (瑗) abandoned Míngzhōu (洺州),
and Shāndōng (山東) fell into chaos.
Qí Wáng (齊王) Yuánjí (元吉) was ordered to quell it.
An imperial edict pardoned those who surrendered,
but the masses did not believe it.
When Jiànchéng (建成) arrived,
he released the captives,
comforting and dismissing them,
and the common people were joyful.
The bandits were afraid
and fled by night.
The troops pursued and fought,
but Hēità (黑闥)'s forces were still strong.
So, he released the prisoners and had them tell each other: 'Take off your armor and return to your hometowns.
If your wives and children were captured,
they have already been released.'
The masses then dispersed,
some even binding their leaders and surrendering,
and thus Hēità (黑闥) was captured."
We observe that although Gāozǔ (高祖) was not benevolent,
he would not have
the idea of "emptying Shāndōng (山東)."
The historians solely wished to attribute merit to Tàizōng (太宗),
and in doing so, they greatly maligned Gāozǔ (高祖).
We now adopt [accounts from] the *Gémìng Jì* (革命記) and the *Xīnshū* (新書).
The grand army crossed the bridge to pursue Hēità (黑闥),

Shàn'ān (Shàn'ān) sent several assassins who pretended to be on a fishing boat.
Those who saw them did not suspect anything,
so they killed Fǎmíng (Fǎmíng) and left.
59 On the day Jiǎshēn,
Shūzhōu Zǒngguǎn Zhāng Zhènzhōu (Zhāng Zhènzhōu) and others attacked Chén Dāngshì (Chén Dāngshì), a general of Fǔ Gōngshí (Fǔ Gōngshí), at Huángshā in Yóuzhōu,
and routed them.
In the 3rd year of Wǔdé, Nánxúzhōu was established from Jīngxiàn of Xuānzhōu,
and soon after renamed Yóuzhōu.
60 On the day Dīnghài,
the Emperor hunted in Huáyīn.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
he welcomed and honored Qín Wáng Shìmín (Qín Wáng Shìmín) at Zhōngwǔ Dùn.
Qín Wáng (Qín Wáng) returned from Bìngzhōu.
Láo (勞),
pronounced "lì dào".
In the 60th year, twelfth month,
on the *Guǐmǎo* day,
the Pacification Commissioner, Lǐ Dàliàng, lured Zhāng Shàn'ān,
and captured him.
Lǐ Dàliàng attacked Zhāng Shàn'ān in Hóngzhōu.
They lined up across a river from each other,
and spoke to each other from a distance.
Lǐ Dàliàng explained to him the consequences of fortune and misfortune.
Zhāng Shàn'ān said:
"I, Shàn'ān, initially had no rebellious intentions.
I was simply misled by my generals and soldiers.
I wish to surrender, but I fear I will not be spared."
Lǐ Dàliàng said:
"If Commander-in-chief Zhāng has a mind to surrender,
then you and I are one family."
Thereupon, he crossed the water alone on horseback into Zhāng Shàn'ān's formation,
shook hands with Zhāng Shàn'ān and spoke with him,
showing no suspicion.
Zhāng Shàn'ān was greatly pleased,
and then promised to surrender.
Soon after, Zhāng Shàn'ān, with several dozen horsemen, went to Lǐ Dàliàng's camp.
Lǐ Dàliàng stopped his horsemen outside the gate,
and led Zhāng Shàn'ān inside
to speak.
After a long while,
Zhāng Shàn'ān took his leave.
Lǐ Dàliàng ordered his warriors to seize him.
All of Zhāng Shàn'ān's horsemen fled.
When those in Zhāng Shàn'ān's camp heard of it,
they were greatly enraged,
and came with all their forces,
intending to attack Lǐ Dàliàng.
Lǐ Dàliàng sent someone to convey to them, saying:
"I am not detaining Commander-in-chief.
The Commander-in-chief, with a loyal heart, returned to the nation,
and told me: 'If I return to the camp,
I fear my generals and soldiers might have disagreements
and I might be controlled by them.'
Therefore, he voluntarily stayed and did not leave.
Why are you angry with me?"
His followers then cursed loudly again, saying:
"Commander-in-chief Zhāng sold us out to ingratiate himself with others."
Thereupon, they all dispersed.
Lǐ Dàliàng pursued and attacked,
capturing many.
He sent Zhāng Shàn'ān to Cháng'ān.
Zhāng Shàn'ān claimed he had not been in communication with Fǔ Gōngshí.
The emperor pardoned his crime
and treated him well.
When Fǔ Gōngshí was defeated,
letters of correspondence with Zhāng Shàn'ān were discovered,
whereupon Zhāng Shàn'ān was killed.
In the 61st year, on the *Jiǎyín* day,
the imperial carriage arrived at Cháng'ān.
In the 62nd year, on the *Jǐsì* day,
the Tujue attacked Dìngzhōu.
The provincial troops attacked and repelled them.
In the 63rd year, on the *Gēngshēn* day,
the Báijiǎn and Báigǒu Qiāng both sent envoys to offer tribute.
"Báijiǎn"
should perhaps be
"Báilán."
The "Suí Shū" (History of the Suí Dynasty) 'Attached States' section mentions tribes such as Báilán and Báigǒu,
whose customs are roughly similar to the Dǎngxiàng.
They were sometimes subjugated by the Tǔyùhún
or attached to other affiliated states.
The "Xīn Shū" (New History) states: The Báilán Qiāng,
whom the Tǔbō called Dīnglíng,
bordered the Dǎngxiàng to their west
and Dūomí to their east.
They had ten thousand skilled warriors,
were brave in battle,
and skilled at making weapons.
In the 6th year of Wǔdé,
their envoys came to court.
The following year, their territory was established as Wéi and Gōng prefectures.
The Báigǒu Qiāng bordered Dōnghuìzhōu
and had only about a thousand skilled warriors.
pronounced *shū lì*.
1 Spring,
first month.
Following the old system of Zhōu and Qí,
one Grand Impartial Judge was appointed in each prefecture.
A Grand Impartial Judge was set up in each prefecture,
following the system of Wèi and Jìn adopted by Zhōu and Qí.
They assessed social standing and ranks,
with the most eminent person from the prefecture's prominent families appointed to the position,
without specific rank or salary.
2 On the *Rénwǔ* day,
Zhào Jùnwáng Xiàogōng attacked a detached general of Fǔ Gōngshí in Cōngyáng
and defeated him.
Cōngyáng County: In the Hàn dynasty, it belonged to Lújiāng Commandery.
The Liáng dynasty established Cōngyáng Commandery.
The Suí dynasty abolished the commandery and renamed it Tóng'ān County,
belonging to Lúzhōu.
pronounced *shí*.
"將" (*jiàng*),
pronounced *jí liàng*.
"樅" (*cōng*),
pronounced *qī róng*.
3 On the *Gēngyín* day,
Dèng Tóngyǐng, a man from Zōuzhōu, killed Governor Lǐ Shìhéng and rebelled.
In the early Táng dynasty, Zōuzhōu was established using Zōupíng and Chángshān counties of Qízhōu.
4 On the *Bǐngshēn* day,
Wéi and Gōng prefectures were established on the territory of the Báigǒu and other Qiāng tribes.
Wéizhōu,
Wéichuān Commandery,
was established for the surrendered Báigǒu Qiāng households
at the old city of Jiāng Wéi.
Its territory was the Rǎnmáng land beyond the frontiers of Shǔ Commandery in the Hàn dynasty.
The Shǔ generals Jiāng Wéi and Mǎ Zhōng campaigned against the Wénshān Qiāng here,
and their old forts remained.
Gōngzhōu
was Xīgōngzhōu,
later renamed Zuòzhōu.
Also, among the Jīmí prefectures administered by Róngzhōu Dūdū Fǔ, there was Qūzhōu,
originally Suí's Gōngzhōu.
It was abolished during the Suí unrest,
and re-established in the 1st year of Wǔdé upon the opening of Nánzhōng.
In the 8th year, it was renamed Qūzhōu,
located in the former Zhūtí Commandery,
which is not this one.
Líu Xù said: Wéizhōu
is the land of the ancient Xīróng.
Its southern border reaches Jiāngyáng,
the Mínshān mountains stretch endlessly to the west,
its extent unknown.
To the north, one sees Lǒngshān,
with accumulated snow like jade.
To the east, one sees Chéngdū
as if at the bottom of a well.
Its land borders Shíniǔshān,
where Yǔ the Great of Xià was born.
Its city is on an isolated peak of the Mínshān mountains,
facing the river on three sides,
about four hundred *lǐ* from Chéngdū.
Dù Yòu said: Wéizhōu is two hundred sixty *lǐ* north of the current prefecture.
5 Second month.
Fǔ Gōngshí sent troops to besiege Yóuzhōu.
Governor Zuǒ Nándāng fortified the city and defended himself.
Sòng Bái said: Jīng County of Xuānzhōu;
in the 2nd year of Táng Wǔdé, Nánxúzhōu was established here.
In the same year, it was renamed Yóuzhōu.
They broke it.
Zhào Jùnwáng Xiàogōng attacked Fǔ Gōngshí's Quètou Garrison
and captured it.
The "Xīn Zhì" (New Records) states: Quètou Garrison is in Nánlíng County of Xuānzhōu.
6 On the *Dīngwèi* day,
King Jiànwǔ of Gāolì sent an envoy to request the imperial calendar.
An envoy was sent to enfeoff Jiànwǔ as King of Liáodōng Commandery and King of Gāolì;
King Fúyú Zhāng of Báijì as King of Dàifāng Commandery;
and King Jīn Zhēnpíng of Xīnluó as King of Lèlàng Commandery.
7 The Láo of Shǐzhōu rebelled.
Shǐzhōu,
Pǔ'ān Commandery,
later renamed Jiànzhōu.
"獠" (*liáo*),
pronounced *lǔ hào*.
8 On the *Jǐyǒu* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"In all prefectures, those who have mastered one classic or more and are not yet appointed to office
shall all be reported by name;
schools shall be established in prefectures, counties, and townships alike."
9 On the *Rénzǐ* day,
the Deputy Commander-in-chief of the Expeditionary Army, Quán Wéndàn, defeated Fǔ Gōngshí's faction in Yóuzhōu
and captured their four garrisons, including Méihuí.
10 On the *Dīngsì* day,
the emperor visited the Guózǐjiān (Imperial Academy),
held a ceremony to honor Confucius;
and issued an edict for all imperial princes and sons of nobles to attend school.
11 On the *Wùwǔ* day,
the Grand Commander-in-chief was renamed Grand Military Governor's Office (Dà Dūdū Fǔ).
On the 12th day of the Jǐwèi month,
Gāo Kāidào’s general, Zhāng Jīnshù, killed Kāidào and surrendered.
Kāidào saw that all under Heaven was settled
and wished to surrender,
but, having repeatedly gone back on his word, he dared not.
Gāo Kāidào had previously surrendered and then rebelled again,
knowing he had the fault of being fickle.
*Shù*,
pronounced like *jué*.
Thus, he had no intention of surrendering.
His generals and soldiers were all people from Shāndōng;
missing their homeland,
they all had thoughts of defection.
Kāidào selected several hundred brave warriors,
called them "adopted sons" (*jiǎzǐ*),
and kept them constantly within his chambers,
making Jīnshù their leader.
Hence, Liú Hēità’s former general, Zhāng Jūnlì, who had sought refuge with Kāidào,
secretly plotted with Jīnshù to take Kāidào.
Jīnshù sent several of his partisans into the chambers,
to play games with the *jiǎzǐ*.
Towards evening,
they secretly cut their bowstrings,
hid swords and spears under the beds.
To "close the eyes" (瞑) means
to embrace (one's sleep) and hurry out.
When one sleeps, one's eyes close and one is "closed-eyed" (瞑).
*Suò*,
pronounced like *sè-jué*.
*Míng*,
pronounced like *mò-dìng*.
When they attacked Kāidào’s chambers,
the *jiǎzǐ* were about to resist,
but their bowstrings were all cut,
and their swords and spears were already gone;
they scrambled out to surrender.
Jūnlì also lit fires outside to signal in response,
causing panic and confusion inside and out.
Kāidào knew he could not escape,
so he donned his armor, took his weapons, and sat in the hall,
drinking heavily with his wives and concubines while listening to music.
The crowd, awed by his bravery,
dared not approach.
As dawn approached,
Kāidào hanged himself,
and his wives, concubines, and all his sons then committed suicide.
Jīnshù arrayed his troops,
rounded up all the *jiǎzǐ* and beheaded them,
and also killed Jūnlì;
the dead numbered over five hundred.
He sent an envoy to surrender,
and an imperial edict established Guīzhōu in his territory.
Guīzhōu was named after the Guīshuǐ River.
*Guī*,
pronounced like *jù-wéi*.
On the Rénxū day,
Jīnshù was appointed Grand Administrator of Běiyànzhōu.
Guīzhōu was Guīchuān Commandery,
with its seat at Huáiróng County.
The Northern Qí established Běiyànzhōu,
originally administered from Huáiróng.
The Táng had already established Guīzhōu in the territory of Huáiróng,
and further honored Jīnshù with the title of Grand Administrator of Běiyànzhōu.
*Yàn*,
pronounced like *yīn-jiān*.
On the 13th day of the Wùchén month,
the Líao of Yángzhōu and Jízhōu rebelled,
capturing Jìnchéng in Lóngzhōu.
Yángzhōu was Yángchuān Commandery,
with its seat at Xīxiāng County.
Xīxiāng was Hán Chénggù County.
The Shǔ established Xīxiāng County.
Later, the Northern Wèi established Yángzhōu there,
naming it after the river.
*Yáng*,
pronounced *xiáng*.
Jízhōu was Fúyáng Commandery.
In the first year of Wǔdé,
it was established by separating Nánjiāng from Liángzhōu, and Fúyáng, Chángchí, and Báishí from Bāzhōu.
Lóngzhōu was Bāxī Commandery,
the land of Hán Lángzhōng.
Liú Xù said: The Western Wèi established Lóngzhōu at Lángzhōng.
The Suí made it Bāxī Commandery.
The Táng restored it to Lóngzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: It was named for its high and undulating terrain.
The *Diǎnlǜe* of the Later Wèi states: This prefecture historically had the strong and perilous Lóngchéng,
and so Lóngzhōu was established.
Jìnchéng County was also Lángzhōng territory.
The Liáng established Mùlán Commandery.
The Western Wèi abolished the commandery,
renaming Xīchōngguó to Jìnchéng.
*Láo*,
pronounced *lǔ-hào*.
In this month,
Dù Fúwēi, the Grand Tutor and Prince of Wú, passed away.
When Fú Gōngshí rebelled,
he falsely claimed Fúwēi’s command to deceive his followers.
When Gōngshí was pacified,
Zhàoqún Wáng Xiàogōng, unaware of the deception,

An imperial edict ordered the posthumous removal of Fúwēi’s name
and the confiscation of his wives and children.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
knowing he had been wronged,
he pardoned him
and restored his official rank and title.
In the third month of the 15th year,
the regulations were initially established.
The Tàiwèi, Sītú, and Sīkōng were designated as the Sāngōng.
Next were the six provinces: Shàngshū, Ménxià, Zhōngshū, Mìshū, Diànzhōng, and Nèishì.
Next was the Yùshǐtái.
Next were the nine courts, from Tàicháng to Tàifǔ:
Tàicháng, Guānglù, Wèiwèi, Zōngzhèng, Tàipú, Dàlǐ, Hónglú, Sīnóng, and Tàifǔ.
In total, there were nine courts.
Next was the Guózǐxué.
Next was the Tiāncè Shàngjiàngfǔ.
Next were the fourteen guards, from Zuǒ-Yòu Wèi to Zuǒ-Yòu Lǐngwèi.
The twelve guards, along with the Zuǒ-Yòu Jiānménwèi, made up the fourteen guards.

A princely residence (Wángfǔ) had a Fù, Zīyì Cānjūn, Yǒu, Wénxué, Dōng-Xī Gé Jìjiǔ, Chángshǐ, Sīmǎ, Yuàn, Shǔ, Zhǔbù, Shǐ, Jìshì, Lùshì Cānjūn, Lùshì, seven Cáo Cānjūn (Gōng, Cāng, Hù, Bīng, Qí, Fǎ, Shì), Cānjūnshì, Xíngcānjūn, and Diǎnqiān.
A kingdom (Wángguó) had a Guólìng, Dànóngwèi-Chéng, Lùshì, Diǎnwèi, Shèrén, Xuéguānzhǎng, Shíguānzhǎng, Mùzhǎng, and Diǎnfǔzhǎng.

20 In the early stages, the Fútián Rent and Corvée Law was established:
For adult males (dīng) and middle-aged men (zhōng zhī mín),

Widows and concubines had theirs reduced by seven-tenths.
In all cases, two-tenths were designated as hereditary land (shìyè),
and eight-tenths as personal allocation (kǒufēn).
Each dīng annually paid rent
of two shí of grain.

They were liable for twenty days of corvée labor annually.

and I fear many will respond to him.
You should go yourself,
and when you return,
I will establish you as Crown Prince.
I cannot emulate Suí Wéndì and personally execute my son.
I will enfeoff Jiànchéng as King of Shǔ.
Shǔ's forces are weak.
In the future, if he can serve you,
you should spare him;
if he cannot serve you,
it will be easy for you to take him!"
The Emperor, considering Rénzhìgōng 仁智宮 to be in the mountains,
feared a sudden attack by bandits.
At night,
he led his guards out of the mountains to the south,
traveling several tens of *lǐ*.
Officials and subordinates of the Eastern Palace
followed.
He ordered them all to form teams of thirty men
and divided the troops to surround and guard them.
The next day,
he returned to Rénzhìgōng 仁智宮.
The Kǎoyì 考異 says: The Shílù 實錄 states:
"When Gāozǔ 高祖 left the mountains,
Jiànchéng 建成 was distressed and angry,
lying beneath his tent.
Dù Yān 杜淹, a staff officer of the Tiāncè 天策, requested to use the chaos to attack him.
Jiànchéng's 建成's entourage also made this request,
but the present Emperor rejected them all and did not accept."
The Tángtǒngjì 唐統紀 says:
"When Tàizōng 太宗 came out from within,
he passed by Jiànchéng's 建成's tent at night.
He estimated that Jiànchéng's 建成's guards and attendants numbered only ten men.
They all came and knelt, holding Tàizōng's 太宗's feet,
saying: 'The matter today
awaits the King's command.
If you wish to eliminate him,
now is the time.'
Tàizōng 太宗 rebuked them and stopped them.
Afterwards, he returned and spoke of the matter to his palace officials.
All the civil and military officials advanced and said: 'Wéngàn 文幹 plotted treason as the Heir Apparent,
which is known throughout the world.
To use palace officials to achieve this
perfectly accords with Heaven's will.'
Tàizōng 太宗 said: 'I have just received the benevolent command.
How can I immediately turn back on it?
If there is any transgression,
you speak to him;
surely, there is no such reason.'
The palace officials again requested,
but he ultimately refused and did not listen."
According to this, at that time, Gāozǔ 高祖 had no intention of executing Jiànchéng 建成,
so how would his attendants dare to kill him without authorization?
This account is not adopted now.
After Shìmín 世民 departed,
Yuánjí 元吉 and his concubines repeatedly interceded for Jiànchéng 建成.
Fēng Déyí 封德彞 again made efforts to resolve the situation from outside.
The Emperor's intention thereupon changed,
and he again sent Jiànchéng 建成 back to the capital to take up his post.
He only reproached him for the discord among brothers,
placing the blame on Prince Royal's Middle Assistant Wáng Guī 王珪 and Left Guard General Wéi Tǐng 韋挺.
The Left and Right Guard Generals were in charge of the political decrees concerning the Eastern Palace's feather guard troops and weapons,
a position of the senior fourth rank.
*Shuài* 率,
read as *suǒ lǜ* 所律.
Both were exiled to Cuīzhōu 巂州.
Tǐng 挺 was
Chōng's 沖's son.
Wéi Chōng 韋沖 served Suí Wéndì 隋文帝,
pacified rebellious Hú 胡,
went to the campaign at Chángchéng 長城,
and also achieved merit in the south.
After Luòyáng 洛陽 was pacified,
Dù Yān 杜淹 had been unable to secure an appointment for a long time,
and wished to serve Jiànchéng 建成.
Fáng Xuánlíng 房玄齡, fearing Yān's 淹's many cunning schemes
and that he might teach and guide Jiànchéng 建成,
thereby becoming more detrimental to Shìmín 世民,
therefore spoke to Shìmín 世民,
and introduced him into the Tiāncèfǔ 天策府.
5 The Tūjué 突厥 raided Wǔzhōuchéng 武周城 in Dàizhōu 代州.
Wǔzhōuxiàn 武周縣,
during the Hàn 漢, belonged to Yànménjùn 雁門郡.
It was abolished during the Wèi 魏 and Jìn 晉.
Later Wèi 后魏, it belonged to Dàijùn 代郡.
Suí 隋 abolished it and incorporated it into Yúnnèixiàn 雲內縣 of Shuòzhōu 朔州.
Dù Yòu 杜佑 said: The administrative seat of Shuòzhōu 朔州 Mǎyìjùn 馬邑郡 was Shànyángxiàn 善陽縣,
which had the Qín 秦 Mǎyìchéng 馬邑城 and Wǔzhōusài 武周塞.
*Jué* 厥,
read as *jiǔ wù* 九勿.
6 Autumn,
seventh month,
on the *jǐsì* 己巳 day,
Yuàn Jūnzhāng 苑君璋, with the Tūjué 突厥, raided Shuòzhōu 朔州.
Commander Qín Wǔtōng 秦武通 attacked and repelled them.
7 Yáng Wéngàn 楊文幹 attacked and captured Níngzhōu 寧州.
Sòng Bái 宋白 said: Níngzhōu 寧州 takes its name from "peace and tranquility."
The Jiǔyùzhì 九域志 says: "North to Qìngzhōu 慶州 is one hundred twenty *lǐ*."
Bǎijiābǎo 百家堡 is in Mǎlíngxiàn 馬嶺縣 of Qìngzhōu 慶州.
All his followers dispersed.
On the *guǐyǒu* 癸酉 day,
Wéngàn 文幹 was killed by his own subordinate
and his head was sent to the capital.
Yǔwén Yǐng 宇文穎 was captured
and executed.
8 On the *dīngchǒu* 丁丑 day,
Liáng Shīduō's 梁師都's provisional administration officer Bái Fúyuàn 白伏願 surrendered.
9 On the *wùyín* 戊寅 day,
the Tūjué 突厥 raided Yuánzhōu 原州.
Níngzhōu 寧州 Governor Lù Dàshī 鹿大師 was dispatched to rescue it.
Yáng Shīdào 楊師道 was also dispatched to advance towards Dàmùgēnshān 大木根山.
On the *gēngchén* 庚辰 day,
the Tūjué 突厥 raided Lǒngzhōu 隴州.
Protector-General Yùchí Jìngdé 尉遲敬德 was dispatched to attack them.
10 The Tǔyùhún 吐谷渾 raided Mínzhōu 岷州.
On the *xīnsì* 辛巳 day,
the Tǔyùhún 吐谷渾 and Dǎngxiàng 党項 raided Sōngzhōu 松州.
*Tǔ* 吐,
from *tūn* 暾 in entering tone.
*Gǔ* 谷,
pronounced *yù* 浴.
11 On the *guǐwèi* 癸未 day,
the Tūjué 突厥 raided Yīnpán 陰盤.
Yīnpánxiàn 陰盤縣,
during the Hàn 漢, belonged to Āndìng 安定.
During the Jìn 晉, it belonged to Jīngzhào 京兆.
Later Wèi 后魏 established Píngliángjùn 平涼郡.
During the Suí 隋 and Táng 唐, it belonged to Jīngzhōu 涇州.
After the Táng 唐, Yīnpán 陰盤 was renamed Pānyuán 潘原.
12 On the *jiǎshēn* 甲申 day,
Fúzhōu 扶州 Governor Jiǎng Shànhé 蔣善合 attacked the Tǔyùhún 吐谷渾 at Chìmózhèn 赤磨鎮 in Sōngzhōu 松州,
defeating them.
13 On the *jǐchǒu* 己丑 day,
Tūlìshè 吐利設 of the Tūjué 突厥 and Yuàn Jūnzhāng 苑君璋 raided Bìngzhōu 幷州.
14 On the *jiǎzǐ* 甲子 day,
the imperial carriage returned to the capital.
15 Someone advised the Emperor, saying:
"The reason the Tūjué 突厥 repeatedly raid Guānzhōng 關中
is because daughters, jade, and silks are all in Cháng'ān 長安.
If Cháng'ān 長安 were burned and no longer served as the capital,
then the Hú 胡 raiders would cease naturally."
The Emperor considered this to be true,
and dispatched Palace Secretary Yǔwén Shìjí 宇文士及 to cross Nánshān 南山 to Fán 樊 and Dèng 鄧,
to survey habitable lands.
Crossing Cháng'ān 長安 Nánshān 南山 and emerging in Shāngzhōu 商州
leads directly to Fán 樊 and Dèng 鄧.
*Xíng* 行,
read as *xià mèng* 下孟.
Heir Apparent Jiànchéng 建成, Qíwáng Yuánjí 齊王元吉, and Péi Jì 裴寂 all approved of this plan.
Xiāo Yǔ 蕭瑀 and others, though knowing it was unfeasible, dared not remonstrate.
Qínwáng Shìmín 秦王世民 remonstrated, saying:
"The incursions of the Róngdí 戎狄
have existed since ancient times.
Your Majesty, through your sacred martial prowess, rose to power
and brightly occupied the Central Plain.
With a million elite troops,
your conquests are unrivaled.
How can you, due to Hú 胡 raiders disturbing the border,
hastily move the capital to avoid them,
bringing shame upon the four seas
and becoming a laughingstock for a hundred generations!
Huò Qùbìng 霍去病, a mere general of the Hàn 漢 court,
still aspired to annihilate the Xiōngnú 匈奴.
Moreover, I, your servant, am humbly entrusted with the defense of the realm.
I beg for a few years' time,
and I request to bind Xiélì's 頡利's neck
and present him at the palace gates.
If this does not succeed,
then moving the capital will not be too late."
The Emperor said:
"Good."
Jiànchéng 建成 said:
"In the past, Fán Kuài 樊噲 wanted to lead one hundred thousand men to sweep through the Xiōngnú 匈奴.
This incident is recorded in Volume 12, Third Year of Hàn Huìdì 漢惠帝."
Shìmín 世民 said:
"Circumstances differ,
and military tactics vary.
Fán Kuài 樊噲 was a mere young upstart;
what is he worth mentioning!
Within ten years,
Mòběi 漠北 will certainly be pacified.
This is no
empty boast!"
This laid the groundwork for Tàizōng's 太宗's destruction of the Tūjué 突厥.
Jiànchéng 建成 and his concubines then jointly slandered Shìmín 世民, saying:
"Although the Tūjué 突厥 have repeatedly caused border troubles,
they retreat once bribed.
Qínwáng 秦王 outwardly uses the pretense of repelling invaders,
but inwardly seeks to command all military authority
to achieve his plot of usurpation!"
The Emperor was hunting south of the capital,
and the Crown Prince, Qín Wáng, and Qí Wáng all accompanied him.
The Emperor ordered his three sons to race and shoot to determine a winner.
Lǐ Jiànchéng had a Hú horse,
which was strong and fat but prone to stumble.
He gave it to Lǐ Shìmín, saying,
"This horse is very swift.
It can clear a ravine several *zhàng* wide.
You are a good rider,
try riding it."
Lǐ Shìmín rode it to chase deer.
The horse stumbled,
and Lǐ Shìmín leaped and stood a few steps away.
The horse rose,
and he rode it again.
This happened three times.
He looked at Yǔwén Shìjí and said,
"He intends to kill me with this.
Life and death are fated;
what harm can it do?"
Lǐ Jiànchéng heard of this,
and then ordered a concubine to slander Lǐ Shìmín to the Emperor,
saying,
"Qín Wáng himself said,
'I have the mandate of Heaven,
and am destined to be the lord of the world;
how could I die a wasteful death!'"
The Emperor was greatly enraged.
He first summoned Lǐ Jiànchéng and Lǐ Yuánjí,
then summoned Lǐ Shìmín to enter.
He rebuked him, saying,
"The Son of Heaven has his own mandate of Heaven,
which cannot be sought through wisdom or strength.
Why are you so eager to seek it?"
Lǐ Shìmín removed his cap, kowtowed,
and requested to be handed over to the judicial authorities for investigation.
The Emperor's anger did not subside.
It so happened that an official reported a Tújué invasion.
The Emperor then changed his expression, comforted and encouraged Lǐ Shìmín,
ordered him to don his cap and belt,
and consulted with him about the Tújué.
In the intercalary month,
on the day *jǐ wèi*,
an edict ordered Lǐ Shìmín and Lǐ Yuánjí to lead troops out of Bīnzhōu to resist the Tújué.
The Emperor saw them off at Lánchí.
Lánchí
was the place where Qín Shǐhuáng encountered robbers.
The *Shǐjì* commentary says: According to the *Dìlǐ Zhì*,
there was Lánchí Gōng in Wèichéng Xiàn.
The *Zhèngyì* says: According to the *Kuòdì Zhì*,
Lánchí Pō is the ancient Lánchí,
located within Xiányáng Xiàn.
The *Qínjì* says: Shǐhuáng diverted the Wèi River to form a pond,
built islands like Péngyíng,
and carved a stone whale,
two hundred *zhàng* long;
it was the place where he encountered robbers.
He immediately ordered Lǐ Shìmín to suppress them.
After the matter was settled,
the suspicion and animosity intensified.
In the beginning,
at the end of the Suí dynasty, Wéi Rénshòu of Jīngzhào was the Judicial Clerk of Shǔjùn.
According to the *New Book of Official Ranks*: The Judicial Staff Officer of the Law Bureau in various prefectures
was in charge of trying cases and applying the law,
supervising bandits,
and managing the confiscation of stolen goods and bribes.
There was also a Staff Officer (*cānjūnshì*),
and a note says: In the early Wǔdé period, the traveling clerk (*xíngshūzuǒ*) was renamed traveling staff officer (*xíngcānjūn*),
and soon after changed to Staff Officer (*cānjūnshì*).
Thus, the clerk (*shūzuǒ*) was the same as the staff officer (*cānjūn*) position.
Wéi Rénshòu still faced west to pay homage to the Buddha before dying.
History records that Wéi Rénshòu's judgment in punishments
made people feel they were not wronged.
is pronounced *yúwěi*.
Cuàn Hóngdá led the southwest Yi to submit.
The court sent envoys to pacify them,
but they were generally greedy and tyrannical,
which troubled the distant people,
and some rebelled.
At that time, Rénshòu was the Chief Clerk (*zhǎngshǐ*) of Cuīzhōu Military Governor (*dūdū*).
The Emperor heard of his reputation
and ordered him to inspect and administer Nánníngzhōu Military Governorship (*dūdū*),
with his office temporarily in Yuècuī.
Cuīzhōu
was Yuècuī Jùn.
'Cuī' (*巂*)
is pronounced *suǐ*.
'Zhǎng' (*長*),
is pronounced *zhīliǎng*.
Rénshòu's nature was broad and generous,
with discernment and magnanimity.
Having received the order,
he led five hundred soldiers to Xīěrhé.
He traveled thousands of *lǐ* around,
and the chieftain leaders of the Mán and Yí all submitted upon hearing of him,
coming to see Rénshòu.
Rénshòu, by imperial authority, established seven prefectures and fifteen counties,
appointing their chieftain leaders as prefects and county magistrates.
According to the *Old Book of Geographical Records*,
in that year Xīníng, Yù, Xīpíng, Lì, Nányún, Mó, and Nánníng seven prefectures were established.
The *Zhì* also mentions Xīpíngzhōu,
also established in that year.
'Shuài' (*帥*),
is pronounced *suǒlèi*.
The Mán and Yí were pleased and submitted.
When he was about to return,
all the chieftain leaders said,
"The Emperor sent you, Duke, to be the Military Governor of Nánníng;
why are you leaving so soon?"
Rénshòu used the excuse that cities and fortifications had not yet been built.
The Mán and Yí then led each other to build a city for Rénshòu,
and erected official residences.
It was completed in ten days.
Rénshòu then said,
"I received an edict only to patrol and pacify;
I dare not stay."
The Mán and Yí cried and saw him off,
and then each sent their sons and younger brothers to pay tribute.
On the day *rén xū*,
Rénshòu returned to court.
The Emperor was greatly pleased
and ordered Rénshòu to move his garrison to Nánníng,
and station troops there.
Yuàn Jūnzhāng led the Tújué to invade Shuòzhōu.
In the eighth month,
on the day *wù chén*,
the Tújué invaded Yuánzhōu.
On the day *jǐ sì*,
the Tǔyùhún invaded Shànzhōu.
Shànzhōu was Xīpíng Jùn,
the capital of the Tǔfà clan.
'Shàn' (*鄯*),
is pronounced *shízhàn*.
On the day *rén shēn*,
the Tújué invaded Xīnzhōu.
On the day *bǐng zǐ*,
they invaded Bìngzhōu;
the capital was put on high alert.
On the day *wù yín*,
they invaded Suīzhōu.
Suīzhōu
was Diāoyīn Jùn.
Diāoyīn was an ancient county,
belonging to Shàngjùn in the Hàn dynasty.
It is now the Hengshān area north of Yánzhōu.
Sūn Mǐn says: Suīzhōu
was inhabited by the Bái Dí during the Spring and Autumn period,
was Shàngjùn in Qín,
the Later Wèi established Shàngzhōu,
and then changed it to Suīzhōu,
named after Suīdé Xiàn.
At this time,
the two Qaghans, Jiélì and Tūlì, led their entire nations in an invasion.
Their camps stretched continuously as they advanced south.
Qínwáng Shìmín led troops to resist them.
It happened that Guānzhōng had suffered prolonged rain,
making grain transport impossible,
the soldiers were exhausted from campaigns,
and their weapons and equipment were worn out and dilapidated.
The imperial court and the army were all worried.
Shìmín encountered the barbarians in Bīnzhōu.
He marshalled his troops, ready to fight.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
the Qaghan led over ten thousand cavalry and suddenly arrived west of the city.
They arrayed themselves on Wǔlǒngbǎn,
striking fear into the officers and soldiers.
Shìmín said to Yuánjí:
"Now the barbarian cavalry are acting aggressively;
we cannot show them weakness.
We must fight them.
Can you come with me?"
Yuánjí said fearfully:
"The barbarians' posture is like this,
how can we lightly sally forth?
If by any chance we suffer a defeat,
will regret be able to avert it?"
Shìmín said:
"If you dare not go out,
I will go alone.
You stay here and watch."
Shìmín went out alone to display his might to the Tūjué
and to internally subdue Yuánjí's heart.
He declared:
"Our state and the Qaghan have made peace and are kin.
Why do you break the agreement
and deeply invade our territory?
I am Qínwáng.
If the Qaghan can fight,
come out alone and fight me;
if you come with a multitude,
I will confront you directly with these hundred horsemen."
Jiélì could not gauge him,
so he smiled and did not respond.
Jiélì had long respected Qínwáng's divine martial prowess,
fearing that he challenged with a hundred horsemen
but had a large army ambushed, ready to encircle and attack him.
Therefore, he dared not respond.
He sent a rider to tell Tūlì:
"You made an alliance with me before,
promising mutual aid in emergencies.
Now you lead troops to attack me.
Why is there no 'incense and fire' sentiment?"
In ancient times, oaths were sworn to Heaven, Earth, mountains, rivers, ghosts, and spirits,
merely by smearing blood;
in later generations, some swore oaths before spirits,
and some swore oaths before Buddhas,
which is when the matter of "incense and fire" began.
Qínwáng used this to sow doubt in Jiélì's heart.
Tūlì feared that he would be suspected by Jiélì because of this,
so he also dared not respond.
As they were about to cross the ditch,
Jiélì saw Shìmín lightly sally forth,
and also heard the words about "incense and fire,"
suspecting Tūlì and Shìmín had a plot.
So he sent someone to stop Shìmín, saying:
"Your Highness need not cross.
I have no other intention;
I merely wish to reaffirm and solidify our alliance with Your Highness."
Thereupon, he led his troops to retreat slightly.
After this, the continuous rain intensified.
Shìmín said to his generals:
"What the barbarians rely on are bows and arrows.
Now, prolonged heavy rain has continued for a long time,
their sinews and glue are all loosened,
making their bows unusable,
as if a flying bird has its wings broken.
We live in houses and eat cooked food,
our swords and spears are sharp and strong.
Xī
means 'firm' or 'strong.'
If we do not seize this opportunity,
what else shall we wait for?"
So, he secretly led his army out by night,
advancing through the rain,
which greatly astonished the Tūjué.
Shìmín also sent someone to persuade Tūlì with arguments of advantage and disadvantage.
Tūlì was pleased
and obeyed.
Jiélì wanted to fight,
but Tūlì disagreed.
Thereupon, Tūlì and his jiābìtèlè, Ashǐnà Sīmó, were sent to meet Shìmín,
requesting peace and kinship.
Shìmín granted it.
Sīmó
was Jiélì's paternal cousin.
Tūlì thereupon entrusted himself to Shìmín,
requesting to become sworn brothers.
Shìmín also treated him with kindness and favor,
made an alliance with him, and he departed.
This laid the groundwork for Tūlì's later surrender.
On the Gēngyín day,
Qízhōu cìshǐ Chái Shào defeated the Tūjué at Dùyánggǔ.
Dùyángshān is in Fúfēngxiàn, Qízhōu.
Kǒng Yǐngdá's Shīpǔ states: Zhōuyuán is
the land south of Qíshān,
belonging to Dùyáng.
Its terrain is rugged,
but the plains are fertile.
Dùyáng
was a Hàn dynasty county,
belonging to Fúfēng.
It had Dùyángshān,
and north of the mountain was Dùyánggǔ.
On the Rénshēn day,
the Tūjué Ashǐnà Sīmó came for an audience.
The emperor invited him to ascend to his imperial couch
and comforted him.
Sīmó's appearance resembled that of a Hú,
not like a Tūjué.
Therefore, Chǔluó suspected he was not of the Ashǐnà clan.
Throughout the reigns of Chǔluó and Jiélì,
he was always a jiābìtèlè,
but never got to command troops or be appointed a shè.
After entering the court,
he was granted the title of Héshùnwáng.
On the Dīngyǒu day,
Zuǒ Púshè Péi Jì was sent as an envoy to the Tūjué.
21st, ninth month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
Jiāng Zǐlù from Rìnán rebelled.
Rìnánjùn
was Dézhōu,
later renamed Huānzhōu.
22nd, on the Guǐmǎo day,
the Tūjué raided Suízhōu.
Dūdū Liú Dàjù attacked and defeated them,
capturing three tèlè.
Winter,
tenth month,
on the Jǐsì day,
the Tūjué raided Gānzhōu.
23rd, on the Xīnwèi day,
the emperor hunted in the southern mountains of Hù.
Hùxiàn belongs to Jīngzhào,
located at the foot of the southern mountains,
sixty lǐ north of Cháng'ān city.
Hù,
pronounced "hù."
On the Guǐyǒu day,
he visited Zhōngnán.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Tàiyīshān in Wǔgōngxiàn
was, in ancient texts, considered Zhōngnánshān,
located southwest of Wǔgōngxiàn.
It is observed that the southwestern mountains of Hù and Cháng'ān are all called Zhōngnánshān;
"Zhōng" (終)
is also written as
"Zhōng" (中).
24th, the Tǔyùhún and Qiāng people raided Diézhōu,
capturing Héchuān.
Diézhōu was Héchuānjùn,
its seat was Diéchuan.
Since the Qín and Hàn dynasties, it had been a stronghold for various Qiāng tribes.
Later, Emperor Wǔ of Later Zhōu expelled the Tǔyùhún
and, taking the meaning of "overlapping mountains,"
established Diézhōu.
Héchuānxiàn:
Later Zhōu established Xījiāngjùn,
Suí abolished it and made it a county.
Its seat was Tǔyùhún Mǎmùchéng.
In the third year of Wǔdé of Táng, it was moved to Jiāoshùchéng.
Tǔ,
rhymes with tūn in rising tone.
Gǔ,
rhymes with yù.
25th, on the Bǐngzǐ day,
the emperor visited Lóuguān
and offered sacrifices at Lǎozǐ's temple.
In Zhōuzhìxiàn, Qízhōu, there are Lóuguān and Lǎozǐ's temple.
Guān,
pronounced like gǔwán.
On the Guǐwèi day,
grand sacrifices (tàiláo) were offered at Emperor Wén of Suí's mausoleum.

Upon arriving at the prefecture,

summoned relatives and old friends,
and feasted with them,
with disheveled hair and sitting cross-legged,
as if he were still a commoner,

Afterwards, he distributed gold and silk as gifts,
wept,
and bade them farewell,

"Today, Zhāng Zhènzhōu can still happily drink with old friends.
After tomorrow,
the Grand Administrator of Shūzhōu will govern the populace.
The etiquette between ruler and subject will separate us,
and we can no longer be friends."
From then on, when relatives and old friends violated the law,
he showed no leniency whatsoever,

18 On the *guǐmǎo* day,
for the first time, the Grand Secretariat was ordered to inspect the weights and measures of all *zhōu*.
To inspect their lightness and heaviness, smallness and largeness.
According to Táng regulations: All lengths were based on the medium-sized black millet grains of the north.
The width of one millet grain was a *fēn*,
ten *fēn* made an *cùn*,
ten *cùn* made a *chǐ*,
one *chǐ* and two *cùn* made a *dàchǐ* (large *chǐ*),
ten *chǐ* made a *zhàng*.
All volumes were based on the medium-sized black millet grains.
Containing 1,200 millet grains was a *yuè*,
two *yuè* made a *hé*,
ten *hé* made a *shēng*,
ten *shēng* made a *dǒu*,
three *dǒu* made a *dàdǒu* (large *dǒu*),
ten *dǒu* made a *hú*.
All weights and balances were based on the medium-sized black millet grains.
The weight of one hundred millet grains was a *zhū*,
twenty-four *zhū* made a *liǎng*,
three *liǎng* made a *dàliǎng* (large *liǎng*),
sixteen *liǎng* made a *jīn*.
For the volume system,
the *yuè* was not used by both public and private sectors.
The divisions within a *hé*
included the finer units of *chāo* and *cuō*.

Chéng Dàchāng (程大昌) said: Dù Yòu’s (杜佑) *Tōngdiǎn*, in narrating the taxes of the Six Dynasties and discussing their general system, said: "Their measure of three *shēng* was equal to one *shēng* of today,
their weight of three *liǎng* was equal to one *liǎng* of today,
and their *chǐ* of one *chǐ* and two *cùn* was equal to one *chǐ* of today."

“The Buddha is in the Western Regions;
their teachings are distant.
Chinese translations of foreign texts
indulge in false claims.
They cause the disloyal and unfilial to shave their heads and bow to rulers and parents,
and idlers and parasites to change their clothes to escape taxes and levies.
They falsely proclaim the Three Evil Paths (sāntú),
and erroneously spread the Six Paths (liùdào).
Buddhists consider hell, hungry ghosts, and animals as the three evil paths,
saying that those who do evil will surely fall into them.
They also add Asuras, heavenly deities, and earthly spirits as the six paths.
They deceive the common folk.
They claim to repent past sins,
and make empty promises of future blessings;
giving ten thousand coins,
they hope for a ten-thousand-fold return;
observing a fast for one day,
they expect a hundred days' provisions.
Thus, they lead the ignorant astray,
making them seek merit blindly,
not fearing prohibitions,
and easily violating laws;
some commit heinous crimes,
fall into the net of justice,
and then in prison worship the Buddha,
hoping to be absolved of their crimes.
Moreover, birth and death, longevity and short life,
are due to nature;
punishment and reward, power and fortune,
pertain to the ruler;
poverty and wealth, nobility and lowliness,
are brought about by one's deeds.
Yet the foolish monks, through their deception,
attribute everything to the Buddha.
They usurp the ruler's authority,
and seize the power of creation.
Their harm to governance
is truly lamentable!
From Xī and Nóng
down to the Hàn dynasty,
there was no Buddhist Dharma.
Rulers were enlightened, ministers loyal,
and their reigns were long and enduring.
Emperor Míng of Hàn first established foreign gods,
and Sānmén from the Western Regions
themselves transmitted their Dharma.
This matter is found in Volume 45, the eighth year of Yǒngmíng of Emperor Míng of Hàn.
The state had strict laws
that forbade Chinese people from arbitrarily shaving their heads.
By the time of Fú and Shí,
Qiāng and Hú tribes disrupted China,
rulers were mediocre, ministers sycophantic,
governance cruel, and reigns short.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng and Xiāng of Qí
serve as clear mirrors.
Referring to Emperor Wǔ of Liáng starving to death in Táichéng,
and Wénxiāng of Qí being assassinated by a servant who prepared meals.
Their numbers exceed one hundred thousand;
they cut silk and fabric,
dress clay figures,
competing in malevolent enchantments,
bewildering the myriad people.
I request that they be matched for marriage;
this would create over one hundred thousand households,
producing boys and girls,
raised for ten years,
and educated for twelve years,
which could provide enough soldiers.
The four seas would be free from the calamity of being eaten away,
and the common people would know where authority and fortune reside.
Then the customs of delusion and enchantment would naturally be reformed,
and the transformation to simplicity and honesty would revive.
I secretly recall Zhāngchóu Zǐtuó's (Zhāngchóu Zǐtuó) memorial in the Qí dynasty stating:
'Monks and nuns,
their multitude harms the state,
and the extravagance of temples and pagodas
waste gold and silk.'
Shāmén,
or Sāngmén,
also similar in sound,
collectively refer to monks (sēng),
all foreign words.
Sēng
is translated as 'harmonious multitude,'
Sāngmén as 'stilling the mind,'
Bǐqiū
as 'begging;'
for lay believers in the Daoist Dharma,
males are called Yōupósaì,
and females Yōupóyí.
Those who are Shāmén
first cultivate the ten precepts,

Gǔ-Sǒu made Shùn dig a well.

被 (bèi)

“Divination is for resolving doubts;

Now we follow the Jiù Tángshū.
Shì-Mín ordered Wú-Jì to secretly summon Fáng Xuán-Líng and others,

Fáng Xuán-Líng’s words

He said to Jìng-Dé:

Jìng-Dé went

Jìng-Dé also arrived via another path.
On the day Jǐwèi,

Fù Yì secretly memorialized:

The Emperor handed this memorial to Shì-Mín.

The Emperor perused it

He replied:

明 (míng)
refers to the next day.

Xuánwǔ-Mén

Yuánjí drew his bow and shot at Shìmín,

The reason it did not reach its full extent

呼 (hū)

Jìng Xiǎnjùn served in Northern Qí,

Wànchè raised a clamor, intending to attack the Qín Fǔ,

The Emperor was then boating on the Hǎichí (Sea Pond).

Jìngdé, donning armor and holding a spear,

The Emperor was greatly surprised

The Emperor said to Péi Jì and others:

Xiāo Yǔ and Chén Shúdá said:

King Qín's achievements cover the universe,

If Your Majesty places him in the position of Yuánliáng
(Yuánliáng refers to the Crown Prince),
瑀 (yǔ)
is pronounced "yǔ" (like yǔ).

According to the Tàijí Gōngtú (Map of the Tàijí Palace) in the commentary,

幾 (jī)
is pronounced "jūxī fān" (like jū-xī).
He sobbed for a long time.
Jiànchéng's sons, Ānlù Wáng Chéngdào, Hédōng Wáng Chéngdé, Wǔ'ān Wáng Chéngxùn, Rǔnán Wáng Chéngmíng, and Jùlù Wáng Chéngyì,

On that day,

In the fourth month of that year,

"All matters shall be handled by King Qín."
On the day Xīnyǒu,

Chén Guāng 陳光 said: To establish the eldest legitimate son as heir

However, the reason Gāo Zǔ 高祖 possessed the empire

With the suspicion of status and the pressure of power,

If Gāo Zǔ 高祖 had possessed the sagacity of Wén Wáng 文王,

Since this could not be so,
Tài Zōng 太宗 initially wished to wait for the other to make the first move,

If this had happened,
then the matter would have been unavoidable,
and still preferable.
But then, being pressed by his subordinates,

Rú Chún 如淳 said: "To kill and shed blood profusely is called 'wading through blood' (dié xuè 蹀血)."
Shī Gǔ 師古 said: "Dié 蹀

Dié 蹀,
pronounced dú jiá 徒頰.
This brought criticism for a thousand ages.
What a pity!
The founder of an enterprise and progenitor of a lineage,
is the model for his descendants.
The successions of Zhōng Zōng 中宗, Míng Huáng 明皇, Sù Zōng 肅宗, and Dài Zōng 代宗,
were they not pointed to and used as justification?
That Míng Huáng 明皇 is referred to by his imperial title instead of his temple name

During the latter reigns of Zhōng Zōng 中宗 and Sù Zōng 肅宗,

All the gold, silks, and sundry implements of Qí Wáng's 齊王 kingdom were bestowed upon Jìngdé 敬德.
According to Táng 唐 regulations: the kingdom of a Prince (Qīn Wáng 親王) had a Kingdom Bureau (Guósī 國司),

The Groom of the Imperial Stable (Xǐmǎ 洗馬), Wèi Zhēng 魏徵, had often advised the Crown Prince, Jiànchéng 建成, to eliminate Qín Wáng 秦王 early.
When Jiànchéng 建成 was defeated,
Shìmín 世民 summoned Zhēng 徵 and said:

Everyone was fearful for him, but
Zhēng 徵 remained composed,

"If the former Crown Prince had followed my advice early,

Shìmín 世民 had always valued his talent,
so he changed his demeanor, treated him with respect,

The Principal Clerk to the Grand Tutor (Zhānshì Zhǔbù 詹事主簿),
a rank of from seven upper (cóng qī pǐn shàng 從七品上),

Wáng Guī 王珪 and others were exiled to Xīzhōu 巂州.
Xī 巂,
pronounced suǐ 髓.
Shìmín 世民 ordered the release of hunting falcons and dogs from the imperial park,
stopped tributes from all regions,

The governmental decrees were simple and strict,
and the entire court and populace greatly rejoiced.
Qūtú Tōng 屈突通 was appointed Left Grandee Secretary of the Shǎndōng 陝東 Circuit Regional Bureau (Shǎndōng Dào Xíngtái Zuǒ Púshè 陝東道行臺左僕射),

Dòu Guǐ 竇軌, the Grandee Secretary of the Yìzhōu 益州 Regional Bureau, was at odds with the Regional Bureau Secretaries Wéi Yúnqǐ 韋雲起 and Guō Xíngfāng 郭行方.
Yúnqǐ's 雲起 younger brother, Qìngjiǎn 慶儉, and many of his clan served the Crown Prince, Jiànchéng 建成.

Tǔ 吐,
pronounced tūn 暾.
Yù 谷,

Initially,

Jūnkuò was formerly a village bandit,
brave, fierce, and cunning.
Yuán trusted and relied on him wholeheartedly,

Crown Prince Jiànchéng plotted to harm Qínwáng,
and secretly allied with Yuán.
After Jiànchéng died,
an imperial edict dispatched the Tōngshì Shèrén Cuī Dūnlǐ to summon Yuán via express post.
The Tōngshì Shèrén
was an official position similar to the Qin Dynasty's Yèzhě.
During the Jìn Dynasty, one Shèrén and one Tōngshì were appointed,
subordinate to the Zhōngshū.
In the Eastern Jìn, they were called Tōngshì Shèrén.
In the Táng Dynasty, it was a senior sixth-grade position.
They were in charge of introducing officials and those offering apologies to the emperor at court and in the palace courtyard.
Whenever close ministers entered to serve,
or civil and military officials took their places,
they would guide their entry and exit.
Whenever tribute memorials came from the four directions,
or barbarians offered tribute,
they would receive and present them.
Yuán consulted with Jūnkuò.
Jūnkuò wanted to capture Yuán to claim merit,
so he persuaded him, saying:
“If Your Highness enters [the capital],
you will certainly not escape unharmed.
Now you command tens of thousands of troops,
how can you answer the summons of a lone envoy,
and cast yourself into a net? ”
Thereupon, they wept together.
Yuán said:
“I now entrust my life to you, Duke;
the undertaking is decided. ”
He then seized Dūnlǐ,
and questioned him about secret affairs in the capital;
Dūnlǐ refused to yield,
so Yuán imprisoned him.
He dispatched express riders to call up troops,
and also summoned Yānzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Shēn to Jì,

During the Suí Dynasty, Liáoxī Jùn was established in the territory of Yíngzhōu at the old city of Rǔluó.
In the first year of Wǔdé, it was renamed Yānzhōu.
In the sixth year,

In the sixth year of Wǔdé,
Lǐ Yì entered court from Yōuzhōu.
Wáng Shēn was the Chángshǐ,
effectively managing the affairs of the prefecture,
and the people of Yōuzhōu had always trusted and obeyed him.
Yuán intended to rebel,
which is why he summoned him to plan.
燕,

詵,

“Wáng Jūnkuò is fickle and unreliable;

Yuán could not decide.
Jūnkuò, knowing this,

The crowd all replied:

Only Yuán remained,
