eighth, Kāiguó Xiànzǐ,
with an actual income of five hundred households,
of the superior first rank (zhèng wǔ pǐn shàng);
ninth, Kāiguó Xiànnán,
with an actual income of three hundred households,
of the superior junior fifth rank (cóng wǔ pǐn shàng).
For all enfeoffed households,
the rate was based on three adult males and above,
with one-third of the annual rent going to the imperial court.
Those who received actual enfeoffments
obtained true households distributed across various prefectures.
9 Initially,
Xiāo Yǔ recommended Fēng Déyǐ to the Former Emperor (Shànghuáng),
who appointed Fēng Déyǐ as Zhōngshū Lìng.
When the Emperor (Shàng) ascended the throne,
Xiāo Yǔ was Left Grand Minister (Zuǒ Púshè),
and Fēng Déyǐ was Right Grand Minister (Yòu Púshè).
After deliberations were settled,
Fēng Déyǐ repeatedly reversed his stance
before the Emperor,
which led to a rift between them.
At that time, Fáng Xuánlíng and Dù Rúhuì were newly in power,
and both distanced themselves from Xiāo Yǔ and favored Fēng Déyǐ.
During the early administration of Tàizōng,
with the wisdom of Fáng and Dù,
and the integrity of Xiāo Yǔ,
they did not become close,
but rather favored Fēng Déyǐ.
This was probably because Xiāo Yǔ's straightforwardness
made him difficult to work with during times of crisis and uncertainty,
while Fēng Déyǐ's cunning and craftiness
meant that if one was not close to him,
one could not ascertain his true intentions.
Later prime ministers,
without any discernment in their hearts,
merely spoke of being close to honorable men (jūnzǐ)
and distant from petty men (xiǎorén),
and none were able to succeed.
Subsequently, Xiāo Yǔ submitted a memorial discussing this,
but his language was vague and distant,
which displeased the Emperor.
Coincidentally, Xiāo Yǔ and Chén Shúdá had a furious dispute before the Emperor.
On the day *gēngchén*,
both Xiāo Yǔ and Chén Shúdá were impeached for disrespect
and dismissed from office.
The *Kǎoyì* (Critical Annotations) states: The old account relates,
"Tàizōng considered Xuánlíng and others to have rendered great service,
which displeased the Emperor,
and so he was dismissed to his home.
Soon after, he was appointed Junior Mentor (Shàoshī),
and again became Left Grand Minister (Zuǒ Púshè),
but was dismissed for his furious dispute with Chén Shúdá."
However, according to the *Shílù* (Veritable Records), the dispute occurred before he was made Junior Mentor,
and we follow that account now.
10 On the day *jiǎshēn*,
Péi Jǔ, the Minister of Revenue (Mínbù Shàngshū), memorialized,
"For the people who have suffered the brutal devastation of the Tujue,
I request that each household be given one bolt of silk."
The Emperor said,
"I govern my subordinates with sincerity and trust.
I do not wish to have a hollow reputation for compassion and relief without the actual substance.
Households vary in size;
how can we give aid uniformly? "
Thereupon, the distribution was calculated based on the number of mouths.
11 Initially,
the Former Emperor (Shànghuáng) wished to strengthen the imperial clan (zōngshì) to secure the realm.
Thus, the Emperor's second cousins and third cousins,
those with the same great-great-grandfather being second cousins,
and those with the same high-great-grandfather being third cousins.
The character *cóng* (從),
pronounced *cái yòng fān*.
Even young children were made Wáng,
numbering several tens of people.
Enfeoffing members of the imperial clan as Jùnwáng,
as seen in volume 190, year five.
"Is extensively enfeoffing members of the imperial clan
beneficial to the realm?"
Fēng Déyǐ replied,
"In previous eras, only imperial sons and brothers were made Wáng.
Apart from those with great achievements,
none became Wáng.
The Former Emperor (Shànghuáng) strengthened relations within the nine clans (jiǔzú)
and extensively enfeoffed the imperial clan.
Since the two Hàn dynasties, there has never been such a large number as there is now.
With high titles and ranks,
many corvée laborers are supplied."
Corvée labor,
refers to guards, servants, and menial workers of that kind.
The Emperor said,
"Indeed.
I, as the Son of Heaven,
am here to nourish the common people.
How can I burden the common people to support my own clan? "
In the eleventh month,
on the day *gēngyín*,
all Jùnwáng of the imperial clan were demoted to Xiàngōng,
except for a few who had rendered meritorious service.
12 On the day *bǐngwǔ*,
the Emperor discussed the cessation of banditry with his attendant officials.
Someone suggested using harsh laws to forbid it.
The Emperor smiled faintly
A smile that does not change one's facial expression is a faint smile (shěn).
*Shěn* (哂),
pronounced *shì rěn fān*.
"The reason people become bandits
is due to heavy taxes and burdensome labor,
and the greed of officials.
When hunger and cold press upon them,
they have no time to consider integrity and shame.
I shall reduce extravagance and expenses,
lighten corvée and decrease taxes,
and select incorruptible officials.
If the people have surplus food and clothing,
they will naturally not become bandits.
Why use harsh laws? "
From then on, several years later,
the realm was at peace,
nothing was picked up if dropped on the road,
outer doors were not closed,
and merchants and travelers slept in the wilderness.
The Emperor also once said to his attendant officials,
"A ruler relies on the state,
and the state relies on the people.
To exploit the people to serve the ruler
is like cutting off one's flesh to fill one's belly:
the belly is full, but the body dies.
The ruler is rich, but the state perishes.
Therefore, the troubles of a ruler
do not come from outside;
they often originate from within himself.
If desires are abundant, expenses will be vast;
if expenses are vast, taxes will be heavy;
if taxes are heavy, the people will suffer;
if the people suffer, the state will be endangered;
if the state is endangered, the ruler will be lost.
I constantly ponder this,
and thus I dare not indulge my desires."
13 In the twelfth month,
on the day *jǐsì*,
Dòu Guǐ, the Grand Governor of Yìzhōu (Yìzhōu Dàdūdū), memorialized, claiming that the Luáo had rebelled.
In the sixth month of that year,
the Grand Executive Bureau (Dàxíngtái) was abolished,
and Grand Governorships (Dàdūdūfǔ) were established.
Thereafter, the various prefectural governorships (zhōudūdūfǔ) were divided into three grades: superior, middle, and inferior.
Grand Governors of large prefectures were of the junior second rank (cóng èr pǐn),
their Chief Clerks (Zhǎngshǐ) were of the junior third rank (cóng sān pǐn),
and their Marshals (Sīmǎ) were of the junior fourth rank (cóng sì pǐn).
Governors of middle prefectures were of the first rank (zhèng sān pǐn),
their Vice-Governors (Biéjià) were of the first fourth rank (zhèng sì pǐn),
their Chief Clerks were of the superior first rank (zhèng wǔ pǐn shàng),
and their Marshals were of the inferior first rank (zhèng wǔ pǐn xià).
Governors of inferior prefectures were of the junior third rank (cóng sān pǐn),
and their Vice-Governors, Chief Clerks, and Marshals were all successively reduced by one rank.
The character *Luáo* (獠),
pronounced *lǔ hào fān*.
The Emperor said,
"The Luáo live nestled in mountains and forests,
occasionally emerging to pilfer.
This is their usual custom.
If the local governors can manage them with benevolence and trust,
they will naturally submit and obey.
How can one lightly deploy weapons of war,
and hunt their people
like birds and beasts? Is this the intention of being a parent to the people? "
He ultimately did not permit it.
14 The Emperor said to Péi Jì,
"Recently, many have submitted memorials discussing affairs of state.
I have pasted them all on the walls of my chamber,
so I can view them as I come and go.
Every time I consider how to govern,
sometimes I do not sleep until deep into the night.
You and your colleagues should also diligently attend to your duties,
to fulfill this intention of mine."
The Emperor was diligent in seeking good governance.
He frequently invited Wèi Zhēng into his private chambers
to ask about what was gained and lost.
Wèi Zhēng spoke everything he knew,
and the Emperor always gladly accepted it.
The Emperor sent envoys to muster troops.
Fēng Déyí submitted a memorial, saying:
"Even if 'middle males' have not yet reached eighteen,
those whose physiques are strong and large
may also be mustered."
According to Táng dynasty regulations, a commoner aged sixteen was a 'middle male' (zhōngnán),
at eighteen they became a 'full male' (chéngdīng),
and at twenty-one they were a 'full adult' (dīng),
assigned to labor service.
When the imperial edict was issued,
Wèi Zhēng firmly insisted that it was unacceptable
and refused to sign the edict.
According to Táng regulations,
a Secretary of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén) signs edicts.
Wèi Zhēng was then a Grand Master Remonstrant (Jiànyì Dàfū).
Did Tàizōng also make him co-sign?
The Emperor was angry,
summoned him, and reproached him, saying:
"Those 'middle males' who are strong and large
are merely cunning commoners feigning illness to avoid conscription and service.
What harm is there in taking them,
yet you insist so firmly!"
Wèi Zhēng replied:
"The strength of an army lies in governing it correctly,
not in its multitude.
If Your Majesty takes the strong and healthy,
and governs them with the right Way,
it will be enough to be unrivaled in the world.
Why must you take many weak and frail ones to increase a mere number?
Moreover, Your Majesty always says: 'I govern the world with sincerity and trust,
wishing to make all my officials and commoners free from deceit.'
Yet, you have been on the throne for only a short time,
and you have already broken your word several times!"
The Emperor was astonished and said:
"How have I broken my word?"
Wèi Zhēng replied:
"When Your Majesty first ascended the throne,
you issued an edict saying: 'All outstanding debts to the government
are to be entirely waived.'
The relevant officials believed that debts owed to the Qín Prince's Household (Qínfǔ Guósī)
were not government property
and continued to demand them as before.
Your Majesty, as the Prince of Qín, ascended to be the Son of Heaven.
How could the property of your princely household
not be government property!
You also said: 'The Guānzhōng region is exempted from two years of rent and taxes,
and the regions outside Guānzhōng are granted one year of remission.'
But then, an imperial edict followed, stating: 'For those who have already performed labor or paid taxes,
the exemption will begin next year.'
After they had dispersed and returned home,
taxes were again levied,
which naturally caused discontent among the common people.
Now that goods have already been collected,
you are again conscripting them into the army.
How can this be called 'starting next year'?
Furthermore, Your Majesty relies on the prefects and magistrates (shǒuzǎi) to govern the world with you.
You normally inspect them casually
and entrust everything to them.
Yet, when it comes to mustering troops,
you alone suspect them of deceit.
Is this what is meant by 'governing with sincerity and trust'?"
The Emperor was pleased and said:
"Previously, I suspected you of not understanding state affairs because of your obstinacy.
Now, your discussion of the general principles of the state
indeed reveals their essence and importance.
If imperial decrees are not trustworthy,
then the common people will not know what to follow.
How then can the world be governed?
My error is profound!"
Thereupon, he did not conscript the 'middle males'
and bestowed upon Wèi Zhēng a golden urn.
The Emperor heard of Zhāng Xuánsù, the Secretary for Records (lùshì cānjūn) of Jǐngzhōu.
Jǐngzhōu was
the land of Gé County (Géxiàn) in Hàn dynasty Píngyuán Commandery (Píngyuán Jùn).
The Suí dynasty established Gōnggāo County (Gōnggāo Xiàn),
which belonged to Guānzhōu.
When Táng pacified Hébĕi,
Jǐngzhōu was established by partitioning Gōnggāo.
The Secretary for Records of a superior prefecture (shàngzhōu lùshì cānjūn) was of rank seven upper,
in charge of auditing and checking the accounts of the provincial offices.
The Secretary for Records was in charge of receiving and dispatching affairs
and also checking for errors.
The Emperor asked him about the way of governance.
Zhāng Xuánsù replied:
"The Suí emperor was fond of personally managing all affairs
and did not entrust them to his ministers.
The ministers were fearful
and only knew how to receive instructions and carry them out,
none daring to disobey.
For one person's wisdom to decide the affairs of the entire world,
even if gains and losses were half and half,
the errors would already be numerous.
With sycophancy from below and concealment from above,
how could it avoid ruin?
If Your Majesty can truly carefully select your ministers
and assign them their duties,
sitting back in serene majesty (Gāo Gǒng Mù Qīng) and examining their successes and failures to administer rewards and punishments,
what worry is there that the realm will not be well-governed!
Moreover,
I observe that in the chaos at the end of the Suí dynasty,
those who wished to contend for the world were no more than a dozen or so people.
The rest all protected their hometowns and families,
awaiting a virtuous ruler to return to.
From this, I know that few common people actually desire chaos;
it is simply that the ruler cannot bring them peace."
The Emperor praised his words
and promoted him to Imperial Household Remonstrant (Shìyùshǐ).
Zhāng Yùngǔ, formerly the Archivist (jìshì) of Yōuzhōu and an Attendant (zhí) in the Central Secretariat, presented the 'Great Treasure Admonition' (Dàbǎo Zhēn).
In the Táng dynasty, there were no Archivists in the various prefectures;
only royal principalities (wángguó) had Archivist Advisers (jìshì cānjūn),
of rank six upper.
Yùngǔ was likely an Archivist when Prince Yuán of Lújiāng (Lújiāng Wáng Yuán) supervised Yōuzhōu.
According to Táng regulations,
if one's official rank was insufficient
but one entered a secretariat in another capacity, they were called an Attendant.
The Emperor
at that time was responsible for reviewing and annotating.
The admonition said: "The Sage receives the Mandate,
rescuing the drowning and bringing prosperity to the distressed.
Thus, one person governs the world;
the world is not to serve one person."
It also said:
"You may make your nine-layered palace grand within,
yet your dwelling place is no more than knee-room.
Those ignorant and confused
adorn their terraces with jade and their chambers with pearls.
You may array the 'Eight Delicacies' (bāzhēn) before you,
yet what you eat is no more than enough to suit your taste.
The Zhōu Rites: the provisioner,
used eight kinds of rare foods.
Commentary says: 'rare foods'
refers to chún'áo, chúnwú, páotún, páozāng, dǎozhēn, zì, áo, and gānpáo.
Chún is pronounced
zhī chún.
Wú is pronounced
mò hú,
also wǔ yóu.
Zāng is pronounced
zuò láng.
Páo is pronounced
lì diāo.
They pile up the dregs and make ponds of wine."
It further said:
"Do not be dull and ignorant,
nor be overly scrutinizing and seemingly clear.
Though the dangling beads of your ceremonial cap (miǎnliú) obstruct your sight, you see what is unformed.
Though the yellow cotton plugs (tǒukuàng) fill your ears, you hear the soundless."
The dangling beads in front of the ceremonial cap
serve to obscure keen sight.
The yellow cotton plugs in the ears
serve to block keen hearing.
Shīgǔ said: "They are made of yellow silk and cloth in a circular shape,
hung by two cords from the ceremonial cap,
dangling beside both ears,
to show that one does not listen to external matters."
Tǒu is pronounced
tā kǒu.
Sāi is pronounced
xī zé.
He was given a bundle of silk.
Táng regulations: For any grant of ten lengths of fabric,
the standard was three bolts of plain silk,
three pieces of coarse cloth,
and four bundles of cotton.
If it was ten lengths of assorted colored silks,
then two bolts of thin silk,
two bolts of spun silk,
two bolts of twill,
and four bolts of patterned silk.
If brocade and colored silks were granted to foreign guests,
for ten lengths,
it would be one piece of brocade,
two bolts of twill,
four bolts of patterned silk,
and four bundles of cotton.
All seasonal clothes specified as 'one set' were given in full;
'one pair' was given in reduced quantity.
At the winter solstice assembly,
those designated to receive bundles of silk of differing amounts:
officials of rank five and above received five bolts,
those of rank six and below received two bolts.
Imperial ladies received according to their husbands or sons.
Zhāng Yùngǔ was promoted to Grand Judge Assistant (Dàlǐ Céng),
rank six upper,
in charge of presiding over divisions of the temple's affairs.
15 The Emperor [Gāozǔ 高祖] summoned Fù Yì 傅奕
and gave him food.
He said:
"The memorial you submitted earlier
almost brought disaster upon me.
This incident is recorded in the previous volume in the sixth month of that year.
'Jī' 幾
is pronounced 'jū yī'.
You should speak your mind fully in all such matters;
do not be deterred by past events."
The Emperor once said to Yì 奕:
"The teachings of Buddhism
are profound and worthy of emulation.
Why are you alone unable to comprehend their principles?"
He replied:
"Buddha was merely a shrewd and cunning person from the Western Regions,
who deluded and dazzled the people of that land.
In China, perverse individuals
have taken the profound theories of Zhuāngzǐ 莊子 and Lǎozǐ 老子,
embellished them with monstrous and illusory tales,
and used them to deceive the ignorant populace.
This is of no benefit to the people
and is harmful to the state.
It is not that I do not understand;
I simply disdain to study them."
The Emperor was quite pleased with this.
16 The Emperor was concerned that many officials were taking bribes.
To twist the law and accept bribes is called 'qíu' 賕.
'Qíu' 賕
is pronounced 'qíu'.
A clerk of the Sīmén 司門 [Board of Gates] accepted one bolt of silk.
The Sīmén Láng 司門郎 [Director of the Board of Gates]
belonged to the Xíngbù 刑部 [Ministry of Punishments],
and was in charge of the records and administration of all gates and passes of the empire, as well as the entry and exit of people.
There were six such clerks.
According to Táng 唐 regulations,
a bolt of cloth was one 'chǐ bā cùn' 尺八寸 [about 58 cm] wide and four 'zhàng' 丈 [about 13 m] long.
Péi Jǔ 裴矩, the Shàngshū 尚書 [Minister] of the Mínbù 民部 [Ministry of Revenue], advised:
"The crime of an official taking bribes
indeed deserves death;
but if Your Majesty sends people to tempt them, and they accept,
you are entrapping people into violating the law.
I fear this is not what is meant by 'guide them with virtue,
and regulate them with ritual'."
This quotes Confucius's words from the Analects.
'Dào' 道
is pronounced 'dǎo'.
The Emperor summoned all civil and military officials of the fifth rank and above and announced:
"Péi Jǔ 裴矩 can argue forcefully in his official capacity
and does not merely assent superficially.
If every matter were handled this way,
why should we worry about not achieving good governance!"
Chén Guāng 臣光 [Sīmǎ Guāng 司馬光] says: The ancients had a saying: "When the ruler is enlightened, the ministers are upright."
Péi Jǔ 裴矩 was obsequious to the Suí 隋 but loyal to the Táng 唐.
This was not a change in his nature;
if the ruler dislikes hearing of his faults,
loyalty transforms into obsequiousness; if the ruler enjoys hearing straightforward words,
obsequiousness transforms into loyalty.
Thus, we know that the ruler is the gnomon,
and the ministers are the shadow;
when the gnomon moves,
the shadow follows.
17 In this year,
Imperial Prince Lángshā Jùnwáng Kè 長沙郡王恪 was advanced to Hán Wáng 漢王 [Prince of Hàn], and Yíyáng Jùnwáng Yòu 宜陽郡王祐 was advanced to Chǔ Wáng 楚王 [Prince of Chǔ].
18 The three kingdoms of Xīnluó 新羅, Bǎijì 百濟, and Gāolì 高麗 had an ancient feud.
The Běishǐ 北史 [History of the Northern Dynasties] says: Xīnluó 新羅 was originally of the Jìnhán 辰韓 lineage,
located southeast of Gāolì 高麗,
also called Qínhán 秦韓.
Tradition holds that during the Qín 秦 dynasty, people fleeing forced labor
came to Mǎhán 馬韓,
and were allotted the eastern border to live in,
hence the name Qínhán 秦韓.
Originally there were six states,
which gradually divided into twelve,
and Xīnluó 新羅 was one of them.
Some say that after Wèi Guānqiū Jiǎn 魏毌丘儉 defeated Gāolì 高麗,
they fled to Wòjú 沃沮,
and later reestablished their state.
Those who remained became Xīnluó 新羅,
also possessing the lands of Wòjú 沃沮, Bùnài 不耐, Hán 韓, and Huì 濊.
Its king was originally a Bǎijì 百濟 person,
who fled from the sea to Xīnluó 新羅,
and subsequently became king of that state,
a vassal of Bǎijì 百濟;
later, it grew strong
and thus became an enemy of Bǎijì 百濟.
Bǎijì 百濟 attacked Gāolì 高麗,
and came to request aid.
Xīnluó 新羅 sent all its troops and defeated them.
From then on, they continuously attacked each other.
Later, the king of Bǎijì 百濟 was captured
and killed,
intensifying the animosity.
'Lì' 麗
is pronounced 'lì zhī'.
The Emperor sent Zhū Zǐshē 朱子奢, Assistant Instructor of the Guózǐ 國子 [Imperial Academy], to convey his intentions.
In the fourth year of Xiánníng 咸寧 of Jìn Wǔdì 晉武帝 [278 CE], the Guózǐ Xué 國子學 [Imperial College] was established,
with one Jìjiǔ 祭酒 [Libationer] and one Bóshì 博士 [Erudite],
and fifteen Zhùjiào 助教 [Assistant Instructors] to teach the students.
In the tenth year of Tàiyuán 太元 of Xiàowǔ 孝武 [385 CE],
the number of Assistant Instructors was reduced to ten.
Under the Táng 唐, there were five Assistant Instructors,
of rank 'cóng liùpǐn shàng' 從六品上 [senior sixth rank],
who were in charge of assisting the Erudites in teaching the classics.
Tàizōng Wénwǔ Dàshèng Dàguǎngxào Huángdì Shàngzhīshàng 太宗文武大聖大廣孝皇帝上之上
His personal name was Shìmín 世民,
the second son of Gāozǔ 高祖.
The Emperor was initially posthumously honored as Wén Huángdì 文皇帝 [Emperor Wén],
with the temple name Tàizōng 太宗;
in the fifth year of Xiánhéng 咸亨 [674 CE], he was posthumously honored as Tàizōng Wénwǔ Shèng Huángdì 太宗文武聖皇帝 [Emperor Wénwǔ Shèng of Tàizōng];
in the eighth year of Tiānbǎo 天寶 [749 CE], he was posthumously revered as Tàizōng Wénwǔ Dàshèng Huángdì 太宗文武大聖皇帝 [Emperor Wénwǔ Dàshèng of Tàizōng];
in the thirteenth year [754 CE],
he was again honored with the title Tàizōng Wénwǔ Dàshèng Dàguǎngxào Huángdì 太宗文武大聖大廣孝皇帝 [Emperor Wénwǔ Dàshèng Dàguǎngxào of Tàizōng].
First year of Zhēngguān 貞觀
(Dīnghài 丁亥, 627)
1 Spring,
First month,
Yǐyǒu 乙酉
The era name was changed.
2 Dīnghài 丁亥
The Emperor hosted a banquet for his officials,
and the "Qín Wáng Pò Chén Yuè" 秦王破陳樂 [Music of the Prince of Qín Defeating the Enemy] was performed.
The Emperor said:
"When I was entrusted with leading the expedition,
this song circulated among the people.
Although it lacks the elegance of civil virtue,
my achievements were made through it,
and I dare not forget my origins."
Fēng Déyí 封德彝 said:
"Your Majesty pacified the realm with divine military prowess;
how can civil virtue compare?"
The Emperor said:
"Rebellions are quelled by military means;
stability is maintained by civil means.
The use of civil and military means
depends on the times.
Your statement that civil means are inferior to military means
is mistaken!"
Déyí 德彝 prostrated himself and apologized.
3 Jǐhài 己亥
An edict was issued:
"From now on, whenever officials from the Zhōngshū 中書 [Central Secretariat] and Ménxià 門下 [Chancellery] and those of the third rank and above enter the chambers to discuss matters,
Censorate officials shall be commanded to accompany them,
to remonstrate whenever there is a fault."
Chéng Dàchāng 程大昌 says: The Táng 唐 Xīnèi Tàijí Diàn 西內太極殿 [Western Palace Grand Ultimate Hall]
was where court was held on the first and fifteenth days of the month;
it was the main hall.
North of the Tàijí Diàn 太極殿 was the Liǎngyí Diàn 兩儀殿,
where court was held on regular days.
In the eastern and western corridors of the Tàijí Diàn 太極殿 were the two Shànggé 上閤 [Upper Chambers],
meaning both chambers had doors for entry,
and one could then turn north to enter the Liǎngyí Diàn 兩儀殿.
This was the system for entering the chambers during the time of Tàizōng 太宗.
After Gāozōng 高宗,
emperors mostly resided in the Dōngnèi 東內 [Eastern Palace],
holding court in the Xiānzhèng Qiándiàn 宣政前殿,
which was called 'Yá' 衙 [court],
and the 'Yá' 衙 had guards;
holding court in the Zǐchén Biàndiàn 紫宸便殿 [Purple Palace Side Hall]
was called 'rù gé' 入閤 [entering the chambers].
When the emperor did not hold court in the Xiānzhèng Qiándiàn 宣政前殿 but in the Zǐchén Biàndiàn 紫宸便殿,
he would summon guards from the main 'Yá' 衙 [court],
and enter through the chamber door.
Officials waiting for court at the guard posts
would then follow and enter for an audience,
which was called 'rù gé' 入閤.

4 The Emperor ordered Chángsūn Wújí 長孫無忌, Shàngshū 尚書 [Minister] of the Lìbù 吏部 [Ministry of Personnel], and others, together with scholars and legal officials, to revise and deliberate on the law code.
Fifty articles punishable by strangulation were mitigated to cutting off the right foot.
The Emperor still found this too cruel,
saying:
"Corporal punishment has been abolished for a long time;
there should be something to replace it."
Péi Hóngxiàn 裴弘獻, Cānjūn 參軍 [Staff Officer] of the Fǎ Cáo 法曹 [Judicial Section] of Shǔ Wáng 蜀王 [Prince of Shǔ],
According to Táng 唐 regulations,
princes had seven sections for meritorious service, granaries, households, military, cavalry, law, and clerks,
each with a Staff Officer of rank 'zhèng qīpǐn shàng' 正七品上 [senior seventh rank].
proposed exile for three thousand 'lǐ' 里 and forced labor for three years.
An imperial edict adopted this.
The Kǎoyì 考異 [Investigation of Differences] states: Both the Xīn Xíngfǎ Zhì 新刑法志 [New Treatise on Penal Law] and Jiù Xíngfǎ Zhì 舊刑法志 [Old Treatise on Penal Law] say
"forced labor for two years."
We now follow Wáng Pǔ's 王溥 Huìyào 會要.
5 The Emperor considered Dài Zhòu, a Grandee in the Ministry of War, to be loyal, pure, public-spirited, and upright.
The Grandee in the Ministry of War
was in charge of managing accounts and the ranks and grades of all military officers in the empire, as well as the names and numbers of the guard garrisons.
The Emperor, seeing that many candidates for office fraudulently claimed hereditary privileges,
issued an edict ordering them to confess voluntarily,
with death as the penalty for those who did not confess.
Not long after,
a case of fraudulent claim came to light,
and the Emperor wished to execute him.
Zhòu remonstrated,
"According to the law, he should be exiled."
The Emperor angrily said,
"Are you trying to uphold the law and make me break my word?"
He replied,
"An edict arises from momentary joy or anger,
but the law is what the state uses to establish great trust throughout the empire.
Your Majesty is indignant at the many deceptions of the candidates,
and therefore wishes to kill him.
But knowing that it is not permissible,
if you then decide the case according to the law,
this is to suppress a small indignation and preserve great trust."
The Emperor said,
"If you can enforce the law,
what more worries do I have!"
Zhòu repeatedly defied the Emperor and enforced the law,
speaking like a gushing spring.
The Emperor always followed his advice,
and there were no wrongful incarcerations in the empire.
6 The Emperor ordered Fēng Déyí to recommend worthy individuals,
but for a long time, no one was recommended.
The Emperor questioned him,
and he replied,
"It's not that I haven't tried my best,
but there are no extraordinary talents at present!"
The Emperor said,
"A gentleman uses people like tools,
each according to their strengths.
How could the rulers of ancient times who achieved good governance
have borrowed talent from a different era?
The real problem is one's own inability to recognize talent;
how can one slander an entire generation of people!"
Déyí was ashamed and withdrew.
Dù Yān, the Censor-in-Chief, memorialized,
"There might be delays or errors in the documents of various departments.
I request that censors be sent to inspect them in those departments."
The Emperor asked Fēng Déyí about this,
who replied,
"Officials are appointed and duties divided,
each with their own responsibilities.
If there are indeed transgressions,
the censors should naturally impeach them;
but if they were to visit all departments
and search for flaws and defects,
it would be too cumbersome and trivial."
Yān remained silent.
The Emperor asked Yān,
"Why are you not arguing anymore?"
He replied,
"In the affairs of the world,
one must be entirely impartial.
If it is good, one follows it.
What Déyí said
truly grasps the essence.
I am sincerely convinced
and dare not persist in error."
The Emperor was pleased and said,
"If all of you can be like this,
what more worries do I have!"
7 Chángsūn Shùndé, the General of the Right Valiant Guard, accepted silk as a gift from someone.
When the matter came to light,
the Emperor said,
"If Shùndé truly benefits the state,
I would share the national treasury with him;
why would he be so greedy as this!"
Still cherishing his past achievements,
the Emperor did not punish him,
but merely bestowed upon him several dozen bolts of silk in the palace courtyard.
Hú Yǎn, the Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, said,
"Shùndé violated the law by accepting bribes;
his crime is unforgivable.
How can you bestow silk upon him again?"
The Emperor said,
"If he has human nature,
the humiliation of receiving silk
is more severe than suffering a punishment;
if he knows no shame,
he is merely an animal,
what good would killing him do!"
8 On the day Xīchǒu,
Lǐ Yì, Prince of Yānjùn and General Tiānjíe, rebelled in Jīngzhōu.
The Yízhōu circuit was designated as the Tiānjíe Army,
with one general appointed.
Yān,
read as jiān.
When Yì first came to court,
in the fifth year of Wǔdé (622 CE),
Yì led his troops to join Crown Prince Jiànchéng in attacking Liú Hēitá.
Then he came to court.
Cháo,
read as zhāo.
When Qin Prince's attendants arrived at his camp,
Yì beat them without cause.
The Retired Emperor was furious,
arrested Yì and imprisoned him,
but later released him.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Yì felt uneasy internally.
A demon sorcerer from Cáozhōu, Lǐ Wǔjiè,
told Yì,
"Your noble aura has appeared!"
and persuaded him to rebel.
Yì then falsely claimed to have received a secret edict
and ordered his troops to enter the capital.
He then led his troops to Bīnzhōu.
Zhào Cíhào, the Administrator of Bīnzhōu, rushed out to meet him.
The Administrators of various prefectures
were also known as Deputy Prefects.
An edict ordered Chángsūn Wújí, Minister of Personnel, and others to serve as Grand Field Marshals to suppress him.
When Zhào Cíhào heard that the imperial army was approaching,
he secretly plotted with the Commander Yáng Jí.
The plot was discovered,
and Yì imprisoned Cíhào.
Jí, outside the city, noticed the change,
and led his troops to attack.
Yì's forces collapsed,
he abandoned his wife and children,
and was about to flee to the Tujue.
Upon reaching Wūshì,
his subordinates beheaded him
and sent his head to Cháng'ān.
His younger brother Shòu,
who was the Governor of Lìzhōu,
was also executed.
9 Initially,
during the chaos at the end of the Suí dynasty,
heroes rose up everywhere,
gathering followers and occupying territories,
vying for supremacy among themselves.
When the Táng dynasty arose,
they successively submitted.
The Retired Emperor rewarded and honored them by demarcating and establishing prefectures and counties for them,
thus the number of prefectures and counties
doubled compared to the Kāihuáng and Dàyè eras.
The Emperor, seeing that there were few common people but many officials,
wished to reform this abuse.
In the second month,
he ordered a major consolidation and reduction,
and according to the geographical convenience of mountains and rivers,
divided the empire into ten circuits: first was Guānnèi,
second Hénán,
third Hédōng,
fourth Héběi,
fifth Shānnán,
sixth Lǒngyòu,
seventh Huáinán,
eighth Jiāngnán,
ninth Jiànnán,
tenth Língnán.
Jīngzhào, Tóng, Huá, Shāng, Qí, Bīn, Lǒng, Jīng, Yuán, Níng, Qìng, Fū, Fāng, Dān, Yán, Líng, Huì, Yán, Xià, Suí, Yín, Fēng, Shèng formed the Guānnèi circuit.
Luò, Rǔ, Shǎn, Guó, Zhèng, Huá, Xǔ, Yǐng, Chén, Cài, Biàn, Sòng, Bó, Xú, Háo, Sù, Yùn, Qí, Cáo, Pú, Qīng, Zī, Dēng, Lái, Dì, Yǎn, Hǎi, Yí, Mì formed the Hénán circuit.
Pú, Jìn, Jiàng, Fén, Xí, Bīng, Nánfén, Liáo, Qìn, Lán, Shí, Xīn, Dài, Shuò, Wèi, Zé, Lù formed the Hédōng circuit.
Huái, Mèng, Wèi, Bó, Xiāng, Wèi, Chán, Bèi, Xíng, Míng, Cí, Héng, Jì, Shēn, Zhào, Cāng, Jǐng, Dé, Yì, Dìng, Yōu, Zhuó, Yíng, Mò, Yān, Tán, Yíng, Píng formed the Héběi circuit.

Jīng, Xiá, Guī, Kuí, Lǐ, Lǎng, Zhōng, Fú, Wàn, Xiāng, Táng, Suí, Dèng, Jūn, Fáng, Yǐng, Fù, Jīn, Liáng, Yáng, Lì, Fèng, Xīng, Chéng, Fú, Wén, Bì, Bā, Péng, Tōng, Kāi, Lóng, Guǒ, Qú formed the Shānnán circuit.
Qín, Wèi, Hé, Shàn, Lán, Jiē, Táo, Mín, Kuò, Dié, Dàng, Liáng, Guā, Shā, Gān, Sù formed the Lǒngyòu circuit.
Yáng, Chǔ, Chú, Hé, Shòu, Lú, Shū, Guāng, Qí, Huáng, Ān, Shēn formed the Huáinán circuit.

Rùn, Cháng, Sū, Hú, Háng, Mù, Yuè, Qú, Wù, Kuò, Tái, Fú, Jiàn, Quán, Xuān, Shè, Chí, Hóng, Jiāng, È, Yuè, Ráo, Xìn, Qián, Jí, Yuán, Fǔ, Tán, Héng, Yǒng, Dào, Chēn, Shào, Qián, Chén, Yí, Sī, Bó formed the Jiāngnán circuit.
Yì, Jiā, Méi, Qióng, Jiǎn, Zī, Kuí, Yǎ, Nánhuì, Yì, Wéi, Sōng, Yáo, Gōng, Róng, Zǐ, Suí, Mián, Jiàn, Hé, Lóng, Pǔ, Yú, Líng, Róng, Lú formed the Jiànnán circuit.

Guǎng, Fān, Xún, Cháo, Nánkāng, Lóng, Duān, Xīn, Fēng, Nándàng, Chūn, Luó, Nánshí, Gāo, Nánhé, Yá, Zhèn, Yōng, Nánfāng, Nánjiǎn, Chún, Qīn, Nányǐn, Xiàng, Téng, Guì, Wú, Hè, Lián, Nánkūn, Jìng, Lè, Nángōng, Róng, Róng, Láo, Nánlín, Nánfú, Nányuè, Nányì, Jiāo, Lù, Fēng, Ài, Nándé formed the Língnán circuit.
10 In the third month,
on the day Guǐsì,
the Empress, leading the inner and outer ladies, personally attended the silkworms.
Inner ladies
were female officials in the palace,
ranging from noble consort to attendant,
also divided into nine ranks.
There were six ranks of outer ladies: the mothers and wives of princes, princely heirs, and princely commanderies were [rank 1],
mothers and wives of ducal peers of the first rank were Guo Furen (Lady of the State),
mothers and wives of officials of the third rank and above were Jun Furen (Lady of the Commandery),
mothers and wives of officials of the fourth rank were Jun Jun (Lady of the Commandery),
mothers and wives of officials of the fifth rank were Xiàn Jun (Lady of the County),
and mothers and wives of honorary officials of the fourth rank with a title
were Xiāng Jun (Lady of the Township).
Generally, outer ladies attended court
according to the rank of their husband or son.
According to the Táng system,
the Empress would offer sacrifices to the Ancestress of Silkworms on the auspicious Sī day of the last month of spring,
and then personally gather mulberry leaves.
The treatise on carriages and attire states: When the Empress personally attended the silkworms,
she wore a juyī,
made of yellow silk gauze.
Shuài,
read as lǜ.
11 In the intercalary month,
on the first day, Guǐchǒu,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the 12th day of the Rénshēn month,
the Emperor said to Tàizǐ Shǎoshī Xiāo Yǔ:
“When I was young, I loved bows and arrows.
I acquired more than ten excellent bows,
and thought there could be nothing better.
Recently, I showed them to a bow craftsman,
who then said, ‘None of these are made of good material.’
I asked him why,
and the craftsman replied: ‘If the heartwood is not straight,
then the grain will all be askew.
Even if the bow is strong, the arrow it shoots will not fly straight.’
Only then did I realize that my previous discernment was not precise.
I used bows and arrows to bring order to the four directions,
yet my understanding of them was still incomplete.
How much more so for the affairs of the world!
How could I possibly know everything about them!”
Thereupon, he ordered京官of the fifth rank and above—
“Jīngguān” meaning
officials holding positions in the capital—
to be frequently summoned
to inquire about the suffering of the common people
and the successes and failures of governance.
On the 13th, the Dūdū of Liángzhōu, Chánglè Wáng Yòu Liáng,
was rough and violent by nature.
His entourage of over a hundred people
were all good-for-nothing youths,
who harassed and abused the common people.
Moreover, he engaged in mutual trade with the Qiāng and Hú.
Someone accused Yòu Liáng of harboring ulterior motives.
The Emperor dispatched Zhōngshūlìng Yǔwén Shìjí by express post to replace him
and investigate his affairs.
His entourage, in fear,
plotted to abduct Yòu Liáng and flee to the Northern barbarians,
and also intended to kill Shìjí and occupy Héxī.
Again, someone reported their conspiracy.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Guǐsì day,
Yòu Liáng was granted death.
In the fifth month,
Yuàn Jūnzhāng led his followers to surrender.
Originally,
Jūnzhāng had led the Tūjué to conquer Mǎyì,
killing Gāo Mǎnzhèng.
This incident is recorded in volume 190, Gāozǔ Wǔdé 6th year.
“Jué” (厥),
read as “jiǔ wù fān”.
Héng'ān Zhèn in Suí’s Shuòzhōu Yúnnèi County
was Pingchéng, the capital of the Later Wèi.
The Táng later established Yúnzhōu and Yúnzhōng County there.
“Héng” (恆),
read as “hù dēng fān”.
Many abandoned Jūnzhāng and surrendered.
Jūnzhāng, in fear,
also surrendered,
requesting to defend the northern border to atone for his crimes.
The Former Emperor (Shànghuáng) agreed.
Jūnzhāng requested a sworn covenant.
The Former Emperor sent Yuán Pǔ, a native of Yànmén, to bestow upon him a golden tablet (quàn).
Yànmén County was part of Dàizhōu,
the land of Hàn’s Guǎngwǔ County.
Jūnzhāng hesitated and was indecisive.
Guō Zǐwēi of Héng'ān persuaded Jūnzhāng, saying:
“Héng'ān has strategic terrain and strong fortifications.
The Tūjué are currently powerful,
and you should rely on them to observe the situation,
rather than surrendering immediately to others.”
Jūnzhāng then arrested Yuán Pǔ and sent him to the Tūjué,
and rejoined them.
They frequently raided with the Tūjué.
By this time,
seeing Xiélì’s chaotic rule,
Jūnzhāng knew he could not be relied upon,
and so he led his followers to surrender.
Yuàn Jūnzhāng and Liú Wǔzhōu rose together,
and only now did he surrender.
“Ruì” (芮),
name of an ancient state.
On the 15th, someone submitted a memorial requesting the removal of sycophantic officials.
The Emperor asked:
“Who are these sycophantic officials?”
The person replied:
“Your servant dwells in the countryside
and cannot precisely know the individuals.
I wish Your Majesty would speak with all your officials,
perhaps feigning anger to test them.
Those who uphold justice and do not yield
are upright officials.
Those who fear your might and comply with your wishes
are sycophantic officials.”
The Emperor said:
“The ruler
is the source;
the officials
are the stream.
To muddy the source and yet expect the stream to be clear
is impossible.
If the ruler himself resorts to deceit,
how can he demand uprightness from his subordinates!
I intend to govern the world with utmost sincerity.
I have always privately felt shame for previous emperors and kings who resorted to cunning and petty tricks in dealing with their subordinates.
Although your strategy is good,
I will not adopt it.”
In the sixth month,
on the Xīnsì day,
Yòu Púshè Mìmíng Gōng Fēng Déyí passed away.
According to the rules for posthumous titles:
“Ming” (明) means insightful and far-sighted.
The commentary says: He was close to being self-reliant and decisive.
On the Rénchén day,
Tàizǐ Shǎoshī Xiāo Yǔ was again appointed Zuǒ Púshè.
Xiāo Yǔ had been dismissed from office last year.
read as “fú yòu fān”;
similarly for subsequent “fù” (復).
“Shǎo” (少),
read as “shǐ zhào fān”.
pronounced as “yǔ”.
On the Wùshēn day,
the Emperor discussed with his attendant officials the longevity of Zhōu and Qín.
Xiāo Yǔ replied:
“Zhòu was unprincipled,
and King Wǔ campaigned against him.
Zhōu and the Six States were innocent,
yet Shǐhuáng annihilated them.
Although the way they gained the empire was the same,
the hearts of the people were different.”
The Emperor said:
“You know one aspect,
but not the other.
Zhōu gained the empire
and further cultivated benevolence and righteousness.
Qín gained the empire
and increasingly valued deception and force. This is why their lifespans differed.
Indeed, the empire might be acquired through perverse means,
but it cannot be maintained without following the Way.”
Yǔ apologized for his inadequacy.
There was a severe drought in Shāndōng.
An imperial edict ordered relief where needed,
and remission of this year’s rent and taxes.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Rénzǐ day,
Lìbù Shàngshū Zhǎngsūn Wújí was appointed Yòu Púshè.
Wújí and the Emperor were commoner friends,
and he was also an imperial relative.
He had rendered meritorious service in establishing the dynasty.
Wújí
was the Empress’s brother,
and was credited for assisting in the execution of Jiànchéng and Yuánjí.
“Zhǎng” (長),
read as “zhī liǎng fān”.
No other official received such courteous treatment.
The Emperor had repeatedly wanted to appoint him as prime minister.
Ōuyáng Xiū said: The Táng, following the Suí system,
had the heads of the three departments – Shàngshūlìng, Shìzhōng, and Zhōngshūlìng – jointly deliberate on national affairs.
This was the role of the prime minister.
Later, since Tàizōng was Shàngshūlìng,
subordinates avoided daring to hold that position.
Therefore, the Púshè became the chief official of the Shàngshū Department,
and together with the Shìzhōng and Zhōngshūlìng, they were called prime ministers.
Since their rank and status were so exalted,
the Emperor did not wish to lightly bestow it upon people.
Thus, he often had other officials hold the prime ministerial role under a different title,
such as Dù Yān, who, as Lìbù Shàngshū, participated in discussing court affairs,
and Wèi Zhēng, who, as Mìshūjiān, participated in court affairs.
They were called “Cānyì Déshī” (Participator in Discussing Successes and Failures) or “Cānzhī Zhèngshì” (Participator in Political Affairs), and other such names,
which were not singular,
but all held the duties of prime minister.
“Shù” (數),
read as “suǒ jiǎo fān”.
The Empress said to the Emperor: “I occupy the position of Empress in the inner palace,
and my family’s honor and favor are extreme.
I truly do not wish for my brothers to again hold national political power.
Lǚ, Huò, and Shàngguān
serve as a bitter warning to us.
I hope Your Majesty will observe this with compassion!”
The Emperor did not heed her,
and ultimately appointed him.
21 Initially,
the Türks were pure and simple by nature,
and their governance was simple and brief.
However, Jíelì Kèhán obtained the Chinese man Zhào Déyán,
and entrusted him with affairs.
Déyán monopolized power and authority,
and frequently changed old customs,
making governance burdensome and harsh.
The people of the state began to be displeased.
Jíelì also preferred to trust various Hu people while alienating the Türks.
The Hu people were greedy and avaricious,
often disloyal,
causing warfare to erupt annually.
He frequently raised armies to attack those who rebelled,
thus there was no peaceful year.
Gèng,
gōng héng fān.
Hǎo,
hū dào fān.
Mào,
mò běi fān.
(Snow) reached several feet deep,
many livestock died,
and for successive years there was famine,
leaving all the people frozen and starving.
Jíelì's expenditures were insufficient,
so he heavily taxed various tribes.
As a result, there was internal and external discontent and resentment,
many tribes rebelled,
and his military gradually weakened.
Many who spoke on affairs requested to attack them.
The Emperor asked Xiāo Yǔ and Zhǎngsūn Wújí,
saying:
"Jíelì, his ruler and ministers are dim-witted and tyrannical;
their downfall is certain.
If we attack them now,
we have just made an alliance with them;
if we do not attack,
I fear we will miss the opportunity.
What should be done?"
Yǔ requested to attack them.
Wújí replied:
"To abandon faith and weary the people when the barbarians have not violated our borders
is not the act of a king's army."
The Emperor then stopped.
22 The Emperor asked his high-ranking officials for a long-term strategy for the state.
Xiāo Yǔ said:
"The Three Dynasties endured long through their feudal system,
while Qín stood alone and perished quickly."
The Emperor considered this to be true,
and thus discussions about establishing a feudal system began.
23 The Yellow Gate Imperial Attendant Wáng Guī had a secret memorial,
which he gave to the Attendant Counselor Gāo Shìlián,
but Shìlián suppressed it and did not report it.
The Emperor heard of this.
In the eighth month,
on the day of wù xū,
Shìlián was sent out as the Grand Commandant of Ānzhōu.
24 In the ninth month,
on the first day of gēng xū,
there was a solar eclipse.
25 On the day of xīn yǒu,
the Central Secretariat Director Yǔwén Shìjí was dismissed and made Palace Supervisor,
and the Censor-in-Chief Dù Yān participated in court governance.
The participation of other officials in governmental affairs began from this point.
Yān recommended the Supernumerary Official of the Board of Punishments, Dí Huáidào.
The Lang in the Board of Punishments
assisted the Minister and Vice Minister,
upholding their regulations and laws,
and discerning the severity of crimes.
Dí,
dīng lǐ fān,
is a surname;
in the Later Wèi there was Dí Zhēn.
【Yán:
"Dí"
changed to
"Zhì."
(Dù Yān) replied:
"When Yángdì was about to travel to Jiāngdū,
he summoned all officials to ask for advice on whether to go or stay.
Huáidào was a Principal Official in the Board of Civil Office.
Táng inherited the Suí system,
where all departments under the Minister had Principal Officials,
ranking ninth grade, upper class.
I personally witnessed it."
The Emperor said:
"You praise Huáidào as such,
why did you not remonstrate yourself?"
He replied:
"At that time, I did not hold an important position,
and I knew that remonstrance would not be heeded,
so to die in vain would be useless."
The Emperor said:
"You knew Yángdì could not be remonstrated with,
why did you serve in his court?
Since you served in his court,
how could you not remonstrate?
When you served Suí,
you could perhaps say your position was low;
later, you served Wáng Shìchōng,
becoming distinguished and prominent,
how could you still not remonstrate?"
He replied:
"I did not fail to remonstrate with Shìchōng,
but he simply did not listen."
The Emperor said:
"If Shìchōng were virtuous and accepted remonstrance,
he would not have lost his state;
if he were tyrannical and rejected remonstrance,
how did you escape calamity?"
Yān could not reply.
The Emperor said:
"Today you hold a respected position;
can you remonstrate now?"
He replied:
"I am willing to dedicate my life."
The Emperor laughed.
26 On the day of xīn wèi,
the Commandant of Yōuzhōu, Wáng Jūnkuò, plotted rebellion
and died en route.
Jūnkuò, while in the prefecture,
was arrogant, indulgent, and committed many unlawful acts.
He was summoned to the capital.
The Chief Clerk, Lǐ Xuándào,
who was a nephew of Fáng Xuánlíng,
entrusted Jūnkuò with a letter.
Jūnkuò privately opened it,
but not recognizing the cursive script,
suspected it was reporting his crimes.
When he arrived at Wèinán,
(Later Wèi established Wèinán Commandery between Xīnfēng and Zhèngxiàn.
Suí abolished the commandery and made it a county,
subordinate to Jīngzhào Yǐn,
located 115 lǐ east of Cháng'ān.)
he was about to flee to the Türks
but was killed by commoners.
27 The chieftains of Língnán, Féng Àng and Tán Diàn, et al., attacked each other.
Tán,
a surname;
Diàn,
a given name.
Genealogical records: Records of Shǔ say: In Jìn there was General Zhengdong Tán Bā.
Qiú,
cí yóu fān.
Zhǎng,
zhī liǎng fān.
Various prefectures reported Àng's rebellion,
numbering in the tens.
The Emperor ordered General Lìn Mó and others to mobilize troops from dozens of prefectures in Jiāng and Líng to suppress him.
Wèi Zhēng remonstrated, saying:

must be reviewed by officials of the fourth rank and above from the Zhongshū Shěng and Ménxià Shěng,
from the heads and deputies of the two departments down to the Jiànyì Dàfū (諫議大夫, Censor-in-chief).
This was to prevent unjust and excessive punishments.
Shortly after, when the prisoner Zhèng Shànguǒ (鄭善果, Inspector of Qízhōu) was brought forward,
the Emperor said to Hú Yǎn:
"Although Zhèng Shànguǒ is guilty,
his official rank is not low.
How can he be made to stand with common prisoners?
From now on, when officials of the third rank and above commit crimes,
there is no need to bring them before the court.
Let them await orders in the Cháotáng (朝堂, imperial court chambers)."
To the left and right of the Chéngtiānmén (承天門) of the Tàijí Gōng (太極宮) were the east and west Cháotáng.
"Cháo" (朝),
pronounced "zhí yáo fān";
the same below.
10 Within the Guānnèi (關內) region, there was a drought and famine.
Many people sold their children to obtain food and clothing.
On the day Jǐsì,
an edict was issued to use gold and silk from the imperial treasury to redeem them,
returning them to their parents.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
an edict was issued, stating that due to last year's continuous rain,
and this year's drought and locusts,
a general amnesty would be granted to the empire.
The edict briefly stated:
"If the year's harvest is abundant,
and the empire is at peace,
may disaster be transferred to Our person,
to preserve the myriad states.
This is Our wish,
and We would accept it without reluctance."
Coincidentally, there was rain in the affected areas,
and the people were greatly pleased.
11 Summer,
fourth month,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
an edict was issued stating that
"during the chaos at the end of the Suí dynasty,
followed by famine,
exposed corpses filled the fields,
distressing people's hearts and eyes.
It is proper to order local officials to collect and bury them."
12 Earlier, Tūlì Kèhán (突利可汗) of the Tūjué (突厥) had established his royal court directly north of Yōuzhōu,
ruling the eastern flank.
Dozens of tribes, including the Xī (奚) and Xī (霫), largely rebelled against the Tūjué and surrendered [to the Táng].
Xiélì Kèhán (頡利可汗) blamed him for losing these people.
When the Xuēyántuó (薛延陀), Huíhé (回紇), and other tribes defeated Yùgǔ Shè (欲谷設),
Xiélì sent Tūlì to suppress them.
Tūlì's army was again defeated,
and he fled back on a light cavalry.
Xiélì was enraged,
detained him for more than ten days, and flogged him.
Tūlì resented this,
and secretly wished to rebel against Xiélì.
Xiélì repeatedly demanded troops from Tūlì,
but Tūlì refused to provide them
and submitted a memorial requesting to enter the court.
The Emperor said to his attendants:
"In the past, the Tūjué were powerful,
commanding a million archers,
and they encroached upon the central plains.
Because of this, they became arrogant and lost their people.
Now, they themselves request to enter the court.
If not in dire straits,
would they do such a thing?
When We heard this,
We were both happy and fearful.
Why so?
When the Tūjué decline, the borders will be secure,
hence Our joy.
However, if We should stray from the right path,
in the future We too will become like the Tūjué.
How can We not be fearful?
You, Our ministers, should not hesitate to offer harsh remonstrances,
to assist Us in Our shortcomings."
Xiélì dispatched troops to attack Tūlì.
On the day Dīnghài,
Tūlì sent an envoy to request aid.
The Emperor deliberated with his ministers, saying:
"We and Tūlì are sworn brothers,
and when he is in trouble, We cannot fail to help him."
The brotherhood [sworn between them],
the event is seen in the previous volume, Gāozǔ, Wǔdé seventh year.
This refers to the oath at Wèiqiáo (渭橋),
seen in the previous volume, Wǔdé ninth year.
Dù Rúhuì (杜如晦, Minister of War) said:
"The Róngdích (戎狄) are untrustworthy and will eventually break their agreements.
If we do not take advantage of their disorder now to conquer them,
there will be no time for regret later.
'Seizing the disordered and humiliating the fallen'
is a phrase from the admonition of Zhònghuǐ (仲虺)."
The character '夫' (fū)
is pronounced 'fú'.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
the chieftain of the Qìdān (契丹) led his tribes to surrender.
Xiélì sent an envoy requesting to exchange Liáng Shīduō (梁師都) for the Qìdān.
The Emperor said to the envoy:
"The Qìdān are a different race from the Tūjué.
Now that they have come to surrender,
why do you demand them?
Shīduō is a man of the central plains,
he stole Our land
and oppressed Our people.
The Tūjué received and sheltered him.
When We raised an army to punish him,
you always came to his rescue.
He is like a fish swimming in a pot.
How can We worry that he won't become Ours?
Even if We could not capture him,
We would still never exchange him for people who have surrendered and joined Us."
Prior to this,
the Emperor knew that the Tūjué government was in disarray
and could not protect Liáng Shīduō.
He sent a letter to persuade him,
but Shīduō did not comply.
The Emperor sent Liú Mín (劉旻, Grand Administrator of Xiàzhōu) and Liú Lánchéng (劉蘭成, Sīmǎ) to scheme against him.
Mín and others repeatedly sent light cavalry to trample his crops,
widely spread disinformation,
and alienated his lord and ministers.
His state gradually weakened,
and those who surrendered followed one after another.
His famous generals Lǐ Zhèngbǎo (李正寶) and others plotted to capture Shīduō.
The plot was leaked,
and they fled to the Táng.
Because of this, suspicion grew between Shīduō and his subordinates.
Mín and others knew that Shīduō could be taken,
and submitted a memorial requesting troops.
The Emperor sent Chái Shào (柴紹, Right Guard General-in-Chief) and Xuē Wànjūn (薛萬均, Deputy Director of the Palace Attendants) to attack him,
and also sent Mín and others to occupy the eastern city of Shuòfāng to press him.
The capture of the eastern city is seen in Volume 190, Wǔdé fifth year.
Liú Lánchéng kept his flags lowered and drums muffled, not sallying forth.
Shīduō fled during the night.
Lánchéng pursued and attacked him,
defeating him.
The Tūjué sent a large army to rescue Shīduō.
Chái Shào and others encountered the Tūjué a few tens of *lǐ* before reaching Shuòfāng.
They fought fiercely,
heavily defeating them,
and then besieged Shuòfāng.
The Tūjué dared not rescue them,
and food ran out in the city.
On the day Rén'yín,
Shīduō's paternal cousin, Luòrén (洛仁), killed Shīduō
and surrendered the city.
Liáng Shīduō
had raised an army at the end of the Dàyè era of the Suí dynasty,
and was destroyed at this time.
The character '從' (cóng)
is pronounced 'cái yòng fān'.
13 Tàicháng Shǎoqīng Zǔ Xiàosūn
believed that the music of the Liáng and Chén dynasties contained too many Wú and Chǔ elements,
and that the music of the Zhōu and Qí dynasties contained too many Hú and Yí elements.
Therefore, he harmonized the northern and southern styles,
and, by examining ancient sounds,
created the Táng Yǎyuè,
comprising eighty-four modes, thirty-one pieces, and twelve *hé*.
Each *lǜ* has seven tones,
and the twelve *lǜ* comprise eighty-four modes in total.
The Suí dynasty had fourteen Huángxià pieces.
Zǔ Xiàosūn composed twelve *hé*,
in accordance with the perfect number of Heaven,
making a total of thirty-one pieces.
The twelve *hé* are:
1. Yùhé,
2. Shùnhé,
3. Yǒnghé,
4. Sùhé,
5. Yōnghé,
6. Shòuhé,
7. Shūhé,
8. Tàihé,
9. Zhāohé,
10. Xiūhé,
11. Zhènghé,
12. Chénghé.
Diào
is pronounced *tuó diào fān*.
Hé is pronounced as written.
The Hàn dynasty had a Xiélǜ Dūwèi,
who wore the seals and ribbons of a two-thousand-stone official.
The Táng dynasty's Xiélǜ Láng
was of the senior eighth rank,
subordinate to the Tàicháng Sì.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Zǔ Xiàosūn and others presented the new music.
The Emperor said:
"Rites and music
are merely teachings established by the sages based on human emotions.
How can the prosperity or decline of governance
depend on these?"
Yùshǐ Dàfū Dù Yān said:
"When Qí was about to fall,
the *Bànlǚ Qǔ* was composed.
During the time of Northern Qí,
Yáng Jùnzhī composed many six-character songs,
which were licentious and clumsy.
They were widely circulated among the people
and known as *Yáng Wǔ Bànlǚ*.
The *Yùshù Hòutíng Huā* was composed.
Dù Yòu said: 'The *Yùshù Hòutíng Huā*,
'Tángtáng Huánglí Liú',
and 'Jīnchāi Liǎngbìn Chuí'
were all created by Chén Hòuzhǔ.
He constantly sang and harmonized poetry with palace female scholars and court officials.
Tàilè Lìng Hé Xū selected the most frivolous and alluring among them to create this piece.
Those who heard it on the road wept sorrowfully.
How can it be said that the prosperity or decline of governance does not lie in music!"
The Emperor said:
"Not so.
Music can indeed move people,
so joyous people feel joy upon hearing it,
and sorrowful people feel sorrow upon hearing it.
Joy and sorrow reside in people's hearts,
not in the music itself.
When a government is on the verge of collapse,
the people are bound to be distressed,
and thus feel sorrow upon hearing music.
Now, both pieces exist.
If I play them for you,
will you be sorrowful?"
Yòuchéng Wèi Zhēng said:
"The ancients said, 'Rites, oh rites!
Are they merely jade and silk?
Music, oh music!
Are they merely bells and drums?'
The *Lúnyǔ* records Confucius' words.
They do not lie in sounds."
Your subject Guāng says: I have heard that Chuí could accurately draw circles and squares with his eyes,
and estimate curves and straight lines with his mind.
Chuí
was a skilled craftsman of ancient times.
Duó
is pronounced *tú luò fān*.
What he used to teach people
were always merely compasses and squares.
The sages attained without effort and understood without thought,
yet they could not impart this to others.
What they used to impart to others
were always merely rites and music.
Rites
are what the sages practiced;
music
is what the sages delighted in.
The sages practiced uprightness and delighted in harmony,
and furthermore desired to share this with all under Heaven,
and transmit it for a hundred generations.
It was then that they created rites and music.
Therefore, when a craftsman takes Chuí's compasses and squares and applies them to objects,
this is also Chuí's achievement.
When a ruler takes the rites and music of the Wǔdì and Sānwáng and applies them to the world,
this is also the governance of the Wǔdì and Sānwáng.
The Wǔdì and Sānwáng
have been gone for a long time.
Yet later generations, upon seeing their rites, know what they practiced;
upon hearing their music, know what they delighted in,
as clearly as if they still existed in the world.
Is this not the achievement of rites and music!
Indeed, rites and music have a root and an embellishment.
Central harmony
is the root;
external sounds
are the embellishment.
Neither can be abandoned.
The former kings upheld the root of rites and music;
it never left their hearts for an instant.
They performed the embellishment of rites and music;
it never left their persons for an instant.
It arose in the inner chambers,
manifested in the court,
extended to the villages and neighbors,
reached the feudal lords,
and flowed throughout the world.
From sacrifices and military campaigns to eating, drinking, and daily life,
they were never outside the scope of rites and music.
After decades or centuries of this,
then benevolent governance spread thoroughly,
and phoenixes came to appear.
If one lacks the root and merely has the embellishment,
practicing it for one day and abandoning it for a hundred,
to seek to change customs and transform habits
is indeed difficult.
This is why Emperor Wǔ of Hàn established the Xiélǜ
and sang of heavenly omens.
This was not unbeautiful,
yet it could not avert the imperial edict of sorrow.
(See the Basic Annals).
He examined the *lǜlǚ*.
This was not unrefined,
yet it could not save him from the disaster of Jiàntái.
(Wáng Mǎng ordered Liú Xīn to determine the *lǜlǚ*,
and Xīhé was in charge of them.
Bān Gù included this in his Treatise on Pitch-pipes and Calendars.
The affair of Jiàntái is found in the biography of the King of Huáiyáng in the Hàn dynasty.)
Jiàn
is pronounced *zǐ lián fān*.
He tuned metal and stone instruments.
This was not unthorough,
yet it could not quell the disaster of Píngyáng.
(Emperor Wǔ of Jìn ordered Xún Xù to standardize the bells and pitch-pipes.
The disaster of Píngyáng refers to the disgrace of Emperors Huái and Mǐn.)
He was not unperceptive,
yet he could not avert the humiliation of Táichéng.
(The four instruments refer to the "Four 通".
The event is found in Volume 145, Tiānjiān first year.
The humiliation of Táichéng is found in Volume 162, Tàiqīng third year.)
Although the Shùn music called Sháo,
the Yǔ music called Xià,
the Tāng music called Hù,
and the Zhōu Wǔwáng music called Wǔ
exist in the world
(Xià
is pronounced *hù yǎ fān*.
Hù
is pronounced *hù gù fān*),
they are not enough to commend it.
They cannot even transform a single man,
let alone all under Heaven!
This is like taking Chuí's compasses and squares
but having no skilled worker or materials,
sitting and waiting for an object to be made –
it will never happen.
How then could the decadent and confused rulers of Qí and Chén,
with their music of a dying state,
if briefly played in the court,
possibly change the sorrow and joy of an entire age?
(Zhàn
is synonymous with Zàn.
Lè
is pronounced *luò*.)
How easily he spoke
and how boldly he criticized the sages!
As for ritual, it is not merely a matter of dignified demeanor;
however, without dignified demeanor, ritual cannot be put into practice.
As for music, it is not merely a matter of sounds;
however, without sounds, music cannot be made manifest.
Take the example of a mountain:
it is not permissible to call a single clod of earth or a single stone a mountain;
yet, if all the earth and stones are removed,
where would the mountain be?
Thus it is said:
"Without a root, nothing can stand;
without form, nothing can proceed."
This records the words concerning ritual vessels.
How is this different from seeing a fist-sized rock and belittling Mount Tài (Tài Shān)?
If what is said were true,
then all the music created by the Five Emperors (Wǔ Dì) and Three Kings (Sān Wáng) would be mere fantasy.
"When a noble man (Jūnzǐ) comes across something he does not know,
he should leave it unquestioned."
The Analects (Lún Yǔ) records these words of Kǒngzǐ.
On the 14th day of the Wùzǐ month,
the Emperor (Shàng) said to his attending officials:
"I have read the collected works of Emperor Yáng (Yáng Dì) of Suí.
His writings are profound and extensive;
he also knew that Yáo (Yáo) and Shùn (Shùn) were right and Jié (Jié) and Zhòu (Zhòu) were wrong.
Yet, why were his actions so contrary?"
Wèi Zhēng (Wèi Zhēng) replied:
"Even if a ruler is sagely and wise,
he should still humble himself to accept others,
so that the wise will offer their strategies,
and the brave will exhaust their strength.
Emperor Yáng (Yáng Dì) relied on his exceptional talent,
became arrogant and self-serving.
Thus, he recited the words of Yáo (Yáo) and Shùn (Shùn) with his mouth, but committed the deeds of Jié (Jié) and Zhòu (Zhòu) with his body.
He was utterly unaware of this until his downfall."
The Emperor (Shàng) said:
"The past is not distant;
it serves as a teacher for us!"
On the 15th, there were locusts in the capital region (Jīnèi).
On the Xīnmǎo day,
the Emperor (Shàng) entered the imperial garden,
passing north of the Xuánwǔ Gate (Xuánwǔ Mén) into the Forbidden Garden (Jìn Yuàn).
He picked up several locusts
and prayed over them, saying:
"The people depend on grain for their lives,
and you eat it.
Better to eat my lungs and intestines instead."
He raised his hand as if to swallow them.
His attendants remonstrated, saying:
"Such a foul creature might cause illness."
The Emperor (Shàng) said:
"I am suffering this calamity for the people;
why should I avoid illness?"
He then swallowed them.
In that year,
the locusts did not become a disaster.
On the 16th, the Emperor (Shàng) said:
"Every time I preside over court,
if I wish to utter a word,
I never fail to think thrice,
fearing it might harm the people.
This is why I do not speak much."
Dù Zhènglún (Dù Zhènglún), a Gěishìzhōng (Gěishìzhōng) and Zhī Qǐjū Shì (Zhī Qǐjū Shì), said:
"My duty is to record words.
In ancient times, there were Left (Zuǒ) and Right (Yòu) Scribes.
When the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) spoke, the Left Scribe (Zuǒ Shǐ) recorded it;
when he acted, the Right Scribe (Yòu Shǐ) recorded it.
The Suí dynasty first established the Qǐjū Shèrén (Qǐjū Shèrén) position.
In the second year of Zhēnguàn (Zhēnguàn),
the Qǐjū Shèrén (Qǐjū Shèrén) was abolished,
and its duties were transferred to the Ménxià Shěng (Ménxià Shěng),
where two Qǐjū Láng (Qǐjū Láng) officials were appointed.
Those who held this concurrently with other posts
were called Zhī Qǐjū Zhù (Zhī Qǐjū Zhù) or Zhī Qǐjū Shì (Zhī Qǐjū Shì).
I must record your words;
it is not only for fear of harm in the present,
but also lest they incur criticism from later generations."
The Emperor (Shàng) was pleased
and bestowed upon him 200 bolts of silk.
On the 17th, the Emperor (Shàng) said:
"Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ Dì) of Liáng (Liáng) and his officials only discussed suffering and emptiness (kǔ kōng);
what they discussed was solely ascetic practices and empty stillness.
Officials were unable to ride horses.
When Emperor Yuán (Yuán Dì) was besieged by the Zhōu (Zhōu) army,
he was still lecturing on Lǎozǐ (Lǎozǐ),
with officials in military attire listening.
This incident is recorded in volume 165, during the third year of Chéngshèng (Chéngshèng) of Emperor Yuán (Yuán Dì) of Liáng (Liáng).
What I favor
is only the Way of Yáo (Yáo), Shùn (Shùn), Zhōu (Zhōu), and Kǒng (Kǒng).
I consider it like a bird having wings,
or a fish having water;
losing them means death,
they cannot be absent even for a moment."
On the 18th, concerning Péi Qiántōng (Péi Qiántōng), the Prefect of Chénzhōu (Chénzhōu),
he was an old acquaintance of Emperor Yáng (Yáng Dì) of Suí,
yet he committed regicide.
This incident is recorded in volume 185, during the first year of Wǔdé (Wǔdé) of Emperor Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ).

there should be

He had been repeatedly pardoned,
luckily escaping extermination of his clan,
but he could not still be allowed to govern the people.
Thus, an imperial edict stripped him of his office
and banished him to Huānzhōu (Huānzhōu).
In the first year of Zhēnguàn (Zhēnguàn),
Rìnán Commandery (Rìnán Jùn) of Dézhōu (Dézhōu) was renamed Huānzhōu (Huānzhōu).
"I rid the Suí (Suí) court and established Great Táng (Táng),"
he considered this his achievement,
and showed some signs of discontent.
When he fell from grace,
he died of resentment and anger.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,

an edict ordered Niú Fāngyù (Niú Fāngyù), Prefect of Láizhōu (Láizhōu), Xuē Shìliáng (Xuē Shìliáng), Prefect of Jiàngzhōu (Jiàngzhōu), Táng Fèngyì (Táng Fèngyì), Commandant-Long史 of Guǎngzhōu (Guǎngzhōu), and Yuán Lǐ (Yuán Lǐ), Martial Teeth Cavalry Commander (Wǔyá Lángjiàng) of Suí (Suí), all members of Yǔwénhuàjí's (Yǔwénhuàjí) faction, to be stripped of their offices and exiled to the frontier.
On the 20th, the Emperor (Shàng) said to his attending officials:
"There is an ancient saying: 'Amnesty is a blessing for villains,
but a misfortune for noble men (jūnzǐ).'
'Two amnesties in a year
make good people silent.'
Indeed, nurturing weeds harms good grain;
pardoning the guilty harms good citizens.
Therefore, since my ascension to the throne,
I have not wished for frequent amnesties,
fearing that villains would rely on them to casually violate the laws and regulations!"
