Hou Xietian Tai
Second year of Zhēnguàn (Zhēnguàn)
(Wùzǐ, 628)
1. In the ninth month,
on the Bǐngwǔ day,
it was first ordered that retired officials
should rank above those currently holding their respective ranks.
According to the Táng Huìyào (Táng Huìyào),
an edict at that time stated that civil and military officials, both inside and outside the court, who retired due to old age,
should attend court
and rank above those currently holding their respective ranks.
Guān (guān), read as gǔ wán.
2. The Emperor (Shàng) said:
"Recently, I have seen my sycophantic officials repeatedly submit memorials congratulating me on auspicious omens.
If families are well-provided and the people are content, but there are no auspicious omens,
it does not prevent one from being like Yáo (Yáo) and Shùn (Shùn);
if the common people are anxious and resentful, but there are many auspicious omens,
it does not prevent one from being like Jié (Jié) and Zhòu (Zhòu).
During the time of the Later Wèi (Hòu Wèi) dynasty,
officials burned entwined trees
and boiled white pheasants to eat them;
how could this be considered a time of utmost peace and order?"
On the Dīngwèi day,
an edict stated:
"From now on, only major auspicious omens may be reported in memorials."
According to the Rites and Regulations (Yí Zhì Lìng),
all auspicious stars (Jǐng Xīng) and auspicious clouds (Qìng Yún) are considered major auspicious omens,
of which there are sixty-four types;
white wolves and red rabbits are considered superior auspicious omens,
of which there are thirty-eight types;
dark ravens and red geese are considered medium auspicious omens,
of which there are thirty-two types;
auspicious grains (Jiā Hé), magic mushrooms (Zhī Cǎo), and entwined trees (Mù Lián Lǐ) are considered minor auspicious omens,
of which there are fourteen types.
Only inform the relevant authorities.
The Táng Liùdiǎn (Táng Liùdiǎn) states: The Director (Lángzhōng) of the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù),
whenever auspicious omens appear,
shall identify their names and types.
A pair of magpies had built a nest on a tree
that looked like a waist drum.
Attendants congratulated the Emperor.
The Emperor (Shàng) said:
"I always mocked Emperor Yáng (Yáng Dì) of Suí for his fondness of auspicious omens.
Auspiciousness lies in acquiring worthy individuals;
what is there to celebrate about this?"
He ordered the nest to be destroyed
and the magpies released into the wild.
3 It rained little that day.
The Palace Attendant, Lǐ Bǎiyào, submitted a memorial, saying:
“Although palace women were released in previous years,
I secretly hear that there are still many useless palace women
in the Grand Emperor Emeritus’s palace and the Yètíng Palace.
Not only do they waste food and clothing in vain,
but the accumulation of Yin energy
is also sufficient to cause drought.”
The Emperor said:
“It is indeed pitiable for women to be confined deep in the palace.
After sweeping and cleaning,
what else are they used for?
They should all be released
and allowed to seek partners.”
Thereupon, the Emperor dispatched the Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, Dài Zhòu, and the Remonstrance Official, Huánshuǐ Dù Zhènglún.
Huánshuǐ county
was established in the sixth year of Jiàndé of Zhōu by dividing the northeastern border of Línzhāng,
and belonged to Wèizhōu.
Huán
is pronounced as Yúyuán.
Over three thousand people were released both before and after this.
4 On the day Jǐwèi,
the Tujue raided the border.
Some court officials requested the repair of the ancient Great Wall.
The ancient Great Wall
was built by Qín Méngtián.
From Hàn to Suí,
many fortifications were built along the border,
but none of the Great Wall’s extension was like that of Qín.
Cháo
is pronounced as Zhíyáo.
The Emperor said:
“The Tujue suffer continuous calamities.
Jiélì does not fear and cultivate virtue,
his tyranny grows ever more severe,
and his own kin attack each other.
His demise is imminent.
I am about to clear the desert for you,
why bother the people to repair distant fortifications!”
5 On the day Rénshēn,
Dòu Jìng, formerly the Minister of Agriculture, was appointed Governor of Xiàzhōu.
While Jìng was at the Ministry of Agriculture,
the Vice Minister Zhào Yuánkǎi was skilled at amassing wealth.
Jìng disdained him
and loudly declared to his officials:
The officials of the Ministry of Agriculture
include Assistant Ministers and Chief Clerks,
and the Directors and Assistant Directors of the four departments of Shànglín, Tàicāng, Gōudùn, and Dǎoguān.
Tàicāng, Yǒngfēng, Lóngmén, and other granaries.
The Superintendencies of Sīzhú, Qìngshàn, Shímén, Wēnquán Tāng, and others,
the General Superintendency of the capital’s palaces and gardens,
the Superintendencies of various parks and gardens,
the Superintendencies of the four sides of the park,
the Superintendency of Jiǔchénggōng,
the Superintendencies of various salt ponds,
and the Superintendencies of various military colonies.
Each has a Deputy Superintendent and an Assistant Superintendent.
The General Superintendency of the park also has a Chief Clerk.
The Superintendencies of various salt ponds and military colonies do not have Deputy Superintendents.
“Emperor Yáng of Suí was extravagant and imposed heavy taxes,
so the Ministry of Agriculture could not do without you.
Today’s Son of Heaven is frugal and loves the people,
so what use are you now!”
Yuánkǎi was greatly shamed.
6 The Emperor asked Wáng Guī:
“Why have those who governed states in recent times been increasingly inferior to those of ancient times?”
He replied:
“In the Hàn era, Confucianism was esteemed,
and prime ministers were often scholars of the Classics,
thus customs were pure and honest.
In recent times, literature has been valued over Confucianism,
and laws have been incorporated,
this is why governance has increasingly declined.”
The Emperor assented to this.
7 In winter,
tenth month,
the Grand Censor and participant in court affairs, Ānjí Xiānggōng Dù Yān, passed away.
8 The Governor of Jiāozhōu, Suí’ān Gōng Shòu, was punished for his greed.
Suí’ān Gōng Shòu
was of the imperial clan.
Liánpíng Gōng Zhí
was summoned to the court,
and instructed with,
“Jiāozhǐ has long lacked a suitable person,
and requires your governance and pacification.”
Zǔ Shàng bowed in thanks and departed,
but then regretted it,
and declined on the pretext of an old illness.
The Emperor sent Dù Rúhuì and others to convey his will, saying:
“Even commoners uphold their promises,
to uphold one’s promises
is to value one’s promises.
Once a promise is made to someone,
it must be fulfilled.”
Zǔ Shàng firmly refused.
On the day Wùzǐ,
the Emperor again granted him an audience
and instructed him, but Zǔ Shàng remained unyielding.
The Emperor was greatly angered and said:
“If my emissaries do not comply,
how can I govern!”
He ordered him to be beheaded in the court hall.
According to the Cabinet’s map of Tàijígōng: the East and West Court Halls were on the left and right of Chéngtiānmén.
Chéngtiānmén
was the outer court.
In front of the East Court Hall was the Fèishí,
and in front of the West Court Hall was the Dēngwéngǔ.
Another day,
when discussing with his attendants
“what kind of person was Emperor Wénxuān of Qí?”,
Wèi Zhēng replied:
“Wénxuān was violent and tyrannical,
yet if someone disputed with him,
and the reasoning of the matter was sound, he would follow it.
There was the former Governor of Qīngzhōu, Wèi Kǎi, who returned from an embassy to Liáng,
and was appointed Governor of Guāngzhōu,
but he refused to go.
Yáng Zūnyàn reported this.
Wénxuān was angry,
summoned him, and rebuked him.
Kǎi said: ‘I previously held a major prefecture.
After returning from the embassy,
having rendered service without fault,
I was given a smaller prefecture.
This is why I refuse to go.’
Wénxuān looked at Zūnyàn and said: ‘His words are reasonable,
you may pardon him.’
This was his strength.”
Yáng Yīn,
courtesy name Zūnyàn,
served as prime minister to Emperor Wénxuān of Qí,
and was greatly trusted and favored.
“Indeed.
Although Lú Zǔshàng had earlier transgressed the duty of a subject,
my killing him was also too violent.
By this account,
I am inferior to Wénxuān!”
He ordered the restoration of his official rank and hereditary privilege.
Restoring his official rank
meant that his son or grandson could receive hereditary privilege.
According to the Táng system,
for all hereditary privileges: a first-rank official’s
son received a junior seventh rank, upper grade;
a second-rank official’s
son received a junior seventh rank, lower grade;
a third-rank official’s
son received a senior seventh rank, upper grade;
a junior third-rank official’s
son received a senior seventh rank, lower grade;
a senior fourth-rank official’s
son received a junior eighth rank, upper grade;
a junior fourth-rank official’s
son received a junior eighth rank, lower grade;
a senior fifth-rank official’s
son received a senior eighth rank, upper grade;
a junior fifth-rank official’s son, and the sons of imperial princes,
received a senior eighth rank, lower grade.
Officials of the third rank and above
could extend privilege to their great-grandsons;
officials of the fifth rank and above
could extend privilege to their grandsons.
A grandson’s rank was one grade lower than a son’s,
and a great-grandson’s rank was one grade lower than a grandson’s.
A posthumous official’s rank was one grade lower than a regular official’s,
but those who died in service were treated the same as regular officials.
The sons of commandery and county princes were treated the same as a junior fifth-rank official’s grandson.
The sons of county marquises and above were one grade lower.
The sons of a second-rank meritorious official were another grade lower.
The grandsons of the two former kings were treated as a senior third-rank official.
Wèi Zhēng’s appearance was not extraordinary, not exceeding that of an average person,
but he had courage and resourcefulness,
and was good at changing the ruler's mind.
He often risked offending the Emperor with bitter remonstrance;
sometimes, when the Emperor was very angry,
Wèi Zhēng’s expression remained unchanged,
and the Emperor would also calm his intimidating demeanor.
The ruler's authority
is weightier than thunder and lightning.
To "calm intimidating demeanor"
means like when the rain clears, the thunder and lightning also withdraw their power.
Later, he
said to the Emperor:
“People say Your Majesty wanted to go to Nánshān,
and preparations outside were all complete,
but then you didn't go.
Why is that?”
The Emperor smiled and said:
“Originally I did have that intention,
but I was afraid of your scolding,
so I stopped halfway.”
The Emperor once acquired a fine hawk,
and held it on his arm.
Seeing Wèi Zhēng approach,
he hid it in his bosom.
Wèi Zhēng presented his matters for so long without stopping
that the hawk eventually died in his bosom.
9 In the eleventh month,
on the Xīnyǒu day,
the Emperor sacrificed at Huánqiū.
In the first year of Wǔdé,
it was decreed that every winter solstice,
Hào Tiān Shàngdì should be sacrificed to at Huánqiū,
with Jǐng Huángdì as consort.
10 In the twelfth month,
on the Rénwǔ day,
Wáng Guī, a Palace Secretary, was appointed acting Attendant Councilor.
The Emperor once resided at leisure,
and conversed with Wáng Guī.
A beautiful woman attended at his side.
The Emperor pointed to her and said to Wáng Guī:
“This is a concubine of Lújiāng Wáng Yuàn.
Lújiāng Wáng Yuàn rebelled and died;
see juan 191, the 9th year of Wǔdé.”
Wáng Guī rose from his mat and said:
“Does Your Majesty consider it right
or wrong to have taken this woman from Lújiāng?”
The Emperor said:
“Having killed a man and taken his wife,
why do you ask about right or wrong!”
Wáng Guī replied:
“In the past, Qí Huánggōng knew that the reason Guō Gōng perished
was that he approved of good but could not employ it.
However, he discarded the person who spoke these words,
and Guǎn Zhòng considered him no different from Guō Gōng.
Qí Huánggōng passed by the ruins of the Guō clan
and asked the elders:
‘Why did Guō perish?’
They replied:
‘It approved of good and disliked evil.’
The Duke said:
‘If, as you say,
how did it come to perish?’
They replied:
‘It approved of good but could not employ it,
and disliked evil but could not remove it;
this is why it perished.’
Your subject believes that the sagely mind considers this to be correct.”
The Emperor was pleased,
and immediately sent her away,
returning her to her relatives.
The textual criticism states: The Shílù and the Xīn Jiù Shū all say,
“Though the Emperor did not send this beautiful woman away, he greatly valued his words.”
By examination, Tàizōng was a wise ruler;
since he valued Wáng Guī’s words,
how could he then disregard them and not act upon them!
Moreover, this person merely served at his side generally,
and was not a favored or famous individual.
What affection would Tàizōng have had to keep her!
Therefore, this account follows Zhēnguān Zhèngyào.
The Emperor ordered Zǔ Xiàosūn, a Lesser Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, to teach music to the palace women.
As his teaching was not to the Emperor's liking,
the Emperor reprimanded him.
Wēn Yànbó and Wáng Guī remonstrated, saying:
“Zǔ Xiàosūn is an elegant scholar.
To now make him teach music to palace women,
and then to censure him,
your subjects humbly believe this is improper.”
The Emperor angrily said:
“I have placed you gentlemen as my trusted advisors;
you should exhaust your loyalty and uprightness in serving me.
Instead, you side with inferiors and deceive your superior,
speaking on behalf of Zǔ Xiàosūn!”
Wēn Yànbó bowed and offered his apologies.
Wáng Guī did not bow,
saying:
“Your Majesty reproaches your subject for loyalty and uprightness;
are the words your subject now speaks personal bias?
This is Your Majesty having failed your subject,
not your subject having failed Your Majesty!”
The Emperor was silent and let the matter drop.
The next day,
the Emperor said to Fáng Xuánlíng:
“Since ancient times, it has truly been difficult for emperors to accept remonstrance.
I reprimanded Wēn Yànbó and Wáng Guī yesterday,
and I regret it to this day.
You gentlemen must not, because of this, fail to speak your mind completely.”
11 The Emperor said:
“Those who govern the people for me
are solely the Dūdū and Cìshǐ.
I always list their names on a screen
and observe them whether sitting or lying down.
When I learn of their good or bad conduct in office,
I note it beneath their names,
to prepare for their demotion or promotion.
County magistrates are especially close to the people
and must be chosen carefully.”
He then ordered all officials, civil and military, of the fifth rank and above,
to each recommend suitable candidates for county magistrate,
and report their names.
12 The Emperor said:
“Recently there have been cases of slaves accusing their masters of rebellion.
This is a corrupt practice.
Indeed, conspiracy to rebel cannot be done alone;
it must be shared with others.
Why worry that it won't be exposed?
Why must we rely on slaves to report it?
From now on, any slave who accuses his master
shall not be accepted,
and shall moreover be beheaded.”
13 Tǒngyèhù Kèhán of the Western Tūjué was killed by his paternal uncle.
The uncle then established himself
as Mòhèduō Hóu Qūlì Sīpí Kèhán.
The people of the country did not submit.
The Nǔshǐbì tribes supported Níshú Mòhèshè as Khagan.
The Western Tūjué had five Nǔshǐbì tribes,
and Níshú was also a tribal chief of Yīchuò.
Diélì Tèlēi, son of Tǒngyèhù,
fled the disaster from Mòhèduō
and took refuge in Kāngjū.
Níshú welcomed and enthroned him
as Yǐpí Bōluó Sìyèhù Kèhán.
He and Mòhèduō attacked each other,
engaging in ceaseless warfare,
and both sent envoys to request marriage.
The Emperor did not permit it,
saying:
“Your country is currently in chaos,
and the ruler and ministers are not yet settled.
How can you speak of marriage!”
He further instructed them to each maintain their territories
and not attack each other again.
Thereupon, all the various states in the Xīyù and the Chìlè tribes who had formerly been vassals of the Western Tūjué all rebelled against them.
Historians say that at this time, Fúhuá was in heaven,
and both the Eastern and Western Tūjué were in disorder.
14 Many tribes on the northern border of the Tūjué rebelled against Xiélì Kèhán and defected to Xuēyántuó.
They jointly enthroned their Qíjīn, Yínán, as Khagan,
but Yínán dared not accept.
The Emperor was planning to deal with Xiélì,
so he sent General of Agile Cavalry Qiáo Shīwàng, by a secret route, bearing an imperial edict to appoint Yínán as Zhēnzhū Pígā Kèhán,
and bestowed upon him drums and standards.
Yínán was greatly pleased,
sent envoys to pay tribute,
and established his court at the foot of Mount Yùdūjūn in the Great Desert.
His territory extended east to Mòhé,
west to the Western Tūjué,
south to the desert,
and north to the Jùlún River.
The Huíhé, Bá yě gǔ, Ādiē, Tóngluó, Púgǔ, and Xí tribes all became his subordinates.
Historians say that as the Tūjué declined, Xuēyántuó grew strong north of the desert.
1 In spring,
in the first month,

on the day Guǐhài,

Initially, there was a discussion about the location of the ceremonial field.
Gěishìzhōng Kǒng Yǐngdá said:
"According to the Rites,
the Son of Heaven ploughs the ceremonial field in the southern suburb,
and the feudal lords in the eastern suburb.
Even Emperor Wǔ of Jìn used the southeast.
Now, to do it in the eastern part of the city
does not conform to ancient rites."
The Emperor said:
"Rites are based on human sentiments;
how can there be a constant in them?
Moreover, the Book of Yú states: 'Order the works of the east.'
This shows that Yáo and Shùn respectfully imparted the proper season for people,
which was already in the east.
Furthermore, riding a blue carriage and carrying a dark ploughshare
is to conform to the qi of spring,
hence we know it corresponds to the east.
And since I reside in the land of Shàoyáng,
ploughing in the eastern suburb
is probably fitting."
Thereupon, it was settled.
According to the text, the Emperor called himself residing in the land of Shàoyáng,

Xuánlíng was intelligent and knowledgeable in governance,

18 Fáng Xuánlíng and Wáng Guī were in charge of the evaluations of inner and outer officials.
The Táng evaluation system: For all chiefs of the hundred bureaus,
their subordinates' merits and demerits were assessed annually,
and they were categorized into nine grades.
Officials within the 流內 (liú nèi) [of the bureaucracy]
were ranked by four excellences: 1. Their virtue and integrity were renowned;
2. They were clear, cautious, and manifestly upright;
3. They were fair and commendable;
4. They were diligent and unflagging.
Beyond these excellent qualities,
there were twenty-seven "bests":
1. Offering appropriate suggestions and replacing the inappropriate,
picking up omissions and filling gaps,
was the best for close attendants;
2. Selecting and evaluating personnel,
promoting all those with talent and goodness,
was the best for selection officials;
3. Praising the pure and condemning the turbid,
with praise and criticism always appropriate,
was the best for evaluation officials;
4. Ritual systems and ceremonies,
always conforming to the classics,
was the best for ritual officials;
5. Musical tones harmonizing perfectly,
without losing rhythm,
was the best for music officials;
6. Decisions made without delay,
with granting and taking reasonable,
was the best for judgment officials;
7. Troop management was orderly,
with guards faultless,
was the best for palace guards;
8. Soldiers were well-trained and disciplined,
and military equipment fully prepared,
was the best for commanding officers;
9. Investigations and interrogations uncovered the truth,
and judgments were impartial,
was the best for judicial officials;
10. Collating and proofreading were precise and thorough,
with clear editing and finalizing,
was the best for correcting officials;
11. Receiving directives and presenting memorials,
with clear and quick expression,
was the best for conveying and presenting officials;
12. Instruction and guidance were effective,
with students completing their studies,
was the best for education officials;
13. Rewards and punishments were strict and clear,
and battles were always victorious,
was the best for military generals;
14. Rituals and righteousness were promoted and practiced,
making their jurisdiction pure and clear,
was the best for political and educational officials;
15. Records were detailed and precise,
with both wording and reason well-executed,
was the best for literary and historical officials;
16. Investigations and inspections were precise and thorough,
and impeachments were always appropriate,
was the best for rectifying officials;
17. Inspection and review were clear,
with no hidden errors detected,
was the best for supervising officials;
18. Official duties were well-managed,
and provisions and services were robust and complete,
was the best for inspecting officials;
19. All assigned tasks were completed,
and laborers had no complaints,
was the best for labor officials;
20. Plowing and weeding were done on time,
and harvests met targets,
was the best for garrison farm officials;
21. Storage was careful,
and receipts and disbursements were clear,
was the best for warehouse officials;
22. Astronomical calculations of waxing and waning,
with precise research into principles,
was the best for calendar officials;
23. Astrological observation, medicine, and divination,
with many effective results,
was the best for arcane arts officials;
24. Inspection and control were effective,
and travelers faced no obstructions,
was the best for pass and ferry officials;
25. Markets were undisturbed,
and illicit activities were suppressed,
was the best for market officials;
26. Livestock were well-fed and multiplied,
with abundant reproduction,
was the best for pasturage officials;
27. Borders were peaceful and orderly,
and city walls and moats were well-maintained,
was the best for frontier defense officials.
One "best" and four excellences constituted "upper-upper";
one "best" and three excellences constituted "upper-middle";
one "best" and two excellences constituted "upper-lower";
no "best" but two excellences constituted "middle-upper";
no "best" but one excellence constituted "middle-middle";
duties roughly managed,
with no excellences or "bests" heard of,
constituted "middle-lower";
acting on personal likes and dislikes,
with judgments contrary to reason,
constituted "lower-upper";
turning from public duty to private gain,
with official duties neglected or deficient,
constituted "lower-middle";
serving as an official with flattery and deceit,
and manifest corruption and greed,
constituted "lower-lower."
All evaluations were gathered at the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng),
and then announced by grade before being presented to the emperor.
The emperor ordered Hóu Jūnjí to investigate this.
Wèi Zhēng remonstrated, saying:
"Fáng Xuánlíng and Wáng Guī are both veteran ministers of the court,
always trusted by Your Majesty for their loyalty and uprightness.
With so many evaluations,
how could there not be one or two inappropriate ones among them?
Examining their intentions,
they were ultimately not acting out of personal bias.
If the investigation finds fault in their conduct,
then none of them can be trusted,
and how could they again hold important responsibilities?
Furthermore, Wàn Jì has been in the evaluation hall constantly recently,
yet he never raised any objections or corrections;
it was only when he himself was not evaluated
that he began to make his arguments.
This is merely to incite Your Majesty's anger,
not to exhaust his sincerity in serving the state.
Even if an investigation finds truth in his claims,
it will not significantly benefit the court;
if his claims are baseless,
it will merely diminish Your Majesty's trust in your high ministers.
What your subject cherishes is the system of governance,
not daring to show partiality to these two ministers."
The emperor then dropped the matter and did not pursue it.
19 Púzhōu (Púzhōu) Inspector Páng Xiāngshòu was dismissed for corruption.
He pleaded that he had once served in the staff of Qínwáng (Qínwáng);

and wished to allow him to return to his former post.
Wèi Zhēng remonstrated, saying:
"The Qínwáng's attendants,
both inside and outside the court, are very numerous.
I fear that everyone will rely on personal favor,
which would deter those who wish to do good."
The emperor gladly accepted this,
and said to Páng Xiāngshòu:
"When I was Qínwáng,
I was the lord of one establishment;
now occupying the great position,
I am the lord of the four seas,
and cannot solely favor old acquaintances.
Since a high minister holds such a stance,
how dare I defy him!"
He bestowed silk upon him and sent him away.
Páng Xiāngshòu wept as he departed.

The Emperor said:

In the past, Qín Shǐhuáng performed the Fēngshàn sacrifice.
See *Shǐhuáng* 28th Year, scroll 7.
Would later generations consider Emperor Wén's virtue to be inferior to Qín Shǐhuáng's?
Moreover, to serve Heaven, one sweeps the ground and makes offerings.

is a great return to Heaven.

taking the position of *yáng*.
To sweep the ground and make offerings
is to show its plainness.'
Can erecting a few feet of earth
then allow one to express sincerity and reverence?"
However, his ministers continued to request it tirelessly.
The Emperor also wished to comply,

*Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù*, the *Tángshū Zhì*, and the *Táng Tǒngjì* all state that Tàizōng himself did not wish to perform the Fēngshàn sacrifice.

but Zhēng remonstrated and he stopped.
The intentions are quite different,
so both accounts are preserved here.
"Do you not wish me to perform the Fēngshàn sacrifice
because my achievements are not yet great?"
He replied:
"They are great!"
"Is my virtue not profound?"
He replied:
"It is profound!"
"Is China not peaceful?"
He replied:
"It is peaceful!"
"Are the four barbarian tribes not submissive?"
He replied:
"They are submissive!"
"Are the harvests not abundant?"
He replied:
"They are abundant!"
"Have auspicious signs not arrived?"
He replied:
"They have arrived!"
"Then why is it impossible to perform the Fēngshàn sacrifice?"
He replied:
"Although Your Majesty possesses these six conditions,
yet, after the great chaos at the end of the Suí dynasty,
the population has not recovered,
and the granaries are still empty.
If the imperial carriage tours eastward,
with a thousand chariots and ten thousand cavalry,
the supply and lodging expenses
are not easy to bear.

then all nations will gather,
and the rulers of distant barbarian tribes

plundering heavily before leaving.
The Kingdom of Yānqí bordered Gāochāng to the east.
This laid the groundwork for the expedition against Gāochāng.
On the Xīnwèi day
of the 12th month, an imperial banquet was held for officials of the third rank and above in the Dānxiāo Diàn.
The Emperor calmly remarked:
"The peace and order within and beyond the capital
are all due to the efforts of you, my lords and ministers.
However, Suí Yángdì's might extended over the barbarians and the Huáxià,
Xiélì ruled across the northern wilderness,
and Tǒngyèhù dominated the Western Regions;
now all have perished.
This is what I and you, my lords, have personally witnessed,
so do not boast of strength and prosperity and become complacent!"
On the 13th, the Xī Tūjué Sìyèhù Kèhán dispatched troops to attack Xuēyántuó,
but was defeated by Xuēyántuó.
Sìyèhù was by nature suspicious and cruel, and trusted slander.
There was Yìlì Kèhán,
who had the most accomplishments.
Yìlì
was a minor Kèhán of the Xī Tūjué.
"狠" (hěn)
is read as hù kěn.
He was executed,
and consequently, all the tribes felt insecure.
Sìyèhù also harbored jealousy towards Níshú, the son of Mòhèshè,
and secretly planned to kill him.
Níshú fled to Yānqí.
The tribes of Shèbēidáguān and Nǔshībì attacked him.
The old tradition writes
"設卑達官."
The *Kǎoyì* says: The new tradition writes
"沒卑達干."
We follow the old tradition here.
He soon died.
Sìyèhù was established as seen in the third year of the previous volume.
"騎" (qí)
is read as qí jì.
"卒" (zú)
is read as zǐ xù.
This was Duōlù Kèhán,
who sent envoys to pledge allegiance.
On the Dīngyǒu day,
Liú Shànyīn, the Junior Minister of the Hónglú, was sent to establish Duōlù as Xīlìbì Duōlù Kèhán.
In the intercalary month,
on the Yǐmǎo day,
the Emperor held a banquet for his close ministers in the Dānxiāo Diàn.
Zhǎngsūn Wújì said:
"Wáng Guī and Wèi Zhēng
were formerly enemies,
as they served the Crown Prince Yǐn and
advised him to plot against Your Majesty."
The Emperor said:
"Zhēng and Guī served with all their hearts;
that is why I employ them.
However, whenever Zhēng remonstrates,
and I do not follow,
he never responds when I speak to him.
Why is that?"
Wèi Zhēng replied:
"Your subject believes the matter to be unacceptable,
hence the remonstrance;
if Your
Majesty does not follow and your subject responds,
then the matter will proceed,
thus I dare not respond."
The Emperor said:
"Even if you respond and then remonstrate again,
what harm is there?"
He replied:
"In ancient times, Shùn cautioned his ministers: 'You must not agree to my face,
and then have dissenting words later.'
This is from the words of Yì and Jì in the *Shūjīng*.
If one merely agrees to the face,
how could that be the intention of Jì and Qì serving Shùn?"
The Emperor laughed heartily and said:
"People say Wèi Zhēng's demeanor is unconstrained and rude,
but to me, he appears even more charming.
It is precisely for this reason!"
Zhēng rose,
bowed and thanked, saying:
"Your Majesty opens me up to speak,
thus your subject can fully express his foolish thoughts;
if Your Majesty were to refuse and not accept,
how would your subject dare to repeatedly offend your imperial countenance?"
On the Wùchén day,
Yú Shìnán, the Junior Supervisor of the Secretariat, presented his "Shèngdé Lùn" (Treatise on Sage Virtue).
The Emperor bestowed a handwritten edict,
stating:
"Your treatise is too lofty.
How dare I compare myself to the ancients?
I am merely a little better than those of recent times.
However, you have only seen its beginning,
and do not know its end.
If I can be as careful at the end as at the beginning,
then this treatise can be transmitted;
but if not,
I fear it will only make later generations laugh at you!"
In the 9th month,
on the Jǐyǒu day,
the Emperor visited the Qìngshàn Gōng,
which was his former residence at birth.
The old residence of Gāozǔ's military achievements was made into Qìngshàn Gōng.
He composed a poem.
Lǚ Cái of Qīngpíng, the Palace Assistant Secretary,
Qīngpíng County
belonged to Bózhōu.
Liú Xù says: Originally Bèiqiū County in the Hàn dynasty,
called Qīngpíng in the Suí.
named it the "Gōngchéng Qìngshàn Yuè" (Music of Accomplishment and Auspiciousness).
He had eight rows of child dancers perform the "Jiǔgōng zhī Wǔ" (Dance of Nine Accomplishments).
A grand banquet was held,
with the "Pòchén Wǔ" performed concurrently in the courtyard.
Lǚ Cái had an ingenious mind,
so he was ordered to set the poem he composed to music for wind and string instruments, to be performed as a musical piece.
Sixty-four child dancers, wearing "Jìndé Guān" (Crowns of Advanced Virtue),
purple trousers and jackets,
long sleeves,
lacquered topknots,
and straw sandals, performed the dance,
known as the "Jiǔgōng Wǔ."
Their movements were steady and graceful,
symbolizing civil virtue.
The "Pòchén Yuè" (Music for Breaking the Enemy Formation),
known as the "Qīdé Wǔ" (Dance of Seven Virtues),
involved striking and thrusting back and forth,
with vigorous and forceful movements,
symbolizing martial prowess.
"陳" (chén)
is read as zhèn.
Tóngzhōu
was Fēngyì Prefecture.
"尉" (wèi)
is read as yū wù.
Jìngdé angrily said:
"What achievement do you have, to sit above me!"
Rènchéng Wáng Dàozōng, who sat below him,
tried to mollify him.
Jìngdé punched Dàozōng,
almost blinding him in one eye.
The Emperor was displeased and dismissed the banquet,
saying to Jìngdé:
"I saw Hàn Gāozǔ execute meritorious ministers,
and I often censured him for it.
Therefore, I wish to share wealth and honor with you, my lords,
and ensure that your descendants do not perish.
However, you have repeatedly broken the law in your official capacity,
which makes me realize that Hán and Péng being chopped into pieces
was not Gāozǔ's fault.
The laws of the state
are only rewards and punishments;
undeserved favors
cannot be repeatedly granted.
Strive to cultivate and restrain yourself,
lest you invite future regret!"
From then on, Jìngdé became fearful and disciplined himself.
In winter,
on the Yǐmǎo day
of the 10th month,
the imperial carriage returned to the capital.
The Emperor attended the Retired Emperor at a banquet in the Dà'ān Gōng.
The Emperor and the Empress personally presented food, drink, and personal items,
and the banquet concluded late into the night.
The Emperor personally carried the sedan chair for the Retired Emperor to the palace gate.
The Retired Emperor did not allow it,
and ordered the Crown Prince to take his place.
Xiélì Kèhán of the Tūjué was downcast and dispirited,
often weeping with his family,
and his appearance was emaciated.
The Emperor saw this and pitied him.
As Guózhōu had abundant deer,
in the first year of Yìníng, Guózhōu and Guójùn were established by dividing two counties from Hóngnóng.
Sòng Bái said: The *Dìwáng Shìjì* states that
there were three Guó: Zhōu enfeoffed Guó Zhòng in Xīguó,
which is the land of Guózhōu;
he enfeoffed Guó Shú in Dōngguó,
which is today Chénggāo;
Pínglù in Shǎnjùn is Běiguó.
So, Xiélì was made the Governor of Guózhōu;
Xiélì declined,
not wishing to go there.
On the Guǐwèi day,
he was again appointed General-in-Chief of the Right Guard.
In the 11th month,
on the Xīnsì day,
Qìbì tribal chieftain Hélì led more than six thousand households of his tribe to Shāzhōu and surrendered.
An edict ordered them to be settled between Gānzhōu and Liángzhōu,
and Hélì was appointed General of the Left Leader Guard.
On the 20th *gēngyín* day,
Chen Shúdá (陳叔達), the Grand Master of Remonstrance, Left, was appointed Minister of Rites.
The Emperor said to Shúdá (叔達):
"During the Wǔdé (武德) era, you offered forthright advice."
(See Volume 191, Gāozǔ (高祖) Wǔdé (武德) 9th year.)
*Dǎng* (讜)
(pronounced *dǎng* [黨]),
means good and forthright words.
He replied:
"Your servant witnessed the Suí (隋) dynasty's father and son slaughtering each other,
leading to chaos and ruin.
My words that day
were not for Your Majesty,
but for the sake of the state! "
On the 21st, in the twelfth month,
on the *guǐchǒu* day,
the Emperor discussed the fundamentals of security and danger with his attendant ministers.
Wēn Yànbó (溫彥博), the Minister of the Central Secretariat, said:
"I humbly wish that Your Majesty would always be as you were at the beginning of the Zhēngguān (貞觀) era,
then all would be well."
The Emperor said:
"Have I been negligent in governing lately?"
Wèi Zhēng (魏徵) said:
"At the beginning of the Zhēngguān (貞觀) era,
Your Majesty was intent on frugality
and tirelessly sought remonstrance.
Lately, construction and repairs have been somewhat excessive,
and those who remonstrate sometimes contradict your will.
This is the difference!"
The Emperor clapped his hands and laughed heartily, saying:
"Indeed, this is true."
On the 22nd *xīnwèi* day,
the Emperor personally reviewed the prisoners,
and seeing those condemned to death,
he pitied them,
released them to return home,
expecting them to return to face death in the autumn of the following year.
He then issued an edict that all death row prisoners in the empire
should be released,
to come to the capital at the appointed time.
In this year,
three hundred thousand Qiāng (羌) from the Dǎngxiàng (党項) tribe, both before and after, submitted to the empire.
Officials from the *gōngqīng* (公卿) and below repeatedly requested the Fēngshàn (封禪) ceremony.
The Emperor instructed them, saying:
"I have an old respiratory illness,
and I fear that ascending a high place would exacerbate it.
You gentlemen should speak no more of this."
On the 25th, the Emperor said to his attendant ministers:
"Lately, when I make decisions, I sometimes do not always adhere to the laws and regulations.
You gentlemen consider these matters small
and no longer press your advice.
However, all matters, without exception, grow from small to large.
This is the beginning of danger and ruin.
In the past, Guān Lóngpáng (關龍逄) died for his loyal remonstrance,
and I grieve for this every time.
Emperor Yáng (煬帝) perished due to his arrogance and tyranny,
which you gentlemen personally witnessed.
You gentlemen should always contemplate the demise of Emperor Yáng (煬帝) for me,
and I will always remember the death of Guān Lóngpáng (關龍逄) for you.
What then need we fear about ruler and ministers not preserving each other!"
On the 26th, the Emperor said to Wèi Zhēng (魏徵):
"When selecting officials,
one must not act hastily.
(Zhū Yuánhuì (朱元晦) said: *zàocì* (造次)
means a time of urgency and carelessness.
*Zào* (造) is pronounced *qī dào* [七到翻].)
If gentlemen are all appointed,
but if even one petty person is employed,

He replied:
"Indeed.
When the empire is not yet settled,
one focuses solely on talent,
without examining conduct;
but once chaos is pacified,
then those without both talent and conduct cannot be employed."
(Looking at this,
after the empire is settled,
how can one not be careful in selecting officials!)
On the 1st, in spring,
in the first month,

I request that the capture of Liú Wǔzhōu (劉武周), Xuē Rénguǒ (薛仁果), Dòu Jiàndé (竇建德), Wáng Shìchōng (王世充), and others be depicted."
The Emperor said:
"They were all heroes of their time,

If they were to see their former lords in a state of humiliation,

Yǔ (瑀) apologized, saying:

Wèi Zhēng (魏徵), wishing the emperor to cease military endeavors and cultivate civil arts,

On the 3rd, Lǐ Chúnfēng (李淳風) of the Bureau of Astronomy, from Yǒng Rén (雍人),
(Yǒng (雍) county

Lǐ Chúnfēng (李淳風) then reported: "Shùn (舜) used the *xuánjī* (璿璣) and *yùhéng* (玉衡) to regulate the seven celestial bodies,

The *Zhōu Lǐ* (周禮) states that the earth-gnomon was used to rectify the shadow of the sun and determine the center of the earth,
which showed evidence of the sun's movement along the ecliptic.
By the end of the Zhōu (周) dynasty,
this instrument was lost.
Hàn (漢) astronomer Luò Xiàhóng (洛下閎) made a celestial
sphere.
Later, Jiǎ Kuí (賈逵) and Zhāng Héng (張衡) also had such instruments,
but their calculations and observations of the seven luminaries
all followed the equator.
According to observation, at winter solstice it is furthest south,
and at summer solstice furthest north,
while the equator is always fixed in the middle.
It
seems
that the armillary sphere has lacked an ecliptic for a long time."
The Emperor found his explanation unusual
and thus decreed its construction.
The instrument
had three layers, inner and outer.
The base rested on a level foundation,
and the top was shaped like a cross,
with tortoise feet supporting the ends,
to hold four indicators.
One was called the Liùhé (六合) instrument,
with a double track for the celestial equator,
a golden ecliptic track,
and a golden regular track,
interconnected within the four cardinal points,
showing the twenty-eight lunar mansions, the ten
heavenly
stems, and three hundred sixty-five degrees of celestial longitude and latitude.
The second was called the Sānchén (三辰) instrument,
with a diameter of eight feet,
having a *xuánjī* (璿璣) track,
and the sun,
moon,
and celestial mansions'
paths
displayed,
rotating within the Liùhé (六合) instrument.
The third was called the Sìyóu (四游) instrument,
with a circular
dark
pivot, connected to the *yùhéng* (玉衡) movable tube, which passed through and constrained the rules and compasses.
Furthermore, the dark
pivot's
southern *jǔ* (矩) marked the earth's axis,
rotating laterally within,
with the *yùhéng* (玉衡) between the dark pivots,
moving north and south,
looking up to observe the celestial bodies,
and looking down to identify the instrument's shadow measurements.
All were made of bronze.
On the 4th, in summer,
in the fifth month,

"To obtain skilled craftsmen is to serve the affairs of the state.

"Xié"
is pronounced *yē*.
The Táng system: The Minister of Works is a third-rank official.

16 The Emperor asked Wèi Zhēng:
"Ministers' memorials are often insightful,
but when summoned for audience, they often speak disorderly.

He replied:
"I observe that when officials of various departments submit memorials,

But when they stand before Your Majesty,
they cannot articulate even a third of what they intended.
Moreover, remonstrators contradict intentions and touch upon taboos.
'Fú'
is the same as 'fú' (咈).
How could they dare to express their full feelings?"
Because of this, the Emperor's demeanor and words towards his ministers became even warmer.
He once said:
"Emperor Yáng was often suspicious and wary,
and when holding court, often said little to his ministers.
I am not like that;
I treat my ministers as closely as if we were one body."

3 The Emperor wished to dispatch high officials as Cȟùzhì Dàshǐ to various circuits,
but he had not found the right people.
Lǐ Jìng recommended Wèi Zhēng.
The Emperor said:
“Zhēng constantly advises me on my shortcomings,
and I cannot be without him by my side for even a single day.”
So he ordered Jìng and Tàicháng Qīng Xiāo Yǔ, and a total of thirteen others, to travel throughout the realm,
“to observe whether senior officials are worthy or unworthy,
to inquire about the hardships of the common people,
to show respect to the elderly,
to relieve the poor,
and to release those long imprisoned,
so that wherever the envoys arrive,
it will be as if I had personally witnessed it.”
4 In the third month,
on the day Gēngchén,
the Emperor visited Jiǔchéng Gōng.
5 In summer,
in the fifth month,
on the first day, Xīnwèi,
there was a solar eclipse.
6 Initially,
Fúyùn, the Kèhán of Tǔyùhún,
[pronunciation notes omitted]
had not returned [from a previous raid],
and greatly plundered Shànzhōu before departing.
The Emperor sent an envoy to rebuke him,
summoning Fúyùn to court.
He claimed illness and did not come,
still seeking a marriage alliance for his son Zūnwáng.
The Emperor agreed,
ordering him to personally come for the bride.
Zūnwáng again did not come,
so the marriage was broken off.
Fúyùn then sent troops to raid Lán and Kuò prefectures.
[notes omitted]
Believing in the counsel of his minister, Tiānzhùwáng,
he repeatedly violated the border.
He also detained Zhào Dékǎi, an envoy from Táng.
The Emperor sent envoys to remonstrate with him
ten times.
He also summoned Fúyùn's envoys,
and personally explained to them the consequences of fortune and misfortune from the throne.
But Fúyùn ultimately showed no change of heart.
In the sixth month,
he dispatched Zuǒ Xiāowèi Dàjiàngjūn Duàn Zhìxuán as Xīhǎidào Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn,
and Zuǒ Xiāowèi Jiàngjūn Fán Xīng as Chìshuǐdào Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn,
leading border troops and the forces of the Qìbì and Dǎngxiàng to attack him.
[notes omitted]

[notes omitted]

7 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
there were great floods between Shāndōng, Hénán, Huái, and Hǎi.
8 The Emperor repeatedly invited the Retired Emperor to escape the summer heat at Jiǔchéng Gōng.
The Retired Emperor, because Suí Wéndì had died there,
detested it.
[notes omitted]
[notes omitted]

Dàmíng Gōng was constructed.
[notes omitted]
Before it was completed, the Retired Emperor fell ill,
and was unable to reside there.
9 On the day Xīnchǒu,
Duàn Zhìxuán attacked Tǔyùhún,
defeating them.
He pursued the fleeing enemy for over eight hundred *lǐ*,
stopping more than thirty *lǐ* from Qīnghǎi.
[notes omitted]
[pronunciation notes omitted]
10On the day Jiǎzǐ,
the Emperor returned to the capital.
11Yòu Púyè Lǐ Jìng requested to retire due to illness,
and it was granted.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Xīnwèi,
Jìng was appointed Tèjìn,
with his titles and peerage remaining as before.
His emoluments, allowances, officials, and soldiers were all to be provided as before,
and once his illness slightly improved,
he was to come to the Ménxià and Zhōngshū [departments] every two or three days to 平章政事 (deliberate on government affairs).
[notes omitted]
On the 12th day of the *jiǎshēn* (甲申) month,
the Tǔfān Zānpǔ, Qìzōngnòngzàn (棄宗弄讚),
an alternative account states: In the *Tàizōng Shílù* (太宗實錄),
"Zānpǔ" (贊普)
is written

In the *Gāozōng Shílù* (高宗實錄),
"Qìzōng" (棄宗)
is written

again requested a marriage alliance.
Tǔfān (吐蕃) was southwest of Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾),
and in recent times, it had grown stronger,
gradually encroaching upon other states,
with a vast territory
and hundreds of thousands of crack troops,
yet it had never communicated with China.
Its king was called Zānpǔ (贊普),
and by custom, surnames were not spoken.
All royal family members were called Lùn (論),
and all official families were called Shàng (尚).
Tǔfān (吐蕃) was originally a branch of the Xīqiāng (西羌),
numbering about one hundred and fifty tribes,
scattered between the Hé (河), Huáng (湟), Jiāng (江), and Mín (岷) rivers.
Among them were the Fāqiāng (發羌) and Tángmáo (唐旄), etc.,
who had never communicated with China,
residing west of the Xīzhī (析支) River.
Their ancestor was called Hútíbóxīyě (鶻提勃悉野),
who was brave and resourceful.
He gradually annexed the various Qiāng (羌) tribes
and occupied their land.
Fān (蕃) and Fā (發) sound similar,
hence his descendants were called Tǔfān (吐蕃) and had the surname Bósūyě (勃窣野).
Some say: They were descendants of Tūfà Wūgū (禿髮烏孤) of Southern Liáng (南涼).
His two sons,
Fánní (樊尼)
and Rùtán (傉檀),
were destroyed by Qǐfú Chìpán (乞伏熾盤).
Fánní (樊尼) led his remaining forces to surrender to Jǔqú Méngxùn (沮渠蒙遜).
When Jǔqú (沮渠) destroyed Fánní (樊尼),
he led troops to cross the river westward,
passed over Jīshí (積石) Mountain,
and subsequently brought the various Qiāng (羌) under his control.
Their custom was to call a strong hero "Zàn" (贊),
and a man "Pǔ" (普),
hence their ruler was called Zānpǔ (贊普).
Their land was eight thousand *lǐ* (里) directly west of Cháng'ān (長安),
and five hundred *lǐ* (里) from Shànshàn (鄯善).
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: Tǔfān (吐蕃)
are descendants of the Tūfà (禿髮) clan,
the name corrupted to Tǔfān (吐蕃).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Fánní (樊尼) fled to Jǔqú Méngxùn (沮渠蒙遜),
who appointed him Administrator of Línsōng (臨松) Commandery.
When Jǔqú (沮渠) was destroyed,
he established a state in the western lands
and changed his surname to Bósūyě (勃窣野).
People at the time called an administrator "Zànfǔ" (贊府),
which was corrupted to Zānpǔ (贊普).
Tǔ (吐),
from *tūn* (暾) in the entering tone.
Its neighbors feared it.
The Emperor sent the envoy Féng Déxiá (馮德遐) to comfort and conciliate them.
On the 13th day of the *dīnghài* (丁亥) month,
Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) raided Liángzhōu (涼州).
On the *jǐchǒu* (己丑) day,
an imperial edict was issued to launch a major campaign against Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾).
An alternative account states: The old tradition says:
"Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) detained Zhào Dékǎi (趙德楷).
Tàizōng (太宗) sent envoys to declare his will more than ten times,
but they showed no sign of repentance.
In the ninth year,
an edict ordered Lǐ Jìng (李靖) and others to attack."
In the *Tàizōng Shílù* (太宗實錄),
on the *jǐchǒu* (己丑) day,
Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) detained our messenger Zhào Dékǎi (趙德楷),
and this edict was immediately issued.
In the twelfth month,
Lǐ Jìng (李靖) and others were sent.
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄).
According to the old tradition,
the detention of Dékǎi (德楷) happened earlier;
according to the *Shílù* (實錄),
envoys were first sent to declare the imperial will,
then Dékǎi (德楷) was detained,
and an edict to attack was immediately issued.
We now include both.
Because of his old age,
it was difficult to burden him.
*Zhòng* (重),
means difficult.
Because of his old age, it was difficult to burden him with matters of military expedition.
*Jiāng* (將),
pronounces as *jiàng*.
*Wèi* (為),
pronounces as *wèi*.
He requested to go;
the Emperor was greatly pleased.
In the twelfth month,
on the *xīnchǒu* (辛丑) day,
Jìng (靖) was made Grand General of the Xīhǎi (西海) Marching Army,
to command all forces.

The Minister of War, Hóu Jūnjí (侯君集), was made Army Commander of the Jīshí (積石) Route; the Minister of Justice, Rènchéng Wáng Dáozōng (任城王道宗), was made Army Commander of the Shànshàn (鄯善) Route; the Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州), Lǐ Dàliàng (李大亮), was made Army Commander of the Qiěmò (且末) Route; the Governor of Mínzhōu (岷州), Lǐ Dáoyàn (李道彥), was made Army Commander of the Chìshuǐ (赤水) Route; the Prefect of Lìzhōu (利州), Gāo Zèngshēng (高甑生), was made Army Commander of the Yánzé (鹽澤) Route.
Xīhǎi (西海), Shànshàn (鄯善), and Qiěmò (且末) were all names of commanderies established by the Suí (隋) dynasty after defeating Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾).
Jīshí (積石) Mountain was in the Suí (隋) dynasty's Héyuán (河源) Commandery.
Chìshuǐ (赤水) City was also in Héyuán (河源) Commandery.
The Salt Lake was in Xīhǎi (西海) Commandery.
Rèn (任),
pronounced *rén*.
Shàn (鄯),
pronounced *shàn*.
Qiě (且),
pronounced *qiě*.
On the 14th, the Emperor sought to appoint Zhèng Rénjī's (鄭仁基) daughter, a *tōngshì shèrén* (通事舍人) of the Suí (隋) dynasty, as a *chōnghuá* (充華).
*Chōnghuá* (充華) was an old title.
The Tang (唐) dynasty's six palace offices did not include this position.
When the envoy bearing the册 (册) was about to depart,
Wèi Zhēng (魏徵) heard that she had previously been promised in marriage to a scholar, Lù Shuǎng (陸爽),
and immediately submitted a memorial remonstrating against it.
The Emperor heard of it and was greatly surprised,
issuing a handwritten edict deeply criticizing himself,
and ordering the cancellation of the envoy's departure.
Fáng Xuánlíng (房玄齡) and others reported:
"The promise of marriage to the Lù (陸) clan
had no clear evidence,
and since the great ceremony was about to take place,
it should not be stopped."
Shuǎng (爽) also submitted a memorial stating that there had never been any discussion of marriage.
The Emperor said to Zhēng (徵):
"The various officials might attempt to curry favor;
but Shuǎng (爽) also stated his case,
why is this?"
He replied:
"They believe that although Your Majesty outwardly dismisses it,
you might secretly add punishment or condemnation,
hence they had no choice but to do so."
The Emperor smiled and said:
"Outsiders might indeed think so.
Does my word not inspire complete trust to this extent!"
On the 15th, Huángfǔ Désān (皇甫德參), the Chief Clerk of Zhōngmóu (中牟),
Zhōngmóu (中牟) County,
belonged to Hénán (河南) Commandery during the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
to Xíngyáng (滎陽) Commandery during the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
and to Guǎngwǔ (廣武) Commandery during the Later Wèi (魏) dynasty,
serving as its administrative seat;
in the tenth year of Kāihuáng (開皇) of the Suí (隋) dynasty,
it was renamed Jiáchéng (郟城) County,
in Dàyè (大業) it was renamed Pǔtián (圃田) County,
and in the third year of Wǔdé (武德) of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
it was again named Zhōngmóu (中牟).
The Chief Clerk
was the assistant to the magistrate, managing county affairs.
The Chief Clerk of a superior county was of rank eight, lower class;
those of medium and inferior counties each dropped one rank in difference.
reported: "The construction of Luòyáng (洛陽) Palace
burdens the people;
the collection of land rent
is excessive;
the custom of high coiffures
is likely influenced by the palace."
The Emperor was angry
and said to Fáng Xuánlíng (房玄齡) and others:
"Does Désān (德參) want the state to not employ a single person,
not collect a single *dǒu* (斗) of rent,
and all palace women to have no hair,
only then will he be satisfied!"
He intended to punish him for the crime of slander.
Wèi Zhēng (魏徵) remonstrated:
"Jiǎ Yì (賈誼), during the reign of Emperor Wén (文) of Hàn (漢), submitted a memorial
saying, 'There is one thing to weep bitterly over,
and two things to shed tears over.'
See volume 14, sixth year of Emperor Wén (文) of Hàn (漢).
If he could not move the heart of the ruler,
it is what is called 'the words of a madman, from which the sage chooses.'
The *Hànshū* (漢書), Lǐ Zuǒchē (李左車) has this saying.
The Emperor said:
"If I punish this man,
then who will dare to speak again!"
So he bestowed twenty bolts of silk.
Another day,
Zhēng (徵) reported:
"Your Majesty has recently not been fond of straightforward speech.
Although you reluctantly tolerate it,
it is not as open-minded as before."
The Emperor then gave him even more generous rewards
and appointed him Censor-Investigator (*jiānchá yùshǐ* 監察御史).
16 In the sixteenth year [of the reign], Zhōngshū Shèrén Gāo Jìfǔ (高季輔) submitted a memorial:
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: In *Zhēngguàn Zhèngyào* (貞觀政要),
Jìfǔ’s (季輔) memorial is placed in the third year [of Zhēngguàn];
in *Huìyào* (會要), it is in the eighth year.
According to old accounts: Jìfǔ (季輔) was appointed Yùshǐ (御史) in the early years of Zhēngguàn (貞觀),
and successively transferred to Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人).
Therefore, it is placed here according to *Huìyào* (會要).
"Low-ranking officials in the provinces
have not yet received their stipends;
with hunger and cold pressing upon them,
it is difficult to maintain their integrity.
Now that the granaries are gradually full,
it is advisable to appropriately increase their generous provisions.
Only then can they be held accountable for not being greedy,
and strict prohibitions be imposed.
Furthermore,
Mìwáng Yuánxiǎo (密王元曉) and others are all Your Majesty's younger brothers.
I have observed the Emperor's sons bowing to their paternal uncles,
and the uncles returning the bows,
which disrupts the order of seniority (zhāomù).
It is advisable to instruct them in proper etiquette."
When the memorial was presented,
the Emperor approved of it.
17 The Western Tujue (突厥) Duōlù Kèhán (咄陸可汗) died.
His younger brother, Tóng'é Shèlì (同娥設立),
became Shābōluó Dìlìshī Kèhán (沙鉢羅咥利失可汗).
1 In spring,
in the first month,
the Dǎngxiàng (党項) who had previously submitted to the court all rebelled and returned to Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾).
In the third month,
on the day *gēngchén*,
the Qiāng (羌) of Táozhōu (洮州) rebelled and entered Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾),
killing the Cìshǐ (刺史) Kǒng Chángxiù (孔長秀).
2 On the day *rénchén*,
a general amnesty was granted throughout the empire.
3 On the day *yǐyǒu*,
Yánzé Dào Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn (鹽澤道行軍總管) Gāo Zèngshēng (高甑生) attacked the rebellious Qiāng (羌)
and defeated them.
4 On the day *gēngyín*,
an edict was issued stating that the people's wealth should be divided into three classes,
but the details were not exhaustive,
and it should be divided into nine classes.
*Táng Huìyào* (唐會要) states: In the sixth year of Wǔdé (武德),
in the third month,
an order was issued for all households in the empire to assess their assets
and categorize them into three classes.
Now, dividing them into nine classes
means that each of the three classes is further divided into upper, middle, and lower.
5 The Emperor said to Wèi Zhēng (魏徵):
"Qí Hòuzhǔ (齊後主) and Zhōu Tiānyuán (周天元) both heavily taxed the common people
and lavishly provided for themselves,
collapsing when their resources were exhausted.
This is like a glutton eating his own flesh;
when the flesh is gone, he dies.
How foolish!
However, which of these two rulers was superior or inferior?"
He replied:
"Qí Hòuzhǔ (齊後主) was weak and indecisive,
with governance emanating from many sources;
Zhōu Tiānyuán (周天元) was arrogant and tyrannical,
with power and authority concentrated in himself.
Although both led to the downfall of their states,
Qí Hòuzhǔ (齊後主) was still inferior."
6 In summer,
in the intercalary fourth month,
on the day *guǐyǒu*,
Rènchéngwáng Dàozōng (任城王道宗) defeated Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) at Kùshān (庫山).
Fúyǔn (伏允), the Kèhán (可汗) of Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾), burned all the wild grasses
and fled into the desert (qì) with light troops.
*Qì* (磧) is pronounced *qì* (七迹翻).
"The horses have no grass and are thin and weak;
it is not advisable to advance deep into enemy territory."
Hóu Jūnjí (侯君集) said:
"No.
Earlier, when Duàn Zhìxuán’s (段志玄) army returned,
as soon as they reached Shànzhōu (鄯州),
the barbarians had already arrived at its city walls.
This was because the barbarian state was still intact,
and its people served them.
Now, after a single defeat,
they are scattered like rats and birds,
their scouts are cut off,
and their rulers and subjects are separated,
fathers and sons lost to each other.
Taking them will be easier than picking up straws.
If we do not seize this opportunity,
we will surely regret it later."
Lǐ Jìng (李靖) agreed with him.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The old biography of Dàozōng (道宗) says:
"Dàozōng (道宗) strongly requested pursuit,
and Lǐ Jìng (李靖) approved,
but Jūnjí (君集) did not agree."
Jìng’s (靖) biography says:
"The army reached Fúsìchéng (伏俟城),
and Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) burned the wild grasses to starve our army,
retreating to Dàfēichuān (大非川).
All the generals said:
'The spring grasses have not yet grown,
and the horses are already emaciated;
we cannot advance against the enemy.'
Only Jìng (靖) was determined to advance
deep into enemy territory,
and thus crossed the Jīshíshān (積石山)."
According to the *Shílù* (實錄):
"After the victory at Kùshān (庫山),
the Kèhán (可汗) planned to enter the desert to avoid the government army.
Dàozōng (道宗) again said:
'Bǎihǎi (柏海) is near the source of the river,
and few have reached it since ancient times.
Since the bandits have fled west,
their whereabouts are unknown.
Duàn's (段) current advance
relies on the strength of the horses.
Now the horses are weary and provisions are scarce,
making a distant advance difficult.
It is better to go to Shànzhōu (鄯州) for now,
and after the horses have recovered,
plan further offensives.'
Jūnjí (君集) said:
'Not so.
When Duàn Zhìxuán (段志玄) previously merely reached Shànzhōu (鄯zhou),
the enemy forces immediately arrived at the city walls,
because their country was still intact,
and their fierce followers resisted orders.
Now, after a single defeat,
their scouts are also cut off,
their rulers and subjects are separated,
and fathers and sons are estranged.
Taking advantage of their fear and desperation,
capturing them is like picking up something that has fallen.
Although Bǎihǎi (柏海) is far away,
we can march straight there.'
Jìng (靖) again agreed with him."
The biography of Dàozōng (道宗) contradicts the *Shílù* (實錄).
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄). Jūnjí (君集) and Rènchéngwáng Dàozōng (任城王道宗) took the southern route.
On the day *wùzǐ*,
Jìng’s (靖) subordinate, Xuē Gū'ér (薛孤兒), defeated Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) at Mántóushān (曼頭山),
beheaded their famous prince,
and captured a large quantity of livestock
to serve as military provisions.
On the day *guǐsì*,
Jìng (靖) and others defeated Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) at Niúxīnduī (牛心堆).
*Shuǐjīngzhù* (水經註) states: The Huángshuǐ (湟水) flows east from Línqiāngxiàn (臨羌縣),
joins the Lóngjūchuān (龍駒川) water,
then flows east to join the Jìnchāngchuān (晉昌川) water,
then flows east to join the Chángníngchuān (長寧川) water,
then flows east to join the Niúxīnchuān (牛心川) water;
this water originates from the distant mountains in the southwest,
flows northeast past Niúxīnduī (牛心堆),
then flows east past the west of Xīpíngtíng (西平亭),
and then flows northeast into the Huángshuǐ (湟水).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: *Shílù* (實錄):
"On the day *guǐsì*,
Lǐ Jìng (李靖), Hóu Jūnjí (侯君集), Rènchéngwáng Dàozōng (任城王道宗) and others defeated Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) at Chìshuǐyuán (赤水源)."
According to the text above, after Kùshān (庫山), the troops and horses were divided into two routes:
Jìng (靖) took the northern route out of Mántóushān (曼頭山)
and crossed Chìshuǐ (赤水);
Jūnjí (君集) and Dàozōng (道宗) took the southern route,
passing through Luózhēngǔ (破邏真谷).
Therefore, Jūnjí (君集) and Dàozōng (道宗) were not present at the Battle of Chìshuǐ (赤水).
We now delete their names.
Furthermore, the biography of Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) states that their Gāochāngwáng Mùróng Xiàojùn (高昌王慕容孝儁) was captured,
but it is unknown in which battle;
we also delete this.
In mid-summer, frost fell,
and they passed through Luózhēngǔ (破邏真谷),
where there was no water.
People gnawed ice,
and horses ate snow.
In the fifth month,
Fúyǔn (伏允) was overtaken at Wūhǎi (烏海).
*Suí Zhì* (隋志) states: Hèyuánjùn (河源郡) has Wūhǎi (烏海),
west of Hàn Kūshān (漢哭山).
They inflicted a great defeat,
capturing their famous prince.
Xuē Wànjūn (薛萬均) and Xuē Wànchè (薛萬徹) again defeated Tiānzhùwáng (天柱王) at Chìhǎi (赤海).
Chìhǎi (赤海) is probably the deep and wide part of Chìshuǐ (赤水).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The old biography of Wànchè (萬徹) says Chìshuǐyuán (赤水源),
and the biography of Qìbì Hélì (契苾何力) says Chìshuǐchuān (赤水川).
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄).
7 The Tàishàng Huáng (太上皇) had suffered from a stroke since last autumn.
On the day *gēngzǐ*,
he passed away at the Chuígǒngdiàn (垂拱殿).
*Jiùshū Dìjì* (舊書帝紀) states: He passed away at the Chuígǒngqiándiàn (垂拱前殿) of Dà'āngōng (大安宮) at the age of seventy.
On the day *jiǎchén*,
officials requested the Emperor to take charge of military and national affairs in accordance with the last will,
but the Emperor refused.
On the day *yǐsì*,
an edict was issued for Tàizǐ Chénggān (太子承乾) to manage governmental affairs in the Eastern Palace.
8 In the Battle of Chìshuǐ,
Xuē Wànjūn and Xuē Wànchè advanced with light cavalry,
but were surrounded by the Tǔyùhún.
Both brothers were struck by spears,
lost their horses, and fought on foot.
Six or seven tenths of their cavalry died.
Zuǒ Lǐngjūn Jiàngjūn Qìbì Hélì led several hundred cavalry to rescue them,
fighting with all his might and courage.
Wherever he went, they crumbled,
and Wànjūn and Wànchè thus escaped.
Lǐ Dàliàng defeated the Tǔyùhún at Shǔhún Shān;
the mountain is west of Chìhǎi.
Jiàngjūn Zhíshī Sīlì defeated the Tǔyùhún at Jūrú Chuān.
Lǐ Jìng commanded the various armies, passing through Jīshí Shān and Hélùn,
reaching Qiěmò,
and exploring its western borders.
He heard that Fúyǔn was in Tūlún Chuān.
A textual variant states: The Biography of Tǔyùhún says:
"Fúyǔn fled west to Túlún Qì."
This is probably Tūlún Chuān,
a mere phonetic variation in the barbarian language.
We now follow the Biography of Qìbì Hélì.
Qìbì Hélì wanted to pursue and attack him.
Xuē Wànjūn, cautioned by his previous defeat,
firmly argued against it.
Hélì said:
"The barbarians have no walled cities;
they move with water and grass.
If we do not attack them when they are gathered together,
once they disperse like clouds,
how can we overthrow their lair again?!"
He personally selected over a thousand elite cavalry
and headed directly for Tūlún Chuān.
Wànjūn then led his troops to follow him.
There was a lack of water in the desert,
so the officers and soldiers stabbed their horses and drank their blood.
They attacked and destroyed Fúyǔn's headquarters,
beheading several thousand people
and capturing over two hundred thousand livestock.
Fúyǔn escaped alone,
but his wife and children were captured.
Hóu Jūnjí and others advanced past Xīngsù Chuān,
reaching Bǎihǎi,
then returned to rejoin Lǐ Jìng's army.
Dàníng Wáng Shùn,
nephew of the Suí imperial clan and Fúyǔn's legitimate son,
served as a Shìzhōng
in Suí.
He had been unable to return for a long time.
Fúyǔn established his attendant
son as太子 (Tàizǐ).
When he returned,
he always felt discontent.
Shùn's return is mentioned in Volume 187, Gāozǔ Wǔdé 2nd year.
Yàng,
pronounced like "yǎng."
The people of the country were in extreme distress,
resenting Tiānzhù Wáng.
Shùn, capitalizing on popular sentiment,
executed Tiānzhù Wáng
and offered the entire country's surrender.
Fúyǔn fled into the desert with over a thousand cavalry.
After more than ten days,
his followers gradually dispersed completely,
and he was killed by his subordinates.
The people of the country enthroned Shùn as Kèhán.
On the day Rénzǐ,
Lǐ Jìng reported the pacification of Tǔyùhún.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
an edict restored their state,
appointing Mùróng Shùn as Xīpíng Jùnwáng and the Chéqugǔlǚ
Wūgāndòu Kèhán.
The emperor worried that Shùn might not be able to command his people,
so he ordered Lǐ Dàliàng to lead several thousand elite troops as his support.
9 In the sixth month,
on the day Jǐchǒu,
the officials again requested the emperor to resume governing.
The emperor agreed,
but still entrusted minor matters to the Tàizǐ,
who was quite capable of hearing and deciding cases.
Thereafter, whenever the emperor went on an excursion,
he always left the Tàizǐ to guard the capital and supervise the state.
10 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
Yánzé Dào Xíngjūn Fù Zǒngguǎn Liú Démǐn attacked the rebellious Qiāng,
defeating them.
11 On the day Dīngsì,
an edict stated:
"The imperial mausoleum shall follow the precedent of Hàn Chánglíng.
Chánglíng
is the mausoleum of Hàn Gāozǔ.
Huángfǔ Mì said: Chánglíng is one hundred and twenty步 (bù) wide from east to west,
and thirteen zhàng high.
Fáng Xuánlíng said it was nine zhàng high.
Perhaps the units of measurement differed between ancient and modern times.
The deadline is too short,
and the work cannot be completed.
Mìshū Jiān Yú Shìnán submitted a memorial,
stating:
'Sages buried their parents sparingly,
not out of filial impiety,
but out of deep thought and foresight,
believing that lavish burials only serve to burden their parents,
and therefore did not do so.
Formerly, Zhāng Shìzhī said: "If there is anything desirable within,
even if one bars Nánshān, there will still be openings."
See Volume 14, Hàn Wéndì 3rd year.
Zhāng Shìzhī's words
are a plan for eternity.'
See Volume 31, Hàn Chéngdì Yǒngshǐ 1st year.
Truly, they accord with ultimate reason.
I humbly believe that Your Majesty's sagely virtue surpasses that of Táng and Yú,
yet in the lavish burial of your parents, you take Qín and Hàn as your model.
Your humble servant secretly believes Your Majesty should not do this.
Even if gold and jade are not buried,
later generations will only see such a large mound
and how could they know
there is no gold or jade?!
Moreover, the mourning period has already been observed according to Bālíng.
This refers to observing the thirty-seven-day mourning period according to Hàn Wéndì's dying edict.
I fear this is not appropriate.
I humbly wish that according to Bái Hǔ Tōng
Bān Gù and others compiled the six-volume Bái Hǔ Tōng Yì.
the regulations for objects and rituals be largely reduced,
and a stone inscription be erected beside the mausoleum,
with another copy written
and stored in the ancestral temple,
to serve as a perpetual law for descendants.'
The memorial was submitted
but not acknowledged.
Shìnán again submitted a memorial,
stating:
'Hàn emperors began constructing their mausoleums upon their ascension,
some taking over fifty years.
Now, to accomplish decades of work in a few months,
I fear human effort may be insufficient.'
The emperor then handed Shìnán's memorial to the relevant officials,
ordering them to deliberate on its appropriateness.
Fáng Xuánlíng and others discussed,
believing:
'Hàn Chánglíng is nine zhàng high,
and Yuánlíng is six zhàng high.
Yuánlíng
is the mausoleum of Hàn Guāngwǔ.
Gāo
is pronounced in the departing tone.
Three rèn would be too low;
we request to follow the system of Yuánlíng.'
This was adopted.
12 On the day Xīnhài,
an edict stated:
'In the early days of the nation's founding,
the system for ancestral temples was incomplete.
Now that the ancestral tablets are to be moved and enshrined,
the officials of ritual should deliberate on it.'
Jiànyì Dàfū Zhū Zǐshē requested the establishment of three Zhāo and three Mù positions, leaving the position of Tàizǔ vacant.
Thereupon, the Tàimiào was enlarged and renovated,
enshrining Hóngnóng Fǔjūn and Gāozǔ, along with the four old ancestral tablets, making a total of six chambers.
Hóngnóng Fǔjūn's taboo name was Chóngěr.
Liáng Wáng Lǐ Hào's posthumous title was Wǔzhāo.
He cannot be considered the progenitor;
the emperor followed this.
13 The Dǎngxiàng raided Diézhōu.
14 When Lǐ Jìng attacked the Tǔyùhún,
he lavishly bribed the Dǎngxiàng
to act as guides.
The Dǎngxiàng chieftain Tuòbá Chìcí came
and said to the generals:
'The Suí people are untrustworthy and love to plunder us.
If your armies now have no ulterior motives,
I request to supply your provisions.
If not,
I will occupy strategic points to block your armies' path.'
The generals made an oath with him and sent him away.
Chìshuǐ Dào Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn Lǐ Dàoyàn marched to Kuòshuǐ.
Kuòshuǐ is within the jurisdiction of the Dǎngxiàng jīmí Kuòzhōu.
He attacked them,
capturing several thousand cattle and sheep.
Thereupon, the various Qiāng grew resentful and angry,
gathering at Yěhú Xiá.
Dàoyàn could not advance.
Chìcí attacked him,
and Dàoyàn suffered a great defeat,
with tens of thousands dead,
retreating to secure Sōngzhōu.
Zuǒ Xiāowèi Jiàngjūn Fán Xīng delayed and missed the military deadline,
resulting in many lost soldiers.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
Dàoyàn and Xīng were both punished with a reduced death sentence and exiled to the frontier.
The Emperor dispatched envoys to comfort the generals at Dàdǒubágǔ.
Xuē Wànjūn disparaged Qìbì Hélì
and claimed all the credit for himself.
Hélì, unable to bear his indignation,
drew his sword and rose,
intending to kill Wànjūn.
The generals intervened and stopped him.
When the Emperor heard of it,
he reproached Hélì.
Hélì fully explained the situation,
recounting how he had rescued Wànjūn's brothers from encirclement in the Battle of Chìshuǐ and how Wànjūn had now disparaged him.
The Emperor wished to dismiss Wànjūn from office and bestow it upon Hélì.
Hélì firmly declined,
saying:
"If Your Majesty dismisses Wànjūn from office because of me,
the ignorant Hú (barbarians)
will believe Your Majesty favors Hú over Hàn,
leading to mutual false accusations
and widespread rivalry.
Moreover, it will make the Hú people think all generals are like Wànjūn,
fostering a contempt for the Hàn."
The Emperor approved of this and desisted.
Soon after, he ordered him to guard the Northern Gate
and inspect the affairs of the garrison camps.
The Northern Gate
was the Xuánwǔmén.
According to the Huìyào,
in the twelfth year of Zhēnguān, Left and Right Garrison Camps were established at Xuánwǔmén,
led by generals of various guards,
their soldiers being called Fēiqí.
Hélì's inspection of the garrison camps
must have been an event after the twelfth year,
as the history explicitly states.
15 Gāo Zèngshēng, the Dūdū of Mínzhōu and Commander-in-Chief of the Yánzé Route Army, was late for his military deployment.
Lǐ Jìng prosecuted him.
Zèngshēng resented Jìng
and falsely accused Jìng of rebellion.
The investigation found no grounds for the charge.
In the eighth month,
on the day Gēngchén,
Zèngshēng was sentenced to a reduced penalty of banishment to the frontier.
Someone said:
"Zèngshēng is
a meritorious official of Qínfǔ;
his crime should be pardoned."
The Emperor said:
"Zèngshēng disobeyed Lǐ Jìng's orders
and then falsely accused him of rebellion.
If this can be pardoned,
where then shall the law be applied?
Moreover, since the state rose from Jìnyáng,
there have been many meritorious officials.
If Zèngshēng is pardoned,
then everyone will break the law,
and how can it be forbidden again?
I have never forgotten his former achievements,
but because of this, I dare not pardon him."
From then on, Lǐ Jìng kept his doors shut and refused visitors;
even relatives were not allowed to see him without permission.
Lǐ Jìng served Tàizōng,
yet still faced such difficulties;
how difficult it must be to dwell at the height of fame and achievement!
16 The Emperor wished to visit the imperial mausoleums in person.
The imperial mausoleums
refer to Xiànlíng.
Fú Gù (or other officials) remonstrated, and he desisted.
17 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Yǐhài,
the Chǔyuè for the first time sent envoys to pay tribute.
The Chǔyuè and Chǔmì
were both separate tribes of the Western Tūjué.
18 On the day Gēngyín,
Emperor Tàiwǔ was buried at Xiànlíng.
Xiànlíng is eighteen lǐ east of Sānyuán County, Jīngzhào.
Empress Mù was interred with him.
Empress Tàimù Dòu Shì
was initially buried at Shòu’ānlíng;
now she is interred with Xiànlíng.
19 In the eleventh month,
on the day Gēngxū,
an edict was issued to discuss establishing a temple for Gāozǔ in Tàiyuán.
The Grand Secretary Yán Shīgǔ argued,
believing:
"The ancestral temple should be in the capital.
During the Hàn dynasty, establishing temples in commanderies and states
was not in accordance with rites."
So, it was stopped.
20 On the day Wùwǔ,
Xiāo Yǔ, Grand Master of Guanglù, was appointed Tèjìn,
and again allowed to participate in government affairs.
Xiāo Yǔ had ceased to be involved in court affairs,
as seen in the previous scroll, Zhēnguān Four.
Fù (復),
pronounced Fú Yòu.
"After the sixth year of Wǔdé,
Gāozǔ had thoughts of deposing and establishing (a new heir) but had not yet decided.
I was not tolerated by my brothers,
and indeed feared that my great achievements would not be rewarded.
This man
cannot be swayed by profit,
nor intimidated by death;
he is truly a minister of the state!"
Therefore, he bestowed a poem upon Yǔ, saying:
"Strong winds reveal sturdy grass;
chaos discerns loyal ministers."
He also said to Yǔ:
"Your loyalty and uprightness,
no ancient person surpassed;
however, being too clear about good and evil
sometimes leads to errors."
Yǔ bowed twice in thanks.
Wèi Zhēng said:
"Yǔ stands isolated against the multitude;
only Your Majesty knows his loyalty and steadfastness.
If he had not met with a sagacious and enlightened ruler,
it would have been difficult for him to escape!"
21 Lǐ Jìng, Tèjìn,
The Táng Liùdiǎn states: A First Rank B official is called Tèjìn.
The commentary notes: The Two Hàn and Wèi dynasties used it as an additional office,
serving alongside one's original office,
without officials or attendants.
It was of the Second Rank,
ranking after all the Dukes,
and above Kāifǔ Piàojí.
South of the Yangtze, it was always a concurrent office;
in Liáng, it was the seventeenth rank.
In Northern Qí,
Tèjìn was of the Second Rank;
in Suí, Tèjìn was a First Rank B sinecure office,
and Táng followed this.
requested to wear everyday clothes
and attend the main hall, according to the imperial dying injunctions;
it was not permitted.
22 Gāndòu Kèhán of Tǔyùhún had long been a hostage in China,
and his people were not loyal to him.
He was eventually killed by his subordinates.
His son, King Yàn Nuògěbō, was enthroned.
As Nuògěbō was young,
the powerful ministers contended for power,
and the state fell into great disorder.
In the twelfth month,
an edict ordered Hóu Jūnjí, Minister of War, and others to lead troops to assist him.
Envoys were first sent to persuade them to resolve the situation;
those who did not obey the edict
were to be pacified as appropriate.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Jiǎwǔ,
the Emperor began to personally attend to government affairs.
2 Xīnchǒu,
Āshǐnà Shè'ěr of the Tujue (突厥) Tàshè was appointed General-in-chief of the Left Swift Cavalry Guard.
Shè'ěr
was the son of Chǔluó Kèhán.
At the age of eleven,
he became known for his wisdom and strategy.
The Kèhán appointed him Tàshè,
establishing his banner north of the Qì [desert],
and together with Yùgǔshè, he jointly governed the various Bùlè tribes.
He held office for ten years,
and never once imposed taxes or levies.
The various shè (設) sometimes scorned him for not being able to accumulate wealth and power.
Shè'ěr said,
"If the tribes are prosperous,
that is enough for me."
The various shè felt ashamed and submitted.
The Tujue called those sons and younger brothers who commanded troops "shè."
There was more than one person commanding troops simultaneously with Shè'ěr,
hence the term "various shè."
He attacked and defeated Yùgǔshè;
the account of this event can be found in Volume 192, first year [of Zhēnguān].
He led the remaining troops to take refuge in the western frontier.
After Xiélì Kèhán perished,
as mentioned in the previous volume, fourth year [of Zhēnguān],
Duōlù Kèhán and his brother fought for the throne.
The account of this event can be found in the same place.
He led his army to attack and defeat the Western Tujue,
seizing nearly half of their territory,
with over ten thousand troops.
He proclaimed himself Dábù
Kèhán.
Shè'ěr then said to the various tribes,
"The first to cause chaos and break our nation
was Xuēyántuó.
I shall avenge our former Kèhán and annihilate them."
All the tribes remonstrated, saying,
"Having just acquired the western regions,
it would be wise to remain and pacify them.
If we were to suddenly abandon them and depart afar,
the Western Tujue will certainly come and reclaim their former territory."
Shè'ěr did not heed their advice,
and attacked Xuēyántuó north of the Qì [desert],
engaging in battle for over a hundred days.
Just then, Diélìshī Kèhán was established,
as mentioned in the previous volume, eighth year [of Zhēnguān].
Many deserted Shè'ěr and returned.
They returned to Diélìshī.
Shè'ěr suffered a great defeat
and fled to take refuge in Gāochāng.
Only a little over ten thousand families of his old army remained,
and fearing the pressure from the Western Tujue,
he then led his troops to surrender.
An imperial edict settled his tribes north of Língzhōu,
and Shè'ěr remained in Cháng'ān.
He married the imperial sister, Nányáng Cháng Gōngzhǔ.
Both the Old and New Histories record
"Héngyáng Cháng Gōngzhǔ."
Yángzhǎng,
pronounced in two ways.
3 Guǐchǒu,
Zhào Wáng Yuánjǐng was transferred to be Jīng Wáng,
Lǔ Wáng Yuánchāng to be Hàn Wáng,
Zhèng Wáng Yuánlǐ to be Xú Wáng,
Xú Wáng Yuánjiā to be Hán Wáng,
Jīng Wáng Yuánzé to be Péng Wáng,
Téng Wáng Yuányì to be Zhèng Wáng,
Wú Wáng Yuánguǐ to be Huò Wáng,
Bīn Wáng Yuánfèng to be Guó Wáng,
Chén Wáng Yuánqìng to be Dào Wáng,
Wèi Wáng Língkuí to be Yān Wáng.
All above were imperial younger brothers.
Yuè Wáng Tài was made Wèi Wáng,
Yān Wáng Yòu was made Qí Wáng,
Liáng Wáng Yīn was made Shǔ Wáng,
Tán Wáng Yùn was made Jiǎng Wáng,
Hàn Wáng Zhēn was made Yuè Wáng,
Shēn Wáng Shèn was made Jǐ Wáng.
All from Kè downwards were imperial sons.
Yān,
pronounced 'yīn' (因肩翻).
Yīn,
pronounced 'yīn' (於今翻).
Tán,
pronounced 'tán' (音談).
Yùn,
pronounced 'yùn' (於粉翻).
In the second month,
Yǐchǒu,
Yuánjǐng was appointed Grand Administrator of Jīngzhōu,
Yuánchāng Grand Administrator of Liángzhōu,
Yuánlǐ Grand Administrator of Xúzhōu,
Yuánjiā Grand Administrator of Lùzhōu,
Yuánzé Grand Administrator of Suízhōu,
Língkuí Grand Administrator of Yōuzhōu,
Kè Grand Administrator of Tánzhōu,
Tài Grand Administrator of Xiāngzhōu,
Yòu Grand Administrator of Qízhōu,
Yīn Grand Administrator of Yìzhōu,
Yùn Grand Administrator of Ānzhōu,
Zhēn Grand Administrator of Yángzhōu.
Tài did not proceed to his post,
so Zhāng Liàng, Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Gold and Purple Seal,
acted as Grand Administrator.
According to the Tang system,
when appointing officials,
if the rank was low but the proposed position high, it was called shǒu (守, acting as);
if the rank was high but the proposed position low, it was called xíng (行, acting).
Now, Zhāng Liàng acting as Grand Administrator followed the precedent of the Song and Qi dynasties where princes overseeing regions had "acting" officials,
which is different from the xíng used in general official appointments.
In his treatment of scholar-officials,
he was specially ordered to establish a separate Literature Institute in his residence,
allowing him to invite scholars himself.
This was to lay the groundwork for Tài's bid for the Eastern Palace.
4 In the third month,
Dīngyǒu,
Nuòhēbō, King of Tǔyùhún, sent an envoy to request the promulgation of the calendar and the adoption of an era name.
He also requested that his sons and younger brothers be sent to serve at court,
and both requests were granted.
Dīngwèi,
Nuòhēbō was appointed Prince of Héyuán Commandery and Wūdìyěbáqín Dòukèhán.
5 Guǐchǒu,
when the various princes departed for their fiefs,
the Emperor bade them farewell, saying,
"How can I not wish for the affection of brotherhood to allow us to always be together!
But due to the gravity of the world [responsibilities],
it cannot be otherwise.
I can still have more sons,
but brothers cannot be obtained again."
