He then shed tears and choked up, unable to stop.
When the Emperor shed tears and choked up,
was he perhaps thinking of the affairs of Jiànchéng and Yuánjí?
6 In summer,
sixth month,
Rénshēn,
Wēn Yànbó was appointed Right Executive of the Department of State Affairs,
and Tàicháng Qīng Yáng Shīdào was appointed Grand Councillor (Shìzhōng).
7 Shìzhōng Wèi Zhēng repeatedly requested to become a titular official (sǎnguān) due to an eye ailment.
Sǎn,
pronounced 'sǎn' (悉亶翻).
Wèi Zhēng was appointed Special Advanced Rank (Tèjìn),
and remained in charge of the Department of the Palace Chancellery.
Although he no longer held the position of Shìzhōng, he was still made responsible for the affairs of the Department of the Palace Chancellery.
He participated in discussions of successes and failures,
and for crimes punishable by exile or heavier,
he was to thoroughly investigate and report to the throne;
his emoluments, stipends, and staff were the same as those of an active official.
Tèjìn
was a titular official.
His emoluments, stipends, and staff being the same as active officials
was a way of showing honor to the worthy.
8 Empress Zhǎngsūn was by nature benevolent, filial, frugal, and simple.
She was fond of reading
and often leisurely discussed ancient events with the Emperor,
offering advice and suggestions that provided immense benefit.
Sometimes the Emperor would angrily scold palace women for minor offenses;
the Empress would also feign anger,
requesting to personally investigate and interrogate them,
then ordering them imprisoned.
After the Emperor's anger subsided,
she would slowly plead their case.
Consequently, within the palace,
there were no unjust or excessive punishments.
Yùzhāng Gōngzhǔ lost her mother early.
The Empress took her in and raised her,
treating her with more loving care than her own children.
Yùzhāng Gōngzhǔ
was the Emperor's daughter,
and later married Táng Yìshí.
Wèi,
pronounced 'wèi' (于偽翻).
Hú,
pronounced 'hú' (苦本翻).
Sàng,
pronounced 'sàng' (息浪翻).
The Empress personally attended to her and nursed her,
giving up her own medicinal meals to provide for her.
Everyone in the palace loved and respected her.
She always prioritized humility and frugality when instructing her sons.
Suí'ān Fūrén, the太子's wet nurse,
According to Tang regulations,
the太子's wet nurse was enfeoffed as a Commandery Lady.
Mùzhōu
was Suí'ān Commandery.
noticed that the Eastern Palace lacked certain furnishings
and requested to petition for more.
The Empress refused,
saying,
"For the太子,
the concern lies in failing to establish virtue
and failing to achieve renown.
Why worry about a lack of furnishings?"
The emperor fell ill,
and for several years he did not recover.
Empress Zhǎngsūn attended to him,
never leaving his side day or night.
She constantly kept poison medicine tied to her sash,
saying,
"If anything untoward were to happen,
it would be unrighteous for me to live alone."
The empress had long suffered from a respiratory illness.
The year before last, she accompanied the emperor on a visit to Jiǔchénggōng.
When Chái Shào and others reported a rebellion in the middle of the night,
the emperor donned his armor and went out to the courtyard to inquire about the situation.
The empress, despite her illness, followed him.
Those around her tried to stop her,
but the empress said,
"Since the emperor is already alarmed,
how can I remain at ease?"
From then on, her illness became much worse.
The Crown Prince said to the empress,
"All medicines have been exhausted, but your illness does not improve.
Please ask the emperor to pardon criminals and allow people to enter the monastic life,
hoping to gain blessings from the unseen world."
The empress said,
"Life and death are determined by fate,
not by wisdom or strength.
If doing good brings blessings,
then I would not do evil;
if it is not so,
what good is a futile request?
Pardons are a major affair of the state,
and should not be frequently issued.
Daoism and Buddhism are heterodox teachings
that harm the state and afflict the people.
The emperor has always avoided them;
how can I, a mere woman, cause the emperor to do what he has avoided?
If you insist on doing as you say,
I would rather die quickly!"
The Crown Prince dared not make the proposal,
but secretly spoke of it to Fáng Xuánlíng.
Fáng Xuánlíng reported it to the emperor.
The emperor pitied her
and wished to issue a pardon for her sake,
but the empress firmly refused it.
When her illness became critical,
she bid farewell to the emperor.
At that time, Fáng Xuánlíng had been censured and sent home.
The empress said to the emperor,
"Fáng Xuánlíng has served Your Majesty for a long time.
He is cautious and discreet,
and his ingenious plans and secret strategies
have never been divulged.
Unless there is a major fault,
I hope you will not abandon him.
My own clan members
have attained their positions and salaries through flimsy connections,
as the Hàn Shū says: 'not having the kinship of jiāfú.'
Zhāng Yàn says: 'Jiā
is the reed leaf.
Fú
is the white skin inside the leaf.'
Jìn Zhuó says: 'Fú
is the white skin inside the reed.'
All these are analogies for something light and thin.
Shīgǔ says: 'Jiā
is the reed.
Fú
is the extremely thin white skin inside its stalk.'
Jiāfú is an analogy that is obvious.
Fú
has the sound of fú.
Zhāng Yàn's 'white skin inside the leaf' is incorrect.
They are easily brought to ruin and danger.
To ensure their descendants' preservation,
be careful not to place them in positions of power and importance.
It is enough for them merely to serve the court as imperial relatives.
Given how even the virtuous Wú Jì could not protect himself,
the empress's concerns were indeed profound and far-reaching.
Yì,
read as chì.
Chǔ,
read as chānglǚ.
Cháo,
read as zhíyáo.
'One cannot harm others by dying'
uses the meaning of the words of Chéng Zǐgāo recorded in the Tán Gōng.
Just make a grave by relying on a mountain,
and use only earthenware and wood for the implements.
Furthermore, I wish Your Majesty to draw near to gentlemen,
keep away from petty men,
accept loyal remonstrance,
dismiss slanderous sycophants,
lighten labor services,
and stop hunting excursions.
Even if I am buried in the netherworld,
I will truly have no regrets.
There is no need for our children
to come;
seeing their sorrow
would only disturb one's mind."
Then she took out the poison medicine from her clothing and showed it to the emperor, saying,
"When Your Majesty was ill,
I vowed to follow your carriage in death.
I simply could not assume the position of Empress Lǚ."
The affairs of Empress Lǚ are found in the Hàn Jì.
Chéng,
read as shéngzhèng.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
she passed away in Lìzhèngdiàn.
The Jiégé manuscript's map of Tàijígōng shows: East of the East Shànggémén is Wànchūndiàn;
east of Wànchūndiàn is Lìzhèngdiàn.
The Táng Liùdiǎn states: North of Tàijídiàn is Liǎngyídiàn;
east of Liǎngyídiàn is Wànchūndiàn.
Left of Liǎngyídiàn is Xiànchūnmén;
left of Xiànchūnmén is Lìzhèngmén;
inside of which is Lìzhèngdiàn.
The empress once compiled thirty volumes of Nǚzé,
collecting examples of ancient women's successes and failures.
She also wrote a discourse refuting Empress Mǎ,
who, despite her virtue during the reign of Emperor Míng of Hàn, failed to restrain her relatives,
allowing them to become powerful and prominent in court,
merely warning them that "their carriages were like flowing water and horses like dragons."
This can be found in volume 46, second year of Jiànchū, Emperor Zhāng of Hàn.
Bó,
read as běijiǎo.
Cháo,
read as zhíyáo.
When she passed away, the palace officials presented her Nǚzé.
In the internal offices of Táng,
there was a Gōngzhèng,
who rectified transgressions.
The Tóngshǐ
recorded merits and faults.
The Liùdiǎn states: The Shàngyíjú has two Sījì,
responsible for teaching classics and history.
The one who presented Nǚzé
was likely the Sījì.
The emperor showed it to his close ministers, saying,
"This book by the empress
is sufficient to serve as a model for a hundred generations.
It is not that I do not understand the Mandate of Heaven and indulge in useless sorrow,
but rather that upon entering the palace, I will no longer hear words of admonition.
I have lost a good assistant,
hence I cannot forget her!"
Thereupon, he summoned Fáng Xuánlíng
and reinstated him to his position.
eighth month,
day Bǐngzǐ.
The emperor said to his close ministers,
"I opened the path for frank speech
to benefit the state.
However, recently, many who submit memorials expose trivial matters about others.
From now on, if anyone does this again,
I will punish them as slanderers."
eleventh month,
day Gēngwǔ.
Empress Wéndé was buried at Zhāolíng.
Zhāolíng
is sixty *lǐ* northwest of Lǐquán Xiàn, Jīngzhào.
The Táng Liùdiǎn states: West of the inner Tàijídiàn,
next to the north is Zhūmíngmén;
to the left of the gate is Qiánhuàmén;
to the right is Sùzhāngmén;
west of Sùzhāngmén is Huīzhèngmén,
also called Liǎngyídiàn,
which was the ancient inner court.
East of Chéngtiānmén is Chánglè mén;
entering north through Gōnglǐmén,
and further north through Qiánhuàmén,
is the palace interior.
West of Chéngtiānmén is Yǒng'ānmén;
entering north through Ānrénmén,
and further north through Sùzhāngmén,
is the palace interior.
Shì Jí wanted to open the inner camp;
Zhì Xuán closed the gates and did not admit them,
saying,
"The camp gates cannot be opened at night."
The messenger said,
"I have a handwritten imperial decree here."
Zhì Xuán said,
"One cannot distinguish genuine from fake in the middle of the night."
He kept the messenger until morning.
The emperor heard of it and sighed, saying,
"He is a true general!"
The emperor again composed an inscription and carved it on stone,
stating:
"The empress was frugal.
Her dying wish was for a simple burial,
believing that 'the minds of thieves
only seek precious treasures.
If there are no precious treasures,
what more could they seek?'
My original intention
was also like this.
A ruler takes the world as his home.
Why must things be kept inside the imperial tomb
to be considered his own?
Now, using Mount Jiǔzōng as the mausoleum,
the stone-carving laborers number only a little over a hundred,
and the work was completed in a few tens of days.
No gold or jade is hidden,
and the figures of people, horses, and vessels
are all made of earth and wood,
merely providing the form.
This may hopefully cause villains and thieves to cease their intentions,
ensuring peace for both the living and the deceased.
This shall serve as a model for descendants for a hundred generations."
The emperor, unable to stop thinking of the empress,
had a tiered pavilion built in the imperial garden
to gaze upon Zhāolíng.
He once invited Wèi Zhēng to ascend with him
and made him look at it.
Wèi Zhēng looked intently and said:
"I am dim-sighted
and cannot see it."
The emperor pointed it out to him.
Wèi Zhēng said:
"I thought Your Majesty was gazing at Xiànlíng.
If it is Zhāolíng,
then I certainly see it."
The emperor wept
and had the pavilion demolished for his sake.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Wùyín,
Jūjùbō and Gāntáng sent envoys to offer tribute.
Jūjùbō was north of the Cōnglíng mountains,
two
thousand eight hundred *lǐ* from Guāzhōu.
Gāntáng was south of the Great Sea.
Jūjùbō
was also called Jūjùpán;
it was the country of Zǐhé during the Hàn dynasty.
Gāntáng was south of the Western Sea,
its people were from Kūnlún.
Both countries were in the Western Regions.
The envoy,
*shū lì fān*.
"When China is peaceful,
the four barbarians naturally submit.
However, I cannot be without fear.
In the past, Qín Shǐhuáng's power shook the Hú and Yuè,
but his dynasty perished in the second generation.
It is solely up to you, gentlemen, to rectify my shortcomings."
Wèi Wáng Tài was favored by the emperor.
Some said that officials of the third rank and above often treated Wèi Wáng lightly.
The emperor was angered.
He summoned officials of the third rank and above,
and sternly reprimanded them, saying:
"During the time of Suí Wéndì,
officials of the first rank and below were all tripped up by the imperial princes.
Were they not the sons of the Son of Heaven?!
I merely do not allow my sons to act recklessly.
I hear that officials of the third rank and above all treat him lightly.
If I were to indulge him,
would he not be able to humiliate you gentlemen?!"
Fáng Xuánlíng and others all bowed in fear and profusely apologized.
Wèi Zhēng alone spoke with a stern expression, saying:
"I venture to say that among current officials,
there is certainly no one who dares to treat Wèi Wáng lightly.
According to ritual,
a subject and a son are one and the same.
In the *Chūnqiū*,
even a minor royal envoy
is ranked above the feudal lords.
*Chūnqiū*: Xī, seventh year,
the duke met with the royal envoy, Qí Hóu, Sòng Gōng, Wèi Hóu, Xǔ Nán, Cáo Bó, Chén Shìzǐ Kuǎn, Zhèng Shìzǐ Huá, and formed an alliance at Táo.
*Gōngyáng Zhuàn* says: What is a royal envoy?
A humble person.
Why is he ranked above the feudal lords?
It is the command of the former king.
Your Majesty honors and respects this.
If the imperial discipline were completely broken,
that would be another matter;
but with a sagely and enlightened ruler above,
Wèi Wáng certainly has no reason to insult or humiliate officials.
Suí Wéndì indulged his sons,
allowing them to act with much impropriety,
and they were eventually all annihilated.
Is that an example to follow?!"
The emperor was pleased and said:
"Such reasonable words
must be obeyed.
I, in my private affection, forgot public righteousness.
My previous anger
seemed unquestionable to myself,
but upon hearing Wèi Zhēng's words,
I realized my reasoning was flawed.
How can a ruler speak so carelessly!"
The emperor said:
"Laws must not be frequently changed.
Frequent changes lead to confusion,
and officials cannot remember them all.
Moreover, inconsistencies between earlier and later laws
allow corrupt officials to commit wrongdoing.
From now on, any changes to laws
should be carried out with utmost care and prudence."
Quán Wànjì, the Censor for Reviewing Documents, submitted a memorial:
"Silver deposits in Xuān and Ráo prefectures have greatly increased.
If mined,
several million *mín* can be obtained annually."
The emperor said:
"I, being the Son of Heaven,
am not lacking in wealth.
My only regret is not having good advice that can benefit the people.
Rather than gaining several million *mín*,
how much better it is to gain one virtuous talent!
You have never recommended a worthy person nor dismissed an unworthy one,
but only speak of the benefits of silver tax.
In the past, Yáo and Shùn cast jade discs into mountains
and threw pearls into valleys.
Lù Jiǎ's *Xīnyǔ* says: Sages do not use pearls and jade but value their bodies.
Therefore, Shùn abandoned gold in jagged mountain cliffs,
and discarded pearls and jade in the rivers of the Five Lakes,
to curb lustful and evil desires.
The event is seen in volume 57, Hàn Língdì Guānghé first year.
*Zàng*,
*cú làng fān*.
On that day,
Quán Wànjì was dismissed
and sent home.
15 That year,
the title tǒngjūn was changed to zhé chōng dūwèi,
and biéjiāng to guǒyì dūwèi.
According to the Táng system: A zhé chōng dūwèi of an upper prefecture was of the senior fourth rank, upper grade;
of a middle prefecture, senior fourth rank, lower grade;
of a lower prefecture, senior fifth rank, lower grade.
A guǒyì dūwèi of an upper prefecture was of the junior fifth rank, lower grade;
of a middle prefecture, senior sixth rank, upper grade;
of a lower prefecture, junior sixth rank, lower grade.
Gēng,
read as gōnghéng.
Jiàng,
read as jíliàng.
Six hundred and thirty-four fǔ were established,
with two hundred and sixty-one in Guānnèi,
all subordinate to the various wèi and the six shuài of the Dōnggōng.
The six shuài of the Dōnggōng were: the Zuǒ Wèi Shuài and Yòu Wèi Shuài,
modeled after the Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn and Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn of the upper yǎmén;
the Zuǒ Zōng Wèi Shuài and Yòu Zōng Wèi Shuài,
modeled after the Zuǒ Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn and Yòu Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn;
and the Zuǒ Jiānmén Shuài and Yòu Jiānmén Shuài,
modeled after the Zuǒ Jiānmén Jiāngjūn and Yòu Jiānmén Jiāngjūn.
Later, the Zuǒ Yúhòu Shuài and Yòu Yúhòu Shuài were also established,
modeled after the Zuǒ Jīnwú Jiāngjūn and Yòu Jīnwú Jiāngjūn;
and the Zuǒ Nèi Shuài and Yòu Nèi Shuài,
modeled after the Zuǒ Qiānnú Jiāngjūn and Yòu Qiānnú Jiāngjūn.
Together, they were called the Ten Shuài.
A middle fǔ had a thousand men,
a lower fǔ eight hundred men.
Three hundred men formed a tuán,
with a xiàowèi;
fifty men formed a duì,
with a zhèng;
ten men formed a huǒ,
with a zhǎng.
Each man had a set amount of armor, weapons, and provisions,
all self-provided,
and stored in the arsenal.
When there was an expedition, they were supplied.
Men became soldiers at twenty,
and were exempt at sixty.
Those skilled in horsemanship and archery were called yuèqí.
Yuèqí
means they were so strong and brave as to be able to leap over obstacles.
Qí,
read as qí jì.
Every year in the last month of winter,
the zhé chōng dūwèi would lead his subordinates in military drills,
and those who needed horses would be given money by the government to buy them.
All those who were to perform guard duty rotated turns.
The Ministry of War assigned turns based on distance:
those from afar had fewer turns, those from nearby more frequently,
and everyone rotated after one month.
At that time, the regulation was:
within five hundred lǐ, five turns;
a thousand lǐ, seven turns;
one thousand five hundred lǐ, eight turns;
two thousand lǐ, ten turns;
beyond that, twelve turns.
If selected to remain for permanent guard duty,
within five hundred lǐ, seven turns;
a thousand lǐ, eight turns;
two thousand lǐ, ten turns;
beyond that, twelve turns.
Shàng,
read as shípáng.
Shù,
read as suǒjiǎo.
Gēng,
read as gōnghéng.
1 In the spring,
first month,
Yuán Yù, Prince of Huì, was moved to become Prince of Dèng,
and Yuán Míng, Prince of Qiáo, to become Prince of Shū.
2 On the day of Xīnmǎo,
Kè, Prince of Wú, was appointed Dūdū of Ānzhōu;
Zhì, Prince of Jìn, Dūdū of Bìngzhōu;
and Shèn, Prince of Jì, Dūdū of Qínzhōu.
When they were about to depart for their posts,
the Emperor bestowed upon them a letter of admonition, saying:
"I wished to give you precious ornaments,
but I fear it would only increase your arrogance and extravagance.
It is better to have this one piece of advice."
3 The Emperor began construction of the Fēishān Palace.
Observing that the Míngdé Palace and the Xuánpǔ Courtyard of Fēishān Palace were abandoned next year to provide housing for the people of Luòyáng whose homes were damaged by floods,
we know that Fēishān Palace was also in Luòyáng.
On the day of Gēngzǐ,
Wèi Zhēng, a tèjìn, submitted a memorial,
in which he argued:
"Emperor Yáng, relying on his wealth and power,
did not foresee future calamities.
He indulged in extreme extravagance and desire,
causing the common people to suffer,
to the extent that he died by the hands of others,
and the state became a ruin.
Your Majesty has brought order out of chaos and restored righteousness.
You should reflect on how the Suí lost
and how we gained.
You should dismantle their lofty buildings
and be content with humble palaces.
If you build upon their foundations and expand,
or adopt their old practices and add embellishments,
this would be to replace chaos with chaos,
and calamity will surely come.
It is easy to lose what is hard to gain;
how can one not be mindful of this!"
4 Fáng Xuánlíng and others had previously received an imperial edict to compile the laws and statutes.
They believed:
"According to the old laws,
if brothers lived separately, their official immunity did not extend to each other,
yet those implicated in rebellion were all sentenced to death;
while grandparents and grandchildren enjoyed immunity,
they were only to be exiled.
Considering the rites and common sense,
this was deeply unsatisfactory.
Now, in compiling the laws,
grandparents, grandchildren, and brothers who are implicated
are all to be sentenced to penal servitude."
This was adopted.
From then on, compared to ancient times, more than half of the death penalties were abolished,
and the whole empire praised this.
Fáng Xuánlíng and others compiled five hundred articles of law,
establishing twenty grades of criminal penalties:
five levels of chī punishment,
from ten to fifty blows;
five levels of zhàng punishment,
from sixty to one hundred blows;
five levels of tú punishment (penal servitude),
from one year to three years;
three levels of liú punishment (exile),
from one thousand lǐ to three thousand lǐ;
two types of death penalty,
strangulation and decapitation.
Seventy-one articles reduced exile to penal servitude.
In total, the cumbersome was removed, the harmful eliminated,
and severe punishments lightened
in countless ways.
They also established over one thousand five hundred and ninety articles of administrative regulations.
According to the old system of Wǔdé,
the Ceremony of Offerings to Confucius was held at the Imperial Academy,
with Duke Zhōu as the Former Sage and Confucius as the co-sacrificer.
Fáng Xuánlíng and others proposed to stop sacrificing to Duke Zhōu,
making Confucius the Former Sage
and Yán Huí the co-sacrificer.
They also edited the imperial edicts and regulations since Wǔdé,
retaining seven hundred articles,
which were promulgated at this time.
They also standardized the length and width of jiā (cangue), niǔ (handcuffs), qián (pincers), suǒ (chains), zhàng (large stick), and chī (small stick).
A device shackling the neck was called a jiā;
one shackling the hands, a niǔ.
Qián
was to bind with iron clamps.
Suǒ
was to shackle with iron chains.
A zhàng
was three chǐ and five cùn long,
with knots smoothed off.
An interrogation zhàng
had a large end diameter of three fēn and two lí,
and a small end of two fēn and two lí.
A regular zhàng
had a large end diameter of two fēn and seven lí,
and a small end of one fēn and seven lí.
A chī zhàng
had a large end diameter of two fēn,
and a small end of one and a half fēn.
Niǔ,
read as nǚjiǔ.
Since the death of Zhāng Yùngǔ,
as seen in Volume 5 of the previous scroll,
there were instances where officials erred by being too lenient,
but they were not punished.
The Emperor once asked Liú Déwēi, the Dàlǐ Qīng:
"Why has the legal net become somewhat tighter recently?"
He replied:
"This depends on Your Majesty,
not on your humble officials.
If the ruler prefers leniency, it will be lenient;
if strictness, it will be strict.
The law states: an error of undue leniency results in a three-grade reduction in punishment,
an error of undue severity results in a five-grade reduction.
Now, if one errs by being too lenient, there is no consequence,
but if one errs by being too severe, one incurs a grave offense.
Therefore, officials seek to protect themselves
and compete to apply the laws strictly.
It is not that they are instructed to do so,
but out of fear of punishment.
If Your Majesty were to judge strictly according to the law just once,
this trend would immediately change."
The Emperor was pleased
and followed his advice.
From then on, judicial rulings were fair and balanced.
5 The emperor wished to emulate the Hàn Dynasty's practice of preparing imperial tombs in advance,
to spare his descendants the sudden toil and expense.
He also intended for a frugal burial,
fearing his descendants might follow the custom of extravagance.
In the second month,
on a Dīngsì day,
he personally set out his final wishes,
to use a mountain as his mausoleum,
just large enough to contain the coffin.
6 On a Jiǎzǐ day,
the emperor traveled to Luòyáng Gōng.
7 The emperor arrived at Xiǎnrén Gōng.
The Suí Zhì states: In Shòu'ān County, Hénán, there was Xiǎnrén Gōng,
built by Yángdì in the first year of Dàyè.
There were officials who were reprimanded.
Wèi Zhēng admonished:
"Your Majesty has reprimanded officials for failing to make provisions.
I fear that this will spread like a wildfire,
and in the future, the common people will not be able to live in peace.
This is surely not the original intention of Your Majesty's tour.
In the past, Yángdì prompted commanderies and counties to present food,
and judged their abundance or scarcity as a basis for rewards and punishments.
(See volume 183, Dàyè year 12.)
Your Majesty witnessed this personally,
how can you wish to imitate it?"
The emperor was startled and said:
"Without you, I would not have heard these words."
He then said to Zhǎngsūn Wújí and others:
"When I passed through here in the past,
I bought food and ate,
and rented lodging to sleep.
Now, the provisions are like this,
how can I complain of insufficiency?"
8 In the third month,
on the first day, a Bǐngxū day,
there was a solar eclipse.
9 On a Gēngzǐ day,
the emperor held a banquet in the Western Park of Luòyáng Gōng,
boating on Jīcuì Chí.
Luòyáng's Western Park
extended north to Běimáng,
west to Xiàoshuǐ,
and south bordered a branch canal of the Luòshuǐ.
The Gǔ and Luò rivers met there.
Fearing floods,
three dikes were built to control them: one called Jīcuì,
the second Yuèpō,
and the third Shàngyáng.
The park wall had a circumference of one hundred twenty-six *lǐ*.
"Yángdì built this palace garden,
incurring the resentment of the people.
(The construction of the Western Park is seen in volume 180, Dàyè year 1.)
This was precisely because individuals like Yǔwén Shù, Yú Shìjī, and Péi Yùn were flatterers within,
and shielded the emperor's sagacity from outside.
How can one not be warned by this!"
According to Suí Yángdì, in the second year of Dàyè,
Yǔwén Kǎi was ordered to build Luòyáng's Western Park.
"Shù"
should probably be
"Kǎi".
10 Fáng Xuánlíng and Wèi Zhēng presented one hundred thirty-eight chapters of new rituals determined by the emperor.
On a Bǐngwǔ day,
an imperial edict commanded their implementation.
11 Wáng Guī, the Minister of Rites, was appointed as tutor to Wèi Wáng TàI.
In the early Táng Dynasty, following the system of Wèi and Jìn,
each prince was assigned one tutor.
During the Kāiyuán era, this was changed to *fù*.
The emperor said: "You should serve Guī as you serve me."
Whenever TàI saw Guī,
he would first bow.
Guī also conducted himself as a tutor.
Guī's son, Jìngzhí, was married to Nánpíng Gōngzhǔ.
The princess
was the emperor's daughter.
When princesses married,
they generally did not observe filial duties towards their parents-in-law.
Guī said:
"Now the emperor is enlightened and clear-sighted,
acting always in accordance with ritual and law.
My acceptance of the princess's audience
is not for personal honor,
but to complete the beauty of the state."
Thereupon, he and his wife sat in their proper places,
and instructed the princess to hold a basket and perform the ritual of washing and presenting food.
After this, princesses began to observe proper wifely rituals,
starting with Guī.
12 Many officials again requested the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices.
In the fifth year,
emissaries from various prefectures, gathered for court, requested the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices.
In the sixth year,
civil and military officials requested them.
Now, various officials requested them again.
Fù (復),
pronounced Fú Yòu.
Fáng Xuánlíng made the final decision.
13 Summer,
fourth month,
on a Jǐmǎo day,
Wèi Zhēng submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Many rulers begin well,
but few endure to the end.
Is it because it is easy to acquire but difficult to maintain?
It is probably because in dire distress, one exerts sincerity to serve subordinates to the utmost,
but in peace and comfort, one becomes arrogant and takes things lightly.
When one serves subordinates to the utmost, even Hú and Yuè are of one mind.
When one takes things lightly, even one's close relatives become estranged.
Although one may awe them with authority and anger,
they merely feign obedience, but their hearts are not submissive.
If a ruler can truly, when seeing desirable things, think of contentment;
when about to undertake construction, think of knowing when to stop;
when in a high and perilous position, think of humility;
when nearing fullness, think of moderation;
when encountering ease and pleasure, think of restraint;
when in peace and security, think of future troubles;
when guarding against obstruction, think of extending invitations for counsel;
when disliking slander and evil, think of rectifying oneself;
when bestowing ranks and rewards, think of avoiding excess due to joy;
when imposing punishments, think of avoiding abuse due to anger –
*Jiàn* (僭),
means exceeding proper limits;
*Làn* (濫),
means excessive.
And if one selects the worthy and appoints the capable,
then one can govern by non-action,
why then must one labor one's spirit and exhaust one's body to take over the responsibilities of all officials?"
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ, reviewed by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command
Hòu Xué Tiān Tái
Zhēngguàn Shíyī Nián
(Dīngyǒu, 637)
1 In the fifth month,
on a Rénshēn day,
Wèi Zhēng submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Your Majesty's resolve to do good is not as it was in former times;
your willingness to correct errors upon hearing them has somewhat diminished compared to before.
Reprimands and punishments have accumulated,
and your authority and anger have become somewhat severe.
Thus, I know that 'nobility does not necessarily lead to arrogance, and wealth does not necessarily lead to extravagance,'
is not an empty saying.
The Shū, Zhōuguān, states: 'Rank does not necessarily lead to arrogance,
and emoluments do not necessarily lead to extravagance.'
Kǒng Ānguó commented: 'Arrogance comes unbidden with nobility,
and extravagance comes unbidden with wealth.'
Wèi Zhēng quoted this.
Comparing this to today,
how can it be considered comparable?
Yet, Suí, by its wealth and strength, stirred itself to danger,
while we, by our smallness and weakness, kept still and found peace.
The principles of peace and danger
are clearly before our eyes.
In the past, before Suí fell into disorder,
it believed it would never fall into disorder;
before it perished,
it believed it would never perish.
Thus, levies and corvée were endless,
and campaigns never ceased,
to the point that disaster was about to strike, yet it had not yet awakened.
Indeed, for reflecting one's form, nothing is like still water;
for reflecting failure, nothing is like a lost state.
I humbly wish that Your Majesty would take Suí as a mirror,
abandon extravagance and embrace frugality,
draw close to the loyal and distance the treacherous,
and in this time of peace,
practice the reverence and frugality of former days.
Then, being completely good and perfect,
there would truly be nothing left to praise.
Indeed, acquiring is truly difficult,
but maintaining is very easy.
If Your Majesty was able to achieve what is difficult,
how could you not preserve what is easy?"
2 In the sixth month,
Yú Gōnggōng Wēn Yànbó, the Right Grand Councilor, passed away.
Yànbó had long managed state affairs,
tirelessly engaging in all that he knew.
The emperor said to his attendant ministers:
"Because of his worries for the state,
Yànbó exhausted his spirit.
I have seen his decline
for two years now.
I regret not allowing him to enjoy ease and comfort,
thereby cutting short his natural lifespan!"
3 On a Dīngsì day,
the emperor visited Míngdé Gōng.
In the second year of Xiǎnqìng,
the Supervisorate of Míngdé Gōng
was renamed the Supervisorate of the Southern Front of the Eastern Capital Park.
4 On a Jǐwèi day,
an imperial edict mandated that the twenty-one princes, including Jīng Wáng Yuánjǐng, the Governor-General of Jīngzhōu, who were appointed as regional inspectors (*cìshǐ*),
should all have their positions inherited by their descendants.
On a Wùchén day,
fourteen meritorious officials, including Zhǎngsūn Wújí, were also appointed as regional inspectors,
with their positions also hereditary;
unless there was a major offense,
they were not to be dismissed.
5 On the day Jǐsì,
Xǔwáng Yuánxiáng was moved to become Jiāngwáng.
6 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Guǐwèi,
there was heavy rain,
and the Gǔ River and Luò River overflowed into Luòyáng Gōng.
According to Táng Liùdiǎn,
the imperial city of Luòyáng
was created by order of Suí Dàyè’s second year, with Yáng Sù and Yǔwén Kǎi relocating the old capital to build it.
To the south, it directly faced the mouth of Yīquè;
to the north, it leaned against the stronghold of Mángshān;
to the east, it extended beyond the east of the Chán River;
and to the west, it crossed beyond the west of the Jiàn River.
The Luò River flowed through the capital,
symbolizing the Milky Way.
It was eighteen lǐ east of the old capital.
The imperial city was connected to the Imperial Park in the west,
where the Gǔ River and Luò River met.
Later, in Xuánzōng’s Kāiyuán twenty-fourth year,
because the Gǔ River and Luò River occasionally overflowed,
exhausting the people's labor,
the inner treasury was used to hire workers
to build three dikes to defend against them:
one was called Jīcuì,
the second Yuèpō,
and the third Shàngyáng.
After this, the two rivers caused no more labor-intensive troubles.
Over six thousand people drowned.
7 Wèi Zhēng submitted a memorial,
stating:
“Wénzǐ said: ‘When words are believed to be the same, trust precedes the words;
when orders are carried out as the same, sincerity is beyond the orders.’
Hàngshū Yìwénzhì says: Wénzǐ,
a disciple of Lǎozǐ,
was a contemporary of Kǒngzǐ.
Your Majesty,
for over ten years,
yet the transforming influence of your virtue has not yet spread widely
because your feelings towards your subordinates have not been fully sincere and trustworthy.
Now, in establishing governance and achieving good order,
you must entrust it to gentlemen (jūnzǐ);
but when there are successes or failures,
you sometimes consult petty men (xiǎorén).
Your treatment of gentlemen is respectful but distant,
while your interaction with petty men is casual and intimate.
Intimacy allows all words to be spoken,
but distance prevents feelings from reaching Your Majesty.
Even people of average intelligence
are not without minor wisdom!
However, their talents are not suited for governing the state,
and their foresight does not extend far.
Even if they exert all their effort and sincerity,
they still cannot avoid failure,
to say nothing of those who harbor treachery within;
how can their harm not be profound!
Even a gentleman cannot be without minor faults,
but if these do not harm the righteous path,
they can be overlooked.
If one is called a gentleman but then doubted for their trustworthiness,
how is this different from setting up a straight tree and doubting that its shadow is crooked!
If Your Majesty can truly carefully select gentlemen,
and trust them with propriety,
what worry is there that the state will not be well-governed!
Otherwise,
the time of peril and ruin
cannot be guaranteed.”
The Emperor bestowed a personal edict of praise, saying:
“After Jìn Wǔdì pacified Wú,
his will became arrogant and lazy.
Hé Zēng, who held the highest position of táisī,
could not offer direct remonstrance,
but privately spoke to his descendants,
boasting of his own wisdom.
This matter is found in volume eighty-seven, Jìn Huáidì’s Yǒngjiā third year.
Having received your remonstrance,
I know my faults.
I shall place it on my table and desk, comparing it to Xián and Wéi.”
This refers to the stories of Dǒng Ānyú and Xīmén Bào.
8 On the day Yǐwèi,
the imperial carriage returned to Luòyáng,
returning from Míngdé Gōng to Luòyáng Gōng.
“The Luòyáng Gōng, damaged by water,
will be slightly repaired,
just enough to be habitable.
All other materials
will be given to those in the city whose homes were destroyed.
Order all officials to submit memorials,
speaking openly about my faults.”
On the day Rén'yín,
Míngdé Gōng and the Xuánpǔ Yuàn of Fēishān Gōng were abolished,
and their resources were given to those affected by the flood.
9 In the eighth month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ,
the Emperor said to his attendants:
“Those who submitted memorials all said that I hunted too frequently.
Now, the world is at peace,
but military preparedness cannot be forgotten.
I occasionally hunt with my retinue in the Imperial Park.
This causes no trouble for the people;
what harm is there in that!”
Wèi Zhēng said:
“The former kings only feared not hearing their faults.
Since Your Majesty allows them to submit memorials,
you should let them express themselves freely.
If their words are valuable,
they will naturally benefit the state;
if they are not valuable,
they will cause no harm.”
The Emperor said:
“Your words are correct.”
He rewarded them all and sent them away.
10 The Supervising Censor, Mǎ Zhōu, submitted a memorial,
thinking:
"The Three Dynasties and the Hàn dynasty,
the longest-lasting endured for eight hundred years,
the shortest not less than four hundred.
This was truly because their benevolence bound people's hearts,
and people could not forget their past.
From then on,
the longest-lasting lasted for sixty years,
the shortest for merely twenty-odd years.
They were all without benevolence towards the people,
and thus their foundations were not solid.
Your Majesty ought to restore the achievements of Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ,
and establish a foundation for your descendants for ten thousand generations.
How can you merely maintain the present!
The current population is less than one-tenth of that of the Suí dynasty,
yet those conscripted for service see brothers depart and return,
continuously succeeding each other on the roads.
Although Your Majesty has issued gracious edicts,
ordering a reduction in these burdens,
construction works never cease,
so how can the people find rest!
Therefore, officials merely process documents,
without any actual implementation.
In the past, Emperors Wén and Jǐng of Hàn
were respectful and frugal, nurturing the people.
Emperor Wǔ inherited their abundant resources,
and thus was able to indulge in extravagance and desire without leading to chaos.
If Emperor Gāo Zǔ had been immediately succeeded by Emperor Wǔ,
how could the Hàn dynasty have endured for long!
This is a firm conclusion.
The imperial carriages, equipment, and the attire of the various princes, princesses, and consorts made in the capital and the four regions,
are not considered frugal by critics.
'If one does not rise early and strive for great distinction,
later generations will still become indolent.'
Zuǒ Zhuàn quotes the inscription on the 'chán dǐng' as saying this.
Dù Yù's commentary says: 'Mèi'
means 'dàn',
to rise early.
'Pī'
means 'great'.
It means to rise early and strive for great distinction,
yet later generations will still become indolent.
'Fú',
pronounced 'fú'.
Knowing the people's sufferings,
and it is still like this,
how much more so for the Crown Prince, who grew up in the deep palace,
and has not experienced outside affairs.
'Gèng',
pronounced 'gōng-héng'.
After ten thousand years [i.e., after your reign],
this is indeed what Your Majesty ought to worry about.
Your subject observes that since ancient times,
when the common people are troubled and resentful,
gathering into bandits and thieves,
there has been no country that did not perish.
Even if the ruler wishes to make amends,
they cannot fully recover.
Therefore, one should make reforms while it is still possible to reform,
and not regret after it is already lost.
Yōu and Lì once laughed at Jié and Zhòu;
Emperor Yáng also laughed at Zhōu and Qí.
Do not let later generations laugh at the present as the present laughs at Emperor Yáng!
At the beginning of the Zhēngguān reign,
there was famine throughout the land;
a *dǒu* of rice was worth a bolt of silk,
yet the common people did not complain,
knowing that Your Majesty was worried and had not forgotten them.
Now, for consecutive years, harvests have been abundant;
a bolt of silk can buy more than ten *hú* of millet,
yet the common people complain and sigh,
knowing that Your Majesty no longer thinks of them,
and is undertaking many non-urgent projects.
Since ancient times,
the rise and fall of a nation
has not depended on the amount of accumulated wealth,
but on the suffering or happiness of the common people.
Let us use recent examples to verify this:
The Suí dynasty stored provisions in Luòkǒu Granary, and Lǐ Mì profited from it.
The Eastern Capital accumulated cloth and silk, and Shì Chōng utilized it.
The treasuries of the Western Capital were also used by the state,
and are not yet exhausted even today.
Accumulation of wealth is indeed indispensable,
but it must be collected when people have surplus strength,
and then gathered.
One must not forcefully levy it to enrich enemies and bandits.
As for frugality to relieve the people,
Your Majesty personally practiced it at the beginning of the Zhēngguān reign.
To do so today
is certainly not difficult.
If Your Majesty truly desires a long-term plan,
you need not seek far into antiquity;
simply return to the state of the beginning of the Zhēngguān reign,
and the world will be extremely fortunate.
Your Majesty's favor and treatment of the various princes
is somewhat excessive.
At this time, Wèi Wáng Tàii was favored by the Emperor,
hence Zhōu mentioned it.
This must be deeply considered.
Furthermore,
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi loved Chén Sī Wáng,
yet when Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he imprisoned the various princes,
albeit without physical fetters.
This event is seen in the annals of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn and Emperor Wén of Wèi.
'Léi',
pronounced 'lì-zhuī'.
'Xiè',
pronounced 'xī-liè'.
Zhū Yuánhuì said: 'Léi'
is a black rope.
'Xiè'
means to bind.
In ancient times, prisons used black ropes to bind criminals.
This was precisely how they inflicted suffering.
Also,
the peace and order of the common people
depend solely on the Governors and County Magistrates.
If suitable people are selected and employed,
then Your Majesty can sit with folded hands and do nothing.
Currently, the court only values internal officials and lightly regards the selection of officials for the provinces and counties.
Governors are often military men,
or capital officials who failed in their duties are appointed to external posts.
In remote areas,
the selection of personnel is even more lenient.
Therefore, the common people are not yet at peace,
probably due to this."
When the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor praised its excellence for a long time,
and said to his attendants:
"For Governors, I shall select them myself;
for County Magistrates,
I should issue an edict for officials of
the capital and above to each nominate one person."
11 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Guǐchǒu,
an edict was issued that all deceased meritorious officials and imperial relatives should be buried alongside the imperial mausoleums.
The Táng system stipulated: all meritorious officials and close relatives who requested burial alongside the imperial mausoleum were permitted to do so,
arranged with civil and military officials separated to the left and right.
If imperial concubines were buried alongside,
the mausoleum households would construct their tombs.
The Táng Huìyào records that among those buried alongside Zhāolíng,
there were imperial consorts, princesses, imperial sons-in-law, meritorious nobles, and those whose ancestors were buried alongside while their descendants followed in burial,
as well as barbarian rulers who served in the imperial guard and were buried alongside.
Their names were very numerous,
in accordance with this edict.
12 The Emperor hunted in the Luòyáng Yuàn.
The Táng Liùdiǎn states: Luòyáng Yuàn is located west of the capital city,
north to Běimáng,
west to Xiàoshuǐ,
south bordered by a branch of the Luòshǔi,
with the Gǔ and Luò rivers converging within it.
It was seventeen *lǐ* on the east side,
thirty-nine *lǐ* on the south side,
fifty *lǐ* on the west side,
and twenty *lǐ* on the north side,
with a total circumference of one hundred and twenty-six *lǐ*.
The Emperor drew his bow four times,
killing four boars.
A boar charged forward,
reaching the stirrup of his horse;
the Minister of Revenue, Táng Jiǎn, dismounted and wrestled with it.
The Emperor drew his sword and killed the boar,
then looked back and smiled, saying:
"Isn't the Chief Clerk of Tiāncè watching the supreme general strike down a foe?"
During the Wǔdé reign,
the Emperor established the Tiāncè Shàngjiāng Commandery,
with Táng Jiǎn as its Chief Clerk.
'Zhǎng',
pronounced 'zhī-liǎng'.
'Jiāng',
pronounced 'jí-liàng'.
'Xié',
pronounced 'yē'.
Táng Jiǎn replied:
"Emperor Gāo Zǔ of Hàn gained the empire on horseback,
but did not govern it on horseback."
This is Lù Jiǎ's admonition to Emperor Gāo Zǔ of Hàn.
'Zhì',
pronounced 'zhí-zhī'.
"How can one again display heroic spirit against a mere beast!"
The Emperor was pleased,
and stopped the hunt for him,
soon after promoting him to Guānglù Dàfū.
13 Wu Wáng Kè (吳王恪), the Grand Governor of Ānzhōu, frequently went out hunting,
which greatly inconvenienced the residents;
Imperial Censor Liǔ Fàn (柳範) impeached him.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
Kè was dismissed from office and
300 households were confiscated.
The Emperor said:
"The chief clerk, Quán Wànjì (權萬紀), served my son
but failed to rectify him,
so he deserves to die."
Liǔ Fàn said:
"Fáng Xuánlíng (房玄齡) served Your Majesty,
yet he could not stop your hunting.
How can Wànjì alone be blamed?"
The Emperor was furious,
flung his sleeves, and went inside.
After a long while,
he summoned Fàn alone and said:
"Why did you criticize me directly?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty is benevolent and wise;
your subject dares not but speak with foolish honesty."
There is an ancient saying: "If the ruler is benevolent, his ministers are upright."
It also says: "If the ruler is enlightened, his ministers are upright."
This is why Liǔ Fàn spoke as he did.
14 In the eleventh month,
on the Xīnmǎo day,
the Emperor visited Huáizhōu;
on the Bǐngwǔ day,
he returned to Luòyáng Gōng.
15 The daughter of the late Grand Governor of Jīngzhōu, Wǔ Shìhuò (武士彠),
was fourteen years old.
The Emperor heard of her beauty
and summoned her into the imperial harem,
making her a cáirén.
This laid the foundation for the Wǔ clan to disrupt the Táng dynasty.
Huò (彠),
pronounced yī guó fān.
The Discernment of Differences states: According to the Old Annals of Zétiān,
she was eighty-three at the time of her death.
The Tánglì, Jiāo Lù's Tángcháo Niándàijì, Tǒngjì, Mǎ Zǒng's Tángnián Xiǎolù, Shèngyùntú, and Huìyào all state eighty-one.
Tánglù and Zhèngyào say
she entered the palace in the thirteenth year of Zhēngguān.
Based on Wǔ Shì's entry into the palace at age fourteen.
Now, following Wú Jìng's Zétiān Shílù, which states eighty-two,
she is placed in this year.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the Yǐwèi day,
Lǐbù Shàngshū Wáng Guī (王珪) reported:
"It is improper for officials of the third rank and above to dismount when encountering a princely king on the road.
This is not according to ritual."
The Emperor said:
"You gentlemen are merely exalting yourselves and belittling my sons."
Tèjìn Wèi Zhēng (魏徵) said:
"The princely kings rank below the Three Dukes.
Officials of the third rank are all Nine Ministers and Eight Seats.
For them to dismount for kings
is indeed inappropriate."
The Emperor said:
"The span of a person's life is unpredictable.
Should the Crown Prince unfortunately pass away,
how can we know that the princely kings will not one day become the masters of your generation?
How can they be slighted?"
At that time, Crown Prince Chéngqián (承乾) had a foot ailment,
and Wèi Wáng Tài (魏王泰) was favored;
Emperor Tàizōng's words
indeed harbored the intention of replacing Chéngqián with Tài.
Yāo (夭),
pronounced yú shào fān.
"From the Zhōu dynasty onward,
succession has always been from son to son,
not from brother to brother.
This is to prevent younger sons from harboring ambitions
and to stem the source of disaster and chaos.
This is something rulers should deeply guard against."
Thereupon, the Emperor followed Guī's suggestion.
2 Lìbù Shàngshū Gāo Shìlián (高士廉), Huángmén Shìláng Wéi Tǐng (韋挺), Lǐbù Shìláng Línghú Défēn (令狐德棻), and Zhōngshū Shìláng Cén Wénběn (岑文本) completed the compilation of the Shìzúzhì
and presented it to the Emperor.
Before this,
the prominent clans from Shāndōng, such as the Cuī, Lú, Lǐ, and Zhèng families,
liked to boast about their prestigious origins.
Even if their fortunes had declined over generations,
if other clans wished to form marriage alliances with them,
the Báihǔtōng states: Hūn (昏) refers to performing rites at dusk,
hence called hūn.
Yīn (姻) refers to a woman relying on her husband,
hence called yīn.
Xián says: The wife's father is called hūn,
and the son-in-law's father is called yīn.
Some would abandon their native place and falsely claim a prominent clan name,
or brothers of equal standing would humble each other through their wives' families.
The Emperor detested this.
He ordered Shìlián and others to thoroughly examine all genealogies in the realm,
verify them against historical records,
ascertain their authenticity,
distinguish their generational order,
rank them into grades,
commend loyal and virtuous individuals,
demote treacherous and rebellious ones,
and divide them into nine ranks.
Shìlián and others ranked Huángmén Shìláng Cuī Míngàn (崔民幹) as the first.
The Emperor said:
"Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn, along with Xiāo, Cáo, Fán, and Guàn, all rose from commoners in the villages.
Yet you gentlemen still admire them as heroes and worthies.
Is it about hereditary official positions?
The Gāo clan only partially occupied Shāndōng;
Liáng and Chén were confined to Jiāngnán.
Although they had some notable figures,
what is there to speak of?
Moreover, their descendants' talents and conduct are weak,
and their official positions have declined.
Yet they still arrogantly boast about their family origins,
peddling their ancestors' names,
relying on wealth and power,
abandoning integrity and forgetting shame.
I don't know why the people of the world value them!
Now, officials of the third rank and above
have achieved their noble and prominent positions
either through virtue,
merit,
or literary accomplishment.
Those old clans of a declining era
are truly not worth admiring!
Yet people seek to marry into them,
and even if they offer much gold and silk,
they are still treated arrogantly by them.
I do not understand why this is."
Jiě (解),
means 'to explain'.
"You should abandon superficial reputation and seek substance,
yet you still rank Cuī Míngàn as the first.
This is to belittle my official ranks and cater to popular sentiment."
He then ordered a revision,
specifically using the current dynasty's official ranks as the basis for hierarchy.
Thus, the imperial clan was placed first,
followed by the imperial relatives by marriage,
and Cuī Míngàn was demoted to the third rank.
In the sequence of the nine ranks,
the imperial clan was the "upper-upper,"
the imperial relatives by marriage were the "upper-middle,"
and Cuī Míngàn was the "upper-lower."
One thousand six hundred and fifty-one families
were announced throughout the realm.
3 In the second month,
on the Yǐmǎo day,
the imperial carriage returned west;
it returned west to Cháng'ān from Luòyáng.
Huán (還),
pronounced cóng xuān fān,
also pronounced as the character itself.
On the Guǐhài day,
he visited Héběi
to observe the Dǐzhù rock.
After returning west,
he visited Héběi County en route.
Héběi County,
in Hàn and Jìn, belonged to Hédōng Commandery.
Later, the Wèi established Héběi Commandery.
The Suí abolished the commandery
and restored it as a county,
belonging to Púzhōu.
In the river south of the county is Dǐzhù Mountain.
In the first year of Zhēngguān,
Héběi County was transferred to Shǎnzhōu.
The Kuòdìzhì states: Héběi County in Shǎnzhōu
was originally Dàyáng County in Hàn.
4 On the Jiǎzǐ day,
the Láozǐ of Wūzhōu rebelled,
capturing over three thousand men and women.
In the first year of Zhēngguān,
Wūzhōu was established by dividing Lóngbiāo County from Chénzhōu.
Láo (獠),
pronounced lǔ hào fān.
5 On the Yǐchǒu day,
the Emperor offered sacrifices at Yǔ Miào;
on the Dīngmǎo day,
he arrived at Liǔgǔ
to inspect the salt lake.
Yǔ's capital was Ānyì;
later generations established a temple there.
Ānyì has a salt lake,
so Liǔgǔ must also be in Ānyì.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
he arrived at Púzhōu.
The Prefect Zhào Yuánkǎi (趙元楷) ordered the elders to wear yellow gauze single garments to welcome the imperial carriage
and elaborately decorated the government offices and towers.
He also fed over a hundred sheep and several hundred fish to present to the imperial relatives.
The Emperor rebuked him, saying:
"When I tour Hè and Luò,
everything I need
is supplied from the treasury.
What you have done is the corrupt practice of the fallen Suí dynasty."
On the Jiǎxū day,
he visited Chángchūn Gōng.
6 On *wùyín* (day 55 of the 60-day cycle),
an edict said:
"Although Yáo Jūnsù, the former Eagle Striking Commander of the Suí dynasty,
was like a jackal barking at Yáo,
and lacked the intention to turn his weapons around (to defect),
yet in a strong wind, sturdy grass
truly demonstrates a heart that endures the cold of the year;
he may be posthumously granted the title of Inspector of Púzhōu,
and his descendants should be sought out and reported."
7 In the intercalary month,
on the *gēngchén* (day 17 of the 60-day cycle) new moon,
there was a solar eclipse.
8 On *dīngwèi* (day 44 of the 60-day cycle),
the imperial carriage arrived at the capital, Jīngshī.
9 In the third month,
on *xīnhài* (day 48 of the 60-day cycle),
Dèng Shìlóng, an assistant to the Director of the Imperial Library, submitted a memorial requesting the collection of His Majesty's writings.
The Emperor said:
"As for my pronouncements,
those beneficial to the people
are all recorded by the historians,
sufficient to achieve immortality.
If they are
of no benefit,
what use is collecting them!
The father and son of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng, the Last Lord of Chén, and Emperor Yáng of Suí all had collections of their writings circulated in the world,
but how did that save them from ruin!
For a ruler, the worry is not having virtuous governance;
what use are writings!"
Thereupon, he did not permit it.
10On *bǐngzǐ* (day 13 of the 60-day cycle),
because of the birth of an imperial grandson,
a banquet was held for officials of the fifth rank and above in the Eastern Palace.
The Emperor said:
"Before the Zhēngguān era,
managing the empire with me was the achievement of Xuánlíng.
Since the Zhēngguān era,
correcting faults and rectifying errors
has been the achievement of Wèi Zhēng."
Both were bestowed with ceremonial swords.
The Emperor said to Wèi Zhēng:
"How does my governance compare to previous years?"
He replied:
"The awe and virtue that are imposed
are far greater than in the early Zhēngguān era;
but in terms of the people's joyful submission, it is not as good."
The Emperor said:
"Distant regions fear my might and admire my virtue,
hence they come to submit;
if it is not as good,
how can this be achieved?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty, previously, you were worried about the empire being ungoverned,
hence your virtue and righteousness renewed daily;
now, you consider the empire being governed as peaceful,
hence it is not as good."
The Emperor said:
"What I do now
is still the same as in previous years,
how is it different?"
He replied:
"At the beginning of the Zhēngguān era, Your Majesty
feared that people would not admonish,
and constantly encouraged them to speak,
and in the interim, you were pleased and followed their advice.

The Táng (唐) system for visiting a mausoleum was: an interim palace was set up
ten *lǐ* from the mausoleum,
seats were arranged in the purification chamber,
a small temporary residence (xiǎo cì, 小次) was set up southwest of the path to the mausoleum,
and a large temporary residence (dà cì, 大次) southwest of the main burial chamber (qǐn, 寢).
Attendant ministers' residences were southwest of the large temporary residence,
and those in accompanying positions had their residences further to the southwest,
all facing east.
Civil officials were to the north,
military officials to the south,
and the envoys for court assemblies further to their south,
all arranged according to the suitability of the terrain.
When the emperor arrived at the interim palace,
which was the purification chamber,
the mausoleum director presented the jade tablet for signature.
The imperial seat was placed at the southeastern corner of the mausoleum,
facing west.
If there were hills or ridges obstructing, arrangements were made according to the terrain.
Another seat was placed southeast of the eastern steps of the main hall of the main burial chamber,
facing west,
with the honored stand and offerings arranged southeast of the hall's door.
All officials, accompanying imperial family members, and guest envoys were positioned to the left and right of the spirit path.
At the main burial chamber, they were arranged in their respective positions in front of the large temporary residence.
On that day, five *kè* before dawn,
the imperial yellow standard guard was arrayed at the mausoleum.
Three *kè* before dawn,
the officials in charge of the ceremony, imperial relatives of the fifth rank and above, and guest envoys who were to accompany took their positions.
The emperor, in plain attire, rode on horseback under a parasol and fan,
with attendant ministers riding alongside,

Leaving the residence to reach his position,

then bowed twice again.
All those in position bowed twice,
then bowed twice again.

the Tài Cháng Qīng (太常卿) requested permission to depart.
The emperor bowed twice,
then bowed twice again.
The Fèng Lǐ (奉禮) said,
"Permission granted."
All those in position bowed twice.
The emperor returned to the small temporary residence,
rode on horseback to the large temporary residence,
where guards stood in formation awaiting his departure.
All officials, imperial relatives, and guest envoys stood in order in front of the residence.
The emperor walked to the south gate of the main burial chamber.
The guards stopped,
and he entered.
Passing through the eastern side chamber,
he advanced to the southeastern position on the palace steps,

ascended from the eastern stairs,

He entered to inspect the clothing and articles,

The emperor bowed twice,

"For several years, Gāochāng

Han (汗),

8 In the summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day of Wùyín (戊寅),
the Emperor proceeded to Jiǔchéng Gōng (九成宮).
Originally,
Jiéshèrài (結社率), the younger brother of Tūlì Kèhán (突利可汗) of the Tūjué, had accompanied Tūlì to the court
and successively held the position of Zhōngláng Jiāng (中郎將).
At home, he was dissolute
and resented Tūlì for ostracizing him.
He then falsely accused Tūlì of rebellion,
and the Emperor, for this reason, held him in low regard
and did not promote his rank for a long time.
Jiéshèrài secretly allied with his former tribesmen,
gathering over forty people.
They planned, when the Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng 晉王) left the palace at the fourth drum,
to open the gates and clear the way,
gallop into the palace gates,
and head directly for the imperial tent,
which could lead to a great achievement.
On the day of Jiǎshēn (甲申),
he took Hèluóhú (賀邏鶻), Tūlì's son, and waited in ambush outside the palace at night.
It happened to be a strong wind,
and the Prince of Jìn had not yet come out.
Jiéshèrài, fearing dawn,
then attacked the traveling palace,
climbing over four layers of curtains.
Bows and arrows were fired indiscriminately,
and dozens of guards died.
Zhéchōng (折衝) Sūn Wǔkāi (孫武開) and others led their troops in a fierce counterattack.
After a long time,
they retreated,
galloping into the imperial stables (御廄),
stealing over twenty horses.
They fled north,
crossed the Wèi (渭) River,
intending to run to their tribe.
They were pursued and captured,
and then executed.
Hèluóhú was pardoned
and exiled to the distant frontier (Lǐngbiǎo 嶺表).
9 On the day of Gēngyín (庚寅),
Wǔhóu Jiāngjūn (武候將軍) Shàngguān Huáirén (上官懷仁) was sent to attack the rebellious Láo (獠) people in the four prefectures of Bā (巴), Bì (壁), Yáng (洋), and Jí (集).
He pacified them,
capturing over six thousand men and women.

"Your Majesty's ambition and conduct,

"In recent years,

It is even said: 'If the common people have nothing to do, they become arrogant and unruly;
if they are kept busy with labor, they are easy to manage.'

This, I fear, is not the ultimate wisdom for founding a state."
The Emperor greatly praised and admired him,

Básīmí (拔悉彌),
is likely Básīmì (拔悉蜜),
west of Gélúolù (葛邏祿).
Bómǎ (駁馬),
also called Bìlà (弊剌),
or Èluózhī (遏羅支),
was directly north of Tūjué (突厥),
fourteen thousand *lǐ* (里) from the capital,
its northern limit reaching the sea.
They plowed fields with horses.
Although they raised horses, they did not ride them.
They relied on mare's milk and kumis for food.
The horses were all dappled,
hence the country's name.
Jiégǔ (結骨),
was the ancient Jiānkūn Guó (堅昆國),
west of Yīwú (伊吾),
north of Yānqí (焉耆),
beside the Báishān (白山).
Jiānkūn (堅昆),
later corrupted to Jiégǔ (結骨),
gradually known as Hégǔ (紇骨),
also Hégēsī (紇扢斯),
and Xiágē sī (黠戞斯).
Huǒxún (火燖),
or Huòlìxímí (貨利習彌),
or Guòlì (過利),
resided on the south bank of the Wūxǔ Shuǐ (烏滸水),
bordered Persia to the southwest,
and Tūjué (突厥) to the northwest.
Bó (駁),
read as Běi Jiǎo (北角).
Xún (燖),
read as Xú Yán (徐鹽).
Yīliè (伊列),
was an ancient Xīyù (西域) country during the Hàn (漢) period,
north of Kāngjū (康居).
Chén Tāng (陳湯) consulted with Gān Yánshòu (甘延壽) about Zhìzhī (郅支) saying:
"Attack Yīliè (伊列) to the north,
and take Ānxī (安息) to the west."
This is the proof.
*Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The biography of Shābōluó Yèhù (沙鉢羅葉護) says:
"Its eastern border was the Yīliè Hé (伊列河)."
However, the biography of Yǐpí Duōlù (乙毗咄陸) says:
"West of the Yīliè Hé (伊列河) belonged to Duōlù (咄陸),
and east of it belonged to Diēlìshī (咥利失)."
Since Shābōluó Yèhù (沙鉢羅葉護) occupied Diēlìshī's (咥利失) territory,
it should say its western border was the Yīliè Hé (伊列河).
It is currently unknown which of the two accounts is incorrect,
so it merely states that Yīliè Shuǐ (伊列水) was the boundary.
1 Spring,
first month,
jiǎyín (甲寅) day,
the Emperor visited the residence of Wèi Wáng Tà (魏王泰).
He pardoned prisoners in Cháng'ān (長安), Yōngzhōu (雍州), from capital offenses downwards,
exempted Yánkāng Lǐ (延康里) from this year's land tax and levies,
and bestowed gifts upon Tà (泰)'s officials, staff, and elders in the same *lǐ* (里), with varying grades.
Wèi Wáng Tà (魏王泰)'s residence was in Yánkāng Lǐ (延康里) within Cháng'ān Chéng (長安城).
It is noted that Yōngzhōu (雍州) had two red counties,
Cháng'ān (長安) and Wànnián (萬年), both administered within Cháng'ān Chéng (長安城).
Now, only the Cháng'ān (長安) prisoners were pardoned,
presumably because Yánkāng Lǐ (延康里) belonged to Cháng'ān Xiàn (長安縣)'s jurisdiction.
Yōng (雍),
read as Yū Yòng (於用).
Pì (辟),
read as Pí Yì (毗亦).
2 In the second month,
on the *Dīngchǒu* day,
the Emperor went to the Guózǐjiān,
to observe the *shìdiàn* ceremony.
According to records, the Táng Guózǐjiān was located west of Ānshàngmén.
Under the Táng system, *shìdiàn* ceremonies were performed for Wénxuān Wáng in mid-spring and mid-autumn,
always on the first *Dīng* and first *Wù* days of the month,
with the *Jìjiǔ*, *Sīyè*, and *Bóshì* performing the three libations.
The *Jìjiǔ* and those below, down to the most distinguished students, were granted silk in varying amounts.
The *Zhōuguān* recorded positions like *Shīshì* and *Bǎoshì*.
The Hàn dynasty first established the positions of *Jìjiǔ* and *Bóshì*;
the Jìn dynasty first established the Guózǐxué.
The Táng Guózǐ Jìjiǔ,
a third-rank official,
was in charge of the national policies for Confucian education and guidance.
The Emperor frequently visited the Guózǐjiān,
ordering discussions and lectures.
Students who could clearly expound on one major classic or more were eligible for official appointments.
To select officials, the Táng dynasty
regarded the *Lǐjì* and *Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Zhuàn* as major classics,
the *Shī*, *Yílǐ*, and *Zhōulǐ* as medium classics,
and the *Yì*, *Shàngshū*, *Chūnqiū Gōngyáng Zhuàn*, and *Gǔliáng Zhuàn* as minor classics.
*Shù* (數),
pronounced *suǒ jiǎo fān*.
*Yǐshàng* (已上),
pronounced *shí zhǎng fān*.
The number of students was increased to a full 2,260 members.
Even those from the garrison camps and flying cavalry
were assigned *Bóshì*
to teach them classics.
Those who could master the classics
were allowed to participate in the imperial examinations.
Consequently, scholars from all directions gathered in the capital,
and even chieftains from Gāolí, Bǎijì, Xīnluó, Gāochāng, and Tǔbō sent their sons and younger brothers to request entry into the national academy.
Those who attended lectures reached over 8,000 people.
As the Emperor found that scholarly theories were numerous
and textual interpretations complex,
he ordered Kǒng Yǐngdá and other scholars to compile and edit the commentaries on the Five Classics,
calling it the *Zhèngyì*,
and commanded scholars to study it.
The *Wǔjīng Zhèngyì* is still circulated today.
*Zhuàn* (撰),
pronounced *shì miǎn fān*.
*Shū* (疏),
pronounced *suǒ qù fān*.
*Lìng* (令),
pronounced *lì dīng fān*.
3 On the *Rénwǔ* day,
the Emperor went to the Lìshān Hot Springs;
on the *Xīnmǎo* day,
he returned to the palace.
4 On the *Yǐwèi* day,
an imperial edict was issued to seek out descendants of renowned scholars of recent times: Huángfǔ Kǎn and Chǔ Zhòngdū of the Liáng dynasty;
Xióng Ānshēng and Shěn Zhòng of the Zhōu dynasty;
Shěn Wén'ā, Zhōu Hóngzhèng, and Zhāng Jī of the Chén dynasty;

Dòuzhōu Road Commander Dǎng Rénhóng attacked the rebellious *lǎo* people of Luódòu,
defeating them

the kingdom of Liúguǐ sent envoys to pay tribute.
It was 15,000 *lǐ* from the capital,
bordering the Northern Sea,
south of Mòhé.
The kingdom of Liúguǐ was
directly northeast of Hēishuǐ Mòhé,
north of the Small Sea.
It was surrounded by the sea on three sides,
bordering Moyè Mòhé to the south.
Sailing southeast for fifteen days
