Its people lived scattered across islands,
many in marshy areas.
They initially submitted to Bǎijì,
then later to Xīnluó;
they were an Eastern Yi people.
Dù Yòu said: "The kingdom of Liúguǐ is north of the Northern Sea."
*Shǐ* (使),
pronounced *shū lì fān*.
pronounced *mò*.
pronounced *hé*.
They arrived after three translations.
The Emperor appointed their envoy, Yú Zhì, as a Cavalry Commandant.
7 On the *Bǐngchén* day,
a Níngshuò Grand Envoy was established to protect the Tūjué.
8 In summer,
the fifth month,
on the *Rényín* day,
Lǐ Língkuí, Prince of Yān, was transferred to be Prince of Lǔ.
9 The Emperor was about to visit Luòyáng,
and ordered Minister of Works Yán Lìdé to survey a suitable location for a summer retreat.
In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the *Gēngwǔ* day,
Xiāngchéng Palace was built in the western mountains of Rǔzhōu.
Qín established the *Jiàngzuò*,
in charge of constructing and repairing palaces,
a system unchanged through the dynasties.
Hàn Jǐngdì established the *Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng*.
Under Táng, he was a third-rank official,
in charge of national construction, timber, and artisan policies.
The New Records state: "During the Zhēngguān era,
Qīngshǔ Palace was built south of Mínggāoshān in Línrǔ County, Rǔzhōu."
According to records, the Rǔ River bordered Guǎngchéng Zé.
He was Lìběn's elder brother.
Yán Lìběn
served as Chancellor during Gāozōng's reign.
10 Gāochāng King Qú Wéntài, upon hearing that Táng troops were mobilized,
said to his people:
"Táng is seven thousand *lǐ* away from us,
with two thousand *lǐ* of sandy deserts in between,
where there is no water or grass. The cold wind is like a knife,
and the hot wind is like fire.
How can they bring a large army here!
When I previously went to court,
(I went to court and saw volume 193, four years.)
The cities were desolate,
not comparable to the time of Suí.
pronounced *qī jī fān*.
*Cháo* (朝),
pronounced *zhí yáo fān*.
If they come to attack me now,
if they dispatch many troops, their provisions will not suffice;
if it's less than thirty thousand,
my strength can control them.
We should rest and await their exhaustion,
and reap the benefits of their weariness.
If they halt their troops outside the city,
within twenty days,
their food will run out, and they will surely retreat.
Then we will pursue and capture them.
What is there to worry about!"
However, when he heard that Táng troops had reached the *Qìkǒu*,
he became worried and fearful, not knowing what to do.
He fell ill and died,
and his son Qú Zhìshèng ascended the throne.
When the army reached Liǔgǔ,
(The New Records state: "From Jiāohé County, Xīzhōu, going north 210 *lǐ* reaches Liǔgǔ ferry.")
The people of the kingdom had all gathered there.
The generals requested to attack them,
but Hóu Jūnjí said:
"No,
the Son of Heaven sent me to punish Gāochāng because of its disrespect.
To attack people amidst ruins and tombs
is not the conduct of an army sent to seek justice."
Thereupon, they advanced with drums beating.
Upon reaching Tiánchéng,
(The *Kǎo Yì* states: "The *Shílù* writes 'Tiándìchéng,'
now following the old accounts.
According to records, Tiánchéng is Tiándìchéng.
When Qú Jiā was King of Gāochāng,
he established the Tiándì Grand Administrator
and enfeoffed his two sons:
one as Duke of Jiāohé,
and the other as Duke of Tiándì.
The New Book states: 'Tiándìchéng
is the land where the Hàn *Wùjǐ Xiàowèi* governed.'
Sòng Bái said: 'Gāochāng County in Xīzhōu
was originally the land of Jìn's Tiándì County.'
The *Yúdì Zhì* states: 'In the second year of Jìn Xiánhé (327 CE),
Gāochāng Commandery was established,
and Tiándì County was founded.
Táng renamed it Gāochāng County.')
It did not fall immediately.
They attacked it the next morning,
and captured it by noon,
seizing over 7,000 men and women.
With Zhonglangjiang Xīn Liáo'ér as the vanguard,
they marched through the night
towards the capital city.
Gāochāng resisted but was defeated;
the main army followed and
reached the city walls.
Zhìshèng 致書於君集曰：
“The one who offended the Son of Heaven
was the former king.
The heavenly punishment was inflicted,
and he has already passed away.
Zhìshèng succeeded to the throne not long ago,
may Sàngshū have pity and investigate!”
Jūnjí replied:
“If you can repent of your mistakes,
you should surrender yourself at the military gate.”
Zhìshèng still did not come out.
Jūnjí ordered the moats to be filled and attacked the city.
Stones rained down,
and all the people in the city stayed indoors.
They also built a cháo chē,
ten zhàng high,
to look down into the city.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says: “The King of Chǔ ascended a cháo chē to observe the Jìn army.”
The Shì Wén says: “A war chariot as high as a nest,
used to observe the enemy.”
Dù Yù says: “A turret was built on top of the chariot.”
Dù Yòu’s explanation was seen previously.
高 (gāo),
pronounced jū áo.
瞰 (kàn),
pronounced kǔ làn.
All pronounced.
Previously,
Wéntài had allied with the Khagan of the Western Tūjué,
promising mutual assistance in times of emergency.
The Khagan sent his Yèhù to garrison Kèhánfútú City.
Yèhù
was a high official of the Tūjué,
the chief of the ministers.
From Jiāohé City to Fútú City was three hundred seventy lǐ.
When Jūnjí arrived,
the Khagan was afraid and fled west for over a thousand lǐ,
and the Yèhù surrendered the city.
Zhìshèng was in dire straits.
On the day guǐ yǒu,
he opened the gates and surrendered.
Gāochāng, since Qū Jiā established the state,
passed through nine generations,
and perished after one hundred thirty-four years.
降 (jiàng),
pronounced hù jiāng.
Its twenty-two cities were captured,
with eight thousand forty-six households,
and seventeen thousand seven hundred people.
Kǎo Yì says: “The old tradition says,
‘eight thousand households,
thirty-seven thousand seven hundred people,’
now following the Veritable Records.”
Five hundred lǐ from north to south.
The emperor wished to make Gāochāng into prefectures and counties.
Wèi Zhēng remonstrated, saying:
“When Your Majesty first ascended the throne,
Wéntài and his wife were the first to come to court.
Wéntài entered court for four years.
Therefore, the former king was punished.
The guilt should stop with Wéntài;
it would be appropriate to comfort its people,
preserve its altars of soil and grain,
and re-establish his son.
Then Your Majesty’s prestige and virtue would extend to distant lands,
and all the Four Barbarians would joyfully submit.
Now, if you covet its land to make it into prefectures and counties,
you will constantly need over a thousand men to guard it,
changing them every few years.
Three or four out of ten of those who travel back and forth will die.
Providing clothing and supplies,
separating from relatives,
after ten years,
Lǒngyòu will be depleted.
Your Majesty will ultimately not gain a handful of grain or a foot of silk from Gāochāng to assist the Central Kingdom.
This is what is called scattering what is useful to serve what is useless.
Your servant does not see its propriety.”
The emperor did not heed.
In the ninth month,
its land was made Xīzhōu,
and Kèhánfútú City was made Tíngzhōu.
Xīzhōu governed Gāochāng County,
which was the former king’s court of Han Chēshī.
Tíngzhōu governed Jīnmǎn County,
which was the later king’s court of Han Chēshī.
Sòng Bái said: “The two prefectures are four hundred fifty lǐ apart.”
On the day yǐ mǎo,
the Ānxī Dūhù Fǔ was established at Jiāohé City,
and troops were left to garrison it.
Jūnjí captured Gāochāng King Zhìshèng and his officials and heroes, and returned.
At this point, the Tang territory extended east to the sea,
west to Yānqí,
south to Línyì,
and north to the Great Desert,
all made into prefectures and counties.
In total, it was nine thousand five hundred ten lǐ from east to west,
and ten thousand nine hundred eighteen lǐ from north to south.
When Hóu Jūnjí was campaigning against Gāochāng,
he sent an envoy to make an agreement with Yānqí to join forces.
Yānqí was pleased
and obeyed.
After Gāochāng was defeated,
the King of Yānqí went to the military gate to meet Jūnjí,
and also said that three cities of Yānqí had previously been seized by Gāochāng.
Jūnjí memorialized to return all the people of Yānqí plundered by Gāochāng.
Gāochāng’s plundering of Yānqí was seen in year six.
In the winter of the 11th year,
tenth month,
on the day jiǎ xū,
Jīng Wáng Yuánjǐng and others again submitted a memorial requesting the Fēngshàn sacrifices,
but the emperor did not allow it.
Previously,
Lǔ Níng, the Chéncāng Zhéshōng Dūwèi, was imprisoned for a crime.
Relying on his high rank,
he insulted and cursed Liú Rén'guǐ, the Chéncāng Wèi.
Chéncāng County
belonged to Qízhōu.
According to Tang regulations: a county magistrate (wèi) in a capital prefecture was of junior ninth rank, lower grade;
in an upper county, junior ninth rank, upper grade;
in middle and lower counties, junior ninth rank, lower grade.
The prefectural office reported this.
The emperor was enraged
and ordered him to be executed,
but was still not appeased,
saying:
“What kind of county magistrate
dares to kill my Zhéshōng!”
He ordered Rén'guǐ to be summoned to Cháng'ān for questioning face-to-face.
Rén'guǐ said:
“Lǔ Níng insulted your servant in front of the common people in this way,
your servant was truly indignant and killed him.”
His words and demeanor were calm.
Wèi Zhēng, attending at his side,
said:
“Does Your Majesty know why the Suí dynasty perished?”
The emperor said:
“Why?”
Zhēng said:
“At the end of the Suí dynasty,
the common people were strong and insulted officials,
just like Lǔ Níng.”
Lǔ Níng’s official position was Zhéshōng,
he was originally a commoner of Chéncāng.
Rén'guǐ was promoted to Lìyáng Chéng.
Emperor Gāo of Hàn buried Taishang Huang on the north mound of Lìyáng,
named Wànnián Líng,
and changed Lìyáng to Wànnián County,
which was still in use until the Suí dynasty.
When the Tang established its capital in Cháng'ān,
Suí’s Dàxīng County was renamed Wànnián,
and the old Wànnián County was renamed Lìyáng,
belonging to Jīngzhào.
A county magistrate (chéng) in a Tang capital prefecture was of principal eighth rank, lower grade.
The emperor was about to go to Tóngzhōu for a hunt.
Rén'guǐ submitted a memorial, saying:
“This autumn has seen a great harvest,
but the people have only harvested one or two tenths of it.
Making them serve the hunting activities,
repairing roads and bridges,
would require one or two ten thousand labor units,
which would truly hinder farming.
I wish Your Majesty would delay your imperial visit for ten days,
waiting until they finish their work,
then both public and private interests would benefit.”
The emperor granted an imperial rescript praising and accepting it.
He was soon transferred to be Xīn'ān Lìng.
The Xīn'ān Jun was established in the early Tang,
and in the first year of Zhēngguān,
the commandery was abolished and made into a county,
belonging to Luòzhōu.
According to Tang regulations: a county magistrate (lìng) in a capital prefecture was of principal sixth rank, lower grade;
in an upper county, junior sixth rank, upper grade;
in a middle county, principal seventh rank, upper grade;
in a lower county, junior seventh rank, lower grade.
On the day yǐ wèi,
the emperor went to Tóngzhōu;
on the day gēng xū,
he returned to the palace.
On the day bǐng chén,
the Tubō Zānpǔ sent his minister Lù Dōngzàn to offer five thousand liǎng of gold and several hundred precious curios,
to request a marriage alliance.
The emperor promised to give Princess Wénchéng to him as a wife.
Princess Wénchéng was a daughter of the imperial clan.
妻 (qī),
pronounced qī xì.
14th day of the 11th month.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day, the new moon occurred.
It was the Winter Solstice.
The Emperor offered sacrifices in the Southern Suburb.
At that time, the *Wùyín* calendar designated the *guǐhài* day as the new moon.
For the *Wùyín* calendar, see Volume 187, Wǔdé 3rd year.
"Ancient calendars began the day at *zǐ* half-hour.
This year, the *jiǎzǐ* day's new moon coincided with the Winter Solstice.
However, Fù Rénjūn, the former Grand Astrologer, subtracted a little too much from the remainder,
making *zǐchū* the new moon,
thus creating a discrepancy of three *kè*.
This deviates from the true celestial position;
please re-examine and correct it."
The consensus of the assembly was that Rénjūn's calculation of the new moon was slightly off,
while Chúnfēng's calculations were precise.
They requested to follow Chúnfēng's proposal,
and it was granted.
15th day of the *dīngmǎo* day.
The officials of rites submitted a request to increase the mourning period for great-grandparents to *qīcuī* for five months,
and for the legitimate son's wife to *qī*.
A brother's wife, a husband's younger brother, a younger brother's wife, a husband's elder brother, and a maternal uncle should all observe *xiǎogōng* mourning.
This was granted.
According to the New Annals:
"Great-grandparents"
is written as
"great-great-grandparents."
The old mourning period was *qīcuī* for three months.
The legitimate son's wife previously observed *dàgōng* mourning.
The wives of other sons previously observed *xiǎogōng* mourning.
Now, the wives of other sons are to observe *dàgōng* mourning.
And for a brother's wife, a husband's younger brother, a younger brother's wife, a husband's elder brother, and a maternal uncle, who previously observed *sī* mourning,
all are now to observe *xiǎogōng* mourning.
*Qī*
is pronounced *zī*.
*Cuī*
is pronounced *shì huí*.
16th day of the *bǐngzǐ* day.
All officials again memorialized requesting the *fēngshàn* sacrifices,
and an imperial edict granted it.
He further ordered various scholars to meticulously determine the ceremonial procedures;
Wéi Tǐng, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and others were appointed as *Fēngshàn* envoys.
17th day. Wéi Yuánfāng, an Assistant Director of the Bureau of Gates, delayed the issuance of a travel pass for a palace attendant.
In the Táng dynasty, the Director of the Bureau of Gates was in charge of the registers of entry and exit for all gates and passes in the empire.
There were twenty-six passes throughout the empire,
which served to separate the interior from the exterior,
to divide the Huá from the Yí,
to establish strategic defenses,
and to guard against evil and maintain order.
Anyone wishing to cross a pass
first had to apply to the Bureau of Gates of the Ministry of Justice for a travel pass.
A "palace attendant"
referred to those who served as attendants in the forbidden palace,
i.e., eunuchs.
In the Táng dynasty, there was no fixed number of palace attendants.
Anyone without official rank
was called a palace attendant
and was subordinate to the Director of the Palace Secretariat.
The Emperor was enraged
and demoted Yuánfāng to Magistrate of Huáyīn.
Huáyīn county belonged to Huázhōu.
“Huá”
is pronounced *hù huà*.
"When emperors are greatly angered,
they must not act rashly.
Previously, for a palace attendant,
an imperial edict was issued overnight;
the matter was treated like a military secret,
who would not be startled and terrified?
Moreover, the eunuch class
has historically been difficult to manage;
careless words
easily lead to trouble and harm.
Sending them on distant missions alone
is deeply inappropriate.
This trend must not be allowed to grow;
it should be treated with utmost caution."
The Emperor accepted his words.
18th day. Wéi Cōng, Assistant Minister of the Left, pointed out that the price of timber from the Court of the Imperial Granaries was higher than in the private market,
and memorialized that it indicated embezzlement.
The Emperor summoned Sūn Fúgā, Minister of the Grand Court of Justice, to record the crimes of the Court of the Imperial Granaries.
Fúgā said:
"The Court of the Imperial Granaries is not guilty."
The Emperor was surprised
and asked for the reason. He replied:
"It is only because official timber is expensive
that private timber is cheap.
If official timber were cheap,
private timber would have no reason to be cheap.
I only see that the Court of the Imperial Granaries understands the greater good,
and I do not know its fault."
The Emperor understood
and repeatedly praised his astuteness.
He turned to Wéi Cōng and said:
"Your understanding and judgment are far inferior to Fúgā's."
19th day of the 12th month.
On the *dīngyǒu* day.
Hóu Jūnjí presented captives at Guāndé Hall.
Guāndé Hall
was an archery hall.
Comparing it with the map of the Tàijí Palace,
the archery hall was north of Yíchūn Gate.
There was a grand banquet for three days.
Subsequently, Zhìshèng was appointed General of the Left Wǔwèi and Duke of Jīnchéng Commandery.
The Emperor acquired musicians from Gāochāng
and entrusted them to the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
increasing the nine-part music to ten-part music.
The Táng Liùdiǎn states: For all grand banquets,
ten sets of musical performances were arranged in the courtyard,
to accommodate both Huá and Yí.
The first was the Banquet Music,
which included the dances of Jǐngyún Music, Qìngshàn Music, Pòzhèn Music, and Chéngtiān Music;
the second was Qīng Music;
the third was Xīliáng Music;
the fourth was Tiānzhú Music;
the fifth was Gāolì Music;
the sixth was Qūcí Music;
the seventh was Ānguó Music;
the eighth was Shūlè Music;
the ninth was Gāochāng Music;
and the tenth was Kāngguó Music.
When Jūnjí defeated Gāochāng,
he privately took its treasures.
The officers and soldiers, knowing this,
competed in theft,
and Jūnjí could not stop them.
He was impeached by the relevant authorities,
and an imperial edict sent Jūnjí and others to prison.
Cén Wénběn, Secretariat Drafter, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Gāochāng was misguided,
and Your Majesty ordered Jūnjí and others to conquer it,
which they did.
Yet, within ten days,
they were all handed over to the Grand Court of Justice.
Although Jūnjí and the others brought this upon themselves,
I fear that people within the empire will suspect that Your Majesty only records their faults and overlooks their merits.
I have heard that when dispatching generals and armies,
the main objective is to defeat the enemy.
If they can defeat the enemy,
even if they are greedy, they should be rewarded;
if they suffer defeat,
even if they are incorruptible, they should be punished.
Thus, Lǐ Guǎnglí and Chén Tāng of the Hàn,
Wáng Jùn of the Jìn,
and Hán Qínhǔ of the Suí,
though they had committed crimes,
the rulers, recognizing their achievements,
all granted them titles and rewards.
For Lǐ Guǎnglí's case, see Volume 20, Hàn Wǔdì, Tàichū 4th year.
For Chén Tāng's case, see Volume 29, Hàn Yuándì, Jìngníng 1st year.
For Wáng Jùn's case, see Volume 81, Jìn Wǔdì, Tàikāng 1st year.
For Hán Qínhǔ's case, see Volume 177, Suí Wéndì, Kāihuáng 9th year.
Among generals and commanders,
the incorruptible and cautious are few,
while the avaricious are many.
Therefore, the Duke of Huángshí's 'Art of War' states:
'Employ the intelligent,
employ the brave,
employ the greedy,
employ the foolish.
Thus, the intelligent are happy to establish their achievements,
the brave love to fulfill their ambitions,
the greedy are eager to pursue their profit,
and the foolish do not consider their own deaths.'
I humbly pray that you record their minor contributions,
and overlook their major transgressions,
so that Jūnjí may once again ascend to court ranks
and resume his service.
Although he may not be an upright and pure official,
he is still a greedy and foolish general.
In this way, Your Majesty, though bending the law, your virtue will shine even brighter,
and Jūnjí and others, though pardoned, their faults will be even more evident."
The Emperor then released them.
There was also someone who accused Xuē Wànjūn of illicitly communicating with a Gāochāng woman.
Wànjūn denied it.
The Gāochāng woman was brought out from the palace and handed over to the Dàlǐ,
to confront Wànjūn.
Wèi Zhēng admonished, saying:
“Your minister has heard, ‘The lord employs his ministers with propriety;
the minister serves his lord with loyalty.’
This is recorded in the Analects as Kǒngzǐ’s reply to Lǔ Dìnggōng.
Indeed, what is gained is slight,
but what is lost is grave.
In the past, Qín Mù shared drinks with a horse thief.
Qín Mùgōng’s horse had been lost,
and three hundred peasants from Qíxià found it and ate it together.
Officials pursued and apprehended them,
intending to punish them according to the law.
The duke said:
‘A jūnzi does not harm people for the sake of livestock.
I have heard that eating horse meat without drinking wine
is harmful to people.’
Then he gave them wine to drink.
Later, when Mùgōng attacked Jìn,
the three hundred men heard that Mùgōng was surrounded by Jìn forces.
They brandished their blades and fought to the death,
to repay the kindness of being given horse meat,
whereupon Mùgōng captured the Jìn Hóu and returned.
飲,
read Yú Jīn fān.
The Shuō Yuàn states: Chǔ Zhuāngwáng hosted a banquet for his ministers.
As evening fell,
and the drinking was in full swing,
the candles went out.
There was a man who pulled at a beauty’s clothes.
The beauty grabbed and broke off his cap-string,
and told the king to quickly bring light so that
the man with the broken cap-string could be identified.
The king said:
‘I gave people wine,
causing them to become drunk and commit impropriety.
How can I uphold a woman’s virtue and yet humiliate a scholar!’
So he ordered his attendants, saying:
‘Today, when drinking with me,
anyone who does not break off their cap-string will not be considered to have enjoyed themselves.’
All the ministers broke off their cap-strings before the lights were brought.
They enjoyed themselves to the fullest and then dispersed.
Later, when Jìn and Chǔ fought,
one minister was always at the forefront,
engaging five times and capturing heads five times, repelling the enemy,
and ultimately winning.
Zhuāngwáng was surprised and asked about it.
It turned out to be the man who had broken his cap-string that night, repaying the king.
How can Your Majesty fall short of these two rulers!”
The Emperor immediately released him.
Hóu Jūnjí’s horse suffered from maggots [AS-FBED] in its forehead.
The Grand Army Controller, Zhào Yuánkǎi, personally touched its pus with his finger and sniffed it.
虫[AS-FBED]中,
read zhí zhòng fān;
虫食曰虫[AS-FBED]中.
齅,
read xǔ jiù fān.
He was demoted to Kuòzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yǒngjiā Jùn:
In the ninth year of Suí Kāihuáng, Chǔzhōu was established;
in the thirteenth year, it was renamed Kuòzhōu.
劾,
read hù gài fān,
also hù dé fān.
When Gāochāng was pacified,
all the generals immediately received their rewards.
However, the Grand Army Controller, Āshǐnà Shè'ér, having no imperial edict,
alone refused to accept.
Only when a separate edict was issued,
did he accept it,
and what he took were only the old, weak, and worn-out items.
The Emperor praised his integrity and prudence,
and bestowed upon him the precious sword obtained from Gāochāng and a thousand bolts of miscellaneous silks.
On the 20th day of the guǐmǎo month,
the Emperor hunted at Fánchuān.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Fánchuān is in Hàn Dù Xiàn,
also called Fán Xiāng.
When Hàn Gāozǔ arrived at Lìyáng,
because Fán Kuài’s merit in destroying Fèiqiu was the greatest,
he was granted a fief in this area,
hence it was named Fánchuān.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Fánchuān,
also named Yùsù Chuān,
is thirty-five lǐ south of Wànnián Xiàn.
On the yìsì day
he returned to the palace.
On the 21st, Wèi Zhēng submitted a memorial,
believing that:
“The ministers in court,
who are entrusted with crucial responsibilities,
though their duties are heavy,
are not yet fully trusted.
Therefore, some people doubt themselves,
and harbor a perfunctory attitude.
Your Majesty is lenient in major matters,
but strict in minor offenses,
assigning blame and expressing anger on the spur of the moment,
which cannot avoid showing likes and dislikes.
Indeed, entrusting great ministers with overall principles
and holding minor officials accountable for minor matters,
is the way of governance.
Now, in entrusting them with their positions,
great ministers are valued while minor officials are slighted;
yet when matters arise,
minor officials are trusted while great ministers are doubted.
To trust those who are slighted,
and doubt those who are valued,
how can one then seek to achieve good governance?
How can it be achieved!
If great officials are appointed to high positions,
but their minor faults are sought out,
then scribes and clerks,
following the imperial will, will become a trend,
manipulating laws and documents,
to unjustly establish their guilt.
If they explain themselves,
it is assumed they do not acknowledge their guilt;
if they remain silent,
it is assumed their transgressions are all real.
They are stuck in a dilemma,
unable to clear themselves.
The Shī (Sāngróu) says: ‘jìntuì wéi gǔ.’
Note: Gǔ
means ‘plight.’
Falsehood and deceit will become a custom!”
The Emperor accepted his advice.
On the 22nd, the Emperor said to his attendants:
“Although I have pacified the world,
it is very difficult to maintain it.”
Wèi Zhēng replied:
“Your minister has heard that it is easier to win a battle than to hold onto victory.
Your Majesty’s statement today
is a blessing for the imperial ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain!”
On the 23rd, the Emperor heard that the Right Shùzǐ, Zhāng Xuánsù, had repeatedly offered earnest remonstrances in the Eastern Palace.
He promoted him to Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū,
and acting Zuǒ Shùzǐ.
The Crown Prince once beat a drum in the palace.
Xuánsù knocked on the palace gate and remonstrated sharply.
The Crown Prince brought out his drum
and destroyed it in front of Xuánsù.
The Crown Prince had long not appeared before his officials.
Xuánsù remonstrated, saying:
“The court selects outstanding and virtuous men to assist Your Highness’s noble virtue.
Now, a month passes without seeing your palace officials.
How can this be of even the slightest benefit?
Furthermore, there are only women in the palace.
I wonder if there is anyone among them as capable as Fán Jī?”
Fán Jī
was a concubine of Chǔ Zhuāngwáng.
Zhuāngwáng was fond of hunting.
Fán Jī, because of this, refused to eat the meat of birds and beasts.
She scornfully laughed at Yúqiū Zǐ.
Yúqiū Zǐ was shamed by this
and recommended Sūn Shú'áo as prime minister.
Zhuāngwáng then became a hegemon.
Zhāng Xuánsù (張玄素) was an assistant clerk in the Ministry of Justice when he was young.
The Emperor once asked him in court, saying:
"What office did you hold in the Suí (隋) dynasty? "
He replied:
"County Magistrate (Xiànwèi 縣尉)."
He asked again:
"Before you were a Magistrate, what office did you hold? "
He replied:
"Outside the official ranks (Liúwài 流外)."
According to the Suí (隋) system of official ranks,
this was equivalent to the Táng (唐) system of selecting officials outside the official ranks (Liúwài Quán 流外銓).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: According to the Táng (唐) system,
one Lángzhōng (郎中) of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù 吏部)
was in charge of evaluating the ranks and grades of all civil officials in the empire.
Another was in charge of the minor selection (Xiǎoquán 小銓),
which also had nine grades,
generally called "acting appointments" (Hángshǔ 行署).
Because these were outside the nine ranks,
they were called "selection outside the official ranks" (Liúwài Quán 流外銓),
and also "minor selection" (Xiǎoxuǎn 小選).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: In the Sòng (宋) and Qí (齊) dynasties, those outside the official ranks
began with the record keepers (Lùshì 錄事) of the various Guards and the assistant clerks (Lìngshǐ 令史) of the Five Ministries.
"Which department? "
Zhāng Xuánsù (張玄素) was ashamed of this,
and could barely walk after leaving the court,
his face like dead ash.
The Grand Master Remonstrant (Jiànyì Dàfū 諫議大夫) Chǔ Suíliáng (褚遂良) submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"If a ruler can treat his ministers with courtesy,
then he can make them exert their full strength.
Although Zhāng Xuánsù (張玄素) came from humble origins,
Your Majesty valued his talent
and promoted him to the third rank (sānpǐn 三品),
to assist and support the Crown Prince (Huángchǔ 皇儲).
How can you again question his background in front of the assembled ministers!
To discard the past favor
and inflict a moment's shame,
making him feel repressed in his heart,
how can you expect him to uphold his integrity and die for righteousness? "
The Emperor said:
"I also regret this question;
your memorial deeply accords with my heart."
Chǔ Suíliáng (褚遂良)
was the son of Chǔ Liàng (褚亮).
Chǔ Liàng (褚亮)
first served Xuē Jǔ (薛舉),
and during the Wǔdé (武德) reign,
was an academician of the Academy of Literary Studies (Wénxuéguǎn Xuéshì 文學館學士).
Sūn Fújiā (孫伏伽) sometimes openly recounted past events in a large assembly,
concealing nothing.
Historians say that Sūn Fújiā's (孫伏伽) broad-mindedness surpassed that of Zhāng Xuánsù (張玄素).
Gā (伽),
pronounced qiú jiā.
Zuò (坐),
pronounced cú wò.
24 Jiǎ Chóng (賈崇), the Prefect (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Dài Prefecture (Dàizhōu 戴州), reported that some people in his jurisdiction had committed the Ten Abominations (Shí È 十惡).
The articles of the Ten Abominations are: First, plotting rebellion (móu fǎn 謀反);
second, plotting great sedition (móu dà nì 謀大逆);
third, plotting treason (móu pàn 謀叛);
fourth, plotting atrocious rebellion (móu è nì 謀惡逆);
fifth, unfilial conduct (bù dào 不道);
sixth, great disrespect (dà bù jìng 大不敬);
seventh, unfilial piety (bù xiào 不孝);
eighth, disharmony (bù mù 不睦);
ninth, unrighteousness (bù yì 不義);
tenth, internal disorder (nèi luàn 內亂).
The Emperor said:
"In ancient times, the great sages Táng (唐) and Yú (虞),
though honored as Sons of Heaven,
could not transform their own sons;
how much more so for Chóng (崇) as a Prefect,
can he alone make his people universally good?
If he were demoted because of this,
then prefectures and counties would mutually cover up [crimes]
and release criminals.
From now on, if there are people in any prefecture who commit the Ten Abominations,
do not impeach the Prefect,
but only order him to diligently investigate,
and apply punishment according to law,
so as to suppress evil and wickedness."
25 The Emperor personally supervised a military drill.
Seeing that the formations were not in order,
he ordered General-in-Chief Zhāng Shìguì (張士貴) to cane the Middle-Ranked Generals (Zhōnglángjiàng 中郎將) and others;
angered that the caning was light,
he demoted Zhāng Shìguì (張士貴) to a clerk.
Wèi Zhēng (魏徵) remonstrated, saying:
"The duty of a general
is to be the claws and teeth of the nation;
making him wield a cane
is already not in accordance with later law,
how much more so to demote him to a clerk for a light caning! "
The Emperor immediately released him.
26 Many who spoke to the throne requested the Emperor to personally review memorials and reports,
to prevent obstruction.
The Emperor asked Wèi Zhēng (魏徵) about this,
who replied:
"These people do not understand the overall situation.
If Your Majesty must personally attend to every single matter,
not only affairs of the court,
but also those of the prefectures and counties would have to be personally attended to."
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ (王崇武), collated by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖) and Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
by imperial decree.
Hòu Xué Tiāntái (後學天台)
The 15th year of Zhēngguān (貞觀)
(Xīnchǒu 辛丑, 641 CE)
1 Spring,
First month,
on the Jiǎxū (甲戌) day,
Lù Dōngzàn (祿東贊) of Tǔbō (吐蕃) was appointed General-in-Chief of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Dàjiāngjūn 右衞大將軍).
The Emperor praised Lù Dōngzàn (祿東贊) for his skillful responses,
and offered him the daughter of the Duàn (段) family, who was the granddaughter of Princess Lángyá (Lángyá Gōngzhǔ 琅邪公主);
he declined, saying:
"In my country, I already have a wife,
betrothed by my parents,
whom I cannot abandon.
Moreover, the Zānpǔ (贊普) has not yet been able to meet the Princess,
how dare a humble minister marry first! "
The Emperor esteemed him even more,
but wishing to treat him with great favor,
ultimately did not respect his wishes.
Historians say that even a barbarian could conduct himself with propriety,
yet the Central Kingdom (Zhōngguó 中國) could not treat him with propriety.
On the Dīngchǒu (丁丑) day,

Liú Dàozōng (劉道宗), Prince of Jiāngxià (Jiāngxià Wáng 江夏王) and Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū 禮部尚書), was ordered to take a special envoy to escort Princess Wénchéng (Wénchéng Gōngzhǔ 文成公主) to Tǔbō (吐蕃).
The Zānpǔ (贊普) was greatly pleased,
and upon meeting Liú Dàozōng (劉道宗),
performed all the rites due to a son-in-law.
He admired the beauty of the clothing and ceremonial guards of the Central Kingdom (Zhōngguó 中國),
built a separate city and palace for the Princess to reside in,
and himself wore fine silks to meet the Princess.
His countrymen all smeared their faces with赭 (ochre),
and the Princess disliked it.
The Zānpǔ (贊普) issued an order to prohibit it;
he also gradually reformed their suspicious and violent nature,
sending his sons and younger brothers to the Imperial Academy (Guóxué 國學)
to study the Odes (Shī 詩) and the Documents (Shū 書).
2 On the Yǐhài (乙亥) day,
Hóu Lìbì Kèhán (侯利苾可汗) of the Tūjué (突厥)
for the first time led his tribes across the river.
He had received the imperial edict the previous year,
and only now crossed the river.
Jué (厥),
pronounced jiǔ wù.
Bì (苾),
pronounced pí bì.
Kě (可),
pronounced as an entering tone from kān.
Hàn (汗),
pronounced hán.
Shuài (帥),
read as lǜ.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: The former Dìngxiāng City (Dìngxiāng Chéng 定襄城)
is about three hundred li north of Mǎyì Commandery (Mǎyì Jùn 馬邑郡) in Shuò Prefecture (Shuòzhōu 朔州).
He had forty thousand victorious soldiers and ninety thousand horses,
and furthermore memorialized, saying:
"Your servant, undeservedly blessed with grace,
has become the chief of my tribe.
I wish that my descendants for generations
may be a dog for the state,
guarding and barking at the northern gate.
If Xuē Yántuó (薛延陀) invades,
I request to bring
my family inside the Great Wall."
An imperial edict granted this.
3 The Emperor was about to visit Luòyáng (洛陽),
and ordered the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ 皇太子) to oversee the state,
leaving the Right Executive Assistant (Yòupúshè 右僕射) Gāo Shìlián (高士廉) to assist him.
On the Xīnsì (辛巳) day,
they arrived at Wēntāng (溫湯).
There is a Wēntāng (溫湯) at Líshān (驪山) in Xīnfēng (新豐);
there is a Wēntāng (溫湯) Prefecture in Huázhōu (華州).
Hoping that the Emperor would be alarmed and stop,
arrows were shot at the imperial temporary palace (xínggōng 行宮) at night,
five of which reached the sleeping quarters;
all were deemed great sedition.
The Ten Abominations,
the second is plotting great sedition.
The commentary says: This refers to plotting to destroy ancestral temples, imperial tombs, and palaces.
The Xíngtǒng Yì (刑統議) says: People covered by this article
transgress moral principles and defy the natural order,
violating the Dao and going against virtue.
There is no greater insubordination,
hence it is called "great sedition."
To be "judged as great sedition"
does not mean directly committing the crime of great sedition,
but because their actions transgress moral principles and defy the natural order, they are judged with the crime of great sedition.
In the third month,
on the day *wùchén*,
the emperor visited Xiāngchénggōng.
The area was already oppressively hot,
and moreover, there were many venomous snakes.
On the day *gēngwǔ*,
Xiāngchénggōng was abolished,
and its land was distributed among the common people.
Yán Lìdé was dismissed from office.
(The construction of Xiāngchénggōng is mentioned in the previous volume, previous year.)
4. In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the first day, *xīnmǎo*,
an edict was issued stating that in the second month of the coming year, a ceremony would be held at Tài Shān.
5. The emperor, noting that recent divination books on yin and yang
contained numerous errors and fabrications,
ordered Lǚ Cái, a *Tàicháng Bóshì*,
to review them. (Hàn dynasty's Shūsūn Tōng was a *bóshì*,
subordinate to the *tàicháng*.
During the Suí and Táng dynasties, this was considered a very prestigious position.)
(A *tàicháng bóshì*
was of the senior seventh rank,
in charge of the rituals of the five rites,
basing them on the laws and institutions of the former kings,
adapting and modifying them as times changed.)
He compiled forty-seven volumes in total.
On the day *jǐyǒu*,
the book was completed
and presented to the emperor.
Lǚ Cái wrote prefaces for all of them,
substantiating them with classics and histories.
In his preface to *Zhái Jīng*,
he stated:
"Recently, shamans
arbitrarily divided the five surnames,
such as Zhāng and Wáng as *shāng*,
Wǔ and Yǔ as *yǔ*,
seemingly for phonetic harmony.
As for classifying Liǔ as *gōng*
and Zhào as *jiǎo*,
it is even more incongruous.
Sometimes people from the same surname
are divided into *gōng* and *shāng*;
sometimes poly-syllabic surnames
cannot be categorized as *zhēng* or *yǔ*.
This shows that these matters are not based on ancient records
and their principles are perverse."
In his preface to *Lù Mìng*,
he stated:
"Books on destiny and fortune
often contain statements that sometimes prove true,
leading people to believe them.
However, it has never been heard that the soldiers buried alive at Chángpíng
all committed the 'three punishments'.
(In the Battle of Chángpíng,
450,000 people died.)
(The three punishments: *yín* punishes *sì*,
*sì* punishes *shēn*,
*shēn* punishes *yín*;
*chǒu* punishes *xū*,
*xū* punishes *wèi*,
*wèi* punishes *chǒu*;
*zǐ* punishes *mǎo*,
*mǎo* punishes *zǐ*.
Also, *chénchén*, *wǔwǔ*, *yǒuyǒu*, *hàihài*
are called 'self-punishment'.)
Why must they all correspond to the 'six harmonies'?
(*Zǐ* harmonizes with *chǒu*,
*yín* harmonizes with *hài*,
*mǎo* harmonizes with *xū*,
*chén* harmonizes with *yǒu*,
*sì* harmonizes with *shēn*,
*wǔ* harmonizes with *wèi*.)
When Hàn Guāngwǔ revived the dynasty,
many people from Nányáng became prominent.
Yet, those born at the same time and of the same parents often have different lifespans and fates.
According to the system, Lǔ Zhuāng Gōng should have been poor and lowly,
and also sickly, short, and ugly,
yet he achieved longevity.
Qín Shǐ Huáng, according to the system, should have had no official titles,
and even if he gained wealth,
he would have few servants, and his life would have a beginning but no end.
Hàn Wǔ Dì and Hòuwèi Xiàowén Dì both, according to the system, should have had no official titles.
Sòng Wǔ Dì's fortune and destiny both fell into 'emptiness and void'.
(*Jiǎjǐ* in *shēnyǒu*,
*yǐgēng* in *wǔwèi*,
*bǐngxīn* in *chénsì*,
*dīngrén* in *yínmǎo*,
*wùguǐ* in *zǐchǒu* and *xūhài*
are called 'road-blocking emptiness and void'.
*Jiǎzǐ* cycle's *xūhài*,
*Jiǎxū* cycle's *shēnyǒu*,
*Jiǎshēn* cycle's *wǔwèi*,
*Jiǎwǔ* cycle's *chénsì*,
*Jiǎchén* cycle's *yínmǎo*,
*Jiǎyín* cycle's *zǐchǒu*
are called 'cycle-midst emptiness and void'.)
Even if he had a second son,
the system dictated he should die young.
These are all clear examples of the inaccuracy of fortune-telling."
In his preface on burials,
he stated:
"The *Xiàojīng* says: 'Divining the burial site and interring them there,'
implying that once the grave is finished,
(Dù Yù says: *zhūn*
means thick.
*xī*
means night.
'Thick night'
is synonymous with 'long night'.
*Zhūn*
is pronounced *zhū lún*.)
and as towns and markets change
and springs and rocks encroach,
what cannot be known in advance
is therefore divined with tortoise shells and milfoil.
In recent years, some choose the month and day,
or select tomb sites,
believing that a single mistake
will bring disaster upon the living and the dead.
According to the rites: emperors, feudal lords, and high officials all have specific monthly periods for burial,
which means the ancients did not choose months and days.
In ancient times, the Son of Heaven was buried after seven months,
and all within the same jurisdiction attended;
feudal lords after five months,
and allies attended;
high officials after three months,
and those of the same rank attended.
(*Dīngsì*
buried Duke Dìng.
It rained,
so they could not bury him.
On *wùwǔ*,
it was late afternoon,
and only then could they bury him.)
This shows that they did not choose days.
When Zhèng buried Duke Jiǎn,
the house of the tomb official was in the way.
If it were demolished, the burial could take place in the morning;
if not demolished, it would be noon before the burial.
Zǐchǎn did not demolish it,
which shows that they did not choose times.
Ancient burials were all to the north of the capital,
and the burial grounds had fixed locations,
which shows that they did not choose sites.
Now, burial books claim that the wealth, poverty, longevity, or early death of descendants
are all caused by the chosen burial site.
However, Zǐwén served as *Lìngyǐn* and was dismissed three times;
Liǔxiàhuì served as *Shìshī* and was demoted three times.
Their graves
were never moved.
Yet, ignorant common folk
and deceptive shamans utter nonsense,
leading people, at the moment of grief,
to choose burial sites hoping for official titles;
and in times of bitter sorrow,
to select burial times to gain wealth.
Some say one should not weep on a *chén* day,
so they smile at mourners.
Some say that those of the same zodiac sign are taboo at the grave,
so they wear festive clothes and do not send off their parents.
Nothing corrupts teaching and ruins etiquette
more than this!"
All the diviners hated his words,
but those with understanding
considered them sound arguments.
6. On the day *dīngsì*,
Guǒyì Dūwèi Xí Jūnmǎi, leading 120 elite cavalry, attacked Tǔyùhún's Chancellor Xuān Wáng,
defeating him
and slaying him and his three brothers.
Initially,
Chancellor Xuān Wáng controlled the government
and secretly plotted to attack Princess Hónghuà.
(The emperor gave a female member of the imperial clan as Princess Hónghuà,
marrying her to Tǔyùhún.)
Nuògēbō, hearing of this,
fled with light cavalry to Shànshànchéng.
(Suí Yáng Dì defeated Tǔyùhún
and established four commanderies.
Shànshàn Commandery's seat was Shànshànchéng,
which was the ancient city of Lóulán.)
(*Jì*
is pronounced *qíjì*.)
(*Shàn*
is pronounced *shízhàn*.)
Therefore, Xí Jūnmǎi was sent to punish Xuān Wáng.
The people of the kingdom were still disturbed,
so Hùbù Shàngshū Táng Jiǎn and others were sent to comfort and pacify them.
7. In the fifth month,
on the day *rénshēn*,
elders from Bīngzhōu came to the palace gate, requesting that after the emperor's *fēngshàn* ceremony at Tài Shān,
he return and visit Jìnyáng.
The emperor granted their request.
8. On the day *bǐngzǐ*,
Baekje reported the death of its king, Fúyú Zhāng,
and an envoy was dispatched to confer a title on his heir, Yìcí.
9 On the day of Jǐyǒu,
a comet appeared in Tàiwēi.
The Grand Astrologer, Xuē Yí, reported,
“It is not yet appropriate to perform the *Fēng* sacrifice in the East.”
On the day of Xīnhài,
Chǔ Suìliáng, the Palace Reporter, also said the same;
on the day of Bǐngchén,
an edict was issued to halt the *Fēngshàn* sacrifices.
10Yú Zhìníng, the Crown Prince’s *Zhānshì*, suffered the loss of his mother,
but was soon reinstated in his position.
According to the *Huìyào*,
the system in the Wǔdé era stipulated that
civil officials who lost their parents
were permitted to leave office.
*Qǐfù* means
to raise one from the mourning mat and clod of earth and restore one's official post,
also called *duóqíng* (forcibly overriding one's natural feelings).
This hindered agricultural work;
he also enjoyed the music of Zhèng and Wèi.
Zhìníng remonstrated,
but was not heeded.
Moreover, he doted on eunuchs,
who were constantly by his side.
Zhìníng submitted a memorial,
stating:
“Since Yìyá,
there has been more than one instance of eunuchs causing the downfall of the state.
Now Your Highness shows favor to these individuals,
allowing them to slight those of official attire.
This cannot continue.”
The Crown Prince employed his charioteers and others,
not allowing them to rotate duties for half a year.
The *Diǎn* of the Tàipúsì had a *Ji* office,
with one hundred charioteers.
Formerly, they rotated between the two palaces.
The *Liùdiǎn* states that
the Tàizǐpúsì had a *Ji* and animal husbandry office,
with fifteen *yìyù* (assistant charioteers)
and thirty *jiàshì* (drivers).
The New Book renders it
“Dágēzhī.”
The Crown Prince was furious,
and sent assassins Zhāng Sīzhèng and Gēgān Chéngjī to kill him.
The two entered his residence
and saw Zhìníng sleeping on a mat with a clod for a pillow.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: "Sleeping on a mat and using a clod as a pillow
means that a filial son dwells in a mourning hut,
sleeping on a mat,
and resting his head on a clod of earth."
*Chǔ*
is pronounced like "chāng lǚ."
11Shābōluó Yèhù Kèhán of the Western Tujue frequently sent envoys to offer tribute.
In autumn,
seventh month,
on the day of Jiǎxū,
Zhāng Dàshī, General of the Left Leader Guard, was ordered to carry the imperial insignia and proceed to his domain to enthrone him as Kèhán,
and bestow upon him a drum and a *dáo* banner.
The Emperor also ordered the envoy to bring much gold and silk,
and travel through various countries to purchase good horses.
Wèi Zhēng remonstrated, saying:
“To purchase horses before the Kèhán's position is settled,
they will surely think that Your Majesty’s true intent is to buy horses,
and that establishing the Kèhán is merely a pretext.
If the Kèhán is successfully enthroned,
his gratitude will surely be shallow;
if he is not enthroned,
the resentment will be truly deep.
When other nations hear of this,
they will also slight the Middle Kingdom.
Even if horses are purchased,
they will not be excellent.
If we can ensure their peace and stability,
then horses from all nations
will arrive without being sought.”
The Emperor was pleased and ceased the activity.
Yǐpí Duōlù Kèhán and Shābōluó Yèhù attacked each other.
Yǐpí Duōlù gradually grew stronger,
and many nations in the Western Regions submitted to him.
Before long,
Yǐpí Duōlù sent the *Tútún* of Shíguó to attack Shābōluó Yèhù,
captured him and brought him back,
and killed him.
*Tútún*
is a Tujue official title,
whose holders were dispatched to oversee various countries.
Shābōluó Yèhù’s enthronement is mentioned in Volume 13.
*Jǐ*
is pronounced like "jū qǐ."
12On the day of Bǐngzǐ,
the Emperor pointed to the palace roof and said to his attendant ministers:
“Governing the world is like building this house.
Once the construction is complete,
do not frequently alter or move things.
If one were to change a single rafter,
or even adjust one tile,
the constant treading and shaking
would surely cause damage.
If one seeks extraordinary achievements,
changes laws and regulations,
and is inconstant in their virtue,
there will be much labor and disturbance.”
13The Emperor sent Chén Dàdé, the *Zhífāng Lángzhōng*, as an envoy to Gāolì;
*Zhífāng*
was in charge of maps of the world, and the numbers of city walls, garrisons, and beacon towers,
distinguishing the distances of various states and the submission of the four barbarians.
All matters concerning the regions of the five directions,
the establishment and abolishment of capitals,
and boundary disputes,
were to be managed and rectified by them.
*Shǐ*
is pronounced like "shū lì."
*Lì*
is pronounced like "lì zhī."
On the day of Jǐhài,
he returned from Gāolì.
When Dàdé first entered its territory,
he wished to learn about its mountains, rivers, and customs.
In every city he visited,
he gave silk and brocade to the local governors,
saying:
“I have a deep fondness for mountains and rivers.
If there are scenic spots here,
I would like to see them.”
The governors were pleased
and guided him on his travels,
leaving no place unvisited.
He frequently encountered Chinese people,
who told him:
“Our homes are in such-and-such commandery.
At the end of the Suí dynasty, we joined the army
and were captured by Gāolì.
Gāolì gave us local women as wives,
and we live interspersed with the Gāolì people.
Almost half of us are here.”
Then he asked about the welfare of their relatives.
Dàdé deceived them, saying:
“All are well.”
They all wept and told each other.
Several days later,
those from Suí who looked towards him and cried
covered the countryside.
Dàdé reported to the Emperor, saying:
“Their nation, upon hearing of Gāochāng’s demise,
is greatly fearful.
Their diligence in hosting and observing us
exceeded the usual measure.”
The Emperor said:
“Gāolì was originally the land of four commanderies.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn established the four commanderies of Líntún, Zhēnfān, Lèlàng, and Xuántú,
and Gāolì now possesses their land.
They will certainly mobilize their entire nation to defend it.
If we also send a naval force from Dōnglái,
proceeding by sea towards Píngyǎng,
with combined land and sea forces,
taking it will not be difficult.
However, the prefectures and counties of Shāndōng are still suffering and have not yet recovered,
and I do not wish to burden them!”
Observing the Emperor’s words,
he already harbored the intention to conquer Gāolì.
*Zhài*
is pronounced like "zé jiè."
14On the day of Yǐsì,
the Emperor said to his attendant ministers:
“I have two joys and one fear.
Recent years have seen abundant harvests,
and a *dǒu* of millet in Cháng'ān costs only three or four *qián*—
this is one joy.
The northern barbarians have long been submissive,
and there is no danger on the borders—
this is the second joy.
When there is peace and order, extravagance and pride are easily generated;
when there is extravagance and pride, peril and ruin quickly follow—
this is my one fear.”
15In winter,
tenth month,
on the day of Xīnmǎo,
the Emperor held a military hunt at Yīquè;
on the day of Rénchén,
he visited Sōngyáng.
Yīquè County,
formerly called Xīnchéng,
was renamed in the 18th year of Kāihuáng of Suí;
it has the Yīquè pass.
Sōngyáng County,
formerly called Yǐngyáng,
was changed to Wǔlín in the 6th year of Kāihuáng of Suí,
then to Lúnshì in the 18th year,
and to Sōngyáng in the 1st year of Dàyè;
it has Mount Sōnggāo.
Both belonged to Luòzhōu.
On the day of Xīnchǒu,
he returned to the palace.
16 Lǐ Shìjì
served as the Grand Administrator of the Protectorate-General of Bīngzhōu for sixteen years. His orders were carried out, and prohibitions were enforced,
and both the Chinese and barbarian people were won over and submitted to him.
The Emperor said:
“The Suí Yángdì [Emperor Yáng of Suí] overworked his people
to build the Great Wall as a defense against the Tūjué,
but ultimately gained nothing.
I merely placed Lǐ Shìjì at Jìnyáng, and the border dust does not stir.
How magnificent
is this Great Wall!”
In the eleventh month,
on the day Gēngshēn,
Shìjì was appointed Minister of War.
17 On the day Rénshēn,
the imperial carriage returned west to Cháng'ān.
18 The Zhēnzhū Kèhán of Xuēyántuó heard that the Emperor was preparing for the eastern封 (Fēng) ceremony [at Tài Shān],
and said to his subordinates:
“When the Son of Heaven performs the Fēng ceremony at Tài Shān,
all the soldiers and horses will follow,
and the border regions will certainly be empty.
At this time, I will seize Sīmó
as easily as pulling down a rotten tree.”
Thereupon, he ordered his son Dàdùshè to raise 200,000 soldiers from the Tóngluó, Púgǔ, Huíhè, Mòhé, and Xī tribes,
totaling 200,000,
to cross south of the desert,
station them at Báidào Chuān,
and occupy Shànyáng Lǐng to attack the Tūjué.
Shànyáng Lǐng
is north of Shànyáng Xiàn in Shuòzhōu.
Sīmó led his tribes into the Great Wall,
secured Shuòzhōu,
and sent an envoy to report the emergency.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
the Emperor ordered Zhāng Jiǎn, the Governor of Yíngzhōu, to lead his cavalry and the Xī, Xī, and Qìdān troops to press on their eastern border;
appointed Lǐ Shìjì, Minister of War, as the Commander-in-chief of the Shuòzhōu Route Army,
leading 60,000 soldiers
and 1,200 cavalry,
to encamp at Yǔfāng;
appointed Lǐ Dàliàng, Right Grand General of the Guard, as the Commander-in-chief of the Língzhōu Route Army,
leading 40,000 soldiers
and 5,000 cavalry,
to encamp at Língwǔ;
Língwǔ Xiàn belongs to Língwǔ Jùn of Língzhōu.
The character 將兵 (jiāngbīng) [in the phrase before Lǐ Dàliàng’s appointment]
is read as liàngfān [not jiāngbīng as in leading soldiers].
He [Lǐ Dàliàng] was appointed Commander-in-chief of the Qìngzhōu Route Army,
advancing from Yúnzhōng;
and Lǐ Xíyù, Governor of Liángzhōu, was appointed Commander-in-chief of the Liángzhōu Route Army,
advancing from their west.
When the generals bade farewell,
the Emperor cautioned them, saying:
“The Xuēyántuó, relying on their strength and prosperity,
crossed the desert southwards,
traveling thousands of *lǐ*.
Their horses are already fatigued and lean.
The way of deploying troops is
to advance quickly when advantageous,
and retreat quickly when disadvantageous.
The Xuēyántuó failed to catch Sīmó unprepared
and strike quickly.
Sīmó entered the Great Wall,
and they did not retreat quickly.
I have already ordered Sīmó to burn and clear the autumn grass.
Their provisions will be exhausted daily,
and they will find nothing in the wilderness.
Recently, scouts reported
that their horses have almost completely gnawed the bark and branches of trees.
You and Sīmó should form pincers,
and there is no need to fight quickly.
Wait until they are about to retreat,
then strike with full force at once,
and you will surely defeat them.”
19 In the twelfth month,
on the day Wùzǐ,
the imperial carriage arrived at the capital.
20 On the day Jǐhài,
the Xuēyántuó sent an envoy to request an audience
and propose a peace marriage with the Tūjué.
On the day Jiǎchén,
Lǐ Shìjì defeated the Xuēyántuó at Nuòzhēn Shuǐ.
From the ancient city of Yúnzhōng,
traveling northwest about 400 *lǐ*,
one reaches Nuòzhēn Shuǐ.
The character 見 (jiàn) [in the phrase “見薛延陀” (jiàn Xuēyántuó)]
is read as xiánbiànfān.
The character 敗 (bài) [in the phrase “李世勣敗薛延陀” (Lǐ Shìjì bài Xuēyántuó)]
is read as bǔmàifān.
The Xuēyántuó attacked Shābōluó and Āshǐnà Shè'ěr of the Western Tūjué,
and achieved victory in both cases through infantry combat.
When they were about to invade,
they extensively taught infantry combat,
making five men a squad.
One man held the horses,
and four men fought in front.
If they won the battle, they were given horses to pursue the fleeing enemy.
Thereupon, Dàdùshè led 30,000 cavalry to approach the Great Wall,
intending to attack the Tūjué,
but Sīmó had already fled.
Knowing he could not achieve his objective,
he sent someone to climb the wall and curse them.
Just then, Lǐ Shìjì arrived with the Táng army,
raising dust that filled the sky.
Dàdùshè was alarmed and led his troops to flee north from Chìkē Luò.
Shìjì selected 6,000 elite cavalry from his command and the Tūjué,
and intercepted them via a direct route,
crossing Báidào Chuān,
and caught up with them at Qīng Shān.
Dàdùshè had fled for several days
and reached Nuòzhēn Shuǐ.
He ordered his troops to turn and fight,
forming a battle line ten *lǐ* long.
The Tūjué had fought them earlier
but were defeated and fled back.
Dàdùshè pursued them, taking advantage of his victory,
and encountered the Táng army.
The Xuēyántuó fired ten thousand arrows simultaneously,
and many Táng horses died.
Shìjì ordered all his soldiers to dismount,
grasp long spears,
and charge straight forward.
The Xuēyántuó forces disintegrated.
The Deputy Commander Xuē Wànchè, with several thousand cavalry, rounded up those who held the horses.
Deprived of their horses, the Xuēyántuó
did not know what to do.
The Táng army attacked them relentlessly,
beheading over 3,000
and capturing more than 50,000 prisoners.
Dàdùshè escaped,
but Wànchè could not catch him.
When his troops reached Mòběi [north of the desert],
they encountered heavy snow,
and eight or nine tenths
of the people and livestock froze to death.
Lǐ Shìjì returned his army to Dìngxiāng.
The Sījié tribe of the Tūjué, who lived at Wǔtái, rebelled and fled.
Wǔtái
was originally Lǜsī Xiàn of Tàiyuán during the Hàn dynasty,
long abandoned.
Later, the Northern Wèi renamed it Lǘyí.
At the beginning of the Dàyè era [of Suí],
it was renamed Wǔtái.
There is Wǔtái Shān there;
it belongs to Dàizhōu.
When Shìjì’s army returned,
they attacked them from both sides
and completely exterminated them.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
the Xuēyántuó envoy bade farewell.
The Emperor said to him:
“I agreed with you and the Tūjué to take the Great Desert as the border.
If anyone invaded,
I would punish them.
You, relying on your own strength,
crossed the desert to attack the Tūjué.
Lǐ Shìjì led only a few thousand cavalry,
and you were already in such a predicament!
Go back and tell your Kèhán:
For all your actions, consider the advantages and disadvantages,
and choose wisely what is appropriate.”
21 The Emperor asked Wèi Zhēng:
“Why have court officials lately
not discussed matters?”
He replied:
“If Your Majesty sincerely accepts advice,
there will certainly be those who speak.
However, few officials serve the country,
while many cherish their own lives.
They fear punishment,
which is why they do not speak.”
The Emperor said:
“Indeed.
If a subject speaks persuasively but offends the imperial will,
it often leads to execution or banishment. How is that different from treading on fire and water or braving sharp blades?
Therefore, Yǔ bowed to wise counsel,
and his ‘Three Counsels’ were recorded.”
Fáng Xuánlíng and Gāo Shìlián met Dòu Désù, the Junior Supervisor of the Lesser Treasury, on the road.
Qín established the Lesser Treasury,
which was in charge of taxes from mountains and marshes.
Under Hàn, it was in charge of precious goods in the inner palace treasury.
Liáng first made it a Minister,
Suí changed it to Supervisor.
Under Táng, it was a third-rank official,
and the Junior Supervisor was a fourth-rank official.
It was in charge of supplying the needs of all artisans and craftsmen.
All garments and equipage for the Son of Heaven,
and the ceremonial attire for all officials,
preparing and providing materials for display,
were all provided by his subordinates.
"What construction is ongoing near the North Gate?"
Désù reported this to the Emperor.
The Emperor was angry,
and reproached Xuánlíng and others, saying:
"You only know about the affairs of the Southern Gate.
What concern is a small construction project at the North Gate
to you?"
The main imperial court of Táng was in the south,
hence it was called the Southern Gate (Nányá).
Xuánwǔmén was in the north,
and was called the North Gate (Běimén).
Liú Fēng's "Shǐshǐ" says: A banner with a tusks design is
the essence of a general.
Whenever such a banner is first erected,
it must be on an auspicious day.
An auspicious day
is a day whose earthly branch, in terms of the Five Elements,
is one where the upper element overcomes the lower element.
Also, the "Shàngshū" says: "Gate banners are two with eight flaps,
red in color,
the great general's gate banners,
leading out in front of the general's column."
Also, the "Huángdì Chūjūn Jué" says: "A banner with a tusks design
is the essence of a general;
golden drums
are the spirit of a general."
"Zhōulǐ: Sīcháng Zhíchóng" states: "For military gatherings, a banner-gate is erected."
If a banner serves as a gate,
it is a banner-gate (qímén).
Later generations' armies thus established gate-banner generals (yámén jiàng),
and also gate-banner troops (yábīng).
Those who commanded these troops
were called Guarding-Gate Commissioners (yāyá).
As for the morning and evening assemblies in government offices,
and the two audiences for military officials,
they were also called "yá".
Once the term became common,
even the Son of Heaven's main hall for receiving audiences
was also called the main "yá" (zhèngyá).
Wèi Zhēng stepped forward and said:
"I do not know why Your Majesty blames Xuánlíng and others,
nor do I know what Xuánlíng and others have to apologize for!
Xuánlíng and others are Your Majesty's limbs, ears, and eyes.
How could there be anything in internal or external affairs that they should not know?
If the ongoing construction is correct,
they should assist Your Majesty in completing it;
if it is wrong,
they should request Your Majesty to stop it.
To inquire of the responsible officials
is reasonable and proper.
I do not know for what crime they are blamed,
nor for what crime they should apologize!"
The Emperor was greatly ashamed.
22 The Emperor once presided over court and said to his attendants:
"As the ruler of men,
I always combine the duties of a general and a minister."
Zhāng Xíngchéng, Acting Palace Censor, withdrew and submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"Yǔ did not boast, and thus no one in the world contended with him.
The 'Shū' says: Shùn said to Yǔ, 'You do not boast,
thus no one in the world contends with you in ability;
you do not brag,
thus no one in the world contends with you in merit.'
Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo fān;
same below.
Jiāng,
pronounced jí liàng fān.
Xiàng,
pronounced xī liàng fān.
Ér shàng,
pronounced shí zhǎng fān.
This humble subject is truly unworthy of Your Majesty's favor;
however, it is not necessary to say this in court.
For the Lord of Ten Thousand Chariots,
to compete in merit and ability with humble subjects,
your subject secretly believes Your Majesty should not do."
The Emperor greatly approved.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Yǐchǒu,
Wèi Wáng Tài presented the "Kuòdì Zhì".
Tài was fond of learning.
His chief clerk, Sū Xù, persuaded Tài,
saying that ancient worthy kings all attracted scholars to compile books.
Therefore, Tài memorialized to request its compilation.
At that time, Tài memorialized to invite Xiāo Déyán, Yán Yìn, Jiǎng Yàqīng, Xǔ Yǎn, and others to his residence to compile it.
Hào,
pronounced hū dào fān.
Shuì,
pronounced shū ruì fān.
He extensively invited talents of the time,
and people gathered in great numbers,
his residence gate was like a marketplace.
Tài's monthly allowance exceeded that of the Crown Prince.
Chǔ Suìliáng, Grand Master Remonstrant, submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"Sages established rites,
honoring the legitimate heir and demeaning the illegitimate.
A Crown Prince should not have exclusive use of certain items,
but share them with the king.
The 'Zhōulǐ' says: 'The king and the Crown Prince share all food,'
but for other garments and items,
the Crown Prince shares them all.
Huì,
pronounced gǔ wài fān.
He should not exceed the legitimate heir,
this is to prevent the spread of suspicion and doubt,
and eliminate the source of disaster and chaos.
If those who should be close are alienated,
and those who should be honored are demeaned,
then the deceit of flattering villains
will seize the opportunity to act.
In the past, Empress Dòu of Hàn favored Liáng Xiàowáng,
who eventually died of sorrow;
see 'Hàn Jǐngdì Jì'.
Sè,
pronounced xì zé fān.
Zú,
pronounced zǐ xù fān.
It also almost led to disaster.
See 'Xuāndì, Yuándì Jì'.
Jī,
pronounced jū xī fān;
same below.
It is appropriate to show him the rules of propriety,
and instruct him in humility and frugality,
thus making him a good vessel.
This is what is meant by 'the teaching of the sage accomplishes without strictness.'"
This quote from Kǒng Zǐ is recorded in the "Xiàojīng".
The Emperor also ordered Tài to move to Wǔdédiàn.
Wèi Zhēng submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"Your Majesty loves Wèi Wáng,
and always wishes for his safety and well-being.
It is proper to always restrain his extravagance and arrogance,
and not place him in suspicious circumstances.
Now moving him to this palace,
which is west of the Eastern Palace,
Hǎilíng once resided there.
Yuánjí was posthumously enfeoffed as Hǎilíng Cìwáng.
Although the times and circumstances are different,
I fear that Wèi Wáng's heart may not rest easy there."
The Emperor said:
"This almost led to an error."
He immediately sent Tài back to his residence.
2 On the day Xīnwèi,
those condemned to death were exiled to Xīzhōu,
while those who committed crimes punishable by banishment or penal servitude were assigned to border garrisons,
each according to the severity of their crime, for a fixed term of years.
3 An imperial edict ordered a census of all unregistered vagrants nationwide,
to be completed by the end of next year.
Fù means
to be registered.
4 Cén Wénběn, concurrently a Palace Censor, was made Palace Censor (Zhōngshū Shìláng),
exclusively in charge of confidential matters.
There were two positions for Palace Censor.
At this time, only Wénběn was employed,
hence he exclusively handled confidential matters.
5 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Rénzǐ,
the Emperor said to the remonstrance official Dàfū Chǔ Suíliáng:
“You are familiar with the records of daily life (Qǐjūzhù).
The Táng Liù Diǎn states that from Emperor Xiàndì of Hàn and onwards from the Western Jìn dynasty,
all emperors had Qǐjūzhù,
which were all recorded by imperial historians.
