why?'
He replied,
'In the past, King Wén [Wénwáng] set aside Bóyìkǎo and established King Wǔ [Wǔwáng];
Wēizǐ set aside his grandson Tún and established Yǎn.
Zhòngzǐ also followed the ancient way.'
Zǐyóu asked Kǒngzǐ about it,
who said,
'No,
establish the grandson.'
I will certainly not replace the legitimate heir with a concubine's son,
thus opening the door to usurpation!"
2 Zhèng Wénzhēn Gōng Wèi Zhēng was critically ill.
The Emperor [Shàng] sent messengers to inquire about him,
bestowing medicines,
who could be seen one after another on the road.
He also sent Colonel Lǐ Ānyǎn to stay at Wèi Zhēng's residence,
reporting his condition constantly.
The Emperor [Shàng] further went with the Crown Prince [Tàizǐ] to his residence,
pointing to Princess Héngshān, expressing his desire to marry her to Wèi Zhēng's son, Shúyù.
On the day of wùchén,
Wèi Zhēng passed away.
The Emperor [Shàng] ordered all officials of the ninth rank and above to attend the funeral,
providing feathered canopies and drums and trumpets,
and to be buried alongside Zhaolíng.
His wife, Lady Péi [Péi Shì], said,
"Wèi Zhēng was frugal and simple in life.
To bury him now with first-rank feathered regalia [yǔyí] is not the wish of the deceased."
She declined all of it,
and the coffin was carried in a plain cart for burial.
The Emperor [Shàng] ascended the Western Tower of the Imperial Park,
which was the Western Tower of Cháng'ān's forbidden park.
The Emperor [Shàng] personally composed the epitaph [bēi wén]
and also wrote it on stone.
The Emperor [Shàng] continuously thought of Wèi Zhēng,
and said to his attendant officials,
"People use copper as a mirror [jìng],
by which they can straighten their clothes and caps;
they use history as a mirror,
by which they can see the rise and fall [of dynasties];
they use people as a mirror,
by which they can know their gains and losses.
With Wèi Zhēng gone,
I have lost one mirror!"
3 Yù [Hù] County Commander Yóu Wénzhī accused the Area Commander of Dàizhōu, Liú Lánchéng, of plotting rebellion.
On the day of wùshēn,
Liú Lánchéng was sentenced to be cut in half at the waist.
General of the Right Wǔhóu, Qiū Xínggōng, dug out Liú Lánchéng's heart and liver and ate them.
The Emperor [Shàng] heard of it and reprimanded him, saying,
"Liú Lánchéng plotted rebellion,
and the state has its standing laws [chángxíng].
How could it come to this!
If you considered it loyalty and filial piety,
then the Crown Prince [Tàizǐ] and the various princes would have eaten it first;
how could it fall to you, sir?"
Qiū Xínggōng was ashamed and bowed in apology.
4 In the second month,
on the day of rénwǔ,
the Emperor [Shàng] asked Grand Master Remonstrant Chǔ Suìliáng,
"When Shùn made lacquerware,
more than ten people remonstrated."
The Shuō Yuàn states: Yáo abdicated the empire,
and Shùn received it.
He made drinking vessels,
cutting and shaping wood,
and then lacquered them black.
The feudal lords considered this extravagant,
and thirteen states refused to submit.
Chǔ Suìliáng replied,
"Extravagance is
the root of danger and destruction.
If lacquerware is not stopped,
then eventually it will be made of gold and jade.
Loyal officials love their ruler [jūn],
and must prevent such tendencies from the start.
If disaster and chaos have already formed,
there will be nothing left to remonstrate about."
The Emperor [Shàng] said,
"Indeed.
If I have faults,
you too should remonstrate against them at their inception.
I have seen that previous emperors [dìwáng] who rejected remonstrance
often said, 'It has already been done,'
or, 'It has already been promised,'
and ultimately refused to change.
If this is the case,
can one hope to avoid danger and destruction?"
At that time, many imperial princes who served as Area Commanders [dūdū] and Regional Inspectors [cìshǐ] were very young.
Chǔ Suìliáng submitted a memorial,
saying,
"Emperor Xuān of Hàn [Hàn Xuāndì] said, 'Those who will govern the world with me,
are surely the excellent two-thousand-pic officials!'"
See Volume 24, second year of Dìjié of Hàn Xuāndì.
[Zhì,
same as zhì,
pronounced zhí lì.]
[Shàng,
pronounced shí zhǎng.]
[Zhì,
pronounced zhí zhī.]
"They do not yet know how to govern,
so it would be better to keep them in the capital for now,
teaching them the classics and arts [jīngshù],
and sending them out when they are older."
The Emperor [Shàng] considered it correct.
5 On the day of rénchén,
Zhāng Liàng, the Crown Prince's [Tàizǐ] Chamberlain, was appointed Area Commander [dūdū] of Luòzhōu.
Hóu Jūnjí had been subjected to arrest despite his merits (see Volume on the fourteenth year of the Emperor's [Shàng] reign).
[Xià,
pronounced xiá jià.]
When Zhāng Liàng was sent out to Luòzhōu,
Hóu Jūnjí provoked him, saying,
"Who is it that is suppressing you?"
Zhāng Liàng said,
"If not you, then who else!"
Hóu Jūnjí said,
"Since I pacified a state,
I have encountered displeasure as large as a house;
how could I have the energy to suppress you?"
He then rolled up his sleeves and said,
"I am so depressed I can barely live!
Can you rebel?
I will rebel with you!"
Zhāng Liàng secretly reported this.
The Emperor [Shàng] said,
"You and Hóu Jūnjí are both meritorious officials.
When you spoke, there was no one else present.
If he were arrested,
Hóu Jūnjí would certainly not submit.
In that case,
the outcome of the matter is uncertain.
You should not speak of it for now."
The Emperor [Shàng] treated Hóu Jūnjí as before.
6 The Area Commander [dūdū] of Fūzhōu, Yùchí Jìngdé, submitted a memorial requesting to retire.
On the day of yǐsì,
Yùchí Jìngdé was appointed Kãifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
requiring attendance at court once every five days.
[Cān,
is like cháo.]
7 On the *dīngwèi* day,
the Emperor said:
"A ruler has but one mind,
but many attack it.
Some by courage and strength,
some by eloquent speech,
some by flattery,
some by treachery and deceit,
some by desires and cravings—
they flock to attack it,
each seeking to sell themselves
to gain favor and emolument.
Should the ruler be slightly negligent
and accept one of them,
then danger and ruin will follow.
This is why it is difficult."
8 On the *wùshēn* day,
the Emperor ordered paintings of meritorious officials Zhào Gōng Zhǎngsūn Wújí, Zhàojùn Yuán Wáng Xiàogōng,
(Posthumous title rules: "Great achievements and grand virtue" is called Yuán;
"Excelling in goodness and practicing virtue" is called Yuán.)
Rúhuì was initially enfeoffed as Càiguó Gōng;
after his death,
he was transferred to Lái Guó Gōng.
(Posthumous title rule: "Fond of integrity and self-restraint" is called Jié.)
Yún,
the sound is *yún*;
similarly below.
Chái Shào should
be Xǔ Shào.
Xiāng Gōng Liú Zhènghuì, Jǔ Gōng Táng Jiàn, Yīng Gōng Lǐ Shìjì, Hú Zhuàng Gōng Qín Shúbǎo, and others in the Língyān Gé.
Those whose noble titles are recorded but not their posthumous titles are
still alive;
those whose noble titles and posthumous titles are recorded are
already dead.
The *Nánbù Xīnshū* says: The Língyān Gé is beside the Sānqīng Diàn in the Western Palace,
and the portraits of the meritorious officials all face north.
Inside the pavilion, there is an inner partition;
the inner side facing north depicts high-ranking marquises and kings,
and the outer side of the partition lists other meritorious officials in order.
Chéng Dàchāng says: Inside the pavilion, there are three partitions in total.
The innermost layer depicts high-ranking chancellors,
the outer layer depicts high-ranking marquises and kings,
and the outermost layer lists other meritorious officials in order.
Although these three partitions are divided internally and externally,
the images of the meritorious officials depicted all face north.
Perhaps it is because it is beside the Sānqīng Diàn,
and facing north is a sign of respect!
I say that facing north
is the etiquette for ministers,
not because it is beside the Sānqīng Diàn.
9 Qízhōu Dūdū Qí Wáng Yòu,
was naturally frivolous and impetuous.
His maternal uncle, Shàngchéng Zhícháng Yīn Hóngzhì, persuaded him, saying:
(The Shàngchéng Jú
belongs to the Diànzhōng Jiān,
with Fèngyù
and Zhícháng.
They manage the horses in the internal and external stables,
distinguishing their quality and supervising their trainers.)
Chéng,
read *shéngzhèng fān*.
Zhǎng,
read *zhīliǎng fān*.
Shuō,
read *shūruì fān*.
"Your Majesty has many brothers;
after the Emperor's thousand autumns and ten thousand years,
you should acquire brave warriors for self-defense."
Yòu considered this true.
Hóngzhì then recommended his wife's elder brother, Yàn Hóngxìn.
Yòu was pleased with him,
generously bestowed gold and jade,
and had him secretly recruit assassins.
The Emperor selected upright and resolute men to assist the various princes,
serving as Zhǎngshǐ and Sīmǎ,
to report any transgressions of the princes.
Yòu was intimate with petty men
and fond of hunting.
Zhǎngshǐ Quán Wànjì repeatedly admonished him,
but he did not listen.
Brave warriors Zǎn Jūnmó and Liáng Měngbiāo gained Yòu's favor.
Wànjì impeached and expelled them all,
but Yòu secretly recalled them,
favoring them even more.
The Emperor frequently sent letters severely reprimanding Yòu.
Wànjì feared that they would both incur punishment,
and said to Yòu:
"If Your Highness can truly reform,
I, Wànjì, request to go to court and report it."
Thereupon, he itemized Yòu's misdeeds
and pressured him to submit a memorial confessing them.
Yòu was afraid and complied.
When Wànjì arrived at the capital,
he reported that Yòu would surely repent and change.
The Emperor was very pleased,
encouraged Wànjì,
and enumerated Yòu's past faults,
cautioning him with an imperial edict.
When Yòu heard this,
he was greatly enraged and said:
"The Zhǎngshǐ has betrayed me!
He advised me and then claimed it as his own merit."
(It means Wànjì advised Yòu to confess,
and then claimed it as his own merit for assisting,
which is being betrayed.)
The Emperor, considering Xiàowèi Jīngzhào Wéi Wénzhèn to be careful and upright,
appointed him as Diǎnjūn of Yòu's princely establishment.
(In the Táng dynasty, each princely establishment had Xiàowèi.
Each Xiàowèi led two Lǚshuài.
Princely estates and retinues each had two Diǎnjūn,
of rank five, first class,
and two Fùdiǎnjūn,
of rank five, second class,
in charge of leading the Xiàowèi and below in guarding and escorting duties.)
Xiào,
read *hùjiào fān*.
Yòu also disliked him.
Wànjì was narrow-minded
and strictly restrained Yòu with severity.
He did not allow him to leave outside the city gates,
released all his falcons and hounds,
and banished Jūnmó and Měngbiāo, preventing them from seeing Yòu.
It happened that a clod of earth fell at Wànjì's residence one night.
Wànjì thought Jūnmó and Měngbiāo were plotting to murder him,
so he arrested them all,
sent an urgent report to the capital,
and also impeached dozens of others who had committed misdeeds with Yòu.
The Emperor dispatched Xíngbù Shàngshū Liú Déwēi to investigate.
The evidence was quite conclusive,
so an edict ordered Yòu and Wànjì to both come to court.
Yòu, having accumulated much resentment,
then conspired with Yàn Hóngxìn's elder brother, Hóngliàng, and others to murder Wànjì.
Wànjì, complying with the edict, set off first.
Yòu sent Hóngliàng and more than twenty horsemen to pursue him
and shot him dead.
Yòu's partisans collectively coerced Wéi Wénzhèn, wanting him to join the conspiracy.
Wénzhèn refused,
fled for several *lǐ*,
but was overtaken
and killed.
The officials and subordinates trembled with fear,
bowed their heads and prostrated themselves on the ground,
none daring to look up.
Yòu then privately appointed officials such as Shàng Zhùguó and Kāifǔ,
opened the treasury to bestow rewards,
drove the populace into the city,
repaired armor, weapons, towers, and battlements,
and established offices such as Tuòdōng Wáng and Tuòxī Wáng.
Officials and common people abandoned their wives and children, secretly escaping at night by rope, one after another,
which Yòu could not prevent.
(Escaping the city by rope at night,
fearing contamination by the rebellious faction.)
Dié,
read *dáxié fān*.
Zhuì,
read *chíwèi fān*.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
an edict ordered Bīngbù Shàngshū Lǐ Shìjì and others to mobilize troops from Huái, Luò, Biàn, Sòng, Lù, Huá, Jì, Yùn, and Hǎi prefectures to suppress him.
The Emperor bestowed a personal letter upon Yòu, saying:
"I often warned you not to associate with petty men;
this is precisely why."
Yòu summoned Yān Hóngliàng and five others to sleep in his chamber.
The remaining partisans were divided into groups to command the soldiers and people,
patrolling the city and defending themselves.
Yòu feasted and drank with Hóngliàng and others every night,
thinking he had achieved his ambitions.
During their jesting,
when the imperial army was mentioned,
Hóngliàng and others said,
"Your Highness need not worry!
Hóngliàng and others will hold a wine cup in our right hand,
and with our left hand, we will wield swords for Your Highness to sweep them away!"
Yòu was pleased,
believing it to be truly so.
He sent proclamations to all the counties,
but none were willing to follow.
At this time, Lǐ Shìjì’s troops had not yet arrived,
but the forces from Qīng, Zī, and other prefectures had already gathered at its border.
Zīzhōu,
Zīchuān Commandery.
In Wǔdé first year (618 CE),
Zīchuān was separated from Qízhōu and established as a commandery.
The *Táng Liù Diǎn* (Six Canons of the Tang Dynasty) states: a princely establishment had a Military Affairs Counselor (*bīngcáo cānjūn*),
exclusively in charge of military officials’ records, evaluations, ceremonial guards, temporary assignments, and other matters.
Among Yòu’s attendants, as well as the officials and common people not involved in the conspiracy, there was none who did not respond.
On *gēngshēn*,
at night,
drums rattled on all four sides,
their sound audible for dozens of *lǐ*.
Among Yòu’s partisans, those who lived outside [the palace]
were all killed by the crowd with gathered blades.
Yòu asked what the sound was,
and his attendants deceived him, saying,
"Duke Yīng has already led the Flying Cavalry (*fēiqí*) onto the city wall."
Lǐ Shìjì was enfeoffed as Duke Yīngguó.
Flying Cavalry (*fēiqí*)
were the troops garrisoned at the northern gate.
*Gǔi* (紿),
pronounced *dàng hài*.
pronounced *qí jì*;
same below.
Yòu and Hóngliàng donned armor and wielded weapons, entering the chamber,
closing the doors to resist the battle.
Háng Mǐn and over a thousand others surrounded them.
From dawn until noon,
they could not conquer them.
Háng Mǐn said to Yòu,
"Your Highness was formerly an imperial son,
but now you are a national rebel.
If you do not surrender quickly,
you will immediately become ashes."
Thereupon, he ordered firewood to be piled up, intending to burn them.
Yòu spoke to Háng Mǐn from the window, saying,
"I will open the door immediately,
but I only worry about Yān Hóngliàng and his brother dying."
Háng Mǐn said,
"I will surely protect them."
Yòu and the others then came out.
Some gouged out Hóngliàng’s eyes and threw his eyeballs to the ground;
the rest [of the rebels] were clubbed, their legs broken, and then killed.
Yòu was apprehended and brought before the government office (*yáqián*) to be displayed to the officials and common people.
Returning,
he was locked in the east wing.
Qízhōu was entirely pacified.
On *yǐchǒu*,
an imperial edict ordered Lǐ Shìjì and others to cease military operations.
Yòu arrived at the capital,
and was granted death at the Inner Palace Service Bureau (*Nèishì Shěng*).
The *Xīng Jīng* (Canon of Stars) states that there are four stars for eunuchs,
located west of the Emperor's Seat in the Heavenly Market Enclosure.
The *Zhōu Guān* (Officials of Zhou) mentions the offices of *xiàngbó* and *sìrén*,
all inner officials.
In the Former Hàn, palace officials often used scholars,
but in the Later Hàn, eunuchs began to be used as palace officials.
The Jìn Dynasty established the Great Chief of the Imperial Women’s Quarters (*Dà Chángqiū Qīng*) as an official for the empress’s palace,
using eunuchs for it.
The Suí Dynasty had the Inner Palace Service Bureau (*Nèishì Shěng*),
which Emperor Yáng of Suí changed to the Director of the Imperial Women’s Quarters (*Chángqiū Jiān*).
In the early Wǔdé reign,
it was restored to the Inner Palace Service Bureau (*Nèishì Shěng*).
The rest were not investigated.
When Yòu first rebelled,
Luó Shítou, a man from Qízhōu, confronted him, enumerating his crimes.
He advanced with a spear,
intending to stab him,
but was killed by Yān Hóngliàng.
Yòu led his cavalry to attack Gāocūn.
Gāo Jūnzhuàng, a villager, shouted reproaches at Yòu from afar, saying,
"The Sovereign wielded a three-foot sword to win the empire!
The myriad people received his virtue
and look up to him as to Heaven.
Your Highness suddenly drives hundreds of people from the city, intending to rebel and offend your ruler and father!
This is no different from trying to shake Mount Tài with one hand.
How greatly you overestimate yourself!"
Yòu ordered an attack,
captured him,
but was ashamed and could not kill him.
An imperial edict posthumously granted Shítou the title of Grand Administrator (*cìshǐ*) of Bózhōu.
Jūnzhuàng was made Magistrate (*lìng*) of Yúshè.
In the Yìníng first year (617 CE) of the Suí Dynasty,
the township county of Shàngdǎng was divided
and Yúshè County was established,
belonging to Bìngzhōu.
In Wǔdé first year (618 CE),
it belonged to Hánzhōu.
In the second year, Yúzhōu was established.
In the sixth year,
the prefecture was abolished,
and Yúshè belonged to Liáozhōu.
pronounced *páng gè*.
He was enfeoffed as Duke of Nányáng Commandery.
Those who conspired with him to apprehend Yòu received official rewards commensurate with their contributions.
The Emperor examined Yòu’s family documents and memorials,
and found a remonstrance from the Archivist (*jìshì*) Sūn Chǔyuē of Jiāchéng.
Jiāchéng was the former Jiā County of Yǐngchuān Commandery in the Hàn Dynasty.
The Later Wèi Dynasty established Jiāchéng County and Lóngshān County.
In the early Kāihuáng reign of the Suí Dynasty,
Lóngshān was renamed Rǔnán.
In the eighteenth year,
Rǔnán was renamed Fǔchéng.
In the early Dàyè reign,
Fǔchéng was renamed Jiāchéng,
incorporating the territory of the Later Wèi’s Jiāchéng.
Shīgǔ said: *jiā* (郟),
pronounced *jiá*.
*Chǔ* (處),
pronounced *chāng lǘ*.
He was successively promoted to Academician-in-waiting of the Central Secretariat (*Zhōngshū Shèrén*).
On *gēngwǔ*,
Quán Wànjǐ was posthumously granted the title of Area Commander-in-chief (*Dūdū*) of Qízhōu,
awarded the noble title of Duke of Wǔdū Commandery,
and given the posthumous epithet Jìng.
Wéi Wénzhèn was made General of the Left Militant Guard (*Zuǒ Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn*),
and awarded the noble title of Duke of Xiāngyáng County.
10 In the beginning, Crown Prince Chénggān was fond of music, women, and hunting.
His behavior was extravagant.
Fearing that the Emperor would find out,
he often discussed loyalty and filial piety with his palace officials,
sometimes even to the point of tears.
Upon returning to his palace,
he would act wantonly and intimately with his young attendants.
When a palace official intended to remonstrate,
the Crown Prince would first anticipate their intention,
immediately greet them with a bow,
compose himself, sit upright,
admit his faults,
and speak eloquently in self-reproach,
leaving the palace official no time to bow and respond.
The palace was secretive,
and outsiders did not know [what was happening],
so at first, contemporary opinion generally praised him as worthy.
The Crown Prince made an eight-foot bronze furnace
and a six-section large tripod.
He recruited runaway slaves to steal horses and cattle from the common people.
Runaway slaves (*wángnú*)
refers to officials’ slaves who had absconded.
He shared the meat with his favored servants.
He also liked to imitate Turkic speech and their clothing.
He selected five of his attendants who resembled Turks to form a "flock" (*luò*),
braided their hair, wore sheepskins, and herded sheep.
He made five wolf-head banners and flags,
set up a yurt (*qiónglú*),
and the Crown Prince positioned himself within it,
gathering the sheep and cooking them.
He drew his scabbard knife and cut the meat, eating it with them.
He once said to his attendants,
"I will pretend to die as a Khagan,
and you all shall perform the mourning rites."
Thereupon, he lay stiffly on the ground.
The crowd all wailed and cried,
rode horses in circles,
approached his body,
and gashed their faces.
After a long while,
the Crown Prince suddenly got up and said,
"Should I one day possess the empire,
I shall lead tens of thousands of cavalry to hunt west of Jīnchéng.
"Jīnchéng"
should probably be
"Jīnhé."
*Shuài* (帥),
read as *shuài*.
pronounced *qí jì*.
I will entrust myself to Sīmó.
If I were to perform a single act,
I would not be second to anyone."
He meant that if he could command troops for Sīmó
and take charge of a single expedition,
he would surely distinguish himself.
The historian speaks of Chénggān's madness and foolishness.
Zuǒ Shùzǐ Yú Zhìníng and Yòu Shùzǐ Kǒng Yǐngdá repeatedly admonished the Crown Prince.
The Emperor commended them
and bestowed gold and silk upon the two men to encourage and stimulate the Crown Prince.
Subsequently, Yú Zhìníng was promoted to Zhānshì.
Yú Zhìníng and Zuǒ Shùzǐ Zhāng Xuánsù repeatedly submitted memorials, strongly admonishing the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince secretly sent men to kill them,
but they did not succeed.
Hánwáng Yuánchāng's actions were often unlawful.
Yuánchāng
was the Emperor's younger brother.
Because of this, he harbored resentment and discontent.
The Crown Prince was close to him,
playing games together morning and evening.
They divided their attendants into two teams,
with the Crown Prince and Yuánchāng each commanding one.
They wore felt armor,
wielded bamboo spears,
arranged their formations, and shouted as they engaged in battle,
striking and stabbing until blood flowed,
taking this as entertainment.
If anyone disobeyed orders,
they would strip them naked and beat them with a stick.
"Pī" refers to their hands and feet;
"zhuā" means to pull them to a tree and beat them with a stick.
"Zhuā"
is pronounced zhì guā.
The Crown Prince also said,
"If I were to become Emperor today,
tomorrow I would set up a camp of ten thousand men in the imperial park,
and divide command with Hánwáng.
Watching them fight,
would that not be enjoyable!"
He further said,
"When I am Emperor,
I will indulge my desires to the fullest.
If there are any who admonish me, I will immediately kill them.
It will be no more than killing a few hundred people,
and the populace will naturally settle down."
Wèiwáng Tàì had many artistic and technical skills
and was favored by the Emperor.
Seeing that the Crown Prince had a foot ailment,
he secretly harbored the ambition to usurp the succession.
He humbled himself before scholars to gain a good reputation.
The Emperor ordered Huángmén Shìláng Wéi Tǐng to act as the administrator of Tàì's residence.
Later, he ordered Gōngbù Shàngshū Dù Chǔkè to replace him.
Both men conspired with Tàì to win over court officials.
Dù Chǔkè sometimes carried gold to bribe influential figures,
and then persuaded them, saying that Wèiwáng was intelligent
and ought to be the heir apparent.
Civil and military officials
each found their own patrons,
secretly forming factions.
The Crown Prince feared their pressure,
and sent someone to impersonate a registrar of Tàì's residence to submit a sealed memorial,
which contained only accusations of Tàì's wrongdoings.
An imperial edict was issued to apprehend the culprit,
but he was not caught.
The Crown Prince privately favored Chēngxīn, a music boy from the Tài Cháng temple.
A "music boy"
refers to a boy skilled in playing music,
officially registered with the Tài Cháng temple.
Chēngxīn
was his name.
The old histories' biography of Chénggān states: There was a musician from the Tài Cháng temple,
just over ten years old,
with a beautiful appearance,
skilled in singing and dancing.
Chénggān particularly favored him,
calling him Chēngxīn.
Daoist priests Qín Yīng and Wéi Língfú practiced heterodox arts
and gained the Crown Prince's favor.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he was greatly enraged,
and had Chēngxīn and the others arrested and killed.
Several people died as a result of implication,
and the Crown Prince was reprimanded severely.
The Crown Prince believed that Tàì had reported him,
and his resentment and anger grew even stronger.
He constantly thought of Chēngxīn,
built a room in the palace,
erected his statue,
and offered sacrifices morning and evening,

wolf,

Cáo Dàgū's *Nǚjiè* says: To give birth to a son like a wolf,

Wújí replied:

Wújí's protection of the Crown Prince was utmost;

He ordered Lǐ Shìjì to lead fifteen thousand infantry and cavalry to array on the western ridge;
Zhǎngsūn Wújí was to lead eleven thousand elite troops as a surprise force,
to emerge from a narrow valley north of the mountain to strike their rear.
The Emperor himself led four thousand infantry and cavalry,
with drums and horns,
and lowered banners,
ascending the northern mountain.
He commanded all armies to charge forth simultaneously upon hearing the drums and horns.
He then ordered the appropriate officials to set up a surrender tent beside the imperial court.
On the *wǔwǔ* day,
Yánshòu and others, seeing only Lǐ Shìjì's formation,
mustered their troops, intending to fight.
The Emperor, observing dust rising from Wújí's army,
ordered the drums and horns to sound,
and the banners to be raised.
All armies advanced with shouts and drumrolls.
Yánshòu and the others were greatly alarmed
and wanted to divide their forces to resist,
but their formation was already in disarray.
Coincidentally, there was thunder and lightning;
just as battle was joined, thunder and lightning arrived.
Lóngmén was
in the territory of Hàn's Píshì County.
Later, the Northern Wèi called it Lóngmén County
and also established Lóngmén Commandery.
The Suí abolished the commandery
and made the county subordinate to Púzhōu.
In the early Wǔdé reign of the Táng,
it became the seat of Tàizhōu.
In the seventeenth year of Zhēnguàn, the prefecture was abolished
and it became subordinate to Jiàngzhōu.
Xuē Rén’guì responded to the recruitment call from among the common households.
He charged into the enemy formation with a great shout,
invincible wherever he went.
The Gāolì soldiers scattered,
and the main army pressed on.
The Gāolì army was utterly routed,
beheading more than twenty thousand.
The Emperor, seeing Rén’guì,
summoned him and appointed him Yóujī Jiāngjūn.
According to Táng regulations,
among the martial scattered ranks,
Yóujī Jiāngjūn
was of the lower fifth rank.
He was the sixth-generation descendant of Āndū.
Xuē Āndū, as a general,
was renowned for his bravery between Sòng and Wèi.
He was known by his courtesy name.
Yánshòu and others, with their remaining forces, fortified themselves by the mountains.
The Emperor ordered all armies to besiege them.
Zhǎngsūn Wújí completely dismantled the bridges
and cut off their retreat.
On the *jǐwèi* day,
Yánshòu and Huìzhēn, leading their thirty-six thousand eight hundred men, requested to surrender.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
"Lǐ Jì reported, 'If Your Majesty had not personally come,
your minister and Dàozōng, leading tens of thousands of men, would have attacked Ānshì City without success.
Yánshòu and the others, with over a hundred thousand, would have advanced with drawn spears.
The soldiers inside the city would have again opened their gates and come out.
Your minister, trying to save both head and tail,
would have been defeated in an instant,
and surely bound by Yánshòu and others and sent to Píngyǎng,
to be laughed at by Mòlízhī and others.
Today, your minister dares to thank Your Majesty for the grace of his life.'
The Emperor, who was always informal with Jì,
smiled and nodded. "
However, Jì later led troops alone to conquer Gāolì;
why would Tàizōng necessarily have to go personally?
This is not the historian's embellishment,
but Jì's flattery.
Therefore, we do not adopt this.
They advanced on their knees,
prostrated themselves, and begged for their lives.
The Emperor addressed them, saying,
"Young men of the Eastern Yi,
prancing around the seacoast,
when it comes to breaking through the strong and deciding victory,
naturally you are inferior to old men.
From now on, do you dare to fight the Son of Heaven again?"
They all prostrated themselves on the ground, unable to reply.
The Emperor selected three thousand five hundred chiefs, from *nuòsà* downwards,
granted them military ranks,
and resettled them in the interior.
The rest were all released
and sent back to Píngyǎng.
They all raised both hands and struck their foreheads to the ground,
their joyful shouts heard tens of *lǐ* away.
Three thousand three hundred Mòhé were captured
and all buried alive,
because the Mòhé had breached the formation.
Fifty thousand cattle,
ten thousand suits of iron armor,
and other equipment in similar quantities were captured.
Gāolì was utterly terrified.
Afterwards, Huángchéng and Yínchéng were both evacuated by their own garrisons,
and for hundreds of *lǐ* there was no trace of human habitation.
The Emperor sent a swift dispatch to the Crown Prince,
and also wrote to Gāo Shìlián and others, saying,
"I, as a general, am like this.
What do you think?"
The historian says that Emperor Tàizōng had a heart of self-congratulation.
"Jiāng" (將)
is pronounced "liàng".
According to old histories,
the mountain was originally named Liùshān.
"Gēng" (更)
is pronounced "héng".
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the *xīnwèi* day,
the Emperor moved his camp to the eastern ridge of Ānshì City.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
an edict was issued to mark the bodies of the fallen soldiers,
to be returned with the army.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
Gāo Yánshòu was appointed Hónglú Qīng,
and Gāo Huìzhēn was appointed Sīnóng Qīng.
Zhāng Liàng's army passed beneath Jiàn’ān City.
The ramparts were not yet firm,
and many soldiers were out gathering firewood or grazing livestock.
Gāolì soldiers suddenly arrived,
and the army was thrown into chaos.
Liàng was naturally timid,
but he sat on his *húchuáng*,
staring straight ahead without speaking.
Seeing this, his officers and men
mistook it for bravery.
The Director-General, Zhāng Jīnshù, and others sounded the drums, mustered their troops, and attacked the Gāolì forces,
defeating them.
In the eighth month,
on the *jiǎchén* day,
a scout captured Mòlízhī's spy, Gāo Zhúlí.
He was brought to the army gate with his hands tied behind his back;
"reverse-tied" means both hands were tied behind the back.
"Qí" (騎)
is pronounced "jì".
"Dié" (諜)
is pronounced "xié";
likewise below.
Untying him, the Emperor asked,
"Why are you so thin?"
He replied,
"I secretly traveled by road,
and haven't eaten for several days."
The Emperor ordered food to be given to him,
and said,
"You are a spy;
you should quickly report back.
Convey this message for me to Mòlízhī:
if he wants to know the news from our army,
he can send someone directly to my presence.
Why bother with the hardships of secret travel?"
Zhúlí was barefoot;
the Emperor gave him sandals and sent him away.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
the camp was moved south of Ānshì City.
While the Emperor was outside Liáo,
whenever he set up camp,
he only made sure the scouts were clear,
and did not build trenches or ramparts.
Although they approached the city,
the Gāolì never dared to come out to raid or plunder.
The soldiers marched singly and camped in the open like in China.
The historian says that the Emperor's might awed distant lands.
This is what is meant by "a good general does not array."
When the Emperor
attacked Gāolì,
the Xuēyántuó sent envoys to offer tribute.
The Emperor said to them,
"Tell your Khagan:
'Kě' (可)
enters the *rùshēng* from 'kān'.
'Hán' (汗)
is pronounced 'hán'.
If you are capable of being a marauder,
you should come quickly!"
Zhēnzhū Kèhán was terrified,
sent envoys to apologize,
and also requested to dispatch troops to assist the army.
The Emperor refused.
When Gāolì was defeated at Zhùbì Shān,
Mòlízhī sent the Mòhé to persuade Zhēnzhū,
tempting him with great benefits.
Zhēnzhū was intimidated and dared not move.
In the ninth month,
on the *rénshēn* day,
Zhēnzhū died.
The Emperor observed mourning for him.
Initially,
Zhēnzhū asked that his eldest illegitimate son, Yèmǎng, be made Dúlìshī Kèhán,
to reside in the east
and govern the various tribes;
and his legitimate son, Báhuò, be made Sìyèhù Kèhán,
to reside in the west
and govern the Xuēyántuó.
An imperial edict granted this,
and they were both appointed with ritual ceremonies.
Yèmǎng was impetuous and prone to disturbance,
and lightly used military force,
disagreeing with Báhuò.
When Zhēnzhū died,
they came to attend the funeral.
After the burial,
Yèmǎng feared that Báhuò intended to harm him,
and returned to his own部 first.
Báhuò pursued and killed him,
then established himself as Jiélìjùlǐ Xuēshāduōmí Kèhán.
This laid the foundation for the rebellion and downfall of the Xuēyántuó.
2 When the Emperor had conquered Báiyán,
he said to Lǐ Shìjì:
“I have heard that Ānshì City is perilous and its soldiers are elite,
and its city lord is courageous and capable.
During the rebellion of Mòlíchī,
the city garrison did not submit,
and Mòlíchī attacked but could not take it,
and therefore came to terms with it.
Jiàn'ān's soldiers are weak and their provisions are few.
If we strike unexpectedly,
we will certainly conquer it.
You can first attack Jiàn'ān.
Once Jiàn'ān falls,
Ānshì will be in our grasp.
This is what is called in military strategy, ‘There are cities that should not be attacked.’ ”
This is a statement from Sūnzǐ Bīngfǎ.
“Jiàn'ān is in the south,
and Ānshì is in the north.
Our army's provisions are all in Liáodōng.
If we now bypass Ānshì and attack Jiàn'ān,
and if the enemy cuts off our supply route,
what will we do?
It is better to first attack Ānshì.
Once Ānshì falls,
we can then advance triumphantly and take Jiàn'ān.”
The Emperor said:
“With you as a general,
how can I not adopt your strategy?
Do not jeopardize my affairs!”
Shìjì then attacked Ānshì.
When the people of Ānshì saw the Emperor's banners and chariots,
they would immediately mount the city walls and beat drums and shout.
The Emperor was angry.
Shìjì requested that on the day the city was captured,
all men and women be buried alive.
When the people of Ānshì heard this,
they defended even more resolutely,
and the attack prolonged without success.
Gāo Yánshòu and Gāo Huìzhēn petitioned the Emperor, saying:
“We, your servants, have entrusted ourselves to the great nation,
and dare not fail to offer our sincerity.
We wish for the Son of Heaven to achieve great success early,
so that we, your servants, may see our wives and children again.
The people of Ānshì cherish their families,
and each fights for himself,
so it is not easy to capture them swiftly.
Now, with more than 100,000 Gāogōuryě troops,
we are disheartened at the sight of your banners.
The people of our country are terrified.
The nousà of Wūgǔ City is old and infirm,
and cannot hold out.
If you move your troops to confront it,
it will be conquered by morning to evening.
The other small cities along the way
will surely flee at the mere sight of you.
Then, gather their supplies and provisions,
advance triumphantly,
and Píngyǎng will surely not hold.”
Yǐn Chén also said:
“Zhāng Liàng's troops are in Shāchéng.
Shāchéng is Bīshā City.
Taking advantage of Gāogōuryě's panic,
combine forces to capture Wūgǔ City,
cross the Yālǜ River,
and proceed directly to Píngyǎng.
Success lies in this campaign.”
The Emperor was about to follow this advice,
but only Zhǎngsūn Wújì believed:
“The Son of Heaven's personal campaign
is different from that of ordinary generals;
one should not take risks and seek fortune.
Now, the enemies in Jiàn'ān and Xīnchéng
still number 100,000.
If we head towards Wūgǔ,
they will all follow close behind us.
It is better to first defeat Ānshì,
take Jiàn'ān,
and then advance rapidly.
This is a foolproof strategy.”
The Emperor then stopped.
When Tàizōng pacified the empire,
he often achieved victory through ingenious tactics.
Only in the Liaodong campaign
did he seek to defeat the enemy with a foolproof plan,
which is why he achieved no success.
The various armies urgently attacked Ānshì.
The Emperor heard the sounds of chickens and pigs in the city,
and said to Lǐ Shìjì:
“The siege has lasted a long time,
and the smoke and fires in the city have diminished daily.
Now, the chickens and pigs are very noisy;
this must be a feast for the soldiers,
intending to launch a night attack on us.
We should prepare our troops strictly.”
That night,
several hundred Gāogōuryě men descended the city walls by rope.
The Emperor heard of it,
personally went to the city wall,
summoned troops to attack swiftly,
beheading several tens of them,
and the Gāogōuryě retreated.
Jiāngxiàwáng Dàozōng supervised the troops in building an earthen mound at the southeastern corner of the city,
gradually approaching the city walls.
The city also heightened its walls to resist it.
Soldiers fought in shifts,
six or seven engagements daily.
Battering rams and catapult stones
destroyed their watchtowers and battlements.
Pào,
same as pào,
pronounced pǐ mào fān.
Huài,
pronounced guài.
Dàozōng was wounded in the foot;
the Emperor personally applied acupuncture for him.
The construction of the mound continued day and night without cease,
for a total of sixty days,
employing 500,000 laborers.
The mountaintop was several *zhang* from the city,
overlooking the city below.
Dàozōng ordered Guǒyì Fù Fú'ài to lead troops to garrison the mountaintop to prepare for the enemy.
The mountain collapsed,
pressing against the city,
and the city wall crumbled.
It happened that Fú'ài had privately left his post.
Several hundred Gāogōuryě men sallied out from the breach in the wall,
then captured and occupied the earthen mound,
entrenching themselves there.
The Emperor was furious,
beheaded Fú'ài for public display,
and ordered his generals to attack it,
but they could not take it in three days.
Dàozōng went barefoot to the imperial banner to request punishment.
The Emperor said:
“Your crime deserves death,
but I recall that Emperor Wǔ of Han killed Wáng Huī,
see volume 18, Yuánguāng 2nd year.
Duke Mù of Qín sent Mèng Míng to lead an army to campaign eastward,
and he was twice defeated by the Jìn army.
Duke Mù again employed Mèng Míng.
Mèng Míng improved his administration,
led an army to attack Jìn,
and the Jìn people dared not sally forth,
thus he dominated the Xīróng.
Therefore, I especially pardon you.”
Because of the early cold in Liáozuǒ,
the grass withered and the water froze,
making it difficult for soldiers and horses to stay long.
Moreover, provisions were about to run out.
On Guǐwèi day,
an imperial edict commanded the army to return.
The households of Liáo and Gài prefectures were first relocated across the Liáo River.
Then the army displayed its might before Ānshì City and then withdrew.
Everyone in the city stayed hidden and did not come out.
The city lord ascended the wall to bid farewell.
The Emperor praised his steadfast defense,
bestowed upon him one hundred bolts of silk.
Jiān,
refers to silk woven from combined threads.
He ordered Lǐ Shìjì and Jiāngxiàwáng Dàozōng to lead forty thousand infantry and cavalry as the rearguard.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
[the Emperor] arrived in Liáodōng.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
[he] crossed the Liáo Shuǐ.
The Liáo Zé was muddy and flooded,
making it impossible for chariots and horses to pass.
He ordered Zhǎngsūn Wújí to lead ten thousand men
to cut grass and fill the road.
Where the water was deep, chariots were used as bridges.
The Emperor personally tied firewood to his horse’s saddle to assist in the labor.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the *bǐngshēn* day, the first day of the lunar month,
the Emperor reached Púgōu and halted his horse,
supervising the troops filling the road as they crossed the Bócuò Shuǐ.
Púgōu and Bócuò Shuǐ
were both within the Liáo Zé.
Many soldiers died from being wet and cold.
An imperial edict ordered fires to be lit along the road to await them.
In total, during the campaign against Gāolì,
ten cities were captured: Xuántú, Héngshān, Gàimóu, Mómǐ, Liáodōng, Báiyán, Bīshā, Màigǔ, Yínshān, and Hòuhuáng.
Seventy thousand households from the three prefectures of Liáo, Gài, and Yán were resettled in Zhōngguó.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* (Veritable Records) states,
"Seventy thousand households from the three prefectures were moved into the interior,
before and after."
The imperial edict of the *guǐchǒu* day (later in the record) states,
"Ten thousand households were captured,
with one hundred eighty thousand people."
This presumably includes those who were not resettled.
Over forty thousand heads were taken,
nearly two thousand soldiers died,
and seven or eight out of ten warhorses perished.
The Emperor, saddened by his failure to achieve success,
deeply regretted it,
and sighed,
"If Wèi Zhēng had been alive,
he would not have let me undertake this campaign!"
He ordered a fast courier to offer a *shàoláo* sacrifice to Wèi Zhēng,
and re-erected the stele he had composed,
(the overturning of the stele is seen in Volume 17 of the previous scroll).
Rewards were bestowed.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
[the Emperor] arrived in Yíngzhōu.
Yíngzhōu is two thousand nine hundred ten *lǐ* from Luòyáng.
He ordered the officials concerned to prepare a *tàiláo* sacrifice,
and personally wrote the text for the sacrifice,
weeping in deep sorrow.
When [Wèi Zhēng's] parents heard of it,
they said,
"Our son died, and the Son of Heaven wept for him;
what regret could he have in death!"
The Emperor said to Xuē Rén’guì,
"All my generals are old.
I seek a new, brave, and valiant man to lead them,
and none is like you.
I am not pleased to have gained Liáodōng;
I am pleased to have gained you."
On the *bǐngchén* day,
the Emperor heard that the Crown Prince was about to arrive for the welcoming,
and, with three thousand *fēijì* (light cavalry), galloped into Línyú Guān.
Línyú Xiàn was in Hàn's Liáoxī Jùn.
The Táng *Zhì* states
that Yíngzhōu had the Yúguān Shǒuzhuō Chéng.
Dù Yòu said: Línyú Guān is one hundred eighty *lǐ* east of the city of Lúlóng Xiàn in Píngzhōu.
*Qí*,
is pronounced *qí jì fān* (a phonetic annotation).
Shīgǔ said: Yú,
pronounced *yù*.
When the Emperor departed Dìngzhōu,
he pointed to his brown robe and said to the Crown Prince,
"Only when I see you
will I change this robe."
In Liáo Zuǒ,
even during the intense heat and sweating,
he did not change it.
By autumn,
it was worn out and damaged.
His attendants requested him to change it,
but the Emperor said,
"Many soldiers' clothes are tattered.
Is it right for me alone to wear new clothes?"
At this point,
the Crown Prince presented new clothes,
and he finally changed it.
The Gāolì civilians captured by all the armies, fourteen thousand people,
were first gathered in Yōuzhōu
and were to be rewarded to the soldiers.
The Emperor pitied their separation of fathers, sons, husbands, and wives,
and ordered the officials concerned to assess their value,
and redeem them all with money and cloth to become commoners.
The sound of their cheers
did not cease for three days.
In the eleventh month,
on the *xīnwèi* day,
the imperial carriage arrived in Yōuzhōu.
The Gāolì civilians welcomed him east of the city,
bowing, dancing, shouting, and wailing,
writhing on the ground,
with dust filling the view.
On the *gēngchén* day,
passing through the border of Yìzhōu, Sīmǎ Chén Yuánshú had people store fire seeds and cultivate vegetables in underground chambers to present to the Emperor;
The Emperor disliked his flattery
and dismissed Yuánshú from office.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
the imperial carriage arrived in Dìngzhōu.
On the *dīnghài* day,
Lìbù Shàngshū Yáng Shīdào was demoted to Gōngbù Shàngshū
because many of those he appointed were not talented.
On the *rénchén* day,
the imperial carriage departed Dìngzhōu.
In the twelfth month,
on the *xīnchǒu* day,
the Emperor fell ill with a carbuncle
and traveled in a walking sedan chair.
On the *wùshēn* day,
he arrived in Bìngzhōu.
The Crown Prince sucked the carbuncle for the Emperor

On the *xīnhài* day,
the Emperor's illness healed,
and all the officials offered congratulations.
When the Emperor campaigned against Gāo Lí,
he ordered Zhíshī Sīlì, the Grand General of the Right Leader Guard, to lead the Turks and encamp north of Xià Zhōu to guard against Xuē Yántuó.
After Duōmí Kèhán of Xuē Yántuó had been enthroned,
seeing that the Emperor had gone on campaign and not yet returned,
he led his troops to raid Hénán.
Hénán
refers to the south of the Yellow River,

Sīlì feigned weakness and retreated,
luring them to advance deeply.
When they reached the border of Xià Zhōu,
he arrayed his formation and waited for them.
Xuē Yántuó suffered a great defeat,
and Sīlì pursued them for over six hundred *lǐ*,
displaying his might north of the desert before returning.
磧,
pronounced *qì* (qi4).
還,

*huán* (huan2).
*Kǎo Yì* says: The *Gāozōng Shílù* records:

Its meaning points to Zhēnxhū as Yántuó.

but this text says the invasion came in winter,

On the *Jǐwèi* day,

pronounced *yín* (yin2).

鄜,
pronounced *fū* (fu1).

"Granted self-termination"

*Kǎo Yì* says: The *Shílù* records:
"Huángmén Shìláng Chǔ Suíliáng falsely accused him, saying: 'There is no need to worry about the affairs of the state.

and execute any ministers with dissenting ambitions,
and things will naturally be settled.'
When Tàizōng recovered from his illness,
he issued an edict asking about the reason.
Jì replied truthfully.
Suíliáng persisted in his accusation.
Jì invoked Zhōngshū Lìng Mǎ Zhōu to clear himself.
Tàizōng questioned Zhōu,
and Zhōu's reply was no different from what Jì had stated.
The Emperor used this to interrogate Suíliáng;
but he still insisted on the accusation,
and Zhōu avoided the truth,
so Jì was condemned."
However, such an act is not what a normal person would do.
Suíliáng was a loyal and upright minister,
and had no previous animosity.
How could he have gone so far?
It is probably that Xǔ Jìngzōng disliked Suíliáng,
and therefore, when compiling the *Shílù*, attributed Jì's death to Suíliáng.
We do not adopt this version now.

distinguishing their proper uses.
When there was an affair, they would request them from within the palace,

They stored the left half and issued the right half,

The first was the Bronze Fish Tally,

The second was the Relay Tally,

The third was the Personal Fish Tally,
used for distinguishing rank
and responding to summons.
The fourth was the Wooden Tally,
used for reinforcing garrisons
and carefully managing receipts and disbursements.
The fifth was the Banner and Staff,
used for entrusting competent individuals
and granting authority for rewards and punishments.
The system for Fish Tallies was:
within the imperial domain,
three on the left and one on the right;
outside the imperial domain,
five on the left and one on the right.
The left ones were kept within the court,
the right ones were issued outside.
When put into use,
the first one was taken as the starting point.
Subsequent affairs requiring use
were dispatched in sequence,
circling back to the beginning.
For major affairs, an imperial edict was also issued;
for minor affairs, only a tally was sent in a sealed case,
and an envoy was dispatched to match and execute it.
The system for Relay Tallies was:
for the crown prince acting as regent, there were Double Dragon Tallies,
ten on each side.
For the commander of the capital, there was the Qílín Tally.
Twenty on the left,
and nineteen on the right.
For the east, the Azure Dragon Tally;
for the west, the Zōu'yú Tally;
for the south, the Vermilion Bird Tally;
for the north, the Black Tortoise Tally.
Four on the left and three on the right.
The left ones were sent to the interior,
the right ones were issued to the exterior.
The system for Personal Tallies was:
two on the left and one on the right.
The crown prince used jade,
princes used gold,
and common officials used copper,
worn as decoration.
Those with names engraved
were returned upon leaving office;
those without engraving
were passed down and worn.
The system for Wooden Tallies was:
for the crown prince acting as regent,
within the imperial domain,
three on each side;
outside the imperial domain,
five on each side.
For common officials acting as garrison commanders,
ten on each side.
The system for Banners and Staffs was:
when appointing a grand commander or dispatching envoys to the four directions,
they were requested and granted.
The banner was for exclusive authority over rewards,
the staff for exclusive authority over executions.
All other matters were handled by the Crown Prince.

1. In the spring,
the first month,
Gāoshìlián (高士廉), Grandee Minister-Attendant of the Bureau of Administration (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī) and Duke Wénxiàn (文獻公) of Shēn (申), was critically ill.

He led his attendants out through the Xīng'ān Gate (興安門).
According to the *Six Canons* (六典),
the Dàmíng Palace (大明宮) has five gates on its south side,
the one next to the west being the Xīng'ān Gate (興安門).
However, before the Zhēnguān (貞觀) era,

Could it be that the Emperor departed from the Yǒng'ān Palace (永安宮) and exited through the Xīng'ān Gate (興安門)?
According to the biography of Gāoshìlián (高士廉) in the *Old Book* (舊書): The Emperor exited the Xīng'ān Gate (興安門),

From the Dàmíng Palace's (大明宮) Xīng'ān Gate (興安門) to the imperial city's Yánxǐ Gate (延喜門),

His Majesty presided in Cuìwēi Hall,

"Since ancient times, even if emperors pacified the central states,
they could not subjugate the Róng and Dí.
My talent does not match that of the ancients, yet my achievements surpass theirs.
I myself do not understand the reason;
let all of you speak your minds truthfully."
The assembled officials all declared:
"Your Majesty's merits and virtues are like Heaven and Earth;
the myriad things cannot adequately describe them."
His Majesty said:
"Not so.
The reason I have been able to achieve this
is merely due to five matters.
Ancient emperors often envied those superior to themselves;
I, however, when I see another's goodness,
regard it as if I possess it myself.
People's actions and abilities
cannot be entirely perfect;
I always discard their shortcomings
and utilize their strengths.
Rulers often, when advancing the worthy, wish to hold them close to their bosom,
and when dismissing the unworthy, wish to cast them into a ravine.
I, however, when I see the worthy, respect them,
and when I see the unworthy, pity them,
so the worthy and unworthy each find their proper place.
Rulers often dislike uprightness,
secretly punishing and openly executing,
which has occurred in every generation.
Since I ascended the throne,
upright gentlemen
stand shoulder to shoulder in court,
and I have never dismissed or reprimanded a single one.
Since ancient times, all valued the central states
and despised the Yí and Dí;
I alone love them equally.
Therefore, all their tribes lean on me as on their parents.
These five things
are the reasons why I have achieved today's success."
He turned to Chǔ Suíliáng (褚遂良) and said:
"You once served as a historian—

no longer concurrently holding a historical post,

He replied:
"Your Majesty's abundant virtue cannot be fully recorded.

is surely a humble sentiment."

"What did Xuánlíng say?"
He replied:
"Xuánlíng, upon hearing that Lǐ Wěi was appointed Shàngshū,
merely said, 'Lǐ Wěi has a beautiful beard and whiskers.'"
The Emperor immediately changed Wěi's appointment to Governor of Luòzhōu.
A textual variant note says: The Táng History states:
"Before long,
Wěi was reassigned as Crown Prince Zhànshì."
We now follow the old biography.
16 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Niú Jìndá (牛進達) and Lǐ Hǎi'àn (李海岸) entered Gāogōulí territory.
They fought over a hundred battles,
none without victory,
attacked Shíchéng (石城),
and captured it.
They advanced to the foot of Jīlìchéng (積利城),
where more than ten thousand Gāogōulí soldiers sallied out to fight.
Hǎi'àn defeated them,
beheading two thousand.
17 His Majesty, finding Cuìwēi Palace precipitous and narrow,
unable to accommodate the hundred officials,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
issued an edict to construct Yùhuá Palace anew in Fènghuáng Valley
of Yíchūn.
Yùhuá Palace is forty Lǐ west of Yíchūn County.
On the day Gēngxū,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
18 In the eighth month,
on the day Rénxū,
an edict stated that because Xuēyántuó had newly submitted,
and major construction projects had been repeatedly undertaken,
coupled with floods in Héběi,
the Fēngshàn ceremony for the next year would be suspended.
19 On the day Xīnwèi,
the Gǔlìgàn (骨利幹) sent envoys to offer tribute;
on the day Bǐngxū,
Gǔlìgàn was established as Xuánquē Prefecture,
and its Sījīn (俟斤) was appointed as its Governor.
Among the Tiělè tribes, Gǔlìgàn was the furthest.
There, the days are long and the nights short;
after sunset,
as the sky turns dusky,
by the time a lamb's spleen is cooked,
the sun has already risen again.
Gǔlìgàn resided north of the Hànhǎi Sea
and produced fine horses.
Its territory stretched north to the sea,
making it the farthest from the capital.
Further north, crossing the sea,
the days are long and nights short,
which is close to the place where the sun rises.
The character "復" (fù),
read "fú yòu fān" (扶又翻).
A textual variant note says: The Shílù and Táng History both read
"sheep scapula (羊胛)."
Monk Yīxíng's (一行) Commentary on the Dàyǎn Calendar, as well as the Old Astronomical Treatise and Táng Tǒngjì, all read
"spleen (脾)."
The New Astronomical Treatise says:
"To cook,
sheep thigh (羊髀)."
We note that specifically saying "lamb's spleen"
is because it cooks easily.
If one were to cook lamb scapula or thigh,
even in China,
it would not be tender even after a whole night.
We now follow the Commentary on the Dàyǎn Calendar.
On the *jǐchǒu* day (20th),
Duàn Zhìchōng (段志沖), a man from Qízhōu (齊州), presented a sealed memorial,
requesting the Emperor to transfer governance to the Crown Prince.
When the Crown Prince heard of this,
worry showed on his face,
and he spoke with tears streaming down.
Zhǎngsūn WúJì (長孫無忌) and others requested that Zhìchōng (志沖) be executed.
The Emperor issued an imperial rescript, saying:
"The Five Peaks soar into the sky,
and the Four Seas stretch across the earth.
Accepting filth and harboring illness
does not diminish their height or depth.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* (左傳) says: 'Rivers and marshes receive filth,
mountains and wilds harbor disease.'
*Gèng* (亙)
is pronounced *gǔdèng fān*.
This means he wished for the Son of Heaven to abdicate.
This is his straightforwardness;
if he has no fault,
then this is his madness.
It is like a foot of mist obscuring the sky,
which does not detract from its vastness;
or an inch of cloud dotting the sun,
how does it diminish its brightness!"
On the *dīngyǒu* day (21st),
the imperial prince Lǐ Míng (李明) was established as Prince of Cáo (曹王).
Míng's (明) mother was Lady Yáng (楊氏),
who was the daughter of Cháo Lì Wáng (巢剌王) and
was favored by the Emperor.
When Empress Wéndé (文德皇后) died,
the Emperor wanted to establish Lady Yáng (楊氏) as Empress.
Wèi Zhēng (魏徵) remonstrated, saying:
"Your Majesty is currently comparing your virtue to that of Táng (唐) and Yú (虞),
why would you burden yourself with a Chén Yíng (辰嬴)!"
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* (左傳) says: Prince Yǔ (圉) of Jìn (晉) was a hostage in Qín (秦).
Duke Mù (穆公) of Qín (秦) gave him a daughter in marriage.
When Yǔ (圉) was about to flee back,
he said to her:
"Will you return with me?"
Lady Yíng (嬴氏) dared not follow,
and Yǔ (圉) subsequently fled back.
When Prince Chóng'ěr (重耳) of Jìn (晉) entered Qín (秦),
Duke Mù (穆公) of Qín (秦) presented five daughters,
Huái Yíng (懷嬴) was among them,
and she was called Chén Yíng (辰嬴).
Jiǎ Jì (賈季) said: "Chén Yíng (辰嬴) was favored by two lords," which refers to this.
*Lèi* (累)
is pronounced *lìruì fān*.
Soon after, Lǐ Míng (李明) was made the heir to Yuánjí (元吉).
On the *wùxū* day (22nd),
an imperial edict commanded Wáng Bōlì (王波利), the Prefect of Sòngzhōu (宋州), and others to dispatch workers from the twelve prefectures south of the Yangtze to build several hundred large ships,
intending to use them for an expedition against Gāolì (高麗).
The twelve prefectures were Xuān (宣), Rùn (潤), Cháng (常), Sū (蘇), Hú (湖), Háng (杭), Yuè (越), Tái (台), Wù (婺), Kuò (括), Jiāng (江), and Hóng (洪).
*Sōu* (艘)
is pronounced *sūzāo fān*.
*Lì* (麗)
is pronounced *lìzhī fān*.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the *gēngchén* day,
Núlā Chuòfú Sīyǒu (奴剌啜匐俟友), leading more than ten thousand people from his tribe, surrendered and submitted.
The Núlā (奴剌) tribe resided between Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) and Dǎngxiàng (党項).
*Lā* (剌)
is pronounced *láidá fān*.
*Chuò* (啜)
is pronounced *zhìlüè fān*.
*Fú* (匐)
is pronounced *púběi fān*.
*Sī* (俟)
is pronounced *qúzhī fān*.
*Shuài* (帥)
is read as *shuài*;
similarly below.
In the eleventh month,
Chēbí Kèhán (車鼻可汗) of the Tujue (突厥) sent envoys to pay tribute.
Chēbí (車鼻) was named Húbó (斛勃),
originally of the same Tujue (突厥) clan,
and had been a minor Khagan for generations.
After Xiélì's (頡利) defeat,
the remaining Tujue (突厥) wanted to enthrone him as the Great Khagan,
but at that time, Xuē Yántuó (薛延陀) was strong,
and Chēbí (車鼻) dared not accept,
so he led his followers to submit to them.
Someone advised Xuē Yántuó (薛延陀):
"Chēbí (車鼻) is of noble lineage,
possesses courage and strategy, and is supported by the masses.
He might become a future menace,
it is better to kill him."
Chēbí (車鼻) learned of this
and fled.
Xuē Yántuó (薛延陀) sent several thousand cavalry to pursue him,
but Chēbí (車鼻) rallied his troops and fought,
thoroughly defeating them.
He then established his headquarters north of Jīnshān (金山),
where his territory was extremely difficult to access on three sides,
with only one side passable by chariots and cavalry,
and its soil was vast and flat.
The remaining Tujue (突厥) gradually rallied to him,
and within a few years, his fighting force reached thirty thousand men,
often raiding Xuē Yántuó (薛延陀).
When Xuē Yántuó (薛延陀) was defeated,
Chēbí's (車鼻) power further expanded.
He sent his son Shābōluótè Lè (沙鉢羅特勒) to visit,
and also requested to personally come to the court.
An edict dispatched General Guō Guǎngjìng (郭廣敬) to summon him.
Chēbí (車鼻) merely used flattering words,
having no intention of coming at all,
and ultimately did not arrive.
*Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The *Shílù* (實錄) states,
"An edict dispatched Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn (雲麾將軍) Ān Diàozhē (安調遮) and Yòu Túnwèi Lángjiāng (右屯衞郎將) Hán Huá (韓華) to welcome him.
Chēbí (車鼻) merely adorned his words,
initially having no intention of coming.
Hán Huá (韓華) was about to recruit the Gēluólù (歌邏祿) to jointly ambush him.
Chēbí (車鼻) discovered their plot,
and Hán Huá (韓華) and Chēbí's (車鼻) son Zhìbì Tèlè (陟苾特勒) shot each other to death.
Diàozhē (調遮) was also killed."
Now we follow the Old Tujue (突厥) biography.
On the *guǐmǎo* day (25th),
Prince Tàizhōu (泰州) of Shùnyáng (順陽) was transferred to be Prince of Pú (濮王).
On the *rénzǐ* day (26th),
the Emperor's illness recovered,
and he held court every three days.
In the twelfth month,
on the *rénshēn* day,
Zhào Mó (趙磨), the chieftain of Xīzhào (西趙), leading over ten thousand households, submitted and joined.
Their land was established as Míngzhōu (明州).
South of Dōngxiè (東謝) were the Xīzhào Mán (西趙蠻),
extending west to Kūnmíng (昆明),
and south to the Xī'ěrhé (西洱河).
The mountain caves were deep and treacherous,
and the Zhào (趙) clan had been chieftains for generations.
*Qiú* (酋)
is pronounced *cíyóu fān*.
*Zhǎng* (長)
is pronounced *zhīliǎng fān*.
Kūcí Wáng (龜茲王) Fádié (伐疊) died,
and his younger brother Hēlíbùshībì (訶黎布失畢) ascended.
He gradually neglected his duties as a vassal
and encroached upon neighboring countries.
The Emperor was angered,
and on the *wùyín* day,
issued an edict to send the Emissary with Imperial Insignia, Grand General of the Kūnqiū Dào (崑丘道) Expeditionary Army.
It has been passed down since ancient times
that there is Kūnlúnshān (崑崙山) in the Western Regions,
where the source of the river lies.
Also, the *Ěryǎ* (爾雅) says: "Three sections make up Kūnlúnqiū (崑崙丘),"
hence it is called Kūnqiū Dào (崑丘道).
*Shǐ* (使)
is pronounced *shūlì fān*.
He was also commanded to link up with the thirteen prefectures of Tiělè (鐵勒), Tujue (突厥), Tǔbō (吐蕃), and Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) to advance and suppress them.
King Gāolì (高麗) sent his son Mòlízhī Rènwǔ (莫離支任武) to apologize,
and the Emperor accepted it.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Jǐchǒu,
the Emperor composed "Dìfàn" (Models for an Emperor) in twelve chapters and bestowed it upon the Crown Prince.

Its chapters were titled: "The Sovereign's Character" (Jūntǐ), "Establishing Kinship" (Jiànqīn), "Seeking the Worthy" (Qiúxián), "Scrutinizing Officials" (Shěnguān), "Accepting Admonition" (Nàjiàn), "Removing Slanderers" (Qùchán), "Guarding Against Complacency" (Jièyíng), "Honoring Frugality" (Chóngjiǎn), "Rewards and Punishments" (Shǎngfá), "Promoting Agriculture" (Wùnóng), "Reviewing Military Affairs" (Yuèwǔ), and "Esteeming Culture" (Chóngwén).
He further said:
“Cultivating oneself and governing the state,
all are contained therein.
Should I suddenly pass away,
I shall have nothing more to say.”
He also said:
“You should further seek out the wise kings of antiquity as your teachers.
As for me,
I am not worthy of imitation.
Indeed, if one takes a superior model,
one will only achieve the middle;
if one takes a middle model,
one will inevitably fall to the lower.
Since I ascended the throne,
I have committed many errors:
brocades, silks, pearls, and jade have constantly been before me;
palaces and pavilions have frequently been constructed;
dogs, horses, hawks, and falcons have been brought from far and wide;
I have traveled in all four directions,
causing much trouble and expense for provisions and lodgings.
These are all my grave faults;
do not consider them correct and imitate them.
However, I have broadly benefited the common people,
and my contributions are many;
I have founded and established this land of China,
and my achievements are great.
My benefits are many and my faults few,
hence the people do not resent me;
my achievements are great and my transgressions minor,
hence my enterprise does not fall.
Yet, compared to absolute perfection and goodness,
I am indeed much ashamed.
You do not have my diligence and effort, yet you inherit my wealth and nobility.
If you strive to do good,
then the state will barely be secure;
if you are arrogant, lazy, extravagant, and self-indulgent,
then your own person will not be preserved.
Moreover, that which is slow to achieve but quick to fail
is the state;
that which is easy to lose but difficult to gain
is the position of power.
How can one not cherish it!
How can one not be cautious!”
Tàizōng personally enumerated his own faults and shortcomings to admonish the Crown Prince.
This may be called truly exemplary.
However, the Crown Prince suffered from being weak and fond of inner chambers,
yet not a single word touched upon this to warn and stimulate him.
It is truly said that people do not know the faults of their own children!
The character 易 (yì)
should be
read as 豉 (chǐ).
2 The illness of Mǎ Zhōu, Grand Councillor and concurrent Right Chief Administrator, worsened.
The Emperor personally prepared medicine for him;
he sent the Crown Prince to visit and inquire after him.
On the day Gēngyín,
he passed away.
3 On the day Wùxū,
the Emperor went to the hot springs at Líshān.
4 On the day Jǐhài,
Cuī Rénshī, a Palace Secretary, was appointed Vice Director of the Chancellery
and given a concurrent role in privy council affairs.
5 King Jīn Shàndé of Xīnluó passed away.
Her sister, Zhēndé, was appointed Pillar of the State,
ennobled as Prince of Lèlàng Commandery,
and an envoy was dispatched to confer the title.
6 On the day Bǐngwǔ,
an imperial edict appointed Xuē Wànchè, Grand General of the Right Martial Guard, as Grand Field Commander of Qīngqiū Circuit.
Péi Xíngfāng, General of the Right Guard, was his deputy.
They were to lead over thirty thousand troops, as well as tower-ships and warships,
sailing from Láizhōu to attack Gāolì.
7 Zhǎngsūn Wújí was appointed Provisional Grand Councillor, and concurrently took charge of the affairs of the Department of State Affairs and the Chancellery.
Zhǎngsūn Wújí thus oversaw the affairs of the three central departments.
8 On the day Wùshēn,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
9 The Jiégǔ had never communicated with China since ancient times.
Dù Yòu said: "The Jiégǔ are three thousand *lǐ* northwest of the Huíhé."
In the second month,
their Qīlìfā Shībóqū'āzhàn came to court.
The people of their state were all tall,
with red hair and green eyes;
those with black hair were considered inauspicious.
The Emperor hosted them at the Tiānchéng
Palace
and said to his attendant ministers:
“In the past, at Wèiqiáo, I cut off the heads of three Tūjué leaders,
and considered it a great achievement—
this refers to the ninth year of Wǔdé,
when Xiélì encroached upon Biànqiáo.
But why do you not find it strange now!”
Shībóqū'āzhàn requested to be appointed to one official post,
saying, “to return holding a tablet of office
would truly be a blessing for a hundred generations.”
On the day Wùwǔ,
Jiégǔ was established as the Jiānkūn Area Command,
and Shībóqū'āzhàn was appointed Grand General of the Right Garrison Guard and Jiānkūn Area Commander,
subordinate to the Yànrán Protectorate.
Furthermore, the tribe of Āshǐdé Shíjiàn Sījīn was established as Qílián Prefecture,
subordinate to the Yíngzhōu
Area Commander.
At this time, the rulers of the various barbarian tribes, large and small, vied to send envoys to offer tribute and appear before the Emperor.
The roads were constantly busy.
Each New Year's Day audience,
there were usually several hundred or a thousand people.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
the Emperor granted an audience to the envoys of the various Hu tribes
and said to his attendant ministers:
“Emperor Wǔ of Hàn exhausted his army for over thirty years,
fatiguing China,
and what he gained was little;
how can that compare to today, where we pacify them with virtue,
making the lands of 'barren hair' entirely into registered households!”
Lù Démíng's *Jīngdiǎn Shìwén* states: "Sīmǎ says: 'Qióngfà' (barren hair)
refers to the land without vegetation beneath the North Pole."
Cuī says: "It is the northern land without vegetation."
Based on this, *máo* (hair)
refers to grass.
Geographical texts state: "Mountains take grass and trees as their hair."
10 The Emperor constructed the Yùhuá Palace.
Chéng Dàchāng said: "Yùhuá Palace is in Yíjūn County, Fāngzhōu."
Only the hall where he resided was covered with tiles;
the rest were thatched.
However, it was fully equipped with palaces for the Crown Prince and various offices,
encompassing mountains and valleys.
The expenses already amounted to billions.
On the day Yǐhài,
the Emperor went to the Yùhuá Palace.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
he hunted at Huáyuan.
Huáyuan, Yíjūn, and Tóngguān
were the lands of Yúnyáng and Duìyǔ in the Hàn dynasty.
The Later Wèi established Běiyōng Prefecture in Huáyuan;
the Western Wèi renamed it Yí Prefecture
and also established Běidì Commandery.
In the early Kaihuang era of the Suí dynasty,
the commandery was abolished;
in the early Daye era,
the prefecture was abolished,
and the county was made subordinate to Jīngzhào.
In the early Táng, Yí Prefecture was re-established.
In the 17th year of Zhēngguān,
the prefecture was abolished,
and Huáyuan was again made subordinate to Jīngzhào.
11 Cuī Rénshī, Vice Director of the Chancellery, was implicated because someone lodged a complaint against him from outside the palace.
Rénshī failed to report it.
He was dismissed from office
and exiled to Liánzhōu.
Liánzhōu
was the land of Guìyáng and Yángshān in the Hàn dynasty.
The Liáng dynasty established Yángshān Commandery.
The Suí dynasty established Liánzhōu.
In the early Daye era,
the prefecture was abolished and became Xīpíng Commandery.
The Táng dynasty re-established it as Liánzhōu.
Liánzhōu is three thousand six hundred sixty-five *lǐ* south of the capital.
*Kǎoyì* (Textual Research) states: "The old tradition
says 'exiled to Gōngzhōu'.
Now we follow the new and old imperial annals."
12 In the third month,
on the day Jǐchǒu,
the Juluóbó tribe of the Hànhǎi Area Command was divided to establish Zhúlóng Prefecture.
13 On the day Jiǎwǔ,
the Emperor said to his attendant ministers:
“I have spent my youth and adult life amidst military campaigns
and am quite skilled at estimating the enemy.
Now, in the campaign at Kūnqiū, the two tribes of Chùyuè and Chùmì, and Jiélièdiānnàlì, who holds power in Qiūcí, are always indecisive and hesitant.
They will certainly be the first to surrender.
Nǔshībì will be next.”
“Nǔshībì”
should be written as
“Bùshībì”,
who was the King of Qiūcí.
14 On the day Gēngzǐ,
Empress Xiāo of Suí passed away.
An imperial edict restored her title and rank,
and she was posthumously granted the epithet Mǐn.
An official of the third rank was dispatched to supervise her burial,
and ceremonial carriages and imperial guards were provided
to escort her to Jiāngdū,
where she was interred with Emperor Yáng.
15 Chōngróng (Consort) Xú Huì of Chángchéng
The Táng Huìyào (Essential Records of the Tang) states: According to the old system,
Zhaoyí, Zhaoróng, Zhaoyuàn, Xiūyí, Xiūrúng, Xiūyuàn, Chōngyí, Chōngróng, Chōngyuàn each had one person,
forming the Nine Pín (Consorts),
of the second rank.
In the third year of Tàikāng (282 CE) during the reign of Jìn Wǔdì,
Chángchéng county was established by dividing Wūchéng,
subordinate to Wúxīng Commandery.
This is today's Chángxīng County in Húzhōu.
Huì
was the daughter of Xú Xiàodé.
When the western campaign against Qiūcí was launched,
and construction projects like Cuìwēi and Yùhuá
followed one after another,
with clothes and ornaments being quite extravagant,
she submitted a memorial to remonstrate,
the gist of which was:
"Using finite agricultural labor
to fill an endless giant wave;
plotting to acquire unobtained foreign populations,
while losing our established army.
In ancient times, Qín Huáng (First Emperor of Qin) annexed the Six States,
which instead hastened the foundation of his downfall and ruin.
Jìn Wǔ (Emperor Wu of Jin) suddenly possessed the three regions,
which instead led to a legacy of collapse and defeat.
The three regions of Wèi, Shǔ, and Wú stood in a tripod formation,
until Jìn unified them.
Abandoning virtue and making light of the state,
seeking profit and forgetting danger,
is this not caused by indulging desires and giving free rein to passions?
Therefore, it is known that vast territory is not the art of permanent stability,
and exhausting the people is indeed the source of easy rebellion."
She also said:
"Although thatched huts indicate frugality,
they still cause exhaustion from wood and stone construction;
even if labor is hired,
there are inevitably inconveniences and troubles."
She also said:
"Precious curios and ingenious crafts
are the axes that destroy a nation;
pearls, jade, brocade, and embroidery
are truly mind-bewitching poisons."
She also said:
"If rules are made for frugality,
one still fears extravagance;
if rules are made for extravagance,
how can future generations be controlled?"
The Emperor praised her words
and treated her with great respect.
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ, collated by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by Imperial Edict
Later Scholars Tiāntái
The 22nd year of Zhēngguān
(Wùshēn, 648 CE)
1 Summer,
Fourth month,
Dīngsì.
Liáng Jiànfāng, the Right Wǔhóu General, attacked the Mán (barbarians) outside Sōngzhōu
and defeated them.
The various Mán tribes outside Sōngzhōu relied on mountains and valleys for their defenses,
which also belonged to the ancient Nánzhōng region.
They were named thus because they were outside Sōngzhōu.
The New Records state: The Mán outside Sōngzhōu are beyond the borders of Chāngmíng County in Xīzhōu.
Previously,
Liú Bóyīng, the Grand Administrator of Xīzhōu, had memorialized:
"The various Mán tribes outside Sōngzhōu have temporarily submitted but then rebelled again.
I request an expedition to punish them,
to open the route to Xī'ěr and Tiānzhú."
This was the route that Hàn Wǔdì had wished to open,
but which was obstructed by Kūnmíng.
Xīzhōu was
the land of the Qióngdū Yí in the Han dynasty.
Hàn Wǔdì established Yuèxī Commandery there.
Later, Zhōu Wǔdì established Yánzhōu,
which became Xīzhōu in the Tang.
Xī,
pronounced suǐ.
Shàng,
pronounced zhǎng.
Zhàn,
same as zàn.
Jiàng,
pronounced jiàng.
Fù,
pronounced fù.
Ěr,
pronounced èr.
Thirteen zhōu (prefectures): Yì, Méi, Róng, Zǐ, Lì, Mián, Suí, Bā, Lú, Qú, Dá, Jí, Yú.
Jiànfāng defeated them,
killing and capturing over a thousand people.
The various Mán were terrified
and fled into the mountains and valleys.
Jiànfāng sent envoys to explain the advantages and disadvantages to them,
and they all came to submit.
In total, seventy tribes,
with 109,300 households, came forward.
Jiànfāng appointed their chieftains, such as Méng Hé, as county magistrates,
each governing their own tribe,
and none were displeased.
He then sent envoys to Xī'ěrhé.
The New Book states: The Mán route to Xī'ěrhé
runs three thousand lǐ from Lángzhōu.
At that time, Jiànfāng sent a surprise force fifteen hundred lǐ from Xīzhōu to their territory.
They had prepared boats to flee,
but the envoy enlightened them with his authority and trustworthiness,
and Shèng Suì then requested to surrender.
In that land, there were dozens of surnames such as Yáng, Lǐ, Zhào, Dǒng,
each occupying a prefecture,
the larger ones with six hundred,
the smaller ones with two or three hundred households.
There was no great ruler,
and they were not unified.
Although their language was slightly different,
their livelihoods and customs
were generally the same as those of the Central Plains.
They claimed to be all Hàn people originally,
the only difference being that their year began in the twelfth month.
2 Jǐwèi.
Qìdān Rǔhèzhǔ Qǔ Jù led his people to submit to the interior.
The chieftains of Xī and Qìdān were all called Rǔhèzhǔ.
Qì,
pronounced qì,
also chī.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Qǔ Jù was appointed Cìshǐ (Prefect)
and placed under the Yíngzhōu Grand Administrator's Office.
3 Jiǎzǐ.
Gǔ Shéngǎn, the commander of Wūhú Garrison,
Wūhú Garrison should have been established on Wūhú Island in the sea.
Traveling northeast by sea from Dēngzhōu,
one passes Dàxiè Island, Guīxīn Island, and Yū Island before reaching Wūhú Island;
then another three hundred lǐ north across Wūhú Sea.
The Genealogical Records state: When Zhōu Tàiwáng left Bīn for Qí,
he was called Gǔ Gōng,
and thus the surname was adopted.
He encountered five thousand Gāolì infantry and cavalry
and defeated them in battle at Yìshān.
"Yìshān"
is written as
"Héshān" in the New Book.
Jiàng,
pronounced jiàng.
Lì,
pronounced lì.
Qí,
pronounced qí.
Over ten thousand Gāolì troops attacked Shéngǎn's boats.
Shéngǎn set an ambush
and defeated them again before returning.
4 Previously,
Yǐpí Duōlù Kèhán of the Western Tūjué
had appointed Āshǐnà Hèlǔ as Yèhù (Jabghu),
residing near the Duōluósī River,
fifteen hundred lǐ north of Xīzhōu,
commanding the five tribes of Chùyuè, Chùmì, Shǐsū, Gēluólù, and Shìbì.
Yǐpí Duōlù fled to Tuǒhuǒluó.
See volume 196, 16th year.
His tribes dispersed.
Yǐhài.
Hèlǔ led his remaining several thousand tents to submit to the interior.
An edict ordered them to be settled in Mòhè City in Tíngzhōu.
Sixty lǐ west of Xīyán City in Tíngzhōu, there was a Shābō City guard post,
which was probably Mòhè City;
because Hèlǔ was later established as Shābōluó Yèhù Kèhán,
the city name was changed.
Chù,
pronounced chǔ.
Hèlǔ, hearing that Tang forces were campaigning against Qiūcí,
requested to serve as a guide
and then came to court with several dozen cavalry.
The Emperor appointed him commander-in-chief of the Kūnqiū Road expeditionary force
and sent him off with a generous feast and gifts.
This laid the groundwork for Hèlǔ's later rebellion.
5 Fifth month,
Gēngzǐ.
Wáng Xuáncè, the Chief Clerk of the Right Wèilǜ (Palace Guard), attacked King Āluónàshùn of Dì'nàfúdì
and severely defeated him.
The ten Commander-in-Chief offices of the Eastern Palace
each had a Chief Clerk,
of the senior seventh rank.
The New Book writes
"Nàfúdì Āluónàshùn,"
without the character
"Wáng" (King).
Lǜ,
pronounced lǜ.
At first,
the king of Central Tiānzhú, Shīluóyìduō, had the strongest army,
and all four Tiānzhú kingdoms submitted to him.
The country of Tiānzhú
was the Shēndú kingdom of the Hàn dynasty.
It was also called Mógātuó
or Póluómén.
It was nine thousand six hundred *lǐ* from the capital,
located south of the Cōnglǐng Mountains,
with a circumference of thirty thousand *lǐ*.
It was divided into five Tiānzhú: Eastern, Western, Southern, Northern, and Central.
Southern Tiānzhú bordered the sea;
Northern Tiānzhú was near the snowy mountains;
Eastern Tiānzhú bordered the sea
and adjoined Fúnán and Línyì;
Western Tiānzhú adjoined Jìbīn and Bōsī;
Central Tiānzhú was at the junction of the four Tiānzhú.
Its capital city was called Chábóhéluó Chéng.
Dù Yòu said: Tiānzhú
is a Sāi tribe.
Yán Shīgǔ said: Sāi
means *shì*.
All these countries sent envoys to pay tribute.
When Shīluóyìduō died,
the country fell into great chaos.
His minister Āluónàshùn declared himself king
and sent Hú soldiers to attack Xuáncè.
Xuáncè, leading thirty followers, fought them.
They were no match
and were all captured.
Āluónàshùn plundered all the tribute items from the various countries.
Xuáncè escaped and fled during the night,
reaching the western border of Tǔbō.
He sent letters to summon soldiers from neighboring countries.
Tǔbō dispatched one thousand two hundred elite soldiers,
and Nípó Guó sent over seven thousand cavalry to assist him.
Nípóluó Guó was directly west of Tǔbō in Lèlíng Chuān,
and was a vassal of Tǔbō.
Tǔ,
from *tūn* in the entering tone.
Qí,
read *qí jì*.
After three days of continuous fighting,
they utterly defeated them,
beheading over three thousand people,
and nearly ten thousand drowned in the water.
Āluónàshùn abandoned the city and fled.
He then gathered his remaining forces
and returned to fight with Shīrén;
they were again defeated,
and Āluónàshùn was captured.
The remaining forces, supporting their ruler and the crown prince,
blocked the Gāntuówèi Jiāng.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* says: Kūnlún Shān,
which the Buddhists call Ānòudá Shān,
from its northeast corner issues the Hé Shuǐ,
which curves from its southeast to flow into Púchāng Hǎi.
From Púchāng Hǎi, it flows underground
and emerges south of Jīshí to become the river of China.
West of Kūnlún Shān,
a great river issues forth,
called the Xīntóu Hé,
which flows southwest through Wūcháng Guó,
then southeast through Zhōng Tiānzhú Guó,
also called the Héng Hé,
then west past the north of the four great stupas,
and then west past the north of Tuówèi Guó.
The so-called Gāntuówèi Jiāng is probably this one.
The enemy forces collapsed,
and their ruler and crown prince were captured,
along with twelve thousand men and women.
Thereupon, Tiānzhú was shaken,
and five hundred eighty-odd cities, towns, and settlements surrendered.
Āluónàshùn was brought back as a captive.
Xuáncè was appointed Cháosàndàfū.
Táng system: civil non-official rank Cháosàndàfū,
junior fifth rank, lower grade.
Cháo,
read *zhí yáo*.
Sàn,
read *xī dàn*.
6th month.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
the Báixī tribe was established as Jūyán Zhōu.
On the *guǐyǒu* day,
the Grand Master of Remonstrance Sòng Gōng Xiāo Yǔ passed away.
The Grand Court of Imperial Sacrifices proposed the posthumous title
"Dé" (Virtuous),
while the Department of State Affairs proposed
"Sù" (Reverent).
The posthumous title rules of Duke Zhōu state: "One of resolute virtue and successful achievements is called *Sù*."
Shì,
read *shí lì*.
"Posthumous titles
