are records of conduct;
one must obtain the truth of their actions,
so he can be posthumously called Zhēnbiǎn Gōng."
Hè Chēn's posthumous title rules state: "One who follows the straight path unyielding is called *Zhēn*;
one who is thrifty and without virtue is called *Biǎn*;
one with a narrow mind and harsh policies is called *Biǎn*."
The emperor had previously married Princess Xiāngchéng, the daughter of Xiāo Yǔ.
The emperor wanted to build a separate residence for her,
but the princess firmly declined,
saying:
"A wife serving her parents-in-law
should attend to them day and night.
If I were to live in a separate residence,
there would be many deficiencies."
The emperor then ordered that the residence be built within Xiāo Yǔ's estate.
The emperor, seeing that Gāolì was exhausted and weakened,
discussed launching an expedition next year with three hundred thousand troops
to conquer it in one fell swoop.
Some suggested that a large army campaigning eastward
would require provisions for a whole year,
which could not be carried by beasts of burden,
so ships and vessels should be prepared for water transport.
At the end of the Suí dynasty, Jiànnán alone was free from bandits and invaders.
Recently, during the Liáodōng campaign,
Jiànnán was again not involved,
and its people were wealthy.
It would be appropriate to have them build ships.
The emperor agreed.
Autumn,
7th month.
He dispatched Qiáng Wěi, the Chief Clerk of the Right and Left Guards of the Imperial Palace,
The Right and Left Guards of the Imperial Palace
were also divided into Left and Right,
each with a Chief Clerk.
These were the Left and Right Qiānniú Fǔ.
Qiáng,
read *qí liǎng*,
a surname.
(The ships) could be a hundred *chǐ* long,
and half that in width.
He separately sent envoys to survey waterways,
from Wū Xiá to Jiāng and Yáng,
heading towards Láizhōu.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Qūlìchuò, the prime minister of Western Tūjué, requested to lead his subordinate tribes to attack Qūcí.
At first,
Lǐ Jūnxiàn, Duke of Wǔlián County and General of the Left Wǔwèi Guard, was stationed at Xuánwǔ Mén.
Wǔlián County at that time belonged to Shǐ Zhōu;
Shǐ Zhōu was later renamed Jiàn Zhōu.
Wǔ'ān County,
in Hàn belonged to Wèi Jùn,
in Jìn to Guǎngpíng Jùn,
in Later Zhōu and Suí to Míng Zhōu.
The Generals of the Left and Right Wǔwèi Guards were generals of the Southern Yamēn guards;
being stationed at Xuánwǔ Mén
meant being in charge of guarding the Northern Gate.
The grand astrologer divined, saying:
"A female ruler will prosper."
There was also a secret prophecy circulating among the populace, saying:
"After three generations of Táng,
a female Wǔ king will possess the empire."
The emperor disliked this.
One day, during a banquet with his military officials in the palace,
they played a drinking game.
In a drinking game,
one person acts as the *lìngbó*,
and the others follow in turn.
The text below where they each state their nicknames
refers to this drinking game.
Jūnxiàn declared his nickname was Wǔniáng.
The emperor was startled,
then laughed and said:
"What kind of woman
is so brave and strong!"
Furthermore, because Jūnxiàn's official title and feudal domain both contained the character
"Wǔ,"
the emperor intensely disliked him,
and later sent him out as the Prefect of Huá Zhōu.
There was a commoner named Yuán Dàoxìn,
who claimed to be able to abstain from food
and understood Buddhist teachings.
Jūnxiàn deeply respected and trusted him,
and frequently met with him,
speaking privately.
An imperial censor reported that Jūnxiàn was colluding with a sorcerer
and plotting rebellion.
On the *rénchén* day,
Jūnxiàn was executed,
and his family property was confiscated.
The Emperor secretly asked the Grand Astrologer, Lǐ Chúnfēng:
"Are the prophecies mentioned in the secret texts
truly real?"
He replied:
"Your servant, having observed the celestial phenomena above,
and studied the calendar and computations below,
can confirm that this person is already in Your Majesty's palace,
and is a close relative.
From now, in no more than thirty years,
she will rule the world,
and almost all of the Táng descendants will be killed.
The signs are already established."
The Emperor said:
"What if we kill all those who seem to fit the description?"
Lǐ Chúnfēng replied:
"What is decreed by Heaven
cannot be defied by man.
The sovereign will not die,
and you would only kill many innocents in vain.
Furthermore, from now on, in thirty years,
that person will be old,
and it is hoped that she will have some compassion,
making the disaster perhaps less severe.
If we were to capture and kill her now,
Heaven might instead raise a vigorous person who would unleash their bitter resentment,
and I fear that Your Majesty's descendants
would have no survivors!"
The Emperor then stopped the plan.
The Grand Minister of Works, Liáng Wénzhāo Gōng Fáng Xuánlíng, who was left to guard the capital,
became critically ill.
The Emperor summoned him to Yùhuá Palace.
He was carried in a shoulder-borne litter into the hall,
and only disembarked beside the imperial throne.
They wept together.
He was then kept at the palace.
When the Emperor heard he was slightly better, joy showed on his face;
when he worsened, the Emperor became worried and gaunt.
Fáng Xuánlíng told his sons:
"I have received great kindness from the Emperor.
Now the world is at peace,
except for the ongoing eastern expedition.
All the ministers dare not remonstrate.
If I know this and do not speak,
I will have an unforgivable fault even in death."
He then submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Lǎozi said: 'Knowing contentment avoids humiliation;
knowing when to stop avoids danger.'
Your Majesty's achievements, fame, power, and virtue are sufficient.
Expanding territory and opening frontiers can now cease.
Furthermore, whenever Your Majesty decides on a serious criminal case,
you invariably order three reviews and five reports,
eat plain meals,
and stop music.
(Seen in 193 scrolls, 5 years.)
Now you drive innocent soldiers
to face the blade,
causing their brains and guts to be splattered on the ground.
Is this not uniquely lamentable?
Careful and cautious use of punishment
shows the importance of human life.
Eagerly using military force
forgets the importance of human life.
(Comparing that with this,
Fáng Xuánlíng's words can be said to be profound, incisive, and clear.)
If they are causing harm, they may be punished.
If they are harassing the people,
they may be annihilated.
If in the future they could become a threat to Zhōngguó,
they may be eliminated.
But now, without these three conditions, to vex Zhōngguó
internally to wipe out the shame of previous generations,
and externally to avenge Xīnluó,
is this not valuing the trivial
and suffering a great loss?
(Speaking of this,
it is clearly seen that Gāolì need not be conquered.
Among the ministers at court at that time who remonstrated against the eastern expedition,
none could match this.
This flowed from his loyalty and earnestness.)
pronounced yú wěi.) Burning the ships at Língbō
and disbanding the recruited troops
will naturally bring joy and reliance to Huá and Yí,
bringing peace to distant lands and stability to nearby ones.
Your servant will soon be in the grave.
If I may be granted the recording of this mournful plea—
(The Analects: Zēngzǐ was ill,
Mèng Jìngzǐ visited him.
Zēngzǐ said:
'When a bird is about to die,
its cries are mournful;
when a man is about to die,
his words are good.')
Fáng Xuánlíng's son Yí'ài was married to the Emperor's daughter, Gāoyáng Gōngzhǔ.
The Emperor said to the princess:
"He is so critically ill,
yet he can still worry about our country."
The Emperor personally visited him,
held his hand to bid farewell,
and was overwhelmed with grief.
On the day of Guǐmǎo,
he passed away.
Liǔ Fāng commented: Fáng Xuánlíng assisted Tàizōng in pacifying the empire.
And until the end of his time as prime minister,
for a total of thirty-two years,
he was known throughout the world as a worthy prime minister;
yet there were no visible traces of his deeds,
his virtue was indeed paramount.
Therefore, when Tàizōng settled chaos and disorder, Fáng and Dù did not claim credit.
When Wáng and Wèi were good at remonstrating, Fáng and Dù deferred to their wisdom.
When Yīng and Wèi were skilled commanders, Fáng and Dù followed their path.
(Xīn Zàn wrote
"Fáng and Dù complemented with culture.")
pronounced jí liàng.)
They attributed good deeds to the sovereign.
To be a loyal minister of Táng,
how fitting!
In the eighth month,
on the first day, Jǐyǒu,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the day of Dīngchǒu,
an imperial edict ordered the Yuèzhōu Military Command and Wù, Hóng, and other prefectures to build 1,100 warships and double-hulled boats.
(Dōngyáng Commandery,
during the Suí's pacification of Chén,
Wùzhōu was established.)
pronounced fǔ wàng.)
pronounced sū zāo.)
On the day of Xīnwèi,
Zhíshī Sīlì, Grand General of the Left Guards, was sent out through Jīnshān Pass to attack the remaining bandits of Xuēyántuó.
In the ninth month,
on the day of Gēngchén,
Āshǐnà Shè'ěr, Grand Commander of the Kūnqiūdao Expeditionary Army, attacked Chùyuè and Chùmì,
defeated them,
and all their remaining forces surrendered.
On the day of Guǐwèi,
Xuē Wànchè and others returned from campaigning against Gāolì.
Wànchè, while in the army,
was arrogant and overbearing.
Péi Xíngfāng reported his resentment and disaffection,
for which he was stripped of his rank
and exiled to Xiàngzhōu.
(Péi Xíngfāng was Xuē Wànchè's deputy in the eastern campaign,
as seen in the previous scroll, last year.)
(Xiàngzhōu,
the land of Tánzhōng Zhōngliú County in the Hàn dynasty.
In the Suí, it was Guìlín County of Shǐ'ān Commandery.
In the Táng, Wǔdé 4th year,
Xiàngzhōu Guìlín Commandery was established,
named after Xiàngshān.)
On the day of Jǐchǒu,
Xīnluó reported being attacked by Bǎijì,
who captured thirteen of their cities.
On the day of Jǐhài,
Chǔ Suìliáng, Attendant Secretary of the Yellow Gate, was appointed Chancellor of the Central Secretariat.
Qiáng Wěi and others levied commoners to build ships,
the corvée extending to the mountain tribes.
The tribes of Yǎ, Qióng, and Méi three prefectures rebelled.
On the day of Rén'yín,
Zhāng Shìguì, Governor of Màozhōu, and Liáng Jiànfāng, General of the Right Guards, were sent with over 20,000 troops from Lǒngyòu and Xiázhōng to attack them.
The people of Shǔ suffered from the ship-building corvée.
Some begged to pay money to hire people from Tánzhōu to build ships;
the Emperor permitted this.
Prefectural and county officials pressed them severely,
so much so that people sold their fields and houses, and even their children, yet could not meet the demands.
Grain prices soared,
causing unrest throughout Jiànwài.
(South of Jiànmén Pass is called Jiànwài,
similar to how inside the capital is 'inside' and outside is 'all the Zhūxià'.)
Chángsūn Zhīrén, Vice Minister of Agriculture, was sent by express courier to inspect.
Zhīrén reported:
"The people of Shǔ are weak
and cannot endure such arduous labor.
One large ship costs 2,236 rolls of silk in labor wages.
The timber already felled in the mountains
has not yet been fully dragged out,
and now ship wages are being levied again.
These two matters combined
are unbearable for the people.
It is advisable to show them greater care."
The Emperor then decreed that all ship wages in Tánzhōu should be paid by the government.
In winter,
tenth month,
on the day of Guǐchǒu,
the imperial carriage returned to the capital.
The 21st year. Wū-Hé (烏紇), the nephew of Tú-Mí-Dù (吐迷度) of the Huí-Hé (回紇), married his aunt (Tú-Mí-Dù's wife).
Wū-Hé and Jù-Lù-Mò-Hè-Dá-Guān (俱陸莫賀達官) Jù-Luó-Bó (俱羅勃)
were both sons-in-law of Qí-Bì Kè-Hán (車鼻可汗) of the Tū-Juē (突厥).
They conspired to kill Tú-Mí-Dù and return to Qí-Bì.
At night, Wū-Hé led more than ten cavalrymen to attack Tú-Mí-Dù,
and killed him.
Yuán Lǐ-Chén (元禮臣), the Deputy Protector-General of Yàn-Rán (燕然), sent someone to entice Wū-Hé,
promising to recommend him as the Protector-General of Hàn-Hǎi (瀚海).
Wū-Hé, with light cavalry, went to Lǐ-Chén to express his gratitude.
Lǐ-Chén seized and executed him,
and reported it.
The Emperor, fearing the dispersion of the Huí-Hé tribes,
dispatched Cuī Dūn-Lǐ (崔敦禮), the Minister of Personnel, to pacify them.
After a long time,
Jù-Luó-Bó came to see the Emperor,
who kept him and did not send him back.
The Huí-Hé consequently weakened again.
見,
賢遍翻.
The 22nd year. Ā-Shǐ-Nà Shè-Ěr (阿史那社爾), having defeated Chǔ-Yuè (處月) and Chǔ-Mì (處密),
led his troops from west of Yān-Qí (焉耆) towards the northern border of Qū-Cí (龜茲).
He divided his forces into five routes,
striking unexpectedly.
Xuē-Pó-Ā-Nà-Zhī (薛婆阿那支), the King of Yān-Qí, abandoned his city and fled to Qū-Cí,
defending its eastern border.
Shè-Ěr sent troops to pursue and attack him,
capturing and executing him.
(In) the 16th year,
Guō Xiào-Kè (郭孝恪) defeated Yān-Qí
and enthroned Lì-Pó-Zhǔn (栗婆準) as king.
However, Ā-Nà-Zhī killed him.
Now, the criminal is captured.
The New Book says: Lì-Pó-Zhǔn's younger brother Pó-Gā-Lì (婆伽利) was enthroned as king.
This follows the Old Book.
從,
才用翻.
Qū-Cí was greatly alarmed,
and most of its defending generals abandoned their cities and fled.
Shè-Ěr advanced and encamped at Qì-Kǒu (磧口),
three hundred *lǐ* from its capital city.
"Qì-Kǒu" (磧口),
in the Old and New Books, is written as
"Qì-Shí" (磧石).
The capital of Qū-Cí was the city of Yī-Luó-Lú (伊邏盧),
which relied on Bái-Shān (白山) to its north,
also called Ā-Jié-Tián-Shān (阿羯田山).
將,
即亮翻.
磧,
七迹翻.
Cáo Jì-Shú (曹繼叔), the Right Guard General, was next in command.
Arriving at Duō-Hè-Chéng (多褐城),
Hē-Lì-Bù-Shī-Bì (訶利布失畢), the King of Qū-Cí, and his chief ministers Nà-Lì (那利) and Jié-Liè-Diān (羯獵顛), led fifty thousand troops to resist the attack.
As soon as the blades met,
Wēi (威) led his troops in a feigned retreat.
Qū-Cí pursued with all its forces,
marching thirty *lǐ*,
where they met Jì-Shú's army.
Qū-Cí was frightened
and was about to retreat.
Jì-Shú pressed the attack,
and Qū-Cí suffered a great defeat,
pursued for eighty *lǐ*.
The 23rd year, on the *Jiǎ-Xū* (甲戌) day.
Pó-Rùn (婆閏), son of Tú-Mí-Dù of the Huí-Hé and former General of the Left Tun-Wèi, was appointed General of the Left Xiāo-Wèi, Grand Sī-Lì-Fā, and Protector-General of Hàn-Hǎi.
The 24th year, in the eleventh month.
On the *Gēng-Zǐ* (庚子) day.
Kū-Gē (窟哥), leader of the Qì-Dān (契丹), and Kě-Dù-Zhě (可度者), leader of the Xī (奚), both led their respective tribes to submit to the Tang court.
The Qì-Dān tribe was established as Sōng-Mò Fǔ (松漠府).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: The land of Sōng-Mò
is north of Liǔ-Chéng (柳城) Commandery.
Also, their separate leaders, Dá-Jī (達稽) and others, were made into Qiao-Luò (峭落) and other nine prefectures,
each with its Rǔ-Hé (辱紇) chief as *Cì-Shǐ* (刺史).

Qiao-Luò Zhōu (峭落州), Wú-Féng Zhōu (無逢州), Yǔ-Líng Zhōu (羽陵州), Bái-Lián Zhōu (白連州), Tú-Hé Zhōu (徒何州), Wàn-Dān Zhōu (萬丹州), Pǐ-Lí Zhōu (疋黎州), Chì-Shān Zhōu (赤山州), and Sōng-Mò Fǔ (松漠府) formed the nine prefectures.
峭,
七笑翻.
Kě-Dù-Zhě was appointed as a Protector-General;
also, his separate leaders Ā-Huì (阿會) and others were made into Ruò-Shuǐ (弱水) and other five prefectures,
each also with its Rǔ-Hé chief as *Cì-Shǐ*.
Ruò-Shuǐ Zhōu (弱水州), Qí-Lí Zhōu (祁黎州), Luò-Huái Zhōu (洛⿰王褱州), Tài-Lǔ Zhōu (太魯州), Kě-Yě Zhōu (渴野州).
On the *Xīn-Chǒu* (辛丑) day,
the office of Eastern Yi Commandant was established in Yíng-Zhōu (營州).
The 25th year, in the twelfth month.
On the *Gēng-Wǔ* (庚午) day.
The Grand Prince completed the construction of Dà-Cí-Ēn Sì (大慈恩寺) for Empress Wén-Dé (文德).
The Xī-Jīng Zá-Jì (西京雜記) says: In the outer city of Xī-Jīng (西京), the third bridge east of Zhū-Què Jiē (朱雀街), the first street east of the Imperial City is Jìn-Yè Fāng (進業坊),
the old site of the Suí dynasty's Wú-Lòu Sì (無漏寺).
The Grand Prince built the temple on this site
to pray for Empress Wén-Dé.
The bamboos and trees were deep and secluded,
making it the most popular sightseeing spot in the capital.
The Yōng-Lù (雍錄) says: Cí-Ēn Sì (慈恩寺) is on the third street east of Zhū-Què Jiē (朱雀街),
the fifteenth *fāng* from north to south,
named Jìn-Chāng Fāng (進昌坊).
The temple faces the Huáng-Qú (黃渠) to the south,
with deep and secluded bamboos and trees.
為,
于偽翻.
The 26th year. After the defeat of King Bù-Shī-Bì (布失畢) of Qū-Cí,
he fled and defended the capital city.
Ā-Shǐ-Nà Shè-Ěr advanced and pressured it.
Bù-Shī-Bì, with light cavalry, fled west.
Shè-Ěr captured his city
and made Guō Xiào-Kè (郭孝恪), the Protector-General of Ān-Xī (安西), defend it.
Sū Hǎi-Zhèng (蘇海政), the *Cì-Shǐ* of Shā-Zhōu (沙州), and Xuē Wàn-Bèi (薛萬備), the *Shàng-Niǎn Fèng-Yù*, led elite cavalry to pursue Bù-Shī-Bì.
After marching six hundred *lǐ*,
Bù-Shī-Bì, in desperation,
defended Bō-Huàn Chéng (撥換城).
From the Ān-Xī Protectorate, he went west through Zhè-Juē Guān (柘厥關),
crossed the Bái-Mǎ Hé (白馬河) for over four hundred *lǐ* to reach Bō-Huàn Chéng.
騎,
奇寄翻.
帥,
讀曰率;
下同.
In the intercalary month,
on the *Dīng-Chǒu* (丁丑) day,
it was captured,
and Bù-Shī-Bì and Jié-Liè-Diān (羯獵顛) were captured.
Nà-Lì (那利) escaped and fled,
secretly leading the forces of the Western Tū-Juē, along with his national troops, numbering over ten thousand,
to attack Xiào-Kè.
Xiào-Kè was encamped outside the city.
Some Qū-Cí people informed him,
but Xiào-Kè did not pay attention.
Nà-Lì arrived suddenly.
Xiào-Kè led his thousand-plus men to enter the city,
but Nà-Lì's forces had already scaled the walls.
The surrendered Hu (胡) people inside the city colluded with them
and jointly attacked Xiào-Kè.
Arrows and blades rained down like showers.
Xiào-Kè could not resist,
and as he was about to retreat,
he died at the west gate.
There was great chaos in the city.
Cuī Yì-Chāo (崔義超), the *Cāng-Bù Láng-Zhōng*,
*Cāng-Bù Láng* (倉部郎),
was in charge of managing all granaries,
receiving taxes,
and issuing stipends.
It belonged to the Ministry of Revenue.
Yì-Chāo served in the army with this official title.
He defended military supplies and provisions,
and fought against Qū-Cí in the city.
Cáo Jì-Shú (曹繼叔) and Hán Wēi (韓威) also encamped outside the city
and attacked from the northwest corner of the city.
Nà-Lì retreated after a night,
with over three thousand heads taken.
The city finally stabilized.
After more than ten days,
Nà-Lì again led over ten thousand Qū-Cí people from north of the mountains towards the capital city.
North of the mountains,
it refers to the north of Bái-Shān (白山).
趣,
七喻翻.
He was greatly defeated,
with eight thousand heads taken.
Nà-Lì fled alone on horseback.
The Qū-Cí people captured him
and presented him at the army gate.
Ā-Shǐ-Nà Shè-Ěr successively captured five of their major cities.
He dispatched Quán Zhī-Fǔ (權祗甫), the *Láng-Jiàng* of the Left Guard, to various cities
to explain the consequences of resistance and the benefits of submission.
All surrendered, leading each other.
In total, over seven hundred cities were obtained,
and tens of thousands of captive men and women.
Shè-Ěr then summoned their elders,
proclaimed the might and authority of the nation,
and explained the intention of punishing the guilty.
He enthroned the King's younger brother, Yè-Hù (葉護), as King;
the Qū-Cí people were greatly pleased.
The Western Regions were shocked and alarmed.
The Western Tū-Juē, Yú-Tián (于闐), and Ān-Guó (安國) vied to offer camels, horses, and military provisions.
Shè-Ěr carved a stone inscription to record his achievements and then returned.
The 27th year, on the *Wù-Yín* (戊寅) day.
Ā-Shǐ-Nà Hè-Lǔ (阿史那賀魯), the Commander-in-Chief of the Kūn-Qiū (崑丘) Expeditionary Army and General of the Left Xiāo-Wèi, was appointed Ní-Fú-Shā-Bó-Luó Yè-Hù (泥伏沙鉢羅葉護),
bestowed with a drum and banner,
and tasked with subduing the unsubdued of the Western Tū-Juē.
Giving Hè-Lǔ wings would only hasten his rebellion.
正速其叛耳.
驍,
堅堯翻.
纛,
徒到翻.
The 28th year, on the *Guǐ-Wèi* (癸未) day.
Jīn Chūn-Qiū (金春秋), the Chief Minister of Xīn-Luó (新羅), and his son Wén-Wáng (文王) came to meet the Emperor.
Chūn-Qiū was the younger brother of Zhēn-Dé (真德).
The Emperor appointed Chūn-Qiū as *Tè-Jìn*,
and Wén-Wáng as General of the Left Wǔ-Wèi.
Chūn-Qiū requested to change their robes and caps to follow the Chinese style.
The Emperor then brought out winter clothes from the palace and bestowed them upon him.
1 Spring.
First month.
On the *xīnhài* day,
Bùshībì (King of Qiūcí) and his chancellor Nàlì, among others, arrived at the capital.
The Emperor reprimanded them but then released them,
appointing Bùshībì as Left Commandant-in-chief of the Martial Guard.
2 The Mòzhī and other Man barbarians from the southwest submitted,
and their territory was organized into four prefectures: Bàng, Wàng, Lǎn, and Qiū,
subordinate to the Lángzhōu Protectorate-general.
The Mòzhī Man barbarians were to the west of the Cuàn Man barbarians.
"Lángzhōu"
should be
"Lángzhōu".
In the first year of Wǔdé,
the Nánzhōng region was opened up,
and Nánníngzhōu was re-established.
In the eighth year of Zhēngguān,
it was renamed Lángzhōu,
as its territory was originally the state of Yèláng.
3 As the Emperor Chēbí Kèhán of the Tujue did not come to court,
the Emperor dispatched Gāo Kǎn, Commandant-in-chief of the Right Agile Guard, to lead troops from the Huíhét, Púgǔ, and other tribes to attack him.
When the troops entered his territory,
the various tribes successively came to surrender.
Tǔdūn Féiluóchá of the Báxīmì surrendered,
and his territory was established as Xīnlízhōu.
The old histories state: Chēbí's eldest son, Jiémàntuó,
who formerly governed the Báxīmì tribe,
sent his son Ānshuò to court.
The Emperor praised him
and established Xīnlízhōu for him.
朝,
pronounced *zhí yáo fān*.
降,
pronounced *hù jiāng fān*.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Gāozōng Shílù* states:
"Initially,
Chēbí Kèhán of the Tujue sent his son Chēbōluó to pay tribute.
Tàizōng sent an envoy to summon him,
but he did not come.
Tàizōng was furious,
and dispatched Gāo Kǎn, Commandant-in-chief of the Right Agile Guard, to lead troops from the Huíhét, Púgǔ, and other tribes to attack him.
His subordinate tribes successively came to surrender.
His son Jiémàntuó, who formerly governed the Báxīmì tribe,
wept and advised his father,
pleading to return to the state;
Chēbí did not listen.
Jiémàntuó then rebelled against his father and came to surrender,
and his territory was established as Xīnlízhōu."
The old biographies state:
"In the twenty-third year,
Gāo Kǎn, Commandant-in-chief of the Right Agile Guard, was secretly dispatched to lead troops from the Huíhét, Púgǔ, and other tribes to attack him.
Their chieftains, Gēluólù Nízhí Quēsìlìfā, Nǎibásèfú, Chǔmùkūn, Mòhèduōsìjīn, and others,
led their tribes,
rebelled against Chēbí,
and successively came to surrender.
Chēbí's eldest son Jiémàntuó, who formerly governed the Báxīmì tribe,
before Chēbí was defeated,
sent his son Ānshuò to court.
Tàizōng praised him,
appointed him General of the Left Tun Guard,
and re-established Xīnlízhōu to govern his people."
Now we follow the *Tàizōng Shílù*.
4 Second month.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
the Yáochí Protectorate-general was established.
This was named after the story in the *Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn* where the Queen Mother of the West feasted King Mù by the Yáochí Pool.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
Āshǐnà Hèlǔ, General of the Left Guard, was appointed Protector-general of Yáochí.
5 Third month.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
the Fēngzhōu Protectorate-general was established,
and Lǐ Sùlì, Protector-general of Yànrán, concurrently served as Protector-general.
6 The drought of last winter
finally ended with rain.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
the Emperor, despite his illness, went outside the Xiǎndào Gate
and granted a general amnesty.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
the Crown Prince was ordered to attend to government affairs at the Jīnyè Gate.
According to the *Táng Liùdiǎn*: The City Gate Supervisors were in charge of the gates of the capital city, the imperial city, and the palaces.
The Míngdé and other gates were city gates;
the Zhūquè and other gates were imperial city gates;
the Chéngtiān and other gates were palace city gates;
the Jiādé and other gates were palace gates;
the Tàijí and other gates were hall gates.
All gates leading to the interior
were similar to the Shànggémén.
Were Xiǎndào and Jīnyè
also gates leading to the interior?
The maps and gazetteers could not record them all.
7 Summer.
Fourth month.
On the *yǐhài* day,
the Emperor travelled to Cuìwēi Palace.
8 The Emperor said to the Crown Prince:
"Lǐ Shìjì has abundant talent and wisdom,
but you have no personal favor with him,
so I fear you cannot win his submission.
I shall now demote him.
If he departs immediately,
after my death,
you shall appoint him Grand Councilor,
and trust him closely.
If he hesitates and looks back,
then you must kill him."
Fifth month.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
Lǐ Shìjì, who was concurrently Third Rank Official of the Central Secretariat and Chancellery, was made Protector-general of Diézhōu;
Shìjì received the edict
and left without going home.
Historians say that Tàizōng used stratagems to control Lǐ Shìjì,
and Shìjì also served his sovereign with cunning.
Dù Yòu said: Diézhōu is 1,340 *lǐ* from the capital.
Sūn Miǎn said: From Qin to Wei,
various Qiāng tribes occupied Diézhōu.
Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu expelled the Qiāng tribes
and then established Diézhōu,
naming it after the overlapping mountains.
9 On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Lǐ Jìng, Kaīfǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Duke Jǐngwǔ of Wèi, passed away.
10 The Emperor's illness worsened,
and the Crown Prince stayed by his side day and night,
sometimes not eating for several days,
his hair even turning white.
The Emperor wept, saying:
"You are so filial and loving;
what regret could I have in death!"
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
as his illness became critical,
Chángsūn Wújí was summoned into the Hánfēng Hall.
The Hánfēng Hall
was in the Cuìwēi Palace.
The Emperor reached out and stroked Wújí's chin.
Wújí cried,
overwhelmed with grief;
the Emperor was unable to say anything,
and then ordered Wújí to leave.
On the *jǐsì* day,
Wújí and Chǔ Suìliáng were again summoned into the imperial bedchamber.
The Emperor said to them:
"I now entrust all future affairs to you, my lords.
The Crown Prince is benevolent and filial,
as you all know;
guide him well!"
He said to the Crown Prince:
"With Wújí and Suìliáng here,
you need not worry about the world!"
He further said to Suìliáng:
"Wújí has been utterly loyal to me;
my possession of the world
is largely due to his efforts.
After my death,
do not let slanderous people alienate him."
He then ordered Suìliáng to draft his dying edict.
Shortly after,
the Emperor passed away.
He was fifty-three years old.
The Crown Prince embraced Wújí's neck,
wailing almost to the point of collapse.
Wújí, wiping away tears,
requested to arrange all matters to stabilize the internal and external situation.
The Crown Prince continued to mourn inconsolably.
Wújí said:
"His Majesty entrusted the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain to Your Highness;
how can you merely weep like a common man!"
Thus, the news of the Emperor's death was kept secret.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
Wújí and others requested the Crown Prince to return first,
accompanied by flying cavalry, elite soldiers, and veteran generals.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
the Crown Prince entered the capital city;
the Grand Emperor's imperial palanquin,
with guards as on ordinary days,
followed the Crown Prince and arrived,
stopping at the Liǎngyí Hall.
Yú Zhìníng, Left Chief Clerk to the Crown Prince, was appointed Grand Councilor.
Zhāng Xíngchéng, Minor Supervisor of the Household of the Crown Prince, concurrently served as Grand Councilor.
Gāo Jìfǔ, Acting Minister of Personnel, Right Chief Clerk, and concurrently Vice Minister of Personnel, was concurrently appointed Chief Minister of the Central Secretariat.
On the *rénshēn* day,
the Emperor's death was announced at the Tàijí Hall,
the dying edict was proclaimed,
and the Crown Prince ascended the throne.
The Tàijí Hall,
the main court of the Western Palace,
was where the death was announced,
and the Crown Prince ascended the throne before the coffin.
No delays were permitted;
ordinary minor affairs
were delegated to the responsible officials.
All kings serving as Protector-generals or Prefects
were permitted to attend the funeral rites,
except for Pú Wáng Tài.
The campaign in Liaodong and all construction projects were halted.
Hundreds of people from the Four Barbarian tribes who served at court or came to pay tribute,
upon hearing the news of the death, all wailed,
cut their hair, gashed their faces, and cut their ears,
their blood spilling onto the ground.
In the sixth month,
on the *jiǎxū* day,
Gāozōng ascended the throne
and granted a general amnesty to the empire.
On the 11th, *dīngchǒu* day,
Lǐ Jì, the Dudū of Diézhōu, was appointed Tèjìn, Jiǎnjiào Luòzhōu Cìshǐ, and Luòyáng Gōng Liúshǒu.
Lǐ Shìjì removed
the character "Shì"
to avoid
offending Tàizōng's personal name.
The character "shǒu"
is also pronounced "shòu" (in some contexts).
Previously,
Tàizōng's personal name
was not to be avoided by those who did not use it in combination with other characters;
now,
however, officials whose names offended the late emperor's taboo name were changed.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: In the Qūlǐ,
the taboo is observed after the final wailing.
The commentary says: It is out of respect for the names of ghosts and spirits.
To taboo
is to avoid.
The living do not avoid each other's names.
The Marquis of Wèi was named È,
and a Dàfū was also named È.
The lord and his minister shared the same name,
and the Chūnqiū does not condemn it.
According to Zhāo 7th year,
the Marquis of Wèi, È, died.
The Gǔliáng Zhuàn says: In Zhāo 1st year, there was Wèi Qí È.
Why is the Marquis of Wèi È mentioned now?
This means that a lord and his minister had the same name,
and a *jūnzǐ* does not usurp a name given by another's parents.
On the 13th, *guǐwèi* day,
Zhǎngsūn WúJì was appointed Tàiwèi,
concurrently Jiǎnjiào Zhōngshū Lìng,
and he was to oversee the affairs of the Shàngshū and Ménxià two departments.
WúJì firmly declined to oversee the affairs of the Shàngshū department.
The emperor granted his request,
and further ordered that as Tàiwèi, he would be accorded the rank equivalent to Sān Pǐn of Zhōngshū and Ménxià.
According to Táng regulations, the Sān Gōng were of the first rank.
Since WúJì was already Tàiwèi,
to order him to be equivalent to Sān Pǐn of Zhōngshū and Ménxià
was an error in the court's deliberation at the time.
On the *guǐsì* day,
Lǐ Jì was appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and concurrently Sān Pǐn of Zhōngshū and Ménxià.
When Āshǐnà Shè'ěr broke Qūcí,
the Xíngjūn Zhǎngshǐ Xuē Wànbèi requested to use the military might to persuade the King of Yútián, Fúshéxìn, to pay homage to the court.
Shè'ěr agreed.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the *jǐyǒu* day,
Fúshéxìn followed Wànbèi to the court.
An imperial edict ordered him to pay respects at the imperial coffin.
In the eighth month,
on the *guǐyǒu* day,
at night,
an earthquake occurred.
Jìnzhōu was especially affected,
and more than five thousand people were crushed to death.
On the 16th, *gēngyín* day,
Emperor Wén was buried in Zhāolíng.
Zhāolíng is located sixty *lǐ* northwest of Lǐquán Xiàn, Jīngzhào, on Jiǔzōng Shān.
After Táng Tàizōng,
ministers and sons generally referred to their lord by his miàohào.
Is this not because children, subjects, and common people also felt that his shìhào were too numerous and not factual,
and that the ancient meaning of "ancestors having merit and patriarchs having virtue" was fading?
The emperor sent someone to convey his predecessor's intention not to allow it.
Fourteen leaders of barbarian tribes, such as Xiélì, who had been captured and subdued by the late emperor,
all had their images carved in stone
with their names inscribed and placed inside the Běisīmǎ Mén.
On the 17th, *dīngyǒu* day,
Lǐbù Shàngshū Xǔ Jìngzōng proposed that the shrine of Hóngnóng Fǔjūn should be demolished.
Hóngnóng Fǔjūn
was Chóng'ěr, the Tàishǒu of Hóngnóng during the Wèi dynasty,
and was Gāozōng's seventh-generation ancestor.
The close relationship having ended, the shrine should be demolished.
The emperor agreed.
The Tàimiào had east and west side chambers,
flanking the main chamber on both sides,
hence they were called side chambers.
In the ninth month,
on the *yǐmǎo* day,
Lǐ Jì was appointed Zuǒ Púshè.
This was to carry out the late emperor's administrative decree.
In winter,
the tenth month,
the various Tūjué tribes were organized into five prefectures, such as Shèlì, subordinate to the Yúnzhōng Dūdūfǔ.
The five prefectures were Shèlìzhōu, Sīpìzhōu, Āshǐnàzhōu, Chuòzhōu, and Báidēngzhōu.
The history only records Sūnóngzhōu, Ādézhōu, Zhíshīzhōu, and Báyánzhōu;
the other two prefectures are missing.
On the 20th, *yǐhài* day,
the emperor asked Dàlǐ Qīng Táng Lín about the number of prisoners.
He replied:
"There are currently fifty-odd prisoners,
only two of whom deserve death."
The emperor was pleased.
The emperor once reviewed prisoners.
Many sentenced by the former minister cried out claiming injustice,
while those sentenced by Lín were uniquely silent.
The emperor, surprised, asked the reason.
A prisoner said:
"Those sentenced by Minister Táng
are inherently without injustice."
The emperor sighed for a long time,
saying:
"A judge should be like this, shouldn't he!"
The emperor appointed Zānpǔ Nòngzàn of Tǔbō as Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn established three Dūwèi:
Fèngchē Dūwèi,
Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
and Qí Dūwèi.
During the Táng, Qí Dūwèi became an honorary official title,
Fùmǎ Dūwèi was bestowed upon those who married princesses,
and Fèngchē Dūwèi was no longer appointed.
The Zānpǔ wrote to Zhǎngsūn WúJì and others, saying:
"The Son of Heaven has just ascended the throne.
If there are disloyal subjects, I shall lead troops to your country to suppress and eliminate them."
Tǔbō, upon Tàizōng's death,
already harbored intentions of underestimating the Middle Kingdom.
In the twelfth month,
an edict ordered Púwáng Tài to establish an official residence and retain officials,
and his carriages, clothing, and precious foods
were to be given exceptional preferential treatment.
Gāozōng Tiānhuáng Dàshèng Dàhóngxiào Huángdì Shàngzhīshàng
His personal name was Zhì,
his courtesy name Wéishàn,
and his childhood name Zhìnú.
He was Tàizōng's ninth son.
In the first year of Wénmíng,
he was given the posthumous title Tiānhuáng Dàdì,
and his temple name was Gāozōng;
in the eighth year of Tiānbǎo,
he was granted the honorific title Gāozōng Tiānhuáng Dàshèng Huángdì;
in the thirteenth year,
he was granted the honorific title Gāozōng Tiānhuáng Dàshèng Dàhóngxiào Huángdì.
The first year of Yǒnghuī
(*gēngxū*, 650 CE)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the *xīnchǒu* day,
the era name was changed.
2. On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Empress Wáng was established.
The Empress
was the granddaughter of Sīzhèng.
Wáng Sīzhèng, while defending Yǐngchuān for Western Wèi,
was captured by Eastern Wèi.
3. On the *jǐwèi* day,
Zhāng Xíngchéng was appointed Shìzhōng.
4. On the *xīnyǒu* day,
the emperor summoned the court assembly envoys
and said:
"I have just ascended the throne.
All matters inconvenient to the people should be fully presented.
If not fully presented, seal and resubmit your memorial."
From then on, ten Cìshǐ were summoned daily into the inner chamber
to be asked about the hardships of the people
and their governance.
A man from Luòyáng, Lǐ Hóngtài, falsely accused Zhǎngsūn WúJì of plotting rebellion.
The emperor ordered his immediate execution.
WúJì and Chǔ Suìliáng worked together to assist in governance.
The emperor also respected them both,
humbly listening to them.
Considering the emperor's trust and reliance on the two in such a manner,
Empress Wǔ slandered and removed them,
yet she did not regret even if it meant falling into an abyss.
The transformation of wise women into owls and kites has long been so.
The people were prosperous and peaceful,
displaying remnants of the Zhēngguān era's spirit.
5. Tàizōng's daughter, Princess Héngshān, was to marry a member of the Zhǎngsūn clan.
The officials believed that since the period of public mourning had ended,
the marriage could take place in the autumn of that year.
Yú Zhìníng memorialized, saying:
"Emperor Wén of Hàn established regulations
primarily for the benefit of the people of the empire.
The princess's mourning attire was originally *zhǎncuī*.
Even if the mourning period is removed according to custom,
how can her feelings be changed according to custom?
I request that the marriage await the completion of the three-year mourning period."
The emperor agreed.
6. In the second month,
on the *xīnmǎo* day,
Imperial Prince Xiào was enfeoffed as Xǔwáng,
Shàngjīn as Wáng,
and Sùjié as Yōngwáng.
Emperor's concubine Zhèng gave birth to Xiào;
Yáng gave birth to Shàngjīn;
and Xiāo Shúfēi gave birth to Sùjié.
Yōng
is pronounced *yōng*.
7 In summer,
in the fifth month,
on the day Rénxū,
Tǔbō Zànpǔ Nòngzàn died.
His eldest son had died early,
so his grandson was established as Zànpǔ.
The Zànpǔ was young and weak,
and all government affairs were decided by the Guóxiàng Lù Dōngzàn.
Lù Dōngzàn was intelligent, clear-sighted, and serious,
and adept at military strategy.
The reason Tǔbō became strong
and brought the Dī and Qiāng under its sway
was all due to his schemes.
8 In the sixth month,
Gāo Kǎn attacked the Tūjué
and reached Mount Āxī.
Chēbí Kèhán summoned the troops of all the tribes, but none responded.
He fled with a few hundred cavalry.
Kǎn led his elite cavalry in pursuit to Mount Jīn,
captured him, and returned,
and all his followers surrendered.
9 Initially,
Āshǐnà Shè'ěr captured Bùshībì, the King of Qiūcí,
and established Bùshībì’s younger brother as king.
This event is recorded in Tàizōng’s Zhēnguān 26th year.
Their chieftains vied for succession,
attacking each other.
In autumn,
in the eighth month,
on the day Rénwǔ,
an imperial edict restored Bùshībì as King of Qiūcí,
sent him back to his country,
and pacified his people.
10 In the ninth month,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
Gāo Kǎn brought Chēbí Kèhán to the capital.
He was released
and appointed Zuǒ Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn.
His remaining followers were settled at Mount Yùdūjūn.
處,
昌呂翻.
Gāo Kǎn was appointed Wèijiāngjūn.
The Táng did not have a Wèijiāngjūn;
there must be a missing character
above the character Wèi.
The single Dānyú and Hànhǎi Dūhùfǔ were established.
The Dānyú Dūhùfǔ administered the three Dūdūfǔ of Lángshān, Yúnzhōng, and Sānggān,
and fourteen prefectures including Sūnóng;
the Hànhǎi Dūhùfǔ administered seven Dūdūfǔ including Hànhǎi, Jīnhuī, and Xīnlí,
and eight prefectures including Xiān'è;
each with their chieftains appointed as Cìshǐ and Dūdū.
The Xīnshū records
“twenty-four prefectures of Sūnóng,”
while the Jiùshū records
“fourteen prefectures.”
It is also examined that later in Diàolù 1st year,
when the Wēnfù and Fèngzhí tribes rebelled,
all twenty-four prefectures rebelled in response,
so the character
“èr” (two)
is correct.
However, among the prefectures administered by the Dānyú Dūhùfǔ recorded in historical accounts,
there are four prefectures including Sūnóng,
five prefectures including Shèlì, and four prefectures including Yùshè, Yìshī, Bēishī, and Chìlüè under the Sānggān Fǔ,
and three prefectures including Hèlǔ, Gélào, and Diē under the Hūyán Fǔ,
totaling only nineteen prefectures.
The other five prefectures are missing
and cannot be verified.
There were also the two Dūdū of Dìngxiāng and Hūyán, but no Dūdū of Lángshān.
This indicates that their establishment, abolition, separation, and combination
cannot be detailed.
The Lángshān Fǔ
was abolished and became a prefecture in Xiǎnqìng 3rd year.
“Jīnhuī”
should be
“Jīnwēi.”
The Hànhǎi Dūhùfǔ administered six Dūdūfǔ: Hànhǎi, Jīnwēi, Xīnlí, Yōulíng, Guīlín, and Jiānkūn,
one of which is missing;
and eight prefectures: Xiān'è, Jùnjī, Yúwú, Jīluò, Jūyán, Zhìyán, Yúxī, Húnhé, and Zhúlóng.
Sòng Bái said: The Zhènwǔ Jūn was formerly the Dānyú Dūhùfǔ,
which was Shènglè Xiàn of the Hàn Dìngxiāng Jùn.
It was south of Mount Yīnshān and north of the Yellow River,
one hundred and twenty *lǐ* southwest to Dōng Shòuxiáng Chéng.
The Hànhǎi Dūhùfǔ was later moved to the main territory of the Huíhè.
乾,
音干.
11 On the day Guǐhài,
the emperor went hunting.
He encountered rain
and asked the Jiànyì Dàfū Chānglè Gǔnàlǜ:
“How can an oiled coat be made so that it does not leak?”
Zhīgǔzǐ said: The system of oiled silk and oiled hats
only began in Chén.
樂,
音洛.
“If it is made of tiles,
it will certainly not leak.”
The emperor was pleased
and stopped the hunt for him.
12 Lǐ Jì firmly requested to resign his post.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Wùchén,
Jì was relieved of his post as Zuǒ Púyè,
and appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
13 On the day Jǐwèi,
Wèi Sīqiān of Yángwǔ,
a Jiānchá Yùshǐ,
Yángwǔ Xiàn,
belonged to Hénán Jùn during the Hàn dynasty.
Since the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Xíngyáng Jùn.
監,
工銜翻.
The Zhōngshū was in charge of receiving tributes from the four directions and communicating memorials,
hence there were interpreters.
劾,
戶概翻,
又戶得翻.
Sīqiān reported:
“The establishment of appraised prices
is to meet the needs of the state.
How can transactions by officials
be fixed according to these appraisals!
Ruìcè distorted documents,
deceived his superiors by colluding with subordinates;
his crime deserves execution.”
On that day,
Suíliáng was demoted to Cìshǐ of Tóngzhōu,
and Ruìcè to Cìshǐ of Xúnzhōu.
Sīqiān’s given name was Rén Yuē,
but he was known by his courtesy name.
14 In the twelfth month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
Xiè Wànsuì, Dūdū of Zǐzhōu, Xiè Fǎxīng, Dūdū of Yǎnzhōu, and Lǐ Mèngcháng, Dūdū of Qiánzhōu, attacked the rebellious Liáo of Yǎnzhōu.
“Zǐzhōu”
should be
“Zāngzhōu.”
In Wǔdé 3rd year,
Xiè Lóngyǔ, a chieftain of the Zāngkē Mán, surrendered,
and Zāngzhōu was established in his territory.
“Yǎnzhōu”
should be
“Chōngzhōu.”
In Wǔdé 3rd year,
it was established for a separate tribe of the Zāngkē Mán.
Yǎnzhōu
was also a Mán prefecture,
established in Zhēnguān 4th year.
All belonged to the Qiánzhōu Dūdùfǔ.
黔,
音琴.
獠,
魯皓翻.
They were killed by the Liáo.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Yǐsì,
Huángmén Shìláng Yǔwén Jié and Zhōngshū Shìláng Liǔ Shì were both appointed Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
Shì
was the nephew of Hēng.
Liǔ Hēng
was the grandson of Qìngzhī, Zuǒ Púyè of the Bureau of Personnel in the Western Wèi,
and the son-in-law of Dòu Dàn.
Hēng’s wife was the daughter of Princess Xiāngyáng.
2 Āshǐnà Hèlǔ,
Zuǒ Xiāowèi Jiāngjūn and Dūdū of Yáochí, gathered scattered people,
and his camps gradually prospered.
Hearing of Tàizōng’s death,
he plotted to seize Xī and Tíng two prefectures.
Luò Hóngyì, Cìshǐ of Tíngzhōu, knew of his plot
and reported it in a memorial.
The emperor sent Tōngshì Shèrén Qiáo Bǎomíng to rush and comfort him.
Bǎomíng persuaded Hèlǔ
to send his eldest son Diéyùn to serve in the imperial guard,
and he was appointed Yòu Xiāowèi Zhōnglángjiāng.
Soon after, he was sent back.
Diéyùn then persuaded his father to lead his people west,
defeated Yǐpí Shèkuì Kèhán,
and absorbed his followers.
He established his headquarters at Shuānghé and Qiānquán.
From Shuānghé southwest to Hèlǔ’s main camp was two hundred *lǐ*.
Qiānquán belonged to the territory of the Shíguó,
and was also southwest of Hèlǔ’s main camp.
The Xīnshū says: Four hundred *lǐ* west of Suzhōng Chéng to Qiānquán,
the land stretches over two hundred *lǐ*,
south of the snowy mountains,
three sides are flat land,
with many springs,
hence its name.
The five Chuài of Duōlù and the five Sījīn of Núshībì all submitted to him.
He had hundreds of thousands of soldiers
and allied with Yǐpí Duōlù Kèhán.
The Chǔyuè, Chǔmì, and various Xīyù kingdoms mostly joined him.
Diéyùn was appointed Mòhèduō Yèhù.
3 Bógālì, King of Yānqí, died.
The people of the country memorialized to request the restoration of the former king Tūqízhī.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
an imperial edict conferred on Tūqízhī the title of Yòu Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn
and sent him back to his country.
4 The Cìshǐ of Jīnzhōu, Prince Téng Yuán-Yīng, was arrogant, extravagant, and dissolute.
While mourning,
he hunted without restraint.
He frequently opened the city gates at night,
disturbing the common people.
Sometimes he would shoot people with a slingshot,
or bury people in the snow for amusement.
The emperor sent him a letter of severe reprimand,
and further said:
"There are many ways
to find pleasure.
How can the degenerate ruler of Jìn be a model for you!
The Zǔo Zhùan states:
'Dùke Lìng-Gōng of Jìn was not a true lord.
He shot people with a slingshot from his terrace to watch them dodge the pellets.'
I cannot
bring the prince to justice.
So now I will record the prince's conduct in the 'Lower Superior' category in the official assessment to shame his heart."
Yuán-Yīng and Prince Jiǎng Yùn were both fond of accumulating wealth.
The emperor once bestowed five hundred bolts of silk upon each of the princes,
but these two princes alone did not receive any.
He issued an edict saying:
"Téng Shú and Jiǎng Xiōng are perfectly capable of managing their own affairs
and do not need gifts.
Give them two carts of hemp to serve as strings for their cash."
The two princes were greatly ashamed.
5 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Shābōluó Kèhán of the Western Tūjué invaded Tíngzhōu,
capturing Jīnlǐngchéng and Púlèixiàn.
From Jiāohéxiàn in Xīzhōu, traveling eighty lǐ north into a valley,
then another one hundred thirty lǐ through Liǔgǔ,
crossing Jīnshālǐng,
and one hundred sixty lǐ to Púlèixiàn in Tíngzhōu.
It belonged to Xīzhōu,
then later to Tíngzhōu,
and was later renamed Hòutíngxiàn.
An imperial edict appointed Zuǒwǔhóu
Dàjiāngjūn Liáng Jiànfāng and Yòuxiāowèi Dàjiāngjūn Qìbì Hélì as Gōngyuèdào Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn.
Gōngyuèchéng is over a thousand lǐ west of Tíngzhōu.
Gū and Wú Rén were made deputies.
Thirty thousand regular army troops were dispatched from Qín, Chéng, Qí, and Yǒng Prefectures.
Chéngzhōu was
the land of Hàn Wǔdū Shànglù and Xiàbiàn.
The Later Wèi established Qiúchí Jùn there.
Hányáng Jùn was Nánqínzhōu.
The Western Wèi renamed it Chéngzhōu.
Yǒngzhōu was
Jīngzhào Jùn.
Yǒng is pronounced
yu-yong fan.
6 On Guǐsì,
an edict ordered the officials of rites and scholars to deliberate on the system of the Míngtáng,
and to associate Gāozǔ with the Five Celestial Emperors.
Tàizōng was to be associated with the Five Human Emperors.
The Five Celestial Emperors:
the note is already found in volume seventy-nine, Jìn Wǔdì Tàishǐ second year.
The Five Human Emperors: Dàhào, the Eastern Emperor; Shàohào, the Western Emperor; Yándì, the Southern Emperor; Zhuānxū, the Northern Emperor; and Huángdì, the Central Emperor.
7 In the eighth month,
on Jǐsì,
Yú Zhìníng was appointed Zuǒpúyè,
Zhāng Xíngchéng as Yòupúyè,
and Gāo Jìfǔ as Shìzhōng.
Zhìníng and Xíngchéng continued to hold the third rank of Zhōngshūménxià Sānpǐn.
8 On Jǐmǎo,
the Báishuǐ Mán of Lángzhōu rebelled,
attacking Mázhōu.
The Báishuǐ Mán, adjacent to Qīnglíng and Nòngdòng,
were subordinate to Lángzhōu.
Mázhōu
was established in the twenty-second year of Zhēnguàn by splitting from Lángzhōu.
9 In the ninth month,
on Guǐsì,
Yùhuágōng was abolished and converted into a Buddhist temple.
On Wùxū,
Jiǔchénggōng was renamed Wànniángōng.
10 On Gēngxū,
Lú Wéncāo, an escort officer of the Zuǒwǔhóu, scaled a wall and stole items from the Zuǒcáng.
The emperor considered that an escort officer's duty was to maintain discipline.
The Zuǒ- and Yòuwǔhóu
were in charge of patrolling the palace and capital day and night
to apprehend illegal activities.
They had a guard of sixty men from the three guards for escort,
and sixty-six additional escort archers.
The Zuǒ- and Yòucáng
were first established in Jìn,
and the Táng continued the system without change.
Each had one director.
Sòng Bái said: "According to Táng regulations, the Zuǒ- and Yòujīnwú had an escort guard of one hundred forty men,
filled by personnel from the three guards.
The Zuǒcáng managed the national treasury,
and the Yòucáng managed national treasures and wealth."
Cáng is pronounced
zu-lang fan.
The emperor ordered his execution.
Jiànyì Dàfū Xiāo Jūn remonstrated:
"Wéncāo's crime is indeed difficult to excuse,
but the law does not warrant death."
The emperor then pardoned Wéncāo from death
and, looking at his attendants, said:
"This is truly a remonstrating official!"
11 In the intercalary month,
Zhǎngsūn Wújí and others presented the revised Lùlìngshì.
On Jiǎxū,
an edict ordered its promulgation throughout the four quarters.
12 The emperor said to the prime ministers:
"I hear that local officials
still tend to consider people's feelings in their actions,
often not being entirely impartial."
Zhǎngsūn Wújí replied:
"How can one say there is none of this?
However, acting wantonly and bending the law
is something they truly dare not do.
As for minor acts of gaining favor,
I fear Your Majesty may not even be able to avoid them."
As Wújí was the emperor's maternal uncle assisting in governance,
whatever he said,
the emperor always accepted it with approval.
13 In winter,
in the eleventh month,
on Xīnyǒu,
the emperor performed the sacrifice at the Southern Suburb.
14 On Guǐyǒu,
an edict stated:
"From now on, any officials in the capital or outer prefectures who present eagles, falcons, dogs, or horses
shall be punished."
15 On Wùyín,
the Qiāng chief Dǒng Xīfèngqiú of Tèlàng and the Qiāng chief Bǔ Yánmò of Pìhuì each led over ten thousand households of their tribes to Móuzhōu to submit.
Both Tèlàng and Pìhuì were 'raw' Qiāng.
In this year,
thirty-two prefectures, including Pénglǔ, were established in their territory,
subordinate to the Dūdūfǔ of Móuzhōu.
Qiú is pronounced
zi-you fan.
Yán is pronounced
yu-lian fan.
Shuài,
read as lǜ.
Zhǒng is pronounced
zhang-yong fan.
16 The Mán chiefs Lǐ Bǎochéng and others from Dòuzhōu and Yìzhōu rebelled.
Yìzhōu was
the land of Hàn Měnglíngxiàn.
Liáng established Yǒngyè Jùn.
Suí renamed it Huáidéxiàn,
subordinate to Lóngzhōu.
In the fifth year of Wǔdé of Táng,
Nányìzhōu was established.
In the second year of Zhēnguàn,
it was named Yìzhōu.
17 The Dà Zǒngguǎn of Lángzhōu, Zhào Xiàozǔ, attacked the Báishuǐ Mán.
The Mán chieftains Tūmó Pú and Jiǎnmí Yú led their forces to occupy strategic positions and resist.
Xiàozǔ defeated and beheaded them all.
Coincidentally, there was a heavy snowfall,
and the Mán suffered from hunger and cold,
nearly all dying.
Xiàozǔ submitted a memorial, stating:
“During the Zhēngguān reign, the Wū Mán of Kūnzhōu were attacked,
and for the first time Qīnglíng and Nòngdòng were established as prefectures and counties.
Kūnzhōu was
the land of the Hàn dynasty’s Yìzhōu Commandery.
The Suí dynasty established Kūnzhōu,
but it was abandoned due to chaos.
In the early Wǔdé reign of the Táng dynasty,
Nánzhōng was opened,
and it was re-established.
The two Cuàn Mán of Zhèdōng,
from Qǔzhōu and Jìngzhōu southwest to Kūnchuān, Qǔè, Jìnníng, Yùxiàn, Ānníng, extending to Lónghé Chéng,
are collectively known as the Xī Cuàn Bái Mán.
From the two streams of Mǐlù and Shēngmá,
south to Bùtóu,
they are called the Dōng Cuàn Wū Mán.
Qīnglíng
was established as a county by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
belonging to Yuèkuí Commandery.
Nòngdòng County belonged to Yìzhōu Commandery.
During the Jìn dynasty, both belonged to Yúnnán Commandery,
and later to Xīngníng Commandery.
During the Suí chaos,
they were cut off from China.
The Táng dynasty established Máozhōu in the territory of Qīnglíng,
and Póuzhōu in the territory of Nòngdòng.
Bólòng belonged to the jurisdiction of the Hàn dynasty’s Yǒngchāng Commandery.
In the seventh year of Táng Wǔdé,
Nányúnzhōu was established.
In the eighth year of Zhēngguān,
it was renamed Kuāngzhōu.
We wish to make them submit.
The area west of Bólòng borders Huángguā, Yèyú, and Xīěhé.
Yèyú was also established as a county by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
There is Yèyú Zé there,
belonging to Yìzhōu Commandery.
In the Later Hàn, it belonged to Yǒngchāng Commandery,
and in the Jìn, to Yúnnán Commandery,
later divided to belong to Dōnghéyáng Commandery.
There are many there, as in the Shǔchuān,
but no great chieftains.
They are fond of forming feuds.
Now, having broken the army of Báishuǐ,
I request permission to advance west and pacify them as circumstances permit.”
The emperor granted the request.
18 In the twelfth month,
on the Rénzǐ day,
Chùyuè Zhūxié Gūzhù killed the Zhāowèishǐ Shàn Dàohuì,
and allied with the Tujue Hè Lǔ.
19 In this year,
Báijì sent envoys to pay tribute.
The emperor admonished them,
saying, “Do not attack Xīnluó and Gāolì.
Otherwise,
I will send troops to attack you.”
1 In spring, in the first month,
on the Jǐwèi day (which was the first day of the month),
Tǔyùhún, Xīnluó, Gāolì, and Báijì all sent envoys to pay tribute.
2 On the Guǐhài day, Liáng Jiànfāng, Qìbì Hélì, and others severely defeated Chùyuè Zhūxié Gūzhù at Láoshān.
The New Book states: Láoshān is also called Dǔpú.
To its northeast lies Wūdégān Shān,
a fifteen-day journey by horse.
Jiànfāng sent his deputy commander Gāo Déyì with light cavalry to pursue him,
traveling over five hundred *lǐ*,
and captured Gūzhù alive,
beheading nine thousand heads.
When the army returned,
the imperial censor impeached Liáng Jiànfāng for having sufficient military strength to pursue and attack,
but delaying and not advancing;
and Gāo Déyì for ordering the purchase of horses
and taking the best ones for himself.
The emperor, considering Jiànfāng and others meritorious,
released them without punishment.
Dàlǐ Qīng Lǐ Dàoyù memorialized, stating:
“The horses taken by Déyì are of extraordinary strength and stamina.
I request that they be truly kept in the *zhōng ji*.”
*Zhōng ji*
is akin to saying *nèi ji*.
“Dàoyù is a legal official,
and presenting horses is not his duty.
He wrongly hoped to please me.
Is it that my actions are not trusted by my officials?
I am reproaching myself,
so I will not demote Dàoyù again.”
3 On the Jǐsì day, Chǔ Suìliáng, the Cìshǐ of Tóngzhōu, was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
4 On the Bǐngzǐ day, the emperor offered sacrifices at the Tàimiào;
on the Dīnghài day, he offered sacrifices to the Xiānnóng,
and personally tilled the Jiètián.
The Hàn ritual: The Son of Heaven personally tills the Jiètián in the first month,
and offers sacrifices to the Xiānnóng.
Xiānnóng is Shénnóng.
Sacrifices are made with a grand animal offering,
and all officials participate.
According to Táng regulations,
the Son of Heaven offers sacrifices to the Xiānnóng on a propitious Hài day in the first month of winter,
and then proceeds with the tilling.
5 In the second month, on the Jiǎyín day,
the emperor ascended the Ānfúmén Tower.
The Táng Liùdiǎn states: The two gates on the west side of the imperial city of Cháng'ān are
the northern one called Ānfú,
and the southern one called Shùnyì;
Ānfú is directly west of the imperial city's Kāiyuǎnmén.
On the Yǐmǎo day,
the emperor said to his attendant officials:
“Yesterday I ascended the tower,
intending to observe popular sentiment and the extravagance or frugality of customs,
not for entertainment.
I heard that the Hú people are good at playing a game of *jīju* (polo).
The *ju* is made of leather
and filled with soft material,
now called *qiúzi*.
Yesterday, as soon as I ascended the tower,
there were some Hú playing *jīju*,
thinking that I was very fond of it.
The actions of an emperor
should not be taken lightly.
I have already burned this *ju*,
hoping to prevent the Hú people from harboring such expectations,
and also to serve as a warning.”
6 In the third month, on the Xīnsì day,
Yǔwén Jié was appointed Shìzhōng,
Liǔ Shì as Zhōngshū Lìng,
and Hán Yuàn of Sānyuán, the Bīngbù Shìláng, was appointed Shǒu Huángmén Shìláng and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
7 In summer, in the fourth month,
Zhào Xiàozǔ severely defeated the southwestern Mán,
beheading Mòshèng, the chieftain of Xiǎo Bólòng,
and capturing Yáng Chéngdiān, the chieftain of Dà Bólòng.
All the others were gathered in fortified strongholds;
the large ones had tens of thousands of people,
the small ones several thousands.
Xiàozǔ defeated and subjugated them all,
and the southwestern Mán were thus pacified.
8 On the Jiǎwǔ day, Péng Sīwáng Yuánzé, Cìshǐ of Lǐzhōu, passed away.
9 In the sixth month, on the Wùshēn day,
the Bīngbù Shàngshū Cuī Dūnli and others were dispatched to lead ten thousand infantry and cavalry from Bìng and Fén to Màozhōu.
Màozhōu,
according to examination of the old and new gazetteers, is not found there;
it should be located in the former territory of Xuē Yántuó.
Qíliánzhōu was established to settle them.
10 In autumn, in the seventh month,
on the Dīngsì day,
Lǐ Zhōng, Prince of Chén, was established as the Crown Prince,
and a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
Empress Wáng had no sons.
Liǔ Shì, scheming for the empress,
considering Lǐ Zhōng’s mother, Lady Liú, to be of humble status,
advised the empress to establish Lǐ Zhōng as crown prince,
hoping he would be close to her;
externally, he hinted to Zhǎngsūn Wújí and others to request this from the emperor.
The emperor agreed.
On the Yǐchǒu day,
Yú Zhìníng was appointed concurrent Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
Zhāng Xíngchéng as concurrent Junior Tutor,
and Gāo Jìfǔ as concurrent Junior Guardian.
11 On the Dīngchǒu day, the emperor asked Hùbù Shàngshū Gāo Lǚxíng:
“How many households were added last year?”
Hùbù Shàngshū was formerly Mínbù Shàngshū,
changed to avoid Emperor Tàizōng’s taboo name.
*Jìnhù*
means newly added households.
“Last year, a total of one hundred and fifty thousand households were added.”
The emperor then asked about the current number of households compared to the Suí dynasty.
Lǚxíng memorialized:
“During the Kāihuáng reign of the Suí dynasty,
there were 8.7 million households.
Currently, there are 3.8 million households.”
*Jìnjīn*
is equivalent to *dāngjīn* (current),
a term often used by Táng people.
He was the son of Shìlián.
12 In the ninth month, Shǒu Zhōngshū Shìláng Lái Jì was appointed Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
In the 13th year (of the Zhēn'guān era),
the eleventh month,

The Emperor had also bestowed extraordinary gifts upon Wújí's officials and illegitimate children;

If Wújí wished to block his improper desire,

This laid the groundwork for Wújí's downfall.

If we look at Níshú's biography,

8 Lǐ Yìfǔ, the Zhōngshūlìng, was favored by the Emperor.

Dù Zhènglún, also a Zhōngshūlìng, always regarded himself as superior due to seniority.

Héngzhōu was
the land of Guǎngyù Gāoliáng in the Hàn dynasty.
In the seventh year of Tàikāng under Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,

Suí established Jiǎnzhōu,

In the early Wǔdé period of Táng,

It was 5,539 lǐ from the capital (Jīngshī),

the land of the three Hàn counties of Niúbì, Diànjiāng, and Zīzhōng.

and also established Pǔzhōu.
Suí abolished the prefecture (zhōu),
making the county belong to Zīyáng Commandery.
In the second year of Wǔdé of Táng,
Pǔzhōu was re-established.
It was 2,360 lǐ from the capital (Jīngshī),
and 3,203 lǐ from Dōngdū.

If Your Majesty still doubts this,
I fear it will not be a blessing for the state. "
The Kǎoyì says: The Shílù states:
"Lǐ Fèngjié from Luòyáng submitted a sealed memorial accusing Wéi Jìfāng, Prince's Gentleman-of-the-Household, and Lǐ Cháo, Investigating Censor, of colluding with court nobles
and forming a clique.
An imperial edict commanded Lǐ Jìngzōng and Xīn Máojiāng, Attendant Censor, to interrogate them.
Lǐ Jìngzōng pressed them very hard,
and Wéi Jìfāng, under pressure,
stabbed himself
but did not die.
They also searched Lǐ Fèngjié
and found a private letter
titled 'To Zhào Shī.'
Lǐ Jìngzōng then memorialized, saying: 'Zhào Shī
is Zhǎngsūn Wújì.
He secretly used veiled language
to frame loyal and good people,
seeking an opportunity to rebel.'
The Emperor was startled and said: 'How could this be?
Perhaps evil people have plotted maliciously,
causing minor suspicions and obstructions.
As for immediately rebelling,
I still doubt it.'
Lǐ Jìngzōng memorialized, saying: 'Your subject has investigated thoroughly from beginning to end.
Since Lǐ Fèngjié mentioned 'Zhào Shī,'
and a forged letter was also found,
which Wéi Jìfāng wrote,
it immediately raised suspicion that Zhǎngsūn Wújì intended to rebel.
He had them secretly plot discord
and eliminate loyal officials and close relatives.
If this plan succeeded,
power would naturally revert to Zhǎngsūn Wújì.
The traces are already evident.
If Your Majesty still has doubts,
I fear it will not be a blessing for the state.' "
The Old Biography of Zhǎngsūn Wújì says:
"Lǐ Jìngzōng sent someone to submit a sealed memorial,
claiming that Investigating Censor Lǐ Cháo was colluding with Zhǎngsūn Wújì to rebel.
An imperial edict commanded Lǐ Jìngzōng and Xīn Máojiāng to interrogate them."
The Tánglì and Tǒngjì are largely similar to the Shílù.
It is noted that Lǐ Fèngjié was the accuser.
How could the interrogators search Lǐ Fèngjié's house instead?
And whose private letter was it that was 'To Zhào Shī'?
If it was Wéi Jìfāng's letter,
how could it be in Lǐ Fèngjié's house?
If it was in Lǐ Fèngjié's house,
Lǐ Fèngjié should have produced it to bring the charge.
Why wait for a search to find it?
Also, since it was stated that Zhào Shī was Zhǎngsūn Wújì,
then it was a real letter to Zhǎngsūn Wújì.
How could it be called a 'forged letter'?
The Shílù narrates this matter quite carelessly,
with discrepancies from beginning to end,
making it impossible to know the full truth.
Therefore, only the general meaning has been extracted.
What the Old Biography states,
although concise,
does not fit, as Gāozōng initially had no suspicion of Zhǎngsūn Wújì.
Thus, when Lǐ Hóngtài accused Zhǎngsūn Wújì of rebellion,
Gāozōng immediately executed him.
Why would he specifically order Lǐ Jìngzōng to interrogate him in Lǐ Fèngjié's case?
Furthermore, the Shílù came earlier and is detailed,
while the biographies came later and are abbreviated.
Therefore, it cannot be taken as conclusive either.
"My family has been unfortunate;
relatives have repeatedly harbored dissenting intentions.
In previous years, Princess Gāoyáng plotted rebellion with Fáng Yí'ài,
as seen in the third year of Yǒnghuī in the previous volume.

If this matter is true,

He replied:

Zhǎngsūn Wújì conspired with the late Emperor to seize the empire;

He has been Chancellor for thirty years;
Zhǎngsūn Wújì served as Chancellor from the beginning of Zhēnguān,
to now over thirty years.
If he were to suddenly rise up,
whom would Your Majesty send to oppose him?
Now, thanks to the spiritual power of the imperial ancestral temple,
and Heaven's hatred of evil,
by investigating a minor matter,
a great villain has been exposed.
This is truly a blessing for the empire.
Your subject secretly fears that if Zhǎngsūn Wújì learns of Wéi Jìfāng's self-stabbing,
he will be driven to desperate measures,
raise his sleeves and make a call,
and his confederates will flock like clouds,
which will surely bring worry to the imperial ancestral temple.
Your subject once saw Yǔwén Huàjí, whose father Yǔwén Shù was deeply trusted by Emperor Yáng,
bound by marriage,
and entrusted with court affairs.
After Yǔwén Shù's death,
Yǔwén Huàjí again commanded the imperial guards.
One night he revolted in Jiāngdū,
first killing those who did not support him.
Your subject's family also suffered from that disaster.
At that time, ministers like Sū Wēi and Péi Jù,
all danced before his horse,
fearing only that they would not be quick enough.
At dawn, the Suí dynasty was overthrown.
This event is found in volume 186, first year of Gāozǔ Wǔdé.
I beg Your Majesty to act swiftly!"
The Emperor ordered Lǐ Jìngzōng to conduct a further, careful examination.
The next day,
Lǐ Jìngzōng again memorialized, saying:
"Last night, Wéi Jìfāng already admitted to rebelling with Zhǎngsūn Wújì.
Your subject further asked Wéi Jìfāng: 'Zhǎngsūn Wújì is a close relative of the state,
favored and trusted by successive emperors.
What cause for resentment does he have to rebel?'
Wéi Jìfāng replied: 'Hán Yuàn once told Zhǎngsūn Wújì:
"Liǔ Shì and Chǔ Suìliáng advised you to establish Prince Liáng as太子 (crown prince).
Now that Prince Liáng has been deposed,
the Emperor also suspects you,
which is why Gāo Lǚxíng has been sent out of the capital."
Gāo Lǚxíng
is Zhǎngsūn Wújì's nephew (son of his maternal aunt).
Last year he was sent out to be the Administrator of Yìzhōu.
He gradually began to make plans for his own safety.
Later, seeing Zhǎngsūn Xiáng also sent away,
and Hán Yuàn disgraced,
he plotted rebellion day and night with Wéi Jìfāng and others.'
Your subject has compared and verified the statements,
and they all match.
I request that they be arrested according to law."
The Emperor again wept and said:
"If my maternal uncle truly is like that,
I simply cannot bear to kill him.
What will the world say of me,
what will future generations say of me!"
Lǐ Jìngzōng replied:
"Bó Zhāo
was the maternal uncle of Emperor Wén of Hàn.
When Emperor Wén came from Dài,
Bó Zhāo also rendered service.
His crime was merely murder,
yet Emperor Wén had all officials wear plain clothes and weep before executing him.
This is recorded in the Account of Emperor Wén of Hàn.
Now Zhǎngsūn Wújì has forgotten the great kindness of two dynasties
and plots to usurp the state.
His crime cannot be spoken of in the same breath as Bó Zhāo's.
Fortunately, the treacherous plot has revealed itself,
and the rebels have confessed.
Why does Your Majesty hesitate,
and not make an early decision!
The ancients said: 'If you hesitate to act when you should,
you will suffer its ill effects instead.'
This is a Daoist saying.
Duàn means 'to decide,'
Dīngluàn-fān.
There is no room for delay.
Zhǎngsūn Wújì is a treacherous hero of our time,
in the same vein as Wáng Mǎng and Sīmǎ Yì.
If Your Majesty delays even a little longer,
your subject fears that trouble will arise right under your nose,
and it will be too late for regret!"
The Emperor thought this was right,
and ultimately did not summon Zhǎngsūn Wújì for questioning.
