“Shì (Shì) was repeatedly demoted to Assassin of Àizhōu (Àizhōu),
and Gāozōng (Gāozōng) had him killed in Àizhōu (Àizhōu).”
We now follow the Veritable Records.
They opened and examined the body, then returned.
To open the coffin and inspect his corpse.
“還” (Huán),
pronounced cóng xuān,
also as written.
The “Kǎoyì” (Kǎoyì) states: The Old Biography of Yuàn (Yuàn) says:
“He died in office in the fourth year.
The next year,
Zhǎngsūn Wú-Jì (Zhǎngsūn Wú-Jì) died,
and an envoy was sent to kill him.
By the time the envoy arrived,
Yuàn (Yuàn) was already dead.”
The Biography of Chǔ Suìliáng (Chǔ Suìliáng) says:
“He died in office in the third year.
Two years later, his official titles were posthumously stripped.”
The Veritable Records may have mentioned Wú-Jì (Wú-Jì) being banished to Qiánzhōu (Qiánzhōu) and then his end.
However, many books place it in this month,
likely because the Veritable Records and the Chronological Records state that on the seventh month, xīnwèi,
an envoy was sent to force Wú-Jì (Wú-Jì) to hang himself.
According to the Long Calendar,
the seventh month began on bǐngzǐ,
and there was no xīnwèi,
so it cannot be relied upon.
All close relatives were banished to Lǐngnán (Lǐngnán) as slaves.
Zhǎngsūn Xiáng (Zhǎngsūn Xiáng), Assassin of Chángzhōu (Chángzhōu), was sentenced to strangulation for communicating with Wú-Jì (Wú-Jì).
Chángzhōu (Chángzhōu) is two thousand eight hundred forty-three lǐ southeast of the capital,
and one thousand nine hundred eighty-three lǐ from the Eastern Capital.
“處” (Chǔ),
pronounced chānglǚ.
Tánzhōu (Tánzhōu) was the territory of Tíxī (Tíxī) County, Yúyáng (Yúyáng) Commandery, during the Hàn (Hàn) dynasty.
Later, the Northern Wèi (Wèi) established Ānzhōu (Ānzhōu),
which the Northern Zhōu (Zhōu) later renamed Xuánzhōu (Xuánzhōu).
In the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng (Kāihuáng) of the Suí (Suí) dynasty, it was renamed Tánzhōu (Tánzhōu).
In the early Dàyè (Dàyè) era,
the prefecture was abolished and became Ānlè (Ānlè) Commandery.
The Táng (Táng) restored it as Tánzhōu (Tánzhōu).
It is two thousand five hundred sixty-seven lǐ northeast of the capital,
and one thousand eight hundred forty-four lǐ from the Eastern Capital.
The “Kǎoyì” (Kǎoyì) states: The Táng Tǒngjì (Táng Tǒngjì) and Tánglì (Tánglì) both say
“Zhǎngsūn Ēn” (Zhǎngsūn Ēn).
The New Book says
“clan younger brother Ēn” (Ēn).
In the Tǒngjì (Tǒngjì) and Tánglì (Tánglì),
Zhǎngsūn Quán (Zhǎngsūn Quán) was banished to Cuīzhōu (Cuīzhōu),
and the county magistrate, hoping to please the emperor, killed him,
placed after this.
The Veritable Records state,
“Quán (Quán) was banished to Cuīzhōu (Cuīzhōu).
Xǔ Jìngzōng (Xǔ Jìngzōng) feared that his nephew Zhào Chímǎn (Zhào Chímǎn) would cause trouble,
so he killed Chímǎn (Chímǎn).”
This means Quán’s (Quán) banishment to Cuīzhōu (Cuīzhōu) happened earlier.
We now follow this.
10th month, 8th month.
On the day Rénzǐ,
Li Yìfǔ (李義府), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Pǔzhōu (普州), was appointed concurrently Shàngshū (尚書) of Lìbù (吏部) and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn (同中書門下三品).
As Yìfǔ (義府) gained power,
he claimed descent from Zhàojùn (趙郡)
and established lineage connections with the various Lǐ (李) clans.
Many scoundrels, leveraging his authority,
prostrated themselves, calling him elder brother or uncle.
Lǐ Chóngdé (李崇德), a Jǐshìzhōng (給事中), had initially included Yìfǔ (義府) in his family genealogy.
However, when Yìfǔ (義府) was demoted and sent out as Cìshǐ (刺史) of Pǔzhōu (普州),
Chóngdé (崇德) immediately removed him.
Yìfǔ (義府) heard of this and bore a grudge.
When he returned to power as chancellor,
he had someone falsely accuse Chóngdé (崇德) of a crime.
Chóngdé (崇德) was imprisoned
and committed suicide.
11th month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
thirteen individuals from the Zhǎngsūn (長孫) and Liǔ (柳) clans who had been demoted due to Wújí (無忌) and Shì (奭) were restored.
Gāo Lǚxíng (高履行) was demoted to Cìshǐ (刺史) of Yǒngzhōu (永州).
Yǒngzhōu (永州) was formerly Línglíng Jùn (零陵郡).
When the Suí (隋) dynasty conquered Chén (陳),
Yǒngzhōu (永州) was established.
It is 3,274 lǐ (里) south of the capital
and 3,665 lǐ (里) from the Eastern Capital.
Nine individuals from the Yú (于) clan were demoted.
From then on, governance fell to the Empress.
12th month, 9th month.
An imperial edict established 127 prefectures and counties in the kingdoms of Shí (石), Mǐ (米), Shǐ (史), Dà'ān (大安), Xiǎo'ān (小安), Cáo (曹), Báhànnà (拔汗那), Yìdá (悒怛), Shūlè (疏勒), and Zhūjūbàn (朱駒半).
The Kingdom of Mǐ (米)
is also called Mímò (彌末)
or Mǐmòhè (弭秣賀).
It is 100 lǐ (里) north of Kāngguó (康國).
Its king ruled from Bōxīdé Chéng (鉢息德城).
Dà'ān (大安)
is also called Bùhuò (布豁)
or Bǔhē (捕喝).
It was called Niǔmì (忸密) during the Yuánwèi (元魏) period.
It is 400 lǐ (里) northeast of Xiǎo'ān (小安)
and borders the Wūxǔ Hé (烏滸河) to the west.
Its capital is Hémì Chéng (河謐城),
which was the old territory of Jì Wáng (罽王), a minor chieftain of Kāngjū (康居).
Xiǎo'ān (小安)
is also called Dōng'ān (東安)
or Hēhàn (喝汗).
It is located on the sunny side of the Nàmì Shuǐ (那密水),
about 200 lǐ (里) east of the river.
Its capital is Hēhàn Chéng (喝汗城).
Cáo (曹) also had Eastern, Western, and Middle parts.
Dōngcáo (東曹) was located on the shady side of Bōxī Shān (波悉山),
the territory of Hàn Èrshī Chéng (漢貳師城).
It is 400 lǐ (里) north to Shí (石),
west to Kāng (康),
and northeast to Níngyuǎn (寧遠).
Wèicáo (魏曹) is also 400 lǐ (里).
Xīcáo (西曹) was the Kingdom of Cáo (曹) during the Suí (隋) dynasty.
It bordered Shǐ (史) and Bōlán (波覽) to the south.
Its capital was Sèdǐhén Chéng (瑟底痕城).
Zhōngcáo (中曹) was located at Jiādǐzhēn Chéng (迦底真城).
Báhànnà (拔汗那)
is Níngyuǎn (寧遠),
also called Pāhàn (鏺汗).
It was called Pòluònà (破洛那) during the Yuánwèi (元魏) period.
It is 8,000 lǐ (里) from the capital
and located at Xījiān Chéng (西鞬城),
north of Zhēnjū Hé (真珠河).
Later it split into two: one ruled from Hūmèn Chéng (呼悶城),
the other from Èsāi Chéng (遏塞城).
The Kingdom of Yìdá (悒怛)
is a branch of the Dàyuèzhī (大月氏) of the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
The Dàyuèzhī (大月氏) were dispossessed by the Wūsūn (烏孫),
passed west through Dàyuān (大宛),
and attacked and subjugated Dàxià (大夏).
Dàxià (大夏) is Tǔhuǒluó (吐火羅).
Yēdá (嚈噠)
is a surname.
Later generations used the surname for the country,
which became corrupted to Yìdá (悒怛).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Yēdá (嚈噠)
is sometimes said to be a branch of Gāochē (高車),
or a branch of Dàyuèzhī (大月氏).
Yìdá (悒怛) is also a branch of Dàyuèzhī (大月氏).
As Dù Yòu (杜佑) stated,
Yēdá (嚈噠) and Yìdá (悒怛) seem to be two different countries.
Shūlè (疏勒)
is also called Qiēshā (佉沙).
It is over 9,000 lǐ (里) from Cháng'ān (長安).
Yì (悒)
is pronounced Yì (邑).
Dá (怛)
is pronounced Dāgē (當割).
13th month, Winter,
10th month.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
the Crown Prince came of age and underwent the capping ceremony.
An amnesty was granted to the empire.
The ceremony of the Crown Prince coming of age
is fully detailed in the Lǐ Zhì (禮志) of the Xīnshū (新書).
14th month.
Initially, Tài Zōng (太宗) disliked the scholars from Shāndōng (山東) who prided themselves on their family status
and often demanded high dowries for marriage.
He ordered the revision of the Shìzú Zhì (氏族志) to demote them by one rank.
Princesses and imperial sons-in-law were all chosen from the families of meritorious officials,
without considering the Shāndōng (山東) clans.
However, the families of Wèi Zhēng (魏徵), Fáng Xuánlíng (房玄齡), and Lǐ Jì (李勣) frequently intermarried with them,
often influencing them,
thus their old prestige did not diminish.
Within some clans,
they were further divided into certain branches and households,
with vast differences in status.
Lǐ Yìfǔ (李義府) sought a marriage alliance for his son but failed to obtain it.
He resented this,
and therefore, using the late emperor's decree,
he advised the current emperor to correct this malpractice.
On the day Rénxū,

an imperial edict was issued decreeing that the descendants of Lǐ Bǎo (李寶) of Lǒngxī (隴西), Wáng Qióng (王瓊) of Tàiyuán (太原), Zhèng Wēn (鄭溫) of Xíngyáng (滎陽), Lú Zǐqiān (盧子遷), Lú Hún (盧渾), and Lú Fǔ (盧輔) of Fányáng (范陽), Cuī Zōngbó (崔宗伯) and Cuī Yuánsūn (崔元孫) of Qīnghé (清河), Cuī Yì (崔懿) of Bólíng (博陵) from Former Yān (燕), and Lǐ Kǎi (李楷) of Zhàojùn (趙郡) from Jìn (晉)
were not permitted to intermarry among themselves.
Furthermore, the amount of property accepted as dowry for marrying daughters throughout the empire was standardized,
and the practice of accepting péimén cái (陪門財) was forbidden.
Péimén cái (陪門財)
refers to cases where a daughter's family had low status,
and the family seeking marriage was an unsuitable match,
so they were made to pay a sum to compensate for the family's status.
Ultimately, it could not be prohibited.
Sometimes daughters were secretly taken to their husband's family,
or old maids remained unmarried,
refusing to marry outside their clan.
Those of declining lineage and those not recognized in the genealogy
often falsely claimed to be "forbidden marriage families"
to increase their prices.
This was to take a large amount of péimén cái (陪門財).
Zhāo (昭)
is pronounced Shìzhāo (市招).
15th month, Intercalary month.
On the day Wùyín,
the Emperor departed the capital,
ordering the Crown Prince to oversee the state.
The Crown Prince, longing for his parents,
people long for their parents when young,
was immediately summoned to the imperial temporary residence.
On the day Wùxū,
the imperial carriage arrived at the Eastern Capital.
16th month, 11th month.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
Xǔ Yǔshī (許圉師) was appointed Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) and Jiǎnjiào Shìzhōng (檢校侍中).
Sàn (散)
is pronounced Xīdàn (悉亶).
Qí (騎)
is pronounced Qíjì (奇寄).
17th month, On the day Wùwǔ,
Shìzhōng (侍中) and concurrent Zuǒshùzǐ (左庶子) Xīn Màojiāng (辛茂將) passed away.
18th month, Sījié Sìjīn Dūmàn (思結俟斤都曼), leading the three kingdoms of Shūlè (疏勒), Zhūjùbō (朱俱波), and Yēbāntuó (謁般陀), rebelled.
The Xīnshū (新書) renders it as
“Hēpántuó” (喝盤陀),
or “Hàntuó” (漢陀),
or “Kěguǎntán” (渴館檀),
also called “Kěluótuó” (渴羅陀).
From southwest Shūlè (疏勒), entering Jiànmò Gǔ (劍末谷) up to Bùrěn Lǐng (不忍嶺) for 600 lǐ (里),
is their country.
It is 4,500 lǐ (里) from Guāzhōu (瓜州),
directly southwest of Zhūjùbō (朱俱波),
and near Xuándù Shān (懸度山).
Sì (俟)
is pronounced Qúzhī (渠之).
Shuài (帥)
is read as Shuài (率).
On the day Guǐhài,
Sū Dìngfāng (蘇定方), the Dàjiàngjūn (大將軍) of Zuǒxiāowèi (左驍衞), was appointed Ānfǔ Dàshǐ (安撫大使) to suppress them.
19th month, Lú Chéngqìng (盧承慶) was appointed Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn (同中書門下三品).
20th month, Xuē Rén’guì (薛仁貴), the Zhōnglángjiàng (中郎將) of Yòulǐngjūn (右領軍), and others fought against Gāolí (高麗) general Wēn Shāmén (溫沙門) at Héngshān (橫山)
and defeated them.
21st month, Sū Dìngfāng’s (蘇定方) army reached Yèyè Shuǐ (業葉水).
Traveling west about 300 lǐ (里) from Tíngzhōu Lúntái Xiàn (庭州輪臺縣),
one reaches the Yèyè Hé (業葉河).
Dìngfāng (定方) selected 10,000 elite soldiers and 3,000 cavalry and galloped to surprise them.
They marched 300 lǐ (里) in one day and one night.
At dawn,
they reached the city walls.
Dūmàn (都曼) was greatly alarmed.
They fought outside the city.
Dūmàn (都曼) was defeated
and retreated to defend his city.
By evening,
the other armies arrived in succession.
They then besieged the city,
and Dūmàn (都曼), in fear, surrendered.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Sū Dìngfāng (蘇定方) presented the captives at Gānyáng Diàn (乾陽殿).
Gānyáng Diàn (乾陽殿) was in Luòyáng Gōng (洛陽宮).
Sū Dìngfāng (蘇定方) requested, saying:
"Your servant promised him his life,
so Dūmàn (都曼) surrendered.
I wish for his remaining life to be spared."
The Emperor said:
"We will bend the law to uphold your trust, General."
So he was pardoned.
2 On the day jiǎzǐ (甲子),
the Emperor departed from Dōngdū (東都);
in the second month,
on the day xīnsì (辛巳),
he arrived at Bìngzhōu (幷州).
The distance from Dōngdū (東都) to Bìngzhōu (幷州) was 808 *lǐ*.
On the day bǐngwǔ (丙午),
the Empress hosted a banquet for relatives, old friends, and neighbors in the cháotáng (朝堂),
and for women in the nèidiàn (內殿),
distributing gifts according to rank.
Empress Wǔ (武后)
was from Wénshuǐ Xiàn (文水縣) of Bìngzhōu (幷州).
Wherever the Son of Heaven traveled,
there was a cháotáng (朝堂).
When Tài Zōng (太宗) attacked Gāolì (高麗),
he set up a reception tent for surrender on the side of the cháotáng (朝堂),
which is this.
The Empress's residence was called the nèidiàn (內殿).
Cháo (朝),
pronounced as zhí yáo.
"All women in Bìngzhōu (幷州) aged eighty or above
were enfeoffed as Jùn Jūn (郡君)."
Jùn Jūn (郡君) had distinctions of 正四品 (zhèng sì pǐn), 從四品 (cóng sì pǐn), and 正五品 (zhèng wǔ pǐn).
3 Bǎijì (百濟), relying on aid from Gāolì (高麗),
frequently invaded Xīnluó (新羅);
King Chūnqiū (春秋) of Xīnluó (新羅) submitted a memorial requesting rescue.
On the day xīnhài (辛亥),
Sū Dìngfāng (蘇定方), the Grand General of the Left Guards of the Military (左武衞大將軍), was appointed Grand Commander of the Shénqiū Dào (神丘道) expeditionary army.
The *New Book* writes
"Shénbīng Dào (神兵道)."
He led 100,000 troops by land and sea to attack Bǎijì (百濟).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: Both Sū Dìngfāng's (蘇定方) biography in the *Old Book* and the *Xīnluó Zhuàn* (新羅傳) state that Dìngfāng (定方) was the Grand Commander of Hóngjīn Dào (熊津道).
The biography of Dìngfāng (定方) in the *Shílù* (實錄) also agrees.
Now we follow the *Shílù* (實錄) for this year and the Basic Annals of the *New Tang History*.
Also, the *Old Basic Annals* and the *Tang Calendar* both state,
"In the twelfth month of the fourth year, on the day guǐhài (癸亥),
Dìngfāng (定方) was appointed Grand Commander of Shénqiū Dào (神丘道),
and Liú Bóyīng (劉伯英) was appointed Commander of the Yúyí Dào (嵎夷道) expeditionary army."
However, Dìngfāng (定方) was at that time campaigning against Dūmàn (都曼),
and had not yet become Grand Commander of Shénqiū Dào (神丘道).
Both the *Old Book* and the *Tang Calendar* are mistaken.
Now we follow the *Shílù* (實錄).
Taking advantage of the *Yáo Diǎn* (堯典)
which says, "Settled in Yúyí (嵎夷) and called it Yánggǔ (暘谷),"
it was named.
And they joined forces with him.
4 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day bǐng
yín (丙寅),
the Emperor departed from Bìngzhōu (幷州);
on the day guǐsì (癸巳),
he arrived at Dōngdū (東都).
In the fifth month,
the Hébì Gōng (合璧宮) was constructed.
At this time, the Bāguān Gōng (八關宮) was renamed Hébì Gōng (合璧宮),
located within the Dōngdū (東都) gardens.
On the day rénxū (壬戌),
the Emperor visited the Hébì Gōng (合璧宮).
5 On the day wùchén (戊辰),
Àshǐdé Shūbīn (阿史德樞賓), the Dudufu of Dìngxiāng (定襄都督), Yántuó Tījīn (延陀梯真), the General of the Left Guards of the Military (左武候將軍)—
Tījīn (梯真)
was of the Xuē Yántuó (薛延陀) lineage,
hence he took it as his surname—
and Qián (岍),
same as,
which is Lěngjìng Shān (冷徑山).
The Xī (奚) and Qìdān (契丹) relied on this mountain for their defense,
its territory being south of the Huáng Shuǐ (潢水)
and north of Huánglóng (黃龍).
Furthermore, the Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (尚書右丞) Cuī Yúqìng (崔餘慶) was appointed as envoy to oversee the troops of the three tribes.
The Xī (奚) soon dispatched envoys to surrender.
Shūbīn (樞賓) and others were then appointed commanders of the Shāzhuān Dào (沙磚道) expeditionary army
to attack the Qìdān (契丹).
They captured Àbùgù (阿卜固), the Dudufu of Sōngmò (松漠), and sent him to Dōngdū (東都).
6 In the sixth month,
on the first day gēngwǔ (庚午),
there was a solar eclipse.
7 On the day jiǎwǔ (甲午),
the imperial carriage returned to Luòyáng Gōng (洛陽宮).
8 Liáng Wáng Zhōng (梁王忠), the Prefect of Fángzhōu (房州),
as he grew older,
became quite uneasy.
Sometimes he secretly wore women's clothing to guard against assassins;
he also frequently divined his own fortune.
Someone reported his affairs, and
in autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day yǐsì (乙巳),
Zhōng (忠) was deposed as a commoner
and exiled to Qiánzhōu (黔州),
imprisoned in the former residence of Chéngqián (承乾).
In the seventeenth year of Zhēngguān (貞觀) of Tài Zōng (太宗),
Crown Prince Chéngqián (承乾) was exiled to Qiánzhōu (黔zhou).
Qián (黔),
pronounced as qín.
9 On the day dīngmǎo (丁卯),
Lú Chéngqìng (盧承慶), Minister of the Department of Finance (度支尚書) and Joint Manager of Affairs with the Chancellery (同中書門下三品), was dismissed from office for mismanagement of levies.
The Minister of the Department of Finance (度支尚書)
was responsible for all matters concerning labor services, taxes, tribute,
expenditure calculations,
and the standards for the increase or decrease of stored goods.
All these were consulted with him.
Now, his mismanagement of levies
showed he was not competent for his position,
hence he was dismissed from his office.
Diào (調),
pronounced as tú diào.
10 In the eighth month,
Lù Dōngzàn (祿東贊) of Tǔbō (吐蕃) sent his son Qǐzhèng (起政) to lead troops to attack Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾),
because Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) had submitted to the Tang.
Tǔ (吐),
pronounced like tūn in entering tone.
Yù (谷),
pronounced like yù.
11 Sū Dìngfāng (蘇定方) led his troops from Chéngshān (成山), crossing the sea.
Bǎijì (百濟) held the mouth of the Hóngjīn Jiāng (熊津江) to resist them.
Dìngfāng (定方) advanced and defeated them;
several thousand Bǎijì (百濟) soldiers died,
the rest scattered and fled.
Dìngfāng (定方) advanced by both land and sea,
heading straight for their capital city.
The *Northern History* states: The capital of Bǎijì (百濟) was Jùbá Chéng (俱拔城),
also called Gùmá Chéng (固麻城).
Outside it were five other regions:
the central region was called Gǔshā Chéng (古沙城),
the eastern region was called Dé'ān Chéng (得安城),

In this year,
it was changed to Sīxiàn Dàfū,
a rank of zhèng wǔpǐn shàng,
assisting the Dàsīxiàn,
and upholding the national constitution and regulations to maintain order in the court.
Hái is pronounced hù gài fān;
also hù dé fān.

The emperor decreed that their merits should redeem their crimes,

Qìbì Hélì, the Grand General of the Zuǒ Xiāowèi, was appointed Tiělè Dào Ānfǔshǐ,
with Jiāng Kè, General of the Zuǒwèi, as his deputy,
to pacify the remaining tribes.
Hélì selected 500 elite cavalry and
galloped into the midst of the nine clans.
The barbarians were greatly alarmed.
Hélì then said:
"The state knows that you were all coerced.
Your crimes are pardoned.
The guilt lies with the chieftains;
once they are captured, the matter is settled."
The tribes were greatly pleased and
jointly seized their Yèhù, Shè, Tèlè, and over 200 others, handing them over to Hélì.
Hélì enumerated their crimes and executed them,

6 On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
the imperial carriage departed from Dōngdū;
on the *xīnhài* day,
the Emperor visited Púzhōu;
in summer,
the fourth month,
on the *gēngshēn* new moon day,
he arrived at Jīngshī.
7 On the *xīnsì* day,
the Pénglái Palace was built.
The Pénglái Palace was the Dàmíng Palace,
also called Dōngnèi.
Chéng Dàchāng said: The Dàmíng Palace grounds
were originally the shooting range on the northeast side of the rear garden of the Tàijí Palace,
located on Lóngshǒu Hill.
In the early years of Tàizōng's reign, the Yǒng'ān Palace was built on that site
to provide a summer retreat for the Tàishàng Huáng.
Although it was once renamed Dàmíng Palace,
the Tàishàng Huáng continued to reside in the Dà'ān Palace
and never moved in.
In the second year of Lóngshuò,
Gāozōng suffered from *fēngbì* (rheumatism)
and disliked the low-lying Tàijí Palace,
so he undertook repairs on the Dàmíng Palace,
renamed it Pénglái Palace,
taking the Pénglái Pond behind the hall as its name,
and carried out its construction.
8 In the fifth month,
on the *bǐngshēn* day,
Xǔ Yǔshī was made Zǔoxiàng.
9 In the sixth month,
on the *yǐchǒu* day,
an initial decree ordered monks, nuns, Daoist priests, and female officials to show respect to their parents.
10 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the *wùzǐ* new moon day,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the empire.
11 On the *dīngsì* day,
Liú Rénzhǐ, the Dūdu of Xióngzhīn, and Liú Rénzhuǐ, the Cìshǐ of Dàifāng Prefecture, thoroughly defeated Baekje to the east of Xióngzhīn,
and captured Zhēnxiàn City.
Initially,
Rénzhǐ, Rénzhuǐ, and others were stationed in Xióngzhīn City.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Last year, Dàochēn and Fúxìn besieged Rénzhǐ in the administrative city of Baekje.
Now it is said they are still in Xióngzhīn City.
Perhaps they are the same city.
Otherwise, after the siege was lifted,
they moved their encampment to Xióngzhīn City.
Due to the order
"The Píngyǎng army has returned.
One city cannot be held alone.
You should evacuate and join Silla.
If Jīn Fǎmǐn relies on your continued presence as a garrison,
you should temporarily stay there.
If he does not need you,
then you should return by sea."
The officers and soldiers all wished to return west.
Rénzhuǐ said:
"As ministers, in pursuing the interests of the state,
one should be prepared to die without wavering.
How can we first think of our private interests!
The Emperor wishes to destroy Gāolì,
and so first punished Baekje,
leaving troops to guard it,
controlling its heartland.
Although remnant bandits are rampant, our defenses are very strict.
We should sharpen our weapons and feed our horses,
striking when they least expect it;
there is no reason not to be victorious.
After victory,
the soldiers' hearts will be at ease.
Then we can divide our forces to occupy strategic points,
expand our positions,
send swift reports to the court,
and request additional troops.
When the court knows of our success,
they will surely order generals and dispatch armies.
As soon as reinforcements arrive,
the wicked villains will be annihilated.
Not only will we not abandon our success,
but we will also permanently pacify the lands across the sea.
Now, if the Píngyǎng army has already returned,
and Xióngzhīn is also evacuated—
'evacuated'
refers to moving the army to Silla,
or to the army returning west—
and we soon leave again,
when will the fleeing rebels of Gāolì
ever be eliminated!
Moreover, we are now in the center of enemy territory with only one city.
If we were to make any move,
we would be captured.
Even if we entered Silla,
we would still be mere guests.
Should things not go as desired,
regret would be too late.
Furthermore, Fúxìn is cruel, perverse, and tyrannical,
and the king and his ministers are suspicious of each other,
about to slaughter one another.
It is precisely right to stand firm and observe the changes,
taking advantage of the opportune moment.
We must not move."
The multitude followed his advice.
At that time, Baekje King Fēng and Fúxìn believed that Rénzhǐ and others were isolated in a city without support,
so they sent envoys to tell them:
"When will the Grand Envoy and others return west?
We shall send someone to see you off."
Rénzhǐ and Rénzhuǐ knew they were unprepared,
so they suddenly launched an attack,
capturing Zhīluó City and the stockades of Yǐnchéng, Dàshān, and Shājǐng,
killing and capturing many,
and dividing their troops to guard them.
Fúxìn and others, considering Zhēnxiàn City strategically important,
reinforced its defenses.
Rénzhuǐ waited until they were slightly relaxed,
led the Silla troops to approach the city at night,
scaled the walls by clinging to grass,
and by dawn,
entered and occupied the city,
thus opening a route for transporting provisions to Silla.
Rénzhǐ then submitted a memorial requesting more troops.
An imperial edict ordered 7,000 soldiers from Zī, Qīng, Lái, and Hǎi prefectures to proceed to Xióngzhīn.
The historian comments that Liú Rénzhuǐ was able to endure steadfastly and seize opportunities,
awaiting reinforcements to fully pacify Baekje.
Fúxìn monopolized power,
and he and Baekje King Fēng gradually became suspicious of each other.
Fúxìn feigned illness,
lying in a cave chamber,
intending to wait for Fēng to visit him and then kill him.
Fēng knew of this,
and led his trusted followers to ambush and kill Fúxìn;
it was indeed as Liú Rénzhuǐ had predicted.

Lóngshuò, Second Year
1 In the eighth month,
on the *rénchén* day,
Xǔ Jìngzōng was appointed Tàizǐ Shàoshī, Tóng Dōngxī Tái Sānpǐn, and Zhī Xī Tái Shì.
(Also) Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn, and Zhī Zhōngshū Shì.
2 In the ninth month,
on the *wùyín* day,
a decree was first issued that officials of the eighth and ninth ranks should wear blue.

the tenth month,
on the *dīngyǒu* day,
the Emperor visited the Lìshān Hot Springs,
and the Crown Prince supervised the state;
on the *dīngwèi* day,
he returned to the palace.

Shàngguān Yí of Shǎn, Xītái Shìláng, was appointed Tóng Dōngxī Tái Sānpǐn.
Xītái Shìláng
is Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Shǎn
is read as *shīrǎn*.

an imperial edict proclaimed that in the first month of the fourth year, rites would be performed at Tàishān,
and furthermore, in the second month of the coming year, the Emperor would visit Dōngdū.
6 Xǔ Yǔshī (許圉師), the Left Chancellor, had a son named Zìrán (自然) who was a Fèngniǎn Zhícháng (奉輦直長).
He hunted and encroached upon people's fields.
Fèngniǎn Zhícháng (奉輦直長)
is the same as Shàngniǎn Zhícháng (尚輦直長).
The Zhícháng (直長) of the six bureaus in the palace
held a rank of junior seventh grade.
In the Lóngshuò (龍朔) reign, the Shàngniǎn Jú (尚輦局) was renamed Fèngniǎn Jú (奉輦局).
Xiàng (相),
read *xiàng*.
Zhǎng (長),
read *zhǎng*.
Zìrán (自然) shot them with a whistling arrow.
Xǔ Yǔshī (許圉師) flogged Zìrán (自然) one hundred strokes but did not report it.
The field owner went to the Sīxiàn (司憲) to lodge a complaint.
The Sīxiàn Dàfū (司憲大夫), Yáng Déyì (楊德裔), did not handle it.
Yuán Gōngyú (袁公瑜), a Xītái Shèrén (西臺舍人), sent someone to change their name and submit a sealed memorial to expose it.
Xītái Shèrén (西臺舍人)
is the same as Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人).
Wéi (為),
read *wèi*.
Shàng (上),
read *shàng*.
"Xǔ Yǔshī (許圉師) is a Chancellor,
oppressing the common people,
concealing it and not reporting it.
Is this not 'wielding power and authority'?"
Xǔ Yǔshī (許圉師) bowed and said:
"Your subject occupies a pivotal position,
serving Your Majesty with integrity.
I cannot fully satisfy everyone's wishes,
and therefore I am attacked and exposed by others.
As for those who 'wield power and authority',
some hold strong armies in their hands,
or personally reside in important garrisons.
Your subject, as a civil official,
serves Your Sagely Majesty.
I only know how to keep to myself behind closed doors;
how would I dare to 'wield power and authority'?"
The Emperor angrily said:
"Are you resentful that you have no troops?!"
Xǔ Jìngzōng (許敬宗) said:
"A subject like this
commits a crime for which even execution is insufficient."
The Emperor immediately ordered him to be led out.
An imperial edict specially dismissed him from office.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The Old Annals state:
"On the *xīnwèi* (辛未) day of the eleventh month,
Xǔ Yǔshī (許圉師) was imprisoned."
The New Annals state:
"On the *xīnwèi* (辛未) day of the eleventh month,
Xǔ Yǔshī (許圉師) was demoted to Qínzhōu Cìshǐ (虔州刺史)."
Now, according to the *Shílù* (實錄),
on the *xīnwèi* (辛未) day,
he was dismissed from office.
After a long time,
he was demoted to Qínzhōu Cìshǐ (虔州刺史).
In the Old Annals,
the demotion to Qínzhōu Cìshǐ (虔州刺ǐ) was in the second month of the third year.
The New Annals are mistaken.

Xùlún (旭輪) later changed his name to Dàn (旦),

the people of Hébĕi (河北) were burdened by military service and levies.

He was ordered to dispatch the two Khans, Xīngxīwáng (興昔亡) and Jìwǎngjué (繼往絕), with their troops to accompany him.

"Míshè (彌射) is plotting rebellion; I request his execution."

So, he falsely claimed an imperial edict,

Xīngxīwáng (興昔亡) led his followers to receive the gifts,
and Hǎizhèng (海政) captured and beheaded them all.
His two tribes, Shǔníshī (鼠尼施) and Básaigān (拔塞幹), fled.

was one of the five tribes of Duōlù (咄陸);
Básaigān Sìjīn (拔塞幹俟斤)
was one of the five tribes of Nǔshībì (弩失畢).

read *zhǎng*.

And pacified them.
When the army returned
to Shūlè (疏勒),
the Southern Gōngyuè (弓月) tribe again led the forces of Tǔbō (吐蕃) there,
intending to fight the Táng (唐) troops.
Hǎizhèng (海政), with his army weary, dared not engage in battle.
He bribed Tǔbō (吐蕃) with military supplies
and made a peace agreement before returning.
Because of this, all the various tribes considered Xīngxīwáng (興昔亡) to have been wronged,
and each harbored disloyal sentiments.
Jìwǎngjué (繼往絕) soon died,
leaving the Ten Surnames without a leader.
Ashǐnà Dūzhī (阿史那都支) and Lǐ Zhēfú (李遮匐) gathered their remaining followers and allied with Tǔbō (吐蕃).
This set the stage for Dūzhī (都支) and Zhēfú (遮匐) to unite their armies and rebel.
10 In this year,
the Western Tūjué (突厥) raided Tíngzhōu (庭州).
The Cìshǐ (刺史), Lái Jì (來濟), led troops to resist them,
saying to his men:
"I have long been due to die;
fortunately, I have been preserved until today.
I must repay the nation with my life."
He then did not remove his armor,
and charged into the enemy, dying in battle.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Zhèng Réntài (鄭仁泰), the Zuǒwǔwèi Jiāngjūn (左武衞將軍), campaigned against the remaining remnants of the rebellious Tiělè (鐵勒),
and completely pacified them.
2 On the *yǐyǒu* (乙酉) day,
Lǐ Yìfǔ (李義府) was appointed Ròuxiàng (右相).
Ròuxiàng (右相)
was the same as Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令).
3 In the second month,
the Yànrán Dūhù Fǔ (燕然都護府) was moved to Huíhé (回紇)
and renamed Hànhǎi Dūhù (瀚海都護).
The former Hànhǎi Dūhù (瀚海都護) was moved to the old city of Yúnzhōng (雲中)
and renamed Yúnzhōng Dūhù (雲中都護).
The Yànrán Dūhù (燕然都護) was established in Zhēnguān (貞觀) twenty-first year,
found in volume one hundred ninety-eight.
The Hànhǎi Dūhù (瀚海都護) was established in Yǒnghuī (永徽) first year,
found in volume one hundred ninety-nine.
Yān (燕),
read *yān*.
Gēng (更),
read *gēng*.
All prefectures north of the Qì (磧) were subordinated to Hànhǎi (瀚海);
those south of the Qì (磧) were subordinated to Yúnzhōng (雲中).
The Yúnzhōng Dūhù Fǔ (雲中都護府) was administered from Jīnhé (金河),
which was the old city of Yúnzhōng (雲中) from the Qín (秦) and Hàn (漢) dynasties.
It was three hundred seventy *lǐ* (里) northeast of Shuòzhōu (朔州).
In Líndé (麟德) first year,
it was renamed Chányú Dàdūhù Fǔ (單于大都護府).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: The Chányú Dūhù Fǔ (單于都護府) was one hundred twenty *lǐ* (里) south of Yúlín Jùn (榆林郡)
and three hundred fifty *lǐ* (里) southeast of Mǎyì Jùn (馬邑郡).
Qì (磧),
read *qì*.
4 In the third month,
Xǔ Yǔshī (許圉師) was again demoted to Qínzhōu Cìshǐ (虔州刺史).
Qínzhōu (虔州) was four thousand seventeen *lǐ* (里) southeast of the capital,
and three thousand four hundred *lǐ* (里) from Dōngdū (東都).
Xǔ Yǔshī's (許圉師) sons Wénsī (文思) and Zìrán (自然) were both dismissed from office.
5 Lǐ Yìfǔ (李義府), the Ròuxiàng (右相) and Héjiān Jùngōng (河間郡公),
was in charge of official selection.
Relying on the power of the Empress,
he specialized in selling offices,
and the selection process was in disarray.
Complaints filled the roads.
The Emperor heard about this to some extent
and casually said to Lǐ Yìfǔ (李義府):
"Your son and son-in-law are quite careless
and commit many unlawful acts.
I am still covering for you,
so you should admonish them!"
Lǐ Yìfǔ (李義府) instantly changed color,
his neck and cheeks swelling.
He said:
"Who told Your Majesty?"
The Emperor said:
"I only said what I said;
why must you demand from me where I heard it?"
Lǐ Yìfǔ (李義ǔ) showed no remorse at all
and slowly walked away.
From then on, the Emperor was displeased.
The diviner Dù Yuánjì (杜元紀) told Yìfǔ (義府) that his residence had a "prison aura"
and that it would be advisable to accumulate 200,000 strings of cash to suppress it.
Yìfǔ (義府) believed this,
and his extortion became even more urgent.
While Yìfǔ (義府) was in mourning for his mother,
he was granted leave for weeping on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month.
He would invariably travel in disguise with Yuánjì (元紀) outside the eastern city gate,
ascend ancient tombs,
and observe the atmospheric colors.
Some reported that Yìfǔ (義fǔ) was secretly observing signs of misfortune,
harboring ulterior motives.
He also sent his son, the Yòu Sīyìláng Jīn (右司議郎津), to summon Yán (延), the grandson of Zhǎngsūn Wújí (長孫無忌),
from whom he accepted 700 strings of cash,
in exchange for appointing Yán (延) as Sījīnjiān (司津監).
In the Táng (唐) Eastern Palace,
there were four Sīyìláng (司議郎),
of正六品上 (zhèng liù pǐn shàng) rank,
in charge of submitting memorials and keeping records.
In the Lóngshuò (龍朔) era, Sīyìláng (司議郎) was renamed Zuǒ Sīyìláng (左司議郎),
and Tàizǐ Shèrén (太子舍人) was renamed Yòu Sīyìláng (右司議郎).
In the Hàn (漢) dynasty, there was a Dūshuǐzhǎng (都水長),
subordinate to Zhǔjué (主爵),
responsible for all ponds and marshes.
Later, it was changed to Shǐzhě (使者),
and in the Later Hàn (後漢), it was changed to Hédīyèzhě (河隄謁者).
The Jìn (晉) dynasty established the Dūshuǐtái (都水臺),
with one Shǐzhě (使者)
in charge of boats and oars.
The Liáng (梁) dynasty changed it to Tàizhōuqīng (太舟卿).
Northern Qí (北齊) also called it Dūshuǐtái (都水臺).
The Suí (隋) dynasty changed it to Dūshuǐjiān (都水監),
and Táng (唐) followed suit.
In the Zhēnguān (貞觀) era, it was changed to Shǐzhě (使者),
of 從六品 (cóng liù pǐn) rank.
In the first year of Lóngshuò (龍朔),
it was changed to Sījīnjiān (司津監),
responsible for the regulations concerning rivers, ferries, and bridges.
Summer,
fourth month,
on the day Yǐchǒu (乙丑),
Yìfǔ (義府) was imprisoned.
The Sīxíng Tàichángbó Liú Xiángdào (司刑太常伯劉祥道) was dispatched with Yùshǐ (御史) and Xiángxíng (詳刑) officials to jointly interrogate him.
Sīxíng Tàichángbó (司刑太常伯)
was the equivalent of Xíngbù Shàngshū (刑部尚書).
Xiángxíng (詳刑)
was the Dàlǐ (大理).
From the Yǒnghuī (永徽) era onwards in the Táng (唐) dynasty,
major cases were jointly investigated by officials from the Shàngshū Xíngbù (尚書刑部), Yùshǐtái (御史臺), and Dàlǐsì (大理寺),
known as the Three Courts (三司).
All charges were substantiated.
On the day Wùzǐ (戊子),
an imperial edict stripped Yìfǔ (義府) of his titles
and exiled him to Cuīzhōu (巂州).
Jīn (津) was stripped of his titles
and exiled to Zhènzhōu (振州).
All his sons and sons-in-law were stripped of their titles
and exiled to Tíngzhōu (庭州).
The court and the common people alike celebrated.
Someone wrote a *lùbù* (露布) [open report] titled "Liú Xiángdào (劉祥道), Commander of the Hékàndào (河間道) Army, Defeats the Great Bandit Lǐ Yìfǔ (李義府) at Tóngshān (銅山)."
Lǐ Yìfǔ (李義府) was a native of Hékàn (河間),
hence the name.
*Shuài* (帥) is pronounced *suǒ lèi fān* (所類翻).
Yìfǔ (義府) had taken many people's slaves.
When he fell,
they all scattered back to their homes.
Thus, his *lùbù* (露布) said:
"Slaves were mixed and scattered,
each knowing their home and eagerly returning."
This is a statement of the satisfaction of the people at that time with Yìfǔ's (義府) downfall,
and the *Tōngjiàn* (通鑑) recorded it as a lesson for future generations.
Scholars, when composing texts, often have a precedent.
When Emperor Gāo (高) of Hàn (漢) built Xīnfēng (新豐) for the Tàishàng Huáng (太上皇),
later generations recorded the event,
and the text said:
"Chickens and dogs were mixed and scattered,
each knowing their home and eagerly returning."
This phrase has a clear origin.
On the day Yǐwèi (乙未),
the Jīlín Dàdūdūfǔ (雞林大都督府) was established in the state of Xīnluó (新羅),
with Jīn Fǎmǐn (金法敏) as its head.
On the day Bǐngwǔ (丙午),
the Hányuándiàn (含元殿) of Péngláigōng (蓬萊宮) was completed.
The Emperor began to move his imperial retinue and reside there,
renaming the former palace the Xīnèi (西內).
The "renamed palace"
refers to the Tàijígōng (太極宮),
where the sovereign had resided since the Wǔdé (武德) era.
From this point onwards,
it was called the Xīnèi (西內).
*Gēng* (更) is pronounced *gōng héng fān* (工衡翻).
On the day Wùshēn (戊申),
he began to hold court in the Zǐchéndiàn (紫宸殿).
The main hall of Péngláigōng (蓬萊宮) was called Hányuándiàn (含元殿).
North of Hányuándiàn (含元殿) was Xuānzhèngdiàn (宣政殿).
North of Xuānzhèngdiàn (宣政殿) was Zǐchénmén (紫宸門),
inside which was Zǐchéndiàn (紫宸殿),
which was the main hall of the inner court.
Fifth month,
on the day Rénwǔ (壬午),
Wú Jūnjiě (吳君解), the chieftain of the Mán (蠻) in Liǔzhōu (柳州), rebelled.
Liǔzhōu (柳州) was the territory of the Hàn (漢) Tánzhōng (潭中) county.
The Suí (隋) dynasty established Máipíng (馬平) county.
In the fourth year of Táng (唐) Wǔdé (武德),
Nánkūnzhōu (南昆州) was established.
In the eighth year of Zhēnguān (貞觀), it was renamed Liǔzhōu (柳州).
Tǔbō (吐蕃) and Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) attacked each other.
Each sent envoys to present memorials arguing their case
and came seeking assistance in turn.
*Tǔ* (吐) is pronounced *cóng tūn rù shēng* (從暾入聲).
*Gǔ* (谷) is pronounced *yù* (音浴).
*Shǐ* (使) is pronounced *shū lì fān* (疏吏翻).
*Shàng* (上) is pronounced *shí zhǎng fān* (時掌翻).
*Gēng* (更) is pronounced *gōng héng fān* (工衡翻),
meaning "in turns."
Suǒhégùi (素和貴), a minister of Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾), committed a crime
and fled to Tǔbō (吐蕃),
where he fully revealed the strengths and weaknesses of Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾).
Tǔbō (吐蕃) sent troops to attack Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾)
and greatly defeated them.
Hébō (曷鉢), the Khagan of Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾), and Princess Hónghuà (弘化公主), leading several thousand tents, abandoned their country and fled to depend on Liángzhōu (涼州),
requesting to be resettled in the interior.
The *Táng Huìyào* (唐會要) states: Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾), from the end of Yǒngjiā (永嘉),
first crossed the Táoshuǐ (洮水) westward
and established a state in the former territory of the Qiāng (羌) people.
In the third year of Lóngshuò (龍朔),
it was destroyed by Tǔbō (吐蕃),
a total of 350 years.
*Shuài* (帥) is read as *lǜ* (率);
the same applies below.
Duógu Qīngyún (獨孤卿雲), Xīn Wénlíng (辛文陵) and other generals of the Yòu Wǔwèi (右武衛) were dispatched to station troops in the two prefectures of Liáng (涼) and Shàn (鄯)
to guard against Tǔbō (吐蕃).
Sixth month,
on the day Wùshēn (戊申),
Sū Dìngfāng (蘇定方), Grand General of the Zuǒ Wǔwèi (左武衛), was appointed Ānjí Dàshǐ (安集大使),
to command all armies
as reinforcements for Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾).
Lù Dōngzàn (祿東贊) of Tǔbō (吐蕃) was stationed at Qīnghǎi (青海).
He sent the envoy Lùn Zhōngzǒng (論仲琮) to appear before the Emperor.
In the early days of the Tǔbō (吐蕃) state,
there were Dàlùn (大論) and Xiǎolùn (小論) to govern state affairs,
and later it became a noble surname.
*Jiàn* (見) is pronounced *xián biàn fān* (賢遍翻).
He also requested a peace marriage.
The Emperor did not permit it.
Liú Wénxiáng (劉文祥), a Langzhong of the Zuǒwèi (左衞), was sent as an envoy to Tǔbō (吐蕃),
carrying an imperial letter rebuking them.
10. Autumn,
eighth month,
on the day Wùshēn (戊申),
the Emperor, observing that military campaigns had been waged in Hǎidōng (海東) for several years,
that the common people were distressed by conscription and levies,
and that many soldiers had died in battle or drowned,
issued an edict to cease the construction of ships in the thirty-six prefectures.
Sīyuán Tàichángbó Dòu Déxuán (司元太常伯竇德玄) and others
were dispatched.
Sīyuán Tàichángbó (司元太常伯)
was the equivalent of Hùbù Shàngshū (戶部尚書).
They were to inquire into the suffering of the people
and to assess and dismiss officials.
Déxuán (德玄) was the great-grandson of Yì (毅).
Dòu Yì (竇毅) was the father of Empress Tàimù (太穆皇后).
11. Ninth month,
on the day Wùwǔ (戊午),
Sūn Rénshī (孫仁師), the Xióngjīndào Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn (熊津道行軍總管) and Yòu Wēiwèi Jiàngjūn (右威衞將軍), and others, defeated the remaining forces of Báijì (百濟) and the Japanese army at Báijiāng (白江),
capturing their stronghold of Zhōuliúchéng (周留城).
Initially,
Liú Rén-yuàn and Liú Rén-guǐ had already conquered Zhēnxìan City.
Conquering Zhēnxìan City
is mentioned in Volume Two.
They crossed the sea to assist them.
Jiàng,
pronounced like "liàng";
same below.
Rén-shī combined his forces with Rén-yuàn and Rén-guǐ,
and their power greatly increased.
The various generals, seeing Gā-lín City's strategic location for both land and water,
wished to attack it first.
Rén-guǐ said:
"Gā-lín is steep and fortified.
A hasty attack will injure our soldiers,
while delaying will prolong the campaign.
Jú-liú City
is the rebels' lair,
where all the evildoers gather.
To eliminate evil, one must strike at the root."
These are the words of the *Tài Shì*.
"If we conquer Jú-liú,
the other cities will surrender on their own."
Thereupon, Rén-shī and Rén-yuàn, along with the Sīnxīluó King Fǎ-mǐn, led the land forces forward.
Rén-guǐ, with the separate general Dù Shuǎng and Fúyú Lóng, led the naval forces and grain ships from Xióngzhīn into Bái-jiāng,
to rendezvous with the land forces,
and together they advanced towards Jú-liú City.
They encountered Wō troops at Bái-jiāng-kǒu,
winning all four battles,
and burned four hundred of their ships.
The smoke and flames scorched the sky,
and the seawater all turned red.
Bǎijì King Fēng escaped and fled to Gāolì.
Princes Zhōng-shèng and Zhōng-zhì, leading their followers, surrendered.
Bǎijì was completely pacified,
except for the separate general Chí Xìn-shòu who held Rèn-cún City
and did not surrender.
Initially,
Hēichǐ Cháng-zhī, a man from the western part of Bǎijì,
was over seven *chǐ* tall,
valiant, brave, and resourceful.
He served Bǎijì as a Dáshuài and concurrently a commander of a district,
similar to a Cìshǐ in China.
Sīnxīluó officials had sixteen ranks;
Zuǒpíng was the first rank,
Dáshuài the second rank.
Each of the five regions had one Fānglǐng,
held by a Dáshuài;
a region had ten districts,
and a district had three commanders,
held by a Déshuài;
Déshuài was the fourth rank.
The official system of Bǎijì
was generally similar to Sīnxīluó.
Shuài,
pronounced "suǒ lèi fān".
Cháng-zhī led his subordinates and surrendered with the others.
Dìng-fāng imprisoned their king and crown prince,
let his soldiers plunder,
and many able-bodied men died.
Cháng-zhī was afraid,
and with a dozen or so of his close associates, escaped back to his original territory,
gathered the scattered remnants,
secured Rèn-cún Mountain,
and built stockades to defend themselves.
Within a month, over thirty thousand people had joined him.
Dìng-fāng sent troops to attack them.
Cháng-zhī resisted fiercely,
and the Táng army suffered a defeat.
Cháng-zhī recaptured over two hundred cities,
and Dìng-fāng, unable to overcome him, returned.
Cháng-zhī and the separate general Shāzhā Xiàng-rú,
Shāzhā,
is a foreign compound surname.
Zhā,
pronounced "zhì jiā fān".
After Bǎijì was defeated,
both led their troops to surrender.
Liú Rén-guǐ ordered Cháng-zhī and Xiàng-rú to lead their own troops,
take Rèn-cún City,
and assisted them with provisions and weapons.
Sūn Rén-shī said:
"These people have the hearts of beasts;
how can they be trusted?"
Rén-guǐ said:
"I observe that both men are loyal, brave, and resourceful,
and uphold trust and righteousness.
It's just that those they previously relied on
were not the right people.
Now is precisely the time for them to be grateful and prove their worth;
there's no need to doubt."
He then supplied them with provisions and weapons,
and dispatched a portion of his troops to follow them.
They attacked and captured Rèn-cún City,
and Chí Xìn-shòu abandoned his wife and children
and fled to Gāolì.
An imperial edict commanded Liú Rén-guǐ to lead troops and garrison Bǎijì,
and recalled Sūn Rén-shī and Liú Rén-yuàn.
After the ravages of war in Bǎijì,
every house was devastated and deserted,
and corpses filled the fields.
Rén-guǐ first ordered the burial of bones,
registered households,
reorganized villages,
appointed officials,
opened up roads,
built bridges,
repaired dikes and weirs,
restored reservoirs,
encouraged farming and sericulture,
provided relief to the poor,
cared for orphans and the elderly,
established Táng altars to the gods of land and grain,
and promulgated the correct calendar and imperial taboos.
Everything was accomplished according to Rén-guǐ's will,
truly illustrating the saying, "Where there's a will, there's a way."
Jiāng,
pronounced "jū liáng fān".
Yì,
pronounced "yú jì fān".
Zhǎng,
pronounced "zhī liǎng fān".
Zhèn,
pronounced "jīn rěn fān".
The entire territory was settled, with each person content in their occupation.
Afterwards, he established military colonies,
stored up provisions,
trained soldiers,
to plan the conquest of Gāolì.
When Liú Rén-yuàn arrived at the capital,
the Emperor asked him:
"When you were in Hǎidōng,
your memorials and reports were always
appropriate and well-reasoned.
Moreover, they were elegantly written.
You are fundamentally a military man;
how are you able to be like this?"
Rén-yuàn replied:
"This was all the work of Liú Rén-guǐ;
it was not within my capabilities."
The Emperor was pleased,
and promoted Rén-guǐ by six ranks.
Merits have grades,
and official positions have ranks.
He ordered a mansion to be built for him in Cháng'ān,
generously rewarded his wife and children,
and sent an envoy with an imperial rescript to commend and encourage him.
Shàngguān Yí said:
"Rén-guǐ, despite being dismissed and demoted, was still able to serve with utmost loyalty.
Dismissed and demoted
refers to serving in the military as a commoner to prove oneself.
He can truly be called a *jūnzǐ*!"
12 Winter,
Tenth Month,
on the *Xīnsì* day, the first day of the month,
an imperial edict commanded the Crown Prince to inspect the memorials from various bureaus inside Guāngshùn Gate every five days.
According to the *Táng Liù Diǎn*: Dàmíng Palace,
Zǐchén Hall was the main audience hall for court.
The south face of the hall was called Zǐchén Gate,
the left side Chóngmíng Gate,
and the right side Guāngshùn Gate.
All matters were entrusted to the Crown Prince for decision.
13 Twelfth Month,
on the *Gēngzǐ* day,
an imperial edict announced the change of the era name for the coming year.
14 On the *Rén'yín* day,
Gāo Xián, the Protector-General of Ānxī, was appointed as the General-in-Chief of the Expeditionary Army,
leading troops to attack Gōngyuè to rescue Yútián.
15 In this year,
Dàshí attacked Bōsī and Fúlǐn
and defeated them.
Fúlǐn
was the ancient Dàqín Kingdom.
It was located on the Western Sea,
also called the Hǎixī Kingdom.
It was forty thousand *lǐ* from the capital,
directly north of the Tūjué Kěsà tribe,
bordered by the sea to the west,
and contiguous with Bōsī to the southeast.
Dù Yòu said: Dàqín
was the Lǐqían Kingdom of the Former Hàn.
Lǐn,
pronounced "lì jǐn fān"
and also "lì zhèn fān".
*Lèi Piān* writes Fólǐn.
Dàshí swallowed up various Hú tribes,
with over four hundred thousand victorious soldiers.
The first year of Lǐndé (Lǐndé Yuánnián)
(*Jiǎzǐ*, 664 CE).
Last year, a unicorn was seen in Jiàngzhōu,
and a麒麟 horn was also seen in front of the Hànyuán Hall,
thus the era name was changed.
1 Spring,
First Month,
on the *Jiǎzǐ* day,
the Yúnzhōng Protectorate-General was renamed the Chányú Grand Protectorate-General,
and Yīn King Xù-lún was appointed Chányú Grand Protector-General.
Initially,
Lǐ Jìng (李靖) defeated the Tūjué (突厥).
See Volume 193, Taizōng (太宗) Zhēnguān (貞觀) fourth year.
Jué (厥),
do not read as Wù (勿).
The Ashǐdé (阿史德) clan was their leader.
By this time,
their tribes had gradually grown numerous,
and the Ashǐdé (阿史德) clan went to the imperial court
to request that, according to Hú (胡) custom, a亲王 (qīnwáng) be established as a Kèhán (可汗) to govern them.
The Emperor summoned them for an audience
and said:
"The Kèhán (可汗) of today
is the Chányú (單于) of old."
Therefore, it was renamed the Chányú Dūhùfǔ (單于都護府),
and Yīn Wáng (殷王) remotely held the office.
2 In the second month,
on the day Wùzǐ (戊子),
the Emperor proceeded to Wànnián Gōng (萬年宮).
In Yǒnghuī (永徽) first year,
Jiǔchéng Gōng (九成宮) was renamed Wànnián Gōng (萬年宮).
3 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Rénzǐ (壬子),
Wèi Zhōu (衞州) Cìshǐ (刺史) Dàoxiào Wáng (道孝王) Yuánqìng (元慶) passed away.
4 On the day Bǐngwǔ (丙午),
Wèi Zhōu (魏州) Cìshǐ (刺史) Xún Gōng (郇公) Xiàoxié (孝協) was found guilty of corruption
and granted death.
Sīzōngqīng (司宗卿) Lǒngxī Wáng (隴西王) Bóyì (博乂) submitted a memorial stating that Xiàoxié's (孝協) father, Shúliáng (叔良), died in service to the state.
Sīzōngqīng (司宗卿)
is the same as Zōngzhèngqīng (宗正卿).
Shúliáng (叔良)
was the grandson of Tàizǔ (太祖).
During Gāozǔ's (高祖) time,
Shúliáng (叔良) attacked the Tūjué (突厥)
and died from a stray arrow.
Xún (郇),
pronounced Xún.
(Bóyì (博乂) feared) that the lineage would be cut off.
The Emperor said:
"The law of uniform application
does not differentiate based on closeness or distance.
The Hàn Shū (漢書) says: Xiāo Hé (蕭何) made laws,
discussing them as if drawing a single line.
The commentary says: 'Drawing a single line'
means orderly and uniform.
Even the Crown Prince is not exempt.
Xiàoxié (孝協) has one son;
why worry about the lack of descendants to carry on the sacrifices?"
Xiàoxié (孝協) ultimately took his own life at his residence.
5 In the fifth month,
on the day Wùshēn (戊申), the first day of the month,
Suí Zhōu (遂州) Cìshǐ (刺史) Xǔ Dào Wáng (許悼王) Xiào (孝) passed away.
Xiào (孝)
was the Emperor's son,
born of a concubine.
6 On the day Yǐmǎo (乙卯),
the Yáo Zhōu Dūdūfǔ (姚州都督府) was established in Nòngdòng Chuān (弄棟川) of Kūnmíng (昆明).
Liú Xù (劉昫) says: The Yúnnán (雲南) county of Hàn (漢) Yìzhōu Jùn (益州郡)
was the ancient Diān Guó (滇國),
and in the Later Hàn (後漢) it belonged to Yǒngchāng Jùn (永昌郡).
The Shǔ (蜀) Liú (劉) clan divided Yǒngchāng (永昌) into Jiànníng Jùn (建寧郡),
and also divided Yǒngchāng (永昌) and Jiànníng (建寧) to establish Yúnnán Jùn (雲南郡),
with its seat of governance in Nòngdòng (弄梀).
The Jìn (晉) changed it to Jìnníng Jùn (晉寧郡),
and also established Níng Zhōu (寧州).
In Wǔdé (武德) fourth year,
Ānfǔ Dàshǐ (安撫大使) Lǐ Yīng (李英) established Yáo Zhōu (姚州) because many people in this prefecture were surnamed Yáo (姚).
Now it has been elevated to a Dūdūfǔ (都督府),
governing thirty-two prefectures.
7 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Dīngwèi (丁未), the first day of the month,
an imperial edict proclaimed that in the first month of the third year, sacrifices would be offered at Dàizōng (岱宗).
8 In the eighth month,
on the day Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
the imperial carriage returned to the capital,
proceeding to the old residence.
The old residence
was where the Emperor lived when he was Jìn Wáng (晉王).
On the day Rénwǔ (壬午),
he returned to Pénglái Gōng (蓬萊宮).
9 On the day Dīnghài (丁亥),
Sīliè Tàichángbó (司列太常伯) Liú Xiángdào (劉祥道) was concurrently appointed Yòu Xiàng (右相).
Sīliè Tàichángbó (司列太常伯)
is the same as Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書).
Dàsīxiàn (大司憲)
is the same as Yùshǐ Dàfū (御史大夫).
Sīyuán Tàichángbó (司元太常伯)
is the same as Hùbù Shàngshū (戶部尚書).
Zuǒ Xiàng (左相)
is the same as Shìzhōng (侍中).
In the 10th winter,
the 10th month,
on the *gēngchén* day,
Jiǎnjiào Xióngzhīn Dūdū Liú Rén'guǐ reported:
"Your servant has observed that among the remaining garrison troops,
many are weak and emaciated,
few are brave and strong.
Their clothes are poor and ragged,
they only think of returning west,
and have no desire to exert themselves.
Your servant asked them, 'Previously, when you were west of the sea,
I saw the common people eagerly volunteering,
competing to join the army,
some even offering to provide their own clothes and provisions,
calling it
"righteous conscription."
Why are the soldiers today like this?'
They all said, 'Today, the government is different from before,
and people's hearts are also different.
In previous campaigns to the east and west,
those who died for the royal cause
were all granted imperial envoys for condolences and sacrifices,
and posthumously awarded official titles and ranks.
Sometimes, the official titles and ranks of the deceased were transferred to their sons and younger brothers,
and all who crossed the Liáohǎi [sea]
were granted one promotion in merit.
Since the 5th year of Xiǎnqìng,
conscripted men have repeatedly crossed the sea,
but the government does not record them,
nor does anyone inquire about those who die.
(*Shuíhé* [誰何]
means to question;
to ask who they are
and why they died.)
As for the strong and wealthy,
by paying bribes to those who accompany and follow the officials,
they all manage to escape by fleeing and hiding.
(It means that when county officials recruit people for the army,
the accompanying clerks and soldiers
accept bribes from wealthy commoners,
concealing them
so they can escape and hide.
According to the 4th year of Yuánhé,
the Yùshǐ Tái reported: 'Recently, the number of attendants accompanying regular officials entering the Guāngfàn Mén and Zhōngshū Shěng has been quite large.')
(*Cāncóng* [參從] refers to the number of attendants.)
(*Cāncóng* [參從]
is similar to *cānzhú* [參逐].)
Once conscripted, they had to go immediately.
Recently, during the fierce battles to defeat Baekje and Pyeongyang—
(For the defeat of Baekje, see the earlier volume, Xiǎnqìng 5th year.)
(For the fierce battle at Pyeongyang, see Lóngshuò 2nd year.)
(*Bèi* [被],
pronounced *pí*.)—
they were promised endless rewards and honors;
but upon reaching the west bank,
all they heard of were shackles and imprisonment.
Their rewards and merits were confiscated and stripped,
and they were pursued by prefectures and counties,
unable to sustain themselves.
Public and private affairs were in dire straits,
too numerous to fully recount.
Because of this, even on the day they set out from west of the sea, there were already those who deserted or self-mutilated,
not just when they reached overseas.
Furthermore,
they originally took pride in their military ranks and merits from conscription;
but in recent years, those on campaigns
are all made to perform labor like hauling, even those with merit ranks,
their hardships being no different from commoners.
The common people are unwilling to join the army,
mostly for these reasons.'
Your servant further asked:
'In the past, soldiers who remained in garrison for five years
were still able to make ends meet.
Now, you have only been here for one year,
why are you so destitute and exposed?'
They all replied:
'When we first left home,
we were only ordered to prepare provisions for one year;
now it has been two years,
and there is no date for return.'
Your servant inspected the clothes left by the soldiers;
they are barely sufficient for this winter.
From next autumn onwards,
there will be no preparations at all.
Your Majesty keeps them overseas,
desiring to annihilate Gāogōuryǒ and Baekje.
Gāogōuryǒ's old factions lend support,
and though the Wō people are distant,
they also act in concert.
If there are no garrison troops,
it will again become one state.
Now, relying on garrison defense
and establishing military farms,
what is needed are soldiers united in purpose and virtue.
But with the multitude holding these views,
how can success be hoped for?
Unless there are changes and reforms,
and generous comfort and reward are given—
(Dǒng Zhòngshū said: 'If a *qín* or *sè* is out of tune,
it must be adjusted and restrung.')
(*Gēng* [更], pronounced *gōnghéng*.)
(*Láo* [勞], pronounced *lìdào*.)—
if the current arrangements prior to today merely continue,
I fear the army will grow weary and old,
and there will be no day for achieving results.
Perhaps no one has spoken these unpalatable truths
to Your Majesty exhaustively,
so your servant bares his heart
and risks death to present this memorial."
The emperor deeply accepted his words,
and dispatched Yòu Wēiwèi Jiāngjūn Liú Rén'yuàn to lead troops across the sea to replace the old garrison forces.
He also commanded Rén'guǐ to return with them.
Rén'guǐ said to Rén'yuàn:
"The state has an army deployed overseas,
intending to manage Gāogōuryǒ,
which is no easy task.
Now, the harvest is not yet complete,
but the military officials and soldiers are all departing at once,
and the military commander is also returning.
The barbarians have only recently submitted,
and the hearts of the people are not yet settled;
changes will surely arise.
It would be better to keep the old troops for now,
gradually letting them finish the harvest,
prepare provisions,
and send them back in stages;
(*Jiéjí* [節級]

they should not return yet."
Rén'yuàn said:

(*Zhǔn* [准]

([⿰⺘亶] is probably a character that was intended to be rendered, but without the appropriate context or a definition, it's impossible to assign a meaning or Pinyin. It seems to be a notation for a variant character, like 准 being a variant of 準.)
Rén'guǐ said:

The next year,
the *Shílù* states that Xióngzhīn Dūwèi Fúyú Lóng allied with Jīn Fǎmǐn.
We follow this account.)
In the 11th year,
initially,
Wǔ Hòu was able to humble herself and endure humiliation,

Therefore, the emperor overruled dissenting opinions and established her;
but once she gained power,
she wielded authority arbitrarily.
Whenever the emperor wanted to do something,
he was always controlled by the empress.
The emperor could not bear his resentment.
There was a Daoist priest, Guō Xíngzhēn,

The eunuch Wáng Fúshèng exposed him.
The emperor was furious,

Yí then said:

The emperor also agreed,
and immediately ordered Yí to draft an imperial edict.
The attendants rushed to inform the Empress.
The Empress immediately went to the Emperor to plead her case.
The draft imperial edict was still with the Emperor.
The Emperor felt ashamed and could not bear it,
so he treated her as before.
Fearing that the Empress might still resent him,

"I originally had no such intention;

Yí had previously served as a consultant to Chén Wáng,

Zhōng was established as Crown Prince by Chén Wáng.
The consultant-cavalry commander of a princely establishment

In the twelfth month,

Zuǒ Sùjī

All were implicated for conspiring with Yí.
From then on, whenever the Emperor attended to state affairs,

No matter the size of the affair,

The great power of the empire

Dismissals, promotions, executions, and pardons

The Son of Heaven merely folded his hands.
Both inside and outside the court, they called them the "Two Sages."
The Kǎoyì states: "The Táng Lì:

The Crown Prince's Right Zhōnghù and Acting Xītái Shìláng, Yuè Yànwěi.

the Left Shìjí, Lù Dūn xìn.

Inner ladies of rank: from the third rank down to female attendants,

"For the Shèshǒu sacrifice, the Empress serves as the secondary offerer."

Zhāng Gōngyì of Shòuzhāng, lived with nine generations of his family.

She said to Wéiliáng and the others:

Lóngzhōu
was ancient Jiāngyóu,

Háozhōu
was the land of Zhōnglí County during the Han dynasty.

The Liang dynasty established Běixú Prefecture.

The Tang dynasty called it Háozhōu.
Shǐzhōu was 1,662 *lǐ* from the capital,
and 2,560 *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
Lóngzhōu was 2,660 *lǐ* from the capital,
and 3,115 *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
Háozhōu was 2,150 *lǐ* from the capital,
and 1,313 *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
They died of sorrow.
Yuánshuǎng was banished to Zhènzhōu for an offense and died there.
Lady Hánguó and her daughter, due to the Empress, had free access to the forbidden palace,
and both received the Emperor's favor.
Lady Hánguó soon died.
Her daughter was granted the title Lady Wèiguó.
The Emperor wished to make Lady Wèiguó a palace concubine,
but found it difficult due to the Empress and remained undecided.
The Empress hated this.
It so happened that Wéiliáng, Huáiyùn, and prefects from various prefectures came to Mount Tài for the imperial audience.
They followed to the capital.
Wéiliáng and the others offered food.
The Empress secretly placed poison in the salted meat paste
and had Lady Wèiguó eat it.
She died suddenly.
The Empress then blamed Wéiliáng and Huáiyùn.
On the day Dīng Wèi,
they were executed,
and their surname was changed to Fù (蝮).
Huáiyùn's elder brother Huáiliàng had died early.
His wife, Lady Shàn, was particularly disrespectful to Lady Róngguó.
Because of Wéiliáng and the others, she was confiscated into the imperial harem.
Lady Róngguó ordered the Empress to flog her with a thorny whip for another offense,
until her flesh was completely gone and her bones were exposed, and she died.
8 In the ninth month,
Páng Tóngshàn severely defeated the Gāolì army.
Quán Nánshēng led his troops to join Tóngshàn.
An imperial edict appointed Nánshēng as Grand Master of Imperial Counsel and Grand Military Governor of Liáodōng,
concurrently Pacification Commissioner of Píngyǎng Circuit,
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Xuántú Commandery.
9. On the *wùzǐ* day,
Liú Xiángdào (劉祥道), Grand Master of Gold and Purple with Glorious Happiness, and retiring Duke Xuān (宣) of Guǎngpíng (廣平), passed away.
His son, Liú Qíxián (劉齊賢), succeeded him.
Qíxián was a righteous and upright man,
and the Emperor greatly esteemed him.
He was appointed Sīmǎ (司馬) of Jìnzhōu (晉州).
General Shǐ Xīngzōng (史興宗) once accompanied the Emperor on a hunt in the imperial park.
He mentioned that Jìnzhōu produced excellent goshawks,
and since Liú Qíxián was currently the Sīmǎ,
he requested that Qíxián be sent to capture them.
The Emperor said:
"Is Liú Qíxián a goshawk catcher?
Why do you treat him with such a request?!"
10. In winter,
in the twelfth month,
on the *jǐyǒu* day,
Lǐ Jì (李勣) was appointed Grand Commander of the Líaodōng (遼東) Circuit Expeditionary Army.
Hǎo Chǔjùn (郝處俊) of Ānlù (安陸), Junior 常伯 (Chángbó) of the Bureau of Officials, was made his deputy.
Ānlù County (安陸縣)
belonged to Jiāngxià (江夏) Commandery during the Hàn (漢) Dynasty.
During the Sòng (宋) Dynasty, it was partitioned to Ānlù Commandery.
During the Suí (隋) and Táng (唐) Dynasties, it belonged to Ānzhōu (安州).
Chǔ (處)
is pronounced *chānglǚ* (*昌呂*) reversed.
Páng Tóngshàn (龐同善) and Qìbì Hélì (契苾何力) concurrently served as Deputy Grand Commanders of the Líaodōng Circuit Expeditionary Army and concurrently Grand Commissioners of Pacification as before.
The various commanders of land and naval forces and the grain transport commissioners, Dòu Yìjī (竇義積), Dúgū Qīngyún (獨孤卿雲), Guō Dàifēng (郭待封), and others,
were all to receive orders from Jì.
The taxes and tributes from all the prefectures north of the Yellow River were to be sent to Líaodōng (遼東) for military provisions.
Dàifēng (待封)
was the son of Guō Xiàokè (郭孝恪).
Guō Xiàokè (郭孝恪) served Emperor Tàizōng (太宗)
and died in battle at Qiūcí (龜茲).
Jì (勣) wanted to go with his son-in-law, Dù Huáigōng (杜懷恭) of Jīngzhào (京兆),
to seek meritorious service.
Huáigōng declined, citing poverty.
Jì provided for him.
He again declined, citing lack of servants and horses,
and Jì again provided for him.
With no further excuses, Huáigōng
fled and hid in the Qíyáng (岐陽) mountains,
telling people:
"The Duke wants to make an example of me."
When Jì heard this,
he shed tears and said:
"Dù Láng (杜郎) is unrestrained" –
people at that time still called a son-in-law *láng* (郎).
Then he stopped (the attempt).
1. In spring,
in the first month,
the Emperor plowed the imperial field.
The officials presented plows and shares
that were adorned with carvings.
The Emperor said:
"Plows and shares are held by farmers.
How can they be so elaborate?"
He ordered them to be changed.
Afterwards, he plowed,
and stopped after nine pushes.
Regarding the system of plowing the imperial field,
the Yuèlìng (月令) and Zhèng Xuán's (鄭玄) commentary on the Zhōulǐ (周禮)
both state that the Son of Heaven plows three pushes.
Lú Zhí's (盧植) commentary on the Lǐjì (禮記) says: "The Son of Heaven plows the imperial field,
launching once and pushing the plow nine times."
This account uses Lú's (盧) theory.
Tuī (推)
is pronounced *tǔléi* (*吐雷*) reversed.
2. After the circulation of the Qiánfēng Quánbǎo (乾封泉寶) coins,
grain and silk became exceedingly expensive,
and merchants ceased operations.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
an imperial edict abolished them.
3. In the second month,
on the *dīngyǒu* day,
Lǐ Yīn (李愔), Prince Dào (悼) of Fúlíng (涪陵), passed away.
Yīn (愔)
was the Emperor's younger brother.
Fú (涪)
is pronounced *fú* (浮).
Yīn (愔)
is pronounced *yújiē* (*於今*) reversed.
4. On the *xīnchǒu* day,
Wànnián Palace (萬年宮) was renamed Jiǔchéng Palace (九成宮).
In the second year of Yǒnghuī (永徽),
Jiǔchéng Palace had been renamed Wànnián Palace.
Fù (復)
is pronounced *fúyòu* (*扶又*) reversed,
or as written.
5. The twelve prefectures of uncivilized Qiāng (羌) were conquered by Tǔbō (吐蕃).
In the third month,
on the *wùyín* day,
they were all abolished.
6. The Emperor repeatedly criticized his attendant officials for not recommending worthy people,
and none dared to respond.
Lǐ Ānqī (李安期), Junior 常伯 (Chángbó) of the Bureau of Officials, replied:
"The world is never without worthy people,
nor do humble officials dare to conceal them.
Junior 常伯 (Chángbó) of the Bureau of Officials
is equivalent to Shìláng (侍郎) of the Ministry of Personnel.
Shǎo (少)
is pronounced *shǐzhào* (*始照*) reversed.
Those who slander have already labeled them as factions;
those who are stagnated and not yet promoted cause those in office to be punished first.
This is why everyone strives to keep silent!
If Your Majesty truly treats them with utmost sincerity,
who would not wish to recommend those they know?
This depends on Your Majesty,
not on humble officials."
The Emperor deeply agreed with this.
Ānqī (安期)
was the son of Lǐ Bǎiyào (李百藥).
Lǐ Bǎiyào (李百藥)
was the son of Délín (德林).
Bǐ (比)
is pronounced *pízhì* (*毗至*) reversed.
7. In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the *yǐmǎo* day,

Yáng Hóngwǔ (楊弘武) and Dài Zhìdé (戴至德), both Shìláng (侍郎) of the Western Chancellery, Lǐ Ānqī (李安期), Grand Master of Rectification and concurrently Shìláng (侍郎) of the Eastern Chancellery, Zhāng Wénguàn (張文瓘) of Chānglè (昌樂), Shèrén (舍人) of the Eastern Chancellery, and Zhào Rénběn (趙仁本) of Héběi (河北), Junior 常伯 (Chángbó) of the Bureau of Officials and concurrently Grand Master of Rectification, were all appointed to the third rank of the Eastern and Western Chancelleries.
In Lóngshuò (龍朔), the title Gěishìzhōng (給事中) was changed to Dōngtái Shèrén (東臺舍人),
and Jiànyì Dàfū (諫議大夫) to Zhèngjiàn Dàfū (正諫大夫).
Lè (樂)
is pronounced *luò* (洛).
[Yáng Hóngwǔ (楊弘武)] was a disciple of Yáng Sù (楊素),
who was prominent and noble during the Suí (隋) Dynasty.
[Dài Zhìdé (戴至德)] was the elder brother's son of Dài Zhòu (戴冑).
Dài Zhòu (戴冑) was Prime Minister to Emperor Tàizōng (太宗).
Shàngyáng Palace (上陽宮) was located in the southwest corner of Luòyáng (洛陽) palace city.
To the south, it overlooked the Luò River (洛水),
to the west, it was separated by the Gǔ River (穀水),
to the east was the palace city,
and to the north, it connected to the forbidden garden.
The main gate and main hall within the palace all faced east.
The main gate was called Tíxiàng (提象),
and the main hall was called Guānfēng (觀風).
Within it were nine separate halls, pavilions, and observatories.
To the west of Shàngyáng,
across the Gǔ River (穀水),
was the Western Shàngyáng Palace (西上陽宮).
A rainbow bridge spanned the Gǔ River (穀水)
for imperial travel.
With ten thousand horses in the imperial stables,
the granaries gradually emptied.
Zhāng Wénguàn (張文瓘) remonstrated, saying:
"The lesson of the Suí (隋) Dynasty is not far off.
May Your Majesty not cause resentment among the common people."
The Emperor accepted his words
and reduced the number of imperial horses by several thousand.
8. In autumn,
in the eighth month,
on the *jǐchǒu* day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
9. On the *xīnhài* day,
Lǐ Ānqī (李安期), Shìláng (侍郎) of the Eastern Chancellery and concurrently of the third rank of the Eastern and Western Chancelleries, was sent out as Administrator of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Jīngzhōu (荊州)
was 1,730 *lǐ* southeast of the capital,
and 1,335 *lǐ* to the Eastern Capital.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: "Jīngzhōu (荊州)
was the land of Nánjùn (南郡) during the Qín (秦) Dynasty.
During the Hàn (漢) Dynasty, it was Línjiāng (臨江) Kingdom.
During the Eastern Jìn (晉), Jīngzhōu (荊州) was established as a crucial military command,
analogous to the partition of Shǎnxī (陝西) during the Zhōu (周) Dynasty.
During the Táng (唐) Dynasty, it was a Grand Military Governorship."
10. In the ninth month,
on the *gēngshēn* day,
due to a prolonged illness,
the Emperor ordered Crown Prince Hóng (弘) to oversee the state.
11. On the *xīnwèi* day,
Lǐ Jì (李勣) captured Xīnchéng (新城) of Gāolì (高麗),
and ordered Qìbì Hélì (契苾何力) to defend it.
When Jì (勣) first crossed the Liáo River (遼),
he said to his generals:
"Xīnchéng (新城) is a strategic stronghold on Gāolì's (高麗) western border.
If we do not capture it first,
the other cities will not be easy to take."
He then attacked it,
and the city dwellers, Shī Fūchóu (師夫仇) and others, bound the city lord and opened the gates to surrender.
Jì (勣) then led his troops to advance and attack,
and sixteen cities
all fell.
Páng Tóngshàn (龐同善) and Gāo Kǎn (高侃) were still at Xīnchéng (新城),
when Quán Nánjiàn (泉男建) sent troops to raid their camp.
Xuē Rén’guì (薛仁貴), General of the Left Wǔwèi (武衞), repelled them.
Kǎn (侃) advanced to Jīnshān (金山)
and fought with Gāolì (高麗)
but was at a disadvantage.
Gāolì (高麗) pursued their advantage,
but Rén’guì (仁貴) led his troops in a flanking attack,
inflicting a great defeat.
Over 50,000 heads were severed;
the New History (新書) states 5,000 heads were severed.
The three cities were later all converted into prefectures.
8 On the guǐyǒu day,
the imperial carriage returned to the capital.
9 In the ninth month,
on the guǐsì day,
Lǐ Jì captured Píngrǎng.
After Lǐ Jì had taken Dàxíng Chéng,
all the armies that had set out on other routes met with Lǐ Jì.
They advanced to Yālù Zhà.
Gāolì dispatched troops to resist,
but Lǐ Jì and others fought fiercely,
defeating them utterly.
They pursued the fleeing enemy for over two hundred *lǐ*,
and captured Rǔyí Chéng.
Cities either fled or surrendered one after another.
Qìbì Hélì had previously led his troops to the foot of Píngrǎng City,
and Lǐ Jì's army followed.
They besieged Píngrǎng for over a month.
Gāolì King Zàng sent Quán Nánchǎn, leading ninety-eight chieftains,
to Lǐ Jì with white banners to surrender.
Lǐ Jì received them with courtesy.
Quán Nánjiàn still kept the gates closed and resisted,
frequently dispatching troops to engage in battle,
but they were all defeated.
Nánjiàn entrusted military affairs to the monk Xìnchéng.
Xìnchéng secretly sent someone to Lǐ Jì,
requesting to act as an inside agent.
Five days later,
Xìnchéng opened the gates,
and Lǐ Jì unleashed his troops to climb the walls amidst war cries.
He burned the city's *sìyuè*.
"Yuè"
should be
"jiǎo"
or else
"zhōu".
Nánjiàn did not die;
he was captured.
Gāolì was completely pacified.
10 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the wùwǔ day,
Lukayīta, a Brahman from the kingdom of Wútú, was appointed Huáihuà Dàjiāngjūn.
Wútú Guó,
also called Wūcháng,
is directly south of Tiānzhú.
It is six hundred *lǐ* east of Bólǜ
and four hundred *lǐ* west of Jìbīn.
Bāluómén means
monk.
The Táng dynasty established the Huáihuà Dàjiāngjūn,
a third-rank official,
to be conferred upon barbarian officials.
The emperor was about to consume elixirs.
Hǎo Chùjùn, Shìláng of the Dōngtái, remonstrated, saying:
"Life and death are decreed by fate;
they cannot be prolonged by medicine.
At the end of the Zhēngguān era,
the former emperor took medicines from Nāluóěrsuōpómèi,
but they had no effect.
When he was critically ill,
the famous physicians knew not what to do.
The critics blamed Suōpómèi,
and were about to execute him publicly,
but fearing ridicule from the *Róng* and *Dí*, they stopped.
The matter of Suōpómèi can be found in the previous volume, Xiǎnqìng 2nd year.
I wish Your Majesty would examine this deeply."
The emperor then stopped.
11 When Lǐ Jì was about to arrive,
the emperor ordered Gāo Zàng and others to be first presented at Zhāolíng,
with full military regalia,
playing triumphal music.
They entered the capital
and were presented at the Tàimiào.
In the twelfth month,
on the dīngsì day,
the emperor received the captives at Hányuán Diàn.
The main hall of the eastern palace was called Hányuán Diàn.
The Táng Liù Diǎn states: Hányuán Diàn is on the eastern foot of Lóngshǒu Shān.
Its steps are over forty *chǐ* higher than the ground.
It is over four hundred paces south of Dānfèng Mén.
Its width from east to west is five hundred paces.
In front of the hall, there are three tiers of jade steps.
Each tier extends with a *chítóu*.
Below it is the Lóngwěi Dào,
winding and curving
seven times in all.
He was pardoned and made Sīpíng Tàichángbó,
with the special appointment of Yuánwài,
and holding full official status (*tóngzhèng*).
Sīpíng Tàichángbó
was the same as Gōngbù Shàngshū.
According to the old records,
in the fifth year of Yǒnghuī,
Jiǎng Xiàozhāng, Fèngyù of the Shàngyào Bureau, was specially appointed Yuánwài,
and still held full official status.
The practice of Yuánwài Tóngzhèng
began from this time.
Sīzǎi Shàoqīng
was the same as Guānglù Shàoqīng.
Quán Nánshēng was made Yòuwèi Dàjiāngjūn.
Lǐ Jì and others
received various awards and titles.
Quán Nánjiàn was exiled to Qiánzhōng,
and Fúyú Fēng was exiled to Língnán.
Gāolì's five divisions, one hundred seventy-six cities, and over six hundred ninety thousand households
were divided into nine Dūdufǔ
and forty-two Zhōu.
Xīnchéng Zhōu, Liáochéng Zhōu, Gēwù Zhōu, Wèilè Zhōu, Shèlì Zhōu, Jūsù Zhōu, Yuèxǐ Zhōu,
Qùdàn Zhōu, Jiàn'ān Zhōu; there were nine Dūdufǔ in total.
Of the forty-two Zhōu,
those preserved in records
are only Nánsū, Gàimóu, Dàinà, Cāngyán, Mó Mǐ, Jīlì, Líshān, Yánjīn, Mùdǐ, Ānshì, Zhūběi, Shílí, Fúniè, and Bàihàn, fourteen Zhōu in total.
The Āndōng Dūhùfǔ was established in Píngrǎng to govern them.
Their meritorious chieftains were promoted to Dūdu, Císhǐ, and Xiànlìng,
and governed jointly with Chinese officials.
Xuē Rénguì, Yòuwēi Wèi Dàjiāngjūn, was appointed Jiǎnjiào Āndōng Dūhù,
commanding twenty thousand troops to pacify the region.
On the dīngmǎo day,
the emperor offered sacrifices at Nánjiāo,
announcing the pacification of Gāolì,
with Lǐ Jì serving as the secondary offerer.
On the jǐsì day,
he paid respects at the Tàimiào.
12 Liú Yányòu, Wèinán Wèi,
at a young age, passed the *jìnshì* examination.
Wèinán Xiàn
belonged to Yōngzhōu.
It was Wèinán Jùn in the Later Wèi,
and was abolished as a county in the Later Zhōu.
Guàn
is pronounced gǔwán.
Among the counties of Táng Yōngzhōu,
Wànnián and Cháng'ān were *chìxiàn*,
and the remaining counties were *jīxiàn*.
The Liù Diǎn states: counties within the city were *jīngxiàn*,
and counties outside the city were *jīxiàn*.
"Your Excellency is still young in years,
yet you have already attained such great renown.
You should humble yourself somewhat,
and not always stand out above others."
Historians say Lǐ Jì loved people with virtue.
13 At that time, there was an imperial edict
stating that if soldiers of the Liaodong campaign fled,
and did not surrender within the time limit, or surrendered and then fled again,
they would be executed,
and their wives and children would be confiscated.
The Crown Prince submitted a memorial,
stating:
"There are many such cases: some fall ill and cannot keep up with their units,
and flee out of fear;
some are captured by bandits while gathering firewood;
some are lost at sea;
some penetrate deep into enemy territory and are wounded or killed.
Military law is severe,
and fellow squad members fear being implicated and punished,
so they immediately report them as deserters.
In the midst of military campaigns,
there is no time for investigation,
and based solely on the reports from squad leaders, notifications are sent to the relevant authorities,
and their wives and children are confiscated by the government.
The actual circumstances are pitiable.
The *Shū* says: 'Rather than kill the innocent,
it is better to err on the side of not killing in accordance with normal rules.'
These are the words from the *Dàyǔ Mú* chapter of the *Shū*.
The commentary says: *Jīng*
means 'normal' or 'constant'.
It is better to err by not applying the normal punishment
than to wrongly harm the innocent and good.
Exempt them from confiscation and enslavement."
This was adopted.
14 On the jiǎxū day,
Jiāng Kè, Sīróng Tàichángbó, concurrently served as Jiǎnjiào Zuǒxiàng.
Yán Lìběn, Sīpíng Tàichángbó, held the office of Yòuxiàng.
15 In this year,
the capital, Shāndōng, Jiāng, and Huái regions suffered drought
and famine.
1 In spring,
the second month,
on the xīnyǒu day,
Zhāng Wénguàn was appointed Dōngtái Shìláng.
Lǐ Jìngxúan of Qiáo, Yòusùjī and Jiǎnjiào Tàizǐ Zhōnghù, was appointed Xītái Shìláng.
Qiáo Xiàn was part of Bózhōu.
Previously, officials of the third rank did not have their titles included in the official designation,
but from this time on, they began to be included.
2 Guǐhài,
Lú Chéngqìng, the Prefect of Yōngzhōu, was appointed Sīxíng Tàichángbó.
Chéngqìng often evaluated internal and external officials.
There was one official who supervised transport,
and lost rice due to a storm.
Chéngqìng evaluated him, saying:
"Supervising transport and losing provisions earns a 'middle-lower' evaluation."
The man's expression was composed,
and he withdrew without a word.
Chéngqìng respected his refined composure,
and changed the annotation, saying:
"Beyond his control, earning a 'middle-middle' evaluation."
He showed neither joy
nor words of shame.
Chéngqìng changed it again, saying:
"Unaffected by favor or disgrace, earning a 'middle-upper' evaluation."
3 In the third month,
Bǐngxū,
Hǎo Chǔjùn, the Shìláng of Dōngtái, was appointed Tóng Dōng-Xītái Sānpǐn.
4 Dīnghài,
an edict decreed the system for the Míngtáng: its base would be octagonal,
its roof circular,
covered with pure yang jade leaves.
Its gates, walls, steps,
window lattices, lintels, pillars,
brackets, and corbels.
The Shuōwén states: those in the wall are called yǒu (牖),
those in the roof are called chuāng (窗).
The Shìmíng states: Chuāng (窗),
means cōng (聰),
referring to the ability to see outside from within.
Líng (櫺),
pronounced Lú Jīng,
refers to the space between the balusters in a window partition.
Méi (楣),
is the roof eaves.
The Shuōwén states: Méi (楣),
is the edge of the roof.
Máo Huǎng states: the horizontal timber under the rafters is called méi.
Zhù (柱),
is a pillar.
Yǎng (枊),
pronounced Yú Gāng.
Diagonal rafters are called fēiyǎng.
Jié (楶),
pronounced Zǐ Jié,
is a capital on a beam.
Jī (枅),
pronounced Jiān Xī,
is a roof corbel,
used to support purlins.
Gǒng (栱),
pronounced Jū Sǒng,
is a large wedge,
also a bracket.
After the edict was issued,
public opinion remained undecided,
and it coincided with a famine,
so it ultimately was not built.
5 In the summer,
in the fourth month,
on Jǐyǒu (the first day of the month),
the Emperor proceeded to Jiǔchénggōng.
6 Many Gāolì people were defecting.
An imperial order relocated thirty-eight thousand two hundred Gāolì households to the south of Jiāng and Huái,
and to the vacant lands in the various prefectures of Shānnán and Jīngxī.
The poor and weak among them were left
to guard Āndōng.
7 In the sixth month,
on Wùshēn (the first day of the month),
there was a solar eclipse.
8 In the autumn,
in the eighth month,
on Dīngwèi (the first day of the month),
an edict was issued for the Emperor to proceed to Liángzhōu in the tenth month.
At that time, Lǒngyòu was desolate,
and many advisors thought it was not appropriate for an imperial tour.
When the Emperor heard of this,
on Xīnhài,
he held court in Yánfú Diàn.
There was a Yánfú Diàn in Jiǔchénggōng.
"Since ancient times, emperors
have never failed to conduct inspection tours,
therefore I wish to inspect distant customs.
If it is indeed impossible,
why not state it to my face,
rather than retreat and speak behind my back?
Why is this?"
From the prime ministers downwards, no one dared to reply.
Lái Gōngmǐn, the Xiángxíng Dàfū, alone stepped forward and said:

According to Táng regulations: the Twenty-four Bureaus of the Shàngshū province,

Broadly, the selection methods of the Táng dynasty
involved judging people by their physical appearance (shēn), speech (yán), calligraphy (shū), and judgment (pàn).
The Táng method of selecting people had four criteria: The first was shēn,
which required a dignified and imposing physique.
The second was yán,
which required eloquent and precise speech.
The third was shū,
which required elegant and vigorous standard script.
The fourth was pàn,
which required excellent literary reasoning.
Initially, when candidates assembled for examination,
their shū and pàn were observed.
After the examination, for the evaluation (quān),
their shēn and yán were scrutinized.
After the evaluation, for the appointment (zhù),
their suitability and convenience were inquired about.
After the appointment, for the proclamation (chàng),
the assembly was gathered and informed.
Then they were categorized into grades,
and the Púshè first reviewed them.
Then they were submitted to the Ménxià,
where the Gěishìzhōng read them,
the Shìláng examined them,
and the Shìzhōng scrutinized them.
Those found unsuitable were rejected and sent back.
Once scrutinized,
they were then reported to the Emperor.
The officials in charge received the imperial edict and carried it out,
issuing each a credential,
called a gàoshēn.

with no more than one *chǐ* of movement from the original position.
