one had to carry five *hú* of rice
and walk twenty paces.

Qí,

were called Báicuì.
Those who passed these grades could be appointed without limit.
For officials in the prefectures and counties of Qiánzhōng, Lǐngnán, and Mínzhōng,
they were not under the Lìbù,
but the Dūdū was entrusted to select local people for appointment.
All officials were assessed annually based on their performance,
and for those of the sixth rank and below,
four assessments constituted a full term.

on the day *gēngwǔ*,
the Tǔyùhún were moved to the south of the Hàowěi River in Shànzhōu.
According to the *Hàn Shū* Geography Treatise, the Hàowěi River flows east to Yǔnwú and enters the Huáng River.
Yǔnwú
became Lóngzhī County of Shànzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: The Hàowěi River emerges from outside the passes northwest of Yǔnwú,
flows east past the old city of Hàowěi County to its south,
and then flows further east to join the Huáng River.
The common people call it the Gémén River.
Tǔ,
rhymes with *tūn* entering tone.
Gǔ,
pronounces as *yù*.
Shàn,
pronounces as *shízhàn*.
Hào,
pronounces as *gào*.
Wěi,
pronounces as *mén*.
They were not settled in their dwellings,
and the land in Shànzhōu was narrow,
so they were soon moved to Língzhōu.
Their tribes were used to establish Ānlèzhōu.
At that time, Ānlèzhōu was established on the territory of Míngshā County in Língzhōu.
Lè,
pronounces as *luò*.
Kě,
rhymes with *kān* entering tone.
Hàn,
pronounces as *hán*.
4 On the day *jǐmǎo*,
the Grand Councilor, Duke of Yǒng'ān Commandery, Jiāng Kè, passed away.
5 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day *gēngwǔ*,
the Emperor went to the Hébì Palace.
6 Tǔfān dispatched its high minister Zhòng Cóng to present tribute.
The Emperor asked him about Tǔfān customs.
He replied:
"Tǔfān has barren land and a cold climate,
and its customs are simple and unrefined.
However, its laws and regulations are strict and orderly,
and superiors and subordinates are of one mind.
Discussions about affairs always begin from below,
and actions are taken based on what benefits the people.
This is why it can endure for a long time."
The Emperor pressed him about the annexation of Tǔyùhún
(see the previous volume, Lóngshuò 3rd year)
and the defeat
(rhymes with *qùjí*)
(see the previous volume, Xiánhéng 1st year)
(rhymes with *bǔmài*) of Xīyù,
stating that since Tǔfān had destroyed Tǔyùhún
and conquered Xīyù,
bandits would soon press upon Liángzhōu.
(Zhòng Cóng replied):
"Your servant received orders only to present tribute;
military matters
are not what I have heard of."
The Emperor richly rewarded him and sent him away.
On the day *guǐwèi*,
the Emperor sent Huáng Rénsù, the Director of Waterways, as envoy to Tǔfān.
7 In autumn,
in the eighth month,
on the day *rénwǔ*,
the Special Advancement, Duke of Gāoyáng Commandery, Xǔ Jìngzōng, passed away.
Yuán Sīgǔ, a Taichang scholar, argued:
"Jìngzōng abandoned his eldest son in a desolate frontier
and married his young daughter to barbarian tribes.
According to the methods of bestowing posthumous titles,
'when name and reality are at odds, it is called *miù*,'
so I request the posthumous title *miù*."
Jìngzōng's grandson, the Palace Aide to the Crown Prince, Yànbó, argued that Sīgǔ held a grudge against the Xǔ family
and requested a change of posthumous title.
Wáng Fúzhì, a Taichang scholar, argued,
believing that:
"Gain or loss is for a single morning,
but glory or disgrace for a thousand years.
Taichang scholars, when proposing posthumous titles,
all base their praise or criticism on their accomplishments and conduct.
Great deeds are given great names,
and small deeds small names.
(Zài,
pronounces as *zǐhài*.)
One should adhere to the law and strict standards.
If not,
the principle cannot be overridden."
Dài Zhìdé, the Minister of Revenue, said to Fúzhì:
"Duke Gāoyáng held such high appointments and favor,
why should his posthumous title be *miù*?"
He replied:
"In the past, Hé Céng, the Minister of Works of Jìn, was both loyal and filial,
but merely because he consumed ten thousand cash daily,
Qín Xiù gave him the posthumous title of 'Miù.'
(See volume 80, Jìn Wǔdì Xiánníng 4th year.)
Xǔ Jìngzōng's excessive indulgence in food, drink, and women surpassed this,
so to give him the posthumous title 'Miù'
would not be unfair to the Xǔ family."
An imperial edict ordered all officials of the fifth rank and above to deliberate further.
Yáng Sījìng, the Minister of Rites, argued:
"According to the methods of bestowing posthumous titles,
'one who corrects mistakes after committing them is called *gōng*,'
so I request the posthumous title *gōng*."
The imperial edict followed this.
Xǔ Jìngzōng had previously memorialized to exile his son Āng to Língnán,
and also married his daughter to the son of Fēng Āng, a barbarian chieftain,
accepting much wealth from them,
which is why Sīgǔ brought it up in his discussion.
Fúzhì
was the father of Bó.
(For Wáng Bó,
see volume 200, Lóngshuò 1st year.)
8 In the ninth month,
on the day *guǐmǎo*,
Wáng Xián, the Prince of Pèi, was moved to become the Prince of Yōng.
9 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day *jǐwèi*,
an imperial edict commanded the Crown Prince to oversee the state.
10 On the day *rénxū*,
the imperial carriage departed from the Eastern Capital.
11 In the eleventh month,
on the day *wùzǐ*, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
12 On the day *jiǎchén*,
the imperial carriage arrived at the capital.
13 In the twelfth month,
Gāo Kǎn battled the remaining forces of Gāogōuryǒ
at Báishuǐshān and defeated them.
Sīllá dispatched troops to aid Gāogōuryǒ,
but Kǎn attacked and defeated them.
14 On the day *guǐmǎo*,
Liú Rén'guǐ, Left Senior Scribe, was appointed Concurrent Minister of the Secretariat and Chancellery (third rank).
15 The Crown Prince rarely met with his palace officials.
Xíng Wénwěi of Quánjiāo, the Aide to the Directorate of Palace Kitchens, on his own initiative reduced the provisions of meals.
(The Director of the Eastern Palace Directorate of Palace Kitchens was of Upper Sixth Rank;
the Aide
was of Upper Eighth Rank:
both were responsible for presenting and tasting meals.
Quánjiāo County at the time belonged to Chúzhōu.)
The Crown Prince replied in writing,
apologizing due to frequent illness and little leisure time when attending the Emperor,
and commended and accepted his intention.
Soon after,
the post of Right Scribe was vacant.
The Emperor said:
"Xíng Wénwěi served my son,
and was able to reduce meals to offer remonstrance;
he is an upright scholar."
He was promoted to Right Scribe.
Once, during a banquet, the Crown Prince
ordered his palace officials to perform "throwing down."
(Among the Táng court music performances were plate dancing, wheel dancing, tall stilts, bell jumping, throwing down, sword jumping, and sword swallowing,
all inherited from the Liáng dynasty.
The Suí dynasty established the Crown Prince's Inner Guard Bureau,
patterned after the Imperial Household Grand Militias,
responsible for the Crown Prince's personal guards and attendance.
In Lóngshuò, it was renamed the Left and Right Fèngyù Guards.)
(Suài,
pronounces as *suǒlǜ*.)
(Xíng Wénwěi said): "There are performers for 'throwing down.'
If your servant were to obey this order,
I fear it would not be a way to support Your Highness."
The Crown Prince thanked him.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he bestowed upon him a hundred bolts of excellent silk,
and he was soon promoted to General of the Left Qiānniú Guard.
(The Qiānniú sword
was the sovereign's personal defensive sword,
taking its meaning from Zhuāngzǐ's anecdote of Páo Dīng dismembering thousands of oxen
without dulling his sharp blade.
The Later Wèi had Qiānniú guards,
responsible for night watch and attendance.
Suí Yángdì established the Guards Bureau,
which the Táng dynasty renamed the Qiānniú Bureau.)
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day *bǐngchén*,
Zhèng Huìwáng Yuán Yì, the Prefect of Jiàngzhōu, passed away.
2 In the third month,
on the day *bǐngshēn*,
an imperial edict commanded Liú Rén'guǐ and others to revise the national history,
because much of what Xǔ Jìngzōng and others had recorded was inaccurate.
3 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day *bǐngzǐ*,
the imperial carriage went to the Jiǔchéng Palace.
4 In the intercalary fifth month,
Lǐ Jǐnháng, Grand General-in-Chief of the Right and Grand Administrator of Yānshān Dao, thoroughly defeated the Goguryeo rebels west of Hùlú Hé.
Hú Qiáo said: "North of Hēichēzǐ,
there are Niútí Tūjué (Ox-hoof Turks),
who have human bodies and ox feet.
Their land is extremely cold;
the river is called Hù Hé.
In summer and autumn, the ice is two feet thick;
in autumn and winter, the ice reaches the bottom.
They constantly burn vessels to melt the ice
before they can drink."
I note, according to the biography of Liú Rén'guǐ in the Old Book of Tang,
that this Hùlú Hé should be in the southern border of Goguryeo,
north of Xīlluó's Qīchóngchéng.
Yān
is pronounced with the sound of jiān;
the same below.
The remaining troops all fled to Xīlluó.
At that time, Lǐ Jǐnháng's wife, Lady Liú, was staying in Fánnú Chéng.
Goguryeo led the Mòhé to attack it.
Lady Liú donned armor and led the troops to defend the city.
After a long time,
the barbarians retreated.
The Emperor praised her achievements
and enfeoffed her as Lady of Yānguó.
Lǐ Jǐnháng
was the son of Tūdìjī, a Mòhé man.
Tūdìjī is mentioned in volume 189, Gāozǔ Wǔdé fourth year.
He was feared by all the barbarian tribes.
5 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Wùzhōu suffered a great flood,
drowning five thousand people.
6 In the eighth month,
on the day Xīchǒu,
the Emperor, suffering from malaria,
ordered the Crown Prince to receive memorials from all departments at Yánfú Diàn.
7 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Rénwǔ,
Yán Lìběn, Grand Imperial Secretary, passed away.
8 On the day Yǐsì,
the imperial carriage returned to the capital.
9 In the twelfth month,
on the day Bǐngwǔ,
the two kings of Gōngyuè and Shūlè submitted.
During the reign of Xīngxīwáng Kèhán of the Western Tūjué,
the various tribes scattered,
and Gōngyuè and Āxījí both rebelled.
Āxījí is Āxījié,
one of the five chiefs of the Nǔshīpì.
See volume 200, Xiǎnqìng second year.
Gōngyuè allied with Tǔbō in the south
and recruited Yànmàifèn in the north.
Yànmàifèn
was also a Tīelè tribe,
residing by Déyì Hǎi.
Yàn
is pronounced with the sound of Yúdiàn;
mài
is pronounced with the sound of Miánjiàn.
They surrendered.
The Emperor dispatched Xiāo Sìyè, Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials, to lead troops to suppress them.
Before Sìyè's troops arrived,
Gōngyuè, in fear,
along with Shūlè, both came to court;
the Emperor pardoned their crimes
and sent them back to their countries.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Rénwǔ,
Liú Rén'guǐ, Left Supervising Secretary and concurrently Grand Minister of the Secretariats, was appointed Grand Administrator of Jīlíndao.
The Emperor designated the state of Xīlluó as Jīlínzhōu.
Troops were dispatched to attack Xīlluó.
At that time, Fǎmǐn, King of Xīlluó, had already taken in the Goguryeo rebels,
and also occupied the former territory of Báijì,
stationing men to guard it.
The Emperor was greatly enraged,
and issued an edict to strip Fǎmǐn of his official titles and ranks;
his younger brother Rénwèn, General-in-Chief of the Right Guard Extra-rank and Duke of Línhǎi Commandery, who was in the capital,
was enthroned as King of Xīlluó
and sent back to his country.
2 In the third month,
on the day Xīnhài, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
3 After Hèlán Mǐnzhī had incurred disfavor,
the Empress memorialized to summon Wǔ Yuánshuǎng's son, Chéngsì, from Lǐngnán.
In the first year of Gānfēng,
Yuánshuǎng had been exiled to Zhènzhōu.
Chéngsì was appointed Shàngyī Fèngyù;
the Shàngyī Fèngyù
belonged to the Diànzhōng Shěng,
overseeing imperial clothing,
detailing its regulations,
and distinguishing its names and numbers.
In the fourth month,
on the day Xīnmǎo,
he was promoted to Zōngzhèng Qīng.
4 In autumn,
in the eighth month,
on the day Rénchén,
Xuānjiǎn Gōng was posthumously honored as Xuān Huángdì,
and his mother, Lady Zhāng, as Xuānzhuāng Huánghòu;
Yìwáng as Guāng Huángdì,
and his mother, Lady Jiǎ, as Guāngyì Huánghòu.
Xī, Commander of Jīnmén Town in the Later Wèi,
was the ancestor of Tàizǔ Hǔ,
and was posthumously titled Xuānjiǎn Gōng;
Tiāncì, Banner Master of Wèi,
was the father of Tàizǔ Hǔ,
and was posthumously titled Yìwáng.
Tàimù Huánghòu was honored as Tàimù Shén Huánghòu;
Wén Huángdì as Tàizōng Wénwǔ Shèng Huángdì,
and Wéndé Huánghòu as Wéndé Shèng Huánghòu.
The Emperor was to be called Tiānhuáng,
and the Empress Tiānhòu,
to avoid the titles of the former Emperor and former Empress.
This was actually to exalt themselves,
using the pretext of avoiding the titles of the former Emperor and former Empress;
this was Wǔ Hòu's intention.
Zhī chēng
is pronounced with the sound of Chǐzhèng.
A general amnesty was granted throughout the realm.
5 On the day Wùxū,
an imperial edict stated:
"Civil and military officials of the third rank and above shall wear purple robes
with gold and jade belts;
fourth rank shall wear dark scarlet robes
with gold belts;
fifth rank shall wear light scarlet robes
with gold belts;
sixth rank shall wear dark green robes,
seventh rank shall wear light green robes,
both with silver belts;
eighth rank shall wear dark blue robes,
ninth rank shall wear light blue robes,
both with鍮石 (brass-like stone) belts;
鍮石 resembles gold but is not gold.
Tōu
is pronounced with the sound of Tuōhóu.
No copper or iron belts.
Aside from commoners,
no one is permitted to wear yellow."
"Aside from commoners"
refers to merchants, artisans, and various other households.
6 In the ninth month,
on the day Guǐchǒu,
an edict ordered the restoration of the official titles and ranks of Zhǎngsūn Shèng and Zhǎngsūn Wújí.
Zhǎngsūn Yì, great-grandson of Wújí, was to inherit the title Duke of Zhào,
and Wújí's coffin was permitted to return
for burial with the imperial family at Zhāolíng.
Wújí had his official titles and ranks stripped and died;
see volume 200, Xiǎnqìng fourth year.
7 On the day Jiǎyín,
the Emperor presided at Xiángluán Gé.
According to the biography of Hǎo Chùjùn in the old histories,
Xiángluán Gé was east of Hányuán Diàn.
In the Six Statutes of the Tang,
Hányuán Diàn was flanked by two pavilions:
the left was called Xiángluán,
the right Qīfèng.
Below these two pavilions
were the east and west court halls.
The music was divided into eastern and western "friends" (factions),
with Yōngwáng Xián presiding over the eastern friends,
and Zhōuwáng Xiǎn over the western friends,
competing for victory as entertainment.
Hǎo Chùjùn remonstrated, saying:
"The two princes are still young in years,
their ambitions and interests not yet settled.
They should be taught to 'share pears and yield dates.'
Emperor Yuán of Liáng wrote these words in a letter to the King of Wǔlíng.
Lè
is pronounced luò.
Shào
is pronounced with the sound of Shīzhǎo.
Tuī
is pronounced with the sound of Tǔléi.
Now, by dividing them into two factions,
competing and showing off against each other,
the actors and petty people
will speak without restraint,
and I fear they will dispute for victory and defeat,
mocking and being rude,
which is not conducive to promoting rites and righteousness
and encouraging harmony and closeness."
The Emperor, startled, said:
"Your Excellency has far-sighted wisdom,
not matched by ordinary people."
He immediately stopped it.
On that day,
Lǐ Bì, Minister of the Court of the Imperial Guards, died suddenly at the banquet.
For this, the general feast was canceled for one day.
8 In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the *bǐngwǔ* day (the first day of the month),
the imperial carriage departed from the capital.
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
a hunting expedition was held at Qǔwǔyuán of Huàshān.
Huàshān is south of Huàyīn County in Huàzhōu.
Qǔwǔyuán is at the foot of Huàshān.
華 (Huá),
is pronounced *hù huà fān*.
On the *wùchén* day
reached Dōngdū.
9 Zhāng Jūnchè and others, *lùshì cānjūn* of Jīzhōu, falsely accused the Prefect Jiǎng Wáng Yùn and his son, the Prince of Rǔnán Commandery Wěi, of plotting rebellion.
An imperial edict ordered *tōngshì shèrén* Xuē Sīzhēn to rush by courier to investigate it.
In the twelfth month,
on the *guǐwèi* day,
Yùn, in fear,
hanged himself.
The Emperor, knowing he was innocent,
deeply grieved for him,
and executed Jūnchè and three others.
10 On the *wùzǐ* day,
King Fúshéxióng of Yútián came to court.
11 On the *xīnmǎo* day,
King Bēilùsī of Bōsī came to court.
12 On the *rènyín* day,
the Empress Tiānhòu submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The sacred lineage of the State
originates from Xuányuán Huángdì.
Lǎozǐ's surname was Lǐ and given name was Ěr.
Tángzǔ
in the first year of Qiánfēng,
honored him as Xuányuán Huángdì.
上 (*shàng*),
pronounced *shí zhǎng fān*;
the same below.
Each year during the examination of the classics,
it should be based on the *Xiàojīng* and *Lúnyǔ* for policy questions.
She also requested,
"From now on, if a father is alive,
one should observe three years of *qīcuī* mourning for one's mother.
According to ancient rites,
if the father was alive,
one observed one year of mourning for the mother.
為 (*wèi*),
pronounced *yú wěi fān*.
pronounced *zī*.
衰 (*cuī*),
pronounced *cāng huí fān*.
Officials in the capital of the eighth rank and above
should have their stipends appropriately increased."
京官 (Jīngguān),
means officials in the capital.
量 (*liáng*),
pronounced *liáng*.
(This memorial) comprised twelve articles.
The imperial edict praised her,
and all were implemented.
13 In this year,
there was a certain Liú Xiǎo,
who submitted a memorial discussing the selection of officials,
stating:
"Currently, the selection bureau considers 'inspection and verification' as impartiality.
'Inspection and verification'
refers to assessing their merits and faults,
checking for false names,
discovering concealment of deceit,
and preventing improper promotion or demotion.
They completely fail to consider their moral character and abilities.
Moreover, many rely on others for their essays and judgments.
Furthermore,
the Board of Rites, in recruiting scholars,
exclusively uses literary composition as the standard for ranking.
Consequently, scholars throughout the realm
abandon moral conduct and pursue literary arts.
Some, who ascend to the *jiǎkē* (highest rank) in the morning, fall into criminal punishment by evening.
Even if they recite ten thousand words daily,
what relevance does it have to governing principles?
理體 (lǐtǐ),
means the principles of governance.
行 (*xíng*),
pronounced *xià mèng fān*.
pronounced *qī yù fān*;
the same below.
pronounced *pí yì fān*.
It is insufficient to transform people.
Moreover, dedicating one's heart to flowers and trees,
and exhausting one's brush on mist and clouds,
to make this the prevailing custom,
how is this not a great error?
People's pursuit of fame
is like water flowing downwards;
if the superior has a preference,
the inferiors will surely go to extremes.
If Your Majesty prioritizes moral conduct in selecting officials,
and treats literary arts as secondary,
then many talented individuals will rush like thunder,
and the four quarters will be stirred like the wind!"
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the *bǐngyín* day,
the kingdom of Yútián was established as the Píshā Dūdūfǔ.
Its territory was divided into ten prefectures,
and Wèichí Fúshéxióng, the King of Yútián, was appointed Píshā Dūdū.
2 On the *xīnwèi* day,
Tǔbō sent its high official Lùn Tǔhúmí to request peace,
and also to ask to renew friendly relations with Tǔyùhún.
pronounced with the *rùshēng* from *tūn*;
the same below.
pronounced *fú yòu fān*.
pronounced *yù*.
3 In the second month,
Liú Rénguǐ heavily defeated the forces of Xīnluó at Qīzhòngchéng.
He also sent Mòhé by sea
to raid the southern borders of Xīnluó,
capturing and killing a great number.
Rénguǐ led his troops back.
An edict appointed Lǐ Jǐnxíng as *Āndōng Zhènfǔ Dàshǐ*,
to garrison Mǎixiāo City in Xīnluó to manage the situation.
He won all three battles.
Xīnluó then sent envoys to offer tribute,
and to apologize.
The Emperor pardoned them,
and restored Xīnluó King Fǎmǐn's official title and爵 rank.
Jīn Rénwèn returned midway,
and was re-enfeoffed as Duke of Línhǎi Commandery.
4 In the third month,
on the *dīngsì* day,
the Empress Tiānhòu offered sacrifice to the First Silkworm at the southern side of Mángshān.
Han rituals: In the third month, when mulberries first grow,
the Empress personally picks mulberries in the silkworm house within the imperial park,
raises over a thousand sheets of silkworms,
and offers a *zhōngláo* sacrifice of sheep and pigs.
According to the *Xùhàn Zhì*: In the third month,
the Empress leads the wives of high officials and feudal lords to raise silkworms,
and offers sacrifice to the First Silkworm,
with a *shǎoláo* ceremony.
The commentary states: The current Silkworm Goddess is called Yuànshū
[Yǔ]yù Shì Gōngzhǔ.
Tang system: The Empress sacrifices once a year,
on an auspicious *sì* day in late spring,
offering to the First Silkworm,
and then personally picks mulberries.
The Shǔ commentary states: *Tōngdiǎn*: The First Silkworm is
Tiānsì.
All officials and tributary envoys also attend.
5 The Emperor suffered greatly from dizziness.
There was a discussion about having the Empress Tiānhòu temporarily manage state affairs.
Hàochǔjùn, *zhōngshū shìláng tóng sānpǐn*, said:
"The Son of Heaven governs external affairs,
and the Empress governs internal affairs;
this is the way of Heaven.
The 'Hūn Yì' in the *Lǐjì* states: The Son of Heaven listens to the teachings for men,
the Empress listens to the submission of women;
the Son of Heaven governs the *yáng* way,
the Empress manages *yīn* virtue;
the Son of Heaven listens to external governance,
the Empress listens to internal duties.
When teachings and submission become custom,
and internal and external are harmonious,
the state is well-governed;
this is called abundant virtue.
Even if there is a young ruler,
the Empress is not permitted to preside over court,
in order to prevent the emergence of chaos.
This matter is found in Volume 69, third year of Huángchū of Wèi Wéndì.
Shall we not pass it down to our descendants, but entrust it to the Empress Tiānhòu?"
Lǐ Yìyǎn of Chānglè, *zhōngshū shìláng*, said:
"Chǔjùn's words are utterly loyal.
Your Majesty should heed them!"
The Emperor then stopped the discussion.
6 The Empress Tiānhòu frequently brought in literati such as Yuán Wànqǐng, *zhùzuò láng*.
Tang *zhùzuò láng*,
fifth rank, upper grade,
responsible for compiling steles, eulogies, and sacrificial texts,
subordinate to the Mìshū Shěng.
In Lóngshuò, *qǐjū láng* was changed to *zuǒshǐ*.
(They wrote) over a thousand *juǎn* in total.
Court memorials and documents from all bureaus,
she secretly had them participate in deciding,
to share the power of the prime ministers.
People at the time called them the "Scholars of the North Gate."
They did not pass through the Southern Offices, but entered and exited through the North Gate,
hence the name.
(He) was the son of Zǐyì.
Liú Zǐyì served in Suí,
known for his scholarship and conduct.
7 Summer.
In the fourth month,
on the day Gēngchén,
Wéi Hóngjī, the Minor Controller of Agriculture, was made Controller of Agriculture.
Wéi Hóngjī also oversaw agricultural settlements in the Eastern Capital [Luòyáng],
and received an imperial edict to repair and renovate the palaces and gardens.
When a eunuch committed an offense in the gardens,
Wéi Hóngjī flogged him
before reporting the matter to the emperor.
The emperor thought he was capable
and bestowed upon him several tens of bolts of silk,
saying:
“If there are further offenders,
you may flog them immediately;
there is no need to report it.”
8 Previously,
Zhào Huái of Cháng'ān, General of the Left Qianniu, married Princess Chánglè, a daughter of Emperor Gāozǔ,
and they had a daughter who became the wife of Zhōu Wáng Xiǎn.
The princess was quite favored by the emperor,
but Empress Tiānhòu disliked her.
On the day Xīnsì,
she was deposed,
imprisoned in the Bureau of Palace Attendants,
and given provisions for the living.
Guards were posted to watch for smoke from her chimney,
but after several days, no smoke emerged.
They opened the door to look,
and found she had died and decomposed.
Zhào Huái was demoted from Cìshǐ of Dìngzhōu to Cìshǐ of Kuòzhōu,
and the princess was ordered to accompany him to his post,
thus cutting off her court visits.
9 Crown Prince Hóng was benevolent, filial, humble, and cautious,
and the emperor loved him dearly.
He treated scholar-officials with respect,
and people both inside and outside the court were devoted to him.
Empress Tiānhòu was then asserting her ambitions,
and the Crown Prince’s petitions
frequently went against her will.
Wù
means "to go against."
Shuò
is pronounced suǒ jiǎo fān.
Wù
is pronounced wǔ gù fān.
Princesses Yìyáng and Xuānchéng
were daughters of Xiāo Shúfēi,
and because their mother had incurred imperial displeasure,
they were imprisoned in the YèTíng [Bureau of Palace Women],
and remained unmarried past the age of thirty.
The Crown Prince, seeing this, was shocked and saddened.
He immediately petitioned for them to be released and married off,
and the emperor granted it.
Empress Tiānhòu was furious,
and on that very day married the princesses to Quán Yì and Wáng Suìgǔ, both Imperial Bodyguards.
The three guard divisions—Qīn, Xūn, and Yì—all served in rotation.
Shàng
is pronounced shí zhǎng fān.
On the day Jǐhài,
the Crown Prince died in Habì Palace.
People at the time believed Empress Tiānhòu had poisoned him.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: The *New History*, Basic Annals says:
“On the day Jǐhài,
Empress Tiānhòu killed the Crown Prince.”
The *New Biography* says:
“The Empress was about to achieve her ambitions,
but Hóng’s petitions frequently went against her will.
While accompanying the emperor to Habì Palace,
he encountered poison and died.”
The *Táng Calendar* says:
“Hóng was benevolent, filial, intelligent, and decisive,
and deeply loved by the emperor.
Since being made Crown Prince,
he respectfully treated high ministers and great scholars,
never placing himself in a position of error.
By petitioning for the marriage of the two princesses,
he lost favor with Empress Tiānhòu,
and did not die a natural death.”
The *Shílù* [Veritable Records] and *Old Biography* both do not mention Hóng encountering poison.
According to Lǐ Bì’s statement to Emperor Sùzōng:
“Emperor Gāozōng had eight sons,
Emperor Ruìzōng being the youngest.
The four sons born to Empress Tiānhòu were ranked according to their birth,
thus Emperor Ruìzōng was the fourth.
The eldest was Emperor Xiàojìng,
who served as regent Crown Prince, benevolent, intelligent, filial, and fraternal.
Empress Tiānhòu was then planning to rule the court,
so she poisoned Emperor Xiàojìng
and established Yōng Wáng Xián as Crown Prince.”
The *New History* is likely based on this and the *Táng Calendar*.
Regarding Hóng’s death,
the matter is difficult to clarify.
We merely state that people at the time believed Empress Tiānhòu poisoned him,
treating a doubtful matter as doubtful.
On the day Rén'yín,
the imperial carriage returned to Luòyáng Palace.
In the fifth month,
on the day Wùshēn,
an edict was issued:
“I was about to abdicate the throne to the Crown Prince,
but he fell ill and could not recover.
It is fitting to declare his former appointment
and bestow upon him an honorable posthumous name.
He shall be posthumously titled Emperor Xiàojìng.”
This marks the beginning of an emperor’s son being posthumously titled emperor.
Shì
is pronounced shén zhì fān.
In the sixth month,
on the day Wùyín,
Yōng Wáng Xián was established as Crown Prince,
and a general amnesty was declared throughout the empire.
10 Empress Tiānhòu disliked Wáng Shàngjīn, Cìshǐ of Cízhōu.
Sòng Bái says: Cízhōu
was the state of Qiángjiùrú in the Spring and Autumn period,
and Běiqū County in the Han dynasty.
In the Suí dynasty, it was Fénzhōu.
In the first year of Wǔdé of the Táng dynasty,
it was Xīfénzhōu.
In the fifth year,
it was renamed Nánfénzhōu.
In the eighth year of Zhēnguān,
Nánfénzhōu was renamed Cízhōu,
because the prefecture was near Cíwū Fort,
hence the name.
Sūn Miǎn says: Named after Císhì County.
Shàngjīn
was born to Lady Liú, a concubine of the emperor.
Wù
is pronounced wū lù fān.
Autumn,
in the seventh month,
Wáng Shàngjīn was dismissed from office
and settled in Lǐzhōu.
11 In the eighth month,
on the day Gēngyín,
Emperor Xiàojìng was buried at Gōnglíng.
Gōnglíng
is located on Àolái Mountain in Gōushì County, Luòzhōu,
which was renamed Tàipíng Mountain.
12 On the day Wùxū,
Dài Zhìdé was made Right Púyè.
On the day Gēngzǐ,
Liú Rénlǐ was made Left Púyè,
both retaining their concurrent titles of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn as before.
Zhāng Wénguàn was made Shìzhōng,
Hǎo Chǔjùn was made Zhōngshū Lìng;
Lǐ Jìngxuán was made Lìbù Shàngshū and concurrently Zuǒ Shùzǐ,
retaining his concurrent title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn as before.
Liú Rénlǐ and Dài Zhìdé took turns receiving petitions.
Rénlǐ always promised [resolution] with pleasing words,
while Zhìdé would always challenge [the petitioners] based on reason,
never granting or denying outright.
However, for those with genuine grievances,
he would secretly memorialize and argue on their behalf.
Because of this, all contemporary praise went to Rénlǐ.
When asked the reason,
Zhìdé said:
“Power and authority belong to the ruler;
how can a subject usurp them!”
The emperor heard this
and greatly esteemed him.
There was an old woman who wished to present a petition to Rénlǐ
but mistakenly went to Zhìdé.
Before Zhìdé finished reading it,
the woman said:
“I thought this was the sensible Púyè,
but it turns out to be the insensible Púyè!
Give me back my petition!”
Zhìdé smiled and handed it back to her.
People at the time praised him as a man of integrity.
Wénguàn also concurrently held the post of Dàlǐ Qīng [Minister of the Court of Judicial Review] at the time.
When prisoners heard of his transfer,
they all wept bitterly.
Wénguàn was by nature stern and upright.
In discussions and memorials from various departments,
he frequently corrected and refuted them,
and the emperor greatly trusted him.
In the first year of Yífèng
(Bǐngzǐ, 676)
The reign title was changed in the eleventh month of this year.
1 Spring,
in the first month,
on the day Rénxū,
Jì Wáng Lún was transferred to become Xiāng Wáng.
2 The Luó in Nàzhōu rebelled.
According to Táng regulations,
Nàzhōu was established in the second year of Yífèng by opening mountain caves,
and it belonged to the Dūdūfǔ of Lúzhōu.
Luó
is pronounced lǔ hào fān.
3 In the second month,
on the day Jiǎxū,
the Āndōng Dūhù Fǔ was moved to the old city of Liáodōng.
A textual variant states: The Shílù records that
in the first year of Xiánhēng,
Yáng Fǎng and Gāo Kǎn attacked Ān Shùn,
and first captured the Āndōng Dūhù Fǔ,
moving it from Píngrǎng Chéng to Liáodōng Zhōu.
On the day Jiǎxū in the second month of the first year of Yífèng,
due to the rebellion of the remaining Gāogōuryě populace,
the Āndōng Dūhù Fǔ was moved to Liáodōng Chéng.
It is likely that the mention of moving the commandery in the first year of Xiánhēng
refers to its ultimate completion;
the mention of the Gāogōuryě rebellion in the first year of Yífèng
is the reason for its relocation.
The Huìyào does not contain the matter of moving the commandery in the first year of Xiánhēng.
This year it says it was moved to the old city of Liáodōng,
and we follow this account now.
All
officials of the Eastern Office were dismissed.
The Xióngjīn Dūdū Fǔ was moved to the old city of Jiàn'ān;
those households from Bǎijì who were previously moved to Xú, Yǎn, and other zhōu
were all settled in Jiàn'ān.
4 Tiānhòu encouraged the emperor to perform the Fēng sacrifice on Sōngshān, the Central Peak;
on the day Guǐwèi,
an edict was issued stating that there would be a ceremony at Sōngshān this winter.
Sōngshān, the Central Peak,
is in Yángchéng Xiàn, Hénán.
5 On the day Dīnghài,
the emperor visited the hot springs of Rǔzhōu.
Fifty lǐ southwest of Liáng Xiàn, Rǔzhōu, there are hot springs
where rice can be cooked.
There is also the Huángnǚ Tāng.
The emperor established a hot spring lodge.
6 In the third month,
on the day Guǐmǎo,
Lái Héng, the Huángmén Shìláng, and Xuē Yuánchāo, the Zhōngshū Shìláng, were both appointed Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
Héng was
Jì's elder brother;
Yuánchāo was
Shōu's son.
Lái Jì was utterly loyal and died on the frontier.
Xuē Shōu served Tàizōng during his early career.
Héng,
pronounced hù dēng.
7 On the day Jiǎchén,
the emperor returned to the Eastern Capital.
8 In the intercalary month,
the Tǔbō raided Shàn, Kuò, Hé, and Fāng zhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Chángfēn Xiàn of Diézhōu
was formerly occupied by the Tǔyùhún.
In the third year of Wǔchéng of Zhōu,
the various Qiāng were expelled,
and the land was first acquired.
A city was then built at Sānjiāo,
and the Gānsōng Fáng was established.
It also became Sānchuān Xiàn,
administered under Chángxiāng Jùn.
In the third year of Jiàndé,
Sānchuān was renamed Chángfēn Xiàn,
and Fāngzhōu was still established,
with the county belonging to it.
It was named for the abundance of fragrant grasses in the area.
The Suí abolished the zhōu,
and the Táng re-established it.
Tǔ,
pronounced with the entering tone of tūn.
Shàn,
pronounced shí zhàn.
Xīngzhōu,
was the land of Jǔ Xiàn, Wǔdū, in the Hàn dynasty.
The Later Wèi renamed it Luèyáng Xiàn.
South of the Yangtze, it was the vassal kingdom of Wǔxīng.
The Later Wèi made it Wǔxīng Jùn,
established Xīngzhōu,
and renamed Luèyáng Xiàn to Shùnzhèng Xiàn.
Fèngzhōu was
the land of Gùdào Héchí Xiàn in the Hàn dynasty.
The Jìn dynasty was occupied by the Qiúchí Dī.
The Later Wèi established Liángquán Xiàn,
and Emperor Fèi of Western Wèi established Fèngzhōu.
Shàn,
pronounced shí zhàn.
Jiān,
pronounced gǔ xián.
Jiāng,
pronounced jí liàng.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
an edict was issued stopping the Fēng sacrifice on Sōngshān
due to the Tǔbō encroaching on the frontier.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
Lúo Zhōumù Zhōu Wáng Xiǎn was appointed Táozhōudào Xíngjūn Yuánshuài,
leading twelve Dūguǎn, including Gōngbù Shàngshū Liú Shěnlǐ;
and Bìngzhōu Dàdūdū Xiāng Wáng Lún was appointed Liángzhōudào Xíngjūn Yuánshuài,
leading Qìbì Hélì, the Zuǒwèi Dàjiāngjūn, and others,
to suppress the Tǔbō.
Neither of the two princes went.
9 On the day Gēngyín,
the imperial carriage returned westward.
10On the day Jiǎyín,
Lǐ Yìyǎn, the Zhōngshū Shìláng, was appointed Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
11On the day Wùwǔ,
the imperial carriage arrived at Jiǔchéng Gōng.
12In the sixth month,
on the day Guǐhài,
Gāo Zhìzhōu of Jìnlíng, the Huángmén Shìláng, was appointed Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
13In the autumn,
in the eighth month,
on the day Yǐwèi,
the Tǔbō raided Diézhōu.
14On the day Rényín,
an imperial edict stated:
"The Dūdū Fǔs of Guì, Guǎng, Jiāo, and Qián
have recently been appointing local officials, but the selection has not been precise enough.
From now on, every four years, officials of the fifth rank and above, who are upright, shall be sent as envoys,
and Yùshǐ shall accompany them for the appointments."
People at the time called this "Southern Selection."
15In the ninth month,
on the day Rénshēn,
the Dàlǐ reported that Quán Shàncái, the Zuǒwēiwèi Dàjiāngjūn, and Fàn Huáiyì, the Zuǒjiānmén Zhōnglángjiàng, had mistakenly cut down cypress trees at Zhāolíng,
and their crime merited dismissal;
the emperor specifically ordered their execution.
Dí Rénjié of Tàiyuán, the Dàlǐ Céng, reported:
"The crime of these two men does not warrant death."
Tàiyuán was
Jìnyáng Xiàn of the Hàn dynasty.
The Suí renamed it Tàiyuán Xiàn,
and made Lóngshān Xiàn, established by the Later Qí, into Jìnyáng Xiàn,
both belonging to Bìngzhōu.
"If I do not kill Shàncái and others for cutting down the mausoleum cypresses,
then I will be unfilial."
Rénjié stubbornly persisted,
and the emperor changed countenance,
ordering him to leave.
Rénjié said:
"To offer frank remonstrance despite offending the emperor
has always been considered difficult.
I believe it is difficult when encountering Jié and Zhòu,
but easy when encountering Yáo and Shùn.
Now, the law does not prescribe death, yet Your Majesty specifically orders their execution;
this means the law will not be trusted by the people,
and what will people do with their hands and feet!
Moreover, Zhāng Shìzhī once said: 'If someone were to steal a handful of earth from Chánglíng,
how would Your Majesty handle it?'
Shìzhī's words
can be found in Volume 14, in the third year of Hàn Wéndì.
Póu,
pronounced bó hóu.
Chǔ,
pronounced chāng lǚ.
What will future generations say of Your Majesty!
I dare not obey the edict,
for fear of implicating Your Majesty in unrighteousness,
and also because I would be ashamed to face Shìzhī in the underworld."
The emperor's anger gradually subsided,
and the two men were dismissed
and exiled to Língnán.
A few days later,
Rénjié was promoted to Shìyùshǐ.
Previously,
when Rénjié was a Fǎcáo in Bìngzhōu,
his colleague Zhèng Chóngzhì was to be sent on a mission to a distant region.
Chóngzhì's mother was old and ill.
Rénjié said:
"With his mother in such a state,
how can he be made to worry for ten thousand lǐ!"
He went to Lìn Rénjī, the Chángshǐ,
and requested to take his place.
Rénjī had long been at odds with Lǐ Xiàolián, the Sīmǎ,
and said to each other:
"How can we not feel ashamed!"
Thus, they became harmonious.
16In the winter,
in the tenth month,
the imperial carriage returned to the capital.
17th *dīngyǒu* (of the sexagenary cycle),
the *xiá* sacrifice was offered at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
Following the proposal of Shǐ Càn, a Grand Academy *Bóshì*,
the *xiá* sacrifice was performed three years after the *dì* sacrifice,
and the *dì* sacrifice two years after the *xiá*.
Ōuyáng Xiū said: The *dì* and *xiá* sacrifices
are major sacrifices.
The *xiá* sacrifice is for all ancestors, according to their *zhāomù* order, to share a meal with the Grand Ancestor,
while the *dì* sacrifice is to scrutinize their relative seniority,
this is the meaning of the *dì* and *xiá* sacrifices.
However, those who established the rites erred in this,
leading to differing timeframes,
and ancestors being out of their proper position.
Scholars could not determine what to follow.
The *Lǐ* (Book of Rites) states: "A *xiá* every three years,
a *dì* every five years."
The *Zhuàn* (Commentaries) states: "Two *yīn* sacrifices every five years."
In the 10th month of the 3rd year of Shangyuán of Gāozōng's reign, a *xiá* was due,
but officials debated the timeframe.
Shǐ Càn and others proposed,
that the *xiá* be performed after the new sovereign's mourning period concluded,
and the *dì* in the following year.
Thereafter,
the two sacrifices would be performed every five years.
That is, five years between successive *dì* sacrifices,
and the *xiá* would always be three years after a *dì*,
and the *dì* always two years after a *xiá*.
In the 8th year of Duke Xuān of Lǔ,
the *dì* sacrifice was offered to Duke Xī.
This was after the three-year mourning period concluded with a *xiá*,
followed by a *dì* the next year,
and then another *dì* in the 8th year.
In the 20th year of Duke Zhāo, a *dì* was performed,
and then again in the 25th year;
this is ascertainable.
At the time, because his words were based on classical texts,
they were followed.
Under the Táng system: The *Guózǐ Bóshì* (Imperial College Doctor),
was of 正五品上 (senior fifth rank, upper class),
responsible for teaching students who were sons and grandsons of civil and military officials of the second rank and above, or great-grandsons of royal princes of the second rank and above.
The *Tàixué Bóshì* (Grand Academy Doctor),
was of 正六品上 (senior sixth rank, upper class),

responsible for teaching students who were sons and grandsons of civil and military officials of the fifth rank and above, sons and grandsons of *jùn* and *xiàn* officials, or great-grandsons of officials of the junior third rank.
*Xiá*,
read *hú jiá*.
*Càn*,
read *cāng àn*.
*Dì*,
read *dà jì*.
18th, Li Sujié, Prince of Xún,
was the son of Xiāo Shúfēi. He was intelligent, alert, and fond of learning.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān disliked him,
and demoted him from *Qízhōu Cìshǐ* to *Shēnzhōu Cìshǐ*.
Shēnzhōu
was the land of Hàn's Píngshì and Méngxiàn counties.
During the Jìn dynasty, Yìyáng Commandery was established by division.
During the Southern Qí, Sīzhōu was established.
Later Wèi changed it to Yǐngzhōu.
Later Zhōu changed it to Shēnzhōu.
Suí changed it to Yìzhōu.
Táng restored it to Shēnzhōu.
Qízhōu was 315 *lǐ* west of the capital,
and 1,170 *lǐ* to the Eastern Capital.
Shēnzhōu was 1,796 *lǐ* to the capital,
and 943 *lǐ* to the Eastern Capital.
An imperial decree stated:
"Sùjié already has an old illness,
so there is no need for him to come to court."
However, Sùjié actually had no illness.
Feeling that he had been unable to enter and pay respects for a long time,
he wrote a "Discourse on Loyalty and Filial Piety."
Zhāng Jiànzhī, the *Cāngcáo Cānjūn* of the princely establishment, secretly sealed the discourse and submitted it.
The Empress, upon seeing it,
falsely accused him of bribery and corruption.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
he was demoted and enfeoffed as the Prince of Póyáng,
and settled in Yuánzhōu.
Jiànzhī submitted the sealed discourse
hoping to move the Emperor's heart,
how could he know that this only hastened Sùjié's punishment!
Yuánzhōu was 3,580 *lǐ* southeast of the capital,
and 2,161 *lǐ* to the Eastern Capital.
19th, 11th month,
on the *rénshēn* day,
the era name was changed,
and a general amnesty was granted throughout the empire.
20th, on the *gēngyín* day,
Lǐ Jìngxuán was appointed *Zhōngshūlìng*.
21st, 12th month,
on the *wùwǔ* day,
Lái Héng was appointed *Hénándào Dàshǐ*,
Xuē Yuánchāo was appointed *Héběidào Dàshǐ*,
Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Yānlíng Cuī Zhìtì and Guózǐ Sīyè Zhèng Zǔxuán were appointed *Jiāngnándào Dàshǐ*.
In the 3rd year of Dàyè of the Suí dynasty,
the *Guózǐ Sīyè* position was first established.
In Táng, it was from 從四品下 (junior fourth rank, lower class),
with duties similar to the *Jìjiǔ*.
*Shǐ*,
read *shū lì*.
*Yān*,
read *yè wǎn*,
also *yú jiàn*,
also pronounced *yǎn*.
1st, Spring,
1st month,
on the *yǐhài* day,
the Emperor plowed the *jiètián*.
2nd, Initially,
Liú Rén'guǐ led his troops back from Xióngjīn.
Refer to the 2nd year of Líndé in the previous volume.
He dared not linger,
and soon returned to court.
2nd month,
on the *dīngsì* day,
Gāo Zàng, the *Gōngbù Shàngshū*, was appointed *Liáodōngzhōu Dūdū*,
enfeoffed as King of Cháoxiǎn,
and sent back to Liáodōng to
pacify the remaining Gāolì populace.
Those Gāolì who were previously in various prefectures were all sent back with Zàng.
Furthermore, Fúyú Lóng, the *Sīnóng Qīng*, was appointed *Xióngjīn Dūdū*,
enfeoffed as King of Dàifāng,
and also sent back to pacify the remaining Bǎijì populace.
The Āndōng Dūhùfǔ was moved to Xīnchéng to govern them.
Last spring,
the Āndōng Dūhùfǔ was moved to the old city of Liáodōng,
and now it was moved again to Xīnchéng.
*Tǒng*,
read *tā zòng*.
Lóng was ordered to reside in the territory of Gāolì.
When Zàng arrived in Liáodōng,
he plotted rebellion,
secretly colluding with the Mòhé.
He was summoned back,
exiled to Qióngzhōu, where he died.
His people were scattered and resettled in various prefectures of Hénán and Lǒngyòu.
The poor were left to live around Āndōng City.
The old city of Gāolì was absorbed by Xīnhuá.
The remaining populace scattered into Mòhé and Tūjué.
Lóng also dared not return to his homeland in the end,
and thus the Gāo and Fúyú clans perished.
3rd, 3rd month,
on the *guǐhài* *shuò* day,
Hǎo Chǔjùn and Gāo Zhìzhōu were both appointed *Zuǒshùzǐ*,
and Lǐ Yìyǎn was appointed *Yòushùzǐ*.
Summer,
4th month,
Zhāng Dà'ān, the *Zuǒshùzǐ*, was appointed *Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn*.
Dà'ān was the son of Gōngjǐn.
Zhāng Gōngjǐn was a meritorious official of Emperor Tàizōng's court.
4th, An imperial edict stated that due to drought in Hénán and Hébĕi,
Imperial Censor-in-chief Cuī Mì and others were dispatched in different routes to inquire and provide relief.
Shìyùshǐ Liú Sīlì of Nínglíng submitted a memorial:
Nínglíng County,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Chénliú Commandery.
From Cáo Wèi to Yuán Wèi, it belonged to Qiáojùn.
It was abolished during the Later Qí.
In the 6th year of Kāihuáng of Suí, it was re-established
and belonged to Sòngzhōu.
*Zhèn*,
read *jīn rěn*.
*Shàng*,
read *shí zhǎng*.
*Shū*,
read *suǒ jù*.
"Now, as wheat ears ripen and silkworms mature,
agricultural work is in full swing.
When imperial envoys tour and offer comfort,
people are all excited and applauding,
forgetting their household tasks,
hoping for this imperial grace.
They gather to greet them,
causing no small disruption to their work.
Since it involves relief distribution,
records must be kept.
The original intention was to provide comfort,
but it becomes more troublesome.
It is hoped that relief distribution be entrusted to the prefectures and counties,
and when autumn tasks are light,
envoys be sent out to commend or criticize."
After the memorial was presented,
Mì and the others did not proceed.
5 In the fifth month,

(The Western Tūjué (突厥) Shābōdiélìshī Kèhán (沙鉢咥利失可汗) divided his country into ten tribes,

Xíngjiǎn (行儉) selected his elite cavalry,

Sìyè (嗣業) and others had previously won many battles,

Coinciding with a heavy snowfall,
the Tūjué (突厥) launched a night raid on their camp.
Sìyè (嗣業) hastily withdrew his camp and fled.
His troops then fell into great disorder,
and were defeated by the barbarians.
The number of dead was countless.
Dàzhì (大智) and Jǐngjiā (景嘉) led the infantry, fighting as they retreated,

Sìyè (嗣業) was spared death

Dàzhì (大智) and Jǐngjiā (景嘉) were both dismissed from office.
The Tūjué (突厥) raided Dìngzhōu (定州).
The Prefect, Prince Huò (霍) Yuán Guǐ (元軌), ordered the city gates opened and the banners lowered.
The barbarians suspected an ambush,
became frightened, and fled under the cover of night.
Lǐ Jiāyùn (李嘉運) of that prefecture conspired with the barbarians.
When the matter was exposed,
the Emperor ordered Yuán Guǐ (元軌) to thoroughly investigate his accomplices.
Yuán Guǐ (元軌) said:
"With strong enemies on our borders,
people's hearts are uneasy.
If too many are arrested and imprisoned,
it will only drive them to rebellion."
So, he executed only Jiāyùn (嘉運),
and questioned no one else.
He then impeached himself for violating the imperial decree.
The Emperor read the memorial with great joy,
and said to the messenger:
"I too regret it.
If not for the Prince,
Dìngzhōu (定州) would have been lost!"
Thereafter, whenever there were important matters in the imperial court,
the Emperor often secretly sent edicts to him for advice.

Xíng (陘),

Yǒnglóng (永隆) 1st year
(*gēngchén* (庚辰), 680 CE)
(According to the Huìyào (會要),
on the 23rd day of the 8th month of this year,

Hēishān (黑山) is also named Shāhúshān (殺胡山).

He brought their heads and surrendered.
Originally,
when Xíngjiǎn (行儉) marched to Shuòchuān (朔川),

I observe that Shuòzhōu (朔州) in the Táng (唐) dynasty governed Shànyáng Xiàn (善陽縣),
which was the territory of Hàn (漢) Dìngxiāng Xiàn (定襄縣).

From Shuòzhōu (朔州) to the Chányú Fǔ (單于府) was three hundred fifty-seven lǐ (里).
Based on the encampments of Péi Xíngjiǎn's (裴行儉) army,
he first arrived at Shuòzhōu (朔州) and then north of the Chányú Fǔ (單于府),

"The way of warfare
values sincerity in treating soldiers and
cleverness in controlling enemies.
The provisions of Xiāo Sìyè (蕭嗣業) were plundered by the Tujue (突厥 a few days ago,
and his soldiers suffered from cold and hunger,
hence their defeat.
Now the Tujue (突厥) will surely plot this again,
so we should deceive them."
Thereupon, he faked three hundred provision carts,
with five strong warriors hidden in each cart,
each holding a mòdāo (陌刀) and a strong crossbow.
Mòdāo (陌刀)
is a great saber;
one stroke of the saber could kill several people.
The Táng Liù Diǎn (唐六典) states: Mòdāo (陌刀)
is a long saber,
held by infantry,
perhaps the ancient zhǎnmǎjiàn (斬馬劍).
The Shì Míng (釋名) states: Nǔ (弩),
means "anger" (怒),
because it has an angry force.
Its handle is called an "arm" (臂),
resembling a human arm.
The part that hooks the string is called a "tooth" (牙),
resembling teeth.
Outside the "tooth" (牙) is the "frame" (郭),
which is the frame of the "tooth" (牙).
Combined, it is named a "mechanism" (機),
meaning its ingenuity is like a mechanism;
it also refers to the pivot of a door,
opening and closing with precision.
Chéng (乘),
read as shéng zhèng.
Moreover, he ambushed elite troops in strategic defiles to wait for them.
When the barbarians indeed arrived,
the weak soldiers abandoned the carts and scattered.
The barbarians drove the carts to water and grass,
unbridled their horses to graze,
and intended to take the provisions.
The strong warriors leaped out from the carts
and attacked them.
The barbarians fled in panic,
and were again intercepted by the ambush,
almost all of them were killed or captured.
From then on, whenever provisions were transported,
the barbarians dared not approach.
When the army reached north of the Chányú Fǔ (單于府),

they set up camp.
After the trenches were completed,
Xíngjiǎn (行儉) urgently ordered them to move to a high ridge.
All the generals said that the soldiers had already settled down
and should not be moved again.
Xíngjiǎn (行儉) did not comply,
and urged them to move.
That night,
a storm suddenly arrived,
and the previous camp site
was more than a zhàng (丈) deep in water.
The generals were astonished and convinced.
When asked why,
Xíngjiǎn (行儉) smiled and said:
"From now on, just follow my orders;
there is no need to ask how I knew."
Once Fèngzhí (奉職) was captured,
the remaining rebels fled to secure Lángshān (狼山).
Lángshān (狼山)
was where the right wing tribes of the Gēluólù (歌邏祿) resided.
In the first year of Yǒnghuī (永徽),

After settling the remaining bandits,

The textual variant states: The Shílù (實錄) says:

According to the ninth month of the third year of Yífèng (儀鳳),

This matter is quite similar.
The old biography of Jìngxuán (敬玄)
records only one defeat,
not a second.
Chángzhī's (常之) biography states:
"During Yífèng (儀鳳),
he accompanied Jìngxuán (敬玄) in attacking the Tǔbō (吐蕃),

At that time, Zànpó (贊婆) and others were encamped at Liángfēichuān (良非川).
Chángzhī (常之) attacked the bandit camp by night,
routing them,
and was promoted to Dàshǐ (大使)."
These events seem to be simultaneous.
The new biography of Jìngxuán (敬玄)
records a battle at Qīnghǎi (青海) and another battle at Huángchuān (湟川),
totaling two defeats.
Chángzhī's (常之) biography: In the third year of Yífèng (儀鳳),
he attacked Bádì Shè (跋地設).
During Tiáolù (調露),
he attacked Zànpó (贊婆).
The Táng Lì (唐曆) and Tǒngjì (統紀) both have no record of Jìngxuán's (敬玄) defeat this year.
Furthermore, the Shílù (實錄) states,
in the eighth month of this year, on the day Dīngsì (丁巳),
Jìngxuán (敬玄) was demoted to Hénzhōu Cìshǐ (衡州刺史).
From Xīnsì (辛巳) to Dīngsì (丁巳)
is only thirty-seven days.
Jiǎ Dān (賈耽)'s Huánghuá Sìdá Jì (皇華四達記) states that from Cháng'ān (長安) to Shànzhōu (鄯州) is about one thousand seven hundred lǐ (里).
At that time, Gāozōng (高宗) was also in Dōngdū (東都).
If Jìngxuán (敬玄) was defeated and then
repeatedly submitted memorials claiming illness,
and only after receiving a reply did he come
to Dōngdū (東都),
it would certainly take several days before he was demoted,
which could not be contained within thirty-seven days.
Therefore, I have omitted Jìngxuán's (敬玄) defeat at Huángchuān (湟川)
and simply state that the Tǔbō (吐蕃) raided Héyuán (河源),
and Chángzhī (常之) attacked and repelled them.
Now, according to Liú Xù (劉昫)'s Táng Shū Dìlǐ Zhì (唐書地理志),
Shànzhōu (鄯州) is one thousand nine hundred thirteen lǐ (里) west of the capital.
Chángzhī (常之) considered Héyuán (河源) a strategic point
and wanted to station troops there,
but transport was difficult and distant.
So, he extensively set up over seventy beacon stations and garrisons,
opened over five thousand qǐng (頃) of military farmland,
yielding over five million dàn (石) annually,
thus ensuring preparedness for both war and defense.
Previously,
Jiànnán conscripted soldiers in Mòuzhōu.
In the southwest, Ānróngchéng was built
to cut off the Tǔbō’s route to the various Mán tribes.
Sòng Bái said: Mòuzhōu was originally the country of Rǎnmáng,
which the Hàn dynasty opened up as Wènshān Jùn.
The Huáyáng Guózhì states: In the third year of Dìjié of Emperor Xuān,
the Báimǎ Qiāng of Wǔdū rebelled.
Luò Wǔ was sent to pacify them.
The officials and people of Wènshān went to Wǔ to accuse themselves, saying
that taxes had been levied twice in one year to an extreme degree,
and the border people were poor
and unable to provide.
They requested the reduction of the prefecture.
Consequently, Wènshān Jùn was abolished,
and a Dūwèi was re-established.
The present-day zhōu is the Hàn dynasty’s Shǔ Jùn, Wènjiāng Xiàn.
In the third year of Pǔtōng of the Liáng dynasty,
Shéngzhōu was established.
It was named after the “rope” (shéng) used to make bridges on the road to Táoguān.
In the Later Zhōu dynasty, it became Wènzhōu,
and Wènshān Xiàn was established.
The Táng dynasty renamed it Mòuzhōu,
taking its name from Mòuzī Shān within its borders.
Its city was captured
and occupied by soldiers.
From then on, all the Xiīr Mán tribes surrendered to the Tǔbō.
The Tǔbō seized all the lands of Yángtóng, Dǎngxiàng, and the various Qiāng tribes.
To the east, they bordered the zhōu of Liáng, Sōng, Mòu, Xī, etc.
To the south, they neighbored Tiānzhú.
To the west, they captured Kūcí, Shūlè, and the other Four Garrisons.
To the north, they reached the Tūjué.
Their territory spanned over ten thousand *lǐ*,
and among all the Hú peoples,
none could compare in their prosperity.
On the day of Bǐngshēn,
Jiāng Wáng Yuánxiáng, the Cìshǐ of Zhèngzhōu, passed away.
Zhèngzhōu was
the land of Xíngyáng Xiàn during the Hàn dynasty.
Hàn Xíngyáng belonged to Hénán Jùn.
The Jìn dynasty divided it into Xíngyáng Jùn.
The Later Wèi dynasty belonged to Běiyùzhōu.
Later, Zhèngzhōu was established.
In the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng of the Suí dynasty, it was renamed Guǎnzhōu.
In the early years of Dàyè,
it was again called Zhèngzhōu.
The remaining forces of the Tūjué besieged Yúnzhōu.
Yúnzhōu was
the land of Píngchéng Xiàn during the Hàn dynasty.
During the Later Wèi dynasty, it was the capital of Dài.
Under the Northern Qí and Later Zhōu dynasties, it was Hèngān Zhèn.
In the seventh year of Zhēngguān,
Yúnzhōu and Dìngxiāng Xiàn were established.
Zhé
is the same as Zhé.
In the eighth month,
on the day of Dīngwèi,
the Emperor returned to Dōngdū.
Lǐ Jìngxuán, the Zhōngshū Lìng and Jiǎnjiào Shànzhōu Dūdū,
after his army was defeated,
repeatedly claimed illness and requested to return.
The Emperor granted his request.
Upon his arrival,
he had no illness and went to the Zhōngshū to attend to affairs.
The Emperor was enraged, and
on the day of Dīngsì,
demoted him to Cìshǐ of Héngzhōu.
Héngzhōu was
the land of Líng Xiàn, Zhēngyáng, Lèiyáng, and Chálíng Xiàn during the Hàn dynasty.
The Wú dynasty established Xiāngdōng Jùn.
The Liáng and Chén dynasties established Héngshān Jùn.
When the Suí dynasty pacified the Chén,
Héngzhōu was established.
It is three thousand four hundred and three *lǐ* southeast of the capital,
and two thousand seven hundred and sixty *lǐ* to Dōngdū.
Tàizǐ Xián heard secret discussions in the palace,
suggesting that Xián was born to Tiānhòu’s elder sister, Hánguófūrén.
He became inwardly suspicious and fearful.
Míng Chóngyǎn, trusted by Tiānhòu for his witchcraft,
often secretly claimed
"the Crown Prince is unfit to succeed,
and Yīngwáng resembles Tàizōng in appearance."
He also said,
"Xiāngwáng has the noblest physiognomy."
Tiānhòu once ordered the scholars of the Běimén to compile the Shàoyáng Zhèngfàn.
Yán Yánzhī’s Qūshuǐ Shī Xù states: "Propriety nurtures virtue in Shàoyáng."
The commentary says: "The Eastern Palace

Shào
is pronounced like "zhào."
She also frequently wrote letters to admonish and criticize him,

When Chóngyǎn died,

The Crown Prince was quite fond of sensual pleasures,

Dàoshēng also confessed that the Crown Prince had ordered him to kill Chóngyǎn.
The Emperor had always loved the Crown Prince

Tiānhòu said:
"For a son to harbor rebellious intentions

Great righteousness demands the extermination of relatives;

On the day of Jiǎzǐ,

His armor was then burned south of Tiānjīnqiáo to display it to the officials and common people.
Liú Xù said: Dōngdū
was the royal city of Zhōu,
the capital where King Píng moved eastward.
The old city is in the northeast corner of the present park.

In the first year of Dàyè of the Suí dynasty,
a new capital was built eighteen *lǐ* west of the old Luòchéng,

It is backed by Mángshān to the north,

A bridge was built over the Luò, called Tiānjīnqiáo.

Liú Nàiyán, the Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ, had compiled a collection of humorous writings (páixié jí) and presented it to Xián.

"Even when teaching people with the Six Classics,

It is eight thousand six hundred and six *lǐ* to the capital,

Scout cavalry reported their arrival with dust rising to the sky.
The generals and soldiers were all terrified.
Xíngjiǎn said,

A short while later,
Fúniàn indeed led his chieftains, with Wēnfù bound, to the army gate to plead for punishment.
Xíngjiǎn completely pacified the remaining Tujue factions

Āshǐnà Fúniàn, Āshǐdé Wēnfù, and fifty-two others were executed in the marketplace.
After recording the solar eclipse on the bǐngyín day of the tenth month,

This means there were two bǐngyín days in the tenth month.
This is an error in the old historical records,
which the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn followed,

The New History records that the reign era was changed on the yǐchǒu day of the ninth month of that year.
Perhaps the presentation of captives on the rénxū day

In the previous year, Xíngjiǎn was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Dìngxiāng Dào Expeditionary Army to suppress the Tujue,

Originally,

Péi Yán was jealous of Xíngjiǎn's achievements,

(This event is seen in Volume 81, first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jin.)

At this time, the reign era was changed due to the birth of the imperial grandson Chóngzhào.

Lántián County,

(The Ministry of Personnel was in charge of examining the ranks and grades of civil officials throughout the empire.)

Póu

That man smiled and assented.

(Miǎn,

A great wind arose,

The Emperor looked at his wounds and sighed;

With the vastness of the empire,

and between the two capitals, the dead lay piled on the roads,

'Jiān',
pronounced 'gǔ xián'.
"Your Majesty performed the Fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài,

Since the deaths of Chǔ Suìliáng and Hán Yuàn,

The note says: 'Wútóng'

'Jī',

13The emperor sent eunuchs to transport exotic bamboo along the Jiāng River,

The eunuchs, loading the bamboo onto boats,

When they passed through Jīngzhōu,

and submitted a strongly worded memorial,

"Transporting exotic items from distant places
and causing trouble along the roads

Furthermore,

The emperor said to Empress Tiānhòu:

According to the old system: all nine-rank officials with actual duties
also held an honorary rank (sànwèi),
which was called their "original rank" (běnpǐn).
Their actual duties were assigned according to their talent,
sometimes moving from a relaxed position to a demanding one,
or from a high-ranking position to a lower one.
Their transfers and appointments
were irregular and inconsistent.
Honorary ranks, however, were universally determined by family connections (mén yīn) and rank,
and then advanced based on meritorious service (láokǎo).
The Wǔdé regulations stipulated that officials with actual duties who were relieved of their honorary posts
would be "jiān" (兼, concurrent) if they were one rank short of their honorary rank.
Those with low-ranking actual duties were not relieved of their honorary posts.
The Zhēnguān regulations stipulated that those with high-ranking actual duties were "shǒu" (守, provisional),
and those with low-ranking actual duties were "xíng" (行, acting).
They still held their honorary ranks.
Those who were one rank short were still "jiān" as before.
Sometimes they held honorary official posts,
sometimes they were "shǒu,"
combining these uses.
Holding two actual posts was also considered "jiān,"
which was quite confusing.
In the second year of Xiánhēng (671),
all were uniformly designated "shǒu."
The "jiān" (兼) for being one rank short
is read gǔ niàn;
the "jiān" (兼) for holding two actual posts
is read gǔ tián.
The character is the same, but the pronunciation is different.

Disperse the qi immediately upon sensation.
Nǎohù,
also known as Hélú (合顱),
is one and a half cuns behind the strong part of the occipital bone.
Needling is forbidden,

It is traditionally said that when Mínghè pricked, a slight amount of blood came out,
