and the three prefectures of Yáng 揚, Rùn 潤, and Chǔ 楚 were pacified.
Chén Yuè 陳嶽 commented: "If Jìngyè 敬業 had adopted Wèi Sīwēn 魏思溫's strategy,
and advanced directly to Héluò 河洛,
focusing solely on the task of restoration,
then even if his army was defeated and he was killed,
loyalty and righteousness would still reside in him.
But he vainly hoped for the imperial aura of Jīnlíng 金陵,
truly making him a rebel.
What else could he expect but defeat!
When Jìngyè 敬業 rose,
he made Jìngyóu 徐敬猷 lead five thousand soldiers
up the west bank of the river,
to seize territory in Hézhōu 和州.
Gāo Zǐgòng 高子貢 of Lìyáng 歷陽, former scholar of the Hóngwénguǎn 弘文館, led several hundred men from his hometown to resist him,
and Jìngyóu 徐敬猷 could not advance westward.
For his merit, he was appointed Cháosàndàfū 朝散大夫 and Chéngjūn Zhùjiào 成均助教.
Lìyáng 歷陽 County in the Han 漢 dynasty belonged to Jiǔjiāng 九江 Commandery.
The Jin 晉 dynasty established Lìyáng 歷陽 Commandery.
When the Northern Qí 北齊 and Liáng 梁 dynasties made peace,
Hézhōu 和州 was established,
and the Suí 隋 and Tang 唐 dynasties followed this.
Later, the Guózǐjiān 國子監 was changed to Chéngjūn Jiān 成均監.
According to the *Tang Liùdiǎn* 唐六典: In the Hóngwénguǎn 弘文館,
scholars were from rank five or higher.
A Guózǐ Zhùjiào 國子助教 was merely from rank 6a,
responsible for assisting the doctors in teaching the classics.
Cháosàndàfū 朝散大夫 was from rank 5b.
Shuài 帥 is read as 'lǜ' 率.
Cháo 朝 is pronounced 'zhí yáo fān' 直遙翻.
Sàn 散 is pronounced 'xī dǎn fān' 悉亶翻.
32 On *dīngmǎo* 丁卯,
Guō Dàijǔ 郭待舉 was dismissed and made Zuo Shùzǐ 左庶子.
Wèi Fāngzhì 韋方質, Lúantái Shìláng 鸞臺侍郎, was made Fènggé Shìláng 鳳閣侍郎 and Tóng Píngzhāngshì 同平章事.
Fāngzhì 韋方質 was the grandson of Yúnqǐ 雲起.
Wèi Yúnqǐ 韋雲起 served between the Suí 隋 and Tang 唐 dynasties.
33 In the twelfth month,
Liú Jǐngxiān 劉景先 was again demoted to Yuánwài Chángshǐ 員外長史 of Jízhōu 吉州,
and Guō Dàijǔ 郭待舉 was demoted to Cìshǐ 刺史 of Yuèzhōu 岳州.
Yuèzhōu 岳州 is two thousand two hundred and thirty-seven *lǐ* 里 southeast of the capital,
and one thousand eight hundred and sixteen *lǐ* 里 to the Eastern Capital.
Initially,
Péi Yán was imprisoned.
Chéng Wùtǐng (單于道安撫大使, 左武衛大將軍), the Protector-General of Shànyú Dào and Grand General of the Left Martial Guard, secretly submitted a memorial to clarify his case,
which displeased the Empress Dowager.
Wùtǐng had always been on good terms with Táng Zhīqí and Dù Qiúrén.
Someone slandered him, saying,
"Wùtǐng is colluding with Péi Yán and Xú Jìngyè."
On the day Guǐmǎo,
the Left Eagle-Bearer General Péi Shàoyè was sent to execute him in the army.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Táng Tǒngjì* says:
"Afterward, the Empress Dowager was furious,
and summoned her ministers, saying: 'I have done no wrong to the world.
Do all my ministers know this?'
The ministers said: 'Yes.'
The Empress Dowager said: 'I served the former Emperor for over twenty years,
and my concern for the world was extreme!
The high officials and nobles,
I bestowed their wealth and positions;
the peace and happiness of the world,
I nurtured it.
When the former Emperor abandoned his ministers,
he entrusted the world to me,
not loving himself but loving the common people.
Now, the leaders of rebellion
all come from generals, prime ministers, and ministers.
How deeply have you wronged me!
Moreover, among you, are there any entrusted veteran ministers
who are more stubborn and difficult to control than Péi Yán?
Are there any noble descendants of generals
who can gather more fugitives than Xú Jìngyè?
Are there any veteran generals holding military power
who can surely win battles more than Chéng Wùtǐng?
These three men
were highly regarded by the people,
and were disadvantageous to me,
yet I was able to execute them.
If any of you can surpass these three,
then you should do so immediately;
otherwise,
you must change your hearts and serve me,
lest you become a laughingstock of the world.'
The ministers kowtowed,
not daring to look up,
and said: 'We will do whatever the Empress Dowager commands.'
I fear Empress Wǔ would not have been so frivolous."
This account is not accepted.
When the Tujue heard of Wùtǐng's death,
they feasted and celebrated everywhere;
they also erected a shrine for Wùtǐng,
and whenever they went on an expedition,
they would pray there.
The Empress Dowager, considering Wáng Fāngyì (夏州都督), the Military Governor of Xiàzhōu, was associated with Wùtǐng in office
and they were previously close,
and also being a close relative of the deposed empress,
summoned him to prison,
exiled him to Yázhōu, where he died.
The *Jiùzhì* says: Yázhōu is seven thousand four hundred and sixty *lǐ* from the capital,
and six thousand three hundred *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
Chuígǒng First Year
(Yǐyǒu, 685)
1 Spring,
First Month,
on the first day Dīngwèi,
a general amnesty was granted to the empire,
and the era name was changed.
2 The Empress Dowager, considering Xú Sīwén loyal,
specifically exempted him from guilt by association,
and appointed him Junior Lord of the Imperial Stables.
"Guilt by association" means
being implicated in a crime due to one's relatives or party.
Guāngzhái changed the Grand Minister of the Imperial Stables to Junior Lord of the Imperial Stables.
"Jìngyè changed the surname of the minister to Wǔ;
I will not take it back now."
3 On the day Gēngxū,
Qiān Wèidào was appointed Minister of the Interior.
The Minister of the Interior
is the Chancellor.
4 On the day Wùchén,
Liú Rénguǐ (文昌左相, 同鳳閣鸞臺三品, 樂城文獻公), the Left Chancellor of the Wénchāng Bureau, Minister-Director of the Phoenix and Luan Terrace, and Duke Wénxiàn of Yuèchéng, passed away.
The Left Chancellor of the Wénchāng Bureau
is the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
5 Second Month,
on the day Guǐwèi,
an imperial edict stated:
"Regarding the Dengwengu (Drum of Complaint) and Feishi (Pulpit Stone) placed in the imperial court,
the Dengwengu is in the western court,
and the Feishi is in the eastern court.
Cháo,
pronunciation: zhí yáo fān.
If anyone beats the drum or stands by the stone,
the Censor is to receive their petition and report it."
6 On the day Yǐsì,
Wǔ Chéngsì (春官尚書) and Péi Jūdao (秋官尚書) were appointed.
Guāngzhái changed the Ministry of Rites to Ministry of Spring,
and the Ministry of Punishments to Ministry of Autumn.
Shàng,
pronunciation: chén yáng fān.
Sì,
pronunciation: xiáng lì fān.
Right Grand Master of Rectification,
is the Right Grand Censor.
7 Ashǐnà Gǔdǔlù and other Tujue tribes frequently invaded the border.
Chúnyú Chùpíng (左玉鈐衛中郎將), the Colonel of the Left Jade Token Guard, was appointed Area Commander of Yángqǔ Dào
to attack them.
8 Shěn Jūnliàng (正諫大夫, 同平章事), Grand Master of Remonstrance and Administrator of Affairs, was dismissed.
9 Third Month,
Cuī Chá (正諫大夫, 同平章事), Grand Master of Remonstrance and Administrator of Affairs, was dismissed.
10On the day Bǐngchén,
Lúlíng Wáng was moved to Fángzhōu.
The *Jiùzhì* says: Fángzhōu
is one thousand one hundred and ninety-five *lǐ* south of the capital,
and one thousand one hundred and eighty-five *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
Dù Yòu says: Fángzhōu
was the land of the ancient states of Mí and Yōng.
In the Spring and Autumn period, Chu Zǐ defeated the Mí army at Fángzhǔ,
which is this place.
During Cao Wèi, it was Zhúshān County of Xīnchéng Commandery.
Then the ancient state of Yōng
was Shàngyōng County in Qin and Han dynasties.
11On the day Xīnyǒu,
Wǔ Chéngsì was dismissed.
12On the day Xīnwèi,
the Chuígǒng Ge (Regulations) were promulgated.
13Among the court officials, some who were demoted went to the prime minister to complain.
The Minister of the Interior, Qiān Wèidào, said:
"This is the Empress Dowager's decision."
Liú Yīzhī (同中書門下三品), Minister-Director of the Central Secretariat and Chancellery, said:
"Changes in office due to guilt by association
are made upon the ministers' petitions."
When the Empress Dowager heard this,
Summer,
Fourth Month,
on the day Bǐngzǐ,
Wèidào was demoted to Prefect of Qīngzhōu,
and Yīzhī was promoted to Grand Master of the Palace.
Grand Master of the Palace
is of the senior fourth rank.
Liú Yīzhī's original post was Sīmǎ of the Yù Wáng Palace.
Sīmǎ of a princely palace
is of the junior fourth rank.
"The sovereign and ministers are one body;
how can one attribute bad things to the sovereign
and take credit for good things oneself!"
14On the day Guǐwèi,
the Tujue raided Dàizhōu;
Chúnyú Chùpíng led troops to relieve it;
reaching Xīnzhōu,
they were defeated by the Tujue,
with over five thousand casualties.
15On the day Bǐng
wǔ,
Péi Jūdao was appointed Minister of the Interior.
Wáng Dézhēn (納言), the Grand Remonstrance Secretary, was exiled to Xiàngzhōu.
Xiàngzhōu is four thousand nine hundred and eighty-nine *lǐ* from the capital.
16On the day Jǐyǒu,
Sū Liángsì (冬官尚書), the Minister of Winter Works, was appointed Grand Remonstrance Secretary.
Guāngzhái changed the Ministry of Works to Ministry of Winter.
17On the day Rénxū,
an edict ordered all officials from the ninth rank and above, both inside and outside the capital, as well as the common people,
to recommend themselves.
This meant that those with talent could speak for themselves to seek advancement.
Lìng,
pronunciation: lì dīng fān.
18On the day Réngshēn,
Wéi Fāngzhì was appointed Minister-Director of the Phoenix and Luan Terrace.
19Sixth Month,
Wéi Dàijià (天官尚書), the Minister of Heaven Works, was appointed Minister-Director of the Phoenix and Luan Terrace.
Guāngzhái changed the Ministry of Personnel to Ministry of Heaven.
He was the elder brother of Wànshí.
20The Tóngluó, Púgù, and other tribes rebelled.
Liú Jìngtóng (左豹韜衛將軍), General of the Left Leopard-Pounce Guard, was dispatched with cavalry from Hexi to go out to Jūyán Hǎi to suppress them.
North of Shāndān County in Gānzhōu, crossing the Zhāngyè River,
heading northwest,
out of the Hélí Shān gorge,
along the eastern bank of the river,
winding northeast for a thousand *lǐ*,
there was the Níngkòu Army,
northeast of the army was Jūyán Hǎi.
Qí,
pronunciation: qí jì fān.
An imperial order provisionally established the Anběi Protectorate at Tóngchéng to receive those who surrendered.
Tóngchéng
was the Tóngchéng Garrison of Shāndān,
renamed Níngkòu Army in the second year of Tiānbǎo.
Jiàng,
pronunciation: hù jiāng fān.
21Autumn,
Seventh Month,
on the day Jǐyǒu,
Wèi Xuántóng (文昌左丞), the Left Vice Director of Wénchāng Bureau, was appointed Attendant-in-ordinary of the Luan Terrace and Minister-Director of the Phoenix and Luan Terrace.
The Left Vice Director of Wénchāng Bureau
is the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
22An edict declared that from now on, when sacrificing to Heaven and Earth,
Gāozǔ, Tàizōng, and Gāozōng would all be seated as co-sacrificers;
this was according to the proposal of Yuán Wànqǐng and others, Attendants-in-ordinary of the Phoenix Bureau.
23Ninth Month,
on the day Dīngmǎo,
Wáng Guǒ (廣州都督), the Military Governor of Guǎngzhōu, suppressed the rebellious獠 (Láo) tribes.
In the winter of the 24th year,
the eleventh month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
Wéi Dàijià, Shàngshū of the Tiānguān, was appointed Grand Commander of the Yànrán Dao Expeditionary Army to suppress the Tǔbō.
Initially,
after the deaths of Xī Tūjué's Xīngxīwáng Kěhàn and Jìwǎngjué Kěhàn,
the Ten Surnames were left without a lord,
and many tribes dispersed or perished.
Therefore, the Empress Dowager promoted Yuánqìng, the son of Xīngxīwáng and a Zhōnglángjiàng of the Zuǒ Bàotāo Wèi Yìfǔ,
(All the Táng guards had a Yìfǔ Zhōnglángjiàng and Lángjiàng.)
to be
(Liàng is pronounced like “Liàng.”)
concurrently the Dūhù of Kūnlíng,
inheriting the title of Xīngxīwáng Kěhàn and taking charge of the Five Duōlù tribes.
In the 25th year, Chén Zǐ'áng of Shèhóng, a Zhèngzì of the Líntái,
(During the Guāngzhái era, the Mìshūshěng was renamed Líntái. Zhèngzì was a junior ninth-rank official,
responsible for correcting texts.)
stated:
(Shèhóng County
belonged to Zǐzhōu,
and was part of the territory of the Hàn's Qī County.
Later, the Later Wèi divided it to establish Shèjiāng County,
because six lǐ east of Lóulǚ Tān there was Shèjiāng.
The Western Wèi mistakenly changed it to Shèhóng.)
"The imperial court dispatches envoys to inspect the four directions;
unsuitable individuals should not be appointed.
Also, for Cìshǐ and Xiànlìng,
careful selection is essential.
In recent years, the common people have been exhausted by military campaigns;
they must be brought to peace."
His summary said:
"If envoys are not carefully chosen,
then promotions and demotions will be unclear,
punishments will be unjust,
factions will advance,
and the upright will retreat.
It would only cause the common people to repair roads
and welcome and send off officials,
without any benefit.
The proverb says: 'To know a person,
observe those whom he employs.'
This must not be treated lightly."
He further said:
"The Zǎixiàng are Your Majesty's heart and mind;
the Cìshǐ and Xiànlìng are Your Majesty's hands and feet.
No one has ever been able to govern alone without a heart, mind, hands, and feet!"
He also said:
"The world contains a crisis,
from which good fortune and calamity arise.
When the crisis is calm, there is good fortune;
when the crisis stirs, there is calamity.
The common people are this crisis.
If the common people are at peace, they enjoy their lives;
if they are not at peace, they regard death lightly.
If they regard death lightly, there is nothing they will not do.
Rebellious villains will exploit the opportunity,
and the world will fall into chaos!"
He further said:
"Suí Yángdì did not know that the world contained a crisis,
but trusted greedy and sycophantic officials,
hoping to gain advantages from the barbarians,
and consequently perished.
How great a lesson is that!"
The Empress Dowager renovated the old Báimǎ Sì
and appointed the monk Huáiyì as its abbot.
Yáo Sīlián said: During the reign of Hàn Míngdì,
Buddhist scriptures were carried by a white horse from the Western Regions to Luòyáng,
and thus the Báimǎ Sì was established.
Wèi Shōu said: The Hàn established the Báimǎ Sì west of Yōngguān in Luòchéng.
This refers to the old Luòchéng;
the Táng's Luòchéng
was relocated by the Suí.
Huáiyì, a native of Hù,
originally named Féng Xiǎobǎo,
sold medicine in the Luòyáng market.
He was introduced by Gāozǔ's daughter,
Princess Qiānjīn,
to the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager, wishing him to have access to the forbidden palace,
had him ordained as a monk
and named him Huáiyì.
Because his family was humble,
she ordered him to be united in clan with the Fùmǎ Dūwèi Xuē Shào,
and commanded Shào to treat him as a paternal uncle.
(Xuē Shào was married to Princess Tàipíng, the Empress's daughter.)
More than ten eunuchs attended him;
commoners who encountered him would all flee and avoid him.
If anyone came close,
he would strike them on the head until it bled,
abandon them,
and leave them to their fate.
When he saw Daoist priests, he would beat them mercilessly,
and then shave their heads before leaving.
All high-ranking officials prostrated themselves before him.
Wǔ Chéngsì and Wǔ Sānsī treated him with the deference of servants,
even holding his reins for him,
while Huáiyì regarded them as if they were nothing.
He gathered many unruly youths,
ordained them as monks,
and they committed crimes with impunity;
no one dared to speak out.
Féng Sīxù, a Yòutái Yùshǐ,
(Yòutái was the Yòusùzhèngtái.)
repeatedly tried to punish him according to the law,
but Huáiyì ordered his attendants to beat Féng Sīxù,
nearly killing him.
In the 1st year of spring,
the first month,
the Empress Dowager issued an edict to restore governance to the Emperor.
Rùizōng knew that the Empress Dowager was not sincere,
and submitted a memorial firmly declining;
the Empress Dowager then resumed presiding over court and issuing decrees.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the empire.
In the 2nd month,
on the Xīnwèi day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
Lǐ Xiàoyì, the Dà Jiàngjūn of the Yòuwèi, having defeated Xú Jìngyè,
enjoyed significant prestige.
Wǔ Chéngsì and others resented him
and frequently slandered him to the Empress Dowager,
leading to his demotion to Cìshǐ of Shīzhōu.
In the 3rd month,
on the Wùshēn day,
the Empress Dowager ordered the casting of bronze remonstrance boxes:
The east box, named
"Yán'ēn,"
was for submitting rhapsodies, eulogies, and requests for advancement;
the south box, named
"Zhāojiàn,"
was for comments on the successes and failures of court governance;
the west box, named
"Shēnyuān,"
was for those with grievances or injustices;
and the north box, named
"Tōngxuán,"
was for reporting celestial phenomena, disasters, and secret military plans.
The four boxes
corresponded to their respective cardinal directions and colors.
(Zhèngjiàn refers to the Jiànyì Dàfū.)
In the first year of Chuígǒng,
one Zuǒ Bǔquē and one Yòu Bǔquē were established,
both of junior seventh rank;
and two Zuǒ Shíyí and two Yòu Shíyí,
both of junior eighth rank.
They were responsible for offering remonstrance to the emperor and stood after the Zuǒ Shǐ and Yòu Shǐ.
The Zuǒ Bǔquē and Zuǒ Shíyí belonged to the Ménxiàshěng,
while the Yòu Bǔquē and Yòu Shíyí belonged to the Zhōngshūshěng.)
(Shíguān means guarantor.)
When Xú Jìngyè rebelled,
Bǎojiā, the son of Shì Yùshǐ Yú Chéngyè, taught Xú Jìngyè to construct knife-carts and crossbows.
When Xú Jìngyè was defeated, Bǎojiā barely escaped.
The Empress Dowager wanted to know everything happening among the people,
so Bǎojiā submitted a memorial,
requesting the casting of bronze boxes to receive secret memorials from throughout the empire.
The device was a single chamber,
with four internal compartments,
each with an opening at the top
to receive memorials, allowing them to enter but not be removed.
The Empress Dowager approved of this.
(The Kǎoyì states: The Tǒngjì and Tánglì both say the bronze boxes were made in the eighth month.
We follow the Shílù and Jiù Běnjì here.
Also, the Cháoyě Qiānzài mentions
"Yú Sīxuǎn,"
saying: "The Empress wanted to make the boxes,
and summoned artisans,
but no one could make them.
Sīxuǎn responded to the imperial decree and made them,
which perfectly matched the design,
and so they were used."
We follow the Yùshǐtái Jì here.)
Bǎojiā's enemy submitted a complaint to the box,
accusing him of making weapons for Xú Jìngyè,
which killed many imperial soldiers,
and so Bǎojiā was executed.
The Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) had, since Xú Jìngyè's (Xú Jìngyè) rebellion,
suspected that many people in the empire were plotting against her.
Moreover, she had long monopolized state affairs,
and her private conduct was not proper.
Knowing that members of the imperial clan and high officials harbored resentment and discontent,
and were not truly submissive,
she wished to carry out a great slaughter to overawe them.
Thus, she widely opened the door for informants.
When someone reported a secret,
subordinate officials were not allowed to question them;
all were given post horses.
According to Tang (Táng) regulations: traveling by relay carriage meant four relays a day,
traveling by post horse meant six relays a day.
For those provided with horses,
a first-rank official received eight horses,
a second-rank six horses,
a third-rank five horses,
fourth and fifth-rank four horses,
sixth-rank three horses,
and seventh-rank and below two horses.
For those provided with relay carriages,
a first-rank official received ten horses,
a second-rank nine horses,
a third-rank eight horses,
fourth and fifth-rank four horses,
sixth and seventh-rank two horses,
and eighth and ninth-rank one horse.
For those of third rank and above summoned by imperial decree,
four horses were provided;
for fifth-rank, three horses;
and for sixth-rank and below, there were differences.
One relay
was thirty *lǐ* (lǐ).
The Tang Six Statutes (Táng Liùdiǎn) state: for fourth and fifth-rank officials,
regular provisions included seven dishes,
two *shēng* (shēng) of fine rice daily,
two *shēng* and three *gé* (gé) of wheat (mài),
one and a half *shēng* of wine,
one-third of a sheep's worth of meat,
two melons,
and salt, *chǐ* (chǐ), scallions, ginger, mallow, and leeks in varying amounts.
The New Tang History (Xīn Táng Zhì) states: for fifth-rank provisions,
miscellaneous expenses amounted to six hundred coins per month.
Even farmers and woodcutters
could be summoned for an audience,
and were provided for in the guest house.
The guest house
belonged to the Registrar (Diǎnkèlìng) of the Court of State Ceremonials (Hónglúsì).
"Provided for" means
given provisions.
"Seen"
is pronounced *xián biàn fān*.
Those seen were promoted to official positions without following the usual order,
and those without real information were not questioned.
Consequently, informants from all directions arose like swarms of bees,
and everyone stood on tiptoe, holding their breath in fear.
There was a Hu (Hú) man, Suǒ Yuánlǐ (Suǒ Yuánlǐ),
who understood the Empress Dowager's (Tàihòu) intentions.
He reported a secret, was summoned for an audience,
and was promoted to Guerrilla General (Yóujī Jiāngjūn),
ordered to investigate cases in the imperial prison.
Suǒ Yuánlǐ (Suǒ Yuánlǐ) was cruel by nature;
when interrogating one person, he would invariably force them to implicate dozens or hundreds of others.
The Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) repeatedly summoned and rewarded him to amplify his authority.
Thereupon, Zhōu Xìng (Zhōu Xìng) of Cháng'ān (Cháng'ān), a Director of the Ministry of Personnel (Shàngshū Dūshì),
in the Tang (Táng) Ministry of Personnel (Shàngshū Dūshěng), there was a Director (Dūshì)
who managed the Masters of Offices (Zhǔshì) and Clerks (Lìshǐ) of various departments.
"Shàng"
is pronounced *chén yáng fān*.
and Lái Jùnchén (Lái Jùnchén) of Luòyáng (Luòyáng), a Grand Judge (Píngshì) of the Ministry of Justice (Sīxíng),
followed one after another. Zhōu Xìng (Zhōu Xìng) was successively promoted to Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice (Qiūguān Shìláng),
and Lái Jùnchén (Lái Jùnchén) was successively promoted to Assistant Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
They privately kept hundreds of ruffians,
specializing in reporting secrets.
To frame someone,
they would invariably have multiple places report simultaneously,
with identical details.
Lái Jùnchén (Lái Jùnchén) and Wàn Guójùn (Wàn Guójùn) of Luòyáng (Luòyáng), a Grand Judge of the Ministry of Justice (Sīxíng Píngshì),
during Guāngzhái (Guāngzhái), the Grand Court of Justice (Dàlǐ) was renamed the Ministry of Justice (Sīxíng). A Grand Judge (Píngshì) was of rank eight, class one,
and was responsible for going on missions to investigate and impeach.
taught their followers to ensnare the innocent,
fabricating charges of rebellion,
constructing and arranging the narratives
with all their intricate details.
When the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) received reports from informants,
she would immediately order Suǒ Yuánlǐ (Suǒ Yuánlǐ) and others to investigate them.
They competed to devise cruel interrogation methods,
giving them names such as
"Setting the Hundred Pulses" (Dìng Bǎimài),
"Sudden Earth Roar" (Tūdì Hǒu),
"Grieving Dead Pig" (Sǐzhū Chóu),
"Seeking to Destroy a Family" (Qiú Pòjiā),
and "Reversal is Real" (Fǎn Shì Shí).
Some involved using a beam to bind the hands and feet and then rotating it,
which was called
"Phoenix Spreading Its Wings" (Fènghuáng Shàichì);
others involved tying an object around the waist,
and pulling the cangue forward,
which was called
"Donkey Colt Pulling Up a Stake" (Lǘjū Bájué);
or forcing the person to kneel and hold a cangue,
with bricks stacked on top of it,
which was called
"Immortal Presenting Fruit" (Xiānrén Xiànguǒ);
or making them stand on a high piece of wood,
and pulling the tail of the cangue backward,
which was called
"Jade Maiden Ascending the Ladder" (Yùnǚ Dēngtī);
or hanging them upside down with a stone tied to their head,
or pouring vinegar into their nose,
or placing an iron ring [AS-98BB] around their head and inserting wedges,
to the point where some had their brains split and marrow spill out.
Each time a prisoner was captured,
they would first display their torture instruments to them,
causing them to tremble and sweat,
and confess falsely at the mere sight.
Whenever an amnesty was declared,
Lái Jùnchén (Lái Jùnchén) would invariably order the prison guards to first kill the serious offenders,
and then announce the amnesty.
The Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) considered this loyalty,
and increasingly favored and trusted them.
Both inside and outside the court, these few individuals were feared
more than tigers and wolves.
Chén Zǐ'áng, Rectifier of Characters in the Lín Tái, submitted a memorial:
He believed:
"Those in charge, whether quickly or slowly, respectfully engage in their duties, but they were the first to stir up trouble and instigate disaster.
They seek to put an end to the source of evil,
exhaust its partisans,
and thus cause Your Majesty to greatly open the imperial prisons,
re-establish severe punishments.
Anyone with a trace of suspicion,
or whose statements implicate others,
is exhaustively pursued, arrested, investigated, and interrogated.
This has led to treacherous people being deluded [or misleading others],
taking advantage of the danger to falsely accuse each other,
reporting ambiguous suspicions,
hoping to gain titles and rewards.
This, I fear, is not the intention of punishing crimes and comforting the people.
Your servant humbly observes that the people of the world today
have longed for peace for a long time.
Therefore, even though the rebellion in Yángzhōu
lasted almost fifty days,
the empire remained tranquil,
not a speck of dust stirred.
Your Majesty does not strive for profound silence to relieve the weary people,
but instead employs severe punishments, thereby disappointing their hopes.
Your servant, dull and ignorant,
harbors great perplexity.
I humbly observe that among those who report secrets from various regions,
prisoners number in the hundreds and thousands.
Yet, when their cases are fully investigated,
not one in a hundred is proven true.
Your Majesty, being benevolent and forgiving,
moreover bends the law to tolerate them,
thereby allowing the party of evil-doers to maliciously plot against each other,
and a mere glance of displeasure is enough to be labeled a secret informant.
When one person is accused,
hundreds fill the prisons.
Envoys apprehend suspects,
and officials in carriages are as numerous as market-goers.
Some say that Your Majesty loves one person and harms a hundred.
The people of the world are anxious and expectant,
not knowing where to find peace.
Your servant has heard that at the end of the Suí dynasty,
the world was still peaceful.
Yáng Xuán'gǎn started a rebellion,
but failed in less than a month.
The evils of the empire
had not yet reached the point of collapse,
and the hearts of the common people [zhēng rén]
still hoped for a peaceful livelihood [lè yè].
Zhēng rén [蒸人],
is the same as zhēng mín [蒸民].
To avoid Emperor Tàizōng's taboo name,
the character
'mín' (民)
was changed
to 'rén' (人).
Lè (樂)
is pronounced luò.
Yet, Fán Zǐgài, the Minister of War, was allowed to exclusively carry out massacres,
thoroughly persecuting partisans.
None of the brave gentlemen within the seas [of the empire]
escaped calamity;
so much so that people were slaughtered like hemp,
and blood flowed like a lake.
This event is recorded in Volume 182, in the 9th year of Dàyè.
Only then did thoughts of rebellion arise,
and thus heroes and outstanding figures rose together, and the Suí clan perished.
Once a major inquisition begins,
it is impossible to avoid abuses.
The wronged lament and sigh,
affecting the harmony of qi,
leading to epidemics,
followed by floods and droughts.
Once people lose their livelihoods,
thoughts of disaster and rebellion will arise fearfully.
Ancient enlightened kings were cautious and deliberate with penal laws,
precisely fearing this.
In the time of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, when the Wūgǔ case arose,
it caused the crown prince to flee,
and troops clashed in the palace.
Millions of innocent people were killed,
and the imperial ancestral temple was almost overthrown.
Fortunately, Emperor Wǔ received a letter from the Three Elders of Húguān,
and suddenly became enlightened.
He exterminated the three clans of Jiāng Chōng.
This event is recorded in Volume 22, in the 2nd and 3rd years of Zhēnghé of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
Jǐ (幾)
is pronounced jū yī.
Only then did the empire become peaceful.
The ancients said: 'That which happened before, if not forgotten,
serves as a teacher for what is to come.'
These are the words of Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān in the Shǐjì.
The Empress Dowager did not listen.
5. In summer,
fourth month,
the Empress Dowager cast a grand ritual vessel (Dàyí)
and placed it at the North Palace Gate.
The North Palace Gate was outside Xuánwǔmén.
6. Cén Chángqiàn was made Nèishǐ.
In the sixth month,
on the day Xīnwèi,
Sū Liángsì was made Zuǒ Xiàng,
and Wéi Dàijià, concurrently Píng Zhāngshì, was made Yòu Xiàng.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
Wéi Sīqiān was made Nàyán.
Sū Liángsì encountered the monk Huái Yì in the court.
Huái Yì acted arrogantly and showed no deference.
Liángsì was furious and
ordered his attendants to seize and drag him away,
striking his cheek dozens of times.
Huái Yì complained to the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager said:
"Āshī should use the North Gate for entry and exit.
The Southern Court is where the prime ministers come and go.
Do not offend them."
The Empress Dowager claimed that Huái Yì had ingenious skills,
and therefore allowed him into the palace to carry out construction.
Wáng Qiúlǐ of Chángshè, a Bǔ Quē, submitted a memorial.
Chángshè
was a Hàn county.
Suí changed its name to Yǐngchuān.
In the 4th year of Wǔdé, it reverted to its old name
and was part of Xǔzhōu.
Shàng (上)
is pronounced shí zhǎng.
"In the time of Emperor Tàizōng,
there was Luó Hēihēi, skilled at playing the Pípá.
Emperor Tàizōng castrated him to be a servant [gěi shǐ],
and had him teach the palace women.
If Your Majesty believes Huái Yì has ingenious skills [qiǎo xìng],
and wishes to employ him in the palace,
your servant requests that he be castrated,
so as not to corrupt the palace chambers."
The memorial was shelved and not acted upon.
7. In autumn,
ninth month,
on the day Dīngwèi,
Hú Sèluó, son of the Western Tujue chieftain Jìwǎngjué Kèhán, was made Right Yùqínwèi Jiāngjūn,
inheriting the title of Jìwǎngjué Kèhán and leading the Wǔnǔshī Bì tribes.
8. On the day Jǐsì,
Yōngzhōu reported that a mountain had spontaneously emerged southeast of Xīnfēng County.
Xīnfēng was renamed Qìngshān County.
Xīnfēng had belonged to Jīngzhào since the Hàn dynasty.
Yú Wénjùn of Jiānglíng submitted a letter:
Jiānglíng County was part of Jīngzhōu.
"When the atmospheric qi is not harmonious, cold and heat occur together.
When human qi is not harmonious, warts and tumors grow.
When the terrestrial qi is not harmonious, hills and mounds appear.
Now, Your Majesty, as a female ruler, occupies the yang position,
reversing the roles of rigid and flexible [gāng róu].
Therefore, the terrestrial qi is blocked and obstructed,
and mountains emerge as a disaster.
Your Majesty calls it 'Auspicious Mountain' (Qìngshān),
but your servant believes it is not auspicious.
Your servant humbly believes that you should reflect upon yourself and cultivate virtue to respond to Heaven's warning.
Otherwise,
calamity and misfortune will ensue!"
The Empress Dowager was enraged,
and banished him to the region beyond the ridge (Lǐngwài).
Later, he was killed by the Six Routes Commissioners.
The Six Routes Commissioners are mentioned in Volume 205, in the 2nd year of Chángshòu.
Shǐ (使)
is pronounced shū lì.
9. The Tujue invaded.
Hēichǐ Chángzhī, Grand General of the Zuǒ Yīngyángwèi, resisted them.
Upon reaching Liǎngjǐng,
he encountered over three thousand Tujue soldiers.
Seeing the Táng troops,
they all dismounted and donned their armor.
Chángzhī charged them with over two hundred cavalry,
and they all abandoned their armor and fled.
At dusk, a large Tujue force arrived.
Chángzhī ordered fires to be lit in his camp,
and fires also started to the southeast.
The barbarians suspected there were supporting troops,
and so they fled during the night.
10. Dí Rénjié was the Inspector of Níngzhōu.
Guō Hàn of Jìnlíng, Censor of the Right Bureau, inspected Lǒngyòu,
and investigated and impeached many people wherever he went.
Upon entering Níngzhōu territory,
the roads were filled with elders singing praises of the Inspector's virtues.
Hàn recommended him to the court,
and he was summoned to be Dōngguān Shìláng.

Chuígǒng 3rd Year
(Dīnghài, 687)
1. In the spring,
in the intercalary first month,
on the *dīngmǎo* day,
the imperial prince Chéngměi was enfeoffed as King Héng.
At the time of Rùizōng, he was made emperor,
so Chéngměi and others were all imperial princes.
Héng
is pronounced *hù dēng fān*.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The Táng history, old imperial annals, and new biographies all record
"Chéngyì."
We now follow the *Shílù*.
Lóngfàn was made King Wèi,
and Lóngyè was made King Zhào.
2. In the second month,
on the *bǐngchén* day,
the Tujue (Turks) Gǔdǔlù and others raided Chāngpíng.
Chāngpíng
was a county in the Later Hàn,
belonging to Guǎngyáng Commandery.
In the Suí dynasty, it belonged to Zhuójùn;
in the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Yōuzhōu.
3. In the third month,
on the *yǐchǒu* day,
Nàyán Wéi Sīqiān retired as Grand Master of the Middle (Tàizhōng Dàfū).
4. In the summer,
in the fourth month,
Sū Liángsì was ordered to remain as Administrator of the Western Capital.
At that time, Shàngfāng Jiān Péi Fěigōng supervised the Imperial Parks.
Guāngzhái changed the Shǎofǔ Jiān to Shàngfāng Jiān.
The Imperial Parks were
the parks of the Western Capital.
Liángsì said:
"In the past, Gōngyí Xiū, when he was minister of Lǔ,
was still able to pull up mallow and dismiss the weaving women."
Dǒng Zhòngshū said: Gōngyí Xiū, when he was minister of Lǔ,
went to his home
and saw silk being woven.
He became angry and left.
His wife ate in the house and consumed mallow;
he was displeased and pulled up her mallow.
He said:
"I have already received a salary.
How can I also take the profits of the garden laborers and the weaving women?"
Xiàng
is pronounced *xī liàng fān*.
Qù
is pronounced *qiāng lǚ fān*.
So it stopped.
5. On the *rénxū* day,
Péi Jūdào was made Nàyán.
In the fifth month,
on the *bǐngyín* day,
Xiàguān Shìláng Zhāng Guāngfǔ of Jīngzhào was made Fènggé Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
6. Fènggé Shìláng and Tóng Fènggé Luántái Sānpǐn Liú Yīzhī secretly said to Fènggé Shèrén Jiǎ Dàyǐn of Yǒngnián:
Yǒngnián
was originally Qǔliáng County in the Hàn dynasty.
In the Wèi dynasty, it was the administrative seat of Guǎngpíng Commandery.
In the Suí dynasty, the commandery was abolished and it became Guǎngpíng County,
later renamed Jīzé.
In the first year of Rénshòu, it was renamed Yǒngyuán
[year]
to avoid the taboo name of Crown Prince Guǎng.
In the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Míngzhōu.
"Since the Empress Dowager has deposed the incompetent and established the intelligent,
why does she still preside over court and issue decrees?
It would be better to restore the rightful ruler
to pacify the hearts of the world."
Dàyǐn secretly reported this.
The Empress Dowager was displeased.
She said to her attendants:
"Yīzhī was brought up by me."
Liú Yīzhī rose from a scholar of the Northern Gate to a minister,
hence this statement.
Someone falsely accused Yīzhī of receiving gold from Sūn Wànróng, the Governor of Guīchéng Prefecture.
In the twenty-second year of Zhēngguān,
Guīchéng Prefecture was established for a separate tribe of Qìdān,
belonging to Sōngmò Dūdū Fǔ.
Fù
is pronounced *fú yòu fān*.
The Empress Dowager ordered Wáng Běnlì, the Prefect of Sùzhōu, to investigate him.
Běnlì declared the imperial edict to him.
Yīzhī said:
"If it does not pass through the Fènggé and Luántái,
how can it be called an imperial edict?"
The Empress Dowager was greatly enraged,
considering it an act of resisting the imperial envoy.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
he was granted death at his home.
When Yīzhī was first imprisoned,
Rùizōng submitted a memorial to plead on his behalf.
His friends and relatives all congratulated him.
Yīzhī said:
"This is precisely what will hasten my death."
Before his execution,
he bathed.
His demeanor was calm and composed.
He drafted his memorial of thanks himself,
completing several pages instantly.
Líntái Láng Guō Hàn
(Guāngzhái changed Mìshū Láng to Líntái Láng).
The Tàizǐ Gōng Sījīng Jú had one Tàizǐ Wénxué,
a rank six official,
responsible for attending to literary matters.
When the Empress Dowager heard of this,
she demoted Hàn to Sīfǎ of Wūzhōu,
and Sījūn to Sīcāng of Bòzhōu.
In the eighth year of Zhēngguān,
Wūzhōu was established from Lóngbiāo County of Chénzhōu.
In the ninth year,
Bòzhōu was established from Zāngkē County of the Suí dynasty's Zāngkē Commandery.
The old gazetteer states: Wūzhōu
is four thousand one hundred ninety-seven *lǐ* south of the capital,
and three thousand nine hundred *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
Bòzhōu
is four thousand four hundred fifty *lǐ* south of the capital,
and four thousand nine hundred sixty *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
7. In the autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the *rénchén* day,
Wèi Xuántóng was appointed acting Nàyán.
8. The native households of Lǐngnán used to pay half taxes.
Liú Yányòu, the Protector of Jiāozhǐ, made them pay full taxes.
The native households refused,
and Yányòu executed their leaders.
Their followers, Lǐ Sīshèn and others, revolted,
attacking and breaking into the Annam Protectorate city.
In the first year of Tiáolù under Gāozōng,
Jiāozhōu Dūdū Fǔ was changed to Ānnán Dūhù Fǔ.
Lǐ
is pronounced *lǐ*.
Cáo Xuánjìng, the Sīmǎ of Guìzhōu, led troops to suppress Sīshèn and others,
and beheaded them.
9. The Tujue (Turks) Gǔdǔlù and Yuánzhēn raided Shuòzhōu.
Hēichǐ Chángzhī, the Grand Commander of the Yànrán Circuit, was dispatched to attack them,
with Zuǒ Yīngyáng Dà Jiāngjūn Lǐ Duōzuò as his deputy.
They utterly defeated the Tujue at Huánghuāduī,
which means Huángguāduī.
According to Shuòzhōu, there is a Huánghuāduī
in Shénwǔ Chuān.
All the Tujue scattered and fled north of the desert.
Duōzuò's family had been chieftains of the Mòhé for generations.
He entered the imperial guard through military merit.
Whenever Hēichǐ Chángzhī received rewards,
he distributed them among his officers and soldiers.
When a good horse of his was injured by a soldier,
his officials requested that the soldier be flogged.
Chángzhī said:
"How can I flog imperial soldiers for a private horse?"
He ultimately did not question it.
10. In the ninth month,
on the *jǐmǎo* day,
Yáng Chūchéng of Guózhōu falsely claimed to be a Military Attendant (Lángjiāng),
and forged an imperial decree in the marketplace to recruit people to welcome King Lúlín from Fángzhōu.
The matter was discovered,
and he was executed.
11. In the winter,
in the tenth month,
on the *gēngzǐ* day,
Cuàn Bǎobì, the Zhōnglángjiāng of the Right Imperial Guard, fought against the Tujue (Turks) Gǔdǔlù and Yuánzhēn.
His entire army was lost,
and Bǎobì escaped alone on a light cavalry horse.
Bǎobì saw Hēichǐ Chángzhī's success,
and submitted a memorial requesting to pursue the remaining bandits to their lair.
An edict ordered him to consult with Chángzhī
and provide distant support.
Bǎobì wanted to claim the merit for himself,
so he did not wait for Chángzhī.
He led thirteen thousand elite soldiers ahead,
traveled over two thousand *lǐ* outside the pass,
and launched a surprise attack on their tribe.
Upon arrival,
he first sent someone to inform them,
allowing them to prepare thoroughly.
In the ensuing battle,
he was defeated.
The Empress Dowager executed Bǎobì.
She changed Gǔdǔlù's name to Bùzúlù.
12. Wèi Xuántóng was ordered to remain as Administrator of the Western Capital.
13 Wǔ Chéngsì (武承嗣) also sent someone to falsely accuse Lǐ Xiàoyì (李孝逸) of saying
"My name contains 'rabbit' (兔),
a rabbit
is a creature of the moon,
and thus I possess a heavenly destiny (天分)."
This implied he was destined to be the Son of Heaven.
Fēn (分),
read Fúwèn.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Wùyín (戊寅),
he was reprieved from death, stripped of his official title,
and exiled to Dānzhōu (儋州), where he died.
Dānzhōu (儋州)
was formerly Dān'ěr Xiàn (儋耳縣);
Dānzhōu (儋州) was established in the fifth year of Wǔdé (武德).
According to old gazetteers: Dānzhōu (儋州) was seven thousand four hundred and forty-two *lǐ* (里) from the capital.
Dān (儋),
read Túgān.
Zú (卒),
read Zǐxù.
*Kǎoyì* (考異) states: *Xīnjì* (新紀) says:
"On the *jǐhài* (己亥) day of the fifth month of the first year of Tiānshòu (天授),
Liánggōng Lǐ Xiàoyì (梁公李孝逸) was killed.
Xiàoyì (孝逸) was initially enfeoffed as Liángjùn Gōng (梁郡公);
for his achievements in suppressing Xú Jìngyè (徐敬業),
he was re-enfeoffed as Wúguó Gōng (吳國公);
in the third year of Chuíyǒng (垂拱),
he was reprieved from death and stripped of his official title,
then banished to Dānzhōu (儋州).
His noble rank should have been abolished then."
*Xīnchuán* (新傳) says:
"He was exiled to Dānzhōu (儋州) and died (薨)."
The *Jì* (紀) and *Chuán* (傳) contradict each other.
*Tánglì* (唐曆) says:
"On the eleventh day of the fourth month, Yìzhōu Chángshǐ Lǐ Xiàoyì (益州長史李孝逸) was executed.
This was also an old appointment."
*Tǒngjì* (統紀) says,
"Lǐ Xiàoyì (李孝逸) and his associates Cuī Yuánfǎng (崔元昉) and Péi Ānqī (裴安期) were executed."
*Tánglì* (唐曆) says,
"And his associates Cuī Zhīxián (崔知賢), Dǒng Yuánfǎng (董元昉), and Péi Ānqī (裴安期), etc."
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄) and *Jiùchuán* (舊傳).
14 The Empress Dowager wanted to dispatch Wéi Dàijià (韋待價) to lead troops to attack the Tǔbō (吐蕃).
*Kǎoyì* (考異) states: *Shílù* (實錄) says,
"On the *rénchén* (壬辰) day of the twelfth month,
Dàijià (待價) was appointed Grand Commander of Ānxī Dào (安息道),
to oversee thirty-six commanders in an expedition against the Tǔbō (吐蕃)."
It does not state how the expedition fared in victory or defeat.
In the fifth month of the first year of Yǒngchāng (永昌),
it again says
"Dàijià (待價) was ordered to attack the Tǔbō (吐蕃),
and in the seventh month, he was defeated at Yínshíjiā Hé (寅識迦河)."
However, his main biography (本傳) does not mention him leading troops on two occasions,
so this matter is now deleted.
"Please follow the old system and dispatch Censors to supervise the army."
The Empress Dowager said:
"In ancient times, enlightened rulers dispatched generals
and entrusted them with all matters outside the palace gate.
Recently, I have heard that when Censors supervise the army,
all military matters, great or small, must be reported and approved.
For those below to control those above
is not a standard institution;
furthermore, how can one then hold them accountable for their achievements?"
Thereupon, she abolished the practice.
15 In this year,
there was a great famine throughout the realm,
particularly severe in Shāndōng (山東) and Guānnèi (關內).
1 Spring,
first month,
on the *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) day,
three ancestral temples for Gāozǔ (高祖), Tàizōng (太宗), and Gāozōng (高宗) were established in Shéndū (神都),
with seasonal sacrifices performed according to the rites of the Western Temples.
The Western Temples (西廟) were the imperial ancestral temples in the Western Capital (西京).
The Empress Dowager ordered the responsible officials to deliberate on the number of ancestral temple chambers for honoring ancestors.
Sīlǐ Bóshì (司禮博士) Zhōu Cóng (周悰) requested seven chambers.
Guāngzhái (光宅) changed the Tàicháng (太常) office to Sīlǐ (司禮).
Historians say Zhōu Cóng's (周悰) request
was to curry favor and accommodate the Empress Dowager's wishes.
Chūnkuān Shìláng (春官侍郎) Jiǎ Dàyǐn (賈大隱) memorialized:
"According to the Rites,
the Son of Heaven has seven ancestral temples,
feudal lords have five temples,
a principle that has not changed for a hundred generations.
Now Zhōu Cóng (周悰) cites alternative, frivolous opinions
and widely spreads strange anecdotes,
merely promoting the current provisional ceremonies of the regency,
not adhering to the established national norms.
The Empress Dowager personally received the charge and entrustment,
glorifying the great way.
The number of ancestral temple chambers for honoring ancestors should be according to the number for feudal lords,
and the national ancestral temples should not be altered arbitrarily."
The Empress Dowager then desisted.
2 In the reigns of Tàizōng (太宗) and Gāozōng (高宗),
there were repeated intentions to build a Míngtáng (明堂).
Various scholars debated its design,
but it remained undecided and was abandoned.
When the Empress Dowager assumed regency,
she deliberated its design solely with the Northern Gate Scholars (北門學士),
without consulting other scholars.
The scholars believed that the Míngtáng (明堂) should be located in the *bǐngsì* (丙巳) auspicious direction of the capital,
between three and seven *lǐ* (里) from the city.
The Empress Dowager considered it too far from the palace.
In the second month,
on the *gēngwǔ* (庚午) day,
the Qiányuán Diàn (乾元殿) was demolished,
and a Míngtáng (明堂) was built on its site.
Monk Huáiyì (懷義) was appointed its commissioner,
and tens of thousands of people were conscripted for the labor.
3 Summer,
fourth month,
on the *wùxū* (戊戌) day,
Tàizǐ Tōngshì Shèrén (太子通事舍人) Hǎo Xiàngxián (郝象賢) was killed.
According to the Tang system,
Tàizǐ Tōngshì Shèrén (太子通事舍人) held the rank of regular seventh grade, lower class,
and was responsible for guiding palace officials for audiences and conveying greetings.
He was the grandson of Chǔjùn (處俊).
Initially,
the Empress Dowager harbored resentment towards Chǔjùn (處俊),
referring to his remonstrance with Gāozōng (高宗) in the second year of Shàngyuán (上元).
The Empress Dowager ordered Zhōu Xìng (周興) to interrogate him,
which led to the condemnation of Hǎo Xiàngxián's (郝象賢) clan.
Hǎo Xiàngxián's (郝象xián) family went to the court hall,
to plead their innocence to Jiānchá Yùshǐ (監察御史) Rèn Xuánzhí (任玄殖) of Lè'ān (樂安).
Lè'ān (樂安) Commandery
was in Dìzhōu (棣州).
Cháo (朝),
read Zhíyáo.
Jiān (監),
read Gǔxián.
Rèn Xuánzhí (任玄殖) was dismissed from office for this.
At his execution, Hǎo Xiàngxián (郝象賢)
cursed the Empress Dowager vehemently,
exposing hidden scandals in the palace,
snatching firewood from market vendors to strike the executioners;
the Jīnwǔ (金吾) soldiers collectively killed him.
The Empress Dowager ordered his body to be dismembered,
his father's and grandfather's tombs to be exhumed,
and their coffins destroyed and bodies burned.
Thereafter, throughout the Empress Dowager's reign,
when legal officials executed someone,
they would first plug their mouth with a wooden ball.
4 Wǔ Chéngsì (武承嗣) had a white stone carved with the inscription:
"The Sacred Mother (聖母) descends upon the people,
establishing an eternal imperial enterprise."
The end was filled with purple stone mixed with medicines.
On the *gēngwǔ* (庚午) day,
he had Táng Tóngtài (唐同泰) of Yōngzhōu (雍州) present a memorial dedicating it.
During the Suí (隋) dynasty, it was Jìngzhào Jùn (京兆郡),
renamed Yōngzhōu (雍州) in the first year of Wǔdé (武德).
Yōng (雍),
read Yúyòng.
The Empress Dowager was pleased,
naming the stone "Precious Chart" (寶圖).
She promoted Táng Tóngtài (唐同泰) to Yóujī Jiāngjūn (遊擊將軍).
In the fifth month,
on the *wùchén* (戊辰) day,
an edict proclaimed that she would personally perform the *bàiluò* (拜洛) ritual,
to receive
the "Precious Chart" (寶圖);
and conduct the Nánjiāo (南郊) ritual,
to offer thanks to Hào Tiān (昊天);
after the rites were completed,
she would ascend the Míngtáng (明堂)
and hold court for her officials.
She ordered the governors (*dūdū*) and prefects (*cǐshǐ*) of all prefectures, as well as members of the imperial clan and maternal relatives,
to gather in Shéndū (神都) ten days before the *bàiluò* (拜洛) ritual.
On the *yǐhài* (乙亥) day,
the Empress Dowager was given the exalted title of Shèngmǔ Shénhuáng (聖母神皇).
5 Sixth month,
on the *dīnghài* (丁亥) *shuò* (朔) day,
there was a solar eclipse.
6 On the *rénchén* (壬寅) day,
the Three Seals of Shénhuáng (神皇) were made.
7 Dōngyáng Dàcháng Gōngzhǔ (東陽大長公主) had her enfeoffment and income reduced,
and she and her two sons were exiled to Wūzhōu (巫州).
The Princess
was the daughter of Tàizōng (太宗).
Zhǎng (長),
read Zhīliǎng.
The Empress Dowager disliked her
because Gāo Shì (高氏) was the maternal clan of Zhǎngsūn Wújí (長孫無忌).
8 Jiāngnán Dào (江南道) Pacification Commissioner (*Xúnfǔ Dàshǐ*) and Dōngguān Shìláng (冬官侍郎) Dí Rénjié (狄仁傑), finding many excessive temples (*yíncí*) in Wú (吳) and Chǔ (楚),
memorialized to burn over one thousand seven hundred of them,
leaving only four temples: those of Xià Yǔ (夏禹),
Wú Tàibó (吳太伯), Jì Zhā (季札), and Wǔ Yuán (伍員).
9 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the dìngsì day,
an amnesty was granted to the empire.
The name
"Bǎotú"
was changed
to "Tiānshòu Shèngtú";
the Luòshuǐ River was renamed Yǒngchāng Luòshuǐ,
its deity was enfeoffed as Xiǎnshèng Hóu,
granted the additional title of Tèjìn,
fishing was prohibited,
and sacrifices to it were made equivalent to those for the Four Great Rivers (Sìdú).
According to the Táng system,
the Five Sacred Mountains (Yuè) and the Four Great Rivers (Dú) were designated as middle-level sacrifices.
The "Shèngtú Quán" [sacred diagram spring]
had Yǒngchāng County established beside it.
Sōngshān Mountain was also renamed Shényuè,
its deity was enfeoffed as Tiānzhōng Wáng,
appointed Tàishī, Shǐchíjié, and Shényuè Dàdūdū,
and pasturage was prohibited.
Furthermore, because an auspicious stone had been found earlier in the Sìshuǐ River,
the Sìshuǐ River was renamed Guǎngwǔ.
Sìshuǐ
was the Hàn dynasty's Chénggāo County,
part of Hénán Jùn;
during the Later Wèi, it was Chénggāo Jùn,
where the Dōngzhōng Fǔ was established;
in the 18th year of the Kāihuáng reign of the Suí dynasty, Chénggāo was changed to Sìshuǐ,
belonging to Zhèngzhōu.
Within the county's borders was Guǎngwǔ,
where the Chǔ and Hàn armies were stalemated.
Later, the county's name was changed to match her surname.
Sì
is pronounced "sì."
The Grand Empress Dowager secretly plotted a revolution,
gradually eliminating members of the imperial clan.
Hán Wáng Yuánjiā, Inspector of Jiàngzhōu; Huò Wáng Yuánkuǐ, Inspector of Qīngzhōu; Lǔ Wáng Língkuí, Inspector of Xíngzhōu; and Yuè Wáng Zhēn, Inspector of Yùzhōu
Yùzhōu was
the land of the Hàn dynasty's Rǔnán Jùn;
the Later Wèi established Yùzhōu,
which the Táng continued;
however, the Táng's Yùzhōu did not encompass all the land of the Hàn's Rǔnán Jùn.

And Yuánkuǐ's son, Jiāngdū Wáng Xù, Inspector of Jīnzhōu; Guó Wáng Fèng's son, Dōngguǎn Gōng Róng, Inspector of Shēnzhōu; Língkuí's son, Fànyáng Wáng Aǐ; and Zhēn's son, Lángyá Wáng Chōng, Inspector of Bózhōu—
all were known for their talent and good conduct among the imperial clan,
and the Grand Empress Dowager particularly feared them.
Yuánjiā and the others felt insecure internally,
and secretly harbored the ambition to restore the former order.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The old tradition,
"seventh month of the third year of Chuíyǒng,"
is incorrect.
Now we follow the *Shílù*.
Zuǎn fabricated a letter to Zhēn saying:
"The empress (meaning the Grand Empress Dowager) is increasingly ill,
and should be treated quickly;
if it continues until winter,
it may become an incurable disease."
And when the Grand Empress Dowager summoned the imperial clan to court at the Míngtáng,
the various princes, in turn, alarmed each other saying:
"The Divine Empress intends, during the great sacrifice,
to have informers denounce us,
arrest all members of the imperial clan,
and execute them without exception."
Zuǎn fraudulently produced an imperial sealed letter to Chōng saying:
"I am held in confinement,
the various princes should each raise troops to rescue me."
Chōng also fraudulently produced an imperial sealed letter saying:
"The Divine Empress intends to transfer the Lí clan's imperial rule to the Wǔ clan."
In the eighth month,
on the rényín day,
Chōng summoned Chief Clerk Xiāo Décóng and others to recruit soldiers.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Shílù* records it as the bǐngwǔ day,
presumably based on the day the report arrived.
The old tradition and the *Běnjì* record it as the rényín day.
Considering that Chōng died on the wùshēn day,
and the *Shílù* also states
"Chōng raised an army and was defeated seven days later,"
then the rényín day is correct;
we follow this now.
They were ordered to each raise troops and collectively advance towards Shéndū.
When the Grand Empress Dowager heard of this,
she appointed Qiū Shénjì, General of the Left Jīnwú, as the Grand Commander of the Qīngpíngdào Expeditionary Army to suppress him.
Bózhōu had Qīngpíng County,
which was the Hàn's Bèiqiū County,
renamed by the Suí.
Chōng recruited over five thousand soldiers,
and intended to cross the river to seize Jìzhōu;
he first attacked Wǔshuǐ.
Wǔshuǐ was
the land of the Hàn's Dōngjùn Yángpíng County;
the Suí renamed it Qīngyì,
and also divided Qīngyì to establish Wǔshuǐ County;
under the Táng, it belonged to Bózhōu.
Jì,
pronounced "zǐ lǐ fān."
Mǎ Xuánsù, Magistrate of Shēn,
Shēn was
also the land of the Hàn's Yángpíng County.
Later Qí renamed it Lèpíng,
the Suí in the sixth year of Kāihuáng restored it to Yángpíng,
in the eighth year changed it to Qīngyì,
and in the sixteenth year established Shēnzhōu;
in early Dàyè,
the zhōu was abolished and became Shēn County;
under the Táng, it belonged to Wèizhōu.
Fearing that his strength was insufficient,
he entered Wǔshuǐ
and closed the gates to defend.
Chōng pushed carts of straw to block its south gate,
and using the wind, set them on fire,
intending to rush in with the fire;
but as the fire started, the wind shifted,
Chōng's army could not advance,
and thus their morale was dampened.
Dǒng Xuánjì of Tángyì
Tángyì was
a Hàn county,
abolished during the Later Wèi,
the Suí re-established it by dividing Qīngyáng County,
and it belonged to Bózhōu.
said to people:
"Lángyá Wáng is fighting against the state;
this is rebellion!"
When Chōng heard this,
he beheaded Xuánjì and displayed his head to the public.
The crowd was terrified and scattered into the tall grass,
unable to be stopped;
only a few dozen household servants and close attendants remained.
Chōng fled back to Bózhōu,
and on the wùshēn day,
upon reaching the city gate,
he was killed by the gatekeepers.
The *Kǎoyì* states: Qiū Shénjì's biography says:
"He was killed by the officer Wú Xīzhì and the commoner Mèng Qīngbàng."
Now we follow the *Shílù* and Chōng's biography.
When Qiū Shénjì arrived in Bózhōu,
the officials, dressed in mourning clothes, came out to greet him,
but Shénjì
slaughtered them all,
destroying over a thousand households in total.
Yuèwáng Zhēn (越王貞) heard that Chōng (沖) had risen [in revolt],
and also raised troops in Yùzhōu (豫州).
He sent troops to capture Shàngcài (上蔡).
Shàngcài (上蔡) county,
during the Hàn (漢) dynasty, belonged to Rǔnán Jùn (汝南郡).
Later Wèi (魏) called it Línrǔ (臨汝).
In the early Kāihuáng (開皇) era of the Suí (隋) dynasty, it was renamed Wǔjīn (武津).
In the early Dàyè (大業) era, it was called Shàngcài (上蔡).
In the Táng (唐) dynasty, it belonged to Yùzhōu (豫州).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states
it was fifty-five *lǐ* (里) north of the prefecture.
On the *bǐngchén* (丙辰) day,
[the imperial court] appointed Zuǒ Bàotāo Dàjiāngjūn Qū Chóngyù (左豹韜大將軍麴崇裕) as Zhōngjūn Dàzǒngguǎn (中軍大總管),
and Cén Chángqiàn (岑長倩) as Hòujūn Dàzǒngguǎn (後軍大總管),
leading one hundred thousand troops to suppress him.
It also appointed Zhāng Guāngfǔ (張光輔) as Zhūjūn Jiédù (諸軍節度).
Chōng's (沖)
household registration was removed,
and his surname changed to Huǐ (虺) clan.
Zhēn (貞) heard of Chōng's (沖) defeat
and wanted to shackle himself and go to the imperial court to apologize.
It so happened that Fù Yánqìng (傅延慶), whom he had appointed as Xīncài Lìng (新蔡令)
Xīncài (新蔡) county,
from the Hàn (漢) dynasty onwards, belonged to Rǔnán Jùn (汝南郡).
In the Táng (唐) dynasty, it belonged to Yùzhōu (豫州).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states
it was one hundred and sixty *lǐ* (里) east of the prefecture.
Zhēn (貞) then declared to the masses:
"Lángxié (琅邪) has already broken through Wèi (魏) and Xiāng (相) prefectures,
with two hundred thousand troops,
who will arrive day and night."
He dispatched troops from the subordinate counties, totaling five thousand,
divided into five camps,
and had Péi Shǒudé (裴守德), the Rǔnán Xiànchéng (汝南縣丞), and others lead them.
Rǔnán (汝南) county,
formerly called Shàngcài (上蔡),
was renamed Rǔyáng (汝陽) in the early Dàyè (大業) era of the Suí (隋) dynasty.
It was attached to Yùzhōu (豫州).
All the officials he appointed were coerced and threatened;
none had the will to fight.
Only Shǒudé (守德) conspired with him.
Zhēn (貞) married his daughter to him,
appointed him Dàjiāngjūn (大將軍),
and entrusted him with his innermost confidence.
Zhēn (貞) had Daoist priests and monks chant scriptures to pray for success,
and his attendants and warriors all wore talismans to ward off weapons.
When Qū Chóngyù (麴崇裕) and his army reached forty *lǐ* (里) east of Yùzhōu (豫州) city,
Zhēn (貞) sent his youngest son Guī (規) and Péi Shǒudé (裴守德) to resist them.
Their army collapsed and returned.
Zhēn (貞) was greatly afraid,
closed the gates, and defended himself.
When Chóngyù (崇裕) and others arrived below the city walls,
his attendants said to Zhēn (貞):
"How can Your Highness sit and await slaughter and humiliation!"
Zhēn (貞), Guī (規), Shǒudé (守德), and his wife all committed suicide.
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The Shílù (實錄) says,
"On the *gēngxū* (庚戌) day,
Zhēn (貞) raised troops.
In the ninth month,
on the *bǐngyín* (丙寅) day,
Yùzhōu (豫州) was pacified."
It also says,
"He raised troops and was defeated in twenty days."
From *gēngxū* (庚戌) to *bǐngyín* (丙寅) is only seventeen days.
This is probably based on the date the reports arrived.
Earlier,
Fànyáng Wáng (范陽王) Ài (藹) sent an envoy to Zhēn (貞) and Chōng (沖), saying:
"If the various kings from all four directions rise simultaneously,
there is nothing that cannot be accomplished."
The various kings came and went, making agreements,
but before it was settled, Chōng (沖) launched his revolt first.
Only Zhēn (貞) responded hastily.
The other kings all dared not act,
hence the defeat.
When Zhēn (貞) was about to raise troops,
he sent an envoy to tell Shòuzhōu Cìshǐ (壽州刺史) Zhào Huái (趙懷).
Huái's (懷) wife, Chánglè Chánggōngzhǔ (常樂長公主)
Chánglè Gōngzhǔ (常樂公主) was
Gāozǔ's (高祖) daughter.
*Shǐ* (使),
pronounced as *shū lì fān* (疏吏翻);
same below.
pronounced *luò* (洛).
*Cháng* (長),
pronounced *zhī liǎng fān* (知兩翻).
[said:] "Tell Yuèwáng (越王) for me:
In the past, when Suí Wéndì (隋文帝) was about to usurp the Zhōu (周) imperial house,
Yùchí Jiǒng (尉遲迥),
a nephew of Zhōu (周),
was still able to raise troops to save the state.
This event is found in volume one hundred seventy-four, under the fourteenth year of Tàijiàn (太建) of Chén Xuāndì (陳宣帝).
*Wèi* (尉),
pronounced *yū wù fān* (紆勿翻).
His might shook the entire realm,
truly a loyal and heroic figure.
How much more so for you, the various kings,
sons of the former emperor!
How can you not have the state at heart!
Now the Lǐ (李) clan is as precarious as morning dew.
If you, the various kings, do not abandon life to uphold righteousness,
but still hesitate and do not act,
what are you waiting for?!
means to wait.
A true man should be a ghost of loyalty and righteousness;
do not die in vain."
After Zhēn's (貞) defeat,
the Empress Dowager wanted to execute all the kings, such as Hán (韓) and Lǔ (魯).
She ordered Jiānchá Yùshǐ (監察御史) Sū Xiàng (蘇珦) of Lántián (藍田) to investigate their secret denunciations.
Xiàng (珦) interrogated them,
but found no clear evidence.
Some accused Xiàng (珦) of colluding with Hán (韓) and Lǔ (魯).
The Empress Dowager summoned Xiàng (珦) to question him,
but Xiàng (珦) argued fearlessly and did not yield.
The Empress Dowager said:
"You are a man of great character.
I will find another task for you.
This case does not require you."
So she ordered Xiàng (珦) to oversee the army in Héxī (河西),
and instead had Zhōu Xìng (周興) and others investigate.
Thereupon, Hánwáng Yuánjiā (韓王元嘉), Lǔwáng Língkuí (魯王靈夔), Huáng Gōngzhuàn (黃公譔), and Chánglè Gōngzhǔ (常樂公主) were arrested in Dōngdū (東都),
coerced, and all committed suicide.
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The old tradition says:
"Língkuí (靈夔) was exiled to Zhènzhōu (振州)
and hanged himself."
Now we follow the Shílù (實錄).
"Huǐ" (虺)'s
close relatives and associates were all executed.
Dì Rénjié (狄仁傑), Wénchāng Zuǒchéng (文昌左丞), was appointed Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (豫州刺史).
In Guāngzhái (光宅), Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞) was renamed Wénchāng Zuǒchéng (文昌左丞).
There were six or seven hundred families liable for punishment,
and five thousand individuals whose property was confiscated.
The Sīxíng (司刑) urged that the executions be carried out.
The Sīxíng Sì (司刑寺) was the Dàlǐ Sì (大理寺).
pronounced as *cù* (促).
[Rénjié (仁傑) said:] "They were all misled and implicated by mistake.
I wish to make a formal plea,
but it might seem like I am defending rebels;
yet to know and not speak,
I fear would go against Your Majesty's benevolent intent."
The Empress Dowager specifically pardoned them,
and they were all exiled to Fēngzhōu (豐州).
When they passed through Níngzhōu (寧州),
the elders of Níngzhōu (寧州) welcomed and comforted them, saying:
"Did our Governor Dì (狄) save you?"
They held hands and wept beneath the Tablet of Virtue,
and held a three-day fast before continuing their journey.
At that time, Zhāng Guāngfǔ (張光輔) was still in Yùzhōu (豫州).
His officers and soldiers, relying on their merits, made many demands,
but Rénjié (仁傑) did not comply.
Guāngfǔ (光輔) angrily said:
"Does the prefectural governor disrespect the Grand Marshal?"
Rénjié (仁傑) said:
"The one who brought chaos to Hénán (河南) was only Yuèwáng Zhēn (越王貞).
Hénán (河南)
should be Rǔnán (汝南).
I wish Zhēn (貞) lived for ten thousand years!"
Guāngfǔ (光輔) questioned his words.
Rénjié (仁傑) said:
"Your Excellency commanded three hundred thousand troops,
and the only one you executed was Yuèwáng Zhēn (越王貞).
When the people in the city heard the government army approaching,
those who climbed over the walls to surrender formed paths on all four sides.
Your Excellency allowed your officers and soldiers to commit atrocities and plunder,
killing those who had already surrendered to claim merit,
causing blood to stain the fields red.
If this is not Zhēn (貞) living for ten thousand years, then what is it?!
I only regret not having the imperial sword of office to
strike your Excellency's neck.
Even death would be like returning home!"
Guāngfǔ (光輔) could not refute him.
He returned [to the capital]
and reported Rénjié's (仁傑) insubordination,
so Rénjié (仁傑) was demoted to Fùzhōu Cìshǐ (復州刺史).
From a high-ranking prefecture, he was demoted to a lower-ranking prefecture,
and moved from a nearby prefecture to a distant one.
The old records state: Yùzhōu (豫州)
was one thousand five hundred forty *lǐ* (里) from the capital,
and six hundred seventy *lǐ* (里) from Dōngdū (東都);
Fùzhōu (復州)
was one thousand eight hundred *lǐ* (里) southeast of the capital,
and one thousand five hundred eighteen *lǐ* (里) from Dōngdū (東都).
On the *dīngmǎo* (丁卯) day,
Zuǒ Sùzhèng Dàfū Qiān Wèidào (左肅政大夫騫味道) and Xiàguān Shìláng Wáng Běnlì (夏官侍郎王本立) were both appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
11 When the Grand Empress Dowager summoned the imperial clan members to attend court at the Míngtáng,
Dōngguǎn Gōng Róng secretly sent an envoy to ask Chéngjūn Zhùjiào Gāo Zǐgòng.
Gāo Zǐgòng said:
"If you go, you will surely die."
Róng then claimed illness and did not attend.
When Yuè Wáng Zhēn raised an army,
he sent an envoy to make an alliance with Róng.
Róng, in a panic, could not respond.
Forced by his officials,
he arrested the envoy and reported the matter.
He was promoted and appointed Yòu Zànshàn Dàfū.
In the Táng dynasty, the Zǒuzuǒ, Yòu Zànshàn Dàfū of the Eastern Palace
held the senior fifth rank.
They were responsible for conveying orders, admonishing for faults, assisting in ceremonies, and teaching the classics to the various princes.
Implicated by his faction,
in winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Jǐhài,
he was executed in the marketplace,
and his family's property was confiscated.
Gāo Zǐgòng was also executed for his involvement.
Jìzhōu Cìshǐ Xuē Yǐ, Yǐ's younger brother Xù, and Xù's younger brother Fùmǎ Dūwèi Shào
all conspired with Lángyá Wáng Chōng.
When Yǐ heard that Chōng had raised an army,
he made weapons
and recruited men.
When Chōng was defeated,
he killed Lùshì Cānjūn Gāo Zuǎn to silence him.
In the early Wǔdé period of Táng, the Zhōuzhǔbù was renamed Lùshì Cānjūn,
responsible for rectifying errors
and overseeing seals.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
Yǐ and Xù were executed.
Shào, due to Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ,
was given one hundred strokes of the rod
and starved to death in prison.
Shào, as the emperor's son-in-law, was spared capital punishment.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Yǐyǒu,
Sītú and Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Huò Wáng Yuánguǐ was implicated in conspiring with Yuè Wáng,
dismissed from office and exiled to Qiánzhōu.
According to old records: Qiánzhōu
is 3,193 *lǐ* south of the capital,
and 3,277 *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
Qián
is pronounced *qín*.

15 On the day Xīnhài,

It was 294 *chǐ* high and 300 *chǐ* square.
It had three stories in total: the lower story represented the four seasons,

On top

Inside was a giant pillar ten *wéi* in circumference,

Below was an iron channel,

The iron channel was for water circulation.
A banquet was held and rewards were given to all officials,

1. In spring,

His words were gentle and his meaning profound,

Someone reproached Chǔyuàn for her exceptional frugality and simplicity,

"What is valued in wealth and nobility

Now you alone adhere to diligence and hardship,

Chǔyuàn replied:
"I loved propriety when I was young,
and now I practice it.
Is this not living as I wish?
Looking at women throughout history,
all have been praised for their reverence and frugality,
and condemned for extravagance and indulgence.
I fear bringing disgrace to my parents,

Wealth and nobility are fleeting things,

Everyone was ashamed and convinced.
