and to change his surname to Wǔ (武).
The Empress Dowager loved him and
renamed him Yán'ān Dàzhǎng Gōngzhǔ (延安大長公主).
In the ninth month, on the day of Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
Fù Yóuyì (傅遊藝) of Jí (汲), a Shìyùshǐ (侍御史) –
Jí Xiàn (汲縣)
belonged to Hénèi Jùn (河內郡) in the Han (漢) dynasty.
Since the Jin (晉) dynasty, it was attached to Jí Jùn (汲郡).
In the Eastern Wei (東魏), Yìzhōu (義州) was established.
The Sui (隋) abolished it and made it Jí Xiàn (汲縣).
In early Zhēnguān (貞觀),
the seat of Wèizhōu (衞州) was moved there.
– requested to change the dynastic title to Zhōu (周)
and to bestow the imperial surname Wǔ (武).
The Empress Dowager did not grant it
but promoted Yóuyì (遊藝) to Jǐshìzhōng (給事中).
Thereupon, over sixty thousand people, including all officials, imperial relatives, distant and near commoners, tribal chiefs of the four barbarians, monastics, and Daoist priests,
all submitted memorials in accordance with Yóuyì's (遊藝) request.
The Emperor also submitted a memorial, personally requesting the surname Wǔ (武).
On the day of Wùyín (戊寅),
the sycophantic ministers reported: “A phoenix flew from the Míngtáng (明堂) into the Shàngyáng Gōng (上陽宮),
then gathered on a wútóng (梧桐) tree at the Zuǒtái (左臺)
– Zuǒtái (左臺) was the Zuǒsùzhèng Tái (左肅政臺) –
and then flew southeast.
Also, tens of thousands of red sparrows gathered in the court hall.”
On the day of Gēngchén (庚辰),
the Empress Dowager approved the requests of the Emperor and the sycophantic ministers.
On the day of Rénwǔ (壬午),
she ascended the Zétiān Lóu (則天樓)
– which was the Zétiān Ménlóu (則天門樓).
She changed the Tang (唐) dynasty to Zhou (周)
and changed the era name.
The era name was changed to Tiānshòu (天授).
On the day of Yǐyǒu (乙酉),
she was granted the honorable title Shèngshén Huángdì (聖神皇帝).
The Emperor was made the Huángsì (皇嗣)
and given the surname Wǔ (武).
The Crown Prince was made the Huángsūn (皇孫).
On the day *bǐngxū*
the Seven Ancestral Temples of the Wǔ clan were established in Shéndū.
Wǔ Wénwáng of Zhōu was posthumously honored as Shǐzǔ Wén Huángdì,
and his consort, Sī Shì, as Wéndìng Huánghòu.
Sī
refers to Tàisī.
According to genealogical records, the Sī surname originated from Gǔn.
His consort, Jiāng Shì, was honored as Kāngruì
Huánghòu.
The empress’s distant ancestor was Jī Zhōu,
and this was a great deception of the spirits.
Would Wénwáng truly accept sacrifices for those who were not his legitimate descendants?
The consort was titled Chéngzhuāng Huánghòu.
Zhào Sùgōngwáng was titled Sùzǔ Zhāngjìng Huángdì.
Wèi Yìkāngwáng was titled Lièzǔ Zhāo'ān Huángdì.
Zhōu Ānchéngwáng was titled Xiǎnzǔ Wénmù Huángdì.
Zhōngxiào Tàihuáng was titled Tàizǔ Xiàomíng Gāohuángdì.
All their consorts received posthumous titles corresponding to their husbands’
and were called empresses.
Wǔ Chéngsì was enfeoffed as Wèi Wáng,
Wǔ Sānsī as Liáng Wáng,
Wǔ Yōuníng as Jiànchāng Wáng.
Wǔ Shìhuò's elder brother's grandsons—Yōuguī, Chóngguī, Zàidé, Yōujì, Yìzōng, Sìzōng, Yōuyí, Yōuwàng, Yōuxù, and Yōuzhǐ—were all enfeoffed as Jùnwáng.
All paternal aunts and elder female cousins were granted the title of Chánggōngzhǔ.
Furthermore, Shǐ Wùzī of Lìyáng, Sī Bīn Qīng, was appointed Nàyán.
In Guāngzhái, Hónglú was renamed Sī Bīn.
Lìyáng Xiàn
belonged to Dānyáng Jùn during the Hàn dynasty.
The Eastern Jìn followed this.
When Suí conquered Chén,
Dānyáng Jùn was abolished,
and Lìyáng Xiàn was made part of Xuānzhōu.
Lì
is pronounced *lì*.
Fù Yóuyì, Gěishìzhōng, was made Luántái Shìláng and Píngzhāngshì.
Yóuyì, along with Cén Chángqiàn, Zhāng Qiánxù, Yòu Yùqínwèi Dàjiāngjūn, Qiū Shénjì, Zuǒ Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn, and Lái Zǐxún, Shìyùshǐ, were all granted the surname Wǔ.
Qín Kèqián had urged the Empress Dowager to initiate the revolution,
hence he was first made Nèishǐ.
Within a year, Yóuyì successively wore green, blue, vermilion, and purple robes,
rising from the ninth rank to the third rank
within a single year.
Yī
is pronounced *yì*.
An edict was issued to change Zhōu to Jùn.
Someone said to the Empress Dowager:
"Your Majesty abolishing Zhōu at the beginning of the revolution is inauspicious."
The Empress Dowager immediately withdrew the order.
Shǐ Wùzī and ten others were ordered to
tour
and inspect the various circuits.
The Empress Dowager enfeoffed her brother's grandsons, Yánjī and six others, as Jùnwáng.
16 In the winter,
on the tenth month,
the day *jiǎzǐ*,
Zōng Qínkè, Jiǎnjiào Nèishǐ, was demoted to Zūnhuà Wèi for corruption.
Zūnhuà Xiàn belonged to Qīnzhōu,
established in the twentieth year of Kāihuáng of the Suí dynasty.
He was exiled to the Lingnan region for his illicit gains.
17 On the day *dīngmǎo*,
the exile Wéi Fāngzhì was killed.
*Kǎoyì* states: "The old tradition says:
'He was exiled to Dānzhōu and died soon after.'"
This account follows the *Tǒngjì* and *Xīn Běnjì*.
18 On the day *xīnwèi*,
Xíng Wénwěi, Nèishǐ, was demoted to Zhēnzhōu Cìshǐ for colluding with Zōng Qínkè.
Zhēnzhōu was
the territory of Yèláng Jùn during the Hàn dynasty.
In the sixteenth year of Zhēnguān, a mountain cave was opened,
and Zhēnzhōu and Yèláng Xiàn were established from the old Bòzhōu city.
It was named because of Lóngzhēn Shān within the county's boundaries.
The old gazetteer states: Zhēnzhōu is 4,100 *lǐ* from the capital,
and 3,700 *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
When an imperial envoy arrived at the prefecture,
he was called a zhìshǐ because he was sent by imperial edict,
similar to saying zhàoshǐ.
Shǐ
is pronounced *shǐ*.
He immediately hanged himself.
19 On the day *rénshēn*,
an edict was issued for each of the two capitals and various prefectures to establish a Dàyún Sì temple,
to store the *Dàyún Jīng*,
and to have monks ascend the high seat to explain it.
The nine monks who compiled commentaries, including Yún Xuān, were all granted the title of Xiàngōng,
and were also given purple *jiāshā* and silver tortoise pouches.
Western foreign monks wore clothes of coarse hair,
which were called *jiāshā*.
When they flowed into China,
they were made of silk and cloth.
Ordinary monks all wore black robes,
only those who were granted purple were allowed to wear purple.
Jiā
is pronounced *jiā*;
shā
is pronounced *shā*.
According to Táng regulations,
officials were given personal fish tallies
to distinguish their ranks
and for responding to summons.
Gāozōng gave personal silver fish pouches to those of the fifth rank and above
to prevent fraudulent summons,
requiring them to be matched upon entering and leaving;
those of the third rank and above had gold-decorated pouches.
During Chuígǒng,
Dūdū and Cìshǐ began to be granted fish tallies.
In the second year of Tiānshòu,
the custom of wearing fish tallies was changed to wearing tortoise tallies.
Thereafter, those of the third rank and above had tortoise pouches decorated with gold,
fourth rank with silver,
and fifth rank with copper.
At the beginning of Zhōngzōng's reign, tortoise pouches were abolished,
and fish tallies were reissued.
20 An edict was issued that all Wǔ clan members throughout the empire were exempt from taxes and labor services.
21 The Ten Tribes of the Western Tujue,
having been repeatedly invaded by the Eastern Tujue since Chuígǒng—
the Eastern Tujue referring to Gǔdùlù and others—
Hú Sèluó, Měngchí Dūhù Jìwǎngjué Kèhán, gathered their remaining 60,000 to 70,000 people and moved them to reside in the interior.
He was appointed Yòu Wèi Dàjiāngjūn
and renamed Jiézhōngshìzhǔ Kèhán.
Kè
is pronounced with the entering tone of *kān*.
Hán
is pronounced *hán*.
22 Lǐ Xíngbāo, Cìshǐ of Dàozhōu, and his brothers were implicated by cruel officials
and were sentenced to extermination of their clan.
Xú Yǒugōng, Qiūguān Lángzhōng, firmly argued against it but could not succeed.
Zhōu Xìng, Qiūguān Shìláng, impeached Yǒugōng for
releasing
prisoners, deeming it a capital offense.
*Kǎoyì* notes: "The old and new biographies both place Yǒugōng's defense of Xíngbāo after his defense of Péi Xíngběn.
However, Xíngběn's offense occurred in the first month of the first year of Chángshòu,
by which time Zhōu Xìng had already been demoted and died.
Xíngbāo was implicated for plotting to restore the Lǐ clan,
which must have been after the revolution.
Thus, it is placed at the end of this year."
Yǒugōng was also dismissed from office.
However, the Empress Dowager greatly respected Yǒugōng,
and after a long time,
he was reinstated as Shìyùshǐ.
Yǒugōng prostrated himself, tears streaming, and firmly declined, saying:
"I have heard that a deer runs in the mountains and forests, yet its life hangs in the kitchen.
Circumstances make it so.
Your Majesty appoints me as a judicial official,
and I dare not pervert Your Majesty's law.
I shall surely die in this office."
The Empress Dowager insisted on conferring the appointment,
and those who heard of it, near and far, congratulated each other.
23 In this year,
Quán Xiànchéng, Yòu Wèi Dàjiāngjūn, was made Zuǒ Wèi Dàjiāngjūn.
The Empress Dowager brought out gold and jewels,
and ordered five of the best archers from the northern and southern imperial guards to compete for them.
Xiànchéng came in first,
but yielded to Xuē Duōmó, Yòu Yùqínwèi Dàjiāngjūn.
Duōmó, in turn, yielded to Xiànchéng.
Xiànchéng then memorialized, saying:
"Your Majesty commanded the selection of skilled archers.
Now many are not Hàn officials.
I fear the four barbarian tribes may slight the Hàn."
Quán Xiànchéng was
the son of Quán Nánshēng of Gāolì.
Xuē Duōmó was
of Xuē Yántuó descent,
hence the statement.
The Empress Dowager approved and followed his advice.
1 In the first month,
on the day *guǐyǒu* (the first day of the month),
the Empress Dowager first received the honorable title in the Wànxiàng Shéngōng.
Hàn Āidì called himself Chén Shèng Liú Tàipíng Huángdì,
and honorable titles perhaps originated from this.
It was especially contrary to ancient practice for the Empress Dowager, a female ruler, to receive an honorable title.
Thereafter, Xuánzōng, from the third year of Xiāntiān to the thirteenth year of Tiānbǎo,
over fifty years,
received honorable titles six times,
and rulers eventually regarded it as common practice.
On the day *jiǎxū*,
the Altars of Land and Grain were relocated to Shéndū.
On the day *xīnsì*,
the spirit tablets of the Wǔ clan were enshrined in the Tàimiào.
The Táng Tàimiào in Cháng'ān
was renamed Xiǎngdé Miào.
In the four seasons, only Gāozǔ and subsequent emperors were honored,
while the remaining
four chambers were closed and not honored.
The four chambers were those for Xuāndì, Yuándì, Guāngdì, and Jǐngdì.
In the fourth year of Chuígǒng,
the Chóngxiān Miào was established.
On the day *yǐyǒu*
(winter solstice),
a grand ceremony was held in the Míngtáng,
offering sacrifices to Hàotiān Shàngdì,
with all other deities accompanying the sacrifice.
The ancestors of the Wǔ clan were honored as co-sacrificers,
and the three Táng emperors also co-sacrificed.
2 Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng zhī Dàfū Shì, Lǐ Sìzhēn, seeing the rampant cruelty of corrupt officials,
submitted a memorial
stating:
“Currently, accusations are in disarray,
mostly false and rarely true.
I fear there are wicked individuals secretly plotting to sow discord between Your Majesty and your ministers.
In ancient times, when a case was concluded,
the Gōngqīng would participate in the hearing,
and the king would pardon three times
before carrying out the execution.
The ‘Wáng Zhì’ records: when a verdict is reached,
the historian informs the Zhèng that the case is concluded,
and the Zhèng hears it;
the Zhèng then informs the Dà Sīkòu that the case is concluded,
and the Dà Sīkòu hears it beneath a thorny tree;
the Dà Sīkòu then informs the king that the case is concluded,
and the king orders the Sāngōng to participate in the hearing;
the Sāngōng then inform the king that the case is concluded,
and the king pardons three times
before imposing the punishment.
Once an investigation and interrogation are finalized,
the legal authorities should follow the judgment
and not allow re-interrogation.
However, sometimes decisions are made unilaterally on the spot,
without being reported to the throne again.
If this is the case,
power rests with the ministers,
which is not a cautious and deliberate method.
If there happens to be an injustice,
how can it be known?
Moreover, to allow a ninth-rank official to be solely entrusted with investigation and review,
wielding the power of life and death,
and usurping the sovereign’s authority,
with investigations not handled by the Qiūguān,
and reviews not passing through the Ménxià,
the state's vital instruments
are lightly entrusted to others.
I fear this will become a calamity for the state.”
The Empress Dowager did not listen.
3 Ráoyáng Wèi Yáo Zhēnliàng and several hundred others submitted a memorial requesting to bestow the honorific title “Shàng Shèng Dàshén Huángdì,”
but it was not granted.
4 Shìyùshǐ Lái Zǐxún falsely accused Shàngyī Fèngyù Liú Xínggǎn and his brothers of plotting rebellion,
and they were all executed.
5 Spring,
first month.
Dìguān Shàngshū Wǔ Sīwén and 2,800 Cháojíshǐ
submitted a memorial requesting the封 (fēng) of Mount Sōng.
Mount Sōng
is Sōngshān.
Cháo (朝),
reads zhí yáo.
6 On the day Jǐhài,
the officials of the Táng Xìngníng, Yǒngkāng, and Yǐnlíng agencies were abolished.
Emperor Yuán’s mausoleum was called Xìngníng,
and Emperor Jǐng’s mausoleum was called Yǒngkāng.
Xìngníng Mausoleum was in Xiányáng,
and Yǒngkāng Mausoleum was eighteen lǐ north of Sānyuán.
All Táng mausoleums had one Lìng,
of the senior fifth rank;
two Fǔ,
four Shǐ,
four Zhǔyī,
four Zhǔniǎn,
four Zhǔyào,
three Diǎnshì,
and two Zhǎnggù.
There was also one Línglìng,
in charge of the mountain mausoleum,
who led the mausoleum households to guard it;
a Céng served as his deputy.
7 Zuǒ Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn Qiū Shénjì was executed for his crimes.
8 Nàyán Shǐ Wùzī, together with Lái Jùnxún, interrogated the case of Liú Xínggǎn.
Jùnxún memorialized that Wùzī was close to Xínggǎn and
intended to suppress evidence of his rebellion.
The Empress Dowager ordered Jùnxún to interrogate him as well.
Wùzī committed suicide in fear.
9 Someone accused Wénchāng Yòuchéng Zhōu Xīng of colluding with Qiū Shénjì.
The Empress Dowager ordered Lái Jùnxún to interrogate him.
Jùnxún and Xīng were discussing a case over a meal,
and Jùnxún said to Xīng:
“Many prisoners do not confess.
What method should be used?”
Xīng replied:
“This is very easy!
Take a large jar,
heat it all around with charcoal,
make the prisoner go inside,
and there’s nothing they won’t confess!”
Jùnxún then summoned a large jar,
heated it with fire as Xīng described,
then stood up and said to Xīng:
“There is an internal case to interrogate you, my brother.
Please enter this jar!”
Xīng, terrified, kowtowed and confessed his guilt.
By law, he should have died,
but the Empress Dowager pardoned him.
In the second month,
Xīng was exiled to Lǐngnán,
and on the way,
he was killed by his enemies.
Xīng, Sǔo Yuánlǐ, and Lái Jùnxún competed in their cruelty and harshness.
Xīng and Yuánlǐ each killed several thousand people,
and Jùnxún ruined over a thousand families.
Yuánlǐ’s cruelty was particularly severe,
so the Empress Dowager also had him killed to satisfy public demand.
10 Zuǒ Wèi Dàjiāngjūn Qiānchéng Wáng Wǔ Yōují was transferred to become Dìng Wáng.
11 Guāngshùn, son of the late Crown Prince Xián, was established as Yìfēng Wáng.
Kǎoyì says: It was previously recorded as Ānlè Wáng.
Now following Tánglì and Tǒngjì.
12 On the day Jiǎzǐ,
the Empress Dowager decreed that the mausoleum of the founding ancestor be named Délíng,
the mausoleum of the ancestral Rùizǔ be named Qiáolíng,
the mausoleum of the ancestral Yánzǔ be named Jiélíng,
the mausoleum of the ancestral Sùzǔ be named Jiǎnlíng,
the mausoleum of the ancestral Lièzǔ be named Jìnglín,
the mausoleum of the ancestral Xiǎnzǔ be named Yǒnglín,
and changed Zhāngdélíng to Hàolíng,
and Xiǎnyìlíng to Shùnlíng.
13 Lǐ Jūnxiàn’s official title and rank were posthumously restored.
Jūnxiàn’s execution is recorded in Volume 199, Tàizōng Zhēnguān 22nd year.
14 Summer,
fourth month,
on the first day, Rén Yín,
there was a solar eclipse.
15 On the day Guǐmǎo,
an edict was issued stating that Buddhism paved the way for revolution,
referring to the Dàyúnjīng.
16 Jiàn'ān Wáng Yōu Yí was ordered to remain in Cháng'ān as acting governor.
17 On the day Bǐngchén,
a large bell was cast
and placed at the North Gate.
18 Fifth month.
Cén Chángqiàn was appointed Wǔwēi Dào Xíngjūn Dàzǒngguǎn
to attack Túbō.
He was recalled midway,
and the army ultimately did not march out.
19 Sixth month.
Zuǒ Sùzhèng Dàfū Gé Fǔyuán was appointed Dìguān Shàngshū.
Xìngpǔ says: The Gé surname
is descended from Yǔn Gé;
the Dōngguān Hànjì mentions Shìyùshǐ, Dōngpíng Xiàng Gé Bān.
Sīhuì
was the son of Yànhuì.
Lè Yànhuì is mentioned in Volume 200, Gāozōng Xiǎnqìng 1st year.
20 Autumn,
seventh month.
Hundreds of thousands of households from Guānnèi were moved to populate Luòyáng.
21 Eighth month,
on the day Wùshēn,
Nàyán Wǔ Yōuníng was dismissed and made Zuǒ Yǔlín Dàjiāngjūn;
Xiàguān Shàngshū Ōuyáng Tōng was appointed Sīlǐ Qīng.
Guāngzhái changed Tàicháng to Sīlǐ.
22 On the day Gēngshēn,
Yùqín Wèi Dàjiāngjūn Zhāng Qiánxù was killed.
Lái Jùnxún interrogated Qiánxù’s case,
and Qiánxù pleaded his innocence to Xú Yǒugōng;
Jùnxún, angered,
ordered guards to hack him to death with knives
and displayed his head in the market.
23 Yìfēng Wáng Guāngshùn, Sì Yōng Wáng Shǒulǐ, Yǒng'ān Wáng Shǒuyì, Chángxìn Xiànzhǔ, and others were all granted the surname Wǔ.
According to Táng regulations: Sīwáng and Jùnwáng were of the senior first rank.
Guāngshùn and his brothers were all sons of Zhānghuái Tàizǐ Xián.
Sì (嗣),
reads xiáng lì.
Yōng (雍),
reads yú yòng.
They had not left their residences for over ten years.
Shǒulǐ and Shǒuyì
were Guāngshùn’s younger brothers.
24 Someone accused Dìguān Shàngshū Wǔ Sīwén of initially colluding with Xú Jìngyè.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Sīwén was exiled to Lǐngnán
and his original surname, Xú, was restored.
Sīwén’s change of surname is mentioned in the previous volume, Guāngzhái 1st year.
25 Ninth month,
on the day Yǐhài,
Qízhōu Cìshǐ Yún Hóngsì was killed.
Lái Jùnxún interrogated him
without asking a single charge (kuǎn).
A “kuǎn” is a confession that comes from the prisoner’s mouth in a court statement.
Kuǎn (款) means sincerity,
meaning everything spoken is sincere and true.
He instead fabricated a case and memorialized it.
The killing of Zhāng Qiánxù was also done in the same manner.
Imperial edicts approved all of them,
and the people of the realm were silenced.
26 Luántái Shìláng, Tóng Píngzhāngshì Fù Yóuyì dreamed of ascending the Zhànlù Diàn.
He told a confidant about it,
who then reported him.
On the day Rénchén,
he was imprisoned
and committed suicide.
On the 27th day, *guǐsì*,
Wǔ Yōuníng (武攸寧), Prince of Jiànchāng (建昌) and Grand General of the Left Yǔlín Guard, was made Nàyán (納言).
Dí Rénjié (狄仁傑), Sīmǎ (司馬) of Luòzhōu (洛州), was made Dìguān Shìláng (地官侍郎),
and, along with Péi Xíngběn (裴行本), Dōngguān Shìláng (冬官侍郎), was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
The Grand Empress Dowager said to Rénjié:
"When you were in Rǔnán (汝南),
you governed very well."
This refers to when he was Governor of Yùzhōu (豫州) in Chuígǒng (垂拱) 4th year.
Rénjié bowed and said:
"If Your Majesty considers me to have erred,
I request to correct it;
if you know me to have no fault,
that is my good fortune.
I do not wish to know the names of those who slandered me."
The Grand Empress Dowager praised him deeply.
Earlier,
Zhāng Jiāfú (張嘉福) of Xiūwǔ (脩武), Fènggē Shèrén (鳳閣舍人),
instigated several hundred people, including Wáng Qìngzhī (王慶之) from Luòyáng (洛yáng), to submit a memorial
requesting the establishment of Wǔ Chéngsì (武承嗣) as Crown Prince.
Cén Chángqiàn (岑長倩), Right Chancellor of Wénchāng (文昌) and Tóng Fènggē Luántái Sānpǐn (同鳳閣鸞臺三品), considered that since the Imperial Heir was in the Eastern Palace,
such a proposal was inappropriate.
He memorialized, requesting a severe rebuke for those who submitted the memorial,
and a notice to dismiss them.
The Grand Empress Dowager also asked Gé Fǔyuán (格輔元), Dìguān Shàngshū (地官尚書) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Fǔyuán firmly stated it was not permissible.
Because of this, they greatly displeased the Wǔ (武) clan.
Therefore, Chángqiàn was exiled to campaign against Túbō (吐蕃) in the west.
Before he arrived,
he was recalled
and imprisoned.
Chéngsì also slandered Fǔyuán.
Lái Jùnchén (來俊臣) also coerced Chángqiàn’s son, Língyuán (靈原),
to implicate several tens of people, including Ōuyáng Tōng (歐陽通), Sīlǐ Qīng (司禮卿) concurrently serving as Pàn Nàyán Shì (判納言事),
all of whom were said to be co-conspirators in rebellion.
When Tōng was interrogated by Jùnchén,
all kinds of torture were applied,
but he ultimately did not change his testimony.
Jùnchén then forged Tōng's confession.
In winter,
10th month,
on the day *jǐyǒu*,
Chángqiàn, Fǔyuán, Tōng, and others were all executed.
Wáng Qìngzhī (王慶之) saw the Grand Empress Dowager.
The Grand Empress Dowager said:
"The Imperial Heir is my son.
How can he be deposed?"
Qìngzhī replied:
" 'Spirits do not accept sacrifices from non-kin;
people do not sacrifice to non-clansmen.'
This is a saying of Hú Tū (狐突), a great official of Jìn (晉), from the *Zuǒzhuàn* (左傳).
How can the Lǐ (李) clan be made heir?"
The Grand Empress Dowager instructed him to leave.
Qìngzhī prostrated himself,
crying and pleading to the death, refusing to leave.
The Grand Empress Dowager then gave him a sealed paper, saying:
"If you wish to see me,
show this to the gatekeepers."
After this, Qìngzhī repeatedly sought an audience.
The Grand Empress Dowager became rather angry with him
and ordered Lǐ Zhāodé (李昭德), Fènggē Shìláng, to give Qìngzhī a beating with a staff.
Zhāodé led him out beyond Guāngzhèng Gate (光政門).
The Luòyáng (洛yáng) imperial city had three south-facing gates;
the central one was called Yìngtiān (應天),
the left Xīngjiào (興教),
and the right Guāngzhèng (光政).
"This scoundrel wants to depose my Imperial Heir
and establish Wǔ Chéngsì,"
he said, and ordered him to be beaten.
Blood flowed from his ears and eyes,
and then he was beaten to death with the staff.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The old account says:
"In the early part of Yánzài (延載) era,
Zhāng Jiāfú (張嘉福), Fènggē Shèrén, ordered Wáng Qìngzhī (王慶之) from Luòyáng to lead several hundred frivolous and wicked youths to the palace gate
and submit a memorial requesting the establishment of Wǔ Chéngsì as Crown Prince,
but Zétiān (則天) did not permit it."
The *Táng Lì* (唐曆) states that Zhāodé
was demoted from Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) to Língshuǐ Wèi (淩水尉) of Zhènzhōu (振州) in Yǒngchāng (永昌) 1st year.
The *Shílù* (實錄) states that he first became Chancellor in Chángshòu (長壽) 1st year.
The old account says that Qìngzhī was beaten to death after Zhāodé became Chancellor.
According to the *Yùshǐ Táijì* (御史臺記),
Zhāodé transferred from Zhōngchéng (中丞) to Fènggē Shìláng.
He was probably briefly demoted to Língshuǐ and then soon recalled to serve as Fènggē Shìláng.
The beating to death of Qìngzhī,
according to the *Yùshǐ Táijì*,
occurred when he was Fènggē Shìláng,
not after he became Chancellor.
The old account might have mistakenly recorded Zàichū (載初) as Yánzài.
Qìngzhī's memorial might have been submitted in the Zàichū (載初) year.
The *Shílù* mentions it in connection with the deaths of Cén Chángqiàn and Gé Fǔyuán.
We now consult the *Shílù*, *Yùshǐ Táijì*, and the old accounts.
Zhāodé then spoke to the Grand Empress Dowager, saying:
"The Heavenly Emperor was Your Majesty's husband;
the Imperial Heir is Your Majesty's son.
Your Majesty holds the empire personally,
and it should be transmitted to your descendants for a myriad generations.
How can a nephew be made heir?
From ancient times, there has never been a case of a nephew becoming emperor and building a temple for his aunt!
Moreover, Your Majesty received the Heavenly Emperor's trust and entrustment.
If you give the empire to Chéngsì,
then the Heavenly Emperor will not receive blood sacrifices."
The Grand Empress Dowager also considered this to be true.
Zhāodé was the son of Gānyòu (乾祐).
Lǐ Gānyòu (李乾祐) was the one who rescued Péi Rénkuǐ (裴仁軌) in the early years of Zhēnguān (貞觀).
On the 29th day, *rénchén*,
Lè Sīhuì (樂思晦), Luántái Shìláng (鸞臺侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, and Lǐ Ānjìng (李安靜), Right General of the Guards, were killed.
Ānjìng was the grandson of Gāng (綱).
Lǐ Gāng (李綱) was known for his upright and steadfast character between the Suí (隋) and Táng (唐) dynasties;
Ānjìng can be said to have brought no shame to his ancestor.
All the princes and hundred officials submitted memorials urging her to ascend the throne,
but Ānjìng alone, with a stern expression, refused.
When he was imprisoned,
Lái Jùnchén interrogated him about his rebellious acts.
Ānjìng said:
"As an old official of our Táng imperial house,
if I must be killed, then kill me!
If you ask about rebellion,
I truly have nothing to answer."
Jùnchén eventually killed him.
Wáng Xún zhī (王循之), a Grand Student, submitted a memorial
requesting leave to return home.
The Grand Empress Dowager granted it.
Dí Rénjié said:
"I have heard that a ruler reserves only the power of life and death for himself;
all other matters are entrusted to the relevant officials.
Thus, the Left and Right Chancellors do not handle cases below that of a common criminal;
the Left and Right Prime Ministers only judge cases of exile and above,
because such matters are gradually becoming more important.
That student's request for leave is a matter for the丞 (*céng*) and 簿 (*bù*) officials."
The *céng* (丞) in the Táng Guózǐjiān (唐國子監丞) was from rank 6, lower grade, responsible for judicial matters in the Guózǐjiān;
the *zhǔbù* (主簿) was from rank 7, lower grade.
"Then will all matters in the empire be exhausted by imperial edicts?
If you must not deny his wish,
please simply issue a general regulation for all."
The Grand Empress Dowager approved of this.
Punctuation by Hè Chāngjìn (賀昌㣥), re-checked by Wáng Chóngwǔ (王崇武) and Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
Compiled by imperial order by Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光).
