Chángshòu (長壽) 1st year
(*rénchén*, 692)
In the 4th month of this year,
the reign title was changed to Rúyì (如意);
in the 9th month,
it was changed to Chángshòu.
Before the 4th month, it was still Tiānshòu (天授) 3rd year.
1 In the 1st month,
on the first day, *wùchén*,
the Grand Empress Dowager offered sacrifices at Wànxiàng Shéngōng (萬象神宮).
2 In the 12th month,
Xiá (瑕), son of the late King Wèichí Fúshéxióng (尉遲伏闍雄) of Yútián (于闐), was established as King of Yútián.
3 In spring,
the first month,
on the dìngmǎo day,
the Empress Dowager [Wǔ Zé Tiān] granted an audience to the people recommended by the巡撫使 xúnfǔshǐ (circulating pacification commissioners).
She sent the xúnfǔshǐ to present a memorial to the Emperor (referring to the Empress Dowager herself, who was effectively ruling as empress regnant) in the first year of Tiānshòu [690 CE].
Jiàn (見) means to present a memorial.
Xián (賢) is pronounced like biànfān (遍翻).
Shǐ (使) is pronounced like shūlì fān (疏吏翻).
All were promoted and employed.
The most distinguished were provisionally appointed as Fènggě Shèrén (鳳閣舍人) or Gěishì Zhōng (給事中).
The next best were provisionally appointed as Yuánwàiláng (員外郎), Shìyùshǐ (侍御史), Bǔquē (補闕), Shíyí (拾遺), or Jiàoshūláng (校書郎).
A Táng Dynasty Jiàoshūláng was
a 正九品上 zhèng jiǔ pǐn shàng (Senior Ninth Rank) official.
Kǎoyì (考異) states: Tǒngjì (統紀) records:
"In the second month of the second year of Tiānshòu [691 CE],
sixty people from the ten circuits, including Wáng Shānlíng (王山齡), the magistrate of Shí'ài County,
were promoted to Shíyí or Bǔquē.
Twenty-four people, including Huò Xiànkě (霍獻kě), the lùshì cānjūn (錄事參軍) of Huáizhōu, were made Yùshǐ.
Twenty-four people, including Xú Xīn (徐昕), the lùshì cānjūn of Bìngzhōu, were made Zhùzuò Zuǒláng (著作佐郎) or Píngshì (評事).
Twenty-two people, including Cuī Xuāndào (崔宣道), the Wèiwèi (尉) of Nèihuáng, were made wèizuǒ (衞佐)."
It is suspected that this refers to the same event.
At the time, people made up a saying:
"Bǔquē were carried by the cartload,
Shíyí were measured by the peck;
Róngzhāi Suíbǐ (容齋隨筆) considers this saying to originate from Zhāng Zhuó (張鷟).
The Jiàoshūláng were thrown into the bowl."
A recommended person, Shěn Quánjiāo (沈全交), continued it, saying:
"The xúnfǔshǐ (巡撫使) are like dust in the heart,
blinding the sagely and divine Emperor."
Mài hú (麥[AS-FBEE]胡)
is pronounced like hùwú fān (戶吳翻),
meaning wheat husks sticking together.
Mī (眯)
is pronounced like mòlǐ fān (莫禮翻),
meaning something entering the eye;
Lǎo Zǐ (老子) said: "broadcasting chaff to blind the eye."
Someone impeached him for slandering the court,
requesting that he be flogged in the court hall
and then handed over to the law.
The Empress Dowager laughed and said:
"As long as you, my officials, do not make arbitrary appointments,
why worry about what people say!
His crime should be pardoned."
The impeacher was greatly ashamed.
Although the Empress Dowager made arbitrary grants of emoluments and positions to win the hearts of the people,
those who were not up to the task
were soon demoted,
or even subjected to punishment and execution.
Wielding the power of punishment and reward to govern the empire,
with policies originating from herself,
she was discerning and decisive.
Therefore, the heroes and worthies of the time competed to serve her.
4 Guō Bà (郭霸) of Lújiāng, the Nínglíng Magistrate, used flattery to gain favor with the Empress Dowager.
Nínglíng County belonged to Sòngzhōu.
It was originally Níngchéng of Wèi during the Warring States period.
Hàn Gāozǔ (漢高祖) changed its name to Nínglíng County.
Lújiāng was the land of Lóngshū County in the Hàn Dynasty,
belonging to Lújiāng Commandery.
Liáng established Húzhōu there.
Suí abolished the prefecture and made it Lújiāng County,
belonging to Lúzhōu.
Kǎoyì (考異) states: Xīn Zhuàn (新傳)
names him Hóngbà (弘霸).
Jiù Zhuàn (舊傳) and Yùshǐ Tái Jì (御史臺記) both give his single name as Bà.
Only Tǒngjì (統紀) in the first year of Yánzài (延載) says Hóngbà.
Qiānzài (僉載) says he responded to the call for revolution,
probably referring to this time.
Now we follow Tái Jì (臺記).
When Zhōngchéng (中丞) Wèi Yuánzhōng (魏元忠) fell ill,
Bà went to visit him.
He then tasted his feces
and happily exclaimed:
"If the Grandee's feces were sweet, it would be worrisome;
Zhōngchéng (中丞) being called Grandee (大夫 dàfū)
is an over-appellation.
There is no harm."
Yuánzhōng greatly loathed him,
and reported it to everyone he met.
5 On the wùchén day,
Yáng Zhíróu (楊執柔), the Xiàguān Shàngshū (夏官尚書), was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
Zhíróu was
the grandson of Gōngrén's younger brother.
The Empress Dowager employed him because of his relation to her mother's family.
The Empress Dowager's mother was from the Yáng clan.
Shàng (尚)
is pronounced like chényáng fān (辰羊翻).
6 Initially,
Emperor Yáng of Suí built the Eastern Capital.
See volume 180, first year of Dàyè.
Yáng (煬)
is pronounced like yángliàng fān (羊亮翻).
It only had short walls.
By this time,
Lǐ Zhāodé (李昭德), the Fènggě Shìláng (鳳閣侍郎), began to build it [the outer city wall].

7 Lái Jùnchén (來俊臣), the Zuǒ Tái Zhōngchéng (左臺中丞), falsely accused Rèn Zhīgǔ (任知古), Dí Rénjié (狄仁傑), Péi Xíngběn (裴行本), the Sìlǐ Qīng (司禮卿) Cuī Xuānlǐ (崔宣禮), the former Wénchāng Zuǒchéng (文昌左丞) Lú Xiàn (盧獻), the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) Wèi Yuánzhōng (魏元忠), and Lùzhōu Cìshǐ (潞州刺史) Lǐ Sìzhēn (李嗣真) of treason.
Before this,
Lái Jùnchén had submitted a memorial requesting an imperial edict
that anyone who confessed to treason upon the first interrogation would have their death penalty commuted.
When Zhīgǔ and the others were imprisoned,
Jùnchén used this to entice them.
Rénjié replied:
"The Great Zhōu has revolutionized,
and all things are renewed.
We, the old officials of the Táng house,
are willing to accept execution.
Treason is a fact!"
Jùnchén then slightly eased their treatment.
Pànguān (判官) Wáng Déshòu (王德壽) said to Rénjié:
A pànguān was Jùnchén's subordinate.
"Shàngshū (尚書), your death penalty is certainly commuted.
Déshòu is already under your command,
and wishes to gain a small promotion.
Would you trouble the Shàngshū to implicate Yáng Zhíróu (楊執柔)?
Is that permissible?"
Rénjié said:
"May Heaven and Earth send Dí Rénjié to do such a thing!"
He struck his head against a pillar,
blood flowing over his face.
Déshòu was frightened and apologized to him.
Hóu Sīzhǐ (侯思止) interrogated Wèi Yuánzhōng (魏元忠).
Yuánzhōng's tone and manner were unyielding.
Sīzhǐ was enraged
and ordered him dragged backward.
Yuánzhōng said:
"I am ill-fated,
like falling from a donkey,
with my foot caught in the stirrup,
being dragged by it."
Sīzhǐ became even angrier
and dragged him further.
Yuánzhōng said:
"Hóu Sīzhǐ,
if you need Wèi Yuánzhōng's head, then cut it off.
Why must you make me confess to treason!"
Once Dí Rénjié confessed to treason,
the authorities awaited the order for execution,
no longer maintaining strict precautions.
Rénjié tore his quilt fabric and wrote a plea of injustice,
placing it inside his padded clothes.
He said to Wáng Déshòu:
"The weather is hot now,
please give these padded clothes to my family to remove the padding."
Déshòu agreed.
Rénjié's son, Guāngyuǎn (光遠), obtained the letter
and carried it to report the situation,
and was granted an audience.
Empress Zétiān (則天) read it
and questioned Jùnchén about it.
He replied:
"When Rénjié and the others were imprisoned,
your servant never removed their caps or belts.
They slept and lived quite peacefully.
If there were no factual basis,
how would they have confessed to treason!"
The Empress Dowager sent Tōngshì Shèrén (通事舍人) Zhōu Lín (周綝) to inspect them.
Jùnchén temporarily returned Rénjié and the others their caps and belts,
arranged them standing to the west,
and had Lín observe them.
Lín dared not look directly,
only looking east and mumbling affirmations.
Jùnchén then forged a memorial of thanks for their commuted death sentence in the names of Rénjié and others,
and had Lín present it.
Yuè Sīhuì’s son, not yet ten years old,
was confiscated into the Sīnóng.
Sīhuì's death is recorded in the previous volume, previous year.
(The son) was summoned for an audience.
The Tàihòu asked about the situation.
He replied,
"My father is dead,
and my family is ruined.
I only lament that Your Majesty's laws are being manipulated by Lái Jùnchén and others.
If Your Majesty does not believe my words,
I beg you to select loyal and upright court officials whom Your Majesty has always trusted,
forge a confession of rebellion, and hand it over to Lái Jùnchén.
There will be none who do not confess to rebellion."
The Tàihòu's mind was somewhat enlightened.
She summoned Rénjié and others,
and asked,
"Why did you confess to rebellion?"
They replied,
"If we did not confess,
we would have already died from torture."
The Tàihòu said,
"Why did you write a memorial expressing gratitude for being granted death?"
They replied,
"There was no such thing."
She brought out the memorial to show them,
and then knew it was a deception.
Thereupon, these seven clans were released.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
(Dí) Zhīgǔ was demoted to Jiangxià Ling,
(Dí) Rénjié to Péngzé Ling,
(Cuī) Xuānlǐ to Yílíng Ling,
(Lǐ) Yuánzhōng to Fúlíng Ling,
and (Lú) Xiàn to Xīxiāng Ling.
Jiāngxià
was originally the territory of Shāxiàn County in the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to Jiāngxià Jùn.
The Jìn dynasty changed Shāxiàn to Shāyáng.
The Jiāng and Hàn rivers met west of the county,
and it was called Xiàruì in the Chūnqiū period,
and Xiàkǒu in the Jìn and Sòng dynasties.
The Sòng dynasty established Jiāngxià Jùn,
governing from here.
The Suí dynasty established Jiāngxià Xiàn based on the commandery name.
Under the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Èzhōu.
Péngzé
was a Hàn county,
belonging to Yùzhāng.
The Suí dynasty renamed it Lóngchéng.
The Táng dynasty restored its name to Péngzé,
belonging to Jiāngzhōu.
Fúlíng Xiàn
belonged to Bā Jùn in the Hàn dynasty.
Liú Shǔ established Fúlíng Jùn.
In the Suí dynasty, Fúlíng Xiàn
belonged to Yúzhōu.
In the first year of Wǔdé of the Táng dynasty, Fúzhōu was established as the prefectural seat.
Xīxiāng was the territory of Chénggù Xiàn in the Hàn dynasty.
The Shǔ dynasty established Xīxiāng Xiàn.
The Later Wèi made it the seat of Yángzhōu.
Xià,
pronounced like *yǎ*.
Fú,
pronounced like *fú*.
Lái Jùnchén and Wǔ Chéngsì repeatedly pleaded for their execution,
but the Tàihòu did not permit it.
Lái Jùnchén then solely claimed that Xíng Běn’s crimes were particularly severe,
and requested his execution.
Xú Yǒugōng, a Lángzhōng of the Qiūguān, refuted this,
believing that
"a sagacious ruler has the grace of granting new life.
Lái Jùnchén is unable to comply,
thereby diminishing this grace and trust."
Huò Xiànkě of Guìxiāng, a Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ,
(Guìxiāng was where) the Later Wèi dynasty, by dividing the western border of Guǎntáo,
established Guìxiāng Xiàn in Zhàochéng.
In the seventh year of Jiàndé of the Zhōu dynasty, it was moved thirty *lǐ* southeast from Zhàochéng,
making Kǒng Sījítì Sì the county seat.
In the second year of Dàxiàng, Wèizhōu was established in the county.
spoke to the Tàihòu, saying:
"If Your Majesty does not kill Cuī Xuānlǐ,
I beg to perish before you."
He knocked his head against the steps of the hall,
and blood flowed, staining the ground,
to show that a subject should not be partial to his relatives.
The Tàihòu did not listen to any of it.
Xiànkě always wrapped his wound with green silk,
subtly revealing it beneath his *fútóu*.
(The *Xù Shì Shǐ* says): In the Three Dynasties, commoners wrapped their hair with black silk.
Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu cut it into four flaps,
naming it *fútóu*.
Mǎ Zhōu requested to tie the front flaps more securely.
On the day Jiǎxū,
Xuē Qiānguāng, a Bǔquē, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The method of selection
should genuinely acquire real talent.
The choices made
affect moral transformation.
Currently, those selected
all claim to seek recommendations,
competing vigorously,
and complaining without shame.
As for those whose talents are sufficient to govern a state,
they are merely made to take policy examinations;
those who are capable of repelling enemies
are only tested on archery.
In the past, Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, upon seeing Sīmǎ Xiāngrú’s *fù*,
regretted not living in the same era.
Yet, after placing him in court,
he ended up as a Wényuán Lìng,
knowing he was not fit for the responsibilities of a Gōngqīng.
When Wú Qǐ was about to go to battle,
his attendants presented a sword.
Wú Qǐ said: 'A general brandishes the drum and wields the drumstick,
making decisions when facing the enemy.
The duty of a single sword
is not a general's business.'
If that is the case, how can superficial literary accomplishments be sufficient to assist the times,
or good archery be sufficient to defeat the enemy!
The key lies in civil officials assessing their conduct and ability,
military officials observing their courage and strategy,
evaluating their performance in office,
and rewarding or punishing those who make recommendations, that is all."
Lái Jùnchén sought gold from Quán Xiànchéng, the Zuǒ Wèi Dà Jiàngjūn.
When he did not get it,
he falsely accused him of rebellion,
and he was imprisoned.
On the day Yǐhài,
he was strangled to death.
On the day Gēngchén,
Lǐ Yóudào, Sīxíng Qīng and Jiǎnjiào Shǎnxīn Zhìshǐ, was appointed Dōngguān Shàngshū and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
In the second month,
on the day Jǐhài,
over ten thousand people from the Tǔbō Dǎngxiàng tribes submitted to the court.
Tǔ,
*tǔn* with entering tone.
Dǎng,
*dǐlǎng* pronunciation.
On the day Wǔwǔ,
Yuán Zhìhóng, Qiūguān Shàngshū, was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Qiūguān
refers to the Xíngbù.
In summer,
fourth month,
on the day Bǐngshēn,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the empire.
The reign era was changed to Rúyì.
The first year of Rúyì begins here.
In the fifth month,
on the day Bǐngyín,
a ban was issued against all slaughtering of animals and catching of fish and shrimp throughout the empire.
The Jiānghuái region suffered drought
and famine.
People could not gather fish and shrimp,
and many died of starvation.
Zhāng Dé, a Yòu Shíyí,
whose son was three days old,
secretly slaughtered a lamb to host his colleagues.
Dù Sù, a Bǔquē, concealed a piece of meat pie,
and submitted a memorial to report him.
The next day,
the Tàihòu, facing the court,
said to Zhāng Dé:
"I heard you had a son,
and I am very happy."
Zhāng Dé bowed in gratitude.
The Tàihòu said:
"Where did you get the meat from?"
Zhāng Dé kowtowed and confessed his crime.
The Tàihòu said:
"I banned slaughtering,
but this does not apply to auspicious or inauspicious occasions.
However, from now on, when you invite guests,
you should also choose your company carefully."
She then brought out Dù Sù's memorial to show him.
Dù Sù was greatly ashamed,
and the entire court wished to spit in his face.
Hésū, a Tǔbō chieftain, led his tribes to request submission to the court.
Zhāng Xuányù, the Yòu Yùlíng Wèi Jiàngjūn, was appointed Ānfǔshǐ
and led twenty thousand elite soldiers to welcome them.
In the sixth month,
when the army reached west of Dàdù Shuǐ,
Hésū's plot was exposed
and he was captured by his own people.
Zǎnchuí, a chieftain of another tribe, led over eight thousand Qiāng Mán people to submit.
Zhāng Xuányù established Lái Chuānzhōu for their tribes and returned.
In the 16th *xīnhài* year,
Wànnián Chief Secretary Xú Jiān submitted a memorial,
arguing:
“The classics speak of the method of 'five hearings',
and the ordinances include the request for 'three reviews'.
See volume 193 of the *Zhenguàn* Fifth Year of Emperor Tài Zōng.
If an envoy obtains the facts,
he is to immediately execute the sentence.
Human life is of utmost importance;
death brings no second life.
Should one in ten thousand be unjustly accused,
and their cries silenced as their entire clan is exterminated,
would that not be grievous!
This is not sufficient to suppress villains and rebels or clarify the law;
it merely serves to extend power and authority, and breed suspicion and fear.
I hope that this kind of judgment be abolished,
and that cases be reviewed according to the law.
Furthermore,
the selection of judicial officers
should be made with greater care.
Those who administer the law with leniency and fairness,
and are praised by the populace,
I wish Your Majesty would draw near and appoint them;
those who act with profound cruelty,
and fail to meet public expectations,
I wish Your Majesty would distance and remove them.”
Jiān
was the son of Qí Dǎn.
The *Xiàguān* Assistant Minister Lǐ Zhāodé secretly spoke to the Empress Dowager, saying:
“Wèi Wáng Wǔ Chéngsì's power is too great.”
*Xiàguān*
is the Ministry of War.
Sì,
read as *xiáng lì*.
“He is my nephew,
which is why I entrust him with my innermost thoughts.”
Zhāodé said:
“How does the relationship of a nephew to an aunt
compare to that of a son to a father?
Even a son may usurp or assassinate his father,
let alone a nephew!
Now, Chéngsì is not only Your Majesty's nephew
and a Prince,
but also a Chancellor;
his power rivals that of the sovereign.
I fear Your Majesty will not long remain secure in your heavenly position!”
The Empress Dowager was startled and said:
“I had not thought of that.”
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the *wùyín* day,
Wǔ Chéngsì, former Left Chancellor of Wénchāng and concurrently *Fènggérántái Sānpǐn*, was made a Special Grandee;
Nàyán Wǔ Yōuníng was made *Dōngguān Shàngshū*;
Yáng Zhíròu, *Xiàguān Shàngshū* and concurrently *Píngzhāngshì*, was made *Dìguān Shàngshū*;
all were dismissed from political affairs.
Cuī Yuánzōng of Xīnzhèng, *Qiūguān Shìláng*, was made *Luántái Shìláng*;
*Qiūguān*
is the Ministry of Justice.
Xīnzhèng
was the capital of the State of Zhèng in the Spring and Autumn period.
After Zhèng Wǔgōng moved east with King Píng of Zhōu,
he established his city between Guó and Kuài.
This is what Duke Zhuāng meant by
“Our former lord newly settled here.”
This is it.
In the Han dynasty, it was Xīnzhèng County,
subordinate to Hénán Commandery.
It was abolished in Wèi and Jìn,
and re-established in the 16th year of *Kāihuáng* in the Suí dynasty,
subordinate to Zhèngzhōu.
Yáo Shú, Acting *Tiānguān Shìláng*, was made Left Assistant of Wénchāng;
*Xiàguān*
is the Ministry of War.
*Fènggé*
is the Central Secretariat.
*Tiānguān*
is the Ministry of Personnel.
The name *Shàngshū* was changed to Wénchāng.
Shú,
read as *shū yù*.
Along with Cuī Shénjī, *Sībīn Qīng*,
*Dìguān*
is the Ministry of Revenue.
*Sībīn Qīng*
is the *Hónglú Qīng*.
*Kǎoyì* says: The old biography of Zhāodé states:
“He passed the *Míngjīng* examination and was successively promoted to *Fènggé Shìláng*.
In the second year of *Chángshòu*, *Xiàguān Shìláng* was added,
and Zhāodé was appointed to it;
that same year,
he was promoted to *Fènggé Luántái Píngzhāngshì*.”
The new annals, tables, and biographies all state,
“Zhāodé was promoted from *Xiàguān Shìláng* to *Fènggé Shìláng* concurrently *Píngzhāngshì*.”
Presumably, Zhāodé moved from *Fènggé* to *Xiàguān*,
and from *Xiàguān* returned to *Fènggé*.
The biography of Lóu Shīdé states:
“In the first year of *Chángshòu*, *Xiàguān Shìláng* was added.”
We follow this now.
“Cuī Shénjī”
is written as
“Cuī Jī”
in the Veritable Records.
We follow the new annals and tables here.
He was the grandson of Yáo Sīlián;
Yáo Sīlián served the Suí and Táng dynasties.
He was the younger brother of Lǐ Jìngxuán.
Lǐ Jìngxuán was a chancellor during Emperor Gāozōng's reign.
On the *xīnsì* day,
Wáng Xuán, Grand Architect of Construction, was made *Xiàguān Shàngshū* and concurrently *Píngzhāngshì*.
During *Guāngzhái*, the Directorate of Works was changed to Directorate of Construction.
Xuán,
read as *sì xuān*.
The Empress Dowager said:
“Since I entrusted Zhāodé,
I have been able to sleep peacefully.
He shoulders my burdens,
you must not speak of this again.”
At this time,
cruel officials were rampant,
and all officials walked on tiptoes in fear of them.
Only Zhāodé publicly exposed their wicked deeds in court.
The Empress Dowager was fond of auspicious omens.
Someone presented a white stone with red markings.
The officials in power questioned its peculiarity,
and the man replied:
“It is because of its 'red heart' (loyalty).”
Zhāodé angrily said:
“If this stone has a red heart,
are all other stones rebellious?”
Those around him all laughed.
Hú Qìng from Xiāngzhōu wrote on the belly of a turtle with vermillion lacquer, saying:
“May the Son of Heaven live for ten thousand, ten thousand years.”
He went to the palace gate to present it.
Zhāodé scraped it all off with a knife,
and memorialized to have him prosecuted according to the law.
The Empress Dowager said:
“His intention was not evil.”
She ordered his release.
The Empress Dowager kept a cat,
and had it live with a parrot.
She displayed them to the officials;
before everyone had seen them,
the cat, being hungry,
attacked and ate the parrot.
The Empress Dowager was very ashamed.
From the *Chuígǒng* era onwards,
the Empress Dowager employed cruel officials,
first executing several hundred members of the imperial clan and esteemed relatives of the Táng,
followed by several hundred families of high officials.
As for governors (*Cǐshǐ*), commanders (*Lángjiàng*), and below,
their numbers were countless.
Whenever an official was appointed,
the palace maids would secretly whisper to each other:
“Palace maids”
refers to official maids guarding the palace gates.
“The ghost servants are here again.”
Within not even a month,
they would inevitably be arrested and their families exterminated.
Yán Shànsī of Cháoyì, Censor *Jiānchá Yùshǐ*,
the Later Wèi dynasty divided Fèngyì to establish Chéngchéng Commandery,
and also established Nánwǔquán County.
The Western Wèi changed it to Cháoyì County.
During the Suí and Táng, it was subordinate to Sīzhōu.
*Jiān*,
read as *gǔ xián*.
Cháo,
read as *zhí yáo*.
At that time, informants were innumerable.
The Empress Dowager, also weary of the constant accusations,
ordered Shànsī to investigate.
He found over 850 people who had falsely confessed to crimes.
The faction of those who framed people was thus weakened.
They then conspired to frame Shànsī,
and he was exiled to Huānzhōu.
Old records state: From Huānzhōu to the capital, it was 12,452 *lǐ* by land,
and 17,000 *lǐ* by water.
To the Eastern Capital, it was 11,595 *lǐ* by land,
and 16,220 *lǐ* by water.
Sòng Bái said: Huānzhōu
is Rìnán Commandery.
It is where Yáo banished Huāndōu to Chóngshān.
This is it.
Soon after, he was recalled to be *Húnyí Jiāncéng*.
The Empress later changed the Directorate of Astronomy to the Directorate of Armillary Spheres.
*Céng*
is a subordinate official of the seventh rank, lower grade.
Fù,
read as *fú yòu*.
Hún,
read as *hù běn*.
His courtesy name was used.

The Grand Remonstrance Official, Zhū Jìngzé (朱敬則), from Xīnzhèng, submitted a memorial, reasoning that the Empress Dowager had originally relied on severe punishments and intimidation to suppress dissent.
Now that the revolution was complete,
and the public mind settled,
it was appropriate to reduce punishments and promote leniency.
He thus presented a memorial,
arguing:
"Lǐ Sī (李斯), as Prime Minister of Qín,
employed harshness, treachery, and deceit to slaughter the feudal lords.
He failed to understand the need to change to leniency and harmony,
which ultimately led to collapse.
This was the calamity of not knowing how to adapt.
This matter is recorded in the 'Qín Annals'.
上,
時掌翻.
相,
息亮翻.
卒,
子恤翻.
Lù Jiǎ (陸賈) and Shūsūn Tōng (叔孫通) persuaded [Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖)] with rites and righteousness,
and the dynasty lasted for twelve generations.
This was the virtue of knowing how to adapt.
Since the beginning of the Wénmíng (文明) era,
when heaven and earth were in a state of 'Tún' and 'Méng' (屯蒙),
草,
造也;
昧,
蒙也.
The beginning of creation,
started in obscurity and darkness,
signifying the early period when the Empress assumed regency,
changing the era name to Wénmíng,
a time of new beginnings.
Tún (屯) represents the genesis of things,
Méng (蒙) represents the immaturity of things,
indicating that the early period of the Empress's regency
was like the beginning of heaven and earth creating life.
屯,
涉倫翻.
With the 'Four Felons' causing trouble,
'Three Uncles' refers to the kings of Hán (韓), Huò (霍), and others;
'Four Felons' refers to Xú Jìngyè (徐敬業) and others.
四凶,
指徐敬業等.
難,
乃旦翻.
It was impossible to respond to Heaven and comply with man [without strict application of the law],
it was impossible to use appropriate punishments and titles,
and it was impossible to suppress traitors and stop violence.
Therefore, the divine instruments were set up,
and channels for accusations were opened,
meaning the casting of 'guǐ' (匭, censorate boxes) to open the door to secret denunciations.
All hidden intentions were exposed,
and divine power assisted justice.
No guilt remained unpunished,
the populace was peaceful,
and the Zǐchén (紫宸) palace changed its master.
However, hasty actions rarely lead to good results.
This uses the metaphor of walking.
This uses the metaphor of the qín (琴) and sè (瑟).
少,
詩沼翻.
Now, [those instruments] are like the 'chúgǒu' (芻狗) of today.
Chúgǒu (芻狗) are used in sacrifices,
and once the sacrifice is over,
they are discarded.
Weigh what is appropriate for the current times,
and discern what dregs can be discarded.
This uses wine as a metaphor.
One extracts the pure essence and discards the dregs.
Zhuāngzǐ (莊子) said: 'A 'qúlú' (蘧廬) can serve for a night's lodging, but not for long-term residence.'
Guō Xiàng (郭象) annotated: 'Qúlú' (蘧廬)
is a temporary dwelling.
The Shī (詩) says: 'How luxuriant and beautiful, woven into brocade!'
Those slanderers,
they are indeed too much!
去,
羌呂翻.
Block the source of fabricated charges,
sweep away traces of factions,
and make all the people of the world joyful and at ease!
Would that not be delightful!"
The Empress Dowager approved of this,
and bestowed three hundred bolts of silk.
The Palace Censor, Zhōu Jǔ (周矩), submitted a memorial stating:
"The officials in charge of investigation and interrogation all boast of their cruelty.
They 'mud the ears and cage the head' (泥耳籠頭),
'shackle and grind, wedge and spike' (枷研楔[AS-98BB]),
枷研,
refers to using heavy shackles to grind the neck;
楔[AS-98BB],
refers to using an iron collar [AS-98BB] the head and adding a wedge.
楔,
先結翻.
[AS-98BB],
乎角翻.
They hang by their hair and fumigate their ears,
calling it 'prison restraint' (獄持).
Or they starve them for days,
interrogate them slowly through the night,
shaking them day and night,
preventing them from sleeping,
calling it 'night imprisonment' (宿囚).
Since these people are not made of wood or stone,
they will try to save themselves in the moment,
and desperately seek a 'prolonged death.'
賒,
means distant,
signifying that by confessing and facing execution,
it is somewhat 'prolonged' compared to dying in prison.
They all claim that the world is at peace,
why then would one wish to rebel?
Are all the accused heroes,
desiring to become emperors?
No, they simply cannot endure the torture and falsely incriminate themselves.
I beg Your Majesty to investigate this.
Now the entire court is in uneasy suspense,
all believing that Your Majesty is intimate with them in the morning,
but an enemy in the evening,
and thus they cannot feel secure.
The Zhōu (周) dynasty prospered by employing benevolence,
while the Qín (秦) dynasty perished by employing punishment.
I beg Your Majesty to ease punishments and employ benevolence,
and the world will be exceedingly fortunate!"
The Empress Dowager largely adopted his words,
and the severity of judicial prisons gradually declined.
The 'Kǎoyì' (考異) states: The 'Yùshǐ Tái Jì' (御史臺記) records:
"After his memorial was presented,
he was appointed Sìgōng (司功) of Luòzhōu (洛州)."
The old biography of Xuē Huáiyì (薛懷義) states:
"Jǔ impeached Huáiyì,
and Jǔ was promoted to Yuánwàiláng (員外郎) of Tiānguān (天官).
He was eventually framed by Huáiyì,
imprisoned, and dismissed from office."
The 'Yùshǐ Tái Jì' also states:
"At that time, the election department of Tiānguān was in disorder,
so an imperial edict commanded Jǔ to oversee it.
The Attendant-in-Waiting, Lǐ Jǐng (李景), who was controlled by Jǔ,
then had him appointed Yuánwàiláng (員外郎),
but he was not proficient in official duties,
and from then on, he was demoted."
According to the old biography, Jǔ's impeachment of Xuē Huáiyì occurred later.
If he was appointed Sìgōng (司功) of Luòzhōu (洛zhōu) this year,
he should not have impeached Huáiyì again.
However, the old biography places Jǔ's memorial in the second month of the first year of Zàichū (載初).
At that time, the judicial prisons had not yet ceased,
so it is mentioned here after Zhū Jìngzé's (朱敬則) memorial.
Though the Empress Dowager was advanced in years,
she was skilled at adorning herself,
so much so that even those around her did not perceive her decline.
On the day Bǐngxū (丙戌),
an edict announced that her teeth had fallen out and grown back.
In the ninth month,
on the day Gēngzǐ (庚子),
she held court at Zétiānmén (則天門),
granted a general amnesty,
and changed the era name.
It was at this point that the era name was changed to Chángshòu (長壽),
and from this point onwards was the first year of Chángshòu.
An edict established Běidū (北都, Northern Capital) in Bīngzhōu (幷州).
On the day Guǐchǒu (癸丑),

the Co-Prime Ministers Lǐ Yóudào (李遊道), Wáng Xuán (王璿), Yuán Zhìhóng (袁智弘), Cuī Shénjī (崔神基), Lǐ Yuánsù (李元素), the Attendant of the Ministry of Rites Kǒng Sīyuán (孔思元), and the Grand Administrator of Yìzhōu (益州) Rèn Lìnghuī (任令輝),
were all framed by Wáng Hóngyì (王弘義)
and exiled to Lǐngnán (嶺南).
The Left Yǔlín Zhōnglángjiàng (左羽林中郎將), Lái Zǐxún (來子珣), was implicated in an incident and exiled to Àizhōu (愛州),
where he soon died.
Àizhōu (愛州) was eight thousand eight hundred *lǐ* (里) from the capital,
and eight thousand one hundred *lǐ* (里) from the Eastern Capital.
將,
即亮翻.
卒,
子恤翻.
Earlier,
Wáng Xiàojié (王孝傑) of Xīnfēng (新豐), serving as Deputy Commander-in-Chief under Liú Shěnlǐ (劉審禮) in the campaign against Tǔbō (吐蕃),
was captured by Tǔbō along with Shěnlǐ.
Xīnfēng (新豐) County belonged to Yōngzhōu (雍州),
and was later renamed Zhāoyìng (昭應) County.
The capture of Liú Shěnlǐ (劉審禮)
is recorded in Volume 202, Gāozōng (高宗) Yífèng (儀鳳) 3rd year.
吐,
從暾入聲.
[The Tǔbō chieftain remarked:] "His appearance resembles my father."
He was treated with great courtesy,
and later managed to return,
successively promoted to Right Yīngyángwèi Jiàngjūn (右鷹揚衞將軍).
During Guāngzhái (光宅), the Left and Right Wǔwèi (武衞) were changed to Left and Right Yīngyángwèi (鷹揚衞).
[Wáng Xiàojié (王孝傑)] knew their strengths and weaknesses.
Coincidentally, the Grand Protector of Xīzhōu (西州), Táng Xiūjǐng (唐休璟), requested to retake the Four Garrisons of Qiūcí (龜茲), Yútián (于闐), Shūlè (疏勒), and Suìyè (碎葉).
An imperial edict appointed Xiàojié (孝傑) as Commander-in-Chief of the Wǔwēi Army (武威軍),
to lead troops with the Grand General of the Wǔwèi (武衞), Āshǐnà Zhōngjié (阿史那忠節), to attack Tǔbō.
At this time, since the Wǔwèi (武衞) had been changed to Yīngyángwèi (鷹揚衞),
Zhōngjié (忠節) should not have been referred to by the old official title.
Could it be that historians continued to use the old official titles when writing?
將,
又音如字.
In the tenth month,
on the day Bǐngxū (丙戌),
they decisively defeated Tǔbō
and recaptured the Four Garrisons.
The Protectorate-General to Pacify the West (Ānxī Dūhùfǔ, 安西都護府) was re-established in Qiūcí (龜茲),
and troops were dispatched to garrison it.
1 In the first month,
on the *rénchén* day,
the Empress Dowager offered sacrifices at the Wànxiàng Shéngōng,
with Wèi Wáng Chéngsì as the secondary offerer,
and Liáng Wáng Sānsī as the final offerer.
The Empress Dowager herself composed the music for the Shéngōng,
using nine hundred dancers.
2 A maidservant named Tuán'ér, who was favored and trusted by the Empress Dowager,
bore a grudge against the Crown Prince.
She then slandered the Crown Prince's wife, Liú Shì, and Dé Dòu Shì, accusing them of practicing witchcraft.
On the *guǐsì* day,
Dé and the Crown Prince's wife went to the Jiāyù Diàn to pay respects to the Empress Dowager.
After they withdrew,
they were both killed simultaneously.
An alternative account states: According to the New Standard History:
"On the *guǐhài* day of the twelfth month,
the Crown Prince's wife, Liú Shì, and Dé Dòu Shì, were killed."
The old tradition says
"the second day of the first month,"
which is followed here.
Here we note that Dé Dòu Shì was the mother of Xuánzōng.
Her whereabouts are unknown.
Dé
was a great-granddaughter of Kàng.
Dòu Kàng was
a paternal cousin of Tàimù Huánghòu.
She dared not speak,
and in the presence of the Empress Dowager,
her demeanor was natural.
Tuán'ér again sought to harm the Crown Prince.
Someone reported her intentions to the Empress Dowager,
who then had Tuán'ér killed.
At this time,
informers would entice people's servants to accuse their masters,
in order to gain rewards.
Dé's father, Xiàochén, was the Inspector of Rùnzhōu.
He had a slave who falsely performed strange phenomena to frighten Dé's mother, Páng Shì.
Páng Shì was scared,
and the slave requested to offer sacrifices at night to dispel the evil.
He then revealed the matter.
The case was assigned to the Supervising Censor of Lóngmén, Xuē Jìchàng, to investigate.
Jìchàng falsely reported,
claiming that Páng Shì and Dé had jointly engaged in curses,
and first wept uncontrollably,
then said:
"What Páng Shì did
is something a subject and son cannot bear to speak of."
The Empress Dowager promoted Jìchàng to Gěishìzhōng.
Páng Shì was to be beheaded.
Her son, Xījiān,
went to the Imperial Censor, Xú Yǒugōng, to plead her case.
Yǒugōng sent a dispatch to the relevant department to suspend the execution,
and submitted a memorial arguing,
that she was innocent.
Jìchàng reported Yǒugōng for being partial to and supporting the wicked and rebellious,
and requested that he be handed over to the law.
The legal authorities sentenced Yǒugōng to be hanged.
The clerks reported this to Yǒugōng.
Among the Imperial Censors,
there were seventeen clerks.
*Shàng*,
at this time pronounced *fān*.
*Chù*,
pronounced *chānglǚ fān*.
"Am I the only one to die,
while everyone else lives forever!"
After eating,
he covered his face with a fan and went to sleep.
People thought Yǒugōng was merely putting on a brave face,
and must be inwardly fearful.
They secretly watched him,
and found he was sound asleep.
The Empress Dowager summoned Yǒugōng,
and welcomed him, saying:
"When you adjudicated cases recently,
why did you make so many mistaken releases?"
He replied:
"Mistaken releases are
a minor fault of a subject;
cherishing life is
a great virtue of a sage."
To mistakenly release someone from punishment is called a "mistaken release."
*Bǐ*,
pronounced *pízhì fān*.
*Hào*,
pronounced *hūdào fān*.
Because of this, Páng Shì's death sentence was commuted,
and she and her three sons were all exiled to Lǐngnán.
Xiàochén was demoted to Sīmǎ of Luózhōu,
and Yǒugōng was also dismissed from office.
An alternative account states: According to the old biography of Yǒugōng:
"Yǒugōng, as a Censor,
was dismissed from office due to Páng Shì's case,
and soon after was reinstated as Lángzhōng of Zuǒsī."
Biography of Dòu Xiàochén:
"In the second year of Chángshòu,
Páng Shì was framed by cruel officials."
Records of the Yùshǐ Tái:
"Yǒugōng, from Yuánwàiláng of Qiūguān,
was dismissed from office and exiled as a result of Páng Shì's case.
A little over a month later,
he was appointed Censor."
According to the Veritable Records,
Yǒugōng,
"at the beginning of Tiānshòu,
was successively appointed Sīxíng Chéng and Qiūguān Yuánwàiláng,
gradually promoted to Lángzhōng.
Later he was dismissed due to official business.
In the first year of Wànsuì Tōngtiān,
he was promoted to Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ."
This is followed here.
3 On the *wùshēn* day,
Yáo Shú submitted a memorial requesting that the Chancellors be ordered to compile a *Shízhèng Jì*.
The Essentials of the Assembly: Shú believed that the directives and instructions of emperors and kings
should not be lacking in written record,
and that historians, being distant,
had no means of recording them.
He requested that from now on,
for all important military and state policies discussed,
one Chancellor should compile and record them,
to be called the *Shízhèng Jì*.
This was granted.
The *Shízhèng Jì* began from this point.
4 In the twelfth month,
on the *dīngmǎo* day,
the Imperial Grandson Chéngqì was enfeoffed as Shòuchūn Wáng;
the Prince of Héng, Chéngyì, as Héngyáng Wáng;
the Prince of Chǔ, Lóngjī, as Línzī Wáng;
the Prince of Wèi, Lóngfàn, as Bālíng Wáng;
the Prince of Zhào, Lóngyè, as Péngchéng Wáng.
All were sons of Ruìzōng.
5 In spring,
first month,
on the *gēngzǐ* day,
Lóu Shīdé, the Shìláng of Xiàguān, was made Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
Shīdé was broad-minded, generous, pure, and prudent,
and never took offense.
He and Lǐ Zhāodé entered court together.
Shīdé was stout and walked slowly.
Zhāodé waited for him repeatedly but he did not arrive,
so he angrily cursed:
"You rustic!"
Shīdé slowly smiled and said:
"If Shīdé is not a rustic,
then who should be one?"
His younger brother was appointed Inspector of Dàizhōu.
As he was about to depart,
Shīdé said to him:
"I hold the position of Chancellor,
and you are now a provincial governor.
Our honor and favor are excessive,
and people will resent it.
How will you save yourself?"
His brother knelt respectfully and said:
"From now on, even if someone spits on my face,
I will merely wipe it off,
hoping not to cause you worry."
Shīdé said with a look of concern:
"This is precisely what worries me!
If someone spits on your face,
they are angry with you;
if you wipe it off,
you are going against their intention,
thereby increasing their anger.
Now, spit,
if not wiped, dries by itself.
You should smile and accept it."
6 On the *jiǎyín*

day, former Director of the Imperial Manufactories, Péi Fěigōng (裴匪躬), and Internal Grandee, Fàn Yúnxiān (范雲仙), were腰斩 (sliced in half at the waist) in the marketplace for privately meeting with the Imperial Heir.
Guāngzhái (光宅) changed the Less Minister of the Imperial Treasury to Director of the Imperial Manufactories.
The Bureau of Internal Retainers had six Internal Grandees,
ranked Lower Fifth Grade,
which was the position of the Han Grandee Attendants.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: "The old biography of Lái Jùnchén (來俊臣) says:
'Lái Jùnchén arrested Zhāng Qiánxù (張虔勗) and Fàn Yúnxiān (范雲仙) at the Luòyáng (洛陽) prefecture office.
Zhāng Qiánxù (張虔勗) and others, unable to endure the suffering,
brought their own accusations to Xú Yǒugōng (徐有功).
Lái Jùnchén (來俊臣) ordered guards to kill them with a flurry of knives.
Fàn Yúnxiān (范雲仙) also spoke,
recounting his service to previous emperors,
claiming the officials were unjust.
Lái Jùnchén (來俊臣) ordered his tongue to be cut off.
The common people were terrified,
and no one dared to speak.'"
According to records, Zhāng Qiánxù (張虔勗) was killed in the second year of Tiānshòu (天授).
Fàn Yúnxiān (范雲仙) was executed this year for meeting the Imperial Heir.
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄).
There were also accusations that the Imperial Heir harbored secret rebellious intentions.
The Empress Dowager ordered Lái Jùnchén (來俊臣) to interrogate his attendants.
The attendants, unable to withstand the torture,
all wished to falsely implicate themselves.
Ān Jīnzàng (安金藏) of Jīngzhào (京兆), a craftsman of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
at that time, high officials were not allowed to see the Imperial Heir,
only Ān Jīnzàng (安金藏) and other craftsmen were allowed to be nearby.
He said, "Since Your Majesty does not believe my words,
I ask to cut open my heart to prove that the Imperial Heir is not rebellious."
He immediately drew his personal knife and cut open his chest,
all his internal organs protruded,
and blood flowed over the ground.
The Empress Dowager, hearing of this,
ordered him to be carried into the palace,
and had doctors place his internal organs back,
sewing him up with mulberry bark thread,
and applying medicine.
He did not revive until the next day.
The Empress Dowager personally visited him,
sighing,
"My son cannot clear his own name,
causing you to come to this."
She immediately ordered Lái Jùnchén (來俊臣) to stop the investigation.
She stopped the case,
and no longer interrogated him.
7 The practice of examining candidates on Lǎozǐ (老子) was abolished,
and replaced with examining them on the *Chénguǐ* (臣軌), compiled by the Empress Dowager.
8 In the second month,
on the *bǐngzǐ*
day, King Zhèngmíng (政明) of Xīnlúo (新羅) died.
An envoy was sent to enthrone his son, Lǐ Hóng (理洪), as king.
9 On the *yǐhài*
day, the wearing of brocade among the people was forbidden.
Hóu Sīzhǐ (侯思止), an imperial censor, secretly hoarded brocade.
Lǐ Zhāodé (李昭dé) investigated him
and had him beaten to death in the court.
10 Someone accused exiles in Língnán (嶺南) of plotting rebellion.
The Empress Dowager dispatched Wàn Guójùn (萬國俊), a Judicial Reviewer, acting as a Supervising Censor, to investigate them.
Wàn Guójùn (萬國俊) arrived in Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
summoned all the exiles,
and falsely issued an imperial decree ordering them to commit suicide.
The exiles cried out, refusing to comply.
Wàn Guójùn (萬國俊) herded them to a bend in the river
and executed all of them,
killing over three hundred people in one morning.
He then fabricated evidence of rebellion,
returned to report,
and stated that exiles in other circuits
must also harbor resentment and rebellious intentions,
and should be executed early.
The Empress Dowager was pleased and promoted Wàn Guójùn (萬國俊) to Grand Master for Discussion and Acting Imperial Censor.
She then dispatched Liú Guāngyè (劉光業), Adjutant of the Right Flank Guard's Military Bureau,
(*Note: In the fourth year of Wǔdé (武德), the Left and Right Flank Guards were already renamed Left and Right Guards.
It is suspected
that the character 'yì' (翊)
is superfluous.*)
The Adjutant of the Military Bureau was in charge of the roster of military officers of the five bureaus on guard duty,
receiving their names and numbers,
and the Grand General would assign them.
In the Tang capital, each imperial park had four side supervisors,
each with one supervisor,
ranked Lower Sixth Grade;
one deputy supervisor,
ranked Lower Seventh Grade;
and one assistant,
ranked Lower Eighth Grade.
Each was in charge of the palaces, gardens, and ponds within their respective side of the imperial park, as well as planting and repairs;
the assistant handled the supervisor's affairs.
And Qū Zhēnjūn (屈貞筠), Adjutant of the Right Wǔwēi (武威) Guard's Military Bureau, both acting as Supervising Censors,
to various circuits to investigate exiles.
Liú Guāngyè (劉光業) and others, seeing Wàn Guójùn (萬國俊) rewarded for mass killings,
vied to emulate him.
Liú Guāngyè (劉光業) killed seven hundred people,
Déshòu (德壽) killed five hundred people,
and the rest killed no less than a hundred each,
with long-term exiles for miscellaneous offenses also perishing with them.
The Empress Dowager was somewhat aware of the excess,
and issued an edict:
"All exiles in the six circuits who are still alive, along with their families, are permitted to return to their hometowns."
Wàn Guójùn (萬國俊) and others also died in succession,
or were punished and exiled.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Shílù* (實錄) says that
Liú Guāngyè (劉光業) and others also received instructions from Fù Yóuyì (傅遊藝), Attendant Gentleman of Luántái (鸞臺).
However, Fù Yóuyì (傅遊藝) had already died in the second year of Tiānshòu (天授).
The old biography of Fù Yóuyì (傅遊藝) states that Fù Yóuyì (傅遊藝) requested Zétiān (則天) to dispatch six circuit envoys.
Although he died afterwards,
his plan was eventually followed.
Empress Wǔ (武) originally sent only one envoy, Wàn Guójùn (萬國俊).
Wàn Guójùn (萬國俊) returned and reported that exiles in other circuits were also rebellious,
hence five more envoys were sent.
How could Fù Yóuyì (傅遊藝) have known in advance that six circuit envoys would be dispatched!
This is an example of 'all evil being attributed to one person.'
Pān Yuǎn's (潘遠) *Jìwén* (紀聞) states:
"Lǐ Qínshòu (李秦授), a Remonstrance Official, was on duty in the Central Secretariat,
and presented a memorial saying: 'Your Majesty, since ascending the throne,
has executed and dismissed members of the Lǐ (李) clan and various high officials.
Their families and relatives are exiled outside,
by my estimation, there are tens of thousands of them.
If they were to conspire together suddenly
and gather for rebellion,
catching Your Majesty by surprise,
I fear the state would be in grave danger.
The prophecy says:
"The one who replaces Wǔ (武) is Liú (劉)."
Now, Liú (劉) sounds like Liú (流), which means exile.
If Your Majesty does not eliminate these people,
I fear the calamity will run deep.'
The Empress accepted his advice.
She summoned him at night,
saying: 'Your name is Qínshòu (秦授), Heaven has granted you to me (授朕),
how you have enlightened my heart!'
She immediately appointed him Director of the Bureau of Merit,
also giving him charge of drafting imperial edicts,
bestowed a crimson sash,
ten female entertainers,
and an equivalent amount of gold and silk.
She conspired with him to dispatch ten imperial envoys to the ten circuits,
ostensibly to comfort the exiles,
but in reality, she gave secret edicts to the local governors
to kill those who were exiled.
After the Empress judged that the exiles were dead,
she again sent envoys to pacify the exiles, saying:
'I previously dispatched ten circuit envoys
to comfort the exiles,
why did the envoys not understand my intentions,
acting with great cruelty and violence!
Let those envoys who presumptuously killed exiles, along with the local officials, be chained by their necks,
brought to the place where the exiles were harmed and executed,
to appease the deceased souls.
All exiles who are still alive or detained for other matters,
along with their families, are to be released and returned home.' "
However, at that time, only the Língnán (嶺南) circuit was targeted for execution.
Because of Wàn Guójùn's (萬國俊) report,
five more circuit envoys were dispatched,
not ten circuit envoys simultaneously.
How could there have been exiles in the nearby ten circuits!
Since Wàn Guójùn (萬國俊) was rewarded for mass killings,
the other envoys either died of illness,
or were themselves exiled for other crimes,
there is no reason they would have been executed together.
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄) and old biographies.
11 Lái Jùnchén (來俊臣) falsely accused Sū Gàn (蘇幹), Minister of Public Works,
claiming he conspired with Wáng Chōng (王沖), Prince of Lángyá (琅邪), in Wèizhōu (魏州).
Wáng Chōng (王沖) raised an army,
as seen in the *Chuígǒng* (垂拱) fourth year in the previous volume.
In the fourth month,
on the *yǐwèi*
day, he was killed.
12 In the fifth month,
on the *guǐchǒu*
day, the Hé (河) river in Dìzhōu (棣州) overflowed.
13 In autumn,
the ninth month,
on the *dīnghài* day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.

14 Wèi (魏) Prince Chéngsì (承嗣) and five thousand others submitted a memorial requesting an additional honorific title: Jīnlún Shèngshén Huángdì (金輪聖神皇帝, Sacred and Divine Emperor of the Golden Wheel).
On the *yǐwèi*
day, the Empress Dowager ascended the Wànxiàng Shéngōng (萬象神宮, Palace of Ten Thousand Forms of the Divine),
received the honorific title,
and issued a general amnesty.
The Seven Treasures, including the Golden Wheel, were made.
The Seven Treasures
are: the Golden Wheel Treasure,
the White Elephant Treasure,
the Female Treasure,
the Horse Treasure,
the Jewel Treasure,
the Minister of War Treasure,
and the Minister of Treasury Treasure.
They were displayed in the palace courtyard.
In the *gēngzǐ* year,
Emperor Zhāo'ān (昭安皇帝) was posthumously honored as Emperor Húnyuán Zhāo'ān (渾元昭安皇帝);
Emperor Wénmù (文穆皇帝) as Emperor Lìjí Wénmù (立極文穆皇帝);
Emperor Xiàomíng Gāo (孝明高皇帝) as Emperor Wúshàng Xiàomíng Gāo (無上孝明高皇帝).
Empresses followed the imperial titles.
Later, she further posthumously honored her three generations.
15 In the *xīnchǒu* year,
Yáo Shú (姚璹), who was Wénchāng Zuǒchéng (文昌左丞) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事), was made Sībīnqīng (司賓卿),
and his involvement in state affairs ceased.
Dòulú Qīnwàng (豆盧欽望), who was Sībīnqīng, was made Nèishǐ (內史).
The *Xīnshū Zǎixiàng Shìxì Biǎo* (新書宰相世系表) states: The Dòulú clan's original surname was Mùróng (慕容).
After Mùróng Jīng (慕容精), Prince of Běidì (北地王), surrendered to the Later Wèi (後魏),
the northern people called those who returned and submitted
"dòulú" (豆盧),
and thus they adopted it as their surname.
Lù Yuánfāng (陸元方) of Wú (吳), who was Qiūguān Shìláng (秋官侍郎), was made Luántái Shìláng (鸞臺侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Jùyuán (巨源)
was the great-great-grandson of Xiàokuān (孝寬).
Wèi Xiàokuān (韋孝寬) served the Yǔwén (宇文) clan as a famous general.
The first year of Yánzài (延載)
The era name was changed in the fifth month of this year.
1 In the first month,
on the *bǐngxū* day,
the Empress Dowager offered sacrifices at the Wànxiàng Shéngōng (萬象神宮).
2 The Tujue Khan Gǔdùlù (骨篤祿) died.
His son was young,
so his younger brother Mòchuò (默啜) enthroned himself as Khan.
In the twelfth month,
on the *jiǎxū* day,
Mòchuò raided Língzhōu (靈州).
3 The Shīwèi (室韋) rebelled.
The *Běishǐ* (北史) states: The Shīwèi are probably of the same kind as the Qìdān (契丹).
Those in the south are Qìdān,
those in the north are Shīwèi.
The *Xīnshū* (新書) states: The Shīwèi
are a distinct branch of the Qìdān,
on the northern frontier of the Dōnghú (東胡),
probably descendants of the Dīnglíng (丁零).
Their territory is based at Huánglóng (黃龍),
bordering the Náoyuè River (峱越河) to the north,
seven thousand *lǐ* northeast of the capital,
east of the Hēishuǐ Mòhé (黑水靺鞨),
west of the Tujue,
south of the Qìdān,
and north of the sea.
Their state has no sovereign.
Only the great chieftains are all called Mòhèduō (莫賀咄),
governing their tribes and being subservient to the Tujue.
4 In spring,
the first month,
Lóu Shīdé (婁師德) was appointed Jiǎnjiào Yíngtián Dàshǐ (檢校營田大使) for the Héyuán (河源) and other armies.
5 In the second month,
Wáng Xiàojié (王孝傑), Grand Commander of the Wǔwēi Dao (武威道), defeated the Tubo Bólùn Zànrèn (㪍論贊刃)
and the Tujue Khan Tuízǐ (俀子) and others at Lěngquán (冷泉) and Dàlǐng (大嶺).
Tuízǐ
was installed by the Western Tujue tribe.
*Tuí* (俀)
is pronounced *tuǐ*,
meaning weak.
Dàlǐng
is a valley name.
Hán Sīzhōng (韓思忠), Protector of Suìyè (碎葉), defeated Níshú Sīhòu (泥熟俟斤) and over ten thousand others.
6 On the *gēngwǔ* day,
the monk Huáiyì (懷義) was appointed Dàiběi Dào Xíngjūn Dàzǒngguǎn (代北道行軍大總管).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Shílù* (實錄) and *Xīnjì* (新紀) both say
"Fá Nìdào" (伐逆道).
Now following the old biography of Huáiyì.
7 On the *sānyuè jiǎshēn* day,
Sū Wèidào (蘇味道), who was Fènggé Shèrén (鳳閣舍人), was made Fènggé Shìláng (鳳閣侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Lǐ Zhāodé (李昭德) was Jiǎnjiào Nèishǐ (檢校內史).
The monk Huáiyì was further appointed Shuòfāng Dào Xíngjūn Dàzǒngguǎn (朔方道行軍大總管),
with Lǐ Zhāodé as Zhǎngshǐ (長史)
and Sū Wèidào as Sīmǎ (司馬),
leading Chìbì Míng (契苾明), Cáo Rénshī (曹仁師), Shāzhà Zhōngyì (沙吒忠義), and eighteen other generals to attack Mòchuò.
Before they departed,
the barbarians retreated and so the expedition was halted.
Zhāodé once discussed matters with Huáiyì,
and misunderstood his intent,
whereupon Huáiyì struck him.
Zhāodé was terrified and begged for forgiveness.
8 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the *rénxū* day,
Wáng Xiàojié, who was Xiàguān Shàngshū (夏官尚書) and Wǔwēi Dào Dàzǒngguǎn (武威道大總管), was made Tóng Fènggé Luántái Sānpǐn (同鳳閣鸞臺三品).
9 In the fifth month,
Wèi Wáng Chéngsì (魏王承嗣) and over twenty-six thousand others presented an honorific title, "Yuègǔ Jīnlún Shèngshén Huángdì" (越古金輪聖神皇帝).
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
she presided at the Zétiānmén Tower (則天門樓) to receive the honorific title,
granted a general amnesty,
and changed the era name.
10 During the Tiānshòu (天授) era,
Péi Huáigǔ (裴懷古) of Shòuchūn (壽春), a Jiānchá Yùshǐ (監察御史), was dispatched to pacify and settle the southwestern barbarians.
In the sixth month,
on the *guǐchǒu* day,
Xūnqī (薰期), a chieftain of the Yǒngchāng (永昌) barbarians, led over two hundred thousand households to submit.
Within Yáozhōu (姚州) there were Yǒngchāng barbarians,
residing in the territory of Yǒngchāng Commandery (永昌郡).
"Xūnqī"
is written as "Dǒngqī" (董期) in the *Xīnshū*.
*Jiān* (監),
pronounced *gān* (ancient reading).
*Qiú* (酋),
pronounced *qiú*.
11 In Hénèi (河內) there was an old nun residing at Lízhǐ Temple (麟趾寺) in Shéndū (神都), who, with Wéi Shífāng (韋什方) and others from Sōngshān (嵩山), deluded the masses with sorcery and falsehoods.
The nun called herself Jìngguāng Rúlái (淨光如來),
claiming she could know the future.
Shífāng claimed to have been born in the Wú (吳) era of Chìwū (赤烏).
There was also an old Hu (胡) man who claimed to be five hundred years old,
saying he had seen Master Xuē (薛師) for two hundred years.
The monk Huáiyì was originally Fèng Xiǎobǎo (馮小寶).
The Empress Dowager had him related to Xuē Shào (薛紹) by marriage,
hence the old Hu called him Master Xuē.
The Empress Dowager greatly trusted and respected him,
bestowing the surname Wǔ (武) upon Shífāng.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the *guǐwèi* day,
Shífāng was made Zhèngjiàn Dàfū (正諫大夫) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
The imperial edict stated:
"Surpassing Guǎngchéng (廣成) of the Xuān era."
Zhuāngzǐ (莊子) states: Guǎngchéngzǐ resided atop Kōngtóng (崆峒).
The Yellow Emperor (黃帝) stood downwind and inquired about the Way.
Guǎngchéngzǐ said:
"I have cultivated my body for one thousand two hundred years,
and my form has never decayed."
The Yellow Emperor's name was Xuānyuán (軒轅), hence the Xuān era.
Gě Hóng (葛洪) states: Héshànggōng (河上公),
whose name is unknown,
during the reign of Emperor Wén (文帝) of Hàn (漢), built a thatched hut by the river.
Emperor Wén consulted him about Lǎozǐ (老子).
Héshànggōng said:
"I have annotated this scripture for over one thousand seven hundred years."
*Cháo* (朝),
pronounced *zhāo* (ancient reading).
Shífāng requested to return to the mountains,
and an edict dismissed him and sent him away.
12 On the *wùchén* day,
Wáng Xiàojié was appointed Hànnèi Dào Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn (瀚內道行軍總管),
still under the command of Xuē Huáiyì (薛懷義), Shuòfāng Dào Xíngjūn Dàzǒngguǎn.
13 On the *jǐsì* day,
Yáo Shú, who was Sībīn Shàoyù (司賓少卿), was made Nàyán (納言).
Yáng Zàisī (楊再思) of Yuánwǔ (原武), who was Zuǒ Sùzhèng Zhōngchéng (左肅政中丞), was made Luántái Shìláng.
Dù Jǐngjiǎn (杜景儉), who was Luòzhōu Sīmǎ (洛州司馬), was made Fènggé Shìláng.
Both were Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
1 In the first month,
on the *xīnsì* day,
the Empress Dowager added the title Císhì Yuègǔ Jīnlún Shèngshén Huángdì.
There was a general amnesty throughout the realm,
and the era name was changed to Zhèngshèng.

2 Zhōu Yǔnyuán, along with司刑少卿 Sīxíng Shǎoqīng Huángfǔ Wénbèi, memorialized that Nèishǐ Dòulú Qīnwàng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Wéi Jùyuán, Dù Jǐngjiǎn, Sū Wèidào, and Lù Yuánfāng had colluded with Lǐ Zhāodé
and failed to rectify the situation.
Qīnwàng was demoted to Zhàozhōu.
The Old Records state: Zhàozhōu is 1,842 *lǐ* northeast of the capital,
and 1,033 *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The Old Annals and Biographies,
and the New Annals, Tables, and Biographies
all record
"Fūzhōu."
The *Tǒngjì* records
"Yíngzhōu."
The *Shílù* and *Tánglì* record
"Línzhōu,"
which is followed here.
Línzhōu was established in the fifth year of Zhēngguān to settle the raw Qiāng,
and it was subordinate to Sōngzhōu Dūdūfǔ.
In the sixteenth year, a mountain cave was opened and Zhēnzhōu was established,
subordinate to Qiánzhōu Dūdūfǔ.
The Old Records state: Zhēnzhōu is 3,480 *lǐ* from the capital,
and 4,200 *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
Zhēn,
pronounced *cè shēn fān*.
Yuánfāng was demoted to Sūizhōu Cìshǐ.
The Old Records state: Jízhōu,
is 1,425 *lǐ* southwest of the capital,
and 2,600 *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
Sūizhōu,
is 1,000 *lǐ* northeast of the capital,
and 1,819 *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
3 Previously,
after the Míngtáng was completed,
the Empress Dowager ordered the monk Huáiyì to create a large lacquered cloth Buddha statue.
Its little finger alone could accommodate dozens of people.
A Tiāntáng was constructed north of the Míngtáng to house it.
When the hall was first built,
it was destroyed by wind.
It was rebuilt,
with 10,000 laborers working daily,
collecting timber from rivers and mountains.
Over several years,
the expenditures amounted to tens of millions,
exhausting the imperial treasury.
Huáiyì spent money like dirt,
and the Empress Dowager indulged him entirely,
asking no questions.
Whenever he held a Wúzhēhuì,
he spent 10,000 *mín* of cash.
Men and women gathered like clouds,
and he would scatter ten cartloads of money,
causing them to scramble for it,
trampling each other, resulting in deaths.
Many public and private fields and residences in various places
became possessions of monks.
Huáiyì grew somewhat tired of entering the palace
and often resided at Báimǎsì.
The strongmen he ordained as monks numbered over a thousand.
Shìyùshǐ Zhōu Jǔ suspected a conspiracy
and strongly requested an investigation.
The Empress Dowager said:
"You may withdraw for now;
I will immediately order him to go."
When Jǔ reached the Censorate,
Huáiyì also arrived,
riding his horse directly to the steps and dismounting,
then lay on a couch with his belly exposed.
Jǔ summoned officials to investigate him,
but Huáiyì quickly leaped onto his horse and rode away.
Jǔ fully reported the situation,
and the Empress Dowager said:
"This monk has a wind illness;
he is not worth questioning.
As for the monks he ordained,
you may deal with them as you see fit."
All were exiled to distant prefectures.
Jǔ was promoted to Tiānguān Yuánwàiláng.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
a Wúzhēhuì was held at the Míngtáng.
The ground was dug into a pit
five *zhàng* deep.
Palaces were constructed of colored silks,
and all the Buddha statues were drawn out from the pit,
said to have emerged from the earth.
Cattle were also slaughtered for their blood,
which was used to paint a large statue head,
two hundred *chǐ* tall,
said to have been painted by Huáiyì with blood from his knee.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
the statue was displayed south of Tiānjīnqiáo,
and a vegetarian feast was held.
At that time, Yùyī Shěn Nánqiú
The *Táng Liùdiǎn* states: The Shàngyàojú is subordinate to the Diànzhōngshěng,
with four Shìyùyī
of rank six, upper grade.
Qiú,
pronounced *qiú*.
Huáiyì was secretly resentful.
