one by one falling into the gap.
The chasm was ten thousand *zhàng* deep,
the corpses were level with the cliff.
Not a single horse returned,
no soldier came back alive.”
Zhāng Zhuó’s accounts often exaggerate the facts,
so we do not entirely adopt them here.
The Empress Dowager posthumously bestowed official titles and ranks upon Xiàojié.
She sent an envoy to execute Hónghuī and display his head as a warning.
Before the envoy arrived,
Hónghuī was pardoned for achieving a meritorious deed.
Wǔ Yōuyí’s army was stationed at Yúyáng.
Yúyáng
was the administrative seat of the Qín’s Yòuběipíng Commandery.
In the Suí, it was Yúyáng County,
belonging to Yōuzhōu,
located 210 *lǐ* east of Yōuzhōu.
The army was terrified
and dared not advance.
The Qìdān, emboldened by their victory, raided Yōuzhōu,
captured cities and towns,
and plundered officials and commoners.
Yōuyí dispatched generals to attack them,
but failed.
Yán Zhīwēi and Tián Guīdào were jointly sent as envoys to the Tūjué,
to enthrone Mòchuò as Khagan.
Kě
is pronounced “cóng kān rù shēng.”
Hán
is pronounced “hán.”
They arbitrarily bestowed him with scarlet robes and silver belts,
and moreover reported:
“When barbarian envoys arrive in the capital,
they should be generously entertained.”
Guīdào reported:
“The Tūjué have been rebellious for many years,
and are now regretting their past.
It is proper to await the Holy Grace’s leniency.
Now Zhīwēi rashly gave him robes and belts,
leaving the imperial court with no further additions to make.
It is fitting to order him to return to his original attire and await imperial favor.
Furthermore,
minor barbarian envoys
are not worthy of lavish entertainment.”
The Empress Dowager approved of this.
Zhīwēi met Mòchuò,
danced,
and licked the tip of his boots.
Guīdào merely bowed with a long salute and did not prostrate.
Mòchuò imprisoned Guīdào
and intended to kill him.
Guīdào’s demeanor and expression remained unyielding;
he rebuked Mòchuò for his insatiability
and explained the consequences of good and ill fortune.
Ābō Dágān Yuánzhēn said:
The Tūjué had twenty-eight ranks of officials,
from Shè to Dágān,
all hereditary.
This refers to Āshǐdé Yuánzhēn.
“An envoy from a great nation
cannot be killed.”
Mòchuò’s anger slightly subsided,
but he detained him and did not send him back.
Previously,
in the Xiánhēng era,
Tūjué defectors
were settled in the six prefectures of Fēng, Shèng, Líng, Xià, Shuò, and Dài.
At this time,
Mòchuò demanded the defectors from the six prefectures and the land of the Shányú Dūhùfǔ,
along with grain seeds, silk fabrics, farming tools, and iron.
The Empress Dowager did not permit it.
Mòchuò was enraged,
and his words were insolent and disrespectful.
Yáo Shú and Yáng Zàisī, considering that the Qìdān had not yet been subdued,
requested to grant Mòchuò’s demands.
Lǐ Qiáo of Zànhuáng, Líntái Shàojiān and Zhī Fènggé Shìláng, said:
Líntái Shàojiān was the same as Mìshū Shàojiān.
Zànhuáng County
was established in the Suí,
belonged to Zhàozhōu,
and was named after Zànhuáng Mountain.
Shào
is pronounced “shī zhào.”
“Barbarians are greedy and untrustworthy.
This is what is meant by ‘lending weapons to bandits and supplying food to thieves.’”
This was a saying of Lǐ Sī of Qín.
Shú and Zàisī insisted on granting them,
so several thousand households of defectors from the six prefectures were all driven out and given to Mòchuò,
along with 40,000 *hú* of grain seeds,
50,000 *duàn* of various colored silks,
3,000 sets of farming tools,
40,000 *jīn* of iron,
and permission for intermarriage was also granted.
Mòchuò consequently became even stronger.
Tián Guīdào had just been able to return
and debated with Yán Zhīwēi before the Empress Dowager.
Guīdào believed that Mòchuò would definitely break his promise
and that one could not rely on a marriage alliance,
and that preparations should be made.
Zhīwēi believed that the marriage alliance would definitely be secure.
The "Kǎo Yì" (Examination of Differences) says: The old biography of Guīdào states:
"At the beginning of Shènglì,
Mòchuò requested peace,
and Yán Zhīwēi was sent as an envoy to enfeoff him as Lìgōng Bàoguó Kèhán.
Zhīwēi gave red robes to the envoys,
but Guīdào submitted a memorial stating it was impermissible.
When Mòchuò was about to arrive at the Dānyú Dūhùfǔ,
Guīdào was ordered to act as Sìbīn Qīng to welcome and comfort him.
Mòchuò requested the six Hú prefectures,
which was not granted,
so he then detained Guīdào."
The "Tūjué Zhuàn" (Biography of the Tujue) says:
"Lǐ Jìnzhōng's grandson, Wànróng, captured Yíngfǔ,
and Mòchuò requested to conquer the Qìdān for the state,
which was granted.
Mòchuò's forces gradually grew,
and Zétiān sent an envoy to enfeoff him as Lìgōng Bàoguó Kèhán."
The "Cháoyě Qiānzài" says:
"Guīdào was Zhīwēi's deputy.
When he met Mòchuò,
he did not bow.
Mòchuò hung him upside down,
intending to kill him.
Yuánzhēn remonstrated,
and he was then released."
According to the eighth month of Shéngōng First Year,
Yáo Shú was demoted to Yìzhōu Zhǎngshǐ.
Thus, the giving of grain and silk to him
must have been before this,
not at the beginning of Shènglì.
The "Shílù" (Veritable Records) states:
"In Wànsuì Tōngtiān First Year,
ninth month,
on the dìngmǎo day,
because Mòchuò was not associated with the Qìdān rebellion,
Yán Zhīwēi was sent as an envoy to enfeoff him as Qiānshàn Kèhán."
At that time, he was not yet Lìgōng Bàoguó Kèhán.
The enfeoffment with this title
is not in the "Shílù,"
so it is not known when exactly it occurred.
Now, because the Qìdān were not yet pacified and
Yáo Shú had not yet left,
this is appended here.
Guīdào was Zuǒwèi Lángjiàng at court;
how could he have participated in the debate about Mòchuò?
It was probably while on the road, seeing Zhīwēi's actions, that he submitted his memorial.
The events are preserved by collecting credible accounts from various books.
9 In the summer,
fourth month,
the nine tripods were cast and completed,
and moved to the Tōngtiān Gōng.
The Yùzhōu tripod was one zhàng and eight chǐ tall,
and could hold 1,800 dàn;
the other provincial tripods were one zhàng and four chǐ tall,
and could hold 1,200 dàn.
The Yùzhōu tripod was uniquely tall and large,
as it represented Shéndū Jī.
Gāo (high) is pronounced like "kāo" (犒).
In total, 560,700 catties of copper were used.
The Empress Dowager wished to coat them with 1,000 liǎng of gold.
Yáo Shú said:
"The nine tripods are divine artifacts,
more precious for their natural essence.
Moreover, I observe their brilliant and variegated colors mixing together,
not needing a golden color for dazzling splendor."
The Empress Dowager followed his advice.
They were pulled in from Xuánwǔmén,

with the chancellors and various princes leading over 100,000 palace guards from the northern and southern divisions, along with large oxen and white elephants from within the palace, to pull them together.
10 The former Yìzhōu Zhǎngshǐ, Wáng Jíshàn, had retired.
When the Qìdān rebelled
and Shāndōng was in unrest,
he was appointed as Huázhōu Cìshǐ.
The Empress Dowager summoned him
and asked about the gains and losses of the court.
Jíshàn presented over ten crucial points for governance and peace.
The Empress Dowager said:
"Matters in outer prefectures are trivial; these are fundamental.
You cannot leave."
On the guǐyǒu day,
he was kept as Nèishǐ.
11 On the guǐwèi day,
Wǔ Yìzōng, the Yòujīnwúwèi Dàjiāngjūn, was appointed as Shénbīngdào Xíngjūn Dàzǒngguǎn,
and with Hé Jiāmì, the Yòubàotāowèi Jiāngjūn, led troops to attack the Qìdān.
In the fifth month,
on the guǐmǎo day,
Lóu Shīdé was again appointed as Qīngbiāndào Fùdàzǒngguǎn,
and Shāzhā Zhōngyì, the Yòuwǔwēiwèi Jiāngjūn, as Qiánjūn Zǒngguǎn.
Shāzhā
is a barbarian surname.
Zhā is pronounced like "chūjiā" (初加).
Earlier,
there was a Zhū Qiányí
who submitted a memorial saying:
"Your servant dreamt that Your Majesty's lifespan reached 800 years."
He was immediately appointed Shíyí.
He then claimed
"to have dreamt that Your Majesty's white hair turned black again,
and fallen teeth grew anew."
He was promoted to Jiàbù Lángzhōng.
The Jiàbù Láng in the Táng Dynasty was in charge of the official records of national carriages, palanquins, vehicles, post stations, ⿸广既牧,
and the various livestock of the Sīmǎ,
distinguishing their entry and exit,
and managing their names and numbers.
Shàng (上) is pronounced like "shízhǎng" (時掌);
the same applies below.
He submitted another memorial saying:
"I heard Sōngshān call out 'Long live!'"
He was bestowed with a crimson suàndài.
In the early Táng, officials of the third rank and above were given gold-decorated knives and whetstones;
those below the first rank received hand towels and suàndài.
After Kāiyuán,
all officials wore suàndài during the New Moon and Full Moon court audiences,
and outer officials on administrative days,
each according to the color of their robes,
but not on other days.
Shǐ (使) is pronounced like "shūlì" (疏吏).
He wore it over a green gown.
When troops were mobilized to suppress the Qìdān,
an imperial edict commanded capital officials to provide one horse for the army,
to be compensated with a fifth-rank official position.
Qiányí bought a horse and submitted it,
repeatedly presenting memorials requesting promotion.
The Empress Dowager disliked his greed and meanness.
In the sixth month,
on the yǐchǒu day,
an edict ordered his horse to be returned
and him to be expelled back to his hometown.
12 Qiáo Zhīzhī of Fēngyì, a Yòusī Lángzhōng, had a beautiful concubine named Bìyù.
Zhīzhī did not marry because of her.
Wǔ Chéngsì borrowed her to teach his own concubines,
then kept her and did not return her.
Zhīzhī wrote "Lǜzhū Yuàn" (Lǜzhū's Lament) and sent it to her.
Jìn's Shí Chóng had a beloved concubine named Lǜzhū.
Her story can be found in Volume 83, Jìn Huìdì Yǒngkāng Third Year.
Chéngsì found the poem on her sash
and was furious.
He incited cruel officials to make false accusations,
and his clan was exterminated.
The "Kǎo Yì" says: "Táng Lì" (Tang Calendar) states:
"On the tenth day of the second month of Tiānshòu First Year,
Qiáo Zhīzhī was executed."
The "Xīn Běnjì" (New Imperial Annals) states:
"In the eighth month,
on the rénxū day,
Yòusī Lángzhōng Qiáo Zhīzhī was killed."
Lú Zàngyòng's "Chénshì Biézhuàn" and Zhào Dān's "Chén Zǐáng Jīngdé Bēi" all state:
"The Qìdān rebelled in Yíngzhōu.
Jiàn'ān Jùnwáng Wǔ Yōuyí personally commanded the army.
An imperial edict specifically summoned Zuǒbǔquē Qiáo Zhīzhī and Gōng to participate in military deliberations.
After the army was disbanded,
because his father was old,
he submitted a memorial requesting to return and attend to him."
Yōuyí's campaign against the Qìdān was in Wànsuì Tōngtiān First Year,
and the Qìdān were pacified the following year.
Chén Zǐáng's collected works include a poem "Xī Huán Zhì Sànguān Dá Qiáo Bǔquē Shī" (Returning West to Sanguan, Answering Vice-Secretary Qiao), which says:
"In the past, you served the barbarian horses,
I was able to serve the military banners.
Hand in hand we journeyed through the desert,
distant from Guānhé, Yōu, and Yān.
Sighing on this day of return south,
I still hear of the northern frontier guard."
It is suspected that Zhīzhī's death was after Shéngōng Year.
However, "Táng Lì," "Tǒng Jì," and "Xīn Jì" all place Zhīzhī's execution in Tiānshòu First Year.
Now, based on Zǐáng's poem, there must be no error,
but it says
"I still hear of the northern frontier guard,"
implying the army had not yet been disbanded.
Furthermore, Empress Wǔ said that after Lái Jùnchén's death,
no one dared to rebel.
Therefore, it is placed here.
According to "Cháoyě Qiānzài,"
Zhīzhī was falsely accused by people incited by Wǔ Chéngsì over the matter of the maid Bìyù,
and was executed in the south market,
his family ruined and property confiscated.
At this time, Zhīzhī was on the frontier;
presumably, Chéngsì harbored resentment towards him earlier,
and only now had him killed.
13 Sīpú Shàoqīng Lái Jùnchén
in Guāngzhái changed the Tàipú to Sīpú.
If a civil servant or commoner had a beautiful wife or concubine,
he would use every means to take her;
sometimes he would have someone falsely accuse them of a crime,
forging imperial edicts to seize their wives.
The number of people framed and executed before and after this
was countless.
From the chancellors downward,
he would list their names and seize them.
The 'Kǎoyì' states: 'Cháoyě Qiānzài' says:
"Jùnchén once gathered his confederates at Lóngmén on the third day of the third month,
erected a stone, inscribed the names of court officials on it, and divined by it.
He ordered them to throw stones at it from a distance;
whoever's name fell over would be the first to be accused.
By evening,
the stone thrown at Lǐ Zhāodé did not hit."
This is not adopted here.
Jiānchá Yùshǐ Lǐ Zhāodé had always detested Jùnchén,
and had also publicly humiliated Qiūguān Shìláng Huángfǔ
Bèi.
The two jointly slandered Zhāodé with plotting rebellion,
and he was imprisoned.
Jùnchén wanted to frame the Wǔ clan princes and Princess Tàipíng,
and also wanted to falsely accuse the Imperial Heir Apparent and Prince Lúlíng of conspiring with the northern and southern imperial guards in rebellion.
Hoping to usurp state power through this,
Wèi Suìzhōng from Hédōng reported him.
The Wǔ clan and Princess Tàipíng were terrified,
jointly exposed his crimes,
and he was imprisoned.
The authorities sentenced him to the death penalty.
The Empress Dowager wanted to pardon him,
the memorial was submitted for three days,
but not issued.
Wáng Jíshàn said:
"Jùnchén is ferocious, cunning, greedy, and tyrannical,
he is the nation's chief evil.
If he is not removed,
he will certainly destabilize the court."
The Empress Dowager was touring the imperial garden,
Jí Xù held the reins.
The Empress Dowager asked about external affairs,
and he replied:
"Outsiders only wonder why Lái Jùnchén's memorial has not been issued."
The Empress Dowager said:
"Jùnchén has rendered service to the state;
I am still considering him."
Xù said:
"Yú Ānyuǎn accused Huī Zhēn of rebellion,
and indeed he rebelled later.
Zhēn's affair can be found in the previous volume, Chuígǒng fourth year.
Jùnchén gathers desperadoes,
frames good people,
his ill-gotten gains are like mountains,
and the spirits of the wronged block the roads.
He is a thief of the state;
why should he be spared!"
The Empress Dowager then issued his memorial.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
Zhāodé and Jùnchén were both executed in the marketplace.
At that time, everyone mourned Zhāodé and rejoiced at Jùnchén's fate.
His enemies vied to eat Jùnchén's flesh,
it was all gone in an instant.
They gouged out his eyes and peeled off his face,
cut open his belly and pulled out his heart,
trampling him into mud.
The Empress Dowager knew that the world hated him,
so she issued an edict detailing his crimes,
adding:
"He deserves the punishment of exterminating the entire clan,
to appease the anger of the common people.
His family should be confiscated according to the law."
Civil servants and commoners congratulated each other in the streets, saying:
"From now on, those who sleep will finally have their backs stick to their mats."
Jùnchén, for reporting Qílián Yào's achievements,
was rewarded with ten slaves.
Jùnchén inspected the Sīnóng's slave women;
there were none he desired.
The 'Táng Liùdiǎn' states that
the Sīnóngchéng manages all official household slaves,
when males and females come of age,
they are first paired within their own group.
If granted, their wives and children are allowed to follow;
if involved in confiscation,
they are assigned to various departments according to their abilities,
and skilled women enter the Yètíng.
He wanted skilled singers and dancers
to be rewarded as 'singing mouths'.
So he had someone falsely accuse Hú Sèluó of rebellion.
Thousands of chieftains came to the imperial court, cutting their ears and lacerating their faces to plead their innocence.
When Jùnchén was executed,
they were then spared.
While Jùnchén was in power,
the Bureau of Appointments would accept his requests for irregular appointments,
sometimes several hundred people at each selection.
When Jùnchén fell,
the Shìlángs all confessed.
The Empress Dowager rebuked them,
and they replied:
"We have failed Your Majesty,
and deserve death!
Our disruption of state law
only concerns our own lives;
defying Jùnchén's words
would immediately lead to the extermination of our clans."
The Empress Dowager then pardoned them.
The Shànglín Lìng Hóu Mǐn
(the Shànglín Shǔlìng was a subordinate of the Táng Sīnóng,
rank seven lower,
in charge of imperial gardens and county lands,
all planting of fruit trees and vegetables for court assemblies and sacrifices,
and storing ice in late winter were his responsibility).
His wife, Lady Dǒng, advised him, saying:
"Jùnchén is a national traitor,
destined to fail soon.
You should keep your distance from him."
Mǐn followed her advice.
Jùnchén was angered,
and sent him out as Wǔlóng Lìng.
(Wǔlóng County belonged to Tiánzhōu,
established in a barbarian cave.
Old texts write
"Wǔlóng"
and say the year of its establishment or abolishment is unknown.
Also, Fúzhōu has Wǔlóng County,
established in the second year of Wǔdé by splitting from Fúlíng.)
His wife said:
"Go quickly, do not linger!"
When Jùnchén fell,
his associates were all exiled to Lǐngnán,
but Mǐn alone was spared.
The Empress Dowager summoned Yú Ānyuǎn to be Shàngshí Fèngyù,
and promoted Jí Xù to Yòusùzhèng Zhōngchéng.
14 Zōng Chǔkè, as acting Xiàguān Shìláng, was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
15 Wǔ Yìzōng's army reached Zhàozhōu.
Hearing that Qìdān general Luò Wùzhěng's several thousand cavalry were approaching Jìzhōu,
Yìzōng was afraid
and wanted to flee south.
Someone said:
"The barbarians have no baggage train;
they rely on raiding for supplies.
If we hold our ground and defend,
they will inevitably disperse,
and we can then strike them,
achieving great merit."
Yìzōng did not listen,
retreated to Xiāngzhōu,
abandoning a large amount of military supplies and weapons.
The Qìdān then massacred Zhàozhōu.
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
Sūn Wànróng was killed by his slave.
When Wànróng defeated Wáng Xiàojié,
he built a fortress 400 *lǐ* northwest of Liǔchéng in a strategic location,
leaving his old, weak, and women there,
along with the captured weapons and assets.
He made his brother-in-law, Yǐ Yuānyǔ, guard it,
and led his elite troops to raid Yōuzhōu.
Fearing that the Tujue Mòchuò might attack from behind,
he sent five men to Hēishā,
(Hēishā was
the Tujue court.
The word
'yǔ' is pronounced 'niú jù'.)
saying to Mòchuò:
"I have already defeated Wáng Xiàojié's million-strong army;
the Tang people are terrified.
I invite the Khagan to take advantage of this victory and together capture Yōuzhōu."
Three men arrived first;
Mòchuò was pleased
and bestowed crimson robes upon them.
The other two arrived later;
Mòchuò was angry at their delay
and was about to kill them.
The two men said:
"Allow us one word before we die."
Mòchuò asked their reason;
the two men revealed the Qìdān's true intentions.
Mòchuò then killed the first three men and bestowed crimson robes upon the two,
making them guides,
and dispatched troops to seize Qìdān's new city,
killing Xǔ Qīnmíng, the captured governor of Liángzhōu, to sacrifice to heaven.
After besieging the new city for three days,
he conquered it.
(The new city
was the one previously built by the Qìdān,
northwest of Liǔchéng.)
He sent Yǐ Yuānyǔ to report to Wànróng.
At that time, Wàn Róng was still holding out against the Táng forces.
When the army heard of it,
they were terrified.
The Xī people rebelled against Wàn Róng.
Yáng Xuánjī, General-in-chief of the Divine Army, attacked from the front,
while the Xī troops attacked from the rear.
They captured his general Hé Āxiǎo.
Wàn Róng's army was utterly routed,
and he fled eastward with several thousand light cavalry.
Zhāng Jiǔjié, General-in-chief of the vanguard, dispatched troops to intercept him on the road.
Wàn Róng was in dire straits,
and fled with his slave to the east of Lùshuǐ.
The Bāoqīushuǐ flows from outside the frontier,
passing south through Yōuzhōu Lùxiàn,
and is called Lùshuǐ.
He sighed,
"If I now return to Táng,
my crime is already great.
To return to the Tūjué is also death;
to return to Xīnluó is also death.
Where shall I go?"
His slave beheaded him and surrendered,
displaying his head at the gate of the Sìfāngguǎn.
The Hàn dynasty had the Gāojiē Mányídǐ (Barbarian Residence of Gāojiē).
The Later Wèi dynasty established residences for envoys from various states.
Later, four lodges were built to accommodate those who surrendered from the four directions.
This matter is found in Volume 149, during the first year of Pǔtōng of Liáng Wǔdì.
During Suí Yángdì's reign, the Sìfāngguǎn was established outside the Jiànguómén gate
to receive envoys and guests from the four directions.
Each managed affairs related to their respective foreign states and mutual trade,
and was subordinate to the Hónglú Sì.
The Táng dynasty placed the Sìfāngguǎn under the Zhōngshūshěng,
with the Tōngshì Shèrén in charge.
Xiāo,
read as "jiān yáo fān".
On the 16th day, wùzǐ,
Tejìn Wǔ Chéngsì and Chūn Guān Shàngshū Wǔ Sānsī were both appointed Tóng Fènggéláántái Sānpǐn.
On the 17th day, xīnmǎo,
an imperial edict stated that since the Qìdān had just been pacified,
Wǔ Yìzōng, the Prince of Hénèi, Lóu Shīdé, and Dí Rénjié, the Cìshǐ of Wèizhōu, were ordered to proceed along separate routes to pacify Héběi.
Wherever Yìzōng went, he was cruel.
If any people who had been coerced by the Qìdān returned,
Yìzōng considered them rebels,
and would eviscerate them alive to extract their gallbladders.
Earlier,
Hé Āxiǎo was fond of killing,
and the people of Héběi had a saying about him:
"Only these two Hés,
kill the most people."
Wǔ Yìzōng, enfiefed as Prince of Hénèi,
together with Hé Āxiǎo, constituted
"the two Hés".
In the seventh month of autumn,
on the dìngyǒu day,
Kūnmíng submitted,
and Dòuzhōu was established.
Wǔ Chéngsì and Wǔ Sānsī were both dismissed from political affairs.
On the gēngwǔ day,
Wǔ Yōuyí returned triumphantly from Yōuzhōu.
Wǔ Yìzōng memorialized, requesting that all the Héběi commoners who had followed the rebels should be exterminated.
Wáng Qiúlǐ, a Zuǒ Shíyí, argued vehemently in court, saying:
"These people have always been unprepared for war,
and were unable to resist the rebels;
if they followed them to survive, how could they have had any intention of rebelling against the state?
Yìzōng, with an army of several hundred thousand strong,
fled at the mere sight of the enemy,
allowing the rebel hordes to proliferate.
Now he wants to blame these misguided people from the countryside.
As a disloyal minister,
I request that Yìzōng be executed first to apologize to Héběi!"
Yìzōng was unable to respond.
Dù Jǐngjiàn, Sīxíng Qīng, also memorialized:
"These were all people coerced into compliance;
I request that they all be pardoned."
The Empress Dowager agreed.
In the eighth month,
on the bǐngxū day,
Yáo Shú, Nàyán, was demoted to Yìzhōu Chángshǐ due to an incident.
Dòu Lúqīnwàng, Tàizǐ Gōngyǐn, was appointed Wénchāng Yòuxiàng and Fènggéláántái Sānpǐn.
During the Tiānshòu era, Tàizǐ Zhānshì was changed to Tàizǐ Gōngyǐn.
Above "Fènggéláán"
should be the character
"tóng".
The 'Kǎoyì' (Textual Differences) states: The new table says,
"On the gēngzǐ day,
Dí Rénjié was additionally appointed Nàyán,
Wǔ Sānsī was appointed Jiǎnjiào Nèishǐ,
and Qīnwàng was appointed Wénchāng Yòuxiàng, Tóng Sānpǐn."
The old biographies and the new chronicles do not contain this.
There is no gēngzǐ day in this month.
The appointments of Rénjié and Sānsī are in the following year.
The new table mistakenly duplicates entries.
In the ninth month,
on the rénchén day,
a grand banquet was held at Tōngtiāngōng,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed.
The era name was changed to Shéngōng.
On the gēngxū day, Lóu Shīdé was appointed Shǒu Nàyán.
On the jiǎyín day,
the Empress Dowager said to her attendant ministers:
"Recently, Zhōu Xīng and Lái Jùnchén handled cases,
implicating many court officials, claiming they were plotting rebellion;
the state has its established laws,
how could I dare to violate them!
In between, I doubted their veracity,
and had trusted officials question them in prison.
I obtained their written confessions,
all of which they admitted themselves.
I had no doubts.
Since Xīng and Jùnchén died,
no more rebellions have been heard of.
Does this not mean that those who died previously were unjustly accused?"
Yáo Yuánchóng, Xiàguān Shìláng, replied:
"Since the Chuígǒng era, those who died for plotting rebellion
were mostly framed by Xīng and others,
who sought to gain merit for themselves.
When Your Majesty had trusted officials question them,
these officials could not even guarantee their own safety,
how would they dare to waver?
If the questioned individuals had retracted their confessions,
they would have feared brutal torture,
so it was better to die quickly.
Thanks to Heaven enlightening Your Sacred Heart,
Xīng and others have been executed.
I, your subject, with a hundred lives, guarantee to Your Majesty
that from now on, no officials, internal or external, will rebel again.
If there is even a slight factual instance,
I request to suffer the crime of knowing without reporting it."
The Empress Dowager was pleased and said:
"In the past, the chancellors all went along with their schemes,
trapping me as a ruler of cruel punishments.
Hearing what you have said,
it deeply accords with my heart."
She bestowed a thousand strings of cash upon Yuánchóng.
At that time, many people petitioned for Wèi Yuánzhōng's redress,
and the Empress Dowager recalled him to serve as Sùzhèng Zhōngchéng.
Yuánzhōng had been condemned to public execution or exile four times.
The 'Kǎoyì' states: The old biography says he was exiled three times,
but this account follows the Yùshǐ Tái record.
According to the New Book: Yuánzhōng, as Luòyáng Lìng,
was implicated in Zhōu Xīng's case and sentenced to death,
but was exiled due to his merits in pacifying Yáng and Chǔ.
After more than a year,
he was framed by Lái Jùnchén
and was about to be executed,
but the Empress Dowager sent Wáng Yǐnkè to proclaim an edict pardoning him.
This constitutes two incidents.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn records Wáng Yǐnkè's proclamation of pardon in the first year of Yǒngchāng.
Then in the first year of Chángshòu, he was again imprisoned and demoted.
This constitutes three incidents.
Later, in the third year of Cháng'ān, he was again demoted to Gāoyào Wèi.
This constitutes four incidents.
It is unknown what the Yùshǐ Tái record states.
The Empress Dowager asked:
"Why were you often slandered in the past?"
He replied:
"I am like a deer,
and those who weave accusations desire my flesh for soup.
How can I avoid them!"
In winter,
in the intercalary tenth month,
on the jiǎyín day,
Dí Rénjié, Dūdú of Yōuzhōu, was appointed Láántái Shìláng,
and Dù Jǐngjiàn, Sīxíng Qīng, was appointed Fènggé Shìláng,
both with the title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Rén Jié submitted a memorial
stating:
"Heaven created the Four Yi (barbarians),
all outside the territories established by the former kings.
Thus, to the east, they are blocked by the dark sea;
to the west, they are hindered by the moving sands;
to the north, they are separated by the great desert;
and to the south, they are obstructed by the Wǔ Lǐng (Five Ranges).
This is how Heaven limits the Yi-Di (barbarians) and separates the Middle Kingdom from the outside.
Since the records of the classics,
and the reach of civilization,
what the Three Dynasties could not reach,
the State has now entirely embraced.
The poets praised the 'light expedition' to Tàiyuán,
and the spread of civilizing influence to the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
The ode 'Lìu Yuè'
describes King Xuān's northern expedition.
Its verses say:
'We lightly attacked the Xiǎnyǔn,
reaching as far as Tàiyuán.'
And the ode 'Hàn Guǎng'
praises King Wén's Way extending to the southern states,
and its civilizing influence reaching the regions of the Jiāng and Hàn.
These are all within the realm of our State.
If, however, one uses military force beyond our borders,
seeking achievement in distant lands,
exhausting the treasury's resources to contend for barren lands,
gaining people who cannot increase revenue,
acquiring land that cannot be cultivated,
merely pursuing the reputation of having distant barbarians wear our attire,
and neglecting the art of consolidating the foundation and pacifying the people—
this is the path taken by Qín Huáng and Hàn Wǔ,
not the enterprise of the Five Emperors and Three Kings.
The First Emperor exhausted his military might,
striving to expand territory,
causing countless deaths,
which led to rebellion throughout the empire.
(The matter is found in Qín Jì.)
The common people were impoverished,
and bandits rose up like swarms of bees.
In his later years, he regretted and realized his error,
ceased military campaigns and suspended forced labor,
and thus was able to be blessed by Heaven.
(The matter is found in Hàn Wǔdì Jì.)
The expenses were increasingly vast,
with garrisons to the west in the Four Garrisons,
and to the east in Āndōng.
Levies increased daily,
and the people were exhausted and impoverished.
Now, there is famine east of the passes,
Shǔ and Hàn are seeing people flee,
and south of the Jiāng and Huái,
levies are relentless.
People no longer have their livelihoods,
and are gathering to become bandits.
If the foundation is shaken,
the troubles will be deep.
The reason for all this
is striving for the barren lands of the Mán and Mò,
deviating from the Way of nourishing the common people.
In the past, Emperor Yuán of Hàn accepted the counsel of Jiǎ Juānzhī and abolished Zhūyá Commandery.
(The matter is found in volume 28, during the second year of Chūyuán.)
(The matter is found in volume 25, during the second year of Yuánkāng.)
This was out of concern for the toil of the people.
Recently, during the Zhēngguān era, the Jiǔxìng (Nine Surnames) were pacified,
and Lǐ Sīmó was made Khagan,
to govern the various tribes.
(See volume 190, Zhēngguān 13th year.)
When they surrendered, they were placated,
embodying the principle of 'removing the fallen and securing the existing.'
(The 'Zhòng Huǐ zhī Gào' says: 'Remove the fallen and secure the existing, and the state will prosper.')
('Bāng nǎi qí chāng.')
('Tuī,'
is pronounced 'tǔ léi.')
This is a recent excellent precedent,
a historical example regarding border affairs.
I humbly suggest that Āshǐnà Húluósè be established as Khagan,
entrusting the Four Garrisons to him,
thus continuing the line of the extinct Gāo clan,
(referring to Gāolì).
This would save military expenditure in distant lands,
and concentrate armed forces along the frontier.
If the Yi-Di have no fear of invasion or insult, then that will suffice.
Why must we seek out their lairs,
and contend with ants over trivial matters?
We should simply instruct the border troops
to maintain strict defenses,
send out distant scouts,
gather provisions,
and wait for them to expose themselves,
then strike them.
By waiting in ease for the weary, our soldiers' strength will be doubled;
by defending as masters against guests, we will have the advantage;
by strengthening our walls and clearing the fields, the invaders will gain nothing.
Naturally, if the two bandits penetrate deep, they will face difficulties;
if they enter shallowly, they will gain no spoils.
If this is done for several years,
the two captives can be subdued without battle."
(The "two bandits" and "two captives" both refer to the Tūjué and Tǔbō.)
Discerning individuals agreed with this.
26 Lǐ Qiáo, a Shèláng of the Fènggé and concurrently in charge of the Tiānguān elections,
first established several thousand supernumerary officials.
27 Previously, the calendar officials designated this month as the first month and the twelfth month as an intercalary month.
The Empress Dowager desired that the winter solstice fall on the first day of the first month, Jiǎzǐ.
Therefore, she issued an edict stating,
"To remove the last day of the month yet still see the moon
is to contradict the heavenly order.
(To 'remove the last day' refers to the last day of the previous month.)
The coming month shall be the first month."
Shènglì First Year
(Wùxū, 698 CE)
1 In the first month,
on the first day, Jiǎzǐ,
the winter solstice,
the Empress Dowager held a sacrifice at the Tōngtiān Palace.
(A textual variant states: The 'Shílù' records:
"In the first month,
on Rénxū,
a sacrifice was held at Tōngtiān Palace."
According to the long calendar,
the first day of the first month of this year was Rénxū.
The 'Shílù' is mistaken.
We now follow the Táng Lì, Tǒng Jì, and the new Běnjì.)
The era name was changed.
2 Zōng Chǔkè, the Shìláng of Xiàguān, was dismissed from his administrative post.
3 In spring,
the second month,
on Yǐwèi,
Dòu Lúqīnwàng, the Yòuxiàng of Wénchāng and concurrently Sānpǐn of Fènggé Luántái, was dismissed and appointedtàizǐ Bīnkè (Guest of the Crown Prince).
4 Wǔ Chéngsì and Sānsī sought to be made Crown Prince,
repeatedly sending people to persuade the Empress Dowager, saying:
"Since ancient times, no Son of Heaven has ever taken someone of a different surname as his heir."
The Empress Dowager was undecided.
Dí Rénjié frequently spoke to the Empress Dowager in a gentle manner, saying:
"Emperor Wén weathered wind and rain,
personally braving sharp blades,
to bring peace to the empire,
and transmitted it to his descendants.
The Great Emperor entrusted his two sons to Your Majesty.
(Emperor Gāozōng was posthumously titled Tiānhuáng Dàdì.)
(The 'two sons' refers to the Prince of Lúlíng and the Imperial Heir.)
Would it not be against Heaven's will to deny them?
Moreover, which is closer: aunt and nephew, or mother and son?
(The Empress Dowager to Chéngsì and Sānsī is aunt and nephew.)
(To the Prince of Lúlíng and the Imperial Heir, she is mother and son.)
Then, after a thousand autumns and ten thousand years, if you establish your sons, they will be enshrined in the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
and the succession will be endless.
If you establish your nephew,
it has never been heard of a nephew becoming Son of Heaven and enshrining his aunt in the temple."
The Empress Dowager said:
"This is My family affair,
you need not concern yourself with it."
Rén Jié replied:
"A king regards the four seas as his family;
within the four seas,
who is not a subject or maidservant?
What is not Your Majesty's family affair?
The ruler is the head,
and ministers are the limbs;
by definition, they are one body.
Moreover, I hold the position of prime minister;
how can I not concern myself with it?"
He further urged the Empress Dowager to recall the Prince of Lúlíng.
(The Prince of Lúlíng was moved to Jūnzhōu in Guāngzhái First Year, and to Fángzhōu in Chuí Gǒng First Year.)
The Empress Dowager's mind began to awaken.
Another day,
she again said to Rén Jié:
"I dreamed of a large parrot with both wings broken.
What does it mean?"
He replied:
"'Wǔ' is Your Majesty's surname;
the 'two wings' are your two sons.
If Your Majesty raises your two sons,
then both wings will flap."
From then on, the Empress Dowager had no intention of establishing Chéngsì or Sānsī.
When Sūn Wànróng besieged Yōuzhōu,
he sent a manifesto to the imperial court saying:
"Why do you not return Lúlíng Wáng to me?"
Jí Xū, Zhāng Yìzhī, and Chāngzōng all served as attendants of the Kònghè Jiān.
The Kònghè Jiān was established that year to accommodate favored close associates.
Xū casually advised the two of them, saying:
"Your brothers enjoy such favor and honor,
not obtained through virtue or achievement.
Many in the empire look askance and gnash their teeth.
Without great service to the empire,
how can you protect yourselves?
I secretly worry for you!"
The two were afraid,
and tearfully asked for a plan.
Xū said:
"The gentry and common people of the empire have not forgotten the virtue of Táng,
and all desire the return of Lúlíng Wáng.
The Sovereign is advanced in years,
and the great enterprise must be entrusted to someone;
the Wǔ clan's princes are not the intended recipients.
Why do you not gently persuade the empress to establish Lúlíng Wáng as the heir, thereby securing the hopes of the populace!
If you do this,
not only will you avoid disaster,
but you can also long preserve your wealth and honor."
The two thought this was a good idea,
and seized opportunities to speak to the Grand Empress Dowager about it repeatedly.
The Grand Empress Dowager knew the plan originated from Xū,
so she summoned and questioned him.
Xū again fully explained the advantages and disadvantages to the Grand Empress Dowager,
and her mind was then made up.
The Kǎoyì says: There is a biography of Dí Liánggōng in the world,
which claims Lǐ Yōng compiled it.
Its language is crude and exaggerated,
likely not by Yōng.
It says:
"The Empress accepted the counsel of the Wǔ clan,
intending to shift the imperial succession,
planning to establish Wǔ Sānsī as the heir apparent,
and relocate Lúlíng Wáng to Fánglíng.
The Wǔ clan secretly plotted,
offering advice day and night, saying: 'Your Majesty's surname is Wǔ,
it is proper to establish a Wǔ as heir;
there has never been an emperor who took someone of a different surname as their successor.'
The Empress having already agreed,
she ceremoniously asked her ministers: 'I am advanced in age,
and the nation has no heir.
Now I wish to choose a worthy person,
who would be suitable?
Although I may have someone in mind,
it ultimately depends on your collective deliberation.'
Many of the prime ministers, hearing the plan was already decided,
tailored their words to her wishes;
only Rénjié stood back silently,
without a single word.
The Empress asked: 'You alone have no words,
you must have a different opinion.'
The Duke replied: 'I do.
Observing the celestial phenomena above,
there are no signs of a change in sovereign;
examining the hearts of the people below,
they are truly not tired of Táng virtue.'
The Empress said: 'How do you know this?'
The Duke replied: 'Recently the Xiōngnú invaded the frontier;
Your Majesty sent Liáng Wáng Sānsī to recruit in the cities,
and after more than a month,
fewer than a thousand men were gathered.
Afterward, Lúlíng Wáng followed,
and in less than twenty days,
the number exceeded fifty thousand.
From this, one can see that
the hearts of the people have not left.
If Your Majesty wishes to continue the succession,
other than Lúlíng Wáng,
the rest are truly not what your subject knows of.'
The Empress was enraged,
and ordered her attendants to escort him out."
However, at that time Lúlíng Wáng was the Marshal of Hébĕi,
after he had been established as Crown Prince,
and moreover, at that time Ruìzōng was the Imperial Heir.
If Rénjié requested Lúlíng Wáng to succeed to the throne,
it would mean advising the Grand Empress Dowager to depose and establish an heir.
This is certainly not credible.
Perhaps Rénjié advised recalling Lúlíng Wáng, who was closely related as mother and son yet imprisoned in Fánglíng,
to attend upon her,
which is plausible.
The Tánbīnlù says:
"In the second year of Shènglì,
in the twelfth month,
Zhāng Yìzhī's brothers were excessively favored and honored,
and fearing they would not be preserved whole,
they sought counsel from Tiānguān Shìláng Jí Xū.
Xū said: 'Your brothers have received deep grace,
but without great service to the empire,
few throughout history have been preserved whole.
There is only one plan;
if you can implement it,
why stop at preserving your family,
you will also enjoy the enfeoffment of land;
apart from this,
it is not what Xū can devise.'
Yìzhī's brothers wept and pleaded for it.
Xū said: 'The empire has longed for Táng virtue for a long time,
the Sovereign is advanced in years,
and the Wǔ clan's princes are clearly not the intended recipients.
Why do you not gently request the establishment of Lúlíng Wáng,
to secure the hopes of the living?'
Yìzhī then seized opportunities to speak of it repeatedly,
and Empress Wǔ's mind then changed;
once she knew Xū was the initial planner,
she summoned and questioned Xū.
Xū said: 'Lúlíng Wáng and Xiāng Wáng are both Your Majesty's sons;
Gāozōng deeply entrusted them to Your Majesty;
it is solely for Your Majesty to decide.'
Empress Wǔ's mind was then made up."
The Yùshǐtái Jì says:
"Zétiān established the Kònghè Fǔ,
and Xū, Yìzhī, and Chāngzōng served together in the府
and Xū was intimate with Chāngzōng.
Chāngzōng, feeling his favor and honor were excessive,
feared he would not be preserved whole,
and sought counsel from Xū,"
and so on,
as in the Tánbīnlù.
Probably, the Grand Empress Dowager favored and trusted the Wǔ clan,
and purged the Lǐ clan;
even her own son Lúlíng Wáng was deposed and exiled to Fánglíng.
Therefore, Rénjié advised recalling him to attend upon her,
to strengthen the Lǐ clan,
and suppress the Wǔ clan.
Zhāng and Jí were not capable of devising plans for the Táng dynasty;
they merely sought their own benefit.
If the Imperial Heir (Ruìzōng) were to remain established,
what merit would they have!
Therefore, they advised the Grand Empress Dowager to establish Lúlíng Wáng as Crown Prince,
and the Grand Empress Dowager followed their advice.
Thus, the desire to recall Lúlíng Wáng was Rénjié's intention;
establishing him as Crown Prince was
Zhāng and Jí's plan.
The Tánbīn states the second year of Shènglì and refers to Xū as Tiānguān Shìláng;
the Táijì refers to Ruìzōng as Xiāng Wáng;
both are errors.
The Xīn Dí Rénjié Zhuàn says:
"Zhāng Yìzhī once casually asked for a plan for self-preservation.
Rénjié said: 'Only by advising the recall of Lúlíng Wáng can disaster be avoided.'"
Considering Rénjié, how could he speak of this in depth with Yìzhī!
The Dí Liánggōng Zhuàn also says:
"After a period of ten days,
the Duke was summoned,
and the Empress said: 'Last night I dreamt I was playing Liùbó with someone,
and I repeatedly could not win.
Why is this?'
He replied: 'Not winning at Liùbó
is probably because there are no sons in the palace.
This is the will of Heaven,
using this to show Your Majesty.
How can the position of heir remain vacant for long?'
The Empress said: 'This is my family matter,
decided within my heart;
how can you be allowed to participate!'
Rénjié replied: 'Your subject hears that a king takes the empire as his family,
and within the four seas,
all are subjects and concubines.
What is not Your Majesty's family matter!
The ruler is the head,
the ministers are the limbs;
how can your subject not participate!'
She again ordered him to be escorted out,
and ultimately did not accept his advice."
However, at that time the Imperial Heir (Ruìzōng) was in the palace,
so it was incorrect to say there were no sons or that the heir's position had been long vacant.
The Cháoyě Qiānzǎi says:
"Zétiān once dreamt of a parrot,
with magnificent feathers,
but both its wings were broken.
She asked her prime ministers about it,
and all the Dukes were silent.
Nèishǐ Dí Rénjié said: 'The parrot (Wǔ 鵡)
is Your Majesty's surname (Wǔ 武).
Its two wings being broken
refers to Your Majesty's two sons, Lúlíng Wáng and Xiāng Wáng.
If Your Majesty raises these two sons,
both wings will be complete.'
Wèi Wáng Chéngsì and Wǔ Sānsī's necks all turned red.
Later, the Qìdān revolted,
besieging Yōuzhōu,
and sent a manifesto to the imperial court saying: 'Return Lúlíng Wáng and Xiāng Wáng to us!'
Zétiān then remembered Dí Gōng's words,
and said to him: 'You once interpreted a dream for me;
now it has come true.
I wish to establish a Crown Prince,
which would be best?'
Rénjié said: 'Your Majesty has worthy sons internally,
and worthy nephews externally.
To choose between them wisely
rests in Your Majesty's imperial heart.'
Zétiān said: 'I have my own sacred sons;
what are Chéngsì and Sānsī but a mere skin ailment!'
Chéngsì and others, afraid,
covered their ears and fled.
An edict was immediately issued to recall Lúlíng.
Hénèi Wáng and others memorialized,
requesting that he not be allowed to enter the capital city,
but be settled in Lóngmén.
The rebels grew even stronger,
conquering Jìzhōu.
Zétiān was alarmed,
and thereupon established Lúlíng Wáng as Crown Prince,
to serve as Grand Marshal.
Initially,
when troops were recruited, none responded.
When it was heard that the Crown Prince was going forth,
Běimángshān Tón had so many soldiers that it was full,
with no room for people;
the rebels then dispersed on their own. "
According to this, Rùizōng was not yet Xiāng Wáng at that time.
Furthermore, if Rénjié had said there was a worthy son within and
a worthy nephew outside,
that would have been holding two positions.
Now, we select the credible parts from various accounts and preserve them.
In the third month,
on the Jǐsì day,
it was said that Lúlíng Wáng was ill,
and Xú Yànbó of Xiáqiū, Assistant Director of the Bureau of Public Works, was dispatched.
Xiáqiū,
formerly Xiáyì of Lǔ during the Spring and Autumn period,
Jìn and Sòng established Yǎnzhōu here.
In the thirteenth year of Kāihuáng of Suí,
Xiáqiū county was established,
subordinate to Yǎnzhōu.
On the Wùzǐ day,
Lúlíng Wáng arrived at Shéndū.
The Kǎoyì states: The Tǒngjì says:
"On the Gǔichǒu day,
Xú Yànbó, Assistant Director of the Bureau of Public Works, was dispatched to Fángzhōu
to summon Lúlíng Wáng and his children to the capital for medical treatment."
The Dǐ Liánggōng Zhuàn states:
"Later, ten palace women were secretly sent to Fángzhōu
to convey an imperial edict saying: 'My son is here.
Let the palace women go and attend him.
The chief officials of the prefecture and county
are commanded to allow them to enter and exit frequently without intermingling.'
Secretly, one palace woman was ordered to take the place of Lúlíng Wáng;
Lúlíng Wáng was ordered to wear the palace women's clothes,
and return with the old number,
without the prefecture and county realizing.
After several days, he reached the capital,
and none of the court officials
were aware of it."
The Jiù Zhuàn states:
"When Lúlíng Wáng returned to the palace from Fánglíng,
the Empress Dowager concealed him behind a curtain,
and then summoned Dǐ Rénjié,
speaking of Lúlíng.
Rénjié spoke passionately and sincerely,
tears flowing as he spoke.
She then quickly brought Lúlíng out,
saying to Rénjié: 'I return your Crown Prince.'
Rénjié descended the steps, weeping and congratulating her.
After this,
he memorialized, saying: 'The Crown Prince has returned to the palace,
but no one knows.
How can public opinion assess right from wrong?'
Zétiān thought this was right,
and so Middle Zōng was reinstated at Lóngmén,
and formally welcomed back,
moving everyone with joy."
The Dǐ Liánggōng Zhuàn states:
"The Empress had an audience in a small hall,
with a curtain drawn behind her,
concealed on the left and right,
so that outsiders could not know.
She then ordered the Duke to sit at the foot of the steps,
saying: 'The matter discussed earlier
was indeed not small.
Waking and sleeping, I have pondered it repeatedly,
and considering your words,
I realize more and more that the reasoning is not too far off.
My intention is for loyal subjects to serve their lord;
why should there be much opposition?
Today,
we must change our previous views.
The position of the empire rests on your single word.
If you agree with my wishes, both will be preserved;
if you go against my heart, both will perish!'
The Duke calmly said: 'What Your Majesty speaks of,
the position of the Son of Heaven,
can be exclusively held.
But as far as I know,
this is the position of Tàizōng Wénwǔ Huángdì!
How can Your Majesty claim it for yourself?
Tàizōng risked his life in battle,
governing the four seas.
The reason he did not complain of toil
was for his descendants,
how could it be for Wǔ Sānsī?
Your Majesty is the Empress of Dàdì.
When Dàdì fell ill,
he temporarily allowed Your Majesty to supervise the state;
after Dàdì passed away,
it should have reverted to the legitimate heir.
Your Majesty then usurped the divine instruments [of power]
for more than ten years.
Now that succession is being discussed,
how can it be changed again?
Furthermore, who is closer, an aunt or a mother?
Who is nearer, a son or a nephew?'
And so on.
Thereupon, the Empress sighed and shed tears,
ordered her attendants to draw aside the curtain,
patted the Duke's back with her hand,
and exclaimed loudly: 'You are not my subject,
but a subject of the Táng dynasty and its altars of grain and soil!'
Turning to Lúlíng Wáng, she said: 'Bow to the Elder of the State!

The Empress said: 'Immediately prepare what has been said,
and proclaim it inside and outside the court.

The Duke, wiping his tears, said: 'Since ancient times,
how can there be a Son of Heaven secretly substituted?

is known throughout the realm;
that he is now inside [the palace],
even I do not know.
If I am to follow the edict,
should it be like the incident of Wèi Tàizǐ,
how will Your Majesty clear my name?'
The Empress said: 'How can he return to Fánglíng now?
Just settle him at Shíxiàng Yì,
prepare the imperial carriage,
arrange the hundred officials,
and welcome him there.'
Thereupon, shouts of 'Long live!' arose,
and the position of Crown Prince was finally settled."
Now, if Wǔ Hòu had secretly summoned Lúlíng Wáng,
and the ten palace women knew her plan,
the journey from Luòyáng to Fánglíng was very long,
how could no outsiders know at all?
Furthermore,
how could the Shílù invent the story of Xú Yànbó going to welcome him,
and record the date of Lúlíng Wáng's arrival from Fángzhōu,
if it were false?
Also,
if the position of Crown Prince had already been settled at that time,
how could it be that from the third month to the ninth month he was only just established as Crown Prince?
Probably, after Lúlíng arrived,
the Empress Dowager wished to establish him based on seniority,
and the Imperial Heir also yielded his position because of this,
hence the half-year delay.
Now, all accounts based on the Shílù are taken as correct.

on the Dīngsì (丁巳) day,
he was dismissed."
Previously, it was not stated that Jùyuán (巨源) was a Zuǒxiàng (左相).
Neither the Jiùjì (舊紀) nor the biographies mention it.
It is likely that Zuǒchéng (左丞) was mistakenly written as Zuǒxiàng (左相).
On the Yǐsì (乙巳) day,
the Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu 太后) went to Sōngshān (嵩山);
in spring,
the first month,
on the Dīngmǎo (丁卯) day,
she went to Wēntāng (溫湯) in Rǔzhōu (汝州);
on the Wùyín (戊寅) day,
she returned to Shéndū (神都).
The Sānyánggōng (三陽宮) was built at Shícóng (石淙) in Gàochéng (告成).
Sānyánggōng (三陽宮) was one hundred and sixty *lǐ* (里) from Luòchéng (洛城).
In the first year of Wànsuì Dēngfēng (萬歲登封),
Dōngdū Yángchéng Xiàn (東都陽城縣) was renamed Gàochéng (告成),

Cóng (淙) is pronounced
"zàng zōng fān" (藏宗翻),

7. In the second month,
on the Yǐwèi (乙未) day,
Dòu Lúqīnwàng (豆盧欽望), Tóng Fènggé Luántái Sānpǐn (同鳳閣鸞臺三品), was dismissed and made Tàizǐ Bīnke (太子賓客).
8. In the third month,
Xuānchāo (宣超), Prince of Qīnghǎi (Qīnghǎi Wáng 青海王) of Tuyuhun (Tǔyùhún 吐谷渾), was made Wūdì Yěbáqínzhōng Kèhán (烏地也拔勤忠可汗).
Xuānchāo (宣超) was
the grandson of Nuòhépō (諾曷鉢).
9. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Wùshēn (戊申) day,
the Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu 太后) went to Sānyánggōng (三陽宮) to escape the summer heat.
A Hu (胡) monk invited the imperial carriage to observe the burial of a relic.
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu 太后) consented.
Dī Rénjié (狄仁傑) knelt before the horse and said,
"Buddha is a god of the barbarians (yídí 夷狄),
not worthy of the Lord of All Under Heaven (Tiānxià zhī Zhǔ 天下之主) humbling herself.
That Hu (胡) monk is deceitful,
merely wishing to attract Your Majesty to bewilder people near and far.
The mountain road is dangerous and narrow,
not allowing for an escort,
which is not suitable for Your Majesty to visit."
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu 太后) returned halfway, saying,
"To fulfill the integrity of Our loyal official."
10. In the fifth month,
on the Jǐyǒu (己酉) *shuò* (朔),
there was a solar eclipse.
11. The Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu 太后) had the monk Hú Chāo (胡超) from Hóngzhōu (洪州) compound an elixir of immortality.
It took three years to complete,
and cost an enormous sum.
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu 太后) took it,
and her illness slightly improved.
On the Guǐchǒu (癸丑) day,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the reign title was changed to Jiǔshì (久視);
the title Tiāncè Jīnlún Dàshèng (天冊金輪大聖) was abolished.
12. In the sixth month,
the Kònghè Fǔ (控鶴府) was changed to Fèngchén Fǔ (奉宸府),
and Zhāng Yìzhī (張易之) was made Fèngchénlìng (奉宸令).
Whenever the Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu 太后) held a private banquet in the inner palace,
she would invite the Wǔ (武) relatives, Yìzhī (易之), and his younger brother Mìshūjiān (祕書監) Chāngzōng (昌宗) to drink, gamble, and jest.
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu 太后) wished to conceal these activities,
so she ordered Yìzhī (易之), Chāngzōng (昌宗), and scholars like Lǐ Qiáo (李嶠) to compile the Sānjiào Zhūyīng (三教珠英) in the inner palace.
The three teachings (sānjiào 三教) were
Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism.
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu 太后) ordered Chāngzōng (昌宗) to wear a feathered robe,
play the *shēng* (笙),
and ride a wooden crane in the courtyard;
the scholars all composed poems to praise him.
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu 太后) also selected many handsome young men to serve as Fèngchén Nèigòngfèng (奉宸內供奉).
Yòubǔquē (右補闕) Zhū Jìngzé (朱敬則) remonstrated, saying,
"Your Majesty already has Yìzhī (易之) and Chāngzōng (昌宗) as inner favorites,
which is sufficient.
Recently, I heard that Hóu Xiáng (侯祥) and others, the Zhǎnglǐ (長史) of the Yòujiānménwèi (右監門衞)
(Tang (Táng 唐) dynasties, each of the various guard prefectures had a Zhǎnglǐ (長史),
from rank six upper,
each overseeing the affairs of the various departments in their prefecture.
Jiān (監) is pronounced
'gǔ xián fān' (古銜翻).
are brazen and shameless,
seeking to become Fèngchén Nèigòngfèng (奉宸內供奉).
Their lack of decorum and propriety
overflows into the court's hearing.
Your servant's duty is to remonstrate,
and I dare not not report this."
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu 太后) praised him, saying,
"If not for your frank words,
We would not have known this."
She bestowed upon him one hundred bolts of silk.
Yìzhī and Chāngzōng competed in extravagance.
Their younger brother, Chāngyí, was the Prefect of Luòyáng.
Any requests for patronage were granted without exception.
Once, during an early court session,
there was a candidate named Xuē
who offered fifty *liǎng* of gold along with a petition, stopping Chāngyí's horse to bribe him.
Chāngyí accepted the gold.
Upon reaching the imperial court,
he handed the petition to Tiānguān Shìláng Zhāng Xī.
Several days later,
Xī lost the petition
and asked Chāngyí about it.
Chāngyí cursed him, saying:
"You incompetent fellow!
I don't remember either.
Just give it to anyone named Xuē."
Xī was frightened.
He withdrew
and searched for all sixty-some people named Xuē among the candidates,
and arranged for all of them to be appointed to official positions.
Xī
was the nephew of Wénguàn.
(Zhāng Wénguàn is mentioned in scroll 201, during Gāozōng's Qiánfēng second year).
13 Initially,
the Khitan general Lǐ Kǎigù,
skilled in using [AS-FEEB] [AS-FBED] a lasso and in mounted archery and wielding a long spear,
whenever he charged into battle formations,
was like a falcon entering a flock of sparrows,
scattering all before him.
In the Battle of Huángzhāng,
Zhāng Xuányù and Má Rénjié were both [AS-FEEB] [AS-FBED] by him.
(This event is mentioned in the previous scroll, Wàansuì Tōngtiān first year).
He also served as a Khitan general
and repeatedly defeated Tang forces.
When Sūn Wànróng died,
both men surrendered.
The authorities accused them of delayed surrender
and petitioned for their entire families to be executed.
Dí Rénjié said:
"Kǎigù and the others are all exceptionally brave and fierce.
They were able to exert their utmost for their former master,
so they will certainly be able to exert their utmost for us.
If we treat them with virtue,
they can all be used by us."
He then requested that they be pardoned.
His close associates all tried to stop him,
but Rénjié said:
"If it benefits the state,
why should I scheme for myself!"
The Empress Dowager followed his advice
and pardoned them.
He also requested that they be given official posts.
The Empress Dowager appointed Kǎigù as Zuǒ Yùqínwèi Jiāngjūn

Jiǔshì first year
(Gēngzǐ, 700 AD)
1. Autumn,
seventh month.
Captives were offered at Hánshū Diàn.
Lǐ Kǎigù presented the Khitan captives.
Hánshū Diàn was located within Sānyáng Gōng.
(He was) granted the surname Wǔ.
He summoned the high officials and ministers for a joint banquet.
(To) "summon the high officials and ministers"
refers to summoning generals and commanders for a joint banquet.
"This is the achievement of the Duke."
When he was about to be rewarded, he replied:
"This is due to Your Majesty's awe-inspiring power
and the utmost efforts of the generals and commanders.
What achievement have I?"
He firmly declined to accept.
2. Intercalary month,
Wùyín.
The imperial carriage returned to the palace.
(It returned) from Sānyáng Gōng to Luòyáng Gōng.
3. Jǐchǒu.
Tiānguān Shìláng Zhāng Xī was appointed Fènggé Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Luántái Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Lǐ Qiáo was dismissed as Chéngjūn Jìjiǔ.
Xī
was Qiáo's maternal uncle,
which is why Qiáo was dismissed from political affairs.
4. Dīngyǒu.
The Tubo general Qūmǎng Bùzhī invaded Liángzhōu
and besieged Chāngsōng
(Tǔ, from tūn entering tone;
Jiàng, read as liàng).
Chāngsōng County was the Cāngsōng County of Hàn Wǔwēi Commandery;
Lǚ Guāng changed it to Chāngsōng.
Yuángǔ.
Qūmǎng Bùzhī's troops and armor were splendid and bright.
Xiūjǐng said to his generals:
"Now that Zhūlún is dead,
(Zhūlún's death is mentioned in the previous scroll, Shènglì second year),
he is not accustomed to military affairs.
Though they appear elite,
they are actually easy to deal with.
I request to break them for you all."
He then put on his armor and was the first to charge into the formation,
winning six battles consecutively.
The Tubo forces fled in disarray.
Two thousand five hundred heads were cut off,
and two subordinate generals were captured before returning.
5. Sīfǔ Shàodī Yáng Yuánhēng,
(In Guāngzhái first year,
Tàifǔ Sì was renamed Sīfǔ Sì).
Both (Yuánhēng and Yuánxǐ) were the sons of Hóngwǔ.
(Yáng Hóngwǔ is mentioned in scroll 201, Gāozōng's Qiánfēng second year).
Yìzhī spoke to the Empress Dowager:
"Yuánxǐ
is a member of Yáng Sù's clan.
Yáng Sù and his son
were rebellious ministers of the Suí dynasty.
Their descendants should not serve at court."
The Empress Dowager followed his advice.
Rènyín,
an edict was issued:
"Yáng Sù and all his brothers, sons, and grandsons are forbidden from holding positions in the capital."
Yuánhēng was demoted to Mùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Yuánxǐ to Bèi
zhōu Cìshǐ.
Mǎ Hēluó rebelled during the time of Hàn Wǔdì,
yet Mǎ Yuán rose to prominence during the restoration of the Eastern Hàn.
Shěn Chōng betrayed Wáng Dūn,
yet Shěn Jìn devoted his life to Sīmǎ.
Evil should stop with the perpetrator himself.
To punish a minister from a different era and abandon all his descendants
is surely born of temporary affection or aversion,
merely using this pretext as an excuse.
Mùzhōu is three thousand six hundred fifty-nine *lǐ* southeast of the capital,
and two thousand eight hundred twenty-one *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
Bèizhōu is one thousand seven hundred eighty-two *lǐ* northeast of the capital,
and nine hundred ninety-three *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
6. Gēngxū.
Wèi Yuánzhōng was appointed Lǒngyòu Zhūjūn Dàshǐ
to attack Tubo.
On Gēngshēn,
the Tàihòu desired to construct a large statue,
ordering all monks and nuns in the realm to contribute one *qián* daily to assist in its undertaking.
Dī Rénjié submitted a memorial to remonstrate,
its summary stating:
"The *jiālán* of today,
their scale exceeds that of palaces.
The labor does not employ spirits,
but solely relies on conscripting people;
materials do not come from heaven,
but must ultimately be extracted from the earth.
If the common people are not harmed,
from where will these be obtained!"
He also said:
"Wandering monks all rely on Buddhist teachings,
misleading and deluding the living;
in neighborhoods and streets, there are often *jīngfāng*,
and in markets, *jīngshè* are also erected.
Cuī Bào's Gǔjīn Zhù states: *Huán*,
a city wall; *huì*,
a city gate.
*Huán*,
pronounced hù guān;
*huì*,
pronounced hù duì.
Their demands press more heavily than official taxes;
what is required for Buddhist rituals
is more stringent than imperial edicts."
He also said:
"Liáng Wǔ and Jiǎn Wén's almsgiving and donations were boundless,
yet when the three Huái rivers surged with waves,
and the Five Ridges rose in smoke,
(using Emperor Tàizōng's words from an edict),
they could not save themselves from the disaster of peril and demise.
The character *chà*
is pronounced chū xiá.
How could there be troops to serve the sovereign!"
He also said:
"Though monks' money is collected,
a hundred (parts collected) will not cover one (part of the cost).
Since the Venerable Countenance is so vast,
it cannot be left exposed;
to cover it with a hundred layers
still leaves concern that it won't be entirely covered.
As for the remaining halls and chambers,
they cannot be entirely absent.
The Tathāgata established his teachings
with compassion as the main principle,
(Buddhists refer to the Buddha as the Tathāgata).
Is this for the sake of empty embellishment!"
He also said:
"Recently, floods and droughts have been out of season,
and currently, the frontiers are not yet peaceful.
If official funds are spent
and manpower is exhausted,
should trouble arise in a corner (of the realm),
how will it be remedied!"
The Tàihòu said:
"You instruct me to do good,
how can I go against you!"
She then halted the project.
In the 8th month, Àxíjí Bólù rebelled.
(Àxíjí
is the Àxíjié of the Five *Sìjīn* of the Xī Tūjué Nǔshībì;
Bólù
is his name).
His army reached Suìyè.
Bólù plundered by night near the city and departed.
Sīyè led cavalry to pursue him,
but was instead defeated.
Yáng Míng led the forces of the Xī Tūjué Hú Sèluó to attack his city.
For more than ten days,
they could not capture it.
In the 9th month,
Bólù feigned surrender.
Sīyè lured and beheaded him,
and then captured his followers.
In the 9th month, the Tàihòu trusted and highly valued the Nèishǐ, Duke Liáng Wénhuì, Dī Rénjié.
No other minister could compare to him;
she always referred to him as *Guólǎo* and did not address him by name.
Rénjié was fond of directly and publicly remonstrating in court,
and the Tàihòu always yielded her will and followed him.
Once, when accompanying the Tàihòu on an outing,
a gust of wind blew Rénjié's headcloth off,
and his horse was startled and could not be stopped.
The Tàihòu ordered the Tàizǐ to pursue him, grasp the bridle, and stop it.
Rénjié repeatedly requested to retire due to old age and illness,
but the Tàihòu did not permit it.
When he came for an audience,
she always stopped him from bowing.
(The character *jiàn*
is pronounced xián biàn.)
"Whenever I see you bow, sir,"
she said, "I too feel a pain in my body."
She also excused him from night duty,
and instructed his colleagues, saying:
"Unless it is a major military or state affair,
do not trouble him."
On Xīnchǒu,
he passed away.
The Tàihòu wept and said:
"The court is empty!"
From then on, whenever there was a major court matter
and the multitude (of officials) could not decide,
the Tàihòu would sigh and say:
"Why has Heaven taken away my *Guólǎo* so early!"
The Grand Empress Dowager once asked Dī Rénjié:
"I wish to find a fine scholar to employ.
Who would be suitable?"
Dī Rénjié replied:
"I am not sure for what purpose Your Majesty wishes to employ him?"
The Grand Empress Dowager said:
"I wish to employ him as a chancellor or minister."
Dī Rénjié responded:
"For literary grace and refinement,
Sū Wèidào and Lǐ Qiáo are certainly among the chosen.
If you must have a truly outstanding and extraordinary talent,
then there is Zhāng Jiǎnzhī, the Prefect of Jīngzhōu.
Although that man is old,
he has the talent of a chancellor."
The Grand Empress Dowager promoted Zhāng Jiǎnzhī to Luòzhōu Sīmǎ.
To advance from a Prefect of a major prefecture to a Sīmǎ of Shénzhōu [Luòzhōu] was
therefore called a "promotion."
She asked Dī Rénjié again,
who replied:
"The Zhāng Jiǎnzhī I recommended earlier
has not yet been employed."
The Grand Empress Dowager said:
"He has already been transferred."
He replied:
"The one I recommended is fit to be a chancellor,
not a Sīmǎ."
Thereupon, he was transferred to Qiūguān Shìláng;
after a long time,
he was eventually appointed as chancellor.
Dī Rénjié also recommended several dozen people, including Xiàguān Shìláng Yáo Yuánchóng, Jiānchá Yùshǐ Qū'ā Huán Yànfàn, and Tàizhōu Cìshǐ Jìng Huī.
[Qí]
In the sixth year,
the prefecture was abolished;
it must have been re-established at this time.
Kǎo Yì says: The biography of the Duke of Liáng states:
"Zhāng Jiǎnzhī, Huán Yànfàn, Jìng Huī, Cuī Xuánwěi, and Yuán Shùjǐ were all recommended by the Duke.
The Duke once, after finishing his meal,
said to the Five Dukes: 'My only regret is that I am old and feeble,
and my body will perish before the morning dew.
I will not be able to witness the grand achievements of the Five Dukes.
I hope you will all cherish yourselves
and act with your whole hearts.'
The Five Dukes understood and saw clearly,
comprehending the Duke's intention in advance.
When the Duke was ill in bed,
the Five Dukes visited to inquire about his health.
They conversed by chance for a whole day,
but not a single word was exchanged.
A moment later,
tears flowed and soaked his pillow,
but they merely looked at each other.
When the Five Dukes withdrew,
they were all puzzled by the reason.
Yuán Shùjǐ said: 'Perhaps his strength is waning,
and he needs to discuss family matters?'
Zhāng Jiǎnzhī said: 'I have never heard of a great sage abandoning national affairs for family matters.'
After a short while,
he summoned Zhāng Jiǎnzhī, Yuán Shùjǐ, and Huán Yànfàn, the three Dukes, to enter,
while the other two Dukes stood outside the door,
and said: 'My silence earlier
was because of those two Dukes.
These two Dukes can be decisive but cannot be discreet.
If we had discussed it with them beforehand,
the matter would certainly have leaked out.
Once it leaked,
the state would be destabilized and the family would perish.
By that time, if they were not involved,
the matter would also not be accomplished.
Liángwáng Sānsī holds power;
he must be apprehended first before action can be taken.
Otherwise,
it will certainly bring about
great disaster.'
After Dī Gōng's death,
more than a year later,
the Five Dukes secretly met in a secluded place,
recounted the Duke's words from that time,
and renewed their covenant.
After the feast was cleared,
they looked at each other, wanting to speak,
but it was not yet the time,
fearing they would betray their previous promise.
They wanted to speak but stopped again,
this happened several times.
Huán Yànfàn then began to recount his words.
Before he had even finished speaking,
they heard a sound outside the windows
like thunder,
and in a moment, wind and rain came,
making it impossible to distinguish things nearby.
The cushions they were sitting on were all thrown down the steps.
The Five Dukes were trembling with fear,
not knowing what to do.
They then said to each other: 'This is Dī Gōng's utmost loyalty and integrity,
borrowing this spiritual manifestation to alarm the public,
not wanting us to discuss this matter prematurely.
It is not yet the time,
and we must not speak of it again.'
After a short while,
the sky cleared and the sun shone brightly,
no different from before.
After Yìzhī and others were executed,
Yuán Shùjǐ said to Zhāng Gōng: 'There was a dying wish
to apprehend Sānsī first.
How can we abandon it?'
Zhāng Gōng said: 'Once the major task is accomplished,
this is something on the chopping block;
how can it escape!'
Later, Liángwáng secretly conspired within the palace,
and the Five Dukes were indeed slandered by him,
and all suffered exile.
The years of their rise and fall,
and the pattern of the old agreement, were hardly different."
However, Zhāng Jiǎnzhī and the other five happened to be in office at the same time,
working together to establish their achievements.
How could Dī Rénjié have known these events in advance,
and specifically recommended these five people,
intending for them to assist in establishing the Crown Prince?
Furthermore, if Yìzhī and others were ripe for execution,
and the Crown Prince was in a position to be established,
Dī Rénjié, as chancellor,
would he have waited five years later,
and required Zhāng Jiǎnzhī and others to act then?
This is likely the biographer, due to the five men's achievement of restoring power,
fabricating the story,
saying they were all recommended by Dī Rénjié
and received instruction from him.
Such bizarre and groundless statements
are not accepted now.
The old biographies only mention the names of three people: Zhāng Jiǎnzhī, Huán Yànfàn, and Jìng Huī.
We follow that now.
Someone once said to Dī Rénjié:
"The peaches and plums of the empire
are all at your gate."
Chéng Dàchāng's Yǎn Fánlù: Zhào Jiǎnzǐ said to Yáng Hǔ:
"Only the worthy can repay kindness;
the unworthy cannot.
One who plants peaches and plums
rests in summer
and eats in autumn;
one who plants caltrops
cannot rest in summer
and gets pricked in autumn.
What you have gained now
are caltrops."
The current practice of referring to recommended scholars as peaches and plums
is all based on this.
"Recommending worthies is for the state,
not for private gain."
In the beginning,
Dī Rénjié was the Prefect of Wèizhōu.
(See volume 205, Wànsuì Tōngtiān first year).
The common people erected a shrine for him during his lifetime.
Later, his son Dī Jǐnghuī became the Sīgōng Cānjūn of Wèizhōu,
and his greed and tyranny caused distress to the people,
so people destroyed his statue.
The historian states that Dī Rénjié was utterly loyal,
thereby encouraging all subjects in the empire;
it says that because Dī Jǐnghuī was greedy and tyrannical, his shrine was destroyed,
thereby warning all sons in the empire.
10th winter,
10th month,
Xīnhài day,
Wèi Yuánzhōng was appointed Grand Commander of the Xiāoguān Road,
to guard against the Tūjué.
Xiāoguān is located in the Pinggao County of Yuánzhōu.
In the sixth year of Zhēngguān,
Tūjué surrendered households were settled in Yuánzhōu,
governing from Tālóu City in Pínggāo.
Gāozōng established Tālóu County,
which was abolished in the first year of Shénlóng,
and Xiāoguān County was established in its place.
Jue,
pronounced Jiǔwù.
11th Jiǎyín day,
an imperial edict restored the 1st month as the 11th month,
and the 1st month as the 1st month.
The matter of making the 11th month the 1st month is found in volume 204, Tiānshòu first year.
Making the 1st month the 1st month
adopted the Xià calendar's Jiànyín.
Fù,
pronounced Fúyòu.
12th Dīngsì day,
Nàyán Wéi Jùyuán was dismissed.
Wénchāng Yòuchéng Wéi Ānshí was appointed Luántái Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
Nàyán is
Shìzhōng.
Wénchāng Yòuchéng is
Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
Luántái is
Ménxià.
He was the grandson of Wéi Jīn.
The death of Wéi Jīn during the Suí dynasty is found in volume 185, Gāozǔ Wǔdé first year.
At that time, Wǔ Sānsī and the Zhāng Yìzhī brothers held power,
and Ānshí frequently reprimanded them to their faces.
Once, while attending a banquet in the Forbidden City,
Yìzhī invited several people, including the Shuǐ merchant Sòng Bàzi, to sit and gamble with them.
Ānshí knelt and reported, saying:
"Merchants are a base class,
and should not be allowed to participate in this gathering."
He motioned to the attendants to expel them,
and everyone present turned pale;

Quánjié County,

Cháng'ān first year
(Xīnchǒu, 701)
In this year, the era name was changed to Cháng'ān starting in the tenth month.

a wife who commits one of the seven reasons for divorce is abandoned: one, childlessness;

four, garrulousness;

1 In spring,
the first month,
on the *yǐyǒu* day,
the Martial Examinations were first established.
The system of Martial Examinations
included selections based on long-distance archery, mounted archery, foot archery, flat archery, tube archery, mounted spearmanship, levering a gate-bar, weightlifting, and physique.
The *Táng Liùdiǎn* states: "Martial examinees are assessed in seven categories: First, long-distance archery.
Those who shoot thirty arrows in long-distance archery and do not miss outside the third courtyard are rated excellent.
Entering the central courtyard is 'superior,'
entering the next courtyard is 'next superior,'
and entering the outer courtyard is 'next.'
Second, mounted archery.
Hitting the target with every shot is 'superior';
hitting sometimes and missing sometimes is 'next superior';
and missing all shots is 'next.'
Third, mounted spearmanship.
Hitting three or four targets is 'superior';
two targets is 'next superior';
one target or missing entirely is 'next.'
Fourth, foot archery.
Hitting the straw man accurately is 'next superior';
hitting but not according to the rules,
or following the rules but not hitting, is 'next.'
Fifth, talent and appearance.
Those six *chǐ* or more in height are 'next superior';
those below are 'next.'
Sixth, speech.
Those with inspiring demeanor fit to command are 'next superior';
those without are 'next.'
Seventh, weightlifting,
referring to levering a gate-bar.
Typically, five repetitions are rated excellent."
All those who achieved high ranks were reported by name.
