All insects and creatures that can squirm they take for food.
Líao, pronounced lǔ hào.
had attacked and occupied prefectures and counties.
The court sought a capable official to pacify them.
Zhū Jìngzé praised the Minister of the Bureau of Feudal Grants, Péi Huáigǔ, for his literary and military talents
(The Táng Minister of the Bureau of Feudal Grants was in charge of the nation's enfeoffments
and belonged to the Ministry of Personnel).
He was consequently appointed Commissioner for Recruitment, Pacification, and Suppression.
As soon as Huáigǔ reached the mountain pass,
he sent letters explaining the consequences of fortune and misfortune.
Qiàn and others came to surrender,
stating
"We were oppressed by officials,
and thus raised troops to save ourselves."
Huáigǔ rode lightly to meet them.
His attendants said:
"The Yi and Líao are untrustworthy;
do not take them lightly."
Huáigǔ said:
"I rely on loyalty and trustworthiness,
which can move gods,
let alone people!"
He then proceeded to their camp.
The bandit multitude was greatly pleased
and returned all the goods they had plundered.
The chieftains of various caves, who had previously maintained neutrality,
all came to submit,
and the entire Lingnan region was pacified.
In this
year,
emissaries were dispatched to inspect prefectures and counties according to six articles.
18 All the southern tribes of Tǔbō rebelled.
Zànpǔ Qì Nǔ Xī Lòng personally led an attack against them,
and died in the army.
After his death,
his son Xù Fān succeeded him.
His sons contended for the succession,
and after a long time,
the people of the country enthroned his son Qì Lì Suō Zàn as Zànpǔ,
who was seven years old.
Historians say that after Zhū Lùn died,
the power of Tǔbō gradually declined.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Bǐng Shēn,
Ā Shǐ Nà Huái Dào, General of the Right Wǔwèi, was enfeoffed as Khan of the Western Tūjué Ten Tribes.
Huái Dào was
the son of Hú Sè Luó.
2 On the day Dīng Wèi,
Sānyáng Palace was demolished,
and its materials were used to build Xīngtài Palace on Wàn'ān Mountain.
Wàn'ān Mountain is forty *lǐ* southwest of Shòu'ān County in Luòzhōu.
The Empress Dowager was invited to visit it every year,
and the construction costs were enormous,
causing suffering to the common people.
Lú Zàngyòng, Left Shíyí, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Many close officials on your left and right consider compliance to be loyalty,
and all officials in the court take offense as a warning,
causing Your Majesty to be unaware that the common people are losing their livelihoods,
which harms Your Majesty's benevolence.
If Your Majesty can truly use the hardship of the people as an excuse,
issue an edict to stop it,
then the whole world will know that Your Majesty suffers for yourself and loves the people."
It was not followed.
Zàngyòng was
the younger grandson of Chéngqìng.
See Lú Chéngqìng in Volume 200, Xiǎnqìng 2nd year.
3 On the day Rén Zǐ,
Wéi Sìlì, Shìláng of Tiānguān, was made Fènggé Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Tiānguān was
the Ministry of Personnel.
Sì,
read as Xiáng Lì.
4 Lǐ Jiǒngxiù, Shìláng of Xiàguān and Tóng Fènggé Luántái Sānpǐn, frequently accepted bribes.
Mǎ Huáisù, Jiānchá Yùshǐ, impeached him.
Xiàguān was
the Ministry of War.
Fènggé and Luántái were
the Central Secretariat and the Chancellery.
Jiǒng,
read as Hù Qǐng.
Jiān,
read as Gǔ Xián.
Hái,
read as Hù Gài,
also read as Hù Dé.
On the day Guǐ Hài,
Jiǒngxiù was demoted to Cìshǐ of Lúzhōu.
During the Suí dynasty, the Hézōu of Liáng and Zhōu was renamed Lúzhōu.
The Táng dynasty continued this.
According to old gazetteers: Lúzhōu was
2,387 *lǐ* southeast of the capital,
and 1,569 *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
5 On the day Rén Shēn,
Zhū Jìngzé, Zhèngjiàn Dàfū and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, retired due to old age and illness.
As prime minister, Jìngzé
prioritized the selection of personnel,
and paid no attention to other minor matters.
6 The Empress Dowager once discussed with the prime ministers about the Cìshǐ and Xiànlìng.
In the third month,
on the day Jǐ Chǒu,
Lǐ Qiáo, Táng Xiūjǐng, and others memorialized:
"We humbly observe that in the court and among the people, near and far,
no one fails to value internal officials
and despise external posts.
Whenever a governor is appointed,
they repeatedly plead against it.
Recently, those sent to external posts
are mostly demoted or implicated individuals;
the lack of clarity in customs
is truly due to this.
We hope that virtuous and capable individuals will be carefully selected from the ministries,
to govern the major prefectures,
and together improve public administration.
Your subjects request to withdraw from our close attendance
and set an example for the other officials."
The Empress Dowager ordered them to write down their names and drew lots,
obtaining Wéi Sìlì and Yáng Zàisī, Yùshǐ Dàfū, and eighteen others.
On the day Guǐ Sì,
an edict was issued appointing each to concurrently serve as Cìshǐ with their original official rank.
Sìlì became Cìshǐ of Biànzhōu.
According to old gazetteers: Biànzhōu was
1,350 *lǐ* east of the capital,
and 401 *lǐ* from the Eastern Capital.
Only Xuē Qiānguāng, Cìshǐ of Chángzhōu, and Sīmǎ Huáng, Cìshǐ of Xúzhōu, were exempt.
7 On the day Dīng Chǒu,
Píng'ēn Wáng Chóngfú was transferred to be Qiáo Wáng.
8 Zōng Chǔkè, Shìláng of Xiàguān, was made Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
9 Sū Wèidào, Fènggé Shìláng and Tóng Fènggé Luántái Sānpǐn, requested leave to return home and bury his father.
An edict ordered the prefectures and counties to provide for the funeral arrangements.
Wèidào was
a native of Luánchéng County, Zhàozhōu.
He overused corvée labor.
Xiāo Zhìzhōng, Jiānchá Yùshǐ, impeached him,
and he was demoted to Cìshǐ of Fángzhōu.
The former Emperor Yuán of Táng
was Cìshǐ of Fūzhōu during the Tiānhé reign of Zhōu,
and established horse stables in Zhōngbù County.
In the 2nd year of Wǔdé of Emperor Gāozǔ,
Fángzhōu was established by dividing Zhōngbù and Fūchéng from Fūzhōu.
He was a great-grandson of Yǐn.
See Xiāo Yǐn in Volume 170, Chén Xuāndì, Tàijiàn 2nd year.
Jiān,
read as Gǔ Xián.
Hái,
read as Hù Gài,
also read as Hù Dé.
10 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Rén Xū,
Wéi Ānshí, Tóng Fènggé Luántái Sānpǐn, was made Zhī Nàyán,
and Lǐ Qiáo was made Zhī Nèishǐ Shì.
11 The Empress Dowager visited Xīngtài Palace.
12 The Empress Dowager again taxed all monks and nuns in the realm
to create a great statue at Báisīmǎ Bǎn,
ordering Wǔ Yōuníng, Chūnguān Shàngshū, to supervise the work.
The expenses were enormous.
Lǐ Qiáo submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Among the registered households in the realm,
the poor and weak are numerous.
There are currently over 170,000 strings of cash for statue making.
If this were to be distributed,
giving one thousand to each person,
it would aid over 170,000 households.
This would alleviate the hardships of hunger and cold,
reduce the toil of corvée labor,
conform to the compassionate hearts of all Buddhas,
and embody the nurturing intent of the sacred ruler.
Both humans and gods would be pleased,
and the merits would be boundless.
How can future karmic connections
compare to present rewards?"
Zhāng Tíngguī, Jiānchá Yùshǐ, submitted a memorial remonstrating:
"Your subject, in discussing current policies,
believes that the borders should be prioritized,
treasuries accumulated,
and manpower nurtured;
in discussing Buddhist teachings,
relief from suffering should be prioritized,
all phenomena eliminated,
and non-action upheld.
I humbly wish that Your Majesty would discern your subject's foolishness,
act according to the Buddha's intent,
prioritize reason,
and not reject words because of the person."
The Empress Dowager consequently ceased the project,
and moreover summoned Tíngguī,
greatly commending and comforting him.
13 Yáo Yuánchóng, Fènggé Shìláng and Tóng Fènggé Luántái Sānpǐn, firmly requested to return home to attend to his elderly mother.
In the sixth month,
on the day Xīn Yǒu,
Yuánchóng was made acting Zhǎngshǐ of Xiāng Wáng's residence,
with his rank and position remaining equivalent to Sānpǐn.
14 On the day Yǐ Chǒu,
Cuī Xuánwěi, Shìláng of Tiānguān, was made Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
15 Wéi Sìlì, Fènggé Shìláng, Tóng Píngzhāngshì, and concurrently Cìshǐ of Biànzhōu, was summoned to Xīngtài Palace.
16 On the day Dīng Chǒu,
Lǐ Qiáo was made Tóng Fènggé Luántái Sānpǐn.
Qiáo himself requested to be relieved from the post of Nèishǐ.
17 On the day Rén Wǔ,
Yáo Yuánchóng, Zhǎngshǐ of Xiāng Wáng's residence, was concurrently made Zhī Xiàguān Shàngshū and Tóng Fènggé Luántái Sānpǐn.
18 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Bǐng Xū,
Yáng Zàisī, when serving as a Chancellor,
focused entirely on flattery to gain favor.
Zhāng Tóngxiū, the Palace Secretary of the Bureau of Rites,
who was the elder brother of Yìzhī,
once summoned high-ranking officials for a feast.
When the wine was flowing freely,
he playfully said to Zàisī:
"Minister Yáng's face resembles a Gāolí person."
Zàisī was delighted,
immediately cut paper and pasted it on his headscarf,
wore his purple robe inside out,
and performed the Gāolí dance.
The Táng dynasty's ten musical ensembles included Gāolí performers,
with four dancers;
Yáng Zàisī probably emulated them to perform this dance.
At that time, some people praised Zhāng Chāngzōng's beauty
saying:
"Sixth Master's face resembles a lotus flower."
Zàisī alone said:
"Not so."
Chāngzōng asked him why,
and Zàisī replied:
"Rather, the lotus flower resembles Sixth Master."
On the 19th jiǎwǔ day,
the Empress Dowager returned to the palace.
On the 20th yǐwèi day,

Zhāng Tóngxiū, the Palace Secretary of the Bureau of Rites, Zhāng Chāngqī, the Prefect of Biànzhōu, and Zhāng Chāngyí, the Junior Supervisor of the Imperial Workshops, were all imprisoned on charges of embezzlement.
Orders were given for the Left and Right Censorates to jointly interrogate them;
On the bǐngshēn day,
an imperial edict stated
that Zhāng Yìzhī and
Zhāng Chāngzōng, who had been abusing their power,
should also be jointly interrogated.
On the xīnchǒu day,
Jiǎ Jìngyán, the Judicial Reviewer of the Court of Judicial Review, reported:
"Zhāng Chāngzōng forcibly purchased a commoner's land."
Guāngzhái era changed Dàlǐ Zhèng (Judicial Reviewer of the Court of Judicial Review) to Sīxíng Zhèng,
a fifth-rank official,
in charge of participating in discussions on criminal cases and reviewing legal codes.
An imperial decree said:
"Approved."
On the yǐsì day,
Lǐ Chéngjiā, the Grandee Secretary, and Huán Yànfàn, the Censor-in-chief, reported:
"Zhāng Tóngxiū's brothers embezzled a total of over four thousand strings of cash,
and Zhāng Chāngzōng should, by law, be dismissed from office."
Chāngzōng reported:
"I have rendered service to the state;
my offense does not warrant dismissal."
The Empress Dowager asked the Chancellors:
"Has Chāngzōng rendered service?"
Yáng Zàisī said:
"Chāngzōng compounded a divine elixir,
which Her Majesty found effective when taken;
this is a service of the highest order."
The Empress Dowager was pleased,
pardoned Chāngzōng's crime,
and restored him to his office.
Dài Lìngyán, a Left Remonstrance Official, wrote the "Ode to the Two-Legged Fox" to satirize Zàisī,
implying that Zàisī was as cunning and seductive as a fox,
only with two legs.
On the 21st bǐngwǔ day,
Zōng Chǔkè, the Vice-Minister of the Ministry of War and a Grand Chancellor, was found guilty,
demoted to Governor of Yuánzhōu,
and appointed Commander-in-chief of the Língwǔ Dao Expeditionary Army.
On the 22nd guǐchǒu day,
Zhāng Tóngxiū was demoted to Assistant Magistrate of Qíshān.
The Later Wèi dynasty divided the Fúfēng Yōng County to establish Píngqín Commandery.
The Western Wèi dynasty changed it to Qíshān Commandery.
The Suí dynasty abolished the commandery and made it a county,
subordinate to Qízhōu.
Wéi Ānshí, the Vice-Minister of the Bureau of Palace Affairs, Director of the Palace Secretariat, and Chancellor of the Third Rank, impeached Zhāng Yìzhī and others for their crimes.
An imperial edict ordered Ānshí and Táng Xiūjǐng, the Right Senior Tutor and Chancellor of the Third Rank, to interrogate them.
The matter was not concluded when events changed.
In the eighth month,
on the jiǎyín day,
Ānshí was concurrently appointed acting Prefect of Yángzhōu.
The "Kǎoyì" notes: The Táng chronicle states
"the 5th day, wùwǔ."
We follow the factual record here.
On the gēngshēn day,
Xiūjǐng was concurrently appointed Governor of Yōuyíng and Protector-General of Āndōng.
As Xiūjǐng was about to depart,
he secretly said to the Crown Prince:
"The two Zhāngs, relying on imperial favor, are disloyal and rebellious;
they will certainly cause trouble.
Your Highness should be prepared."
On the 23rd, Yáo Yuánchóng, the Chief Administrator of the Prince of Xiāng's Household and concurrently Director of the Ministry of War, and Chancellor of the Third Rank, submitted a memorial:
"I serve the Prince of Xiāng;
it is inappropriate for me to manage military affairs.
Xiàguān (Ministry of War) is the Ministry of Military Affairs,
hence this statement.
Xiāng is pronounced xìliàng.
I fear it would not benefit the Prince."
On the xīnyǒu day,
he was reassigned as Minister of the Ministry of Rites,
with other duties remaining unchanged.
Yuánchóng's courtesy name was Yuánzhī.
At that time, the Turkic chieftain Chìliè Yuánchóng rebelled,
and the Empress Dowager ordered Yuánchóng to use his courtesy name (as his official name).
On the 24th, after the Turkic Mòchuò had established friendly relations,
on the wùyín day,
the Prince of Huáiyáng, Wǔ Yánxiù, was finally sent back.
Wǔ Yánxiù's detention is mentioned in Volume 245, Shènglì 1st year.
On the 25th, in the ninth month,
on the rénzǐ day,
Yáo Yuánzhī was appointed Commander-in-chief of the Língwǔ Dao Expeditionary Army;
On the xīnyǒu day,
Yuánzhī was appointed Pacification Commissioner of the Língwǔ Dao.
As Yuánzhī was about to depart,
the Empress Dowager ordered him to recommend officials from the outer court suitable for Chancellorship.
Outer court (wàisī)
refers to officials of various ministries in the outer court.
"Zhāng Jiǎnzhī is profound and resourceful,
capable of making important decisions,
and moreover, he is already old;
Your Majesty should employ him urgently."
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the jiǎxū day,
Zhāng Jiǎnzhī, the Vice-Minister of the Ministry of Justice, was appointed Grand Chancellor.
He was nearly eighty years old at the time.
On the 26th yǐhài day,
Wéi Sìlì was appointed acting Prefect of Wèizhōu,
with other duties remaining unchanged.
On the 27th rénwǔ day,
Fáng Róng of Hénán, the Chief Administrator of Huáizhōu, was appointed Grand Chancellor.
On the 28th, the Empress Dowager ordered each Chancellor to recommend candidates for Member of the Secretariat of a Board (Yuánwàiláng).
Wéi Sìlì recommended Cén Xī,
the Duke of Guǎngwǔ, saying:
"My only regret is that his uncle, Chángqiàn, is a burden."
Chángqiàn's death is mentioned in Volume 244, Tiānshòu 2nd year.
Lèi is pronounced lìruì;
same below.
"If one truly possesses talent,
what kind of burden could this be!"
So, he was appointed Member of the Secretariat of the Ministry of Personnel.
The "Táng Liù Diǎn" states: The Zhōu official system had "shàngshì" among the subordinates of the Grand Tutor,
which is likely the role of today's Yuánwàiláng.
The Sòng dynasty's official ranks included Yuánwàiláng,
which was considered a good promotion to Shàngshūláng.
In the 6th year of Kāihuáng (586 AD) under Emperor Wén of the Suí dynasty,
the twenty-four bureaus of the Ministry of Personnel
each had one Yuánwàiláng,
a rank of junior sixth grade,
meaning it was an additional official (láng) beyond the principal staff of the bureau.
In the 3rd year of Dàyè (607 AD) under Emperor Yáng,
the Yuánwàilángs of the twenty-four bureaus were abolished,
with one official reduced from each bureau,
and one Chéngwùláng was established,
with the same duties as the Kāihuáng era's Yuánwàiláng,
known as Xuǎnbù Chéngwùláng.
The Táng dynasty's various bureaus of the Ministry of Personnel each had a Yuánwàiláng,
with the Ministry of Personnel having two.
Tiānguān
is the Ministry of Personnel.
On the 29th, in the eleventh month,
on the dīnghài day,
Wéi Chéngqìng, the Vice-Minister of the Ministry of Personnel, was appointed Vice-Minister of the Bureau of Palace Affairs and Grand Chancellor.
On the 30th guǐmǎo day,
Lǐ Qiáo, the Libationer of the Directorate of Education and Chancellor of the Third Rank, was dismissed and appointed Minister of the Ministry of Land.
On the 31st, in the twelfth month,
on the jiǎyín day,
an edict ordered the abolition of all newly established offices since Dàzú era.
On the 32nd bǐngchén day,
Wéi Sìlì, the Vice-Minister of the Bureau of Palace Affairs and Grand Chancellor, was dismissed and appointed Libationer of the Directorate of Education,
with his position as acting Prefect of Wèizhōu remaining unchanged;
this was because his elder brother, Chéngqìng, had entered the Chancellery.
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) was gravely ill,
residing in the Chángshēng Yuàn.
Chángshēng Yuàn
was the Chángshēng Diàn.
The following year, the Five Princes (Wǔ Wáng) executed the two Zhāngs (Èr Zhāng),
advancing to the Chángshēng Diàn where the Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) was sleeping.
This is the same place.
Generally, all sleeping palaces in the Táng dynasty were called Chángshēng Diàn.
This Chángshēng Diàn, where Empress Wǔ (Wǔ Hòu) was gravely ill,
was a sleeping palace in the Luòyáng Palace (Luòyáng Gōng).
When Emperor Sùzōng (Sùzōng) was critically ill,
Prince Yuè (Yuè Wáng) was granted a guard with armor in the Chángshēng Diàn;
this was a sleeping palace in the Dàmíng Palace (Dàmíng Gōng) in Cháng'ān.
What Bái Jūyì (Bái Jūyì) referred to in his "Song of Everlasting Regret" (Chánghèn Gē) as
"On the seventh day of the seventh month, in the Chángshēng Diàn,
in the middle of the night, when no one was around to overhear their private whispers,"
was the Chángshēng Diàn in the Huáqīng Palace (Huáqīng Gōng).
Only Zhāng Yìzhī (Zhāng Yìzhī) and Zhāng Chāngzōng (Zhāng Chāngzōng) attended her side.
When her illness slightly abated,
閒
is pronounced as written.
"[The] Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) and Prince Xiàng (Xiàng Wáng)
are benevolent, intelligent, filial, and friendly,
capable of attending to your medicine.
Palace matters are grave,
I humbly request that no outsiders be permitted to enter or exit."
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) said:
"Zhāng Déqīng (Zhāng Déqīng), your intentions are kind."
Yìzhī (Yìzhī) and Chāngzōng (Chāngzōng), seeing the Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) critically ill,
feared disaster would befall them.
They enlisted their partisans
and secretly prepared for it.
Repeatedly, people wrote anonymous letters and posted them on major thoroughfares,
saying,
"The Yìzhī (Yìzhī) brothers are plotting rebellion."
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) ignored all of them.
On the day Xīnwèi,
Yáng Yuánsì (Yáng Yuánsì) from Xǔzhōu
reported that
"Chāngzōng (Chāngzōng) once summoned the diviner Lǐ Hóngtài (Lǐ Hóngtài) to read his fortune.
Hóngtài (Hóngtài) said Chāngzōng (Chāngzōng) had the physiognomy of an emperor
and advised him to build a Buddhist temple in Dìngzhōu,
which would cause the people of the world to submit."
The "Examination of Discrepancies" (Kǎoyì) states: The "Veritable Records" (Shílù) say:
"In the autumn of the fourth year of Cháng'ān,
Yuánsì (Yuánsì) reported this,
and the Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) ordered Fènggé Shìláng Wéi Chéngqìng (Wéi Chéngqìng) to investigate."
According to the records, on the Dīnghài day of the eleventh month,
Chéngqìng (Chéngqìng) first became Fènggé Shìláng.
Now we follow the Táng Calendar (Tánglì).
Shénqìng (Shénqìng) was the brother of Shéngjī (Shéngjī).
Chéngqìng (Chéngqìng) and Shénqìng (Shénqìng) reported:
"Chāngzōng (Chāngzōng) admitted that 'Hóngtài's (Hóngtài) words were promptly reported to the throne,'
and according to the law, those who confess first are pardoned;
the law
pardons the crime of those who confess themselves.
Chéngqìng (Chéngqìng) and Shénqìng (Shénqìng) wished to use this clause to clear Chāngzōng (Chāngzōng) of his crime.
首
is also read as *shòu*.
We request that he be arrested and punished according to the law."
Sòng Jǐng (Sòng Jǐng) and Dàlǐchéng Fēng Quánzhēn (Fēng Quánzhēn) reported:
"Chāngzōng (Chāngzōng) enjoys such favor and honor,
yet he again summoned a diviner to read his fortune.
What more does he seek!
Hóngtài (Hóngtài) claimed to have divined 'pure qián' (chúnqián),
the hexagram of an emperor.
If Chāngzōng (Chāngzōng) considered Hóngtài (Hóngtài) to be a deceiver,
why did he not seize and hand him over to the authorities!
Although he claims to have reported it to the throne,
it ultimately concealed malicious intent,
and according to the law, he should be beheaded and his family property confiscated.
We request he be taken to prison
and his crime thoroughly investigated!"
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) did not respond for a long time.
Jǐng (Jǐng) then said:
"If he is not immediately arrested and detained,
I fear it will disturb the public mind."
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) said:
"You should halt the investigation for now."
"Halt the matter,
and do not investigate for now."
When Jǐng (Jǐng) withdrew,
Zuǒ Shíyí Lǐ Yōng (Lǐ Yōng) of Jiāngdū (Jiāngdū) stepped forward and said:
Jiāngdū county was part of Yángzhōu.
"I just observed Sòng Jǐng's (Sòng Jǐng) memorial;
his aspiration is to secure the state,
not to seek personal gain.
I beg Your Majesty to approve his memorial!"
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) did not listen.
Soon, she issued an edict for Jǐng (Jǐng) to investigate in Yángzhōu.
She also ordered Jǐng (Jǐng) to investigate the corruption of Yōuzhōu Dūdū Qūtú Zhòngxiáng (Qūtú Zhòngxiáng).
She further ordered Jǐng (Jǐng) to assist Lǐ Qiáo (Lǐ Qiáo) in pacifying Lǒng (Lǒng) and Shǔ (Shǔ).
Jǐng (Jǐng) refused to go on any of these missions,
memorializing:
"According to established practice,
if a provincial or county official commits a crime,
a high-ranking one is investigated by a Shìyùshǐ,
a low-ranking one by a Jiānchá Yùshǐ.
The Zhōngchéng should not be sent on missions unless they involve major military or state affairs.
Now, there is no unrest in Lǒng (Lǒng) and Shǔ (Shǔ);
I do not understand why Your Majesty sends me outside.
I dare not obey these commands."
The "Examination of Discrepancies" (Kǎoyì) states: The "Records of the Censorate" (Yùshǐtái Jì) say:
"Yìzhī (Yìzhī) and Chāngzōng (Chāngzōng) hoped that after Jǐng (Jǐng) left on his mission,
they could submit a memorial to have Jǐng (Jǐng) executed."
However, if Yìzhī (Yìzhī) and his cohorts could indeed memorialize for Jǐng's (Jǐng) execution,
then why would they have to wait until he left on a mission to do so!
This was likely because Jǐng (Jǐng) was then requesting the arrest and detention of Chāngzōng (Chāngzōng),
so the Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) wanted to send Jǐng (Jǐng) away to disperse the matter.
Jǐng (Jǐng) was insistent on the arrest and detention,
hence his refusal to go;
the Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) realized she was in the wrong,
hence she did not force him to go.
Otherwise,
if Jǐng (Jǐng) refused to go without cause,
how could the Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) not punish him for resisting her imperial command!
It also says:
"At that time, Jǐng's (Jǐng) family had a social gathering,
and Yìzhī (Yìzhī) and his group planned to assassinate him that evening.
Someone secretly warned Jǐng (Jǐng),
who escaped in a government carriage to another place and was spared."
However, if such an event truly occurred,
how could Jǐng (Jǐng) not report it to the Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu)!
If there was no such event,
then it was mere rumor.
This account is not accepted here.
Sīxíng Shǎoqīng Huán Yànfàn (Huán Yànfàn) submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Chāngzōng (Chāngzōng), without merit, enjoys great favor,
yet harbors malicious intentions
and brings calamity upon himself.
This is the wrath of Heaven descending;
if Your Majesty cannot bear to execute him,
it will be an inauspicious defiance of Heaven.
Furthermore, since Chāngzōng (Chāngzōng) claimed to have reported it,
he should not have continued his association with Hóngtài (Hóngtài),
allowing him to seek blessings and avert disaster.
This shows he had no remorse from the beginning.
The reason he reported it
was to claim prior disclosure if the matter came to light,
and if it did not, to await the opportune moment for rebellion.
This is a treacherous minister's cunning scheme.
If he can be pardoned,
then who is worthy of punishment!
Moreover, the matter has already been brought up twice,
and Your Majesty has pardoned him each time without inquiry,
causing Chāngzōng (Chāngzōng) to become increasingly conceited and believe his plan successful,
and the world also believes he is destined not to die.
This is Your Majesty fostering his rebellion.
If this rebellious minister is not executed,
the state will perish.
I request that the case be handed over to the Luántái, Fènggé, and Three Judicial Departments (Sān Sī)
for a thorough investigation and judgment of his crime!"
The Three Judicial Departments (Sān Sī)
refer to the Shàngshū Xíngbù, Dàlǐ Sì, and Yùshǐtái.
According to the Táng system,
for major cases, the Dà Sān Sī were summoned for investigation and judgment,
and the Zhōngshū and Ménxià were also ordered to participate in the inquiry.
There was no reply.
Cuī Xuánwěi also repeatedly spoke about it.
The Empress Dowager ordered the judicial authorities to deliberate on his crime.
Xuánwěi's younger brother, the Judicial Minor Prefect Cuī Biàn,
sentenced him to capital punishment.
Sòng Jǐng again memorialized to have Zhāng Chāngzōng arrested and imprisoned.
The Empress Dowager said:
"Chāngzōng has already personally memorialized this."
He replied:
"Chāngzōng was pressed by anonymous accusations,
and in desperation, he reported himself,
forced by circumstances.
Moreover, for rebellion and high treason,
there is no allowance for initial confession to grant immunity.
If Chāngzōng is not subjected to severe punishment,
what good are the national laws!"
The Empress Dowager gently tried to mollify him.
Jǐng's voice and demeanor became even more severe, saying:
"Chāngzōng has received extraordinary favor,
and I know that speaking out will bring disaster,
but righteousness stirs within my heart,
and I will have no regrets even if I die!"
Yáng Zàisī, fearing that he would offend the Empress Dowager's will,
hastily announced the imperial decree for him to leave.
Jǐng said:
"The Holy Ruler is here,
there is no need for the Chancellor to rashly announce imperial decrees!"
The Empress Dowager then approved his memorial,
and sent Chāngzōng to the Censorate.
Jǐng stood in the court and interrogated him;
before the matter was concluded,
the Empress Dowager sent a palace envoy to summon Chāngzōng and specially pardoned him by imperial decree.
Jǐng sighed and said:
"If I don't first smash that little fellow's head open,
I will forever carry this regret."
The Empress Dowager then ordered Chāngzōng to go to Jǐng to apologize,
but Jǐng refused to see him.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Yùshǐ Táijì*, *Tánglì*, and *Jiùzhuàn* all state
"arrested and interrogated Yìzhī and others."
However, Jǐng only interrogated Chāngzōng about the matter of physiognomy;
there was no reason to involve Yìzhī.
Therefore, this is not adopted now.
The *Jiù Zhāng Yìzhī Zhuàn* says:
"Sòng Jǐng requested to interrogate Yìzhī,
Zétiān seemingly agreed,
then soon issued an imperial decree for Sòng Jǐng to go to Yōuzhōu to interrogate the Governor Qūtú Zhòngxiáng;
and ordered the Minister of Rites, Cuī Shénqìng, to comply with her will,
to exonerate the Chāngzōng brothers."
The *Tánglì* says,
"Huán Yànfàn submitted a memorial but it was not accepted,
and Jǐng was immediately dispatched on a mission."
However, Jǐng's biography says:
"A special decree pardoned Yìzhī,
and he was still ordered to go to Jǐng to apologize."
This means that when Chāngzōng was pardoned by imperial decree,
Jǐng was in the capital,
and was not dispatched on a mission.
The *Shílù* says
"ordered Wéi Chéngqìng and Cuī Shénqìng to investigate and interrogate with Jǐng,"
which must mean that Jǐng upheld the correctness of his crime while Shénqìng leniently treated it,
not that Shénqìng only began to interrogate him after Jǐng had been dispatched on a mission.
The *Jiù Sòng Jǐng* and *Yìzhī Zhuàn* contradict each other.
We now follow the *Yùshǐ Táijì*.
The Left Censor-in-chief, Huán Yànfàn, and the Right Censor-in-chief, Yuán Shùjǐ of Dōngguāng, together recommended Yáng Jiào, a Director in the Palace Administration, to be a Censor.
In Guāngzhái, the Left and Right Censorates were established,
each with a Grandee, Censor-in-chief, and Supervising Censor.
Dōngguāng County,
in the Han dynasty, belonged to Bóhǎi Commandery;
in the Tang dynasty, it belonged to Cāngzhōu.
The Director in the Palace Administration held a rank of principal ninth grade, upper,
responsible for impeaching palace officials

"What if Jiào is not fond of aggressive duties?"
Yànfàn said:
"When selecting people for office,
why must we wait for what they desire!
For what they do not desire,
it is even more necessary to give it to them,
in order to foster the tradition of taking on difficult tasks,

So, he was promoted to Supervising Censor of the Right Censorate.
Jiào was
the great-great-grandson of Yáng Xiūzhī.
Yáng Xiūzhī served in Gāo Qí and achieved high prominence.
Previously, Lǐ Qiáo and Cuī Xuánwěi memorialized:

many people were rebellious,

The Judicial Minor Prefect Huán Yànfàn also memorialized on this matter,
submitting ten memorials both before and after.
The Empress Dowager then agreed.
Zhōngzōng Dàhé Dàshèng Dàzhāoxiào Huángdì's personal name

He was later renamed Zhé,

In the first year of Jǐngyún (710),

he was posthumously honored as Dàhé Dàshèng Huángdì.
In the thirteenth year (754),
he was posthumously honored as Dàhé Dàshèng Dàzhāoxiào Huángdì.

The "Kǎo Yì" (Textual Differences) states: The old biography of Lǐ Zhàn says:

According to Liú Zǐxuán's "Zhōngzōng Shílù", "Táng Lì", and "Tǒng Jì", all attribute this to Wáng Tóngjiǎo's words,

Lǐ Zhàn

Outwardly, this does not diminish the honor and favor shown to meritorious officials,
but inwardly, it truly strips them of power."
The Emperor considered this to be true.
On the day of jiǎwǔ,
Shìzhōng Qí Gōng Jìng Huī was made Píngyáng Wáng,
Huán
Yànfàn as Fúyáng Wáng,
Zhōngshū Lìng Hànyáng Gōng Zhāng Jiǎnboshī as Hànyáng Wáng,
Nányáng Gōng Yuán Shùjǐ as Nányáng Wáng,
Tèjìn, Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn Bólíng Gōng Cuī Xuánwěi as Bólíng Wáng.
Kǎoyì says: Tǒngjì says:
"The Empress Dowager was skilled at adorning herself,
so even with her grandchildren by her side, her age was not apparent.
However, when she was in Shàngyáng Gōng,
she no longer combed her hair or washed her face, and her appearance was haggard and emaciated.
When the Emperor entered to see her,
he was greatly alarmed.
The Empress Dowager wept, saying:
'I welcomed you from Fánglíng,
and indeed entrusted the realm to you,
but the five bandits, greedy for merit,
have frightened me to this state.'
The Emperor wept uncontrollably,
prostrated himself, and begged forgiveness for his grave sins.
From this, Sānsī and others were able to carry out their scheme."
However, Zhōngzōng was dull, vulgar, and unkind.
Even if the Empress Dowager disfigured herself and wept,
it would not necessarily move his heart.
The reason he distanced himself from and suspected the five kings
was simply that he heeded the words of Empress Wéi and Sānsī.
Therefore, this account is not adopted.
The relative ranks of the five kings
are not consistently ordered.
The Shílù states
that when Zhāng Yìzhī was executed, Zhāng Jiǎnboshī was the leader.
When iron certificates were bestowed, Cuī Xuánwěi was the leader.
When they were enfeoffed as kings and later demoted to Sīmǎ or exiled, Jìng Huī was always the leader.
Old accounts and the edict restoring their offices during Kāiyuán both list Huán Yànfàn as the leader.
According to the fourth year of Cháng'ān,
in the sixth month,
Xuánwěi was Luántái Shìláng and Píngzhāngshì.
In the tenth month,
Zhāng Jiǎnboshī, formerly Qīuguān Shìláng, was Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
In the eleventh month,
he served as Fènggé Shìláng.
At the time of Yìzhī's execution,
only these two were prime ministers.
In the first month of the first year of Shénlóng,
Yuán Shùjǐ, formerly Sīxíng Shǎoqīng, became Fènggé Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
On the day of gēngxū,
Zhāng Jiǎnboshī was Xiàguān Shàngshū,
Xuánwěi served as Nèishǐ,
Jìng Huī and Huán Yànfàn both became Nàyán.
In the third month,
Shùjǐ served as Zhōngshū Lìng.
In the fourth month,
Jiǎnboshī became Zhōngshū Lìng,
Jìng Huī became Shìzhōng.
The promotions of the five kings followed this sequence.
It is suspected that the Shílù merely considered Jiǎnboshī the leader because he was the mastermind of Yìzhī's execution.
Huī and Yànfàn were both Shìzhōng.
It is suspected that Shìzhōng ranked above Zhōngshū Lìng,
hence when the memorials to remove the Wǔ clan and to dismiss them from political duties were made, Huī was listed as the leader.
When the iron certificates were bestowed,
Xuánwěi had already been granted Tèjìn.
Huī and others were granted Tèjìn only when they were dismissed from their political duties,
while Xuánwěi remained as before.
It is suspected that although Tèjìn was a nominal rank, its official grade was the highest,
hence Xuánwěi was listed as the leader.
Yànfàn and Huī were both Shìzhōng,
but Yànfàn suffered the most severe calamity.
It is suspected that the Kāiyuán edict and the historians specifically listed him as the leader,
not necessarily according to their actual rank at the time.
During the reigns of Tiānhòu and Zhōngzōng,
Shìzhōng was suspected to rank above Zhōngshū Lìng.
They were bestowed with gold, silk, saddles, and horses,
and ordered to attend court on the first and fifteenth day of each month.
Additionally, Yànfàn was granted the surname Wéi,
sharing the same clan as the Empress.
Soon after, Xuánwěi was again appointed Jiǎnxiào Yìzhōu Zhǎngshǐ, and entrusted with the duties of the Dūdū.
Later, he was changed to Liángzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yìzhōu was 2,379 lǐ southwest of the capital,
and 3,216 lǐ from Dōngdū.
Liángzhōu was 1,223 lǐ from the capital,
and 2,078 lǐ from Dōngdū.
Those who were not allied with the Wǔ clan were removed,
and those who had been expelled by the five kings were reinstated.
All major power ultimately reverted to Sānsī.
The five princes requested the reduction of the fiefdoms of the Wǔ clan's princes,
and sought someone to draft a memorial.
No one in the assembly was willing to do it.
Cén Xī, a Shě Rén of the Central Secretariat, drafted it,
and the language was very strong and passionate.
Bì Gòu of Yǎnshī, a Shě Rén of the Central Secretariat, whose turn it was to read the memorial,
spoke with a clear and stern countenance.
After Wǔ Sānsī gained power,
Cén Xī was demoted to Bìshū Shǎojiān,
and Bì Gòu was sent out as the Cìshǐ of Rùnzhōu.
Rùnzhōu is
2,821 *lǐ* southeast of the capital,
and 1,797 *lǐ* from the eastern capital.
Zhào Lǚwēn, Cìshǐ of Yìzhōu,
was the elder brother of Huán Yànfàn's wife.
When Huán Yànfàn executed the two Zhāng brothers,
he claimed Zhào Lǚwēn was involved in the conspiracy,
and summoned him to be Sīnóng Shǎoqīng.
Zhào Lǚwēn gave two maidservants to Huán Yànfàn.
When Huán Yànfàn was dismissed from his government duties,
Zhào Lǚwēn took back the maidservants.
The Emperor commended Sòng Jǐng's loyalty and uprightness,
and repeatedly promoted him to Huángmén Shìláng.
Wǔ Sānsī once entrusted Sòng Jǐng with a matter,
but Sòng Jǐng sternly refused him, saying:
"Now that the Empress Dowager has restored her son to rule,
Your Highness should retire to your residence as a marquis.
How can you still interfere with court affairs?
Do you not recall the affair of Zhāng Yīzhī and Zhāng Chāngzōng?!"
On the 27th, Wéi Ānshí was appointed concurrent Jiǎnxiào Zhōngshūlìng,
Wèi Yuánzhōng concurrent Jiǎnxiào Shìzhōng.
Lǐ Zhàn was also appointed Yòu Sànqí Chángshì,
Zhào Chéng'ēn as Guānglù Qīng,
and Yáng Yuányǎn as Wèiwèi Qīng.
Earlier,
Yáng Yuányǎn, realizing that Wǔ Sānsī was increasingly influential,
requested to resign from office and become a monk,
but the Emperor refused.
Jìng Huī heard of it
and laughed, saying:
"If I had known earlier,
I would have advised the Emperor to permit it,
to shave off his barbarian head!
Wouldn't that be wonderful?!"
Yáng Yuányǎn had a thick beard, resembling a barbarian,
hence Jìng Huī's jest.
Yáng Yuányǎn said:
"Once achievements are made and fame attained,
not to withdraw will lead to danger.
This was truly a heartfelt request."
"Zhōng" (衷)
means sincerity.
"Yóuzhōng" (由衷)
means words spoken from a sincere heart.
Jìng Huī understood his meaning
and was startled and displeased.
When Jìng Huī and others incurred punishment,
Yáng Yuányǎn alone was spared.
On the 28th, Shàngguān Jiéyú advised Empress Wéi to follow Empress Wǔ Zétiān's precedent,
memorializing to request that gentlemen and commoners throughout the realm observe three years of mourning for their birth mother.
She also requested that commoners be registered as *dīng* at age twenty-three
and exempted from corvée at fifty-nine.
According to the Táng system,
one became a *dīng* at twenty-one
and was considered old at sixty.
Imperial edicts granted all these requests.
On the 29th, *Guǐmǎo*,
an edict was issued
degrading the Wǔ princes.
Wǔ Sānsī, Prince of Liáng, was enfeoffed as Prince of Déjìng;
Wǔ Yōujì, Prince of Dìng, was enfeoffed as Prince of Lèshòu.
Both were demoted to county princes.
Déjìng County belonged to Xiàzhōu;
Lèshòu County belonged to Shēnzhōu.
This was to satisfy the public.
On the 30th, *Jiǎchén*,
Táng Xiūjǐng was appointed Zuǒ Púshè,
retaining his concurrent title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
Dòulú Qīnwàng was appointed Yòu Púshè.
In the 31st, sixth month,
*Rénzǐ*,
Péi Sīshuō, Grand General of the Left Xiāowèi, was appointed Grand Commander of the Língwǔ Army,
in preparation against the Turks.
On the 32nd, *Guǐhài*,
an imperial order was issued to Yòu Púshè Dòulú Qīnwàng:
for important military and state affairs,
the Zhongshusheng and Menxiasheng should deliberate together.
Previously,
the Púshè was a chief chancellor,
but later often concurrently held positions in the Zhongshusheng and Menxiasheng.
They would handle court affairs in the morning
and provincial matters in the afternoon.
"Provincial matters"
referred to matters of the Shangshusheng.
Dòulú Qīnwàng was solely a Púshè
and dared not involve himself in state affairs,
hence this imperial order.
Thereafter, those appointed solely as Púshè
no longer served as chancellors.
Wéi Ānshí was also appointed Zhōngshūlìng,
Wèi Yuánzhōng as Shìzhōng,
and Yáng Zàisī as Jiǎnxiào Zhōngshūlìng.
On the 33rd, *Dīngmǎo*,
Emperor Xiàojìng was enshrined in the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
and given the temple name Yìzōng.
The former Crown Prince Hóng, posthumously titled Emperor Xiàojìng,
was the Emperor's elder brother.
On the 34th, *Wùchén*,
the Luò River overflowed,
affecting over two thousand households.
In the 35th, autumn,
seventh month,
*Xīnsì*,
Wéi Jùyuán, Tutor to the Crown Prince, was appointed Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn,
retaining his post as Resident Administrator of the Western Capital.
On the 36th, Tèjìn Hányáng Wáng Zhāng Jiǎnzhī memorialized to request permission to return to Xiāngzhōu to recuperate from illness.
On *Yǐwèi*,
Zhāng Jiǎnzhī was appointed Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu,
not overseeing provincial affairs,
but granted full salary.
According to the Táng system,
Tèjìn was a rank 2a official,
and a Commandery Prince was rank 1b.
Those of rank 1b were given the salary of rank 1a:
a monthly salary of 8,000 (cash),
food allowance of 1,800,
and miscellaneous expenses of 1,200.
A Cìshǐ of a superior prefecture was rank 3b,
with a monthly salary of 5,100,
and miscellaneous expenses of 900.
The 37th, Henan and Hebei seventeen prefectures experienced great floods.
In the eighth month,
*Wùshēn*,
an edict sought frank advice due to the floods.
Sòng Wùguāng of Xīhé, a Cānjūn of the Right Wèi Qí Cáo, submitted a memorial.
In the Táng system, the Wèi prefectures had four Cānjūn offices: Cāng, Bīng, Qí, and Zhòu.
The Qí Cáo Cānjūn was responsible for the accounts and rearing of miscellaneous domestic and foreign animals.
All prefectural horses on duty
were divided into seven shifts by distance,
changed monthly,
and supplied to those leaving the imperial city by imperial decree.
Xīhé County belonged to Fénzhōu.
Qí (騎)
is pronounced *qíjì* (奇寄).
Shàng (上)
is pronounced *shízhǎng* (時掌).
Shū (疏)
is pronounced *suǒqù* (所去).
"Water is of the *yīn* category,
an omen of servants and concubines.
I fear there are those in the inner court interfering with outer court governance;
their sprouts should be utterly cut off.
Now the continuous rain does not stop,
yet the neighborhood gates are closed to avert it,
leading the common people to call the neighborhood gates 'chancellors,'
meaning the court uses them to regulate *yīn* and *yáng*.
Sòng Bái said: 'According to Táng regulations,
during prolonged rain, the northern gates of the wards and markets were closed to pray for clear weather.'
The Crown Prince is the root of the nation;
a virtuous and capable person should be chosen and established early.
Moreover,
the imperial relatives are too powerful, such as Wǔ Sānsī and others;
their crucial positions should be relieved,
and they should be generously endowed with stipends.
Furthermore,
Zhèng Pǔsī and Yè Jìngnéng, by petty skills, have usurped high positions;
they are also parasites of court governance."
The memorial was submitted,
but not heeded.
On the 38th, *Rénxū*,
Lady Zhào was posthumously granted the title Empress Gōng.
(The death of Lady Zhào is mentioned in volume 202, Gāozōng Shàngyuán 2nd year.)
The "Record of Discrepancies" states: "The old basic annals say
'*Jiǎzǐ*,'
but now follows the Veritable Records."
In the 39th, ninth month,
*Rénwǔ*,
the Emperor sacrificed to Hào Tiān Shàngdì and Huáng Dìqí at the Míngtáng,
with Gāozōng as co-sacrificer.
40 Initially,
the Emperor was in Fánglíng,
and the restrictions imposed by the provincial authorities were very severe.
The Prefects, Zhāng Zhījiǎn of Hédōng and Cuī Jìngsì of Língchāng,
Hédōng,
was formerly Púbǎn.
It commanded Hédōng Commandery.
The Suí dynasty abolished the commandery
and renamed Púbǎn as Hédōng County.
The Táng dynasty followed this
and it commanded Púzhōu.
The Suí dynasty divided Suānzǎo County
to establish Língchāng County,
named after the river ford.
Under the Táng, it belonged to Huázhōu.
Jiǎn,
pronounced Jiǔniǎn.
provided ample supplies.
The Emperor appreciated this,
and promoted Zhāng Zhījiǎn from Prefect of Bèizhōu to General of the Left Guard,
bestowing upon him the title of Fànyáng Gōng.
Cuī Jìngsì had already died,
so his son Wāng was sought out.
As he was addicted to alcohol
and unfit for official duties,
he was appointed to a Fifth-rank sinecure.
According to the Táng Liùdiǎn,
Emperor Suí Yángdì established the title of Cháoqǐng Dàfū as a 正五品 (zhèng wǔ pǐn) sinecure.
Emperor Suí Wéndì established the title of Cháosàn Dàfū as a 正四品 (zhèng sì pǐn) sinecure;
Emperor Yángdì changed it to 從五品下 (cóng wǔ pǐn xià).
41 The burial of Wéi Xuánzhēn, Prince of Shàngluò, was changed,
and all the ceremonies followed the precedents set for the Prince of Tàiyuán.
Wǔ Shìhuò was enfeoffed as Prince of Tàiyuán.
42 On Guǐsì,
Wéi Jùyuán, Prince's Retainer and concurrently Third-Rank Official in the Central Secretariat and Chancellery, was dismissed as Minister of Rites,
because his paternal cousin Ānshí had become Chief Minister.
43 Jì Chùnà, General of the Left Guard and from Shàngguī, was concurrently made acting Grand Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud,
because Chùnà had married the elder sister of Wǔ Sānsī's wife.
44 In winter,
in the tenth month,
Táng Xiūjǐng was ordered to remain as acting defender of the capital.
45 On Guǐhài,
the Emperor visited Lóngmén;
on Yǐchǒu,
he hunted in Xīn'ān and returned.
46 On Xīnwèi,
Wèi Yuánzhōng was made Chief Minister,
and Yáng Zàisī was made Attendant Counselor.
47 In the eleventh month,
on Wùyín,
the assembled ministers conferred upon the Emperor the honorific title Yìngtiān Huángdì,
and upon the Empress the title Shùntiān Huánghòu.
On Rénwǔ,
the Emperor and Empress
paid respects and offered thanks at the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
and a general amnesty was declared throughout the empire;
Xiāngwáng and Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ had their actual stipends increased,
both reaching ten thousand households.
48 On Jǐchǒu,
the Emperor ascended the Southern Tower of Luòchéng.
Southwest of Luòyáng's imperial city was the Luòchéng Gate,
and inside the gate was the Luòchéng Hall.
The "Splashing Cold Barbarian Play" was also known as the "Begging Cold Barbarian Play,"
originally from the Western Regions of the barbarians, Kāngguó.
In the eleventh month, they would beat drums and dance to beg for cold,
taking pleasure in splashing water on each other.
This practice only began in the last month of winter at the end of Empress Wǔ's reign.
The Emperor said,
"If one plans for the season, the cold will come as desired.
Qīngyuán County belonged to Bīngzhōu.
The Suí dynasty established it at the site of the ancient Gěngyáng City,
naming it after water.
The Book of Great Plan says: 'Plan for the season, and the cold will come as desired.'
The commentary says: 'If the ruler can plan, then the seasonal cold will obey it.'
Ruò
means 'to obey.'
Shàng,
pronounced Shícháng.
Shū,
pronounced Suǒqù.
Beat drums and dance in the streets to seek it!"
The memorial was submitted
but not accepted.
49 On Rén'yín,
Zétiān passed away in the Shàngyáng Palace,
at the age of eighty-two.
Her dying injunction stipulated:
"Remove the imperial title,
and be referred to as Zétiān Dàshèng Huánghòu.
The clans of Wáng and Xiāo, and the relatives of Chǔ Suìliáng, Hán Yuàn, and Liǔ Shì are all pardoned."
When Empress Wǔ was enthroned,
Empress Wáng and Xiāo Shúfēi were deposed and confined,
and did not die a natural death.
Chǔ Suìliáng and Hán Yuàn died for their remonstrances.
Liǔ Shì died as a relative of Empress Wáng,
and all their relatives were exiled.
While the Emperor was in mourning,
Wèi Yuánzhōng temporarily took charge of the prime minister's duties for three days.
Yuánzhōng had always enjoyed a reputation for loyalty and uprightness,
and the court and common people relied on him;
Wǔ Sānsī feared him,
and so, forging the Empress Dowager's dying will,
he consoled Yuánzhōng
and bestowed upon him an actual stipend of one hundred households.
Yuánzhōng received the edict,
choked with emotion and wept,
and those who saw it said:
"The matter is settled!"
knowing that he would no longer dare to debate the affairs of the Wǔ clan.
In the twelfth month,
on Dīngmǎo,
the Emperor first held audience with his ministers in the Tóngmíng Palace.
50 When the Empress Dowager was to be interred with the Emperor at Qiánlíng,
Yán Shànsī, Grand Master of Remonstrance, submitted a memorial,
arguing:
"The Xuan Palace of Qiánlíng has a stone gate,
its seams sealed with iron.
To open this gate now
would require carving and chiseling.
The way of the spirits
values subtlety and profound mystery.
Mobilizing the masses to exert effort
may cause great disturbance and irreverence.
Moreover, joint burial is not an ancient practice;
among the imperial tombs of the Hàn dynasty,
empresses were often not buried together.
It was only from the Wèi and Jìn dynasties onwards
that some began to be interred together.
I hope that a propitious site near Qiánlíng can be chosen for a separate tomb.
If the spirits have awareness,
the netherworld paths will naturally converge;
if they have no awareness,
what benefit is there in joining them?"
This was not accepted.
51 In this year,
the Ministry of Revenue reported that there were six million one hundred and fifteen thousand households
and thirty-seven million one hundred and fourteen thousand odd individuals in the empire.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on Wùxū,
Lǐ Qiáo, Minister of Personnel, was made concurrently Third-Rank Official in the Central Secretariat and Chancellery,
and Yú Wéiqiān, Central Secretariat Drafter, was made concurrently Administrator of Affairs.
2 In the intercalary month,
on Bǐngwǔ,
an edict stated:
"The princesses Tàipíng, Chángníng, Ānlè, Yíchéng, Xīndū, Dìng'ān, and Jīnchéng shall all establish residences
and appoint their own staff."
From Chángníng downwards, all were imperial daughters.
Lè,
pronounced Luò.
3 Wǔ Sānsī, fearing Jìng Huī, Huán Yànfàn, and Yuán Shùjǐ who were still in the capital,
on Yǐmǎo,
sent them out as Prefects of Huázhōu, Míngzhōu, and Yùzhōu respectively.
According to old records,
Huázhōu was one thousand four hundred and forty lí from the capital,
and five hundred and thirty lí from the Eastern Capital.
Míngzhōu was one thousand five hundred and eighty-five lí northeast of the capital,
and eight hundred and fifty-seven lí from the Eastern Capital.
Yùzhōu was one thousand five hundred and forty lí from the capital,
and six hundred and seventy lí from the Eastern Capital.
A note on discrepancies says: The Veritable Records, New Annal, and New and Old Biographies do not mention the year and month of Cuī Xuánwěi and Huī et al. being sent out as prefects.
Only the Old Annal, Tǒngjì, and Tánglì mention these three individuals.
It is probable that Xuánwěi had already been sent out earlier,
but the exact time is unknown.
However, when Huī et al. were demoted to Grand Administrator,
they were prefects of Lángzhōu, Bózhōu, Yǐngzhōu, and Jūnzhōu,
so they must have been moved again later.
Tánglì and Tǒngjì believe this occurred after Wáng Tóngjiǎo's execution,
which is followed here.
4 The monk Wànhuí of Mínxiāng was granted the title Fǎyún Gōng.
Wànhuí's surname was Zhāng.
Initially,
his mother prayed to the Guānyīn statue and conceived Huí.
Huí was born foolish,
only able to speak at the age of eight or nine.
Even his parents treated him like a pig or dog.
His elder brother was conscripted for military service in Ānxī,
and communication was cut off.
His parents sent him to inquire,
and one day,
he set out in the morning with his provisions
and returned home in the evening.
His parents found this extraordinary.
Hóngnóng was ten thousand lí from Ānxī,
and because he returned from ten thousand lí,
he was named Wànhuí.
Empress Wǔ bestowed upon him a brocade robe and a golden belt.
5 On Jiǎxū,
the chieftain Wūzhìlè of the Tūqíshī was made Prince of Huáidé Commandery.
6 In the second month,
on Yǐwèi,
Wéi Jùyuán, Minister of Punishments, was made concurrently Third-Rank Official in the Central Secretariat and Chancellery, and was further permitted to establish family relations with the Empress.
7 On the day *bǐngshēn*,
monk Huìfàn and nine others were all granted the fifth-grade rank,
and bestowed the titles of commandery and county dukes.
Daoist priests Shǐ Chóng'ēn and others were
granted the fifth-grade rank,
appointed *Guózǐ Jìjiǔ*,
with the status of full official.
The *Táng Huìyào* states: In the fifth year of Yǒnghuī,
Jiǎng Xiàozhāng was appointed *Shàngyào Fèngyù*,
an "outside-the-quota" special appointment,
still with the status of a full official.
The system of "outside-the-quota" officials began from this point.
8 Twenty officials from the Left and Right Bureaus and internal and external offices, of fifth grade and above, were selected as Inspecting Envoys for the Ten Circuits.
They were entrusted with observing officials, pacifying the people,
recommending worthy individuals, and rectifying prisons.
They were replaced every two years,
and promoted or demoted based on their merits and faults.

Jiāng Shīdù of Wèizhōu, the *cìshǐ* of Yìzhōu; Mǎ Huáisù, the *yuánwàiláng* of the Ministry of Rites; Yuán Qiányào of Línzhāng, the *diànzhōng shìyùshǐ*; Lú Huáishèn of Língchāng, the *jiānchá yùshǐ*; and Lǐ Jié of Fúyáng, the *wèiwèi shàoqīng*, all participated.
Wèixiàn,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Wèijùn.
At that time, it belonged to Wèizhōu.
Emperor Mǐn of Jìn, due to a naming taboo on the character *yè*,
changed Yè to Línzhāng.
At that time, Yèchéng had already fallen and been destroyed.
Later Zhào restored it as Yèxiàn.
The Eastern Wèi divided Yè, Nèihuáng, Chìqiū, and Féixiāng,
and established Línzhāngxiàn,
which belonged to Wèijùn.
During Zhōu, Suí, and Táng, it belonged to Xiāngzhōu.
Fúyáng
was the land of Wǔ'ānxiàn during the Hàn dynasty.
The Later Zhōu established Fúyángxiàn,
which belonged to Xiāngzhōu.
The character *fú*
is pronounced *fǔ*.
9 In the third month,
on the day *jiǎchén*,
Wéi Ānshí, the *zhōngshūlìng*, was dismissed and made *Hùbù Shàngshū*.
Sū Huái, the *Hùbù Shàngshū*, was made *Shìzhōng* and Western Capital *Liúshǒu*.
Sū Huái
was the father of Tǐng.

promising them immunity from death. He then exiled Huī to Qióngzhōu.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù initially said
"Jiāzhōu,"
and later said
"Cuīzhōu."
The Xīn Běnjì records "Jiāzhōu."
The Jiù Chuán records "Cuīzhōu."
Now we follow the Tǒngjì and Xīn Chuán.
Jiǎnzhī was exiled to Lóngzhōu.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé,
after the pacification of Xiāo Xiǎn,
Lóngshuǐ Xiàn of the Suí dynasty's Yǒngxī Jùn was designated as Lóngzhōu.
"Lóng" (瀧)
is pronounced "suǒ jiāng fān."
Rángzhōu.
The Suí general Liú Fāng first opened this route.
In the twelfth year of Zhēnguān,
following Liú Fāng's old path,
they reached Jiāozhǐ,
expanded into the barbarian territories,
and established Rángzhōu.
The prefecture was southwest of Yùlín and east of Jiāozhǐ.
To the north was Rángshuǐ,
after which the prefecture was named.
In the twelfth year of Zhēnguān,
Lǐ Hóngjié opened up the territories of the uncivilized tribes,
and established Huánzhōu,
named after the Huánwáng Kingdom,
which belonged to the Língnán Dào.
Gǔzhōu
was also established by Lǐ Hóngjié in the barbarian territories.
All were exiled beyond the Líng mountains.
Chéngjiā was promoted to Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and advanced to the rank of Xiāngwǔ Jùngōng.
Tán was appointed Xíngbù Shàngshū.
Lǐ Cháoyǐn was appointed Wénxǐ Lìng.
Sānsī then influenced the Crown Prince to submit a memorial
requesting the extermination of the three clans of Wěi and the others.
The Emperor did not permit it.
Zhōngshū Shèrén Cuī Shí advised Sānsī,
"If Huī and the others return north someday,
they will eventually become a future problem.
It would be better to send an envoy with a false edict to kill them."
Sānsī asked who could be sent.
Shí recommended Dàlǐ Zhèng Zhōu Lìyòng.
Lìyòng had previously been disliked by the Five Princes and
demoted to Jiāzhōu Sīmǎ.
So Lìyòng was appointed acting Yòutái Shìyùshǐ
and sent as an envoy to Líng'ài.
By the time he arrived,
Jiǎnzhī and Xuánwěi had already died.
He encountered Yànfàn in Guìzhōu,
and ordered his attendants to bind him,
drag him over bamboo splinters
until his flesh was stripped to the bone,
and then beat him to death.
He found Huī,
disemboweled him and killed him.
Shùjǐ had always worn gold;
Lìyòng forced him to drink wild Gě (Gelsemium) juice.
Běncǎo: Gōuwěn
is also called Yěgé.
Táo Hóngjǐng said: It is said to hook people's throats when ingested.
After investigation,
these are two different substances,
but it is not clear why.
Língbiǎo Lùyì says: Yěgé
is a poisonous herb,
commonly called Húmàn Cǎo.
If accidentally ingested, sheep's blood is used as an antidote.
Chén Zàngqì said: If people eat its leaves
and drink cold water, they will die,
as cold water activates its poison.
The local people feed Yěgé to people,
without giving them cold water,
until they become fat.
Then they are given cold water to drink,
leading to death.
They hung the corpse on a tree;
the dripping juice caused fungi to grow on the ground.
These were collected
and called Jūnyào (fungus medicine),
which was more potent than Yěgé.
Unable to withstand the toxic rage,
Shùjǐ clawed at the ground,
his fingernails almost entirely gone,
and was then beaten to death.
Upon Lìyòng's return,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Xuē Jìchǎng was repeatedly demoted to Dānzhōu Sīmǎ
and died by drinking poison.
Sān Sī, having killed the five princes,
wielded power over the sovereign.
He often said:
"I do not know who in this age are called good people
and who are called evil people.
But those who are good to me are good people,
and those who are evil to me are evil people."

At that time, Zōng Chǔkè, the Minister of War; Zōng Jìnqīng, the Grand Master of Works; Jì Chùnà, the Grand Minister of the Imperial Treasury; and Gān Yuánjiǎn, the Minister of the Court of Diplomatic Receptions, were all Sān Sī's wings.

Zhōu Lìyòng, the Palace Censor; Rǎn Zǔyōng, the Supervising Censor; Lǐ Jùn, the Assistant Minister of the Imperial Stud; Sòng Zhīxùn, the Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments; and Yáo Shàozhī, the Investigating Censor, were all Sān Sī's eyes and ears.
People at the time called them the "Five Dogs."
In the ninth month of the 25th year,
on the day Wùwǔ,
Lǐ Huáiyuǎn, Left Palace Aide and Grand Administrator of the Secretariat-Chancellery, passed away.
Initially,
Lǐ Qiáo was the Vice Minister of Personnel.
Wishing to establish personal favors
and seeking to become a chancellor again,
he proposed to greatly increase the number of supernumerary officials
and widely appoint his noble and powerful relatives and acquaintances.
After he became chancellor,
the selection process became disordered,
and the imperial treasury diminished.
He then presented another memorial speaking of the abuses of excessive official appointments
and requested to resign.
The emperor consoled him and did not permit it.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
the imperial carriage departed from the Eastern Capital.
Zhāng Rényuàn, former Acting Administrator of Bìngzhōu, was appointed Acting Grand General of the Left Palace Guard and Administrator of Luòzhōu.
On the day Wùxū,
the imperial carriage arrived at the Western Capital.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Yǐsì,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the empire.
On the 27th day, Bǐngchén,
Dòu Cóngyī, Governor of Púzhōu, was appointed Governor of Yōngzhōu.
Cóngyī was
the son of Dòu Déxuán.
Dòu Déxuán is mentioned in volume 201, during Gāozōng's Líndé 1st year.
To avoid the taboo name of the empress's father,
he changed his name to Cóngyī,
and was often sycophantic towards the powerful and noble.
Princess Tàipíng contended with a Buddhist monastery over a mill.
Lǐ Yuánhóng, Household Registrar of Yōngzhōu, ruled in favor of the monastery.

According to Tang regulations, the Household Department's Household Registrar and Counselor was in charge of household registers, accounting records, travel permits, exemption certificates, various corvée services, arrears, status of free and unfree people, fodder, inns, marriages, land disputes, and honoring the filial and fraternal.
He was repeatedly ordered to change his judgment.
Yuánhóng wrote a large inscription after his judgment, saying:
"The Southern Mountains may move,
but this judgment shall not!"
Cóngyī could not overturn it.
Yuánhóng was
the son of Lǐ Dàoguǎng.
Lǐ Dàoguǎng is mentioned in volume 205, during Empress Wǔ's Wànsuì Tōngtiān 1st year.
Initially,
Zhèng Pǔsī, Director of the Imperial Library, offered his daughter to the imperial harem.
Cuī Rìyòng of Língchāng, an Investigating Censor, impeached him for it,
but the emperor did not heed.
Pǔsī gathered a faction in Yōng and Qí prefectures,
plotting rebellion.
When the matter came to light,
Sū Huái, the Western Capital Commissioner, arrested and imprisoned him,
thoroughly investigating the case.
Pǔsī's wife, a Lady Dìwǔ, had gained favor with the empress through necromancy.
The emperor issued an edict to Huái not to investigate.
When the imperial carriage returned to the Western Capital,
Huái argued strongly in court,
but the emperor suppressed Huái and protected Pǔsī.
Fàn Xiànzhōng, the Supervising Censor, stepped forward and said:
"I request that Sū Huái be executed!"
The emperor said:
"For what reason?"
He replied:
"Huái, as a senior minister overseeing the capital,
failed to execute Pǔsī first
and then report it,
allowing him to confuse the sacred ear of the emperor. His crime is grave.
Furthermore,
Pǔsī's rebellious intentions are clear,
yet Your Majesty bends the law to defend him.
I have heard that 'the king will not die.'
Is this what it means?
I wish to be granted death first;
I cannot serve Pǔsī by facing north."
Wèi Yuánzhōng said:
"Sū Huái is an honorable man;
he does not use unjust punishments.
Pǔsī's crime warrants death by law."
The emperor, having no choice,
on the day Wùwǔ,
exiled Pǔsī to Dānzhōu.
All his remaining accomplices were executed.
In the twelfth month of the 29th year,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
Mòchuò of the Tujue invaded Míngshā.
Língzhōu had Míngshā Commandery.
In the 2nd year of Wǔdé,
Huìzhōu was established from Míngshā County.
In the 6th year of Zhēnguān,
the prefecture was abolished,
and Huánzhōu was established instead,
named after the winding great river.
In the 9th year, the prefecture was abolished,
and the county was returned to Língzhōu.
In that year, it was invaded by Mòchuò,
and its administration was moved to the old Fēng'ān City.
Sòng Bái said: Míngshā was originally part of Hàn's Fùpíng County.
Later Zhōu established Huìzhōu there,
soon after establishing Míngshā Garrison.
Suí established Huánzhōu,
named after the surrounding mountains.
Here, people and horses walking on the sand produced a sound
different from other sands,
hence it was called Míngshā (Singing Sand).
The army was defeated,
and over six thousand people died.
On the day Dīng
sì,
the Tujue advanced and invaded Yuán, Huì, and other prefectures.
In the 2nd year of Wǔdé, Xīhuìzhōu was established from the Huìníng Garrison of Píngliáng Commandery.
In the 8th year of Zhēnguān, it was renamed Huìzhōu.
Officials who showed loyalty and righteousness were exempted from punishment.
Guō Yuánzhèn, Grand Protector of Ānxī, visited the tent of Wūzhìlè of the Tūqíshī to discuss military affairs.
There was a great wind and snow.
Yuánzhèn stood before the tent,
speaking with Wūzhìlè.
After a long time,
the snow grew deep,
but Yuánzhèn did not move his feet.
Wūzhìlè was old
and could not withstand the cold.
The meeting concluded, and he passed away.
His son, Suōgě, gathered troops and was about to attack Yuánzhèn.
Xiè Wǎn, the Vice Envoy and Palace Censor, knew of this
and advised Yuánzhèn to flee during the night.
Yuánzhèn said:
"I treat people with sincerity.
What is there to doubt or fear?
Moreover, I am deep within enemy territory.
Where would I flee to?"
He lay down peacefully and did not move.
The next morning,
he entered and wept,
very sorrowfully.
Suōgě was moved by his righteousness
and treated Yuánzhèn as before.
On the day Wùxū,
Suōgě was appointed to succeed as Governor of Wòlùzhōu and Prince of Huáidé.
In the 1st year of Gāozōng's Xiǎnqìng reign, the Wòlùzhōu Commandery was established from the Suōgě Mòhè tribe of the Tūqíshī.
Wò is
pronounced Wūmò.
Princess Ānlè, relying on imperial favor, was arrogant and unrestrained.
She sold offices and perverted justice,
her power influencing the court and the countryside.
Sometimes she would write imperial edicts herself,
concealing the text,
and have the emperor sign them.
The emperor would smile and comply,
never even looking.
She personally requested to be made Crown Princess.
Although the emperor did not agree,
he also did not rebuke her.
A "Kǎo Yì" (Textual Research) states: The Tǒng Jì records:
"Princess Ānlè privately requested to depose the Crown Prince and establish herself as Crown Princess.
The emperor asked Wèi Yuánzhōng about this.
Yuánzhōng said: 'The Crown Prince is the heir apparent of the state,
the foundation of the people's lives.
Since he is innocent,
how can he be arbitrarily removed?
And to make the princess Crown Princess!
What title would the consort receive then?
The people of the empire would surely be greatly astonished and bewildered.
I fear this is not a path to the princess's own peace.'
The princess, knowing this,
then memorialized: 'Yuánzhōng
is a stubborn country bumpkin from Shandong.
How can he be fit to discuss grand national expediency, protocols, and preferences?
My mother's son became the Son of Heaven;
how can it be unacceptable
for me, a princess,
to become Crown Princess?'"
However, even if Zhōngzōng was foolish,
how could he not know that establishing a Crown Princess was impossible?
Why would he need Yuánzhōng's words?
We now follow the old tradition.
Jǐnglóng 1st year
(Dīngwèi, 707 CE).
The reign name was changed in the ninth month of this year.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day *gēngxū*,
an edict was issued stating that due to the incursions of the Tujue (Turk) Möchuò on the frontier,
officials, both internal and external, were commanded to each submit a strategy for pacifying the Tujue.
Lú Fú, Right Reminder, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Xì Gǔ delighted in ritual and music,
and was dedicated to poetry and literature,
becoming the Grand Marshal of Jìn.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states: When Duke Wén of Jìn reviewed his troops at Bèilú,
he organized three armies
and sought a Grand Marshal.
Zhào Shuāi said:
'Xì Gǔ would be suitable.
Your servant has often heard his words;
he delights in ritual and music and is dedicated to poetry and literature.
Poetry and literature
are the repository of righteousness;
ritual and music
are the standard of virtue;
virtue and righteousness
are the foundation of benefit.
Your Lord should test him.'
So Xì Gǔ was made to command the Central Army.
帥 (*shuài*) is pronounced *suǒ lèi fān*.
He established the achievement of pacifying Wú.
(See Volume 81, Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, *Tàikāng* First Year.)
Do not rely on the courage of a single man.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states: 'The center holds the power, the rear is strong.'
The commentary says: 'The central army controls strategy.'
The talent of a brave general
is fundamentally insufficient to bear a great responsibility.
Furthermore,
in the battle of Míngshā,
the commander-in-chief fled first.
The defeat at Míngshā
also refers to Shāzhà Zhōngyì.
驍 (*xiāo*) is pronounced *jiān yáo fān*.
將 (*jiàng*) is pronounced *jí liàng fān*.
If rewards and punishments are clear,
there will be no enemy that does not submit.
Furthermore,
for the regional governors of border prefectures,
their personnel should be carefully selected,
so that they can drill their soldiers and chariots,
accumulate provisions and grain,
repel invaders when they come,
and prepare for them when they depart.
Last year, the four quarters suffered from drought,
making it difficult to raise an army.
We should manage internal affairs before extending to external ones,
pacify those nearby to attract those far away,
and wait until the granaries are full
and the soldiers are trained,
then launch a major expedition to suppress them."
The Emperor approved of this.
2 In the second month,
on the day *bǐngxū*,
the Emperor dispatched Wǔ Yōujì and Wǔ Sānsī to Qíng Líng to pray for rain.
Soon after, rain fell,
and the Emperor was pleased.
An edict was issued to restore the Wǔ clan's Chóng'ēn Temple and the Hào Líng and Shùn Líng.
(After the Emperor was restored to the throne,
the Wǔ clan's Chóngzūn Temple was renamed Chóng'ēn Temple;
when the Empress Dowager died,
the Chóng'ēn Temple was abolished.
Hào Líng and Shùn Líng,
see Volume 204, *Tiānshòu* Second Year.)
The *Kǎoyì* states: "The old basic annals record,
'On the *jǐsì* day of the first month,
Wǔ Yōujì and Wǔ Sānsī were dispatched to Qíng Líng to pray for rain to Empress Zétiān.'
The new basic annals record,
'On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
a prefect and an assistant were established for the Póudé Róngxiān Mausoleum.'
According to the *Cháng Lì*,
the first month began on *gēngzǐ*,
and there was no *jǐsì*;
the second month began on *gēngwǔ*,
and there was no *jiǎwǔ*.
Now we follow the *Shílù*."
The mausoleum was called Róngxiān;
last year, the Empress's father, Wéi Xuánzhēn, was posthumously enfeoffed as the King of Fēng.
Yáng Fú, Doctor of the Grand Court, said:
"All grand ancestral temples take sons of seventh rank and below as斋郎 (*zhāiláng*) (temple attendants).
Now, Chóng'ēn Temple takes sons of fifth rank.
I do not know what the Grand Ancestral Temple should do?"
The Emperor ordered that the Grand Ancestral Temple should also follow the standard of Chóng'ēn Temple.
Fú said:
"To equate a minister with the ruler is already presumptuous and rebellious,
how much more so to equate the ruler with a minister!"
The Emperor then stopped.
3 On the day *gēngyín*,
an imperial edict changed the Zhōngxīng Temples and Daoist temples in all prefectures to Lóngxīng.
(The *Táng Huìyào* states: In the first year of *Shénlóng*,
an imperial edict commanded that each prefecture throughout the realm establish a Dàtáng Zhōngxīng Temple and Daoist temple.)
觀 (*guān*) is pronounced *gǔ wán fān*.
This demonstrated that after succeeding the Wǔ clan,
their policies were not changed.
It was believed that
"the words 天 (*tiān*), 地 (*dì*), 日 (*rì*), 月 (*yuè*), etc.,
(see Volume 204, Empress Wǔ, *Tiānshòu* First Year, for the changed characters)
were lightly disturbed by the treacherous ministers Jìng Huī and others from the former regulations;
now, abolishing them would not benefit the purification,
while preserving them would bring glory to filial piety and governance.
Furthermore,
the edict of the first year of *Shénlóng* stated that
for matters above one (rank),
all should follow the precedents of *Zhēnguān*.
How can we neglect the current maternal model
and honor the distant ancestral virtue!"
When the memorial was presented,
the Emperor personally wrote a commendation.
(Historians say Emperor Zhōngzōng had no sense of right or wrong.)
4 In the third month,
on the day *gēngzǐ*,
Tubó dispatched its chief minister, Xīxūn Rè, to offer tribute.
吐 (*tǔ*) has the pronunciation *cóng tūn rù shēng*.
5 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day *xīnsì*,
Princess Jīnchéng, the daughter of Yōng Wáng Shǒulǐ, adopted by the Emperor, was given in marriage to the Tubó Zanpu.
6 In the fifth month,
on the day *wùxū*,
Zhāng Rényuàn, Grand General of the Left Guards, was appointed Grand Commander of Shuòfāng Circuit,
to prepare against the Tujue.
7 Due to the drought and high grain prices,
the Emperor summoned Jǐ Chùnà, Minister of the Imperial Treasury, to discuss the matter.
The next day,
Wǔ Sānsī sent Jiāyè Zhìzhōng, who managed the affairs of the Grand Astrologer, to report:
"That night,
Shètí entered the Tàiwēi Palace.
(The *Xìng Pǔ* states: Jiāyè is an Indian surname.
迦 (*jiā*) is pronounced *jū gā fān*.
The *Jìn Tiānwén Zhì* states: The six stars of Shètí are directly south of the Dipper's handle,
presiding over the establishment of seasons
and observing auspicious omens.
Sānsī specially used Zhìzhōng to contrive this to flatter (the Emperor).)
There is the Seat of the Great Emperor within the Tàiwēi Palace."
The Emperor considered this to be true.
(Historians say the Emperor was foolish and dim-witted, and was deceived by his subordinates.)
見 (*jiàn*) is pronounced *xián biàn fān*.
For this revelation from the celestial phenomena,
he was granted one set of robes
and sixty bolts of silk.
8 In the sixth month,
on the first day, *dīngmǎo*,
there was a solar eclipse.
9 Táng Jiǔzhēng of Jìnchāng, the Commander for Punitive Expeditions of Yáoxī Circuit and Censor, attacked the rebellious barbarians of Yáo Prefecture,
and defeated them.
(Jìnchāng was the territory of Míng'ān County in Dūnhuáng Commandery during the Hàn dynasty.
The Zhāng clan of Héxī established Jìnchāng Commandery.
During the Suí dynasty, Guā Prefecture was established,
and Míng'ān was renamed Chánglè County.
In the fourth year of *Wǔdé*, Chánglè was again renamed Jìnchāng County.)
巂 (*suí*) has the sound *suí*.
使 (*shǐ*) is pronounced *shū lì fān*.
監 (*jiān*) is pronounced *gǔ xián fān*.
10 The Empress disliked Crown Prince Zhòngjùn because he was not her natural son.
(Zhòngjùn was born of a concubine;
historians have lost her surname.)
惡 (*è*) is pronounced *wū lù fān*.
Shangguān Jiéyú, for the sake of Sānsī,
whenever she drafted edicts,
would exalt the Wǔ clan.
Princess Ānlè and her consort, Wǔ Chóngxùn, General of the Left Guards, often insulted the Crown Prince,
sometimes calling him a slave.
Chóngxùn also encouraged the Princess to speak to the Emperor,
requesting the deposition of the Crown Prince
and the establishment of herself as Imperial Grand Daughter.
The Crown Prince accumulated much dissatisfaction.
In autumn,
seventh month,
on the xīnchǒu day,
the Crown Prince, along with the Grand General of the Left Yǔlín, Lǐ Duōzuò, and generals Lǐ Sīchōng, Lǐ Chéngkuàng, Dúgū Yī,
Shāzhà Zhōngyì, and others,
forged an imperial edict and mobilized over three hundred Yǔlín cavalrymen.
They killed Sān Sī and Chóngxùn at their residences,
along with more than ten of their relatives and partisans.
They also sent the Grand General of the Left Jīnwú, Chéng Wáng Qiānlǐ, and his son, Tiānshuǐ Wáng Xǐ, to guard the gates of the palace city with separate detachments of troops.
The Crown Prince and Duōzuò led their troops, cut through the barriers at Sùzhāng Mén, and entered.
They pounded on the gates, demanding to seize Shàngguān Jiéyú.
Jiéyú shouted loudly,
"It appears their intention is to first seize Wǎnwán,
Wǎnwán,
is the given name of Shàngguān Jiéyú.
and then come for the Empress."
The Emperor then ascended the Xuánwǔ Mén Tower with Empress Wéi, Ānlè Gōngzhǔ, and Shàngguān Jiéyú to avoid the attacking forces.
He ordered the Grand General of the Right Yǔlín, Liú Jǐngrén, to lead over a hundred Fēiqí soldiers to station below the tower for self-defense.
Yáng Zàisī, Sū Huái, and Lǐ Qiáo, along with the Minister of War Zōng Chǔkè and the Left Guard General Jì Chùnà, mustered over two thousand troops and stationed them in front of Tàijí Diàn,
closing the gates and defending themselves.
Duōzuò arrived first below Xuánwǔ Lóu,
intending to ascend the tower,
but the imperial guards resisted him.
Duōzuò and the Crown Prince hesitated,
holding their troops and not fighting,
hoping the Emperor would question them.
Yáng Sīxù of Shíchéng, the Director of the Palace Affairs Bureau (Gōngwéi Lìng), was by the Emperor's side.
According to Táng regulations: the Director of the Gōngwéi Bureau was a junior seventh-rank official,
subordinate to the Nèishì Shěng,
responsible for attending to the palace,
and managing the keys for entry and exit.
Shíchéng County belonged to Luózhōu,
and was the land of Hán Hépǔ County.
Liú Xù said: Sòng general Tán Dàojì built Shíchéng at the mouth of the Língluó Jiāng.
Later, Luózhōu was established there,
and in Táng, Shíchéng County was established.
Ōuyáng Xiū said: It was named after the Shíchéng River.
Duōzuò's son-in-law, Yěhūlì, a Major of the Yǔlín, was the vanguard commander.
Sīxù drew his blade and cut him down.
Tǐng
means to draw.
The Emperor leaned over the railing and said to Duōzuò's thousand cavalrymen,
"You are all my long-standing guards!
Why do you follow Duōzuò in rebellion!
If you can kill the rebels,
you need not worry about not gaining wealth and rank!"
Thereupon, the thousand cavalrymen killed Duōzuò, Chéngkuàng, Yīzhī, and Zhōngyì.
The remaining troops scattered.
Chéng Wáng Qiānlǐ and Tiānshuǐ Wáng Xǐ attacked Yòu Yánmíng Mén,
(Refer to the old map of Tàijí Gōng:
to the left of Tàijí Diàn was Zuǒ Yánmíng Mén,
to the right was Yòu Yánmíng Mén).
They failed and died.
The Crown Prince fled with a hundred cavalrymen to Zhōngnán Shān, and upon reaching Hùxī,
only a few individuals were still with him.
They rested under a forest,
where he was killed by his own followers.
The Emperor offered his head to the Tàimiào and sacrificed it before the coffins of Sān Sī and Chóngxùn,
then displayed it in the court.
Chéng Wáng Qiānlǐ's surname was changed to Fù Shì.
All his accomplices were executed.
None of the Crown Prince's palace staff dared to approach his corpse,
only Níng Jiāxù, the County Magistrate of Yǒnghé, took off his clothes to wrap the Crown Prince's head and cried bitterly.
He was demoted to Assistant County Magistrate of Xīngpíng.
Yǒnghé
was the land of Hán Húdié County.
Later Zhōu established Línhé County and Línhé Jùn.
Suí abolished the commandery
and renamed the county Yǒnghé.
In Táng, it belonged to Xízhōu.
Dié
is pronounced zhǐ shè.
"Xīngpíng"
is written as
"Píngxīng" in the New History.
Píngxīng
was the land of Hán Gāoyào County.
Sòng established Píngxīng County,
