the repetition of 'Táng' (堂)
is an omen that the Táng (唐) dynasty will receive the Mandate again.'
Zhèng Qiáo (鄭樵) said: 'Tángtáng' (堂堂)
was composed by Chén Hòuzhǔ (陳後主),
and Gāozōng (高宗) of Táng (唐) often sang it.
The world sang 'Wǔmèi Niáng' (娬媚娘);
after Yǒnghuī (永徽),
people sang the 'Wǔmèi Niáng' (娬媚娘)曲 (qǔ).
It is likely that this曲 (qǔ) already existed during the Suí (隋) dynasty.
Wǔ (娬),
pronounced 'wǔ' (武).
The world sang 'Yīngwáng Shízhōu' (英王石州);
this song is not found in historical records.
Zhōng (忠) was initially enfeoffed as Yīngwáng (英王),
so he fabricated this to be an omen for receiving the Mandate.
The world sang 'Sāng Tiáo Wéi' (桑條韋).
At the end of Yǒnghuī (永徽),
a folk song in the villages included 'Sāng Tiáo Wéi yě' (桑條韋也) and 'Nǚ Shí Wéi yě' (女時韋也).
In the 'Yuè Zhì' (樂志): Zhōng (忠) then fabricated this to be a testament to the empress's virtues,
that she specialized in silkworm rearing and mulberry cultivation,
providing for ancestral temple affairs.
He presented twelve pieces of 'Sāng Wéi Gē' (桑韋歌).
'She presides over silkworm and mulberry affairs,
and reverently presents twelve pieces of 'Sāng Wéi Gē' (桑韋歌),
requesting them to be compiled into the Music Bureau,
to be performed when the empress sacrifices to the First Silkworm Deity.'
Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿) Zhèng Yīn (鄭愔) further elaborated on this.
The Emperor was pleased
and bestowed generous rewards upon them all.
3 Yòu Bǔ Quē (右補闕) Zhào Yánxǐ (趙延禧) submitted a memorial:
"The Zhōu (周) and Táng (唐) dynasties are unified,
and their auspicious omens are identical.
Therefore, Gāozōng (高宗) enfeoffed Your Majesty as Zhōuwáng (周王);
in the 2nd year of Xiǎnqìng (顯慶),
the Emperor was enfeoffed as Zhōuwáng (周王),
and in the 2nd year of Yífèng (儀鳳),
he was transferred to be enfeoffed as Yīngwáng (英王).
Táng Tàitài (唐同泰) presented the 'Luòshuǐ Tú' (洛水圖).
It is found in scroll 204, from the 3rd year of Chuígǒng (垂拱) of Wǔ Hòu (武后).
Though a hundred generations may be known.'
Your Majesty succeeded Zétiān (則天),
and your descendants will rule the empire for a hundred generations."
The Emperor was pleased
and promoted Yánxǐ (延禧) to Jiànyì Dàfū (諫議大夫).
4 On the day Dīnghài (丁亥),
Xiāo Zhìzhōng (蕭至忠) submitted a memorial,
arguing:
"Favored individuals should only be enriched with gold and silk,
and fed with fine meat.
Public offices must not be used for private gain.
Now, official positions are already numerous,
and their occupants have doubled,
yet their demands are still not satisfied, increasing daily.
Your Majesty bestows immeasurable favors,
while close relatives make endless requests,
selling offices for personal profit
and perverting the law for private interests.
Within the bureaus and temples,
officials of all ranks are abundant.
When not busy, they neglect their duties;
when relying on their power, they openly violate regulations.
They merely occupy official positions in vain,
bringing no benefit to current governance."
Although the Emperor appreciated his intentions,
he ultimately did not implement them.
5 In the third month,
on the day Bǐngchén (丙辰),
Shuòfāngdào Dà Zǒngguǎn (朔方道大總管) Zhāng Rényuàn (張仁愿) built three Shòuxiángchéng (受降城) on the river.
The Central Shòuxiángchéng (中受降城) was on the north bank of the Yellow River,
over 1,300 li south of Shuòfāng (朔方),
and the Anběi Dūhùfǔ (安北都護府) was established there.
The Eastern Shòuxiángchéng (東受降城) was 200 li northeast of Shèngzhōu (勝州),
over 1,600 li southwest of Shuòfāng (朔方).
The Western Shòuxiángchéng (西受降城) was 80 li north of Fēngzhōu (豐州), outside the Yellow River,
over 1,000 li southeast of Shuòfāng (朔方).
Sòng Qí (宋祁) said: The Central City (中城) was directly south of Shuòfāng (朔方),
the Western City (西城) was directly south of Língwǔ (靈武),
and the Eastern City (東城) was directly south of Yúguān (榆關).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: The Eastern Shòuxiángchéng (東受降城) was 120 li northeast of Chányú Dūhùfǔ (單于都護府),
400 li southeast of Shuòzhōu (朔州),
8 li southwest across the river to Shèngzhōu (勝州),
and 300 li west to the Central Shòuxiángchéng (中受降城).
This was originally the land of Hàn (漢) Yúnzhōng Jùn (雲中郡).
The Central Shòuxiángchéng (中受降城) was 200 li northwest of Tiāndé Jūn (天德軍),
400 li south of Línzhōu (麟州),
and 500 li north of Qìkǒu (磧口).
This was originally the land of Qín (秦) Jiǔyuán Jùn (九原郡),
in Yúlín (榆林).
Hàn (漢) renamed it Wǔyuán (五原).
In the 10th year of Kāiyuán (開元), the Anběi Dà Dūhùfǔ (安北大都護府) was established here.
The Western Shòuxiángchéng (西受降城) was 80 li southeast across the river to Fēngzhōu (豐州),
700 li southwest to Dìngyuǎn Chéng (定遠城),
and 300 li northeast to Qìkǒu (磧口).
Jiàng (降),
read 'hù jiāng' (戶江).
Initially,
the Shuòfāng (朔方) army and the Tujue (突厥) used the river as their border.
North of the river was the Fúyún Cí (拂雲祠),
the shrine was on Fúyún Duī (拂雲堆),
thus it was named after it.
Jué (厥),
read 'jiǔ wù' (九勿).
They (the Tujue) would first visit the shrine to pray,
graze their horses, and prepare their soldiers before crossing the river.
At that time, Mòchuò (默啜) had taken all his troops to attack Tūqíshī (突騎施) in the west.
Rényuàn (仁愿) requested to seize the opportunity to take the lands south of the desert,
and build three Shòuxiángchéng (受降城) north of the river,
connected from end to end,
to cut off their route for southern incursions.
Tàizǐ Shàoshī (太子少師) Táng Xiūjǐng (唐休璟) believed
that "since the Hàn (漢) dynasties, we have always been blocked by the great river to the north.
Now building cities in enemy territory
might exhaust the people and waste resources,
and ultimately be taken by the barbarians."
Rényuàn (仁愿) insisted stubbornly,
and the Emperor finally agreed.
Rényuàn (仁愿) submitted a memorial requesting to keep soldiers whose annual tour of duty had ended to help with the project.
Those frontier soldiers whose annual tour had ended and were supposed to return
were kept to help with the city construction.
Rényuàn (仁愿) captured them all
and executed them at the foot of the city walls.
The army trembled with fear,
and the construction was completed in sixty days.
The Fúyún Cí (拂雲祠) was designated as the central city,
about 400 li from each of the eastern and western cities.
All occupied strategic points.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: The Eastern Shòuxiángchéng (東受降城) was originally the land of Hàn (漢) Yúnzhōng Jùn (雲中郡),
the Central Shòuxiángchéng (中受降城) was originally the land of Qín (秦) Jiǔyuán Jùn (九原郡),
and the Western Shòuxiángchéng (西受降城) was probably the old administrative seat of Hàn (漢) Línhé Xiàn (臨河縣).
North of Niútóu Cháonà Shān (牛頭朝那山).
For Cháonà Shān (朝那山),
see the note in scroll 203, Gāozōng (高宗) Hóngdào (弘道) 1st year.
Lùn Gōngrén (論弓仁), the Zuǒ Yùqínwèi Jiāngjūn (左玉鈐衞將軍), was appointed Shuòfāng Jūn Qiánfēng Yóuyì Shǐ (朔方軍前鋒遊弈使),
to guard Nuòzhēn Shuǐ (諾真水) as a patrolling defense.
A Yóuyì Shǐ (遊弈使)
leads patrolling troops for reconnaissance.
From the Central Shòuxiángchéng (中受降城) 200 li west to Dàtóng Chuān (大同川),
then 240 li north to Bùyuè Duō Shān (步越多山),
then 300 li northeast to Dìgēdá Chéng (帝割達城),
then northeast to Nuòzhēn Shuǐ (諾真水).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Yóuyì (遊弈)
involves selecting valiant and skilled individuals from the army who are familiar with mountains, rivers, springs, and wells to serve.
They patrol outside the garrisons day and night,
capturing people for questioning;
their deputies and sub-generals
are all experienced military personnel
and skilled riders and archers.
Shǐ (使),
read 'shū lì' (疏吏).
Shuòfāng (朔方) was no longer raided,
and tens of thousands of garrison troops were reduced.
Rényuàn (仁愿) built the three cities
without installing barbicans or defensive structures.
Yōngmén (壅門)
refers to the ancient xuánmén (懸門).
Some say: Walls were built outside the gate to obstruct the city gate;
this is today's wèngchéng (甕城).
Beyond the wèngchéng (甕城),
there were also bāguà qiáng (八卦牆) and wànrén dí (萬人敵),
all for obstructing the city gates.
Fàn Zǔyǔ (范祖禹) said: Zhāng Rényuàn (張仁愿) built three Shòuxiángchéng (受降城)
without installing wèngmén (甕門), qǔdí (曲敵), or zhàngé (戰格).
Rényuàn (仁愿) said:
"Military strategy values offense
and disfavors defense.
When the enemy arrives,
we should unite our strength and go out to battle.
Anyone who looks back at the city
should still be executed.
Why use defensive preparations
and breed a timid desire to retreat?!"
Later, Cháng Yuánkǎi (常元楷) became the Shuòfāng Jūn Zǒngguǎn (朔方軍總管)
and first built the yōngmén (壅門).
People therefore esteemed Rényuàn (仁愿) and disfavored Yuánkǎi (元楷).
6 Summer,
fourth month,
guǐwèi,
four Grand Academicians (Dà Xuéshì) were appointed to the Xiūwén Guǎn,
eight Direct Academicians (Zhí Xuéshì),
and twelve Academicians (Xuéshì).
Li Jiǎo and others, who were good writers from among the high officials and nobles down, were selected for these positions.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé,
the Xiūwén Guǎn was established in the Ménxià Shěng.
In the ninth year,
it was renamed Hóngwén Guǎn.
Those of the fifth rank and above were called Academicians (Xuéshì);
those of the sixth rank and above were called Direct Academicians (Zhí Xuéshì).
There were also Literary Direct Academicians (Wénxué Zhíguǎn),
all concurrently held by officials with other posts.
After Empress Wǔ's Chuígǒng era,
the prime ministers concurrently held the affairs of the institute,
known as Institute Heads (Guǎnzhǔ).
In the first year of Shénlóng,
to avoid the taboo name of Emperor Xiàojìng,
it was renamed Zhāowén Guǎn.
In the second year, it was renamed Xiūwén Guǎn.
Shàngguān Zhāoróng persuaded the Emperor to appoint four Grand Academicians (Dà Xuéshì) to symbolize the four seasons,
eight Direct Academicians (Zhí Xuéshì) to symbolize the eight seasonal divisions,
and twelve Academicians (Xuéshì) to symbolize the twelve hours.
Whenever imperial relatives gathered for banquets,
the Academicians (Xuéshì) would all attend,
composing poems and matching verses.
Shàngguān Zhāoróng was made to rank them as first, second, etc.
In Northern Qí, the new regulations of Héqīng mentioned Zhāoróng,
who was one of the eighty-one imperial concubines.
In the Táng dynasty, the position of Zhāoróng was second to Zhāoyí,
ranked second among the nine ranks.
In the winter of this year,
Shàngguān Jiéyú was made Zhāoróng.
Those who attended the banquets
were only officials from the Zhōngshū Shěng and Ménxià Shěng, along with a few long-serving princes (wáng gōng) and imperial relatives;
only for grand banquets
were the eight high ministers (bā zuò), nine high officials (jiǔ liè), and officials of the fifth rank and above from various departments invited to participate.
Consequently, the whole empire was swept up in a competition for literary brilliance,
and loyal and upright scholars (rúxué zhōngdǎng zhī shì) found no path to advancement.
7 Autumn,
seventh month,
guǐsì,
Zhāng Rényuàn, Grand General of the Left Túnwèi Guard and Grand Commander-in-Chief of the Shuòfāng Circuit, was made to hold the third rank of the Zhōngshū Shěng and Ménxià Shěng concurrently.
8 Jiǎwǔ,
Lǚ Yuántài, the County Magistrate (wèi) of Qīngyuán, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The frontiers are unsettled,
garrisons never cease,
soldiers suffer hardships,
and transportation is exhausting.
Yet, the construction of Buddhist temples
increases daily and monthly,
straining the people and squandering wealth,
without end.
In ancient times, Huángdì, Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ established their virtue and left their names solely through frugality, benevolence, and righteousness.
Since the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
pagodas and temples have arisen competitively,
and chaos and disorder have followed one another.
This is because their preferences were misplaced,
extravagance competed upwards,
and the people could not bear their fate.
I humbly wish that the funds for construction
be diverted to cover the expenses of the frontiers,
so that beacon fires may cease permanently,
and all living beings become prosperous and abundant.
Then, the compassionate giving of the Tathāgata (Rúlái)
and his egalitarian heart,
what could surpass this!"
When the memorial was presented,
it was not heeded.
9 Princess Ānlè, Princess Chángníng, the Empress's sister Lady Chéngguó Fūrén, Shàngguān Jiéyú, Shàngguān Jiéyú's mother Lady Pèiguó Fūrén Zhèng, and the Shanggōng Shāi and Hèlóu
— In the Táng palace, there were six Shang (shàng),
whose duties were like those of the Six Ministers (Lù Shàngshū).
There were two Shanggōng,
of the principal fifth rank,
in charge of guiding the Empress (Zhōnggōng),
and supervising the four departments of Records (Sījì), Speeches (Sīyán), Books (Sībáo), and Gates (Sīwéi).
Hèlóu was later executed by Prince Línzī.
Yuè is pronounced Luò.
Jiéyú is pronounced jiēyú.
— all used their influence to seek favors and accept bribes.
Even butchers, vendors, and slaves
— Zānghuò refers to male and female slaves.

a male slave is called zāng,
and a female slave is called huò;
in the northern suburbs of Yān,
a man who marries a female slave is called zāng,
and a woman who marries a male slave is called huò.
— they would issue secret imperial decrees to grant official positions,
delivered slanted (xiéfēng) to the Zhōngshū Shěng.
At the time, people called them
"slanted-seal officials" (xiéfēng guān).
For thirty thousand cash, one could become a monk or nun.
The number of yuánwài, tóngzhèng, shì, shè, jiǎnxiào, pàn, and zhī officials amounted to several thousands.
At that time, there were officials extra to the regular establishment (yuánwài),
officials extra to the regular establishment with the same rank (yuánwài tóngzhèng),
probationary officials (shì guān),
acting officials (shè guān),
and inspecting officials (jiǎnxiào guān).
Pàn
refers to "pàn mou guān shì" (judging the affairs of a certain official);
Zhī
refers to "zhī mou guān shì" (knowing the affairs of a certain official).
They formed four categories of selection (sì quán),
with tens of thousands of candidates each year.
Shàngguān Jiéyú and many other palace women established external residences,
entering and exiting without restraint.
Court officials often associated with them
to seek advancement.
Princess Ānlè was particularly arrogant and domineering;
many officials, including prime ministers, rose through her patronage.
She competed with Princess Chángníng in building residences,
— Princess Chángníng was the Emperor's daughter,
married to Yáng Shènjí —
emulating the imperial palace,
but surpassing it in exquisite craftsmanship.
Princess Ānlè requested Kūnmíng Chí.
The Emperor refused,
as it was a source of livelihood for the common people (púyú suǒ zī).
The Princess was displeased,
so she instead seized commoners' land to create Dìngkūn Chí,
extending for several li.
The Xīn Shū says: Dìng means "it can be contended with."
The Cháoyě Qiānzǎi states: Dìngkūn Chí was forty-nine li square,
extending directly to the Southern Mountains.
Kǎoyì says: The Xīn Zhuàn states forty-nine li,
extending directly to the Southern Mountains,
which probably includes the Princess's land.
Now we follow the old account.
Its waters were drawn to resemble Tiānjīn.
Tiānjīn refers to the Celestial River (Tiānhé).
The Hétú Kuòdì Xiàng says: The essence of the river ascends to become the Celestial Han (Tiānhàn).
Zhèng Xuán says: The Celestial River is the essence of water vapor,
its refined light circulating in the heavens.
Yáng Quán's Wùlǐ Lùn says: Stars are the essence of primordial qi;
Han is the essence of water.
When qi manifests and becomes visible,
its essence floats upwards,
winding and flowing,
named the Celestial River,
also known as Yúnhàn.
Hence it was named Dìngkūn.
Ānlè possessed a woven skirt
worth one hundred million cash.
Its flowers, plants, birds, and beasts
were all like millet grains.
Whether viewed directly or obliquely,
in sunlight or in shadow,
each appeared as a different color.
The Emperor was fond of polo (jīqiú),
and consequently, this custom became fashionable.
The imperial sons-in-law Wǔ Chóngxùn and Yáng Shènjí even sprinkled oil to construct polo grounds.
Shènjí was Gōngrén's great-grandson.
Gōngrén was Yáng Shīdào's elder brother.
The emperor, empress, and princesses frequently constructed Buddhist temples.
Zǔo Shíyí (左拾遺) Xīn Tìfǒu (辛替否) of Jīngzhào (京兆) submitted a memorial advising against this,
which briefly stated:
"Your servant has heard that in ancient times when officials were established,
their numbers were not necessarily complete,
but scholars possessed perfect conduct,
families had integrity and frugality,
the imperial court had surplus income,
and the common people had surplus food.
Now I observe that Your Majesty rewards a hundredfold,
increases official positions tenfold,
so much so that gold and silver are insufficient for their seals,
and bundles of silk are inadequate for their bestowals.

They exhaust the strength of the people,
squander their wealth,

they love a few children but incur three resentments.
This causes the soldiers on the frontiers not to exert their full strength,
and the officials at court not to be fully loyal.
If the people disperse,
how can one rely on holding only those one loves?
How can one rely on holding only those one loves?
The ruler takes the people as the foundation;
when the foundation is solid, the state is tranquil.
The 'Song of the Five Sons' in the Shūjīng (書經) says: 'The people are the foundation of the state;
when the foundation is solid, the state is tranquil.'
It further said:
"If constructing temples is necessarily considered the principle of governance,

At this time, all "slanted-seal officials" (xiéfēng guān, 斜封官) were appointed without passing through the two central ministries (liǎng shěng, 兩省),
and the two ministries dared not object,
merely transmitting the edicts to the relevant offices.
Lǐ Cháoyǐn (李朝隱), a Yuánwàiláng (員外郎) of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù, 吏部), consecutively thwarted over 1,400 such appointments.
Although resentment and slander were rampant,
Lǐ Cháoyǐn (李朝隱) paid no heed whatsoever.
10th Winter,
10th month,
on the day of Jǐyǒu (己酉),
Wǔ Píngyī (武平一), a Zhíxuétì (直學士) of the Xiūwénguǎn (修文館) and Qǐjūshèrén (起居舍人), submitted a memorial requesting the reduction of the power and favor of imperial relatives.
He dared not explicitly name the Wèi (韋) clan,
but only requested the reduction of his own family's influence.
The emperor issued a gracious edict refusing his request.
Wǔ Píngyī's (武平一) personal name was Zhēn (甄),
but he was known by his courtesy name (zì, 字);
he was the son of Zàidé (載德).
During the peak of the Wǔ (武) clan's power,
Zàidé (載德) was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yǐngchuān (潁川).
11th month,
on the day of Gēngshēn (庚申),
Sāgē (娑葛), the chieftain of the Túqíshī (突騎施), declared himself Khan,
killed Fèng Jiābīn (馮嘉賓), the Táng (唐) envoy and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞),
and dispatched his younger brother Zhēnǔ (遮努) and others to lead troops to invade the frontier.
Initially,
Sāgē (娑葛) had replaced Wūzhìlè (烏質勒) in leading the multitude.

They frequently attacked each other.

As Zhōngjié (忠節) traveled to Bōxiān (播仙) City,
Zhōu Yǐtì (周以悌), the Jīnglüèshǐ (經略使) and Yòuwēiwèijiāngjūn (右威衞將軍), persuaded him, saying:

is pronounced shū lì fān;
same for jiànshǐ (間使) below.)
(Shuō (說)
is pronounced shū ruì fān.)
"The state does not grudge high offices and prominent titles in waiting for you
because you have a multitude of tribes.
If you now go to court empty-handed,
you will be merely an old Hu barbarian.
Not only will you not preserve your favor and emoluments,
but your life and death will also be controlled by others.
Currently, the chancellors Zōng Chǔkè (宗楚客) and Jǐ Chǔnà (紀處訥) are in power.
It would be better to heavily bribe these two lords
to request permission to remain and not proceed,
then dispatch Ānxī (安西) troops and enlist the Tǔbō (吐蕃) to attack Sāgē (娑葛).
Seek Āshǐnà Xiàn (阿史那獻) to be Khan to rally the Ten Surnames.
(Xiàn (獻)
was the grandson of Āshǐnà Míshè (阿史那彌射)
and the son of Yuánqìng (元慶).)
(Dù Huán's (杜環) Jīngxíngjì (經行記) states: The kingdom of Báhànnà (拔汗那) is a thousand lǐ (里) south of Tánluósī (怛邏斯),
separated by mountains to the east,
over two thousand lǐ (里) from Shūlè (疏勒),
and over a thousand lǐ (里) west of Shíguó (石國).)
You would also gain revenge.
Compared to going to court,
how can they be spoken of on the same day!"
Guō Qián'guàn (郭虔瓘),
a native of Lìchéng (歷城),
(Lìchéng (歷城) County
belonged to Jìnán (濟南) Commandery during the Hàn (漢) and Jìn (晉) dynasties,
and was associated with Qízhōu (齊州) since the Later Wèi (後魏) dynasty.)
Zhōngjié (忠節) agreed with his words,
and sent a secret envoy to bribe Chǔkè (楚客) and Chǔnà (處訥),
requesting to follow Yǐtì's (以悌) strategy.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
the ceremony was completed.
The Empress's retinue was borrowed.
According to the *Táng Liùdiǎn* (Six Institutes of the Táng Dynasty),
the palace officials of the Six Bureaus,
the Shàngfú Bureau had officials for controlling the retinue (*sīzhàng*), managing the retinue (*diǎnzhàng*), and commanding the retinue (*zhǎngzhàng*),
who were responsible for matters concerning ceremonial feather banners and imperial guards.
Furthermore, according to the Táng system,

the Empress rode in a heavy-pheasant carriage (*zhòngzhái*), a lesser-pheasant carriage (*yànzhái*), a pheasant carriage (*zháichē*), an tranquil carriage (*ānchē*), a four-directional viewing carriage (*sìwàngchē*), and a gold-root carriage (*jīngēnchē*);
while a princess rode in a lesser-pheasant carriage (*yànzháichē*),
which was one rank lower than the Empress.
At this time, it was probably the heavy-pheasant carriage (*zhòngzhái*) and the Empress's ceremonial retinue that were borrowed.
Ānguó Xiāngwáng was ordered to block the carriage.
On the *gēngchén* day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* and the Old and New Histories all state
"a general amnesty on the *jǐmǎo* day."
Now, following the *Jǐnglóng Wénguǎnjì*,
it was the day after the ceremony was completed.
(He was also appointed) Right Guard General.
On the *xīnsì* day,
a banquet was held for the officials in the Liǎngyí Hall.
The princess was ordered to come out and pay respects to the dukes and ministers.
All the dukes and ministers prostrated themselves on the ground and kowtowed.
On the 13th *guǐwèi* day,
Niú Shījiǎng battled Suǒgē of the Tūqíshī tribe at Huǒshāochéng.
Shījiǎng's army was defeated and lost.
Suǒgē then captured Ānxī.
The Ānxī Dūhùfǔ
was at that time located in Qūcí.
He sent an envoy to present a memorial,
requesting the head of Zōng Chǔkè.
Chǔkè then again memorialized to replace Guō Yuánzhèn with Zhōu Yǐtì to command the troops,
and to summon Yuánzhèn back to court;
to appoint Āshǐnà Xiàn as the Khaghan of the Ten Tribes,
and to station troops in Yānqí to suppress Suǒgē.
Suǒgē sent a letter to Yuánzhèn,
stating:
"I initially had no ill will towards Táng,
but I am an enemy of Quēchuò.
Minister Zōng received gold from Quēchuò,
wishing to unjustly destroy the Pòrú tribe.
Vice Censor Féng and Protector Niú came one after another."
"Minister Zōng" refers to Chǔkè;
"Vice Censor Féng" refers to Jiābīn;
"Protector Niú" refers to Shījiǎng.
Each refers to their official title.
"I also heard that Shǐ Xiàn is about to come."
"Shǐ Xiàn" refers to Āshǐnà Xiàn,
a simplified way of speaking.
"I fear there will be no day of peace.
I beg the Grand Envoy to discuss a resolution."
Yuánzhèn presented Suǒgē's letter to the throne.
Chǔkè was enraged,
and memorialized that Yuánzhèn had ulterior motives.
He was summoned,
and was about to be punished.
Yuánzhèn had his son Hóng Jiāndào present a memorial detailing his situation,
requesting to remain to pacify the Western regions,
not daring to return.
Zhōu Yǐtì was eventually exiled to Báizhōu because of this,
and Yuánzhèn was again appointed to replace Yǐtì,
Suǒgē's crime was pardoned,
and he was enfeoffed as the Khaghan of the Fourteen Tribes.
The Western Tūjué originally had ten tribes;
now, Yànmiè, Gěluólù, Mòhédágān, and Dūmózhī were added to make fourteen tribes.
The 14th (day): Shàngguān *Jiéyú* was made *Zhāoróng*.
The 15th (day): In the twelfth month,
Yáo Tíngyún, the Imperial Censor-in-chief, memorialized:
"Recently, I have observed that various departments do not adhere to the legal codes and regulations;
all matters, large or small, are reported to Your Majesty.
I have heard that a ruler entrusts his ministers,
and ministers uphold the law.
The myriad affairs are numerous and complex,
making it impossible to review them all.
How can it be that repairing a water culvert
or cutting down a dead tree
all require Your Majesty's personal decision!
From now on, if it is a major national affair or something not covered by regulations,
it may be reported for Your Majesty's decision.
For all other matters, dispose of them according to the law.
If anyone deliberately creates doubts or delays,
causing errors or negligence,
I hope Your Majesty will order the censors to impeach them."
This was adopted.
The 16th (day): On the *dīngsì* day, the last day of the year,
an edict ordered the Zhongshū and Ménxià departments, along with the scholars, various princes, and imperial sons-in-law, to enter the inner palace to "guard the year" (celebrate New Year's Eve).
Courtyard torches were set up,
wine was served,
and music was played.
*Gé* means
inner hall.
Such a "guarding the year" banquet
did not exist in ancient times.
Yǔ Jiānwú of the Liáng dynasty wrote in his New Year's Eve poem:
"Let's pour some cypress-leaf wine,
and try to offer the five-pungent-herb dish."
This indicates that such customs already existed in Jiāngzuǒ,
but had not yet reached the point where ruler and ministers enjoyed themselves together so freely.
Suí Yángdì was extravagant and lustful.
Every New Year's Eve,
dozens of "volcanoes" were set up in front of the palace halls,
all made from agarwood roots.
Each "mountain" burned several carts of agarwood.
When the fire dimmed, it was doused with *jiǎjiān* (a type of perfumed oil),
causing flames to rise several *zhàng* high.
The fragrance could be smelled for dozens of *lǐ*.
In a single night,
over two hundred carts of agarwood
and over two hundred *dàn* of *jiǎjiān* were used.
Ōuyáng Xiū's poem:
"In the Suí palace, agarwood fires guarded the night,"
refers to this.
The Emperor's doing this
was a precursor to the fall of Suí.
The Emperor said to the Imperial Censor-in-chief Dòu Cóngyī:
"I heard that you have been without a consort for a long time,
which greatly concerns me.
Tonight is New Year's Eve,
I shall arrange a marriage for you."
Cóngyī simply assented and bowed in gratitude.
Soon after, inner attendants led candle lanterns, screen partitions (*bùzhàng*), and gold-threaded silk fans from the west corridor and ascended.
The official of the *nèishì* (inner attendant)
in Táng was ranked from upper fourth grade,
responsible for serving within the palace and transmitting messages in and out of the inner quarters.
The Later Wèi called them *Chángqiū Qīng*,
Northern Qí called them *Zhōngshìzhōng*,
Later Zhōu called them *Sīnèi Shàngshì*,
Suí called them *nèishì*,
and Táng followed this.
The prestige of palace eunuchs
reached its peak with this.
If they had extraordinary achievements or distinguished service,
they would be appointed Grand General,
while still holding the office of *nèishì*.
*Shàng* (ascended) is
*shí zhǎng fān*.
*Huāchāi* (flower hairpins):
According to Táng regulations, the clothing of noblewomen included *díyī* (pheasant robes),

which were worn by inner noblewomen when receiving investiture, performing sericulture rites, and attending court assemblies; and by outer noblewomen for marriage, receiving investiture, performing sericulture rites, and grand court assemblies.
They were green in color,
embroidered with pheasants,
arranged in sequence on the robe and skirt,
with nine grades of 重.
First rank had nine grades of pheasants and nine trees of *huāchāi*;
second rank had eight grades of pheasants and eight trees of *huāchāi*;
third to fifth ranks all decreased by one.
*Lǐyī* (ceremonial robes) were
worn by inner noblewomen for regular attendance, and by outer noblewomen for court attendance, formal visits, and ceremonial gatherings.
Their regulations were the same as *díyī*,
with the addition of a double pendant (*shuāngpèi*) and a small ribbon (*xiǎoshòu*),
and slippers (*lǚ*) instead of clogs (*xì*).
*Rén Yī*
*yú jì fān*.
The Emperor ordered Cóngyī to recite several poems for "removing the fan."
At wedding nights for Táng people,
there were "makeup urging poems" (*cuīzhuāngshī*) and "fan-removing poems" (*quèshànshī*).
Lǐ Shāngyǐn's "Fan-removing Poem for Scholar Dǒng" says:
"Do not bring the painted fan out from the curtain,
obscuring the spring mountains and hindering the talented man.
If you say that roundness is the bright moon,
then the osmanthus flowers must be allowed to bloom within it."
(She) removed the flower hairpins and changed her clothes before coming out.
Cóngyī looked closely,
and it was none other than Empress Wáng, the old wet nurse,
who was originally a barbarian maid.
The Emperor and his attendants laughed heartily.
An edict enfeoffed her as Jǔguó Fūrén,
and married her as Cóngyī's wife.
People commonly called the husband of a wet nurse
"*āfù*" (foster father).
Whenever Cóngyī had an audience or presented memorials,
he referred to himself as
"Yìshèng Huánghòu's *āfù*."
People at the time called him
"Guófù" (national foster father).
Cóngyī was delighted and showed a proud demeanor.
In the 1st (year),
spring,
first month,
on the *dīngmǎo* day,
an imperial edict established the Shèngshàn Temple in Guǎngdōng.
According to records, there was already a Shèngshàn Temple in Xījīng,
and also a Shèngshàn Temple in Dōngdū,
both built by the Emperor
to pray for blessings for Empress Wǔ Hòu.
The 2nd (day):
Chángníng, Ānlè, and other princesses often allowed their servants and slaves to plunder the common people's sons and daughters, making them slaves.
Yúan Cóngzhī, the Supervising Censor, arrested and imprisoned them,
prosecuting them.
The princesses complained to the Emperor,
and the Emperor personally wrote an edict to release them.
Cóngzhī memorialized, saying:
"If Your Majesty allows slaves to plunder good people,
how can you govern the empire!"
The Emperor still released them.
3 In the second month,
on the day Jǐchǒu,
His Majesty went to Xuánwǔmén
and, with his close ministers, watched palace women playing tug-of-war.
They used a hemp rope and large bamboo poles, divided into teams, and pulled for water.
This was called tug-of-war,
to determine victory or defeat.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Tángjì* states:
"watched palace women's grand feast."
Now we follow the *Shílù*.
The dukes and ministers acted as merchants,
conducting transactions with them,
which then led to disputes
and disrespectful language.
His Majesty and the Empress watched this for their amusement.
4 On the day Bǐngshēn,
Supervising Censor Cuī Wǎn, standing before the court, impeached Zōng Chǔkè and Jì Chǔnè for secretly communicating with the nomadic tribes [róngdí],
accepting their bribes,
and thereby causing border troubles.
He said they accepted bribes from Quēchuò Zhōngjié,
which led to the change of allegiance of Suōgá.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Jǐnglóng Wénguǎnjì* states:
"Supervising Censor Cuī Wǎn, formally dressed,
impeached Grand Academician and Minister of War, Duke of Yǐng, Zōng Chǔkè, and Attendant Counselor Jì Chǔnè, before the court.
At that time, Chǔkè was in the ranks [of officials] and
reported, 'I, being incompetent and presumptuous,
occupy a position of great importance.
Both internal and external factions are conspiring;
I have reported this beforehand,
and Your Majesty's divine judgment is expected.'
His Majesty nodded [in agreement]
and said to Wǎn, 'I know about Chǔkè's matter.
Leave for now;
wait until after the court session.'
After the court session,
Wǎn then continued his report;
an imperial edict ordered an inquiry in the Western Secretariat.
The Central Secretariat and the Department of the Imperial Chancellery reported no misconduct;
if there was any further instruction, he would be reinstated.
Originally,
Suōgá and his father were hereditary enemies with Āshǐnà Zhōngjié.
Suōgá repeatedly requested the state to eliminate Zhōngjié,
and the Protector-General of Ānxī, Guō Yuánzhèn, submitted a memorial requesting to comply with his petition.
Zōng Chǔkè firmly insisted,
saying, 'Zhōngjié serves the nation with utmost sincerity,
guarding Yùguān.
If we allow Suōgá to eliminate him,
I fear it would not be in line with the principle of strengthening the strong and rescuing the weak.'
His Majesty therefore did not permit it.
Before long, Suōgá killed the Imperial Censor FÉng Jiābīn and Palace Attendant Censor Lǚ Shǒusù,
destroyed Zhōngjié,
and harassed the Four Garrisons.
At that time, Zhōu Yǐtì, the Commander of the Suìyè Garrison, led several hundred garrison soldiers and inflicted a great defeat on them,
recapturing Zhōngjié's and Yútián's people, totaling tens of thousands, that had been invaded.
When the report arrived,
His Majesty was greatly pleased,
appointed Yǐtì as General of the Left Tunwei,
and appointed Yuánzhèn as the Strategic Commissioner of the Four Garrisons;
an imperial edict formally reprimanded Yuánzhèn.
Zōng [Chǔkè] proposed sending elite troops,
ordering Yǐtì and Guō Qián'guàn to campaign in the north,
and also inviting the Túbō and various Western Regions tribes to coordinate a joint attack on Suōgá;
the Right Censor-in-Chief Xiè Wǎn argued against it, saying it was not feasible.
Afterwards, peace was eventually made with him.
Suōgá, hearing of the previous proposal,
became very resentful,
and then sent Yuánzhèn a document,
stating that Zōng had previously taken gold from Zhōngjié.
His Majesty asked him about this,
and Zōng reported the entire previous matter.
At that time, Princesses Tàipíng and Ānlè, due to their noble birth, power, and favor,
each formed factions,
secretly vying for power and usurping authority.
From the crucial officials to the prime ministers, all were divided into two groups.
At that time, Tàipíng was particularly at odds with Zōng,
and therefore instigated Wǎn to impeach him;
the rumor that he took gold from Suōgá
was incorrect."
Now we follow the *Shílù* and the record.
When a high-ranking minister was impeached,
he would bend down and walk out quickly.
'Fǔ' (俛) means to bow the head;
'lóu' (僂) means to stoop the back.
'Lóu',
pronounced 'lì zhǔ fān'.
At this point,
Chǔkè became even more enraged and showed his displeasure,
asserting his loyalty and integrity,
claiming he was slandered by Wǎn.
His Majesty did not pursue the inquiry,
but ordered Wǎn and Chǔkè to become sworn brothers to reconcile their differences.
People at the time called him
"the Son of Heaven who reconciles disputes."
5 On the day Rén'yín,
Wéi Jùyuán was appointed Left Minister of the Department of State Affairs,
Yáng Zàisī was appointed Right Minister of the Department of State Affairs,
both with the concurrent title of *Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn*.
6 His Majesty frequently held banquets and gatherings with his close ministers and scholars,
ordering each to display their artistic skills for amusement.
Minister of Works Zhāng Xī danced *Tán Róngniáng*;
Grand Architect Zōng Jìnqīng danced *Húntuō*.
Chángsūn Wújì made *húntuō* felt caps from black sheep's wool,
and many people imitated them,
calling them "Duke Zhào's *húntuō*,"
which were then developed into a dance.
In the early Ruòyì reign,
a folk song went:
"Yellow deer, yellow deer, hidden in the grass,
bend your bow and shoot, injuring you."
This was also developed into a dance.
This is what is now called the "Divine Incantation of India."
Guō Shānyùn of Hédōng, Assistant Director of the Directorate of Education, alone said:
"I have no skills [to display],
please allow me to sing ancient poems."
His Majesty permitted it.
Shānyùn then sang "Lùmíng" and "Xīshuài."
"Lùmíng" is for feasting loyal ministers and honored guests;
"Xīshuài" takes the meaning of enjoying pleasure without excess.
However, Shānyùn wished to display his own learning
and align himself with Confucian scholarship,
rather than truly guiding the sovereign towards goodness.
His Majesty bestowed an imperial edict upon Shānyùn,
praising his intentions,
and granted him a set of seasonal attire.
His Majesty also once hosted a banquet for his attendant ministers,
asking each to compose a *huíbō* poem.
At that time, during the inner banquet, emboldened by wine,
the attendant ministers generally rose to perform the *huíbō* dance,
hence they were asked to compose *huíbō* poems.
Some sought honor and emolument for themselves.
Remonstrance Official Lǐ Jǐngbó said:
"The wine goblet at that time
was a *huíbō*.
My humble duty lies in admonishment.
Having attended the banquet for more than three cups [of wine]..."
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states: When a minister attends his lord at a banquet,
he should not drink more than three cups;
more than three cups
is not proper.
His Majesty was displeased.
Xiāo Zhìzhōng said:
"This is truly an admonishing official."
7 In the third month,
on the day Wùwǔ,
Zōng Chǔkè was appointed Director of the Central Secretariat,
Xiāo Zhìzhōng was appointed Attendant Counselor,
and Wéi Sìlì, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, was appointed Vice Director of the Central Secretariat, with the concurrent title of *Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn*.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The new table states:
"Sìlì held the post of Minister of War."
Now we follow the *Shílù*.
Cuī Shí was intimate with Grand Concubine Shàngguān,
so the Grand Concubine recommended him as prime minister.
Yànzhāo,
was from Zhāngyè.
Zhāngyè
was formerly the land of the Xiongnu King Húnxié.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn established Zhāngyè Commandery and Lùdé County there.
Yīng Shào says: It covers the arms of the state,
hence called Zhāngyè.
Lùdé,
where the commandery seat was located, was also a Xiongnu king's title.
The Jìn dynasty changed Lùdé to Yǒngpíng.
The Later Wèi established Zhāngyè Commandery.
In the 17th year of Kāihuáng of the Suí dynasty,
Yǒngpíng was changed to Jiǔquán.
In the early Dàyè period, it was changed to Zhāngyè County.
Since the Western Wèi, its territory
served as the administrative seat of Gānzhōu,
named after the Gānjùn Mountain in the prefecture.
Lù (觻)
is pronounced 'lù'.
At that time, government edicts issued from multiple sources,
and superfluous officials abounded.
People said that there was no place for "three-worthless" officials to sit,
referring to prime ministers, censors, and supernumerary officials.
Wéi Sìlì submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Recently, a great many temples have been built,
with an emphasis on grandeur and beauty.
Large ones cost hundreds of thousands of coins,
small ones three to five tens of thousands,
the total expenditure certainly exceeding ten million.
Manpower is exhausted and worn out,
and groans of complaint fill the roads.
The essence of Buddhism
lies in subduing the body and mind;
how can it be about carving and painting wood and earth
to boast of magnificence?
If, by any chance, floods or droughts strike,
or the Róngdí cause trouble,
even if 'dragon-elephants' are as numerous as clouds,
what salvation will there be?
Furthermore,
the number of households with enfeoffments
is very large.
When I inquired with the Hùbù yesterday,
they said it required over 600,000 *dìng*;
with two bolts of silk per *dìng*,
it totals over 1.2 million bolts.
The system at the beginning of the Táng dynasty
was one *dìng* paying two bolts of silk annually.
The annual *yōng* silk tax
was usually no more than one million bolts,
and sometimes as little as 600,000 or 700,000 bolts.
Compared to the income of enfeoffed households,
the state's revenue is remarkably small.
Only those with the merit of assisting in the founding of the dynasty
should be granted territories with symbolic partitioning.
In the early days of the state,
there were no more than twenty or thirty meritorious officials who received enfeoffments.
Now, those who receive enfeoffments due to imperial favor number over a hundred.
More than half of the state's taxes and tributes
go to private households.
While private households have a surplus,
which merely increases their extravagance,
the public treasury is insufficient,
leading to anxiety and peril.
How can this be considered a sound method
for governing the state?
The goods from enfeoffed households
are collected directly by the various families.
Their servants, relying on their power,
bully the *zhōu* and *xiàn* officials,
demand excessive 'head-wrapping' fees,
and engage in trade,
causing trouble and coercion,
the suffering from which is unbearable.
It would be better to calculate the amount per *dìng* and deliver it all to the Tàifǔ,
and have the enfeoffed families receive it from the Zuǒzàng.
This would be better for the matter."
(This means it would be better than enfeoffed families collecting it themselves.)
"The number of supernumerary officials
is several times that of regular posts.
The clerks in government offices
are exhausted by attending to them,
and the government treasuries and granaries
are depleted by providing for them.
Furthermore,
*cìshǐ* and *xiànlìng* officials
have, in recent years,
not been selected with care.
Capital officials who have committed offenses or have low reputations are sent to govern *zhōu*,
while those selected by the Lìbù who are old and infirm and lack writing skills are appointed as *xiànlìng*.
With such people governing,
how can one expect them to guide and transform the people?
I hope that from now on,
only officials of the Sānshěng, Liǎngtái, and those of the fifth rank and above with clear reputations should be appointed,
(Liǎngtái
refers to the Zuǒ Yùshǐtái and Yòu Yùshǐtái.)
then the world will be well governed."
The Emperor did not heed.
8. On *wùyín*
(this day), Wéi Wēn, Shàngshū of the Lǐbù, was appointed Tàizǐ Shàobǎo and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
Zhèng Yīn, Tàicháng Qīng, was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
According to a note,
"Zhèng Yīn, Lìbù Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì."
Also, upon examining the New History's annals,
on this year, month, and day, it states
"Zhèng Yīn, Tàicháng Shàoyǐng, serving as Lìbù Shìláng and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì."
Thus, it is known that the transcriber of the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn mistakenly wrote *shàngshū* instead of *shìláng*.
(He was the empress's brother.)
9. Tàicháng Bóshì Táng Shào believed that the Wǔ clan's Hàolíng and Shùnlíng each had 500 households guarding them,
which was the same number as Zhāolíng.
The tombs of Liáng Xuānwáng and Lǔ Zhōngwáng had five times more guard households than those of imperial princes.
(Liáng Xuānwáng was Wǔ Sānsī;
Lǔ Zhōngwáng was Wǔ Chóngxùn.)
(The establishment of the Bāodé Miào is mentioned in the first year of the preceding volume.)
(The Emperor) did not listen.
Shào
was the grandson of Lín.
(Táng Lín served Gāozǔ, Tàizōng, and Gāozōng.)
10. Zhōngshū Shìláng concurrently acting as Lìbù Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Cuī Shí, and Lìbù Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Zhèng Yīn, both managed the selection of officials.
They ingratiated themselves with powerful individuals,
engaged in widespread bribery,
retained people beyond the official quotas,
and were insufficient in their appointments.
They preemptively used up vacancies from three years in advance.
The corruption of the selection system
reached its extreme during our Sòng dynasty.
The Lìbù's appointments
typically involved three people for one official position:
one who held the position,
one who was yet to arrive,
and one who was waiting for it.
For slightly desirable positions,
there was more than just one person waiting for it.
How could it be limited to merely preemptively using three years of vacancies?
Shí's father, Yì, was a Sīyè.
He accepted money from candidates.
Shí, unaware of this,
released them from the "long name list."
(In the second year of Gāozōng's Zǒngzhāng era,
Péi Xíngjiǎn first established the "long name list" (*cháng míng bǎng*).
All candidates who assembled at the Lìbù,
those who were accepted stayed,
those who were not accepted were released.)
(Sòng Bái said: The *cháng míng bǎng* determined who stayed and who was released;
those who stayed entered the selection process,
those who were released could not enter the selection process.)
"Your trusted associate received a certain bribe,
why did you not grant him an official position?"
Shí angrily said,
"Who is this trusted associate?
I will seize him and beat him to death!"
The person said,
"Do not beat him to death,
for it will cause you sorrow."
Shí was greatly ashamed.
Shìyùshǐ Jìn Héng and Jiānchá Yùshǐ Lǐ Shàngyǐn jointly impeached them (Cuī Shí and Zhèng Yīn) in court.
They were both put in prison,
and Jiānchá Yùshǐ Péi Cuǐ was ordered to investigate.
Princess Ānlè secretly urged Cuǐ to be lenient in their case.
Cuǐ, however, again impeached them in court.
In the summer,
the fifth month,
on *bǐngyín* (this day),
Yīn was spared death
and exiled to Jízhōu.
Shí was demoted to Jiāngzhōu Sīmǎ.
(Old records state: Jiāngzhōu is
2,948 *lǐ* southeast of the capital,
and 2,197 *lǐ* to the eastern capital.)
The next day,
Shí was appointed Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
(Old records state: Xiāngzhōu is
from the capital to the eastern capital.)
Yīn became Jiāngzhōu Sīmǎ.
11. In the sixth month,
Yòu Púyè and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn Yáng Zàisī passed away.
12. In the autumn,
seventh month,
Tūqíshī Suōgé sent an envoy to request surrender.
On *gēngchén* (this day),
he was appointed Qīnhuà
Kèhán
and given the name Shǒuzhōng.
13. In the eighth month,
on *jǐ*
*yǒu* (this day),
Lǐ Qiáo was appointed Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn,
Wéi Ānshí was appointed Shìzhōng,
and Xiāo Zhìzhōng was appointed Zhōngshū Lìng.
Zhìzhōng's daughter married Cuī Wúbì, the nephew of the Empress.
On the wedding day,
the Emperor was the host for the Xiāo family,
and the Empress was the host for the Cuī family.
People at the time called it
"the Son of Heaven marrying off a daughter,
and the Empress taking a daughter-in-law."
14 In the first half of the first month, when the sacrifices to the Southern Suburb were to be held,
on the *Dīngyǒu* day,

Zhù Qīnmíng (祝欽明), the Libationer of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ 國子祭酒), and Guō Shānyùn (郭山惲), the Director of Studies of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Sīyè 國子司業), submitted a memorial, stating:
"In ancient times, during major sacrifices,
the empress performed the libation and presented offerings with a jade goblet.
The empress should assist in the sacrifices to Heaven and Earth."
Táng Shào (唐紹) and Jiǎng Qīnxù (蔣欽緒), Academicians of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Bóshì 太常博士), refuted this,
believing:
"Zhèng Xuán's (鄭玄) commentary on the 'Inner Attendant' (Nèisīfú 內司服) chapter of the *Rítuals of Zhōu* (Zhōulǐ 周禮)
only mentions assisting in sacrifices to former kings and former dukes,
but contains no text about assisting in sacrifices to Heaven and Earth.
The empress should not assist in the sacrifices to the Southern Suburb."
The 'Inner Steward' (Nèizǎi 內宰) chapter of the *Rítuals of Zhōu* states: For major sacrifices,
if the empress performs the libation and presentation, she is assisted.
The same applies to the jade goblet.
The commentary says: This refers to sacrifices at the ancestral temple,
where after the king has performed the libation and gone out to welcome the sacrificial animal,
the empress then follows to perform the libation.
"Presentation"
means presenting raw and cooked offerings,
and the empress also follows to make the presentation.
"Jade goblet"
means when the representative of the deceased has finished eating,
and the king has rinsed the representative's mouth,
the empress makes the secondary offering,
and the goblet used for this is adorned with jade.

Furthermore, the 'Inner Attendant' (Nèisīfú 內司服) chapter states: "She is in charge of the six robes of the queen: the *huīyī*, *yúdí*, *quēdí*, *júyī*, *zhǎnyī*, and *ruányī* (褘衣、揄狄、闕狄、鞠衣、展衣、褖衣) with plain gauze."
The commentary says: The *huīyī*, *yúdí*, and *quēdí*
are all sacrificial robes.
When accompanying the king in sacrificing to former kings, she wears the *huīyī*;
when sacrificing to former dukes, she wears the *yúdí*;
and when sacrificing at minor rites, she wears the *quēdí*.
Those of this age who have *guīyī*
are likely following a remnant custom of the three *dí* robes.
According to the *Rítuals of Zhōu*,
what the 'Inner Steward' referred to as "major sacrifices" specifically meant sacrifices at the ancestral temple.
Zhù Qīnmíng (祝欽明) and others, based on the Táng (唐) system that considered Heaven and Earth and the ancestral temple as equally "major sacrifices,"
then twisted the meaning of "major sacrifices" in the *Rítuals of Zhōu* to flatter Empress Wéi (韋后).
Moreover, Zhèng (鄭)'s interpretation in the *Rítuals of Zhōu* of "libation," "presentation," and "jade goblet"
refers to three stages of the ceremony during the sacrifice;
now Qīnmíng (欽明) says "the empress performs the libation and presentation with a jade goblet,"
which also goes against Zhèng's (鄭) interpretation,
creating his own theory.
祼, pronounced *guàn*.
駮, pronounced *bó*.
Yánguān (鹽官),
in Hán (漢) times, was the territory of Hǎiyán (海鹽).
There was formerly an official in charge of salt,
and Wú (吳) subsequently established it as a county name.
In Táng (唐) times, it was subordinate to Hángzhōu (杭州).
"The sacrifice to Heaven primarily focuses on the primordial ancestor,
and is not accompanied by ancestral mothers,
therefore the empress should not participate in the sacrifice."
Wéi Jùyuán (韋巨源) finalized the ritual protocols,
requesting to follow Qīnmíng's (欽明) proposal.
The Emperor assented,
making the empress the secondary officiant.
He also made daughters of chancellors the "Fasting Maidens" (zhāiniáng 齋娘),
to assist in holding the wooden and bamboo sacrificial vessels.
Qīnmíng (欽明) further wished to make Princess Ānlè (安樂公主) the final officiant,
but Shào (紹) and Qīnxù (欽緒) strongly objected,
so it was stopped;
Jùyuán (巨源) acting as Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi 太尉) was made the final officiant.
Qīnxù (欽緒) was a native of Jiāoshuǐ (膠水).
Jiāoshuǐ (膠水) was,
in Hán (漢) times, the territory of the kingdom of Jiāodōng (膠東國).
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn (晉武帝) established Chángguǎng Commandery (長廣郡).
Later, Wèi (魏) made it the seat of Guāngzhōu (光州).
In the first year of Rénshòu (仁壽) of Suí (隋),
Chángguǎng (長廣) was renamed Jiāoshuǐ (膠水) County,
subordinate to Láizhōu (萊州).
15 On the *Jǐsì* day,
the Emperor visited Dìngkūn Pond (Dìngkūnchí 定昆池),
ordering his retinue to compose poems.
Lǐ Rìzhī (李日知), the Huangmen Shilang (黃門侍郎), wrote in his poem:
"My wish is that you occasionally consider the ease of those dwelling here,
and not let it be said that the creators are toiling."
When Ruìzōng (睿宗) ascended the throne,
he said to Rìzhī (日知):
"At that time,
even I dared not speak such words."
Ruìzōng's (睿宗) words
likely referred to the fear of Princess Ānlè's (安樂公主) influence at that time.

on the *Wùchén* day,
Sū Huái (蘇懷) was appointed Right Grandee Secretary (Yòu Púyè 右僕射) and concurrently Jointly in Charge of the Secretariat-Chancellery (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn 同中書門下三品).
17 Princesses Tàipíng (太平) and Ānlè (安樂) each formed factions,
mutually slandering each other,
which troubled the Emperor.
In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the *Guǐhài* day,
the Emperor said to Wǔ Píngyī (武平一), a Scholar of the Bureau of Cultivated Literature (Xiūwénguǎn Zhí Xuéshì 修文館直學士):
"Recently I hear that many close relatives and nobles, both inside and outside the court, are not harmonious.
By what method can they be reconciled?"
Píngyī (平一) believed:
"This is due to treacherous and flattering individuals secretly causing discord.
It is appropriate to admonish them deeply and banish the cunning and insidious.
If this still does not stop,
I humbly wish that Your Majesty would look beyond immediate concerns,
suppress leniency and uphold strictness,
demonstrate awareness of prohibitions,
and not allow evil to accumulate."
The Emperor bestowed silk upon Píngyī (平一) but was unable to use his words.
18 The Emperor summoned former Scholars of the Bureau of Cultivated Literature (Xiūwénguǎn Xuéshì 修文館學士) Cuī Shí (崔湜) and Zhèng Yīn (鄭愔) to attend the grand ceremony.
On the *Yǐchǒu* day,
the Emperor sacrificed to the Southern Suburb,
granted a general amnesty to the empire,
including the Ten Abominations, all of which were pardoned;
the Ten Abominations are usually not pardonable by acts of grace.
Those Fasting Maidens (zhāiniáng 齋娘) who had husbands
were all reassigned to official posts.
19 On the *Jiǎxū* day,
Dòulú Qīnwàng (豆盧欽望), Kaifu Yitong Sansi (開府儀同三司) and Pingzhang Junguo Zhongshi (平章軍國重事), passed away.
The title Pingzhang Junguo Zhongshi (平章軍國重事)
likely began with Dòulú Qīnwàng (豆盧欽望).
20 On the *Yǐhài* day,
the Tǔbō (吐蕃) Zānpǔ (贊普) dispatched his minister Shàng Zànduō (尚贊咄) and over a thousand people to meet Princess Jīnchéng (金城公主).
21 Sòng Wùguāng (宋務光), Censor-in-chief and Inspector of Hénán Circuit (Hénándào Xúnchásǐ Jiānchá Yùshǐ 河南道巡察使、監察御史), submitted a memorial, stating
"At that time, there were over 140 families enjoying actual enfeoffment (shífēng 食實封).
According to Táng (唐) regulations: those enjoying actual enfeoffment
received true households,
all of which had three or more adult males,
and one part went to the state.
The Kaìyuán (開元) fixed regulations
limited it to three adult males,
and all taxes and levies went entirely to the enfeoffed family.
All the most fertile lands were allocated,
or one enfeoffment was divided among several prefectures;
but Princesses Tàipíng (太平) and Ānlè (安樂) further took those with high wealth and many adult males,
exploiting them excessively and harshly,
so that those designated as enfeoffed households suffered more than those under corvée labor.
Huázhōu (滑州), where silk gauze was produced (
the 'Six Codes of Táng' (Táng Liùdiǎn 唐六典) states
Huázhōu (滑州) contributed square-patterned silk gauze),
particularly suffered from this abuse,
and many people fled;
I request that the enfeoffed households be slightly redistributed among other prefectures.
Furthermore,
the envoys collecting enfeoffment taxes troubled both public and private affairs;
I request that this be attached to the land tax and poll tax,
and paid annually."
The Emperor did not heed him.
22 At this time, all exiles were allowed to return,
but Qíáo Wáng Chóngfú (譙王重福), the Prefect of Jūnzhōu (均州), alone was not permitted to return.
Chóngfú (重福) was exiled to Jūnzhōu (均州); see the first year of Shénlóng (神龍) in the preceding scroll.
重, pronounced *zhòng*.
"Your Majesty kindled firewood and performed rites,
sacrificed to the Supreme Heaven in the suburbs.
All the common people received pardon,
yet this child of the people (chìzǐ 赤子) is specifically rejected.
Chìzǐ (赤子) refers to Chóngfú (重福) himself.
Is it truly like this?
All those in the empire who hear this shed tears for your subject.
How much more so Your Majesty's merciful thoughts,
should you not pity your subject's wandering plight!"
"Wandering plight" (qīhuáng 栖遑) means separation, anxiety, and distress.
No reply was given.
23 Táng Xiūjǐng (唐休璟), former Right Grandee Secretary (Yòu Púyè 右僕射) who had retired,
was over eighty years old, yet still keen to advance,
and married the adopted daughter of the Head of the Palace Ladies (Hèlóu Shànggōng 賀婁尚宮) for his son.
In the twelfth month,
on the *Rénchén* day,
Xiūjǐng (休璟) was appointed Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàoshī 太子少師) and concurrently Jointly in Charge of the Secretariat-Chancellery (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn 同中書門下三品).
24 On the *Jiǎwǔ* day,
the Emperor visited the Hot Springs at Líshān (Líshān Wēntāng 驪山溫湯);

A separate estate served as a manor.
He was granted the title Duke Xiāoyáo (Xiāoyáo Gōng 逍遙公).
The affair of Wéi Xiòng (韋敻) can be found in scroll 167, third year of Yǒngdìng (永定) of Emperor Gāozǔ of Chén (陳高祖).
敻, pronounced *xiōng*.
He was a distant relative of the Empress.
Because of this, he received especially significant attention and rewards.
On the *Yǐsì* day,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
In that year,
Guānzhōng suffered a famine,
with a dou of rice costing a hundred coins.
Grain was transported from Shāndōng, Jiāng, and Huái to the capital,
but eight or nine out of ten oxen died.
Many officials requested that the imperial carriage return to the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū),
but Empress Wéi, whose family was originally from Dùlíng,
was unwilling to move east.
So she had the shaman Péng Jūnqīng and others tell the Emperor,
"This year is unfavorable for eastward travel."
When others spoke of it again,
the Emperor angrily said,
"How can there be an emperor who chases after food!"
So the matter was dropped.
Ruìzōng Xuánzhēn Dàshèng Dàxīng Xiàohuángdì, whose personal name
was Dàn,
was the eighth son of Gāozōng.
His initial name was Xùlún,
later he removed the character Xù and was named Lún,
and later still his name was changed to Dàn.
Initially, his posthumous title was Dàshèng Zhēnhuángdì,
and his temple name was Ruìzōng;
in the eighth year of Tiānbǎo,
he was posthumously honored as Xuánzhēn Dàshèng Huángdì;
in the thirteenth year,
he was further honored as Xuánzhēn Dàshèng Dàxīng Xiàohuángdì.
In the first year of Jǐngyún
(gēngxū, 710 AD),
in the sixth month of that year, the reign title was changed to Tánglóng,
and in the seventh month, it was again changed to Jǐngyún.
In spring,
in the first month,
on the night of bǐngyín,
Zhōngzōng and Empress Wéi secretly went to the market to observe the lanterns,
and also allowed several thousand palace women to go out and roam,
many of whom did not return.
The Emperor ordered Jì Chùnà to escort Princess Jīnchéng to Tǔbō,
but Chùnà declined;
he then ordered Zhào Yànzhāo,
and Yànzhāo also declined.
On dīngchǒu,
he ordered the Grand General of the Left Xiāowèi, Yáng Jǔ, to escort her.
On jǐmǎo,
the Emperor personally escorted the princess to Shǐpíng;
in the second month,
on guǐwèi,
he returned to the palace.
When the princess arrived in Tǔbō,
the Zānpǔ built a separate city for her to reside in.
On gēngxū,
the Emperor visited the Líyuán Ball Court.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Líyuán was north of Guānghuàmén.
Guānghuàmén was
the first gate at the western end of the southern side of the Forbidden Park,
west of Fānglín and Jǐngyào gates.
Zhōngzōng ordered scholars to enter through Fānglínmén,
gather at Líyuán,
and divide into teams for tug-of-war;
thus Líyuán was west of Tàijígōng,
within the Forbidden Park.
In the second year of Kāiyuán,
Xuánzōng established the Jiàofāng at Péngláigōng,
and personally taught ritual music,
referring to the students as Líyuán Dìzǐ.
By the middle of Tiānbǎo,
the Yíchūn Běiyuàn was established in the Eastern Palace,
and several hundred palace women were appointed as Líyuán Dìzǐ.
Líyuán was a place for practicing music,
and those taught beforehand were called dìzǐ.
In all cases, Péngláigōng and Yíchūnyuàn
were not within Líyuán.
Wéi Jùyuán and Táng Xiūjǐng, being old and frail,
stumbled over a rope and fell to the ground,
unable to rise for a long time;
the Emperor, Empress, and princesses watched,
and laughed heartily.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
on bǐngxū,
the Emperor visited Fānglínyuán.
According to records, the Táng Forbidden Park was extensive;
the entire Han Cháng'ān capital city
was within the Táng park,
and the Cáojú (canal) first received water from the Fēng River,
flowed north, then bent into the Forbidden Park and flowed east,
then bent again, flowed north, and entered the Wèi River.
The parkland extended from the east of the Cáojú,
to the west of the Dà'ānpálace walls,
reaching south to be level with the palace city,
with three gates arranged to the south,
the middle one being Fānglín.
Entering the Forbidden Park from Fānglínmén,
that area was known as Fānglínyuán.
Cherries,
according to the Éryǎ, were called xiējīngtáo.
The trees provided much shade,
ripened before other fruits,
were as large as a thumb,
round and red,
and sweet in taste.
Each cluster typically had ten to twenty fruits,
with pits the size of beans.
Because they were held in the mouths of orioles,
they were also called hántáo.
Initially,
during the reign of Zétiān,
a well in the home of Wáng Chún, a commoner in the eastern corner of Cháng'ān city, overflowed,
forming a large pond several tens of qǐng in size,
called Lóngqìngchí.
The pond was south of Lóngqìngfāng.
Chéng Dàchāng said: The rise of emperors,
if accompanied by auspicious signs, has its own logic,
but many accounts are fabricated.
The Liùdiǎn records that in Lóngqìngfāng there was a well
that suddenly gushed forth to form a small pond,
tens of zhàng in circumference,
often with clouds and mist,
or a yellow dragon emerging from it.
By the Jǐngyún period,
water secretly re-emerged,
and the pool gradually expanded,
so the local residents all moved away,
and it became a vast Lóngchí.
However, after my detailed examination,
the Cháng'ān Zhì states: Lóngchí was south of Yuèlóngmén,
originally flat ground,
but since the early Chuígǒng era,
due to rainwater and floods, it became a small stream;
later, water from the Lóngshǒuqú canal was diverted to irrigate it,
and it expanded daily.
By the Jǐnglóng period,
it stretched for several qǐng,
and was several zhàng deep,
often associated with stories of clouds and dragons,
and later came to be called Lóngchí.
The Zhì also states: In the southeast corner outside the Suí city was the Lóngshǒuyàn (weir),
from which the Chǎnshǔi was divided and flowed north to Chánglèpō,
where it divided into two canals,
the western one flowing southwest from Yǒngjiāfāng past Xīngqìnggōng.
Thus, Xīngqìng's ability to transform flat ground into Lóngchí
was actually due to the power of diverting the Chǎn River.
However, the account in the Liùdiǎn
completely omits the fact of diverting the Chǎn,
instead saying that initially a well overflowed,
and later a spring emerged,
combining two waters to form this pond,
attributing it entirely to natural transformation.
Shòuchūn Wáng Chéngqì,
Línzī Wáng Lóngjī,
Héngyáng Wáng Chéngyì,
Bālíng Wáng Lóngfàn,
Péngchéng Wáng Lóngyè.
These five princes were all sons of the Emperor.
"They always possessed the imposing air of emperors,
which has become particularly strong recently."
On yǐwèi,
the Emperor visited Lóngqìngchí.
The Kǎoyì states: The Jǐnglóng Wénguǎnjì believes it was the twelfth day of that month.
According to the Chánglì,
the first day of this month was rénwǔ.
We now follow the Shílù and Běnjì.
He feasted his attendant officials
and dispelled the omens by floating boats and playing with elephants.
Láng Jí, from Dìngzhōu, submitted a memorial,
stating,
"Empress Wéi and Zōng Chǔkè are about to commit rebellion."
Empress Wéi informed the Emperor, who had him beaten to death.
In the fifth month,
on dīngmǎo,
Yàn Qīnrong, the Sībīng Cānjūn of Xǔzhōu from Yǎnshī, again submitted a memorial,
stating,
"The Empress is promiscuous
and interferes in state affairs.
In the Táng dynasty, Sībīng Cānjūn (Staff Officer in charge of military affairs) in various prefectures managed the selection of military officials, weapons, and armaments,
gate keys and locks,
military defenses and beacon towers,
as well as post stations and hunting.
Yàn is pronounced with a jiān fān tone.
Fù is pronounced with a fú yòu fān tone.
Shàng is pronounced with a shí zhǎng fān tone.
Princess Ānlè, Wǔ Yánxiù, and Zōng Chǔkè are conspiring to endanger the imperial ancestral temple."
The Emperor summoned Qīnrong to question him in person.
Qīnrong kowtowed and spoke forcefully,
his expression unwavering;
the Emperor remained silent.
Zōng Chǔkè forged an imperial edict and ordered the Fēiqí (Flying Cavalry) to beat him to death,
throwing him onto the stone in the palace courtyard,
where he died with a broken neck.
Chǔkè shouted in satisfaction.
Although the Emperor did not pursue the inquiry,
he was quite displeased and uneasy;
from this, Empress Wéi and her faction began to fear.
This provided the prelude to Empress Wéi's regicide.
7 On the day Jǐmǎo,
the Emperor hosted a banquet for his close officials.
Zhù Qīnmíng (祝欽明), the chancellor of the Guózǐ (國子祭酒), voluntarily performed the Eight Winds Dance.
He shook his head and rolled his eyes,
displaying all sorts of grotesque postures.
What Zhù Qīnmíng called the Eight Winds Dance
was not what Zòng Zhòng (衆仲), a grand master of Lǔ (魯) in the Spring and Autumn period, meant by a dance that regulated the eight tones and expressed the eight winds.
He merely borrowed the name of the eight winds to perform various lewd and ugly acts.
Nowadays, people refer to licentious and irredeemable behavior as "wind" (風).
This is what Qīnmíng (欽明) meant by the Eight Winds.
Qīnmíng (欽明) was always renowned for his Confucian scholarship.
Lú Zàngyòng (盧藏用), the vice minister of the Lìbù (吏部侍郎), privately remarked to the various scholars:
"Master Zhù's (祝公) Five Classics are utterly swept away!"
The various scholars mentioned
were the scholars and resident scholars of the Xiūwén Guǎn (修文館學士及直學士).
8 Mǎ Qínkè (馬秦客), a Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), due to his medical skills,
and Yáng Jūn (楊均), a Guānglù Shǎoqīng (光祿少卿), due to his culinary expertise,
both frequently entered and exited the palace inner quarters
and were favored by Empress Wéi (韋后).
Fearing exposure and execution,
Sàn (散),
pronounced like "sī dǎn."
Qí (騎),
pronounced like "qí jì."

on the day Rénwǔ,
Emperor Zhōngzōng (中宗) died in the Shénlóng Diàn (神龍殿).

Shénlóng Diàn (神龍殿) was named after the era name.

To its left was the Shénlóng Mén (神龍門),
and inside it was the Shénlóng Diàn (神龍殿).
Yuè (樂),

Dàn (餤),

Empress Wéi (韋后) secretly withheld the news of the mourning
and personally took charge of all government affairs.
On the day Guǐwèi,
she summoned the various chancellors to the Forbidden City
and conscripted fifty thousand provincial troops to garrison the capital city.
She appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉) Wéi Jié (韋捷) and Wéi Guàn (韋灌),
Wéi Jié (韋捷) was married to Princess Chéng'ān (成安公主), daughter of Emperor Zhōngzōng (中宗).
Wéi Guàn (韋灌) was married to Princess Dìng'ān (定安公主).
Xuán (璿)

Pèi Tán (裴談), the minister of the Xíngbù (刑部尚書), and Zhāng Xī (張錫), the minister of the Gōngbù (工部尚書), were both appointed Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn (同中書門下三品),

Zhāng Jiāfú (張嘉福), the minister of the Lìbù (吏部尚書), Cén Xī (岑羲), the vice minister of the Zhōngshū (中書侍郎), and Cuī Shí (崔湜), the vice minister of the Lìbù (吏部侍郎), were all appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
Xī (羲)

Princess Tàipíng (太平公主) and Shàngguān Zhāoróng (上官昭容) conspired to draft an imperial edict
to establish Wēn Wáng Chóngmào (溫王重茂) as crown prince,
with the empress regent overseeing government affairs,
and Xiāng Wáng Dàn (相王旦) participating in political discussions.
Zōng Chǔkè (宗楚客) secretly said to Wéi Wēn (韋溫):
"The Prince of Xiāng (相王) assisting in government is inappropriate according to principle.
Furthermore, regarding the Empress,
it is not customary for a sister-in-law and brother-in-law to communicate privately."
This refers to the saying in the Qúlǐ (曲禮).
Xiāng (相),

Thereupon, he led the various chancellors to petition the empress to oversee court affairs

Sū Huái (蘇⿰王褱) said:
"How can an imperial will be altered!"
Wēn (溫) and Chǔkè (楚客) were enraged.
Huái (⿰王褱) became fearful and complied,
so the Prince of Xiāng (相王) was appointed Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
the imperial coffin was moved to the Tàijí Diàn (太極殿).
The main palace in the western inner compound was called the Tàijí Diàn (太極殿).
The Empress assumed regency,
granted a general amnesty to the empire,
and changed the era name to Tánglóng (唐隆).
Xiāng Wáng Dàn (相王旦) was promoted to Tàiwèi (太尉),
Yōng Wáng Shǒulǐ (雍王守禮) was made Bīn Wáng (豳王),
and Shòuchūn Wáng Chéngqì (壽春王成器) was made Sòng Wáng (宋王),
to conform with public expectation.
Wéi Wēn (韋溫) was ordered to take overall charge of the internal and external garrison troops and horses.
On the day Dīnghài,
Emperor Shāng (殤帝) ascended the throne,
at the age of sixteen.
The Empress was honored as Empress Dowager.
Lady Lù (陸氏) was made empress.
On the day Rénchén,
Jǐ Chǔnè (紀處訥) was ordered to hold the imperial insignia and patrol the Guānnèi Dào (關內道).
Cén Xī (岑羲) was assigned to the Hénán Dào (河南道),
and Zhāng Jiāfú (張嘉福) to the Héběi Dào (河北道).

Zōng Chǔkè (宗楚客), together with Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿) Wǔ Yánxiù (武延秀), Sīnóng Qīng (司農卿) Zhào Lǚwēn (趙履溫), Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (國子祭酒) Yè Jìngnéng (葉靜能), and other members of the Wéi (韋) clan, jointly urged Empress Wéi (韋后) to follow the precedents of Empress Wǔ (武后).
They intended to follow Empress Wǔ's (武后) precedent of changing the dynastic name.
The Southern Army (南軍) consisted of the sixteen guards' armies.
The Northern Army (北軍) consisted of the Yǔlín (羽林) and Wànqí (萬騎).
Táigé (臺閣) referred to the various bureaus of the Shàngshū (尚書).
They extensively gathered partisans
and formed internal and external alliances.
Chǔkè (楚客) also secretly submitted a memorial citing prophecies,
stating that the Wéi (韋) clan ought to reform the Táng (唐) dynasty.
They plotted to murder Emperor Shāng (殤帝),
were deeply wary of the Prince of Xiāng (相王) and Princess Tàipíng (太平公主),
and secretly conspired with Wéi Wēn (韋溫) and Princess Ānlè (安樂公主) to eliminate them.
The Prince of Xiāng's (相王) son, Línzī Wáng Lóngjī (臨淄王隆基),
had previously been dismissed from his post as Biejia of Lùzhōu (潞州別駕).
According to Táng (唐) regulations: Biejia of a superior prefecture was of rank four lower;
of a middle prefecture, rank five lower;
of an inferior prefecture, rank five upper.
He secretly gathered brave and capable men
and plotted to restore the dynasty.
Initially,
Emperor Tàizōng (太宗) selected valiant men from official households and foreign tribes,
dressed them in tiger-patterned clothes,
rode leopard-patterned saddles,
and had them accompany him on hunts,
shooting birds and beasts before his horses.
These were called the Bǎiqí (百騎).
During Empress Zétiān's (則天) time, their number was gradually increased to Qīanqí (千騎)
and they were subordinate to the left and right Yǔlín (羽林).
Emperor Zhōngzōng (中宗) called them Wànqí (萬騎)
and established commissioners to lead them.
Lóngjī (隆基) had befriended the heroes among them.
Cuī Rìyòng (崔日用), the vice minister of the Bīngbù (兵部侍郎), had always been close to the Wéi (韋) and Wǔ (武) clans.
He was on good terms with Zōng Chǔkè (宗楚客).
Knowing Chǔkè's (楚客) plot,
and fearing that disaster would befall him,
he sent Pǔrùn (普潤), a monk from Bǎochāng Sì (寶昌寺), to secretly visit Lóngjī (隆基) to inform him
and urge him to act quickly.
Lóngjī (隆基) then, with Princess Tàipíng (太平公主) and her son Xuē Chóngjiǎn (薛崇暕), the court attendant of the Wèiwèi (衞尉卿),
Zhōng Shàojīng (鍾紹京) from Gàn (贛人), the general supervisor of the Yuàn (苑總監),
Zhōng Shàojīng (鍾紹京) was the general supervisor of the Western Capital's imperial park.
The Táng (唐) capitals each had one general supervisor of the imperial park,
of rank five lower,
in charge of the palaces, gardens, and ponds within the imperial park,
overseeing all birds, fish, fruits, and trees.
Gànxiàn (贛縣),
in Hàn (漢) belonged to Yùzhāng Jùn (豫章郡),
in Wú (吳) and Jìn (晉) belonged to Lúlíng Jùn (廬陵郡),
from Sòng (宋) onwards it was the administrative seat of Nánkāng Jùn (南康郡),
and in Táng (唐) it was part of Qiánzhōu (虔州).
Gàn (贛),
Shīgǔ (師古) pronounced "gǔ àn,"
Liú Xù (劉昫) pronounced "gǔ làn."
and Má Sìzōng (麻嗣宗), the commanding officer of the Lìrén Fǔ (利仁府折衝),
Táng (唐) Yōngzhōu (雍州) had one hundred and thirty-one prefectures,
one hundred and twenty of which were outside the capital.
The Lìrén Fǔ (利仁府) must have belonged to Yōngzhōu (雍州).
Wéi Bō (韋播) and Gāo Sōng (高嵩) had repeatedly flogged the Wànqí (萬騎)
to establish their authority,
and the Wànqí (萬騎) all resented them.
Guǒyì (果毅) Gé Fúshùn (葛福順) and Chén Xuánlǐ (陳玄禮) saw Lóngjī (隆基) and complained to him.
Lóngjī (隆基) subtly suggested that they should eliminate the Wéi (韋) clan,
and they all eagerly offered to die for the cause.
Lǐ Xiānfú (李仙鳧), a Guǒyì (果毅) of the Wànqí (萬騎), also joined the conspiracy.
Someone suggested that Lóngjī (隆基) should inform the Prince of Xiāng (相王),
but Lóngjī (隆基) said:
"We are doing this for the sake of the dynasty.
If the mission succeeds, the blessings will go to the Prince.
If it fails, I will die for it,
without implicating the Prince.
If I inform him now and he agrees,
then the Prince will be involved in a dangerous affair.
If he does not agree,
then the great plan will be ruined."
Thus, he did not inform him.
Historians say that Lóngjī (隆基) had great strategic foresight,
which is why he was able to quell the internal rebellion.
Bài (敗),
pronounced like "bǔ mài."
On the day Gēngzǐ,
in the late afternoon,
Lí Lóngjī, in plain clothes, with Liú Yōuqú and others, entered the Forbidden Park.
The Táng Forbidden Park was north of the imperial city.
The park city measured twenty-seven lǐ from east to west
and thirty lǐ from north to south.
To the east, it reached the Bàshuǐ;
to the west, it connected to the old Cháng'ān city;
to the south, it adjoined the capital city;
and to the north, it rested against the Wèishuǐ.
Within the park were twenty-four detached palaces, pavilions, and viewing platforms.
The old Hàn Cháng'ān city, thirteen lǐ from east to west,
was all incorporated into the park.
Wèi Shàojīng regretted
and wanted to refuse,
but his wife, née Xǔ, said:
“To sacrifice oneself for the country,
the gods will surely assist.
Moreover, the conspiracy was long ago settled.
Even if you don't act now,
how can you escape?!”
Wèi Shàojīng then hastened out to bow and pay respects.
Lí Lóngjī clasped his hand and had him sit.
Wèi Shàojīng hastening out to bow and pay respects
showed his reverence for Lí Lóngjī;
Lí Lóngjī clasping his hand and having him sit
showed his humility
and aimed to secure his loyalty.
By night,
Gě Fúshùn and Lǐ Xiānfú both arrived at Lí Lóngjī's location,
requesting passwords to proceed.
Whenever troops were deployed, camps established, or attacks launched,
passwords were obtained from the commander-in-chief to prepare for emergencies
and for mutual identification.
Stars scattered like snow,
and Liú Yōuqú said:
“Heaven's will is thus;
the opportunity must not be lost!”
Gě Fúshùn drew his sword and went directly into the Yǔlín camp,
beheading Wéi Xuán, Wéi Bō, and Gāo Sōng as a warning,
saying:
“Empress Wéi poisoned the former Emperor
and plotted to endanger the state.
Tonight, we shall together execute all Wéis.
Those whose names are mentioned and those who are taller than a horse whip shall all be slain;
this means all Wéi men and women, adults, and those taller than a horse whip shall all be slain.
Dare anyone harbor ambivalence or aid the rebellious faction,
their crime will extend to their three clans.”
The Yǔlín soldiers all joyfully obeyed.
Then, the heads of Wéi Xuán and the others were sent to Lí Lóngjī.
Lí Lóngjī took a light to examine them,
and then, with Liú Yōuqú and others, exited the southern gate of the park.
The southern gate of the Forbidden Park
was directly opposite the Xuánwǔmén of the palace city.
They carried axes and saws with them.
Lí Lóngjī ordered Gě Fúshùn to lead the left division of ten thousand cavalry to attack Xuándémén,
and Lǐ Xiānfú to lead the right division of ten thousand cavalry to attack Báishòumén.
Báishòumén was Báishòutà,
which is what Dù Fǔ's “Běizhēng” poem refers to as
“the solitary Báishòutà,”
and it,
along with Xuándémén, were among the inner palace gates.
Jiàng
is read jiàng;
the same below.
They then let out a great shout.
Gě Fúshùn and others together killed the gate guards
and broke through the gates to enter.
Lí Lóngjī arrayed his troops outside Xuánwǔmén.
After three drumbeats,
hearing the shouting,
he led the supervisors-general and Yǔlín soldiers to enter.
The guards stationed in the Tàijídiàn to protect the imperial coffin,
these were the southern guards,
all donned armor and responded.
Empress Wéi, confused and terrified, fled into the Fēiqíjìng.
A Fēiqí soldier beheaded her and presented it to Lí Lóngjī.
Princess Ānlè was looking in a mirror and drawing her eyebrows
when soldiers beheaded her.
Wǔ Yánxiù was beheaded outside Sùzhāngmén.
The Inner General Hèlóu Shì was beheaded west of the Tàijídiàn.
At that time, Empress Wéi appointed women as Inner Generals,
which was likely Hèlóu Shànggōng.
Initially,
Shàngguān Zhāoróng had her maternal cousin, Wáng Yù, appointed as Zuǒ Shíyí.
The sisters of one's mother are called maternal cousins.
Cóng
is read cóng.
“The Wǔ clan,
abandoned by Heaven,
cannot be revived.
Now, Jíeyú is attached to Wǔ Sānsī;
this is a path to clan extermination.
I hope my aunt will consider this!”
Zhèng Shì used this to warn Zhāoróng,
but Zhāoróng did not listen.
When Crown Prince Lǐ Chóngjùn raised troops to punish Wǔ Sānsī
and sought Zhāoróng –
the details are in the previous volume, Jǐnglóng First Year –
Suǒ
is read suǒ;
the same below.
Zhāoróng reflected on Wáng Yù's words;
from then on, her heart inclined towards the imperial house,
and she and Princess Ānlè each formed their own factions.
When Zhōngzōng died,
Zhāoróng drafted an imperial edict to establish Prince Wēn,
with Prince Xiāng assisting in government.
However, Zōng [Chǔkè] and Wéi [Hòu] altered it.
When Lí Lóngjī entered the palace,
Zhāoróng held a candle and led palace women to welcome him,
showing the drafted edict to Liú Yōuqú.
Liú Yōuqú spoke on her behalf,
but Lí Lóngjī did not permit it
and had her beheaded beneath the banner.
At that time, the young Emperor was in the Tàijídiàn.
Liú Yōuqú said:
“The multitude pledged tonight to enthrone Prince Xiāng;
why not decide early?”
Lí Lóngjī hurriedly stopped him,
and then rounded up and beheaded all Wéis within the palace, those guarding the gates,
and those who were habitually close confidants of Empress Wéi.
By dawn,
everything inside and outside was settled.
On the day Xīnsì,
Lí Lóngjī went out to see Prince Xiāng,
bowing his head to apologize for not having informed him first.
Prince Xiāng embraced him, weeping, and said:
“The altars of state and the imperial ancestral temple did not fall to the ground;
this is your strength.”
Thereupon, Prince Xiāng was welcomed in to assist the young Emperor.
The palace gates and the capital city gates were closed.
Ten thousand cavalry were dispatched to arrest all relatives and partisans of the Wéi clan.
The Crown Prince's Junior Protector and Minister of Central Secretariat and Chancellery of the Third Grade, Wéi Wēn, was beheaded north of the East Market.
The Central Secretariat Director, Zōng Chǔkè, wearing mourning clothes and riding a green donkey, escaped.
Upon reaching Tōnghuàmén,
the gatekeepers said:
“Duke,
you are Minister Zōng.”
He took off his cloth cap,
was seized and beheaded,
and his younger brother Jìnqīng was also beheaded.
Kǎoyì states: Tàishàng Shílù says:
“Zōng Chǔkè was beheaded outside Chūnmíngmén.”
Now following Qiānzài.
Tàishàng Lù,
“Jìnqīng was killed at Dìnglíng.”
Upon examination, Dìnglíng
was Zhōngzōng's mausoleum,
which did not exist at that time;
so it is not adopted here.
Qù
is read qù.
The common people were appeased.
Táng Liùdiǎn states: On the west side of the imperial city were two gates:
the northern one was Ānfúmén, the southern one Shùnyìmén.
Ānfúmén directly faced Kāiyuǎnmén to its west.
Zhào Lǚwēn spent the nation's wealth to serve Princess Ānlè,
building mansions and residences for her,
and constructing terraces and digging ponds without ceasing.
He wore a purple tunic
and used his neck to pull the Princess's calf-cart.
When the Princess died,
Zhào Lǚwēn rushed to the foot of Ānfúlóu to dance and shout “Long Live!”
Before his voice faded,
Prince Xiāng ordered ten thousand cavalry to behead him.
The common people resented his forced labor
and eagerly cut off his flesh until it was all gone.
The Palace Secretary, Prince Yōng of Biàn,
married the younger sister of Empress Wéi, Lady Chóngguó.
Chóng
is an ancient state name.
Yōng
was the grandson of Fèng.
Fèng
was the son of Gāozǔ.
His family advised him to flee and hide,
but Jùyuán said:
“I am a high minister;
