how can I hear of trouble and not respond?!”
He went out to the capital street
and was killed by the rebellious soldiers,
then eighty years old.
Thereupon, the heads of Mǎ Qínkè, Yáng Jūn, Yè Jìngnéng, and others were displayed,
and Empress Wéi's corpse was exposed in the market.
Cuī Rìyòng led soldiers to execute the Wéis in Dùqū.
South of the Táng capital city,
the Wéi and Dù clans resided there,
hence called Wéiqū and Dùqū.
A saying went:
“The Wéi and Dù of the city's south
are but five inches from Heaven.”
At that time, the Wéi clan's prestige was strong,
encroaching upon Dùqū and residing there.
Xiāo
is read xiāo.
Jiàng
is read jiàng,
also pronounces as jiāng.
Many of the Dù clan were wrongly killed.
On this day,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the empire,
stating:
"The head of the rebellious bandits has been executed;
as for the remaining factions, no questions will be asked."
Línzī Wáng Lóngjī was made Píng Wáng,
concurrently overseeing the inner and outer imperial stables.
Píng Wáng insisted that Píngzhōu be the name of his state,
because he had indeed pacified an internal rebellion,
and thus he was honored with this name.
According to the Six Statutes, the Shàngchéng Fèngyù
was in charge of the horses of the inner and outer imperial stables.
First were the Left and Right Fēihuáng Stables;
second were the Left and Right Jíliáng Stables;
third were the Left and Right Lóngméi Stables;
fourth were the Left and Right Táotú Stables;
fifth were the Left and Right Kuàití Stables;
sixth were the Left and Right Tiānyuàn Stables.
During the Kāiyuán era,
the six imperial stables within the palace were called Fēilóng, Xiánglín, Fèngyuàn, Yuānlán, Jíliáng, and Liùlóng;
two other stables were Bēnxīng and Nèijū.
Outside the palace were the Left Fēi, Right Fēi, Left Wàn, and Right Wàn stables, making four;
and the Dōngnán Nèi and Xīnán Nèi stables, making two.
The Left and Right Wings
were what were formerly called the Left Wànqí and Right Wànqí.
Zhōng Shàojīng was appointed Shǒuzhōngshū Shìláng,
and Liú Yōuqíu was appointed Shǒuzhōngshū Shèrén,
both participating in advising on state affairs.
Má Sìzōng served as Yòujīnwú Wèi Zhōnglángjiàng.
The Wǔ clan members
were almost entirely executed, exiled, or banished.
The Wǔ clan members should have been entirely executed or banished by this time.
However, the historian wrote "almost entirely" because
Yōuxù and Píngyī were able to avoid power and distant influence,
and Wǔ Huì was still sufficient to cause the disaster of the killing of the three sons.
Lìbù Shàngshū Tóng Píngzhāngshì Zhāng Jiāfú, having traveled to Huáizhōu,
was arrested and beheaded there.
According to old records,
Huázhōu
was 180 *lǐ* east of the capital.
Huáizhōu
was 969 *lǐ* east of the capital.
Huá
is pronounced *hù huà fān*.
On *Rén'yín*,
Liú Yōuqíu was in the Tàijí Diàn.
A palace woman and an eunuch asked Yōuqíu to draft an imperial edict to enthrone the Empress Dowager.
Yōuqíu said:
"The state is in great difficulty,
people's hearts are uneasy,
and the imperial tomb is not yet finished.
To hastily enthrone an Empress Dowager
is not permissible!"
Píng Wáng Lóngjī said:
"Do not speak lightly of this."
Envoys were dispatched to the ten circuits with imperial edicts to convey soothing messages,
and also to Jūnzhōu to console Qiáo Wáng Chóngfú.
Dòu Cóngyī was demoted to Háozhōu Sīmǎ.
According to old records,
Háozhōu
was 2,150 *lǐ* southeast of the capital.
During Zhōngzōng's reign,
Tàipíng, Ānlè, and seven other princesses all established administrative offices with officials.
On *Guǐmǎo*,
Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ transmitted the young emperor's command,
requesting to yield the throne to Xiàng Wáng.
Xiàng Wáng steadfastly declined.
Píng Wáng Lóngjī was made Diànzhōngjiān and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
Sòng Wáng Chéngqì was made Zuǒwèi Dàjiāngjūn.
Héngyáng Wáng Chéngyì was made Yòuwèi Dàjiāngjūn.
Bālíng Wáng Lóngfàn was made Zuǒyǔlín Dàjiāngjūn.
Péngchéng Wáng Lóngyè was made Yòuyǔlín Dàjiāngjūn.
Guānglù Shàoqīng Sìdào Wáng Wēi was appointed Jiǎnjiào Yòujīnwú Wèi Dàjiāngjūn.
Wēi
was Yuánqìng's grandson.
Dào Wáng Yuánqìng
was Gāozǔ's son.
Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ's son Xuē Chóngxùn was made Yòuqianniú Wèi Jiāngjūn.
Lóngjī had two servants,
Wáng Máozhòng and Lǐ Shǒudé,
both agile and skilled in archery and horsemanship,
who always attended him by his side.
When Lóngjī entered the imperial park,
Máozhòng hid and did not follow.
He only returned several days after the matter was settled.
Lóngjī did not blame him,
but instead promoted him to general.
Máozhòng
was originally from Gāolì.
This lays the groundwork for Wáng Máozhòng's future favor and subsequent downfall.
Lì
is pronounced *lì zhī fān*.
According to old records: Qìnzhōu
was 1,025 *lǐ* northeast of the capital.
Qìn
is pronounced *qī zhèn fān*.
Zhōngshū Lìng Xiāo Zhìzhōng was demoted to Xǔzhōu Cìshǐ.
According to old records,
Xǔzhōu
was 1,200 *lǐ* east of the capital.
Zhōngshū Shìláng Tóng Píngzhāngshì Zhào Yànzhāo was demoted to Jiàngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Lìbù Shìláng Tóng Píngzhāngshì Cuī Shí was demoted to Huázhōu Cìshǐ.
Liú Yōuqíu spoke to Sòng Wáng Chéngqì and Píng Wáng Lóngjī, saying:
"Xiàng Wáng previously occupied the imperial throne,
and the hopes of the multitude rest on him."
In the first year of the Sìshèng era,
Zétiān deposed Zhōngzōng and enthroned Xiàng Wáng.
When the revolution occurred,
the King was made the imperial heir.
Shǔ
is pronounced *zhī yù fān*.
"The affairs of the family and state are weighty.
How can Xiàng Wáng still adhere to minor principles
and not promptly ascend the throne to stabilize the empire!"
Lóngjī said:
"The King's nature is peaceful and indifferent;
he does not allow state affairs to trouble his mind."
"State affairs" (*dàishì*) means "worldly affairs" (*shìshì*), used to avoid the taboo of Tàizōng's personal name.
"He still yields to others,"
meaning he yielded to Empress Wǔ,
and also yielded to Zhōngzōng.
"How could he take his place?"
Yōuqíu said:
"The will of the people cannot be defied.
Even if the King wishes to remain aloof and content with his own virtue,
what about the altars of soil and grain (the state)?"
Chéngqì and Lóngjī entered to see Xiàng Wáng,
and spoke extensively about the matter.
Xiàng Wáng then assented.
On *Jiǎchén*,
the young emperor stood facing west in the eastern corner of the Tàijí Diàn.
Xiàng Wáng stood beside the imperial coffin.
Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ said:
"The Emperor wishes to yield this position to his uncle.
Is this acceptable?"
Yōuqíu knelt and said:
"The state has experienced many difficulties.
The Emperor is benevolent and filial,
following the footsteps of Yáo and Shùn.
This is truly in line with ultimate impartiality.
Xiàng Wáng will take on a heavy responsibility,
and his compassion and love are especially profound."
Then, with the young emperor's imperial edict, the throne was transmitted to Xiàng Wáng.
At that time, the young emperor was still on the throne.
Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ stepped forward and said:
"The hearts of the empire have already turned to Xiàng Wáng.
This is not a child's seat!"
Thereupon, she pulled him down.
Ruìzōng ascended the throne,
held court at Chéngtiān Mén,
and declared a general amnesty throughout the empire.
The main western gate of the inner city of the capital was called Chéngtiān Mén.
Zhōng Shàojīng was made Zhōngshū Lìng.
When he was young,
Zhōng Shàojīng served as Sīnóng Lùshì.
All nine ministries of the Táng dynasty had *Lùshì* officials,
of the ninth rank,
which were probably outside the regular official stream.
Shǎo
is pronounced *shī zhào fān*.
He arbitrarily dispensed rewards and punishments;
everyone disliked him.
Tàicháng Shàoqīng Xuē Jì advised him to submit a memorial showing humility and deference.
Shàojīng followed this advice.
Jì entered and spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"Although Shàojīng has rendered meritorious service,
he inherently lacks talent and virtue.
Having risen from a mere clerk,
to suddenly be elevated to the position of chief minister
might compromise the esteemed reputation of the sagacious court."
The *Shī* says: "Illustrious Shī Yǐn,
the people all look up to you."
On *Bǐngwǔ*,
he was reappointed Hùbù Shàngshū,
and soon after was sent out as Shǔzhōu Cìshǐ.
According to old records,
Shǔzhōu was 3,332 *lǐ* from the capital.
9. The emperor was about to establish an heir apparent.
Sòng Wáng Chéngqì was the legitimate eldest son,
but Píng Wáng Lóngjī had rendered great service.
The emperor was hesitant and could not decide.
Chéngqì declined, saying:
"If the state is at peace, the legitimate eldest son takes precedence.
If the state is in peril, the one who has rendered service takes precedence.
If we deviate from what is appropriate,
the whole world will be disappointed.
I would rather die than be placed above Píng Wáng."
He tearfully and firmly requested this for several days.
Many high officials also argued that Píng Wáng's achievements were great and he should be established.
Liú Yōoqiú said:
"I have heard that those who remove the calamities of the world
should enjoy the blessings of the world.
Píng Wáng rescued the altars of grain and soil from danger
and saved the sovereign and his kin from difficulty.
In terms of merit, none is greater;
in terms of virtue, none is more worthy.
There is nothing to doubt."
The emperor agreed with him.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
Píng Wáng Lóngjī was established as the Heir Apparent.
The *Kǎoyì* (Textual Research) states: Liú Zǐxuán first compiled the *Tàishàng Huáng Shílù* (Veritable Records of the Retired Emperor),
covering up to the abdication.
Later, he compiled the *Ruìzōng Shílù* (Veritable Records of Emperor Ruìzōng),
covering up to Qiáolíng.
The texts are quite different.
The *Ruìzōng Lù* and the Old Annals both say,
"On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
the Heir Apparent was established."
Now, the *Tàishàng Huáng Lù* is followed.
[This was] not permitted.
10. Empress Wǔ Dàshèng Fù (Wǔ Zétiān) had her former title restored as Tiānhòu.
Yōng Wáng Xián was posthumously honored with the title Zhānghuái Tàizǐ.
The deposition of Xián is seen in Volume 202, Gāozōng, Yǒnglóng first year.
Yōng,
pronounced *yúyòng*;
similarly below.
11. On the *wùshēn* day,
Sòng Wáng Chéngqì was made Yōngzhōu Mù, Yángzhōu Dàdūdū, and Tàizǐ Tàishī.
12. Wēn Wáng Chóngmào was kept in the inner residence.
[This was] out of fear that some scoundrels might use him to cause trouble.
13. Xuē Jì, the Tàicháng Shàocīng, was made Huángmén Shìláng
and participated in deliberating state affairs.
Jì was skilled in calligraphy
and had served the emperor at his princely mansion.
His son, Bóyáng, married Xiānyuán Gōngzhǔ.
Xiānyuán Gōngzhǔ
was a daughter of the emperor,
later enfeoffed as Jīngshān Gōngzhǔ.
14. Wǔ Sānsī and Wǔ Chóngxùn were posthumously stripped of their peerage and posthumous titles,
their coffins were hacked open and their corpses exposed,
and their graves were leveled.
15. Yáo Yuánzhī, the Xǔzhōu Cìshǐ, was made Bīngbù Shàngshū and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
Wéi Sìlì, the Sòngzhōu Cìshǐ, and Xiāo Zhìzhōng, the Xǔzhōu Cìshǐ, were made Zhōngshū Lìng.
Zhào Yànzhāo, the Jiàngzhōu Cìshǐ, was made Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Cuī Shí, the Huázhōu Cìshǐ, was made Lìbù Shìláng.
All of them were Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
16. Sòng Zhīwèn, the Yuèzhōu Zhǎngshǐ,
and Rǎn Zǔyōng, the Ráozhōu Cìshǐ,
for fawning upon Wéi and Wǔ,
were all banished to the Lingnan region.
17. On the *jǐyǒu* day,
Héngyáng Wáng Chéngyì was established as Shēn Wáng.
Bālíng Wáng Lóngfàn as Qí Wáng.
Péngchéng Wáng Lóngyè as Xuē Wáng.
Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ's actual enfeoffment was increased to ten thousand households.
Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ was astute and resourceful with many strategies.
Empress Wǔ thought she was like herself,
and thus among her children, she alone was favored and loved,
and was quite involved in secret plans.
However, she still feared Empress Wǔ's strictness
and dared not openly wield power and influence.
When Zhāng Yìzhī was executed,
the princess was instrumental.
The execution of Zhāng Yìzhī is seen in Volume 207, Zhōngzōng, Shénlóng first year.
Empress Wéi and Ānlè Gōngzhǔ both feared her.
She also joined the Heir Apparent in executing the Wéi clan.
Having repeatedly rendered great service,
she was increasingly respected.
The emperor often consulted with her on major state affairs.
Whenever she came to present matters,
they would sit and talk for a long time.
Sometimes, if she did not attend court,
the prime ministers would go to her residence to consult her.
Whenever the prime ministers presented matters,
the emperor would invariably ask,
"Have you discussed this with Tàipíng?"
And then he would ask, "Have you discussed this with Sānláng?"
Only then would he approve it.
Sānláng
referred to the Heir Apparent.
There was nothing the princess desired that the emperor would not grant.
From the prime ministers downwards,
promotions and demotions depended on her single word.
The number of other recommended scholars who rapidly rose to prominent official positions was countless.
Her power overshadowed the sovereign,
and those who flocked to her gate
were like a marketplace.
Her sons, Xuē Chóngxíng, Chóngmǐn, and Chóngjiǎn, were all enfeoffed as kings.
Their fields and gardens spread throughout the nearby suburbs.
They collected and purchased various objects and artworks,
from as far as Lǐng and Shǔ,
with transporters constantly streaming along the roads.
Their residences and provisions
rivaled those of the imperial palace.
18. Láng Jí and Yān Qīnrong were posthumously granted the title of Jiànyì Dàfū.
19. Autumn,
seventh month,
on the *gēngxū* day, the first day of the month,
Wéi Yuèjiāng was posthumously granted the title of Xuānzhōu Cìshǐ.
The death of Wéi Yuèjiāng is seen in the previous volume, Zhōngzōng, Shénlóng second year.
20. On the *guǐchǒu* day,
Cuī Rìyòng, the Bīngbù Shìláng, was made Huángmén Shìláng
and participated in deliberating state affairs.
21. The former Heir Apparent Chóngjùn's title and rank were posthumously restored.
The death of Heir Apparent Chóngjùn is seen in the previous volume, Zhōngzōng, Jǐnglóng first year.
His official positions and peerage were restored.
The matter of the Five Kings is seen in the previous volume, Shénlóng second year.
Qiānlǐ and Duōzuò died together with Chóngjùn,
seen in Jǐnglóng first year.
22. On the *dīngsì* day,
Sòng Jǐng, the Luòzhōu Zhǎngshǐ, was made Jiǎnjiào Lìbù Shàngshū and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
Cén Xī was dismissed and made Yòusànqí Chángshì,
concurrently Xíngbù Shàngshū.
Jǐng and Yáo Yuánzhī worked together to reform the corrupt policies of Zhōngzōng,
promoting loyal and upright individuals,
and dismissing the unworthy.
Rewards and punishments were entirely just,
and solicitations were ineffective.
The state administration was rectified and revived.
At that time, everyone unanimously believed
that the spirit of Zhēngguān and Yǒnghuī had returned.
23. On the *rénxū* day,
Cuī Shí was dismissed and made Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
Zhāng Xī was made Jiàngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Xiāo Zhìzhōng was made Jìnzhōu Cìshǐ.
The old gazetteer states: Jìnzhōu
is 725 *lǐ* northeast of the capital.
Zhào Yànzhāo was made Sòngzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
Yáo Yuánzhī concurrently held the title of Zhōngshū Lìng.
Lǐ Qiáo, the Bīngbù Shàngshū and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn, was demoted to Huáizhōu Cìshǐ.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Tàizǐ Shàoshī and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn Táng Xiūjǐng retired.
Zhāng Rényuàn, the Yòu Wǔwèi Dàjiāngjūn and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn, was dismissed and made Zuǒwèi Dàjiāngjūn.
24. Cuī Rìyòng, the Huángmén Shìláng and Cānzhī Jīwù, and Xuē Jì, the Zhōngshū Shìláng and Cānzhī Jīwù, argued before the emperor.
Jì said:
"Rìyòng is fickle and in the past sided with Wǔ Sānsī;
he is not a loyal minister.
Selling out friends to claim merit;
he is not a righteous scholar."
Rìyòng said:
"Although I had faults in the past,
I have now rendered great service."
Rendering great service
refers to the plot to execute the Wéi clan,
which Rìyòng initiated.
[Jì] referred to Jì's son, Bóyáng, who married a princess.
"Is this not being fickle?"
The emperor therefore dismissed both of them.
On the *wùchén* day,
Rìyòng was made Yōngzhōu Zhǎngshǐ,
and Jì was made Zuǒsànqí Chángshì.
25. On the *jǐsì* day,
a general amnesty was granted to all under heaven,
and the era name was changed.
The era name was changed to Jǐngyún.
All were pardoned.
26. On the *yǐhài* day,
the Wǔ clan's Chóng'ēn Miào and Háolíng, Shùnlíng were abolished.
Zhōngzōng, Jǐnglóng first year, restored the Wǔ clan's tombs and temples.
Ānlè Gōngzhǔ was demoted to Bèinì Shùrén (Commoner of Rebellion).
27. When Empress Wéi oversaw the court,
Zhèng Yīn, the Lìbù Shìláng, was demoted to Jiāngzhōu Sīmǎ.
He secretly passed through Jūnzhōu
and conspired with Qí Wáng Chóngfú, the Cìshǐ, and Zhāng Língjūn of Luòyáng
to raise an army to execute the Wéi clan.
Before they acted, the Wéi clan was defeated.
Chóngfú was transferred to Jízhōu Cìshǐ.
Before he departed,
Língjūn persuaded Chóngfú, saying:
"Your Highness holds the position of the legitimate eldest son,
and should be the Son of Heaven.
Although Xiàng Wáng has rendered service,
he should not succeed to the throne.
The officials and commoners of the Eastern Capital
all wish for Your Highness to come.
If you secretly enter Luòyáng
and mobilize the troops of the Left and Right Tunying camps—
the Eastern Capital had Left and Right Tunying camps to guard the palace city—
taking control of the Eastern Capital
would be like descending from heaven.
Then, you can take Shǎnxia Zhōu to the west
and Hénán Běi to the east;
the whole world can be settled with a wave of your hand."
Chóngfú agreed.
Língjūn (靈均) then secretly plotted with Yīn (愔),
gathering dozens of followers.
At that time, Yīn (愔) had been demoted from Assistant Director of the Imperial Library to Prefect of Yuánzhōu (沅州).
In the second year of Tiānshòu (天授) of Empress Wǔ (武),
Wūzhōu (巫州) was renamed Yuánzhōu (沅州).
According to old gazetteers: Yuánzhōu (沅州)
is 4,197 *lǐ* (里) south of the capital,
and 3,900 *lǐ* (里) from the Eastern Capital.
They drafted an edict
to establish Zhòngfú (重福) as emperor,
changing the reign title to Zhōngyuán Kèfù (中元克復).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The *Tàishàng Huáng Shílù* (太上皇實錄) states:
"The reign title was changed to Zhōngzōng Kèfù Yuánnián (中宗克復元年)."
We now follow the *Xīnshū* (新書).
Wēn Wáng (溫王) was to be made皇tài dì (皇太弟, imperial younger brother of the crown prince),
Yīn (愔) was to be Left Chancellor and oversee civil affairs both internal and external,
Língjūn (靈均) was to be Right Chancellor and Tiānzhù Dàjiàngjūn (天柱大將軍, Great General Pillar of Heaven) and oversee military affairs,
and Yán Shànsī (嚴善思), Right Attendant-in-ordinary, was to be Minister of Rites and oversee the Ministry of Personnel.
Zhòngfú (重福) and Língjūn (靈均) falsely claimed to be on an imperial express journey to the Eastern Capital.
Yīn (愔) had already prepared a reception at the residence of the Imperial Son-in-law Pèi Xùn (裴巽) to await Zhòngfú (重福).
The magistrate of Luòyáng (洛陽) County faintly heard of their plot.
Collated and punctuated by Qí Sīhé (齊思和) and reviewed by Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐)
Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
compiled by imperial command
Hòu (後) Xué (學) Tiāntái (天台)
Jǐngyún (景雲) first year
(Gēngxū (庚戌), 710)
1. In the eighth month,
on the day *Gēngyín* (庚寅),
[they] went to Xùn's (巽) residence to investigate.
This follows from the previous volume's "The magistrate of Luòyáng (洛陽) County faintly heard of their plot."
The magistrate rushed out,
informing the acting grand marshal;
all officials fled and hid.
Only Cuī Rìzhī (崔日知), Chief Administrator of Luòzhōu (洛州), led troops to suppress them.
Lǐ Yōng (李邕), Acting Palace Censor, encountered Zhòngfú (重福) at Tiānjīn Qiáo (天津橋);
his followers already numbered several hundred.
[Lǐ Yōng (李邕)] galloped to the encampment
and announced:
"Qiáo Wáng (譙王) offended the former emperor" —
(meaning Zhòngfú (重福) offended Zhōngzōng (中宗)) —
"and was exiled to Jūnzhōu (均州).
This is certainly an act of rebellion;
you gentlemen should perform meritorious deeds to gain wealth and honor."
He also informed the Imperial City.
(This refers to the Imperial City of the Eastern Capital.)
Zhòngfú (重福) first hurried to the Left and Right Imperial Guards' camps.
Soldiers in the camps shot at him,
arrows falling like rain.
He then turned back and rushed to the Zuǒyè Mén (左掖門, Left Flank Gate),
intending to seize the acting grand marshal's troops.
Seeing the gate closed,
he was enraged
and ordered it to be burned.
Before the fire could ignite,
soldiers from the Left Imperial Guard camp came out to press him.
Zhòngfú (重福), in distress,
spurred his horse out of Shàngdōng (上東).
(*Rán* (然)
is the same as *rán* (燃).)
(*Jiǒng* (窘)
is pronounced *qú yún*.)
Shàngdōng (上東)
is the Shàngdōng Mén (上東門) of Luòchéng (洛城, Luoyang City),
the first gate from the north on the east side.
The next day,
the acting grand marshal sent out a large force to search for him.
Zhòngfú (重福) plunged into the Cáo Qú (漕渠, Grand Canal) and drowned.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: Both the *Ruìzōng Shílù* (睿宗實錄) and the old *Běnjì* (本紀) state
"On the day *Guǐsì* (癸巳), Zhòngfú (重福) rebelled."
We now follow the *Tàishàng Huáng Shílù* (太上皇實錄).
Rìyòng (日用) was his paternal cousin.
For his merits, he was appointed acting grand marshal of the Eastern Capital.
Zhèng Yīn (鄭愔) was ugly and had a bushy beard.
After his defeat,
he combed his hair into a bun
and wore women's clothing,
hiding in a carriage.
When captured
and interrogated,
his legs trembled and he could not speak.
Zhāng Língjūn (張靈均), his demeanor unchanged,
looked at Yīn (愔) and said,
"That I undertook this matter with such a person,
it is no wonder we failed!"
Both he and Yīn (愔) were executed in the Eastern Capital market.
Initially,
Yīn (愔) attached himself to Lái Jùnchén (來俊臣) and gained advancement.
When Jùnchén (俊臣) was executed,
he attached himself to Zhāng Yìzhī (張易之).
When Yìzhī (易之) was executed,
he attached himself to the Wéi (韋) clan.
When the Wéi (韋) clan fell,
he again attached himself to Qiáo Wáng (譙王) Zhòngfú (重福),
eventually suffering extermination of his clan.
The historians say that although Zhāng Língjūn (張靈均) was a man who delighted in misfortune and loved chaos,
he could still face death without flinching.
As for Zhèng Yīn (鄭愔),
constantly shifting between sycophancy and treachery,
heedless of consequences in pursuit of profit,
and yet so terrified of death,
how could he be fit to manage important affairs!
[Yán Shànsī (嚴善思)] was exiled to Jìngzhōu (靜州).
Jìngzhōu (靜州) in Língnán (嶺南)
had already been renamed Fùzhōu (富州) during the Zhēngguān (貞觀) era.
This Jìngzhōu (靜州) belonged to Jiànnán (劍南);
in the first year of Yífèng (儀鳳),
Nánhézhōu (南和州) was established from Xītáng (悉唐) County of Xīzhōu (悉州).
In the second year of Tiānshòu (天授) of Empress Wǔ (武),
it was renamed Jìngzhōu (靜州).
Yán Shànsī (嚴善思) was spared death and exiled here;
he had long relied on favored courtiers,
and now, involved in rebellion, he still managed to escape with his life.
2. The Wànqí (萬騎, Ten Thousand Cavalry), relying on their meritorious service in suppressing the Wéi (韋) clan,
became very violent and lawless.
The people of Cháng'ān (長安) suffered from this.
An edict ordered them all to be transferred to outer official posts.
It also stopped the practice of making household slaves into Wànqí (萬騎).
The practice of household slaves becoming Wànqí (萬騎)
must have originated after Yǒngchāng (永昌).
They were assigned to the Left and Right Yǔlín (羽林, Imperial Guard).
3. Yáo Yuánzhī (姚元之), Sòng Jǐng (宋璟), and Grand Censor Bì Gòu (畢構) memorialized:
"All 'slanted appointment' officials from the previous reign should be dismissed."
The emperor agreed.
On the day *Guǐsì* (癸巳),
several thousand "slanted appointment" officials were dismissed.
(Information on "slanted appointment" officials can be found in the previous volume, Zhōngzōng (中宗) Jǐnglóng (景龍) third year.)
4. Pèi Tán (裴談), Minister of Justice and Concurrent Grand Councillor, was demoted to Prefect of Púzhōu (蒲州).
According to old gazetteers: Púzhōu (蒲州)
is 324 *lǐ* (里) northeast of the capital.
(*Shàng* (尚)
is pronounced *chén yáng*.)
5. Sū Ānhéng (蘇安恆) was posthumously granted the title of Remonstrance Official.
(Sū Ānhéng's (蘇安恆) death is mentioned in volume 208, Zhōngzōng (中宗) Shénlóng (神龍) first year.)
(*Héng* (恆)
is pronounced *hù dēng*.)
6. In the ninth month,
on the day *Xīnwèi* (辛未),
Táng Xiūjǐng (唐休璟), former Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince who had retired, was appointed Grand Commander of the Shuòfāng (朔方) Circuit.
7. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day *Jiǎshēn* (甲申),
Yáo Yuánzhī (姚元之) and Sòng Jǐng (宋璟), Commissioners of Rites, memorialized:
(During the Táng (唐) dynasty, whenever there was a national mourning,
a chancellor would be appointed Commissioner of Rites
to manage affairs related to imperial tombs and ancestral temples.)
(*Shǐ* (使) is pronounced *shū lì*.)
"The spirit tablet of the late Emperor
should be enshrined in the Grand Ancestral Temple.
We request that the spirit tablet of Yìzōng (義宗) be moved to the Eastern Capital
and a separate temple be built for it."
This was approved.
(Yìzōng's (義宗) enshrinement in the temple is mentioned in volume 208, Zhōngzōng (中宗) Shénlóng (神龍) first year.)
8. On the day *Yǐwèi* (乙未),
Empress Tiānhòu's (天后) honorific title was posthumously restored to Dàshèng Tiānhòu (大聖天后).
9. On the day *Dīngyǒu* (丁酉),
Xuē Nè (薛訥), Grand Envoy for Frontier Defense and Military Commissioner of Yōuzhōu (幽州), was appointed Grand General of the Left Wǔwèi (武衞) and concurrent Area Commander-in-chief of Yōuzhōu (幽州).
(The title *Jiédùshǐ* (節度使, military commissioner) originated with Nè (訥).)
10. Princess Tàipíng (太平公主), deeming the Crown Prince young,
initially thought little of him.
However, she later became wary of his sagacity and martial prowess,
and wished to select a more dim-witted and weak successor to establish her power for longer.
She frequently spread rumors,
saying,
"The Crown Prince is not the eldest,
and therefore should not be established."
On the day *Jǐhài* (己亥),
an edict was issued to admonish all within and without the court,
to quell the frivolous discussions.
The Princess constantly spied on the Crown Prince's actions,
and even the slightest detail was reported to the emperor.
Many of the Crown Prince's close attendants
also served as the Princess's informants,
causing the Crown Prince deep unease.
(This laid the groundwork for the future execution of Princess Tàipíng (太平公主) and her partisans.)
11. [Lǐ] Zhòngjùn, the former Crown Prince, was posthumously granted the谥号 (shìhào) of Jiémǐn.
Wéi Còu, the Taifǔ Shǎoqīng, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"For those whom rewards and punishments do not reach,
their conduct is examined and a posthumous title is established to praise or condemn them.
The former Crown Prince [Lǐ] Zhòngjùn,
with Lǐ Duōzuò and others, raised an army and entered the palace.
Zhōngzōng ascended Xuánwǔmén to avoid them.
The Crown Prince, astride his horse, directed his troops with composure.
But when his followers turned their weapons,
[Lǐ] Duōzuò and others died,
and the Crown Prince then fled and hid.
If the palace guards had not held their ground,
the calamity would have been unbearable!
The next day,
Zhōngzōng wept tears like rain.
'Wept tears like rain'
means tears falling like rain.
Officials of the Zhōngshū and Ménxià departments were called Gōngfèngguān.
The danger was of this magnitude.
Now the sacred dynasty grants him a ceremonial burial,
and bestows the posthumous title of Jiémǐn.
I am secretly perplexed by this.
Indeed, it is the ritual for a subject [or] son [that] when passing a temple, one must dismount;
when passing a superior's position, one must hasten.
When Hàn Chéngdì was Crown Prince,
he dared not cross the imperial road.
When Hàn Chéngdì was Crown Prince,
he initially resided in Guìgōng.
Yuándì once urgently summoned him.
The Crown Prince exited Lónglóumén,
not daring to cross the imperial road.
He went west to Zhíchéngmén,
and only when he could cross there did he do so.
He then returned and entered Zuòshìmén.
The emperor was delayed by him
and asked why.
He replied with the circumstances.
Thereupon, an order was issued that the Crown Prince might cross the imperial road.
To ride a horse before the emperor
is extremely impolite.
If he is praised for executing Wǔ Sānsī and his son,
then raising an army to punish treacherous officials and honor the sovereign father would be acceptable.
But now, [Lǐ Zhòngjùn] wished to seize power himself.
This is to compete with [Wǔ] Sānsī in treachery.
How is that worthy of praise?
If he is praised for wishing to depose the Wèi clan,
then at that time, the Wèi clan's treacherous actions were not yet clear,
and the great principle had not yet been severed.
To depose them without Zhōngzōng's command
would be to coerce one's father and depose one's mother.
How could that be permissible?
Hàn Lì Tàizǐ was trapped by Jiāng Chōng's slanders.
In anger, he killed [Jiang] Chōng.
Although he raised an army and engaged in battle,
it was not to besiege or coerce his sovereign father.
He died after his army was defeated.
This event is found in volume 22, Wǔdì, Zhēnghé 2nd year.
He was only later reburied,
and was still posthumously titled Lì.
See volume 24, Xuāndì, Běnshǐ 1st year.
I fear that future rebellious subjects and unfilial sons
might cite this as a precedent,
opening the source of rebellion and defiance.
This is not how one clarifies good and condemns evil.
'Zhāng'
means 'clear';
'dàn'
means 'ill.'
It means to make clear what is good
and to condemn what is evil.
'Dàn'
is pronounced 'dīng dàn.'
[Lǐ] Duōzuò and others, who raised an army with [Lǐ] Zhòngjùn,
were not guiltless.
Your Majesty may pardon them now.
But to name it 'snow' (to vindicate them)
is also something I am uneasy about."
The Emperor greatly approved of his words.
However, the executive officials believed that the imperial decree had already been issued,
and would not be retroactively changed.
They merely halted the posthumous appointments of [Lǐ] Duōzuò and others.
12. In the eleventh month,
on the day Wùshēn (the first day of the month),
Yáo Yuánzhī was made Zhōngshūlìng.
13. On the day Jǐyǒu,
Xiàohé Huángdì was buried in Dìnglíng.
Dìnglíng is fifteen lǐ northwest of Fùpíngchéng in Yōngzhōu.
The court debated that since Empress Wèi was guilty,
she should not be interred with him.
The former Yīngwáng's wife, a woman of the Zhào clan, was posthumously titled Hé Sīshùn Shèng Huánghòu.
Her burial site was sought,
but no one knew where it was. Her death is recorded in volume 202, Gāozōng, Shàngyuán 2nd year.
According to Tang regulations, a empress had three types of ceremonial robes: wēiyī, jūyī, and tànyī.
Wēiyī
was the robe for receiving official appointments, assisting in sacrifices, and major court assemblies.
It was made of deep blue woven silk,
embroidered with hūi birds
on a red background,
in five colors,
with twelve layers.
It had a plain gauze undershirt,
a fǔ collar,
scarlet gauze cuffs,
and a knee-cover matching the robe's color.
It was edged with a cù collar,
decorated with zhái patterns
of three types.
It included a blue gown and a leather belt,
a large belt matching the robe's color,
and a biyao, button, pendant, and ribbon similar to those of the Son of Heaven.
It was worn with blue stockings
and slippers adorned with golden slippers.
She was interred with him in Dìnglíng.
14. On the day Rénzǐ,
Wéi Ānshí, the Shìzhōng, was dismissed and made Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo.
Sū Huái, the Zuǒ Púyè and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn, was dismissed and made Shǎofù.
15. On the day Jiǎyín,
Pèi Yán's official titles were posthumously restored.
Previously, Pèi Yǒuxiān had escaped from Língnán,
was given one hundred strokes,
and exiled to Běitíng.
Upon reaching his place of exile,
he accumulated wealth and acted as a knight-errant,
often sending retainers to spy on affairs in the capital.
When Empress Wǔ executed exiled persons (Pèi Yán had died and [Pèi] Yǒuxiān had been exiled to Língnán,
see volume 203, Wǔ Hòu, Guāngzhái 1st year;
the execution of exiled persons is in volume 205, Chángshòu 2nd year),
'xún'
is pronounced 'xiū zhèng'.
he fled to Húzhōng.
The Běitíng Dūhù pursued and captured him,
imprisoning him and reporting it.
When the envoy arrived,
all other exiled persons had been killed.
[Pèi] Yǒuxiān had not yet been killed, awaiting a report.
Subsequently, Empress Wǔ issued an edict to appease the exiled persons;
those who had not yet died were all allowed to return.
Thus, [Pèi] Yǒuxiān was able to return.
At this time, when [Pèi] Yán's descendants were sought,
only [Pèi] Yǒuxiān remained, and he was appointed Zhànshìcéng.
A Zhànshìcéng,
a regular sixth-rank senior official,
was responsible for managing affairs of the Zhànshìfǔ.
16. On the day Rénxū,
Wáng Tóngjiǎo's official titles were posthumously restored.
Wáng Tóngjiǎo's death is recorded in volume 208, Zhōngzōng, Shénlóng 2nd year.
17. On the day Gēngwǔ,
Xǔ Wénzhēn Gōng Sū Huái passed away.
An edict ordered his son, Tǐng, to be reinstated as Gōngbù Shìláng,
but Tǐng firmly declined.
The Emperor sent Lǐ Rìzhī to convey the imperial decree,
but [Lǐ] Rìzhī returned without speaking,
reporting:
"I saw his sorrow and extreme grief,
and could not bear to speak, fearing he might collapse and die."
The Emperor then allowed him to observe the full mourning period.
18. In the twelfth month,
on the day Guǐwèi,
the Emperor appointed his two daughters, Xīchéng Gōngzhǔ and Lóngchāng Gōngzhǔ, as female Daoist officials,
to bring blessings to Tiānhuáng Tàihòu.
He also intended to build a Daoist temple west of the city.
Níng Yuántì, the Jiànyì Dàfū, submitted a memorial, stating:
"In the previous dynasty, the rebellious commoner's beloved daughters, due to their arrogance and extravagance, met with disaster.
Xīnchéng and Yídu, being of common birth and living modestly, were preserved.
Xīnchéng Gōngzhǔ married Wǔ Yánhuī,
and Yíchéng Gōngzhǔ married Péi Xùn;
both were daughters of Zhōngzōng.
It is inappropriate to extensively construct temples and monasteries,
which exhausts the people and wastes resources.
Liáng Wǔdì suffered defeat in the past,
and the late emperor brought disaster upon himself later.
The clear mirror is not far away.
Now that the two princesses have entered the Daoist path,
a temple will be built for them.
It should not be overly grand or extravagant,
inviting criticism from all quarters.
Furthermore,
the monks whom the previous dynasty had befriended
are still around.
They should be dismissed and kept away."
The Emperor read it and found it good.
19 The eunuch Lǘ Xīngguì 閭興貴 committed an offense, which was brought before Lǐ Cháoyǐn 李朝隱, the Magistrate of Cháng'ān 長安.
Cháoyǐn 朝隱 imprisoned him.
The Emperor heard of this,
summoned Cháoyǐn 朝隱,
and praised him, saying:
"You are the Magistrate of Chìxiàn 赤縣.
If you can act like this,
what more worries do I have!"
Thereupon, he went to the Chéngtiānmén 承天門,
assembled all the civil and military officials and the emissaries from various prefectures,
and announced Cháoyǐn's 朝隱's actions.
He also issued an imperial decree stating:
"When eunuchs encounter a lenient and gentle era,
they invariably wield power and authority.
I have reviewed previous records,
and each time I have sighed with regret.
That someone can fulfill my intentions
is truly this man.
He may be promoted one rank to Tàizhōng Dàfū 太中大夫,
and granted a 'superior-middle' evaluation (zhōngshàngkǎo 中上考) and a hundred bolts of silk."
20 On the day Rénchén 壬辰,
the Xī 奚 and Qì 霫 violated the frontier,
plundered Yúyáng 漁陽 and Yōngnú 雍奴,
and departed through the Lúlóng Pass 盧龍塞.
Yúyáng 漁陽 County originally belonged to Yōuzhōu 幽州.
In the first year of Shénlóng 神龍 of Zhōngzōng 中宗, it was separated to belong to Yíngzhōu 營州.
Yōngnú 雍奴 County,
since the Hàn 漢 dynasty, belonged to Yúyáng Commandery 漁陽郡.
Under the Suí 隋, it belonged to Zhuó Commandery 涿郡.
Under the Táng 唐, it belonged to Yōuzhōu 幽州.
Lúlóng 盧龍
was Húirú 肥如 County during the Hàn 漢 dynasty,
belonging to Liáoxī Commandery 遼西郡.
In the eighteenth year of Kāihuáng 開皇 of the Suí 隋,
its name was changed to Lúlóng 盧龍,
belonging to Běipíng Commandery 北平郡.
Under the Táng 唐, it was part of Píngzhōu 平州.
The character Qì 霫 is pronounced with 'er li' (而立) as the fanqie.
Not translated.
Not translated.
21 According to old regulations,
officials of the third rank and above were appointed by cèshū 冊書 (enfeoffment letters),
those of the fifth rank and above by zhìshū 制書 (imperial decrees),
and those of the sixth rank and below by chǐshū 敕書 (imperial edicts).
The Táng 唐 imperial pronouncements had seven types: first, cèshū 冊書;
second, zhìshū 制書;
third, wèiláo zhìshū 慰勞制書 (consolatory imperial decrees);
fourth, fāchǐ 發敕 (issued edicts);
fifth, chǐzhǐ 敕旨 (imperial rescripts);
sixth, lùnshì chǐshū 論事敕書 (imperial edicts on specific matters);
seventh, chǐdié 敕牒 (imperial dispatches).
Civil appointments belonged to the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù 吏部),
and military appointments to the Ministry of War (Bīngbù 兵部).
The Shàngshū 尚書 (Minister) was called Zhōngquán 中銓,
and the Shìláng 侍郎 (Vice-Minister) was called Dōngquán 東銓 or Xīquán 西銓.
This was known as the 'Three Selections' (sānquán 三銓).
When favorites gained power,
selections became muddled,
and there was no longer any discipline.
By this time,
Sòng Jǐng 宋璟 was appointed Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū 吏部尚書),
and Lǐ Yì 李乂 and Lú Cóngyuàn 盧從愿 were appointed Vice-Ministers.
All of them feared no powerful person,
and the path for requests and favors was cut off.
Among the more than ten thousand who assembled,
those retained after the Three Selections were no more than two thousand.
People admired their fairness.
Yáo Yuánzhī 姚元之 was appointed Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū 兵部尚書),
and Lù Xiàngxiān 陸象先 and Lú Huáishèn 盧懷慎 were appointed Vice-Ministers,
and military selections also became well-ordered.
Cóngyuàn 從愿 was a nephew of Chéngqìng 承慶.
Lú Chéngqìng 盧承慶
is mentioned in volume 200, fourth year of Xiǎnqìng 顯慶 of Gāozōng 高宗.
He was the son of Yuánfāng 元方.
Lù Yuánfāng 陸元方
is mentioned in volume 205, first year of Zhèngshèng 證聖 of Tiānhòu 天后.
22 The Supervising Censor Ní Ruòshuǐ 倪若水 of Gǎochéng 藁城
(Gǎochéng 藁城 County
belonged to Zhēndìng 真定 Kingdom in the Former Hàn 漢,
to Jùlù 鉅鹿 Commandery since the Later Hàn 漢,
and to Héngzhōu 恆州 under the Táng 唐)
was eager to please the ruler and feigned illness for him.
This refers to his request for Empress Wéi 韋 Hòu to perform the secondary offering at the suburban sacrifice.
Shān Yùn 山惲 was the Chángshǐ 長史 (Chief Administrator) of Kuòzhōu 括州.
The old gazetteer states: Ráozhōu 饒州
is 3,263 *lǐ* southeast of the capital.
Kuòzhōu 括州 later became Chǔzhōu 處州,
4,278 *lǐ* southeast of the capital.
23 The Supervising Censor Yáng Fú 楊孚,
when impeaching and rectifying, did not avoid the powerful and influential.
The powerful and influential defamed him.
The Emperor said:
"When a hawk attacks a cunning rabbit,
one must rescue it quickly, otherwise it will surely be bitten in return.
It is the same when an Censor rectifies evil and wickedness.
If the ruler does not protect them,
they will also be devoured by evil and wickedness."
Fú 孚 was the grand-nephew of Emperor Wén of Suí 隋 Wéndì 隋文帝.
24 The posts of Jiédu 使 (Military Commissioner), Zhīdù 使 (Fiscal Commissioner), and Yíngtián 使 (Agricultural Colony Commissioner) for Héxī 河西 were established,
governing the seven prefectures of Liáng 涼, Gān 甘, Sù 肅, Yī 伊, Guā 瓜, Shā 沙, and Xī 西,
with its seat of governance in Liángzhōu 涼州.
According to Táng 唐 regulations,
all frontier armies in the empire
had a Zhīdùshǐ 支度使 to calculate the use of military provisions, grain, and weapons.
If a Jiédù 使 did not concurrently hold the Zhīdù 使 position,
the Zhīdù 使 formed its own office.
If they did concurrently hold it,
then the Jiédù 使 handled the fiscal management himself.
Whenever border defense, garrisoning, and transportation were insufficient,
agricultural colonies (túntián 屯田) were established to increase military supplies,
and thus there were Yíngtiánshǐ 營田使.
The character Shǐ 使 is pronounced with 'shū lì' (疏吏) as the fanqie.
Not translated.
The character Dù 度 is pronounced with 'tú luò' (徒洛) as the fanqie.
Not translated.
25 The Bùmán 㣥蠻 of Yáozhōu 姚州
had previously submitted to Tǔbō 吐蕃. The Acting Supervising Censor Lǐ Zhīgǔ 李知古 requested to dispatch troops to attack them.
Once they surrendered,
he again requested to build cities,
establish prefectures and counties,
and heavily tax them.
Huángmén Shìláng 黃門侍郎 (Vice-Minister of the Chancellery) Xú Jiān 徐堅 thought this was not advisable.
Full stop.
Zhīgǔ 知古 dispatched troops from Jiànnán 劍南 to build cities,
and then intended to execute their chieftains and
plunder their women and children to be slaves.
The Bùmán 㣥蠻 were resentful and angry.
The Mán 蠻 chieftain Páng Míng 傍名 led Tǔbō 吐蕃 to attack Zhīgǔ 知古,
killed him,
and sacrificed his body to heaven.
As a result, the road between Yáo 姚 and Cuì 巂 was cut off
and remained impassable for years.
The Anxī Dūhù 安西都護 (Protector-General of Anxi) Zhāng Xuánbiǎo 張玄表 encroached upon and plundered the northern border of Tǔbō 吐蕃.
Although Tǔbō 吐蕃 resented this, they had not yet severed their peace and kinship relations.
So they bribed Yáng Jǔ 楊矩, the Dūdu 都督 (Military Governor) of Shànzhōu 鄯州,
to request the Jiǔqǔ 九曲 land in Héxī 河西 as a bathing and toiletry estate (tāngmùyì 湯沐邑) for the princess.
Jǔ 矩 memorialized to grant it to them.
Jiǔqǔ 九曲 was
three hundred *lǐ* from Jīshí Army 積石軍,
where the water was sweet and the grass fertile,
suitable for animal husbandry.
This was likely the area of the Greater and Lesser Yú Valleys (Dà-Xiǎoyú Gǔ 大小榆谷) of the Hàn 漢 dynasty.
Tǔbō 吐蕃 established cities such as Hóngjì 洪濟 and Dàmò Mén 大漠門 to guard it.
The historian records this as a foreshadowing of Yáng Jǔ's 楊矩's later regret and suicide.
The character Shàn 鄯 is pronounced with 'shí zhàn' (時戰) as the fanqie,
and also sounds like 'shàn' (善).
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Guǐchǒu 癸丑,
Moquò 默啜, the Khagan of the Tūjué 突厥, sent an envoy to request peace.
This was granted.
2 On the day Jǐwèi 己未,
Guō Yuánzhèn 郭元振, the Tàipú Qīng 太僕卿 (Minister of the Imperial Stud), and Zhāng Yuè 張說, the Zhōngshū Shìláng 中書侍郎 (Vice-Minister of the Chancellery), were both appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì 同平章事.
3 Wēn Wáng 温王 (Prince of Wen) Chóngmào 重茂 was made Xiāng Wáng 襄王 (Prince of Xiang),
and assigned as Cìshǐ 刺史 (Prefect) of Jízhōu 集州.
A Zhōnglángjiàng 中郎將 (General of the Household) was dispatched with five hundred soldiers to guard him there.
The old gazetteer states: Jízhōu 集州
is 1,425 *lǐ* southwest of the capital.
The character Jiāng 將 is pronounced with 'jí liàng' (即亮) as the fanqie.
Not translated.
4 On the day Yǐchǒu 乙丑,
Lady Liú 劉 Shì was posthumously honored as Sùmíng Huánghòu 肅明皇后,
and her mausoleum named Huìlíng 惠陵.
Lady Dòu 竇 Shì was honored as Zhāochéng Huánghòu 昭成皇后,
and her mausoleum named Jìnglíng 靖陵.
Both were re-interred through calling back their spirits (zhāohún zàng 招魂葬) south of the Eastern Capital city.
The two deaths are mentioned in volume 205, second year of Wǔ Hòu 長壽 武后.
Their temple was named Yíkūn Miào 儀坤廟.
The Huìyào 會要 states that
Yíkūn Miào 儀坤廟 was in Qīnrén Lǐ 親仁里.
They were the mothers of the Crown Prince.
5 Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ 太平公主 formed a faction with Dòu Huáizhēn 竇懷貞, the Chángshǐ 長史 (Chief Administrator) of Yìzhōu 益州, and others,
intending to endanger the Crown Prince.
She had her son-in-law, Táng Jùn 唐晙, invite Wéi Ānshí 韋安石 to her residence.
Ānshí 安石 firmly declined to go.
The Emperor once secretly summoned Ānshí 安石
and said:
"I hear that all in the court are inclining towards the Eastern Palace (Crown Prince).
You should investigate this."
He replied:
"How can Your Majesty utter such words of a doomed state!
This must be a scheme of Tàipíng 太平 (Princess Taiping).
The Crown Prince has rendered service to the state,
is benevolent, wise, filial, and fraternal, which is known throughout the realm.
I beg Your Majesty not to be misled by slanderous words."
The Emperor started, saying:
"I understand;
you need not say more."
At that time, the princess was secretly listening behind the curtain.
She then used false accusations to incriminate Ānshí 安石,
intending to have him arrested and investigated.
Thanks to Guō Yuánzhèn 郭元振 saving him,
he escaped.
The Gōngzhǔ, again, once rode in her carriage and invited the Zǎixiàng to within Guāngfànmén.
The Táng Liùdiǎn says: The western corridor in front of Xuānzhèngdiàn is called Yuèhuámén.
To the west of the gate is the Zhōngshūshěng.
To the west of the Shěng is the north-south street.
To the south, it directly leads to Zhāoqìngmén,
which exits at Guāngfànmén.
This is where Hán Yù prostrated himself beneath Guāngfànmén to present a letter to the Zǎixiàng.
Everyone turned pale.
Sòng Jǐng spoke out firmly, saying:
"The Dōnggōng has rendered great service to all under Heaven.
He is the true master of the Zōngmiào and Shèjì.
How can the Gōngzhǔ suddenly have such a proposal?"
Jǐng and Yáo Yuánzhī secretly spoke to the Shàng, saying:
"Sòngwáng is Your Majesty's eldest son.
Bīnwáng is Gāozōng's eldest grandson.
Bīnwáng Shǒulǐ
is the son of Zhānghuáitàizǐ Xián.
Zhǎng (meaning ‘eldest’)
is pronounced in two ways.
This will cause the Dōnggōng to be uneasy.
Please send both Sòngwáng and Bīnwáng out as Cìshǐ,
and dismiss Qí and Xuē Erwáng from their posts as Zuǒ Yǔlín and Yòu Yǔlín,
making them Zuǒshuài and Yòushuài to serve the Tàizǐ."
When the Wèi clan was first pacified,
the Erwáng commanded the Yǔlín.
The Dōnggōng had five commanders (wǔshuài),
which were divided into Zuǒ and Yòu ten commanders (shíshuài).
This refers to the Zuǒ Wèishuài and Yòu Wèishuài.
The Shàng said:
"I have no other brothers;
only Tàipíng, my one sister.
How can she be exiled to the Eastern Capital!
As for the other princes, you may decide their fate."
Thereupon, an edict was first issued, stating:
"From now on, no princes or Fùmǎ are permitted to command the Imperial Guard.
Those currently in office shall all be reassigned to other posts."
Jiàn (meaning 'currently in office')
is pronounced Xián Biàn.
After a while,
the Shàng said to his attendants:
"Diviners say that within five days, urgent troops will enter the palace.
You gentlemen, prepare for this for me."
Zhāng Yuè said:
"This must be slanderers attempting to sow discord with the Dōnggōng.
I wish Your Majesty would make the Tàizǐ supervise the state,
then the rumors will naturally cease."
Yáo Yuánzhī said:
"What Zhāng Yuè said
is the ultimate strategy for the Shèjì."
The Shàng was pleased.
Yuè (meaning 'pleased')
is the same as yuè.
In the second month,
on the day Bǐngzǐ, the first day of the month,
Sòngwáng Chéngqì was made Cìshǐ of Tóngzhōu,
and Bīnwáng Shǒulǐ was made Cìshǐ of Bīnzhōu.
The Old Gazetteer says: Tóngzhōu is
255 lǐ northeast of the capital;
Bīnzhōu is
493 lǐ northwest of the capital.
Xuēwáng Lóngyè, the Dàjiàngjūn of the Yòu Yǔlín, was made Yòu Wèishuài.
Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ was placed in Púzhōu.
On Dīngchǒu,
the Tàizǐ was ordered to supervise the state.
The appointment of officials of the sixth rank and below, and sentences of penal servitude and below,
were all to be handled by the Tàizǐ.
The Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ Cuī Lì and the Tàizǐ Zhōngyǔn Xuē Zhāosù spoke to the Shàng, saying:
"The xiéfēngguān were all appointed by the late Emperor,
and their imperial favor has already been bestowed.
Xiéfēngguān,
see the second year of Jǐnglóng in the previous volume.
To strip them all away in one morning
would highlight the faults of the late Emperor
and incur resentment for Your Majesty.
Now, public opinion is boiling,
spread throughout the realm,
which might lead to extraordinary changes."
Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ also spoke of this,
and the Shàng agreed.
On Wùyín,
an edict was issued:
"All officials appointed through xiéfēng biéchì,
who were previously suspended from their posts,
shall all be reinstated according to their talents."
Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ, hearing of the plans of Yáo Yuánzhī and Sòng Jǐng,
was furious,
and reproached the Tàizǐ.
The Tàizǐ, in fear,
memorialized that Yuánzhī and Jǐng were alienating his paternal aunt and brothers.
Gū (paternal aunt)
refers to Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ;
Xiōng (brothers)
refers to Sòngwáng and Bīnwáng.
Jiān (meaning 'alienate')
is pronounced Gǔ Xiàn.
On Jiǎshēn,
Yuánzhī was demoted to Cìshǐ of Shēnzhōu,
and Jǐng was demoted to Cìshǐ of Chǔzhōu.
The Old Gazetteer says: Shēnzhōu is 1,796 lǐ from the capital;
Chǔzhōu is
2,501 lǐ southeast of the capital.
On Bǐngxū,
the appointments of Sòngwáng and Bīnwáng as Cìshǐ were also rescinded.
The Zhōngshū Shèrén and Cānzhījīwù Liú Yōuqíu was dismissed and made Hùbù Shàngshū;
Wéi Ānshí, the Tàizǐ Shàobǎo, was made Shìzhōng.
Ānshí and Lǐ Rìzhī replaced Yáo and Sòng in governance.
From then on, the administration became disorganized again,
returning to the state of the Jǐnglóng era.
Liǔ Zé, former Cānjūn of Kǎicáo in the Yòu Shuàifǔ, submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"The xiéfēngguān were all promoted through the influence of servants and concubines;
how could this be the intention of Xiàohé?
Zhōngzōng's posthumous title was Xiàohé Huángdì.
Shuài
is pronounced Suǒ Lǜ.
Shàng (meaning 'to present')
is pronounced Shí Zhǎng.
Shū (meaning 'memorial')
is pronounced Suǒ Qù.
Everyone under Heaven praised the clarity of the previous decision.
To suddenly reinstate all of them,
blurring the distinction between good and bad,
and allowing them to attack each other,
how can Your Majesty's governance lack consistency!
Commentators all say that Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ ordered the Hu monk Huìfàn to improperly promote these people,
misleading Your Majesty.
Your subject fears that small matters will accumulate into great ones,
leading to no small disaster."
The Shàng did not listen.
Zé was
Hēng's grandson.
Liǔ Hēng served Suí as Wángwū Zhǎng,
returned to Gāozǔ,
who gave him his granddaughter Dòu as a wife.
He served Tàizōng through several reigns,
rising to the position of Jiǎnjiào Qízhōu Cìshǐ.
The Zuǒ and Yòu Wànqí and the Zuǒ and Yòu Yǔlín constituted the four Northern Gate armies,
commanded by Gě Fúshùn and others.
In the third month,
Sòngwáng Chéngqì's daughter was made Jīnshān Gōngzhǔ,
promised in marriage to Tūjué Mòchuò.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on Jiǎshēn,
Sòngwáng Chéngqì offered to resign from his post as Sītú.
This was permitted,
and he was made Tàizǐ Bīnkè.
Wéi Ānshí was made Zhōngshū Lìng.
The Shàng summoned his ministers of the third rank and above,
and said:
"I have always cherished a simple and detached nature,
not valuing the position of the Son of Heaven.
Formerly, as the Heir Apparent,
and again as the Imperial Younger Brother,
I declined both positions.
See Volume 204, Tiānshòu first year, for being Heir Apparent;
see Volume 208, Shénlóng first year, for declining the position of Imperial Younger Brother.
Sì (meaning 'heir')
is pronounced Xiáng Lì.
Chǔ (meaning 'position')
is pronounced Chāng Lǚ.
What do you think?"
None of the ministers responded.
The Tàizǐ sent his Yòu Shùzǐ Lǐ Jǐngbó to firmly decline,
but it was not permitted.
The Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ Hé Féngyáo, who sided with Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ,
said to the Shàng:
"Your Majesty's age is not yet advanced;
you are still relied upon and looked up to by all under Heaven.
How can you suddenly do this!"
Thereupon, the Shàng stopped.
On Wùzǐ,
an edict was issued:
"All political matters shall be handled by the Tàizǐ.
As for military matters, death sentences, and appointments of officials of the fifth rank and above,
all must first be discussed with the Tàizǐ,
and then reported to me."
On Xīnmǎo,
Lǐ Rìzhī was appointed Shìzhōng.
On Rén’yín,
a general amnesty was granted to all under Heaven.
In the fifth month,
the Tàizǐ requested to yield the throne to Sòngwáng Chéngqì.
This was not permitted.
He requested to recall Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ to the capital.
This was permitted.
On Gēngxū,
an edict was issued:
"The tombs of Empress Zétiān's parents shall remain as Hàolíng and Shùnlíng,
and officials shall be appointed according to their scale."
For the abolition of the two Wǔ family tombs, see the first year in the previous volume.
Liàng
is pronounced liáng.
In the 17th year, Xīnyǒu,
Xīchéng Commandery was renamed Jīnxiān Gōngzhǔ,
and Lóngchāng Commandery was renamed Yùzhēn Gōngzhǔ.
Temples were built for each of them.
The two temples, Jīnxiān Guān and Yùzhēn Guān, were both built in Fǔxīng Fāng within the capital city.
Yùzhēn Guān
was originally the old residence of Dòu Dàn,
and faced Jīnxiān Guān.
Gèng
is pronounced gōng héng fān.
Several million manpower were used.
The Right Sànqí Chángshì, Wèi Zhīgǔ, and the Huángmén Shìláng, Lǐ Yì, remonstrated,
but were not heeded.
Sàn
is pronounced xī dàn fān.
Qí
is pronounced qí jì fān.
In the 18th year, Rénxū,
the Diànzhōng Jiān, Dòu Huáizhēn, was made Yùshǐ Dàfū and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
The monk Huìfàn, relying on Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ's influence,
forcibly seized people's property.
The Yùshǐ Dàfū, Xuē Qiānguāng, and the Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ, Mùróng Xún, impeached him.
The Princess complained to the Emperor,
who then demoted Qiānguāng to Qízhōu Cìshǐ.
The Kǎoyì states: The Tǒngjì says:
"The Jiānchá Yùshǐ, Mùróng Xún, impeached the monk Huìfàn of Xīmíng Sì,
because he had illicit relations with the palace woman Zhāng,
who was Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ's wet nurse,
and encroached upon the property of the common people.
The Emperor thought that an Yùshǐ should not avoid the powerful and noble;
seeing the Princess leave to reside in Púzhōu,
he dared to impeach her.
While she was present, he said nothing,
which appeared to be an attempt to sow discord among the family.
Consequently, he was demoted to Mìzhōu Yuánwài Sīmǎ."
Now we follow the old transmission.
In the 20th year, envoys were dispatched to inspect the Ten Circuits.
In the 18th year of Tàizōng's Zhēngguān era,
seventeen circuits were sent on inspection tours.
In the early days of Wǔ Hòu's Chuí Gǒng era,
nine circuits were also sent on inspection tours.
In the second year of Tiānshòu, ten circuits were again dispatched as Fǔwěi envoys.
At this time, they were divided into Ten Circuit Àncháshǐ,
to oversee the prefectures and commanderies with integrity,
changing every two years.
Shǐ
is pronounced shū lì fān.
They were then divided into Eastern and Western Circuits;
Lǒngyòu was also divided into Héxī Circuit.
In the sixth month,
on the day Rénwǔ,
the empire was again divided, establishing twenty-four Dūdū in Biàn, Qí, Yǎn, Wèi, Jì, Bīng, Pú, Fū, Jīng, Qín, Yì, Tóng, Suì, Jīng, Qí, Tōng, Liáng, Xiāng, Yáng, Ān, Mǐn, Yuè, and Hóng, Tán.
In the first year of Wǔdé,
Shǔjùn was renamed Yìzhōu.
Tóngzhōu
was the land of Hàn Fúxiàn.
During the Eastern Jìn, Bāxī Jùn was established.
During the Western Wèi, it was called Tóngzhōu.
In the Kàihuáng era of the Suí dynasty, it was renamed Tóngzhōu.
In the early Dàyè era, the prefecture was abolished and became Jīnshān Jùn.
In the early Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty, it was again called Tóngzhōu.
Also, in the second year of Wǔdé, Mǐnzhōu was established in Mǐnxiàn.
In the 13th year of Kāiyuán, Mǐnzhōu was renamed Fúzhōu.
Fū
is pronounced fū.
Only Luò and the nearby Jīzhōu were not subordinate to the Dūdū Fǔ.
Yōng, Huá, Tóng, Shāng, Qí, Bīn formed the Jīngjī;
Luò and Rǔ formed the Dūjī.
"The Dūdū exclusively held the power of life and death,
and their authority was too great.
If the wrong person was appointed,
the harm would be considerable.
Now, the Yùshǐ, though low in rank, are highly esteemed.
By regularly inspecting,
corruption will naturally be curbed."
Later, the Dūdū were eventually abolished,
and only the Ten Circuit Àncháshǐ were retained.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day Guǐsì,
Shàngguān Zhāoróng was posthumously restored to her title with the posthumous epithet Huìwén.
Her position as Zhāoróng was restored, and a posthumous epithet was added.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
because a withered persimmon tree at Gāozǔ's former residence revived,
a general amnesty was granted throughout the empire.
At that time, an imperial edict stated that Xīngshèng Sì was Gāozǔ's old residence,
and there was a persimmon tree that had withered and died during the Tiānshòu era.
By this time, it had revived,
so a great amnesty was granted to the empire.
Fù
is pronounced fú yòu fān,
and also as written.
On the day Jǐsì,
the Right Yùshǐ Dàfū, Xiè Wǎn, was made Shuòfāng Dàzǒngguǎn.
Wǎn inspected and reviewed the frontier troops of the Three Cities.
The Three Cities
are the Sān Shòuxiángchéng.
Xiè
is pronounced hù mǎi fān.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
the Zhōngshū Lìng, Wéi Ānshí, was made Zuǒ Púshè concurrently Tàizǐ Bīnke, and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ, because Ānshí did not side with her,
elevated him with a nominal title,
effectively removing his real power.
In the ninth month,
on the day Gēngchén,
Dòu Huáizhēn was made Shìzhōng.
Every time Huáizhēn left court,
he would visit Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ's residence.
At this time, the construction of Jīnxiān Guān and Yùzhēn Guān was underway.
Many officials remonstrated,
but Huáizhēn alone encouraged its completion,
personally supervising the work.
People at the time said that Huáizhēn had previously been the Empress's Ápèi.
This matter is mentioned in the second year of Zhōngzōng's Jǐnglóng era in the previous volume.
Pèi
is pronounced zhèng shē fān.
Táng princesses had Yìsī Lìng and Chéng,
who managed the income and expenditure of their household's wealth and goods, and matters of land taxation and enfeoffment.
The Kǎoyì states: The Ruìzōng Shílù says:
"On the day Yǐmǎo,
Yùshǐ Dàfū Dòu Huáizhēn was made Shìzhōng."
The Tàishàng Huáng Shílù says:
"On the day Gēngchén,
Yùshǐ Dàfū, Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn Dòu Huáizhēn was made Shìzhōng,
and oversaw the affairs of Jīnxiān and Yùzhēn Gōngzhǔ's Yìsī."
The Old Annals record, on the day Jǐmǎo,
Huáizhēn was made Shìzhōng.
The New Annals and New Tables record,
"On the day Yǐhài,
Huáizhēn was appointed Shìzhōng."
According to the records, the first day of this month was Guǐyǒu,
and there was no Yǐmǎo.
Moreover, because Huáizhēn personally supervised the construction of the two temples,
people at the time said:
"Dòu Púshè was previously the Empress's Guópèi,
and is now the Princess's Yìchéng."
He was not truly in charge of the Yìsī.
Now we follow the Old Annals.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Jiǎchén,
the Emperor ascended the Chéngtiān Mén,
and summoned Wéi Ānshí, Guō Yuánzhèn, Dòu Huáizhēn, Lǐ Rìzhī, and Zhāng Yuè to announce an imperial decree,
rebuking them for
"numerous shortcomings in governance and education,
droughts and floods causing calamities,
the public treasury becoming increasingly depleted,
and the number of officials daily increasing.
Although this is due to Our lack of virtue,
it is also because Our assistants are not talented.
Ānshí is appointed Zuǒ Púshè and Dōngdū Liúshǒu,
Yuánzhèn is appointed Lìbù Shàngshū,
Huáizhēn is appointed Zuǒ Yùshǐ Dàfū,
Rìzhī is appointed Hùbù Shàngshū,
Yuè is appointed Zuǒ Chéng,
and all are dismissed from participating in government affairs."
Lìbù Shàngshū Liú Yōuqíu was made Shìzhōng.
Right Sànqí Chángshì Wèi Zhīgǔ was made Zuǒ Sànqí Chángshì.
Tàizǐ Zhànshì Cuī Shí was made Zhōngshū Shìláng.
All were made Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
Zhōngshū Shìláng Lù Xiàngxiān was made Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
These were all Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ's wishes.
Xiàngxiān was pure and simple,
with few desires,
and his discourse was lofty and profound,
highly esteemed by people of his time.
Shí secretly served Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ.
The Princess wanted to promote him to Prime Minister,
but Shí requested to be promoted alongside Xiàngxiān.
The Princess disagreed,
but Shí said:
"If so, then I also dare not accept."
The Princess then spoke to the Emperor on his behalf,
but the Emperor was unwilling to employ Shí.
The Princess pleaded with tears,
and only then did he accede.
The Kǎoyì states: The Cháoyě Qiānzài says:
"Shí's wife was beautiful,
and both of his two daughters were favored by the Crown Prince.
People at the time posted a placard saying:
'He entrusted his mediocre talent to the Princess's residence,
and presented his seductive women to the Eastern Palace.'"
This is not adopted here.
27 Yòu Bǔquè Xīn Tìfǒu presented a memorial,
stating:
"Since ancient times, those who lost the Way, ruined their states, and destroyed their families,
spoken words are not as good as personal experience,
and hearing is not as good as witnessing with one's own eyes;
I ask to speak about what Your Majesty has personally witnessed.
Emperor Tàizōng,
was Your Majesty's ancestor.
He restored order from chaos,
using the Grand Historian's (Tàishǐ Gōng) phrase 'restoring order to a chaotic world and returning to righteousness.'
Officials were not appointed idly,
wealth was not unjustly wasted;
he did not build many temples and monasteries, yet he had blessings,
he did not ordain many monks and nuns, yet he had no disasters.
Heaven and Earth bestowed blessings,
winds and rains were timely,
('Ruò'
means 'in accordance with'.)
barbarians readily submitted,
he enjoyed a long reign,
and his name soared for ten thousand ages.
Why does Your Majesty not take this as a model to emulate!
Emperor Zhōngzōng,
Your Majesty's brother,
abandoned the legacy of his ancestors,
and yielded to the will of women;
several thousand people without ability received emoluments,
and over a hundred families without merit were ennobled;
the building of temples never ceased,
costing hundreds of billions in wealth and goods,
the ordination of people was endless,
hundreds of thousands were exempted from taxes and corvée;
what was expended increased daily,
and what was collected decreased daily;
he snatched food from the mouths of the common people to feed the greedy and cruel,
stripped clothes from the bodies of ten thousand people to plaster earth and timber for construction.
Thereupon men resented and gods were angered,
the masses rebelled and kin deserted,
floods and droughts arrived together,
both public and private coffers were exhausted,
his reign was not long,
and disaster reached him personally.
Why does Your Majesty not take this as a warning and change!
Since recent times,
floods and droughts have followed one another,
compounded by frost and locusts,
people have nothing to eat.
No relief has been heard of,
but for two daughters, temples are being built,
using over a million strings of cash.
(Referring to the two temples, Jīnxiān and Yùzhēn.)
('Wèi'
is pronounced "yú wěi fān".)
How much are the expenses within and outside the court,
that over a million strings of cash are lightly spent
to supply useless projects!
Your Majesty exterminated the Wéi clan, but did not abandon the evils of the Wéi clan;
can you bear to abandon the laws of Emperor Tàizōng,
yet cannot bear to abandon the policies of Emperor Zhōngzōng!
Moreover, when the Wéi clan was in power, Your Majesty and the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ),
were anxious and in danger day and night,
gnashing your teeth at the powerful villains;
(Gǒngxiōng
refers to Wéi Wēn, Zōng Chǔkè, and others.)
yet you do not change their ways.
I fear there will again be those who gnash their teeth at Your Majesty.
If that is the case, then why did Your Majesty hate the powerful villains and punish them!
Formerly, when the late Emperor (Xiāndì) pitied the rebellious one,
(The Emperor posthumously demoted Princess Ānlè (Ānlè Gōngzhǔ) to a commoner for rebellion,
thus she is referred to as such.)
('Bèi'
is pronounced "pú nèi fān"
and also "pú mò fān".)
Zhào Lǚwēn renovated gardens for her,
exhausted the national treasury,
and depleted manpower.
The mansion was completed but there was no time to live in it,
the garden was completed but there was no time to wander in it,
and she herself was killed and confiscated.
Those who now build extravagant temples,
are surely not acting on the original intentions of Your Majesty or the Princesses (Gōngzhǔ),
but most likely there are followers of Zōng and Zhào who encourage them,
and this must be investigated.
If Your Majesty does not stop these projects,
I fear the sorrow and resentment of the people
will not be less than during the previous dynasty.
Everyone knows of the disaster and ruin but dares not speak,
for if they speak, punishment and execution will follow.
Wéi Yuèjiāng, Yān Qīnróng, and others like them,
were punished by the previous court,
but Your Majesty rewarded them.
Is it not that Your Majesty knows straightforward words are beneficial to the state!
What I now say,
is also the straightforwardness of the previous court;
may Your Majesty please observe it."
Although the Emperor could not follow the advice,
he praised its keen directness.
28 Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Hé Féngyáo, acting Hónglú Qīng,
was sent as an envoy to the Tūjué,
and persuaded Mòchuò, saying:
"The Chǔmì and Jiānkūn, having heard that the Khagan (Kèhán) has entered into a marriage alliance with Táng,
will all surely submit.
Why does the Khagan not adopt Táng hats and belts,
so that all the Hu may know it,
would that not be splendid!"
Mòchuò assented,
and the next day,
wearing a pútóu and a purple robe,
he faced south and prostrated twice,
declaring himself a subject.
(The pútóu and purple robe
were the attire of Táng officials of the third rank or higher.)
(The pútóu originated in the Hòu Zhōu
and was convenient for military matters.)
(During Emperor Tàizōng's time,
Mǎ Zhōu presented a proposal,
stating that according to ritual, there was no text for wearing robes without a formal border,
and requested adding borders to sleeves and cuffs.)
('Shuō'
is pronounced "shū ruì fān".)
('Pú'
is pronounced "fáng yù fān".)
('Yī'
is pronounced "yú jì fān".)
In the eleventh month,
on the day Wùyín,
he arrived in the capital.
Féngyáo, for his merit on the envoy mission,
was promoted to Hùbù Shìláng.
29 On the day Rénchén,
an order was issued for all people of the realm to enter the army at twenty-five years old,
and be exempted at fifty-five.
30 In the twelfth month,
on the day Guǐmǎo,
Xīngxīwáng Kèhán Āshǐnà Xiàn was appointed as Envoy to Reconcile the Ten Surnames.
31 The Emperor summoned the Daoist priest Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn from Tiāntái Mountain.
(Línhǎi Records: Tiāntái Mountain is remarkably towering and eminent,
with eight layers,
appearing as one when viewed,
18,000 zhàng high,
and 800 lǐ in circumference.
It also has flying springs,
dropping a thousand rén.
At that time, it was within the borders of Tángxīng County, Táizhōu.
In the first year of Jiànlóng of Tàizǔ of our dynasty,
Tángxīng County was first changed to Tiāntái County.
The mountain is now over twenty lǐ west of the county seat.)
He replied:
"The Way,
is to decrease again and again,
until reaching wúwéi.
How could one be willing to toil one's mind to learn various arts and techniques!"
The Emperor said:
"To govern oneself through wúwéi is indeed lofty,
but what about governing the state?"
He replied:
"The state is like the body;
if one follows the natural course of things and has no selfish thoughts in one's heart,
then the world will be well-governed."
The Emperor sighed, saying:
"The words of Guǎngchéng,
cannot be surpassed."
(Guǎngchéngzǐ resided on Kōngtóng Mountain,
and the Yellow Emperor (Huángdì) stood downwind to ask about the Way.)
The Emperor agreed to his words. Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Lú Zàngyòng pointed to Zhōngnán Mountain,
(Chéng Dàchāng said: Zhōngnán Mountain stretches across Guānzhōng,
its southern face beginning in Qín and Lǒng in the west,
and extending eastward to Lántián.
Yōng, Qí, Méi, Hù, Cháng'ān, and Wànnián are all about 800 lǐ apart,
and what continuously stands to their south
is all this one mountain.
Máo Gōng said: Zhōngnán
is the famous mountain Zhōngnán of Zhōu;
Zhōngnán is Zhōngnán.
Guānzhōng Records say: it means it is located in the middle of the heavens and south of the capital.)
"There are many excellent spots here,
why must it be Tiāntái Mountain!"
Chéngzhēn replied:
"In my humble opinion,
this is merely a shortcut to officialdom!"
(Zàngyòng once lived in seclusion on Zhōngnán Mountain and
was summoned to be Zuǒ Shíyí during Empress Zétiān's time,
which is why Chéngzhēn said this.)
Emperor Xuánzōng Zhìdào Dàshèng Dàmíng Xiàohuángdì, first part of the highest grade.
His taboo name was Lóngjī,
and he was the third son of Emperor Ruìzōng.
(This posthumous title
was determined in the first year of Guǎngdé.)
First year of Xiāntiān
(Rénzǐ, 712)
(In the eighth month of this year, the era name was only then changed to Xiāntiān.)
1 In spring,
in the first month,
the *Kǎoyì* (Textual Variations) states: The *Xīnjì* (New Annals) and *Biǎo* (Tables)
say, "In the *rénchén* year,
Lù Xiàngxiān was made *Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn*."

Up to this point, Zēng proposed: The Yǒuyú clan offered the *dì* sacrifice to Huángdì and the *jiāo* sacrifice to Kù;
the Xiàhòu clan offered the *dì* sacrifice to Huángdì and the *jiāo* sacrifice to Gǔn.
The *jiāo* sacrifice and the ancestral temple
both included the *dì* sacrifice.
When the *dì* sacrifice was performed in the temple, the ancestors were feasted together with the great ancestor.
When the *dì* sacrifice was performed at the suburban altar, the earthly deities and all *wàng* (mountain and river spirits) were feasted together at the round mound,
with the progenitor participating in the sacrifice.
This was a great sacrifice for a major event,
not an ordinary one.
The *Sānfǔ Gùshì* (Old Stories of the Three Commanderies) states: At sacrifices at the round mound,

At the time, everyone considered Zēng's words correct.

When Chóngfú was defeated,
