but Zhāng Yuè (張說) and Liú Yōuqíu protected him, and he was spared.
Afterwards, Shí attached himself to Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ
and plotted with the Princess to remove Yuè (說) from his political duties,
making him Zuǒ Chéng (左丞) with concurrent duties in the Eastern Capital.
When Yōuqíu was exiled to Fēngzhōu,
Shí subtly influenced Guǎngzhōu Dūdū (廣州都督) Zhōu Lìzhēn (周利貞)
to have him killed.
Fēngzhōu
belonged to the Guǎngzhōu Dūdūfǔ.
Jùn (晙) knew of the plot
and detained Yōuqíu, not sending him on.
Lìzhēn repeatedly sent official documents demanding his surrender,
but Jùn did not respond.
Lìzhēn reported this to the court.
Shí repeatedly pressured Jùn to send Yōuqíu.
Yōuqíu said to Jùn:
"You are resisting the powerful officials to protect an exile.
You cannot possibly succeed,
and will only implicate yourself."
He earnestly requested to go to Guǎngzhōu.
Jùn said:
"The crime you are accused of is not one that would cause friends to abandon you.
If I am implicated because of you,
I will have no regrets."
He ultimately delayed and did not send him.
Yōuqíu thus escaped death.
24 In the ninth month,
on the first day Dīngmǎo (丁卯),
there was a solar eclipse.
25 on the *xīnmǎo* day,
the imperial prince, Sīshēng, was appointed Prince of Shǎn.
Sīshēng's mother, Lady Yáng,
was the great-granddaughter of Yáng Shìdá.
Yáng Shìdá served the Suí dynasty,
reaching the office of Nàyán.
His mother raised him.
26 In winter,
on the tenth month,
on the *gēngzǐ* day,
the Emperor visited the Grand Ancestral Temple
and granted a general amnesty.
27 On the *guǐmǎo* day,
the Emperor traveled to Xīnfēng
and hunted at the foot of Lìshān.
28 On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Jīnshān of the Shātuó sent envoys to offer tribute.
The Shātuó were
a branch of the Chǔyuè,
with the surname Zhūyé.
29 In the eleventh month,
on the *yǐyǒu* day,
two thousand cavalry from Xī and Qìdān raided Yúyáng.
Sòng Jǐng, the Grand Governor of Yōuzhōu, closed the city gates and did not sally forth.
The barbarians plundered extensively and then departed.
30 The Former Emperor issued an imperial edict dispatching the Emperor to inspect the borders,
from Hé and Lǒng in the west,
to Yān and Jì in the east,
to select generals and train soldiers.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Sòng Jǐng, the Grand Governor of Yōuzhōu, was appointed Grand Commander of the Left Army;
Xuē Nà, the Governor of Bìngzhōu, was appointed Grand Commander of the Central Army;
and Guō Yuánzhèn, Grand Commander of Shuòfāng and Minister of War, was appointed Grand Commander of the Right Army.
31 In the twelfth month,
Lǐ Rìzhī, Minister of Justice, requested to retire.
While in office, Rìzhī
managed affairs successfully without resorting to flogging.
There was a clerk in the Ministry of Justice
who, having received an imperial order three days prior,
forgot to execute it.
Rìzhī was angered.
He called for a staff
and gathered the subordinate officials, intending to flog the clerk.
But then he said to him,
"If I flog you,
everyone in the world will surely say that you were capable of provoking Lǐ Rìzhī's anger
and receiving Lǐ Rìzhī's flogging,
making you incomparable to other men.
Even your wife and children will abandon you."
So he released him.
All the clerks were moved and delighted;
none dared to transgress.
If there was any delay or error,
the multitude would collectively admonish him.
The first year of Kāiyuán
(*guǐchǒu*, 713)
The regnal year was only changed in the twelfth month of this year.
1 In spring,
on the first month,
on the *yǐhài* day,
an edict stated:
"From now on, guardsmen shall enlist at twenty-five
and be discharged at fifty.
Yǔlín Fēiqí will all be selected from and supplemented by guardsmen."
2 Xiāo Zhìzhōng, Minister of Personnel, was appointed Zhongshūlìng.
3 The Emperor's border inspection was postponed,
and the recruited soldiers were dispersed.
They were scheduled to reassemble in the eighth month,
but the journey ultimately did not take place.
4 In the second month,
on the night of the *gēngzǐ* day,
the gates were opened and lamps lit.
According to the biography of Yán Tǐngzhī in the Old Book: on the full moon of the first month of Xiāntiān 2nd year,
the Buddhist monk Pólùo requested that the gates be opened at night to light thousands of lamps.
In the first year,
the Emperor received the imperial abdication,
but there was no time to grant a general celebration to the empire.
So this was done retrospectively.
*Pú*,
pronounced *pú*.
The Former Emperor and the Emperor ascended the gate tower to observe.
This continued from night into day,
for more than a month in total.
The Emperor's extravagance had already manifested itself here.
*Jì*,
pronounced *qǐfān*.
It was believed:
"A general celebration is something people benefit from,
a gathering for collective joy.
Now, however, the strength of ten thousand people is wasted
to fund a hundred spectacles,
which is not how to glorify sagely virtue and beautify moral transformation."
So it was stopped.
5 Initially,
after Gāolì fell (see Gāolì's fall in Juan 201, Gāozōng's Zǒngzhāng 1st year),
and when Lǐ Jìnzhōng rebelled (see Lǐ Jìnzhōng's rebellion in Juan 205, Wǔ Hòu's Wànsuì Tōngtiān 1st year),
(according to Fēngsú Tōng: the Dà surname, a descendant of Dàtíngshì; Dàkuǎn was the teacher of Zhuāndì.
According to Lǐ Jì: Dàlián was skilled in mourning rites, a son of the Eastern Yí.
Thus, the Dà surname among the Eastern Yí has a long history.)
the people of that area, *zhāngyǒngfān* (chapter 勇翻),
relied on natural barriers for defense.
When Jìnzhōng died,
Empress Wǔ sent General Lǐ Kǎigù to suppress his remaining followers.
Kǎigù attacked Qǐsì Běiyǔ,
beheaded him,
and led his troops across Tiānménlǐng,
pressing towards Zuòróng.
(Xīn Shū: Tiānménlǐng is three hundred *lǐ* north of the Tǔhùzhēn River.)
Kǎigù was thoroughly defeated,
barely escaping with his life.
Zuòróng then led his people eastward to Dōngmóushān,
built a city, and resided there.
(Dōngmóushān is on the border of the Yìlóu kingdom, located two thousand *lǐ* directly east of Yíngzhōu.
The Nán-Běi (border with?) Xīnluó was the Níhé River,
stretching to the sea in the east,
and Qìdān in the west.)
*Shuài*,
read *shuài*.
People from Gāolì and Mòhé gradually joined him,
expanding his territory to two thousand *lǐ* square,
with over one hundred thousand households,
and tens of thousands of trained soldiers.
He declared himself King of Zhèn State
and allied with the Tūjué.
At that time, both Xī and Qìdān had rebelled,
and the roads were blocked,
so Empress Wǔ was unable to launch an expedition.
When Zhōngzōng ascended the throne,
he sent the Supervising Censor Zhāng Xíngjí to appease them.
Zuòróng sent his son to serve at court.
Up to this point,
Zuòróng was appointed Grand General of the Left Xiāowèi and Prince of Bóhǎi Commandery;
his dominion was designated Hūhàn Prefecture,
with Zuòróng concurrently serving as its Grand Governor.
The Mòhé subsequently flourished;
from this point on, they ceased to be called Mòhé
and exclusively adopted the name Bóhǎi.
6 On the *gēngshēn* day,
an imperial edict declared Yán Tǐngzhī's loyalty and uprightness to all officials,
and he was richly rewarded.
7 In the third month,
on the *xīnsì* day,
the Empress personally offered silk to the silkworms.
(According to old regulations, there was a ceremony for the Empress to sacrifice to the first silkworms and personally pick mulberry leaves.
Under the Later Zhōu dynasty,
the Empress had twelve grades of clothing, and for picking mulberries, she wore a *bǎo* robe.
Under the Táng dynasty,
the Empress wore a *júyī*, made of yellow patterned silk, for the silkworm ceremony.
*Kǎo Yì* states: the *Xuánzōng Shílù* omits events from the second and third months of this year.
The imperial edict for sacrificing to the first silkworms was on the *dīngmǎo* day of the third month,
but the Táng calendar continued this error,
stating
"on the *xīnsì* day of the first month,
the Empress sacrificed to the first silkworms."
The *Tàishàng Huáng Lù* states:
"on the *xīnsì* day of the third month,
the Empress personally offered silk to the silkworms.
Since Sīshèng and Guāngzhái,
this ritual had been abandoned,
but it was reinstated at this time."
The *Tàishàng Huáng*, *Ruìzōng Shílù*, and the old chronicles all say
"*xīnmǎo*."
According to the imperial decree,
"the sacrifice to the first silkworms will be held on the eighteenth day of this month."
The first day of this month was *jiǎzǐ*.
We now follow the *Xuánzōng Shílù*.)
8 Yáng Xiàngrú
, the commandant of Jìnlíng, submitted a memorial on current affairs,
which stated in summary:
"Emperor Yáng, relying on his strength,
did not concern himself with the affairs of the time.
Although imperial edicts were issued frequently,
their words and deeds were contradictory.
His words were like Yáo and Shùn,
but his actions were like Jié and Zhòu.
He threw away the vastness of the whole empire in one toss."
He also said:
"The Suí dynasty perished by indulging in desires,
while Emperor Tàizōng prospered by suppressing desires.
I wish Your Majesty would carefully choose between them!"
He further said:
"No ruler fails to favor the loyal and upright and detest the flattering and wicked.
Yet, the loyal and upright are often estranged,
and the flattering and wicked are often intimate,
to the point of overthrowing the state and endangering themselves without realizing it.
Why is this?
It is truly because the loyal and upright often go against one's wishes,
while the flattering and wicked often comply with one's desires.
Accumulated opposition breeds resentment,
and accumulated compliance breeds affection.
This is why intimacy and estrangement are divided.
An enlightened ruler is not like this.
They cherish opposition to attract loyal and virtuous individuals,
and detest compliance to get rid of the flattering and wicked.
Then the achievements of peace and prosperity of Emperor Tàizōng
will not be far off!"
He also said:
"Indeed, laws should be concise yet effective in prohibition,
and punishments should be light yet certain to be carried out.
As Your Majesty is now greatly promoting virtue
and widely implementing new policies,
please abolish all petty and trivial regulations
and overlook minor transgressions.
If minor transgressions are overlooked, there will be no vexatious strictness.
If major crimes are not let slip, then evildoers will be stopped.
If it is concise and difficult to violate,
and lenient yet able to control,
then it will be good."
The Emperor read it and praised it.
9 Earlier,
the construction of the Dàmíng Palace was not yet finished.
In summer,
in the fifth month,
on the day Gēngyín,
an imperial edict was issued to halt it due to the busy farming season,
to wait for the slack months.
"Slack months"
refers to the period after the farming work is completed and harvested.
10 In the sixth month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
Guō Yuánzhèn, the Minister of War, was given the concurrent title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
The "Kǎo Yì" (Textual Differences) states: In the sixth month,
on the day Xīnchǒu,
Guō Yuánzhèn was made Tóng Sānpǐn.
A note below states: The old record places it on Bǐngchén,
but now we follow the "Ruìzōng Shílù" (Veritable Records of Emperor Ruìzōng).
According to the "Kǎo Yì,"
the main text of the "Tōngjiàn" should change
"Bǐngchén"
to
"Xīnchǒu."
11 Princess Tàipíng, relying on the power of the Former Emperor,
exerted her influence in government affairs.
She had a rift with the Emperor,
and five out of the seven chancellors
came from her faction.
The "Kǎo Yì" states: The "Táng Lì" (Tang History) says:
"There were seven chancellors,
four of whom came from her faction;
the Son of Heaven stood alone without support."
The "New" and "Old Biographies" both state:
"Seven chancellors,
five came from the Princess's faction."
According to the records, at this time Dòu Huáizhēn, Xiāo Zhìzhōng, Cén Xī, Cuī Shí, were in league with the Princess.
Those who did not align with the Princess were
Guō Yuánzhèn, Wèi Zhīgǔ, and Lù Xiàngxiān, three individuals.
Xuē Jì was the Crown Prince's Junior Guardian,
not a chancellor.
Perhaps the "New" and "Old Biographies" both counted Lù Xiàngxiān among them,
while the "Táng Lì" did not count Lù Xiàngxiān.
A large majority were aligned with her,
and with Dòu Huáizhēn, Cén Xī, Xiāo Zhìzhōng, Cuī Shí, as well as Xuē Jì, the Crown Prince's Junior Guardian, Xīnxīng Wáng Jìn, the Prefect of Yōngzhōu,

Cháng Yuánkǎi, the Grand General of the Left Yǔlín, Lǐ Cí, who was in charge of the Right Yǔlín General's affairs, Lǐ Qīn, the General of the Left Jīnwú, Lǐ Yóu, the Shěrrén of the Central Secretariat, Jiǎ Yīngfú, the Right Sànqí Chángshì, Táng Jùn, the Honglú Qīng, and the monk Huìfàn and others, plotted to depose and enthrone.
They also conspired with the palace maid Yuan to put poison in the red arrowroot powder and present it to the Emperor.
Táo Hóngjǐng says: Chìjiàn (red arrowroot)
is also a type of ganoderma;
its stem is red like an arrow shaft,
leaves grow at its tip,
its root is like a human foot,
or like a taro corm,
and it has twelve "children" guarding it.
Its shoots are made into powder;
long-term consumption benefits qi and strength,
makes one vigorous and healthy,
lightens the body and increases longevity.
Shěn Kuò says: Chìjiàn
is the seedling of Tiānmá (gastrodia elata).
The root sends up a straight shoot,
the shoot bears seeds that mature and fall,
then descend through the stem
to grow in the soil.
Chìjiàn refers to the shoot,
and its use has the effect of entering the interior from the exterior.
Tiānmá refers to the root,
and its use has the principle of reaching the exterior from the interior.
The "Běncǎo Tújīng" (Illustrated Classic of Materia Medica) says: Chìjiàn
has a hollow stem,
growing up from the middle,
with small pointed leaves adhering to the stem,
and forming a spike at the tip,
bearing flowers and seeds the size of beans.
Its seeds do not fall until summer,
but instead penetrate the hollow stem to grow secretly in the soil.
(Jìn) was the grandson of Délíang.
Délíang was
the younger brother of Chángpíng Wáng Shúliáng,
and was enfeoffed as Xīnxīng Wáng at the beginning of Wǔdé.
They conspired together.
Wáng Jū said to the Emperor:
"The situation is urgent,
we must act quickly."
Zhāng Yuè, the Left Censor-in-chief, sent someone from Dōngdū to present a saber to the Emperor,
implying that the Emperor should make a decisive cut.
Cuī Rìyòng, the Prefect of Jīngzhōu, entered to report on affairs,
and said to the Emperor:
"Tàipíng has been plotting rebellion for some time.
When Your Majesty was in the Eastern Palace,
you were still a subject.
If you wished to suppress her,
you needed strategy and effort.
Now that you have ascended to the Great Throne,
merely issue an imperial edict,
who would dare not obey?
If by some chance the traitors succeed,
how can regret help then!"
The Emperor said:
"What you say is true;
I am just afraid of alarming the Former Emperor."
Rìyòng said:
"The Son of Heaven's filial piety lies in bringing peace to the four seas.
If the treacherous succeed,
then the state will become ruins.
Where then would his filial piety be!
Please first secure the Northern Army,
The Northern Army
refers to the Left and Right Yǔlín and the Left and Right Wànqí.
Then the Former Emperor will not be alarmed."
The Emperor considered it so.
Rìyòng was appointed Shìláng of the Ministry of Personnel.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Wèi Zhīgǔ reported that the Princess intended to launch a rebellion on the fourth day of this month.
The "Kǎo Yì" states: The "Shànghuáng Lù" (Record of the Former Emperor) says:
"The Princess plotted against the Emperor,
intending to replace the current Emperor with an imperial prince
and monopolize power,
scheduled for the seventh day of this month.
The current Emperor secretly learned of this,
and ordered his guards to execute her."
According to records, the first day of this month was Rénxū,
and Xuánzōng executed her on the third day, Jiǎzǐ.
We now follow the "Xuánzōng Lù."
At that time, the Emperor was receiving court officials at the Wǔdé Hall,
so they intended to break in and cause a disturbance.
The Tàijí Hall in the Western Palace served as the main front gate;
from the north gate, it was referred to as the South Gate.
At the beginning of the Jǐngyún era,
the Left and Right Wànqí, together with the Left and Right Yǔlín, were designated the Four Armies of the Northern Gate,
and Left and Right Lóngwǔ Generals were appointed
to lead the Wànqí,
with a rank of From the Third Grade.
Guǒyì Lǐ Shǒudé and others finalized the plan to execute her.
Jiǎo was
the great-grandson of Mó.
Jiāng Mó is mentioned in Volume 184, Yìníng first year of Suí Gōngdì.
(Rén) was the grandson of Jìng's younger brother Kèshī.
Lǐ Kèshī also had military achievements.
(Lìshì) was the son of Rénjiǎo.
Lìshì was
a native of Pānzhōu.
Pānzhōu was ancient Xī'ōu and Luòyuè territory;
during the Hàn dynasty, it belonged to the commandery of Hépǔ.
During the Eastern Jìn dynasty, Dìngzhōu Commandery was established;
the Suí abolished the commandery and made it a county;
in the fourth year of Wǔdé of Táng, Nándàngzhōu was established;
in the eighth year of Zhēnguān, it was renamed Pānzhōu,
named after the Pān River.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
the Emperor, acting on Wáng Máozhòng's (王毛仲) suggestion, acquired excellent horses and three hundred soldiers.
From
Wǔdé Diàn (武德殿), he entered Qiánhuà Mén (虔化門).
To the west of the inner Tàijí Diàn (太極殿), the north gate was called Zhūmíng Mén (朱明門).
The left gate was called Qiánhuà Mén (虔化門).
The right gate was called Sùzhāng Mén (肅章門).
To the east of Qiánhuà Mén (虔化門) was Wǔdé Xīmén (武德西門).
Inside the gate was Wǔdé Diàn (武德殿).
First, they were beheaded.
Yīngfú (膺福) and Yóu (猷) were captured in the Inner Guest Hall and brought out.
The Sīfāng Guǎn (四方館) belonged to the Zhōngshū Shěng (中書省),
so the Inner Guest Hall was located there.
The Zhōngshū Shěng (中書省) was to the right of Tàijí Mén (太極門).
Yīngfú (膺福) and Yóu (猷) were both officials of the Zhōngshū Shěng (中書省).
The East and West Imperial Courts were inside Chéngtiān Mén (承天門),
divided into left and right.
"Cháo" (朝)
is pronounced "zhí yáo" (直遙).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The *Xuánzōng Shílù* (玄宗實錄) records it as
"the *yǐchǒu* day."
According to *Qiānzài* (僉載),
"Cháng Yuánkǎi (常元楷) was executed on the third day of the seventh month."
We now follow the *Ruìzōng* (睿宗) and *Shànghuáng Shílù* (上皇實錄).
The *Tánglì* (唐曆), the new and old *Běnjì* (本紀), and the old biography of Wáng Jū (王琚) state:
"Jū (琚), along with Qí Wáng Fàn (岐王範), Xuē Wáng Yè (薛王業), Jiāng Jiǎo (姜皎), Wáng Máozhòng (王毛仲), and others, participated in suppressing the rebels.
They arrived at Chéngtiān Mén (承天門) with armored cavalry.
At that time, Ruìzōng (睿宗) heard the sounds of drums and shouts,
summoned Guō Yuánzhèn (郭元振) to ascend Chéngtiān Lóu (承天樓),
issued an edict to close the gates,
and ordered Assistant Imperial Censor Rèn Zhīgǔ (任知古) to recruit several hundred men at the Imperial Court,
but they were not allowed to enter."
A short while later,
Jū (琚) and others arrived at the tower with Xuánzōng (玄宗).
The *Tàishànghuáng Shílù* (太上皇實錄) states:
"The princess planned to have Cháng Yuánkǎi (常元楷) enter through the north gate with the Yǔlín (羽林) troops on the seventh day of this month.
Dòu Huáizhēn (竇懷貞) and others would raise troops in the Southern Offices to respond.
The current Emperor secretly learned of this matter,
immediately ordered the Left and Right Forbidden Armies to exit the north gate,
summoned Cháng Yuánkǎi (常元楷) and Lǐ Cí (李慈),
and executed them below the palace gate.
Returning to Chéngtiān Mén (承天門),
he seized Cén Xī (岑羲) and Xiāo Zhìzhōng (蕭至忠),
and executed them in the Imperial Court."
The old biography of Xiāo Zhìzhōng (蕭至忠) says:
"Zhìzhōng (至忠) hastily fled into a mountain temple,
and after several days,
he was captured and put to death."
This is likely a mistake, attributing Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ's (太平公主) affair to Zhìzhōng (至忠).
We now follow the *Xuánzōng Shílù* (玄宗實錄).
The *Cháoyě Qiānzài* (朝野僉載) says:
"Yǔlín Jiāngjūn (羽林將軍) Cháng Yuánkǎi (常元楷) obtained his official position through informing on others for three generations.
On the third day of the seventh month of Xiāntiān (先天) two years,
Kǎi (楷) was executed for rebellion,
and his family and property were confiscated."
The *Xuánzōng Shílù* (玄宗實錄) says:
"When the Emperor executed the villains and rebels,
Ruìzōng (睿宗) feared a palace coup,
and took his place at Chéngtiān Mén (承天門),
issuing orders to the Southern Offices' soldiers to guard against any unforeseen events.
Guō Yuánzhèn (郭元振) led his troops as guards,
ascended the tower, and reported: 'The Emperor has already issued an edict to execute Dòu Huáizhēn (竇懷貞) and others.
Your Majesty need not worry.'
Ruìzōng (睿宗) was greatly pleased."
We now select what is credible from these accounts.
She hanged herself.

and her surname was changed to Dú (毒).
When the Emperor Emeritus heard of the change,
he ascended Chéngtiān Mén Lóu (承天門樓).
Guō Yuánzhèn (郭元振) reported,

The Emperor soon arrived at the tower.
The Emperor Emeritus then issued an edict condemning Huáizhēn (懷貞) and others,
and consequently pardoned the world,
except for the rebels and their close relatives.
Xuē Jì (薛稷) was granted death in Wànnián Yù (萬年獄).
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
the Emperor Emeritus issued an edict:
"From now on, all military, state, administrative, and penal matters
shall be decided by the Emperor.
I shall now live a life of non-action and cultivate my aspirations,
to fulfill my long-cherished wish."
On this day,
he moved to Báifú Diàn (百福殿).
The *Táng Liùdiǎn* (唐六典) says: To the right of Liǎngyí Diàn (兩儀殿) is Yíqiū Mén (宜秋門).
To the right of Yíqiū Mén (宜秋門) is Báifú Mén (百福門).
Inside it is Báifú Diàn (百福殿).
Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ (太平公主) fled into a mountain temple,

She was granted death at home.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The new biography states,
"emerged three days later."
The *Tàishànghuáng Shílù* (太上皇實錄) says:
"When the princess heard of the uprising,

We now follow the new and old biographies and the *Ruìzōng Shílù* (睿宗實錄).
Xuē Chóngjiǎn (薛崇簡) was specifically spared death because he had been whipped multiple times for admonishing his mother.
He was granted the surname Lǐ (李),
and his official rank and titles remained unchanged.
Chóngjiǎn (崇簡)
is

27 On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Tubò sent its minister to seek peace.
28 On the *rénchén* day,
Yáo Yuánzhī was concurrently made Zǐwēi Lìng.
Yuánzhī avoided the imperial honorific title Kāiyuán,
and reverted his name to Chóng.
Yáo Yuánzhī's original name was Yuánchóng.
In the fourth year of Cháng'ān under Empress Wǔ, he was ordered to use his courtesy name.
Now he reverted to his old name,
omitting the character Yuán.
Fù,
pronounced *fù*.
29 An imperial edict stated:
“All officials serving as governors, prefects, and protectors-general,
after their personal audience and farewells,
shall exit through the side gate to await further instructions.”
The eastern palace had left and right side gates,
and beyond the left and right side gates
were the left and right imperial guards of the Jīnwǔ.
30 Yáo Chóng (姚崇) had just become prime minister.
Zhāng Yuè (張說), the Zǐwēi Lìng (紫微令), was afraid,
and so secretly went to Qí Wáng (岐王) to ingratiate himself.
Kuǎn (款)
means sincerity.
When Chóng (崇) was at the informal audience hall,
he walked with a slight limp.
The emperor asked,
"Do you have a foot ailment?"
He replied,
"Your servant has a heart ailment,
not a foot ailment."
The emperor asked the reason.
He replied,
"Qí Wáng (岐王) is Your Majesty's beloved younger brother,
and Zhāng Yuè (張說) is a high official,
yet he secretly takes a carriage into the prince's residence.
I fear he may be misled,
and thus I worry about it."
On the day Guǐchǒu (癸丑),
Yuè (說) was demoted to become the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Xiāngzhōu (相州).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Sōngchuāng Zálù (松窗雜錄) states:
"When Yáo Chóng (姚崇) was prime minister,
one day he was at an informal audience in the private hall,
and he lifted his right foot not very lightly.
The emperor said, 'Do you have a foot ailment, my lord?'
Chóng (崇) replied, 'Your servant has a heart ailment,
not a foot ailment.'
He then presented a few hundred words detailing Zhāng Yuè's (張說) crimes.
The emperor said angrily, 'You return to the Central Secretariat;
you should issue an edict and, together with the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞), investigate this matter.'
But Yuè (說) did not know this yet.
It happened that a scarlet-robed official reported that three *kè* after noon,
Yuè (說) rode his horse home first.
Chóng (崇) urgently called Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) Lǐ Línfǔ (李林甫) and gave him the previous edict.
Línfǔ (林甫) said to Chóng (崇), 'Yuè (說) is full of stratagems;
this will surely trouble him.
It would be best to send him to a harsh place.'
Chóng (崇) said, 'When a chancellor commits a crime,
it is not advisable to press too hard.'
Línfǔ (林甫) then said, 'If you cannot bear it,
then Yuè (說) will be unharmed.'
Línfǔ (林甫) only gave the edict to a minor censor,
who reported that his horse had fallen on the way.
A month or so before Yuè (說) was impeached by Chóng (崇),
there was a scholar who taught in his household,
and who was intimate with Yuè's (說) most favored maidservant.
They were caught in the act of adultery,
and this was reported to Yuè (說).
Yuè (說) was extremely angry
and intended to pursue a thorough investigation at the Jīngzhào Yǐn (京兆尹).
The scholar spoke in a stern voice, saying, 'Unable to control one's desire at the sight of beauty
is a common human failing.
You, honored as a prime minister,
surely have times of urgent need for people,
why are you so parsimonious over one maidservant?'
Yuè (說) found his words remarkable and released him,
also giving him the maidservant to take with him.
The scholar disappeared,
and for more than ten days, nothing was heard of him.
Suddenly one day he directly visited Yuè (說),
with a worried expression on his face, and said, 'I am grateful for your kindness,
and it has been long since I should have thanked you.
Now I hear that you are being framed by Prime Minister Yáo (姚),
and an external investigation is about to be launched.
You do not know this,
and danger is imminent.
I wish to obtain something you cherish most,
to use a stratagem with the Ninth Princess,
and she will surely be able to secure your immediate release.'
Yuè (說) then listed and pointed out what he cherished,
but the scholar said, 'None of these are sufficient to resolve your difficulty.'
He then pondered for a long time,
and suddenly said, 'Recently, someone sent me a night-glowing curtain from Jīlín Jùn (雞林郡) as a token of goodwill.'
The scholar said, 'My task is accomplished.'
He then asked for a few lines in Yuè's (說) own handwriting,
earnestly stating his situation,
and then rushed out.
By night,
he arrived at the Ninth Princess's residence.
The scholar fully conveyed Yuè's (說) words,
and also used the night-glowing curtain as a gift,
and moreover said to the princess, 'Does His Majesty not remember that when he was Crown Prince, he thought of always bestowing favor upon Chancellor Zhāng (張)?
And now, on the contrary, he is fulfilling the wishes of those who are unfavorably disposed towards Chancellor Zhāng (張)!'
The next morning,
the princess sought an audience
and fully presented the matter.
The emperor was moved,
and then urgently ordered Gāo Lìshì (高力士) to go to the Yùshǐ Tái (御史臺) and proclaim that the previous investigation
should all be dismissed.
The scholar was never seen again by Chancellor Zhāng (張)."
This account also seems to originate from someone who enjoys such stories.
Furthermore, Yuán Chóng (元崇) was dismissed as prime minister in the fourth year of Kāiyuán (開元),
and Línfǔ (林甫) only became Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) in its fourteenth year.
We now follow the Xīn Zhuàn (新傳).
On the day Jiǎyín (甲寅),
Lú Huáishèn (盧懷shèn), the Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎), was appointed Tóng Zǐwēi Huángmén Píngzhāng Shì (同紫微黃門平章事).
Punctuation by Qí Sīhé (齊思和), re-collated by Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
Compiled by imperial command.
Hòu Xué Tiāntái (後學天台)
Second year of Kāiyuán (開元)
(Jiǎyín (甲寅), 714 CE)
1 Spring,
First month,
on the day Rénshēn (壬申),
an edict stated:
"Select capital officials with talent and discernment to be appointed Dūdū (都督) or Cìshǐ (刺史).
Dūdū (都督) and Cìshǐ (刺史) with records of good governance shall be appointed as capital officials.
Capital officials are those in court service.
This shall be a permanent rule."
2 On the day Jǐmǎo (己卯),
Lú Huáishèn (盧懷慎) was appointed Jiǎnjiào Huángmén Jiān (檢校黃門監).
Last year, the Ménxià Shěng (門下省) was renamed Huángmén (黃門),
and the Shìzhōng (侍中) was renamed Jiān (監).
Jiǎnjiào Huángmén Jiān (檢校黃門監)
is Jiǎnjiào Shìzhōng (檢校侍中).
3 According to the old system,
both court and popular music
were administered by the Tàicháng (太常).
The emperor was highly skilled in music and rhythm.
He believed that the Tàicháng (太常), as the office of rites and music,
should not manage entertainers and variety performers;
so he established the Zǔoyòu Jiàofāng (左右教坊) to teach popular music,
appointing Fàn Jí (范及), a right Xiāowèi Jiāngjūn (驍衞將軍), as its envoy.
He also selected several hundred musicians
and personally taught court music in the Líyuán (梨園),
referring to them as
"Emperor's Líyuán (梨園) Disciples."
The Líyuán (梨園) was in the imperial garden,
and its note has been seen before.
He also selected female entertainers
and established the Yíchūn Yuàn (宜春院).
The Yíchūn Yuàn (宜春院) was presumably inside the Yíchūn Mén (宜春門) of the Western Palace,
near the Shè Diàn (射殿).
Lǐbù Shìláng (禮部侍郎) Zhāng Tíngguī (張廷珪) and Suānzǎo Wèi (酸棗尉) Yuán Chǔkè (袁楚客) both submitted memorials,
believing that
"Your Majesty is in the prime of his life;
you should promote classical studies,
draw close to upright scholars,
and value simplicity;
and be deeply wary of delighting in wanton music and being fond of hunting."
Although the emperor could not act on their advice,
he
praised them all.
4 Since the time of Zhōngzōng (中宗),
powerful relatives had competed to establish Buddhist temples,
requesting to ordain people as monks,
often with false pretenses;
wealthy households and able-bodied men often shaved their heads to evade labor service,
filling every locality.
Yáo Chóng (姚崇) submitted a memorial, stating:
"Fútú Chéng (佛圖澄) could not preserve Zhào (趙);
Shí Hǔ (石虎) respected Fútú Chéng (佛圖澄),
but after Chéng (澄) died, Zhào (趙) perished.
Yáo Xīng (姚興) revered Jiūmóluóshí (鳩摩羅什),
but after Xīng (興) died, Qín (秦) perished.
They could not escape disaster.
If only the common people are peaceful and happy,
that is true blessing;
why ordain deceitful individuals without reason,
thereby corrupting the proper Dharma!"
The emperor followed his advice.
On the day Bǐngyín (丙寅),
he ordered the relevant authorities to purge monks and nuns throughout the empire,
and over 12,000 fraudulent individuals were returned to lay life.
5 Initially,
the Dūdū of Yíngzhōu administered Liǔchéng to pacify the Xī and Qìdān.
During the reign of Zétiān,
Dūdū Zhào Wénhuì misgoverned,
and the Xī and Qìdān attacked and captured it.
See volume 205, Wǔhòu Wànsuì Tōngtiān first year.
契,
pronounced Qī Qì fān,
also Chī.
翽,
pronounced Hū Huì fān.
According to old records,
Yúyángchéng was two hundred *lǐ* east of Yōuzhōu.
"The Mòhé, Xī, and Xī all greatly desire to surrender to Táng.
It is precisely because Táng has not re-established Yíngzhōu
that they have no one to rely on
and are harassed by Mòchuò,
hence they temporarily attach themselves to him.
If Táng re-establishes Yíngzhōu,
they will lead each other to submit and assimilate."
Xuē Nà, the Chángshǐ of Bìngzhōu and Jiédù Dàshǐ of Héróng, Dàwǔ and other military prefectures, believed this.
The Dàwǔ Army was north of Dàizhōu,
later renamed Dàtóng Army.
使,
pronounced Shū Lì fān.
Yíngzhōu was re-established.
The emperor also intended to punish the Qìdān
due to the defeat at Lěngxíng.
The defeat at Lěngxíng is seen in the previous volume, Xiāntiān first year.
On *Jiǎshēn*,
Nà was appointed Tóng Zǐwēi Huángmén Sānpǐn,
and commanded troops to attack the Qìdān.
All the officials then dared not speak.
6 Wáng Xiāntóng, maternal uncle of Xuē Wáng Yè,
harassed and brutalized the common people.
The Yùshǐ impeached him.
Yè pleaded on his behalf,
and an imperial edict ordered the Zǐwēi and Huángmén to re-examine the case.
Yáo Chóng, Lú Huáishèn, and others memorialized:
"Xiāntóng's crimes are clear,
and the Yùshǐ's statements are not fabricated.
He must not be released."
The emperor followed their advice.
From then on, powerful relatives restrained themselves.
7 In the second month,
on *Gēngyín* (the first day of the month),
the imperial astrologer reported that the sun was supposed to be eclipsed but was not.
Yáo Chóng presented a memorial of congratulations,
requesting it be recorded in the historical annals.
This was granted.
8 On *Yǐwèi*,
the Tūjué Khān Mòchuò dispatched his son Tóng'é Tèlè and his brother-in-law Huǒbá Jiélìfā,
and Shí Āshībì to lead troops to besiege the Běitíng Dūhùfǔ.
Dūhù Guō Qián'guàn defeated them.
Tóng'é, on a single horse, pressed near the city wall.
Qián'guàn ambushed brave warriors by the roadside,
who suddenly attacked and beheaded him.
The Tūjué requested all military provisions in exchange for Tóng'é,
but upon learning of his death,
they wept bitterly and departed.
9 On *Dīngwèi*,
an imperial edict stated:
"From now on, no new Buddhist temples shall be built anywhere.
For old temples that are dilapidated and need repair,
submit a petition to the competent authorities for inspection,
and then permission will be granted."
10In the intercalary month,
Wáng Jùn, the Hónglú Shàopíng and Shuòfāng Jūn Fù Dà Zǒngguǎn, was additionally appointed Ānběi Dà Dūhù and Shuòfāng Dào Xíngjūn Dà Zǒngguǎn.
All armies at Fēng'ān, Dìngyuǎn, Sān Shòuxiángchéng, and nearby were ordered to be under Jùn's command.
Within Língzhōu's territory were the Fēng'ān and Dìngyuǎn armies,
outside the Yellow River.
In Wǔdé fourth year,
Fēng'ān County was established by partitioning the Huíyǐn County of Fēngzhōu.
In Zhēnguān thirteenth year,
it was abolished and merged into Huíyǐn.
Dù Yòu said: The Fēng'ān Army was one hundred eighty *lǐ* west of Língwǔ, outside the Yellow River;
the Dìngyuǎn Army was two hundred *lǐ* northeast of Língwǔ, outside the Yellow River.
臚,
pronounced Líng Rú fān.
晙,
pronounced Zǐ Jùn fān.
降,
pronounced Hù Jiāng fān.
Dù Yòu said: Ānběi Fǔ was three hundred fifty *lǐ* east to Yúlín,
eight hundred *lǐ* south to Shuòfāng,
three hundred fifty *lǐ* west to Jiǔyuán,
and seven hundred *lǐ* north to the Huíhé border.
11On *Dīngmǎo*,
the Ten Circuits Investigating Commissioners were re-established.
The Ten Circuits Investigating Commissioners had been abolished
in the previous year, as seen in the previous volume.
復,
pronounced Fú Yòu fān.
使,
pronounced Shū Lì fān.
12The emperor remembered Xú Yǒugōng's just application of the law.
On *Yǐhài*,
his son, Dàlǐ Sīzhí Lùn, was appointed Gōnglíng Lìng.
Dòu Xiàochén's son, Guānglù Qīng Bīngōng Xījiān and others requested to cede their official ranks to Lùn to repay his virtue.
The matter of Dòu Xiàochén is seen in volume 205, Wǔhòu Chángshòu second year.
諶,
pronounced Shì Rén fān.
瑊,
pronounced Gǔ Xián fān.
According to Táng regulations: Dàlǐ Sīzhí was from Rank 6, Upper;
Qīnwáng Fǔ Sīmǎ was from Rank 4, Lower.
13On *Bǐngzǐ*,
Shēn Wáng Chéngyì requested that his household's Lùshì Yán Chǔguī be appointed as his household's Cānjūn.
Táng Qīnwáng Fǔ Lùshì was from Rank 9, Upper,
and an official outside the regular stream.
Cānjūn was
Regular Rank 7, Upper.
Yáo Chóng and Lú Huáishèn memorialized:
"We previously received an imperial decree
stating that any requests from princes and imperial sons-in-law, unless written as a personal imperial edict, should not be acted upon."
They cited this recent decree to block the request.
It should be returned to the competent authorities.
If, due to personal favor,
official positions can be granted as a kindness,
it would be repeating recent occurrences,
Recent occurrences refer to the abuses of excessive official appointments during the Zhōngzōng reign.
The matter was thus dropped.
From then on, requests through personal connections were ineffective.
14Tūjué Shí Āshībì, having lost Tóng'é,
dared not return.
On *Kuǐwèi*,
he came to defect with his wife,
and was appointed Yòuwèi Dà Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as Yànběi Jùnwáng.
His wife was named Jīnshān Gōngzhǔ.
15Someone accused Tàizǐ Shàobǎo Liú Yōoqiú and Tàizǐ Zhānshì Zhōng Shàojīng of making resentful remarks.
They were sent to the Zǐwēi Shěng for interrogation,
but Yōoqiú and others did not admit guilt.
Yáo Chóng, Lú Huáishèn, and Xuē Nà said to the emperor:
"Yōoqiú and others are all meritorious officials.
Having just taken up idle positions,
it is natural for people to feel a little dejected.
Their achievements were great,
and their honors deep.
If they are suddenly imprisoned,
it might alarm those far away."
On *Wùzǐ*,
Yōoqiú was demoted to Mùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Shàojīng to Guǒzhōu Cìshǐ.
Guǒzhōu was the territory of Hàn's Ānhàn County.
Sòng established Nándàngqú Jùn in the former city of Ānhàn.
Suí abolished the commandery,
renamed Ānhàn County as Nánchōng County,
which belonged to Lóngzhōu.
In Wǔdé fourth year,
Guǒzhōu was established.
Old records state: Mùzhōu was three thousand six hundred fifty-nine *lǐ* southeast of the capital.
Guǒzhōu was two thousand five hundred fifty-eight *lǐ* from the capital.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The biography of Yōoqiú says:
"Yáo Chóng had always been jealous of him,
so he memorialized that Yōoqiú was frustrated in his idle position
and also made resentful remarks,
and was demoted to Mùzhōu Cìshǐ."
The biography of Shàojīng says:
"Yáo Chóng had always disliked Shàojīng's character,
and thus memorialized that Shàojīng had expressed resentment,
and he was demoted to Miánzhōu Cìshǐ."
We now follow the *Shílù*.
Last year Wáng Jū was sent to inspect the northern armies.
行,
pronounced Xià Mèng fān.
還,
pronounced Cóng Xuān fān,
also as written.
Zézhōu was one thousand thirty *lǐ* northeast of the capital.
16An imperial edict stated:
"Zhōu Lìzhēn, Cìshǐ of Fúzhōu, and twelve others,

all cruel officials during the reign of Tiānhòu (Wǔ Zétiān)—Zhōu Lìzhēn, Péi Tán, Zhāng Qīzhèng, Zhāng Sījìng, Wáng Chéngběn, Liú Huī, Yáng Yǔn, Kāng Wěi, Fēng Xúnxíng, Zhāng Zhīmò, Wèi Suízhōng, Gōngsūn Yǎn, Zhōng Sīlián, a total of thirteen people—
涪,
pronounced Fú.
should be banished to the countryside,
never to hold office again."
17Dū Dàn, chieftain of the Ten Surnames of the Western Tūjué, rebelled.
In the third month,
on *Jǐhài*,
Āshǐnà Xiàn, Jiédùshǐ of Qìxī, captured the garrisons of Suìyè and others,
captured and beheaded Dū Dàn,
and received the surrender of over twenty thousand households from his tribe.
18 The Grand Censor Jiāng Huì (姜晦) reported that Zōng Chǔkè (宗楚客) and others had altered Zhōngzōng’s (中宗) dying wishes.
This incident can be found in chapter 209, Ruìzōng’s (睿宗) Jǐngyún (景雲) first year.
At that time, Jiāng Huì was also a chancellor,
but he was unable to rectify the situation.
He therefore ordered the Supervising Censor Guō Zhèn (郭震) to impeach them.
He also said that Yàn Zhāo (彥昭) had adopted the shamaness Zhào (趙) as an aunt,
dressed in women's clothes,
and went with his wife by carriage to her home.
On the jiǎchén day,
Ān Shí (安石) was demoted to Assistant Administrator of Miǎnzhoū (沔州);
Sì Lì (嗣立) was demoted to Assistant Administrator of Yuèzhōu (岳州);
Yàn Zhāo (彥昭) was demoted to Assistant Administrator of Yuánzhōu (袁州).
The old gazetteer states: Yuèzhōu (岳州)
is 2,227 lǐ southeast of the capital;
Yuánzhōu (袁州)
is 3,580 lǐ southeast of the capital.
Miǎn (沔)
is pronounced “mí yǎn.”
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The biography of Yàn Zhāo (彥昭) states:
“Yáo Chóng (姚崇) had always disliked Yàn Zhāo’s (彥昭) character.”
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄).
Chúzhōu (滁州),
in the Han dynasty, was the territory of Quánjiāo (全椒) County.
South of the Yangtze River, it was divided into the two Qiaozhou (譙州) (Southern and Northern) and Xīnchāng (新昌) Commandery.
During the Sui dynasty, Southern Qiaozhou (南譙州) was renamed Chúzhōu (滁州).
The old gazetteer states: Chúzhōu (滁州)
is 2,564 lǐ southeast of the capital.
Chú (滁)
is pronounced “chú.”
Huì (晦) further reported that Ān Shí (安石) had once overseen Dìnglíng (定陵),
Dìnglíng (定陵)
being Zhōngzōng’s (中宗) mausoleum.
He was summoned to a lower prefecture to face charges of embezzlement.
Ān Shí (安石) sighed, saying:
“This only means they wish me dead.”
He died in anger and resentment.
Huì (晦)
was Jiǎo’s (皎) younger brother.
19 The Heavenly Pivot (Tiānshū 天樞) was demolished.
The construction of the Heavenly Pivot (Tiānshū 天樞) is mentioned in chapter 205, Wǔ Hòu’s (武后) Yánzài (延載) first year.
It took more than a month to complete.
Earlier,
Empress Wéi (韋后) had also erected a stone platform on Tiānjiē (天街),
several *zhàng* high,
to praise her achievements.
Tiānjiē (天街) is the Zhūquè (朱雀) Street in the capital.
Xiān (先)
is pronounced “xī jiǎn.”
Gāo (高)
is pronounced “gǔ hào.”
20 In summer,
fourth month,
on the xīnsì day,
the Turkic Khagan Mòchuò (默啜) again sent envoys to propose marriage,
calling himself
"Gānhé Yǒngqīng Tàifùmǎ (乾和永清太駙馬), Tiānshàng Déguǒbào Tiānnán (天上得果報天男), Tūjué Shèngtiān Gǔduōlù Kèhán (突厥聖天骨咄祿可汗)."
Tiānnán (天男)
means "Son of Heaven."
Duō (咄)
is pronounced “dāng mò.”
21 In the fifth month,
on the jǐchǒu day,
due to famine,
all supernumerary, probationary, and acting officials were dismissed.
Supernumerary officials
are one type;
probationary officials
are a second type;
acting officials
are a third type.
They were dismissed
because they were redundant
and consumed stipends.
No more appointments were to be made.
These three categories of officials,
henceforth, unless there were military achievements or a special imperial decree for their appointment,
the Ministries of Personnel (Lìbù 吏部) and War (Bīngbù 兵部) were not to make appointments.
22 On the jǐyǒu day,
the Tǔbō (吐蕃) Chancellor Bèndá Yán (坌達延)
Tǔ (吐)
is pronounced “tūn rùshēng.”
Xiàng (相)
is pronounced “xī liàng.”
Bèn (坌)
is pronounced “pú dùn.”
requested that Xiè Wǎn (解琬) be sent first to Héyuán (河源) to demarcate the borders between the two states,
and only then would an alliance be formed.
Wǎn (琬) had previously served as the Grand Commander of Shuòfāng (朔方),
which is why the Tǔbō (吐蕃) requested him.
Prior to this, Wǎn (琬) had retired as Grand Master of Gold and Purple with Glorious Happiness (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū 金紫光祿大夫).
He was recalled and appointed as Left Remonstrance Official (Zuǒ Sànqí Chángshì 左散騎常侍) and dispatched.
The emperor also ordered the chancellor to reply to Bèndá Yán’s (坌達延) letter
to appease him.
Wǎn (琬) submitted a memorial, stating
that the Tǔbō (吐蕃) must be secretly harboring plans for rebellion, and requested that 100,000 troops be stationed in Qín (秦), Wèi (渭), and other prefectures as a precaution.
Historians say that Xiè Wǎn’s (解琬) insights
far surpassed those of Cuī Hànpéng (崔漢衡).
Shàng (上)
is pronounced “shí zhǎng.”
23 The Yellow Gate Supervisor (Huángmén Jiān 黃門監) Wèi Zhīgǔ (魏知古),
originally a minor official,
was promoted by Yáo Chóng (姚崇)
until they served as chancellors together.
Chóng (崇) slighted him,
requesting Zhīgǔ (知古) to act as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū 吏部尚書) and oversee the selection process in the Eastern Capital.
The Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū 吏部尚書) Sòng Jǐng (宋璟) was sent to the Chancellery (Ménxiàshěng 門下省) for "official vetting."
According to Tang regulations: for all civil and military officials below the sixth rank,
proposals for appointments from the Ministries of Personnel (Lìbù 吏部) and War (Bīngbù 兵部) must pass through the Chancellery (Ménxiàshěng 門下省),
where their rank and qualifications are assessed,
and their talents and abilities evaluated,
to determine their suitability;
if the proposed position is inappropriate,
they are returned and reassessed based on their merits or shortcomings,
this is called "official vetting."
Xuǎn (選)
is pronounced “xū juàn.”
Chóng’s (崇) two sons, who were serving in the Eastern Capital,
presuming on their father's favor with Zhīgǔ (知古),
extensively abused their power and sought favors.
When Zhīgǔ (知古) returned,
he reported everything.
Another day,
the emperor casually asked Chóng (崇):
“What are your sons’ talents and dispositions like?
What offices do they hold now?”
Chóng (崇) perceived the emperor’s intent
and replied:
“I have three sons;
two are in the Eastern Capital,
they are greedy and indiscreet;
they must have sought favors from Wèi Zhīgǔ (魏知古),
I have not yet had a chance to ask them.”
The emperor had initially thought Chóng (崇) would certainly cover for his sons.
Upon hearing Chóng’s (崇) reply,
he happily asked:
“How did you know this?”
He replied:
“When Zhīgǔ (知古) was obscure,
I nurtured him as one would an egg and winged fledgling.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* (左傳) says: Chǔ Zǐxī (楚子西) said to Bái Gōngshèng (白公勝):
‘Shèng (勝) was like an egg,
and I nurtured him until he grew wings.’
I believed that Zhīgǔ (知古) would certainly be grateful to me
and tolerate their wrongdoings,
which is why they dared to solicit him.”
The emperor then considered Chóng (崇) selfless,
and felt Zhīgǔ (知古) had betrayed Chóng (崇),
intending to dismiss him.
Chóng (崇) earnestly pleaded:
“My sons are unworthy and have violated Your Majesty’s laws.
It is already fortunate that Your Majesty has pardoned their crimes;
if Zhīgǔ (知古) were dismissed because of me,
the world would surely consider Your Majesty partial to me,
which would harm your sagely governance.”
The emperor eventually agreed after a long while.
On the xīnhài day,
Zhīgǔ (知古) was dismissed as Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū 工部尚書).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The old biography of Zhīgǔ (知古) states:
“In the second year, he returned to the capital.
The emperor frequently consulted him,
showing him great favor.
Soon after, he was appointed Purple Phoenix Administrator (Zǐwēi Lìng 紫微令).
Yáo Chóng (姚崇) deeply resented and feared him,
secretly slandering and defaming him,
whereupon he was appointed Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū 工部尚書)
and relieved of his political duties.”
The new biography also states
“he was changed from Yellow Gate Supervisor (Huángmén Jiān 黃門監) to Purple Phoenix Administrator (Zǐwēi Lìng 紫微令).”
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄), which states that Zhīgǔ (知古) was dismissed from political duties as Yellow Gate Supervisor (Huángmén Jiān 黃門監);
the reason for his dismissal
follows the old account of Liǔ (柳) family.
Sòng Wáng Chéngqì,
Shēn Wáng Chéngyì
were the Emperor's elder brothers.
Qí Wáng Fàn
and Xuē Wáng Yè
were his younger brothers.
Bīn Wáng Shǒulǐ
was his paternal cousin.
The Emperor was by nature loving and friendly,
a quality unmatched by emperors of recent generations.
When he first ascended the throne,
he had a long pillow and a large quilt made,
and slept with his brothers.
Every morning, the princes would pay their respects at the side gate,
and afterwards, they would gather for banquets and drinks,
engage in cockfighting,
play polo,
or hunt in the nearby suburbs,
and enjoy themselves at their villas.
Imperial envoys constantly came and went on the roads to inquire about their well-being.
After the Emperor finished court,
he often went out to amuse himself with the princes.
While in the palace,
they would bow and kneel to each other as if among family.
In eating, drinking, and daily life,
they shared everything.
Five tents were set up in the palace hall,
where the Emperor and the princes took turns residing.
Sometimes they would discuss literature and compose poetry,
interspersed with drinking, gambling, and hunting.
Sometimes the Emperor would personally play string and wind instruments;
Chéngqì was skilled at the flute,
and Fàn was skilled at the pípa.
They would take turns performing with the Emperor.
If any of the princes fell ill,
the Emperor would go without food all day,
and without sleep all night.
Once, when Yè was ill,
the Emperor was presiding over court.
In a short while,
messengers returned ten times.
The Emperor personally boiled medicine for Yè.
A gust of wind blew the fire,
accidentally singeing the Emperor's beard.
His attendants were alarmed and rushed to help him.
The Emperor said,
"As long as the Prince drinks this medicine and recovers,
why regret a beard?"
Chéngqì was especially respectful and cautious.
He never discussed current political affairs
or formed close associations with others.
The Emperor trusted and valued him all the more,
thus preventing slanderous remarks from finding an entry point.
However, he was solely
kept for entertainment with music and women,
and was not entrusted with any official duties.
Censorious officials, seeing Chéngqì's high status,
requested that he be sent out as an prefectural governor, following old precedents.
In the sixth month,
on the *Dīngsì* day,
Sòng Wáng Chéngqì was concurrently appointed as the Prefect of Qízhōu.
According to old records: Qízhōu
is 315 *lǐ* west of the capital.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* and old biographies state
"Yōuzhōu."
Now, we follow the *Tánglì* and old annals.
Guózhōu is 430 *lǐ* west of the capital.
For other prefectural matters,
all responsibilities were entrusted to the Senior Assistants.
Senior Assistants
are the *Zhǎngshǐ* and *Sīmǎ*.
On the *Bǐngyín* day,
Tǔbō sent its Prime Minister, Shàng Qīnzàng, to present a treaty.
Shàng
is a noble surname of Tǔbō.
The Emperor, seeing the extravagant customs,
in autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the *Yǐwèi* day,
issued an edict:
"Imperial carriages, garments, and gold and silver utensils
should be ordered to be melted down by the proper authorities
to supply military and national needs.
As for pearls, jade, brocade, and embroidery,
they are to be burned in front of the palace.
From the Empress downwards,
none are permitted to wear pearls, jade, brocade, or embroidery."
On the *Wùxū* day,
an imperial decree stated:
"Regarding the belts worn by all officials and their wine vessels, horse bits, and stirrups:
officials of the third rank and above
are permitted to adorn them with jade;
fourth rank with gold;
fifth rank with silver.
All others are prohibited from doing so.
Women's attire shall follow that of their husbands or sons."
Husbands or sons
means husband *or* son.
"They are permitted to be dyed black.
From this day forth, no one in the realm shall collect pearls or jade,
or weave brocade and embroidered items.
Violators shall be flogged one hundred strokes,
and the artisans shall have their punishment reduced by one degree."
According to Tang law: One hundred strokes of flogging
means twenty strokes on the buttocks.
Reduced by one degree means eighty strokes.
Your servant Guāng says: At the beginning, when Emperor Míng wanted to establish good governance,
he was able to discipline himself and practice such frugality.
Yet, in his later years, he still failed due to extravagance.
How profound is the ease with which extravagance can ensnare people!
The *Shī* says:
"Few are they who have a beginning,
and are capable of a finish."
This is a line from the *Shī Dàng*.
*Yì*
is pronounced like *shǐ*.
*Xiǎn*
is pronounced like *xǐqiǎn*.
Xuē Nè, along with the Left Guardian General Dù Bīnke and Dìngzhōu Prefect Cuī Xuāndào, led an army of sixty thousand
out of Tánzhōu to attack the Qìdān.
Bīnke believed
that "it is difficult to succeed if soldiers, in the height of summer, burdened with armor,
carrying provisions,
penetrate deep into enemy territory."
Nè said,
"In the height of summer, the grass is lush,
and lambs and calves are abundant.
Small sheep are called *gāo*,
small cattle are called *dú*.
*Zī*
is pronounced *jīnzhī*,
meaning 'to be born.'
This is precisely the opportune moment given by heaven;
we must not miss the chance
to annihilate the barbarians in one strike."
They marched until they reached a mountain gorge at Luánshuǐ.
Jìzhōu Xióngwǔ Army traveled 120 *lǐ* northeast to Yánchéng Shǒuzhuō,
then crossed the Luánhé to the northeast.
*Luán*
is pronounced *luòguān*.
The Tang army attacked from the mountains,
but suffered a great defeat,
with eight or nine tenths of their soldiers killed.
Nè escaped with several dozen cavalrymen, breaking through the encirclement.
The barbarians mocked him,
calling him
"Xuē Pó."
Common people call an old woman *pó*.
This implies that Xuē Nè was as old and timid as an old woman.
Xuāndào, leading the rearguard,
fled upon hearing of Nè's defeat.
Nè attributed the blame to Xuāndào and eight other Hu generals, including Lǐ Sījìng.
An imperial decree ordered all of them to be executed in Yōuzhōu.
On the *Gēngzǐ* day,
an imperial edict exempted Nè from the death penalty,
but stripped him of his offices and titles.
Only Dù Bīnke's crime was pardoned.
On the *Rényín* day,
Guō Qián'guàn, the Protector-General of Běitíng, was appointed as the Prefect of Liángzhōu and Jìedùshǐ of the various armies and prefectures of Hexi.
Zhōng Shàojīng,
Prefect of Guǒzhōu, harbored resentment and discontent,
and repeatedly submitted memorials making unfounded predictions of good and ill fortune.
On the *Yǐsì* day,
he was demoted to Prefect of Zhēnzhōu.
On the *Dīngwèi* day,
Xiāng Wáng Chóngmào, Prefect of Fángzhōu, passed away.
Court was suspended for three days,
and he was posthumously granted the title of Emperor Shāng.
Because he was enthroned by the Wèi clan,
he was still posthumously titled Emperor.
*Zhòng*
is pronounced *zhílóng*.
*Cháo*
is pronounced *zhíyáo*.
On the *Wùshēn* day,
all officials' families were forbidden from interacting with monks, nuns, and Daoist priests.
On the *Rénzǐ* day,
the private casting of Buddha statues and copying of scriptures were prohibited.
32 Sòng Wáng Chéngqì and others requested to offer their residence in the Xīngqìng Ward as a detached palace.
On a jiǎyín day,
an imperial edict permitted it.
Construction of Xīngqìng Gōng (Xīngqìng Palace) began.
Xīngqìng Gōng
was later called Nánnèi (Southern Inner Palace).
It was southeast of the Imperial City,
east of the capital,
directly south of Dōngnèi (Eastern Inner Palace).
From Dōngnèi to Nánnèi,
there was a covered walkway between two walls.
It passed through Tōnghuà Mén and reached Nánnèi.
When the sovereign traveled between the two palaces,
outsiders did not know.
It surrounded the palace side.
The residences of Níng Wáng and Qí Wáng were in Ānxīng Fāng,
and the residence of Xuē Wáng was in Shèngyè Fāng.
The two wards were connected,
both west of Xīngqìng Gōng.
Níng Wáng was Sòng Wáng.
Huán
is pronounced huàn.
On its west, it was inscribed
"Huā'è Xiānghuī zhī Lóu" (The Tower of Flowers and Calyxes Shining Together),
and on its south,
"Qínzhèng Wùběn zhī Lóu" (The Tower of Diligent Governance and Fundamental Matters).
When the Emperor occasionally ascended the tower
and heard the princes playing music,
he would summon them to ascend the tower and feast together,
or he would visit their residences and enjoy himself thoroughly,
bestowing generous rewards.
33 On an yǐmǎo day,
Qí Wáng Fàn was appointed concurrent Cìshǐ of Jiàngzhōu,
and Xuē Wáng Yè concurrent Cìshǐ of Tóngzhōu.
The "Kǎoyì" (Textual Differences) states: The "Shílù" (Veritable Records) says,
"In the eighth month,
on an yǐmǎo day."
According to the "Chánglì" (Long Calendar),
the first day of the eighth month was a bǐngchén day.
The "Shílù" is incomplete from this point onwards;
we now supplement it with the "Tánglì" (Tang Calendar) and old editions of the "Běnjì" (Basic Annals).
Cycles continued.
34 A rumor circulated among the people
that the Emperor was selecting women to fill the Yètíng (imperial harem).
Upon hearing this,
in the eighth month,
on an yǐchǒu day,
the Emperor ordered the relevant officials to prepare carriages and oxen at Chóngmíng Mén.
The "Táng Liùdiǎn" (Six Institutes of Tang) states: Zǐchén Diàn of Dàmíng Gōng
was the main hall for imperial court meetings.
South of the hall was Zǐchén Mén,
to the left of Zǐchén Mén was Chóngmíng Mén,
and to the right was Guāngshùn Mén.
The imperial edict said:
"Within the imperial bedchambers,
they are still ordered to be dismissed;
among the common people,
this should be well known."
35 On an yǐhài day,
Tibetan generals Bèndá Yán and Qǐlì Xú led a host of 100,000 to invade Líntáo,
stationed troops at Lánzhōu,
and reached Wèiyuán,
just as Xiè Wǎn had predicted.
Mínzhōu Yìyuè Xiàn,
ancient Líntáo Xiàn,
was renamed Wèiyuán in Yìníng the second year.
It was the Shǒuyáng Xiàn of Hàn Lǒngxī.
Later, Wèi divided Lǒngxī and established Wèiyuán Jùn,
and also changed Shǒuyáng to Wèiyuán Xiàn.
Táng made the county subordinate to Wèizhōu.
Jiāng
is pronounced liàng.
Bèn
is pronounced púdùn.
Shuài
is read as shuài;
same below.
Táo
is pronounced tǔdāo.
Xuē Nà was ordered to provisionally assume the post of Zuǒ Yǔlín Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Imperial Forest Army) in commoner's clothes
and serve as Lǒngyòu Fángyùshǐ (Defense Commissioner of Lǒngyòu).
Because Xuē Nà had his official titles and ranks removed due to the defeat at Luánhé,
he was therefore ordered to provisionally assume office in commoner's clothes and go to Lǒngyòu.
Shǐ
is pronounced shūlì;
same below.
Chánglè
was the territory of Hàn Guǎngzhì Xiàn.
Cáo Wèi divided Guǎngzhì and established Yíhé Xiàn.
Lǐ Gǎo established Liángxìng Jùn here.
Suí established Chánglè Zhèn.
In the fifth year of Wǔdé, the zhèn was changed to a xiàn
and belonged to Guāzhōu.
Xiāo
is pronounced jiāoyáo.
Lè
is pronounced luò.
On a xīnsì day,
brave warriors were extensively recruited
to go to Hé and Lǒng to be trained by Nà.
Initially,
Shànzhōu Dūdū (Regional Governor of Shànzhōu) Yáng Jǔ ceded the land of Jiǔqǔ to Tubo.
This event is recorded in the previous volume, Ruìzōng, Jǐngyún the first year.
Shàn
is pronounced shízàn,
also shàn.
Tubo grazed their livestock there,
and then used it to invade.
Jǔ repented, became afraid, and committed suicide.
36 On an yǐyǒu day,
Tàizǐ Bīnkè (Guest of the Crown Prince) Xuē Qiānguāng presented the inscription for the Yùzhōu cauldron, which had been made by Empress Wǔ.
Empress Wǔ cast the Jiǔzhōu dǐng (Nine Cauldrons),
and personally composed the inscriptions.
"The August Heavens bestow their gaze,
and now establish a grand foundation."
The "Tōngdiǎn" (Comprehensive Institutions) records the inscription for the Yùzhōu cauldron as:
"Xī and Nóng first emerged,
Xuān and Hào met their time,
Táng and Yú followed in their footsteps,
Tāng and Wǔ seized the moment.
The empire is brilliantly settled,
within its borders, peace and prosperity reign.
The August Heavens bestow their gaze,
and now establish a grand foundation."
Yáo Chóng submitted a memorial congratulating the Emperor,
and also requested that it be proclaimed to the historiographers
and announced throughout the empire.
Your servant Guāng says:
The failure to verify the solar eclipse was the fault of the Grand Astrologer;
yet the ruler and ministers congratulated each other,
which is to deceive Heaven.
To select an accidental text and consider it an auspicious omen is the flattery of a minor official;
yet the prime minister then confirms it,
which is to insult his ruler.
Deceiving Heaven above,
and insulting his ruler below —
that even Míng Huáng, with his brilliance,
and Yáo Chóng, with his wisdom,
could not avoid this,
is it not regrettable!
37 In the ninth month,
on a wùshēn day,
the Emperor visited the hot springs at Líshān.
38 An imperial edict stated that abundant harvests harmed farmers,
and ordered all prefectures to repair the constant-level granary system.
During Tàizōng's time, righteous granaries and constant-level granaries were established
to prepare for famine.
After Gāozōng,
they were gradually borrowed to cover other expenses,
and by the Shénlóng era, they were almost depleted.
At this time, they were re-established.
Those unsuitable for storage
were not included in this rule.
39 The Turkic Khagan Mòchuò was old
and his tyranny grew worse.
On a rénzǐ day,
the Qígěluó and other tribes surrendered at Liángzhōu.
40 In winter,
the tenth month,
Tubo again invaded Wèiyuán.
On a bǐngchén day,
the Emperor issued an edict intending to personally lead an expedition,
mobilizing over 100,000 soldiers
and 40,000 horses.
41 On a wùwǔ day,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
42. *Jiǎzǐ* (戊辰 year).
Xuē Nà (薛訥) and the Tubo (吐蕃) fought at Wǔjiē (武街).
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* (水經註) states: Wǔjiē (武街) City is located northwest of Báishí Mountain (白石山), east of Hàn Dídào County (漢狄道縣).
In the Táng (唐) dynasty, it was the Wǔjiē驛 (武街驿) post station,
and along with Dàlái Valley (大來谷), both belonged to the territory of Líntáo (臨洮) and Wèiyuán (渭源) Counties.
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: The Wǔjiē驛 (武街驿) post station is in the western border of Wèizhōu (渭州).
At that time, Wáng Jùn (王晙), Taipú Shàofú (太僕少卿) and Lǒngyòu Jìnmùshǐ (隴右㣥牧使), led his contingent of two thousand men to meet with Nà (訥) and strike the Tubo (吐蕃).
Bèndáyán (坌達延) led ten thousand Tubo (吐蕃) soldiers and encamped in Dàlái Valley (大來谷).
Jùn (晙) selected seven hundred brave warriors,
dressed them in Hú (胡) clothing,
and launched a night attack.
He placed many drums and horns five *lǐ* (里) behind them.
The vanguard met the enemy and shouted loudly,
while the men in the rear beat drums and blew horns in response.
The captives (i.e., Tubo soldiers) thought a large army had arrived,
were terrified,
and killed and wounded each other.
The dead numbered in the tens of thousands.
Nà (訥) was at Wǔjiē (武街) at the time,
twenty *lǐ* (里) from Dàlái Valley (大來谷),
and the Tubo (吐蕃) army blocked the intervening space.
Jùn (晙) again launched a night attack,
the Tubo (吐蕃) army was utterly routed,
and only then was he able to link up with Nà's (訥) army.
They pursued the fleeing enemy to Táo River (洮水),
and fought again at Chángchéng Castle (長城堡).
Qín (秦) built the Great Wall,
starting from Líntáo (臨洮),
hence the name of the castle.
is pronounced *fú yòu fān*.
Before and after, tens of thousands of people were killed or captured.
Wáng Hǎibīn (王海賓), the Fēng'ān Jūnshǐ (豐安軍使), died in battle.
*Wùchén* (戊辰 year).
Yáo Chóng (姚崇), Lú Huáishèn (盧懷慎) and others reported:
"Previously, the Tubo (吐蕃) took the Yellow River as their border.
In the *Shénlóng* (神龍) era, they married a princess (i.e., Jīnchéng Gōngzhǔ 金城公主),
and then crossed the river to build cities,
establishing the Dúshān (獨山) and Jiǔqǔ (九曲) two armies.
This was the Jiǔqǔ (九曲) land given by Yáng Jǔ (楊矩).
They also built a bridge over the river.
Now that the Tubo (吐蕃) have rebelled,
the bridge should be destroyed and the cities demolished."
This was granted.
Wáng Hǎibīn's (王海賓) son, Zhōngsì (忠嗣), was appointed Cháosàn Dàfū (朝散大夫) and Shàngniǎn Fèngyù (尚輦奉御),
and raised in the palace.
43. *Jǐsì* (己巳 year).
The Turkic Khagan Mòchuò (默啜) again sent an envoy to request marriage.
The Emperor (上) promised to receive the princess next year.
44. The Húlùwū (胡祿屋) and other tribes of the Turkic Ten Surnames (突厥十姓) went to Běitíng (北庭) to surrender.
These were the Western Turks.
is pronounced *hù jiāng fān*;
the same applies below.
45. *Yǐyǒu* (乙酉 year).
Wèi Chíhuái (尉遲⿰王褱), the Zuǒxiāowèi Lángjiàng (左驍衞郎將), was ordered to go as an envoy to Tubo (吐蕃)
to convey greetings to Jīnchéng Gōngzhǔ (金城公主).
The Tubo (吐蕃) sent their minister Zōng'é Yīnmáo (宗俄因矛)
to the Táo River (洮水) to request peace,
using the rites of an equal state.
The Emperor (上) did not permit it.
From then on, they violated the border year after year.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The *Tánglì* (唐曆) states:
"In the seventh month, *Dīngchǒu* (丁丑) day, of the fourth year,
due to last year's defeat, the Tubo (吐蕃) sent their minister Sòng'é Yīnmáo (宋俄因矛) to the frontier to request peace.
They relied on their military strength
and demanded the rites of an equal state.
The Son of Heaven was angered by this."
According to this, from this point to the fourth year (i.e., a different fourth year),
it was not "last year."
Since it says they requested peace due to defeat, how can it then say they relied on their military strength?
Since it says the Son of Heaven was angered,
why was their peace request granted in the eighth month of that very year?
We now follow the old tradition.
46. In the eleventh month,
*Xīnmǎo* (辛卯 day),
Emperor Shāng (殤皇帝) was buried.
47. *Bǐngshēn* (丙申 day).
Xiè Wǎn (解琬), the Zuǒsànqí Chángshì (左散騎常侍), was sent to Běitíng (北庭) to convey greetings to the surrendering Turks
and handle matters as he saw fit.
48. In the twelfth month,
*Rénxū* (壬戌 day),
Shātuó (沙陀) of Jīnshān (金山) came to court.
49. *Jiǎzǐ* (甲子 day).
The Lǒngyòu Jiédù Dàshǐ (隴右節度大使) was established,
administering the twelve prefectures of Shàn (鄯), Fèng (奉), Hé (河), Wèi (渭), Lán (蘭), Lín (臨), Wǔ (武), Táo (洮), Mín (岷), Guō (郭), Dié (曡), and Dàng (宕).
should be
is a superfluous character.
should be
should be
Línzhōu (臨州) was originally the Dídào (狄道) territory of Hàn (漢) Lǒngxī (隴西).
The Jìn (晉) dynasty established Wǔshǐ Commandery (武始郡).
