19 The Empress's brother-in-law, Shàngyī Fèngyù (Service Official of the Imperial Robes) Zhǎngsūn Xīn, disagreed with Yùshǐ Dàfū Lǐ Jié over a trivial matter.

The Diànzhōng Shěng (Palace Domestic Service) had six bureaus: Shàngshí (Imperial Food), Shàngyào (Imperial Medicine), Shàngyī (Imperial Robes), Shàngshè (Imperial Residences), Shàngchéng (Imperial Carriages), and Shàngniǎn (Imperial Palanquins),
each with two Fèngyù.
The Shàngyī Fèngyù were in charge of providing the Emperor's clothing,
detailing its regulations,
distinguishing its types and quantities, and supplying it for imperial use.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Xīn and his brother-in-law Yáng Xiānyù ambushed Jié in a neighborhood alley and beat him.
Jié submitted a memorial to protest, saying:
"Though my hair and skin have been harmed, causing physical pain,
my official hat and robes have been insulted, which truly disgraces the nation."
The Emperor was furious
and ordered Xīn to be beaten to death with a staff in the imperial court
to apologize to all officials.
He then issued an imperial edict to comfort Jié, saying:
"Xīn and his associates are close relatives of mine,
but I failed to instruct them,
allowing them to violate the dignity of officials.
Although they have been put to extreme punishment,
it is not enough to atone for their crime.
You should maintain your integrity and detest evil,
and not let these villains trouble your mind."
2 On the day Dīnghài,
Sòng Wáng (Prince of Song) Chéngqì changed his name to Xiàn,
and Shēn Wáng (Prince of Shen) Chéngyì changed his name to Huī.
The two princes changed their names because the character chéng offended the posthumous title of Empress Zhāochéng.
Gēng (更),
pronounced gōng héng fān.
3 On the day Yǐyǒu,
Lǒngyòu Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of Longyou) Guō Qián'guàn memorialized that
eight of his servants, including Shí Liángcái, all had military achievements,
and requested that they be appointed Yóujī Jiāngjūn.
According to Tang regulations: Yóujī Jiāngjūn was a rank 5b official.
Lú Huáishèn and others memorialized:
"Guō Qián'guàn, relying on his minor achievements,
brazenly insults the standard regulations
by requesting a fifth-rank position for his servants.
This truly disrupts discipline
and cannot be permitted."
The Emperor agreed.
4 On the day Bǐngwǔ,

Zēng Wáng (Prince of Zeng) Sìzhēn was appointed Ānběi Dàdūhù (Grand Protector-General of Anbei) and Ānfǔ Hédōng Guānnèi Lǒngyòu Zhūfān Dàshǐ (Commissioner for Pacifying the Various Barbarians of Hedong, Guannei, and Longyou).
According to both the New and Old Books,
this was Tán Wáng Sìzhí,
and referring to him as Zēng Wáng Sìzhēn
is an error.
Also, both the New and Old Books mistakenly refer to Ānběi as Ānxī.
This is also an error.
Shǐ (使),
pronounced shū lì fān;
the same below.

Shǎn Wáng (Prince of Shan) Sìshēng was appointed Ānxī Dàdūhù (Grand Protector-General of Anxi) and Ānfǔ Héxī Sìzhèn Zhūfān Dàshǐ (Commissioner for Pacifying the Various Barbarians of the Four Garrisons of Hexi),
with Ānxī Dūhù Guō Qián'guàn as his deputy.
Both princes did not leave the palace.
The practice of princes remotely holding jiédù (military governorships) began here.
5 In the second month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
the Emperor visited the Lìshān hot springs.
6 The Tǔbō besieged Sōngzhōu.
7 On the day Dīngmǎo,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
8 On the day Xīnwèi,
Shàngshū Yòuchéng (Right Assistant of the Department of State Affairs) Ní Ruòshuǐ was appointed Cǐshǐ of Biànzhōu and concurrent Hénán Cǎifǎngshǐ (Investigating Commissioner for Henan).
The Táng Huìyào states: On the nineteenth day of the second month of the twenty-second year of Kāiyuán,
the first ten Dào Cǎifǎng Chǔzhì Shǐ (Investigating and Disposing Commissioners for the Circuits) were established.
According to this,
Cǎifǎngshǐ were established first,
and Cǎifǎng Chǔzhì Shǐ were only established in the twenty-second year.
The Old Gazeteer says: Biànzhōu,
1350 li east of the capital.
Talented and reputable officials from the capital were chosen for this position,
but at that time, literati still slighted external appointments.
Yángzhōu Cǎifǎngshǐ Bān Jǐngqiàn was appointed Dàlǐ Shàogīng (Minor Minister of the Court of Judicial Review) and passed through Dàliáng.
The seat of Biànzhōu in the Tang Dynasty was Jùnyí Xiàn,
which was ancient Dàliáng.
He stood and watched their travelling dust
for a long time before returning,
saying to his subordinates:
"This journey for Master Bān,
how is it different from ascending to immortality!"
9 On the day Guǐyǒu,
Sōngzhōu Dūdū (Governor of Songzhou) Sūn Rénxiàn attacked the Tǔbō beneath the city
and heavily defeated them.
The Emperor (Shàng) once sent eunuchs to Jiangnán to fetch egrets (jiāo qíng) and Mandarin ducks (xī zhì),
intending to place them in the imperial park.
Wherever the envoy went, there was trouble and disturbance.
Passing through Biànzhōu,
Ní Ruòshuǐ submitted a memorial, saying:
"Now is the busy season for farming and sericulture,
yet birds are being captured to supply the amusement of the imperial gardens and ponds.
Transported from afar, from Jiāng and Lǐng,
by land and water,
they are fed with fine grains and meat.
Spectators along the road,
how can they not consider that Your Majesty values birds cheaply over people!
Your Majesty should consider the phoenix a common bird,
and the qílín a common beast,
let alone egrets and Mandarin ducks –
what are they worth valuing!"
The Emperor (Shàng) personally issued an edict thanking Ní Ruòshuǐ,
bestowed forty bolts of silk,
and released the birds.
Locusts again rose in great numbers in Shāndōng.
Yáo Chóng again ordered their capture.
Ní Ruòshuǐ said:
"Locusts are a natural disaster,
not within the power of humans to overcome.
It is appropriate to cultivate virtue to avert them.
During Liú Cōng's time,
they were often caught and buried,
but the harm became even greater."
He resisted the censor (yù shǐ) [who was enforcing the order],
and did not obey his command.
Yáo Chóng wrote a dispatch to Ní Ruòshuǐ, saying:
"Liú Cōng was a false ruler,
whose virtue could not overcome calamity;
today is a sacred dynasty,
where calamity cannot overcome virtue.
In ancient times, good governors [ensured] locusts did not enter their territory.
If cultivating virtue alone could prevent them,
would those [past rulers] have been without virtue to cause such a thing!"
Ní Ruòshuǐ then dared not defy [the order].
In summer,
in the fifth month,
on the jiǎ chén day,
an imperial edict instructed envoys to thoroughly investigate the diligence or laziness of state and county officials in catching locusts,
and report their names.
Due to this, although locust plagues occurred for successive years,
they did not lead to widespread famine.
Someone spoke to the Emperor (Shàng), saying:
"This year's selection and appointment of officials is excessively broad,
and county magistrates (xiàn lìng) are not talented."
When they came to express gratitude (xiè),
the Emperor (Shàng) summoned all the county magistrates to the court of Xuānzhèng Diàn.
The main hall of Dàmíng Gōng was called Hányuán Diàn,
and north of it was Xuānzhèng Diàn.
Only Wéi Jì, the magistrate of Juànchéng, was first in rhetoric and reasoning.
Juànchéng was an ancient county.
During the Hàn dynasty, it belonged to Jìyīn Jùn.
In the Later Hàn, it was the seat of Yǎnzhōu.
In the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Púyáng Jùn.
In the Táng dynasty, it was under Púzhōu.
Juàn
is pronounced "jí yuàn fān".
He was promoted from a jǐn xiàn to a cì chǐ xiàn.
And the officials were made magistrates.
"Bǎi"
should be
"shí".
Lú Cóngyuàn, the Assistant Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shìláng), was demoted to Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yùzhōu.
Lǐ Cháoyǐn was demoted to Governor of Huázhōu.
The Old Gazetteer states: Huázhōu was 1,440 lǐ from the capital.
Cháo
is pronounced "zhí yáo fān".
The Record of Divergences (Kǎo yì) says: The biography of Wéi Jì states,
"He was asked one policy question on how to bring peace to the people (ān rén cè)."
Now following the Tánglì.
The biography of Lú Cóngyuàn says:
"The Emperor (Shàng) summoned all newly appointed county magistrates,
tested them simultaneously in the palace court,
and those who failed the examination
were all sent back to study."
The Tánglì states the examination was in the fourth month,
and the demotion of Lú Cóngyuàn and Lǐ Cháoyǐn was in the fifth month.
Lǐ Cháoyǐn's biography says:
"In the spring of the fourth year,
because the appointed county magistrates were not the right people,
he was demoted."
Now following the Tánglì.
Furthermore, Wéi Jì's biography says:
"At that time, someone secretly memorialized to the Emperor (Shàng), saying: 'This year's selection and appointment of officials by the Ministry of Personnel is excessively broad,
county magistrates are not talented,
and there has been no proper selection at all.'
On the day the county magistrates came to give thanks for their appointments,
they were led into the palace court and asked a policy question on bringing peace to the people (ān rén cè).
Among the more than one hundred who were tested,
only Wéi Jì's policy was first.
Some did not even write anything on the paper.
Wéi Jì was promoted to magistrate of Lǐquán.
More than twenty people returned to their old posts.
Forty-five people were sent back to study."
Now also following the Tánglì.
Both Lú Cóngyuàn and Lǐ Cháoyǐn were renowned for being competent.
The historians (shǐ) considered Lú Cóngyuàn and Lǐ Cháoyǐn competent,
so the earlier statement [about incompetence] must be wrong.
Chēng
is pronounced "chǐ zhèng fān".
During the reign of Gāozōng,
Mǎ Zài and Péi Xíngjiǎn were most famous in the Ministry of Personnel.
People at the time said, "Before, the Ministry of Personnel had Mǎ and Péi;
later, it had Lú and Lǐ."
Wéi Jì
was the son of Wéi Sìlì.
Wéi Sìlì,
son of Wéi Sīqiān,
served as prime minister (xiāng) during the Cháng'ān era.
There was a Hú person who memorialized that there were many pearls, kingfisher feathers, and rare treasures in Hǎinán.
Hǎinán refers to the various kingdoms of Línyì, Fúnán, and Zhēnlà.
Shàng
is pronounced "shí zhǎng fān".
He then spoke of the profits from maritime trade (shì bó).
He also wished to go to Shīzi Guó.
Shīzi Guó
was a country adjacent to Tiānzhú,
located in the southwest sea.
It originally had no human inhabitants,
only ghosts, spirits, and dragons resided there.
Merchants from various countries came to trade together.
The ghosts and spirits did not show their forms,
but merely displayed precious treasures,
indicating their appropriate price.
Merchants took them according to the price.
The land was mild and pleasant,
with no distinction between winter and summer.
People from various countries, hearing of the delights of its land,
consequently flocked there.
Some even settled down,
and it eventually became a great nation.
They were able to train and raise lions,
hence the country was named after them.
[He wanted to] place them in the imperial harem (gōng yè).
The Emperor (Shàng) ordered Surveillance Censor (Jiānchá Yùshǐ) Yáng Fànchén to accompany the Hú person to seek them.
Yáng Fànchén calmly submitted, saying:
"Your Majesty, two years ago, you burned pearls, jade, and brocades,
indicating you would no longer use them.
How do the things now sought differ from those burned?
That maritime trade (shì bó) competes with merchants for profit,
which is hardly the manner of a king.
The nature of Hú medicines
is largely unknown to the Central Kingdom;
how much more so Hú women (Hú yù),
are they suitable to be placed in the imperial harem (gōng yè)?
Indeed, the censor (yù shǐ) is the eyes and ears of the Son of Heaven.
If there are important military or state affairs,
although I would brave the burning miasma,
I would not decline even if it meant death.
This is merely a Hú person trying to dazzle and flatter,
with no benefit to Your Majesty's sagely virtue.
I secretly fear this is not Your Majesty's true intention.
I beg you to consider it carefully."
The Emperor (Shàng) immediately admitted his fault,
consoled him, and dismissed the matter.
In the sixth month,
on the guǐ hài day,
the Retired Emperor (Shàng Huáng) passed away in Bǎifú Diàn.
He was fifty-five years old.
The Record of Divergences (Kǎo yì) says: The records of Ruìzōng and Xuánzōng both state jiǎ zǐ.
As it says below,
"on the jǐ sì day,
during Ruìzōng's first seven-day ritual (yī qī zhāi),
Princess Wàn'ān was ordained as a female Daoist priestess (nǚ dàoshì)."
Now following the Old Annals (jiù běn jì) and Tánglì.
On the jǐ sì day,
the Emperor (Shàng) made his daughter, Princess Wàn'ān, a female official,
wishing to accumulate blessings for the departed.
On the 15th guǐyǒu,
Báyè Gù cut off the head of Tújué Khagan Mòchuò and presented it.
At that time, Mòchuò had attacked Báyè Gù in the north,
thoroughly defeating them at Dúlè Shuǐ.
Relying on his victory, he returned lightly,
without preparing for defense.
He encountered Xiézhìlüè, a remnant soldier from Báyè Gù,
who suddenly emerged from Liǔlín
and killed him.
The army collapsed and scattered,
with native soldiers fleeing,
hence they were called "remnant soldiers."
Fù
is pronounced fú yòu fān.
Bèng
is pronounced běi mèng fān.
Zǐjiàng
means a junior general.
According to Táng regulations,
each army was to have one Grand General,
eight secretaries (bié zòu),
sixteen personal attendants (jiàn).
Two deputies
managed military affairs;
the number of secretaries and attendants was half that of the Grand General.
Two adjudicators (pànguān),
four clerks (diǎn).
Four Commanders-in-chief (zǒngguǎn),
two overseeing the Left and Right Yúhóu,
two overseeing the Left and Right Yāyá,
each with five attendants.
Eight Sub-generals (zǐjiàng)
were responsible for dividing the ranks and formations,
distinguishing signals from drums and gongs, and deployments,
each with two attendants.
The *Kǎoyì* (Critical Review of Differences) states: The Tánglì writes
"Bóyè Gù,"
but we follow the *Shílù* (Veritable Records).
The Tánglì also states,
"Língquán led Tèlè Huíhè tribesmen to kill Mòchuò at Dúlè Hé,"
but we follow the old tradition (jiùzhuàn).
The old tradition states,
"The envoy to the barbarians was Hǎo Língjiǎn,"
but we follow the Tánglì.
Furthermore, both the new and old *Jì* (Annals) state that Mòchuò was killed on the guǐyǒu day of the sixth month,
and the Tánglì also places it in the sixth month.
The *Xuánzōng Shílù* (Veritable Records of Emperor Xuánzōng) records
an imperial edict to the surrendered Tújué on the wùyín day of the seventh month, stating:
"Taking advantage of their weakness,
they have been swiftly eliminated.
A reward has already been established
for whoever can capture Mòchuò."
This was likely before the report of his death had arrived.
His head was hung in the public street.
The Báyè Gù, Huíhè, Tóngluó, Xí, and Púgù five tribes all surrendered,
and were settled north of Dàwǔ Jūn.
Mòchuò's son, the Xiǎo Kèhán, was enthroned,
but Gǔduōlù's son Quètèlè attacked and killed him.
Gǔduōlù was Gǔdúlù,
Mòchuò's elder brother,
who rebelled in the second year of Yǒngchún
and died in the second year of Tiānshòu.
Mòchuò had succeeded him.
(Quètèlè) then enthroned his elder brother, the Zuǒxián Wáng Mòjílián,
who became Píjiā Kèhán.
The people of the state called him
"Xiǎoshā" (Little Killer).
Píjiā firmly offered the state to Quètèlè,
but Quètèlè did not accept;
so, he was made Zuǒxián Wáng,
in sole charge of the military.
16 In autumn,
seventh month,
on the rénchén day,
Chén Zhēnjié and Sū Xiàn, Imperial Academicians of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, noting that the seven chambers of the Tàimiào (Imperial Ancestral Temple) were full,
requested to move Emperor Zhōngzōng's spirit tablet to a separate temple,
and to enshrine Emperor Ruìzōng's spirit tablet in the Tàimiào;
this was granted.
They further proposed moving Empress Zhāochéng to be enshrined with Emperor Ruìzōng,
while Empress Sùmíng remained enshrined at Yíkūn Miào.
Empress Sùmíng was
Emperor Ruìzōng's primary wife.
Empress Zhāochéng was
secondary; she was elevated to be enshrined with Emperor Ruìzōng because she gave birth to the emperor,
while Empress Sùmíng was worshipped in a separate temple.
This was not in accordance with ritual propriety.
For Yíkūn Miào,
see the previous volume, second year of Jǐngyún.
On the yǐsì day,
Emperor Zhōngzōng's temple was established west of the Tàimiào.
17 On the xīnwèi day,
Lǐ Shīhuó of the Qìdān and Lǐ Dàpú of the Xī led their respective tribes to surrender.
During Empress Wǔ's Wànsuì Tōngtiān era,
the Xī and Qìdān had rebelled.
After the emperor's enthronement,
Sūn Quán and Xuē Nà successively suffered military defeats,
yet the two barbarian groups dared not take advantage of their victories to invade Zhōngguó,
but instead led their people to surrender.
This was because Zhōngguó's power was strong
and thus commanded their submission.
Pú
is pronounced pú.
Shuài
is read as lǜ.
Jiàng
is pronounced hù jiāng fān;
same below.
Their eight tribal chieftains
were appointed Cìshǐ (prefects).
In the late Zhēnguān era,
the Qìdān Dájī Bù was made Qiàoluò Zhōu,
the Gēbiàn Bù Tánhàn Zhōu,
the Dúhuó Bù Wúféng Zhōu,
the Fēnwèn Bù Yǔlíng Zhōu,
the Tūbiàn Bù Rìlián Zhōu,
the Ruìxī Bù Túhé Zhōu,
the Zhuìjīn Bù Wàndān Zhōu,
and the Fú Bù Pǐlí and Chìshān two prefectures,
totaling six tribes and ten prefectures, including Sōngmò Fǔ.
Now, their chieftains were again made Cìshǐ.

Lǐ Dàpú was appointed Ráolè Jùnwáng (Prince of Raole Commandery), acting Yòujīnwú Dàjiāngjūn (General-in-chief of the Right Arm of the Golden Guard), and concurrent Ráolè Dūdū (Military Governor of Raole).
Lǐ Shīhuó
was Lǐ Jìnzhōng's paternal cousin.
Lǐ Jìnzhōng was the one who rebelled during the Wànsuì Tōngtiān era.
Lè
is pronounced luò.
Cóng
is pronounced cái yòng fān.
18 The Tǔbō again requested peace;
the emperor permitted it.
19 After Tújué Mòchuò died,
the Xī, Qìdān, Báyè Gù, and other tribes all pledged allegiance internally,
and Túqíshī Sūlù again proclaimed himself Khagan.
Many Tújué tribes were scattered,
and Píjiā Kèhán was concerned about this.
He therefore summoned Tūnyùgǔ, Mòchuò's trusted aide,
to be his chief strategist.
Tūnyùgǔ was over seventy years old,
possessed great wisdom and strategy,
and the people of the state trusted and respected him.
Many Tújué surrendered households living in the Héqǔ (River Bend) region,
the bend of the Northern River,
Chǔ
is pronounced chāng lǚ fān.
rebelled again and returned to him.
Bìngzhōu 長史 Wáng Jùn
memorialized, “These people have only come to surrender because their state is in chaos
and disarray.
If their homeland becomes peaceful,
they will surely rebel and leave again.
Now, if we settle them in the Héqu area,
these people are cunning and difficult
to control.
They often disregard the restrictions of the military districts and prefectures,
raising troops to plunder.
We hear that many of those who have fled are already in communication with the 'lǔ' [referring to the Turks] and
exchanging detailed information.
This is like raising these people to be spies.
As days and months pass,
their treachery will deepen,
and they will spy on our border vulnerabilities,
becoming a great menace.
When the 'lǔ' cavalry raids south,
they will surely act as internal collaborators,
pressing upon our military districts and prefectures.
Attacked from both inside and out,
even if we had Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè,
we would not be able to win.
I propose that around the change of autumn and winter,
we gather a large army,
explain the advantages and disadvantages to them,
provide them with provisions,
and relocate them to the interior.
After twenty years,
their old customs will gradually change,
and they will all become formidable soldiers.
Although there might be temporary hardship,
there will be lasting peace.
Recently, border-guarding officials and those sent beyond the frontier
have offered many flattering words,
none of which are true.
Some say the northern 'lǔ' are destroyed,
others say the surrendered households are settled.
All wish to parade their own achievements,
not truly dedicating themselves to the state.
I hope you will examine these 'sharp-tongued' individuals.
Confucius said,
‘I detest those with sharp tongues who overthrow states and families.’
Opponents will surely say, ‘The state previously settled surrendered households in Héqu
and they all found peace.’
This refers to the time of Zhēnguān.
However, the circumstances are different now,
and this must be observed.
Previously,
after Xiélì was defeated,
the surrendered had no treacherous intentions,
hence long-term peace without incident.
Now, the northern 'lǔ' still exist,
meaning though Mòchuò is dead,
Bǐgā has risen.
Some harbor gratitude towards them,
or have relatives among them.
Why would they be happy to come south?
Compared to that time,
it is certainly not the same.
That time
refers to the Zhēnguān period.
Lè
has the pronunciation luò.
Relocating them to the interior
is the best policy.
Stationing many soldiers and horses,
making extensive preparations,
with Huá and Yí mixed together,
leading to public hardship and vast expenses,
is the second best.
Just as it is today
is the worst.
I hope you will carefully consider these three strategies,
choose the most advantageous, and implement it.
Even if some escape during the relocation,
those we gain will all belong to Táng.
If they are kept until the river freezes,
I fear there will certainly be trouble.”
The memorial was submitted
but not yet answered.
The surrendered households Diēsītài and Āxīlàn, among others, indeed rebelled.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the jiǎchén day,
Shìfāng Grand Protector Xuē Nà was ordered to dispatch troops to pursue and suppress them.
Wáng Jùn led the Bìngzhōu troops west across the river,
marching day and night,
pursuing the rebels.
He defeated them,
beheading and capturing three thousand individuals.
Earlier,
Shànyú Vice-Protector Zhāng Zhīyùn had confiscated all weapons from the surrendered households,
ordering them to cross the river southward.
The surrendered households resented and were enraged by this.
Censor Zhongchéng Jiāng Huì was the border inspector.
The surrendered households complained that they had no bows and arrows
and thus could not hunt.
Jiāng Huì returned them all.
Once the surrendered households got their weapons back,
they rebelled.
Zhāng Zhīyùn was unprepared
and fought them at Qīnggāng Lǐng.
Qīnggāng Lǐng is north of Fāngqú County in Qìngzhōu,
and south of Língzhōu.
They wanted to deliver Zhāng Zhīyùn to the Tujue.
When they reached the border of Suízhōu,
General Guō Zhīyùn, with Shìfāng troops, ambushed them
and severely defeated their forces at Hēishān Hūyán Gǔ.
The 'lǔ' then released Zhāng Zhīyùn and departed.
The Emperor, seeing that Zhāng Zhīyùn had suffered a military defeat,
had him executed and his head displayed to the public.
After Bǐgā Kèhán acquired Sītài and others,
he wished to raid south.
Tūn Yùgǔ said,
“The Táng ruler is heroic and sagacious,
the people are harmonious, and the year is bountiful.
There is no opening yet;
we cannot act.
Our forces have only recently gathered;
our strength is still weak.
We should rest and recuperate for a few years
before we can observe the changes and make a move.”
Bǐgā also wanted to build cities
and establish Buddhist and Daoist temples.
Tūn Yùgǔ said,
“This cannot be done.
The population of the Tujue is sparse,
not even one percent of the Táng.
The reason we can be their enemy
is precisely because we follow water and grass,
have no fixed abode,
make hunting our profession,
and everyone is skilled in warfare.
When strong, we advance to raid and plunder;
when weak, we flee and hide in mountains and forests.
Even if Táng troops are numerous,
they have no way to apply their strength.
If we build cities and settle,
changing our old customs,
a single setback
will surely lead to our destruction.
The teachings of Buddhism and Daoism
instruct people to be benevolent and weak;
they are not methods for military victory.
They should not be promoted.”

In the eighth month,
the Rites of the Rural Archery and Drinking Ceremony were promulgated to the prefectures and counties,
mandating their performance every year in the twelfth month.
According to the Tang dynasty's Rites of the Rural Archery and Drinking Ceremony,
the Cìshǐ served as the host.
They would first invite retired villagers of virtue to consult.
The most virtuous would be the guest,
the next in virtue would be the secondary guest (Jiè),
and the next would be the various common guests,
who would all participate in the ceremony.
In counties, the magistrate (Lìng) served as the host.
One venerable elder from the countryside, aged sixty or above and of good reputation, would be the guest;
the next one would be the Jiè;
the next three would be the three common guests;
and the next would be the various common guests.
Those aged sixty received three servings (Dòu),
seventy received four servings,
eighty received five servings,
and ninety, along with the host, all received six servings.
Once the host, guest, Jiè, three common guests, and various common guests had ascended [to their places]
and were seated,
the musicians carrying zithers (Sè) would ascend from the steps and take their positions,
playing "Lù Míng."
When the song ended,
the reed pipes (Shēng) entered and stood below the hall, facing north,
playing "Nán Gāi."
Then, alternating songs were sung:
first "Nán Yǒu Jiā Yú,"
with the reed pipes playing "Chóng Qiū."
Then, they would perform a combined musical piece, "Zhōu Nán Guān Suī" and "Shào Nán Què Cháo."
The Master of Ceremonies (Sī Zhèng) ascended from the western steps,
announced the rites,
raised the drinking horn (Zhì),
and admonished them with the essentials of loyalty and filial piety.
The host, guest, Jiè, and all below them would bow twice.
After the libations and toasting were completed,
unlimited drinking (Wú Suàn Jué)
and unlimited music (Wú Suàn Yuè) would ensue.

Sòng Jǐng memorialized:
"For old friendships and private favors,
there are established precedents,
but official appointments and qualifications
are not without public principles.
Rénchēn, due to his old favor,
has already received a preferential promotion.
If he were to receive another extraordinary award now,
it would be unlike other people;
furthermore, he is from the Empress's clan,
Wáng Rénchēn
was probably a distant relative of Rénjiǎo.
Yú,
means 'multitude'.
If there is no transgression,
he should, according to regulations, be retained,
but I request he be noted for a slightly more preferential appointment according to his qualifications."
The Emperor agreed.
The selected candidate Sòng Yuánchāo claimed to the Lìbù that he was the paternal uncle of Shìzhōng Jǐng,
hoping to receive preferential treatment.
Jǐng heard of this
and sent a dispatch to the Lìbù saying:
"Yuánchāo is Jǐng's third cousin once removed.
'Third cousin once removed'
means they share a great-great-grandfather.
Xià,
read *xiájia fān*.
Xuǎn,
read *xūjuàn fān*.
Cóng,
read *cáiyòng fān*.
I do not see him often.
I dare not conceal him because of his seniority,
nor do I wish to harm public interest with private matters.
Previously, there was no mention,
and he would have followed the general rule,
but since a claim has been made,
it is necessary to correct the deviation;
I request he be dismissed."
Yuánchāo had hoped to receive preferential treatment,
but now he could not be retained for appointment;
this is what is meant by "correcting a wrong by overdoing it."
Níng Wáng Xiàn memorialized, requesting a minor official position for the selected candidate Xuē Sìxiān,
and the matter was sent down to the Zhongshū and Ménxià.
Jǐng memorialized:
"Sìxiān has twice been selected as a *zhāiláng*.
Although he is not clearly qualified to be retained,
due to his noble kinship,
he should indeed be given a minor official rank.
During the Jǐnglóng era,
there were often 'black edicts' for appointments,
called 'slanted seals'.
Since the Emperor's ascent to power,
such practices have been abolished.
Every reward given
and every official appointed
must be based on merit and talent,
and all must pass through the Zhongshū and Ménxià.
The way of ultimate impartiality
can only be practiced by the Sage.
Sìxiān is fortunate to be related by marriage,
but we should not bend the law for him.
Allow your servants to discuss and hopefully refer him to the Lìbù for consideration,
without issuing a formal imperial edict."
The Emperor agreed.
Previously,
*cháojíshǐ* often brought goods into the capital,
and when spring approached for their return,
many were promoted;
Sòng Jǐng memorialized that all should be ordered to return their goods to eradicate this malpractice.
13 This year,
a Jìnnán Jiéduǎnshǐ was established,
overseeing twenty-five prefectures including Yìzhōu and Péngzhōu.
1 Spring,
the first month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
Zuǒ Sǎnqí Chángshì Chǔ Wúliàng died.
According to the *Tōngjiàn* precedent,
only for a duke or high official is *hōng* (薨) used,
while for other officials and nobles, *zú* (卒) is used.
Here, Chǔ Wúliàng’s death is recorded with *zú*
because Zhěng Bǐyìshū had not yet been completed,
and Yuán Xíngchōng was subsequently appointed,
hence it is recorded as the beginning of the undertaking.
*Kǎoyì* says: The old basic annals state:
"On the first day of the first month, Jiǎzǐ,
the Crown Prince came of age;
on the day Rénshēn,
Yòu Sǎnqí Chángshì Chǔ Wúliàng died."
According to the *Chánglì*,
the first day of the first month was Jiǎyín;
Jiǎzǐ was the eleventh day.
The *Tánglì* also says,
"On the day Rénshēn, Wúliàng died."
We now follow the *Shílù*.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
Yuán Xíngchōng, Yòu Sǎnqí Chángshì, was ordered to revise and compile the imperial library collection.
2 Shìzhōng Sòng Jǐng, disliking those who were guilty yet ceaselessly made groundless appeals,
handed them all over to the Yùshǐtái for investigation.
He said to Zhōngchéng Lǐ Jǐndù:
"Release those who admit their guilt and no longer appeal;
detain those who continue to appeal."
Consequently, many people harbored resentment.
It happened to be a drought with a *bá* (drought demon);
entertainers performed a *bá* skit before the Emperor,
asking the *bá*:
"Why have you come out?"
It replied:
"I follow the instructions of the Prime Minister."
They asked again:
"For what reason?"
The *bá* said:
"There are over three hundred people with grievances,
the Prime Minister has imprisoned and suppressed them all,
so the *bá* has no choice but to emerge."
The Emperor privately thought this was true.
At that time, Jǐng and Zhōngshū Shìláng, Tóng Píngzhāngshì Sū Tíng, proposed a strict prohibition on counterfeit currency.
Counterfeit currency was particularly rampant in the Jiāng-Huái region.
Jǐng appointed Jiānchá Yùshǐ Xiāo Yǐnzhī as an envoy to confiscate counterfeit money.
Yǐnzhī was severe and disruptive,
filling the roads with complaints and lamentations.
The Emperor then demoted Yǐnzhī.
On the day Xīnsì,
Jǐng was dismissed and made Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and Tíng was made Lǐbù Shàngshū.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Tánglì* states "
on the twenty-eighth day, Xīnmǎo,"
and the old annals state "
Jǐmǎo."
However, there was no Xīnmǎo in this month.
We now follow the *Shílù*.
Bìngzhōu Chángshǐ Zhāng Jiāzhēn was made Zhōngshū Shìláng,
and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Thereupon, the currency ban was relaxed,
and counterfeit money circulated again.
3 The second month,
on the day Wùxū,
Imperial Prince Mǐn died,
and was posthumously granted the title Huái Wáng.
This Huái Wáng's princely title derived from a prefecture.
4 On the day Rénzǐ,
an imperial edict stated that no labor was more burdensome than military service;
once one became a guard,
one was not relieved until sixty years old.
It was appropriate to shorten the age limit
and allow the common people to serve in rotation.
5 Summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Bǐngwǔ,
envoys were dispatched to bestow imperial appointments upon the kings of Wūzhǎng, Gǔduō, and Jùwèi.
These three kingdoms were all west of Dàshí.
Wūzhǎng is Wūcháng,
also known as Wūtú.
Gǔduō is east of Huòshā,
sometimes called Āduōluó,
its capital is Sīzhùjiànchéng.
Jùwèi,
sometimes called Shāngmí,
its capital is Āshétuōshīduōchéng,
located north of the Bólǜ River in the Great Snow Mountains.
The climate is cold,
and people dwell in caves in winter.
Duō,
pronounced mò.
The three kingdoms did not submit,
so they were praised.
6 The fifth month,
on the day Xīnyǒu,
the Ten Dao Inspectors were reinstated.
The abolition of inspectors is discussed in the fifth year of the previous volume.
7 On the day Dīngmǎo,
Yuán Qiányào was appointed Shìzhōng,
and Zhāng Jiāzhēn was appointed Zhōngshū Lìng.
Qiányào memorialized:
"Powerful families mostly hold metropolitan official positions,
causing talented individuals to remain obscure in the provinces.
My three sons are all in the capital;
I request that two of them be sent out."
The Emperor agreed.
Consequently, an edict was issued praising Qiányào's impartiality,
instructing civil and military officials to emulate him,
whereupon over a hundred people were sent out.
Zhāng Jiāzhēn was strong and astute in administration,
but headstrong and self-willed.
Zhōngshū Shèrén Miáo Yánsì and Lǚ Tàiyī, Kǎogōng Yuánwàiláng Yuán Jiājìng, and Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ Cuī Xùn were all promoted by Jiāzhēn,
and often discussed state affairs with him.
These four individuals somewhat usurped power,
and people at the time said:
"The Duke Lìng's four outstanding talents are Miáo, Lǚ, Cuī, and Yuán."
8 The sixth month,
the Chán and Gǔ rivers overflowed,
drowning nearly two thousand people.
9 The surrendered Tújué households of Púgù Dūdū Sháomó and Diē tribes lived scattered near Shòuxiángchéng.
Shuòfāng Dàshǐ Wáng Jùn reported that they were secretly colluding with the Tújué
and plotting to seize the military city,
and secretly memorialized to request their execution.
He lured Sháomó and others to a banquet at Shòuxiángchéng,
where he ambushed and killed them all.
Nearly all the surrendered households in Héqu had perished.
The Báyìgù and Tóngluó tribes living near Dàtóng and Héngyě armies,
hearing of this, were all terrified.
Dàtóng Jūn is Dàwǔ Jūn,
renamed in the first year of Wǔ Hòu's Dàzú era.
Dù Yòu says: It is three hundred *lǐ* north of Dàizhōu,
and over eight hundred *lǐ* from Bìngzhōu.
Jùn,
pronounced *jùn*.
Yòu,
pronounced *yǒu*.
Hōng,
pronounced *hǒng*.
Bìngzhōu Chángshǐ, Tiānbīng Jiéduǎn Dàshǐ Zhāng Yuè, rode with twenty cavalry,
bearing an imperial staff to their tribes to appease them,
and even spent the night in their tents;
his deputy Lǐ Xiàn, believing that barbarian trust was unreliable,
urgently wrote to stop him.
Yuè wrote back:
"My flesh is not yellow sheep,
so I will not fear being eaten;
nor will I fear being stabbed."
(Northerners call deer "yellow sheep."
) "One does not worry about a wild horse."
(Things that are not raised by families or in pastures, but are born and grow wild, are called wild horses.
The *Analects* records Zǐzhāng's words.)
The Báyìgù and Tóngluó thus became settled.
10Winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Xīnsì,
the Emperor traveled to Chángchūn Gōng;
on the day Rénwǔ,
he hunted in Xiàguī.
The emperor strictly forbade the various princes
from associating with their retainers.
Péi Xūjǐ (裴虛己), Guanglù Shàogīng (光祿少卿) and Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉), feasted and caroused with Qí Wáng Fàn (岐王範),
and also privately possessed texts of prognostication and apocrypha.
On the day Wùzǐ (戊子),
Xūjǐ (虛己) was exiled to Xīnzhōu (新州),
and his princess was divorced.
Ruìzōng's (睿宗) daughter, Huòguó Gōngzhǔ (霍國公主),
had been married to Xūjǐ (虛己).
According to old records: Xīnzhōu (新州) was 5,052 *lǐ* (里) from the capital.
In the Táng (唐) Tàicháng Sì (太常寺), there were six Tàizhù (太祝),
of the senior ninth rank.
Tíngqí (庭琦) was demoted to Sīhù (司戶) of Yǎzhōu (雅州),
and È (諤) was made Chéng (丞) of Shānchí (山茌).
Shānchí Xiàn (山茌縣),
in the Hàn (漢) and Jìn (晉) dynasties, belonged to Tàishān Jùn (泰山郡);
in the Sòng (宋) dynasty, it belonged to Dōng Tàiyuán Jùn (東太原郡);
in the Suí (隋) dynasty, it was abolished and merged into Chángqīng Xiàn (長清縣) of Jìzhōu (濟州);
in the first year of Wǔdé (武德), Shānchí Xiàn (山茌縣) was re-established,
belonging to Qízhōu (齊州).
*Shǔ* (數),
pronounced *suǒ jiǎo*.
He said to his attendants,
"My brothers and I have no estrangement,
but those who strive for gain forcefully attach themselves to us.
I will never blame my brothers for this."
The emperor had once been unwell,
and Wéi Bīn (韋賓), the younger brother of Xuē Wáng Yè (薛王業), was Nèizhíláng (內直郎).
According to the *Táng Liùdiǎn* (唐六典): The Eastern Palace had the Nèizhí Jú (內直局),
with two Nèizhíláng (內直郎),
who were in charge of seals, umbrellas, fans, tables, cases, and clothing,
with duties comparable to a Shàngniǎn Fèngyù (尚輦奉御).
When the matter was discovered,
Bīn (賓) was beaten to death,
and Xún (恂) was demoted to Cìshǐ (刺史) of Jǐnzhōu (錦州).
In the second year of Wǔ Hòu's (武后) Chuígǒng (垂拱) era, Jǐnzhōu (錦州) was established using land from Máiyáng Xiàn (麻陽縣) of Chénzhōu (辰州) and by opening mountain caves.
The emperor descended the steps and grasped Yè's (業) hand, saying,
"If I harbor suspicion against my brothers,
may Heaven and Earth strike me down."
He then feasted and drank with him,
and comforted and appeased him,
ordering him to return to his position.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Yǐmǎo (乙卯),
the emperor returned to the capital.
On the day Xīnwèi (辛未),
the Tūjué (突厥) raided Gānzhōu (甘州), Liángzhōu (涼州) and other prefectures.
Liángzhōu (涼州) was 500 *lǐ* (里) west of Gānzhōu (甘州).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: According to the Táng (唐) calendar,
the Tūjué (突厥) raid on Liángzhōu (涼州) was in the ninth month.
The old *Tūjué Zhuàn* (突厥傳) says:
"In the eighth year, in winter,
Wáng Jùn (王晙), Yùshǐ Dàfū (御史大夫), became Shuòfāng Dà Zǒngguǎn (朔方大總管),
and submitted a memorial requesting a western campaign against the Bāxīmì (拔悉密),
and mobilizing the Xī (奚) and Qìdān (契丹) tribes in the east.
The plan was to enter with several routes of Shuòfāng (朔方) troops in early autumn of the following year,
to attack the Tūjué (突厥) royal camp
on the Jīluò Hé (稽落河)."
According to the records, Wáng Jùn (王晙) was Dūdū (都督) of Yōuzhōu (幽州) this month.
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄) and *Jiùjì* (舊紀).
They plundered the Qìbì (契苾) tribe and left.
During the Zhēnguān (貞觀) era,
the Qìbì (契苾) came to surrender,
and their tribe was settled in Liángzhōu (涼州).
pronounced *qī qì*.
pronounced *pí bì*.
Earlier,
Wáng Jùn (王晙), Shuòfāng Dà Zǒngguǎn (朔方大總管), had memorialized to request the mobilization of the Bāxīmì (拔悉密) from the west.
The chieftain of the Bāxīmì (拔悉密) was of the Āshǐnà (阿史那) clan,
likely a branch of the Tūjué (突厥) people,
residing in Běitíng (北庭).
*Xiān* (先),
pronounced *xī jiàn*.
The plan was to attack Bǐjiā's (毗伽) royal camp on the Jīluò Shuǐ (稽落水) this autumn.
Jīluò Shuǐ (稽落水) probably originated from Jīluò Shān (稽落山).
[Bǐjiā (毗伽)] was greatly alarmed.
Tūnyùgǔ (暾欲谷) said,
"There is no need to fear.
The Bāxīmì (拔悉密) are in Běitíng (北庭),
very far from the Xī (奚) and Qìdān (契丹), so they cannot reinforce each other.
The Shuòfāng (朔方) army also cannot come here.
If they do manage to come,
wait until they are about to arrive,
then move the royal camp three days' journey north.
The Táng (唐) army will run out of food and leave on its own.
Moreover, the Bāxīmì (拔悉密) are fickle and greedy for profit;
upon hearing Wáng Jùn's (王晙) plan,
they will surely be pleased and arrive first.
Jùn (晙) and Zhāng Jiāzhēn (張嘉貞) are not on good terms,
and Jùn's (晙) memorials often do not receive approval,
so he will surely not dare to send out troops.
History states that the plans of those in court and on the border were not in harmony,
and were spied upon by the barbarians.
When the Bāxīmì (拔悉密) arrive alone,
we can attack and capture them;
the situation is very easy."
Indeed, the Bāxīmì (拔悉密) then sent troops to press the Tūjué (突厥) royal camp,
but the Shuòfāng (朔方) and the Xī (奚) and Qìdān (契丹) armies did not arrive.
The Bāxīmì (拔悉密) were afraid,
and withdrew.
Bǐjiā (毗伽) wanted to attack them,
but Tūnyùgǔ (暾欲谷) said,
"These people are a thousand *lǐ* (里) from home;
they will fight to the death,
so they cannot be attacked directly yet.
It is better to pursue them with troops."
Two hundred *lǐ* (里) from Běitíng (北庭),
Tūnyùgǔ (暾欲谷) divided his troops and secretly went ahead to surround Běitíng (北庭),
then unleashed his soldiers to attack the Bāxīmì (拔悉密),
thoroughly defeating them.
The Bāxīmì (拔悉密) forces scattered and fled,
heading for Běitíng (北庭),
but could not enter,
and were all captured by the Tūjué (突厥).
Tūnyùgǔ (暾欲谷) led his troops back,
exiting Chìtíng (赤亭),
and plundering sheep and horses from Liángzhōu (涼州).
Yáng Jìngsù (楊敬述) dispatched his deputy generals Lú Gōnglì (盧公利) and judge Yuán Chéng (元澄) to lead troops to intercept and attack them.
Tūnyùgǔ (暾欲谷) said to his troops,
"I have come riding on victory;
Jìngsù (敬述) sending out troops means we will surely defeat them."
When Gōnglì (公利) and others arrived at Shāndān (刪丹),
Shāndān Xiàn (刪丹縣),
in the Hàn (漢) dynasty, belonged to Zhāngyè Jùn (張掖郡);
in the Later Hàn (後漢) and Jìn (晉) dynasties, it belonged to Xī Jùn (西郡);
in the Later Wèi (後魏), it was called Shāndān (山丹);
in the Suí (隋) dynasty, it was again called Shāndān (刪丹),
belonging to Gānzhōu (甘州).
The Táng (唐) army was greatly defeated,
and Gōnglì (公利) and Chéng (澄) escaped with their lives.
Bǐjiā (毗伽) was thus greatly strengthened,
acquiring all of Mòchuò's (默啜) forces.
The Qìdān (契丹) court official Kětūgān (可突干) was brave and skilled, gaining the hearts of the people,
and Lǐ Suōgù (李娑固) was suspicious and fearful,
wishing to remove him.
That year,
Kětūgān (可突干) raised an army to attack Suōgù (娑固),
and Suōgù (娑固) was defeated and fled to Yíngzhōu (營州).

Xǔ Qīndàn (許欽澹), Dūdū (都督) of Yíngzhōu (營州), sent Xūe Tài (薛泰), Āndōng Dūhù (安東都護), to lead five hundred elite soldiers with Xī Wáng Lǐ Dàpú (奚王李大酺) to support Suōgù (娑固) in attacking [Kětūgān (可突干)].
They were defeated in battle,
Suōgù (娑固) and Lǐ Dàpú (李大酺) were both killed by Kětūgān (可突干),
and Xūe Tài (薛泰) was captured alive.
Yíngzhōu (營州) was greatly alarmed.
Xǔ Qīndàn (許欽澹) moved his army into Yúguān (渝關).
Kětūgān (可突干) enthroned Yùgān (鬱干), Suōgù's (娑固) paternal cousin, as ruler,
and sent envoys to request pardon.
The emperor pardoned Kětūgān's (可突干) crimes,
appointed Yùgān (鬱干) as Sōngmò Dūdū (松漠都督),
and Lǐ Dàpú's (李大酺) younger brother Lǔsū (魯蘇) as Ráolè Dūdū (饒樂都督).
In spring,
in the first month,
an imperial decree stripped Yáng Jìngsù (楊敬述) of his official titles and ranks,
due to the defeat at Shāndān (刪丹).
He was still to serve as *zhūshǐ* (諸使).
*Zhūshǐ* (諸使) refers to Jiédù (節度), Zhīdù (支度), Yíngtián (營田) envoys, and the like.
On the day Bǐngchén (丙辰),
Púzhōu (蒲州) was renamed Hézhōng Fǔ (河中府),
and central government officials were established,
entirely on par with Jīngzhào (京兆) and Hénán (河南).
On the day Bǐngyín (丙寅),
the emperor visited the Lìshān (驪山) hot springs;
on the day Yǐhài (乙亥),
he returned to the palace.
Yǔwén Róng (宇文融), Jiānchá Yùshǐ (監察御史), submitted a memorial, stating
that household registers throughout the realm were fraught with escaped and displaced persons,
and much trickery and falsity existed,
requesting a thorough investigation.
Róng (融) was the great-grandson of Yǔwén Jí (宇文㢸).
Yǔwén Jí (宇文㢸) is mentioned in volume 172 under Chén Xuāndì (陳宣帝) Tàijiàn (太建) seven years.
*Jiān* (監),
pronounced *gǔ xián*.
*Shàng* (上),
pronounced *shí zhǎng*.
the character *gǔ bì*.
The emperor approved it.
In the second month,
on the day Yǐyǒu (乙酉),
an imperial edict instructed the relevant authorities to deliberate on methods for recruiting and gathering displaced persons and for investigating trickery and falsity, and to report their findings.
3. Yǐchǒu,
the office fields were confiscated.
Tang dynasty civil and military officials had official land allotments:
first rank, twelve qǐng;
second rank, ten qǐng;
third rank, nine qǐng;
fourth rank, seven qǐng;
fifth rank, six qǐng;
sixth rank, four qǐng;
seventh rank, three qǐng and fifty mù;
eighth rank, two qǐng and fifty mù;
ninth rank, two qǐng.
All were granted land within a hundred *lǐ*.
Dūdū (governors-general) of various prefectures, Dūhù (protector-generals), and officials in imperial princes' mansions:
second rank, twelve qǐng;
third rank, ten qǐng;
fourth rank, eight qǐng;
fifth rank, seven qǐng;
sixth rank, five qǐng;
seventh rank, four qǐng;
eighth rank, three qǐng;
ninth rank, two qǐng and fifty mù.
Officials of frontier garrisons (zhèn),
military posts (shù), passes (guān), ferries (jīn), sacred mountains (yuè), and rivers (dú):
fifth rank, five qǐng;
sixth rank, three qǐng and fifty mù;
seventh rank, three qǐng;
eighth rank, two qǐng;
ninth rank, one qǐng and fifty mù.
In the eleventh year of Zhēnguān,
as the office fields were encroaching upon the common people,
an imperial edict commanded that escaped and returned impoverished households
be granted, according to the amount of office land,
two dòu of grain per mù,
which was called "land rent."
Soon after, due to floods and droughts, this was again abolished.
4. In the second month,
on Wùyín,
the Emperor arrived at the Eastern Capital.
5. In summer,
in the fourth month,
on Jǐhài,
Zhāng Yuè was concurrently appointed *Jiān zhī Shuòfāng Jūn Jiédùshǐ*.
6. In the fifth month,
the Yī and Rǔ rivers overflowed,
drowning several thousand households.
7. In the intercalary month,
on Rénshēn,
Zhāng Yuè went to Shuòfāng to inspect the frontier.
8. On Jǐchǒu,
the daughter of the Yúyáo County Princess, of the Mùróng clan, was enfeoffed as the Yānjùn Princess
and married to Yùgān, the King of Qìdān.
9. In the sixth month,
on Dīngsì,
the Yellow River breached its banks in Bózhōu.
An imperial order commanded Ànchásǐ Xiāo Sōng and others to manage it.
Sōng
was the grandson of Liáng Míngdì.
The later Liáng ruler Kuí's posthumous title was Míngdì.
(The character *zhì* (治)
is pronounced *zhí zhī fān*.)
10. On Jǐsì,
an edict ordered the expansion of the Tàimiào (Imperial Ancestral Temple) to nine chambers,
and the spirit tablet of Zhōngzōng was moved back to the Tàimiào.
(Zhōngzōng had been moved to a separate temple,
as seen in the fifth year of the previous volume.)
11. In autumn,
in the eighth month,
on Guǐmǎo,
Péi Jǐngxiān, the magistrate of Wǔqiáng,
(Wǔqiáng
was the Wǔsuì County of Héjiān in the Hàn dynasty;
in the Jìn dynasty, its name was changed to Wǔqiáng;
in the Tang dynasty, it belonged to Jìzhōu.)
his actions came to light,
and he fled.
The Emperor was enraged
and commanded that he be publicly executed.
Dàlǐ Qīng Lǐ Cháoyǐn memorialized that Jǐngxiān's ill-gotten gains were all acquired through begging and extortion,
and his crime did not warrant death.
Furthermore,
his great-grandfather Jí had performed great services in establishing the dynasty.
During the Zàichū era, his family was ruined for no crime.
(According to the biography of Péi Jí,
Jí's grandson Chéngxiān
was killed by cruel officials during Empress Wǔ's reign.)
Now, as his legitimate descendant,
he should be pardoned from death and
banished to a remote wilderness.
His memorial roughly stated:
"Ten generations pardoned for virtuous deeds,
his achievements indeed deserve to be recorded.
(The *Zuǒzhuàn* states that Jìn Qí Xī asked Shū Xiàng:
'The stability of the state,
even so, will be pardoned for ten generations.')
His circumstances may be pitiable."
An imperial edict commanded that he be beaten to death.
Cháoyǐn further memorialized:
"The power of life and death
rests solely with the ruler;
however, there are regulations for the severity of punishments,
which officials must uphold.
If now, a crime of begging and extortion
is immediately punished with execution,
then for future violations of the law that deserve a penalty,
what greater punishment could be applied?
Therefore, for the sake of the state, we cherish the law,
and we expect to abide by the written statutes;
we dare not make the law conform to individuals,
and show partial compassion for Jǐngxiān's life."
He also said:
"If Jí's merits are entirely discarded,
and Jǐngxiān's crime is specially aggravated,
then what is there to praise about the wisdom of Shū Xiàng?
The ghost of Ruò'áo,
will it not starve?"
(This is a saying by Zǐwén, the *Lìngyǐn* of Chǔ, in the *Zuǒzhuàn*.)
Jǐngxiān was given one hundred blows with a staff
and exiled to an evil place in Lǐngnán.
(The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
"Initially,
the Emperor ordered him to be publicly executed,
but Lǐ Cháoyǐn insisted on memorializing against it.
Another edict was then issued stating 'publicly beaten to death,'
and Cháoyǐn again memorialized,
whereupon he was exiled to Lǐngnán."
It seems the Emperor originally intended to behead him.)
12. Méi Shūyān, the rebel leader in Ānnán, and others besieged prefectures and counties.
Pyàojì Jiāngjūn (General of Agile Cavalry) concurrently Nèishì (Palace Attendant) Yáng Sīxù was sent to suppress them.
Sīxù recruited barbarians and their sons,
gathering over a hundred thousand soldiers.
He launched a surprise attack,
greatly defeating them,
beheading Shūyān,
piling up the corpses to form a *jīngguān* (mound of skulls) before returning.
13. Originally,
when the Emperor executed the Wéi clan,
Empress Wáng was quite involved in the secret plot.
However, after he ascended the throne for several years,
her beauty faded and his affection waned.
Wǔ Huì (Consort Wǔ) was favored,
and secretly harbored the ambition to usurp her position.
The Empress was displeased
and sometimes spoke disrespectfully to the Emperor.
The Emperor became increasingly displeased,
and secretly conspired with Bìshū Jiān (Palace Librarian) Jiāng Jiǎo to depose the Empress because she had no son.
Jiǎo leaked this conversation.
Sī Těng Wáng Jiào
(According to the *Xīnshū*,
Těng Wáng Yuán Yīng died,
and his eldest son Xiūqí succeeded him as Chánglè Wáng,
dying in prison during the Chuígǒng era.
In the early Shénlóng era,
his youngest son Xiūxìn's son Shè succeeded.
There was no Sī Těng Wáng Jiào.)
(The *Xīnshū* biography of Jiāng Jiǎo states that
Jiǎo leaked palace secrets
and was impeached by Sī Pú Wáng Jiào.)
(Furthermore, according to the *Xīnshū*,
Tàizōng's son Wèi Wáng Tài fell from grace,
later enfeoffed as Pú Wáng,
and died.
His son Xīn succeeded,
but was implicated by cruel officials during Empress Wǔ's reign
and demoted.
In the early Shénlóng era,
his son Jiào succeeded as king.)
Therefore,
"Sī Těng Wáng Jiào"
should be
"Sī Pú Wáng Jiào"
(明矣 meaning 'it is clear').
memorialized this.
The Emperor was furious.
Zhāng Jiāzhēn, seeking to please the Emperor, fabricated his crime,
saying:
"Jiǎo speaks idly of omens."
On Jiǎxù,
Jiǎo was given sixty blows with a staff
and exiled to Qīnzhōu.
His younger brother, Lìbù Shìláng (Vice Minister of Personnel) Huì, was demoted to Sīmǎ of Chūnzhōu.
(Old records state: Chūnzhōu
is six thousand four hundred forty-eight *lǐ* southeast of the capital.)
Jiǎo died on the way.
On Jǐhài,
an imperial edict stated:
"Members of the imperial clan, maternal relatives, and imperial sons-in-law,
unless they are close relatives, are not permitted to visit each other.
As for diviners, physiognomists, and fortunetellers,
none are permitted to enter or exit the homes of officials."
On the 14th day of the *jǐmǎo* night,
Zuǒ Lǐngjūn Bīngcáo Quán Chǔbì and his faction, including Lǐ Qísǔn, started a rebellion.
They established Quán Chǔbì’s nephew, Liáng Shān, as Guāngdì,
falsely claiming he was the son of Xiāngwáng.
In the second year of Jǐngyún,
Zhòngmào was re-enfeoffed as Xiāngwáng.
They sought the Liúshǒu Wáng Zhìyīn,
but could not find him.
By dawn,
the encampment's soldiers had collapsed on their own,
and Quán Chǔbì and others were executed,
their heads sent to Dōngdū.
Wáng Zhìyīn died of fright.
Quán Chǔbì
was the nephew of Huái’ēn.
Quán Huái’ēn, as an official,
was known for his strict competence.
Bù (怖)
is pronounced *pǔbù fān*.
He was the son of Jǒng Xiù.
Lǐ Jǒngxiù first appeared in volume 106, in the first year of Wǔ Hòu's Shéngōng era.
Jǒng (迥)
is pronounced *hùqǐng fān*.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
Wáng Yí, the Hénán Yǐn, was dispatched to the capital [Jīngshī]
to investigate and offer condolences.
On the 15th day, *guǐwèi*,
Tǔbō besieged the king of Xiǎobólǜ, Méijǐn Máng.
Xiǎobólǜ is three hundred *lǐ* northwest of Dàbólǜ,
over nine thousand *lǐ* from the capital [Jīngshī],
and three thousand *lǐ* east-southeast of the Tǔbō Zānpǔ's court.
"Bólǜ
is the western gate of Táng.
If Bólǜ falls, the entire Xīyù will belong to Tǔbō."
Sōng then dispatched Shūlè Fùshǐ Zhāng Sīlǐ to lead four thousand Fān and Hàn infantry and cavalry to rescue them.
According to the Xīnshū,
Zhāng Sōng is Zhāng Xiàosōng.
Shǐ (使)
is pronounced *shūlì fān*.
Jiàng (將)
is pronounced *jíliàng fān*.
Qí (騎)
is pronounced *qíjì fān*.
They joined Méijǐn Máng to strike Tǔbō,
utterly defeating them,
killing and capturing tens of thousands.
From then on, for several years,
Tǔbō dared not encroach upon the border.
Wáng Yí managed Quán Chǔbì’s case,
which implicated many people,
and it remained unresolved for a long time.
The Emperor then appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Sòng Jǐng as Xījīng Liúshǒu.
Upon Sòng Jǐng’s arrival,
he only executed a few key conspirators,
and reported that the rest should be pardoned.
Kāng Dàibīn’s remaining followers, led by Kāng Yuànzǐ, rebelled,
proclaiming themselves Khans.
Zhāng Yuè dispatched troops to pursue, suppress, and capture them,
and his faction was completely pacified.
Over fifty thousand residual Hú from the six prefectures of Héqǔ were relocated to the prefectures of Xǔ, Rǔ, Táng, Dèng, Xiān, and Yù.
In the eighth year of Zhēngguān,
Yīzhōu Xiāngchéng Jùn was renamed Rǔzhōu.
Tángzhōu
was the land of Bǐyáng, Húyáng, and Píngshì in the eastern border of Hàn Nányáng Jùn.
The Later Wèi established Dōngjīngzhōu in Bǐyáng,
which was later changed to Chāngzhōu,
then to Huáizhōu,
and the Suí changed it to Xiǎnzhōu.
In the fifth year of Wǔdé,
because the commandery had Tángchéng Shān,
it was renamed Tángzhōu.
In the third year of Kāiyuán,
Xiānzhōu was established from Yèxiāngchéng of Rǔzhōu, Fāngchéng of Tángzhōu, Xīpíng of Yùzhōu, and Wǔyáng of Xǔzhōu.
Previously,
there were usually over six hundred thousand border garrison troops.
Zhāng Yuè, seeing no strong enemies at the time,
proposed disbanding over two hundred thousand of them to return to farming.
The Emperor was skeptical,
and Zhāng Yuè said:
"Your subject has long been at the frontier,
and fully understands the situation. Generals merely use them for self-defense and private labor.
If it is to defend against enemies and achieve victory,
there is no need to keep an excessive number of troops that hinder agricultural work.
If Your Majesty is still skeptical,
I request to guarantee it with my entire family of a hundred lives."
The Emperor then consented.
Initially,
the Fǔbīng of the various guards,
from adulthood, joined the army,
and were exempt at sixty,
but their families were not exempt from miscellaneous labor.
Gradually, they became impoverished and weak,
and almost all fled.
The common people suffered from this.
Zhāng Yuè suggested
recruiting strong men to serve as imperial guards [Sùwèi],
without regard to background or corvée.
By offering generous provisions,
those who had fled would surely contend to enlist.
The Emperor agreed.
Within ten days,
thirteen thousand elite soldiers were obtained,
distributed among the various guards,
and rotated in service.
The division between soldiers and farmers
began from this point.
Historians say that the drawbacks of the Táng's troop-raising system began with Zhāng Yuè.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the *guǐchǒu* day,
Qiányuán Diàn was again designated as Míngtáng.
The Dōngdū Míngtáng was again designated as Qiányuán Diàn,
seen in the previous volume, the fifth year.
Fù (復)
is pronounced *fúyòu fān*.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
the Emperor visited Shòu’ān Xìngtài Gōng.
Shòu’ān
was the land of ancient Xīn’ān Jiǔqǔ.
The Later Wèi established Gāntáng Xiàn,
and in the fourth year of Suí Rénshòu, it was changed to Shòu’ān Xiàn,
belonging to Luòzhōu.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
he returned to the palace.
The Emperor wished to display military might in the northern frontier.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Qínzhōu Dūdū Zhāng Shǒujié and others were appointed as various guard generals.
In the eleventh month,
on the *yǐwèi* day,
for the first time, chancellors were ordered to collectively receive an actual enfeoffment of three hundred households.
The Táng Huìyào states: The old system was that
all meritorious officials granted actual enfeoffment [shífēng]
would first have their household count determined by *kèhù*.
Prefecture and county officials, along with state and township officials, would keep records
and supply their rent and taxes.
Each would correspond to the allocated rent and taxes.
Distant and near prefecture and county officials would collect their fees [jiǎozhí]
and then remit them to the state and township officials.
The *dīng* (adult male laborers) were treated similarly,
and those who entered the state or township collected their corvée [yōng].
Former Guǎngzhōu Dūdū Péi Zhòuxiān was imprisoned.
The Emperor discussed his crime with the chancellors.
Zhāng Jiāzhēn suggested flogging him,
but Zhāng Yuè said:
"I have heard that 'punishment does not extend to high officials.'
This is a saying from the Qūlǐ.
Shàng (上)
is pronounced *shípú fān*.
This is also how integrity and shame are fostered.
Therefore, a *shì* (scholar-official) can be killed but not disgraced.
This is a saying from the Rúxíng.
I heard that Jiāng Jiǎo was flogged in the imperial court.
Jiāng Jiǎo's official rank reached the third grade,
and he also had minor merits.
If he committed a crime deserving death, he should die;
if deserving exile, he should be exiled.
How could he be lightly subjected to flogging and humiliation,
treated like a common servant!
The incident with Jiāng Jiǎo is in the past and cannot be undone,
but Péi Zhòuxiān, according to the facts, deserves exile.
How can we repeat the previous mistake!"
The Emperor deeply agreed with him.
Zhāng Jiāzhēn was displeased,
and upon retreating, said to Zhāng Yuè:
"Why debate the matter so profoundly!"
Zhāng Yuè replied:
"A chancellor
serves when the time comes.
If all the great ministers of the state can be flogged and humiliated,
I only fear that it will eventually extend to us.
My words are not for Péi Zhòuxiān,
but for the gentlemen of the entire realm."
Zhāng Jiāzhēn had no reply.
In the twelfth month,
on the *gēngzǐ* day,
the daughter of Shíxìng Kèhán Āshǐnà Huáidào was made Princess Jiāohé.
In the fourth year of Wǔ Hòu's Cháng'ān era,
Āshǐnà Huáidào was invested as Shíxìng Kèhán.
The Emperor was about to visit Jìnyáng,
and then return to Cháng'ān.
Zhāng Yuè spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"On the sandbanks of Fényīn, there is a Hàn-era Hòutǔ Ancestral Temple.
The establishment of the Hòutǔ Ancestral Temple is mentioned in volume 20, in the fourth year of Hàn Wǔdì's Yuándǐng era.
Shuí (脽) is pronounced *yīnshuí*.
Your Majesty should take advantage of this imperial tour to repair it
and pray for grain for the farmers."
The Emperor agreed.
25. In the first month, Princess Yǒngmù (永穆公主) was about to be married.
Princess Yǒngmù married Wáng Yáo (王繇).
The monk Yī Xíng (一行) remonstrated, saying:
"Empress Wǔ (武后) had only one daughter, Tàipíng (太平),
and therefore her trousseau was especially lavish.
Eventually, this led to her downfall due to arrogance."
Princess Tàipíng (太平公主) first married Xuē Shào (薛紹) and met her downfall at the beginning of the Kāiyuán (開元) era.
"Zú (卒)"
is pronounced "xù" (恤).
The Emperor immediately stopped the preparations.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the day Jǐsì (己巳),
the imperial carriage departed from the Eastern Capital for a northern tour.
On the day Gēngchén (庚辰),
they arrived at Lùzhōu (潞州), where taxes and corvée were remitted for five years.
This was because the Emperor had once served as a Sub-Prefect (biéjià, 別駕) in Lùzhōu (潞州).
"Fù (復)"
is pronounced "fāngmù" (方目).
On the day Xīnmǎo (辛卯),
they arrived at Bìngzhōu (幷州), where the Northern Capital was established.
Bìngzhōu (幷州) was renamed Tàiyuán Fǔ (太原府),
and its governor (cìshǐ, 刺史) was made an Yin (尹).
In the second month,
on the day Wùshēn (戊申),
they returned to Jìnzhōu (晉州).
2. Zhāng Yuè (張說) and Zhāng Jiāzhēn (張嘉貞) were at odds.
It so happened that Jiāzhēn's (嘉貞) younger brother, Zhāng Jiāyòu (張嘉祐), the General of the Right Wǔwèi (右金吾將軍), was implicated in a corruption case.
Yuè (說) advised Jiāzhēn (嘉貞) to wait outside in plain clothes to atone for his guilt.
On the day Jǐyǒu (己酉),
Jiāzhēn (嘉貞) was demoted to Governor (cìshǐ, 刺史) of Yōuzhōu (幽州).
3. On the day Rénzǐ (壬子),
sacrifices were offered to Hòutǔ (后土) at Fényīn (汾陰).
On the day Yǐmǎo (乙卯),
Wáng Tóngqìng (王同慶), the Magistrate of Píngyáo (平遙), was demoted to Commandant (wèi, 尉) of Gàn (贛).
Píngyáo (平遙) was originally Píngtáo (平陶) County of Hàn (漢) Dynasty's Tàiyuán (太原) Commandery.
Later, the Northern Wèi (北魏) avoided the national taboo name [of Emperor Dàozǔ Tuòbá Guì (道祖拓跋珪)'s father, Tuòbá Shí (拓跋寔)],
and changed Píngtáo (平陶) to Píngyáo (平遙).
During the Zhōu (周) and Suí (隋) dynasties, it belonged to Jièzhōu (介州);
in the Táng (唐) Dynasty, it belonged to Fénzhōu (汾州).
"Gàn (贛)"
is pronounced "gàn" (紺).
He caused trouble and annoyance to the common people.
4. On the day Guǐhài (癸亥),
Zhāng Yuè (張說) was additionally appointed concurrently as Minister of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng, 中書令).
5. On the day Jǐsì (己巳),
the Tiānbīng (天兵), Dàwǔ (大武) and other armies were disbanded.
The Dàtóng (大同) Army was made the Jiedushi (jiédùshǐ, 節度使) for the region north of Tàiyuán (太原),
overseeing the ten prefectures of Tàiyuán (太原), Liáo (遼), Shí (石), Lán (嵐), Fén (汾), Dài (代), Xīn (忻), Shuò (朔), Wèi (蔚), and Yún (雲).
In the third year of Wǔdé (武德),
Lèpíng (樂平), Liáoshān (遼山), Píngchéng (平城), and Shí'ài (石艾) from Bìngzhōu (幷州) were separated
to establish Liáozhōu (遼州).
In the eighth year, it was called Jīzhōu (箕州).
In the first year of Xiāntiān (先天), to avoid the Emperor's given name, it was changed to Yízhōu (儀州).
It was not until the third year of Zhōnghé (中和) that it was restored to Liáozhōu (遼州).
This is written according to the later established prefectural name.
"Lán (嵐)"
is pronounced "lúhán" (盧含).
"Wèi (蔚)"
is pronounced "yūwù" (紆勿).
6. In the third month,
on the day Gēngwǔ (庚午),
the imperial carriage arrived at the capital.
7. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ (甲子),

Wáng Jùn (王晙), Minister of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū, 吏部尚書), was appointed Minister of the Ministry of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū, 兵部尚書) and given the concurrent title "Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn" (同中書門下三品).
8. In the fifth month,
on the day Jǐchǒu (己丑),
Wáng Jùn (王晙) was additionally appointed Grand Commissioner of the Shuòfāng (朔方) Army (jiédù dàshǐ, 節度大使),
to inspect the various armies of Héxī (河西), Lǒngyòu (隴右), Hédōng (河東), and Héběi (河北).
9. The Emperor established the Lìzhèng Shūyuàn (麗正書院),
gathering men of letters.
Since the Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏) dynasties,
there had been the office of "Mìshū" (祕書, Director of the Imperial Library).
Liáng (梁) stored all books inside the Wéndé Diàn (文德殿).
The Northern Qí (北齊) had "Wénlín Guǎn Xuéshì" (文林館學士),
and the Northern Zhōu (北周) had "Línzhǐ Diàn Xuéshì" (麟趾殿學士),
all responsible for writing and compiling.
The Suí (隋) Dynasty made two copies, one main and one secondary, of all books,
storing them in the palace,
while the rest filled the outer cabinet of the Imperial Library (mìshū wàigé, 祕書外閣).
Emperor Yáng (煬帝) stored books in the east and west wings of the Guānwén Diàn (觀文殿) in the Eastern Capital.
From the Yánjiā (延嘉) era of the Hàn (漢) Dynasty to the Suí (隋) Dynasty, the "Mìshū" (祕書) office managed maps and documents,
and books within the imperial forbidden area
were sometimes included.
When Tàizōng (太宗) was a prince,
he established eighteen scholars.
Afterwards, the Hóngwén (弘文) and Chóngwén (崇文) Academies both had scholars.
In the fifth year of Kāiyuán (開元), four categories of books were copied in the Qiányuán Diàn (乾元殿),
and a "Qiányuán Yuàn Shǐ" (乾元院使) was established,
with four "Kānzhèng Guān" (刊正官) and eight "Zhīshū Guān" (知書官),
separately managing the books of the four divisions.
In the sixth year, it was renamed Lìzhèng Xiūshū Yuàn (麗正修書院),
with a "Shǐ" (使) and "Jiǎnjiào Guān" (檢校官) appointed,
and the "Xiūshū Guān" (修書官) were renamed "Lìzhèng Diàn Xuéshì" (麗正殿學士).
In the eighth year, "Wénxué Zhí" (文學直) were added,
and "Xiūzhuàn" (修撰), "Jiàolǐ" (校理), "Pànzhèng" (判正), and "Jiàokān Guān" (校勘官) were also added.
In the eleventh year, "Lìzhèng Yuàn Xiūshū Xuéshì" (麗正院修書學士) were established.
In the thirteenth year, the Lìzhèng Xiūshū Yuàn (麗正修書院) was changed to the Jíxián Diàn Shūyuàn (集賢殿書院).
Those of fifth rank or above were "Xuéshì" (學士),
and those of sixth rank or below were "Zhí Xuéshì" (直學士).
One Prime Minister (zǎixiàng, 宰相) served as "Xuéshì Zhī Yuànshì" (學士知院事),
and one Palace Attendant (chángshì, 常侍) served as "Fù Zhī Yuànshì" (副知院事).
Additionally, one "Pànyuàn" (判院) was appointed,
and one "Yāyuàn Zhōngshǐ" (押院中使).
Also established were "Jíxián Yuàn Shìjiǎng Xuéshì" (集賢院侍講學士) and "Shìdú Zhí Xuéshì" (侍讀直學士).
Later, "Xiūzhuàn Guān" (修撰官), "Jiàolǐ Guān" (校理官), "Dàizhì Guān" (待制官), "Liúyuàn Guān" (留院官), "Zhī Jiǎntǎo Guān" (知檢討官), "Wénxué Zhí" (文學直) and similar positions were added.
Kuàijī (會稽) County was under Yuèzhōu (越州).
Gǔchéng (鼓城) County was the land of the Hàn (漢) Dynasty's Línpíng (臨平) and Xiàqǔyáng (下曲陽) Counties.
The Suí (隋) Dynasty separated Gāochéng (槀城),
and established Xīyáng (昔陽) County five li east of the old city of Xiàqǔyáng (下曲陽).

In the Táng (唐) Dynasty, it belonged to Dìngzhōu (定州).

Zhāng Yuè (張說) was made the "Xiūshū Shǐ" (修書使) to oversee it all.
The responsible officials provided generous supplies.
Lù Jiān (陸堅) of Luòyáng (洛陽), a Scholar of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén, 中書舍人), believed that these institutions were useless to the country,

The "Kǎoyì" (考異) states: The old tradition records
"Xú Jiān" (徐堅),

"From ancient times, when the nation was at peace, emperors

10. In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the day Guǐmǎo (癸卯),
an imperial edict stated:
"The previous order to investigate and round up fugitives

All under heaven are to be treated equally;
they should each follow their own desires.
Let the local prefectures and counties settle them peacefully,
allowing them to pursue their livelihoods."
11. On the day Wùshēn (戊申),
Xuān Huángdì (宣皇帝) was posthumously honored with the temple name Xiànzǔ (獻祖),
and Guāng Huángdì (光皇帝) with the temple name Yìzǔ (懿祖).
Xuān Huángdì's (宣皇帝) personal name was Xī (熙);
he was the great-grandson of Gǎo (暠), King Wǔzhāo (武昭) of Liáng (涼),
the grandson of Xīn (歆), King of Liáng (涼王),
and the son of Zhòng'ěr (重耳), Grand Administrator (tàishǒu, 太守) of Hóngnóng (弘農).
Guāng Huángdì's (光皇帝) personal name was Tiāncì (天賜);
he was the eldest son of Xuān Huángdì (宣皇帝).
12. Previously,
the Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾), fearing the strength of the Tǔbō (吐蕃),
had been their vassal for several years.
In the ninth month,
on the day Rénshēn (壬申),
they led their people to Shāzhōu (沙州) and surrendered.
Zhāng Jìngzhōng (張敬忠), the Jiedushi (jiédùshǐ, 節度使) of Héxī (河西), accepted and appeased them.
13. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Dīngyǒu (丁酉),

The "Yōnglù" (雍錄) states: The Lìshān Wēntāng (驪山溫湯) is 150 paces south of Líntóng (臨潼) County,
directly northwest of Lìshān (驪山).
The "Shídào Zhì" (十道志) states: There are three spring sources;
one of them is the Huángtáng Shíjǐng (皇堂石井), built by Yǔwén Hù (宇文護) of the Northern Zhōu (北周).
Emperor Wén (文帝) of Suí (隋) further repaired the buildings
and planted over a thousand pines and cypresses.
In the eighteenth year of Zhēnguān (貞觀),
an imperial edict ordered Yán Lìběn (閻立本) to construct palaces and imperial baths,

In that same year, it was renamed Wēnquán Gōng (溫泉宮) and rebuilt.
On the day Jiǎyín (甲寅),
the Emperor returned to the palace.
14 In the eleventh month,
Lǐyí Shǐ Zhāng Shuō and others memorialized,

This was due to the establishment of the Lǐyí Shǐ for suburban sacrifices.
In the early Wǔdé period, regulations were set:
Jǐngdì was paired in the round mound (Yuánqiū),
and Yuándì in the Mingtáng.
During the Zhēnguān reign, Gāozǔ was enshrined in the Yuánqiū.
In the second year of Yǒnghuī, Tàizōng was also enshrined in the Mingtáng.
In the early Chuígǒng reign, Yuán Wànqǐng’s proposal was adopted,
and Gāozōng was enshrined in the Yuánqiū.
From then on, in the rites of suburban sacrifice,
the three ancestors were all paired.
The three ancestors
refer to Gāozǔ, Tàizōng, and Gāozōng.
使 (shǐ),

The Tánglì states:
“On the day Wùyín was the winter solstice,

According to the Chánglì,

蘄 (qí),
pronounced qú xī.

Now we follow the Shílù.
18 In this year,
Zhāng Shuō memorialized to change the name of the Zhèngshìtáng to Zhōngshū Ménxià,

According to the old system: the Chief Ministers (Zǎixiàng) usually deliberated affairs in the Ménxià Shěng,

19 Earlier,
Jiānchá Yùshǐ Dù Xiān of Púyáng, while investigating matters, traveled to Tūqíshī.

buried it under his tent,

Zhōngshū Shèrén Gāo Jìfǔ said

Thereafter, land rent was given to capital officials in spring and autumn,

Provincial officials were one rank lower than capital officials.
First rank was 50 dàn per rank.
Second and third ranks were 30 dàn per rank.
Fourth and fifth ranks were 20 dàn per rank.
Sixth and seventh ranks were 5 dàn per rank.
Eighth and ninth ranks were 2.5 dàn per rank.
Those in charge of grain were paid in salt.
Officials with specific duties also had fánggé and shùpú.
First rank had 96 fánggé.
Second rank had 72.
Third rank had 48.
Fourth rank had 32.
Fifth rank had 24.
Sixth rank had 15 shùpú.
Seventh rank had 4.
Eighth rank had 2.

Provincial officials were distinguished by upper, middle, and lower classifications of zhōu, fǔ, and xiàn.

The Tang system stipulated

Sòng Bái said:
The Tang system stipulated

Chēng,

tenth month,
