They were divided among the Twelve Guards,
totaling 120,000 men, organized into six shifts.

The Emperor personally selected eleven officials of high repute from various departments to be *Cǐshǐ* (Prefects), including Dàlǐ Qīng Yuán Guāngyù (Grand Judge Yuán Guāngyù), Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Yáng Chénglìng (Assistant Minister of the Left Yáng Chénglìng), and Bīngbù Shìláng Kòu Cǐ (Vice Minister of War Kòu Cǐ).
He ordered the prime ministers, various princes, heads of various departments, *Táiláng* (Secretaries of the Grand Secretariat), and *Yùshǐ* (Censors)
The "heads of various departments" refer to
the heads of the ministries, courts, and directorates.
"Táiláng"
refers to the Shàngshū Láng.
Before this, the Shàngshū had been renamed Zhōngtái.
The presence of "Táiláng and *Yùshǐ*" means
that officials from all three departments must have gathered.
The character *zhǎng* (長) is pronounced *zhīliǎng fān* (知兩翻).
The character *cǐ* (泚) is pronounced *cǐ* (且禮翻),
also *cǐ*.
The arrangements were very grand.
The Emperor bestowed imperial meals upon them.
The Tàicháng (Court of Imperial Sacrifices) prepared music.
The "imperial meals" refer to
the daily regular meals for the emperor, managed by the Shàngshí Fèngyù.
The "Tàicháng prepared music" means
that the Tàicháng was ordered to prepare music.
If all the music of the Tàicháng were to be prepared,
including court music, military bands, the two civil and military dances, and the ten types of music,
it would likely not be possible for a farewell banquet to have them all.
The Nèifāng (Inner Bureau)
refers to the Nèijiàofāng (Imperial Music Bureau),
which was the bureau of female entertainers from the Yīchūn Yuàn (Yīchūn Courtyard) selected and established in the second year of Kāiyuán.
The character *jì* (妓) is pronounced *qúqǐ fān* (渠綺翻).
They were bestowed gifts.
Yuán Guāngyù (源光裕)
was the grand-nephew of Yuán Qiányào (源乾曜).
Third month,
on the Jiǎwǔ day,
Tàizǐ Sìqiān (Crown Prince Sìqiān) was renamed Hóng (鴻).
Tán Wáng Sìzhēn (Prince Sìzhēn of Tán) was moved to become Qìng Wáng (Prince Qìng)
and renamed Tán (潭).
Shǎn Wáng Sìshēng (Prince Sìshēng of Shǎn) was moved to become Zhōng Wáng (Prince Zhōng)
and renamed Jùn (浚).
Zēng Wáng Sìzhēn (Prince Sìzhēn of Zēng) was moved to become Dì Wáng (Prince Dì)
and renamed Qià (洽).
È Wáng Sìchū (Prince Sìchū of È) was renamed Juān (涓).
Juàn Wáng Sìxuán (Prince Sìxuán of Juàn) was moved to become Róng Wáng (Prince Róng)
and renamed Huàng (滉).
Additionally, his sons Jū (琚)
was made Guāng Wáng (Prince Guāng),
Wéi (濰) was made Yí Wáng (Prince Yí),
Yún (澐) was made Yǐng Wáng (Prince Yǐng),
Zé (澤) was made Yǒng Wáng (Prince Yǒng),
Qīng (清) was made Shòu Wáng (Prince Shòu),
Huí (洄) was made Yán Wáng (Prince Yán),
Shù (沭) was made Shèng Wáng (Prince Shèng),
and Yì (溢) was made Jì Wáng (Prince Jì).
On the Bǐngshēn day,
Yùshǐ Dàfū Chéng Xíngzhàn (Censor-in-Chief Chéng Xíngzhàn) memorialized:
"Among the cruel officials of the Zhōu dynasty,
Lái Jùnchén (來俊臣) and twenty-two others,
whose crimes were particularly severe,
their descendants should all be permanently banned from office.
Fù Yóuyì (傅遊藝) and three others,
whose crimes were less severe,
their descendants should not be allowed to hold high positions."
The Emperor followed this.
Fénzhōu Cǐshǐ Yáng Chénglìng (Prefect Yáng Chénglìng of Fénzhōu) did not wish for an external appointment.
According to old records, Fénzhōu was 1,206 *lǐ* from the capital.
He said to himself,
"My appointment as a prefect has its reasons."
The Emperor heard of this and became
angry.
On the Rén Yín day,
he was demoted to Mùzhōu Biéjià (Assistant Administrator of Mùzhōu).
Zhāng Yuè (張說) drafted the Fēngshàn rituals and presented them.
Summer,
fourth month,
on the Bǐngchén day,
the Emperor held a banquet with officials from the Zhōngshū Ménxià (Central Secretariat and Chancellery) and scholars of ritual at the Jíxiān Diàn (Gathering of Immortals Hall).
The Emperor said:
"Immortals are a baseless legend,
which I do not value.
The wise are tools for governing.
Now that I am holding this banquet with you,
it should be renamed Jíxián Diàn (Gathering of the Worthy Hall)."
According to the Táng Liù Diǎn, the Luòyáng Palace had three south-facing gates.
The middle one was called Yìngtiān,
the left Xīngjiào,
and the right Guāngzhèng.
Inside Guāngzhèng was Guǎngyùn.
North of that was Míngfú.
West of Míngfú was Chóngxián Mén (Chóngxián Gate).
Inside that was the Jíxián Diàn (Gathering of the Worthy Hall).
Officials of the sixth rank and below served as *Zhí Xuéshì* (Resident Academicians).
Zhāng Yuè (張說) was appointed Director of the Academy,
and Xú Jiān (徐堅), the Yòu Sǎnqí Chángshì (Right Remonstrance Official), was his deputy.
The Emperor wished to make Zhāng Yuè a *Dà Xuéshì* (Grand Academician);
Zhāng Yuè firmly declined, and so it was stopped.
Zhāng Yuè (張說) feared that the Tūjué might take advantage of the Emperor's eastern tour to invade,
and proposed increasing border defenses.
He summoned Bīngbù Lángzhōng Péi Guāngtíng (Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs Péi Guāngtíng) to discuss it.
Péi Guāngtíng said:
"The Fēngshàn sacrifices
are meant to proclaim success.
Now we are about to ascend to heaven.
The *Jì* (Record) says: 'Ascend to heaven by means of a famous mountain.'
The commentary states: 'This refers to the Fēng sacrifice on Tài Shān.'
This is not a way to manifest great virtue."
Zhāng Yuè said:
"Then what should be done?"
Péi Guāngtíng said:
"Among the Four Barbarians,
the Tūjué are the most powerful.
They have repeatedly sought peace through marriage alliances,
but the court has kept them at arm's length,
not yet definitively agreeing.
Now, send an envoy
to invite their chief minister to accompany the Fēng sacrifice on Tài Shān.
They will surely accept the command with joy.
If the Tūjué come,
then none of the Róng Dí (northern and western barbarians) chieftains will fail to come.
Then we can furl our banners and silence our drums,
and rest easy without worry."
Zhāng Yuè said:
"Excellent,
that is something I did not think of."
He immediately memorialized and put it into practice.
Péi Guāngtíng
was the son of Péi Xíngjiǎn (裴行儉).
Péi Xíngjiǎn served Emperor Gāozōng,
was discerning in his selection of officials,
and achieved fame and merit as a general.
The Emperor dispatched Yuán Zhèn
from the Zhōngshū Zhíshěng to the Zhōngshū Shěng with another official post,
calling it Zhíshěng.
This refers to the official duties of the Zhíshěng today.
He issued an imperial edict to the Tūjué,
saying,
"Lú and líng are read as fān."
He held a banquet
and said to Zhèn:
"The Tǔfān
are a dog breed;
the Xīróng
were anciently called Quǎnróng (Dog-Rong),
hence the Tǔfān are called a dog breed.
They were originally slaves of the Tūjué;
in the barbarian language, 'slave'
is like 'subject' in the Huá language.
Why is it that the Tūjué have repeatedly sought marriage alliances but have never been permitted?
And I also know that all princesses who have gone to the Tǔfān are not daughters of heaven;
why question authenticity now!
It is just that having repeatedly requested and not obtained,
I am ashamed to face the various barbarian tribes."
Zhèn promised to present a memorial on their behalf.
Xiǎoshā then sent his chief minister Āshǐdé Jiélìfā to present tribute,
and he subsequently accompanied the Emperor's eastern tour.
9 In the fifth month,
on the day Gēngyín,
the rebel leader Liú Dìnggāo, leading his followers, attacked the Tōngluò Gate by night;
they were all captured and executed.
10 In autumn,
in the eighth month,
Zhāng Yuè discussed the ceremonies for the Fēngshàn sacrifices,
requesting that Ruìzōng be associated with the Supreme Earth Spirit;
this was granted.
11 In the ninth month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
the Emperor said to his chancellors:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals do not record auspicious omens,
but only note the abundance of harvests."
He decreed that from now on, prefectures and counties were not to present auspicious omens again.
12 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Guǐchǒu,
a water-powered armillary sphere was constructed.
On it were displayed the various constellations.
Water was poured to drive the wheel,
causing it to rotate by itself,
completing one revolution in a day and night.
Separately, two wheels were placed,
entangled outside the sphere,
to which the sun and moon were attached,
moving against the heavens,
with appropriate speed.
Every time the heavens rotated one circle westward,
the sun moved one degree eastward,
and the moon moved thirteen degrees and seven-nineteenths of a degree.
After twenty-nine rotations, the sun and moon met,
and after three hundred sixty-five rotations, the sun completed its circuit of the heavens.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: "Heaven's day and night are divided by the rising and setting of the sun;
man's day and night are bounded by dusk and dawn.
Two and a half kè before sunrise is dawn;
two and a half kè after sunset is dusk.
If five kè are subtracted from night to add to day,
then day will be five kè longer than night.
Ancient and modern calendrical methods and what the Grand Astrologer observed
all state that the day of the summer solstice is sixty-five kè,
and night is thirty-five kè;
the day of the winter solstice is forty-five kè,
and night is fifty-five kè;
the day of the spring and autumn equinoxes is fifty-five kè,
(The character
'five'
is suspected to be superfluous below;
the same applies below.)
and night is fifty-five kè: this is an unchangeable rule.
However, the Grand Astrologer's current refined observation method
differs from the regular method by half a kè.
From the spring equinox to the summer solstice, the day gradually lengthens, increasing by nine and a half kè;
from the summer solstice to the autumn equinox, the decrease is similar.
From the autumn equinox to the winter solstice, the day gradually shortens, decreasing by ten and a half kè;
from the winter solstice to the spring equinox, the increase is also similar.
Moreover, between each khí,
the number of kè increased or decreased varies,
sometimes more, sometimes less,
so it cannot be uniformly applied as a rate.
In the early Hàn dynasty, they could not ascertain this precisely,
so they used a rate of increasing or decreasing one kè every nine days.
During the reign of Hédì, Huò Róng first requested to change this.
Half was underground,
and two wooden figures were also set up.
A drum was beaten every kè,
and a bell was struck every chén.
The mechanisms were all hidden inside a cabinet."
13 On the day Xīnyǒu,
the imperial carriage departed from the Eastern Capital.
All officials, noble relatives, and chieftains of the Four Barbarians followed.
At each stop,
within several tens of lǐ, people and animals covered the wilds,
and the officials' supply wagons, laden with provisions,
stretched for hundreds of lǐ without interruption.
The Sīmǎ Fǎ says: "The Xiàhòushì called a niǎn a yúchē,
the Yīn called it a Húnúchē,
and the Zhōu called it a zīniǎn."
A niǎn had one axe, one chisel, one shovel, one hoe;
a Zhōu niǎn added two planks and two rammers.
It also says: "For the Xiàhòushì, twenty men pulled a niǎn;
for the Yīn, eighteen men pulled a niǎn;
for the Zhōu, fifteen men pulled a niǎn."
Jiǎ Gōngyàn said: "A niǎn is used to bundle and carry baggage."
I note that what the Sīmǎ Fǎ and Jiǎ Gōngyàn say
all refers to military niǎn;
what is referred to here as niǎn载 (niǎn zài)
includes all kinds of objects.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
they arrived at the foot of Mount Tàishān.
The Emperor rode his horse up the mountain.
The Kǎoyì states: "The Shílù, Tánglì, and Tǒngjì all say,
'equipped with the imperial carriage,
ascended Mount Tàishān'."
The Kāitiān Chuánxìn Jì says:
"When the Emperor was about to perform the Fēng sacrifice on Mount Tàishān,
Yìzhōu presented a white mule.
The Emperor personally rode it,
unaware of the fatigue of ascending and descending;
as soon as it descended the mountain,
it died without illness,
and was posthumously titled 'General White Mule'."
I note that Mount Tàishān cannot be ascended by imperial carriage,
and the white mule is rather strange.
We now follow the old records.
Only the Emperor, accompanied by the chancellors and ritual officials, ascended,
while the imperial guards were arrayed for over a hundred lǐ at the foot of the mountain.
The Emperor asked Hè Zhīzhāng, Minister of the Board of Rites:
"Why were the jade tablets of previous dynasties
kept secret?"
He replied:
"Perhaps they secretly sought immortality,
and therefore did not wish people to see them."
The Emperor said:
"I merely pray for blessings for the common people."
Thereupon, he brought out the jade tablets
and showed them to all his ministers.
On the day Gēngyín,
the Emperor sacrificed to Hàotiān Shàngdì on the mountain.
All ministers sacrificed to the Five Emperors and a hundred gods at an altar at the foot of the mountain;
the rest followed the precedents of the Gānfēng era.
Details can be found in Volume 101, Gāozōng, Gānfēng First Year.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
he sacrificed to the Supreme Earth Spirit at Shèshǒu.
On the day Rénchén,
the Emperor held court in the tent-palace.
In the field, consecutive tents formed a palace,
hence it was called a tent-palace.
朝 is pronounced zháo.
He enfeoffed the god of Mount Tàishān as Tiānqí Wáng,
raising his ritual status by one grade above the Sāngōng.
According to ancient regulations,
the Four Peaks were considered equivalent to the Sāngōng.
Zhāng Yuè appointed many officials from the Two Secretariats.
The Two Secretariats were
the Zhōngshū Shěng and the Ménxià Shěng.
After the rituals, he granted favors,
often promoting them to the fifth rank and above, but neglecting other officials.
Zhōngshū Shèrén Zhāng Jiǔlíng remonstrated,
but was not heeded.
Furthermore,
the accompanying soldiers
were only given honorary titles but no material rewards,
which caused resentment both inside and outside the court.
14 Initially,
at the end of the Suí dynasty, all state horses were plundered by bandits and the Róngdí.
In the early Táng, only three thousand mares and stallions were obtained from Chì'àn Zé,
and moved to Lǒngyòu.
The Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud, Zhāng Wàansuì, was ordered to manage them.
Kǎoyì states: Tǒngjì records that Wàansuì managed the imperial pastures for three generations,
and his kindness and trustworthiness were known throughout Lǒngyòu.
Therefore, the people of Lǒngyòu referred to the age of a horse (mǎ suì) as "chǐ" (teeth),
which was to avoid a naming taboo of the Zhāng clan.
According to Gōngyáng Zhuàn, Jìn Xiàngōng said to Xún Xī:
"The teeth of my horses are already long."
Thus, the practice of calling horse age "chǐ" (teeth)
has a precedent.
From the Zhēnguàn to the Líndé eras,
the horse population bred to seven hundred thousand head,
divided into eight fāng and forty-eight jiān,
each with a commissioner appointed to oversee it.
According to Táng regulations,
a jiān with five thousand horses was a superior jiān;
with three thousand or more, a medium jiān;
with one thousand or more, an inferior jiān.
In the Líndé era, eight commissioners were appointed
to collectively manage the jiān and fāng.
The four prefectures of Qín, Lán, Yuán, Wèi, and the Héqǔ region
had a total of forty-eight jiān.
The Southern Commissioner had fifteen jiān,
the Western Commissioner had sixteen jiān,
the Northern Commissioner had seven jiān,
the Yánzhōu Commissioner had eight jiān,
and the Lánzhōu Commissioner had two jiān.
West of the capital, in Lǒngyòu, there were seven horse fāng,
with three Lǒngyòu Commissioners appointed to lead them.
Ōuyáng Xiū said: Eight fāng were established
in the thousand-li wide area between Bīn, Qí, Jīng, and Níng.
One was Bǎolè,
two Gānlù,
three Nánpǔrùn,
four Běipǔrùn,
five Qíyáng,
six Tàipíng,
seven Yílù,
and eight Āndìng.
The land for these eight fāng totaled one thousand two hundred thirty qǐng,
and commoners were recruited to cultivate it to provide fodder.
The horses of the eight fāng belonged to the forty-eight jiān;
but as the horses became too numerous and the land too narrow to accommodate them,
eight jiān were further divided
and established in the spacious wilderness of Héxī.
After the Chuígǒng era,
more than half of the horses were secretly lost.
When the Emperor first ascended the throne,
there were two hundred forty thousand imperial horses.
He appointed the Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud, Wáng Máozhòng, as Commissioner of Inner and Outer Imperial Stables,
with Vice-Minister Zhāng Jǐngshùn as his deputy.
By this time, there were four hundred thirty thousand horses,
and cattle and sheep in comparable numbers.
When the Emperor performed the Eastern Feng Sacrifice,
tens of thousands of imperial horses followed,
separated by color into herds,
looking like clouds and brocade from a distance.
The Emperor praised Máozhòng's achievements,
and on the guǐsì day,
bestowed upon Máozhòng the honorary title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
On the jiǎwǔ day, the imperial carriage departed from Tài Shān;
on the gēngshēn day,
the Emperor
visited Kǒngzǐ's residence to offer sacrifices.
When the Emperor returned,
arriving at Sòngzhōu,
he feasted his entourage on an upper floor,
and Prefect Kòu Cǐ was among them.
While the wine was flowing,
the Emperor said to Zhāng Yuè:
"Previously, I frequently dispatched imperial envoys to tour the various circuits
to investigate the conduct of officials, good or bad.
Now, having visited the various prefectures during the Feng and Shan sacrifices,
I realize that many of these envoys have failed me.
Wáng Qiū, the Prefect of Huáizhōu,
offered nothing but official provisions.
Cuī Miǎn, the Prefect of Wèizhōu,
provided no embroidered silks for entertainment,
showing me his frugality.
Péi Yàoqīng, the Prefect of Jìzhōu,
submitted a memorial of several hundred words,
all of which were admonitions and criticisms.
The two prefectures of Huáizhōu and Wèizhōu are in Héběi.
Jìzhōu is administered from Jùyě.
The Emperor's journey to Tài Shān
allowed him to be greeted by the imperial carriage both going and returning.
Then it would not be sufficient to report success.'
I always keep it at my side,
and also use it to caution those around me.
Such men as these three
do not burden the people to gain favor;
they are truly good officials."
He turned to Kòu Cǐ and said:
"Previously, there were also many who complained to me about insufficient food and drink.
I know that you do not seek reputation among those around you."
He then personally raised his wine cup and bestowed it upon him.
The chancellors, leading the attendant officials, rose to offer congratulations,
and everyone on the upper floor shouted "Long live the Emperor!"
Consequently, Wáng Qiū was made Shàngshū Zuǒchéng,
Cuī Miǎn was made Sànqí Shìláng,
and Péi Yàoqīng was made Prefect
of Dìngzhōu.
Yàoqīng
was the seventh-generation descendant of Shúyè.
In the twelfth month,
on the yǐsì day,
the Emperor returned to the Eastern Capital.
15 The Tūjué Xiélìfā
asked to return home; the Emperor bestowed rich gifts upon him and sent him off,
but ultimately did not consent to a marriage.
16 Wáng Máozhòng was favored by the Emperor,
and officials flocked to him.
When Máozhòng was marrying off his daughter,
the Emperor asked what he needed.
Máozhòng replied: "All matters are prepared,
but I lack guests."
The Emperor said:
"Can Zhāng Yuè, Yuán Qiányào, and their like not be invited?"
He replied:
"Them, I can get."
The Emperor said:
"I know there is only one person you cannot get to come,
and that must be Sòng Jǐng."
He replied:
"Indeed."
The Emperor smiled and said:
"Tomorrow, I will summon guests for you."
The next day,
the Emperor said to the chancellors:
"My servant Máozhòng has a wedding.
You and all other high-ranking officials should go to his residence."
It was already noon,
but the guests dared not raise their chopsticks,
waiting for Jǐng.
After a long while,
he finally arrived,
first holding wine and bowing towards the west to express thanks,
thanking the Emperor for his command to come,
not for Máozhòng.
He then quickly claimed stomach pains and returned home.
Jǐng's uprightness
grew even stronger with age.
17 Prior to this,
the Qìdān King Lǐ Tǔgān and Kětúgān again grew suspicious of each other.
Lǐ Tǔgān came with the princess seeking refuge,
not daring to return.
He was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Liáoyáng,
and kept as a guard at the imperial residence.
During the Emperor's eastern tour,
Shào Gù came to the imperial temporary residence,
and consequently followed to Tài Shān,
where he was appointed Grand General of the Left Forest of Feathers Guard and Commissioner for Pacification and Control of the Jìngzhé Army.
Four years later,
the Qìdān surrendered,
and the Jìngzhé Army was established in Sōngmò Fǔ,
with its chief serving as Commissioner for Pacification and Control.
This implies that the Central Plains army did not move, yet the Qìdān surrendered on their own,
pacified and subdued from afar without direct confrontation.
The Emperor was suspicious that the examinations for selection by the Ministry of Personnel were unfair.
As the selection period was imminent,
Yǔwén Róng (宇文融), the Grand Censor, secretly memorialized,
requesting that the Ministry of Personnel be divided into ten examination boards.
On the Jiǎxū day,
Sū Tǐng (蘇頲), Minister of Rites, and nine others were put in charge of the Ministry of Personnel's selection process.
When the trial judgment was about to conclude,
they were immediately summoned into the Forbidden Palace to make the final decisions.
The Minister and Vice-Ministers of Personnel were not allowed to participate.
Wú Jīng (吳兢), Left Shùzǐ, submitted a memorial,
arguing:
"Your Majesty has wrongly accepted slanderous accusations,
and does not trust your officials.
This is not the way of a ruler who governs the people with sincerity and inspires loyalty.
In the past, Chén Píng (陳平) and Bǐng Jí (邴吉),
prime ministers of the Hàn dynasty,
did not concern themselves with the details of finances or grain,
nor did they inquire about those who died in brawls.
The matter of Chén Píng is found in Volume 13, first year of Hàn Wéndì's reign.
The matter of Bǐng Jí is found in Volume 26, third year of Hàn Xuāndì's Shénjué era.
How then can Your Majesty personally undertake the task of selection?
As for all written examinations for candidates,
I request that they be entrusted to the responsible officials,
and that these ten examination boards be discontinued."
Although the Emperor did not immediately comply,
the old system was restored the following year.
In this year,
a dòu of rice in the Eastern Capital cost fifteen coins,
while in Qīng-Qí it cost five coins,
and millet three coins.
Yútián King Wèichí Tiào (尉遲眺) secretly conspired with the Tujue and other Hu tribes to rebel.
Dù Xiān (杜暹), Vice Protector-General of Ānxī, dispatched troops to capture and execute him,
and then established a new king.
Punctuation by Qí Sīhé (齊思和), collated by Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
by imperial decree.
Hòu Xué Tiāntái (後學天台)
The 14th year of Kāiyuán
(Bǐngyín, 726)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the Guǐwèi day,
Lǐ Shàogù (李邵固), King of Sōngmò of Qìdān, was re-established as King of Guǎnghuà,
and Lǐ Lǔsū (李魯蘇), King of Ráolè of Xī, as King of Fèngchéng.
The Emperor bestowed his maternal nephew's daughter, Lady Chén, with the title of Princess Dōnghuá,
and married her to Shàogù.
He also bestowed Wéi Shì (韋氏), daughter of Princess Chéng'ān, with the title of Princess Dōngguāng.
Princess Chéng'ān was
the daughter of Zhōngzōng,
who was married to Wéi Jié (韋捷).
2. Zhāng Yuè (張說) memorialized:
"Among the current Five Rites,
the revisions made during the Zhēngguàn and Xiǎnqìng eras
have resulted in considerable discrepancies,
some of which have yet to be properly reconciled.
I propose that we, along with the scholars, discuss ancient and modern practices,
and then revise and implement them."
The Emperor approved.
3. The Líáo (獠) people of Fēnglíng in Yōngzhōu, led by Liáng Dàhǎi (梁大海) and others, rebelled, seizing Bīnzhōu and Héngzhōu.
Fēnglíng was originally a mountainous aboriginal stronghold,
gradually developed during the Táng dynasty,
and only established as a county after the Qiányuán era.
Bīnzhōu
was the territory of Lǐngfāng County in the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to Yùlín Commandery.
The Liáng dynasty established Lǐngfāng Commandery.
The Suí dynasty abolished the commandery and made it a county,
belonging to Yùzhōu.
In the early Táng, it belonged to Nánfāngzhōu.
In the fifth year of Zhēngguàn, Bīnzhōu was established by division.
Héngzhōu
was the territory of Guǎngyù and Gāoliáng Counties in the Hàn dynasty.
East of the Jiāng River, Níngpǔ Commandery was established.
The Suí dynasty abolished the commandery and made it a county,
belonging to Yùzhōu.
In the early Táng, Jiǎnzhōu was established by division,
and in the eighth year of Zhēngguàn, its name was changed to Héngzhōu.
On the Jǐyǒu day,
Eunuch Yáng Sīxù (楊思勗) was dispatched to lead troops to suppress them.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The old records state
"Gēngxū day, first day of the month,"
now following the *Shílù*.
4. The Emperor summoned Cuī Yǐnfǔ (崔隱甫), Prefect of Hénán,
intending to appoint him.
However, Zhāng Yuè (張說), Grand Counselor of the Secretariat, disdained his lack of literary talent
and proposed him as Grand General of the Golden Guard.
Cuī Rìzhī (崔日知), former Palace Supervisor, was on good terms with Yuè,
and Yuè recommended him as Grand Censor.
The Emperor did not follow this advice.
On the Bǐngchén day,
Rìzhī was appointed Grand General of the Left Feathered Forest Guard.
On the Dīngsì day,
Yǐnfǔ was appointed Grand Censor.
From then on, Yǐnfǔ harbored resentment towards Yuè.
Yuè possessed talent and intelligence but was fond of bribes.
When officials reported matters that did not accord with his views,
he often reprimanded them face-to-face,
even to the point of scolding.
He disliked Yǔwén Róng (宇文融), the Grand Censor,
and was troubled by his excessive power.
As Yǔwén Róng held a position in the Censorate
and also served as Vice Minister of Revenue,
his power was indeed excessive.
Yuè often suppressed him.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng (張九齡), Secretary of the Secretariat, said to Yuè:
"Yǔwén Róng enjoys imperial favor and wields power,
being eloquent and skilled in stratagem, he must not be underestimated."
Yuè replied:
"What can a mere rat do!"
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Rénzǐ day,
Yǐnfǔ, Róng, and Lǐ Línfǔ (李林甫), another Grand Censor, jointly impeached Yuè,
accusing him of
"consulting diviners about stars,
showing favoritism and extravagance,
and accepting bribes."
An imperial edict ordered Yuán Qiányào (源乾曜), Wéi Kàng (韋抗), Minister of Justice, and Míng Guī (明珪), Minor Administrator of the Grand Court of Justice,
to jointly investigate the matter with Yǐnfǔ and others at the Censorate.
Línfǔ was
the great-grandson of Shúliáng.
Shúliáng, Prince Chángpíng,
was a cousin of Gāozǔ.
He was also the son of Wéi Ānshí's (韋安石) paternal cousin.
Wéi Ānshí served Empress Wǔ and Zhōngzōng successively,
and was demoted and died in the early Kāiyuán era.
Cóng (從), pronounced cái yòng fān.
On the Dīngsì day,
Lǐ Yuánhóng (李元紘), Vice Minister of Revenue, was appointed Secretary of the Secretariat and Concurrent Grand Councilor.
Yuánhóng was known for his integrity and frugality,
which is why the Emperor appointed him as prime minister.
5. Yuán Qiányào and others investigated Zhāng Yuè.
The accusations appeared to have some basis.
The Emperor sent Gāo Lìshì (高力士) to check on Yuè.
Lìshì returned and reported:
"Yuè, with disheveled hair and dirty face,
sitting on straw,
eating from an earthenware vessel,
is terrified and awaiting punishment."
The Emperor felt pity for him.
Lìshì then spoke of Yuè's contributions to the state,
and the Emperor agreed.
On the Gēngshēn day,
Yuè was merely dismissed from his post as Grand Counselor of the Secretariat,
but his other positions remained unchanged.
6. On the Dīngmǎo day,
Lǐ Fàn (李範), Prince Qí and Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince, died.
He was posthumously honored with the title Prince Huìwén.
The Emperor abstained from meat for several weeks because of his death,
and only resumed normal meals after
officials repeatedly memorialized to urge him.
7. On the Dīnghài day,
Zhāng Xiàosōng (張孝嵩), Prefect of Tàiyuán, memorialized,
"There is a man named Lǐ Zǐqiáo (李子嶠)
who claims to be an imperial son,
saying he was born in Lùzhōu,
and his mother's name was Zhào."
The Emperor ordered him to be beaten to death.
8. On the Xīnchǒu day,
armies were stationed in the five prefectures of Dìng, Héng, Mò, Yì, and Cāng to guard against the Tujue.
The Běipíng Army was stationed in Dìngzhōu,
the Héngyáng Army in Héngzhōu,
the Tángxīng Army in Mòzhōu,
the Gāoyáng Army in Yìzhōu,
and the Hénghǎi Army in Cāngzhōu.
Héng (恆), pronounced Hù Dēng fān.
9. The Emperor wanted to make Wǔ Huì (武惠) empress,
but some memorialized, saying:
"The Wǔ clan is an irreconcilable enemy;
how can one of them be made the nation's mother?
It is widely rumored that Zhāng Yuè seeks credit for establishing an empress
as a stratagem to regain his position as prime minister.
Furthermore, the Crown Prince is not born of Huì,
and Huì herself has sons.
If she ascends to the imperial throne,
the Crown Prince will surely be in peril."
The Emperor then desisted.
However, in the palace, her ceremonial rank
was exactly as that of an empress.
10. In the fifth month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
the Ministry of Revenue reported that this year there were 7,069,565 households
and 41,419,712 individuals.
11. In autumn,
the seventh month,
there were great floods in Hénán and Hénán Běi,
with thousands drowned.
12. In the eighth month,
on the Bǐngwǔ day (the first day of the month),
Wèizhōu reported that the river had overflowed.
13th day of the 9th month.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Dù Xiān, Vice Grand Protector of Ānxī and Military Governor of Qīxī, was appointed Concurrent Commissioner of State Affairs.
Qī [character],
read as "qī" in Qī Jì.
Xiān [character],
read as "xiān" in Xī Lián.
Ever since Wáng Xiàojié recovered the Four Garrisons,
See the recovery of the Four Garrisons in Zǐzhì Tōngjiàn, scroll 205, Wǔ Hòu’s Chángshòu first year.
and the Tang army of 30,000 was stationed there,
the common people suffered from their service.
Among those who served as Grand Protectors,
only Tián Yángmíng, Guō Yuánzhèn, Zhāng Sōng, and Xiān had good governance,
and were praised by the people.
14th day of winter,
10th month.
On the day Gēngshēn,
the Emperor went to Guǎngchéng Hot Spring in Rǔzhōu.
Kǎoyì says: Línghú Huán’s Dàizōng Shílù states:
“The Emperor was born on the 13th day of the 10th month in Kaiyuan 14th year.
At that time, Xuánzōng was visiting the hot springs of Rǔzhōu.
A person skilled in observing vital energies said,
‘There is the vital energy of an Emperor in the palace.’
Xuánzōng returned to the palace on that very day,
and Dàizōng was born that night.”
According to Xuánzōng Shílù,
the Emperor only went to the hot springs on the 16th day of this month, Gēngshēn,
and returned to the palace on the day Jǐsì,
which differs from Dàizōng Shílù.
The Old Annals state,
“He was born on the 13th day of the 12th month.”
The Old Empress Biographies say:
“Empress Zhāngjìng, née Wú, was enslaved in the Imperial Harem due to her father’s case.
In Kaiyuan 23rd year,
Xuánzōng visited the residence of Prince Zhōng.
Seeing that the Prince’s attire and surroundings were simple and sparse,
without any concubines or attendants,
he ordered General Gāo Lìshì to select palace women from the Imperial Harem to bestow upon him,
and Empress Wú was among those registered.
The next year,
Emperor Dàizōng was born,
and she passed away in the 18th year.”
Considering that Dàizōng was born in this year,
but it says Empress Wú was bestowed upon Prince Zhōng in the 23rd year and passed away in the 18th year,
it is likely a mistake, confusing the 13th year with the 23rd year.
Next, Liǔ Shì’s Jiùwén states:
“Sùzōng, while in the Eastern Palace, was framed by Lǐ Línfǔ,
and his situation was precarious on several occasions.
Before long,
his beard and hair turned white.
Once, during an early court audience,
the Emperor saw him and said with a somber expression,
‘You may return to your residence;
I will visit you.’
When the Emperor arrived,
he noticed that the palace courtyard and halls were unswept,
the musical instruments were covered in dust,
and there were no singing girls among the attendants.
The Emperor was moved by this sight.
He ordered Gāo Lìshì to summon the Imperial Harem officials to inspect the registers and select three women.
These were then bestowed upon the Crown Prince,
and Empress Zhāngjìng, née Wú, was among those selected,
and she gave birth to Dàizōng.”
However, in Kaiyuan 23rd year,
Lǐ Línfǔ had just become chancellor.
In the 25th year, Crown Prince Yīng was deposed.
It was in the 26th year that Sùzōng was established as Crown Prince.
The Wéi Jiān case, framed by Lǐ Línfǔ, only began in Tiānbǎo 5th year.
The events recorded in Jiùwén [Old Accounts]
are all fictitious and exaggerated,
and the dates do not match.
Xīnshū Hòuchuán adopted all of this,
but we do not include any of it here.
According to historical records, the Hàn dynasty’s Guǎngchéng Park was located within the borders of Liángxiàn in Tang Rǔzhōu,
and there were hot springs there.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
he returned to the palace.
15th day of the 12th month.
On the day Dīngsì,
the Emperor went to Shòu'ān [County] and hunted in Fāngxiùchuān.
On the day Rénxū,
he returned to the palace.
Yáng Sīxù attacked the rebellious tribes,
capturing alive over 3,000 people, including Liáng Dàhǎi,
and returned after beheading 20,000.
In this year,
the Hēishuǐ Mòhé sent envoys to appear at court.
The Hēishuǐ Mòhé were southwest of the Liúguǐ Kingdom,
and the Jurchens are their descendants.
Mòhé [characters],
read as "mòhé".
Jiàn [character],
read as "xiánpiàn".
Then a Chángshǐ was appointed to govern them.
“Chángshǐ” [character]
should perhaps be
“Chánglì”.
Rénwéi [characters],
read as "yúwěi".
Bóhǎi Mòhé King Wǔyì said:
“The Hēishuǐ [Mòhé] enters Tang [territory],
and the route passes through our border.
In the past, they asked for a Tǔtún from the Tujue.
The Tujue established Tǔtúns to govern various tributary states.
Jué [character],
read as "jiǔwù".
Now, they did not inform us but asked Tang for an official.
This must be a conspiracy with Tang,
intending to attack us from front and rear.”
He dispatched his younger half-brother Mén Yì and his maternal uncle Rèn Yǎ with troops to attack the Hēishuǐ.
Mén Yì had once been a hostage in Tang.
He remonstrated, saying:
“The Hēishuǐ requested an official from Tang,
and we attack them on that account;
this is rebelling against Tang.
Tang
is a great nation.
In the past, when Gāolì was in its prime,
with strong forces of over 300,000,
it did not obey Tang’s commands,
and was swept away without a trace.
Swept away without a trace,
meaning the state was destroyed without any survivors.
See the annals of Tàizōng and Gāozōng.
Lì [character],
read as "lìzhī".
Once we become enemies with Tang,
this is the path to national destruction.”
Wǔyì did not heed him,
and forcibly sent him.
When Mén Yì reached the border,
he again sent a letter strongly remonstrating.
Wǔyì was enraged,
and sent his cousin Dà Yīxià to replace him as general,
recalling [Mén Yì],
intending to kill him.
Mén Yì abandoned his troops
and fled through a secret path to surrender.
He was appointed by imperial decree as General of the Left Swift Cavalry.
Wǔyì sent an envoy to submit a memorial enumerating Mén Yì’s crimes,
requesting his execution.
The Emperor secretly sent Mén Yì to Ānxī.
He detained Wǔyì’s envoy
and sent a separate report saying
that Mén Yì had been exiled to Língnán.
Wǔyì, knowing this,
submitted a memorial stating,
“A great nation should show people trustworthiness;
how can it engage in such deception?”
He steadfastly requested Mén Yì’s execution.
The Emperor held Hónglú Shàoqīng Lǐ Dàosuì and Yuán Fù responsible for failing to supervise their subordinates,
leading to the leak,
and both were demoted.
There were two Shàoqīngs in each of the Nine Courts of Tang.
The Hónglú Sī was in charge of foreign guests,
hence the leak was deemed a crime.
Lú [character],
read as "língrú".
Shào [character],
read as "shǐzhào".
Your servant Sīmǎ Guāng says:
The way for a sovereign to subdue the four barbarians
is through awe and trust alone.
Mén Yì was punished for his loyalty,
and sought refuge with the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven should investigate the injustice, reward Mén Yì, and punish Wǔyì—this is the principle of governance.
Even if he could not launch an expedition,
he should still have justly declared Mén Yì innocent.
Now, Emperor Xuánzōng’s authority could not subdue Wǔyì,
nor could his benevolence protect Mén Yì.
Instead, he resorted to the deceptive words of a petty person, thus embarrassing himself before a small nation.
Then he punished the Hónglú officials for the leak.
Is this not shameful!
18 Dù Xiān (杜暹) was appointed as the Protector-General of Ānxī (安西).
The Princess Jiāohé (交河公主) of the Túqíshī (突騎施) sent her牙官 (yáguān) with a thousand horses to Ānxī (安西) for mutual trade.
The envoy announced the princess's decree,
whereupon Dù Xiān (杜暹) angrily said:
"The daughter of Āshǐnà (阿史那),
Princess Jiāohé (交河公主),
is the daughter of Āshǐnà Huáidào (阿史那懷道)."
He flogged her envoy
and detained him.
The horses died out in the snow.
Sūlù (蘇祿), the Khagan of Túqíshī (突騎施), was furious,
and he dispatched troops to raid the Four Garrisons.
At this time, Dù Xiān (杜暹) had entered the court.
疏吏翻.)
直遙翻;
下同.)
The garrisons fortified themselves and held fast.
The people, livestock, and stores of the Four Garrisons
were all plundered by Sūlù (蘇祿),
and Ānxī (安西) barely survived.
Soon after, Sūlù (蘇祿) heard that Dù Xiān (杜暹) had become a chancellor,
and he gradually withdrew.
He then sent an envoy to offer tribute.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day of Xīnchǒu (辛丑),
Wáng Jūnzhì (王君ㄓ), the Military Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州), defeated the Tǔbō (吐蕃) west of Qīnghǎi (青海).
Initially,
the Tǔbō (吐蕃), relying on their strength,
sent letters using the etiquette of rival states.
(This event is recorded in volume 211, year 2.)
The Emperor was always angry about this.
Upon returning from the Eastern Sacrifice,
Zhāng Yuè (張說) said to the Emperor:
"The Tǔbō (吐蕃) are disrespectful,
and it would indeed be fitting to punish and exterminate them.
However, having been engaged in continuous warfare for over ten years,
Gān (甘), Liáng (涼), Hé (河), and Shàn (鄯)
have suffered unbearable hardships.
Although our armies have repeatedly achieved victories,
what we gain does not compensate for what we lose.
I hear they regret their past actions and seek peace.
I wish Your Majesty would accept their submission
to relieve the people on the border."
The Emperor said:
"I will discuss this with Wáng Jūnzhì (王君ㄓ)."
Zhāng Yuè (張說) withdrew
and said to Yuán Qiányào (源乾曜):
"Wáng Jūnzhì (王君ㄓ) is brave but lacks strategy;
he always seeks quick gains.
If the two nations achieve peace and kinship,
how will he earn merit?
My advice will surely not be followed."
When Wáng Jūnzhì (王君ㄓ) came to court,
he indeed requested to pursue a deep punitive expedition.
Last winter,
Xīnuòluó (悉諾邏), the Tǔbō (吐蕃) general, raided Dàdòugǔ (大斗谷)
and advanced to attack Gānzhōu (甘州),
burning and plundering before leaving.
Wáng Jūnzhì (王君ㄓ) estimated their troops were exhausted
and led his soldiers to pursue them.
There was heavy snowfall,
and many of the barbarians froze to death.
They retreated west from Jīshí Jūn (積石軍).
(West of Kuòzhōu (廓州)'s Dáhuà (達化) County is Jīshí Jūn (積石軍),
originally Jìngbiān Zhèn (靜邊鎮),
which became a military garrison in the second year of Yífèng (儀鳳).
To its east is Huángshā Shù (黃沙戍).)
Wáng Jūnzhì (王君ㄓ)
burned the grass along the road.
When Xīnuòluó (悉諾邏) reached Dàfēichuān (大非川),
he wanted to rest his soldiers and horses,
but the wild grass was all gone,
and more than half of his horses died.
Wáng Jūnzhì (王君ㄓ) and Zhāng Jǐngshùn (張景順), the Military Governor of Qínzhōu (秦州), pursued them,
catching up with them west of Qīnghǎi (青海).
They crossed the ice.
Xīnuòluó (悉諾邏) had already left,
but they defeated his rear guard,
capturing countless wagons, sheep, and horses, and returned.
Wáng Jūnzhì (王君ㄓ) was promoted to Grand General of the Left Yǔlín (左羽林) for his meritorious service,
and his father Shòu (壽) was appointed to the position of 少府監 (shàofǔjiān) and allowed to retire.
From then on, the Emperor was even more dedicated to border affairs.
2 Initially,
Liú Zōngqì (劉宗器) of Luòyáng (洛陽) memorialized,
requesting to block the old Biànkǒu (汴口) of the Sìshuǐ (汜水)
and to divert the Yellow River into the Biàn (汴) at Yíngzé (熒澤).
(In the fourth year of Kāihuáng (開皇) of the Suí (隋) dynasty, Guǎngwǔ (廣武) County was established from Xíngyáng (滎陽).
In the first year of Rénshòu (仁shòu), it was renamed Yíngzé (熒澤)
and belonged to Zhèngzhōu (鄭州).)
時掌翻.)
悉則翻;
下同.)
音祀.)
皮變翻.)
By this time,
the new canal had become blocked and impassable.
Liú Zōngqì (劉宗器) was demoted to garrison commander of Ānhuái (安懷) in Xúnzhōu (循州).
The Emperor ordered Fàn Ānjí (范安及), the Grand Master of Works, to mobilize 30,000 people from Hénán (河南), Huái (懷), Zhèng (鄭), Biàn (汴), Huá (滑), and Wèi (衞) to dredge the old canal,
which was completed in ten days.
3 Cuī Yǐnfǔ (崔隱甫), the Censor-in-Chief, and Yǔwén Róng (宇文融), the Vice Censor-in-Chief,
feared that Zhāng Yuè (張說), the Right Chancellor, would be reinstated.
They repeatedly memorialized to disparage him,
each forming their own factions.
The Emperor detested this.
In the second month,
on the day of Yǐsì (乙巳),
he decreed that Zhāng Yuè (張說) should retire,
Cuī Yǐnfǔ (崔隱甫) be dismissed from office to attend to his mother,
and Yǔwén Róng (宇文融) be sent out as the Governor of Wèizhōu (魏州).
4 On the day of Yǐmǎo (乙卯),
an imperial decree stated:
"For household members who have fled from various prefectures,
if, after being surveyed and verified by the勸農使 (quànnóngshǐ), they flee again,
they shall, upon arrival, pay the current year's rent and corvée labor according to the standard of commoners,
and those subject to conscription shall be drafted first."
5 In summer,
the fifth month,
on the day of Guǐyǒu (癸酉),
the Emperor appointed all his sons, including Qìngwáng Tán (慶王潭), as Regional Governors, Prefects, Military Governors, Commissioners, Grand Protector-Generals, and Commissioners of Strategic Affairs,
though they did not actually leave the capital.
Initially,
Taizōng (太宗) loved Jìnwáng (晉王),
who became Gāozōng (高宗) when he took charge.
Yùwáng (豫王), being the youngest son of Empress Wǔ (武后), also did not leave the inner palace.
It was not until he became Xiàngwáng (相王) from being the Imperial Heir
that he first left the inner palace.
During Zhōngzōng's (中宗) reign,
Qiáowáng (譙王) fell out of favor
and was banished to an outer prefecture.
Wēnwáng (溫王), at seventeen,
still resided in the forbidden palace.
(Qiáowáng (譙王) was Chóngfú (重福).)
(Wēnwáng (溫王) was Chóngmào (重茂).)
Ten princes' residences were attached to the imperial park wall.
On the fifth street east of Zhūquè (朱雀) Street was Ānguó Sì (安國寺).
East of the temple, a large residence was attached to the imperial park wall,
where the ten princes were housed.
The ten princes were
Qìng (慶), Zhōng (忠), Dì (棣), È (鄂), Róng (榮), Yí (儀), Tái (台), Yǐng (潁), Yǒng (永), and Jì (濟).
Later, the six princes, Shèng (盛), Shòu (壽), Chén (陳), Fēng (豐), Cháng (常), and Liáng (涼),
were also enfeoffed and moved into the inner residence,
making it the Sixteen Princes' Residences.
Eunuchs guarded them,
and they attended the daily audience in the enclosed palace area.
From then on, they no longer left the inner palace.
Although they established offices with officials and led frontier commands,
only their tutors were allowed in to give lessons.
Other officials of the princes' establishments
only reported their names and paid respects annually.
Officials of their frontier commands
did not even report their names.
As the number of imperial grandsons gradually increased,
the Bǎisūn Yuàn (百孫院) was also established.
The Crown Prince also did not reside in the Eastern Palace
but always stayed in a separate residence favored by the imperial carriage.
6 The Emperor ordered the palace women, from concubines downwards, to raise silkworms in the palace,
wishing them to understand women's work.
On the day of Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
the summer solstice,
he bestowed silk upon high-ranking officials and close attendants,
one coil per person.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: According to Tang statutes,
six liǎng of cloth or silk constituted a dùn (屯),
five liǎng of silk constituted a qú (絇),
and three jīn of hemp constituted a lì (綟).
It is unknown what the weight of a silk lì (綟) was.
