7 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day of Wùyín (戊寅),
the Yellow River overflowed in Jìzhōu (冀州).
8 On the day of Jǐmǎo (己卯),
Xǔ Wénxiàn Gōng Sū Tǐng (許文憲公蘇頲), the Minister of Rites, passed away.
9 In the ninth month,
on the day Bǐngzǐ,
the Tubo generals Xīnuòluó Gōnglù and Zhúlóng Mǎngbùzhī captured Guāzhōu,
seized the Cìshǐ Tián Yuánxiàn and Wáng Jūnxuánbǐ’s father, who was the former Jǐedùshǐ of Héxī,
and advanced to attack Yùmén Jūn.
Wáng Jūnxuánbǐ’s father, Shòu, had retired from his post as Shàofǔ Jiān and resided in his hometown.
Yùmén Jūn was two hundred lǐ west of Sùzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Xīmén County of Sùzhōu,
during the Hàn dynasty, the Yùmén Guān garrison was abolished,
its people were moved here,
hence it was called Yùmén County.
The Shímén Pass wound through the mountains
for twenty lǐ,
and all the rivers flowed north into Yánxīng Hǎi.
An envoy returned to Liángzhōu,
and said to Jūnxuánbǐ:
“The general has always pledged loyalty and bravery to the state,
why not fight a battle!”
Jūnxuánbǐ climbed the city wall, looked west, and wept,
but ultimately dared not send out troops.
Mǎngbùzhī separately attacked Chánglè County.
Sòng Bái said: Chánglè County belonged to Guāzhōu,
it was the territory of Yíhé Jùn during the Wèi dynasty,
and Liángxīng County during the Former Liáng dynasty.
Liáng Wǔzhāo Wáng established Chánglè Zhèn east of Sānwēi Shān,
and in the fifth year of Wǔdé of the Táng dynasty, it was renamed Chánglè County.
When Guāzhōu fell,
Xīnuòluó assembled all his troops to jointly attack it.
After more than ten days,
the Tubo forces were exhausted,
and unable to conquer it,
they sent someone to persuade them to surrender;
but they did not comply.
The Tubo said:
“Since Your Excellency will not surrender,
you should gather the wealth in the city and present it to us,
and we will withdraw.”
Shīshùn requested the soldiers to remove their clothes;
Xīnuòluó realized there was no wealth,
so he led his troops away,
and destroyed the city of Guāzhōu.
Shīshùn immediately opened the gates,
collected weapons,
and repaired the defenses;
the barbarians indeed sent elite cavalry back,
observed the city,
saw that it was prepared,
and then left.
Tián Yuánxiàn could not defend Guāzhōu, but Jiǎ Shīshùn could defend Chánglè.
Indeed, the defense and preservation depend on the person.
Fù,
read as fú yòu fān.
Chān,
read as chǒu lián fān,
also chǒu yàn fān.
He was from Qízhōu.
10 Initially,
when the Tujue Mòchuò was powerful,
he forcefully seized the land of the Tiělè,
so the four tribes of Huíhè, Qìbì, Sījié, and Hún crossed the desert and migrated to the area between Gānzhōu and Liángzhōu to avoid him.
When Wáng Jūnxuánbǐ was of humble status,
he traveled among the four tribes,
and was looked down upon by them;
when he became the Jǐedùshǐ of Héxī,
he disciplined them with law.
The four tribes felt humiliated and resentful,
and secretly sent envoys to the Eastern Capital to lodge a complaint.
Jūnxuánbǐ hastily sent an urgent report
stating: “The four tribes are difficult to control,
and secretly harbor rebellious intentions.”
The emperor sent an imperial envoy to investigate,
but the tribes could not get justice.
Thereupon, Hànhǎi Dàdūdū Huíhè Chéngzōng was exiled to Rángzhōu,
Hún Dàdé to Jízhōu,
Hèlán Dūdū Qìbì Chéngmíng to Téngzhōu.
Téngzhōu
was the territory of Cāngwú and Měnglíng Counties during the Hàn dynasty,
Yǒngpíng Jùn was established during the Jìn dynasty,
and Téngzhōu was established during the Suí dynasty.
Huíhè Fúdìnán was appointed Hànhǎi Dàdūdū.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
Lǐ Lìngwèn, the Yòu Sànqí Chángshì, was demoted to Fǔzhōu Biéjià.
According to old records: Fǔzhōu is
three thousand three hundred and twelve lǐ southeast of the capital.
11 On the day Bǐngxū,
Píjiā Kèhán of the Tujue sent his great minister Méilù Chuò to present tribute.
When the Tubo invaded Guāzhōu,
they sent a letter to Píjiā,
wishing to jointly invade with him.
Píjiā also presented their letter.
The emperor praised him,
and allowed trade at the Western Shòuxiáng Chéng,
where tens of thousands of bolts of silk and cloth were brought annually to trade for military horses,
to aid the army,
and also to serve as breeding stock for imperial pastures.
As a result, the national horses became stronger.
12 In the intercalary month,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
the Tubo Zànpǔ and Tūqíshī Sūlù besieged Ānxī Chéng.
Zhào Yízhēn, the Ānxī Fù Dàdūhù, attacked and defeated them.
13 Hùshū, a kinsman of Huíhè Chéngzōng and Hànhǎi Sīmǎ,
gathered his partisans to avenge Chéngzōng.
At that time, the Tubo sent an envoy through a secret path to the Tujue,
and Wáng Jūnxuánbǐ led elite cavalry to intercept them at Sùzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: In the first year of Rénshòu of the Suí dynasty, Sùzhōu was established by dividing Fúlù County of Gānzhōu.
It was two hundred lǐ southeast to Chìliǔ Jiān of Gānzhōu,
and three hundred and forty lǐ southwest to Ānlè Fēng at the border of Guāzhōu.
When they reached Gǒngbǐ Yì south of Gānzhōu,
Hùshū’s hidden troops suddenly attacked,
seized Jūnxuánbǐ’s banners and insignia,
first killed his Pànguān Sòng Zhēn,
and dissected his heart, saying:
“You were the primary schemer.”
Jūnxuánbǐ led several tens of his attendants in fierce combat.
From morning till dusk,
all his attendants died.
Hùshū killed Jūnxuánbǐ,
carried his corpse and fled to Tubo;
the Liángzhōu troops pursued and caught up with him,
Hùshū abandoned the corpse and fled.
Kǎoyì says: The old tradition states:
“After the Huíhè killed Jūnxuánbǐ,
the emperor ordered Guō Zhīyùn to suppress them.”
However, Zhīyùn had already died in the ninth year,
and Jūnxuánbǐ had taken over the defense of Liángzhōu;
the old tradition is mistaken.
14 On the day Gēngshēn,
the imperial carriage departed from the Eastern Capital.
In winter,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
it arrived at the Western Capital.
The character “winter”
is missing the two characters
“tenth month”
below it.
15 On the day Xīnsì,
Wáng Yī of Xìn'ān, the Zǔo Jīnwú Wèi Dàjiāngjūn, was appointed Fù Dàshǐ of Shuòfāng Jǐedù, etc.
Yī
was the grandson of Kè.
Wú Wáng Kè
was the son of Tàizōng.
Yī,
read as xū wéi fān.
At that time, Wáng Jūnxuánbǐ had just suffered a defeat,
and Hé and Lǒng were shaken.
Sōng appointed Péi Kuān, the Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng, as Pànguān,
and together with Jūnxuánbǐ’s Pànguān Niú Xiānkè, managed military and political affairs,
and the people’s morale gradually stabilized.
Kuān
was Tsǔi’s cousin.
Xiānkè was originally a minor official from Qún'gū.
Qún'gū County,
during the Former Hàn dynasty, belonged to Běidì Jùn;
during the Later Hàn and Jìn dynasties, it belonged to Āndìng Jùn.
The Later Wèi dynasty established Zhàopíng Jùn,
and the Later Zhōu dynasty abolished the Jùn,
making the county subordinate to Jīngzhōu.
Liú Xù said: Jǐedùshǐ appointed two Pànguān,
their rank is not yet seen.
Qún,
read as rú lún fān.
Gū,
read as gōng hū fān.
He was Jūnxuánbǐ’s trusted confidant.
Sōng also proposed appointing Zhāng Shǒuguī, the Jiànkāng Jūnshǐ of Hébĕi, as Guāzhōu Cìshǐ.
Jiànkāng Jūn was located in the Qílián Shān, one hundred and ninety lǐ northwest of Gānzhōu.
Hébĕi County belonged to Shǎnzhōu.
When the planks were just erected,
the poem says: shrink the planks to carry.
Planks on both sides,
earth placed inside and rammed.
Gàn
also refers to planks.
Kǒng Ānguó said: The sides are called gàn.
Shuài,
read as lǜ.
The people in the city looked at each other, their faces drained of color,
and no one had the will to fight.
Shǒuguī said:
“Their numbers are great, ours are few,
and we are the remnants of a disaster;
we cannot confront them with arrows and blades,
we must win with a clever strategy.”
So he set up a feast and played music on the city wall.
The barbarians suspected they were prepared,
dared not attack, and retreated.
Shǒuguī then unleashed his troops to attack them,
and the barbarians fled in defeat.
Shǒuguī then repaired the city,
gathered the scattered people,
and all resumed their former occupations.
The imperial court praised his achievements,
made Guāzhōu a Dūdū Fǔ,
and appointed Shǒuguī as Dūdū.
Xīnuòluó’s prestige was very high,
so Xiāo Sōng sent a counter-intelligence agent to Tubo,
claiming that Xīnuòluó was colluding with the Central Kingdom.
The Zànpǔ summoned and executed him;
the Tubo thereupon declined somewhat.
16th, 12th month.
On the day Wùyín,
an imperial edict was issued concerning the threat of the Tǔbō on the border.
It ordered 56,000 regiment soldiers from the Lǒngyòu Circuit and various army corps,
and 40,000 regiment soldiers from the Héxī Circuit and various army corps.
The Fǔbīng system was abolished.
All methods were to be employed to organize civilian militias,
which were called
"Tuánbīng."
Ten thousand soldiers from Shuòfāng gathered at Huì Zhōu to defend against autumn incursions.
By early winter,
as there were no raids, they were dismissed.
If the barbarians invaded,
troops would be sent out from both front and rear to attack them.
17th, on the day Yǐhài,
the Emperor visited the Lǐshān Hot Springs.
On the day Bǐngxū,
he returned to the palace.
1st year, Spring.
1st month.
On the day Rén'yín,
Zhào Yízhēn, Deputy Grand Protector-General of Ānxī, defeated the Tǔbō at Qǔzǐ Chéng.
2nd. On the day Jiǎ'yín,
Yǔwén Róng, the Cìshǐ of Wèizhōu, was appointed Hùbù Shìláng and concurrently Cìshǐ of Wèizhōu,
serving as Xuānfǔshǐ of Hébĕi Circuit.
The office of Xuānfǔshǐ began with this.
The character "使" (shǐ)
is read like "疏吏" (shūlì);
the same below.
3rd. On the day Yǐmǎo,
Chén Hángfàn, a Láo from Chūn and Lóng prefectures, and Féng Lín and Hé Yóulǔ, Láo from Guǎngzhōu, revolted,
capturing over forty cities.
Hángfàn proclaimed himself emperor,
Yóulǔ styled himself Dìngguó Dàjiāngjūn,
and Lín styled himself Nányuè Wáng,
intending to occupy the Lǐngbiǎo region.
The inner attendant Yáng Sīxù was ordered to dispatch troops from Guìzhōu and nearby circuits north of the Lǐng to suppress them.
4th. On the day Bǐng'yín,
Yǔwén Róng, the Cìshǐ of Wèizhōu, was appointed concurrently Jiǎnjiào Bìanzhōu Cìshǐ,
serving as the commissioner for the nine rivers, canals, dikes, and weirs in Hénán and Hébĕi.
Róng requested to use the old channels of the Nine Rivers from the Yǔgòng to open rice fields,
and to reduce the cost of land transport,
with the government collecting the profit.
His projects were incessant,
but many did not succeed.
5th. 2nd month.
On the day Rénshēn,
Zhāng Yuè, who had retired as Shàngshū Yòuchéngxiàng, was appointed concurrently Jíxián Diàn Xuéshì.
Although Yuè had resigned from state affairs,
he specialized in literary and historical duties.
Whenever there was a major event in court,
the Emperor would often send an imperial envoy to consult him.
History records that Zhāng Yuè's favor did not wane.
The character "尚" (shàng)
is read like "辰羊" (chényáng).
The character "相" (xiàng)
is read like "息亮" (xīliàng).
The character "說" (yuè)
is read as "悅" (yuè).
The character "使" (shǐ)
is read like "疏吏" (shūlì).
6th. On the day Rénchén,
the Kuòqí were renamed the Zuǒyòu Yǔlín Jūn Fēiqí.
The Kuòqí were mentioned in the 13th year of the previous volume.
The character "彍" (kuò)
is read like "虛郭" (xūguō),
or "古郭" (gǔguō).
The character "騎" (qí)
is read like "奇寄" (qíjì).
7th. Autumn.
7th month.
Xīmòlǎng, a great general of the Tǔbō, raided Guāzhōu.
The character "吐" (tǔ)
is read with the entering tone of "暾" (tūn).
The character "將" (jiàng)
is read like "即亮" (jíliàng).
On the day Yǐsì,
Xiāo Sōng, Jìedùshǐ of Héxī, and Zhāng Zhōngliàng, Jìedùshǐ of Lǒngyòu, greatly defeated the Tǔbō at Kēbō Gǔ.
According to the "New Book of Tang, Account of Tǔbō,"
Kēbō Gǔ should be west of Qīnghǎi.
A textual variant states: "Shílù," "Tánglì," and "Xiāo Sōng Zhuàn" write
"Zhāng Zhìliàng."
Now following the old "Běnjì" and "Tǔbō Zhuàn."
They captured their Dàmò Mén Chéng,
Dàmò Mén Chéng is in Jiǔqǔ.
They burned their Luòtuó Qiáo (Camel Bridge) and returned.
8th. 8th month.
On the day Yǐsì,
Tèjìn Zhāng Yuè presented the Kāiyuán Dàyǎn Lì (Dàyǎn Calendar),
and it was put into use.
Monk Yīxíng derived the Dàyǎn numbers to establish methods,
and in response to celestial phenomena, solstices, and eclipses, created the new calendar,
hence it was called Dàyǎn Lì.
The character "上" (shàng)
is read like "時掌" (shízhǎng).
9th. On the day Xīnmǎo,
Dù Bīnke, Zuǒ Jīnwú Jiāngjūn, defeated the Tǔbō below Qílián Chéng.
Qílián Chéng is in Qílián Shān, Zhāngyè Xiàn, Gānzhōu.
Xiāo Sōng sent Bīnke with four thousand strong crossbowmen to attack them.
The battle lasted from chén (7-9 AM) to dusk.
The Tǔbō were utterly defeated,
and one of their great generals was captured.
The barbarians scattered and fled into the mountains,
their cries echoing all around.
10th. Winter.
10th month.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
the Emperor visited the Lǐshān Hot Springs.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
he returned to the palace.
A textual variant states: "Shílù"
says "12th month, Dīngmǎo."
It also says
"visited the Wēnquán Gōng (Hot Springs Palace)."
It does not mention his return.
"Tánglì" says,
"On Dīngmǎo, visited the hot springs;
on Dīngchǒu, returned to the palace."
Since he already visited the hot springs this month,
this might be a repetition,
and is not adopted.
11th. 11th month.
On the day Guǐsì,
Xiāo Sōng, Deputy Ambassador of the Héxī Jìedù, was appointed Bīngbù Shàngshū and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
12th. 12th month.
On the day Bǐng'yín,
an imperial edict stated:
"Long-serving soldiers have no fixed return date,
which is difficult for people to endure.
It is appropriate to divide them into five rotations,
sending one rotation home each year for rest and bathing,
and after five years, rewarding them with five promotions."
13th. That year,
an imperial decree mandated that household registers be fixed every three years,
divided into nine grades.
14th. Yáng Sīxù marched against Chén Hángfàn.
Upon reaching Lóngzhōu,
he defeated them,
capturing Hé Yóulǔ and Féng Lín.
Hángfàn fled to the two caves of Yúnjì and Pánliáo.
Sīxù pursued and captured him alive,
and then executed him.
In total,
six tens of thousands of heads were decapitated.
Sīxù was a stern man;
subordinate officers dared not look up when reporting to him.
Therefore, wherever he deployed troops, he achieved success.
However, he was cruel by nature.
Of the captives he took,
some had their faces flayed alive,
others had knives used to cut their hairlines,
tearing off their scalps.
The barbarians feared him.
1st year, Spring.
2nd month.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
Zhāng Shǒusù, Dūdū of Xīzhōu,
defeated the Southwestern Man,
capturing Kūnmíng and Yánchéng.
Kūnmíng Xiàn belonged to Xīzhōu,
it was the territory of Hàn's Dìngzuò Xiàn.
Later, the Northern Zhōu established Dìngzuò Zhèn.
In the 2nd year of Wǔdé, it was changed to Kūnmíng Xiàn,
because its land was adjacent to Kūnmíng.
The county had salt and iron,
and a city was built to protect them,
hence it was also called Yánchéng.
The character "巂" (xī)
is pronounced like "髓" (suǐ).
2nd. 3rd month.
Zhāng Shǒuguī, Dūdū of Guāzhōu, and Jiǎ Shīshùn, Cìshǐ of Shāzhōu, attacked the Dàtóng Army of the Tǔbō,
and greatly defeated it.
3 On the day *Jiǎyín*,
Wé Yī, Prince of Xìn'ān and Jìedùshǐ of Shuòfāng, attacked the Tǔbō's Shíbǎo City
and captured it.
Previously,
the Tǔbō had seized Shíbǎo City,
garrisoned it with troops,
and harassed the area west of the Yellow River (Héyòu).
The Emperor commanded Wé Yī to discuss with the Jìedùshǐ of Héxī and Lǒngyòu how to attack and retake it.
All the generals thought that Shíbǎo was strategically located in a perilous place and the route was long;
if they attacked and failed to capture it,
they would have no way to return themselves.
They suggested it would be better to hold their troops and observe the opportune moment.
Wé Yī did not listen.
He led his troops deep into enemy territory,
quickly attacked and captured it.
Then
he divided his troops to garrison strategic points,
preventing the barbarians from advancing.
From then on, the various armies in Hélǒng conducted patrols,
expanding their territory by over a thousand *lǐ*.
When the Emperor heard this,
he was greatly pleased,
and renamed Shíbǎo City as Zhènwǔ Jūn.
From Shànchéng County in Shànzhōu, going 120 *lǐ* west to Báishuǐ Jūn,
then 60 *lǐ* southwest to Dìngróng City,
then seven *lǐ* south across a gully was Shíbǎo City,
which was originally the Tǔbō's Tiěrèn City.
Sòng Bái said: Shíbǎo City is west of Lóngzhī County.
On all four sides are cliffs several thousand *rèn* high.
The stone path winds and twists,
three or four *lǐ* long.
Thirty *lǐ* west is Chìlǐng.
更 (gēng, meaning change),
pronounced like HÉNG in the fanqie method.
4 On the day *Bǐngchén*,
Yáng Yáng, Guózǐ Jìjiǔ, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The provincial office has proposed limiting the number of candidates who pass the *Míngjīng* and *Jìnshì* examinations throughout the empire
to no more than one hundred each year.
I have observed that those who enter officialdom from outside the regular ranks
number more than two thousand each year,
while *Míngjīng* and *Jìnshì* cannot even account for one-tenth of that.
This means that scholars who diligently pursue their studies and profession are not as successful in obtaining office as petty clerks.
I fear that Confucian traditions will gradually decline,
and integrity and shame will diminish daily.
If the number of people entering officialdom is too high,
then all categories should be reduced,
not just *Míngjīng* and *Jìnshì*."
He also proposed:
"When various
departments administer the *Míngjīng* examination,
they do not focus on understanding the main points of composition and rhetoric,
but instead exclusively seek difficult-to-know facts,
asking about obscure lines from classics or isolated sentences, or specific dates;
I request that from now on, only plain texts be used for the examination."
The Tang dynasty's examination categories for selecting officials
included *Jìnshì*
and *Míngjīng*.
For the *Míngjīng* examination,
candidates first answered questions on a text,
then orally answered ten questions on the general meaning of the classics,
and three questions on current affairs policies.
Based on the clarity and breadth of their essays, they were graded as *shàngshàng*, *shàngzhōng*, *shàngxià*, *zhōngshàng*;
those four grades constituted "passing the examination" (*jíyǐn*).
For the *Jìnshì* examination,
candidates answered five questions on current affairs policies,
and one major classic text.
Those who passed all classic and policy questions were in the *jiǎdì* (first class);
those who passed four policy questions and more than four classic questions were in the *yǐdì* (second class).
The *Tōngdiǎn* states: According to the Tang system,
for *tiējīng* (text-pasting examination),
the two ends of the studied classic were covered,
with only one line left open in between.
Paper was cut to make the "paste,"
usually consisting of three characters.
This was adjusted over time, sometimes increased or decreased,
and the criteria for passing varied.
Sometimes passing meant getting four, five, or six characters correct.
5 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day *Gēngwǔ*,
the *dì* sacrifice was performed at the Tàimiào.
In the early Tang,
during the *xiá* sacrifice, the generations (zhāomù) were sequenced,
but during the *dì* sacrifice, each was worshipped in their own chamber.
By this time,
Wéi Tāo, Shàoyī of the Tàicháng Temple, and others memorialized,
saying: "If
this is done, the *dì* sacrifice will be no different from an ordinary offering.
We request that in both the *dì* and *xiá* sacrifices, the generations be sequenced."
This was adopted.
Wéi Tāo
was the nephew of Wéi Ānshí.
6 In the fifth month,
on the day *Rénchén*,
the ten circuits and the Ancha Shǐ for the Jīng and Dū prefectural areas were re-established.
Yōng, Tóng, Huá, Shāng, Qí, and Bīn constituted the Jīngjī (Capital Prefectural Area);
Luò and Rǔ constituted the Dūjī (Secondary Capital Prefectural Area).
Twelve years prior,
the Ancha Shǐ for the various circuits had been abolished;
now they were re-established.
复 (fù, meaning re-establish),
pronounced like fúyòu in the fanqie method,
or as written (rújì).
7 Initially,
Zhāng Yuè, Zhāng Jiāzhēn, Lǐ Yuánhóng, and Dù Xiān successively served as chancellors and held power.
Yuán Gānyào, adhering to prudence and integrity,
always deferred matters to Zhāng Yuè and others,
merely assenting and affixing his signature.
Lǐ Yuánhóng and Dù Xiān often disagreed on matters,
leading to animosity,
and they impeached each other.
The Emperor was displeased.
In the sixth month,
on the day *Jiǎxū*,
Dù Xiān, Huángmén Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was demoted to Jīngzhōu Chángshǐ;
Lǐ Yuánhóng, Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was demoted to Cáozhōu Cìshǐ.
According to old records,
Cáozhōu
was 1,453 *lǐ* northeast of the capital.
Yuán Gānyào was only made Zuǒ Chéngxiàng.
In the early Kaiyuán era,
the Shàngshū Zuǒ and Yòu Púyè were renamed Zuǒ and Yòu Chéngxiàng.
In the early Tang,
the office of Púyè oversaw everything,
and was truly the prime minister.
By the first year of Zhōngzōng's Shénlóng era, Dòulú Qīnwàng served solely as Púyè,
not daring to involve himself in political affairs.
Thereafter, those appointed solely as Púyè no longer managed political affairs.
Although they held the title of Chéngxiàng,
it was no longer the function of the Chéngxiàng of the early Tang.
Now, Yuán Gānyào was only made Zuǒ Chéngxiàng,
meaning he was merely Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
and no longer involved in political affairs.
Péi Guāngtíng, Bīngbù Shìláng, was made Zhōngshū Shìláng,
also Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Xiāo Sōng was appointed concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng,
remotely overseeing Héxī.
He remotely held the title of Héxī Jìedùshǐ.
8 Initially, Wáng Máozhòng, Kāifǔ, entered into a marriage alliance with Gé Fúshùn, Lóngwǔ Jiāngjūn.
Wáng Máozhòng was trusted by the Emperor,
and his words were always heeded.
Therefore, many of the generals of the Northern Gate attached themselves to him,
their promotions and demotions dependent on his commands.
Qí Hǎn, Lìbù Shìláng, took an opportunity to speak to the Emperor, saying:
"Gé Fúshùn commands the imperial guards;
what Gé Fúshùn commanded
were the Wànqí (Ten Thousand Cavalry),
hence the statement.
Wáng Máozhòng is a petty man;
excessive favor will breed wickedness.
If precautions are not taken early,
I fear it will become a future problem."
The Emperor was pleased and said:
"I know of your loyalty.
I will consider the matter slowly."
Qí Hǎn said:
"If the ruler is not discreet, he will lose his minister."
This is from the *Yì Dàzhuàn*.
It happened that Má Chá, Dàlǐ Chéng, was demoted for an offense to Xīngzhōu Biéjià.
According to old records,
Xīngzhōu was 948 *lǐ* from the capital.
Qí Hǎn went out of the city to see him off,
and incidentally mentioned his admonition given within the palace.
Má Chá was by nature frivolous and cunning,
and he immediately reported it to the Emperor.
The Emperor was furious,
summoned Qí Hǎn, and rebuked him, saying:
"You doubted my discretion,
and then spoke of it to Má Chá.
How is that discreet?
Moreover, Má Chá has always been of bad character;
surely you knew that?"
Qí Hǎn bowed his head and apologized.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day *Dīngsì*,
an imperial edict was issued:
"Qí Hǎn and Má Chá conspired against the chancellors
and sowed discord between ruler and minister.
Qí Hǎn is demoted to Liángdé Chéng of Gāozhōu;
Má Chá is demoted to Huánghuà Wèi of Xúnzhōu."
Liángdé was also part of Hàn's Hépǔ County territory.
Wú established Gāoliáng Commandery.
Chén divided it to establish Wùdé County,
later renamed Liángdé.
Xúnzhōu was the land of Hàn's Bùshān and Ālín.
Liáng established Guìpíng Commandery in the Bùshān area.
Suí abolished the commandery and made it a county.
Suí also established Huánghuà County in the Ālín area,
which Suí later abolished and merged into Guìpíng.
In the seventh year of Zhēnguān, Xúnzhōu was established,
with its seat in Guìpíng,
and Huánghuà County was re-established and belonged to it.
9 In the eighth month, on the
guǐhài day,
the Emperor hosted a banquet for the civil and military officials below the Huā'è Lóu to celebrate his birthday.
Kǎoyì says: The Shílù states,
“The first day of the eighth month was guǐhài.”
According to the Chánglì,
the first day of this month was jǐwèi;
guǐhài
was the fifth day.
Gù Kuàng’s poem says:
“On the fifth night of the eighth month, the auspicious qi is new,
Empress Zhaochéng gave birth to the Holy Man.”
The Shílù is incorrect.
It was requested that the fifth day of the eighth month each year be designated as Qiānqiū Jié,
proclaimed throughout the realm,
and everyone should feast and celebrate.
The imperial banquet on the Sānɡ Jié began from this time.
Later, Qiānqiū Jié was changed to Tiāncháng Jié.
During the reigns of Dézōng, Shùnzōng, Xiànzōng, and Mùzōng, no such festival names were established.
Lì,
pronounced lì dīng fān.
Lè,
pronounced luò.
Since ancient times,
the community rites have been held on wù days.
10On the gēngchén day,
Zhāng Jiāzhēn, Minister of Works, passed away.
Zhāng Jiāzhēn did not concern himself with managing family property.
When someone advised him to buy fields and houses,
Zhāng Jiāzhēn said:
“I am noble enough to be a general and a prime minister,
why should I worry about cold and hunger!
If I were to incur guilt,
even with fields and houses,
they would be of no use.
I have seen officials widely occupying good land,
and on the day of their death,
it merely serves as capital for their dissolute sons and younger brothers for wine and women.
I do not take this.”
Those who heard him agreed.
11On the xīnsì day,
an imperial edict was issued because many commoners were privately minting counterfeit coins.
From this point, private sale of copper, lead, and tin, and making vessels of copper was prohibited;
those who mined copper, lead, and tin,
the government would purchase it from them.
12Yǔwén Róng was quick-witted and astute.
He was eloquent in his responses,
and gained the Emperor's favor through his management of finance and tribute.
He began to widely establish various agencies,
competing to accumulate wealth.
Because of this, the various officials gradually lost their proper duties, and the Emperor's extravagance increased.
Historians say that during the reign of Táng Xuánzōng,
the opening of avenues for profit began with Yǔwén Róng.
He was hasty and talkative,
and fond of boasting.
When he was in a prime ministerial position,
he told people:
“If I remain in this position for a few months,
there will be no troubles within the four seas.”
Xìn'ān Wáng Yī,
was favored by the Emperor due to his military achievements,
specifically for his success in pacifying Shíbǎo Chéng.
When Yī came to court,
Róng had Censor Lǐ Yín impeach him,
which was leaked to Yī’s close associates.
When Yī heard of it,
he reported it to the Emperor first.
The next day,
Yín’s memorial indeed arrived,
and the Emperor was enraged.
In the ninth month, on the
rénzǐ day,
Róng was demoted to Inspector of Rǔzhōu.
Kǎoyì says: The old tradition states:
“Palace Censor Lǐ Zhòu was summoned by post-horse to arrest Yī for imprisonment.
After Yī successfully pleaded his case,
Róng was demoted for being partial to Lǐ Zhòu.”
Now we follow the Tánglì.
From the jiǎxū day of the sixth month
to the rénzǐ day of the ninth month,
it was only ninety-nine days.
All these were rooted in Róng.
13In winter,
the tenth month,
on the wùwǔ day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse,
not full, like a hook.
14After Yǔwén Róng incurred guilt,
the national expenditure became insufficient.
The Emperor remembered him again,
and said to Péi Guāngtíng:
“All of you spoke of Róng's wickedness.
I have already dismissed him.
Now the national expenditure is insufficient,
what shall we do!
How can you assist me?”
Guāngtíng and the others were afraid and could not respond.
Coincidentally, a sealed report arrived accusing Róng of bribery and corruption,
and he was further demoted to Magistrate of Pínglè.
Pínglè County,
was the territory of Lìpǔ in Cāngwú Commandery during the Hàn dynasty.
In the Jìn dynasty, Pínglè County was established,
belonging to Shǐ'ān Commandery.
In the Táng dynasty, Zhaozhōu was separately established;
there is Pínglè River.
Lè,
pronounced luò.
Kǎoyì says: The Tánglì states:
“Péi Guāngtíng and others instigated the relevant officials to impeach him,
accumulating bribes amounting to millions.”
The old tradition states:
“Péi Guāngtíng was concurrently Grand Censor,
and also impeached Róng for forming factions and his son receiving bribes, among other things.”
Now we follow the Shílù and Tǒngjì.
The Tánglì also states
“the yìwèi day of the tenth month.”
According to the Chánglì,
the first day of the tenth month was wùwǔ,
there was no yìwèi.
Now we follow the Tǒngjì.
Jiǎng Cén, Vice Minister of the Court of Agriculture, memorialized that Róng had embezzled millions of official funds in Biànzhōu.
An edict ordered a thorough investigation of the matter,
and Róng was exiled to Yánzhōu.
In the second year of Diàolù of Gāozōng,
Yánzhōu was established by separating parts of Héng and Guì Prefectures,
named after its location north of Yángāng.
Zhì,
pronounced zhí zhī fān.
15In the eleventh month, on the
xīnmǎo day,
the Emperor traveled to visit the five imperial tombs of Qiáo, Dìng, Xiàn, Zhāo, and Qián;
the order of visiting the five tombs
was based on the relative proximity and sequence of the imperial carriage's route.
On the wùshēn day,
he returned to the palace;
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the realm,
and half of the land tax for this year was remitted for all commoners.
16In the twelfth month, on the
xīnyǒu day,
the Emperor visited the Xīnfēng Hot Springs;
on the rénshēn day,
he returned to the palace.
Xīnfēng Hot Springs are the Lìshān Hot Springs,
Lìshān is in Xīnfēng County.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Kǎoyì says: The Shílù states:
“On the guǐyǒu day,
the Emperor presided over the court audience in the Hányuán Diàn to receive congratulations.”
According to the Chánglì,
the first day of this month was bǐngxū,
there was no guǐyǒu.
The events in the Shílù for this year differ from the Běnjì, Tánglì, and Tǒngjì;
the jiǎzǐ day of the first month is entirely erroneous;
it is suspected that this book had missing parts,
and later generations added to it.
The Xīnjì only relies on the Jiùjì,
and completely disregards the Shílù for this year.
It also states:
“On the dīngsì day,
he personally welcomed the qi in the eastern suburbs,
and issued an edict,
‘All prisoners in the realm who were not pardoned by ordinary amnesties before the fifth day of the first month of the eighteenth year,
shall all be pardoned and released.’ ”
However, there was no dīngsì day in this month;
all other books and the Huìyào contain no record of the Emperor personally welcoming the qi in the eighteenth year.
The Tánglì places it on the bǐngzǐ day, the seventh day of the first month of the twenty-sixth year.
The Tǒngjì places it in the first month of the twenty-sixth year.
The Shílù on the dīngchǒu day of the first month of the twenty-sixth year also records the welcoming of qi and a grand amnesty.
The wording of that edict and the scope of its benevolence
are similar to this year;
perhaps the Shílù mistakenly duplicated it here.
Now we do not adopt it.
On the xīnmǎo day,
Péi Guāngtíng was made Shìzhōng.
2 In the second month, on the
guǐyǒu day,
an initial decree allowed officials to take ten-day rests in the spring month,
to choose scenic spots for recreation, meaning they were to seek out beautiful places to travel and feast.
There were twelve banquets in total,
each granted five thousand strings of cash;
the Emperor sometimes invited their returning riders to stay and drink in the Huā'è Lóu,
alternately having them get up and dance,
and they left after enjoying themselves to the fullest.
3 In the third month, on the
dīngyǒu day,
official service land was reinstated for metropolitan officials.
The collection of service land is mentioned in Volume 10.
4 Summer,
fourth month.
Kǎoyì says: The Shílù says:
“On the day Yǐsì,
the imperial carriage visited Wēnquán Gōng.
On the day Dīngwèi,
he returned from Wēnquán Gōng.”
According to the Chánglì,
the first day of this month was Yǐmǎo,
so there were no Yǐsì or Dīngwèi days.
Neither the Jiùjì nor the Tánglì mentions a visit to Wēnquán.
Therefore, we do not adopt this account.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
the outer wall of Xījīng was built,
and it was completed in ninety days.
5 On the day Yǐchǒu,
Péi Guāngtíng was appointed concurrently Lìbù Shàngshū.
Previously,
the selection bureau, when assigning officials,
only considered their ability,
sometimes promoting them out of sequence,
or leaving them to grow old in lower positions.
Some, after more than twenty years of official career, had not received emoluments.
Furthermore,
there was no clear hierarchy for zhōu and xiàn offices,
sometimes moving from large to small,
or experiencing initial long periods
followed by distant postings,
all without a fixed system.
Guāngtíng first proposed using a system based on qualifications and seniority,
with each official, after being dismissed from office, accruing a certain number of “selections” to be gathered.
This meant that after an official was dismissed from office,
he would be subject to a certain number of selections;
these were ranked by quantity and gathered at the Lìbù.
Those in lower positions with more selections,
regardless of their ability,
would be appointed once their selections were met.
There were annual limits on advancement through ranks,
and no one was allowed to overstep.
Unless penalized,
all would be promoted, never demoted.
This was the same as the Tíngniángé of Cuī Liàng in the Later Wèi dynasty,
which was followed and implemented,
and remains so to this day.
Many talented individuals
have grown old in ordinary positions.
This was called
“Shèngshū,”
but all talented individuals complained and sighed.
Sòng Jǐng argued against it but could not prevail.
Guāngtíng also mandated that officials outside the regular civil service in acting capacities also had to be reviewed by the Ménxià Shěng.
6 Fifth month.
Tǔbō sent an envoy with a letter to the border, seeking peace.
7 Initially,
the Khitan king, Lǐ Shàogù, sent Kětūgān to present tribute,
but Tóngpíngzhāngshì Lǐ Yuánhóng treated him discourteously.
Zuǒchéngxiàng Zhāng Yuè said to others:
“The Xī and Khitan will surely rebel.
Kětūgān is cunning and defiant,
and has dominated his nation's politics for a long time;
the people are attached to him.
This refers to the hearts of the Khitan people.
Qì,
pronounced qī qì,
also chī.
Hěn,
pronounced hù kěn.
They will certainly not return.”
On the day Jǐyǒu,
Kětūgān assassinated Shàogù,
and led his people, along with coercing the Xī multitude, to defect to the Tūjué.
Xī king Lǐ Lǔsū, his wife Wéi Shì, and Shàogù’s wife Chén Shì all fled to the court.
History confirms the words of Zhāng Yuè.
Wéi and Chén were both Chinese women given in marriage as princesses to the two barbarians,
as recorded in the fourteenth year mentioned above.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Jiàng,
pronounced hù jiāng.
Jué,
pronounced jiǔ wù.
It was also ordered that Zhōngshū Shèrén Péi Kuān, Jǐshìzhōng Xuē Kǎn, and others should be dispatched to Guānnèi, Hédōng, and Hénánběi to recruit brave warriors.
Sixth month.
Kǎoyì says: The Tángcháo Niándàijì says:
“Initially,
Péi Guāngtíng married Wǔ Sānsī’s daughter,
and Gāo Lìshì had an affair with her.
Guāngtíng had administrative talent,
and Lìshì promoted him,
thus he became a chancellor.
Contemporaries despised this,
and Sòng Jǐng and Wáng Jùn would perform the Huíbōyuè dance after drinking as a jest.
Guāngtíng was troubled by this,
so he memorialized: ‘More than thirty zhōu across the empire lack cìshǐ.
Peace has reigned for a long time,
and people are unwilling to serve as external officials.
I request that senior officials concurrently hold external offices and serve as cìshǐ to enhance their prestige.’
Thereupon, Jǐng was nominated for Yángzhōu,
Jùn for Wèizhōu,
Lù Xiàngxiān for Jīngzhōu,
and more than ten others in total.
Xiāo Sōng firmly memorialized: ‘The empire’s affairs are critical;
we rely on experienced and virtuous old ministers to inquire into gains and losses.
If we lose all of them,
then the imperial court will be empty.’
The Emperor then understood
and stopped the plan.”
According to the Shílù,
in the intercalary sixth month of this year,
“Prince Heir Apparent Junior Guardian Lù Xiàngxiān was concurrently appointed Jīngzhōu Zhǎngshǐ,”
but Jǐng and Jùn were never appointed external officials.
Therefore, we do not adopt this account.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Zhōngwáng Jùn, the Dàdūhù of Shányú, was appointed concurrently Xīběidào Xíngjūn Yuánshuài,
with Yùshǐ Dàfū Lǐ Cháoyǐn and Jīngzhàoyǐn Péi Zhǒuxiān as his deputies,
leading eighteen Zǒngguǎn to suppress the Xī and Khitan.
Jùn was ordered to meet the officials at Guāngshùn Mén.
Zhāng Yuè, upon retreating,
said to the academicians Sūn Tì and Wéi Shù:
These were academicians of the Jíxián Shūyuàn.
“I once observed the portrait of Tàizōng;
it remarkably resembles Zhōngwáng.
This is a blessing for the nation.”
Kětūgān plundered Pínglú.
The vanguard commander, Zhāngyè Wū Chéngcǐ, defeated him at Nàlù Shān.
In the early Kaiyuán era,
Pínglú Jūn was established in Yíngzhōu.
Cǐ,
pronounced qiě lǐ,
also cǐ.
Nà,
pronounced nú gé.
Kǎoyì says: Hán Yù’s Wū Shì Xiān Miào Bēi says:
“Shàngshū, whose taboo name was Chéngqià,
during the Kaiyuán era commanded the Pínglú Vanguard Army,
repeatedly defeating the Xī and Khitan,
and participated in the battle of Nàlù,
driving away Kětūgān.”
The Xīn Chuán says:
“Chéngcǐ,
during the Kaiyuán era, along with his cousin Chéng'ēn, both served as Pínglú vanguards,
deeply brave and decisive,
known as the ‘Two Dragons of the Camp Gate.’”
According to this,
Chéngcǐ and Chéngqià are the same person.
We now follow the Xīn Shū.
8 On the day Rénwǔ,
the Luò River overflowed,
drowning over a thousand households in Dōngdū.
9 Autumn,
ninth
month.
On the day Dīngsì,
Zhōngwáng Jùn was concurrently appointed Hédōngdào Yuánshuài,
but he ultimately did not take up the post.
10 The Túbō troops were defeated several times and grew afraid,
so they sought a peace alliance.
Zhōngwáng's companion Huángfǔ Wéimíng
was a companion to a prince of Táng,
from rank five, upper grade,
responsible for attending and offering admonitions.
The Emperor said:
"The Zànpǔ once sent me a letter that was disrespectful and arrogant.
Túbō requested to be treated with the rites due to a rival state."
(See volume 211, second year.)
Cóng,
read as qiān róng.
Yí,
read as yú jì.
Bèi,
read as pú nèi,
also pú mò.
Wéimíng replied:
"When the Zànpǔ was first installed in the early Kaiyuán reign,
he was still young and immature.
In the third year of Cháng'ān of Wǔ Hòu,
the Zànpǔ was enthroned,
being only seven years old.
He was still young in the early Kaiyuán reign.
Zhì,
read as zhí lì.
This was probably fabricated by border generals,
hoping to provoke Your Majesty's anger.
When there are troubles on the frontier,
generals and officials can use this as an opportunity to embezzle state property,
and falsely report achievements to gain honors and titles.
These are all benefits for treacherous ministers,
not blessings for the state.
If the conflict continues unresolved,
it will cost a thousand gold a day.
The Art of War says: 'Raising an army of a hundred thousand [men]
costs a thousand gold a day.'
If Your Majesty would sincerely send an envoy to visit the Princess
(referring to Princess Jīnchéng),
shǐ,
read as shū lì;
the shǐ and qiǎn shǐ below are pronounced the same.
and have him kowtow and declare himself a subject,
permanently ending the border troubles,
would this not be a superior strategy for managing the barbarians!"
The Emperor was pleased,
and ordered Wéimíng and the Imperial Attendant Zhāng Yuánfāng to go as envoys to Túbō.
The Zànpǔ was greatly delighted,
and brought out all the imperial edicts received since the Zhēngguàn era to show Wéimíng.
In winter,
the tenth month,
he dispatched his minister Lùn Míngxīliè to accompany Wéimíng to present tribute.
(Kǎoyì says: In the Shílù,
"On the guǐsì day of the seventh month of the nineteenth year,
Túbō sent its minister Míngxīliè to court
to request a reaffirmation of the peace and good relations,
and also presented a letter"
and so on.
According to the Chánglì,
the first day of the seventh month of the nineteenth year was dìngwèi,
and there was no guǐsì day.
We now follow the Tánglì, the Jiù Běnjì, and the Túbō Zhuàn.)
"Your nephew has for generations married princesses,
and our righteousness is that of one family.
In between, Zhāng Xuánbiǎo and others first raised troops to raid and plunder.
During Wǔ Hòu's time,
Zhāng Xuánbiǎo was the Protector-General of Ānxī,
and he and Túbō mutually invaded and plundered.
Chāo,
read as chǔ jiāo.
Your nephew deeply understands the distinction between superior and inferior,
how could he dare to be disrespectful!
It was precisely because border generals colluded
that I incurred the displeasure of my uncle;
I repeatedly sent envoys to court,
but they were all obstructed by border generals.
Now, I have received the honor of a distant envoy,
who has come to visit the princess,
and your nephew cannot express his joy and gratitude enough.
If we can restore our former good relations,
I will have no regrets even unto death!"
From then on, Túbō again submitted.
11 On the gēngyín day,
the Emperor visited Fèngquán Hot Springs;
on the guǐmǎo day,
he returned to the capital.
There was Fèngquán Mansion in Méi County, Qí Prefecture.
12 On the jiǎyín day,
Hùmìwáng Luózhēntán came to court
and was kept for imperial guard duty.
Hùmì is sometimes called Dámosītiědì,
or Huòkǎn.
It is what Yuánwèi called Bōhé,
also the old territory of Tuǒhuǒluó.
It is directly northeast of the capital, over nine thousand lǐ away,
bordering the Wūhǔ River to the north,
and lying on the route from the Four Garrisons into Tuǒhuǒluó.
13 In the eleventh month,
on the dīngmǎo day,
the Emperor visited Líshān Hot Springs;
on the dīngchǒu day,
he returned to the palace.
14 In this year,
only twenty-four capital crimes were reported nationwide.
15 Tūqíshī sent envoys to present tribute.
The Emperor entertained them at Dānfènglóu,
which was the tower of Dānfèngmén.
The main gate of the Dàmíng Palace in the Eastern Inner Palace was called Dānfèngmén.
The two envoys vied for precedence.
The Tūjué said:
"Tūqíshī is a small state,
originally a subject of Tūjué,
and cannot be placed above us."
The Tūqíshī said:
"Today's banquet
is set for us,
and we cannot be placed below them."
So the Emperor ordered curtains to be set up on the east and west.
Tūjué was placed on the east,
and Tūqíshī on the west.
16 Wáng Máozhòng, Kǎifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Dūshǐ of the Nèi-Wài Xián Jiānmù and Húoguógōng,
was in charge of the twelve inner and outer stables, eight breeding farms, and forty-eight prefectural pastures,
as well as the Shāyuàn and other pastures,
all under his command,
hence "Dūshǐ."
His arrogance and profligacy grew daily,
but the Emperor always tolerated him.
Máozhòng was close to Zuǒlǐngjūn Dàjiàngjūn Gě Fúshùn, Zuǒjiānmén Jiàngjūn Táng Dìwén, Zuǒwǔwèi Jiàngjūn Lǐ Shǒudé, Ròuwēiwèi Jiàngjūn Wáng Jǐngyào, and Gāo Guǎngjì.
Fúshùn and others, relying on his influence,
often acted unlawfully.
Máozhòng sought the position of Bīngbù Shàngshū but did not get it,
and his displeasure showed in his words and demeanor,
which caused the Emperor to be displeased.
At this time,
the Emperor greatly favored and trusted eunuchs,
who were often appointed as third-rank generals.
Yáng Sīxù and Gāo Lìshì were among them.
When they traveled as imperial envoys through various prefectures,
officials served them, fearing they would not be diligent enough.
The bribes they received
were no less than a thousand strings of cash for the smallest amounts;
consequently,
half of the fields and gardens in the capital's suburbs
were in the possession of officials.
(Cānbàn means
either one-third
or half.)
Sīxù frequently led troops on campaigns;
Yáng Sīxù often campaigned in Língnán,
and all were successful.
Emperor Míng did not consider it a disgrace to have eunuchs serve as great national teachers,
and even honored and promoted them.
Jiàng,
read as jí liàng.
But Máozhòng regarded high-ranking and influential eunuchs as if they were nothing;
those of very low rank,
"shèn"
should be
"qí",
he would openly curse and insult like servants.
Wǔ,
read as wǔ gù.
Lì,
read as lì zhì.
It so happened that when Máozhòng's wife gave birth to a child,
three days later,
the Emperor ordered Lìshì to bestow upon them a generous amount of wine, food, gold, and silk,
and also granted the child a fifth-rank official position.
When Lìshì returned,
the Emperor asked:
"Is Máozhòng pleased?"
He replied:
"Máozhòng held his infant in his arms and showed it to your servant, saying: 'How can this child not be worthy of a third-rank official position!'"
The Emperor was greatly enraged and said:
"When the Wéi clan was executed,
this scoundrel was ambivalent in his heart.
(The incident is found in volume 209, first year of Jǐngyún of Ruìzōng.)
Today he dares to resent me with an infant!"
Lìshì then said:
"The Northern Gate slaves
(Wáng Máozhòng and Lǐ Shǒudé were both imperial slaves),
and Gě Fúshùn and others all came from the Wànqí (Ten Thousand Cavalry).
Zhōngzōng appointed household slaves to the Wànqí,
hence the remark.
If they are not eliminated early,
they will surely cause great trouble."
The Emperor feared that his faction might be alarmed and rebel.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Rénxū,
an imperial decree was issued.
It merely stated that Máo Zhòng was disloyal and resentful,
and demoted him to Assistant Prefect of Rángzhōu.
Fúshùn, Dìwén, Shǒudé, Jǐngyào, and Guǎngjì were all demoted to Assistant Prefects of distant prefectures.
Máo Zhòng’s four sons were all demoted to Army Supervisors in distant prefectures.
Dozens of people were implicated.
When Máo Zhòng arrived at Yǒngzhōu,
an order was sent to grant him death.
According to old records,
Yǒngzhōu
was 3,274 lǐ south of the capital.
From this time, the eunuchs’ power grew even stronger.
Gāo Lìshì was especially favored and trusted by the Emperor.
The Emperor once said:
“When Lìshì is on duty,
I sleep soundly.”
Therefore, Lìshì often stayed within the palace,
rarely going to his outer residence.
Memorials and petitions from all directions
were first presented to Lìshì,
and then submitted to the Emperor;
Lìshì would decide on minor matters himself,
his influence extending both within and outside the court.
Chéng Bóxiàn, the Grand General of Jīnwú, and Féng Shàozhèng, the Director of the Lesser Treasury, became sworn brothers with Lìshì.
When Lìshì’s mother, Lady Mài, died,
Bóxiàn and others unbound their hair and received condolences,
beating their chests and wailing,
more so than for their own relatives.
Lìshì married the daughter of Lǚ Xuánwù of Yíngzhōu,
and Xuánwù was promoted to Shaoqīng,
while his sons and nephews all became Wangfu (Prince’s Tutors).
In the Táng dynasty, the Wangfu
were officials of the third rank,
responsible for assisting, supporting, and guiding,
and correcting the princes’ mistakes.
The court and commoners vied to offer sacrifices.
From his residence to the tomb,
carriages and horses were ceaseless.
However, Lìshì was cautious and respectful,
so the Emperor continued to trust him completely.
2 On the day Xīnwèi,
Cui Lín, the Hónglúqīng, was sent as an envoy to Tǔbō.
Lín
was the son of Shénqìng.
Cuī Shénqìng had advanced in service during the reign of Empress Wǔ.
The character “Lú”
is pronounced as "líng rú" in reverse.
The character “Shǐ”
is pronounced as "shū lì" in reverse;
the same below.
Yú Xiūliè submitted a memorial,
arguing:
“The King of Dōngpíng, a close relative of Hàn,
requested the Shǐjì and various philosophical works, but Hàn still did not grant them.
When Yǔ, King of Dōngpíng, Emperor Chéng of Hàn’s brother, came to court,
he submitted a memorial requesting various philosophical works and the Grand Historian’s Records.
The Emperor
asked Grand General Wáng Fèng about this.
Fèng said:
‘The works of various philosophers sometimes go against canonical principles and criticize the sages,
or they explain ghosts and spirits and believe in strange phenomena.
The Grand Historian’s Records contain stratagems of the Warring States period, involving vertical and horizontal alliances and cunning tactics.
At the beginning of the Hàn dynasty,
the strategies and extraordinary schemes of strategists,
celestial omens and disasters,
and the topography of strategic passes,
are all unsuitable for feudal kings
and should not be given to them.’
So, they were not given.
Now, our nation’s enemy
is to be given these books,
allowing them to learn military strategies and tactics,
which will only increase their deceptions and trickery,
and is not beneficial to the Middle Kingdom.”
The matter was referred to the Zhōngshū Ménxià for deliberation.
Péi Guāngtíng and others memorialized:
“Tǔbō is ignorant, stubborn, and foolish,
long rebellious and newly submitted.
Since they have made a request,
granting them poetry and books
may gradually civilize them through our teachings,
spreading our influence far and wide.
Xiūliè only knows that books contain words of strategy and deceit,
but does not know that loyalty, trustworthiness, propriety, and righteousness
all originate from books.”
The Emperor said:
“Good!”
And so, they were given.
Xiūliè
was the great-great-grandson of Zhìníng.
Yú Zhìníng served Emperor Tàizōng and Emperor Gāozōng,
and incurred the wrath of Empress Wǔ.
3 On the day Bǐngzǐ,
the Emperor personally plowed the land beside Xīngqìng Palace,
covering a full three hundred paces.
4 In the third month,
Què Tèlè, the Left Worthy Prince of the Turks, died. A letter of condolence was granted.
Què Tèlè had killed Mòchuò’s son and installed Píjiā,
wielding great authority in his country,
hence the letter of condolence was granted.
5 On the day Bǐngshēn,
it was first ordered that temples for Tàigōng be established in both capitals and all prefectures,
with Zhāng Liáng as co-worshipper.
Famous generals of antiquity were selected
to make up the Ten Philosophers;
Zhāng Liáng was to be co-worshipped,

along with Tián Rángjū, the Grand Sīmǎ of Qí; Sūn Wǔ, the General of Wú; Wú Qǐ, the Administrator of Xīhé in Wèi; Lè Yì, the Lord of Chāngguó in Yān; Bái Qǐ, the Lord Wǔ’ān of Qín; Hán Xìn, the Marquis of Huái’yīn in Hàn; Zhūgě Liàng, the Chancellor of Shǔ; Lǐ Jìng, the Shàngshū Yòupúyè and Duke of Wèiguó; and Lǐ Jì, the Sīkōng and Duke of Yīngguó.
The character “Jiāng”
is pronounced as "jí liàng" in reverse.
The ceremony was like that for Confucius.
The worship of Wǔchéng Wáng began from this point.
Your minister Guāng says:
“To govern the world is called ‘Wén’ (civil),
and to quell chaos is called ‘Wǔ’ (martial).
Since ancient times, there has never been anyone who did not possess both of these
and yet was called a sage.
Therefore, the Yellow Emperor, Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, Yī Yǐn, and Duke of Zhōu all had achievements in military campaigns.
Although Confucius was not given a chance to serve,
he was still able to repel the Láiyí
and drive back the Fèirén.
He said:
‘When I fight, I conquer.’
When Duke Dìng of Lǔ met Qí at Jiágǔ,
Confucius acted as assistant.
Qí sent Láiyí to threaten the Duke of Lǔ with weapons.
Confucius said:
‘Soldiers, move back!
Two rulers are forming a friendly alliance,
and barbarians are disrupting it with weapons.
This is not how the ruler of Qí commands the feudal lords.’
The Marquis of Qí heard this and
immediately had them withdrawn.
And when he temporarily acted as chancellor,
he was about to dismantle the three cities.
Thereupon, the Shúsūn clan dismantled Hòu.
The Jì clan was about to dismantle Fèi.
Gōngshān Bùniǔ and Shúsūn Zhé led the Fèirén to attack Lǔ.
Zhòngní ordered Shēn Jùxū and Lè Qí to attack them.
The Fèirén retreated north,
and the people of the state pursued them,
defeating them at Gūmiè.
The two (Gōngshān Bùniǔ and Shúsūn Zhé) fled to Qí.
Thus, Fèi was dismantled.
Confucius also said:
‘When I fight, I conquer;
when I sacrifice, I receive blessings.’
Fèi,
pronounced as mì.
Confucius is worshipped by scholars
because of the ritual of honoring former sages and former teachers.
Since the beginning of humankind,
there has been no one like Confucius.
How could Tàigōng be allowed to compete with him?
In ancient times, when a campaign was launched,
the Grand Sītú was commanded to instruct soldiers in chariots and armor,
to bare their arms and legs,
and to decide archery and charioteering contests,
recording the words of the royal regulations.
‘Yǒu fā’ refers to a military commander dispatching troops,
teaching them the etiquette of riding war chariots and wearing armor.
‘Luǒ gǔ gōng’ and ‘jué shè yù’ refer to putting on clothing and exposing their arms and shins,
making them practice archery and charioteering
to decide victory and defeat
and display courage and strength.
‘Luǒ’
is pronounced as "lì guǒ" in reverse.
None of this was outside of learning.
The Lǔ Sòng chapter of the Shījīng, ‘Pànshuǐ’, says:
‘How imposing are the tiger-like ministers,
presenting captives in the Pàn palace;
their virtuous inquiries are like Gāotáo,
presenting prisoners in the Pàn palace.’
‘Shòuchéng’ refers to accepting the conclusion of judicial cases.
The aim was to prioritize propriety and righteousness over courage and strength.
A gentleman with courage but without righteousness causes chaos,
and a common person with courage but without righteousness becomes a thief;
The Analects record Confucius’s words.
What would they not do?
From Sūn Wǔ and Wú Qǐ downwards,
all prevailed by courage and strength,
and surpassed others by cunning and deceit.
How could they be counted among the ranks of sages and worthies and be called ‘Wǔ’?
To then falsely include them in the list of the Ten Philosophers,
and make them teachers for future scholars;
if Tàigōng has a spirit,
he would surely be ashamed to share sacrifices with them.”
6 In the fifth month,
on the day Rénxū,
the shrines of the Five Sacred Peaks’ True Sovereigns were first established.
Chéng Dàchāng’s Yǎnfánlù states: In the 19th year of Kāiyuán,
Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn said:
“The current shrines of the Five Sacred Peaks are for mountain and forest spirits,
not for the truly divine sovereigns.”
An imperial edict commanded that one True Sovereign shrine be established at each.
Dù Yòu said: In the 9th year of Kāiyuán,
the Tiāntái Daoist Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn said:
“The current shrines of the Five Sacred Peaks are for mountain and forest spirits,
not for the truly divine sovereigns.
The Five Sacred Peaks all have their grotto-heavens,
with Realized Persons of Shàngqīng descending to assume their posts.
Mountains, rivers, wind, and rain,
the order of yīn and yáng energies,
are all managed by them;
their crowns, robes,
attendant deities, and immortals
all have established ranks.
I request that separate places for fasting and sacrifice be established.”
The Emperor was impressed by his words,
and thus issued an edict for each of the Five Sacred Peaks to establish a True Sovereign shrine.
7 In autumn,
the ninth
month,
on the day Xīnwèi,
Tǔbō sent its minister, Lùn Shàngtuōgǔ, to have an audience
and requested to establish a mutual market at Chìlǐng;
this was granted.
8 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Bǐngshēn,
the Emperor visited the Eastern Capital.
9 Someone accused Zhāng Shěnsù, the Dūdū of Kuízhōu who was from Xièxiàn, of corruption.
Xièxiàn
belonged to Hézhōng Fǔ.
During the Yuán Wèi dynasty, Xièxiàn was divided to establish Yúxiāng Xiàn.
In the 17th year of Zhēngguàn, Xièxiàn was abolished and merged into Yúxiāng.
In the 20th year, Xièxiàn was re-established and Yúxiāng was abolished.
In the 2nd year of Tiānshòu,
Xièxiàn was again divided to establish Yúxiāng Xiàn,
making them two distinct counties.
Kuí
is pronounced suǐ.
Xiè
is pronounced huìmǎi fān.
The grand marshal Dǒng Yuánlǐ led 700 soldiers to surround Wāng,
killed the accuser,
and said to Wāng:
“If you report Shěnsù well, you will live;
otherwise, you will die.”
Just then, relief troops arrived
and attacked and beheaded Dǒng Yuánlǐ.
Wāng then reported Shěnsù for rebellion.
In the twelfth month,
Shěnsù was executed,
and his family property was confiscated.
This laid the groundwork for Shěnsù’s two sons to seek revenge later.
10 The Luò River in the imperial garden was dredged;
this work ceased after sixty days.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Yǐmǎo,
Wéi, Prince of Xìn'ān and Deputy Grand Commander of Shuòfāng Jiedu, was made Deputy Grand Commander of the Hédōng and Héběi expeditionary forces,
leading troops to attack the Xī and Qìdān;
on the day Rénshēn,
Péi Yàoqīng, the Household Minister of Revenue, was made Deputy Grand Commander.
2 In the second month,
on the day Guǐyǒu (the first day of the month),
there was a solar eclipse.
3 The Emperor recalled the loyalty and valor of General Ān Jīnzàng of the Right Swift Cavalry Guard.
Jīnzàng’s story is found in volume 205, in the 2nd year of Empress Wǔ’s Chángshòu reign.
Xiāo
is pronounced jiānyáo fān.
He was granted the title Duke of Dàiguó,
and steles were erected at the Eastern and Western Sacred Peaks
to commemorate his achievements.
Jīnzàng eventually died of old age.
4 Wéi, Prince of Xìn'ān, leading Péi Yàoqīng and Zhào Hánzhāng, the Jiedu envoy of Yōuzhōu, divided their forces to attack the Qì
dān.
Hánzhāng encountered the barbarians,
who fled at the sight of them.
Wū Chéngcǐ, the vanguard general of Pínglú, said to Hánzhāng:
“These two barbarian tribes
are formidable enemies.
Their flight yesterday
was not out of fear,
but to lure us.
We should hold our troops and observe their movements.”
Hánzhāng disagreed
and fought the barbarians at Báishān.
Báishān was where the Wūhuán lived during the Later Hàn dynasty,
located in the great wilderness outside Wǔyuǎn Pass.
Chéngcǐ separately led his troops out to their right flank,
attacked the barbarians,
and routed them.
On the day Jǐsì,
Wéi and others thoroughly defeated the Xī and Qìdān,
capturing and beheading many.
Kǎoyì states: The Tánglì records it as
“Gēngchén.”
We now follow the Shílù.
The remaining remnants went into hiding in the mountains and valleys.
Lǐ Shīsuǒgāo, the chieftain of the Xī, came to surrender with over five thousand households.
Wéi led his troops back.
Lǐ Shī was granted the title Prince of Guīyì,
appointed Dūdū of Guīyì Zhōu,
and his tribe was relocated within the borders of Yōuzhōu.
During the Zǒngzhāng reign of Gāozōng,
Guīyì Zhōu was established for surrendered Xīnnú households at Guǎngyángchéng in Liángxiāng Xiàn.
It was later abolished,
and is now re-established to settle Lǐ Shī’s tribe.
5 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Yǐhài,
a banquet was held for all officials at Shàngyáng Dōngzhōu.
Shàngyáng Gōng faced the Luò River to the south,
and the Luò River was channeled to form a central island east of the palace.
The Emperor returned in a palanquin,
with a continuous line of attendants on the road.
6 In the sixth month,
on the day Dīngchǒu,
Wéi, Prince of Xìn'ān, was promoted to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
The Emperor ordered Péi Yàoqīng to carry 200,000 bolts of silk to be distributed among the meritorious Xī officials.
Yàoqīng said to his followers:
“The barbarians are greedy.
Now, carrying valuable goods deep into their territory,
we must be prepared.”
So he ordered them to set out earlier than planned,
advancing along separate routes.
In a single day,
the distribution was completed.
The Tūjué and Shìwéi indeed dispatched troops to block the narrow passes,
intending to plunder the goods.
By the time they arrived,
Yàoqīng had already returned.
Zhào Hánzhāng was accused of embezzling huge sums,
was flogged in the imperial court,
and exiled to Rángzhōu,
where he died on the way.
7 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Xiāo Sōng reported:
“Since sacrificing to Hòutǔ,
we have repeatedly enjoyed bountiful harvests.
It would be fitting to perform a thanksgiving sacrifice upon returning to the capital.”
The Emperor agreed.
The sacrifice to Hòutǔ is mentioned in the previous volume, 11th year.
Returning to the capital
means returning to the Western Capital.
Sài
is pronounced xiāndài fān.
8 An imperial edict ordered Péi Guāngtíng and Xiāo Sōng to separately command the Left and Right Flank armies.
This refers to commanding the Left and Right Flank armies of the Southern Yá.
9 In the eighth month,
on the day Xīnwèi (the first day of the month),
there was a solar eclipse.
10 Previously,
the Emperor had ordered Zhāng Yuè and various scholars to revise and finalize the Wǔlǐ.
After Yuè's death,
Xiāo Sōng succeeded him.
Wáng Zhòngqiū, the Imperial Diarist, requested to follow the Míngqìng rituals.
Míngqìng is Xiǎnqìng;
to avoid the taboo name of Zhōngzōng,
it was changed to Míngqìng.
All sacrifices were to Hào Tiān Shàngdì;
Sōng also requested to follow the Shangyuán edict,
that when the father is alive, one should wear three years of mourning (Qīcuī) for the mother.
All these requests were granted.
According to ritual,
when the father is alive, one wears one year of mourning for the mother;
at the beginning of Kāiyuán,
Chǔ Wúliáng had indeed already raised this point.
Wéi
is pronounced yúwěi fān.
Qī
is pronounced zī.
Cuī
is pronounced cānghuí fān.
Tàizōng paired with Yú (for rain sacrifice) and the Earth God of Shénzhōu;
Ruìzōng paired with the Míngtáng.
In the ninth month,
on the day Yǐsì,
the new rites were completed,
and the Emperor approved them.
Shàng
is pronounced shípáng fān.
11 Bóhǎi King Wǔyì of the Mòhé sent his general Zhāng Wénxiū to lead sea pirates to raid Dēngzhōu,
killing the Prefect Wéi Jùn.
The Emperor ordered General Gě Fúshùn of the Right Leader Cavalry to raise troops and attack them.
Last spring,
Gě Fúshùn had been demoted for his association with Wáng Máozhòng,
but now he was again serving as an imperial guard.
This was because after Máozhòng had been executed,
Fúshùn and others were reinstated.
In the 9th year of Kāiyuán,
Wáng Jùn was demoted to Zǐzhōu,
but soon after was reinstated as a Shàngshū,
and again served in a border post;
this matter was similar.
12 On the day Rénzǐ,
Niú Xiānkè, the Jìedùshǐ of Héxī, was promoted six ranks.
Previously,
when Xiāo Sōng was in Héxī,
he entrusted military and civil administration to Xiānkè.
Xiānkè was honest and diligent,
and excelled in his position.
Sōng repeatedly recommended him,
and eventually Xiānkè replaced Sōng as Jìedùshǐ.
13 In winter,
10th month,
on the day Rénwǔ,
the Emperor departed from the Eastern Capital.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
he visited Lùzhōu.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
he arrived at the Northern Capital.
11th month,
on the day Gēngshēn,
he sacrificed to the Hòutǔ at Fēnyīn,
which was at the suggestion of Xiāo Sōng.
12th month,
on the day Xīnwèi,
he returned to the Western Capital.
14 This year,
the Jìedùshǐ of Yōuzhōu, concurrently the Cǎifǎng Chǔzhìshǐ of Héběi, was granted additional command over the sixteen prefectures of Wèi, Xiāng, Luò,
Bèi, Jì, Wèi, Shēn, Zhào, Héng, Dìng, Xíng, Dé, Bó, Dì, Yíng, Mò, as well as the Āndōng Dūhùfǔ.
Dézhōu
was the territory of Hàn's Āndé, Guǎngchuān, and Píngchāng.
A Píngyuán Commandery had been established there previously;
at this time, Dézhōu was established.
The Āndōng Dūhùfǔ
was at this time administered from Píngzhōu.
處 (chǔ),
read as chāng-lǚ.
使 (shǐ),
read as shū-lì.
恆 (héng),
read as hù-dēng.
鄚 (mò),
pronounced mò.
15 The empire had seven million eight hundred sixty-one thousand two hundred thirty-six households,
and forty-five million four hundred thirty-one thousand two hundred sixty-five mouths.
1 In spring,
1st month,
on the day Yǐsì,
Empress Sùmíng was inducted into the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
and the Yíkūn Temple was demolished.
The worship of Sùmíng in the Yíkūn Temple
is mentioned in volume 211, fourth year.
2 On the day Dīngsì,
the Emperor visited the Lìshān Hot Springs.
3 The Emperor sent Dà Ményì to Yōuzhōu to raise troops
to attack Bóhǎi King Wǔyì.
A textual variant states: the New Book's biography of Wū Chéngcǐ says:
"Kětūgān killed his king Shàogù,
and surrendered to the Tujue;
the Xī also fell into disorder.
This year,
the Xī and Qìdān invaded.
An imperial edict ordered Chéngcǐ to attack them,
defeating them at Nàlùshān."
It also says:
"Bóhǎi's Dà Wǔyì led troops to Mǎdūshān,
and plundered cities and towns.
Chéngcǐ blocked key routes,
digging trenches and piling large stones for four hundred *lǐ*,
thereby allowing the displaced people to return to their homes and rest a little,
discarding their armor to farm,
and saving annual expenditures on transport of money."
According to Hán Yù's stele inscription for Wū Zhòngyìn's temple,
narrating about Zhòngyìn's father Chéngqià, it says:
"He repeatedly defeated the Qìdān,
fought at Nàlù,
chased Kětūgān to the Bóhǎi region,
and reached Mǎdūshān,
where officials and common people fled and lost their livelihoods.
The Shàngshū led his troops to block their path,
digging trenches across plains and piling stones,
for four hundred *lǐ*,
both deep and high by three *zhàng*.
The invaders could not advance,
the people returned to their residences,
and thirty million cash were saved annually."
It is suspected that the New Book's biography of Chéngcǐ was based on this stele.
However, neither the New nor Old Imperial Annals, nor the Bóhǎi biography, mention Wǔyì's invasion reaching Mǎdūshān.
Perhaps the Hán stele's phrase
"chased Kětūgān to the Bóhǎi region,
reaching Mǎdūshān"
means he defeated and pursued Kětūgān to the Bóhǎi region,
and chased him to Mǎdūshān.
In the 21st year,
Guō Yīngjié fought Kětūgān at Dūshān.
Therefore, Dūshān was likely Qìdān territory.
The flight and displacement of officials and common people
were probably due to Kětūgān's invasion,
and it is the same incident as above;
the New Book mistook it.
However, it is unknown what other texts the rest of the New Book's biography of Chéngcǐ is based on.
On the day Gēngshēn,
Jin Sīlán,
Taiboku Yuànwàiqīng, was dispatched as an envoy to Xīnluó.
Sīlán
was a royal hostage from Xīnluó,
residing in the capital,
holding the office of Taiboku Qīng,
established as an adjunct.
A heavy snowfall of over a *zhàng* occurred,
blocking mountain roads.
More than half of the soldiers died,
and he returned without accomplishing his mission.
Wǔyì's resentment towards Ményì did not cease;
he secretly sent assassins to attack Ményì south of Tiānjīnqiáo.
Ményì did not die.
The Emperor ordered Hénán to search for and apprehend the bandit party,
and killed them all.
Hénán
refers to Hénán Fǔ.
刺 (cì),
read as qī-yì.
4 2nd month,
on the day Dīngyǒu,
Princess Jīnchéng requested the erection of a stele at Chìlǐng to mark the boundary between Táng and Tǔbō.
This was granted.
This laid the groundwork for later severing peace with Tǔbō and the destruction of the Chìlǐng stele.
5 3rd month,
on the day Yǐsì,
Shìzhōng Péi Guāngtíng passed away.
Tàicháng Bóshì Sūn Wǎn proposed:
"Guāngtíng adhered to formalities
and failed in the way of encouragement and reward.
I request his posthumous name be 'Kè'."
His son Zhěn disputed this,
and the Emperor bestowed the posthumous name Zhōngxiàn.
The Emperor asked Xiāo Sōng who could replace Guāngtíng.
Sōng was good friends with Yòusànqí Chángshì Wáng Qiū
and intended to recommend him.
However, Wáng Qiū firmly deferred to Yòuchéng Hán Xiū.
Sōng then spoke to the Emperor about Hán Xiū.
Since Xiāo Sōng was able to act on Wáng Qiū's suggestion and recommend Hán Xiū,
making it possible for them to work together harmoniously,
then Qiū's goodness was in fact Sōng's goodness.
On the day Jiǎyín,
Hán Xiū was appointed Huángmén Shìláng and Tóngpíngzhāngshì.
Hán Xiū was a stern and upright man,
not seeking personal glory or profit.
When he became prime minister,
he greatly met the expectations of the time.
Initially,
Sōng thought Hán Xiū was gentle and mild,
believing him easy to control,
and thus introduced him.
However, when they worked together,
Hán Xiū upheld justice and was unyielding,
and Sōng gradually grew to dislike him.
Sòng Jǐng sighed and said:
"I never expected Hán Xiū could be like this!"
Whenever the Emperor held banquets in the palace or hunted in the imperial gardens,
if there was any slight transgression,
he would immediately say to his attendants:
"Does Hán Xiū know?"
As soon as he finished speaking,
a remonstrance memorial would arrive.
The Emperor once looked in the mirror, silent and unhappy.
His attendants said:
"Since Hán Xiū became prime minister,
Your Majesty has become considerably thinner than before.
Why not dismiss him?"
The Emperor sighed and said:
"Although my appearance is thinner,
the empire will surely prosper.
Xiāo Sōng always reported things in a way that pleased me,
but after he retired,
I could not sleep soundly.
Hán Xiū always strenuously argued,
but after he retired,
I could sleep soundly.
I employ Hán Xiū
for the sake of the state,
not for my own sake."
There was a dwarf attendant named Huáng Ruǎn,
who was astute and quick-witted.
The emperor often leaned on him when walking,
calling him
"Human Stool."
He was greatly favored and generously rewarded.
One day, he returned late in the evening.
The emperor was surprised.
He replied:
"When I entered the palace earlier,
I met a bandit-catching official on the road who contended with me for the path.
I shoved him off his horse,
hence my lateness."
Then he descended the steps and kowtowed.
The emperor said:
"As long as there are no memorials from outside,
you have nothing to worry about."
A moment later,
the Jīngzhào submitted a report about the incident.
The emperor immediately shouted at Huáng Ruǎn to be cast out
and handed him over to the authorities to be beaten to death.
6 In the intercalary month,
on the Guǐyǒu day,
Guō Yīngjié, Deputy Commander-in-Chief of Yōuzhōu Circuit, fought the Khitan at Dūshān
and was defeated and died.
At that time, the Jìedù
Xuē Chǔyù had sent Yīngjié with ten thousand elite cavalry and surrendered Xī to attack the Khitan,
stationing them outside Yúguān.
"Yú"
should be written as
"Yú."
This Yúguān is between Yíng and Píng,
what the ancients called the strategic pass of Línyú.
The Hànshū Yīnyì says: "Yú"

There was also a Yúguān in the territory of Táng's Shèngzhōu.
In the two passes of Suí's Yúlín Commandery,
there were
"Yú"
and
"Yú"
with different characters.
Historians' transcription has been confused and indistinct,
thus a detailed distinction is made here.
Jiāng [將],
read as lìang fān.
Qí [騎],
read as qí jì fān.
Xiáng [降],
read as hù jiāng fān;
the same below.
The Xī held both ends,
scattering and fleeing to secure positions.
The Táng troops were at a disadvantage,
and Yīngjié died in battle.
The remaining six thousand-plus men still fought desperately,
but when the barbarians showed them Yīngjié's head,
they still did not surrender
and were all killed by the barbarians.
Chǔyù
was Nà's younger brother.
7 In summer,
in the sixth month,
on the Guǐhài day,
an edict was issued:
"From now on, officials chosen for their talent, achievements, and conduct
shall be entrusted to the Lìbù to be promoted and employed as needed;
those outside the official ranks who are nominated for service no longer need to be introduced through the Ménxià."
Although this edict existed,
the authorities, finding it convenient to adhere to the established hierarchy,
still followed it.
Historians spoke of Péi Guāngtíng's flawed system,
which later generations continued to follow,
unable to reform it.
There were seventeen thousand six hundred and eighty-six officials from the Three Mentors downwards.
According to Táng regulations,
Grand Tutor, Grand Preceptor, and Grand Guardian were the Three Mentors.
And the paths to officialdom were numerous,

8 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the Yǐchǒu first day,

Cǐ as Yì Wáng,
Cuǐ as Chén Wáng,
Chéng as Fēng Wáng,

Cóng as Liáng
Wáng,

10For a long time, there had been continuous rain in Guānzhōng, and grain was expensive.
The emperor was about to travel to the Eastern Capital [Dōngdū].
He summoned the Jīngzhào Yǐn, Péi Yàoqīng, to consult with him.
Péi Yàoqīng replied:
"Guānzhōng is where the imperial enterprise arose,
and it should remain so for a hundred generations;
but because the land is narrow and grain is scarce,
the imperial retinue sometimes travels to the Eastern Capital to relieve the burden.
I have heard that during the Zhēngguān and Yǒnghuī eras,
the official stipends were not large,
and each year twenty to thirty thousand *shí* of grain were transported from Guāndōng,
which was sufficient for sustenance,
allowing the imperial retinue to live in peace.
Now, expenditures have greatly expanded,
and transport volume is several times what it was before,
yet it is still insufficient,
thus causing Your Majesty to frequently brave cold and heat to care for the people of the west.
Now, if all the Sīnóng's rental grain were transported to the Eastern Capital,
and from there transport by canal,
gradually filling Guānzhōng,
if Guānzhōng had several years' worth of reserves,
then there would be no worries about floods or droughts.
Moreover, the people of Wú are not accustomed to river transport,
and stops are made everywhere,
and after a long time,
secret theft occurs.
I request to establish a granary at the river mouth.
The river mouth [Hékǒu]
is the mouth where the Biànshuǐ reaches the Yellow River.
The Hékǒu Granary was called Wǔláo Granary.
Officials should hire carriers themselves to transport goods in stages into the Yellow River and Luò River.
Furthermore, establish one granary each to the east and west of Sānmén.
Yǔ carved the Dǐzhù,
and two rocks appeared in the water like pillars,
hence it was called Dǐzhù.
When the Yellow River water reached this point,
it divided into three branches flowing between them,
hence it was also called Sānmén.
At that time, Jíjīn Granary was established to the east of Sānmén,
and Yán Granary to the west.
If the water was dangerous, they would stop;
if the water was clear, they would proceed.
Or they would open mountain roads,
transporting by cart,
at that time, an eighteen-li mountain road was carved out alongside Sānmén for land transport,
to avoid the danger of Dǐzhù.
This would save enormous expenses.
Along the banks of the Yellow River and the Wèi River,
there are old Hàn and Suí granaries,
and repairing them would not be difficult."
The emperor deeply approved of his words.
11In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Gēngxū day,
the emperor visited the Lìshān Hot Springs;
on the Jǐwèi day,
he returned to the palace.
12On the Wùzǐ day,
Left Chancellor Sòng Jǐng retired [zhìshì]
and returned to the Eastern Capital.
13Hán Xiū frequently argued with Xiāo Sōng before the emperor,
openly pointing out Sōng's shortcomings,
which displeased the emperor considerably.
Sōng then requested to resign,
and the emperor said:
"I am not yet tired of you;
why are you leaving in such a hurry?"
He replied:
"I have received profound grace,
and as chancellor, I have been remiss in my duties,
having reached the pinnacle of wealth and honor.
While Your Majesty is not yet tired of me,
I can respectfully withdraw;
if Your Majesty were already tired of me,
I would not even be able to save my head,
how could I satisfy myself!"
Then he shed tears.
Xiāo Sōng adopted a pleading posture,
both to preserve his own favor and emoluments,
and also to undermine Hán Xiū.
The emperor said:
"You may go for now;
I will consider it slowly."
On the Dīngsì day,
Sōng was dismissed as Left Chancellor,
and Xiū was dismissed as Minister of Works [Gōngbù Shàngshū].
Péi Yàoqīng, the Jīngzhào Yǐn, was made Yellow Gate Attendant [Huángmén Shìláng],
and former Vice Director of the Central Secretariat [Zhōngshū Shìláng] Zhāng Jiǔlíng, who was then observing mourning for his mother,
was reinstated as Vice Director of the Central Secretariat,
both concurrently serving as Grand Councillor [Tóng Píngzhāngshì].
14 That year,
the empire was divided into Jīngjī, Dūjī, Guānnèi, Hénán, Hédōng, Héběi, Lǒngyòu, Shānnán Dōngdào, Shānnán Xīdào, Jiànnán, Huáinán, Jiāngnán Dōngdào, Jiāngnán Xīdào, Qiánzhōng, and Língnán,
totaling fifteen circuits.
Each was assigned a Cǎifǎngshǐ [Investigator],
to investigate illegal activities according to six principles.
The two Jī circuits were overseen by a Zhōngchéng,
while all others were led by selected worthy Cìshǐ [Prefects].
The Jīngjī Cǎifǎngshǐ was based within the western capital (Xījīng),
and the Dūjī Cǎifǎngshǐ was based in the eastern capital (Dōngdū).
The Guānnèi Cǎifǎngshǐ was held by a court official (Jīngguān).
The Hénán Cǎifǎngshǐ was based in Biànzhōu,
Hédōng in Púzhōu,
Héběi in Wèizhōu,
Lǒngyòu in Shànzhōu,
Shānnán Dōngdào in Xiāngzhōu,
Shānnán Xīdào in Liángzhōu,
Huáinán in Yángzhōu,
Jiāngnán Dōngdào in Sūzhōu,
Jiāngnán Xīdào in Hóngzhōu,
Qiánzhōng in Qiánzhōu,
Jiànnán in Yìzhōu,
and Língnán in Guǎngzhōu.
Later, there were instances where border command Jìdù [military commissioners] also served as Cǎifǎngshǐ,
in which case the Guānzhōng Circuit was certainly not limited to court officials,
and the administrative seats of the various circuit Cǎifǎngshǐ also could not be strictly fixed to a specific location.
Thus, there was no abolition or change to the office.
Only major reforms to old regulations
required reporting for approval;
all other matters could be handled at convenience,
acting first and reporting later.
15 Yáng Chónglǐ, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàifù Qīng),
was the son of Yáng Zhèngdào.
Yáng Zhèngdào was
the grandson of Emperor Yáng of Suí [Dynasty],
and the son of Qí Wáng Jiǎn.
No one who served as Tàifù before or after him could equal him.
At that time, peace had prevailed for a long time,
and wealth and goods were piled high like mountains.
Anything that passed through Minister Yáng’s hands
was without exception exquisite and beautiful.
Each year, through auditing and simplification,
several million strings of cash were saved.
That year,
he retired as Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū),
being over ninety years old.
The Emperor asked the Chancellors:
“Among Chónglǐ’s sons,
who can succeed his father?”
They replied:
“Chónglǐ has three sons:
Shènyú, Shènjǐn, and Shènmíng.
All are honest, diligent, and talented,
but Shènjǐn is superior.”
The Emperor then promoted Shènjǐn from Magistrate of Rǔyáng to Censor (Jiānchá Yùshǐ),
in charge of the receipts and disbursements of the Tàifù.
Shènmíng was appointed acting Censor (shè Jiānchá Yùshǐ),
in charge of the receipts and disbursements of the Hánjiā Granary.
The Hánjiā Granary was located in Dōngdū.
Jiān,
pronounced like ‘gōng hán fān’.
The Emperor was very pleased with this.
Shènjǐn proposed that for silk and cloth submitted by the various prefectures that were stained, soiled, or torn,
the prefectures concerned should be ordered to pay replacement money for the estimated value,
and these funds be used to purchase light goods.
From then on, taxes and levies began to become burdensome.

Kāiyuán twenty-second year
