1 Spring,
first month.
On the day Jǐsì,
the Emperor departed Xījīng.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
he arrived at Dōngdū.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng came from Sháozhōu to have an audience,
requesting to complete his mourning period;
this was not permitted.
2 Second month.
On the day Rén'yín,
Qínzhōu experienced successive earthquakes,
destroying almost all public and private buildings.
More than four thousand officials and common people were crushed to death.
The Emperor ordered Left Chancellor Xiāo Sōng to provide relief.
3 The geomancer Zhāng Guǒ claimed to possess immortal arts,
deceiving people by saying that he served as Attendant (Shìzhōng) during the time of Yáo,
and was now several thousand years old.
He frequently traveled in the Hénɡshān mountains,
which at that time belonged to the jurisdiction of Hénɡyáng County, Dìngzhōu.
Kuáng,
pronounced like ‘jū kuàng fān’.
Hénɡ,
pronounced like ‘hù dēng fān’.
He was summoned repeatedly but did not come.
Wéi Jì, the Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu, recommended him.
The Emperor sent Xú Jiào, Secretary of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén), with an imperial letter (Xǐshū) to invite him.
On the day Gēngyín,
he arrived at Dōngdū,
entering the palace in a palanquin.
He was treated with great favor and courtesy.
4 Zhāng Jiǔlíng requested that private coin casting not be prohibited.
Third month.
On the day Gēngchén,
an imperial edict ordered all officials to discuss the matter.
Péi Yàoqīng and others all said:
“Once this door is opened,
we fear that common people will abandon agriculture for profit,
and the proliferation of counterfeit and inferior coins will worsen.”
Since Empress Wǔ’s reign,
there had been many bad coins among the populace,
which the government could not prohibit.
“If copper is taxed for labor in lieu of service,
then official minting can succeed.
If costs are calculated and wages estimated,
then private casting will not be profitable.
This is easy and sustainable,
simple and difficult to falsify.
Moreover, as for money,
its value lies in its circulation,
profit is not in its quantity.
Why wait for private casting to have enough for use!”
Liú Zhì, Recording Officer (Lùshì Cānjūn) of the Right Palace Guard (Yòu Jiānmén), said:
The sixteen guards of the Táng dynasty all had Lùshì Cānjūn,
who held a rank of Zheng Bā Pǐn Xià (Junior Eighth Rank, Lower Grade),
and were in charge of receiving matters from various offices and external affairs of the five directorates,
auditing and copying records,
and issuing paper and pens.
Jiān,
pronounced like ‘gǔ hán fān’.
“If people are wealthy, they cannot be encouraged by rewards;
if they are poor, they cannot be restrained by intimidation.
If private casting is permitted,
the poor will certainly be unable to do it.
I fear that the poor will become poorer and be exploited by the rich,
and the rich will become richer and indulge their desires.
During the reign of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
Wú Wáng Bì's wealth was comparable to that of the Son of Heaven,
which was caused by his minting of coins.”
This matter is recorded in Chapter 14, Emperor Wén of Hàn, fifth year.
Bì,
pronounced like ‘pǐ bèi fān’.
Liè,
pronounced like ‘lì chuò fān’.
Zhì
was the son of Zǐxuán.
Liú Zǐxuán

fourth month.
On the day Rénchén,
Xìn'ān Wáng Yī, the Jìdùshǐ of Shuòfāng, was additionally appointed as Cǎifǎng Chǔzhìshǐ of Guānnèi Dào,
and given command over twelve more prefectures, including Jīng and Yuán.
6 Lìbù Shìláng Lǐ Línfǔ,
was obsequious and full of cunning schemes.
He deeply cultivated relationships with eunuchs and the imperial family,
observing the emperor's every move,
leaving nothing unknown to him.
Because of this, whenever he had an audience,
his responses always pleased the emperor,
who was delighted with him.
At that time, Wǔ Huì's favor eclipsed the entire harem,
and she gave birth to Shòu Wáng Qīng,
whom none of the other princes could rival,
and the crown prince gradually fell out of favor.
Lǐ Línfǔ then used a eunuch to speak to Wǔ Huì,
expressing his desire to fully protect Shòu Wáng;
Wǔ Huì was grateful to him,
secretly assisting him from within,
and thus he was promoted to Huángmén Shìláng.
The Examination of Differences states: The old tradition says:
"Initially,
Shìzhōng Péi Guāngtíng's wife, a daughter of Wǔ Sānsī,
was cunning and resourceful,
and had a private relationship with Lǐ Línfǔ.

Xuánzōng ordered Zhōngshū Lìng Xiāo Sōng to choose a chancellor;

Xiāo Sōng presented Yòuchéng Hán Xiū.
Xuánzōng approved of him,
and ordered a decree to be drafted.
Gāo Lìshì immediately leaked the information to Lady Wǔ,
who then instructed Lǐ Línfǔ to inform Hán Xiū.
After Hán Xiū became chancellor,
he was very grateful to Lǐ Línfǔ and
was at odds with Xiāo Sōng.
He then recommended Lǐ Línfǔ as capable of being chancellor,
and Wǔ Huì secretly assisted him.
Consequently, Lǐ Línfǔ was appointed Huángmén Shìláng,
and Xuánzōng's favor and trust in him deepened. "
However, Péi Guāngtíng's wife
was merely a widow.
How could she dare to immediately recommend her private lover to replace her husband as chancellor!
Hán Xiū was upright,
and even if he received early notice from Lǐ Línfǔ,
he would certainly not have recommended him as chancellor.
Therefore, this account is not adopted here.
On the day Wùzǐ,
Péi Yàoqīng was appointed Shìzhōng,
Zhāng Jiǔlíng as Zhōngshū Lìng,
and Lǐ Línfǔ as Lǐbù Shàngshū and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
This laid the groundwork for Lǐ Línfǔ gaining power and the deposition of the Crown Prince.
Yán Zhēnqīng's memorial states:
"After Tiānbǎo,

Lǐ Línfǔ would anticipate the emperor's wishes and make proposals,
making Xuánzōng surprised and delighted, as if Lǐ Línfǔ were divine.
With this power,
his favor and trust grew daily. "
7 The emperor planted wheat in the imperial park,
and led the crown prince and others to personally weed it.
He said:
"This is for offering to the ancestral temples,
so I dared not but do it myself.
Moreover, I want to make you all know the hardships of farming. "
He also distributed it widely to his attending officials, saying:
"Recently, I sent people to inspect the crops in the fields,
but they often did not report the truth,
so I planted it myself to observe. "
In the matter of planting and cultivation,
Heaven may not provide timely rain or sunshine,
and the earth may not have equal fertility or barrenness,
and human effort may also be insufficient,
thus the harvest varies in abundance.
If the ruler does not interfere with the farming season,
and people can exert their full effort,
then the land will have no wasted resources.
Why must one wait until one has planted oneself to observe the truth?

10 The emperor appointed Péi Yàoqīng as Jiānghuái, Hénán Zhuǎnyùnshǐ.

which originated from Buddhism.
*Gài*,
read *gǔ tài*.
In the 1st year, spring,
the first month,
Lǐ Guòzhé (李過折), the Qìdān (契丹) military commander, came to present the victory report.
An imperial edict appointed Guòzhé (過折) as Prince of Běipíng (北平),
and Acting Governor-General of Sōngmòzhōu (松漠州).
*Kǎoyì* states: The *Shílù* (實錄) says
"concurrently Vice-Commissioner of the Yōuzhōu (幽州) Jìedùshǐ (節度使)".
The old *Chuán* (傳) says
"awarded *tèjìn* (特進) and Acting Governor-General of Sōngmòzhōu (松漠州)".
Considering that although Guòzhé (過折) had merit,
the Táng (唐) would not necessarily have allowed him to be the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Yōuzhōu (幽州).
We now follow the old *Chuán* (傳).
On the *yǐhài* day,
the Emperor personally tilled the sacrificial field,
and stopped after nine pushes.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) states: In this year, when the Emperor personally tilled,
the officials presented the ceremonial regulations: the Son of Heaven pushed three times,
the high ministers pushed nine times,
and commoners tilled to the end of the furrow.
The Emperor wished to emphasize the tilling of the sacrificial field,
so he advanced to plow more than fifty paces,
stopping only at the end of the ridge.
*Tuī*,
read *tǔ léi*.
A general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire,
and the imperial capital feasted for three days.
"Imperial capital"
refers to the Eastern Capital, Luòyáng (洛陽).
*Pú*,
pronounced *pú*.
The Emperor attended a feast at Wǔfènglóu (五鳳樓),
where the spectators were boisterous and crowded.
Music could not be performed,
and the Jīnwǔ (金吾) guards' white staves fell like rain,
but they could not control the crowd.
The Emperor was troubled by this.
Gāo Lìshì (高力士) reported that Yán Ānzhī (嚴安之), Assistant Magistrate of Hénán (河南), was strict in governance.
A Táng (唐) Assistant Magistrate of an Imperial Prefecture was of the seventh rank, lower grade.
*Lǐ* (理)
means governance.
The Táng (唐) avoided the character
*zhì* (治),
and changed it to
He requested to send him to control the situation.
The Emperor agreed.
When Ānzhī (安之) arrived,
he drew a line on the ground around the area with his tablet, saying:
"Those who transgress this line shall die!"
Thereafter, for the entire three days,
people pointed to his line to warn each other,
and no one dared to violate it.
At that time, governors and county magistrates from within three hundred *lǐ* were ordered to lead their respective musicians to gather beneath the tower,
and compete for superiority.
The Governor of Huáizhōu (懷州) transported hundreds of musicians in carriages,
all dressed in embroidered robes.
The oxen pulling the carriages were all shaped like tigers, leopards, rhinoceroses, and elephants.
The *Shī Dà Dōng* (詩大東) says: "Look at that Niu (牽牛) (Altair),
it does not draw a cart."
The commentary says: *Fú* (服)
refers to a female animal used for pulling.
*Xiāng* (箱)
refers to the carriage box of a large cart.
The commentary further says: The space between the two shafts is called *xiāng* (箱).
The *Fǔ Tián* (甫田) says: "Then seek ten thousand *xiāng* (箱)."
The *Shū Chuán* (書傳) says: "Length sufficient to fill a *xiāng* (箱)."
This refers to the place inside a carriage where things are stored.
Qiū Shì (丘氏) says: *Fú xiāng* (服箱)
is like saying "to drive a cart."
*Yī*,
read *yú jì*.
They sang in unison the song "Yú Wěi" (于蒍).
Lǔshān (魯山),
ancient Lǔ County,
was the place to which Liú Lěi (劉累), the dragon-breeder, migrated during the time of Kǒngjiǎ (孔甲) in the Xià (夏) dynasty.
During the Hàn (漢) dynasty, it was Lǔyáng County,
part of Nányáng Commandery.
Later, during the Wèi (魏) dynasty, Lǔyáng Commandery was established.
During the Suí (隋) dynasty, it reverted to Lǔ County,
part of Rǔzhōu (汝州).
During the Táng (唐) dynasty, it was Lǔshān County,
named because
the county had Lǔshān (魯山) mountain.
Thus it was named.
"Yú Wěi" (于蒍)
was a song composed by Déxiù (德秀).
*Wěi*,
read *wéi wěi*.
*Kǎoyì* states: *Mínghuáng Zá Lù* (明皇雜錄) writes
"Yú Wěi" (于蒍),
while the new *Chuán* (傳) writes
"Yú Wěi Yú" (于蒍于).
Its meaning is not detailed.
We now follow *Zá Lù* (雜錄).
"The people of Huáizhōu (懷州),
are they in utter misery?"
The Governor was immediately appointed a *sǎnguān* (散官).
A *sǎnguān* (散官)
had no actual duties.
*Sǎn*,
read *sū hàn*.
All scholars and officials admired his noble conduct.
In the 2nd month, the Emperor praised Zhāng Shǒuguī's (張守珪) achievements
and wanted to make him a chancellor.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng (張九齡) remonstrated, saying:
"The chancellor (zǎixiàng 宰相) is one who acts on behalf of Heaven to govern all things;
it is not an office for rewarding merits."
The Emperor said:
"If I give him the title but do not allow him to perform the duties,
would that be permissible?"
He replied:
"No, it would not.
Titles and authority cannot be bestowed upon others;
these are the sovereign's exclusive prerogatives."
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* (左傳) records Confucius's words.
"Your Majesty should consider if you make him chancellor;
what if he then completely eliminates the Xī (奚) and Jué (厥)?"
Xī (奚) and Jué (厥)
refer to the Xī (奚) and Tūjué (突厥).
*Juē*,
read *jiǔ wù*.
The Emperor then stopped (the discussion).
In the second month,
Shǒuguī (守珪) went to the Eastern Capital to present the victory report.
He was appointed General-in-Chief of the Right Yǔlín (羽林),
concurrently Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
His two sons were granted official posts,
and he received very generous rewards.
3 In the beginning,
the Palace Censor, Yáng Wāng (楊汪), had already killed Zhāng Shěnsù (張審素).
The details of this matter can be found in the nineteenth year of the previous volume.
Zhāng Shěnsù’s two sons, Huáng (瑝) and Xiù (琇), were both young,
and were exiled to the Lingbiao (嶺表) region as punishment.
They soon escaped and returned,
plotting to seize an opportunity to avenge their father.
In the third month,
on the Dīngmǎo (丁卯) day,
they personally killed Wànqǐng (萬頃) in the capital city,
tying a memorial to an axe,
stating the injustice suffered by their father.
They intended to go beyond the Jiāng (江) region to kill those who had conspired with Wànqǐng (萬頃) to frame their father.
When they reached the Sìshuǐ (汜水),
they were apprehended by the authorities.
Many debaters argued that the two sons' father had died unjustly,
and that as young men, their filial devotion and ferocity enabled them to avenge their father,
and therefore they ought to be treated with compassion and pardoned.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng (張九齡) also wished to spare their lives.
Péi Yàoqīng (裴耀卿) and Lǐ Línfǔ (李林甫) believed that if this were done,
it would undermine the national law.
The emperor also agreed,
saying to Jiǔlíng (九齡):
"The feelings of a filial son
mean that he would not hesitate to die for righteousness.
However, to pardon someone for murder,
this path cannot be opened."
He then issued an imperial edict which stated:
"The state establishes laws
with the aim of stopping killing.
If each were to follow their own filial aspirations,
who would not be someone acting out of filial devotion!
Turning to revenge again and again,
what would be the limit to it!
Gāoyáo (咎繇) acted as a judge,
and the law must be enforced.
Even Zēngshēn (曾參) killing someone
would not be forgivable.
They should be handed over to Hénán Fǔ (河南府) to be beaten to death."
The officials and common people all pitied them,
composing elegies for them,
which they posted on the crossroads.
The city residents collected money to bury them on Mount Běimáng (北邙),
fearing that Wànqǐng’s (萬頃) family might exhume them.
Therefore, several decoy tombs were made.
Many tombs were created to mislead,
so that no one would know the true location of their burial.
4 In the early Táng (唐) dynasty,
the actual enfeoffment of princesses was limited to three hundred households.
During the reign of Zhōngzōng (中宗), Princess Tàipíng (太平公主) reached five thousand households,
generally limited to seven able-bodied men (per household for tax purposes).
Since the Kàiyuán (開元) era,
imperial sisters were limited to one thousand households,
and imperial daughters to half of that,
all limited to three able-bodied men.
All imperial sons-in-law were appointed to supernumerary third-rank official positions,
but were not entrusted with actual duties.
The income from the princesses' fiefs was so little
that they could not even afford proper carriages and attire.
Some attendants remarked that it was too meager.
The emperor said:
"The rents and taxes of the common people
are not my personal possessions.
Warriors exert their utmost strength and face death,
their rewards do not exceed bolts of silk;
what merit do women have
to enjoy so many households?
Furthermore, I wish to make them aware of frugality."
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Princess Xiányí (咸宜公主) was about to be married.
Princess Xiányí (咸宜公主) was married to Yáng Huí (楊洄).
The princess
was the daughter of Wǔ Huì (武惠).
Thereupon, all princesses had their households increased to one thousand.
5 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Wùshēn (戊申) day,
the Tūqíshī (突騎施) raided Běitíng (北庭) and Ānxī Bōhuàn Chéng (安西撥換城).
6 In the intercalary month,
on the Rénwǔ (壬午) day, the new moon,
there was a solar eclipse.
The `Kǎoyì` (考異) states: The old records say
"eleventh month,
Rénshēn (壬申) day, new moon."
According to the `Chánglì` (長曆),
the new moon of the eleventh month was on a Rénzǐ (壬子) day.
We now follow the `Shílù` (實錄) and `Tánglì` (唐曆).
7 In the twelfth month,
on the Yǐhài (乙亥) day,
the daughter of Yáng Xuányǎn (楊玄琰), the former Registrar of Shǔzhōu (蜀州), was enfeoffed as the consort of Shòuwáng (壽王).
She was taken into the emperor's harem to lay the groundwork for national disorder.
The `Kǎoyì` (考異) states: The `Shílù` (實錄) records the enfeoffment text,
saying
"the eldest daughter of Xuánjiǎo (玄璬)."
According to Chén Hóng's (陳鴻) `Chánghèn Gē Chuán` (長恨歌傳), it says:
"An imperial edict ordered Gāo Lìshì (高力士) to secretly search the outer palace,
and he found Yáng Xuányǎn's (楊玄琰) daughter at Shòuwáng's (壽王) residence."
The old `Yáng Guì Zhuàn` (楊貴傳) states:
"Xuányǎn's (玄琰) daughter was orphaned early,
and was raised by her paternal uncle Xuánjiǎo (玄璬)."
It also states:
"Someone reported that Xuányǎn's (玄琰) daughter was unrivaled in beauty in her generation
and ought to be summoned for an audience.
At the time, she wore the robes of a Daoist priestess,
and was called Tàizhēn (太真)."
The new biography states:
"She was initially for Shòuwáng (壽王), etc.,
then summoned into the forbidden palace,
which was the emperor's own idea.
She was granted a position as a female official,
named Tàizhēn (太真),
and Shòuwáng (壽王) was married to the daughter of Wéi Zhāoxùn (韋昭訓) instead,
and Tàizhēn (太真) gained favor."
The old histories probably concealed this.
She was the great-granddaughter of Wāng (汪).
Yáng Wāng (楊汪) is mentioned in volume 183, in the twelfth year of Suí Yángdì's (隋煬帝) Dàyè (大業) era.
8 In this year,
the Khitan (契丹) king Guòzhé (過折) was killed by his minister Nèilǐ (涅禮),
along with his sons.
One son, Lìgān (剌乾), escaped by fleeing to Āndōng (安東).
Nèilǐ (涅禮) reported that
Guòzhé (過折) had employed cruel and tyrannical punishments,
causing widespread unrest,
which was why he killed him.
The emperor pardoned his crime,
and appointed Nèilǐ (涅禮) as the Dūdū (都督) of Sōngmò (松漠),
and also sent him a letter of reprimand saying:
"Your barbarian laws often show no righteousness towards your sovereign.
It has been this way since ancient times,
and I am aware of it.
However, Guòzhé (過折) was your king.
To kill him as soon as he commits an offense,
is it not difficult to be a king like this?
I just fear that if you become king,
later generations will do the same.
Always unable to protect oneself,
who would wish to be king!
You should also consider future consequences,
how can you merely seek immediate gratification!"
The Turks soon led troops eastward to invade the Xī (奚) and Khitan (契丹),
and Nèilǐ (涅禮) and Xī (奚) King Lǐ Guīguó (李歸國) defeated them.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the Gēngyín (庚寅) day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Throughout the empire, runaway households
are permitted to surrender by the end of this year.
Those with existing property shall be returned to their original residence,
while those without shall await further instructions.
If they do not surrender within the deadline,
special envoys will be dispatched to search for them,
and they will be dispersed and assigned to various armies."
2 Gài Jiāyùn (蓋嘉運), the Grand Protector of Běitíng (北庭), attacked the Tūqíshī (突騎施)
and greatly defeated them.
3 In the second month,
on the Jiǎyín (甲寅) day,
newly appointed county magistrates were entertained in the imperial court.
The emperor composed an essay, "New Admonitions for Magistrates and Chiefs,"
which he bestowed upon all county magistrates in the empire.

the names of the imperial princes were changed:

Tán (潭) to Cóng (琮),
Jùn (浚) to Yú (璵),

Miǎn (沔) to Lǐ (理),

5 The old system dictated that
the Examiner of Merit, Yuánwàiláng (員外郎), was in charge of testing candidates for imperial examinations.
There was a scholar-official, Lǐ Quán (李權),
who insulted the Yuánwàiláng (員外郎) Lǐ Áng (李昂).
Debaters argued that the Yuánwàiláng’s (員外郎) rank was too low
to command the respect of the masses.
In the third month,
on the Rénchén (壬辰) day,
an imperial edict stipulated that from now on, the Minister of Rites, Shǐláng (侍郎), would be entrusted with testing candidates for imperial examinations.

6 Zhāng Shǒuguī sent Pínglú Tǎojī Shǐ (Pacification and Suppression Commissioner of Pínglú), Zuǒ Xiāowèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Valiant Guard) Ān Lùshān, to suppress the rebellious Xī and Qìdān tribes.
Lùshān, presuming on his bravery, advanced rashly,
and was defeated by the barbarians.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the Xīnhài day,
Shǒuguī submitted a memorial requesting his execution.
As Lùshān was about to be executed, he cried out:
“Does Dàfū (Grandee) not wish to destroy the Xī and Qìdān?
Why then kill Lùshān!”
Shǒuguī also cherished his valor and bravery,
so he instead had him arrested and sent to the capital.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng appended a comment, saying:
“In the past, Ráng Jū executed Zhuāng Jiǎ.
The Shǐjì (Records of the Grand Historian) states: Qí Jǐnggōng sent Sīmǎ Ráng Jū to be a general.
Ráng Jū said:
‘I wish to have one of Your Lordship’s favored ministers supervise the army.’
Jǐnggōng sent Zhuāng Jiǎ.
Jiǎ was always arrogant and esteemed.
Ráng Jū made an appointment with him
to meet at the army gate at noon.
He only arrived at dusk.
Ráng Jū, because Jiǎ was late,
executed him
to command the three armies.
‘Pī’,
pronounced pǐ-mí,
means to judge.
People nowadays call it pīpàn (critique).
Sūn Wǔ presented his art of war to King Hélǘ of Wú.
The King of Wú said:
‘Can you try drilling a small number of troops with women?’
He replied:
‘Yes.’
Thereupon, he brought out one hundred and eighty palace beauties,
divided them into two teams,
and made the King’s two favorite concubines each a team leader,
all holding halberds.
After the commands were issued,
repeatedly and clearly stated,
he then beat the drum.
The women on the right burst into laughter.
Master Sūn said:
‘If commands are not followed,
and orders are not clearly understood,
it is the general’s fault.’
He again repeatedly and clearly stated the orders and beat the drum,
but the women on the left again burst into laughter.
Master Sūn executed the left and right team leaders to demonstrate,
used their seconds in command as team leaders, and beat the drum again.
The women, whether kneeling or standing, front or back, left or right, all conformed to the established rules and measures.
Thereupon, the King of Wú knew that Master Sūn was capable in using troops,
and made him a general.
Lùshān should not be spared death.”
The Emperor, cherishing his talent,
issued an imperial order to dismiss him from office,
allowing him to lead as a commoner.
Jiǔlíng strongly argued,
saying:
“Lùshān lost control and suffered a defeat;
by law, he must be executed.
Moreover, I observe that his appearance shows signs of rebellion;
if he is not killed, he will certainly become a future calamity.”
The Emperor said:
“You must not, like Wáng Yíbǔ recognizing Shí Lè,
wrongfully harm a loyal and good man.”
When Shí Lè of Jìn was fourteen,
he followed people from his village to trade in Luòyáng,
and leaned and whistled at the Shangdong Gate.
Wáng Yǎn saw him and found him extraordinary,
and turning to his attendants, said:
“That Húchú (barbarian youth) just now,
I observed that his voice and gaze reveal an extraordinary ambition;
I fear he will cause trouble for the world.”
He hurriedly sent someone to apprehend him,
but Lè had already left.
Kǎoyì (Investigation of Differences) states: Xuánzōng Shílù (Veritable Records of Emperor Xuánzōng) says:
“In the fourth month,
on the Xīnhài day,
Zhāng Shǒuguī memorialized that Lùshān, in commanding the army, lost control,
and diminished military prestige,
requesting that he be executed according to military law.
This was permitted.
As Lùshān was about to be executed, he raised his voice and said: ‘The two barbarian tribes are not yet pacified.
How can you bear to kill a brave man?
Is this for Dàfū’s plan?’
Shǒuguī, because Lùshān had once achieved victory in capturing enemies alive,
hearing his words,
then spared him,
and reported it.”
Sùzōng Shílù (Veritable Records of Emperor Sùzōng) says:
“Lùshān was a Yáláng (broker) in the border markets.
His theft of sheep was discovered.
Shǒuguī was enraged,
pursued and captured him,
and intended to beat him to death.
Lùshān cried out loudly: ‘Dàfū does not wish to destroy the Xī and Qìdān, the two barbarian tribes,
but instead kills a brave man!’
Shǒuguī admired his appearance,
and was impressed by his words,
so he released him.”
Yáo Rǔnéng’s work, Lùshān Shìjì (Record of Lùshān’s Deeds),
describes the sheep theft incident similarly to the Sùzōng Shílù.
It also says:
“In the twenty-first year,
Shǒuguī ordered Lùshān to report on affairs.
Zhōngshū Lìng (Minister of the Central Secretariat) Zhāng Jiǔlíng saw him,
and said to Shìzhōng (Grand Councillor) Péi Guāngtíng: ‘This Hu (barbarian) will bring chaos to Yōuzhōu.’”
It also says:
“In the twenty-fourth year,
Lùshān was a Pínglú general,
and suffered a defeat while suppressing the Xī and Qìdān.
Shǒuguī memorialized requesting his execution.
Jiǔlíng appended a comment, saying: ‘When Ráng Jū went to war,
he certainly executed Zhuāng Jiǎ.
When Sūn Wǔ issued orders,
he also executed palace women.
If Shǒuguī’s military orders are to be enforced,
Lùshān should not be spared death.’
Xuánzōng cherished his bravery and sharpness,
and merely ordered his dismissal from office,
allowing him to serve as a commoner.
Jiǔlíng insisted on his execution,
but Xuánzōng said: ‘Are you, Minister, like Wáng Yíbǔ recognizing Shí Lè,
making an arbitrary judgment that Lùshān will be difficult to control?’
In the end, he did not execute him.”
Sūn Qiáo’s work, Xīzhāi Lù (Record of the Western Study),
its preface says:
“Why did Zhāng Shǒuguī cause Ān Lùshān to rebel?
It was due to pardoning his punishment and disobeying instructions, thereby accumulating the cause of disaster.
Lùshān was a subordinate general of Zhāng Shǒuguī.
He once violated orders,
and Zhāng Qǔjiāng (Zhāng Jiǔlíng) ordered Shǒuguī to execute him,
but he did not comply,
which indeed led to chaos in the world.
Therefore, the book says:
‘Zhāng Shǒuguī caused Ān Lùshān to rebel.’”
The Old Biography of Zhāng Jiǔlíng states:
“Zhāng Shǒuguī sent his deputy general Ān Lùshān to suppress the Xī and Qìdān.
He was defeated,
arrested and sent to the capital,
with a request to apply the imperial law.
Jiǔlíng presented an impeachment, saying: ‘When Ráng Jū went to war,
he certainly executed Zhuāng Jiǎ.
When Sūn Wǔ taught warfare,
he also executed palace women.
If Shǒuguī’s military orders are to be enforced,
Lùshān should not be spared death.’
The Emperor specifically spared him.
Jiǔlíng memorialized, saying: ‘Lùshān has the ambition of a wolf cub,
and his face shows signs of rebellion.
I request to kill him for his crime,
hoping to eliminate future troubles.’
The Emperor said: ‘You, Minister, must not, because of Wáng Yíbǔ knowing the story of Shí Lè,
wrongfully harm a loyal and good man.’
He was then released and returned to the frontier.”
The New Biography’s account of Péi Guāngtíng is similar to the Shìjì (Record of Deeds).
The account of being arrested and sent to the capital is similar to the Old Biography.
The Old Biography of Lùshān’s account of the sheep theft is similar to the Shìjì,
but without the incident of defeat and request for execution.
The New Biography is also similar.
The Old Biography also says:
“In the twentieth year,
Shǒuguī became the Jiédù Shǐ (Military Governor) of Yōuzhōu,
and Lùshān’s sheep theft was discovered.”
However, Péi Guāngtíng died in the twenty-first year.
In the winter of that year,
Jiǔlíng only then became a chancellor.
Therefore, the statement that he spoke with Guāngtíng
is an error.
Sūn Qiáo’s statement
“Qǔjiāng ordered Shǒuguī to execute him”
is even more inaccurate.
According to the Shílù,
in the twenty-first year,
Shǒuguī was still in Lǒngyòu establishing boundary markers with the Tǔbō,
and had not yet reached Yōuzhōu.
The Old Biography’s statement
“became Jiédù in the twentieth year”
is also an error.
Moreover, if Lùshān had only just become a Yáláng in the border markets,
how could Shǒuguī have known that he would eventually bring chaos to the world,
and release him instead of killing him!
How could Sūn Qiáo immediately accuse him of the crime of rebellion!
If it is as in the Old Biography of Jiǔlíng,
that Shǒuguī arrested and sent him to the capital,
and Xuánzōng himself pardoned him,
then what crime did Shǒuguī commit that people of that time blamed him?
If it is said that he deserved death twice for sheep theft and for losing troops,
how could Lùshān escape death twice merely by speaking?
If it is as in the Xuánzōng Shílù,
that Shǒuguī memorialized requesting to enforce the law,
received permission,
but was moved by a single statement
and immediately spared him,
then Shǒuguī would surely not dare to be so easily contradictory.
Moreover, how could Jiǔlíng have seen his face,
to say that his face showed signs of rebellion?
If it is said that Shǒuguī never memorialized requesting to enforce the law,
Thus, in Zhāng Jiǔlíng’s collected works, there is an imperial edict bestowed upon Zhāng Shǒuguī, which says:
“Ān Lùshān and others lightly regarded my military might,
without proper deliberation,
leading to losses.
It is fitting that they be executed;
since you have carried this out,
it aligns with military law.”
Another imperial edict bestowed upon the Pínglú generals and soldiers says:
“The execution of Ān Lùshān
was due to excessive underestimation of the enemy.
Do not be intimidated or weak because of this,
lest you lose future opportunities.”
This indicates that at that time, it was indeed permitted to execute him.
If it is said that Zhāng Shǒuguī spared him on his own initiative,
contrary to Xuánzōng’s wishes,
then there is another imperial edict bestowed upon Zhāng Shǒuguī, which says:
“Ān Lùshān is brave but lacks strategy,
thus leading to defeat.
His armor and supplies were plundered,
frustrating our military power.
Considering his underestimation of the enemy,
he ought to receive severe punishment.
However, upon first hearing of his valiant fighting,
there was also an inclination to execute;
but as the barbarians have not yet been eliminated,
military orders must be flexible.
Therefore, we will not abandon him for a single defeat,
intending to utilize his future effectiveness.
However, to impose no slight reprimand
would also offer no deterrent.
It is fitting that he be temporarily suspended from office,
and serve as a common soldier.
You should further review the original situation
and may deal with it as appropriate.”
Now, by referencing various texts,
it appears that when Lùshān suffered a defeat,
Shǒuguī submitted a memorial requesting the application of military law.
Hence, the former edict said:
“Since you have carried this out,
it aligns with military law.”
It also said:
“The execution of Lùshān
was due to excessive underestimation of the enemy.”
This seems to imply that Shǒuguī had already executed him.
Subsequently, Shǒuguī was moved by what he had said
and regretted his bravery.
He was unwilling to kill him,
but to spare him, he had already memorialized the court.
Moreover, he feared that he could not satisfy the hearts of the generals and soldiers.
Perhaps the report had not yet arrived,
so he apprehended and sent him to the capital,
allowing the emperor to decide for himself,
hoping that the emperor would see his talent and strength and pardon him.
This is similar to Chén Píng apprehending Fán Kuài
or Wèi Qīng imprisoning Sū Jiàn.
The emperor consequently wished to pardon him,
but Jiǔlíng firmly remonstrated, saying:
“If Shǒuguī’s military orders are to be carried out,
Lùshān should not be spared death.”
This also impeached Shǒuguī for not making a decisive judgment outside the frontier,
but rather apprehending him to pass the buck to the emperor.
Jiǔlíng, seeing him because of this,
said
“he has the physiognomy of a rebel.”
The emperor ultimately wished to pardon him,
so Jiǔlíng had no choice but to draft the imperial edict, saying:
“You should further review the original situation
and deal with it as appropriate.”
Upon receiving this edict, Shǒuguī
immediately spared him
and reported it.
This aligns with the Xuánzōng Shílù (Veritable Records of Emperor Xuánzōng)
and is somewhat more consistent with human nature.
Ān Lùshān
was originally a miscellaneous Hu from Yíngzhōu,
initially named Ā Luòshān.
His mother
was a shaman;
the Xīn Shū (New Book) says: Lùshān’s original surname was Kāng.
His mother lived among the Tujue,
prayed to Yà Luòshān,
what the barbarians called the god of battle,
and gave birth to Lùshān,
hence he was given that as his courtesy name;
he adopted his mother’s surname Ān.
Ā (阿) is pronounced like "wū gé."
Luò (犖) is pronounced like "lǚ jiǎo."
His mother took him and married again to the Tujue, Ān Yányǎn.
When their tribe was scattered and broken,
he and Yányǎn’s nephew Sīshùn fled together,
hence he adopted the surname Ān and was named Lùshān.
There was also Shǐ Sūgān,
who lived in the same neighborhood as Lùshān
and was born one day apart.
The Kǎoyì (Investigation of Differences) says: Old traditions say:
“Sīmíng was born on New Year’s Eve,
Lùshān was born on New Year’s Day.”
According to Lùshān’s biography:
“On the twentieth day of the first month of the tenth year of Tiānbǎo,
the emperor and Guì (the Imperial Consort) celebrated Lùshān’s birthday.”
This is not accepted now.
They were very close,
both serving as intermediaries in mutual markets,
and were known for their bravery.
Yáláng (牙郎) means a broker;
the prices of goods from north and south
were determined by their word,
after which trade would commence.
Lùshān would often go out with a few riders,
capturing dozens of Qìdān and returning.
He was cunning
and adept at gauging human emotions.
Shǒuguī loved him
and raised him as a son.
Sūgān once absconded into the Xī territory with official debts,
and was captured by a Xī patrol,
who intended to kill him.
Sūgān deceived them, saying:
“I am
an envoy of peace and marriage from the Táng.
If you kill me,
disaster will befall your country.”
The patrol believed him
and sent him to the royal tent.
When Sūgān saw the Xī king,
he made a long bow but did not prostrate himself.
Although the Xī king was angry,
he feared the Táng
and dared not kill him,
treating him with the courtesy due to a guest.
He sent a hundred men with Sūgān to the imperial court.
Sūgān said to the Xī king:
“Although the men your majesty sends are numerous,
judging by their abilities, none are capable of seeing the Son of Heaven.
I hear your majesty has an excellent general named Suǒgāo;
why not send him to the imperial court?”
Suǒgāo
was actually the title of a chieftain among the Xī,
not a person’s name.
There was previously Lǐ Shī Suǒgāo.
Jiàng (將) is pronounced like "jì liàng."
Cháo (朝) is pronounced like "zhí yáo."
When Sūgān was about to reach Pínglú,
he first sent someone to tell the military commander Péi Xiūzǐ:
“The Xī envoy Suǒgāo is coming with elite troops,
claiming to go to the imperial court,
but in reality intending to attack the military city.
It is advisable to make careful preparations and
deal with it proactively.”
Xiūzǐ then prepared the military forces and went out to meet them.
Upon reaching the residence,
he buried all the accompanying soldiers alive
and seized Suǒgāo, sending him to Yōuzhōu.
Zhāng Shǒuguī considered Sūgān to have performed meritorious service
and memorialized to have him appointed as Guǒyì,
and he was successively promoted to general.
Later, he entered the court to report on affairs.
The emperor spoke with him,
was pleased,
and bestowed upon him the name Sīmíng.
The Ān-Shǐ incident began here.
7 The son of Wǔ Yōuwàng, Sīmǎ of Liánzhōu, Wǔ Wēnshèn,
was executed by caning for colluding with powerful nobles.
When the emperor pacified the Wéi clan,
Wǔ Yōuwàng was demoted and died.
Shèn (眘) is pronounced like "shí rèn."
On the Yǐchǒu day,
Xìn'ān Wáng Yī, Jìedùshǐ of Shuòfāng and Hédōng, was demoted to Cìshǐ of Qúzhōu.
Guǎngwǔ Wáng Chénghóng was demoted to Biéjià of Fángzhōu.
Xué Zìquàn, Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu, was demoted to Biéjià of Lǐzhōu.
All were implicated for their association with Wǔ Wēnshèn.
Chénghóng
was the son of Shǒulǐ.
Bīnwáng Shǒulǐ
was the son of Zhānghuái Tàizǐ Xián.
On the Xīnwèi day,
Wáng Jū, Cìshǐ of Púzhōu, was demoted to Cìshǐ of Tōngzhōu,
for exchanging letters with Yī.
8 In the fifth month,
the sorcerer Liú Zhìchéng from Lǐquán rebelled,
seizing and plundering passers-by,
intending to advance towards Xiányáng.
Villagers ran to inform the county officials,
who burned bridges and cut off roads to resist them.
His followers then dispersed,
and within a few days,
all were captured and executed.
9 In the sixth month,
the monthly payment of salary in cash to all officials was first implemented.
10 Initially,
the Emperor, on account of the amnesty following the Jìtián ceremony,
commanded the relevant officials to discuss increasing the offerings of biāndòu at the ancestral temples and those whose mourning attire regulations were not yet settled.
Tàicháng Qīng Wéi Tāo (韋縚) memorialized, requesting twelve biāndòu for each seat in the ancestral temples.
Bīngbù Shìláng Zhāng Jūn (張均) and Zhífāng Lángzhōng Wéi Shù (韋述) deliberated, saying:
"Sages know that the filial son's feelings are deep and that the types of offerings are limitless;
therefore, they established regulations and limits.
Human preferences and tastes are fundamentally without fixed standards,
and private banquets change with the times;
thus, the sages brought everything back to ancient customs.
Qū Dào (屈到) loved water caltrops (jì),
but Qū Jiàn (屈建) did not offer them,
believing that one should not impose private desires upon state rituals.
The Guóyǔ records: 'Qū Dào of Chǔ loved water caltrops.
When he fell ill,
he summoned his clan elders and instructed them, saying:
"When you sacrifice to me, you must use water caltrops." '
However, at the end of the mourning period (xiáng),
when the clan elders were about to offer water caltrops,
Qū Jiàn ordered them to be removed,
saying:
'A lord has an ox offering (niúxiǎng);
a grandee has a sheep offering (yángkuì);
a scholar has a pig and dog offering (túnquǎn zhī diàn);
and commoners have fish and roasted meat offerings (yúzhì zhī jiàn).
As for biāndòu, dried meat, and mincemeat (púhǎi),
these are shared by all from top to bottom.
One does not present rare delicacies,
nor display excessive luxuries,
nor impose one's private desires upon the state rituals.'
Thereupon, they were not used.
Jì (芰),
pronounced Qí Jì fān.
Líng (蔆),
also known as jì.
The Shuōwén says: 'Chǔ calls it jì;
Qín calls it xièhóu (薢茩).
Nowadays, people commonly just say língjì.'
The Wǔlíng Jì states: 'Those with four or three corners are called jì;
those with two corners are called líng.'
Hào (好),
pronounced Hū Dào fān.
Qù (去),
pronounced Qiāng Lǚ fān.
All are used for sacrifices.
If we arbitrarily exceed the old system,
where would the limits be?
The Shū Jīng says: 'Millet and grain are not fragrant;
only luminous virtue is fragrant.'
This refers to the words of King Chéng (成王) commanding Jūn Chén (君陳).
If one seeks to commune with spirits without method, based on what one is accustomed to in daily life,
why must one cling to ancient ways?
Then fǔguǐ could be removed, and pányúbēi'àn would be used instead;
and Sháo (韶) and Huò (濩) music could cease, while kōnghóuzhēngdí would be played.
Shùn's music is called Sháo;
Tāng's music is called Huò.
Kōnghóu:
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (漢武帝) had musician Hóu Tiáo (侯調) make it;
some say Hóu Huī (侯輝) made it.
Now, its shape is like a smaller sè (瑟),
with seven strings,
played with a plectrum like a pípa.
The Jiù Tángshū says: 'Kōnghóu is Hú music.'
Emperor Líng of Hàn (漢靈帝) was fond of it.
It is curved and long,
with twenty-three strings,
held vertically against the chest,
played with both hands simultaneously.
Commonly known as
'bò kōnghóu'.
The Fèngshǒu Kōnghóu had an added neck and seven frets (zhěn),
made by Zhèng Shànzǐ (鄭善子),
and presented during the Kāiyuán (開元) era.
Its shape was like a Ruǎn Xián (阮咸),
with a small lower sounding board but a large body,
and a small side cutout,
for ease of holding.
Another account says: 'Kōnghóu originated from the music of Zhèng (鄭) and Wèi (衛).
Because it was the music of a doomed state,
it was called "empty state marquis" (kōngguó zhī hóu),
or also Kǎnhóu.'
The Fēngsú Tōng says: 'During the time of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Qiū Zhòng (丘仲) made the flute (dí).'
According to the Zhōu Lǐ,
the Shēng Shī (笙師) was in charge of teaching chí (篪) and suì (遂).
It also says
it originated from the Qiāng people.
The hengdí (橫笛) described by Mǎ Róng (馬融) in the Later Hàn (後漢) was
hollow,
bottomless,
with two holes cut at one end,
and five holes coming out on its back,
very similar to today's chìbā.
Lǐ Shàn (李善) annotated it,
saying: 'The seven-holed one is now one chǐ and four cùn long;
this is today's hengdí.'
What the Tàicháng Gǔchuī Bù (太常鼓吹部) calls 'héngchuī' (橫吹)
is not the one described by Mǎ Róng.
Mǎ Róng's ode says:
'Jīng Fáng (京房) had a clear understanding of musical temperament,
so he added one hole to the original four;
the hole Jīng Fáng added came out from the back,
thereby completing the five notes (shāngshēng wǔyīn).'
Shěn Yuè's (沈約) Sòng Shū also says that
Jīng Fáng completed its five notes.
The commentary on the Shēng Shī in the Zhōu Lǐ by Dù Zǐchūn (杜子春) says: 'Chí and suì (篪遂) are the five-holed suì (遂) played nowadays.'
Judging by what Mǎ Róng and Shěn Yuè recorded,
the ancient suì (遂) should not have had five holes,
so Dù Zǐchūn's statement
is not necessarily correct.
Today's Sān Lǐ Tú (三禮圖) depicts the suì (遂) horizontally placed and having five holes;
I do not know what classical source this comes from.
Suì (遂)
is the same as dí.
Fǔ (簠),
pronounced Fǔ.
Guǐ (簋),
pronounced Jū Wěi fān.
What would future generations observe?
Spirits
are those who approach people with clarity and intelligence;
they do not seek abundance and grandeur.
If one deviates from ritual,
what good is even much?
How can we abandon the ritual classics to follow popular customs?
Moreover, a gentleman loves people with ritual,
not seeking mere agreement;
how much more so in the ancestral temple,
how dare we forget the old regulations!"
Tàizǐ Bīnkè Cuī Miǎn (崔沔) deliberated, saying:
"The rise of sacrifices
began in remote antiquity.
When people ate raw meat and drank blood,
there were offerings of hair and blood.
Before there was qūniè,
there were offerings of black wine (xuánjiǔ).
The Sīxuǎn Shì (司烜氏) used a mirror to draw clear water from the moon for xuánjiǔ.
Niè (糵),
pronounced Yú Liè fān.
Ritual objects gradually became complete;
however, respect for the way of the spirits
must not be abandoned.
The contents of biāndòu, fǔguǐ, zūnléi
were all contemporary dishes of the Zhōu people,
their use extending to banquets and entertaining guests.
Yet, when Duke of Zhōu (周公) established the rituals,
these were offered to gods and spirits alongside hair and blood and xuánjiǔ.
The state establishes its teachings based on ritual,
and sets its standards according to the times.
During the seasonal sacrifices in the pure temple,
ritual dishes are fully displayed,
following the Zhōu system.
For example, fǔguǐ, biāndòu, xínggēng, and similar items.
Zhuàn (饌),
pronounced Chú Liàn fān,
also Chú Huǎn fān.
Contemporary seasonal dishes are prepared,
following the Hàn (漢) method.
For example, Shúsūn Tōng (叔孫通) requested the offering of 'sweet cherries' (hántáo).
Shàng (上),
pronounced Shí Zhǎng fān.
This is about presenting distant items.
New items must always be offered,
in accordance with the seasonal calendar.
Within the imperial parks,
what is harvested from personal farming;
during hunting seasons,
what is personally shot;
none are eaten before being offered,
showing utmost sincerity and reverence.
If this is done to such an extent,
what more can be added?
We should simply reiterate instructions to the relevant officials
to not be negligent or lazy,
then fresh, delicious, and rich offerings
will all be present,
without necessarily increasing the number of biāndòu."
From this point onwards,
the opinions of all these individuals
were based on and reiterated the old rituals.
However, the Emperor still wished to proportionately increase the variety of dishes.
Wéi Tāo (韋縚) again memorialized, requesting that six biāndòu be added to each chamber,
and that each season they be filled with new fruits and rare delicacies;
this was approved.
Tāo (縚) further memorialized:
"Regarding mourning rites, 'For a maternal uncle (舅, jiù),
three months of sīmá (緦麻) mourning.
For a maternal aunt (從母, cóngmǔ) and maternal grandparents (外祖父母, wàizǔfùmǔ), all wear xiǎogōng (小功) for five months.'
Maternal grandparents are of utmost importance,
yet their mourning attire is the same as for a maternal aunt;
maternal aunts (姨, yí) and maternal uncles (舅, jiù) are of the same degree,
but their mourning attire differs in severity.
Yí (姨)
is the same as cóngmǔ (從母).
Cóng (從)
is pronounced cái yòng.
If affection is severed, there is no mourning for each other;
the maternal uncle's wife (舅母, jiùmǔ) comes to join the outer clan,
but is not treated with the same reverence as those who share a hearth.
I humbly believe that the ancient meaning is still somewhat inadequately expressed,
and I request that maternal grandparents be elevated to dàgōng (大功) for nine months,
and maternal aunts and maternal uncles both to xiǎogōng (小功) for five months,
and paternal first cousins once removed (堂舅, tángjiù), maternal first cousins once removed (堂姨, tángyí), and maternal uncle's wife (舅母, jiùmǔ) all be elevated to tǎnmǐan (袒免)."
The Five Mourning Rites (五服, Wǔfú) stop at sīmá (緦麻);
beyond this there is the attire of tǎnmǐan (袒免).
Tǎn (袒) means
to partially remove one's garment and expose one's shoulder;
mǐan (免) means
to take a piece of cloth one cun wide,
pass it from the back of the neck forward and cross it over the forehead,
then turn it back and wrap it around the topknot.
Tǎn (袒)
is pronounced dàn.
Mǐan (免)
is pronounced wèn.
Cuī Miǎn (崔沔) deliberated, saying:
"The way of rectifying the family
cannot be divided;
to bring together a single principle,
the truth reverts to the main lineage.
Therefore, within the family there are qī (齊) and zhǎn (斬) [mourning rites],
while outside all are sīmá (緦麻);
the added title of 'venerated' [for maternal kin]
does not exceed one degree.
This is the unchangeable way of the former kings.
I wish to uphold the clear imperial decree of the eighth year,
and follow the ancient rites completely."
The imperial decree mentioned by Cuī Miǎn
is found in volume 212, seventh year;
the reference to the "eighth year"
includes the year before the emperor's accession to the throne.
Wéi Shù (韋述) deliberated, saying:
"The Commentary on Mourning Rites (喪服傳) states: 'Birds and beasts know their mothers but not their fathers.
Commoners say,
"What are parents
indeed!"
Scholars in cities, however, know to revere their deceased parents;
grandees and learned scholars know to revere their ancestors.'
The sages thoroughly understood the Way of Heaven and were generous towards ancestors and deceased parents,
tied together clans and cherished their descendants.
The mother's side of the family compared to the main lineage
cannot be treated equally;
this is clear.
If now maternal grandparents and maternal uncles have their mourning increased by one degree,
and paternal first cousins once removed and maternal aunts are included in the mourning code,
then what will be the difference between inner and outer relatives?
Neglecting rites to indulge emotions
focuses on trivialities.
The ancient legislators,
knowing that human emotions are easily swayed,
feared the gradual loss of rites.
They distinguished between similarities and differences,
making the heavy and light rites disparate,
wishing that later generations would never mix them up.
The subtle intent lies here;
how could it be without reason!
If it can be increased,
it can also be decreased;
if the former sages can be gainsaid,
then the classics of rites can be destroyed.
The institutions of the former kings
are called the 'constant principles' (彞倫, yílún).
Yí (彞)
means 'constant'.
Lún (倫)
means 'principle and order'.
Yet we still fear their loss and fall;
if their order is disturbed even once,
how can it be stopped!
I request that the mourning rites be set according to the Yílǐ (儀禮) [book]."
Yáng Zhòngchāng (楊仲昌), Supervising Secretary of the Board of Rites (禮部員外郎), deliberated, saying:
The Lang (郎) of the Board of Rites (禮部) in the Táng (唐) dynasty was in charge of the Five Rites (五禮),
outlining their ceremonies and distinguishing their names and numbers.
"Zhèng Wénzhēn Gōng (鄭文貞公) Wèi Zhēng (魏徵) first increased the mourning for maternal uncles to xiǎogōng (小功) for five months.
Although Wénzhēn (文貞) was worthy,
Zhōu (周) and Kǒng (孔) were sages.
If a worthy man can change the words of sages,
what can later scholars follow?
I secretly fear that inner and outer relations will become disordered,
and the close and distant will lose their proper sequence,
and what will not be reached by the flow of emotion!
Formerly, Zǐlù (子路) did not observe mourning for his sister,
and Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said:
'The former kings established rites
so that people walking the Way
would not be able to bear [such omissions].'
Zǐlù (子路) then observed mourning.
This is seen in the Jì Tángōng (記檀弓).
The Jì (記) says:
'Do not lightly dispute the rites.'
This is from Lǐqì (禮器).
Together with the sun and moon,
the worthy follow them;
how dare we diminish or add to them!"
An imperial edict stated:
"Since maternal aunts and maternal uncles already observe xiǎogōng (小功),
a maternal uncle's wife should not be entirely reduced [in mourning];
she should observe sīmá (緦麻).
Paternal first cousins once removed and maternal first cousins once removed should observe tǎnmǐan (袒免)."
Jūn (均)
was the son of Yuè (說).
In the 11th year,
8th month,
on the day Rénzǐ (壬子),
it was Qiānqiū Jié (千秋節),
and all officials presented precious mirrors.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng (張九齡) believed that one uses a mirror to see one's own appearance,
and uses people to see auspicious and inauspicious omens.
So he narrated the origins of the rise and fall of previous generations,
compiling five volumes [of writings],
titled Qiānqiū Jīnjìnglù (千秋金鏡錄),
and presented them;
the emperor bestowed a letter of commendation.
On the day Jiǎyín (甲寅),
the Tūqíshī (突騎施) sent their high official Húlù Dágān (胡祿達干) to request surrender,
which was granted.
Lǐ Shìzhī (李適之), Censor-in-chief (御史大夫),
was the grandson of Chénggān (承乾).
Due to his talent and ability, he gained favor with the emperor,
and repeatedly argued on behalf of Chénggān (承乾);
on the day Jiǎxū (甲戌),
Chénggān (承乾) was posthumously granted the title of Héngshān Mǐnwáng (恆山愍王).
Chénggān's (承乾) dethronement is seen in volume 197, Tàizōng Zhēnguān (太宗貞觀) 17th year.
Shù (數)
is pronounced suǒ jiǎo.
Wéi (為)
is pronounced yú wěi.
Héng (恆)
is pronounced hù dēng.
On the day Yǐhài (乙亥),
Biàn Āiwáng Jǐng (汴哀王璥) passed away.
In winter,
10th month,
on the day Wùshēn (戊申),
the imperial carriage departed from the Eastern Capital (東都).
Earlier,
an edict had ordered a journey to the Western Capital (西京) on the second day of the second month of the following year.
However, there were strange occurrences in the palace,
so the next day,
the emperor summoned the chancellors
and immediately discussed returning west.
Péi Yàoqīng (裴耀卿) and Zhāng Jiǔlíng (張九齡) said:
"The autumn harvest is not yet finished;
please wait until mid-winter."
Lǐ Línfǔ (李林甫) secretly knew the emperor's intention.

"In the tenth month, on the day bǐngwǔ,
the emperor, while holding court,
inquired about prisoners in the capital.
Officials reported there were fifty people.
He showed a joyful expression
and issued an edict saying: 'Recently, in the thorny thicket area,
magpies have come to nest.
Now, tallying all criminal cases,
it barely exceeds fifty.
Xíngbù Shìláng Zhèng Shǎowēi and others are each granted a superior-medium evaluation.'"
It is unclear whether these two are one event or two events.
This entry follows the old record.
The emperor ordered Lǐ Línfǔ and Niú Xiānkè, along with judicial officials, to revise the Lǜlìng Géshì. Upon completion,
in the ninth month,
on the day rénshēn,
it was promulgated.
12 Previously,
many dozens of prefectures on the northwest frontier stationed heavy troops.
The land taxes and military farm produce were insufficient to support them,
so the method of "hédí" (purchase at a fixed price) was first used.
One Péng Guǒ,
through Niú Xiānkè, presented a proposal,
requesting the implementation of the "dí" (purchase) method in Guānzhōng.
On the day wùzǐ,
an imperial edict stated that due to a good harvest and low grain prices harming farmers,
the emperor ordered an increase of twenty to thirty percent above the current market price,
to "hédí" several million hù of millet from the Eastern and Western Jī each.
The Eastern Jī
refers to the Dūjī.
The Western Jī
refers to the Jīngjī.
Dí is pronounced "tā lì" (tāli) (Pinyin: dí).
From then on, the reserves in Guānzhōng overflowed,
and the imperial carriage no longer made trips to the Eastern Capital.
On the day guǐsì,
an imperial edict stated that taxes from Hénán and Héběi that were due to be delivered to Hánjiā and Tàiyuán Granaries,
according to Lǐ Bì's biography,
the Tàiyuán Granary was west of Shǎnzhōu.
13 Tàicháng Bóshì Wáng Yú
submitted a memorial requesting the establishment of an Altar to the Green Emperor to welcome spring;
it was approved.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day xīnchǒu,
an edict was issued that from now on, on Lìchūn, the emperor would personally welcome spring in the eastern suburb.
At that time, the emperor was quite fond of worshipping spirits and ghosts,
so Wáng Yú specialized in the rites of sacrifice and worship to gain favor.
The emperor was pleased with him,
and appointed him Shìyùshǐ,
also in charge of the Císì Shǐ.
Wáng Yú's prayers sometimes involved burning paper money,
resembling shamanistic practices.
Since the Hàn dynasty, it was customary to bury money with the dead.
Later, common folk gradually used paper to represent money for ghostly affairs.
Shǐ is pronounced "shū lì" (shūlì) (Pinyin: shǐ).
Xī is pronounced "xíng dí" (xíngdí) (Pinyin: xí).
14 On the day rénshēn,
the emperor visited the Lìshān Hot Springs.
On the day yǐyǒu,
he returned to the palace.
15 On the day jǐchǒu,
Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Guǎngpíng Wénzhēn Gōng Sòng Jǐng passed away.
16 In the twelfth month,
on the day bǐngwǔ,
Huì Wǔ Shì passed away,
and was posthumously granted the title of Zhēnshùn Huánghòu.
17 This year,
the emperor ordered Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng Kāng Qiānsù
to go to the Eastern Capital to demolish the Míngtáng.
"Qiān"
is
the same as
"qiān" (愆),
it is a zhòuwén character.
The Xīnshū Lǐyuè Zhì writes
"Qiānsù."
"To demolish it would be strenuous for the people, so I request to remove the upper layer,
making it ninety-five chǐ lower than the old one,
and it shall still be the Qiányuán Diàn."
This was approved.
18 At first, it was ordered that the land tax (zū), labor service (yōng), and textile tribute (diào), as well as the commercial tax (zīkè),
should all be paid in local produce to the capital.
The Zūyōngdiào for the Western Capital and Eastern Capital
was the law of Gāozǔ and Tàizōng;
the Zīkè was definitely a law from the Kāiyuán era onwards.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day yǐhài,
Niú Xiānkè was appointed Shìzhōng.
2 On the day dīngchǒu,
the emperor welcomed the qi (vital energy) of spring east of the Chǎnshuǐ.
3 An edict was issued that since enough long-term frontier soldiers had been recruited,
from now on, no more garrison troops should be dispatched,
and those already there should be allowed to return.
4 It was ordered that schools be established in every prefecture, county, and village throughout the empire.
5 On the day rénchén,
Lǐ Línfǔ was appointed Lǒngyòu Jiédù Fùdàshǐ,
and Shànzhōu Dūdū Dù Xīwàng was appointed Zhī Liúhòu.
In the second month,
on the day yǐmǎo,
Niú Xiānkè was concurrently appointed Hédōng Jiédù Fùdàshǐ.
Niú Xiānkè had previously held the position for Shuòfāng,
and now also concurrently held Hédōng.
6 On the day jǐwèi,
Zhēnshùn Huánghòu was buried at Jìnglíng.
Wǔ Huì was posthumously named Zhēnshùn Huánghòu.
Jìnglíng was forty lǐ southeast of Jīngzhào Wànnián Xiàn.
7 On the day rénxū,
an imperial edict stated that the Hú people of the six Héqú prefectures, who had been dispersed among various prefectures by Kāng Dàibīn,
were permitted to return to their ancestral lands.
Yòuzhōu was established between Yán and Xià
to settle them.
The relocation of the six Hú prefectures is mentioned in volume 212, year 10.
Now, the land of the six Hú prefectures was consolidated to form Yòuzhōu.
Old records: Yòuzhōu was one thousand one hundred lǐ from the capital.
Xià is pronounced "hù yǎ" (hùyǎ) (Pinyin: Xià).
Chǔ is pronounced "chāng lǚ" (chānglǚ) (Pinyin: chǔ).
8 In the third month,
Tǔbō invaded Héxī.
Jìedùshǐ Cuī Xīyì attacked and defeated them.
Shànzhōu Dūdū and Zhī Lǒngyòu Liúhòu Dù Xīwàng attacked Tǔbō's Xīnchéng,
and captured it.
Its territory was established as Wēiróng Jūn.
Wēiróng Jūn was 350 *lǐ* northwest of Xīngxiù Chuān in Shànzhōu.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The old records state
"Wēiwǔ Jūn,"
but we now follow the *Shílù*.
9 In the summer,
the fifth month,
on the *Yǐyǒu* day,
Lǐ Línfǔ concurrently held the post of Héxī Jìedùshǐ.
He already held Lǒngyòu,
and now also concurrently held Héxī.
On the *Bǐngshēn* day,
Cuī Xīyì was made Hénán Yǐn.
Xīyì, recalling his breach of faith with Tǔbō,
due to breaking the alliance with Qǐlìxú,
died not long after.
10 After Prince Yīng had died,
Lǐ Línfǔ repeatedly advised the Emperor to establish Prince Shòu Mào.
The Emperor considered Prince Zhōng Yú to be older,
and moreover benevolent, filial, respectful, and cautious,
and also fond of learning.
He intended to establish him,
but hesitated for over a year, unable to decide.
He reflected that his age was gradually advancing,
three sons had been executed on the same day,
and the heir had not yet been determined.
He was often uneasy and unhappy,
and his sleep and appetite diminished because of it.
Gāo Lìshì seized an opportunity to ask the reason.
The Emperor said:
"You,
my old servant,
how can you not fathom my thoughts!"
Lìshì said:
"Is it not because the young master has not yet been decided?"
The Emperor said:
"Indeed."
He replied:
"Why should *Dàjiā* trouble your sacred heart so much?
Just choose the eldest and establish him;
who would dare to contend again!"
The Emperor said:
"You are right!
You are right!"
From this, the decision was made.
In the sixth month,
on the *Gēngzǐ* day,
Yú was established as太子 (Crown Prince).
11 On the *Xīnchǒu* day,
Xiāo Jiǒng, the Qízhōu Cìshǐ, was made Héxī Jìedùshǐ to oversee *liúhòu* affairs;
Dù Xīwàng, the Shànzhōu Dūdū, was made Lǒngyòu Jìedùshǐ;
Wáng Yù, the Tàipú Qīng, was made Jiànnán Jìedùshǐ.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The old records state
"Wáng Hào,"
but we now follow the *Shílù* and *Tánglì*.
The Chìlǐng stele that had been erected was also destroyed.
The erection of the stele
is recorded in volume 21 of the previous scroll.
12 Türgeš Khaghan Sūlù,
was always modest and frugal.
Whatever he gained from battles,
he would distribute among his various tribes,
keeping no private wealth.
Because of this, the populace happily served him.
After marrying a Tang princess,
he also secretly communicated with the Tujue and Tǔbō.
The Tujue and Tǔbō each gave him a daughter in marriage.
Sūlù made the daughters of the three states his *kědūn*,
and also established several sons as *yèhù*.
His expenses gradually increased,
and because of this, he no longer distributed what was gained from battles.
In his later years, he suffered from paralysis,
and one hand was crippled.
The various tribes became disloyal.
The chieftains Mòhè Dágān and Dūmó Dù were the strongest of the two tribes.
Their tribes were further divided into Yellow Surname and Black Surname.
They were at odds with each other.
The Türgeš people who called themselves descendants of Suōgá were the Yellow Surname,
and Sūlù's tribe was the Black Surname.
They killed him.
Dūmó Dù initially conspired with Mòhè Dágān,
but then differed with him again.
He established Sūlù's son Gǔchuò as Tuǒhuǒxiān Khaghan to gather the remaining populace,
and fought against Mòhè Dágān.
Mòhè Dágān sent an envoy to report to Qìxī Jìedùshǐ Gài Jiāyùn.
*Qì*
is pronounced *qī jī fān*.
Tuǒhuǒxiān and Dūmó Dù occupied Suìyè Chéng.
The Black Surname Khaghan Ěrwēitèlè occupied Dáláshī Chéng.
Suìyè Chuān is a thousand *lǐ* long,
and its western part belongs to Dáláshī Chéng.
That city originally belonged to the Shí State,
which often garrisoned troops there.
*Gài*
is pronounced *gǔ hè fān*.
*Qí*
is pronounced *qí jì fān*.
*Kě*
is from *kān* in the entering tone.
*Hàn*
is pronounced *hán*.
*Dá*
is pronounced *dāng gē fān*.
*Luó*
is pronounced *láng zuǒ fān*.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Tánglì* states
"Héngluósī."
We now follow the *Shílù*.
13 When the Crown Prince was about to receive his investiture,
the ceremonial procedures included *zhōngyán*, *wàibàn*, and the *jiàngshāpáo*.
According to Tang regulations,
on the day the Emperor observed a grand sacrifice and fasted,
at one *kè* after the water clock began dripping in the daytime,
the Shìzhōng would present a tablet requesting *zhōngyán*.
All guards would enter and arrange themselves in the palace courtyard.
Civil and military officials of the fifth rank and above would wear *kùzhé* and attend.
All attending officials would wear their ritual attire.
All fasting attendant officials would tie their ceremonial pendants
and proceed to the gate to welcome the Emperor.
At two *kè*,
the Shìzhōng would present a tablet for *wàibàn*.
The imperial carriage would then emerge for court assemblies.
The various guards would stand at attention.
When all officials were arrayed and ready,
the Shìzhōng would also announce *wàibàn*,
without requesting *zhōngyán*.
When the Emperor was about to depart,
seven *kè* before the carriage set off, one drum would be struck for the first *yán*.
Five *kè* before, two drums would be struck for the second *yán*.
The Shìzhōng would present a tablet requesting *zhōngyán*.
The responsible officials would arrange the imperial guard of honor.
Two *kè* before, three drums would be struck for the third *yán*.
The various guards would sequentially enter and stand in the palace courtyard.
All officials would stand in the court hall.
The Shìzhōng, Zhōngshū Lìng, and others would welcome the Emperor at the western steps.
The Shìzhōng would present the imperial seal.
The Chénghuáng Lìng would lead the way to the south-facing western steps of the Tàijí Diàn.
The Qiānniú Jiāngjūn would hold a long saber and stand in front of the path, facing north.
The Huángmén Shìláng would stand in front of the attendant officials,
with two chanters.
After *wàibàn*,
the Tàipú Qīng would adjust his robes and ascend,
standing upright and holding the reins.
The imperial carriage would emerge and ascend the path.
The Empress Dowager and Empress also had *zhōngyán* and *wàibàn*,
all presented by the Shàngyí.
For the Crown Prince's *zhōngyán* and *wàibàn*,
the Zuǒshùzǐ would present the tablet.
When the Emperor wore the Tōngtiān Guān,
he would wear the *jiàngshāpáo*.
This was the attire for receiving court felicitations on the winter solstice, returning from sacrifices, feasting all officials, and honoring the elderly.
When the Crown Prince wore the Yuǎnyóu Guān,
he also wore the *jiàngshāpáo*.
This was the attire for visiting court and returning to the palace, attending court on the New Year's Day and the first day of each month, and for *shìdiàn* ceremonies.
A memorial was submitted requesting to change these.
Zuǒchéngxiàng Péi Yàoqīng proposed to abolish *zhōngyán*,
change *wàibàn* to *wàibèi*,
and change *jiàngshāpáo* to *zhūmíngfú*.
In the autumn,
the seventh month,
on the *Jǐsì* day,
the Emperor proceeded to the Xuānzhèng Diàn
to invest the Crown Prince.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Yuán Zài's *Sùzōng Shílù* records:
"On the *Rénchén* day of the seventh month of the 27th year,
the ceremony was held."
We now follow the *Xuánzōng Shílù*.
The Crown Prince's carriage arrived at the palace gate.
On this occasion,
the Crown Prince did not ride in the carriage,
but walked from his palace.
On this day,
there was a general amnesty throughout the empire.
On the *Jǐmǎo* day,
Prince Zhōng's consort Wéi Shì was invested as the Crown Princess.
14 Dù Xīwàng led the forces of Shànzhōu to seize the river bridge from Tǔbō,
and built Yánquán Chéng on the left bank of the river.
Tǔbō dispatched 30,000 troops to engage them.
Xīwàng's forces were few and no match,
and all the generals and soldiers were fearful.
Zuǒwēiwèi Lángjiāng Wáng Zhōngsì led his unit to charge their formation first.
Wherever he went, the enemy gave way,
killing several hundred men,
and the enemy formation fell into disarray.
Xīwàng unleashed his troops to press the attack,
and the enemy suffered a great defeat.
Zhènxi Jūn was established at Yánquán.
Zhènxi Jūn was 180 *lǐ* west of Hézhōu.
15 In the eighth month,
on the *Xīnsì* day,
Bóhǎi Wáng Wǔyì died,
and his son Qīnmào succeeded him.
16th, 9th month,
on the day Bǐngshēn, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
17th, Initially,
during the Yífèng era,
Tubó conquered and occupied Ānróngchéng.
Previously,
Jiànnán had built and garrisoned Ānróngchéng west of Máozhōu,
to press against Tubó's southern border.
The Qīng Qiāng (wild Qiāng) guided Tubó to seize it,
and they subsequently defended it.
They then incorporated all the Mán of Xī'ěrhé,
and to the east, bordered Sōng, Máo, and Cuì.
Tang repeatedly attacked it,
but could not conquer it.
The Jiànnán Jiédùshǐ, Wáng Yù, built two cities on its side,
and stationed his army below Púpólǐng.
The Xīnshū (New History) writes
"Péngpólǐng".
This place is outside the Snow Mountains,
which is what Dù Fǔ's poem refers to as
"next, take Péngpó, the city beyond the snow".
This is it.
Tubó sent a large army to rescue Ānróngchéng,
and Yù's forces were greatly defeated,
with thousands of casualties.
The Kǎoyì (Discrepancies Examination) states: The old account says,
"tens of thousands of officers and soldiers
were all annihilated by the bandits."
We now follow the Shílù (Veritable Records).
Provisions, weapons, and military supplies were all abandoned.
Yù was demoted to Guāzhōu Cìshǐ,
and then further demoted to Gāoyào Wèi, where he died.
18th, On the day Wùwǔ,
Méng Guīyì of Nánzhào was enfeoffed as Yúnnán Wáng.
The Shuǐjīngzhù (Commentary on the Classic of Waterways) states: Yúnnánjùn was originally the territory of Yúnshānxiàn,
and the commandery was established by the Shǔ Liú family in the second year of Jiànxīng.
From Tang's Róngzhōu Kāibiānxiàn, it is seventy lǐ south to Qǔzhōu,
and another two thousand five hundred lǐ to Yúnnánchéng.
Guīyì's ancestors were originally from the territory of the Āiláoyí.
The Āiláoyí
submitted to the Han during Emperor Míng's time.
To the southeast, they bordered Jiāozhǐ,
and to the northwest, Tubó.
In the Mán language, "king" is called Zhào.
There were originally Six Zhào: namely Méngshè,
Méngyuè,
Yuèxī,
Lángqióng,
Yàngbèi,
and Yuèdàn.
The Kǎoyì states: The Xīnshū (New History) says
"The Six Zhào are Méngcuì, Yuèxī, Lángqióng, Dèngxiǎn, Shīlàng, and Méngshè."
We now follow Dòu Pāng's Yúnnán Biélù (Separate Record of Yúnnán).
None could unify them;
succeeding dynasties maintained this division to weaken their power.
Méngshè was the southernmost,
hence called Nánzhào.
During Emperor Gāozōng's reign,
Méngshè's Xìnuóluó first paid tribute.
Xìnuóluó had Luóshèng,
Luóshèng had Shènglúopí,
and Shènglúopí had Píluóhé.
Píluóhé gradually became powerful,
while the Five Zhào were weak.
He had also achieved merit in defeating the Mǐhé Mán.
Mǐhé is Xī'ěrhé.
Mǐ,
pronounced nǎi lì fān.
He sought to unify the Six Zhào into one.
Yù pleaded for him,
and the imperial court granted it,
also bestowing the name Guīyì.
Thereupon, he used military might to subdue all the Mán.
Those who did not comply were eliminated.
He then defeated Tubó,
and moved his residence to Dàhéchéng.
After this, it eventually became a border threat.
The affairs of Nánzhào began here.
Their ancestors were a separate branch of the Wūmán.
In the Yi language, mountain slopes are called Hé,
hence it was called Dàhéchéng.
Zú,
pronounced zǐ xù fān.
19th, Winter,
10th month,
on the day Wùyín,
the Emperor visited Lìshān Wēnquán;
on the day Rénchén,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
20th, In this year,
along the route between Xījīng and Dōngdū,
over a thousand imperial traveling palaces were built.
21st, The Zuǒ and Yòu Yǔlín were divided to establish the Lóngwǔjūn,
to which the Wànqíyíng was subordinate.
22nd, Qí Hǎn, the Rùnzhōu Cìshǐ, reported:
"From Guābù to cross the river involves a detour of sixty lǐ.
I request to cross the river directly from Jīngkǒudài,
and after digging twenty-five lǐ through Yīlóuhé, one would reach Yángzǐxiàn,
where an Yīlóudài can be established."
This was granted.
1st, Spring,
1st month,
on the day Rényín,
Prince Róng Wǎn, the Lǒngyòu Jiédù Dàshǐ, was ordered to inspect and manage the various armies in his domain,
and to select and recruit thirty to fifty thousand strong men from Guānnèi and Hédōng,
to proceed to Lǒngyòu for defense and interception.
If there were no invaders by the end of autumn,
they would be allowed to return.
2nd, All ministers requested to add the honorific title "Shèngwén";
2nd month,
on the day Jǐsì,
it was granted.
Thereupon, a general amnesty was declared,
and the people's land tax for this year was waived.
3rd, Summer,
4th month,
on the day Guǐyǒu,
an imperial edict stated:
"All matters of yin-yang and numerology,
except for divination concerning marriages, funerals, and selections,
are prohibited."
4th, On the day Jǐchǒu,
Niú Xiānkè was appointed Bīngbù Shàngshū兼 Shìzhōng (Minister of War and concurrently Grand Councilor),
and Lǐ Línfǔ was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū兼 Zhōngshūlìng (Minister of Personnel and concurrently Grand Councilor),
to manage the selection of civil and military officials.
This meant that Niú Xiānkè managed the selection of military officials,
and Lǐ Línfǔ managed the selection of civil officials.
Xuǎn,
pronounced xū juàn fān.
5th, 6th month,
on the day Guǐyǒu,
Lǐ Shìzhī, the Yùshǐ Dàfū, was concurrently appointed Yōuzhōu Jiédùshǐ.
Zhào Kān and Bái Zhēntuóluó, generals of Yōuzhōu, falsely invoked the order of Jiédùshǐ Zhāng Shǒuguī,
to have Wū Zhīyì, the Pínglújūn Shǐ, attack the remaining rebels of Xī in the north of Héngshuǐ;
Héngshuǐ should be
"Huángshuǐ".
The Xīnshū (New History) writes
"Huángshuǐ",
while the biography of Zhāng Shǒuguī in the Jiùshū (Old History) writes
"Huángshuǐ",
which we now follow.
Huángshuǐ is in Liáoguó,
now within the borders of Línhuángfǔ.
The Zhì (Treatise) says,
from Yíngzhōu, crossing Sōngxínglǐng and going four hundred lǐ north, one reaches Huángshuǐ.
Shǐ,
pronounced shū lì fān.
Jiàng,
pronounced jí liàng fān.
Bái Zhēntuóluó falsely claimed an imperial decree to pressure him.
Zhīyì, having no choice, led his army out.
He met the barbarians,
initially won, then lost.
Shǒuguī concealed the defeat,
reporting a victory.
The matter was somewhat revealed.
The Emperor ordered Niú Xiāntóng, the Nèi Yèzhě Jiān, to investigate it.
Nèi Yèzhě Jiān, a Tang official of rank six lower,
was in charge of internal proclamations and the assemblies of imperial relatives and noblewomen,
registering their numbers and sending them to the Nèishìshěng.
Blame was attributed to Bái Zhēntuóluó,
who was forced to hang himself.
Xiāntóng was favored by the Emperor,
and the other eunuchs resented him,
jointly revealing his transgressions.
The Emperor was enraged.
On the day Jiǎxū,
he ordered Yáng Sīxù to beat him to death with a staff.
Sīxù bound him,
beat him hundreds of times with a staff,
cut out his heart,
and cut his flesh to eat it.
Shǒuguī was demoted to Kuòzhōu Cìshǐ.
Xiāo Sōng, the Tàizǐ Tàishī, had once bribed Xiāntóng with several qǐng of good land south of the city.
Lǐ Línfǔ exposed this,
and Sōng was demoted to Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
6th, Autumn,
8th month,
on the day Yǐhài,
Gài Jiāyùn, the Qīxī Jiédùshǐ, captured Tukīshī Khagan Tǔhuǒxiān.
Qī,
pronounced qī jì fān.
Gài,
pronounced gǔ hé fān.
Tǔhuǒxiān came out to battle,
was defeated and fled,
and was captured at Hèluólǐng.
He dispatched Fūméng Língchá, the Shūlè Zhènshǒushǐ, and Āxīlàndágān, the King of Báhànnà, to secretly lead troops to suddenly enter Táláshīchéng,
capturing the Black-Clothed Khagan Ěrwēi.
Then they entered Yèjiànchéng,
took Princess Jiāohé,
(the matter of Princess Jiāohé began in volume 212, 11th year),
and their might shook the western border.
7 On the day *rénwǔ*,
the Tǔbō attacked the Bácǎo and Ānrén garrisons, among others.
The Bácǎo garrison was west of the Wèirú River.
Also,
the Ānrén garrison was west of Xīngsù Chuān in Shànzhōu.
The Wèirú River is in Xiāoguān county, Yuánzhōu,
and at this time, Tǔbō troops could not have reached it.
It is suspected
that "Bácǎo Jūn"
should be
"Báishuǐ Jūn."
8 On the day *jiǎshēn*,
Kǒngzǐ was posthumously granted the title Wénxuān Wáng.
Previously,
when sacrifices were made to the Former Sage and Former Teacher,
Zhōugōng sat facing south,
and Kǒngzǐ sat facing east.
A decree stated:

His disciples were posthumously granted titles of Gōng, Hóu, or Bó.
