9 In the ninth month,
on the day *wùwǔ*,
the Chǔmùkūn, Shǔníshī, Gōngyuè, and other tribes that had formerly belonged to the Tūqíshī,
all led their multitudes to pledge allegiance to the court,
and furthermore requested to resettle within the jurisdiction of Ānxī.
10The crown prince's name was changed to Shào.
11In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day *xīnsì*,
the Míngtáng in Dōngdū was renovated.
According to the old imperial annals,
the Míngtáng was renovated by converting the Qiányuán Diàn in Dōngdū.
12On the day *bǐngxū*,
the emperor visited Lìshān Hot Springs;
in the eleventh month,
on the day *xīnchǒu*,
he returned to the palace.
13On the day *jiǎchén*,
the Míngtáng was completed.
14 Zhāng Yòu (張宥), the Jiànnán (劍南) Military Commissioner,
being a civil official, was not accustomed to military affairs.
He entrusted all military administration to the Vice Commissioner of Militias, Zhāngqí Gānqióng (章仇兼瓊).
According to old records,
the position of Commissioner of Militias was established after the Shàngyuán (上元) period.
My research into the Táng (唐) system shows
that wherever there were organized militia forces,
a Commissioner of Militias would be appointed.
At this time, Shǔ (蜀) had organized militia forces in the five prefectures of Lí (黎), Yǎ (雅), Qióng (邛), Yì (翼), and Mào (茂) for defense,
hence the appointment of a Vice Commissioner of Militias.
After the Ān (安)-Shǐ (史) Rebellion,
Commissioners of Militias were established in all prefectures.
He (Zhāngqí Gānqióng) spoke at length about how Ānróng Chéng (安戎城) could be captured,
and the Emperor was pleased.
On the dìngsì (丁巳) day,
Yòu (宥) was appointed Guānglù Qīng (光祿卿).
In the twelfth month,
Gānqióng (兼瓊) was appointed Jiànnán (劍南) Military Commissioner.
15 Initially,
after the mourning period for Ruìzōng (睿宗) ended,
a *xiá* (祫) ceremony was held at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
From then on, a *xiá* (祫) ceremony was held every three years,
and a *dì* (禘) ceremony every five years.
This year,
a *dì* (禘) ceremony had already been held in the summer,
and a *xiá* (祫) was due again in the winter.
The Grand Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng, 太常) deliberated, considering that frequent sacrifices would be irreverent,
and requested to suspend this year's *xiá* (祫) ceremony.
From then on, it was to be counted as one *xiá* (祫) and one *dì* (禘) every five years in total.
This was approved.
Historians say that this arrangement conforms to the principle of performing two major sacrifices every five years.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the guǐsì (癸巳) day,
the Emperor visited the Lìshān (驪山) Hot Springs.
On the gēngzǐ (庚子) day,
he returned to the palace.
2 In the second month,
Zhāng Jiǔlíng (張九齡), the Chángshǐ (長史) of Jīngzhōu (荊州), passed away.
Although the Emperor had dismissed Jiǔlíng (九齡)
for disagreeing with his will,
(*wǔ*, 忤, is pronounced *wú*),
he still loved and respected the man.
Whenever a chancellor recommended an official,
he would ask:
"Does his demeanor match Jiǔlíng's (九齡)?"
3 In the third month,
on the dīnghài (丁亥) day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
4 Zhāngqí Gānqióng (章仇兼瓊) secretly conspired with Zhái Dūjú (翟都局), a Tubó (吐蕃) official in Ānróng Chéng (安戎城), and Dǒng Chéngyàn (董承晏), the Assistant Prefect of Wéizhōu (維州).
He had Dūjú (都局) open the city gates to let in Táng (唐) troops,
kill all the Tubó (吐蕃) generals and soldiers,
and then had Censor Xǔ Yuǎn (許遠) lead troops to guard it.
Yuǎn (遠)
was the great-grandson of Jìngzōng (敬宗).
During the Yǒnghuī (永徽) and Xiǎnqìng (顯慶) periods,
Xǔ Jìngzōng (許敬宗) achieved high office as a chancellor through cunning and obsequiousness.
During the Ān (安)-Shǐ (史) Rebellion,
Yuǎn (遠) was able to die for his country as a loyal minister.
Historians therefore recorded his lineage to encourage ministers.
5 On the jiǎyín (甲寅) day,
Gài Jiāyùn (蓋嘉運) entered the court to present a report of victory.
The Emperor pardoned Tǔhuǒxiān's (吐火仙) crime
and appointed him General-in-Chief of the Left Golden Guard (Zuǒ Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn, 左金吾大將軍).
Jiāyùn (嘉運) requested to enthrone Āshǐnà Huáidào's (阿史那懷道) son, Xīn (昕), as the Kèhán (可汗) of the Ten Surnames (Shíxìng, 十姓).
This was granted.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The old tradition says:
"Jiāyùn (嘉運) wanted to enthrone Huáidào's (懷道) son, Xīn (昕), as Kèhán (可汗) to pacify them,
but Mòhè Dágān (莫賀達干) disagreed,
saying: 'Suppressing Sūlù (蘇祿)
was originally my primary strategy.
If Shǐ Xīn (史昕) is enthroned as ruler,
how will the state reward me?'
So, Shǐ Xīn (史昕) was not enthroned.
Instead, Mòhè Dágān (莫賀達干) was ordered to command the masses.
In the twenty-seventh year (of Kāiyuán),
Jiāyùn (嘉運) went to the capital to present captives,
and also ordered Tǔhuǒxiān (吐火仙) to be presented at the Grand Ancestral Temple."
The *Huìyào* (會要) states:
"In the twenty-ninth year,
Xīn (昕), the grandson of Jiěsèluó (解瑟羅) and son of Huáidào (懷道), was enthroned as Kèhán (可汗),
and troops were dispatched to escort him.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo (天寶),
Xīn (昕) reached Jùnán Chéng (俱南城) southwest of Suìyè (碎葉),
where he was killed by Mòhèduō Dádān (莫賀咄達干).
In the third year,
Mǎ Língchá (馬靈詧), the Ānxī (安西) Military Commissioner, beheaded him (Mòhèduō Dádān),
and enthroned another chieftain as Yīdì Mǐlǐ Gǔduōlù Pígā Kèhán (伊地米里骨咄祿毗伽可汗)."
According to the *Shílù* (實錄):
"In the twenty-eighth year of Kāiyuán (開元),
in the third month,
on the jiǎyín (甲寅) day,
Gài Jiāyùn (蓋嘉運) presented Tǔhuǒxiān (吐火仙) as a captive.
In the fourth month,
on the xīnwèi (辛未) day,
Xīn's (昕) wife, Lady Lǐ (李氏), was enfeoffed as Princess Jiāohé (交河 Gōngzhǔ).
In the twelfth month, on the yǐmǎo (乙卯) day,
Mòhè Dágān (莫賀達干), the Kèhán (可汗) of the Tūqíshī (突騎施), led his wife, children, and over a hundred chieftain leaders to submit.
Previously,
Mòhè Dágān (莫賀達干) and Wūsū Wànluòshàn (烏蘇萬洛扇) had incited various tribes to rebel against us.
The Emperor ordered Gài Jiāyùn (蓋嘉運) to proclaim benevolence and persuade them,
and they all came to surrender."
The *Xīnzhuàn* (新傳) says:
"Dágān (達干) refused to enthrone Xīn (昕),
and immediately incited his tribes to rebel.
An imperial edict ordered Jiāyùn (嘉運) to persuade them,
so he (Mòhè Dágān) led his wife and children to surrender,
and was then commanded to lead their masses.
Several years later,
Xīn (昕) was again enthroned as Kèhán (可汗)
and escorted by troops.
Xīn (昕) reached Jùlán Chéng (俱蘭城)
where he was killed by Mòhèduō (莫賀咄).
Mòhèduō (莫賀咄) enthroned himself as Kèhán (可汗),
and Fūméng Língchá (夫蒙靈詧), the Ānxī (安西) Military Commissioner, executed him."
If the old tradition is true,
that Jiāyùn (嘉運) immediately appointed Mòhè Dágān (莫賀達干) as Kèhán (可汗) to command the masses,
then Mòhè (莫賀) should not have rebelled again.
Furthermore, the enthronement of a Kèhán (可汗) must be by imperial decree of the court.
How could Jiāyùn (嘉運) simply enthrone him beyond the frontier?
If he was not yet made Kèhán (可汗),
then the *Shílù* (實錄) in the twelfth month should not have referred to him as Mòhè Dágān (莫賀達干), the Kèhán (可汗) of the Tūqíshī (突騎施).
If the *Huìyào* (會要) is true,
that Xīn (昕) was enthroned as Kèhán (可汗) only in the twenty-ninth year,
then the *Shílù* (實錄) in the fourth month of the twenty-eighth year should not have already referred to Xīn (昕) as the Kèhán (可汗) of the Ten Surnames.
After Gài Jiāyùn (蓋嘉運) pacified the Tūqíshī (突騎施),
he immediately memorialized to enthrone Xīn (昕) as the Kèhán (可汗) of the Ten Surnames,
which is why Mòhè Dágān (莫賀達干) was not appeased and rebelled.
Emperor Míng (明皇) then made Mòhè Dágān (莫賀達干) a minor Kèhán (可汗),
only to command the Tūqíshī (突騎施) masses,
and sent Jiāyùn (嘉運) to persuade him,
which is why he surrendered.
However, Xīn (昕) was the Kèhán (可汗) of the Ten Surnames,
commanding all the tribes,
so Emperor Míng (明皇) sent troops to escort him,
and he was killed by Mòhè Dágān (莫賀達干).
This might be what happened.
But the *Shílù* (實錄) is abridged,
so I dare not make definitive judgments.
Therefore, I have briefly gathered what is seen in various books,
and recorded the general outline.
In the fourth month,
on the xīnwèi (辛未) day,
Xīn's (昕) wife, Lady Lǐ (李氏), was enfeoffed as Princess Jiāohé (交河 Gōngzhǔ).
6 In the sixth month,
the Tubó (吐蕃) besieged Ānróng Chéng (安戎城).
7 The Emperor highly praised Gài Jiāyùn's accomplishments,
and appointed him as Jìedùshǐ of Héxī and Lǒngyòu,
entrusting him with the strategy against Tǔbō.
Gài Jiāyùn, presuming upon imperial favor, lingered,
and did not depart in a timely manner.
Gài Jiāyùn relied on his frontier achievements to endear himself to the sovereign;
this was drifting along with the current at the top.
While in the capital, he indulged in wine and women and did not immediately proceed to his post;
this was drifting along with the current at the bottom.
The historian's use of the two words "liúlián" (lingered)
is profound!
Thinking:
"Your servant recently served in the same rank as Gài Jiāyùn.
Observing his actions,
he certainly possesses abundant courage and ferocity,
yet his words and demeanor are boastful and arrogant.
I fear he will find it difficult to succeed.
In the past, Mó'áo felt complacent after the campaign of Púsāo,
and ultimately lost the Chǔ army.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states: Chǔ's Mó'áo, Qū Xiá, after defeating the Yún army at Púsāo,
again attacked Luó.
Dòu Bóxī, seeing him off, said:
'Mó'áo will surely be defeated;
his stride is high,
and his heart is not firm.'
He then saw the Lord of Chǔ.
The Lord of Chǔ went in and told his consort, Dèng Màn.
Dèng Màn said:
'Mó'áo is complacent after the campaign of Púsāo,
and will act on his own.
If Your Majesty does not keep him in check and encourage him,
will he not neglect to prepare?'
Mó'áo indeed did not prepare.
When he reached Luó,
Luó and Lúróng jointly attacked him with two armies,
and utterly defeated him.
Nǐu,
read Nǚjiǔ.
Lù Démíng said: Sāo,
pronounced xiāo,
also pronounced shēn.
Zú,
read zǐxù.
Your servant secretly worries about this.
Moreover, the autumn defense is not far off,
and he has not yet specified a departure date.
If he only leaves when the matter is urgent,
then the officers and soldiers will not yet be acquainted with each other.
How can he control the enemy?
Furthermore, a general receiving orders
proceeds through the 'ominous gate' and sets out;
yet now he is indulging in drink morning and night.
This is surely not the heart of one who worries about the nation and loves its people.
If he cannot change,
it would be advisable to quickly dispatch him to advance on the road,
and further beg for Your Sacred Grace to strictly instruct and encourage him."
The Emperor then urged Gài Jiāyùn to proceed.
Afterwards, Gài Jiāyùn ultimately achieved nothing.
Gài Jiāyùn was small-minded and easily satisfied,
his ambition and spirit having grown lazy.
How could he achieve anything?
8 Autumn,
eighth month,
on the day Jiǎxū,
Yōuzhōu reported a victory over the Xī and Qìdān.
9 Winter,
tenth month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ,

10 Tǔbō raided Ānróngchéng and Wéizhōu;

Ānróngchéng was renamed Píngróng.
11 Eleventh month,
Niú Xiānkè was dismissed as Jìedùshǐ of Shuòfāng and Hédōng.
12 The Tūqíshī Mòhè Dágān heard that Āshǐnà Xīn was made Kèhán,

"The initial execution of Sūlù was my plan;

how am I to be rewarded?"
Thereupon, he led his various tribes in rebellion.
The Emperor then appointed Mòhè Dágān as Kèhán,

and ordered Gài Jiāyùn to persuade and appease him.
Twelfth month,

13 Jīnchéng Gōngzhǔ passed away;
the events concerning Jīnchéng Gōngzhǔ began in chapter 280, Jǐnglóng first year of Zhōngzōng.
Furthermore, he requested peace,
but the Emperor did not grant it.
14 In this year,
there were 1,573 counties in the empire,
8,412,871 households,
and 48,143,609 mouths.
The price of a *hú* of rice in Xīyīng and Dōngdū was less than 200 cash,
and a bolt of silk was also the same.
The empire was prosperous and peaceful;
travelers, even for ten thousand *lǐ*, did not carry a single weapon.
Despite the peace and stability of Kāiyuán,
the population still did not reach the peak of the Hàn dynasty.
Since the rise of the Táng,
there have been fewer days of order and more days of chaos.
1 Spring,
first month,
on the day Guǐsì,
the Emperor visited the Lìshān Hot Springs.
2 On the day Dīngyǒu,
an edict stated:
"Previously, in cases of famine in various prefectures,
it was always necessary to wait for a report and approval
before granaries could be opened for relief.
Chéngqián,
like today's 'cóngqián' (in the past);
ránshǐ,
like today's 'ránhòu' (afterwards).
How could this rescue those in dire straits?
From now on, the chief officials of the prefectures and counties, along with the Cǎifǎngshǐ, are entrusted to provide relief as appropriate and then report it to the throne."
3 On the day Gēngzǐ,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
〠4 The Emperor dreamt that Xuányuán Huángdì told him:
"I have an image located more than a hundred *lǐ* southwest of the capital.
You should send someone to seek it,
and I shall meet you at Xīngqìng Gōng."
The events of Sòng's Dàzhōng Xiángfú
were all taught by Táng Mínghuáng.
Zhōuzhì Xiàn,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Fúfēng;
later, the Northern Wèi merged it into Wǔgōng,
then soon restored it.
In the Northern Zhōu, it was Zhōunán Jùn;
the Suí abolished the commandery,
placing Zhōuzhì Xiàn under Yōngzhōu;
in the Táng, it belonged to Qízhōu.
Sū Shì said: "The Guānshān Pavilion,
now Chóngshèng Guān,
was the old residence of Yǐn Xǐ.
At the foot of the mountain is the Shòujīng Tái,
which still exists."
Shǐ,
read shūlì.
Zhōuzhì,
pronounced zhōu zhì.
Guān,
read gǔwán;
same below.
In the intercalary fourth month,
it was welcomed and placed in Xīngqìng Gōng.
Fifth month,
an order was given to paint true likenesses of Xuányuán,
and distribute them to the Kāiyuán Guān in various prefectures.
5 Sixth month,
400,000 Tǔbō troops invaded,
reaching Ānrén Jūn.
"Ānrén Jūn"
should be
"Ānrén Jūn."
6 Autumn,
seventh month,
on the day Bǐngyín,
the Tūjué sent an envoy to announce the death of Dēnglì Kèhán.
Initially,
Dēnglì had two paternal uncles
who divided command of the armed forces,
known as the Left and Right Shà.
Dēnglì was troubled by the exclusive power of the two Shà.
He plotted with his mother,
lured the Right Shà,
and beheaded him,
personally leading his troops.
The Left Shà, Pàn Quètèlè, mustered troops and attacked Dēnglì,
killing him.
He then enthroned the son of Píjiā Kèhán as Kèhán;
shortly after, he was killed by Gǔduō Yèhù,
who then enthroned his younger brother.
Soon after, he also killed him,
and Gǔduō Yèhù enthroned himself as Kèhán.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The old tradition states:
"The Left Shà enthroned himself as Wūsūmǐshī Kèhán."
The *Tánglì* and new biographies both state
"Pàn Quètèlè's son was Wūsūmǐshī Kèhán,
enthroned at the beginning of Tiānbǎo";
this is followed now.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
Sūn Lǎonú, the Left Yǔlín General, was ordered to persuade and appease the Huíhé, Gěluólù, Bábàmì, and other tribes.
7 On the day Yǐhài,
the Luòshuǐ in Dōngdū overflowed,
drowning over a thousand people.
8 Ān Lùshān, Pinglú's Commissioner of Military Affairs,
was cunning,
and skilled at serving people.
Many praised him.
Those around the emperor who went to Pínglú,
Lùshān heavily bribed all of them.
Because of this, the emperor increasingly considered him worthy.
Zhāng Lìzhēn, the Censor-in-chief, became the Investigator of Héběi.
When he arrived at Pínglú,
Lùshān painstakingly served Lìzhēn,
and even those around him received bribes.
When Lìzhēn returned to court,
he lavishly praised Lùshān's merits.
In the eighth month,
on the *yǐwèi* day,
Lùshān was appointed Governor of Yíngzhōu,
and concurrently Commissioner of Pínglú Army.
A note on discrepancies says: The Veritable Records state that
in this year,
"in the eighth month, on the *yǐwèi* day,
Ān Lùshān, Deputy Military Commissioner of Yōuzhōu, was appointed Prefect of Yíngzhōu,
and concurrently Commissioner of Pínglú, Bóhǎi, and Hēishuǐ Armies."
The Old Annals state:
"Ān Lùshān, Deputy Military Commissioner of Yōuzhōu, was appointed Prefect of Yíngzhōu,
and Deputy Military Commissioner of Pínglú Army."
The *Huìyào* states:
"In the twenty-eighth year,
Wáng Húxī was appointed Military Commissioner of Pínglú,
which thus became a fixed post."
According to old biographies,
Lùshān went from Commissioner of Military Affairs of Pínglú to Commissioner of Pínglú Army.
Perhaps the title "Commissioner of Military Affairs of Pínglú" was merely an additional title to his "Deputy Military Commissioner of Yōuzhōu."
The Veritable Records' inclusion of the character
is an error.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo,
Pínglú was first made a military commission.
The *Huìyào* is mistaken.
The Táng referred to the Xī and Qìdān as the "Two Fān."
9 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the *bǐngshēn* day,
the emperor visited the Lìshān Hot Springs.
10On the *rénchén* day,
Běitíng and Ānxī were divided into two military commissions.
11In the eleventh month,
on the *gēngxū* day,
Shǒulǐ, Prince of Bīn and Minister of Works, passed away.
Shǒulǐ was mediocre and untalented.
However, whenever it was about to rain or clear up,
Shǒulǐ would always predict it first,
and it would always be accurate.
The princes of Qí and Xuē told the emperor:
"Brother Bīn has a special skill."
The emperor asked the reason,
to which he replied:
"I have no special skill.
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's time, because of Zhānghuái,
I was imprisoned in the palace for over ten years.
(Shǒulǐ's imprisonment is mentioned in volume 204, Empress Wǔ's Tiānshòu first year.)
I developed a very thick scar on my back.
When it is about to rain, it feels heavy and stuffy;
when it is about to clear up, it feels light and refreshed.
This is how I know."
He then wept, soaking his robes,
and the emperor also felt saddened by this.
12On the *xīnyǒu* day,
the emperor returned to the palace.
13On the *xīnwèi* day,
Xiàn, Prince of Níng and Grand Commandant, passed away.
The emperor was particularly grief-stricken,
saying:
"The empire
was my brother's empire;
my brother firmly yielded it to me.
(This event is mentioned in volume 210, Ruìzōng's Jǐngyún first year.)
Wǎn (惋) is pronounced like *wǔguàn*.
A common posthumous title is not sufficient for him."
So he was posthumously titled Emperor Ràng.
His son, Lùyángwáng Jìn,
submitted a memorial tracing his father's original intention,
humbly declining to accept the imperial title.
The emperor did not permit it.
On the day of the funeral,
imperial robes were brought out,
which were the robes of an emperor.
The document was signed
"Lóngjī Bái" (隆基白);
his tomb was also named Huìlíng.
(Huìlíng is ten *lǐ* northwest of Fèngxiān County in Tóngzhōu.)
He was interred there.
14In the twelfth month,
on the *yǐsì* day,
Tǔbō massacred Dálhuà County.
(Dálhuà was the ancient land of Jiāohé.
The Later Zhōu established Dálhuà Commandery and County.
The Suí abolished the commandery,
assigning the county to Kuòzhōu.
One hundred and twenty *lǐ* west of the county was Jiāohé City.)
Gài Jiāyùn was unable to resist them.
It was exactly as Péi Yàoqīng had said.

The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The Old Annals say,
"In the tenth month, on Wùyín (戊寅), he visited the Hot Springs Palace;
in the eleventh month, on Yǐmǎo (乙卯), he returned to the palace,"
which is consistent with the Shílù (實錄).
"In the twelfth month, on Wùshēn (戊申), he again visited the Hot Springs Palace;
on Bǐngchén (丙辰), he returned to the palace,"
is not in the Shílù (實錄).
According to the twelfth month, Bǐngyín (丙寅) was the first day of the month,
so there were no Wùshēn (戊申) or Bǐngchén (丙辰) days.
The Táng (唐) Calendar says:
"In the eleventh month, on Wùshēn (戊申), he visited the Hot Springs Palace;
on Bǐngchén (丙辰), he returned to the capital,"
which is also different from the Shílù Běnjì (實錄本紀).
Therefore, neither is adopted here.

Historians say that the Tang ruler was deluded and mad, while his officials were obsequious and flattering.

Zhōngsì (忠嗣) had been proud of his bravery in his youth.
When he governed the frontier regions,
he focused solely on maintaining stability and securing the borders,
often saying:
"A general in times of peace
should only comfort and train his soldiers,
and not exhaust the strength of the Middle Kingdom to seek personal glory."
He had a lacquered bow weighing 150 catties,
which he always kept in its quiver
to demonstrate his reluctance to use it.
The army constantly thought of battle day and night,
but Zhōngsì (忠嗣) often sent spies to look for opportune moments.
Only when victory was assured
would he dispatch his troops,
thus ensuring success in every expedition.
Having concurrently controlled the two circuits,
from Shuòfāng (朔方) to Yúnzhōng (雲中),
a frontier of several thousand *lǐ*,
all strategic locations
were garrisoned with castles and fortresses,
extending the territory by several hundred *lǐ* in each direction.
The border people believed that no general

they all falsely confessed,
The case was concluded in an instant,
and examination of the prisoners showed no signs of torture.
In the sixth month,
on the day of Xīnhài (辛亥),

an imperial edict reproached the Vice Ministers (Shìláng, 侍郎) and Lang Officers (Lángguān, 郎官) who had been in charge of personnel selection (quán, 銓) and presided over the Southern Bureau (Náncáo, 南曹) in the past, but then pardoned them.
In the second year of Kàichéng (開成) of Wénzōng (文宗),
the Prime Minister (Zǎixiàng, 宰相) Lǐ Shí (李石) presented a new regulation (xuǎngé, 選格) for the Southern Bureau (Náncáo, 南曹) which he had finalized.
The Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù, 吏部) requested the addition of one Langzhong (Lángzhōng, 郎中) to the Southern Bureau (Náncáo, 南曹),
and a separate seal,
with
"Seal of the Newly Established Southern Bureau"
as its inscription.
Originally, the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù, 吏部) had its Lang Officials (Lángguān, 郎官) preside over the Southern Bureau (Náncáo, 南曹),
but during the Kàichéng (開成) era, a Lang (Láng, 郎) was specifically appointed for the Southern Bureau (Náncáo, 南曹).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: The Southern Bureau (Náncáo, 南曹) was established in the second year of Zǒngzhāng (總章),
when the Comptroller of Appointments (Sīliè Chángbó, 司列常伯) Lǐ Jìngxuán (李敬玄) proposed its creation.
Before its establishment,
personnel selection matters were handled internally.
According to old customs,
there were two rotation halls (zhuǎntīng, 轉廳).
In the first year of Jiànzhōng (建中),
Vice Minister (Shìláng, 侍郎) Shào Yuè (邵說) impeached and removed Wáng Xuān (王鋗), the Langzhong (Lángzhōng, 郎中) of the Southern Bureau (Náncáo, 南曹), after which
the rotation hall system (zhuǎntīng, 轉廳) ceased.
In the eleventh year of Zhēnyuán (貞元),
Vice Minister (Shìláng, 侍Láng, 郎) Dù Huángcháng (杜黃裳) requested to reinstate the rotation hall (zhuǎntīng, 轉廳) according to the old precedent.
Later, and so on,
same as above.
Qiào (誚),
rhymes with cái and xiào.
(Jí Wēn, 吉溫) was Jūn's (均) elder brother;
Wēn (溫)
was Xù's (頊) nephew.
Jí Xù (吉頊) gained favor and was promoted during the time of Empress Wǔ (武后).
Wēn (溫) first served as Magistrate (Chéng, 丞) of Xīnfēng (新豐).
Tàizǐ Wénxué (太子文學) Xuē Nì (薛嶷) recommended Wēn's (溫) talent.
The Táng Liùdiǎn (唐六典) states: The Wei (魏) dynasty established the Tàizǐ Wénxué (太子文學).
When Wèi Wǔ (魏武) was Chancellor (Chéngxiàng, 丞相),
he appointed Sīmǎ Xuānwáng (司馬宣王) as Wénxué Yuàn (文學掾),
who was greatly trusted by the Crown Prince (Shìzǐ, 世子).
He, along with Wú Zhì (吳質), Zhū Shuò (朱鑠), and Chén Qiē (陳㣥), formed the four friends of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Sìyǒu, 太子四友).
After the Jin (晉) dynasty, it was no longer established.
It was not until the third year of Jiàndé (建德) in the Later Zhou (後周) that
ten Tàizǐ Wénxué (太子文學) were appointed,
but later abolished.
In the Xiǎnqìng (顯慶) era of the Tang (唐) dynasty,
two Tàizǐ Wénxué (太子文學) were first established,
subordinate to the Sījīng Jú (司經局),
responsible for managing classics and literature,
attending to literary matters,
and compiling classics.
The work of copying, binding, and dyeing,
and the number of writing brushes and supplies,
were all estimated and managed by them.
Nì (嶷),
rhymes with yú and lì.
Gù Nì (顧嶷) said:
"This is a bad person.
I will not employ him."
Xiāo Jiǒng (蕭炅) became the Prefect of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn, 河南尹)
and was once involved in a case.
The Xītái (西臺) sent Wēn (溫) to investigate it.
Xītái (西臺) refers to the Censorate of the Western Capital (Xījīng Yùshǐtái, 西京御史臺).
Later, Wēn (溫) became the Magistrate (Chéng, 丞) of Wànnián (萬年).
Not long after, Jiǒng (炅) became the Jīngzhào Yǐn (京兆尹).
Wēn (溫) had always been associated with Gāo Lìshì (高力士).
When Lìshì (力士) returned from the palace,
Wēn (溫) knew that Jiǒng (炅) would surely go to offer his thanks for the appointment.
So he went to Lìshì (力士) first,
chatted and joked with him,
and shook hands very happily.
Jiǒng (炅) arrived later.
Wēn (溫) feigned surprise and avoided him.
Lìshì (力士) called out:
"Jí Qī (吉七) (Seventh Jí) doesn't need to avoid me."
Jí Wēn (吉溫) was the seventh son.
"This is also an old friend of mine."
He called Wēn (溫) back and
had him sit with Jiǒng (炅).
Jiǒng (炅) treated him very respectfully,
not daring to hold a grudge over previous matters.
Another day,
Wēn (溫) visited Jiǒng (炅) and said:
"Previously, I did not dare to violate the national laws.
From now on, I wish to serve you wholeheartedly."
Jiǒng (炅) then became very friendly with him
and appointed him as the Judicial Officer (Fǎcáo, 法曹).
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The Tánglì (唐曆) says:
"Wēn (溫) was involved in major interrogations,
relying on the law to collude with evil,
and manipulating people's lives for over ten years.
He was cunning and slanderous by nature,
cruel and fearless.
Anyone who displeased him in the slightest
would surely be implicated and entrapped.
If he wanted to solidify a relationship,
even with princes and high-ranking officials,
he could quickly become intimate with them.
Initially,
Xiāo Jiǒng (蕭炅) was imprisoned for corruption,
and Wēn (溫) thoroughly investigated his crime.
Later, when Wēn (溫) was the Magistrate (Xiàn Chéng, 縣丞) of Wànnián (萬年),
Jiǒng (炅) was appointed Jīngzhào Yǐn (京兆尹).
Wēn (溫) met Jiǒng (炅) at Gāo Lìshì's (高力士) residence,
and they formed a strong bond,
becoming as close as glue and lacquer.
Jiǒng (炅) appointed him as Judicial Officer (Fǎcáo, 法曹)
and recommended him to Línfǔ (林甫).
Wēn's (溫) advancement was, in turn, due to Jiǒng's (炅) influence."
The Jiùzhuàn (舊傳) says:
"When Jiǒng (炅) was the Prefect of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn, 河南尹),
he was involved in a matter.
The Jīngtái (京臺) dispatched Wēn (溫) to investigate and interrogate him,
and Wēn (溫) was unyielding.
When Wēn (溫) was selected for a new post,
Jiǒng (炅) had already become the Jīngzhào Yǐn (京兆尹).
He was first assigned as the Constable (Wèi, 尉) of Wànnián (萬年),
and immediately took up the post.
People feared for him."
Now, these two accounts are combined for use.
When Línfǔ (林甫) wanted to eliminate those who did not support him,
he sought out skilled judicial officers.
Jiǒng (炅) recommended Wēn (溫) to Línfǔ (林甫);
Línfǔ (林甫) was overjoyed to have him.
Wēn (溫) often said:
"If I meet a true confidant,
even the white-browed tiger of Nánshān (南山) is not enough to bind."
At that time, there was also Luó Xīshì (羅希奭) from Hángzhōu (杭州),
who was a harsh and severe official.
Línfǔ (林甫) brought him in,
promoting him from Secretary of the Censorate (Yùshǐtái Zhǔbù, 御史臺主簿) to Palace Attendant Censor (Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ, 殿中侍御史).
The Secretary of the Censorate (Yùshǐtái Zhǔbù, 御史臺主簿) in the Tang (唐) dynasty was of rank seven upper,
responsible for seals, receiving and dispatching documents,
checking for errors,
and overseeing official kitchens and imperial archives.
They fabricated and completed cases,
from which no one could escape.
People at the time called them
"Luó's (羅) pincers and Jí's (吉) net."
To bind things with iron pliers is called qián (鉗).
Qián (鉗),
rhymes with qí and lián.
7 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day of Rénwǔ (壬午),
Wèi Zhāoxùn's (韋昭訓) daughter was enfeoffed as the Princess Consort of Shòu Wáng (壽王).
In the eighth month,
on the day *Rényín*,
Lady Yáng Tàizhēn was enfeoffed as *Guìfēi*.
A textual variant note says: The *Tǒngjì* states:
"In the eighth month, the female Daoist Yáng Shì was enfeoffed as *Guìfēi*."
The *Běnjì* has
"*Jiǎchén*",
and the *Tánglì* has
"*Jiǎyín*".
Now, based on the *Shílù*,
"on *Rényín*, her father Xuán Yǎn and others were posthumously granted official titles."
*Jiǎchén* and *Jiǎyín* both fall later,
so it is possible that the enfeoffment occurred before the posthumous grants.
The new *Běnjì* also says
"in the eighth month, on *Rényín*, Tàizhēn was established as *Guìfēi*,"
so we follow this.
Her uncle Xuán Guī was made *Guānglù Qīng*,
her cousin Shēn was made *Diànzhōng Shàojiān*,
and Qí was made *Fùmǎ Dūwèi*.
On *Guǐmǎo*,
Princess Wǔhuì's daughter was enfeoffed as Tàihuá Gōngzhǔ,
and Qí was ordered to marry her.
A textual variant note says: The *Shílù* and old biographies both consider Shēn and Qí to be second cousins,
and Guózhōng to be a paternal cousin of the grandfather's generation (from the same great-grandfather).
If so, then a paternal cousin of the grandfather's generation is also a second cousin.
During the time of bestowing imperial favor,
why were Shēn and Qí promoted but not Guózhōng?
The new biography calls him a paternal cousin (*zōngxiong*).
The *Tánglì* states Shēn was Xuán Yǎn's son.
Even if he wasn't his son,
compared to Guózhōng, he must have been somewhat closer;
yet he is merely called a cousin.
The old biography states Qí was a *Shìyùshǐ*.
Now we follow the *Shílù*.
They were all granted mansions in the capital,
and their favor and prestige were magnificent.
Yáng Zhāo,
a paternal cousin of *Guìfēi*'s grandfather's generation,
was uneducated and lacked moral conduct,
and was scorned by his kinsmen.
He served in the army in Shǔ,
and became the *Xīndū Wèi*.
When his term was up,
being poor, he could not return home on his own.
Xiānyú Zhòngtōng, a rich man from Xīnzhèng, often provided him with provisions.
Xīndū county
belonged to Guǎnghàn prefecture in the Hàn dynasty.
Liáng established Shǐkāng Commandery,
and Western Wèi abolished the commandery.
In the eighteenth year of Kāihuáng of Suí, Xīndū was renamed Xīnglè,
and soon the county was abolished.
In the early Táng, it was re-established
and belonged to Shǔ prefecture.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé, Nánbù and Xiāngrú counties were separated
and Xīnchéng county was established.
Soon, to avoid the name of the Crown Prince Yǐn,
it was renamed Xīnzhèng,
and at that time belonged to Lángzhōng Commandery.
Zhāo frequented his family's home,
and consequently had an affair with his second daughter.
Xiānyú Zhòngtōng, whose given name was Xiàng,
went by his courtesy name.
He was quite learned
and possessed talent and wisdom.
Zhāngqiú Jiānqióng, the *Jiànnán Jiédùshǐ*, appointed him as a *Cǎifǎng Zhīshǐ*.
A textual variant note says: The *Tánglì* states:
"He was a *Jiédù Xún Guān*."
According to the surviving stele for Zhòngtōng written by Yán Zhēnqīng,
it says
"he was a *Cǎifǎng Zhīshǐ*,"
so we follow this.
Under the Táng *Cǎifǎng* and *Jiédù Shǐ* and other envoys, their staff included *Pànguān*, *Zhīshǐ*, *Zhǎngshūjì*, *Tuīguān*, *Xúnguān*, and *Yátū*, etc.
The Sòng dynasty first established the system
that *Shūjì* and *Zhīshǐ* could not be simultaneously appointed;
those with official background became *Shūjì*,
and those without became *Zhīshǐ*.
Jiānqióng once leisurely said to Zhòngtōng:
"Currently, I alone am highly favored by the Emperor.
If I do not have internal support,
I will certainly be endangered by Lǐ Línfǔ.
I hear that the Yáng family has recently gained favor,
but people dare not attach themselves to them yet.
If you can go to Cháng'ān for me and forge ties with their family,
I will have no worries."
Zhòngtōng replied:
"I am a man of Shǔ and have never traveled to the capital.
I fear I might spoil your affairs.
I will find another person for you."
He then recounted Zhāo's background.
Jiānqióng met Zhāo,
who was impressive in appearance and quick-witted in speech.
Jiānqióng was greatly pleased,
immediately appointed him *Tuīguān*,
and their interactions became increasingly intimate.
Then he sent someone to present spring silk to the capital.
As they were about to part,
he said:
"There is a small amount of goods in Pí,
enough for a day's provisions.
When you pass through,
you may take them."
When Zhāo arrived in Pí,
Jiānqióng sent trusted confidants to give him a large quantity of exquisite Shǔ goods,
worth ten thousand strings of cash.
Zhāo was overjoyed beyond expectation,
traveling day and night.
Upon reaching Cháng'ān,
he visited all his female cousins (the sisters of *Guìfēi*),
presenting them with the Shǔ goods,
saying:
"These are gifts from His Excellency Zhāngqiú."
At that time, the second daughter had recently become a widow.
Zhāo then took lodging in her chamber,
dividing the Shǔ goods with her.
Thereupon, the Yáng family praised Jiānqióng day and night.
They also said Zhāo was skilled at *chūpú* (a dice game),
and introduced him to the Emperor.
He was allowed to enter and exit the Forbidden Palace with the *Gōngfèng Guān*.
The Táng system: Officials of the Central Secretariat and Chancellery were all *Gōngfèng Guān*.
External officials permitted to enter for audience with court officials were called *Zhàngnèi Gōngfèng*.
Those who followed the ranks of the Hanlin Academy officials were called *Hànlín Gōngfèng*.
Eunuchs were called *Nèi Gōngfèng*.
There were also court officials who served in the Forbidden Palace.
8 In the ninth month,
on *Guǐwèi*,
Wéi Jiān, the Prefect of Shǎn Commandery and Transport Commissioner for Jianghuai taxes and tributes, was made *Xíngbù Shàngshū*.
His various commissions were abolished.
Yáng Shènjīn, the *Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng*, replaced him.
Wéi Jiān's wife, Jiāng Shì,
was the daughter of Jiǎo,
and the niece of Línfǔ's maternal uncle.
Thus, Línfǔ was close to her.
When Jiān gained imperial favor for his success in water transport,
he developed aspirations to become a chancellor
and was also on good terms with Lǐ Shìzhī.
Línfǔ, therefore, disliked him,
and thus transferred him to a high-sounding official post,
but in reality stripped him of his power.
9 Ān Lùshān wished to gain favor through military achievements on the border.
He repeatedly raided the Xī and Qìdān.
The Xī and Qìdān each killed their princesses and rebelled.
Lùshān attacked and defeated them.
10 Huángfǔ Wéimíng, the *Lǒngyòu Jiédùshǐ*, battled the Túbō at Shíbǎo Castle.
He was defeated by the barbarians,
and his deputy general Chǔ Chèn died in battle.
11 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on *Jiǎwǔ*,
Ān Lùshān reported:
"Your servant attacked the Qìdān and reached Běipíng Commandery."
Běipíng Commandery
was Píngzhōu.
He then ordered a temple to be built.
He also reported that on the day of the dedication ceremony,
fungi grew on the temple's main beam.
The *Tōngjiàn* does not speak of anomalies,
yet it records the events of Ān Lùshān's birds eating locusts and fungi growing on the temple beam,
to show Lùshān's deceit
and Emperor Míng's delusion.
12 On *Dīngyǒu*,
the Emperor visited the Lìshān hot springs.
The emperor, 13, appointed Wáng Hóng (王鉷), a Lángzhōng (郎中) of the Hùbù (戶部), as the Hùkǒu Sèyì Shǐ (戶口色役使),
and issued an edict granting the common people exemptions (fùchú 復除).
Wáng Hóng (王鉷) then proposed to levy the cost of their cartage and transportation,
greatly inflating the monetary amounts.
He also made them purchase light goods from their home commanderies,
so that what the common people paid was actually far more than if they had not received the exemption.
According to the old system,
those serving on the border were exempted from their land tax (zūyōng 租庸),
and the term of service was six years.
At that time, the border generals were ashamed of their defeats,
and all soldiers who died were not reported,
nor were their names removed from the registers.
Guànjí (貫籍)
refers to the register of one's native place.
Since those who had names on the register but were no longer present were all considered to be evading taxes,
all their land tax (zūyōng 租庸) was levied for the period beyond the six years of border service according to the registers.
In some cases,
thirty years of back taxes were levied,
and the people had no one to complain to.
The emperor had been on the throne for a long time,
and his expenses became increasingly extravagant.
Awards and gifts in the imperial harem were without limit,
and he did not wish to frequently draw from the Zuǒcáng (左藏) and Yòucáng (右藏).
During the Táng (唐) dynasty, there were the Zuǒcáng (左藏) and Yòucáng (右藏).
Cáng (藏)
is pronounced "cú làng fān".
The annual tribute extra revenue
amounted to a hundred million,
stored in the Nèikù (內庫),
to supply banquets and gifts within the palace.
He said,
"These all do not come from the land tax (zūyōngdiào 租庸調),
and are not related to official expenditures."
The emperor considered Wáng Hóng (王鉷) capable of enriching the nation,
and treated him with even greater favor.
Wáng Hóng (王鉷) was eager to exploit the people to gain favor,
causing widespread complaints both inside and outside the court.
On the day Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
Wáng Hóng (王鉷) was appointed Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) and Jīngjī Cǎifǎng Shǐ (京畿采訪使).
Yáng Zhāo (楊釗) attended a banquet in the forbidden palace,
exclusively managing the accounts of the Chūpú (樗蒲) game,
meticulously checking and verifying them.
The emperor admired his astuteness,
saying,
"A good Dùzhī Láng (度支郎)."
The Táng (唐) Dùzhī Láng (度支郎) was in charge of determining the amount of rent and taxes (zūfù 租賦) in the empire,
the suitability of abundant or scarce local products,
and the benefits of water and land routes.
Each year, they would calculate the income and estimate the expenditure,
regulating the speed of transport, collection, and submission according to fixed procedures.
All agreements for purchasing grain (héxí 和糴) and goods (héshì 和市) were made by assessing their value,
balancing the goods of the empire to benefit the people.
All items such as gold, silver, precious treasures, silk, and brocade,
were used to offset labor service (yōngdiào 庸調) for their manufacture.
For all water and land transport by boats and carriages throughout the empire,
regulations were established based on the weight, value, ease, and difficulty of the foot-toll (jiǎozhí 腳直).
For all border armies in the empire, there was a Zhīdu Shǐ (支度使)
to account for the use of military provisions, grain, and weapons.
Annual expenses were all reported to the Dùzhī (度支) for accounting,
based on the emperor's long-standing directives.
Dù (度)
is pronounced "tú luò fān".
This office was also assigned to Wáng Hóng (王鉷),
who then recommended himself to serve as Pànguān (判官).
14th day of the twelfth month,
on the day Wùxū (戊戌),
the emperor returned to the palace.
He returned from the Wēnquán Gōng (溫泉宮).
Huán (還)
is pronounced "cóng xuān fān",
and also as written.
In the fifth year
(Bǐngxū 丙戌, 746)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the day Yǐchǒu (乙丑),
Huángfǔ Wéimíng (皇甫惟明), the Jiédu Shǐ (節度使) of Lǒngyòu (隴右), was concurrently appointed Jiédu Shǐ (節度使) of Héxī (河西).
Lǐ Shìzhī (李適之) was naturally careless and unrestrained.
Lǐ Línfǔ (李林甫) once said to Lǐ Shìzhī (李適之),
"There are gold mines in Huàshān (華山);
extracting from them could enrich the nation,
but the emperor is not aware of this yet."
Another day,
Lǐ Shìzhī (李適之) mentioned this during an audience with the emperor.
The emperor asked Lǐ Línfǔ (李林fǔ) about it,
who replied,
"Your subject has known of this for a long time,
but Huàshān (華山) is His Majesty's natal mountain,
where the imperial aura resides.
The imperial inscription on the Huáyùe (華嶽) stele states: 'When I, the humble one, was born,
it was in the year Jǐnxū (景戌),
the middle month of autumn.
I received the abundant virtue of Shǎohào (少皞),
and was in harmony with the natal mountain Tàihuá (太華).
Therefore, I often dream of the spiritual peak,
and have divine communion.'
Lǐ Línfǔ (李Línfǔ) knew this intention,
and thus misled Lǐ Shìzhī (李適之) to entrap him.
Wáng (王)
is pronounced "yú kuàng fān".
Therefore, I dared not speak of it."
The emperor believed Lǐ Línfǔ (李林fǔ) was devoted to him,
and thought Lǐ Shìzhī (李適之) was not thorough in his considerations,
saying to him,
"From now on, when you report matters,
you should first discuss them with Lǐ Línfǔ (李林fǔ).
Do not be hasty or reckless."
Lǐ Shìzhī (李適之) was thus constrained.
After Lǐ Shìzhī (李適之) lost imperial favor,
and Wéi Jiān (韋堅) lost power,
they became even closer,
which Lǐ Línfǔ (李林fǔ) resented more.
Initially,
the establishment of the Crown Prince was not Lǐ Línfǔ's (李林fǔ) intention.
This event is mentioned in volume 210, Kaiyuan 26th year.
He always harbored the ambition to destabilize the Eastern Palace;
and Wéi Jiān (韋堅)
was also the Crown Prince's elder brother.
Huángfǔ Wéimíng (皇甫惟明) had once been a friend to Zhōngwáng (忠王),
as mentioned in volume 213, Kaiyuan 18th year.
Upon entering the capital to present a victory report,
he saw Lǐ Línfǔ (李林fǔ) monopolizing power,
and his mood was quite displeased.
At that time, while seeing the emperor,
he subtly advised the emperor to remove Lǐ Línfǔ (李林fǔ) when there was an opportune moment.
Tǔ (吐)
is pronounced "cóng tūn rù shēng".
Yīn jiàn (因見)
is pronounced "xián biàn fān".
Jiān (間)
is pronounced "gǔ xiàn fān".
Qù (去)
is pronounced "qiāng lǚ fān".
He made Yáng Shènjīn (楊慎矜) secretly observe their actions.
It happened on the night of the Lantern Festival in the first month
that the Crown Prince went out for a stroll
and met Wéi Jiān (韋堅).
Wéi Jiān (韋堅) also met Huángfǔ Wéimíng (皇甫惟明) in the room of a Daoist priest at the Jǐnglóng Guān (景龍觀).
The Jǐnglóng Guān (景龍觀) was in the Chóngrén Fāng (崇仁坊) of Cháng'ān (長安) city.
It was northwest of Shēn Gōng Gāoshìlián Zhái Zuǒjīnwú Wèi (申公高士廉宅西北左金吾衞).
In the first year of Shénlóng (神龍),
it was incorporated into Chángníng Gōngzhǔ Zhái (長寧公主宅).
After Wéi Shùrén (韋庶人) was defeated,
it was established as a Daoist temple,
and named after the reign title of Zhōngzōng (中宗).
Guān (觀)
is pronounced "gǔ wán fān".
It was considered inappropriate for Wéi Jiān (韋堅), as a member of the imperial family,
to be close to a border general.
Lǐ Línfǔ (李林fǔ) then reported that Wéi Jiān (韋堅) and Huángfǔ Wéimíng (皇甫惟明) had conspired
to jointly establish the Crown Prince.
Wéi Jiān (韋堅) and Huángfǔ Wéimíng (皇甫惟明) were imprisoned.
Lǐ Línfǔ (李林fǔ) instructed Yáng Shènjīn (楊慎矜), together with Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) Wáng Hóng (王鉷) and Jīngzhào Fǔ Fǎcáo (京兆府法曹) Jí Wēn (吉溫), to jointly interrogate them.
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The old biography of Lǐ Línfǔ (李林fǔ) says:
"Lǐ Línfǔ (李林fǔ) secretly ordered Yáng Shènjīn (楊慎矜) to watch for Wéi Jiān's (韋堅) weaknesses,
and then report to the emperor."
The biography of Yáng Shènjīn (楊慎矜) says:
"When Wáng Hóng (王鉷) interrogated Wéi Jiān (韋堅),
Yáng Shènjīn (楊慎矜) stood neutrally and observed,
which Wáng Hóng (王鉷) resented,
and Lǐ Línfǔ (李林fǔ) also bore a grudge."
The two biographies contradict each other.
We now follow the Tánglì (唐曆).
On the day Guǐyǒu (癸酉),
an imperial edict was issued,
blaming Wéi Jiān (韋堅) for persistently seeking advancement
and demoting him to Jìnyún Tàishǒu (縉雲太守).
Jìnyún Jùn (縉雲郡) was originally Guā Zhōu (括州) Yǒngjiā Jùn (永嘉郡),
and its name was changed in the first year.
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The old records
say "demoted to Kuòcāng Tàishǒu (括蒼太守)."
We now follow the Shílù (實錄) and old biographies.
(Huángfǔ Wéimíng (皇甫惟明) was) demoted to Bōchuān Tàishǒu (播川太守).
Bōchuān Jùn (播川郡) is Bō Zhōu (播州).
2 Wáng Zhōngsì was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Héxī and Lǒngyòu,
concurrently overseeing the affairs of Shuòfāng and Hédōng Jìedù.
When Zhōngsì was initially in Shuòfāng and Hédōng,
whenever there were border markets,
he would overvalue the price of horses.
When the various Hú people heard of this,
they vied to sell horses to Táng.
Zhōngsì bought them all.
As a result, there were few Hú horses,
and Táng's army became stronger.
When he was transferred to Lǒngyòu and Héxī,
he again requested to transfer nine thousand horses from Shuòfāng and Hédōng to reinforce them,
and their army also became strong.
Zhōngsì wielded four credentials,
controlling ten thousand *lǐ*;
all of the empire's elite troops and important strongholds
were in his grasp.
He fought the Tǔbō at Qīnghǎi and Jīshí,
winning great victories in both.
He also campaigned against the Tǔyùhún at Mòlí Jūn,
capturing their entire tribe and returning.
Tǔ,
pronounced with the *tūn* entering tone.
Gǔ,
pronounced *yù*.
3 Summer,
fourth month,
*Guǐwèi* day.
Xī tribal chief Suōgù was made Zhāoxìn Wáng,
and Qìdān tribal chief Kǎiluò was made Gōngrén Wáng.
4 On the *Jǐhài* day,
an edict was issued:
"From now on, in the four *Mèng* months,
auspicious days shall be chosen to offer sacrifices to Heaven and Earth and the Jiǔgōng."
5 After Wéi Jiān and others were demoted,
Left Chancellor Lǐ Shìzhī was afraid,
and requested a less critical position for himself.
On the *Gēngyín* day,
Shìzhī was made Tàizǐ Shàobǎo,
and relieved of governmental affairs.
His son, Wèiwèi Shàoqīng Zhà, once prepared a grand feast and invited guests,
but the guests feared Lǐ Línfǔ,
and not a single person dared to attend all day.
6 Ménxià Shìláng and Chóngxuán Guǎn Dàxuéshì Chén Xīliè was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
The Later Wèi established the Chóngxuán Shǔ,
in charge of monks, nuns, Daoist priests, and Daoist priestesses.
The Suí placed the Chóngxuán Shǔ under the Hónglú.
The Táng established supervisors for various temples and monasteries,
under the Hónglú,
with one supervisor for each temple or monastery;
in the Zhēnguān period,
the temple and monastery supervisors were abolished.
In the second year of Shàngyuán,
the Qīyuán Jiān was established,
but soon abolished;
in the twenty-fifth year of Kāiyuán,
the Chóngxuán Xué was established at the Xuányuán Huángdì Miào;
in the first year of Tiānbǎo,
one Bóshì and one Zhùjiào were appointed in both capitals.
In the second year,
the Chóngxuán Xué was renamed Chóngxuán Guǎn,
the Bóshì were renamed Xuéshì,
and the Zhùjiào were renamed Zhí Xuéshì;
a Dàxuéshì was established,
held by the prime minister,
overseeing the Xuányuán Gōng and Daoist temples in both capitals.
Chén Xīliè, a native of Sòngzhōu,
advanced through lecturing on Lǎo and Zhuāng,
and specialized in using tales of immortals, talismans, and auspicious omens to ingratiate himself with the emperor.
Lǐ Línfǔ, seeing that Xīliè was favored by the emperor
and was docile and easy to control,
therefore recommended him as chancellor;
all governmental affairs were decided by Línfǔ,
and Xīliè merely offered his consent.
According to custom,
chancellors would not leave until six *kè* after noon;
Línfǔ submitted a memorial, stating that
as there was peace and no trouble,
he would return home at *Sì* hour,
and all military and state affairs were decided in his private residence;
the chief clerk merely took the completed documents to Xīliè to sign his name.
7 Fifth month,
on the *Rénzǐ* day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
8 On the *Yǐhài* day,
Zhāngchóu Jiānqióng, Jìedùshǐ of Jiànnán, was made Hùbù Shàngshū;
this was due to the influence of the various Yáng family members.
9 Autumn,
seventh month,
on the *Bǐngchén* day,
an imperial decree stated:
"Many exiled officials delay on the journey.
From now on, demoted officials must travel more than ten post stations per day."
After this, many exiled individuals did not complete their journey intact.
10 Yáng Guìfēi was favored.
Whenever she rode a horse, Gāolìshì would hold the reins and hand her the whip.
Seven hundred artisans specializing in weaving and embroidery were exclusively dedicated to her distinguished residence.
Officials inside and outside the court vied to present her with vessels, clothing, rare treasures, and curiosities.
Zhāng Jiǔzhāng, Jīnglüèshǐ of Lǐngnán,
and Wáng Yì, Chángshǐ of Guǎnglíng.
Guǎnglíng Commandery
is Yángzhōu.
Cháng,
pronounced in two ways.
Jiǔzhāng was promoted to the third rank,
and Yì entered as Hùbù Shìláng;
the whole empire followed suit.
The common people sang:
"Rejoice not at the birth of a son, grieve not at the birth of a daughter,
for now you see daughters making the family's façade."
Whenever people build a house,
those who come from outside,
seeing its broad and spacious lintel,
consider it a magnificent sight.
This means the Yáng family was exalted because of the birth of a daughter.
Some say: a door is propped up by its lintel,
meaning that daughters can support the household.
Each year, an order was given to Lǐngnán to dispatch *lìzhī* by post-horse.
From Sū Shì and others,
all say that at this time *lìzhī* was dispatched from Fúzhōu,
not Lǐngnán.
Its color and taste remained unchanged.
Bái Jūyì said: *lìzhī* grows between Bā and Xiá.
Its tree form is round like a canopy,
its leaves are like holly,
its flowers like oranges,
blooming in spring.
Its fruit is like vermilion,
ripening in summer.
Its clusters are like grapes,
its pits like loquats,
its skin like red silk,
its membrane like purple gauze,
its pulp white as ice and snow,
its juice sweet and sour like *lǐlào*.
Generally as described,
but in reality, it is even better.
If separated from its branch,
its color changes in one day,
its fragrance changes in two days,
and after four or five days, its color, fragrance, and taste are all gone.
At this point,
because of her jealous and fierce insubordination,
the Emperor was enraged
and ordered her to be sent back to the residence of her brother, Xiān.
On this day,
the Emperor was displeased.
By midday,
he still had not eaten,
and his attendants, acting without pleasing him,
were arbitrarily flogged.
Gāo Lìshì wanted to test the Emperor's intentions,
so he requested that all the stored provisions in the court be loaded and sent to Guì,
totaling over a hundred carts.
The Emperor personally divided his imperial meals to bestow upon her.
At night,
Lìshì secretly submitted a memorial requesting to welcome Guì back to the court,
and so the forbidden gates were opened for her to enter.
The Táng Liùdiǎn states: "The Chéngménláng is in charge of the regulations for the opening and closing of all gates of the capital city, the imperial city, and the palaces.
When the dawn drum is beaten at Chéngtiānmén,
a quarter of an hour after the bell is struck,
when the drum sound ceases,
the Imperial City gates open.
When the first 'dōng dōng' drum sound ceases,
the Palace City gates and the Zuǒyánmíngmén, Yòuyánmíngmén, and Gānhuàmén open.
When the second 'dōng dōng' drum sound ceases,
the Palace Hall gates open.
At night,
when the first 'dōng dōng' drum sound ceases,
the Palace Hall gates close.
When the second 'dōng dōng' drum sound ceases,
the Palace City gates close,
as do the Zuǒyánmíngmén, Yòuyánmíngmén, and Imperial City gates.
The opening and closing of the Capital City gates
occur at the same moment as the Imperial City gates.
When the drum is beaten at Chéngtiānmén,
it is always according to the markers of the clepsydra;
the drum is beaten when the marker arrives.
Only when the plaque on the clepsydra reaches the designated point
does the drum sound cease.
For all keys to the closed Imperial City gates,
they are taken out before Yǒu (5-7 PM)
and brought in after Xū (7-9 PM).
For the keys to the open gates,
they are taken out after Chǒu (1-3 AM)
and brought in when night ends.
For the keys to the closed Capital City gates,
they are taken out after Shēn (3-5 PM)
and brought in before Zǐ (11 PM-1 AM).
For the keys to the open gates,
they are taken out after Zǐ (11 PM-1 AM)
and brought in before Mǎo (5-7 AM).
If it is not the designated time,
but there is an order to open or close,
one must go to the閤 to report,
and open or close only upon imperial decree and matching of tally.
For palace gates and city gates,
if there is an imperial edict to open them at night,
the recipient of the edict must fully record the gates to be opened
and declare and send the record to the Zhōngshūménxià."
Zì,
pronounced like "lǐ".
No one else in the Hòugōng was allowed to enter.
Jiāngzuò Shǎojiàng Wèi Lán and Bīngbù Yuánwàiláng Wèi Zhī pleaded the case of injustice for their brother, Jiān,
and moreover invoked the Crown Prince in their argument.
The Emperor grew even more enraged.
The Crown Prince, fearing,
submitted a memorial requesting a divorce from her,
begging not to set aside the law because of kinship.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Jiān was again demoted to Jiāngxià Biéjià.
Jiāngxià Jùn
is Èzhōu.
The old gazetteer states: "Èzhōu
is two thousand three hundred forty-six lì southeast of the capital."
Xià,
pronounced like "yǎ".
However, the Emperor knew the Crown Prince was always filial and respectful,
so his condemnation and anger did not reach him.
Lǐ Línfǔ thereupon said that Jiān and Lǐ Shìzhī and others were forming a faction.
A few days later,
Jiān was exiled to Línfēng,
Shìzhī was demoted to Yíchūn Tàishǒu,
Tàicháng Shǎoqīng Wèi Bīn was demoted to Bālíng Tàishǒu,
the Heir to Xuēwáng, Juàn, was demoted to Yílíng Biéjià,
Suīyáng Tàishǒu Péi Kuān was demoted to Ānlù Biéjià,
Hénán Yǐn Lǐ Qíwù was demoted to Jìnglíng Tàishǒu.
Línfēng Jùn was originally Fēngzhōu Guǎngxìn Jùn;
its name was changed to Jùn in the first year [of Tiānbǎo].
Yíchūn Jùn
is Yuánzhōu.
Bālíng Jùn
is Yuèzhōu.
Yílíng Jùn
is Xiázhōu.
Ānlù Jùn
is Ānzhōu.
Jìnglíng Jùn
was originally Fùzhōu Miǎnyáng Jùn;
its name was changed to Jùn in the first year [of Tiānbǎo].
The old gazetteer states: "Fēngzhōu is four thousand five hundred ten lì by water and land from the capital;
Yuèzhōu, two thousand two hundred thirty-seven lì;
Xiázhōu, one thousand eight hundred eighty-eight lì;
Ānzhōu,
two thousand fifty-one lì southeast of the capital;
Fùzhōu, one thousand eight hundred lì."
Bīn,
pronounced "bīn".
Juàn,
pronounced "quǎn".
Bīn
is Ānshí's son.
Juàn
is Yè's son,
and Jiān's nephew.
Juàn's mother was also ordered to accompany Juàn to his post.
Wèi Ānshí served under the reigns of Wǔ Hòu, Zhōngzōng, and Ruìzōng.
Yè
is the Emperor's younger brother.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Wùxū,
the Emperor visited Lìshān Hot Springs;
in the eleventh month,
on the day Yǐsì,
he returned to the palace.
Zànshàn Dàfū Dù Yǒulín.
In the Táng dynasty, Zànshàn Dàfū,
ranked principal fifth grade, upper class,
was in charge of reciting admonitions and offering remonstrances to the Crown Prince.
In the Táng dynasty, the Crown Prince's inner officials included
Liángdì,
ranked principal third grade.
Dì,
pronounced "jì".
Jì was wild and careless by nature,
fond of fame and reputation,
and enjoyed associating with heroes and outstanding individuals.
Zīchuān Tàishǒu Péi Dūnfù recommended him to Běihǎi Tàishǒu Lǐ Yōng.
Běihǎi Jùn
is Qīngzhōu.
When Jì arrived in the capital,
he became friends with Zhùzuò Láng Wáng Zēng and others,
all of whom were famous scholars of the time.
Jì was not on good terms with his wife's family
and wanted to implicate them,
so he spread rumors,
accusing Yǒulín of falsely claiming prophecies and omens,
colluding with the Eastern Palace,
and making direct references to the imperial chariot.
Línfǔ ordered Jīngzhào Shìcáo Jí Wēn and the Censor to investigate it.
Shìcáo Sīshì Cānjūnshì
was in charge of ferries, bridges, boats, carts, residences, and craftsmanship.
Wēn ordered Jì to implicate Zēng and others to the Censorate.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Jiǎxū,
Yǒulín, Jì, and Zēng and others were all beaten to death.
Their bodies piled up in Dàlǐ Temple.
The Kǎoyì states: "Both the Jiùjì and the Tánglì record
'Xīnwèi'.
Now we follow the Shílù."
The Shílù says,
"Jì and his associates were all executed,"
while the imperial edict states:
"The extreme penalty is leniently spared,
and they are to suffer the punishment of flogging.
As for Wáng Zēng and others,
each shall receive one hundred heavy flogs.
Dù Yǒulín and Liǔ Jì, considering their minor kinship,
are especially spared capital punishment,
to be flogged once,
and demoted to Xīnxīng Wèi in Língnán."
Jí Wēn's biography, however, says:
"Jì and others were beaten to death,
their bodies piled up at Dàlǐ Sì."
Presumably, although the edict granted flogging,
in reality, they all died under the flogging.
Inside and outside the court, people trembled with fear.
The Heir to Guó Wáng, Jù, was demoted to Yìyáng Sīmǎ.
Yìyáng Jùn
is Shēnzhōu.
The old gazetteer states: "Shēnzhōu is one thousand seven hundred ninety-six lì from the capital."
He was Yōng's son.
Gāozǔ's son,
Guó Wáng Fèng;
Fèng's legitimate grandson was the Heir to Guó Wáng, Yōng.
The Crown Prince's Liángdì was also dismissed to become a commoner.
On the *yǐhài* [day],
Wáng Jū (王琚), the Grand Administrator of Yèjùn (鄴郡), was demoted to Commandant of Jiānghuá (江華) for embezzlement.
Yèjùn
was originally Wèijùn (魏郡) of Xiāngzhōu (相州).
It was renamed in the first year [of Tiānbǎo (天寶)].
Jiānghuájùn (江華郡)
was Dàozhōu (道州).
He and Lǐ Yōng (李邕) both considered themselves veterans [of the court],
having been away for a long time.
They felt discontent.
Lǐ Línfǔ (李林甫) disliked them for relying on their talent and acting presumptuously,
so he used various pretexts to remove them.
Wáng Jū had served the Emperor in the Eastern Palace
and assisted in the decision to execute Princess Tàipíng (太平公主).
*È* (惡) [here] is read *wū lù fān*.
In the sixth year
(*dīnghài* (丁亥), 747),
in spring,
the first month,
on the *xīnsì* [day],
Lǐ Yōng and Péi Dūnfù (裴敦復) were both beaten to death with staves.
Yōng's talent and skill were exceptional.
Lú Zàngyòng (盧藏用) often said to him:
"You are like Gānjiàng (干將) and Mòyé (莫邪) [famous swords],
difficult to contend with,
yet ultimately susceptible to being chipped or broken."
Yōng could not heed this advice.
Línfǔ further memorialized to dispatch censors to the places of banishment to grant death to Huángfǔ Wéimíng (皇甫惟明), Wéi Jiān (韋堅) and his brothers, and others.
Luó Xīshì (羅希奭) traveled from Qīngzhōu (青州) to Língnán (嶺南),
killing those who had been exiled and banished along the way.
Xīshì had already killed Lǐ Yōng in Qīngzhōu,
and then proceeded to Língnán.
The document authorizing the requisition of horses arrived in Yíchūn (宜春).
Wherever the censor went,
the commanderies and counties along the route supplied post horses,
hence the document for requisitioning horses arrived before him.
[They were ordered to] take poison and commit suicide.
When [Luó Xīshì] reached Jiānghuá,
Wáng Jū took poison but did not die.
Hearing that Xīshì had arrived,
he immediately hanged himself.
Xīshì then took a detour through Ānlù (安陸),
intending to terrify Péi Kuān (裴寬) to death.
Kuān prostrated himself before Xīshì, begging for his life.
Xīshì passed through without spending the night,
and thus [Kuān] was spared.
Lǐ Shìzhī's (李適之) son Zhà (霅) brought his father's coffin to the Eastern Capital.
Lǐ Línfǔ ordered someone to falsely accuse Zhà,
and he was beaten to death with a staff in Hénánfǔ (河南府).
Fáng Guǎn (房琯), Supervising Secretary, was demoted to Grand Administrator of Yíchūn for being on good terms with Shìzhī.
Guǎn
was the son of Róng (融).
Fáng Róng is mentioned in volume 207 during Wǔ Hòu's (武后) Cháng'ān (長安) fourth year.
Línfǔ's hatred for Wéi Jiān did not cease.
He sent envoys to commanderies and counties along the Yellow River, Jiāng (江), and Huái (淮) rivers to seek out Jiān's crimes,
arresting
and imprisoning *gāngdiǎn chuánfū* (綱典船夫).
The prisons overflowed.
Ten boats constituted one *gāng*.
The *gāng* here refers to an official,
and *diǎn chuánfū* (典船夫) refers to
the boatmen who tow or pilot boats.
The arrests extended to neighbors,
all of whom died naked in the government offices.
This continued until Línfǔ's death.
On the *dīnghài* [day],
the Emperor performed offerings at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
On the *wùzǐ* [day],
he jointly sacrificed to Heaven and Earth at the southern suburban altar,
and granted a general amnesty.
An edict was issued exempting the people from this year's land tax.
It was also ordered to commute sentences of strangulation and decapitation.
The Emperor desired the reputation of cherishing life,
so he ordered that all those sentenced to strangulation or decapitation be given severe staff beatings and banished to Língnán;
however, the officials often beat them to death.
He also ordered that throughout the realm, one should wear mourning for three years for a remarried mother.
The Emperor wished to widely recruit talented individuals from across the realm,
ordering that all who possessed one or more skills should proceed to the capital.
Lǐ Línfǔ feared that commoners might expose his villainy in their policy discussions,
so he advised:
"Most candidates are lowly and ignorant.
I fear their rustic words may sully the sagely hearing."
Thereupon, he ordered the chief officials of commanderies and counties to carefully test and train them.
Those who were clearly outstanding
were to have their names recorded and sent to the Department of State Affairs,
which would then be entrusted with a re-examination,
supervised by the Censor-in-Chief.
Those whose names and abilities truly matched were to be reported to the throne.
Subsequently, all who arrived were tested with poetry, *fù* (賦), and essays,
and not a single person passed.
Línfǔ then submitted a memorial congratulating the Emperor that there were no overlooked talents in the wilds.
On the *wùyín* [day],
Ān Lùshān (安祿山), Military Governor of Fànyáng (范陽) and Pínglú (平盧), was concurrently appointed Censor-in-Chief.
Lùshān was stout and corpulent,
his belly hanging below his knees.
He often claimed his belly
weighed three hundred *jīn*.
Outwardly, he appeared foolish and straightforward, but inwardly he was cunning and shrewd.
He often kept his general Liú Luògǔ (劉駱谷) in the capital to spy on the court's intentions,
reporting all movements;
if there was to be a memorial,
Luògǔ would write it for him.
Each year, he continuously presented captives, various livestock, rare birds, exotic beasts, and precious treasures along the road,
exhausting the commanderies and counties with their transport.
Before the Emperor, Lùshān
responded with quick wit,
mixed with humor.
The Emperor once playfully pointed at his belly and said:
"What is inside this barbarian's belly?
How can it be so large!"
He replied:
"There is nothing else,
only a loyal heart!"
The Emperor was pleased.
He was also once ordered to meet the Crown Prince,
but Lùshān did not bow.
His attendants urged him to bow, but Lùshān stood with cupped hands and said:
"Your subject is a barbarian,
unaccustomed to court etiquette.
I do not know what office the Crown Prince holds?"
The Emperor said:
"This is the Heir Apparent.
After I pass away,
he will replace me as your ruler."
Lùshān said:
"Your subject is foolish.
Until now, I only knew of Your Majesty alone,
and did not know there was also an Heir Apparent."
Only then, out of necessity,
did he bow.
The Emperor believed this to be true,
and loved him even more.
The Emperor once held a banquet at Qínzhèng Lóu (勤政樓).
All officials were seated below the building,
but for Lùshān alone, a screen with golden roosters was set up in the eastern chamber of the imperial seat.
*Zhàng* (障) is a seated screen,
decorated with painted golden roosters.
*Wèi* (為) is read *yú wěi fān*.
The screens were rolled up to show his special favor and honor.
He ordered Yáng Xiān (楊銛), Yáng Qí (楊錡), and the three sisters of Guì (貴) [Consort Yáng Guìfēi] to establish fraternal relationships with Lùshān.
Lùshān was allowed to enter and exit the Forbidden Palace,
and consequently requested to become Guì's foster son.
When the Emperor and Guì were seated together,
Lùshān first bowed to Guì.
The Emperor asked why,
and he replied:
"Barbarians honor their mother before their father."
The Emperor was pleased.
Lǐ Línfǔ, seeing Wáng Zhōngsì's (王忠嗣) merits and fame grow daily,
feared he would become prime minister,
and became jealous of him.
Ān Lùshān secretly harbored rebellious intentions.
Under the pretext of defending against invaders,
he built Xióngwǔ Chéng (雄武城).
There was a Xióngwǔ (雄武) garrison in Guǎnghàn Chuān (廣漢川) of Jìzhōu (薊州).
He requested Zhōngsì to assist in the construction,
intending to retain his troops.
Zhōngsì went ahead of schedule,
did not meet Lùshān, and returned,
repeatedly stating that Lùshān would surely rebel;
Línfǔ disliked him even more.
This was the root cause of Wáng Zhōngsì's eventual disgrace.
*Xiān* (先) is read *xī jiàn fān*.
*Shù* (數) is read *suǒ jiǎo fān*.
*Shàng* (上) is read *shí zhǎng fān*.
*È* (惡) is read *wū lù fān*.
In the fourth month,
Zhōngsì firmly declined the concurrent appointments as Military Governor of Hédōng (河東) and Shuòfāng (朔方),
which was granted.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the *jǐyǒu* [day],
the Emperor visited Lìshān (驪山) Hot Springs.
A different account states: The Old Annals and Táng Records both record it as
"*wùshēn*" (戊申),
which is followed here.
6 Wáng Zhōngsì, the Jìedùshǐ of Héxī and Lǒngyòu, appointed his subordinate general Gēshū Hàn as the Deputy Commissioner of Dàdòu Army,
and Lǐ Guāngbì as the Military Commissioner of Héxī and concurrently Commissioner of Chìshuǐ Army.
A Military Commissioner
was a frontline military position in a Jìedùshǐ's headquarters,
holding overall military authority,
a very important responsibility.
After Zhìdé,
the Chief Military Commissioners often became prospective commanders of Fānzhèn.
將,
read as liàng.
使,
read as shǐ.
The Wǔnǔshīfù of Western Tūjué had Gēshū Què Sìjīn.
騎,
read as qí.
酋,
read as qiú.
長,
read as zhǎng.
He was the son of Qìdān King Kǎiluò,
and in the early Kàiyuán period,
Lǐ Kǎiluò was enfeoffed as the King of Qìdān.
Zhōngsì sent Hàn to attack Túbō.
A colleague was made his deputy,
but he was arrogant and refused to be used.
Hàn flogged him to death,
causing terror in the army.
Through successive merits, he rose to be the Deputy Jìedùshǐ of Lǒngyòu.
Every year, when the wheat in Jīshí Army was ripe,
Túbō would invariably come to harvest it,
and no one could stop them.
The border people called it
"Túbō Wheat Farm."
Hàn first ambushed troops by its side.
When the barbarians arrived,
he cut off their retreat,
and attacked them from both sides.
Not a single person returned,
and from then on, they dared not come again.
The emperor wished to make Wáng Zhōngsì attack Túbō's Shíbǎo City.
Shíbǎo City fell,
see the previous volume, Kàiyuán 29th year.
Shíbǎo is dangerously fortified, and Túbō guards it with their entire nation.
Now, to station troops beneath it
cannot conquer it without killing tens of thousands of people.
I fear that what is gained will not compensate for what is lost.
It would be better to sharpen our weapons and feed our horses,
wait for an opportune moment,
and then seize it."
The emperor was displeased.
General Dǒng Yánguāng volunteered to lead troops to capture Shíbǎo City.
The emperor ordered Zhōngsì to divide his forces to assist him.
Zhōngsì had no choice but to obey the edict,
but he did not fully meet Yánguāng's desires,
and Yánguāng resented him.
Lǐ Guāngbì said to Zhōngsì:
"You, Grand Master, out of love for your soldiers,
do not wish to complete Yánguāng's achievement.
Before the mid-Táng period,
generals and commanders were generally called Grand Master.
As Bái Jūyì's poem says,
'military officials are called Grand Masters,'
this is it.
In reality, you have undermined his strategy.
How do I know this?
Now, you give him tens of thousands of troops but do not offer heavy rewards.
How can the soldiers be willing to exert themselves for him?
However, this is the Son of Heaven's intention.
If he fails,
he will surely blame you, Grand Master.
Your military treasury is overflowing.
Why are you reluctant to offer tens of thousands of bolts of silk to stop their slanderous tongues?"
Zhōngsì said:
"Now, to contend for a single city with tens of thousands of troops,
even if we gain it, it is not enough to control the enemy;
if we do not gain it, it does no harm to the state.
Therefore, I, Zhōngsì, do not wish to do it.
If I, Zhōngsì, am now punished,
the Son of Heaven will at most demote me to a general of the Jīnwú or Yǔlín Guards, to return to the imperial guard.
Next, at most, I would be an Senior Aide in Qiánzhōng.
The entire Qiánzhōng circuit is inhabited by a mix of Xīxī and Yáo barbarians from mountain valleys.
Those who are demoted but do not cross the mountains are placed there.
Senior Aide refers to
Chángshǐ or Sīmǎ.
黔,
pronounced qín.
General Lǐ,
you truly care for me,
but my resolve is firm,
do not speak of it again."
Guāngbì said:
"Before, I feared it would be a burden to you, Grand Master,
so I dared not but speak.
Now, you, Grand Master, are able to act as the ancients did,
which is beyond my capabilities."
Thereupon, he hastened out.
Yánguāng failed to conquer the city by the deadline,
and reported that Zhōngsì had obstructed the military plan.
The emperor was enraged.
Lǐ Línfǔ then instructed Wèi Lín, the Assistant Administrator of Jìyáng, to accuse Zhōngsì, saying:
"Zhōngsì once said, 'I was raised in the palace since childhood,
and was close to the Prince Zhōng.'"
In Wǔdé 4th year, Lú County of Dōngpíng was divided to establish Jì Prefecture.
It was Suí's Jìběi Commandery.
In Tiānbǎo 1st year, its commandery name was changed to Jìyáng Commandery.
When Zhōngsì was nine years old,
his father Hǎibīn died in battle at Wèiyuán Chángchéng Fort.
The Emperor raised Zhōngsì in the palace,
and the Crown Prince, then Prince Zhōng,
associated with him.
Wèi Lín was previously the Governor of Shuò Prefecture.
Zhōngsì was the Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng,
and Shuò Prefecture was under his jurisdiction.
Therefore, Lín was made to slander him,
to show that the accusation had a source.
濟,
pronounced jì.
An imperial edict summoned Zhōngsì to court,
entrusting his case to the Three Judicial Offices for investigation.
The emperor heard of Gēshū Hàn's reputation,
summoned him to Huáqīng Palace,
conversed with him,
and was pleased.
In the 11th month,
on the Xīnmǎo day,
Hàn was appointed Acting Governor of Xīpíng
and concurrently Jìedùshǐ of Lǒngyòu.
Ān Sīshùn, the Jìedùshǐ of Shuòfāng, was appointed Acting Governor of Wǔwēi Commandery
and concurrently Jìedùshǐ of Héxī.
Xīpíng Commandery was
Shàn Prefecture.
Wǔwēi Commandery was
Liáng Prefecture.
7 Yáng Shènjīn, the Assistant Minister of Revenue and concurrently Censor-in-Chief, was highly favored by the emperor.
Lǐ Línfǔ gradually grew jealous of him.
Shènjīn and Wáng Hóng's father, Jìn,
were maternal cousins.
Shènjīn was close to Hóng when they were young,
and Hóng's entry into the Censorate
was largely due to Shènjīn's recommendation.
When Hóng was promoted to Censor-in-Chief,
Shènjīn still addressed him by his given name when speaking to him.
Hóng, relying on his good relationship with Línfǔ,
became somewhat displeased.
Shènjīn seized Hóng's official land.
Both were Censors-in-Chief,
so he seized Hóng's official land and appropriated it.
Shènjīn once spoke of this to others;
Hóng held a deep grudge against him.
Shènjīn still treated him with his former familiarity,
and once privately discussed prophetic books with him.
Shènjīn was friends with the diviner Shǐ Jìngzhōng.
Jìngzhōng said that the world would soon be in chaos,
and advised Shènjīn to buy an estate in Línrǔ Mountain as a refuge.
Línrǔ Commandery was originally Xiāngchéng Commandery of Yī Prefecture.
In Zhēnguān 8th year, Yī Prefecture was renamed Rǔ Prefecture.
In Tiānbǎo 1st year, the commandery name was changed to Línrǔ Commandery.
Shènjīn disliked this [omen],
惡,
pronounced wù.
and asked Jìngzhōng about it.
Jìngzhōng requested to perform an exorcism,
setting up a Taoist ritual site in the backyard.
After returning from court, Shènjīn
would always sit naked in it, wearing shackles.
The bleeding stopped after ten days,
and Shènjīn was grateful to him.
Shènjīn had a maid named Míngzhū,
who was beautiful.
Jìngzhōng often looked at her,
so Shènjīn gave her to Jìngzhōng.
As she was being transported by carriage past his elder sister Liǔ's residence,
his sister invited Jìngzhōng upstairs
and asked for the beautiful woman in the carriage.
Jìngzhōng dared not refuse.
The next day,
his sister entered the palace,
bringing Míngzhū with her.
The emperor saw her and was surprised,
asking where she came from.
Míngzhū told him the truth in full.
The emperor believed Shènjīn and the diviner were practicing witchcraft,
disliked it,
and harbored anger, but had not yet acted.
Yáng Zhāo 楊釗 informed Yáng Hóng 楊鉷.
Yáng Hóng 楊鉷 was secretly pleased,
and consequently treated Shèn Jīng 慎矜 with contempt;
Shèn Jīng 慎矜 grew angry.
Lǐ Línfǔ 李林甫, knowing that Yáng Hóng 楊鉷 and Shèn Jīng 慎矜 had a grudge,
secretly enticed Yáng Hóng 楊鉷 to scheme against him.
Yáng Hóng 楊鉷 then sent someone with a rumor to report
"Shèn Jīng 慎矜 is the grandson of Suí Yángdì 隋煬帝,
Shèn Jīng 慎矜,
is the great-great-grandson of Suí Yángdì 隋煬帝.
His family possesses a book of prophecies,
plotting to restore his ancestral enterprise."
The Emperor was greatly enraged,
arrested Shèn Jīng 慎矜 and imprisoned him,
ordering the Ministry of Justice, the Grand Court of Revision, and Attendant Censor Yáng Zhāo 楊釗, along with Palace Attendant Censor Lú Xuàn 盧鉉, to jointly interrogate him.
Tài fǔ Shà qīng 太府少卿 Zhāng Xuān 張瑄
had been recommended by Shèn Jīng 慎矜.
Lú Xuàn 盧鉉 falsely accused Zhāng Xuān 張瑄 of having discussed prophecies with Shèn Jīng 慎矜.
He was subjected to a hundred forms of torture,
but Zhāng Xuān 張瑄 refused to confess.
So they bound his feet with wood,
and had someone pull his cangue handle,
drawing it forward,
causing his body to stretch several feet longer,
his waist to become thin to the point of breaking,
and blood to pour from his eyes and nose,
yet Zhāng Xuān 張瑄 still did not confess.
They also sent Jí Wēn 吉溫 to arrest Shǐ Jìngzhōng 史敬忠 in Rǔzhōu 汝州.
Shǐ Jìngzhōng 史敬忠 and Jí Wēn's 吉溫 father had always been good friends,
and when Jí Wēn 吉溫 was young,
Shǐ Jìngzhōng 史敬忠 often held and caressed him.
When he was captured,
Jí Wēn 吉溫 did not speak to him,
but locked his neck,
covered his head with cloth,
and drove him before his horse.
Upon reaching Xīshuǐ 戲水,
Xīshuǐ 戲水 is east of Xīnfēng 新豐.
Xī 戲,
pronounced xǔyí.
Jí Wēn 吉溫 said: "Yáng Shènjīng 楊慎矜 has already confessed and admitted his guilt.
You only need to make one confession.
If you understand what is desired, you will live;
otherwise, you will surely die.
When we reach Wēntāng 溫湯,
you will not be able to confess."
Wēntāng 溫湯 is now Huìchāng 會昌.
At that time, Huìchāng Xiàn 會昌縣 was established below the Wēnquán Gōng 溫泉宮.
Shǒu 首,
pronounced shìjiù,
means to confess one's crime.
Some say
shǒu 首
is pronounced as written.
Shǐ Jìngzhōng 史敬忠 pleaded, "Qī Láng 七郎,
give me a piece of paper."
Jí Wēn 吉溫 did not respond.
Ten-odd *lǐ* (li) from Wēntāng 溫湯,
Shǐ Jìngzhōng 史敬忠 pleaded earnestly,
so Jí Wēn 吉溫 allowed him to write three pages under a mulberry tree.
His confession was entirely in accordance with Jí Wēn's 吉溫 wishes.
Jí Wēn 吉溫 then slowly said,
"Elder, please do not be offended!"
And he rose and bowed to him.
Upon reaching Huìchāng 會昌,
in the first year of Tiānbǎo 天寶,
Lìshān 驪山 was renamed Huìchāng Shān 會昌山.
Three years later,
because Xīnfēng Xiàn 新豐縣 was far from Huáqīng Gōng 華清宮,
Huìchāng Xiàn 會昌縣 was established by dividing Xīnfēng 新豐 and Wànnián 萬年.
That year,
Wēnquán 溫泉 was renamed Huáqīng Gōng 華清宮.
The hot springs were developed into pools,
palaces were arranged around the mountain,
and a *luóchéng* 羅城 (outer defensive wall) was built,
with a hundred offices and ten residences established.
Shǐ Jìngzhōng 史敬忠 was used as a witness.
Shèn Jīng 慎矜 confessed to everything,
but the book of prophecies could not be found.
Lǐ Línfǔ 李林甫 was worried,
so he sent Lú Xuàn 盧鉉 into Cháng'ān 長安 to search Shèn Jīng's 慎矜 home.
Lú Xuàn 盧鉉 slipped the book of prophecies into his sleeve, entered a dark room,
then emerged cursing, saying,
"This rebel deeply hides secret records!"
Upon reaching Huìchāng 會昌,
he showed it to Shèn Jīng 慎矜.
Shèn Jīng 慎矜 sighed,
"I do not keep books of prophecy.
How could this be in my house?
I am destined to die, that is all."
On *dīngyǒu* 丁酉 (day),
Shèn Jīng 慎矜 and his elder brother, Shàofǔ Shàojiān 少府少監 Shèn Yú 慎餘, and Luòyáng Lìng 洛陽令 Shèn Míng 慎名, were granted self-execution;
Shǐ Jìngzhōng 史敬忠 was given one hundred strokes of the staff,
and his wife and children were all exiled to Lǐngnán 嶺南;
Zhāng Xuān 張瑄 was given sixty strokes of the staff,
exiled to Línfēng 臨封,
and died at Huìchāng 會昌.
Although SÌ Guó Wáng Jù 嗣虢王巨 was not involved in the conspiracy,
he was punished for being acquainted with Shǐ Jìngzhōng 史敬忠.
He was dismissed from office
and placed in Nánbīn 南賓.
Nánbīn Jùn 南賓郡,
Zhōngzhōu 忠州,
originally Línjiāng Xiàn 臨江縣 of Bājùn 巴郡.
In the second year of Suí Yìníng 隋義寧, Línzhōu 臨州 was established.
In the eighth year of Zhēnguān 貞觀, it was renamed Zhōngzhōu 忠州.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo 天寶, it was changed to a Commandery.
According to old records,
Zhōngzhōu 忠州
is 2,122 *lǐ* (li) south of the capital.
When Shèn Míng 慎名 heard the imperial decree,
his expression did not change;
he wrote a letter to bid farewell to his elder sister.
Shèn Yú 慎餘 clasped his hands, pointed to the sky, and hanged himself.
The Three Judicial Bureaus investigated Wáng Zhōngsì 王忠嗣.
The Emperor said,
"My son resides deep within the palace;
how could he conspire with outsiders?
This must be false."
*Kǎo Yì* 考異 says: The new biography states
that Lǐ Línfǔ 李林甫 repeatedly reported that the Crown Prince intended to conspire against the Emperor, and so forth.
However, although Lǐ Línfǔ 李林甫 desired to harm the Crown Prince,
he would not admit it himself.
This is not adopted now.
When Gēshū Hàn 哥舒翰 came to court,
some advised him to bring much gold and silk to save Wáng Zhōngsì 王忠嗣.
Gēshū Hàn 哥舒翰 said,
"If integrity still exists,
Duke Wáng 王公 will surely not die unjustly;
if it is about to perish,
what good would many bribes do?"
So he traveled with a single bag.
The Three Judicial Bureaus reported that Wáng Zhōngsì's 王忠嗣 crime deserved death.
Gēshū Hàn 哥舒翰, who had only recently gained the Emperor's favor,
vigorously argued the injustice of Wáng Zhōngsì's 王忠嗣 case,
and furthermore requested to use his own official rank and titles to redeem Wáng Zhōngsì's 王忠嗣 crime.
The Emperor rose
and entered the inner palace.
Gēshū Hàn 哥舒翰 kowtowed and followed him,
speaking with tears.
The Emperor was moved to understanding.
On *jǐhài* 己亥 (day),
Wáng Zhōngsì 王忠嗣 was demoted to Hànyáng Tàishǒu 漢陽太守.
Hànyáng Jùn 漢陽郡,
Miǎnyáng Zhōu 沔州.
Lǐ Línfǔ 李林甫 repeatedly initiated major cases,
establishing a separate interrogation court in Cháng'ān 長安.
Because Yáng Zhāo 楊釗 had kinship with the inner court (*yè tíng* 掖庭),
frequently entering and exiting the forbidden palace,
his words were often heard,
so Lǐ Línfǔ 李林ǔ drew him in as an ally
and promoted him to Censor.
Any matter that even slightly involved the Eastern Palace,
he would point out and make Yáng Zhāo 楊釗 report and impeach,
then hand it over to Luó Xīshì 羅希奭 and Jí Wēn 吉溫 for interrogation.
Yáng Zhāo 楊釗 thus indulged his personal desires,
and hundreds of families were framed, implicated, and executed,
all initiated by Yáng Zhāo 楊釗.
Fortunately, the Crown Prince was benevolent, filial, cautious, and quiet,
and Zhāng Jì 張垍 and Gāo Lìshì 高力士 always protected him before the Emperor,
so Lǐ Línfǔ 李林甫 ultimately could not sow discord.
In the twelfth month,
on *rénxū* 壬戌 (day),
commoners from Féngyì 馮翊 and Huáyīn 華陰 were conscripted to build Huìchāng Chéng 會昌城,
establishing a hundred offices.
Huáyīn Jùn 華陰郡,
Huázhōu 華州.
Féngyì Jùn 馮翊郡,
Tóngzhōu 同州.
Huá 華,
pronounced hùhuà.
An *mǔ* 畝 (mu) of land was worth a thousand gold.
On *guǐhài* 癸亥 (day),
the Emperor returned to the palace.
On *bǐngyín* 丙寅 (day),
the Emperor ordered all officials to inspect the annual tribute items from across the empire at the Department of State Affairs,
and afterward, all of them were loaded into carts and bestowed upon Lǐ Línfǔ's 李林甫 family.
Sometimes the Emperor did not hold court,
and all officials gathered at the gate of Lǐ Línfǔ's 李林甫 residence,
leaving the Censorate and other departments empty.
Although Chén Xīliè 陳希烈 was in his office,
