not a single person came to visit him.
Lǐ Línfǔ's 李林甫 son, Lǐ Xiù 李岫, was Jiāngzuò Jiān 將作監 (Director of the Imperial Works).
In early Táng 唐, it was called Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng 將作大匠.
During Lóngshuò 龍朔, it was renamed Shàngōng Jiān 繕工監.
During Guāngzhái 光宅, it was renamed Yíngshàn Jiān 營繕監.
During Shénlóng 神龍, it was restored to Jiāngzuò Jiān 將作監.
He once accompanied Lǐ Línfǔ 李林甫 on a stroll through the back garden,
pointed to the laborers, and said to Lǐ Línfǔ 李林甫,
"Father, you have long held the reins of power,
and enemies fill the empire.
Should disaster strike one day, would these [laborers] be able to help?"
Lǐ Línfǔ 李林ǔ was displeased and said,
"The situation is already like this;
what can be done?"
Previously,
all the chancellors conducted themselves with virtue and measure,
not relying on power or prestige.
Their retinue numbered no more than a few people,
and commoners sometimes did not avoid them.
Lín Fǔ, believing he had made many enemies,
constantly feared assassins.
When he went out, he had over a hundred cavalry and infantry,
forming left and right wings.
The Golden Guards cleared the streets,
and his vanguard was several hundred paces ahead.
Nobles and officials scurried to get out of the way.
At home, he had multiple gates and reinforced walls,
with stone paving the ground,
and boards placed within the walls,
as if defending against a great enemy.
He moved his bed several times each night,
and even his family members did not know its location.
The lavishness of the chancellors' retinues
began with Lín Fǔ.
12 Initially,
General Gāo Xiānzhī,
originally a man from Gāolì,
joined the army in Ānxī.
Xiānzhī was valiant and fierce,
skilled in horsemanship and archery.
The Jìedùshǐ Fúméng Língchá repeatedly recommended him until he reached the positions of Ānxī Fùdūhù and Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ,
serving concurrently as Sìzhèn Jiédufùshǐ.
The Tǔbō married a daughter to the King of Xiǎobólǜ.
Xiǎobólǜ was over nine thousand *lǐ* from Cháng'ān,
and three thousand *lǐ* from the Tǔbō Zànpǔ's court.
*Qī*
rhymes *qī xì fān*.
All of them were subservient to Tǔbō,
and their tributes ceased.
Previous Jìedùshǐ had campaigned against them,
but none could conquer them.
An imperial decree appointed Xiānzhī as Xíngyíng Jiéduǐshǐ,
to lead ten thousand cavalry to campaign against them.
From Ānxī, they traveled for over a hundred days
until they reached Tèlèmǎnchuān.
The army was divided into three routes.
Tèlèmǎnchuān was where the kingdom of Wǔshìní was located.
The three routes were: one through the North Valley Road,
one through the Chìfó Road,
and Xiānzhī himself took the Hùmì Road.
From Hùmì Lèchéng south to the capital of Xiǎobólǜ was five hundred *lǐ*.
Liányúnbǎo relied on the mountain to the south
and the Suōlèchuān to the north for its defense.
Unexpectedly, the Tang army arrived suddenly,
causing great alarm.
They resisted battle from the mountain,
with projectiles raining down like arrows.
Xiānzhī appointed Commander Gāolíng Lǐ Sìyè as the General of Mó Dāo,
and ordered him:
"You must break the barbarians
before midday."
Sìyè, holding a flag,
led the *mó dāo* soldiers, climbed the dangerous terrain first, and fought bravely.
From *chén* to *sì*,
they utterly defeated them.
*Kǎoyì* states: The old biography of Sìyè says
"Tiānbǎo sixth year."
Now we follow the Veritable Records and Fēng Chángqīng's biography.
Over a thousand prisoners were captured;
the rest fled and scattered.
The imperial envoy Biān Lìngchéng, having entered deep into enemy territory,
was afraid and dared not advance.
Biān Lìngchéng was the supervisor of the army at the time.
*Shǐ*
rhymes *shū lì fān*.
He advanced again.
Three days later,
they reached Tǎnjūlǐng.
They descended a steep slope of over forty *lǐ*.
In front was Ānúyuè City.
Xiānzhī feared that the soldiers would dread the danger
and be unwilling to descend,
so he first sent men in Hu clothing to pretend to be defenders of Ānúyuè City, welcoming their surrender,
saying:
"Ānúyuè sincerely submits to Tang,
and the rattan bridge over the Suōyí River has already been cut."
The Suōyí River
is the Ruòshuǐ.
The King of Xiǎobólǜ resided in Nièduō City,
by the Suōyí River.
*Suō*
rhymes *sù hé fān*.
The rattan bridge
was the path to Tǔbō.
Xiānzhī feigned joy,
and the soldiers then descended.
Three more days later,
the greeters from Ānúyuè City indeed arrived.
The next day,
Xiānzhī entered Ānúyuè City.
He dispatched General Xí Yuánqìng with a thousand cavalry to go ahead,
saying:
"When Xiǎobólǜ hears that the main army is coming,
its ruler, ministers, and people will surely flee into the mountains and valleys.
Just call them out,
and give them silk as if bestowed by imperial decree.
When the high ministers arrive,
bind them all and await me."
Yuánqìng did as he was told,
binding all the high ministers.
The King and the Tǔbō princess escaped into a stone cave;
they could not be captured.
When Xiānzhī arrived,
he executed several high ministers who had sided with Tǔbō.
The rattan bridge was still sixty *lǐ* from the city.
Xiānzhī urgently dispatched Yuánqìng to cut it.
As soon as it was finished,
a large Tǔbō army arrived,
but it was too late.
The rattan bridge was as wide as an arrow.
It required great effort to repair it,
and a full year to rebuild it.
In the eighth month,
Xiānzhī captured the King of Xiǎobólǜ and the Tǔbō princess and returned.
In the ninth month,
he reached Liányúnbǎo,
together with Biān Lìngchéng.
At the end of the month,
he reached Bōmìchuān
and sent an envoy to present a report.
A report of victory was submitted to the capital.
*Shǐ*
rhymes *shū lì fān*.
Upon reaching Héxī,
this Héxī
is Báimǎhéxī,
from Ānxī westward, passing Zhèjuéguān and crossing the Báimǎ River.
No one came to greet and comfort them.
*Yī*
means "all" or "everything."
*Láo*
rhymes *lì dào fān*.
"You Gāolì slave who eats dog feces!
By whose favor did you get your official positions,
yet you dared to submit a victory report
without waiting for my instructions!
Gāolì slave!
Your crime deserves execution,
but I cannot bear to do so because you have just achieved a merit!"
Xiānzhī merely apologized.
Biān Lìngchéng reported that Xiānzhī had ventured ten thousand *lǐ* deep,
achieved extraordinary merit,
and was now worried about dying at any moment.
Punctuation by Qí Sīhé, collated by Niè Chóngqí.
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command.
Hòu Xué Tiāntái
Tiānbǎo sixth year
(Dīnghài, 747)
1 In the twelfth month,
on the Jǐsì day,
the Emperor appointed Xiānzhī as Ānxī Sìzhèn Jiéduǐshǐ,
and summoned Língchá to court.
Língchá was greatly frightened.
When Xiānzhī saw Língchá,
he still rushed and bowed as before.
Língchá became even more frightened.
The Fùdūhù Jīngzhào Chéng Qiānlǐ, the Yáyá Bì Sīchēn, and the Xíngguān Wáng Tāo and others.
Yáyá means
to manage all affairs within the Jìedùshǐ's headquarters.
Xíngguān
refers to an official sent by the commander to travel between the capital and neighboring regions, or to inspect counties and prefectures within the jurisdiction.
*Chēn*
rhymes *chǒu lín fān*.
Xiānzhī confronted Qiānlǐ and Sīchēn, saying:
"Your faces are like men,
but your hearts are like women,
why is that?"
He also grabbed Tāo and others,
intending to flog them,
but later released them all,
saying:
"What I have always resented about you
I wished not to say,
fearing you would harbor worries;
now that I have spoken it,
there is nothing left to worry about."
The army then became settled.
At first,
Gāo Xiānzhī was the Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ.
Fēng Chángqīng, a man from Yīshì,
was orphaned and poor in his youth.
He was thin and had a prominent birthmark on his eye,
and one foot was shorter than the other.
He sought to be Gāo Xiānzhī's aide,
but was not accepted.
Fēng Chángqīng waited daily for Gāo Xiānzhī to come and go,
not leaving his gate.
After dozens of days,
Gāo Xiānzhī reluctantly kept him.
It happened that the Dáxī tribe rebelled.
Fūméng Língchá sent Gāo Xiānzhī to pursue them,
and he almost completely annihilated them.
Fēng Chángqīng privately drafted a victory report and showed it to Gāo Xiānzhī,
which contained everything Gāo Xiānzhī wished to say.
From this, everyone in the prefecture was impressed by him.
When Gāo Xiānzhī became Jìedùshǐ,
he immediately appointed Fēng Chángqīng as Pànguān.
When Gāo Xiānzhī went on campaigns,
Fēng Chángqīng often served as Liúhòu.
Among the subordinates of Tang commissioners,
the Pànguān ranked next to the Fùshǐ,
and fully managed the affairs of the prefecture.
Moreover, when a Jìedùshǐ was on campaign,
or entered the court,
or died and had not yet been replaced,
there was always someone designated to manage the Liúhòu affairs.
Later, this was known as the Jìedù Liúhòu.
In our dynasty, the Liúhòu was renamed Chéngxúanshǐ,
and was held by those whose qualifications did not yet warrant appointment as Jìedùshǐ.
Gāo Xiānzhī treated him like a brother,
entrusting him with household affairs,
and his authority was felt throughout the army.
Fēng Chángqīng once went out,
and Dé Quán rode his horse from behind, charging past him.
When Fēng Chángqīng arrived at the Shǐyuàn (commissioner's office),
the Shǐyuàn
was where the Liúhòu handled affairs.
The Jìedùshǐ also handled affairs in his private residence,
or sometimes went to the Shǐyuàn.
Shǐ,
read as suō lì.
Each time he passed a door,
he closed it.
When he arrived,
Fēng Chángqīng stood up from his seat and said:
"Chángqīng originally came from humble origins,
as the Lángjiàng knows.
Today, the Zhōngchéng has appointed me as Liúhòu.
How can the Lángjiàng so arrogantly ride past me in front of everyone!"
Then he shouted at him:
"The Lángjiàng must die temporarily to enforce military discipline."
Zàn,
same as zàn.
He fell face down,
and was dragged out.
Gāo Xiānzhī's wife and wet nurse cried loudly outside the door to save him,
but it was too late.
They reported the situation to Gāo Xiānzhī,
who, upon reading it,
exclaimed in shock:
"Is he already dead?"
When he saw Fēng Chángqīng,
he did not speak further,
and Fēng Chángqīng did not apologize.
The army was filled with fear and awe.
The historians say that Fēng Chángqīng was capable of managing military administration,
also because Gāo Xiānzhī did not let personal affection interfere with the law.
Tì,
read as tà lì.
Since the rise of the Tang dynasty,
frontier commanders were all loyal and upright famous officials,
who were not appointed for long terms,
did not hold distant concurrent posts,
and did not command multiple regions.
Those with distinguished achievements often entered the court as prime ministers.
Examples include Lǐ Jìng, Lǐ Jì, Liú Rén'guǐ, and Lóu Shīdé.
Since the Kāiyuán era,
Xuē Nà, Guō Yuánzhèn, Zhāng Jiāzhēn, Wáng Jùn, Zhāng Yuè, Dù Xiān, Xiāo Sōng, Lǐ Shìzhī, etc.,
also all entered the court as prime ministers from being frontier commanders.
Shuài,
read as suǒ lèi.
Even talented strategists like Āshǐnà Shè'ěr and Qìbì Hélì were not given sole command of large armies,
but always had high officials appointed as their commissioners to control them.
When Shè'ěr attacked Gāochāng,
Hóu Jūnjí was the Yuánshuài.
When Hélì attacked Gāolì,
Lǐ Jì was the Yuánshuài.
Jiàng,
read as jí liàng.
Qì,
read as qī qì.
Bì,
read as pí bì.
Shǐ,
read as suō lì.
The Son of Heaven had the ambition to conquer the four barbarian tribes,
and frontier generals were not replaced for over ten years,
thus beginning long-term appointments.
Wáng Jùn, Guō Zhīyùn, and Zhāng Shǒuguī are examples of this.
As for prime ministers, Xiāo Sōng and Niú Xiānkè,
began to hold distant concurrent posts.
Matters concerning various princes can be found in volume 213, Kāiyuán 15th year.
Matters concerning Xiāo Sōng can be found in the 17th year,
and matters concerning Niú Xiānkè can be found in volume 214, 24th year.
This marked the beginning of concurrent command of multiple regions.
Matters concerning Gài Jiāyùn can be found in volume 214, Kāiyuán 28th year.
Matters concerning Wáng Zhōngsì can be found in the preceding volume, 5th year.
Gài,
read as gǔ hé.
Because the "Hu" (barbarians) were uneducated,
he (Lǐ Línfǔ) memorialized, saying:
"Civil officials as generals are timid in facing arrows and stones.
It is better to use humble, uncultured 'Hu' people.
Hán,
refers to lowly and humble.
Jùn,
refers to those who once engaged in farming.
Jùn is pronounced jùn.
Humble families are isolated and without factions.
If Your Majesty truly wins their hearts with kindness,
they will certainly be able to die for the court."
The emperor was pleased with his words,
and thus began to use Ān Lùshān.
By this time,
all the Jìedùshǐ of the various circuits were "Hu" people.
Ān Lùshān, Ān Sīshùn, Gēshū Hàn, Gāo Xiānzhī,
were all "Hu" people.
The balance of power in the realm became skewed,
eventually leading to Lùshān overthrowing the empire,
all due to Lǐ Línfǔ's scheme to monopolize favor and secure his position.
The 7th year
(Wùzǐ, 748)
Summer,
4th month,
Xīnchǒu day,
Gāo Lìshì, the Zuǒ Jiānmén Dàjiàngjūn and Zhī Nèishìshěngshì, was promoted to Piàojì Dàjiàngjūn.
The position of Zhī Nèishìshěngshì began from this time.
According to Tang regulations: there were twenty-nine ranks of merit and prestige,
and Piàojì Dàjiàngjūn was the highest,
of the first rank.
Jiān,
read as gǔ xián.
Piào,
read as pǐ miào.
Qí,
read as qí jì.
Everyone within and outside the court feared him.
The crown prince also called him "elder brother,"
various princes and dukes called him "uncle" (wēng),
and consort-officials directly called him "father" (yé).
Lǐ Línfǔ, Ān Lùshān, and their ilk all used him to gain positions as generals and prime ministers.
His family's wealth was immeasurable.
He built Bǎoshòu Temple in the Western Capital.
When the temple bell was completed,
Gāo Lìshì held a vegetarian feast to celebrate it,
and the entire court gathered.
If Sòng Jǐng were alive,
he would certainly not have attended this gathering.
Cháo,
read as zhí yáo.
He donated a hundred strings of cash,
and those seeking favor donated up to twenty *chu*,
with the least being no fewer than ten *chu*.
However, his nature was cautious and he made few mistakes,
he was good at observing the times and adapting,
and dared not be arrogant or overbearing.
Therefore, the emperor always trusted and employed him,
and the scholar-officials did not resent him.
2 In the fifth month,
on the day Rénwǔ,
the assembled officials presented the honorific title of Kāiyuán Tiānbǎo Shèngwén Shénwǔ Yìngdào Huángdì to the Emperor;
a general amnesty was declared,
and the people were exempted from rent and labor service for the coming year.
One descendant of the Later Wèi was chosen to be among the Sānkè.
The Sānkè and the descendants of the Èrwáng are
explained previously.
Dù Yòu said: When the Zhōu obtained the empire,
they enfeoffed the descendants of the two kings, Xià and Yīn,
and also enfeoffed the descendant of Shùn,
calling them Kè.
Kè
means reverence;
the meaning is derived from those whom the king reveres,
hence they are called Sānkè.
In the thirteenth year of Tiānbǎo,
the high officials debated, saying: Regarding the Sānkè and Èrwáng,
there are three theories.
The first theory says
that before the Èrwáng,
the descendants of the Three Dynasties should be established as the Sānkè.
This is based on the Lèjì
which states: "King Wǔ, after conquering Shāng,
did not dismount before enfeoffing the descendants of Huángdì, Yáo, and Shùn.
After dismounting, he enfeoffed the descendants of Xià and Yīn."
This is the basis.
The second theory says
that before the Èrwáng,
only one dynasty was preserved,
combining the Èrwáng to form the Sānkè.
This is based on the Zuǒzhuàn,
which states: "Hú Gōng was merely enfeoffed to complete the Sānkè,"
illustrating that the kings revered two previous kings,
and enfeoffed one more dynasty to complete the Sānkè.
The third theory says
that the descendants of the Èrwáng constitute one Kè,
the parents of the empress constitute two Kè,
and the rulers of the Yí Dī barbarians constitute three Kè.
This is based on
the saying, "The king has three who are not his subjects."
These are the theories.
Cuī Líng'ēn of Liáng said: Among the three theories, the first is superior.
Examining the Èrwáng and Sānkè,
there is no direct text in the classics.
Líng'ēn, basing his argument on the Lǐjì,
concluded that all five dynasties were to be preserved.
I fear this might not be sound.
The Lǐjì says: One should not honor more than two generations.
As for the third generation,
although distant and difficult to emulate as a model,
how could their descendants not be recorded?
Therefore, they are also preserved,
merely to show reverence for their ways.
Thus, they are called Sānkè.
Hence the Zuǒzhuàn says:
"Hú Gōng was enfeoffed to complete the Sānkè."
This is sufficient to know that there were no five generations.
Moreover, from antiquity until now,
all have considered the Three Dynasties as the Sānkè.
Based on this,
it is likely that the descendants of the Later Wèi, along with the descendants of Zhōu and Suí, were to be the Sānkè.
The next year,
the descendant of Wèi was subsequently removed;
the explanation for this will be found later.
3 In the sixth month,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
Ān Lùshān was bestowed with an iron certificate.
4 Yáng Zhāo, an assistant director of the Ministry of Finance and concurrently a Supervising Censor, was skilled at discerning the Emperor's likes and dislikes and pandering to them.
He rapidly rose through the ranks by accumulating wealth,
holding more than fifteen commissions within a year.
On the day Jiǎchén,
he was promoted to Palace Assistant Secretary and concurrently Censor-in-Chief,
specializing in overseeing the affairs of the Ministry of Finance.
His favor and influence grew daily.
Sū Miǎn commented: Offices are established and duties divided,
each with its own jurisdiction.
Governance, when consistent, is easy to maintain; affairs, when rooted in their fundamentals, are difficult to go astray.
For long-term principles,
what else can one rely on?
Yet treacherous ministers spoke widely of profit to gain favor,
established many commissions to demonstrate their influence,
exploited the common people for heavy levies,
and presented fabricated figures in their reports.
The Emperor's heart became more indulgent and extravagant,
and the people's resentment turned into disaster.
This caused the Emperor's officials to hold their positions without their proper duties,
and receive high salaries without fulfilling their functions.
Yǔwén Róng initiated this trend,
Yáng Shènjīn and Wáng Xióng subsequently followed his path,
and Yáng Guózhōng ultimately completed the chaos.
Confucius said: Better to have thieving ministers than ministers who accumulate wealth.
The Great Learning records: A family with a hundred chariots
does not employ ministers who accumulate wealth;
rather than having ministers who accumulate wealth,
it is better to have thieving ministers.
The cart in front has already overturned,
yet the tracks behind remain unchanged.
How difficult it is to achieve fundamental transformation!
5 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Gēngxū,
the Emperor visited the Huáqīng Palace.
6 In the eleventh month,
on the day Guǐwèi,
the Emperor enfeoffed his noble sister, who was married to the Cuī family, as Hánguó Fūrén;
the one married to the Péi family as Guóguó Fūrén;
and the one married to the Liǔ family as Qínguó Fūrén.
All three women possessed talent and beauty.
The Emperor called them "aunties,"
and they had free access to the palace inner quarters,
all receiving imperial favor,
their power shaking the world.
Whenever court ladies came for an audience,
Princess Yùzhēn and others would yield and not dare to take their seats.
Princess Yùzhēn was the daughter of Ruìzōng.
Any requests or solicitations from them
were welcomed by the prefectural and county offices,
even more strictly adhered to than imperial decrees.
Gifts and tributes from all directions
converged on their doors,
fearing only to be last,
making their gates like a marketplace morning and evening.
The marriages of the princes in the Ten Princely Residences and the Hundred Descendants' Academy
(for Ten Princely Residences and Hundred Descendants' Academy,
see volume 213, Kāiyuán 15th year)
all went as desired.
What the Emperor bestowed and what was offered from all directions
was divided among the five families as one.
They vied to build mansions,
making them extremely grand and beautiful,
the cost of a single hall
often exceeding ten million.
Once built,
if they saw someone else had something superior,
they would immediately demolish theirs and rebuild.
Guóguó Fūrén was particularly extravagant and uninhibited.
One day,
she led workers and laborers to forcibly enter Wéi Sìlì's residence,
immediately tore down the old house,
and built a new mansion for herself,
only giving Wéi's family ten *mǔ* of vacant land.
When the central hall was completed,
she summoned plasterers,
agreeing to pay two million cash.
They then requested a reward for their skill.
Guóguó Fūrén rewarded them with five hundred bolts of crimson silk,
but they scoffed and ignored it,
saying:
"Please take ants and lizards,
count them and place them in the hall.
If even one is lost,
we will not dare to accept the payment."
7 In the twelfth month,
on the day Wùxū,
someone said that Xuányuán Huángdì had descended upon the Chaoyuan Pavilion.
The Emperor then built the Lǎojūn Hall at the Huáqīng Palace,
and to the north of the hall built the Chaoyuan Pavilion.
Because someone said Lǎojūn descended there,
it was renamed Jiàngshèng Pavilion.
Xīnfēng County was abolished and incorporated into Zhāoyìng County.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
the Emperor returned to the palace
from the Wēnquán Palace.
The character "還" (huán)
is read with the same sound as "xuán,"
and also pronounced as it is written.
8 Gēshū Hàn built the Shénwēi Army base on the Qīnghǎi Lake.
When the Tǔbō arrived,
Hàn defeated them.
He also built a city on Lóngjū Island in the middle of Qīnghǎi Lake.
The character "吐" (tǔ)
is pronounced with the entering tone of "tūn."
Qīnghǎi Lake is eight or nine hundred *lǐ* in circumference.
It contains a mountain.
Mares must be led to mate on it when the ice has formed,
and the following year colts are born,
known as "dragon steeds,"
hence it is called Lóngjū Island.
The Tǔbō thereafter kept their distance and dared not approach Qīnghǎi Lake.
9 In this year,
Guīyì, the king of Yúnnán, died.
His son Géluófèng succeeded him,
and appointed his son Fèng Jiāyì as the Administrator of Yángguā Prefecture.
Eighth year
(Jǐchǒu, 749)
1 In spring,
the second month,
on the day of Wùshēn,
the Emperor led all officials to inspect the Zuǒcáng.
The Táng Liùdiǎn states: The Zhōulǐ has an Outer Treasury Junior Official (wàifǔ zhōngshì)
who is in charge of the external treasury and storehouses,
managing the income and expenditure of state currency
to supply all goods and meet state needs.
There are also Senior and Junior Officials for Currency (zhíbì shàngshì, zhōngshì)
who are in charge of currency income.
These positions are equivalent to the current Zuǒcáng officials.
By the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
they were divided among the Sīnóng and Shàofǔ.
In the Later Hàn dynasty,
among the subordinate officials of the Shàofǔ, there was a Prefect and Assistant of the Central Treasury Office (zhōngcángfǔ lìng, chéng),
who managed the currency, silks, gold, silver, and goods in the central treasury.
The Wèi clan followed this system.
In the Jìn dynasty, the Shàofǔ's subordinate officials included Left and Right Treasury Prefects (zuǒ, yòucáng lìng).
In the Eastern Jìn, there were nine Imperial Censors (Yùshǐ),
each in charge of a department (cáo).
There was a Treasury Censor (kùcáo yùshǐ).
Later, the Treasury Department was further divided,
establishing an Outer Left Treasury (wài zuǒkù) and an Inner Left Treasury (nèi zuǒkù).
Emperor Wén of Sòng abolished the Outer Left Treasury,
and the Inner Left Treasury was simply called the Left Treasury.
The Qí, Liáng, and Chén dynasties had a Right Treasury (yòucángkù) but no Left Treasury.
The Northern Qí's Tàifǔsì administered the Left and Right Treasury Prefects and Assistants (zuǒ, yòucáng lìng, chéng).
The Later Zhōu had Outer Treasury Senior and Junior Officials (wàifǔ shàngshì, zhōngshì).
The Suí dynasty had Left and Right Treasury Office Prefects and Assistants (zuǒ, yòucángshǔ lìng, chéng).
The Táng dynasty's Zuǒcáng included the Eastern Treasury (dōngkù), Western Treasury (xīkù), and Court Treasury (cháotángkù),
and also the Eastern Capital Treasury (dōngdūkù).
I observe in the Yōnglù: In Tàijí Gōng, there was an Eastern Left Treasury (dōng zuǒcángkù)
and a Western Left Treasury (xī zuǒcángkù).
The Eastern Treasury was east of Gōnglǐ Mén,
and the Western Treasury was west of Ānrén Mén.
In Dàmíng Gōng, there was a Left Treasury (zuǒcángkù),
located to the left of Líndé Diàn.
There was also a Right Treasury Office Prefect (yòucángshǔ lìng)
who managed the treasures and miscellaneous goods of the state.
However, the regular revenue of taxes and levies (fùdiào) from across the empire, in cash and goods,
all went to the Zuǒcáng.
The character 藏 (cáng)
is pronounced "cú làng" in fǎnqiè;
the 帑藏 (tángcáng) below is pronounced the same.
At this time, the prefectures and counties were prosperous and wealthy.
Granaries and storehouses accumulated grain and silk,
often in the tens of thousands.
Yáng Zhāo submitted a memorial requesting that local sales of grain be converted into light currency (qīnghuò),
and that conscription taxes (dīngzū) and land taxes (dìshuì) all be converted into cloth and silk to be transported to the capital.
He repeatedly reported that the imperial treasuries (tángcáng) were overflowing,
unparalleled in ancient and modern times.
Therefore, the Emperor led his officials to view them,
and bestowed upon Zhāo a purple robe and golden fish ornament to reward him.
Since the Emperor considered the national treasury to be abundant and overflowing,
he regarded gold and silk as dirt,
and bestowed gifts upon favored noble families
without any limit.
2 In the third month,
Zhāng Qíqiū, the military governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Shuòfāng Circuit, etc., built the Héngsài Army (Héngsài Jūn) at Mùlà Shān, over five hundred lǐ northwest of Zhōng Shòujiàng Chéng.
He appointed Guō Zǐyí, a native of Zhèng, as the commander of the Héngsài Army (Héngsài Jūnshǐ), who was originally the commander of the Zhènyuǎn Army (Zhènyuǎn Jūnshǐ).
The Héngsài Army was originally named Kědūn Chéng.
According to Sòng Bái's Xù Tōngdiǎn: The Héngsài Army
was initially established in Fēihú.
Later it was moved to Wèizhōu.
In the sixth year of Kāiyuán (718 CE), Zhāng Jiāzhēn moved it south of Dà'ān Chéng in the ancient Dàijùn Commandery,
to serve as a support for the Jiǔxìng tribes.
In the twelfth year of Tiānbǎo (753 CE), it was renamed Tiāndé Jūn.
Comparing various books,
the Héngsài Army is actually the Héngyě Army (Héngyě Jūn).
The first year of Tiānbǎo records
“The Hédōng Jiédù [Circuit] administers the Héngyě Army,”
which was the one moved in the sixth year of Kāiyuán.
The Héngsài Army built here is at Kědūn Chéng.
The Zhènyuǎn Army was within the territory of Shànyú Fǔ.
Zhèngxiàn [County]
belonged to Jīngzhào in the Hàn dynasty.
The Later Wèi established Dōngyōngzhōu,
and merged Huàshānxiàn [County].
The Western Wèi renamed it Huàzhōu.
In the early Kāihuáng period of the Suí dynasty, the commandery was abolished.
In the early Dàyè period, the prefecture was abolished,
and Zhèngxiàn County was re-established,
belonging to Jīngzhào.
In the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Huàzhōu.
The character 使 (shǐ)
is pronounced "shū lì" in fǎnqiè.
The character 降 (jiàng)
is pronounced "hù jiāng" in fǎnqiè.
The character 剌 (là)
is pronounced "lú dá" in fǎnqiè.
3 In summer,
the fourth month,
Zhào Fèngzhāng, the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Xiánníng
Xiánníngjùn was originally Dānzhōu Dānyángjùn;
in the first year, the commandery name was changed.
The character 守 (shǒu)
is pronounced "shì yòu" in fǎnqiè.
His memorial had not yet arrived,
but Línfǔ knew about it.
He insinuated to the Imperial Censors to arrest him,

4 Previously,
all zhé冲 fǔ had wooden tallies and bronze fish tallies.
When the imperial court mobilized troops,
it would issue an imperial rescript, a tally, and a fish tally.
According to the Táng system: bronze fish tallies were used to raise armies.
Within the royal domain (wáng jī),
the left half was three, and the right half was one;
outside the royal domain,
the left half was five, and the right half was one.
The left halves were used when operating externally,
with the first one used as the initial one,
and for subsequent matters requiring a second mobilization, it would be issued again,
cycling repeatedly.
As for the system of wooden tallies,
if the crown prince (tài zǐ) was supervising the state (jiān guó),
then within the royal domain,
both the left and right halves would each be three;
outside the royal domain,
both the left and right halves would each be five.
For various officials guarding (zhèn shǒu) regions,
both the left and right halves would each be ten.
The Táng Liù Diǎn states: The Fú Bǎo Láng was in charge of tallies and seals.
Wooden tallies were so named
to emphasize the importance of regional defense (zhèn shǒu)
and to ensure caution in issuing and receiving them.
When the imperial carriage (chē jià) was on a tour of inspection (xún xìng),
and the crown prince (huáng tài zǐ) was supervising the state,
if there were military forces (bīng mǎ) to be deployed,
wooden tallies would be used.
All expeditions, including those involving armies and leading forces of five hundred men and five hundred horses or more,
were issued wooden tallies.
For officials below the Sān Gōng,
the resident administrators of the two capitals (liǎng jīng liú shǒu) and those in various prefectures (zhōu) who had military forces to deploy,
wooden tallies were also issued.
Bronze fish tallies were so named
because they were used to raise armies
and to facilitate the change of commanders (shǒu zhǎng).

The resident administrators of the two capitals, as well as various prefectures, various armies, zhé冲 fǔ, garrisons (zhuō bīng zhèn shǒu zhī suǒ) in various places, and palace overseers (gōng zǒng jiān),
were all issued fish tallies.
Chéng Dàchāng's Yǎn Fán Lù states that
in the Táng era,
in addition to the left fish tally, an imperial rescript (chì dié) would also accompany it,
hence it was also called a "fish document" (yú shū).
"先" (xiān) is
read as "sì jiàn fān".
"下" (xià) is
read as "xiá jià fān".
After that, they were dispatched.
Since the recruitment and establishment of the Guō Jì,
see Volume 212 for Guō Jì in Kaiyuan Thirteenth Year.
"彍" (guō)
is pronounced "guō",
and also "huò".
For those who died or deserted,
the responsible officials no longer replenished their numbers.
Their six packhorses and oxen, equipment, and dry rations
were nearly completely depleted.
Soldiers from the fǔ bīng who were stationed as imperial guards
were called "shì guān" (attendant officials),
meaning they served as the emperor's bodyguards.
Later, many of these primary guards were lent out to individuals,
who used them like slaves.
The people of Cháng'ān were ashamed of this,
to the extent that they used it to revile each other.
The Jì Rú Xíng states: "Now the common people revile each other with 'rúp' (scholars)."
The commentary states: "They taunt each other with 'rúp',
hence they tease each other."
"Gòu bìng" (revile)
is similar to "chǐ rǔ" (humiliate).
Dù Yù states: "To tease and make one ashamed is 'jìn'."
"詬" (gòu)
is pronounced "gòu",
and also "hū hòu fān".
Furthermore, many were harshly exploited by frontier generals,
who profited from their deaths by confiscating their property.
Consequently, all those who were supposed to serve as fǔ bīng fled and hid,
so that by this time, there were no soldiers to hand over.
In the fifth month,
on the guǐ yǒu day,
Lǐ Línfǔ memorialized to halt the issuance of "yú shū" (fish documents) by the zhé冲 fǔ,
after which the fǔ bīng consisted only of officials.
Under the Táng fǔ bīng system,
ten men constituted a "huǒ",
and each "huǒ" had a leader.
Each "huǒ" was equipped with six packhorses.

Generally, each "huǒ" had one set of tools, one black cloth tent, one iron cooking pot, one horse trough, one cloth manger, one spade, one pickaxe, one chisel, one pestle, one basket, one axe, one pair of pincers, and one saw;
two armor stands;
and two sickles.
Fifty men constituted a "duì".
Each "duì" was equipped with one fire drill,
one breast-rope for horses,
three head-halters and three fetters.
Each man was equipped with one bow,
thirty arrows,
one quí, one horizontal saber, one whetstone, one large awl, one felt cap, one felt saddlebag, and one pair of gaiters.
Nine dòu of wheat rations
and two dòu of rice
were all self-provided.
Their armor and military equipment were stored in the arsenal.
When there was a military expedition,
they would be inspected and issued these items.
For those on rotation as imperial guards (fān shàng sù wèi),
only bows, arrows, and horizontal sabers were provided.
Now, all these are depleted and ruined,
no longer as they were.
Moreover, there were no promotions for years,
and even literati (shì dà fū) considered it shameful to serve.
As for the system of guō jì,
after the Tiānbǎo era,
it also gradually changed and became obsolete.
Those who answered the call for recruitment were all peddlers from the marketplace (shì jǐng) and unruly youths.
Kǒng Yǐngdá states: "Bái Hǔ Tōng says: 'Markets are formed by wells,
hence they are called shì jǐng.'"
Yìng Shào's Tōng Sú Wén says: "'Shì' means 'rely';
relying on it to support the elderly and young
ensures they do not lack."
Popular saying about shì jǐng,
refers to those who went to the market washing their items to be fragrant and clean at the well,
and adorning themselves,
before going to the market.
We carefully examine that in ancient times, twenty mù constituted a "jǐng",
and because markets were established for trade,
they were called "shì jǐng".
Thus, it originally referred to trade within the well-field (jǐng tián) system,
so the markets in the capital cities were also called "shì jǐng".
According to the Rítu system, nine men constituted a "jǐng".
Yìng Shào's statement that twenty mù constitute a "jǐng"
is based on Shào's reference to the Hàn Shū Shí Huò Zhì, where one "jǐng" consisted of eight households,
each household having one hundred mù of private land
and ten mù of public land,
with the remaining twenty mù used for wells, stoves, huts, and dwellings,
hence he mentioned twenty mù.
The formation of markets by wells
might be as Shào stated.
At that time, peace had lasted for a long time,
and many commentators believed that China's military forces could be reduced.
Consequently, commoners possessing weapons were prohibited.
If a son became a military official,
his father and elder brothers would disown him.
Fierce generals and elite soldiers
were all gathered in the northwest,
and China had no military preparedness.
5 Lǐ Hún and others, hermits of Tài Bái Shān, submitted a memorial, stating:
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù states: "Wǔ Gōng Xiàn has Tài Yī Shān,
ancient texts refer to it as Zhōng Nán,
also called Zhōng Nán,
also called Tài Bái Shān,
located south of Wǔ Gōng Xiàn,
two hundred lǐ from Cháng'ān,
its height is unknown.
The popular saying goes:
'Wǔ Gōng, Tài Bái,
three hundred lǐ from heaven.'"
Dù Yàn Yuǎn states: "Tài Bái Shān connects to Wǔ Gōng Shān in the south,
it is the most outstanding and majestic among all mountains,
with accumulated snow in winter and summer,
appearing dazzling white when viewed."
The Suí Zhì states: "Tài Yī Shān is in the vicinity of Zhōu Zhì Xiàn."
The Xīn Zhì states: "Tài Bái Shān is in Méi Xiàn."
They stated that in Jīn Xīng Dòng there was a jade tablet with an inscription, a symbol of the sagely ruler's blessings and longevity.
The emperor ordered Yù Shǐ Zhōng Chéng Wáng Xiē to enter Xiān Yóu Gǔ to seek it, and he found it.
The emperor, seeing that auspicious omens followed one another,
all due to the glorious achievements of his ancestors,
in the sixth month,
on the wù shēn day,
bestowed the holy ancestral title "Dà Dào Xuán Yuán Huáng Dì" upon his holy ancestor.
He posthumously titled Gāo Zǔ as "Shén Yáo Dà Shèng Huáng Dì".
Tài Zōng was posthumously titled "Wén Wǔ Dà Shèng Huáng Dì".
Gāo Zōng was posthumously titled "Tiān Huáng Dà Shèng Huáng Dì".
Zhōng Zōng was posthumously titled "Xiào Hé Dà Shèng Huáng Dì".
Ruì Zōng was posthumously titled "Xuán Zhēn Dà Shèng Huáng Dì".
Dòu Tài Hòu and others below her were all posthumously titled "Shùn Shèng Huáng Hòu".
6 On the xīn hài day,
Xíng Bù Shàng Shū and Jīng Zhào Yǐn Xiāo Jiǒng, due to corruption, was demoted to Rǔ Yīn Tài Shǒu.
Rǔ Yīn Jùn
is Yǐng Zhōu.
11th year, *xīnmǎo* (751 CE),
Hermit Cuī Chāng (崔昌) submitted a memorial, saying:
"The state should succeed the Zhōu (周) and Hàn (漢) dynasties,
using the element Earth to replace Fire.
The Zhōu (周) and Suí (隋) were both 'intercalary' (or 'illegitimate') reigns,
and their descendants should not be considered as the successors of the Two Kings."
The matter was sent down to the high officials for a collective discussion.
Xuéshì (學士) of the Jíxián Diàn (集賢殿), Wèi Bāo (衞包), submitted a memorial, saying:
"On the night of the collective discussion,
four stars gathered in the Tail constellation (*wěi* 尾),
which clearly shows Heaven's will."
Thereupon, the Emperor ordered a search for the descendants of the Yīn (殷), Zhōu (周), and Hàn (漢) to be the Sān Kè (三恪),
and abolished the titles of Dukes of Hán (韓), Jiè (介), and Xī (酅).
Hán (韓) was
a descendant of the Yuán Wèi (元魏).
Jiè (介) was
a descendant of the Hòu Zhōu (後周).
Xī (酅) was
a descendant of the Suí (隋).
Xī (酅) is pronounced *hù guī* (戶圭) in reverse.

Kǒng Yǐngdá (孔穎達) said: "According to the ancient *Zuǒshì Chuán* (左氏傳) commentary on the *Chūnqiū* (春秋), the Zhōu (周) house enfeoffed the descendants of the Two Kings of Xià (夏) and Yīn (殷) as high dukes (*shànggōng* 上公),
and enfeoffed the descendants of the Huángdì (黃帝), Yáo (堯), and Shùn (舜),
calling them the Sān Kè (三恪)."
Zhèng Shì (鄭氏) said: "The preserved descendants of the Two Kings
were commanded to perform sacrifices to Heaven in the manner of the Son of Heaven,
to offer sacrifices to their founding ancestors, the kings who received Heaven's mandate,
and to independently observe their own calendar, reign names, and colors of dress.
*Kè* (恪)
means 'respect.'
Out of respect for their former sages, their descendants were enfeoffed,
and they were no different from other feudal lords,
and could not be compared to the descendants of Xià (夏) and Yīn (殷)."
Bāo (包) was a Yuánwàiláng (員外郎) of the Yúbù (虞部).
12th year, Winter,
10th month,
*gēngshēn* day,
the Emperor visited Huáqīng Gōng (華清宮).
13th year, Wáng Xuányì (王玄翼), a recluse from Tàibái Shān (太白山), submitted a memorial claiming to have seen Xuányuán Huángdì (玄元皇帝),
who said that the Bǎoxiān Dòng (寶仙洞) contained the Miàobǎo Zhēnfú (妙寶真符).
*Kǎoyì* (考異) states: "According to the old records,
'Wáng Xiāng (王鉷) reported that Xuányì (玄翼) saw Xuányuán (玄元) in Bǎoxiān Dòng (寶仙洞).
Xiāng (鉷) was sent with Zhāng Jūn (張均), Wáng Chuí (王倕), Wáng Jì (王濟), Wáng Yì (王翼), and Yuè Líng (嶽靈) to the cave,
where they found a jade casket, the *Shàngqīng Hùguó Jīng* (上清護國經), precious talismans, and records, which they presented.'"
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄).
(These items) were obtained.
At that time, the Emperor honored Daoism
and yearned for immortality;
thus, people everywhere competed to report auspicious omens and portents,
and ministers submitted congratulatory memorials every month without fail.
Lǐ Línfǔ (李林甫) and others all requested to convert their residences into Daoist temples
to pray for the Emperor's longevity,
and the Emperor was pleased.
14th year, Ān Lùshān (安祿山) repeatedly lured the Xī (奚) and Qìdān (契丹),
arranged banquets for them,
and gave them *làngdàng* (莨菪) wine.
The *Běncǎo* (本草) states: "The seeds of *làngdàng* (莨菪) grow by the sea and in river valleys;
they are now found everywhere.
The seedlings and stems are about two to three *chǐ* high;
the leaves resemble those of *dìhuáng* (地黃) and *hónglán* (紅藍), etc.,
but are three fingers wide.
They bloom in the fourth month with
purple flowers.
The stems are covered with white hairs.
They bear fruit in the fifth month,
with a husk in the shape of a poppy capsule,
like a small pomegranate.
The seeds inside are extremely fine,
bluish-white like grains of rice,
and very poisonous.
If boiled for one or two days, they sprout.
When used to brew wine,
their toxicity is even greater."
*Wèi* (為) is pronounced *yú wěi* (于偽) in reverse;
the *wèi* (為) below is pronounced the same.
*Yǐn* (飲) is pronounced *yú zhèn* (於鴆) in reverse.
*Làng* (莨)
has the sound *làng* (浪).
*Dàng* (菪)
has the sound *dàng* (蕩).
(He massacred) several thousand people,
sending their chiefs' heads
as tribute,
doing this several times.
At this time, he requested to come to court.
The Emperor ordered the relevant authorities to first build a residence for him in Zhāoyìng (昭應).
At that time, all the princes and dukes privately built residences in Zhāoyìng (昭應),
but only Lùshān (祿山), by imperial favor,
was ordered by the authorities to build a residence.
*Qiú* (酋) is pronounced *cí yóu* (慈由) in reverse.
*Zhǎng* (長) is pronounced *zhī liǎng* (知兩) in reverse.
*Cháo* (朝) is pronounced *zhí yáo* (直遙) in reverse.
Yáng Zhāo's (楊釗) brothers and sisters all went to welcome him,
their carriages and parasols covering the fields.
The Emperor himself went to Wàngchūn Gōng (望春宮) to await him.
On *xīnwèi* day,
Lùshān (祿山) presented eight thousand Xī (奚) captives.
The Emperor ordered that they be recorded as "superior of superiors" in the annual evaluation.
Before this, Lùshān (祿山) was permitted to mint coins in five furnaces in Shànggǔ (上谷).
Lùshān (祿山) then presented a sample of one thousand *mín* of coins.
15th year, Yáng Zhāo (楊釗)
was the nephew of Zhāng Yìzhī (張易之).
He submitted a memorial requesting the rehabilitation of Yìzhī's (易之) brothers.
The execution of Yìzhī's (易之) brothers is recorded in Volume 207, Emperor Zhōngzōng's (中宗) Shénlóng (神龍) 1st year.
On *gēngchén* day,
an edict cited the merit of Yìzhī's (易之) brothers in welcoming Emperor Zhōngzōng (中宗) from Fánglíng (房陵).
Welcoming Emperor Zhōngzōng (中宗)
was not initiated solely by the two Zhāng (張) brothers;
the matter is recorded in Volume 206, Empress Wǔ's (武后) Shènglì (聖曆) 1st year.
*Kǎoyì* (考異) states: "The *Táng Lì* (唐曆) records it as the 25th day of the 7th month."
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄).
Because a *túchèn* (圖讖) contained the phrase
"gold knife" (*jīndāo* 金刀),
Zhāo (釗) requested to change his name.
The Emperor bestowed upon him the name Guózhōng (國忠).
16th year, 12th month,
*yǐhài* day,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
17th year, Wáng Nándé (王難得), the Yóuyì Shǐ (遊弈使) of Guānxī (關西), attacked the Tǔbō (吐蕃),
captured five bridges,
and seized Shùdūn Chéng (樹敦城).
Nándé (難得) was appointed Báišuǐ Jūnshǐ (白水軍使).
18th year, Gāo Xiānzhī (高仙芝), the Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of the Ānxī Sìnzhèn (安西四鎮), feigned a peace agreement with Shíguó (石國),
then led his troops to attack it,
captured its king and his people, and returned,
killing all the old and weak.
Xiānzhī (仙芝) was greedy by nature,
and plundered over ten *hú* of *sèsè* (瑟瑟, an emerald-like gem),
five or six camel-loads of gold,
and other goods, horses, and various merchandise in comparable amounts,
all of which went into his personal household.
This laid the groundwork for the prince of Shíguó (石國) to instigate and entice various states to defeat Xiānzhī's (仙芝) army.
*Chēng* (稱) is pronounced *chǐ zhèng* (尺證) in reverse.
19th year, Yáng Guózhōng (楊國忠) was indebted to Xiānwú Zhòngtōng (鮮于仲通).
Xiānwú Zhòngtōng (鮮于仲通) provided financial support to Guózhōng (國忠)
and also promoted him;
this matter is recorded in the previous volume, 4th year.
Zhòngtōng (仲通) was narrow-minded and impetuous by nature,
thus losing the hearts of the barbarian tribes.
According to custom,
the Nánzhào (南詔) always visited the Dūdū (都督) with their wives and children.
When passing through Yúnnán (雲南),
Zhāng Qiántuó (張虔陀), the Administrator of Yúnnán (雲南), always had illicit relations with them.
Moreover, he made many demands.
Gēluófèng (閤羅鳳), the King of Nánzhào (南詔), refused to comply.
Qiántuó (虔陀) sent people to insult him,
and secretly reported his crimes.
Gēluófèng (閤羅鳳) was furious and resentful.
In this year,
he raised an army and rebelled,
attacked and captured Yúnnán (雲南),
killed Qiántuó (虔陀),
and took thirty-two barbarian prefectures (*yízhōu* 夷州).
*Yízhōu* (夷州)
refers to the subordinate and tributary prefectures of the southwestern barbarians that had adopted Chinese civilization.
10th year
(*xīnmǎo*, 751 CE)
1st month,
Spring,
on *rénchén* day,
the Emperor offered sacrifices at the Tàiqīng Gōng (太清宮).
On *guǐsì* day,
he offered sacrifices at the Tàimiào (太廟).
On *jiǎzǐ* day,
he jointly sacrificed to Heaven and Earth at the southern suburban altar,
granted a general amnesty to the empire,
and remitted the land tax for the current year throughout the empire.
The text above mentions *rénchén* and *guǐsì*,
and the text below mentions *dīngyǒu*.
Therefore,
"*jiǎzǐ*" (甲子)
should probably be written as
"*jiǎwǔ*" (甲午).
2nd month,
on *dīngyǒu* day,
Lǐ Línfǔ (李林甫) was appointed to remotely command the Shuòfāng Jiédùshǐ (朔方節度使),
with Lǐ Wěi (李暐), the Hùbù Shìláng (戶部侍郎), appointed to manage affairs in his stead.
3rd month,
on *gēngzǐ* day,
the five households of the Yáng (楊) clan went on a night outing.
Yáng Xiān (楊銛), Qí (錡), and the three ladies of Hán (韓), Guó (虢), and Qín (秦) constituted the five households.
"Guǎngpíng" (廣平)
is written as "Guǎngníng" (廣寧) in the *Xīnshū* (新書).
The Princess
was the Emperor's daughter.
*Cóng* (從) is pronounced *cái yòng* (才用) in reverse.
The Princess fell from her horse.
Chéng Chāngyì (程昌裔), the imperial son-in-law, dismounted to help her up
and was also whipped several times.
The Princess tearfully complained to the Emperor.
The Emperor had a Yáng (楊) family slave beaten to death for this.
The next day,
Chāngyì (昌裔) was dismissed from office
and forbidden from attending court.
4 The Emperor commanded the officials to construct a residence for Ān Lùshān in the Qīnrén Ward,
issuing an imperial decree that it should be built with utmost grandeur,
without regard for cost.
When it was completed,
it was fully furnished with canopies, curtains, and utensils,
filling it completely.
There were two beds inlaid with white sandalwood,
each ten *zhàng* long
and six *chǐ* wide.
The *Běncǎo Tú Jīng* states: Sandalwood is like regular *tán* wood,
growing in the Nánhǎi region,
with varieties of yellow, white, and purple.
帟,
pronounced *yì*.
長,
pronounced *zhí liàng* (rising tone) when meaning 'long'.
The tent measured one *zhàng* by six *chǐ*.
All kitchen utensils were adorned with gold and silver;
there were two gold rice jars,
and two silver rinsing basins.
A rinsing basin
is used for washing rice.
There was one woven silver-thread basket and one silver-thread strainer.
Other items were similar.
Even the Emperor's personal possessions and regalia
scarcely surpassed them.
The Emperor often ordered his eunuchs to supervise the construction for Lùshān,
護,
meaning to oversee.
使,
pronounced *shū lì* (falling tone);
same below.
Often admonishing them, saying:
"The barbarian's eyes are large;
do not let him laugh at me."
When Lùshān moved into his new residence,
he held a banquet
and requested an imperial decree to invite the chancellors to his residence.
On that day,
the Emperor wished to play polo downstairs,
but quickly cancelled the game
and ordered the chancellors to attend.
Daily, he sent the various Yáng family members to select scenic spots and feast with him,
accompanied by music from the Líyuán and Jiàofāng.
Líyuán refers to the Emperor's Líyuán Disciples.
Jiàofāng refers to the Inner Jiàofāng.
Sometimes, fresh game was caught during hunts in the imperial park,
and he would immediately send eunuchs on horseback to bestow it upon him,
in an endless stream along the road.
On the *Jiǎchén* day,
Lùshān's birthday,
the Emperor and Guì bestowed a generous amount of clothing, precious artifacts, wine, and food.
Three days later,
Lùshān was summoned into the Forbidden Palace.
Guì wrapped Lùshān in a large swaddling cloth made of brocade,
and had palace women carry him in a colorful palanquin.
When the Emperor heard the joyful laughter from the inner palace,
he asked the reason,
and his attendants replied that Guì was performing the "washing of Lù-child" ceremony for the third day.
The Emperor went to observe it himself,
and was pleased.
He bestowed gold and silver coins upon Guì for the "washing ceremony,"
and again richly rewarded Lùshān.
They parted when the merriment was complete.
From then on, Lùshān's entry and exit from the palace were unrestricted;
sometimes he dined opposite Guì,
and sometimes he did not leave until dawn,
leading to scandalous rumors outside,
yet the Emperor did not suspect him.
5 Gāo Xiānzhī, the Jìedùshǐ of Ānxī, came to court,
presenting the captured Qíkěhàn of the Tūqíshī, the chieftains of the Tǔbō, the King of Shíguó, and the King of Qièshī.
Xiānzhī was promoted to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Soon after, Xiānzhī was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Héxī,
replacing Ān Sīshùn.
Sīshùn instigated the Hu tribes to cut their ears and gash their faces to plead for him to remain.
An imperial edict then allowed Sīshùn to remain in Héxī.
6 Ān Lùshān sought to concurrently hold the position of Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng.
In the second month,
on the *Bǐngchén* day,
Hán Xiūmín, the Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng, was made Zuǒ Yǔlín Jiāngjūn,
and Lùshān was appointed to replace him.
Jí Wēn, a Lángzhōng of the Hùbù, seeing Lùshān's favor,
also attached himself to him,
and they pledged brotherhood.
He advised Lùshān, saying:
"Although Prime Minister Lǐ, the Right Chancellor, is currently close to you, the Third Brother,
in the first year of Tiānbǎo,
the title of Shìzhōng was changed to Zuǒ Xiàng, and Zhōngshū Lìng to Yòu Xiàng.
Lǐ Línfǔ was then the Right Chancellor, holding the office of Zhōngshū Lìng;
the character "丞"
is superfluous.
Ān Lùshān was the third brother.
說,
pronounced *shì ruì* (falling tone).
Although Wēn is currently serving under you,
he will never achieve a super-promotion.
If you, elder brother, recommend Wēn to the Emperor,
Wēn will then report that you are capable of great responsibility,
and together we can oust Línfǔ,
and you will surely become chancellor."
Lùshān was pleased by his words,
and repeatedly praised Wēn's talent to the Emperor.
The Emperor also forgot his previous words.
When Lùshān took charge of Hédōng,
he consequently proposed Wēn as Fùshǐ and Zhī Liúhòu of the Jìedùshǐ,
and Zhāng Tōngrú, a Dàlǐ Sīzhí, as Liúhòu Pànguān.
Dàlǐ Sīzhí is a senior sixth-rank official.
Tōngrú held the position of Sīzhí while serving as Hédōng Liúhòu Pànguān.
Thereafter, Jìedùshǐ and their subordinates sometimes held concurrent titles of Liùcáo Shàngshū,
sometimes officials of the Three Departments,
and sometimes Sāngōng and Sānshī.
Their subordinates also typically held concurrent court positions of sixth rank and below,
known as "concurrently holding office."
Huáng Cóng said: When external officials concurrently hold office,
they might have honorary censorate titles
or acting appointments.
Honorary censorate titles ranged from Jiānchá Yǔshǐ to Yǔshǐ Dàfū,
and acting appointments from Guózǐ Jìjiǔ to Sāngōng.
This was the system during the Táng and Five Dynasties.
At this time,
Yáng Guózhōng was Yǔshǐ Zhōngchéng,
and was enjoying imperial favor and wielding power.
When Lùshān ascended and descended the palace steps,
Guózhōng always supported him.
Lùshān and Wáng Hóng were both Dàfū,
and Hóng's authority was second only to Lǐ Línfǔ.
When Lùshān met Línfǔ,
his demeanor was quite arrogant.
Línfǔ, feigning another matter, summoned Dàfū Wáng.
When Hóng arrived,
he bowed and prostrated himself with great deference.
Lùshān involuntarily lost his composure,
and his expression became increasingly respectful.
When Línfǔ spoke with Lùshān,
he always managed to discern Lùshān's thoughts
and speak them first,
which astonished and convinced Lùshān.
Lùshān was contemptuous of all the high officials,
but he alone feared Línfǔ.
Every time he met him,
even in the depths of winter,
he would sweat profusely, soaking his clothes.
Línfǔ then invited him to sit in the Zhōngshū Hall,
spoke to him gently,
and took off his own robe to cover him.
Lùshān was deeply grateful,
and spoke his mind without reservation,
calling Línfǔ "Shíláng" (Tenth Master).
Línfǔ was the tenth.
Whenever Liú Luògǔ came from Cháng'ān,
he would always ask:
"What did Shíláng say?"
If the words were favorable, he would be pleased;
but if he only said
"tell Dàfū Ān,
he needs to be more careful in his duties!"
he would immediately turn his hand and pound the bed, saying:
"Alas!
I am ruined!"
Having concurrently taken charge of the three garrisons,
Lùshān now independently issued rewards and punishments,
becoming increasingly arrogant and dissolute.
He harbored inner fear
due to his previous failure to pay homage to the Crown Prince (this matter is recorded in volume 6 above).
Moreover, seeing the military preparations lax and deficient,
he began to entertain thoughts of despising the Central Plains.
The Kǒngmùguān Yán Zhuāng
(Kǒngmùguān was a clerical position in the衙前 administration,
first appearing in the Táng Dynasty;
it meant that all matters of the office,
every detail,
had to pass through their hands)
and the Zhǎng Shūjì
(whose position was below that of Pànguān,
similar to the ancient Jìshì Cānjūn)
incited him to rebellion.
Ān Lùshān (安祿山) kept over eight thousand surrendered Tóngluó (同羅), Xī (奚), and Qìdān (契丹) people,
calling them
"Yèlòuhé" (曳落河).
Yèlòuhé (曳落河),
in the Hú (胡) language, means "brave warriors."
Along with over a hundred household servants,
all were fierce and skilled in battle,
each capable of facing a hundred.
He also kept tens of thousands of warhorses,
amassed many weapons,
and secretly dispatched Hú (胡) merchants to various circuits to trade,
annually delivering several million in precious goods.
He privately manufactured crimson and purple robes and fish pouches,
numbering in the millions.
He regarded Gāo Shàng (高尚), Yán Zhuāng (嚴莊), Zhāng Tōngrú (張通儒), and general Sūn Xiàozhé (孫孝哲) as his trusted confidants.
Shǐ Sīmíng (史思明), Ān Shǒuzhōng (安守忠), Lǐ Guīrén (李歸仁), Cài Xīdé (蔡希德), Niú Tíngjiè (牛廷jiè), Xiàng Rùnrǒng (向潤容),
Lǐ Tíngwàng (李庭望), Cuī Qiányòu (崔乾祐), Yǐn Zǐqí (尹子奇), Hé Qiānnián (何千年), Wǔ Lìngxún (武令珣), Néng Yuánhào (能元皓),
Tián Chéngsì (田承嗣), Tián Qiánzhēn (田乾真), and Āshǐnà Chéngqìng (阿史那承慶) were his fangs and claws (i.e., his vanguard generals).
Gāo Shàng (高尚) was
a person from Yōngnú (雍奴).
Yōngnú (雍奴)
was renamed Wǔqīng (武清) in the first year of Tiānbǎo (天寶) and
belonged to Fányáng Jùn (范陽郡).
This is written using the old county name.
He possessed considerable literary talent,
briefly traveled in Héshuò (河朔),
was poor and unsuccessful,
and often sighed, saying:
"How can Gāo Bùwēi (高不危) undertake a great endeavor and die,
or chew on grass roots to survive!"
Ān Lùshān (安祿山) brought him into his staff,
allowing him access to his private chambers.
Gāo Shàng (高尚) managed memorials and reports,
while Yán Zhuāng (嚴莊) handled accounts and documents.
Zhāng Tōngrú (張通儒) was
Zhāng Wànsuì's (張萬歲) son;
Zhāng Wànsuì (張萬歲)
was in charge of the imperial pastures in early Táng (唐).
Zhāng Tōngrú (張通rú) could not possibly be his son;
perhaps he was his grandson;
otherwise, there was another Zhāng Wànsuì (張萬歲).
Tián Chéngsì (田承嗣) was a Qìdān (契丹).
His family had been minor officers in Lúlóng (盧龍) for generations.
Ān Lùshān (安祿山) appointed him as his vanguard military commissioner.
Once, during a heavy snow,
Ān Lùshān (安祿山) inspected the camps.
When he reached Tián Chéngsì's (田承嗣) camp,
it was so quiet as if deserted.
He entered and inspected the soldiers,
finding not a single one absent.
Ān Lùshān (安祿山) greatly esteemed him for this.
7 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Rénwǔ (壬午),
Xiānyú Zhòngtōng (鮮于仲通), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Jiànnán (劍南), attacked the Southern Mán (蠻) of Nánzhào (南詔)
and was utterly defeated at Lúnán (瀘南).
This refers to the south of the Lúshuǐ (瀘水).
In the first year of Chuígǒng (垂拱) of Empress Wǔ (武),
Chángchéng Xiàn (長城縣) was established,
belonging to Yáozhōu (姚州),
and was renamed Lúnán Xiàn (瀘南縣) in early Tiānbǎo (天寶).
The examination of discrepancies states: The biography of Yáng Guózhōng (楊國忠) says:
"When the southern Mán (蠻) hostage Gěluófèng (閤羅鳳) fled back and was not captured,
the emperor was enraged
and wanted to punish them.
Yáng Guózhōng (楊國忠) recommended Xiānyú Zhòngtōng (鮮于仲通) from Làngzhōu (閬州) to be the Yìzhōu Zhǎngshǐ (益州長史),
ordering him to lead eighty thousand elite troops to attack the Southern Mán (蠻)."
However, the biography of Nánzhào (南詔) states:
"In the seventh year,
Méng Guīyì (蒙歸義) died,
and an imperial edict made Gěluófèng (閤羅鳳) succeed him as King of Yúnnán (雲南),"
and does not mention him ever being a hostage who fled back.
In the ninth year,
Yáozhōu (姚州) rebelled because Zhāng Qiántuó (張虔陀) had invaded them.
At that time, Xiānyú Zhòngtōng (鮮于仲通) was already Yìzhōu Zhǎngshǐ (益州長史).
Yáng Guózhōng's (楊國忠) biography contradicts the Nánzhào (南詔) biography.
Both the Old and New Histories are like this,
which is probably an error.
They advanced to Qǔzhōu (曲州) and Jìngzhōu (靖州).
The army was divided into two routes;
one route went out from Róngzhōu (戎州),
and the other route went out from Xīzhōu (嶲州).
From Kāibiān Xiàn (開邊縣) in Róngzhōu (戎州), one would travel seventy *lǐ* (里) west to Qǔzhōu (曲州);
from Xīzhōu (嶲州), one would travel over eight hundred *lǐ* (里) southwest to cross the Lúshuǐ (瀘水).
Qǔzhōu (曲州) was originally Gōngzhōu (恭州) in the Suí (隋) dynasty,
the ancient land of Zhūtí (朱提),
renamed Qǔzhōu (曲州) in the eighth year of Wǔdé (武德).
Jìngzhōu (靖州) belonged to Xiézhōu (協州) in the Suí (隋) dynasty,
the ancient land of Yèláng (夜郎),
and Jìngzhōu (靖州) was established by dividing Xiézhōu (協州) in early Wǔdé (武德).
Xī (嶲)
pronounced suǐ.
(Gěluófèng (閤羅鳳) confessed his) crime,
requested the return of the captives and plunder,
and to rebuild Yúnnán (雲南) city before departing.
The previous year,
Nánzhào (南詔) had attacked and captured Yúnnán (雲南) city.
There must have been destruction,
so he requested to rebuild the city to apologize.
"Now, a large Túbō (吐蕃) army is at our border.
If you do not grant our request,
I will submit to Túbō (吐蕃),
and Yúnnán (雲南) will no longer belong to Táng (唐)."
Zhòngtōng (仲通) refused
and imprisoned his envoy.
The army advanced to the Xīěrhé (西洱河),
where they fought Gěluófèng (閤羅鳳).
The army was utterly defeated;
sixty thousand soldiers died.
Zhòngtōng (仲通) barely escaped with his life.
Yáng Guózhōng (楊國忠) concealed the defeat
and still reported his battle merits.
The examination of discrepancies states: The Tánglì (唐曆) says,
"Ordered Zhòngtōng (仲通) to take charge of the *jiédù* (節度) affairs as a commoner,"
which is absent from old biographies.
Considering that the defeat was concealed and merits reported,
how could he then assume office as a commoner?
He built a Jīngguān (京觀) (monument of enemy corpses),
and subsequently became a vassal of Túbō (吐蕃) in the north.
In the Mán (蠻) language, a younger brother is called
"Zhōng" (鍾).
Túbō (吐蕃) appointed Gěluófèng (閤羅鳳) as
"Zānpǔ Zhōng" (贊普鍾),
giving him the title "Eastern Emperor"
and a golden seal.
Gěluófèng (閤羅鳳) inscribed a stele at his national gate,
stating that he rebelled against Táng (唐) out of necessity,
and also said:
"My ancestors served Táng (唐) for generations
and received their titles and fiefs.
Future generations may return to Táng (唐);
they should point to this stele to show the Táng (唐) envoy
that my rebellion was not my original intention."
Afterwards, during the reign of Dézōng (德宗),
Yìmóxún (異牟尋) eventually returned to Táng (唐).
Fù (復)
is pronounced fú yòu.
An imperial edict was issued to massively recruit soldiers from the two capitals, Hénán (河南), and Hénán Běi (河北) to attack Nánzhào (南詔).
People heard that Yúnnán (雲南) had much malaria and other diseases,
and eight or nine tenths of the soldiers died before even fighting,
so no one was willing to enlist.
Yáng Guózhōng (楊國忠) dispatched censors to various routes to capture people
and send them to the army in shackles.
According to the old system,
commoners with achievements were exempt from conscription and labor.
Since many soldiers were being levied at that time,
Yáng Guózhōng (楊國忠) proposed to first recruit those with high achievements.
Consequently, those departing were sorrowful and resentful,
and their parents, wives, and children saw them off,
with cries of lamentation filling the fields everywhere.
8 When Gāo Xiānzhī (高仙芝) captured the king of Shíguó (石國),
the prince of Shíguó (石國) fled to various Hú (胡) tribes
and fully reported Xiānzhī's (仙芝) deception, enticement, greed, and cruelty.
All the Hú (胡) tribes were enraged
and secretly allied with Dàshí (大食) (the Arabs) to jointly attack the Four Garrisons.
Xiānzhī (仙芝), hearing this,
led thirty thousand Fān (蕃) (non-Han) and Hàn (漢) troops to attack Dàshí (大食),
penetrating over seven hundred *lǐ* (里) deep
to the city of Héngluōsī (恆羅斯),
sometimes written as
"Dáluōsī Chéng" (怛羅斯城).
After a five-day standoff,
the Gěluólù (葛羅祿) (Karluk) tribe rebelled.
Gěluólù (葛羅祿)
is also Gěluólù (葛邏祿).
Xiānzhī (仙芝) was utterly defeated,
almost all his soldiers died,
with only a few thousand remaining.
Lǐ Sìyè (李嗣業), the General of the Right Wēiwèi (右威衞), advised Xiānzhī (仙芝) to flee overnight.
The road was narrow and obstructed,
with the Bábànnà (拔汗那) (Ferghana) troops in front,
blocking the path with people and animals.
Bábànnà (拔汗那) was accompanying Xiānzhī (仙芝) in attacking Dàshí (大食) at the time.
Sāi (塞)
is pronounced sì zé.
Lǐ Sìyè (李嗣業) wielded a large staff and struck them,
causing both people and horses to die,
allowing Xiānzhī (仙芝) to pass.
The generals and soldiers lost each other.
The detached general, Yáng Duàn Xiùshí,
of Yángjùn, originally Lǒngzhōu Lǒngdōngjùn,
whose name was changed in the first year [of Tiānbǎo].
There was Yángxiàn,
presumably established by the Northern Wèi.
“Tǐng”
is read as dài dǐng.
“Jiàng”
is read as jí liàng;
the same applies below.
“Gòu” is read as kǒu jiān.
He reproached, saying,
“To flee first from the enemy is cowardice;
to save oneself and abandon the multitude
is inhumanity.
Even if you fortunately succeed in escaping,
will you not be ashamed?”
Sīyè grasped his hand and apologized to him,
and stayed to resist the pursuing soldiers,
gathering the scattered troops.
They both escaped.
Upon returning to Ānxī,
he spoke to Xiānzhī,
who appointed Xiùshí concurrently Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ
and his own Pànguān.
9. In the eighth month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
the armory caught fire,
burning thirty-seven thousand weapons.
Kǎoyì says: The Tánglì records forty-seven thousand,
but we follow the Shílù here.
10. Ān Lùshān led sixty thousand troops from three circuits
(Yōuzhōu, Pínglú, and Hédōng).
He used two thousand Xī cavalry as guides.
After traveling over a thousand *lǐ* past Pínglú,
they reached the Tǔhùzhēn River,
where they encountered rain.
From the northeast of Xióngwǔjūn, they crossed the Luánhé.
There was the ancient Lúlóngzhèn,
and the Dǒujìnglíng.
From the north of ancient Lúlóng, passing through Jiǔjìnglíng, Shòumǐchéng, and Zhānghóng’ài,
they crossed Shílǐng,
and reached the Xī King’s encampment, six hundred *lǐ* away.
Then, to the northeast, following the Tǔhùzhēnhé for five hundred *lǐ*,
they reached the Xī and Qìdān royal encampments.
They also went out from the northeast of Yānlèxiàn in Tánzhōu, one hundred eighty-five *lǐ*,
to the Chángchéngkǒu,
and then eight hundred *lǐ* north there was the Tǔhùzhēnhé,
which was the Xī King’s royal encampment.
When they reached the Qìdān royal encampment,
the Qìdān were greatly alarmed.
At that time, it had been raining for a long time,
and the sinews and glue of the bows and crossbows were all slack.
The general Hé Sīdé said to Lùshān:
“Although our troops are numerous,
having traveled a long distance, they are exhausted
and truly unusable.
It would be better to keep our weapons sheathed and rest our soldiers to confront them.
In no more than three days,
the barbarians will surely surrender.”
Lùshān was furious and intended to execute him.
Sīdé requested to go ahead as a vanguard and die in battle.
Sīdé resembled Lùshān in appearance.
The barbarians eagerly attacked,
killing him,
thinking they had captured Lùshān,
and their courage doubled.
The Xī then rebelled
and joined forces with the Qìdān,
attacking the Táng army from both sides,
killing and wounding almost all of them.
They shot at Lùshān,
hitting his saddle,
breaking his coronet and hairpin,
and he lost his shoes.
He fled with only twenty horsemen under his command.
It happened to be night,
and the pursuing cavalry dispersed,
allowing him to enter Shīzhōu.
In the third year of Zhēnguàn,
Shīzhōu was established with the Shìwéi tribe,
governed from the abandoned Yángshīzhèn in Yíngzhōu.
“Fù”
is read as fú yòu.
“Shè”
is read as ér yì.
“Zhòng”
is read as zhú zhòng.
“Zhě”
is read as ér shè.
Gējiě were presumably those who came and surrendered from the Türks.
“Jiě”
is read as hù mǎi.
Shǐ Sīmíng, the Pínglú Bīngmǎshǐ, was afraid
and fled into the mountain valleys for nearly two *xún*,
gathering scattered soldiers,
obtaining seven hundred men.
Shǐ Dìngfāng, the Pínglú garrison commander, led two thousand elite troops to rescue Lùshān.
The Qìdān withdrew,
and Lùshān was thus saved.
Upon arriving at Pínglú,
all his subordinates had perished,
and he did not know what to do.
Shǐ Sīmíng emerged and met Lùshān.
Lùshān was delighted,
stood up,
and grasped his hand, saying,
“With you,
what more can I worry about!”
Sīmíng withdrew and said to others,
“If I had come out earlier,
I would have already been executed along with Gējiě.”
The historian says that Shǐ Sīmíng’s wisdom and resourcefulness surpassed Ān Lùshān’s.
Lùshān ordered Sīmíng to repel them.
11. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Rénzǐ,
the Emperor went to Huáqīnggōng.
12. Yáng Guózhōng had Xiānyú Zhòngtōng submit a memorial requesting that he remotely oversee Jiànnán.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Bǐngwǔ,
Guózhōng was appointed Jiànnán Jiédùshǐ.
The eleventh year
(Rénchén, 752)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the day Dīnghài,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
2. In the second month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
officials were ordered to issue grain, silk, and hundreds of thousands of *mín* of treasury money
in the two markets to exchange for bad currency.
Kǎoyì says: The Old Records and Tánglì both write
“Guǐyǒu,”
but we follow the Shílù here.
Jiāng and Huái had much bad currency.
Noble relatives and great merchants often exchanged one good coin for five bad ones,
transporting them to Cháng’ān.
The markets could not withstand the harm.
Therefore, Lǐ Línfǔ memorialized requesting a prohibition,
with the government undertaking the exchange.
The deadline was one month,
and those who did not surrender them to the government would be punished.
Thereupon, merchants were in an uproar,
finding it inconvenient.
The multitude collectively blocked Yáng Guózhōng’s horse to voice their complaints.
Guózhōng spoke to the Emperor on their behalf,
who then re-ordered that coins not cast from lead or tin, nor those with holes,
could all be used as before.
3. In the third month,
Ān Lùshān dispatched two hundred thousand Fān and Hàn infantry and cavalry to attack the Qìdān,
intending to avenge the humiliation of the previous autumn.
Originally, the Türks’ Ābùsī had surrendered.
This event is mentioned in the first year of the previous volume.
“Jiàng” is read as hù jiāng.
He was granted the surname and personal name Lǐ Xiànzhōng,
and gradually promoted to Shuòfāng Jiédù Fùshǐ,
and granted the title Fèngxìn Wáng.
Xiànzhōng had talent and strategy
and did not wish to be subservient to Ān Lùshān.
Lùshān resented him.
At this time,
he memorialized requesting that Xiànzhōng lead tens of thousands of Tuóngluó cavalry
to attack the Qìdān with him.
Xiànzhōng feared he would be harmed by Lùshān,
and informed his acting commander Zhāng Wěi,
requesting to memorialize to stay and not go.
Wěi did not permit it.
Ān Lùshān governed Hédōng, and Zhāng Wěi was the acting commander.
Wěi only knew how to attach himself to Lùshān.
How could he possibly plead for Ābùsī?
(Ābùsī) rebelled and returned to Mòběi.
Lùshān then halted his troops and did not advance.
4. On the day Yǐsì,
the Lìbù was renamed Wénbù,
the Bīngbù was renamed Wǔbù,
and the Xíngbù was renamed Xiànbù.
5. Wáng Xié, the Hùbù Shìláng, Yùshǐ Dàfū, and Jīngzhàoyǐn,
grew increasingly powerful and favored,
holding over twenty concurrent positions.
Next to his residence were offices for these commands,
with documents piled high.
Clerks seeking his signature for a single character
would wait for days without making progress.
Imperial envoys bearing gifts were constantly at his door.
Even Lǐ Línfǔ feared and avoided him.
Línfǔ’s son, Xiù, was Jiāngzuòjiān,
and Xié’s son, Zhǔn, was Wèiwèi Shàopǐng.
Both served in the Forbidden Palace.
Zhǔn often bullied Xiù,
and Xiù always deferred to him.
Zhǔn (準) once led his followers past Fùmǎ Dōuwèi Wáng Yáo (駙馬都尉王繇).
Wáng Yáo (王繇)
was the son of Tóngjiǎo (同皎).
Shuài (帥)
is read as lǜ (率).
Guò (過)
is pronounced gōng hé fān (工禾翻).
Zhǔn (準), holding a sling, hit Yáo’s (繇) cap,
breaking his jade hairpin,
as a prank.
Soon after, Yáo (繇) invited Zhǔn (準) to a banquet;
Yáo’s (繇) esteemed Yǒngmù Gōngzhǔ (永穆公主)

3. In the early Táng dynasty,
imperial edicts and decrees were all drafted by officials of the Central Secretariat and the Chancellery who were skilled in writing.
After Qiánfēng,
scholars such as Yuán Wànqǐng and Fàn Lǚbīng were first summoned to draft various literary pieces.
They would often wait at the North Gate for imperial instructions,
and people at the time called them
"North Gate Scholars."
During the reign of Zhōngzōng,
Shàngguān Zhāoróng monopolized this responsibility.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
the Hànlín Academy was first established,
close to the imperial court.
Men of letters were invited,
down to monks and Daoists,
and masters of calligraphy, painting, zithers, chess, and numerology were all accommodated there.
They were called
"Dàizhào" (Academicians-in-waiting).
Zhāng Jūn, Minister of Personnel, and his younger brother Zhāng Jì, Grand Minister of Ceremonies, both served as Dàizhào in the Hànlín Academy.
In the Táng dynasty,
when the Emperor was at Dàmíng Palace,
the Hànlín Academy was inside the Right Yíntái Gate;
when at Xìngqìng Palace,
the Academy was inside the Jīnmíng Gate;
if in the Western Palace,
the Academy was inside the Xiǎnfú Gate;
if in the Eastern Capital or Huáqīng Palace,
there were also places for the Dàizhào.
Those who served as Dàizhào
included those with literary and scholarly talents,
as well as accomplished monks, Daoists, diviners, ritual officiants, practitioners of various arts, calligraphers, and chess players.
They were housed in separate academies and provided for,
and they retired in the evening.
Among them, literary and scholarly talents were most esteemed.
Since the Emperor's ascension,
Zhāng Yuè, Lù Jiān, Zhāng Jiǔlíng, Xú Ānzhēn, Zhāng Jì, and others were summoned into the Forbidden City
and called
"Hànlín Dàizhào."
The sovereign is supreme,
handling myriad affairs daily.
Reports come from all directions,
and responses to memorials and petitions from both within and outside the court,
or imperial edicts issued from the palace,
are written by the imperial hand.
They also assist in their review,
which is called
"shì cǎo" (drafting).
Therefore, four people were usually selected to be on duty for consultation.
After Zhìdé,
with many military affairs throughout the realm,

These officials were named
"Hànlín Xuéshì" (Academicians of the Hànlín Academy).
To be selected for this position

Similar to the six Vice Ministers of the Central Secretariat, six Academicians were appointed,
and from them, one person with long service and great virtue was chosen as the Chancellor of the Academy (*Chéngzhǐ*),
because he alone was entrusted with secret imperial commands.
Dèzōng was fond of literature
and made the selection particularly difficult.
After Zhēnyuán,
many who served as Academicians or Chancellors later became Grand Counselors (*Zǎixiàng*).
'Shàng' (尚)
should be read as 'cháng' (常).
'Jì' (垍)
