Jì to Lúxī Sīmǎ,
and Jì's younger brother, Gěishìzhōng Chà, to Yíchūn Sīmǎ.
Jiàn'ān Jùn,
during the Suí dynasty, was Quánzhōu;
during the Táng dynasty, it was renamed Mínzhōu,
and Quánzhōu was separately established.
The emperor renamed Mínzhōu Fúzhōu Chánglè Jùn,
and established Jiànzhōu as Jiàn'ān Jùn.
Lúxī Jùn was Chénzhōu.
According to old records: Jiàn'ān Jùn
is four thousand nine hundred and thirty-five *lǐ* southeast of the capital.
Lúxī Jùn
is three thousand four hundred and five *lǐ* slightly east of south of the capital.
Chà (埱)
is pronounced Chāng-liù.
*Kǎoyì* states: *Tánglì* says:
"Jì once assisted in protocol and ceremonies,
conducting himself with grace and measure.
The emperor was pleased with him.
The next day,
he said to Jì: 'I will dismiss Xīliè as chancellor,
and replace him with you.'
Jì replied: 'I dare not.'
Guì was present,
and told Guózhōng to dismiss him."
The old biography of Jì states:
"During the Tiānbǎo era,
Xuánzōng once visited Jì's private residence,
and said to Jì: 'Xīliè has repeatedly declined state affairs.
Among those I might choose to replace him,
who is suitable?'
Jì was startled and did not respond.
The emperor immediately said: 'No one is better than my beloved son-in-law.'
Jì descended the steps to express his gratitude.
Yáng Guózhōng heard this and disliked him.
When Xīliè was dismissed as chancellor,
Wéi Jiànsu was put forward to replace Jì,
and Jì felt deeply disappointed."
According to the imperial annals,
on the day of Dīngyǒu in the third month,
Jì was demoted,
but Wéi Jiànsu only took charge of government affairs in the eighth month.
Therefore, the statement that Jì was deeply disappointed
in the old biography is mistaken.
*Mínghuáng Zálù* states:
"The emperor visited Zhāng Jì's residence
and said to Jì: 'Among the central and outer ministers, who are capable of being prime ministers?
Tell me all of them;
I will appoint and employ them.'
Jì hesitated and did not respond.
The emperor said: 'Indeed, none are like my beloved son-in-law.'
Jì descended the steps and bowed.
The emperor said: 'I will immediately make the appointment.'
After more than a month,
Jì felt quite discontent,
suspecting that he had been thwarted by Lǐ Línfǔ.
It happened that Lùshān came from Fányáng for an audience.
Lùshān secretly bribed Guì,
seeking to be appointed Píngzhāngshì,
but the emperor did not allow it.
Jì then at his private residence fully recounted: 'When the emperor previously visited my residence,
he personally promised to make me chancellor,
and that I would serve alongside you, My Lord.
Now that this has changed,
I must have been thwarted by treacherous ministers.'
Lùshān became greatly resentful and angry.
The next day, when he sought an audience,
he shed tears and asked for forgiveness.
The emperor consoled and encouraged him for a long time,
then asked him the reason.
Lùshān fully reported what Jì had told him.
The emperor ordered Gāo Lìshì to send him back,
and also heard of his discontent.
Because of this, the emperor was angry."
However, Lǐ Línfǔ was already dead at this time, so this is also an error.
Gēshū Hàn also assessed the merits of his subordinate generals.

An imperial edict appointed Huǒbá Guīrén, one of the ten generals of Lǒngyòu, a Grand Master for Court Discussion (Tèjìn), Governor-General of Huǒbázhōu, and Prince of Yānshān Commandery, as General-in-Chief of Cavalry (Piāoqí Dàjiàngjūn).
Ten generals,
was also the title of military commanders in the Tang dynasty from the mid-period onwards.
Huǒbá,
was a separate tribe of the Tujue.
Huǒbázhōu was established during the Kāiyuán era.
According to Tang regulations: Grand Master for Court Discussion (Tèjìn),
was a civil honorary rank (wén sànjiē),
of senior second grade (zhèng èr pǐn).
General-in-Chief of Cavalry (Piāoqí Dàjiàngjūn),
was a military honorary rank (wǔ sànjiē),
of junior first grade (cóng yī pǐn).
Yān,
rhymes with jiān.
Piāo,
rhymes with pǐ miào.
Qí,
rhymes with qí jì.

Chéng Rúqiú, the Administrator of Líntáo; Fán Yáng Lǔ Jiǒng, the Deputy Commissioner for Attack; and Hún Wéimíng, the Governor-General of Gāolán Prefecture, were all promoted to General of Cloud Cavalry (Yúnhuī Jiàngjūn).
During the Zhēnguān era,
the Tiele surrendered,
and Gāolán Governor-General’s Office was established for the Hún tribe.
General of Cloud Cavalry (Yúnhuī Jiàngjūn),
was a military honorary rank (wǔ sànjiē),
of senior third grade (cóng sān pǐn shàng).
Táo,
rhymes with tǔ dāo.
Shǒu,
rhymes with shì yòu.
Qiú,
sounds like qiú.
Jiǒng,
rhymes with huǒ jiǒng.
Yīngyì,
was the son of Zhīyùn.
Hàn also memorialized to appoint Wǔ, the son of Yán Tǐngzhī, as Military Commissioner’s Aide (Jiédù Pànguān);
Lǚ Yīn of Hédōng as Fiscal Aide (Zhīdù Pànguān);
Gāo Shì, formerly the Magistrate of Fēngqiū, as Chief Secretary (Zhǎngshūjì);
and Qū Huán of Ānyì as a separate general (biéjiàng).
Hédōng Commandery,
was Púzhōu.
According to Tang regulations: border armies had Fiscal Commissioners (Zhīdùshǐ),
to manage the use of military provisions and weapons.
Their subordinates included Aides (Pànguān) and Inspectors (Xúnguān).
Fēngqiū County,
had belonged to Chénliú since the Han and Jin dynasties.
In the Tang, it belonged to Biànzhōu.
Ānyì County,
belonged to Púzhōu.
Genealogy records: Chéng Shī, son of Duke Mù of Jin, was enfeoffed in Qūwò,
and his descendants took the surname Qū.
During the Han, there was Qū Qiān, Administrator of Dàijùn;
and in the "Biographies of Money-makers," there was Qū Shú.
Yīn,
rhymes with yī zhēn.
9 Chéng Qiānlǐ captured Ābùsī,
presented him at the imperial court,
and he was executed.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
Qiānlǐ was appointed General-in-Chief of the Left/Right Militant Guard (Jīnwú Dàjiàngjūn),
and Fēng Chángqīng was given acting authority as Protector-General of Běitíng and Military Commissioner of Yīxī.
10In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the Guǐsì day,
Ā Lùshān memorialized that he had attacked the Xī and defeated them,
capturing their king, Lǐ Rìyuè.
11In the sixth month,
on the 乙chǒu day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse,
which was not total, appearing like a hook.
12Lǐ Mì, the Palace Censor and acting Military Commissioner of Jiànnán—
Yáng Guózhōng held the position of Military Commissioner of Jiànnán,
and appointed Mì as acting commissioner.
Mì,
sounds like mì,
also sounds like fú.
Gélúofèng lured him deep into the territory,
to Dàhé City.
The New Book writes
"Tàihé City."
【In the 12-line edition, it is correctly written
"Tài";
the 11-line edition of Yi is the same;
Kong's edition is the same;
Xiong's collation is the same.
】In the Yi language, "pítuó" refers to a mountain slope, hence Dàhé (Great Slope),
which was Gélúofèng's residence.
Jiāng,
rhymes with jí liàng.
Yòu,
sounds like yòu.
Mì's provisions ran out,
and seven or eight tenths of his soldiers died from malaria and starvation.
He then led them back,
but the Man pursued and attacked them.
Mì was captured,
and the entire army was annihilated.
Yáng Guózhōng concealed this defeat,
and instead reported a victory,
sending even more troops from China to attack them.
The cumulative death toll reached nearly two hundred thousand;
including the defeat of Xiānyú Zhòngtōng,
the death toll reached this number.
Jī,
rhymes with jū yī.
The Emperor once said to Gāo Lìshì:
"I am old now.
Court affairs are entrusted to the prime ministers,
and border affairs to the generals.
What more do I have to worry about!"
Lìshì replied:
"I hear that Yúnnán has suffered numerous military losses,
and also that the border generals command excessively large armies.
How will Your Majesty control them!
I fear that once disaster strikes,
it will be irreparable.
How can you say you have no worries!"
The Emperor said:
"You need not speak,
I will consider it slowly."
Gāo Lìshì's words—
how could Emperor Míng not be moved by them in his heart!
The impending disaster was simply
left to unavoidable fate,
hoping only that he himself would not live to see it.
13In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the Guǐchǒu day,
Gēshū Hàn memorialized: two commanderies, Táoyáng and Jiāohé, and the Shéncè Army, were to be established in the newly opened Jiǔqū territory.
Chéng Rúqiú, Administrator of Líntáo, was concurrently appointed Administrator of Táoyáng,
and made Commissioner of the Shéncè Army.
Táoyáng and Jiāohé Commanderies
were both established southwest of Táozhōu and Kuòzhōu.
Kuòzhōu,
originally Jiāohé Commandery,
was renamed Níngsài Commandery in the first year of Tiānbǎo.
The Shéncè Army was established in Móhuán Chuān, eighty li west of Táozhōu.
The New Book states: Jiāohé Commandery was established west of Jīshí.
Jiāo,
rhymes with jiān yáo.
14Yáng Guózhōng was jealous of Chén Xīliè.
Xīliè repeatedly submitted memorials to resign his position.
The Emperor wanted to replace him with Jí Wēn, the Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Military Affairs (Wǔbù Shìláng),
but Guózhōng, because Wēn was associated with Ān Lùshān,
memorialized that he was unsuitable.
He recommended Wéi Jiànsù, the Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Personnel (Wénbù Shìláng),
who was mild-mannered and easy to control.
In the eighth month,
on the Bǐngxū day,
Xīliè was appointed Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàishī)
and dismissed from political affairs.
Chén Xīliè subsequently harbored resentment for this and later surrendered to the rebels.
The "Kǎoyì" (Textual Research) states: The Old Biography of Jiànsù says:
"At that time, Yáng Guózhōng wielded power.
The Left Prime Minister, Chén Xīliè, feared his authority and favor.
In all matters, he merely assented,
not daring to express his own opinions.
Xuánzōng knew this
and was displeased.
In the thirteenth year of Tiānbǎo,
in autumn,
it rained for over sixty days.
The Son of Heaven, believing that perhaps the prime ministers were not fulfilling their duties,
and seeing this ominous sign,
ordered Yáng Guózhōng to diligently seek out upright scholars.
At that time, Jí Wēn, Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Military Affairs, was enjoying imperial favor.
The Emperor intended to employ him.
Guózhōng, seeing Wēn as a retainer of Lùshān,
feared his power and influence,
and memorialized to halt the matter.
Guózhōng consulted Dòu Huá and Sòng Yù, Secretariat Drafters,
and Huá and Yù said that Jiànsù was composed
and gentle and easy to control.
The Emperor also considered that he had served in the princely establishment
and had old favors,
and agreed."
Xīliè's Biography says:
"Guózhōng wielded power,
and was secretly jealous of him.
So he brought Wéi Jiànsù into the same rank
and dismissed Xīliè from political affairs."
According to this, if Emperor Míng disliked Xīliè for flattering Guózhōng,
he should have chosen a firm and upright person himself.
How could he still seek a prime minister from Guózhōng!
Here, we follow Xīliè's Biography.
15 Since last year, floods and droughts have occurred in succession,
and there was a great famine in Guānzhōng.
Yáng Guózhōng disliked Jīngzhàoyǐn Lǐ Xiàn for not supporting him,
and attributed the disaster to Xiàn.
In the ninth month,
Xiàn was demoted to the Administrator of Chángshā.
Xiàn
was the son of Yī.
Xìn'ān Wáng Yī,
at the beginning of the Kāiyuán reign, was favored by the emperor for his military merits.
Yī,
read like "xū wéi."
Guózhōng presented the best of the harvested grains,
saying:
"Although there was much rain,
it did not harm the crops."
The emperor believed this to be true.
Fúfēng Tàishǒu Fáng Guǎn reported a flood in his jurisdiction.
Fúfēng Jùn
was Qízhōu.
Sòng Bái said: According to the old system of the Táng dynasty,
there were two Shìyùshǐ,
each in charge of investigations in the east and west.
They were also assigned to various bureaus in the capital and to various circuits and prefectures,
divided into eastern and western jurisdictions;
on odd-numbered days, the Táiyuàn handled affairs,
and on even-numbered days, the Diànyuàn handled affairs.
There were also Jiānchá Yùshǐ sent out to investigate and interrogate,
known as Tuīshì Yùshǐ.
No one in the empire dared to report disasters.
Gāo Lìshì was attending at his side,
and the emperor said:
"The continuous heavy rains do not cease..."
Jiǎ Gōngyàn said: Rain for three days or more is considered "yín" (excessive).
[Gāo Lìshì] replied:
"Since Your Majesty granted power to the chancellor,
rewards and punishments have been without order,
and yin and yang have lost their balance.
How would your subject dare to speak!"
The emperor was silent.
16 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day of Yǐyǒu,
the emperor visited Huáqīng Gōng.
17 In the eleventh month,
on the day of Jǐwèi,
two Nèishìjiān were appointed,
holding the rank of zhèng sān pǐn.
According to the Táng system,
eunuchs were not allowed to exceed the third rank;
four Nèishì were appointed,
holding the rank of cóng sì pǐn shàng.
The highest a palace official could reach
was this,
and it was not until this emperor that the system was broken.
Yáng Sīxù for military merits,
Gāo Lìshì for imperial favor,
were all appointed Dàjiāngjūn,
reaching the rank of cóng yī pǐn,
yet still called honorary officials (xūn guān).
Now, the appointment of Nèishìjiān as zhèng sān pǐn
means they are functional officials (zhíshì guān).
18 Hédōng Tàishǒu and concurrent Běndào Cǎifǎngshǐ Wéi Zhì,
older brother of Bīn,
was refined and highly renowned.
Yáng Guózhōng feared he would become chancellor,
and had someone accuse Zhì of corruption.
The case was sent to the Yùshǐ for investigation.
Zhì bribed Zhōngchéng Jí Wēn
to seek help from Ān Lùshān,
but this was again exposed by Guózhōng.
In the intercalary month,
on the day of Rén'yín,
Zhì was demoted to Guìlǐng Wèi,
and Wēn to Lǐyáng Zhǎngshǐ.
Guìlǐng
was the territory of Hàn's Línhè Xiàn,
Suí established Guìlǐng Xiàn,
and Táng it belonged to Hèzhōu.
Lǐyáng Jùn
was Lǐzhōu.
Old records state: Lǐyáng Jùn
was one thousand eight hundred and ninety-three *lǐ* southeast of the capital.
Moreover, it was said that Guózhōng was slanderous and jealous.
The emperor did not question either matter.
19 On the day of Wùwǔ,
the emperor returned to the palace.
20 In this year,
the Hùbù reported that there were three hundred and twenty-one prefectures in the empire,
one thousand five hundred and thirty-eight counties,
sixteen thousand eight hundred and twenty-nine townships,
nine million sixty-nine thousand one hundred and fifty-four households,
and fifty-two million eight hundred and eighty thousand four hundred and eighty-eight people.
The prosperity of the Táng dynasty's households and population
reached its peak at this time.
Fourteenth year
(Yǐwèi, 755)
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Sūpí Prince Xīnuòluó left Tǔbō and surrendered.
The Xīnshū states: Sūpí
was a powerful tribe of Tǔbō.
Luó, read like "láng zuǒ."
2 In the second month,
on the xīnhài day,
Ān Lùshān sent his deputy general Hé Qiānnián to submit a memorial to the throne,
requesting to replace thirty-two Hàn generals with Fān generals.
The Emperor ordered the immediate issuance of a Huà (画, "drawing" or "plan").
What is a Huà?
It means ordering the Zhōngshū (中書) to issue a Fārì Chì (發日敕, "edict issued on the day").
This was done after requesting the imperial approval (Yù Huà 御画) for execution.
The Táng Liùdiǎn (唐六典) states: "The Zhōngshū is in charge of the emperor's words,
and there are seven types of these edicts.
The fourth is called Fārì Chì,
which precisely refers to an edict issued with imperial approval."

It was used for increasing or decreasing officials, abolishing or establishing prefectures and counties, dismissing or remitting official titles and ranks, and appointing officials of the sixth rank and below.
Jiāng (將)
is pronounced as liàng.
Wéi Jiànshù said to Yáng Guózhōng:
"Lùshān has harbored rebellious intentions for a long time.
Now he has this request,
his rebellion is clear.
Tomorrow, I, Jiànshù, will speak my mind forcefully;
if the Emperor does not agree,
you should follow up."
Guózhōng agreed.
On the rénzǐ day,
Guózhōng and Jiànshù had an audience.
The Emperor greeted them and said:
"Do you gentlemen harbor suspicions about Lùshān?"
Jiànshù then strongly stated that Lùshān's rebellion already showed signs,
and his request should not be granted.
The Emperor was displeased;
Guózhōng hesitated and dared not speak.
The Emperor ultimately granted Lùshān's request.
On another day,
Guózhōng and Jiànshù said to the Emperor:
"We have a strategy that can passively thwart Lùshān's scheme.
If we now appoint Lùshān as Píngzhāng Shì (平章事),
summon him to the capital,
appoint Jiǎ Xún as the Fànyáng Jiédùshǐ (范陽節度使),
Lǚ Zhīhuì as Pínglú Jiédùshǐ (平盧節度使),
and Yáng Guānghuì as Hédōng Jiédùshǐ (河東節度使),
then his power will be naturally divided."
The Emperor agreed.
A decree was drafted,
but the Emperor held it and did not issue it.
Instead, he dispatched the palace envoy Fǔ Qiúlín to bestow rare fruits upon Lùshān,
secretly observing his movements.
Fǔ (輔)
is a surname.
In the Zuǒzhuàn (左傳),
Jìn (晉) had a grandee named Fǔ Luò (輔躒).
Also, Zhì Guǒ (智果) separated his clan to form the Fǔ (輔) clan.
This passage refers to the incident of bestowing sweet fruits upon Lùshān, as cited in the Kǎoyì (考異) earlier.
Qiú (璆)
is pronounced qiú.
Upon his return,
he greatly exaggerated Lùshān's utmost loyalty to the state,
claiming he had no ulterior motives.
The Emperor said to Guózhōng and others:
"Lùshān,
I treat him with sincerity,
he certainly has no disloyal intentions.
The two barbarian tribes in the northeast
rely on his suppression.
I will guarantee it myself,
you gentlemen need not worry!"
The matter was thus dropped.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù (實錄) records:
"In the first month,
on the xīnsì day,
Lùshān submitted a memorial requesting to replace thirty Hàn generals with Fān generals.
The Emperor sent the palace envoy Yuán Sīyì to deliver it to the Zhōngshū,
ordering them to prepare the 'Huà' immediately
and write out the appointment document.
Yáng Guózhōng and Wéi Jiànshù said to each other: 'Rumors spread that Lùshān harbors rebellious intentions,
and now he requests to replace Hàn generals;
his rebellion is clear.'
They then requested to present the matter.
Upon seeing the Emperor,
the Emperor first said: 'Do you gentlemen harbor suspicions about Lùshān?'
Guózhōng and others immediately ran down the steps,
shedding tears and fully stating Lùshān's rebellious intentions,
then left, leaving Lùshān's memorial before the Emperor.
A moment later,
the Emperor again ordered Yuán Sīyì to announce: 'This one memorial,
let us provisionally approve it.
I will slowly plan for it.'
Guózhōng received the imperial edict.
Thereafter, every time Guózhōng had an audience,
he never failed to earnestly plead for the matter.
Guózhōng said: 'I have a strategy that can resolve this difficulty.
I humbly hope that a decree be issued to make Lùshān Left Púyè (左僕射) and Píngzhāng Shì (平章事),
summon him to the imperial court,
and have Jiǎ Xún and others divide and command the three circuits.'
The Emperor agreed to it.
After the decree was drafted,
it was held and not issued.
The Emperor secretly ordered Fǔ Qiúlínn to send sweet fruits,
privately observing his situation.
Upon his return,
he firmly stated that there was no issue,
and the decree was then dropped.
Earlier, when the Emperor summoned the prime ministers for an audience,
he always placed white silk (bái má 白麻, for drafting edicts) in front of their seats.
When Qiúlínn returned,
the Emperor then said to his prime ministers:
'Lùshān certainly has no disloyal intentions.
I have already burned the decree.'
Later, when Qiúlínn's acceptance of a bribe from Lùshān was exposed,
the Emperor, during a sacrifice at the Dragon Hall,
sent him to prepare offerings,
accusing him of impiety,
and then ordered his左右 (attendants) to beat him to death;
it was only then that he began to suspect Lùshān."
The Lùshān Shìjì (祿山事迹) states:
"The request not to replace Hàn generals with Fān generals,
the discussion of Lùshān's rebellious state,
and the request to summon Lùshān to the capital,
were all the intentions of Wéi Jiànshù;
Guózhōng had no part in it.
He even said to Jiànshù: 'Lùshān came from humble beginnings,
and now holds a position above the masses.
He is naturally envied and mistrusted at this time,
hence the suspicions.'
Jiànshù said: 'If you truly hold this view,
the state is in peril.'
When about to earnestly discuss the matter before the Emperor,
Jiànshù made an agreement: 'If the matter is not resolved,
you must follow up.'
Guózhōng did not say a single word,
bowed and retreated.
Jiànshù returned to the Zhōngshū,
weeping and sobbing.
This was nothing else;
Guózhōng wanted Lùshān to rebel quickly
to prove his own foresight."
Sòng Jù's Xuánzōng Xìng Shǔ Jì (宋巨玄宗幸蜀記) states:
"In the spring of that year,
in the second month,
on the twenty-second day, xīnhài,
Lùshān sent Hé Qiānnián to submit a memorial requesting to replace thirty-two Hàn generals with Fān generals to command the troops.
On that day,
the prime ministers Wéi Jiànshù and Yáng Guózhōng were in the secretariat.
Jiànshù looked distraught.
Guózhōng asked: 'Elder Hall (堂老, a polite address for Jiànshù), why are you so sad?'
Jiànshù said: 'Lùshān's rebellious state
is known by everyone on the road.
Now to replace Hàn generals with Fān chieftains,
means chaos is about to break out.
As we hold this position,
how can we not be sad!'
Guózhōng was also at a loss for a long time,
then said: 'Whether to grant or deny
rests upon the imperial decision;
how can we make right or wrong of it!'
Jiànshù said: 'Knowing the emergence of disaster but being unable to prevent it,
what use is such a prime minister!'
Tomorrow, when we meet the Emperor,
I will certainly plead earnestly,
hoping for a slight chance.
If he does not agree,
you must follow up.'
Guózhōng said: 'If the matter does not succeed,
I fear offending the Emperor's face in vain,
thereby inviting trouble upon myself.'
Jiànshù said: 'If one dies for speaking rightly,
it is still better than conforming and clinging to life.'
The next day, rénzǐ,
the two prime ministers entered for an audience.
Jiànshù said: 'Lùshān secretly harbors rebellious schemes,
and the signs are already manifest,'
then kowtowed and wept for a long time.
Guózhōng merely bowed, hesitated,
and offered no further help.
The Emperor was displeased
and then discussed other matters.
After they retreated to the secretariat,
Jiànshù said to Guózhōng: 'The Sacred Will has not changed;
what plan shall we adopt?'
Guózhōng said: 'Lùshān may not necessarily have rebellious intentions;
it is merely that he is slandered and envied by the times,
leading to suspicions.'
Jiànshù said: 'If you hold this view,
the state is in peril.'
He then sorrowfully fell silent.
On the twenty-fourth day, guǐchǒu,
the Emperor again sent Sīyì to announce an imperial edict,
ordering: 'For now, proceed according to this.
The matters you gentlemen discussed
will be deliberated separately later.'
From then on, Jiànshù repeatedly memorialized about Lùshān's sinister conduct.
On the first day of the third month, jǐwèi,
Jiànshù requested that Lùshān be appointed Tong Zhongshu Menxia Píngzhāng Shì (同中書門下平章事)
and summoned to the imperial court.
When Fǔ Qiúlínn delivered the sweet fruits,
Lùshān deceived Qiúlínn saying: 'The Emperor is old,
trusting improperly.
Guózhōng and his kind
are merely seeking personal glory.
If I were to present unpalatable advice or bitter medicine,
with my heart,
The matter will be of no benefit.
Now, wishing to display military might and strongly remonstrate,
thereby showing signs of Yùquán,
this intention is decided.'
Lùshān presented gifts to QiúLín.
After QiúLín had received the gold and silk,
and returned,
he memorialized, saying: 'Lùshān is utterly loyal and serves the country,
he certainly has no disloyal intentions,
and I particularly hope that Your Majesty will not worry about Dōngběi.'
The Emperor approved of it,
and said to his prime ministers: 'Lùshān, I personally guarantee him,
you need not worry!'
JiànSù rose and said: 'Your servant has offended the imperial decree,
and presumed to disrespect a high official,
my crime deserves ten thousand deaths.
However, even a foolish person in a thousand considerations,
may sometimes hit upon one correct point,
I beg Your Majesty to carefully examine it.' "
The rest is generally consistent with what is narrated in the *shílù* and historical accounts.
Considering that Lùshān was just then bribing QiúLín,
to conceal his traces of rebellion,
how would he suddenly utter rebellious words in front of him?
Furthermore, Guózhōng had frequently stated that Lùshān intended to rebel,
how could he not be of the same mind as JiànSù at this juncture?
This is probably what is meant by "all evils in the world are attributed to him."
Now, we select the credible parts.
He was a native of Huáyuan.
At that time, he was the jiédù fùshǐ.
3 Gēshū Hàn, the jiédùshǐ of Lǒngyòu and Héxī, came to court,
and on the way, he contracted a stroke,
so he remained in the capital,
staying at home and not going out.
4 In the third month,
on the *xīnsì* day,
the jǐshìzhōng Péi Shìyān was ordered to convey imperial goodwill to Héběi.
5 In summer,
in the fourth month,
Ān Lùshān memorialized that he had defeated the Xī and Qìdān.
6 On the *guǐsì* day,
Prince Xīnuòluó of Sūpí was appointed Huáiyìwáng,
and was bestowed the name Lǐ Zhōngxìn.
7 Ān Lùshān returned to Fányáng.
Every time the court sent envoys,
he would feign illness and not go out to welcome them.
He would conspicuously display his military preparations,
and only then meet them.
When Péi Shìyān arrived in Fányáng,
it took more than twenty days before he was granted an audience,
and there was no longer the decorum of a subject.
Yáng Guózhōng sought day and night for evidence of Lùshān's rebellion,
and ordered the Jīngzhàoyǐn to surround his residence.
The *Kǎoyì* says: *Sùzōng Shílù* states:
"Yáng Guózhōng sought day and night for evidence of Ān Lùshān's rebellion,
sometimes fabricating imperial edicts to besiege his residence with troops,
or ordering prefectures and counties to arrest his retainers Lǐ Qǐ, Ān Dài, Lǐ Fānglái, and others.
All of these were secretly investigated and interrogated by Shìyùshǐ Zhèng Ángzhī,
and quietly clubbed to death.
Because Qìngzōng was married to a Princess and
also served at the capital,
he secretly reported this to his father,
and Lùshān grew even more fearful."
The *Táng Lì* states:
"This summer,
Jīngzhàoyǐn Lǐ Xiàn was demoted to Línglíng Tàishǒu.
Previously, Yáng Guózhōng had sent his retainers Jiǎn Áng and Hé Yíng to investigate Ān Lùshān's secret affairs,
ordering the Jīngzhàoyǐn to surround and apprehend people at his residence.
They captured Ān Dài, Lǐ Fānglái, and others with evidence of Lùshān's rebellion,
and had Shìyùshǐ Zhèng Ángzhī strangle them.
Lùshān was enraged
and sent Yán Zhuāng to submit a memorial in his own defense,
detailing more than twenty charges against Yáng Guózhōng.
The Emperor feared he would cause trouble,
and so shifted the blame to Lǐ Xiàn to appease him."
The *Ān Lùshān Shìjì* is similar to the *Táng Lì*,
and additionally states:
"He ordered Jīngzhàoyǐn Lǐ Xiàn to arrest Lǐ Qǐ, Ān Dài, Lǐ Fānglái, and others at his residence;
he also demoted Jí Wēn to Lǐyáng Zhǎngshǐ
to provoke Lùshān's anger,
hoping he would rebel quickly.
The Emperor ultimately did not realize this."
The *Xuánzōng Xìngshǔ Jì* is similar to the *Shìjì*.
According to Lǐ Xiàn's biography:
"In the twelfth year [of Tiānbǎo],
it rained for more than sixty days consecutively.
Yáng Guózhōng blamed the Jīngzhàoyǐn [Lǐ Xiàn],
and he was demoted to Chángshā Tàishǒu."
The *Xīn Zōngshì Zǎixiàng Chuán* states:
"Yáng Guózhōng sent his retainers Jiǎn Áng and Hé Yíng to uncover Ān Lùshān's secret affairs,
and hinted to the Jīngzhào [Yǐn] to apprehend people at his residence.
They captured Ān Dài, Lǐ Fānglái, and others with evidence of Lùshān's rebellion,
and strangled them.
Lùshān was enraged
and submitted a memorial in his own defense.
The Emperor, fearing trouble,
sent Lǐ Xiàn out as Línglíng Tàishǒu."
We now follow the *Shílù*.
They were sent to the Yùshǐ Tái prison
and secretly killed.
Lùshān's son Qìngzōng was married to the imperial daughter, Princess Róngyì,
and served at the capital.
He was Tàipú Qīng in the capital
and was allowed to attend audiences with the other court officials.
Lùshān grew even more fearful.
In the sixth month,
the Emperor, because his son was getting married,
sent a handwritten edict inviting Lùshān to observe the ceremony.
Lùshān declined, citing illness, and did not come.
Autumn,
seventh month,
Lùshān memorialized, offering three thousand horses,
with two attendant grooms for each horse,
and dispatched twenty-two barbarian generals to escort them.
He intended to launch a surprise attack on the capital with them.
A memorial was submitted requesting:
"Inform Lùshān that the presentation of chariots and horses should wait until winter,
and the court will provide the grooms itself,
without bothering his army."
At this, the Emperor gradually understood,
and began to suspect Lùshān.
At the same time, the matter of Fǔ Qiúlín taking bribes was also exposed,
and the Emperor, using another pretext, had him beaten to death.
The Emperor sent the palace envoy Féng Shénwēi with a handwritten edict to inform Lùshān,
as advised by Xún Cè;
it also said:
"We have just built a new bath for you.
Since the sixth year of Tiānbǎo,
baths at Huáqīng Gōng have been continuously built,
with wells, pools, terraces, and pavilions
arranged around the valley.
The imperial bath is called Jiǔlóng Diàn,
also known as Liánhuā Tāng."
The *Mínghuáng Zálù* states:
"When Emperor Mínghuáng visited Huáqīng Gōng,
new baths were extensively built,
magnificent and beautiful in their construction.
Ān Lùshān, from Fányáng,
presented fish, dragons, ducks, and geese made of white jade,
along with a stone bridge and lotus flowers.
Their carving was so exquisite
as to be almost superhuman.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and ordered them to be displayed in the bath,
with the stone bridge spanning across the bath,
and the lotus flowers just emerging from the water's surface.
When the Emperor arrived there,
he took off his clothes, intending to enter,
but the fish, dragons, ducks, and geese all seemed to shake their scales and raise their wings,
appearing as if they were about to fly.
The Emperor was alarmed
and immediately ordered them to be removed,
but the lotus flowers remain to this day.
He also once had dozens of long baths built in the palace,
their roofs all circular and paved with patterned stones.
Silver-inlaid lacquer boats and white fragrant wood boats
were placed within them.
Even the oars
were adorned with pearls and jade.
Also, in the baths, mountains of lapis lazuli and aloeswood were piled up,
to represent Yíngzhōu and Fāngzhàng."
The *Jīnyángmén Shī Zhù* states: "Besides the two baths for officials in the palace,
there were also other baths,
sixteen long baths.
These were frequently bestowed upon various concubines and consorts;
their length and width were not comparable to the other baths,
paved with patterned jade and dense stones.
In the center was a jade lotus flower holding the water,
spraying to form a pool.
Also, embroidered ducks and geese
were placed in the water.
The Emperor would sometimes float small engraved boats among them
to amuse himself.
To the west of this was the Tàizǐ Tāng,
further west was the Yíchūn Tāng,
and further west were sixteen long baths.
Today, only the Tàizǐ and Shàoyáng baths remain.
There was also the Yùnǚ Diàn Tāng,
which is where the Shíxīnghén Tāng and Yùmíngwèng Tāng are now derived from."
pronounced *wéi* (于偽翻).
When Shénwēi arrived in Fányáng to declare the imperial edict,
Lùshān sat on the bed, rising slightly,
but did not bow.
He said:
"Is the Saint secure?"
"Saint"
refers to the Emperor.
read as *wěn*.
Many Tang inscriptions write
the character "穩" (*wěn*)
as
"The horses need not be presented;
I will definitely arrive at the capital in the tenth month."
He then ordered his attendants to lead Shénwēi to the guesthouse
and did not see him again.
After several days,
he sent him back,
without any memorial.
When Shénwēi returned,
he saw the Emperor and wept, saying:
"Your servant almost didn't make it back to see Your Majesty!"
8 Eighth month,
Xīnmǎo,
the taxes of rent and labor for this year were remitted for the common people.
9 Winter,
tenth month,
Gēngyín,
the Emperor visited Huáqīng Gōng.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The old annals say Rénchén,
but we now follow the *Shílù* and the new annals.
Ān Lùshān (安祿山) monopolized the administration of the three *dào* (道),
secretly harboring rebellious intentions
for nearly ten years.
As the Emperor had treated him generously,
he intended to rebel only after the Emperor's demise.
It happened that Yáng Guózhōng (楊國忠) and Lùshān were displeased with each other.
Guózhōng repeatedly stated that Lùshān was about to rebel,
but the Emperor did not listen.
Guózhōng frequently provoked him with various incidents,
wishing him to rebel quickly to gain the Emperor's trust.
Lùshān, from this, decided to rebel suddenly.

He secretly plotted only with the *kǒngmùguān* (孔目官) and *tàipúchéng* (太僕丞) Yán Zhuāng (嚴莊), the *zhǎngshūjì* (掌書記) and *túntiányuánwàiláng* (屯田員外郎) Gāo Shàng (高尚), and General Āshǐnà Chéngqìng (阿史那承慶).
None of the other generals or aides knew of it,
but they were puzzled that since the eighth month,
he had frequently feasted his soldiers
and fattened his horses and sharpened his weapons.
There happened to be an official returning from the capital to report on affairs.
Lùshān forged an imperial decree,
summoned all the generals, and showed it to them, saying:
"There is a secret imperial edict
commanding me, Lùshān, to lead troops into the capital to punish Yáng Guózhōng.
Gentlemen, you should immediately follow the army."
The crowd looked at each other in astonishment,
none daring to speak otherwise.
In the eleventh month,
on the *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) day,
Lùshān mobilized his subordinate troops and those of the Tóngluó (同羅), Xī (奚), Qìdān (契丹), and Shìwéi (室韋), totaling one hundred fifty thousand men,
claiming two hundred thousand,
and rebelled in Fànyáng (范陽).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: Píng Zhìměi's (平致美) *Jìmén Jìluàn* (薊門紀亂) says:
"From the eighth month of that year onwards,
he consoled and instructed his soldiers,
and sharpened spears and halberds,
which was quite different from the norm.
Discerning people secretly found it strange.
At this point,
Lùshān led his troops to depart at night.
Before leaving,
he ordered his subordinate officials and others, saying: 'The reporting official Hú Yì (胡逸) has returned from the capital,
bearing a secret imperial edict,
sending me, Lùshān, to lead my personal troops and horses to the court.
Do not let that person know.
Gentlemen, do not be surprised,
please follow the army.'
'That person'
likely refers to Yáng Guózhōng."
Lǚ Zhīhuì (呂知誨), the Deputy Military Commissioner of Pínglú (平盧), was guarding Pínglú.
The general Gāo Xiùyán (高秀yán) was guarding Dàtóng (大同).
Two hundred *lǐ* (里) west of Zhōng Shòujiàng Chéng (中受降城) was Dàtóng Chuān (大同川).
Also, north of Dàizhōu (代州) was Dàtóng Jūn (大同軍),
over eight hundred *lǐ* from Tàiyuán (太原).
*Xīn Zhì* (新志) says: Dàtóng Jūn
was in Shuòzhōu (朔州), Mǎyì Xiàn (馬邑縣).
According to Sòng Bái's (宋白) *Xù Tōngdiǎn* (續通典): Dàtóng Chuān, west of Zhōng Shòujiàng Chéng,
was the old ruins of Suí (隋) dynasty Dàtóng Chéng.
In the fifth year of Kaiyuán (開元), Dàtóng Jūn was established thirty *lǐ* east of Shànyáng Xiàn (善陽縣) to guard the frontier.
Mǎyì Xiàn was also established within the army,
directly north of Dàizhōu.
The next morning,
Lùshān exited south of Jìchéng (薊城),
conducted a grand review and swore in his troops,
using "punishing Yáng Guózhōng" as his pretext,
and posted a notice in the army saying:
"Those who express dissenting opinions or incite the soldiers
shall be executed along with their three clans!"
Thereupon, he led his troops south.
Lùshān rode in an iron chariot,
with elite infantry and cavalry,
raising smoke and dust for a thousand *lǐ*,
and their war cries shook the earth.
*Yú* (轝)
is the same as *yú* (輿).
*Qí* (騎)
is pronounced *qí jì fān*.
*Zào* (譟)
is pronounced *sū dào fān*.
The common people had not known warfare for generations,
and suddenly hearing of the uprising in Fànyáng,
both near and far were shocked and dismayed.
Héběi (河北) was entirely under Lùshān's jurisdiction,
as Lùshān also held the title of Investigating Commissioner of Héběi Dào.
People disintegrated at the mere sight,
local officials either opened the gates and welcomed them,
or abandoned their cities and fled,
or were captured and killed,
with none daring to resist him.
Lùshān had first dispatched generals Hé Qiānnián (何千年) and Gāo Miǎo (高邈) with twenty Xī (奚) cavalry,
ostensibly to present skilled archers,
who traveled by post to Tàiyuán.
On the *yǐchǒu* (乙丑) day,
Yáng Guānghuì (楊光翽), the Deputy Resident Administrator of Běijīng (北京), came out to welcome them,
and was subsequently abducted.
The *Kǎoyì* states: *Sùzōng Shílù* (肅宗實錄) says:
"He first ordered Qiānnián to lead several thousand strong men,
falsely claiming to present captives,
with a thousand carts
packed with banners, spears, armor, and weapons,
to wait in advance at Héyáng Qiáo (河陽橋)."
It does not state how they were used later.
Furthermore, Qiānnián was at that time going to Tàiyuán to seize Yáng Guānghuì,
and did not have time to go to Héyáng.
This is therefore not adopted.
*Jìmén Jìluàn* says:
"In this month, on the *jiǎwǔ* (甲午) day,
Guānghuì was captured."
However, in this month there was a *jiǎzǐ* day,
how could there be a *jiǎwǔ*!
This is also not adopted.
Dōng Shòujiàng Chéng (東受降城) also reported Lùshān's rebellion.
The Emperor still thought it was a fabrication by those who hated Lùshān,
and did not believe it.
On the *gēngwǔ* (庚午) day,
the Emperor heard that Lùshān had indeed rebelled,
and then summoned the chancellors to discuss it.
Yáng Guózhōng looked pleased and virtuous;
the Shǔ (蜀) version reads
"looked pleased,"
which should be followed.
"Now, only Lùshān himself has rebelled;
the generals and soldiers do not wish to.
Within ten days,
his head will surely be presented to the imperial court."
The Emperor thought this was true,
but the senior officials looked at each other, their faces losing color.
The Emperor sent the Grand Master Bì Sīchēn (畢思琛) to Dōngjīng (東京),
and the Jinwu General Chéng Qiānlǐ (程千里) to Hédōng (河東),
each to recruit tens of thousands of men,
to spontaneously organize and resist him.
On the *xīnwèi* (辛未) day,
Fēng Chángqīng (封常清), the Military Commissioner of Ānxī (安西), came to court.
The Emperor asked him for a strategy to suppress the rebels.
Chángqīng declared boldly:
"Now, peace has lasted for a long time,
so people are intimidated by the rebels at first sight.
However, events have their proper order and opposition,
and circumstances have their strange changes.
I request to ride quickly to Dōngjīng,
open the armories,
recruit brave warriors,
and cross the Hé (河) with whips and horses.
I will calculate the days and present the head of the rebellious Hu (胡) beneath the imperial palace!"
The Emperor was pleased.
On the *rénshēn* (壬申) day,
Chángqīng was appointed Military Commissioner of Fànyáng and Pínglú.
Chángqīng immediately traveled by post to Dōngjīng to recruit soldiers.
Within ten days,
he gathered sixty thousand men.
He then broke the Héyáng Qiáo,
as a defensive measure.
On the *jiǎxū* (甲戌) day,
Lùshān arrived south of Bólíng (博陵).
Bólíng Jùn (博陵郡)
was originally Dìngzhōu (定州), Gāoyáng Jùn (高陽郡);
in the first year of Tiānbǎo (天寶), its name was changed to Bólíng Jùn.
*Jiù Zhì* (舊志) says: Bólíng Jùn
was two thousand nine hundred six *lǐ* northeast of the capital.
He accused Guānghuì of supporting Yáng Guózhōng,
and executed him as a public display.
The *Kǎoyì* states: *Xìng Shǔ Jì* (幸蜀記) says:
"On the nineteenth day, *jiǎxū*,
he arrived south of Zhēndìng (真定)
and encountered Yáng Guānghuì."
According to *Táng Lì* (唐曆):
"Lùshān sent the elite cavalry Hé Qiānnián and others to abduct Guānghuì and bring him back.
They met in Bólíng Jùn,
and killed him."
It is likely that *Xìng Shǔ Jì* mistakenly took Dìngzhōu for Zhēndìng.
*Lùshān Shìjī* (祿山事迹) says:
"In the ninth month of that year, on the *jiǎwǔ* day,
the head of Yáng Guānghuì, Prefect of Tàiyuán, arrived."
However, Lùshān only rebelled in the eleventh month,
so *Shìjī*'s statement that Guānghuì was captured in the ninth month
is an error.
Zhōng Zhì (忠志), a Xī man,
was adopted by Lùshān as his foster son.
He also appointed Zhāng Xiànchéng (張獻誠) as acting Prefect of Bólíng.
Xiànchéng
was the son of Shǒuguī (守珪).
Zhāng Shǒuguī (張守珪) had nurtured Lùshān, which was indeed the root of the disaster.
Ān Lùshān reached Gǎo Chéng.
Chángshān太shǒu Yán Gǎoqīng, being unable to resist,
went with Chángshǐ Yuán Lǚqiān to welcome him.
Lùshān immediately bestowed upon Gǎoqīng gold and purple vestments,
and kept his sons and younger brothers as hostages,
ordering him to continue guarding Chángshān.
Chángshān Jùn
was originally Héng Zhōu’s Héngshān Jùn.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo, its name was changed.
Liú Xù said: The old seat of Chángshān Jùn was Yuán Shì.
Wèi Dàowǔ ascended Chángshān Jùn and looked north towards Ānlè Lěi.
He found it beautiful
and thus moved the seat of the commandery to Ānlè Chéng.
This is the present-day Zhōu Chéng.
Wèi Shōu’s Zhì states
that there is Ānlè Lěi in Jiǔmén Xiàn.
Zhì
is pronounced zhì.
(These hostages were to) guard against all armies coming from the west.
The armies coming from the west
refers to the Hédōng troops advancing east through Jǐngxíng Kǒu.
Xíng
is pronounced xíng.
Lùshān pointed at his clothes and said to Lǚqiān,
"Why are you wearing this?"
Lǚqiān understood his meaning
and secretly plotted with Gǎoqīng to raise an army to attack Lùshān.
Gǎoqīng was
Yán Sīlǔ’s great-great-grandson.
Yán Sīlǔ was
Yán Zhītuī’s son
and Yán Shīgǔ’s father.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
the emperor returned to the palace.
Táipú Qīng Ān Qìngzōng was beheaded.
Róngyì Jùnzhǔ was granted permission to commit suicide.
Ān Sīshùn, the Shuòfāng Jiédùshǐ, was appointed Hùbù Shàngshū.
Sīshùn’s younger brother, Yuánzhēn, was made Táipú Qīng.
Guō Zǐyí, Shuòfāng Yòuxiāng Bīngmǎshǐ and Jiǔyuán Tàishǒu, was made Shuòfāng Jiédùshǐ.
Jiǔyuán Jùn
was Fēng Zhōu.
Tàiyuán was the Northern Capital,
hence an Yǐn was appointed.
(A Jiédùshǐ) was put in charge of Chénliú and thirteen other commanderies,
with Wèiwèi Qīng Yīshì Zhāng Jièrán appointed to this position.
Chénliú Jùn
was Biàn Zhōu.
Kǎoyì says: The Shílù states that Jièrán was Biàn Zhōu Cìshǐ;
the Jiùjì states that Jièrán was Chénliú Tàishǒu.
According to this period, there was no Cìshǐ.
Guō Nà was currently Tàishǒu.
Jièrán was simply a Jiédùshǐ.
For commanderies directly in the path of the rebels,
Fángyùshǐ were appointed for the first time.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Róng Wáng Wǎn was made marshal,
with Yòujīnwǔ Dàjiāngjūn Gāo Xiānzhī as his deputy,
to command all armies in the eastern campaign.
Money and silk from the inner treasury were issued,
and 110,000 troops were recruited in the capital.
They were called Tiānwǔ Jūn.
They gathered in ten days
and were all sons of the marketplace.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
Gāo Xiānzhī, leading the Fēiqí, Guòqí, newly recruited troops, and border troops stationed in the capital, a total of 50,000 men,
set out from Cháng'ān.
The emperor sent the eunuch Jiānmén Jiāngjūn Biān Lìngchéng to supervise his army,
which was stationed at Shǎn.
11On the day Dīnghài,
Ān Lùshān crossed the river from Língchāng.
Língchāng Jùn
was originally Huá Zhōu’s Dōng Jùn.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo, its name was changed.
In one night,
the ice merged like a floating bridge,
and thus Língchāng Jùn fell.
The Jiùzhì says: Língchāng Jùn
is 1,440 lǐ from the capital
and 530 lǐ from the Eastern Capital.
No one knew his numbers,
and he devastated everywhere he passed.
Zhāng Jièrán had only been in Chénliú for a few days when
Lùshān arrived.
Jièrán armed the soldiers and ascended the city walls,
but the troops were terrified
and could not hold it.
On the day Gēngyín,
Tàishǒu Guō Nà surrendered the city.
Lùshān entered the northern outer city.
Hearing of Ān Qìngzōng’s death,
he cried aloud,
"What crime did I commit
that my son should be killed!"
At that time, nearly ten thousand surrendered Chénliú generals and soldiers lined the road.
Lùshān killed them all to vent his rage,
and beheaded Zhāng Jièrán at the army gate.
Kǎoyì says: The Jiùjì states:
"On the day Xīnmǎo,
Chénliú Jùn fell."
Lùshān Shìjì states:
"On the day Gēngwǔ,
Chénliú Jùn fell,
and the heads of Zhāng Jièrán, Lìfēi Yuán Yú, and others were sent."
Now we follow the Shílù.
(Lùshān) then guarded Chénliú.
The Jiùzhì says: Chénliú Jùn
is 1,350 lǐ east of the capital
and 401 lǐ from the Eastern Capital.
12On the day Rénchén,
the emperor issued an edict declaring his intention to personally lead the campaign.
The troops from Shuòfāng, Héxī, and Lǒngyòu stationed outside their fortresses
were all to proceed to the imperial camp,
with their Jiédùshǐ personally leading them.
They were ordered to gather within twenty days.
13Initially,
Píngyuán Tàishǒu Yán Zhēnqīng,
Píngyuán Jùn was established during the Hàn.
In the Táng, it became Dé Zhōu.

at dusk,

After a short while,
Gāo Miǎo returned from Yōuzhōu

Qiānnián said to Gǎoqīng:
"Now the Grand Protector wishes to dedicate his strength to the imperial court.

sending proclamations to Zhào and Wèi,
and cutting off the vital arteries of Yān and Jì.

'Lǐ Guāngbì is leading ten thousand infantry and cavalry out of Jǐngxíng;'

without strong armor or sharp weapons,
and it will be difficult to withstand the elite troops from Shānxī.'

and west of Hán Pass was Shānxī.

Xiànchéng will surely lift the siege and flee.

Kǎoyì states: "Héluò Chūnqiū says:
