It also said: "Now Héběi is prosperous and abundant,
the common people are rich,
and in terms of attire, rituals, and music,
there is no equal in the world.
Confucius said:
'In a village of ten households,
there must be loyal and trustworthy people.'
In a state of ten thousand families,
it is not without heroes.
If they were to gather and unite,
would they not become a future trouble?
I humbly submit that you should strengthen your vanguard,
make your rearguard strict,
and proceed cautiously wherever you go.
Also, carefully examine the map;
wherever there are narrow passes,
you must strengthen defenses;
carefully select good officials
and entrust them with vital responsibilities.
From Luò eastwards,
consider it already yours.
Extensively gather fodder and grain,
and repair armor and weapons;
send proclamations to the Western Capital,
and they will rally at the mere mention.
If the Táng dynasty's mandate has not changed,
and the royal orders are still effective,
and the ruler and ministers conspire together,
and the officials and common people rush to serve,
then strengthen your troops at Gǒng and Luò,
occupy Āocāng to the east,
overlook the Bái Mǎ Ford to the south,
and guard Fēihú Pass to the north.
You will naturally contend with the imperial court
and occupy one region.
If the glorious mandate has shifted,
and the songs of praise are attached to you,
then you should advance rapidly to Qí and Yōng,
water your horses in the Wèi River,
and the common people will submit.
Who could surpass Your Excellency!'
Lù Shān was greatly pleased,
bestowed Gǎoqīng with official robes and attire,
and kept him as the Chángshān Grand Protector concurrently Wǔjūn Regiment Commander,
stationed at Jǐngxíng Pass.
He left one hundred Tóngluó and Yèluòhé troops,
each with one chieftain.
The prefectures of Zhào, Xíng, Míng, Xiàng, Wèi, and others
were all replaced.
When Cāng, Yíng, and Shēn did not follow Lù Shān,
Zhāng Xiànchéng besieged Shēnzhōu for over a month without taking it.

Former Zhàozhōu Sīhù Bāo Chǔsuì, former Yuánshì尉 Zhāng Tōngyōu, Gǎo Chéng Xiàn尉 Cuī Ānshèng, and Héngzhōu Zhǎngshǐ Yuán Lǚqiān and others jointly submitted a letter persuading Gǎoqīng, saying: 'You, esteemed Duke, bear great honor,
and hold the position of a regional governor,
yet you abandon a perfectly safe and excellent strategy,
and tread a path of certain death.
You seek immediate gratification
and forget the future troubles for your descendants.
We secretly believe this is not worthy of you, esteemed Duke.
If you now defy Lù Shān's command,
recruit an army of one hundred thousand,
stock up on fodder,
accumulate grain,
divide and guard strategic points,
and greatly raise your prestige,
open the Jǐngxíng road,
and combine forces with the Eastern Capital—
if you do this,
then your great achievements and glorious deeds
would be beyond words!
Rashly advancing with blind talk
is utterly useless.
Our souls vanish towards Dōngdài,
we first harbor worries of being butchered and torn apart;
our hearts bow to Běichén,
wishing to establish a loyal and faithful example."
Gǎoqīng read the letter
and was greatly pleased.
Thereupon, it was unanimously decided
to falsely use Lù Shān's order to summon the Jǐngxíng garrison troops to Héngzhōu for a feast.
Each chieftain was granted three hundred bolts of silk,
one horse,
one set of gold and silver utensils,
and one beautiful woman.
The rest were generally granted ten thousand bolts of goods.
The feast was held at Jiāotóng Post Station south of the prefecture.
From dawn to dusk,
hundreds of courtesans and musicians were also used to please them.
Secretly, poison was placed in the wine,
and they were given to drink,
making them completely drunk.
They perceived nothing,
so all their weapons were seized,
and they were all bound.
The next day,
they were all beheaded,
and their bodies were discarded into the Hútuó River."
Yīn Liàng's biography of Yán Gǎoqīng says:
"When Lù Shān rebelled,
Gǎoqīng had no recourse,
so he and Zhǎngshǐ Yuán Lǚqiān visited him in Gǎo Chéng county.
Lù Shān, knowing that Gǎoqīng had once been his judicial officer,
falsely issued an imperial edict granting him a purple gold fish purse,
making him self-guard Chángshān Commandery,
and taking his grandson Dàn and disciple Xún as hostages.
Bǐchóng郡刺史 Jiǎng Qīncòu guarded Tǔmén with 7,000 elite soldiers from Zhàojùn.
Gǎoqīng made an appointment with
Jiǎng Qīncòu,
summoning him under a private pretext.
When Gǎoqīng returned home,
on the way,
he pointed to his clothes and said to Lǚqiān: "These are things that bring harm to one's body.
Although Lùshān claims to be executing the corrupt officials around the emperor,
he is in fact rebelling.
You and I have served the Táng for generations,
and hold positions as provincial officials.
How can we follow him in rebellion!"
Lǚqiān's countenance changed with sorrow,
and after a long sigh of emotion,
he said: "What should be done?
I will obey whatever you command,
and dare not disobey."
Gǎoqīng then sent someone to inform Tài yuán Yǐn Wáng Chéngyè that Qīncòu had been killed,
awaiting his response in case of emergency.
Wáng Chéngyè also sent a reply.
Fearing a leak,
Gǎoqīng pretended not to be involved in affairs,
delegating most governance to Lǚqiān.
They did not meet all day,
only sending his son Quánmíng back and forth to convey messages.
He summoned the former Zhēndìng Magistrate Jiǎ Shēn, the recluse Quán Huàn, and Guō Zhòngyōng to Lǚqiān's place to conspire.
It happened that Gǎoqīng's paternal cousin, Zhēnqīng, held Píngyuán,
and had killed Duàn Zǐguāng.
He sent Gǎoqīng's niece Lú Tì, along with a secretly delivered proclamation from Lùshān, which was intended to buy allegiance.
Gǎoqīng was overjoyed
and hid Lú Tì at his home.
Before Lú Tì arrived,
Gǎoqīng had already sent someone to summon Qīncòu under a private pretext.
When he arrived,
Gǎoqīng excused himself saying: "It is late,
and there might be other bandits tonight.
The city gates are closed.
Please wait until tomorrow morning to meet."
He then dispatched Cānjūn Féng Qián, Zōngshì Lǐ Jùn, Língshòu Wèi Lǐ Qīmò, and the local man Zhái Wàndé to meet Qīncòu at the relay station.
Late at night, when Qīncòu was deeply drunk,
they hacked him to death with an axe;
all the soldiers at Tǔmén were dispersed.
Previously, Lùshān had sent his confidant, the pseudo-Jīnwǔ Jiāngjūn Gāo Miǎo, to levy troops in Fányáng.
His route passed through Chángshān,
and Gǎoqīng, after scouting, learned of this.
On that day,
Miǎo arrived at Mǎnchéng station.
Gǎoqīng ordered Cuī Ānshí and Féng Qián to kill him.
Several of Miǎo's advance guards arrived first,
and were promptly killed.
Then Miǎo was captured alive
and sent to the prefecture.
When Hé Qiānnián approached carelessly,
Ānshí cut off the path of travelers from the south
and rushed to Lǐquán station to await Qiānnián.
He also decapitated his men and captured him alive, just like Miǎo.
Before noon,
the two villains were brought together.
According to the Sùzōng Shílù:
"When Gǎoqīng first heard that Lùshān had raised an army in Fányáng,
he summoned Chángshǐ Yuán Lǚqiān, former Zhēndìng Magistrate Jiǎ Shēn, and Nèi qiū Chéng Zhāng Tōngyōu, and said to them: 'Now Lùshān's cavalry from Yōu and Bīng has passed Chángshān in a single day,
heading towards Luòyáng,
with the ambition to usurp the throne.
The Son of Heaven is in Cháng'ān,
and is just about to levy troops from all over the realm
to march east and punish the rebels.
It will be too late.
If the rebel army arrives suddenly,
we will surely become their captives.
It is better, before their scheme fully develops,
to gather righteous volunteers,
hold Tǔmén to the west,
connect with Héshuò to the north,
and await rescue from within the realm.
This will, on the one hand, secure the nation,
and on the other, preserve our loyalty as officials.
This is the best plan.'
Thereupon, on that very day, he recruited over a thousand soldiers,
ordered Lǚqiān to lead troops to garrison Tǔmén,
ordered Jiǎ Shēn to guard the eastern road,
and Zhāng Tōngyōu to defend the prefectural city.
The rebel general Lǐ Guīrén ordered his brother Qīncòu to lead 5,000 infantry and cavalry to first garrison Tǔmén,
and also ordered his troops to be subordinated to Gǎoqīng.
He also sent his cavalry general Gāo Miǎo to report to Lùshān,
ordering him to hasten his march.
Scouts learned of this plot and reported it to Gǎoqīng.
Gǎoqīng summoned Lǚqiān and informed him.
Lǚqiān said: 'The matter is urgent.
If Qīncòu is not executed soon,
the plan will not succeed.'
So, they falsely summoned Qīncòu,
ordering him to come to the prefecture to discuss affairs,
and ordered Lǚqiān to assign officials to await him.
Qīncòu arrived at the prefecture at night.
Gǎoqīng ordered him to rest at the relay station,
then sent Cānjūn Lǐ Xún, Féng Qián, Xiànwèi Lǐ Qīmò, and others to entertain Qīncòu at the station.
When he was drunk, they killed him that night.
Lǚqiān brought Qīncòu's head to Gǎoqīng.
Gǎoqīng and Lǚqiān rejoiced at the success of the deed,
yet also feared the coming of the rebels,
and wept together.
Gǎoqīng wiped away his tears and encouraged Lǚqiān, saying: 'If a great man's name is not recorded in history,
what is the point of being alive!
You and I have served the Táng for generations;
how could we seek temporary peace under the Hú Jié?
As long as we die without disgrace,
what regrets could we have!'
After a moment,
Gǎochéng Wèi Cuī Ānshí reported that Gāo Miǎo had returned from Lùshān's location
and had lodged in the territory of Shànggǔ Commandery.
He also sent Féng Qián and the county official Zhái Wàndé, along with Ānshí, to devise a strategy.
The next morning,
several of Miǎo's cavalry arrived first at the station,
and Féng Qián buried them all.
Miǎo arrived shortly after.
Féng Qián deceived him, saying: 'The Grand Protector is preparing music to welcome you.'
Miǎo had no doubts
and dismounted in the hall.
Féng Qián, Ānshí, and others directed the officials
to strike him repeatedly with sticks.
Miǎo fell,
and was captured alive.
Soon after,
the southern border reported that Hé Qiānnián had come from Dōngdū and lodged in Zhàojùn.
Ānshí and Wàndé waited for him in advance at the Lǐquán station south of the prefecture.
When Qiānnián arrived
and learned that Miǎo had been captured,
he ordered his cavalry to fight Ānshí,
but was defeated.
Qiānnián was also captured alive
and sent to the prefecture along with Miǎo."
The Old Biography states:
"When Lùshān captured Dōngdū,
Gǎoqīng was inspired by his loyalty,
fearing that if the rebels seized Tóngguān,
the imperial house would immediately be in danger.
At that time, his cousin Zhēnqīng was the Grand Protector of Píngyuán.
He sent a messenger to inform Gǎoqīng,
proposing that they raise righteous armies together,
to cut off the rebels' retreat route from two sides,
thereby alleviating the pressure of the western invaders.
Gǎoqīng then conspired with Chángshǐ Yuán Lǚqiān, former Zhēndìng Magistrate Jiǎ Shēn, former Nèiqiū Chéng Zhāng Tōngyōu, and others to close Tǔmén and turn against the rebels.
Lùshān sent Jiǎng Qīncòu and Gāo Miǎo to lead a force of 5,000 to guard Tǔmén.
Gǎoqīng wanted to execute Qīncòu
to open the path at Tǔmén.
At that time, Qīncòu's army was attached to Chángshān Commandery,
and Qīncòu had sent Gāo Miǎo to Yōuzhōu and he had not yet returned.
Gǎoqīng sent an official to summon Qīncòu to the commandery to discuss affairs.
On the night of the twenty-second of that month,
Qīncòu arrived
and was housed in the relay station.
During the welcoming feast, when he was deeply drunk,
Yuán Lǚqiān, Cānjūn Féng Qián, Xiànwèi Lǐ Qīmò, and the strongman Zhái Wàndé were ordered to kill Qīncòu.
In the middle of the night,
Lǚqiān brought Qīncòu's head to Gǎoqīng,
and they both shed tears,
rejoicing at the success of the undertaking.
That night,
Gǎochéng Wèi Cuī Ānshí reported that Gāo Miǎo had returned and reached Mǎnchéng.
He immediately ordered Féng Qián, Zhái Wàndé, and Ānshí to go and plan against him.
The next morning,
several of Miǎo's cavalry arrived at Gǎochéng station,
and Ānshí killed them all.
Shortly after, Miǎo arrived.
Ānshí deceived him, saying: 'The Grand Protector has prepared wine and music at the relay station.'
As Miǎo was dismounting in the hall,
Féng Qián and others captured and bound him.
On that day,
the rebel general Hé Qiānnián came from Dōngdū to Zhàojùn.
Féng Qián and Zhái Wàndé ambushed him at Lǐquán station.
When Qiānnián arrived,
he was also captured.
On the same day, the two rebel generals were bound and brought back to the commandery."
In consideration: When Lùshān first advanced south from Fányáng with hundreds of thousands of troops,
Chángshān was directly in his path.
If Gǎoqīng had not obeyed his orders,
and had immediately resisted him with only a thousand people,
he would have been instantly annihilated.
How could he have continued to hold his old commandery?
Moreover, at that time, Lùshān still claimed to be executing Yáng Guózhōng,
and had not yet usurped the imperial title.
If Gǎoqīng had welcomed him at Gǎochéng
and accepted his golden-purple attire,
he would likely not have been able to avoid it.
What is stated in the Sùzōng Shílù
is probably to preserve the integrity of a loyal official.
However, Gǎoqīng was loyal, upright, and resolute,
sacrificing his body for the country,
giving up his life for righteousness.
He is rarely matched in history.
How could he possibly have written a memorial to flatter Lùshān,
comparing himself to Hàn Gāo and Wèi Wǔ,
and devising strategies for territorial division and annexation?
Even those with rudimentary knowledge would surely know this is not true.
Indeed, Bāo Xū was the son of Chǔ Suì.
He wanted to claim that Gǎoqīng initially had no intention of fighting the rebels and establishing loyalty,
and that it was due to his father's memorial advising him to succeed,
in order to magnify his father's achievements.
Upon examining the memorial from Gǎoqīng to Lùshān recorded by him,
Chǔ Suì and others submitted a letter from Gǎoqīng.
Tián Chéngsì submitted a memorial from Shǐ Cháoyì.
Their literary styles were identical,
which is sufficient to know that they were all drafted by Bāo Xū.
Furthermore, Zhāng Tōngyōu's brother was a rebel leader,
and he also instigated Wáng Chéngyè to seize Gǎoqīng's achievements.
Ultimately, due to his perfidy, he was executed;
such were his actions.
Yet Bāo Xū claimed that he had initially joined Chǔ Suì in submitting a letter to persuade Gǎoqīng to be loyal and righteous,
which is even harder to believe.
The old accounts say:
"Qīn Còu and Gāo Miǎo jointly defended Tǔmén.
Qīn Còu dispatched Miǎo to Yōuzhōu."
Since the two generals held military power and were stationed together at Tǔmén,
how could Qīn Còu dispatch Miǎo to Yōuzhōu?
Now, following Yīn Liàng's biography of Gǎoqīng,
it was Lùshān himself who dispatched Miǎo to recruit soldiers, and that is correct.
The Héluò Chūnqiū says:
"Liú Tóngluó and Yèlèhé one hundred men."
They were stationed at Jǐngxíng,
blocking the forces from west of the mountains.
This was a crucial task,
how could a hundred men defend it?
Yīn's biography says
"seven thousand men defended Tǔmén."
These seven thousand men could not have been bound by Lǚ Qiān in a single night either.
Probably Lùshān left a hundred elite soldiers as Qīn Còu's trusted inner circle and enforcers,
while the rest were militia and those forced to join,
thus Lǚ Qiān was able to intoxicate them with wine,
execute Qīn Còu and the hundred men, and disperse the rest.
The Héluò Chūnqiū says
"poison was placed in the wine."
However, at the time, Lǚ Qiān and others drank with Qīn Còu.
How could poison be placed only in the guest's wine?
We do not accept this now.
Both the old accounts and Yīn's biography state that Qīn Còu's surname was Jiǎng.
We now follow the biographies of Xuánzōng and Sùzōng, and the Táng Lì, which state his surname was Lǐ.
Xuánzōng Shílù:
"In the twelfth month, on the Jǐhài day,
Gǎoqīng killed the rebel general Lǐ Qīn Còu,
seized Hé Qiānnián and Gāo Miǎo, and sent them to the capital."
According to Jǐhài,
it was the fifteenth day.
However, Zhēnqīng executed Duàn Ziguāng on the Rén Yín day.
Rén Yín
was the eighteenth day.
After Zhēnqīng killed Ziguāng,
he then reported to Gǎoqīng to jointly raise a righteous army.
Now we follow the old accounts,
placing the killing of Qīn Còu on the twenty-second day, Bǐngwǔ.
Sùzōng Shílù also says:
"After Gǎoqīng executed Qīn Còu and others,
he then sent envoys to publicize throughout the commanderies,
saying: 'The emperor has now appointed Prince Róng as Grand Marshal,
Gēshū Hàn as deputy,
and is mobilizing four hundred thousand troops from across the realm
to march eastward and suppress the rebellion.'"
However, according to the shílù,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
Hàn was first appointed Deputy Grand Marshal.
Calculating to Bǐngwǔ,
Chángshān would not yet have known this.
We do not accept this now.
The Héluò Chūnqiū says
"thirteen commanderies all raised righteous armies and submitted to the court."
Yīn Liàng's Yán Shì Xíngzhuàng, the old biography of Yán Zhēnqīng, and the Táng Lì all say
"seventeen commanderies submitted."
Presumably, the Héluò Chūnqiū did not count Píngyuán, Jǐngchéng, Héjiān, and Ráoyáng, which were pacified earlier.
The Yán Shì Xíngzhuàng says:
"Only six commanderies did not submit."
At that time, Wèijùn had not yet been subdued either.
This likely refers to the final count.
Only Fányáng, Lúlóng, Mìyún, Yúyáng, Jí, and Yè were the six commanderies.
Consulting the Táng Zhì, there is no Lúlóng Jùn;
this must be the former Běipíng Jùn of Píngzhōu renamed Lúlóng Jùn.
Mìyún Jùn,
originally Ānlè Jùn of Tánzhōu,
had its commandery name changed in the first year of Tiānbǎo.
Yúyáng Jùn,
Jìzhōu.
Jí Jùn,
Wèizhōu.
Gǎoqīng also secretly sent someone into Fányáng
to recruit Jiǎ Xún.
Mǎ Suì from Jiáchéng persuaded Xún, saying:
Jiáchéng was the land of Jiá Xiàn in Yǐngchuān under the Hàn.
Later, the Northern Wèi established Lóngshān Xiàn and Nányáng Xiàn.
In the early Kǎihuáng era of the Suí,
Lóngshān was renamed Rǔnán;
in the eighteenth year, Rǔnán was renamed Fǔchéng,
and Nányáng was renamed Qīchéng.
In the early Dàyè era,
Fǔchéng was renamed Jiáchéng,
and Qīchéng was abolished and merged into it.
Jiá,
pronounced jiá.
Shuō,
pronounced shuì.
"Lùshān has betrayed his benefactor and committed rebellion.
Even if he seizes Luòyáng,
he will eventually be annihilated.
If you execute the generals who disobey orders,
and return Fányáng to the state,
shaking his very foundations,
this would be an unparalleled achievement."
Xún agreed,
but hesitated and did not act immediately.
His subordinate Niú Rùnróng learned of this,
and reported it to Lùshān.
Lùshān sent his confederate Hán Cháoyáng to summon Xún.
Cháoyáng arrived in Fányáng,
led Xún aside for a private conversation,
and had strongmen strangle him,
exterminating his clan;
he appointed his subordinate Niú Tíngjiè to manage Fányáng's military affairs.
Shǐ Sīmíng and Lǐ Lìjié led ten thousand Fān and Hàn infantry and cavalry to attack Bólíng and Chángshān.
Mǎ Suì fled into the Xīshān mountains;
the Xīshān mountains of Fányáng Jùn
connect in the south with the various mountains of Shànggǔ and Zhōngshān.
He managed to escape.
At first, Lùshān wanted to personally lead an attack on Tóngguān.
When he reached Xīn'ān,
he heard of disturbances in Hébĕi and returned.
Kǎo Yì says: Xuánzōng Shílù:
"In the fifteenth year,
in the first month,
on the Rénxū day,
Lùshān was about to attack Tóngguān,
and reached Xīn'ān.
Hearing that it was prepared, he returned."
However, Lùshān captured the Eastern Capital on the Dīngyǒu day of this month.
From Dīngyǒu to Rénxū was twenty-six days.
It was not a surprise attack on an undefended position.
How could he only learn of its preparedness upon reaching Xīn'ān?
Presumably, with the disturbance in Chángshān, the route to Yōu and Jì was cut off,
hence he was afraid and returned.
We now follow the Sùzōng Běnjì.
Hénèi Jùn,
Huáizhōu.
On the Wùshēn day,
Prince Róng Wǎn died.
He was posthumously honored with the title Crown Prince Jìnggōng.
In this year,
the Tubo Zānpǔ Qīlísūlónglièzàn died.
His son Suōsīlónglièzàn succeeded him.
Tǔ,
from the entering tone of tūn.
Zú,
pronounced zǐxù.
Suō,
pronounced sùhuó.
Sùzōng Wénmíng Wǔdé Dàshèng Dàxuān Xiàohuángdì, whose personal name was Hēng,
was the third son of Xuánzōng.
His original name was Sìshēng;
in the fifteenth year of Kāiyuán, his name was changed to Jùn;
in the twenty-third year, it was changed to Yú;
in the twenty-eighth year, it was changed to Shào;
in the third year of Tiānbǎo, it was changed to Hēng.
In the first year of Zhìdé
(Bǐngshēn, 756),
in the seventh month of this year,
the Crown Prince ascended the throne in Língwǔ,
and the era name was changed to Zhìdé.
1. In spring,
in the first month,
on the Yǐmǎo day, the first day of the month,
Lùshān proclaimed himself Emperor of Great Yàn,
changed the era name to Shèngwǔ,
and appointed Dáxī Xún as Shìzhōng and Zhāng Tōngrú as Zhōngshū Lìng.
Kǎo Yì says: The Xìngshǔ Jì says:
"Xún was made Left Chancellor,
and Tōngrú Right Chancellor."
We now follow the Shílù.
2. Lǐ Suí arrived in Suīyáng,
with tens of thousands of troops.
On the Bǐngchén day,
Suí was appointed Hénán Jiédùshǐ.
This year marked the first establishment of the Hénán Jiédùshǐ,
headquartered in Biànzhōu,
overseeing thirteen commanderies: Chénliú, Suīyáng, Língchāng, Huáiyáng, Rǔyīn, Qiáo, Jìyīn, Púyáng, Zīchuān, Lángyá, Péngchéng, Línhuái, and Dōnghǎi.
Suī,
pronounced suī.
Shǐ,
pronounced shùlì;
same below.
Xǔ Yuǎn had previously served in Shǔ,
but offended Zhāngchóu Jiānqióng,
and was demoted to Gāoyào Wèi.
The histories frame Xǔ Yuǎn's steadfast defense of Suīyáng as an important basis.
Wáng Qīyào, a man from the commandery, was appointed Yáqián Zǒngguǎn.
3 Yán Gǎoqīng sent his sons, Quánmíng and Jiǎ Shēn, along with Zhái Wàndé, to present the head of Lǐ Qīncòu, and Hé Qiānnián and Gāo Miǎo, to the capital.
Zhāng Tōngyōu tearfully pleaded, saying,
"My elder brother, Tōngyōu, has fallen into enemy hands,
believing it to be Tōngrú.
I wish to save my clan."
Gǎoqīng, out of pity, agreed to it.
When they reached Tàiyuán,
Tōngyōu wanted to ingratiate himself with Wáng Chéngyè,
so he instructed them to detain Quánmíng and others.
He altered their memorial,
claiming much credit for himself,
slandering Gǎoqīng,
and sent a separate envoy to present it.
Gǎoqīng had raised an army just eight days prior,
and his defenses were incomplete,
when Shǐ Sīmíng and Cài Xīdé both led their troops to the city walls.
The Kǎoyì states: The Hélúo Chūnqiū says:
"On the *yǐwèi* day of the twelfth month,
Sīmíng and Xīdé both arrived at the city walls."
Gǎoqīng only killed Lǐ Qīncòu on the *bǐngwǔ* day.
To say *yǐwèi*
is an error.
Now we follow other accounts.
Chéngyè, having stolen his credit,
stood to benefit from the city's fall,
and thus held back his troops without providing aid.
Gǎoqīng fought day and night,
until his provisions and arrows were exhausted.
On the *rénxū* day,
the city fell.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù says:
"On the *guǐhài* day,
the city fell."
The Hélúo Chūnqiū:
"On the first day of the first month,
the city fell."
The Old Biography of Sīmíng:
"On the sixth day of the first month,
Chángshān was besieged;
on the ninth day,
it was captured."
Now we follow Xuánzōng Shílù, Tánglì, Jiùjì, and the Biography of Gǎoqīng.
Gǎoqīng and Yuán Lǚqiān were captured and sent to Luòyáng.
The Jiùzhì: Chángshān Commandery is one thousand seven hundred and sixty *lǐ* northeast of the capital,
and one thousand one hundred and thirty-six *lǐ* from the eastern capital.
Xuánzōng was greatly pleased,
appointing Chéngyè as Grand General of the Yǔlín Army,
and hundreds of his subordinates received official posts and titles.
Yán Gǎoqīng was summoned to be Minister of the Imperial Guard.
Before the imperial order arrived,
Chángshān had already fallen.
When Gǎoqīng arrived in Luòyáng,
Lùshān rebuked him, saying,
"You were merely a household registrar in Fànyáng.
I recommended you to be a staff officer,
and in just a few years, you were promoted to Prefect.
Gǎoqīng was a household registrar in Fànyáng.
Lùshān memorialized for him to be an agricultural affairs staff officer,
and acting Prefect of Chángshān.
Gǎoqīng glared and cursed, saying,
"You were originally a sheep-herding Hu slave from Yíngzhōu!
The Son of Heaven promoted you to Military Commissioner of three circuits,
showing unparalleled favor.
What wrong did he do to you that you rebelled?
My family has been loyal subjects of Tang for generations,
and our positions and salaries all come from Tang.
Even though you recommended me,
how could I join you in rebellion!
I am fighting a rebel for the country!
I only regret not having decapitated you.
How can you say I rebelled?
You stinking Hu dog,
why don't you kill me quickly!"
Lùshān was furious,
and he bound Gǎoqīng and Yuán Lǚqiān to a pillar on Zhōngqiáo Bridge and executed them.
Gǎoqīng and Lǚqiān cursed without faltering until their death.
More than thirty members of the Yán family were put to death by sword and saw.
After Shǐ Sīmíng, Lǐ Lìjié, and Cài Xīdé captured Chángshān,
they led their troops to attack the commanderies that had not submitted,
destroying everything in their path.
Consequently, Yè, Guǎngpíng, Jùlù, Zhào, Shànggǔ, Bólíng, Wén'ān, Wèi, Xìndū, and other commanderies were again occupied by the rebels.
Jùlù Commandery is Xíngzhōu.
Xìndū Commandery is Jìzhōu.
Wén'ān Commandery is Mòzhōu.
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu fān.
Sīmíng and others besieged it.
Lǐ Huàn, the Judicial Supervisor of Héjiān, with seven thousand men, and Lǐ Wěi, the Chief Administrator of Jǐngchéng, who sent his son Sī with eight thousand men to relieve it,
were all defeated by Sīmíng.
4 The Emperor ordered Guō Zǐyí to lift the siege of Yúnzhōng,
return to Shuòfāng,
raise more troops, and advance to capture the eastern capital.
He selected one capable general to divide his forces and first emerge through Jǐngxíng,
to pacify Héběi.
Zǐyí recommended Lǐ Guāngbì.
On the *guǐhài* day,
Guāngbì was appointed Military Commissioner of Hédōng,
and ten thousand Shuòfāng soldiers were assigned to him.
The Kǎoyì states: Dù Mù's Biography of Zhāng Bǎogāo says:
"When Ān Lùshān rebelled,
Ān Sīshùn, Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng, a younger paternal cousin of Lùshān, was given death,
and an imperial edict appointed Guō Fényáng to replace him.
Ten days later,
another edict appointed Lǐ Línchuái with imperial credentials,
to divide half of the Shuòfāng troops,
and march east into Zhào and Wèi.
During Sīshùn's time,
Fényáng and Línchuái were both staff generals,
and the two did not get along.
Though they shared meals,
they always looked at each other askance,
without exchanging a single word.
When Fényáng replaced Sīshùn,
Línchuái wished to flee,
but before he could decide,
the edict arrived,
dividing Fényáng's troops for an eastern campaign.
Línchuái entered and requested, saying,
'I am ready to die,
but I beg for the safety of my wife and children.'
Fényáng rushed down,
took his hand, and sat with him on the dais,
saying, 'Now the country is in chaos and the ruler has moved.
Without you, we cannot campaign in the east.
How can this be a time for private grudges!'
He summoned all the military officials,
brought out the imperial edict, and read it,
following its instructions.
When they parted,
they clasped hands and wept,
encouraging each other with loyalty and righteousness."
However, at that time, Xuánzōng had not yet fled to Shǔ,
and Tang's authority still prevailed throughout the land.
If an imperial decree appointed Guāngbì as Military Commissioner,
how would Zǐyí dare to prevent him!
Dù Mù perhaps obtained this from erroneous hearsay.
Now we follow the Family Biography of Fényáng and the Old Biography.
5 On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Gēshū Hàn was promoted to Left Minister of Works and concurrently Grand Councilor,
with other titles unchanged.
6 A Military Commissioner of Nányáng was established,
with Rǔ Jiǒng, Prefect of Nányáng, appointed to the post.
He was to lead fifty thousand men from Língnán, Qiánzhōng, and Xiāngyáng to garrison Yèběi,
as a precaution against Ān Lùshān.
Jiǒng memorialized for Xuē Yuàn to be Prefect of Yǐngchuān and concurrently Defense Commissioner.
Nányáng Commandery is Dèngzhōu.
Xiāngyáng Commandery is Xiāngzhōu.
Yè County,
at that time, belonged to Rǔzhōu.
Yǐngchuān Commandery is Xǔzhōu.
Jiǒng,
pronounced huǒ jiǒng fān.
Jiāng,
pronounced jí liàng fān.
Qián,
pronounced qín.
Yè,
pronounced shì shè fān.
Yuàn,
was the elder brother of the former crown prince, Yīng;
Jiān,
was the great-grandson of Páng Yù.
Páng Yù,
left Sui and joined Tang as a general.
Páng,
pronounced pí jiāng fān.
7 On the *yǐchǒu* day,
Ān Lùshān sent his son Qìngxù to raid Tóngguān;
Gēshū Hàn repelled him.
8 On the *jǐsì* day,
Yán Zhēnqīng was promoted to Vice Minister of Revenue and concurrently Defense Commissioner of his commandery;
Zhēnqīng appointed Lǐ Wěi as his deputy.
9 In the second month,
on the *bǐngxū* day,
Lǐ Guāngbì was promoted to Prefect of Wèijùn and concurrently Investigating Commissioner of Héběi Circuit.
10 Shǐ Sīmíng and others besieged Ráoyáng for twenty-nine days
but failed to take it.
Lǐ Guāngbì led over ten thousand Fān and Hàn infantry and cavalry, and three thousand crossbowmen from Tàiyuán, out of Jǐngxíng.
On the Jǐhài day,
they reached Chángshān.
Three thousand Chángshān militiamen killed the Hú soldiers
and captured Ān Sīyì, who surrendered.
Lǐ Guāngbì said to Ān Sīyì,
"Do you know that you deserve to die?"
Ān Sīyì did not respond.
Lǐ Guāngbì said,
"You have been in battle for a long time.
Looking at my troops here,
can they contend with Shǐ Sīmíng?
Now, what strategy should I adopt?
If your plan is sound,
I will not kill you."
Ān Sīyì said,
"Your Lordship's men and horses have come a long way and are exhausted.
If you suddenly encounter a large enemy,
I fear it will not be easy to resist.
It would be better to move the army into the city,
prepare defenses early,
first assess victory and defeat,
and then send out troops.
Although the Hú cavalry are formidable,
they cannot maintain a strong position for long.
If they gain no advantage,
their morale will drop and their hearts will disengage.
At that time, we can plan our attack.
Shǐ Sīmíng is now in Ráoyáng,
not two hundred Lǐ from here."
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: from Zhēndìng to Ráoyáng is two hundred thirty-five Lǐ.
Sīyì was likely referring to where Sīmíng had pitched his camp.
"I reckon his vanguard will certainly arrive by tomorrow morning,
and the main army will follow.
This cannot be overlooked."
Lǐ Guāngbì was pleased,
released him from his bonds,
and immediately moved his army into the city.
When Shǐ Sīmíng heard that Chángshān was not defended,
he immediately lifted the siege of Ráoyáng.
The next day, before dawn,
his vanguard had already arrived,
and Shǐ Sīmíng and others followed,
totaling over twenty thousand cavalry,
advancing directly to the city walls.
Lǐ Guāngbì sent five thousand infantry out from the east gate to fight.
The rebels held the gate and did not retreat.
Lǐ Guāngbì ordered five hundred crossbowmen on the city wall to fire simultaneously.
The rebels retreated slightly.
Then he sent out a thousand crossbowmen, divided into four squads,
ensuring their arrows were fired one after another.
The rebels could not withstand them
and withdrew their army to the north side of the road.
Lǐ Guāngbì sent out five thousand troops to form a spear-wall on the south side of the road,
arrayed along the Hūtúo River.
The rebels repeatedly engaged in cavalry charges,
but Lǐ Guāngbì's soldiers shot at them.
More than half of their men and horses were hit by arrows,
so they retreated
to rest briefly and await their infantry.
A villager informed the rebels that five thousand rebel infantry were coming from Ráoyáng,
having marched one hundred seventy Lǐ day and night,
and had reached Féngbì south of Jiǔmén,
where they were probably resting.
Jiǔmén county was subordinate to Chángshān Commandery,
located east of the commandery.
Sòng Bái said: The Zhànguó Cè states: it originally had nine chambers where people resided,
and Zhào Wǔlíng Wáng changed it to Jiǔmén county.
Qì,
pronounced as lì.
[Lǐ Guāngbì's men] hid their flags and drums,
advanced stealthily along the water,
and reached Féngbì.
The rebels were just having a meal.
They launched their troops in a surprise attack,
killing them all without exception.
When Shǐ Sīmíng heard this,
he lost momentum
and retreated into Jiǔmén.
At that time, Chángshān had nine counties:
Zhēndìng, Gāochéng, Shíyì, Jiǔmén, Xíngtáng, Jǐngxíng, Píngshān, Huòlù, and Língshòu,
a total of nine counties.
Only Jiǔmén and Gāochéng were occupied by the rebels.
Lǐ Guāngbì sent his deputy general Zhāng Fèngzhāng with five hundred soldiers to garrison Shíyì.
Shíyì county, since the Hàn dynasty, was subordinate to Chángshān Commandery,
located southwest of the commandery.
The garrison here was larger than in other counties
to keep open the road to Tàiyuán.
Sòng Bái said: The Suí dynasty changed Hàn's Shàngqǔyáng county to Shíyì;
later moved Shíyì to Jǐngxíng county,
and established Héngyáng county at the old Shíyì county site,
named for being on the south side of Héngshān.
Thus, this Shíyì was in Jǐngxíng.
11 The Emperor appointed Wú Wáng Zhī as the Grand Administrator of Língchāng and the Overseer of Military Affairs for Hénán.
"The Emperor"
refers to Xuánzōng.
Shǐ, pronounced as shū lì.
He had two thousand troops.
Earlier, Yáng Wànshí, the Grand Administrator of Qiáojùn, had surrendered the commandery to Ān Lùshān,
forcing Zhāng Xún, the Magistrate of Zhēnyuán from Hédōng, to serve as his Assistant,
going west to meet the rebels.
When Zhāng Xún arrived in Zhēnyuán,
he led officials and common people in weeping at the Xuányuán Huángdì Temple.
Yōngqiū county,
in Hàn and Jìn, was subordinate to Chénliú Commandery;
in Latter Wèi, to Tāngxià Commandery;
in Suí, to Liáng Commandery;
in Táng, to Biànzhōu.
Qiáojùn,
Bózhōu.
Lǎozǐ,
a native of Kǔxiàn,
had a temple there;
the Táng emperors considered him their ancestor,
hence the county was renamed Zhēnyuán.
The Jiǔyù Zhì: The county is seventy Lǐ west of Qiáojùn.
Shuài,
pronounced as lǜ.
Several thousand officials and common people were happy to follow him.
Zhāng Xún selected a thousand elite soldiers and went west to Yōngqiū,
where he joined Jiǎ Bēn.
Previously,
Lìnghú Cháo, the Magistrate of Yōngqiū, had surrendered the county to the rebels.
The rebels appointed him general
and sent him east to attack the Huáiyáng relief force at Xiāngyì,
defeating them.
Huáiyáng Commandery,
Chénzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Xiāngyì county
was the land of Sòng Xiāngniú in the Spring and Autumn period.
Duke Xiāng of Sòng was buried there,
hence it was called Xiānglíng.
His tomb is now in the northwest corner of the county.
Qín Shǐhuáng, finding Chéngkuāng county low and damp,
moved it to Xiānglíng;
and because
the character "líng"
violated a taboo,
he changed it to Xiāngyì.
[The Huáiyáng soldiers] were captured at Yōngqiū
and were about to be killed, but they went to see Lǐ Tíngwàng.
The Huáiyáng soldiers then killed their guards.
Lìnghú Cháo abandoned his wife and children and fled.
Thus, Jiǎ Bēn was able to enter Yōngqiū in the interim.
On the Gēngzǐ day,
Lìnghú Cháo led elite rebel troops to attack Yōngqiū.
Jiǎ Bēn went out to fight,
was defeated and died.
Zhāng Xún fought bravely and repelled the rebels,
then took command of Jiǎ Bēn's troops,
styling himself the Vanguard Commander of Wú Wáng.
In the third month,
on the Yǐmǎo day,
Lìnghú Cháo, along with rebel generals Lǐ Huáixiān, Yáng Cháozōng, Xiè Yuántóng, and others, numbering over forty thousand, suddenly arrived at the city walls.
The troops were afraid;
none had a firm resolve.
Zhāng Xún said,
"The rebel army is elite and underestimates us.
If we attack them by surprise now,
they will surely be routed.
When the rebels' momentum is slightly broken,
then the city can be defended."
He then sent a thousand men to man the city walls;
he himself led a thousand men,
divided into several squads,
opened the gates, and launched a突襲 (sudden attack).
Zhāng Xún personally led his soldiers,
directly charging the rebel lines.
Men and horses scattered,
and the rebels retreated.
The next day,
they advanced again to attack the city,
setting up a hundred trebuchets surrounding the city,
destroying all the towers and battlements.
Zhāng Xún erected wooden barricades on the city wall to resist them.
When the rebels climbed like ants,
Zhāng Xún tied up bundles of reeds, soaked them in grease,
set them on fire, and threw them down.
The rebels could not climb up.
Whenever an opportunity arose,
he sent out troops to attack them,
or sometimes descended at night to raid their camp.
For over sixty days,
after more than three hundred battles, large and small,
eating in armor,
fighting again with wounds bandaged,
the rebels were finally defeated and fled.
Zhāng Xún pursued them, capitalizing on the victory,
captured two thousand Hú soldiers, and returned.
His military reputation greatly increased.
12 Initially,
Hùbù Shàngshū Ān Sīshùn knew of Lù Shān's rebellious intentions,
and therefore went to court to report them.
When Lù Shān rebelled,
the Emperor, because Sīshùn had reported it first,
did not punish him.
Gēshū Hàn, who had long had a rift with him,
a matter detailed in the previous volume, Tiānbǎo 10th year,
seized him at the pass gate and presented him [to the Emperor],
enumerating Sīshùn's seven crimes
and requesting his execution.
On the day Bǐngchén,
Sīshùn and his younger brother, Tàipú Qīng Yuánzhēn, were both executed,
and their family members were exiled to outside the嶺 Lǐng mountains.
Yáng Guózhōng was unable to save them,
and from this, he began to fear Hàn.
13 Guō Zǐyí arrived at Shuòfāng,
gathered more elite soldiers,
and on the day Wùwǔ,
advanced his army to Dài.
This Dài
refers to Dàizhōu.
14 On the day Wùchén,
Wú Wáng Zhī attacked Xiè Yuántóng,
putting him to flight,
and was appointed Chénliú Tàishǒu and Hénán Jiédùshǐ.
15 On the day Rénwǔ,
Lǐ Guāngbì, the Hédōng Jiédùshǐ, was appointed Fànyáng Zhǎngshǐ and Hébĕi Jiédùshǐ.
Yán Zhēnqīng was additionally appointed Hébĕi Cǎifǎngshǐ.
Zhēnqīng appointed Zhāng Dàn as his zhīshǐ.
Previously, a guest from Qīnghé, Lǐ È,
aged over twenty,
requested aid from Zhēnqīng on behalf of the people of his prefecture,
saying:
"You were the first to uphold the great righteousness,
and the various prefectures of Hébĕi rely on you as their Great Wall.
Now Qīnghé,
your western neighbor—
Qīnghé Jùn
is Bèizhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Dézhōu,
230 lì southwest to Bèizhōu.—
is called 'the Northern Treasury of All Under Heaven';
it currently has over three million bolts of cloth,
over eight hundred thousand bolts of silk,
over three hundred thousand strings of cash,
and over three hundred thousand hú of grain.
In the past, when Mòchuò was suppressed,
all weapons and armor were stored in the Qīnghé treasury—
this refers to the time of Wǔ Hòu.
Chuò is pronounced 'zhì luè'.
Zhù is pronounced 'dīng lǚ'.—
Each item can supply one need—
'thing' here refers to 'need'.—
and over one hundred thousand people.
I estimate that its wealth is sufficient to triple that of Píngyuán,
and its military strength is sufficient to double that of Píngyuán.
If you would truly provide it with soldiers,
pacify and possess it,
and make these two prefectures your heartland,
then the remaining prefectures would be like limbs,
all obeying your command."
Zhēnqīng said:
"Píngyuán's troops have only recently gathered
and are not yet trained;
they might not even be sufficient for self-preservation,
how can we afford to help a neighbor!
However,
if I were to grant your request,
then what would you do?"
È replied:
"Qīnghé sent me to convey this message to you,
not because its own strength is insufficient and it borrows your army to test the enemy,
but also to observe the clarity of a great worthy's
righteousness.
Now, looking up at your noble intention,
there is no decisive word or determined expression,
how dare I hastily speak of what I would do!"
Zhēnqīng was impressed by him
and wanted to provide him with troops.
The others believed È was young and reckless,
that it would merely divide their military strength,
and that nothing would be achieved.
Zhēnqīng reluctantly declined him.
È went to his lodging,
and again wrote a letter persuading Zhēnqīng,
stating:
"Qīnghé has abandoned the rebellion and pledged allegiance,
offering grain, silk, and weaponry to support the army,
yet you refuse to accept it and doubt it.
After I turn back,
Qīnghé will not be able to stand alone;
it will certainly have to rely on someone,
and will become a strong enemy to your west.
Will you then have no regrets?"
Zhēnqīng was greatly startled
and immediately went to his lodging,
lending him six thousand soldiers;
he accompanied him to the border
and bid him farewell with a handshake.
Zhēnqīng asked:
"The troops have already departed;
can you now tell me what you intend to do?"
È said:
"I heard that the imperial court has dispatched Chéng Qiānlǐ with a hundred thousand elite soldiers to exit Guōkǒu to suppress the rebels—
Guōkǒu
is west of Hándān Xiàn in Míngzhōu,
likely the same as the dangerous pass of Húguān.
Also, according to the Old Book of Tang: Guōkǒu
is in the western mountains of Xiāngzhōu.
Guō is pronounced 'guō'.—
but they cannot advance.
Now, I should lead the troops to first attack Wèijùn,
capture Yuán Zhītài, the Tàishǒu appointed by Lù Shān,
reinstate the old Tàishǒu Sīmǎ Chuí,
and make him the master of the southwest;
then divide the troops to open Guōkǒu,
allowing Chéng Qiānlǐ's army to pass through,
and subsequently suppress those prefectures and counties north of Jí and Yè, up to Yōulíng, that have not yet submitted—
Yōulíng
refers to Yōuzhōu.
We will combine our forces of one hundred thousand,
approach Mèngjīn from the south,
divide our troops along the river,
occupy strategic strongholds,
and control their escape route to the north.
I estimate that the government forces attacking from the east are no less than two hundred thousand,
and the Hénán righteous armies advancing west are also no less than one hundred thousand.
You should merely petition the court to hold fast to their defenses and avoid battle;
within a month or so,
the rebels will certainly experience internal collapse and mutual conflict."
Zhēnqīng said:
"Excellent!"
He ordered Lùshì Cānjūn Lǐ Zéjiāo and Píngyuán Lìng Fàn Dōngfù to lead these troops—
Píngyuán Xiàn
belonged to Píngyuán Jùn;
the ancient seat of Píngyuán Jùn was here,
its old city is twenty-five lì southwest of the current county.
The current county seat
was a city built by the Northern Qí.
At that time, Píngyuán Jùn's seat was Āndé Xiàn.
Sòng Bái said: Tángyì Xiàn,
belonged to Bópíng Jùn,
originally the land of the two Hàn counties, Qīng Xiàn and Fāgān;
in the 16th year of Kāihuáng of the Suí dynasty, Tángyì Xiàn was established here,
named after the old city of Tángyì to the northwest of the county.—
The combined forces of the three prefectures fought all day,
and the Wèi army was utterly defeated,
with over ten thousand heads decapitated,
over a thousand prisoners captured,
a thousand horses obtained,
and abundant military supplies.
Zhītài fled to Jíjùn, and Wèijùn was subsequently captured, greatly boosting the army's morale.
At that time, Hèlán Jìnmíng (賀蘭進明), the Grand Administrator of Běihǎi (北海), also raised an army.
Yán Zhēnqīng (顏真卿) wrote to summon him to join forces.
Běihǎi Commandery
was in Qīngzhōu (青州).
Yán Zhēnqīng arrayed his troops to meet him.
They saluted each other,
and wept on horseback,
their sorrow moving the ranks.
Hèlán Jìnmíng encamped south of Píngyuán (平原) city,
resting his soldiers and horses.
Yán Zhēnqīng consulted him on every matter,
and thus military authority gradually shifted to Hèlán Jìnmíng.
Yán Zhēnqīng did not take this amiss.
Yán Zhēnqīng attributed the merit of Tángyì (堂邑) to Hèlán Jìnmíng,
and Hèlán Jìnmíng submitted a memorial detailing his achievements,
making choices as he wished.
An imperial edict appointed Hèlán Jìnmíng as the Commander of Hébĕi (河北),
and selected Jiāo Dōngfú (交冬馥) for a slight promotion in rank;
those who distinguished themselves in Qīnghé (清河) and Bópíng (博平) were not recorded.
Hèlán Jìnmíng attacked Xìndū Commandery (信都郡).
After a long time,
he failed to conquer it.
Lùshì Cānjūn (錄事參軍) Zhǎng'ān (長安) Wǔ Qí (第五琦) advised Hèlán Jìnmíng to generously offer gold and silks to recruit brave warriors,
and thus he conquered it.
The “Kǎoyì” (考異) states: The “Yánshì Xíngzhuàng” (顏氏行狀) says:
"Hèlán Jìnmíng suffered a defeat beneath Xìndū city,
and an imperial edict ordered him punished;
the Duke [Yán Zhēnqīng] released him,
sending him to the traveling court.
Hèlán Jìnmíng's survival
was due to the Duke's protection."
Now we follow the old biography.
Also, the “Tánglì” (唐曆) states:
"On the *yǐyǒu* (乙酉) day of the third month,
Yán Zhēnqīng was appointed Commissioner of Hébĕi (河北 Cǎifǎngshǐ, 採訪使).
At that time, Hèlán Jìnmíng raised a righteous army,
crossed the Yellow River northward,
and jointly formulated strategies with Yán Zhēnqīng.
In the sixth month,
Yán Zhēnqīng defeated Yuán Zhītài (袁知泰) at Tángyì (堂邑)."
Hèlán Jìnmíng's second capture of Xìndū,
and the “Tǒngjì” (統紀) all place it in the third month.
The old record places the defeat of Yuán Zhītài
and the capture of Xìndū
both in the sixth month.
However, there was no *yǐyǒu* (乙酉) day in the third month;
*yǐyǒu* (乙酉)
was the second day of the fourth month.
Now we follow the “Tǒngjì” (統紀).
Lǐ Guāngbì (李光弼) and Shǐ Sīmíng (史思明) faced each other for more than forty days.
Shǐ Sīmíng cut off the grain supply route to Chángshān (常山).
There was a shortage of fodder in the city;
horses ate straw mats.
Lǐ Guāngbì used five hundred carts to fetch fodder from Shíyì (石邑).
*Zhī* (之),
means "to go".
*Chéng* (乘),
reads *shéng zhèng* (繩證).
A thousand crossbowmen guarded them,
forming a square formation as they marched,
and the rebels could not seize it.
Cài Xīdé (蔡希德) led his troops to attack Shíyì (石邑),
but Zhāng Fèngzhāng (張奉璋) repulsed him.
Lǐ Guāngbì sent an envoy to request urgent help from Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀).
Guō Zǐyí led his troops out from Jǐngxíng (井陘).
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the *rénchén* (壬辰) day,
he reached Chángshān (常山)
and joined forces with Lǐ Guāngbì.
Their combined Fān (蕃) and Hàn (漢) infantry and cavalry totaled over one hundred thousand.
On the *jiǎwǔ* (甲午) day,
Guō Zǐyí and Lǐ Guāngbì fought Shǐ Sīmíng and others south of Jiǔmén (九門) city.
Sòng Bái (宋白) states: Jiǔmén (九門) county
was a Zhào (趙) city in the Warring States period.
The “Zhànguócè” (戰國策) says it originally had nine chambers for residence,
and Zhào Wǔlíngwáng (趙武靈王) renamed it Jiǔmén county.
Zhōnglángjiàng (中郎將) Hún Jiān (渾瑊) shot and
killed Lǐ Lìjié (李立節).
Hún Jiān (瑊)
was the son of Shì Zhī (釋之).
Shǐ Sīmíng gathered his remaining troops and fled to Zhào Commandery (趙郡),
and Cài Xīdé (蔡希德) fled to Jùlù (鉅鹿).
Shǐ Sīmíng went from Zhào Commandery to Bólíng (博陵).
At that time, Bólíng had already surrendered to the imperial army,
and Shǐ Sīmíng slaughtered all the commandery officials.
The people of Héshuò (河朔) suffered from the rebels' cruelty and tyranny,
forming groups wherever they went,
many as numerous as twenty thousand,
the fewest being ten thousand,
each establishing camps to resist the rebels.
When Guō Zǐyí's and Lǐ Guāngbì's armies arrived,
they eagerly came out to offer their services.
On the *gēngzǐ* (庚子) day,
Zhào Commandery was attacked;
in one day,
the city surrendered.
Many soldiers engaged in plunder.
Lǐ Guāngbì sat at the city gate,
collected what was seized,
and returned it all to the people,
who were greatly pleased.
Guō Zǐyí captured four thousand men alive,
released them all,
and beheaded Lùshān's (祿山) Grand Administrator Guō Xiànqiú (郭獻璆).
Lǐ Guāngbì advanced to besiege Bólíng (博陵).
After ten days,
he failed to capture it,
and led his troops back to Héngyáng (恆陽) for provisions.
Héngyáng (恆陽)
was Héngshān Commandery (恆山郡),
named so because its territory was south of Mount Héng (恆山).
The Táng (唐) dynasty established the Héngyáng Army (恆陽軍) north of the commandery.
Also, Bólíng Commandery (博陵郡) had Héngyáng county (恆陽縣),
which was the Hàn (漢) dynasty's Shàngqǔyáng (上曲陽) county,
renamed Héngyáng county by the Suí (隋) dynasty,
located ten *lǐ* west of Bólíng.
*Héng* (恆),
reads *hù dēng* (戶登).
*Huán* (還),
reads *cóng xuān* (從宣),
also pronounced as the character itself.
Yáng Guózhōng (楊國忠) asked Zuǒ Shíyí (左拾遺) Bópíng (博平) Zhāng Gǎo (張鎬) and Xiāo Xīn (蕭昕) who among the scholars could be made a general.
Zhāng Gǎo and Xiāo Xīn recommended Zuǒ Zànshàn Dàfū (左贊善大夫) Yǒngshòu (永壽) Lái Tián (來瑱).
In the second year of Wǔdé (武德), Yǒngshòu county (永壽縣) was established by dividing Xīnpíng (新平),
belonging to Bīnzhōu (邠州).
*Tián* (瑱),
reads *tā jiàn* (他見).
On the *bǐngwǔ* (丙午) day,
Lái Tián was appointed Grand Administrator of Yǐngchuān (潁川).
The rebels attacked it repeatedly,
and Lái Tián defeated many rebels before and after,
and was promoted to Defense Commissioner of his commandery.
People called him
"Lái Jiáotiě" (來嚼鐵, Lái the Iron-chewer).
Ān Lùshān (安祿山) sent Pínglú (平盧) Military Commissioner Lǚ Zhīhuì (呂知誨) to entice Āndōng (安東) Vice Grand Protector Mǎ Língchá (馬靈詧),
and then killed him.
Mǎ Língchá (馬靈詧)
was Fūméng Língchá (夫蒙靈詧).
In the second year of Kāiyuán (開元),
the Āndōng Grand Protectorate was moved to Píngzhōu (平州);
in the second year of Tiānbǎo (天寶),
it was moved to the old commandery city of Liáoxī (遼西).
*Yòu* (誘),
reads *yáng jiǔ* (羊久).
Wǔzhì (武陟)
was the territory of Hàn (漢) Huái (懷) county.
In the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng (開皇) of the Suí (隋) dynasty, Wǔzhì county (武陟縣) was established by division.
At that time, it belonged to Hénèi Commandery (河內郡).
Envoys were sent across the sea to communicate with Yán Zhēnqīng,
requesting to capture Fányáng (范陽) to prove their loyalty.
Yán Zhēnqīng sent his adjutant Jiǎ Zài (賈載) with provisions and soldiers' clothing to assist them.
Yán Zhēnqīng at that time had only one son, Pǒ (頗),
who was just over ten years old,
and sent him to Kènú (客奴) as a hostage.
When the imperial court heard of this,
Kènú was appointed Pínglú Military Commissioner,
and given the name Zhèngchén (正臣);
Xuánzhì (玄志) was appointed Āndōng Vice Grand Protector,
and Dǒng Qín (董秦) was appointed Pínglú Bingmǎshǐ (兵馬使).
Nányáng (南陽) Military Commissioner Lǔ Jiǒng (魯炅) erected a stockade south of the Zhìshǔi (滍水).
Ān Lùshān's generals Wǔ Lìngxún (武令珣) and Bì Sīchēn (畢思琛) attacked it.
Punctuation by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖), reviewed by Hé Zīquán (何茲全), Gù Jié​gāng (顧頡剛), and Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
Compiled by imperial order.
后 学 天 台 (Hòu Xué Tiāntái)
The first year of Zhìdé (至德元年)
(*bǐngshēn*, 756 CE)
1 In the fifth month,
on the Dīngsì day,
the forces of Guǎng collapsed,
fleeing to take refuge in Nányáng.
The rebels then besieged them.
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies, Zhāng Jì, recommended Guó Wáng Jù, the Administrator of Yílíng, as a man of courage and strategy.
The Emperor summoned Wú Wáng Zhī to be the Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud,
and appointed Jù as the Administrator of Chénliú and Qiáojùn, and Jìedùshǐ of Hénán.
He also concurrently commanded Hé Lǚguāng, the Jìedùshǐ of Lǐngnán,
Chénliújùn,
and Biànzhōu.
Qiáojùn,
and Bózhōu.
These were the administrators of the two prefectures.
In this year, the Five Prefectural Jinglǜ Táojī Shǐ was promoted to Lǐngnán Jìedùshǐ,
governing Guǎng, Sháo, Xún, Cháo, Kāng, Lóng, Duān, Xīn, Fēng, Chūn, Qín, Luó, Pān, Gāo, and Sī
[ēn]
[téng] prefectures,
with its seat in Guǎngzhōu.
Zhào Guózhēn, the Jìedùshǐ of Qiánzhōng,
Zhào Guózhēn
was a descendant of Zhào Jūndào, a chieftain of the Zāngkē Bìebù Chōngzhōu barbarians.
Yáng Guózhōng concurrently held the Jìedù of Jiànnán.
Because Guózhēn possessed strategy,
he was appointed Dūdū of Qiánzhōng,
guarding the Five Streams for over ten years.
While the empire was in turmoil,
his commandery alone remained peaceful.
According to the Xīnshū Fāngzhèn Biǎo: in the 26th year of Kāiyuán,
a Wǔxī Zhūzhōu Jīnglǜ Shǐ was established in Qiánzhōu.
In the 14th year of Tiānbǎo,
it was expanded to include the Shǒuzhuō Shǐ.
In the 4th year of Dàlì under Dàizōng,
the Dūdù Tuánliàn Shǒuzhuō Guānchá Chǔzhì Shǐ of Chén, Xī, Wū, Jǐn, and Yè prefectures was first established.
In the 3rd year of Yuánhé under Xiànzōng,
the Guānchá of Qiánzhōu was expanded to include Fúzhōu.
At the end of the Táng dynasty,
a Jiézhèn was first established in Qiánzhōu.
It is suspected that Zhào Guózhēn had not yet been made a Jiézhèn at this time.
By the following year,
the Tōngjiàn records the establishment of the Qiánzhōng Jìedù,
which must have a basis.
Guózhēn
was originally from the Zāngkē Yi.
On the Wùchén day,
Jù led his troops out from Lántián,
heading towards Nányáng.
When the rebels heard of this,
they lifted the siege and fled.
2 Lìnghú Cháo again led his troops to attack Yōngqiū.
Cháo and Zhāng Xún were old acquaintances,
and they greeted each other under the city walls as if in peacetime.
Cháo then tried to persuade Xún, saying:
"The fate of the empire is sealed.
Why do you stubbornly defend a precarious city,
for whom?"
Xún replied:
"You always prided yourself on loyalty and righteousness.
Where is your loyalty and righteousness
in your actions today?"
Cháo felt ashamed and withdrew.
3 Guō Zǐyí and Lǐ Guāngbì returned to Chángshān,
and Shǐ Sīmíng gathered tens of thousands of scattered soldiers and pursued them.
Zǐyí selected elite cavalry to challenge them repeatedly.
After three days,
they reached Xíngtáng,
which was the Xíngtáng county south of Hàn,
belonging to Chángshān Jùn.
Jiǔyù Zhì: 55 lǐ north of the commandery.
Then they retreated.
Zǐyí took advantage of this,
and again defeated them at Shāhé.
Shāhé is between Xīnlè and Xíngtáng counties.
Bàī,
pronounced Mài.
Ān Lùshān again sent two myriad infantry and cavalry north to join Sīmíng,
and also sent Niú Tíngjiè to dispatch over ten thousand troops from Fányáng and other prefectures to assist Sīmíng,
totaling over fifty thousand men,
with the Tóngluó and Yèluòhé comprising one fifth.
When Zǐyí reached Héngyáng,
Sīmíng arrived shortly after.
Zǐyí dug deep trenches and built high ramparts to await them;
when the rebels came, he defended;
when they left, he pursued them.
By day he displayed his troops,
and by night he raided their camp,
giving the rebels no rest.
After several days,
Zǐyí and Guāngbì deliberated, saying:
"The rebels are weary;
we can now engage in battle."
Kǎoyì says: Hélùo Chūnqiū attributes this to Guāngbì,
while Fényáng Jiāchuán attributes it to Zǐyí.
It was probably a joint deliberation between the two.
On the Rénwǔ day,
they fought at Jiāshān.
According to the Old History, Ān Lùshān's biography: Jiāshān is east of Chángshān Jùn.
Wèi Shōu's Dìxíng Zhì: There is Jiāshān in Shàngqǔyáng county, Zhōngshān Jùn.
Shàngqǔyáng
was Táng's Héngyáng.
Kǎoyì says: The Shílù states
"sixth month, Rénwǔ day."
According to Chánglì,
the first day of the sixth month was Guǐwèi;
the Rénwǔ day
was the twenty-ninth day of the fifth month.
Fényáng Jiāchuán and the Old Lùshān biography also state
"sixth month,
fought at Jiāshān."
Hélùo Chūnqiū says:
"On the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month,
Guāngbì defeated the rebels at Jiāshān."
Now, following the Shílù, the month has been changed.
They beheaded forty thousand,
and captured over a thousand prisoners.
Sīmíng fell from his horse,
and fled on foot with bare head and feet.
By evening,
he returned to his camp leaning on a broken spear,
and then fled to Bólíng;
Guāngbì then besieged him,
and the army's morale greatly rose.
Thereupon, over ten prefectures in Hébĕi all killed the rebel defending generals and surrendered.
The Yúyáng road was again cut off.
Yúyáng
refers to Fányáng.
Fányáng Jùn
was Yōuzhōu.
Later, Jìzhōu Yúyáng Jùn was also established,
and the two commanderies began to have distinct boundaries.
However, the Fányáng Jìedù still commanded Yōu, Yì, Píng, Tán, Guī, Yān, and other prefectures,
so the rebel's true stronghold was indeed Fányáng.
At this time, Tang people often used Fányáng and Yúyáng interchangeably.
Bái Jūyì's poem
"The war drums of Yúyáng shake the earth"
uses Fányáng interchangeably with Yúyáng.
Before this, Yán Gǎoqīng had returned Chángshān to the rightful government,
and the Yúyáng road was cut off;
Gǎoqīng was defeated, and it was re-opened.
Now Guō and Lǐ defeated Shǐ Sīmíng,
so it was cut off again.
Many were captured by the government forces,
and all the officers and soldiers whose families were in Yúyáng felt unsettled.
Lùshān was greatly alarmed.
He summoned Gāo Shàng and Yán Zhuāng and scolded them, saying:
"For several years you urged me to rebel,
claiming it would be foolproof.
Now, defending Tōngguān,
we cannot advance for months,
the northern road is cut off,
all the armies are closing in from four directions,
and all I possess are merely a few prefectures like Biàn and Zhèng.
Where is this foolproof plan?
From now on, do not come to see me!"
Shàng and Zhuāng were terrified,
and for several days dared not see him.
Tián Gānzhēn came down from the pass,
and spoke to Lùshān on behalf of Shàng and Zhuāng, saying:
"Since ancient times, emperors who built great enterprises
all experienced victories and defeats.
How could it be achieved in one go?
Although there are many army camps in the four directions now,
they are all newly recruited, disorganized multitudes,
who have not yet experienced battle formations.
How can they contend with our elite troops from Jìběi?
There is no need to worry deeply!
Shàng and Zhuāng are both founding meritorious officials.
If Your Majesty suddenly cuts them off,
which general, upon hearing this,
would not feel inner fear?
If superiors and subordinates become disunited,
your servant secretly fears for Your Majesty's safety!"
Lùshān was pleased, saying:
"Āhào,
you have been able to relieve my worries."
He immediately summoned Shàng and Zhuāng,
set up a lavish banquet,
and personally sang for them to accompany the wine,
treating them as before.
Āhào
was Gānzhēn's courtesy name.
Lùshān discussed abandoning Luòyáng
and returning to Fányáng,
but his decision was not yet made.
At this time,
the whole realm, regarding Yáng Guózhōng's arrogance and indulgence as the cause of rebellion,
was filled with bitter resentment.
Moreover,
Lù Shān started his rebellion under the pretext of executing Guózhōng.
Wáng Sīlǐ secretly advised Gēshū Hàn
to submit a memorial requesting Guózhōng's execution,
but Hàn did not agree.
Sīlǐ then suggested taking thirty cavalry to kidnap him
and kill him at Tóngguān.
Hàn said:
"If that were to happen,
it would be Hàn rebelling,
not Lù Shān."
Someone persuaded Guózhōng:
"Now the court's main forces are all in Hàn's hands.
If Hàn were to raise his banner and point it westward,
wouldn't that be dangerous for you, sir?"
Guózhōng was greatly alarmed,
and so he memorialized:
"Although the large army at Tóngguān is strong,
there are no reinforcements behind it.
Should it suffer a defeat,
the capital would be in peril.
I request that three thousand 'youngsters' from the imperial pastures be selected and trained within the park."
At that time, the soldiers of the imperial pastures, Wǔfāng, and Jìnyuàn
were generally called "youngsters."
He had Lǐ Fúdė and other generals from the Jiànnán army lead them.
He also recruited ten thousand men to garrison Bāshàng,
appointing his confidant, Dù Gānyùn, to command them.
The stated purpose was to resist the rebels,
but in reality, it was to guard against Hàn.
When Hàn heard this,
he also feared being plotted against by Guózhōng.
So he submitted a memorial requesting that the Bāshàng army be subordinate to Tóngguān.
In the sixth month,
on the day Guǐwèi,
he summoned Dù Gānyùn to the pass
and, on some pretext, executed him.
Guózhōng grew even more fearful.
At this time, someone reported that Cuī Gānyòu was in Shǎn,
with fewer than four thousand troops,
all weak and unprepared,
stating that this was Lù Shān's stratagem to sow discord.
Shǎn,
pronounced Shī Rǎn fān.
Hàn memorialized, saying:
"Lù Shān has long been skilled in warfare.
Now that he has just become a rebel,
how could he be unprepared?
He must be feigning a weak army to lure us.
If we go,
we will fall right into his trap.
Furthermore, the rebels have come a long way;
their advantage lies in a quick battle.
The government army holds a strategic position to block them;
its advantage lies in holding firm.
Moreover, the rebels are cruel and have lost popular support;
their military strength is dwindling daily,
and internal discord is imminent.
If we take advantage of this,
we can capture them without fighting.
The key is to achieve success;
why must we rush?
Now, many of the troops levied from various circuits have not yet assembled;
please wait for them."
Guō Zǐyí and Lǐ Guāngbì also memorialized, saying:
"We request to lead our forces north to capture Fányáng,
overturning their lair,
and holding the rebels' wives and children hostage to lure them,
and the rebels will surely collapse internally.
The large army at Tóngguān
should only hold its ground to wear them out,
and must not sally forth rashly."
Guózhōng suspected Hàn of plotting against him,
and spoke to the Emperor,
saying that since the rebels were currently unprepared,
Hàn's hesitation
would cause them to lose the opportunity.
The Emperor believed this to be true,
and continuously dispatched eunuchs to urge him on,
one after another.
Hàn had no choice.
He beat his chest and wept bitterly.
On the day Bǐngxū,
he led his troops out of the pass.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
they encountered Cuī Gānyòu's army on the western plains of Língbǎo.
Língbǎo County was renamed;
see volume 215, Tiānbǎo first year.
To the south, it bordered the mountains;
to the north, it was blocked by the river,
a narrow pass seventy *lǐ* long.
On the day Gēngyín,
the government army and Gānyòu engaged in battle.
Gānyòu had hidden troops in the dangerous terrain.
Hàn and Tián Liángqiū floated in a boat on the river to observe the military situation.
Seeing that Gānyòu's troops were few,
they urged the various armies to advance.
Wáng Sīlǐ and others led fifty thousand elite troops in the vanguard.
Páng Zhōng and others led the remaining hundred thousand troops to follow.
Hàn, with thirty thousand troops, ascended a northern mound by the river to observe them,
beating drums to boost their morale.
Gānyòu's deployed troops numbered no more than ten thousand;
in groups of tens and fives,
scattered like stars,
sometimes sparse, sometimes dense,
sometimes advancing, sometimes retreating.
The government army looked on and laughed.
Gānyòu kept his elite troops in strict formation,
arrayed behind them.
Once the armies engaged,
the rebels lowered their banners as if about to flee.
The government army relaxed
and was unprepared.
In a moment,
the hidden troops were unleashed.
The rebels, from the high ground, rolled down wood and stones,
killing a great many officers and soldiers.
The path was narrow;
the soldiers were packed together,
unable to use their spears and lances.
Hàn drove horse-drawn felt chariots as a vanguard,
intending to charge the rebels with them.
Past noon,
a strong east wind suddenly picked up.
Gānyòu used dozens of hay chariots to block the felt chariots' path,
then set them ablaze.
The smoke and flames
blinded the government troops,
who wildly killed each other,
believing the rebels to be in the smoke,
and gathered bows and crossbows to shoot into it.
As dusk fell,
their arrows were exhausted,
and only then did they realize there were no rebels there.
Gānyòu dispatched elite Tongluó cavalry to cross from the southern mountains
and attack the government army from the rear.
The government army was thrown into disarray, head to tail,
not knowing where to defend,
and thus suffered a crushing defeat.
Some abandoned their armor and hid in the mountains and valleys;
others pushed each other into the river and drowned.
The clamor shook heaven and earth,
and the rebels pressed their advantage.
When the rearguard saw the vanguard defeated,
they all disintegrated.
The army north of the river, seeing this, also routed.
Hàn alone, with a few hundred cavalry under his command, fled.
He crossed the river west of Shǒuyángshān and entered the pass.
Shǒuyángshān should be Shǒushān;
the character
"yáng"
is superfluous.
Shǒushān is in Púzhōu, Hédōng County,
facing Jīngshān in Húchéng County across the river.
Both were two *zhàng* wide
and one *zhàng* deep,
and men and horses that fell into them
filled them up in a moment.
The remaining troops trampled over them to cross.
Only a little over eight thousand soldiers managed to enter the pass.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
Gānyòu advanced and attacked Tóngguān,
capturing it.
Gé Shūhán 哥舒翰 arrived at the Guānxī 關西 relay station,
unfurled a banner to gather scattered soldiers,
hoping to re-garrison Tóngguān 潼關.
Fān Jiàng 蕃將 Huǒbá Guīrén 火拔歸仁 and others, with over a hundred cavalry, surrounded the station,
entered and said to Hàn 翰:
"The rebels are here!
Please, Your Excellency, mount your horse."
Hàn 翰 mounted his horse and left the station.
Guīrén 歸仁 led his men in prostration and said:
"You abandoned an army of 200,000 in one battle!
What face do you have to see the Son of Heaven again?
Moreover, have you not seen Gāo Xiānzhī 高仙芝 and Fēng Chángqīng 封常清?"
He meant that defeated generals were certainly executed.
The incident is found in the upper volume of the previous year.
Hàn 翰 refused and
wanted to dismount.
Guīrén 歸仁 tied his feet to the horse's belly with hair,
and as for the generals who would not comply,
he seized them all and took them east.
At that time, the rebel general Tián Gānzhēn 田乾真 had already arrived,
so he surrendered to him,
and they were all sent to Luòyáng 洛陽.
Ān Lùshān 安祿山 asked Hàn 翰:
"You always belittled me."
The incident is found in volume 216, Tiānbǎo 天寶 eleventh year.
Hàn 翰 prostrated himself and replied:
"Your subject's mortal eyes failed to recognize a sage.
Now the empire is not yet pacified.
Lǐ Guāngbì 李光弼 is in Chángshān 常山,
Lǐ Zhī 李祗 is in Dōngpíng 東平.
Lǐ Zhī 李祗
refers to Wúwáng Zhī 吳王祗.
If Your Majesty keeps your subject
and allows him to summon them with a short letter,
they will all submit within days."
Lùshān 祿山 was greatly pleased,
and appointed Hàn 翰 as Sīkōng 司空 and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì 同平章事.

He seized him and beheaded him.
Hàn 翰 wrote letters to summon the generals,
but they all wrote back to rebuke him.
Lùshān 祿山 knew it was ineffective,
so he imprisoned him in the imperial garden.
This was the imperial garden of the Eastern Capital.
Thereupon, the defense commissioners of Hédōng 河東, Huáyīn 華陰, Fēngyì 馮翊, and Shàngluò 上洛 all abandoned their prefectures and fled.

Huá 華,
pronounced Hù Huà.
On that day,
Hàn's 翰 subordinates came to report the emergency.
The emperor did not grant an audience in time,

By evening,
the peace fires did not arrive.
According to the Liùdiǎn 六典: In the Tang dynasty, where beacon towers were established for garrisons,
they were generally about thirty *lǐ* apart.
Every night at dusk,
a plume of smoke was lit,

At this time, the defending troops had already collapsed,
and no one was left to light the fires.
On the *Rénchén* 壬辰 day,
the emperor summoned the chancellors to deliberate.
Yáng Guózhōng 楊國忠, having personally held the governorship of Jiànnán 劍南,
upon hearing of Ān Lùshān's 安祿山 rebellion,
immediately ordered his deputy, Cuī Yuán 崔圓, to secretly prepare provisions
in case of emergency, intending to flee there.
At this point, he was the first to propose the strategy of fleeing to Shǔ 蜀.
The emperor approved.
On the *Guǐsì* 癸巳 day,
Guózhōng 國忠 assembled the hundred officials in the imperial hall,
where they were terrified and wept.
When asked for strategies, they all simply assented and did not respond.
Guózhōng 國忠 said:
"People have been reporting Lùshān's 祿山 rebellion for ten years,
but the emperor did not believe it.
Today's events
are not the fault of the chancellors."
After the court session,
when the court was dismissed,
the imperial guards of the three Left and Right Guards who stood in attendance all went off duty.
[The officials] did not know where to go,
and the streets and markets were desolate.
Guózhōng 國忠 sent Hán 韓 and Guó 虢 into the palace
to persuade the emperor to enter Shǔ 蜀.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
barely one or two tenths of the officials attended court.
The Emperor ascended the Qínzhèng Lóu,
and issued an edict,
stating that he intended to lead a personal campaign.
Those who heard it did not believe it.
Wèi Fāngjìn, the Jīngzhào Yǐn, was appointed Yùshǐ Dàfū and concurrent Zhìdùn Shǐ;
Cuī Guāngyuǎn of Língchāng, the Jīngzhào Shàoyǐn, was appointed Jīngzhào Yǐn,
and made concurrent Xījīng Liúshǒu;
General Biān Lìngchéng was put in charge of the palace keys.
Under the pretext that Yǐngwáng Qǐ, the Jiànnán Jiédù Dàshǐ, was about to proceed to his post,

On that day,
the Emperor moved his retinue to the Northern Palace.
Cháng'ān, the capital of the Táng dynasty,
designated the Tàijí Gōng as the Western Palace,
the Dàmíng Gōng as the Eastern Palace,
and the Xīngqìng Gōng as the Southern Palace.
The Northern Palace would therefore be inside the Xuánwǔ Mén.
Furthermore, speaking geographically,
moving the retinue from the Xīngqìng Gōng back to the Dàmíng Gōng,
with the Xīngqìng Gōng in the south
and the Dàmíng Gōng in the north,
also led to the Dàmíng Gōng being referred to as the Northern Palace.
The Kǎo Yì says: The Xìng Shǔ Jì states:

When the Emperor was about to mount his horse,
Yáng Guózhōng remonstrated,
saying: 'You should diligently guard the ancestral temples;

Wéi Jiànsu fought hard,
arguing: 'The rebel forces are pressing close,
people's hearts are not firm,

Wèi Fāngjìn was promoted to Yùshǐ Dàfū,
and made concurrent Qiánlù Zhīdùn Shǐ."
We note that when the rebels captured Tóngguān,
and the imperial carriage was about to leave,
people's hearts were already in peril;
how could there have been more drum-beating and grass-burning to alarm them!
Guózhōng had long harbored the plan to "seek refuge in Shǔ,"
and Jiànsu was introduced by him;
how could there have been such a dispute before the Emperor!
This is likely Sòng Jù wanting to credit Jiànsu,
making the matter almost a fabrication.
We do not adopt it here.
Lóngwǔ Dàjiāngjūn Chén Xuánlǐ was ordered to organize the Six Armies,
given generous gifts of money and silk,
and nine hundred excellent horses were selected.
Outsiders were all unaware of this.
On the Yǐwèi day,
at dawn,

the Emperor, accompanied only by his noble sisters, imperial princes, princesses, imperial grandsons, Yáng Guózhōng, Wéi Jiànsu, Wèi Fāngjìn, Chén Xuánlǐ, along with trusted eunuchs and palace attendants, departed through Yánqiū Mén.
Yánqiū Mén
was the western gate of the Táng Cháng'ān imperial park.
Chéng Dàchāng's Yōng Lù contains a map indicating important places of the Hàn and Táng dynasties.

The Shǐ Jì Xuánzōng contains words fit for a ruler.
Qiāo,
pronounced Zǐ-xiǎo.
Liǎn,
pronounced Lì-shàn.

The third was the Xūn Zhàng,

The fourth was the Yì Zhàng,

after the roll call was completed,
the inner gates opened,

the Emperor walked into the Dōngxù Mén,

The inner and outer guard formations

On days when regular attendance was suspended,

Cuī Guāngyuǎn and Biān Lìngchéng led people to extinguish the fire,

Guāngyuǎn sent his son, Dōng Xiàn, to see Lùshān,

The Emperor passed over the pontoon bridge.
Yáng Guózhōng sent men to burn the bridge.
The Emperor said:

why should we cut off their path!"
He kept the Director of the Inner Bureau, Gāo Lìshì,

Xuánzōng first established the post of Director of the Inner Bureau,

Pū,

is forty *lǐ* west of the capital city.
Wàngxián Palace
is east of the county.
Imperial envoys were sent to summon provisions,

*Húbǐng*
are today's *zhēngbǐng*.
Gāo Sìsūn said: *Húbǐng*
means they are made with sesame seeds.

Mixed with wheat and beans,
the imperial grandchildren vied to scoop it up with their hands and eat it.
In an instant, it was all gone,
and they still weren't full.

"Upon reaching Wàngxián Lodge,
the imperial horse fell ill.

*Xìng Shǔ Jì*:

all those in the imperial retinue were hungry.

rested under a tree,

then embraced the Emperor's feet,
weeping and gently admonishing him,

*Sùzōng Shílù*:

put *húbǐng* in his sleeves,

*Tiānbǎo Luànlí Jì*:
"On the eleventh day of the sixth month,
the imperial cortege headed to Shǔ.
Upon reaching Wàngxián Palace,

The old and young then eagerly carried and brought pots of gruel,

It was first given to the soldiers;

According to this, the Emperor went to Shǔ on the ninth day.
Wēn Yú's statement
"eleventh day"
is incorrect.
The rest combines the accounts.
He comforted and rewarded them.
Everyone wept,
and the Emperor also wiped away tears.

certainly not just one day;

as seen in the upper volume of that year's record.
This led to Your Majesty's displacement.
This is why the former kings diligently sought out loyal and upright individuals to broaden their understanding,

Your subject still remembers Sòng Jǐng as prime minister,

Consequently, outside the palace gates,
Your Majesty knows nothing.

The Emperor said:
"This is due to My lack of discernment,

He comforted him and sent him away.
Soon after, the Department of Imperial Food presented the imperial meal.

Only then did he eat.

Jīnchéng County,
part of Jīngzhào,

On the day of Bǐngshēn,

Wéi È, the Jīngzhào Sīlù, stepped forward and said:

“Now the anger of the multitude is difficult to defy.
