If you hesitate and do not act,
nor make preparations,
once Chángshān falls,
how can Xìndū remain untouched!"
Chéng'ēn did not agree.
Xiānyùn again said:
"General, if you do not heed my humble words,
it must be because you fear having too few soldiers.
Now, the people are not living peacefully
and all wish to repay the nation.
They are gathering together,
occupying villages.
If you offer rewards to recruit them,
100,000 can be raised within ten days;
combined with the over 3,000 Shuòfāng armored soldiers,
it will be sufficient to accomplish royal affairs.
If you abandon a vital strategic point to others,
and reside in a place open on all sides while feeling secure,
referring to the land of Xìndū,
which is flat and open in all directions,
not a place where one can reside in security.
That is the path to defeat."
Chéng'ēn remained indecisive.
Chéng'ēn
was the elder cousin of Chéngcǐ.
Wū Chéngcǐ is mentioned in Volume 213, Kāiyuán 20th year.
Cǐ
is pronounced cǐ,
also qiělǐ.
The Kǎoyì states: Hán Yù's Wūshì Xiānmiào Bēi says:
"Chéng'ēn
was Chéngqià's elder brother."
We now follow the New Biography.
That month,
Shǐ Sīmíng and Cài Xīdé led 10,000 troops south to attack Jiǔmén.
Within ten days,
Jiǔmén feigned surrender,
hiding armored soldiers on the city walls.
Sīmíng ascended the wall,
and the hidden troops attacked him;
Sīmíng fell from the wall,
a deer-horn impediment injuring his left flank.
That night,
he fled to Bólíng.
Yán Zhēnqīng
sent a sealed memorial in a wax pellet to Língwǔ.
Zhēnqīng was appointed Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū) and concurrently Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Dàfū),
retaining his previous titles of Commissioner for Héběi Suppression, Investigation, and Disposition,
and a general amnesty decree was also sent,
likewise in a wax pellet.
Zhēnqīng distributed it among the various prefectures of Héběi
and also sent people to distribute it in Hénán, Jiāng, and Huái.
From this, the various circuits first learned that the Emperor had ascended the throne in Língwǔ,
and their patriotism became even stronger.
Guō Zǐyí and others
led 50,000 troops from Héběi to Língwǔ.
The military prestige of Língwǔ then began to flourish,
and people had hopes of restoration.
In the eighth month,
on Rénwǔ day, the first day of the lunar month,
Zǐyí was appointed Minister of War (Wǔbù Shàngshū) and Língwǔ Chief Administrator,
and Lǐ Guāngbì was appointed Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū) and Northern Capital Resident-General.
Empress Wǔ in Tiānshòu 1st year designated Tàiyuán as the Northern Capital;
Zhōngzōng in Shénlóng 1st year abolished it;
Kāiyuán 11th year re-established it;
Tiānbǎo 1st year called it Běijīng;
that year it was again called Northern Capital.
The rest remained as before.
Guāngbì, with 5,000 troops from Jǐngchéng and Héjiān, proceeded to Tàiyuán.
Earlier,
Wáng Chéngyè, the Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng, had neglected military and administrative affairs.
The imperial court sent Shìyùshǐ Cuī Zhòng to take over his troops.
Soon after, an imperial envoy was sent to execute Wáng Chéngyè.
Cuī Zhòng had treated Wáng Chéngyè with contempt and disrespect,
which Guāngbì had always found displeasing.
At this time,
an imperial edict ordered Guāngbì to take over the troops.
When Cuī Zhòng saw Guāngbì,
he showed no courtesy,
nor did he hand over the troops promptly.
Guāngbì was enraged,
arrested and beheaded him.
The troops were terrified.
*Kǎoyì* (Investigation of Discrepancies) states: *Sùzōng Shílù* (Veritable Records of Emperor Sùzōng):
"In the eighth month,
on the day *rénwǔ*,
Zǐyí and Guāngbì both decisively defeated the rebels at Jiāshān in Chángshān Commandery.
Zǐyí and others, having received an imperial edict,
led 50,000 soldiers and horses from Héběi;
Zǐyí was appointed to a certain official position,
and Guāngbì to a certain official position."
*Fényáng Jiāchuán* (Family Biography of Fényáng) states:
"On the eighth day of the sixth month,
Shǐ Sīmíng was defeated below Jiāshān.
The Duke (Gōng) said to Guāngbì: 'The rebels are scattered,
and what remains of them is insignificant.
We can march southward without hindrance
to pacify the empire.'
In that month,
they departed from Héngyáng
and arrived at Chángshān.
The imperial envoy Xíng Yán'ēn arrived,
bearing an edict to take the Héběi route,
sweeping south.
Coincidentally, Gēshū Hàn was defeated,
Xuánzōng fled to Shǔ,
and Sùzōng went to Shuòfāng.
Upon hearing this, the Duke
alone led 50,000 elite troops and rushed to Sùzōng's temporary residence.
Xuánzōng issued an edict
for Sùzōng to succeed to the imperial throne;
Sùzōng received the edict with sobs,
unable to control his grief.
The Duke remonstrated, saying this and that,
and knelt to present the Son of Heaven's seal.
On the thirteenth day of the seventh month, Sùzōng ascended the imperial throne.
On the twenty-seventh day,
an imperial decree was issued: 'He (the Duke) may be appointed Wǔbù Shàngshū and Píngzhāngshì.'"
*Xìngshǔ Jì* (Record of the Flight to Shǔ) states:
"On the eleventh day of the sixth month,
Xuánzōng summoned Guō Zǐyí to the capital,
and Lǐ Guāngbì remained to defend Tàiyuán."
*Héluò Chūnqiū* (Annals of Hédōng and Luòyáng) states:
"On the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month,
the rebels were decisively defeated at Jiāshān.
On the twenty-sixth day,
the encampment was destroyed.
On the twenty-seventh day,
an imperial edict arrived at Héngyáng,
stating: 'Tóngguān has fallen,
the imperial carriage has gone to Jiànnán,
and the Crown Prince has also gone to Língwǔ.'
Consequently, the army withdrew and entered Jǐngxíngkǒu."
*Bīnzhì* (Records of Bīnzhoū) states:
"On the eighth day of the sixth month,
Shǐ Sīmíng was defeated at Jiāshān.
Coincidentally, Tóngguān fell,
and the two Dukes (Gōng) returned with their armies."
*Tánglì* (Tang Calendar) states:
"On the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month,
Zǐyí and Guāngbì were both granted the title of Píngzhāngshì.
An edict also ordered Zǐyí to gather his troops and proceed to Shuòfāng,
and Guāngbì to Tàiyuán."
*Héluò Chūnqiū* also states:
"When Guāngbì arrived at Tàiyuán,
he killed Wáng Chéng'ēn [sic for Wáng Chéngyè]
and firmly defended Jìnyáng."
The old annals (Jiùjì) are consistent with the Veritable Records (Shílù).
*Zǐyí Chuán* (Biography of Zǐyí) states:
"In the seventh month,
Sùzōng ascended the throne.
As the rebels occupied the two capitals,
he planned their recovery,
and issued an edict for Zǐyí to return with his army.
In the eighth month,
Zǐyí and Guāngbì led 50,000 infantry and cavalry from Héběi."
*Guāngbì Chuán* (Biography of Guāngbì) states:
"Sùzōng was organizing his forces in Língwǔ,
and sent the imperial envoy Liú Zhìdá to summon Guāngbì and Zǐyí to his temporary residence."
It also states:
"He led 5,000 soldiers from Jǐngchéng and Héjiān to Tàiyuán."
*Xuánzōng Shílù* (Veritable Records of Emperor Xuánzōng) states:
"In the sixth month,
on the day *rénwǔ*,
Guāngbì and Zǐyí defeated Shǐ Sīmíng at Jiāshān."
*Jiùjì* (Old Annals) states:
"In the sixth month,
the first day was *guǐwèi*.
On the day *gēngyín*,
Gēshū Hàn was defeated at Língbǎo.
On the same day,
Guāngbì defeated Shǐ Sīmíng at Jiāshān."
The biographies of Zǐyí and Guāngbì both state
"sixth month,"
without a specific day.
The various accounts regarding Lǐ and Guō's affairs differ thus.
According to the *Suìshuòlì* (Calendar of Year-Starts),
the first day of the sixth month was *guǐwèi*,
which is consistent with the *Jiùjì*.
The *Xuánzōng Shílù* stating *rénwǔ*
is an error.
The *Sùzōng Shílù* states
"eighth month, *rénwǔ*,"
which was the first day of the month (shuòrì).
Zǐyí and Guāngbì both decisively defeated the rebels at Jiāshān,
and led their soldiers and horses from Héběi,
being appointed to certain official positions.
Presumably, *rénwǔ* was the day of their appointment,
and the preceding events were mentioned in passing.
*Fényáng Jiāchuán* and *Bīnzhì* both state that Sīmíng was defeated on the eighth day of the sixth month,
which is consistent with the *Jiùjì*.
The *Jiāchuán* stating that he advised Sùzōng to ascend the throne
and presented the seal
is probably not true.
Gēshū Hàn was defeated on the eighth day of the sixth month,
and it would have taken at least ten days for the news to reach Héběi.
Sùzōng ascended the throne on the thirteenth day of the seventh month.
If they returned with their armies on the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month,
how could they have reached Língwǔ by the thirteenth day of the seventh month?
*Héluò Chūnqiū*,
stating the rebels were defeated on the twenty-fifth day,
is inconsistent with all other accounts
and is probably too late.
Now, based on the old *Xuánzōng Jì*, *Fényáng Jiāchuán*, *Bīnzhì*, and *Tánglì*,
all stating that Shǐ Sīmíng was defeated on the eighth day of the sixth month,
this should be followed.
*Xìngshǔ Jì*
stating that on the eleventh day
Xuánzōng summoned Zǐyí and Guāngbì,
this might be true.
However, both biographies state that Sùzōng summoned them.
It is probable that the two men were in Héběi,
heard that Tóngguān was undefended,
and had already gathered their armies and were on their way to face the crisis,
when they encountered Sùzōng's imperial envoy,
and consequently hastened to Língwǔ.
We now follow the old biographies.
*Tánglì* places the appointment of prime ministers on the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month,
*Fényáng Jiāchuán* on the twenty-seventh,
and *Sùzōng Shílù* on the first day of the eighth month.
The three accounts are not far apart.
*Zǐyí Chuán* states the eighth month,
and although it has no day,
it generally corresponds with the *Shílù*.
We now follow the *Shílù*.
According to the old biographies,
Guāngbì also went to Língwǔ.
It is suspected that all the Shuòfāng troops followed Sùzōng,
hence Guāngbì only led the Héběi troops to Tàiyuán.
*Héluò Chūnqiū*'s dates are particularly sparse,
and its statement about killing Wáng Chéng'ēn [sic for Wáng Chéngyè]
and firmly defending Jìnyáng
must be an error.
The Khagan of Huíhé and the Zānpǔ of Tǔbō successively sent envoys requesting to assist the nation in attacking the rebels.
They were feasted, rewarded, and sent away.
On the day *guǐwèi*,
the Former Emperor (Shànghuáng) issued an edict
pardoning the empire.
*Kǎoyì* states: *Xuánzōng Shílù* and *Jiùjì* both state
"eighth month, first day *guǐwèi*,"
while *Sùzōng Shílù*, *Tánglì*, *Jiùjì*, and *Chánglì* all state
"first day *rénwǔ*."
We now follow the latter.
At this time, the Former Emperor (Shànghuáng) did not yet know that the Crown Prince had ascended the throne in Língwǔ.
Hélán Jìnmíng, the Grand Administrator of Běihǎi, sent Lùshì Cānjūn Wǔ Qí to Shǔ to report on affairs.
Wǔ Qí spoke to the Former Emperor (Shànghuáng),
thinking:
"Now that we are employing military forces,
financial resources are urgent.
Most of the financial resources are produced in Jiāng and Huái.
I beg Your Majesty to grant me an office,
which can ensure the military does not lack supplies."
The Former Emperor (Shànghuáng) was pleased
and immediately appointed Wǔ Qí as Jiānchá Yùshǐ and Jiānghuái Zūyōngshǐ (Commissioner of Taxes and Labor for Jiāng and Huái).
In the eleventh year of Kāiyuán,
Yǔwén Róng was appointed Jùdāng Zūyōng Dìshuìshǐ (Commissioner for Administering Land Taxes and Labor),
which was the beginning of this Zūyōngshǐ office.
Afterwards, Wéi Jiān and Yáng Guózhōng successively held this position.
Shǐ Sīmíng again attacked Jiǔmén.
On the day *xīnmǎo*,
he captured it,
killing several thousand people;
he then led his troops east to besiege Gāochéng.
33 Lǐ Tíngwàng (李庭望) led over 20,000 Fān (蕃) and Hàn (漢) troops to attack Nínglíng (寧陵) and Xiāngyì (襄邑) to the east.
That night,
he set up camp thirty *lǐ* (里) from Yōngqiū (雍丘) city.
Zhāng Xún (張巡) led 3,000 light infantry to ambush them,
decisively defeating them,
killing and capturing more than half.
Tíngwàng (庭望) gathered his troops and fled under cover of night.
34 On *guǐsì* (癸巳),
an envoy from Língwǔ (靈武) arrived in Shǔ (蜀).
The enthronement on *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) in the seventh month
had occurred thirty days prior to this.
Only now did the envoy reach Shǔ (蜀).
"My son has responded to Heaven and followed the people;
what more do I have to worry about!"
On *dīngyǒu* (丁酉),
an edict was issued:
"From now on, imperial edicts shall be called *gào* (誥),
and memorials and petitions shall refer to the Supreme Emperor (太上皇).
All military and national affairs within the four seas
shall first await the Emperor's (皇帝) decision and approval,
then be reported to me;
once the Upper Capital (上京) is recovered,
I will no longer be involved in affairs."
On *jǐhài* (己亥),
the Supreme Emperor (上皇) appeared at the imperial court,
and ordered Wéi Jiànsu (韋見素), Fáng Guǎn (房琯), and Cuī Huàn (崔渙) to take the imperial seal and jade tablets to Língwǔ (靈武) to transfer the throne.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Sùzōng Shílù* (肅宗實錄) says:
"On *guǐwèi* (癸未),
a memorial from the Emperor (上) arrived in Shǔ (蜀)."
The *Xuánzōng Shílù* (玄宗實錄) says:
"On *guǐwèi* (癸未) the first day of the eighth month,
an amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
At that time, the Crown Prince (皇太子) had already reached Língwǔ (靈武),
and was enthroned on *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) in the seventh month.
The roads were treacherous,
and memorials and petitions had not yet arrived.
When this edict was issued,
a few days later,
the northern envoy arrived,
fully presenting the earnest pleas of the ministers and the Crown Prince's (太子) refusal to accept the throne.
On *xīnmǎo* (辛卯),
an edict was issued,
referring to him as the Supreme Emperor (太上皇).
On *gēngzǐ* (庚子),
Wéi Jiànsu (韋見素) and others were dispatched to convey the imperial tablets."
We follow the old records and the *Tánglì* (唐曆) here.
35 On *xīnchǒu* (辛丑),
Shǐ Sīmíng (史思明) captured Gǎochéng (藳城).
36 In the past,
whenever the Supreme Emperor (上皇) held grand banquets,
he would first arrange the Imperial Secretariat's (太常) court music, both seated and standing ensembles,
followed by military bands, Hu (胡) music, the Bureau of Music (教坊), and various popular entertainment and acrobatics from prefectures and counties.
The Imperial Secretariat's (太常) court music
was the music established by Zǔ Xiàosūn (祖孝孫) and Zhāng Wénshōu (張文收) in the early Táng (唐) dynasty.
Xuánzōng (玄宗) divided the music into two sections: standing performances below the hall,
called Lìbù Jì (立部伎);
and seated performances above the hall,
called Zuòbù Jì (坐部伎).
There were eight Lìbù (立部) pieces: 1. Ānwǔ (安舞);
2. Tàipíng Yuè (太平樂);
3. Pòzhèn Yuè (破陣樂);
4. Qìngshàn Yuè (慶善樂);
5. Dàdìng Yuè (大定樂);
6. Shàngyuán Yuè (上元樂);
7. Shèngshòu Yuè (聖壽樂);
8. Guāngshèng Yuè (光聖樂).
There were six Zuòbù (坐部) pieces: 1. Yàn Yuè (燕樂);
2. Chángshòu Yuè (長壽樂);
3. Tiānshòu Yuè (天授樂);
4. Niǎo Gē Wànsuì Yuè (鳥歌萬歲樂);
5. Lóngchí Yuè (龍池樂);
6. Xiǎo Pòzhèn Yuè (小破陣樂).
Drum and wind music (鼓吹)
were the *náogē* (鐃歌) and *gǔchuī* (鼓吹) pieces managed by the Director of the Drum and Wind Office (鼓吹署令).
Hu (胡) music
included the music of Qiūcí (龜茲), Shūlè (疏勒), Gāochāng (高昌), and Tiānzhú (天竺).
The Bureau of Music (教坊)
referred to the Inner Bureau of Music (內教坊) and the ceremonial music of the Liyuan (梨園).
Prefectures and counties (府縣)
referred to Jīngzhàofǔ (京兆府) and the two red counties, Cháng'ān (長安) and Wànnián (萬年).
Sànlè (散樂)
were miscellaneous performances.
Pú (酺) is pronounced *pú*.
Shānchē (山車) were
carriages on which elaborate structures were built,
decorated with colorful silk,
resembling mountains and forests.
Lùchuán (陸船) were
bamboo and wood bound together into the shape of a boat,
decorated with silk and colors,
with people arranged inside,
and carried on land.
During Xuánzōng's (玄宗) time,
Yáng Jìngshù (楊敬述), the Jìdùshǐ (節度使) of Héxī (河西), presented the *Níshang Yǔyī Qǔ* (霓裳羽衣曲) in twelve movements.
While all other compositions abruptly ended,
only the *Níshang Yǔyī Qǔ* (霓裳羽衣曲) ended with a gradually slowing tempo.
According to popular legend,
the Emperor (帝) had traveled to the Moon Palace,
where he saw hundreds of celestial maidens
dancing in a vast courtyard.
The Emperor (帝) memorized the music
and upon his return, composed the *Níshang Yǔyī Wǔ* (霓裳羽衣舞).
This is incorrect.
Horses were trained to hold a cup in their mouths and offer a toast (銜盃上壽);
The Emperor (帝) had a hundred horses,
lavishly adorned,
divided into left and right,
placed on triple-tiered platforms,
and they would dance dozens of *qīngbēi* (傾盃) pieces;
strong men would lift the platforms,
and the horses would remain motionless.
Liú Xù (劉昫) states: The Emperor (帝) personally entered the training ground,
brought out thirty *diémǎ* (蹀馬) horses,
and performed the *Qīngbēi Yuè Qǔ* (傾杯樂曲),
where the horses would toss their heads and wag their tails,
moving in rhythm.
He also set up three-tiered wooden beds,
rode the horses onto them,
and clapped and danced.
Sometimes they would bow,
sometimes they would dance.
Ān Lùshān (安祿山) saw this and was delighted.
After conquering Cháng'ān (長安),
he ordered the search and arrest of musicians,
the transportation of musical instruments and dance costumes,
and the driving of all the dancing horses, rhinoceroses, and elephants to Luòyáng (洛陽).
Your subject Guāng (光) says: Sages consider virtue as beauty,
and benevolence and righteousness as joy;
therefore, even with thatched huts and earthen steps,
coarse clothing and meager food,
they are not ashamed of their humility,
but rather fear excessive provisions that would burden the people and squander wealth.
Mínghuáng (明皇), relying on the era of peace,
did not consider future troubles.
He exhausted his ears and eyes with amusements,
and pushed the limits of vocal and instrumental skill,
believing that no emperor or wealthy person could surpass him,
wishing that none before him could reach his level,
and none after him could exceed it.
This was not merely for his own pleasure,
but also to show off to others.
How could he know that a great bandit was nearby,
already harboring covetous designs,
ultimately leading to the imperial carriage fleeing,
and the common people plunged into misery.
It is thus understood that for a ruler to display extravagance and luxury to others
is merely to invite great bandits.
37 Lùshān (祿山) hosted a banquet for his ministers at Níngbì Chí (凝碧池).
The *Táng Liùdiǎn* (唐六典) states: within the Imperial Gardens (禁苑) of Luòyáng (洛陽) were the Fāngshù (芳樹) and Jīngǔ (金谷) pavilions,
and the Níngbì (凝碧) pond.
The disciples of the Liyuan (梨園) often sighed and wept.
The Liyuan (梨園) disciples are mentioned in Volume 211, second year of Kāiyuán (開元).
The musician Léi Hǎiqīng (雷海清) could not bear his grief and indignation,
threw his instrument to the ground,
and wept bitterly facing west.
Lùshān (祿山) was enraged,
bound him in front of the Shìmǎ Diàn (試馬殿),
and dismembered him.
Lùshān (祿山) heard that many common people had stolen treasury goods during the chaos.
After taking Cháng'ān (長安),
he ordered a massive three-day search,
and all their private wealth was plundered.
He also ordered prefectures and counties to investigate and prosecute,
leaving no item, however small, untraced,
leading to widespread arrests and investigations,
endlessly implicating others.
The common people were greatly disturbed,
and increasingly yearned for the Táng (唐) dynasty.
After the Emperor left Mǎwéi and traveled north,
the common people spread rumors that the Crown Prince was gathering troops in the north to retake Cháng'ān.
The people of Cháng'ān longed for this day and night,
and sometimes they would startle each other, saying,
“The Crown Prince's grand army has arrived!”
Then they would all flee,
and the markets and streets would become empty.
The rebels, seeing dust rise from the north,
would invariably be startled and wish to flee.
In the Jīngjī region, heroes often killed rebel officials,
remotely responding to the loyalist army;
they were executed but would rise again,
succeeding each other without end,
and the rebels could not suppress them.
From the start, the Jīngjī, Fū, and Fáng regions, all the way to Qí and Lǒng, joined them.
By this time, everything beyond the West Gate was an enemy encampment.
The West Gate
refers to the west gate of Cháng'ān city.
To the south, they did not exit Wǔguān;
to the north, they did not pass Yúnyáng.
Yúnyáng county
belonged to Fēngyì during the Hàn dynasty,
to Běidì Commandery during the Later Wèi dynasty,
and to Jīngzhào from the Suí dynasty onward.
Wǔgōng county
belonged to Fúfēng during the Hàn and Jìn dynasties,
and to Jīngzhào during the Suí and Táng dynasties.
Zhī
means "to go."
Shàngjīn
was the territory of Chánglì county in Hànzhōng during the Hàn dynasty;
Liáng established Nánluò Prefecture there;
the Later Wèi changed its name to Shàng Prefecture;
the Suí abolished the prefecture and made it Shàngjīn county;
the Táng dynasty made it part of Shāng Prefecture.
These were all the achievements of Xuē Jǐngxiān.
38In the ninth month,
on the day Rénzǐ,
Shǐ Sīmíng besieged Zhàojùn.
On the day Bǐngchén,
he captured it;
he then besieged Chángshān.
After ten days,
the city fell,
and several thousand people were killed.
39Jìanníng Wáng Tán
was brave and decisive by nature,
possessing talent and strategy.
He accompanied the Emperor on his northward journey from Mǎwéi.
The troops were few and weak,
and they frequently encountered bandits;
Tán personally selected valiant men
to guard the Emperor in front and behind,
fighting bloody battles to protect him.
If the Emperor sometimes missed a meal,
Tán would weep uncontrollably,
and all in the army looked up to him.
The Emperor wished to make Tán the Generalissimo of the Imperial Forces (Tiānxià Bīngmǎ Yuánshuài)
and have him lead all generals in an eastern campaign.
Lǐ Bì said:

The poems Bǎn (板) and Dàng (蕩)
satirize the great decay of the Zhōu (周) dynasty,
and the lack of moral order and literary culture in the world.
Later generations often cite these two poems
to describe great chaos in the world.
Máo Shì Zhuàn (毛氏傳) says: Bǎn (板) means
'to go against.'
The Zhèng Yì (正義) says: The Shì Xùn (釋訓) states that
Bǎn (板) means
'perverse.'
Perversity means 'to go against and deviate,'
hence it means 'to go against.'
Zhèng (鄭) said: Dàng (蕩) means
'the appearance of laws and regulations being abolished and ruined.'
Those he (Guǎn) has employed are all of the superficial and ostentatious faction,
truly comparable to Wáng Yǎn (王衍)!
If Your Majesty employs him as chancellor,
I fear it will not be a blessing for the state.
Moreover, when Guǎn (琯) was in the southern court assisting the Former Emperor,
he arranged for Your Majesty and the various princes to separately control the military commissions of the various circuits.
This matter is found in the previous volume.
The Emperor was enthroned at Língwǔ (靈武)
and then moved to Péngyuán (彭原),
a region north of Guānshān (關山).
The Former Emperor was in Chéngdū (成都),
a region south of Guānshān (關山),
hence it was called the Southern Court.
He also placed his private partisans in various circuits,
entrusting them with great power.
This refers to Lǐ Xiàn (李峴), Lǐ Chéngshì (李承式), Dèng Jǐngshān (鄧景山), and others.
Thus, he did not lose his wealth and status;
how can this be the act of a loyal minister!"
From this, the Emperor distanced himself from him.
The Kǎo Yì (考異) states: The Táng Lì (唐曆) says:
"The Emperor, seeing Fáng Guǎn (房琯) had a great reputation,
humbled himself to await him
and treated him with extra courtesy.
Guǎn (琯) was sincere and outspoken,
also taking the world's affairs as his own responsibility,
doing everything he knew needed to be done.
Those he recommended were all renowned scholars of the time.
He detested evil too much,
and indeed had the bearing of a chancellor.
However, in terms of governing the world,
he was not skilled.
Later, he often directly contradicted the imperial will,
and though the Emperor tolerated him due to his high reputation,
he gradually could no longer accommodate him.
Guǎn (琯) then requested to lead an army as marshal,
and this was granted."
We follow the Shílù (實錄) here.
According to the Kǎo Yì (考異),
the Emperor's estrangement from Guǎn (琯)
was not solely due to Jìnmíng's (進明) words.
Fáng Guǎn (房琯) submitted a memorial,
requesting to personally lead troops to retake the two capitals;
the Emperor granted it,
adding the titles of Commander-in-Chief with Imperial Credentials, Pacification and Defense Commissioner of Xī Jīng (西京) and the Pú (蒲) and Zhāng (漳)
passes, and other such military commissioners.
Guǎn (琯) requested to select his own staff,
appointing Dèng Jǐngshān (鄧景山), Vice Censor-in-Chief, as his deputy,
Lǐ Yī (李揖), Minister of Revenue, as his Army Commander,
and Liú Zhì (劉秩), Remonstrance Official, as his Strategist.
After they had departed,
he further ordered Wáng Sīlǐ (王思禮), Minister of War, to act as his deputy.
Guǎn (琯) entrusted all military affairs to Lǐ Yī (李揖) and Liú Zhì (劉秩);
both were scholars
and unfamiliar with military matters.
Xián (閑) means
'skilled.'
"Though the rebels' Yèluòhé (曳落河) are many,
how can they stand against my Liú Zhì (劉秩)!"
Guǎn (琯) divided his forces into three armies: he had Brigadier General Yáng Xīwén (楊希文) lead the southern army,
entering via Yíshòu (宜壽);
in the first year of Tiānbǎo (天寶),
Zhōuzhì (盩厔) County was renamed Yíshòu (宜壽),
belonging to Fèngxiáng (鳳翔) Commandery.
[The middle army entered] via Wǔgōng (武功);
Lǐ Guāngjìn (李光進) led the northern army,
entering via Fèngtiān (奉天).
Guāngjìn (光進) was
Guāngbì's (光弼) younger brother.
He appointed Hèlánd Jìnmíng (賀蘭進明) as Military Commissioner of Hénán (河南).
see previous volume.
Qiáo (璬),
pronounced like "gōng" (公) and "liǎo" (了) combined.
He bowed at the horse's head,
but Qiáo (璬) did not stop him;
Yuán (圓) resented this.
Qiáo (璬) administered for two months,
and the officials and people found peace under him.
Yuán (圓) memorialized to dismiss Qiáo (璬),
sending him back to his private residence;
the capital had ten residences
to house princes who had not yet left the palace.
At this time in Chéngdū (成都),
the temporary palace served as the private residence.
Yuán (圓) replaced him.
Huán (峘) was
Xiàn's (峴) elder brother.
The Former Emperor then ordered Qiáo (璬) and Chén Wáng (陳王) Guī (珪) to go to the Emperor to convey greetings and comfort;
by this time,
they saw the Emperor at Péngyuán (彭原).
Yán Wáng (延王) Fēn (玢) followed the Former Emperor into Shǔ (蜀),
but failed to catch up with the imperial carriage;
the Former Emperor was angry
and wanted to execute him.
Hànzhōng Wáng (漢中王) Yǔ (瑀) saved him,
so Fēn (玢) was also ordered to go to the Emperor.
Línghú Cháo (令狐潮) and Wáng Fúdé (王福德) again led over ten thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Yōngqiū (雍丘).
Zhāng Xún (張巡) sallied forth to attack,
utterly defeating them and
beheading several thousand;
the rebels fled.
and on the Gēngzǐ (庚子) day,
they reached Biànqiáo (便橋).
On the Xīnchǒu (辛丑) day,
the two armies encountered the rebel general Ān Shǒuzhōng (安守忠) at Chéntāoxié (陳濤斜) in Xiányáng (咸陽).
Chéntāozé (陳濤澤) is
east of Xiányáng (咸陽) County,
and its path slopes out,
hence called Chéntāoxié (陳濤斜).
Moreover, Sòng Mǐnqíu's (宋敏求) Tuì Cháo Lù (退朝錄) quotes a Táng (唐) literati's collected works saying: Táng (唐) palace women's tombs were called gōngrén xié (宮人斜),
and in the four mid-months of the seasons,
envoys were sent to offer sacrifices there.
If so, then Chéntāoxié (陳濤斜),
might it also be named after a burial ground for palace women?
They used chariot warfare,
with two thousand ox-carts, flanked by cavalry and infantry;
the rebels, with the wind at their backs, raised a clamor,
terrifying all the oxen.
The rebels set fire to them,
causing great chaos among people and animals,
and over forty thousand government troops were killed or wounded,
with only several thousand surviving.
On the Guǐmǎo (癸卯) day,
Guǎn (琯) personally led the southern army into battle,
and was again defeated.
The southern army was
the Yíshòu (宜壽) army.
When the Emperor heard of Guǎn's (琯) defeat,
he was furious.
Lǐ Mì (李泌) interceded for him,
and the Emperor then pardoned him,
treating Guǎn (琯) as before.
He appointed Xuē Jǐngxiān (薛景仙) as Deputy Military Commissioner of Guānnèi (關內).
Chéngcǎi's (承寀) mission to the Uighurs is described in the ninth month of the previous volume.
Dūn (敦),
pronounced like "tú" (徒) and "mén" (門) combined.
They sent their noble official with Chéngcǎi (承寀) and Púgù Huái'ēn (僕固懷恩) to come together
and see the Emperor at Péngyuán (彭原).
The Emperor treated their envoy with great courtesy and sent him back,
bestowing upon the Uighur woman the title Princess Píjiā (毗伽).
10 Yǐn Zǐqí (尹子奇) besieged Héjiān (河間),
for over forty days without taking it.
Shǐ Sīmíng (史思明) led his troops to join him.
Yán Zhēnqīng (顏真卿) dispatched his general, Hé Lín (和琳), with twelve thousand men to relieve Héjiān (河間).
Sīmíng (思明) intercepted and attacked them,
capturing him,
and subsequently took Héjiān (河間).
He seized Lǐ Huàn (李奐) and sent him to Luòyáng (洛陽),
where he was killed.
They also captured Jǐngchéng (景城).
The Prefect, Lǐ Wěi (李暐), threw himself into the Zhànshuǐ (湛水) and died.
The Xīn Shū (新書) states he threw himself into the Hé (河) and died.
Lè'ān (樂安) immediately surrendered the entire commandery.
Lè'ān Jùn (樂安郡) [is]
Dìzhōu (棣州).
Once Jǐngchéng (景城) had fallen,
Lè'ān (樂安) was isolated and cut off,
and immediately surrendered to the rebels.
This was probably because the people's hearts were filled with fear,
and the city's lord could not defend it.
Before the troops even arrived,
Yán Zhēnqīng (顏真卿) knew his strength was insufficient to resist.
On the day Rén Yín (壬寅),
he abandoned the commandery and fled south across the Hé (河).
Sīmíng (思明) then used the Píngyuán (平原) troops to attack Qīnghé (清河) and Bópíng (博平),
taking them both.
Qīnghé Jùn (清河郡) [is]
Bèizhōu (貝州).
Bópíng Jùn (博平郡) [is]
Bózhōu (博州).
The Kǎo Yì (考異) says: The Hélòu Chūnqiū (河洛春秋) says:
"Cài Xīdé (蔡希德) led troops to attack Bèizhōu (貝州),
and Bèizhōu (貝州) fell.
He attacked Bózhōu (博州),
and after five days,
the city fell."
We now follow the Sùzōng Shílù (肅宗實錄).
Chéng'ēn (承恩)
surrendered,
personally guiding Sīmíng (思明) into the city,
and handing over the horses and storehouses,
three thousand horses and ten thousand troops.
Xìndū Jùn (信都郡) [is]
Jìzhōu (冀州).
Having surrendered,
Hù Jiāngfān (戶江翻) (the population scattered).
The history says Wū Chéng'ēn's (烏承恩) military strength was sufficient for defense.
Lùshān (祿山) restored his official titles and ranks.
The auxiliary general of Ráoyáng (饒陽), Zhāng Xìng (張興) of Shùlù (束鹿),
could lift a thousand jūn (鈞) (a heavy weight) and
was also intelligent and discerning.
The rebels attacked Ráoyáng (饒陽),
and for a full year could not take it.
Ráoyáng (饒陽) was attacked,
this event began in volume 217, during the Tiānbǎo (天寶) fourteenth year.
The Kǎo Yì (考異) says: This matter comes from the Hélòu Chūnqiū (河洛春秋).
It previously said
"the rebels attacked Shēnzhōu (深州),
for a month without taking it."
Later it said
"Xìng (興) fought and defended for a full year, and the city walls grew stronger."
The previous mention of "a month" refers to
this current siege;
the later mention of "a full year"
calculates the total duration of both earlier and later periods.
Sīmíng (思明) concentrated his forces to besiege it.
All external relief was cut off.
The Prefect, Lǐ Xì (李系), was in dire straits,
and threw himself into a fire and died.
The city then fell.
Sīmíng (思明) captured Xìng (興),
stood him before his horse,
and said:
"General, you are truly a brave man.
Are you willing to share wealth and honor with me?"
Xìng (興) said:
"Xìng (興)
is a loyal minister of Táng (唐),
and certainly has no reason to surrender.
Now I am but a person with a few moments left to live."
Zhāng Xìng (張興)'s will was set on certain death,
he said his life was measured in a brief span of time.
Sīmíng (思明) said:
"Try to speak."
Xìng (興) said:
"The sovereign treated Lùshān (祿山)
with kindness like a father to a son,
no other minister could compare.
Yet he did not repay this kindness,
but instead raised an army to point at the palace,
plunging the common people into misery.
How can a true man, unable to eliminate the凶逆 (ferocious rebels),
then turn north to become their subject!
I have a small plan;
can Your Excellency listen to it?
The reason Your Excellency follows the rebels
is for wealth and honor.
This is like a swallow nesting in a curtain."
Quoting Wú Jìzhá's (吳季札) words from the Zuǒ Zhuàn (左傳).
"Why not seize the opportunity to eliminate the rebels,
turn misfortune into blessing,
and long enjoy wealth and honor?
Would that not be splendid!"
Sīmíng (思明) became enraged,
ordered him to be tied to a wooden stake,
and sawn to death.
He cursed incessantly,
until he died.
As the history states,
among the twenty-four commanderies of Hébĕi (河北),
only Zhāng Xìng (張興) could be called a righteous scholar.
Each time the rebels captured a city,
all the clothing, treasures, and women in the city were plundered by them.
As for the men,
the strong ones were made to carry burdens,
while the weak, sick, old, and young were all playfully killed with knives and spears.
Lùshān (祿山) initially gave Sīmíng (思明) three thousand soldiers,
to pacify Hébĕi (河北).
By this time,
Hébĕi (河北) had all submitted to him.
According to history, Shǐ Sīmíng (史思明) was in a standoff with Guō (郭) and Lǐ (李) at Chángshān (常山) and Bólíng (博陵),
so Lùshān (祿山) must have repeatedly increased his troops.
It was when Guō (郭) and Lǐ (李) entered Jǐngxíng (井陘)
that Sīmíng (思明) was able to take Hébĕi (河北).
This is likely the rebel faction praising his talent, which the historian did not remove.
He garrisoned it with a mix of Hu (胡) soldiers.
Sīmíng (思明) returned to Bólíng (博陵).
Yǐn Zǐqí (尹子奇) led five thousand cavalry across the river,
raided Běihǎi (北海),
intending to move south to seize Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮).
It happened that the Huíhé Kèhán (回紇可汗) sent his minister Gēluózī (葛邏支) with troops to assist.
Luó (邏),
read Láng Zuǒ fān (郎佐翻).
Zǐqí (子奇) heard of this,
and hastily led his troops back.
11In the twelfth
month,
on the day Wù Wǔ (戊午),
the Huíhé (回紇) arrived at Dàihàn Gǔ (帶汗谷).
The Xīn Shū (新書) states
"Hūyán Gǔ (呼延谷)",
which is probably a phonetic shift.
Hàn (汗),
pronounced Hán (寒).
On the day Xīn Yǒu (辛酉),
they fought the Tóngluó (同羅) and rebel Hú (胡) at the north of Yúlín Hé (榆林河).
Yúlín Jùn (榆林郡) [is]
Shèngzhōu (勝州),
the great river runs north of it.
They beheaded thirty thousand and
captured ten thousand,
and the Héqū (河曲) area was all pacified.
Zǐyí (子儀) returned his army to Luòjiāo (洛交).
Luòjiāo Jùn (洛交郡) [was]
originally Fūzhōu Shàngjùn (鄜州上郡);
in the first year of Tiānbǎo (天寶) the commandery name was changed.
12The emperor ordered Cuī Huàn (崔渙) to convey his regards to Jiāngnán (江南),
and concurrently oversee elections.
13Lìnghú Cháo (令狐潮) led over ten thousand troops and encamped north of Yōngqiū (雍丘) city.
Zhāng Xún (張巡) ambushed and attacked them,
severely defeating them,
and the rebels then fled.
14 Yǒng Wáng Lín
lost his mother when he was young.
Lín
was the son of Guō Shùnyí,
who died early.
[Sùzōng] often held him while sleeping.
He followed the Retired Emperor into Shǔ.
The Retired Emperor ordered his sons to divide the superintendence of all the military governorships in the empire;
this matter is found in the seventh month of the previous volume.
[Sùzōng] thought this was not advisable;
the Retired Emperor did not listen.
Lín was given command of the military governorships of four circuits,
and was stationed in Jiānglíng.
At that time, the taxes and levies from the Jiāng and Huái regions were piled up like mountains in Jiānglíng.
Lín recruited tens of thousands of brave warriors,
spending vast sums daily.
Lín had grown up in the inner palace
and had no experience of human affairs.
His son, Xiāngchéng Wáng Yáng,
possessed courage and strength
and was fond of military matters.
With Xuē Liú and others as his strategists,
Lín believed that the empire was in great chaos,
and only the south was intact and wealthy.
As Lín held the armies of four circuits,
with a territory spanning several thousand *lǐ*,
he should occupy Jīnlíng.
Kāng said: Chǔ Wēiwáng buried gold to suppress the regal aura,
hence it was called Jīnlíng.
This would be like the precedents of the Eastern Jìn dynasty.
The Emperor heard of this
and issued an edict for Lín to return to Shǔ for an audience;
Lín did not comply.
Lǐ Xiàn, the Administrator of Jiānglíng, resigned due to illness and went to the imperial temporary residence.
Lín was about to raise troops;
Xiàn did not wish to be implicated in his calamity.
He happened to explain the advantages and disadvantages of Jiāngdōng
and also spoke of the certainty of Lín's defeat.
In the twelfth month,
a Military Commissioner of Huáinán was established,
governing twelve prefectures including Guǎnglíng,
with Gāo Shì appointed to the post.
A Military Commissioner of Huáinán Xīdào was established,
governing five prefectures including Rǔnán,
with Lái Tián appointed to the post.

The Huáinán Military Commissioner governed Yángzhōu Guǎnglíng Prefecture, Chǔzhōu Shānyáng Prefecture, Chúzhōu Quánjiāo Prefecture, Hézhōu Lìyáng Prefecture, Shòuzhōu Huáinán Prefecture, Lúzhōu Héféi Prefecture, Shūzhōu Tóng'ān Prefecture, Guāngzhōu Yìyáng Prefecture, Qízhōu Qíchūn Prefecture, Ānzhōu Ānlù Prefecture, Huángzhōu Qí'ān Prefecture, Shēnzhōu Yìyáng Prefecture, and MiǎNzhōu Hànyáng Prefecture,
totaling thirteen.
The Huáinán Xīdào Military Commissioner governed Càizhōu Rǔnán Prefecture, Zhèngzhōu Xíngyáng Prefecture, Xǔzhōu Yǐngchuān Prefecture, Guāngzhōu Yìyáng Prefecture, and Shēnzhōu Yìyáng Prefecture.
The above are all based on the "Table of Frontier Commands" in the *New History*.
However, Yìyáng and Yìyáng already belonged to the Huáinán Military Command;
this should be investigated.
"Table of Frontier Commands": In the second year of Zhìdé,
a Defender-General of Jiāngdōng was established,
with his seat in Hángzhōu.
This refers to the area east of the Zhèjiāng River.
Wéi Zhì's military command
probably referred to the Jiāngnán Dōngdào.
Its jurisdiction also included Zhèdōng and Zhèxī, as well as the prefectures of Shēng, Xuān, and Shè.
15 Ān Lùshān sent troops to attack Yǐngchuān.
The city had few soldiers
and no supplies.
The Prefect Xuē Yuàn and Administrator Páng Jiān resisted with all their strength.
Within a hundred *lǐ* around the city, all the houses and trees were destroyed.
After a year,
no relief troops arrived.
Lùshān sent Āshǐnà Chéngqìng to reinforce the attack.
They fought fiercely day and night for fifteen days.
The city fell,
and Yuàn and Jiān were captured and sent to Luòyáng.
Lùshān bound them on the ice by the Luò River,
and they froze to death.
16 The Emperor asked Lǐ Bì,
"Now that the enemy is so strong,
when can peace be restored?"
He replied,
"I observe that the rebels transport all the captured women, children, gold, and silk to Fányáng.
How can this indicate an ambition to dominate the four seas?
Now, only a few barbarian generals are in their service;
among the Chinese, only Gāo Shàng and a few others are with them;
the rest are all coerced followers.
In my estimation,
in no more than two years,
there will be no more rebels in the empire."
The Emperor said,
"Why?"
He replied,
"The rebel's most skilled generals are no more than Shǐ Sīmíng, Ān Shǒuzhōng, Tián Gānzhēn, Zhāng Zhōngzhì, Āshǐnà Chéngqì, and a few others.
If we now order Lǐ Guāngbì to advance from Tàiyuán through Jǐngxíng,
and Guō Zǐyí from Féngyì into Hédōng,
then Sīmíng and Zhōngzhì will not dare to leave Fányáng and Chángshān,
and Shǒuzhōng and Gānzhēn will not dare to leave Cháng'ān.
Thus, two armies will tie down their four generals,
leaving only Chéngqì with Lùshān.
I request that Your Majesty order Zǐyí not to capture Huáyīn,
so that the roads to the two capitals remain open.
Your Majesty, with the troops you have conscripted, should encamp at Fúfēng,
and with Zǐyí and Guāngbì, alternately attack them.
If they rescue the head, we strike the tail;
if they rescue the tail, we strike the head,
making the rebels travel thousands of *lǐ*,
exhausting them in their hurried movements.
We will always be rested while they are weary.
When the rebels arrive, we avoid their vanguard;
when they depart, we exploit their weakness.
We will not attack cities
or block roads.
Next spring, order Jiànníng to be the Grand Envoy of Fányáng Military Command,
and he should come out of Sāiběi.
With Guāngbì, they will form a pincer movement from north and south to take Fányáng.
Bì wishes Jiànníng to proceed from Líng and Xià, along with the fortresses of Fēng, Shèng, Yún, and Shuò,
directly strike Guī and Tán,
attacking Fányáng from the north.
Guāngbì will take Héng and Dìng from Tàiyuán,
attacking Fányáng from the south.
If the rebels retreat, they will have nowhere to go;
if they stay, they will find no peace.
Then, the main armies will converge from all sides and attack them;
they will certainly be captured."
If Sùzōng had adopted Bì's strategy,
how could Shǐ Sīmíng have again become a threat to Guān and Luò?
At that time, Zhāng Liángdì and Lǐ Fǔguó were in collusion,
and both disliked Bì.
Jiànníng Wáng Tán said to Bì,
"Sir, you recommended me to His Majesty,
allowing me to fulfill my duty as a subject and son.
I have no way to repay your kindness,
so please allow me to eliminate a danger for you."
Bì said,
"What is it?"
Tán spoke of Liángdì.
Bì said,
"This is not something a son should say.
I ask Your Highness to put it aside
and not consider it first."
Tán did not comply.
17 On the *Jiǎchén* day,
Yǒng Wáng Lín led his troops
on an eastern tour,
advancing down the Jiāng River.
His military display was very grand,
yet he had not revealed his intention to establish an independent regime.
Lǐ Xīyán, the Prefect of Wújùn and Investigating Envoy of Jiāngnán Dōnglù, sent a flat dispatch to Lín,
questioning his intention of leading troops eastward.
Lín was enraged
and divided his forces, sending his general Hún Wéimíng to attack Xīyán in Wújùn,
and Jì Guǎngchēn to attack Lǐ Chéngshì, the Administrator of Guǎnglíng and Investigating Envoy of Huáinán, in Guǎnglíng.
Lín advanced to Dāngtú.
Xīyán sent his generals Yuán Jǐngyào and Yán Jìngzhī, the Prefect of Dāntú, to lead troops to resist him.
The present-day Dāngtú
was originally the territory of Hàndānyáng County.
The Jìn dynasty separated Dānyáng and established Yúhú County.
Emperor Chéng, seeing that refugees from Jiāngběi Dāngtú County had settled in Yúhú,
renamed it Dāngtú County
and nominally established Huáinán Commandery there.
The Suí dynasty abolished Huáinán Commandery,
and the county belonged to Dānyáng Commandery.
The Táng dynasty belonged to Xuānchéng Commandery.
Dāntú County was subordinate to Rùnzhōu Dānyáng Commandery.
The Táng dynasty never named a commandery Dāntú.
"Tú"
should be
"Yáng".
Shǒu,
also pronounced "shì".
Lín attacked and beheaded Jìngzhī as a warning.
Jǐngyào and Chéngqì both surrendered to Lín,
causing a great tremor throughout Jiāng and Huái.
Gāo Shì, Lái Tián, and Wéi Zhì met in Ānlù,
formed an alliance, and swore to their troops to suppress him.
Wéi Zhì was probably en route to his post,
heard of the change midway,
and so met in Ānlù.
Jiàng,
also pronounced "gōng".
Tián,
pronounced "tián".
18 The King of Yútián, Shèng, heard that Ān Lùshān had revolted.
He ordered his brother, Yào, to manage state affairs
and personally led five thousand troops to provide aid.
The Emperor praised him
and appointed him Grandee Extraordinary and concurrently Palace Overseer.
19 Lìnghú Cháo and Lǐ Tíngwàng attacked Yōngqiū.
After several months, they had not taken it,
so they established a prefecture,
and built a city north of Yōngqiū
to cut off its provisions and aid.
The rebels often numbered tens of thousands,
while Zhāng Xún's forces were barely a thousand,
yet he won every battle.
Guó Wáng Jù, the Jìedùshǐ of Hénán, was encamped at Péngchéng
and appointed Xún as Vanguard Commander.
That month,
Lǔ, Dōngpíng, and Jìyīn fell to the rebels.
Péngchéng Jùn was
Xúzhōu.
Lǔ Jùn was
Yǎanzhōu.
Dōngpíng Jùn was
Yùnzhōu.
Jì
(pronounced Zǐ Lǐ). [The rebels] intended to attack Nínglíng
and cut off Xún's retreat.
Xún then evacuated Yōngqiū
and garrisoned Nínglíng to await them.
It was then that he first met Xǔ Yuǎn, the Tàishǒu of Suīyáng.
On that day,
Yáng Cháozōng arrived northwest of Nínglíng city.
Xún and Yuǎn fought him,
engaging in dozens of clashes day and night,
and thoroughly defeated him,
beheading over ten thousand enemies.
The corpses choked the Biàn River as they floated downstream,
and the rebels gathered their forces and fled by night.
An imperial edict appointed Xún as Hénán Jìedù Fùshǐ.
Xún, seeing that his officers and soldiers had performed meritorious service,
sent an envoy to Guó Wáng Jù to request blank credentials and gifts.
Jù only provided thirty blank credentials for Zhéchōng and Guǒyì ranks,
but no gifts.
Xún wrote a letter rebuking Jù,
but Jù did not respond.
20 That year,
the Běihǎi Jìedùshǐ was established,
governing Běihǎi and three other prefectures;
specifically Qīngzhōu's Běihǎi Jùn,
Mìzhōu's Gāomì Jùn,
Dēngzhōu's Dōngmóu Jùn,
and Láizhōu's Dōnglái Jùn.
[Another Jìedùshǐ] governed Shàngdǎng and two other prefectures;
specifically Lùzhōu's Shàngdǎng Jùn,
Zézhōu's Chángpíng Jùn,
and Qìnzhōu's Yángchéng Jùn.
[Another Jìedùshǐ] governed Shàngluò and three other prefectures.
Specifically Shāngzhōu's Shàngluò Jùn,
Jīnzhōu's Ānkāng Jùn,
and Qízhōu's Fèngxiáng Jùn.
The gazetteer of border garrisons only lists three prefectures;
the remaining one needs to be investigated.
East of Méi Xiàn in Fèngxiáng Jùn, there was originally Xīngpíng Jūn,
which was subsequently designated a Jíezhèn.
21 The Tǔbō captured the Stone Fortress, Hundred Valley Fortress, and Eagle's Nest Fortress, which belonged to the Wēiróng, Shénwēi, Dìngròng, Xuānwēi, Zhìshèng, Jīntiān, and Tiānchéng Armies.
Dìngròng Jūn was north of the Stone Fortress,
seven lǐ across a ravine.
One hundred and forty lǐ southwest of Kuòzhōu were Hóngjì Qiáo and Jīntiān Jūn;
eighty lǐ southeast of these was Hundred Valley Fortress.
Eighty lǐ west of Hézhōu, in Suǒgōng Chuān, was Tiānchéng Jūn;
over one hundred lǐ west of that was Eagle's Nest Fortress.
All were established in the thirteenth year of Tiānbǎo.
22 Initially,
Fàn Zhēnlóng, King of Línyì, was murdered by his minister Móhāmànduōgēdú,
who completely exterminated the Fàn clan.
According to the New Book,
this event occurred in the nineteenth year of Zhēnguān.
It is recorded here as an initiating event.
The Fàn clan had ruled Línyì for generations since the Jìn dynasty,
and was extinguished at this point.
The people of the kingdom enthroned the daughter of their King Tóulí as queen.
The queen could not govern the state,
so they instead enthroned Zhūgě Dì, Tóulí's cousin,
calling him Huán Wáng,
and married him to the queen.
The Second Year
(Dīngyǒu, 757)
1 Spring,
first month,
the Former Emperor issued an edict
appointing Lǐ Lín, Shàngshū of the Xiànbù, as Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
to oversee all central government offices,
and commanded Cuī Yuán to convey the edict to Péngyuán.
Lín
was a descendant of Yìzǔ.
Yìzǔ Guāng Huángdì,
whose taboo name was Tiānxī,
was the father of Tàizǔ.
Lín
was a descendant of Qǐdòu, Yìzǔ's second son.
2 Since Ān Lùshān raised his army,
his eyesight had gradually deteriorated,
and by this time he could no longer see anything.
He also suffered from carbuncles,
which made his temperament even more irritable and violent.
His attendants and servants,
if they displeased him even slightly,
were often flogged,
or sometimes killed.
After declaring himself emperor,
he remained secluded in the forbidden palace,
and his senior generals rarely saw him,
all communications being handled through Yán Zhuāng.
Although Zhuāng held high office and power,
he too was not spared from flogging.
The eunuch Lǐ Zhū'ér suffered particularly frequent floggings.
The Old Book states: Lǐ Zhū'ér
was from a Qìdān tribe.
He served Lùshān from his early teens
and was very intelligent and clever.
Lùshān, holding a blade, completely removed his genitals,
and several pints of blood spurted out.
He was on the verge of death,
but Lùshān applied ash and fire to the wound,
and he recovered after a full day.
Having become a eunuch,
he then gained Lùshān's trust.
Lùshān's favorite concubine, Duan Shì,
had a son, Qìng'ēn,
whom Lùshān intended to make his successor instead of Qìngxù.
Qìngxù constantly feared death,
not knowing what to do.
Zhuāng said to Qìngxù:
"There are things that must be done;
the time must not be missed."
Qìngxù replied:
"If you, Elder Brother, undertake something,
how dare I not respectfully follow?"
He also said to Zhū'ér:
"Have you counted the floggings you've received before and now?
If you don't accomplish this great deed,
your death is imminent!"
Zhū'ér also agreed.
Zhuāng and Qìngxù stood outside the tent with weapons at night.
Zhū'ér, holding a knife, went straight into the tent
and stabbed Lùshān in the abdomen.
Those around were terrified
and dared not move.
Lùshān felt for a knife by his pillow
but did not find it.
The Old Book states: Lùshān's eyes could not see,
and there was always a knife by his bed.
He said:
"It must be a family traitor."
Several pints of his intestines had already flowed out,
and he died.
They dug a hole several feet deep beneath the bed,
wrapped his corpse in felt, and buried it,
warning those in the palace not to reveal it.
On the morning of Yǐmǎo,
Zhuāng announced outside
that Lùshān was critically ill.
He established Jìn Wáng Qìngxù as crown prince,
who soon ascended the imperial throne,
honored Lùshān as Tàishàng Huáng,
and then announced his death.
Qìngxù was dim-witted and weak,
and his speech was disordered.
Zhuāng, fearing the multitude would not accept him,
kept him from seeing people.
Qìngxù spent his days indulging in wine for pleasure,
treated Zhuāng as an elder brother,
made him Yùshǐ Dàfū and Fèngyì Wáng,
and all matters, great or small,
were decided by him.
He generously bestowed official titles and ranks upon the generals to win their favor.
3 The Emperor calmly said to Lǐ Bì:
"Guǎngpíng has been the Yuánshuài for over a year,
now I want to appoint Jiànníng to command the entire expedition;
but I fear the power would be divided.
What about establishing Guǎngpíng as the Tàizǐ?"
What about it?"
He replied:
"Your subject has indeed spoken of this before.
Military matters are pressing,
and must be dealt with immediately;
as for family affairs,
we should wait for the Shànghuáng.
Otherwise,
how will later generations understand Your Majesty's intention in ascending the throne at Língwǔ?
There must be someone who wants to create a rift between your subject and Guǎngpíng;
your subject asks to speak to Guǎngpíng about it,
and Guǎngpíng will also certainly not dare to accept it."
Bì left,
and informed Guǎngpíng Wáng Chú,
who said:
"This gentleman deeply understands His Majesty's heart,
and wishes to subtly help him achieve his virtuous intention."
He then entered,
and firmly declined,
saying:
"Your Majesty has not yet served the Shànghuáng morning and evening,
how could your subject dare to accept the position of Tàizǐ!
I wish to wait for the Shànghuáng to return to the palace;
that would be my good fortune."
The Emperor rewarded and comforted him.
Lǐ Fǔguó was originally a Fēilóng Xiǎo'ér;
all attendants of the stables, pastures, Wǔfāng, and Imperial gardens
were called Xiǎo'ér.
Lǐ Fǔguó, as a eunuch slave, served as a Xiánjiù Xiǎo'ér.
He served in the Tàizǐ Gōng,
and the Emperor trusted him completely.
Fǔguó was outwardly respectful, cautious, and spoke little, but inwardly cunning and treacherous.
Seeing that Zhāng Liángdì was favored,
he secretly ingratiated himself with her,
and they acted in collusion.
Jiànníng Wáng Tán frequently denounced the crimes and evils of the two before the Emperor.
The two slandered him to the Emperor, saying:
"Tán resents not being made the Yuánshuài.
Because Tán was not appointed Yuánshuài,
(See previous volume, ninth month of previous year).
The Emperor was enraged,
and ordered Tán to commit suicide.
Kǎoyì says: The Yèhóu Jiāzhuàn states:
"Sùzōng traveled north from Mǎwéi,
arriving at Tóngguān Xiàn,
and ate at the home of the local gentry Lǐ Qiān.
Zhāng Liángdì claimed to have a stomach ache and could not ride a horse,
so she left her young daughter at Lǐ Qiān's home and departed.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he sent someone to fetch her.
The person sent to fetch her perhaps had other stories (rumors),
which Jiànníng heard and frequently spoke about."
Jiùzhuàn states:
"Tán repeatedly said that Liángdì was quite autocratic,
and colluded with Hùguó inside and outside (the court),
wanting to undermine the imperial heir."
It is unknown which is correct.
The Shílù and the Xīn Jiù Běnjì all have no record of the year and month of Tán's death.
The Lièzhuàn states:
"Tán died,
and in the winter of the following year,
Guǎngpíng Wáng recaptured the two capitals."
If so, then Tán died in the first year of Zhìdé.
According to the Yèhóu Jiāzhuàn:
"The Emperor calmly said: 'Guǎngpíng has been Yuánshuài for a year;
now I want to appoint Jiànníng as Yuánshuài.'"
This means that Tán was still alive in the second year of Zhìdé.
It also states:
"Dàizōng sent an envoy to Péngyuán to receive Tán's remains."
Therefore, it is placed here.
"Hùguó"
should be
"Fǔguó".
Chú planned to remove Fǔguó and Liángdì,
but Bì said:
"No,
Your Highness, have you not seen the disaster of Jiànníng?"
Chú said:
"I humbly worry about you, Sir."
Bì said:
"Bì has an agreement with the Emperor.
It means the Emperor promised Bì
that when the rebels are pacified, he would permit me to carry out my noble aspirations (to retreat to the mountains).
(See previous volume, ninth month of previous year).
Then I will leave and return to the mountains,
and will probably escape calamity."
Chú said:
"If you leave, Sir,
then Chú will be in even greater danger."
Bì said:
"Your Highness, just fulfill your filial duties as a son.
Liángdì is just a woman;
if Your Highness accommodates and complies with her,
what can she possibly do!"
I observe that the reason Dàizōng ultimately avoided the calamity of Empress Zhāng
was by using Lǐ Bì's words.
4 The Emperor said to Bì:
"Now Guō Zǐyí and Lǐ Guāngbì are already Chancellors.
If they recapture the two capitals
and pacify the realm,
then there will be no official positions to reward them with.
What should be done?"
He replied:
"In ancient times, official positions were for employing the capable,
and titles of nobility were for rewarding merit.
Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
although commanderies and counties were used to govern the people,
nevertheless, if there was merit, they were bestowed with land (symbolized by mao-tu),
to be passed down to their descendants.
This was true for the Zhōu and Suí dynasties as well.
In the early Táng,
as Guāndōng had not yet been fully secured,
all enfeoffments and titles were merely nominal,
and those who were granted actual enfeoffment
only received silk and cloth.
Under the Táng system: for those granted actual enfeoffment,
for every household, the annual tax of one able-bodied man was granted to them.
Tàizōng wanted to restore the ancient system,
but the high officials disagreed, and it was stopped.
(See volume 195, 13th year of Zhēnguàn).
Now, to reward merit with official positions has two harms:
if one is not talented, affairs will be ruined;
if one's power is too great, they will be difficult to control.
Therefore, meritorious officials who hold high offices
do not make long-term plans for their descendants,
but rather seize momentary power to seek personal gain,
stopping at nothing.
If Ān Lùshān had been granted a hundred-li state,
he would also have cherished it to pass on to his descendants,
and would not have rebelled.
As for the current plan,
when the realm is pacified,
nothing is better than to divide titles and land to reward meritorious officials.
Then, even a large state
would not exceed two or three hundred li,
comparable to a small commandery today.
How could it be difficult to control!
For subjects, this would be a benefit for ten thousand generations."
The Emperor said:
"Excellent!"
5 The Emperor heard that troops from Ānxī, Běitíng, and various countries including Báhannà and Dàshí had arrived at Liáng and Shàn.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
he visited Bǎodìng.
Bǎodìng Jùn
was originally Āndìng Jùn in Jīngzhōu;
its commandery name was changed last year.
Shàn.
6 On the Bǐngyín day,
5,000 Jiànnán troops led by Jiǎ Xiù and others plotted rebellion.
General Xí Yuánqìng and Línqióng Tàishǒu Liǔ Yì suppressed and executed them.
Línqióng Jùn
is Qióngzhōu.
Qióng.
7 Héxī Bīngmǎshǐ Gài Tínglún,
together with the Jiǔxìng Shānghú of Wǔwēi, Ān Ménwù and others, killed Jiédùshǐ Zhōu Bì,
and gathered 60,000 followers.
Within the great city of Wǔwēi,
there were seven small forts.
Wǔwēi Jùn,
which is Liángzhōu,
had its seat of government in Gūzāng.
The old city was built by the Xiōngnú,
seven li from north to south,
and three li from east to west.
When the Zhāng clan occupied Héxī,
they also built four more forts,
each measuring a thousand paces (along its walls/perimeter),
making five with the old city.
It is unknown who built the remaining two forts.
Two of the forts held firm in defense.
Zhīdù Pànguān Cuī Chēng and Zhōngshǐ Liú Rìxīn attacked them with troops from the two forts.
After seventeen days,
they pacified it.
8 Shǐ Sīmíng (史思明) led troops from Bólíng (博陵),
Cài Xīdè (蔡希德) from Tàiháng (太行),
Gāo Xiùyán (高秀巖) from Dàtóng (大同),
Niú Tíngjiè (牛廷介) from Fànyáng (范陽),
a total of 100,000 soldiers,
to attack Tàiyuán (太原).
All of Lǐ Guāngbì’s (李光弼) elite troops had been dispatched to Shuòfāng (朔方),
leaving fewer than ten thousand conscripts and hastily assembled militias.
Sīmíng (思明) believed that Tàiyuán (太原) could be taken easily,
and once captured,
he would press on to take Shuòfāng (朔方), Hé (河), and Lǒng (隴).
All the generals in Tàiyuán (太原) were afraid,
and discussed repairing the city walls to await the enemy.
Guāngbì (光弼) said:
"The city of Tàiyuán (太原) has a circumference of forty *lǐ*.
The capital city of Tàiyuán (太原),
with the Fén (汾) River on its left and the Jìn (晉) River on its right,
and Qiánqiū (潛丘) in the middle,
is four thousand three hundred twenty steps long,
two thousand one hundred twenty-two steps wide,
and has a circumference of fifteen thousand one hundred fifty-three steps.
The palace city is in the northwest of the capital city,
with a circumference of two thousand five hundred twenty steps.
East of the Fén (汾) is called the East City,
built in the eleventh year of Zhēnguān (貞觀) by Chief Clerk Lǐ Jī (李勣).
Between the two cities is called the Middle City,
built by Empress Wǔ (武后).
When it says the combined East City is forty *lǐ* in circumference,
it only refers to the capital city.
This is to trap ourselves before even seeing the enemy."
Thereupon, he led soldiers and civilians to dig moats outside the city to strengthen its defenses.
He made hundreds of thousands of mud bricks,
but the衆 (multitude) did not know their purpose;
when the rebels attacked the city from outside,
Guāngbì (光弼) used them to reinforce the ramparts from within,
patching any damage as it occurred.
Sīmíng (思明) sent men to obtain siege equipment from Shāndōng (山東),
protected by three thousand Hú (胡) soldiers,
when they reached Guǎngyáng (廣陽).
Guǎngyáng (廣陽)
was the Xiààngyì (上艾) county in the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
later renamed Shíài (石艾) county in the Later Hàn (後漢),
and changed its name in the first year of Tiānbǎo (天寶),
belonging to Tàiyuán (太原) Prefecture.
Jǐngxíng (井陘) Pass was to its east,
Wěizé (葦澤) Pass to its northeast,
both routes connecting to Shāndōng (山東).
He killed all of them.
Sīmíng (思明) besieged Tàiyuán (太原)
for over a month without success.
He then selected fierce and elite soldiers as skirmishers,
cautioning them:
"When I attack the north, you secretly advance to the south;
when I attack the east, you advance to the west.
If there's an opening, seize it."
However, Guāngbì's (光弼) military discipline was strict and orderly;
even in places not directly attacked by the rebels,
patrols never slackened,
so the rebels could not enter.
Guāngbì (光弼) offered rewards to recruit people in the army;
if anyone had a minor skill,
he would employ them,
making use of their abilities,
so that everyone's talent was utilized.
He found three money artisans from the Ānbiān (安邊) army,
skilled in tunneling.
The Ānbiān (安邊) army was stationed in Xīngtáng (興唐) county, Wèizhōu (蔚州).
Wèizhōu (蔚州) had a copper foundry,
and a money bureau,
hence there were money artisans.
At this time, he obtained three of them.
Guāngbì (光弼) sent men to pull the rebels' feet from the tunnel,
and executed them at the city wall.
From then on, the rebels always looked at the ground when moving.
The rebels built scaling ladders, assault ramps, and earthen mounds to attack the city.
Guāngbì (光弼) dug tunnels to counter them,
causing them to collapse as they neared the city.
When the rebels first pressed the city hard,
Guāngbì (光弼) built large cannons,
which fired huge stones,
killing more than twenty people with a single shot.
Two or three tenths of the rebels died,
so they retreated their camp to several tens of steps away,
to a place beyond the range of the cannons.
Pào (礮),
pronounced *pǐ mào* (匹貌).
Guāngbì (光弼) sent someone to feign an agreement with the rebels,
setting a date to surrender.
The rebels were delighted and
made no preparations.
Guāngbì (光弼) had tunnels dug all around the rebel camp,
propping them with wood.
On the appointed day,
Guāngbì (光弼) arrayed his troops on the city walls,
and sent a subordinate general with several thousand men to go out,
appearing to surrender.
All the rebels' eyes were fixed on them.
Suddenly, the ground in the camp collapsed,
killing over a thousand people.
The rebel forces were startled and chaotic,
and the government troops, beating drums and shouting, attacked them,
capturing and killing tens of thousands.
Coincidentally, Ān Lùshān (安祿山) died,
and Qìngxù (慶緒) ordered Sīmíng (思明) to return and guard Fànyáng (范陽),
leaving Cài Xīdè (蔡希德) and others to besiege Tàiyuán (太原).
9 Qìngxù (慶緒) appointed Yǐn Zǐqí (尹子奇) as the Prefect of Biànzhōu (汴州) and Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hénán (河南).
On the *jiǎxū* (甲戌) day,
Zǐqí (子奇) led 130,000 soldiers from Guī (歸), Tán (檀), Tóngluó (同羅), and Xī (奚) to attack Suīyáng (睢陽).
Guī (歸)
should be written as Guī (媯),
which is Guīzhōu (媯州).
Many unofficial histories by Táng (唐) people write Guī (歸) and Tán (檀),
which is likely a mistake.
Qù (趣),
pronounced *qī yù* (七喻).
Suī (睢),
pronounced *suī* (雖).
Xún (巡) led troops from Nínglíng (寧陵) into Suīyáng (睢陽).
It is forty-five *lǐ* from Nínglíng (寧陵) east to Suīyáng (睢陽).
Combined with Yuǎn's (遠) troops, there were six thousand eight hundred men.
The rebels advanced with all their forces to press the city.
Xún (巡) exhorted and encouraged his generals and soldiers,
fighting fiercely day and night,
sometimes engaging in twenty battles in a single day;
in sixteen days,
they captured over sixty rebel generals
and killed over twenty thousand soldiers,
which greatly boosted the morale of their forces.
Yuǎn (遠) said to Xún (巡):
"I am timid
and not skilled in military matters.
You possess both wisdom and courage.
I request to defend for you,
and you fight for me."
After this,
Yuǎn (遠) only managed military provisions
and repaired combat equipment,
handling communications from within,
while all fighting and strategy came from Xún (巡).
The rebels then fled that night.
10 Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) believed that Hédōng (河東) was situated between the two capitals,
and if Hédōng (河東) was secured, then the two capitals could be targeted.
Hédōng (河東) Commandery,
Púzhōu (蒲州).
Advancing from Hédōng (河東) to attack and capture Tóngguān (潼關)
would cut off the road to the two capitals,
after which they could be targeted.
On the *dīngchǒu* (丁丑) day,
Zǐyí (子儀) secretly sent men into Hédōng (河東)
to conspire with Táng (唐) officials who had fallen into rebel hands,
so that when the government troops arrived,
they would act as an internal support.
11 Initially,
Liú Zhèngchén (劉正臣), the Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of Pínglú (平盧), returned defeated from Fànyáng (范陽).
This event is mentioned in the previous volume, previous year.
Lùshān (祿山) appointed his partisan Xú Guīdào (徐歸道) as Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of Pínglú (平盧).
Xuánzhì (玄志) then, with the Pínglú (平盧) general Hóu Xīyì (侯希逸), attacked and killed him.
He also dispatched Cavalry Commissioner Dǒng Qín (董秦) to lead troops across the sea on reed rafts,
and together with General Tián Shéngōng (田神功), attacked Píngyuán (平原) and Lè'ān (樂安),
subduing them.
Lǐ Xiǎn (李銑), the Fánghé Zhāotǎoshǐ (防河招討使), by imperial decree, appointed Qín (秦) as the Prefect of Píngyuán (平原).
12 In the second month,
on the *wùzǐ* (戊子) day,
the Emperor arrived at Fèngxiáng (鳳翔).
13 Guō Zǐyí 郭子儀 led troops from Luòjiāo 洛交 to Qū Hédōng 趣河東.
Sòng Bái 宋白 said: Fūzhōu 鄜州 was Luòjiāo Jùn 洛交郡.
In the Hàn 漢 dynasty, it was the territory of Diāoyīn 雕陰 in Shàngjùn 上郡.
In the Later Wèi 後魏, it was Dōngqínzhōu 東秦州,
then changed to Běihuázhōu 北華州.
Emperor Fèi 廢帝 changed it to Fūzhōu 鄜州,
named after Fūzhì 鄜畤.
In the Suí 隋 dynasty, the seat of government was moved from Xìngchéng 杏城 to Wǔjiāochéng 五交城.
In the Tiānbǎo 天寶 era, it was changed to Luòjiāo Jùn 洛交郡,
with its seat in Luòjiāo Xiàn 洛交縣,
named after the confluence of the Luòshǔi 洛水.
Qù 趣,
pronounced Qī Yù (七喻).
Féngyì Jùn 馮翊郡
was Tóngzhōu 同州.
By taking both Pú 蒲 and Tóng 同,
he could control Hédōng 河東 and Hexī 河西,
and with a plan for Guān 關 and Shǎn 陝,

Jǐchǒu 己丑:
Hán Mǐn 韓旻, the Registrar of Hédōng 河東, and others revolted in Hédōng Chéng 河東城 and welcomed the imperial army.

Xīn Zhì 新志 says: The Hùcáo Sīhù Cānjūnshì 戶曹司戶參軍事 [Registrar of the Ministry of Revenue] was in charge of household registers, account books, travel permits, exemptions, miscellaneous corvée, arrears, free and unfree persons, fodder, inns, marriages, land disputes, and the commendation of filial piety and fraternity.
Cuī Gānyòu 崔乾祐 climbed over the city wall and escaped,
then mustered soldiers from north of the city to attack the city
and resist the imperial army.
Zǐyí 子儀 defeated them.
Gānyòu 乾祐 fled,
Zǐyí 子儀 pursued and attacked him,

and capturing five thousand people.
Gānyòu 乾祐 reached Ānyì 安邑.
Ānyì Xiàn 安邑縣
was then part of Jiězhōu 解州.
Half entered,
they closed the gates and attacked them,

Gānyòu 乾祐 had not yet entered,

Báijìng Lǐng 白逕嶺

14 After the Emperor reached Fèngxiáng 鳳翔 for ten days,

The ordinary and tribute levies from Jiāng-Huái 江淮 also arrived at Yángchuān 洋川 and Hànzhōng 漢中.
The ordinary and tribute levies from Jiāng-Huái 江淮
went up the Hàn 漢 river to Liáng-Yáng 梁洋.
Diào 調,
pronounced Tú Diào (徒弔).

Shǐ 使,
pronounced Shū Lì (疏吏).
Those who escaped from the rebels came day and night without ceasing.
After the Western army had rested and settled,
Lǐ Bì 李泌 requested to send the troops from Ānxī 安西 and Xīyù 西域,
as previously planned, to block the northeast,
and from Guī 歸 and Tán 檀, take Fányáng 范陽 from the south.
The Emperor said:
"Now the main forces have gathered,
and the ordinary levies have also arrived.
We should seize the momentum of our troops and strike at their heart,
but instead lead the army several thousand *lǐ* to the northeast
to first take Fányáng 范陽.
Is that not too circuitous?"
He replied:
"If we use these troops now to directly take the two capitals,
we will certainly succeed.
However, the rebels will surely regain strength,
and we will again be in distress.
This is not a strategy for lasting peace."
The Emperor asked:
"Why is that?"
He replied:
"Those we rely on now
are all border-guarding troops from the northwest and various Hu 胡 tribes.
They are accustomed to cold but fear heat.
If we take advantage of their fresh vigor
to attack Lùshān's 祿山 already aging army,
we will surely defeat them.
The spring air in the two capitals is already deep,
and the rebels will gather their remaining forces,
flee back to their lairs.
The land east of the passes is hot,
and the imperial army will certainly be exhausted and long to return home,
so they cannot be kept.
When the rebels rest their troops and feed their horses,
waiting for the imperial army to leave,
they will surely come south again.
In that case, the end of the war will not be in sight.
It would be better to use them first in the cold regions,
eliminate their lairs,
then the rebels will have nowhere to return,
and their roots will be forever severed."
The Emperor said:
"I am anxious about my parents and siblings,
I am eager to recover the two capitals
and welcome back the Supreme Emperor."
This meant he absolutely could not follow Bì's 泌 plan.

Shǐ 使,

Ān Shǒuzhōng 安守忠 and others raided Wǔgōng 武功.

Guī 媯,
pronounced Jū Wéi (居為).

He garrisoned Jǐngxíng Kǒu 井陘口.

18 Wùxū 戊戌:
Yǒng Wáng Lín 永王璘 was defeated and died,
and his partisans, such as Xuē Liú 薛鏐, were all executed.
At that time, Lǐ Chéngshì (李成式) and Lǐ Xiǎn (李銑), the Investigating Commissioner for Héběi (河北), combined their forces to attack Lín (璘).
Xiǎn's (銑) army numbered several thousand.
They encamped at Yángzǐ (揚子).
Yángzǐ (揚子)
was originally a garrison,
belonging to Jiāngdū (江都) county.
Emperor Gāozōng (高宗) abolished the garrison and established Yángzǐ (揚子) county,
which is now the seat of Zhēnzhōu (真州).
The Xīn Shū (新書) writes
“Péi Nìè Shù (裴卄[AS-FBEC]戍)”.
They encamped at Guābù (瓜步),
displaying a great many banners
arrayed along the bank of the river.
Lín (璘) and his son Yáng (瑒) climbed the city wall to observe them,
and only then showed signs of fear.
Jì Guǎngchēn (季廣琛) summoned his generals and said:
“We have followed the prince here.
Heaven's mandate has not been fulfilled,
and human plans have already collapsed.
It is better, before the armies clash,
to make an early decision about whether to stay or leave.
To die by the sword
would make us rebels forever.”
All the generals agreed.
Thereupon, Guǎngchēn (廣琛) fled with his direct subordinates to Guǎnglíng (廣陵),
and Hún Wéimíng (渾惟明) fled to Jiāngníng (江寧).
In that year, Shēngzhōu (昇州) Jiāngníng (江寧) Commandery was established from Dānyáng (丹陽) county's Jiāngníng (江寧).
The current seat of Zhēnzhōu (真州)
was Táng's (唐) Báishā (白沙) Garrison,
which at that time belonged to Guǎnglíng (廣陵) Commandery.
The source is unknown.
That evening,
the army north of the river displayed many torches,
their light reflecting in the water,
each appearing as two.
Lín's (璘) army also responded with fires.
Lín (璘) thought the government army had already crossed the river,
and so he hastily took his family and subordinates and secretly fled.
When morning came,
no one was seen to have crossed.
He then re-entered the city, gathered his troops,
prepared boats, and departed.
Chéngshì's (成式) general Zhào Kǎn (趙侃) and others crossed the river and reached Xīnfēng (新豐).
The Xīn Shū (新書) states
“Xīnfēnglíng (新豐陵)”.
Upon examining the location, it is within the Jìnlíng (晉陵) boundary,
likely the name of a Southern Dynasties imperial tomb.
Kǎn (侃) and others fought back,
shooting Yáng (瑒) in the shoulder,
and Lín's (璘) army consequently collapsed.
Lín (璘) and Xiānqí (仙琦) gathered the remaining forces
and fled south to Póyáng (鄱陽).
Póyáng (鄱陽) Commandery
is Ráozhōu (饒州).
Wishing to flee south to the Lǐngbiǎo (嶺表) region,
Huángfǔ Shēn (皇甫侁), the Investigating Commissioner of Jiāngxī (江西),
Jiāngxī (江西)
is the Jiāngnánxī (江南西) Circuit.
Historians simply call it Jiāngxī (江西).
Shēn (侁)
is pronounced suǒ zhēn.
captured him
and secretly killed him at a post station.
Yáng (瑒) also died in the chaos of battle.
Shēn (侁) sent men to escort Lín's (璘) family back to Shǔ (蜀).
The Emperor said:
“Since Shēn (侁) captured my brother alive,
why did he not send him to Shǔ (蜀) but instead secretly kill him?”
Consequently, Shēn (侁) was dismissed and not reappointed.
19 Gēngzǐ (庚子)
Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) dispatched his son Gàn (旰) and the Army Commander Lǐ Sháoguāng (李韶光), and General Wáng Zuò (王祚) to cross the river and attack Tóngguān (潼關).
They defeated it.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Shílù (實錄) states:
“In the third month,
Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Shuòfāng (朔方), greatly defeated the rebels at Tóngguān (潼關).”
The Fényáng (汾陽) family chronicle says:
“On the 28th day of the first month,
he sent his kinsman Huáiwén (懷文) to secretly recruit Guō Jùn (郭俊) and Gǒu Wénjùn (苟文俊) to enter Hédōng (河東),
to gather loyalists,
and to arrange with the main army a time to turn against the city.
The Duke then advanced his army out of Luòjiāo (洛交)
and divided his troops to take Féngyì (馮翊).
On the 11th day of the second month,
Guō Jùn (郭俊) and others, seeing the main army was about to arrive,
lit fires in the middle of the night,
and cut down a thousand elite soldiers from Yōu (幽) and Tán (檀).
Cuī Gānyòu (崔乾祐) subsequently escaped by climbing down a rope.
Gānyòu (乾祐) had previously stationed troops in an abandoned mansion north of the city,
and then used three thousand soldiers to attack the city,
while personally leading five thousand cavalry and infantry in ambush within the pass city.
The Duke sent Gàn (旰) and Púgù Huái'ēn (僕固懷恩) and others to attack them first.
The rebels were greatly defeated
and hastily burned the bridge;
our army trampled on it and was destroyed.
Gānyòu (乾祐) abandoned the pass city
and fled along Báijìnglǐng (白涇嶺),
whereupon Hédōng (河東) Commandery was recovered.”
The Old Biography of Zǐyí (子儀) says:
“In the third month of the second year,
Zǐyí (子儀) greatly defeated the rebels at Tóngguān (潼關),
and Cuī Gānyòu (崔乾祐) retreated to defend Pújīn (蒲津).

At that time, Zhào Fù (趙復), the magistrate of Yǒnglè (永樂), Hán Mín (韓旻), the Administrative Officer of Hédōng (河東), Xú Jiǒng (徐炅), the Commander of Troops, and Lǐ Zàngfēng (李藏鋒), a kinsman, had fallen into rebel hands
and were in Púzhōu (蒲州).
The four secretly conspired
to act as an internal應 (yìng) when the imperial army arrived.
When Zǐyí (子儀) attacked Púzhōu (蒲州),
Zhào Fù (趙復) and others cut down the rebels defending the parapets
and opened the gates to admit Zǐyí (子儀).
Gānyòu (乾祐) and several thousand of his subordinates fled north to Ānyì (安邑).
The common people feigned surrender.
When half of Gānyòu's (乾祐) troops had entered,
they lowered the portcullis and attacked them.
Gānyòu (乾祐) had not yet entered,
and thus managed to escape east.
Zǐyí (子儀) then recovered the Yǒngfēng (永豐) granary in Shǎnjùn (陝郡).
From then on, there were no more raids or plunder between Tóng (潼) and Shǎn (陝).”
The Tánglì (唐曆) says:
“Zǐyí (子儀) recovered Púzhōu (蒲州)
and then launched a surprise attack to take Tóngguān (潼關).”
However, Tóngguān (潼關) is south of Hédōng (河東) and Féngyì (馮翊).
If Hédōng (河東) and Féngyì (馮翊) were not yet defeated,
how could Tóngguān (潼關) be taken first?
Moreover, the Shílù (實錄) says:
“Hédōng (河東) was taken in the third month,”
but then records events from after the second month of Wùxū (戊戌),
which is inconsistent with the Old Biography.
Now we follow the Fényáng (汾陽) family chronicle and the Tánglì (唐曆).
Ān Qìngxù (安慶緒) dispatched troops to relieve Tóngguān (潼關).
Guō Gàn (郭旰) and others were greatly defeated,
with over ten thousand dead.
Lǐ Sháoguāng (李韶光) and Wáng Zuò (王祚) died in battle.
Púgù Huái'ēn (僕固懷恩) clung to his horse's head and floated across the Wèishǔi (渭水),
retreating to defend Hédōng (河東).
Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Fényáng (汾陽) family chronicle says:
“The pseudo-Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Guānxī (關西), Ān Shǒuzhōng (安守忠), arrived with his troops.
On the 29th,
the Duke ordered Púgù Huái'ēn (僕固懷恩) and Wáng Zhòngshēng (王仲昇) to deploy south of Yǒngfēng (永豐) granary.
By evening,
after a hundred battles,
ten thousand heads were taken.
Lǐ Sháoguāng (李韶光) and Wáng Zuò (王祚) fought to the death.”
The Tánglì (唐曆) says:
“Zǐyí (子儀) launched a surprise attack to take Tóngguān (潼關) and Tóngzhōu (同州),
massing troops at Tóngguān (潼關) to defend it.
The rebel general Lǐ Guīrén (李歸仁) came to relieve it.
Zǐyí (子儀) fought
and suffered a great defeat,
with over ten thousand dead,
retreating to defend Hédōng (河東).
Guīrén (歸仁) then attacked and captured Tóngzhōu (同州);
the刺shǐ (cìshǐ) Xiāo Bēn (蕭賁) died there,
and the entire city was massacred.”
The Old Biography of Púgù Huái'ēn (僕固懷恩) says:
“Huái'ēn (懷恩) retreated to the Wèishǔi (渭水),
without boats,
and crossed by clinging to horses.
Barely half survived,
fleeing back to Hédōng (河東).”
However, if Zǐyí (子儀) did not obtain Féngyì (馮翊), the western route would be impassable.
Later, he was ordered to go to Fèngxiáng (鳳翔),
passing through Féngyì (馮翊) on his way,
meaning Féngyì (馮翊) was not captured.
Tóngguān (潼關)
was the route between the two capitals,
which the rebels were bound to contest.
If Zǐyí (子儀) had not been defeated,
why would he abandon Tóngguān (潼關) and not defend it?
Now, we refer to the credible parts of various historical texts and preserve them.

The officers and soldiers were all inspired and requested to fight with fervor.

and capturing five thousand.

fourth month,

north to Fèngxiáng.

Almost all were killed or wounded,

Báiqú
was opened by Bái Gōng of Hàn,

is pronounced *jué*.
Chéng Dàchāng's *Yōnglù* contains an illustrated map of important Hàn and Táng locations: west of the Táng imperial city was the Cáogú,
which flowed south from the Fēng River,

bent and flowed east,
