then bent again and flowed north,
entering the Wèi River.
The Qīngqú was east of the Cáogú,
directly east of the old Dù Nánchéng of Qín,
which is north of Xiāngjī Sì.
The government army did not advance.
In the fifth month, on the *Guǐchǒu* day,
Shǒuzhōng feigned retreat,
and Zǐyí pursued him with his entire army.
The rebels formed a long snake formation with nine thousand swift cavalry.
When the government army attacked,
the head and tail formed two wings,
attacking the government army from both sides.
The government army suffered a great rout.
The judicial officer Hán Yè and the supervising commissioner Sūn Zhīgǔ were both captured by the rebels,
and all military supplies and equipment were abandoned.
Zǐyí retreated to secure Wǔgōng,
and a general alert was declared throughout the capital and provinces.
At this time, the imperial treasury had no reserves,
and the imperial court solely used official titles and ranks to reward merit.
When generals went on campaigns,
they were all given blank official patents,
ranging from *kāifǔ*, *tèjìn*, *lièqīng*, *dàjiàngjūn*, down to *zhōngláng* and *lángjiàng*,
allowing names to be filled in as needed.
Afterwards, it was even allowed to confer official titles and ranks by official letters,
some reaching the status of kings of different surnames.
"Official letters" refers to
giving a letter as proof before an official patent was issued.
It was used as a token of trust.
The distinction of official rank and position was no longer considered.
After the defeat at Qīngqú,
official titles and ranks were again used to gather scattered soldiers.
Fearing their disintegration
and that they might return to the rebels out of fear of punishment,
they were again rallied with official titles and ranks.
*Fù*
is pronounced *fúyòu*.
One *dàjiàngjūn* patent
could barely buy one drunken spree.
All who enlisted in the army
were entirely clothed in purple and gold,
to the extent that there were even servants of court officials dressed in purple and gold,
claiming to be high officials,
yet performing menial tasks.
The abuse of official honors
reached its extreme at this point.
In the 26th year, Fáng Guǎn was by nature lofty and simple.
At that time, the nation faced many difficulties,
but Guǎn often claimed illness and did not attend court,
not paying attention to his official duties.
Daily, he and his *shùzǐ* Liú Zhì, and *jiànyì dàfū* Lǐ Yī,
would engage in high-flown discussions on Buddhism and Taoism,
or listen to his retainer Dǒng Tínglán play the *qín*.
Tínglán used this to greatly exploit his influence.
An imperial censor impeached Tínglán for corruption.
On the *Dīngsì* day,
Guǎn was dismissed to become太子少師 (Tàizǐ Shàoshī).
Fáng Guǎn, having lost the battle, did not reflect on how to make amends.
His dismissal to a sinecure position
was still a light punishment.
The Emperor often had several hundred monks perform a *dàocháng* within the palace,
reciting Buddhist scriptures day and night.
Hào remonstrated, saying:
"An emperor should cultivate virtue to quell chaos and bring peace to the people.
I have never heard that feeding monks can achieve great peace!"
The Emperor agreed with him.
In the 27th year, on the *Gēngshēn* day,
the Retired Emperor posthumously honored the Emperor's mother, Yáng, as Yuánxiàn Empress.
[She was]
the great-granddaughter of Suí Nàyán Shì Dá.
In the early Jǐngyún era, she entered the Eastern Palace as a *liángyuán*, and was indeed the mother of the Emperor.
28 Shānnán Dōngdào Jiédùshǐ Lǔ Gǒng defended Nányáng.
The rebel generals Wǔ Lìngxún and Tián Chéngsì successively attacked it.
Food ran out in the city.
A single rat was worth several hundred coins.
Those who starved to death lay piled upon each other.
The Emperor sent the eunuch general Cáo Rìshēng to convey his solicitude.
Because he was a eunuch and a general,
he was therefore called a "eunuch general."
He could not enter.
Rìshēng requested to enter alone on horseback to deliver the imperial message,
but Xiāngyáng Tàishǒu Wèi Zhòngxī refused.
Just then, Yán Zhēnqīng arrived from Hébĕi.
In the fourth month of the summer of this year,
Yán Zhēnqīng had already traveled north from Jīng-Xiāng to Língwǔ.
Cáo Rìshēng's arrival at Xiāngyáng
was probably before the fourth month.
"General Cáo disregards myriad deaths to deliver the Emperor's command;
why obstruct him!
Even if he does not succeed,
it is merely the loss of one envoy;
if he succeeds,
then the hearts of the entire city will be firm."
Rìshēng went with ten cavalrymen.
The rebels feared their sharpness
and dared not approach.
The people in the city thought hope was lost,
but when they saw Rìshēng,
they were overjoyed.
Rìshēng again went to Xiāngyáng for them to obtain provisions,
and with a thousand men, transported the provisions into the city.
The rebels could not stop them.
Gǒng was besieged for a full year.
The rebels besieged Nányáng in the fifth month of the previous year,
and it had been a full year by now.
His strength was exhausted and he could no longer hold out.
On the night of Rénxū,
he opened the city gates and led the remaining several thousand soldiers to break through the siege,
fleeing to Xiāngyáng.
Chéngsì pursued him,
fighting for two days,
but could not defeat him and returned.
At that time, the rebels wanted to invade Jiāng and Hàn to the south;
thanks to Gǒng's holding of the crucial pass,
the south was preserved.
29 Sīkōng Guō Zǐyí went to the palace to request self-demotion,
due to the defeat at Qīngqú.
On Jiǎzǐ,
Zǐyí was appointed Zuǒ Púyè.
30 Yǐn Zǐqí increased his troops and besieged Suīyáng even more urgently.
Zhāng Xún, inside the city, beat drums and arranged his troops at night,
as if about to launch a sortie.
The rebels heard this
and remained on alert until dawn.
When it was light,
Xún then put his weapons away and stopped the drums.
The rebels used flying towers to overlook the city,
saw nothing,
and so doffed their armor to rest.
Xún, with general Nán Jìyún,
Nán
is a surname.
In the Zhōu dynasty there was Nán Zhòng,
and in the Lǔ state there was the Grand Master Nán Yí.
directly charged into the rebel camp,
reaching Zǐqí's standard.
Great chaos erupted in the camp,
and over fifty rebel generals were beheaded,
and over five thousand soldiers were killed.
Xún wanted to shoot Zǐqí but did not recognize him.
He then sharpened reeds into arrows;
those struck by them rejoiced,
thinking Xún had run out of arrows,
and ran to tell Zǐqí,
thus revealing his appearance.
He ordered Jìyún to shoot him,
hitting his left eye,
and nearly capturing him.
Zǐqí then withdrew his army and retreated.
31 In the sixth month,
Tián Gānzhēn besieged Ānyì.
At that time, the rebel general Yáng Wùqīn of Shǎnjùn secretly planned to return to the imperial side.
Hédōng Tàishǒu Mǎ Chéngguāng supported him with troops.
Wùqīn killed the generals in the city who did not agree with him,
and turned over the city to surrender.
Gānzhēn lifted the siege of Ānyì
and fled.
32 General Wáng Qùróng, due to a private grudge, killed the magistrate of his own county.
He deserved death.
Wáng Qùróng
was from Fùpíng.
On Rénchén,
an imperial edict pardoned him from death,
allowing him to serve in Shǎnjùn as a commoner.
At that time, Shǎnjùn had just been recovered,
located between the two capitals,
and was thus an area the rebels were bound to attack.
The Emperor wished to pardon Qùróng from death and make use of his abilities,
without considering the damage to national law.
Kǎoyì says: The Shílù states:
"served in Hé'dōng Chéngtiān Jūn."
According to the Jiǎ Zhì Jí,
it was Shǎnjùn.
We follow this now.
A memorial was submitted,
stating:
"Qùróng behaved atrociously,
killing the lord of his own county.
The Yì says: 'When a minister murders his lord,
or a son murders his father,
it is not due to a single morning or evening's cause,
but rather it has gradually accumulated.'
This is from the Wényán commentary to the Kūn Hexagram of the Yì.
It can be said to be the birth of gradual accumulation.
Some argue that Shǎnjùn has just been recovered,
and cannot be defended without such a man.
However, if there were no others like Qùróng,
how could others also hold out firmly?
If Your Majesty pardons someone from capital punishment for a single skill like using a cannonball,
then among the various armies, those with extraordinary skills
are truly numerous.
They will certainly rely on their abilities,
offending superiors wherever they are;
how then will you stop them!
If you only spare Qùróng but execute the others,
then the laws are inconsistent and you are enticing people to commit crimes.
Now, you cherish the talent of one Qùróng and do not kill him,
but you will surely kill ten men of Qùróng's talent;
will not the harm be even greater?
Indeed, Qùróng is a rebellious and disorderly person.
How can someone be rebellious here and orderly there,
disorderly in Fùpíng and orderly in Shǎnjùn,
disloyal to his county lord and not disloyal to the great lord?
I humbly hope that the enlightened ruler will preserve the long-term and the greater good,
then chaos and rebellion will be settled in no time."
The Emperor submitted this matter
and ordered the hundred officials to discuss it.
The Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince, Wéi Jiàn-sù (韋見素), and others deliberated,
holding that:
"Law is a great norm of Heaven and Earth;
even emperors dare not arbitrarily kill,
so
the power of your subjects is exceeding that of the sovereign.
If Qù-róng (去榮) kills a person but does not die,
then all those in the army with skills
will also consider themselves safe from worry
and act violently wherever they are.
How difficult
would that be for those who govern commanderies and counties!
Your Majesty is the lord of all under Heaven;
your love should be without distinction between close and distant.
What benefit is there
in gaining one Qù-róng (去榮) and losing the myriad common people!
According to the law,
killing one's local county magistrate
is listed among the Ten Abominations.
In the early Táng (唐) dynasty,
Fáng Xuán-líng (房玄齡), based on the Suí (隋) dynasty's laws,
established the articles of the Ten Abominations: First, plotting rebellion (móu fǎn 謀反);
second, plotting great sedition (móu dà nì 謀大逆);
third, plotting treason (móu pàn 謀叛);
fourth, plotting malevolent sedition (móu è nì 謀惡逆);
fifth, unfilial conduct (bù dào 不道);
sixth, great irreverence (dà bù jìng 大不敬);
seventh, unfilial piety (bù xiào 不孝);
eighth, discord (bù mù 不睦);
ninth, unrighteousness (bù yì 不義);
tenth, internal disorder (nèi luàn 內亂).
Those who commit the Ten Abominations
may not be granted leniency according to the usual deliberated requests.
The article concerning unrighteousness
is annotated as: referring to killing one's local prefect (fǔ zhǔ 府主), regional inspector (cì shǐ 刺史), or county magistrate (xiàn lìng 縣令);
seeing one's professional teacher (shòu yè shī 受業師);
a clerk or soldier killing an official of the fifth rank or higher in their own department;
and hearing of a husband's death but concealing it without mourning,
or engaging in music, casting off mourning clothes for joy, or remarrying.
If the king's law is not upheld,
human morality will be debased.
We, your subjects, having received the edict,
do not know what to follow.
A state is governed by law,
an army triumphs by law;
with kindness but no authority,
a benevolent mother cannot control her children.
Your Majesty generously supports the soldiers, yet gains little in every battle;
is this not due to a lack of law?
Although Shǎn-jùn (陝郡) is important now,
it is not as urgent as the law.
With law, the whole empire will have no worries and no unconquered foes,
let alone Shǎn-jùn (陝郡)!
Without law, Shǎn-jùn (陝郡) cannot be defended either;
what benefit is there in obtaining it?
Qù-róng (去榮) possesses a minor skill;
Shǎn-jùn (陝郡)'s survival does not depend on him;
the existence or non-existence of the king's law
determines the country's importance.
This is why we, your subjects, sincerely wish Your Majesty to uphold the laws of Zhēn-guān (貞觀)."
The emperor ultimately pardoned him.
He was Zēng (曾)'s son.
Jiǎ Zēng (賈曾) is found in two hundred ten volumes, Xiān-tiān (先天) first year.
33 Hé Tāo (何滔), a local strongman from Nán-chōng (南充), revolted,
seizing Yáng Qí-lǔ (楊齊魯), the defense commissioner of his commandery.
Nán-chōng-jùn (南充郡)
was Guǒ-zhōu (果州).
34 In autumn,
seventh month,
Hé-nán (河南) Military Commissioner Hè-lán Jìn-míng (賀蘭進明) captured Gāo-mì (高密) and Láng-yé (琅邪),
killing over twenty thousand rebels.
35 On the night of Wù-shēn (戊申),
the Shǔ-jùn (蜀郡) soldiers, Guō Qiān-rèn (郭千仞) and others, rebelled.
The Six Armies' Cavalry Commander Chén Xuán-lǐ (陳玄禮) and Jiàn-nán (劍南) Military Commissioner Lǐ Huán (李峘) suppressed and executed them.
36 On Rén-zǐ (壬子),
Yǐn Zǐ-qí (尹子奇) again conscripted tens of thousands of soldiers
and attacked Suí-yáng (睢陽).
Earlier,
Xǔ Yuǎn (許遠) had accumulated sixty thousand *shi* of grain in the city.
Guó (虢) Prince Jù (巨) gave half of it to Pú-yáng (濮陽) and Jì-yīn (濟陰) commanderies.
Yuǎn (遠) strongly objected
but could not prevent it.
Subsequently, Jì-yīn (濟陰), having received the grain,
rebelled with its city,
and by this time, Suí-yáng (睢陽) city had run out of food.
The officers and soldiers received one *hé* of rice per day,
mixed with tea leaves, paper, and tree bark for food.
Meanwhile, the rebels' supply lines were open,
and even when defeated, they could recruit again.
The Suí-yáng (睢陽) officers and soldiers, dying off, were not replenished;
aid from other armies failed to arrive,
and the soldiers dwindled to one thousand six hundred men,
all too hungry and sick to fight.
Thus, they were besieged by the rebels.
Zhāng Xún (張巡) then repaired defensive structures to resist them.
The rebels constructed cloud ladders (yún tī 雲梯),
their form like a half rainbow.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: They used large timbers as a base,
with six wheels underneath,
and a double-pronged frame above.
The frame held a retractable ladder,
each section one *zhàng* and two *chǐ* long,
with four rungs,
the rungs four *chǐ* apart.
They could slightly recoil and extend, retracting and advancing mutually,
moving through the clouds to observe the city.
There was also a city-scaling ladder (shàng chéng tī 上城梯),
with twin rollers at its head,
propped against the city wall to ascend,
called the "flying cloud ladder" (fēi yún tī 飛雲梯).
They pushed it to the city wall,
intending to climb in.
Xún (巡) had three holes dug in the city in advance.
When the ladder was about to reach,
from one hole, a large timber was extended,
with an iron hook at its end,
which hooked the ladder to prevent it from retreating.
From another hole, a timber was extended
to prop it, preventing it from advancing.
From the third hole, a timber was extended,
with an iron cage holding fire at its end,
to burn the ladder.
The ladder broke in the middle,
and all the soldiers on it were burned to death.
The rebels also used hook carts (gōu chē 鉤車) to hook the sheds and pavilions on the city wall.
Sheds and pavilions were
wooden structures built on the city wall,
extending four or five *chǐ* outside the city wall.
They had roofs
to shelter from wind and rain,
where warriors resided
to overlook and defend against external enemies.
People today call them 'enemy towers' (dí lóu 敵樓).
All of them collapsed.
Xún (巡) used large timbers,
with a chain at the end,
and a large ring at the end of the chain.
He pressed it onto the hook heads,
and used leather carts to pull them into the city,
where he cut off the hook heads and released the carts to go.
The rebels then built wooden donkeys (mù lǘ 木驢) to attack the city.
Xún (巡) melted liquid metal (jīn zhī 金汁) and poured it on them,
which immediately melted them.
The rebels then piled up earth bags and firewood to create a ramp (dèng dào 磴道) at the northwest corner of the city,
intending to scale the wall.
Xún (巡) did not directly contest them.
Every night,
he secretly threw pine kindling (sōng míng 松明) and dry straw (gān gǎo 乾藳) into it.
Pine kindling means
dried pine that retains its oil,
which can be lit for illumination.
*Gān* (乾) is pronounced *gān*.
The rebels did not notice this.
Taking advantage of this, he led his army out for a major battle,
and had men carry fire with the wind to burn the ramp.
The rebels could not save it.
After more than twenty days,
the fire finally extinguished.
Everything Xún (巡) did
was executed promptly and resourcefully as the occasion demanded.
The rebels admired his wisdom
and dared not attack again.
They then dug three layers of moats outside the city
and erected wooden palisades to guard against Xún (巡).
Xún (巡) also dug moats inside to resist them.
37 On Dīng-sì (丁巳),
the rebel general Ān Wǔ-chén (安武臣) attacked Shǎn-jùn (陝郡).
Yáng Wù-qīn (楊務欽) died in battle,
and the rebels then massacred Shǎn (陝).
With an isolated city situated between powerful enemies,
and no external relief,
it was inevitable that it would suffer massacre.
38 Cuī Huàn (崔渙) was in Jiāng-nán (江南) selecting and appointing officials,
and many unqualified persons were chosen.
In the eighth month,
Huàn (渙) was dismissed and made Grand Administrator of Yú-háng (餘杭).
Háng-zhōu (杭州)
was Yú-háng-jùn (餘杭郡).
The Suí (隋) dynasty established Háng-zhōu (杭州) in Yú-háng (餘杭) county.
Later, it moved its seat from Yú-háng (餘杭) to Qián-táng (錢唐),
and later still moved it to Liǔ-pǔ (柳浦),
which is the current prefectural city.
Yú-háng (餘杭)
was an ancient county in the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
The *Huán-yǔ Jì* (寰宇記) says: Yǔ (禹) disembarked here,
and thus it was named Yú-háng (餘杭).
39 Zhāng Hào (張鎬) was appointed concurrently as Military Commissioner and Investigating Commissioner of Hé-nán (河南) and other areas,
replacing Hè-lán Jìn-míng (賀蘭進明).
40 Xǔ Shūjì (許叔冀), the Grand Administrator of Língchāng (靈昌), was besieged by rebels.
No relief troops arrived, so
he led his troops and fled to Péngchéng (彭城).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Shílù (實錄) states:
"He led his troops south to Suīyáng Jùn (睢陽郡)."
According to the Zhāng Zhōngchéng Zhuàn (張中丞傳), it says:
"Xǔ Shūjì (許叔冀) was in Qiáo Jùn (譙郡)."
It is probable that Shūjì (叔冀) intended to go to Suīyáng (睢陽),
but was besieged by rebels,
and so fled to Péngchéng (彭城) and Qiáo Jùn (譙郡).
We now follow the Xīnjì (新紀).
41 Of the soldiers of Suīyáng (睢陽) who survived the deaths and injuries,
there were only six hundred men.
Zhāng Xún (張巡) and Xǔ Yuǎn (許遠) divided the city to defend it.
Xún (巡) defended the northeast,
and Yuǎn (遠) defended the southwest.
They shared tea leaves and paper with their soldiers,
and no longer descended from the city walls.
When rebel soldiers attacked the city,
Xún (巡) persuaded them with arguments of loyalty and rebellion,
and often they abandoned the rebels and surrendered,
fighting to the death for Xún (巡).
In total, there were over two hundred such men.
At this time,
Xǔ Shūjì (許叔冀) was in Qiáo Jùn (譙郡),
Shàng Héng (尚衡) was in Péngchéng (彭城),
and Hèlán Jìnmíng (賀蘭進明) was in Línhuái (臨淮).
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (漢武帝) established Línhuái Jùn (臨淮郡).
Later, Emperor Míng of Hàn (漢明帝) renamed it Xiàpī (下邳),
and its territory was vast.
During the Liáng (梁) dynasty, Gāopíng Jùn (高平郡) was established on the land of Hàn Xú Xiàn (漢徐縣).
In the eighteenth year of Kāihuáng (開皇) of the Suí (隋) dynasty,
the commandery was abolished and became Xúchéng Xiàn (徐城縣),
belonging to Sīzhōu (泗州) Xiàpī Jùn (下邳郡).
At that time, the seat of Sīzhōu (泗州) was Sùyù (宿預).
In the fourth year of Cháng'ān (長安) of Empress Wǔ (武后),
two villages from the southern border of Xúchéng (徐城) were carved out,
and Línhuái Xiàn (臨淮縣) was established at Shāshú (沙熟) and Huáikǒu (淮口).
In the twenty-third year of Kāiyuán (開元),
the seat of Sīzhōu (泗州) was moved to Línhuái (臨淮).
In the first year of Tiānbǎo (天寶),
it was renamed Línhuái Jùn (臨淮郡).
The city was shrinking day by day,
so Xún (巡) ordered Nán Jìyún (南霽雲) to lead thirty cavalrymen to break through the siege
and report the emergency to Línhuái (臨淮).
When Jìyún (霽雲) left the city,
tens of thousands of rebels blocked him.
Jìyún (霽雲) charged directly into their ranks,
riding and shooting right and left.
The rebels were scattered,
and only two cavalrymen were lost.
Upon arriving at Línhuái (臨淮),
he met Jìnmíng (進明).
Jìnmíng (進明) said:
"Today, the fate of Suīyáng (睢陽) is unknown;
what good would it do for troops to leave?"
Jìyún (霽雲) replied:
"If Suīyáng (睢陽) falls,
Jìyún (霽雲) begs to die to atone to the Grandee.
Moreover, once Suīyáng (睢陽) is captured,
Línhuái (臨淮) will be next.
It is like skin and hair depending on each other;
how can we not save it?"
Jìnmíng (進明) admired Jìyún's (霽雲) bravery,
but did not heed his words.
He forcibly detained him,
prepared food and entertainment,
and invited Jìyún (霽雲) to sit.
Jìyún (霽雲) was filled with righteous indignation,
weeping as he spoke:
"Jìyún (霽雲) came here,
and the people of Suīyáng (睢陽) have not eaten for over a month!
Even if Jìyún (霽雲) wanted to eat alone,
he could not swallow it.
Grandee, sitting here with a strong army,
watching Suīyáng (睢陽) fall,
without any intention to share the disaster and relieve the suffering,
how can this be the act of a loyal subject or a righteous gentleman?"
Thereupon, he bit off one of his fingers to show Jìnmíng (進明).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: Hán Yù (韓愈), in his postscript to the Zhāng Zhōngchéng Zhuàn (張中丞傳), says:
"He then drew his saber and cut off a finger,
blood profusely dripping,
to show Hèlán (賀蘭).
Everyone present was greatly astonished,
all deeply moved,
and wept for Yún (雲)."
According to Liǔ Zōngyuán's (柳宗元) Jìyún Bēi (霽雲碑), it says:
"He bit his own finger and said: 'This is enough to eat.'"
We now follow the old biography.
"Since Jìyún (霽雲) cannot convey the wishes of his commander,
I request to leave a finger to show my trustworthiness upon returning to report."
Many in the assembly wept for him.
Jìyún (霽雲), realizing that Jìnmíng (進明) had no intention of dispatching troops,
thereupon left.
Upon reaching Nínglíng (寧陵),
he, together with Lián Tǎn (廉坦), the City Commandant, led three thousand infantry and cavalry.
Zhāng Xún (張巡) entered Suīyáng (睢陽) from Nínglíng (寧陵),
likely having Lián Tǎn (廉坦) defend Nínglíng Chéng (寧陵城).
City Commandant (城使)
was a position appointed by Xún (巡).
The character 'jiāng' (將)
is pronounced 'liàng' (亮).
The character 'shǐ' (使)
is pronounced 'shū lì' (疏吏).
On the night of Wùshēn (戊申),
they braved the siege,
fighting and advancing,
until they reached the city walls.
A great battle ensued,
destroying the rebel camp.
Besides those killed or wounded,
only a thousand men managed to enter the city.
The officials and officers within the city, knowing that no relief would come,
all wept bitterly.
The rebels, knowing that reinforcements were cut off,
tightened their siege even more.
Initially,
Fáng Guǎn (房琯) was chancellor,
and he disliked Hèlán Jìnmíng (賀蘭進明).
This matter was mentioned in the tenth month of the previous year.
The character 'è' (惡)
is pronounced 'wū lù' (烏路).
He appointed Xǔ Shūjì (許叔冀) as Jìnmíng's (進明) Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ (都知兵馬使),
both also concurrently holding the title of Yùshǐ Dàfū (御史大夫).
Shūjì (叔冀), relying on the elite troops under his command,
and holding a rank equal to Jìnmíng (進明),
did not submit to his authority.
Therefore, Jìnmíng (進明) dared not divide his troops,
not only because he envied Xún (巡) and Yuǎn's (遠) achievements,
but also because he feared being attacked by Shūjì (叔冀).
History says that Fáng Guǎn (房琯), out of personal resentment towards Jìnmíng (進明),
used Xǔ Shūjì (許叔冀) to restrain him,
preventing him from dividing his troops to rescue Xún (巡) and Yuǎn (遠).
However, with Jìnmíng's (進明) talent,
even if he had dispatched troops,
he might not necessarily have been able to achieve victory.
42 On Wùchén (戊辰),
the Emperor rewarded and entertained the generals,
and sent them to attack Cháng'ān (長安).
He said to Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀):
"Whether this enterprise succeeds or fails
depends on this expedition!"
He replied:
"If this expedition is not victorious,
your subject will surely die for it."
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Fényáng Jiāchuán (汾陽家傳) states:
"On the twenty-third day of the intercalary eighth month,
Sùzōng (肅宗) presented the axe to Dàizōng (代宗),
instructing him to execute the chief villain,
and decreed that the Duke (Guō Zǐyí) be Deputy Commander-in-chief.
On the twenty-third,
they departed from Fèngxiáng (鳳翔)."
The Shílù (實錄) states:
"On Dīnghài (丁亥) in the ninth month,
the Marshal led one hundred and fifty thousand troops and took leave to depart."
It also says:
"On Wùzǐ (戊子),
the Uighur Yèhù (葉護) arrived at Fúfēng (扶風)."
It is likely that Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) first set out on the twenty-third day of the intercalary month to encamp at Fúfēng (扶風),
and Guǎngpíng (廣平) only departed on the twelfth day of the ninth month.
43 On Xīnwèi (辛未),
Yùshǐ Dàfū Cuī Guāngyuǎn (御史大夫崔光遠) defeated the rebels at Luògǔ (駱谷).
Guāngyuǎn's (光遠) Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬) Wáng Bólún (王伯倫) and Pànguān (判官) Lǐ Chūn (李椿) led two thousand men to attack Zhōngwèi Qiáo (中渭橋),
killing a thousand rebel bridge guards.
They pressed their advantage to Yuànmén (苑門).
This was the Yuànmén (苑門) of Cháng'ān (長安).
They fled back
and encountered them north of the park.
In the ensuing battle,
Bólún (伯倫) was killed, and Chūn (椿) was captured and sent to Luòyáng (洛陽).
However, from then on, the rebels no longer encamped at Wǔgōng (武功).
44 The rebels repeatedly attacked Shàngdǎng (上黨),
but were always defeated by Jiédùshǐ Chéng Qiānlǐ (節度使程千里).
Cài Xīdé (蔡希德) again led his troops to besiege Shàngdǎng (上黨).
Shàngdǎng Jùn (上黨郡)
was Lùzhōu (潞州).
This set the stage for Chéng Qiānlǐ's (程千里) capture.
Collated by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖) and re-proofread by Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
Compiled by Imperial Edict
Hòuxué Tiāntái (後學天台)
Second Year of Zhìdé (至德)
(Dīngyǒu, 757)
Mì said:
"The reason Your servant speaks this
is not to fault the past,
but rather to make Your Majesty cautious about the future.
Formerly, Empress Tiānhòu had four sons.
The eldest was Crown Prince Hóng.
When Empress Tiānhòu was planning to assume imperial authority,
she detested his intelligence
and poisoned him to death.
(See volume 202, Gāozōng, Shàngyuán 2nd year.)
Xián became inwardly anxious and fearful,
and composed the 'Yellow Platform Melon Song,'
hoping to enlighten Empress Tiānhòu.
Empress Tiānhòu did not listen,
and Xián eventually died in Qiánzhōng.
(For Xián's deposition, see volume 202, Yǒnglóng 1st year;
for his death, see volume 203, Wǔ Hòu, Guāngzhái 1st year.)
Zú,
read Xù.
Qián,
read Qín.
'The melons ripen, the seeds fall apart: one pluck makes the melon good,
a second pluck makes the melon scarce,
a third pluck is still acceptable,
but with a fourth pluck, you return home with only the vine!'
Now Your Majesty has already made one pluck.
Be careful not to pluck again!"
The Emperor was startled and said:
"How can this be!
You record these words,
and I shall write them on my sash."
He replied:
"Your Majesty only needs to remember it in your heart,
why must it be displayed externally!"
At this time, Guǎngpíng Wáng had performed great deeds,
and Liángdì was jealous of him.
She secretly instigated rumors,
which is why Mì brought this up.
Guō Zǐyí led Fān and Hàn troops to pursue the rebels to Tóngguān,
beheaded five thousand,
and captured the two commanderies of Huáyīn and Hóngnóng.
Over a hundred captives were presented from Guāndōng,
and an imperial edict ordered them all to be executed.
The Supervising Censor Lǐ Miǎn spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"Now that the chief villain has not yet been eliminated,
half the empire has been defiled by the rebels.
Hearing of Your Majesty's ascension,
they all wish to cleanse their hearts to submit to the sacred transformation.
If we execute them all now,
it is to drive them to follow the rebels."
The Emperor immediately ordered them to be pardoned.
In winter,
10th month,
on the Dīngwèi day,
Tán
Tíngyáo arrived in Shǔ.
On the Rénzǐ day,
Xīngpíng Jūn reported: they defeated the rebels at Wǔguān
and captured Shàngluò Jùn.
At that time, Wáng Nándé commanded the Xīngpíng Jūn.
The Tǔbō captured Xīpíng.
Xīpíng Jùn
is Shànzhōu.
Yǐn Zǐqí had besieged Suīyáng for a long time.
Food in the city was exhausted,
and there was a discussion to abandon the city and flee east.
Zhāng Xún and Xǔ Yuǎn deliberated,
considering:
"Suīyáng is the safeguard of Jiāng and Huái.
If we abandon it and leave,
the rebels will surely take advantage of their victory to advance rapidly,
which means there will be no Jiāng and Huái."
(Kǎoyì says: Tang people all attributed the preservation of Jiāng and Huái to Xún and Yuǎn's merit.
According to this, although Suīyáng was on the path to Jiāng and Huái,
with the city already under siege,
if the rebels wanted to take Jiāng and Huái,
they could bypass it.
How could Suīyáng block them?
It is probably because Xún was skilled in military strategy,
and the rebels feared Xún as a future threat,
so they dared not cross south without destroying Xún.)
"Fleeing will certainly not succeed."
"In ancient times, the feudal lords of the Warring States
still rescued and assisted each other."
(Refers to the states in the Spring and Autumn period, where allies would rescue and assist each other in times of urgency.)
"All the commanders,"
(refers to Zhāng Hào, Shàng Héng, Xǔ Shūjì, etc.)
"Shuài,"
(read Suǒlèi).
"When tea and paper were exhausted,
they then ate horses;
when horses were exhausted, they netted sparrows and dug for rats;
when sparrows and rats were also exhausted,
Xún brought out his beloved concubine,
killed her, and fed her to his soldiers.
Yuǎn also killed his slave;
then they gathered the women in the city and ate them,
followed by old and weak men.
People knew they would surely die,
but none rebelled.
Only about four hundred people remained."
On the Guǐchǒu day,
the rebels scaled the city walls.
The generals and soldiers were ill
and unable to fight.
Xún bowed twice to the west and said:
"Your servant's strength is exhausted,
and I cannot preserve the city.
Since I cannot repay Your Majesty in life,
in death I shall become a vengeful ghost to kill the rebels!"
(Ghosts without a place to return to become malevolent spirits.)
Xún and Yuǎn were both captured.
Yǐn Zǐqí asked Xún:
"I heard that in every battle your eye corners tore and your teeth shattered.
Why is that?"
Xún said:
"My ambition is to swallow the traitorous rebels,
but my strength is simply insufficient."
Zǐqí used a knife to pry open his mouth and look,
and only three or four teeth remained.
Zǐqí admired his actions
and wanted to spare his life.
His followers said:
"He is a man who upholds integrity;
he will never be used by us.
Moreover, he has won the hearts of the soldiers;
keeping him alive
will lead to future trouble."
So, Nán Jìyún, Léi Wànchūn, and thirty-six others were all executed together.
(Kǎoyì says: The New Biography states:
"When Guó Wáng Jù fled to Lín Huái,
Xún had a sister who married into the Lù family.
She intercepted Jù, advising him not to go,
but he did not heed her.
She was given a hundred pieces of silk,
but refused them.
She mended and sewed for Xún among the ranks,
and in the army, she was called 'Aunt Lù.'
She was killed before Xún."
However, Jù was in Péngchéng.
If he fled to Lín Huái,
and Sister Lù was in Suīyáng city,
how could she intercept him?
Therefore, this is not adopted.)
Their expressions did not change;
they were composed as usual.
Xǔ Yuǎn was taken alive to Luòyáng.
When Xún first defended Suīyáng,
his soldiers numbered barely ten thousand,
and the residents in the city were also several tens of thousands.
Xún met each one and asked their names;
thereafter, there was no one he did not recognize.
In total, there were over four hundred major and minor battles,
in which twelve thousand enemy soldiers were killed.
Xún's method of deploying troops did not follow ancient practices.
When teaching formations,
he ordered each commander to teach according to their own understanding.
"Běnjiàng"
refers to the commander of one's own unit.
"Chén"
is read as zhèn.
Xún said:
"Now when fighting the Húlǔ,
they gather like clouds and scatter like birds,
their tactics are inconstant.
Within a few steps,
the situation can change.
Responding quickly to circumstances
happens in an instant,
and to always consult the commanding general
means the opportunity is missed;
this is not understanding the变化 of military tactics.
Therefore, I make soldiers understand the general's intent,
and generals understand the soldiers' feelings.
When dispatched, they advance
like the hand directing the fingers.
When soldiers and generals are accustomed to each other,
each person fights for themselves,
isn't this acceptable!"
Since raising the army,
all weapons, armor, and equipment were taken from the enemy,
never self-made.
In every battle,
if the officers and soldiers retreated or scattered,
Xún would stand at the battle site
and say to the officers and soldiers:
"I will not leave here;
you must return for me and fight to the death."
None of the officers and soldiers dared not return,
and they fought to the death,
ultimately defeating the enemy.
He also treated people with sincerity,
with no suspicion or concealment;
facing the enemy, he adapted to changes,
producing endless unexpected strategies;
his orders were clear,
rewards and punishments were trustworthy,
and he shared the hardships of heat and cold with the populace.
Therefore, his subordinates vied to exert their utmost effort.
Zhāng Hào heard that Suīyáng was under urgent siege,
and advanced rapidly, doubling his pace.
Zhāng Hào replaced Hèlán Jìnmíng,
see August in the upper volume.
According to the Xīnshū Fāngzhèn Biǎo,
Zhedōng and Zhexī did not establish Jiedùshǐ until the next year.
At that time, Cuī Huàn was in Zhedōng,
and Lǐ Xīyán was in Zhexī,
neither were Jiedùshǐ.
As for Huáinán, it was Lǐ Chéngshì,
and Běihǎi was still occupied by the rebel general Néng Yuánhào.
However, a Běihǎi Jiedùshǐ had already been established the previous year,
meaning that even though Běihǎi had not yet been recovered, a Běihǎi commander had already been appointed.
[Zhāng Hào] ordered them to jointly rescue it.
Xiǎo was always arrogant and obstinate,
and did not accept Hào's orders.
By the time Hào arrived,
Suīyáng city had already fallen three days prior.
Hào summoned Xiǎo,
and had him beaten to death with a staff.
The Kǎoyì states: The old biography writes
"Háo Zhōu Cìshǐ,"
the new biography writes
"Háo Zhōu Cìshǐ,"
and the Tǒngjì writes
"Bó Zhōu Cìshǐ."
According to Háo Zhōu is in Huáinán,
far from Suīyáng.
Bó Zhōu borders Suīyáng,
it must be Bó Zhōu.
Now we follow the Tǒngjì.
I note that the Tōngjiàn changed the Tǒngjì's Bó Zhōu to Qiáo Jùn,
because the commanderies had not yet been restored to prefectures at this time.
Readers should be aware of this.
Zhāng Tōngrú and others gathered the remaining troops and fled to defend Shǎn,
fleeing east from Cháng'ān to defend Shǎn.
He sent his Yùshǐ Dàfū Yán Zhuāng to lead them,
joining Tōngrú to resist the imperial army,
with the old troops, infantry and cavalry, still numbering one hundred and fifty thousand.
"Old troops"
refers to the troops led by Zhāng Tōngrú and others who fled east from Xījiīng.
On the jǐwèi day,
Prince Guǎngpíng arrived at Qǔwò.
This is not the Qǔwò sealed to Jìn Zhuāngshú in the Spring and Autumn period;
its location is between Hóngnóng and Língbǎo counties.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: Thirteen li east of Hóngnóng county is Hǎoyáng Tíng,
and further east is Qǔwò City.
He then stationed his army north of the ridge.
Guō Zǐyí and others encountered the rebels at Xīndiàn;
according to the old records,
Xīndiàn is west of Shǎn City.
Zǐyí and others initially fought them
unsuccessfully,
and the rebels pursued them down the mountain.
The Huíhé attacked their rear from the southern mountain,
firing more than ten arrows amidst the yellow dust.
The rebels looked back in alarm and said:
"The Huíhé are here!"
Then they routed.
The imperial army and the Huíhé attacked them from both sides,
and the rebels suffered a great defeat,
with corpses covering the field.
Yán Zhuāng, Zhāng Tōngrú, and others abandoned Shǎn and fled east.
Prince Guǎngpíng Chù and Guō Zǐyí entered Shǎn City,
and Púgù Huáiēn and others pursued them along separate routes.
Yán Zhuāng first entered Luòyáng to inform Ān Qìngxù.
On the gēngshēn night,
Qìngxù led his followers out of the Yuànmén,
which was the Eastern Capital's Yuànmén.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù has no date for the Battle of Xīndiàn,
but only says:
"Zǐyí and Sīyè and others arrived at Xīndiàn,
met the rebels,
greatly defeated them,
pursued them over fifty li to the north,
with men and horses piled upon each other,
weapons, spears, and armor abandoned along the road from Shǎn to Luò City, leaving no empty space.
On gēngshēn,
Qìngxù fled,
that night,
he led his followers from the Eastern Capital's Yuànmén and fled to Héběi.
On rěnxū,
Marshal Guǎngpíng Wáng and Zǐyí recovered Shǎn Jùn."
The Fényáng Family Records state:
"In the ninth month,
Ān Qìngxù hastily sent his generals from Luò to Shǎn,
gathering the defeated soldiers,
still numbering one hundred and fifty thousand.
On the fourth day of the tenth month,
they arrayed along the mountain west of Shǎn.
They relied on the high ground to strike downwards,
while our army advanced uphill to attack.
The rebels stood firm and did not move.
The Duke [Guō Zǐyí] feigned retreat,
drawing them down the mountain,
and sent the Huíhé to cross the ravine and perilous paths to attack their rear.
The rebels were then defeated;
ninety thousand heads were taken,
and ten thousand people were captured."
The Fényáng Family Records also state:
"On the fourth day of the tenth month, the rebels were defeated west of Shǎn,
and Luòyáng was recovered on the eighth day."
The Niándàijì states:
"In the tenth month,
on the jǐwèi day,
the rebels were defeated at Xīndiàn.
On the xīnyǒu day,
Qìngxù heard of the army's defeat,
and led his followers to Xiāngzhōu."
The Jiù Jì states:
"On the gēngshēn day,
Qìngxù fled to Héběi.
On the rěnxū day,
Prince Guǎngpíng entered Dōngjīng."
The Xīn Jì states:
"On the wùshēn day,
the rebels were defeated at Xīndiàn,
and Shǎn Jùn was captured.
On the rěnzǐ day,
Dōngjīng was recovered."
Note that the distance between Shǎn and Luò is almost three hundred li.
The Fényáng biography and Xīn Jì are too early,
and the Shílù's rěnxū for recovering Shǎn Jùn is too late.
We now follow the Niándàijì and Xìng Shǔ Jì.
Xǔ Yuǎn died at Yǎnshī.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù and old biographies all say:
"Yǐn Zǐqí captured and sent him to Luòyáng,
where he was imprisoned with Gēshū Hàn and Chéng Qiānlǐ in the Kèshěng.
When Ān Qìngxù was defeated,
crossed the Héběi and fled,
he ordered Yán Zhuāng to kill them all."
The Zhāng Zhōngchéng Biography states:
"Xiānglǐ Zào's eulogy says:
'The late Imperial Censor Zhāng and Xǔ, two gentlemen of Tang,
as the city of Suīyáng fell during their defense,
Lord Zhāng was killed,
while Lord Xǔ was captured by the Jié rebels,
unable to find death,
and forced to surrender, reaching Yǎnshī County,
where he was also killed by soldiers.'"
We now follow this.
On the rěnxū day,
Prince Guǎngpíng Chù entered Dōngjīng.
The Huíhé were still not satisfied,
and Chù was troubled by this.
The elders requested to offer ten thousand rolls of fine silk to bribe the Huíhé,
and only then did the Huíhé stop.
9 The envoy from Chéngdū returned.
This returnee
was Dàn Tíngyáo.
“Huán” (還)
is pronounced xuán.
“You should provide for me in Jiànnán,
I will not return.”
The Emperor was anxious and fearful,
not knowing what to do.
Later, another envoy arrived;
this refers to the eunuch who returned with the congratulatory memorial from the officials.
“When the Retired Emperor first received the memorial requesting his return to the Eastern Palace,
he was distraught and could not eat,
wishing not to return.
But when the officials’ memorial arrived,
he was greatly pleased,
ordered food and music,
and issued an edict setting the date of his departure.”
This was the day set for his journey east to the capital.
“All this is due to your efforts!”
Bì asked repeatedly to return to the mountains.
The Emperor firmly tried to keep him,
but could not succeed,
so he allowed him to return to Héngshān.
Héngshān
is thirty *lǐ* west of Héngshān County, Héngyáng Commandery,
and is the Southern Peak.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn considered Huòshān as the Southern Peak;
Emperor Wén of Suí considered Héngshān as the Southern Peak.
According to Bì’s biography,
Bì wished to live in seclusion on Héngshān,
and an imperial edict granted this.
He was given the provisions of a third-rank official.
10 On *guǐhài* day,
the Emperor departed from Fèngxiáng,
and sent Grand Tutor Wéi Jiànsu to Shǔ
to welcome the Retired Emperor.
11 On *yǐchǒu* day,
Guō Zǐyí sent Left Army Horse Commander Zhāng Yòngjì and Right Wǔfēng Commander Hún Shìzhī to lead troops to take Héyáng and Hénèi.
Yán Zhuāng came to surrender.
The people of Chénliú killed Yǐn Zǐqí
and the entire commandery surrendered.
Tián Chéngsì besieged Lái Tián in Yǐngchuān
and also sent an envoy to surrender.
Guō Zǐyí responded slowly,
so Chéngsì rebelled again
and, along with Wǔ Lìngxún, both fled to Héběi.
An edict appointed Tián as Hénán
Military Commissioner.
12 On *bǐngyín* day,
the Emperor arrived at Wàngxián Palace.
The *Yōnglù* states: Wàngxián Palace
is a few *lǐ* east of Xiányáng County.
On *dīngmǎo* day,
the Emperor entered the Western Capital.
The common people came out of the city gates to welcome him,
forming an unbroken line for twenty *lǐ*,
dancing, leaping, and shouting “Long live!”
Some were weeping.
The Emperor entered and resided in Dàmíng Palace.
In the first year of Xiánhēng of Gāozōng,
Pénglái Palace was renamed Dàmíng Palace,
which was the Eastern Inner Palace.
Hányuán Hall
was the front hall of the Eastern Inner Palace,
located inside Dānfèng Gate.
It was surrounded by soldiers,
and officials were made to inspect it.
The Imperial Ancestral Temple had been burned by the rebels,
so the Emperor wore plain clothes and wept towards the temple for three days.
On this day,
the Retired Emperor departed from Shǔjùn.
13 Ān Qìngxù fled to secure Yèjùn,
renamed Yèjùn to Ānchéng
Prefecture,
and changed the reign title to Tiānchéng.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Tánglì* says the reign title was changed to Tiānhé.
The *Jìmén Jìluàn* says the reign title was changed to Zhìchéng,
which differs from the reign titles in the *Shílù*.
Both are preserved in the *Jìnián* and *Tōngpǔ*.
Here, we follow the *Shílù*.
His infantry numbered no more than a thousand men,
and generals like Āshǐnà Chéngqìng scattered to Chángshān, Zhàojùn, and Fányáng.
Within ten days,
Cài Xīdé from Shàngdǎng,
Tián Chéngsì from Yǐngchuān,
and Wǔ Lìngxún from Nányáng
each led their respective troops to rejoin him.
He also recruited people from various prefectures in Héběi,
and his forces reached sixty thousand,
and his military power revived.
14 When Guǎngpíng Wáng Chú entered the Eastern Capital,
over three hundred officials, including Chén Xīliè, who had accepted appointments from Ān Lùshān and his son,
all wore plain clothes, grieved, and wept, asking for punishment.
Chú, by imperial decree, released them,
and soon ordered them to proceed to the Western Capital.
On *jǐsì* day,
Cuī Qì ordered them to go to the court hall to request punishment.
This was the court hall of the Eastern Inner Palace,
located to the left and right of Hányuán Hall.
The left was called the Eastern Court Hall,
the right the Western Court Hall.
“Cháo” (朝)
is pronounced zhí yáo.
Then they were arrested and imprisoned in Dàlǐ and Jīngzhào prisons.
Those officials, clerks, and attendants from prefectures and counties who had been forced by the rebels to pursue and arrest people
were all arrested and imprisoned.
“Suǒyóu rén” (所由人)
refers to those with supervisory duties;
“zhīchéng rén” (祗承人)
refers to those who merely followed orders and served as attendants.
Initially,
Zhēn Jì of Jíjùn,
a man of integrity,
lived in seclusion on Qīngyán Mountain.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* says: Jíjùn’s Suíxīng County has Cāngyán Mountain.
Suíxīng County would have been merged into Jí County during the Táng dynasty.
“Zhēn” (甄)
is pronounced zhī rén.
“Cāo” (操)
is pronounced qī dào.
“Xíng” (行)
is pronounced xià mèng.
He served as a secretary.
This was during the Tiānbǎo era.
He feigned a wind illness
and was carried home.
When Lùshān rebelled,
he sent Cài Xīdé with two executioners,
their swords sheathed, to summon him.
Jì stretched out his neck, awaiting the sword.
Xīdé informed Lùshān that he was genuinely ill.
Later, Ān Qìngxù also sent men to forcibly carry him to the Eastern Capital.
After more than a month,
Guǎngpíng Wáng Chú pacified the Eastern Capital.
Jì rose
and went to the army gate to present himself.
Chú sent him to the capital,
and the Emperor ordered him to be housed in the Three Judicial Offices.
At that time, the Three Judicial Offices were investigating those who had accepted rebel official titles and ranks,
so Jì was housed in the Three Judicial Offices’ residence,
and those who had accepted rebel official titles and ranks were made to prostrate themselves before him.
“Guǎn” (館)
is pronounced guàn.
This was to shame those who had accepted rebel official titles and ranks.

it was all Chéng'ēn's (承ēn) doing.
It is very good that he was killed."
At this time, the "three ministries" (sānsī 三司) debated the crimes of officials who had fallen into the hands of the rebels. Their findings reached Fànyáng (范陽).
Sīmíng (思明) said to his generals:
"Chén Xīliè (陳希烈) and his ilk are all high-ranking officials of the imperial court.
The Former Emperor (Shànghuáng 上皇) abandoned them and fled to Shǔ (蜀),
and now they still cannot escape death.
How much more so for us, who originally rebelled with Ān Lùshān (安祿山)!"
Sīmíng (思明) used this to incite his generals and soldiers.
Sīmíng (思明) complied with their wishes and ordered his judge Gěng Rénzhì (耿仁智) and his colleague Zhāng Bùjīn (張不矜) to write a memorial saying:
"If Your Majesty does not execute Guāngbì (光弼) for your servant,
then your servant will lead his troops to Tàiyuán (太原) to execute him himself."
Bùjīn (不矜) drafted the memorial and showed it to Sīmíng (思明).
When it was about to be sealed in its box –
all memorials were sealed in boxes.
The person who wrote the memorial reported this to Sīmíng (思明).
Sīmíng (思明) ordered the two men seized and beheaded.
Rénzhì (仁智) had served Sīmíng (思明) for a long time.
Sīmíng (思明) felt pity and
wanted to spare his life.
He summoned him again and
said:
"I have employed you for nearly thirty years.
Today, it is not I who have wronged you."
Rénzhì (仁智) shouted loudly:
"Every man must die once.
To die with loyalty and righteousness
is a good way to die.
Now, to follow the grand general in rebellion
is merely to prolong one's life by a few years.
How can that compare to a swift death!"
Sīmíng (思明) was enraged,
beat him indiscriminately,
and his brains flowed onto the ground.
The historians say that Gěng Rénzhì (耿仁智) abandoned the rebellious and followed the righteous,
preserving his integrity with his death.
pronounced "huǒ gù fān" (火故翻).
Wū Chéngcǐ (烏承玼) fled to Tàiyuán (太原).
Lǐ Guāngbì (李光弼) memorialized to have him made Chānghuà Jùnwáng (昌化郡王) (Prince of Chānghuà Commandery)
and appointed Shílǐng Jūnshǐ (石嶺軍使) (military commissioner of Shílǐng).
The Shílǐng Army (石嶺軍) was in Xiùróng (秀容) county, Xīnzhōu (忻州).
23. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day of bǐngxū (丙戌),
the "Dāng Shí Dàqián" (當十大錢) (ten-cash coins) were first minted.
The inscription read
"Qiányuán Zhòngbǎo" (乾元重寶).
The Qiányuán (乾元) coins had a diameter of one cùn (寸),
each string weighed ten jīn (斤),
and circulated alongside the Kāiyuán Tōngbǎo (開元通寶) coins.
24. On the day of dīnghài (丁亥),
the Huíhé (回紇) Khagan (Kèhán 可汗) was invested with the title Yīngwǔ Wēiyuǎn Píjiā Què Kèhán (英武威遠毗伽闕可汗),
and the emperor's youngest daughter, Princess Níngguó (寧國公主), was married to him.
Diànzhōngjiān (殿中監) (Director of the Palace Administration) Hánzhōng Wáng Yǔ (漢中王瑀) (Prince Yǔ of Hánzhōng) was appointed as the envoy for the investiture ceremony,
and Yòusī Lángzhōng (右司郎中) (Director of the Right Department of the Ministry of Personnel) Lǐ Xùn (李巽) was his deputy.
Zuǒ Púshè (左僕射) (Left Grand Master of Remonstrance) Péi Miǎn (裴冕) was ordered to escort the princess to the border.
On the day of wùzǐ (戊子),
Xiānyú Shúmíng (鮮于叔明), Yuánwàiláng (員外郎) (Supernumerary Official) of Sīxūn (司勳) (Ministry of Merits), was appointed as Yǔ's (瑀) deputy.
Shúmíng (叔明) was
the younger brother of Zhòngtōng (仲通).
During the Tiānbǎo (天寶) era,
Xiānyú Zhòngtōng (鮮于仲通) allied himself with Yáng Guózhōng (楊國忠)
and attained high and prominent positions.
On the day of jiǎzǐ (甲子),
the emperor escorted Princess Níngguó (寧國公主) to Xiányáng (咸陽).
The princess bid farewell, saying:
"The affairs of the state are important.
Even if I die, I will have no regrets."
The emperor shed tears and returned.
When Yǔ (瑀) and others arrived at the Huíhé (回紇) royal tent,
the Khagan (Kèhán 可汗), dressed in a reddish-brown robe and a barbarian cap,
sat on a couch inside the tent.
His guard of honor was very strict.
He led Yǔ (瑀) and the others to stand outside the tent.
Yǔ (瑀) stood without bowing.
The Khagan (Kèhán 可汗) said:
"I and the Heavenly Khagan (Tiān Kèhán 天可汗) are rulers of two nations.
There are proper courtesies between a ruler and his subject.
Why do you not bow?"
Yǔ (瑀) and Shúmíng (叔明) replied:
"Previously, when the Táng (唐) dynasty married into various nations,
they always gave women of the imperial clan as princesses.
Today, the Son of Heaven, because the Khagan (Kèhán 可汗) has rendered meritorious service,
personally gives his own born daughter as wife to the Khagan (Kèhán 可汗).
The benevolence and courtesy are extremely great.
How can the Khagan (Kèhán 可汗), as a son-in-law, be arrogant towards his father-in-law
and receive the investiture sitting on a couch!"
The Khagan (Kèhán 可汗) changed his demeanor,
stood up, and received the investiture.
The next day,
the princess was established as Khatun (Kèdūn 可敦).
Since the establishment of the state by the Tujue (Tūjué 突厥),
the Khagan (Kèhán 可汗) referred to his principal wife as Kehedun (Kèhèdūn 可賀敦).
25. On the day of yǐwèi (乙未),
Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) entered the court.
The "Kǎo Yì" (考異) (Examination of Differences) states: The "Shílù" (實錄) (Veritable Records) states:
"Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) captured the rebel general Ān Tàiqīng (安太清) and sent him to the palace."
However, in the first year of Shàngyuán (上元),
Lǐ Guāngbì (李光弼) recaptured Huáizhōu (懷州)
and first captured Tàiqīng (太清).
The "Shílù" (實錄) is mistaken.
The "Tánglì" (唐曆) (Tang Calendar), "Běnjì" (本紀) (Annals), etc., all lack this information.
The old biography of Zǐyí (子儀) states:
"In the seventh month,
he defeated the rebels on the river,
captured Ān Shǒuzhōng (安守忠),
and presented him."
Other books also lack this,
so we do not adopt it here.
26th day of the 8th month,
on the day Rén-yín,
Xǔ Shūjì, Jìedùshǐ of Qīng, Dēng, and five other prefectures, was made Jìedùshǐ of Huá, Pú, and six other prefectures.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù records,
"Jì Guǎngchēn, Jìedùshǐ of Qīng, Xú, and five other prefectures,
Xǔ Shūjì, Jìedùshǐ of Qīng, Dēng, and five other prefectures."
I observe: How could Qīngzhōu belong to two Jìedùshǐ?
Furthermore, Guǎngchēn was previously Jīngzhōu Chángshǐ;
in the fifth month of this year, he became Yòu Chángshì.
In the ninth month, when An Qìngxù was being suppressed,
the Shílù refers to him as Zhèng-Cài Jìedùshǐ.
The Fényáng Jiāchuán calls him Huáixī, Jīng, Lǐ.
The Jiù Jì refers to him as Jīngzhōu.
He never garrisoned Qīng or Xú.
The Shílù's mention of Qīng and Xú here
is likely an error.
I observe that in the Xīnshū Fāngzhèn Biǎo,
in the first year of Zhìdé, the Qīng-Mì Jìedùshǐ was established,
administering the four commanderies of Běihǎi, Gāomì, Dōngmóu, and Dōnglái.
In the first year of Qiányuán,
the Qīng-Mì Jìedù added the two prefectures of Huá and Pú.
The Qīng-Mì Jìedù
is the same as the previously mentioned Běihǎi Jìedù,
which administered the four prefectures of Qīng, Mì, Dēng, and Lái.
Adding Huá and Pú,
this makes it a Jìedùshǐ of six prefectures.
If Qīng and Dēng (two of the five prefectures) were to add Huá and Pú (two prefectures),
then it would be seven prefectures,
which does not match the number.
27th day, on the day Gēng-xū,
Lǐ Guāngbì entered court.
On the day Bǐng-chén,
Guō Zǐyí was appointed Zhōngshūlìng,
and Guāngbì was appointed Shìzhōng.
On the day Dīng-sì,
Zǐyí proceeded to the military camp.
28th day, the Huíhé sent their minister Gǔchuò Tèlè and Dìdé with three thousand cavalry to assist in suppressing An Qìngxù.
The Emperor ordered Púgù Huái'ēn, Shuòfāng Zuǒ Wǔfēngshǐ, to lead them.
29th day of the 9th month,
on the first day Gēng-wǔ,
Zhào Cǐ, Yòu Yǔlín Dàjiàngjūn, was made Jìedùshǐ of Pú, Tóng, and Guó (three prefectures).
Last year, the Hézhōng Jìedùshǐ was established,
administering Pú, Jiàng, and seven other prefectures.
Now, Zhào Cǐ is Jìedùshǐ only of Pú, Tóng, and Guó (three prefectures).
This is probably because, at a time of military uprising,
commanders were separately appointed to guard strategic passes,
and the increases, decreases, divisions, and combinations of their jurisdictions
were adjusted as circumstances required.
30th day, on the day Bǐng-zǐ,
Wáng Zhòngshēng, Zhāotǎo Dǎngxiàng Shǐ, beheaded the Dǎngxiàng chieftain Tuòbá Róngdé,
and sent his head.
After Zhēnguān,
Túbō gradually grew strong.
The Dǎngxiàng and Tuòbá tribes, fearing oppression,
requested to move inland.
An edict ordered the establishment of the Jìngbiānjūnzhōu in Qìngzhōu to settle them.
The Fāngchí Dūdūfǔ was also established in the vicinity of Huái'ān County, Qìngzhōu,
administering ten small prefectures,
to settle the Yělì clan of the Dǎngxiàng.
Since Zhìdé,
as the Central Plains fell into chaos,
the Dǎngxiàng consequently plundered Bīn and Níng (two prefectures).
31st day, when An Qìngxù first arrived at Yè,
although his factions were scattered,
he still held seven commanderies and over sixty cities,
namely Jí, Yè, Zhào, Wèi, Píngyuán, Qīnghé, and Bópíng,
a total of seven commanderies.
Qìngxù did not attend to governmental affairs,
specializing instead in building terraces, ponds, and tower-ships, and indulging in heavy drinking.
His grand ministers Gāo Shàng, Zhāng Tōngrú, and others vied for power discordantly,
and there was no longer any discipline.
Cài Xīdé had talent and strategy,
and his troops were elite,
but he was strong-willed
and fond of speaking frankly.
Tōngrú slandered him and had him killed;
several thousand men under his command all fled,
and the various generals resented him and refused to serve him.
Cuī Gānyòu was made Tiānxià Bīngmǎshǐ,
in overall command of the inner and outer armies.
Gānyòu was obstinate and fond of killing,
and the soldiers were not attached to him.
On the day Gēng-yín,

Guō Zǐyí of Shuòfāng, Lǔ Jiǒng of Huáixī, Lǐ Huàn of Xīngpíng, Xǔ Shūjì of Huá-Pú, Lǐ Sìyè of Zhènxī-Běitíng, Jì Guǎngchēn of Zhèng-Cài, and Cuī Guāngyuǎn of Hénán—seven Jìedùshǐ—and Dǒng Qín, Pínglú Bīngmǎshǐ, were ordered to lead 200,000 infantry and cavalry to suppress Qìngxù.
Lǐ Guāngbì of Hédōng and Wáng Sīlǐ of Guānnèi-Zélù were also ordered to join.
Wáng Sīlǐ was previously Guānnèi Jìedùshǐ;
at this time, he concurrently held the Zélù Jìedùshǐ,
garrisoned in Lùzhōu.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù mentions Lǐ Huàn,
but not Cuī Guāngyuǎn,
and says there were nine Jìedùshǐ in total.
The Fényáng Jiāchuán mentions Guāngyuǎn,
but not Huàn,
and also mentions Xuē Jiānxùn, Hédōng Bīngmǎshǐ.
Probably the Shílù omitted Guāngyuǎn,
and the Fényáng Chuán omitted Huàn's name.
Jiānxùn was likely a subordinate general of Guāngbì,
whom Guāngbì sent ahead to Yèchéng
before his own arrival.
The Fényáng Chuán also refers to Jiǒng as Xiāng-Dèng,
and Guǎngchēn as Huáixī, Jīng-Lǐ.
The Jiù Běnjì states,
"Guǎngchēn was Jīngzhōu."
Now we follow the Shílù.
The Fényáng Chuán also says,
"The Duke departed Luò on the twelfth day of the ninth month;
the army crossed the river eastward."
Now we follow the Shílù,
which refers to Gēng.
This was the twenty-first day.
I observe that
"shè gēng"
should be written as
"gēngyín."
As they were difficult to command under one head,
no grand marshal was appointed.
The various armies advanced in parallel,
with several hundred thousand infantry and cavalry,
but without a grand marshal,
their orders were not unified,
which is why there was the defeat at Ānyáng.
The title Guānjūnrǒng began from this point.
32nd day, on the day Guǐ-sì,
Guǎngzhōu reported: Dàshí and Bōsī besieged the prefectural city.
Guǎngzhōu's seat was Nánhǎi County,
originally Pānyú County of Han.
The armies of the two nations plundered the storehouses,
burned residences,
and then departed by sea.
33rd day of winter,
10th month,
on the day Jiǎ-chén,
the Crown Prince was formally invested.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù records:
"A general amnesty for the empire may be granted.
Recently, grand ceremonies have been frequently held,
and special favors repeatedly bestowed,
repeatedly cleansing [the empire] from end to end.
However, fearing that recently some might still be detained in prison,
all prisoners below the rank of death row throughout the empire
are to be released without exception."
I observe: If it is called a "general amnesty,"
then all death sentences are pardoned.
How could it only pardon crimes below the rank of penal servitude?
I suspect that
"A general amnesty for the empire may be granted"
is a superfluous phrase.
Therefore, I do not record the amnesty.
Initially,
in the year the Crown Prince was born,
Yùzhōu presented auspicious grain.
Thus, it was considered an omen,
and his name was changed to Yù.
Gēng (更) is pronounced gōng-héng.
From this point onward, no further gifts were bestowed.
By this time,
new large coins had just been minted,
which were the Qiányuán Zhòngbǎo coins.
34 Guō Zǐyí 引兵自杏園濟河,
東至獲嘉.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Wèizhōu Jíxiàn 有杏園鎮.
Huòjiā Xiàn,
本汲縣之新中鄉.
漢武帝 Hàn Wǔdì 行幸至此,
聞獲呂嘉,
因置獲嘉縣.
唐屬懷州.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Huòjiā Xiàn,
在衞州西九十里.
斩首四千級,
捕虜五百人.
Tàiqīng 走保衞州,
Zǐyí 進圍之.
丙午,
遣使告捷.
Lǔ Jiǒng 自陽武濟,
Jì Guǎngchēn, Cuī Guāngyuǎn 自酸棗濟.
Yángwǔ Xiàn,
武德四年置於故原武城,
屬鄭州.
Qìngxù 悉舉鄴中之衆七萬救衞州,
分三軍,
以崔乾祐 Cuī Gānyòu 將上軍,
田承嗣 Tián Chéngsì 將下軍,
Qìngxù 自將中軍.
Zǐyí 使善射者三千人伏于壘垣之內,
令曰:
「我退,
賊必逐我,
汝乃登壘,
鼓譟而射之.」
既而與 Qìngxù 戰,
偽退,
賊逐之,
至壘下,
伏兵起射之,
矢如雨注,
賊還走,
Zǐyí 復引兵逐之,
Qìngxù 大敗.
獲其弟慶和 Qìnghé,
殺之.
遂拔衞州.
Qìngxù 走,
Zǐyí 等追之至鄴,
Xǔ Shúji, Dǒng Qín, Wáng Sīlǐ 及河東兵馬使 Xuē Jiānxùn 皆引兵繼至.
Qìngxù 收餘兵拒戰於愁思岡 Chóusīgāng.
Chóusīgāng,
在鄴城西.
據歐史,
在相州湯陰縣.
Xuē Jūzhèng 曰: 湯陰縣界有一岡,
土人謂之愁死岡.
考異曰: 汾陽 Fényáng 家傳:
「十月五日,
戰愁岡.」
據實錄,
「癸丑,
Zǐyí 破賊,
擒安慶和 Ān Qìnghé.」
癸丑,
十四日也,
蓋捷奏始到.
前後斬首三萬級,
捕虜千人.
Qìngxù 乃入城固守,
Zǐyí 等圍之.
Qìngxù 窘急,
遣薛嵩 Xuē Sōng 求救於史思明 Shǐ Sīmíng,
且請以位讓之.
Sīmíng 發范陽 Fányáng 兵十三萬欲救鄴,
觀望未敢進,
先遣李歸仁 Lǐ Guīrén 將步騎一萬軍于滏陽 Fǔyáng.
磁州治滏陽,
南至鄴城六十里.
35甲寅,
上皇 Shànghuáng 幸華清宮 Huáqīng Gōng;
十一月,
丁丑,
還京師.
36 Cuī Guāngyuǎn 拔魏州.
魏州,
治漢元城縣郭下.
又置貴鄉縣,
與元城為二縣.
丙戌
以前兵部侍郎蕭華 Xiāo Huá 為魏州防禦使.
會史思明 Shǐ Sīmíng 分軍為三,
一出邢 Xíng、洺 Míng,
一出冀 Jì、貝 Bèi,
一自洹水 Huánshuǐ 趣魏州.
洹水縣,
漢長樂縣地.
魏郡國志曰: 周建德六年,
分臨漳縣東北置洹水縣,
在魏州西.
趣,
七喻翻.
十二月,
癸卯,
敕以光遠領魏州刺史.
37甲辰,
置浙江西道節度使 Zhèjiāng Xīdào Jiédùshǐ,
領蘇 Sū、潤 Rùn 等十州,
以昇州刺史韋黃裳 Wéi Huángshang 為之.
浙西道節度使兼江寧軍使,
領昇 Shēng、潤 Rùn、宣 Xuān、歙 Shè、饒 Ráo、江 Jiāng、蘇 Sū、常 Cháng、杭 Háng、湖 Hú 十州,
治昇州.
庚戌
置浙江東道節度使 Zhèjiāng Dōngdào Jiédùshǐ,
領越 Yuè、睦 Mù 等八州,
以戶部尚書李峘 Lǐ Huán 為之.
浙東道節度使領越 Yuè、睦 Mù、衢 Qú、婺 Wù、台 Tái、明 Míng、處 Chǔ、溫 Wēn 八州,
治越州.
此宜參考下卷上元元年都統李峘 Lǐ Huán 註.
38己未,
㣥臣請上尊號曰乾元大聖光天文武孝感皇帝 Qiányuán Dàshèng Guāngwén Wǔxiàogǎn Huángdì,
許之.
39 Shǐ Sīmíng 乘崔光遠 Cuī Guāngyuǎn 初至,
引兵大下,
光遠使將軍李處崟 Lǐ Chùyín 拒之.
賊勢盛,
處崟連戰不利,
還趣城.
賊追至城下,
揚言曰:
「處崟召我來,
何為不出!」
光遠信之,
腰斬處崟.
處崟,
驍將,
衆所恃,
既死,
衆無鬬志.
姚聳夫 Yáo Sǒngfū 若在,
未必能為宋保守河南,
而聳夫之死,
宋人惜之.
李處崟 Lǐ Chùyín 若在,
未必能為唐保守魏州,
而處崟之死,
唐人惜之.
以兩敵相持而自戮鬬將,
乃自翦其手足也.
丁卯,
Sīmíng 陷魏州,
所殺三萬人.
40平盧節度使 Pínglú Jiédùshǐ 王玄志 Wáng Xuánzhì 薨,
上遣中使往撫將士,
且就察軍中所欲立者,
授以旌節.
高麗人 Gāolí Rén 李懷玉 Lǐ Huáiyù 為裨將,
殺玄志之子,
推侯希逸 Hóu Xīyì 為平盧軍使.
希逸之母,
懷玉姑也,
故懷玉立之.
立侯希逸 Hóu Xīyì 者李懷玉 Lǐ Huáiyù,
而逐侯希逸 Hóu Xīyì 者亦李懷玉 Lǐ Huáiyù 也.
懷玉後賜名正己 Zhèngjǐ.
節度使由軍士廢立自此始.
Chén Guāng said: Indeed, when people are born, they have desires,
without a ruler, there will be chaos.
The words of the 'Charge of Zhònghuǐ' in the Shū state.
From the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords down to the ministers, grand masters, scholars, and common people,
there are distinctions between the noble and the humble,
and ranks between the great and the small.
Like the strands of a net supporting each other,
the 'Charge of Yuè' in the Shū says:
"Like a net on its main rope,
it has threads but is not entangled."
Jiǎ Yì said:
"Like the body commanding the arms,
the arms commanding the fingers,
none fail to obey and follow."
And those below have no covetous desires.
In the Zhōu Yì, it says:
"Heaven above, marsh below:
Lǚ (Treading)."
The Commentary on the Image says:
"The noble man thereby distinguishes between high and low,
and settles the will of the people."
This is what is meant.
The reason a ruler can possess his officials and people,
is that the eight levers of power reside with him.
The Zhōu Lǐ says:
"The King uses the eight levers to control his many officials: First are ranks,
to control their nobility;
second are emoluments,
to control their wealth;
third are grants,
to control their favor;
fourth is placement,
to control their conduct;
fifth is life,
to control their good fortune;
sixth is seizure,
to control their poverty;
seventh is dismissal,
to control their offenses;
eighth is execution,
to control their transgressions."
If the power of both sides is equal,
how can he command those below him?
Emperor Sùzōng encountered the decline of the Táng dynasty in its middle period,
and fortunately restored the state.
It was appropriate for him to rectify the rites between high and low to govern the four directions;
yet he indulged in temporary peace,
and gave no thought to long-term calamity.
When he appointed generals and commanders,
to govern the frontier regions, this was a major affair of the state,
but he entrusted a mere envoy,
to act according to the sentiments of the ranks,
without regard for their worthiness or unworthiness,
granting positions only to those who desired them.
From then on,
this accumulated habit became the norm.
Rulers and ministers followed and upheld it,
considering it a good strategy,
calling it "gū xī" (appeasement).
Gū (姑)
means "temporarily";
xī (息)
means "peace";
it means seeking temporary peace.
When a commander was killed or expelled,
their crime was not punished,
but their position was instead conferred upon the perpetrator.
Thus, ranks and emoluments, dismissal and appointment, life and death, granting and seizing,
these are precisely the eight levers of power mentioned in the Zhōu Lǐ.
Zhì (治)
is pronounced as zhí (直).
Yú (予)
is read as yǔ (與).
How can the genesis of chaos
ever be brought to an end?
Moreover, those who possess a state,
reward the good and punish the evil.
Thus, those who do good are encouraged,
and those who do evil are chastised.
If a subordinate kills and expels his superior,
what greater evil is there than this!
Yet they are allowed to wield banners and battle-axes,
to command a region as its chief.
This is rewarding them.
When evil is rewarded,
what evil will they not commit?
The Shū says:
"Be far-sighted in your plans."
The words of the 'Kāng Gào' in the Shū.
Yóu (猷)
means "plan."
"If plans are not far-reaching,
great remonstrances are necessary."
The lines from the 'Dà Yǎ Bǎn' in the Shī.
"If a man has no far-reaching thoughts,
he will have anxieties close at hand."
Seen in the Lúnyǔ.
How can such anxieties and calamities be enumerated?
Because of this, subordinates constantly watch their superiors with greedy eyes,
and if they find an opportunity, they attack and exterminate them;
while superiors constantly fear their subordinates with trepidation,
and if they find an opportunity, they ambush and slaughter them.
These two phrases fully capture the situation of the fānzhèn and generals/soldiers in the late Táng.

There is no mutual preservation and nurturing for a plan of shared benefit and long-term existence.
If this is the case, can peace be achieved in the world?
Trace its path to disaster,
it began here.

Máo Cháng said: Lì (厲)
means "evil."

In ancient times, the governance of armies was always based on ritual.
Thus, at the Battle of Chéngpú, Jìn Wéngōng,
seeing that his army, young and old, observed ritual,
knew they could be used.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says: Jìn and Chǔ fought at Chéngpú.
The Marquis of Jìn ascended the ruins of Yǒuxīn to observe the army,

Zhì (治)

If soldiers are allowed to disrespect their subordinate officers,

Jiǎ Yì's treatise on "Lián Bì,"
expresses precisely this meaning.
From this, chaos and rebellion continuously arose,

and the people fell into misery,
with no one to appeal to.
This lasted for over two hundred years,

Tàizǔ began to establish military laws,

Thus, order was maintained between high and low,

Tíng (庭)

Recent scholars define bù tíng as not coming to court,

The realm was at peace,
and the myriad people truly prospered,

Is this not a far-sighted plan?

on the day rénzǐ,
there was a lunar eclipse,
total.
According to the Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals), solar eclipses are recorded,
but lunar eclipses are not.
The sun
symbolizes the sovereign.
This is recorded due to Empress Zhāng's tyranny.
The record states: If the male teachings are not cultivated,
and yang matters are not properly handled,
a chastisement appears in heaven,
and the sun is eclipsed;
if the wife's obedience is not cultivated,
and yin matters are not properly handled,
a chastisement appears in heaven,
and the moon is eclipsed.
Therefore, when there is a solar eclipse,
the Son of Heaven wears plain clothes and attends to the duties of the six officials,
rectifying the yang affairs of the realm;
when there is a lunar eclipse,
the empress wears plain clothes and attends to the duties of the six palaces,
rectifying the yin affairs of the realm.
Thus, the Son of Heaven and the empress
are like the sun and the moon,
yin and yang,
mutually dependent for their completion.
Therefore, subsequent lunar eclipses are all recorded above the catalog.

(Qìngxù 慶緒), not knowing what to do,
