6 On *Jiǎshēn* (甲申),
fifteen men, including Guǒchuò Tèlè (骨啜特勒) and Dìdé (帝德) of the Huíhú (回紇), rushed back to the Western Capital from Xiāngzhōu (相州).
The Emperor feasted them in the Zǐchén (紫宸) Hall.
Sòng Mǐnqíu's (宋敏求) *Cháng'ān Zhì* (長安志): North of Xuānzhèng (宣政) Hall is the Zǐchén (紫宸) Gate;
inside the gate is Zǐchén (紫宸) Hall,
which is the main hall of the inner court.
On *Gēngyín* (庚寅),
Guǒchuò Tèlè (骨啜特勒) and others took their leave to return to their mobile camp.
7 On *Xīnmǎo* (辛卯),
Lìfēi Yuánlǐ (荔非元禮) was appointed Governor (刺史 *cìshǐ*) of Huáizhōu (懷州),
and acting Military Governor (節度使 *jiéduōshǐ*) of the Western Circuit and Běitíng (北庭) Mobile Camp.
Yuánlǐ (元禮) again appointed Duàn Xiùshí (段秀實) as his Military Governor's Staff Officer (節度判官 *jiéduō pànguān*).
8 On *Jiǎwǔ* (甲午),
Lǚ Yīn (呂諲), Vice Minister of the Ministry of War (兵部侍郎 *bīngbù shìláng*), was given the concurrent title "Equal to Grand Chancellor" (同平章事 *tóng píngzhāngshì*).
On *Yǐwèi* (乙未),

Miáo Jìnqīng (苗晉卿), Central Secretariat Vice Minister (中書侍郎 *zhōngshū shìláng*) and "Equal to Grand Chancellor" (同平章事 *tóng píngzhāngshì*), was made Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (太子太傅 *tàizǐ tàifù*);
Wáng Yú (王璵) was made Minister of Punishments (刑部尚書 *xíngbù shàngshū*).
Both were dismissed from their governmental duties.
Lǐ Xiàn (李峴), Prefect of Jīngzhào (京兆尹 *jīngzhàoyǐn*), was made acting Minister of Personnel (吏部尚書 *lìbù shàngshū*);

Lǐ Kuí (李揆), Drafter in the Central Secretariat (中書舍人 *zhōngshū shèrén*) and concurrently Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites (禮部侍郎 *lǐbù shìláng*), was made Central Secretariat Vice Minister (中書侍郎 *zhōngshū shìláng*);
and Wǔ Qí (第五琦), Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue (戶部侍郎 *hùbù shìláng*), were all given the concurrent title "Equal to Grand Chancellor" (同平章事 *tóng píngzhāngshì*).
The Emperor's favor towards Xiàn (峴) was especially deep,
and Xiàn (峴) also took economic governance as his personal responsibility.
Many major military and national affairs were decided solely by Xiàn (峴).
Because Lǐ Fǔguó (李輔國) was jealous of Xiàn (峴),
he could not remain in the position of chancellor for long, which laid the groundwork for this.
Lǐ Fǔguó (李輔國) requested to select five hundred Imperial Forest cavalrymen for patrol duty.
Lǐ Kuí (李揆) submitted a memorial, saying:
"In the past, the Western Hàn (漢) dynasty used the Southern and Northern armies to counterbalance each other.
Thus, Zhōu Bó (周勃) entered the Northern Army through the Southern Army,
and thereby pacified the Liú (劉) clan.
Zhōu Bó (周勃) pacifying the Liú (劉) clan
is recorded in the *Hàn Gāohòu Jì* (漢高后紀).
Lǐ Kuí (李揆) states that Bó (勃) entered the Northern Army through the Southern Army;
examining the details,
it may not have been so.
Civil and military were separated,
to watch and inspect each other.
Now, if the Imperial Forest guards replace the Jinwú (金吾) guards in patrolling at night,
should an unusual change suddenly occur,
how will it be controlled!"
Thereupon, the plan was stopped.
The Jīnwú (金吾) Guard
belonged to the Southern Administration (*Nán yá* 南牙);
the Yǔlín (羽林) Guard
belonged to the Northern Administration (*Běi yá* 北牙).
The Jīnwú (金吾) were in charge of patrols and surveillance.
Lǐ Fǔguó (李輔國) wanted to use the Yǔlín (羽林) army to usurp their duty,
which is why Lǐ Kuí (李揆) spoke out against it.
朝 (*Zhāo*)
is pronounced *zhí yáo fān* (直遙翻).
9 On *Bǐngshēn* (丙申),
Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) was appointed Grand Marshal (元帥 *yuánshuài*) of the Eastern Domain, Shāndōng (山東), and Hédōng (河東) circuits,
and acting Commander of the Eastern Capital (東京留守 *dōngjīng liúshǒu*).
The Eastern Domain (*Dōngjī* 東畿)
refers to the Eastern Capital domain.
Shāndōng (山東)
refers to Hénán (河南) and Héběi (河北).
Hédōng (河東)
extends from Pú (蒲) and Jiàng (絳) in the south to Bìng (幷) and Dài (代) in the north.
(He was) concurrently appointed Military Governor (節度使 *jiéduōshǐ*) of Shǎn (陝), Guó (虢), and Huàzhōu (華州).
Lái Tiàn (來瑱) was transferred to Héxī (河西),
but before he departed,
the army at Xiāngzhōu (相州) was routed,
so he was made to garrison Shǎn (陝) to guard the passes.
However, Tiàn (瑱) was soon transferred to Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
華 (*Huá*)
is pronounced *hù huà fān* (戶化翻).
10Summer,
Fourth month.
On *Gēngzǐ* (庚子),
Wáng Sīlǐ (王思禮), Military Governor (節度使 *jiéduōshǐ*) of Zélu (澤潞), defeated Shǐ Sīmíng's (史思明) general Yáng Mín (楊旻) east of Lùchéng (潞城).
Lùchéng (潞城) County
belonged to Lùzhōu (潞州),
established in the 16th year of Kāihuáng (開皇) in the Suí (隋) dynasty,
and was the town of the Viscount of Lù (潞子) in the Spring and Autumn period.
*Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志): Lùchéng (潞城)
is forty *lǐ* northeast of Lùzhōu (潞州).
11 Tàizǐ Zhānshì Lǐ Fǔguó
had, ever since the emperor was in Língwǔ,
taken charge of the affairs of the Yuánshuài Xíngjūn Sīmǎ,
attended directly in the imperial tent,
proclaimed imperial edicts and commands,
handled memorials from the four directions,
the imperial seals and tallies,
and the morning and evening military signals.
Everything was entrusted to him.
When they returned to the capital,
he exclusively managed the imperial guards,
and often resided in the inner residence.
The inner residence
was located within the forbidden palace,
and was the quarters where Fǔguó stayed.
After that, all matters were implemented
only after the prime ministers and various bureaus, when presenting affairs out of their normal schedule,
consulted with Fǔguó and received his instructions.
He often settled all affairs of the realm at Yíntáimén.
Yōng Lù (雍錄) records: According to the six canons and the Dàmínggōng Map,
there were the Left and Right Yíntáimén.
The Left Yíntáimén was directly east of Zǐchéndiàn,
and the Right Yíntáimén was directly west of Zǐchéndiàn.
Furthermore, examining the Dàmínggōng Map in the pavilion edition,
inside the Right Yíntáimén were the Hànlín Yuàn and Líndédiàn,
and further east, passing through the Nèishì Biéshěng, Yányīngdiàn, and Guāngshùnmén, one would then reach Zǐchéndiàn.
From the Left Yíntáimén, entering westward,
one would pass through Wēnshì, Yùtángdiàn, and Língqǐdiàn before reaching Zǐchéndiàn.
Zǐchéndiàn was behind Xuānzhèngdiàn,
in the very center of Dàmínggōng.
The Right Yíntáimén was on the west side of the palace city,
and the Left Yíntáimén was on the east side of the palace city.
Judging by their location,
they were directly east and west of Zǐchéndiàn.
Fǔguó verbally issued imperial edicts,
which were then written down and sent out for implementation,
and after the matter was concluded, it was reported to the emperor.
He also set up dozens of investigators
to secretly listen for and investigate minor matters among the people,
and immediately conduct inquiries;
if there was something to be pursued or seized,
none of the various bureaus dared to refuse.
For serious prisoners in the Yùshǐtái and Dàlǐsì,
if their trials were not yet finished,
Fǔguó would summon them to Yíntái
and release them immediately.
When the Three Judicial Offices, prefectures, and counties interrogated prisoners,
they all first went to Fǔguó to consult and seek instructions;
the severity of punishment was at his discretion,
and he would act in the name of imperial edicts,
with no one daring to disobey.
The eunuchs dared not address him by his official title,
but all called him Wǔláng.
Lǐ Kuí, a prominent clan member from Shāndōng,
when he saw Fǔguó, performed the rites of a junior to an elder,
and called him Wǔfù.
Lǐ Kuí’s lineage originated from Lǒngxī,
but his ancestors settled as guests in Xíngyáng,
and thus became a prominent clan in Shāndōng.
Lǐ Fǔguó
was the fifth (son).
When Lǐ Xiàn became prime minister,
he prostrated himself before the emperor,
arguing that all imperial edicts should originate from the Zhōngshū,
and fully exposing Fǔguó’s usurpation of power and corrupt governance.
The emperor was moved and enlightened,
and praised his uprightness;
Fǔguó’s conduct
was greatly altered,
and his investigators were dismissed.
Fǔguó subsequently yielded the Xíngjūn Sīmǎ position,
requesting to return to his original post.
His original post
was Tàizǐ Zhānshì.
An imperial edict stated:
"Previously, due to the urgent military and state affairs,
verbal edicts were sometimes issued for disposition.
All kinds of requisitions and punishments of prisoners by flogging or exile are from now on to be entirely suspended.
Unless officially proclaimed,
they shall not be carried out.
All internal and external affairs
shall return to their respective responsible offices.
The Yīngwǔ Jūn Yúhòu and the various envoys of the Six Armies, and various bureaus, etc.,
who previously might have, due to disputes,
independently pursued and arrested,
Yīngwǔ Jūn were the elite archers before the imperial palace,
with a Yúhòu placed to command them.
The Six Armies
were the six armies of the Northern Gate.
The various envoys
were the internal envoys.
The various bureaus
were the internal bureaus.
Shǐ (使) is pronounced shǐ.
Lùn (論) is pronounced lún.
Tái (臺) refers to Yùshǐtái.
Fǔ (府) refers to Jīngzhàofǔ.
are to report by presenting a detailed memorial.
All laws and regulations, with the exception of the Ten Abominations, murder, rape, theft, and forgery,
all other troublesome [regulations] are to be entirely abolished,
and the Zhōngshū and Ménxià are instructed, together with judicial officials, to thoroughly deliberate and finalize [revisions] and report them."
Fǔguó consequently resented Xiàn.
Kǎoyì says: The biography of Lǐ Xiàn in the Shílù states:
"At that time, Lǐ Fǔguó exclusively commanded the military power within the forbidden palace;
imperial decrees sometimes did not originate from the Zhōngshū.
Xiàn sharply exposed this situation.
Sùzōng greatly praised him,
and immediately issued an edict
in accordance with Xiàn’s memorial.
Consequently, Fǔguó’s authority was curtailed,
and Fǔguó greatly resented him."
This is likely the same edict.
12 On the jiǎchén day,
the Jiedushi for Chén, Zhèng, and Bó was established,
with Dèngzhōu Cìshǐ Lǔ Jiǒng appointed to it;
Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Shàng Héng was appointed Jiedushi of the seven prefectures of Qīng and Mì;
the seven prefectures were
Qīng, Mì, Dēng, Lái, Zī, Yí, Hǎi.
Jiǒng (炅) is pronounced jiǒng.
Each was also to defend and guard their borders.
Chén, Zhèng, and Bó had never before had a Jiedushi stationed,
Lǔ Jiǒng was made their Jiedushi from Nányáng.
Shàng Héng was promoted from Péngchéng to govern the seven prefectures of Qīng and Mì.
The Xīngpíng Army was originally established in Shǐpíng County, Yōngzhōu;
Lǐ Huàn was at the mobile camp at the time,
and was made to command the three prefectures of Yù, Xǔ, and Rǔ.
These were all temporary divisions of commands,
not a fixed system.
When the nine jiedushis were defeated at Xiāngzhōu,
the troops under Lǔ Jiǒng were especially notorious for looting.
Hearing that Guō Zǐyí had retreated to camp by the river,
and Lǐ Guāngbì had returned to Tàiyuán,
Jiǒng was ashamed and fearful,
and died by drinking poison.
13 Shǐ Sīmíng proclaimed himself Emperor of Great Yān,
changed the era name to Shùntiān,
enthroned his wife Lady Xīn as empress,
and his son Cháoyì as Huái Wáng.
He appointed Zhōu Zhì as prime minister,
and Lǐ Guīrén as general.
He renamed Fányáng to Yānjīng,
and the various prefectures to commanderies.
14 On the wùshēn day,
Hónglú Qīng Lǐ Bàoyù was appointed Jiedushi of Zhèng, Chén, Yǐng, and Bó.
Bàoyù
was a descendant of Ān Xìngguì.
Ān Xìngguì is mentioned in Volume 187, Gāozǔ Wǔdé 2nd year.
He had repeatedly achieved military merits,
and personally declared his shame at sharing the same surname as Ān Lùshān,
hence he was granted the surname Lǐ.
15 The Huíhé Pígā Quē Kèhán died.
His eldest son Yèhù had previously been murdered,
so the people of the country enthroned his youngest son,
who became Dēnglǐ Kèhán.
The Huíhé wanted to have Princess Níngguó follow him in death.
The princess said:
"The Huíhé admire the customs of China,
and therefore marry Chinese women.
If they wish to follow their own customs,
why did they need to form a marriage alliance from ten thousand *lǐ* away!"
Nevertheless, she also gashed her face and wept for him.
According to the customs of Mòběi,
when someone died, the corpse was kept in a tent;
children, grandchildren, and relatives, both male and female, would each slaughter oxen and horses,
arrange them in front of the tent as offerings,
ride horses around the tent seven times,
then go to the tent entrance,
gash their faces with knives,
and weep,
with blood and tears flowing together.
This was done seven times,
and then they stopped.
Wéi (為) is pronounced wèi.
Lí (剺) is pronounced lí.
16 The investigating officials of the Mǎfāng (horse stables) in Fèngxiáng were robbed.
An investigating official
is an official in charge of the horse stables.
Tiānxìng County
was originally the ancient Yōng County.
In the second year of Zhìdé (757 CE),
it was renamed Fèngxiáng,
and Tiānxìng County was also established,
subordinate to Fèngxiáng Prefecture.
Lǐ Fǔguó had always emerged from the Fēilóng (Flying Dragon) Camp,
Lǐ Fǔguó was originally a boy in the Fēilóng Camp.
(The officials) were innocent.
(The emperor) also ordered Cúi Bóyáng, the Censor-in-chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng), Lǐ Yè, the Vice Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shìláng), and Quán Xiàn, the Grand Judge (Dàlǐ Qīng), to interrogate them.
This was what the Táng system called the "Minor Three Judicial Offices."
Yet
they did not confess.
(The emperor) then ordered Máo Ruòxū of Tàipíng, a Supervising Censor (Shìyùshǐ), to interrogate them.
Tàipíng County
was subordinate to Jiàng Prefecture.
Emperor Tàiwǔ of Wèi established Tàipíng County.
The Zhōu Dynasty changed it to Tàipíng,
named after Tàipíng Pass City.
He sought to please Lǐ Fǔguó,
and blamed Yífǔ.
Bóyáng was enraged,
summoned Ruòxū and reprimanded him,
intending to impeach him.
Ruòxū first reported himself to the emperor,
and the emperor hid Ruòxū behind a curtain.
Bóyáng arrived shortly after,
saying that Ruòxū had colluded with the eunuch
The emperor was furious,
and shouted at him to leave.
Bóyáng was demoted to County Commandant (Wèi) of Gāoyào,
Xiàn was demoted to County Commandant of Guìyáng.
Guìyáng
was a Hàn Dynasty county.
During the Suí and Táng Dynasties, it was subordinate to Lián Prefecture.
"Below the嶺 (ridge)"
refers to various counties south of the mountain range.
The historical records lost the names of the counties to which Yè and Xiàng were demoted,
hence it is said they were all demoted to county commandants below the嶺.
(Yífǔ) was exiled to Bō Prefecture.
Lǐ Xiàn, the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) and Grand Imperial Chancellor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì), memorialized that Bóyáng was innocent
and that the punishment was too severe.
The emperor considered this factionalism.
In the fifth month,
on the Xīnsì day,
Xiàn was demoted to Inspector (Cǐshǐ) of Shǔ Prefecture.
Hán Zémù, the Grand Master of Remonstrance (Yòu Sànqí Chángshì), was granted an audience.
Sàn
is pronounced "sì dǎn".
Qí
is pronounced "qí jì".
"(The emperor said) 'Lǐ Xiàn wanted to wield exclusive power.
Now that he is demoted to Shǔ Prefecture,
I feel that I have been too lenient in applying the law.'"
(Zémù) replied,
"Lǐ Xiàn spoke frankly;
he did not seek exclusive power.
Your Majesty's leniency
will only enhance your sacred virtue."
Ruòxū was soon appointed Censor-in-chief,
and his authority shook the court.
17 On the Rénwǔ day,
Xǔ Shúji, the Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Huá and Pú, was appointed Inspector of Biàn Prefecture,
and concurrently Military Commissioner of Huá, Biàn, and other seven prefectures.
The Xīnshū Fāngzhèn Biǎo (New Book's Table of Frontier Commands) states: The Biàn-Huá Military Commissioner administered Huá Prefecture,
controlling five prefectures: Huá, Pú, Biàn, Cáo, Sòng.
(He) served as Deputy Commissioner.
18 In the sixth month,
on the Dīngsì day,
the command of Bīn and Níng and other nine prefectures was established by dividing the Shuòfāng command.
The Fāngzhèn Biǎo states: In the ninth year of Kāiyuán (721 CE), the Shuòfāng Military Commissioner was established,
administering the Dàdūhùfǔ of Shányú, and the six prefectures of Xià, Yán, Suí, Yín, Fēng, Shèng,
the two armies of Dìngyuǎn and Fēng'ān,
and the three Xúiángchéng (Receiving Surrender Cities).
In the tenth year (722 CE),
the three prefectures of Lǔ, Lí, Qì were added.
In the twenty-second year (734 CE),
it concurrently served as the Investigator and Administrator of Guānnèi Circuit,
and the twelve prefectures of Jīng, Yuán, Níng, Qìng, Lǒng, Fú, Fāng, Dān, Yán, Huì, Yòu, Lín were added.
Kuāng and Cháng two prefectures were subordinate to Qìng Prefecture;
Ānlè and Chánglè two prefectures were subordinate to Yuán Prefecture.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo (742 CE),
Bīn Prefecture was added.
In the first year of Qiányuán (758 CE),
the Zhènwǔ Military Commissioner was established by dividing the Běidàdūhùfǔ,
and the two prefectures of Lín, Shèng.
In this year,
the Guānnèi Military Commissioner was abolished,
the administration of Shányú Dàdūhù was terminated,
and Jīng, Yuán, Níng, Qìng, Fāng, Fú, Dān, Yán were made subordinate to the Bīnnníng command.
Bīn Prefecture was originally Bīn Prefecture.
In the thirteenth year of Kāiyuán (725 CE), because the character
resembled the character
it was renamed Bīn.
19 Yú Cháo'ēn, the Commissioner of the Imperial Carriages and Armies (Guānjūnrúngshǐ), disliked Guō Zǐyí.
Taking advantage of his defeat,
he slandered him to the emperor.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
the emperor summoned Zǐyí back to the capital,
and appointed Lǐ Guāngbì as the new Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng and Marshal of the Armies (Bīngmǎ Yuánshuài).
The Kǎoyì (Textual Studies) says: The Bīn Zhì (Record of Bīn) says:
"In the fourth month,
Sùzōng sent Chancellor Zhāng Gōnghào to the Eastern Capital
to comfort and encourage the various armies.
Duke Guō prepared a feast for the army,
but Duke Zhāng did not sit down and left.
The army was displeased,
and rumors spread among factions.
Ten days later,
an imperial envoy was sent to recall Duke Guō."
The Fényáng Jiāchuán (Family Chronicle of Fényáng) says:
"In the sixth month,
the Duke came to court in the capital,
and thrice declined the position of Marshal.
The emperor permitted it.
Then an edict was issued appointing Lǐ Guāngbì to replace the Duke as Deputy."
The Duàn Gōng Biéchuan (Separate Biography of Duke Duàn) says:
"In the fifth month,
Lǐ Guāngbì replaced Zǐyí as Deputy Marshal,
guarding the Eastern Capital."
Now, based on the Shílù (Veritable Records) which states that in the seventh month, Zhào Wáng Jì was appointed Marshal,
it is mentioned together here.
They intercepted the imperial envoy, requesting to keep Zǐyí.
Zǐyí deceived them, saying,
"I am only seeing off the imperial envoy;
I haven't left yet."
Thereupon, he leaped onto his horse and departed.
Guāngbì wished to have an imperial prince as his deputy.
On the Xīnsì day,
Zhào Wáng Jì was appointed Grand Marshal of all Armies (Tiānxià Bīngmǎ Yuánshuài),
and Guāngbì served as his deputy.
The Kǎoyì says: The Jiù Chuán (Old Biography) says:
"Sīmíng unleashed his troops in Hénán.
Guāngbì was promoted to Grand Preceptor (Tàiwèi) and concurrently Grand Chancellor (Zhōngshū Lìng),
replacing Guō Zǐyí as Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng and Deputy Grand Marshal,
with command over the eastern armies."
The Xīn Chuán (New Biography) says:
"The emperor forgave the generals' faults,
and appointed Guāngbì concurrently as Grand Administrator (Zhǎngshǐ) of Yōuzhōu Dàdūdūfǔ and Commissioner of all Provisional Camps (Zhī Zhū Dào Jiédù Xíngyíng Shì),
and also replaced Zǐyí as Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng.
Not long after,
he became Deputy Grand Marshal of all Armies."
According to the Shílù,
Guāngbì was promoted to Grand Preceptor and Grand Chancellor after the defeat of Shǐ Sīmíng in the first year of Shàngyuán (760 CE),
and became Governor (Dūdū) of Yōuzhōu in the eighth month of this year.
The month and day of his replacement of Zǐyí to command Shuòfāng are not in the Shílù.
The imperial edict stated:
"You should serve as deputy for the expedition,
and also receive the honor of a divided command."
This probably refers to this very time.
Guāngbì rushed to the Eastern Capital with five hundred cavalry from Hédōng.
At night,
he entered their camp.
Guāngbì managed the army with strict order.
Upon his arrival,
as soon as his orders were issued,
the soldiers, fortifications, banners, and morale all transformed.
The history states that when Guāngbì entered the Shuòfāng army,
all the arrangements followed Zǐyí's old system,
only the orders were made stricter and more orderly.
Zhì
is pronounced "zhí zhī".
(The soldiers) feared Guāngbì's strictness.
The Army Commissioner of the Left Wing, Zhāng Yòngjì, was stationed at Héyáng.
Guāngbì summoned him with a dispatch.
Yòngjì said:
"The Shuòfāng army
is not a rebellious army.
We entered by night;
why is there such suspicion of us?"
He plotted with his generals to break into Dōngjīng with elite troops,
drive out Guāngbì,
and invite Zǐyí.
He ordered his soldiers to don armor and mount their horses,
holding gags in their mouths, to await orders.
The Grand Supervisor of Army Commissioners, Púgù Huái'ēn, said:
"At the collapse at Yèchéng,
Grand Duke Guō was the first to leave.
Observing Huái'ēn's words here,
then what Bīnzhì said can also be trusted.
Therefore, his military authority was revoked.
Now, to drive out Grand Duke Lǐ and forcefully invite Guō Gōng,
this is rebellion.
How can this be done?"
The Right Wǔfēng Commander, Kāng Yuánbǎo, said:
"If you use your troops to invite Grand Duke Guō,
the court will surely suspect that Grand Duke Guō instigated you to do it,
which would ruin his family.
What wrong has Grand Duke Guō's hundred mouths done to you?"
Yòngjì then stopped.
Huái'ēn's words here,
and Kāng Yuánbǎo's words, are all correct.
If the generals had followed Zhāng Yòngjì in evil,
and Shǐ Sīmíng's troops had arrived again,
the Táng cause would have been in peril.
Yòngjì arrived alone on horseback to pay his respects.
Guāngbì reprimanded Yòngjì for not arriving on time when summoned,
and beheaded him,
ordering his subordinate general, Xīn Jīnggǎo, to take command of his troops.
Kǎoyì says: The old accounts say:
"Yòngjì, presuming on Zǐyí's leniency,
and fearing Guāngbì's orders,
had considerable disagreement with his generals,
wanting to delay his troops.
Guāngbì rode out with several thousand cavalry to Sīshuǐ Xiàn.
Yòngjì rode alone to pay his respects,
and was immediately beheaded at the camp gate.
The generals were intimidated into submission,
and Xīn Jīnggǎo was appointed in his place.
He then pursued the Grand Army Commissioner, Púgù Huái'ēn.
Huái'ēn, afraid,
arrived earlier than scheduled."
Bīnzhì says:
"On the twenty-third day of the fifth month,
an imperial edict appointed Lǐ Gōng, the Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng, to replace Zǐyí as commander of all armies.
After Lǐ Gōng received the order,
he arrived at Dōngdū with five hundred cavalry from Hédōng.
That night,
he entered his army.
Zhāng Yòngjì, who was in Héyáng,
heard of it and said: 'The Shuòfāng army
are not rebels;
why such suspicion?'
He wanted to lead elite cavalry to break into Dōngdū,
drive out Lǐ Gōng,
and invite Guō Gōng.
Lǐ Gōng knew of this,
so he remained in Dōngdū,
and memorialized to request that troops be dispatched to Héyáng.
In the tenth month of winter,
Sīmíng led his troops across the river.
Lǐ Gōng said: 'If Sīmíng crosses the river,
he will surely aim for Luòchéng.
I should guard Wǔláo Guān
and display troops on Guǎngwǔ Yuán to await him.'
He then led his army east to Sīshuǐ Xiàn.
He dispatched orders to summon the generals at Héyáng.
Yòngjì arrived late,
and Lǐ Gōng enumerated his crimes and executed him,
appointing Xīn Jīnggǎo to take his place.
The next day,
he led his army into Héyáng."
According to the Shílù,
Guāngbì was Vice Marshal in this month,
and only moved his army to Héyáng in the ninth month.
20 Púgù Huái'ēn arrived next.
Guāngbì invited him to sit
and conversed with him.
The history says that Lǐ Guāngbì treated Púgù Huái'ēn with more favor than other generals.
The gatekeeper reported:
"Five hundred Fān and Hún cavalry have arrived."
Fān and Hún
refer to various foreign tribes and the Hún tribe.
Huái'ēn walked out,
summoned his subordinate generals,
and feigned anger, saying:
"I told you not to come,
how dare you disobey!"
Guāngbì said:
"The soldiers follow their generals,
what crime have they committed?"
He ordered that they be given beef and wine.
The history says that Huái'ēn arrived prepared before seeing Guāngbì,
and Guāngbì, though aware of his intentions, tolerated him without revealing it.
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu fān.
21 Wáng Sīlǐ,
the Jìedùshǐ of Lùqìn,
Wáng Sīlǐ was Jìedùshǐ of Zé, Lù, and Qìn prefectures.
History sometimes calls it Zélù,
sometimes Lùqìn.
Qìn,
pronounced qī zhèn fān.
was appointed Grand Administrator of Běijīng and Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng.
This was to replace Lǐ Guāngbì.
Originally,
at the defeat at Tóngguān (the incident is found in volume 118, the first year of Zhìdé),
a cavalryman from Zhōuzhì, Zhāng Guāngshèng, dismounted and gave him a horse.
When asked his name,
he left without saying.
Sīlǐ secretly remembered his appearance,
but could not find him.
When he arrived in Hédōng,
someone slandered Xīn Yúnjīng, the Cìshǐ of Dáizhōu and from Héxī.
Yúnjīng,
a native of Jīnchéng, Lánzhōu,
belonged to the Héxī circuit.
Yúnjīng was afraid
and did not know what to do.
Guāngshèng, who was then under Yúnjīng's command,
said:
"Guāngshèng once did a kindness for Grand Duke Wáng,
and has never dared to speak of it,
ashamed to seek reward for it.
Now that my lord is in distress,
Guāngshèng requests to go see Grand Duke Wáng,
and will surely resolve this for my lord."
Yúnjīng was pleased and sent him.
Guāngshèng paid respects to Sīlǐ.
Before he could speak,
Sīlǐ recognized him and said:
"Ah!
Are you not my old friend?
How late we meet!"
Guāngshèng told him the truth.
Sīlǐ was greatly pleased,
took his hand,
and wept, saying:
"That I am where I am today
is all due to your effort."
Sīlǐ meant that
Guāngshèng gave him a horse,
saved him from battle,
and thus he had his present fortune.
He invited him to sit on the same couch,
and they vowed to be brothers.
Guāngshèng then calmly spoke of Yúnjīng's injustice.
Sīlǐ said:
"Yúnjīng's fault is not small,
but today I will forgive him especially for an old friend."
On that very day, he promoted Guāngshèng to Army Commissioner,
and bestowed upon him abundant gold, silk, fields, and residences.
Zhāng Guāngshèng's conduct towards Wáng Sīlǐ
can be called that of a noble person.
However, his later service to Dézōng,
when he harbored resentment and longing for a lost position,
led him to surrender himself to Zhū Cǐ.
How contradictory were his actions then!
22 On the Xīnmǎo day,
Púgù Huái'ēn, the Vice Jìedùshǐ of Shuòfāng and Palace Supervisor, was concurrently appointed Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
and advanced to the title of Prince of Dàníng Commandery.
Huái'ēn served as vanguard under Guō Zǐyí,
his bravery surpassing all three armies,
and he had numerous military achievements before and after,
thus he was rewarded.
23 In the eighth month,
on the Yǐsì day,
Xiāngzhōu generals Kāng Chǔyuán and Zhāng Jiāyán seized the prefecture and rebelled.
The Cìshǐ, Wáng Zhèng, fled to Jīngzhōu.
Chǔyuán declared himself "Hegemon King of Nánchǔ."
24 The Huíhé, seeing that Princess Níngguó had no son,
allowed her to return.
On the Bǐngchén day,
she arrived at the capital.
The princess's marriage to the Huíhé is mentioned in the previous volume, last year.
25 On the Wùwǔ day,
the Emperor sent General Cáo Rìshēng to Xiāngzhōu to console Kāng Chǔyuán and persuade him.
Wáng Zhèng was demoted to Chief Administrator of Ráozhōu,
and Zhāng Guāngqí, the Minor Minister of the Court of the Imperial Granaries, was appointed Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu.
Chǔyuán did not comply.
26 On the Rénxū day,
Lǐ Guāngbì was appointed Grand Administrator of Yōuzhōu and Jìedùshǐ of Hébĕi and other regions.
This was to enable him to recover Hébĕi, as well as Yōu and Yān.
27 In the ninth month,
on the Jiǎwǔ day,
Zhāng Jiāyán launched a surprise attack and captured Jīngzhōu.
Dù Hóngjiàn, the Jìedùshǐ of Jīngnán, abandoned the city and fled.
Upon hearing this, the officials of Lǐ, Lǎng, Yǐng, Xiá, and Guī prefectures
scrambled to hide in the mountains and valleys.
At that time, the Jìedùshǐ of Jīngnán governed ten prefectures: Jīng, Lǐ, Lǎng, Yǐng, Fù, Kuí, Xiá, Zhōng, Wàn, and Guī.
On the 28th, *wùchén*,
an order was again issued for Jiàngzhōu to mint large *qiányuán zhòngbǎo* coins.
In the Tang dynasty, coins were minted,
generally in ninety-nine furnaces throughout the realm,
and of these, thirty furnaces were in Jiàngzhōu.
As for the remaining furnaces,
some were separated by rivers and mountains,
or had fallen to bandits and rebels,
so at that time, coin minting largely depended on Jiàngzhōu.
One coin was worth fifty;
the large coin had a diameter of one *cùn* and two *fēn*,
and its inscription also read
"乾元重寶" (*Qiányuán Zhòngbǎo*).
The outer rim on the reverse was a double rim.
Each string weighed twelve *jīn*,
and was called *zhòngléng qián*.
*Zhòng*
is pronounced like *lóng* reversed.
Previously, the military forces had received no stipends,
so it was decided to issue them their winter provisions in new coins.
Winter provisions
refer to the stipends and allowances that various officials were entitled to receive in winter.
On the 29th, *dīnghài*,
Cuī Guāngyuǎn, the Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent, was appointed as the Pacification Commissioner of Jīng and Xiāng,
and concurrently served as the Supreme Commander of Troops for Shānnán Dōngdào;
Wáng Zhòngshēng, the Military Governor of Chén, Yǐng, Bó, and Shēn, was appointed as the Military Governor of Shēn, Miǎn, and other five prefectures,
and was placed in charge of the mobile forces for Huáinán Xīdào.
At that time, the Military Governor of Huáixī administered the five prefectures of Shēn, Guāng, Shòu, Ān, and Miǎn.
Shǐ Sīmíng ordered his son Shǐ Cháoqīng to guard Fányáng,
and commanded the grand administrators of various prefectures, each leading three thousand soldiers, to follow him towards Hénán.
They were divided into four routes,
and he sent his general Línghú Zhāng, leading five thousand soldiers, to cross the river from Líyáng and take Huázhōu.
Sīmíng himself would go via Púyáng,
Shǐ Cháoyì via Báigāo,
and Zhōu Zhì via Húliáng, to cross the river.
Báigāo and Húliáng were both crucial ferry crossings
on the northwest bank of Huázhōu.
*Liáng*
is sometimes written as
"梁" (*liáng*).
*Pú*
is pronounced *bǔ*.
Lǐ Guāngbì was inspecting the various camps along the Yellow River,
and hearing of this,
returned to Biànzhōu.
He said to Xǔ Shúji, the Military Governor of Biàn and Huá:
"If you, Grandee, can hold Biànzhōu for fifteen days,
I will then bring troops to rescue you."
Shúji agreed.
Guāngbì returned to Dōngjīng.
When Sīmíng reached Biànzhōu,
Shúji engaged him in battle,
but was defeated.
He then surrendered to Sīmíng, along with Dǒng Qín, the Prefect of Púzhōu, and his generals Liáng Pǔ, Liú Cóngjiàn, and Tián Shéngōng.
Xǔ Shúji indeed followed Zhāng Gǎo's words.
(Sīmíng) ordered him and his general Lǐ Xiáng to guard Biànzhōu;
he treated Dǒng Qín generously,
seized his wife and children,
and kept them at Chánglú as hostages.
Chánglú
was the territory of Hàn Cānhù County,
renamed Chánglú County in the Later Zhōu dynasty,
and belonged to Cāngzhōu at that time.
*Zhì*
is pronounced *zhì*.
Shéngōng
was from Nángōng;
Nángōng
was an ancient county in the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to Jìzhōu.
Soon after,
Shéngōng attacked Déxìn
and beheaded him.
Cóngjiàn escaped and fled.
Shéngōng led his troops to surrender.
Sīmíng, taking advantage of his victory, attacked Zhèngzhōu to the west.
Zhèngzhōu was Xíngyáng Commandery.
Upon arriving at Luòyáng,
he said to Wéi Zhì, the Resident Commissioner:
"The rebels are advancing with their victory,
it is advantageous to hold back the troops, not to rush into battle.
Luòchéng cannot be defended,
what is your plan, honored sir?"
Zhì requested to leave troops in Shǎn
and retreat to defend Tóngguān,
holding the strategic pass to blunt their advance.
Guāngbì said:
"When two enemies face each other,
advance is valued and retreat is feared.
If we now abandon five hundred *lǐ* of land without reason,
the rebel's momentum will only grow.
It is better to move the army to Héyáng,
connect with Zé and Lù to the north,
advance if advantageous,
and retreat to defend if not advantageous,
with internal and external support,
preventing the rebels from invading westward.
This is the 'ape's arm' strategy.
An ape's arm can extend and lengthen,
and can contract and shorten,
hence the simile.
I, Guāngbì, am not as good as you;
when it comes to military matters,
you are not as good as I, Guāngbì."
Zhì had no reply.
The Judge Wéi Sǔn said:
"Dōngjīng is the imperial residence,
how can the Grand Councilor not defend it?"
(Note: Lǐ Guāngbì was already *Sīkōng* at the beginning of Zhìdé,
and became *Shìzhōng* in Qiányuán first year,
which is why Wéi Sǔn addressed him thus.)
"If we defend it,
then Fùshuǐ, Èlǐng, and Lóngmén should all have troops stationed there.
Fùshuǐ has the strategic importance of Chénggāo.
Èlǐng is in Dēngfēng County.
Lóngmén is Yīquè.
*Fù*
is pronounced *sì*.
is pronounced like *nì* and *gè* combined.
Can you defend all of them?"
Thereupon, he issued a dispatch to Resident Commissioner Wéi Zhì, ordering him to lead the officials of Dōngjīng westward into the pass,
and dispatched Hénán Magistrate Lǐ Ruòyōu to lead the officials and common people out of the city to avoid the rebels,
thus emptying the city.
Guāngbì led his soldiers to transport oil, iron, and other supplies to Héyáng for defense,
with Guāngbì bringing up the rear with five hundred cavalry.
At this time, Sīmíng's scouting parties had already reached Shíqiáo.
His generals asked:
"Should we proceed north from Luòchéng,
or advance by Shíqiáo?"
Guāngbì said:
"Advance by Shíqiáo."
(Note: *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states that the Gǔshǔi river flows eastward north of Luòyáng's Guǎngmò Gate,
which was the Hàn dynasty's Gǔ Gate.
It flows eastward beneath the Shíqiáo bridge of Jiànchūn Gate,
which is the Shàngdōng Gate.
This refers to the gates of Hàn and Jìn Luòchéng,
not the Luòchéng relocated in the Suí and Tang dynasties.
The area of Shàngdōng Gate
became a garrison in the Tang dynasty.)
Guāngbì held a torch and proceeded slowly,
his units were firm and orderly.
The rebels pursued him,
but dared not press close.
"Pursued him" means
they hoped he would become panicked and collapse.
"Dared not press close" means
because he was stern and orderly, difficult to assault.
(Note: When Guō Zǐyí retreated from Fúshuǐ to defend Héyáng,
his forces numbered tens of thousands.
When Lǐ Guāngbì arrived at Héyáng,
he had twenty thousand soldiers.
How could there be such a discrepancy in numbers?
This is because after Zhāng Yòngjì's death,
many of the Shuòfāng soldiers, fearing punishment, scattered and fled.)
Guāngbì inspected the defenses
and assigned his soldiers,
all of which were meticulously prepared.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Sīmíng entered Luòyáng,
but the city was empty,
and he gained nothing.
Fearing that Guāngbì would attack his rear,
he dared not enter the palace,
but retreated to camp south of Báimǎsì,
and built a crescent-shaped fort south of Héyáng to resist Guāngbì.
(Note: Shǐ Sīmíng, while riding the wave of victory to attack Héyáng,
first built the crescent fort
because he feared an unexpected setback in battle.)
When Sīmíng arrived at Luòyáng,
Zhèng and Huá prefectures and others had already fallen.
(*Tōngjiàn* follows existing historical texts,
and neglected to revise and correct this.)
In the winter,
tenth month,
on the *dīngyǒu* day,
an imperial edict was issued for a personal expedition against Shǐ Sīmíng;
however, the court officials submitted a memorial advising against it,
and so it was stopped.
32 Sīmíng (史思明) led his troops to attack Héyáng (河陽).
He sent his valiant general Liú Lóngxiān (劉龍仙) to challenge them below the city walls.
Lóngxiān, relying on his bravery,
raised his right foot onto his horse's mane,
and insultingly cursed Guāngbì (光弼).
Guāngbì looked at his generals and said:
"Who can capture this man?"
Púgù Huái'ēn (僕固懷恩) requested to go.
Guāngbì said:
"This is not something a great general should do."
Guāngbì's words were fitting,
and Huái'ēn was indeed convinced.
"Brigadier General Bái Xiàodé (白孝德) can go."
Guāngbì summoned and questioned him.
Xiàodé requested to go.
Guāngbì asked:
"How many soldiers do you need?"
He replied:
"I request to go alone and take him."
Guāngbì admired his resolve,
but still asked what he needed.
He replied:
"I wish to select fifty cavalrymen to leave the camp gate as a reserve force,
and also ask the main army to beat drums and shout to boost morale."
Guāngbì patted his back and sent him off.
He praised his courage,
and especially his strategy for defeating the enemy.
He spurred his horse and advanced through the chaotic current.
To cross the current chaotically is called "亂" (luàn).
Huái'ēn congratulated him, saying:
"He will win."
Guāngbì said:
"Their weapons have not yet clashed,
how do you know?"
Huái'ēn said:
"Watching him calmly hold the reins,
I know he is perfectly safe."
Lóngxiān saw him approaching alone
and greatly underestimated him;
as he drew a little closer,
Lóngxiān was about to move,
but Xiàodé waved his hand to him,
as if he had not come as an enemy,
so Lóngxiān stopped, unsure what to make of it.
When he was ten paces away,
he spoke to him,
and Lóngxiān cursed insultingly as before.
Xiàodé rested his horse for a long time.
"Resting the horse" (息馬) means
to allow the horse's strength to fully recover before battle.
"Does the bandit recognize me?"
Lóngxiān said:
"Who are you?"
He said:
"I
am Bái Xiàodé."
Lóngxiān said:
"What kind of dog or pig is that!"
Xiàodé let out a great shout,
wielded his spear, spurred his horse, and charged him.
Drums beat and shouts rose from the city walls,
and the fifty cavalrymen followed.
Lóngxiān had no time to shoot an arrow
and ran in circles on the embankment.
Xiàodé pursued and caught him,
cut off his head,
and carried it back with him.
Lóngxiān relied on his bravery and underestimated the enemy,
while Xiàodé attacked him by surprise,
hence his victory.
Xiàodé
was originally a Hú (胡) person from Ānxī (安西).
Sīmíng had over a thousand fine horses,
which he brought daily to the sandbar south of the river to bathe,
rotating them constantly to display their large numbers.
Guāngbì ordered the collection of mares from his army,
obtaining five hundred,
and tethered their foals inside the city.
When Sīmíng's horses reached the water's edge,
he released all the mares.
The horses neighed incessantly,
and Sīmíng's horses all swam across the river,
and were driven into the city at once.
The stallions longed for the mares,
and all crossed the river at once.
This was merely a small trick.
Sīmíng could not control them,
as they were blocked by the river.
Sīmíng arranged several hundred warships,
and launched fire ships ahead of them, following,
intending to use the current to burn the pontoon bridge.
Guāngbì had already stored several hundred long poles, each a hundred feet long,
supported at their base by large timbers,
with felt-wrapped iron forks at their tips,
to meet the fire ships and fork them.
The ships could not advance
and soon burned themselves out.
He also used the forks to resist the warships,
and from the bridge, fired catapult stones at them.
Those hit all sank,
and the bandits were defeated and withdrew.
Sīmíng [史思明] saw troops at Héqīng [河清],
desiring to cut off Guāngbì's [光弼] supply route.
Guāngbì [光弼] encamped at Yěshuǐdù [野水渡] to prepare for this.
As dusk fell,
he returned to Héyáng [河陽],
leaving a thousand soldiers,
and sent his subordinate general Yōng Xīhào [雍希顥] to guard the palisade,
saying:
"The enemy generals Gāo Tínghuī [高庭暉], Lǐ Rìyuè [李日越], and Yù Wénjǐng [喻文景]
are all capable of fighting ten thousand men.
Yù [喻]
is a surname.
The Xìngpǔ [姓譜] states: In the Eastern Jìn [東晉] there was Yù Guī [喻歸],
who compiled the Héxī Jì [河西記].
I will leave now;
you are to wait here.
If the enemy arrives,
do not engage them in battle.
If they surrender,
then come with them."
The generals did not understand his intention,
and all secretly mocked him.
Soon after, Sīmíng [思明] indeed said to Lǐ Rìyuè [李日越]:
"Lǐ Guāngbì [李光弼] is skilled at defending cities,
but now he is out in the open,
he will surely be captured.
You, with your iron cavalry, cross the river tonight,
and seize him for me.
If you fail,
then do not return."
Rìyuè [日越] led five hundred cavalry and arrived at the palisade in the morning.
Xīhào [希顥] blocked the moat and rested his troops,
humming and whistling, looking at each other.
Rìyuè [日越] found it strange,
finding their lack of fighting spirit strange.
"Is the Sīkōng [司空] present?"
Lǐ Guāngbì [李光弼] had been promoted to Sīkōng [司空] and Shìzhōng [侍中],
hence the address.
"He left last night."
"How many troops?"
He replied:
"A thousand men."
"Who is the general?"
He replied:
"Yōng Xīhào [雍希顥]."
Rìyuè [日越] pondered for a long time,
and said to his subordinates:
"Now we have missed Lǐ Guāngbì [李光弼];
if we return with Xīhào [希顥],
I will surely die.
It is better to surrender."
So he asked to surrender.
Xīhào [希顥] brought him to see Guāngbì [光弼],
who treated him generously,
and entrusted him with important matters.
Gāo Tínghuī [高庭暉] heard of this,
and also surrendered.
Someone asked Guāngbì [光弼]:
"How was it so easy to make two generals surrender?"
Guāngbì [光弼] said:
"This is merely human nature.
Sīmíng [思明] always regretted not being able to engage in open battle.
Hearing that I was outside,
he thought I could surely be captured.
Rìyuè [日越], failing to capture me,
would dare not return.
Tínghuī's [庭暉] talent and bravery surpassed Rìyuè's [日越].
Hearing that Rìyuè [日越] was favored and entrusted,
he would surely think of supplanting him."
This is called skillfully using one's weaknesses.
Sūn Bìn [孫臏] said:
"A skilled warrior takes advantage of the situation and guides it to his benefit."
Dàizhōu [代州] had Wǔtáifǔ [五臺府].
On the day of Jǐhài [己亥],
Tínghuī [庭暉] was made Yòuwǔwèi Dàjiāngjūn [右武衞大將軍].
The Guǒyì [果毅] of the various Fǔ [府] in Táng [唐]
had a relatively low rank;
a Dàjiāngjūn [大將軍] of the various Wèi [衞]
was of the third rank.
The Kǎoyì [考異] states: The Xīn Zhuàn [新傳] says:
"In the first year of Shàngyuán [上元] (760),
Guāngbì [光弼] accepted the surrender of the rebel generals Gāo Huī [高暉] and Lǐ Rìyuè [李日越]."
According to the Jǐhài [己亥] day of this month,
Gāo Tínghuī [高庭暉] was granted Tèjìn [特進].
It is suspected that he is Gāo Huī [高暉].
On the Dīngsì [丁巳] day,
Lǐ Rìyuè [李日越] was again granted Tèjìn [特進].
This means they had both already surrendered this month.
The Xīn Zhuàn [新傳] is incorrect.
The Bīn Zhì [邠志] states:
"In the third month of the second year,
Sīmíng [思明] led his forces south,
and ordered his son Cháoyì [朝義] to besiege Héyáng [河陽].
On the first day of the fourth month,
Sīmíng [思明] captured Luòchéng [洛城].
In the fifth month of the first year of Shàngyuán [上元],
Sīmíng [思明] demonstrated his military might at Héqīng [河清],
declaring: 'I shall cross the river
and cut off their supply route.
When the three cities run out of food,
they will fall without attack.'
Duke Lǐ [李公] heard of this,
and encamped at Yěshuǐdù [野水渡].
As dusk fell,
he returned to his camp."
This also contradicts the Shílù [實錄].
We now follow the Shílù [實錄].
Sīmíng [思明] again attacked Héyáng [河陽].

Xuē (鞾)

Traditionally,

"Battle

Lǐ Fǔguó had always been of humble origin,

Lǐ Fǔguó's words here

the Shànghuáng will enjoy eternal peace,

An 'imperial edict by forgery'

'Qiū' (湫)

Since the officers and soldiers blocked the road with bared blades,

'Remain well'

Yán'ēn 延恩 presented the imperial edict to Zhǎn 展.

"I, Zhǎn 展, have risen from Cénliú Cānjūn 陳留參軍

One could say I have become powerful too quickly.
Jiāng-Huái 江淮 is where the land tax and levies come from,
and it is now a crucial responsibility.
I, Zhǎn 展, have no meritorious service,
nor am I a close relative or a worthy person.
How can such an extraordinary favor be bestowed upon me overnight?
Is it not perhaps that some slanderer has sowed discord?"
Thereupon, tears streamed down his face.
Yán'ēn 延恩 was afraid,

"You, Gong 公, have always been known for your talent and prestige.

Zhǎn 展 said:
"If the matter is truly not deceptive,

A saying goes:
"To act deceitfully, one's efforts become daily more futile."
This referred to Xíng Yán'ēn 邢延恩.
