If people had accumulated ten *hú* of grain,
they would stand trembling, awaiting their fate,
or gather in mountains and marshes to become bandits,
and the prefectures and counties could not control them.
6 In the *jiànmǎo* month,
on the *xīnhài* *shuò*,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the empire.
Jīngzhào was again designated as Shàngdū,
Hénán as Dōngdū,
Fèngxiáng as Xīdū,
Jiānglíng as Nándū,
and Tàiyuán as Běidū.
Last year, Xījīng and Nándū were abolished.
*Fù* is pronounced
*fú yòu fān*,
and also sounds like the character itself.
7 Nuólà attacked Chénggù.
Chénggù Xiàn,
since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Hànzhōng.
*Là* is pronounced
*lái dá fān*.
8 Earlier,
Wáng Sīlǐ was the Jiédùshǐ of Hédōng,
and his provisions and stores were abundant.
Besides provisioning the army,
he had accumulated a million *hú* of rice,
and memorialized to deliver 500,000 *hú* to the capital.
After Sīlǐ died,
Wáng Sīlǐ was stationed in Tàiyuán in Qiányuán first year;
his death should have occurred last year.
His governance became lax,
and he trusted his subordinates.
Within a few months,
most of the stores were depleted,
with only over ten thousand *hú* of stale rice remaining.
This means the remaining rice was only this amount.
Déng Jǐngshān was appointed to replace him.
When Jǐngshān arrived,
he audited the expenditures and receipts,
and found that many generals and soldiers had embezzled funds,
causing fear among them all.
A deputy general was condemned to death for a crime.
The generals pleaded for him,
but Jǐngshān refused.
The deputy general's brother offered to die in his place,
which was also refused.
He then offered one horse to redeem his brother from death,
and this was granted.
The generals were enraged, saying:
"Are we not even worth a single horse?!"
Thereupon they revolted.
On the *guǐchǒu* day,
they killed Jǐngshān.
The Emperor believed that Jǐngshān's mismanagement led to the rebellion,
and did not further investigate the rebels,
instead sending an envoy to appease them.
The generals requested that Xīn Yúnjīng, the Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ and Cǐshǐ of Dàizhōu, be appointed Jiédùshǐ.
Yúnjīng then memorialized to appoint Zhāng Guāngshèng as Cǐshǐ of Dàizhōu.
Zhāng Guāngshèng had been kind to Xīn Yúnjīng,
as seen in the previous scroll, Qiányuán second year.
9 Jìngzhōu had no reserves,
the people were starving,
and taxes could not be levied.
The soldiers' food and stipends were insufficient.
Lǐ Guózhēn, the acting commander-in-chief of various circuits including Shuòfāng, repeatedly reported the situation in memorials;
the imperial court did not reply,
and the army was full of complaints.
“Jīzā” means to sigh with worry and complain to the emperor.
A “tújiāng”
is one who leads brave and aggressive soldiers.
“Tújiāng”
is pronounced liàng fān.
“Tomorrow, we will repair the commander-in-chief’s residence.
Each of you bring a shovel and a basket,
and await orders at the gate.”
The soldiers were all enraged
and said:
“Are the brave men of Shuòfāng merely house-repairers!”
On the day Yǐchǒu,
Yuán Zhèn led his followers in rebellion,
burning the gate of the governor’s compound.
Guózhēn fled to prison;
Yuán Zhèn captured him,
placed soldier’s food before him,
and said:
“Eat this and be exploited for your labor,
is that acceptable!”
Guózhēn said:
“Regarding repairing the residence, there is none of that.
Regarding military provisions, I have repeatedly memorialized, but there has been no reply,
which you gentlemen all know.”
The crowd wanted to retreat.
Yuán Zhèn said:
“As for today’s matter,
why ask any further!
If the commander-in-chief does not die,
then we will die.”
Thereupon, he drew his blade and killed him.
The expeditionary forces of Zhènxī and Běitíng were stationed in Yìchéng.
Yìchéng County
belonged to Jìngzhōu,
originally Hàn’s Jìng County,
later called Běijìng County in the Northern Wèi.
In Suí’s Kāihuáng eighteenth year,
it was renamed Yìchéng,
because the Marquis of Yì in the Spring and Autumn period had his fief here.
They elevated the adjutant Bái Xiàodé to Jiedushi,
and the imperial court consequently granted him the title.
10 On the day Wùchén,
Wáng Zhòngshēng, the Jiedushi of Huáixī, fought Xiè Qīnràng, a general of Shǐ Cháoyì, beneath the walls of Shēnzhōu.
He was captured by the rebels,
and Huáixī was shaken with fear.
Coincidentally, Hóu Xīyì, Tián Shéngōng, and Néng Yuánhào were attacking Biànzhōu,
so Cháoyì recalled Qīnràng’s troops to rescue it.
11 The various armies of Jìngzhōu continued their plundering,
and the imperial court feared they would join forces with the rebel army in Tàiyuán and ally with the rebels.
As they could not be subdued by the newly appointed generals,
on the day Xīnwèi,
Guō Zǐyí was made Fényáng Wáng,
and appointed acting deputy marshal of the Shuòfāng, Hézhōng, Běitíng, Lùzé Jiedushi expeditionary forces, concurrently commander of the Xīngpíng and Dìngguó armies.
Forty thousand bolts of silk, fifty thousand bolts of cloth, and sixty thousand *shi* of rice were dispatched from the capital to supply the Jìng army.
In the third month (Jiànchén yuè),
on the day Gēngyín,
Zǐyí was about to depart.
At that time, the Emperor was unwell,
and no minister was able to see him.
Zǐyí requested, saying:
“Your old servant has received orders
and is about to die outside.
If I do not see Your Majesty,
my eyes will not close in peace.”
The Emperor summoned him into his sleeping quarters
and said:
“The affairs of Hédōng
are entirely entrusted to you, my dear official.”
Shǐ Cháoyì sent troops to besiege Lǐ Bàoyù in Zézhōu.
Zǐyí dispatched the Dìngguó army to relieve him,
whereupon they withdrew.
12 The Emperor summoned Lái Diàn, the Jiedushi of Shānnán Dōngdào, to the capital;
Diàn was content in Xiāngyáng,
and his generals and soldiers also loved him,
so he implicitly encouraged his subordinate officers to memorialize to keep him.
When he reached Dèngzhōu,
he was ordered to return to his post.
Lǚ Yīn, Jiedushi of Jīngnán, Wáng Zhòngshēng, Jiedushi of Huáixī, and eunuchs traveling back and forth all said
“Diàn is skillfully winning the hearts of the people,
and it is feared he will be difficult to control in the long run.”
The Emperor then carved out Shāng, Jīn, Jūn, and Fáng and established a separate observer-commissioner,
ordering Diàn to govern only six prefectures.
Shānnán Dōngdào governed nine prefectures: Xiāng, Dèng, Suí, Táng, Ān, Jūn, Fáng, Jīn, and Shāng.
Now, four prefectures are separated,
leaving only five prefectures.
To say he governs six prefectures,
could it be that he added one prefecture to the two prefectures of Yǐng and Fù?
Diàn resented this,
held back his troops and did not provide aid,
and Zhòngshēng was eventually defeated and killed.
The acting military commissioner Péi Róng plotted to usurp Diàn’s position,
secretly memorializing that Diàn was stubborn and difficult to control,
requesting to attack him with troops.
The Emperor considered it plausible.
On the day Guǐsì,
Diàn was appointed Jiedushi of Huáixī and the sixteen prefectures of Hénán.
The “Kǎoyì” states: The old biography does not have “Rǔ” and says fifteen prefectures.
Now, we follow the authentic record.
This was actually intended to eliminate him.
A secret edict was issued appointing Róng to replace Diàn as the defense commissioner of Xiāng, Dèng, and other prefectures.
13 On the day Jiǎwǔ,
Núlā invaded Liángzhōu,
and the observer-commissioner Lǐ Miǎn abandoned the city and fled.
At that time, the observer-commissioner of Shānnán Xīdào had his office in Liángzhōu.
The Jiedushi of Shānnán Xīdào governed thirteen prefectures: Liáng, Yáng, Jí, Bì, Wén, Tōng, Bā, Xīng, Fèng, Lì, Kāi, Qú, and Péng.
“Bīn”
is pronounced mí pín fān.
“Shǐ”
is pronounced shū lì fān.
The “Kǎoyì” states: The *Sùzōng Shílù* records it as
“Xīyè.”
The *Dàizōng Shílù* has a biography
and records it as
“Xīràng.”
We follow this now.
14 On the day Bǐngshēn,
the Dǎngxiàng invaded Fèngtiān.
15 Lǐ Fǔguó resented Xiāo Huá because he failed to obtain the position of chancellor.
The incident of failing to obtain the chancellorship is recorded in the *Shàngshàngyuán* second year, eighth month.
“Xiāng”
is pronounced xì liàng fān.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
Yuán Zài, a vice minister of the Ministry of Revenue, was made Jingzhao尹.
Zài went to Fǔguó and firmly declined,
Fǔguó understood his intention.
On the day Rén Yín,
Táo Ruì, the Minister of the Court of Agricultural Supervision, was made Jingzhao尹.
Fǔguó stated that Xiāo Huá was abusing his power
and requested that his chancellorship be revoked,
but the Emperor did not consent.
Fǔguó insisted repeatedly,
and finally the Emperor agreed,
and then brought in Yuán Zài to replace Huá.
The “Kǎoyì” states: The old biography of Huá says:
“When Sùzōng was ill in bed,
Fǔguó falsely issued an edict to dismiss Huá from chancellorship.”
Now, we follow Fǔguó’s biography.
On the day Wùshēn,
Huá was dismissed and made Minister of Rites,
and Zài was appointed *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*,
retaining his former posts as Commissioner of Finance and Transport.
16 In the fourth month (Jiànsì yuè),
on the first day Gēngxū,
“Jiànsì yuè”
is the fourth month.
17 On the day Rénzǐ,
Cuī Shēn, the Prefect of Chǔzhōu, memorialized, claiming
that there was a nun named Zhēnrú,
who in a trance ascended to heaven,
met the Heavenly Emperor,
and was given thirteen precious jade pieces,
who said:
“There are calamities in the Central Plains;
use these to quell them.”
All the ministers memorialized their congratulations.
18 On the day Jiǎyín,
the Retired Emperor passed away in the Shénlóng Diàn.
The Shénlóng Diàn
was likely where Zhōngzōng resided during the Shénlóng period,
and thus the hall was named after it.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
his coffin was moved to the Tàijí Diàn.
The Emperor, being ill,
expressed his grief in the inner palace,
while all the ministers expressed their grief in the Tàijí Diàn.
The inner palace
was the Emperor's sleeping quarters in the Dàmíng Gōng.
The Tàijí Diàn
was the front hall of the Western Palace,
where the deceased Emperor resided.
On the day Bǐngchén,
Miáo Jìnqīng was ordered to act as the chief minister for the funeral.
The Emperor had been ill since mid-spring.
Hearing of the Retired Emperor's demise,
he mourned,
and his illness worsened.
Thereupon, he ordered the Crown Prince to oversee the state.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
an edict was issued to change the reign title;
the reign title was changed to Bǎoyīng.
All the month designations remained as before;
a general amnesty was granted to the empire.
19 Initially,
Empress Zhāng (Zhāng Hòu) and Lǐ Fǔguó (Lǐ Fǔguó) were in league with each other,
wielding exclusive power and authority,
as seen in Volume 77, Qiányuán (Qiányuán) second year.
Later, a rift emerged.
The Inner Archery Commissioner (Nèi Shèshēng Shǐ), Chéng Yuánzhèn (Chéng Yuánzhèn) of Sānyuán (Sānyuán), a eunuch, was a partisan of Fǔguó (Fǔguó).
Because a eunuch commanded the archers,
he was called the Inner Archery Commissioner.
The empress summoned the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) and said:
"Lǐ Fǔguó (Lǐ Fǔguó) has long commanded the palace guard (jìnbīng);
imperial edicts all issue from him;
he dared to force the Sacred Emperor (Shèng Huáng) to move.
Xuánzōng (Xuánzōng) was honored with the title Sacred Emperor of Heaven (Shèng Huáng Tiāndì).
Those he fears are I and the Crown Prince.
Now the Lord (Zhǔshàng) is dying;
the imperial decree says:
'The illness daily worsens,
already in extremis.' "
It means the illness progresses day by day,
lingering and not leaving the body.
"He must be executed."
The Crown Prince wept and said:
"Your Majesty (Bìxià) is gravely ill;
both are old and meritorious ministers of Your Majesty;
to execute them suddenly without warning
will surely cause shock and alarm,
which I fear cannot be endured."
The empress said:
"In that case, the Crown Prince may return for now;
I will reconsider slowly."
After the Crown Prince left,
the empress summoned Wáng Xì (Wáng Xì) of Yuè (Yuè) and said:
"The Crown Prince is too soft and weak
to execute the treacherous minister;
can you do it?"
He replied:
"I can."
Xì (Xì) then ordered the Supervisor of the Inner Attendants (Nèi Yèzhě Jiān), Duàn Héngjùn (Duàn Héngjùn), to select over two hundred brave and strong eunuchs,
and armed them behind the Chángshēng (Chángshēng) Palace.
On the *yǐchǒu* (yǐchǒu) day,
the empress, using the Lord's (Shàng) command, summoned the Crown Prince.
Yuánzhèn (Yuánzhèn) knew of her plot,
secretly informed Fǔguó (Fǔguó), and laid an ambush at the Língxiāo (Língxiāo) Gate to await him.
Yōng Lù (Yōng Lù): According to the *Liù Diǎn Dàmínggōng Tú* (Liù Diǎn Dàmínggōng Tú), west of Xuánwǔ (Xuánwǔ) Gate on the north side of the palace city is the Qīngxiāo (Qīngxiāo) Gate.
The *Géběn Dàmínggōng Tú* (Géběn Dàmínggōng Tú) has Língyún (Língyún) Gate.
He reported the danger.
The Crown Prince said:
"There can be no such thing;
the Lord (Zhǔshàng) is gravely ill and has summoned me;
how can I fear death and not go?"
Yuánzhèn (Yuánzhèn) said:
"The affairs of the state (shèjì) are grave;
the Crown Prince absolutely cannot enter."
He then led troops to escort the Crown Prince to the Fēilóng Kuì (Fēilóng Kuì).
The Fēilóng Kuì (Fēilóng Kuì)
was one of the six stables within the palace (zhàngnèi liùxián).
Chéng Dàchāng (Chéng Dàchāng) said: It was outside Xuánwǔ (Xuánwǔ) Gate.
That night,
Fǔguó (Fǔguó) and Yuánzhèn (Yuánzhèn) commanded troops to the three palaces,

arrested Wáng Xì (Wáng Xì) of Yuè (Yuè), Duàn Héngjùn (Duàn Héngjùn), and Zhū Guānghuī (Zhū Guānghuī), the Acting Commissioner of the Inner Attendants (Zhī Nèi Shìshěng Shì), and over a hundred others,
and imprisoned them.
By order of the Crown Prince, the empress was moved to a side palace.
At this time, the Lord (Shàng) was in the Chángshēng (Chángshēng) Palace.
Envoys forced the empress to descend from the palace,
and she, along with dozens of her attendants, was confined to the rear palace.
Eunuchs and palace women were all terrified and scattered.
On the *dīngmǎo* (dīngmǎo) day,
the Lord (Shàng) passed away.
He was fifty-two years old.
That day,
Fǔguó (Fǔguó) first led the Crown Prince, dressed in plain mourning attire, to the Jiǔxiān (Jiǔxiān) Gate to meet the prime ministers (zǎixiàng).
According to the *Géběn Dàmínggōng Tú* (Géběn Dàmínggōng Tú),
north of the Yòuyíntái (Yòuyíntái) Gate on the west side of the palace city is the Jiǔxiān (Jiǔxiān) Gate,
and further north, turning east, is the Língyún (Língyún) Gate.
Xiàng (Xiàng) is read *xīliàng* (xīliàng).
They bowed and wept,
relating how, since the Supreme Emperor's (Shàng Huáng) passing,
there had been many troubles in the palace,
and no auxiliary ministers had been seen.
The order for the Crown Prince to supervise the state (jiānguó) was before the *jiǎzǐ* (jiǎzǐ) day,
but on *yǐchǒu* (yǐchǒu) there was already an internal disturbance.
Once it was settled,
the order was then carried out.
Jiān (Jiān) is read *gǔxián* (gǔxián).
On the *wùchén* (wùchén) day,
the mourning rites for the Great Departed Emperor (Dàxíng Huángdì) were commenced at the Liǎngyí (Liǎngyí) Palace,
and his last will was proclaimed.
Sùzōng (Sùzōng) passed away in the east inner sleeping chamber,
but the mourning rites were commenced in the west inner court (nèi cháo),
following the precedent of the Supreme Emperor (Shàng Huáng).
The Supreme Emperor's (Shàng Huáng) coffin was in the west inner front palace.
On the *jǐsì* (jǐsì) day,
Dàizōng (Dàizōng) ascended the throne.
20 Gāo Lìshì (Gāo Lìshì) was pardoned and returned,
reaching Lǎngzhōu (Lǎngzhōu).
In the first year of Shàngyuán (Shàngyuán), Gāo Lìshì (Gāo Lìshì) was exiled to Wūzhōu (Wūzhōu),
and was pardoned and returned to Lǎngzhōu (Lǎngzhōu).
From Lǎngzhōu (Lǎngzhōu) to the capital (Jīngshī) was still 2,259 *lǐ*.
The pardon was the *jiǎzǐ* (jiǎzǐ) amnesty.
Huán (Huán) is read *cóngxuān* (cóngxuān), also pronounced as written.
He wailed in grief,
vomited blood, and died.
Lìshì (Lìshì)'s exile is seen in Volume 77, first year of Shàngyuán (Shàngyuán).
Háo (Háo) is read *hùdāo* (hùdāo).
Zú (Zú) is read *zǐxù* (zǐxù).
21 On the *jiǎxū* (jiǎxū) day,
the imperial son, Fèngjié (Fèngjié) King Shì (Shì), was made Grand Marshal of All Armed Forces (Tiānxià Bīngmǎ Yuánshuài).
Fèngjié (Fèngjié) is a county name;
the Former Lord (Xiān Zhǔ) of Shǔ (Shǔ) changed Fúfù (Fúfù) County to Fèngjié (Fèngjié) County.
Shuài (Shuài) is read *suǒlèi* (suǒlèi).
22 Lǐ Fǔguó (Lǐ Fǔguó), relying on his achievements, became even more arrogant,
openly telling the Lord (Shàng):
"Your Majesty (Dàjiā) need only reside within the palace;
external affairs will be handled by this old servant."
He spoke this openly before the Lord (Shàng),
without any fear or restraint.
Héng (Héng) is read *hùmèng* (hùmèng).
Chǔ (Chǔ) is read *chānglǚ* (chānglǚ).
Fèn (Fèn) is read *fúwèn* (fúwèn).
Because he was then in command of the palace guards,
he was outwardly honored.
On the *yǐhài* (yǐhài) day,
Fǔguó (Fǔguó) was honored with the title Shàngfù (Shàngfù) and was not addressed by his given name.
Tài Gōng (Tài Gōng) of Qí (Qí) assisted King Wǔ (Wǔ Wáng) of Zhōu (Zhōu)
and was called Shī Shàngfù (Shī Shàngfù);
now this title was bestowed upon a palace attendant to show favor.
All ministers, when entering and exiting, first went to Fǔguó (Fǔguó),
and he calmly accepted it.
Historians say Lǐ Fǔguó (Lǐ Fǔguó) was brutal and foolish.
Chǔ (Chǔ) is read *chānglǚ* (chānglǚ).

The Acting Commissioner of the Inner Attendants (Zhī Nèi Shìshěng Shì) Zhū Guānghuī (Zhū Guānghuī), along with the Inner Regular Attendant (Nèi Chángshì) Dàn Tíngyáo (Dàn Tíngyáo), the mountain man Lǐ Táng (Lǐ Táng), and over twenty others, were all exiled to Qiánzhōng (Qiánzhōng).
From Zhū Guānghuī (Zhū Guānghuī) downwards,
all were attendants of the Great Departed (Dàxíng).
Jiān (Jiān) is read *gǔxián* (gǔxián).
Dàn (Dàn) is read *túlǎn* (túlǎn).
Qián (Qián) is read *qímǐn* (qímǐn).
23 Initially,
Lǐ Guózhēn (Lǐ Guózhēn) governed the army strictly,
and the officers and soldiers of Shuòfāng (Shuòfāng) were unhappy,
all missing Guō Zǐyí (Guō Zǐyí);
thus Wáng Yuánzhèn (Wáng Yuánzhèn) took advantage of this to rebel.
When Zǐyí (Zǐyí) arrived at the army,
Yuánzhèn (Yuánzhèn) considered it his own accomplishment.
Zǐyí (Zǐyí) said:
"You are on the border of enemy territory;
Jiàngzhōu (Jiàngzhōu) is bordered on the east by Hénán (Hénán).
At that time, the rebels also occupied Héyáng (Héyáng) and Hénèi (Hénèi),
hence the saying.
If the rebels seized the opportunity,
Xìn (Xìn) means 'gap' or 'opportunity'.
Jiàng (Jiàng) is read *jíliàng* (jíliàng).
I am a prime minister (zǎixiàng);
how can I accept a private soldier!"
In the fifth month,
on the *gēngchén* (gēngchén) day,
Yuánzhèn (Yuánzhèn) and forty of his co-conspirators were arrested
and all executed.
Xīn Yúnjīng (Xīn Yúnjīng), hearing of this,
also investigated and arrested dozens of those who had killed Dèng Jǐngshān (Dèng Jǐngshān),
and executed them.
From then on, the various prefectures (zhèn) of Hédōng (Hédōng) generally obeyed the law.
Guō Zǐyí (Guō Zǐyí) executed Wáng Yuánzhèn (Wáng Yuánzhèn), and the various prefectures of Hédōng (Hédōng) all obeyed the law,

while Púgǔ Huái'ēn (Púgǔ Huái'ēn) divided the various prefectures of Héběi (Héběi) and distributed them to Tián Chéngsì (Tián Chéngsì) and others, leading to the disaster of the vassal prefectures (fānzhèn).
How cautious one must be in employing people!
24 On the *rénwǔ* (rénwǔ) day,
Lǐ Fǔguó (Lǐ Fǔguó) was made Sīkōng (Sīkōng) concurrently Grand Chancellor (Zhōngshū Lìng).
25 The Dǎngxiàng (Dǎngxiàng) plundered Tóngguān (Tóngguān) and Huáyuan (Huáyuan).
26 On the *jiǎshēn* (jiǎshēn) day,
Hóu Xīyì (Hóu Xīyì), Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ) of Pínglú (Pínglú), was made Military Governor of Pínglú (Pínglú), Qīng (Qīng), Zī (Zī), and other six prefectures.
The six prefectures were Qīng (Qīng), Zī (Zī), Qí (Qí), Yí (Yí), Mì (Mì), and Hǎi (Hǎi).
Zīzhōu (Zīzhōu)'s seat of government was Zīchuān (Zīchuān),
originally Bānyáng (Bānyáng) County in the Hàn (Hàn) dynasty.
The Sòng (Sòng) dynasty relocated Qīnghé (Qīnghé) Commandery and Bèiqiú (Bèiqiú) County there.
During the Wèi (Wèi) dynasty, it was Dōngqīnghé (Dōngqīnghé) Commandery.
The Suí (Suí) dynasty established Zīzhōu (Zīzhōu),
named after the Zī (Zī) River.
On the 27th, *yǐyǒu* day,
Wáng Shì (王適), Prince of Fèngjié (奉節), was transferred to be the Prince of Lǔ (魯).
On the 28th,
Wú (吳), the Emperor's late mother, was posthumously honored as Empress Dowager.
Wú (吳) served Sùzōng (肅宗) in the Eastern Palace,
gave birth to the present Emperor, and then passed away.
On the 29th, *rénchén* day,
Xiāo Huá (蕭華), Minister of Rites, was demoted to *sīmǎ* of Xiázhōu (峽州).
Yuán Zǎi (元載) sought to align with Lǐ Fǔguó's (李輔國) intentions,
and Fǔguó (輔國) was displeased with Huá (華).
On the 30th, an imperial edict declared that all *Qiányuán* (乾元) large and small coins should be worth one (of previous currency) each.
The people then began to settle down.
The people found the two-denomination *Qiányuán* (乾元) coins inconvenient;
see the previous volume, *Qiányuán* (乾元) second year.
Shǐ Cháoyì (史朝義) had besieged Sòngzhōu (宋州) for several months.
Food in the city was exhausted,
and it was about to fall.
Lǐ Cén (李岑), the prefect, was at a loss.
Suí Chéngguǒyì (遂城果毅) Liú Chāng (劉昌) of Kāifēng (開封) said:
Yìzhōu (易州) has Suí Chéngfǔ (遂城府).
Kāifēng (開封) and Hànxiàn (漢縣)
belonged to Biànzhōu (汴州) under the Táng (唐).
The old Hàn (漢) county was fifty *lǐ* south of the present county.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: After the Tiānbǎo (天寶) era,
frontier commanders, relying on imperial favor,
would readily request appointments.
Such as "separate commander" or "valiant general" for Suí Chéngfǔ (遂城府) in Yìzhōu (易州) or Āntáifǔ (安臺府) in Fángzhōu (坊州)
—each imperial decree would appoint over a thousand people.
"There are still several thousand *jīn* of yeast in the granary.
Please grind it for food.
In no more than twenty days,
Grand Marshal Lǐ (李) will surely rescue us."
Grand Marshal Lǐ (李) refers to Guāngbì (光弼).
Chāng (昌) requested to hold out.
Lǐ Guāngbì (李光弼) arrived at Línhuái (臨淮).
His generals, believing Cháoyì's (朝義) forces were still strong,
requested to withdraw south to protect Yángzhōu (揚州).
Guāngbì (光弼) said:
"The court relies on me for its safety or peril.
If I retreat again,
what hope does the court have?
Moreover, I will attack when they least expect it.
How will the rebels know whether my forces are many or few?"
He then proceeded directly to Xúzhōu (徐州)
and sent Tián Shénggōng (田神功), the Military Commissioner of Yǎn-Yùn (兗鄆), to attack Cháoyì (朝義),
inflicting a great defeat.
Previously,
Tián Shénggōng (田神功), having conquered Liú Zhǎn (劉展) (see
Shénggōng (神功) conquered Liú Zhǎn (劉展) in the first month of last year.
The character "先" (xiān)
is pronounced *xī* (悉) and *fán* (翻).
The same applies below.)
Shàng Héng (尚衡), Prince Consort and Grand Master, and Yīn Zhòngqīng (殷仲卿), Grand General of the Left Yǔlín (羽林), were attacking each other in Yǎn (兗) and Yùn (鄆).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: Héng (衡) became Military Commissioner of Zīqīng (淄青) in the first year of Shàngyuán (上元).
In the fifth month of this year,
Tián Shénggōng (田神功) moved from Zīqīng (淄青) to Yǎn-Yùn (兗鄆).
In the sixth month,
Héng (衡) moved from Prince Consort and Grand Master to Grand Master Remonstrant.
In the seventh month,
Zhòngqīng (仲卿) moved from Grand General of the Left Yǔlín (羽林) to Grand Master of Ceremonies.
The reason they could still attack each other in Yǎn (兗) and Yùn (鄆)
is probably that Héng (衡) had not yet left Zīqīng (淄青),
and Zhòngqīng (仲卿) was also there.
Although they had new appointments,
they were unwilling to enter the court.
Fearing his formidable reputation,
Shénggōng (神功) immediately returned to Hénán (河南).
This Hénán (河南) refers to the entire Hénán (河南) circuit.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The old biography states:
"Cháoyì (朝義), capitalizing on his victory at Běimáng (北邙),
invaded thirteen prefectures including Shēn (申) and Guāng (光).
He personally led his elite cavalry to besiege Lǐ Cén (李岑) in Sòngzhōu (宋州).
The officers and soldiers were all afraid,
and requested to withdraw south to protect Yángzhōu (揚州).
Guāngbì (光弼) went directly to Xúzhōu (徐州) to stabilize the situation
and sent Tián Shénggōng (田神功) to defeat him."
It also says:
"Initially,
when Guāngbì (光弼) was about to go to Línhuái (臨淮),
he traveled along the road, carried in a palanquin due to illness.
The supervising envoy, seeing that Yuán Cháo (袁晁) was disturbing Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮),
and that Guāngbì (光弼) had few troops,
requested to protect Rùnzhōu (潤州) to avoid his vanguard.
Guāngbì (光弼) did not comply,
and went directly to Sìzhōu (泗州).
Guāngbì (光弼) had not yet reached Hénán (河南).
After Tián Shénggōng (田神功) pacified Liú Zhǎn (劉展),
he lingered in Yángfǔ (揚府).
Shàng Héng (尚衡) and Yīn Zhòngqīng (殷仲卿) were attacking each other in Yǎn (兗) and Yùn (鄆),
and Lái Tián (來瑱) was resisting in Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
When Guāngbì (光弼) arrived at Xúzhōu (徐州) with light cavalry,
Shǐ Cháoyì (史朝義) retreated.
Tián Shénggōng (田神功) immediately returned to Hénán (河南).
Shàng Héng (尚衡), Yīn Zhòngqīng (殷仲卿), and Lái Tián (來瑱) all feared his formidable reputation
and successively came to the capital."
According to this, since Guāngbì (光弼) sent Tián Shénggōng (田神功) to defeat Cháoyì (朝義),
Shénggōng (神功) must have already returned.
The *Shílù* (實錄) (Veritable Records) states that
Yuán Cháo (袁晁) only captured Táizhōu (臺州) in the eighth month of this year.
Even if he had already disturbed Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮) at that time,
going from Sìzhōu (泗州) to Rùnzhōu (潤州)
could not be called "avoiding his vanguard."
We now follow the new biography.
While Guāngbì (光弼) was in Xúzhōu (徐州),
he personally decided only on military matters.
All other public affairs
were entrusted to the Assistant Official Zhāng Càn (張傪).
Càn (傪) was skilled and swift in official duties,
managing affairs with fluidity.
When generals reported matters,
Guāngbì (光弼) often ordered them to discuss with Càn (傪).
The generals served Càn (傪) as if he were Guāngbì (光弼) himself.
Because of this, the army was well-ordered,
and the eastern realm was pacified.
Previously,
Tián Shénggōng (田神功) had risen from a junior officer to Military Commissioner.
(In the sixth month of last year, Tián Shénggōng (田神功) was appointed Military Commissioner of Yǎn-Yùn (兗鄆) from Commander of Pínglú (平盧) forces.)
Shénggōng (神功) would receive all salutations on equal terms.
But when he saw Guāngbì (光弼) and Càn (傪) treating each other with equal ceremony,
he was greatly astonished.
He then bowed to all his subordinates, saying:
"Shénggōng (神功) comes from the ranks
and does not understand proper etiquette.
Why did none of you gentlemen speak up
and allow Shénggōng (神功) to commit this error?"
The historian comments that fierce military commanders can be transformed by etiquette,
and those in superior positions should set an example with their own conduct.
"行" (xíng)
is pronounced *hù* (戶) and *gāng* (剛).
On the 32nd, *dīngyǒu* day,
a general amnesty was granted.
On the 33rd, the imperial prince Máo (邈), Prince of Yìchāng (益昌), was made Prince of Zhèng (鄭).
(During the Tiānbǎo (天寶) era, Lìzhōu (利州) was renamed Yìchāng Jùn (益昌郡).)
Jué (迥) was made Prince of Hán (韓).
On the 34th, Lái Tián (來瑱), hearing of his transfer to Huáixī (淮西),
was greatly alarmed.
He submitted a memorial saying:
"There are no provisions in Huáixī (淮西).
Please allow me to wait until after the wheat harvest before moving."
He also subtly encouraged his officers to keep him.
Lái Tián (來瑱), wielding his followers to pressure the emperor,
desired to seek another exemption—would he succeed?
On the *rén'yín* day,
Tián (瑱) was reinstated as Military Commissioner of Shānnán Dōngdào (山南東道).
On the 35th, Chéng Yuánzhèn (程元振), Vice Envoy of Fēilóng (飛龍), plotted to usurp Lǐ Fǔguó's (李輔國) power.
He secretly advised the Emperor
to gradually curb Fǔguó's (輔國) authority.
In the sixth month,
on the *jǐwèi* day,
Fǔguó (輔國) was relieved of his duties as Grand Marshal and Minister of War.
His other positions remained unchanged.
Yuánzhèn (元振) was appointed acting Grand Marshal
and Fǔguó (輔國) was moved to reside in an outer mansion.
Since the time of Sùzōng (肅宗),
Lǐ Fǔguó (李輔國) had always resided in the inner quarters of the Forbidden City.
Fǔguó (輔國) began to feel apprehensive and
submitted a memorial declining his position.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Fǔguó (輔guó) was dismissed from his concurrent post as Grand Chancellor
and his noble title was advanced to Prince of Bólù (博陸).
Fǔguó (輔guó) entered to express his gratitude,
choking with indignation, and said:
"This old slave has failed to serve my young master properly.
I request to return to the underworld to serve the late emperor!"
The Emperor still comforted and dismissed him.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The old biography states:
"Fǔguó (輔guó) wished to enter the Secretariat to present a memorial of thanks.
The gatekeeper stopped him, saying:
'Since the Grand Mentor has been dismissed from his chancellorship,
he should not enter this gate again.'
Fǔguó (輔guó) was indignant and said:
'This old slave is worthy of death, having failed to serve my young master properly.
I request to return to the underworld to serve the late emperor.'
The Emperor still responded with a gracious edict."
However, this was a statement made to the Emperor,
not to the gatekeeper.
We now follow the *Táng Jì* (唐紀).
On the 36th, *rénxū* day,
Yán Wǔ (嚴武), Vice Minister of War, was appointed Military Commissioner of Xīchuān (西川).
Thirty-seven. Péi Rǒng (裴茙), the Defense Commissioner of Xiāng and Dèng, was stationed at Gǔchéng.
Gǔchéng
was the land of Zhúyáng (筑陽) County during the Hàn dynasty,
and the Jìn dynasty established Yìchéng (義成) Commandery and Yìchéng County there.
In the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng (開皇) of the Suí dynasty,
the commandery was abolished,
and the county was renamed Gǔchéng,
because of the Gǔchéng Mountain in its territory.
Péi Rǒng then led his two thousand subordinates along the Hàn River towards Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
On the *jǐsì* day,
he arrayed his troops north of the Gǔ River.
Lái Tiān (來瑱) met them with his troops,
asking why they had come.
Péi Rǒng replied:
"The Minister (尚書) has not accepted the imperial decree,
so we have come.
If he accepts the replacement,
we will respectfully lay down our arms."
Lái Tiān said:
"I have already received imperial favor,
and am to remain in command here;
how can there be any replacement!"
He then took out the imperial decree and his commission to show them.
Péi Rǒng was astonished and confused.
Lái Tiān and his deputy commissioner Xuē Nányáng (薛南陽) deployed their troops to attack from both sides,
thoroughly defeating them.
They pursued and captured Péi Rǒng at Shēnkǒu (申口).
There is Shēnkǒu Town in Xúnyáng (洵陽) County, Jīn Prefecture.
Péi Rǒng was granted death.
The *Kǎo Yì* (考異) states: The old biography of Péi Rǒng says:
"Lái Tiān prepared a feast at the river crossing to await him.
Péi Rǒng initially declared he was merely asking for passage to the capital,
but upon seeing Lái Tiān,
he immediately claimed to be his replacement,
and wished to assume office.
Lái Tiān replied: 'I (Lái Tiān) have already received the imperial decree
and am reinstated in this position.'
Péi Rǒng was bewildered,
and explained to his subordinates: 'These words must be false.'
He then led his men to shoot at Lái Tiān's army,
and subsequently engaged Lái Tiān's troops in battle.
Péi Rǒng's army was utterly defeated."
However, if Lái Tiān had set up a feast to meet him,
how could Péi Rǒng have suddenly shot at Lái Tiān's army and engaged in battle?
Now we follow Lái Tiān's biography.
Thirty-eight. On the *yǐhài* day,
Liú Yàn (劉晏), the Prefect of Tōng Prefecture,
Liú Yàn was demoted to Tōng Prefecture in November of the previous year.
was appointed Commissioner of Revenue, Transport, Salt and Iron, and Coinage.
Thirty-nine. In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the *rénchén* day,
Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) was made Overall Commander of the military camps of Shuòfāng (朔方), Hédōng (河東), Běitíng (北庭), and the military governors of Lù (潞), Yí (儀), Zé (澤), Qìn (沁), Chén (陳), Zhèng (鄭), etc.
At this time, Lù, Yí, Zé, Qìn, Chén, and Zhèng were constituted as one military region,
with Lǐ Bàoyù (李抱玉) as the military governor.
This was because Lǐ Bàoyù had previously, as military governor of Chén and Zhèng, been suppressing rebels in the field,
and after Lǐ Guāngbì's (李光弼) defeat at Máng Mountain,
Lǐ Bàoyù fled to Zé Prefecture.
Chén and Zhèng were cut off by the rebels,
so the imperial court then made him military governor of the four prefectures of Lù, Yí, Qìn, and Zé.
Forty. On the *guǐsì* day,
Xú Zhīdào (徐知道), the Army Commander of Jiànnán (劍南), rebelled.
He guarded strategic points with his troops,
resisting Yán Wǔ (嚴武),
who could not advance.
Forty-one. In the eighth month,
Xíng Jì (邢濟), the Prefect of Guì Prefecture, attacked the Western Yuán (西原) rebel leaders Wú Gōngcáo (吳功曹) and others,
and pacified them.
Forty-two. On the *jǐwèi* day,
Xú Zhīdào was killed by his general Lǐ Zhōnghòu (李忠厚),
and Jiànnán was entirely pacified.
Forty-three. On the *yǐchǒu* day,
Lái Tiān, the Military Governor of Shānnán Dōngdào (山南東道), came to the capital to apologize for his offense,
and the emperor treated him with exceptional courtesy.
Forty-four. On the *jǐsì* day,
Guō Zǐyí came to the capital from Hédōng.
At that time, Chéng Yuánzhèn (程元振) wielded great power,
and was jealous of Guō Zǐyí's great achievements and important position,
frequently slandering him to the emperor.
Guō Zǐyí felt uneasy,
and submitted a memorial requesting to resign from the posts of Deputy Marshal and Military Governor.
The emperor comforted and appeased him,
so Guō Zǐyí remained in the capital.
Forty-five. Yuán Cháo (袁晁), a rebel leader from Tái Prefecture, captured and occupied various prefectures in Zhèdōng (浙東),
and changed the era name to Bǎoshèng (寶勝).
The *Kǎo Yì* states: Liǔ Càn's (柳璨) *Zhèng Rùn Wèi Lì* (正閏位曆) and Sòng Xiáng's (宋庠) *Jìyuán Tōngpǔ* (紀元通譜) both record the era name as Shēngguó (昇國).
Now we follow the New History.
Lǐ Guāngbì dispatched troops to attack Yuán Cháo in Qú Prefecture.
Qú Prefecture
was the land of Gūmiè (姑蔑) during the Spring and Autumn period, belonging to Yuè.
Qín established Tàimò (太末) County there,
Hàn divided it to establish Xīn'ān (新安) County,
and Jìn renamed it Xìn'ān.
Táng established Qú Prefecture,
named after the Sānqú Mountain.
In ancient times, a flood divided the mountain into three paths,
hence it was called Sānqú.
(斂) *liàn*, read *lìshàn fān*.
Forty-six. On the *yǐhài* day,
Lǔ Wáng Shì (魯王适) was transferred to become Yōng Wáng (雍王).
Forty-seven. In the ninth month,
on the *gēngchén* day,
Lái Tiān was appointed Minister of War, Grand Chancellor (*Tóng Píngzhāngshì*), and concurrently Military Governor of Shānnán Dōngdào.
Forty-eight. On the *yǐwèi* day,
Chéng Yuánzhèn was promoted to Grand General of Agile Cavalry (驃騎大將軍) and concurrently Director of the Palace Secretariat (內侍監).
Forty-nine. Péi Miǎn (裴冕), the Left Prime Minister, was made Commissioner of Imperial Tombs.
During the construction of the imperial tombs,
the Táng dynasty established the position of Commissioner of Imperial Tombs,
held by a Chancellor.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
Péi Miǎn was demoted to Prefect of Shī Prefecture.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: According to the *Dàizōng Shílù* (代宗實錄):
"Hán Yǐng (韓穎), the Secretary of the Imperial Library, and Liú Xuǎn (劉烜), a Secretariat Drafter, were skilled at observing stars and calendars.
During the Qiányuán (乾元) era, they served as Imperial Academicians,
and received considerable imperial favor.
They were also close to Lǐ Fǔguó (李輔國).
At that time, the emperor was deeply worried about the imperial tombs,
and widely sought divination.
Hán Yǐng and others could not be precise and careful,
making arbitrary predictions of good or ill.
Because of this, they were found guilty,
and exiled to Língnán (嶺南).
After they departed,
they were granted death on the way.
Initially,
Péi Miǎn, as Left Prime Minister,
often discussed current affairs.
He was subsequently concurrently appointed Grand Master of Censors
and served as Commissioner of Imperial Tombs.
Because Lǐ Fǔguó held great power and favor,
Péi Miǎn then recommended Lǐ Fǔguó's trusted confidant Liú Xuǎn as an assessor,
secretly aligning himself with Lǐ Fǔguó.
When Liú Xuǎn was found guilty,
Péi Miǎn was implicated."
Now we follow the old biography of Chéng Yuánzhèn.
In the 50th year, the Emperor sent the court envoy Liú Qīngtán
to Huíhé to renew their old friendship
and to conscript troops to attack Shǐ Cháoyì.
When Qīngtán arrived at their court,
Huíhé's Dēnglǐ Kèhán had already been lured by Cháoyì,
who said,
"The Táng dynasty has successively suffered great bereavements;
now the Central Plains are without a ruler,"
referencing the successive deaths of Xuánzōng and Sùzōng.
Thus, he lied that the Central Plains were without a ruler.
The Kèhán believed him.
Qīngtán delivered the imperial edict, saying:
"Although the former emperor has departed this world,
the present emperor, who inherited the succession,
is the former Guǎngpíng Wáng,
who, together with Yèhù, recovered the two capitals."
This event is recorded in volume 220, second year of Zhìdé.
This refers to the three fortresses of Shuòfāng.
Having the intention to slight Táng,
he therefore humiliated Qīngtán.
Qīngtán sent an envoy to report the situation
and also said,
"The entire Huíhé nation, with 100,000 troops, is approaching!"
The capital was greatly alarmed.
The Emperor sent the Palace Commissioner Yào Zǐ'áng to comfort them south of Xīnzhōu.
Originally,
Píjiā Què Kèhán sought a marriage for Dēnglǐ.
Sùzōng gave his daughter, Púgù Huái'ēn's daughter, in marriage to him,
becoming Dēnglǐ Kèdūn.
The Kèhán requested to meet Huái'ēn.
Huái'ēn was then in Fénzhōu.
The Emperor ordered him to go and meet him.
Huái'ēn told the Kèhán that the Táng family's grace and trust should not be betrayed.
The Kèhán was pleased,
sent an envoy to present a memorial,
requesting to assist the state in attacking Cháoyì.
The Kèhán wished to enter through Púguān,
exit through Shāyuàn, and head east from Tóngguān.
Yào Zǐ'áng persuaded him, saying:
"Guānzhōng has suffered repeated military conflicts and famine.
The prefectures and counties are desolate,
with nothing to supply you.
I fear the Kèhán will be disappointed.
The rebel troops are all in Luòyáng.
Please enter from Tǔmén, take Xíng, Míng, Huái, and Wèi to the south,
and acquire their resources to equip your army."
The Kèhán did not agree.
He then requested
"to descend south from Tàiháng and occupy Héyīn,
choking the rebels' throat."
Kě,
from kān, entering tone.
Hán,
pronounced hán.
Háng,
hù gāng fān.
Yān,
pronounced yān.
He again requested
"to cross the river from Dàyángjīn in Shǎnzhōu."
North of Shǎnxiàn in Shǎnzhōu is Dàyángguān,
a vital crossing point of the Yellow River.
This is where, as recorded in the Zuǒzhuàn, Qín Mèngmíng attacked Jìn,
crossing from Máojīn,
and burying the bodies at Yáo,
also known as Shǎnjīn.
Shǎn,
shī rǎn fān.
"and advance together with the various armies."
So, they agreed to this.
The Suí dynasty established Tàiyuán Granary
in the Hédōng region.
History states that Huíhé's interest lay in China's treasures,
and they dared not lightly engage the rebels.
Yuán Cháo captured Xìnzhōu.
Xìnzhōu was
originally Gèyáng Xiàn of Wú's Póyáng Jùn.
Chén changed Gèyáng to Yìyáng.
In the first year of Táng Qiányuán,
Yìyáng from Ráozhōu, Chángshān and Yùshān from Qúzhōu, and parts of Jiànzhōu and Fúzhōu were separated to establish Xìnzhōu,
with its seat in Shàngráo Xiàn,
named after being adjacent to Xiàráozhōu.
Hence the county's name.
Cháo,
chí yáo fān.
In winter,
tenth month,
Yuán Cháo captured Wēnzhōu and Míngzhōu.
Wēnzhōu was Yǒngjiā Jùn,
with its seat in Yǒngjiā Xiàn.
Míngzhōu was Yúyáo Jùn,
with its seat in Mò Xiàn,
which is today's Yínxiàn.
Yōng Wáng Shì was appointed Grand Marshal of the World's Troops.
On xīnyǒu,
he departed,
appointing the concurrently serving Palace Censor-in-Chief Yào Zǐ'áng and Wèi Jū as Commanders of the Left and Right Wing Armies,
Wéi Shàohuá, a Secretariat Drafter, as Pànguān,
and Lǐ Jìn, a Supervising Secretary, as Director of Military Affairs.
They were to rendezvous with the various Jìedùshǐ and Huíhé at Shǎnzhōu
to advance and attack Shǐ Cháoyì.
The Emperor wanted to make Guō Zǐyí Shì's deputy,
but Chéng Yuánzhèn and Yú Cháo'ēn obstructed it, and it was stopped.
Púgù Huái'ēn, Jìedùshǐ of Shuòfāng, was given the concurrent title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì and Prefect of Jiàngzhōu,
commanding the various armies as acting deputy to Shì.
Jiàngzhōu was
Jiàng Jùn.
At that time, the Shuòfāng army was stationed in Jiàngzhōu,
so Huái'ēn was given the title of Prefect.
This laid the groundwork for Huái'ēn's future rebellion, relying on his achievements.
When the Emperor was in the Eastern Palace,
he was deeply displeased by Lǐ Fǔguó's tyranny.
Upon ascending the throne,
he did not wish to execute him publicly, considering Fǔguó's merit in killing Empress Zhāng.
On the night of rénxū,
a thief entered his residence,
stole Fǔguó's head and an arm, and departed.
Kǎoyì states: Old traditions say:
"A thief killed Lǐ Fǔguó,
carrying away his head and arm."
Tǒngjì states:
"Fǔguó was disrespectful to Mínghuáng.
When the Emperor was in the Eastern Palace,
he heard of it and was quite angry.
When he ascended the throne,
Fǔguó again rendered meritorious service,
making it difficult to execute him publicly.
He secretly ordered someone to assassinate him,
cut off his head,
discarded it in a latrine,
and also cut off his right arm,
which was then rushed to offer sacrifice at Tàilíng.
No one, inside or outside the court, understood.
Later, Dù Jì, Prefect of Hángzhōu, told people: 'I once knew a warrior who was a Yámén general,
who said: I am the one who harmed Shàngfù.'"
We now follow the old tradition.
An imperial envoy was sent to inquire after his family,
a wooden head was carved for his burial,
and he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor.
Grand Tutor
is one of the Three Ducal Ministers.
On bǐngyín, the Emperor ordered Púgù Huái'ēn, along with his mother and wife, to go to the expeditionary camp.
At that time, Dēnglǐ came with Huái'ēn's daughter,
so Huái'ēn's mother and wife were sent to the expeditionary camp to strengthen the bond.
Yōng Wáng Shì arrived at Shǎnzhōu.
The Huíhé Kèhán was encamped north of the river.
Shì, with his subordinates, accompanied by dozens of horsemen, went to meet him.
The Kèhán criticized Shì for not prostrating and bowing.
Yào Zǐ'áng replied that ritual did not require such an action.
Chēbí, a Huíhé general, said:
"The Son of Heaven of Táng and the Kèhán have sworn to be brothers.
To Yōng Wáng, the Kèhán
is an uncle.
How can he not prostrate and bow?"
Zǐ'áng said:
"Yōng Wáng is
the eldest son of the Son of Heaven,
and is now the Grand Marshal.
How can the Crown Prince of China prostrate and bow to a foreign Kèhán!
Moreover, both imperial bodies are in coffins,"
"both imperial bodies" refers to the Retired Emperor and the Former Emperor,
neither of whom had been buried yet.
After a long argument,
Chēbí ordered Zǐ'áng, Wèi Jū, Wéi Shàohuá, and Lǐ Jìn each to be flogged one hundred times.
As Shì was young and inexperienced,
he was sent back to his camp.
Jū and Shàohuá died that very night.
On wùchén, the various armies departed from Shǎnzhōu.
Púgù Huái'ēn and the Huíhé Zuǒ Shā served as the vanguard,
Guō Yīngyì, Jìedùshǐ of Shǎnxī,
Fāngzhèn Biǎo: In the first year of Shàngyuán,
the Jìedùshǐ of Shǎn, Guó, and Huá was renamed Jìedùshǐ of Shǎnxī.
Shǐ,
shū lì fān.
entered from Miǎnchí;
Lǐ Bàoyù, Jìedùshǐ of Lùzé, entered from Héyáng;
Lǐ Guāngbì, Vice Grand Marshal of Hénán and other routes, entered from Chénliú;
they entered along separate routes to attack Luòyáng.
Kǎoyì states: Records of Dàizōng:
"On wùchén,
Marshal Yōng Wáng led Púgù Huái'ēn and other armies, as well as the Huíhé forces, to depart from Shǎnzhōu to attack the east.
Yīngyì and Cháo'ēn were left as rearguard.
On that day,
an edict also ordered the Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng to enter via the Zézhōu route."
We now follow the Tánglì and the old biography of Cháoyì.
On xīnwèi,
Huái'ēn's army encamped at Tóngguǐ.
Yǒngníng Xiàn in Hénán was
the territory of Tóngguǐ Xiàn during the Later Zhōu dynasty,
where Tóngguǐ City was located.
Shǐ Cháoyì heard that the imperial army was approaching,
and deliberated with his generals.
Āshǐnà Chéngqìng said:
"If the Táng come with only Hàn troops,
it would be advisable to engage them with all our forces;
but if they come with the Huíhét together,
their vanguard will be irresistible,
and it would be advisable to retreat and defend Héyáng to avoid them."
Cháoyì did not follow this advice.
On the day Rénshēn,
the imperial army reached the northern suburbs of Luòyáng,
and detached troops to take Huáizhōu;
on the day Guǐyǒu,
they captured it.
In the previous year's defeat at Mángshān,
Héyáng and Huáizhōu had both fallen to the rebels.
The northern suburbs of Luòyáng
were outside Mángshān.
On the day Yǐhài,
the imperial army arrayed itself at Héngshuǐ.
According to old records: Héngshuǐ
was in the northern suburbs of Luòyáng.
The Jīnrén Territory Map shows a Héngshuǐ Inn in Mèngjīn County.
Chén,
pronounced as zhèn;
the following characters 恩陳, 陳於, 賊陳, 陳 are all pronounced the same way.
They erected palisades to fortify themselves,

attacking from both inside and outside,
and utterly routed them.
Cháoyì mustered his 100,000 elite soldiers to rescue them,

The imperial army swiftly attacked them,

The Zhènxī Jìedùshǐ, Mǎ Lín, said:

Attacking the array but failing to break it,

hence the statement "the situation is critical."
Shǐ,
read as shū lì fān.
Lín,
read as lí zhēn fān.
He seized two shields from the rebels.
Pái,
in ancient times called shǔn,
between the Jìn and Sòng dynasties called péng pái.
Southerners made them of leather interwoven with bamboo
to defend against enemies,
northerners made them of wood.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn: Lè Qí brought disaster upon himself with a poplar shield,
indicating that the use of wood in the north was already ancient.
The rebels' left and right flanks collapsed,
and the main army advanced into them,
the rebel forces were utterly defeated;
they fought their way to Shíliúyuán and Lǎojūmiào,
where the rebels were again defeated;
men and horses trampled each other,
filling Shàngshū Gǔ,
60,000 heads were cut off,
and 20,000 prisoners were captured.
Cháoyì fled eastward with a few hundred light cavalry.
Huái'ēn advanced and captured the Eastern Capital and Héyáng City,

and released them by imperial decree.
Huái'ēn left the Huíhét Khān to encamp at Héyáng,
and ordered his son, Yòuxiāng Bīngmǎshǐ Yáng, and Shuòfāng Bīngmǎshǐ Gāo Fǔchéng, to lead over 10,000 infantry and cavalry to pursue Cháoyì, taking advantage of their victory.
Upon reaching Zhèngzhōu,
they fought two more battles, both victorious.
When Cháoyì arrived at Biànzhōu,
his Chénliú Jìedùshǐ, Zhāng Xiànchéng, closed the gates and resisted him.
Cháoyì fled to Púzhōu,
and Xiànchéng opened the gates and surrendered.
The Huíhét entered the Eastern Capital,
looting and killing indiscriminately,
with tens of thousands dead,
and fires burned for more than ten days without ceasing.
The Shuòfāng and Shéncè armies also considered the Eastern Capital, Zhèng, Biàn, and Rǔ prefectures to be rebel territory,
and plundered wherever they went,
only stopping after three months.
If Guō and Lǐ had been the commanders,
how could such disaster have occurred!
The officials and common people all wore paper clothes.
The Huíhét placed all the treasures they had plundered in Héyáng,
leaving their general Ān Kè to guard them.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Dīngchǒu,
a victory report reached the capital.
Cháoyì crossed the Yellow River north from Púzhōu.
Huái'ēn advanced and attacked Huázhōu,
capturing it,
and pursued and defeated Cháoyì at Wèizhōu.
Cháoyì's Suīyáng Jìedùshǐ, Tián Chéngsì, and others led over 40,000 troops to join Cháoyì,
and again came to resist battle;
Púgù Yáng defeated them,
and advanced rapidly to the east of Chānglè.
Cháoyì led Wèizhōu troops to battle,
but was again defeated and fled.
Chānglè,
an ancient Hàn county,
belonged to Wèizhōu.
Later Táng, to avoid taboos,
changed its name to Nánlè.
Lè,
pronounced luò.
Shuài,
read as lǜ.
Héngyáng Jìedùshǐ, Zhāng Zhōngzhì, surrendered the five prefectures of Zhào, Héng, Shēn, Dìng, and Yì to Hédōng Jìedùshǐ, Xīn Yúnjīng.
Sōng was
the son of Chǔwáng.
Chǔ Yù was
the younger brother of Xuē Nà.
Observing their formations,
Sōng and the others were all replaced;
shortly after,
Púgù Huái'ēn reinstated them all.
Because of this, Bàoyù and Yúnjīng suspected Huái'ēn of disloyalty,
and each submitted a memorial stating so.
The imperial court secretly made preparations for it;
Huái'ēn also submitted a memorial to clear himself,
and the emperor comforted and encouraged him.
On the day Xīnsì,
an imperial edict stated:
"Those in the Eastern Capital and Hénán and Héběi who accepted pseudo-appointments
will not be questioned at all."
This laid the groundwork for Qīng, Jì, Wèi, and Yōu to each seize the prefectures and counties they possessed and pass them down through generations.
56 On the day Jǐchǒu,
Liú Yàn, the Hùbù Shìláng, was concurrently appointed Hénándào Shuǐlù Zhuǎnyùn Dūshǐ.
In Rùizōng's Xiāntiān second year,
Lǐ Jié was appointed Shǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,
concurrently serving as Shuǐlù Yùnshǐ.
The Shuǐlù Yùnshǐ began from this point.
By Kāiyuán second year,
Jié was appointed Hénán Shàoyǐn,
concurrently serving as Shuǐlù Yùnshǐ.
In Tiānbǎo twelfth year,
Cuī Wúbì, the Shǎnjùn Tàishǒu, was appointed commissioner,
Yáng Guózhōng was appointed commissioner,
and the Shuǐlù Zhuǎnyùn Dūshǐ began at this point.
57 On the day Dīngyǒu,
Zhāng Zhōngzhì was appointed Chéngdéjūn Jìedùshǐ,
commanding the five prefectures of Héng, Zhào, Shēn, Dìng, and Yì.
He was granted the imperial surname Lǐ
and the given name Bǎochén.
Earlier,
when Xīn Yúnjīng was leading his troops to march out of Jǐngxíng and Chángshān,
his deputy general, Wáng Wǔjùn, advised Bǎochén, saying:
"Now the Hédōng troops are elite and sharp.
Fighting far from their borders is something we cannot contend with.
Moreover, we, with few, face many,
and with the wrong cause, meet the right cause.
If we fight, we will certainly disperse;
if we defend, we will certainly collapse.
You should plan for this."
Bǎochén then dismantled his defenses
and offered the five prefectures in surrender.
When he was reinstated as Jìedùshǐ,
he considered Wǔjùn's strategy to be excellent,
and promoted him to Xiānfēng Bīngmǎshǐ.
Wǔjùn was
originally Qìdān,
and his initial name was Mònuògān.
This was the basis for Wáng Wǔjùn to exterminate the Zhāng clan and gain Chéngdé.
Qì,
pronounced qī qì fān,
also pronounced chī.
Guō Zǐyí, considering Púgù Huái'ēn's achievement in pacifying Héshuò,
requested to yield the position of Fù Yuánshuài to him.
On the day Jǐhài,
Huái'ēn was appointed Héběi Fù Yuánshuài,
and was further granted Zuǒ Púyè concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng, Chányú, Zhèn Běi Dà Dūhù, and Shuòfāng Jìedùshǐ.
Shǐ Cháoyì fled to Bèizhōu.
He united with his great general Xuē Zhōngyì and other two military governors,
Púgǔ Yáng pursued him to Línqīng.
Línqīng
was Qīngyuān County in the Hàn dynasty.
The Later Wèi dynasty renamed it Línqīng.
During the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Bèizhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is one hundred and fifty lǐ north of Wèizhōu.
Yáng set up an ambush and routed him.
The Huíhé arrived again,
the government army's morale was greatly boosted,
and they pursued him.
A great battle took place southeast of Xiàbó.
Xiàbó
was a Hàn dynasty county,
and at that time belonged to Shēnzhōu.
Piles of corpses flowed downstream.
Cháoyì fled to Mòzhōu.
The Kǎoyì states: The Héluò Chūnqiū says:
“Cháoyì was defeated
and fled back to Fányáng,
passing through Héngshuǐ.
Púgǔ Yáng led fifteen myriad of Fān and Hàn troops, catching up with Cháoyì and engaging in battle,
defeating him.
That summer into autumn, there was severe rain.
Ponds and lakes overflowed.
Lǐ Jiéchéng, the military commissioner of Hédōng, and Lǐ Lìngchóng, a general of the Chéngdé Army, both commanded elite troops,
and also came to pledge allegiance,
competing to act as pincers.
The boats on the Zhānghé River and other ferries
were all captured.
Cháoyì sent someone to deliver a message,
but it was not answered.
He then ordered scattered hiring of boats,
but they were all plundered,
and all four routes were cut off.
Some generals requested to fight,
others requested to surrender,
Cháoyì was displeased.
Tián Chéngsì submitted a memorial to Cháoyì, saying: 'Your subject has heard that when the military forces are evenly matched,
success or failure is decided by the general;
when the numbers are unequal,
total annihilation depends on strategy.
In the past, Lord Liú was defeated at Báidì,
Cáo Gōng was defeated at Chìbì,
Lù Xùn and Huáng Gài both achieved victory through strategy.
Now, the armies under your command
are all exhausted,
the guest and host forces are vastly different,
and the labor and rest strengths are unequal.
If they are driven to battle,
no advantage is seen.
I request to use fifty chariots to set up three chariot camps north of the ancient Xià Kāngwáng City.
On each chariot, set up a shed and barrier,
with inverted spears for defense.
On each chariot, place two armored soldiers,
armed and hidden.
The accompanying women and children are arranged in the tents.
The baggage trains are arranged separately in each camp.
Behind the camps, select twenty thousand men
to form a crescent array.
Whenever the enemy is numerous and we are few,
this array is to be set up.
If there are natural defenses on the left and right,
this array is also to be set up.
If there are surprise forces on the left and right,
this array is also to be set up.
Let valiant generals command each.
The left army marches southeast,
the right army marches southwest,
staying more than ten lǐ from the chariot camps.
In front of the camps, select five thousand elite soldiers
to form a goose-wing array,
to engage in battle.
If they do not win,
they retreat behind the crescent array.
Once the vanguard has retreated,
the enemy will surely reach the chariot camps.
Coveting the treasures and valuables,
they will surely attack and seize them.
Wait until their troops are dispersed
and their formation is broken.
Then, with drums beating in unison,
the front and rear armies will arrive simultaneously.
Pixiū will fight bravely,
and shield-bearers will rush forward.
The left army marches west,
the right army marches east,
both taking the south of the ancient city,
so that head and tail are connected.
When the ambush is launched,
the enemy will surely be startled.
The arrival of the rear army
will naturally cut them off.
With the front and rear unable to rescue each other,
and the central army encountering elite troops,
their uniforms will be in disarray.
What else can they expect but defeat!
Let Wén Jǐngyì command the left army,
Dá Yúyìgǎn command the right army,
and Your Excellency personally command the central army.
If it is not victorious,
this old subject requests to use five thousand weak soldiers to swallow them for Your Excellency.'
Cháoyì read the memorial with great pleasure,
and then adopted his plan.
The government army was defeated,
losing over three thousand men.
Púgǔ Yáng was greatly shocked,
and retreated several tens of lǐ.
Because of this, Cháoyì was able to reach Mòzhōu.
After Cháoyì defeated the government army,
his prestige was restored.
All those he summoned
did not dare to disobey him.
He gathered boats and ships,
and connected rafts,
first ferrying the baggage,
and then the old and weak.
He then marched the army southward,
as if to attack.
Púgǔ Yáng ordered his officers and soldiers to guard their respective divisions to resist his vanguard.
Cháoyì then organized his troops
and crossed to the north all at once.
Púgǔ Yáng also connected boats and ships,
crossing at night to pursue them.”
Now following the old biography of Huái'ēn.
They then besieged Cháoyì in Mòzhōu.

58In the twelfth month,
on the day Gēngshēn,
Tàizǔ was first enshrined as a co-sacrificant with Heaven and Earth.
In the first year of Wǔdé of Gāozǔ, an edict was issued: for the annual sacrifices at the Round Mound and Square Mound,
Tàizǔ Jǐngdì was to be enshrined as a co-sacrificant.
In the second year of Qiánfēng of Gāozōng,
Gāozǔ and Tàizōng were both enshrined as co-sacrificants.

arguing that Shényáo, being the lord who received the mandate,
was not the first enfeoffed ruler,
and thus should not be Tàizǔ to be enshrined as a co-sacrificant with Heaven and Earth.
Tàizǔ Jǐngdì was first enfeoffed in Táng,

Dàizōng Ruìwén Xiàowǔ Huángdì, Superior First Class
His initial name was Shú,
later changed to Yù.
He was Sùzōng's eldest son.
After his passing,
it was debated to grant him the temple name Shìzōng.
To avoid the taboo name of Tàizōng,
it was changed to Dàizōng.
Guǎngdé First Year
(guǐmǎo, 763)
This year, the reign title was only changed in the seventh month.
Details can be found in the next volume.
1 Spring,
first month,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
Empress Wú, the Tàihòu, was posthumously honored as Zhāngjìng Huánghòu.
Empress Wú, the Tàihòu, was the emperor's birth mother.
2 On the day Guǐwèi,
Liú Yàn, the Guózǐ Jìjiǔ, was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
His duties as Dùzhī and other commissioners remained as before.
3 Initially,
Lái Tián was in Xiāngyáng.
Chéng Yuánzhèn had made some requests,
which Lái Tián did not comply with.
When Chéng Yuánzhèn became chancellor,
last year he added the title Tóng Píngzhāngshì to Lái Tián.
Wáng Zhòngshēng, while among the rebels,
survived by capitulating.
After the rebellion was quelled, he returned
and was on good terms with Yuánzhèn.
He impeached Tián for conspiring with the rebels,
which led to Zhòngshēng being trapped by them.
On the day Rén'yín,
Tián was stripped of his official titles and ranks,
exiled to Bōzhōu,
and ordered to commit suicide on the way.
Because of this, all the frontier governors gnashed their teeth at Yuánzhèn.
This serves as background for the frontier governors fearing Chéng Yuánzhèn and not daring to diligently serve the emperor.
4 Shǐ Cháoyì (史朝義) repeatedly went out to battle,
but was defeated every time.
Tián Chéngsì (田承嗣) persuaded Cháoyì (朝義)
to personally go to Yōuzhōu (幽州) to raise troops
and return to relieve Mòzhōu (莫州).
Chéngsì (承嗣) volunteered to remain guarding Mòzhōu (莫州).
Cháoyì (朝義) agreed,
and selected five thousand elite cavalry to break out of the encirclement through the northern gate.
Once Cháoyì (朝義) had departed,
Chéngsì (承嗣) immediately surrendered the city,
sending Cháoyì’s (朝義) mother, wife, and son to the government army.
Thereupon, Púgù Chǎng (僕固瑒), Hóu Xīyì (侯希逸), Xuē Jiānxùn (薛兼訓), and others led a host of thirty thousand in pursuit.
They caught up at Guīyì (歸義).
Guīyì (歸義)
was in the territory of Yìxiàn (易縣) during the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
belonging to Zhuōjùn (涿郡).
During the Northern Qí (北齊), it was abolished and merged into Mòxiàn (鄚縣).
In the fifth year of Wǔdé (武德) [622 CE],
Guīyì (歸義) and Běiyìzhōu (北義州) were established;
in the first year of Zhēnguān (貞觀) [627 CE],
both the prefecture and county were abolished.
In the eighth year [634 CE],
Guīyì (歸義) County was re-established,
belonging to Yōuzhōu (幽州).
According to Sòng Bái’s (宋白) *Xù Tōngdiǎn* (續通典),
Táng (唐) Guīyì (歸義) County was north of Wǎqiáo (瓦橋) Pass.
Cháoyì (朝義) was defeated and fled.
At that time, Lǐ Huáixiān (李懷仙), Cháoyì’s (朝義) Fànyáng (范陽) Military Commissioner, had already offered to surrender through the imperial envoy Luò Fèngxiān (駱奉仙).
He dispatched his commander of troops, Lǐ Bàozhōng (李抱忠), with three thousand soldiers to garrison Fànyáng (范陽) County.
Fànyáng (范陽) County
was Hàn (漢) Zhuōxiàn (涿縣),
the seat of Zhuōjùn (涿郡).
Cáo Wèi (曹魏) Emperor Wén (文帝) changed Zhuōjùn (涿郡) to Fànyángjùn (范陽郡).
Suí (隋) abolished Fànyángjùn (范陽郡),
re-establishing Zhuōjùn (涿郡) at Jìxiàn (薊縣),
with Zhuōxiàn (涿縣) belonging to it.
In the seventh year of Wǔdé (武德) [624 CE],
Zhuōxiàn (涿縣) was renamed Fànyáng (范陽) County,
still belonging to Yōuzhōu (幽州);
in the first year of Tiānbǎo (天寶) [742 CE],
Yōuzhōu (幽州) Zhuōjùn (涿郡) was renamed Fànyángjùn (范陽郡),
so the old city of Jì (薊) was also called Fànyáng (范陽).
Historians distinguish it with the character for county,
and its location was south of Jì (薊).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: "It is 160 *lǐ* (里) south to Mòzhōu (莫州)."
