As the government army was approaching,
Cháoyì (朝義) sent someone to inform Bàozhōng (抱忠) of his intention to leave the main army at Mòzhōu (莫州) and come with light cavalry to raise troops for relief.
He then reproached him with the principle of loyalty between sovereign and minister.
Bàozhōng (抱忠) replied:
"Heaven does not bless Yān (燕),
and the Táng (唐) court has been restored.
Now that we have submitted to Táng (唐),
how can we be treacherous again?
Are you not ashamed before the three armies?
A true man disdains to use cunning schemes against others.
I advise you to choose your course of action early to save yourself.
Furthermore, Tián Chéngsì (田承嗣) must have already rebelled.
Otherwise,
how could the government army have reached this place?"
Cháoyì (朝義) was greatly frightened and
said:
"I have not eaten since this morning.
Can you not at least provide me with a meal?"
Bàozhōng (抱忠) then ordered food to be set out east of the city.
Thereupon, the Fànyáng (范陽) people under Cháoyì’s (朝義) command
all bowed in farewell and departed.
Cháoyì (朝義) merely wept.
He alone, with several hundred Hu (胡) cavalry, ate and then departed.
He fled east to Guǎngyáng (廣陽),
but Guǎngyáng (廣陽) refused him entry.
He wished to enter the Xī (奚) and Qìdān (契丹) territories to the north.
Upon reaching Wēnquánzhà (溫泉柵) —
according to the biographies of Huái'ēn (懷恩) in the Old and New Books,
Wēnquánzhà (溫泉柵) was northeast of Shíchéng (石城) County in Píngzhōu (平州) territory.
Qì (契) is pronounced *qī qǐ*
and also *chī*.
Zhà (柵) is pronounced *cè gé*.
Cháoyì (朝義), desperate,
hanged himself in the forest.
Huáixiān (懷仙) took his head and offered it.
Púgù Huái'ēn (僕固懷恩) and all the armies returned.
On *jiǎchén* (甲辰) day,
Cháoyì’s (朝義) head arrived at the capital.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Héluò Chūnqiū* (河洛春秋) says:
"Cháoyì (朝義) fled east to Guǎngyáng (廣陽) Commandery,
but was refused entry.
He went north through Lùxiàn (潞縣) and Yúyáng (漁陽),
intending to submit to the two border tribes.
Upon reaching Yúguān (榆關),
Lǐ Huáixiān (李懷仙) sent an envoy to recall him.
He returned to Yúyáng (漁陽) and passed through
from Lùxiàn (潞縣) to outside the Āpó (阿婆) Gate east of Yōuzhōu (幽州) city.
In the Wūlǘ (巫閭) spirit temple,
he and his brother were both strangled to death.
Their heads were then delivered to Luò Fèngxiān (駱奉仙).
One day later,
all the armies learned of it
and returned to the foot of Mòzhōu (莫州) city."
The old biography of Púgù Huái'ēn (僕固懷恩) says:
"In the third month of the second year of Bǎoyìng (寶應) [763 CE],
Cháoyì (朝義) reached Wēnquánzhà (溫泉柵) in Shíchéng (石城) County, Píngzhōu (平州).
Desperate,
he fled into a long forest and hanged himself.
Huáixiān (懷仙) sent his wife's younger brother, Xú Yǒujì (徐有濟), to present his head."
The *Shǐ Cháoyì Zhuàn* (史朝義傳) says:
"In the first month of the second year [763 CE],
Lǐ Huáixiān (李懷仙) captured him alive in Mòzhōu (莫州),
sent a message of surrender,
and presented his severed head at the imperial palace."
The *Shílù* (實錄) says:
"On the *jǐhài* (己亥) day of the eleventh month of the first year of Bǎoyìng (寶應) [762 CE],
Púgù Huái'ēn (僕固懷恩) reported: 'Yōuzhōu (幽州) is pacified,
and all the prefectures and counties north of the Yellow River are pacified.
Shǐ Cháoyì (史朝義) was killed by rebellious soldiers
and his head sent to the capital.'"
The old annals say:
"In the tenth month of the second year of Bǎoyìng (寶應) [763 CE],
all the prefectures and commanderies north of the Yellow River were pacified.
Lǐ Huáixiān (李懷仙) surrendered with Yōuzhōu (幽州),
and Tián Chéngsì (田承嗣) surrendered with Wèizhōu (魏州)."
Shěn Jìjì’s (沈既濟) *Jiànzhōng Shílù* (建中實錄) says:
"In the first month of the second year [763 CE],
the rebel general Lǐ Huáixiān (李懷仙) captured Cháoyì (朝義) and surrendered,
and Shāndōng (山東) was pacified."
The *Táng Lì* (唐曆) says:
"On the *jiǎchén* (甲辰) day of the first month,
Lǐ Huáixiān (李懷仙) captured Shǐ Cháoyì (史朝義),
severed his head,
and presented it at the imperial palace.
He surrendered with all his territories."
The *Niándàijì* (年代記) says:
"On the *jǐhài* (己亥) day of the twelfth month of the first year of Bǎoyìng (寶應) [762 CE],
Púgù Huái'ēn (僕固懷恩) reported: 'Shǐ Cháoyì (史朝義) was killed by rebellious soldiers
and his head sent to the capital.'
On the *jiǎshēn* (甲申) day of the first month of the second year [763 CE],
Cháoyì’s (朝義) severed head arrived at the palace."
The new annals say:
"On the *jiǎshēn* (甲申) day of the first month of the first year of Guǎngdé (廣德) [763 CE],
Cháoyì (朝義) committed suicide,
and his general Lǐ Huáixiān (李懷仙) surrendered with Yōuzhōu (幽州)."
According to the records, the various armies surrounded Cháoyì (朝義) at Mòzhōu (莫州)
already at the end of the eleventh month of the previous year,
and the *Héluò Chūnqiū* (河洛春秋) states that the siege lasted forty days.
Huái'ēn’s (懷恩) old biography also states that the attack and defense lasted over a month.
Thus, Cháoyì’s (朝義) death
must clearly have occurred in the first month of this year.
All books state that Cháoyì (朝義) was killed in the first month of this year,
but the *Shílù* (實錄) places it in the eleventh month of the first year,
and the old annals follow this,
also omitting the character for "eleventh month."
Huái'ēn’s (懷恩) biography mistakenly gives the third month instead of the first month.
*Jiǎshēn* (甲申) is the tenth day of the first month;
*jiǎchén* (甲辰)
is the thirtieth day.
The new principal annals are probably based on the *Niándàijì* (年代記),
but the *Niándàijì* (年代記) also agrees with the *Shílù* (實錄) that Cháoyì (朝義) died on the *jǐhài* (己亥) day of the eleventh month in the winter of the first year.
If he was killed in the first month,
his head should not have arrived in Cháng'ān (長安) by the tenth day.
It is suspected that he committed suicide on *jiǎshēn* (甲申),
and his head was sent to the palace on *jiǎchén* (甲辰).
The new annals only use the *Niándàijì’s* (年代記) *jiǎshēn* (甲申) arrival at the palace as the date of suicide,
but it is unknown what this is based on.
Now, following the *Táng Lì* (唐曆),
his head arrived in the capital on *jiǎchén* (甲辰).
5 In the intercalary month,
on the night of *jǐyǒu* (己酉) day,
fifteen Huíhú (回紇) people violated Hánguāng (含光) Gate,
crashing into Hónglú (鴻臚) Temple.
The gate guards dared not stop them.
6 On the guǐhài day,
Xuē Sōng (薛嵩), a surrendered general of Shǐ Cháoyì (史朝義), was made Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of the six prefectures of Xiāng (相), Wèi (衞), Xíng (邢), Míng (洺), Bèi (貝), and Cí (磁).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Cízhōu (磁州),
originally the land of Guǎngpíng (廣平) County in the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
was where Emperor Wǔ (武) of the Zhōu (周) dynasty established Fúyáng (滏陽) County and Chéng'ān (成安) Commandery.
In the tenth year of Kāihuáng (開皇) of the Suí (隋) dynasty,
the commandery was abolished,
and Cízhōu (磁州) was established.
In the first year of Wǔdé (武德) of the Táng (唐) dynasty, Cízhōu (磁州) was established by dividing Xiāngzhōu (相州).
In the first year of Zhēnguān (貞觀),
the prefecture was abolished.
After Xuē Sōng (薛嵩) obtained the jíe (節),
he again submitted a memorial requesting the establishment of Cízhōu (磁州) with Fúyáng (滏陽) from Xiāngzhōu (相州) and Hándān (邯鄲) and Wǔ'ān (武安) from Míngzhōu (洺州).
Cí (磁)
is pronounced like "qiáng zhī" in reverse.
Xiāng (相)
is pronounced like "xī liàng" in reverse.
Wèizhōu (魏州)
was the land of Wèijùn (魏郡) in the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
Bózhōu (博州)
was Liáochéng (聊城) County of Dōngjùn (東郡) in the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
Dézhōu (德州)
was the land of Píngyuánjùn (平原郡) in the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
The Suí (隋) dynasty established Dézhōu (德州)
and named it after Āndé (安德) County.
The Fányáng Jìedùshǐ (范陽節度使) was renamed Yōuzhōu Jìedùshǐ (幽州節度使).
At that time, Pínglú (平盧) had already fallen,
and he also concurrently held the title of Lúlóng Jìedùshǐ (盧龍節度使).
Sōng (嵩) and others welcomed Púgù Huái'ēn (僕固懷恩),
bowed before his horse,
and begged to serve him in the army.
Huái'ēn (懷恩) also feared that his favor would wane once the rebels were pacified,
so he petitioned to keep Sōng (嵩) and others, including Lǐ Bǎochén (李寶臣), to command Héběi (河北) separately,
to be his own allies.
The court was also weary of military conflicts,
hoping for peace,
and thus granted their requests.
The Héběi (河北) fānzhèn (藩鎮)
became arrogant and uncontrollable from this point onward.
7 The Huíhé (回紇) Dēnglǐ (登里) Khān (可汗) returned to his country.
Wherever his troops passed, they plundered.
If their provisions were slightly unsatisfactory,
they would kill people,
without any scruples.
Lǐ Bàoyù (李抱玉), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Chénzhèng (陳鄭) and Zélù (澤潞), wanted to send officials to set up stations,
but everyone declined due to apprehension.
Only Zhào Chéngwèi (趙城尉) Mǎ Suì (馬燧) volunteered to go.
In the first year of Yìníng (義寧) of the Suí (隋) dynasty,
Zhàochéng (趙城) County was established by dividing Huòyì (霍邑),
belonging to Jìnzhōu (晉州).
Suì (燧) first sent someone to bribe their chief,
making an agreement to prevent plunder.
The chief gave him a flag and said:
"If anyone violates the order,
you may execute them yourself."
Suì (燧) took condemned prisoners as his attendants.
If there was a slight violation of the order,
he immediately beheaded them.
The Huíhé (回紇) looked at each other, startled.
Those who passed through his territory all clasped their hands and obeyed the rules.
Bàoyù (抱玉) was impressed by him.
Suì (燧) then persuaded Bàoyù (抱玉), saying:
"When I spoke with the Huíhé (回紇),
I learned their true intentions quite well.
Púgù Huái'ēn (僕固懷恩) is arrogant and disrespectful, relying on his achievements.
His son Yáng (瑒) is brave but reckless.
Now, with the establishment of four commanders internally,
the four commanders
refer to Tián Chéngsì (田承嗣), Lǐ Bǎochén (李寶臣), Lǐ Huáixiān (李懷仙), and Xuē Sōng (薛嵩).
they will surely have ambitions to spy on Hédōng (河東) and Zélù (澤潞).
It is advisable to be deeply prepared."
Bàoyù (抱玉) agreed with this.
8 Initially,
Liáng Chóngyì (梁崇義) from Cháng'ān (長安), a Yǔlín (羽林) archer, followed Lái Tián (來瑱) to garrison Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
and was repeatedly promoted to Yòubīngmǎshǐ (右兵馬使).
Chóngyì (崇義) was brave and strong,
able to bend iron and straighten hooks;
he was resolute and spoke little,
and won the hearts of the people.
When Tián (瑱) went to court,
he ordered his generals to garrison various prefectures.
When Tián (瑱) died,
all the garrisons fled back to Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Páng Chōng (龐充), the Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬), led two thousand soldiers to Hénán (河南).
This was because Lái Tián (來瑱) had previously sent Páng Chōng (龐充) to the Hénán (河南) field headquarters to assist in the campaign against Shǐ Cháoyì (史朝義).
Hearing of Tián's (瑱) death,
he led his troops back to attack Xiāngzhōu (襄州).
Lǐ Zhāo (李昭), the Zuǒbīngmǎshǐ (左兵馬使), resisted him,
and Chōng (充) fled to Fángzhōu (房州).
Chóngyì (崇義) led his garrison troops back from Dèngzhōu (鄧州).
He, Zhāo (昭), and Deputy Commissioner Xuē Nányáng (薛南陽) deferred to each other for leadership.
After a long time, no decision was made,
and the crowd all said:
"The army cannot be without Lord Liáng (梁) as its commander."
So, Chóngyì (崇義) was chosen as the commander.
Chóngyì (崇義) soon killed Zhāo (昭) and Nányáng (南陽),
and reported the situation.
The Emperor was unable to punish him.
On the jiǎchén day of the third month,
Chóngyì (崇義) was appointed Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (襄州刺史) and Shānnán Dōngdào Jìedù Liúhòu (山南東道節度留後).
When a fānzhèn (藩鎮) in the Táng (唐) dynasty appointed a commander,
if they had not yet been granted the banner and staff,
they were first made Jìedù Liúhòu (節度留後).
This sets the stage for Liáng Chóngyì's (梁崇義) defiance and death in Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
A temple was established for him.
He did not reside in Tián's (瑱) official residence or main hall.
9 On the xīnyǒu day,
the Zhìdào Dàshèng Dàmíng Xiàohuángdì (至道大聖大明孝皇帝) was buried at Tàilíng (泰陵).
Tàilíng (泰陵)
is on Jīnsù (金粟) Mountain, twenty lǐ (里) northeast of Fèngxiān (奉先) County in Tóngzhōu (同州).
On the gēngwǔ day,
the Wénmíng Wǔdé Dàshèng Dàxuān Xiàohuángdì (文明武德大聖大宣孝皇帝) was buried at Jiànlíng (建陵).
Jiànlíng (建陵)
is on Wǔjiāng (武將) Mountain, eighteen lǐ (里) northeast of Lǐquán (醴泉) County in Jīngzhào (京兆).
10 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the gēngchén day,
Lǐ Guāngbì (李光弼) reported the capture of Yuán Cháo (袁晁),
and all of Zhèdōng (浙東) was pacified.
At that time, Cháo (晁) had gathered nearly two hundred thousand people,
attacking various prefectures and counties.
Guāngbì (光弼) sent his subordinate general Zhāng Bóyí (張伯儀) to lead troops to suppress them.
Bóyí (伯儀)
was from Wèizhōu (魏州).
11 Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) repeatedly memorialized, saying:
"The Tǔbō (吐蕃) and Dǎngxiàng (党項) should not be overlooked;
preparations should be made early."
His words were not heeded,
setting the stage for the two foreign groups to invade the capital.
Shù (數)
is pronounced like "suǒ jiǎo" in reverse.
Shàng (上)
is pronounced like "shí zhǎng" in reverse;
the same applies below.
12 On the xīncǒu day,
Li Zhīfāng (李之芳) and others, concurrently Yùshǐ Dàfū (御史大夫), were sent as envoys to Tǔbō (吐蕃).
They were detained by the barbarians
and only returned after two years.
Shǐ Jiū (史究) explains it.
13 Several ministers repeatedly submitted memorials requesting the establishment of a crown prince.
In the fifth month,
on the guǐmǎo day,
an imperial edict was issued, permitting discussion after the autumn harvest.
14 On the dīngmǎo day,
an edict was issued to divide the various prefectures of Héběi (河北): Yōu (幽), Mò (莫), Guī (媯), Tán (檀), Píng (平), and Jì (薊) were put under the administration of Yōuzhōu (幽州);
Héng (恆), Dìng (定), Zhào (趙), Shēn (深), and Yì (易) were put under the administration of Chéngdé Jūn (成德軍);
Xiāng (相), Bèi (貝), Xíng (邢), and Míng (洺) were put under the administration of Xiāngzhōu (相州);
Wèi (魏), Bó (博), and Dé (德) were put under the administration of Wèizhōu (魏州);
Cāng (滄), Dì (棣), Jì (冀), and Yíng (瀛) were put under the administration of Qīngzī (青淄);
Huái (懷), Wèi (衞), and Héyáng (河陽) were put under the administration of Zélù (澤潞).
Since Tián Chéngsì (田承嗣) and Lǐ Língyào (李靈耀) successively rebelled,
the administration of these various garrisons
no longer adhered to this system.
4 The Tǔfān entered Dàzhèn Pass,
capturing Lán, Kuò, Hé, Shàn, Táo, Mín, Qín, Chéng, Wèi and other prefectures.
They seized all the lands of Héxī and Lǒngyòu.
Lán, Kuò, Qín, Wèi and other prefectures
were precisely the lands of Héxī and Lǒngyòu,
which had already been captured by the Tǔfān.
The historian, because of their entry into Dàzhèn Pass, recorded it in full.
Lánzhōu was
Hàn Jīnchéng Commandery.
During the Suí dynasty, Lánzhōu was established,
named after Gāolán Mountain.
Kuòzhōu was
the southern boundary of Hàn Xīpíng Commandery.
The Former Liáng established Huánghé Commandery in its territory.
The Later Wèi established Táohé Commandery.
In the fifth year of Jiàndé of the Zhōu dynasty,
the land south of the Hé River was taken and Kuòzhōu was established,
named after the meaning of "kuòqīng" (to clear away).
Hézhōu was
Hàn Báohǎn County.
Zhāng Jùn of the Former Liáng divided it and established Hézhōu.
Shànzhōu was
the land of Hàn Pòqiāng and Yǔnwú Counties.
After the Táng pacified Xuē Jǔ,
Shànzhōu was established.
Táozhōu was
governed from Hàn Táoyáng City,
established in the early Bǎodìng era of the Zhōu dynasty.
Mínzhōu was
the land of Qín Líntáo County.
In the tenth year of Dàtǒng of the Later Wèi, Mínzhōu was established,
named after Mínshān to its south.
Qínzhōu was
governed from Chéngjì Xiǎnqīn Chuān,
retaining the name of the former prefecture from the Wèi and Jìn dynasties.
Chéngzhōu was
ancient Xīróng territory.
Later, the Jiāng clan of Qiānmǔ Róng resided there.
Still later, it became the Báimǎ Dī Kingdom.
During the Hàn dynasty, it was Wǔdū Commandery.
During the Jìn dynasty, it was Chóuchí Commandery.
The Later Wèi changed it to Nánqínzhōu.
The Western Wèi changed it to Chéngzhōu.
Wèizhōu was
governed from Hàn Xiāngwǔ County,
established by the Later Wèi.
The borders were expanded,
connecting with the Western Regions,
and all were placed under dūdū, fǔ, zhōu, and xiàn.
During the Kāiyuán era,
Shuòfāng, Lǒngyòu, Héxī, Ānxī, and Běitíng jiédùshǐ were established to govern them.
Annually, able-bodied men from Shāndōng were conscripted as garrison soldiers,
silk and cloth were used as military supplies,
military colonies were opened,
rations were supplied,
supervisory pasturages were set up,
and horses and cattle were raised.
Military cities and patrol posts
stretched for ten thousand *lǐ*, visible one from another.
When Ān Lùshān rebelled,
all the elite border troops were conscripted to aid the capital,
called "Xíngyíng" (mobile camps).
The remaining troops were few and weak,
and the Hú barbarians gradually encroached upon them.
Within a few years,
dozens of prefectures in the northwest successively fell,
and from Fèngxiáng westward,
and Bīnzhōu northward,
all adopted the "left lapel" (barbarian attire).
The historian states why the Táng lost Hé and Lǒng.
5 Initially,
Púgù Huái'ēn received an imperial edict to meet the Huíhé Kèhán in Tàiyuán.
Xīn Yúnjīng, the Jiédùshǐ of Hédōng, knowing that the Kèhán was Huái'ēn's son-in-law,
feared that they might conspire to attack the military headquarters,
so he closed the city gates and defended himself,
also failing to feast the troops.
After Shǐ Cháoyì was pacified,
an edict ordered Huái'ēn to escort the Kèhán out of the frontier.
When they passed through Tàiyuán on their way back,
Yúnjīng again closed the city gates and did not communicate with them.
Huái'ēn was enraged
and fully reported the situation in a memorial,
but received no reply.
Huái'ēn stationed tens of thousands of Shuòfāng troops in Fénzhōu,
and sent his son, Yùshǐ Dàfū Yáng, with ten thousand men to station in Yúcì.
Subordinate generals Lǐ Guāngyì and others were stationed in Qí County.
[Qí]
Both were ancient Hàn counties,
belonging to Tàiyuán.
Lǐ Huáiguāng and others were stationed in Jìnzhōu,
Zhāng Wéiyuè and others in Qìnzhōu.
Huáiguāng was
originally a Mòhé from Bóhǎi,
surnamed Rú.
As a general of Shuòfāng,
he was granted the imperial surname for his merits.
When the imperial envoy Luò Fèngxiān arrived in Tàiyuán,
Yúnjīng cultivated a close relationship with him,
and told him that Huái'ēn was conspiring with the Huíhé,
and that his rebellion was evident.
Fèngxiān returned,
passing by Huái'ēn.
Huái'ēn drank with him in front of his mother.
His mother repeatedly reproached Fèngxiān, saying:
"You and my son pledged to be brothers,
but now you are close to Yúnjīng.
How can you be two-faced!"
The Táng people referred to turncoats as "two-faced."
After the Zhēnyuán era,
the Báigǒu and other Qiāng from the Xīshān of Jiànnán submitted,
were granted cattle and grain,
provided with means of livelihood,
and given official positions and salaries,
all hereditary.
However, they secretly colluded with the Tǔfān,
and were commonly called the "two-faced Qiāng."
This is the evidence.
Huái'ēn rose to dance,
and Fèngxiān presented him with "chántóu cǎi" (head-wrapping silk).
When Táng people gathered for banquets,
and someone danced when intoxicated,
it was customary to present them with silk items as a gift,
called "chántóu."
Singing girls and courtesans who danced at banquets also received "chántóu" and shouts of appreciation,
which is what Dù Fǔ's poem refers to as
"after the dance, brocade wrapped around the head."
Hān, pronunciation Hù Gān Fān.
[He] said:
"Tomorrow is Duānwǔ Festival,
we should celebrate with another day of drinking."
Fèngxiān insisted on leaving.
Huái'ēn hid his horse.
Fèngxiān said to his attendants:
"This morning he reprimanded me,
and now he hides my horse. He intends to kill me!"
At night,
he scaled the wall and fled.
Huái'ēn was surprised,
and immediately sent his horse to chase him back.
In the eighth month,
on the day Guǐwèi,
Fèngxiān arrived in Cháng'ān
and reported Huái'ēn's rebellion.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
"On Guǐwèi,
Huái'ēn turned his army around,
stopping at Fénzhōu,
delaying and not advancing.
Supervising Commissioner Luò Fèngxiān reported it.
The emperor, considering his great merits, did not punish him,
but issued a benevolent edict to comfort him."
It also says:
"Huái'ēn stationed his army at Fén.
Supervising Commissioner Luò Fèngxiān, during a public banquet,
made pointed remarks.
Huái'ēn had already conceived treasonous intentions
and retorted brazenly.
Fèngxiān left without informing him
and reported it to the emperor by express messenger.
The emperor, tolerating him due to his great merits,
reprimanded Fèngxiān and sent him out,
treating Huái'ēn as before.
Huái'ēn feared Fèngxiān
and felt increasingly uneasy."
*Bīnzhì* says:
"In the second year of Bǎoyìng,
after Hèshuò was pacified,
an edict ordered Xīn Yúnjīng, Jiédùshǐ of Tàiyuán, and Púgù Huái'ēn, each with their armies, to escort the Huíhé back to their territory.
After exiting Jìn Pass,
Duke Xīn led his light cavalry and entered Tàiyuán first.
Huái'ēn was angry that he had not been informed,
saying: 'Duke Xīn is suspicious of me.'
When the Huíhé arrived,
Duke Xīn lodged them outside the city
and provided cattle and wine to feast them.
Huái'ēn wanted to use the Huíhé to inspect the city walls
and secretly guided the Huíhé to request to visit the Buddhist temples.
Duke Xīn granted permission.
Upon entering the city,
they saw soldiers arrayed in all the streets.
The barbarians were greatly alarmed
and scattered and left."
We now follow the old biography of Huái'ēn.
[Huái'ēn] requested the execution of Yúnjīng and Fèngxiān.
The emperor questioned neither,
but issued a benevolent edict to reconcile them.
Huái’ēn, from the time the war began,
believed that since Lù Shān rebelled in Shuòfāng,
he raised an army to suppress it,
until the time the rebels were pacified.
Forty-six members of his family died for the nation's cause,
his daughter was married to a distant land,
referring to her marriage to the Huíghé Khagan.
He recovered the two capitals,
pacified Hénán and Héběi,
his merits were unmatched,
yet he was framed by others.
His indignation and resentment were extremely deep.
He submitted a memorial to protest his innocence,
stating:
"Yesterday, I received an imperial edict to escort the Khagan back to his country.
I exhausted my family's wealth
to enable him to start his journey.
When we reached the north of the mountains,
Yún Jīng and Fèng Xiān closed their cities and did not come out to greet him,
and even ordered secret thefts.
The Huíghé became resentful and angry,
urgently wanting to unleash their troops.
I exerted myself to mediate,
only then were we able to pass beyond the frontier.
Yún Jīng and Fèng Xiān, fearing that I had already submitted a report,
then falsely claimed to be making preparations,
and colluded with Lǐ Bǎoyù.
When I calmly reflect on this,
their crimes are six-fold: Formerly, when the Tóngluó rebelled,
I swept clean the Héqu region for the former emperor,
this is one;
My son, Bīn, was captured by the Tóngluó,
he found an opportunity to escape and return,
I executed him to command the loyalty of the soldiers,
this is two;
Both events are recorded in volume 218, Sùzōng, Zhìdé Yuánzài.
Bīn,
read bēi jīn fān.
Jiàn,
read gǔ xiàn fān.
Marrying a daughter to a foreign barbarian,
for the sake of national harmony and kinship,
and pacifying the enemies,
this is three;
My son Yáng and I, disregarding death,
served the nation with our lives,
this is four;
Héběi had newly submitted,
the Jiedushi
refers to Tián Chéngsì, Lǐ Bǎochén, Lǐ Huáixiān, and others.
I pacified them to reassure the wavering,
this is five;
I persuaded the Huíghé
to come to our aid in times of emergency.
After the world was pacified,
I escorted them back to their country,
this is six.
Since I bear these six crimes,
I truly deserve ten thousand executions.
I can only swallow my hatred in the netherworld,
and carry my grievance through the ages.
What more can I plead!
I have received profound kindness,
and day and night I think of presenting myself before Your Majesty,
meaning he wanted to enter the court.
If the court does not declare my crime,
which of the Jiedushi in the various circuits
will not be suspicious and fearful!
Recently I heard an edict summoned several people,
Tang people generally referred to "summoning" as "pursuing"; this can be seen from the various unofficial histories cited in the Kǎoyì.
They truly fear the slanderous mouths of the palace eunuchs,
and will unjustly suffer Your Majesty's execution;
It is not merely that Your humble servant is disloyal,
but rather that perverse elements are at Your side.
The situation between ruler and minister at that time
was indeed as Huái’ēn said.
His words were not without basis,
but Your Majesty eventually had no place
to put
him, and instead
favored and trusted him even more;
all because those of the same kind banded together,
blinding the sage's hearing.
I secretly heard that when people from the four directions sent memorials,
Your Majesty always said to discuss it with the Grand Marshal of Cavalry.
Grand Marshal of Cavalry
refers to Chéng Yuánzhèn.
Piào,
read pǐ miào fān.
Qí,
read qí jì fān.
Or they were detained for several months without returning,
increasing suspicion and obstruction far and wide.
As for my Shuòfāng generals and soldiers,
their achievements are the highest.
They were the masters of the former emperor's restoration,
and Your Majesty's former officials during the time of adversity.
Yet they have not received any special commendation,
but instead slanderous and jealous words are believed.
Zǐyí has already been suspected,
and now I am also being slandered.
When the bow is stored, the birds are gone;
this is indeed not empty talk.
An ancient saying goes:
'When high-flying birds are gone,
good bows are stored away;
when cunning rabbits are dead,
hunting dogs are cooked;
when enemy states are broken,
strategists perish.'
This means that when applied to present events,
it is not empty talk.
Jiǎo,
meaning to entrust.
Falsely claiming rebellion to heavily slander.
Citing the story of Zhào Gāo to compare with the eunuchs.
Moreover, if we merely let things slide,
I truly cannot protect my family,
how can Your Majesty secure the nation!
Huái’ēn's true feelings
can be seen here.
Honest advice grates on the ear but benefits one's actions;
an ancient saying.
I wish to enter the court openly,
but I fear the generals and soldiers will hold me back.
Now, under the pretext of inspecting Jìn and Jiàng,
I will linger there.
I beg Your Majesty to specifically send a messenger to Jiàngzhōu to inquire about me,
and I will set off with him immediately."
In the ninth month,
on the day Rénxū,
the emperor sent Péi Zūnqìng to Huái’ēn to convey an imperial decree,
and to observe his intentions.
When Huái’ēn saw Zūnqìng,
he embraced his feet, weeping and complaining of his grievances.
Zūnqìng spoke of the emperor's great kindness,
hinting for him to enter the court.
Huái’ēn agreed.
His deputy general, Fàn Zhìchéng, thought it was inadvisable,
saying:
"You believe his sweet words.
If you enter, you will become Lái Tián,
and will never return!"
The next day,
Huái’ēn saw Zūnqìng,
using fear of death as an excuse,
and asked to send one of his sons to court.
Zhìchéng again thought it was inadvisable,
so Zūnqìng returned.
The Censor-in-chief Wáng Yì returned from a mission to Huíghé.
Huái’ēn had previously communicated with the Khagan,
and feared Yì would disclose his affairs,
so he detained him.
When the Tubo invaded,
the border generals reported the emergency,
but Chéng Yuánzhèn did not relay any of it.
In winter,
the tenth month,
the Tubo attacked Jìngzhōu.
The prefect, Gāo Huī, surrendered the city to them,
and then served as their guide,
leading the Tubo deeper into the territory.
After passing Bīnzhōu,
the emperor first heard of it.
On the day Xīnwèi,
they attacked Fèngtiān and Wǔgōng,
shaking the capital with fear.
An edict appointed Yōng Wáng Shì as Grand Marshal of Guānnèi,
and Guō Zǐyí as Vice Marshal,
to garrison Xiányáng to defend against them.
Zǐyí had been idle for a long time.
In the eighth month of Bǎoyì Yuánzài,
Guō Zǐyí had entered the court from Hédōng,
and had since remained in the capital.
Now, when he was summoned, he recruited
twenty horsemen and set off.
When he reached Xiányáng,
the Tubo commander, with over 200,000 troops of Tuyuhun, Dǎngxiàng, Dǐ, and Qiāng,
spread out for dozens of *lǐ*,
had already crossed the Wèi River from Sīzhúyuán.
There was a Sīzhúyuán in Zhōuzhì county, Fèngxiáng prefecture.
This is the place referred to in the Hànshū, Wáng Mǎng biography, as Huò Hóng relying on the *mangzhu*.
Sū Shì said: Zhōuzhì has an official bamboo garden,
by the water,
extending for dozens of *lǐ* without interruption,
which is what is called Sīzhú.
Zǐyí sent his judge and Palace Assistant Secretary, Wáng Yánchāng, to submit a memorial to the emperor,
requesting more troops.
Chéng Yuánzhèn obstructed him,
and he was never granted an audience.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
Lǚ Yuèjiāng, the Commander of Troops of the Wèiběi Field Army,
leading two thousand elite soldiers, defeated the Tubo west of Zhōuzhì.
On the day Yǐhài,
the Tubo attacked Zhōuzhì.
Yuèjiāng again fought vigorously,
but his troops were exhausted,
and he was captured by the enemy.
The Emperor was mustering troops,
but the Tǔbō had already crossed the makeshift bridge.
In a panic, not knowing what to do,
on the day of Bǐngzǐ,
he fled to Shǎnzhōu.
Officials hid and scattered,
and the six armies dispersed.
Guō Zǐyí heard of this
and quickly returned from Xiányáng to Cháng'ān.
By the time he arrived,
the imperial carriage had already departed.
The Emperor had barely exited the Yuànmén
and crossed the Chǎnshuǐ.
According to Tang records, the Forbidden Park
encompassed the area north of Dàmínggōng,
extending east to the Chǎnshuǐ.
However, sources like the Yǒnglù and Cháng'ānzhì
state that there was no gate on the east side of the Forbidden Park leading out to the Chǎnshuǐ.
It was likely that he exited through the Guāngtàimén.
Xié Fēngwáng Gǒng and ten other princes were coerced into going west to welcome the Tǔbō.
They encountered Zǐyí inside the Kāiyuǎnmén.
The Kāiyuǎnmén was the first gate on the northern part of the western wall of Cháng'ān city.
Xiànzhōng dismounted
and said to Zǐyí:
"Now that the Emperor has moved east,
the nation is without a ruler.
You, Lìnggōng, are the Grand Marshal."
Guō Zǐyí was the Zhōngshūlìng,
hence referred to as Lìnggōng.
Zǐyí did not respond.
Gǒng interjected, saying:
"Why do you not speak?"
Zǐyí reprimanded him
and sent troops to escort the traveling court.
On the day of Dīngchǒu,
the imperial carriage arrived at Huázhōu.
Officials had fled and scattered,
with no one left to provide supplies,
and the accompanying generals and soldiers suffered from cold and hunger.
Coincidentally, Guān Jūnróng Shǐ Yú Cháo'ēn was leading the Shéncèjūn from Shǎn to meet them.
The Emperor then went to Cháo'ēn's camp.
Fēngwáng Gǒng saw the Emperor at Tóngguān.
The Emperor did not blame him.
He retired to the tent,
where he made disrespectful remarks.
Attendant ministers proposed to execute him,
so he was granted death.
On the day of Wùyín,
the Tǔbō entered Cháng'ān.
Gāo Huī, along with the Tǔbō general Mǎ Zhòngyīng and others, enthroned Chéng
hóng, the grandson of the late Bīn Wáng Shǒulǐ, as emperor.
They changed the reign title,
appointed various officials,
and made former Hànlín Xuéshì Yú Kěfēng and others their chancellors.
The Tǔbō plundered the imperial treasuries and markets,
and burned down houses,
leaving Cháng'ān desolate and empty.
Miáo Jìnqīng, sick and lying at home,
was carried in by people,
and coerced.
Jìnqīng kept his mouth shut and did not speak,
and the barbarians dared not kill him.
At this time, the scattered soldiers of the six armies plundered everywhere,
and the gentry and common people, avoiding the chaos,
all entered the mountains and valleys.
On the day of Xīnsì,
the Emperor arrived at Shǎn,
and officials gradually began to arrive.
Guō Zǐyí led thirty horsemen from Yùsùchuān, following the mountains eastward.
He said to Wáng Yánchāng:
"Most of the fleeing soldiers from the six armies are in Shāngzhōu.
Now, quickly go and gather them.
Shāngzhōu,
whose administrative seat is Shàngluòxiàn,
is two hundred eighty-one lì from the capital.
Within a few days,
we will head north from Lántián towards Cháng'ān,
and the Tǔbō will surely flee."
Passing Lántián,
he met Yuánshuài Dūyúhòu Zāng Xīràng and Fèngxiáng Jiédùshǐ Gāo Shēng,
obtaining nearly a thousand soldiers.
Wǔguān
is in the northwest of Shāngzhōu,
south of Lántiánxiàn in Yōngzhōu.
Tǔ
is pronounced in the entering tone from tūn.
Guò
is pronounced gǔ hé,
also gǔ wò.
Shǐ
is pronounced shū lì.
Jìn
is pronounced qí jìn.
"When the fleeing soldiers reach Shāngzhōu,
the officials will surely hide, and the people will be in chaos."
He sent Yánchāng to proceed directly into Shāngzhōu to pacify them.
The generals were in the midst of letting their troops pillage violently,
but hearing of Zǐyí's arrival,
they were all overjoyed and obeyed his orders.
Zǐyí feared that the Tǔbō would press towards the imperial carriage,
so he left troops at Qīpán.
Dù Yòu said: Qīpán
is what Wáng Mǎng called
"the fortress of ràoliù, blocking the south from Jīngchǔ."
Ràoliù means
that it is obstructed and winding on all sides,
with water winding around and flowing,
now called Qīpán, Shí'èrhèn.
Chéng
is pronounced chéng zhèng.
Tǔ
is pronounced in the entering tone from tūn.
By the time he reached Shāngzhōu,
he had gathered troops along the way,
including the defense troops at Wǔguān, totaling four thousand men.
The army's morale slightly revived.
Zǐyí then wept as he exhorted the generals and soldiers to jointly wipe away the national shame
and recapture Cháng'ān.
They were all moved and agreed to obey orders.
Zǐyí requested Tàizǐ Bīnkè Dìwǔ Qí to be the Liángliàoshǐ
to supply the army with food.
The Emperor issued an edict to Zǐyí,
fearing that the Tǔbō would move east towards Tóngguān,
summoning Zǐyí to the traveling court.
Zǐyí submitted a memorial stating:
"If I do not retake the capital, I will have no face to see Your Majesty.
If I deploy troops to Lántián,
the barbarians will surely not dare to move eastward."
The Emperor permitted it.
Fūyán
Jiédù Pànguān Duàn Xiùshí persuaded Jiédùshǐ Bái Xiàodé to lead troops to the rescue.
In the first year of Shàngyuán,
the Wèiběi and Fūfāng Jiédùshǐ were established,
governing Fū, Fāng, Dān, and Yán four prefectures,
with its administrative seat in Fāngzhōu.
Tǔ
is pronounced in the entering tone from tūn.
Tóng
is pronounced tóng.
Shuō
is pronounced shì ruì.
Nàn
is pronounced nǎi dàn.
Moving south towards the Jīngjī,
Lǐ Sìyè came from the Western Regions to the rescue at the beginning of Zhìdé,
and Bái Xiàodé came from Fūfāng to the rescue during the Guǎngdé crisis.
Both were initiated by Duàn Xiùshí,
whose loyalty and righteousness were truly innate.
The Tubo, having already enthroned Guǎngwǔ Wáng Chénghóng,
desired to plunder the city's scholars, women, and artisans,
then gather their forces and return to their own country.
Zǐyí sent the Left Yǔlín Grand General, Zhǎngsūn Quánxù, with two hundred cavalry to Lántián to observe the Tubo's movements.
He ordered Dìwǔ Qí to act as the Jīngzhào Yǐn
and accompany him.
He also ordered Zhāng Zhījié, commander of the Bǎoyìng Army, to follow with troops.
When Quánxù reached Hán Gōng Duī,
he beat drums and displayed banners by day,
and lit many fires by night,
to create suspicion among the Tubo.
The former Guānglù Qīng, Yīn Zhòngqīng, gathered nearly a thousand people,
held Lántián,
and acted in concert with Quánxù.
With over two hundred cavalry, he directly crossed the Chǎnshuǐ.
The Tubo were afraid,
and the common people also deceived them, saying:
"Guō Línggōng has arrived from Shāngzhōu with an countless large army!"
The barbarians believed it,
and gradually withdrew their troops.
Quánxù then sent the Shèshēng general, Wáng Fǔ, into the city to secretly gather several hundred youths,
who beat drums and shouted loudly on Zhūquè Street at night.
The Tubo were terrified and panicked,
and on the *gēngyín* day,
they all fled.
*Kǎoyì* says: The old "Tǔbō Zhuàn" says:
"Zǐyí led his retainers, several hundred men, and his family and servants, south into Niúxīnggǔ,
with several hundred camels, horses, carts, and oxen.
Zǐyí lingered,
uncertain where to go.
The Supervisor-General of the Army, Zhōngshū Shèrén Wáng Yánchāng, and the Inspector-Censor Lǐ È, said to Zǐyí: '
As commander-in-chief, with the Emperor in distress abroad,
and the Tubo's power pressing daily,
how can you remain secure in the valley?
Why not head south to Shāngzhōu
and gradually proceed to the Emperor's temporary residence?'
Zǐyí immediately agreed.
Yánchāng said: 'The Tubo will know you are heading south,
and will surely dispatch troops to press you.
If you take the main road,
the situation will be perilous.
It is better to take the Yùshān road and depart,
catching them by surprise.'
Zǐyí again agreed.
Zǐyí's entourage numbered over a thousand people.
The valley was narrow and confined,
stretching for over a hundred *lǐ*,
making it impossible for people to gallop.
Yánchāng and È feared being pursued on the narrow path,
and that those in front and behind would not be able to help each other.
Upon reaching Dàohuí Kǒu,
they separated from Zǐyí,
crossed steep ravines,
ascended Qī Pán,
and proceeded to Shāngzhōu.
Earlier,
Zhāng Zhījié, a commander of the Six Armies, with several hundred men under his command, had fled from the capital to Shāngzhōu,
and had been extensively plundering the assets and saddled horses of court officials, gentry, and residents who had sought refuge
for some days.
When Yánchāng and È arrived,
they persuaded Zhījié, saying: '
As a general in command of the imperial guard,
your army has been defeated, yet you have not gone to the Emperor's temporary residence,
and you have allowed your subordinates to pillage. Where will you go?
Now Guō Línggōng,
the commander-in-chief,
is already about to reach Luònán.
If you reorganize your soldiers,
explain to them the consequences,
invite Línggōng to rally them,
and plan to retake Cháng'ān,
this will be an extraordinary achievement for you.'
Zhījié was greatly pleased.
At that time, several other generals, such as Zāng Xīràng, Gāo Shēng, Péng Tǐyíng, and Lǐ Wéishēn,
each with dozens of cavalry of their own retainers and household troops,
arrived one after another,
and also followed their plan,
all joining to form an army,
agreeing not to commit violence.
Yánchāng remained in the army to oversee the agreement.
È, with several cavalry, went to welcome Zǐyí,
and met him over ten *lǐ* from Luònán.
They then returned with Zǐyí to Shāngzhōu.
All the generals were overjoyed
and complied with his regulations.
When the Tubo were about to enter the capital,
the former Guānglù Qīng, Yīn Zhòngqīng, escaped the disaster,
reached Lántián,
and gathered a hundred or so defeated soldiers and brave volunteers,
fortifying Lántián to resist the Tubo.
His forces gradually grew
to a thousand men.
After Zǐyí arrived in Shāngzhōu,
he recruited men to scout the enemy's situation,
and the Yǔlín General Zhǎngsūn Quánxù requested to go.
When Quánxù reached Hán Gōng Duī,
Zhòngqīng, having allied with the government army,
grew even stronger in power,
and thus they acted in concert.
Zhòngqīng led over two hundred cavalry on a reconnaissance mission,
directly crossing the Chǎnshuǐ.
The Tubo were afraid,
and asked the common people,
who all deceived them, saying: 'Guō Línggōng has an innumerable grand army.'
The invaders believed it,
and thus withdrew their troops and returned."
The "Fényáng Jiāchuán" says:
"The Duke, with thirty cavalry, followed Yùsù Chuān,
skirting the mountains eastward.
The Duke looked west towards the national gate,
weeping uncontrollably,
and said to Yánchāng: 'For the *shèrén*'s plan,
how can the nation be restored?'
Yánchāng sobbed and could not reply.
The Duke said to him: 'I reckon the generals and scattered soldiers will surely flee to Shāngyú.
If we quickly gather the scattered soldiers,
and also the Wǔguān soldiers,
within a few days,
we will reappear in Lántián,
set up a deceptive army,
wave banners,
and encamp at Hán Gōng Duī.
The Tubo will surely fear us and retreat,
then we will quickly pursue them together.'
Passing Lántián,
the Duke discussed with Yánchāng, saying: 'When scattered soldiers reach Shāngzhōu,
if officials do not maintain order,
then the army will be in chaos and the people will disperse.'
He sent Yánchāng by a secret path to spend the night in Shāngzhōu.
It was indeed as he had discussed.
Yánchāng, using the Duke's words, rallied and pacified them,
and the chaos ceased,
and the dispersed returned."
Now, this is followed.
He led over three hundred cavalry under his command eastward.
Upon reaching Tóngguān,
the defending general Lǐ Rìyuè captured and killed him.
On the *rénchén* day,
an edict appointed Yuán Zài as Provisional Commander-in-chief of the Army,
and Dìwǔ Qí as Jīngzhào Yǐn.
On the *guǐsì* day,
Guō Zǐyí was appointed Western Capital Retainer.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Zǐyí departed from Shāngzhōu.
On the *jǐhài* day,
Yú Cháoēn's subordinate Huángfǔ Wēn was appointed Shǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Zhōu Zhìguāng was appointed Huázhōu Cìshǐ.
This laid the groundwork for Zhōu Zhìguāng's defiance in Huázhōu.

and was feared by people even more than Lǐ Fǔguó (李輔國).
Chéng Yuánzhèn (程元振) was jealous of and sought to harm
all generals who had achieved great merits.

Chéng Yuánzhèn (程元振) failed to report it in time,
causing the Emperor to flee in haste.
The Emperor issued an edict summoning troops from all circuits,
but Lǐ Guāngbì (李光弼) and others all resented Chéng Yuánzhèn (程元振) for being in power at court,
so none arrived.
Everyone, both inside and outside the court, gnashed their teeth but dared not speak.
Liǔ Kàng (柳伉), a doctor of the Grand Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Tàicháng Bóshì (太常博士), submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The Quǎnrong (犬戎) violated the passes and crossed the Long (隴) mountains,

plundering the palace,
burning the imperial tombs.

and entrusted power to close attendants,

thereby creating great disaster.

Your Majesty, looking at the illness of today,
how did it come to this?
If you truly wish to preserve the ancestral temples and the altars of grain and soil,

Send all inner attendants to various prefectures.

hence called 'inner attendants'.
At that time, Yú Cháo'ēn (魚朝恩) commanded the Shéncè Army (神策軍).
Issue an edict acknowledging fault,
saying: 'If the world permits Us to reform and correct Our mistakes,

if it is believed that We are incorrigible,

Let the world go where it pleases.'
If this is done,
and troops do not arrive,
people are not moved,
and the world is not convinced,
then I request to close my gate and be cut into a thousand pieces to apologize to Your Majesty."
The Emperor, considering Chéng Yuánzhèn (程元振) had once rendered protective service,
The protective service is mentioned in the previous volume, Baoying (寶應) first year.
On the day Xīnchǒu (辛丑),

8 Wáng Fǔ (王甫) proclaimed himself the Prefect of Jīngzhào (京兆尹),

appointed officials,
and acted tyrannically in Cháng'ān (長安).
On the day Rén Yín (壬寅),
Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) arrived west of the Chǎn River (滻水).
Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) arrived west of the Chǎn River (滻水),
meaning he had already crossed the Chǎn River (滻水)

Someone told Zǐyí (子儀) that
the city was impenetrable.
Zǐyí (子儀) did not listen,

The "Kǎoyì" (考異) states: The "Shílù" (實錄) says:
"A military general, Wáng Fǔ (王甫), and others,
enticed several hundred young ruffians in Cháng'ān (長安),
gathered the drums from the six streets at Zhūquè Street (朱雀街),
and beat them loudly.
Tǔbō (吐蕃) heard this, were terrified,
and fled during the night."
The "Fényáng Jiāchuán" (汾陽家傳) says:
"The archer general, Shèshēng Jiāng (射生將), Wáng Fǔ (王撫),
was fierce and powerful.
He proclaimed himself Grand Master of Remonstrance, Yùshǐ Dàfū (御史大夫),
commanded five hundred cavalry and two thousand infantry,
and appointed his own officials,
planning a rebellion.
On the day Jiǎwǔ (甲午),
the Duke departed from Shāngzhōu (商州);
in the eleventh month of winter, on the day Rén Yín (壬寅),
the Duke was positioned to the right of the Chǎn River (滻水).
Wáng Fǔ (王撫), knowing of the Duke's arrival,
set up a firm formation within the city,
with spears and halberds like a forest,
giving commands from within,
holding his armor and not coming out.
People advised the Duke that he absolutely could not enter,
but the Duke advanced slowly with thirty horsemen,
not showing the slightest fear,
and ordered someone to shout for Wáng Fǔ (王撫).
Wáng Fǔ (王撫) responded by prostrating himself,
and the unruly mob
dispersed at once."
The "Bīnzhì" (邠志) says:
"Duke Guō (郭公) was stationed in Shāngzhōu (商州).
On the first day of the twelfth month,
he led over fifty thousand troops out of Lántián (藍田),
and encamped a hundred li from the city.
Rumors spread within the city
that a large army was approaching,
terrifying the Western Róng (西戎).
On the third day,
Mǎ Jiā Xiǎo'ér (馬家小兒), Zhāng Xiǎojūn (張小君), Lǐ Jiǔzhǎn (李酒盞), and the archer official Wáng Fǔ (王甫), among over five hundred others,
at midnight,
gathered the drums from the six streets and entered the inner city,
striking the drums like thunder in Tiānmén Street (天門街),
and then divided their forces to hoist banners at various gates.
Tǔbō (吐蕃) believed a large army had arrived during the night,
and fled in unison.
Xiǎojūn (小君) sent a report to Duke Guō (郭公).
On the seventh day,
Duke Guō (郭公) entered the capital with his entire army,
arresting Xiǎojūn (小君), Jiǔzhǎn (酒盞), Wáng Fǔ (王甫), and others,
and rebuked them, saying: 'My army had not yet arrived,
yet you used deception to frighten Tǔbō (吐蕃).
When Tǔbō (吐蕃) discovers this, they will be enraged with you,
burn and destroy the palace,
and depart leisurely.
Is this not due to you!'
He ordered them to be beheaded.
He then reported that he had defeated the rebels and recovered the city."
The "Jiù Zǐyí Chuán" (舊子儀傳) says:
"Quán Xù (全緒) sent the former imperial guard general Wáng Fǔ (王甫) into Cháng'ān (長安),
secretly conspiring with local heroes to provide internal support.
One day,
they simultaneously beat drums on Zhūquè Street (朱雀街),
and the Tǔbō (吐蕃) army fled in panic."
It also says:
"The archer general Wáng Fǔ (王撫) proclaimed himself Prefect of Jīngzhào (京兆尹),
gathered two thousand troops,
and caused chaos in the capital.
Zǐyí (子儀) summoned Wáng Fǔ (王撫)
and killed him.
An imperial edict appointed Zǐyí (子儀) as acting Administrator of Jīngchéng (京城 Liúshǒu, 留守)."
The "Tǔbō Chuán" (吐蕃傳) says:
"The remaining Tǔbō (吐蕃) forces were still in the city.
Military general Wáng Fǔ (王撫) and Grand Master of Remonstrance, Yùshǐ Dàfū (御史大夫), Wáng Zhòngshēng (王仲昇) led troops into the park,
beating drums and shouting loudly.
Zhòngqīng's (仲卿) troops also entered the city,
and the Tǔbō (吐蕃) all fled."
If what the "Bīnzhì" (邠志) says is true,
then Zǐyí (子儀) killed Wáng Fǔ (王撫) and claimed his credit.
It is unlikely that Zǐyí (子儀) would have done such a thing.
Zǐyí's (子儀) achievements and deeds
are highly praised by ancient and modern people.
Líng Zhǔn (淩準), in his writings,
often attacked his shortcomings,
which suggests a possible old grudge,
and therefore cannot be entirely trusted.
We now follow the "Fényáng Jiāchuán" (汾陽家傳) and the old biography of Zǐyí (子儀).
Bái Xiàodé (白孝德) and Zhāng Yùnqí (張蘊琦), the Regional Commander of Bīnníng (邠寧 Jiédu Shǐ, 節度使), led troops to encamp in the metropolitan counties (Jīxiàn, 畿縣).
The Jīngzhào (京兆) Prefecture administered twenty counties.
Wànnián (萬年) and Cháng'ān (長安) were designated "red counties" (Chìxiàn, 赤縣), and the remaining counties were all "metropolitan counties" (Jīxiàn, 畿縣).
The capital region (Jīngjī, 京畿) was then pacified.
9 The eunuch Lǚ Tàiyī (呂太一), who was the Director of Shipping (Shìbó Shǐ, 市舶使) in Guǎngzhōu (廣州), raised troops and started a rebellion.
The Táng (唐) dynasty established the Director of Shipping (Shìbó Shǐ, 市舶使) in Guǎngzhōu (廣州) to collect profits from merchant ships. At that time, eunuchs served in this role.
"舶" (bó)
is pronounced "bái" (白).
The "Jiùzhì" (舊志) says: Guǎngzhōu (廣州) is two hundred and forty li west of Duānzhōu (端州).
The government forces suppressed it.
10 The Túbō returned to Fèngxiáng.
The Jiedùshǐ Sūn Zhízhí closed the city gates and resisted them.
The Túbō besieged it for several days.
The Zhènxī Jiedùshǐ Mǎ Lín heard that the imperial carriage had gone to Shǎn Prefecture
and led over a thousand elite cavalry from Héxī to respond to the crisis.
Fighting his way to Fèngxiáng,
he found the Túbō besieging the city.
Lín led his troops, holding their bows fully drawn and facing outwards,
and burst into the city.
Without doffing his armor,
he emerged from the city to fight with his back to it.
On a lone horse, he advanced ahead of his soldiers and fought fiercely,
capturing and beheading thousands before returning.
The next day,
the barbarians again pressed close to the city, requesting battle.
Lín opened the xuánmén (hanging gate) to await them.
Dù Yù said: The xuánmén
is installed on the inner city gate.
According to the gates of border cities today,
leaves (doors) are set up for opening and closing.
As for the xuánmén,
it is installed outside the gate threshold,
usually suspended and not lowered.
When invaders arrive, it is lowered to block the gate,
serving as a secure double-closure.
(The Túbō) said:
"This general does not fear death;
we should avoid him."
So they departed,
settling in the areas of Yuán, Kuài, Chéng, and Wèi.
Yuán Prefecture was
Gāopíng Commandery;
Kuài Prefecture was
Kuàiníng Commandery;
Chéng Prefecture was
Tónggǔ Commandery.
All of them occupied strategic points in the Hérlǒng region to overlook the Táng territory.
11 In the twelfth month,
on the day Dīnghài,
the imperial carriage departed Shǎn Prefecture.
The Zuǒchéng Yán Zhēnqīng requested that His Majesty first visit the imperial mausoleums and temples
before returning to the palace.
Yuán Zài did not comply.
Zhēnqīng angrily said:
"How can the imperial court bear for you, Xiànggōng, to ruin it again!"
Zài thus bore a grudge against him.
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
His Majesty arrived at Cháng'ān.
Guō Zǐyí led the city officials and various armies to welcome him east of the Chǎn River,
prostrating themselves to await punishment.
His Majesty consoled him, saying:
"I did not employ you early enough,

12 Yú Cháo'ēn was appointed Tiānxià Guānjūnrónɡ Xuānwèi Chǔzhìshǐ,
commanding the palace guards.
His power and favor were unparalleled.
Yú Cháo'ēn, due to his service in welcoming and escorting His Majesty in Shǎn Prefecture,
received excessive power, responsibility, and imperial favor.
Getting Yú when leaving the journey
is like getting a tiger when getting rid of a poisonous snake.
處 (chǔ),
read Chānglǚ fān.
使 (shǐ),

朝 (cháo),
read Zhíyáo fān.
He stationed troops to guard against the Túbō.

Miáo Jìnqīng was appointed Tàibǎo,

Zōngzhèngqīng Lǐ Xiàn was appointed Huángmén Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
After Zūnqìng's departure,
Yuán Zài's power grew even greater.
He used bribes to establish ties with the eunuch Dǒng Xiù,

Whatever His Majesty's intentions were,
zhǔshū is
a provincial clerk.
峴 (xiàn),
read Hùdiǎn fān.
屬 (shǔ),
read Zhīyù fān.
he understood His Majesty's subtle intentions,

a person from Jīn Prefecture.
Jīn Prefecture was
Ānkāng Commandery.
14 After the Túbō departed,
Guǎngwǔ Wáng Chénghóng fled and hid in the wilderness.

16 The Túbō captured the three prefectures of Sōng, Wéi, and Bǎo, and the two newly built cities of Yúnshān.
Sōng Prefecture was Jiāochuān Commandery,
named after the Gānsōng Ridge in its commandery boundary.
In the 28th year of Kāiyuán,
Fèng Prefecture and Yúnshān Commandery were established from Dìnglián of Wéi Prefecture.
In the 8th year of Tiānbǎo,

1 Spring,
first month,
on the day Rényín,
an imperial edict stated that Chéng Yuánzhèn had changed his clothes and moved stealthily,
planning disloyalty,

His Majesty remembered Yuánzhèn's accomplishments,

Jiànnán was divided into Dōngdào and Xīdào,

The Examination of Differences states: Old traditions say:
"Wǔ was Jīngzhào Shàoyǐn.
Because Shǐ Sīmíng blocked the roads with his army,
he did not proceed to his post,
but was sent out as Cìshǐ of Mián Prefecture,
then promoted to Dōngchuān Jiedùshǐ.
The Supreme Emperor's edict combined the two Chuān circuits into one,
and Wǔ was appointed Jiànnán Jiedùshǐ."
New traditions say:
"Wǔ was Shàoyǐn.
Implicated by Fáng Guǎn,
he was demoted to Bā Prefecture.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Dōngchuān."
The rest is the same as the old traditions.
However, Sīmíng blocking the roads in Hé and Luò
should not have prevented Jīngzhào Shàoyǐn from taking up his post!
This year was when Dōngchuān and Xīchuān were first combined into one circuit;
how could it be combined by the Supreme Emperor's edict!
Both new and old traditions are mistaken.
3 On the day Bǐngwǔ,
Jiǎnjiào Xíngbù Shàngshū Yán Zhēnqīng was dispatched to comfort the Shuòfāng mobile army.
When His Majesty was in Shǎn,
Yán Zhēnqīng requested to issue an imperial decree to summon Púgù Huái'ēn,
but His Majesty did not allow it.
Now,
His Majesty ordered Zhēnqīng to persuade Huái'ēn to come to court.
He replied:
"When Your Majesty was in Shǎn,
if your servant had gone and reproached him with loyalty and righteousness,
making him rush to aid,
he might still have had reason to come.
Now that Your Majesty has returned to the palace,
if he advances, it will not be to serve the emperor,
and if he retreats, he cannot abandon his troops.
If summoned,
would he be willing to come!
Moreover, those who say Huái'ēn is rebellious
are only Sīn Yúnjīng, Luò Fèngxian, Lǐ Bǎoyù, and Yú Cháo'ēn, four people.
All other courtiers
say he has been wronged.
Your Majesty would do better to replace Huái'ēn with Guō Zǐyí;
then he can be brought to submission without battle."
At that time, Lǐ Bǎozhēn, Biejia of Fén Prefecture,
who was Bǎoyù's paternal cousin,
knew Huái'ēn had rebellious intentions
and escaped to the capital.
His Majesty was then worried about Huái'ēn,
summoned Bǎozhēn to ask for advice,
and he replied:
"This is not worth worrying about.
The officers and soldiers of Shuòfāng miss Guō Zǐyí
as children miss their fathers and elder brothers.
Huái'ēn deceives his troops by saying
that Guō Zǐyí has already been killed by Yú Cháo'ēn,
and the troops believe him,
so they are used by him.
If Your Majesty truly appoints Zǐyí to lead Shuòfāng,
they will all come without being summoned."
His Majesty agreed with him.
4 On the Jiǎyín day,
Dù Hóngjiàn, the Minister of Rites,
according to the Táng Huìyào, states: "During Emperor Gāozǔ’s abdication,
Wēn Dàyǎ, along with Dòu Wēi and Chén Shúdá, participated in establishing the rituals and ceremonies.
From then until the early Kāiyuán reign,
those who participated in establishing the rituals and ceremonies were not officially titled,
making it impossible to review their contributions.
In the ninth year of Kāiyuán,
Wéi Shùo was appointed Guózǐ Sīyè,
and also oversaw the ritual affairs of the Tàicháng Temple.
From this point until the twenty-third year,
his official position was changed four times,
eventually reaching Tàicháng Qīng,
and he always retained the oversight of ritual affairs.
It was not until the ninth year of Tiānbǎo
that the office of Lǐyí Shǐ was first established,
with Crown Prince Zuǒshùzǐ Wéi Shù as its first occupant."
The character 使 (shǐ)
is pronounced shū lì fān. He said:
“From now on, for the sacrifices at the Yuánqiū and Fāngqiū altars, please use Tàizǔ as the co-sacrificer;
for the grain prayer, use Gāozǔ;
for the grand rain ceremony, use Tàizōng;
and for the Míngtáng, use Sùzōng.”
This was approved.
According to Tang regulations: the winter solstice sacrifice was at the Yuánqiū altar,
the summer solstice sacrifice at the Fāngqiū altar,
the mid-spring prayer for grain,
the mid-summer rain ceremony,
and the late-autumn grand sacrifice at the Míngtáng.
The use of Sùzōng as co-sacrificer
was in accordance with the principle of honoring one's father.
5 On the Yǐmǎo day,
Yōng Wáng Shì was established as the Crown Prince.
6 When the Tubo invaded Cháng'ān,
deserting soldiers from various armies and unruly youths from the countryside gathered to become bandits.
After the Tubo left,
they still hid and lurked in the five valleys of Nánshān, such as Zǐwǔ.
The character 吐 (tǔ)
is pronounced tūn rù shēng.
The Nánshān south of Cháng'ān
extends west to the borders of Qízhōu
and east to the borders of Guózhōu.

Zǐwǔ Gǔ, Xié Gǔ, Luò Gǔ, Lántián Gǔ, and Hénglǐng Gǔ.

7 Tián Chéngsì, Jìedùshǐ of Wèibó, requested to name his command "Tiānxióng Jūn,"

killed Jiéchéng,

The character 還 (huán)

“Huái’ēn and his son have truly wronged me deeply.

and the army on the Fén River will surely not cause trouble.”
Fénshàng
refers to Fényáng,

Zǐyí was appointed Deputy Grand Marshal of Guānnèi and Hédōng, and Jìedùshǐ of Hézhōng, among other titles.
When Huái’ēn’s officers and soldiers heard this,
they all said:

Yàn was implicated for his contact with Chéng Yuánzhèn.
When Yuánzhèn was punished,
Xiàn had contributed
to the matter,
and thus incurred the animosity of the eunuchs.
Lǐ Xiàn had served Sùzōng as prime minister

The character 峴 (Xiàn)

Wáng Jìn, Right Sànqí Chángshì, was appointed Huángmén Shìláng,

The character 散 (sàn)
is pronounced xī dǎn fān.
The character 騎 (qí)

is pronounced Jìn.
This was a prelude to Wáng Jìn’s allegiance to Yuán Zǎi and their eventual joint execution.
10 On the Dīngmǎo day,
Guō Zǐyí was appointed Shuòfāng Jìedù Dàshǐ.
In the second month,
Zǐyí arrived at Hézhōng.
Ten thousand youths from Yúnnán were garrisoned at Hézhōng.
Their commanders were greedy and their soldiers violent,
causing trouble for the entire prefecture.
Zǐyí executed fourteen men
and flogged thirty,
and peace was thus restored to the prefecture.
11 On the Guǐyǒu day,
the Emperor offered sacrifices at the Tàiqīng Temple.
The Tàiqīng Temple
was built by Xuánzōng.
The character 朝 (cháo)
is pronounced zhí yáo fān.
On the Jiǎxū day,
he offered sacrifices at the Tàimiào.
On the Yǐhài day,
he worshipped Hào Tiān Shàngdì at the Yuánqiū altar.
12 Púgù Yáng besieged Yúcì,

He sent an urgent request for troops from Qíxiàn,

Lǐ Guāngyì was garrisoned at Qíxiàn;

The troops could not advance.

Those at the rear
were the ones who could not keep up with the main body of troops.
The character 射 (shè)
is pronounced ér yì fān;
the following characters 乃射 and 射之 are pronounced the same.
“General, why do you shoot people?”
Yù said:

Death is but one thing;
what harm is there in shooting them!”
Bái Yù and Jiāo Huī wanted to kill Yáng

and the Hu people said:

and all the soldiers became resentful and angry,

That evening,

His mother said:

Huái’ēn did not reply,
bowed twice, and left.
His mother, brandishing a knife, chased him, saying:
“I will kill this traitor for the state
and take his heart to apologize to the three armies!”
Huái’ēn fled quickly
and escaped,
then, with three hundred of his subordinates,
crossed the Hé River and fled north.
From Fénzhōu, he crossed the river to the west,
headed north,
and made for Língzhōu.
At that time, Hún Shìzhī (渾釋之), the commander of Shuòfāng, was guarding Língzhōu (靈州).
Huái'ēn's (懷恩) summons arrived,
stating that his entire army was returning to the garrison.
Shìzhī (釋之) said:
"No,
this must be a collapse of the troops."
He was about to refuse them,
but his nephew, Zhāng Sháo (張韶), said:
"Perhaps he has suddenly changed his plans
and is returning to the garrison with his troops;
how can we not admit them?"
Shìzhī (釋之) was undecided.
Huái'ēn (懷恩) moved quickly,
arriving before his scouts,
so Shìzhī (釋之) had no choice but to admit him.
