You shall lead them to attack Língwǔ (靈武).
Then Huái'ēn (懷恩) will have to consider turning back.
This is also a special strategy to save the capital!"
Wéndá (文達) then led his troops to attack Cuīshābǎo (摧砂堡) and Língwǔxiàn (靈武縣),
taking both.
Cuīshābǎo (摧砂堡)
was northwest of Yuánzhōu (原州).
As for Língwǔ (靈武),
the Later Zhōu (周) established Jiàn'ānxiàn (建安縣).
Later, Lìchéngjùn (歷城郡) was also established.
In the third year of Kāihuáng (開皇) of the Suí (隋) dynasty, the commandery was abolished.
In the eighteenth year, Jiàn'ān (建安) was renamed Guǎngrùn (廣閏).
In the ninth year of Rénshòu (仁壽), it was again renamed Língwǔ (靈武)
and belonged to Jīngzhōu (涇州).
When Huái'ēn (懷恩) heard of this,
he abruptly returned from Yǒngshòu (永壽).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Yǒngshǒuxiàn (永壽縣)
belonged to Bīnzhōu (邠州).
In the first year of Wǔdé (武德),
a county was established on Yǒngshòuyuán (永壽原),
and named after the plain.
(Bǎi Wéndá (柏文達) was) greatly defeated,
and nearly half of his soldiers died.
Wéndá (文達) led the remaining troops back to Liángzhōu (涼州),
entering in tears.
Zhìliè (志烈) met him, saying:
"This expedition contributed to the peace of the capital.
What does it matter if soldiers die?"
The soldiers resented his words.
Not long after,
the Túbō (吐蕃) besieged Liángzhōu (涼州),
and the soldiers refused to fight for him.
Zhìliè (志烈) fled to Gānzhōu (甘州),
where he was killed by the Shātuó (沙陀).
The Shātuó (沙陀) bore the surname Zhūyé (朱耶)
and lived in the Shātuóqì (沙陀磧) for generations,
hence their name.
The Shātuó (沙陀) first appear here.
35 In the eleventh month,
on the *Dīngwèi* day,
Guō Zǐyí entered the court from his field headquarters.
Guō Xī, who was in Bīnzhōu,
allowed his soldiers to commit violence.
The *Jiédùshǐ*, Bái Xiàodé, was troubled by this,
but for Zǐyí's sake,
dared not speak.
Duàn Xiùshí, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, volunteered to be appointed *Dū Yúhòu*.
The *Yúhòu*
was an ancient office of *hóuyǎn*.
*Yú*
means to guard against danger.
*Hòu*
means to watch and observe.
After being in office for a month,
seventeen of Xī's soldiers entered the market to get wine,
and stabbed the vintner with a blade.
A vintner
is one who brews wine;
people today call him a *jiǔ dàgōng*.
*Cì*
is pronounced *qī yì*.
Xiùshí lined up his soldiers, took the heads of the seventeen men, mounted them on spears,
and planted them at the market gate.
Xī's entire camp erupted in a great clamor,
fully armored.
Xiàodé was struck with fear,
and summoned Xiùshí, saying:
"What shall we do?"
Xiùshí said:
"It's nothing serious.
I beg to go and resolve it."
Xiàodé sent dozens of men to accompany him,
but Xiùshí dismissed them all,
and selected one old, crippled man
*Zào*
is pronounced *zé zào*.
*Bì*
is pronounced *bǐ yì*,
meaning severely lame.
When the armored men came out,
Xiùshí laughed as he entered,
saying:
"Why arm yourselves for killing an old soldier?
I have brought my head with me."
"Old soldier"
is what Xiùshí called himself.
He meant he had brought his head,
ready for them to chop it off.
Then he admonished them, saying:
"Has the *Chángshì* failed you?
Has the Deputy Marshal failed you?"
The Deputy Marshal
refers to Zǐyí.
*Shuài*
is pronounced *suǒ lèi*.
*Bài*
is pronounced *bǔ mài*.
Xiùshí reproached them, saying:
"The Deputy Marshal's achievements fill heaven and earth.
You should consider his ultimate reputation.
Now the *Chángshì* allows his soldiers to commit violent acts,
which will lead to chaos.
Chaos will implicate the Deputy Marshal.
If the chaos originates from the *Chángshì*,
then how much of the Guō family's glory
will remain?"
Before he had finished speaking,
Xī bowed twice and said:
"Sir, you have kindly instructed Xī in the right way.
[This is a sentence break.]
How dare I not obey!"
He looked around and shouted at his subordinates:
"All of you, disarm!
Disperse and return to your fire-groups!
Anyone who dares to make noise shall die!"
Xiùshí then stayed overnight in the camp.
Xī did not undress the entire night,
and ordered the sentries to beat the *tuò* (clapper) to guard Xiùshí.
In the morning,
they both went to Xiàodé's quarters,
apologizing for their failings,
[This is a sentence break.]
and requesting to amend their errors.
36 Xuē Jǐngxiān, the *Wǔgǔ Fángyùshǐ*, campaigned against the Nan Mountains bandits,
but failed to defeat them for several months.
The Emperor ordered Lǐ Bàoyù to suppress them.
The bandit chief Gāo Yù was the strongest.
Bàoyù dispatched the *Bīngmǎshǐ*, Lǐ Chóngkè, with four hundred cavalry to enter from Yángzhōu,
and surprise them at Táoguó Chuān,
where they were utterly defeated.
Yù fled to Chénggù.
On the *Gēngshēn* day,
Zhāng Xiànchéng, the *Shānnánxī Dào Jiédùshǐ*, captured Yù
and presented him to the court.
All other bandits were suppressed.
37 In the twelfth month,
on the *Yǐchǒu* day,
Guō Zǐyí was appointed *Shàngshū Lìng*.
Zǐyí believed:
"Since Tài Zōng held this office,
successive emperors have not reinstituted it,
and recently the Crown Prince also held it.
It is not an office suitable for a humble subject like me."
He firmly declined,
refused the appointment,
and returned to his post in Hézhōng.
38 In this year,
the Ministry of Revenue reported: 2.9 million households,
and 16.9 million people.
Historians say that after the chaos and disturbances,
the number of households and people decreased by seven or eight tenths compared to peaceful times.
39 The Emperor sent Yútián King Shèng back to his kingdom.
Shèng firmly requested to remain as a palace guard,
entrusting the kingdom to his brother Yào.
Shèng had ordered his brother Yào to govern the kingdom in his stead,
while he himself led troops to assist in the defense.
(See volume 219, Zhìdé Yuánzǎi.)
*Tián*
is pronounced *tú xián* and also *tú jiàn*.
Shèng was granted the title *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*
and bestowed the noble rank of King of Wǔdū.
The First Year of Yǒngtài
(765, *Yǐsì* year)
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the *Guǐmǎo* day, the first day of the month,
the reign title was changed;
a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
2 On the *Wùshēn* day,
Lǐ Bàoyù, the *Chénzhèng*, *Zélù Jiédùshǐ*, was additionally appointed *Fèngxiáng*, *Lǒngyòu Jiédùshǐ*.
Lǐ Bàoyù at that time was garrisoning his *Chénzhèng*, *Zélù Xíngyíng* troops west of the capital,
hence the additional appointment as *Fèngxiáng*, *Lǒngyòu Jiédùshǐ*.
Bàoyù, realizing that there were disturbances in Shāndōng,
and that Shàngdǎng was a military thoroughfare,
and moreover, after the devastation and chaos,
the land was barren and the people impoverished,
had no means to support the army.
So he registered the populace,
selecting one able-bodied man from every three *dìng* (adult males),
exempting them from rent and labor service,
providing them with bows and arrows,
and having them practice archery during agricultural slack seasons.
At the end of the year, a comprehensive test was conducted.
Shǐ Zhào said: This means a general review and test of military preparations.
*Huòguāng Zhuàn*: *Dū Yì Láng*.
Mèng Kāng said: *Dū*
means a test.
According to Han regulations,
commanderies and kingdoms conducted a comprehensive test in the eighth month
to review military preparations.
Within three years,
he obtained 20,000 elite soldiers.
Since no provisions were expended,
the state coffers were full,
and he thus dominated Shāndōng.
Because of this, the infantry of Zélù were regarded as the best among all circuits.
This laid the groundwork for Lǐ Bàozhēn to control the various rebels with the Zélù army.
3 In the second month,
on the *Wùyín* day,
the Dǎngxiàng raided Fùpíng
and burned the Dìnglíng Palace.
4 On the *Gēngchén* day,
Yí Wáng Suí passed away.
5 In the third month,
on the *rénchén* day,

an order was issued for thirteen civil and military officials, including Left Executive Secretary Péi Miǎn and Right Executive Secretary Guō Yīngyì, to attend the court for consultation at the Jíxián Diàn.
During the Yǒnghuī reign,
two scholars from the Hóngwén Guǎn were ordered to attend court daily for consultation at the west gate of the Wǔdé Diàn.
In the first year of Wénmíng,
an edict ordered one incorruptible official of the fifth rank or above from the capital bureaucracy to attend court daily for consultation at the Zhāngshàn and Míngfú Gates.
Towards the end of Xiāntiān,
two envoys from the morning assembly (*cháojíshǐ*) of the sixth rank or above were further ordered to attend court for consultation along with the imperial procession (*suízhàng dàizhì*).
At this time, meritorious officials who had been relieved of their military governorships (*jiézhì*),
having no official duties,
were ordered to attend court for consultation at the gate of the Jíxián Diàn.
Sòng Bái said: In this year,

an edict summoned Left Executive Secretary Péi Miǎn, Right Executive Secretary Guō Yīngyì, Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent Péi Zūnqìng, Acting Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent and Censor-in-Chief Yuán Zhízhí, Grand Administrator of the Heir Apparent and Censor-in-Chief Zāng Xīràng, Left Palace Counsellor Chàng Cuǐ, Acting Minister of Justice Wáng Áng, Gāo Shēng, Acting Minister of Works and Manager of Departmental Affairs Cuī Huàn, Vice Minister of Personnel Lǐ Jìshī, Wáng Yánchāng, Vice Minister of Rites Jiǎ Zhì, and Tutor to the Prince of Jìng, Wú Lìngyáo, to attend court for consultation at Jíxián.
Because meritorious officials had been relieved of their military governorships,
and had no official duties,
they were made to attend court for consultation in the imperial library,
interspersed with literary scholars,
as a mark of imperial favor.
"Your Majesty has summoned me and others to attend for consultation to be available for questioning;
this is a great virtue of the Five Emperors.
Recently, although Your Majesty tolerated their straightforwardness, their words were not recorded;
there was the name of tolerating subordinates,
but no substance of listening to admonitions.
This caused those who admonished to gradually close their mouths and eat their fill,
inviting each other to become officials for salary.
This is why loyal and upright people sigh secretly,
and I too am ashamed of it.
Now, military campaigns have continued without cease for ten years,
and people's livelihoods [resources]
are exhausted from their looms.
Those who command troops have mansions extending across streets and lanes,
and their servants are sated with wine and meat,
while the poor and emaciated are conscripted into service,
their very skin and marrow exploited.
In Cháng’ān city, there are robberies and assassinations in broad daylight,
and officials dare not question them.
Government is disordered, duties are neglected,
generals are corrupt, soldiers are violent,
and all affairs of state are in disarray,
like boiling porridge or entangled flax.
In the eras of Táng and Yú, there was the office of 'all affairs.'
Kǒng Ānguó said: *kuí*
means to measure.
To measure all affairs,
and manage all officials.
This 'all affairs'
refers to the affairs of all officials.
*Jí*
is pronounced with the initial *q* and final *ji*.
*Jiāng*
is pronounced with the initial *ji* and final *liàng*.
*Lā*
is pronounced with the initial *l* and final *dá*.
The officials concerned dare not report this to Your Majesty,
enduring poison and swallowing pain,
destitute and without recourse.
If Your Majesty does not at this time contemplate methods to remedy this,
I am truly fearful.
Currently, only Shuòfāng and Lǒngxī face the threat of the Tǔbō and Púgù;
the troops of Bīn, Jīng, and Fèngxiáng are sufficient to deal with them.
Beyond these,
east to the sea,
south to Pānyú,
*Tǔ*
is pronounced with the initial *tūn* entering tone.
*Bīn*
is pronounced *bīnjīn*.
*Jì*
is pronounced *qíjì*.
*Pānyú*
is pronounced *Pānyú*.
there are no minor thefts, yet the troops are not disbanded.
The wealth of the empire is drained,
the grain of the empire is exhausted,
to supply useless armies.
I do not know the reason for this.
If one were to 'be mindful of danger in times of peace,'
it would be possible to fortify strategic locations,
station garrisons for defense,
and furlough all the rest,
using the provisions of grain, stores, and supplies
to alleviate the contributions and taxes of the weary populace.
Annually, half of the national tax could be reduced.
How can Your Majesty hesitate to make changes,
causing the suffering of the entire realm to worsen day by day?!"
The emperor was unable to adopt his advice.
6 On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Lǐ Bàoyù was appointed Grand Councillor (*Tóng Píngzhāngshì*),
continuing to guard Fèngxiáng as before.
7 On the *gēngxū* day,
Tǔbō sent an envoy to request peace.
An edict ordered Yuán Zài and Dù Hóngjiàn to make an alliance with them at Xīngtáng Sì.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Ānguó Sì is in Chánglè Fāng, the fourth street east of Zhūquè Jiē.
Xīngtáng Sì is in a different *fang* southwards.
It was built in the eighth year of Kāiyuán.
The *Huìyào* says: Xīngtáng Sì is in Dàníng Fāng.
In the first year of Shénlóng,
Princess Tàipíng built it for the Empress Dowager as Wǎngjí Sì.
In the twentieth year of Kāiyuán, it was renamed Xīngtáng Sì.
*Shǐ*
is pronounced *shūlì*.
*Zài*
is pronounced *zǔhài*,
also as the character itself.
"What about Tǔbō's request for an alliance?"
He replied:
"The Tǔbō benefit from our lack of preparedness.
If they come unexpectedly,
the state cannot be defended."
Lack of preparedness
means not being ready.
He also dispatched troops to patrol Jīngyuán to spy on them.
8 This spring there was no rain,
and a *dǒu* of rice cost a thousand coins.
9 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the *dīngchǒu* day,
Censor-in-Chief Wáng Yì was appointed Commissioner for Tax Money of All Circuits (*Zhūdào Shuìqiánshǐ*).
Péi Xǔ, the Commissioner for Land Tax, Tribute, and Salt and Iron for Hédōng Circuit, came to court to report on affairs.
The emperor asked:
"How much revenue does the liquor monopoly bring in annually?"
Xǔ was silent for a long time.
The emperor asked him again,
and he replied:
"I have come from Hédōng.
Everywhere I passed, I saw that soybeans and grain had not yet been sown,
and farmers were worried and resentful.
I thought that when Your Majesty saw me,
you would first ask about the people's suffering,
but instead you demanded of me profits.
That is why I did not dare to answer."
The emperor apologized to him
and appointed him Vice Director of the Left Department (*Zuǒsī Lángzhōng*).
Xǔ
was the son of Kuān.
Péi Kuān served Xuánzōng.
10 On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Yán Wǔ, the Military Governor of Jiànnán, passed away.
Wǔ had held three governorships in Jiànnán.
According to the record, in the second year of Zhìdé, after Cháng’ān was recovered,
Wǔ was appointed Military Governor of Jiànnán and Dōngchuān.
The Retired Emperor issued an edict combining the two circuits of Jiànnán into one,
and appointed Wǔ as Administrator of Chéngdū (*Chéngdū Yǐn*)
and Military Governor of Jiànnán.
Later,
he was recalled to court.
Last year,
Wǔ was again appointed to guard Jiànnán.
In total, he served twice as Military Governor of Jiànnán,
receiving three appointments in total.
In the second year of Guǎngdé, the *Kǎoyì* states that the combination of Dōngchuān and Xīchuān was not by edict of the Retired Emperor.
Indeed, in the second year of Zhìdé, Jiànnán was divided into Dōngchuān and Xīchuān.
In this year, when the Retired Emperor returned to the capital,
Dōngchuān and Xīchuān were combined into one circuit,
which must not have been by edict of the Retired Emperor.
The *Tōngjiàn* records in the first year of Qiányuán that Yán Wǔ was demoted to Bāzhōu;
in the first year of Bǎoyìng, it records that Yán Wǔ, Minister of War, was made Military Governor of Xīchuān;
and in the second year of Guǎngdé, it records the combination of Dōngchuān and Xīchuān,
and Yán Wǔ, Palace Counsellor, was made Military Governor.
According to the *Tōngjiàn* records,
Wǔ was Military Governor of Jiànnán twice.
Now it says he governed Jiànnán three times;
this would imply he was previously appointed to Dōngchuān,
only then could it be three.
Since the *Tōngjiàn* does not adopt from the old and new histories,
it should not record the section about being appointed to Dōngchuān.
However, to say Wǔ governed Jiànnán three times
requires further extensive research.
According to the record in the next volume about Wǔ's use of Cuī Gàn,
he was only governor of Jiànnán twice.
The *Tángshū* probably made this error
due to Dù Fǔ's poem,
which contains the line,
"The imperial favor gave him three *jié* [appointments] before and after."
Zhāng Yí, the Prefect of Zǐzhōu, did not quite meet his expectations,
so he summoned and flogged him to death.
However, the Tǔbō feared him
and dared not invade his territory.
His mother repeatedly cautioned him against his arrogance and brutality,
but Wǔ did not listen.
When he died,
his mother said:
"Now I am finally saved from becoming a government slave!"
She meant that Wǔ's arrogance and brutality
would lead to crimes of rebellion,
and calamity would surely extend to his mother.
Now that he was dead, she knew she was spared.
11th of the 5th month,
on the day Guǐchǒu,
Guō Yīngyì, the Right Prime Minister, was appointed Jìannán Military Commissioner.
This set the stage for Guō Yīngyì's death at the hands of Cuī Hàn.
射 (Shè),
read Yín Xiè.
使 (Shǐ),
read Shū Lì.
12The wheat harvest in the imperial domain was abundant.
Fěi Qí, the Governor of Jīngzhào, requested to tax the people's fields,
taking one-tenth of the produce from ten *mǔ*.
He said:
"This is the ancient law of the 'one-tenth'."
The historian says Fěi Qí cleverly invoked ancient laws to deceive the emperor.
琦 (Qí),
pronounced Qí.
13Hóu Xīyì, the Pínglú Military Commissioner, was stationed in Zīqīng.
Hóu Xīyì's stationing in Zīqīng began in the first year of Shàngyuán, as recorded in the previous volume.
使 (Shǐ),
read Shū Lì;
same below.
He built pagodas and temples,
which caused hardship to the military and the prefectures.
Lǐ Huáiyù, the Army Commander, gained the support of the troops.
Xīyì became jealous of him
and used an incident to relieve him of his military post.
Xīyì lodged with a shaman outside the city.
The soldiers closed the city gates and refused to let him in,
acclaiming Huáiyù as their commander.
Xīyì fled to Huázhōu,
submitted a memorial asking for punishment,
and an imperial edict pardoned him
and summoned him back to the capital.
Autumn,
7th month,
on the day Rénchén,
Lǐ Miǎo, the Prince of Zhèng, was appointed Grand Military Commissioner of Pínglú and Zīqīng.
Miǎo
was an imperial prince.
He was granted the name Zhèngjǐ.
At that time, Lǐ Bǎochén,
the Chéngdé Military Commissioner, Tián Chéngsì,
the Wèibó Military Commissioner, Xuē Sōng,
the Xiāngwèi Military Commissioner, and Lǐ Huáixiān,
the Lúlóng Military Commissioner,
had gathered the remnants of Ān Shǐ's followers.
Each commanded tens of thousands of elite soldiers,
trained their armies, fortified their cities,
and appointed their own civil and military officials.
They did not pay tribute or taxes,
and they all formed marriage alliances with Liáng Chóngyì, the Shānnán Dōngdào Military Commissioner, and Zhèngjǐ,
supporting each other.
The imperial court focused solely on appeasement
and could no longer control them.
Although they were nominally provincial vassals,
they were merely kept in check by loose reins.
The historian, using the event of Lǐ Zhèngjǐ expelling Hóu Xīyì, describes in detail the tyranny of the regional military governors.
復 (Fù),
read Fú Yòu.
將 (Jiàng),
read Jì Liàng.
朝 (Cháo),
read Zhí Yáo.
14On the day Jiǎwǔ,
Shēngpíng Gōngzhǔ, the emperor's eldest daughter, was married to Guō Ài, the son of Guō Zǐyí.
15Shěn Shì, the crown prince's mother,
was from Wúxīng;
Wúxīng
is Húzhōu.
See volume 218, the first year of Sùzōng's Zhìdé era.
When the emperor recaptured Luòyáng,
see volume 221, the second year of Qiányuán.
She had not yet been brought back to Cháng'ān;
then Shǐ Sīmíng again captured Luòyáng,
see volume 121, the second year of Qiányuán.
After the emperor ascended the throne,
he sent envoys to search for her widely,
but without success.
On the day Jǐhài,
a nun named Guǎngchéng from Chóngshàn Temple in Shòuzhōu falsely claimed to be the crown prince's mother.
Upon investigation,
she was found to be the former wet nurse of the Shàoyáng Courtyard.
The Dàmíng Palace had a Shàoyáng Courtyard,
where the crown prince resided.
尼 (Ní),
read Nǚ Yí.
少 (Shào),
read Shī Zhào.
169th month,
on the day Gēngyín, the first day of the month,
one hundred tall altars were set up at Zīshèng and Xīmíng Temples.
According to 'Bǎi Gāozuò',
these were one hundred-foot tall altars.
'Táng Huìyào' states: Zīshèng Temple was in Chóngrén Ward,
originally the residence of Zhǎngsūn Wújí.
In the third year of Lóngshuò,
it was established as a nunnery for the blessings of Empress Wéndé.
In the fourth year of Xiánhēng,
it was converted back into a monastery.
Xīmíng Temple was in Yánkāng Ward,
originally the residence of Yáng Sù, Duke of Yuè.
During the Zhēnguān era, it was bestowed upon Púwáng Tài.
After Tài's death,
it was established as a temple.
This refers to the Hùguó Rénwáng Jīng (Sutra of Humane Kings for the Protection of the Country).
People were dressed as bodhisattvas and ghosts,
led by musicians and ceremonial guards.
All officials welcomed them outside Guāngshùn Gate
and followed them to the temples.
17Púgù Huái'ēn enticed the Huíhé, Tǔbō, Tǔyùhún, Dǎngxiàng, and Núlà
with several hundred thousand troops to invade together.
He ordered the Tǔbō generals Shàng Jiésī Zànmó and Mǎ Chóngyīng to advance towards Fèngtiān via the northern route.
The Dǎngxiàng commanders Rèn Fū, Zhèng Tíng, Hǎo Dé, and others were to advance towards Tóngzhōu via the eastern route.
Sòng Bái said: Rèn Fū
was a former general of Shuòfāng.
趣 (Qù),
read Qī Yù;
same below.
The Huíhé followed the Tǔbō,
and Huái'ēn then followed them with Shuòfāng troops.
Guō Zǐyí sent the Army Supervisor, Zhào Fù, to report to the emperor:
"The barbarians are all cavalry;
they come like flying,
and should not be underestimated.
I request that the various regional military commissioners—Lǐ Bǎoyù of Fèngxiáng, Lǐ Guāngtíng of Huápú, and Bái Xiàodé of Bīnnìng—
'Lǐ Guāngtíng'
should probably be
'Lǐ Guāngjìn'.
At this time, Lǐ Guāngtíng, Hǎo Tíngyù, and Lǐ Zhōngchén were each in their own commanderies;
the others were all garrisoned in separate positions west of the capital.
Many of the regional forces did not dispatch troops promptly.
Lǐ Zhōngchén was playing *jīqiú* with his generals.
Upon receiving the edict,
he immediately ordered preparations for departure.
His generals and supervising eunuchs all said:
"An army's march must choose an auspicious day."
Zhōngchén angrily replied:
"If one's parents are in urgent danger,
how can one choose a day before saving them?!"
He immediately led his troops onto the road that day.
Huái'ēn encountered a sudden illness midway and returned.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
he died at Míngshā.
The 'Kǎoyì' states: The old biography of Huái'ēn says:
"Huái'ēn led the Huíhé and Shuòfāng troops in a continuous advance.
Upon reaching Míngshā County,
he fell ill and was carried back;
on the 9th day of the 9th month,
he died in Língwǔ."
According to the 'Chánglì',
the 9th month began on the day Gēngyín.
The day Dīngyǒu
was the 8th day.
Both 'Tánglì' and 'Bīnzhì' state
"on the 8th day of the 9th month,
Huái'ēn died in Língzhōu."
We now follow the 'Shílù'.
His adjutant, Xú Huángyù, killed him.
Fàn Zhìchéng then killed Huángyù and took command of his troops.
Huái'ēn defied orders for three years,
twice leading barbarian invaders,
becoming a great menace to the country—referring to the invasions of last year and this year.
Previous imperial edicts never stated that he had rebelled.
When the emperor heard of his death,
he said sadly:
"Huái'ēn did not rebel;
he was merely misled by those around him!"
The Túfān reached Bīnzhōu.
Bái Xiàodé held the city by defending it.
On the jiǎchén day,
the Emperor ordered the prime ministers and the chief officials of various departments.
The Six Bureaus had Shàngshū,
the Temples had Qīng,
the Directorates had Jiān,
all serving as chief officials of various departments.
They played music,
seeking blessings from the Buddha.
A force of 100,000 Túfān reached Fèngtiān,
and the capital was shaken with fear.
Hún Jiān, the commander of the Shuòfāng army,
and Bái Yuánguāng, the commander of the punitive expedition, had previously garrisoned Fèngtiān.
When the barbarians first arrayed their camps,
Hún Jiān led two hundred elite cavalry to charge them,
placing himself at the forefront of his soldiers.
The barbarian host crumbled.
Hún Jiān, seizing a barbarian general, leapt on his horse and returned.
None of his attendant cavalry were struck by arrows or spears.
The soldiers on the city walls watched this,
and their courage began to rally.
On the yǐsì day,
the Túfān attacked again.
The barbarians suffered heavy casualties.
After several days,
they gathered their troops and returned to their camps.
Hún Jiān led his troops to raid them by night,
killing over a thousand people.
In total, he engaged the barbarians in more than two hundred battles,
beheading five thousand.
On the bǐngwǔ day,
the lectures of the Hundred High Seats were abolished.
Guō Zǐyí was summoned from Hézhōng
and ordered to garrison Jīngyáng.
On the jǐyǒu day,
Lǐ Zhōngchén was ordered to garrison Dōngwèiqiáo,
Lǐ Guāngjìn to garrison Yúnyáng,
Mǎ Lín and Hǎo Tíngyù to garrison Biànqiáo,
Lǐ Bàoyù to garrison Fèngxiáng,
the Inner Court Eunuch Luò Fèngxiān and General Lǐ Rìyuè to garrison Zhōuzhì,
Zhōu Zhìguāng, the Jiedushi of Tónghuá, to garrison Tóngzhōu,
Dù Miǎn, the Jiedushi of Fūfáng, to garrison Fāngzhōu.
The Emperor personally led the Six Armies to garrison within the Imperial Park.
On the gēngxū day,
an edict was issued for a personal expedition.
On the xīnhài day,
Yú Cháo'ēn requested a search of the city,
confiscating private horses from officials and commoners.
He ordered all men in the city to wear black
and form military units.
All but one of the city gates were blocked.
The officials and commoners were greatly alarmed,
and many escaped by climbing walls and digging holes.
Officials could not stop them.
Yú Cháo'ēn wanted to escort the Emperor to Hézhōng to avoid the Túfān.
Fearing that various officials would not agree,
one morning,
when the hundred officials entered court,
they stood in line for a long time.
The palace gate did not open.
The palace gate refers to the East and West Upper Palace Gates.
A declaration was made:
"The Túfān have repeatedly invaded the imperial environs.
The imperial carriage wishes to proceed to Hézhōng.
What do you think?"
The high officials were all astonished and did not know how to respond.
There was a Supervising Secretary Liú,
who alone stepped out of line and retorted loudly:
"Is the imperial envoy rebelling?
Tang people called eunuchs 'imperial envoys'.
Shǐ (使) is pronounced '疏吏' (shū lì).
Instead of uniting to resist the invaders,
you suddenly wish to coerce the Son of Heaven to abandon the ancestral temples and the altars of grain and soil and leave.
If this is not rebellion, what is it?"
Yú Cháo'ēn was startled, disheartened, and withdrew,
and the matter was thus dropped.
Supervising Secretary Liú stood firm in upholding righteousness in court and could not be swayed like this.
Moreover, he was an official of the Two Provinces,
yet the historians lost his name.
What was the purpose of the Tang dynasty establishing a Historiography Institute?
The `Kǎoyì` states: The New Biography of Yú Cháo'ēn says:
"Púgù Yáng attacked Jiàngzhōu,
and sent Yáo Liáng to occupy Wēn,
luring the Huíhé to capture Héyáng.
Cháo'ēn dispatched Lǐ Zhōngchéng to attack Yáng,
with Huò Wén Yáng supervising him;
Wáng Jǐngcén to attack Liáng,
with Wáng Xīqiān supervising him.
They defeated Yáng at Wànquán and
captured Liáng alive.
Gāo Huī and others led the Túfān to invade.
He sent Liú Déxìn to attack and slay them.
Therefore, Cháo'ēn, due to the repeated victories of his subordinates,
secretly prided himself.
At this time, Guō Zǐyí, having achieved the meritorious service of stabilizing the realm,
ranked first among all subjects.
Cháo'ēn envied him in his heart,
and taking advantage of the defeat at Xiāngzhōu,
he slandered and disparaged him.
Sùzōng did not heed his words,
yet still dismissed Zǐyí's troops
and kept him in the capital.
When Dàizōng ascended the throne, he and Chéng Yuánzhèn
jointly intensified the slander.
The Emperor had not yet realized their true nature,
and Zǐyí was greatly worried.
Soon after, the Túfān captured the capital,
and ultimately his strength was needed,
and the imperial house was once again secure.
Cháo'ēn felt inwardly ashamed,
and so advised the Emperor to move to Luòyáng,
wishing to keep the Róngdǐ at a distance.
While the hundred officials were in court,
Cháo'ēn emerged with over ten armed men and said: 'The barbarians have invaded the imperial domain.
We wish to proceed to Luòyáng.
What say you?'
The prime ministers had not yet responded.
A close official interjected, saying: 'Is the imperial envoy rebelling?
The troops currently garrisoned are sufficient to resist the invaders.
Why suddenly coerce the Son of Heaven to abandon the ancestral temples?'
Cháo'ēn's expression was dejected,
and Zǐyí also deemed it inappropriate,
so it was stopped."
Lǐ Zhào's `Guóshǐ Bǔ` says:
"During Dàizōng's reign, the hundred officials
stood in line for a long time,
but the palace gate did not open.
Yú Cháo'ēn suddenly emerged with over ten men wielding bare blades,
and declared: 'The Western Barbarians have repeatedly invaded the imperial environs.
We wish to proceed to Hézhōng.
What do you think?'
The prime ministers and those below were flustered and did not know how to respond.
Supervising Secretary Liú,
whose name is not recorded,
stepped out of line and retorted loudly: 'Is the imperial envoy rebelling?'
And so on.
Thus, the proposal to move the capital was stopped."
Upon examination, Púgù Yáng attacked Yúcì,
and it is not heard that he attacked Jiàngzhōu.
Gāo Huī was captured by Lǐ Rìyuè,
and it is not heard that he was slain by Liú Déxìn.
Cháo'ēn wished to proceed to Hézhōng,
and it is not heard that he wished to proceed to Luòyáng.
Since it says 'repeatedly invaded the imperial environs',
it must be the later Túfān invasion.
What the `New Book` states,
it is not known what book it is based on.
Now we follow the `Guóshǐ Bǔ`.
From the bǐngwǔ day to the jiǎyín day,
heavy rain did not stop,
thus the barbarians could not advance.
The Túfān shifted their troops to attack Lǐquán.
The Dǎngxiàng plundered Báishuǐ to the west.
Báishuǐ County was
the land of Sùyì in the Hàn dynasty.
In the second year of Tàihé of the Later Wèi dynasty,
Báishuǐ County and Báishuǐ Commandery were established.
The Suí dynasty abolished the commandery and kept the county.
In the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Tóngzhōu.
On the dīngsì day,
the Túfān heavily plundered tens of thousands of men and women and then left,
burning houses and
trampling nearly all the crops in their path.
Zhōu Zhìguāng led his troops to intercept and attack them,
defeating them north of Chéngchéng,
and then pursued them northward to Fūzhōu.
Sòng Bái says: Fūzhōu was
the land of Diāoyīn in Shàngjùn during the Hàn dynasty.
In the eleventh year of Tàihé of the Later Wèi dynasty,
Dōngqínzhōu was established.
In the second year of Xiàochāng,
it was renamed Běihuázhōu.
In the second year of Fèidì,
it was renamed Fūzhōu,
named after Fūzhì.
The `Jiùyù Zhì` says: Fūzhōu is
four hundred fourteen li southeast of Tóngzhōu.
Chéngchéng County is
ninety li north of Tóngzhōu.
Fāngzhōu was Hàn Qúsōu County,
the seat of the Commander of Zhōngbù.
In the Later Wèi dynasty, it belonged to Fūzhōu.
In the seventh year of Tiānhé of the Zhōu dynasty,
Emperor Yuán served as governor of Fūzhōu,
and established horse stables here.
Emperor Gāozǔ of the Táng dynasty then established Fāngzhōu,
named after the horse stables.
The `Jiùyù Zhì` says: Fāngzhōu is
one hundred ten li north of Fūzhōu.
Fū is
pronounced fū.
They then killed Zhāng Lín, the Prefect of Fūzhōu,
buried Dù Miǎn's eighty-one family members alive,
and burned over three thousand houses in Fāngzhōu.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Jǐwèi day,
the Sūtra lectures were resumed at Zīshèng Sì.
The Tǔbō retreated to Bīnzhōu.
There they met the Huíhú
and again united to invade.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
they reached Fèngtiān.
The Kǎoyì states: The Bīnzhì states:
“In the eighth month,
Huái'ēn led the various barbarians to invade.
In the ninth month,
an imperial edict ordered Guō Gōng to attack them.
He deployed his army at Jīngyáng.
The Huíhú camped north of the Jīng River,
ten lǐ away from us.
Cháo'ēn requested to attack the Huíhú.
Guō Gōng said: ‘My past relationship with the Huíhú was quite intimate.
Their current invasion
must be due to some reason.
I intend to guide them and inquire,
and they may surrender without battle.’
Cháo'ēn spread rumors, claiming Guō Gōng was colluding with Huái'ēn,
and secretly led various armies to set up camps on the Wèi River.
Guō Gōng's memorials did not reach the emperor for more than ten days.
Guō Gōng's sons in Cháng'ān heard of this
and sent the junior general Qiáng Yǔ to inform Guō Gōng of public opinion.
Guō Gōng secretly made his way to court for an audience,
and also reported the public sentiment.
The emperor said: ‘There is no such thing.’
On the same day, he ordered him to proceed to Jīngyáng.
Cháo'ēn was astonished and said: ‘Guō Gōng is truly a noble person;
I doubted him earlier,
and I am truly a petty man.’ ”
However, the Huíhú did not arrive at Jīngyáng in the ninth month.
They only reached Fèngtiān on the Xīnyǒu day of the tenth month.
On the Bǐngyín day, Jīngyáng was besieged.
On the Dīngmǎo day, Zǐyí had already allied with them.
From beginning to end, it was only seven days.
How could there have been a situation where memorials did not reach the emperor for over ten days?
Zǐyí was the marshal,
facing a strong enemy.
How could he abandon his army and go to court?
The Fényáng Family Record also has no mention of him going to court at this time.
Therefore, this account is not adopted.
On the Guǐhài day,
the Dǎngxiàng burned the official residences and civilian homes in Tóngzhōu and departed.
On the bǐngyín day,
the Huíhé and Tǔbō combined forces and besieged Jīngyáng.
Zǐyí ordered his generals to set up strict defenses but not to engage in battle.
As evening fell,
the two barbarian forces retreated and encamped on Běiyuán,
which was to the north of Jīngyáng.
On the dīngmǎo day,
they again came to the city walls.
At this time,
the Huíhé and Tǔbō had heard of Púgù Huái'ēn's death,
and had already begun to contend for superiority,
not being harmonious with each other.
They camped in separate divisions,
and Zǐyí knew this.
The Huíhé were to the west of the city.
Zǐyí sent his vanguard general Lǐ Guāngzàn and others to persuade them.
A vanguard general
was a general at the forefront,
commanding the marshal's personal guards.
"Shuì"
is pronounced "shì ruì fān";
"wǎng shuō" below is the same.
The Huíhé did not believe them,
saying:
"Is Duke Guō truly here?
You are deceiving us.
If he is indeed here,
can we see him?"
Guāngzàn returned and reported this.
Zǐyí said:
"Our forces are currently outnumbered,
and it is difficult to win by force.
In the past, we had a very close agreement with the Huíhé.
It would be better to step forward personally and persuade them;
we can subdue them without battle."
His generals requested to select five hundred elite cavalry to serve as his escort.
Zǐyí said:
"This would only be detrimental."
Guō Xī reined in his horse and admonished him, saying:
"They
are tigers and wolves!
My lord
is the marshal of the state!
How can you offer yourself as bait to the barbarians!"
Zǐyí said:
"If we fight now,
both father and son will die, and the state will be in peril.
If I go and speak to them with utmost sincerity,
perhaps I will be fortunate enough to be followed,
which would be a blessing for all under heaven!
If not,
then I will perish, but my family will be preserved."
Such was Zǐyí's careful consideration of advantages and disadvantages and his weighing of their importance.
"Go!"
He then, with a few horsemen, opened the gate and rode out,
sending someone to shout:
"The Grand Councilor is coming!"
Zǐyí was at that time the Zhōngshū Lìng,
hence the shout "Grand Councilor."
Their great commander, Héhúlù Dūdu Yàogěluó,
who was the Khan's younger brother,
stood in front of the formation, holding a bow with an arrow nocked.
Zǐyí removed his helmet, took off his armor, threw down his spear, and advanced.
The Huíhé chieftains looked at each other and said:
"It is him!"
They all dismounted and bowed down in a row.
Zǐyí also dismounted,
stepped forward and grasped Yàogěluó's hand,
and reproached him, saying:
"You Huíhé rendered great service to Tang,
referring to how they raised troops to help Tang pacify Ān and Shǐ.
How could you break your promise,
penetrate deep into our territory,
and invade and press upon the Jīxiàn counties—
the counties belonging to the Tang capital,
counties adjacent to the city walls were 'Red' (chì),
and 'Secondary Red' (cìchì).
For example, Zhāoyìng, Fèngtiān, Lǐquán and other counties were 'Secondary Red.'
The rest were Jīxiàn counties.
To form animosity,
betray kindness, and aid a traitorous minister,
how foolish is that!
Moreover, Huái'ēn rebelled against his sovereign and abandoned his mother—
referring to Huái'ēn blocking troops in Fén and Jiàng,
then defecting to Língwǔ,
abandoning his mother in Fénzhōu.
Now I have come forward personally,
letting you seize and kill me.
My officers and soldiers will surely fight to the death against you."
Yàogěluó said:
"Huái'ēn deceived me,
saying that the Tiān Kèhán had already died,
and that the Grand Councilor had also passed away,
and that Zhōngguó was without a ruler.
That is why I dared to come with him.
Now I know that the Tiān Kèhán is in Shàngdū—
since the Zhēnguān era, the rulers of the four barbarian tribes requested Tàizōng to be the Tiān Kèhán;
thereafter, the barbarians generally referred to the Son of Heaven as the Tiān Kèhán.
Shàngdū
is Cháng'ān.
Huái'ēn was also killed by Heaven,
how could we possibly want to fight with the Grand Councilor!"
Zǐyí then persuaded him, saying:
"The Tǔbō are lawless,
taking advantage of the disorder in our country.
They disregarded the relationship of maternal uncle and nephew—
Tǔbō married Tang princesses,
forming nations related as maternal uncle and nephew.
'Fù'
is pronounced 'fú yòu fān.'
'Shuō'
is pronounced 'shì ruì fān.'
They burned and plundered our Jīdiàn.
The wealth they plundered cannot be fully transported;
horses, cattle, and various livestock
stretch for hundreds of lǐ,
spreading across the plains.
This is Heaven bestowing it upon you.
Preserve your army and continue good relations,
defeat the enemy to gain wealth.
For your plan,
what could be more advantageous than this!
You must not miss this opportunity."
Yàogěluó said:
"I was misled by Huái'ēn.
My failure to you is truly deep.
Now I ask to exert all my strength for you,
to attack the Tǔbō to atone for my transgression.
However, Huái'ēn's son
is the Kèdūn's brother;
I wish you would spare him and not kill him."
Zǐyí agreed.
The Huíhé spectators
formed two wings,
advancing slightly.
Zǐyí's subordinates also advanced,
but Zǐyí waved his hand to make them retreat.
Then he took wine and drank with the chieftains.
Yàogěluó made Zǐyí first hold the wine to swear an oath.
Zǐyí poured a libation on the ground and said:
"Long live the Emperor of Great Tang!
Long live the Huíhé Khan!
Long live the generals and ministers of both nations!
Whoever breaks this oath
shall perish before the battle array,
and their family □ □."
When the cup reached Yàogěluó,
he also poured a libation on the ground and said:
"As the Grand Councilor swore!"
Thereupon, all the chieftains were greatly pleased and said:
"Previously, we had two shamans accompany the army.
The shamans said this journey would be very peaceful and safe,
that we would not fight with Tang,
and would see a great man and return.
Now it has indeed come true."
Zǐyí presented them with three thousand bolts of colored silk,
which the chieftains divided to reward the shamans.
Zǐyí finally concluded the agreement and returned.
When the Tǔbō heard of this,
that night,
they withdrew their troops and fled.
The Huíhé sent their chieftain Shíyěnà and five others to have an audience with the Emperor.
Yào Gěluó led his troops to pursue the Túbō.
Zǐyí sent Bái Yuánguāng to lead elite cavalry to go with them.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
they fought on the western plain of Língtái
and thoroughly defeated them.
Língtái
was the territory of Hán Qūngū County during the Hàn dynasty.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo,
its name was changed to Língtái.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Língtái County
is ninety lǐ east of Jīngzhōu.
The Old History states:
The place where the Túbō were defeated
was fifty lǐ west of Língtái County,
a place called Chìshānlǐng.
Four thousand men and women who had been plundered were recovered.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
they again defeated them east of Jīngzhōu.
Kǎoyì says: The Shílù says:
"In the tenth month,
the Túbō retreated to Bīnzhōu,
met the Huíhé,
and again combined to act as bandits.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
they plundered Fèngtiān.
On the day Yǐhài,
the Huíhé, because Púgù Huái'ēn had died,
wavered towards the Túbō.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Guō Zǐyí rode alone to the Huíhé army,
removed his helmet, and spoke with the Huíhé general,
reproaching him for breaking the agreement,
and then made an alliance with him.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
six Huíhé chiefs, including Shíyěnà, came to court.
On the day Gēngchén,
Zǐyí sent Bái Yuánguāng to lead elite troops to join several thousand Huíhé soldiers and thoroughly defeat more than a hundred thousand Túbō troops on the western plain of Língtái County."
Fényáng Jiāchuán says:
"On the eighth day of the tenth month,
the Túbō and Huíhé jointly besieged Jīngyáng,
encamping on the northern plain.
That night,
the Duke ordered each flank to clear two paths,
intending to fight the next morning.
The next day,
the bandits arrived again,
with even more soldiers and armor.
The Duke sent Lǐ Guāngzàn and others, who were generals from the yáqián, to go out and persuade them,
but they did not accept,
requesting a decisive battle.
The Duke, seeing the strength of the bandit cavalry,
and also the disparity in numbers,
with his isolated army having no reinforcements,
ordered the camp gate to be opened,
and rode out on a single horse.
Mǎ Xī, a Lángzhōng of the Ministry of War, and Chén Hóng, a Yuánwàiláng of the Ministry of Rites, followed him at that time on a single horse each.
Yào Gěluó, the Huíhé Héhúlù Dūdū and Prime Minister, stood before the formation,
with his bow drawn, facing them.
The Duke advanced and shouted at him, saying so-and-so.
Yào Gěluó and others were bewildered and ashamed,
prostrated themselves and begged for forgiveness,
and thereupon made an alliance with him.
When the Túbō heard of this,
in the middle of the night,
they withdrew their troops and fled.
The Huíhé Yào Gěluó and others quickly pursued them.
The Duke sent Bái Yuánguāng and others to follow.
On the fifteenth day,
they reached Língtái
and defeated more than one hundred thousand troops of Shàng Jiéxī.
On the eighteenth day,
they again defeated them east of Jīngzhōu."
The Old Zǐyí Zhuàn says:
"Zǐyí arrived from Hézhōng,
encamped at Jīngyáng,
and the bandit cavalry had already converged.
Zǐyí's army numbered over ten thousand men,
while the various barbarians surrounded them several times over.
Zǐyí ordered Lǐ Guózhěn and Gāo Shēng to resist them to the east,
Wèi Chǔyù to guard their south,
Chén Huíguāng to guard their west,
Zhū Yuáncóng to guard their north,
and Zǐyí himself led two thousand armored cavalry, appearing and disappearing on all sides.
The barbarians saw him and asked: 'Who is this?'
They were told: 'It is Guō Línggōng.'
The Huíhé said: 'Is Línggōng alive?
Púgù Huái'ēn said that the Heavenly Khagan had abandoned the four seas,
and Línggōng had also passed away,
and that China had no master,
so we came with him.
Now Línggōng is alive, is the Heavenly Khagan alive?'
They were told: 'The Emperor lives for ten thousand years without limit.'
The Huíhé all said: 'Huái'ēn deceived us.'
Zǐyí again sent someone to inform them, saying so-and-so.
The Huíhé said: 'We thought Línggōng was dead;
if not,
why would we have come here!
If Línggōng truly lives,
how can we see him?'
Zǐyí was about to go out,
but his generals remonstrated.
Zǐyí said: 'Our strength is truly no match now,
and sincerity can move spirits,
let alone these barbarians!'"
The Huíhé Zhuàn says:
"Túbō general Mǎ Zhòngyīng and others began to withdraw in the tenth month,
returning via the old route of Bīnzhōu.
Huíhé chief Luódágān and others led their troops of over two thousand cavalry to Jīngyáng to request surrender.
Zǐyí allowed it,
leading several thousand men in armor with bows drawn.
The Huíhé interpreter said: 'We did not come with ill intent;
we wish to see Línggōng.'
Zǐyí said: 'I am Línggōng.'
The Huíhé said: 'Please remove your armor.'
Zǐyí then took off his helmet and spear armor,
spurred his horse forward and advanced alone.
The Huíhé chiefs looked at each other and said: 'It is he!'
They immediately dismounted and bowed in a row.
Zǐyí also dismounted,
held the hands of the Huíhé general Héhúlù Dūdū Yào Gěluó and others,
and reproached them, saying: 'The state knows the Huíhé have rendered service
and has amply rewarded you.
Why did you break the agreement
and invade our royal domain!
I ought to fight you,
why surrender now!
I, myself, entered your camp,
allowing you to capture me at will,
my subordinate officers and soldiers must fight you.'
The Huíhé interpreter again said: 'Huái'ēn was faithless
and came to report to the Khagan, saying:
"The Son of Heaven of Táng has now gone to Jiānghuái,
and Línggōng no longer commands troops."
That is why we dared to come.
Now we know that the Heavenly Khagan is still in the capital,
and Línggōng is a general,
and Huái'ēn has been killed by Heaven.
We now ask to pursue and kill the Túbō,
seize their sheep and horses,
to repay the nation's kindness.' "
Bīn Zhì says:
"On the twenty-fourth day of the tenth month,
the Huíhé approached Jīngyáng,
arraying themselves west of the city,
and sent Chinese speakers to say: 'Who is the general in the city?'
The military official replied: 'It is Guō Línggōng.'
The barbarians said: 'Guō Línggōng is dead;
you are deceiving us.'
Duke Guō heard this,
and went alone with five or six of his household retainers in ordinary clothes.
His son Xī and others pulled his horse to stop him,
but the Duke struck their hands and said: 'Go.'
He sent someone to inform the barbarians,
then reined in his horse and approached them.
The Huíhé looked closely and said: 'It is he!'
They all dismounted and bowed,
saying: 'At first we did not know Línggōng was still alive;
may we surrender today?'
Duke Guō entered their ranks
and drank wine with them.
The barbarians again requested, saying: 'We fear we will not be trusted;
we wish to attack the Túbō to prove our loyalty.'
Duke Guō agreed.
The Huíhé attacked the Túbō
and pursued them.
On the thirtieth day,
they defeated the Fān troops at Língtái,
killing over ten thousand men before departing."
According to the Chánglì, the first day of the tenth month was Jǐwèi,
the third day was Xīnyǒu,
and the nineteenth day was Dīngchǒu.
If what the Shílù says is true,
how could hundreds of thousands of Huíhé and Túbō troops enter the capital region
and stay for seventeen days without any attack or battle?
At that time,
Chén Hóng was in Zǐyí's army,
and the dates he recorded are closer to the truth.
Now, for the dates of the two barbarians besieging Jīngyáng,
Zǐyí making an alliance with the Huíhé,
and defeating the Túbō,
all follow the Fényáng Jiāchuán.
For the events,
various records are consulted, and the most credible ones are chosen.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Púgù Huái'ēn's generals Zhāng Xiūcáng and others surrendered.
On the day Xīnsì,
an edict was issued to cease the imperial expedition,
and the state of alert in the capital was lifted.
18. Earlier,
Sùzōng appointed Guō Yīng-yì (郭英乂), the Military Commissioner of Shǎnxī, to command the Shéncè Army,
and assigned the palace attendant Yú Cháo-ēn (魚朝恩) to supervise the army.
When Yīng-yì entered court to become a Minister (Púyè),
Cháo-ēn took sole command of it.
When the Emperor traveled to Shǎn,
Cháo-ēn led the troops in Shǎn and the Shéncè Army to escort him,
all of whom were called the Shéncè Army,
and the Son of Heaven went to their camp.
When the capital was pacified,
Cháo-ēn brought the army back to the Forbidden City,
commanding it himself.
However, he had not yet gained an equal footing with the Northern Army.
The Northern Army
refers to the Six Armies of the Northern Gate.
Cháo-ēn, with the Shéncè Army, followed the Emperor and encamped in the imperial gardens.
Their power gradually became formidable,
and they were divided into Left and Right Divisions,
taking precedence over the Northern Army.
The historians state that this was how the Shéncè Army's might and prosperity began.
19. Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀), fearing that Púgù Míngchén (僕固名臣) and Lǐ Jiànzhōng (李建忠) — all of whom were valiant generals under Huái'ēn (懷恩) — might defect to foreign tribes,
requested to recruit them.
Míngchén
was Huái'ēn’s nephew,
and was at the time in the Huíhét (回紇) camp.
The Emperor issued an edict pardoning the crimes of all former generals who had rendered meritorious service,
ordering the Huíhét to send them over.
On the day Rénwǔ,
Míngchén surrendered with over a thousand cavalrymen.

Zǐyí sent Mùróng Xiūzhēn (慕容休貞), Grand Master of Cavalry with Independent Rank and concurrently Minister of Works (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), with a letter to admonish the Dǎngxiàng (党項) chiefs Zhèng Tíng (鄭庭) and Hǎo Dé (郝德) and others,
all of whom came to Fèngxiáng (鳳翔) to surrender.
20. On the day Jiǎshēn,
Zhōu Zhìguāng (周智光) came to the imperial court to present his victory report,
and returned to his post after two nights.
Zhìguāng’s crime of unauthorized killing had not yet been dealt with,
referring to the crime of killing Zhāng Lín (張麟) and the family of Dù Miǎn (杜冕).
*Zhì* (治) is pronounced *zhí zhī* (直之).
21. On the day Yǐyǒu,
Húlù Dūdū (胡祿都督) and over two hundred other Huíhét entered for an audience.
They were given over ten thousand bolts of silk and cloth as gifts both before and after;
the imperial treasuries became empty,
and the salaries of all officials were taxed to provide for them.
Punctuated by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖), reviewed by Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐)
Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
Compiled by Imperial Edict
Later, Xúe Tiāntái (學天台)
Yǒngtài First Year
(Yǐsì, 765 CE)
1. In the intercalary tenth month,
on the day Yǐsì,
Guō Zǐyí entered the court.
Zǐyí, considering that Língwǔ (靈武) had just been recovered,
Púgù Huái'ēn (僕固懷恩) had died,
and Língwǔ was just recovered,
and that the barbarian tribes were not yet settled,
requested that Lù Sìgōng (路嗣恭) be appointed as the commander of the Shuòfāng (朔方) army provisions, to be stationed at Sānyuán.
*Jūnnliángshǐ* (軍糧使)
is the same as *liángliàoshǐ* (糧料使).
The death of Yáng Zhìliè (楊志烈) is mentioned in the previous volume, Guǎngdé Second Year.
The Emperor agreed to all of his requests.
2. On the day Dīngwèi,
all officials requested to surrender their official land (zhífántián) to be used for army provisions.
According to Táng regulations: officials of the first rank were granted twelve *qǐng* of official land,
second rank ten *qǐng*,
third rank nine *qǐng*,
fourth rank seven *qǐng*,
fifth rank six *qǐng*,
sixth rank four *qǐng*,
seventh rank three *qǐng* and fifty *mǔ*,
eighth rank two *qǐng* and fifty *mǔ*,
ninth rank two *qǐng*.
All were allocated land within one hundred *lǐ*.
For governors (Dūdū), protectors (Dūhù) of various prefectures, and officials of princely establishments: second rank twelve *qǐng*,
third rank ten *qǐng*,
fourth rank eight *qǐng*,
fifth rank seven *qǐng*,
sixth rank five *qǐng*,
seventh rank four *qǐng*,
eighth rank three *qǐng*,
ninth rank two *qǐng* and fifty *mǔ*.
For officials of garrisons (Zhèn), outposts (Shù), passes (Guān), ferries (Jīn), and sacred mountains and rivers (Yuè Dú): fifth rank five *qǐng*,
sixth rank three *qǐng* and fifty *mǔ*,
seventh rank three *qǐng*,
eighth rank two *qǐng*,
ninth rank one *qǐng* and fifty *mǔ*.
For Commanders (Zhōnglángjiàng) of the Three Guards and Commandants (Zhéchōng Dūwèi) of upper-grade *fǔ*: six *qǐng*;
middle-grade *fǔ*: five *qǐng* and fifty *mǔ*;
lower-grade *fǔ* and Commanders (Lángjiàng): five *qǐng*.
For Commanders of Valor (Guǒyì Dūwèi) of upper-grade *fǔ*: four *qǐng*;
middle-grade *fǔ*: three *qǐng* and fifty *mǔ*;
lower-grade *fǔ*: three *qǐng*.
For Chief Clerks (Zhǎngshǐ) and Deputy Commanders (Biéjiàng) of upper-grade *fǔ*: three *qǐng*;
middle-grade and lower-grade *fǔ*: two *qǐng* and fifty *mǔ*.
For Palace Masters of Soldiers (Diǎnjūn) in princely establishments: five *qǐng* and fifty *mǔ*;
Deputy Palace Masters of Soldiers (Fù Diǎnjūn): four *qǐng*;
Imperial Bodyguards (Qiānniú Bèishēn Zuǒyòu) and Imperial Bodyguards (Qiānniú Bèishēn): three *qǐng*.
For Military Clerks (Bīngcáo) of upper-grade *fǔ* commandants: two *qǐng*;
middle-grade and lower-grade *fǔ*: one *qǐng* and fifty *mǔ*.
For Commanders of Arranged Armies (Lièjūn Xiàowèi): one *qǐng* and twenty *mǔ*;
Company Commanders (Lǚshuài): one *qǐng*;
Platoon Leaders (Duìzhèng Fù): eighty *mǔ*.
For princes and below,
there was also permanent land (yǒngyètián) of one hundred *qǐng*.
For officials with specific duties (zhíshìguān): first rank sixty *qǐng*;
Princely Duke (Jùnwáng) and officials with specific duties of secondary first rank: fifty *qǐng*;
State Duke (Guógōng) and officials with specific duties of secondary second rank: thirty-five *qǐng*;
Commandery Duke (Jùngōng) and officials with specific duties of secondary third rank: twenty-five *qǐng*;
County Duke (Xiàngōng) and officials with specific duties of secondary third rank: twenty *qǐng*;
Marquis (Hóu) and officials with specific duties of secondary fourth rank: twelve *qǐng*;
Viscount (Zǐ) and officials with specific duties of secondary fifth rank: eight *qǐng*;
Baron (Nán) and officials with specific duties of secondary fifth rank: five *qǐng*;
sixth and seventh ranks: two *qǐng* and fifty-eight *mǔ*;
eighth and ninth ranks: two *qǐng*.
For Supreme Pillar of the State (Shàng Zhùguó): thirty *qǐng*;
Pillar of the State (Zhùguó): twenty-five *qǐng*;
Supreme Defender-General (Shàng Hùjūn): twenty *qǐng*;
Defender-General (Hùjūn): fifteen *qǐng*;
Supreme Light Chariot Commandant (Shàng Qīngchē Dūwèi): ten *qǐng*;
Light Chariot Commandant (Qīngchē Dūwèi): seven *qǐng*;
Supreme Cavalry Commandant (Shàng Qí Dūwèi): six *qǐng*;
Cavalry Commandant (Qí Dūwèi): four *qǐng*;
Valiant Rider Commandant (Xiāoqí Wèi) and Flying Rider Commandant (Fēiqí Wèi): eighty *mǔ*;
Cloud Rider Commandant (Yúnqí Wèi) and Martial Rider Commandant (Wǔqí Wèi): sixty *mǔ*.
Unofficial officials (sǎnguān) of fifth rank and above
were given the same as officials with specific duties of the corresponding rank.
3. On the day Wùshēn,
Lù Sìgōng (路嗣恭), Attendant Gentleman of the Board of Revenue (Hùbù Shìláng), was appointed Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng.
Sìgōng cleared thorny thickets,
established military offices,
and his authority and commands were greatly enforced.
4. On the day Jǐyǒu,
Guō Zǐyí returned to Hézhōng.
Zǐyí returned to his post in Hézhōng after an audience in the capital.
The character *huán* (還)
is pronounced *suān* (宣),
and also sounds as written.
5. Earlier,
Yán Wǔ (嚴武), the Military Commissioner of Jiànnán, memorialized to appoint General Cuī Gǎn (崔旰) as Prefect of Lìzhōu.
At that time, Shu (蜀) had just been in chaos,
with mountain bandits blocking the roads;
Gǎn suppressed and pacified them.
When Wǔ was again stationed in Jiànnán,
he bribed Zhāng Xiànchéng (張獻誠), the Military Commissioner of Shānnán Xīdào, to request Gǎn.
Lìzhōu
was the ancient town of Jūhóu (苴侯),
and in the Qín and Hàn dynasties, it was the land of Jiāmáng (葭萌).
In the Shǔ Hàn dynasty, it was called Hànshòu (漢壽) County;
in the Jìn dynasty, Jìnshòu (晉壽);
in the Liáng dynasty, Lízhou (黎州),
soon changed to Lìzhōu;
in the Tiānbǎo era, it became Yìchāng (益昌) Commandery;
in the Qiányuán era, it reverted to Lìzhōu.
It was under the jurisdiction of Shānnán Xīdào.
*Gǎn* (旰) is pronounced *gǔ dàn* (古旦).
Gǎn
went to Wǔ.
Wǔ made him Prefect of Hànzhōu,
and ordered him to lead troops to attack the Tǔbō (吐蕃) in the Western Mountains,
consecutively capturing several of their cities,
reclaiming hundreds of *lǐ* of land.
Hànzhōu
was the land of Hànluò (漢雒) County, Shífāng (什方), and Miánzhú (綿竹);
the Táng dynasty established Hànzhōu in the Chuígǒng (垂拱) era;
in the Tiānbǎo era, it became Déyáng (德陽) Commandery;
in the Qiányuán era, it reverted to a prefecture.
Wǔ died,
as mentioned in the previous volume, April.
Guō Yīnggān (郭英幹), the Overall Commander of Military Affairs (Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ),
who was Yīng-yì’s younger brother,
along with Guō Jiālín (郭嘉琳), the Grand Commander of the Vanguard (Dū Yúhòu), both requested that Yīng-yì be appointed Military Commissioner.
Gǎn was at that time the Overall Commander of Military Affairs for the Western Mountains,
and together with his subordinates, he requested that General Wáng Chóngjùn (王崇俊) be appointed Military Commissioner.
It happened that the imperial court had already appointed Yīng-yì.
Yīng-yì therefore bore a grudge against Gǎn.
A few days after arriving in Chéngdū,
he falsely accused Chóngjùn of a crime and executed him.
He summoned Gǎn back to Chéngdū,
but Gǎn declined, citing his duty to defend against the Tǔbō and that he could not yet return.
Yīng-yì became even angrier,
cutting off his provisions to distress him.
Gǎn moved deeper into the mountains.
Yīng-yì personally led troops to attack him,
ostensibly to assist Gǎn in defending.
Coincidentally, there was heavy snow,
and the mountain valleys were several *chǐ* deep.
Many soldiers and horses froze to death.
Gǎn launched a surprise attack,
and Yīng-yì was utterly defeated,
collecting his remaining troops,
which numbered barely a thousand, and returned.
Yīng Yì 英乂's administration was
harsh, cruel, arrogant, and extravagant.
He showed no concern for his soldiers,
and the hearts of the people were alienated and resentful.
When Xuánzōng 玄宗 left Shǔ 蜀,
he converted his temporary palace into a Daoist temple,
and cast a golden image of himself.
Yīng Yì 英乂 loved the lush beauty of its bamboo and trees,
so he memorialized to have it made into a military camp.
Consequently, he moved the golden image away
and resided there himself.
Gàn 旰 declared that Yīng Yì 英乂 was rebelling, saying,
"If not,
why would he move the golden image and reside in its place?"
Thereupon, he led his部部 of over five thousand men to attack Chéngdū 成都.
On the day Xīnsì 辛巳,
they fought west of the city,
and Yīng Yì 英乂 was soundly defeated.
Gàn 旰 then entered Chéngdū 成都
and massacred Yīng Yì 英乂's family.
Yīng Yì 英乂 fled alone on horseback to Jiǎnjiuān 簡州.
Sòng Bái 宋白 said: Jiǎnjiuān 簡州
was the land of Niúbì Xiàn 牛鞞縣 in the Hàn 漢 dynasty.
In the third year of Rénshòu 仁壽 of the Suí 隋 dynasty (603),
Yáng'ān 陽安 and Píngquán 平泉 of Yìzhōu 益州,
and Zīyáng 資陽 of Zīzhōu 資州 were separated
to establish Jiǎnjiuān 簡州.
The prefecture had the Láijiǎn Chí 賴簡池 pond,
from which it took its name.
Yīng Yì 英乂's head was sent to Gàn 旰.
The military commanders Bó Màolín 柏茂琳 of Qióngzhōu 邛州, Yáng Zǐlín 楊子琳 of Lúzhōu 瀘州, and Lǐ Chāngnáo 李昌巎 of Jiànzhōu 劍州,
Sòng Bái 宋白 said: Qióngzhōu 邛州
was Línqióng Xiàn 臨邛縣 in the Hàn 漢 dynasty.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng 梁 Wǔlíng Wáng Jì 武陵王紀 established Qióngzhōu 邛州,
taking its name from the Qiónglái Shān 邛來山 mountains on its southern border.
Lúzhōu 瀘州
was Jiāngyáng Xiàn 江陽縣 in the Hàn 漢 dynasty.
Liáng 梁 established Lúzhōu 瀘州,
taking its name from the Lúshuǐ 瀘水 river.
Jiànzhōu 劍州
was Zǐtóng Xiàn 梓潼縣 of Guǎnghàn 廣漢 in the Hàn 漢 dynasty.
Liáng 梁 established Ānzhōu 安州.
The Western Wèi 西魏 changed it to Shǐzhōu 始州.
In the second year of Xiāntiān 先天 of the Táng Đường dynasty (713),
it was changed to Jiànzhōu 劍州,
taking its name from Jiàngé 劍閣.
Náo 巎
is pronounced "nuo dao" (slave-knife) [in fanqie].
The "Kǎo Yì" 考異 (Examination of Differences) states: The Táng Lì 唐曆 (Tang Calendar) writes it as
"Lǐ Chāngkuí 李昌夔";
we now follow the "Shílù" 實錄 (Veritable Records).
There was great chaos in Shǔ 蜀.
Gàn 旰
was a native of Wèizhōu 衛州.
6. Gù Yáo 顧繇, the magistrate of Huáyúan 華原, memorialized that
Yuán Zài 元載's son Bóhé 伯和 and others were abusing their power and accepting bribes.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Wùxū 戊戌,
Yáo 繇 was exiled to Jǐnzhōu 錦州.
Sòng Bái 宋白 said: In the second year of Chuígǒng 垂拱 of the Táng 唐 dynasty (686),
the land of Máyáng Xiàn 麻陽縣 of Chénzhōu 辰州 was separated,
and mountain caves were opened,
to establish Jǐnzhōu 錦州.
The old gazetteer states: Jǐnzhōu 錦州 was three thousand five hundred *lǐ* from the capital.
7. Since the Rebellion of Ān Lùshān 安祿山 and Shǐ Sīmíng 史思明,
the halls and rooms of the Guózǐjiān 國子監 had fallen into disrepair,
and many soldiers were occupying them.
Jìjiǔ 祭酒 Xiāo Xīn 蕭昕 memorialized,
"Schools cannot be allowed to fall into disuse."
The first year of Dàlì 大曆
(Bǐngwǔ 丙午, 766)
This year, in the eleventh month,
the reign title was changed.
1. Spring,
first month,
on the day Yǐyǒu 乙酉,
an edict ordered the restoration and enrollment of students at the Guózǐjiān 國子監.
2. On the day Bǐngxū 丙戌,

Liú Yàn 劉晏, Minister of Revenue, was appointed Commissioner of Transport, Ever-Normal Granaries, Coinage, and Salt and Iron for Dūjī 都畿, Hénán 河南, Huáinán 淮南, Jiāngnán 江南, Húnán 湖南, Jīngnán 荊南, and Shānnán Dōngdào 山南東道.
Fěi Qí 第五琦, Attendant Official, was appointed Commissioner of Transport for Jīngjī 京畿, Guānnèi 關內, Hédōng 河東, Jiànnán 劍南, and Shānnán Xīdào 山南西道,
to separately manage the empire's revenue and taxation.
3. Zhōu Zhìguāng 周智光 arrived at Huázhōu 華州.
(Zhōu Zhìguāng 周智光 returned to Huázhōu 華州,
see last year in the previous volume.)
The emperor summoned him,
but he did not come. The emperor ordered Dù Miǎn 杜冕 to follow Zhāng Xiànchéng 張獻誠 to Shānnán 山南 to avoid him.
Zhìguāng 智光 sent troops to Shāngshān 商山 to intercept them,
but failed to catch them.
Knowing his crimes were serious, Zhìguāng 智光
gathered desperadoes and idle youths.
Their numbers reached tens of thousands.
He allowed them to plunder to win their favor.
He illegally detained twenty thousand *hú* of grain transported to Guānzhōng 關中,
and often killed envoys from藩鎮 *fānzhèn* (military governorships)
and seized their tribute.
4. Second month,
on Dīnghài 丁亥, the first day of the month,
a ceremony to honor Confucius was held at the Guózǐjiān 國子監.
According to Táng 唐 regulations: Sacrifices to Wénxuān Wáng 文宣王 (Confucius) were held in mid-spring and mid-autumn.
These were always performed on the *shàngdìngwù* 上丁戊
[days?]
with the Jìjiǔ 祭酒, Sīyè 司業, and Bóshì 博士 performing the three libations.
The prime minister was ordered to lead the *chángcān guān* 常參官
(*Chángcān guān* 常參官
refers to officials who attended court daily for regular audiences.
According to Táng 唐 regulations,
civil officials of the fifth rank and above, as well as officials serving in the two secretariats, censors, assistant secretaries, and Grand Astrologers attended court daily,
and were called *chángcān guān* 常參官.
Military officials of the third rank and above had audience every three days,
and were called *jiǔcān guān* 九參官.
Those of the fifth rank and above and newly appointed
*zhézhōng* 折衝
were called *liùcān guān* 六參官.
Students of the Hóngwén 弘文 and Chóngwén 崇文 Academies and the Guózǐjiān 國子監 attended four times a year.
All princes who came to court and those specially summoned by imperial grace attended daily.
As for civil and military officials of the ninth rank and above, and descendants of the two former dynasties,
they attended only on the first and fifteenth day of the month.)
The commander,
Yú Cháo'ēn 魚朝恩, led the generals of the Six Armies to listen to the lectures.
His adopted sons and disciples all wore vermilion and purple robes as students.
After Cháo'ēn 魚朝恩 became prominent,
he studied to lecture on the classics and write essays.
Though he could barely hold a brush to distinguish sentences and phrases,
he immediately declared himself talented in both civil and military arts,
and no one dared to oppose him.
On the day Xīnmǎo 辛卯,
an order was issued to the relevant authorities to repair the Guózǐjiān 國子監.
5. Yuán Zài 元載, monopolizing power,
feared that memorialists would expose his private misdeeds.
He therefore requested:
"When any official discusses matters,
they must first report to their superior,
the superior reports to the prime minister,
and then it is submitted to the emperor."
He also issued an imperial decree to all officials, saying:
"Recently, the various departments have been submitting too many memorials,
and what they say often involves slander.
Therefore, the superiors and prime ministers are entrusted to first determine their feasibility."
The Grand Secretary of the Ministry of Punishments, Yán Zhēnqīng
presented a memorial,
believing:
"The staff officials and censors are Your Majesty's ears and eyes.
Now, to make those who discuss affairs first report to the prime minister
is to deliberately cover up your own ears and eyes.
Your Majesty is troubled by slander from treacherous officials,
why not examine the truth and falsehood of their words!
If what they say is indeed false, they should be executed;
if it is indeed true, they should be rewarded.
Not bothering to do this,
but allowing the world to say that Your Majesty is weary of the bother of listening and reviewing,
using this as a pretext to block the path of remonstrance and contention,
your servant secretly feels pity for Your Majesty because of this!
Emperor Tàizōng wrote in the 'Gate Guard Regulations':
The thirty-three chapters of the Táng Regulations

comprise sections on the various departments of the Department of State Affairs, as well as the Secretarial Bureau, the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, the Court of the Imperial Granaries, the Court of Imperial Entertainments, the Court of the Imperial Treasury, the Court of the Imperial Stud, the Court of the Imperial Manufactories, and the gate guards and palace guards, and accounts.
For those with urgent memorials,
the gate guards and the palace guard officers are to usher them in to present their memorials.
According to the Táng system: for the gate register,
officials within the 'stream' (i.e., appointed officials) recorded their official rank and name,
those outside the 'stream' recorded their age and appearance.
The register was changed once a month;
it was not removed unless there was a transfer or dismissal.
For those without a gate register,
if they had an urgent memorial,
the gate guards and palace guard officers would usher them in to present it.
'Zhàngjiā' (仗家)
refers to the executive officers of the five palace guard divisions.
'Lìdīng' (力丁) is the pronunciation of 'lìdīng' (力丁),
'fān' (翻) is the pronunciation of 'fān' (翻).
This was to prevent obstruction.
After the Tiānbǎo era,
when Lǐ Línfǔ was prime minister,
he deeply hated those who spoke out,
so people communicated with glances on the roads.
The emperor's intentions did not reach below,
and the feelings of those below did not reach above;
there was obstruction and muffled silence.
Shǐ Zhào said: 'Ānyú' (喑嗚)

Kǒng Yǐngdá said: There are two methods, large and small, for the number *yì*. For the small number,

ten myriad (*wàn*) is *yì*,

For the large number,
ten thousand (*wàn*) is the multiplier:
counting by *wàn* up to *wàn*,
that is, ten thousand *wàn* is *yì*;
then counting by *yì* up to *wàn*,
ten thousand *yì* is *zhào*.
(A memorial) stated in brief:
