following the mistaken schemes of your attendants,
harming the great governance of the imperial kings.
Your minister secretly laments this for Your Majesty!"
All were ignored and no replies were given.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Yǐngjí* states that
the first memorial was submitted on the 25th day of the eighth month, and the later memorial on the 12th day of the ninth month.
Now, this is mentioned in the context of the temple construction.
Initially,
the Emperor enjoyed sacrificial rites,
but did not place much importance on Buddhism.
Yuán Zài, Wáng Jìn, and Dù Hóngjiàn became chancellors;
all three favored Buddhism.
Jìn was particularly devout,
not eating meat or blood.
"荤" (*hūn*)
means pungent vegetables.
"血" (*xuè*)
refers to taking blood from slaughtered animals.
"好" (*hào*)
is pronounced *hào*.
The Emperor once asked them,
"Buddhist teachings speak of retribution;
is it truly real or not?"
Zài and others memorialized:
"The state's destiny and fortune are enduring;
without virtues and karma cultivated in past lives,
how could this be achieved!
With fortune and karma already fixed,
even if there are occasional minor disasters,
they ultimately cannot cause harm.
This is why Ān Lùshān and Shǐ Sīmíng, though their rebellion was raging, both met with calamity from their sons;
this refers to Ān Qìngxù killing Lùshān, and Shǐ Cháoyì killing Sīmíng.
(And they) died from illness upon leaving the city;
the Huíhé and Tǔbō launched major invasions deep into our territory,
but retreated without battle.
These events are all seen in the previous volume, last year.
How can it be said that there is no retribution!"
From then on, the Emperor deeply believed in it,
and often fed over a hundred monks within the palace;
when invaders approached, he would order monks to recite the *Rénwáng Jīng* to ward them off.
This refers to the *Hùguó Rénwáng Jīng*.
The foreign monk Bùkōng
rose to the rank of Minister and Director,
was ennobled as Duke of the State,
entered and exited the palace,
and his influence shifted that of powerful nobles.
Much fertile land and profitable assets in the capital region reverted to Buddhist monasteries.
An imperial edict forbade flogging or dragging monks and nuns anywhere in the realm.
The Jīngé Temple was built on Wǔtái Mountain.
Wǔtái Mountain in Xīnzhōu's Wǔtái County
is traditionally regarded by Buddhists as the *bodhimaṇḍa* of Mañjuśrī.
A detailed note will be seen later.
The expenditure was enormous,
"enormous" meaning "countless billions."
This refers to the large number *yì*.
Dozens of monks from Wǔtái
were dispatched to various regions
to seek funds for its construction.
Zài and others often attended the Emperor during his leisure,
frequently discussing Buddhist affairs.
As a result, officials and common people, both inside and outside the court, followed their example and were transformed,
all abandoning worldly affairs to serve the Buddha,
and governance and laws became increasingly disordered.
7 In the eighth month,
on the *gēngchén* day,
Lǐ Bàoyù, Jìedùshǐ of Fèngxiáng and other circuits, Left Executive, and Acting Chancellor, came to court.
Lǐ Bàoyù served as Jìedùshǐ of Chénzhèng, Zélù, Fèngxiáng, and other circuits, defending against the Tǔbō.
His words were firm and precise.
"確" (*què*)
means firm
and solid.
On the *guǐchǒu* day,
he again offered to resign from the post of Fèngxiáng Jìedùshǐ,
but was not permitted.
8 On the *dīngyǒu* day,
Dù Hóngjiàn fed a thousand monks,
because he had returned safely from his mission to Shǔ.
9 In the ninth month,
tens of thousands of Tǔbō troops besieged Língzhōu,
and their raiding cavalry reached Pānyuán and Yílù.
Pānyuán
was originally Gǔyīnpán County;
in Tiānbǎo 1st year,
it was renamed Pānyuán and belonged to Jīngzhōu.
The capital was put on alert.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Zǐyí moved his garrison to Fèngtiān.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The Fényáng family records state:
"On the 17th day of the eighth month,
the Tǔbō arrived west of Jīng.
On the 27th day,
an edict ordered him to lead ten thousand elite soldiers to join Mǎ Lín and attack them."
We now follow the *Shílù*.
The *Shílù* states:
"On the *jiǎyín* day,
(the Tǔbō) raided Língzhōu.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
they raided Yílù."
This is likely based on the date the reports arrived.
We now follow the *Tánglì*.
10 The mountain barbarians captured Guìzhōu,
expelling its Prefect, Lǐ Liáng.
11In winter,
tenth month,
on the *wùyín* day,
Lù Sìgōng, Jìedùshǐ of Shuòfāng, defeated the Tǔbō beneath the walls of Língzhōu.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Tánglì* states:
"In the ninth month,
the Tǔbō besieged Língwǔ.
On the *wùshēn* day,
Sìgōng defeated the Tǔbō."
According to the *Chánglì*,
the *wùshēn* day
was the first day of the ninth month.
We now follow the *Shílù*.
The Tǔbō withdrew.
The 12th month.
On the *gēng-chén* day,
bandits broke into the tomb of Guō Zǐyí’s father.
They were pursued,
but not caught.
People thought that Yú Cháo'ēn had always resented Guō Zǐyí,
and suspected him of orchestrating it.
When Guō Zǐyí entered the court from Fèngtiān,
the imperial court worried he would cause trouble.
Guō Zǐyí had an audience with the emperor,
and when the emperor spoke of the matter,
Guō Zǐyí wept and said:
"I have commanded troops for a long time,
but could not prevent violence.
Many soldiers dug up people's tombs.
This happening today
is a punishment from Heaven,
not a human act."
The court was then pacified.
That year,
Zhènxī was again changed to Ānxī.
(Zhènxī's change is seen in volume 220, the first year of Sùzōng’s Zhìdé reign.)
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu fān.
The King of Xīnlüó, Xiàn Yīng, died.
His son Gān Yùn was enthroned.
Spring,
first month.
On the *yǐ-chǒu* day,
the emperor visited Zhāngjìng Temple
and ordained a thousand monks and nuns.
Tán, the Prince of Jiànníng, was posthumously granted the title of Prince of Qí.
(Tán's death is seen in volume 219, the second year of Zhìdé.)
Second month.
On the *guǐ-sì* day,
Liú Qià, the Infantry and Cavalry Commander of Shāng Zhōu, killed Yīn Zhòngqīng, the Defense Commissioner,
and soon pacified the region.
On the *jiǎ-wǔ* day,
Guō Zǐyí prohibited unauthorized horse riding in the army.
The son of Lady Nányáng's wet nurse violated the prohibition.
(Guō Zǐyí’s wife was enfeoffed as Lady Nányáng.)
His sons tearfully pleaded with Guō Zǐyí,
and also mentioned the arrogance of the Capital Commandant.
(Yǔwén Tài, when serving as prime minister for the State of Wèi,
established the position of Commandant-Inspector General,
and later generations followed this,
establishing the office of Commandant.)
Héng,
pronounced hù mèng fān.
The next day,
Guō Zǐyí discussed the matter with his subordinates and sighed,
saying:
"My sons
are all slaves!
They do not appreciate their father's Capital Commandant, but pity their mother's wet nurse's son.
If not slaves, then what are they!"
On the *gēng-zǐ* day,
Lady Dúgū of the imperial harem was made a noble consort (Guìfēi).
Third month.
On the *yǐ-sì* day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
Summer,
fourth month.
On the *wù-yín* day,
Zhāng Xiànchéng, the Jìedùshǐ of Shānnán Xīdào,
due to illness, recommended his cousin, General of the Right Yǔlín Zhāng Xiàngōng, to replace him,
and the emperor permitted it.
On the *rén-yín* day,
Cuī Gàn, the Jìedùshǐ of Xīchuān, came to court.
Earlier,
the emperor sent an imperial envoy to summon Lǐ Bì from Héngshān.
(Bì's return to Héngshān is seen in volume 220, the second year of Zhìdé.)
He was again bestowed with the golden and purple robes.
(Bì followed Sùzōng to Língwǔ,
and was already bestowed with the golden and purple robes.
After returning to Héngshān,
he reverted to his original plain clothes,
and now he was again bestowed with them.)
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu fān.
(The Pénglái Hall was north of the Zǐchén Hall.
North of the Pénglái Hall was the Tàiyè Pool,
and in the pool was Pénglái Mountain.)
Wéi,
pronounced yú wěi fān;
the later "wéi Bì" is the same.
(A "hànshān" was casual wear for banquets.
Now, both noble and humble wore it,
only the Son of Heaven used yellow to distinguish himself.
The *Zhì Gǔ Zǐ* says: In the court of Yān,
the imperial robes and crown had a white gauze undergarment,
and a clear robe,
both resembling the "hànshān",
used for sacrifices and communicating with spirits.
When Hàn Gāozǔ fought Xiàng Yǔ,
his inner garment was soaked with sweat,
so it was renamed "hànshān",
and both noble and humble wore it.)
Yī,
pronounced yú jì fān.
Guò,
pronounced gǔ hé fān.
(Jǐi and Shè refer to the Jǐshìzhōng and Zhōngshū Shèrén,
both Tang officials of the fifth rank, primary.)
All were consulted.
The emperor also had Yú Cháo'ēn build an outer residence for Lǐ Bì at Báihuātún,
so he could meet with relatives and old friends.
The emperor wished to appoint Lǐ Bì as Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
but Lǐ Bì firmly declined.
The emperor said:
"The burdens of state affairs
prevent us from meeting morning and evening.
It is indeed better to reside close by for now.
Why must there be an official appointment before one is prime minister!"
Later, during the Duānwǔ Festival,
princes, dukes, and princesses each presented gifts.
The emperor said to Lǐ Bì:
"Why do you, sir, alone have nothing to offer?"
Lǐ Bì replied:
"Living in the forbidden palace,
from my cap to my shoes, all are bestowed by Your Majesty.
All that remains is my own person,
what can I offer!"
The emperor said:
"What I seek is precisely this."
Lǐ Bì said:
"My person is not Yours, Your Majesty,
then whose is it?"
The emperor said:
"The late emperor wished to make you prime minister but could not.
(Seen in volume 218, the seventh month of Sùzōng’s Zhìdé first year.)
It shall be as I wish,
it will not be yours!"
Lǐ Bì said:
"What does Your Majesty wish me to do?"
The emperor said:
"I want you to eat meat and drink wine,
have a family,
receive official salary and rank,
and be a common person."
Lǐ Bì wept and said:
"I have abstained from grain for over twenty years,
why must Your Majesty force me to abandon my resolve!"
The emperor said:
"What good are tears?
You are within the nine layers of the palace,
where do you intend to go?"
He then ordered an imperial envoy to bury Lǐ Bì's parents,
and also arranged for Lǐ Bì to marry a daughter of the Lú clan.
(The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Yè Hóu Jiā Chuán* says:
"In the first year of Yǒngtài, on the Duānwǔ Festival,
the emperor ordered Bì to eat meat and marry."
Later it says:
"The monk Āzú secretly placed felt shoes
in Zǐchén.
The emperor wanted the palace women to guard the lamps and candles.
Bì said: 'I have been here for six or seven years.'"
It also says
"moreover, he had just been granted a marriage."
From the emperor's enthronement to Yǒngtài was
only four years.
It also says,
"because of this, he suffered slander,
and Yuán Zài then used the matter of Yú Cháo'ēn to expel him."
Thus, his marriage and Yú Cháo'ēn's execution were not far apart.
Now, everything is based on the posthumous bestowal of the title Chéngtiān.)
A residence was granted in Guāngfú Ward,
and Lǐ Bì was ordered to reside there for several days,
and for several days at Pénglái Yuan.
The emperor spoke with Lǐ Bì about Tán, the Prince of Qí,
and wished to greatly honor him posthumously.
Lǐ Bì requested that, following the precedent of Qí and Xuē, he be posthumously granted the title of Crown Prince.
The emperor wept and said:
"My brother first proposed the plan at Língwǔ
and achieved the revival of the dynasty.
(The event is seen in volume 219, the first year of Sùzōng’s Zhìdé.)
With utmost loyalty and filial piety,
he was harmed by slanderers.
Had he still been alive,
I would certainly have made him the Imperial Younger Brother (tàidì).
Now I should elevate him to an imperial title,
fulfilling my long-cherished wish."
On the *yǐ-mǎo* day, an edict was issued,
posthumously conferring on Tán the title of Emperor Chéngtiān.
On the *gēng-shēn* day,
he was buried at Shùnlíng.
When Cuī Gàn came to court,
he appointed his brother Kuān as Acting Jìedùshǐ.
(In the fourth month of this year, on the *rén-yín* day,
Cuī Gàn came to court.)
Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
When the imperial court heard of this,
they added the title Jiǎnjiào Gōngbù Shàngshū to Cuī Gàn,
bestowed upon him the name Níng,
and sent him back to his post.
11th month (June),
on the day Rénchén,
Zhū Xīcǎi (朱希彩), commander of the Yōuzhōu (幽州) forces, Zhū Cǐ (朱泚) of Chāngpíng (昌平), vice-commissioner of the military governor,
and Cǐ’s (泚) brother Tāo (滔) jointly killed the military governor Lǐ Huáixiān (李懷仙).
Xīcǎi (希彩) declared himself acting military governor.
In the intercalary month,
Lǐ Bǎochén (李寶臣), military governor of Chéngdé (成德) Army, sent a general with troops to attack Xīcǎi (希彩).
They were defeated by Xīcǎi (希彩);
the imperial court had no choice but to pardon him.
On the day Gēngshēn,
Wáng Jìn (王縉) was appointed acting military governor of Lúlóng (盧龍);
on the day Dīngmǎo,
Xīcǎi (希彩) was appointed acting
military governor of Yōuzhōu (幽州).
12 Cuī Kuān (崔寬) fought Yáng Zǐlín (楊子琳)
several times without success.
In autumn,
7th month,
Rèn Shì (任氏), a concubine of Cuī Níng (崔寧), contributed several hundred thousand in family wealth
to recruit several thousand soldiers.
She led them to attack Zǐlín (子琳)
and defeated him;
Zǐlín (子琳) fled.
13 On the day Yǐhài,
Wáng Jìn (王縉) went to Yōuzhōu (幽州).
Zhū Xīcǎi (朱希彩) mustered a large force and made strict preparations to receive him.
Jìn (縉) proceeded calmly,
and Xīcǎi (希彩) greeted him with great respect.
Jìn (縉) realized that he could ultimately not be controlled,
so he rewarded the army
and returned after about ten days.
14 The Khagan of the Huíhé (回紇) died.
On the day Gēngchén,
Xiāo Xīn (蕭昕), Right Sanqí Chángshì (右散騎常侍), was appointed envoy for condolence and sacrifice.
Sàn (散),
formerly Dàn (亶) fān.
Qí (騎),
Qíjì (奇計) fān.
Xīn (昕),
Xǔjīn (許斤) fān.
Shǐ (使),
Shūlì (疏吏) fān.
“I have rendered great service to Táng (唐).
Why does Táng (唐) break its promise,
buying my horses
but not returning their value in time?”
Xīn (昕) said:
“The service of the Huíhé (回紇)
has already been repaid by Táng (唐).
When Púgù Huái'ēn (僕固懷恩) rebelled,
the Huíhé (回紇) assisted him,
joining forces with the Tǔbō (吐蕃) to invade
and menace our capital region.
After Huái'ēn (懷恩) died
and the Tǔbō (吐蕃) fled,
then the Huíhé (回紇) became afraid and requested peace.
Our Táng (唐) did not forget their past services,
extended kindness, and let them go.
This event is found in the previous volume, Yǒngtài (永泰) First Year.
Not a single horse remained unpaid.
It was the Huíhé (回紇) who broke the agreement,
how could Táng (唐) have lost faith?”
The Huíhé (回紇) were ashamed,
treated him with great courtesy, and sent him back.
15 On the day Bǐngxū,
an Ullambana basin was sent from the palace and bestowed upon Zhāngjìng Sì (章敬寺).
The Buddhist Ullambana Sūtra says: Mùlián Bǐqiū (目連比丘) saw his deceased mother in the realm of hungry ghosts.
Mùlián (目連) reported to the Buddha: On the full moon day of the seventh month,
one should, for parents of seven generations who are in distress,
prepare a hundred flavors and five fruits to place in a basin,
offer them to the Buddhas of the ten directions,
and then receive food.
The Mènghuá Lù (夢華錄) says: During the Zhōngyuán (中元) festival,
paper effigies and colorful clothes are sold.
A bamboo stand, tripod-shaped like a lamp nest,
is called an Ullambana basin.
Paper money and clothes are hung on it
and burned.
The Shìshì Yàolǎn (釋氏要覽) says: Fàn (梵) (Sanskrit) word Yúlán (盂蘭) means here ‘basin to save from hanging upside down.’
Lù Yóu (陸游) says: It is customary on the full moon day of the seventh month to prepare vegetarian food to offer to ancestors,
weave bamboo into basins and bowls,
store paper money,
and burn it with a bamboo stalk,
calling it an Ullambana basin.
Alas!
For Dàizōng (代宗) to do this, where then were the divine spirits of the seven ancestral temples?
The honorific title was inscribed on a banner,
and all officials welcomed and paid respects at Guāngshùn Mén (光順門).
The Géběn Dàmínggōng Tú (閣本大明宮圖) says: Guāngshùn Mén (光順門) is west of Zǐchén Mén (紫宸門).
Inside Guāngshùn Mén (光順門) are Míngyì Diàn (明義殿) and Chénghuān Diàn (承歡殿).
16 In the 8th month,
on the day Rénxū,
a Tǔbō (吐蕃) army of 100,000 attacked Língwǔ (靈武).
On the day Dīngmǎo,
Tǔbō (吐蕃) Shàng Zànmó (尚贊摩) with 20,000 troops attacked Bīnzhōu (邠州);
the capital was put on high alert;
Mǎ Lín (馬璘), military governor of Bīnníng (邠寧), defeated them.
Tǔ (吐),
from tūn (暾) entering tone.
Bīn (邠),
Bīnmín (卑旻) fān.
Shǐ (使),
Shūlì (疏利) fān.
Lín (璘),
Lízhēn (離珍) fān.
17 On the day Gēngwǔ,
Xīn Yúnjīng (辛雲京), military governor of Hédōng (河東) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事), passed away.
Wáng Jìn (王縉) was appointed acting military governor of Hédōng (河東),
with other duties remaining as before.
18 In the 9th month,
on the day Rénshēn,
Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) was ordered to lead 50,000 troops to garrison Fèngtiān (奉天) to prepare for the Tǔbō (吐蕃).
19 On the day Dīngchǒu,
Jì Wáng Huán (濟王環) passed away.
Huán (環)
was Emperor Xuánzōng’s (玄宗) son.
Jì (濟),
Zǐlǐ (子禮) fān.
20 On the day Rénwǔ,
Bái Yuánguāng (白元光), a cavalry general of Shuòfāng (朔方), attacked the Tǔbō (吐蕃)
and defeated them.
On the day Rénchén,
Yuánguāng (元光) again defeated 20,000 Tǔbō (吐蕃) troops at Língwǔ (靈武).
Lǐ Bàoyù (李抱玉), military governor of Fèngxiáng (鳳翔), sent Lǐ Shèng (李晟) of Líntáo (臨洮), commander of the Right Army, to lead 5,000 soldiers to attack the Tǔbō (吐蕃).
Shèng (晟) said:
“By force, 5,000 is not enough;
by strategy, it is too many.”
So he led 1,000 men
out of Dàzhèn Guān (大震關);
upon reaching Líntáo (臨洮),
he slaughtered the Tǔbō (吐蕃) Dìngqín Bǎo (定秦堡).
Líntáo (臨洮)
is Táozhōu (洮州).
The Tǔbō (吐蕃) intended to annex Qin (秦) territory,
hence they built a fortress in Táozhōu (洮州)
and named it Dìngqín (定秦) (Pacifying Qin).
Táo (洮),
Túdāo (徒刀) fān.
Shèng (晟),
Chéngzhèng (承正) fān.
He returned after capturing the barbarian fortress commander Mùróng Gǔzhǒng (慕容谷種).
When the Tǔbō (吐蕃) heard of this,
they lifted the siege of Língzhōu (靈州) and departed.
On the day Wùxū,
the capital’s alert was lifted.
21 Lǐ Hù (李岵), prefect of Yǐngzhōu (潁州), offended Línghú Zhāng (令狐彰), military governor of Huábó (滑亳), due to a certain matter.
Zhāng (彰) sent Yáo Shì (姚奭), a judicial commissioner of the military governorship, to inspect Yǐngzhōu (潁州),
and consequently replace Hù (岵) in charge of the prefecture’s affairs,
also saying:
“If Hù (岵) does not accept the replacement,
kill him.”
Hù (岵) learned of this,
and then incited his officers and soldiers to anger,
making them kill Shì (奭).
More than a hundred people died with Shì (奭).
Hù (岵) fled to seek refuge with Tián Shéngōng (田神功), military governor of Hénán (河南), in Biànzhōu (汴州).
In winter,
10th month,
on the day Yǐsì,
Zhāng (彰) submitted a memorial detailing the situation,
and Hù (岵) also submitted a memorial to defend himself.
The Emperor ordered Gěishìzhōng (給事中) Hèruò Chá (賀若察) to investigate.
22 On the day Dīngmǎo,
Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) came to court from Fèngtiān (奉天).
23 In the 11th month,
on the day Dīnghài,
Zhū Xīcǎi (朱希彩), acting military governor of Yōuzhōu (幽州), was made military governor.
24 Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) returned to Hézhōng (河中).
From Fèngtiān (奉天) he came to court,
then returned to Hézhōng (河中).
Huán (還),
from xuān (宣) fān.
Also pronounced as written.
Mǎ Lín (馬璘) garrisoned the four frontier troops in Bīnníng (邠寧),
but lacked the strength to resist.
However, Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) with the heavy forces of Shuòfāng (朔方) was stationed in Hézhōng (河中),
deep in a peaceful inland area.
Thus, he discussed with Zǐyí (子儀) and other generals
to move Lín (璘) to govern Jīngzhōu (涇州),
and have Zǐyí (子儀) with the Shuòfāng (朔方) forces govern Bīnzhōu (邠州),
saying:
“If the borderlands are desolate and ruined,
and military expenses are insufficient,
then we will use taxes from inland territories and transport gold and silk to assist them.”
All the generals agreed.
In the 12th month,
on the day Jǐyǒu,
Mǎ Lín (馬璘) was moved to be military governor of Jīngyuán (涇原),
and the three prefectures of Bīn (邠), Níng (寧), and Qìng (慶) were subordinated to Shuòfāng (朔方).
Lín (璘) went ahead to establish Jīngzhōu (涇州), appointing Dù Yúhòu (都虞候) Duàn Xiùshí (段秀實) as acting military governor of Bīnzhōu (邠州).
Initially,
the soldiers of the Four Garrisons (Sì Zhèn) and Běitíng, having traveled far to aid the central plain in its difficulties,
as recorded in volume 219 under the first year of Zhìdé.
Nán (難),
read dàn.
They were repeatedly relocated.
The Four Garrisons passed through Biàn, Guó, and Fèngxiáng.
Běitíng passed through Huái, Jiàng, and Fū before reaching Bīn.
They had accumulated considerable weariness and hardship.
When they were moved to Jīngzhōu,
everyone grumbled and complained.
Wáng Tóngzhī (王童之), the commissioner of swords, axes, soldiers, and horses, plotted a rebellion,
scheduling it to erupt at the sound of the morning watch on the Xīnyǒu day.
The "morning watch" (dàn jǐngyán) means
sounding the drum at dawn to alert the populace.
The Rítuals of Zhōu calls this fāxù,
and people today call it cuán diǎn.
Someone reported him;
Xiùshí (秀實) feigned summoning the timekeeper,
and angrily rebuked him,
saying he had missed his watch,
ordering him to report back every shift.
The "timekeeper" (zhǎng lòu zhě)
refers to the soldiers who guard the clepsydra.
Lìng (令),
read lìdīng.
Gēng (更),
read gōnghéng.
Consequently, it was dawn by the fourth shift,
and Tóngzhī (童之) could not carry out his plan.
Xiùshí (秀實) wished to suppress him, but the signs of rebellion had not yet been fully revealed,
fearing that the army would suspect an injustice.
The informant then said,
"Tonight they intend to burn the hay in the horse stables,
and use the ensuing fire rescue as an opportunity to rebel."
In the middle of the night,
a fire indeed broke out.
Xiùshí (秀實) ordered all those walking in the army to stop,
and those sitting not to rise.
Everyone was to arrange their formations
and strictly guard vital points.
Tóngzhī (童之) reported and requested to help put out the fire,
but was refused.
At dawn,
Tóngzhī (童之) and eight of his confederates were captured,
and all were beheaded.
An order was issued, saying:
"Those who relocate again shall be exterminated; those who spread rumors shall be punished!"
Then they were moved to Jīng.
The historian says that Duàn Xiùshí (段秀實) was able to quell the rebellion.
Lìng (令),
read lìdīng.
On the 25th day of Guǐhài,
Xīchuān defeated more than ten thousand Tǔbō soldiers.
Tǔ (吐),
from tūn (暾) in entering tone.
On the 26th day, Xǔ Gǎo (許杲), the acting military governor of Pínglú,
Kǎoyì says: The old tradition renders it as

Cuī Yuán (崔圓), the military governor of Huáinán, ordered his deputy Zhāng Wànfú (張萬福) of Yuánchéng to act as the prefect of Háozhōu.
When Gǎo (杲) heard this,
he immediately led his troops away,
stopping at Dāngtú.
This Dāngtú county
belonged to Tàipíngzhōu during the Sòng dynasty,
and was originally the territory of Dānyáng county in the Hàn dynasty.
According to the Hànshū Dìlǐzhì,
Dāngtú belonged to Jiǔjiāng Commandery.
During the reign of Emperor Chéng of Jìn,
a Dāngtú Qiáo county was established for the refugees from Dāngtú county north of the river who crossed the river,
and it then became actual territory.
The emperor summoned Wànfú (萬福),
appointing him as the prefect of Hézhōu and acting defense commissioner of the marching army,
to suppress Gǎo (杲).
When Wànfú (萬福) arrived at the prefecture,
Gǎo (杲) was fearful and
moved his army to Shàngyuán.
According to Shàngyuán,
it was Jīnlíng of Chǔ,
Mòlíng of Qín,
Jiànyè of Wú,
and Jiànkāng of the Eastern Jìn.
Jìn divided Mòlíng and established Línjiāng county.
In the early years of Tàikāng,
it was again renamed Jiāngníng.
In the second year of Shàngyuán of Sùzōng, it was renamed to its present name,
belonging to Shēngzhōu.
Shǐ (使),
read shūlì.
After Xǔ Gǎo (許杲) left Háozhōu,
he crossed the river south and camped at Dāngtú.
When Zhāng Wànfú (張萬福) arrived at Lìyáng and pressed him,
he again moved to Shàngyuán,
and then from Shàngyuán crossed the river north,
plundering Chǔzhōu.
Before reaching Huáiīn,
Gǎo (杲) was driven out by his general Kāng Zìquàn (康自勸).
Zìquàn (自勸) amassed troops and continued to plunder,
following the Huái River eastward.
Wànfú (萬福) doubled his march to pursue and kill him,
with only two or three tenths escaping.
Yuánfǔ (元甫) intended to generously reward the officers and soldiers.
Wànfú (萬福) said:
"The government-supported soldiers (guānjiàn) always consume clothing and provisions needlessly,
without performing any service.
Since soldiers and farmers are now separate,
the county officials spend clothing and provisions to support the army,
calling them guānjiàn (官健), which means 'strong men supported by the government'.
According to the Táng Liùdiǎn: besides the imperial guards,
all armies in the empire had jiànér (健兒).
Previously, jiànér (健兒) in the army all had a fixed term of service,
and their repeated comings and goings were quite arduous and detrimental.
In the fifteenth year of Kāiyuán,
an imperial edict stated that since there were no major concerns in the empire,
it was fitting to allow the people to rest.
From now on,
all military garrisons, based on their level of activity, urgency, and strategic importance, shall establish defensive jiànér (健兒) forces,
recruiting strong and willing men from among various types of conscripts and tenant households to serve as jiànér (健兒) and remain long-term in border armies.
They shall receive annual additional regular stipends and grants,
and also permanent preferential treatment.
Their families, if willing to join them,
are permitted to move to the military prefectures,
and each shall be granted land and housing.
The people benefited from this,
and both the court and the provinces achieved peace,
permanently free from conscription duties.
This discusses the benefits of separating soldiers and farmers at that time,
but the harm of maintaining an army ultimately became incurable,
persisting to this day.
There is no need for excessive rewards;
I request that one-third be used."
1 Spring,
first month,
on the day of Bǐngzǐ,
Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) entered the court for an audience.
Yú Cháo'ēn (魚朝恩) invited him to visit Zhāngjìng Temple.
Yuán Zài (元載) feared they would conspire,
so he secretly sent Guō Zǐyí's (郭子儀) military clerk to inform Zǐyí (子儀) that:
"Cháo'ēn (朝恩) is plotting against your excellency."
Zǐyí (子儀) did not listen.
The clerk also informed the various generals.
Three hundred officers and soldiers requested to wear armor under their clothes to accompany him.
Dù Yù says: "Zhōngjiǎ" (衷甲)
means worn under the clothing.
Cóng (從),

similarly below.
"I am
a high minister of the state.
He has no imperial decree;
how would he dare harm me!
If he came with an imperial decree,
what would you all intend to do?"
So he went with only a few household retainers.
Cháo'ēn (朝恩) welcomed him,
surprised by the small number of his followers.
Zǐyí (子儀) told him what he had heard,
and also said:
"I fear it might trouble your excellency's management."
Cháo'ēn (朝恩) patted his chest, clasped his hands, and wept, saying:

6 Yáng Zǐlín (楊子琳) having been defeated and returned to Lúzhōu (瀘州),

Wèi Bóyù (衞伯玉), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Jīngnán (荊南), wanted to ally with him

Liú Chāngyì (劉昌裔) of Yángqǔ (陽曲)
(Old records: In the Former Hàn (漢) dynasty, Yángqǔ (陽曲) County,

Sòng Bái (宋白) said: In the ninth year of Tàihé (太和) of the Later Wèi (魏) dynasty,

In the fourth year of Bǎodìng (寶定),

Jiě County was established east of the present Yúxiāng (虞鄉) city,

On the day Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
the princess bid farewell
and arrived at the Huíhé (回紇) royal tent.
The Huíhé (回紇) came and said:
"Táng (唐) agreed to trade horses with us,
but once they entered,
the tribute given to us was insufficient.
We will take it from your envoys."
Hán (涵) was frightened
and dared not reply.
He looked at Jìn (晉),
who said:
"We do not lack horses to trade with you,
but have our gifts to you not been exceedingly generous?
Your horses arrive annually,
and we count the hides and return the funds,
without considering their life or death,
paying the full price for the horses.
The Son of Heaven, mindful of your merits,
thus issued an edict prohibiting invasion and infringement.
All the barbarian tribes fear our great nation and your alliance with us,
none daring to dispute it.
That your fathers and sons live in peace and your horses thrive,
who but us made it so?"
Thereupon, all of their people encircled Jìn (晉) and bowed.
Then they led each other to face south, lined up, and bowed,
all raising both hands and saying:
"We dare not harbor any ill intentions towards the great nation."
(This is the eulogy of Jìn (晉) written by his clerk Hán Yù (韓愈);
his words may contain some exaggeration.)
*Shuài* (帥)
is pronounced *lǜ* (率).
8 On the day Wùshēn (戊申),
Wáng Jìn (王縉) submitted a memorial declining the positions of Deputy Grand Marshal, Commander-in-Chief, and Campaign Commissioner.
9 On the day Xīnyǒu (辛酉),
Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) moved from Hézhōng (河中) to Bīnzhōu (邠州).
His elite troops all followed him,
while the remaining troops were led by his subordinate generals
and divided to guard Hézhōng (河中) and Língzhōu (靈州).
The soldiers had long been settled in Hézhōng (河中)
and were quite unhappy about the relocation,
many often fleeing back from Bīn (邠).
Yán Yǐng (嚴郢), the Army Adjutant, who was in charge of the retained headquarters,
captured them all,
executed their leaders,
and only then did the morale of the troops stabilize.

the ninth month,

Cháng Qiānguāng (常謙光), the Left-Behind Commander of Shuòfāng (朔方), defeated them.
11 Wáng Wúzòng (王無縱), Zhāng Fèngzhāng (張奉璋), and others, the commanders of the Hédōng (河東) army, relied on their merits and became arrogant and haughty.
Regarding Wáng Jìn (王縉) as a mere scholar,
they slighted him
and frequently violated regulations.
Jìn (縉) received an imperial edict to dispatch troops to Yánzhōu (鹽州) for autumn defense.
(Yánzhōu (鹽州) was the territory of Hàn (漢) Wǔyuán (五原) Commandery.
In the Suí (隋) dynasty, Yánzhōu (鹽州) was established,
with its seat in Wǔyuán (五原) County.
The present-day prefecture's southern boundary reaches the northern border of Mǎlíng (馬嶺) County in Qìngzhōu (慶州),
which was the territory of Hàn (漢) Mǎlíng (馬嶺) County.)
Fèngzhāng (奉璋) lingered and did not advance,
while Wúzòng (無縱), citing other matters,
brazenly entered Tàiyuán (太原) city;
Jìn (縉) captured and executed them all,
along with seven of their associates.
Almost all the fierce and recalcitrant generals were eliminated,
and the military headquarters finally became peaceful.
12 In winter,
the tenth month,
Cháng Qiānguāng (常謙光) reported that the Tǔbō (吐蕃) had raided Míngshā (鳴沙),
for a distance of forty *lǐ* (里) from end to end.
is pronounced with the entering tone, like *tūn* (暾).)
Míngshā (鳴沙) County
belonged to Língzhōu (靈州)

Zǐyí (子儀) personally led his troops to Qìngzhōu (慶州).
Hearing that the Tǔbō (吐蕃) had retreated,
he returned.
13 Dù Hóngjiàn (杜鴻漸), the Grand Master of the Golden Seal and Grand Councillor, resigned his position due to illness.
On the day Rénshēn (壬申),
this was granted;
on the day Yǐhài (乙亥),
he died.
Hóngjiàn (鴻漸) was gravely ill and ordered a monk to shave his head,
leaving instructions for a pagoda to be built for his burial.
14 On the day Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
Péi Miǎn (裴冕), the Left Grand Master, was appointed Grand Councillor.
Previously,
Yuán Zài (元載) was the Commander of Xīnpíng (新平).
Miǎn (冕) had once recommended him,
so Zài (載) nominated him to be chancellor,
also benefiting from his old age and illness which made him easy to control.
At the moment of receiving the appointment,

Zài (載) rushed to help him up
and offered words of thanks on his behalf.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Wùxū (戊戌),

1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Jǐsì (己巳),
Qiāng (羌) chieftain Bái Duìpéng (白對蓬) and others each led their tribes to submit to the court.

2 Yú Cháo'ēn (魚朝恩), the Commissioner for Inspecting Military Affairs, Consoling, and Disposing, General-in-Chief of the Left Gate Guard, concurrently Commander of the Shéncè (神策) Army, and Director of the Palace Eunuchs,
exclusively controlled the forbidden troops,
enjoying unparalleled favor and trust.
The Emperor often discussed military and state affairs with him,
and his influence dominated the court and country.
Cháo'ēn (朝恩) enjoyed freely discussing current politics in public gatherings,
insulting and humiliating the chancellors.
Although Yuán Zài (元載) was eloquent,
he also stood in silent deference, not daring to respond.
The Shéncè Dūyúhóu, Liú Xīxiān,
and Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ, Wáng Jiàhè,
both enjoyed the favor of Yú Cháo'ēn.
Xīxiān advised Cháo'ēn to establish a prison in the Northern Army.
The Left and Right Shéncè Armies,
Left and Right Yǔlín Armies,
and Left and Right Lóngwǔ Armies
were all referred to as the Northern Army.
說 (shuō)
is pronounced 'shì ruì' (式芮).
相 (xiāng)
is pronounced 'xī liàng' (息亮).
暹 (xiān)
is pronounced 'xī lián' (息廉).
They were falsely accused of crimes and
arrested and imprisoned in dungeons.
They were interrogated and tortured until they confessed,
and their family property was confiscated and taken into the army.
The informers and captors were also rewarded.
The area was highly restricted and secret,
so no one dared to speak.
Whenever Cháo'ēn presented a memorial to the emperor,
he expected it to be approved without fail.
If there were any court affairs that did not go his way,
he would become angry and say,
"Are there any affairs in the world that are not decided by me?!"
The emperor heard of this
and was displeased.
Yú Cháo'ēn's adopted son, Lìnghuī, was still young,
serving as an Nèigěishǐ.
He wore green.
According to Táng regulations, there was no fixed number of Nèigěishǐ,
and they belonged to the Nèishìshěng.
All those without official rank
were called Nèigěishǐ,
in charge of the records of goods entering through various gates.
Sòng Bái said: in charge of the records of goods entering and leaving through various gates.
衣 (yī)
is pronounced 'yú jì' (於既).
Lìnghuī reported this to Cháo'ēn.
The next day, Cháo'ēn saw the emperor and said,
"My son's official rank is low,
and he is being bullied by his peers.
I beg you to bestow upon him a purple robe."
Before the emperor could reply,
the relevant officials had already presented a purple robe.
Lìnghuī put it on,
bowed, and thanked him.
The emperor forced a smile and said,
"For my son to wear purple
truly fits his heart's desire."
Yuán Zài secretly understood the emperor's intentions.
Seizing the opportunity, he memorialized that Yú Cháo'ēn was arrogant, abusive, and rebellious,
間 (jiān)
is pronounced 'gǔ xiàn' (古莧).
and requested his removal.
The emperor also knew that the whole empire resented and was angry at him,
so he instructed Zài to devise a plan.
Whenever Cháo'ēn entered the palace,
he always had the Shèshēng Jiāng, Zhōu Hào, escort him with a hundred men for self-protection.
He also had his partisan, Huángfǔ Wēn, the Jiédùshǐ of Shǎnzhōu, hold military power outside as support.
Zài bribed them heavily to win them over,
so the emperor heard every one of Cháo'ēn's secret plots and confidential words,
but Cháo'ēn was unaware of it.
On the day of Xīnmǎo,
Zài, planning for the emperor,
transferred Lǐ Bàoyù to be the Jiédùshǐ of Shānnán Xīdào,
and appointed Wēn as the Jiédùshǐ of Fèngxiáng.
This outwardly increased their power,
but in reality, it brought Wēn closer to assist Zài himself.
Zài also requested to divide Méi, Guó, Bǎojī, Hù, and Zhōuzhì to Bàoyù,
and Xīngpíng, Wǔgōng, Tiānxīng, and Fúfēng to the Shéncè Army.
Xīngpíng,
formerly known as Shǐpíng,
was renamed Jīnchéng in the first year of Jǐnglóng (707 AD).
In the second year of Zhìdé (757 AD),
it was renamed Xīngpíng
and belonged to Jīngzhàofǔ.
Cháo'ēn, however, did not suspect Zài in the least,
and remained as arrogant and overbearing as before.
3 On the day of Rénchén,
Zhāng Yánshǎng, the Hénán Yǐn, was promoted to Dōngjīng Liúshǒu.
The position of Fùyuánshuài of Hénán and other circuits was abolished,
and their troops were placed under the Liúshǒu.
Yánshǎng was the son of Jiāzhēn.
Zhāng Jiāzhēn served as chancellor during the Kāiyuán period.
4 In the second month,
on the day of Wùxū,
Lǐ Bàoyù moved his garrison to Zhōuzhì,
to be stationed at Zhōuzhì to also govern Shānnán.
He extensively plundered the markets of Fèngxiáng,
which only settled down after several days.
5 Liú Xīxiān somewhat sensed the emperor's change of mind
and reported it to Yú Cháo'ēn,
who then began to feel suspicion and fear.
However, whenever the emperor saw him,
his favor and courtesy became even greater,
which made Cháo'ēn feel secure.
When Huángfǔ Wēn arrived in the capital,
Yuán Zài detained him and did not send him away.
He then secretly conspired with Wēn and Zhōu Hào to execute Cháo'ēn.
The Kǎoyì says: The Bīn Annals say:
"In the spring of the fifth year,
an edict summoned Guō Gōng for Hánshí,
saying that during the prosperous year and festive season, he wished to enjoy himself with his great ministers.
At this time, intending to execute Cháo'ēn, he hinted to Guō Gōng,
'The Shuòfāng Army
has performed services for the state.
It would be appropriate for several thousand veteran soldiers to enter the court,
so that I may reward them at a banquet
and thus get to know them.'
In the first month,
Guō Gōng entered the court with three thousand armored men.
Yú Cháo'ēn invited Guō Gōng to visit Zhāngjìng Temple,
and Guō Gōng accepted.
Prime Minister Yuán Gōng, fearing they might conspire,
had the Bīn officials subtly urge Guō Gōng not to go.
A Bīn official rushed from the Zhongshū to inform Guō Gōng, saying, 'The Military Commissioner may act unfavorably towards you,'
and also informed his generals.
Soon after, Cháo'ēn's envoy arrived.
As Guō Gōng was about to leave,
three hundred armored soldiers requested to accompany him,
wishing to be prepared for any emergency.
Guō Gōng angrily said, 'I am a great minister.
Unless he has a secret imperial edict,
how would he dare to harm me?!
If it is the emperor's command,
what could you all do?!'
He went alone with about ten servants.
Cháo'ēn waited for him and exclaimed in surprise,

Today's Hánshí,
according to the solar terms, is at the end of mid-spring.
Qīngmíng is at the beginning of the third month.
Thus, the fire ban is also a Zhōu dynasty system.

which created a rift.
When Cháo'ēn was executed,
I happened to be gravely ill,
and thus could not enter the court,
a shame and regret in life and death.
I am now certainly not to recover.
My warehouses and livestock
have already been sealed and registered.
The generals and soldiers in the army,
and the officials in the prefectures and counties,
are awaiting orders in their places.
I respectfully observe that Liú Yàn, Minister of Personnel, and Lǐ Miǎn, Minister of Works, are capable of being entrusted with important matters.
I wish that they be quickly appointed to replace me.
My sons, Jiàn and others,
are now ordered to return to their private residence in the Eastern Capital.”
After Zhāng passed away,
the generals and soldiers wanted to install Jiàn,
but Jiàn swore he would die rather than comply,
and his entire family returned west.
In the third month,
on the bǐng-zǐ day,
Lǐ Miǎn was appointed Jiedushi of Yǒngpíng.
3 Xú Hào and Xuē Yōng, both Vice Ministers of Personnel,
were partisans of Yuán Zài and Wáng Jìn.
Háo's concubine's younger brother, Hóumòchén Fù, was the Commandant of Měiyuán.
Hào instructed Dù Jì, the Governor of Jīngzhào, to falsely report him as excellent in managing the postal service.
“Zòu yōu” (奏優, memorializing excellence)
means reporting that the postal stations'
supply of carriages, horses, fuel, fodder, and provisions
was abundant and never lacking,
and superior to other counties.
Shǔ,
read as “yù” in “zhī yù.”
Fù was impeached by Lǐ Qīyún, the Censor-in-Chief.
An imperial edict ordered Yú Shào of Wànnián, Vice Minister of Rites, and others to investigate.
Shào reported that Yōng's crime occurred before the amnesty,
and thus should be pardoned,
which angered the Emperor.
Summer.
In the fifth month,
on the yǐ-yǒu day,
Hào was demoted to Biejia of Míngzhōu,
and Yōng to Inspector of Shèzhōu.
On the bǐng-xū day,
Jì was demoted to Inspector of Hángzhōu,
and Shào to Chief Administrator of Guìzhōu.
The court began to be rectified.
Míngzhōu
was four thousand one hundred lǐ southeast of the capital.
Shèzhōu
was three thousand six hundred sixty-seven lǐ southeast of the capital.
Hángzhōu
was three thousand five hundred fifty-six lǐ southeast of the capital.
Guìzhōu
was four thousand seven hundred sixty lǐ by land and water from the capital.
Shè,
pronounced “shè.”
Háng,
read as “gāng” in “hù gāng.”
Zhǎng,
read as “liǎng” in “zhī liǎng.”
The *Kǎoyì* (Critical Analysis) says: The *Shílù* (Veritable Records) states:
“Hóumòchén Fù was Commandant of Měiyuán.”
The old biography of Lǐ Qīyún states:
“Hóumòchén Fù, Commandant of Huáyuán,
was moved to Commandant of Cháng'ān
for his excellent management of postal transport.”
It also states:
“When Qīyún impeached Hào and others,
the Emperor hesitated and did not make a decision.
During a lunar eclipse,
the Emperor asked its cause.
He replied: ‘Your servant has heard that a solar eclipse calls for cultivating virtue,
and a lunar eclipse calls for cultivating punishment.
Currently, the crimes of deceiving the emperor and engaging in private interests have not been rectified;
this is Heaven's warning to Your sagely majesty.’
The Emperor was enlightened by this,
and all involved with Fù were demoted and exiled.
From this point, the imperial administration was invigorated,
and all official matters became orderly.”
However, the lunar eclipse occurred on the jǐ-chǒu day,
which was not at this time.
Therefore, this account is not adopted.
4 On the xīn-mǎo day,
Liú Máo, Prince of Zhèng, passed away.
He was posthumously honored as Zhāojìng Crown Prince.
Máo
was the son of the Emperor's second elder brother.
5 Since the Qián-yuán reign, the Huí-hú
had annually sought peace and market trade.
For each horse, forty bolts of silk were exchanged,
often reaching tens of thousands of horses.
The horses were all old, emaciated, and useless.
The court suffered from this,
and often could not purchase the full number requested.
Huí-hú envoys awaiting departure or arriving subsequently were constantly present at the Hóng-lú-sì.
By this time,
the Emperor, wishing to please them,
ordered that all be purchased.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the xīn-chǒu day,
the Huí-hú took their leave to return home,
carrying gifts and horse payments
that required over a thousand carts.
6 In the eighth month,
on the jǐ-wèi day,
sixty thousand Tú-bō cavalry raided Líng-wǔ,
trampled the autumn crops, and departed.
The Kǎo-yì states: The Fén-yáng family chronicle says:
"In the eighth month,
five thousand Tú-bō cavalry reached the Qī-jí-qú Canal south of Líng-zhōu.
Gōng dispatched Wēn Rú-yǎ, Cóng-zhèng, and others to reinforce the army and rescue them.
In the ninth month,
they were greatly defeated."
Now we follow the Shí-lù.
7 On the xīn-wèi day,
Zhū Cǐ, military governor of Yōu-zhōu, sent his younger brother Tāo with five thousand elite cavalry to Jīng-zhōu to defend against autumn raids.
Since Ān Lù-shān’s rebellion,
Yōu-zhōu troops had never been used.
When Tāo arrived,
the Emperor was greatly pleased
and rewarded them generously.
8 On the rén-shēn day,
the Huí-hú again sent the envoy Chì-xīn with ten thousand horses to request mutual trade.
9 In the ninth month,
on the rén-wǔ day,
Gē-shū Huǎng, prefect of Xún-zhōu, killed Lǚ Chóng-bēn, the military governor of Lǐng-nán,
and rebelled, occupying Lǐng-nán.
10 On the guǐ-wèi day,
a man from Jìn-zhōu named Xún Mó
braided his hair with hemp,
carried a bamboo basket and a rush mat,
and wept in the eastern market.
When people asked his reason,
he replied:
"I wish to present thirty characters,
each character representing one matter.
If my words are not worth adopting,
please wrap my corpse in the mat,
place it in the basket,
and abandon it in the wilderness."
The Jīng-zhào reported this.
The Emperor summoned him for an audience,
bestowed new clothes upon him,
and lodged him in the Kè-shěng.
At that time, a Kè-shěng was established at the ancient Yín-tái-mén gate,
where those whose petitions from the four directions had not yet been dispatched, those who had submitted memorials with dissenting views, and foreign guests whose requests had not yet been answered,
were all lodged.
There were usually several hundred people.
Guǎn,
reads as gǔ-wán.
"Tuán"
meant: please dismiss the Tuán-liàn envoys of all prefectures.
"Jiān"
meant: please dismiss the Jiān-jūn envoys of all circuits.
11 Tián Chéng-sì, military governor of Wèi-bó, built an ancestral shrine for Ān and Shǐ and their sons,
calling them the Four Sages,
and also sought to become a chancellor.
The Emperor ordered the court eunuch Sūn Zhī-gǔ, while on an imperial mission, to implicitly persuade him to destroy it.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the jiǎ-chén day,
Chéng-sì was promoted to Tóng-píng-zhāng-shì to commend him.
12 Líng-zhōu defeated over ten thousand Tú-bō troops.
One hundred thousand Tú-bō troops raided Jīng and Bīn.
Guō Zǐ-yí dispatched Hún Jiān, the commander of the Shuò-fāng army, with five thousand infantry and cavalry to resist them.
On the gēng-shēn day,
they battled at Yí-lù.
Sòng Bái said: Yí-lù
was originally the territory of Qún-gū county in the Hàn dynasty.
In the second year of Xī-píng of the Later Wèi,
Dōng-yīn-pán county was established by dividing Qún-gū county.
In the first year of Fèi-dì,
it was renamed Yí-lù county because it bordered Yí-lù-chuān to the south.
The Jiǔ-yù-zhì states: Yí-lù is sixty lǐ west of Bīn-zhōu.
The Kǎo-yì says: The Shí-lù records
"jiǎ-zǐ,"
which was probably the day the memorial arrived.
The Bīn-zhì says
"the eighteenth day,"
which matches the Táng-lì.
Now we follow this.
"Wàng-lǔ,"
end of sentence.
The veteran generals Shǐ Kàng, Wēn Rú-yǎ, and others held Jiān in low regard
and did not obey his orders.
Jiān summoned them to attack the barbarians,
but they were already drunk.
Seeing the abatis,
they said:
"In open battle,
what use are these!"
and ordered them to be removed.
They ordered the cavalry to charge the barbarian formation,
but they could not penetrate it and returned.
The barbarians pursued and pressed them,
and the government army was greatly defeated.
Seven or eight tenths of the soldiers died,
and over a thousand residents were plundered by the Tú-bō.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Mǎ Lín (馬璘) fought the Tǔbō (吐蕃) at Yáncāng (鹽倉)
and was defeated again.
Yáncāng (鹽倉)
is west of Jīngzhōu (涇州) city.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Bīn Zhì* (邠志) says:
"In the tenth month,
the Western戎 (Róng) raided Bīn (邠).
Mǎ Gōng (馬公), the Jīngyuán (涇原) Military Commissioner, attacked them.
Guō Gōng (郭公) sent his general Hún Jiān (渾瑊) with five thousand infantry and cavalry to act as a pincer.
On the eighteenth day,
our army ascended Huángbèi Yuán (黃萯原).
When they saw the Tǔbō (吐蕃),
Jiān (瑊) quickly led his troops forward to occupy a strategic pass,
and also set up chevaux de frise and spears to block their rapid charge.
Shǐ Kàng (史抗), Wēn Rúyǎ (溫儒雅) and five or six other veteran generals, being arrogant and conceited,
disdained the chief general
and drank heavily.
Jiān (瑊) sent for them;
when they arrived,
they were all drunk.
Seeing the chevaux de frise and spears,
they said: 'When you see the enemy in the open field, you must attack! What is the point of setting these up!'
They ordered them removed.
As the Róng (戎) forces arrayed,
Kàng (抗) and others ordered the cavalry commanders to charge the enemy.
When they returned,
they charged their own army.
The Tǔbō (吐蕃) pursued them from behind and entered,
and our army was utterly defeated.
Only two or three tenths of the soldiers survived."
The *Fényáng Jiāchuán* (汾陽家傳) says:
"In the tenth month,
the four Tǔbō (吐蕃) Military Commissioners passed through Jīngchuān (涇川),
crossed south of Géchuan (閣川),
and united their forces at the Wèihé (渭河).
The Duke (Gōng) sent Hún Jiān (渾瑊) and others to connect front and back to await them.
On the twenty-fourth day,
a great battle was fought at Chángwǔ Chéng (長武城).
Our army suffered a crushing defeat.
Jiān (瑊) and others broke through
and thus escaped."
The *Táng Lì* (唐曆) says:
"On the eighteenth day,
the Tǔbō (吐蕃) raided Bīnzhōu (邠州).
Jiān (瑊) fought them at Yílù (宜祿),
and the government army was severely defeated.
On the twenty-second day,
Mǎ Lín (馬璘) led out troops to attack them
and was defeated again.
On the twenty-seventh day, the *jǐsì* day,
Lín (璘) sent troops to hack at the Tǔbō (吐蕃) camp
and broke it.
On the twenty-eighth day, the *gēngwǔ* day,
an edict ordered the troops from various circuits to gather and garrison the western suburbs.
On the first day of the eleventh month,
the Tǔbō (吐蕃) retreated."
Duàn Gōng Biéchuán (段公別傳) says:
"In the eighth year, on the twenty-third day of the tenth month of winter,
the Quǎnrong (犬戎) invaded.
A great battle was fought at Yáncāng (鹽倉).
Our army and the forces of Hún Jiān (渾瑊), the Shuòfāng (朔方) Army Commissioner, combined their strength in a concerted attack.
However, the various armies responsible for autumn defense retreated at the sight of the enemy.
Consequently, our army was at a disadvantage."
Today, we follow the *Bīn Zhì* (邠志), *Táng Lì* (唐曆), and *Duàn Gōng Jiāchuán* (段公家傳).
The events follow the *Shílù* (實錄) and *Jiùchuán* (舊傳),
and also draw from various other books.
As dusk fell and he had not yet returned,
Jiāo Lìngchén (焦令諶), the Jīngyuán (涇原) Army Commissioner, and others, along with the routed soldiers, rushed into the gate.
Someone advised the Army Supervising Secretary Duàn Xiùshí (段秀實) to man the city walls and defend,
but Xiùshí (秀實) said:
"The Grand Marshal's whereabouts are unknown;
we should go forth and strike the barbarians.
How can we merely preserve ourselves!"
He summoned Lìngchén (令諶) and others and reprimanded them, saying:
"According to military law,
if the supreme commander is lost,
all under his command must die.
Have you gentlemen forgotten your duty to die!"
Lìngchén (令諶) and others, in fear and trembling, bowed and begged for his command.
Xiùshí (秀實) then dispatched all the city's untouched soldiers,
arraying them on the eastern plain.
He also gathered the scattered soldiers,
creating the appearance that they would fight with all their might.
The Tǔbō (吐蕃) feared this
and gradually retreated.
That night,
Lín (璘) was able to return.
Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) summoned his generals and deliberated, saying:
"The fault for the army's defeat lies with me,
not with the generals.
However, the Shuòfāng (朔方) army's elite troops are renowned throughout the world.
Now that they have been defeated by the barbarians,
what strategy can wipe out this disgrace?"
No one responded.
Hún Jiān (渾瑊) said:
"A defeated general
should no longer participate in deliberations.
Nevertheless, I wish to say something about today's events,
solely to address my guilt."
*Lǐ* (理)
means "to govern" or "to deal with."
Zǐyí (子儀) pardoned his crime
and had him lead troops to Qū Cháonà (趣朝那).
After defeating the government army, the barbarians
intended to plunder Lǒng (隴).
Lǐ Guó chén (李國臣), the Yánzhōu (鹽州) Prefect, said:
"The barbarians, emboldened by victory, will surely invade the imperial domain.
If we attack their rear,
the barbarians will surely look back."
So he led his troops to Qū Qínyuán (趣秦原).
The *Kuòdì Zhì* (括地志) says: "Qínzhōu (秦州) Qīngshuǐ (清水) County has Qín Tíng (秦亭) and Qín Gǔ (秦谷),
which are not the fiefdom of the Marquis (Zǐ)."
*Qū* (趣)
is pronounced *qī yù* (七喻).
When the barbarians heard of this,
they reached Bǎichéng (百城)
and turned back.
Bǎichéng (百城)
is the Bǎilǐ Chéng (百里城) in Língtái (靈臺) County, Jīngzhōu (涇州).
All that they had plundered was recovered.
Mǎ Lín (馬璘) also led elite troops to raid the barbarian's baggage train at Pānyuán (潘原),
killing several thousand people.
The barbarians then fled.
In the 13th year, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
Lù Sìgōng (路嗣恭), the Jiāngxī (江西) Observing Commissioner,
was ordered to suppress Gēshū Huàng (哥舒晃).
Previously, Yuán Zǎi (元載) had served as Xīzhōu (西州) Prefect
and understood the terrain of Héxī (河西) and Lǒngyòu (隴右).
At this time,
the Tǔbō (吐蕃) repeatedly made incursions.
Zǎi (載) spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"Since the Four Garrisons and Běitíng (北庭) have been placed under Jīngzhōu (涇州) jurisdiction,
there are no strategic strongholds to defend.
Lǒngshān (隴山) is high and steep,
connecting south to Qínlǐng (秦嶺).
Qínlǐng (秦嶺)
is Shānglǐng (商嶺).
Currently, the western border of the state ends at Pānyuán (潘原),
while the Tǔbō (吐蕃) garrison Cuīshābǎo (摧沙堡).
Yuánzhōu (原州) lies in between,
at the mouth of Lǒngshān (隴山).
To its west are former imperial pastures,
with rich grass and fine water.
Píngliáng (平涼) is to its east.
The Tang dynasty's Yuánzhōu (原州) was governed from ancient Gāopíng (高平),
which controlled the vital Lǒngdào (隴道) pass.
When Hàn Guāngwǔ (漢光武) took Lǒngyòu (隴右),
he first subjugated Gāojùn (高峻) before he could press Kuí Xiāo (隗囂).
Hèlián Bóbó (赫連勃勃) occupied Gāopíng (高平),
using its height to observe Lǒngdōng (隴東) and Lǐngběi (嶺北),
which allowed him to harass Yáo Xīng (姚興).
It is truly a critical strategic location.
Píngliáng (平涼) County belongs to Yuánzhōu (原州).
To its southwest is the Liùpán Guān (六盤關) of Lǒngshān (隴山).
Provisions for the army can be supplied.
The old fortifications still exist,
but the Tǔbō (吐蕃) have abandoned them and do not reside there.
Every year in midsummer,
the Tǔbō (吐蕃) graze their livestock in Qīnghǎi (青海),
far from the frontier.
If we seize this opportunity to build fortifications there,
it could be completed in twenty days.
We should move the Jīngxī (京西) army to garrison Yuánzhōu (原州)
and Guō Zǐyí's (郭子儀) army to garrison Jīngzhōu (涇州) to form its base.
Divide troops to guard Shímén (石門) and Mùxiá (木峽).
Southwest of Yuánzhōu (原州) is Mùxiá Guān (木峽關).
Within the prefecture there is also Shímén Guān (石門關).
Advancing to Ānxī (安西) and occupying the heartland of the Tǔbō (吐蕃),
the court can then rest easy."
He also submitted maps of the terrain
and secretly sent people to Lǒngshān (隴山) to survey the work.
Coincidentally, Tián Shéngōng (田神功), the Biànsòng (汴宋) Military Commissioner, came to court.
The Emperor asked him about it,
and he replied:
"Leading an army and assessing the enemy is difficult even for veteran generals.
How can Your Majesty use the words of a scholar
and expect the whole country to follow them!"
Zǎi (載) soon fell out of favor,
and the matter was dropped.
This laid the groundwork for Yáng Yán (楊炎) to later revive the proposal to fortify Yuánzhōu (原州).
The responsible officials, noting the abundance of 'red-hearted horses' (i.e., loyal, strong horses) among the Huíhé (回紇),
requested to purchase a thousand steeds.
Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) considered this to be too much against their wishes,
and offered to contribute a year's salary to purchase them for the state.
The Emperor did not permit it.
In the eleventh month,
on the *wùzǐ* day,
an order was issued to purchase six thousand horses.

1 Spring,
1st month,
Rén Yín,
Tián Shéngōng died in the capital.
Tián Shéngōng's audience with the emperor is recorded in the previous year of the preceding volume.
2 Lǐlǎng Zhèn'è Shǐ Yáng Yóu traveled downstream from Lǐzhōu,
passing through to Èzhōu.
An imperial edict permitted him to enter the court.
Yóu then traveled upstream on the Hàn Jiāng;
Fùzhōu and Yǐngzhōu both closed their gates and defended themselves.
Fù and Yǐng prefectures are both on the Hàn River.
At this time, they were probably under the jurisdiction of Shānnán Dōngdào.
Shǒu
is also pronounced yì.

Xīn Wèi,
the Xúzhōu army mutinied.
Cìshǐ Liáng Chéng fled over the city wall.
Xúzhōu,
its seat was Péngchéng.
4 Jiànyì Dàfū Wú Sǔn was sent as an envoy to Tǔbō,
where he was detained for several years,
eventually dying of illness among the captives.
Tǔ
is pronounced with the entering tone from tūn.

5 Gēng Chén,
one thousand five hundred soldiers from Biàn and Sòng, who were stationed for autumn defense,
stole treasury funds and deserted.
This was due to the death of Tián Shéngōng.
Jǐ Chǒu,

6 Guǐ Sì,
Guō Zǐyí had an audience with the emperor
and reported:
"Shuòfāng is
the northern gate of the state.
In recent times, the warriors have been depleted,
with only one in ten remaining.
Now, Tǔbō occupies the lands of Hé and Lǒng,
with a multitude of Qiāng and Hún people,
their power is ten times stronger.
I wish that elite soldiers be dispatched from various circuits,

7 3rd month,
Wù Shēn,
Imperial Daughter Yǒnglè Gōngzhǔ was betrothed to Huá, the son of Tián Chéngsì, Jìedùshǐ of Wèibó.
The emperor intended to solidify their loyalty,
but Chéngsì became even more arrogant and disrespectful.
History says that a 'wolf's heart' cannot be tied by favor.
8 Yáng Yóu,
Lǐlǎng Zhèn'è Shǐ, was appointed Táozhōu Cìshǐ and Lǒngyòu Jiédù Bīngmǎshǐ.
9 Summer,
4th month,
Jiǎ Shēn,
Guō Zǐyí resigned and returned to Bīnzhōu.
Zǐyí came to court from Bīn,
and now returns.
Huán
is pronounced xuān,
also pronounced as written.
The text 'Kǎoyì yuē: Táng Lì zuò
"Guǐ Wèi".
Jīn cóng shí lù' is a textual note and is not translated.
He wept profusely.

a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
115th month,
Bǐng Wǔ,
Yáng Yóu arrived in the capital from Lǐzhōu.
In the 1st month of this year, it was already recorded that Yáng Yóu departed Lǐzhōu,
traveled downstream along the river and upstream on the Hàn River,
and now finally reached the capital.
Cháo
is pronounced zhí yáo.
12Jīngyuán Jiédùshǐ Mǎ Lín had an audience,

Bǐng Yín,
Lín was appointed Zuǒ Púshè.
136th month,
Lúlóng Jiédùshǐ Zhū Cǐ sent his younger brother Tāo to present a memorial requesting an audience,
and also requesting to personally lead five thousand infantry and cavalry for autumn defense;
the emperor granted it.
Cǐ
is pronounced qiě lǐ,

Jiàng
is pronounced jí liàng,

14Guǐ Wèi,
the Hu monk Bùkōng of Xìngshàn Sì died.
He was posthumously granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Sīkōng,
enfeoffed as Sùguó Gōng,
and given the posthumous title Dàbiànzhèng Guǎngzhì Bùkōng Sānzàng Héshàng.
Buddhist scriptures state: The Buddha was in Táránài,
first teaching the Sūtras and Sūtra Piṭaka to five people.
The Buddha was in Luóyuèqí,
first teaching the Vinaya Piṭaka to Xūnàtí.
The Buddha was at the Macaque Pond in Píshèlì,
first teaching the Abhidharma Piṭaka to Qíqí.
Five hundred Arhats gathered at night for Abhidharma,
continuously explaining the scriptures;
this is the study of the Three Piṭakas.
Also,
the study of the Three Piṭakas
is Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.
Zú
is pronounced zǐ xù.
Zàng
is pronounced cú làng.
15There was a drought in the capital.
Jīngzhào Yǐn Lí Gàn made an earthen dragon to pray for rain,
and he himself danced with shamans.
After a full month, there was no rain,
so he also prayed to Wénxuān Wáng.
The emperor, hearing of this,
ordered the removal of the earthen dragon
and reduced his meals and expenses.
Autumn,
7th month,
Wù Wǔ,
it rained.
16Zhū Cǐ had an audience.
When he reached Wèizhōu,

Chéngsì secretly ordered something to be buried within Bǎochén's territory,

Kǎoyì says: The old biography of Wáng Wǔjùn states:

Chéngqiàn cursed him
and threw it onto the road.
Wáng Wǔjùn advised him to play with Chéngsì and use him for his own advantage.
Bǎochén said: 'Now there's a rift between me and Chéngsì.
Can I trust him completely?'
Wǔjùn said: 'Your situations are similar, and your troubles are the same.
Turning enemies into father and son
is as easy as a cough and a spit.
If you only spread empty words,
it will be useless.
Now, the palace eunuch Liú Qīngtán is at the驿.
Behead him and send his head to Chéngsì,
and Chéngsì will immediately offer his wife and children as hostages.'
Bǎochén said: 'I cannot do that.'
Wǔjùn said: 'Zhū Tāo is stationed at Cāngzhōu for the state.
Please capture and send him to Chéngsì to gain his trust.'
Bǎochén agreed."
However, Chéngsì was at that moment seeking a resolution with Bǎochén,
so why would he need to capture Tāo to gain trust?
Moreover, Chéngqiàn was still at the relay station,
so why didn't Wǔjùn advise beheading Chéngqiàn instead of Qīngtán?
Bǎochén himself, believing Chéngsì had lured him into jointly taking Yōuzhōu,
therefore attacked Zhū Tāo,
not because of Chéngqiàn's insult.
Now, we follow the Táng Annals.

I (按) note that Dàizōng (代宗) disliked Sìgōng (嗣恭) because he was associated with Yuán Zǎi (元載)
