(Jìn,
pronounced like "Jìn").
He ordered Liú Yàn, the Lìbù Shàngshū, and Lǐ Hán, the Yùshǐ Dàfū, and others to jointly interrogate them.
The leads for questioning all came from within the forbidden palace.
(Wènduān
is like what we call "subject of inquiry" today).
Zài and Jìn both confessed to their crimes.
On that day,
Dǒng Xiù, the Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn and Zhī Nèishì Shěngshì, was first beaten to death inside the forbidden palace.
Then Zài was granted the right to commit suicide in Wànnián County.
Zài asked the official in charge:
"I wish to die quickly!"
The official said:
"Prime Minister, you must endure a little defilement,
please do not mind!"
Then they removed a soiled sock, stuffed it into his mouth, and killed him.
Wáng Jìn was initially also granted the right to commit suicide.
Liú Yàn said to Lǐ Hán and others:
"Traditionally,
severe punishments require a second report to the emperor,
how much more so for a high minister!
Moreover, the law distinguishes between principal and accessory.
(Shǒu
refers to the principal offender).
(Cóng
refers to being implicated).
(Cóng,
pronounced like "cái yòng").
Hán and others agreed.
The emperor then demoted Jìn to Cìshǐ of Kuò Prefecture.
Sòng Bái said:
Kuò Prefecture,
during the Jìn dynasty, was Yǒngjiā Commandery.
The Suí dynasty renamed it Chǔ Prefecture,
and soon after it became Kuò Prefecture,
named after Kuòcāng Mountain.
Liú Xù said:
It is 4,278 lǐ southeast of the capital.
The daughter of Zhōngsì, and his sons Bóhé, Zhòngwǔ, and Jìnéng were all executed.
The authorities confiscated Zài's family property;
there were up to 800 dàn of pepper,
and other items in proportion.
In the 5th year of summer,
in the fourth month,
on the Rénwǔ day,
Yáng Wǎn, the Tàicháng Qīng, was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Cháng Gǔn, the Lǐbù Shìláng, was appointed Ménxià Shìláng,
both concurrently Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Yáng Wǎn was by nature pure, frugal, and simple.
On the day the edict was issued,
the court and the common people celebrated.
Guō Zǐyí was then entertaining guests;
upon hearing the news,
he reduced the musical entertainment by four-fifths.
Lí Gàn, the Jīngzhàoyǐn, whose retinue was very grand,
immediately reduced it,
keeping only ten horsemen.
Cuī Kuān, the Zhōngchéng, whose residence was vast and extravagant,
promptly demolished parts of it.
On the Guǐwèi day,
Yáng Yán, the Lìbù Shìláng, Hán Huí, Bāo Jí,
the Jiànyì Dàfū,
and Hán Huì, the Qǐjū Shèrén, were all demoted.
They were all Zài's partisans.
(Yán
was from Fèngxiáng).
(Zài often befriended one person of literary talent and reputation,
intending to replace himself with that person in the future,
hence Yán was among those demoted).
(Huí
was Huàng's younger brother).
(Huì
was from Nányáng).
The emperor initially wanted to execute Yán and the others,
but Wú Còu repeatedly advised against it and pleaded for them,
so they were only demoted.
On the Dīngyǒu day,
the Tubó invaded Lí and Yǎ Prefectures.
(In the first year of Empress Wǔ's Dàzú era,
Lí Prefecture was established
using Hànyuán and Fēiyuè from Yǎ Prefecture,
and Yángshān from Xī Prefecture).
(Tǔ,
pronounced like "tūn" in entering tone).
8 Yuán Zài (元載), seeing that many officials preferred to serve in the capital,
feared their proximity to himself.
Therefore, he reformed the salary system,
making outer officials well-paid and capital officials poorly paid.
Capital officials were unable to support themselves
and often had to beg for loans from outer officials.
Yáng Wǎn (楊綰) and Cháng Gǔn (常袞) memorialized that the salaries of capital officials were too low.
On the *jǐyǒu* day [of the fourth month],
an imperial edict was issued to increase the salaries of capital officials,
amounting to approximately 156,000 *mín* annually.
According to the *Táng Huìyào* (唐會要): In the 24th year of Kaiyuán (開元) [736 CE],
an imperial decree ordered that the salaries of all officials should be unified into a single category,
all under the name of monthly salary,
and disbursed monthly according to each official's rank:
First rank: thirty thousand [cash],
Second rank: twenty-four thousand,
Third rank: seventeen thousand,
Fourth rank: eleven thousand,
Fifth rank: nine thousand two hundred,
Sixth rank: five thousand three hundred,
Seventh rank: four thousand fifty,
Eighth rank: two thousand four hundred seventy-five,
Ninth rank: one thousand nine hundred seventeen.
By the 12th year of Dàlì (大曆) [777 CE],
the salaries of capital officials were increased: the Sān Shī (三師), Sān Gōng (三公), Shìzhōng (侍中), and Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令) each received one hundred twenty *guànwén* (貫文) monthly.
The Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎) and Ménxià Shìláng (門下侍郎) each received one hundred *guànwén* monthly.
The Dōnggōng Sān Tài (東宮三太) and Zuǒ-Yòu Púshè (左‧右僕射) each received eighty *guànwén*.
The Dōnggōng Sān Shǎo (東宮三少) each received seventy *guànwén*.
The Shàngshū (尚書), Yùshǐ Dàfū (御史大夫), and Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿) each received sixty *guànwén*.
The Chángshì (常侍), Zōngzhèng Qīng (宗正卿), Tàizǐ Zhànshì (太子詹事), and Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (國子祭酒) each received fifty *guànwén*.

The Zuǒ-Yòu Chéng (左‧右丞), as well as the various *shìláng* (侍郎) of various departments, Jǐshě (給舍), Zhōngchéng (中丞), Bīnkè (賓客), Diànzhōng (殿中), Mìshū Jiān (祕書監), Sīnóng Qīng (司農卿) and others, and Jiàngzuò Jiān (將作監) and others, each received forty-five *guànwén*.
The Tàizǐ Èr Shùzǐ (太子二庶子) and Tàicháng Shǎoqīng (太常少卿) each received forty *guànwén*.
The Jiànyì (諫議), and various *shǎoqīng* (少卿) and *shǎojiān* (少監) of various departments, each received thirty-five *guànwén*.
The Guózǐ Sīyè (國子司業), Nèishì (內侍), and Dōnggōng Sān Qīng (東宮三卿) each received thirty *guànwén*.

The Lángzhōng (郎中), Shìyùshǐ (侍御史), Sītiān Jiān (司天監), Shǎozhànshì (少詹事), various Wáng Fù (諸王傅), Guózǐ Bóshì (國子博士), Yùdé (諭德), Zhōngyǔn (中允), Zhōngshě (中舍), and Diànzhōng (殿中), Mìshū (祕書), Tàicháng (太常), Zōngzhèng Chéng (宗正丞) each received twenty-five *guànwén*.
The Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ (殿中侍御史), Zhùzuò Láng (著作郎), Dàlǐ Zhèng (大理正), Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě (都水使者), Zǒngjiān (總監), Nèi Chángshì (內常侍), and Nèi Jǐshì (內給事) each received twenty *guànwén*.
The Yuánwàiláng (員外郎), Tōngshì Shèrén (通事舍人), Qǐjū (起居), and Wángfǔ Zhǎngshǐ (王府長史) each received eighteen *guànwén*.

The Jiānchá Yùshǐ (監察御史), Tái Zhǔbù (臺主簿), Bǔquē (補闕), Wángfǔ Sīmǎ (王府司馬), Sītiān Shǎojiān (司天少監), Tàizǐ Diǎnnèi (太子典內), Tàicháng Bóshì (太常博士) and Zhǔbù (主簿), Zōngzhèng Zhǔbù (宗正主簿), Ménxià Lùshì (門下錄事), and Zhōngshū Zhǔshū (中書主書) each received fifteen *guànwén*.

The Shíyí (拾遺), Sīyì (司議), Tàizǐ Wénxué (太子文學), Mìshū Zhùzuò Zuǒláng (祕書著作佐郎), Guózǐ (國子), Tàixué (太學), Sì Mén (四門), Guǎngwén Bóshì (廣文博士), Dàlǐ Sīzhí (大理司直), Zhànshìfǔ Chéng (詹事府丞), and various Temple (寺) and Directorate (監) Chéng (丞), Yèzhě Jiān (謁者監), and Zhōngshū (中書) and Ménxià Zhǔshì (門下主事) each received twelve *guànwén*.
The Xǐmǎ (洗馬), Zànshàn (贊善), various Temple (寺) and Directorate (監) Zhǔbù (主簿), and Zhànshìfǔ Sīzhí (詹事府司直) each received ten *guànwén*.
The Píngshì (評事) received eight *guànwén*.
Various Jiàozhèng (校正) each received six *guànwén*.
Various Fèngyù (奉御), Jiǔchéng Zǒngjiān (九成總監), various Wáng Zīyì (諸王諮議) and Yǒu (友), and various Líng Lìng (諸陵令) each received six *guànwén* and two hundred *wén*.

The Chéngmén (城門), Fúbǎo (符寶), Guózǐ Zhùjiào (國子助教), Liù Jú Láng (六局郎), Wángfǔ Yuánshǔ (王府掾屬), Tàicháng Shìyī (太常侍醫), Wénxué (文學), Lùshì Cānjūn (錄事參軍), Zhǔbù (主簿), Jìshì (記室), various Wèi (衞) and Liù Jūn Zhǎngshǐ (六軍長史), Liǎng Shì Lìng (兩市令), various Fùzǒngjiān (副總監), Wǔkù Shǔlìng (武庫署令), and Tàigōng Miào Lìng (太公廟令) each received five *guànwén* and three hundred *wén*.

The Tàizǐ Tōngshì Shèrén (太子通事舍人), Dōnggōng Sān Sì Chéng (東宮三寺丞), Tàixué (太學) and Guǎngwén Zhùjiào (廣文助教), Nèifāng Chéng (內坊丞), various Zhízhǎng (直長), Nèisì Bó (內寺伯), Qiānniú Wèi (千牛衞) and various Shuàifǔ Zhǎngshǐ (率府長史), various Líng Chéng (諸陵丞), various Líng Shǔ (諸陵署) and various Wángfǔ Pànsī (諸王府判司), Sīzhú (司竹) and Wēnquán Jiān (溫泉監), Shàngshū Dūshì (尚書都事), Dūshuǐ (都水) and various Zǒngjiān Chéng (總監丞), Sītiāntái Chéng (司天臺丞), Tàizǐ Shìyī (太子侍醫), various Sī Shàngjú Shǔlìng (諸司上局署令), Wángfǔ Guólìng (王府國令), Yuàn Sīmiàn Fùjiān (苑四面副監), and Gōngzhǔ Yìsī Lìng (公主邑司令) each received four *guànwén* and one hundred sixteen *wén*.

The Guózǐ (國子) and Sì Mén Zhùjiào (四門助教), Lǜ (律) and Yīxué Bóshì (醫學博士), Xiélǜ Láng (協律郎), Nèi Yèzhě (內謁者), various Wèi (衞) and Liù Jūn Zuǒ-Yòu Wèishuàifǔ (六軍左‧右衞率府) and other Wèi Zuǒ (衞佐), various Wángfǔ Cānjūn (諸王府參軍), Dànóng (大農), Dūshěng (都省), Bīng (兵), Lì (吏), Lǐ (禮), Fáng Kǎogōng Zhǔshì (房考功主事), Chūnfāng Lùshì (春坊錄事), Sīzhú Fùjiān (司竹副監), various Sī Zhōngjú Shǔlìng (諸司中局署令), Dūshuǐ Zhǔbù (都水主簿), various Sī Shàngjú Shǔ (諸司上局署) and Jiānmiào Sīchéng (監廟司丞), Sītiāntái Língtái Láng (司天臺靈臺郎), Bǎozhāng (保章), Qìhú Zhèng (挈壺正), Tàicháng Zhēnyī (太常針醫) and Yījiān (醫監), and Shàngyī Jú Sīyī (尚醫局司醫) each received two *guànwén* and four hundred seventy *wén*.

The Tàizhù (太祝), Fènglǐ (奉禮), various Xíng Zhǔshì (行主事) in the ministries, Ménxià Diǎnyí (門下典儀), Yùshǐtái (御史臺), Diànzhōng (殿中), Mìshū (祕書), Nèishìshěng (內侍省), Chūnfāng (春坊), Zhànshìfǔ Zhǔshì (詹事府主事), various Temple (寺) and Directorate (監) and various Wèi (衞) and Liù Jūn (六軍) various Sī Lùshì (諸司錄事), various Sī Zhōngjú Shǔchéng (諸司中局署丞) and Dàlǐ Yùchéng (大理獄丞), various Sī Jiànzuò Jiànshì (諸司監作監事), various Shuàifǔ Lùshì (諸率府錄事), Diànzhōngshěng Yīzuǒ (殿中省醫佐), Shíyī (食醫), Fèngniǎn (奉輦), Sīkù (司庫), Sīlǐn (司廩), Fèngchéng (奉乘), Hónglú Sì Zhǎngkè (鴻臚寺掌客), Sīyí (司儀), Tàipú Zhǔchéng (太僕主乘), Nèifāng Diǎnzhí (內坊典直), Sītiāntái Sīchén (司辰), Sīlì Jiān (司曆監), Nèishìshěng Gōngjiào Bóshì (內侍省宮教博士), Dōnggōng Sān Sì Zhǔbù (東宮三寺主簿), Tàicháng Tàilè (太常太樂) and Gǔchuī Chéng (鼓吹丞), Yīzhèng (醫正), Ānmó (按摩), Zhòujìn (呪禁), Bǔshì Bóshì (卜筮博士) and Zhēn (針), Yī (醫), Bǔ Zhùjiào (卜助教), Guózǐ Shū (書) and Suàn Bóshì (算博士) and Zhùjiào (助教), various Wángfǔ Guóchéng (諸王府國丞) and Wèi (尉), and various Zǒngjiān Zhǔbù (總監主簿) each received one *guànwén* and nine hundred seventeen *wén*.
Military officials: The Zuǒ-Yòu Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn (左右金吾大將軍) each received forty-five *guànwén*.
The Liù Jūn Dàjiāngjūn (六軍大將軍) and Zuǒ-Yòu Jīnwú Jiāngjūn (左右金吾將軍) each received forty *guànwén*.
Various Wèi Dàjiāngjūn (諸衞大將軍) and Liù Jūn Jiāngjūn (六軍將軍) each received thirty *guànwén*.
Various Wèi Jiāngjūn (諸衞將軍) each received twenty-five *guànwén*.
Various Wèi (衞) and Liù Jūn Zhōnglángjiàng (六軍中郎將), and various Shuàifǔ Shuài (諸率府率) and Fùshuài (副率) each received ten *guànwén* and five hundred sixty-seven *wén*.
Various Wèi (衞) and Liù Jūn Lángjiàng (六軍郎將), and various Wángfǔ Diǎnjūn Fù (諸王府典軍副) each received nine *guànwén* and two hundred *wén*.
Various Wèi (衞) and Liù Jūn Sījì (六軍司陛), Qiānniú (千牛) and Zuǒ-Yòu Bèishēn (左右備身) each received five *guànwén* and three hundred *wén*.
Various Wèi (衞) and Liù Jūn Zhōnghòu (六軍中候), and Tàizǐ Qiānniú (太子千牛) each received four *guànwén* and one hundred sixty-six *wén*.
Various Wèi (衞) and Liù Jūn Sījiē (六軍司戈), and Tàizǐ Bèishēn (太子備身) each received two *guànwén* and four hundred seventy-five *wén*.
Various Wèi (衞) and Liù Jūn Zhíjiē (六軍執戟) and Chángshàng (長上) each received one *guànwén* and nine hundred seventeen *wén*.
The Jīngzhào Fǔ (京兆府) and various Fǔyǐn (府尹) each received eighty *guànwén*.
The Shǎoyǐn (少尹) and the two Xiàn Lìng (縣令) each received fifty *guànwén*.
The Fèngxīan (奉先), Zhāoyìng (昭應), Lǐquán (醴泉) and other Xiàn Lìng (縣令), and Sīlù (司錄) each received forty-five *guànwén*.
Various Jī Lìng (畿令) each received forty *guànwén*.
The Pànsī (判司) and the two Xiàn Chéng (縣丞) each received thirty-five *guànwén*.
The two Xiàn Bù (縣簿) and Wèi (尉), and the Fèngxīan (奉先) and other Xiàn Chéng (縣丞) each received thirty *guànwén*.
The Fèngxīan Xiàn Bù (奉先縣簿) and Wèi (尉), and various Jī Lìng (畿令) each received twenty-five *guànwén*.
The Jī Bù (畿簿) and Wèi (尉) each received twenty *guànwén*.
The Cānjūn (參軍), Wénxué Bóshì (文學博士), and Lùshì (錄事) each received ten *guànwén*.
In addition to the monthly salaries for regular civil and military officials of all departments,
the Jiǎnjiào Guān Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (檢校官同中書門下平章事)
received one hundred twenty *guànwén* monthly.
The Nèishìshěng Jiān (內侍省監)
received forty-five *guànwén* monthly, making the total annual increase about one hundred fifty-six thousand *guànwén*.
In the fifth month,
on the *xīnhài* day,
an imperial edict was issued to dismiss all Guótuánliàn Shǒuzhuōshǐ (都團練守捉使) in the various prefectures,
except for the Dūtuánliàn Shǐ (都團練使).
It also ordered that unless it was a matter of urgent military necessity,
no commissioner should be allowed to summon prefectural governors (cǐshǐ) or suspend them from their duties
and appoint others to temporarily act in their place.
Furthermore, the troops in the various prefectures were regularized,
all having fixed numbers.
Those who were recruited and provided with family provisions and spring/winter clothing
were called
"Guāngiàn" (官健) [government-maintained soldiers].
Those who were selected from local people,
returned to farming in spring and summer, were recalled in autumn and winter, and provided with personal rations and salted vegetables,
were called
"Tuánjié" (團結) [local militia].
Since the outbreak of war,
the salaries of prefectural and county officials had been inconsistent.
Moreover, Yuán Zài (元載) and Wáng Jìn (王縉) acted based on their personal whims and favoritism,
with some prefectural governors receiving up to a thousand *mín* monthly, while others received only a few tens of *mín*.
By this time,
the salaries of officials from Jiedushi (節度使) down to Zhǔbù (主簿) and Wèi (尉) were finally fixed.
Those with too much were reduced, and those with too little were increased,
creating an ordered hierarchy,
and the legal system was roughly established.
9 On the *gēngwǔ* day [of the fifth month],
the Emperor sent an imperial envoy to excavate Yuán Zài's (元載) ancestral grave,
hack open the coffin, abandon the corpse,
destroy his family temple,
and burn his spirit tablets.
On the *wùyín* day [of the seventh month],
Zhuó Yīngqiàn (卓英倩) and others were all beaten to death.
When Yīngqiàn (英倩) was in power,
his younger brother Yīnglín (英璘) was unruly in their hometown.
When Yīngqiàn (英倩) was imprisoned,
Yīnglín (英璘) seized a strategic location and started a rebellion.
The Emperor dispatched imperial guards to suppress him.
On the *yǐsì* day [of the ninth month],
Sūn Dàopíng (孫道平), the Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Jīnzhōu (金州), attacked and captured him.
10 The Emperor had relied on Yáng Wǎn (楊綰)
to reform corrupt policies. Coincidentally, Wǎn (綰) fell ill.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the *jǐsì* day,
he passed away.
The Emperor mourned him greatly,
and said to his close ministers:
"Heaven does not wish for me to achieve great peace!
Why did it take my Yáng Wǎn (楊綰) so quickly?"
11 In the eighth month,
on the *guǐwèi* day,
Xiānyú Shūmíng (鮮于叔明), the Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of Dōngchuān (東川), was granted the imperial surname Lǐ (李).
12 When Yuán Zài (元載) and Wáng Jìn (王縉) were chancellors,
the Emperor daily bestowed upon them imperial meals from the inner kitchen,
enough to feed ten people,
which then became a custom.
On the *guǐmǎo* day,
Cháng Gǔn (常袞) and Zhū Cǐ (朱泚) memorialized:
"The meal allowance is already too much."
("Cānjīan" (餐錢) [meal money],
is what is called "shíliàojián" (食料錢) [food allowance].
The character *Cǐ* (泚)
is pronounced *zhí* and *lǐ* (直禮) in fanqie,
and also *cǐ* (此) as a tone.
The character *Shàng* (上)
is pronounced *shí* and *zhǎng* (時掌) in fanqie.)
The Emperor agreed to it.
Gǔn (袞) also wanted to decline the *Táng Fēng* (堂封),
but his colleagues disagreed, so he stopped.
According to the Táng (唐) system: the *Táng Fēng* (堂封)
amounted to three thousand six hundred *jiān* (縑) annually.
After Xīngyuán (興元) [784 CE], it was only one thousand one hundred,
but Dēzōng (德宗) soon restored it to its former amount.
It was thought that:
"The court's generous salaries
are for nurturing the worthy.
If one is incapable,
one should resign from office,
not decline the salary."
Your servant Guāng (光) says: A gentleman is ashamed to eat more than others.
Gǔn's (袞) refusal of salary
shows his integrity and sense of shame.
Is this not better than those who cling to office and covet salary?
The *Shī* (詩) says: 'Those gentlemen,
they do not eat in vain!'
This is a line from the *Shī Fádán* (詩伐檀).
Therefore, it should not be criticized too harshly.
13 Yáng Wǎn (楊綰) and Cháng Gǔn (常袞) recommended Yán Zhēnqīng (顏真卿), Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Húzhōu (湖州).
In the first year of Dàlì (大曆) [766 CE], Zhēnqīng (真卿), for attacking Yuán Zài (元載),
was demoted to Biéjià (別駕) of Xiázhōu (峽州).
Soon after, he was re-designated as Sīmǎ (司馬) of Jízhōu (吉州),
and then promoted to Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Fǔzhōu (撫州) and Húzhōu (湖州).
On the *jiǎchén* day [of the ninth month],
he was made Xíngbù Shàngshū (刑部尚書).
Wǎn (綰) and Gǔn (袞) also recommended Guān Bò (關播) from Jí (汲), Pànguān (判官) of Huáinán (淮南).
He was promoted to Dūguān Yuánwàiláng (都官員外郎).
The Dūguān Láng (都官郎) of the Táng (唐) dynasty
was in charge of assigning laborers and registering captives,
providing them with clothing, food, and medicine,
and handling their appeals and clearing their grievances.
They had to know all about the commoners, both public and private, noble and humble,
and belonged to the Xíngbù (刑部) [Ministry of Justice].
14th day of the 9th month,
on the Xīnyǒu day,
Duàn Xiùshí, who was concurrently the Provisional Commissioner of the Four Garrisons and Běitíng military command, and Deputy Jìedùshǐ of Jīngyuán and Zhèngyǐng, was made Jìedùshǐ.
The Yìkǎo (Examination of Differences) says: Duàn Gōng Biézhuàn (Biography of Duke Duàn) says:
"From the time he received the battle-axe, for three to five years,
there were no alarms of beacon fires in the western borders."
It also says:
"The Róng commander Lún Qǐlìtuó admired the Duke's pure virtue,
and dared not invade our territory."
The Jiùzhuàn (Old Biography) also says:
"For three or four years,
the Tǔbō dared not violate the frontier."
However, in this month, the Tǔbō raided Yuánzhōu.
In the 12th month,
Zhū Cǐ repelled the Tǔbō,
and returned from Jīngzhōu.
In the 9th month of the following year,
the Tǔbō threatened Jīngzhōu.
The claim that they "dared not violate the frontier for three or four years"
is probably an embellishment by historians.
He possessed prestige and benevolence,
lived a clean and frugal life,
had no concubines in his household,
and except for public gatherings,
never drank wine or listened to music.
15 The Tǔbō, with 80,000 troops, encamped at Chángzé Jiān, north of Yuánzhōu.
This was Chángzé Chuān (Long Marsh River),
where the Táng had previously established a horse pasture.
Tǔ (in Tǔbō),
is pronounced with the Rùsheng of tūn;
the same below.
On the Jǐsì day,
Fāngqú was defeated.
Fāngqú was
a Hàn dynasty county,
belonging to Běidì Jùn,
later abolished.
In the 3rd year of Shénlóng of Zhōngzōng,
Fāngqú Xiàn was established by dividing Mǎlíng,
and it belonged to Qìngzhōu.
Sòng Bái's Xù Tōngdiǎn says: Lǐngzhōu Fāngqú Zhèn,
Tōngyuǎn Jūn was established in the early Sòng,
the Qín Great Wall was one lí north of the city.
Guō Zǐyí sent his subordinate general Lǐ Huáiguāng to relieve it,
and the Tǔbō retreated.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
the Tǔbō raided Fāngzhōu.
16 In winter,
in the 10th month,
on the Yǐyǒu day,
Cuī Níng, Jìedùshǐ of Xīchuān, reported a great victory over the Tǔbō at Wànghàn Chéng.
The Tǔbō built a city on the western mountains to overlook Shǔ,
hence its name Wànghàn Chéng (City for Gazing at Hàn).
Shǐ (使 in Jìedùshǐ),
is pronounced suō lì.
17 Previously,
due to autumn rains,
much of the salt from the salt ponds in Hézhōng Fǔ was ruined.
Under the administration of Hézhōng Fǔ, Ānyì and Xiè Xiàn
all had salt ponds.
Xiān (先 in Xiānnán),
is pronounced xī jiàn.
On the Dīnghài day,
a report stated that although there was much rain,
it did not harm the salt,
and auspicious salt was still forming.
The Emperor doubted this,
and sent Jiànyì Dàfū Jiǎng Zhèn of Yìxīng to inspect it.
Yìxīng was
the land of Yángxiàn Xiàn in the Hàn dynasty.
The Jìn dynasty established Yìxīng Jùn and Xiàn.
The Suí dynasty abolished the Jùn and kept the Xiàn,
attaching it to Chángzhōu.
18 The Tǔbō raided Yán and Xiàzhōu,
and also Chángwǔ.
Bīnzhōu Yílù Xiàn had Chángwǔ Chéng.
At that time, Guō Zǐyí sent Lǐ Huáiguāng to build Chángwǔ Chéng,
occupying the high ground,
overlooking the Jīng river,
and commanding the pass.
From then on, the Tǔbō dared not lightly trespass.
Sòng Bái says: Chángwǔ Zhèn,
is on the border of Línyóu Xiàn in Fèngxiáng Fǔ,
forty lí west of Jīngzhōu.
Xià (夏 in Xiàzhōu),
is pronounced hù yǎ.
19 Liú Qià of Kuāngchéng, the Yāyá of Yǒngpíng Jūn, was appointed Cìshǐ of Sòngzhōu.
The Yìkǎo says: The Jiù Liú Xuánzuǒ Zhuàn (Old Biography of Liú Xuánzuǒ) says:
"Lǐ Língyào occupied Biànzhōu,
and Qià led troops, taking advantage of his unpreparedness,
and marched straight into Sòngzhōu."
However, Liú Chāng, as the Yáménjiàng of Sòngzhōu, persuaded Lǐ Sēnghuì to surrender,
which means Sēnghuì had already been guarding Sòngzhōu for Língyào,
and the court then appointed him Cìshǐ of Sòngzhōu.
If Sēnghuì had not surrendered,
then Qià could not have obtained Sòngzhōu;
if he had surrendered,
then Qià would not have dared to seize Sòngzhōu.
It is probable that Sēnghuì had already been killed by Lǐ Zhōngchén,
and Qià then led troops to occupy Sòngzhōu.
The old biography wished to attribute this achievement to Qià,
hence it said so,
but it is actually incorrect.
Yǒngpíng Jūn's seat of government was Huázhōu.
20 Lí Gàn, Jīngzhàoyǐn, reported that autumn rains had damaged crops.
Hán Huàng reported that Gàn's statement was inaccurate.
The Emperor ordered the Yùshǐ to investigate.
On the Dīngwèi day,
they returned with a report,
"the damage totaled over 30,000 qǐng."
Liú Zǎo, Magistrate of Wèinán,
Wèinán Xiàn,
belonged to Huázhōu in the early Táng,
but at this time belonged to Yōngzhōu.
Sòng Bái says: Guō Yuánshēng's Shùzhēng Jì says: Wèinán Xiàn
was established by barbarians,
referring to Fú and Yáo.
was said to have flattered Hán Huàng.
Dù (度 in dùluò),
is pronounced tuó luò.
Yùshǐ Zhào Jì's report was consistent with Zǎo's.
The Emperor said:
"The continuous rain was widespread;
how could Wèinán alone be unaffected!"
He then ordered Yùshǐ Zhū Áo to inspect it.
The damage was over 3,000 qǐng.
The Emperor sighed for a long time,
and said:
"A county magistrate is
an official who cares for the people;
even if there is no damage, one should still report damage.
How could one be so unbenevolent!"
Zǎo was demoted to Nánpǔ Wèi.
The Later Wèi divided Qúfén Xiàn to establish Yúquán Xiàn.
The Later Zhōu changed its name to Wànchuān.
The Suí changed it to Nánpǔ.
The Táng dynasty administered Wànzhōu.
But Hán Huàng was not questioned.
21 In the 11th month,
on the Rénzǐ day,
Zhāng Xiàngōng, Jìedùshǐ of Shānnán Xīdào, reported defeating over 10,000 Tǔbō troops at Mínzhōu.
22 On the Bǐngchén day,
Jiǎng Zhèn returned,
and reported that
"the auspicious salt was indeed as Hán Huàng had said,"
and he submitted a memorial congratulating the Emperor,
requesting that it be recorded by the imperial historians
and bestowed with a felicitous name.
The Emperor agreed,
and granted the name Bǎoyìng Língyìng Chí.
The given name was for
the Ānyì pond.
23 In the 12th month,
on the Bǐngxū day,
Zhū Cǐ returned to the capital from Jīngzhōu.
Zhū Cǐ had come to court from Yōuzhōu,
and remained in the capital.
He was then sent on an autumn defense mission and returned.
Huán (還 in huánjīng),
is pronounced cóng xuān,
and also as its original pronunciation.
24 On the Dīnghài day,
Cuī Níng reported defeating over 100,000 Tǔbō troops,
beheading over 8,000.
Tǔ (吐 in Tǔbō),
is pronounced with the Rùsheng of tūn.
25 On the Gēngzǐ day,
Zhū Cǐ was concurrently appointed Jìedùshǐ of Lǒngyòu,
and Supervisor of the Héxī and Zélù Provisional Commands.
26 Lǐ Zhèngjǐ (李正己), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Pínglú (平盧), already held the ten prefectures of Zī (淄), Qīng (青), Qí (齊), Hǎi (海), Dēng (登), Lái (萊), Yí (沂), Mì (密), Dé (德), and Dì (棣).
When Lǐ Língyào's (李靈曜) rebellion occurred,
the armies from various circuits attacked him.
The lands they seized
were each taken for themselves.
Zhèngjǐ (正己) also gained the five prefectures of Cáo (曹), Pú (濮), Xú (徐), Yǎn (兗), and Yùn (鄆).
He then moved his administrative seat from Qīngzhōu (青州) to Yùnzhōu (鄆州),
and made his son, the former Zīzhōu Cìshǐ (淄州刺史) Nà (納), guard Qīngzhōu (青州).
Zhèngjǐ (正己) enforced severe punishments;
no one dared to whisper in groups wherever he ruled.
However, his laws and decrees were uniform,
and taxes were fair and light.
He commanded an army of one hundred thousand,
dominating the east,
and all neighboring feudal states feared him.
At this time, Tián Chéngsì (田承嗣) held the seven prefectures of Wèi (魏), Bó (博), Xiāng (相), Wèi (衞), Míng (洺), Bèi (貝), and Chán (澶).
Chánzhōu (澶州)
was the land of Dùnqīu (頓丘) County in Hán (漢) Dōngjùn (東郡).
In the 16th year of Kāihuáng (開皇) of the Suí (隋) dynasty,
Chányuān (澶淵) County was established by partitioning Dùnqīu (頓丘).
The Táng (唐) dynasty renamed it Chánshuǐ (澶水),
to avoid the taboo name of Gāozǔ (高祖).
In the 4th year of Wǔdé (武德),
Chánzhōu (澶州) was established by partitioning Chánshuǐ (澶水) from Lízhōu (黎州), Dùnqīu (頓丘) from Wèizhōu (魏州), and Guānzhōu (觀州).
In the 1st year of Zhēnguān (貞觀),
the prefecture was abolished.
In the 7th year of Dàlì (大曆),
Tián Chéngsì (田承嗣) petitioned to re-establish Chánzhōu (澶州)
using Dùnqīu (頓丘) and Línhuáng (臨黃) from Wèizhōu (魏州).
Sī (嗣),
pronounced like "Xiánglì".
Xiāng (相),
pronounced like "Xīliàng".
Míng (洺),
pronounced "míng".
Chán (澶),
pronounced like "Shílián".
Each commanded an army of fifty thousand.
Liáng Chóngyì (梁崇義) held the six prefectures of Xiāng (襄), Dèng (鄧), Jūn (均), Fáng (房), Fù (復), and Yǐng (郢),
with an army of twenty thousand.
They were interconnected and intertwined,
and although they nominally served the imperial court, they did not follow its laws and decrees.
They independently controlled official titles, military weapons, taxes, punishments, and executions.
The emperor was lenient and benevolent,
letting them do as they pleased.
If the imperial court repaired a single city
or increased a single soldier,
they would immediately complain,
taking it as a sign of suspicion and disloyalty,
and the work was often suspended because of them.
Yet, within their own territories, they built fortifications and repaired their armies ceaselessly.
Because of this, although they were nominally feudal vassals within the central lands,
they were in reality like the uncivilized Mánmò (蠻貊) tribes in foreign lands.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Xīnyǒu (辛酉),
an imperial edict commanded the destruction of the watermills on the branch canals of the Báiqú (白渠) to irrigate fields.
Shēngpíng (昇平) Gōngzhǔ (公主) had two mills.
She met the emperor
and requested to keep them.
The emperor said,
"I wish to benefit the common people.
If you understand my intention,
you should set an example for the multitude."
The princess destroyed them that very day.
2 On the day Wùchén (戊辰),
the Huíhú (回紇) raided Tàiyuán (太原).
Lǐ Zìliáng (李自良) of Sìshuǐ (泗水), the Yāyá (押牙) of Hédōng (河東), said:
"The elite Huíhú (回紇) troops have come from afar to seek battle;
it is difficult to contend with them directly.
It would be better to build two strongholds on their return path
and garrison them with troops.
When the barbarians arrive,
hold firm in your defenses and do not engage them.
When their forces are exhausted and retreat on their own,
then send out our army to attack them.
With the two strongholds opposing them in front
and our main army pressing them from behind,
there will be no failure."
The Liúhòu (留後) Bào Fáng (鮑防) did not follow this advice and
sent the grand general Jiāo Bóyú (焦伯瑜) and others to meet them in battle.
On the day Guǐyǒu (癸酉),
they encountered the barbarians at Yángqǔ (陽曲)
and were greatly defeated, returning with over ten thousand dead.
The Huíhú (回紇) let their troops loose to plunder extensively.
In the second month,
Zhāng Guāngshèng (張光晟), Dūdū (都督) of Dàizhōu (代州),
defeated them at Yángwǔgǔ (羊武谷),
whereupon they withdrew.
The emperor also did not question the reason for the Huíhú (回紇) invasion,
treating them as before.
3 On the day Jǐhài (己亥),
Tǔbō (吐蕃) sent its general Mǎ Chóngyīng (馬重英) with forty thousand troops to raid Língzhōu (靈州).
Tǔ (吐),
pronounced with the entering tone from "tūn".
Shuài (帥),
read as "shuài".
Shǐ Zhào (史炤) said: The three canals
refer to the Tiánhàn Qú (填漢渠), Yùshǐ Qú (御史渠), and Shàngshū Qú (尚書渠).
Tián (填),
read as "zhèn".
4 In the third month,
on the day Jiǎxū (甲戌),
a Huíhú (回紇) envoy returned.
Passing through Hézhōng (河中),
soldiers from the Shuòfāng (朔方) army plundered his baggage.
These were Shuòfāng (朔方) army soldiers stationed in Hézhōng (河中).
Shǐ (使),
pronounced like "Shūlì".
Guò (過),
pronounced like "Gǔhé",
also like "Gǔwò".
Zī (輜),
pronounced like "Zhuāngchí".
Zhòng (重),
pronounced like "Zhíyòng".
5 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Jiǎchén (甲辰),
Tǔbō (吐蕃) raided Língzhōu (靈州).
Cháng Qiānguāng (常謙光), Liúhòu (留後) of Shuòfāng (朔方), defeated them.
6 In the sixth month,
on the day Wùxū (戊戌),
Zhū Cǐ (朱泚), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Lǒngyòu (隴右), presented a cat and a mouse suckling together without harming each other, considering it an auspicious omen.
Cháng Gǔn (常袞) led all officials in offering congratulations.
However, Cuī Yòufǔ (崔祐甫), Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人), alone did not offer congratulations,
saying:
"Things that go against the norm are omens of disaster.
A cat catching a mouse
is its duty. Now, suckling together
is an omen of disaster.
Why should we congratulate this!
We should warn the judicial officials who fail to investigate treachery and the border officials who fail to repel invaders
in order to comply with the will of Heaven."
The emperor praised him.
Yòufǔ (祐甫)
was the son of Miǎn (沔).
Cuī Miǎn (崔沔)
was a famous minister during the Kāiyuán (開元) era.
Miǎn (沔),
pronounced like "Mǐyǎn".
In the seventh month,
Yòufǔ (祐甫) was appointed to oversee the selection of officials in the Ministry of Personnel.
Yòufǔ (祐甫) frequently argued with Cháng Gǔn (常袞) over public matters,
which caused Gǔn (袞) to dislike him.
This laid the groundwork for Gǔn (袞) to recommend Yòufǔ's (祐甫) demotion.
Xuǎn (選),
pronounced like "Xūjuàn".
Shù (數),
pronounced like "Suǒjiǎo".
È (惡),
pronounced like "Wūlù".
7 On the day Wùwǔ (戊午),
Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) reported that the Huíhú (回紇) were still at the border,
causing fear among the border inhabitants,
and requested to send Hún Jiān (渾瑊), Cìshǐ (刺史) of Bīnzhōu (邠州), with troops to garrison Zhènhǔ (振武) Army.
This was granted.
The Huíhú (回紇) then finally departed.
8 On the day Xīnwèi (辛未),
the Tǔbō (吐蕃) general Mǎ Chóngyīng (馬重英) with twenty thousand troops raided Yán (鹽) and Qìng (慶) prefectures.
Guō Zǐyí (郭子儀) sent Lǐ Huáiguāng (李懷光), Dū Yúhóu (都虞候) of Shuò
fāng (朔方), to attack and repel them.
9 In the eighth month,
on the day Yǐhài (乙亥),
Lǐ Bǎochén (李寶臣), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Chéngdé (成德), requested to revert to his original surname Zhāng (張).
This was granted.
Bǎochén (寶臣) was granted the surname in volume 222, first year of Bǎoyìng (寶應).
Shǐ (使),
pronounced like "Shūlì".
10 The Tǔbō (吐蕃) with twenty thousand troops raided Yín (銀) and Lín (麟) prefectures,
plundering the livestock of the Dǎngxiàng (黨項) and other tribes.
Tǔ (吐),
pronounced with the entering tone from "tūn".
Yínzhōu (銀州),
was the land of Yīnyīn (圁陰) County in Hán (漢) Xīhé (西河) Commandery.
Línzhōu (麟州),
was the land of Hán (漢) and Xīnqínzhōng (新秦中).
Dǎng (黨),
pronounced like "Dǐlǎng".
Xù (畜),
pronounced like "Xǔjiù".
11 The emperor continuously mourned Zhēnyì (貞懿) Hòuhòu (皇后).
Zhēnyì (貞懿) Hòuhòu (皇后)
was Dúgū (獨孤),
and passed away ten years ago.
For many years, he could not bear to bury her.
On the day Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
she was finally interred in Zhuānglíng (莊陵).
Zhuānglíng (莊陵)
is five lǐ (里) northwest of Sānyuán (三原) County in Jīngzhào (京兆).
12th day of the 9th month,
on the *gēngwǔ* day,
a Tubó army of ten thousand cavalry descended Qīngshílǐng,
pressing on Jīngzhōu.
Qīngshílǐng is west of Bǎodìng County in Jīngzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Línjīng City
is ninety *lǐ* northwest of Jīngzhōu,
and Qīngshílǐng is within its borders.
騎 (*qí*)
is pronounced *qíjì*.
13th day of winter,
12th month,
on the *bǐngxū* day,
Liú Yàn was appointed as Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, retaining his positions as Minister of Personnel and Commissioner of Transport and Salt and Iron.
He was to oversee the selection of officials and his commissioner duties as before.
14th day. Guō Zǐyí entered the imperial court.
He ordered his administrative assistant, Dù Huángshang of Jīngzhào, to manage the remaining affairs.
Lǐ Huáiguāng secretly plotted to replace Zǐyí.
He forged an imperial edict,
intending to execute generals such as Wēn Rúyǎ.
Huángshang, discerning the deception,
questioned Huáiguāng about it.
Huáiguāng, sweating, confessed his crime.
Thereupon, for those generals who were difficult to control,
Huángshang, feigning Zǐyí's orders,
sent them all out to other posts,
and the military headquarters became secure.
15th day. Dù Yà, Supervising Secretary, was appointed Jiangxi Circuit Observer.
16th day. The Emperor summoned Lǐ Bì, the administrative assistant for Jiangxi, for an audience.
He spoke to him about Yuán Zài's affair,
saying:
"It has been eight years since I parted with you,
and only now have I been able to execute this scoundrel.
It was thanks to the Crown Prince for revealing his conspiracy.
This credit goes to the Crown Prince. "
語 (*yǔ*)
is pronounced *niújù*.
"I almost didn't see you again."
Bì replied:
"I did indeed speak of this in the past.
Your Majesty, when you knew your servant was not good,
you should have removed him.
Your excessive forbearance
is why it came to this."
The Emperor said:
"Things must be perfectly certain;
one cannot act lightly."
The Emperor then said:
"I personally entrusted you to Lù Sìgōng,
but Sìgōng, acting on Zài's intentions,
memorialized to appoint you as Prefectural Administrator of Qiánzhōu.
When Sìgōng first pacified Língnán,
he presented a glass plate,
nine *cùn* in diameter,
which I considered a supreme treasure.
After Zài's household was broken up,
a glass plate from Sìgōng to Zài was found,
a *chǐ* in diameter.
When he arrives,
I shall discuss it with you."
Bì said:
"Sìgōng, as a person,
is cautious,
good at serving others,
fears power and influence,
and is diligent in official duties but lacks a grasp of the bigger picture.
In the past, as a county magistrate,
he had a reputation for ability.
Lù Sìgōng was initially named Jiànkè.
He served as magistrate of Xiāoguān,
then was successively transferred to Shénwū and Gūzāng counties,
and his performance was rated the best in the realm.
Xuánzōng believed he could follow the example of Hàn Lǔgōng,
and thus bestowed the name.
Because he was used by Zài,
he devoted his full effort to him.
If Your Majesty truly understands and employs him,
he will also devote his full effort to Your Majesty.
As for the Prefectural Administrator of Qiánzhōu,
I myself desired it;
it is not his fault.
Furthermore, Sìgōng has just accomplished a great service,"
meaning the pacification of Língnán.
The Emperor's anger then subsided,
and he appointed Sìgōng as Minister of War.
17th day. Guō Zǐyí considered Zhāng Tán, the Deputy Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng, to be headstrong and rude,
believing that he, as a military man, disrespected him, and thus bore a grudge.
Wú Yào, the *Kǒumùguān* appointed by Zǐyí (
*Kǒumùguān* existed in all prefectures under military commissioners,
to manage all affairs;
it was an administrative position.
The words *yī kǒng yī mù* (one hole, one eye)
indicate all that is managed),
angered Zǐyí,
who falsely accused Tán of inciting the troops
and had him executed.
The Chief Secretary, Gāo Yǐng, strongly argued against it,
but Zǐyí did not listen
and memorialized to demote Yǐng to Prefectural Administrator of Yīshì.
Yīshì County
belonged to Hézhōng Prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: It was originally the land of the Xún State.
Yī Dùn became rich here,
hence the name Yīshì.
Zǐyí regretted it
and fully recommended Yǐng to the court,
saying:
"Wú Yào misled me."
He then expelled him.
History says that Guō Zǐyí corrected his mistakes.
朝 (*cháo*)
is pronounced *zhíyáo*.
18th day. Cháng Gǔn spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"Your Majesty has long desired to employ Lǐ Bì.
In the past, Emperor Xuān of Han, when wishing to appoint someone as a high official,
would first test them by making them govern people.
I request that he first be made a prefect,
so he may thoroughly understand the benefits and harms among the people,
and then be employed after reporting on his governance."
Tài Gōng governed Qí,
and reported on his governance after five months.
Bó Qín governed Lǔ,
and reported on his governance after three years.
Cháng Gǔn used this saying.
1st day of spring,
1st month,
on the *rénxū* day,
Lǐ Bì was appointed Prefect of Lǐzhōu.
2nd day.
2nd month, on the *guǐwèi* day,
Tián Chéngsì, Military Commissioner of Wèibó, passed away.
He had eleven sons,
but he considered his nephew Yuè, the Commander of the Central Army, to be talented,
so he had him oversee military affairs,
with his sons assisting him.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
Yuè was made Acting Military Commissioner of Wèibó.
This set the stage for Tián Xù to kill Yuè.
3rd day. Lǐ Zhōngchén, Military Commissioner of Huáixī,
was greedy, cruel, and licentious.
He often coerced and raped
the beautiful wives and daughters of his officers and officials.
He entrusted all military and administrative affairs to his sister's husband, Zhāng Huìguāng, the Deputy Military Commissioner.
Huìguāng, leveraging his power, was tyrannical,
and the military districts suffered from it.
Zhōngchén further appointed Huìguāng's son as an army commander,
who was even more tyrannical than his father.
Lǐ Xīliè, Commander of the Left Flank,
was a cousin of Zhōngchén
and respected by the populace.
Xīliè, capitalizing on the people's resentment and anger,
in the 3rd month,
on the *dīngwèi* day,
together with General Dīng Gǎo and others,
killed Huìguāng and his son and expelled Zhōngchén.
Zhōngchén fled alone to the capital.
The Emperor, considering his past merits (
when Tubó raided the capital,
Zhōngchén was among the first military commissioners to respond with aid,
and he also had the merit of pacifying Lǐ Língyào),
appointed Xīliè as Prefect of Cáizhōu and Acting Military Commissioner of Huáixī.
This set the stage for Lǐ Xīliè to rebel with Huái and Cài.
He was given command over the additional prefectures of Biàn and Yǐng,
and his headquarters were moved to Biànzhōu.
The Yǒngpíng Army originally governed from Huázhōu.
汴 (*biàn*)
is pronounced *píbiàn*.
4th day. On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Wáng Hóng, Pacification Commissioner of Róngguǎn, was appointed Vice Prefect of Hézhōng and Overseer of Prefectural Affairs.
Líng Zhèng, a subordinate general of the Acting Deputy Supreme Commander of Hédōng, was tyrannical,
and Hóng suppressed him.
Zhèng and his followers attempted to stage a rebellion during the night.
Hóng, knowing this,
purposely shortened the clepsydra by several *kè* to alter their timing,
causing the rebels to be alarmed and
scatter.
He captured Zhèng
and executed him,
and the military headquarters became secure.
5th day. Zhāng Bǎochén, Military Commissioner of Chéngdé, having previously requested to revert to his original surname (
Last year, Bǎochén requested to revert to the surname Zhāng),
again requested a surname bestowed by the Emperor.
In summer,
4th month,
on the *guǐwèi* day,
he was again bestowed the surname Lǐ.
6 In the fifth month,
on the guǐmǎo day,
the Emperor first fell ill.
On the xīnyǒu day,
an edict was issued appointing the Crown Prince as regent.
That evening,
the Emperor passed away in the inner chamber of the Zǐchén Hall.
The Emperor was fifty-two years old.
The Zǐchén Hall was located north of the Xuānzhèng Hall in the Eastern Palace,
and south of the Pénglái Hall.
On the guǐhài day,
Dézōng ascended the throne.
During his period of mourning,
he strictly adhered to ritual and law.
He once summoned Hán Wáng Huí for a meal.
Huí
was Dézōng's younger brother.
Salt and curds were not served.
Mǎchǐ
is purslane.
Là,
pronounced luò;
it is milk curds.
7 Cháng Gǔn was of a rigid and quick temper.
His governance was meticulous and harsh,
failing to win popular support.
At that time, all officials attended the morning and evening mourning rituals.
Gǔn wept to the point of collapse,
and his attendants sometimes had to support him.
Zhōngshū Shèrén Cuī Yòufǔ pointed him out to the crowd and said:
"When a minister weeps before his lord,
is it proper to be supported?"
Gǔn heard this and resented him even more.
When discussing the mourning attire for all officials,
Gǔn believed:
"According to ritual,
a minister wears mourning of 'coarse hemp with unhemmed edges' (zhǎncui) for three years for his sovereign.
Emperor Hàn Wén's provisional regulation
still prescribed thirty-six days.
The matter is recorded in scroll 15, on the seventh year after Emperor Hàn Wén of the Former Hàn.
All followed the Hàn system.
It was not until the mourning of Xuánzōng and Sùzōng
that twenty-seven days were first observed.
Now the imperial will states,
'Officials and common people throughout the realm
shall remove mourning after three days.'
In ancient times, high-ranking officials mourned along with the sovereign.
If the Emperor removes mourning after twenty-seven days,
then all officials at court
should also follow suit."
Yòufǔ believed:
"The imperial will
makes no distinction between court officials and commoners.
Both court and commoners, inside and out,
are all 'throughout the realm.'
All officials in charge
are 'officials and common people.'
Therefore, all should
remove mourning."
They argued vigorously,
their voices and expressions sharp and aggressive.
Gǔn could not tolerate it,
so he impeached Yòufǔ, accusing him of acting on emotion and altering ritual,
and requested his demotion to Cìshǐ of Cháozhōu.
The Emperor deemed it too severe.
In the intercalary month,
on the rénshēn day,
Yòufǔ was demoted to Shǎoyǐn of Hénán.
Initially,
during the reign of Sùzōng,
affairs throughout the realm were pressing.
There were often several Chancellors,
who took turns on duty to make decisions.
Sometimes, when they were on leave or at home,
an edict would instruct the duty officer to sign their name and report it.
From then on, this became common practice.
At that time, Guō Zǐyí and Zhū Cǐ, although Chancellors due to military achievements,
did not participate in court politics.
Gǔn alone occupied the Zhèngshìtáng.
In the early Táng,
the Zhèngshìtáng was in the Ménxiàshěng.
When Péi Yán moved from Shìzhōng to Zhōngshūlìng,
the Zhèngshìtáng was then moved to the Zhōngshūshěng.
The heads of the three departments discussed affairs there.
After Yòufǔ was demoted,
the two presented memorials stating his innocence.
The Emperor asked:
"You previously said he deserved demotion;
now you say he is innocent.
Why is this?"
The two replied that
they had not known initially.
The Emperor, who had just ascended the throne,
considered Gǔn deceitful
and was greatly alarmed.
On the jiǎchén day,
all officials, dressed in mourning attire,
stood in order at the Yuèhuá Gate.
Chéng Dàchāng said: According to the Liùdiǎn,
in front of the Xuānzhèng Hall were two corridors.
Each corridor had its own gate.
The eastern one was called Rìhuá;
to the east of Rìhuá was the Ménxiàshěng.
The western corridor had a gate called Yuèhuá;
to the west of Yuèhuá was the Zhōngshūshěng.
Shuāi,
pronounced cānghuí.
Gǔn was demoted to Cìshǐ of Cháozhōu.
Cháozhōu
was about five thousand *li* from the capital.
Those who heard were shocked and trembled.
Yòufǔ returned after reaching Zhāoyìng.
Zhāoyìng County
was originally Xīnfēng County.
In the second year of Chuígǒng,
it was renamed Yìngshān.
In the first year of Shénlóng,
it reverted to its old name.
Xuánzōng renamed it Zhāoyìng.
Suí Xīnfēng's seat was north of the old Xīnfēng city.
Tiānbǎo Zhāoyìng County's seat was north of the Zhāoyìng Palace.
Huán,
pronounced cóngxun,
also pronounced as written.
The Emperor was then in his period of mourning,
and all government affairs were entrusted to Yòufǔ,
whose proposals were invariably accepted.
Initially,
after Zhìdé,
the realm was at war,
and generals competed for recognition and rewards,
leading inevitably to an excessive number of official titles and ranks.
After Yǒngtài,
the realm gradually became peaceful,
but Yuán Zài and Wáng Jìn held power,
and those from all directions seeking official positions through bribes crowded their gates.
The major appointments came from Zài and Jìn,
minor ones from Zhuó Yīngqiàn and others,
and all left having achieved their desires.
When Cháng Gǔn became Chancellor,
he sought to reform these abuses,
cutting off opportunities for ill-gotten gains.
Petitions from all corners
were entirely rejected;
however, he made no distinctions,
causing both the worthy and the unworthy to be stagnant.
Cuī Yòufǔ replaced him,
desiring to gain public esteem.
He recommended and promoted people constantly,
with no empty days.
He had been Chancellor for less than two hundred days,
yet appointed eight hundred officials.
The Kǎoyì states: The old records say:
"Yòufǔ had been Chancellor for less than a year,
and appointed nearly eight hundred officials,
many of whom were praised as suitable."
Now we follow the Jiànzhōng Shílù.
He ultimately failed to find the right balance.
The Emperor once said to Yòufǔ:
"Some people criticize you,
saying that most of those you appoint are relatives or old acquaintances.
Why is this?"
He replied:
"Your servant selects officials for Your Majesty,
and dares not be anything but thorough and cautious.
If I have never known someone in my life,
how can I be familiar with their talents and conduct to appoint them?"
The Emperor thought this was reasonable.
Your servant Sīmǎ Guāng says: Your servant has heard that in employing people,
there should be no distinction between close and distant, new and old;
only the wise and the unworthy should be discerned.
If a person is not necessarily worthy,
and is employed due to kinship or acquaintance,
this is certainly not impartial.
But if they are indeed worthy,
and are rejected due to kinship or acquaintance,
this is also not impartial.
The worthy people in the world
are certainly not all known by one person alone.
If one must wait to personally know their talents and conduct before employing them,
many capable individuals would be overlooked.
Chancellors of old were not like this.
They proposed people based on public opinion,
and selected them with impartiality.
If the public deemed someone worthy,
even if the Chancellor did not know their details,
they would provisionally employ them.
If they proved ineffective,
then they would be removed;
if effective, they would be promoted.
If the person proposed was suitable, they would be rewarded;
if not suitable, they would be punished.
Promotions, demotions, rewards, and punishments
were all agreed upon by the public,
with not a shred of personal bias from the Chancellor in between.
If this principle were consistently applied,
what need would there be to worry about overlooking the worthy or leaving official posts vacant!
8 An imperial edict ordered the cessation of all non-essential tributes from the four directions.
It also dismissed the Lìyuán envoys and over three hundred musicians.
Those who remained were all assigned to the Tàicháng Temple.

9 Guō Zǐyí, holding the titles of Sītú and Zhōngshū Lìng, concurrently served as Hézhōng Yǐn, Língzhōu Dà Dūdū, Chányú-Zhènběi Dà Dūhù, Guānnèi-Hédōng Fù Yuánshuài, Shuòfāng Jiédù, Guānnèi Zhīdù-Yánchí-Liùchéng Shuǐyùn Dàshǐ, and Yā Fānbù Bìng Yíngtián jí Héyáng Dào Guānchá děng Shǐ.
Hézhōng, Líng, and Xià all had salt ponds.
Shuòfāng had six cities beyond the frontier.
單,
pronounced Chán.
帥,
pronounced shuài.
使,
pronounced shǐ.
His accomplishments and fame were again great,
and his nature was magnanimous.
However, his administration was somewhat lax,
and Dàizōng wished to divide his authority but found it difficult to do so.
The decision remained unresolved for a long time.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
an imperial edict honored Zǐyí as Shàngfù,
just as Tàigōng Wàng was the master and Shàngfù of Zhōu.
Commentators say that "shàng" means "to be revered" and "fù" means "father,"
implying he was a master to the Son of Heaven.
His actual enfeoffment was increased to two thousand households,
with a monthly allowance for fifteen hundred men and feed for two hundred horses.
Over ten of his sons and sons-in-law were promoted in office.
All his concurrent titles of Fù Yuánshuài and other envoys were abolished.
His subordinate general, Lǐ Huáiguāng, the Hédōng and Shuòfāng Dū Yúhòu, was appointed Hézhōng Yǐn and the Jiédùshǐ of Bīn, Níng, Qìng, Jìn, Jiàng, Cí, and Xī.
Cháng Qiānguāng, the Shuòfāng Liúhòu concurrently Língzhōu Chángshǐ, was appointed Língzhōu Dà Dūdū and the Jiédùshǐ of Xīshòuxiángchéng, Dìngyuǎn, Tiāndé, Yán, Xià, and Fēng military prefectures.
Hún Jiān, the Zhènbǔ Jūnshǐ, was appointed Chányú Dà Dūhù and the Jiédùshǐ of Dōng, Zhōng'èr Shòuxiángchéng, Zhènbǔ, Zhènběi, Suíyín, and Línshèng military prefectures.
They were to divide his responsibilities.
10On the day Bǐngxū,
an imperial edict stated:
“Lǐ Yàn, the Cìshǐ of Zézhōu,
presented a drawing of auspicious clouds.
To Us, peace and abundant harvests are propitious omens,
and promoting the worthy and manifesting loyalty are excellent signs.
As for auspicious clouds, spirit ganoderma, rare birds, strange beasts, peculiar grasses, and unusual trees,
how do they benefit the people!
Qīngyún [azure clouds]
are the same as Qìngyún [auspicious clouds].
From now on, if such things occur,
they are not to be presented.”
The Nèi Zhuāngzhái Shǐ reported that the various prefectures had over fourteen thousand hu of official grain tax.
The Emperor ordered it to be distributed to the respective locations for military provisions.
Previously,
various countries had repeatedly presented trained elephants,
totaling forty-two.
The Emperor said:
“Elephants consume much to be fed yet violate their natural disposition.
What use are they!”
He ordered them to be released on the southern side of Jīngshān.
This is what Yǔgòng referred to as
“the Dǎo River reached Qí and extended to Jīngshān.”
In the Táng dynasty,
this area belonged to Fùpíng County of Jīngzhào Prefecture.
All were released;
also, several hundred palace women were released.
At this, both the court and the common people rejoiced.
The soldiers of Zīqīng,
even cast down their weapons and looked at each other, saying:
“A wise ruler has emerged,
should we still rebel!”
11On the day Wùzǐ,
Lǐ Xīliè, the Huáixī Liúhòu, was appointed Jiédùshǐ.
12On the day Xīnmǎo,
Mǎ Suì, the Héyáng Zhèn'è Shǐ, was appointed Hédōng Jiédùshǐ.
Hédōng had suffered the defeat at Bǎijǐng,
referring to the defeat of Bào Fáng last year.
According to the biography of Zhāng Qíxián in the Dōngdū Shìlüè: Bóyǐng [柏井],
is forty lǐ north of the city of Bìngzhōu.
During the Sòng dynasty, Bìngzhōu city was moved to Yángqǔ County.
Suì summoned all the horse herders and servants,
obtaining several thousand men.
After training them for several months,
they all became elite cavalry.
When making armor, he always made three grades—long, medium, and short—
to match what they wore,
for ease of movement.
He also built war chariots;
they carried weapons and armor when moving,
and formed battle formations when stationary,
or blocked strategic points to repel swift charges.
All his equipment was sophisticated and sharp.
Within a year,
he had thirty thousand select soldiers.
He appointed Zhāng Jiànfēng from Yǎnzhōu as his Pànguān,
and appointed Lǐ Zìliáng as Cìshǐ of Dàizhōu,
entrusting them with responsibilities.
13Lí Gàn, the Bīngbù Shìláng,
was cunning, treacherous, and sycophantic,
and was close to the eunuch Tèjìn Liú Zhōngyì.
Zhōngyì's original name was Qīngtán,
and he was arrogant and avaricious, relying on imperial favor.
Both were detested by the masses.
At the time, some said Gàn and Zhōngyì had once advised Dàizōng to establish Dúgū Guì as Empress
and his son Hán Wáng Jióng as Crown Prince.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Gàn secretly went by carriage to Zhōngyì to plot matters.
When the matter was discovered,
on the day Bǐngshēn,
Gàn and Zhōngyì were both stripped of their titles and exiled.
Upon reaching Lántián,
they were granted death.
14Hán Huàng, the Hùbù Shìláng and Pàn Dùzhī, was appointed Tàicháng Qīng.
Liú Yàn, the Lìbù Shàngshū, was appointed Pàn Dùzhī.
Previously, Yàn and Huàng had divided the management of the empire's finances and revenues:
Yàn was in charge of Jiāngnán,
Shānnán, Jiānghuái, and Língnán;
Huàng was in charge of Guānnèi, Hédōng, and Jiànnán.
At this point,
Yàn began to concurrently hold all these responsibilities.
The Emperor had long heard that Huàng was excessively grasping,
so he stripped him of his lucrative authority.
Soon after, he was sent out as Cìshǐ of Jìnzhōu.
Jìnzhōu,
governed Línfén County,
was ancient Píngyáng,
seven hundred twenty-five lǐ northeast of the capital.
In the early Zhìdé era,
Dìwǔ Qí first monopolized salt to support military expenses.
This matter is recorded in volume 219, Zhìdé Yuánzài.
Qí,
pronounced Qí.
Què,
pronounced què.
The system became increasingly precise.
Initially, the annual income was six hundred thousand mín.
In later years, the income exceeded ten times that amount,
yet the people did not feel oppressed.
By the end of the Dàlì era,
the total annual income
was calculated to be twelve million mín,
with salt profits accounting for the greater half.
Salt was used for canal transport wages;
from the Jiāng and Huái rivers to Wèiqiáo,
which is the Eastern Wèiqiáo.
The wages were seven thousand mín.
North of the Huái River,
patrol stations were established,
and capable officials were chosen to manage them.
This facilitated matters without burdening the prefectures and counties.
15In the sixth month,
on the first day, Jǐhài,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
16Cuī Níng, the Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ, and Lǐ Miǎn, the Yǒngpíng Jiédùshǐ, were both appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
17An imperial edict stated:
“For all injustices and grievances in the empire
that prefectures and counties fail to address,
people are allowed to go to the Sānsī Shǐ.
The so-called Sānsī Shǐ
refers to the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng, Zhōngshūshěng Shèrén, and Ménxiàshěng Jǐshìzhōng.
These three officials,
each representing one bureau, would come to the imperial court to receive petitions.
Hence they were called Sānsī.
This is not the Sānsī Shǐ of financial management during the Five Dynasties period.
They would receive petitions at the court daily.
For those cases whose resolutions were not yet satisfactory,
people were allowed to beat the Dēngwén Gǔ [petition drum].
During the Táng dynasty, the Dēngwén Gǔ
was in front of the Western Imperial Hall.
撾,
pronounced zhuā.
And to request the ordination of monks and nuns.”
Thereupon, many people beat the Dēngwén Gǔ.
Péi Xǔ, the Yòu Jīnwú Jiāngjūn, submitted a memorial,
stating:
“The disputes brought by litigants are all trivial matters.
If the Son of Heaven personally handles each one,
then what use are officials!”
The Emperor then returned all cases to the relevant authorities.
18An imperial decree stated:
“The regulations for imperial tombs and mausoleums
must follow generous and substantial standards,
and the imperial treasury must be exhausted to cover their costs.”
Lìnghú Huán, the Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng, submitted a memorial of remonstrance.
Its gist was:
“Your servant humbly reads the last will and testament,
which emphasized frugality and simplicity.
If the standards are generous and substantial,
how can this be the intention of the dying command!”
The Emperor replied with an edict,
whose gist was:
“Not only does this hit upon My shortcomings,
but it also helps to perfect My virtue.
How could I not change upon hearing what is right!”
Huán
was the great-great-grandson of Lìnghú Défēn.
Lìnghú Défēn
served Tàizōng.
棻,
pronounced fēn.
In the 19th *gēngzǐ* year,
Imperial Prince Sòng was made King Xuān,
Mó was made King Shū,
Chén was made King Tōng,
Liàng was made King Qián,
Xiáng was made King Sù.
In the *yǐsì* year,
Imperial Younger Brother Nǎi was made King Yì,
Kuǐ was made King Shǔ.
In the 20th *bǐngwǔ* year,
following the precedent from the *Xiāntiān* era,
two officials of the sixth rank and above, who held esteemed and reputable positions,
even if they were not officials of the Imperial Household Department or the Imperial Guard,
were ordered to take turns on duty each day to serve as *dàizhì* [attendants]
to be available for consultation.
The *Xīnzhì* states: At first,
when Dàizōng ascended the throne,
he ordered capital officials of the fifth rank and above to take turns spending the night in the Secretarial Department and the Chancellery,
to be available for inquiries.
During the *Yǒnghuī* era,
one scholar from the Hóngwénguǎn Academy was ordered to be on daily duty at the west gate of Wǔdé Hall.
In the first year of *Wénmíng*,
an edict ordered one esteemed capital official of the fifth rank and above to be on daily duty at Zhāngshàn and Míngfú Gates.
At the end of the *Xiāntiān* era,
it was further ordered that all *cháojíshǐ* [officials for imperial audience] of the sixth rank and above should attend as *dàizhì* with the imperial procession.
During the *Yǒngtài* era,
when meritorious ministers were relieved of their regional commands [jiézhì]
and had no official duties,
they all served as *dàizhì* at Jíxián Gate,
thirteen individuals in total.
When Cuī Yòufǔ became chancellor,
he proposed that civil officials of the first rank and below should take turns on duty as *dàizhì*.
Subsequently, it was enacted into law
that there should be two *zhèngyá dàizhì* officials each day.
Sòng Bái said: At that time, Yòufǔ memorialized and obtained approval for the original imperial edict that civil officials of the first rank and below should take turns on duty as *dàizhì*.
These *dàizhì* officials,
after the officials presenting memorials had finished,
would then proceed out,
and be granted a place to wait for further instructions in the inner corridor,
and were not dismissed until the *yǒu* hour.
*Lì*,
pronounced like *dīng*.
*Gēng*,
pronounced like *héng*;
the same below.
On the 21st *gēngxū* day,
Zhū Cǐ was appointed Prefect of Fèngxiáng.
The 22nd, Dàizōng showed excessive favor to eunuchs;
those sent on imperial missions to the four quarters
were not restricted in their demands.
He once sent an inner envoy to bestow gifts upon a clan;
upon his return,
when asked about the meager gains,
Dàizōng was displeased,
thinking he had belittled his imperial command;
frightened,
the envoy hastily compensated them with his private possessions.
From then on, inner envoys openly sought bribes and gifts,
without any scruples.
The chancellor once stored money in his inner chamber;
each time a gift was bestowed [from the emperor],
and an imperial decree announced,
none returned empty-handed.
When they traveled through various prefectures and counties on imperial missions,
they would issue documents to extract goods,
treating it as equivalent to taxes,
and all returned heavily laden.
The Emperor was well aware of this abuse.
He sent the inner envoy Shào Guāngchāo to bestow banners and insignia upon Lǐ Xīliè;
Xīliè presented him with servants, horses, seven hundred bolts of silk,
and two hundred *jīn* of yellow tea.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he was enraged,
flogged Guāngchāo sixty times, and exiled him.
Consequently, those inner envoys who had not yet returned,
all secretly discarded their gains in the mountains and valleys;
even if offered,
none dared to accept.
On the 23rd *jiǎzǐ* day,
Wáng Jiàhè, the General in Chief of the Divine Strategy Army and Great General of the Right Leader of the Army, was appointed Director of the Eastern Capital Gardens.
The office of Director of the Eastern Capital Gardens
was the position of Superintendent of Parks in the early Táng dynasty.
He changed his name to Zhìzhēn.
Jiàhè had commanded the imperial guards for over ten years,
his power extending both internally and externally,
and the Emperor feared he might instigate a rebellion.
Cuī Yòufǔ summoned Jiàhè and spoke with him,
detaining him for a long time,
and Xiùguī had already taken up his duties.
The 24th, Lǐ Zhèngjǐ, fearing the Emperor's authority and reputation,
memorialized offering three hundred thousand *mín* in cash.
The Emperor wished to accept it but feared being deceived,
yet had no grounds to refuse it.
Cuī Yòufǔ requested that an envoy be sent to convey imperial greetings to the officers and soldiers of Zīqīng,
and then to bestow upon them the money offered by Zhèngjǐ,
so that every officer and soldier would be grateful for the Emperor's benevolence;
furthermore, all other circuits, hearing of this,
would know that the imperial court did not value wealth.
The Emperor was pleased
and agreed.
Zhèngjǐ was greatly ashamed and submitted.
The empire believed that an era of great peace
could truly be anticipated.
The 25th, Autumn,
seventh month,

the posthumous titles and temple names of the ancestors were all made nine characters.

*Shì*,

9 On the *Jǐyǒu* day,
Ruìwén Xiàowǔ Huángdì was buried at Yuánlíng.
Yuánlíng
is located twenty-five *lǐ* northwest of Fùpíng County, Jīngzhào, on Tánshān.
As the funeral procession was about to depart,
the Emperor went to see it off.
He noticed that the imperial carriage was not on the main imperial road,
but rather pointed slightly between the *dīngwèi* direction.
He asked why.
The officials in charge replied:
"Your Majesty's natal sign is *wǔ*,
and we dared not clash with it."
The Emperor wept, saying:
"How can one deviate the spiritual carriage for personal benefit!"
He ordered the shaft to be repositioned to point directly at *wǔ* and proceed.
Sùzōng and Dàizōng both delighted in Yin-Yang and spirits,
and regardless of the matter's size,
they would consult diviners and shamans.
Thus, Wáng Yǔ and Lí Gàn both gained advancement through heterodox practices.
The Emperor was inherently disbelieving of such things;
for the imperial tomb, he simply chose the seventh month,
as the ritual prescribed: "The Son of Heaven is buried in the seventh month."
He did not select another day.
10 In the eleventh month,
on the *Dīngchǒu* day,
Hán Huàng, the Governor of Jìnzhōu, was appointed Governor of Sūzhōu and Inspector of Zhèjiāng East and West.
11 Qiáo Lín was old and hard of hearing.
When the Emperor occasionally questioned him,
his replies were disorderly,
and his advice was often superficial.
On the *Rénwǔ* day,
Lín was appointed Minister of Works,
thereby dismissed from political affairs.
From then on, the Emperor estranged Zhāng Shè.
Qiáo Lín
had been recommended by Shè.
*Shàng*,
read *chén yáng* fan.
12 After Yáng Yán detained Cuī Níng,
the two became enemies.
Yán, using the pretext that the northern frontier required a high-ranking minister to pacify it,
on the *Guǐsì* day,
appointed Cuī Níng, the Inspector of Jīngjī, as Grand Protector of Shányú and Zhènběi, and Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng,
to guard Fāngzhōu.
He appointed Zhāng Yánshǎng, the Military Commissioner of Jīngnán, as Military Commissioner of Xīchuān.
He also appointed Lǐquán Dù Xīquán, the Commander of the Troops of Língyán Military Commission, to oversee the retention of Líng and Yán Prefectures;
and Zhāng Guāngshèng, the Governor of Dàizhōu, to oversee the retention of Shányú, Zhènwǔ and other cities, and Suí, Yín, Lín, and Shèng Prefectures.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The old records state that
Wáng Xióng was for Zhènwǔ.
Now we follow the Veritable Records.
Since Níng had already been sent to govern the frontier,

Yán wished to usurp Níng's authority,
and also to monitor his actions,
so he allowed all three men to report directly to the throne,
and hinted that they should watch for Níng's transgressions.
13 In the twelfth month,
on the *Yǐmǎo* day,
Sòng, the Prince of Xuān, was established as Crown Prince.
14 According to the old system,
all the gold and silk of the empire were stored in the Zuǒzàng.
The Tàifǔ submitted its numbers quarterly,
and the Bǐbù audited its expenditures and receipts.
The Táng system: Tàifǔ managed granaries and the receipts and expenditures of wealth.
Bǐbù managed accounts.
A Shuǐ commentary says: Táng system: All imperial revenues were deposited in the Zuǒzàng.
Tàifǔ reported the numbers quarterly,
and the Shàngshū Bǐbù audited its expenditures and receipts.
*Zhù*,
read *dīng lǚ* fan.
*Zàng*,
read *cú làng* fan.
*Shàng*,
read *shí zhǎng* fan.
*Bǐ*,
sound *pí*.
At that time, there were many powerful generals in the capital,
who made excessive demands.
Qí could not control them,
so he memorialized to have everything stored in the Dàyíng Nèikù.
The Bǎibǎo Dàyíng Kù [Hundred Treasures Great Abundance Treasury]
began in Xuánzōng's reign;
detailed information can be found in the note for the tenth month of Jiànzhōng fourth year of Dézōng, volume 228.
The Son of Heaven also found it convenient for his own use,
so it remained inaccessible for a long time.
From then on, the empire's public revenue became the ruler's private treasury,
and officials could no longer ascertain its quantity
or audit its increases and decreases,
for nearly twenty years.
Over three hundred eunuchs were in charge of this matter,
all of whom enriched themselves from it,
forming deeply entrenched and
unshakable factions.
Yáng Yán prostrated before the Emperor and said:
"Financial resources are
the great foundation of the state,
the lifeblood of the common people.
Their significance, stability, and danger
all stem from them.
That is why in previous eras, important ministers were entrusted with this matter,
yet sometimes there were still wasteful irregularities.
Now, only palace eunuchs manage the inflows and outflows,
and no high-ranking minister is allowed to know.
The corruption and decay of governance
are no greater than this.
I request that these funds be returned to the relevant officials.
We can calculate the annual needs of the palace,
and a measured amount will be provided,
without any deficiency.
Only in this way
can governance truly be established."
The Emperor immediately issued an edict:
"All financial revenues shall revert to the Zuǒzàng,
following the old system entirely.
Annually, from the total, three to five thousand pieces of the finest quality
shall be transferred to the Dàyíng."
Yán, with a single statement, altered the ruler's intentions,
and commentators praised him for it.
15 On the last day of *Bǐngyín*,
there was a solar eclipse.
16 Wáng Guóliáng, a bandit leader in Húnán, entrenched himself in the mountains as a robber.
The Emperor sent Guān Bō, a supernumerary official of the Department of Justice, to pacify him through persuasion.
The Táng Dūguān Láng
was responsible for registering captives, distributing clothes, food, and medicine, and handling their grievances.
The Emperor asked Bō about the essentials of governance.
He replied:
"The foundation of governance
must be to seek virtuous and sagely people to administer it."
The Emperor said:
"I have recently issued edicts seeking worthy individuals
and sent envoys to search widely.
Surely this can establish good governance!"
Bō replied:
"Those sought by edicts and recommended by envoys are merely scholars adept at prose who seek advancement.
How can truly virtuous and sagely people be willing to be selected merely by official documents?"
The Emperor was pleased.
17 Cuī Yòufǔ fell ill.
The Emperor ordered him to be carried in a sedan chair into the Central Secretariat,
or if he was on leave at his residence,
important matters were decided by consulting him through palace eunuchs.
Dézōng Shénwǔ Xiàowén Huángdì I
His personal name was Shì,
the eldest son of Dàizōng.
The posthumous title rules state: "One who does not act with intimidation when remonstrated with is called Dé,"
meaning he did not use his authority to reject remonstrances;
"One who upholds righteousness and extols goodness is called Dé,"
meaning he praised the good deeds of others.
Jiànzhōng First Year
(*Gēngshēn*, 780 CE)
1 Spring,
first month,
on the *Dīngmǎo* first day,
the reign era was changed.
His ministers respectfully offered him the honorific title Shèngshén Wǔwǔ Huángdì;
a general amnesty was granted.
The Emperor first adopted Yáng Yán's proposal,
"ordering inspectors and governors to assess the property of the common people,
determine their ranks,
and revise it into the Two-Tax System.
Yáng Yán created the Two-Tax System,
where the summer payment was not to exceed the sixth month,
and the autumn payment not to exceed the eleventh month,
determined by the amount of cultivated land in Dàlì fourteenth year.
All other levies were abolished;
anyone collecting even one *qián* beyond the two taxes
would be prosecuted for violating the law."
In the early
Táng dynasty, the method of taxation was called *zū-yōng-diào* (rent, labor, and silk tax).
Those who owned land paid *zū*.
Those with an adult male (body) paid *yōng*.
Those with a household paid *diào*.
Towards the end of Xuánzōng's reign,
the household registers were increasingly damaged
and largely inaccurate.
When the armies rose during the Zhìdé era,
taxes were levied everywhere,
with urgency to collect what was needed,
and no constant standard remained.
The offices responsible for taxation increased in number but were not unified,
each adding new levies arbitrarily,
establishing their own categories.
Old and new taxes accumulated endlessly,
without limit.
Wealthy households had many adult males,
and most of them became officials or monks to avoid taxes and labor service.
Poor households, however, had many adult males,
with no place to hide,
so the upper households were favored while the lower households toiled.
Corrupt officials gradually exploited them,
with daily
and monthly payments,
leading to unbearable hardship.
Most of them fled and became floating households,
with only four or five out of a hundred remaining as permanent residents.
At this point,

Yáng Yán proposed the implementation of the Two-Tax System: first, calculate the annual expenses for each prefecture and county, as well as the amount to be sent to the capital, and then levy these on the people,
determining income based on expenditure.
Households were no longer classified as "host" or "guest,"
but recorded according to their current residence;
people were no longer classified as "adult male" (*dīng*) or "junior male" (*zhōng*),
but differentiated by wealth;
prefectures and counties still distinguished between "host households" (*zhǔhù*) and "guest households" (*kèhù*).
In the third year of Tiānbǎo,
a law had been enacted that males aged eighteen and above were *zhōngnán* (junior males),
and those twenty-three and above were *chéngdīng* (adult males).
量,
read *liáng*.
見,
read *xián biàn*.
The prefectures and counties in question collected one-thirtieth of the tax,
ensuring that permanent residents received no illicit gain.
This means there was no illicit gain from either residence or movement.
僥,
read *jiān yáo*.
Taxes were collected twice, in autumn and summer.
The *zū*, *yōng*, *diào*, and various other labor services were all abolished,
and everything was overseen by the Duòzhī (Ministry of Finance).
The emperor adopted his suggestion,
and, taking advantage of a general amnesty,
ordered its implementation.
2 Initially,
the Left Minister Lǐu Yàn was Minister of Personnel,
and Yáng Yán was a Vice Minister;
they disliked each other.
When Yuán Zài died,
Lǐu Yàn played a significant role.
This event is detailed in the previous volume under Dàizōng, Dàlì 13th year.
載,
read *zǔ hài*,
also as written.
Lǐu Yàn had long held financial power,
and many resented him,
often submitting memorials suggesting the abolition of the Commissioner of Transportation;
there were also rumors that Lǐu Yàn had secretly memorialized Dàizōng, advising him to establish Dúgū as empress.
風言,
means words derived from hearsay.
Yáng Yán, wishing to avenge Yuán Zài,
wept before the emperor and said:
"Lǐu Yàn conspired with Lì Gàn and Lǐu Zhōngyì.
Lì Gàn and Lǐu Zhōngyì died in Dàlì 14th year,
as recorded in the previous volume.
為,
read *yú wěi*.
相,
read *xī liàng*.
Their crime deserves ten thousand deaths."
Cuī Yòufǔ said:
"This matter is vague,
and Your Majesty has already granted a general amnesty;
it is inappropriate to further investigate baseless rumors."
Yáng Yán then proposed:
"The Shàngshūshěng (Department of State Affairs) is the root of national governance.
Recently, various commissioners have been appointed,
usurping its authority.
Now it should be restored to its former state."
The emperor agreed.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
an edict was issued that all national funds and grains should be returned to the Jīnbù (Ministry of Finance) and Cāngbù (Ministry of Granaries).
Táng records: The Jīnbù was in charge of the empire's treasury receipts and disbursements,
as well as affairs concerning capital markets, border markets, peace markets, palace markets, and trade.
The Cāngbù was in charge of the empire's granary reserves,
receipts and disbursements, taxes, stipends, and granary matters.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Jiànzhōng Shílù* states:
"Initially,
during the Dàlì era,
when the emperor resided in the Eastern Palace,
Empress Zhēnyì was then the favored consort,
highly beloved,
and gave birth to Prince Huí of Hán.

Therefore, the eunuch Lǐu Qīngtán, the Administrator of Jīngzhào, Lì Gàn, and other favored attendants wished to establish Zhēnyì as empress,
and moreover claimed that a yellow snake was found in Prince Hán's residence,
taking it as an auspicious omen,

Lǐu Yàn joined their plot,
hoping to achieve extraordinary merit

Wáng Jìn also said to people: 'Lǐu Yàn

The emperor resented this.
At this point,
considering Lǐu Yàn a high official who sided with evil and engaged in treachery,

Using the pretext of his memorials being untrue,

This was recommended by Shěn Jìjì and Yáng Yán,
probably speaking on behalf of Yáng Yán.
We now follow the old biography.

Hóng Jīnglún, the *chùzhìshǐ* for Hébĕi,

heard that Tián Yuè's army numbered seventy thousand men.

"According to the five cities of Shuòfāng,

Lǐ Zhōngchén, as Jiǎnxiào Sīkōng, Tóng Píngzhāngshì, and Fèng Cháoqǐng,

(said): "Your Majesty is noble as the Son of Heaven,

the fourth month,

Military generals and corrupt officials
used this as an excuse to oppress and exploit the common people.

on the first day of the year (Zhèng), Winter Solstice (Zhì), Duānwǔ, and the Imperial Birthday (Jiàngdàn),
all prefectures offered contributions,
known as the "Four Festivals' Offerings."

the Emperor's birthday,

on the day Wùchén,
Wéi Lún was appointed Tài Cháng Qīng;
