The Emperor did not listen to any of them,
saying:
"If this minor scion is not eliminated,
how can I command the realm?"
Wénxǐ sent his general Liú Hǎibīn to submit a memorial.
Hǎibīn addressed the Emperor, saying:
"Your servant was a subordinate of Your Majesty's princely residence.
When the Emperor first appointed the Prince of Yōng as Grand Marshal of all forces in the realm
to suppress Shǐ Cháoyì,
all those in the campaigning army
were his subordinates.
I will certainly present his head to Your Majesty.
However, what Wénxǐ now seeks is merely a jíe (insignia of authority).
I wish Your Majesty would temporarily grant it to him.
Wénxǐ will then surely become complacent,
and my plan can then be put into effect."
The Emperor said:
"Distinctions and instruments of authority cannot be lent to others,
as Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) said.
My jíe cannot be obtained."
He sent Hǎibīn back to inform Wénxǐ,
and continued the attack as before.
The imperial meals were reduced to supply the soldiers.
The officers and soldiers in the city who were due to receive their spring clothes
were given their allotments as usual.
At this, the multitude knew that the Emperor's resolve could not be swayed.
At that time, Tǔbō was on friendly terms with Táng,
and did not dispatch troops.
The city's position became desperate.
On the day Gēngyín,
Hǎibīn and the other generals jointly killed Wénxǐ
and sent his head.
The Kǎoyì states: The Bīn Zhì says:
"An edict ordered Lǐ Huáiguāng and Zhū Cǐ to join forces to execute him.
The army besieged Jīngchéng,
but could not capture it for several months.
Wénxǐ sent his son to seek aid from Tǔbō.
When the Tǔbō forces were about to arrive,
the two generals (Lǐ Huáiguāng and Zhū Cǐ) discussed retreating to avoid them.
The Dū Yóuyì Shǐ (Chief Patrol Commissioner) Hán Yóuhuái argued, saying: 'If the Western Rong come,
the Jīngzhōu populace will surely turn.
It is not righteous to perish for Wénxǐ among the barbarians.'
In the seventh month of autumn,
Western Fān cavalry ascended a height
and signaled to the Jīngzhōu people.
The Jīngzhōu people indeed said: 'Originally, we sought the jiedù (military governorship) for Wénxǐ.
The imperial army launched its punitive expedition,
and if we are in distress, we will surrender to it.
How can we smear our faces with red earth to become people of a foreign land!'
Liú Hǎibīn then killed Wénxǐ
and surrendered with his followers to Cǐ.
Cǐ did not execute anyone,
and the Jīngzhōu people were grateful to him.
The seeds of Cǐ's rebellion also began from this."
However, at this time, Tǔbō was on good terms with Táng,
and there was no event of them coming to aid Wénxǐ.
Moreover, the Shílù states that Jīngzhōu was pacified this month,
while the Bīn Zhì states that the Western Fān arrived in the seventh month.
These contradict each other.
We now follow the Jiànzhōng Shílù.
Since the Emperor's ascension,
Lǐ Zhèngjǐ had been inwardly uneasy,
and sent his staff to report to the court.
At that time, the news of the victory in Jīngzhōu arrived.
The Emperor had them observe Wénxǐ's head before returning.
Zhèngjǐ became even more fearful.
15 In the sixth month,
on the day Jiǎwǔ, the first day of the month,
Ménxià Shìláng (Vice-Director of the Chancellery) and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì (Chancellor) Cuī Yòufǔ died.
16 The occultist Sāng Dàomào submitted a memorial, stating:
"Your Majesty, within a few years, will temporarily face the hardship of leaving the palace.
Your servant observes an aura of the Son of Heaven over Fèngtiān.
It is advisable to heighten and enlarge its city walls to prepare for extraordinary circumstances."
On the day Xīnchǒu,
the Jīngzhào (capital prefecture) was ordered to dispatch several thousand laborers,
mixed with soldiers from the six armies,
to construct the city of Fèngtiān.
The Kǎoyì states: The old tradition says:
"Dàomào was a Dàizhào Hánlín (academician-in-waiting).
In the early Jiànzhōng period,
the Shéncè (Divine Strategy Army) was repairing Fèngtiān city.
Dàomào requested to heighten its walls
and greatly enlarge its scale.
Dézōng (the Emperor) did not heed him.
When Zhū Cǐ's rebellion broke out,
the Emperor hastily fled
to Fèngtiān,
and then remembered Dàomào's words.
At that time, Dàomào had already died,
and an order was given to sacrifice to him."
We now follow the Shílù and Cuī Tíngguāng's Xìng Fèngtiān Lù.
17 In the beginning,
the Húi-hé's customs were simple and honest.
The distinctions between rulers and subjects were not very great.
Therefore, their collective will was unified,
making them strong and invincible.
After they rendered meritorious service to Táng,
referring to the suppression of Ān Shǐ's rebellion,
Dēng-lǐ Kě-hán began to aggrandize himself.
He built palaces to house women,
who were adorned with cosmetics and elaborate embroidery.
This depleted the resources of the Central Kingdom.
Kě,
from kān, entering tone.
Hán,
pronounced hán.
Wéi,
pronounced yú-wěi fān.
When Dài-zōng passed away,
the Emperor dispatched the palace envoy Liáng Wén-xiù to convey his condolences.
Dēng-lǐ was arrogant and did not observe the proper rites.
The Jiǔ-xìng Hú, who were attached to the Húi-hé,
persuaded Dēng-lǐ, saying that the Central Kingdom was rich and prosperous,
and if they attacked it now while it was in mourning,
there would be great profit.
Dēng-lǐ agreed,
intending to invade with his entire nation.
His chancellor, Dùn-mò-hè Dá-gān,
who was Dēng-lǐ's paternal cousin,
remonstrated, saying:
"Táng
is a great nation and
has not wronged us.
The year before last, when we invaded Tài-yuán,
we acquired tens of thousands of sheep and horses.
That could be called a great victory.
The incident is recorded in the previous volume under Dài-zōng, Dà-lì, 13th year.
By the time we returned,
many soldiers had to walk.
Now, if we delve deep with the entire nation,
and should we by chance not win,
where shall we return to?"
Dēng-lǐ did not listen.
Dùn-mò-hè took advantage of the people's reluctance to invade the south,
raised troops, and killed Dēng-lǐ,
along with two thousand Jiǔ-xìng Hú.
He then established himself as Hé-gǔ-duō-lù Pí-gā Kě-hán,
and dispatched his minister Yù-dá-gān to enter the court together with Liáng Wén-xiù,
expressing his desire to be a vassal,
letting his hair grow long without cutting it
in anticipation of an imperial edict.
On the Yǐ-mǎo day,
the Emperor ordered Yuán Xiū, the Shào-yǐn of Jīng-zhào and Lín-zhāng, to enfeoff Dùn-mò-hè as Wǔ-yì Chéng-gōng Kě-hán.
Shào,
pronounced shǐ-zhào fān.
Lín-zhāng county
belonged to Xiàng-zhōu.
Originally part of Yè county,
Emperor Xiào-jìng of Eastern Wèi divided Yè county
and established Lín-zhāng county within Yè city.
The Kǎo-yì states: "According to old traditions:
'Yuán Xiū's wife
was the daughter of Wáng Yì, the Lì-bù Shì-láng.
Due to a minor disagreement, they separated.
Her family appealed,
and the case was sent to the Yù-shǐ Tái for investigation and resolution.
Yuán Xiū delayed and did not respond to the summons,
so he was dismissed and
exiled to Zhēn-zhōu.
After a long time,
he was transferred to Yuè-zhōu.
In the early Jiàn-zhōng period,
Yáng Yán was in power.
Noticing the growing prestige of Yán Yǐng, the Jīng-zhào Yǐn,
he wished to undermine him.
Yán Yǐng
was Wáng Yì's nephew-in-law.
When Yuán Xiū and the Wáng family separated,
Yáng Yán heard rumors of a rift between Yuán Xiū and Yán Yǐng,
so he promoted Yuán Xiū from exile to Jīng-zhào Shào-yǐn,
to have him spy on Yán Yǐng's misdeeds.
After Yuán Xiū had been in office for a long time,
he became close with Yán Yǐng.
Yáng Yán was enraged and
submitted a memorial requesting that Yuán Xiū be appointed concurrently as Yù-shǐ Zhōng-chéng with his current office,
and sent as an envoy to Húi-hé.' "
This account is inconsistent: When Yuán Xiū was an envoy,
the Húi-hé were still respectful and submissive.
Zhāng Guāng-shèng had not yet killed Dǒng Tú.
How could Yáng Yán have known that the Húi-hé wanted to kill Yuán Xiū and sent him?
Therefore, this account is not adopted.
18 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the Bǐng-yín day,
Wáng Guó-liáng, the bandit leader of Shào-zhōu, surrendered.
Guó-liáng was originally a Yá-jiàng in Hú-nán.
Xīn Jīng-gǎo, the Guān-chá-shǐ, sent him to garrison Wǔ-gāng
to defend against the Xī-yuán Mán.
Xīn Jīng-gǎo was greedy and tyrannical.
Wáng Guó-liáng's family was wealthy,
so Jīng-gǎo accused him of a capital crime.
Guó-liáng, fearing for his life,
took control of the county and rebelled.
He allied with the Xī-yuán Mán,
gathered a thousand men,
and plundered prefectures and counties.
A thousand *lǐ* along the lake
were all ravaged by them.
An imperial edict ordered the combined forces of Jīng, Qián, Hóng, and Guì circuits to attack him.
The Jīng-nán Jié-dù-shǐ
governed Jīng-zhōu.
The Qián-zhōng Guān-chá-shǐ
governed Qián-zhōu.
The Jiāng-nán Xī-dào Guān-chá-shǐ
governed Hóng-zhōu.
The Guì-guǎn Jīng-lüè Guān-chá-shǐ
governed Guì-zhōu.
Qián,
pronounced qín.
When Cáo Wáng Gāo became the Hú-nán Guān-chá-shǐ,
he said:
"Driving tired commoners
to execute rebels
is not a wise strategy."
So he sent a letter to Wáng Guó-liáng,
saying:
"General, you did not dare to rebel,
but wished to save your life.
I and you, General, were both framed by Xīn Jīng-gǎo.
The story of Cáo Wáng Gāo is in the previous Dà-lì 14th year.
How could I bear to use weapons against you, General?
If you, General, meet me
and do not surrender quickly,
you will regret it when it is too late."
Wáng Guó-liáng was both happy and afraid,
and sent an envoy to beg for surrender,
yet he was still hesitant.
Cáo Wáng Gāo then impersonated an envoy,
taking one rider,
traveled five hundred *lǐ*,
reached Wáng Guó-liáng's stronghold,
whipped his gate,
and shouted loudly:
"I am Cáo Wáng!
I have come to accept your surrender!"
The entire army was greatly surprised.
Wáng Guó-liáng rushed out,
welcomed him with a bow, and begged for punishment.
Cáo Wáng Gāo took his hand,
pledged brotherhood with him,
completely burned all offensive and defensive equipment,
dispersed his troops,
and sent them back to agriculture.
An imperial edict pardoned Wáng Guó-liáng's crimes
and bestowed upon him the name Wéi-xīn.
According to the New Book, Southern Man Biographies: The Xī-yuán Mán lived south of Guǎng and Róng,
and west of Yōng and Guì.
Their territory spanned thousands of *lǐ*,
and their tribes were numerous.
Since Qián-yuán,
they repeatedly rebelled.
They allied with the Yí-liáo, Liáng Chóng-qiān, Tán Wèn, and the Xī-yuán chief Wú Gōng-cáo, combined their forces, and attacked inland.
They captured Dào-zhōu,
advanced to attack Yǒng-zhōu,
and captured Shào-zhōu.
Xīn Jīng-gǎo sent Wáng Guó-liáng to garrison Wǔ-gāng,
and Guó-liáng also rebelled.
In the early Jiàn-zhōng period,
Xǔ-zhōu was fortified to cut off Xī-yuán,
and Wáng Guó-liáng then surrendered.
Jiàng,
pronounced hù-jiāng fān.
19 On the Xīn-sì day,
the Emperor's mother, Lady Shěn, was posthumously honored as Empress Dowager.
Lady Shěn was selected into Dài-zōng's palace at the end of Kāi-yuán.
During Ān Lù-shān's rebellion,
Xuán-zōng fled from the rebels.
The concubines of the princes who could not follow
were all captured by the rebels
and confined in the Yè-tíng of the Eastern Capital.
When Dài-zōng recaptured the Eastern Capital,
he entered the palace
and found Lady Shěn,
leaving her in the Eastern Capital palace.
When Shǐ Sī-míng recaptured the Eastern Capital,
her whereabouts were subsequently lost.
20 Yǔ Zhǔn, the Jīngnán Jìedùshǐ, following Yáng Yán’s instructions,
impeached Liú Yàn, the Císhǐ of Zhōngzhōu, for having written a letter to Zhū Cǐ seeking rescue,
in which he expressed many grievances and resentments.
He also accused him of summoning and reinforcing local troops,
intending to resist imperial orders.
Zhōngzhōu
was under Jīngnán’s jurisdiction,
which is why Yǔ Zhǔn was able to falsely accuse Liú Yàn.
使 (Shǐ)
is pronounced shū lì fān.
泚 (Cǐ)
is pronounced qiě lǐ fān,
also cǐ.
朝 (Cháo)
is pronounced zhí yáo fān;
the same below.
The Emperor secretly sent an eunuch to Zhōngzhōu to strangle him.
On the jǐchǒu day,
an imperial edict granting him death was issued.
The world felt he was wronged.
Initially,
during the Ān–Shǐ Rebellion,
within a few years,
eight or nine out of ten households and people in the empire were lost.
Most prefectures and counties were occupied by fānzhèn,
and tribute and taxes were not collected.
The imperial treasury was depleted.
As China faced many troubles,
the Róngdí constantly violated the borders every year.
Heavy troops were stationed everywhere,
relying on government support.
The expenses were immeasurable,
and all depended on Yàn to manage them.
Yàn first served as the Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
solely overseeing the various circuits east of Shǎnxī.
In the first year of Bǎoyìng,
Liú Yàn was appointed Dùzhī and Zhuǎnyùn Envoy.
In the second year of Dàizōng’s Guǎngdé reign,
Yàn was appointed Zhuǎnyùn Envoy for Hénán and the Jiāng–Huái regions.
He then dredged the Biànshǔi to open up the benefits of river transport.
陝 (Shǎn)
is pronounced shī rǎn fān.
In his later years, he also held other concurrent positions,
but was dismissed not long after.
Yàn was energetic
and resourceful,
able to adapt to changing circumstances regarding supply and demand,
mastering every subtlety.
He often recruited good runners with high pay,
stationing them within sight of each other,
to report commodity prices from all four directions.
Even from distant places,
reports would reach his office within a few days.
使司 (Shǐsī)
refers to the Zhuǎnyùnshǐsī (Transport Commissioner’s Office).
Everything was within his grasp,
allowing the state to profit without the people suffering from extreme prices, whether high or low.
He often believed:
“Managing all affairs
lies in getting the right people.
Therefore, one must select those who are discerning, astute, diligent, and honest to employ;
as for examining ledgers and records,
and handling money and grain,
these must be entrusted to scholars;
clerks are only to write official documents,
and must not lightly utter a single word.”
He often said:
“If scholars fall into bribery,
they are abandoned by society.
Reputation is valued more than profit,
thus many scholars maintain integrity.
Although clerks may be pure and honest,
they will ultimately gain no prominent honor.
Profit is valued more than reputation,
thus many clerks are corrupt.”
However, only Yàn was able to implement this;
others who tried to imitate him could never achieve it.
Although his subordinate officials were thousands of li away,
they obeyed his orders as if he were present,
and dared not deceive him in their daily conduct or speech.
When powerful and influential figures of the time
recommended relatives or old acquaintances to him,
Yàn would accommodate them,
arranging their salaries
and the speed of their promotions
according to their wishes,
but they were never allowed to hold actual official duties.
For critical and important positions in his depots and granaries,
he would always select the best talents of the era.
Therefore, after Yàn’s death,
many of those who became renowned in managing finances and taxes
were his former subordinates.
Yàn also believed that if the population increased,
then taxes would naturally expand.
Therefore, his financial management
prioritized
loving the people.
In each circuit, he established Zhīyuàn Guān.
Zhīyuàn Guān
were officials in charge of the circuit sub-offices.
They would report the conditions of rainfall, snow, and harvest (good or bad) in the prefectures and counties to the main office.
If the harvest was good, grain would be bought at a high price;
if poor, it would be sold at a low price.
Sometimes, grain would be exchanged for miscellaneous goods for official use,
or sold in areas with abundant harvests.
When a Zhīyuàn Guān first saw signs of a poor harvest,
they would immediately report,
“In a certain month, such and such exemptions are needed;
in a certain month, such and such aid is needed.”
When the time came,
Yàn would not wait for prefectures and counties to apply,
but would immediately memorialize and implement it.
He never failed to respond to the people's urgent needs in a timely manner,
not waiting until they were exhausted, displaced, or starving
before providing relief.
As a result, the people were able to live and work in peace,
and the population thrived.
When Yàn first became Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
the total number of registered households in the empire was no more than two million;
in his last years, it reached over three million.
Where Yàn governed, the population increased;
where he did not, it did not.
Initially, annual revenue from finances and taxes did not exceed four million mǐn;
in his last years, it reached over ten million mǐn.
Yàn exclusively used the salt monopoly system to fund military and state expenditures.
At that time, west of Xǔ, Rǔ, Zhèng, and Dèng,
everyone consumed Hédōng pool salt,
managed by the Dùzhī department;
east of Biàn, Huá, Táng, and Cài,
everyone consumed sea salt,
managed by Yàn.
Yàn believed that too many officials would disturb the people,
so he only established salt officials in salt-producing regions
to collect salt boiled by salt-producing households and resell it to merchants,
letting them transport it wherever they wished.
No further officials were established in other prefectures and counties.
In regions like Jiānglíng, far from salt-producing areas,
official salt was transported and stored there.
If merchants ceased trading and salt became expensive,
it would be sold at a reduced price,
which was called “ever-normal salt.”
Later, he also monopolized tea,
and consequently established ever-normal tea and salt officials.
貯 (Zhù)
is pronounced dīng lǚ fān.
Initially, the profit from salt in Jiāng–Huái was no more than four hundred thousand mǐn;
in his last years, it reached over six million mǐn.
Consequently, state expenditures were sufficient, and the people were not impoverished.
The profit from Hédōng salt was no more than eight hundred thousand mǐn,
and its price was also more expensive than sea salt.
Previously,
for those who transported grain from Guāndōng into Cháng’ān,
because the river currents were swift and fierce,
if one *hú* (bushel) yielded eight *dòu* upon arrival,
it was considered a successful effort
and they received generous rewards.
Liú Yàn believed that the water forces of the Jiāng (Yangzi River), Biàn (River), Hé (Yellow River), and Wèi (River)
were different,
so he designed different types of transport boats
according to what was appropriate,
and trained the漕 *cáo* (canal) soldiers.
Boats from the Jiāng reached Yángzhōu,
boats from the Biàn reached Héyīn,
boats from the Hé reached Wèikǒu,
and from Wèikǒu they reached Tàicāng.
Wèikǒu
refers to the mouth where the Wèi River enters the Hé River.
Goods were transferred and supplied along the way.
From then on, each year, grain transported could reach over a million *hú*,
with not a single *dòu* or *shēng* lost to sinking.
Ten boats formed a *gāng* (fleet),
led by a military general.
If ten transports were completed without loss,
they were given superior merit
and the person was granted an official post.
After several such transports,
all (the generals) had become gray-haired.
Liú Yàn established ten shipyards in Yángzǐ to build boats,
allocating a thousand *mín* of cash for each vessel.
Someone said,
"The actual cost is less than half;
too much is wasted."
Liú Yàn said,
"Not so.
One who considers grand plans must not begrudge small expenses.
All matters must be planned for the long term.
Now that shipyards are first established,
there are many involved in the work.
We must first ensure that their private needs are not constrained,
then the official property will be sturdy.
If we immediately engage in petty calculations over every trifle,
how can it last long?
One day, there will certainly be those who complain that what I provide is too much and will reduce it;
reducing it by half or less might still be acceptable,
but beyond that, transport will become impossible."
Fifty years later,
the authorities indeed reduced it by half.
By the Xiántōng era,
the authorities calculated expenses and allocated funds accordingly,
with no surplus left.
The boats became even more flimsy and easily damaged,
and river transport was subsequently abolished.
Sòng Bái said: After the Wǔdé and Yǒnghuī eras,
Jiāng Xíngběn, Xuē Dàdǐng, and Chǔ Lǎng all stated that river transport could not be fully opened and effective.
Later, Censor Wáng Shīshùn requested to transport grain from Jìn and Jiàng between the Hé and Wèi rivers,
and the Wèiqiáo Granary was first established.
In the early Kāiyuán era,
Lǐ Jié served as the Water Transport Commissioner,
and first greatly developed *cáo* transport affairs.
In the eighteenth year,
Péi Yàoqīng was appointed Jiānghuái Transport Commissioner for his advice on river transport,
with Cuī Xīyì and Xiāo Jiǒng as deputies.
The positions of deputy commissioner for Transport and Salt and Iron began from this point.
In the early Sùzōng era,
Dí Wǔqí gained audience with his proposals on money and grain,
and first established the Jiānghuái Tax and Corvée Commissioner.
In the early Qiányuán era,
the Salt and Iron Commissioner was added,
and the great Salt and Iron Law was first implemented,
collecting taxes on salt from mountains, seas, wells, and stoves,
and establishing supervisory offices and officials.
It was not until Liú Yàn
that the Salt and Iron Commissioner concurrently managed river transport.
Liú Yàn was diligent and hardworking.
Regardless of whether the matter was trivial or urgent,
he would resolve it within a day,
not letting it remain overnight.
Later financial experts could not match him.
21st, eighth month,
*Jiǎwǔ* day,
Zhènwǔ Military Governor Zhāng Guāngshèng killed the Huíhé envoy Dǒng Tú
and over nine hundred other people.
Dǒng Tú was the uncle of Wǔyì Kèhán.
During the reign of Dàizōng,
the Jiǔxìng Hú (Nine Surnamed Hu) often assumed the name of Huíhé,
lived intermingled in the capital,
amassed wealth, and acted violently,
becoming a public and private nuisance along with the Huíhé.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he ordered Dǒng Tú to lead all his followers back to their country,
with abundant baggage.
Upon reaching Zhènwǔ,
they stayed for several months,
demanding extensive provisions and supplies,
consuming a thousand *jīn* of meat daily,
with other items in proportion.
Their woodcutters and herdsmen were allowed to trample and damage orchards and crops,
which the people of Zhènwǔ resented.
Zhāng Guāngshèng wanted to kill the Huíhé
and seize their baggage,
but he feared their strength
and dared not act yet.
The Jiǔxìng Hú heard that their tribe was being purged by the new Kèhán,
and many absconded.
Dǒng Tú guarded against this very strictly.
The Jiǔxìng Hú could not flee,
nor dared they return,
so they secretly offered a plan to Zhāng Guāngshèng,
proposing to kill the Huíhé.
Zhāng Guāngshèng was pleased that their faction was splitting,
and agreed.
The Emperor had been humiliated in Shǎnzhōu –
this event can be found in Volume 222, Bǎoyīng First Year.
Shǎn
pronounced *shī rǎn fān*.
Zhāng Guāngshèng knew the Emperor's intent,
so he memorialized, stating:
"The Huíhé's native tribe is not numerous;
what strengthens them
are the various Hú.
Now we hear that they are preying on each other.
Dùnmòhè has just been enthroned.
Yídìjiàn has an illegitimate son.
Dēnglǐ Kèhán's name was Yídìjiàn.
The country is not yet stable.
If they have no wealth, they cannot command their followers.
If Your Majesty does not seize this opportunity to eliminate them,
but instead returns their people
and gives them wealth,
this is precisely what is meant by 'lending weapons to bandits and providing grain to thieves'."
This quotes Lǐ Sī's remonstrance to Qín Wáng against expelling foreign ministers.
After three memorials,
the Emperor did not permit it.
Zhāng Guāngshèng then sent his deputy general to pass by their guesthouse gate,
deliberately failing to show respect.
Dǒng Tú became enraged,
seized him, and flogged him dozens of times.
Zhāng Guāngshèng rallied his troops and launched a surprise attack,
killing Dǒng Tú along with all the various Hú,
and piled their bodies into a monument of corpses (Jīngguān).
He left only one Hú alive
to return to his country as a witness,
saying:
"The Huíhé flogged and humiliated a great general
and moreover plotted to attack and seize Zhènwǔ,
hence they were executed first."
The Emperor summoned Zhāng Guāngshèng to be Right Gold Seal General,
and sent the court eunuch Wáng Jiāxiáng to convey a letter and gifts.

22nd,

His positions as Military Governor of Lúlóng and Lǒngyòu remained as before.

23rd, *Guǐchǒu* day,
an imperial edict posthumously granted official titles to the Empress Dowager's father, grandfather, elder brother, and younger brother.
For all other male and female clan members who were granted official posts or enfeoffed with land, their household registration documents and appointment certificates
(The character "第"

24 In the ninth month,
on the *rénwǔ* day,
the Directorate for Palace Buildings reported that the corridors of Xuānzhèng Palace were damaged.
In the tenth month, the *kuí gāng* was present,
making repairs impossible.
Diviners were constrained by taboos,
such as *tiāngāng* and *hékuí*.
Generally, in months when *kuí gāng* is present, and in regions to which it is linked,
repairs and constructions are forbidden.
Shǐ Zhào said: "The *kuí gāng*
is the qi of the *Kuí* star of the Big Dipper.
In the tenth month, it is in *xū*,
thus forming *kuí gāng*."
Sòng Bái said: "According to the books of the yin-yang masters,
the first month of winter this year is *kuí gāng*,
which is unfavorable for repairs and construction.
'However, if it does not harm the public or people,
then it is auspicious!
Why ask about the auspicious time and day!' "
So, an order was immediately given to carry out the repairs.
25 Before the Dàlì era,
there were no regulations for taxation, revenue, or salaries.
Senior officials were allowed to monopolize them;
moreover, with Yuán Zài and Wáng Jin holding power,
bribery was openly practiced.
For nearly twenty years, no one in the empire pursued corrupt officials.
*Kǎo Yì* states: *Jiànzhōng Shílù* says
"thirty years,"
which is probably a character error.
He was exiled.
The emperor, considering Xuē Yōng, the Surveillance Commissioner of Xuān-Shè, to be a cultivated veteran official,
summoned him to serve as Left Chancellor (Zuǒ Chéng);
when Yōng left Xuān Province,
he embezzled imperial property amounting to tens of thousands.
Yuán Yǔ, the Palace Censor (Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ), exposed him.
At that time, the two prefectures of Xuān and Shè, situated by mountains and controlling the vital passages of the Yangtze River and lakes,
had separate Surveillance Commissioners established.

pronounced *shū lì fān*.
*Sì*,
pronounced *xiáng lì fān*.
*Shè*,
pronounced *shè*.

pronounced *yùn*,
a surname.
In the tenth month,
on the *jǐhài* day,
he was demoted to County Defender (Wèi) of Liánshān.
Liánshān County
belonged to Lián Prefecture.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn divided Guìyáng to establish Guǎnghuì County,

In the first year of Rénshòu,
it was changed to Liánshān County

He dared not be reckless.
When the emperor first ascended the throne,
he dismissed eunuchs
and placed trust in court officials.
Zhāng Shè entered imperial service through his Confucian scholarship,
and Xuē Yōng ascended to court through his cultured demeanor.
Both subsequently failed due to corruption.
Eunuchs and military generals were able to use this as an excuse,
saying:
"Southern court civil officials' corruption reaches tens of thousands,
yet they accuse us of bringing chaos to the empire.
Is this not deception and trickery?!"
Thereupon, the emperor's heart began to doubt,
and he no longer knew whom to rely upon.
26 Gāo Cān, the Chancellor's Scribe (Zhōngshū Shèrén), requested that several members of the Shěn family be dispatched to search for the Empress Dowager.
On the *gēngyín* day,

it was first ordered that, in addition to the officials on standby,

28 Previously,
when princesses married,
their parents-in-law would bow to them,
and the wives would not return the bow.
The emperor commanded the ritual officials to establish rites for princesses bowing to their parents-in-law and their husband's paternal uncles, elder brothers, and elder sisters.
The parents-in-law would sit and receive the bow in the central hall,
while the elder brothers
and elder sisters would stand and receive the bow in the eastern wing,
according to family rites.
There was a county princess about to be married.
The chosen day was *dīngchǒu*.
On that day,
the emperor's paternal cousin (from his father's generation) died,
so he ordered the marriage to be halted.
The officials concerned reported:
"The arrangements are already complete,
and mourning clothes for a short-lived person are not enough to suspend affairs."
The emperor said:
"You value the cost,
I value the propriety."
In the end, he halted it.
Since the Zhìdé era,
the state had many affairs.
Many imperial princesses, commandery princesses, and county princesses were not married at the appropriate time.
Some had gray hair,
and though residing in the inner palace,
some had not seen the emperor for ten years.
The emperor began to receive these imperial clan women.
"Huá" refers to white strands appearing in the hair.
*Jiàn*,
pronounced *xián biàn fān*.
He offered comfort to those of lower status
and commanded that all of them be married.
The gifts, both large and small,
were all personally inspected by him.
On the two days, *jǐmǎo* and *gēngchén*,
ninety-one county princesses, including those of Yuèyáng,

were even more pleased.
In the fifth month of that year,
Wéi Lún had gone on a second mission to Tubo.
*Tǔ*,
from *tūn* in the entering tone.

1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Wùchén,
Lǐ Bǎochén, the Jiédùshǐ of Chéngdé, passed away.
Héng and Jì
are the Chéngdé Army.
Kǎoyì says: The Jiànzhōng Shílù records:
“On the second month Dīngsì,
Bǎochén died.”
It is suspected that this was the day the report arrived.
We now follow the Dézōng Shílù.
Gǔ Kuàng’s Yànnán Jì says:
“In his later years, Zhōngzhì [Lǐ Bǎochén]
only admitted into his presence people of sorcery and delusion, as well as those who practiced yin-yang, divination, flattery, and opportunism.
They vied to present prophecies,
claiming he would attain an exalted position.
They fabricated crimson grass and divine ganoderma,
and carved names into stones.
They also set up an altar in the courtyard of the rear hall,
practiced abstinence from meat,
and placed gold cups, jade goblets, and silver plates,
claiming that sweet dew and divine wine would spontaneously appear in them.
They also said that heavenly talismans had descended.
Zhōngzhì believed his destiny was aligned with Heaven,
and none of his officials dared to admonish him.
He ordered official documents to be circulated,
announcing to the prefectures and counties: ‘Divine ganoderma and crimson grass,
auspicious signs for a king,
have suddenly grown on the altar,
filling the courtyard with fragrance.
A divine stone has presented an omen,
heavenly talismans have flown down in response,
sweet dew is like honey,
and divine wine overflows the cups.
These were not sought by me,
but arrived spontaneously.
Each prefecture and county under our administration should be informed,
and they should be commanded to acknowledge and
join in the celebration.’
Afterward, these deluded sorcerers daily misled each other, saying: ‘Within days, heavenly deities will descend,
bearing a golden casket and a jade seal,
whereupon you will assume the great position,
bestowed by Heaven.
The four quarters will all submit of their own accord,
without needing conquest,
and the realm will be settled simply by sitting.’
Zhōngzhì was greatly pleased.
He lavishly rewarded them with gold, silver, silk, brocade, and exotic treasures.
The yin-yang practitioners and sorcerers, knowing their deceit,
feared exposure and execution, so
they conspired, saying: ‘Our Duke should drink a decoction of sweet dew and divine ganoderma herb,
which will hasten the descent of the heavenly deities.’
Zhōngzhì completely trusted the sorcerers,
who secretly put poison in the decoction.
After he finished drinking it,
he immediately lost his voice,
and died three days later.”
Traditional accounts also considered this to be true.
However, the sorcerers and deluded individuals
would surely have been hated by the entire administration;
their only reliance was Bǎochén himself.
If they poisoned Bǎochén to death,
while still within the residence,
with nowhere to flee,
how could they have escaped death?
It is likely that even if the sorcerers were foolish,
they would not have done this.
Perhaps people at the time, seeing that Bǎochén had drunk their decoction
and then fell ill and died,
concluded he was poisoned by the sorcerers,
and Gǔ Kuàng simply recorded it.
Because he was young and mentally weak,
he preemptively executed the generals who were difficult to control, such as
Zhāng Xiànchéng, the Cìshǐ of Shēnzhōu,
with more than ten people dying on the same day.
Bǎochén summoned Zhāng Xiàozhōng, the Cìshǐ of Yìzhōu,
but Xiàozhōng did not go.
He sent his younger brother, Xiàojié, to summon him.
Xiàozhōng told Xiàojié to say to Bǎochén:
“What crime have the generals committed that they should be executed one after another?
Xiàozhōng fears death
and dares not go;
nor does he dare to rebel.
It is just like your intention not to attend court.”
Xiàojié wept, saying:
“If so,
Xiàojié will surely die.”
Xiàozhōng said:
“If you go, we will both perish.
As long as I am here,
he will surely not kill you.”
So he returned,
and Bǎochén did not punish him.
Wáng Wǔjùn, the Bīngmǎshǐ,
was of low rank but brave,
so Bǎochén was especially fond of him.
He married his daughter to Wǔjùn’s son, Shìzhēn,
and Shìzhēn in turn cultivated close ties with Bǎochén’s attendants;
thus, Xiàozhōng and Wǔjùn alone remained safe.
The historian says that one should not kill indiscriminately,
and this also set the stage for Xiàozhōng and Wǔjùn’s return to the imperial court.
Fù,
read Fú Yòu Fān.
When he died,
the Kǒngmùguān Hú Zhèn
and the household servant Wáng Tāánú advised Wéiyuè to conceal the death for more than twenty days.

but Hóng did not accept

Initially,

Sì,

He had requested that the imperial insignia be granted to Tián Yuè;

Someone advised:

Dézōng was keen on suppressing the regional governors and made this statement,

Zhǎng,
read Zhī Zhàng fān.
“To appoint or not to appoint is the same.”

Yuè then, along with Lǐ Zhèngjǐ, each sent envoys to Wéiyuè,

Tián Tíngjiè, the Jiédùfùshǐ of Wèibó, said to Yuè:

The Chéngdé Jiédùshǐ governed Héngzhōu,

The former prefect of Dìngzhōu, Gǔ Cóngzhèng,

Furthermore,
His Excellency had a grudge with Yōuzhōu

Tāo and we are within earshot of each other's watchman's clappers

2 Initially,
Gāo Lìshì had an adopted daughter, a widow, who lived in Dōngjīng.

The female official Lǐ Zhēnyī suspected her of being Empress Dowager Shěn,

The Emperor sent eunuchs and palace women to verify her identity.
Her age and appearance were quite similar.
The eunuchs and palace women did not clearly recognize the Empress Dowager,

The woman of the Gāo family declared that she was truly not the Empress Dowager,
but the verifiers became even more suspicious.
They forcibly welcomed her into Shàngyáng Gōng.

carrying the imperial carriage, garments, and utensils, to Shàngyáng Gōng to attend to her.
Those around her coaxed and enticed her in a hundred ways,
and the Gāo woman's heart was swayed,
so she then declared herself to be the one.
The verifiers galloped back to report,
and the Emperor was greatly pleased.
In the second month,
on the Xīnmǎo day,
the Emperor held court on an even-numbered day.
All the officials entered to offer congratulations.
According to Táng regulations: the Son of Heaven received court audiences and congratulations on odd-numbered days.
Now, due to the joy of finding the Empress Dowager,
he therefore held court and received congratulations on an even-numbered day.
Gāo's younger brother, Chéngyuè, was in Cháng'ān.
Fearing that if he did not speak,
he would eventually be punished,
he quickly stated the full story.
The Emperor ordered Gāo Lìshì's adopted grandson Fán Jǐngchāo to go and re-examine her.
Jǐngchāo saw the Gāo woman residing in the inner palace,
acting as the Empress Dowager,
with very strict guards attending her.
Jǐngchāo said to the Gāo woman:
