he often directed and commanded them with a gesture,
making them rush about before him,
and his household treated them as servants.
The safety and peril of the empire depended on him for nearly thirty years.
*Dài*
means "nearly"
or "about to."
Guō Zǐyí rose from Shuòfāng (朔方)
in the first year of Sùzōng's (肅宗) Zhìdé (至德) reign (the same year),
and passed away in the second year of Jiànzhōng (建中).
That year, the *suì* star was in *chóngguāngzuò'è* (重光作噩).
From *róuzhàotūntān* (柔兆涒灘) to *chóngguāngzuò'è*,
it was only twenty-six years,
hence the phrase "nearly thirty years."
He reached the pinnacle of officialdom, yet the populace bore him no ill will.
He indulged in extreme luxury and desire, yet no one criticized him.
He died at the age of eighty-five.
Many of his generals and aides rose to high office
and became famous ministers.
4 On the *rénzǐ* day,
Lǐ Jiāo (李艽), Deputy Military Commissioner of Huái (懷), Zhèng (鄭), and Héyáng (河陽), was appointed Military Commissioner of Héyáng and Huáizhōu (懷州).
Five counties of Dōngjī (東畿) were detached and placed under his jurisdiction.
5 Běitíng (北庭) and Ānxī (安西) had been cut off and isolated since the Tubo (吐蕃) seized Hé (河) and Lǒng (隴).
The seizure of Hé and Lǒng is described in Volume 223, under the first year of Dàzōng's Guǎngdé (廣德) reign.
*Tǔ*
is pronounced with the entering tone of *tūn*.
They had repeatedly sent envoys with memorials,
but none reached the capital,
and communication had been broken for over ten years.
At this time,
envoys were sent through secret paths, passing through various Hu (胡) tribes from among the Huíhé (回紇),
and the emperor commended them.
In autumn,
the seventh month, on the *wùwǔ* day, the first day of the month,
Yuánzhōng (元忠) was granted the title of Grand Protector of Běitíng
and ennobled as Prince of Níngsài Commandery (寧塞郡王).
Níngsài Commandery was in Kuòzhōu (廓州).
Xīn (昕) was ennobled as Prince of Wǔwēi Commandery (武威郡王).
Wǔwēi Commandery was in Liángzhōu (涼州).
Yuánzhōng's surname and personal name
were bestowed by the imperial court;
his original surname was Cáo (曹), and his personal name was Língzhōng (令忠).
Xīn
was Zǐyí's younger brother.
6 Lǐ Xīliè had delayed his advance due to prolonged rain.
The emperor found this strange.
Lú Mì (盧密) said to the emperor:
"Xīliè's delay
is on account of Yáng Yán (楊炎).
He is using Yán's advice to employ Xīliè as a means to sow discord.
It would be better to temporarily relieve Yán from his chancellorship to appease Xīliè.
Once the situation is resolved, he can be reinstated,
with no harm done."
The emperor thought this was correct.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
Yán was appointed Left Palace Secretary (左僕射)
and relieved of his administrative duties.
Zhāng Yì (張鎰), formerly Military Commissioner of Yǒngpíng (永平), was appointed Vice Minister of the Chancellery (中書侍郎) and concurrently Grand Chancellor (同平章事).
Yì was Qíqiū's (齊丘) son.
Cuī Níng (崔寧), Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng, was appointed Right Palace Secretary (右僕射).
*Shè*
is pronounced *yínxiè* (*yínxiè*).
7 On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
the late Yuán Guāngtíng (袁光庭), former Governor of Yīzhōu (伊州), was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Public Works (工部尚書).
Guāngtíng was Governor of Yīzhōu at the end of the Tiānbǎo (天寶) reign.
When the Tubo seized Hé and Lǒng,
Guāngtíng held out for many years.
The Tubo tried a hundred ways to entice him,
but he did not surrender.
Yīzhōu
was administered from Yīwúxiàn (伊吾縣),
the Han-era Yīwúlú (伊吾盧) territory.
*Shàng*
is pronounced *chényáng* (*chényáng*).
*Tǔ*
is pronounced with the entering tone of *tūn*.
*Yòu*
is pronounced *yǒu*.
When the city was about to fall,
Guāngtíng first killed his wife and children,
and then immolated himself.
When Guō Xīn's envoy arrived,
the imperial court first learned of this,
and thus granted him the posthumous official title.
8 On the *xīnsì* day,
Lǐ Huáiguāng, Military Commissioner of Bīnníng (邠寧), was concurrently appointed Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng.
9 On the day of Guǐwèi,
Mǎ Suì, Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng,
Lǐ Bǎozhēn, Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì,
Lǐ Shèng, Shéncè Xiānfēng Dū Zhī Bīngmǎshǐ,
greatly defeated Tián Yuè at Línmíng.
At that time, Yuè attacked Línmíng,
but failed to capture it for months.
The city's food was almost exhausted,
the treasury was depleted,
and many soldiers were dead or wounded.
Zhāng Pī adorned his beloved daughter
and sent her out to bow to the generals and soldiers, saying:
"Gentlemen, you have suffered greatly in defending and fighting.
Pī's family has no other possessions;
I ask to sell this daughter to cover one day's expenses for the generals and soldiers."
Everyone wept
and said:
"We are willing to dedicate our lives to the effort,
and dare not speak of rewards."
Lǐ Bǎozhēn sent an urgent appeal to the court.
An imperial edict ordered Mǎ Suì to lead twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to join Bǎozhēn in attacking Yuè.
It also dispatched Lǐ Shèng with Shéncè troops to go with them.
Another edict ordered Zhū Tāo, Liúhòu of Yōuzhōu, to attack Wéiyuè.
This refers to Lǐ Wéiyuè.
Before Suì's army had emerged from the perilous terrain,
he first sent an envoy with a letter to admonish Yuè,
using conciliatory words.
Yuè thought Suì feared him
and made no preparations.
Suì and Bǎozhēn combined their forces, totaling eighty thousand,
and descended east through Húguān.
A 'Kǎoyì' (collation and discussion) states: The old biography of Tián Yuè says:
"On the third day of the seventh month,
the army descended east from Húguān,
and captured the bandit's Lújiāzhài."
Suì's biography states:
"In the eleventh month,
the army arrived at Hándān."
This might be an error.
We now follow Yuè's biography and 'Yànnánjì'.
They attacked Yuè's detached army
and defeated it.
Yuè was then urgently attacking Línmíng,
and had dispatched five thousand of Lǐ Wéiyuè's troops to assist Yáng Cháoguāng.
The next day,
Suì and others advanced to attack Cháoguāng's stockade.
Yuè led over ten thousand men to relieve it.
Suì ordered his chief general Lǐ Zìliáng and others to defend against them at Shuānggāng.
Shuānggāng
is northwest of Hándān
and west of Línmíng;
it is also known as Lújiātúntuán.
"If Yuè gets through,
you will surely be executed!"
Zìliáng and others fought bravely,
and Yuè's army retreated.
Suì used fire carts to burn Cháoguāng's stockade,
beheaded Cháoguāng,
and captured over five thousand heads and prisoners.
Five days later,
Suì and others advanced their army to Línmíng.
Yuè committed all his forces to a fierce battle,
engaging in over a hundred clashes.
Yuè's army suffered a great defeat,
with over ten thousand heads taken.
A 'Kǎoyì' states: The old biography of Lǐ Shèng:
"Fighting at Línmíng,
all the armies retreated.
Shèng led his troops across the Míngshuǐ,
using the water to cross,
and struck Yuè's army from the flank.
The imperial army recovered its morale,
attacked Yuè,
and greatly defeated him."
According to this,
the battle of Línmíng took place in winter,
which corresponds to Mǎ Suì's biography
"In the eleventh month, the army arrived at Hándān."
The 'Shílù' (Veritable Records) states:
"On the day of Gēngyín in the twelfth month,
Mǎ Suì was promoted to Zuǒ Púyè."
It also says:
"Earlier,
Yuè had dispatched his general Kāng Yīn to lead troops to besiege Xíngzhōu,
and Yáng Cháoguāng to besiege Línmíng.
Suì, Bǎozhēn, and the Shéncè general Lǐ Shèng joined forces to relieve them,
greatly defeating the bandits at Shuānggāng,
beheading Yáng Cháoguāng,
and capturing their chief general Lú Zǐchāng.
Taking advantage of the victory, they advanced their army
and again defeated Yuè at Línmíng.
Therefore, Suì and others were promoted."
According to the 'Shílù',
this battle has no specific month or day,
but is mentioned when Mǎ Suì was promoted.
Now, based on Suì's biography,
Yuè was first defeated at Shuānggāng,
and Yáng Cháoguāng was beheaded.
Five days later,
they advanced to Línmíng.
This is the same as the 'Shílù''s statement that "on the day of Guǐwèi this month, the combined armies defeated Yuè at Línmíng."
The 'Shílù' places this in the winter of this year,
which conflicts with this account.
'Yànnánjì' also states:
"In the seventh month,
Suì and Bǎozhēn's eighty thousand troops
descended east from Lùfǔ through Húguān,
first capturing Hándān's Lújiāzhài;
Cháoguāng died in battle at Línmíng City;
and Yuè was again greatly defeated."
Yuè's retreat occurred before Lǐ Zhèngjǐ's death,
which corresponds to this month in the 'Shílù'.
Regarding the battle of Línmíng,
it is likely that all the armies had already assembled.
If Suì and the others had not yet arrived,
Zhāng Pī certainly could not have defeated Yuè's army alone.
The 'Xīnběnjì' (New Basic Annals) states:
"On the day of Dīngchǒu in the eleventh month,
Mǎ Suì and Tián Yuè fought at Shuānggāng and defeated him."
It is unknown where this date comes from;
it also conflicts with various other texts.
We now follow only the seventh month.
The siege of Xíngzhōu was also lifted.
In the fifth month of that year,
Yuè had sent his general Kāng Yīn to besiege Xíngzhōu.
Yuè's defeat and retreat also lifted the siege.
At this time, Lǐ Zhèngjǐ, Jìedùshǐ of Pínglú, had already passed away.
His son Nà kept it a secret
and managed military affairs.
Yuè sought help from Nà and Lǐ Wéiyuè.
Nà dispatched his chief general Wèi Jùn with ten thousand troops,
and Wéiyuè sent three thousand troops to assist him.
Yuè rallied his scattered soldiers,
obtaining over twenty thousand men,
and encamped at Huánshuǐ.
The Zīqīng army was to his east,
and the Chéngdé army to his west,
supporting each other from head to tail.
Mǎ Suì led the various armies to advance and garrison Yè,
and memorialized asking for Hèyáng troops to assist him.
An edict ordered Lǐ Jiāo, Jìedùshǐ of Hèyáng, to lead troops to meet them.
10 In the eighth month,
Lǐ Nà finally announced his father's death
and memorialized requesting to inherit his father's position.
The Emperor did not permit it.
11 Liáng Chóngyì dispatched troops to attack Jiānglíng.
When they reached Sìwàng,
there is a Sìwàngshān in the east of Suíxiàn, Suízhōu today.
This mountain is the highest,
and one can see in all four directions from it.
He then recalled his troops to Xiāng and Dèng.
Lǐ Xīliè led his army up along the Hàn River
to meet with the troops from various circuits.
Chóngyì sent his generals Zhái Huī and Dù Shàochéng to meet them in battle at Mánshuǐ.
Xīliè greatly defeated them.
He pursued them to Shūkoǔ
and again defeated them.
The two generals requested to surrender.
Xīliè made them lead their troops to first enter Xiāngyáng to comfort and reassure the military and civilians.
Chóngyì closed the city gates and resisted,
but the defenders opened the gates and rushed out,
which could not be stopped.
Chóngyì and his wife threw themselves into a well and died.
Their heads were sent to the capital.
12 Zhū Tāo, Jìedùshǐ of Fányáng, was about to attack Lǐ Wéiyuè
and encamped at Mòzhōu.
Zhāng Xiàozhōng led eight thousand elite soldiers to guard Yìzhōu.
The Jìedùshǐ of Fányáng governed Yōuzhōu,
and Mòzhōu is 280 lǐ south of Yōuzhōu.
Yìzhōu is under the jurisdiction of Chéngdé,
and is 214 lǐ west of Yōuzhōu.
"Wéiyuè is a mere stripling,
daring to defy imperial commands.
Now the Zhāoyì and Hédōng armies have already defeated Tián Yuè.
Lǐ Púyè of Huáiníng has captured Xiāngyáng.
It is estimated that the various armies in Hénán
will turn north morning and night.
The downfall of Héng and Wèi
can be awaited standing.
If you, Sir, can truly be the first to capture Yìzhōu and return to the imperial court,
then the achievement of defeating Wéiyuè will begin with you.
This is a strategy to turn misfortune into fortune."
Xiàozhōng agreed
and sent his staff officer Chéng Huá to Zhū Tāo.
He also sent his recorder and staff officer Dǒng Zhěn to submit a memorial to the Emperor.
Tāo also submitted a memorial to recommend him.
The Emperor was pleased.
In the ninth month,
on the day of Xīnyǒu,
Xiàozhōng was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Chéngdé.
Wéiyuè was ordered to escort the coffin back to court,
but Wéiyuè did not comply.
Xiàozhōng was grateful to Tāo,
and arranged for his son Mào Hè to marry Tāo's daughter,
thus forming a deep alliance.
13 On the day of Rénxū,
Lǐ Xīliè was promoted to Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
14. Initially,
Lǐ Xīliè requested to suppress Liáng Chóngyì.
The Emperor repeatedly praised his loyalty to the court officials.
Lǐ Chéng, the Commissioner of Promotions and Demotions, returned from Huáixī
and said to the Emperor:
"Xīliè will certainly achieve minor successes;
but I fear that after his successes,
he will become arrogant and disloyal,
and will further trouble the imperial court with military campaigns!"
The Emperor did not think so.
After Xīliè had taken Xiāngyáng,
he occupied it for himself,
and the Emperor then remembered Chéng's words.
At that time, Chéng was the Administrator of Hézhōng.
On a jiǎzǐ day,
Chéng was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Shānnán Dōngdào.
The Emperor wanted to send him off with imperial troops,
but Chéng requested to proceed to his post alone on horseback.
Upon reaching Xiāngyáng,
Xīliè housed him in an outer guesthouse,
and threatened him in every possible way.
Chéng swore he would rather die than yield,
whereupon Xīliè plundered all possessions in the entire territory and left.
Chéng governed it for a year,
and the military administration gradually recovered.
Xīliè left a staff officer in Xiāngzhōu
to guard the wealth he had plundered,
and because of this, there were frequent envoys coming and going.
Chéng also sent his trusted aide, Zāng Shúyǎ, to travel between Xǔ and Cài.
Lǐ Xīliè, after returning from Xiāngyáng to Càizhōu,
soon moved his garrison to Xǔzhōu,
so Lǐ Chéng secretly sent people to Xǔ and Cài
to win over his various generals and plan against him.
Together, they secretly plotted against Xīliè.
This laid the groundwork for Zhōu Zēng and others to plot against Xīliè unsuccessfully and die.
15. Initially,
Xiāo Sōng's ancestral temple overlooked Qūjiāng.
Xuánzōng, deeming it a place for entertainment
unsuitable for divine spirits to reside,
ordered it to be moved.
When Yáng Yán became Chancellor,
he disliked Yán Yǐng, the Administrator of Jīngzhào,
and demoted him to Dàlǐ Qīng.
Lú Hàn wanted to trap Yán,
so he brought Yǐng in as Yùshǐ Dàfū.
Earlier,
Yán was about to build his ancestral temple.
First,
he offered all of it.
He entrusted Zhào Huìbó, the Administrator of Hénán, to sell it.
Huìbó bought it to make it an official residence.
Yǐng investigated this
and considered it to have yielded illicit profit.
He summoned Tián Jìn, the Dàlǐ Zhèng, to discuss the law.
According to the Táng Zhì: the Dàlǐ Zhèng,
a junior fifth-rank official,
was responsible for deliberating on legal cases,
rectifying statutes,
and, if a judge's verdict was improper,
correcting it according to the law.
"The law states that
if an overseeing official makes a purchase with illicit profit,
it is treated as extortion
and warrants dismissal from office."
Yán was enraged
and demoted Jìn to Sīmǎ of Héngzhōu.
Héngzhōu is
three thousand four hundred and three lǐ southeast of the capital.
Tián Jìn, a court official, was demoted to Sīmǎ of Héngzhōu.
Yǐng believed that:
"If an overseer steals from himself,
the crime deserves strangulation."
Yán's temple was directly on Xiāo Sōng's temple land,
so Yǐng slandered Yán,
saying
"This land has the aura of a king,
which is why Xuánzōng ordered Sōng to move it;
Yán has ambitious intentions,
which is why he built his temple on that very land."
In winter,
tenth month,
on an yǐwèi day,
Yán was demoted from Zuǒ Púyè to Sīmǎ of Yázhōu.
Before
reaching Yázhōu by a hundred lǐ,
he was strangled to death.
Huìbó was demoted from Administrator of Hézhōng to Wèi of Duōtián, Fèizhōu.
Fèizhōu,
in the Hàn dynasty, was Zāngkē Commandery,
and in the Suí dynasty, was the land of Fúchuān County, Qián'ān Commandery.
In the fourth year of Zhēnguān,
Fúchuān and Fúyáng counties were separated from Sīzhōu
to establish Fèizhōu.
Duōtián County,
in the fourth year of Wǔdé,
was established upon the recommendation of the Administrator of Wùzhōu.
Because the land was somewhat flat,
and cultivated fields were abundant,
it was named Duōtián (meaning "many fields").
In the fourth year of Zhēnguān,
Fèizhōu was renamed Sīzhōu.
In the first year of Qiányuán,
it was restored as Fèizhōu.
It is four thousand seven hundred lǐ south of the capital,
and four thousand nine hundred lǐ from the eastern capital.
It was named after the Fèi River in its jurisdiction.
"Administrator of Hézhōng"
should be
"Administrator of Hénán."
16. On a xīnsì day,
Crown Prince Xiāo Shì was invested.
17. On a guǐmǎo day,
the ancestral spirits were offered to in the Grand Ancestral Temple.
Before this,
since Tàizǔ had taken the principal east-facing position,
Xiànzǔ and Yìzǔ were both stored in the west side-chamber
and not offered to.
Now,
Xiànzǔ was again enshrined facing east and offered to.
18. Lǐ Wèi, the Administrator of Xúzhōu,
was Lǐ Zhèngjǐ's cousin.
When Lǐ Nà encroached upon Sòngzhōu,
Bái Jìgēng of Tàiyuán, the Magistrate of Péngchéng, persuaded Wèi to surrender the prefecture to the imperial court.
Wèi agreed
and sent his acting patrol official Cuī Chéng to present a memorial to the Emperor,
and also to make an oral report,
and also to inform the Chancellors,
that
"Xúzhōu cannot resist Nà alone.
I request to be granted the position of Commissioner of Xú, Hǎi, and Yí prefectures."
Moreover, Hǎi and Yí prefectures
were now both occupied by Nà.
"Wèi, along with Administrators Wáng Shè and Mǎ Wàntōng, has a prior agreement that
if an imperial decree from the court is obtained,
success is assured."
Chéng, having come from outside,
stated he had come from a frontier region.
He first informed Zhāng Yì,
and Yì reported it to Lú Hàn.
Hàn was angered that he had not informed him first
and did not grant his request.
On a wùshēn day,
Wèi was promoted to Yùshǐ Dàfū
and appointed Commissioner to Persuade and Attract.
19. In the eleventh month,
on a wùwǔ day,
Princess Yǒnglè was married to Tián Huá, the Acting Assistant Director of the Department of Personnel Records.
The Emperor did not wish to go against his earlier intention.
Princess Yǒnglè had been promised to Tián Huá,
as mentioned in volume 225, Dàlì 9th year of Dàizōng.
Lè
is pronounced Luò.
20. Wáng Kuǐ of Shǔ
changed his name to Suí.
21. On a xīnyǒu day,
Liú Qià, the Jìedùshǐ of Xuānwǔ;
Qǔ Huán, the Commander of all troops of Shéncè;
Lǐ Chéng of Xiāngpíng, the Administrator of Huázhōu;
and Táng Cháochén, a major general of Shuòfāng,
severely defeated the armies of Zīqīng and Wèibó in Xúzhōu.
According to Lǐ Chéng's biography in the Xīn Shū: Chéng was
from Xiāngpíng, Liáodōng.
From the time of Gāozōng,
the land of Liáodōng had already been abandoned and not possessed by the Táng.
Lǐ Chéng at the time merely had his native place registered as Xiāngpíng, Liáodōng.
Cháo is
pronounced zhí yáo.
Zī is
pronounced zhuāng chí.
Before this,
Lǐ Nà had sent his general Wáng Wēn to join the Wèibó general Xìndū Chóngqìng
to jointly attack Xúzhōu.
Lǐ Wèi sent his staff officer Wēn Rén, Wáng Zhìxīng, to the imperial court to report the emergency.
Wēn,
an ancient county,
belonged to Huáizhōu in early Táng,
and in the second year of Xiǎnqìng,
it was transferred to Luòzhōu.
He arrived in less than five days.
The old records state: Xúzhōu is
two thousand six hundred and four lǐ east of the capital.
The Emperor appointed Cháochén to command it,
and together with Qià, Huán, and Chéng, they relieved the siege.
At that time, the provisions and equipment of the Shuòfāng army had not arrived,
and their flags and uniforms were worn out and shoddy.
The Xuānwǔ people mocked them, saying:
"Can beggars defeat the enemy!"
Cháochén used their words to enrage his soldiers,
and also said:
"The Commander-in-Chief has ordered that
whoever first breaks the enemy camp
shall have all the possessions in the camp."
All the soldiers were indignant and vied to fight.
Chóngqìng and Wēn attacked Péngchéng.
For twenty days they could not take it.
They requested additional troops from Lǐ Nà.
Lǐ Nà dispatched his general Shí Yǐnjīn with ten thousand men to assist them.
The Kǎo Yì says: In the former part of the Shílù, it is written as
"Yǐnjīn,"
and in the latter part as
"Yǐnquán."
We follow the former here.
As dusk approached,
Liú Qià led his army to gradually withdraw.
Yáng Cháoshèng, the cavalry commander of the Shuòfāng army, said to Táng Cháochén:
"You array the infantry with their backs to the mountain
to await the two armies.
I will have the cavalry lie in ambush in the mountain defile.
The bandits, seeing our exposed army isolated,
will surely attack it.
With our hidden troops, we will cut them off at the waist
and surely defeat them."
Táng Cháochén followed his advice.
Chóngqìng and the others indeed led two thousand cavalry across the bridge to the west,
pursuing and attacking the government forces.
The ambushing troops emerged,
striking them from the flank.
Chóngqìng's troops were cut in two,
and they returned in disarray,
blocking the bridge to resist the government forces.
Among their soldiers, some, unable to secure the bridge,
waded across the water.
Yáng Cháoshèng pointed to them and said:
"If they can wade,
why can't we!"
Thereupon, he waded into the water to attack.
Those holding the bridge all fled.
Chóngqìng's troops suffered a great defeat.
Liú Qià and others pressed the attack,
beheading eight thousand men,
with more than half drowning.
The Shuòfāng army captured all their baggage and supplies.
Their flags and uniforms were bright and splendid.
Then they said to the Xuānwǔ people:
"Whose merit, that of Kǒngzǐ [a play on words for "your sons," i.e., the Xuānwǔ troops themselves],
is greater, compared to Sòng's?"
Sòng
refers to the Xuānwǔ troops.
At that time, Sòng and Bó were considered the Xuānwǔ Army.
Liú Qià was appointed Xuānwǔ Jiédùshǐ from his position as Prefect of Sòngzhōu,
hence the saying.
The government forces, emboldened by victory, pursued the routed enemy
to the foot of Xúzhōu city.
The Wèibó and Zīqīng armies lifted the siege and fled.
The grain transport routes of Jiāng and Huái regions began to be unobstructed.
On the 22nd day, Jǐsì,
an imperial edict stripped Lǐ Wéiyuè of his official titles and ranks;
those from his部 who surrendered were
pardoned and rewarded.
On the 23rd day, Jiǎshēn,
Chén Shàoyóu, the Jiédùshǐ of Huáinán, dispatched troops to attack Hǎizhōu.
Its prefect, Wáng Shè, surrendered the prefecture.
Hǎizhōu
was under Lǐ Nà's jurisdiction.
Shǐ,
pronounced as shū lì fān.
Shǎo,
pronounced as shǐ zhào fān.
Jiàng,
pronounced as hù jiāng fān.
In the 24th month, December,
Mǎ Wàntōng, Lǐ Nà's Prefect of Mìzhōu, begged to surrender.
On the Dīngyǒu day,
he was appointed Prefect of Mìzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Mìzhōu is located by the sea,
corresponding to the land of Yúyí in Yǔgòng,
and in the Spring and Autumn period, it was the land of Jǔ and Lǔ.
The prefectural seat
was the Zhūchéng of Lǔ.
In Han, it was Gāomì Kingdom.
In Jin, Dōngguǎn Commandery was established.
Later Wei established Jiāozhōu.
Sui changed it to Mìzhōu,
named after the Mì River within its borders.
On the 25th, Cuī Hànméng arrived in Tǔbō.
Cuī Hànméng was sent as an envoy to Tǔbō;
see the third month of this year in the previous volume.
Tǔ,
pronounced as cóng tūn rù shēng.
He was treated entirely with the rites due to a vassal.
Also,
to the west of Yúnzhōu,
the Hèlánshān should be the boundary.
In the Wǔdài Zhì,
the Hèlánshān is in Hóngjìng County of Língwǔ.
Hóngjìng County
was renamed Bǎojìng by Tang.
Yúnzhōu
should be Língzhōu;
it is a historical error.
On the Dīngwèi day,
Cuī Hànméng sent his staff officer with Tǔbō envoys to submit a memorial to the emperor.
The emperor changed the imperial edict
and the territorial boundaries for them,
all according to their requests.
As the Guāndōng and Héběi regions were engaged in warfare,
there was no time to contend with Tǔbō.
On the 26th, Mǎ Suì was made Wèibó Zhāotǎoshǐ.
On the 1st of spring,
in the first month,
Lǐ Jiāo, the Jiédùshǐ of Héyáng, led troops to press Wèizhōu.
Rèn Lǚxū, Tián Yuè's defending general, feigned surrender,
but then rebelled again.
Wèizhōu
was governed from Jí.
Jiāo,
pronounced as jū bāo fān.
Jiāng,
pronounced as jí liàng fān.
Rèn,
pronounced as rén.
Jiàng,
pronounced as hù jiāng fān.
Fù,
pronounced as fú yòu fān,
and also pronounced as the character itself.
2. Mǎ Suì (馬燧) and the other armies were encamped at Zhāngbīn (漳濱).
Tián Yuè (田悅) sent his general Wáng Guāngjìn (王光進) to build Yuèchéng (月城) to defend Chángqiáo (長橋).
Chángqiáo (長橋)
was on the Zhāngshuǐ (漳水) River.
Yuèchéng (月城)
embraced the river at both ends,
shaped like a crescent moon.
Suì (燧) chained hundreds of chariots with iron chains,
filled them with earth bags,
and blocked the downstream flow.
The water became shallow,
and the armies waded across.
At that time, the army lacked provisions,
and Yuè (悅) and others kept to their deep fortifications and did not engage in battle.
Suì (燧) ordered the armies to carry ten days' provisions
and advance to Cāngkǒu (倉口),
encamping opposite Yuè (悅) across the Huánshuǐ (洹水) River.
Lǐ Bǎozhēn (李抱真) and Lǐ Jiāo (李艽) asked:
"With few provisions, why do we penetrate so deeply?"
Suì (燧) replied:
"Few provisions favor a quick battle.
Now the three garrisons have allied forces but do not fight.
The three garrisons
refer to Wèibó (魏博), Zībó (淄博) (later Zīqīng (淄青)), and Chéngdé (成德).
Jiāo (艽),
pronounced as jū bāo.
Shǎo (少),
pronounced as shǐ shào.
If I were to divide the army to attack their flanks,
Yuè (悅) would surely rescue them,
and then I would be attacked front and back,
and the battle would certainly be unfavorable.
Therefore, I advance to press Yuè (悅),
which is 'attacking what they are sure to save.'
Military strategy has this saying.
I will surely defeat them for you gentlemen."
Then he built three bridges to cross the Huánshuǐ (洹水) River
and challenged them daily,
but Yuè (悅) did not come out.
Suì (燧) ordered the armies to eat at midnight
and secretly led the troops along the Huánshuǐ (洹水) straight to Wèizhōu (魏州),
issuing the order:
"When the enemy approaches, halt and form ranks."
He left a hundred cavalry to beat drums and sound horns in the camp,
and also carried firewood and held fire.
After all the armies had departed,
they stopped the drums and horns and hid by the side;
after Yuè's (悅) army had all crossed,
they burned their bridge.
When the army had marched about ten *lǐ*,
Yuè (悅) heard of it
and led 40,000 infantry and cavalry from Zīqīng (淄青) and Chéngdé (成德) to cross the bridge and attack their rear,
setting fire with the wind
and advancing with shouts and clamor.
Zào (譟),
pronounced as zé zào.
Suì (燧) first cleared a hundred paces of grass and brush in front as a battlefield,
formed ranks to await them,
and recruited more than five thousand brave warriors to form the vanguard.
When Yuè's (悅) army arrived,
the fire died down,
and their morale waned.
Suì (燧) unleashed his troops to attack them,
and Yuè's (悅) army was utterly defeated.
The Shéncè (神策), Zhāoyì (昭義), and Héyáng (河陽) armies retreated slightly.
Shéncè (神策) was Lǐ Shèng's (李晟) army.
Zhāoyì (昭義) was Lǐ Bǎozhēn's (李抱真) army.
Héyáng (河陽) was Lǐ Jiāo's (李艽) army.
They returned to fight
and defeated them again.
When they pursued the fleeing enemy to the river,
the three bridges had already been burned.
The three bridges
were those on the Huánshuǐ (洹水) River.
An innumerable number of people drowned in the water;
over twenty thousand heads were severed,
and over three thousand prisoners were captured.
The corpses lay piled up for more than thirty *lǐ*.
Yuè (悅) gathered over a thousand remnant soldiers and fled to Wèizhōu (魏州).
Mǎ Suì (馬燧) and Lǐ Bǎozhēn (李抱真) were at odds,
and halted their troops at Píngyì Fútú (平邑浮圖).
Yuè (悅) arrived at the south suburb at night.
This was the south suburb of Wèizhōu (魏州).
He waited for the government army,
and after a long time,
as dawn was breaking,
Chángchūn (長春) then opened the gates and let him in.
Yuè (悅) killed Chángchūn (長春)
and defended the city.
There were less than a few thousand soldiers in the city,
and the relatives of the dead
wailed throughout the streets.
Yuè (悅) was worried and fearful,
so he took his saber,
mounted his horse, and stood outside the government office gate.
He assembled all the soldiers and civilians,
and, weeping, said:
"Yuè (悅) is unworthy.
I was recommended and protected by the two venerable elders of Zīqīng (淄青) and Chéngdé (成德),
to succeed my paternal uncle's enterprise.
The two venerable elders were Lǐ Zhèngjǐ (李正己) of Zīqīng (淄青) and Lǐ Bǎochén (李寶臣) of Chéngdé (成德).
Tián Yuè (田悅) treated them as elders.
Paternal uncle
was Tián Chéngsì (田承嗣).
Zī (淄),
pronounced as zhuāng chí.
Sì (嗣),
pronounced as xiáng lì.
Their sons could not inherit.
Yuè (悅) dared not forget the great kindness of the two venerable elders,
and, not measuring my strength,
presumed to defy the imperial decree.
This defeat has come to this,
causing the lives of officials and gentry to be lost.
This is all Yuè's (悅) fault.
Yuè (悅) has an old mother
and cannot commit suicide.
I wish you gentlemen would use this knife to cut off Yuè's (悅) head,
take it out of the city and surrender to Mǎ Púshè (馬僕射),
obtain wealth and honor for yourselves,
and not die with Yuè (悅)!"
Thereupon he threw himself from his horse to the ground.
The generals and soldiers rushed forward to embrace and hold Yuè (悅), saying:
"Shàngshū (尚書) raised an army to pursue righteousness,
not for private gain.
One victory, one defeat,
is common in warfare.
We have received kindness for generations;
how can we bear to hear this!
We wish to serve Shàngshū (尚書) in one battle;
if we do not win, we will follow with our deaths."
Yuè (悅) said:
"Since you gentlemen do not abandon Yuè (悅) for his defeat,
even if Yuè (悅) dies,
how could I dare forget your profound kindness in the afterlife!"
Then he and the generals cut off their hair,
swore to be brothers,
and pledged to live and die together;
they emptied all the treasury and government stores and collected wealth from rich citizens,
obtaining over a million coins,
which they used to reward the soldiers.
The morale of the masses then stabilized.
Tián Yuè (田悅) was good at recovering from defeat; he did not perish.
This is the so-called "even bandits have their code."
He had them organize their ranks and repair defenses,
and the army's morale was restored.
Yuè (悅) did not use Xíng Cáojùn (邢曹俊),
see the previous volume, previous year.
Fù (復),
pronounced as fú yòu,
also pronounced as its original character.
Lǐ Nà (李納)'s army was at Púyáng (濮陽),
pressured by the Hénán (河南) army,
and fled back to Púzhōu (濮州).
Kǎoyì (考異) says: At that time Púzhōu (濮州) administered Juànchéng (鄄城),
and there was a separate Púyáng (濮陽) county.
According to Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志),
Púyáng (濮陽) county was ninety *lǐ* east of Púzhōu (濮州).
Pú (濮),
pronounced as bó mù.
Tián Yuè (田悅) sent his army envoy Fú Lín (符璘) with three hundred cavalry to escort him.
Lín's (璘) father Lìngqí (令奇) said to Lín (璘):
"I am old.
I have observed all those like Ān Lùshān (安祿山) and Shǐ Sīmíng (史思明) who rebelled;
where are they all now!
Can the Tián (田) family last long!
If you take this opportunity to abandon rebellion and follow righteousness,
this will be you spreading your father's name to later generations."
He bit his arm and bid farewell.
Lín (璘) then, with his deputy Lǐ Yáo (李瑤), led his troops to surrender to Mǎ Suì (馬燧).
Yuè (悅) arrested and exterminated Lín's (璘) family,
and Lìngqí (令奇) died cursing and scolding.
Yáo's (瑤) father Zàichūn (再春) surrendered with Bózhōu (博州),
Yuè's (悅) paternal cousin Áng (昂) surrendered with Míngzhōu (洺州),
and Wáng Guāngjìn (王光進) surrendered with Chángqiáo (長橋).
Over ten days after Yuè (悅) entered the city,
Mǎ Suì (馬燧) and the other armies finally arrived at the city walls,
attacked it,
but could not overcome it.
3 On the day of Bǐngyín,
Lǐ Wéiyuè dispatched troops with Méng Yòu to defend Shùlù.
Shùlù
was originally Lùchéng Xiàn.
When Ān Lùshān rebelled,
Xuánzōng changed the county's name to Shùlù to suppress him.
It belonged to Shēnzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is forty-five lǐ west of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Shùlù Xiàn
was originally the land of the Hàn's Xīliáng Xiàn.
Today, sixty lǐ south of the county, the old city of Xīliáng still exists.
They advanced to besiege Shēnzhōu.
Wéiyuè was worried and fearful.
His chief secretary, Shào Zhēn, once again persuaded Wéiyuè
to secretly draft a memorial,
first sending his younger brother Wéijiǎn to court;
then executing those generals who did not obey orders,
and personally going to court.
He would make his father-in-law, Zhèng Shēn, the Prefect of Jìzhōu, temporarily manage the affairs of the Jiedushi
to await the imperial decree.
Once Wéijiǎn had departed,
Méng Yòu learned of his plan
and secretly sent word to Tián Yuè.
Yuè was greatly enraged
and sent his aide Hù Jí to see Wéiyuè,
reprimanding him, saying:
"Shàngshū raised an army
precisely to seek a banner and tally for Dàfū.
This matter was first seen in the second year of the previous volume.
Jí,
pronounced yú jí.
Shàng,
pronounced chén yáng.
Wèi,
pronounced yú wěi;
the 'wéi' below, meaning 'for' or 'to assist', is the same.
Now Dàfū actually believes Shào Zhēn's words,
sends his brother to present a memorial,
and assigns all the crimes of rebellion to Shàngshū,
seeking to clear himself.
What has Shàngshū done to wrong Dàfū to this extent?
If you assist me in beheading Shào Zhēn,
then we shall treat each other as before;
otherwise,
I will sever ties with Dàfū."
The judge Bì Huá spoke to Wéiyuè, saying:
"Tián Shàngshū, for Dàfū's sake, is trapped in a heavy siege.
For Dàfū to betray him overnight
is extremely unrighteous.
Moreover, Wèibó and Zīqīng are militarily strong and rich,
sufficient to resist all under heaven.
The outcome is not yet known.
Why resort to such a duplicitous plan so hastily?"
Wéiyuè was naturally timid
and unable to uphold his previous plan.
So he summoned Shào Zhēn
and beheaded him in front of Hù Jí.
He dispatched ten thousand Chéngdé soldiers
and, together with Méng Yòu, besieged Shùlù.
On the day of Bǐngyín,
Zhū Tāo and Zhāng Xiàozhōng fought with them below Shùlù city.
Wéiyuè suffered a great defeat
and burned his camp before fleeing.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù and the Old Wéiyuè Biography only mention Wéiyuè's one defeat.
According to Tāo's Biography, it says:
"Tāo and Xiàozhōng attacked him
and greatly defeated Wéiyuè at Shùlù.
Tāo ordered a detachment to guard Shùlù
and advanced to besiege Shēnzhōu.
Wéiyuè then led over ten thousand men, along with Tián Yuè's reinforcements, to besiege Shùlù.
Wéiyuè's general Wáng Wǔjùn advanced with three thousand cavalry in battle formation.
Tāo used painted silk to make images of suānní [mythical beasts],
had a hundred brave warriors cover themselves with them,
and with drums and shouts, they rushed forward.
The enemy horses were startled and disordered.
They were then attacked
and greatly defeated.
Wéiyuè burned his camp and fled."
According to this,
Wéiyuè was defeated twice.
The Yànnán Jì states that
Méng Yòu was defeated first,
and Wéiyuè was defeated again later.
This matches Tāo's Biography,
so we follow this account.
Wáng Wǔjùn, the commander of the army, was slandered by his subordinates.
Wéiyuè suspected him,
but valuing his talent,
he could not bear to remove him.
In the battle of Shùlù,
he made Wǔjùn the vanguard,
who secretly deliberated, saying:
"If I defeat Zhū Tāo,
Wéiyuè's military power will be greatly boosted.
When I return,
he will surely kill me."
Therefore, he did not fight with full strength and was defeated.
Zhū Tāo wanted to take advantage of the victory to attack Héngzhōu.
Zhāng Xiàozhōng led his army northwest
and encamped at Yìfēng.
Yìfēng Xiàn
belonged to Dìngzhōu.
Xiàozhōng's generals and aides were all puzzled by this.
Xiàozhōng said:
"Héngzhōu still has many veteran generals;
it should not be taken lightly.
If we press them, they will unite and fight to the death.
If we slacken, they will conspire against each other.
Gentlemen, just observe.
My army at Yìfēng will simply await Wéiyuè's annihilation.
Moreover, Zhū Sītú speaks grandly but has shallow insight;
one can begin with him,
but it is difficult to see things through with him."
Zhū Tāo later indeed proved Zhāng Xiàozhōng right.
He did not dare to advance.
Wéiyuè's general Kāng Rìzhī defected to the nation with Zhàozhōu.
Wéiyuè grew even more suspicious of Wáng Wǔjùn.
Wǔjùn was very afraid.
Someone said to Wéiyuè:
"The former Xiànggōng entrusted his heart to Wǔjùn.
The former Xiànggōng
refers to Lǐ Bǎochén.
Xiàng
is pronounced xī liàng.
And there was also a bond of kinship.
This means Wǔjùn's son Shìzhēn married into the Lǐ clan.
Now, at this time of crisis,
you add suspicion and obstruction.
If not for Wǔjùn,
whom would Dàfū have repel the enemy?"
Wéiyuè thought this was correct,
so he ordered the infantry commander Wèi Chángníng to attack Zhàozhōu together with Wǔjùn.
He also ordered Wáng Shìzhēn to lead troops and lodge them within the prefecture for self-defense.
4 On the day of Guǐwèi,
Shǔ Wáng Suì changed his name to Sù.
5 Chén Shàoyóu, the Jiedushi of Huáinán, captured Hǎi and Mì prefectures.
Lǐ Nà later recaptured them.
6 After Wáng Wǔjùn had left Héngzhōu,
he said to Wèi Chángníng:
“Wǔjùn has luckily escaped the tiger’s mouth today,
and will not return!
We should go north and return to Grand Secretary Zhāng.”
Chángníng said:
“The Grand Master is ignorant and weak,
trusting his close associates.
From the look of things, he will eventually be annihilated by Zhū Tāo.
Now, the Son of Heaven has issued an edict,
that whoever obtains the Grand Master’s head
shall be given his official position and noble rank.
The Censor-in-chief has always been respected by the masses.
Instead of fleeing,
why not turn our weapons against the Grand Master to seize him,
and turn misfortune into fortune?
It’s as easy as turning over one's hand.
If the plan doesn't succeed,
returning to Grand Secretary Zhāng
will not be too late.”
Wǔjùn profoundly agreed with this.
At this time, Wéiyuè sent an Yàojiè, Xiè Zūn, to Zhàozhōu.
An Yàojiè was
also a position of the military governor’s vanguard during the Táng dynasty.
In the second year of Jǐngyún of Zhōngzōng (711 CE),
Xiè Wǎn served as the Grand Commander of Shuòfāng,

and dispatched the Yàojiè officers accompanying the army: Zhāng Guānzōng, the Prefect of Héyáng; Wéi Jǐngjùn, the Magistrate of Féixiāng; and Yú Chùzhōng, the Magistrate of Pǔ'ān, to inspect and verify the soldiers and recruits in the three cities.
Thus, the Yàojiè position in Táng border garrisons was already ancient.
According to the Xīnshū Zhōngyì Zhuàn,
Zhū Cǐ commanded the Yōuzhōu Expeditionary Army
and was the Jīngyuán and Fèngxiáng Military Commissioner.
An edict appointed Cài Tíngyù as the Grand Judge of Dá Lǐ Sì (Court of Judicial Review), serving as Sīmǎ,
and Zhū Tǐwēi as Yàojiè.
Therefore, the Yàojiè
was indeed the military governor’s trusted confidant.
When Zhū Tāo and Wáng Wǔjùn enthroned themselves as kings,
they renamed the Yàojiè position to Chénglìng.
Upon Zūn’s return,
he secretly informed Wáng Shìzhēn.
In the intercalary month,
on the Jiǎchén day,
Wǔjùn and Chángníng led troops from Zhàozhōu back to attack Wéiyuè.
Zūn and Shìzhēn, feigning Wéiyuè’s orders,
opened the city gates to let them in.
At dawn,
Wǔjùn led several hundred cavalrymen in a surprise attack into the prefecture gate.
Shìzhēn responded from within,
killing more than ten people.
Wǔjùn commanded:
“The Grand Master is a rebel.
The generals and soldiers shall surrender.
Those who dare to resist shall be annihilated!”
No one dared to move.
They then captured Wéiyuè,
and arrested Zhèng Shēnn, Bì Huá, Wáng Tānnú, and others,
killing them all.
Wǔjùn, being the son of Wéiyuè’s former envoy—
Lǐ Bǎochén had already died,
hence the mention of the former envoy—
the character shǐ,
pronounced shū lì fān.
Chángníng said:
“When he sees the Son of Heaven,
he will again impute the crime of rebellion to the Censor-in-chief.”
So they hanged him to death,
and sent his head to the capital.
It was exactly as Gǔ Cóngzhèng had said.
In the first year of Guǎngdé of Dàizōng (763 CE),
Lǐ Bǎochén commanded Chéngdé,
which was annihilated after two generations and nineteen years.
Wéiyuè was his brother-in-law,
who had surrendered to Zhū Tāo.
Tāo had him restored to his position.
7 The monopoly on wine was reimposed throughout the empire,
except for Xī Jīng.
The abolition of the wine monopoly can be found in Volume 225, Dàlì 14, 7th month.
Què,
pronounced gǔ yuè fān.
8 In the second month,
on the Wùwǔ day,
Yáng Zhèngyì, the prefect of Dìngzhōu appointed by Lǐ Wéiyuè, surrendered.
At that time, Hébĕi was mostly pacified,
with only Wèizhōu not yet subdued.
The various Hénán armies were attacking Lǐ Nà in Púzhōu,
and Nà’s power was diminishing daily.
The court believed that the empire could be pacified within days.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
Zhāng Xiàozhōng was appointed Military Commissioner of Yì, Dìng, and Cāng three prefectures;
Wáng Wǔjùn was appointed Surveillance Commissioner of Héng and Jì prefectures;
Kāng Rìzhī was appointed Surveillance Commissioner of Shēn and Zhào prefectures.
Dé and Dì two prefectures were assigned to Zhū Tāo,
who was ordered to return to his garrison.
Tāo earnestly requested Shēnzhōu,
but was not granted it.
Because of this, he felt resentment and dissatisfaction,
and remained encamped in Shēnzhōu.
Zhū Tāo had campaigned against Lǐ Wéiyuè,
winning two battles.
When Chéngdé's subordinate territories were divided to reward the surrendered generals,
Tāo did not receive an inch of land.
Furthermore, they wanted him to take Dé and Dì.
This is why Zuǒ Shì knew of King Huán’s mistake concerning Zhèng!
He believed that by personally executing Lǐ Wéiyuè,
his merit was superior to Kāng Rìzhī’s,
yet Xiàozhōng became a military commissioner,
while he and Kāng Rìzhī were both only surveillance commissioners.
He also lost Zhào and Dìng two prefectures,
which also displeased him.
Additionally, an edict granted three thousand dàn of grain to Zhū Tāo
and five hundred horses to Mǎ Suì.
Wǔjùn believed that the court did not want his former associates to be military commissioners—
Wáng Wǔjùn was a veteran general from Héngzhōu,
hence the saying.
They would definitely seize Héng and Jì,
hence the division of grain and horses to weaken them.
Suspicious,
he was unwilling to obey the edict.
Tián Yuè, upon hearing this,
dispatched his secretaries Wáng Yòu and Xǔ Shìzé through secluded paths to Shēnzhōu,
and persuaded Zhū Tāo, saying:
“Sītú, you received an edict to punish Lǐ Wéiyuè.
Within ten days or a month,
you captured Shùlù
and subdued Shēnzhōu.
Wéiyuè’s power was shattered.
Therefore, Grand Master Wáng, benefiting from Sītú’s victorious momentum,
was able to take Wéiyuè’s head.
These are all Sītú’s achievements.
Moreover, the Son of Heaven explicitly issued an edict
stating that all of Wéiyuè’s cities and towns obtained by Sītú
should be annexed to your original garrison.
Now, Shēnzhōu is carved out and given to Rìzhī.
This is abandoning his own trustworthiness.
Furthermore, the current emperor’s ambition is to sweep clean Héquò
and prevent hereditary succession among the regional governors.
He intends to replace all military officials with civil officials.
If Wèi falls,
then Yān and Zhào will be next.
If Wèi survives,
then Yān and Zhào will be free from trouble.
Therefore, if Sītú indeed intends to pity Wèibó’s danger and rescue it,
not only will he gain the righteousness of preserving what is endangered and continuing what is severed,
but it will also be a benefit to his descendants for ten thousand generations.”
When people in the same boat encounter a storm,
even Hú and Yuè people can be made to rescue each other.
Therefore, those skilled in warfare
must first disrupt their alliances.
Bèizhōu
was a subordinate territory of Wèibó.
Tāo, hearing this,
was greatly pleased.
He immediately sent Wáng Yòu back to report to Wèizhōu,
so that the generals and soldiers would know of external aid
and each hold firm.
He also sent his secretary Wáng Zhì
with Xǔ Shìzé to Héngzhōu
to persuade Wáng Wǔjùn, saying:
“Grand Master, you undertook a plan of ten thousand deaths
to execute the rebel leader
and uproot the source of chaos—
meaning the execution of Lǐ Wéiyuè.
How can your achievements be compared with the Grand Master’s on the same day?
