Coincidentally, when Cài Tíngyù and others were demoted,
Zhèng Zhān, a Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ, mistakenly delivered the official documents to Zhāoyì to send them off.
Tíngyù and others had already reached Lántián.
They were summoned back and traveled east.
Tíngyù and others believed they were being arrested and sent to Zhū Tāo.
When they reached west of Língbǎo,
they threw themselves into the river and died.
Língbǎo County
belonged to Shǎnzhōu.
It was ancient Táolín territory.
In the Hàn dynasty, it was Hóngnóng County.
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
it was renamed Língbǎo County.
The old city of Hóngnóng County
is located twenty lǐ southwest of the present county.
Lú Yán was shocked and surprised.
He then memorialized:
"Zhū Cǐ will surely suspect this to be an imperial decree.
I request that a Sānsī envoy be sent to investigate Zhān."
This refers to sending officials from the two provinces and the Yùshǐtái to act as Sānsī envoys
to investigate the case of Zhān and others.
Shǐ,
pronounced like Shū Lì.
"The actions of the Yùshǐ
must be reported to the Dàfū.
I request that Yǐng also be investigated."
Before the case was finalized,
on the Rénwǔ day,
Lú Yán memorialized for Zhān to be beaten to death at the Jīngzhàofǔ;
Yǐng was demoted to Fèizhōu Cìshǐ.
Fèizhōu
was governed from Jiāng'àn in Fúzhōu,
named after the Fèi River in its jurisdiction.
Old records state: Fèizhōu
is 4,700 lǐ south of the capital.
Fèi,
pronounced like Fú Wèi.
The Kǎoyì states: The old biography of Lú Yán says,
"Yǐng was demoted to Huānzhōu Cìshǐ."
We now follow the new biography.
When the emperor first ascended the throne,
Cuī Yǒufǔ was Chancellor.
He devoted himself to promoting leniency and generosity.
Therefore, his governance was widely praised at the time,
and it was considered to have the magnanimity of the Zhēngguān era.
When Lú [Qiú] became Chancellor,
knowing the emperor's suspicious nature,
he used suspicions and insinuations to alienate loyal ministers.
He then began to advise the emperor to rule his subordinates with severity and harshness,
which led to widespread disappointment both inside and outside the court.
17 Chén Shǎoyóu, the Military Commissioner of Huáinán, submitted a memorial,
requesting an increase of two hundred coppers per thousand in the tax revenue of his circuit.
In the fifth month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
an edict was issued to increase the tax revenue in other circuits to be the same as Huáinán;
also, the price of salt was increased by one hundred coppers per dòu.
What was the original price of salt per dòu,
that it was suddenly increased by one hundred coppers?
Who could bear it?
18 Zhū Tāo and Wáng Wǔjùn advanced south from Níngjìn to relieve Wèizhōu.
In the fourth month of that year,
Wáng Wǔjùn advanced to Níngjìn.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
an edict ordered Lǐ Huáiguāng, the Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng, to lead fifteen thousand infantry and cavalry from Shuòfāng and Shéncè to campaign eastward against Tián Yuè,
and also to resist Tāo and others.
When Tāo reached Zōngchéng,
his chief secretary Zhèng Yúnkuí and strategist Tián Jǐngxiān abandoned Tāo and surrendered.
Zōngchéng County
belonged to Wèizhōu,
and was the territory of Hàn's Guǎngzōng County.
Jiàng,
hù jiāng fān.
19 On the day Dīngyǒu,
Mǎ Suì, the Military Commissioner of Hédōng, was granted the additional title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
20 On the day Xīnhài,
the Yìwǔ Army Military Commission was established at Dìngzhōu,
with Yì, Dìng, and Cāng prefectures subordinated to it.
Zhāng Xiàozhōng was appointed to this post.
21 As for Zhāng Guāngshèng's killing of Tūdǒng,
the details can be found in the first year of the previous scroll.
Shèng,
chéng zhèng fān.
Yuán Xiū, the envoy who enfeoffed the Khagan, was recalled to Tàiyuán.
After a long time,
Yuán Xiū was again dispatched to send the four coffins of Tūdǒng, Yìmìshī, and the Greater and Lesser Méilù back to their country.
The Khagan sent his chancellor Xiézi Jiā and others to receive them.
Xiézi Jiā sat in the great tent.
The Xīn Shū Huíhú Zhuàn writes
"Xié gān jiā."
Xiàng,
xī liàng fān.
Xié,
xī jié fān.
Jiā,
qiú jiā fān.
He questioned [Yuán Xiū] about the circumstances of Tūdǒng's murder,
and wanted to kill him several times;
his reception was extremely poor.
After being detained for more than fifty days,
he was finally allowed to return.
The Khagan sent someone to tell him:
"Our countrymen all want to kill you to avenge the grievance,
but my intention is not so.
Your country has already killed Tūdǒng and others,
and if I were to kill you,
it would be like washing blood with blood,
making the stain even worse!
Now, I wash blood with water,
is that not better?
The Táng owes me the price of horses,
one million eight hundred thousand steeds;
you should return it quickly."
He sent his Sǎn zhī Jiāngjūn, Kāng Chìxīn, to accompany Yuán Xiū to the imperial audience.
Yuán Xiū ultimately did not get to see the Khagan before returning.
On the day Jǐ
mǎo,
he arrived in Cháng'ān.
An edict ordered the payment of one hundred thousand bolts of silk and one hundred thousand liǎng of gold and silver as compensation for the horses.
Yuán Xiū was eloquent.
Lú [Qiú] feared that he would gain favor with the emperor,
so before his arrival,
he first appointed him Guānglù Qīng.
This was to lay the groundwork for Yuán Xiū's resentment over meager rewards, leading him to rebel with Zhū Cǐ.
Zhū Tāo and Wáng Wǔjùn’s armies reached Wèizhōu.
Tián Yuè, with oxen and wine, came out to greet them.
The people of Wèi cheered, shaking the earth.
Tāo encamped at Qièshān.
On that day,
Lǐ Huáiguāng’s army also arrived.
Mǎ Suì and others received them with a grand display of military might.
Tāo thought he was being attacked,
and quickly deployed his formation.
Huáiguāng, brave but imprudent,
wanted to attack them before their camp was fully established.
Suì requested that they first allow the officers and soldiers to rest,
and act when an opportune moment presented itself.
Huáiguāng said:
"Once their encampment is established,
it will become a future threat.
This opportunity must not be missed."
So, he attacked Tāo west of Qièshān.
The Wèi Shì Dìjì states: "Fifty *lǐ* northeast of Bóhǎi Gāochéng Xiàn there is Qièshān."
I observe that this Qièshān
should be within Wèizhōu’s territory,
near the Yǒngjì Qú.
"陳" [Chén],
is pronounced *zhèn*.
"燧" [Suì],
sounds like *suì*.
"將" [Jiāng],
is pronounced *jiàng*.
"釁" [Xìn],
is pronounced *xìn*.
"愜" [Qiè],
is pronounced *qiè*.
Tāo’s army collapsed and dispersed;
Huáiguāng watched from his reins,
with a joyful expression.
Soldiers rushed to enter Tāo’s camp to seize treasures and goods.
Wáng Wǔjùn led two thousand cavalry to charge horizontally into Huáiguāng’s army,
dividing the army into two;
Tāo led his troops to follow up,
and the government forces suffered a great defeat.
The number of those driven into the Yǒngjì Qú and drowned was countless.
People trampled on each other,
their bodies piled up like mountains,
causing the water to stop flowing.
Mǎ Suì and others each gathered their troops and secured their fortresses.
That evening,
Tāo and others dammed the Yǒngjì Qú to divert water into Wáng Mǎng’s old river.
Lì Dàoyuán said: "The Hàn Gōuxù Zhì states: ‘The Yellow River was particularly harmful to China,
so Yǔ guided the river from Jīshí,
passed through Lóngmén,
and dug two channels to divert the river.
One was the Luò Chuān,
which is where the river flows today;
the other was the Běidú,
which was cut off during Wáng Mǎng’s time,
so common people call this channel Wáng Mǎng Hé.’"
The next day,
the water was over three *chǐ* deep.
Mǎ Suì was afraid,
and sent an envoy with humble words to apologize to Tāo,
requesting to return to their respective circuits with the other *jiédù*,
and report to the Son of Heaven,
asking to entrust the affairs of Héběi to Wǔláng.
Tāo wanted to agree,
but Wáng Wǔjùn thought it was not permissible;
Tāo did not listen.
In the seventh month of autumn,
Suì and the various armies waded west through the water,
retreating to secure Wèixiàn to resist Tāo.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: "Wèixiàn
is thirty-five *lǐ* west of Wèizhōuchéng."
Wǔjùn thus resented Tāo.
A few days later,
Tāo and others also led their troops to encamp southeast of Wèixiàn,
confronting the government forces across the water.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù says:
"On the *xīnsì* day of the sixth month,
Zhū Tāo and Wáng Wǔjùn’s armies arrived at Wèizhōu.
On that day,
Lǐ Huáiguāng’s army also arrived.
On the *gēngzǐ* day of the seventh month,
Mǎ Suì and the four other *jiédù*’s troops retreated to secure Wèixiàn."
It also says:
"Tián Yuè and others built a dam,
intending to breach the Yù Hé water
and flood Wáng Mǎng’s old river to cut off our supply route.
Suì ordered to inform Huáiguāng that
he wished to retreat,
but Huáiguāng refused.
Bào Zhēn and Shèng also wished to fight to the death to defend.
The rebels built the dam more urgently,
and the situation was pressing.
It happened at night,
so they all retreated together."
The Yànnán Jì states:
"In the sixth month,
Zhū Tāo, Wǔjùn, and Huáiguāng all arrived.
Huáiguāng immediately wanted to fight,
and Mǎ Suì and Bào Zhēn, having no choice,
followed him.
On the sixth day of the seventh month,
Huáiguāng and others attacked Tāo
and defeated him,
but were soon defeated by Wáng Wǔjùn.
That night,
they breached the river to cut off Huáiguāng and others’ path westward.
The next day,
the water was over three *chǐ* deep.
Mǎ Suì had a distant family relationship with Zhū Tāo,
calling Tāo 'my cousin's son' (biǎozhí).
He sent someone to persuade Tāo, saying:
'Old man, I overestimated my strength and with Chancellor Lǐ and others, engaged in battle yesterday.
Grandee Wáng is skilled in battle,
which is known throughout the realm.
If the *Sītú* Wǔláng deliberates,
let this old man and others return to Tàiyuán,
and the other *jiédù* also return to their respective circuits.
We will report this to the Emperor,
and the Héběi region will be for Wǔláng to take.'
Tāo saw Wǔjùn’s victory,
and secretly envied his triumph over himself.
So he said to Wǔjùn: 'Grandee Erxiōng has defeated Huáiguāng and others;
their morale is already low.
Since *Sītú* Mǎ is so humbled,
let them go for now.
To plan gradually later is not too late.'
Wǔjùn said: 'How can four or five *jiédù*,
with an army of over a hundred thousand,
sent to fight rebels,
having just gone through one battle,
be killed fifty thousand men,
and have the face to return and see the Son of Heaven!
Now, they are in distress and deceitfully seeking to retreat.
I estimate they will not get beyond the Míngzhōu boundary
before building fortifications to await us.
Regret will be too late then.'
Tāo knew this clearly in his heart,
but still cut off the water
and released Suì and others.
After they left Wèifǔchéngxià,
they retreated thirty *lǐ*,
then connected with the Wèixiànhé,
and set up camps to confront each other.
Although Tāo felt ashamed and apologized,
Wǔjùn still harbored resentment.
They then advanced together to Wèiqiáohédōngnán,
five *lǐ* from Huáiguāng’s camp."
The relocation of the camp was in mid-seventh month.
The Bīn Zhì states:
"In the summer of the third year,
an imperial edict commanded Huáiguāng to lead five thousand Bīn armored troops and concurrently command all armies for the eastern expedition.
In the sixth month,
the army reached the suburbs of Wèi,
engaged in battle there,
and routed the Yàn forces.
The army entered the rebel camp
and seized their treasures.
Duke Mǎ Suì said: 'I have troubled these rebels for two years.
They arrived in the morning and defeated them in the evening.
What will people say about me!'
So, he gradually withdrew his combat troops to isolate their strength.
Tián Yuè said: 'Mǎ Tàiyuán is jealous of their achievement.
The Shuòfāng army can be attacked.'
So he sent seven hundred infantrymen carrying swords to advance,
taking advantage of our disarray,
pushing them into the river.
Hundreds died,
all elite cavalry.
Duke Mǎ immediately ordered three hundred archers to fight for the bridge
to extricate our army,
so the infantry was not defeated,
but the army’s morale was greatly damaged.
An edict commanded the officials of the Táng court to lead armies from Hénán to rendezvous with them."
The Jiù Tián Yuè Zhuàn states:
"Wáng Wǔjùn, with two thousand cavalry, attacked Huáiguāng’s formation horizontally.
Tāo’s army followed closely,
and the imperial army suffered a great defeat.
People trampled on each other,
and corpses were thrown into the river for twenty *lǐ*,
causing the river water to stop flowing.
Mǎ Suì gathered his army and secured his fortress.
That night,
Wáng Wǔjùn breached the river to divert water into Wáng Mǎng’s old river,
intending to isolate the government forces.
The water was already three *chǐ* deep,
and the supply route was cut off.
The imperial army had no way out,
so they sent someone to inform Zhū Tāo, and so on.
At that time, Wǔjùn was victorious,
and Tāo was secretly jealous of him.
He immediately said: 'Grandee Erxiōng has already defeated the government army.
*Sītú* Mǎ is so humbled.
It is not appropriate to force people into danger.'
Wǔjùn said: 'Suì and others have an army of one hundred thousand,
all renowned officials of the state.
They were defeated in one battle,
bringing shame to the state.
What face do such people have to see the Son of Heaven!
However, I don't mind letting them return.
“but if they do not travel fifty *lǐ*,
they will surely turn against each other.”’”
According to the *Zhǎng Lì*: The first day of the sixth month was *Rénzǐ*;
the first day of the seventh month was *Rénwǔ*.
Thus, *Xīnsì*
was the thirtieth day of the sixth month;
*Gēngzǐ*
was the nineteenth day of the seventh month.
When Zhū Tāo and Lǐ Huáiguāng arrived in Wèi,
Zhū Tāo’s camp had not yet been established.
Lǐ Huáiguāng immediately engaged them in battle.
How could it have been as late as the sixth day of the seventh month?
On the night of the battle at Qièshān,
Wáng Wǔjùn diverted the water.
The next day,
Mǎ Suì and others immediately retreated and fortified Wèixiàn.
How could it have been as late as the nineteenth day?
The dates recorded in the *Shílù* and *Yānnán Jì*
cannot all be relied upon.
However, the *Shílù* mostly bases its records on the dates reports were received,
not knowing on which day the battles or camp movements occurred.
In short, it must have been around the sixth or seventh month,
which is why it only records the retreat and fortification of Wèixiàn in the seventh month.
Zhū Tāo and Wáng Wǔjùn raised troops together.
Their goal was to defeat Mǎ Suì’s army.
How could it be that after winning just one battle,
Zhū Tāo suddenly became wary of Wáng Wǔjùn,
allowed Mǎ Suì to leave,
and thus brought about future trouble for himself?
It was simply that Zhū Tāo lacked foresight,
believed Mǎ Suì and others were not to be feared,
and let them go after they offered humble apologies.
Also, the old biography of Yuè says:
“diverted the river water.”
If the Yellow River were diverted,
there would be no need to build a dam.
If the water were diverted for a whole day,
it would not be just three *chǐ*.
Once diverted,
it could not be blocked again.
We now follow the *Shílù* and say
the Yù River water was diverted,
to irrigate the Wángmǎng River.
23 Lǐ Nà requested aid from Zhū Tāo and others.
Zhū Tāo dispatched Xìndū Chéngqìng, the commander of Wèibó’s forces, to lead troops to assist him.
Lǐ Nà attacked Sòngzhōu,
but failed to capture it.
He sent the commanders Lǐ Kèxìn and Lǐ Qīnyáo to garrison Púyáng and Nánhuá to resist Liú Qià.
24 On *Jiǎchén*,
Lǐ Xīliè, the *Jiédu Duǐ* of Huáiníng, was additionally appointed *Jiédu Duǐ* of Pínglú, Zīqīng, Yǎn Yùn, Dēnglái, and Qízhōu,
to suppress Lǐ Nà.
Mǎ Suì, the *Jiédu Duǐ* of Hédōng, was also additionally appointed *Jiédu Duǐ* of Wèibó, Chán Xiāng.
Lǐ Huáiguāng, the *Jiédu Duǐ* of Shuòfāng and Bīnníng, was given the additional title *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*.
Before this, Huáixī *Jiédù* was changed to Huáiníng Command.
*Yùn* (鄆)
is pronounced *yùn*.
*Suì* (燧)
is pronounced *suì*.
*Chán* (澶)
is pronounced *shí lián fān*.
*Xiāng* (相)
is pronounced *xī liàng fān*.
*Bīn* (邠)
is pronounced *bēi mín fān*.
25 Lǐ Shèng, the *Zhāotǎo Shǐ* of the Shéncè Expeditionary Army, requested to lead his troops north to relieve the siege of Zhàozhōu,
and to divide his forces with Zhāng Xiàozhōng to scheme against Fányáng.
The Emperor permitted it.
Lǐ Shèng led his troops from Wèizhōu north towards Zhàozhōu,
and Wáng Shìzhēn lifted the siege and departed.
Lǐ Shèng remained in Zhàozhōu for three days,
then joined forces with Zhāng Xiàozhōng to advance north and capture Héngzhōu.
26 Lǐ Mèngqiū, the *Sīmǎ* of Yǎnzhōu, raised troops in rebellion.
Yǎnzhōu was
the land of Hàn’s Xiánhuān County.
In the early Wǔdé era of Táng,
Huānzhōu was established.
In the ninth year of Zhēnguàn,
it was renamed Yǎnzhōu.
In the sixteenth year, it was abolished.
Xiánhuān was changed to Huáihuān
and belonged to Huānzhōu.
In the second year of Guǎngdé,
it was established after Huānzhōu was divided.
Fǔ Liángjiāo, the *Ānnán Dūhù*, attacked and beheaded him.
The *Xīnshū Fāngzhèn Biǎo* says: In the first year of Qiányuán,
the *Ānnán Guǎnnèi Jīnglüè Shǐ* was promoted to *Ānnán Jiédù Shǐ*.
27 In the eighth month,
on *Dīngwèi*,
two *Hé
Dōng Xī Shuǐlù Yùn Liǎngshuì Yántiě Shǐ* were appointed;
the *Dùzhī* merely managed their general outline.
28 On *Xīnyǒu*,
Yáo Lìngyán, the *Liúhòu* of Jīngyuán, was appointed *Jiédù Shǐ*.
29 Lú Qiàn, the *Tàishī* of the Crown Prince, wanted to send Yán Zhēnqīng out of the capital.
Yán Zhēnqīng said to him:
“The head of the former *Zhōngchéng* was sent to Píngyuán.
‘*Zhōngchéng*’
refers to my father Yì.
This matter is recorded in volume 217, Tiānbǎo fourteenth year.
Now, Your Excellency, can you not tolerate me?”
Lú Qiàn rose in alarm and bowed,
but his hatred for Yán Zhēnqīng grew even stronger.
30 In the ninth month, on *Guǐmǎo*,
Cuī Hànchéng, the *Diànzhōng Shàojiān*, returned from Tǔbō.
Last year, Cuī Hànchéng was an envoy to Tǔbō.
31 In winter,
the tenth month,
on *Xīnhài*,
Cáo Wánggāo, the *Húnán Guānchá Shǐ*, was appointed *Jiāngnán Xīdào Jiédù Shǐ*.
When Gāo arrived in Hóngzhōu,
he gathered all his generals and advisors,
reviewed their talents,
and obtained commanders such as Yī Shèn and Wáng È.
He promoted them to great generals,
and brought Xǔ Mèngróng, the *Pànguān* of Jīngxiāng, into his headquarters.
Yī Shèn
was from Yǎnzhōu;
Xǔ Mèngróng
was from Cháng’ān.
Yī Shèn had often followed Lǐ Xīliè in suppressing Liáng Chóngyì.
Lǐ Xīliè admired his talent
and wanted to keep him,
but Yī Shèn escaped and returned.
When Lǐ Xīliè heard that Gāo had employed Yī Shèn,
fearing he would become a threat to him,
he sent Yī Shèn seven sets of armor,
falsified a reply letter,
and dropped them at the border.
When the Emperor heard of it,
he sent an imperial envoy to execute Yī Shèn in the army.
Gāo argued on his behalf and cleared his name;
but there was no reply.
Coincidentally, over three thousand Jiang bandits
(Jiang bandits were pirates on the river)
invaded Jiāngnán Xīdào from Húkǒu.
Yī Shèn attacked and routed them,
beheading several hundred before returning,
and thus he was spared.
32 Lú Qǐng, who was in charge of government, knew that the Emperor would definitely appoint another chancellor.
Fearing that this would diminish his own power,
he seized an opportunity to recommend Guān Bō, the *Lìbù Shìláng*, as erudite and upright,
and capable of stabilizing customs.
On *Bǐngchén*,
Guān Bō was appointed *Zhōngshū Shìláng* and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The old biography of Guān Bō says:
“Guān Bō served as *Lìbù Shìláng*,
then was transferred to *Xíngbù Shàngshū*.
In the tenth month,
he was appointed *Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū*, *Zhōngshū Shìláng*, and *Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì*.”
The current *Shílù* states he was made chancellor directly from *Lìbù Shìláng*,
which differs from the biography.
It is suspected that the biography is incorrect.
The next year, he was dismissed from chancellorship
and then changed to *Xíngbù Shàngshū*.
Guān Bō merely bowed respectfully, neither agreeing nor disagreeing.
The Emperor once leisurely discussed matters with the chancellors.
Guān Bō felt he could not agree with something,
stood up wanting to speak,
but was stopped by a glance from the Emperor.
Upon returning to the *Zhōngshū*,
the Emperor said to Guān Bō:
“I brought you here
because you are upright, sincere, and speak little.
Why did you want to open your mouth and speak just now?”
From then on, Guān Bō dared not speak again.
33 On *Wùchén*,
Fán Zé, the *Dūguān Yuánwàiláng*, was dispatched
as an envoy to Tǔbō,
to inform them of the date for forming an alliance.
34 On *Bǐngzǐ*,
Sù Wáng Xiáng passed away.
Xiáng
was an imperial prince.
35 In the eleventh month,
on *Jǐmǎo*, the first day of the month,
Chén Shàoyóu, the *Huáinán Jiédù Shǐ*, was given the additional title *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*.
36 Tián Yuè (田悅) appreciated Zhū Tāo's (朱滔) rescue.
He discussed with Wáng Wǔjùn (王武俊) to enthrone Tāo (滔) as their lord,
and they would serve him as vassals.
Tāo (滔) disagreed,
saying:
"The victory at Qièshān (愜山) was all due to the efforts of Dàfū (大夫) and my second brother."
"Second brother"
refers to Wáng Wǔjùn (王武俊).
Wǔjùn (武俊) [is the] second [brother].
Yōuzhōu (幽州) judicial commissioner Lǐ Zǐqiān (李子千), Héngjì (恆冀) judicial commissioner Zhèng Rú (鄭濡) and others
(A textual variant notes: Old transmissions say
"Lǐ Zǐmóu (李子牟), Zhèng Rú (鄭儒),"
but we follow Yānnánjì (燕南記) here.)
"I request that we, along with Lǐ Dàfū (李大夫) of Yùnzhōu (鄆州), form four states,"
"Lǐ Dàfū (李大夫) of Yùnzhōu (鄆州)"
refers to Lǐ Nà (李納).
"like the feudal lords of old who upheld the chính-shuò (正朔) of the Zhōu (周) house.
We should build an altar and form an alliance.
If anyone violates the agreement,
the multitude will jointly attack him.
Otherwise,
how can we constantly be rebellious subjects,
aimless and without a lord?
If we wage war without a proper justification,
and there are no official titles or ranks as rewards for meritorious service,
what will our generals and officials rely upon or return to?!"
Tāo (滔) and the others all agreed.
Tāo (滔) then proclaimed himself King of Jì (冀),
Tián Yuè (田悅) proclaimed himself King of Wèi (魏),
Wáng Wǔjùn (王武俊) proclaimed himself King of Zhào (趙),
and they further invited Lǐ Nà (李納) to proclaim himself King of Qí (齊).
On that day,
Tāo (滔) and the others built an altar in the army camp,
announced it to Heaven, and received their titles.
(A textual variant notes: The Shílù (實錄) states at the end of the eleventh month:
"This month Zhū Tāo (朱滔) presumptuously proclaimed himself Great King of Jì (冀)."
The Yānnánjì (燕南記) states:
"On the eleventh day of the tenth month,
at the lower camp, altars were built,
ceremonies were arranged,
announcements were made to Heaven,
and they bowed their heads to declare their titles.
On the same day, they were falsely established as kings."
The old Benjì (本紀), Zhū Tāo (朱滔), and Wáng Wǔjùn (王武俊) biographies all say the eleventh month,
but without a day.
Only the Tián Yuè (田悅) biography states,
"the first day of the eleventh month."
We follow this now.)
They called themselves *gū* (孤);
Wǔjùn (武俊), Yuè (悅), and Nà (納) called themselves *guǎrén* (寡人).
Their residences were called *diàn* (殿),
their decrees were called *lìng* (令),
and petitions from subordinates were called *jiān* (牋).
Their wives were called *fù* (婦),
and their eldest sons were called *shìzǐ* (世子).
Each of them designated the prefecture they governed as a *fǔ* (府),
establishing a Liúshǒu (留守) concurrently as Yuánshuài (元帥),
to whom military and political affairs were entrusted;
they also established Eastern and Western Bureaus,
analogous to the Zhōngshū (中書) and Ménxià (門下) provinces;
Left and Right Nèishǐ (內史),
analogous to the Shìzhōng (侍中) and Zhōngshūlìng (中書令);
all other officials imitated the imperial court but changed their names.
Wǔjùn (武俊) appointed Méng Huá (孟華) as Sìlǐ Shàngshū (司禮尚書);
Huá (華) ultimately refused the appointment,
vomited blood, and died.
He appointed the Bingmǎshǐ (兵馬使) Wèi Chángníng (衛常寧) as Nèishǐjiān (內史監).
(The so-called Nèishǐjiān (內史監)
was positioned above the Left and Right Nèishǐ (內史).
*Shǐ* (使) is pronounced *shūlì* (疏吏).)
Chángníng (常寧) conspired to assassinate Wǔjùn (武俊).
Wǔjùn (武俊) had him cut in half at the waist.
Wǔjùn (武俊) sent his general Zhāng Zhōngkuí (張終葵) to raid Zhàozhōu (趙州).
Kāng Rìzhī (康日知) attacked and beheaded him.
Lǐ Xīliè (李希烈) led his three tens of thousands of troops to relocate his garrison to Xǔzhōu (許州).
He sent his close associates to Lǐ Nà (李納)
to conspire with him to jointly attack Biànzhōu (汴州).
He sent an envoy to inform Lǐ Miǎn (李勉),
claiming he had additionally assumed command of Zīqīng (淄青),
and wished to borrow a road to his official post.
Miǎn (勉) had bridges built and provisions prepared for him,
but also made strict defensive preparations.
Xīliè (希烈) ultimately did not arrive.
He also secretly communicated with Zhū Tāo (朱滔) and others.
Nà (納) also frequently sent raiding parties across the Biàn (汴) river to welcome Xīliè (希烈).
Consequently, those transporting goods in the southeast no longer dared to use the Biànqú (汴渠),
but went upstream via the Càishuǐ (蔡水).
(The Càihé (蔡河)
was the ancient Pípágōu (琵琶溝),
in Jùnyí (浚儀) County.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: The Han (漢) transport route
emerged ten *lǐ* (里) from Jùnyí (浚儀),
entered the Pípágōu (琵琶溝),
and joined at Chénzhōu (陳州).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: In the early Jiànzhōng (建中) era,
Dù Yòu (杜佑) changed the transport route.
Ten *lǐ* (里) west from Jùnyí (浚儀),
water was diverted from its southern bank into the Pípágōu (琵琶溝),
passed through the Càihé (蔡河),
and joined the Yǐng (潁) river at Chénzhōu (陳州).
This was the old route of Qin (秦) and Han (漢).
Since the Sui (隋) dynasty opened the Biànhé (汴河),
which facilitated passage to Yáng (揚) and Chǔ (楚),
official transport no longer used this route.
Yòu (佑) was the first to reopen it.
*Shàng* (上) is pronounced *shícháng* (時掌).)
37 In the twelfth month,
on the *dīngchǒu* (丁丑) day,
Lǐ Xīliè (李希烈) proclaimed himself Tiānxià Dū Yuánshuài (天下都元帥), Tàiwèi (太尉), and King of Jiànxīng (建興).
At this time, Zhū Tāo (朱滔) and others had been in confrontation with the imperial army for several months.
The imperial army had its Dùzhī (度支) providing provisions,
and various circuits supplied additional troops,
while Tāo (滔) and Wáng Wǔjùn (王武俊) were isolated deep in enemy territory,
relying entirely on Tián Yuè (田悅) for supplies.
Both guest and host became increasingly exhausted and distressed.
(*Guest*
refers to the armies of Tāo (滔) and Wǔjùn (武俊);
*host*
refers to Tián Yuè (田悅).)
They harbored considerable resentment.
So they conspired together to send an envoy to Xǔzhōu (許州)
to urge Xīliè (希烈) to claim the imperial title.
Xīliè (希烈) then proclaimed himself Tiānxià Dū Yuánshuài (天下都元帥).
38 Sìtiān Shàojiān (司天少監) Xú Chéngsì (徐承嗣) requested a revision of the Jiànzhōng Zhèngyuán Calendar (建中正元曆);
this was approved.
In Qiányuán (乾元) first year,
the Tàishǐjú (太史局) was renamed Sìtiāntái (司天臺),
and its Lìng (令) was renamed Jiān (監),
holding a rank of 正三品 (zhèng sānpǐn).
The Shàojiān (少監)
held a rank of 正四品上 (zhèng sìpǐn shàng),
responsible for observing celestial phenomena and calculating the calendar,
and for divining all unusual occurrences of the sun, moon, stars, wind, clouds, and atmospheric colors
with his subordinates.
During Sùzōng's (肅宗) reign,
Hán Yǐng (韓潁) modified the Dàyǎn Calendar (大衍曆) into the Zhìdé Calendar (至德曆).
In Bǎoyìng (寶應) first year,
Dàizōng (代宗) deemed the Zhìdé Calendar (至德曆) not in accord with the heavens,
and issued an edict to Sìtiāntái (司天臺) officials, including Guō Xiànzhī (郭獻之), to resume using the Lín’dé Yuánjì (麟德元紀),
re-establishing the *suìchā* (歲差) (precession of the equinoxes),
adding and subtracting *chídí jiāohuì* (遲疾交會) (variations in planetary motion) and the *wǔxīng chāshù* (五星差數) (deviations of the five planets),
to reproduce the Dàyǎn (大衍) method,
calling it the Wǔjì Calendar (五紀曆).
By this time,
the *qìshuò jiāshí* (氣朔加時) (solar terms and new moon times) of the Wǔjì Calendar (五紀曆) were slightly later than the actual celestial phenomena,
and the calculated stellar degrees differed considerably from the Dàyǎn (大衍) method.
Therefore, an edict was issued for Chéngsì (承嗣) and others to compile a new calendar, incorporating the principles of Lín’dé (麟德) and Dàyǎn (大衍),
named the Jiànzhōng Zhèngyuán Calendar (建中正元曆).
(*Shào* (少) is pronounced *shǐzhào* (始照).
*Sì* (嗣) is pronounced *xiánglì* (祥吏).
*Gēng* (更) is pronounced *gōnghéng* (工衡).)
Punctuated by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖), proofread by Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐)
Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
by imperial decree
After
Jiànzhōng (建中) Fourth Year
(Kuǐhài (癸亥), 783 CE)
1 Spring,
First month,
on the *dīnghài* (丁亥) day,
Lǒngyòu Jiédùshǐ (隴右節度使) Zhāng Yì (張鎰) made a covenant with the Tubo (吐蕃) minister Shàng Jiézàn (尚結贊) at Qīngshuǐ (清水).
2 On the day *gēngyín*,
Lǐ Xīliè sent his general Lǐ Kèchéng to attack and capture Rǔzhōu,
seizing the *biéjià* Lǐ Yuánpíng.
Yuánpíng
was originally a *pànguān* in Húnán.
He had some talent and skill,
but was arrogant by nature,
dared to speak boastfully,
and loved to discuss military matters.
Guān
Bō considered him extraordinary,
recommended him to the emperor,
believing him to be an instrument fit for a general or prime minister.
As Rǔzhōu was closest to Xǔzhōu,
the *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Rǔzhōu
is 270 *lǐ* southeast of Xǔzhōu.
History states that Guān Bō did not employ the right talent.
*Xiàng*,
read *xīliàng*.
He was in charge of the prefecture.
When Yuánpíng arrived in Rǔzhōu,
he immediately recruited laborers to repair the city walls.
Xīliè secretly sent strong men to enlist and serve,
with hundreds entering,
but Yuánpíng did not notice them.
Xīliè then sent Kèchéng with several hundred cavalry to suddenly arrive at the city walls,
*jiàng*,
read *jíliàng*,
also pronounced as written.
*Qí*,
read *qíjì*.
They tied up Yuánpíng and galloped away.
Yuánpíng was small in stature,
and had no beard.
*Xū*,
ancient character takes its image
from 彡 resembling beard hair.
Later people added
to form
character,
this is merely a vulgar form.
He urinated and defecated on the ground.
Xīliè cursed him, saying:
"The blind prime minister sends you to deal with me,
how dare you despise me so!"
He made the *pànguān* Zhōu Huǎng the *cìshǐ* of Rǔzhōu,
and also sent other generals such as Dǒng Dàimíng to raid in all directions,
capturing Wèishì.
Wèishì County
belonged to Biànzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: 90 *lǐ* south of the prefecture.
*Chāo*,
read *chǔjiāo*.
The government troops were defeated several times by them.
Patrol cavalry reached Péngpó to the west,
causing panic among the officials and people of Dōngdū,
who fled and hid in mountains and valleys.
The *liúshǒu* Zhèng Shúzé took refuge in Xīyuàn.
Dōngdū Xīyuàn
was west of Dōngdū city.
Zhèng Shúzé was probably preparing for an emergency to make it easier to flee west.
*Shǒu*,
read *shìyòu*.
The emperor asked Lú for a plan.
He replied:
"Xīliè is a young and valorous general,
relying on his achievements and being arrogant and presumptuous.
His subordinate generals and advisors dare not admonish or stop him.
If we could truly get an elegant and respected minister
to convey the imperial grace,
and explain the pros and cons of rebellion and obedience, the blessings and misfortunes,
Xīliè would surely change his heart and repent,
and could be subdued without military effort.
Yán Zhēnqīng is an old minister of three courts;
Zhēnqīng served during the Xuán, Sù, and Dài reigns.
*Cháo*,
read *zhíyáo*.
His reputation is weighty throughout the land,
and he is trusted and admired by all.
He is truly the right person!"
The emperor agreed.
On the day *jiǎwǔ*,
he ordered Zhēnqīng to go to Xǔzhōu to convey imperial solace to Xīliè.
When the edict was issued,
the entire court turned pale.
Zhēnqīng traveled by post-horse to Dōngdū.
Zhèng Shúzé said:
"If you go, you will surely not escape.
You should stay a little longer
and await further orders."
Zhēnqīng said:
"It is the emperor's command,
where can I avoid it!"
So he proceeded.
Lǐ Miǎn submitted a memorial saying:
"Losing an elder statesman
would be a disgrace to the state.
Please keep him."
He also sent someone to intercept Zhēnqīng,
but could not reach him in time.
Zhēnqīng wrote to his son,
only instructing him to
"attend to the ancestral temple and care for the orphans."
That was all.
Upon arriving at Xǔzhōu,
intending to proclaim the imperial edict,
Xīliè had over a thousand of his adopted sons surround him and revile him,
Lǐ Xīliè adopted strong men as his sons,
calling them *yǎngzǐ*.
*Huán*,
read *húguàn*.
creating a posture as if to devour him.
Zhēnqīng's feet did not move,
and his expression did not change.
Xīliè hurriedly shielded him with his body,
waved to the crowd to retreat,
housed Zhēnqīng, and treated him with respect.
Xīliè wished to send Zhēnqīng back,
but it so happened that Lǐ Yuánpíng was present.
Zhēnqīng rebuked him,
and Yuánpíng, ashamed, stood up
and secretly reported to Xīliè.
Xīliè's intentions then changed,
and he kept Zhēnqīng, not letting him go.
Zhū Tāo, Wáng Wǔjùn, Tián Yuè, and Lǐ Nà each sent envoys to Xīliè.
They presented memorials declaring themselves vassals
and urged him to assume the imperial title.
The envoys bowed and danced before Xīliè,
saying to him:
“The court has executed meritorious officials,
losing the trust of the empire;
the supreme commander’s divine bravery
and his achievements overshadow the world.
He is already suspected and resented by the court,
and will face the calamity of Hán Xìn and Bái Qǐ.
We wish for you to quickly assume the revered title,
so that the people of the four seas may know where their allegiance lies.”
Xīliè summoned Yán Zhēnqīng and showed him, saying:
“Now the Four Kings have sent envoys to endorse me.
They have done so without prior consultation, yet their actions are identical.”
(As Zhū Tāo was called the King of Jì,
Wáng Wǔjùn the King of Zhào,
Tián Yuè the King of Wèi,
and Lǐ Nà the King of Qí,
Xīliè referred to them as the Four Kings.
The character "使" [shǐ, envoy]
is pronounced *shū lì*.)
“Could it be that I alone am resented by the court and have nowhere to reside?”
Zhēnqīng replied:
“These are four villains,
how can they be called Four Kings!
Does Your Excellency not preserve his achievements,
remaining a loyal official to Táng,
but instead associate with rebellious subjects and traitors,
seeking to be annihilated along with them?”
Xīliè was displeased
and had Zhēnqīng escorted out.
Another day,
he again feasted with the four envoys.
The four envoys said:
“We have long heard of the Grand Tutor’s high reputation.
Now the supreme commander is about to assume the grand title, and the Grand Tutor has just arrived;
this is Heaven granting a prime minister to the supreme commander.”
(Yán Zhēnqīng was the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
so they all addressed him by his official title.
The character "相" [xiàng, prime minister]
is pronounced *xī liàng*.)
“What prime minister!
Do you know of Yán Gǎoqīng, who cursed Ān Lùshān and died?
(The account of Yán Gǎoqīng can be found in Volume 217, Sùzōng, Zhìdé First Year.)
The character "叱" [chì, to scold]
is pronounced *chǐ lì*.)
I am eighty years old,
I know how to die upholding my integrity,
how could I be lured and coerced by you people!”
(Shǐ Zhào said: To move one with profit is called inducement,
to compel one with power is called coercion.
The character "誘" [yòu, induce]
is pronounced *yǒu*.)
Xīliè then ordered ten armored soldiers to guard Zhēnqīng in his residence,
and dug a pit in the courtyard,
saying he intended to bury him alive.
Zhēnqīng remained calm,
and upon seeing Xīliè, said:
(“怡然” [yí rán]
describes a calm and peaceful appearance.)
“Life and death are already decided,
why resort to so many tricks!
Quickly give me a sword,
wouldn’t that satisfy your desire?”
Xīliè then apologized to him.
(The *Kǎo Yì* says: Yán’s biography states:
“When Gōng arrived at Xǔzhōu,
Xīliè repeatedly falsely prepared memorials for Gōng,
petitioning for Biànzhōu dozens of times,
but the Emperor knew and suppressed them.”
The old biography of Zhēnqīng states:
“Xīliè coerced him to write official documents,
asking to clear his name [Xīliè’s],
and requesting to disband his army and horses.
He repeatedly sent Zhēnqīng’s nephew Xiàn and several accompanying clerks to the capital.
The Emperor did not respond to any of them.
Xīliè held a grand banquet for his rebellious faction,
where entertainers ridiculed and insulted the imperial court.
Zhēnqīng flicked his sleeves and rose.
Later, after Zhāng Bóyí suffered a defeat,
Xīliè ordered the display of his head to boast,
and Zhēnqīng wailed bitterly.
Zhōu Céng once planned to enthrone Zhēnqīng,
and thus sent Zhēnqīng to Lóngxīng Sì.”
Based on this, Tāo and others endorsed Xīliè last year.
Zhēnqīng’s mission to Xǔzhōu was in January of this year.
It seems Tāo and others first urged Xīliè to proclaim himself emperor,
but Xīliè only took the titles of Supreme Marshal and King of Jiànxīng.
Therefore, this year Tāo and others again sent Fán Bō and others to urge him to advance, referring to him as the supreme commander.
Zhēnqīng was resolute and steadfast, guarding his integrity even unto death;
how could Xīliè coerce him into writing official documents to clear his [Xīliè’s] name!
The biography’s statement that he [Xīliè]
“falsely prepared memorials”
is correct.)
3 On the day *Wùxū*,
Gēshū Yào, the Grand General of the Left Longwǔ Guard, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Dōngdū and Rǔzhōu.
He was to lead over 10,000 campaigning troops from Fèngxiáng, Bīnníng, Jīngyuán, Fèntiān, and Hǎoshì to attack Xīliè.
(Fèngxiáng, Bīnníng, Jīngyuán
refers to the troops of these three jiedushi garrisons.
Fèntiān and Hǎoshì
refers to the Shéncè army,
which were garrisoned troops.)
Yào marched to Jiāchéng,
where he encountered Xīliè’s vanguard commander Chén Lìzhēn
and defeated him.
Xīliè’s morale was slightly dampened.
(Yào
was the son of Hàn.
At the end of Tiānbǎo,
Ān Lùshān rebelled,
and Gēshū Hàn was defeated and perished at Tóngguān.)
Xīliè sent his general Fēng Yǒulín to occupy Dèngzhōu,
cutting off tribute from the southern route,
and all trade routes were impassable.
On the day *Rényín*,
an imperial edict ordered the construction of a mountain road at Shàngjīn
and the establishment of post stations.
4 In the second month,
on the day *Wùshēn*, the first day of the month,
Cuī Hànhéng, the Hónglú Qīng, was ordered to escort Qūjiá Zàn back to Tǔbō.
(The account of Qūjiá Zàn’s audience first appeared in the previous volume, last year.)
The character "臚" [lú]
is pronounced *líng rú*.)
5 On the day *Bǐngyín*,
Háyáng Sānchéng, Huái, and Wèizhōu were designated as the Háyáng Army.
6 On the day *Dīngmǎo*,
Gēshū Yào captured Rǔzhōu
and arrested Zhōu Huǎng.
7 In the third month,
on the day *Wùyín*,
Cáo Wánggāo, the Jìedùshǐ of Jiāngxī, defeated Lǐ Xīliè’s general Hán Shuānglù at Huángméi
and beheaded him.
On the day *Xīnmǎo*,
he captured Huángzhōu.
At that time, Xīliè’s troops had fortified Cáishān,
which was difficult to attack due to its terrain.
Gāo falsely declared his intention to take Qízhōu from the west,
and led his fleet upstream along the river.
Xīliè’s generals led their troops along the river to engage in battle.
After traveling more than three hundred *lǐ* from Cáishān,
Gāo then released his boats to float downstream,
quickly attacked Cáishān,
and captured it.
Xīliè’s troops returned to rescue it,
but were too late and were defeated.
Gāo then advanced and captured Qízhōu,
and memorialized to appoint Yī Shèn as the Cìshǐ of Qízhōu
and Wáng È as the Cìshǐ of Jiāngzhōu.
8 Huáiníng Dū Yúhòu Zhōu Zēng, Zhèn'è Bīngmǎshǐ Wáng Bīn, Yāyá Yáo Dàn, and Wéi Qīng secretly offered their allegiance to Lǐ Miǎn.
Lǐ Xīliè dispatched Zēng and ten commanders including Kāng Xiùlín with 30,000 troops to attack Gēshū Yào.
They reached Xiāngchéng.
Xiāngchéng County,
in the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Yǐngchuān Commandery;
in the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Xiāngchéng Commandery;
in the Later Zhōu dynasty, Rǔ Zhōu was established;
in the first year of Zhēngguān of Táng,
the prefecture was abolished,
and Xiāngchéng County was made to belong to Xǔ Zhōu;
in the eighth year of Zhēngguān,
Yī Zhōu was made Rǔ Zhōu,
Xiāngchéng still belonged to Xǔ Zhōu;
in the seventh year of Tiānbǎo,
it was again made to belong to Rǔ Zhōu.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Xiāngchéng County
is one hundred and fifty lǐ southeast of Rǔ Zhōu.
Yán Zhēnqīng was appointed Jiédùshǐ,
and Bīn, Dàn, and Qīng were to be his internal agents.
Xīliè learned of this,
and dispatched another general, Lǐ Kèchéng, with 3,000 mule troops.
The Huáixī region had few horses,
so they rode mules into battle,
and were known as the Mule Army,
particularly fierce and swift.
Jiāng,
(jī liàng fān);
chéng jiàng (sound similar),
also sound as written.
Luó,
(luò gē fān).
He killed Zēng,
and also killed Bīn, Dàn, and their faction.
On the day of Jiǎwǔ,
an imperial edict posthumously granted official titles to Zēng and others.
Originally,
Wéi Qīng had an agreement with Zēng and others
that if the plot was exposed, they would not implicate each other,
which is why he alone escaped.
Fearing that disaster would eventually reach him,
Qīng persuaded Xīliè to request aid from Zhū Tāo.
Xīliè dispatched him,
but when he reached Xiāngyì,
he fled to Liú Qià.
Xiāngyì County
belonged to Sòng Zhōu.
At that time, Liú Qià, as Xuānwǔ Jiédù, was stationed in Sòng Zhōu.
The gates were closed for several days;
those of his faction who were raiding Wèishì and Zhèngzhōu heard of it,
and also fled back.
Xīliè then submitted a memorial, blaming Zhōu Zēng and others,
and led his troops back to Càizhōu,
outwardly showing repentance and submission,
but in reality awaiting the aid of Zhū Tāo and others.
Yán Zhēnqīng was placed in Lóngxīng Sì.
The temple was probably in Càizhōu.
On the day of Dīngyǒu,
Zhāng Bóyí, the Jīngnán Jiédùshǐ, fought with Huáiníng troops in Ānzhōu.
Ānzhōu was
the land of Ānlù in the Hàn dynasty.
Bóyí barely escaped with his life,
losing his official staff.
Xīliè sent someone to show his staff and the captives' heads to Yán Zhēnqīng;
Zhēnqīng cried out in sorrow and fell to the ground,
fainted and then revived,
and from then on, he no longer spoke to anyone.
9 Summer,
fourth month.
The Emperor appointed Bái Zhìzhēn, the Shéncèjūnshǐ, as Jīngchéng Zhāomùshǐ,
to recruit imperial guards to suppress Lǐ Xīliè.
Zhìzhēn requested that all who had ever served as Jiédù, Guānchá, or Dū Tuánliàn shǐ,
regardless of whether they were alive or dead,

On the 15th day of the *gēngxū*
day, the tax on dwelling units and the “deduction from *mò*” money laws were first implemented.
At that time, the four armies of Hédōng, Zélù, Héyáng, and Shuòfāng were garrisoned in Wèixiàn,
while the armies of Shéncè, Yǒngpíng, Xuānwǔ, Huáinán, Zhéxī, Jīngnán, Jiāngsì, Miǎn'è, Húnán, Qiánzhōng, Jiànnán, and Língnán encircled the borders of Huáiníng.
“Jiāng”
refers to Jiāngnánxī Dào.
“Sì”
should be
“Xī”.
“Qián”
is pronounced *qín*.
“Huán”
is pronounced *huàn*.
When the armies from various circuits went beyond their borders,
they all relied on the Dùzhī for their provisions.
The emperor showed great solicitude for his soldiers,
and every time they crossed the border,
they were given extra wine and meat.
The grain rations from their home circuits were still provided to their families,
so one man received the rations of three men.
Therefore, the generals and soldiers benefited from this.
Each army merely crossed the border and then stopped.
The *Shū* says:
“When awe overcomes one's affection,
success is truly achieved;
when affection overcomes one's awe,
there is truly no achievement.”
Dèzōng probably did not understand this.
The regular taxes could not meet the demand.
The Pàndùzhī, Zhào Zàn, therefore proposed implementing two laws.
These two laws
are what are called the tax on dwelling units and the “deduction from *mò*” money.
Every two rafters of a house constituted one *jiān*.
An upper-story house was taxed two thousand cash,
a middle-story one a thousand,
and a lower-story one five hundred.
Officials, holding brushes and abacuses,
entered people’s homes to count their numbers.
Shǐ Zhào said: An abacus
is used for calculations.
It was made of bamboo,
one *fēn* in diameter,
six *cùn* long,
with 271 pieces making up one set.
Six pieces formed one grip.
The required payment often amounted to hundreds of *mín*.
Anyone daring to conceal one *jiān*
would be given sixty strokes with a rod,
and the informer would be rewarded fifty *mín* of cash.
What was called the “deduction from *mò*” money was that
for public and private payments and transactions,
the government would retain fifty cash from every *mín*.
For those who gave other goods or traded,
the rate was approximated based on cash value.
Anyone daring to conceal a hundred cash
would be given sixty strokes with a rod,
fined two thousand cash,
and the informer would be rewarded ten *mín* of cash.
All reward money came from the households involved in the offense.
Consequently, cries of sorrow and resentment
filled the distant and near.
On the 16th day of the *dīngmǎo*
day, Chēn Wáng Yú was transferred to become Dān Wáng,
and Fū Wáng Gòu became Jiǎn Wáng.
Both princes
were younger brothers of the emperor.
On the 17th day of the *gēngwǔ*
day, a reply was sent to the Fān Pànguān and Jiānchá Yùshǐ Yú Dí,
“Fān Pànguān”
was a title created for emissaries at the time,
used as an official name.
“Dí”
is pronounced *tú lì fān*.
It stated that the borderlands had been settled,
and requested to send Qūjiá Zàn back to his country.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the *jiǎshēn* day,
Lǐ Kuí, the Lǐbù Shàngshū, was appointed as the Rùfān Huìméng Shǐ.
“Rùfān Mìngguān”
was like “Dáfān”.
On the *rénchén*
day, an imperial edict commanded all generals to swear an oath with Qūjiá Zàn west of the city.
Lǐ Kuí had talent and prestige,
but Lú hated him,
so he made him go to Tǔfān.
Lǐ Kuí said to the emperor:
“Your servant does not fear a distant journey,
but I fear dying on the road
and being unable to deliver your imperial edict!”
The emperor felt pity for him,
and said:
“Kuí, are you not too old!”
He replied:
“To be an envoy to distant barbarians,
one who is not well-versed in court customs is unsuitable.
Moreover, if Kuí goes,
then from this year onwards, those younger than Kuí
will not dare to decline distant missions.”
In the eighth month,
on the *dīngwèi* day,
Lǐ Xīliè led thirty thousand troops to besiege Gēshū Yào in Xiāngchéng.
An imperial edict commanded Lǐ Miǎn and the Shéncè general Liú Déxìn to lead troops to relieve them.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Xīliè’s general Cáo Jìchāng surrendered with Suízhōu,
but was soon killed by his own general Kāng Shúyè.
19 At first,
the Emperor, when he was in the Eastern Palace,
heard of the name of Lù Zhì (陸贄) from Jiāxīng (嘉興), a Censor and Supervising Remonstrator.
Jiāxīng
was the land of Yóuquán (由拳) County during the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
In the third year of Huánglóng (黃龍) of Wú (吳) Emperor Dà (大),
because auspicious grain grew in its land,
it was renamed Héxīng (禾興) County.
Later, to avoid the name of Crown Prince Hé (和),
it was changed to Jiāxīng (嘉興) County.
The Suí (隋) dynasty abolished the county.
In the early Táng (唐) dynasty, it was re-established
and belonged to Sūzhōu (蘇州).
He was summoned to be a Hànlín (翰林) Academician.
Wéi Zhíyì’s (韋執誼) Hànlín (翰林) records state: From the time of Emperor Tàizōng (太宗),
famous scholars and academicians
were occasionally summoned to draft imperial edicts,
but they did not yet have a specific title.
After Qiánfēng (乾封),
they began to be called
“Northern Gate Academicians” (北門學士).
In the early reign of Emperor Xuánzōng (玄宗),
Hànlín (翰林) Expectants (待詔) were established,
responsible for handling memorials and replies from all directions
and composing matching essays.
Later, because all imperial edicts and proclamations went through the Central Secretariat (中書),
and many were delayed,
officials with literary talent and knowledge were selected to reside in the Hànlín (翰林) Academy
to serve special imperial commands.
However, their title was still not fixed;
imperial edicts and proclamations were sometimes still shared with the Jíxián (集賢) Academy.
In the twenty-sixth year of Kāiyuán (開元),
Hànlín (翰林) Expectants began to be called Academicians,
and a separate Academician Academy was built south of the Hànlín (翰林) Academy,
to specifically handle internal imperial commands.
Later, the Eastern Hànlín (翰林) Academy was also established west of the Jīnluan (金鑾) Hall,
following the Emperor’s location.
At that time, the war in the Two Rivers region (兩河) had dragged on for a long time without resolution.
The Two Rivers (兩河)
refer to Hénán (河南) and Héběi (河北).
Zhì (贄) believed that with the troops exhausted and the people suffering,
there was a risk of internal unrest,
so he submitted a memorial,
which briefly stated:
“The key to defeating the enemy
lies in having the right general;
the method of controlling generals
lies in grasping the reins of power.
If the general is not the right person,
even a large army cannot be relied upon;
if the reins of power are lost,
even a talented general cannot be utilized.”
He further said:
“If the general cannot command the troops,
and the state cannot control its generals,
it is not only the drawback of wasting resources and underestimating the enemy,
but also the disaster of uncontrolled self-destruction.”
The Zuǒshì Zhuàn (左氏傳) says: “Soldiers are like fire;
if not restrained,
they will consume themselves.”
“Now, among those who are leaders of rebellion in the Two Rivers (兩河) and Huáixī (淮西),
there are only four or five wicked individuals.
The four or five wicked individuals
refer to Zhū Tāo (朱滔), Wáng Wǔjùn (王武俊), Tián Yuè (田悅) in Héběi (河北),
Lǐ Nà (李納) in Hénán (河南),
and Lǐ Xīliè (李希烈) in Huáixī (淮西).
‘Shuài’ (帥)
is pronounced suǒ lèi fān.
They harbor internal fears and doubts;
in a panic, they lose their direction,
and their situation makes it impossible to stop.
As for the rest of their forces,
they are mostly coerced followers.
Shǐ Zhào (史炤) said: The Shu (書) states that coerced followers are not punished.
Kǒng Yǐngdá (孔穎達) explained: This means those who are coerced to defy royal commands.
I believe that coerced followers
are those who are intimidated by force and coercion,
and are compelled to follow the rebels,
not those who rebel with one mind.
How could they wish to do evil!”
He also said:
“Without relieving immediate worries,
unexpected changes may arise.
The people
are the foundation of the state.
Wealth
is the heart of the people.
If their heart is wounded, their foundation is wounded;
if their foundation is wounded, the branches and trunk will wither.”
He also said:
“If people are unsettled,
changes are hard to predict.
Therefore, swift clumsiness in war is valued,
not clever delay.
If the root is not pacified while efforts are made to fix the branches,
then the very act of fixing
will be the source of disaster.”
He also discussed the strategic importance of Guānzhōng (關中),
stating:
“A ruler accumulates might to display virtue;
partiality leads to danger.
Dwelling in the important to control the light;
holding it in reverse is perverse.
The royal domain
is the foundation of the four quarters.
Emperor Tàizōng (太宗) established garrison militias (府兵)
and assigned them to the imperial guards.
In total, there were over eight hundred garrisons (府),
and nearly five hundred of them were in Guānzhōng (關中).
The whole empire could not rival Guānzhōng (關中),
thus the intent of dwelling in the important to control the light is clear.
As peace gradually lasted,
military preparedness slowly diminished.
Although the garrisons and guards remained, soldiers and chariots were rarely trained.
Thus, Lùshān (祿山) usurped the perverse control,
relying on external strength,
and with one move, caused overwhelming chaos,
and the two capitals could not be defended.
This event is recorded in the fourteenth year of Tiānbǎo (天寶) under Emperor Xuánzōng (玄宗) and the first year of Zhìdé (至德) under Emperor Sùzōng (肅宗).
Each pasturage had horses,
and each prefecture had grain,
which allowed Emperor Sùzōng (肅宗) to achieve a restoration.
After Qiányuán (乾元),
there were successive external threats,

The Tubo (吐蕃) seized the opportunity,

This event is recorded in Volume 223, the first year of Guǎngdé (廣德) under Emperor Dàizōng (代宗).
The concern for deep roots and firm foundations was forgotten.
Internally, Xiáo (殽) and Hán (函) lost their strategic advantage;

At such a time,

Your Majesty, thinking back to this,

Now the forces of Shuòfāng (朔方) and Tàiyuán (太原)

Cunning barbarians scout the borders,
seize opportunities and exploit weaknesses,

I have heard that at the beginning of the campaign against the rebels,

The campaign would not exceed a season,

Those who were considered a problem for the empire in past years,

‘Xié’ (攜)

Thus, it is known that the security of a state lies in its overall situation,

If the situation is secure,

How can Your Majesty not look back at past events,

rectifying the handle of imbalance and neglect to pacify the people,

The people of Hàn said,
"Qín held the tài'ē sword upside down,

Are you exhausting your thoughts and taxing your spirit
in pursuit of endless demands,
and hoping for results that are hard to guarantee?
Currently, in the region between Guān and Fǔ,
conscriptions and levies are already excessive.
Within the imperial palaces and gardens,

The Northern Army is all garrisoned in the imperial park,

Furthermore, figures like Zhū Tāo and Xīliè,

luring wolves,
