I do not know how Your Majesty plans to guard against them!
The rebellions of Yáo Lìngyán and Zhū Cǐ
ultimately turned out as Lù Zhì had predicted.
Fù [the character 复]:
read like fú,
and also pronounced as written.
The Shéncè Six Armies under Lǐ Shèng and others, and the children of Jí Generals who were dispatched,
should all be recalled;
issue a clear edict to Jīng, Lǒng, Bīn, and Níng,
ordering them only to strictly prepare defenses and garrisons,
and further declare that no more levies will be made,
so that they know they can each live securely.
Also, issue a benevolent decree
to abolish miscellaneous taxes like the Jiānjià tax in the capital and its surrounding counties,
then those who have already paid will mitigate their grievances,
and those currently residing there will find peace.
People's hearts will not waver,
and the foundation of the state will naturally be secure."
The Emperor was unable to adopt his advice.
20th day of the Rénxū month,
Cuī Zòng, the Biànxī Transport Commissioner, was concurrently made the Dūliángliàoshǐ for the four military governors of Wèizhōu.
The Biàndōng and Biànxī Transport Commissioners first appeared in the previous volume in the previous year.
The armies of Mǎ Suì, Jìngdōng Military Governor; Lǐ Bàozhēn, Zélù Military Governor; Lǐ Jiāo, Héyáng Military Governor; and Lǐ Huáiguāng, Shuòfāng Military Governor—
at this time were all in the Wèizhōu mobile camp.
Sòng Bái said: During the Jiànzhōng period's military campaigns,
all mobile camps from various circuits that crossed the borders
were supplied by the Dùzhī,
known as "food for troops outside the boundaries."
Moreover, for each army, one official from the Táishěng was assigned to manage its provisions,
known as "Liángliàoshǐ."
I note that in the early Guǎngdé reign of Dàizōng,
Guō Zǐyí, advancing from Shāngzhōu to retake the capital,
requested Wǔ Qí to be the Liángliàoshǐ.
He was Huàn's son.
Cuī Huàn was
Xuánwěi's grandson;
when Xuánzōng fled to Shǔ,
he made him Prime Minister.
21st day of the 9th month,
Bǐngxū day,
Liú Déxìn, a Shéncè general, and Táng Hànchén, a Xuānwǔ general, fought against Lǐ Kèchéng, a Huáiníng general,
and were defeated at Hùjiàn.
At that time, Lǐ Miǎn dispatched Hànchén with ten thousand soldiers to relieve Xiāngchéng.
The Emperor sent Déxìn to lead three thousand volunteers from the families of generals to assist him.
Miǎn reported:
"Lǐ Xīliè's elite troops are all in Xiāngchéng,
and Xǔzhōu is empty.
If we attack Xǔzhōu,
the siege of Xiāngchéng will lift itself."
Last year, Xīliè had moved his headquarters to Xǔzhōu.
The intention was to take advantage of the emptiness to strike at his stronghold,
and then Xīliè would surely abandon the siege of Xiāngchéng to save himself.
Before they were even dozens of lǐ away,
the Emperor sent a palace envoy to rebuke them for disobeying the imperial edict.
The two generals returned in disarray,
without any further scouts.
Kèchéng ambushed them,
killing and wounding more than half.
Hànchén fled to Dàliáng,
and Déxìn fled to Rǔzhōu;
Xīliè's roving troops plundered as far as Yīquē.
Miǎn again sent his general Lǐ Jiān with four thousand men to help defend Dōngdū,
but Xīliè's troops cut off their rear,
and Jiān's army could not return.
The Biàn army was disheartened by this,
and Xiāngchéng became even more precarious.
22nd day, the Emperor, seeing that the various armies attacking Huáiníng were not unified,
Gēngzǐ day, made Shū Wáng Mó the Dūyuánshuài of the Jīngxiāng and other military circuits' mobile camps,
and renamed him Yí;
Xiāo Fù, Minister of the Board of Revenue, was made Chief Administrator;
Kǒng Cháofù, Right Chief Censor, was made Left Sīmǎ;
Fán Zé, Grand Master of Remonstrance, was made Right Sīmǎ.
All other generals and aides were chosen from esteemed figures both inside and outside the court.
Before they could depart,
the mutiny of the Jīng army occurred, and it was halted.
Fù [Xiāo Fù]
was Sōng's grandson;
Xiāo Sōng
was Prime Minister during the Kāiyuán era.
Kǒng Cháofù was the 37th-generation descendant of Kǒngzǐ.
The Emperor dispatched troops from various circuits, including Jīngyuán, to rescue Xiāngchéng.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day of Bǐngwǔ,
Yáo Lìngyán, the Jīngyuán Military Commissioner, arrived at the capital with five thousand troops.
The Kǎoyì states: The old tradition says:
"Lìngyán led five myriad troops from his own town to reinforce."
According to the Fèntiān Jì, it says:
"Gēshū Yào submitted a memorial requesting additional troops,
and the Emperor sent Yáo Lìngyán, the Jīngzhōu Military Commissioner, to reinforce.
Lìngyán originally commanded three thousand,
but requested an increase to five thousand."
This account is now followed.
It was extremely cold,
and many brought their younger relatives,
hoping to receive generous rewards to give to their families.
However, upon arrival,
they received no rewards whatsoever.
On the day of Dīngwèi,
they departed and reached the Chǎnshǔi.
An imperial edict ordered Wáng Gōng, the Metropolitan Governor of Jīngzhào, to feast the troops,
but only coarse grain and vegetable cakes were provided.
The soldiers were enraged,
kicked over and overturned the food,
and then loudly declared:
"We are about to die at the hands of the enemy,
and yet we are not even fed enough.
How can we, with our meager lives, resist the sharp blades!
We heard that the Qiónglín and Dàyíng two treasuries,
during the reign of Xuánzōng,
Wáng Xī served as the Huòkǒu Sèyì Shǐ,
extorting wealth and goods,
and annually contributed ten billion cash,
with treasures of a similar value,
which were deposited into the hundred-treasure Dàyíng Kù,
to be used for the emperor's private banquets, entertainment, and rewards.
So, the Dàyíng Kù already existed during Xuánzōng's time.
Lù Zhì remonstrated with the Emperor, saying:
"Qiónglín and Dàyíng,
such systems have never existed since ancient times.
According to the accounts of elders,
they were all created during the Kāiyuán era.
Ministers who specialized in accumulation,
greedy for power, adorning their craftiness to curry favor,
then said, 'The contributions from the commanderies and states
should be separately managed.
Taxes and levies should be entrusted to the proper authorities
to cover regular expenses;
contributions should belong to the Son of Heaven
to fulfill private requests.'
Xuánzōng was pleased by this,
and newly established these two treasuries,
indulging in extravagance and desires,
sowing the seeds of disaster therein.
Until the loss of the country,
it ultimately served as bait for the bandits."
Thus, it is clear that the treasuries originated with Xuánzōng.
Sòng Bái said: The Dàyíng Kù
is an inner treasury,
managed by eunuchs.
During the Zhìdé era,
Dìwǔ Qí first deposited all rent and taxes into the Dàyíng Kù.
The Son of Heaven found it convenient for receipts and disbursements,
and therefore no longer allowed it to be taken out.
It is better to take it together."
Thereupon, they donned armor, raised banners, beat drums, and shouted,
returning swiftly towards the capital.
Lìngyán, who had entered to bid farewell,
was still within the palace.
Upon hearing this,
he galloped to Chánglèbǎn
and encountered them.
Chánglèbǎn
is west of the Chǎnshǔi,
originally called Chǎnbǎn.
Emperor Wén of Suí disliked the name,
and because it faced Chánglè to the north,
he renamed it Chánglèbǎn,
also known as Chánglèpō.
Lè
is pronounced as luò.
Lìngyán clung to his horse's mane and burst into the unruly soldiers,
shouting:
"Gentlemen, you have miscalculated!
By campaigning east and achieving merit,
what fear is there of not gaining wealth and nobility?
Instead, you are pursuing a plan of clan extermination!"
The soldiers did not listen,
and using their weapons, pushed Lìngyán westward.
From Chánglèbǎn they entered the capital to the west.
two bolts of silk per person.
The crowd grew angrier,
shooting and wounding the imperial envoy.
Another imperial envoy sent to pacify them was also hit,
and the rebels had already reached outside Tōnghuàmén.
Tōnghuàmén
is the first gate from the north on the eastern side of the capital.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Tōnghuàmén
is only two wards north of Dānfèngmén.
The rebels killed him.
The emperor also ordered twenty carts of gold and silk to be brought out as gifts;
but the rebels had already entered the city,
their shouts were tumultuous,
and could no longer be contained.
The common people fled in panic and disarray.
The rebels loudly announced to them:
"Do not be afraid, all of you!
We will not seize your merchandise or pawned goods!
We will not tax your houses or land!"
The Emperor sent Prince Pǔ Yì and Hanlin Academician Jiāng Gōngfǔ to placate and console them.
The rebels had already arrayed themselves outside Dānfèngmén,
and tens of thousands of common people gathered to watch.
Initially,
Bái Zhìzhēn, the commander of the Shéncè Army, was in charge of recruiting imperial guards.
Those who died in the eastern campaign, Zhìzhēn concealed their deaths and did not report them.
Instead, he accepted bribes from wealthy city dwellers and appointed them,
their names were on the military register and they received stipends,
but their persons remained in the markets engaging in trade.
Dùan Xiùshí, the Minister of Agriculture, submitted a memorial saying:
"The imperial guards are not elite,
and their numbers are critically few.
Should trouble arise suddenly,
what can we rely on!"
The Emperor did not listen.
By this time,
the Emperor summoned the imperial guards to resist the rebels,
but not a single person arrived.
The rebels had already broken through the gate and entered.
The Emperor then, with Wáng Guì, Wéi Shú, the Crown Prince, various princes, and Princess Táng'ān, exited through the northern gate of the imperial park.
Wáng Guì tied the imperial seal of transmission into his clothes and followed;
seven or eight tenths of the imperial concubines, princes, and princesses were unable to follow.
Originally,
after Yú Cháo'ēn was executed,
eunuchs no longer commanded troops;
this event is recorded in volume 224, Dàlì fifth year of Dàizōng's reign.
Previously, he had served the Emperor in the Eastern Palace.
By this time,
he led eunuchs and attendants, barely a hundred people, to follow.
He made Prince Pǔ Yì the vanguard,
and the Crown Prince held a weapon to guard the rear.
Guō Shǔ, the Minister of Agriculture, with several tens of his retainers, was hunting in the imperial park.
The forbidden park
was north of the capital,
extending east to the Bàshǔi,
west to the old Cháng'ān city,
south to the capital,
and north bordered by the Wèishǔi.
He greeted them by the roadside,
and then followed with his men.
Shǔ
is the younger brother of Ài.
Ài and Shǔ
are both sons of Guō Zǐyí.
Upon hearing the news,
he led four hundred men under his command to follow,
and then made Jiàn guard the rear.
Jiāng Gōngfǔ clutched the emperor's horse and said:
"Zhū Cǐ once served as the Jīng Commander;
see volume 226, first year.
Shuài
is pronounced suǒ lèi.
He was dismissed and resided in the capital;
this event is recorded in the previous volume, previous year.
Chù
is pronounced chāng lǚ.
I believe that since Your Majesty cannot treat him with sincerity,
it would be better to kill him
to avoid future trouble.
If the rebellious soldiers now enthrone him as their leader,
he will be difficult to control.
Please summon him to accompany us."
In his haste, the Emperor had no time to heed his words,
and said:
"It is too late!"
And so, they proceeded.
That night, they reached Xiányáng,
ate a few spoonfuls of food, and passed through.
At that time, the events were unexpected,
and the officials were all unaware of where the imperial carriage was heading.
Zhī
means to go.
Chéng
is pronounced shéng zhèng.

Bái Zhìzhēn, Wáng Gōng, and Imperial Censor-in-chief Yú Qí, Censor Liú Cóngyī, Vice Minister of Revenue Zhào Zàn, Hanlin Academicians Lù Zhì, Wú Tōngwēi, and others caught up with the Emperor in Xiányáng.
Qí
is the paternal cousin of Dí;
Cóngyī
is the paternal great-grandson of Qíxián.
Liú Qíxián,
son of Xiángdào,
was highly esteemed by Gāozōng for his uprightness.
The bandits entered the palace,
ascended Hányuán Diàn,
and shouted loudly:
"The Son of Heaven has left!
Everyone should seek their own wealth!"
Thereupon, they caused a clamor,
vying to enter the government treasuries,
transporting gold and silk,
and stopping only when utterly exhausted.
The common people, taking advantage of this,
also entered the palace to loot the treasury,
continuing
throughout the night without cessation.
Those who could not enter
plundered along the roads.
Residents of the various wards each led themselves in self-defense.
Yáo Lìngyán plotted with the rebel soldiers, saying:
"Now the multitude is without a master,
and cannot last long.
Grand Marshal Zhū, who resides idly in his private residence,
let us together enthrone him."
The multitude agreed.
They then dispatched several hundred horsemen to welcome Zhū Cǐ at his residence in Jìnchāng Lǐ.
According to the Map of Cháng'ān,
from the capital city, the second ward north of the Dōngjiē, entered through Qǐxià Mén, was called Jìnchāng Fāng.
Kǎoyì says: The old biography of Zhū Cǐ records it as
"Zhāoguó Lǐ,"
but we now follow the Shílù.
Zhū Cǐ, reining his horse and with torches arrayed,
was heralded into the palace,
took residence in Hányuán Diàn,
established strict security,
and set up drums and horns for vigilance.
One account says,
he stationed soldiers for strict guard and defense.
On the morning of Wùshēn,
Zhū Cǐ moved his residence to Báihuá Diàn.
Examining Lǐ Shèng's sequence of retaking the capital city,
Báihuá Diàn was likely near the Gūangtài Mén,
in the northeast corner of Dàmíng Gōng.
Chéng Dàchāng says: Shèng also entered Cháng'ān through Báihuá Mén,
but various sources do not record its location.
Judging from where Shèng's troops reached,
it should be to the east of Dàmíng Dōngyuàn.
He proclaimed:
"The generals and soldiers of Jīngyuán have long been stationed on the frontier,
unfamiliar with court etiquette,
(xián,
means accustomed)
(cháo,
is pronounced zhí yáo fān;
similar below).
causing the imperial carriage to be startled
and depart west on a tour of inspection.
The Grand Marshal has provisionally taken command of the six armies.
All imperial guardsmen of the Shéncè Army and civil and military officials who receive salaries
are to proceed to the Emperor's temporary residence;
those unable to go
should immediately report to their respective offices.
If after three days,
anyone is found unregistered by both parties,
they shall all be executed!"
Thereupon, a hundred officials came out to see Zhū Cǐ,
some advised welcoming the imperial carriage;
Zhū Cǐ was displeased,
and the officials gradually fled.
Yuán Xiū returned from an embassy to the Huíhé,
feeling that his reward was meager,
and resented the imperial court.
(The matter of the meager reward is found in the previous volume, previous year.)
(shǐ,
is pronounced shū lì fān.)
He dismissed others and secretly spoke for a long time,
explaining success and failure to Zhū Cǐ,
citing omens,
and encouraging him to usurp the throne.
Zhū Cǐ was pleased,
but still undecided.
A great number of imperial guards and various armies, carrying white banners, surrendered,
arrayed before the palace gates.
At night, Zhū Cǐ dispatched troops from Yuànmén,
and in the morning, they entered through Tōnghuà Mén,
arriving in an unbroken stream,
with bows drawn and blades exposed,
intending to overawe the populace.
The Emperor remembered Sāng Dàomào's words.
(Dàomào's words are found in Volume 226, first year.)
County officials, upon hearing that the imperial carriage had suddenly arrived,
wished to flee and hide in the mountains and valleys;
the Chief Clerk, Sū Biàn, stopped them.
(Biàn
was the grand-nephew of Liángsì.)
(Sū Liángsì
became a prime minister at the beginning of Empress Wǔ's reign.)
On Jǐyǒu,
Hún Jiān, the Grand General of the Left Imperial Insignia, arrived at Fèngtiān.
Jiān had always commanded great prestige,
and the morale of the populace somewhat stabilized due to their reliance on him.
On Gēngxū,
Yuán Xiū advised Zhū Cǐ to close the ten city gates.
(Cháng'ān, the capital of Tang,
had three gates on the east side of the capital city: Tōnghuà, Chūnmíng, and Yánxīng;
three gates on the south side: Qǐxià, Míngdé, and Ānhuà;
three gates on the west side: Yánqiū, Jīnguāng, and Kāiyuǎn;
and one gate on the north side: Guānghuà.
A total of ten gates.)
Court officials often changed their clothes to those of servants to sneak out.
Xiū also used persuasion and enticement to lure civil and military gentlemen
to join Zhū Cǐ.
Lǐ Zhōngchén, Provisional Sīkōng and concurrently Píngzhāng Shì, had long lost military authority;
Zhāng Guāngshèng, Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud, prided himself on his talent;
both were frustrated and discontent.
(Lǐ Zhōngchén's loss of military authority is seen in Volume 225, Dàizōng Dàlì 14th year.)
(Zhāng Guāngshèng's matter is seen in Volume 236, first year.)
(jiào,
is pronounced gǔ xiào fān.)
(shèng,
is pronounced chéng zhèng fān.)
Jiǎng Zhèn, Vice Minister of Works, fled,
fell from his horse and injured his foot,
and was captured by Zhū Cǐ.
Previously, Xiū was respected for his ability,
Guāngshèng for his integrity,
Zhèn for his purity,
Péng Yǎn, Provisional Director of the Dūguān Bureau, for his literary talent,
and Jìng Gāng, Grand Minister of Ceremonies, for his bravery and strategy;
all were highly regarded by their contemporaries,
and by this time, all were employed by Zhū Cǐ.
Zhāng Tíngzhī and Duàn Chéngjiàn, generals from Fèngxiáng and Jīngyuán, were leading several thousand men to relieve Xiāngchéng.
Before they had exited Tóng Guān,
they heard that Zhū Cǐ had occupied Cháng'ān,
and had killed their grand general Dài Lán, Military Commissioner of Lǒngyòu.
They dispersed and returned to Zhū Cǐ.
Zhū Cǐ had previously commanded Fèngxiáng and Jīngyuán,
so the troops from these two garrisons, upon hearing of the rebellion, all returned to him.
(Tóng,
pronounced tóng.)
(shǐ,
pronounced shū lì fān.)
The plan for rebellion was thus settled.
He appointed Yuán Xiū as Jīngzhào Yǐn and concurrent Pàndùzhī,
and Lǐ Zhōngchén as Huángchéng Shǐ.
(According to the Táng Liù Diǎn: The Imperial City was in the middle of the capital city,
five *lǐ* and
one hundred fifteen *bù* from east to west,
and three *lǐ* and
one hundred forty *bù* from north to south.
On the south side were three gates,
the central one called Zhūquè,
the left Ānshàng,
and the right Hánguāng.
On the east side were two gates,
the northern one called Yánxǐ,
and the southern one Jǐngfēng.
On the west side were two gates,
the northern one called Ānfú,
and the southern one Shùnyì.
Within it,
to the right were the Altar of Land and Grain,
and to the left the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
with the offices of all officials arrayed between them.
Before the Kāiyuán era of the Tang,
the director of city gates was in charge of the opening and closing of the various gates of the Imperial City;
after the middle period,
the office of Huángchéng Shǐ was established.)
The six armies of the imperial guard
were all expected to follow the imperial carriage.
On Xīnhài,
Hún Jiān was appointed Jīngjī Wèiběi Jiédùshǐ,
Bái Zhìzhēn, Commander of the Imperial Hunting Park and traveling Marshal, was appointed Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ,
Línghú Jiàn was appointed Zhōngjūn Gǔjiǎoshǐ,
and Hóu Zhòngzhuāng, Commander of the Imperial Hunting Park for the Shéncè Army, was appointed General of the Left Guard and concurrent Fèngtiān Fángchéng Shǐ.
Zhū Cǐ, seeing that Sī nóng qīng Duàn Xiùshí had long lost control of military power—
Duàn Xiùshí lost military power, see volume 226, first year—
dispatched several dozen horsemen to summon him.
Xiùshí closed his gate and resisted them.
The horsemen scaled the wall and entered,
seizing him by force.
Xiùshí, realizing he could not escape,
said to his family:
"The state is in peril.
Where can I flee?
I must die for the country;
you, my children, should each seek to preserve your lives."
Then he went to see Cǐ.
Cǐ was delighted and said:
"Duke Duàn has come,
my affair is settled."
He invited him to sit and asked for his counsel.
Xiùshí advised him, saying:
"You were originally known throughout the world for your loyalty and righteousness—
referring to Cǐ's ability to relinquish his command and return to court, and to sever ties with his brother Tāo—
(Shuō is pronounced 'shì ruì fān.')
but suddenly became unrestrained,
causing the imperial carriage to flee.
The inadequacy of rewards and gifts
is the fault of the officials in charge;
how could the Son of Heaven know about it?
You should use this to enlighten your generals and soldiers,
show them the consequences of their actions,
welcome the imperial carriage,
and restore it to the palace.
This would be a功 of the greatest magnitude!"
Cǐ was silent and displeased.
However, considering that both he and Xiùshí had been dismissed by the court,
he entrusted his heart to him.
Zuǒ xiāo wèi jiāngjūn Liú Hǎibīn, Jīngyuán dōu yú hòu Hé Mínglǐ, and Kǒngmùguān Qí Língyuè,
all of whom Xiùshí had always held in high regard,
secretly plotted with Xiùshí to assassinate Cǐ
and welcome the imperial carriage.
When the Emperor first arrived at Fèngtiān,
he issued an edict to summon troops from nearby regions for reinforcement.
Someone submitted a memorial, saying:
"Zhū Cǐ was enthroned by rebellious soldiers,
and he is coming to attack the city.
It is advisable to prepare defenses early."
Lú Jiànchǐ angrily declared:
"Zhū Cǐ is loyal and steadfast;
no other minister can compare.
How can you say he joined the rebellion
and wound the heart of a great minister!
I ask to pledge my hundred lives that he will not rebel."
The Emperor also agreed.
He also heard that various ministers were urging Cǐ to welcome the Emperor,
so he decreed that all supporting troops from various circuits should encamp thirty *lǐ* outside the city.
Jiāng Gōngfǔ advised:
"Currently, the imperial guard is few and weak;
we must not be insufficiently vigilant.
If Cǐ is truly loyal and welcomes you,
why fear having many soldiers?
If he is not,
preparation prevents trouble."
The Emperor then summoned all the supporting troops into the city.
Lú Jiànchǐ and Bái Zhìzhēn said to the Emperor:
"Your subjects observe Zhū Cǐ's intentions;
he will surely not rebel.
We request that a great minister be chosen to go to the capital to offer comfort and investigate him."
The Emperor saw that all his
attendant ministers were fearful and hesitant,
none daring to go;
only Jīnwú jiāngjūn Wú Xù requested to go,
and the Emperor was pleased.
Xù retired and told others:
"To eat his salary and avoid his difficulties,
how can one be a minister!
I am fortunate to be related to the imperial family—
(Xù was the brother of Empress Zhāngjìng.)
(Xù is pronounced 'xú lǚ fān.')
(Nán is pronounced 'nǎi dàn fān';
the same below.)
But the entire court lacks ministers who dare face difficulties,
which leaves the Emperor's heart full of vexation!"
(Qiànqiàn means vexed or discontented.)
(Cháo is pronounced 'zhí yáo fān.')
(Qiàn is pronounced 'kǔ diàn fān.')
Cǐ's rebellious intentions were already firm.
Although he feigned obedience and
housed Xù in the guest hall,
he soon killed him.
(Xù was the elder brother of Còu.)
Cǐ sent Jīngyuán bīngmǎshǐ Hán Mín with three thousand elite soldiers,
ostensibly to welcome the imperial carriage,
but in reality to attack Fèngtiān.
At that time, Fèngtiān's defenses were weak.
Duàn Xiùshí said to Qí Língyuè:
"The situation is urgent!"
He made Língyuè falsely produce a tally from Yáo Lìngyán,
ordering Mín to return for now,
saying he should set off with the main army.
As Yáo Lìngyán's seal had not yet been stolen,
Xiùshí inverted the Sī nóng's seal to stamp the tally,
and recruited a swift runner to pursue Mín.
When Mín reached Luòyì—
(Luòyì is a place name.
Shǐ Zhào said it was the relay station at Luògǔ Pass.
I note that if Hán Mín reached the relay station at Luògǔ Pass,
he would have already passed Fèngtiān and gone southwest.
Zhào's explanation is incorrect.
However, the location of Luòyì is unknown.)
Xiùshí said to his co-conspirators:
"If Mín comes,
none of us will survive!
I will directly seize Cǐ and kill him;
if I fail, I will die.
I will never be his subject!"
He then ordered Liú Hǎibīn and Hé Mínglǐ to secretly recruit soldiers within the army,
intending for them to respond from outside.
When Mín's troops arrived,
Cǐ and Lìngyán were greatly alarmed;
Qí Língyuè alone took responsibility and died,
not implicating Xiùshí and the others.
On this day,
Zhū Cǐ summoned Lǐ Zhōngchén, Yuán Xiū, Yáo Lìngyán, and Xiù Shí to discuss the matter of claiming emperorship.
Xiù Shí suddenly rose,
snatched Yuán Xiū's ivory tablet.
In the early Wǔdé reign,
following the old Sui system,
officials of the fifth rank and above held ivory tablets,
those of the third rank and below had tablets that were straight at the back and angled at the front,
while those of the fifth rank and above had tablets curved at the back.
From that time onward,
they were uniformly round at the top and square at the bottom,
never distinguishing.
He cursed loudly,
"Mad bandit!
I regret not having torn you into ten thousand pieces;
how could I join you in rebellion!"
Then he struck Zhū Cǐ with the tablet.
Zhū Cǐ raised his hand to block it,
only for it to hit his forehead,
splashing blood onto the ground.
Zhū Cǐ and Xiù Shí struggled fiercely.
Those nearby were startled and aghast,
not knowing what to do.
Hǎi Bīn dared not advance,
and fled amidst the chaos.
Lǐ Zhōngchén rushed forward to assist Zhū Cǐ,
who was then able to crawl away and escape.
Xiù Shí, knowing the deed could not be accomplished,
said to Zhū Cǐ's partisans,
"I will not rebel with you!
Why don't you kill me!"
The crowd rushed forward to kill him.
Zhū Cǐ, holding his hand to stem the blood with one hand,
and stopping his men with the other, said,
"He is a righteous man!
Do not kill him."
After Xiù Shí died,
Zhū Cǐ wept for him very sorrowfully,
and buried him with the rites of a third-rank official.
According to Tang regulations: the Minister of Agriculture (Sī nóng qīng)
was of the third rank, secondary.
Two days later,
he was captured
and killed.
The "Kǎo Yì" states: Duàn Gōng's "Bié Zhuàn" says:
"On the night of the fifth,
Zhū Cǐ sent the Jiāngyuán generals Lǐ Zhōngchén and Gāo Áng, leading five thousand elite troops to attack Fèngtian.
On the sixth,
the bandit Zhū Cǐ again ordered the Army Commander Hán Mín to lead two thousand cavalry and infantry to follow."
The "Fèngtian Jì" says:
"Xiù Shí and Hǎi Bīn secretly plotted to execute Zhū Cǐ,
pretending to enter
and requesting a private discussion of affairs,
while Hǎi Bīn had placed a dagger in his boot,
intending to act in concert,
but was discovered by the gatekeeper.
Xiù Shí immediately snatched Yuán Xiū's tablet,
and struck him with it."
The "Jiù Cǐ Zhuàn" says:
"Xiù Shí and Liú Hǎibīn plotted to execute Zhū Cǐ,
and also feared that the rebellious soldiers would alarm the imperial carriage,
so they secretly made a bandit tally
to recall the dispatched troops.
By the sixth,
the troops had returned in quick succession.
He then entered to see Zhū Cǐ with Hǎi Bīn,
and explained the principles of loyalty and rebellion,
but Hǎi Bīn took a dagger from his boot,
and was discovered,
thus unable to advance.
Xiù Shí knew he could not be moved by righteousness,
and immediately snatched Yuán Xiū's ivory tablet,
and struck Zhū Cǐ with it."
The "Xiù Shí Zhuàn" says:
"He had an agreement with Hǎi Bīn
that if the situation became urgent, he would assist,
and ordered Míng Lǐ to respond from outside.
When Xiù Shí struck Zhū Cǐ,
Hǎi Bīn and others did not arrive."
Examining this: if Lǐ Zhōngchén and others had already led five thousand men to attack Fèngtian,
then even if Xiù Shí had recalled Mín's troops,
it would have been useless.
Moreover, if Hǎi Bīn had been discovered taking a dagger from his boot by a bandit,
he would have died on the spot;
how could he have escaped again!
If he was discovered by a gatekeeper,
he should also have been captured immediately,
and with the incident clearly known,
the bandits would have been prepared for it,
and Xiù Shí would not have been able to act either!
These several accounts
are all probably hard to believe.
For now, we only preserve what is credible from Duàn Gōng's "Xíng Zhuàng," "Xìng Fèngtian Lù," and the "Jiù Zhuàn."
Míng Lǐ followed Zhū Cǐ to attack Fèngtian,
and again plotted to kill Zhū Cǐ,
and also died.
The history mentions him at the end.
"Fù"
is pronounced "fú yòu."
He regretted that the trust placed in them was not fully realized,
and wept for a long time.
24 Rénzǐ:
Lǐ Chāngnǎo, the Supervisor of the Imperial Treasury (Shàofǔ Jiān), was appointed Jīngjī and Wèinán Military Commissioner (Jiéduúshǐ).
25 Zhāng Yì, Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng and concurrently Grand Minister (Tóng Píngzhāng Shì),
was gentle and slow by nature,
fond of dressing up and maintaining appearances,
but not skilled in military affairs.
Hearing that the emperor was in Fèngtian,
he wished to welcome the imperial carriage.
He prepared clothing, supplies, and wealth,
and presented them to the temporary imperial residence (Xíngzài).
The Rear Camp General (Hòuyíng Jiāng) Lǐ Chǔlín
was a fierce and ruthless man,
feared by the army.
He had previously served Zhū Cǐ
and was highly favored by him.
Qí Yì, the Army Administrator (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ), and his colleague Qí Kàng spoke earnestly to Zhāng Yì, saying,
"If Lǐ Chǔlín is not removed,
he will surely be the cause of rebellion."
Zhāng Yì ordered Lǐ Chǔlín to go garrison Lǒngzhōu.
The "Jiǔ Yù Zhì" states: Fèngxiáng Prefecture is one hundred fifty lǐ west of Lǒngzhōu.
Zhāng Yì was preoccupied with the worries of welcoming the imperial carriage,
believing Lǐ Chǔlín had already departed.
Lǐ Chǔlín rebelled with his partisans that night.
Zhāng Yì climbed down the city wall and fled,
but the rebels pursued and caught him,
killing him.
The Auxiliary Administrator (Pàn Guān) Wáng Zhǎo and others all died.
Qí Yì escaped through a water conduit,
and Qí Kàng disguised himself as a servant carrying burdens and fled,
both escaping death.
Initially,
the emperor, considering Fèngtian too cramped,
wished to proceed to Fèngxiáng.
Xiāo Fù, the Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū), heard of this
and immediately requested an audience,
saying,
"Your Majesty is making a great mistake.
The generals and soldiers of Fèngxiáng were all former subordinates of Zhū Cǐ,
and there must be those among them who share his evil designs.
I am still worried that Zhāng Yì cannot hold out for long;
how can the imperial carriage enter such an unpredictable abyss!"
The emperor said,
"My travel plan is already decided.
I will postpone it for one day for your sake."
The next day,
he heard of the rebellion in Fèngxiáng
and then stopped the plan.
Qí Yì and Qí Kàng both went to Fèngtian.
Qí Yì was appointed Imperial Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng),
and Qí Kàng was appointed Supervising Censor (Shìyùshǐ).
Lǐ Chǔlín appointed himself Military Commissioner
and surrendered to Zhū Cǐ.
Hǎo Tōng, the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Lǒngzhōu, fled to Lǐ Chǔlín.
26 The Tuanlian troops of Shāngzhōu killed their Prefect, Xiè Liángfǔ.
27 Zhū Cǐ entered the Xuānzhèng Hall from the Báihuá Hall.
The Xuānzhèng Hall was north of the Hányuán Hall in the Eastern Palace.
He changed the era name to Yìngtiān.
Guǐchǒu:
Zhū Cǐ appointed Yáo Lìngyán as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Commander-in-Chief of Guānnèi (Guānnèi Yuánshuài);
Lǐ Zhōngchén as Minister of Works (Sīkōng) and concurrently Palace Attendant;
Yuán Xiū as Palace Secretariat Imperial Academician (Zhōngshū Shìláng), concurrently Grand Minister, and Director of Finance (Pàndùzhī);
Jiǎng Zhèn as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shìláng);
Fán Xì as Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shìláng);
Péng Yǎn as Palace Secretariat Drafter (Zhōngshū Shèrén);
and the others, such as Zhāng Guāngshèng, were each granted offices of varying ranks.
He established his brother Tāo as Imperial Younger Brother (Huáng Tàidì).
Yáo Lìngyán and Yuán Xiū jointly managed court affairs.
All of Zhū Cǐ's plans, appointments, removals, military campaigns, and provisions
were reported to Yuán Xiū.
Yuán Xiū advised Zhū Cǐ to eliminate the imperial clan members in the capital to cut off people's hopes,
killing seventy-seven princes, imperial sons, and imperial grandsons.
Soon after, he also appointed Jiǎng Zhèn as Palace Gate Secretariat Imperial Academician (Ménxià Shìláng)
and Lǐ Zǐpíng as Remonstrance Grand Master (Jiànyì Dàfū),
both concurrently Grand Ministers.
Jiǎng Zhèn was worried and fearful,
always carrying a knife, intending to commit suicide,
and also wanted to escape,
but being timid by nature,
he ultimately did not succeed.
Yuán Xiū advised Zhū Cǐ to kill the court officials who were in hiding to intimidate the rest.
Jiǎng Zhèn strenuously saved them,
and many were preserved thanks to him.
Fán Xì drafted the proclamation for Zhū Cǐ.
Once it was completed,
he took poison and died.
Fán Xì, if he had refused Zhū Cǐ's order
not to draft the proclamation,
would have merely died.
To die after drafting the proclamation,
what righteousness is there in that!
When caught by the rebels,
Yǎn refused to eat, feigning illness,
and secretly escaped to safety.
28 Gēshū Yào, having exhausted his provisions,
abandoned Xiāngchéng and fled to Luòyáng.
Lǐ Xīliè captured Xiāngchéng.
29 Li Guān, Right Longwǔ General, with over a thousand palace guards, followed the Emperor to Fèngtiān.
The Emperor entrusted him with recruiting,
and in a few days,
he gathered over five thousand men,
arrayed them in the main thoroughfares,
with their flags and drums strictly ordered.
The city residents were emboldened by this.
When Yáo Lìngyán went east,
Jīngzhōu was to the west,
hence rescuing Xiāngchéng was considered going east.
Yáo Kuàng, Administrator of Húozhōng and acting Jīngzhōu Prefect,
heard that the Emperor had journeyed to Fèngtiān.
He gathered his officers and soldiers and wept bitterly,
inspiring them with loyalty and righteousness.
He dispatched over a hundred carts of armored soldiers and weaponry,
delivering them overnight to the provisional capital.
"Overnight" means traveling
from evening until dawn.
Upon receiving them,
the morale of the soldiers greatly increased.
An imperial edict appointed Yáo Kuàng as Jīngyuán Military Governor of the Four Garrisons and Běitíng Field Army,
and Kuàng as Army Administrator.
30 A few days after the Emperor arrived in Fèngtiān,
Cuī Níng, Right Púshè and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, finally arrived.
The Emperor was extremely pleased,
and offered him exceptional comfort and praise.
Cuī Níng, having governed Xīchuān,
had a formidable reputation.
His arrival in a time of crisis
could stabilize the hearts of the people,
hence the Emperor's extreme pleasure and exceptional comfort and praise.
Láo (勞),
means "to comfort and praise."
Níng said to his confidants:
"The Emperor is brilliant and martial,
quick to accept good advice,
but he was misled by Lú Qǐ,
which brought us to this! "
With that, he shed tears.
Wáng Hóng heard of this,
and conspired with Lú Qǐ to entrap him.
Hóng reported to the Emperor:
"Your servant and Níng both left the capital,
but Níng frequently dismounted to relieve himself,
and took a long time to arrive,
suggesting he was looking around with other intentions."
Coincidentally, Zhū Cǐ issued an edict,
appointing Liǔ Hún, Left Chéng, as Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and Níng as Zhōngshū Lìng.
Liǔ Hún,
from Xiāngyáng,
was at that time in hiding in the mountains and valleys.
Hóng ordered Kāng Zhàn, the Zhöuzhì Commandant, to forge a letter from Níng to Zhū Cǐ,
and present it.
He then slandered Níng, claiming he had allied with Zhū Cǐ,
promising to be an internal accomplice,
which was why he arrived late.
On the Yǐmǎo day,
the Emperor sent a eunuch to lead Níng to a tent,
saying an imperial secret decree was to be announced.
Two strongmen then strangled him from behind.
Everyone inside and outside the court proclaimed his innocence;
the Emperor, hearing this,
pardoned his family.
31 Zhū Cǐ sent an envoy with a letter to Zhū Tāo,
stating:
"The land of Sānqín will be pacified in a matter of days;
the north of the Great River is entrusted to you for elimination and destruction.
I will meet you in Luòyáng."
Tāo received the letter,
displayed it to his army and administration,
and circulated official documents to various circuits,
to boast about himself.
32 The Emperor sent a eunuch to report the difficulties to the Wèixiàn Field Army.
The Wèixiàn Field Army
comprised Mǎ Suì's armies, which were attacking Tián Yuè.
"Nán" (難)
means "difficulties."
Lǐ Huáiguāng led his troops to Cháng'ān.
This paved the way for Lǐ Huáiguāng to rescue Fèngtiān and defeat Zhū Cǐ.
"Shuài" (帥)
is pronounced "shuài."
Mǎ Suì returned to Tàiyuán,
Lǐ Jiù returned to Héyáng.
33 On the Dīngsì day,
Xiāo Fù, Hùbù Shàngshū, was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū;
Liú Cóngyī, Lìbù Lángzhōng, was appointed Xíngbù Shìláng;
Jiāng Gōngfǔ, Hànlín Xuéshì, was appointed Jiànyì Dàfū.
All were concurrently Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
34 Zhū Cǐ personally led his forces to pressure Fèngtiān;
his army was very strong.
He appointed Yáo Lìngyán as Marshal,
with Zhāng Guāngshèng as his deputy.
Lǐ Zhōngchén was appointed Jīngzhào Yǐn and Imperial City Commander,
Chóu Jìngzhōng as Military Governor of Tóng and Huá prefectures and other areas, and King of Tuòdōng,
to defend against the armies east of the pass.
Lǐ Rìyuè was appointed Commander of the Western Vanguard and Strategy Commissioner.
Hán Yóuhuái, Acting Bīnníng Commander,
Lùn Wéimíng, Qìngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Zhái Wénxiù, Supervising Eunuch,
received an imperial edict to lead three thousand troops to resist Cǐ at Biànqiáo,
and they encountered Cǐ at Lǐquán.
Yóuhuái wanted to return quickly to Fèngtiān,
but Wénxiù said:
"If we head towards Fèngtiān,
the rebels will follow.
This would be leading the rebels to pressure the Emperor.
It is better to encamp here.
The rebels will surely not dare to bypass us and proceed to Fèngtiān;
if they disregard us and pass,
then we can attack them from both sides with Fèngtiān."
Yóuhuái said:
"The rebels are strong and we are weak.
If the rebels divide their army to pin us down
and head straight for Fèngtiān,
Fèngtiān's army is also weak,
how can there be a pincer attack!
My urgent move to Fèngtiān now
is to protect the Emperor.
Moreover, our soldiers are hungry and cold, while the rebels have much wealth.
They will tempt our soldiers with promises of gain,
and we cannot prevent it."
Zhái Wénxiù wanted to stay and resist the rebels,
as per the imperial decree.
The talk of a pincer attack
is common military strategy.
To use an imperial decree and common military strategy to control a general
has never failed to make them yield and comply.
If not for Hán Yóuhuái's resolve,
Fèngtiān would have been in peril.
"Yòu" (誘)
is pronounced "yáng jiǔ fān."
Cǐ also arrived shortly after.
The imperial army went out to battle,
but was unsuccessful.
Cǐ's troops vied for the city gate,
wishing to enter;
Hún Jiān and Yóuhuái fought a bloody battle all day.
Inside the gate were several hay carts.
Jiān ordered Gāo Gù, his Yúhòu, to lead armored soldiers to hack at the rebels with long sabers.
Each of them fought like a hundred men.
They dragged the carts to block the gate,
set them on fire,
and the entire army attacked the rebels taking advantage of the fire.
The rebels then retreated.
As night fell,
Cǐ encamped three *lǐ* east of the city.
They sounded watchman's clappers and lit fires,
covering the entire plain.
He ordered the monk Fǎjiān of Xīmíng Temple to construct siege engines,
demolishing Buddhist temples to make ladders and ramming vehicles.
Xīmíng Temple
was located in Yánkāng Fāng in Cháng'ān city,
originally the residence of Súi's Yáng Sù.
Tī (梯)
refers to cloud ladders.
Chōng (衝)
refers to ramming vehicles.
Dàizōng fed monks to protect the state,
but now Zhū Cǐ used a monk to build siege engines to attack Fèngtiān.
"Tuò" (柝)
is pronounced "dá gè fān."
Yóuhuái
said: "The temple timber is all dry firewood;
just prepare fire and wait for it."
Gù
was the great-grandson of Gāo Kǎn.
Gāo Kǎn served Tàizōng and Gāozōng,
and was a meritorious general.
Jiān, Yóuhuái, and others fought fiercely day and night.
The Yōuzhōu troops who were rescuing Xiāngchéng, upon hearing of Cǐ's rebellion,
forced their way through Tóngguān,
and returned to Cǐ at Fèngtiān.
The Yōuzhōu troops
were the Zhū Cǐ's autumn defense troops who came to the capital during Dàizōng's reign.
The garrison soldiers of Pǔrùn were Shéncè troops.
The Emperor (Dàng) spoke with Lù Zhì about the causes of the chaos,
deeply blaming himself.
Lù Zhì said:
"The suffering of today
is all due to your servant's fault."
The Emperor (Dàng) said:
"This is also Heaven's Mandate,
not due to human affairs."
Lù Zhì withdrew,
and submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"Your Majesty’s ambition was to unify the realm,
launching four expeditions against those who did not attend court.
Dù Yù said 'bù tíng' (不庭)
means 'not attending court'.
For those below to serve those above,
all ceremonies are completed in the court.
Another explanation: tíng (庭)
means 'straight';
bù tíng (不庭)
means 'not straight'.
Rebellious generals subsequently stirred up chaos,
and fierce leaders—
referring to Tián Yuè and Lǐ Nà.
Rebellious generals
refer to Zhū Tāo, Lǐ Xīliè, and others.
Qú (渠)
means 'great'.
Jiàng (將),
read as liàng.
This has continued for three years.
In Jiànzhōng (建中) second year,
the hostilities first began,
and by now, it has reached three years.
Taxes and levies grew heavier day by day.
From the capital city
to the remote frontiers,
those who travelled faced the danger of blades,
and those who stayed endured the distress of extortion.
Thus, rebellions arose one after another,
and grievances proliferated.
The fear of extraordinary calamities
was shared by the countless common people.
Only Your Majesty, serene and profound,
has been uniquely unaware,
even allowing fierce soldiers to advance with drums beating,
violating the palace in broad daylight.
Is this not because they seized our opportune moment,
and exploited the people's disunity?
Your Majesty has trusted ministers,
those entrusted with intelligence,
those in the ranks of remonstrance,
and those in charge of defense.
When seeing danger, they could not exhaust their sincerity;
when facing calamity, they could not offer their lives.
What your servant meant by 'the suffering of today
is all due to your servant's fault,'
how could it be merely words?
Your sagely decree also states that the rise and fall of the state
are all due to Heaven's Mandate.
Your servant has heard that what Heaven sees and hears
is all through humans.
The Shū (書) says: 'Heaven sees as my people see;
Heaven hears as my people hear.'
King Wǔ (Wǔ Wáng) recounted Zhòu's (Zhòu) crimes, saying: 'Then he said, "I have the Mandate,"
and did not heed his insults.'
Both are found in the Shàngshū (尚書).
Shù (數),
read as suǒ jù.
The Yì (易) says: 'Observe the conduct to examine the auspiciousness.'
The Yáo Cí (爻辭) of the top nine in the Lǚ (履) hexagram.
Wáng Bì (Wáng Bì) said: 'The auspiciousness of fortune and misfortune
arises from one's conduct.
At the extreme of conduct,
the Way of conduct is perfected,
thus one can observe the conduct and examine the auspiciousness.'
'The manifestations of gain and loss.'
A passage from the Yì Dàzhuàn (易大傳).
Its meaning is clear.
Therefore, the intent of the sagely wise,
as unified in the Six Classics,
all states that fortune and misfortune come from humans,
and does not say that rise and fall are determined by fate.
For human affairs to be well-ordered and Heaven's Mandate to send down chaos,
there has never been such a thing;
for human affairs to be chaotic and Heaven's Mandate to send down peace,
there has also never been such a thing.
Zhèng Xuán (Zhèng Xuán) said: 'Jiàng Kāng' (降康)
means 'sending down the blessings of peace and security'.
The net of punishment gradually tightened,
resources were exhausted,
people's hearts were startled and suspicious,
as if living amidst stormy waves,
restless and unsettled.
From the court officials
down to the common people,
day and night, clans and factions gathered to deliberate,
all fearing that a change would surely occur.
Soon after, the mutiny of the Jīngyuán (涇原) soldiers
indeed confirmed what the multitude had feared.
The people of the capital,
numbering over a hundred million,
certainly do not all know arithmetic
or understand divination books,
yet they clearly understood the cause of the invasion,
which may not be entirely related to Heaven's Mandate.
Your servant has heard that order can give rise to chaos,
and chaos can provide resources for order.
Lǐ (理),
means 'governance'.
People of the Táng (Táng) dynasty avoided the taboo name of Emperor Gāozōng (Gāozōng),
all using lǐ (理) instead of zhì (治).
Some states prosper from many difficulties.
Now, the events of chaos and losing the capital
are in the past and cannot be reversed;
the task of using this to provide resources for order and prospering the state
lies in Your Majesty's diligent effort and careful cultivation.
Why worry about chaotic people,
why fear a difficult fate?
Unceasing diligent effort
is enough to achieve great peace,
why stop at merely sweeping away evil influences
and recovering the palace? "
35 Tián Yuè persuaded Wáng Wǔjùn (Wáng Wǔjùn)
to attack Lǐ Bǎozhēn (Lǐ Bǎozhēn) at Línmíng (臨洺) together with Mǎ Shí (Mǎ Shí).
The marching camp at Wèixiàn (魏縣) having dispersed,
Lǐ Bǎozhēn retreated and garrisoned Línmíng (臨洺).
Shuō (說),
read as shì ruì;

"Línmíng's (臨洺) troops are elite and well-prepared,
not to be underestimated.
If we win the battle and gain territory now,
the profit will go to Wèibó (魏博);
if we do not win,
Héng (恆) and Jì (冀) will suffer great losses.
Yì (易), Dìng (定), Cāng (滄), and Zhào (趙)
are all former territories of the Grand Prefect."
At that time, Zhāng Xiàozhōng (Zhāng Xiàozhōng) occupied Yì (易), Dìng (定), Cāng (滄),
and Kāng Rìzhī (Kāng Rìzhī) occupied Zhàozhōu (趙州).
Wáng Wǔjùn (Wáng Wǔjùn) then bade farewell to Tián Yuè (Tián Yuè)
and returned north with Mǎ Shí (Mǎ Shí).
On the day of Rénxū (壬戌),
Tián Yuè (Tián Yuè) saw Wáng Wǔjùn (Wáng Wǔjùn) off at Guàntáo (館陶).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: Guàntáo (館陶) is forty-five lǐ (里) north of Yuánchéng (元城).
From the generals down to the soldiers,
he gave very generous gifts.
Previously,
Wáng Wǔjùn (Wáng Wǔjùn) had summoned Huíhé (回紇) troops
to cut off the supply routes of Lǐ Huáiguāng (Lǐ Huáiguāng) and others.
Lǐ Huáiguāng (Lǐ Huáiguāng) and others had already gone west,
but the Huíhé (回紇) Dágān (達干), with a thousand Huíhé (回紇) and two thousand assorted barbarians, had just arrived at the northern border of Yōuzhōu (幽州).

wanting to go with them to Hénán (河南) to seize the Eastern Capital,
to meet with Zhū Cǐ (Zhū Cǐ),
promising to bribe them with women and children from Hénán (河南).
He bribed them.
Zhū Tāo (Zhū Tāo) had married a Huíhé (回紇) woman as a concubine,
and the Huíhé (回紇) called him Zhū Láng (朱郎).
Moreover, they were keen on plunder,
so they agreed.

commissioned to compile and edit.

Jiànzhōng 4th year
(Guǐhài, 783)
1. In the eleventh month,
on the Yǐhài day,
Lǒngzhōu was made Fèngyì Jūn,
and Gāo was promoted to Jiedushi.
Chǐ again sent the court eunuch Liú Hǎiguǎng to offer Gāo the Fèngxiáng Jiedushi;
Gāo beheaded him.
Historians say that Wéi Gāo thus rose to prominence.
使 (shǐ),
read shū lì.
泚 (cǐ),
read qiě lǐ.

2. Dù Xīquán, the acting commandant of Língwǔ, Dài Xiūyán, the prefect of Yánzhōu, and Shí Chángchūn, the prefect of Xiàzhōu, joined forces with Lǐ Jiànhuī, the Jiedushi of Wèiběi, bringing an army of ten thousand to reinforce the capital.
The Língwǔ Jiedushi was based in Língzhōu,
Xiàzhōu was based in Shuòfāng Xiàn,
and Yánzhōu was based in Wǔyuán Xiàn;
all were neighboring territories.
The Wèiběi Jiedushi was originally based in Fángzhōu,
but at this time had moved its base to Fūzhōu.
夏 (xià),
read hù yǎ.
The emperor summoned his generals and ministers to discuss which path to take.
Guān Bō and Hún Jiān said:
"The Mògǔ Road is perilous and narrow,
and we fear being intercepted by the rebels.
It would be better to pass north of Qiánlíng,
traveling along Bǎichéng.
The mountain mausoleum has cypress trees planted in rows
to screen and protect the imperial tomb,
hence it is called Bǎichéng.
Sòng Bái said: 'All Tang imperial tombs were encircled with planted cypresses.'
In the eleventh month of Zhēnyuán 6th year,
an imperial edict stipulated that within three *li* on each of the four sides of the cypress cities of the imperial tombs,
no burials were allowed.
過 (guò),
read gǔ hé,
also read gǔ wò.
This would form a pincer attack with the forces in the city,
and also divide the rebel forces."
Lú [Jiàn] said:
"The Mògǔ Road is close.
If we are intercepted by the rebels,
then troops from the city can sally out to meet them.
If we were to go out via Qiánlíng,
we might disturb the imperial tomb."
Hún Jiān said:
"Since Chǐ began attacking the city,
he has cut down the pines and cypresses of Qiánlíng,
continuing day and night.
The disturbance has already been great.
Now the city is in critical danger,
and the relief troops from other circuits have not yet arrived.
Only Xīquán and his men are coming,
and their importance is not trivial.
If they can establish a camp in a strategic location,
then Chǐ can be defeated."
Lú [Jiàn] said:
"When Your Majesty leads an army,
how can it be compared to a rebel!
If we let Xīquán and his men pass there,
it would be to disturb the imperial tomb ourselves."
The emperor then ordered Xīquán and his men to advance through Mògǔ.
On the Bǐngzǐ day,
Xīquán and his troops arrived at Mògǔ,
and indeed they were intercepted by the rebels,
who attacked them from above with large crossbows and huge stones,
causing heavy casualties.
Troops from the city sallied out to meet them,
but were defeated by the rebels.
That evening,
the four armies collapsed
and retreated to defend Bīnzhōu.
Chǐ reviewed their baggage train beneath the city walls;
the accompanying officials looked at each other, paling.
From the rise of the armies in the Two Rivers region to the emperor's relocation,
not a single word of Lú [Jiàn]'s did not harm the state,
yet Dézōng trusted him as before.
How dim-witted and muddled he was!
敗 (bài),
read bǔ mài.
從 (cóng),
read cái yòng.
邠 (bīn),
read bēi mín.
泚 (cǐ),
read qiě lǐ,
also read cǐ.
輜 (zī),
read zhuāng chí.
重 (zhòng),
read zhí yòng.
(Shí Chángchūn was) a person from Xiàzhōu.
Chǐ attacked the city with increasing urgency,
digging trenches around it.
Chǐ moved his camp to Qiánlíng,
from where he could look down into the city,
seeing all movements.
He constantly sent envoys around the city
to entice the soldiers and common people,
laughing at their ignorance of Heaven's mandate.
3. Lǐ Shèng, the Jiedushi of Shéncè and Héběi Campaign Army, recovered from his illness.
In the fifth month of the previous year,
Lǐ Shèng was gravely ill
and returned from Yìzhōu to defend Dìngzhōu;
this event is detailed in the previous volume.
晟 (shèng),
read chéng zhèng.
He led his troops to rush to the rescue.
Zhāng Xiàozhōng, pressed by Zhū Tāo and Wáng Wǔjùn,
relied on Shèng for support,
and did not wish Shèng to depart,
repeatedly attempting to stop him.
Shèng then left his son Píng,
arranging for him to marry Xiàozhōng's daughter,
and also gifted an jade belt to bribe Xiàozhōng's confidants,
asking them to persuade him.
Xiàozhōng then allowed Shèng to return west,
sending his general Yáng Róngguó with six hundred elite soldiers to accompany Shèng.
Shèng led his troops out via Fēihú Pass,
traveling day and night,
and reached Dàizhōu.
Shěn Cúnzhōng said: "The Northern Marchmount, Chángcén,
which is Dàmào Shān,
is half-owned by Qìdān,
with the ridge of Dàmào Shān as the boundary.
Fēihú Road
is west of Mào.
It runs north from Yínyě Zhài, passes Dǎomǎ Guān,
crosses the barbarian border,
then re-enters between Shíménzi and Lìngshuǐ Pù, and then between Píngxíng and Méihuí two strongholds,
reaching Dàizhōu.
This route is now impassable.
Only the route west of Běizhài, passing Chéngtiān Guān,
can reach Hédōng,
but the road is extremely steep and narrow."
According to Cúnzhōng, the so-called territorial boundary
was the boundary divided between the Later Jìn and Qìdān.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
Shèng was appointed Jiedushi of Shéncè Campaign Army.
Historians say that Lǐ Shèng previously was only Jiedushi of the Héběi Shéncè expeditionary forces;
now he was also appointed Jiedushi of the Shéncè campaign forces dispatched to Hénán.
This is how he was able to punish Liú Déxìn.
4. Wáng Wǔjùn and Mǎ Shí attacked Zhàozhōu but could not conquer it.
On the Xīnsì day,
Mǎ Shí returned to Yíngzhōu,
and Wǔjùn escorted him for five *li*,
giving him generous provisions and gifts.
Wǔjùn also returned to Héngzhōu.
5. When the emperor went to Fèngtiān,
Yáo Míngyáng, the Observer of Shǎnxī and Guózhōu,
entrusted military affairs to the Deputy Defense Commissioner Zhāng Quàn,
and went to the temporary imperial residence.
Quàn recruited several tens of thousands of soldiers.
On the Jiǎshēn day,
Quàn was appointed Jiedushi of Shǎnxī and Guózhōu.
6 Zhū Cǐ had besieged Fèngtiān for a month.
In the tenth month of that year,
the Emperor left Fèngtiān.
He had only been in Fèngtiān for a few days when Zhū Cǐ arrived,
and the siege had lasted until this month, making it a full month.
The Emperor once sent a swift messenger out of the city to spy on the rebels.
A "swift messenger" (jiànbù)
is what is today called an "urgent footman" (jíjiǎozǐ).
“To spy” (chān),
pronounced chǒu lián fān.
He knelt and requested a tunic and trousers.
The Emperor searched for them for him but could not find them,
and so he departed with pity and silence.
“Pity” (mǐn) meant
commiserating with his cold;
“silence” (mò) meant
having nothing to say as an excuse.
Whenever the rebels rested,
at night,
people were lowered outside the city walls
to collect turnip roots and bring them in.
The Běncǎo (Materia Medica) says: "Turnips (wújīng) and radishes (lúfú)
are commonly found throughout the north and south.
Wújīng
is Mánjīng;
Lúfú
is Luóbó."
Táo Yǐnjū said: "Lúfú is the Wēnsōng of today;
its roots can be eaten,
but its leaves are not fit to chew.
The roots of Wújīng are finer than Wēnsōng,
but its leaves are similar to Sōng (Chinese cabbage)
and are good to eat."
Rìhuázǐ said: "That which has long stalks, slender leaves, and grows tall is Sōng;
that which has broad, thick, short, and fat leaves and is squat, and has slender stalks, is Wújīng leaves."
Lù Diàn’s Píyǎ says: "According to old sayings,
Sōngcài,
when sown in the north,
in its first year, half becomes Wújīng,
and in the second year, the Sōng seeds are completely gone.
It is the same when Wújīng is sown in the south.
Sōng cannot grow in the northern soil,
just as tangerines and pomelos change when planted north of the Huái River."
Wújīng resembles Sōng but is smaller,
has a stem,
and is also called Fēng,
or Xū.
Shǐ Zhào said: "The Běncǎo Zhù (Annotations to the Materia Medica) says,
Wújīng,
northerners also call Mánjīng;
its roots, leaves, and seeds are of the Sōng category.
The Shī (Classic of Poetry) says: 'Gather Fēng, gather Fěi.'
The Shū (Commentary) says: Lù Jī said,
Fēng
is Wújīng,
and people in Yōuzhōu sometimes call it Jiè (mustard green)."
The Fāngyán says: "Fēngráo
is Wújīng.
People of Chén and Chǔ call it Fēng;
those of Qí and Lǔ call it Ráo;
those of Guānxī call it Wújīng;
and people in the regions of Zhào and Wèi call it Dàjiè (large mustard green)."
“Coarse grain” (lài),
pronounced lú dá fān.
“To watch” (sì),
pronounced xiāng lì fān.
“To lower by rope” (zhuì),
pronounced chí wěi fān.
"I, with my lack of virtue,
have brought myself to peril and ruin,
and it is deserved.
You, my officials, are innocent,
you should surrender early to save your families."
All the officials bowed their heads and wept,
vowing to exert their utmost strength until death.
Therefore, although the officers and soldiers were in distress and urgency, their morale did not wane.
When the Emperor was sojourning in Fèngtiān,
the Superintendent of Provisions, Cuī Zòng, advised Lǐ Huáiguāng to come to his aid.
Cuī Zòng was the Superintendent of Provisions for the marching camp in Wèixiàn.
Zòng collected all the military supplies and came with Huáiguāng.
Huáiguāng marched day and night at double speed,
but upon reaching Hézhōng,
he was exhausted and
rested his troops for three days.
Lǐ Qíyùn, the Prefect of Hézhōng, generously hosted a feast for them.
The army
still wanted to delay.
Cuī Zòng first transported goods and wealth across the river,
and told the troops:
"When we reach Héxī,
everything will be distributed as gifts."
In the eighth year of Kāiyuán,
Héxī County was created by separating the area west of Pújīn from Hédōng County.
They were stationed in Púchéng to the west,
with a force of 50,000 men.
Qíyùn was
Yùn's grandson.
Jiǎngwáng Yùn
was Tàizōng's son.
“Yùn”,
pronounced yú fěn fān.
Lǐ Shèng, as he marched, gathered his troops,
and also crossed the army from Pújīn to Dōngwèiqiáo.
He initially had four thousand soldiers,
but Shèng was skilled at managing and commanding,
sharing hardships with his officers and soldiers.
People were happy to follow him,
and within ten days, his numbers reached over ten thousand.
Shéncè Army Cavalry Commander Shàng Kěgū was attacking Lǐ Xīliè.
He had three thousand men in Xiāngyáng,
and entered to provide aid via Wǔguān,
stationing his army at Qīpán.
He defeated Cǐ's general, Chóu Jìng.
Chóu Jìng
was Chóu Jìngzhōng.
This is written according to the old histories.
“To defeat” (bài),
pronounced bǔ mài fān.
Kěgū
was a branch of the Yǔwén tribe.
Luò Yuánguāng, the Deputy Commander of the Zhènguó Army,
in the first year of Sùzōng’s Shàngyuán reign,
the Zhènguó Army was established in Huázhōu.
He was adopted by Luò Fèngxiān as his son.
He had commanded troops guarding Tóngguān for nearly ten years,
and was respected by all.
Zhū Cǐ sent his general Hé Wàngzhī to raid Huázhōu.
The Prefect Dǒng Jìn abandoned the prefecture and fled to the Emperor's temporary residence.
Wàngzhī occupied the city,
intending to gather troops to cut off the eastern route.
Yuánguāng led the troops from under the pass to attack Wàngzhī,
who fled back to Cháng'ān.
Yuánguāng then stationed his army in Huázhōu,
recruiting soldiers.
Within a few days,
he gained over ten thousand men.
Cǐ repeatedly sent troops to attack Yuánguāng,
but Yuánguāng repelled them all,
so the rebels were unable to advance eastward.
The Emperor then appointed Yuánguāng as Jìedùshǐ of the Zhènguó Army.
The Zhènguó Army Jìedù
was governed from Huázhōu.
Mǎ Suì sent his Military Governor Wáng Quán and his son Huì with five thousand troops to provide aid,
stationing them at Zhōngwèiqiáo.
At this point, the only place Cǐ's faction held was Cháng'ān.
The scouting cavalry of the relief army sometimes reached the foot of Wàngchūnlóu.
Lǐ Zhōngchén and others repeatedly launched attacks but were all defeated,
and sought aid from Cǐ.
Cǐ feared that common people might take advantage of the chaos to plunder.
Wàngchūnlóu was near Chánglè City,
overlooking Guǎngyùntán,
and was built by Xuánzōng.
“Cavalry” (qí),
pronounced qí jì fān.
“To plunder” (chāo),
pronounced chǔ jiāo fān.
Zhū Cǐ was inwardly troubled by Cháng'ān,
so he urgently attacked Fèngtiān.
He ordered the monk Fǎjiān to construct a cloud ladder,
several zhàng in height and width,
wrapped in rhinoceros hide.
Shǐ Zhào said: "Sì (rhinoceros)
is the color of a wild ox but blue,"
another said it was a female rhinoceros.
I (the annotator) observe that in the Shānhǎijīng,
the sì (rhinoceros)
has horns weighing a hundred catties,
and its body weighs a thousand catties.
The Huángdì obtained one
and covered a drum with its hide,
whose sound echoed for a hundred lǐ.
This account is certainly exaggerated.
In the Guóyǔ: Shū Xiàng said: "The Táng Shū killed a sì (rhinoceros)
to make a large suit of armor."
In the Zhōuguān Kǎogōngjì: "Rhinoceros armor lasts a hundred years,
sì (rhinoceros) armor lasts two hundred years."
Sì (rhinoceros) armor was indeed stronger than rhinoceros armor.
In the Zuǒzhuàn: Sòng Huáyuán said: "Rhinoceros and sì (rhinoceros) are still numerous."
Thus, sì (rhinoceros)
were common in the world.
However, sì (rhinoceros) are not commonly seen today.
The historian said that Zhū Cǐ wrapped the cloud ladder in sì (rhinoceros) hide,
but it was nothing more than ox hide.
Sì,
read as 'xù zǐ fān'.
It could hold five hundred strong warriors on top;
those in the city looked upon it with terror.
The Emperor asked his retainers about this,
and Hún Jiān and Hóu Zhòngzhuāng replied:
"We observe that the cloud ladder is very heavy;
if it is heavy, it is easy to get stuck.
We request to dig a tunnel where it approaches,
pile firewood, and store fire to await it."
The Shenwǔjūn envoy Hán Chéng said:
"In the twenty-sixth year of Kāiyuán,
the Left and Right Yǔlín (Armies) were divided
to establish the Left and Right Shénwǔjūn."
Envoy (使),
read as 'shū lì fān'.
"The cloud ladder is a minor trick,
not worth bothering Your Majesty's sacred thoughts.
I request to repel it."
He then measured the direction the ladder would face,
an area thirty paces wide at the northeast corner of the city,
and stored much grease, oil, pine resin, firewood, and reeds upon it.
On the dinghài day,
Zhū Cǐ mustered a large army, beating drums and shouting, to attack the south wall.
Hán Yóuhuái said:
"This is an attempt to divide our strength."
He then led his troops to prepare diligently in the northeast.
On the wùzǐ day,
the north wind was very swift.
Shouting (譟),
read as 'zé zào fān'.
Yóuhuái (⿰王褱),
read as 'gǔ huí fān'.
Swift (迅),
means fast.
The cloud ladder was covered with wet felt,
hung with water bags,
carrying brave warriors to attack the city.
It was flanked by armored carts (fēnwēn),
with men placed beneath them,
carrying firewood and earth to fill the moat and advance,
immune to arrows, stones, and torches.
The rebels concentrated their forces to attack the northeast corner of the city.
Arrows and stones fell like rain,
and the dead and wounded in the city were countless.
Some rebels had already climbed the city wall.
The Emperor and Hún Jiān wept facing each other.
The retainers could only raise their heads and pray to Heaven.
The Emperor gave Hún Jiān over a thousand blank 'gaoshen' from Censor-in-Chief down, each effectively providing five hundred households of revenue.
Blank 'gaoshen' (無名告身)
means 'kōngmíng gaoshen' (empty name 'gaoshen'),
where the names of those with meritorious service would be filled in and issued to them.
'Shíshí' (實食)
refers to 'shíshífēng' (actual enfeoffment).
He also bestowed an imperial edict,
instructing them to fill in the names based on the magnitude of their achievements.
If the 'gaoshen' were insufficient, their ranks would be recorded on their persons.
This means if there were many meritorious individuals
and the more than a thousand 'gaoshen' issued were insufficient to reward their achievements,
then the promotions and honors previously bestowed would be recorded on their persons
as proof,
for issuing 'gaoshen'.
"Today, I will part with you."
He expected Hún Jiān to fight to the death.
The Emperor patted his back,
sobbing uncontrollably.
At that time, the soldiers were cold and hungry,
and also lacked armor.
Hún Jiān comforted and encouraged them,
inspiring them with loyalty and righteousness.
They all shouted and fought bravely.
Hún Jiān was struck by a stray arrow,
Shouting (譟),
read as 'zé zào fān'.
Struck (中),
read as 'zhú zhòng fān'.
He initially did not mention the pain.
At that moment, the cloud ladder rolled over the tunnel,
and one wheel sank deep,
making it unable to advance or retreat.
Fire erupted from underground.
The fire was also what Hún Jiān and others had stored to await the cloud ladder.
People on the city wall threw reed torches,
scattered pine resin,
and poured grease and oil,
their shouts shaking the earth.
In an instant,
the cloud ladder and the people on it were all reduced to ashes,
the stench reaching several lǐ.
The rebels then retreated.
Thereupon, troops sallied forth from all three gates.
At this time, Zhū Cǐ was attacking Fèngtiān city from the east, south, and north,
so troops sallied forth from all three gates to fight.
The rebel forces were greatly defeated,
with thousands dead.
For the wounded officers and soldiers,
the Crown Prince personally dressed their wounds.
As night fell,
Zhū Cǐ attacked the city again.
An arrow fell three paces from the Emperor's presence;
the Emperor was greatly alarmed.
Lǐ Huáiguāng led his troops from Púchéng towards Jīngyáng,
moving west along the northern mountains.
He first dispatched his Cavalry Commander Zhāng Sháo to travel incognito to the temporary imperial residence,
concealing a memorial in a wax pellet.
Sháo arrived at Fèngtiān just as the rebels were attacking the city.
Seeing Sháo,
they took him for a commoner
and drove him to fill the moat with other civilians.
Sháo found an opportunity,
crossed the moat and reached the foot of the city wall, shouting:
"I am an envoy from the Shuòfāng Army!"
People on the city wall lowered a rope to pull him up.
As he was climbing,
he was struck by dozens of arrows.
He managed to retrieve the memorial from his clothes and presented it.
The Emperor was greatly pleased
and had Sháo carried around the city to display him,
and shouts of joy like thunder rose from the four corners.
On the guǐsì day,
Huáiguāng defeated Zhū Cǐ's forces at Lǐquán.
Zhū Cǐ heard of this and was afraid,
so he led his troops and fled back to Cháng'ān.
The multitude believed that if Huáiguāng had not arrived for another three days,
the city would not have been held.
The historian stated that Lǐ Huáiguāng's relief of Fèngtiān's siege
was not without merit.
Cǐ (泚),
read as 'qiě lǐ fān',
also pronounced 'cǐ'.
After Zhū Cǐ retreated,
all the attendants congratulated the Emperor.
Jiǎ Yǐnlín, Cavalry Commander of the Biàn-Huáxíng Army, advised:
"Your Majesty is too impatient
and cannot tolerate others.
If this temperament is not changed,
even if Zhū Cǐ is defeated and perishes,
our troubles will not end!"
The Emperor did not take offense
and praised him greatly.
The Imperial Censor Wànsì Zhù opened up the supply routes through Jīn and Shāng.
With the heavy siege lifted,
tributes and taxes from all circuits followed,
and the state's finances began to recover.
When Zhū Cǐ reached Cháng'ān,
he merely planned for city defense.
At that time, he dispatched people from outside the city
to run around shouting:
"Fèngtiān has fallen!"
hoping to confuse the populace.
Since Zhū Cǐ occupied the wealth of the treasury,
he spared no gold and silk to please his generals and soldiers.
Families of dukes and high officials in the city were all given monthly stipends.
For those of the Shéncè Army and the Six Armies who followed the imperial carriage, or Gē Shūyào, and Lǐ Shèng,
Zhū Cǐ provided their families with grain.
In addition, he repaired and maintained weapons and equipment,
incurring vast daily expenses.
When Cháng'ān was pacified,
the treasury still had surplus reserves.
Those who saw this all retrospectively resented the oppression and heavy taxation by the officials in charge.
Someone said to Zhū Cǐ,
"Your Majesty has received the Mandate of Heaven;
it is inappropriate for the mausoleums and ancestral temples of Táng to remain."
Zhū Cǐ said,
"I once faced north and served Táng;
how could I bear to do such a thing!"
Another said,
"Many official positions are vacant;
please use troops to compel scholars to fill them."
Zhū Cǐ said,
"Forcing appointments upon people will make them fearful.
Just give positions to those who wish to serve;
why must we knock on doors and force people to accept office!"
Zhū Cǐ's only forces were the Fànyáng and Shéncè militia;
the militia,
that is, the tuan jie bing,
the matter is seen in Volume 225, Dàlì 12th year of Dàizōng.
None of them were willing to fight;
they merely guarded the wealth and goods they had plundered,
refusing to go out to battle.
They also secretly plotted to kill Zhū Cǐ,
but the plan did not come to fruition and was abandoned.
Lǐ Huáiguāng was crude and negligent by nature.
He came from Shāndōng to aid in the crisis, from Wèixiàn xíngyíng to aid in the crisis at Fèntiān.
Wèixiàn belongs to Wèizhōu;
its territory is east of the Héshān mountains.
Nàn
is pronounced Dànfān;
the same below.
He also said,
"The chaos in the empire
is all caused by these people!
When I see the emperor,
I will request their execution."
After the siege of Fèntiān was lifted,
he prided himself on his accomplishments,
thinking the emperor would receive him with extraordinary courtesy.
Courtesies that surpassed those given to all other officials are called "extraordinary courtesies."
Lú Jiàn "sighed with indignation along the way,
thinking that the prime minister's deliberations were misguided,
'misguided' is similar to 'losing one's proper place.'
the Capital Mayor's rewards were meager;
that the imperial carriage was forced to flee
was the fault of the three ministers.
The prime minister
refers to Lú Jiàn.
The Minister of Finance
refers to Zhào Zàn.
The Capital Mayor
refers to Wáng Hóng.
Dù
is pronounced Tuóluòfān.
Liǎn
is pronounced Lìshànfān.
Chéng
is pronounced Shéngzhèngfān.
If the emperor were to open his heart and speak truthfully,
inquiring
about gains and losses,
and allow Lǐ Huáiguāng's words to be heard,
would that not be dangerous!"
Dài
means 'danger'.
Fearing this,
he calmly spoke to the emperor, saying,
"Lǐ Huáiguāng's achievements
are such that the state relies on him;
the rebels are disheartened,
all without the will to resist.
If he were allowed to take advantage of the victory to seize Cháng'ān,
then the rebels could be destroyed in one stroke;
this is the momentum of 'splitting bamboo'.
Now, if he is allowed to enter court,
there will surely be a banquet,
delaying for several days,
allowing the rebels to enter the capital,
where they can calmly prepare their defenses,
I fear it will then be difficult to defeat them!"
The emperor agreed.
Huáiguāng prided himself on his accomplishments,
greatly expecting much from the emperor and seeking to fulfill his desires.
Dézōng desired speed,
pressing his subordinates without sympathizing with their toil.
Lú Jiàn's heart
sought to protect himself from blame and manipulated things in between.
Therefore, although they were eager to pacify the rebels,
they unknowingly created another rebel.
Cháo
is pronounced Zhíyáofān.
Lǐ Huáiguāng set a date with Lǐ Jiànhuī, Lǐ Shèng, and Shéncè cavalry commissioner Yáng Huìyuán to jointly take Cháng'ān.
Huáiguāng felt that he had exhausted his sincerity over thousands of *lǐ* to respond to the crisis,
defeated Zhū Cǐ,
and lifted the heavy siege,
yet he could not see the Son of Heaven from such a short distance.
His mood was exceedingly resentful,
and he said,
"I have now been slandered by treacherous ministers;
the situation is clear!"
Thereupon, he led his troops away,
arriving at Lǔdiàn.
Lǔdiàn
is southeast of Fèntiān,
northwest of Chéntāoxié in Xiányáng.

7 Zhāng Fēi, the cavalry commissioner of Xiānánxīshān, led his troops in rebellion,

Bì arrested Zhāng Chóngxiàn and over sixty others and sent them to the capital.
An imperial edict ordered them all to be cut in half at the waist at the military gate of Fūzhōu,
to serve as a warning to the autumn defense troops.
3 Initially,
King Gēluófèng of Yúnnán captured Xīzhōu.
In the first year of Zhìdé of Sùzōng (756 CE),
Xīzhōu fell.
The details are found in volume 218.
Xīlú County,

In the first year of Tiānbǎo (742 CE), it was renamed Xīlú.
He was a native of Xiāngzhōu
and was well-versed in classics and arts.
Gēluófèng greatly admired and valued him.
His son Fèng Jiāyì,
his grandson Yìmóxún, and his great-grandson Xún Mèngcòu all served him as their teacher.
Whenever he taught,
if they turned away, he would whip them.
When Yìmóxún became king,
in the fourteenth year of Dàlì (779 CE),
Yìmóxún ascended the throne.
This is found in volume 226.
The Qīngpíngguān
was the prime minister of the Mán.
Nánzhào officials were called Tǎnchuò,
Bùxiè,
and Jiǔzàn.
They were referred to as Qīngpíngguān.
Their role was to decide the importance of state affairs,

However, state affairs were entirely decided by Huí.
The five men served Huí with great humility and caution.
If they made a mistake,
Huí would whip them.
Yúnnán had a population of several hundred thousand.
Whenever Tǔbō invaded,

Yúnnán suffered greatly from this.
Huí then persuaded Yìmóxún to return allegiance to Táng

Yìmóxún thought this was true,

When Wéi Gāo, the Jìedùshǐ of Xīchuān, arrived at his post,

Yìmóxún secretly sent envoys through these Mán tribes to request submission.
Gāo memorialized:

The eight kingdoms of raw Qiāng: Bái Gǒujūn, Gēlínjūn, Būzūjūn, Nánshuǐjūn, Ruòshuǐjūn, Xīdǒngjūn, Qīngyuǎnjūn, Duōbàjūn—

The Emperor ordered Gāo to first write a letter from a border general to admonish them,

This laid the groundwork for Nánzhào's submission.

"Zhìzhēn

'間' (jiàn),

because his words were not heeded.

Xià,

Xīpíng Wáng.

I say Lǐ Shèng wished to be loyal to his sovereign,

Whenever the Emperor consulted him,

"I wish to make a pact with you."
(This also reveals an aspect of the Emperor's suspicion and jealousy.)

Bì said,

Lǐ Shèng (李晟) and Mǎ Suì (馬燧) have rendered great service to the state,

When Your Majesty appointed Lǐ Huáiguāng (李懷光) as Tàiwèi (太尉), Huáiguāng (懷光) became even more fearful,

Now, Shèng (晟) and Suì (燧) are already sufficiently wealthy and esteemed.

The Emperor said,

Shèng (晟) and Suì (燧) both rose,

The Emperor then said to Bì,

Your Majesty does not consider me untalented,

The duties of a prime minister [宰相] cannot be divided.

According to Tang regulations: there are six Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人),

(The Liùdiǎn [六典] states: six Zhōngshū Shèrén [中書舍人]
are assigned to oversee the six departments.)
All affairs of the realm are to be discussed and decided jointly.

The Emperor laughed and said,

Bì requested the restoration of the abolished prefectural and county officials.

(The word "停" [tíng]

then not only will they not complain,

The Tubo mobilized an army of 100,000 to invade Xīchuān,

Lúběi

Lúshǔi

Tubo initially suspected Yúnnán,

Huìchuān

Yúnnán was enraged

From then on, Yúnnán and Tubo became deeply suspicious of each other,

Tubo, having lost the aid of Yúnnán,
began to weaken in military strength.
However, Tubo had already invaded,
so it divided its troops: 40,000 attacked Liǎnglín and Piāopáng,
30,000 attacked Dōngmán,
and 7,000 attacked Qīngxī Pass.
Qīngxī Pass
was on the border of Xīzhōu.
From the pass southwards, it was 720 *lǐ* to Xīzhōu.
The *Hóngyuán Zhì* states: Qīngxī Pass
was on the southwest border of Lízhōu.
The *Xīn Zhì* states: Lízhōu had eleven strategically important cities in Tóngshān.
Tubo was defeated outside Qīngxī Pass.
On the 21st, Gēngzǐ day,
Princess Xián'ān was formally invested,

In the eleventh month,

From this point onward,
the *Tōngjiàn* consistently used
"Huíhú"
according to previous historical records. On the 22nd, Tubo, ashamed of its previous day's defeat,
