Wéi Gāo ordered Wéi Jìn to guard the strategic city
and supervise all armies to repel them.
Liú Cháocǎi, Military Governor of Xīzhōu, led troops out of the pass and fought continuously.
From Yǐmǎo to Guǐhài,
they were thoroughly defeated.
On the 23rd, Lǐ Bì said to the Emperor:
"The grain transport route from Jiānghuái
relies on Yǒngqiáo as its throat.
This place belongs to Xúzhōu,
and is adjacent to Lǐ Nà.
Xúzhōu and Lǐ Nà's territories are neighboring.
Gāo Míngyìng should inherit the governorship of Xúzhōu,
(beginning of volume 231, Xīngyuán first year.)
He is young,
(Pinyin: shī zhào fān.)
if he seizes Xúzhōu,
then Jiānghuái will be lost,
and from where will the national treasury come?
I request to transfer Zhāng Jiànfēng, Commissioner for Training of Shòu, Lú, and Háo prefectures, to govern Xúzhōu,
and annex Háo and Sì prefectures to his jurisdiction.
Then return Lú and Shòu prefectures to Huáinán.
In this way, Zīqīng will be cautious and the transport route will always be open,
and Jiānghuái will be secure.
Now that Míngyìng is young and foolish and can be replaced,
he should be summoned to become a Commander of the Jinwu Guard.
If by any chance someone else gains control of it,
it will be impossible to control them again."
The Emperor agreed.
Jiànfēng was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Xú, Sì, and Háo prefectures.
Jiànfēng's governance was lenient yet disciplined.
He did not pardon people according to the law;
those who violated the law
were punished without leniency.
On the 24th, Chéng Rìhuá, Jìedùshǐ of Hénghǎi, died.
His son, Huáizhí, appointed himself acting governor.
On the 25th, Tubo repeatedly sent people to entice and coerce Yúnnán.
1. In spring,
the second month,
on the Dīnghài day,
Wéi Gāo sent a letter to Yìmóuxún,
stating:
"The Huíhú have repeatedly requested to assist the Son of Heaven in destroying Tubo together.
If Your Majesty does not decide early,
and is suddenly preempted by the Huíhú,
then the achievements of Your Majesty's ancestors through generations will be in vain.
Moreover, Yúnnán has long suffered humiliation from Tubo.
If you do not seize this opportunity to rely on the power of a great nation to avenge and wipe away the shame,
it will be too late for regret."
2. On the Wùxū day,
Chéng Huáizhí, acting governor of Hénghǎi, was appointed Cāngzhōu Observation Commissioner.
Huáizhí requested to divide Gōnggāo and Jǐngchéng into Jǐngzhōu.
Jǐngchéng County
originally belonged to Cāngzhōu,
in Wǔdé fourth year it belonged to Yíngzhōu,
in Zhēnguān first year it belonged to Cāngzhōu,
in Dàlì seventh year it belonged to Yíngzhōu.
Hénghǎi presumably regained and possessed it after Zhū Tāo's defeat;
later it again belonged to Yíngzhōu.
Gōnggāo
was an ancient county in Hàn,
abolished in Wèi and Jìn.
Suí established Gōnggāo County in the area of Hàn's Gé County;
in Táng it belonged to Cāngzhōu.
The Emperor was pleased and said:
"There has been no such event for thirty years!"
So Xu Shēn, a Yúánwàiláng, was appointed Governor of Jǐngzhōu.
3. Lǐ Bì, Zhongshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, repeatedly begged for a new appointment of chief minister.
The Emperor wanted to use Bān Hóng, Hùbù Shìláng,
but Bì said that although Hóng was honest and strong, he was often hesitant by nature.
He then recommended Dòu Cān as intelligent and agile,
capable of concurrently managing Du zhī Yán Tiě;
and Dǒng Jìn as upright,
suitable for the Ménxià.
The Emperor considered both unsuitable.
Cān
was the great-great-grandson of Dàn.
Dòu Dàn
was the one who, during Wǔdé, advised Qí Wáng Yuánjí to abandon Bìngzhōu.
Jìn was Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
By this time, Bì was seriously ill,
and again recommended the two men.
On the Gēngzǐ day,
Dǒng Jìn was appointed Ménxià Shìláng,
Dòu Cān was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng concurrently Du zhī Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
both with the title Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Bān Hóng was appointed Shàngshū,
continuing as Du zhī Zhuǎnyùn Fùshǐ.
Cān was resolute and stern,
without scholarly learning,
but full of schemes.
Whenever he presented memorials,
the other chief ministers would leave,
and Cān alone would stay behind,
using the pretext of presenting Du zhī matters,
but in fact monopolizing major governmental affairs.
He frequently promoted his relatives and associates to key positions,
using them as his eyes and ears.
Dǒng Jìn merely filled his position.
However, Jìn was a cautious and discreet person.
What he said before the Emperor was never leaked to others.
When his sons and nephews sometimes asked him,
Jìn would say:
"To know whether a chief minister is competent,
look at the peace and danger of the realm.
What is discussed and decided before the Emperor
is not worth mentioning."
The *Kǎoyì* states: Hán Yù wrote in Jìn's biographical account:
"He served as chief minister for five years.
What he memorialized before the Emperor
were all the ways of the Two Emperors and Three Kings,
which had not been spoken of since Qín and Hàn.
After returning home,
he never spoke to others about what he had said to the Emperor.
When his sons and nephews privately asked him,
the Duke said: 'The chief minister's duty
concerns the peace and danger of the realm.
The chief minister's competence or lack thereof can be seen.
To know whether the chief minister is competent or not,
one should observe it thus.
All matters discussed and decided before the Emperor
are not worth mentioning.'
Therefore, his deeds were ultimately not heard of."
Hán Yù, in writing biographical accounts,
would certainly praise good and cover up bad.
His account of Jìn's time as chief minister stops here,
so it can be known that he was compliant, silent, and merely filled his position.
However, his caution and discretion are also commendable.
Here, only a brief extract from the biographical account is taken.
In the third month,
on the *jiǎchén* day,
Lǐ Bì passed away.
Bì possessed strategic intelligence but was fond of talking about immortals and strange tales,
hence he was looked down upon by the world.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Guóshǐ Bǔ* says:
"Lǐ Bì, while serving as chancellor,
took pride in his fantastical claims,
often instructing his household in front of guests to quickly sweep and clean,
'Tonight, Hóngyá Xiānshēng will come to stay.'
Someone gifted him a flask of fine wine,
and when a guest arrived,
he said, 'Mágū sent this wine,
let us share it.'
Before they finished pouring,
the doorkeeper announced, 'Such-and-such Imperial Censor has come to retrieve the flask.'
Bì ordered it to be returned,
showing no trace of shame."
The Old Biography of Bì says:
"When Dézōng first ascended the throne,
he particularly detested shamans, sorcerers, and those who told strange tales.
By the end of the Jiànzhōng era,
when the rebels obstructed the interior,
Sāng Dàomào proposed the idea of defending Fèngtiān,
and the emperor gradually became attentive to auspicious times and taboos,
and he had heard that Bì was skilled in the Way of Ghosts (occult arts),
thus he recalled him from exile,
leading to his great appointment.
The public opinion at the time was not pleased.
When he was in the prime ministership,
he merely adapted to circumstances,
with nothing truly commendable.
He furthermore associated with frivolous individuals like Gù Kuàng and his ilk,
often becoming the butt of jokes and ridicule among court officials,
earning him considerable censure.
Bì was unrestrained and quick-witted in debate,
and fond of grand pronouncements.
From his entry into and exit from the Forbidden City,
he was repeatedly envied and resented by powerful favorites,
but always escaped by his intelligence.
Eventually, through his eloquent and unconstrained discourse,
he enlightened the sagacious sovereign,
thereby rising to the prime ministership.
Initially,
when Bì was exiled to Jiāngnán,
he formed an extraordinary friendship with Liǔ Hún and Gù Kuàng,
composing poetry and finding contentment.
As Hún achieved success earlier,
Bì was able to return to official service in the court.
Kuàng was
a man from Sūzhōu."
However, although Bì was indeed fond of strange tales and immortals,
his knowledge and strategies were truly extraordinary.
As for assisting Sùzōng and Dàizōng in recovering the two capitals,
and refusing the prime ministership to depart,
and the security of Dàizōng and Shùnzōng in the Eastern Palace,
all relied on Bì,
these are his great virtues worthy of respect.
The old biography denounces him too much.
The family biography, written by his son,
though not entirely credible,
cannot be entirely disbelieved either!
Now, we select what is credible and preserve it.
Initially,

3. Liú Xuánzuǒ (劉玄佐), the Military Commissioner of Xuānwǔ (宣武節度使), possessed great authority and strategy.
Each time Lǐ Nà (李納)'s envoy arrived,
Xuánzuǒ (玄佐) would form strong ties with him,
thus he often obtained inside information
and could prepare beforehand;
Nà (納) feared him.
Sūnzǐ (孫子)'s chapter "Five Kinds of Spies" (五間)
includes "using native spies" (因間).
"Using native spies" (因間者)
means using the enemy's own countrymen.
Zhāng Yù (張預) noted: Using a person from the enemy country,
knowing their true intentions,
and employing them,
they can be used for reconnaissance.
Liú Xuánzuǒ (劉玄佐)'s method of controlling Lǐ Nà (李納)
precisely used this tactic.
Weaving one bolt of silk daily,
she said to Xuánzuǒ (玄佐):
"You were originally humble and lowly.
The Son of Heaven has enriched and ennobled you to this extent;
you must repay him with your life."
Thus, Xuánzuǒ (玄佐) never failed in his duty as a subject.
History states that Xuánzuǒ (玄佐) was loyal and obedient,
due to his mother's teaching.
This statement is likely based on his mother's tomb inscription.
Táng (唐) people's tomb inscriptions
were not without excessive praise.
However, such words
are beneficial to worldly morality.
On the day Gēngwǔ (庚午),
Xuánzuǒ (玄佐) passed away.
4. Lǐ Shí (李實), the acting Military Commissioner's Aide (節度判官) of Shānnán East Circuit (山南東道), was in charge of the interim affairs.
He was by nature harsh and mean,
cutting back on the soldiers' clothing and food.
The drum and horn officer, Yáng Qīngtán (楊清潭), led a mob in rebellion.
At night,
they burned and plundered the city,
but uniquely did not violate the home of Cáo Wáng Gāo (曹王皋).
The home of Cáo Wáng Gāo (曹王皋)
had probably already been moved to an external guesthouse,
not residing in the commissioner's official residence.
The next morning,
Commander Xú Chéng (徐誠) climbed over the city wall and entered,
issuing commands and prohibitions,
and only then did the chaos cease;
Qīngtán (清潭) and six others were arrested and executed.
Shí (實) returned to the capital
and was appointed Junior Lord of the Imperial Granaries (司農少卿).
Shí (實)
was the great-great-grandson of Yuánqìng (元慶).
Prince Dào (道王) Xuánqìng (玄慶)
was the son of Gāozǔ (高祖).
On the day Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
Fán Zé (樊澤), the Military Commissioner of Jīngnán (荊南節度使), was appointed Military Commissioner of Shānnán East Circuit (山南東道節度使).
5. Initially,
Dòu Cān (竇參) was the Commissioner of Finance and Transport (度支轉運使),
and Bān Hóng (班宏) was his deputy.
Cān (參) promised Hóng (宏)
that after a year, he would return the commissioner's post to him.
More than a year passed,
and Cān (參) showed no intention of returning it;
Hóng (宏) grew angry.
Zhāng Pāng (張滂), the Junior Lord of the Imperial Granaries (司農少卿),
was recommended by Hóng (宏).
Cān (參) wanted to have Pāng (滂) share control over the salt and iron of Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮),
but Hóng (宏) refused;
Pāng (滂) knew this
and also resented Hóng (宏).
When Cān (參) was alienated by the Emperor,
he then relinquished the post of Finance Commissioner (度支使) to Hóng (宏),
but also did not want all the lucrative power to go solely to Hóng (宏),
so he recommended Pāng (滂) to the Emperor;
Pāng (滂) was appointed Vice Minister of Revenue (戶部侍郎) and Commissioner of Salt and Iron Transport (鹽鐵轉運使),
still subordinate to Hóng (宏) to appease him.
Dòu Cān was secretly cunning and obstinate,
relying on his power and being greedy.
Whenever there was a promotion or demotion,
he often discussed it with his kinsman, Staff Censor Dòu Shēn.
Shēn used his influence to solicit bribes,
and people at the time called him
"the Magpie."
Whenever Dòu Cān promoted or demoted court officials,
he would first discuss it with Shēn.
Shēn would then report it to the person in question in advance,
using this to solicit influence and accept bribes.
The reason people called him "the Magpie" was
that when a family had good news,
a magpie would always chirp first in their courtyard to announce it.
People said to Cān:
"Shēn will surely be a burden to you;
you should dismiss him to quell public criticism."
Cān repeatedly guaranteed that Shēn would do nothing untoward,
and Shēn also did not reform.
Guó Wáng Zézhī, the Great General of the Left Imperial Guard,
was the son of Guó Wáng Jù.
Guó Wáng Jù
was killed by Duàn Zǐzhāng in the second year of Shàngyuán of Sùzōng's reign.
Wú Tōngxuán, the Left Remonstrance Grand Master and Draft Secretary, disagreed with Lù Zhì.
Dòu Shēn feared that Zhì would be promoted,
so he secretly conspired with Tōngxuán and Zézhī to write slanderous letters to undermine Zhì.
The Emperor became aware of all their schemes.
In the summer,
in the fourth month,
on the dìnghài day,
Zézhī was demoted to Sīmǎ of Zhāozhōu.
Zhāozhōu
was the land of Lìpǔ County in the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to Cāngwú Commandery.
In the Jìn dynasty, Pínglè County was established,
belonging to Shǐ'ān Commandery.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé, Lezhou was established,
and in the eighth year of Zhēnguān, it was renamed Zhāozhōu.
Sòng Bái said: North of the commandery is Zhāoshān Gāngtán,
named after the mountain ridge.
According to old records: Zhāozhōu was four thousand four hundred and thirty-six lǐ from the capital.
The Suí dynasty established Quánzhōu,
governing Mǐn County,
with Nán'ān and Pútián Counties belonging to it.
In the second year of Shènglì of Empress Wǔ's reign, Nán'ān, Pútián, and Lóngxī from Quánzhōu were separated to establish Wǔróngzhōu.
In the second year of Jǐngyún, Wǔróng was renamed Quánzhōu,
and the original Quánzhōu in Mǐn was renamed Mǐnzhōu.
In the thirteenth year of Kāiyuán, Mǐnzhōu was again renamed Fúzhōu.
According to old records: Quánzhōu was
six thousand two hundred and sixteen lǐ southeast of the capital.
Soon after, Tōngxuán was granted death.
6 After the death of Liú Xuánzuǒ,
his generals and aides concealed it,
claiming he was ill and requesting a replacement.
The Emperor also kept it secret,
sending an envoy to the army to ask
"if Wú Còu, the Observer of Shǎnxī and Guó, would be a suitable replacement?"
Superintendent Mèng Jiè and Military Administrator Lú Yuàn both deemed it convenient.
Only then was he appointed.
When Còu reached Sǐshuǐ,
Xuánzuǒ's coffin was about to depart.
The army requested that ceremonial guards be prepared.
Yuàn refused,
and also ordered that the implements be kept to await the new envoy.
The officers and soldiers were enraged.
Xuánzuǒ's son-in-law and personal guards were all armored,
and they embraced Xuánzuǒ's son Shìníng, who was wearing mourning attire,
seated him on a high platform,
and
made him acting Military Governor.
They seized city general Cáo Jīn'àn.
A city general
was tasked with leading troops to patrol the city walls,
keeping watch day and night.
They said:
"You all requested Wú Còu!"
So they executed him.
Lú Yuàn escaped.
Shìníng rewarded the officers and soldiers with wealth
and coerced Mèng Jiè to petition the court.
The Emperor consulted the prime ministers,
and Dòu Cān said:
"Now the people of Biàn are using Lǐ Nà to demand a decree.
If we don't grant it,
they will join Nà."
On the gēngyín day,
Shìníng was appointed Xuānwǔ Jiedushi.
The "Kǎo Yì" states: The "Shílù" says:
"Before Shìníng's position was settled,
envoys were sent to communicate with Wáng Wǔjùn, Liú Jì, and Tián Xù.
Since Shìníng had not yet received the imperial edict to take office,
they all detained his envoys."
The "Jiù Zhuàn" says:
"Since Shìníng had not yet received the imperial edict to take office,
they all detained his envoys."
The "Xīn Zhuàn" says:
"The various garrisons did not approve of him
and all detained his envoys."
Therefore, the "Jiù Zhuàn" is correct.
He made a pretense of an inspection tour,
and upon reaching Sòngzhōu,
replaced him with the Commissioner of Military Affairs Liú Yìzhǔn.
The "Kǎo Yì" states: Hán Yù's collected works write
"Yìhuái."
We follow the "Jiù Zhuàn" here.
He was the son of Zhèngchén.
Liú Zhèngchén
was the Jiedushi of Pínglú in the early days of Sùzōng's Zhìdé reign.
7 On the *yǐwèi* day,
Dòu Cān (竇參), Minister of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng 中書侍郎) and co-acting Chancellor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì 同平章事), was demoted to Biejia (別駕) of Chénzhōu (郴州).
The old gazetteer states: Chénzhōu (郴州)
is three thousand three hundred *lǐ* south of the capital.
Chén (郴),
pronounced as *chǒu lín*.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: Liǔ Chéng’s (柳珵) *Shàngqīng Zhuàn* (上清傳) states:
“In the third month of spring in the *rénshēn* year of the Zhēnyuán (貞元) era,
Chancellor Dòu (竇), residing at his mansion in Guāngfú Lǐ (光福里),
was strolling idly in the central courtyard under the moonlight.
His favored maid, Shàngqīng (上清),
said, ‘If I am to report something now,
I must go to the front hall
before I dare speak.’
Chancellor Dòu (竇) promptly went up to the hall.
Shàngqīng (上清) said, ‘There is someone in the courtyard tree.
Fearing he might startle you, my lord,
please take care to avoid him.’
Chancellor Dòu (竇) said, ‘Lù Zhì (陸贄) has long wished to usurp my power and position.
Now that there is someone in the courtyard tree,
my calamity is nigh.
Moreover, whether this matter is reported or not,
I will suffer misfortune
and certainly die in exile on the road.
You are a rare gem among your peers.
When my body dies and my family is ruined,
you will surely become a palace maid.
If the Sacred Sovereign (Shèngjūn 聖君) should inquire,
please speak well on my behalf.’
Shàngqīng (上清) wept and said, ‘If it is truly so,
I shall follow you in life and death.’
Chancellor Dòu (竇) descended the steps and loudly cried, ‘Sir in the tree,
you must be sent by Lù Zhì (陸贄).
If you can spare this old man’s life,
I would not dare fail to richly reward you.’
A voice from the tree responded and descended.
It was a person in rough mourning clothes.
He said, ‘I have a great bereavement at home;
I am very poor
and cannot afford the funeral rites.
I humbly knew that Your Excellency sincerely helps others,
which is why I came by night.
I hope Your Excellency will not be offended.’
The Duke said, ‘All I possess
is a thousand bolts of silk in the hall, which were
originally intended for renovating my private ancestral temple.
May I temporarily bestow them upon you?’
The mourner bowed in thanks.
Chancellor Dòu (竇) reciprocated the courtesy.
He then said, ‘Before I bid farewell to Your Excellency,
please have your attendants throw the bestowed silk outside the wall.
I will wait for it in the street first.’
Chancellor Dòu (竇) acceded to his request
and ordered his servants to ascertain his complete disappearance.
Only at dawn
did he dare return to his bedchamber.
The next day,
the Supreme General of the Guards (Zhí Jīnwú 執金吾) reported the matter first,
and Chancellor Dòu (竇) subsequently reported it.
Dézōng (德宗) sternly said, ‘You are colluding with border generals,
harboring assassins,
and hold the highest position among the Three Dukes (Táidǐng 台鼎);
what more do you seek!’
Chancellor Dòu (竇) bowed his head to the ground and said, ‘I rose from a humble talent in the scribal arts,
and my official position reached the highest ranks.
All of this is due to Your Majesty’s encouragement and promotion,
not from any other person.
Now, unfortunately, it has come to this,
but it is merely the doing of my enemies!
Should Your Majesty suddenly unleash the wrath of thunder,
this minister would deserve ten thousand deaths.’
A palace envoy descended the steps and announced, ‘You may return to your private residence
and await further instructions.’
A month later,
he was demoted to Biejia (別駕) of Chénzhōu (郴州).
At that time, Liú Shìníng (劉士寧), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Xuānwǔ (宣武), established good relations with Chénzhōu (郴州).
The Imperial Censor (Liánshǐ 廉使) submitted a memorial reporting this.
Dézōng (德宗) said, ‘Colluding with border generals,
it is truly evident and proven.’
He banished Duke Dòu (竇公) to Huānzhōu (驩州),
confiscated his family property,
leaving him not even a single hairpin.
He did not even reach the place of exile;
an imperial edict ordered him to take his own life.
Shàngqīng (上清) was indeed registered in the women’s quarters (yètíng 掖庭).
Several years later,
due to her skillful responses
and ability to prepare tea,
she frequently attended the Emperor.
Dézōng (德宗) said to her, ‘There are quite a number of people in the palace.
You are capable;
how did you come to be here?’
Shàngqīng (上清) replied, ‘Your servant was originally a maid in the household of the former Chancellor Dòu Cān (竇參).
Dòu (竇) had lost his wife early,
so your servant was privileged to assist with sweeping and cleaning.
When Dòu’s (竇) family was ruined,
I was fortunate to enter the palace.
Now that I serve the Dragon Countenance (Lóngyán 龍顏),
it is as if I am in heaven.’
Dézōng (德宗) said, ‘Dòu’s (竇) crimes were not limited to harboring assassins;
he also had significant corruption.
Previously, many official silver vessels were seized.’
Shàngqīng (上清) wept and said, ‘From Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞) to Director of the Bureau of Finance (Dùzhī 度支), Minister of Revenue (Hùbù 戶部), and Commissioner of Salt and Iron (Yántiě Shǐ 鹽鐵使),
then to Chancellor,
Dòu (竇) held these positions for a total of six years.
His monthly income was several hundred thousand,
and the irregular rewards and gifts he received before and after were innumerable.
The silver and goods from Chénzhōu (郴州) that were seized for official use
were all imperial grants.
On the day they were registered,
your servant was in Chénzhōu (郴州)
and personally saw the prefecture and county officials, seeking to please Lù Zhì (陸贄),
scrape off the engraved names of frontier officials from the presented silver vessels,
falsely accusing them of being ill-gotten gains.
I humbly beg Your Majesty to verify this.’
Thereupon, an edict was issued to retrieve Dòu’s (竇) confiscated silver vessels.
Upon re-examining the scraped areas,
they were all as Shàngqīng (上清) had stated.
This was in the twelfth year of Zhēnyuán (貞元).
Dézōng (德宗) then asked about the matter of harboring assassins.
Shàngqīng (上清) said, ‘There was truly none.
It was all Lù Zhì’s (陸贄) malicious frame-up,
using others to carry it out.’
Dézōng (德宗) angrily said of Lù Zhì (陸贄), ‘That scoundrel!
I took off his green robe and gave him a purple one,
and I always called him Lù Jiǔ (陸九).
I appointed Dòu Cān (竇參) because it pleased me,
but he made me unjustly kill him.
When power fell into his hands,
he became as weak as a mud ball.’
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued to clear Dòu Cān’s (竇參) name.
At that time, Péi Yánlíng (裴延齡) sensed that Lù Zhì’s (陸贄) favor was waning
and was able to incite slander freely,
and Zhì (贄) ultimately suffered condemnation from which he did not recover.
Later, Shàngqīng (上清) was specifically granted an imperial decree, written in vermilion, to become a female Daoist priestess,
and eventually married Jīn Zhōngyì (金忠義).
The world, because many of Lù Zhì’s (陸贄) disciples achieved prominent positions and fame,
dared not transmit this story,
hence it remained entirely unknown.”
If this account were true,
then Dòu Cān (竇參) was kidnapped.
How could Dézōng (德宗) then say
“harboring assassins”?!
Moreover, Lù Zhì (陸贄) was a wise chancellor;
how could he possibly do this!
Even if he wanted to frame Dòu Cān (竇參),
he had many other methods.
How could he resort to such childish play!
It is utterly contrary to human nature.
Therefore, we do not adopt this account.

Zhào Jǐng (趙憬), Assistant of the Left of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒchéng 尚書左丞), and Lù Zhì (陸贄), Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng 兵部侍郎), were both appointed Minister of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng 中書侍郎) and co-acting Chancellor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì 同平章事).
Jǐng (憬)
was Rénběn’s (仁本) great-grandson.
8 Zhāng Pāng (張滂) requested the old salt and iron account books from Bān Hóng (班宏).
Hóng (宏) refused to give them.
Pāng (滂) and Hóng (宏) together selected officials for the inspectorate offices,
but found no suitable candidates,
leaving many positions vacant.
Pāng (滂) reported to the Emperor, saying:
“If this continues,
official duties will surely be neglected,
and this minister will have no escape from his fault.”
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
the Emperor ordered Hóng (宏) and Pāng (滂) to separately manage the empire’s finances and taxation,
following the precedent of the Dàlì (大曆) era.
In the first year of Dàlì (大曆),
Wǔ Qí (第五琦) and Liú Yàn (劉晏) were ordered to separately manage the empire’s finances and taxation.
The details can be found in Volume 224.
9 On the *rénzǐ* day,
Tǔbō (吐蕃) raided Língzhōu (靈州),
captured the main irrigation channel at Shuǐkǒu (水口),
and destroyed the military farms.
An imperial edict ordered Hédōng (河東) and Zhènwǔ (振武) to relieve them,
and dispatched two thousand soldiers from the Shéncè (神策) Six Armies to garrison Dìngyuǎn (定遠) and Huáiyuǎn (懷遠) cities.
Huáiyuǎn County (Huáiyuǎn Xiàn 懷遠縣) was subordinate to Língzhōu (靈州),
established during the Later Zhōu (Hòu Zhōu 後周) dynasty.
During the Suí (隋) dynasty, Wǔyuán Commandery (Wǔyuán Jùn 五原郡) was within its borders.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Dìngyuǎn County (Dìngyuǎn Xiàn 定遠縣) is two hundred *lǐ* northeast of Língzhōu (靈州).
10Lù Zhì (陸贄) requested that the chief officials of the central government departments (tái shěng chángguān 臺省長官) each nominate their subordinates,
and that their names be recorded in the imperial edict.
In the future, when their performance was evaluated,
the nominators would also be promoted or demoted accordingly.
In the fifth month,
on the *wùchén* day,
an imperial edict was issued to implement Zhì’s (贄) proposal.
Not long after,
someone spoke to the Emperor, saying:
“All whom the various departments recommend are due to personal connections,
or they accept bribes,
and thus true talents are not obtained.”
The Emperor secretly instructed Lù Zhì:
“From now on, there will be a change.
You should choose for yourself;
do not rely on the various departments.”
“Various departments”
refers to the chief officials of the Tái-shěng.
He roughly said:
“In our dynasty, officials of the fifth rank and above
are appointed by imperial edict.
This means the chancellors discuss and propose them for approval.
Officials of the sixth rank and below are appointed by imperial decree.
This means the Lì-bù assesses their talents and assigns them to posts,
and the imperial decree is merely presented for acknowledgment and cannot be rejected.”
For officials of the sixth rank and below, their certificates of appointment
are all marked with
the character “wén” (聞).
Officials such as the Qǐjū, Yí, Bǔ, and Yùshǐ
are still listed among those selected by the Xuǎn-cáo.
This means the Qǐjū Láng, Shèrén, Shíyí, Bǔquè, and Yùshǐ
are all nominated by the Lì-bù.
“Xuǎn” (選)
should be translated.
Abandoning collective deliberation and prioritizing one's own authority,
discarding public recommendations and extending private favors—
this would mean that among the myriad ranks of officials circulating throughout the land,
if they do not emerge from the will of the current chancellors,
they will never be promoted.”
He further said:
“Since this system was put into effect,
only a dozen or so have been recommended.
Evaluating their qualifications and reputation,
they are not ashamed in their official ranks.
Examining their conduct and abilities,
no failures or mistakes have yet been reported.
Yet, critics are quick to voice their opinions,
bothering Your Sacred Intelligence above.
The difficulty of implementing policies
is thus clear!
I request that the accusers be made to specify the details of their claims:
who accepted bribes,
who recommended based on personal connections,
and hand them over to the relevant authorities
to investigate the truth.
Those who made erroneous recommendations must be punished,
and those who slandered the good must also suffer the consequences for their wrongdoing.”
This means they should be counter-sentenced and punished.
“Without adding clarification or inquiry,
privatizing public deliberation,
and not revealing the accuser’s name”—
“Zhǔmíng” (主名)
is the name of the accuser.
“If the guilty are acquitted,
and the wronged and the righteous are treated the same,
upon whom can people rely?!”
Furthermore,
“the chancellors are but a few people;
how can they be thoroughly familiar with so many scholars?
If they were to personally appoint all officials,
they would reasonably need to inquire and consult repeatedly.
This would transform public recommendation into private endorsement,
and replace open promotion with secret lobbying.
Public and private, open and hidden, would reflect upon each other,
and the principles of governance would naturally become evident.”
This is the method of writing.
“However,
the two characters “míngyáng” (明揚)
are derived from the Book of Yú,
and the two characters “àntóu” (闇投)
are derived from the Book of Hàn,
and writing must have its sources.
This is similar to how people are taught to write in recent times;
surely, writing is not limited to just this.
The malpractice only worsens.
Therefore, officials appointed following previous commands
are rarely free from slander.
Although those holding power are not uniform,
and some act on personal sentiments,
it is also because private inquiries are made among intimates,
who then become compromised.
The harm is not distant;
Your Sacred Awareness clearly knows this.”
He further said:
“Today’s chancellors were yesterday’s chief officials of the Tái-shěng;
today’s chief officials of the Tái-shěng are tomorrow’s chancellors.
Their titles are merely temporarily different;
their methods of appointment are certainly not fundamentally distinct.”
“Xíngjǔ” (行舉) means
the chief officials of the Tái-shěng recommend them,
and the chancellors implement it.
“When holding the position of chancellor, one can select from a thousand or a hundred subordinates.
Public opinion is unfathomable,
and its confusion is extreme.
For the respected to grasp the essentials
and the humble to manage the details—
this is why the sovereign chooses their chief ministers,
and the chief ministers choose the chiefs of the various officials.”
“Shùzhǎng” (庶長)
are the chiefs of the various officials.
“If one aims to find the right people,
there is no easier way than this.
To seek talent, breadth is valuable;
to evaluate performance, precision is valuable.
In the past, Zétiān, desiring to win people's hearts,
advanced people without regard to order.”
“Zétiān” (則天)
refers to Empress Wǔ Hòu.
“She also allowed people to recommend their own talents.
However, since accountability and responsibility were strict,
promotions and demotions were swift.
Thus, her era was known for its discerning judgment of people,
and successive dynasties relied on the use of many talented individuals.”
He further said:
“Zétiān’s method of promotion was easy and effective in finding people.
Your Majesty’s rule of careful selection— ”
The Shū Jīng says: “Carefully select your subordinates.”
The Emperor eventually retracted the previous edict and did not implement it.
11 On the day guǐyǒu,
Lǐ Nà, the Jìedùshǐ of Pínglú, passed away.
The army thereupon acclaimed his son, Shīgǔ, as acting Jìedùshǐ.
12 In the sixth month,
over a thousand Tubō cavalry raided Jīngzhōu,
plundering more than a thousand Tiánjūn and departing.
“Tiánjūn” (田軍)
refers to soldiers stationed at agricultural colonies.
13 The Jìedùshǐ of Língnán reported:
“Recently, foreign ships carrying precious and exotic goods
mostly conduct trade in Ānnán.
I wish to send a pànguān to Ānnán to collect these goods
and request that one imperial envoy be sent along with him.”
The Emperor intended to approve it.
Lù Zhì submitted a memorial,
believing that:
“Merchants from distant lands
seek only profit.
Treat them gently, and they will come;
disturb them, and they will leave.
Guǎngzhōu has always been the gathering place for many ships.
Now they suddenly divert to Ānnán.
If it is not due to excessive exploitation,
then it must be because the means of attracting and retaining them have been lost.”
“Xié” (攜)
means to leave;
it means that the way to attract and retain those who leave has been lost.
In the Zuǒ Zhuàn,
Guǎn Zhòng said: “Attract those who depart with propriety.”
In the Lún Yǔ,
Confucius said:
“I have never seen anyone who can see their faults and inwardly accuse themselves.”
The commentary says: “Sòng” (訟)
is like “zé” (責),
meaning people with faults cannot accuse themselves.
The Jì Yuè Lìng records: “Do not engage in extravagant and clever crafts to sway the mind of the superior.”
The commentary: “Dàng” (蕩)
means to stir or move.
“No land is not the king’s land.
Imperial envoys and regional envoys
are all the king’s subjects.
Why must one trust Língnán and reject Ānnán,
or favor imperial envoys and slight regional envoys?
I hope the proposal will be rejected and not implemented.”
14 In the autumn,
seventh month,
on the first day of the cycle, jiǎyín,
Bān Hóng, the Hùbù Shàngshū and Pàndùzhī, passed away.
Lù Zhì requested that Lǐ Xùn, the former Húnán Guānchásǐ, temporarily serve as Pàndùzhī.
The Emperor granted it.
However, later he again wanted to appoint Péi Yánlíng, the Sīnóng Shǎoqīng.
Zhì submitted a memorial,
believing that:
“The current Dùzhī
is responsible for balancing all commodities.
Being stingy creates problems;
being lenient allows for corruption.
Yánlíng is a boastful and petty person;
appointing him will alarm public opinion.
The responsibility for drawing a salary without fulfilling duties
should certainly extend to your humble servant;
the discernment in knowing people
might also harm Your Sacred Awareness.”
The Emperor did not comply.
On the day jǐwèi,
Yánlíng was appointed Pàndùzhī.
This laid the groundwork for Péi Yánlíng to slander Lù Zhì.
More than forty prefectures, including Hénán, Běi, Jiāng, Huái, Jīng, Xiāng, Chén, and Xǔ, suffered extensive flooding.
Over 20,000 people drowned.
Lù Zhì requested that envoys be dispatched to provide relief and consolation.
The emperor said:
"I heard that the damage was very slight.
If we immediately discuss generous relief,
I fear it might lead to deceit and trickery."
Zhì submitted a memorial,
which broadly stated:
"The prevailing flaw of common customs
is to often indulge flattery.
They embellish their words if they anticipate what pleases you,
and downplay matters if they expect what you dislike hearing.
The failure to establish proper preparations
constantly suffers from this."
"Zhìbèi" (制備)
means to make regulations and prepare in advance for each matter.
"Héng" (恆)
is pronounced "hù dēng" (戶登).
"What is spent is wealth and resources;
what is gained is popular support.
If we do not lose the people,
why worry about a lack of resources!"
The emperor agreed to dispatch envoys,
but said:
"Since the tribute and taxes from Huáixī are already deficient,
there is no need to send envoys."
Zhì again submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"Your Majesty has ceased military campaigns and endured humiliation,
pardoning those bandit leaders (qúkuí).
Qú (渠)
means 'great'.
Kuí (魁)
means 'leader'.
It is proper to show compassion and relief.
In ancient times, Qín and Jìn were bitter enemies,
yet Duke Mù still rescued them during their famine.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states: When Jìn suffered famine,
Qín transported grain to them.
When Qín suffered famine,
Jìn closed its markets to grain;
Duke Mù attacked Jìn
and captured Duke Huì.
And when Jìn again suffered famine,
Duke Mù once more supplied them with grain,
saying:
'I resent their ruler, but I pity their people.'
It is solely through virtue and righteousness
that we would rather others wrong us
than we wrong others."
This reverses the words of Cáo Cāo,
thus showing the bearing of an emperor.
Xuānfǔ (宣撫) envoys, including Zhōngshū Shèrén Jīngzhào Xī Zhì, were dispatched to the various circuits affected by the floods.
In the 15th year, Lǐ Shīgǔ, formerly the Prefect of Qīngzhōu, was appointed Military Governor of Pínglú.
In the 16th year, Wéi Gāo attacked
Wéizhōu.
In the first year of Dàizōng's Guǎngdé reign,
Wéizhōu fell to the Tǔbō.
In the 17th year, Lù Zhì submitted a memorial,
stating that the border provisions were inadequate
due to improper arrangements
and unsuitable storage.
The gist of it was:
"What is meant by 'improper arrangements' is that
the garrison soldiers are not subordinate to the defending officials,
and the defending officials are not entirely controlled by the grand marshal.
It even reaches a point where the general of one city
and the soldiers of one brigade
each receive supervision from a court envoy
and each are assigned duties by separate imperial edicts.
The divided garrisons span thousands of lí of land,
yet none cooperate with each other;
the ten myriad troops arrayed along the border
have no strategic planner.
Whenever invaders arrive,
they must first report to the central court for review.
By the time the mobilization and reinforcement orders are received,
the invaders have already won and retreated.
The Tǔbō, when compared to China,
are not unequal in numbers,
nor unmatched in skill.
Yet, they have surplus for attack,
while we lack for defense.
This is because their commands originate from their generals,
while our discipline is controlled by the court;
their forces are united and combined, while ours are divided and scattered.
What is meant by 'unsuitable storage' is that
Your Majesty previously established the 'purchase at the army' and 'harmonious purchase' methods to save on transportation,
stipulating a price double that given to people to encourage agriculture.
When this decree was first implemented,
everyone rejoiced.
This was a method implemented by Lǐ Bì,
details of which can be found
in [volume 232]
of [Zhēnyuán].
But the responsible officials competed in perfunctory actions,
focusing solely on stinginess.
In years of good harvest, they did not collect and store in time;
in times of food scarcity, they suppressed purchases.
This led to powerful families and corrupt officials
conversely manipulating the profit advantage,
buying cheaply from the people, awaiting the scarcity of both public and private sectors.
Moreover, influential figures, close relatives, and itinerant scholars
consigned cheap purchases to military cities,
taking high prices in the capital.
They also often used fine linen and silk to pay.
In the poor border regions, these clothes were too cold to wear,
and there was no market to sell them.
As the superiors had no trust in the subordinates,
the subordinates also responded with deceit.
The prices estimated by the Dùzhī (度支) became higher and higher,
and the grain prices in military cities became more and more expensive.
The Dùzhī regarded the expedient sale of unsalable goods as a meritorious profit,
and the military cities
considered the price increase they obtained as a surplus.
Although inspectorates (xúnyuàn) were established,
they merely became means of personal gain.
On the twelfth day of the twelfth month of the fourth year of Yuánhé,
an imperial edict stated:
'Envoys in distant prefectures
act arbitrarily and violate laws,
which the Táisī (臺司) cannot fully know.
The Zhuǎnyùnshǐ (轉運使) and Dùzhī (度支) all have xúnyuàn,
entrusted with investigating the local envoys and prefecture/county officials
regarding additional taxes beyond the two-tax system, tariffs, and violations of imperial edicts or laws, and reporting these to the Táisī.'
Indeed, Liú Yàn first established xúnyuàn,
extending from the Jiāng-Huái region to the Hé-Wèi region,
and later they were also set up in the various border circuits.
They falsely pointed to 'qūcāng' (囷倉) granaries,
counting their numbers as hundreds of millions,
but upon actual inspection, they were less than hundreds or tens."
It also says:
“The old system, due to the high expenditure in Guānzhōng,
annually transported grain from the east.
There was even a saying: 'A *dǒu* of grain costs a *qián* to transport a *dǒu* of grain.'
Those accustomed to what they saw and heard, but not adaptable to current circumstances,
would say: 'The great affairs of the state
should not account for costs and losses.
Though it is known to be arduous,
it cannot be abolished.'
Those accustomed to immediate benefits but not guarding against distant dangers
would say: 'Every autumn harvest,
just order requisitions within the imperial domain.
This makes the task easy to accomplish,
and also encourages agriculture.'
Your subject believes that the arguments of both parties
have their strengths and weaknesses.
When regulating state expenditures,
it is necessary to weigh their relative importance.
If food is insufficient but wealth is abundant,
then relax accumulation of wealth and focus on filling granaries.
If food is abundant but wealth is insufficient,
then slow down food accumulation and be frugal with currency.
In recent years, Guānfǔ has had repeated bountiful harvests,
and public stores are piled high,
enough for several years.
This summer, the Jiāng and Huái regions suffered from floods,
causing rice prices to double,
and many people became vagrants.
*Liú*
means to wander and migrate.
*Yōng*
means to be hired.
It is appropriate to raise prices to purchase grain, but there is no money.
In Jiāng and Huái, due to high grain prices, people are distressed.
It is appropriate to reduce prices to sell grain, but there is no rice.
Furthermore, to transport what they lack
to augment what is already surplus here—
this is what is called being accustomed to what one sees and hears but not adaptable to current circumstances.
Currently, in Jiāng and Huái, a *dǒu* of rice costs one hundred and fifty *qián*.
Transported to Dōngwèiqiáo,
the freight cost is another two hundred *qián*.
The rice is coarse and stale,
and particularly scorned by the capital.
According to the monthly appraisal of the Market Bureau,
the current Market Office
also submits monthly reports on the rise and fall of commodity prices to the emperor.
Losing nine parts to save one—
taking the rice from Jiāng and Huái,
combined with the freight cost of transportation,
amounts to three hundred and fifty *qián* per *dǒu*.
Yet the price of rice in the capital is only thirty-seven *qián* per *dǒu*.
This is losing nine parts to save one!
Such management of affairs
can be said to be a grave error!
Previously, annually, one million one hundred thousand *hú* of rice were transported from Jiāng, Hú, Huái, and Zhè.
Upon reaching Héyīn, four hundred thousand *hú* were retained,
stored in the Héyīn Granary.
Upon reaching Shǎnzhōu, another three hundred thousand *hú* were retained,
stored in the Tàiyuán Granary.
The remaining four hundred thousand *hú* were delivered to Dōngwèiqiáo.
Currently, the Héyīn and Tàiyuán Granaries still hold over three million two hundred thousand *hú* of rice.
In the counties of Jīngzhào, a *dǒu* of rice costs no more than seventy *qián*.
I request that next year, only three hundred thousand *hú* of rice be transported from Jiāng and Huái to Héyīn.
Héyīn and Shǎnpzhōu will then successively transport it to Dōngwèiqiáo.
The eight hundred thousand *hú* of rice from Jiāng and Huái whose transport is halted
should be entrusted to the Commissioner of Transport to sell in the flood-stricken prefectures and counties at eighty *qián* per *dǒu*,
to aid the poor.
This would yield six hundred and forty thousand *mín* of money
and reduce freight costs by six hundred and ninety thousand *mín*.
I request that the Ministry of Revenue first pay two hundred thousand *mín* to Jīngzhào,
to purchase rice to make up for the deficit in the Wèiqiáo Granary.
Wèiqiáo Granary
is Dōngwèiqiáo Granary.
Increasing the price for purchase will benefit farmers.
This will allow for the purchase of a year's worth of grain for one hundred thousand people,
with a remaining one hundred and four thousand *mín* to be used as the price for next year's requisitions.
The money from Jiāng and Huái rice and freight costs should all be entrusted to the Commissioner of Transport to exchange for *líng*, *juàn*, *shī*, and cotton, to be delivered to the upper capital
to repay the money previously loaned by the Ministry of Revenue."
In the ninth month,
an edict ordered the purchase of grain at high prices in the northwest border regions to fill granaries.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
"A total of three hundred and thirty thousand *hú* of rice was accumulated."
According to Lù Zhì's (陸贄) *Lùn Shǒubèi Zhuàng* (論守備狀), it says:
"Storing provisions at the border without effort,
the number exceeds one million.
The purchases in various garrisons
are now nearing completion."
It also says:
"After another year,
enough provisions for one hundred thousand people for three years can be accumulated."
Probably what the *Shílù* refers to
is this year's quantity,
while Zhì's (贄) memorial calculates up to next spring.
In the winter of the 18th year,
in the eleventh month,
on the *rénzǐ* day of the first quarter,
there was a solar eclipse.
Túbō and Yúnnán increasingly suspected each other.
Whenever Yúnnán troops reached the border,
Túbō would also dispatch troops,
ostensibly in response,
but actually to prepare for them.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Wéi Gāo again sent a letter to the King of Yúnnán,
wishing to jointly attack Túbō,
driving them beyond the Yúnlǐng mountains.
The land of Yúnnán
was originally Yúnnán County of the Hàn dynasty.
During Hàn, it belonged to Yìzhōu Commandery,
and in the Later Hàn, it was partitioned to belong to Yǒngchāng Commandery.
The *Nánzhōng Zhì* says: To the west of Yúnnán County, high mountains are connected.
Among the multitude of mountains,
there is a particularly tall and great mountain,
resembling Tàiyī of Fúfēng.
It is verdant, high, and steep,
connected with clouds and mist.
When one looks at it, its peak is not visible.
It is always overcast and bitterly cold;
even in the peak heat of May, it is not hot.
This is what is called Yúnlǐng.
He wished to construct a great city alone with Yúnnán on the border,
establish garrisons to protect each other,
and forever be one family.
20 The Left Shùzǐ, Jiāng Gōngfǔ, had not been promoted for a long time.
He went to Lù Zhì to seek promotion.
Lù Zhì secretly told him:
"I heard that Chancellor Dòu has repeatedly memorialized to propose you,
but the Emperor did not approve.
Nowadays, people say that when the Emperor's will does not follow what is requested, it means disapproval.
This is a common saying among the Táng people."
Jiāng Gōngfǔ was afraid,
and requested to become a Daoist priest.
The Emperor asked for the reason.
Jiāng Gōngfǔ dared not reveal Lù Zhì's words,
and replied that it was due to Chancellor Dòu's words.
The Emperor was angry that Chancellor Dòu attributed blame to the sovereign.
On the day Jǐsì,
Jiāng Gōngfǔ was demoted to Biejia of Jízhōu,
and a palace envoy was also sent to reprimand Chancellor Dòu.
Jiāng Gōngfǔ, in a suspicious and jealous court, was unable to be content with his fate and duty,
and thereby aggravated the guilt of Dòu Cān.
This too was due to a single word from Lù Zhì.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
"Initially,
Jiāng Gōngfǔ was dismissed as Chancellor and became Left Shùzǐ.
He was excused due to mourning,
and then reappointed as Right Shùzǐ.
He frequently paid private visits to Dòu Cān.
Dòu Cān repeatedly memorialized to propose Jiāng Gōngfǔ for other offices.
The Emperor did not permit it,
and expressed anger towards Jiāng Gōngfǔ.
Jiāng Gōngfǔ was afraid,
and therefore requested to be dismissed from office and become a Daoist priest.
After a long time,
there was no reply.
He then seized an opportunity during an audience in the Yányīng hall to memorialize about it.
The Emperor asked for the reason.
Jiāng Gōngfǔ replied that it was due to Chancellor Dòu's words.
The Emperor understood it,
but Jiāng Gōngfǔ persisted.
The Emperor became furious,
demoted him,
and issued an imperial edict reprimanding Chancellor Dòu for shifting blame to the Emperor."
Jiāng Gōngfǔ's biography says:
"When Lù Zhì was in charge of government affairs,
Jiāng Gōngfǔ, due to their old connection from the Hànlín Academy,
repeatedly asked Lù Zhì for an official position.
Lù Zhì secretly told Jiāng Gōngfǔ: 'I often see Chancellor Dòu of Chēnzhōu,
who said that he has memorialized to propose you several times,
but the Emperor's will did not approve,
and expressed anger towards you.'
Jiāng Gōngfǔ was afraid,
and submitted a memorial requesting to be dismissed from office and become a Daoist priest.
After a long time,
there was no reply.
Later, he again presented his case at court.
Dézōng asked for the reason.
Jiāng Gōngfǔ dared not reveal Lù Zhì's words,
and simply replied with Chancellor Dòu's words.
The Emperor was angry,
demoted Jiāng Gōngfǔ to Biejia of Quánzhōu,
and also sent a palace envoy with an edict to reprimand Chancellor Dòu."
Lù Zhì's biography says:
"Jiāng Gōngfǔ memorialized: 'Dòu Cān once told your servant,
that Your Majesty's anger towards your servant has not ceased.'
Dézōng was angry,
demoted Dòu Cān again,
and eventually put him to death.
At the time, public opinion held that Jiāng Gōngfǔ obtained Dòu Cān's words from Lù Zhì,
and said that Lù Zhì was instrumental
in Dòu Cān's death."
Examining Lù Zhì's memorial requesting that superior officials recommend their subordinates, it says:
"It is also due to privately visiting trusted relatives
who then betray them.
This harm is not distant;
Your Sagely Discernment clearly knows it."
This was to explain Dòu Cān's words.
And at the time of Dòu Cān's death,
Lù Zhì went to great lengths to save and defend him.
From this perspective,
how could Lù Zhì have intended to kill Dòu Cān?
Moreover, when Lù Zhì spoke to Jiāng Gōngfǔ,
how could he have known that Jiāng Gōngfǔ would ask to become a Daoist priest,
and then, before the Emperor, attribute the blame for revealing the words to Dòu Cān?
This was Jiāng Gōngfǔ's intention,
not Lù Zhì's intention.
People at the time,
seeing the rift between Dòu Cān and Lù Zhì,
then made their own conjectures.
The historians who disliked Lù Zhì
therefore assigned the blame to Lù Zhì.
We do not adopt this view now.
21 On the day Gēngwǔ,
Yán Zhèn, Jiedushi of Shānnán Xīdào, reported a victory over the Tǔbō at Fāngzhōu and Hēishuǐbǎo.
22 Initially,
Lǐ Nà, due to the salt profits at Hájiē in Dìzhōu,
fortified and occupied it.
He also garrisoned Sānchàchéng south of Dézhōu,
to open a path to Tián Xù.
When Lǐ Shīgǔ succeeded to the position,
Wáng Wǔjùn, considering him young,
slighted him.
In this month,
Wáng Wǔjùn led his troops to station in Dé and Dì,
intending to seize Hájiē and Sānchàchéng.
Lǐ Shīgǔ sent Zhào Hào to lead troops to resist him.
The Emperor sent a palace envoy to instruct them to stop,
and Wáng Wǔjùn then returned.
23 Initially,
Liú Pēng died.
See volume 232, Zhēnyuán 1st year.
Pēng,
pronounced Pǔméng.
Hōng,
pronounced Hūgōng.
His younger half-brother, Liú Yōng, was by his father's side,
and by his father's command summoned Liú Jì and handed over the military headquarters to him.
Mózhōu administered Mòxiàn,
280 li south of Yōuzhōu.
Yōng,
pronounced Yūyòng.
Yíngzhōu,
Hékān Jùn,
was a large prefecture under the jurisdiction of Yōuzhōu,
its territory being south of Yōuzhōu.
Subsequently, Liú Jì appointed his son as Deputy Grand Commissioner.
The three garrisons of Hèshuò and Zīqīng all appointed their sons as Deputy Grand Commissioner,
making them successor commanders.
Liú Yōng submitted a memorial to the imperial court,
and sent a thousand soldiers for autumn defense.
Liú Jì was enraged,
dispatched troops to attack Liú Yōng,
and defeated him.
24 Bǎi Liángqì, Grand General of the Left Shéncè Army.
The Grand Generals of the Left and Right Shéncè Armies of the Táng dynasty
were of 正二品 (rank 2a).
Shǐ Zhào says: Bǎihuáng Shì,
an ancient imperial title,
later became a surname.
They were descendants of Bǎi Liàng, teacher of Zhuāndì, and Bǎi Chāo, teacher of Dìkù.
The Supervising Eunuch Dòu Wénchǎng disliked him.
It happened that Bǎi Liángqì's wife's relatives got drunk
and lodged in a palace dwelling.
"Palace dwelling"
refers to the residence for those on duty in the palace.
Historians say that eunuchs disliked Bǎi Liángqì's ability to perform his duties,
and therefore fabricated charges against him based on his wife's relatives violating palace security.
On the day Bǐngxū,
Bǎi Liángqì was demoted to Right Lǐngjūn.
From this point, eunuchs began to monopolize military and political power.
This laid the groundwork for eunuchs to wield military power to threaten the Son of Heaven.
The Right Lǐngjūn
was one of the Sixteen Guards.
At that time, the various Guards of the Southern Court
were merely nominal positions.
The Northern Army held control of the imperial guards and had significant power,
hence Bǎi Liángqì's demotion was significant.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the guǐmǎo day,
a tea tax was first levied.
The Èryǎ Shì Mù (Explaining Trees in the Èryǎ) states: "Jiǎ
is bitter tea."
Guō Pú's commentary says: "Its tree is similar in size to a zhǐzi (gardenia),
its leaves grow in winter and can be boiled to make a soup-like drink."
Nowadays, what is picked early is called chá,
what is picked late is called míng,
also known as chuǎn.
The people of Shǔ call it bitter tea, which is correct.
Nowadays, it is generally called chá.
Chá and jiǎ sound similar,
hence the name.
In spring, when tender leaves first sprout,
they are steamed and roasted to remove the bitter liquid,
then powdered,
and only then can they be consumed.
This is vastly different from what was eaten in ancient times.
The Běncǎo Yǎnyì (Expanded Materia Medica) states: "Jìn dynasty's Wēn Jiào submitted a memorial,
contributing one thousand catties of chá
and three hundred catties of míng."
Guō Pú said: "What is picked early is chá,
what is picked late is míng."
Míng is also called chuǎn,
which refers to old tea leaves.
Ancient people called its buds "sparrow tongues" and "wheat grains,"
referring to their extreme tenderness.
There are also new buds
that grow more than an inch long as soon as they sprout,
slightly coarse like needles.
Only long buds are considered top quality,
because their roots and trunk have ample soil nutrients.
As for "sparrow tongues" and "wheat grains,"
they are of lower quality;
previous scholars did not fully recognize this.
History records that the tea tax began here,
thus opening a channel for profit.
All valued its worth,
taxing one-tenth,
in accordance with the request of the Salt and Iron Commissioner, Zhāng Pāng.
Pāng memorialized:
"Last year, tax revenue decreased due to floods,
and expenditures were insufficient.
I request to tax tea to make up the deficit.
From next year onwards,
the money from the tea tax
should be separately stored by the local authorities,
and in the event of floods or droughts,
it should be used to replace the people's land tax."
From then on, an annual tea tax of 400,000 strings of cash was collected,
but it was never used to alleviate floods or droughts.
The idea of a tea monopoly
began with Zhào Zàn,
but it was not implemented until Zhāng Pāng.
Pāng also memorialized:
"Wicked people melt coins to make copperware for profit;
I request to completely prohibit copperware.
Copper mines should be open for people to extract,
but private sales are forbidden."
2 In the second month,
on the jiǎyín day,
Zhāng Shēngyún, the acting military governor of Yìwǔ, was appointed Jiedushi.
3 Initially,
after Yánzhōu had fallen (see volume 232, second year, for the fall of Yánzhōu),
the Tǔbō often blocked Língwǔ
and harassed Fūfáng.
They not only blocked the passage to and from Língwǔ,
but also harassed the people of Fūfáng.
On the xīnyǒu day,
an imperial edict ordered 35,000 soldiers to fortify Yánzhōu.
Kǎoyì says: "The Bīnzì states:
'In the eighth year,
an imperial edict ordered Zhāng Gōngyì to supervise the construction of Yán and Xià cities.
Zhāng Gōngyì memorialized: "To advance and conquer with an army,
it is crucial to rely on brave generals.
Wèi Guāng, a scattered general of the Shéncè Army,
is a native of Shuòfāng,
and his martial arts are unparalleled;
with Guāng,
the task can surely be accomplished."
The Emperor dispatched him.
Zhāng Gōngyì appointed Guāng as the Bīnnìng Cavalry Army Commander.
In the third month,
the army and various forces arrived at Wǔyuán,
camping a hundred li from the city.
Guāng alone, with his cavalry, directly reached the city walls,
broke into and captured the city,
drove out the Tǔbō,
and summoned the various armies to fortify it;
he then led his army westward to plunder the borderlands,
patrolling back and forth,
serving as the eyes and ears for the main army.
The Tǔbō forces kept their distance from the border and dared not enter,
and the government army fortified the two prefectures and returned.'"
The note in Bái Jūyì's Yuèfǔ Yánzhōu
also states:
"In the rénhshēn year of Zhēnyuán,
a special edict ordered its fortification."
However, the Veritable Records place it in the second month of the ninth year.
Presumably, an edict to fortify it was issued last year,
and this year it was attributed to Dù Yànguāng and others.
Its fortification was completed in twenty days;
Dù Yànguāng, the Jiedushi of Yánzhōu, was ordered to guard it,
and Yáng Cháochéng, the Deputy Commissioner of the Shuòfāng Army, was ordered to guard Mùbōbǎo.
Mùbōbǎo
is located within the borders of Fāngqú County in Qìngzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì (Gazetteer of the Nine Regions) states: "Fāngqú,
in the Sòng dynasty, was renamed Tōngyuǎn County,
and Huánzhōu was established,
with Mùbō Town."
Xià and Héxī were pacified.
4 The Emperor sent an envoy to instruct Lù Zhì,
saying
, "For important matters,
do not discuss them with Zhào Jǐng.
Instead, you should seal your handwritten memorials and submit them to me."
He further said,
"Miáo Càn's father, Jìnqīng, served as regent in past years.
During the Bǎoyīng reign
there were repeated national sorrows,
and Jìnqīng served as Prime Minister.
All his sons share names with ancient emperors.
Jìnqīng has ten sons: Fā, Pī, Jiān, Chuí
share names with emperors.
His brothers should also be removed from their external posts,
and not allowed near military garrisons."
He also said,
"Your incorruptibility and prudence are excessive.
You reject all gifts from various circuits,
which I fear will hinder communication.
For items like whips and boots,
accepting them would do no harm."
Lù Zhì submitted a memorial,
the gist of which was:
"The memorial I submitted yesterday
was heard only by Zhào Jǐng.
Your Majesty has already gone to great lengths
to protect it thoroughly.
This suggests that within your innermost circle,
there are still constraints of formality.
When appearances are similar but the substance differs,
it rarely succeeds.
I fear this detracts from the virtue of impartiality.
Shuǎng
means 'mistake'.
The 'Shū' says: 'Do not be reluctant to correct mistakes.'
'Those to be ennobled must be in the court,
and those to be punished must be in the marketplace,'
lest the multitude not see it,
and the matter not be manifest.
The 'Jì' says: 'Those ennobled in court,
share with the multitude;
those punished in the marketplace,
are abandoned by the multitude.'
Cháo,
read zhí yáo fān.
Then the common people will listen without doubt or discussion,
those receiving rewards will feel at ease without shame,
and those undergoing punishment will have no complaints.
This is how the sage kings made their laws and regulations clear
and shared them with all under Heaven.
All accusations
are mostly not credible statements,
beneficial for slander,
and fearful of public debate.
Some say the years are long past,
and it is impossible to investigate;
some say the matter is problematic,
and one must endure it in secret;
some say the evil deeds are not yet exposed,
and one should use other pretexts;
some say simply abandon the person,
why explicitly state the blame and humiliation.
The words all seem reasonable,
but the intent actually encompasses deceit and false accusations.
Harming the good and promoting the wicked,
nothing is worse than this!
If Jìnqīng and his son truly committed great crimes,
then they should be publicly judged by the law;
if they were falsely accused,
how could they be made to suffer secret banishment?
In hearing lawsuits and discerning slander,
one must seek out the truth of the matter and trace the facts.
When the truth is seen and the facts are clear,
and their words are exhausted and their arguments fail,
only then should punishment be applied.
In this way, there will be no wronged people below,
and no mistaken judgments above."
He also said:
"For officials receiving bribes,
even an inch (of illicit gain) merits punishment.
The law states:
'Any supervisory official
who receives property from those under their supervision,
for one chǐ, they shall receive forty strokes of the bamboo.
Any supervisory official who receives property and perverts justice,
for one chǐ, they shall receive one hundred strokes of the heavy bamboo.'
Jiān,
read gǔ hán fān.
Such actions are still strictly forbidden.
How then, can it be permissible for the leader of moral transformation!
'Leader of moral transformation' refers to the Prime Minister, from whom moral transformation originates.
If this continues and worsens,
starting with whips and boots,
it will inevitably reach gold and jade.
Xuē,
same as xuē.
How can one restrain oneself mentally!
There is an ancient saying,
'If one does not see desirable things,
their mind will not be disturbed.'
How can one break off such intentions midway!
It means that once one accepts private gifts,
it becomes difficult to refuse private requests.
The ravines will become a disaster."
He also said:
"If one sometimes accepts
and sometimes rejects,
then those who are rejected will suspect they have been refused and become resentful.
If one consistently refuses to accept,
then everyone will know that non-acceptance is the normal state of affairs,
and what cause for suspicion or obstruction would there be?"
5 Initially,
Dòu Cān hated Zuǒ Sī Lángzhōng Lǐ Xùn,
and had him sent out as Cángzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Dòu Cān was demoted to Chēnzhōu,
Lǐ Xùn became Húnán Guānchásǐ.
Liú Shìníng, Jìedùshǐ of Biànzhōu, sent Dòu Cān fifty bolts of silk.
Lǐ Xùn memorialized that Dòu Cān was colluding with regional governors.
The Emperor was greatly angered
and wished to kill Dòu Cān.
Lù Zhì believed Dòu Cān's crime did not merit death,
so the Emperor stopped.
Soon after, he again sent a eunuch to Lù Zhì, saying:
"Dòu Cān colluded with both those inside and outside the court.
His intentions are unfathomable.
The affairs of the state are grave,
you should quickly submit a document for his disposition."
Lù Zhì submitted a memorial, stating:
"Dòu Cān is a high minister of the court;
executing him without clear cause is unacceptable.
In the past, Liú Yàn's death
was without clear crime,
and to this day, public opinion remains indignant,
allowing rebellious officials to use it as an excuse.
See volume 226, Jiànzhōng first and second years.
The whole world knows this.
As for secretly harboring rebellious plans,
the facts are ambiguous.
If he is not interrogated,
and suddenly subjected to severe punishment,
it will cause considerable alarm.
Dòu Cān and I have no affinity;
the words indicate no close personal relationship.
Fēn,
read fú wèn fān.
I do not seek to save this man,
but rather regret any abuse of the law."
In the third month,
Dòu Cān was further demoted to Huānzhōu Sīmǎ,
and his entire family (males and females) were banished.
The Emperor then ordered the investigation of Dòu Cān's relatives and associates.
Lǐ,
means zhì (govern, manage).
Lù Zhì said: "Crimes have principals and accessories,
and laws have varying degrees of severity.
Shǒu,
refers to the leader.
Cóng,
refers to the followers.
Leaders receive heavier punishment,
followers lighter.
Dòu Cān's relatives and associates should also receive reduced penalties.
Moreover, at the beginning of Dòu Cān's disgrace,
his private associates were already implicated and punished.
Public sentiment has long been settled,
so please do not investigate further."
The Emperor agreed.
The Emperor also wanted to confiscate Dòu Cān's family property.
Lù Zhì said:
"According to the law,
rebels have all their property confiscated,
while corrupt officials are only penalized for the amount they embezzled.
In both cases, the judgment must be finalized and punishment applied,
before confiscation takes place.
Now, the exact crime is not yet detailed,
and Your Majesty has already shown mercy and leniency.
If his family property is confiscated,
I fear it would be sacrificing righteousness for wealth."
At that time, the eunuchs and attendants hated Dòu Cān even more deeply,
and continued to slander him.
Before Dòu Cān reached Huānzhōu,
he was ultimately granted death on the road.
Dòu Shēn was beaten to death,
and all his goods, money, and slaves were sent to the capital.
Chuán,
read zhī liàn fān.
6 Zhāng Shēnglín (張昇璘), the Commissioner of Militia of Hǎizhōu (海州),
younger brother of Shēngyún (昇雲),
and son-in-law of Lǐ Nà (李納),
returned to Dìngzhōu (定州) for his father’s "Great Mourning" (dàxiáng).
Hǎizhōu (海州)
was Dōnghǎi Jùn (東海郡),
subordinate to Zīqīng Xún (淄青巡).
Lín (璘),
pronounced lí zhēn.
Xù (壻),
pronounced xī jì.
Dìngzhōu (定州)
was the administrative seat of the Yìwǔ (義武) commander.
A son observing his father’s mourning
concludes the great mourning after two full years.
Wǔjùn (武俊) reported this.
Summer,
fourth month,
on the Dīngchǒu (丁丑) day,
an edict stripped him of his official rank,
and a palace envoy was dispatched to cane and imprison him.
Dìngzhōu (定州) was wealthy and prosperous,
and Wǔjùn (武俊) had always coveted it.
On this pretext, he dispatched troops to attack and seize Yìfēng (義豐),
plundering over ten thousand people from Ānxǐ (安喜) and Wújí (無極),
and relocating them to Dé (德) and Dì (棣).
Yìfēng (義豐)
belonged to Dìngzhōu (定州).
Ānxǐ Xiàn (安喜縣)
was originally the administrative seat of Dìngzhōu (定州),
which was later moved.
Wújí (無極),
an ancient county of the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
was named after Wújí Shān (無極山).
During the Táng (唐) dynasty, it belonged to Dìngzhōu (定州).
According to the stele of Wújí Shān (無極山), it states:
“Wújí Shān (無極山) came into being with heaven and earth.
From its top to its base,
it is about three lǐ (里) high.
A stone stands as its body,
about twenty-five chǐ (尺) tall.
The stone is green above
and yellowish-white below.
The front is perfectly flat,
wide enough to lay two large mats.”
It is located thirty lǐ (里) southwest of Wújí (無極).
In the second year of Jǐngfú (景福),
Wújí Xiàn (無極縣) was renamed Qízhōu (祁州).
Dì (棣),
pronounced dà jì.
He repeatedly sent envoys to apologize,
and then stopped.
The emperor ordered Lǐ Shīgǔ (李師古) to demolish the Sānchà Chéng (三汊城).
Lǐ Nà (李納) had built Sānchà Chéng (三汊城),
as mentioned last year.
Chà (汊),
pronounced chǔ jià.
However, he constantly gathered fugitives,
and those who had offended the imperial court
were all appeased and employed by him.
7 Fifth month,
on the Jiǎchén (甲辰) day,
Zhào Jǐng (趙憬), the Senior Vice Minister of the Secretariat, was appointed Senior Vice Minister of the Chancellery and concurrently Director of Affairs (Tóng Píngzhāngshì).
Jiǎ Dān (賈耽), the Military Commissioner of Yìchéng (義成), was appointed Right Executive of the Department of State Affairs;
Lú Mài (盧邁), the Right Assistant, retained his original post,

Mài (邁)
was a clan nephew of Hàn (翰).
Jǐng (憬) suspected Lù Zhì (陸贄) of relying on imperial favor

The Hall of Administration was in the Secretariat,
and now Jǐng (憬) was moved to the eastern department,
hence his suspicion that Zhì (贄) was pushing him out.
The Right Executive of the Department of State Affairs belonged to the Chancellery.
Because of this, he had a rift with Zhì (贄).
This was the basis for Zhào Jǐng (趙憬)'s attachment to Péi Yánlíng (裴延齡).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The old biography of Jǐng (憬) says:
“Jǐng (憬) and Lù Zhì (陸贄) jointly managed state affairs.
Zhì (贄) relied on his long tenure in the Forbidden City,
and his special imperial favor,
considering state affairs his own responsibility.
Within a year,
Jǐng (憬) was transferred to Senior Vice Minister of the Chancellery.
Jǐng (憬) thereupon harbored deep resentment,
repeatedly citing eye illness to request leave,
not fully engaging in state affairs,
and thus they were not in harmony.”
According to this, Jǐng (憬)’s transfer to the Chancellery still made him a Chancellor.
Moreover, Jiǎ Dān (賈耽) and Lú Mài (盧邁) were added.
How could Zhì (贄) monopolize power?
Perhaps Jǐng (憬) merely harbored this suspicion.
8 Lù Zhì (陸贄) submitted a memorial discussing six failings in border defense,
believing that:
“Measures are inappropriate,
accountability is lacking,
resources are depleted by excessive troops,
strength is divided by too many commanders,
resentment arises from inequality,
and opportunities are lost through remote control.”
From "measures are inappropriate" onwards,
these are the so-called six failings.
Shàng (上),
pronounced shí zhǎng.
Jiàng (將),
pronounced jí liàng;
same below.
“Guanzhong (關中) garrison soldiers
are unfamiliar with the local customs.
Their bodies suffer in the desolate borderlands,
and their hearts fear the barbarians.
The state supports them like spoiled children,
indulging them like hired hands.
They count the days until their return,
and wait with open mouths to be fed;
some even profit from the defeat of the imperial army,
taking advantage of the chaos to flee eastward;
others abandon towns and cities,
shaking the hearts of those near and far.
Not only are they useless,
they are actually harmful.
Furthermore, there are those who are criminals exiled by punishment,
who are not only disreputable,
but also harbor strong homesickness,
desiring chaos and rejoicing in disaster,
even more so than the garrison soldiers.
This can be called inappropriate measures.
This is the first failing.
Since recently, power has shifted downwards,
and authority has been lost to the court.
The commanders’ orders are rarely enforced in the army,
and the state’s laws and regulations cannot be applied to the commanders.
They are eager to indulge each other,
Zūn (遵),
means shuài (率),
referring to collectively indulging evil.
If one wishes to reward someone who has rendered service,
one fears that those without service will feel discontent;
if one wishes to punish someone who has committed a crime,
one fears that those of similar ilk will feel worried.
Crimes are concealed and not exposed,
while merits are withheld due to suspicion and not rewarded.
The way of indulgence
has reached this extreme.
This causes those who sacrifice their lives and show loyalty to be ridiculed by their peers,
and those who lead troops to be the first to ascend to incur resentment from their soldiers.
Those who ruin armies and damage the state feel no shame or fear,
and those who delay aid and miss deadlines consider themselves intelligent.
This is why righteous scholars are heartbroken,
and brave men lose their will.
This can be called lacking accountability.
This is the second failing.
Every time the barbarians invade,
the generals and commanders shift responsibility to each other,
none daring to take charge.
They exaggerate the enemy’s strength upwards, reporting,
‘We are outnumbered and cannot contend.’
The imperial court fails to investigate,
only striving to conscript and dispatch more troops,
which does not aid in defense,
but only exacerbates the burden of provisioning.
Zhòng (重),
pronounced zhí yòng.
Levies and demands daily increase,
using the wealth of registered households who lose their families and ruin their livelihoods,
along with the profits from salt monopolies and wine taxes by the authorities.
All their income
is annually used for border affairs.
This can be called resources depleted by excessive troops.
This is the third failing.”
The entirety of Tǔbō's victorious soldiers
amounted to merely a dozen or so large commanderies in the Central Plains.
When they moved, the Central Plains feared their numbers and dared not resist.
When they were still, the Central Plains dreaded their strength and dared not invade.
What was the reason for this?
It was truly because the Central Plains had many divisions in its command and control,
while the barbarian hordes had a unified command.
When command is unified,
people's hearts are not divided,
orders are not duplicated,
advances and retreats can be synchronized,
speed and slowness are as desired,
and opportunities are not missed.
"Qiān"
means "to violate" or "to miss."
This is how few become many,
and weak become strong.
Between the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras,
control over the Xīběi (northwestern) and Liǎngfān (two barbarian groups)
rested solely with the three Jiedùshǐ of Shuòfāng, Héxī, and Lǒngyòu.
Since the Zhongxing (restoration) era,
there has been no time for external campaigns.
Those who resisted the Liǎngfān were also merely the four Jiedùshǐ of Shuòfāng, Jīngyuán, Lǒngyòu, and Hédōng.
"Speaking of the Xīběi Liǎngfān"
distinguishes them from the Xī and Qìdān Liǎngfān.
In the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras,
the west was Tǔbō,
and the north was Tūjué.
Since the Zhōngxīng era,
the so-called Liǎngfān were
Tǔbō in the west,
and Huíhé in the north.
There were three envoys who "jiàn yá yǒng jié" (established their banners and held their insignias of authority).
This matter is found in Volume 225, Dàlì 14th year.
"Shǐ"
reads "shū lì."
Their numbers were almost forty.
All received special imperial edicts entrusting them with responsibility,
and each was accompanied by an imperial eunuch supervisor.
Individuals were able to contend with each other,
and none submitted to another.
Each time frontier reports of emergency arrived,
only then were plans made for military action.
Since there was no military law to enforce,
they merely treated each other with the courtesy due to guests.
Now, warfare
relies on morale and momentum;
when morale is gathered, it flourishes;
when scattered, it dissipates;
when momentum is united, it is formidable;
when divided, it is weak.
The current frontier defenses are
weak in momentum and dissipated in morale;
it can be said that strength is divided due to too many generals.
The essential principle for managing military affairs
lies in training and rigorously assessing the quality and inferiority of various ranks to establish a system of clothing and food grades,
so that the capable can strive for advancement,
and the incapable will resign themselves,
thus, though there may be differences in rewards, there will be no cause for discontent.
Currently, in the remote frontier regions,
the soldiers stationed for long periods
are all veterans scarred from countless battles,
enduring extreme hardships year-round.
However, the clothing and rations provided
are only for themselves,
customarily divided among their wives and children,
always showing signs of cold and hunger.
Meanwhile, the garrisons east of the passes
are timid in facing the enemy,
and lax in performing their duties,
yet the clothing and rations they receive
are several grades more generous.
Moreover, there are those who were originally not imperial guards
but frontier soldiers,
whose officers cunningly use flattering words
to request remote attachment to the Shéncè (Divine Strategy) Army.
They do not leave their old posts,
only change their old
names,
and thus enjoy a threefold increase
in the abundance of their stipends.
If their duties are no different yet their provisions vary,
if they haven't forgotten their resentments,
who can avoid indignation?
It can be said that resentment arises from inequality.
Whenever one wishes to select and appoint generals,
one must first investigate their conduct and abilities.
Those who are suitable should be dispatched,
those who are unsuitable should be dismissed,
the doubtful should not be employed,
and those employed should not be doubted.
Thus, "when a general is in the field,
even the sovereign's command may not be obeyed."
These are the words of Sūnzi's Art of War.
However, decisions often come from the imperial heart;
when selecting and appointing military officials,
the priority is to find those who are easily controlled.
Their departments are multiplied to divide their strength,
and their responsibilities are lightened to weaken their resolve.
Consequently, even if it contradicts military strategy, they obey;
even if it goes against expediency, they obey.
When barbarian raiders charge,
they are swift as a storm.
Urgent dispatches reach the court,
but a month passes before a reply is given.
Those defending their territory dare not resist the enemy with few troops,
and those commanding divided garrisons refuse to mobilize without an imperial edict.
By the time the bandits have plundered and retreated,
these officials then report their achievements and victories.
Their losses are reduced from a hundred to one,
and their gains are exaggerated from a hundred to a thousand.
The generals, being fortunate that overall command is with the court,
do not worry about culpability,
and His Majesty, believing that supreme authority rests with himself,
does not investigate the facts.
It can be said that opportunities are lost due to remote control.
These are the six shortcomings.
Your servant humbly believes that the system of commanders and soldiers from various circuits defending against autumn raids should be abolished.
Let the local circuits merely provide clothing and rations,
and recruit frontier soldiers willing to remain, as well as Tǔbō and Hàn youths, to supply them.
Furthermore, more military agricultural colonies should be established,
with the government collecting and storing grain.
When invaders arrive, people will fight for themselves;
when it is time, families will work hard at farming.
How can these people
be compared to those who come and go swiftly?
Moreover, competent civil and military officials should be selected as the three commanders-in-chief for Lǒngyòu, Shuòfāng, and Hédōng,
to jointly command the various Jiedùshǐ along the border.
Those who are not crucial
should be merged as convenience and proximity dictate.
Then, reduce extravagant and superfluous expenses to enrich the treasury,
establish a system of clothing and ration grades to harmonize the populace,
broaden the path of delegation to fully utilize their talents,
and enforce strict standards of reward and punishment to evaluate their performance.
If this is done,
then the Róngdí will be awed and appeased,
and the borders will be peaceful! "
Although the emperor could not entirely follow this advice,
he valued it greatly in his heart.
9 Wéi Gāo sent his grand general Dǒng Miǎn and others to lead troops out to Xīshān,
defeated the Tǔbō forces,

10 On the day of Bǐngwǔ,

11 Yìmóuxún, King of Yúnnán, sent three groups of envoys.
One group departed from Róngzhōu.

was the land of Bódào County, Nán'ān, in the Hàn dynasty.

Southwestward, taking the path through Qú, Xié Zhōu, Nánníng Zhōu, Ānníng, and Yánjǐng, it was 2,300 lǐ to Yángjūmí City, where Nánzhào resided.
Old records state: Róngzhōu
was 3,104 lǐ southwest of the capital.

Each carried raw gold and cinnabar to Wéi Gāo.
Unforged gold ore is called raw gold.
Cinnabar

reads "qín."

They split Gāo's letter into three parts as a token of trust,

and also sent a silk letter to Gāo,
styling himself "Sun of the Táng
King of Yúnnán and Yìdì (sworn brother) of the Tǔbō Zānpǔ, King of Rìdōng."
"Yìdì Rìdōng Wáng."

"Chǔ"
reads "chāng lǚ fān";
