13 The Qiāng queens of Jiànnán and Xīshān, Tāng Lìzhì,
and queens
of other Qiāng tribes.
To their east, they bordered Tǔbō, Dǎngxiàng, and Máozhōu.
To their west, they were subject to Sānbōhē.
To their north, they were distant from Yútián.
They were administered by Yǎzhōu.
The Luónǚ Mán and Báiláng Yí,
who took women as their rulers,
resided in Kāngyán Chuān,
a place surrounded by steep and perilous mountains.
There was a Ruòshuǐ river flowing south.
"Tāng Lìzhì"
is written as
"Tāng Lìxī" in the New History.
The Dùyáng Biān states: The people of the Nǚmán Kingdom,
with their high chignons and golden crowns,
and their bodies adorned with pearl necklaces,
were therefore called Púsàmán.
At that time, entertainers then composed Púsàmán tunes based on this.
All the tribes from Gēlín downwards
were scattered throughout Xīshān.
Xīshān is Xǔeshān.
Today, Wēizhōu, Bǎoníng Xiàn has Xǔeshān,
which connects to Rǔchuān, Báigǒu Lǐng.
It has nine peaks,
with snow that does not melt in spring and summer.
Báigǒu Lǐng is connected to Xǔeshān.
Wēizhōu
was Táng's Wéizhōu.
At this point, each led their people to submit to the court.
Wéi Gāo settled them in Wéi, Bǎo, and Bàzhōu.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo,
he invited the raw Qiāng to submit
and established Bàzhōu.
Lìzhì, Tuóhū, and Pìhé came to court,
were all granted official positions,

14 On Guǐmǎo,
Péi Yánlíng, Minister of the Board of Revenue, reported:
"Since taking charge of the state finance commission,
I have audited over eight million strings of money owed by various prefectures,
collected three million strings of chōuguàn money from various prefectures,
and presented samples of goods worth over three hundred thousand strings.
I request that a separate quarterly treasury for deficiencies, surpluses, and arrears be established to manage these."
"Hào"
means deficit or reduction.
"Shèng"
means surplus or profit.
"Shèng"
is pronounced like "zhèng,"
and also "shí zhèng."
Three months constitute a quarter.
Whenever a quarter ends,
items are deposited into the treasury,
hence it is called a quarterly treasury.
When items are deposited monthly,
it is called a monthly treasury.
The arrears were all debts that poor people could not repay,
merely existing in the records.
The chōuguàn money was used up as soon as it was disbursed.
The presented samples, dyed and refined goods, were all legitimate items of the Left Treasury.
Yánlíng merely established a separate treasury
and exaggerated the numbers to mislead the emperor.
The emperor believed him,
thinking he could enrich the state, and favored him,
but in reality, nothing was added.

money and currency
are what officials create.
This is why the national dynasty's established regulations state:
rent is paid in grain,
corvée (yōng) in raw silk (juàn),
and tribute (diào) in silk (zēng), floss (kuàng), and cloth.
When was it ever forbidden for people to mint coins, or was money ever used as a tax?
The current Two-Tax (Liǎngshuì)
uniquely differs from old regulations.
It merely assesses assets for grading,
then fixes taxes in money and grain.
Temporarily, miscellaneous goods are collected by 'conversion' (zhézhēng),
meaning converting the value of money and grain to collect other miscellaneous goods.
Zhé
is pronounced with the initial 'zhī' and final 'shé'.
Only the expediency of sought-after profit is considered,
without regard for the difficulty of procurement.
What is collected is not what is produced,
and what is produced is not what is collected.
Consequently, some might increase prices to buy what they lack,
or decrease prices to sell what they possess.
One increase, one decrease,
and the loss is already substantial.
We hope that the initial silk and cloth collected for the Two-Tax (Liǎngshuì) in various prefectures in the year it was implemented will be investigated and assessed.
Determine and compare their estimated value with current market prices,
lower what is expensive, raise what is cheap,
and select a median value.
Sum the total amount of money due for tax,
and convert it into an equivalent amount of cloth and silk."
It also states:
"The productive capacity of the land has a great limit.
If one takes with moderation
and uses with frugality,
there will always be enough.
If one takes without moderation
and uses without frugality,
there will always be scarcity.
The abundance or failure of production depends on heaven;
the quantity of resources used depends on humans.
Therefore, the sage kings established systems,
budgeting expenditures according to income.
Even when disasters occurred,
the people below were not in distress.
When righteous governance (lǐhuà) declines,
the opposite occurs.
Lǐhuà
means 'governance and transformation'.
They do not care about what is lacking.
Jié used all under heaven and it was not enough;
Tāng used a seventy-lǐ territory and had a surplus.
This shows that the abundance or scarcity of resources depends on frugality or its absence."
The third point:
regarding the evaluation of chief officials (chánglì) based on increasing households, raising taxes, and opening up fields as performance metrics.
Its summary states:
"Those who govern people rarely manage to extend compassion and empathy,
or embody impartiality and devotion to the nation.
Instead, they alternately offer minor favors,
compete to entice treacherous commoners,
considering the seduction and seizure of neighboring territories as wisdom and intelligence,
and the gathering of fugitives as righteous governance (lǐhuà).
Those who abandon one place for another become newly registered and receive 'relief' (fù).
Cuì
means 'to gather'.
Fù
is pronounced with the initial 'fāng' and final 'mù'.
Fù
means 'to remit' or 'to exempt'.
Only those who cherish their homeland, live in peace,
and have never moved from beginning to end
are made to bear ever-increasing burdens,
with taxes levied ever more heavily.
This causes settled people (dìzhù zhī rén) to constantly shoulder the duties and taxes of the idle and wandering.
How is this different from driving them to relocate,
and teaching them to become deceitful?
This stems from the inability of local administrators (mùzǎi) to be broad-minded and impartial,
each privately favoring their own jurisdiction."
It also states:
"Laws that aim to equalize people,
after a long time, are invariably flawed.
If those who manage them do not know how to maintain and regulate gains and losses appropriately,
then cunning and deceit will emerge
and invariably flourish due to discouragement and encouragement.
I request that a new decree be issued to relevant officials
to thoroughly establish performance evaluations.
If, within a given jurisdiction,
the people become more prosperous,
and the fixed tax quota has a surplus,
let officials be allowed to reduce it proportionally based on household registration,
and use the amount of reduction as a criterion for performance grading.
If the total tax burden in their jurisdiction is compared
and reduced by three-tenths per household, it is considered a top grade;
a two-tenths reduction is next;
a one-tenth reduction is third.
This does not prioritize increasing households as the best performance,
but rather considers reducing the tax quota of settled households (dìzhù hù) by increasing the household quota as the best performance.
For increasing taxes on existing households,
comparisons for rewards and punishments should also be done similarly."
The fourth point:
regarding the urgent and pressing tax deadlines.
Its summary states:
"The establishment of government and nation
is for the purpose of nurturing the people;
levying taxes from the people
is for the purpose of funding the nation.
An enlightened ruler does not prioritize what funds the nation at the expense of what nurtures the people.
Therefore, he must prioritize human affairs and borrow their leisure labor,
ensuring family sufficiency before collecting their surplus wealth."
It also states:
"While silkworm cultivation is still in full swing,
silk taxes are already due.
Before agricultural work is finished,
grain rents are hastily collected.
The severe demands from superior authorities
make the coercion and brutality of subordinate officials even more urgent.
Those who have goods are forced to sell them quickly, losing half their value;
those who have nothing are forced to borrow, paying double in return.
We hope that the deadlines for tax collection will be re-evaluated and determined in detail."
The fifth point:
a request to use tea tax money to establish communal granaries (yìcāng) to prepare for floods and droughts.
Tea tax (shuìchá) is mentioned in the ninth year [of the reign period] above.
"The ancients referred to stockpiles for nine or six years.
The Wáng Zhì records: 'Three years of farming must yield one year's food;
nine years of farming must yield three years' food.'
The nation's expenditure was planned with a thirty-year general system,
budgeting expenditures according to income.
A nation without a nine-year stockpile was called 'insufficient';
without a six-year stockpile, it was called 'urgent';
without a three-year stockpile, it was called 'not truly a nation'.
This was certainly not merely to enrich public granaries
without benefiting the common people (biānméng).
Recently, officials proposed taxing tea,
which annually yields approximately 500,000 guàn.
An imperial edict initially ordered it to be stored in the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù),
to be used to relieve the people during famine.
Now, using it to stockpile grain
perfectly aligns with the previous imperial intention."
Sixth,
it discusses households that consolidate land,
whose private levies are heavier than public taxes.
Its summary says:
"Currently, within the Jīngjī region,
for every mū of land,
the official tax is five shēng,
but private households collect rent, with some amounting to one dàn per mū,
which is twenty times the official tax.
Even for medium-quality land,
the rent is still half of that.
Land belongs to the sovereign,
and cultivation is done by farmers,
yet those who consolidate land
openly profit from it."
It further states:
"It is hoped that for all land occupied,
based on the stipulated limits,
rent prices will be reduced
to benefit the poor.
Laws must be implemented,
but care must be taken not to be overly harsh.
Make the system lenient to suit common customs,
and make the decrees strict to punish violations,
slightly reducing the surplus
and slightly favoring the insufficient.
Loss should not harm the wealthy;
favoring the poor can alleviate destitution.
This is indeed an excellent principle for
settling the wealthy and helping the poor,
and it must not be abandoned."
The Zhōu Lǐ, Dìguān chapter, states: "By six provisions, the myriad people are sustained: first, to be kind to the young;
second, to care for the elderly;
third, to aid the destitute;
fourth, to relieve the poor;
fifth, to comfort the sick;
sixth, to settle the wealthy."
Punctuation by Róng Zhàozǔ, collated by Niè Chóngqí.
Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng
by imperial decree.
Later School Tāi.
Zhēnyuán tenth year
(jiǎxū, 794).
The sixth month,
on the day rěnyín,
Lǐ Bǎozhēn, Jǐedùshǐ of Zhāoyì, died.
His son, Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ Jiān, plotted with Bǎozhēn's maternal nephew Yuán Zhòngjīng,
secretly withholding the news of death.
They forged a memorial from Bǎozhēn,
requesting that Jiān be appointed to his duties.
They also forged a letter from his father
and sent staff officer Chén Róng to Wáng Wǔjùn to borrow money and goods.
Wǔjùn angrily said:
"I was on good terms with your father,
intending to jointly assist the imperial court.
How could I collaborate with you in wickedness!
I heard your father has already passed away.
Nǎi
is like 'rǔ' (you).
Gōng
is like 'wēng' (old man/father).
How dare you inform me,
let alone make demands!"
He sent Róng back,
conveying a message to sternly rebuke Jiān.
Zhì
means 'zhèng' (correct/just).
It means to rebuke him with righteousness.
Wáng Yánguì, Dūyúhòu of the Zhāoyì infantry,
was a native of Liáng in Rǔzhōu.
Liáng County
belonged to Hénán Commandery during the Hàn and Jìn dynasties.
Later, the Northern Wèi established Rǔběi Commandery.
The Suí divided it to establish Chéngxiū County,
while Liáng County remained as before.
The Táng considered Chéngxiū County as part of Rǔzhōu,
so Liáng County was forty-five lǐ southwest of it.
The Emperor learned that Bǎozhēn had died,
and sent inner envoy Dìwǔ Shǒujìn to observe the situation
and entrust military affairs to Wáng Yánguì.
When Shǒujìn arrived at Shàngdǎng,
the Zhāoyì army
was stationed at Shàngdǎng.
Three days later,
Jiān, with armed soldiers, went to Shǒujìn.
Shǒujìn said to him:
"The imperial court already knows that Xiànggōng has passed away.
Juān
means 'qì' (abandon).
It refers to the deceased abandoning their dwelling and departing.
Shìyù should announce the death and observe mourning."
Jiān was startled.
He went out
and said to his generals:
"The imperial court does not allow Jiān to manage affairs.
What do you gentlemen think?"
No one responded.
Jiān was afraid,
so he returned to announce the death
and handed over the official seal and keys to the supervisor of the army.
The envoy seal
was the Jǐedù's seal.
Jiān
is pronounced gǔhán fān.
He announced the oral imperial decree to manage affairs,
orally proclaiming the imperial edict he received,
hence called an "oral decree."
He was urged to proceed to the Eastern Capital
and return to his private residence.
Qù
is read as 'cù'.
Yánguì placed all blame on Zhòngjīng
and arrested and executed him.
An imperial edict appointed Yánguì to provisionally oversee Zhāoyì military affairs.
Yúnnán Wáng Yìmóxún sent his younger brother Còuluóliànd
to present maps, local tribute, and the gold seal bestowed by Tǔbō,
requesting to restore the title Nánzhào.
In the Yi language, 'wáng' (king) is 'zhào'.
Their early leaders were six,
calling themselves Liùzhào:
Méngkuí Zhào,
Yuèxī Zhào,
Làngqióng Zhào,
Déngshǎn Zhào,
Shīlàng Zhào,
and Méngshè Zhào.
Méngshè Zhào was south of the other tribes,
hence called Nánzhào (Southern Zhào).
When it reached Méng Guīyì,
Xuánzōng enfeoffed him as Yúnnán Wáng,
and thus it was called Yúnnán.
On the day guǐchǒu,
Yuán Zī, Lángzhōng of the Cíbù, was appointed envoy to enfeoff Nánzhào.
Kǎoyì states: The Old Nánzhào Biography says:
"In the eighth month of the tenth year,
Còuluóliànd was sent to present the Tǔbō seal."
The New Biography says:
"Yìmóxún allied with Cuī Zuǒshí at Diǎncāngshān
and defeated the Tūjué at Shénchuān.
In the sixth month of the following year,
Yìmóxún was enfeoffed as Nánzhào Wáng."
According to the records,
it was the sixth month of this year;
both New and Old biographies are mistaken.
Wéi Gāo's memorials all refer to him as
"Yúnnán Wáng,"
but Dòu Pāng's Yúnnán Biélù says:
"An edict enfeoffed Yìmóxún as Nánzhào through Yuán Zī."
It was likely in response to his request,
and the name Nánzhào began from this point.
In the Mán language,
'zhào' means 'wáng' (king).
The New Biography's
"Nánzhào Wáng"
is also mistaken.
I note that Yìmóxún defeated Tǔbō at Shénchuān,
but Kǎoyì mistakenly wrote
"Tūjué."
The text says
"Zhēnyuán enfeoffed Nánzhào seal."
When Zī arrived at his kingdom,
Yìmóxún knelt facing north to receive the enfeoffment and seal,
kowtowed and bowed twice.
He then feasted with the envoy,
bringing out two silver píngtuō horse-head plates bestowed by Xuánzōng to show Zī.
He also pointed to an old flute player and singing girl and said:
"This is Kuīcí music bestowed by the Emperor."
The Táng's ten musical ensembles included Kuīcí music,
featuring a tánzhēng, a shùkōnghóu, a pípa, a wǔxián, a héngdí, a shēng, a xiāo, a bìlì, a dálàgǔ, a máoyuángǔ, a dūtángǔ, a hóutígǔ, a jīlóugǔ, a yāogǔ, a dángǔ, and a qí gǔ.
All were single instruments,
with two bronze cymbals,
and four dancers.
Five "directional lions" were arranged,
over a zhàng tall,
decorated with corresponding colors.
Each lion had twelve performers,
wearing painted clothes,
holding red whisks,
with red socks on their heads,
called 'Shīziláng'.
Kuīcí
is pronounced Qiūcí.
Zī said:
"Nánzhào should deeply remember his ancestors,
and generations of descendants should be loyal to the Táng."
Yìmóxún bowed and said:
"How dare I not respectfully obey the envoy's command!"
Zhāng Shēngyún, Jǐedùshǐ of Yìwǔ, was
granted the name Mào Zhāo.
Kǎoyì states: The Old Biography mentions the name change when his father Xiàozhōng died.
The Níandàijì places it in the ninth month of this year.
4 Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Mù Zàn (穆贊) was investigating a bribery case involving officials from the Du zhī (度支) department,
Péi Yánlíng (裴延齡) wanted to exonerate them
and protect the officials,
wishing to clear them of their crimes.
Yánlíng slandered Mù Zàn,
who was demoted to Ráozhōu (饒州) Biejia (別駕).
Courtiers feared Yánlíng and avoided his gaze.
They feared him and dared not look him directly.
He was the son of Níng (寧).
At the end of the Tiānbǎo (天寶) era,
Ān Lùshān (安祿山) rebelled.
Mù Níng (穆寧) raised troops in Héběi (河北) to suppress him.
5 Wéi Gāo (韋皋) reported a victory over the Tǔbō (吐蕃) at Éhéchéng (峨和城).
In the first year of Wǔdé (武德),
Yìzhōu (翼州) was established on the land of Hàn (漢) Cánlíng (蠶陵) County,
and Éhéchéng (峨和城) was within its jurisdiction.
6 Autumn,
seventh month,
Rénshēn (壬申) *shuò* (朔) [first day of the lunar month].
Wáng Yánguì (王延貴) was appointed Zhāoyì (昭義) Liúhòu (留後),
and granted the name Qiánxiū (虔休).
Yuán Yì (元誼), Zhāoyì (昭義) Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬) and acting Míngzhōu (洺州) Cìshǐ (刺史), heard that Qiánxiū (虔休) was made Liúhòu (留後),
and was displeased.
He submitted a memorial requesting that Cí (磁), Xíng (邢), and Míng (洺) be separated into their own commandery.
Most of the elite troops of Zhāoyì (昭義) were in Shāndōng (山東),
the Zhāoyì (昭義) military command was based in Lùzhōu (潞州),
and the three prefectures of Cí (磁), Xíng (邢), and Míng (洺) were referred to as Shāndōng (山東).
The Emperor repeatedly sent eunuchs to admonish him,
but he did not comply.
Xiàhóu Zhòngxuān (夏侯仲宣), the commander of Línmíng (臨洺), surrendered the city to Qiánxiū (虔休).
Qiánxiū (虔休) sent Cízhōu (磁州) Cìshǐ (刺史) Mǎ Zhèngqīng (馬正卿) to lead his subordinate general Shí Dìngfān (石定蕃) and others with five thousand soldiers to attack Míngzhōu (洺州);
Dìngfān (定蕃) led his two thousand troops in defection to Yì (誼),
and Zhèngqīng (正卿) retreated.
An imperial edict appointed Yì (誼) as Ráozhōu (饒州) Cìshǐ (刺史),
but Yì (誼) did not go;
Qiánxiū (虔xiū) personally led troops to attack him,
diverting the Míngshuǐ (洺水) river to flood the city.
7 Huáng Shàoqīng (黃少卿) captured Qīn (欽), Héng (橫), Xún (潯), and Guì (貴) prefectures,
and attacked Sūn Gōngqì (孫公器) at Yōngzhōu (邕州).
8 Ninth month,
Wáng Qiánxiū (王虔休) defeated Yuán Yì's (元誼) troops,
and advanced to take Jīzé (雞澤).
Jīzé (雞澤) was the land of Hàn (漢) Guǎngpíng (廣平) County,
Jīzé (雞澤) County was established in the fourth year of Wǔdé (武德),
belonging to Míngzhōu (洺州).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) states: it is sixty *lǐ* (里) northeast of the prefecture.
9 Péi Yánlíng (裴延齡) submitted a memorial stating that there were too many officials,
and from now on, vacant positions should not be filled for the time being,
so that their salaries could be collected to fill the imperial treasury.
The Emperor wanted to repair Shénlóngsì (神龍寺) Temple,
which required pine trees fifty *chǐ* (尺) tall,
but they could not be found.
Yánlíng (延齡) said:
"Your subject recently saw a valley in Tóngzhōu (同州),
with several thousand trees,
all about eighty *chǐ* (尺) tall."
The Emperor said:
"During the Kāiyuán (開元) and Tiānbǎo (天寶) eras,
even fine timber near the capital was hard to find,
how can it be available now?"
He replied:
"Heaven produces precious materials,
indeed waiting for a sagely ruler to appear.
How could they have been obtained in Kāiyuán (開元) and Tiānbǎo (天寶)?"
Yánlíng (延齡) reported:
"There have been many losses in the Zuǒzàngkùsī (左藏庫司) [Left Storehouse Bureau].
Recently, when an inspection envoy was establishing records,
thirteen thousand *liǎng* (兩) of silver were found in the dirt,
and more than a million pieces of silk and miscellaneous goods."
If pieces of silk and miscellaneous goods
were in the dirt,
they should have already rotted and become unusable.
Even the most foolish person would know this to be a wild fabrication.
As Dézōng (德宗) did not punish him for it,
what further scruples could Yánlíng (延齡) have?
"These are all surplus funds,
and should all be transferred to the miscellaneous treasury for expenditure by special imperial edict."
Tài Fǔ Shàoqīng (太府少卿) Wéi Shàohuá (韋少華) disagreed,
and submitted a strong memorial stating:
"These are all items that have been reported monthly as existing,
please investigate them further."
The high officials requested that the Sānsī (三司) [Three Judicial Offices] thoroughly review the matter;
the Emperor did not allow it,
nor did he punish Shàohuá (少華).
Whenever Yánlíng (延齡) had an audience with the Emperor,
he spoke with unrestrained trickery,
saying things that others dared not say and had never heard,
and Yánlíng (延齡) did so without hesitation.
The Emperor also somewhat knew of his wild fabrications,
but because he was good at slandering people,
hoping to hear about external affairs,
he therefore treated him with intimacy and favor.
Dézōng's (德宗) intimacy and favor towards Péi Yánlíng (裴延齡)
was not only because he hoped to hear about external affairs,
but also because Yánlíng (延齡) offered tributes and indulged his desires.
Because the treacherous minister Péi Yánlíng had the Emperor's favor,
no one dared to speak up.
Only Zhāng Pāng, the Salt and Iron Transport Commissioner, Lǐ Chōng, the Jīngzhào Prefect, and Lǐ Xiān, the Sīnóng Qīng,
whose duties were related,
occasionally testified to his falsehoods.
But Lù Zhì alone took it upon himself
to constantly argue that Péi Yánlíng should not be used.
In the eleventh month,
on the rénshēn day,
Lù Zhì submitted a memorial vehemently denouncing Péi Yánlíng's treachery and deceit,
listing his crimes and wickedness.
Its summary said:
“Yánlíng takes extortion as his long-term strategy,
and deceptive falsehoods as excellent schemes.
He considers exploitation and accumulating resentment as being dedicated to duty,
and suppressing slander and submitting to calumny as fully exerting loyalty.
The Zǔochuán says: The Shàohào clan had an untalented son
who destroyed trust and abandoned loyalty,
adorned evil words with excessive ornamentation,
indulged in slander, sought out wickedness,
and used them to falsely accuse men of great virtue.
The people of the world called him Qióngqí.
He embraces what the sagely wise warn against, considering it his ability and conduct.
He can be called the Gònggōng of Yáo's era.
The Shū Jīng, Yáo Diǎn says: The Emperor said:
‘Who can assist me in my endeavors?’
Huāndōu said:
‘Gònggōng is just now diligently accomplishing his work.’
The Emperor said:
‘Alas!
His words are reverent, but his actions are rebellious;
he seems respectful, but is overbearing.’
Gòng,
pronounced gōng.
The Jiāyǔ says: Kǒngzǐ became the Sīkòu of Lǔ,
and provisionally acted as prime minister.
After seven days, he executed Shàozhèng Mǎo,
killing him below the two watchtowers.
Zǐgòng stepped forward and said:
‘Shàozhèng Mǎo
was a renowned man of Lǔ.
The Master, upon taking charge of government, began by executing him.
Perhaps this was a mistake?’
Kǒngzǐ said:
‘There are five great evils in the world,
and theft is not among them.
First, his mind is perverse and treacherous.
Second, his actions are false and stubborn.
Third, his words are false but eloquent.
Fourth, he remembers ugliness extensively.
Fifth, he agrees with wrong and beautifies it.
If a person possesses any one of these five,
they cannot escape the execution of a gentleman.
And Shàozhèng Mǎo possessed all of them.
His dwelling place was sufficient to gather followers and form a party.
His discourse was sufficient to embellish praise and gain popularity.
His dominance was sufficient to turn right into wrong and stand alone.
This is truly a villainous hero among men,
and one who cannot but be eliminated.’
As days lengthen and months grow,
what is secretly hidden has certainly not been fully revealed,
and what has been exposed is even harder to enumerate completely.”
He also said:
“If Your Majesty suspects he is slandered,
then it is truly fitting to promptly clear his name.
If Your Majesty knows he is wicked,
then how can you cover for him with partiality!”
He also said:
“If Your Majesty merely wishes to protect him,
without ever questioning him,
Yánlíng will think he can deceive and mislead,
and no longer fear introspection.
Moving things from east to west
is then counted as an achievement.
Taking from one place to another
is then called a surplus.
He makes a fool of the imperial court,
as if playing a child's game.”
He also said:
“His ability to deceive and mislead,
and his words of falsehood and trickery,
are employed whenever an opportunity arises,
and uttered as soon as his mouth opens.
There is no day it doesn't happen,
no time it isn't done,
and it is difficult to recount all of it.”
He also said:
“In the past, Zhào Gāo pointed to a deer and called it a horse.
The horse is seen in the eight fascicles of Qín Èr Shì, third year.
The principle is still the same.
How is this like Yánlíng who conceals what exists to make it seem nonexistent,
and points to what is nonexistent and makes it seem to exist?”
He also said:
“Yánlíng's wickedness and madness
have spread throughout the world.
From the high-ranking officials and close ministers
to the lowest commoners and menials,
The Zǔochuán says: Qiānyǐn Wú Yǔ said: ‘The king's ministers are dukes,
the dukes' ministers are grand masters,
the grand masters' ministers are scholars,
the scholars' ministers are common attendants,
the common attendants' ministers are footmen,
the footmen's ministers are servants,
the servants' ministers are household officers,
and the household officers' ministers are menials.’
There are countless people,
but how many are able to speak out to the Emperor!
I, your humble subject,
am in a high and responsible position.
My feelings are stirred in my heart,
and though I wish to cease, I cannot remain silent.”
When the memorial was presented,
the Emperor was displeased,
and treated Péi Yánlíng even more favorably.
In the twelfth month,
Wáng Qiánxiū, taking advantage of the frozen moat,
crossed it and swiftly attacked Míngzhōu.
Yuán Yì led out troops to strike him.
Wáng Qiánxiū was defeated and retreated.
At dusk, the ice thawed,
and more than half of his soldiers died.
Because the Emperor treated Lù Zhì, the Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, favorably
and he knew the Emperor's generosity,
he often strongly argued against anything he deemed improper.
Some of his close associates advised him that he was too outspoken.
Lù Zhì said:
“Above, I do not fail the Son of Heaven;
below, I do not fail my studies.
I have no other concerns.”
Péi Yánlíng daily disparaged Lù Zhì to the Emperor.
When Zhào Jǐng entered the premiership,
Lù Zhì had actually recommended him.
Afterward, Zhào Jǐng bore a grudge against Lù Zhì;
the matter is detailed in the previous fascicles for the eighth and ninth years.
Therefore, Péi Yánlíng was further able to use this to his advantage.
The Emperor consequently trusted Péi Yánlíng and did not approve of Lù Zhì.
Lù Zhì and Zhào Jǐng had agreed to thoroughly expose Péi Yánlíng's treachery and wickedness before the Emperor.
The Emperor's anger showed on his face,
but Zhào Jǐng remained silent.
On the rénxū day,
Lù Zhì was dismissed and made Tàizǐ Bīnkè.
The Kǎoyì says: Hán Yù's Shùnzōng Shílù states:
“Dézōng, having been on the throne for a somewhat long time,
increasingly took the reins of power into his own hands,
and personally handled minute affairs,
losing the proper bearing of a monarch.
The prime ministers were increasingly unable to perform their duties.
However, critics say this was due to Lù Zhì.”
Upon examination, all who served as prime ministers wished to wield sole power;
how could they willingly seek to be deprived of their duties?
Not employing the prime ministers was Dézōng's fault,
and to attribute blame to Lù Zhì,
how could that be human nature!
Moreover, Lù Zhì's memorial on the vacant positions in the imperial court said:
“Recently, the assistant ministers were rarely competent for their posts.
They were excessively tolerated and maintained,
merely filling staff positions,
leading to Your Majesty's weary deliberation,
considering every detail.”
These are words advising Dézōng not to not employ the prime ministers and personally handle minute affairs.
Initially,
Bóhǎi Wén Wáng Qīnmào died.
His son, Hónglín, died young,
so his distant cousin, Yuán Yì, was enthroned.
Yuán Yì was suspicious and cruel,
so the people of the state killed him
and enthroned Hónglín's son, Huá Yǔ.
He was known as Chéng Wáng,
and the reign era was changed to Zhōngxīng.
When Huá Yǔ died,
Qīnmào's youngest son, Sōnglín, was again enthroned.
He was known as Kāng Wáng,
and the reign era was changed to Zhènglì.
Bóhǎi, since Dà Zuòróng established the state during the Kāiyuán period,
and his son, Wǔyì, was enthroned,
became even stronger and more prosperous.
All the northeastern barbarians feared and submitted to him,
and the reign era was changed to Rén'ān.
After five generations, up to Sòng,
although the Yēlǜ frequently waged war,
they could not subjugate Bóhǎi.
Therefore, the Tōngjiàn records its generations in detail.
In the spring,
the second month,
on the yǐsì day,
Sōnglín was formally appointed Dūdu of Hūhànzhōu and King of Bóhǎi.
The Kǎoyì says: The Shílù states:
“On the yǐsì day,
Dà Lǐng Sōnglín was formally appointed King of Bóhǎi Prefecture.”
The current text follows Xīn Zhuàn.
2 After Lù Zhì was dismissed from his chancellorship,
Péi Yánlíng then slandered Lǐ Chōng, the Jīngzhào Yǐn; Zhāng Pāng, the Wèiwèi Qīng; and Lǐ Xiān, the former Sīnóng Qīng, alleging they were Lù Zhì's partisans.
It happened to be a drought,
and Yánlíng memorialized, saying:
"Zhì and his group, having lost power, resentfully said to the crowd,
'The empire is suffering from drought,
and the common people will soon become displaced.
The Duózhī has a large deficit in fodder and provisions for the various armies,
so the army's men and horses have nothing to eat.
What is to be done about this situation!'
They meant to ask what could be done about the current state of affairs.
Their intention was not merely to harm me."
A few days later,
the emperor was hunting in the imperial park,
when a Shéncèjūn soldier happened to complain:
"The Duózhī has not supplied horse fodder."
The emperor believed Yánlíng's words to be true,
and immediately returned to the palace.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Rénxū,
Zhì was demoted to Zhōngzhōu Biéjià;
Chōng to Fúzhōu Zhǎngshǐ;
and Pāng to Tíngzhōu Zhǎngshǐ.
In the 24th year of Kāiyuán,
the mountain caves of Fǔ and Fú two prefectures were opened,
and Tíngzhōu was established.
Old records state: Zhōngzhōu
is 2,122 lí south of the capital.
Tíngzhōu
is 6,173 lí southeast of the capital.
Qióu Zhōu's Bājì says: In the 6th year of Chūpíng of the Later Hàn,
Línjiāng County was established,
belonging to Yǒngníng Commandery.
The ancient city of Línjiāng, east of present-day Zhōngzhōu city, is it.
In the 2nd year of the abdicated emperor of the Later Wèi,
it was renamed Línzhōu,
naming the prefecture after Línjiāng County.
The Suí abolished the prefecture,
merging its territory into Bādōng Commandery.
In the 4th year of Zhēnguān,
Zhōngzhōu was established,
named for its location bordering the Bājiào
and symbolizing loyalty and trustworthiness.
Fúzhōu was
the land of Fúlíng County in the Hàn dynasty.
The Suí established Fúzhōu,
2,350 lí south of the capital.
Shàozhōu is
3,400 lí southeast of the capital.
Sòng Bái said: Shàozhōu
was Zhāolíng County in the Hàn dynasty.
Wú changed it to Shàolíng,
and divided the northern part of Línglíng to form Shàolíng Commandery.
The Suí established Jiànzhōu,
but soon abolished the prefecture,
making Shàolíng County belong to Tánzhōu.
The Táng established Shàozhōu in the 11th year of Zhēnguān.
Initially,
Yáng Chéng was summoned from being a recluse to become a Jiànyì Dàfū,
as seen in Volume 232, year 2.
"Chǔ" (處) is pronounced Chāng Lǚ.
Before he arrived in the capital,
everyone looked forward to his presence,
saying:
"Chéng will surely remonstrate,
and die for his duty."
When he arrived,
the other remonstrance officials busily spoke about trivial matters,
and the Son of Heaven became increasingly annoyed and weary of them.
Meanwhile, Chéng was daily and nightly drinking heavily with his two younger brothers and guests,
so no one could discern his true intentions,
and all thought he had merely gained an empty reputation.
The former Jinshì, Hán Yù of Hénán, wrote "Zhēngchén Lùn" to satirize him,
but Chéng did not care.
If someone wanted to visit Chéng and ask him a question,
"Xiè" (屑) means "clean" or "to care about."
"Zào" (造) is pronounced Qī Dào.
Chéng would immediately force wine upon them.
Sometimes the guests would get drunk first and collapse on the mat,
and sometimes Chéng would get drunk first and lie in a guest's arms,
unable to listen to what the guests said.
When Lù Zhì and others were implicated and demoted,
the emperor's anger had not subsided,
and officials both inside and outside the court were anxious and fearful,
thinking their crimes would be unpredictable,
and no one dared to rescue them.
Chéng heard this and rose, saying:
"We cannot allow the Son of Heaven to trust treacherous officials
and kill innocent people."
He immediately led the Shíyí Wáng Zhòngshū and Guī Dēng, and the Yòubǔquè Xióng Zhíyì and Cuī Bīn, to guard the Yányīng Mén.
Yányīng Mén
is the gate of Yányīng Diàn.
Chéng Dàchāng said: According to the Liùdiǎn,
west of the Xuānzhèng Diàn gate, above the western gate,
is the Yányīng Mén,
and to the left of the gate is Yányīng Diàn.
Therefore, Yáng Chéng, wishing to save Lù Zhì,
arranged with Wáng Zhòngshū and others to guard the gate of Yányīng Diàn and submit a memorial,
prostrating themselves at the gate and refusing to leave.
"Shuài" (帥) is pronounced "shuài".
Zhì and the others were innocent.
The emperor was greatly enraged
and wanted to punish Chéng and his group.
The Crown Prince interceded for them,
and the emperor's anger then subsided,
ordering the prime ministers to persuade and dismiss them.
Thereupon, Jīnwú Jiāngjūn Zhāng Wànfú, hearing that remonstrance officials were prostrating at the gate to remonstrate,
hurried to Yányīng Mén
and loudly declared in congratulation:
"With upright officials in the imperial court,
the empire will surely be at peace!"
He then bowed to Chéng and Zhòngshū and the others,
and afterwards repeatedly shouted,
"Long live peace!
Long live peace!"
Wànfú,
a military man
over eighty years old,
became famous throughout the empire from then on.
Dēng
was the son of Chóngjìng.
Chóngjìng was
well-versed in the family scholarship of mínglǐ,
and served four generations: Xuán, Sù, Dài, and the emperor.
Yáng Chéng said:
"If Yánlíng is made chancellor,
Chéng will take the white edict and destroy it."
According to Táng precedents,
the Zhōngshū used yellow and white hemp paper to distinguish the importance of imperial edicts.
Later, the Hànlín Xuéshì exclusively managed inner edicts.
The Zhōngshū used yellow hemp paper,
while all white hemp paper was kept in the Hànlín Yuàn.
It was used for appointing or dismissing generals and prime ministers, and for gracious decrees of pardon.
Sòng Bái said: According to Táng precedents,
all white hemp edicts were spoken on behalf of the inner court.
They were used for appointing high officials, promoting generals, alleviating disasters, and suppressing rebellions.
The prime minister received them in the main hall.
If it was an edict appointing a prime minister,
the Tōngshì Shèrén would receive the order,
and after all proclamations and commendations were finished,
it would then be sent to the relevant department.

The Hànlín Zhì states: All edicts of pardon, gracious decrees, establishment of empresses, appointment of heirs apparent, major punitive expeditions, appointment or dismissal of the Sāngōng and prime ministers, and appointment of generals,
all use white hemp paper,
and no seal is used.
Drafts are prepared on even-numbered days,
awaiting the palace gate key to enter before being presented.
On odd-numbered days,
all officials line up in the Xuānzhèng Diàn,
and the Shūmì Shǐ leads the document case,
exiting from the East Shànggémén.
If it is for the appointment or dismissal of a prime minister,
it is immediately handed to the Tōngshì Shèrén.
The rest are handed to the Zhōngshū and Ménxià,
and all are proclaimed by the Tōngshì Shèrén.
If matters are urgent,
it can also be on an even-numbered day.
If extremely urgent,
even during holidays,
officials are summoned to declare it.
"Àn" (案) refers to the document case.
"Cè" (冊) refers to the official document of appointment or investiture.
There is also a document case for investiture.
The investiture of princesses also involves the case exiting from the gate.
"Huài" (壞) is pronounced "guài".
There was a Lǐ Fán,
Lǐ Mì's son.
Chéng fully detailed Yánlíng's faults and misdeeds,
intending to discuss them privately.
Because Fán was the son of an old friend,
Yáng Chéng's appointment as Jiànyì was recommended by Lǐ Mì.
Fán directly reported this to Yánlíng.
Yánlíng first went to the emperor
and explained everything himself.
When the memorial entered,
the emperor considered it fabricated
and did not heed it.
3 On the day Bǐngyín,
Yōuzhōu reported a victory over the Xī King Chuòlì and more than 60,000 of his troops.
4 Huíhú (回鶻) Fèngchéng Kèhán (奉誠可汗) died.
He had no son.
The people of the kingdom enthroned his chancellor, Gǔduōlù (骨咄祿), as Kèhán.
Gǔduōlù (骨咄祿)'s original surname was Diē (跌) clan.
He was eloquent and intelligent, with courage and strategic ability.
Since the time of Tiānqīn (天親),
the Huíhú (回鶻) Tiānqīn Kèhán (天親可汗),
was also Gǔduōlù (骨咄祿).
All the great ministers and chieftains feared and submitted to him.
After becoming Kèhán,
he falsely adopted the surname Yàogěluó (藥葛羅) clan.
The Huíhú (回紇) Kèhán's surname was Yàogěluó (藥葛羅).
Gǔduōlù (骨咄祿) abandoned his original surname
and falsely adopted their surname to inherit their kingdom.
Qiú (酋),
pronounced Cíyóu (慈由).
Zhǎng (長),
pronounced Zhīliǎng (知兩).
The young and immature descendants of Tiānqīn Kèhán (天親可汗) and those before him
were all placed inside the Imperial Palace (Quètíng 闕庭).
This refers to the Imperial Palace of the Táng (唐) dynasty.
5 In the fifth month,
on the Dīngchǒu (丁丑) day,
Lǐ Wànróng (李萬榮), who was acting Liúhòu (留後) of Xuānwǔ (宣武), and Wáng Qiánxiū (王虔休), who was Zuǒsīmǎ (左司馬) of Zhāoyì (昭義) and acting Liúhòu (留後), were both made Jiéduáoshǐ (節度使).

Lǐ Zìliáng (李自良), the Jiéduáoshǐ (節度使) of Hédōng (河東), died.
On the Wùzǐ (戊子) day,
Jiānjūn (監軍) Wáng Dìngyuǎn (王定遠) submitted a memorial requesting that Xíngjūnsīmǎ (行軍司馬) Lǐ Yuè (李說) be made Liúhòu (留後).
Yuè (說)
was the fifth-generation descendant of Shéntōng (神通).
Huái'ān Wáng Shéntōng (淮安王神通)
was a cousin of Gāozǔ (高祖),

Yuè (說)
is read as yuè (悅);
the same below.

the Emperor dispatched Mìshūjiān (祕書監) Zhāng Jiàn (張薦) to officially invest Gǔduōlù (骨咄祿), the Huíhú (回鶻) Kèhán, as Ténglǐluó Yǔlù Mò Mìshī Hé Húlù Píjiā Huáixìn Kèhán (騰里邏羽錄沒密施合胡祿毗伽懷信可汗).
8 On the Guǐsì (癸巳) day,
Lǐ Yuè (李說) was appointed Liúhòu (留後) of Hédōng (河東),

Yuè (說) deeply appreciated Wáng Dìngyuǎn (王定遠),
and requested the casting of a Jiānjūn (監軍) seal.
The Jiānjūn (監軍) having a seal started with Dìngyuǎn (定遠).
9 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Bǐngyín (丙寅) day, the first day of the month,
Yáng Chéng (陽城) was demoted from Guózǐ Sīyè (國子司業),

10 Wáng Dìngyuǎn (王定遠), relying on his services to Lǐ Yuè (李說),
monopolized the military and political affairs of Hédōng (河東),
and frequently replaced generals;
Yuè (說) could not fully comply,
which led to a rift between them.
Dìngyuǎn (定遠), out of personal anger, abducted and killed the great general Péng Língyīn (彭令茵),
and buried him in horse manure;
all the officers and soldiers were enraged.
Yuè (說) memorialized on the situation.
When Dìngyuǎn (定遠) heard of it,
he went directly to Yuè (說),
drew his sword, and stabbed him;
Yuè (說) fled and escaped.
Dìngyuǎn (定遠) summoned the generals,
and placed more than twenty imperial edicts and official appointments in a box.
Xiāng (箱),
a bamboo basket.
Zhù (貯),
pronounced Dīnglǚ (丁呂).
"There is an imperial edict
ordering Yuè (說) to proceed to the capital,
and appointing Xíngjūnsīmǎ (行軍司馬) Lǐ Jǐnglüè (李景略) as Liúhòu (留後)."
Lǐ Jǐnglüè (李景略) was resented by Lǐ Yuè (李說),
which likely started here.
Everyone bowed.
The great general Mǎ Liángfǔ (馬良輔) secretly peeked into the box,
and saw that they were all Dìngyuǎn (定遠)'s own appointments and the edicts he had received.
He then waved to the crowd and said:
"These imperial edicts are all fake,
they cannot be accepted."
Dìngyuǎn (定遠) fled up to the Gānyánglóu (乾陽樓).
Gānyánglóu (乾陽樓)
was probably the south gate tower of the Jìnyáng (晉陽) Palace City.
No one responded.
He jumped over the wall and fell,
was injured by a withered stump and died.
11 In the eighth month,
on the Xīnhài (辛亥) day,
Sītú (司徒) concurrently Shìzhōng (侍中), Běipíng Zhuāngwǔ Wáng Mǎ Suì (北平莊武王馬燧) died.
12 In the intercalary month,
on the Wùchén (戊辰) day,
Yuán Yì (元誼) feigned surrender in Míngzhōu (洺州);
Wáng Qiánxiū (王虔休) sent a subordinate general with two thousand men into the city,
and Yì (誼) killed them all.
13 In the ninth month,
on the Dīngsì (丁巳) day,
Wéi Gāo (韋皋) was given the additional title of Yúnnán Ānfǔshǐ (雲南安撫使).

14 Chéng Huáizhí (程懷直), the Jiéduáoshǐ (節度使) of Hénghǎi (橫海),
did not care for his soldiers.
He went hunting in the wilderness
and did not return for several days.
Huáizhí's (懷直) cousin, Huáixìn (懷信), who was a Bīngmǎshǐ (兵馬使),
capitalized on the resentment of the masses

Huáizhí (懷直) fled back to the capital.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Dīngchǒu (丁丑) day,
Huáixìn (懷信) was appointed Liúhòu (留後) of Hénghǎi (橫海).
15 Nánzhào (南詔) attacked and captured Kūnmíng (昆明) City from Tǔbō (吐蕃);
Kūnmíng City (昆明城)
was located northwest of Xīcuàn (西爨),
and had the advantage of salt ponds.
The two Man (蠻) tribes, Shī (施) and Shùn (順),
were both of the Wūmán (烏蠻) stock.
The Shīmán (施蠻) were northwest of Tiěqiáo (鐵橋),
residing in Dàshī Shǎn (大施睒) and Liǎnxún Shǎn (斂尋睒).
The Shùnmán (順蠻) were four hundred *li* northwest of Jiànshǎn (劍睒).
Shǎn (睒),
pronounced Shīrǎn (失冉).
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the Gēngzǐ (庚子) day,
Yuán Yì (元誼), Shí Dìngfán (石定蕃), and others led five thousand soldiers from Míngzhōu (洺州) and more than ten thousand of their family members to Wèizhōu (魏州);

on the Jiǎwǔ (甲午) day,

Lǐ Qíyùn (李齊運), the Xíanjí (閑廄) and Gōngyuàn (宮苑) commissioner, was appointed Lǐbù Shàngshū (禮部尚書).
Lǐ Qíyùn (李齊運) probably held both positions of Xíanjí (閑廄) and Gōngyuàn (宮苑) commissioners concurrently.

Qíyùn (齊運) had no talent, ability, or scholarship,

the fourth month,
on the Gēngwǔ (庚午) day,

it was the Emperor's birthday.
According to custom,
monks and Daoist priests were ordered to lecture and debate in the Líndé Diàn (麟德殿).
From this time on,
Confucian scholars were first ordered to participate.
Wéi Qúmóu (韋渠牟), the Sì mén Bóshì (四門博士), was eloquent and quick-witted in debate.
Liú Fāng (劉芳) of the Later Wèi (魏) reported: in the twentieth year of Tàihé (太和),

Zhèng's (鄭) commentary says: these are the Yúxiáng (虞庠) of the four suburbs of Zhōu (周).
Now, because they are distant,
they are placed at the four gates.
I request that they be moved to the same location as the Tàixué (太學),
which was granted.
The Táng (唐) Official Records: Sìmén Guǎn Bóshì (四門館博士),
first rank seven, upper grade,
were in charge of teaching sons of marquises, counts, viscounts, and barons of the seventh rank and above, as well as sons of commoners who were talented scholars.

he was promoted to Yòubǔquē (右補闕),
and thus began to gain favor.

on the Bǐngshēn (丙申) day,

on the Yǐchǒu day,

the Court Agent supervising the Left Divine Stratagem Army, Dòu Wénchǎng, and the Court Agent supervising the Right Divine Stratagem Army, Huò Xiānmíng, were both appointed as Protector-General of the Palace Army (Hùjūn Zhōngwèi).
The Supervisor of the Left Divine Might Army, Zhāng Shàngjìn, and the Supervisor of the Right Divine Might Army, Jiāo Xīwàng, were both appointed as Central Protector-General (Zhōnghùjūn).
Originally,
the Emperor (Shàng) established six Regional Commanders (Liù Tǒngjūn),
whose status was equivalent to the Six Ministers (Liù Shàngshū),
to accommodate jiedushi who had been dismissed from their posts.
The six Regional Commanders were established in the first year of Xīngyuán.
The matter is detailed in Volume 229.
Chǔ (to accommodate),
read like "chāng lǚ."
By this time,
Wénchǎng subtly suggested to the chancellors that the Regional Commanders should also be announced with white imperial edicts.
Hanlin Academician Zhèng Yīn
submitted a memorial, stating:
"According to established custom, only the enfeoffment of kings and the appointment of chancellors are announced with white imperial edicts.
Now, if it is to be used for appointing Palace Army Protectors,
I do not know if Your Majesty intends this specifically to favor Wénchǎng,
or if it is to become a permanent regulation?"
"Zhù lìng" means
to establish as a fixed regulation.
"During the Wǔdé and Zhēngguān eras,
eunuchs did not exceed the rank of Yuánwài Jiāngjūn Tóngzhèng,
and few wore crimson robes.
Since the Fǔguó era,
the system has deteriorated.
I am now using you;
I cannot say I am unbiased.
If such an imperial edict is again issued to the whole empire,
people will certainly say that you coerced me into doing it."
Wénchǎng kowtowed in apology.
Consequently, his white imperial edict was burned,
and it was ordered that from now on, appointments for Regional Commanders and other such positions would be announced by the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū) through imperial decrees.
The next day,
the Emperor (Shàng) said to Yīn:
"The chancellors dared not refuse the eunuchs;
only after hearing your words did I understand."
At that time, Dòu and Huò's influence was overwhelming, both inside and outside the court.
Many regional governors and military commanders came from the Divine Stratagem Army,
and even high-ranking officials in the Censorate and other ministries were among their protégés.
10 The Jiedushi of Xuānwǔ, Lǐ Wànróng, suffered from paralysis,
and was so confused he knew nothing of affairs.
Huò Xiānmíng recommended Liú Mù, an yáyá (staff officer) of Xuānwǔ, as capable of managing military and governmental affairs.
On the Xīnsì day,
Mù was appointed Acting Army Administrator (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ).
11 Liú Zàn, the Surveillance Commissioner (Guānchásǐ) of Xuān-Shè, died.
Originally,
the Emperor (Shàng) found Fèngtiān to be in financial straits.
Therefore, since his return to the palace, he had been particularly focused on accumulating wealth.
Many regional governors (fānzhèn) offered tributes to gain favor,
all claiming
"tax revenue outside the square and circular systems" (shuìwài fāngyuán).
"Zhē zé chéng fāng, zhuǎn zé chéng yuán" (Folding makes a square, turning makes a circle)
refers to the practice
of diverting and converting
funds beyond the regular taxes
to procure goods and wealth.
"Yòngdù xiànyú" (surplus for expenditure)
actually involved
either withholding regular levies,
or increasing taxes on the populace,
or deducting from official salaries,
or selling vegetables and fruits.
Often,
most of it went into private pockets,
with only one or two tenths actually being presented as tribute.
Lǐ Jiān in Jiāngxī made monthly tributes,
and Wéi Gāo in Xīchuān made daily tributes.
Later, Péi Sù of Jìyuán, the Císhǐ of Chángzhōu, was promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèdōng because of his tributes.
Tributes from Císhǐ began with Sù.
When Liú Zàn died,
the Judge (Pànguān), Yán Shòu, took charge of the remaining affairs.
He exhausted the treasury to present tributes,
and was subsequently appointed Yuánwài Láng of the Ministry of Punishments (Xíngbù Yuánwài Láng).
Tributes from staff officers (mùliáo) began with Shòu.
Shòu was
a native of Shǔ.
The historian could not ascertain his prefecture or county,
so he is merely referred to as "a native of Shǔ."
12 As Lǐ Wànróng was gravely ill,
his son Nǎi became the Commander of Cavalry and Infantry (Bīngmǎshǐ).
On the Jiǎshēn day,
Nǎi assembled the generals and accused Lǐ Zhàn, Yīlóu Shuō, and Zhāng Pī of not being concerned with military affairs,
expelling them to outer counties.
The Emperor (Shàng) dispatched the court envoy Fífth Shǒujìn to Biànzhōu.
As soon as the imperial慰 (xuānwèi) was completed,
over ten soldiers shouted:
"The Bīngmǎshǐ works hard without reward;
who is Liú Mù, to be Xíngjūn Sīmǎ!"
Mù was frightened,
feigned a stroke,
and was carried out.
The soldiers again shouted:
"Warehouse official Liú Shūhé is corrupt in his management!"
They killed and ate him.
They also wanted to hack Shǒujìn,
but Nǎi stopped them.
Nǎi then killed Yīlóu Shuō and Zhāng Pī.
Dèng Wéigōng of Kuāngchéng, the General of the Imperial Guard (Dū Yúhòu), was a fellow villager and close friend of Wànróng,
and Wànróng had always trusted him as a confidant.
Nǎi also relied on him.
At this point,
Wéigōng conspired with the Supervisor of the Army (Jūnjūn), Jù Wénzhēn.
They seized Nǎi
and sent him to the capital.
In the autumn,
seventh month,
on the Yǐwèi day,
Dǒng Jìn, the Deputy Grand Protector of the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū Liúshǒu), was appointed Co-Chancellor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì),
and concurrently Jiedushi of Xuānwǔ.
Wànróng was made Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàobǎo),
and Nǎi was demoted to Sīmǎ of Qiánzhōu.
On the Bǐngshēn day,
Wànróng died.
After Dèng Wéigōng captured Lǐ Nǎi,
he temporarily took charge of military affairs,
believing he would succeed Wànróng.
He did not send anyone to welcome Dǒng Jìn.
After Jìn received the imperial edict,
he immediately set off for the commandery with over ten attendants,
without military escort.
When he reached Zhèngzhōu,
no one came to welcome him.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Zhèngzhōu
is 150 lǐ east of Biànzhōu.
Someone advised Jìn to stay and observe the situation.
A person who came from Biànzhōu
said to Jìn:
"You cannot enter."
Jìn did not respond,
and continued his journey.
Wéigōng was unprepared for Jìn's swift arrival,
and had no time to plan.
When Jìn was over ten lǐ from the city,
Wéigōng then led the generals out to welcome him.
Jìn ordered Wéigōng not to dismount,
and his demeanor was very amiable,
which somewhat reassured Wéigōng.
After entering,
Jìn still entrusted Wéigōng with military and governmental affairs.
Originally,
Liú Xuánzuǒ had increased the troops in Biànzhōu to 100,000,
treating them generously.
Lǐ Wànróng and Dèng Wéigōng always treated them even more generously.
The soldiers became arrogant
and ungovernable.
(Yù,
alternatively written as Yù.)
They encamped under the eaves of the public courtyard,
carrying bows and swords as a precaution,
and were periodically rewarded with wine and meat.
The day after Jìn arrived,
he dismissed them all.
Dǒng Jìn believed
that these soldiers were the confidants of the previous commander.
If he, as the new commander, also relied on them as confidants,
they would not protect him but would instead cause trouble.
By dismissing them, he treated all armies equally
and showed no suspicion or estrangement.
13 On the Wùxū day,
Hán Wáng Huí died.
Huí was
the Emperor's (Shàng) younger brother.
14 On the Rénzǐ day,
an imperial edict was issued
stating that the generals and soldiers of Xuānwǔ, such as Dèng Wéigōng, who had the merit of capturing and sending Lǐ Nǎi,
were each to be promoted in rank and rewarded with money.
Those who were coerced by Nǎi
and forced the imperial envoy (zhìshǐ) were all to be pardoned.
"Xié" (coerced)
refers to
"xié cóng" (coerced followers).
It means Lǐ Nǎi used his power and might to coerce his subordinates to intimidate the imperial envoy.
In the Táng dynasty, imperial envoys were called "chìshǐ" (imperial decree envoys),
or also "zhìshǐ" (imperial command envoys).
"Shǐ"
is read like "shū lì."
15 In the eighth month,
on the Yǐ
wèi day, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.
16 On the Jǐsì day,
Tián Jì'ān was appointed Jiedushi of Wèibó.
17 On the Bǐngzǐ day,
Lù Chángyuán, the Císhǐ of Rǔzhōu, was appointed Acting Army Administrator of Xuānwǔ.
The court debate (cháoyì)
was that Dǒng Jìn was too soft and agreeable,
fearing he could not handle affairs.
"Cháoyì" means
the discussion of the imperial court.
"Duō kě" means
he agreed to all requests from others, unable to make decisions based on principle and law.
Chángyuán was by nature rigid and severe,
often changing old practices.
Jìn initially agreed to all of them,
but once a plan was finalized, he would order it to be stopped.
Because of this, the army remained peaceful.
This lays the groundwork for Chángyuán bringing disaster upon himself due to his rigidity and severity.
18th year, *bǐng xū* day.
Zhào Jǐng, *Ménxià Shìláng* and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*, passed away.
19th year.
Initially, the Emperor did not want to appoint *Jiédùshǐ* for Dài Commandery,
and often personally selected *Xíngjūn Sīmǎ* to serve as a reserve commander.
A *Xíngjūn Sīmǎ*
was responsible for assisting with military administration;
when at home, they would practice hunting,
and when there was military action, they would apply the methods of offense and defense.
Weapons, provisions, military registers, and grants were all under their exclusive control.
*Shuài*,
pronunciation is similar to *lèi*.
Lǐ Shuō was jealous of this.
Méilù, a Uyghur official, came to present tribute.
When passing through Tàiyuán,
Lǐ Shuō hosted a banquet for him.
Méilù disputed the seating order,
and Lǐ Shuō was unable to stop him.
Lǐ Jǐnglüè shouted at him,
and Méilù recognized his voice,
hurried forward, bowed, and said:
"Is this not *Fēngzhōu Lǐ Duāngōng*?"
Lǐ Jǐnglüè rebuked Méilù,
as recorded in Volume 233, 3rd year.
Tang people referred to *Shìyù* as *Duāngōng*.
Lǐ Zhào's *Guóshǐ Bǔ* states: Chancellors referred to each other as *Tánglǎo*,
officials of the Two Departments as *Gélǎo*,
*Shàngshū* as *Yuànzhǎng*,
and *Yùshǐ* as *Duāngōng*.
Méilù then took a lower seat.
Everyone at the banquet fixed their gaze on Lǐ Jǐnglüè.
Lǐ Shuō became even more displeased,
and generously bribed *Zhōngwèi* Dòu Wénchǎng
to have Lǐ Jǐnglüè removed.
Coincidentally, there was a rumor that Uyghur forces were about to invade.
The Emperor was concerned about this,
and since Fēngzhōu bore the brunt of the barbarian attacks,
he sought someone capable of defending it.
Dòu Wénchǎng then recommended Lǐ Jǐnglüè.
In the 9th month,
on the *jiǎ wǔ* day,
Lǐ Jǐnglüè was appointed *Fēngzhōu Dū Fángyùshǐ*.
The remote frontier was cold, the land barren, and the people poor.
Lǐ Jǐnglüè led the troops with diligence and frugality.
After two years,
the reserves were complete and abundant,
and he became powerful in the northern frontier.
20th year. Lú Mài suffered from a stroke.
On the *gēng zǐ* day,
Jiǎ Dān observed a private mourning day.
Private mourning days were the death anniversaries of one's parents, grandparents, and great-grandparents.
It was said that among the chancellors, not a single one was observing a private mourning day.
According to Tang regulations: the *Shàngshūshěng Zhǔshū* was rank 8b,
and *Zhōngshūshěng* was rank 7a.
They were staff of the chancellery.
21st year. On the *bǐng wǔ* day,
Péi Yánlíng, *Hùbù Shàngshū* and *Pàndùzhī*, passed away.
Everyone inside and outside the court congratulated each other,
but the Emperor alone lamented his loss.
22nd year. On the *rén zǐ* day,
Tubo forces raided Qìngzhōu.
23rd year. In winter,
in the 10th month, on the *jiǎ xū* day,
Cuī Sǔn, *Jiànyì Dàfū*, and Zhào Zōngrú, *Jìshìzhōng*, were both appointed *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*.
Cuī Sǔn was the grand-nephew of Cuī Xuánwěi.
Cuī Xuánwěi had the merit of executing the Two Zhāng and restoring Emperor Zhōngzōng.
Therefore, he was appointed.
24th year. In the 11th month,
on the *yǐ wèi* day, Wèi Qúmóu, *Yòu Bǔquē*, was appointed *Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū*.
Since Lù Zhì's demotion,
Lù Zhì was demoted in the 4th month of the previous year.
the Emperor personally selected and appointed all officials from *Yùshǐ*, *Cìshǐ*, and *Xiànlìng* upwards,
with the *Zhōngshūshěng* merely handling documents.
However, deeply secluded in the forbidden palace,
those he trusted were Péi Yánlíng, Lǐ Qíyùn, *Hùbù Lángzhōng* Wáng Shào, *Sīnóng Qīng* Lǐ Shí, *Hànlín Xuéshì* Wèi Zhíyì, and Wèi Qúmóu.
All of them wielded more power than the chancellors,
and their gates were crowded with sycophants.
Wáng Shào was cautious and discreet, causing no harm or benefit;
Lǐ Shí was cunning, treacherous, and rapacious;
Wèi Zhíyì exchanged poems with the Emperor,
was in his twenties,
and was summoned from *Yòu Shíyí* to the Hànlín Academy.
Wèi Qúmóu was frivolous and impetuous in appearance and spirit,
and was particularly favored and intimate with the Emperor.
Whenever the Emperor met with the executive officials,
the audience would not exceed three *kè*.
Wèi Qúmóu's reports often lasted up to six *kè*,
and their laughter and intimate conversations were often heard outside.
Those he recommended were all promoted out of sequence,
and mostly were mediocre and vulgar individuals.
25th year. Dèng Wéigōng, *Xuānwǔ Dū Yúhòu*, felt uneasy internally,
and secretly colluded with over two hundred officers and soldiers to plot a rebellion.
When the plot was discovered, Dǒng Jìn captured and executed all his associates,
and shackled Dèng Wéigōng to be sent to the capital.
On the *jǐ wèi* day,
an imperial edict pardoned him from death,
and he was *ānzhì* in Tíngzhōu.
To be exiled to remote and desolate prefectures and commanderies
was called *ānzhì*.
1st year. In spring,
in the 1st month, on the *rén yín* day,
Tubo sent envoys to request a marriage alliance.
The Emperor, considering Tubo had repeatedly broken treaties,
refused.
2 The Emperor thought that Fāngqú, Hédào, and Mùbō were all important Tǔbō routes,
and desired to fortify them.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Huánzhōu
governs Tōngyuǎn Xiàn,
which was the land of Táng's Fāngqú Xiàn.
It has four towns: Mùbō, Mǎlíng, Shíchāng, and Hédào.
“How many troops will be needed?”
The reply was:
“The Bīnníng troops are sufficient to fortify them;
there is no need to trouble other circuits.”
The Emperor then sent to ask again:
“Previously, when fortifying Yánzhōu—
The fortification of Yánzhōu is discussed in the ninth year of the previous volume.
Fù,
pronounced fú and yòu.
—we could barely accomplish the task.
Now these three fortresses are even closer to the barbarian frontier,
so the troops should be doubled.
But the situation is quite the opposite.
Why is this?”
The reply was:
“The barbarians are all aware of the forces used to fortify Yánzhōu.
Now, if we dispatch troops from this very circuit,
they will arrive at the frontier in less than ten days.
We will catch them by surprise and fortify the places.
The barbarians will think our forces are no fewer than seventy thousand.
Their troops not yet gathered,
they will not dare to lightly come and attack us.
In no more than thirty days,
our fortresses will be completed.
We will leave troops to guard them.
Even if the barbarians arrive,
they will be powerless to do anything.
This is the old stratagem of Wéi Xiàokuān of the Later Zhōu who fortified Fénshí.
We cannot stay long.
Once the barbarians retreat, we will transport fodder and provisions to stock the fortresses.
This is a perfectly safe plan.
If we gather large armies from all circuits,
they would only arrive after more than a month.
The barbarians would also gather their forces and come,
fighting with us.
The outcome of victory or defeat would be unknown.
How would there be time to build fortresses then!”
The Emperor agreed.
In the second month,
Cháoshèng divided his army into three,
each building one fortress.
An army officer said:
“Fāngqú has no wells,
so troops cannot be stationed there.”
The Pànguān, Mèng Zǐzhōu, said:
“During times of peace in Fāngqú,
residents formed markets.
Without wells, how could people gather?”
He ordered the clearing of a dried-up well.
Yuānjǐng
means a disused well.
Yuān,
pronounced wū huān.
Fāngqú Xiàn has a salty river,
which originates from the three places Tǔqiáo, Guīdé Zhōu, and Tóngjiā Gǔ.
Its water is salty and bitter, unfit for consumption.
The sweet river,
west of the city,
originates from the northern border of the Fānbù Bízújiā.
It supplies water for human consumption.
The three fortresses were completed.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù says:
“Previously,
Yáng Cháoshèng of Bīnníng memorialized: 'Fāngqú, Hédào, and Mùbō are all routes for bandits.
I request to fortify these places as a precaution.'
An imperial edict asked: 'How many people are needed?'”
The Bīnzhì says:
“In the spring of the thirteenth year,
an imperial edict asked Duke Yáng: 'Fāngqú, Hédào, and Mùbō are all routes for bandits.
Is it permissible to fortify them?
If you deem it permissible,
how many more troops will be needed?'
On the eleventh day of the second month,
he was reinstated to his original post.
On the fourteenth day,
the imperial decree reached the army.
On the eighteenth day,
the army was dispatched.
On the twenty-sixth day,
the army arrived at Shítáng Gǔ.
On the twenty-eighth day,
the construction of the three fortresses was completed.”
We now follow the Bīnzhì but do not adopt its specific dates.
In the fourth month,
on the day Gēngshēn,
Yáng Cháoshèng's army returned to Mǎlíng.
Táng's Mǎlíng Xiàn
belonged to Qìngzhōu.
Liú Xù said: Mǎlíng
was a Suí county,
governed from Tiānjiābǎo.
In the eighth year of Zhēngguān, it was moved to Xīnchéng,
because there was Mǎlíng Bǎn west of the county.
Sòng Bái said: Yánzhōu governs Wǔyuán,
which was the land of Hàn's Mǎlíng Xiàn.
Now the southern part of the prefecture reaches the northern border of Qìngzhōu's Mǎlíng Xiàn.
Dù Yòu: Mǎlíng Xiàn,
an old Hàn pasturage.
The river valley resembles a horse's neck.
They confronted each other for several days before leaving.
Cháoshèng then fortified Mǎlíng and returned,
expanding the territory by three hundred *lǐ*,
all according to his original plan.
All according to the period he had originally anticipated.
During the Jiànzhōng period,
Shuòfāng troops defeated Lǐ Nà's army.
This was due to Cháoshèng.
Indeed, his wisdom and strategy were worthy of praise.
Huán,
pronounced cóng xuān,
also as written.
3 On the day Gēngwǔ,
Lǐ Fù, the Jiédu Shǐ of Yìchéng, passed away.
On the day Gēngchén,
Yáo Nánzhòng, the Shǎngxué Guāncháshǐ, was appointed Jiédu Shǐ of Yìchéng.
The supervisor of the army, Xuē Yíngzhēn, was holding a grand assembly.
Hearing of this,
he said:
“Master Yáo is a scholar;
how can he be a military talent!”
The Pànguān Lú Tǎn privately told someone:
“Master Yáo, though outwardly gentle,
is very firm within.
If the army supervisor infringes upon him,
he will certainly not tolerate it.
Disaster for the military prefecture
will begin from this point.
I fear I will be detained.”
So he secretly departed by another route.
Nánzhòng indeed requested his presence by official dispatch,
but did not find him,
thus he was spared.
Later, Yíngzhēn and Nánzhòng had a rift,
and many in the staff were demoted for offenses,
some even dying.
This event is detailed sixteen years later.
The historian says Lú Tǎn was almost certainly discerning of the opportune moment.
4 The Tǔbō Zānpǔ Qǐlìzàn died,
and his son Zúzhījiān ascended.
5 In the sixth month,
on the day Rénwǔ,
Wéi Gāo reported that Tǔbō had invaded.
Cánzhōu Cìshǐ Cáo Gāoshì defeated them below Táidēng Chéng.
Táidēng
was a Hàn county,
and in Táng it belonged to Cánzhōu.
From Qīngxīguān southwest to Táidēng is five hundred fifty *lǐ*.
6 Zhāng Màozōng
was concurrently serving as Guanglù Shàoqīng. The practice of appointing supernumerary officials of equal rank
began during the time of Gāozōng.
Màozhāo was then the Jìedùshǐ of Yìwǔ.
Princess Yìzhāng
was the emperor's daughter.
Yìzhāng
is the name of a county
belonging to Chēnzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: This was the territory of Hàn Chēnxian.
At the end of the Suí dynasty, Xiāo Xiǎn divided Chēnxian to establish it.
Màozōng's mother died,
and he submitted a memorial requesting to complete the auspicious marriage ceremony.
The emperor granted it.
In autumn,
in the eighth month,
on the day of Guǐyǒu,
Màozōng was reinstated as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn, with equal rank.
Jiǎng Yì of Yìxīng, a Zuǒ Shíyí, submitted a memorial remonstrating.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* (Veritable Records) records
"Jiǎng Wǔ."
According to old biographies, Yì's original name was Wǔ.
"In times of military urgency,
it was customary in antiquity for those in mourning to serve with a black sash.
I have never heard of an imperial son-in-law being reinstated while in mourning to marry a princess."
The emperor sent an internal envoy to admonish him,
but he did not stop.
So, he was specially summoned for an audience in the Yányīng Hall.
After the mid-Táng period,
the Yányīng Hall was opened for audiences with prime ministers.
Now Jiǎng Yì, as a Shíyí, was specially summoned for an audience.
"Many people in society borrow an auspicious day to marry.
Why are you so rigid in this matter?"
He replied:
"Marriage and mourning are great human relations;
auspicious and inauspicious matters must not be profaned.
Families in obscure alleys
do not know the rites and teachings.
*Wěixiàng*
refers to winding alleys,
meaning they are winding, remote, and humble.
It means they are poor and have lost their parents.
I have never heard of a man borrowing an auspicious day to marry a wife."
Wéi Tóng and Péi Kān, Taicháng Bóshì, again submitted memorials remonstrating.
The emperor was displeased
and ordered the marriage to proceed quickly.
On the day of Xīnsì,
the marriage was completed.
7 In the ninth month,
on the day of Jǐchǒu,
Lú Mài, Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was dismissed due to illness and became Tàizǐ Bīnkè.
8 In winter,
in the tenth month,
Wú Shàochéng, Jìedùshǐ of Huáinán, dug the Dāogōu channel into the Rǔ River.
The Dāogōu,
in both new and old histories, is written as the Sīwěi River.
He did not comply.
Lú Yǒng, the Bīngbù Lángzhōng, was sent to question him.
Shàochéng said:
"Opening this watercourse
is of great benefit to the people."
Yǒng said:
"When the ruler commands, the minister acts.
Even if it is beneficial,
how can a minister presume to act on his own?
You disregard the Son of Heaven's command;
how can you expect your subordinates to obey your commands?"
Shàochéng immediately stopped the project for him.
9 In the twelfth month,
Zhāng Jiànfēng, Jìedùshǐ of Xúzhōu, came to court.
Previously,
the palace would purchase goods from outside,
entrusting officials to manage it
and paying the price accordingly.
*Xiān*
is pronounced *jiàn*.
This was called "palace market" (Gōngshì).
Goods were coercively purchased,
often for less than their original estimated value.
*Gū*
means price.
Several hundred "white lookouts" were placed in the two markets.
"White lookouts"
means that people were sent to look around in the market,
seize goods without paying the original price.
*Bái* means to take without payment.
The "two markets"
were the Eastern Market and Western Market in Cháng'ān city.
The Suí dynasty called the Eastern Market Duìhuì and
the Western Market Lìrén.
When people's goods for sale were inspected,
if "palace market" was mentioned, they would fold their hands and hand them over.
No one dared to question the origin or dispute the price,
often using goods worth one hundred cash to buy items worth several thousand.
They frequently gave out old clothes dyed red or purple, or damaged silk,
torn into small pieces,
and also demanded "tribute" fees and "porterage" fees.
When people brought goods to the market,
*jiāng* means to carry.
It was called "palace market,"
but it was actually seizure.
Merchants with good wares
would hide them deeply.
Whenever an imperial envoy came out,
even those selling drinks or cakes would close their businesses and shut their doors.
Once, a farmer carried firewood on a donkey.
A eunuch, claiming it was for the palace market, took it
and gave him a few feet of silk.
He then demanded the "tribute" fee
and also insisted on the donkey being used to transport the firewood to the inner palace.
The farmer wept,
offering the silk he had received to the eunuch,
but the eunuch refused to accept it,
saying:
"I must have your donkey."
*Xū*
means what one desires.
"I have parents, a wife, and children
who rely on this for food."
It means they rely on this donkey to carry goods for trade,
and only then can they get food.
"If you don't take the payment and leave,
and you still refuse,
then I only have death."
Thereupon, he beat the eunuch.
The street official seized him and reported it.
An imperial edict dismissed the eunuch
and awarded the farmer ten rolls of silk.
However, the palace market system was not changed because of this,
and although censors repeatedly remonstrated,
they were not heeded.
When Jiànfēng came to court,
he fully reported on this.
The emperor was quite pleased and accepted it.
He asked Sū Biàn, Hùbù Shìláng and Pàndùzhī,
who, hoping to please the eunuchs,
replied:
"There are ten thousand idle households in the capital
with no fixed livelihood,
who rely on the palace market for their sustenance."
The emperor believed him,
so all further remonstrances about the palace market were disregarded.
1 In spring,
in the second month,
on the day of Yǐhài,
the armies of Shēn, Guāng, and Cài were named Zhāngyì.
Wú Shàochéng then occupied Huáinán,
which included the three prefectures of Shēn, Guāng, and Cài.
2 In summer,
in the intercalary fifth month,
on the day of Gēngshēn,
Hán Quányì, Jìedùshǐ of Shéncè Xíngyíng, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Xià, Suí, Yín, and Yòu.
Quányì was then stationed at Chángwǔchéng.
An edict ordered him to lead his troops to the new post.
The soldiers, finding Xiàzhōu to be sandy and saline,
*qì* means sandy land.
*lǔ* means saline.
A place of sandy and saline land
where the five grains do not grow.
*Qì*
is pronounced *qī jì*.
were unwilling to relocate.
On the day of Xīnyǒu,
the army mutinied,
killing the Grand General Wáng Qīyán.
Quányì fled over the city wall.
History records that Hán Quányì was cowardly and lacked strategy to command his troops,
only obtaining his position and authority by currying favor with eunuchs.
The troops later settled.
Chóngwén was from Yōuzhōu.
On the day of Bǐngzǐ,
Chóngwén was appointed Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ of Chángwǔchéng.
No imperial edict was issued;
an internal envoy orally proclaimed the appointment.
An official was orally appointed by imperial decree
to command the troops.
History records that Dézōng valued eunuch ministers and lightly regarded imperial edicts.
3 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day of Rénshēn,
Zhào Zōngrú, Gǐshìzhōng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was dismissed and became Yòushùzǐ.
Zhèng Yúqìng, Gōngbù Shìláng, was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
4 In the eighth month,
the positions of Zuǒ and Yòu Shéncè Tǒngjūn were first established.
From this, it is known that the Shéncè army was outside the Six Armies.
Their stipends and rewards were generous.
*Bǐng* means to supply.
Called the "expeditionary camps,"
they were all under the command of the Zhōngwèi.
Their army eventually reached 150,000 men.
5 Jīngzhào Yǐn Wú Còu (吳湊) repeatedly spoke of the abuses of the Palace Market.
The eunuchs said that Còu repeatedly memorialized concerning the Palace Market,
and that it was all due to the schemes of the Yòujīnwú Dūzhī Zhào Qià (趙洽) and Tián Xiùyán (田秀嵓);
on the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Qià and Xiùyán were exiled to Tiāndé Jūn (天德軍).
Dūzhī was
an official of the Jīnwú (金吾) office,
a right-hand position.
6 In the ninth month,
on the *bǐngshēn* day,
Yú Dí (于頔), the Shǎn Guó Guānchásǐ (陝虢觀察使), was made Shānnán Dōngdào Jiédùshǐ (山南東道節度使).
7 On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Wáng Chuí (王倕) passed away.
Chuí was
Sùzōng's son.
Chuí is
pronounced *chuí*.
8 Zhāngwǔ Jiédùshǐ Wú Shàochéng (吳少誠) dispatched troops to plunder Huòshān (霍山) in Shòuzhōu (壽州).
"Zhāngwǔ"
should be
"Zhāngyì" (彰義).
Huòshān was
originally Qiánchéng Xiàn (灊城縣) of Lújiāng (廬江) in the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
During the Liáng (梁) dynasty, Huòzhōu (霍州) was established.
During the Suí (隋) dynasty, Huòshān Xiàn (霍山縣) was established.
In the Táng (唐) dynasty, it belonged to Shòuzhōu.
In the 27th year of Kāiyuán (開元), Huòshān was renamed Shèngtáng (盛唐).
In the early Tiānbǎo (天寶) period, Huòshān Xiàn was re-established by splitting from Shèngtáng.
Its territory now belongs to the Lù'ān Xiàn (六安縣) area of Shòuzhōu.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: In the sixth year of Zhēnyuán (貞元),
Lántián (藍田), Wèiqiáo (渭橋), and other Zhèn'èshǐ (鎮遏使) were first established.
Troops were stationed to guard them.
9 Tàixuéshēng Xuē Yuē (薛約), who studied under Sīyè Yáng Chéng (陽城),
was exiled to Liánzhōu (連州) for speaking out;
Chéng saw him off outside the city.
The emperor, believing Chéng to be colluding with a criminal,
on the *jǐsì* day,
demoted Chéng to Dàozhōu Cìshǐ (道州刺史).
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* (實錄) and the old and new biographies do not have a year or month.
Liǔ Zōngyuán's (柳宗元) *Yáng Gōng Yí'ài Jié* (陽公遺愛碣) says:
"In the fifth month of the fourth year,
the Emperor, with a silver seal and red sash, appointed Gōng Yáng (陽公) as Jiànyì Dàfū (諫議大夫) from his reclusive dwelling.
Seven years later,
his earnest remonstrances reached the court,
and the Emperor particularly praised and admired him,
promoting him to Guózǐ Sīyè (國子司業).
Another four years later, on the *jǐsì* day of the ninth month,
he was sent out to be Dàozhōu Cìshǐ.
Over 160 students from the Imperial Academy, including Jì Cháng (季償) of Lǔjùn (魯郡) and Hé Fān (何蕃) of Lújiāng, abandoned their studies and rushed
to prostrate themselves before the palace gate,
crying out at the gatekeepers and appealing to heaven,
wishing to beg for his restoration.
The imperial court seriously reconsidered the matter,
as per the *jǐsì* edict."
This account is now followed.
When the taxes of the prefecture were not collected,
the Guānchásǐ repeatedly rebuked him.
Chéng wrote his own evaluation, saying:
"My efforts in governing and nurturing the people have been arduous,
but my tax collection policies are clumsy.
My evaluation is 'lower-lower'."
The Guānchásǐ sent a Pànguān (判官) to supervise his taxes.
Upon arriving at the prefecture,
Chéng had already imprisoned himself.
The Pànguān was greatly surprised,
rushed in,
and met Chéng in prison, saying:
"What crime has the Administrator committed!
I was ordered to inquire about your well-being only."
He stayed for a day or two and did not leave,
but Chéng did not
return;
outside the official residence gate, there was an old gate leaf lying horizontally on the ground,
and Chéng sat and slept on it day and night.
The Pànguān felt uneasy and
took his leave.
Afterwards, another Pànguān was sent to investigate him,
but that Pànguān took his wife and children and fled halfway.
Yáng Chéng's renowned virtue
was known and respected by people.
Who was it that did not know him and sent someone to investigate him?
10 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the *dīngyǒu* day,
Tōng Wáng Chén (通王諶) passed away.
11 On the *gēngzǐ* day,
Xiàzhōu Jiédùshǐ Hán Quányì (韓全義) reported defeating the Tǔbō (吐蕃) northwest of Yánzhōu (鹽州).
12 Míngzhōu Zhènjiàng Lì Huáng (栗鍠)
*Xìngpǔ* (姓譜) says: The Lì (栗) surname descends from Lìlù Shì (栗陸氏).
In Hàn Cháng'ān (長安), there was a wealthy family named Lì.
He incited the Shānyuè (山越) to rebel,
attacking and capturing prefectures and counties in eastern Zhèjiāng (浙江).
The Míngzhōu Shānyuè are
the mountain people in the southern border of modern Cíxī (慈溪) and Yínxiàn (鄞縣), and the northwestern border of Fènghuà Xiàn (奉化縣).
Huáng is
pronounced *hù máng fān*,
and also *huáng*.
Yòu is
pronounced *yǒu*.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the *jiǎyín* day,
Yǎ Wáng Yì (雅王逸) passed away.
Yì was
the Emperor's younger brother.
2 In the second month,
on the *dīngchǒu* day,
Xuānwǔ Jiédùshǐ Dǒng Jìn (董晉) passed away;
on the *yǐyǒu* day,
his Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬) Lù Chángyuán (陸長源) was made Jiédùshǐ.
Chángyuán was stern and impatient by nature,
and arrogant due to his talent.
Pànguān Mèng Shúdù (孟叔度) was frivolous, dissolute,
and enjoyed treating officers and soldiers with disrespect;
everyone in the army disliked him.
When Dǒng Jìn passed away,
Chángyuán knew he would be retained as interim commander and
openly declared:
"The officers and soldiers have been lax for too long;
they must be disciplined by law!"
Everyone was afraid.
Someone advised him to distribute money to reward the army,
but Chángyuán said:
"Am I
a Hébèi (河北) bandit,
buying brave soldiers with money to seek a military governorship!"
According to custom,
when a commander died,
soldiers were given cloth to make uniforms.
Chángyuán ordered that they be given its value in money;
Shúdù raised the price of salt,
and lowered the price of cloth,
so each person received no more than two or three *jin* of salt.
The army resented and raged,
but Chángyuán did not prepare for it.
On that day,
the soldiers mutinied,
killed Chángyuán and Shúdù,
carved up and ate them,
and completely destroyed them.
Historians say that Lù Chángyuán's death
was due to the Táng court misusing his talents.
As for Mèng Shúdù, his death was more than deserved.
Having gained the hearts of the people,
a secret letter summoned him;
Yì Zhǔn (逸準) led his troops directly into Biànzhōu (汴州),
and the rebellious crowd was then pacified.
3 Lǐ Qí (李錡), the Chángzhōu Cìshǐ (常州刺史), was appointed Zhèxī Guānchásǐ (浙西觀察使) and Zhū Dào Yántiě Zhuǎnyùnshǐ (諸道鹽鐵轉運使).
Qí was
Guózhēn's (國貞) son.
Xián guǎng jì and Gōngyuànshǐ (宮苑使) Lǐ Qíyùn (李齊運) accepted hundreds of thousands in bribes from him,
and recommended him to the Emperor,
which is why he was appointed.
Qí exploited the people to offer tribute,
and the Emperor was pleased by this.
This laid the groundwork for Lǐ Qí's rebellion in Zhèxī.
4 On the *gēngchén* day,
Zhèdōng Guānchásǐ Péi Sù (裴肅) captured Lì Huáng in Táizhōu (台州)
and executed him.
5 On the *jǐchǒu* day,
Liú Yìzhǔn (劉逸準) was appointed Xuānwǔ Jiédùshǐ
and granted the name Quánliàng (全諒).
6 In the third month,
on the *jiǎyín* day,
Wú Shàochéng dispatched troops to raid Tángzhōu (唐州),
killed Jiānjūn Shào Guócháo (邵國朝) and Zhèn'èshǐ Zhāng Jiāyú (張嘉瑜),
plundered over a thousand common people, and then departed.
7 On the *wǔwǔ* day,
Zhāoyì Jiédùshǐ Wáng Qiánxiū (王虔休) passed away;
on the *wǔchén* day,
Lǐ Yuánchún (李元淳), the Héyáng (河陽) and Huáizhōu (懷州) Jiédùshǐ, was appointed Zhāoyì Jiédùshǐ.
8 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the *guǐwèi* day,
Yī Shèn (伊慎), the Ānzhōu (安州) Cìshǐ, was appointed Ān (安) and Huáng (黃) and other prefectures' Jiédùshǐ.
9 On the *guǐsì* day,
Shānnán Xīdào Jiédùshǐ Yán Zhèn (嚴震) passed away.
10 Yìmóuxún (異牟尋) of Nánzhào (南詔) sent an envoy to agree with Wéi Gāo (韋皋) to jointly attack the Tǔbō.
Gāo, stating that military provisions had not yet been gathered,
requested to wait until another year.
Wéi Gāo possessed wisdom and strategy;
he feared that Nánzhào was only superficially agreeing and did not fully reveal their intentions,
hence he used the excuse of ungathered military provisions.
This can be conveyed to the wise.
11 Shānnán Xīdào Dūyúhòu (都虞候) Yán Lì (嚴礪) flattered Yán Zhèn.
When Zhèn fell ill,
he made Lì interim commander and
recommended him in his will.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the *yǐsì* day,
Lì was appointed Shānnán Xīdào Jiédùshǐ.
12th month, 8th month,
Qū Huán, the Jìedùshǐ of Chén-Xǔ, passed away.
On the day Yǐwèi,
Wú Shàochéng dispatched troops to plunder Lín yǐng.
Lín yǐng
was an ancient county during the Hàn dynasty,
and belonged to Xǔzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: it is sixty *lǐ* southeast of Xǔzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: In the fourth year of Dàyè of the Suí dynasty,
