it was moved from the old city to Lín yǐng Gāo,
a place that was actually a mound.
General Wáng Lìngzhōng was sent with three thousand soldiers to rescue it,
but they were all captured by Shàochéng.
On the day Bǐng
wǔ,
Shàngguān Yuè was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Chén-Xǔ,
and Shàochéng then besieged Xǔzhōu.
Yuè wanted to abandon the city and flee,
but Liú Chāngyì, the Vice Commissioner for Garrison Farms, stopped him, saying:
"The troops in the city are sufficient to deal with the bandits.
Just close the gates and do not engage in battle.
In a few days,
the bandits' morale will naturally wane.
We, by remaining intact, will capitalize on their weariness,
and there is no way we will not be victorious."
*Miè*
means "without".
Chāngyì recruited a thousand brave warriors to dig through the city wall and sortie to attack Shàochéng,
severely defeating him.
The city was thereby preserved.
Chāngyì
was from Yǎnzhōu.
Shàochéng again raided Xīhuá.
Xīhuá
was a Hàn county,
and belonged to Chénzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: it is eighty *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
Ān Guóníng, the Commandant of Chén-Xǔ's military forces, did not get along with Shàngguān Yuè,
and plotted to betray the city and respond to Shàochéng.
Liú Chāngyì executed him by stratagem.
He summoned Ān Guóníng's subordinates,
gave each two bolts of silk,
and set up ambushes in key alleys.
Anyone seen carrying silk was immediately beheaded,
and none escaped.
13th month, On the day Gēngchén,
Liú Quánliàng, the Jìedùshǐ of Xuānwǔ, passed away.
The army, remembering the kindness of Liú Xuánzuǒ,
nominated his nephew, Hán Hóng of Kuāngchéng, the Commandant of Military Forces, to be Acting Jìedùshǐ.
Hóng, leading his troops,
understood their abilities, weaknesses, bravery, and cowardice,
and his directions always ensured they were fit for their tasks.
14th month, On the day Bǐngchén,
an imperial edict was issued to strip Wú Shàochéng of his official titles and ranks,
and ordered all circuits to send troops to suppress him.
15th month, On the day Xīnyǒu,
Hán Hóng was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Xuānwǔ.
Previously,
Shàochéng
had made an agreement with Liú Quánliàng to jointly attack Chén-Xǔ,
and to return Chénzhōu to Xuānwǔ.
Several envoys were still in the guest quarters,
and Hóng had them all driven out and beheaded.
He selected three thousand elite soldiers
to join the various armies and attack Shàochéng near Xǔ.
Shàochéng thereby lost his advantage.
As there was no one to assist him in his evil deeds,
he lost his advantage.
16th month, Winter,
10th month,
On the day Yǐchǒu,
Wáng Yuán of Yōng passed away.
He was the son of the Crown Prince,
and the Emperor loved him as his own son.
When he passed away,
he was posthumously honored as Crown Prince Wénjìng.

17th month, Yú Dí, the Jìedùshǐ of Shānnán Dōngdào, Yī Shèn, the Jìedùshǐ of Ān-Huáng, Wáng Zōng, the Overseer of Shòuzhōu, together with Shàngguān Yuè and Hán Hóng, advanced and attacked Wú Shàochéng,
defeating him repeatedly.
11th month,
On the day Rénzǐ,
Yú Dí reported the capture of Wúfáng and Lángshān.
The Later Wèi established Xiāngchéng Commandery in the territory of Xīpíng of Rǔnán during the Hàn dynasty,
and also established Suìníng County.
In the early years of Dàyè of the Suí dynasty, it was renamed Wúfáng.
Wúfáng
was originally a Hàn county name.
Yìng Shào said: it was originally the state of Fángzi,
which Chǔ enfeoffed to King Fūgài of Wú,
hence it was called Wúfáng.
Lángshān was the territory of Hàn's Ānchāng County.
The Later Wèi established Chū'ān Commandery there.
In the 18th year of Kāihuáng of the Suí dynasty, Ānchāng was renamed Lángshān.
During the Táng dynasty, both belonged to Càizhōu.
During the Sòng dynasty, to avoid the taboo name of the Holy Ancestor,
Lángshān was renamed Quèshān.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Wúfáng
is seventy *lǐ* northwest of Càizhōu.
Lángshān
is seventy-five *lǐ* southwest of Càizhōu.
18th month, 12th month,
On the day Xīnwèi, Hún Jiān, the Zhōngshū Lìng and King of Xiánníng, passed away in Hézhōng.
Hún Jiān was enfeoffed as King of Xiánníng Commandery.
Although he reached the highest positions of general and minister,
he showed no signs of conceit.
Whenever he presented tribute, he would personally inspect it,
and when receiving imperial gifts, he acted as if in the Emperor's presence.
Because of this, he was cherished and loved by the Emperor.
When the Emperor returned from Xīngyuán,
he sought to appease even those with troops in a single prefecture or garrison.
Whenever Jiān presented a report,
it was never rejected;
according to Táng regulations: all reports that were approved
would pass through the Ménxià Shěng and Zhōngshū Shěng;
those not approved
would be shelved and not sent down.
He said, "The Emperor does not doubt me."
Thus, he was able to complete his life with fame and achievement.
19th month, The six Prefectures' Dǎngxiàng, since Yǒngtài, resided in Shízhōu.
After Dàizōng's Yǒngtài era,
it was changed to Dàlì.
The Dǎngxiàng tribes of the six prefectures
were called Yělì Yuèshī,
Yělì Lóng'ér,
Yělì Juélǜ,
Érhuáng,
Yěhǎi,
Yěsū, etc.,
residing in Qìngzhōu, known as the Dōngshān Department,
and in Xiàzhōu, known as the Píngxià Department.
After Yǒngtài,
they gradually migrated to Shízhōu.
The Táng likely established the Yǒng'ān Garrison Commander in Shízhōu
to pacify and control the Dǎngxiàng.
Jiān,
pronounced *gǔ hán fān*.
20th month, Since the various armies attacking Wú Shàochéng had no unified commander,
whenever they deployed,
each person sought their own advantage.
*Guī*
means "to plan".
On the day Yǐwèi,
the various armies collapsed on their own at Xiǎoyǐnshuǐ.
*Yǐn*
is the same as *Yǐn*,
pronounced *yǐn*,
and also *yǐn*.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Yǐng River flows southeast past Lín yǐng County,
where the Xiǎoyǐn River flows into it. It then flows east past the north of Xīhuá County,
then south past the north of Rǔyáng County,
then southeast past the north of Nándùn County,
where the Dàyǐn River comes from the west to flow into it.
Sòng Bái said: Rǔyáng County of Càizhōu
was renamed Yǐnshuǐ in the 17th year of Kāihuáng of the Suí dynasty.
Today, within its borders, there are waters named Dàyǐn and Xiǎoyǐn.
In that same year, Rǔyáng County was also separately established northeast of Shàngcài County.
All these were taken by Shàochéng.
It was then that the idea of appointing a Commander of Pacification and Suppression was first discussed.
21st month, Fifty thousand Tubō troops divided to attack Nánzhào and Xīzhōu.
Yìmóxún and Wéi Gāo each dispatched troops to resist them.
The Tubō returned without success.
1st month, Spring,
1st month,
The four armies of Héng-Jì, Yì-Dìng, Chén-Xǔ, and Héyáng fought against Wú Shàochéng,
but all were disadvantaged and retreated.
Hán Quányì, the Jìedùshǐ of Xiàsuí, originally came from the Shéncè Army.
The Eunuch-in-attendance Dòu Wénchǎng held him in high regard,
recommended him to the Emperor,
and made him command the various armies to suppress Wú Shàochéng.
2nd month,
On the day Yǐyǒu,
Quányì was appointed Commander of Pacification and Suppression for the four fronts of Càizhōu's mobile camp,
and the troops from seventeen circuits all fell under Quányì's command.
This set the stage for Hán Quányì's defeat.
2 After Liú Xuánzuǒ 薨 passed away, the Xuānwǔ Army
made five rebellions in total.
In the eighth year of Zhēnyuán (792), Xuánzuǒ 薨 passed away.
The troops in Biàn refused Wú Còu and installed his son, Shìníng.
Lǐ Wànróng then drove Shìníng out.
In the tenth year (794),
Hán Wéiqīng and others rebelled.
In the twelfth year (796),
Wànróng died,
and his son then rebelled with his troops.
After Dǒng Jìn entered Biàn,
Dèng Wéigōng again plotted rebellion.
In the fourteenth year (798),
Jìn 薨 passed away,
and the troops again rebelled,
killing the acting commander.
There were five rebellions in total.
They made light of their commander-in-chief.
Hán Hóng had been in charge for several months,
and all knew his name;
there was a general, Liú È,
who often led the instigation.
In the third month,
Hóng arrayed his troops at the headquarters gate,
summoned È and three hundred of his partisans,
and enumerated their crimes, saying,
"You have repeatedly participated in rebellions,
considering it an achievement,"
and had them all executed.
Blood flowed on the scarlet path.
From then until Hóng's entry to court
in the fourteenth year of Yuánhé of Xianzōng (819),
Hán Hóng entered court.
Not a single soldier dared to make a ruckus in the city.
3 Xuē Yíngzhēn, the Inspector of Yìchéng, was favored and trusted by the Emperor.
He wished to usurp military and administrative power from the Jìedùshǐ Yáo Nánzhòng,
but Nánzhòng did not comply,
which caused a rift between them.
Yíngzhēn slandered Nánzhòng's staff member, Mǎ Zǒng,
who was demoted to Biejia of Quánzhōu.
Liǔ Miǎn, the Fújiàn Observer, plotted to harm Zǒng to ingratiate himself with Yíngzhēn.
He dispatched his staff member Bǎodǐng Xuē Róng to act as Quánzhōu official,
ordering him to investigate and convict Zǒng.
Róng, however, argued for Zǒng's innocence;
Miǎn was enraged,
summoned Róng,
imprisoned him,
and allowed the guards to freely insult him.
After a full month of this,
he gradually enticed Róng to falsely accuse Zǒng,
but Róng ultimately refused to comply;
Zǒng was thus spared.
Miǎn
was the son of Fāng.
Liǔ Fāng was learned in history
and served Xuánzōng and Sùzōng.
Yíngzhēn repeatedly disparaged Nánzhòng to the Emperor,
and the Emperor grew suspicious.
Yíngzhēn then
dispatched a minor official, Chéng Wùyíng, by fast courier to falsely accuse Nánzhòng of crimes.
Cáo Wénqià, a yájiàng, also reported matters in Cháng'ān.
Knowing this,
he traveled day and night,
catching up with Wùyíng at Chánglè Post Station.
Chánglè Post Station
was on the Chǎnpo east of Cháng'ān city.
In the middle of the night,
he killed Wùyíng
and sank Yíngzhēn's memorial in a latrine;
he then wrote his own memorial exonerating Nánzhòng,
also confessing to the crime of unauthorized killing,
and also wrote a statement to inform Nánzhòng,
and then committed suicide.
The next morning,
the gate was not opened.
The post station attendant forced his way in
and found the memorial and statement beside Wénqià's corpse.
The Emperor heard of this and was greatly impressed.
He summoned Yíngzhēn to court;
Nánzhòng, fearing Yíngzhēn's slanders would deepen,
also requested to come to court.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day of Bǐngzǐ,
Nánzhòng arrived in the capital
and awaited punishment at Jīnwú.
Jīnwú
referred to the Left and Right Guard barracks,
where all officials, internal and external, who were awaiting punishment would report.
He was granted an audience.
The Emperor asked,
"Does Yíngzhēn trouble you?"
He replied,
"Yíngzhēn does not trouble me,
but only disturbs Your Majesty's law.
Moreover, the number of people like Yíngzhēn in the world
is innumerable!
Even if Yáng and Dù were to be reborn,
Yáng and Dù
refer to Yáng Hù and Dù Yù.
Fù
is pronounced fú yòu fān.
achieving the merit of conquest."
The Emperor was silent
and ultimately did not punish Yíngzhēn,
instead continuing to have him manage confidential matters.
Yíngzhēn again told the Emperor:
"All of Nánzhòng's poor governance
was advised by his staff member Mǎ Shǎowēi."
An imperial edict demoted Shǎowēi to Jiāngnán.
The official dispatched an imperial eunuch to escort him,
who pushed him into the river, where he died.
4 Wéi Shìzōng, the Qiánzhōng Observer,
had harsh regulations;
on the day of Dīnghài,
the yájiàng Fù Jìn and others drove him out.
He fled to Shīzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Qiánzhōu
is 411 lǐ northeast of Shīzhōu.
5 King Jìng of Xīnlúo
passed away.
On the day of Gēngyín,
his legitimate grandson Jùnyōng was formally appointed King of Xīnlúo.
6 Hán Quányì had always lacked courage and strategy.
He relied solely on cunning flattery and bribery to win over eunuchs and become a grand marshal.
Whenever military matters were discussed, dozens of eunuchs serving as监军 (military supervisors) would sit in the tent, arguing among themselves,
creating such a clamor that no decision could be reached, and the meeting would be dismissed.
The weather gradually grew hot,
and the soldiers, having been stationed for a long time in marshy terrain,
many fell ill with epidemics.
People's morale was low.
In the fifth month,
on the day of Gēngxū,
he fought against Wú Shàochéng's generals Wú Xiù and Wú Shǎoyáng at the Yīn Nán Guǎnglìyuán.
Yīn Nán
means south of the Yīn River.
The various armies were utterly routed;
Xiù and others took advantage of this,
and Quányì retreated to defend Wǔlóu.
Wǔlóu
is southwest of Yīnshuǐ County.
He was from Qīngchí, Cāngzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Hàn Fúyáng County,
in the eighteenth year of Suí Kāihuáng (598), its name was changed to Qīngchí,
named after the Qīngchí pond southeast of the county.
7 Yú Dí, the Jìedùshǐ of Shānnán Dōngdào, used the campaign against Wú Shàochéng as an opportunity
to greatly recruit warriors,
repair armor and sharpen weapons,
amass wealth,
and freely execute people.
He harbored ambitions to control Hànnán
and made it his business to disrespect his superiors and oppress his subordinates.
The Emperor, at the time, was lenient towards the regional warlords
and, though aware of his actions,
could do nothing about it.
Dí falsely accused Yuán Hóng, the Cìshǐ of Dèngzhōu, of corruption.
In the first year of Zhìdé (756),
the Xiāngyáng Defense Commissioner was promoted to Shānnán Dōngdào Jìedùshǐ,
governing the nine prefectures of Xiāng, Dèng, Suí, Táng, Ān, Jūn, Fáng, Jīn, and Shāng.
In the first year of Zhēnyuán (785),
Dèngzhōu was subordinate to the Eastern Capital Region.
From this, it can be seen
that at this time he again governed Dèngzhōu.
He dispatched an imperial envoy to escort him to Zǎoyáng.
Zǎoyáng
was the land of Hàn Chōnglíng.
The Suí Dynasty established Zǎoyáng County.
In early Táng, it belonged to Tángzhōu.
In the eleventh year of Zhēnguān (637), it was abolished
and belonged to Suízhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is 160 lǐ northwest of the prefecture
and 135 lǐ from Xiāngzhōu.
The imperial envoy rushed back.
Dí memorialized that Hóng's responsibility was too heavy.
The Emperor reinstated Hóng as Jízhōu Zhǎngshǐ;
then Dí dispatched him.
He was also angered by the Judgement Officer Xuē Zhènglún
and memorialized for his demotion to Xiázhōu Zhǎngshǐ;
by the time the imperial edict arrived,
Dí's anger had subsided,
and he again memorialized to retain him as Judgement Officer.
The Emperor complied with each request.
8. Zhāng Jiànfēng, the Jìdùshǐ of Xú, Sī, and Háo, had been garrisoned at Péngchéng for over ten years.
In the fourth year of Zhēnyuán
Zhāng Jiànfēng was stationed at Péngchéng.
He became critically ill
and requested a replacement.
On the Xīnhài day,
Wéi Xiàqīng, the Cìshǐ of Sūzhōu, was appointed Xú, Sī, Háo Xíngjūn Sīmǎ.
When the imperial edict arrived,
Jiànfēng had already passed away.
Xiàqīng
was Zhíyì's paternal grand-cousin.
Zhèng Tōngchéng, the Pàn'guān of Xúzhōu, took charge as Liúhòu.
Fearing that the soldiers might revolt,
and as Zhejiang's troops were passing Péngchéng,
Tōngchéng wanted to bring them into the city as reinforcements.
The soldiers were enraged.
On the Rénzǐ day,
several thousand men chopped down the armory gate,
took out weapons and armor to equip themselves,
surrounded the Yáchéng,
abducted Yīn (Jiànfēng's son and former Cānjūn of Guózhōu) to make him take charge of the military administration,
killed Tōngchéng and several other high-ranking generals, including Duàn Bóxióng,
and shackled the Jiānjūn.
When the emperor heard of this,
he appointed Lǐ Yōng, the Lìbù Yuánwàiláng, as Xúzhōu Xuānwèishǐ.
Yōng went straight to their camp,
summoned the officers and soldiers to proclaim the imperial decree,
explained the consequences of their actions,
removed the shackles from the Jiānjūn,
and had him reinstated.
The rogue faction dared not defy him.
Yīn submitted a memorial styling himself as Bīngmǎ Liúhòu.
Yōng, deeming it not an imperial appointment,
refused to accept it
and made him strike it out,
then accepted it and returned.
9. Língzhōu defeated the Tǔbō at Wūlánqiáo.
According to the Dòngshū Dìlǐzhì, there was Wūlánguān in Wūlánxiàn of Huìzhōu;
the bridge must have been on the Yellow River outside the pass.
10. On the Bǐngyín day,
Wéi Shìzōng re-entered Qiánzhōng.
In the fourth month of this year,
Wéi Shìzōng had been expelled by his Yájiàng, Fù Jìn.
Qián,
pronounced Qín,
also pronounced with Qián as in “qílian”.
11. Lǚ Wèi of Hézhōng, the Húnán Guānchásǐ, memorialized about the embezzlement and bribery of Yáng Lǚ, the Cìshǐ of Yǒngzhōu.
Lǚ, in his memorial, claimed that all the illicit gains were for imperial tribute.
The emperor summoned him to Cháng'ān.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
he ordered the Sānsīshǐ to interrogate him,
questioning him about the destination of the funds.
Lǚ said,
"I have already purchased horses and presented them as tribute."
When further pressed,
"Who was the owner of the horses?
How old were the horses?"
He replied,
"The owner
was a person from the four directions,
and I do not know where he is now.
According to ritual,
to inquire about the age of a road-horse is punishable,"
a saying from Qūlǐ.
His replies were generally like this.
The emperor was pleased with his words of presenting tribute
and released him,
merely dismissing him from office.
Dèzōng's suspicion and jealousy
were such that officials like Yáng Yán and Dòu Cān, who held prime ministerial positions,
were all dismissed for shifting blame onto the emperor,
and not treated as equals.
Yáng Lǚ, who failed due to corruption but claimed to be presenting tribute,
could it be said that he wasn't shifting blame onto the emperor?
Dèzōng was pleased with his words of presenting tribute and absolved him of his crime.
Indeed, a love for wealth
is not a good reputation;
even if a person loves wealth,
if they are accused of loving wealth,
they will surely become indignant and reject it.
Why then did Dèzōng so readily accept this reputation?
My opinion is that after Yáng Lǚ's corruption was exposed,
he must have offered something in order to avoid punishment,
and Dèzōng was not merely pleased with his words.
12. On the Bǐngxū day,
Lǐ Shīgǔ, the Jìdùshǐ of Zīqīng, was granted the title Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
13. The rebellious soldiers of Xúzhōu memorialized on behalf of Zhāng Yīn, requesting a banner and staff of authority,
but the imperial court refused.
Dù Yòu, the Jìdùshǐ of Huáinán, was granted the title Tóng Píngzhāngshì
and concurrently appointed Jìdùshǐ of Xú, Háo, and Sī,
and ordered to suppress the rebellion.
Yòu extensively prepared boats and ships
and sent his Yájiàng Mèng Zhǔn as the vanguard.
They crossed the Huái River but were defeated,
and Yòu dared not advance.
Zhāng Pēi, the Cìshǐ of Sīzhōu, led troops to attack Yǒngqiáo,
but was severely defeated and returned.
The imperial court had no choice but to appoint Yīn as Xúzhōu Tuánliànshǐ,
appointed Pēi as Sīzhōu Liúhòu,
and Dù Jiān, the Cìshǐ of Háozhōu, as Háozhōu Liúhòu,
while also adding Yòu as concurrent Háosī Guānchásǐ.
Háo and Sī were subordinated to Huáinán
to weaken the authority of Xúzhōu.
According to Kǎoyì: The Shílù states,
"On the Guǐmǎo day of the twelfth month,
Sīzhōu and Háozhōu
were ordered to be administered by the Huáinán Guānchásǐ."
This is concluded here.
Jiān
was the fifth-generation descendant of Zhènglún.
Dù Zhènglún was a chancellor during the reigns of Tàizōng and Gāozōng.
When Jiànfēng was critically ill,
Jiān secretly plotted to replace him and rushed from Háozhōu to the prefectural seat.
Lǐ Fān, a staff member, along with his colleagues,
went in to inquire about Jiànfēng's illness.
Upon seeing Jiān outside,
he wept and said,
"The Púyè is critically ill like this,"
Zhāng Jiànfēng was granted the title Púyè,
hence the address.
"Now you abandon your prefecture and come here,
what do you intend to do?
You should leave quickly,
otherwise,
I will report it to the throne."
Jiān was startled and taken aback,
and thus returned directly.
When Jiànfēng died,
Fān returned to Yángzhōu.
Jiān falsely accused Fān in a memorial of unsettling the military morale after Jiànfēng's death.
The emperor was greatly enraged
and secretly decreed to Dù Yòu to have him killed.
Yòu had always held Fān in high regard.
He kept the edict for ten days, unable to bring himself to issue it.
He then led Fān to discuss Buddhist scriptures, saying,
"The Buddha spoke of retribution.
Is there such a thing?"
Fān replied,
"There is."
Buddhist scriptures say that the good and evil deeds performed by humans constitute the 'fruit',
and according to their actions, they are rewarded with fortune or calamity as 'retribution'.
"If this is truly the case,
you should face matters without fear."
He then took out the edict and showed it to Fān.
Fān's expression did not change.
He said,
"This is truly retribution."
Yòu said,
"You must not speak of this outside.
I have already discussed it secretly and pledged a hundred lives to vouch for you."
People refer to their family members as a hundred lives.
Fān was summoned to Cháng'ān.
When the emperor saw Fān's dignified and composed demeanor,
he said,
"How could this person be an evil-doer?"
He immediately appointed him Mìshū Láng.
14. The King of Xīnluó, Jùnyōng, died.
The people of the kingdom enthroned his son, Zhòngxī.
15. In autumn,
seventh month,
Wú Shàochéng attacked Hán Quányì at Wǔlóu.
The various armies were again soundly defeated.
Quányì fled during the night
and sought refuge in the city of Yǐnshuǐ Xiàn.
Yǐnshuǐ Xiàn
was the territory of Rǔyáng Xiàn in the Hàn dynasty.
The Suí dynasty established Yǐnshuǐ Xiàn,
abolishing Rǔyáng and merging it into Yǐnshuǐ.
In the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Chénzhōu.
The Jiǔyùzhì states: It is eighty lǐ southwest of the prefecture.
16. Liú Yuán, the younger brother of Liú Jì, the Jìdùshǐ of Lúlóng, was the Cìshǐ of Zhuōzhōu
but did not obey Jì's orders.
Jì led troops to attack and capture him.
17. Ninth month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
Lú Cán, the Jìdùshǐ of Yìchéng, passed away.
On the Jiǎxū day,
Lǐ Yuánsù, the Shàngshū Zuǒchéng, was appointed to replace him.
Jiǎ Dān said,
"Whenever a Jìdùshǐ is appointed from within the army,
there will inevitably be feelings of love and hate, allegiance and disloyalty,
with joy and fear being equally divided,
thus the hearts of the multitude are often unsettled.
From now on, I wish Your Majesty would only appoint people from the imperial court,
so that there may be no other changes."
The emperor considered this true.
18. Zhèng Yúqìng, the Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, and Yú Xiào, the Hùbù Shìláng and Pàndùzhī, were close friends.
Yúqìng often advised the emperor to follow Xiào's proposals.
The emperor considered this favoritism.
On the Gēngxū day,
Yúqìng was demoted to Chénzhōu Sīmǎ,
and Xiào to Quánzhōu Sīhù.
Xiào
was Dī's elder brother.
19th, *guǐchǒu* day:
Wú Shàochéng (吳少誠) advanced and set up camp several *lǐ* from Yīnshuǐ (溵水).
Hán Quányì (韓全義) again led the various armies to retreat and defend Chénzhōu (陳州).
The Xuānwǔ (宣武) and Héyáng (河陽) forces secretly returned to their respective commands.
Only Mèng Yuányáng (孟元陽), a general from Chénxǔ (陳許), and Sū Guāngróng (蘇光榮), a general from Shéncè (神策), led their respective units to remain at Yīnshuǐ (溵水).
Hán Quányì (韓全義) used deception to lure Xiàhóu Zhòngxuān (夏侯仲宣), a general from Zhāoyì (昭義), Shí Áng (時昂), a general from Yìchéng (義成), and Quán Wénbiàn (權文變), a general from Héyáng (河陽),
along with Guō Xiāng (郭湘), a general from Hézhōng (河中), and others.
He then executed them,
hoping to awe the troops.
When Quányì (全義) reached Chénzhōu (陳州),
the Prefect Liú Chāngyì (劉昌裔) ascended the city wall and said to him:
“The Son of Heaven commanded you to suppress Cáizhōu (蔡州).
Now you have come here.
Chāngyì (昌裔) dares not receive you;
please encamp outside the city.”
Afterward, Chāngyì (昌裔) brought oxen and wine into Quányì’s (全義) camp to犒赏 *kàoshǎng* (reward) the army.
Quányì (全義) was pleasantly surprised
and inwardly respected him.
*Jǐwèi* day:
Mèng Yuányáng (孟元陽) and others fought Wú Shàochéng (吳少誠),
killing over two thousand men.
20th, *gēngshēn* day:
Qí Kàng (齊抗), Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (tàichángqīng 太常卿), was appointed Secretariat Drafter (zhōngshūshèrén 中書舍人) and concurrently Minister (tóngpíngzhāngshì 同平章事).
The *Xīnshū Zǎixiàng Biǎo* (新書宰相表) states: Qí Kàng (齊抗) was appointed Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat (zhōngshūshìláng 中書侍郎) and concurrently Minister (tóngpíngzhāngshì 同平章事).
21st, *guǐhài* day:
Zhāng Yīn (張愔) was appointed acting Military Governor (liúhòu 留後) of Xúzhōu (徐州).
22nd, Winter,
10th month:
Wú Shàochéng (吳少誠) withdrew his troops back to Cáizhōu (蔡州).
Mèng Yuányáng (孟元陽) had blunted his vanguard,
which is why he retreated.
Wéi Gāo (韋皋), hearing that the various armies had achieved nothing in suppressing Shàochéng (少誠),
submitted a memorial stating:
“I request that Hún Jiān (渾瑊) and Jiǎ Dān (賈耽) be appointed Marshals (yuánshuài 元帥)
to command all the armies.”
Hún Jiān (渾瑊) had died in the 12th month of the previous year.
Wéi Gāo (韋皋) must have submitted this memorial before Jiān’s (瑊) death.
“Heavy” (zhòng 重)
means “difficult” (nán 難).
“Issuing from Jīngchǔ (荊楚) to cut down the rebels.”
Wéi Gāo (韋皋) wanted to be a Marshal,
but he merely used grand words to show off to the court.
How could he possibly be willing to leave Xīchuān (西川)?
“To pardon him upon his request for punishment,
and to disband the various armies of the Two Rivers (Liǎnghé 兩河) to allow both public and private sectors to recuperate,
is also a secondary strategy.
If Shàochéng (少誠) one day commits crimes to the fullest and his wickedness ripens,
and he is killed by his subordinates,
then his titles and ranks would again have to be conferred upon them.
This would mean eliminating one Shàochéng (少誠)
only to create another Shàochéng (少誠),
causing endless trouble.”
Jiǎ Dān (賈耽) spoke to the Emperor, saying:
“The rebel's intention is probably to seek imperial grace and forgiveness;
it is likely necessary to open a path for his survival.”
The Emperor followed this advice.
It happened that Shàochéng (少誠) sent a letter and gifts to the supervising imperial army officials, requesting exoneration.
The supervising officials memorialized this.
*Wùzǐ* day:
An edict was issued pardoning Shàochéng (少誠) and the officers and soldiers of Zhāngyì (彰義),
restoring their official ranks and titles.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Shílù* (實錄) (Veritable Records) says:
“In the 9th month, *rén yín* day:
The Chancellors were having an audience in the Yányīng (延英) Hall.
Jiǎ Dān (賈耽) submitted: ‘Just yesterday, Hán Quányì (韓全義) retreated from Wǔlóu (五樓).
The reason the rebels dared not pursue him
must be that they hope for imperial grace and forgiveness.
It is likely necessary to open a path for their survival.’
The Emperor approved this.”
According to our investigation, Quányì (全義) retreated from Wǔlóu (五樓) to defend Yīnshuǐ (溵水).
Shàochéng (少誠) pressed upon Yīnshuǐ (溵水) and set up camp,
and Quányì (全義) again retreated to defend Chénzhōu (陳énzhōu) (陳州).
It was not that they dared not pursue!
It also states:
“The various armies attacked Cáizhōu (蔡州)
but never formed ranks for direct confrontation,
yet the imperial army was repeatedly defeated and routed.
Wú Shàochéng (吳少誠), knowing the imperial army was incapable,
sent a letter and gifts to inform the supervising officials
that he wished to seek exoneration.
The Emperor, having accepted Jiǎ Dān’s (賈耽) proposal,
and also receiving a favorable memorial from the supervising official,
then restored their official ranks and titles.”
According to our investigation, if Shàochéng (少誠) knew the imperial army was incapable,
he would have been even more aggressive in his incursions.
How could he have been willing to seek exoneration from the supervising official?
It is likely that since Shàochéng (少誠) raised his army,
he could not have been without weariness and exhaustion,
hence he sought a period of recuperation.
This is not adopted now.
23rd, *jǐchǒu* day:
Lǐ Yuè (李說), Military Governor (jiédùshǐ 節度使) of Hédōng (河東), died.
*Jiǎwǔ* day:
His Military Administrator (xíngjūnsīmǎ 行軍司馬) Zhèng Dàn (鄭儋) was appointed Military Governor (jiédùshǐ 節度使).
The Emperor sought someone who could replace Dàn (儋).
Yán Shòu (嚴綬), an Assistant Minister (yuánwàiláng 員外郎) of the Ministry of Punishments (xíngbù 刑部), had once offered tribute as a staff member (mùliáo 幕僚).
Regarding Yán Shòu’s (嚴綬) offering of tribute,
the matter is seen in the 12th year (of the reign).
The histories say that Dézōng (德宗) was fond of wealth,
and only remembered the names of those who offered tribute.
Military Administrator (xíngjūnsīmǎ 行軍司馬).
24th:
Tǔbō (吐蕃) was repeatedly defeated by Wéi Gāo (韋皋).
This year, their *nángòng* (曩貢) and *làchéng* (臘城) and other nine *jiédù* (節度) garrisons’ *yīnglóng guān* (嬰籠官) Mǎ Dìngdé (馬定德) led his tribe to surrender.
Dìngdé (定德) had wisdom and strategy.
When the various Tǔbō (吐蕃) generals campaigned,
they all submitted to his plans and schemes.
He often traveled by post to plan affairs.
By this time, due to repeated military disadvantages,
fearing punishment,
he came to defect.

According to the *Old History* (Jiù Shū 舊書), it says: The Tǔbō (吐蕃) chieftain and supervisor of the nine *jiédù* (節度) garrisons including *nángòng* (曩貢) and *làchéng* (臘城), Yīnglóng (嬰籠) Mǎ Dìngdé (馬定德), and his 87 great generals, brought their tribes to surrender.
Dìngdé (定德) had plans and strategies.
Yīnglóng (嬰籠) knew military strategy and the topography of mountains and rivers.
By this time, because his border achievements were not established,
he feared punishment and came to defect.
If this is the case,
then Yīnglóng (嬰籠) is a separate person,
and *yīnglóng guān* (嬰籠官) Mǎ Dìngdé (馬定德) is another person.
Upon consulting character dictionaries,
there is also no
character.
However, what is recorded in the *Tōngjiàn* (通鑑) entirely uses the text from Wéi Gāo’s (韋皋) biography in the *Old History* (Jiù Shū 舊書).
It is likely that Wéi Gāo’s (韋皋) biography and the Tǔbō (吐蕃) biography in the *Old History* (Jiù Shū 舊書) contradict each other.
“Shuài” (帥)
is pronounced “lǜ” (率).
Punctuation by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖), reviewed by Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
Compiled by imperial order by Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光).
Hòuxuétiāntái (後學天台).
17th year of Zhēnyuán (貞元) reign
(*xīnsì*, 801 CE)
1st: Spring,
1st month:
*Jiǎyín* day:
Hán Quányì (韓全義) arrived in Cháng’ān (長安).
Dòu Wénchǎng (竇文場) covered up his defeat,
and the Emperor treated him with great courtesy.
Quányì (全義) claimed to have a foot ailment
and was unable to attend court audiences.
He sent his Administrator (sīmǎ 司馬) Cuī Fàng (崔放) to have an audience.
Fàng (放) admitted Quányì’s (全義) faults
and apologized for his lack of achievement.
The Emperor said:
“Quányì (全義) served as the Commander-in-chief of the Expedition (zhāotǎoshǐ 招討使).
His ability to bring Shàochéng (少誠) to terms
is a great achievement.
Why must he kill people to be considered meritorious?”
Dézōng’s (德宗) ears and eyes were deafened and blinded by the eunuchs in this manner.
*Jiǎxū* day:
Returned to Xiàzhōu (夏州).
2nd:
Wéi Shìzōng (韋士宗) having entered Qiánzhōu (黔州) –
Last year Shìzōng (士宗) again entered Qiánzhōu (黔州), the matter is seen in the previous volume.
“Qián” (黔)
is pronounced *qú jīn* (渠今) according to the fanqie method,
and also *qí lián* (其廉) according to the fanqie method.
– the people’s hearts were greatly disturbed.
Shìzōng (士宗) feared,
so in the 3rd month,
he escaped and fled.
Summer,
4th month:
*Xīnhài* day:
Péi Jí (裴佶), Right Remonstrance Official (yòujiànyìdàfū 右諫議大夫), was appointed Surveillance Commissioner (guānchásǐ 觀察使) of Qiánzhōu (黔州).
3rd:
5th month, *rénxū* day, the first day of the month:
There was a solar eclipse.
4th:
Yáng Cháoshèng (楊朝晟), Military Governor (jiédùshǐ 節度使) of Shuòfāng Bīn, Níng, and Qìng (朔方邠寧慶) –
The Shuòfāng (朔方) forces were divided and stationed in Bīn (邠),
hence it was still prefixed with the Shuòfāng (朔方) army designation, but in reality, it only governed Bīn (邠), Níng (寧), and Qìng (慶) three prefectures.
– *yǐyóu* day:
Died.
Initially,
Hún Jiān (渾瑊) dispatched his Army Marshal (bīngmǎshǐ 兵馬使) Lǐ Cháocǎi (李朝寀) to lead troops to garrison Dìngpíng (定平).
In the 2nd year of Wǔdé (武德), Dìngpíng (定平) county was established by dividing Dìng’ān (定安) county of Níngzhōu (寧州), and it still belonged to Níngzhōu (寧州).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) states: It is 60 *lǐ* south of the prefecture.
“Cháo” (朝)
is pronounced *zhí yáo* (直遙) according to the fanqie method.
“Cǎi” (寀)
is pronounced *cāng zǎi* (倉宰) according to the fanqie method.
“Jiāng” (將)
is pronounced *jí liàng* (即亮) according to the fanqie method.
Cháocǎi (朝寀) requested that his troops be subordinated to the Shéncè (神策) Army.
An edict permitted it.
Yáng Cháoshèng (楊朝晟) was critically ill.
He summoned his subordinates and said,
"I, Cháoshèng (朝晟), will surely not recover.
The appointment of commanders in Shuòfāng (朔方) has often come from within the army itself.
Although this caters to popular sentiment,
it is truly not in line with national principles.
Liú Nánjīn (劉南金), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Níngzhōu (寧州),
is skilled in military affairs.
It would be appropriate to make him acting Jīnxíngjūn (攝行軍)
and interim Zhījūnshì (知軍事).
By the time the imperial court selects a commander,
there will surely be no cause for concern."
He also gave a handwritten letter to the Jiānjūn (監軍), Liú Yīngqiàn (劉英倩).
Yīngqiàn (英倩) reported it to the throne.
The soldiers privately discussed,
"If the imperial court appoints a commander,
we will accept him.
If Master Liú (劉) is appointed,
we will serve him.
If a commander is appointed from another army,
he will certainly bring his own subordinates,
and we will be dismissed.
We will surely resist him."
On the day Jǐchǒu (己丑),
the emperor dispatched a eunuch to investigate the military situation.
Many in the army favored Nánjīn (南金).
On the day Xīnmǎo (辛卯),
the emperor again dispatched Gāopǐn (高品) Xuē Yíngzhēn (薛盈珍) with an imperial edict to Níngzhōu (寧州).
The Táì (唐) Nèishìshěng (內侍省) had one thousand nine hundred and sixty-six Gāopǐn (高品).
pronounced *fú yòu fān (扶又翻)*.
On the day Jiǎwǔ (甲午),
Yíngzhēn (盈珍) arrived at the army
and proclaimed the edict:
"Lǐ Cháocǎi (李朝寀) currently commands the original Shuòfāng (朔方) army.
Now, this army will be merged with it
to strengthen its military might
and awe the Rong and Di (戎狄).
Lǐ Cháocǎi (李朝寀) is to be the commander,
with Nánjīn (南金) as his deputy.
What do the army generals think of this?"
All the generals submitted to the edict.
On the day Bǐngshēn (丙申),
the Dūyúhòu (都虞候), Shǐ Jīng (史經), said to the assembly,
"Master Lǐ (李) has ordered the collection of all bows and sabers and the delivery of two thousand sets of armor and helmets."
All the soldiers said,
"Master Lǐ (李) wishes to bring in two thousand of his own subordinates as his confidants.
Can our wives and children be safe then?"
At night,
they went to Liú Nánjīn (劉南金),
intending to enthrone him as commander.
Nánjīn (南金) said,
"A Jiédùshǐ (節度使) is indeed what I desire,
but it is not permissible without an imperial decree from the Son of Heaven.
Are there no other generals in the army?"
The assembly said,
"Our bows and sabers have all been collected by the government.
Only the Jūnshìfǔ (軍事府) still has armor and weapons.
The Jūnshìfǔ (軍事府)
is where the Zhījūnshì (知軍事) resides."
Nánjīn (南金) said,
"If you gentlemen do not wish for Cháocǎi (朝寀) to be commander,
you should report your sentiments to the imperial envoy.
If you brandish weapons,
that would be defying the imperial edict."
He ordered the gate closed and did not let them in.
The soldiers left
and went to the Bīngmǎshǐ (兵馬使), Gāo Gù (高固).
Gù (固) had fled and hidden.
They searched and found him.
Gù (固) said,
"Gentlemen, if you can follow my words, then it is acceptable."
The assembly said,
"Your command."
Gù (固) said,
"Do not kill anyone,
and do not plunder gold and silk."
The assembly said,
"Understood."
Then they all went to the Jiānjūn (監軍)
and requested to make a report.
The assembly said,
"Since Master Liú (劉) has received an imperial decree to be deputy commander,
he will certainly thwart our plans."
Falsely claiming it was the Jiānjūn's (監軍) order,
they summoned the Jìshì (計事),
and when he arrived, they killed him.
On the day Wùxū (戊戌),
an imperial decree appointed Lǐ Cháocǎi (李朝寀) as Bīnnìng Jiédùshǐ (邠寧節度使).
On that very day,
a messenger reporting the uprising in Níngzhōu (寧州) arrived.
The emperor recalled the imperial decree
and again dispatched Xuē Yíngzhēn (薛盈珍) to investigate the military situation.
On the day Rén'yín (壬寅),
he arrived at the army.
The army requested Gāo Gù (高固).
Yíngzhēn (盈珍) immediately, by imperial order, appointed Gù (固) as Zhījūnshì (知軍事).
Someone spread word that the Wùxū (戊戌) imperial decree had reached Bīnzhōu (邠州).
The Bīn (邠) army was confused
and did not know what to follow.
Xuē Yíngzhēn (薛盈zhen) had already appointed Gāo Gù (高固) as Zhījūnshì (知軍事) of Níngzhōu (寧州),
but then there was also a report that Lǐ Cháocǎi's (李朝寀) imperial decree had reached Bīn (邠).
Therefore, the army stationed in Bīn (邠) was confused and did not know what to do.
They were also on the verge of revolt.
Liúhòu (留後) Mèng Zǐzhōu (孟子周) secretly moved elite troops into the government compound,
feasting the soldiers daily,
internally to win over the hearts of the people,
and externally to intimidate the rebellious faction.
The Bīn (邠) army did not revolt;
this was due to Zǐzhōu's (子周) strategy.
5 Lǐ Qí (李錡) had seized control of the nation's financial power.
(In the fifteenth year, Lǐ Qí (李錡) served as the Salt and Iron Transportation Commissioner for all circuits.
Details are in the previous volume.)
He used bribes to win over powerful officials,
relying on this to become arrogant and unrestrained,
with no scruples.
He embezzled government funds,
and officials under his jurisdiction were successively punished without cause.
Cuī Shànzhēn (崔善貞), a commoner from Zhèxī (浙西), went to the imperial court to present a memorial,
speaking of the abuses of palace markets, imperial tributes, and salt and iron monopolies,
and thus mentioning Qí's (錡) unlawful acts.
The emperor read it
and was displeased.
He ordered Shànzhēn (善貞) to be chained and sent to Qí (錡).
Qí (錡), hearing that he was about to arrive,
first dug a pit by the roadside.
On the day Jǐhài (己亥),
Shànzhēn (善貞) arrived,
and he was thrown into the pit, still in chains,
and buried alive.
Those near and far who heard of it shuddered without cold.
Qí (錡) then sought to ensure his own safety,
increasing the size of his army.
He selected strong and skilled archers, calling them *Wǎnqiáng* (挽強),
meaning they had the strength to draw a strong bow.
(Dù Fǔ's (杜甫) poem:
"To draw a bow, one must draw a strong one.")
Hu (胡) and Xī (奚) captives who had been assigned to Jiāngnán (江南)
were taken in and supported by Qí (錡).
Zhuǎnyùn Pànguān (轉運判官) Lú Tǎn (盧坦) repeatedly remonstrated but Qí (錡) did not change,
so Lú Tǎn (盧坦) and his staff members, Lǐ Yuē (李約) and others, all left.
(Yuē (約)
was Mǐan's (勉) son.
Lǐ Mǐan (李勉) served during the reigns of Sù (肅), Dài (代), and Dé (德) three emperors,
and was prime minister during the Zhēnyuán (貞元) era.)
6 On the day Jǐyǒu (己酉),
Gāo Gù (高固) was appointed Bīnnìng Jiédùshǐ (邠寧節度使).
Gù (固)
was a veteran general
who had won the loyalty of the masses through his magnanimity.
The Jiédùshǐ (節度使) was jealous of him
and relegated him to an inactive position,
where many of his peers slighted and insulted him.
When he was appointed commander,
he took no revenge on anyone,
and the army subsequently became stable.
7 On the day Dīngsì (丁巳),
the Chéngdé Jiédùshǐ (成德節度使), Wáng Wǔjùn (王武俊), passed away.
8 Autumn,
seventh month,
on the day Wùyín (戊寅),
the Tubo (吐蕃) raided Yánzhōu (鹽州).
9 On the day Xīnsì (辛巳),
Wáng Shìzhēn (王士真), the Chéngdé Jiédù Fùshǐ (成德節度副使), was appointed Jiédùshǐ (節度使).
10On the day Jǐchǒu (己丑),
the Tubo (吐蕃) captured Línzhōu (麟州),
killed the Cìshǐ (刺史) Guō Fēng (郭鋒),
razed its walls and fortifications,
and plundered its inhabitants and Dangxiang (党項) tribes before departing.
(Fēng (鋒)
was Yào's (曜) son.
Yào (曜)
was Guō Zǐyí's (郭子儀) son.)
The monk Yán Sù (延素) was captured by the barbarians.
A barbarian general, Xú Shèrén (徐舍人),
said to Yán Sù (延素),
"I am the fifth-generation descendant of Yīnggōng (英公).
(Lǐ Jì (李勣)
was enfeoffed as Yīngguógōng (英國公).)
My great-great-grandfather's attempt to rise in revolt failed,
(referring to Jìngyè (敬業).
Details are in volume 202, Empress Wǔ's Guāngzhái (光宅) first year.)
Although my family has held official positions and commanded troops for generations,
the desire to restore our origins has never been forgotten.
However, our clan is large,
and there was no way for us to extricate ourselves.
Now I will let you return."
Thereupon, he released him.
The emperor sent an envoy to issue an edict to Wéi Gāo (韋皋), ordering him to lead troops deep into Tǔbō (吐蕃) territory to divide their forces
and relieve the northern frontier's woes.
Shū (紓) means
to relieve.
(Wéi Gāo) attacked Tǔbō's Wéi (維), Bǎo (保), and Sōng (松) prefectures, as well as Qī Jī (棲雞) and Lǎo Wēng (老翁) cities.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Bǎo Zhōu (保州) was originally Dìng Lián (定廉) County of Wéi Zhōu (維州).
It bordered Tǔbō (吐蕃) to the south,
and was the outermost frontier against the barbarians.
In the 28th year of Kāiyuán (開元) (740 CE),
the Qiāng (羌) barbarians pledged allegiance, and Fèng Zhōu (奉州) was established.
In Tiānbǎo (天寶) (742-756 CE), it was renamed Yúnshān (雲山) Commandery.
In the 8th year (749 CE),
its administration was moved to Tiānbǎo (天保) Military Command,
and it was renamed Tiānbǎo (天保) Commandery.
It was soon lost,
but in the 1st year of Qiányuán (乾元) (758 CE), it pledged allegiance again,
and was then renamed Bǎo Zhōu (保州).
According to the biography of Wáng Yá (王涯): "The Wēi Fān (威蕃) palisade of Mián Zhōu (綿州) extended west to Qī Jī (棲雞) City."
This was likely in Mào Zhōu (茂州) territory.
Zhèng Dān (鄭儋), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hédōng (河東), died suddenly,
without making arrangements for his successor.
The army was in an uproar,
and other disturbances were imminent.
In the middle of the night,
more than ten horsemen, armed, summoned the administrator and scribe Línghú Chǔ (令狐楚) to the military gate.
The generals surrounded him,
and made him draft a posthumous memorial.
Chǔ (楚), amidst drawn swords,
took up a brush and completed it immediately.
Chǔ (楚) was a member
of Dé Fēn's (德棻) clan.
Línghú Dé Fēn (令狐德棻) served Tàizōng (太宗).
It is suspected
that after the character "zú" (族) [clan],
there were characters like
"sūn" (孫) [grandson]
and
"zēng, xuán" (曾、玄) [great-grandson, great-great-grandson].
Fēn (棻) is pronounced "fú wén fān".
On Wùwǔ (戊午) day,
Yán Shòu (嚴綬), the Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬) of Hédōng (河東), was appointed Jìedùshǐ (節度使).
In the 9th month,
Wéi Gāo (韋皋) reported a major victory over Tǔbō (吐蕃) in Yǎ Zhōu (雅州).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Yǎ Zhōu (雅州) was the territory of Yán Dào (嚴道) County during the Qín (秦) dynasty.
The Later Wèi (後魏) established Měngshān (蒙山) Commandery,
and the Táng (唐) established Yǎ Zhōu (雅州).
According to the "Jùn Guó Zhì" (郡國志),
Hàngyuán (漢源) County has Lí Shān (離山),
which was excavated by Lǐ Bīng (李冰), the administrator of Shǔ (蜀).
Lí (離) is the ancient character for Yǎ (雅).
The prefecture was named after this.
The old gazetteer states: Yǎ Zhōu (雅州) is 2,723 *lǐ* (里) southwest of the capital.
Dòu Wénchǎng (竇文場), the Zuǒ Shéncè Zhōngwèi (左神策中尉), retired.
Yáng Zhìlián (楊志廉), the deputy envoy, replaced him.
Wéi Gāo (韋皋) repeatedly defeated Tǔbō (吐蕃),
fighting and moving a thousand *lǐ*.
He captured seven cities,
five military towns,
burned 150 fortresses,
beheaded over 10,000 enemies,
captured 6,000 prisoners,
and received the surrender of 3,000 households.
He then besieged Wéi Zhōu (維州) and Kūnmíng (昆明) City.
In winter,
10th month,
on Gēngzǐ (庚子) day,
Gāo (皋) was granted the additional titles of Jiǎnjiào Sītú (檢校司徒) and Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令),
and bestowed the title of Nánkāng Jùnwáng (南康郡王).
Nánzhāo (南詔) King Yìmóxún (異牟尋) captured an especially large number of enemies.
The emperor sent an imperial envoy to comfort and appease him.
On Wùwǔ (戊午) day,
Dù Yànxiān (杜彥先), the Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Yán Zhōu (鹽州), abandoned the city and fled to Qìng Zhōu (慶州).
He was pressured by Tǔbō (吐蕃).
Yán Zhōu (鹽州) had only been fortified for eight years by this time.
In spring,
1st month,
King Móluósīnnà (摩羅思那) of Biāo (驃) sent his son Xīlìyí (悉利移) to offer tribute.
The kingdom of Biāo (驃) was 6,800 *lǐ* (里) southwest of Nánzhāo (南詔).
The Xīn Shū (新書) states: Biāo (驃) was ancient Zhūbō (朱波),
2,000 *lǐ* (里) south of Yǒngchāng (永昌),
and 14,000 *lǐ* (里) from the capital.
Biāo (驃) is pronounced "pí zhào fān".
(He) came to audience via Nánzhāo (南詔),
and also presented their music.
Tǔbō (吐蕃) sent their Grand Minister and Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of the Five Eastern Frontier Roads, Lùn Mǎng Rè (論莽熱), to lead 100,000 troops to relieve the siege of Wéi Zhōu (維州).
The Xīchuān (西川) forces occupied strategic heights and set up ambushes to await them.
When Tǔbō (吐蕃) arrived,
they sent a thousand men to challenge.
The barbarians (Tǔbō) pursued them with all their forces.
The ambush was sprung,
and the barbarian forces were greatly defeated.
Lùn Mǎng Rè (論莽熱) was captured,
and more than half of their soldiers died.
Wéi Zhōu (維州) and Kūnmíng (昆明) ultimately did not fall, and (Wéi Gāo's) troops returned.
On Yǐhài (乙亥) day,
Gāo (皋) sent an envoy to present Lùn Mǎng Rè (論莽熱).
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: "The old biography of Wéi Gāo (韋皋) says,
'In the 10th month, an envoy was sent to present Lùn Mǎng Rè (論莽熱).'
Now we follow the Shílù (實錄)."
Péi Sù (裴肅), the Zhédōng Guānchásǐ (浙東觀察使), had already been promoted due to his tribute offerings.
Péi Sù (裴肅) gained a high office (liánchē) through presenting tribute;
the matter is found in Volume 12 of the previous scroll.
Guān Qí Zǒng (官齊總) temporarily managed affairs after him.
According to the Xīn Táng Shū (新唐書): "Sù (肅) died in office.
Qí Zǒng (齊總) temporarily managed affairs after him."
In the 3rd month,
on Guǐyǒu (癸酉) day,
an imperial edict promoted Zǒng (總) to Qú Zhōu Cǐshǐ (衢州刺史).
Xǔ Mèngrǒng (許孟容) of Cháng'ān (長安), a Jǐshìzhōng (給事中), sealed and returned the edict,
saying:
"Qú Zhōu (衢州) has no particular worries,
and Qí Zǒng (齊總) has no outstanding merits.
This sudden extraordinary promotion
deeply alarms public sentiment.
If Zǒng (總) truly has something worthy of record,
I wish that his merits and achievements be clearly documented,
and then he may be promoted and his office changed,
to dispel public doubt."
The edict was then kept in the imperial archives.
On Jǐhài (己亥) day,
the emperor summoned Mèngrǒng (孟容)
and offered him comfort and praise.
In autumn,
7th month,
on Xīnwèi (辛未) day,
Gāo Hóngběn (高弘本), an adviser to Jiā Wáng (嘉王), presented a memorial at the regular court audience.
Jiā Wáng Yùn (嘉王運) was the son of Dàizōng (代宗).
The Zīyì Cānjūn (諮議參軍) was a senior fifth-rank official,
responsible for strategy and deliberation.
According to the Táng (唐) system, the Hányuán (含元) Hall was the main audience hall in the eastern palace,
and the Tàijí (太極) Hall in the western palace.
The Táng (唐) system: "the emperor's residence is called *yá* (衙),
his procession is called *jià* (駕)."
*Yá* (牙) is the same as *yá* (衙).
Bū (逋) means "owing."
On Yǐhài (乙亥) day,
an imperial edict stated:
"From now on, dukes, ministers, and all officials are not to present memorials at the regular court audience.
If there are any presentations,
they should request an audience at the Yányīng (延英) Gate."
Commentators believed:
"Presenting memorials at the regular court audience
has not changed since Wǔdé (武德) (618-626 CE).
This is how public sentiment is conveyed and political affairs are discussed.
Hóngběn (弘本) was ignorant,
and demoting him is acceptable,
but one should not abolish a practice because of a person."
Dù Yòu (杜佑), the Huáinán Jìedùshǐ (淮南節度使), repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to be replaced.
In winter,
10th month,
on Dīnghài (丁亥) day,
Wáng È (王鍔), the Xíngbù Shàngshū (刑部尚書), was appointed Deputy Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Huáinán (淮南) and concurrently Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬).
On Jǐyǒu (己酉) day,
Wáng Qīyào (王栖曜), the Fūfāng Jìedùshǐ (鄜坊節度使), passed away.
Hé Cháozōng (何朝宗), a general of the central army, plotted rebellion.
At night,
he set fires.
Péi Bīn (裴玢), the Dōuyúhòu (都虞候), secretly hid and did not extinguish the fire.
At dawn,
Cháozōng (朝宗) was captured
and executed.
Liú Gōngjì (劉公濟), the Tóng Zhōu Cǐshǐ (同州刺史), was appointed Fūfāng Jìedùshǐ (鄜坊節度使),
and Bīn (玢) was appointed Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬).
In spring,
2nd month,
on Dīnghài (丁亥) day,
Ānhuáng Jūn (安黃軍) was renamed Fèngyì (奉義).
This was to honor Yī Shèn (伊慎).
On Jǐhài (己亥) day,

The next day,
he was carried home and did not emerge.
On the day *jǐchǒu*,
Chén Jiàn, *Cāngbù Lángzhōng* and *Pàndùzhī Àn*, was made *Hézhōng Shàoyǐn*.
In the Táng dynasty, each metropolitan prefecture had one *Yǐn*;
two *Shàoyǐn*,
of rank four, lower grade,
in charge of assisting the prefectural government.
At the end of the year, they would take turns to report accounts.
On the 26th day, *guǐsì*,
Chéng Huáixìn, *Hénghǎi Jūn Jiédùshǐ*, passed away.
His son, Deputy Commander Zhígōng, was made acting commander.
*Kǎoyì* states: The old tradition says:
"When Chéng Huáixìn died,
Huáizhí's son, Zhígōng, took charge as acting commander,
then sent Huáizhí back to Cāngzhōu,
where he died sixteen years later.
Zhígōng succeeded to his father's position,
and the imperial court consequently conferred it upon him."
However, Huáixìn had driven out Huáizhí and usurped his position,
so how could he possibly let Huáizhí's son act as commander?
Furthermore, Dèzōng's Veritable Records contain no mention of this matter,
nor does the abridged version of Shùnzōng's Veritable Records.
It is likely that the old tradition is mistaken.
Only the detailed version states:
"On the day *guǐsì* in the seventh month of the first year of Yǒngzhēn,
Chéng Huáixìn, *Hénghǎi Jūn Jiédùshǐ*, died.
His son, Deputy Commander Zhígōng, was made *Hénghǎi Jūn Jiédùshǐ*."
Lù Suí's Veritable Records of Xiànzōng state:
"On the day *bǐngzǐ* in the fifth month of the first year of Yuánhé,
Chéng Zhígōng, acting commander of Hénghǎi, was made *Jiédùshǐ*."
It is probable that the character
"acting commander" (*liúhòu*)
in the Shùnzōng records
was mistaken for
"commander" (*shǐ*)
only.
On the 27th day, *yǐwèi*,
an edict stated: "As the cumulative illness has not yet recovered,
all military and national affairs
shall temporarily be handled by Crown Prince Chún."
At that time, everyone, both inside and outside the court, resented the Wáng Shūwén faction for its monopolistic power,
and the Emperor also disliked them.
Jù Wénzhēn repeatedly petitioned the Emperor to let the Crown Prince supervise the state.
The Emperor was indeed weary of the myriad affairs of state,
and so agreed.
Dù Huángshang, *Tàicháng Qīng*, was also made *Ménxià Shìláng*,
and Yuán Zī, *Zuǒ Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn*, was made *Zhōngshū Shìláng*,
both concurrently *Píngzhāngshì*.
Jù Wénzhēn and others appointed them because they were old officials.
Dù Huángshang had already assisted the Shuòfāng Army during Dàizōng's reign,
and Yuán Zī was already positioned at court in the early Jiànzhōng period,
hence they were considered old officials.
Gāo Yǐng was made *Xíngbù Shàngshū*,
and both were dismissed from political affairs.
The Crown Prince met the hundred officials in the East Audience Hall.
According to *Táng Liùdiǎn*: The Dàmíng Palace's Hányuán Hall had two adjacent pavilions:
the left was called Xiángluán,
and below Xiángluán Pavilion was the East Audience Hall;
the right was called Qīfèng,
and below Qīfèng Pavilion was the West Audience Hall.
"Cháo",
pronounced *zhí yáo fān*.
The Crown Prince wept,
and did not return the bow.
In the eighth month,
on the day *gēngzǐ*,
an edict stated:
"Let the Crown Prince immediately ascend to the imperial throne;
I shall be called *Tàishàng Huáng*.
Imperial edicts and decrees shall be called *gào*."
On the day *xīnchǒu*,
the *Tàishàng Huáng* moved to the Xīngqìng Palace.
A *gào* changed the era name to Yǒngzhēn.
Consort Wáng, *Liángdì*, was established as *Tàishàng Huánghòu*.
This empress
was the mother of Xiànzōng.
On the day *rènyín*,
Wáng Pī was demoted to *Kāizhōu Sīmǎ*,
and Wáng Shūwén to *Yúzhōu Sīhù*.
Old records state: Kāizhōu
is 1,460 *lǐ* south of the capital.
Yúzhōu
is 2,748 *lǐ* southwest of the capital.
The next year,
Wáng Shūwén was granted death.
On the day *yǐsì*,
Xiànzōng ascended the throne in Xuānzhèng Hall.
Dèzōng's grand funeral was in progress,
and the *Shàng Huáng* was in Xīngqìng Palace,
so he dared not ascend the throne in the front hall.
On the 28th day, *bǐngwǔ*,
Princess Shēngpíng offered fifty female servants.
The princess
was the mother of Guō.
"The *Shàng Huáng* did not accept offerings,
how dare I violate that!"
So he refused them.
On the day *gēngxū*,
Jīngnán offered two hairy turtles.
The Emperor said:
"What I value most are the worthy.
Auspicious grains and divine *zhī* (lingzhi mushrooms)
are all empty commendations.
That is why the *Chūnqiū* does not record auspicious omens.
From now on, whenever there are auspicious signs,
simply report them to the relevant authorities as per regulations.
The Ministry of Rites is in charge of auspicious omens.
And rare birds and strange beasts
are all not to be offered."
On the 29th day, *guǐchǒu*,
Wéi Gāo, *Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ* and Prince Zhōngwǔ of Nánkāng, passed away.
Gāo was in Shǔ for twenty-one years.
In the first year of Zhēnyuán of Dèzōng,
Wéi Gāo replaced Zhāng Yánshǎng as governor of Shǔ.
He made generous tribute to secure imperial favor,
and gave ample rewards to pacify the soldiers.
For the marriages, deaths, and funerals of soldiers,
he provided all expenses.
Because of this, he was able to maintain his position for a long time, and the soldiers were happy to serve him.
He subdued Nánzhào
and crushed the Tǔbō.
Those staff officers who had served for many years and held high positions became *cǐshǐ*.
They would return to the secretariat afterward,
but were never allowed to return to court,
presumably for fear of revealing his methods.
Once the treasury was full,
he would periodically ease the burden on his people,
reducing rents and taxes once every three years.
The people of Shǔ admired his wisdom and strategy, and feared his authority.
Even today, his portrait is drawn and worshipped as a local deity
by every household.
Liú Pì, *Zhīdù Fùshǐ*, appointed himself acting commander.
On the 30th day, the rivers in Wǔlíng and Lóngyáng in Lǎngzhōu overflowed,
sweeping away more than ten thousand households.
Wǔlíng was the territory of Línchuán County in the Hàn dynasty.
During the Suí dynasty, Línchuán was abolished
and Wǔlíng County was established.
In the Táng dynasty, it was subordinate to Lǎngzhōu.
Lóngyáng County
was established by the Wú.
*Jiǔyù Zhì* states: it is eighty *lǐ* southeast of the prefecture.
On the 31st day, *rénwǔ*,
Yī Shèn, *Fèngyì Jiédùshǐ*, came to court.
He came to court from Ānzhōu.
On the 32nd day, *xīnmǎo*,
Hán Quányì, *Xiàsuí Jiédùshǐ*, came to court.
Quányì had been defeated at the Yīnshuǐ River and returned,
not coming for an audience but leaving.
This matter is discussed in the preceding volumes, Zhēnyuán 16th and 17th years.
Hearing of this, the Emperor disliked him.
Quányì, fearing,
then requested to come to court.
On the 33rd day, Liú Pì had his generals submit memorials requesting a *jiéyuè*.
The imperial court did not permit it.
On the day *jǐwèi*,
Yuán Zī was made *Jiànnán Dōng-Xīchuān, Shānnán Xīdào Ānfǔ Dàshǐ*.
On the 34th day, the Ministry of Finance reported that the separate treasuries established by Péi Yánlíng
had all stored items by reducing what was in the main treasury.
It requested they all be returned to the main treasury,
which was granted.
35th day of the Xīnyǒu cycle (day 58 of the sexagenary cycle),
Pān Mèngyáng, Vice Commissioner for Finance, Salt and Iron, and Transport, was dispatched to tour Jiāng and Huái,
inspect the advantages and disadvantages of land tax and monopoly taxes,
and incidentally observe the integrity of officials,
and the sufferings of the common people.
36th day of the Guǐhài cycle (day 60),
Zhèng Yúqìng, Left Censor of the Department of State Affairs, was made Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
37th day of the ninth month,
Wùchén cycle (day 5),
the Commissioner of Rites submitted a memorial, stating:
"The Great Empress Dowager Zēng, née Shěn, is now very old,
and all hope of finding her is gone.
The matter of searching for her was first mentioned in volume 226, during the first year of Dēzōng's Jiànzhōng era.
After three years of searching,
one should wear mourning until the 'middle lifespan' is reached.
Xún Zǔ of Jìn said:
'If one's parents are lost and there is no hope whatsoever,
then mourning should be observed according to the imperial law and customary practice.'
Yǔ Wèizhī said:
'If one's parents were captured by barbarians,
and their survival is unknown,
then every effort should be made to find them.
If the search proves fruitless,
then after three years, it is advisable to marry and take up official posts,
as the lineage must not be broken
and the royal administration cannot be suspended.
However, one should still live in sorrow and simplicity,
not participate in auspicious celebrations,
and wear mourning until the 'middle lifespan' is reached.
If there is rebellion within the realm,
and after pacification and amnesty,
no trace of them can be found,
then it is advisable to establish a mourning period.'
Zhuāngzǐ said: 'Human life has an 'upper lifespan' of one hundred years,
a 'middle lifespan' of eighty,
and a 'lower lifespan' of sixty.'
Wèi
is pronounced 'yú wù fān'.
The Lǐ Jì's Tán Gōng states: 'For the emperor's funeral rites,
a conical mound covers the dragon-drawn carriage,
with an outer coffin,
an axe placed on top of the outer coffin,
and the entire structure covered like a house.'
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states: 'For the emperor's funeral,
the coffin is placed in a dragon-drawn carriage,
with piled wood
and a themed enclosure resembling an outer coffin,
covered like a four-sided roof.
It is completely sealed,
and opened at the time of burial.'
Zǎn
is pronounced 'cái guān fān'.
Therefore, that day should be observed as a day of taboo."
This was adopted.
38th day of the Rénshēn cycle (day 9),
Wéi Zhíyì, Supervisor of the National Histories, memorialized,
proposing that historians begin compiling daily records.
Yè Bóyì said: "In the early Yǒngzhēn era of Táng,
Wéi Zhíyì memorialized:
'Compiling private records is incorrect.
It is requested that each compile a daily record,
and at the end of the month, the academy will finalize it.'
This was adopted.
This is the origin of the daily records."
39th day of the Jǐmǎo cycle (day 16),
Hán Tài, Shencè Staff Officer, was demoted to Inspector of Fǔzhōu;
Hán Yè, Director of the Bureau of Taxation, to Inspector of Chízhōu;
Liǔ Zōngyuán, Assistant Director of the Bureau of Rites, to Inspector of Shàozhōu;
and Liú Yǔxī, Assistant Director of the Bureau of Military Farms, to Inspector of Liánzhōu.
All were partisans of Wáng Pī and Wáng Shūwén.
The old gazetteer states: Fǔzhōu
is 3,312 lǐ southeast of the capital.
Liánzhōu
is 3,665 lǐ south of the capital.
40th day of the winter,
tenth month,
Dīngyǒu cycle (day 34),
Jiǎ Dān, Right Grandee Secretary and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì, died.
41st day of the Wùxū cycle (day 35),
Yuán Zī, Central Secretariat Secretary and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì, was reappointed Tóng Píngzhāng Shì
and made Military Commissioner of Xīchuān;
Liú Pì was summoned to serve as Gěishìzhōng.
42nd Shū Wáng Yì died.
43rd The Grand Minister of Ceremonies deliberated on the posthumous title for the Great Empress Dowager Zēng, suggesting Ruìzhēn Empress.
44th The recluse Luó Lìngzé traveled from Cháng'ān to Pǔrùn,
falsely claiming to have an imperial edict from the Supreme Emperor,
and raised troops from Liú Yǒng, Inspector of Qínzhōu,
and moreover persuaded Yǒng to depose and install a new emperor;
Yǒng arrested him and sent him to Cháng'ān,
where he and his followers were beaten to death.
45th day of the Jǐyǒu cycle (day 46),
the Divine Martial and Filial Emperor Wén was buried in the Chónglíng Mausoleum.
The New History's Imperial Annals records "Divine Martial and Sagely Emperor Wén,"
which should be followed.
Chónglíng is on Cuó'é Mountain,
fifteen lǐ north of Yúnyáng County, Jīngzhào.
46th day of the eleventh month,
Jǐsì cycle (day 6),
the spirit tablets of Empress Ruìzhēn and Emperor Dēzōng were enshrined in the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
Dù Huángcháng and other ritual officials deliberated,
believing:
"The state's system follows that of Zhōu.
Tàizǔ is like Hòujì,
Gāozǔ is like King Wén,
and Tàizōng is like King Wǔ;
none of them are moved.
Gāozōng is beyond the three zhāo and three mù (cycles of ancestral tablets);
we request that his tablet be moved to the west side chamber."
This was adopted.
47th day of the Rénshēn cycle (day 9),
Wéi Zhíyì, Central Secretariat Secretary and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì, was demoted to Judicial Administrator of Yázhōu.
Zhíyì had previously differed with Wáng Shūwén,
and was also Dù Huángcháng's son-in-law,
so his demotion was delayed.
However, when Shūwén was defeated,
Zhíyì also lost his position and influence,
knowing disaster was coming.
Though he was still a chancellor,
he was never at ease,
listless and without spirit.
Upon hearing footsteps,
he would become terrified and change color,
until his demotion.
48th day of the Wùyín cycle (day 15),
Hán Quányì was made Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and retired from office.
49th Liú Pì refused the summons,
blockaded his territory, and defended himself;
Yuán Zī feared his strength
and dared not advance.
The emperor was angered
and demoted Zī to Inspector of Jízhōu.
50th Wǔ Yuánhéng, Right Grand Master of the Household, was reinstated as Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
In the third month of this year,
Wǔ Yuánhéng was demoted from Imperial Censor-in-Chief to Right Grand Master of the Household;
Wáng Shūwén and others had disliked him.
51st The court deliberated that some partisans of Wáng Shūwén, having been appointed inspectors from assistant director positions,
were demoted too lightly;
Jǐmǎo cycle (day 16),
Hán Tài was again demoted to Judicial Administrator of Qiánzhōu,
Hán Yè to Judicial Administrator of Ráozhōu,
Liǔ Zōngyuán to Judicial Administrator of Yǒngzhōu,
Liú Yǔxī to Judicial Administrator of Lǎngzhōu;
The old gazetteer states: Qiánzhōu
is 4,017 lǐ southeast of the capital;
Ráozhōu
is 3,263 lǐ.
Yǒngzhōu
is 3,274 lǐ south of the capital;
Lǎngzhōu
is 2,159 lǐ.
Líng Zhǔn, Inspector of Hézhōu, was made Judicial Administrator of Liánzhōu;
Chéng [AS-82FA], Inspector of Yuèzhōu, was made Judicial Administrator of Chénzhōu.
Táizhōu
is 4,177 lǐ southeast of the capital;
Hézhōu
is 2,683 lǐ;
Yuèzhōu
is 2,237 lǐ.
52nd Huáixìn Kèhán of the Huíhú died,
and Sūn Gǎo, Junior Minister of the Court of Diplomatic Reception, was dispatched to mourn him,
and enfeoff his successor as Ténglǐyěhéjùlù Pígē Kèhán.
Since Huáixìn's ascension,
the Yàogēluó clan of the Huíhú had ended.
After this, historical records consistently mention enfeoffing his successor,
to indicate the descendants of Huáixìn.
53rd day of the twelfth month,
Jiǎchén cycle (day 41),
Yú Dí, Military Commissioner of Shānnán Dōngdào, was granted the title of Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
54th Yī Shèn, Military Commissioner of Fèngyì, was made Right Grandee Secretary.
55th day of the Jǐyǒu cycle (day 46),
Liú Pì, Gěishìzhōng, was made Vice Military Commissioner of Xīchuān, in charge of military affairs.

The Xīchuān Military Commissioner governed the prefectures of Yì, Péng, Shǔ, Hàn, Méi, Jiā, Zī, Jiǎn, Wéi, Mào, Lí, Yǎ, Sōng, Fú, Wén, Lóng, Róng, Yì, Qióng, Cuì, Yáo, Zhè, Gōng, Dāng, Xī, Fèng, Dié, Jìng, etc.,
with his seat in Chéngdū.
However, many of the western prefectures had already fallen to foreign territories.
This was because the military power was not yet capable of suppressing them.
Wéi Dān, Right Remonstrance Official, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"If Pì is released and not punished now,
then the court can only rely on the two capitals for direct command.
Beyond that, who would not rebel?"
The emperor approved of his words.
Rénzǐ cycle (day 49),
Dān was made Military Commissioner of Dōngchuān.
Dān was the fifth-generation descendant of Jīn.
Jīn was the son of Wéi Xiàokuān.
56th day of the Xīnyǒu cycle (day 58),
all officials requested to bestow the honorary title "Yìngqián Shèngshòu Tàishàng Huáng" upon the Supreme Emperor;
and to bestow the honorary title "Wénwǔ Dàshèng Xiàodé Huángdì" upon the present emperor.
The emperor agreed to bestow the Supreme Emperor's honorary title but declined to accept one for himself.
57th day of the Rénxū cycle (day 59),
Zhèng Yīn, Academician of the Hanlin Academy, was made Central Secretariat Secretary and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
58. Dù Jiān [杜兼], a secretary in the Ministry of Justice, was appointed Prefect of Sūzhōu [蘇州].
When Dù Jiān took his leave,
he submitted a memorial saying that Lǐ Qí [李錡] was about to rebel
and would surely play havoc with his clan and ministers.
The emperor agreed with him,
and kept him as a secretary in the Ministry of Personnel.
Punctuation by Róng Zhàozǔ [容肇祖], reviewed by Niè Chóngqí [聶崇岐].
Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng [司馬光]
by imperial decree.
Posterior
Emperor Xiànzōng [憲宗], Zhaowén Zhāngwǔ Dàshèng Zhìshén Xiào Huángdì [昭文章武大聖至神孝皇帝], first part of the first volume.
His personal name was Chún [淳],
later changed to Chún [純].
He was the eldest son of Emperor Shùnzōng [順宗].
In the *Zīzhì Tōngjiàn* [資治通鑑], the posthumous titles of Tang emperors,
from Emperor Xuánzōng [玄宗] onwards,
are all based on the titles conferred at their burial sites and in their imperial edicts.
The emperor's original posthumous title was Shèngshén Zhāngwǔ Xiào Huángdì [聖神章武孝皇帝].
In the third year of Dàzhōng [大中] (849), after the pacification of Héhuáng [河湟],
the reverent posthumous title Zhaowén Zhāngwǔ Dàshèng Zhìshén Xiào Huángdì [昭文章武大聖至神孝皇帝] was first bestowed.
After Zhōngzōng [中宗] and Ruìzōng [睿宗],
only Shùnzōng [順宗], Xiànzōng [憲宗], and Xuānzōng [宣宗] had reverent posthumous titles.
Therefore, they are recorded as such.
The first year of Yuánhé [元和]
(Bǐngxū [丙戌], 806)
1. Spring,
first month.
On the *bǐngyín* [丙寅] day, the first day of the month,
the emperor led his officials to Xīngqìng Gōng [興慶宮] to confer the honorary title on the Retired Emperor.
This was done at the request of all the officials.
The character "帥"
is pronounced "shuài".
The character "上"
is pronounced "shàng" [時掌翻].
2. On the *dīngmǎo* [丁卯] day,
there was a general amnesty,
and the era name was changed.
3. On the *xīnwèi* [辛未] day,
Hán Gāo [韓皋], the Surveillance Commissioner of È'yuè [鄂岳], was appointed Military Governor of Fèngyì [奉義].
In the nineteenth year of Zhēnyuán [貞元] (803) of Emperor Dézōng [德宗], the Ānhuáng [安黃] army was named Fèngyì [奉義]. On the *guǐyǒu* [癸酉] day,
Yī Yòu [伊宥], the Acting Military Governor of Fèngyì [奉義], was appointed Prefect of Ānzhōu [安州] and Acting Prefect of Ānzhōu [安州].
Yī Yòu [伊宥]
was the son of Shèn [慎]. On the *rénwǔ* [壬午] day,
Wáng Shìzhēn [王士真], the Military Governor of Chéngdé [成德], was given the additional title of *Tóng Píngzhāngshì* [同平章事].
4. On the *jiǎshēn* [甲申] day,
the Retired Emperor passed away at Xīngqìng Gōng [興慶宮].
He was forty-six years old.
5. Liú Pì [劉闢], having obtained the *jīngjié* [旌節] (insignia of military authority),
last year, Pì [闢] was appointed acting Military Governor of Xīchuān [西川],
as mentioned in the previous volume.
He sought to concurrently govern the three Chuān [川] regions,
but the emperor did not permit it.
Pì [闢] then dispatched troops to besiege Lǐ Kāng [李康], the Military Governor of Dōngchuān [東川], at Zǐzhōu [梓州].
The Military Governor of Dōngchuān [東川]
governed Zǐ, Jiàn, Mián, Pǔ, Líng, Róng, Suì, Hé, Yú, Lú [梓、劍、綿、普、陵、榮、遂、合、渝、瀘] and other prefectures,
with its seat in Zǐzhōu [梓州].
Zǐzhōu [梓州]
was formerly the territory of Qī Xiàn [郪縣] in the Hàn [漢] dynasty.
Liú Shàn [劉禪] established the Dōngguǎnghàn [東廣漢] Commandery.
Liáng Wǔlíng Wáng Jì [梁武陵王紀] established Xīnzhōu [新州].
During the Suí [隋] dynasty, it became Zǐzhōu [梓州].
Old records state: Zǐzhōu [梓州] was 2090 *lǐ* [里] from the capital.
Sòng Bái [宋白] said: Zǐzhōu [梓州]
was named after the Zǐtóng Jiāng [梓潼江] river.
Lín Yùn [林蘊] of Pútián [莆田], a judicial assistant, strongly advised Pì [闢] against raising troops.
In the fifth year of Wǔdé [武德] (622),
Pútián Xiàn [莆田縣] was established from a part of Nán'ān [南安].
At that time, it belonged to Quánzhōu [泉州].
The *Fēngsú Tōng* [風俗通] says: The Lín [林] surname
originated from Lín Fàng [林放].
Sūn Miǎn [孫愐] said: It originated from Lín Kāi [林開], the second son of Zhōu Píng Wáng [周平王].
In Lǔ [魯], there were Lín Fàng [林放] and Lín Yōng [林雍].
In Qí [齊], there was Lín Yuán [林元].
Lín Yùn [林蘊] was shackled in prison.
He was brought out
and about to be beheaded.
Pì [闢] secretly instructed the executioner not to kill him,
but only to repeatedly sharpen the blade against his neck,
hoping to make him submit and then pardon him.
Lín Yùn [林蘊] shouted at him,
"You wretch!
If you must behead me, then behead me!
Is my neck your whetstone?!"
Pì [闢] looked at his attendants and said,
"He is truly a loyal and brave man!"
Then he demoted him to the post of County Magistrate of Tángchāng [唐昌].
In the first year of Yífèng [儀鳳] (676),
Tángchāng Xiàn [唐昌縣] was established from parts of Jiǔlǒng [九隴], Dǎojiāng [導江], and Pí [郫],
and belonged to Péngzhōu [彭州].
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* [九域志] says: It was twenty-eight *lǐ* [里] west of the prefecture.
The emperor wished to suppress Pì [闢] but was hesitant to use military force.
He considered using military force a serious matter
and dared not try it lightly.
Dù Huángshang [杜黃裳] alone said:
"Pì [闢] is a mad and foolish scholar.
Taking him will be as easy as picking up mustard seeds!
I know that Gāo Chóngwén [高崇文], the Commander of the Shéncè [神策] Army, is brave and capable.
