falsely issued an imperial order, claiming to be the Deputy Commander of the Punitive Expedition (Zhāotǎo Fùshǐ),
and beheaded Lǐ Shēn.
He sent dispatches to Sūzhōu, Hángzhōu, Húzhōu, and Mùzhōu,
inviting them to join the punitive campaign.
Xīn Mì, the Prefectural Governor of Húzhōu, secretly recruited several hundred local youths
and launched a night attack on Zhào Wéizhōng's camp,
beheading him.
Lǐ Sù, the Prefectural Governor of Sūzhōu, was defeated by Yáo Zhì'ān
and delivered alive to Lǐ Qí.
He was bound in fetters and manacles and nailed to the ship's side.
Before reaching Jīngkǒu,
Lǐ Qí was defeated,
and Lǐ Sù was spared.
On the Yǐchǒu day,
an imperial edict stripped Lǐ Qí of his official titles, ranks, and family registration.
Lǐ Qí was
of the imperial clan,
hence his name was recorded in the imperial genealogy.
Troops from Xuānwǔ, Yìníng, and Wǔchāng were summoned.
At this time, there was no Yìníng Army;
the New Book (Xīnshū) writes
"Wǔníng,"
which should be followed.
鄂,
read as wò.
Huáinán troops and Xuānxī troops converged at the border of Xuānzhōu,
using their upstream advantage to threaten Jīngkǒu.
At this time,
the territory of Xuānzhōu extended north to Dāngtú,
reaching the bank of the river.
Zhèdōng troops marched out from Hángzhōu
to suppress the rebellion.
9 Gāo Chóngwén spent a year in Shǔ.
One day, he said to the supervising eunuch (jiānjūn):
"Chóngwén,
a common soldier from Héshuò—
Gāo Chóngwén was from Yōuzhōu.
—has attained this position.
Xīchuān is a place where prime ministers (zǎixiàng) serve and rotate.
Chóngwén has held this position for a long time;
how dare I remain complacent!"
He repeatedly submitted memorials stating:
"Shǔ is peaceful and comfortable,
offering no opportunity to exert my strength.
I wish to dedicate my life to the frontier."
The *Kǎoyì* says: The old biography of Chóngwén says:
"Chóngwén was illiterate,
and was tired of the voluminous documents and inquiries of a great prefecture.
Moreover, in a rich and comfortable place,
there was no opportunity to exert his strength.
He requested to be stationed on the frontier to guard the border,
and his earnest memorials were repeatedly submitted."
The old biography of Wǔ Yuánhéng says:
"Chóngwén managed the army skillfully,
but he was unfamiliar with prefectural and county administration.
The Emperor found it difficult to find a replacement for him."
This account now follows the *Bǔ Guóshǐ*,
supplemented by the old biographies.
On the Dīngmǎo day,
Wǔ Yuánhéng, Minister of the Department of the Palace Gate (Ménxià Shìláng) and Grand Councilor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì),
was appointed Military Commissioner of Xīchuān.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Sūn Guāngxiàn's *Běimèng Suǒyán* says:
"Before Lǐ Déyù, the Grand Preceptor (Tàiwèi), left the academy,
he was renowned for his literary talent,
but he was not keen on taking imperial examinations.
Jífǔ, as prime minister,
encouraged him through relatives and friends.
Zhǎng Wǔ said: 'Good donkeys and horses don't enter the trade.'
Therefore, he was appointed to officialdom based on his inherited status.
When Jífǔ was prime minister,
he and Wǔ, a fellow prime minister,
often disagreed on matters.
Each time he retired from public office,
his expression was displeased.
Zhǎng Wǔ said in a memorial: 'How difficult is it to remove him!'
Then he requested to repair the temple of Dí Liánggōng.
Thereupon, Prime Minister Wǔ gradually sought to be appointed to a frontier post.
His resourcefulness was already known from an early age."
This account now follows the *Shílù* and old biographies.
10Lǐ Qí, considering Xuānzhōu to be rich and fertile,
desired to seize it first. He dispatched his cavalry commander (bīngmǎshǐ) Zhāng Zǐliáng, Lǐ Fèngxiān, and Tián Shàoshìng with three thousand troops to attack it.
The three men knew that Lǐ Qí was doomed to fail,
and conspired with the *yájiàng* Péi Xínglì to overthrow him.
Péi Xínglì was
Lǐ Qí's nephew,
and thus knew all of Lǐ Qí's secret plans.
The three generals encamped outside the city.
Before setting out,
they summoned the soldiers and instructed them, saying:
"Our Commander (Púshè) is in rebellion,
and government troops are gathering from all directions.
The two generals in Chángzhōu and Húzhōu have successively died,
and the situation is dire.
Now he wants us to march far to capture Xuānchéng.
Xuānzhōu was Xuānchéng Commandery.
Wouldn't it be better to abandon the rebel and pledge allegiance,
turning disaster into fortune!"
The troops were pleased
and agreed.
That very night,
they returned and rushed to the city.
Péi Xínglì lit fires and shouted,
responding from within,
and led troops towards the headquarters gate.
Lǐ Qí heard that Zhāng Zǐliáng and others had raised an army and was enraged.
When he heard that Péi Xínglì had responded from within,
he beat his chest and exclaimed:
"What hope do I have left!"
He fled barefoot
and hid beneath a tower.
His personal general (qīn jiàng) Lǐ Jūn led three hundred crack archers (wǎnqiáng) to rush to Shāntíng,
intending to fight;
Péi Xínglì ambushed and beheaded him.
Lǐ Qí's entire household wept.
His attendants seized Lǐ Qí,
wrapped him in a curtain,
lowered him from the city wall,
and shackled him for transport to the capital.
His crack archers and barbarian guards (fānbù luò) fought to kill themselves,
their corpses piled upon each other.
The matter of Lǐ Qí's adoption of crack archers and barbarian guards is seen in the previous volume, Dézōng, Zhēnyuán 17th year.
枕,
read as zhěn.
藉,
read as jiè.
On the Guǐyǒu day,
the local army reported the news.
The local army
refers to the Zhèxī Army.
On the Yǐhài day,
officials offered congratulations in the Zǐchén Hall.
The Zǐchén Hall
is north of the Xuānzhèng Hall.
"It is due to My lack of virtue
that there have been several transgressors in the realm.
This is My shame;
what is there to congratulate!"
The grand councilors deliberated executing Lǐ Qí's relatives within the *dàgōng* mourning degree.
*Dàgōng*
refers to paternal uncles, brothers, sisters;
and above,
refers to relatives within the *jī* mourning degree.
"Lǐ Qí's *dàgōng* relatives
are all descendants of Huái'ān Jìng Wáng.
Huái'ān Wáng Shéntōng's posthumous title was Jìng.
He attended imperial mausoleums and ancestral temples.
Shéntōng raised an army in response to the righteous cause,
and for his merit was interred beside Xiàn Líng and enshrined in Gāozǔ's ancestral temple."
They also wished to execute his brothers.
Yì said:
"Lǐ Qí's brothers
are the sons of the late General Commander Guózhēn.
Guózhēn died in service to the state;
the matter is seen in Volume 222, Sùzōng, Bǎoyìng 1st year."
The grand councilors considered this to be correct.
On the Xīnsì day,
Lǐ Qí's paternal younger brother Lǐ Xiān, the Prefectural Governor of Sòngzhōu, and others were all demoted and exiled.
In the eleventh month,
on the *jiǎshēn* day,
Lǐ Qí arrived in Cháng’ān.
The Emperor was at the Xīng’ān Gate.
The Táng Dàmínggōng had five southern gates,
and Xīng’ān Gate was the first gate coming from the west.
He replied:
“At first, I did not rebel.
It was Zhāng Zǐliáng and others who incited me.”
The Emperor said:
“You were the Marshal.
If Zǐliáng and others plotted rebellion,
why did you not execute them,
and then come to court?”
Lǐ Qí had no reply.
So he and his son, Lǐ Shīhuí, were cut in half at the waist.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
“A few days after Lǐ Qí was executed,
the Emperor dispatched an imperial envoy with two sets of yellow robes,
ordering the relevant officials to collect his body and that of his son,
and bury them with the rites of commoners.”
The *Guóshǐ Bǔ* says:
“When Lǐ Qí was captured,
a maidservant was found accompanying him.
At night, Lǐ Qí would tear his collar and write by himself about his achievements in managing monopolies,
saying he was betrayed by Zhāng Zǐliáng.
He instructed the maidservant: ‘Tie this to your belt.
If I can calmly present my case to the Emperor,
I will surely become a chancellor or a *jiédùshǐ* like Yáng Yì.
If I cannot present it calmly,
I will suffer extreme punishment.
When I die,
you will surely enter the palace.
The Emperor will certainly question you;
you must present this to him.’
When Lǐ Qí suffered execution,
a great fog enveloped the capital for three days without dispersing,
and some heard ghostly wails.
Xiànzōng also received a silk manuscript,
and somewhat suspected that Lǐ Qí was wronged.
From within the palace, two sets of yellow robes were issued as a gift to Lǐ Qí and his son,
and an imperial edict ordered Jīngzhào to collect and bury them.”
In my opinion, Lǐ Qí was arrogant and rebellious;
what injustice could there be?
I now follow the *Shílù*.
The relevant officials requested to demolish Lǐ Qí’s ancestral tombs and temple.
The *Zhōngchéng*, Lú Tǎn, submitted a memorial stating:
“Lǐ Qí and his son have been executed;
their crime has already been atoned for.
In the past, when the Hàn dynasty executed Huò Yǔ,
they did not punish Huò Guāng;
The execution of Huò Yǔ can be found in Volume 25, during the fourth year of Dìjié of Emperor Xuān of Hàn.
It did not extend to Fáng Xuánlíng.
The execution of Fáng Yí’ài can be found in Volume 199, during the fourth year of Yǒnghuī of Gāozōng.
Crimes should not extend to others.”
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* cites the words of Kāng Gào spoken by Jìn Xūchén.
Currently, the *Shàngshū Kāng Gào* does not contain this phrase.
So, they were not demolished.
The relevant officials confiscated Lǐ Qí’s family property and transported it to the capital.
The Hànlín Xuéshì, Péi Jì and Lǐ Jiàng, submitted a memorial,
believing that:
“Lǐ Qí was extravagant and arrogant,
stripping the people of six prefectures to enrich his family,
or unjustly killing them to seize their wealth.
The six prefectures are Rùn, Mù, Cháng, Sū, Hú, and Háng.
Therefore, he was suppressed and executed.
Now, transporting gold and silk to the upper capital
might cause disappointment among people near and far.
We wish to bestow the rebel’s assets upon the people of Zhèxī,
to substitute for this year’s rents and taxes.”
The Emperor praised and sighed for a long time,
and immediately followed their advice.
The Zhāoyì Jiédùshǐ, Lú Cóngshǐ,
secretly communicated with Wáng Shìzhēn and Liú Jì internally,
while outwardly offering strategies to attack Shāndōng.
At that time, Wèibó and Héngjì were east of the Tàiháng Mountains.
The Emperor summoned him back.
Lú Cóngshǐ made an excuse about foraging for provisions in Xíng and Míng,
and did not promptly obey the edict.
After a long time,
he finally returned.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Jiǎng Jiē and Lǐ Sīkōng discussed matters, saying:
“Lǐ Jiàng submitted a memorial:
‘Lú Cóngshǐ’s recent actions have become quite evident.
Feeling uneasy,
he is eager to stir up trouble,
which is why he elaborately presented advantages and disadvantages,
and frequently offered strategies,
hoping to be allowed to use troops to gain a temporary respite.
Now he requests to personally lead soldiers and horses,
intending to go to Xíng and Míng,
under the pretext of obtaining provisions,
but in reality, to mobilize the masses.
His intentions regarding departure and return
are evident.’”
The *Jiù Cóngshǐ Zhuàn* says:
“The previous year, he was in mourning for his father.
The imperial court had not yet discussed his reappointment.
It happened that Wáng Shìzhēn died,
and Lú Cóngshǐ secretly offered a plan to execute Chéngzōng in order to please the Emperor,
and was thus reappointed,
entrusted with achieving success.
When the edict to suppress the rebels was issued,
and the troops set out,
he lingered and did not advance,
secretly colluding with Chéngzōng,
and instructing his soldiers to secretly harbor the rebel insignia.”
In my opinion, on the *wùxū* day of the ninth month of the third year,
Lǐ Jífǔ was dismissed from chancellorship
and sent to govern Yángzhōu.
On the *dīngmǎo* day of the second month of the fourth year,
Zhèng Yīn was dismissed from chancellorship.
On the *yǐyǒu* day of the third month,
Wáng Shìzhēn died,
and Chéngzōng first assumed his position.
On the *rénchén* day of the fourth month,
Lú Cóngshǐ was reappointed.
If Lú Cóngshǐ’s journey to Shāndōng for provisions was at the time he requested to suppress Chéngzōng,
then at that time, Lǐ Jífǔ and Zhèng Yīn had both already been dismissed from chancellorship.
How could there be the matter of slandering Zhèng Yīn?
Moreover, Lú Cóngshǐ’s demotion edict states:
“Furthermore, some years ago, he requested to forage for provisions in Shāndōng.
When ordered to return his troops,
he did not promptly obey the command,
thereby mobilizing his forces,
hoping to foster his own ambitions.
Fortunately, Liú Jì offered loyal and righteous words,
which caused the wicked fellow to abandon his hesitant plans.
Additionally, he extensively slandered neighboring territories,
secretly outlining affairs,
turning things upside down in a hundred ways,
holding everything in his hands.”
If the court had not rejected his request at the time of suppressing Chéngzōng,
how could it have ordered him to return his troops?
Perhaps before Lǐ Jífǔ and Zhèng Yīn were dismissed,
Lú Cóngshǐ had slandered neighboring circuits,
begging for a punitive expedition,
and consequently led his troops out to Shāndōng.
The court ordered him to return his troops,
but he used the excuse of foraging for provisions in Xíng and Míng,
and did not promptly obey the edict.
However, it is unknown in what year and month this event occurred,
who he intended to attack,
and what words Liú Jì spoke that made Lú Cóngshǐ willing to return.
Now, it is mentioned together with Lǐ Jiàng’s discussion on Lǐ Qí’s family property.
The *Xīn Shū* states:
“Lú Cóngshǐ allied with Chéngzōng,
and there was an imperial edict for him to return to Lù.”
This is an error.
Another day,
the Emperor summoned Lǐ Jiàng to the Bathing Hall.
There was a Bathing Hall Palace within the Táng imperial palace,
which Dèzōng had occupied since his reign.
Shěn Kuò said: The Bathing Hall Palace was north of the Hànlín Yuàn.
The Hànlín Yuàn had a separate northern gate
to facilitate answering summons.
According to the Old Book's biography of Péi Yánlíng: Dèzōng said to Yánlíng,
“One beam in the Bathing Hall Palace, where I reside,
due to its age,
appears to be damaged and decaying;
I wanted to replace it but couldn't.”
From this, we know that Dèzōng frequently resided in the Bathing Hall Palace.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Mr. Shěn's statement that the northern gate of the Xuéshì Yuàn
was south of the Bathing Hall
to facilitate answering summons
is a mistake.
The Xuéshì Yuàn was west of the Zǐchén and Pénglái Palaces.
The Bathing Hall Palace was naturally east of Zǐchén,
not south of the Xuéshì Yuàn.
Táng academicians often held audiences in the Bathing Hall Palace.
Lǐ Jiàng's strong criticism of eunuchs
and Liǔ Gōngquán's soaking paper to extend the candle's burn
all took place there.
However, from the Liùdiǎn to Lǚ Tú, this palace is not mentioned.
Shílín Yè Shì said: As for the northern gate of the Xuéshì Yuàn,
being south of the Bathing Hall,
to facilitate answering summons,
this is perhaps not well-considered.
North of the Xuéshì Yuàn was the Hànlín Yuàn,
and north of the Hànlín Yuàn was the Shǎoyáng Yuàn.
Even if the Bathing Hall were here,
it would also be separated by the Sleeping Palace and the Three Palaces,
making it impossible to have a northern gate connected to it.
The imperial library's Táng map, however, includes the Bathing Hall Palace,
and its position is south of the Língqǐ Palace.
As for Língqǐ,
the Cháng'ān Zhì says,
it was east of the Pénglái Palace.
And the Xuéshì Yuàn,
was precisely west of Pénglái.
Since east and west are already separated,
with many other palaces in between,
there is no way a gate could connect them as north and south.
The Cháng'ān Zhì recorded the Bathing Hall Gate, Bathing Hall Palace, and Bathing Hall Courtyard,
and also stated that Wénzōng once summoned Zhèng Zhù in this palace
and held audiences with academicians in the Bathing Hall Palace.
There was also a separate Bathing Hall Courtyard,
also in the same area,
which suggests it must have been in Dàmíng,
but its exact location is not specified.
Therefore, I believe that what the imperial library's map recorded as being south of the Língqǐ Palace
is correct.
And Yuán Zhěn's "Chéngzhǐ Tīng Jì" also provides corroborating evidence;
it states: When the imperial carriage proceeds to the suburban sacrifices,
the Chéngzhǐ can ride his horse,
following from the Bathing Palace through the inner court.
If external guests are granted an audience at Líndé,
they simply wait directly within the forbidden city.
The inner court,
is the Zǐchén Palace.
Táng's suburban sacrifices were all south of the capital city.
When the sovereign went to the suburban sacrifices,
if not exiting through Dānfèng Mén,
they must exit through Chéngtiān Mén,
and certainly would not make a detour out the West Yíntái Mén.
Thus, that the Bathing Hall could lead to the inner court,
and the inner court must lead to Dānfèng Mén,
this principle is certainly verifiable;
it also states that the palace was east of the Pénglái Palace,
which means it was connected to the Zǐchén Palace,
which is also certain.
Therefore, the position in the imperial library's map
and what Yuán Zhěn recorded largely complement each other,
and is highly credible.
As for external guests being seen at Líndé,
since Líndé was next to the east of the Xuéshì Yuàn,
they could stay in the courtyard to wait without needing to follow a procession.
Combining these two statements to imagine the situation,
the Bathing Hall must be east of the Zǐchén Palace,
and not to its west.
"There is something very unusual
that I have recently been unwilling to speak of.
I discussed with Zhèng Yīn an edict for the attendant secretary to return to Shàngdǎng

The Emperor was silent for a long time and then said:

The Emperor also once casually asked Jiàng:

The life and death of subjects
depend on the ruler's pleasure and anger;

they all ponder day and night,
deleting in the morning and reducing in the evening.
By the time it reaches the top,

still fearing it might not come,
let alone punishing it!
Doing so
would silence all under heaven,

The Emperor approved his words and desisted.
The ministers requested to bestow the honorary title of Ruìshèng Wénwǔ Huángdì upon the Emperor;
on Bǐngshēn,
this was permitted.
The Zhoūzhì County Magistrate and Jíxián College Editor, Bái Jūyì, composed over a hundred poems and yuefu,
criticizing current affairs,

the Emperor saw them and was pleased,
summoning him into the Hànlín as an academician.
In the twelfth month,
on Bǐngchén,

On Bǐngyín,

Princess of Pǔníng Commandery.
Pǔníng Commandery of Róng Prefecture.
Qī,
seven xì fān.
"Dí,

Dí,

17 That year,
Lǐ Jífǔ compiled the Yuánhé Guójì Bù (Comprehensive Records of National Accounts for the Yuánhé Reign) and submitted it.
It totaled forty-eight fāngzhèn (regional commands) across the realm,
two hundred ninety-five zhōufǔ (prefectural administrations),
and one thousand four hundred fifty-three xiàn (counties).

Of these, the fifteen dàos (circuits) of Fèngxiáng, Fūfāng, Bīnníng, Zhènwǔ, Jīngyuán, Yínxià, Língyán, Hédōng, Yìdìng, Wèibó, Zhènjì, Fànyáng, Cāngjǐng, Huáixī, and Zīqīng, comprising seventy-one zhōu, did not report household figures.
Fèngxiáng, Fūfāng, Bīnníng, Zhènwǔ, Jīngyuán, Yínxià, and Língyán in Hédōng were all on the frontier.
Yìdìng, Wèibó, Zhènjì, Fànyáng, Cāngjǐng, Huáixī, and Zīqīng were all hereditary fānzhèn.
Therefore, none of them reported household figures
or paid taxes.
In summer,
the household count was hùyǎ (approximately).
One million four hundred forty thousand households,
which was three-quarters fewer than the tax-paying households in the Tiānbǎo reign.
Sòng Bái said: A comparison of the Guójì Bù figures: In the Tiānbǎo reign, there were three hundred fifteen zhōujùn (prefectures and commanderies).
In the Yuánhé reign, the total under administration was two hundred ninety-five.
Compared to Tiānbǎo, the number of zhōujùn expected to pay taxes was ninety-seven fewer.
The total households in the Tiānbǎo reign was eight million three hundred eighty-five thousand two hundred twenty-three.
The total existing households in the Yuánhé reign was two million four hundred forty thousand two hundred fifty-four.
Compared to the Tiānbǎo figures, the total number of tax-paying households was one million nine hundred forty-four thousand six hundred ninety-nine fewer.

In the Tiānbǎo reign, annual revenue from zūshuì (land tax), yōng (corvée), and diào (tribute) was approximately fifty-two million three hundred thousand duān, pǐ, tún, guàn, and shí in cash, grain, silk, cloth, raw silk, and floss silk.

In the Yuánhé reign, the total from liǎngshuì (two-tax system), quéjiǔ (wine monopoly), húdòu (grain tax), yánlì (salt profits), and chálì (tea profits) was thirty-five million fifteen thousand one hundred twenty-eight guàn and shí.
Compared to the revenue received in the Tiānbǎo reign, the tax income was seventeen million fourteen thousand seven hundred seventy guàn and shí fewer.

1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the guǐsì day,
the officials presented the honorable title "Ruìshèng Wénwǔ Huángdì" (Sagacious, Holy, Cultured, Martial Emperor);
an amnesty was granted to the realm.
"From now on, when senior officials arrive at the capital,
they are not permitted to offer tributes."
Liú Guāngqí, who served as Zhī Shūmì (Director of the Privy Council),
In Dàizōng's Yǒngtài reign,
the position of Nèi Shūmìshǐ (Internal Privy Councilor) was established,
held by eunuchs.
Initially, there was no dedicated office,
but only three bays of a building,
used to store documents.
Their duty was solely to receive memorials and reports,
and present them internally to the sovereign.
If the ruler had a decision to make,
it would be announced and passed to the Zhōngshū Ménxià (Central Secretariat and Chancellery) for implementation.
Later, during the Xī and Zhāo reigns,
Yáng Fùgōng and Xīmén Jìxuán wished to seize the power of the chancellors.
They then affixed yellow notes to the back of official documents,
issuing directives for public affairs.
Desiring to share the tributes received,
the Hànlín Xuéshì (Academicians of the Hanlin Academy) Péi Jì and Lǐ Jiàng memorialized,
"The constant arrival of imperial envoys causes trouble.
It would be better to simply send urgent dispatches."
Jídì (急遞),
the chánjù (relay runners) of ancient times,
who traveled at high speed by post-station.
Guāngqí cited old precedents.
The Emperor said:
"If it is a correct precedent, follow it.
If it is incorrect,
why not change it!"
2 Hǎo Cǐ, the defense commander of Línjìng,
stated that Línjìng's terrain was strategically important, with good water and grass.
When the Tǔbō were about to invade,
they would surely encamp there. He spoke to Duàn Yòu, Jīngyuán Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Jīngyuán).
Kǎoyì (Critical Examination) states: Old traditions record
"Duàn Zuǒ,"
new traditions record
"Yòu."
Now following the Shílù (Veritable Records).
From then on, Jīngyuán was secure.
After the Ān-Shǐ Rebellion,
Yuánzhōu fell to the Tǔbō.
Thereafter, Línjìng was made the administrative center.
3 In the second month,
on the wùyín day,
Princess Xián'ān Dàzhǎnggōngzhǔ died in Huíhú.
Péngzhōu,
Xián'ān Commandery.
In the fourth year of Dèzōng's Zhēnyuán reign, Princess Xián'ān was married to the Huíhú,
see volume 233.
Zhǎng (長),
zhī liàng fān (pronunciation note).
Ténglǐ Kèhán of the Huíhú died.
4 On the guǐsì day,
Shúnwáng Zǒng died.
Zǒng
was the Emperor's younger brother.
5 On the xīnhài day,
Lú Tǎn, Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (Censor-in-Chief), memorialized to impeach Liǔ Shèng, former Shānnán Xīdào Jiédùshǐ, and Yán Jìměi, former Zhèdōng Guāncháshǐ, for violating the amnesty by offering tributes.
The Emperor summoned Tǎn and commended him,
saying:
"I have already pardoned their offense; I cannot go back on my word."
Tǎn replied:
"The amnesty order was proclaimed throughout the realm,
this is His Majesty's great trustworthiness.
Shèng and others do not fear His Majesty's law.
How can one maintain a small trustworthiness and abandon a great trustworthiness!"
The Emperor then ordered that what had been presented be returned to the relevant authorities.
6 In summer,
in the fourth month,
the Emperor personally examined candidates for the 'Xiánliáng Fāngzhèng Zhíyán Jíjiàn' (Wise, Upright, Frank, and Outspoken) examination.
Niú Sēngrú, Yīquè Wèi (Magistrate of Yīquè), and Huángfǔ Shí, Lùhún Wèi (Magistrate of Lùhún),
Lùhún County,
was where the Lùhún Róng resided during the Spring and Autumn period.
The Eastern Wèi established Yīchuān Commandery,
administering Nánlùhún County.
It was abolished in early Kāihuáng of the Suí dynasty,
and the county was renamed Fúliú.
In early Dàyè, it was renamed Lùhún.
Under the Táng, it belonged to Luòzhōu.
They spared no words;
Lǐ Zōngmǐn had achieved the Jìnshì degree and was appointed Cānjūn of Huázhōu,
hence referred to as 'former Jìnshì'.
Wéi Guànzhī, Lìbù Yuánwàiláng (Supernumerary Director in the Ministry of Personnel), was the examiner.
Guànzhī ranked them in the highest class.
The Emperor also praised them,
and decreed that
the Zhōngshū (Central Secretariat) should handle their appointments favorably.
Lǐ Jífǔ disliked their frank words
and tearfully complained to the Emperor,
also stating,
"Hànlín Xuéshì Péi Jì and Wáng Yá reviewed the examinations.
Shěnkǎo (careful examination) means review.
Yá was his nephew,
Yá did not mention it first;
Jì had no differing opinions."
The Emperor, having no choice,
dismissed Jì and Yá from their positions as Xuéshì.
Jì was made Hùbù Shìláng (Vice Minister of Revenue),
Yá was made Dūguān Yuánwàiláng (Supernumerary Director in the Ministry of Justice),
and Guànzhī was made Guǒzhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Guǒzhōu).
A few days later,
Guànzhī was further demoted to Bāzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Yá was demoted to Guózhōu Sīmǎ (Judicial Administrator of Guózhōu).
Old records: Guǒzhōu
is two thousand five hundred twenty-eight lǐ from the capital;
Bāzhōu,
two thousand three hundred sixty lǐ;
Guózhōu,
four hundred twenty lǐ.
On the yǐhài day,
Yáng Yúlíng was made Língnán Jiédùshǐ,
also due to having no differing opinions in the examination review.
Sēngrú and others were not appointed for a long time
and each took up positions in various fānfǔ (military governor's administrations).
Sēngrú was the seventh-generation descendant of Hóng;
Niú Hóng served as chancellor in the Suí dynasty.
He was the great-great-grandson of Yuányì;
Zhèngwáng Yuányì was the son of Gāozǔ.
He was the sixth-generation descendant of Fúsì;
Wéi Fúsì is mentioned in volume 182, Suí Yángdì, Dàyè 9th year.
Wéi Guànzhī's original name was Chún,
changed to avoid the Emperor's personal name.
He was from Xīn'ān, Mùzhōu.
Xīn'ān was the land of Hàn Shèxiàn.
Xīn'ān Commandery was established east of the Jiāng River.
The Suí abolished the commandery and made it a county.
In early Dàyè, it was renamed Zhìshān.
In the first year of Táng Wénmíng, it was restored to Xīn'ān.
In the twentieth year of Kāiyuán, it was renamed Huánchún.
In the first year of Yǒngzhēn, it was renamed Qīngxī to avoid the Emperor's personal name.
Here it says Xīn'ān,
the history follows the old county name.
7 On the dīngchǒu day,
the court assembly at Xuānzhèng Diàn on the first day of the fifth month was abolished.
Under the Táng system, New Year's Day and the Winter Solstice were the regular days for receiving court assemblies.
By the seventh year of Zhēnyuán,
an imperial edict stipulated that on the first day of the fifth month each year, the Emperor would meet with all civil and military officials at Xuānzhèng Diàn.
Capital officials of the ninth rank and above,
and outer officials who were in the capital for court reports,
were all to attend.
This was originally because the first day of the fifth month marked the ascendancy of yin,
when the way of subjects and sons grows,
and the way of rulers and fathers declines.
It was not a good month,
thus this ceremony of meeting on that day was initiated.
8. Péi Jūn (裴均), Jīngnán (荊南) Military Commissioner, was made Right Grandee Secretary.
Péi Jūn had always been attached to eunuchs, thus achieving high status.
As Grandee Secretary,
he became very self-important.
Once, when attending court,
he stood out of place.
Vice Censor-in-Chief Lú Tǎn (盧坦) bowed and motioned for him to step back,
but Péi Jūn refused to comply.
Lú Tǎn said,
"Formerly, Yáo Nánzhòng (姚南仲) was Grandee Secretary,
and his place was here."
Péi Jūn replied,
"Who is Nánzhòng?"
Lú Tǎn said,
"He was one who upheld righteousness and did not associate with influential favorites."
Lú Tǎn was soon demoted to Right Palace Assistant.
Péi Jūn had resented him.
9. In the fifth month,
Bái Jūyì (白居易), Hanlin Academician and Left Reminder, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Niú Sēngrú (牛僧孺) and others spoke frankly about current affairs,
were honored with awards and passed the examinations,
yet they were subsequently denounced and banished,
and all appointed as officials outside the passes.
Niú Sēngrú and others were invited to serve in the provincial administrations,
hence they were considered officials outside the passes.
Péi Jì (裴垍) and others, because they did not retract their frank words during the policy questions,
were all condemned and demoted.
Lú Tǎn was demoted to Palace Assistant for several times presenting his official duties.
These several men are all the hope of the present age,
upon whose advancement or retirement the empire judges the prosperity or decline of the times.
If suddenly, without cause, they are all dismissed and abandoned,
everyone above and below will keep silent,
and public sentiment will be turbulent.
Does Your Majesty know this?
Moreover, since Your Majesty has already issued edicts to invite frank speech,
and sought extreme remonstrance,
the replies of Sēngrú and others were as such.
Even if you cannot implement them,
how can you bear to punish and dismiss them?
Formerly, when Dézōng (德宗) first ascended the throne,
he also summoned men of frank speech and extreme remonstrance.
When asked a policy question about drought,
Mù Zhì (穆質) replied, 'According to the precedents of the Two Hàn (漢) Dynasties,
the Three Dukes should be dismissed;
Bǔ Shì (卜式) proposed, 'Hóngyáng (弘羊) should be cooked.'
Dézōng greatly praised him,
promoting him from Commander of a Metropolitan County to Left Rectifier of Omissions.
Outside of the two metropolitan counties,
the rest of Jīngzhào (京兆) Prefecture's counties
were considered metropolitan counties.
Under the Táng (唐) system: in any capital,
the counties within its city walls were metropolitan counties,
and other counties were also metropolitan counties.
If you hastily dismiss them,
I fear it is not in line with the path of succeeding the ancestors!"
Zhì (質)
was the son of Níng (寧).
Mù Níng (穆寧) and Yán Zhēnqīng (顏真卿) jointly suppressed Ān Lùshān (安祿山).
10. On the day of bǐngwǔ (丙午),
the new Khagan of the Huíhú (回鶻) was enfeoffed as Àidēnglǐ Luómìshī Hébǐjiā Bǎoyì Kèhán (愛登里囉汨密施合毗伽保義可汗).
11. Huáng Shǎoqīng (黃少卿), chieftain of the Xīyuán (西原) Man (蠻), requested to surrender.
In the sixth month,
on the day of guǐhài (癸亥),
he was made Governor of Guīshùn (歸順) Prefecture.
Huáng Shǎoqīng's rebellion is mentioned in Volume 234, Dézōng's Zhēnyuán (貞元) 10th year.
12. The Shatuo (沙陀) were renowned among all Hu (胡) peoples for their bravery.
Tubo (吐蕃) placed them in Gānzhōu (甘州).
The Shatuo's surrender to Tubo is mentioned in Volume 233, Zhēnyuán 6th year.
Guān (冠), read as gǔ wán.
They were used as a vanguard.
When Huíhú attacked Tubo
and took Liángzhōu (涼州),
Tubo suspected the Shatuo of disloyalty to Huíhú
and wanted to move them beyond the river.
The Shatuo were afraid.
Their chieftain, Zhūyé Jìnzhōng (朱邪盡忠), and his son Zhíyí (執宜) planned to return to Táng (唐) rule.
They then led their tribe of 30,000
eastward along Wūdéjiàn (烏德鞬) Mountain.
After three days of travel,
a large Tubo pursuing army arrived.
They fought from Táoshuǐ (洮水) to Shímén (石門).
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù (水經註) says: Táoshuǐ enters the Hé (河) at Páohǎn (枹罕).
Páohǎn
was Hézhōu (河州) during the Táng.
Shíménshuǐ (石門水)
is 80 li west of Gāopíng (高平) County.
The Táng established Shíménguān (石門關) here,
which was in the territory of Pínggāo (平高) County, Yuánzhōu (原州).
Jìnzhōng died,
and more than half of his troops perished.
Zhíyí led the remaining force of nearly 10,000 men,
with 3,000 cavalry,
and surrendered at Língzhōu (靈州).
Fàn Xīcháo (范希朝), Military Commissioner of Língyán (靈鹽), heard of this
and personally led his troops to welcome them at the frontier.
He settled them in Yánzhōu (鹽州),
purchased cattle and sheep for them,
expanded their pasturage,
and treated them kindly.
An edict established Yīnshān (陰山) Prefecture,
with Zhíyí as Commander of Troops and Horses.
Not long after,
Gélè Ābō (葛勒阿波), Jìnzhōng's younger brother,
led another 700 men to surrender to Xīcháo.
Jǐ (幾), read as jū qǐ.
From then on,
whenever Língyán undertook a campaign,
the Shatuo were used, and they were victorious wherever they went,
strengthening the Língyán army.
This laid the groundwork for the rise of the Shatuo in Central China.
13. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the first day, xīnsì (辛巳),
there was a solar eclipse.
14. Lú Tǎn (盧坦), Right Palace Assistant, was made Surveillance Commissioner of Xuānshè (宣歙).
When Sū Qiáng (蘇彊) was executed,
Sū Qiáng
was the son-in-law of Liú Pì (劉闢),
and was executed as a rebel in the first year.
Sū Hóng (蘇弘), Sū Qiáng's brother,
returned home of his own accord,
and no one dared to employ him.
Lú Tǎn memorialized:
"Hóng (弘) has talent and character;
he should not be abandoned because of his brother.
I request to appoint him as a staff supervisor."
The emperor said,
"If Sū Qiáng (蘇彊) had not died,
and indeed possessed talent and character,
he could still be used,
let alone his brother!"
When Lú Tǎn arrived at his post,
it was a time of drought and famine,
and grain prices rose daily.
Some requested to suppress prices.
Lú Tǎn said,
"Xuān (宣) and Shè (歙) have limited land and little grain;
they rely on supplies from all directions.
If prices are low,
merchant ships will no longer come,
and the situation will worsen."
Soon, rice was 200 (cash) per dou,
and merchants flocked in.
15. In the ninth month,
on the day of gēngyín (庚寅),
Yú Dí (于頔) was made Minister of Works,
with his concurrent position of Co-administrator of Affairs as before.
Péi Jūn (裴均), Right Grandee Secretary, was given the concurrent title of Co-administrator of Affairs
and made Military Commissioner of Shānnán Dōngdào (山南東道).
Wáng È, Jìedùshǐ of Huáinán, entered the court.
È's family was immensely wealthy,
and he made generous offerings and bribed eunuchs
to seek the title of Píngzhāngshì.
Hànlín Xuéshì Bái Jūyì
believed:
"A chancellor holds the highest position among officials;
it should not be granted without a reputation for integrity and great merit.
Yesterday, Péi Jūn was appointed,
and public opinion was already in an uproar.
Péi Jūn
also sought to curry favor with eunuchs.
If this continues, people like È will all harbor hopes.
If we grant it to all of them,
then the state's institutions will be greatly damaged,
and they will not even be grateful;
if we do not grant it,
then there will be disparity and
possibly resentment.
Once the door to favoritism is opened,
there will be nothing that can be done.
Moreover, È has been in his post for five years.
In the 19th year of Zhēnyuán of Dèzōng's reign,
È became the commander of Huáinán.
With his wealth already sufficient,
he personally came to make offerings.
If he is appointed chancellor,
all the frontier military governors will believe that È obtained it through offerings,
and they will compete to exploit their people,
how can the common folk endure this!"
The matter was subsequently shelved.
Kǎoyì says: According to the old biographies of Lǐ Fān, Quán Déyú, Bái Jūyì's collected works, and Lǐ Jiàng's collected discussions on affairs,
all contain admonitions against granting Wáng È the title of Píngzhāngshì.
Examining their wording and intent,
each pertains to a specific time.
What Jūyì discussed
says
"the people of Huáinán
have no respite day and night,"
and also says
"whether È returns to his post or remains at court,
it is hoped he will not be appointed chancellor."
This was when he had entered the court from Huáinán but had not yet been appointed to Hézhōng.
Quán and Lǐ were both in the Zhōngshū, receiving secret imperial decrees
that said
"he can concurrently hold the chancellorship,"
which was at the time of his initial appointment to Hézhōng.
Lǐ Sīkōng's discussion on affairs says
"within a year or two of arriving in Tàiyuán,
his financial resources were ample,"
which was after his appointment to Tàiyuán and before Lǐ Jiàng became chancellor in the 11th month of the sixth year.
Now, Jūyì's memorial is appended to the time of his initial appointment to Tàiyuán.
Furthermore, the old biography of È states that he was in Huáinán for four years and
entered the court in the second year of Yuánhé.
According to the Veritable Records,
È was stationed in Huáinán in the 19th year of Zhēnyuán.
Jūyì's memorial states
"five years of extortion,"
and also says
"yesterday Péi Jūn was appointed Píngzhāngshì,"
hence it is placed here.
On the 16th day, Rénchén,
Hán Hóng, Jìedùshǐ of Xuānwǔ, was granted the concurrent title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
On the 17th day, Bǐngshēn,
Péi Jì, Hùbù Shìláng, was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Although the emperor had dismissed Jì as Xuéshì due to Lǐ Jífǔ,
in the fourth month of that year,
Jì was dismissed as Xuéshì.
Therefore, he was soon again promoted to chancellor.
Previously,
Dèzōng did not rely on chancellors;
he decided all minor state affairs himself,
which led to people like Péi Yánlíng gaining influence.
While in his princely residence, the emperor
firmly disapproved of this;
upon his accession,
he selected and promoted chancellors,
entrusting them wholeheartedly.
He once said to Jì and others:
"Even with the sagacity of Tàizōng and Xuánzōng,
they still relied on their assistants to achieve good governance."
(This refers to relying on Fáng, Dù, Yáo, and Sòng to achieve the reigns of Zhēnguān and Kāiyuán.)
Lǐ means
governance.
Jì also exhausted his sincerity in assisting.
The emperor once asked Jì:
"What is the most important prerequisite for good governance?"
He replied:
"First, correct one's own heart."
According to the old system,
the common people's tax contributions were threefold: first,
'tribute to the central government'; second,
'sent to the envoy'; third,
'retained by the prefecture'.
At the beginning of Jiànzhōng, the Two-Tax System was established,
when goods were valuable and currency was cheap;
thereafter, goods became cheap and currency valuable,
so the amount the people paid had already doubled their initial burden.
For those 'retained by the prefecture' and 'sent to the envoy', localities further lowered the provincial appraisal
and levied heavy taxes on the people based on the actual appraisal.
'Provincial appraisal' refers to
the price set by the Dūshěng (Central Secretariat).
Liǎn means
to collect (lì shàn fān).
[Jì] memorialized:
"Regarding all goods 'retained by the prefecture' and 'sent to the envoy' throughout the realm,
I request that the provincial appraisal be uniformly used;
as for the Guāncháshǐ,
they should first tax the prefectures under their direct jurisdiction to support themselves,
and if that is insufficient,
then they may tax the prefectures under their command."
Consequently, the people of Jiāng and Huái gradually found some relief.
Previously,
many in power disliked Censors speaking of the successes and failures of contemporary governance,
but Jì alone appreciated them.
Jì's bearing was stern and upright,
and people dared not approach him with private matters.
Once, an old acquaintance traveled a long distance to visit him.
Jì provided generously and
conversed with him in a relaxed and familiar manner.
Taking advantage of an opening, the man requested to be a Pànsī (Judicial Assistant) of Jīngzhào.
Jì said:
"You are not suited for this office,
and I dare not harm the impartiality of the court with private favors for an old acquaintance.
Should there be a blind chancellor who takes pity on you someday,
you might obtain it,
but from Jì, it is impossible."
On the 18th day, Wùxū,
Lǐ Jífǔ, Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì
and concurrently Jìedùshǐ of Huáinán.
Kǎoyì says: The old biography of Jífǔ states:
"Initially,
Péi Jūn was Púyè and Pàn Dùzhī (Commissioner of Finance).
He colluded with powerful favorites
to seek the chancellorship.
Earlier, an imperial examination had been held for the 'straight talk and blunt admonition' category.
Among the successful candidates, some criticized contemporary governance
and offended powerful favorites.
Therefore, Jūn's faction spread rumors that these were all instigated by the current administration,
hoping to destabilize Jífǔ.
Thanks to the secret memorials presented by Censors Lǐ Yuē, Dúgū Yù, Lǐ Zhèngcí, and Xiāo Miǎn,
the emperor's suspicion was dispelled.
Jífǔ had earlier recognized and promoted Yáng Shì'è,
elevating him to Jiānchá Yùshǐ.
Moreover, Lǚ Wēn, Sīfēng Yuánwàiláng, possessed literary talent,
and Jífǔ also cherished and received him.
When Dòu Wù was first appointed Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
he memorialized to request Shì'è be made Shìyùshǐ and
Wēn be made Lángzhōng and
Zhī Zázhì.
Jífǔ was angered that he had not been consulted first,
and that the requested appointments included those with promotions beyond their due rank.
He withheld them for several days,
creating a rift.
Wù then discovered that the diviner Chén Kèmíng frequented Jífǔ's home
and secretly had him arrested and reported the matter.
Xìanzōng questioned him
but found no evidence of wrongdoing.
Jífǔ, knowing that Péi Jì had long been in the Hànlín Academy and was trusted by Xìanzōng,
and would certainly be greatly employed,
secretly recommended Jì to replace himself,
thus planning his own assignment to a frontier post.
In the ninth month of that year,
he was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Huáinán.
While in Yángzhōu,
whenever there were successes or failures in court affairs,
he would secretly memorialize to discuss them."
It is observed that when Niú Sēngrú and others pointed out shortcomings in contemporary governance,
Jífǔ tearfully complained,
and was thus demoted to Kǎofùguān.
Although Péi Jūn and others tried to slander him,
saying that the administration itself instructed candidates to criticize the government's shortcomings,
how could this be plausible!
Jífǔ himself had falsely accused Zhèng Yīn
and demoted Péi Jì and others.
Xìanzōng had seen through his intentions and thus distanced himself from him,
hence his assignment to govern Huáinán.
Later, when his son Déyù took power,
he concealed his predecessor's faults
and revised the Veritable Records,
which is why this account exists.
On the 19th day, Dù Huángshang, Jìedùshǐ of Hézhōng, Jìn, and Jiàng, and Bīn Xuāngōng, passed away.
In winter,
in the twelfth month,
on the day Gēngxū,
a provisional Yuánzhōu was established in Línjīng.
The original Yuánzhōu of the Táng dynasty was initially governed from Pínggāo Xiàn.
In the first year of Guǎngdé, it was lost to Tǔbō.
Mǎ Lín, Jìedùshǐ of Jìngyuán, memorialized to establish a provisional Yuánzhōu at Bǎilǐ Chéng in Língtái.
In the 19th year of Zhēnyuán, its seat was moved to Píngliáng.
By this time,
its seat was moved to Línjīng.
Sòng Bái said: Línjīng
was originally Qiūgǔ Xiàn of the Suí dynasty.
Yì Móuxún, King of Nánzhào, died.
His son, Xún Gěquàn, ascended the throne.
1 Spring,
first month,
on the day Wùzǐ,
King Jiǎn (簡王) died.
Gòu (遘)
was a prince of the Dàizōng (代宗) lineage.
2 Bohai (渤海) King Kāng (康王) Sōnglín (嵩璘) died.
His son Yuán yú (元瑜) ascended the throne,
and changed the reign title to Yǒngdé (永德).
3 The south suffered from drought and famine.
On the day Gēngyín,

Zhèng Jìngdé (鄭敬德), Langzhong (郎中) of the Left Bureau of Personnel (左司), and others were ordered to serve as pacification commissioners for the circuits of Jiāng (江), Huái (淮), Èrzhè (二浙), Jīng (荊), Hú (湖), Xiāng (襄), and È (鄂).
They were to provide relief and comfort.
As they were about to depart,
the Emperor admonished them, saying:
"For every bolt of silk used in my palace,
its number is recorded.
Only when it comes to relieving and saving the common people
do I not account for the expense.
You and your colleagues should understand this intention,
and not just imitate Pān Mèngyáng (潘孟陽) who drank wine and wandered in the mountains."
This matter is mentioned in the first year.
4 Lǐ Fān (李藩), a Gěishìzhōng (給事中) in the Menxià (門下),
whenever imperial edicts had objectionable parts,
he would immediately write a note on the back of the yellow paper.
An official requested to connect it with plain paper.
Lǐ Fān (李藩) said:
"If so,
it would be a memorial,
how could it be called an imperial edict with a note?"
Péi Jì (裴垍) recommended Lǐ Fān (李藩) as having the qualities of a prime minister.
The Emperor considered Zhèng Yīn (鄭絪), Menxià Shìláng (門下侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事), to be complacent and taciturn.
In the second month,
on the day Dīngmǎo,
Zhèng Yīn (鄭絪) was dismissed as Prince's Guest (太子賓客),
and Lǐ Fān (李藩) was promoted to Menxià Shìláng (門下侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章shì).
Lǐ Fān (李藩) spoke about everything he knew,
and the Emperor greatly valued him.
5 Yán Shòu (嚴綬), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hédōng (河東),
had been in command for nine years.
In the seventeenth year of Zhēnyuán (貞元),
Yán Shòu (嚴綬) was in charge of Hédōng (河東),
see previous volume.
Yán Shòu (嚴綬) merely folded his hands.
Péi Jì (裴垍) fully reported his situation,
and requested Lǐ Yōng (李鄘) to replace him.
In the third month,
on the day Yǐyǒu,
Yán Shòu (嚴綬) was made Zuǒ Púshè (左僕射),
and Lǐ Yōng (李鄘), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Fèngxiáng (鳳翔), was made Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hédōng (河東).
6 Wáng Shìzhēn (王士真), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Chéngdé (成德), died.
His son, Vice Commissioner (副大使) Chéngzōng (承宗), appointed himself as Liúhòu (留後).
This laid the groundwork for the suppression of Wáng Chéngzōng (王承宗).
Successive rulers each appointed a Vice Commissioner (副大使),
with the eldest legitimate son filling the role.
When the father died, the son would take over military affairs.
7 The Emperor, due to the prolonged drought,
wished to issue a benevolent edict.
Lǐ Jiàng (李絳) and Bái Jūyì (白居易), Hanlin Academicians (翰林學士), submitted a memorial.
A critical comparison states: Lǐ Sīkōng's (李司空) discussions on affairs and Bái Jūyì's (白居易) collected works both contain this memorial.
Although the wording is slightly different,
the main gist is similar.
It is probably the same memorial submitted jointly.
"To ensure that real benefits reach the people,
nothing is better than reducing their rents and taxes."
They also said,
"After the servants in the palace have been assigned their duties,
their number is still vast.
It is appropriate to economize on expenses,
and in valuing things, follow sentiment."
To feed the palace from public funds
annually costs allowances and gifts,
which is not economizing.
To have many resentful women in the palace
is not following sentiment.
"Prohibit all circuits from levying excessive taxes to offer as tributes."
They also said,
"In Lǐngnán (嶺南), Qiánzhōng (黔中), and Fújiàn (福建), it is customary
to often abduct common people and sell them as slaves.
We beg for a strict prohibition."
In the intercalary month,
on the day Jǐyǒu,
an edict was issued to release prisoners throughout the empire,
remit rents and taxes,
release palace women, cease tributes, and prohibit abduction and sale.
All were according to the requests of the two men.
On the day Jǐwèi,
it rained.
Lǐ Jiàng (李絳) submitted a memorial of congratulations, saying:
"Only then do we know that worrying before the event
leads to no worries;
worrying when the event occurs
is of no help to the event."
8 Initially,
after the faction of Wáng Shūwén (王叔文) was demoted,
the matter first appeared in the previous volume, first year of Yǒngzhēn (永貞).
Although they received amnesty, they were not allowed to be transferred to closer posts.
Lǐ Xùn (李巽), Shàngshū (尚書) of the Ministry of Personnel (吏部) and Supervisor of Salt and Iron Transport (鹽鐵轉運使), memorialized:
"Chéng Guǎ (程[AS-82FA]), Sīmǎ (司馬) of Chēnzhōu (郴州),
has clear and discerning administrative talent.
I request to make him Liúhòu (留後) of Yángzǐ (楊子)."
Yángzǐ (揚子) County in Yángzhōu (揚州),
since the Dàlì (大曆) era,
the Supervisor of Salt and Iron Transport (鹽鐵轉運使) had established an inspection office here,
hence the establishment of a Liúhòu (留後).
Lǐ Xùn (李巽) was meticulous in supervision.
Officials, even a thousand li away,
trembled as if in Lǐ Xùn's (李巽) presence.
Chéng Guǎ (程[AS-82FA]) excelled even more than Lǐ Xùn (李巽) in examining registers and documents,
and was ultimately employed.
9 Wèi Zhēng's (魏徵) great-great-grandson Chóu (稠) was extremely poor.
He mortgaged his old residence to someone for money.
Lǐ Shīdào (李師道), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Pínglú (平盧), requested to redeem it with his private funds.
The Emperor ordered Bái Jūyì (白居易) to draft an edict.
Bái Jūyì (白居yì) memorialized:
"This matter involves encouragement,
and should come from the imperial court.
Who is Lǐ Shīdào (李師道)
to dare to seize this credit?
I hope Your Majesty will order the proper authorities to redeem it with official funds and return it to his descendants."
The Emperor agreed,
and disbursed two thousand strings of cash from the imperial treasury to redeem and bestow upon Wèi Chóu (魏稠),
also prohibiting its mortgage or sale.
Chéng Dàchāng (程大昌) said: Wèi Zhēng's (魏徵) residence was in Dānfèng (丹鳳) Ward,
directly south, within Yǒngxīng (永興) Ward.
The *Huìyào* (會要) states: In the fourth year of Yuánhé (元和),
the Emperor praised Wèi Zhēng's (魏徵) remonstrance,
and ordered an inquiry into his former residence.
It was found that it had been mortgaged and sold, changing hands among several families,
and divided into nine households.
The Emperor disbursed two million from the imperial treasury to redeem it,
returning it to his family,
and prohibited its mortgage and sale.
10 Wáng Chéngzōng's (王承宗) uncle, Shìzé (士則), fearing that disaster would befall the clan due to Wáng Chéngzōng (王承宗) appointing himself,
together with his strategist Liú Qīchǔ (劉栖楚), both returned to the capital.
A critical comparison states: The old tradition says:
"Liú Qīchǔ (劉栖楚) was an official in Zhènzhōu (鎮州),
and Wáng Chéngzōng (王承宗) greatly admired him."
Now following the Veritable Records.
11 Lǐ Jiàng (李絳) and other Hanlin Academicians (翰林學士) memorialized:
"Your Majesty has held the great imperial throne
for four years now,
yet the heir apparent has not been established,
and the ceremonial rites are not performed.
This opens the door to covetous desires,
and goes against the principle of utmost caution.
This is not the way to uphold the ancestral temple and safeguard the state.
We humbly hope Your Majesty will put aside the minor virtue of excessive humility,
and carry out the great and public ceremony."
On the day Dīngmǎo,
an edict was issued to establish Dèngwáng Níng (鄧王寧),
the eldest son, as太子 (tàizǐ).
Níng (寧)
was the son of Concubine Jì (紀美人).
12 On the day Xīnwèi,
Fàn Xīcháo (范希朝), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Língyán (靈鹽), memorialized
to grant six hundred soldiers' clothing and provisions from Tàiyuán (太原)
to the Shātuó (沙陀).
This was permitted.
13th year, in the summer,
4th month,
Péi Jūn, the Jíedùshǐ of Shānnán Dōngdào, relying on the help of an internal official,
presented over 1,500 liǎng of silver vessels after the Decree of Clemency.
In the 1st month of that year,
an amnesty was granted to all under Heaven,
forbidding the presentation of gifts.
"Jūn wishes to test Your Majesty with this;
I wish for it to be refused."
The Emperor immediately ordered the silver vessels to be handed over to the Ministry of Finance.
Soon after, a decree was issued to the Jìnzòuyuàn:
"From now on, all gifts presented by the various circuits
are not to be reported to the Yúshǐ Tái;
if anyone inquires,
their name shall be immediately reported."
Bái Jūyì again spoke about this,
and the research on discrepancies states: Jūyì's collected memorials say:
"I humbly observe that for the past six or seven days,
it has been rumored outside
that there has been a directive
to inform the Jìnzòuyuàn of the various circuits: 'From now on,
any gifts presented
are not to be reported to the Yúshǐ Tái;
if anyone makes inquiries,
their name should be recorded and reported.'
The rumors circulating both inside and outside
have caused no small surprise and alarm.
I humbly surmise that this matter is mostly a false rumor,
but having heard it,
I dare not fail to memorialize."
And so on.
It also says:
"If this is indeed false,
then I hope it will be announced to all, both inside and outside the court,
to make known the imperial will,
and thus stop these false rumors."
According to records, the decrees and edicts prohibiting gift-giving,
issued before and after, were not just one;
it was not limited to the Decree of Clemency in the intercalary 3rd month of last year.
In the 3rd month of last year,
Liǔ Shèng and Yán Jìměi violated the amnesty by presenting gifts,
and were impeached by Lú Tǎn.
Xiànzōng said:
"Jìměi left Yuèzhōu
and then encountered the amnesty decree,"
thereby excusing his crime.
Now, even if Péi Jūn's gifts
were presented before the Decree of Clemency,
it was still after the amnesty.
It was also said:
"He was already on his way before the amnesty decree arrived, so his fault is forgiven."
This indicates that Xiànzōng was deeply misled by the words of his close associates,
outwardly showing disinterest in receiving offerings,
but inwardly desiring them.
If so, what Jūyì heard
was not false;
if it were false,
it would surely have been clarified.
The Shílù and Lǐ Sīkōng's discussions on the matter all regarded this as a virtue of Xiànzōng.
Therefore, I shall set it straight now.
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu.
14th year, the Emperor wished to reform the abuse of hereditary succession in the various circuits of Héběi.
Taking advantage of Wáng Shìzhēn's death, he intended to appoint someone from the court;
if they did not comply, he would dispatch an army to punish them.
Péi Jì said:
"Lǐ Nà was arrogant and disrespectful,
but Lǐ Nà's crime,
by the amnesty decree of Xīngyuán,
was ultimately forgiven.
This refers to him and Lǐ Bǎozhēn defeating Zhū Tāo.
This meant permitting Lǐ Shīdào to succeed.
Encouraging defiance of reason,
they will surely not submit."
Because of this, the discussion remained unresolved for a long time.
The Emperor asked the various imperial scholars,
and Lǐ Jiàng and others replied:
"Who would not be indignant and sigh that Héběi does not follow our civilizing influence,
but to try to conquer it today
might not be achievable.
Chéngdé, since Wǔjùn,
has seen father and son succeed each other for over forty years;
from Jiànzhōng 3rd year when Wáng Wǔjùn first possessed Héng and Jì,
it has been twenty-eight years until now.
They do not consider this a transgression.
Moreover, Chéngzōng has already taken charge of military affairs;
to replace him suddenly,
it is feared he may not obey the imperial edict.
Furthermore, Fànyáng, Wèibó, Yìdìng, and Zībīng, having inherited their territories,
are of the same body as Chéngdé.
When they hear that an outsider is appointed to Chéngdé,
they will surely feel insecure internally,
and secretly conspire to assist each other.
Although Mào Zhāo has requested it,
it may not be sincere.
Now, if the state appoints someone to replace Chéngzōng,
the neighboring circuits will encourage and support him,
benefitting from either outcome.
If the appointed person gains entry,
they will claim it as their own achievement;
if the imperial edict is not obeyed,
they will secretly form alliances.
As for the imperial dignity,
how can we suddenly stop?
We must dispatch armies to attack from all sides.
Their generals and commanders will be granted official ranks and titles,
their soldiers will be given clothing and provisions.
They will hold their troops back, trifle with the enemy,
and merely observe the outcome of the battles,
while all the toil and expense will fall upon the state.
Since Dàlì and Zhēnyuán,
the ills of military campaigns have been precisely like this.
With public and private resources exhausted,
military matters
can hardly be lightly considered."
Tǔtú Chéngcuǐ, the Zuǒjūn Zhōngwèi,
wishing to please the Emperor
and seize Péi Jì's authority,
personally requested to lead troops to suppress them.
Lǐ Shì, the Zōngzhèng Shàogīng, memorialized, stating:
"Chéngzōng must be suppressed.
Chéngcuǐ is a close and trusted minister;
he should be entrusted with the imperial guard,
and made to command all armies;
who would dare not obey?"
The Emperor showed Shì's memorial to the imperial scholars, saying:
"This is a treacherous minister;
knowing that I intend to appoint Chéngcuǐ,
he submitted this memorial.
You gentlemen must remember this;
from now on, do not allow him to be promoted or employed."
To show it to the imperial scholars
was because at that time, anyone who entered the Hànlín
was considered a candidate for immediate imperial assistance.
Therefore, they were made to know his name,
so as not to recommend him.
However, the Emperor knew of Lǐ Shì's flattery,
yet ultimately appointed Chéngcuǐ.
Why was that?
Yù jiāng,
pronounced liàng.
Shàng,
pronounced shítáng.
Lú Cóngshǐ, the Jíedùshǐ of Zhāoyì, suffered the loss of his father.
The court had long not reinstated him.
Cóngshǐ, fearing this,
persuaded the Emperor through Chéngcuǐ
to request to deploy his own army to suppress Chéngzōng.
On the day Rénchén,
Cóngshǐ was reinstated as Zuǒ Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn,
with other positions remaining as before.
15th year, initially,
regarding the Treaty of Píngliáng,
see volume 232, Dézōng, Zhēnyuán 3rd year.
Thereafter, Tǔbō requested peace.
Mì's son, Suí,
went to the palace gate three times, weeping and submitting memorials,
begging to grant their request.
Lù Suí memorialized to request peace with Tǔbō,
his feelings were strong due to his family.
Háo,
pronounced hù dāo.
It was not granted.
By this time,
Tǔbō again requested peace.
Suí again submitted five memorials,
and went to the executive ministers, weeping and requesting it.
Péi Jì and Lǐ Fān also spoke to the Emperor,
requesting to grant their peace;
the Emperor agreed.
In the 5th month,
Xú Fù, the Cíbù Lángzhōng, was dispatched as an envoy to Tǔbō.
16th year, in the 6th month,
Fàn Xīcháo, the Jíedùshǐ of Língyán, was appointed Jíedùshǐ of Hédōng.
The court debated that the Shātuó were in Língwǔ,
close to Tǔbō,
fearing their perfidy.
Also, their tribes were numerous,
and it was feared this would raise grain prices.
Thus, an order was given for them all to follow Xīcháo to Hédōng.
Xīcháo selected 1,200 of their elite cavalry,
named them the Shātuó Army,
appointed an envoy to lead them,
and settled the rest of their people in Dìngxiāng Chuān.
At this time,
Zhíyí first established himself in Huánghuāduī of Shénwǔ Chuān.
Shénwǔ Chuān was within the commandery of Dàijùn and Sānggān county in the Hàn dynasty.
Later Wèi established Shénwǔ Commandery,
and later Zhōu abolished the commandery and made it Shénwǔ County,
subordinate to Shuòzhōu.
At this time, its territory was within the Mǎyì Shànyáng county.
Chù,
pronounced chāng lǚ.
17 Zuǒjūn Zhōngwèi Tǔtū Chéngcuǐ was appointed Gōngdé Shǐ (Commissioner of Merits).
In the early Táng dynasty,
a department for supervising temples and monasteries was established.
All monks, nuns, Daoist priests, and Daoist priestesses in the empire were subject to the Hónglú Sì.
Empress Wǔ (Wǔ Zétiān) placed monks and nuns under the Cíbù.
In the 14th year of Kāiyuán (726),
Daoist priests and Daoist priestesses were placed under the Zōngzhèng Sì.
In the 2nd year of Tiānbǎo (743),
Daoist priests were placed under the Sīfēng.
The Chóngxuán Guǎn (Academy for Honoring Daoism) established the position of Dàxuéshì (Grand Academician),
which was held by a prime minister,
overseeing the Xuányuán Gōng and Daoist temples in both capitals.
In the 4th year of Zhēnyuán (788),
the position of Dàxuéshì in the Chóngxuán Guǎn was abolished.
Zǔoyòu Jiē Dà Gōngdé Shǐ (Grand Commissioners of Merits for the Left and Right Streets) and Dōngdū Gōngdé Shǐ (Commissioner of Merits for the Eastern Capital) were established,
to manage meritorious works,
and these commissioners oversaw the registers and corvée labor of monks and nuns.
In the 2nd year of Yuánhé (807),
Daoist priests and Daoist priestesses were placed under the Zǔoyòu Jiē Gōngdé Shǐ.
The Táng Huìyào states: Ānguó Sì was in the Chánglè Fāng.
In the 1st year of Jǐngyún (710), an imperial edict converted the old residence where Lóngqián had lived into a temple,
and it was named Ānguó after his original enfeoffment.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Chánglè Fāng
was in the fourth street east of Zhūquè Jiē.
It was as tall and standard as the Huàyuè Bēi.
Xuánzōng erected the Huàyuè Bēi in front of the Huàyuè Cí (Mount Hua Temple),
more than fifty feet high.
Huà
is pronounced "hù huà fān".
The emperor requested the academicians to draft the text,
and also said,
"Your subject has already prepared ten thousand strings of cash,
intending to reward them."
The emperor ordered Lǐ Jiàng to do it.
Jiàng submitted a memorial, saying:
"Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng
never erected steles to proclaim their own sagely virtues.
Only Qín Shǐhuáng, during his tours,
carved stones to highly praise himself.
Your Majesty, I am unsure what you intend to emulate!
Moreover, describing the beauty of repairing a temple
is nothing more than making it grand for viewing.
How can this enhance your sagely virtue?"
When the emperor read the memorial,
Chéngcuǐ happened to be by his side.
The emperor ordered the stele pavilion to be pulled down.
Chéngcuǐ said:
"The stele pavilion is very large,
it cannot be pulled down.
Please allow it to be dismantled slowly."
He hoped to delay it,
and find an opportunity to argue again.
The emperor sternly said:
"Use many oxen to pull it down!"
Chéngcuǐ then dared not speak.
In total, one hundred oxen were used to pull it down,
and only then did it collapse.

Hòu Xué Tiān Tái
4th year of Yuánhé
(Jǐchǒu, 809)
1 Autumn,
7th month,
Rénxū day.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Lǐ Yíjiǎn impeached Jīngzhàoyǐn Yáng Píng,
who, when formerly Jiangxi Guāncháshǐ, had been corrupt, extravagant, and presumptuous.
Dīngmǎo day,
Píng was demoted to Línhè Wèi.
Línhè,
a Hàn county,
belonged to Cángwú Jùn,
named after the Línhè River.
Hence the name.
In the Táng dynasty, it was part of Hèzhōu.
He was the great-great-grandson of Yuányì.
Zhèng Wáng Yuányì was
the son of Gāozǔ.
Possessions, fields, and gardens,
which people use to live,
are called assets.
"The old system states that,
unless it is rebellion, their family property should not be confiscated."
The emperor then stopped.
None of Píng's relatives and friends dared to see him off,
except Lìyáng Wèi Xú Huì, who alone went to Lántián to bid him farewell.
Tàicháng Qīng Quán Déyú, who had always been on good terms with Huì,
said to him:
"Your seeing off Yáng Línhè
is truly generous,
but will it not bring trouble upon you?"
He replied:
"Since I was a commoner, I received the recognition and support of Duke Yáng.
Now that he is banished far away,
how can I not bid him farewell?
Even if, for example, you, esteemed Duke, were someday persecuted by slanderers,
would I dare to treat you as a mere passerby?"
Déyú sighed in admiration
and praised him at court.
A few days later,
Lǐ Yíjiǎn recommended him to be Jiānchá Yùshǐ (Investigating Censor).
Huì thanked him, saying:
"I have never in my life had the honor of seeing your face, esteemed Duke.
How did you come to choose me?"
Yíjiǎn said:
"You would not betray Yáng Línhè,
how could you betray the state?"
2 The emperor secretly asked the academicians:
"I now wish to appoint Wáng Chéngzōng as the Liúhòu of Chéngdé,
and separate Dé and Dì two prefectures to form another military circuit (zhèn) to weaken his power.
At the same time, I want Chéngzōng to pay the two taxes,
and request officials,
exactly as Lǐ Shīdào did.
What do you think?"
The matter of Lǐ Shīdào
can be found in the first year of the previous volume.
"Dé and Dì have belonged to Chéngdé
for a long time.
In the early Zhēnyuán period,
Wáng Wǔjùn defeated Zhū Tāo
and took Dé and Dì.
I fear that Chéngzōng and his generals and soldiers will become worried, suspicious, and resentful,
and use this as a pretext.
Moreover, the neighboring circuits are in a similar situation,
each fearing future divisions,
and might secretly instigate trouble.
If, by any chance, they collectively resist,
it would be even more difficult to manage.
I wish you would reconsider."
Lǚ means
"multitude".
Lǚjù means to gather a multitude and resist an imperial order.
Chǔ
is pronounced "chāng lǚ fān".
Sān
is pronounced "xī zàn fān",
and also as written.
Regarding the two taxes and officials,
I wish that an envoy be sent there on the pretext of offering condolences and sacrifices,
and that he personally convey this idea to Chéngzōng,
instructing him to submit a memorial requesting it, following Lǐ Shīdào's precedent,
without letting him know that it originates from Your Majesty's intention.
If this is done,
and he fortunately complies,
it would be reasonable and proper.
If he does not comply,
Your Majesty's dignity would also not be harmed."
The Emperor again asked,
"Now, Liú Jì and Tián Jì'ān are both ill.
If they were to die,
the note on 'wùgù' has been seen in the Hàn Jì.
Shǐ Zhào said: Yán Shīgǔ said: Wùgù
means 'death,'
referring to becoming like a ghost and ceasing to be.
Another explanation is that,
not wishing to explicitly state it,
it merely means that all their possessions have become old.
When will the empire be at peace?
The debaters all say, 'We should seize this opportunity to replace them.
If they do not accept, we should send troops to punitive expedition.
The opportunity must not be lost.'
What do you think?"
The reply was:
"Your humble servants saw Your Majesty conquer Shǔ in the west
and Wú in the east.
Shǔ
refers to Liú Pì.
Wú
refers to Lǐ Qí.
Thus, sycophantic and restless people
'zào'
means impulsive.
'jìng'
means contending.
encouraged the opening of Héběi,
not deeply deliberating or planning far ahead for the state.
Your Majesty also, due to the ease of previous successes, believed their words.
Your servants have pondered this day and night:
the situation in Héběi is different from those two regions.
Why?
Xīchuān and Zhèxī were not places of wavering loyalty;
their neighbors were all ministers who were Your Majesty's 'arms and fingers.'
'Arms and fingers'
uses the meaning of Jiǎ Yì's words,
indicating their obedience.
Their subordinates did not support them,
and Pì and Qí merely lured them with wealth.
Once a large army arrived,
they scattered and disintegrated.
Therefore, your servants also advised Your Majesty to execute them at that time,
because it was a perfectly safe plan.
Chéngdé, however, is not like that.
Internally, it is deeply entrenched and solidified over the years;
externally, it is widely connected and powerful.
'Jiāogù'
means adhering firmly like glue.
'Mànlián'
means spreading and connecting like creeping vines.
They do not understand the principles of loyalty and rebellion between ruler and subject.
If persuaded, they do not comply;
if threatened, they do not submit,

Moreover,

If by any chance other circuits were to collude,

Xīróng

'Jiàn'
is pronounced gǔ xiàn fān;
same below.
Jì and Jì'ān's situations are not different from Chéngzōng's.
If, at the time of their demise,

To deploy troops now,

The achievement of great peace

At that time, Wú Shàochéng was gravely ill.

The situation in Huáixī is different from Héběi.

Your servants wish to abandon the difficult strategy for Héng and Jì,

If by chance Héng and Jì were to go to war

If both northern and southern campaigns were to start,

Jiàng and others' words

Authority would be completely lost.
It would be better to make an early decision

At this time, Héngzhōu had not yet been renamed Zhènzhōu;

Soon after, Chéngzōng, having long not received an imperial decree,

In the eighth month,
on the day of Rénwǔ,

Chéngzōng was initially afraid of the court's punitive expedition,

After receiving imperial clemency,

individuals who secretly persuaded, enticed, and coerced him,

Lǐ Jiàng can be said to have thoroughly seen the true intentions of Tián Jì'ān and Wáng Chéngzōng.
"Jiàn" (間),
pronounced "gǔ xiàn fān."
"Shuì" (說),
pronounced "shì ruì fān."
"Yòu" (誘),
pronounced "yǒu."
"Now, Your Majesty selected Wǔ to be an envoy into rebellious territory,

Shǐ Zhào said: "'Yī'ē' (依阿)

'Liǎngkě' (兩可)

"If this happens,

The emperor, after a long silence, said:
"Perhaps there is some truth to this."
So, he did not pursue the matter.
On the day of Bǐngchén,
Zhènwǔ reported that more than 50,000 Tubō cavalry had reached Fútī Quán.
Shǐ Zhào said: "Fú" (拂),
pronounced "bó wù qiē."
pronounced "tiān lí qiē."
The original text also writes

It is located 300 *lǐ* north of Shòuxiáng Chéng in Fēngzhōu.
On the day of Xīnwèi,
Fēngzhōu reported that over 10,000 Tubō cavalry had reached Dàshígǔ,
plundering the Huíhú who were returning to their country after paying tribute.
The officer Lǐ Yù of the Zuǒ Shéncè Jūn borrowed 8,000 *mín* of money from a rich man in Cháng'ān.
After three full years, he had not repaid it.
The Jīngzhào Yǐn Xǔ Mèngróng arrested and fettered him,

The entire army was greatly astonished.
The Zhōngwèi complained to the emperor,

Mèngróng did not release him.
The imperial envoy arrived a second time,

"Your subject disobeys the imperial edict and

How else can the capital be kept orderly and pure?
Until the money is fully repaid,

The emperor praised his uprightness and allowed it,

The emperor sent an imperial envoy to admonish Wáng Chéngzōng,
ordering him to send Xuē Chāngcháo back to his post;
and ordering him to send Dézhōu back.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day of Guǐwèi,
an imperial edict was issued to strip Chéngzōng of his official titles and ranks,

The Hànlín Xuéshì Bái Jūyì submitted a memorial,

the responsibility should be placed on the generals and commanders.

then Chéngcuǐ is the 'Zhìjiàng.'
'Zhìjiàng' (制將)
means that the advance and retreat of all armies are subject to Chéngcuǐ's command.
'Jiàng' (將),
pronounced 'jí liàng fān.'
Then Chéngcuǐ is the 'Dūtǒng.'
'Dūtǒng' (都統)
refers to the commander-in-chief of all armies,

by the imperial court;

Bái Jūyì's words come from the *Chūnqiū* record
"many fish leak masters,"
and the *Zuǒzhuàn*
"Sùshā Wèi held up the Qí army."
"Moreover, Tǔtū Chéngcuǐ is a eunuch who commands an independent expedition!
During the Chóng and Guān periods,
the Jurchens' insults and actions were precisely like this.
Your subject also fears that Liú Jì, Mào Zhāo, and Xī Cháo, Cóng Shǐ, and even the generals and officers of all circuits will be ashamed to receive commands from Chéngcuǐ.
With their hearts divided,
how can merit be established?
This is aiding Chéngzōng's schemes and thwarting the power of our generals.
Your Majesty, if you remember Chéngcuǐ's diligence and hard work,

if you pity his loyalty,

how can Your Majesty bear to indulge the feelings of subordinates and self-destruct the legal system,
to follow others' desires and diminish your own sagacious wisdom?
Why do you not consider this moment and avoid being ridiculed for ten thousand generations to come?"
At that time, censorial officials and imperial censors repeatedly argued that Chéngcuǐ's official title was too important,

On the day of Wùzǐ,
the emperor held court in the Yányīng Diàn.
Lǐ Yuánsù, Director of the Dùzhī, Lǐ Yǒng, Director of the Yán-Tiě, Xǔ Mèngróng, Jīngzhào Yǐn, Lǐ Yíjiǎn, Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,

If according to Chéngcuǐ's biography,

The next day,

Lǐ Qí said: "Zhí" (跖)

Shīgǔ said: Zhuāng Zhōu said that Zhí
was Liǔxiàhuì's younger brother.
This is an allegory.
"Gōng and Huáng" (龔、黃)
refer to Gōng Suí and Huáng Bà.
pronounced "yú."
"Qiáo" (蹻),
pronounced "jū lüè fān."
pronounced "fú fú fān."
"They create pretexts for suspicion,

On the day of Jǐhài,

8 In the beginning,
Wú Shàochéng favored his grand general, Wú Shàoyáng.

When Wú Shàochéng fell ill

his household servant Xiānyú Xióng'ér falsely used Wú Shàochéng's order to summon Wú Shàoyáng to act as deputy envoy and take charge of military and administrative affairs.
Wú Shàochéng had a son, Yuánqìng;
Wú Shàoyáng killed him.

Wú Shàochéng died,

9 This year,
Nánzhāo King Xún Géquàn died,

10 Tián Jì'ān, hearing that Tǔtū Chéngcuǐ was leading troops to attack Wáng Chéngzōng,
gathered his followers and said,
"The army has not crossed the river for twenty-five years!
Since Dézōng failed to conquer Tián Yuè,

Zhào is a captive,
and Wèi is also a captive.
What strategy should we adopt?"
Among his generals, there was one who "chāo wǔ" spoke.
"Chāo wǔ"
means speaking out of turn.
It means speaking out from among one's peers.
He said, "I wish to borrow five thousand cavalry to relieve your worries."
Tián Jì'ān shouted,
"Excellent!
The troops will definitely go out.
Whoever obstructs them will be executed!"
Tán Zhōng of Jiàng, a staff officer (yájiàng) from Yōuzhōu, was sent by Liú Jì to Wèi.
Knowing their plan, he entered and said to Tián Jì'ān,
"According to my humble opinion,
this plan
will draw the armies of the entire realm.
Why?
Now, the imperial army crosses Wèi to attack Zhào,
not entrusting it to veteran ministers and experienced generals, but solely to palace eunuchs.
'Qí'
means old.
'Sù'
means old, experienced.
The land within the passes (Guānzhōng)
is the ancient land of Qín.

wishing to boast and subdue his subordinates.
'Kuā fú'
means wishing to boast about his own calculations and strategies

In this case, the emperor's plan is inferior to that of his subordinates.
Furthermore,

Feeling both ashamed and angry,
he will certainly employ wise men to devise long-term strategies,

exert all efforts and again cross the river.
Learning from the previous defeat,
he will certainly not bypass Wèi to attack Zhào.
Weighing the severity of the crimes,
he will certainly not prioritize Zhào over Wèi.
Then, the emperor will not act as emperor,
and the subordinates will not act as subordinates.
They will come directly for Wèi."
Tián Jì'ān asked, "Then what should we do?"
Tán Zhōng replied,
"When the imperial army enters Wèi,

then the righteous warriors of Hébĕi will say Wèi betrayed a friend.
If Wèi sides with Zhào,

Wèi cannot bear to accept the reputation of betraying a friend and rebelling against its lord.
If Your Excellency can secretly dismantle the ramparts
and hand over one city to Wèi,
Wèi can then take it and report victory to the Son of Heaven as proof and trust.
This would allow Wèi to serve Zhào in the north
and serve as a minister in the west.
Cháng'ān is west of Wèi.
'Wéi chén' (serve as a minister)
means being able to obey the emperor's command

'Jiǎo jiān'
means the cost is small.

Tián Jì'ān said,
"Excellent!
The arrival of sir
means Heaven favors Wèi."
He then adopted Tán Zhōng's plan,

Tángyáng
was a Hàn county,
belonging to Jùlù Commandery.
In Táng, it belonged to Jìzhōu,
located southwest of the prefecture.
Tán Zhōng returned to Yōuzhōu,
intending to incite Liú Jì to attack Wáng Chéngzōng.
Coincidentally, Liú Jì gathered his generals and said,
"The Son of Heaven knows I resent Zhào.
Now he commands me to attack it.
'Jīn' (now)
should be 'bì' (certainly).
Is attacking or not attacking more beneficial?"
Tán Zhōng quickly replied,
"The Son of Heaven will ultimately not order me to attack Zhào,

Liú Jì angrily said,
"Why don't you directly say that I and Chéngzōng are in rebellion!"
He ordered Tán Zhōng to be imprisoned.
He sent someone to observe the border of Chéngdé,

One day later,
an imperial edict indeed arrived,

Liú Jì then released Tán Zhōng from prison and summoned him, saying,
"It is truly as you judged!"
'Jiě yù'
means releasing the prisoner.
'Duàn'
is pronounced Dīng-luàn.
Tán Zhōng said,
"Lú Cóngshǐ outwardly shows kinship with Yān,
but inwardly resents it.
Outwardly he cuts off Zhào,
but inwardly he colludes with it.
He advised Zhào, saying:
'Yān uses Zhào as a barrier.
Although it resents Zhào,
it will certainly not destroy Zhào,
so there is no need to make preparations.'
First, this shows Zhào that it dares not resist Yān.
Second, it causes Yān to incur the emperor's suspicion.
Since the people of Zhào do not prepare against Yān,
the people of Lù then run to inform the Son of Heaven, saying:
Lú Cóngshǐ governed Lùzhōu,
hence he is called 'person of Lù.'
'Zhào is being attacked but does not prepare against Yān;
this means Yān is secretly colluding with Zhào.'
This is how I knew the Son of Heaven would ultimately not order you to attack Zhào,
and Zhào would not prepare against Yān."
Liú Jì asked, "What should we do now?"
Tán Zhōng replied,
"That Yān and Zhào are enemies
is known to all under heaven.
Since Zhū Tāo,
Yān and Zhào have been hostile.
You sit with all the troops of Yān,
not a single man has crossed the Yìshuǐ.
This merely causes the people of Lù to say that Yān betrays kindness to Zhào
and undermines loyalty to the emperor.
It means that Yān was originally loyal to the emperor, but Lú Cóngshǐ, by his scheme, ruined that loyalty.
'Bài'
is pronounced Bǔ-mài.
'Mài wù qù shǒu yuē shòu.' (Selling goods and letting go of them is called 'shòu'.)
Ultimately, you are painted by the words of private agreement with Zhào,
gaining no virtue from the people of Zhào,
and only generating bad rumors noisily throughout the realm.
Only you, my lord, should carefully consider this!"
Liú Jì said, "I understand."
He then issued an order to his army, saying,
"All will deploy within five days!
Those who lag behind will be minced and displayed!"
Tán Zhōng somewhat possessed the style of a Warring States orator,
but his heart was for Táng.
