*Huán* (還),
pronounced *xuán*,
and also as written.
On the *xīnhài* day,
he was reinstated as Grand General of the Left Guard,
and appointed Commissioner of the Left Army.
*Péi Jì* said:
"*Chéngcuǐ* was the first to advocate for military action,"
(this event is found in the previous volume, 4th month of the previous year).
"He ultimately achieved no success.
Although Your Majesty, due to old favor, does not inflict a public execution upon him,"
(*Tútū Chéngcuǐ* served the Emperor in the Eastern Palace,
hence the mention of old favor).
"Assistant Remonstrants *Duàn Píngzhòng* and *Lǚ Yuányīng* stated that *Chéngcuǐ* deserved to be executed."
*Lǐ Jiàng* reported:
"If Your Majesty does not punish *Chéngcuǐ*,
should there be another general who suffers defeat in the future,
how will he be dealt with?
If he is executed,
then it would be different punishments for the same crime,
and they certainly would not submit.
If he is released,
then who would not prioritize self-preservation and toy with the enemy?
I wish Your Majesty would cut off the grace of not bearing to punish,
and enact the unchangeable law:
reward those with merit,
and execute those who suffer defeat.
This is an unchangeable law throughout history."
Two days later,
*jiān* (間),
pronounced as written.
He was demoted to Director of Military Armaments.
After the mid-Tang period,
various internal bureaus were established,
staffed by eunuchs;
the Director of Military Armaments was one of them.
*Sòng Bái* said: "Military armaments originally belonged to the Military Armaments Directorate.
In the middle period, the Director of Military Armaments was established.
In the 4th year of *Zhēnyuán*, the Imperial Armory was abolished,
and its weapons and equipment were subordinated to the Director of Military Armaments."
17th day of the 10th month, *Péi Jì* contracted a paralytic illness.
The Emperor deeply cherished him,
and imperial envoys continuously traversed the roads to inquire after him.
"One vertical and one horizontal" is the meaning of *pángwǔ*.
18th day of the 10th month, on the *bǐngyín* day,
*Quán Déyú*, Grand Master of Ceremonies, was appointed Minister of Rites and concurrently Grand Councilor.
19th day of the 10th month, *Zhāng Màozhāo*, Military Governor of *Yìwǔ*, requested to resign and be replaced,
wishing to bring his entire clan to the capital.
The various *Héběi* garrisons sent emissaries to persuade him to stop,
but *Màozhāo* did not comply,
submitting four memorials in total;
the Emperor then granted his request.
*Rèn Díjiǎn*, Left Chief Secretary of the Heir Apparent, was appointed Acting Military Governor of *Yìwǔ*.
*Màozhāo* handed over all the official documents, registers, and keys of *Yì* and *Dìng* prefectures to *Díjiǎn*,
and sent his wife and children ahead,
saying:
"I do not wish my descendants to be tainted by these corrupt customs."
After *Màozhāo* left,
in winter,
10th month,
on the *wùyín* day,
the Imperial Messenger *Yáng Bóyù* rebelled,
and imprisoned *Díjiǎn*.
On the *xīnsì* day,
the officers and soldiers of *Yìwǔ* jointly killed *Bóyù*.
The Commander of Forces *Zhāng Zuǒyuán* rebelled again,
imprisoning *Díjiǎn*,
who then begged to return to the capital.
Soon after, the officers and soldiers again killed *Zuǒyuán*,
and acclaimed *Díjiǎn* to take charge of military affairs.
At that time, the treasuries of *Yìdìng* were exhausted,
and the common households (*lǘyán*) were also empty.
(*Zhōulǐ*: "Five households form a *bǐ*,
five *bǐ* form a *lǘ*."
*Yán* (閻)
is the gate of a *lǐ*.)
He then set up coarse meals and ate with the soldiers,
residing under the *jǐmén* for a month.
(The gates of *fānzhèn* administrative offices were arrayed with halberds,
hence they were called *jǐmén*.)
All of them requested *Díjiǎn* to return to his quarters,
and only then did he manage to settle into his position.
The Emperor ordered 100,000 bolts of silk to be bestowed upon the officers and soldiers of *Yìdìng*.
On the *rénchén* day,
*Díjiǎn* was appointed Military Governor of *Yìwǔ*.
*Xiànzōng* used *Rèn Díjiǎn* and gained *Yìdìng*;
*Mùzōng* used *Zhāng Hóngjìng* and lost *Yōuyān*.
How careful one must be when appointing military governors to the border regions!
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
*Zhāng Màozhāo* was appointed Military Governor of *Hézhōng*, *Cí*, *Xí*, *Jìn*, and *Jiàng* prefectures,
and all the accompanying generals and officers were granted official titles.
20th day of the 10th month, Grand General of the Right *Jīnwú*, *Yī Shèn*, bribed Commissioner of the Right Army *Dìwǔ Cóngzhí* with 30,000 *mín* of money,
seeking the position of Military Governor of *Hézhōng*.
*Cóngzhí* feared the matter would be exposed,
and reported it.
11th month,
on the *gēngzǐ* day,
*Shèn* was demoted to General of the Right Guard,
and three people were executed for their involvement.
Previously,
*Shèn* had arrived at the capital from *Ānzhōu*.
(His arrival at the capital is found in the previous volume, 1st year of *Yuánhé*.)
The imperial court had consequently appointed him Prefect of *Ānzhōu*,
but he had not yet been able to depart.
Coincidentally, his mother died in *Cháng'ān*.
*Yòu* coveted military authority,
and did not announce the mourning in time.
*Xī Shìměi*, Observer of *Èyuè*, sent a subordinate on official business through his territory.
*Yòu* came out to greet him,
and then informed him of the unfortunate news,
(unfortunate news,
the news of his mother's death).
He immediately sent him away.
A bamboo palanquin,
is what is called a sedan chair today.
21st day of the 10th month, on the *jiǎchén* day,
*Wáng Xūn* passed away.
*Xūn*
was the Emperor's younger brother.
*Hōng* (薨),
pronounced *hōng* (呼肱翻).
22nd day, Gēngxū [of the 8th month],
Wáng È, formerly the Jiedushi of Hézhōng, was appointed Jiedushi of Hédōng.
Those around the Emperor received substantial bribes from È,
and many praised him.
The Emperor ordered È to concurrently hold the title of Píngzhāngshì,
but Lǐ Fān firmly insisted it was unacceptable.
Quán Déyú said:
"Prime minister is not a position advanced through seniority.
Since the rise of the Táng dynasty,
regional commanders have only received it if they demonstrated great loyalty and merit, or if they were unruly [and the court had no choice].
The court sometimes granted it out of necessity.
Now È has neither loyal service [to his name],
nor is the court in a position of necessity;
why should this title be hastily conferred upon him!"
The Emperor then stopped.
The Kǎoyì says: The old biography of Lǐ Fān states:
"È bribed Quán Shì with tens of millions of coins,
seeking to concurrently become prime minister.
Fān and Quán Déyú were in the Zhōngshū [shě] and
received a secret imperial edict that said: 'Wáng È may concurrently be prime minister;
an immediate draft proposal is required.'
Fān then used his brush to cross out the words 'concurrently be prime minister,'
and
reported back to the Emperor, saying: 'This is not acceptable.'
Déyú paled and said: 'Even if it's not acceptable,
you should write a separate memorial;
how can you use a brush to cross out an imperial edict!'
Fān replied: 'The situation is urgent;
if it goes out today,
it cannot be stopped,
and it's already late in the day,
how can I find time to write another memorial.'
The matter was indeed dropped."
The Huìyào states: "Cuī Xuàn said:
'This is a baseless rumor spread by someone unfamiliar with past practices,
and a mistaken record by the historian.
Since it was a secret imperial edict,
a memorial should have been drafted to express one's views,
certainly not by crossing out the edict with a brush.
Whenever a 'white imperial edict' is to be issued,
if it is discussed in the Zhōngshū and Ménxià,
the documents are submitted the day before,
and then handed to the Hànlín to draft the edict.'
It also states: Fān said:
'The situation is urgent;
if it goes out today,
it cannot be stopped'
which is particularly careless.
This is probably because historians, given Fān's reputation for forthrightness and integrity,
wished to artfully embellish his virtues.
How can this be called 'straightforward writing'!"
The old biography of Déyú states:
"Initially,
when È came to court,
many favored officials praised È,
and the Emperor was about to add the title Píngzhāngshì,
but Lǐ Fān firmly insisted it was unacceptable,
and Déyú subsequently memorialized as stated,
whereupon it stopped."
We now follow this account.
È had administrative talent [and]
was skilled at accumulation and preservation.
Fàn Xīcháo had led the entire Hédōng army to station in Héběi,
saying it was to attack Wáng Chéngzōng.
When È first arrived at the garrison,
his army was less than thirty thousand men,
and his horses no more than six hundred.
After a year,
his troops reached fifty thousand men,
his horses five thousand,
his weapons were sharp and efficient,
and his storehouses were full.
He also presented 300,000 strings of his private wealth.
The Emperor again wished to add the title Píngzhāngshì to È,
but Lǐ Jiàng remonstrated, saying:
"Although È has shown considerable achievements in Tàiyuán,
if he is appointed now because of his offering of private wealth,
what will happen in later generations!"
The Emperor then stopped.
23rd day, Zhōngshū Shìláng
Péi Jì repeatedly resigned his position due to illness;
on Gēngshēn [of the 9th month],
he was dismissed and made Bīngbù Shàngshū.
24th day, in the twelfth month,
Wùyín [of the 12th month],
Zhāng Màozhāo came to court
and requested to move the bones of his ancestors to Jīngzhào.
Zhāng Màozhāo's grandfather Mì and father Xiàozhōng
were both buried in Héběi.
25th day, Rénwǔ [of the 12th month],
Lǚ Yuányīng, an Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng, was appointed Èyuè Guānchásǐ.
Yuányīng once tried to ascend the city wall at night;
the gate was already locked,
and the guards would not open it for him.
His attendants said:
"He is the Zhōngchéng."
The guard replied:
"It is difficult to distinguish true from false at night,
even if he is the Zhōngchéng, it is not permissible."
Yuányīng then returned.
The next day,
he was promoted to an important position.
26th day, Hànlín Xuéshì and Sīxūn Lángzhōng Lǐ Jiàng personally presented his case against Tǔtū Chéngcuǐ's arrogance and tyranny,
speaking with utmost sincerity.
The Emperor's countenance changed, and he said:
"Your words are too extreme!"
Jiàng wept and said:
"Your Majesty has placed me in a position of trust, as your confidant and informant.
If I were to shrink back in fear of those around me,
cherishing my life and not speaking,
then I would be failing Your Majesty;
but if I speak and Your Majesty dislikes hearing it,
then Your Majesty is failing me."
The Emperor's anger subsided,
and he said:
"What you have said is what others cannot say,
allowing me to hear what I have not heard;
you are truly a loyal subject.
In the future, speak fully,
always as you have now."
On Jǐchǒu [of the 12th month],
Jiàng was appointed Zhōngshū Shèrén,
his position as Xuéshì remaining unchanged.
Jiàng once gently admonished the Emperor for accumulating wealth.
The Emperor said:
"Now, dozens of prefectures in the two Hé regions [Héběi and Hénán]
are all beyond the reach of the state's governance,
and thousands of *lǐ* of Hénán and Húi are
lost to the northern barbarians.
Day and night I think of washing away the shame of my ancestors,
but my financial resources are insufficient;
hence, I have no choice but to accumulate.
Otherwise,
my palace expenses are extremely frugal,
what use is much storage!"
After Huáixī was pacified,
the wealth the Emperor had accumulated
merely became capital for extravagance and luxury.
1st year, Spring,
first month,
Jiǎchén [of the 1st month],
Wú Shàoyáng, the Liúhòu of Zhāngyì, was appointed Jiedushi.
2nd day, Gēngshēn [of the 1st month],

Second month,
Rénshēn [of the 2nd month],
Lǐ Fān was dismissed and made Tàizǐ Zhānshì.

4th day, The eunuchs disliked Lǐ Jiàng being in the Hànlín,
so they had him appointed Hùbù Shìláng,
*pàn běn sī*.
*Pàn běn sī* meant *pàn Hùbù zhíshì*.
From the middle of the Táng dynasty onwards,
Hùbù Shìláng sometimes *pàn dùzhī*,
hence *pàn Hùbù* was called *pàn běn sī*;
this *sī* refers to one of the twenty-four offices.
[The Emperor asked:] "'According to custom,
Hùbù Shìláng all present surplus funds;
why do you alone present none?'
He replied:
'Local officials,
who collect heavily from the people to buy personal favors,
are still criticized by all under heaven;
moreover, all that the Hùbù manages
are items in Your Majesty's treasury,
with records for disbursements and receipts,
how could there be a surplus!
If it were to be transferred from the Zuǒzàng to the Nèizàng
as a tribute,
it would be like moving from the Eastern Treasury to the Western Treasury;
your servant dares not follow this corrupt practice.'
From the time of Xuánzōng,
Wáng È annually presented money to fund the Son of Heaven's private banquets,
and this abuse reached its peak with Péi Yánlíng.
[The Emperor] esteemed him even more.
5th day, Yǐsì [of the 2nd month],
the Emperor asked his prime ministers:
"Which should come first in governance, leniency or severity?"
Quán Déyú replied:
"Qín perished due to its cruelty,
and Hàn flourished due to its generosity.
Tàizōng, upon viewing the Míngtáng Diagram,
prohibited striking people on the back;
this event is recorded in volume 193, Zhēngguān 4th year.
*Chì*
is pronounced chǒu lì fān.
There have been several rebellious officials
who all quickly brought about their own downfall,
because the benevolent governance of the ancestors had deeply settled in people's hearts,
and people could not forget it.
Thus, the precedence of leniency and severity can be seen."
The Emperor praised his words.
6 In summer,
in the fourth month,

Péi Jì, the Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū), was appointed Guest of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Bīnkè).
Lǐ Jífǔ disliked this.
7 On the day Gēngwǔ,

Lú Tǎn, the Assistant Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shìláng) and Commissioner of Salt and Iron Transport (Yántiě Zhuǎnyùnshǐ), was appointed Assistant Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shìláng) and Administrator of the Financial Bureau (Pàndùzhī).
Someone accused Xuē Jiǎn, the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Sìzhōu, of being the Commissioner of Water Transport for Dàiběi
and possessing an unusual horse which he did not present (to the emperor).
The matter was sent down to the Financial Bureau (Dùzhī),
which dispatched an inspecting official to investigate.
Before his return,
the emperor grew impatient
and sent Liú Tàixīn, a court official (pǐnguān), to further investigate the matter.
The Tang Imperial Household Department (Nèishìshěng) had 2,932
low-ranking
court officials.
Xīn
is pronounced like "Xǔ Jīn".
"Your Majesty has already sent a responsible official to investigate,
and now you send another court official to follow.
Is it that the high ministers are not as trustworthy as the court officials?
I request to be immediately dismissed."
The emperor recalled Tàixīn.
8 In the fifth month,
Yú Gāomó and Dǒng Xī, former Commissioners for Grain Supply for the Mobile Army (Xíngyíng Liángliàoshǐ),
were with the mobile army.
This refers to the mobile army that was previously sent to attack Héngzhōu.
An edict pardoned them from death;
Gāomó was exiled to Chūnzhōu,
and Xī was exiled to Fēngzhōu.
When they reached Tánzhōu,
both were pursued and given death by imperial envoys.
Chūnzhōu was the territory of Gāoliáng County, Hépǔ Commandery, in the Hàn dynasty.
In the Suí dynasty, it was Yángchūn County of Gāoliáng Commandery.
In the Táng dynasty, Chūnzhōu was established,
6,448 lì southeast of the capital.
Fēngzhōu was
4,510 lì by water and land from the capital.
Tánzhōu was
the ancient Chángshā Commandery.
In the Jìn dynasty, Xiāngzhōu was established.
In the Suí dynasty, it was changed to Tánzhōu,
2,445 lì south of the capital.
It was believed:
"Gāomó and the others deserved death.
If Your Majesty were to execute them publicly in the market and court,"
Hé Yàn said: 'To display a corpse after execution is called sì.'
"Cháo"
is pronounced "zhí yáo".
"You should not have pardoned them and then killed them."
Xī was
Dǒng Jìn's son.
Dǒng Jìn served as Chancellor (Xiāng) under Dèzōng,
and later governed Xuānwǔ.
He died in office.
9 On the day Gēngzǐ,
Lǐ Wéijiǎn, the Grand General of the Right Imperial Guards (Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn), was appointed Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Fèngxiáng.
Lǐ Wéijiǎn was
the younger brother of Wéiyuè.
Previously, there was constant surveillance day and night,
with raids and skirmishes,
giving people no rest.
Wéijiǎn believed that a frontier general should carefully maintain defenses
and store wealth and grain to await invaders,
and should not covet small gains,
provoke incidents to usurp favor,
create trouble to seek功,
or illicitly obtain official rewards.
This is what is meant by "usurping favor".
He prohibited unauthorized entry into Tubó territory.
He cast farm implements
to supply those farmers who could not afford to procure them themselves,
increasing cultivated land by several hundred thousand mù.
For several years in a row, the harvests were abundant,
and both public and private coffers had surplus,
with merchants trading it to other regions.
10 Àdiē Guāngjìn, the Military Governor of Zhènwǔ (Zhènwǔ Jiédùshǐ), was granted the surname Lǐ.
11 In the sixth month,
on the day Dīngmǎo,
Lǐ Jífǔ memorialized:
"From Qín to Suí, there were thirteen dynasties."
Jífǔ's "thirteen dynasties"
counts Qín, Hàn, Wèi, Jìn, Sòng, Qí, Liáng, Chén, Běiwèi, Běiqí, Zhōu, and Suí.
"None are like our present state.
After Tiānbǎo,
the standing army in the central plains,
of those that can be counted, numbered over 800,000.
Of the rest, five or six tenths were merchants, monks, or Daoists who did not cultivate land.
This means that three tenths of the people who labor with their muscles and bones support seven tenths of those who merely await clothing and food.
Currently, the internal and external officials who are paid with tax money number no less than ten thousand.
Of the over three hundred counties in the realm,
many have a single county's territory forming a prefecture (zhōu),
or a single village's populace forming a county (xiàn).
I request an imperial edict for the responsible authorities to carefully consider abolishing or establishing them,
to reduce official positions where possible,
to merge prefectures and counties where possible,
and to limit the avenues for entering officialdom.
Furthermore,
according to the old regulations of the state,
salaries were set by rank.
A first-rank official received a monthly salary of thirty mǐn in cash.
By the Yǒnghuī regulations,
a first-rank official received eight thousand [cash] monthly.
In the 24th year of Kāiyuán,
it was decreed that the salaries and miscellaneous expenses for guards and servants of all officials
be paid monthly,
collectively called 'monthly salary',
with a first-rank official receiving 31,000 cash.
In the early Táng, a first-rank official was given sixty qǐng of official land and seven hundred dàn of grain.
With the increase in the number of commissioners and generous salaries,
since the outbreak of war,
powerful ministers have held multiple concurrent positions as commissioners,
receiving generous monthly salaries,
many times the amount specified in the Kāiyuán regulations.
Powerful ministers received up to nine thousand mǐn in monthly salary,
and prefects (cìshǐ), regardless of the size of their prefecture,
all received one thousand mǐn.
The Xīn Zhì states: 'Powerful ministers sometimes received up to nine hundred thousand,
and prefects also received up to one hundred thousand',
which refers to these figures.
Limits were first set,
as seen in volume 225, Dàlì 12th year of Dàizōng.
They were increased as circumstances changed,
as seen in volume 233, Zhēnyuán 4th year of Dèzōng.
Liàng,
pronounced liáng,
same below.
It is difficult to reduce them.
However, there are still positions that exist in name but are defunct in function,
or positions that have been abolished but their salaries remain,
and between idle and busy positions,
the remuneration varies greatly.
I request an imperial edict for the responsible authorities to carefully examine salaries, provisions, and miscellaneous allowances,
and to determine and report them."
According to records, when Cháng Gǔn was Chancellor,
he increased the stipends for regular officials in the capital and for Inspector-Commissioners (Guāncháchǐ) and Commander-Commissioners (Túantuànliànshǐ) and their deputies in all circuits.
When Lǐ Bì was Chancellor,
he again increased the monthly salaries for all officials and officials within the capital region,
and reinstated annual allowances for manual laborers and miscellaneous expenses.
Grand Generals of the Left and Right Imperial Guards (Zuǒ, Yòuwèi Shàngjiāngjūn) and below also received six types of miscellaneous allowances:
first, grain and rice;
second, salt;
third, private horses;
fourth, manual laborers;
fifth, personal attendants;
and sixth, spring and winter clothing.
Private horses came with fodder and beans;
manual laborers came with monetary allowances;
personal attendants came with grain, rice, and salt;
spring and winter clothing came with cloth, silk, coarse silk, tussah silk, and cotton.
The Grand Generals of the Imperial Hunting Guards (Shèshēng Dàjiāngjūn) and the Divine Strategy Army (Shéncè Dàjiāngjūn) were also given shoes.
Prefectural and county officials received allowances for manual laborers and miscellaneous expenses.
Lǐ Jífǔ requested a thorough review and adjustment of these.
12 In autumn,
in the ninth month,
Liáng Yuè of Fùpíng avenged his father's murder
by killing Qín Gǎo,
then went to the county office to confess and await punishment.
An imperial edict stated:
"Regarding revenge,
according to the Rites Classics, one cannot live under the same sky as one's father's killer."
The Lǐjì says: 'One cannot live under the same sky as one's father's enemy.'
"The Rites and the Law are two matters,
both fundamental to royal teachings.
Given this discrepancy,
it naturally warrants debate.
It is appropriate for the Grand Secretariat (Dūshěng) to convene a discussion and report to Us."
Dūshěng refers to
the Grand Secretariat of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Dūshěng).
It was believed:
"The law has no such article,
not because it is missing.
If revenge is not permitted,
it would harm the heart of a filial son and go against the teachings of the former kings.
If revenge is permitted,
people will rely on this to kill indiscriminately,
and there will be no way to stop such practices.
Therefore, the sages meticulously elucidated its meaning in the classics
but deeply obscured its text in the law.
Their intention was to let legal officials rule solely by law,
while scholars of the classics could cite the classics for discussion.
It is appropriate to establish the regulation as follows:
'Whenever a case of avenging a father's murder occurs,
once the incident is reported,
it shall be fully submitted to the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshūshěng) for collective deliberation and memorialization,
and an appropriate decision shall be made based on the circumstances.'
This way, neither the classics nor the laws will lose their purport."
An imperial edict stated:
"Liáng Yuè shall receive one hundred strokes of the rod and be exiled to Xúnzhōu."
Xúnzhōu was
the ancient territory of Lóngchuān County.
Old records state: 'It was 4,800 lì from the Eastern Capital.'
Adding the distance from the Eastern Capital to the capital,
the distance can be understood.
13 On the day Jiǎyín,
the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù) memorialized in accordance with an imperial edict that a total of 808 internal and external officials,
and 1,769 non-ranking personnel from various departments, had been merged and reduced.
14 In Qiánzhōu, a great flood damaged the city walls and moats.
Investigating Commissioner Dòu Yǐng dispatched the tribal peoples of the mountain streams and caves to repair them.
The Investigating Commissioner of Qiánzhōng governed Zhèn, Jǐn, Shī, Xù, Jiǎng, Yí, Bō, Sī, Fèi, Nán, Xī, and Zhēn Prefectures,
and also had fifty Jīmí Prefectures,
which were mostly the tribal peoples of the mountain streams and caves.
Zhì (治),
pronounced like "zhí" in "zhí zhī fān" (直之翻).
Thereupon, the tribal peoples of Zhèn and Xù Prefectures revolted.
Xùzhōu
was originally Wūzhōu.
In the second year of Tiānshòu, it was changed to Yuánzhōu.
In the thirteenth year of Kāiyuán, because Yuán and Yuán (沅、原) sounded similar,
it was again made Wūzhōu.
In the fifth year of Dàlì, it was renamed Xùzhōu.
*Kǎoyì* says: The old tradition says
"Zhèn and Jǐn Prefectures,"
but we follow the *Shílù* (實錄) here.
It cannot be determined.
On the day Wùwǔ,
Dòu Yǐng was demoted to Inspector of Kāizhōu.
Kāizhōu
was governed from Kāijiāng County,
named after the county,
one thousand four hundred and sixty *lǐ* south of the capital.
15 In winter,
in the eleventh month,
Liú Xīguāng, the Director of the Bow and Arrow Arsenal,
was a Director of one of the Inner Bureaus in the Táng.
The Director of the Bow and Arrow Arsenal was subordinate to the Director of the Military Equipment Arsenal.
sought a position in the frontier commands.

On the day Bǐngshēn,

if he committed any transgression,

16 As the princes of the Sixteen Mansions no longer left their quarters,
*Kǎoyì* says: The new biography of Lǐ Jífǔ writes
"Ten Mansions."
According to the old annals,
from this time until the end of the Táng,
it always says
"Sixteen Mansions."
The new biography is mistaken.
I note that since Kāiyuán,
many imperial sons resided in the Forbidden City.
An imperial edict ordered a large palace to be built adjoining the imperial park,
where they lived in separate courtyards,
known as the Ten Princes' Mansions,
guarded by eunuchs.
They would pay respects to the Emperor's daily life from the adjacent city walls.
Later, they were increased to Sixteen Mansions.
The old history says: In Kāiyuán, a large mansion was built east of Ānguó Temple, adjoining the imperial park,
where they resided in separate courtyards,
known as the Ten Princes' Mansions.
The ten princes were
Qìng, Zhōng, Dì, È, Yí, Yǐng, Yǒng, Róng, Yán, and Jì.
Later, the six princes, Shèng, Yí, Shòu, Fēng,
Héng, and Liáng, were also granted their titles and moved into the inner mansions.
This is the origin of the name Sixteen Mansions.
Those chosen for marriage (to the princesses) were all selected by eunuchs,
who generally advanced through generous bribes.
Lǐ Jífǔ submitted a memorial stating:
"Since ancient times, when marrying a princess, the person was always carefully chosen,
but this has not been the case in recent times."
In the twelfth month,
on the day Rénshēn,
an imperial edict enfeoffed the six daughters of the Prince of Ēn and others as County Princesses,
entrusting the Central Secretariat, the Chancellery, the Court of Imperial Clan Affairs, and the Ministry of Personnel to select those whose family background and talent were suitable for marriage.

Lǐ Jiàng, the Vice Minister of Revenue, was made Central Secretariat Grandee and concurrently Grand Chancellor.
*Kǎoyì* says: The old biography states:
"Tǔtū Chéngcuǐ's favor and trust were unparalleled.
That year,
when Lǐ Jiàng was about to be made chancellor, Chéngcuǐ was sent out as Inspector of Huáinán the day before;

The new biography states:
"Everything Lǐ Jiàng said was heeded by the Emperor,

But Chéngcuǐ's favor was at its height,
and he resented Lǐ Jiàng's advancement,
secretly slandering him.
The Emperor then sent Chéngcuǐ out as Inspector of Huáinán;
the next day,
Lǐ Jiàng was appointed Grand Chancellor."
Now, according to the *Shílù*,
there were fifty-four days between Chéngcuǐ's departure and Lǐ Jiàng's appointment as chancellor.
The old biography's statement
"the next day"
is mistaken.
Many repaired old grievances,
and the Emperor was somewhat aware of this,
hence he promoted Lǐ Jiàng to chancellor.
Lǐ Jífǔ was skilled at flattering the Emperor's wishes,
while Lǐ Jiàng was upright and outspoken,
often arguing before the Emperor.
The Emperor often sided with Lǐ Jiàng and followed his advice,
which caused a rift between the two men.
18 In the intercalary month,
on the first day, Xīnmǎo,
Qiánzhōu reported that the rebel leader Zhāng Bójìng from Zhèn and Xù attacked Bōzhōu and Fèizhōu.
19 Lǐ Shè, a Probationary Attendant of the Crown Prince,
In the Táng, the Crown Prince's Attendants belonged to the Right Spring Chamber,
with eight members, ranked lower seventh grade,
responsible for guiding palace officials in audiences and conveying imperial orders and condolences.
This was an official post.
Lǐ Shè, however, was a probationary official.
submitted a memorial to the imperial suggestion box,
claiming that
"Chéngcuǐ had rendered meritorious service,
and Xīguāng was innocent.

and should not be hastily discarded."
Kǒng Kuí, the Commissioner of the Imperial Suggestion Box and Remonstrance Official, saw his duplicate memorial,
rebuked him and refused to accept it.
Lǐ Shè then offered bribes
and went to Guāngshùn Gate to submit it.
Kǒng Kuí heard of this
and submitted a memorial strongly stating
that "Lǐ Shè was cunning and treacherous, deceiving Heaven,
and requested that he be publicly executed."
On the day Wùshēn,
Lǐ Shè was demoted to Storehouse Supervisor of Xiázhōu.
Xiázhōu was
ancient Yílíng territory.
Shǔ established Yídū Commandery.
Liáng established Yízhōu.
The Later Wèi changed it to Tuòzhōu;
taking the meaning of "opening up" or "expanding."
Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu renamed it Xiázhōu
because the prefecture commanded the entrance to the Three Gorges.
The old gazetteer states: Xiázhōu
is one thousand eight hundred and eighty-eight *lǐ* southeast of the capital.
(Lǐ Shè was) the elder brother of Bó.
Lǐ Bó was then living in seclusion on Shàoshì Mountain.
(Kǒng Kuí was) the son of Cháofù.
Kǒng Cháofù died during Lǐ Huáiguāng's rebellion.
20 On the day Xīnhài,
Huìzhāo Tàizǐ Níng died.
Níng was established as Crown Prince;
see the third month of the fourth year in the previous volume.
21 That year,
the empire had a great harvest,
and a *dòu* of rice sometimes cost only two coins.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Xīnwèi,
Yuán Yìfāng, the Mayor of Jīngzhào, was made Investigating Commissioner of Fūfāng.
Initially,
Yìfāng fawned upon Tǔtū Chéngcuǐ.
Lǐ Jífǔ, wanting to ingratiate himself with Chéngcuǐ,
promoted Yìfāng to Mayor of Jīngzhào.
Lǐ Jiàng disliked Yìfāng's character,
and thus had him removed.
Yìfāng came to express his gratitude,
and then said
that "Lǐ Jiàng showed favoritism to his colleague Xǔ Jìtóng,
appointing him Junior Mayor of Jīngzhào,
and sending me out to Fūfāng,
exercising arbitrary power and deceiving the intelligent Emperor."
The Emperor said:
"I understand Lǐ Jiàng not to be like that.
Tomorrow,
I will question him."
Yìfāng left feeling ashamed and uneasy.
The next day,
the Emperor questioned Lǐ Jiàng, saying:
"Do people indeed have feelings for their colleagues (from the same examination year)?"
He replied:
"Colleagues
are merely people from the nine provinces and four seas who coincidentally passed the same imperial examination.
They may have only met after passing the examination,
so what feelings could there be?
Táng people referred to successful candidates in the same imperial examination as 'colleagues' (同年),
and this is still the case today.
Holding the position of chancellor,
a chancellor's duty is to assess talent and assign duties accordingly.
If a person truly possesses talent,
even if they are among one's brothers or nephews, they should still be employed,
let alone a colleague!
To avoid suspicion and abandon talent
is self-serving,
not public-spirited."
The Emperor said:
"Good,
I knew you would not do that."
He then urged Yìfāng to proceed to his post.
2 The Zhènbǔ Hé
overflowed, destroying Dōngshòuxiáng Chéng.
Dōngshòuxiáng Chéng was by the river,
and when the river overflowed,
the city was thus destroyed.
3 In the third month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
His Majesty was in the Yányīng Diàn.
Lǐ Jífǔ said,
"The world is already at peace.
Your Majesty should enjoy yourself."
Lǐ Jiàng said,
"During the time of Hàn Wéndì, weapons were without sharp edges,
and every family had enough, every person was well-provided.
Yet Jiǎ Yì still considered it like being under a piled-up薪 fire,
not to be called safe.
(See volume 14, Hàn Wéndì's 6th year.)
Over fifty prefectures north and south of the Hé;
the Quǎnrong, with their rank smell,
are close to Jīng and Lǒng,
with beacons frequently alarming us.
(According to the Táng Liùdiǎn: Beacon posts were generally set up
every thirty *lǐ*.
If there were mountains or ridges separating them,
they had to be placed conveniently
so they could be seen from each other,
not necessarily limited to thirty *lǐ*.
Those close to the border
were built with walls, and
each beacon post had one commander and one deputy.
Beacons were lit with one, two, three, or four torches,
varying according to the number of invaders.)
Granaries are empty.
This is precisely the time for Your Majesty to work from dawn till late,
how can it be called peaceful
and quickly indulge in pleasure?"
His Majesty said delightedly,
"Your words perfectly match my intentions."
Upon withdrawing,
he said to his attendants,
"Lǐ Jífǔ only seeks to please;
as for Lǐ Jiàng,
he is a true chancellor!"
His Majesty once asked the chancellors,
"During the Zhēnyuán period, governance was not well-managed.
How did it come to this?"
Lǐ Jífǔ replied,
"Dézōng relied on his own sagely wisdom,
not trusting the chancellors but trusting others,
which allowed wicked officials to take advantage and wield power and influence.
The poor governance
was due to this reason."
His Majesty said,
"However, this may not be entirely Dézōng's fault.
When I was young, I was by Dézōng's side,
and I saw things that went right and wrong,
but the chancellors at that time also did not repeatedly insist on their remonstrances.
They all coveted their stipends and sought easy comfort.
How can we solely blame Dézōng today?
You and your colleagues should take this as a warning.
If there are things that are wrong,
you must strongly remonstrate without ceasing.
Do not fear my displeasure and stop abruptly."
Lǐ Jífǔ once said,
"A subject should not remonstrate too strongly.
(The Zuǒ Zhuàn says: Gōngzhīqí as a person
was timid and could not remonstrate strongly.
Lù Démíng's Yīnyì says: *Qiáng*,
read as *qí liáng fān*,
also *qí liǎng fān*.)
Is this not beautiful?"
Lǐ Jiàng said,
"A subject should bravely speak out with bitter words,
pointing out what is right and wrong.
If one allows the sovereign to fall into evil,
how can one be considered loyal?"
His Majesty said,
"Jiàng's words are correct."
When Lǐ Jífǔ arrived at the Zhōngshū,
he lay down and did not attend to affairs,
only sighing.
If Lǐ Jiàng sometimes did not remonstrate for a long time,
His Majesty would question him, saying,
"Is it that I cannot tolerate it,
or is there truly nothing to remonstrate about?"
Lǐ Jífǔ also once said to His Majesty,
"Rewards and punishments
are the two handles of the ruler,
neither can be abandoned.
Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
your benevolent favors have been profound;
but your awesome punishments have not yet been enforced,
and officials within and outside the court are lax.
I wish you would increase strictness to reinvigorate them."
His Majesty looked at Lǐ Jiàng and asked,
"What do you think?"
He replied,
"The governance of a king
values virtue, not punishment.
How can one abandon Chéng, Kāng, Wén, and Jǐng, and imitate Qín Shǐhuáng and his son?"
His Majesty said,
"That is right."
More than ten days later,
Yú Dí entered for an audience
and also advised His Majesty to impose severe punishments.
A few days later,
His Majesty said to the chancellors,
"Yú Dí is a great wicked official.
He advised me to impose severe punishments.
Do you know his intention?"
They all replied,
"We do not know."
His Majesty said,
"He wishes to make me lose the hearts of the people."
Lǐ Jífǔ's face changed color.
He withdrew, bowed his head, and did not speak or smile for the entire day.
His Majesty considered Yú Dí's words about severe punishments to be wicked,
hence Lǐ Jífǔ was ashamed of his previous misguided words.

Cuī Yuán, *Kùbù Lángzhōng* and *Hànlín Xuéshì*, was appointed *Zhōngshū Shèrén*,

He ordered the speedy remission of their taxes and levies.
His Majesty once discussed the art of governance with the chancellors in the Yányīng Diàn.
It was late in the day,
and very hot.

The chancellors feared His Majesty was tired

His Majesty kept them, saying,

those I associate with are only palace women and eunuchs.

and I do not feel tired at all."
(*Wéilǐ*
is synonymous with *wéizhì*.
The Táng avoided Gāozōng's taboo name,
changing *zhì* to *lǐ*.
*Chù*,
read as *chāng lǚ fān*.
*Lè*,
pronounced *luò*.)

on the Wùxū day,
Tián Jì'ān, Jìedùshǐ of Wèibó, passed away.

Jì'ān married the daughter of Yuán Yì, Cìshǐ of Míngzhōu.

He served as Jìedù Fùshǐ.
The New Records state: Jìedù Fùshǐ was below Xíngjūn Sīmǎ,

He was the son of Tián Tíngjiè.

He was quite learned
and of a respectful and modest nature.
Jì'ān was lewd and cruel,

Jì'ān, believing he was gaining popular support,
sent him out as commander of Línqīng Town,
and
intended to kill him.
Jiāngyù,
read as written.
His body was covered with cautery marks,
only then was he spared.
Jì'ān suffered from wind-illness,
and his killings were unrestrained.
Military administration became chaotic.
Lady Yuán summoned the generals and established Huáijiàn as Fùdàshǐ,
to oversee military affairs,
at the age of eleven.
The Kǎoyì states: The Lùnshìjí recorded
"twelve,"
but we follow the Shílù and old biographies.
He died more than a month later.
Tián Xìng was summoned to be Bùshè Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ.
On the Xīnhài day,
Xuē Píng, Zǒulóngwǔ Dàjiāngjūn, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Zhènghuá,
with the intention of controlling Wèibó.
The emperor discussed the Wèibó matter with the chancellors.
Lǐ Jífǔ requested to send troops to suppress it,
but Lǐ Jiàng believed that Wèibó did not necessarily require military action,
and would naturally return to the imperial court.
Jífǔ vehemently explained why military action was indispensable,
and the emperor said:
“My intention is also thus. ”
Jiàng said:
“I secretly observe that the unruly regional commanders of the Two Rivers
all divided their troops among various generals,
not allowing them to be solely under one person,
fearing that their authority would become too heavy,
and they might seize an opportunity to plot against them.
With the generals having equal power and strength,
none can control the others.
If they wish to form extensive alliances,
then their hearts are not unified,
and their plot will certainly be exposed.
If they wish to rise alone and cause trouble,
then their troops are few and their power weak,
and their plan will certainly not succeed.
Furthermore, with generous rewards
and strict punishments,
the generals are mutually apprehensive,
none daring to act first.
The unruly ones rely on this as a long-term strategy.
However, I secretly ponder,
if there could always be a strict and clear commander who can control the life and death of the generals to oversee them,
then they could roughly maintain stability.
Now, Huáijiàn is a mere child,
unable to make his own decisions,
and the great power of the military administration will certainly fall to someone.
If the generals are treated unequally in generosity and severity,
resentment and anger will certainly arise,
and they will not obey each other.
Then the strategy of dividing troops in the past
will be precisely the cause of today's chaos.
The Tián family will be like a butcher's stall (meaning the entire family will be slaughtered,
their flesh and bones scattered,
like a butcher slaughtering sheep and pigs,
hanging meat on a rack to display for sale).
Why bother with heavenly troops?
The emperor's troops
are called heavenly troops.
What the neighboring provinces detest
is nothing more than this.
If they do not rely on the support of the imperial court to preserve themselves,
then they will immediately become ([AS-FBBB] [AS-FBED]cì)[AS-FBEC] jiǔfěn for the neighboring provinces.
([AS-FBBB] [AS-FBED]Cì)[AS-FBEC] jiǔ
is the same as jī,
the dictionary explains it as finely chopped ginger and garlic.
We can sit and wait for Wèibó to submit itself.
I only wish Your Majesty would hold back your troops and cultivate your prestige,
and strictly order all provinces to select and train soldiers and horses to await further decrees.
Xū
means 'wait'.
In just a few months,
there will certainly be those in the army who offer their services.
At that time,
it will only be up to the imperial court to respond swiftly and promptly,
seizing the opportunity,
not sparing titles and emoluments to reward such people.
This will make the regional commanders of the Two Rivers, upon hearing this,
fear that their subordinates will imitate them to gain the imperial court's rewards,
and they will all be terrified,
competing to be respectful and obedient.
This is what is called 'subduing the enemy without fighting'. ”
The emperor said:
“Excellent! ”
Another day,
Jífǔ again at Yányīng vehemently expounded the benefits of military action,
and also stated that fodder, provisions, gold, and silk were all prepared.
The emperor looked at Jiàng for his opinion.
Gù
means 'to look back'.
“Troops should not be lightly moved.
Two years ago, when Hēngzhōu was suppressed,
twenty thousand troops were dispatched from all sides,
and two divisions of Shéncè troops were also sent from the capital to join them.
The empire was in turmoil,
and the cost was over seven million mín,
yet no success was achieved,
and it became a laughingstock for the empire.
This refers to Tútū Chéngcuǐ's campaign against Wáng Chéngzōng.
Everyone dreads war.
If we again compel them with imperial decrees,
I fear that not only will there be no achievement,
but other troubles might arise.
Furthermore, Wèibó does not necessarily require military action,
the situation is clear.
I wish Your Majesty would not doubt. ”
The emperor straightened himself and slapped the table, saying:
“My decision not to use troops is final. ”
Fǔ
means 'to pat'.
The Kǎoyì states: The New Biography of Jífǔ records:
“When Tián Jì'ān, Jìedùshǐ of Wèibó, was gravely ill,
Jífǔ requested to appoint Xuē Píng as Jìedùshǐ of Yìchéng,
to control Xíng and Míng with heavy troops,
and then submitted a map of the strategic locations in Héběi.
The emperor displayed it on the wall of the Yùtáng Gate,
and whenever discussing Héběi affairs,
he would point to Jífǔ and say: ‘
I consult the map daily, and it is indeed as you predicted.’ ”
However, Xiànzōng ultimately followed Lǐ Jiàng's strategy of not using troops, and Wèibó was pacified,
contrary to what the New Biography says.
Therefore, we do not adopt it here.
“Although Your Majesty has spoken thus,
I fear that after the court session,
there may be others who confuse Your Sacred Hearing. ”
The emperor, with a stern expression and sharp voice, said:
“My resolve is set;
who can confuse me! ”
Jiàng then bowed and congratulated him, saying:
“This is a blessing for the nation. ”
Later, as Tián Huáijiàn was young and weak,
all military and political decisions were made by the family servant Jiǎng Shìzé.
He frequently moved and replaced generals based on personal likes and dislikes,
which angered the multitude.
As the imperial edict had not arrived for a long time,
there was unrest in the army.
Tián Xìng entered the administrative office in the morning,
and several thousand soldiers shouted loudly,
surrounding Xìng and bowing,
requesting him to be the acting military governor (liúhòu).
Xìng was shocked and fell to the ground,
but the crowd did not disperse.
After a long while,
Xìng realized he could not escape,
and so he said to the crowd:
"Are you willing to listen to my words?"
They all said:
"We obey your command."
Xìng said:
"Do not harm the vice-ambassador (fù dàshǐ).
Abide by the laws and decrees of the imperial court,
update the household registers,
and request officials.
Only then is it permissible."
They all said
"Yes."
Xìng then killed Jiǎng Shìzé and over ten others,
and moved Huáijiàn to an outer residence.
In the first year of Dàizōng's Guǎngdé reign (763 CE),
Tián Chéngsì commanded Wèibó.
After four generations,
and forty-nine years, it was extinguished.
Róng Zhàozǔ punctuated, Niè Chóngqí re-collated.
