Yuánhé Seventh Year
(Rénchén, 812 CE)
1 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Yǐwèi day,
the Wèibó army supervisor reported the situation,
reporting how the Wèi army deposed Huáijiàn and established Tián Xìng.
The emperor said to Lǐ Jiàng:
"You understand Wèibó as if it were a tally."
Lǐ Jífǔ requested to send a palace envoy (zhōngshǐ) to express comfort and observe the change,
but Lǐ Jiàng said:
"No.
Now Tián Xìng presents his territory and troops,
sitting and awaiting an imperial edict.
If we do not seize this opportunity to wholeheartedly appease and embrace him,
and bind him with great benevolence,
but instead wait until the imperial envoy arrives there,
brings a memorial from the generals and soldiers asking for the insignia of military governor (jiéyuè),
and only then grant it,
this would be the drawback of the Dàlì and Zhēnyuán eras.
The same applies to other instances of 為 below.
If it does not originate from the emperor,
the generals and soldiers will be valued heavily,
and the imperial court lightly.
Their gratitude would not be comparable to what it could be today.
If this opportunity is lost,
it will be too late to regret!"
Jífǔ had always been allied with the privy councilor (shūmìshǐ) Liáng Shǒuqīan.
Shǒuqīan also spoke on his behalf to the emperor, saying:
"According to precedent,
palace envoys are always sent to offer comfort.
If this commandery alone is without one,
I fear they might not be enlightened."
He meant he feared they might not understand the emperor's intentions.
He wanted to wait for the envoy's return to discuss it.
On the Guǐmǎo day,
Lǐ Jiàng again submitted a memorial:
"The imperial court's gain or loss of grace and prestige
depends on this one action.
This opportunity is precious,
why abandon it?
The advantages and disadvantages are very clear.
I hope the sacred heart will not doubt.
Calculating the journey of Zhōngshùn,
he should have just passed Shǎn,
'Fǔ' (甫) means 'just now'.
it is still reachable."
The emperor was about to grant the position of acting military governor (liúhòu),
but Jiàng said:
"If Xìng is so respectful and obedient,
meaning Xìng abides by the laws and decrees of the imperial court,
updates the household registers,
and requests officials,
which is different from what the Héběi commanderies do,
then there will be no way to make him extraordinarily grateful."
The emperor followed his advice.
On the Jiǎchén day,
Xìng was appointed as Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Wèibó.
Zhōngshùn had not yet returned,
but the imperial edict had already reached Wèizhōu.
Xìng wept with gratitude,
and all the soldiers were overjoyed.
2 On the Gēngxū day,
the emperor changed the names of his imperial sons Kuān to Yùn,
Chá to Cóng,
Huán to Xīn,
Liáo to Wù,
and Shěn to Kè.
3 Lǐ Jiàng further said:
"Wèibó has not received imperial influence for over fifty years.
Wèibó has been stubborn and defiant since Tián Chéngsì,
lasting forty-nine years until now.
The six prefectures,
Wèi, Bó, Bèi, Wèi, Chán, Xiāng,
are a den of rebellion and treachery.
If there is no generous reward exceeding their expectations,
there will be no way to comfort the hearts of the soldiers,
and make the four neighbors admire them.
I request to issue 1.5 million strings of cash from the imperial treasury to bestow upon them."
The eunuchs around the emperor thought,
"What is given is too much.
If there are similar cases in the future,
how will we provide for them?"
The emperor spoke of this to Jiàng,
and Jiàng said:
"Tián Xìng does not covet the benefits of exclusive territory,
and disregards the troubles of his four neighbors,
submitting to the sacred court.
How can Your Majesty begrudge a small expense and abandon a grand strategy,
failing to win the hearts of an entire commandery?
Money, when used up, can be acquired again,
but an opportunity, once lost, cannot be recovered.
Supposing the state were to dispatch 150,000 troops to conquer the six prefectures,
and succeed in a year,
would the cost be limited to just 1.5 million strings of cash?"
The emperor was pleased,
and said:
"The reason I wear coarse clothes and eat simple food,
accumulating wealth,
is precisely to pacify the four directions;
otherwise,
what is the point of merely storing it in the imperial treasury?"
In the eleventh month,
on the Xīnyǒu day,
the Director of the Imperial Edicts (Zhīzhìgào) Péi Dù was sent to Wèibó to offer comfort,
bestowing 1.5 million strings of cash upon the soldiers,
and granting the people of the six prefectures a year of exemption from taxes and labor.
When the soldiers received the rewards,
their cheers were like thunder.
Several envoys from Chéngdé and Yǎnyùn saw this,
looked at each other, turning pale,
and sighed:
"What good does stubborn defiance do after all?"
Yǎnyùn
refers to the Zīqīng and Pínglú armies.
Dù explained to Xìng the righteousness of the relationship between ruler and minister, and between superiors and inferiors.
Xìng listened to him
tirelessly all night,
treating Dù with extreme courtesy.
He requested Dù to visit all the prefectures and counties under his jurisdiction
to announce the imperial decrees.
He memorialized requesting the imperial court to appoint a vice-military governor (jiédù fùshǐ).
An edict appointed Hú Zhèng, a director in the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù Lángzhōng) from Hédōng, to the post.
Xìng also memorialized that ninety official posts in his jurisdiction were vacant,
requesting the responsible authorities to assign candidates,
to implement imperial court laws and decrees,
and to pay taxes.
Those who had built extravagant houses since Tián Chéngsì's time all avoided living in them.
The rulers of Yùn, Cài, and Héng sent traveling persuaders to disseminate their views in various ways.
Tián Xīng ultimately did not listen.
Yùn was
Lǐ Shīdào;
Cài was
Wú Shàoyáng;
and Héng was
Wáng Chéngzōng.
Héng:
Hù dēng fān.
Jiàn:
Gǔ xiàn fān.
Shuō:
Shū ruì fān.
"Our family has long been allied with the Tián clan to mutually protect and assist each other.
Now Xīng is not of the Tián clan,
and has moreover been the first to change the situation in the Two Rivers region"
meaning Tián Xīng faithfully served the imperial court
and changed the old ways of the Two Rivers regional commands.
"We will join forces with Chéngdé to punish him."
Hóng said,
"I do not know the advantages and disadvantages;
I only know to act in accordance with the imperial edict.
If your troops cross the river to the north,
I will then lead my troops east to seize Cáozhōu!"
Cáozhōu was
under Lǐ Shīdào's jurisdiction.
They dared not act.
After Tián Xīng buried Tián Jì'ān,
he sent Tián Huáijiàn to the capital.
On the Xīnsì day,
Huáijiàn was appointed Right General of the Palace Guard.
4 Lǐ Jiàng memorialized that the fertile fields to the left and right of Zhènwǔ and Tiāndé amounted to tens of thousands of qǐng.
He requested to select able officials to open up and establish military colonies there,
which could save expenses and provide sufficient food.
The emperor assented.
Jiàng ordered the Commissioner of Finance, Lú Tǎn, to plan the expenditures.
Within four years,
four thousand eight hundred qǐng of fields were opened,
yielding over forty million hú of grain.
"Thousand"
should be
"ten".
Border defenses relied on this.
5 The emperor once said to the chancellors in the Yányīng Hall,
"You, my ministers, should treasure official positions for Us,
and not use them for your private relatives or old acquaintances."
Lǐ Jífǔ and Quán Déyú both humbly declined, saying they dared not.
Lǐ Jiàng said,
"Cuī Yòufǔ had a saying:
'If they are neither relatives nor old acquaintances,
one cannot fully understand their talent.'
If those one understands thoroughly are still not given official positions,
how much less dare one give them to those one does not understand!
One should only ask whether their talent and capacity match the office.
If, to avoid the suspicion of favoritism towards relatives and old acquaintances,
the sacred dynasty were to lose the benefit of many talented individuals,
this would be the act of a self-serving minister,
not the way of ultimate impartiality.
If those appointed are indeed not the right people,
then the court has its own laws and punishments;
who would dare to escape them!"
The emperor said,
"Indeed, as you say."
6 In this year,
Tǔbō bandits invaded Jīngzhōu,
reaching outside the west gate,
first raiding the Jīngzhōu border,
then advancing to outside Jīngzhōu's west gate.
The emperor was troubled by this.
Lǐ Jiàng memorialized:
"Both the west and north of the capital have Shéncè garrison troops.
The west of the capital comprises
Fèngxiáng, Qín, Lǒng, Yuán, Jīng, and Wèi.
The north of the capital comprises
Bīn, Níng, Dān, Yán, Fū, Fāng, Qìng, Líng, Yán, Xià, Suí, Yín, and Yòu.
The note on garrison troops has already been seen before.
They are stationed there to guard against Tǔbō,
and to assist the Jìedùshǐ as pincers.
Now, however, they are well-fed and well-clothed,
sitting idly and consuming state resources.
Whenever invaders arrive,
and the Jìedùshǐ invites them to advance together,
they say they must first request instructions from the Zhongwèi.
The Táng Shéncè garrison troops were stationed externally
and all belonged to the Left and Right Shéncè Zhōngwèi.
Chù:
Chāng lǚ fān.
Fēn:
Fú wèn fān.
By then, the invaders have already gone far away.
Even if there are truly brave and resolute generals,
who hasten to respond to the command,
the Jìedùshǐ has no power to punish or execute them to control them;
they treat each other as equals,
moving left and right, advancing and retreating,
and none are willing to obey orders.
What good is that!
I request that all the soldiers, horses, provisions, clothing, and weaponry in their respective locations be transferred to the local Jìedùshǐ,
so that commands are unified
like the arm directing the finger.
Then the army's might will be greatly enhanced,
and the invaders will not dare to intrude."
The emperor said,
"We were unaware that old customs were like this.
This must be implemented quickly."
However, the Shéncè Army had been arrogant and unrestrained for a long time
and disliked being subordinated to the Jìedùshǐ.
Ultimately, they were obstructed by the eunuchs and the matter ceased.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the Guǐhài day,
Tián Róng, the Inspector of Bózhōu, was appointed Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
Róng was
Xīng's elder brother.
Róng, being older,
raised and taught him.
Both brothers lost their parents while young,
but the elder brother was somewhat older,
so he raised and taught his younger brother.
Zhǎng:
Zhī zhàng fān.
Jiǎo:
Jìng yě.
Those who compete in archery
consider hitting the target a victory.
Róng returned and whipped him,
saying,
"If you do not conceal yourself,
disaster will soon be upon you!"
Therefore, Xīng was able to preserve himself during times of suspicion and tyranny.
Times of suspicion and tyranny
refer to the time of Tián Jì'ān.
2 Yuán Yú, the Prince Dìng of Bóhǎi, died.
His younger brother, Yán Yì, assumed control of state affairs.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
Yán Yì was made Prince of Bóhǎi.
3 Lǐ Jífǔ and Lǐ Jiàng often debated before the emperor.
Quán Déyú, Minister of Rites and Chancellor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì), remained neutral, neither approving nor disapproving;
the emperor scorned him.
On the Xīnwèi day,
Déyú was dismissed from his chancellorship and retained his original post.
4 On the Xīnmǎo day,
Tián Xīng, the Jìedùshǐ of Wèibó, was bestowed the name Hóngzhèng.
5 Sīkōng and Chancellor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì) Yú Dí had long stayed in Cháng'ān,
feeling dejected and unfulfilled.
In the second year, Dí came to court.
See juan 232.
He claimed to be of the same clan as Liáng Shǒuqiān, the Commissioner of Military Affairs,
and capable of making requests on others' behalf.
Dí instructed his son, Tàicháng Chéng Mǐn, to heavily bribe Zhèng Yán
to seek an assignment as a regional governor.
After a long time,
Zhèng Yán's deception gradually became apparent.
Mǐn, unable to retrieve his bribe,
lured Zhèng Yán's servant away,
dismembered him,
and dumped the body in a latrine.
When the matter was discovered,
Dí, with his son Diànzhōng Shàojiān Jìyǒu and others, dressed in plain clothes and went to Jiànfú Gate to beg for punishment.
The gatekeepers did not let them in;
they retreated,
stood with their backs against the south wall,
and sent someone to submit a memorial.
The Hégémén Office refused it because it lacked an official seal and an imperial pass.
According to Táng regulations: all memorials from the four directions
were received and presented by the Hégémén.
Dí was currently begging for punishment,
and therefore had neither his official seal
nor an imperial pass,
which is why it was not accepted.
The next day,
he returned.
On the Dīngyǒu day,
Dí was demoted to Imperial Tutor to the Prince of Ēn,
and was moreover forbidden from imperial audiences;
Mǐn was exiled to Léizhōu.
According to old records: Léizhōu was
six thousand five hundred and twelve lǐ from the capital.
Several of the official slaves died;
Mǐn died upon reaching Qínlǐng.
He went south from Lántián Pass, crossing Qínlǐng.
The matter involved the monk Jiànxū.
Since the Zhēnyuán [reign] period,
Jiànxū had used his wealth to ingratiate himself with powerful favorites,
accepted bribes from regional governors,
and lived in great luxury,
so officials dared not question him.
By this time,
the powerful favorites vied to speak on his behalf,
and the Emperor wished to release him,
but the Vice President of the Censorate, Xuē Cúnchéng, refused.
The Emperor sent a palace envoy to the Censorate to declare his will, saying:
"I wish to personally question this monk,
not to release him."
Cúnchéng replied:
"If Your Majesty must personally release this monk,
please first kill your servant,
and then take him.
Otherwise,
your servant will never obey the imperial edict."
The Emperor commended him and agreed.
In the third month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
Jiànxū was beaten to death with a staff,
and all his property was confiscated.
A textual comparison notes: The Veritable Records state it was in the second month.
According to the Extended Calendar,
the first day of the second month was Yǐyǒu,
and the first day of the third month was Jiǎyín.
Bǐngchén
was the third day of the third month.
Jiǎzǐ
was when Wǔ Yuánhéng entered to manage government affairs,
which was the eleventh day.
The Veritable Records likely omitted the month.
6 On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Wǔ Yuánhéng, the former Military Governor of Xīchuān and concurrently acting as Grand Councilor, was summoned to manage government affairs.
In the second year of Yuánhé,
Wǔ Yuánhéng had been sent to govern Xīchuān,
and was now recalled.
7 In the summer,
in the sixth month,
there was a great flood.
The Emperor considered this a sign of excessive Yin,
and on the day Xīnchǒu,
he released two hundred palace women.
8 In the autumn,
in the seventh month,
Lǐ Guāngjìn, the Military Governor of Zhènwǔ, requested to repair Shòuxiángchéng,
and also manage the river defenses.
Lǐ (理)
means to govern.
The destruction of Shòuxiángchéng by the river is mentioned in Volume 7, seven years prior.
The old city of Tiāndé was
in Dàtóngchuān, two hundred *lǐ* west of Dōng Shòuxiángchéng.
After Qiányuán,
the Tiāndé garrison was moved to Yǒngjìzhà.
Sòng Bái's *Xù Tōngdiǎn* writes
"Yǒngqīngzhà".
That city
was the old site of Suí's Dàtóngchéng.
"Shòuxiángchéng,
built by Zhāng Rényuàn (the matter is seen in Volume 209, Zhōngzōng's Jǐnglóng first year),
occupies a vital strategic point against the barbarians,
with excellent water and pasture,
making it a beneficial place for border defense.
Now, to avoid river damage,
retreating two or three *lǐ* would suffice.
How can one abandon a strategy for eternal peace for ten thousand generations
to pursue the convenience of temporary cost-saving?
Moreover, the old city of Tiāndé is remote and barren,
far from the river,
so beacon alarms cannot be responded to promptly.
If the barbarians suddenly attack,
there will be no way to know,
which is to needlessly shrink the nation by two hundred *lǐ*."
When the city envoy Zhōu Huáiyì presented the advantages and disadvantages,
it was similar to Jiàng and Tǎn's views.
The Emperor ultimately adopted Jífǔ's strategy,
assigning the cavalry of Shòuxiángchéng to the Tiāndé garrison.
Lǐ Jiàng reported to the Emperor, saying:
"The border armies have only their nominal numbers but no actual strength.
They waste clothing and provisions,
and generals merely use them for private service (by 'private service' is meant
using them for private ends under the guise of public duty).
They are never trained to prepare for unforeseen circumstances.
This is something Your Majesty must keep in mind during times of peace."
At that time, the Shòuxiángchéng military registry nominally listed four hundred men,
but when the Tiāndé garrison took over the troops,
there were only fifty men.
A textual comparison notes: The Veritable Records say:
"Lǐ Guāngjìn requested to repair Dōng Shòuxiángchéng and also manage the river defenses."
It also says:
"The Zhōng Shòuxiángchéng and its subordinate cavalry of one thousand one hundred forty men were assigned to the Tiāndé garrison."
Old records state:
"Lú Tǎn and Lǐ Jiàng jointly deliberated,
believing that the western city, built by Zhāng Rényuàn,
should not be abandoned."
These three accounts differ,
and it is unknown which is correct.
Now it merely says "Shòuxiángchéng,"
with the omission left as doubtful.
Furthermore, Lǐ Sīkōng's discussion of the matter says:
"The central city originally belonged to Zhènwǔ,
with four hundred garrison troops.
At that time, it was ceded to Tiāndé,
and when the transfer occurred, there were only fifty men."
The numbers are so different,
perhaps one thousand one hundred forty men was the total for all three cities.
The rest aligns with this.
Hence, Jiàng's statement.
The Emperor was startled and said:
"Are the border troops truly so empty!
You officials must investigate and review this more closely."
However, the matter ceased when Jiàng was dismissed from his premiership.
9 On the day Yǐsì,
the Tiānwēi Army was disbanded.
In the early Yuánhé period,
the Zuǒ Shénwēi and Yòu Shénwēi were combined into one army,
named the Tiānwēi Army.
The Shénwēi Army
was originally the Palace Front Elite Archers.
10 On the day Dīngwèi,
Zhāng Bójìng, the rebel leader of Chén and Xù, surrendered.
The rebellion of Chén and Xù began in Volume 6.
On the day Xīnhài,
Bójìng was made Administrator of Guīzhōu,
and assigned to be a vanguard for the Jīngnán army.
Wěi (委)
means to entrust,
to assign.
11 Initially,
the Tubo wished to build the Wūlán Bridge.
The New Records state: Wūlán County in Huìzhōu has Wūlán Pass,
southwest of the county.
The Tubo built a bridge over the river.
Shuòfāng often secretly sent people to throw it into the river,
and they could never complete it.
The barbarians knew that Wáng Bì, the Military Governor of Shuòfāng and Língyán, was greedy,
so they first heavily bribed him,
and then concentrated their efforts to complete the bridge,
and also built a crescent-shaped wall to guard it.
From then on, Shuòfāng was too busy defending against invaders to attack.
12 In the winter,
in the tenth month,
the Uyghurs sent troops across the desert to the south,
attacking the Tubo from west of Liǔgǔ.
The New Records state: Two hundred ten *lǐ* north of Jiāohé County in Xīzhōu,
is Liǔgǔ渡.
On the day Rén Yín,
the Zhènwǔ and Tiāndé armies reported that several thousand Uyghur cavalry had reached Pìtí Quán.
Pìtí Quán
is three hundred *lǐ* north of Xī Shòuxiángchéng.
Pì (鷿)
is pronounced fúlì.
Tí (鵜)
is pronounced túxī.
13 Lǐ Jìnxián, the Military Governor of Zhènwǔ,
did not care for his soldiers.
His judicial officer, Yán Chè,
was the son of Yán Shòu (at that time, Yán Shòu was still alive).
Shòu (綬)
is pronounced shòu.
Jìnxián ordered his adjutant Yáng Zūnxiàn to lead five hundred cavalry to Dōng Shòuxiángchéng to prepare for the Uyghurs.
The supplies provided were often overvalued.
Supplies were not given in their original form,
their value was falsely inflated,
and other items were given instead.
Qù (趣)
is pronounced qīyù.
Zūnxiàn stayed indoors,
while his soldiers were exposed to the elements.
The troops grew angry.
That night,
they gathered firewood, encircled his house, and burned it down,
then donned their armor and returned.
On the night of Gēngyín,
they burned the gate and attacked Jìnxián.
Jìnxián scaled the wall and fled.
The soldiers ransacked his home
and also killed Yán Chè.
Jìnxián fled to the Jìngbiān Army.
The Jìngbiān Army was one hundred eighty *lǐ* west of Yúnzhōu.
14 All the officials repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to establish Lady Guō, a woman of virtue, as Empress.
The Emperor believed that her clan was too strong and prosperous.
(She was the daughter of Guō Ài and granddaughter of Guō Zǐyí).
No other women in the palace could be promoted.
The Emperor cited seasonal taboos as an excuse,
and ultimately refused.
15 On the *dīngyǒu* day,
Luò Cháokuān, the supervising commissioner of Zhènwǔ, reported that the rebellious soldiers had been pacified,
and requested clothing for the generals and soldiers.
The Emperor was enraged.
He appointed Zhāng Xù, the Jìedùshǐ of Xiàsuí, as the Jìedùshǐ of Zhènwǔ,
leading two thousand Xiàzhōu troops to their post.
He further ordered Wáng È, the Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng, to bring two thousand troops to join them,
giving him discretion to act as he saw fit.
Luò Cháokuān blamed and killed his general Sū Ruòfāng.
16 Soldiers from Zhènghuá and Wèibó were conscripted to dig a fourteen-li channel in the old course of the Lìyáng River,
to alleviate the flood समस्या in Huázhōu.
The old course of the Great River used to pass east of Lìyáng Mountain,
but later shifted south,
causing problems for Huázhōu.
Therefore, the old river course was re-excavated.
17 The Emperor asked his chief ministers,
"People say that factions are greatly flourishing outside.
Why is this?"
Lǐ Jiàng replied,
"From ancient times, what rulers have most abhorred
is none other than their ministers forming factions.
Therefore, scoundrels who slander upright men invariably accuse them of forming factions.
Why so?
Because 'factions' sounds odious when spoken,
yet leaves no trace when investigated.
Towards the end of the Eastern Hàn dynasty,
all the worthy gentlemen of the realm
were labeled 'partisans' by the eunuchs and imprisoned,
which led to the downfall of the dynasty.
See the records of Emperors Huán and Líng of Hàn.
I wish Your Majesty would deeply discern this!
Indeed, upright men naturally associate with upright men.
How can they be forced to associate with scoundrels
and only then be called not partisan?"
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the *jiǎxū* day,
Wáng È dispatched five thousand soldiers to meet Zhāng Xù at Shànyángzhà.
"Shànyáng"
should be written
"Shànyáng".
The seat of Shuòzhōu in the Táng dynasty was Shànyáng County,
one hundred and twenty *lǐ* northwest of the Chányú Dūhùfǔ.
The stockade was probably erected within the county's borders.
On the *yǐhài* day,
Xù entered the Chányú Dūhùfǔ.
He was the Jìedùshǐ of Zhènwǔ,
governing from the Chányú Dūhùfǔ.
In the second month,
on the *dīngchǒu* day,
Lǐ Jìnxián was demoted to Cìshǐ of Tōngzhōu.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Luò Cháokuān was charged with condoning the rebels,
given eighty strokes with the rod,
stripped of his rank,
and assigned to penal service in Dìnglíng.
"Stripped of his rank"
means deprived of his official grade.
2 Lǐ Jiàng repeatedly resigned his position due to a foot ailment.
On the *guǐmǎo* day,
he was dismissed and made Shàngshū of the Lǐbù.
Previously,
the Emperor wished to appoint Jiàng as chancellor,
and first sent Tǔtū Chéngcuǐ out as the supervising commissioner of Huáinán (see previous volume, sixth year).
(Xiàng,
pronounced *xī liàng fān*;
same below.)
The Emperor recalled Chéngcuǐ,
first dismissing Jiàng from his chancellorship.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
Chéngcuǐ arrived in the capital,
and was again made Commander of the Bow and Arrow Arsenal.
Observing the full course of Lǐ Jiàng's service at court,
one might almost say he possessed the integrity of a great minister.
Chéngcuǐ had been dismissed from the position of zhōngwèi for losing battles and made Commander of the Bow and Arrow Arsenal.
Now he was reinstated to it.
This was Xìanzōng's cunning,
to hold both ends and observe the court's opinion.
Once Lǐ Jiàng was dismissed,
who would dare speak about it again?
3 Lǐ Jífǔ reported:
"The state formerly established the Six Hú Prefectures in the border region of Líng and Yán.
In the first year of Diàolù, in the southern border region of Líng and Xià, the prefectures of Lǔzhōu, Lìzhōu, Hánzhōu, Sàizhōu, Yīzhōu, and Qìzhōu were established for the surrendered Türks,
with Táng people appointed as Cìshǐ,
and these were called the Six Hú Prefectures.
Yánzhōu bordered Líng and Xià.
Yòuzhōu was also established to govern the surrendered households.
During the Tiānbǎo period,
Yòuzhōu was administered from the Jīnglüè Army.
In the fourth year of Cháng'ān,
the Six Hú Prefectures were merged into Kuāng and Cháng prefectures.
In the twenty-sixth year of Kāiyuán,
Kuāngzhōu was abolished,
Huái'ēn County was established,
attached to Yòuzhōu,
and within the county's jurisdiction was the Yúduōlè City.
During the Tiānbǎo period,
Wáng Zhōngsì requested the establishment of the Jīnglüè Army,
located three hundred *lǐ* northeast of the former Yòuzhōu city.
Sòng Bái said: Yòuzhōu was to connect with Tiāndé,
and reinforce Xiàzhōu to the south,
governing from Chángzé County,
which was originally the land of Hán Sānfēng County.
Through neglect, it was eventually abandoned.
Now I request its re-establishment
to prepare against the Huíhé [Uyghurs]
and pacify the Dǎngxiàng."
The Emperor assented.
In summer,
in the fifth month,
on the *gēngshēn* day,
Yòuzhōu was re-established,
administered from the Jīnglüè Army,
and nine thousand troops from the Shéncè garrison in Fúchéng of Fúzhōu were taken to populate it.
In the sixth year of Dàlì,
the Sùróng Army was established in Fúchéng of Fúzhōu.
Previously,
the Huíhé had repeatedly requested a marriage alliance,
but the court, considering the enormous expense of sending a princess,
had not yet agreed.
Lǐ Jiàng, the Shàngshū of the Lǐbù, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The Huíhé are fierce and strong,
and we cannot be unprepared;
Huáixī is in dire straits,
and requires urgent attention.
Now, major counties in Jiāng and Huái,
whose annual tax revenue reaches two hundred thousand *mín*,
are sufficient to cover the cost of marrying off a princess.
Why does Your Majesty begrudge the revenue of one county,
not using it to restrain the strong barbarians?
If the Huíhé are granted the marriage,
they will surely be pleased and without suspicion,
after which we can repair fortifications,
stockpile arms,
and once the border defenses are complete,
we can focus entirely on Huáixī,
ensuring complete success.
Now, since we have not yet granted a princess, the Western City is weakened.
('Western City'
refers to the Western Shòujiàng City.)
Moreover, rebuilding Tiāndé will make the barbarians suspicious.
(This refers to moving Shòujiàng City to Tiāndé.)
Then the remnants of Huáixī will again prolong their existence for months and years!
If by chance barbarian cavalry rides south,
without thirty thousand infantry
and five thousand cavalry,
the state will be unable to resist!
Even if we were to defeat them in a single year,
would the cost not be far greater than that of marrying off a princess?"
The Emperor did not listen.
4 On the *yǐchǒu* day,
Lún, Prince of Guì, passed away.
Lún
was the Emperor's younger brother.
5 In the sixth month,
on the *rényín* day,
Zhāng Hóngjìng, the Jìedùshǐ of Hézhōng, was appointed Shàngshū of the Xíngbù and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Hóngjìng
was the son of Yánshǎng.
Zhāng Yánshǎng served as chancellor under Dèzōng during the Zhēnyuán period.
6 The Hanlin academician, Dúgū Yù,
was the son-in-law of Quán Déyú.
The Emperor admired Yù's talent and beauty, saying:
"Déyú gained Yù as a son-in-law,
am I, on the contrary, inferior to him?!"
Previously, when princesses were married, they were always given to noble relatives or sons of meritorious officials.
The Emperor now for the first time ordered the chief ministers to select sons of high-ranking officials and grandees who were refined and suitable for prestigious positions.
Shǐ Zhào said: "Guàn
means affair.
Qīngguàn
is analogous to qīngzhí (clean official positions)."
Only Dù Yòu's grandson, the Secretary of Deliberations, Dù Cóng, did not decline.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day wùchén,
Cóng was appointed Palace Deputy Supervisor and Fùmǎ Dōuwèi,
and married Princess Qíyáng.
The princess
was the Emperor's eldest daughter,
born to Guō.
In the eighth month,
on the day guǐsì,
the marriage was completed.
The princess possessed virtuous conduct.
The Dù clan was a great family,
with scores of respected elders.
The princess was humble, compliant, and amiable,
following all the family's rites and customs.
For twenty years,
no one ever considered her noble status a cause for pride or arrogance in the slightest.
Upon her arrival,
she consulted with Cóng, saying:
"The servants bestowed by the Emperor
are ultimately unwilling to be humble and submissive.
I request that we send them back
and instead buy humble and lowly servants whom we can command."
Zhìzhǐ
means those who can be controlled and commanded.
7 In the intercalary month,
on the day bǐngchén,
Wú Shǎoyáng, the Military Governor of Zhāngyì, died.
Kǎoyì says: The Shílù (Veritable Records) states
that Shǎoyáng's death occurred between the days jǐchǒu and
rénchén in the intercalary month,
and mentions Yuánjì's burning of Wǔyáng together with it.
The Tǒngjì and Jiùjì (Old Records)
both place Shǎoyáng's death in the ninth month.
According to the old biography, it says:
"After Shǎoyáng's death,
for forty days,
court sessions were not suspended for him."
The Tángjì (Tang Records) states:
"Zhāng Hóngjìng requested to suspend court sessions and posthumously grant an official title to Shǎoyáng."
However, the Shílù
states that "on the day xīnchǒu, Shǎoyáng was posthumously granted the title of Right Executive Assistant."
If so, from jǐchǒu to xīnchǒu
is only twelve days.
How could it be that court sessions were not suspended for forty days?
We now follow the Xīnjì (New Records).
[Wú Shǎoyáng] secretly gathered fugitives,
raised horses and mules,
and from time to time plundered the Tea Mountain of Shòuzhōu to supply his army.
Shòuzhōu had a Tea Mountain.
Chāo (抄),
pronounced chǔ jiāo.
He concealed the death,
reported himself as ill,
and personally managed military affairs.
Since the Emperor pacified Shǔ,
Shǔ was pacified in the early Yuánhé era.
Lǐ Jífǔ, the Military Governor of Huáinán, submitted a memorial, saying:
"In Shǎoyáng's army, superiors and subordinates are estranged.
I request to move the administration to Shòuzhōu to manage this situation."
The Military Governor of Huáinán governed Yángzhōu; he wished to move the administration to Shòuzhōu to strategize against Huáixī.
This matter is found in volumes four and five of the previous scroll.
When Jífǔ became chief minister,
Tián Hóngzhèng submitted to the court with Wèibó.
This matter is found in the seventh year.
The garrison in Héyáng
was originally intended to control Wèibó.
Now that Hóngzhèng has submitted,
Héyáng becomes an internal commandery,
and should not station heavy troops, which would indicate suspicion and obstruction.
On the day xīnyǒu,
Wū Zhòngyìn, the Military Governor of Héyáng, was appointed Prefect of Rǔzhōu,
also serving as Military Governor of Héyáng, Huái, and Rǔ,
and moved his administration to Rǔzhōu.
On the day jǐsì,
Hóngzhèng was given the concurrent title of Right Executive Assistant,
and his army was granted 200,000 strings of cash.
Hóngzhèng said:
"This is not as joyful to me as the relocation of the Héyáng army."
Joyful means
joy at the court's lack of suspicion and prevention against Wèibó.
In the ninth month,
on the day gēngchén,
Lǐ Guāngyán, the Prefect of Míngzhōu, was appointed Prefect of Chénzhōu,
and also Chief Commander of Military Affairs for Zhōngwǔ.
The Jiǔyùzhì (Records of the Nine Regions) says: Chénzhōu
is 190 li southwest of Càizhōu.
Tōng was Zhāng's son.
During Emperor Sùzōng's time,
Línghú Zhāng defected from Shǐ Sīmíng and submitted to the court.
On the day bǐngxū,
Yuán Zī, the Military Governor of Shānnán Dōngdào, was appointed Military Governor of Jīngnán;
Yán Shòu, the Military Governor of Jīngnán, was appointed Military Governor of Shānnán Dōngdào.
Wú Shǎoyáng's administrative assistants Sū Zhào and Yáng Yuánqīng, and general Hóu Wéiqīng, all urged Shǎoyáng to appear at court.
Yuánjì detested this,
killed Zhào,
and imprisoned Wéiqīng.
Yuánqīng had previously presented a memorial in Cháng'ān,
and fully informed Lǐ Jífǔ about the true situation in Huáixī and the strategy for capturing Yuánjì,
requesting to attack him.
At this time, Yuánjì was still concealing the death,
and Yuánqīng advised Jífǔ
to stop all envoys from Cài who came to present memorials,
wherever they were.
Shǎoyáng had been dead for nearly forty days,
and court sessions were not suspended for him.
Instead, the commanders of the garrisons surrounding Cài were replaced,
and troops were increased for readiness.
Yuánjì killed Yuánqīng's wife and four sons and used them as targets for archers.
Dǒng Zhòngzhì, a veteran general of Huáixī and Wú Shǎochéng's son-in-law,
was made Yuánjì's chief strategist.
8 On the day wùxū,
Wáng È, the Military Governor of Hédōng, was given the concurrent title of Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
9 Lǐ Jífǔ said to the Emperor:
"Huáixī is not like Hébĕi;
it has no allies on all four sides.
The state constantly stations hundreds of thousands of troops to guard against it,
and the labor and expense are unbearable.
If we do not seize this opportunity,
it will be difficult to plan later."
The Emperor was about to launch an expedition,
but Zhāng Hóngjìng requested that court sessions first be suspended and an official title be posthumously granted to Shǎoyáng,
and an envoy be sent to offer condolences and grants.
Only after there were signs of his disobedience
should troops then be deployed.
The Emperor agreed and
dispatched Lǐ Jūnhé, a Supernumerary Assistant Minister of Works, to offer condolences and sacrifices.
The Táng Minister of Works
was in charge of the construction projects and regulations for cities, walls, and earthworks.
Troops were dispatched in all directions,
slaughtered Wǔyáng.
Wǔyáng was a county in the Han dynasty,
belonging to Xǔzhōu in the Tang dynasty.
The Jiǔyùzhì says: It is 180 li southwest of the prefecture.
They plundered Lǔshān and Xiāngchéng,
causing shock throughout Guāndōng.
Jūnhé was unable to enter and returned.
10 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day bǐngwǔ,
Lǐ Jífǔ, the Grand Academician of the Central Secretariat and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì, died.
11 On the day rénxū,
Lǐ Guāngyán, the Deputy Military Commissioner of Zhōngwǔ, was appointed Military Commissioner.
On the day jiǎzǐ,
Yán Shòu was appointed Pacification Commissioner of Shēn, Guāng, and Cài,
to oversee the armies of various circuits in attacking Wú Yuánjì.
On the day yǐchǒu,
the Emperor ordered Cuī Tánjùn, the Inner Palace Grandee and Administrator of Provincial Affairs, to supervise his army.
Kǎoyì says: The Shílù writes "Tánjùn".
We now follow the old biography.
On the day wùchén,
Lǚ Yuányīng, the Left Executive Assistant of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Grand Administrator of the Eastern Capital.
12 The Dǎngxiàng raided Zhènwǔ.
13 In the twelfth month,
on the day wùchén,
Wéi Guànzhī, the Right Executive Assistant of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day yǐyǒu,
Hán Hóng was given the concurrent title of Grand Minister of Works.
Hóng governed Xuānwǔ,
and for more than ten years did not come to court,
somewhat proud of his military strength.
The court also did not treat him with loyalty and sincerity.
Wáng È was given the title of
Tóng Píngzhāng Shì,
and Hóng was ashamed that his rank was below È's.
He wrote to Wǔ Yuánhéng,
somewhat revealing his displeasure.
The court was relying on his strategic position to control Wú Yuánjì,
so they promoted him to a higher official rank than È to placate and comfort him.
2 Wú Yuánjì
allowed his troops to plunder, extending
to the Eastern Jī.
On the day Jǐhài,
an imperial decree stripped Yuánjì of his official titles and ranks,
ordering the armies of Xuānwǔ and sixteen other circuits to advance and suppress him.
Yán Shòu attacked the Huáixī forces,
achieving a minor victory.
Not taking precautions,
the Huáixī forces returned and attacked them by night.
In the second month,
on the day Jiǎchén,
Shòu was defeated at Cíqiū.
“Cíqiū”
should be
“Cíqiū”.
It was a county belonging to Tángzhōu,
established by the Suí dynasty by dividing Bǐyáng County,
named after Cíqiū Mountain within the county's borders,
located northeast of the prefecture.
He fled into Tángzhōu and defended it.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Tángzhōu
is three hundred and fifty *lǐ* east to Càizhōu.
He fled and secured the prefectural city;
all the stockades on the border were slaughtered by Huáixī.
On the day Guǐchǒu,
Lǐ Wéntōng, the Grand General of the Left Guards of the Imperial Insignia, was appointed to replace him.
Wéntōng was demoted to Sīhù of Zhāozhōu.
An imperial edict ordered Liǔ Gōngchuò, the Observer of Èyuè, to give five thousand troops to Lǐ Tīng, the Governor of Ānzhōu,
to suppress Wú Yuánjì.
Gōngchuò said:
"Does the court think I am a mere scholar who doesn't understand military matters?"
He immediately petitioned to lead the campaign himself,
which was granted.
When Gōngchuò arrived in Ānzhōu,
Lǐ Tīng, with his quiver and bow case, welcomed him.
Gōngchuò presented him with two official documents, appointing him as the Military Commissioner of Èyuè and the Vanguard Commander of the Expeditionary Army.
He selected six thousand soldiers and assigned them to Lǐ Tīng,
instructing his subordinate commanders:
"Regarding matters of the expeditionary army,
all decisions shall be made by the Commander-in-Chief."
The one who commanded the armies of all divisions
was called the Commander-in-Chief,
as if operating under his banner.
Gōngchuò's commands were strict and orderly,
and he managed military affairs effectively;
none of the generals were unsubmissive.
For soldiers in the expeditionary army,
if their families suffered illness, death, or mourning,
he provided generously.
If a wife committed adultery,
she was drowned in the river.
All the soldiers rejoiced, saying:
"The Vice-Minister manages our homes for us,
how can we not fight to the death!"
Therefore, every battle was a victory.
The horse Gōngchuò rode
kicked and killed a groom.
Gōngchuò ordered the horse to be killed as a sacrifice to the groom.
Someone said:
"The groom himself was not careful.
This is an excellent horse;
it's a pity!"
Gōngchuò said:
"Even if its talent is good, its nature is stubborn.
What is there to regret!"
He killed it nonetheless.
3 Liú Fǔ, a general from Hédōng, killed Yān Chónghàn, the Governor of Fēngzhōu.
Wáng È executed him
and his partisans.
4 The partisans of Wáng Shūwén who were demoted from office
had not been transferred for a full ten years.
In the first year of Yǒngzhēn [805 CE],
the partisans of Wáng Shūwén were banished.
The details can be found in Volume 236.
Liàng
is pronounced liáng.
All were summoned to the capital.
Censors vied to argue against this.
The emperor and Wǔ Yuánhéng also disliked them.
In the third month,
on the Yǐ
Yǒu day,
all were made Cìshǐ of distant prefectures.
Although their offices were advanced, their locations became even more remote.
Liǔ Zōngyuán, Sīmǎ of Yǒngzhōu, was made Cìshǐ of Liǔzhōu;
Liú Yǔxī, Sīmǎ of Lǎngzhōu, was made Cìshǐ of Bōzhōu.
Yǒngzhōu
was ancient Línglíng Jùn.
The Suí dynasty established Yǒngzhōu,
named after the Yǒng river,
3274 lǐ south of the capital.
Liǔzhōu
was in the territory of Hàn Tánzhōng Xiàn.
The Suí dynasty established Mápíng Xiàn.
In the early Táng dynasty, Kūnzhōu was established.
In Zhēnguān, it was renamed Liǔzhōu,
5470 lǐ by water and land from the capital.
Lǎngzhōu
was ancient Wǔlíng Jùn.
The Liáng dynasty established Wǔzhōu.
The Suí dynasty made it Lǎngzhōu,
2159 lǐ southeast of the capital.
Bōzhōu
was the southwestern corner of the territories of the Hàn Yèláng and Qiělán kingdoms.
The Hàn dynasty established Zāngkē Jùn.
The Táng dynasty established Bōzhōu,
4450 lǐ south of the capital.
“Bōzhōu is not a place where people can live,
and Mèngdé’s mother is still alive.”
Liú Yǔxī’s
courtesy name was Mèngdé.
[Liú Yǔxī] wished to petition the court,
hoping to exchange Liǔzhōu for Bōzhōu.
Coincidentally, Censor-in-Chief Péi Dù also spoke for Yǔxī, saying:
“Yǔxī certainly has committed a crime,
but his mother is old,
and for her to be separated from her son by death
is truly pitiful!”
The emperor said:
“A son should be especially careful and disciplined,
so as not to cause his parents worry.
In this regard, Yǔxī is even more blameworthy.”
Dù said:
“Your Majesty is currently attending to the Empress Dowager,
so Yǔxī’s situation should be pitied.”
The emperor paused for a long while,
then said:
“What I said
was to blame those who are sons;
however, I do not wish to hurt his mother’s heart.”
Upon withdrawing,
he said to his attendants:
“Péi Dù’s love for me is truly profound.”
The next day,
Yǔxī was changed to Cìshǐ of Liánzhōu.
Liánzhōu
was in the territory of Hàn Guìyáng Yángshān.
The Táng dynasty established Liánzhōu,
named after Huanglian Ridge south of the prefecture,
3665 lǐ south of the capital.
The Kǎoyì states: According to the old biography of Yǔxī:
“In the tenth year of Yuánhé [815 CE],
he was recalled from Wǔlíng to the capital,
and the prime minister again wished to place him in the Langshǔ.
At that time, Yǔxī composed poems such as ‘Yǒngyóu Xuándū Guān’, ‘Kànhuā’, and ‘Jūnzǐ Shī’,
whose words contained satire.
The powerful officials were displeased,
and he was again sent out as Cìshǐ of Bōzhōu.”
Yǔxī’s collected works record his poem as saying:
“In Xuándū Guān there are a thousand peach trees,
all planted after Master Liú departed.”
However, at that time, all of Wáng Shūwén’s partisans
were appointed Cìshǐ of distant prefectures,
not just Yǔxī alone.
How could it be because of this poem!
It was probably because of this that he got the bad place of Bōzhōu.
The Shílù states:
“Censor-in-Chief Péi Dù memorialized: ‘His mother is old,
and she would surely be separated from this son by death.
Your subject fears this would harm Your Majesty’s reputation for filial governance.’
Xiànzōng said: ‘A son must be especially cautious and prudent,
lest he cause his parents worry.
Yǔxī is even more to be blamed than others.
How can you argue this way, my lord!’
Dù had no reply.
After a long while,
the Emperor changed his expression and said: ‘What I said
was to blame the matter of a son,
but in the end, I do not wish to hurt his loved one’s heart.’
The next day,
Yǔxī was reassigned to Liánzhōu.”
Zhào Yuángǒng’s Táng Jiànzhèng Jí states:
“Péi Dù said: ‘Your Majesty is currently attending to the Empress Dowager,
governing the world with filial piety.
As for Yǔxī,
he truly deserves compassion.’
Xiànzōng then acceded.
The next day,
an imperial decree appointed Yǔxī to Liánzhōu.
Afterwards, he said to his attendants: ‘Péi Dù’s love for me is truly profound.’”
Zhào Lín’s Yīnhuà Lù states:
“At the beginning of Xiànzōng’s reign, Liǔ Zōngyuán and Liú Yǔxī were summoned to the capital.
Soon after, Liǔ was made Cìshǐ of Liǔzhōu,
and Liú was made Cìshǐ of Bōzhōu.
Liǔ, considering that Liú had to attend to his parent,
and that Bōzhōu was the worst place,
requested to exchange it for Liǔzhōu.
The emperor did not permit it.
The prime minister replied: ‘Yǔxī has an elderly parent.’
The emperor said: ‘One only needs to be granted a prefecture;
what does it matter if his mother is alive!’
Péi Jìngōng advanced and said: ‘Your Majesty is currently attending to the Empress Dowager;
it is inappropriate to utter such words.’
The emperor showed a look of shame.
Liú was then changed to Liánzhōu.”
According to Liǔ Zōngyuán’s tomb inscription,
he intended to submit a memorial but had not yet done so;
it was not that it had already been submitted and not permitted.
When Yǔxī was appointed to Bōzhōu,
Péi Dù was not yet a prime minister.
We now follow the Shílù and Jiànzhèng Jí.
Zōngyuán was skilled in writing.
He once wrote the “Zǐrén Zhuàn” (Biography of the Master Carpenter),
in which he stated:
“The master carpenter does not wield axes, adzes, knives, or saws.
He specializes in using strings, compasses, squares, and ink lines to measure the timber,
observe the structure of buildings,
and determine the appropriate heights, depths, roundness, squareness, shortness, and length.
He directs all the artisans,
each to their task,
dismissing those who are not competent.
When the grand edifice is completed,
he alone is credited with the achievement,
and receives three times the salary.
This is similar to a prime minister who governs the world:
establishing principles and regulations, rectifying laws and standards,
selecting the best talents in the land to fit their positions,
settling the people of the land in their occupations,
promoting the capable and dismissing the incompetent.
When all nations are well-governed,
commentators uniquely praise Yī [Yǐn], Fù [Yuè], Zhōu [Gōng], and Shào [Gōng],
while the diligent labor of the hundred officials is not recorded.
Some, perhaps ignorant of the essential principles,
boast of their abilities and seek fame,
personally engaging in minor tasks,
encroaching upon the duties of many officials,
bustling about in the government offices,
while neglecting the greater and more distant matters.
These are those who do not understand the Way of a Prime Minister.”
The “Biography of Guō Tuó, the Tree Planter” also says:
“Everything that Guō Tuó planted
grew and flourished.
Someone asked him,
and he replied: ‘Guō Tuó is not able to make trees long-lived and prolific.
All trees naturally
want their roots to spread out comfortably,
and their soil to remain undisturbed.
Once planted,
do not move them, do not worry about them,
and leave without looking back.
If you plant them as if they were your children,
but leave them as if they were abandoned,
then their natural state will be complete and their inherent nature obtained.
Other planters do not do this;
their roots are cramped and their soil is changed,
they love them with too much affection,
and worry about them with too much diligence.
They inspect them in the morning and touch them in the evening,
and having left, they look back again.
Even worse, they scratch their bark to check if they are alive or dead,
and shake their base to see how sparse or dense they are.
Thus, the trees' natural state becomes alienated day by day.
Although they say they love them,
in reality, they harm them;
although they say they worry about them,
in reality, they treat them as enemies.
That is why they are not like me!
Governance is also like this.
In my village, I have seen those who govern the people,
who like to issue many bothersome commands,
as if they were greatly compassionate, but ultimately bring disaster upon them.
Morning and evening, officials come,
gather the people and command them,
urging their plowing and harvesting,
and supervising their sericulture and weaving.
We common folk stop our meals to labor for officials without rest,
so how can we increase our livelihood and secure our nature?
All their suffering and exhaustion
are due to this reason.’ ”
Dù Yù said: “Zhí
means to be responsible for.”
The “Biography of the Carpenter” uses it to admonish prime ministers,
and the “Biography of the Tree Planter” uses it to admonish governors and magistrates.
Therefore, Wēn Gōng adopted it,
because it provides insight into the art of governance.
5 On a Gēngzǐ day,
Lǐ Guāngyán reported a victory against Huáixī forces at Lín Yǐng.
6 Tián Hóngzhèng sent his son, Bù, with three thousand soldiers to assist Yán Shòu in attacking Wú Yuánjì.
7 On a Jiǎchén day,
Lǐ Guāngyán again reported a victory against Huáixī forces at Nándùn.
Nándùn
was a Han county,
belonging to Rǔnán Commandery,
and in Tang, it belonged to Chén Zhōu.
8 Wú Yuánjì sent envoys to request aid from Héng and Yùn.
Wáng Chéngzōng and Lǐ Shīdào repeatedly submitted memorials requesting a pardon for Yuánjì,
but the Emperor did not comply.
At this time, troops from various circuits were dispatched to attack Yuánjì, but Zhīqīng was not included.
Shīdào sent a major general with two thousand men to head towards Shòuchūn,
ostensibly to assist the imperial army in attacking Yuánjì,
but in reality, to provide aid to Yuánjì.
Shīdào had long harbored dozens of assassins and rogue individuals,
providing them generously.
These men said to Shīdào:
“Of the urgent needs in warfare,
nothing is more important than provisions.
Now, the Héyīn depot accumulates tribute grain and taxes from Jiāng and Huái;
please secretly go and burn it.
Recruit several hundred unruly youths from Dōng Dū,
raid the markets,
and burn the palaces and gates.
Then the court will not have time to attack Cài,
but will first save its own vital areas.
This is also a unique way to save Cài.”
Shīdào agreed.
From then on, bandits and thieves began to arise in various places.
On the evening of a Xīnhài day,
dozens of bandits attacked the Héyīn Transfer and Transport Office,
killing and wounding more than ten people,
and burning over three hundred thousand mín/pǐ of money and silk,
and over thirty thousand hú of grain.
Consequently, public sentiment became fearful.
Many officials requested to withdraw the troops,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
9 The various armies had been attacking Huáixī for a long time without success.
In the fifth month,
the Emperor sent Grand Censor Péi Dù to the field camp to convey greetings and comfort,
and to assess the military situation.
Upon his return, Dù
reported that Huáixī could definitely be taken,
and moreover said:
“Looking at the various generals,
only Lǐ Guāngyán is brave and knows righteousness,
and will certainly achieve merit.”
The Emperor was pleased.
He was pleased because
the report indicated a certainty of victory.
Hán Yù, a secretary of the Ministry of Personnel for Examination and Director of the Imperial Edicts, submitted a memorial,
stating
that: “Huáixī consists of three small prefectures—
The three small prefectures are
Shēn, Guāng, and Cài.
—and it stands against the full strength of the empire;
its defeat can be awaited swiftly.
This is speaking in terms of the relative size and strength.
It merely depends on Your Majesty’s decision to act or not to act.”
He then itemized the advantages and disadvantages of using military force,
believing
that: “Currently, the various circuits each dispatch two or three thousand soldiers,
their strength is weak and isolated,
they are strangers in a foreign land,
and unfamiliar with the enemy,
easily intimidated by rumors.
The generals, treating them as guest soldiers,
give them meager provisions
and assign them arduous tasks;
or they divide their units,
separating soldiers from their commanders.
Isolated in spirit and timid in resolve,
it is difficult for them to achieve success.
Furthermore, their original armies each require provisions and transportation,
and the long distances involved
result in double the labor and expenses.
I hear that in the villages and among the common people in the areas bordering the enemy, such as Chén, Xǔ, Ān, Táng, Rǔ, and Shòu prefectures,
all possess weapons,
are skilled in combat,
and know the enemy’s strengths and weaknesses.
Until now, no arrangements have been made for them,
yet they are willing to provide their own clothing and food
to protect their homelands.
If they were to be recruited,
an army could be formed immediately.
After the enemy is pacified,
it would be easy to send them back to farming.
I beg that all troops from the various circuits be dismissed,
and local people be recruited to replace them.”
He also said:
“The soldiers in Cài Zhōu are all subjects of the state.
If their power is exhausted and they are unable to commit evil,
there is no need for excessive slaughter.”
10On a Bǐngshēn day,
Lǐ Guāngyán reported defeating Huáixī forces at Shí Qū.
Shí Qū
is southwest of Yīnshuǐ County in Chén Zhōu.
Bài
is pronounced bù mài.
Guāngyán could not break out,
so he himself destroyed the palisades on his left and right,
and sent out cavalry to attack them.
Guāngyán personally led several horsemen to charge their formation,
entering and exiting four times.
The bandits all recognized him,
and arrows gathered on his body like hedgehog quills.
His son grabbed the reins to stop him;
lǎn
means to grasp with the hand.
Thereupon, everyone fought to the death,
and the Huáixī forces were utterly routed,
with several thousand killed.
The Emperor considered Péi Dù to be a good judge of character.
11After Lǐ Jífǔ’s death,
the Emperor entrusted all military matters to Wǔ Yuánhéng.
A guest harbored by Lǐ Shīdào said to Lǐ Shīdào:
“The reason the Son of Heaven is so keen on punishing Cài
is because Yuánhéng supports it.
I request to secretly go and assassinate him.
If Yuánhéng dies,
then other prime ministers will not dare to lead this strategy,
and will instead compete to urge the Son of Heaven to withdraw the troops.”
Shīdào thought this was correct,
and immediately provided him with resources and dispatched him.
Wáng Chéngzōng sent his yájiàng, Yǐn Shàoqīng, to report on affairs,
to lobby for Wú Yuánjì.
When Shàoqīng arrived at the Secretariat,
his words and manner were insolent,
and Yuánhéng shouted at him to leave.
Chéngzōng then submitted a memorial slandering Yuánhéng.
In the sixth month,
on the *Guǐmǎo* day,
before dawn,
Wǔ Yuánhéng entered court.
He exited the east gate of Jìng'ān Fāng, where he resided.
Bandits suddenly emerged from the darkness and shot him.
His attendants all scattered and fled.
The bandits seized Wǔ Yuánhéng's horse and led it for more than ten paces before killing him,
taking his skull and departing.
They then entered Tōnghuà Fāng and attacked Péi Dù,
wounding his head.
He fell into a ditch.
Because Péi Dù's felt hat was thick,
he survived.
His servant, Wáng Yì, embraced a bandit from behind and shouted loudly.
The bandit cut off Wáng Yì's arm and fled.
The capital was greatly alarmed.
Thereupon, an edict ordered that when chancellors went out,
Jīnwú cavalrymen with drawn swords and strung bows would be added to guard them.
At every *fāng* gate they passed, challenges and searches were extremely strict.
*Hē*
means to shout.
*Suǒ*
means to search.
*Suǒ*,
pronounced *shān kè fān*;
the same applies to *dà suǒ* below.
The Emperor sometimes remained on the throne for a long time,
but the ranks of officials had not yet assembled.
The bandits left a note for the Jīnwú and the Prefectural and County offices.
*Yí*
means to abandon.
The Left and Right Jīnwú were in charge of patrolling and arresting criminals.
The *fǔ*
and *xiàn*
refer to the Jīngzhào Fǔ and the two *Chìxiàn*.
"Do not be hasty in capturing us;
we will kill you first."
Therefore, those hunting the bandits did not dare to be too urgent.
Xǔ Mèngróng, the Minister of War, met the Emperor and said:
"Since ancient times, there has never been a chancellor lying dead by the roadside without the culprits being caught.
This is a disgrace to the court!"
He then wept.
He also went to the Zhōngshū Shěng, wiping away tears, and said:
"I request that we memorialize to appoint Vice Censor-in-Chief Péi as chancellor,
and conduct a thorough search for the bandit party,
exhausting the source of their wickedness."
On the *Wùshēn* day,
an edict ordered searches and arrests throughout the capital and provinces.
Those who captured bandits would be rewarded with ten thousand strings of cash
and a fifth-rank official position.
Those who dared to shelter them
would have their entire clan exterminated.
Thereupon, a great search was conducted in the capital.
In the homes of high officials and noble families, those with double walls (*fùbì*) or layered rafters (*zhòngliáo*) were all searched.
*Fùbì*
means a partition wall.
*Zhòngliáo*
means a large roof covering a small house,
with rafters laid above and below,
and space between them where things can be stored.
*Liáo*,
pronounced *lǔ hào fān*.
It means rafters.
Shǐ Zhào pronounces it *lián xiāo qiè*.
In the Chéngdé Jūn Presentment Office, there were several soldiers from Héngzhōu, including Zhāng Yàn,
whose conduct was disorderly.
*Wúzhuàng*
means having no good conduct.
*Héng*,
pronounced *hù dēng fān*.
On the *Gēngxū* day,
Shéncè General Wáng Shìzé and others reported that Wáng Chéngzōng had sent Zhāng Yàn and others to kill Wǔ Yuánhéng.
Officials arrested Zhāng Yàn and eight others.
The Emperor ordered Péi Wǔ, the Magistrate of Jīngzhào, and Chén Zhōngshī, the Censor, to interrogate them.
On the *Guǐhài* day,
an edict ordered that Wáng Chéngzōng's three previous memorials be displayed to all officials
to discuss his crimes.
Péi Dù was ill with wounds,
confined to bed for twenty days.
An edict ordered guards to stay at his residence,
and imperial envoys continually inquired about his health.
Some requested that Péi Dù be dismissed from office to appease Héng and Yùn.
The Emperor angrily said:
"If Péi Dù is dismissed from office,
it means the wicked plot has succeeded,
and the court will no longer have any discipline.
My use of Péi Dù alone
is enough to defeat these two rebels."
Historians say that Xiànzōng's clear judgment
was why he succeeded.
On the *Jiǎzǐ* day,
the Emperor summoned Péi Dù to an audience.
On the *Yǐchǒu* day,
Péi Dù was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Péi Dù memorialized:
"Huáixī
is a disease in our vitals,
which must be eliminated.
Moreover, the court has already undertaken to suppress it.
The defiant *fānzhèn* of the two Hé rivers
will observe this as a measure of our strength,
so we cannot stop."
The Emperor agreed
and entrusted all military affairs to Péi Dù,
who pursued the rebels very aggressively.
Initially,
Dézōng was very suspicious and wary.
If court officials visited each other,
the Jīnwú would all secretly observe and report it,
and chancellors dared not receive guests at their private residences.
Péi Dù memorialized:
"Now that the bandits are not yet pacified,
chancellors should invite worthy talents from all quarters to participate in discussions,"
and for the first time requested permission to receive guests at his private residence,
which was granted.
Chén Zhōngshī interrogated Zhāng Yàn and others,
who fully confessed to killing Wǔ Yuánhéng.
Zhāng Hóngjìng doubted the truth of this
and repeatedly told the Emperor,
but the Emperor did not listen.
On the *Wùchén* day,
Zhāng Yàn and five others were executed,
and fourteen of their associates were killed.
Lǐ Shīdào's retainers, however, managed to hide and escape.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The old biography of Zhāng Hóngjìng says:
"Initially,
when bandits killed Wǔ Yuánhéng,
the capital searched for the culprits but did not find them.
At that time, in Wáng Chéngzōng's residence, there were several garrison soldiers, including Zhāng Yàn,
whose conduct was disorderly,
and many suspected them.
An edict ordered them to be handed over to Censor Chén Zhōngshī of the Yùshǐ Tái for interrogation.
They all confessed to their crimes,
as had been rumored in the capital.
Zhāng Hóngjìng doubted their honesty
and repeatedly spoke of it before the Emperor;
Xiànzōng did not listen.
When Tián Hóngzhèng entered Yùnzhōu,
he examined the registers
and found there were also those who had killed Wǔ Yuánhéng.
However, the matter was ambiguous,
with conflicting accounts,
and the truth was never ascertained."
According to the old biography of Lǚ Yuányīng:
"Lǐ Shīdào's generals Zī Jiāzhēn and Mén Chá were captured,
and both claimed to have harmed Wǔ Yuánhéng."
Thus, Wǔ Yuánhéng's death
must have been Lǐ Shīdào's doing.
However, because Wǔ Yuánhéng had reprimanded Yǐn Shàonú,
and Wáng Chéngzōng had submitted memorials slandering Wǔ Yuánhéng,
people at the time all pointed to Wáng Chéngzōng.
We now follow Xuē Túcún's *Hénán Jì*.
12 In autumn,
seventh month,
on the *Gēngwǔ* first day of the month,
Lǐ Guāngjìn, the Military Commissioner of Língwǔ, passed away.
Lǐ Guāngjìn and his younger brother, Lǐ Guāngyán, were very close.
Lǐ Guāngyán married first,
and his mother entrusted him with household affairs.
When their mother died,
Lǐ Guāngjìn married later.
Lǐ Guāngyán had his wife present the keys and seals,
registered the household property,
and returned it to his elder brother's wife (*sì*).
Máo Huǎng said: Dù Yù said: Wives of brothers call each other *sì*.
This is how sisters-in-law address each other,
using age as the distinguishing name.
The elder is called *sì*, the younger *dì*,
regardless of the seniority of their husbands.
Today, it is customary to call an elder brother's wife *sì*
and a younger brother's wife *dì*.
*Sì*,
pronounced *xiáng lǐ fān*.
"The new daughter-in-law served the former mother-in-law,
and the former mother-in-law ordered her to manage the household affairs.
This cannot be changed."
Then they held each other and wept.
13 On the *Jiǎxū* day,
an edict enumerated Wáng Chéngzōng's crimes
and suspended his tribute,
saying:
"We hope he will repent and correct his errors,
and surrender himself.
The time for attack
will await further orders."
14 In the eighth month,
on the *Jǐhài* first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
15 Lǐ Shīdào (李師道) established a branch office (liúhòuyuàn, 留後院) in Dōngdū (東都).
People from his own territory (běndàorén, 本道人) constantly came and went in a disorderly fashion,
and officials dared not question them.
"People from his own territory"
refers to those from Yǎn (兗), Yùn (鄆), Zī (淄), and Qīng (青) prefectures.
The defense troops (fángyùbīng, 防禦兵) were all stationed at Yīquè (伊闕).
Shīdào (師道) secretly brought his soldiers into the office
until there were hundreds of them.
They planned to burn the palace and government buildings,
unleash their troops to kill and plunder.
They had already cooked oxen to feast the soldiers,
and the next day
they were to launch the attack.
One of their junior soldiers went to the Dōngdū (東都) Retainer-Administrator (liúshǒu, 留守) Lǚ Yuányīng (呂元膺) to report the plot.
Yuányīng (元膺) immediately called back the Yīquè (伊闕) troops to surround them.
The bandit multitude burst out,
with the defense troops following close behind,
but not daring to press them.
Lǚ Yuányīng (呂元膺), as the Dōngdū (東都) Defense Commissioner (fángyùshǐ, 防禦使), also served as the Retainer-Administrator (liúshǒu, 留守).
The troops under his command were called defense troops.
They fled towards the mountains.
The "Six Statutes of Tang (Táng Liùdiǎn, 唐六典)" states: Dōngdū (東都) city's south face has three gates:
the central one is called Dìngdǐng (定鼎),
the left is Chángxià (長夏),
and the right is Hòuzài (厚載).
The east face has three gates:
the central one is Jiànchūn (建春),
the southern is Yǒngtōng (永通),
and the northern is Shàngdōng (上東).
The north face has two gates:
the eastern is Ānxǐ (安喜),
and the western is Huī'ān (徽安).
To the west lies the Imperial Park (Jìnyuàn, 禁苑).
The park's west has four gates:
Nányíngqiū (南迎秋),
next Yóuyì (遊義),
next Lóngyān (籠煙),
and the northern Língxī (靈溪).
The "Dissenting Accounts (Kǎoyì, 考異)" states: The "Record of Hénán (Hénán Jì, 河南記)" says:
"The bandit leader Zī Jiāzhēn (訾嘉珍) indeed secretly recruited over one hundred people in the Dōngdū (東都) branch office,
and also manufactured weapons.
All arrangements were made.
Coincidentally, a gatekeeper (ménzǐ jiàn'ér, 門子健兒) committed a minor offense
and was flogged.
He then sent one of his brothers to report to Hénán Fǔ (河南府).
At that time, the two counties were ordered to gather strong men,
all carrying bows, arrows, swords, and staffs,
to surround the office in Xīngdào Fāng (興道坊) multiple times.
The bandit faction was pressed and cornered,
trampling each other.
Arrows rained down from all four sides.
In an instant, they were annihilated.
Then the office buildings were set on fire,
all reduced to ashes."
We now follow the "Veritable Records (Shílù, 實錄)".
The Retainer-Administrator's (liúshǒu, 留守) troops were few and weak.
Yuányīng (元膺) sat at the gate of the Imperial City (Huángchéng, 皇城).
The "Six Statutes of Tang (Táng Liùdiǎn, 唐六典)" states: Dōngdū (東都)'s Imperial City (Huángchéng, 皇城) is in the northwest corner of the capital city.
Its south face has three gates:
the central one is Duānmén (端門),
the left is Zuǒyèmén (左掖門),
and the right is Yòuyèmén (右掖門).
Its east face has one gate,
called Bīnyào (賓耀).
Its west face has two gates:
the southern is Lìjǐng (麗景),
and the northern is Xuānyào (宣耀).
Yuányīng (元膺) probably sat beneath the Zuǒyèmén (左掖門).
He remained composed and unperturbed,
and the capital's people relied on him for their safety.
The southwest of Dōngdū (東都) bordered Dèng (鄧) and Guó (虢).
The "Record of Nine Regions (Jiǔyù Zhì, 九域志)" states: Hénán Fǔ (河南府)
borders Guó Zhōu (虢州) to the southwest at a distance of 325 lǐ (里).
A little further south,
it borders Dèng Zhōu (鄧州) at a distance of 600 lǐ (里).
The people there did not farm,
but specialized in hunting for a living.
Everyone was agile and brave,
called "mountain sheds" (shānshéng, 山棚).
Yuányīng (元膺) offered a heavy reward to capture the bandits.
After several days,
a mountain shed (shānshéng, 山棚) was selling deer.
The bandits encountered him and robbed him.
The mountain shed (shānshéng, 山棚) ran to summon his fellows,
and also led government troops to jointly surround the bandits in a valley,
capturing them all.
Upon examination,
their leader was found
to be the monk Yuánjìng (圓淨) from Zhōngyuè Sì (中嶽寺).
He had previously served as a general for Shǐ Sīmíng (史思明),
was extraordinarily brave and fierce,
and schemed for Shīdào (師道).
He bought much land between Yīquè (伊闕) and Lùhún (陸渾)
to house and feed the mountain sheds (shānshéng, 山棚).
There were also Zī Jiāzhēn (訾嘉珍) and Mén Chá (門察)
who secretly organized their factions and assigned them to Yuánjìng (圓淨).
Yuánjìng (圓淨), with ten million coins from Shīdào (師道),
ostensibly renovated Fógūang Sì (佛光寺),
gathered his gang, and made their plans.
They agreed that Jiāzhēn (嘉珍) and others would secretly launch the attack within the city,
and Yuánjìng (圓淨) would light a fire in the mountains
to gather the mountain sheds (shānshéng, 山棚) from the two counties to enter the city and assist them.
The "two counties"
were Lùhún (陸渾) and Yīquè (伊闕).
When the captors apprehended him,
they swung their hammers at his shins,
but could not break them.
Yuánjìng (圓淨) cursed, saying:
"You rats!
You can't even break a man's shins,
yet you dare to call yourselves brave men!"
He then positioned his own shins
and instructed them how to break them.
At the execution,
he sighed, saying:
"My plans were ruined; I didn't get to make Luò Chéng (洛城) flow with blood!"
The total number of his followers who died was several thousand.
The two generals of the Retainer-Administrator's (liúshǒu, 留守) and Defense forces
were the general of the Retainer-Administrator's (liúshǒu, 留守) troops and the general of the defense troops.
The titles
were official titles privately conferred by Lǐ Shīdào (李師道) to his yámén (衙門) vanguard army commanders,
for whom he issued commissions (tiē, 帖).
Yuányīng (元膺) interrogated Zī Jiāzhēn (訾嘉珍) and Mén Chá (門察).
Only then did he learn that the one who killed Wǔ Yuánhéng (武元衡) was Shīdào (師道).
Yuányīng (元膺) secretly reported this.
He sent the two men in a cage cart to the capital (Jīngshī, 京師).
The emperor had already been campaigning against Wáng Chéngzōng (王承宗)
and did not pursue a thorough investigation.
Yuányīng (元膺) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Recently, the frontier governors (fānzhèn, 藩鎮) have become unruly and disloyal.
There are some who might be pardoned.
However, Shīdào (師道)'s plot to massacre the capital city
and burn the palace
is an act of extreme rebellion,
and he must not be spared."
The emperor agreed;
but as he was currently suppressing Wú Yuánjì (吳元濟)
and cutting off Wáng Chéngzōng (王承宗),
he had no time yet to deal with Shīdào (師道).
This history states the emperor Xiànzōng (憲宗)'s true feelings.
16 On the day Yǐchǒu (乙丑),
Lǐ Guāngyán (李光顏) was defeated at Shíqǔ (時曲).
17 Earlier,
the emperor believed that because Yán Shòu (嚴綬) was in Hédōng (河東),
many of the subordinate generals he sent had achieved merit, referring to Lǐ Guāngyán (李光顏) and others.
Xiāngyáng (襄陽) was the administrative seat of the Shānnán Dōngdào Jiédù (山南東道節度).
Shòu (綬) had no other talents or abilities.
On the day he arrived at the army,
he emptied the treasury
to reward the soldiers.
Years of accumulation
were exhausted in a single day.
He also heavily bribed eunuchs to gain support,
gathering over ten thousand troops from eight prefectures
and stationing them on the border.
The eight prefectures were Xiāng (襄), Dèng (鄧), Táng (唐), Suí (隨), Jūn (均), Fáng (房), Yǐng (郢), and Fù (復).
He achieved no merit whatsoever.
Péi Dù (裴度) repeatedly stated that his army was disorganized.
In the ninth month,
on the day Guǐyǒu,
Hán Hóng was appointed Supreme Commander of all armies in Huaixī.
Hóng enjoyed flaunting his influence
and wished to use the rebels to enhance his own standing.
He did not want Huaixī to be pacified quickly.
The Kǎoyì (Investigation of Differences) states: The old tradition says:
"Hóng, garrisoned in Biànzhōu,
was at a critical juncture facing the rebels of the two rivers.
The imperial court, fearing his disloyal intentions,
wished to entrust military authority to him,
while having Lǐ Guāngyán and Wū Chóngyìn truly lead the charge.
Thus, Hóng was appointed Acting Supreme Commander of the armies in Huaixī.
Though Hóng held the supreme command,
he consistently did not want the armies to achieve merit.
He secretly devised schemes to delay and obstruct,
and whenever a victory was reported,
he would be displeased for several days.
His actions to endanger the state and seek personal gain were like this."
However, Hóng took charge after the accumulated chaos in Xuānwǔ,
brought stability to the region,
and resided amidst powerful bandits,
achieving considerable prestige.
If he had disloyal intentions,
forming alliances with other garrisons and acting defiantly,
it would have been as easy as turning over his hand.
Yet, observing his conduct from beginning to end,
he never failed in his duty as a subject.
If the imperial court suspected him of disloyal intentions and then appointed him as Supreme Commander,
then Guāngyán and Chóngyìn would be further subject to his command,
which would not be a way to guard against him.
Moreover, "displeased for several days"—
what evidence can be found for such a state?
It is feared that the slander exaggerates the truth.
We now follow what is credible.
Hóng wished to win Lǐ Guāngyán's favor.
He searched throughout Dàliáng City and found a beautiful woman.
(The Xuānwǔ Jìdù governed Dàliáng.)
"Suǒ" (索)
is pronounced "shān kè fān."
He adorned her with pearls, jade, gold, and kingfisher feathers,
worth several million cash,
and sent an envoy to present her.
The envoy first delivered a letter to Guāngyán
and held a grand
banquet for the generals and soldiers.
The envoy presented the entertainer,
whose beauty was unparalleled,
astonishing everyone present.
Guāngyán said to the envoy:
"His Excellency (Xiànggōng) pities this traveler Guāngyán
and bestows upon me a beautiful entertainer;
my gratitude for this virtue is truly profound.
However, there are tens of thousands of warriors here,
all having left their homes to come from afar,
braving sharp blades.
How can Guāngyán bear to enjoy pleasure alone with music and beauty!"
Thereupon, he shed tears,
and all those seated wept.
"Zuò" (座)
should perhaps be written as
"zuò" (坐)
for textual consistency.
He sent the entertainer back,
saying:
"Please convey Guāngyán's deepest thanks to His Excellency.
Guāngyán has pledged his life to the state,
vowing not to share the same sun and moon with the rebels.
I will not waver even unto death!"
18 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
Shānnán Dōngdào was first divided into two military governorships.
Lǐ Xùn, Minister of the Board of Revenue, was made Jìdùshǐ of Xiāng, Fù, Yǐng, Jūn, and Fáng.
Gāo Xiáyù, Grand General of the Right Yǔlín Guard, was made Jìdùshǐ of Táng, Suí, and Dèng.
The court debated that Táng bordered Cài,
so Xiáyù was to focus entirely on offense and battle,
while Xùn would allocate resources from the five prefectures to provision him.
19 On the day Xīnchǒu,
Quán Déyú, Minister of the Board of Punishments, memorialized:
"Since the compilation of the 'Gélǜ Lìnglìng Shìlèi' (Categorized Regulations, Statutes, Ordinances, and Orders) in the 25th year of Kāiyuán,
the 'Táng Liùdiǎn' (Six Canons of Tang) describes the names of legal texts as follows:
'Gé' (regulations) in 24 chapters,
'Shì' (forms) in 33 chapters,
'Lǜ' (statutes) in 12 chapters,
and 'Lìng' (ordinances) in 27 chapters.
The 'Huìyào' (Collected Essentials) states: In the 25th year of Kāiyuán, the 'Lǜ' (Statutes) were edited into 12 rolls,
the 'Lǜshū' (Commentaries on Statutes) in 30 rolls,
the 'Shì' (Forms) in 20 rolls,
and the 'Kāiyuán Xīngé' (New Regulations of Kāiyuán) in 10 rolls.
Additionally, 'Gélǜ Lìnglìng Shìlèi' (Categorized Regulations, Statutes, Ordinances, and Orders) in 40 rolls was compiled,
arranged by category for ease of reference.
Recently, it has been abridged into 30 rolls.
I request that it be put into effect."
The emperor assented.
The 'Huìyào' states: In the 19th year of Kāiyuán,
Péi Guāngtíng and others memorialized to instruct the relevant officials to abridge and compile the "Zhǎnghángchì" (Permanent Edicts) issued after the 'Gé' into 6 rolls.
Now, the "Zhǎnghángchì" issued after the 25th year has again been abridged into 30 rolls.
20 Although the emperor had severed Wáng Chéngzōng's tributary relations,
he had not yet issued an edict to punish him.
Tián Hóngzhèng, Jìdùshǐ of Wèibó, stationed troops on his border,
and Chéngzōng repeatedly defeated them.
Hóngzhèng, angered,
submitted a memorial requesting to attack him,
but the emperor did not permit it.
After ten memorials,
he was finally allowed to proceed to Bèizhōu.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
Hóngzhèng's army encamped at Bèizhōu.
21 On the day Gēngxū,
the Eastern Capital reported that bandits had burned Bǎiyá Granary.
Sòng Bái said: Héqīng County has Bǎiyá City.
Dù Yòu said: Bǎiyá City
was built by Hóu Jǐng,
and is west of Héqīng County.
22 In the eleventh month,
