This incident, however, is likely not something Mùzōng could have done.
The *Xùxùn* is mistaken.
We now follow the *Yīnhuà Lù*.
The various armies dispatched to suppress Huáixī numbered nearly ninety thousand.
The Emperor was angry that the generals had achieved no success for so long.
On the *xīnsì* day,
he ordered Liáng Shǒuqīan, *Zhī Shūmì*, to convey his comfort and good wishes,
and then kept him there to supervise the armies,
giving him five hundred blank imperial patents (*kōngmíng gàoshēn*) and gold and silk,
to encourage those who died in service.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Lí Gūangyán and others were first promoted to *jiǎnxiaoguān*,
and the imperial decree severely reprimanded them,
indicating that failure to achieve success would be punished.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Lǐ Wéntōng reported defeating Huáixī troops at Gùshǐ,
beheading over a thousand.
In the twelfth month,
on the *rényín* day,
Chéng Zhígōng reported defeating Chéngdé troops at Chánghé.
Chánghé
was the territory of Hàn Xìndū Guǎngchūan County.
During the Suí dynasty, Chánghé County was established eighty *lǐ* east of Guǎngchūan County.
In the fourth year of Yuánhé, it was moved to Báiqiáo,
and the county seat was established on the west bank of the Yǒngjì River.
In the tenth year, it was again moved to Xiǎohú City east of the river,
belonging to Dézhōu.
Hún Hào, *Yìwǔ Jiédùshǐ*, repeatedly defeated Wáng Chéngzōng in battle,
and then led his entire army to press upon his border,
encamping thirty *lǐ* from Héngzhōu.
Chéngzōng, fearing,
secretly dispatched troops into Hào's territory,
burning and plundering cities and towns.
The people's hearts began to look inward and waver.
Coincidentally, an imperial envoy arrived to urge him to battle.
Hào led his troops to advance and besiege Héngzhōu,
where he fought Chéngzōng
and suffered a great defeat,
fleeing back to Dìngzhōu.
*Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Héngzhōu to Dìngzhōu is one hundred thirty-five *lǐ*.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
an imperial edict appointed Chén Chǔ, *Yìzhōu Cìshǐ*, as *Yìwǔ Jiédùshǐ*.
When the army heard of this,
they plundered Hào and his family's clothes,
leaving them naked.
Chén Chǔ galloped into Dìngzhōu.
Yìzhōu is one hundred forty *lǐ* south to Dìngzhōu.
He collected the clothes from the army to return to Hào,
meaning he collected the clothes of Hào's family that the army had plundered.
Chǔ was from Dìngzhōu
and was Zhāng Màozhāo's nephew.
Historians say that the people of Héshuò were accustomed to rebellion
and only knew to obey the close relatives of their commanders.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
Wáng Yá, *Hànlín Xuéshì*, was appointed *Zhōngshū Shìláng* and *Tóng Píngzhāng Shì*.
Yuán Zī arrived in Tángzhōu,
removed the scouts,
and stopped his troops from invading Wú Yuánjì's territory.
This is what Yuán Zī called
"opening the gate to invite bandits."
The Xīnxīng Stockade
was likely in the northeastern part of Tángzhōu,
newly erected to guard against the Cài people.
Yuánjì no longer paid attention to Zī because of this.
The imperial court learned of it,
and on the *jiǎyín* day,
appointed Lǐ Sù, *Tàizǐ Zhànshì*, as *Táng-Suí-Dèng Jiédùshǐ*.
Sù was Tīng's elder brother.
Both Sù and Tīng were sons of Lǐ Shèng.
41. Initially, a commissioner for river transport on the Huái and Yǐng Rivers was appointed.
The rice from Yáng Zǐyuàn was transported from Huái'yīn, going upstream along the Huái River into the Yǐng River.
It reached Xiàngchéng and entered the Yǐn River.
According to the old histories,
at that time, the rice transport went upstream along the Huái River for forty *lǐ* to Shòuzhōu,
entered the mouth of the Yǐng River,
and then went upstream again to the Shénqiū border of Yǐngzhōu,
a distance of five hundred *lǐ* to Xiàngchéng.
Then it went upstream for another five hundred *lǐ* into the Yǐn River,
and a further three hundred *lǐ* to Yǎnchéng.
Fifty thousand *shí* of rice were obtained,
and five million bundles of fodder.
This saved seventy-six thousand *mín* in costs for the transport via Biàn.
Xiàngchéng was
Xiàng County during the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to Rǔnán Prefecture.
In the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Chénzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: it is seventy *lǐ* southeast of the prefecture.
According to the *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù*,
the Yǐn River
is a branch of the Rǔ River.
The Yǐng River, upon reaching the old Nándùn County,
merged with the Yǐn River.
The Yǐnshuǐ County of the Táng dynasty
was the territory of Rǔyáng County during the Hàn dynasty.
This was to supply the armies attacking Huáixī,
saving over seventy thousand *mín* in costs for the transport via Biàn.
42. On the *jǐwèi* day,
Róngguǎn reported that the Huángdòng barbarians had massacred Yánzhōu.
Róngguǎn administered Róng, Biàn, Bái, Láo, Qīn, Yán, Yú, Tāng, Ráng, and Gǔ prefectures.
Punctuated by Róng Zhàozǔ, revised by Niè Chóngqí.
Compiled under imperial command by
Sīmǎ Guāng.
Later Academy, Tiāntái.
Yuánhé Twelfth Year
(*dīngyǒu*, 817 CE)
1. Spring,
First Month.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
Yuán Zī was demoted to Inspector of Fúzhōu.
Lǐ Suò arrived at Tángzhōu.
The army was still suffering from recent defeats,
and the soldiers were all hesitant to fight.
Suò knew this.
When someone came to greet him,
Suò said to him,
"The Son of Heaven knows that I, Suò, am gentle and weak,
and able to endure humiliation,
which is why he sent me to pacify you all.
As for engaging in battle and seizing territory,
that is not my business."
The troops believed him and felt at ease.
Suò personally inspected the soldiers.
He cared for the wounded and sick,
and did not act with stern authority.
When some spoke of the military administration being lax,
Suò said,
"It is not that I do not know.
Minister Yuán relied solely on kindness and generosity to win over the rebels;
the rebels underestimated him.
Hearing of my arrival,
they will surely increase their defenses.
Therefore, I deliberately show them laxity.
They will surely consider me weak and negligent,
and only then can we plan against them."
The people of Huáixī, having once defeated the two commanders Gāo and Yuán,
slighted Suò due to his previously humble rank,
and thus made no preparations.
This laid the groundwork for Suò to exploit their unpreparedness and capture Cài.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The old account states:
"Suò was profoundly brave and skilled in long-term planning.
He treated his officers with sincerity,
and thus was able to utilize his humble and weak position
to surprise the rebels.
After half a year,
knowing who could be used,
he then planned to attack Cài and
submitted a memorial requesting reinforcements;
an edict granted two thousand cavalry from Hézhōng and Fūfāng to reinforce him."
Zhèng Xiè's *Píng Cài Lù* says:
"On the *jiǎshēn* day of the first month,
the Duke arrived at his command.
Before this,
the soldiers had suffered defeats at Wànshèng, Xiāopí, Tiěchéng, and Xīnxīng;
everyone was fearful
and dared not speak of battle.
The Duke feigned saying,
'Warfare is not what I am capable of.'
Soon after, he secretly summoned his generals to plan the matter.
At this time,
the Duke submitted a memorial requesting a direct assault on Yuán Jì,
and everyone mocked his proposal.
So he sent the Surveillance Commissioner's aide, Wáng Nǐ, to request troops at the court.
An edict ordered two thousand combined cavalry and infantry from Yìchéng, Hézhōng, and Fūfāng to make up the deficiency."
According to this,
it was upon his initial arrival that he requested additional troops.
Also, in the second month,
he immediately captured Dīng Shìliáng and
received the surrender of Wú Xiùlín.
This means he did not wait half a year to know who could be used,
so the old account is likely mistaken.
However, Suò secretly planned to attack Cài,
how could he reveal it first,
and say
"submitted a memorial requesting an attack on Yuán Jì,
and everyone mocked his proposal"?
If that were the case, everyone would know,
which is likely incorrect!
Therefore, we do not adopt it.
2. The Vice Commissioner of Salt and Iron, Chéng [AS-82FA], was dispatched
to oversee financial levies in Jiāng and Huái.
3. The Uighurs repeatedly requested to marry a princess.
The authorities calculated the cost to be nearly five million *mín*.
At that time, the Central Plains were engaged in warfare,
so the Emperor had not yet consented.
In the second month,
on the *xīnmǎo* day (the first day of the month),
the Uighur Manichaean monks were sent back to their country.
Manichaeism first appeared in the two hundred thirty-seventh year (*Yuánnián*).
Shǐ Zhào says: At the beginning of the Yuánhé era,
the Uighurs paid tribute twice,
and it was then that Manichaeism first arrived.
The Manichaeans came to the capital,
and annually frequented the West Market.
Merchants often engaged in illicit dealings with them involving their bags,
and so at this point they were sent back to their country.
This was to delay the marriage.
4. Lǐ Suò planned to attack Cáizhōu
and submitted a memorial requesting additional troops;
an edict granted him two thousand infantry and cavalry from Zhāoyì, Hézhōng, and Fūfāng.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
Suò sent the 'Ten-Leader' Mǎ Shǎoliáng with over ten cavalrymen to patrol.
A 'Ten-Leader' was
a junior officer in the army.
*Luó* (邏),
pronounced *láng zuǒ*.
They engaged in battle
and captured him.
Shìliáng was
a fierce general of Yuán Jì,
who had often been a menace on the eastern border;
referring to the eastern border of Táng and Dèng.
Suò consented to his request (to be released).
Later, he summoned and questioned him.
Shìliáng showed no fear.
Suò said,
"A true man!"
He ordered his bonds to be released.
Shìliáng then said of himself:
"I am not originally a Huáixī soldier.
During the Zhēnyuán era, I was attached to Ānzhōu.
I fought against the Wú clan
and was captured by them.
I thought I would surely die,
but the Wú clan released me and employed me.
I gained a new life through the Wú clan,
so I exerted all my strength for the Wú father and son.
Yesterday, my strength gave out,
and I was captured again by Your Excellency.
I also thought I would surely die,
but now Your Excellency has given me life again.
I beg to devote my life to repay your kindness."
Suò then provided him with clothes and weapons
and appointed him as a 'Capture-Live General.'
5. On the *jǐhài* day,
the Huáixī field army reported the capture of the ancient Gěbó City in Cáizhōu.
The *Hàn Shū* mentions Chénliú's Nínglíng County,
and Mèng Kāng's commentary states: "It was the ancient state of Gěbó,
and Gě Xiāng is its present location."
This must have been a victory report from Hán Hóng.
6. Dīng Shìliáng said to Lǐ Suò:
"Wú Xiùlín commands three thousand men
and occupies Wénchéngzhà.
Wénchéngzhà is
one hundred twenty *lǐ* southwest of Cáizhōu.
According to the *Xù Tōngdiǎn*,
the stockade is within Wúfáng County.
The government forces dare not approach it
because Chén Guāngqià acts as his strategist.
Guāngqià is brave but reckless,
fond of personally engaging in battle.
Please allow me to capture Guāngqià first for Your Excellency,
and then Xiùlín will surrender on his own."
On the *wùshēn* day,
Shìliáng captured Guāngqià and returned.
7 È-Yuè Guānchásǐ Lǐ Dàogǔ led troops out of Mùlíng Guān;
Mùlíng Guān is northwest of Máchéng County, Huángzhōu,
on Mùlíng Shān.
On a jiǎyín day,
[they] attacked Shēnzhōu,
captured its outer wall,
and then attacked the inner citadel.
The defending general in the city led troops out at night to attack them,
and Dàogǔ’s forces were startled and chaotic,
with many dead.
Dàogǔ
was the son of Gāo.
Cáo Chéngwáng Gāo
served in various garrisons like Jiāngxī and Shānnán,
achieving fame and merit.
8 Huáixī had been subjected to warfare for several years,
exhausting its granaries to support the soldiers,
and many people had no food.
They gathered water caltrops, foxnuts, fish, turtles, birds, and beasts to eat,
but these too were depleted.
Five thousand households or more, in total, subsequently surrendered to the government army;
the rebels also worried about their consumption of provisions,
and no longer forbade it.
On a gēngshēn day,
an imperial edict commanded the establishment of temporary counties to settle them,
but the actual counties could not yet be secured,
so temporary counties were provisionally set up to settle the people who had surrendered.
"Chǔ" (處)
is pronounced "chāng lǚ fān".
[Officials] were sent to care for them,
and troops were also stationed to protect them.
9 In the third month,
on an yǐchǒu day,
Lǐ Sù moved his garrison from Tángzhōu to Yíyáng Zhà.
10 Xī Shìměi was defeated at Bǎixiāng,
abandoned his camp, and returned,
with over a thousand soldiers dead.
11 On a wùchén day,
Chéng Zhígōng was granted the name Quán.
12 On a wùyín day,
Wáng Chéngzōng sent twenty thousand troops into Dōngguāng,
cutting off the Báiqiáo road;
Dōngguāng County
belonged to Jǐngzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Dōngguāng
was an old Han dynasty county.
Its old city was twenty *lǐ* east of the county seat.
In the seventh year of Tiānbǎo of the Qí dynasty, it was moved to the old city of the Táo clan, thirty *lǐ* southeast of the present county seat.
In the third year of Kāihuáng of the Suí dynasty, it was again moved to the abandoned old city of Bóhǎi from the Latter Wèi.
Four *lǐ* west of the county seat was the Yǒngjì Qú,
and there was a bridge over the canal,
which was on the road connecting the county to Gōnggāo.
Báiqiáo spanned the Yǒngjì Qú
in Chánghé County, Dézhōu.
"Duàn" (斷)
has the pronunciation "duǎn".
[They] returned with their forces to Cāngzhōu.
Hún Gǎo had already been defeated,
Xī Shìměi was also defeated,
and Chéng Quán had retreated;
Wáng Chéngzōng's talent
was beyond the control of the various commanders.
13 Wú Xiùlín surrendered Wénchéng Zhà to Lǐ Sù.
On a wùzǐ day,
Sù led troops to five *lǐ* west of Wénchéng,
and sent Lǐ Jìnchéng, the prefect of Tángzhōu, with eight thousand armored soldiers to the city walls.
He summoned Xiùlín,
but arrows and stones rained down from the city,
and the troops could not advance.
Jìnchéng returned and reported:
"The rebels are feigning surrender;
they cannot be trusted."
Sù said:
"They are waiting for me to arrive."
He then advanced to the city walls,
and Xiùlín stacked his weapons and prostrated himself at the horses' feet.
Sù patted his back to comfort him,
and accepted the surrender of his three thousand men.
Xiùlín's general Lǐ Xiàn was talented and brave,
so Sù changed his name to Zhōngyì and employed him,
and moved all the women and children to Tángzhōu.
Thereupon, the morale of the Táng and Dèng armies was restored,
and people had the will to fight.
Those who surrendered from the rebel side continuously arrived on the road,
and were settled wherever was convenient for them.
Those who were heard to have parents were given grain and silk and sent away,
saying:
"All of you are royal subjects;
do not abandon your relatives."
All were moved to tears.
All events from this point onwards concern Lǐ Sù.
The government army and the Huáixī army camped on opposite sides of the Yǐnshuǐ,
and the various armies looked at each other hesitantly,
none daring to cross the Yǐnshuǐ.
Wáng Pèi, the Bīngmǎshǐ of Chén-Xǔ, first led five thousand troops across the Yǐnshuǐ,
and occupied a strategic position to form a city.
Thereupon, the Héyáng, Xuānwǔ, Hédōng, Wèibó, and other armies all crossed in succession,
advancing to press Yǎnchéng.
On a dīnghài day,
Lǐ Guāngyán defeated thirty thousand Huáixī troops at Yǎnchéng.
According to Sòng Bái's Xù Tōngdiǎn: Yǎnchéng
is fifty *lǐ* north of Xīpíng County, Càizhōu.
"Bài" (敗)
is pronounced "bǔ mài fān".
Two or three tenths of the soldiers were killed.
All events from this point onwards concern the attack on Yǎnchéng.
On a jǐchǒu day,
Lǐ Sù sent the Shānhé Shíjiàng Dǒng Shǎofēn and others to divide their troops and attack various palisades.
On that day,
Shǎofēn captured Mǎ'ān Shān
and took Lùkǒu Zhà.
At that time, in Dūjī and Táng-Dèng, brave and talented locals were recruited as soldiers to suppress Cài,
known as the Shānhé Zǐdì,
and ten commanders (Shíjiàng) were appointed to lead them.
"Fēn" (玢)
is pronounced "fǔ jīn fān".
Note that when Táng and Cài were at war,
strategic locations along the border
were garrisoned everywhere.
The precise locations of Mǎ'ān Shān and Lùkǒu Zhà
cannot be fully detailed, and forced annotations should not be made.
In the fourth month,
on a xīnmǎo day,
Shānhé Shíjiàng Mǎ Shǎoliáng captured Cáiyá Shān
and seized the Huáixī general Liǔ Zǐyě.
All events from this point onwards also concern Lǐ Sù.
Wú Yuánjì appointed Dǒng Chānglíng of Cài as the magistrate of Yǎnchéng,
and held his mother, Lady Yáng, as hostage.
Lady Yáng said to Chānglíng:
"Dying in obedience is more worthy than living in rebellion.
Dying in obedience
means dying by surrendering.
Living in rebellion
means living by following the rebels.
[Then you will be] a filial son;
if I live through your rebellion,
it would be equivalent to your killing me."
It happened that the government army besieged Qīnglíng,
cutting off the return route to Yǎnchéng.
Qīnglíng
is southwest of Yǎnchéng.
Chānglíng urged them to return to the imperial court.
Huáijīn then requested to surrender to Lǐ Guāngyán, saying:
"The parents, wives, and children of the people in the city are all in Càizhōu.
Please attack the city,
and I will raise a beacon to call for help.
When the relief troops arrive,
you can intercept and attack them,
and the Cài army will surely be defeated.
Then I will surrender,
and my parents, wives, and children might be spared."
Guāngyán agreed.
On an yǐwèi day,
Chānglíng and Huáijīn surrendered the city,
and Guāngyán led troops in to occupy it.
Wú Yuánjì was greatly alarmed upon hearing that Yǎnchéng could not be held.
At that time, Dǒng Zhòngzhì was leading the mule army to defend Huíqǔ.
According to the Xīnshū Lǐ Guāngyán Zhuàn: Huíqǔ
is Jíqǔ,
presumably where the Yǐnshuǐ curved and meandered,
hence the name.
All events from this point onwards also concern Lǐ Guāngyán.
Lǐ Sù's Shānhé Shíjiàng Guī Yǎ and Tián Zhìróng captured Yělú Chéng.
On a bǐngshēn day,
Shíjiàng Yán Shìróng captured the two palisades of Báigǒu and Wènhóng.
The two palisades of Báigǒu and Wènhóng
are both within the borders of Zhēnyáng County, Càizhōu.
Xiāo Liáng established Xīhuáizhōu at Zhēnyáng Báigǒu Duī.
Later, Qí abolished the prefecture and made it Qíxīng Jùn,
then soon abolished the commandery and made it Báigǒu County.
In the early Kāihuáng period of the Suí dynasty, the county was renamed Huáizhōu,
and in the early Dàyè period, it was abolished and merged into Zhēnyáng.
The Suí Zhì states: Zhēnyáng has Wènshuǐ.
On a guǐmǎo day,
Guī Yǎ and Tián Zhìróng defeated Xīpíng.
Xīpíng
was the State of Bó during the Spring and Autumn period,
became Xīpíng County under the Han dynasty,
belonging to Rǔnán Jùn,
and to Càizhōu under the Tang dynasty.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is one hundred five *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
On a bǐngwǔ day,
the Yóuyì Bīngmǎshǐ Wáng Yì defeated Chǔ Chéng.
Chǔ Chéng
is southwest of Rǔyáng County.
Xiāo Liáng established Xīchǔzhōu and Rǔyáng Jùn here.
In the fifth month,
on a xīnyǒu day,
Lǐ Sù sent Liǔ Zǐyě and Lǐ Zhōngyì to raid Lángshān,
capturing its defending general Liáng Xīguǒ.
14 The matter of the six towns campaigning against Wáng Chéngzōng
can be found in Volume 11 of the preceding scroll.
They circled for thousands of *lǐ*,
having no commander,
and also being far apart,
it was difficult to unify their plans and dates.
Because of this, for two years they had no success,
and in conveying supplies over a thousand *lǐ*,
four or five tenths of the oxen and donkeys died.
Liú Zǒng, having acquired Wǔqiáng,
led his troops out of the border only five *lǐ*.
"Out of the border"
means out of the border of Wǔqiáng.
He received 150,000 *mín* from the Ministry of Finance monthly.
Lǐ Féngjí and many court officials said,
"It is advisable to concentrate our forces and first take Huáixī.
Once Huáixī is pacified,
riding on that victorious momentum,
we can turn to take Héng and Jì,
which will be as easy as picking up mustard seeds!"
The Emperor hesitated,
and after a long time, he adopted their suggestion.
The words of Lǐ Féngjí and others
were the same as the words of Wéi Guànzhī and others.
However, Xìanzōng sometimes used their advice and sometimes did not.
Before this, the military advantage had not been diminished,
but now the military advantage had been diminished,
so he had no choice but to follow it.
On *bǐngzǐ*,
the field headquarters in Héběi was disbanded,
and each was allowed to return to their respective garrisons.
15 On *dīngchǒu*,
Lǐ Sù sent Lǐ Róngzōng, the commander of Fāngchéng town, to attack Qīngxǐ City,
and captured it.
Fāngchéng County
was originally the land of Dǔyáng County in the Hàn dynasty.
The Later Hàn changed its name to Shùnyáng,
the Suí changed it to Fāngchéng County,
and the Táng belonged to Táng Prefecture.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: it is 160 *lǐ* north of the prefecture.
The county has Qīngtái Town.
Here it is written as
"Qīngxǐ,"
which is a scribal error.
Whenever Sù captured surrendered soldiers,
he would personally interrogate them in detail.
Because of this, he came to know all the dangers, ease, distance, proximity, truth, and falsehood within the enemy.
Sù treated Wú Xiùlín generously,
and conspired with him to capture Cài.
Xiùlín said,
"If you wish to capture Cài,
it cannot be done without Lǐ Yòu;
Xiùlín is incapable."
Yòu was
a cavalry general from Huáixī,
brave and strategic.
He guarded the Xīngqiáo Stockade.
The Xīngqiáo Stockade
was east of Zhāngchái Village.
*Líng* means
to overwhelm with spirit.
*Bào* means
to oppress with authority.
On *gēngchén*,
Yòu led his soldiers to cut wheat at Zhāngchái Village.
Zhāngchái Village
was sixty *lǐ* east of Wénchéng Stockade.
*Shuài*
is read as *lǜ*.
A *xiāng yúhòu*
managed the troops of the left and right wings.
"You, with three hundred cavalry, ambush them in that forest,
and also send someone to wave banners in front,
as if you are going to burn their wheat stacks.
Yòu has always underestimated the government army,
and will surely come in light cavalry to pursue them.
Then you can launch your cavalry to surprise them,
and you will surely capture him."
Yòngchéng went as told,
and captured Yòu alive, bringing him back.
The generals and soldiers, remembering that Yòu had killed many government soldiers in the past,
vied to request his execution;
Sù did not permit it,
released his bonds,
and treated him with the courtesy due a guest.
At that time, Sù wanted to launch a surprise attack on Cài,
but kept his plan very secret,
summoning only Yòu and Lǐ Zhōngyì to speak privately,
sometimes until midnight.
"Midnight"
means *yèfēn*.
The generals feared that Yòu would cause trouble,
and many advised Sù against it;
but Sù treated Yòu even more generously.
The soldiers were also displeased;
every day, the various armies sent dispatches claiming Yòu was an internal spy for the rebels,
and even stated that those who captured rebel spies fully confirmed this.
This refers to the official documents from the various armies in the field headquarters.
*Dié*
is pronounced *tú xié fān*.

Since the Warring States period,
Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi contended with Confucian scholars,
each criticizing the other.
By the late Hàn dynasty,
Buddhism was added to the mix,
but those who favored it were still few.
From the Jìn and Sòng dynasties onwards,
it became increasingly prevalent and flourishing,
and from emperors to scholars and common people,
none failed to respect and believe in it.
The lower classes feared and admired the rewards and punishments of karma,
while the higher classes debated the concepts of emptiness and existence.
Only Hán Yù abhorred its waste of wealth and misleading of the masses,
and vigorously opposed it;
his words were often too extreme and forceful.
Only the preface he wrote for Master Wénchàng best captured its essence,
saying:
“Birds peck downwards
and look up and around,
beasts live deep in their lairs and seldom emerge,
fearing that others will harm them,
yet they still cannot escape.
The weak are meat,
the strong are eaters.
Now, Wénchàng and I live in peace and eat at leisure,
passing through life and death without worry.
Since we are different from birds and beasts,
how can we not know our origins!”
Tracing their origins,
it is precisely what the Sages established to transmit their teachings to the world.

but they could never completely stop it.
When Tián Hóngzhèng 田弘正 entered Yùn 鄆,
he reviewed Lǐ Shīdào's 李師道 records
and found entries for rewards for killing Wǔ Yuánhéng 武元衡 and others, such as Wáng Shìyuán 王士元, as well as rewards for officials and soldiers at Tóngguān 潼關 and Pújīn 蒲津.
Only then did he realize that in the past, these officials and soldiers had all taken bribes from the rebels,
allowing their schemes.
*Àn* 案
means official document,
also called *àndú* 案牘.
The historian states that the passes and ferries were not effective in preventing treachery,
but rather served to facilitate it.
Péi Dù 裴度 compiled a record of the emperor's diligence and strategic efforts since the campaign in Cài 蔡 and Yùn 鄆 began.
He presented it at an imperial banquet,
requesting that it be officially stamped and given to the historiographers.
He requested that it be stamped from within the forbidden palace and then handed to the historiographers.
"If so,"
the emperor said, "it would seem to come from Our will,
which is not what We desire."
He did not permit it.
The historian commented that Emperor Xiànzōng 憲宗 acted in a manner befitting a monarch in this matter.
In the third month,
on the day *Wùzǐ* 戊子,
Mǎ Zǒng 馬總, the governor of Huázhōu 華州, was appointed military commissioner of Yùn 鄆, Cáo 曹, Pú 濮 and other prefectures.
On the day *Jǐchǒu* 己丑,
Xuē Píng 薛平, military commissioner of Yìchéng 義成, was appointed military commissioner of Pínglú 平盧 and inspector of Zī 淄, Qīng 青, Qí 齊, Dēng 登, Lái 萊 and other prefectures.
From this point onward,
Zīqīng 淄青 exclusively used the title of Pínglú 平盧,
and Yùn 鄆 was soon granted the title of Tiānpíng Jūn 天平軍.
Wáng Suí 王遂, by his harshness, incited rebellion.
The military commissioner of Hénghǎi 橫海, Wū Chóngyìn 烏重胤, memorialized:
"The reason the *fānzhèn* 藩鎮 of Héshuò 河朔 were able to resist imperial commands for over sixty years
is that various prefectures and counties each established garrison commanders to manage affairs,
seizing the authority of the prefects and county magistrates,
and wielding their own power and influence.
If the prefects had each been able to perform their duties,
then even if there were ambitious villains like Ān Lùshān 安祿山 and Shǐ Sīmíng 史思明,
they would certainly not have been able to rebel with a single prefecture alone.
In the three prefectures under my command, Dé 德, Dì 棣, and Jǐng 景,
I have already issued documents returning their duties to the prefects,
and all soldiers in the prefectures are to be led by the prefects."
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day *Bǐngyín* 丙寅,

an imperial edict commanded that the soldiers in the subordinate prefectures under the various provincial military commissioners (*jiédùshǐ* 節度使), regional commanders (*dōutuánliànshǐ* 都團練使), defense commanders (*dōufángyùshǐ* 都防禦使), and frontier commissioners (*jīnglüèshǐ* 經略使),
should all be led by the prefects.
Since the *Zhìdé* 至德 era,
the power of the *jiédùshǐ* 節度使 became immense,
and their subordinate prefectures each established garrison troops,
led by great generals,
whose tyranny became a problem,
which is why Chóngyìn 崇胤 discussed it.
Thereafter, among the various *fānzhèn* 藩鎮 north of the Yellow River,
only Hénghǎi 橫海 was the most obedient to imperial commands,
due to Chóngyìn's 崇胤 proper handling of affairs.
The historian notes that for unstable regions,
the selection of a commander must not be taken lightly.
*Chǔ* 處
is pronounced *chāng lǚ fān* 昌呂翻.
On the day *Xīnwèi* 辛未,
Chéng Fèng 程[AS-82FA], Minister of Public Works (*Gōngbù Shìláng* 工部侍郎) and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì* 同平章事, passed away.
When Péi Dù 裴度 was in office as Grand Counselor,
he spoke without reservation. Huángfǔ Bó's 皇甫鎛 faction secretly undermined him.
On the day *Bǐngzǐ* 丙子,
an edict appointed Dù 度 as *Ménxià Shìláng Tóng Píngzhāngshì* 門下侍郎、同平章事,
and concurrently as military commissioner of Hédōng 河東.
Huángfǔ Bó 皇甫鎛 specialized in enriching himself through extortion and flattery,
and no one dared to speak out,
except for the Remonstrance Official (*Jiànyì Dàfū* 諫議大夫) Wǔ Rúhéng 武儒衡, who submitted a memorial criticizing him.
Bó 鎛 complained to the emperor,
who said:
"You are upset because Rúhéng 儒衡 submitted a memorial;
are you planning to seek revenge!"
Bó 鎛 then dared not speak.
Rúhéng 儒衡
was the son of Yuánhéng's 元衡 paternal cousin.
6 Li Áo [李翺], Editor of the Imperial Historiography Office, memorialized,
"In the third year of Zhēngguān [貞觀] (629 CE), the Historiography Office was established within the Department of the Palace Gate,
with four Editors,
who were responsible for compiling the national history.
'Those who pacify chaos
rely on military achievements;
those who usher in great peace
rely on civil virtue.
Now Your Majesty has already pacified the realm with military achievements.
If you could then reform corrupt practices,
restore the old systems of Gāozǔ [高祖] and Tàizōng [太宗];
employ the loyal and upright without doubt,
and keep the wicked and sycophantic far away;
reform the tax law,
no longer demanding cash but accepting cloth and silk;
(Since the beginning of Jiànzhōng [建中] (780 CE),
Yáng Yán [楊炎] established the Two-Tax System,
no longer requiring people to pay their local produce but demanding cash.)
lighten the burdens of rent and taxes on the people;
strengthen the frontier troops
to deter incursions and raids by the Róngdí [戎狄];
frequently visit and inquire of officials awaiting appointments
to uncover obstructions;
these six points
are the root of governance,
and the means by which great peace arises.
Your Majesty has already been able to accomplish what is difficult;
why would you not do what is easy?
With Your Majesty's heavenly wisdom and supreme sagacity,
if you are not misled by the flattering words of close attendants,
and employ sincere and upright officials,
and together with them initiate great reforms,
success can be achieved without effort.
If this is not made a priority,
I fear that after great achievements,
indulgence and desire are easily born.
Those who offer advice will certainly say: 'The realm is already peaceful,
Your Majesty can rest easy with a tranquil mind,'
if so,
then great peace cannot yet be expected!"
7 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Dīngchǒu [丁丑], the first day of the month,
Tián Hóngzhèng [田弘正] sent the sixteen assassins, including Wáng Shìyuán [王士元], who killed Wǔ Yuánhéng [武元衡].
An imperial edict ordered
that the Metropolitan Prefecture of Jīngzhào [京兆府] and the Censorate thoroughly interrogate them;
all confessed.
(Kuǎn [款]
means sincerity.
It means they confessed truthfully and admitted their guilt.)
However, there were many discrepancies.
Yuánlüè [元略] asked them why,
and they replied:
"Héng [恆] and Yùn [鄆] conspired to send assassins for Wǔ Yuánhéng [武元衡],
but Shìyuán [士元] and the others arrived late.
Hearing that Héng's [恆] mission was already accomplished,
they fraudulently claimed it as their own achievement
and returned to receive rewards.
Now, we consider our guilt to be the same,
and we will ultimately not escape death,
so we confessed."
The Emperor also did not wish to investigate further for accuracy,
and had them all executed.
8 On the day Wùyín [戊寅],
Hán Hóng [韓弘], the Military Commissioner of Xuānwǔ [宣武], finally arrived at court.
(After Cài [蔡] and Yùn [鄆] were pacified,
Hán Hóng [韓弘] finally came to court.)
Hóng [弘] presented three thousand horses,
five thousand bolts of silk,
thirty thousand bolts of various woven fabrics,
and a thousand gold and silver vessels.
The treasury of Biàn [汴] still contained over a million strings of cash,
over a million bolts of silk,
seven thousand horses,
and three million hú [斛] of grain.
The historians say that Hán Hóng [韓弘] was skilled at accumulation.
9 On the day Jǐchǒu [己丑],
all the ministers offered the Emperor the honorific title Yuánhé Shèngwén Shénwǔ Fǎtiān Yìngdào Huángdì [元和聖文神武法天應道皇帝];
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
10 Wáng Suì [王遂], Inspector of Yǎn [兗], Hǎi [海], Yí [沂], and Mì [密],
was originally a finance official.
He was impatient and quick-tempered,
without long-term vision.
At that time, the military prefecture was newly established.
(In the third month of that year,
the four prefectures were just being divided and assigned an Inspector.)
Suì [遂] governed exclusively with harshness and cruelty.
The cangues he used were much larger than the standard ones;
(According to Tang regulations: all cangues were three feet five inches long,
with knots removed.
For interrogations, the large end of the staff measured three fēn three lí [分三釐] in diameter,
and the small end two fēn two lí [分二釐].
For regular use, the large end measured two fēn seven lí [分七釐],
and the small end one fēn seven lí [分七釐].
For flogging, the large end measured two fēn [分],
and the small end one and a half fēn [分有半].)
He would casually call people
"rebels";
furthermore, in the height of summer, he forced soldiers to build official residences,
supervising them with extreme strictness;
the generals and soldiers were resentful.
On the day Xīnmǎo [辛卯],
the conscripted soldier Wáng Biàn [王弁] and four of his followers bathed in the Yíshuǐ [沂水].
(Yízhōu [沂州] administered Línyí Xiàn [臨沂縣],
named after the Línyí River.)
They said:
"Now, if we perform service and commit a crime, we will die.
If we exert ourselves to accomplish something, we will also die.
Dying for accomplishing something,
is that not better?
Tomorrow,
the Chángshì [常侍] and the Deputy Military Supervisor are having a banquet.
All the military commanders are on leave,
and most of the guards are resting.
(Chángshì [常侍]
refers to Wáng Suì [王遂].
Fùshǐ [副使]
refers to the Deputy Inspector.
Zàigào [在告]
means on vacation in their private residences.
Zhíbīng [直兵]
refers to the soldiers on guard duty.)
This is a perfect opportunity."
All four agreed,
and they agreed that if the deed was successful, they would elevate Biàn [弁] to acting commissioner.
On the day Rénchén [壬辰],
Suì [遂] was feasting.
After noon,
Biàn [弁] and the four others burst in.
They took bows and swords from the guardroom entrance,
(Zhífáng [直房]
was the room where the guards resided.)
and killed them.
Suì [遂] and the Military Supervisor fled in a panic.
Biàn [弁] seized Suì [遂],
enumerated his offenses of starting projects in the height of summer
and his cruel and harsh punishments,
and immediately cut him down.
He ordered that the Military Supervisor not be alarmed.
Biàn [弁] then proclaimed himself acting commissioner,
ascended the hall to issue orders,
treated the Military Supervisor as an equal,
and summoned generals and officials to pay their respects.
No one dared to disobey.
The Military Supervisor reported the situation in full.
11 On the day Jiǎwǔ [甲午],
Hán Hóng [韓弘] again presented two hundred fifty thousand bolts of silk,
thirty thousand bolts of coarse silk,
and two hundred seventy silver vessels;
the military commandants of the Left and Right Armies each presented ten thousand strings of cash.
Since the campaign against Huáixī [淮西],
the Ministry of Finance, the Salt and Iron Commission, and various regions vied to make contributions,
which were called
"aid for the army";
when the rebels were pacified, they again made contributions,
which were called
"congratulatory gifts";
later, they again made contributions,
which were called
"aid for rewards";
when the Emperor was given an honorific title, they again made contributions,
which were also called
"congratulatory gifts."
The historians documented the abuses of contributions during the Yuánhé [元和] period.
12 On the day Dīngyǒu [丁酉],
Línghú Chǔ [令狐楚], Military Commissioner of Héyáng [河陽], was appointed Middle Secretariat Attendant and Concurrently Manager of Affairs.
Chǔ [楚] and Huángfǔ Bó [皇甫鎛] were successful candidates in the same year's imperial examination,
so Bó [鎛] recommended him as Chancellor.
(When Péi Dù [裴度] was supervising the army,
Línghú Chǔ [令狐楚] was dismissed from the Hanlin Academy.
Now Huángfǔ Bó [皇甫鎛] brought him in to be chancellor,
also to prevent Péi Dù's [裴度] return to power.)
13 The court heard of the military unrest in Yízhōu [沂州].
On the day Jiǎchén [甲辰],
Cáo Huá [曹華], Prefect of Dìzhōu [棣州], was appointed Inspector of Yí [沂], Hǎi [海], Yǎn [兗], and Mì [密].
14 Hán Hóng repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to remain in the capital.
In the eighth month,
on the day Jǐyǒu,
Hóng was made the Sītú,
concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng.
On the day Guǐchǒu,
Zhāng Hóngjìng, Minister of Personnel, was made Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and concurrently Jiedushi of Xuanwu.
Hóngjìng
was the son of a chancellor;
Hóngjìng
was the son of Zhāng Yánshǎng.
Yánshǎng served as chancellor under Dézōng.
He was dignified and reticent in court.
When the posts of commander for Hédōng and Xuānwǔ were vacant,
the court, considering his long-standing high status and reputation,
appointed him to govern those regions.
Hóngjìng inherited the regions after Wáng È's avaricious rule
and Hán Hóng's strict and fierce governance;
Wáng È governed Hédōng,
Hán Hóng governed Xuānwǔ,
Hóngjìng succeeded both of them.
斂 (liǎn)
is pronounced lì shàn;
the same applies below.
Thus, both superiors and inferiors found peace under him.
Zhāng Hóngjìng's reserved and noble conduct,
while suitable for Bīng and Biàn,
would lead to failure if applied to Yōuyàn.
15 On the day Jǐwèi,
Tián Hóngzhèng came to court,
and the emperor treated him with exceptional generosity.
16 On the day Wùchén,
Xī Shìměi, Jiedushi of Chénxǔ, passed away.
Lǐ Bó, Kuùbù Yuánwàiláng, was appointed as the envoy for condolences and sacrifices.
Bó submitted a memorial saying:
“When your subject passed through Wèinán,
I heard that Chángyuán Township, which formerly had four hundred households,
now has only a little over one hundred households.
Wénxiāng County, which formerly had three thousand households,
now has only one thousand households.
Other prefectures and counties are largely similar.
The reason for this
is that the taxes of fugitive households are apportioned among their neighbors,
causing them to be forced to flee together.
These are all instances of avaricious officials exploiting the lower classes to curry favor with the upper classes,
thinking only of draining the pond
without considering the absence of fish.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū says: If one drains the pond to fish,
one may indeed catch fish,
but there will be no fish next year.
The malpractice of apportioning taxes for fugitives should be abolished.
The property of fugitive households should be used to pay taxes,
and any insufficient amounts should be pardoned.
In just a few years,
everyone will return to agriculture.”
The powerful ministers saw it and disliked it;
the powerful ministers
refer to Huángfǔ Bó.
惡 (è)
is pronounced wū lù.
Bó was sent back to Dōngdū.
17 On the day Guǐyǒu,
Tǔbō raided Qìngzhōu.
Qìngzhōu,
was Hónghuà Commandery during the Suí dynasty.
In the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng, it was renamed Qìngzhōu,
taking its auspicious name from 'qìngměi' (celebratory beauty).
It was the territory of Han dynasty Guīdé and Fùpíng counties.
According to old records, it was five hundred seventy-three *lǐ* northwest of the capital.
18 The court debated raising troops to punish Wáng Biàn,
fearing that Qīng and Yùn would incite each other to rebellion.
Qīng and Yùn, along with Yǎn, Hǎi, Yí, and Mì,
originally formed one military circuit.
Therefore, it was feared they might incite each other to action.
An imperial envoy was dispatched to bestow a document of appointment.
The envoy deceived him, saying:
“Kāizhōu already has people waiting to welcome you along the road;
you, the Liúhòu, should depart quickly.”
Biàn immediately left Yízhōu that day.
His retinue still numbered over a hundred people.
Upon entering Xúzhōu territory,
the number decreased everywhere,
and his followers also gradually scattered.
He was then shackled
and entered the pass riding a donkey.
In the ninth month,
on the day Wùyín,
he was cut in half at the waist in the East Market.
Earlier,
the Yùn army had been divided into three parts and assigned to three military circuits.
This refers to the beginning when Yùn, Qīng, and Yí were divided into three circuits.
先 (xiān)
is pronounced xī jiàn.
The court, believing that the remnants of Shī Dào's faction still harbored sinister intentions,
ordered Cáo Huá to lead the Dìzhōu troops to the garrison to suppress them.
When the generals and soldiers of Yízhōu came to greet him,
Huá appeased them all with kind words,
telling them to enter the city first
to reassure the others.
All the people had no doubts.
Three days after Huá took office,
he hosted a grand banquet for the generals and soldiers.
He hid a thousand armed soldiers under a tent,
then gathered the crowd and addressed them, saying:
“The Son of Heaven, considering the hardships of the Yùn people's relocation,
has granted them special privileges.
The Yùn people should stand on the left,
and the Yí people on the right.”
Once they were positioned,
he ordered all the Yí people to leave.
Then he closed the gate
and said to the Yùn people:
“Wáng Chángshì was appointed commander here by imperial decree;
how could the generals and soldiers dare to harm him?”
Before he finished speaking,
the hidden soldiers emerged,
surrounded and killed them.
One thousand two hundred people died,
and not one escaped.
A red mist, more than ten feet high, lingered between the gates and screens,
only dispersing after a long time.
The aura of the slain soldiers
condensed into a red mist.
Your subject Guāng says: The Spring and Autumn Annals records that King Chu Zhǐqián lured Marquess Cài Bān and killed him in Shēn.
See Duke Zhāo, eleventh year.
般 (bān)
is pronounced bān.
Confucius still deeply condemned it,
disapproving of the deception and execution.
How much more so for the Son of Heaven to lure a common man!
Wáng Suì, with his talent for avarice,
governed newly established territories,
and his harsh and cruel policies led to rebellion.
Wáng Biàn was an ordinary man
who seized the opportunity to rebel.
釁 (xìn)
means 'a crack' or 'opportunity.'
Killing him would have been easier than killing dogs or pigs.
Why was it necessary to use an imperial decree as bait to lure a man?
Moreover, there were only five instigators of the rebellion,
yet Cáo Huá was made to set a trap
and slaughter over a thousand people.
Is this not excessive?
If so, from now on, which soldiers will not suspect their generals,
and how will generals command their soldiers?
Superiors and inferiors will glare at each other,
like enemies gathered together.
Whoever strikes first will be the victor.
When will such disaster and chaos cease?
Alas!
Xiànzōng pacified the usurpers and rebels,
nearly achieving an era of peace and prosperity.
The reason his great endeavor did not last
was due to his opportunistic pursuit of immediate success rather than upholding great trustworthiness.
19 On the day Jiǎchén,
Tián Hóngzhèng was made concurrent Shìzhōng,
and his position as Jiedushi of Wèibó remained unchanged.
Hóngzhèng submitted three memorials requesting to remain,
but the emperor did not permit it.
Hóngzhèng was constantly afraid that if he were to die suddenly,
the Wèi people would follow tradition and appoint a successor from his family.
Therefore, his brothers, sons, and nephews all served in the court,
and the emperor promoted them all to prominent positions.
Official robes of scarlet and purple filled his courtyard,
and people of the time regarded it as an honor.
20 On the day Yǐsì,
the emperor asked his chancellors:
“The governance of Xuánzōng
was orderly first and then chaotic.
Why was this?”
Cuī Gǎn replied:
“Xuánzōng was orderly when he employed Yáo Chóng, Sòng Jǐng, Lú Huáishèn, Sū Tǐng, Hán Xiū, and Zhāng Jiǔlíng.
He became chaotic when he employed Yǔwén Róng, Lǐ Línfǔ, and Yáng Guózhōng.
Thus, the success or failure of employing people
is no small matter.
Everyone considers the rebellion of Ān Lùshān in the fourteenth year of Tiānbǎo as the beginning of chaos,
but your subject alone believes that the dismissal of Zhāng Jiǔlíng as chancellor in the twenty-fourth year of Kāiyuán
and the sole reliance on Lǐ Línfǔ
marked the division between order and chaos.
I wish Your Majesty would take the early years of Kāiyuán as a model,
and the late years of Tiānbǎo as a warning.
This would be a boundless blessing for the altars of soil and grain (the state)!”
Huángfǔ Bó deeply resented this.
Huángfǔ Bó knew himself to be holding the position of chancellor through treachery and flattery,
hence his deep resentment of Cuī Gǎn's words.
In the winter of the 21st year,
in the tenth month,
on the Rénxū day,
Róngguǎn (Rong Commandery) reported that the Annán (Annan) rebel Yáng Qīng (Yang Qing) had captured the Dūhùfǔ (Protectorate-General).
The Annán Dūhùfǔ
was governed from Jiāozhōu (Jiao Prefecture).
Xiàng Gǔ (Xiang Gu),
Dào Gǔ's (Dao Gu's) elder brother,
had lost the people's hearts due to his greed, indulgence, and harshness.
Qīng's family had for generations been barbarian chiefs.
Xiàng Gǔ summoned Qīng to be a Yájiàng (Brigade Commander),
but Qīng was discontent and felt unfulfilled.
Xiàng Gǔ ordered Qīng to lead three thousand soldiers to suppress the Huángdòngmán (Huangdong Man).
The Huángdòngmán were also known as Xīyuánmán (Xiyuan Man).
Those among them whose surname was Huáng (Huang)
were called Huángdòngmán.
Qīng led his troops back at night
and attacked the prefectural city,
capturing it.
Previously,
the barbarian rebel Huáng Shǎoqīng (Huang Shaoqing)
had repeatedly revolted since the Zhēnyuán (Zhenyuan) era.
Péi Xínglì (Pei Xingli), the Guìguǎn (Gui Commandery) Guānchásǐ (Observation Commissioner), and
Yáng Mín (Yang Min), the Róngguǎn Jīnglüèsǐ (Rong Commandery Military Commissioner), seeking to gain merit through a lucky strike,
both requested to suppress him.
The Emperor granted their request.
Kǒng Kuí (Kong Kui), the Lǐngnán Jiédùsǐ (Lingnan Military Governor), repeatedly remonstrated, saying:
"These are mere beasts!
One can only consider their own advantages and disadvantages;
it is not worth discussing right and wrong with them."
The Emperor did not listen.
He heavily mobilized troops from Jiāng (Jiang) and Hú (Hu) to join the Róng and Guì commanderies in suppression.
The soldiers suffered from malaria and other diseases,
and the number of dead was innumerable.
Annán took advantage of this
and then killed the Dūhù (Protector-General).
Xínglì and Mín ultimately achieved nothing,
and the two commanderies were ruined and exhausted,
while Kǒng Kuí's department remained peaceful.
Although the Lǐngnán Jiédù (Lingnan Military Governor) concurrently governed the Five Commanderies,
Guǎngzhōu (Guangzhou) administered its own subordinate prefectures.

Liú Xù (Liu Xu) said: Guangzhou governed the prefectures of Sháo (Shao), Xún (Xun), Gāng (Gang), Hè (He), Duān (Duan), Xīn (Xin), Kāng (Kang), Fēng (Feng), Lóng (Long), Ēn (En), Chūn (Chun), Gāo (Gao), Téng (Teng), Yì (Yi), Dòu (Dou), and Qín (Qin).
Kuí
is pronounced like "qú guī" reversed.
On the Bǐngyín day,
Guì Zhòngwǔ (Gui Zhongwu), the Cǐshǐ (Prefect) of Tángzhōu (Tang Prefecture), was appointed Annán Dūhù.
Yáng Qīng was pardoned
and made Cǐshǐ of Qióngzhōu (Qiong Prefecture).
In the 22nd year,
Lùn Sānmó (Lun Sanmo) and other Tubō (Tibetan) Jiédù (Military Governors), leading 150,000 troops, besieged Yánzhōu (Yan Prefecture).
The Dǎngxiàng (Tanguts) also dispatched troops to assist them.
Lǐ Wényuè (Li Wenyue), the Cǐshǐ, resisted with all his might
for twenty-seven days,
and the Tubō could not overcome them.
Shǐ Fèngjìng (Shi Fengjing), a Yájiàng (Brigade Commander) from Língwǔ (Lingwu),
spoke to Dù Shúliáng (Du Shuliang), the Shuòfāng Jiédùsǐ (Shuofang Military Governor),
requesting three thousand soldiers
with thirty days' provisions
to penetrate deep into Tubō territory and relieve the siege of Yánzhōu.
Shúliáng gave him two thousand five hundred men.
Fèngjìng marched for over ten days
without any news,
and the people of Shuòfāng thought they had all perished.
It was thought that they had perished along with Yánzhōu.
It means "it was unknown when".
The Tubō were greatly alarmed
and scattered.
Fèngjìng fought fiercely,
inflicting a great defeat,
the casualties were innumerable.
It should have been written
"fought fiercely,
greatly defeated them,
and killed or captured innumerable people"
for the meaning to be clear and smooth.
The Tubō feared him.
Both the Old and New Histories write
"Shǐ Jìngfèng (Shi Jingfeng)."
Lǐu Bì (Liu Bi) arrived in Táizhōu (Taizhou),
forcing officials and commoners to gather herbs.
After more than a year,
he found nothing and became afraid.
Bì governed Táizhōu;
see the previous year in the upper scroll.
The Zhèdōng Guānchásǐ (Zhedong Observation Commissioner) arrested and sent him to the capital.
Huángfǔ Bó (Huangfu Bo) and Lǐ Dàogǔ (Li Daogu) protected him,
and the Emperor again made him Dàizhào Hànlín (Academician Attendant);
he took his medicine,
and his thirst and restlessness increased daily.
Péi Lín (Pei Lin), the Qǐjūshèrén (Diarist of the Emperor's Daily Life), submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Those who remove harm from the world receive benefit from the world;
those who share the joy of the world enjoy the blessings of the world.
From the Yellow Emperor to Kings Wén (Wen) and Wǔ (Wu),
all who enjoyed long reigns and lived to old age
followed this principle.
Since last year,
many practitioners of esoteric arts have been recommended in various places,
attracting and introducing each other,
and their numbers have gradually increased.
Even if there truly were immortals in the world,
they would surely hide deep in mountain caves,
fearing only to be known by others.
All who hover at the gates of powerful officials,
boasting with grandiose words and displaying strange tricks to astound the public,
are disloyal individuals seeking profit.
How can one believe their theories and ingest their medicines?
Medicine is for curing illness,
not something to be taken regularly day and night;
moreover, metals and minerals are intensely potent and poisonous,
and further enhanced by fire,
they are truly beyond what human internal organs can withstand.
In ancient times, when a ruler drank medicine,
his minister first tasted it.
This records the words of the Qūlǐ (Book of Rites).
Thus, genuineness and falsehood can be distinguished."
The Emperor was enraged.
In the eleventh month,
on the Jǐhài day,
Lín was demoted to Líng (Magistrate) of Jiānglíng (Jiangling).
Initially,
Flatterers discussed bestowing an honorific title.
Huángfǔ Bó wanted to add the characters
"Xiàodé" (Filial Virtue).
Cuī Qún (Cui Qun), Zhōngshū Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Chancellery) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (Concurrently Chancellor), said:
"When 'sacred' is mentioned, 'filial piety' is already contained within it."
Bó slandered Qún to the Emperor, saying:
"Qún begrudges Your Majesty the two characters
'Xiàodé'."
The Emperor was enraged.
At that time, Bó was responsible for distributing gifts and provisions to the border armies,
which were often not delivered on time,
and much of what was given was old and spoiled.
Chén (陳)
means "old".
The soldiers were resentful and angry,
and rumors circulated that they intended to rebel.
Liúyán (流言)
means "unrestricted talk".
They wanted to kill themselves.
Lǐ Guāngyán (Li Guangyan) was then commanding Bīnnìng (Bīnnìng).
The Emperor did not believe it.
The capital was fearful, and
Qún fully reported the sentiments of both the court and the populace to the Emperor.
Bó secretly told the Emperor:
"The border provisions are all according to old regulations,
but the public sentiment has suddenly become like this
because Qún incites it,
intending to sell himself as upright
and shift the blame to Your Majesty."
The Emperor believed this.
In the twelfth month,
on the Yǐmǎo day,
Qún was appointed Húnán Guānchásǐ (Hunan Observation Commissioner).
At this, both the court and the populace gnashed their teeth at Bó.
Petty men remove gentlemen as a means of securing themselves,
unaware that this is precisely how they endanger themselves.
Wǔ Rúhéng (Wu Ruheng), Zhōngshū Shèrén (Secretariat Drafter),
had integrity and enjoyed speaking frankly.
The Emperor valued him
and treated him with great favor.
Everyone said he would soon become a chancellor.
Lìnghú Chǔ (Linghu Chu) was jealous of him
and sought a way to obstruct him.
So he recommended Dí Jiāncháo (Di Jianchao), the Tuīguān (Investigating Official) of the Shānnán Dōngdào Jiédù (Shannan East Circuit Military Governor), for his talent and conduct.
On the Guǐhài day,
Jiāncháo was promoted to Zuǒ Shíyí Nèigòngfèng (Left Remonstrance Official serving in the Palace).
As his qualifications and seniority were still shallow,
he was not appointed to a principal office,
but ordered to serve in the palace in the rank of Zuǒ Shíyí,
similar to a Lǐxíng (Acting) Censor.
He was a great-grandson of Rénjié's (Renjie's) clan.
Chǔ personally drafted the imperial edict,
strongly stating:
"Empress Tiānhòu (Tianhou) usurped the throne,
and wicked ministers wielded power.
It was thanks to Rénjié's protection of Zhōngzōng (Zhongzong)
that the enlightened ruler was restored."
This matter is seen in the annals of Empress Wu.
It also said:
"Your servant's great-grandfather, Píngyī (Pingyi),
during Empress Tiānhòu's reign,
declined honors and lived out his years."
Píngyī, during Empress Wu's time,
feared calamity and resided on Mount Sōng (Song),
practicing Buddhist methods,
and did not respond to repeated imperial edicts.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Cáo Huá (Cao Hua), the Guānchásǐ (Observation Commissioner) of Yí (Yi), Hǎi (Hai), Yǎn (Yan), and Mì (Mi) Prefectures, requested to move his administrative seat to Yǎnzhōu.
Moved the governance from Yízhōu to Yǎnzhōu.
2 Liú Wù (Liu Wu), the Yìchéng Jiédùsǐ (Yicheng Military Governor), entered court for an audience.
3 Initially,
Tǔtū Chéngcuǐ (吐突承璀), the Deputy Commander of the Left Army, plotted to install Lǐ Wáng Yùn (澧王惲) as crown prince.
The emperor did not permit it.
When the emperor fell ill,
Chéngcuǐ’s (承璀) plot had not yet subsided.
The Crown Prince, hearing of this, became anxious
and secretly sent someone to ask for advice from Sīnóng Qīng Guō Zhāo (司農卿郭釗).
Zhāo (釗) said:
“Your Highness need only devote yourself to filial piety and reverence, and await the outcome.
Do not concern yourself with other matters.”
Zhāo (釗)
was the Crown Prince’s maternal uncle.
The emperor took golden elixirs,
which often made him irritable and angry.
His eunuchs and attendants frequently incurred his wrath,
some even dying,
and everyone felt unsafe.
On *gēngzǐ*,
he suddenly collapsed and died in the Zhōnghé Diàn (中和殿).
He was forty-three years old.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Shílù* (實錄) only says,
“The emperor collapsed in the Zhōnghé Diàn (中和殿) of the Dàmíng Gōng (大明宮).”
The *Jiù Jì* (舊紀) states:
“At the time, the emperor’s sudden collapse
was widely attributed to the eunuch Chén Hóngzhì (陳弘志) committing regicide,
but historians avoided recording it.”
The biography of Wáng Shǒuchéng (王守澄) states:
“When Xiànzōng (憲宗) was gravely ill,
the eunuch Chén Hóngqìng (陳弘慶) and others committed regicide.
Xiànzōng (憲宗) was valiant and martial,
with great power and virtue over people.
The eunuchs kept it secret
and dared not eliminate or investigate,
only stating that the medicine caused a sudden collapse.”
The *Xīn Zhuàn* (新傳) states:
“Shǒuchéng (守澄) and the Inner Regular Attendant Chén Hóngzhì (陳弘志) assassinated the emperor in the Zhōnghé Diàn (中和殿).”
Péi Tíngyù’s (裴廷裕) *Dōngguān Zòujì* (東觀奏記) says:
“Xuānzōng (宣宗) later regretted the cruelty of the merchant-minister at Guāng Líng (光陵),
and Grand Empress Dowager Guō (郭) also died suddenly because of this.”
However, this matter is obscure,
and its truth or falsity cannot be determined.
Therefore, it is only stated that he died suddenly.
They dared not pursue the regicides,
only saying that the medicine took effect,
and outsiders could not ascertain the truth.
The Deputy Commander Liáng Shǒuxiān (梁守謙), along with the eunuchs Mǎ Jìntán (馬進潭), Liú Chéngxié (劉承偕), Wéi Yuánsù (韋元素), Wáng Shǒuchéng (王守澄) and others, jointly established the Crown Prince,
killed Tǔtū Chéngcuǐ (吐突承璀) and Lǐ Wáng Yùn (澧王惲),
and granted fifty *mín* of cash to each soldier of the Left and Right Shéncè Armies (神策軍),
and thirty *mín* to each soldier of the Six Armies and the Wēiyuǎn Army (威遠).
According to the *Xīn Zhì* (新志): the Left and Right Lóngwǔ (龍武),
Left and Right Shénwǔ (神武),
and Left and Right Shéncè (神策) were called the Six Armies.
Now, since the Shéncè Army (神策軍) received a generous cash reward, and there were also the Six Armies,
this indicates that after the mid-Tang period, the Left and Right Yǔlín (羽林), Lóngwǔ (龍武), and Shénwǔ (神武) constituted the Six Armies.
The Wēiyuǎn (威遠) was a separate army.
In the intercalary month,
on *bǐngwǔ*,
Mùzōng (穆宗) ascended the throne in the eastern wing of the Tàijí Diàn (太極殿).
On this day,

he summoned the Hanlin Academicians Duàn Wénchāng (段文昌) and others, as well as the Minister of the Board of War Xuē Fàng (薛放) and the Assistant Director of the Bureau of Carriages Dīng Gōngzhù (丁公著), for an audience in the Sīzhèng Diàn (思政殿).
Considering that the new emperor ascended the throne in the eastern wing of the Tàijí Diàn (太極殿), and the subsequent text mentions ceasing court mourning in the Western Palace,
it is suspected that the Zhōnghé Diàn (中和殿) and Sīzhèng Diàn (思政殿) were both in the Western Inner Palace.
The *Shílù* (實錄) states that Xiànzōng (憲宗) died in the Zhōnghé Diàn (中和殿) of the Dàmíng Gōng (大明宮),
which would place it in the Eastern Inner Palace.
Róng’s (戎) younger brother;
Xuē Róng (薛戎) is mentioned in volume 235 under Dézōng (德宗), Zhēnyuán (貞元) sixteenth year.
A native of Sūzhōu (蘇州);
both were attendants who read for the Crown Prince.
The emperor had not yet begun to govern,
and Fàng (放) and Gōngzhù (公著) often attended within the forbidden palace,
participating in confidential matters.
The emperor wished to appoint them as chancellors,
but the two firmly declined.
4 On *dīngwèi*,
court mourning in the Western Palace was ceased.
The Western Palace
is the Western Inner Palace.
The deceased emperor was in his coffin,
and his subjects mourned morning and evening.
*Lín* (臨)
means to weep.
*Cháo* (朝),
as written,
pronounced *zhìyáo* (陟遙) (*fanqie*).
*Lín* (臨),
pronounced *lìjìn* (力浸) (*fanqie*).
During the Tang, both the Eastern and Western Inner Palaces had Yuèhuá Mén (月華門).
In the Western Inner Palace, within the Tàijí Mén (太極門), the eastern chamber had the Rìhuá Mén (日華門),
and the western chamber had the Yuèhuá Mén (月華門).
In the Eastern Inner Palace, the eastern corridor of the Xuānzhèng Diàn (宣政殿) had the Rìhuá Mén (日華門),
and the western corridor had the Yuèhuá Mén (月華門).
The marketplaces all congratulated each other.
5 The emperor discussed appointing chancellors.
Lìnghú Chǔ (令狐楚) recommended the Censor-in-chief Xiāo Miǎn (蕭俛).
On *xīnhài*,
Miǎn (俛) and Duàn Wénchāng (段文昌) were both appointed Zhongshū Shìláng (中書侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì (同平章事).
Chǔ (楚), Miǎn (俛), and Huángfǔ Bó (皇甫鎛) were all *jìnshì* (進士) of the same year.
The emperor wished to execute Bó (鎛)
because he had supported Tǔtū Chéngcuǐ (吐突承璀) in attempting to install Lǐ Wáng (澧王).
Therefore, he was spared.
On *rénzǐ*,
Liǔ Bì (柳泌) and the monk Dàtōng (大通) were beaten to death.
All other alchemists were exiled to the Lingbiǎo (嶺表) region.
Lǐ Dàogǔ (李道古), the General of the Left Jinwu Guard, was demoted to Sīmǎ (司馬) of Xúnzhōu (循州).
This was because he had recommended Liǔ Bì (柳泌)
and also protected him.
6 On *guǐchǒu*,
Xuē Fàng (薛放) was appointed Minister of Works,
and Dīng Gōngzhù (丁公著) was appointed Gěishì Zhōng (給事中).
7 On *yǐmǎo*,
Grand Empress Guō (郭) was honored as Grand Empress Dowager.
8 On *dīngmǎo*,
the emperor and his officials all discarded their mourning clothes and resumed auspicious attire.
This was in accordance with the last will of Emperor Wén (漢文帝) of Han.
9 Second month.
On *dīngchǒu*,
the emperor ascended the Dānfèng Mén (丹鳳門) tower
and issued a general amnesty.
After the event,
he extensively displayed singers, actors, and various performances inside the gate and watched them.
On *dīnghài*,
the emperor visited the Left Shéncè Army (神策軍) to watch wrestling and various performances.
On *gēngyín*,
Censor Yáng Yúqīng (楊虞卿) submitted a memorial,
stating:
“Your Majesty should grant frequent audiences to your officials,
consult them thoroughly,
and show them kindness in your demeanor,
so that offering loyalty becomes as attractive as pursuing profit,
and discussing governance is like airing grievances.
If this is done and peace and prosperity are not achieved,
it has never happened.”
Zhào Zhīwēi (趙知微) of Héngshān (衡山) also submitted a memorial admonishing the emperor against excessive hunting.
Although the emperor did not adopt their advice,
he did not punish them.
The state of Wú (吳) established Héngshān Xiàn (衡山縣) from Xiāngnán Xiàn (湘南縣).
In the early Tang, it belonged to Tánzhōu (潭州);
in the third year of Shénlóng (神龍), it was transferred to Héngzhōu (衡州).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) states:
It is two hundred thirty *lǐ* northeast of the prefecture.
10On *rénchén*,
Yōngguǎn (邕管) was abolished,
and Yáng Mín (陽旻), the Military Commissioner of Róngguǎn (容管), was ordered to concurrently administer it.
11Guì Zhòngwǔ (桂仲武), the Protector-General of Ānnán (安南), arrived in Ānnán (安南),
but Yáng Qīng (楊清) resisted at the border and refused to admit him.
Qīng (清) was cruel and tyrannical in his punishments,
causing his followers to become disaffected.
Zhòngwǔ (仲武) sent people to persuade the tribal chiefs,
and within a few months,
those who surrendered came in succession,
amassing over seven thousand soldiers.
The court considered Zhòngwǔ (仲wǔ) to be delaying.
On *jiǎwǔ*,
Péi Xínglì (裴行立), the Surveillance Commissioner of Guìguǎn (桂管), was appointed Protector-General of Ānnán (安南).
On *yǐwèi*,
Dù Shìfāng (杜式方), the Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud, was appointed Surveillance Commissioner of Guìguǎn (桂管).
On *bǐngshēn*,
Zhòngwǔ (仲wǔ) was demoted to Governor of Ānzhōu (安州).
12Prince Dān Yú (丹王逾) passed away.
Yú (逾) was a son of Dàizōng (代宗).
13The Tubo (吐蕃) raided Língwǔ (靈武).
14Towards the end of Xiànzōng’s (憲宗) reign,
the Uyghurs sent Hédá Gàn (合達干) to request a marriage alliance with extreme urgency.
Xiànzōng (憲宗) agreed.
In the third month,
on *guǐmǎo*, the first day of the month,
Hédá Gàn (合達干) was sent back to his country.
15The emperor saw the calligraphy of Liǔ Gōngquán (柳公權), the Judicial Commissioner of Xiàzhōu (夏州),
and loved it.
On *xīnyǒu*,
Gōngquán (公權) was appointed Right Reminder and Academician of the Hanlin Academy for Calligraphy.
He was assigned only to attend to calligraphy
and not entrusted with the duty of drafting imperial edicts.
The emperor asked, “How can your calligraphy be so excellent?”
He replied,
“The use of the brush lies in the heart;
if the heart is upright, then the brush is upright.”
The emperor silently changed his expression,
realizing that Gōngquán (公權) was using calligraphy to offer remonstrance.
Gōngquán (公權)
was the younger brother of Gōngchuò (公綽).
16On *xīnwèi*,
the generals and soldiers of Ānnán (安南) opened the city gates to admit Guì Zhòngwǔ (桂仲武),
captured Yáng Qīng (楊清),
and executed him.
Péi Xínglì (裴行立) died upon reaching Hǎimén (海門).
Hǎimén Zhèn (海門鎮)
is southeast of Bóyù Xiàn (博白縣) in Báizhōu (白州).
pronounced *xù* (*fānqiē*).
17The Tubo (吐蕃) raided Yánzhōu (鹽州).
18 Initially,
Yuán Zhěn (元稹), a Yuánwàiláng (員外郎) in the Shànbù (膳部) department, was a Shìcáo (士曹) in Jiānglíng (江陵).
In the fifth year of Yuánhé (元和) of Emperor Xiànzōng (憲宗) [810 CE],
Yuán Zhěn was demoted to Shìcáo (士曹) of Jiānglíng (江陵).
The details can be found in chapter 238.
When the Emperor was in the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng 東宮),
he heard palace maids reciting Zhěn's (稹) poems and praised them.
When he ascended the throne,
Tán Jùn (潭峻) returned to court
and presented over a hundred poems by Zhěn (稹).
The Emperor asked,
"Where is Zhěn (稹) now?"
He replied,
"He is currently a Sǎnláng (散郎)."
A Lángzhōng (郎中) is called a Zhèngláng (正郎),
and a Yuánwàiláng (員外郎) is called a Sǎnláng (散郎).
Sàn (散)
is pronounced "sī dǎn."
In the fifth month,
on the Gēngxū (庚戌) day,
Zhěn (稹) was appointed Cíbù Lángzhōng (祠部郎中) and Zhī Zhìgào (知制誥).
According to Táng (唐) regulations, there were six Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人),
one of whom was Zhī Zhìgào (知制誥).
In the early Kāiyuán (開元) period,
other officials were put in charge of imperial edicts.
Before an official appointment,
they were referred to as concurrently Zhī Zhìgào (知制誥).
Colleagues happened to be eating melons under the閣 (gé),
the Zhōngshū Shěng (中書省) was called Fènggé (鳳閣),
and there was also Zǐwēigé (紫微閣).
Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人) Wǔ Rúhéng (武儒衡) waved his fan and said,
"Where did you just come from,
to gather here so suddenly!"
He was likening Zhěn (稹) to a fly.
Rúhéng (儒衡) maintained his composed demeanor.
19 On the Gēngshēn (庚申) day,
the divine, sagely, accomplished, martial, and filial Emperor was buried in Jǐnglíng (景陵).
Jǐnglíng (景陵)
is twenty *lǐ* (里) northwest of Jīnchìshān (金熾山) in Fèngxiān (奉先) county, Tóngzhōu (同州).
In ancient times, ancestors with merit were called Zǔ (祖), and those with virtue were called Zōng (宗);
Zhōngzōng (中宗) and Gāozōng (高宗) of the Shāng (商) dynasty are examples.
The Western Hàn (漢) dynasty designated Emperor Wén (文) as Tàizōng (太宗),
Emperor Wǔ (武) as Shìzōng (世宗),
and Emperor Xuān (宣) as Zhōngzōng (中宗),
which still somewhat reflected the ancient intention.
From Emperor Míng (明) to Emperor Huán (桓) in the Eastern Hàn (漢) dynasty, all temple names were called Zōng (宗),
which was not in accordance with ancient practice.
Of the seventeen Zōng (宗) of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
people today only refer to
three Zōng (宗).
20 In the sixth month,
Cuī Shùn (崔㣥), the Húnán Guānchásǐ (湖南觀察使), was appointed Lìbù Shìláng (吏部侍郎)
and summoned for an audience in a side hall.
The Emperor said,
"When I was heir apparent,
I knew you served as my support."
The details can be found in chapter 238, seventh year of Yuánhé (元和) of Emperor Xiànzōng (憲宗).
"The late Emperor's intention
had long been entrusted to the sagely and enlightened;
what power did your servant possess!"
Cuī Shùn's (崔㣥) reply
was gentle and upright in tone.
In handling the transition between past and present affairs,
it should be taken as a model.
21 The Empress Dowager resided in Xīngqìnggōng (興慶宮).
On the first and fifteenth day of each lunar month (shuò wàng 朔望),
the Emperor led all officials to the palace to offer congratulations.
The Emperor was by nature extravagant,
so his provision for the Empress Dowager was especially lavish.
After Huáixī (淮西) was pacified, Emperor Xiànzōng's (憲宗) governance declined.
How much more so when Emperor Mùzōng (穆宗) wished to outdo him!
22 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the Yǐsì (乙巳) day,
the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Yùn (鄆), Cáo (曹), and Pú (濮) were designated Tiānpíngjūn (天平軍).
23 Ménxià Shìláng (門下侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事) Línghú Chǔ (令狐楚) was impeached because, as the Shānlíngshǐ (山陵使),
his subordinates stole official property
and also failed to pay workers their wages.
He collected 150,000 *mín* (緡) in additional funds from them and offered it as a surplus.
Complaints filled the roads.
On the Dīngmǎo (丁卯) day,
he was dismissed and made Xuān (宣), Shè (歙), Chí (池) Guānchásǐ (觀察使).
If we consider Línghú Chǔ's (令狐楚) matter as recorded by the historians,
then his dismissal from premiership was indeed correct.
If we consider Emperor Xuānzōng's (宣宗) employment of Línghú Táo (令狐綯),
then Chǔ's (楚) dismissal was wrong.
One who reads history must be able to discern its right and wrong.
Xuānzhōu (宣州) was the territory of Qín Zhāng (秦鄣) Commandery.
During the Hàn (漢) dynasty, it was Dānyáng (丹楊) Commandery.
Emperor Shùn (順) renamed it Xuānchéng (宣城) Commandery.
During the Suí (隋) dynasty, it became Xuānzhōu (宣州).
It is 3,551 *lǐ* (里) southeast of the capital.
Shèzhōu (歙州) was Xīndū (新都) Commandery during the Wú (吳) kingdom.
The Jìn (晉) dynasty renamed it Xīn'ān (新安) Commandery.
During the Suí (隋) dynasty, it became Shèzhōu (歙州).
It is 3,667 *lǐ* (里) southeast of the capital.
Chízhōu (池州) was the territory of Shíchéng (石城) county during the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
Prince Zhāomíng (昭明) of the Liáng (梁) dynasty
renamed it Guìchí (貴池) because its waters produced beautiful fish.
The Táng (唐) dynasty established Chízhōu (池州).
It is 305 *lǐ* (里) east of Xuānzhōu (宣州).
Shè (歙)
is pronounced "shū shè."
24 In the eighth month,
on the Guǐsì (癸巳) day,
