Furthermore, if a trustworthy and authoritative person were chosen as *Jīnglüèshǐ*,
and the situation handled appropriately,
there would naturally be no further incursions or rebellions."
The Emperor was unable to adopt this.
Mùzōng Ruìshèng Wénhuì Xiàohuángdì,
whose personal name was Héng,
was the third son of Xiànzōng.
Chángqìng first year
(*xīnchǒu*, 821)
1. In spring,
first month,
*xīnchǒu*,
the Emperor sacrificed at the Yuánqiū;
a general amnesty was granted throughout the empire,
and the *gǎiyuán* was declared.
All circuits in Hébĕi were ordered to equalize and fix their Two-Tax System assessments.
This was because the various garrisons in Hébĕi had each submitted maps requesting officials
and offering taxes,
hence the order to equalize and fix them.
2. The *Ménxià Shìláng* and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*, Xiāo Miǎn,
was incorruptible and detested evil.
As Chancellor,
he valued official positions highly and was sparing in his promotions.
Wáng Bō, the *Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ*, greatly increased his tributes
and bribed eunuchs,
seeking to become Chancellor. Duàn Wénchāng further supported him;
an imperial edict summoned Bō to the capital.
Miǎn repeatedly argued strenuously in the Yányīng Hall,
stating:
"Bō is treacherous and wicked;
public opinion is raging.
He cannot be allowed to sully the Censorate."
The Emperor did not listen,
so Miǎn resigned his position.
On *jǐwèi*,
Bō arrived at the capital.
On *rénxū*,
Miǎn was dismissed to become *Yòupúshè*.
Miǎn firmly declined the *Púshè* position,
so in the second month,
on *guǐyǒu*,
he was appointed *Lìbù Shàngshū* instead.
3. Liú Zǒng, the *Lúlóng Jiédùshǐ*, having killed his father and elder brother (the account is in volume 238, Xiànzōng's Yuánhé fifth year),
frequently saw his father and elder brother as vengeful spirits;
he often hosted hundreds of monks in his residence for meals,
having them perform Buddhist rituals day and night.
Whenever he retired from official duties, he would stay among them.
If he stayed in another room,
he would be startled and dare not sleep.
In his later years,
his fear became even more intense.
He also saw that Hénán and Hébĕi had all submitted to imperial authority.
On *jǐmǎo*,
he memorialized requesting to abandon his official post and become a monk.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The old biography of Wēn Zào says:
"In Chángqìng first year,
he was sent as an envoy to Héshuò and pleased the Emperor,
being promoted to *Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ*.
Soon after, Liú Zǒng of Yōuzhōu requested that his nine prefectures be subject to imperial command.
Mùzōng selected a suitable envoy,
and some recommended Zào.
He was then appointed *Qǐjū Shèrén*
and concurrently *Tàiyuán, Yōuzhōu, Zhènzhōu Xuānyùshǐ*.
When Zào first arrived in Fányáng,
Liú Zǒng, fully armed, welcomed him in the suburbs.
Zào then proclaimed the imperial edict,
demonstrating the consequences of good and ill fortune.
Zǒng prostrated himself, sweating profusely,
as if a weapon were at his neck.
When Zào returned from his mission,
Zǒng then moved his family to the capital for an audience."
According to the *Shílù*: On *jǐsì* of the first month of Chángqìng first year,
Zào was made *Tàiyuán, Zhènzhōu děng Dào Xuānwèishǐ*.
On *jǐmǎo* of the second month,
Liú Zǒng memorialized requesting to become a monk.
It is calculated that Zào had not yet returned from his mission.
On *guǐhài* of the third month,
Zǒng had already died.
On *dīnghài* of the eighth month,
Wēn Zào, the *Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ*, was made *Qǐjū Shèrén* and concurrently *Zhènzhōu Sìmiàn Zhūjūn Xuānwèishǐ*.
Zào had previously, as *Jīngzhào Sīlù*, pacified the two Hés;
everyone praised his talent,
hence this appointment.
The old biography is mistaken.
4. The Emperor had previously instructed Wáng Bō, the *Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ*, to return to his post,
but Bō repeatedly memorialized requesting to remain in the capital.
It happened that Duàn Wénchāng, the *Zhōngshū Shìláng* and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*, requested to retire.
On *rénshēn*,
Wénchāng was made *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*
and concurrently *Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ*;
Dù Yuányǐng, a *Hànlín Xuéshì*, was made *Hùbù Shìláng* and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*;
Bō was made *Xíngbù Shàngshū*
and concurrently *Yántiě Zhuǎnyùnshǐ*.
Yuányǐng was the sixth-generation descendant of Yān.
Dù Yān was Chancellor during Tàizōng's reign.
5. Bǎoyì Kèhán of Huíhú died.
6. In the third month,
on *guǐchǒu*,
Liú Zǒng was appointed concurrent *Shìzhōng*
and *Tiānpíng Jiédùshǐ*;
Zhāng Hóngjìng, the *Xuānwǔ Jiédùshǐ*, was made *Lúlóng Jiédùshǐ*.
7. On *yǐmǎo*,
Lú Shìméi, acting *Jīngzhào Yǐn*, was made *Yíngmò Guānchásǐ*.
On *dīngsì*,
an imperial edict was issued that all of Liú Zǒng's brothers, sons, and nephews be granted official posts,
and his generals and aides also be promoted exceptionally.
The common people were granted a year's exemption from taxes and labor,
and the soldiers were given one million *mín* of cash.
8. On *wùwǔ*,
the Emperor's younger brothers were enfeoffed: Jǐng as Fūwáng,
Yuè as Qióngwáng,
Qióng as Miǎnwáng,
Yì as Wùwáng,
Yīn as Màowáng,
Yí as Guāngwáng,
Xié as Zīwáng,
Dàn as Qúwáng,
Wǎn as Chánwáng;
the Emperor's sons were enfeoffed: Zhàn as Jǐngwáng,
Hán as Jiāngwáng,
Còu as Zhāngwáng,
Róng as Ānwáng,
Chán as Yǐngwáng.
9. Liú Zǒng earnestly memorialized requesting to become a monk,
and also to convert his private residence into a Buddhist temple.
An imperial edict granted Zǒng the name Dàjué
and the temple the name Bàoyēn,
and dispatched eunuchs with purple monastic robes, the *Tiānpíng Jiéyuè* (credentials of a *Jiédùshǐ*), and the *Shìzhōng Gàoshēn* (patent of appointment) to be bestowed upon him,
allowing him to choose as he wished.
Before the imperial edict arrived,
Liú Zǒng had already shaved his head and become a monk.
The generals and soldiers wanted to stop and keep him.
Liú Zǒng killed more than ten of those who incited the obstruction.
"遮留者" (zhēliúzhě),
means to block the road and stop someone from leaving.
"唱帥者" (chàngshuàizhě),
means to make a call to lead the crowd.
"帥" (shuài),
is read as "率" (shuài).
He handed over his seal and credentials to the acting commissioner Zhāng [something]
and fled.
Zhāng [something] had conspired with Liú Zǒng to kill his father and elder brother.
The army only then became aware of this.
A memorial was submitted stating that Liú Zǒng's whereabouts were unknown.
A "Kǎoyì" (考異) states: The new biography says:
"Liú Zǒng handed the credentials to Zhāng Gāo.
Gāo
was his elder brother,
and served as the Cìshǐ of Zhuōzhōu,
and was Liú Zǒng's father-in-law."
According to the "Shílù" (實錄):
"Zhāng [something], the acting commissioner of Yōuzhōu, memorialized: 'Liú Zǒng has shaved his head and become a monk,
and his whereabouts are unknown.'"
If so, he did not give the credentials to Gāo.
On the day Guǐhài,
he died in the territory of Dìngzhōu.
In the first year of Zhēnyuán of Dèzōng's reign,
Liú Pēng obtained Yōuzhōu.
After three generations,
and thirty-six years, it was extinguished.
The Hanlin Scholar Lǐ Déyù,
was the son of Lǐ Jífǔ.
Because the Zhongshu Shèrén Lǐ Zōngmǐn had once criticized his father in a policy essay,
he resented him.
The details of the criticism are found in volume 237, Xiànzōng, Yuánhé 3rd year.
Yòu Bǔquē Yáng Rǔshì and Lǐbù Shìláng Qián Huī were in charge of the imperial examinations.
Duàn Wénchāng, Jìdùshǐ of Xīchuān, and Hanlin Scholar Lǐ Shēn each wrote letters commending certain jinshì to Qián Huī, whom they knew well.
When the results were posted,
none of those commended by Wénchāng and Shēn passed.
"及第者" (jízhìzhě),
means those who passed the jinshì examination,
called "jízhì" (及第),
meaning their literary skills reached the standard.
Tán's younger brother;
Péi Zhuàn,
Dù's son;
Sū Cháo,
Zōngmǐn's son-in-law;
Yáng Yīnshì,
Rǔshì's younger brother.
Wénchāng reported to the Emperor, saying:
"This year the Ministry of Rites has been extremely unfair."
"殊" (shū),
means "extremely."
"It is said that all who passed are sons of high officials,
with no real talent."
"Táng people referred to lobbying with letters as 'guānjié' (關節),
this term is still used today."
Déyù, Zhěn, and Shēn all said:
"It is indeed as Wénchāng says."
The Emperor then ordered Zhongshu Shèrén Wáng Qǐ and others to re-examine them.
means to review.
To re-examine and select jinshì to verify their true talent is called "fùshì" (覆試).
In the fourth month,
on the day Dīngchǒu,
an edict was issued dismissing Lǎng and ten others.
A "Kǎoyì" states: The biography of Zhèng Tán says:
"Lǎng
passed the first class of jinshì in the first year of Chángqìng."
This probably refers to his initial passing the examination.
Zōngmǐn was appointed Cìshǐ of Jiànzhōu,
Rǔshì as magistrate of Kāijiāng.
Jiāngzhōu
is 2,948 li southeast of the capital.
Jiànzhōu
is 1,662 li south of the capital.
Kāijiāng
was formerly the land of Hàn Qúwū County.
Liáng established Hànfēng County.
Western Wèi changed its name to Yǒngníng County.
Suí changed it to Shèngshān.
In the first year of Guǎngdé, Dàizōng of Táng changed it to Kāijiāng.
It was attached to Kāizhōu.
Someone advised Huī to submit Wénchāng and Shēn's letters of recommendation,
and the Emperor would surely understand.
Huī said:
"If I have no shame in my heart,
then gain and loss are the same to me.
How can I submit people's private letters?
Is that what a gentleman would do?"
He took and burned them.
People at the time admired him for this.
Shēn
was the great-grandson of Lǐ Jìngxuán.
Lǐ Jìngxuán
served as a chancellor during Gāozōng's reign.
He was Bò's younger brother.
From then on, Déyù and Zōngmǐn each formed factions,
constantly attacking each other,
for nearly forty years.
On the day Bǐngxū,
the new ruler of the Huíhú was enfeoffed as Dēngluóyǔlùmìshījùzhǔpígāochóngdé Kèhán.
According to the practice of the "Tōngjiàn,"
the new Huíhú Kèhán was never recorded as "sìjūn" (嗣君, successor ruler).
The "Táng Huìyào" states: The Huíhú Kèhán was enfeoffed as Jūndēnglǐluóyǔlùmìshījùzhǔpígāochóngdé Kèhán.
"囉" (luō),
pronounced "lúhé."
In the fifth month,
on the first day Bǐngshēn,
the Huíhú dispatched over five hundred people, including their Dūdū and Prime Ministers, to escort the princess.
On the day Rénzǐ,
Wáng Bō, the Salt and Iron Commissioner, memorialized: to fix the tea monopoly quota,
adding a tax of fifty per hundred cash.
Yòu Shíyí Lǐ Yù and others submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The tea monopoly only started recently during the troubled times of Zhēnyuán.
See volume 234, Dèzōng, Zhēnyuán 9th year.
It is appropriate to lighten the burden of oppressive taxes;
yet to increase them further,
when will the common people ever get a moment's rest?"
It was not adopted.
On the day Bǐngchén,
Jiànwáng Kè died.
Kè
was the Emperor's younger brother.
On the day Guǐhài,
Princess Tàihé was married to the Huíhú.
The princess
was the Emperor's younger sister.
When Tubó heard that Táng was marrying the Huíhú,
in the sixth month,
on the day Xīnwèi,
they invaded Qīngsàibǎo.
The "Xīnshū Tubó Zhuàn" (新書吐蕃傳) writes it as
"Qīngsàibǎo" (清塞堡).
On the day Wùyín,
the Huíhú memorialized:
"We will dispatch ten thousand cavalry from Běitíng
and ten thousand cavalry from Ānxī
to resist Tubó and welcome the princess."
Originally,
Liú Zǒng had memorialized to divide his territory into three circuits: Yōu, Zhuó, and Yíng as one circuit,
requesting that Zhāng Hóngjìng be appointed Jìdùshǐ;
Píng, Jì, Guī, and Tán as one circuit,
requesting that Xuē Píng, the Pínglú Jìdùshǐ, be appointed Jìdùshǐ;
Yíng and Mò as one circuit,
requesting that Lú Shìméi, the acting Jīngzhào Yǐn, be appointed Guānchásǐ.
The "Shìmíng" (釋名) says: Yōuzhōu is in the north,
a dark and obscure place,
hence called Yōu.
To the southwest of Zhuōzhōu is 120 li.
Yíngzhōu
is named after the Yíngshì constellation.
Yōu and Zhuó are adjacent.
Yíngzhōu governed Liǔchéng,
the distance is extremely far.
Liú Zǒng's proposal to make them one circuit
must have a reason.
Píngzhōu is 200 li west of Jìzhōu.
Jìzhōu is 217 li northwest of Tánzhōu.
Tánzhōu is 250 li west of Guīzhōu.
Yíngzhōu is 210 li north of Mòzhōu.
"玫" (méi),
pronounced "mòhuí."
Hóngjìng had previously been in Hédōng,
and gained popular support through his leniency and simplicity.
Hóngjìng's governorship in Hédōng is found in volume 239, Xiànzōng, Yuánhé 11th year.
The two garrisons of Yōu and Bìng are adjacent.
As the people of Yàn had been rebellious for a long time,
he therefore recommended Hóngjìng to replace him and pacify them.
Píng
was Sōng's son.
Xuē Sōng served as a general under Shǐ Sīmíng,
and surrendered at the beginning of Dàizōng's reign.
As he was entirely loyal to the state,
he was recommended.
Shìméi
was a relative of Liú Zǒng's wife's clan.
Liú Zǒng also carefully selected
the most capable and unruly among his subordinates, such as the Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ Zhū Kèróng and others, and sent them to the capital,
requesting that they be rewarded and promoted,
so that the people of Yàn would aspire to the honors and positions of the imperial court.
He also presented fifteen thousand warhorses.
"征馬" (zhēngmǎ),
means warhorses.
"委" (wěi),
means to abandon.
He was Tāo's grandson.
Zhū Tāo rebelled during the time of Dèzōng.
At this time, the court was immersed in revelry,
paying no attention to the affairs of the realm.
Cuī Zhí and Dù Yuán Yǐng lacked far-sighted strategies,
unaware of the great principles of safety and danger.
They merely wished to elevate and empower Liú Hóng Jìng,
so they only ceded Yíngzhōu and Mòzhōu,
entrusting Shǐ Méi to govern them.
All others were to be under Liú Hóng Jìng's command.
Zhū Kè Róng and others had long been sojourners in the capital,
even resorting to begging for food and clothing.
Daily they went to the Central Secretariat to seek official positions,
but Cuī Zhí and Dù Yuán Yǐng paid no heed to them.
When Liú Hóng Jìng was appointed to Yōuzhōu,
Zhū Kè Róng and his ilk were ordered to return to their original army for service.
All of them became resentful and angry.
Previously,
all Jìedùshǐ in Héběi
personally endured the cold and heat, sharing hardships and comforts with their soldiers.
But when Liú Hóng Jìng arrived,
he was elegant and arrogant,
carried in a palanquin amidst tens of thousands of people.
The Yān people were surprised by this.
"Yà" (訝) means
to see it and be astonished and suspicious.
"Yān" (燕)
is pronounced "yú xián" (於賢)
and similarly below. He only came out to preside over decisions
once every ten days or so.
His guests and military officials rarely heard him speak.
Their feelings and intentions did not connect,
and most governmental affairs were delegated to his staff.
The judicial officers he appointed, such as Wéi Yōng and his kind, were mostly young, frivolous men,
fond of drinking and unrestrained.
Their comings and goings, with attendants shouting ahead, were very grand.
Sometimes they returned at night with torches illuminating the whole street,
all of which the Yān people were unaccustomed to.
An imperial edict granted a million strings of cash to the generals and soldiers,
but Liú Hóng Jìng retained two hundred thousand strings for the military government's miscellaneous expenses.
Wéi Yōng and his kind further cut down the soldiers' rations and allowances,
enforcing it with strict laws.
They frequently reviled and rebuked the officials and soldiers as "rebellious barbarians,"
and told the soldiers:
"Today, the world is at peace.
You who can draw a two-stone bow
are not as good as someone who knows a single character!"
Because of this, everyone in the army was resentful and angry.
To pacify the wild and rough,
to spread moral influence,
and to adapt to their customs and reform their governance is easy to achieve success.
To frighten them with what they have never seen,
and to alarm them with what they have never heard,
rarely fails to invite disaster quickly.

Chángqìng first year
(Xīnchǒu, 821)
1 Autumn.
In the seventh month,
on the jiǎchén day,
Wéi Yōng went out.
He encountered a young general who spurred his horse and charged past his vanguard.
Yōng ordered him to be pulled down,
intending to flog him in the street.
The soldiers from Héshuò were not accustomed to being flogged,
and resisted.
Wéi Yōng wished to govern Yōuyān with the same methods that Liǔ Gōngchuò used to govern Jīngzhào.
However, when Gōngchuò implemented them, they could bring order to the imperial capital,
but when Wéi Yōng implemented them, they invited disaster and caused turmoil,
for the places where they served were different.
“Guàn” (貫)
should be read as “guàn” (慣).
Hóngjìng ordered the army's yúhóu to arrest and investigate him.
That evening,
the soldiers in their camps collectively shouted and created a disturbance,
which the generals and officers could not control.
They then entered the prefectural residence,
plundered Hóngjìng’s valuables and women,
and imprisoned Hóngjìng in the Jìmén Guǎn.
Jìmén Guǎn
was the post-station in Yōuzhōu.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The old tradition records it as
“Zhāng Zōnghòu.”
Now we follow the *Shílù*.
The dùyúhóu was Liú Cāo, and the yāyá was Zhāng Bàoyuán.
The next day,
the soldiers gradually regretted their actions.
They all went to the guesthouse to apologize to Hóngjìng
and requested to change their hearts and serve him.
They asked three times,
but Hóngjìng did not respond.
The soldiers then said to each other,
“The xiànggōng is silent;
this means he will not pardon us.
How can the army be without a commander for even one day!”
So they went together to welcome the old general Zhū Huí
and installed him as liúhòu.
Huí
was Kèróng’s father.
At that time, he was incapacitated by illness and confined to his home.
He excused himself on account of old age and sickness,
requesting that Kèróng be appointed instead;
the crowd agreed.
Someone asked:
“When the rebellious soldiers collectively went to the guesthouse to apologize to Hóngjìng,
if Hóngjìng had been able to act as Rèn Díjiǎn had in Zhōngshān,
could he have quelled the rebellion?”
The reply was:
“No.
Díjiǎn could share hardships with his subordinates,
while Hóngjìng was arrogant, noble, and taciturn.
Hóngjìng’s women were plundered by the soldiers,
and his aides were killed by the soldiers.
Even if the people of Yān could truly change their hearts to serve Hóngjìng,
it would only be establishing an empty title of jiéshuài over fierce generals and brutal soldiers.
With the ferocious and brutal running rampant,
there would be nothing they wouldn't do,
only further humiliation.”
He was not killed.
Chè cursed, saying:
“How dare you rebel?
You will soon be exterminated along with your families!”
The crowd jointly killed him.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
“Chè had only been in office for a few days.
The soldiers did not kill him,
but placed him in the same guesthouse as Hóngjìng.
A few days later,
the soldiers feared that Chè and Hóngjìng might conspire,
and intended to move him elsewhere.
Chè suspected he was about to be executed,
and so spoke loudly, cursing,
and was again killed.”
The old tradition says:
“Later, there was Zhāng Chè,
who returned from a distant mission.
The soldiers, seeing he had committed no offense,
did not wish to harm him,
and intended to bring him to the guesthouse.
Chè did not know their intentions,
and so sought Hóngjìng’s whereabouts,
and greatly cursed the soldiers,
and was also killed by the rebellious soldiers.”
Hán Yù’s epitaph for Chè says:
“Chè held successive official posts, reaching Inspector-Censor of Fányáng Prefecture.
In the second year of Chángqìng,
when the present Prime Minister Niú was Zhōngchéng,
he recommended you, sir, as Yùshǐ.
That prefecture, regretting and not daring to detain him,
sent him away,
but secretly reported: ‘Your servant, upon first arrival, was isolated and timid;
I need strong assistants to succeed.’
Halfway there,
an imperial edict ordered you, sir, to return.
A few days after arriving,
the army rebelled,
resenting the prefectural official, killed them all and imprisoned their commander.
They also agreed: ‘Inspector Zhāng is a worthy man;
there is no need to kill him.
Place him with the commander.’
After more than a month,
they heard that a zhòngguìrén from the capital was arriving.
You, sir, said to the commander: ‘My lord, you must not fail the people of this land.
When the imperial envoy arrives,
you can ask to see him and defend yourself,
and hopefully escape and return.’
Immediately, he pushed the door and sought to leave.
The guards reported this to their leader,
who, along with his followers, was alarmed and said: ‘Inspector Zhāng is loyal and righteous.
He will certainly report these other men to their commander.
It is better to move him to another guesthouse.’
Immediately, they brought you, sir, out with the crowd.
You, sir, came out the door and cursed the crowd, saying: ‘How dare you rebel!
The other day, Wú Yuánjì was beheaded in the eastern market.
Yesterday, Lǐ Shīdào was beheaded in the army.
Those who shared their wickedness, their parents, wives, and children were all slaughtered,
their flesh fed to dogs, rats, kites, and crows.
How dare you rebel!’
He walked and continued to curse.
The crowd feared and detested his words,
could not bear to hear them,
and also worried about an incident,
so they immediately struck you, sir, to death.
You, sir, cursed incessantly until death.
Everyone said: ‘A righteous man!
A righteous man!’
Some collected and buried him, awaiting burial.
According to the old tradition:
“Chè was killed at the time Hóngjìng was imprisoned.”
The *Shílù* says
“a few days later,”
and the epitaph says
“more than a month later.”
The three accounts differ.
It is noted that in this month, on the dīngsì day,
Hóngjìng had already been demoted.
More than a month later, he would have left Yōuzhōu.
Now we follow the *Shílù*,
consulting the epitaph.
I believe Hán Yù’s epitaph accurately records Zhāng Chè’s words when cursing the rebels.
The *Shílù* and old tradition accurately explain Zhāng Chè’s heart when cursing the rebels.
As for the month and day,
the *Kǎoyì* has already made its selection.
2 On the rénzǐ day,
the officials conferred the honorific title of Wénwǔ Xiàodé Huángdì upon the emperor;
there was a general amnesty throughout the realm.
3 On the jiǎyín day,
the Supervising Eunuch of Yōuzhōu reported the army rebellion;
on the dīngsì day,
Zhāng Hóngjìng was demoted to Bīnkè, Fēnsī;
demoted to Tàizǐ Bīnkè,
which meant Fēnsī in the Eastern Capital.
On the jǐwèi day,
he was again demoted to Cìshǐ of Jízhōu.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The old tradition says:
“Demoted to Cìshǐ of Fúzhōu.”
However, he was not transferred to Fúzhōu until the following year.
Now we follow the *Shílù*.
On the gēngshēn day,
Liú Wù, the Jiédu Shǐ of Zhāoyì, was appointed Jiédu Shǐ of Lúlóng.
Wù, seeing Zhū Kèróng's growing power,
petitioned
“to temporarily grant Kèróng the jiéyuè,
and gradually plan for his removal.”
Therefore, Wù was reinstated as Jiédu Shǐ of Zhāoyì.
4 On the xīnyǒu day,
Princess Tàihé departed from Cháng’ān.
5 Initially,
Tián Hóngzhèng received an imperial edict to garrison Chéngdé.
He considered that he had long been at war with the people of Zhèn,
having the blood feud of his father and brothers,
and during Xiànzōng's reign,
Tián Hóngzhèng twice led troops to attack Zhènjì.
He then kept them for self-defense,
and memorialized requesting Dùzhī to supply their rations and rewards.
According to the old system: when troops from various garrisons crossed the border,
Dùzhī would supply their clothes and rations.
He was rigid and narrow-minded,
without foresight,
and thought that Wèi and Zhèn each had their own troops,
fearing to set a precedent,
so he refused to provide.
Hóngzhèng submitted four memorials,
but received no reply;
left with no choice,
he sent the Wèi troops back.
Kǎoyì says: The old biography of Hóngzhèng states:
"He returned in the seventh month,
and died in Wèizhōu."
Wáng Tíngcòu's biography states:
"In the sixth month,
the Wèi troops returned to the garrison."
Cuī Lín's biography says:
"He sent the Wèi soldiers back to the garrison.
Not many days later, Zhènzhōu was in chaos."
We follow this account now.
He was Miǎn's grandson.
Cuī Miǎn
was a famous minister at the beginning of Kāiyuán.
Hóngzhèng was generous to his family,
with dozens of brothers, sons, and nephews in the two capitals,
competing in extravagance.
Hóngzhèng's brothers, sons, and nephews all served at court,
residing separately in the Eastern and Western Capitals.
Hóngzhèng transported goods from Wèi and Zhèn to supply them,
forming a continuous procession on the roads;
the generals and soldiers in Hébĕi were quite displeased.
An imperial edict granted a million strings of cash to the Chéngdé army,
but Dùzhī's transportation was not timely,
and the soldiers became even more discontent.
The Dū zhī Bīngmǎshǐ Wáng Tíngcòu,
originally of the Ābùsī clan of the Huíhú,
Tíngcòu's great-great-grandfather Wǔgē zhī,
was brave and skilled in combat.
Wáng Wǔjùn adopted him as a son,
so he adopted the surname Wáng.
Ābùsī was
executed for rebellion during Tiānbǎo.
種,
Zhāngyǒng fān.
Secretly plotting rebellion,
he constantly picked out minor issues to incite their anger.
Still, because of the Wèi troops,
he dared not act.
After the Wèi troops departed,
on the night of Rénxū,
Tíngcòu gathered his personal guards and rioted at the official residence,
killing Hóngzhèng and his subordinates, aides, and original attendant officers, as well as over three hundred family members.
Tíngcòu declared himself Liúhòu,
and compelled the supervising censor Sòng Wéichéng to memorialize requesting the jiéyuè.
In the eighth month,
on Guǐsì,
Wéichéng reported it,
and the imperial court was shocked.
Cuī Lín was a second cousin to Cuī Zhí,
so at the time, no one dared to speak of his crime.
Initially,
the imperial court replaced the commanders of Wèi and Zhèn.
Yáng Yuánqīng, General of the Left Jīnwú, submitted a memorial,
deeming it inconvenient.
He also went to the prime minister to deeply explain the advantages and disadvantages;
and when Zhènzhōu was in chaos,
the emperor bestowed a white jade belt upon Yuánqīng.
On Xīnwèi,
Yuánqīng was made Jīngyuán Jiédùshǐ.
Yáng Yuánqīng was rewarded for his accurate words,
but this did not help to save Zhènzhōu from chaos.
Ancient sagacious rulers did not merely reward those who spoke;
if their words were feasible,
they would first follow and implement them.
Many families of the Yíngmò generals and soldiers were in Yōuzhōu.
On Rénshēn,
Zhāng Liángzuǒ, the Dū Yúhòu of Mózhōu, secretly led Zhū Kèróng's troops into the city,
and the whereabouts of the prefect Wú Huī were unknown.
Mózhōu,
bordering Yōu and Jì to the north,
thus fell first.
On Guǐyǒu,
Wáng Tíngcòu sent men to kill Wáng Jìnjí, the prefect of Jìzhōu,
and divided his troops to occupy that prefecture.
Lǐ Sù, Jiédùshǐ of Wèibó, heard that Tián Hóngzhèng had been murdered,
and in mourning attire, he instructed his generals and soldiers:
"The reason Wèi people were able to benefit from the sage's civilizing influence
and enjoy peace, prosperity, and joy until now
is due to Duke Tián's efforts.
Now, the people of Zhèn are inhumane,
daring to harm him,
which is to slight Wèi as if it had no capable men.
Gentlemen, you have received Duke Tián's kindness,
how should you repay it?"
Everyone wept mournfully.
Niú Yuányì, prefect of Shēnzhōu,
was a good general of Chéngdé.
Sù sent him a treasured sword and jade belt,
saying:
"My ancestors once established great merits with this sword,"
referring to the pacification of Zhū Cǐ.
"Now I entrust it to you,
strive to eliminate Tíngcòu."
Yuányì displayed the sword and belt to his army,
and replied:
"I vow to fight to the death!"
Sù was about to dispatch troops,
but fell ill,
and could not.
Yuányì
was from Zhàozhōu.
On Yǐhài,
Tián Bù, formerly Jīngyuán Jiédùshǐ, was reinstated as Wèibó Jiédùshǐ,
and ordered to proceed to Zhèn by post.
Bù firmly declined but was not allowed,
and bid farewell to his wife, children, and guests, saying:
"I shall not return!"
He completely dismissed his banners, insignia, and retinue and traveled,
not yet thirty *lǐ* from Wèizhōu,
he disheveled his hair and walked barefoot,
wailing as he entered,
residing in an unadorned room;
his monthly salary of a thousand strings of cash,
he took none of it,
he sold his old property,
obtaining over a hundred thousand strings of cash,
all of which he distributed to the soldiers.
He treated the older former generals as elder brothers.
Given Tián Bù's actions,
he should have been able to win the hearts of the Wèi soldiers,
but ultimately failed,
because the people's hearts were already shaken,
and Bù's prestige and strategy were not commanding.
On Bǐngzǐ,
the Yíngzhōu army rebelled,
seizing the Guānchásǐ Lú Shìméi and the supervising censor and his subordinates, sending them to Yōuzhōu,
where they were imprisoned in the guest house.
Wáng Tíngcòu sent his general Wáng Lì to attack Shēnzhōu,
but failed.
On Dīngchǒu,
an imperial edict commanded the Wèibó, Hénghǎi, Zhāoyì, Hédōng, and Yìwǔ armies to each dispatch troops to the border of Chéngdé.
If Wáng Tíngcòu remained stubbornly unrepentant,
they should immediately advance and suppress him.
Five great generals of Chéngdé, including Wáng Jiǎn,
plotted to kill Wáng Tíngcòu;
the plot was exposed,
and they, along with three thousand of their soldiers, were all killed.
On Jǐmǎo,
Niú Yuányì, prefect of Shēnzhōu, was made Shēnjì Jiédùshǐ.
Shēnzhōu
is eighty-five *lǐ* south of Jìzhōu.
On Dīnghài,
Wēn Zào, Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ, was appointed Qǐjū Shèrén,
and served as the Xuānwèishǐ for the four armies around Zhènzhōu,
traversing through the Zélù, Hédōng, Wèibó, Hénghǎi, Shēnjì, Yìdìng, and other circuits,
to announce the military deadlines.
Zào
was the fifth-generation descendant of Dàyǎ.
When the emperor's ancestor raised an army,
Wēn Dàyǎ was in charge of writing.
On Jǐchǒu,
Péi Dù was made Yōu and Zhèn Two Circuit Zhāofǔshǐ.
On Guǐsì,
Wáng Tíngcòu led Yōuzhōu troops to besiege Shēnzhōu.
6 In the ninth month,
on Yǐsì,
the Xiāngzhōu army mutinied,
killing the prefect Xíng Chǔ.
7 Tǔbō sent its Lǐbù Shàngshū Lùn Nàluó to seek an alliance.
On Gēngxū,
Liú Yuándǐng, Dàlǐ Qīng, was appointed Tǔbō Huìméngshǐ.
8 On the day Rénzǐ,
Zhū Kèróng burned and plundered Yìzhōu, Láishuǐ, Suìchéng, and Mǎnchéng.
Láishuǐ
was the territory of Qiú Xiàn in Zhuōjùn during the Hàn dynasty.
In the first year of Kāihuáng of the Suí dynasty, Fányáng was made a dào,
and Fányáng Xiàn was established here.
In the sixth year,
Fányáng was renamed Gù'ān.
It was abolished in the eighth year,
and Yǒngyáng Xiàn was established again in the tenth year.
In the eighteenth year, it was again renamed Láishuǐ.
The Rites of Zhōu official text on 'Zhífāng' states: "Its rivers are Lái and Yì."
This county was probably named after Láishuǐ.
Lái
is pronounced like 'lái'.
Suìchéng
was the territory of Běixīnchéng Xiàn during the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to the Zhōngshān Guó.
The Later Wèi dynasty established Nányíngzhōu in its territory,
and set up five commanderies and ten dū,
which were later merged into one commandery, Chānglí,
governing Yǒnglè and Xīnchāng two counties.
The Suí dynasty abolished the commandery,
and established Suìchéng Xiàn based on the former Wǔsuì Xiàn.
During the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Yìzhōu.
The Sòng dynasty established Wēilǔ Jūn in Suìchéng Xiàn.
The Jīn dynasty established Suìzhōu in the county,
and Mǎnchéng Xiàn belonged to Bǎozhōu.
9 Since the establishment of the Two-Tax System,
(See the Two-Tax System in volume 226, Démzōng, Jiànzhōng first year.)
goods have daily become lighter (less valuable),
and the taxes paid by the people are three times the initial amount.
An imperial edict ordered all officials to discuss reforming its abuses.
Hùbù Shàngshū Yáng Yúlíng believed:
"Money is used to weigh all goods
and to trade what is available for what is not.
It should circulate widely
and not be hoarded.
Now, the money taxed from the common people is stored in public coffers.
Furthermore,
during the Kāiyuán era, seventy-some furnaces cast money throughout the realm,
yielding a million annually.
The Xīnzhì records: at the end of Tiānbǎo,
there were ninety-nine furnaces in the realm,
thirty in Jiàngzhōu,
ten each in Yáng, Rùn, Xuān, È, and Wèi,
five each in Yì and Chēn,
three in Yángzhōu,
and one in Dìngzhōu.
It seems that at the end of Tiānbǎo, the number was even greater than during Kāiyuán.
The annual income was 150,000,
and it was also accumulated in the homes of merchants
and flowed into the Four Barbarian regions.
Moreover,
before Dàlì, Zīqīng, Tàiyuán, and Wèibó used lead and iron for various trades,
while Língnán used gold, silver, cinnabar, and ivory for various purposes.
Now, all use money.
If this continues,
how can money not become heavy (valuable),
and goods not become light (less valuable)?
It is now fitting that all who pay taxes should use grain and silk,
that more money should be minted, and that hoarding
and export to beyond the frontier be prohibited.
If money leaves the border passes,
it will flow into the barbarian lands."
The imperial court followed this,
and for the first time ordered that all Two-Tax payments be made in cloth, raw silk, and floss silk;
only the salt and wine taxes were to be paid in money.
10 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Bǐngyín,
Wáng Bō, the Salt and Iron Transport Commissioner and Minister of Personnel, was made Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
while retaining his former posts.
As a chancellor, Bō
focused solely on flattery and ingratiation,
never speaking of the safety or danger of the state.
11 Péi Dù was appointed Zhènzhōu Four-Front Field Commander-in-Chief for Pacification.
Du Shúliáng, a General of the Left Palace Guard,
advanced by skillfully serving the powerful and favored.
At that time, the military power of Yōu and Zhèn was flourishing,
and the armies of other circuits dared not advance.
The emperor desired quick success,
and the eunuchs recommended Shúliáng,
appointing him Jiézèdùshǐ of Shēnzhōu and other field camps.
This laid the groundwork for Du Shúliáng's defeat.
12 On the day Guǐyǒu,
the emperor ordered the chancellors and seventeen other high officials to meet with Nèluó of Tǔbō for a covenant west of the city.
Liú Yuándǐng was sent with Nèluó into Tǔbō,
to likewise make a covenant with their chief minister and others.
The Tǔbō kingdom had a Great Minister and a Vice Minister;
historians also recorded them as chancellors.
13 On the day Yǐhài,
Wáng Zhìxīng, the Governor of Yízhōu, was appointed Deputy Military Commissioner of Wǔníng.
Previously,
deputy commissioners were all civil officials.
The emperor, hearing that Zhìxīng possessed courage and strategy,
wished to employ him in Héběi,
and thus favored him with this appointment.
This laid the groundwork for Wáng Zhìxīng's expulsion of his commander, Cuī Yàn.
14 On the day Dīngchǒu,
Péi Dù personally led troops out of the old pass of Chéngtiān Jūn to suppress Wáng Tíngcòu.
Chéngtiān Jūn should be within the borders of Liáozhōu.
The old pass
is Nángzǐguān.
The Sòng dynasty abolished Liáozhōu,
and made Píngchéng and Héshùn two counties into a garrison (zhèn);
Píngdìng Jūn was established from Lèpíng and Píngdìng two counties of Bìngzhōu,
and the two garrisons belonged to it;
Chéngtiān Jūn was made a stronghold (zhài),
belonging to Píngdìng Xiàn.
Píngdìng
was Guǎngyáng Xiàn of the Táng dynasty.
According to Shěn Cúnzhōng's Bǐtán: there are two routes from Zhènzhōu to Hédōng: the Fēihú Route is west of Dàmàoshān.
Dàmàoshān
is the peak of Héngshān.
It goes north from Yínyě Zhài, passes Dàomǎguān, then enters between the two strongholds of Píngxíng and Méihuí via Shíménzǐ and Lìngshuǐ Pù, reaching Dàizhōu.
Since the Shí Jìn ceded territory to the Qìdān,
with Dàmàoshān as the watershed boundary,
this route was no longer passable.
Only the route from Běizhài westward to Chéngtiān Guān
could reach Hédōng,
but the road was extremely steep and narrow.
Sòng Bái said: Chéngtiān Jūn
is on the eastern edge of Tàiyuán,
and it is the key strategic point for the Tǔmén Route.
15 Zhū Kèróng sent troops to raid Wèizhōu.
Guīzhōu is two hundred and forty li southwest of Wèizhōu.
Wèi
is pronounced 'yúwù'.
16 On the day Wùyín,
Wáng Tíngcòu sent troops to raid Wèi
zhōu.
17 On the day Jǐmǎo,
Liǔ Gōngjì, the Governor of Yìzhōu, defeated the Yōuzhōu army at Báishílǐng,
killing over a thousand men.
18 On the day Gēngchén,
Wū Chóngyìn, the Military Commissioner of Hénghǎi Jūn, reported defeating the Chéngdé army at Ráoyáng.
19 On the day Xīnsì,
Tián Bù, the Military Commissioner of Wèibó, led his entire army of thirty thousand men to suppress Wáng Tíngcòu,
encamping south of Nángōng,
and capturing two of their strongholds.
20 Hànlín Xuéshì Yuán Zhěn (翰林學士元稹) and Zhī Shūmì Wèi Hóngjiǎn (知樞密魏弘簡) were deeply intertwined.
[Yuán Zhěn] sought to become prime minister,
and from this, he gained the emperor's favor,
who consulted him on every matter.
Yuán Zhěn (元稹) associated with powerful eunuchs,
losing his integrity.
This was the fault of Xiànzōng (憲宗).
Zhěn (稹),
pronounced zhǐ rěn.
Dù (度) merely believed that these prominent and respected elders,
fearing that they might again achieve great merit and be given important positions,
would hinder his own advancement.
Therefore, many of the military strategies Dù (度) proposed
were obstructed and ruined by Hóngjiǎn (弘簡) from within.
Dù (度) then submitted a memorial vehemently exposing their factional corruption and treachery,
stating:
"Rebellious scoundrels stir up trouble,
startling Shāndōng (山東);
'rebellious scoundrels'
refers to Wáng Tíngcòu (王庭湊) and others.
They disrupt and ruin national governance.
'Treacherous ministers'
refers to Yuán Zhěn (元稹) and others.
Náo (撓),
pronounced nú jiào.
Bài (敗),
pronounced bǔ mài,
meaning 'to bend'.
It is first appropriate to cleanse the court.
Why?
Because troubles have their scales,
and matters for discussion have their priorities.
The rebels of Héshuò (河朔) only disturb Shāndōng (山東);
but the treacherous ministers in the imperial court
will surely bring chaos to the whole empire.
Therefore, the trouble in Héshuò (河朔) is minor,
while the trouble in the imperial court is great.
The minor trouble, your subject and the generals will surely be able to eliminate;
but the great trouble, unless Your Majesty awakens and makes a decisive judgment, cannot be removed.
Now, among all civil and military officials,
inside and outside, of all ranks,
there is none with a conscience who is not indignant.
Fèn (憤),
meaning 'vexation'.
Fèn (忿),
meaning 'anger'.
It is only because their patronage is so deep
that no one dares to confront them,
fearing that calamity will strike before their actions are completed,
not for the sake of the nation's plan,
but for their own well-being.
Since the war began,
the memorials and petitions submitted by your subject
have all been urgent and critical;
but the imperial edicts received
have often been contradictory.
While your subject deeply appreciates Your Majesty's trust,
the instances of suppression and harm inflicted by treacherous ministers are not few.
Your subject has never had animosity or suspicion with these fawning flatterers;
it is precisely because your subject previously requested to travel quickly to the capital
to personally discuss military affairs,
that the treacherous ministers feared and dreaded it most,
afraid that your subject would expose their faults,
and they used every means to stop your subject.
Your subject also requested to advance simultaneously with all the armies,
to attack and suppress as circumstances permitted,
but the treacherous ministers, fearing that your subject might achieve success,
deliberately created obstacles,
delaying for days and hours.
Both advancement and retreat are subjected to constraint.
Jī (羈),
a horse's halter.
Qiān (牽),
an ox's rope.
This illustrates how horses and oxen are always controlled by humans.
They only wish to make your subject lose his position,
to make your subject achieve nothing,
then the order and chaos of the empire,
and the victory or defeat in Shāndōng (山東),
are all disregarded.
For a subject serving his sovereign,
it has come to this!
If the treacherous ministers in the court are all removed,
then the rebels of Héshuò (河朔) will pacify themselves without being attacked;
but if the treacherous ministers in the court remain,
then even if the rebels are pacified, it will be of no benefit.
If Your Majesty perhaps does not believe your subject's words,
I beg you to release your subject's memorial,
and have all officials convene to discuss it.
If they do not accept responsibility,
your subject is willing to suffer punishment."
The memorial was submitted three times.
Although the emperor was displeased,
considering Dù (度) a great minister,
he had no choice.
On the day Guǐwèi (癸未),
he appointed Hóngjiǎn (弘簡) as Gōngjiànkù Shǐ (弓箭庫使)
and Zhěn (稹) as Gōngbù Shìláng (工部侍郎).
Although Zhěn (稹) was removed from the Hànlín Academy,
his favor remained as before.
Zhěn (稹) served as prime minister, laying the groundwork for Fāng (方) in this matter.
21 Sùzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Zhíchén (宿州刺史李直臣) was condemned to death for corruption.
Eunuchs, having received his bribe,
pleaded on his behalf.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Niú Sēngrú (御史中丞牛僧孺) firmly insisted on his execution.
The emperor said:
"Zhíchén (直臣) is talented,
it's a pity!"
Sēngrú (僧孺) replied:
"Those who are untalented
have no greater desire than to be warmly clothed and well-fed to provide for their families;
what is there to worry about?
Laws are established
precisely to restrain talented individuals.
Ān Lùshān (安祿山) and Zhū Cǐ (朱泚) were both more talented than others,
and the law could not restrain them."
The emperor followed his advice.
22 Hénghǎi Jiédùshǐ Wū Chóngyìn (橫海節度使烏重胤) was about to lead his entire army to relieve Shēnzhōu (深州).
At that time, Wáng Tíngcòu (王庭湊) was besieging Niú Yuányì (牛元翼) in Shēnzhōu (深州).
Hénghǎi (橫海) was east of Zhènzhōu (鎮州) and south of Yōuzhōu (幽州).
Knowing that the rebels could not yet be defeated,
he held his troops and watched for an opportune moment.
The emperor was angered,
appointed Dù Shúliáng (杜叔良) as Hénghǎi Jiédùshǐ (橫海節度使),
and transferred Chóngyìn (重胤) to be Shānnán Xīdào Jiédùshǐ (山南西道節度使).
23 Língwǔ Jiédùshǐ Lǐ Jìnchéng (靈武節度使李進誠) reported defeating three thousand Tubó (吐蕃) cavalry below Dàshíshān (大石山).
On the 24th day of the 11th month,
Xīnyǒu,
Xuē Píng, Jìedùshǐ of Zīqīng, reported that the vanguard general Mǎ Tíngyín had rebelled
and was executed.
At that time, the armies of Yōu and Zhèn were attacking Dìzhōu.
Píng dispatched his grand general Lǐ Shūzuǒ to lead troops to relieve it.
Wáng Jì, the Cìshǐ, provided meager supplies and provisions,
which angered the soldiers.
They scattered during the night,
proclaiming Tíngyín as their leader.
As they marched, they gathered more troops, reaching over 7,000 men,
and directly approached Qīngzhōu.
The city had few soldiers
and could not resist.
Píng completely emptied the government treasury and his personal wealth to recruit soldiers,
obtaining 2,000 elite troops.
They met the rebels in battle
and utterly defeated them,
beheading Tíngyín.
Several thousand of his followers died.
Kǎoyì states: Hénánjì records:
"When the Duke of Hánguó was governor of Qīngzhōu,
in the first year of Chángqìng,
an imperial edict summoned troops from several circuits
to punish Chángshān and Pínglú.
Over 2,000 men were dispatched to garrison Wúdì.
Just as they were about to turn back,
a队长 (duìzhǎng) of the Ministry of War stationed in Qīngzhōu, Mǎ Shìduān,
killed his superior,
and then led his troops.
Through coercion and recruitment,
by the time they reached Bóchāng,
they numbered over 10,000 men.
They had already planned to enter Qīngzhōu.
When the Duke of Hán heard of this,
he immediately deliberated on an extermination campaign.
The grand generals advised: 'These rebels are but fierce and stubborn soldiers,
without far-reaching plans.
We can deceive them by saying that the Shàngshū has already gone to the imperial court,
and the generals and officers of the three armies are all eagerly awaiting the Liúhòu.
The rebels will surely believe this,
relax their guard,
and we can ambush and capture them.'
The Duke of Hán greatly approved of this strategy.
Consequently, the rebels no longer harbored any doubts or suspicions.
The next day,
they led their troops and came.
Three sides of troops were ambushed about thirty *lǐ* north of the city.
The rebel forces indeed fell into our encirclement.
With one wave of the signal flag,
infantry and cavalry converged like clouds.
The rebel forces were startled and confused,
not knowing what to do,
and all surrendered.
They were ordered to throw down their spears and shed their armor,
and were herded into Qīngzhōu.
A false order was given for them to return home,
promising that they would not be killed.
Their numbers were then recorded,
clear registers were established.
Three thousand here, two thousand there,
each group stationed in one place.
Frosty blades were unleashed simultaneously,
and the ant-like multitude melted away.
Over 20,000 people
shared the same fate in one day.
The rebel leader Mǎ Shìduān broke through the encirclement and fled,
but was soon pursued and captured at Zōupíng Dùkǒu.
He was dismembered north of the city.
The details of the situation were then reported to the emperor,
and he was subsequently appointed Zuǒ Púyè."
According to the Shílù, it is written as
"Mǎ Tíngyín."
The old biographies write
"Mǎ Láng'er."
Hénánjì writes

he had a fine horse.
When the emperor was Crown Prince,
he sent his attendants to subtly ask for it,
but Tīng, whose duty it was to command the imperial guard,
dared not offer it.
When the position of commander in Hédōng became vacant,
the emperor said:
"Lǐ Tīng did not give me his horse,

And so, he was appointed.
6 Liú Chéngxié, the Supervisor of the Army of Zhāoyì, relied on imperial favor.
When Xiànzōng collapsed,
Liú Chéngxié had been instrumental in establishing Mùzōng,
hence he relied on imperial favor.
He repeatedly insulted Wù in front of the multitude,
and also allowed his subordinates to violate the law.
He secretly conspired with Zhāng Wèn, the Administrator of Cízhōu, to seize Wù and send him to the capital,
replacing him with Wèn.
Wù learned of this
and incited his soldiers to mutiny,
killing Wèn.
They surrounded Chéngxié,
intending to kill him.
His staff officer, Jiǎ Zhíyán, entered
and admonished Wù, saying:
“What you are doing is like this,
do you wish to emulate Sīkōng Lǐ?
In this army, how can it be known that there are none like you?
Lǐ Shīdào was Sīkōng.
Jiǎ Zhíyán was an old subordinate,
hence he still referred to his official title.
He meant Lǐ Shīdào was rebellious.
Liú Wù turned his forces against Shīdào and obtained his credentials.
Now Wù is doing what Shīdào did,
so in the Zhāoyì army, there will also be those who will do what Wù did and seize credentials.
Would you not be laughed at in the underworld?!”
Wù then apologized to Zhíyán
and saved Chéngxié,
imprisoning him in the government office.
A textual critique states: The Veritable Records say:
“Supervisor Liú Chéngxié somewhat relied on imperial favor to encroach upon authority.
He once publicly insulted Wù
and also allowed his subordinates to violate the law.
Wù could not tolerate it.
Another day,
an imperial envoy arrived.
Chéngxié hosted a banquet for him
and invited Wù.
Wù wanted to go.
His左右 (assistants) all said: ‘If you go, you will surely be humiliated by him.’
The army then mutinied.
Wù did not stop them,
and they seized Chéngxié,
killed his two attendants,
and intended to harm Chéngxié as well.
Wù saved him
and he was spared.”
The New Biography of Liú Wù says:
“Chéngxié conspired with the commander Zhāng Wèn to seize Wù and send him to the capital,
to replace him as Jiedúshǐ.
Wù learned of this
and surrounded the Supervisor with troops,
killing a minor official.
His subordinate Jiǎ Zhíyán questioned and rebuked Wù.
Wù immediately waved his troops back,
hid Chéngxié,
and imprisoned him.”
In the New Biography of Zhíyán,
“Zhāng Wèn”
is written as
“Zhāng Wèn.”
Dù Mù’s memorial to Sītú Lǐ also says:
“His army was in great chaos,
killing Zhāng Wèn, the Administrator of Cízhōu.”
It also says:
“Since Wèn had plotted with Chéngxié to kill Wù,

It is likely that the soldiers surrounding Chéngxié was certainly at Wù’s behest,

he claimed it was the action of the multitude of soldiers.
Now, Chéngxié’s name follows the Veritable Records,

Memorials piled up,

8 Wáng Zhìxìng, the Deputy Jiedúshǐ of Wǔníng, led three thousand elite soldiers from the army to suppress Yōu and Zhèn.
His Jiedúshǐ, Cuī Qún, was wary of him

The matter had not yet been reported,

Zhìxìng led his troops into the territory ahead of schedule.
Qún was afraid

he led his troops straight in.

Zhìxìng killed more than ten people who were not with him

There was a Salt and Iron Office at Yǒngqiáo.
Referring to the tribute ships of various circuits in the Biànhé River.
He took two-thirds of everything.
Historians say that in the Tang dynasty, those below were arrogant to those above,
and there was no longer any discipline.

Zhū Kèróng (朱克融), the Military Commissioner of Yōuzhōu (幽州), presented ten thousand horses
and one hundred thousand sheep,
and memorialized that he first requested their value to be used as rewards.
The historian commented that Zhū Kèróng (朱克róng) toyed with the imperial court.
26. The Three Judicial Offices investigated the matter of Yú Fāng (于方) assassinating Péi Dù (裴度),
but found no evidence.
In the sixth month,
on the *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) day,
Dù (度) and Yuán Zhěn (元稹) were both dismissed from chancellorship.
Dù (度) became the Right Executive,
and Zhěn (稹) became the Prefect of Tóngzhōu (同州).
Lǐ Féngjí (李逢吉), the Minister of War, was appointed as Palace Gentleman-in-Waiting and Concurrent Chancellor.
The Dǎngxiàng ravaged Língzhōu and Wèiběi,
plundering official horses.
They had previously ravaged Língzhōu,
and subsequently reached Wèiběi.
The remonstrating officials submitted a memorial, saying:
"Péi Dù is innocent,
and should not be dismissed from his chancellorship.
Yuán Zhěn and Yú Fāng conspired wickedly,
and their punishment is too light."
The Emperor had no choice but to agree.
On the day Rénshēn,
Zhěn's appointment as Changchúngōng Envoy was revoked.
Changchúngōng was in Tóngzhōu.
Yuán Zhěn had been appointed concurrently as an envoy while serving as an external governor;
now this appointment was revoked.
The Tubófàn raided Língwǔ.
On the day Gēngchén,
Yánzhōu reported that Bábá Wànchéng, the Dǎngxiàng military commissioner, requested to surrender.
On the day Rénwǔ,
the Tubófàn raided Yánzhōu.
On the day Wùzǐ,
the Jīnglüè Envoy of Yōngguǎn was reinstated.
Originally,
Zhāng Hóngjìng was the Xuānwǔ Military Governor.
(Hóngjìng succeeded Hán Hóng; see Volume 14 of Xiànzōng, Yuánhé era).
The treasury was depleted.
Lǐ Yuàn succeeded him.
His nature was extravagant.
His rewards and commendations were even less generous than during Hóngjìng's time,
and he also enforced harsh laws and punishments,
which displeased the soldiers.
Yuàn appointed his wife's younger brother, Dòu Yuán, to command the palace guards.
Yuán was arrogant and greedy;
the army detested him.
The牙將 Yájiàng Lǐ Chénzé and others revolted.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the night of Rénchén,
they beheaded Yuán in his tent,
then shouted loudly,
and the entire commandery responded.
Yuàn and one son scaled the city wall and fled to Zhèngzhōu.
(Biànzhōu is 150 *lǐ* west of Zhèngzhōu).
They acclaimed the 都押牙 Dūyāyá Lǐ Yà as Acting Governor.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
Sòngwáng Jié passed away.
Jié was
a son of Shùnzōng.
On the day Wùxū,
the Xuānwǔ Supervising Censor reported a military mutiny.
On the day Gēngzǐ,
Lǐ Yà personally reported that he had provisionally taken charge as Acting Governor.
On the day Yǐsì,
an imperial edict commanded officials of the Three Departments and the Chancellors to deliberate on the affairs of Biànzhōu.
(Officials of the Three Departments refers to those from *yí*, *bǔ*, *shèrén*, *chéng*, *láng* and above).
(The Emperor) granted Lǐ Yà a *jié* (credentials of authority).
Lǐ Féngjí said:
"The matters in Héběi
were certainly unavoidable.
If we now abandon Biànzhōu as well,
then all lands south of the Jiāng and Huái rivers will no longer belong to the state."
Dù Yuányǐng and Zhāng Píngshū argued, saying:
"How can we begrudge a few *chǐ* of *jié*
and not care for the deaths of a whole region!"
The deliberation was undecided.
Coincidentally, the three prefectures of Sòng, Bó, and Yǐng
each submitted a memorial,
requesting a separate commander to be appointed.
(The three prefectures were all under Xuānwǔ's jurisdiction).
(The Emperor) deemed Féngjí's proposal correct,
and dispatched a palace envoy to the three prefectures to offer solace.
Féngjí then requested
"to summon Yà to court as a general,
and appoint Hán Chōng, the Yìchéng Military Governor, to govern Xuānwǔ.
Chōng,
Hóng's younger brother,
has always been lenient and kind, and has won the hearts of the people."
(Hán Hóng governed Xuānwǔ for over twenty years;
the generals and soldiers were devoted to him.
His younger brother also gained popular support through leniency and kindness.
Therefore, Féngjí requested that he replace Yà).
"Then order the armies of Xú and Xǔ to attack his left and right, and the Húar army to press from the north."
(The Xú commander was
Wáng Zhìxīng;
the Xǔ commander was
Lǐ Guāngyán).
The Emperor agreed to all of it.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
Lǐ Yuàn was demoted to Prefect of Suízhōu.
(Suízhōu was ancient Suíguó,
a county in Hàn,
a commandery south of the Jiāng in the Eastern Jìn,
and Suízhōu was established in the Western Wèi.
It is 1388 *lǐ* southeast of the capital).
Lǐ Yà was summoned to be Ròujīnwú General,
but Yà did not obey the imperial edict.
Gāo Chéngjiǎn, the Prefect of Sòngzhōu, executed Yà's envoy.
Yà dispatched two thousand soldiers to attack him,
seizing Nínglíng and Xiāngyì.
(Sòngzhōu is 285 *lǐ* west of Biànzhōu.
Nínglíng is 45 *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
Xiāngyì is slightly north of west of the prefecture).
The rebels had already captured the southern city,
but Chéngjiǎn held the two northern cities
and fought more than ten battles with the rebels.
On the day Guǐchǒu,
Lǐ Guāngyán, the Zhōngwǔ Military Governor, led twenty-five thousand soldiers to suppress Lǐ Yà,
stationing them at Wèishì.
(Wèishì is southwest of Biànzhōu and
northeast of Xǔzhōu).
He did not wait for an imperial edict,
but immediately dispatched troops to attack him.
Yà sent three thousand soldiers to attack Sòngzhōu;
just as they reached the city walls,
on the day Bǐngchén,
Huá counterattacked
and defeated them.
On the day Dīngsì,
Lǐ Guāngyán defeated the Xuānwǔ army at Wèishì,
killing and capturing over two thousand people.
In the eighth month,
on the day Xīnyǒu,
Liú Yuándǐng, the Dàlǐ Qīng, returned from Tubófàn.
(Yuándǐng had been an envoy to Tubófàn last year).
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Hán Chōng entered the territory of Biàn,
and encamped at Qiāntǎ.
(Qiāntǎ should be north of Biànzhōu).
He beheaded over a thousand people,
and the rest of the forces fled.
On the day Rénshēn,
Hán Chōng defeated the Xuānwǔ army at Guōqiáo.
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Xiángfú County in Biànzhōu has Guōqiáo Town).
He advanced his army to Wànshèng.
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Zhōngmóu County in Biànzhōu has Wànshèng Town).
Initially,
after Lǐ Yà became Acting Governor,
he made Lǐ Zhì, the Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ, his trusted confidant.
When Yà was appointed general
but did not obey the imperial edict,
Zhì repeatedly remonstrated but was not heeded.
Coincidentally, Yà developed a carbuncle on his head,
and sent Lǐ Chénzé and others to lead troops to resist Lǐ Guāngyán at Wèishì.
Soon after, imperial armies gathered from all four directions,
and Yà's troops were repeatedly defeated.
Yà's illness worsened,
and he entrusted all military affairs to Lǐ Zhì,
remaining at home.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Zhì and the Supervising Censor Yáo Wénshòu captured Yà
and killed him.
They forged Yà's dispatch
to recall Chénzé and others.
When they arrived,
they were all beheaded.
They seized Yà's four sons and sent them to the capital.
Before Hán Chōng arrived,
Zhì provisionally managed military affairs.
At that time, there were three thousand elite guards,
who were given daily rations of wine and food,
which the resources could not sustain.
Zhì said:
"If Duke Hán, upon his arrival, dismisses them,
then public sentiment will be greatly alienated!
We cannot leave this burden for our commander."
He immediately ordered the cessation of rations and then welcomed Chōng.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Chōng entered Biàn.
On the day Guǐwèi,
Hán Chōng was solely appointed Xuānwǔ Military Governor,
Cáo Huá was appointed Yìchéng Military Governor,
Gāo Chéngjiǎn was appointed Military Governor of Yǎn, Hǎi, Yí, and Mì,
Lǐ Guāngyán was promoted to 겸시중 jiān Shìzhōng (concurrently Grand Mentor),
and Lǐ Zhì was appointed Ròujīnwú General.
After Hán Chōng assumed office,
public sentiment largely stabilized.
He secretly registered over a thousand individuals in the army who had committed evil deeds.
One morning,
he expelled them all, along with their parents, wives, and children,
declaring:
"Anyone who dares to remain within the borders shall be executed."
Consequently, military administration was greatly rectified.
(To eliminate the chaos and remove its root,
then chaos will have no way to arise).
38 In the ninth month,
on the day Wùzǐ,
Dòu Yìzhí (竇易直) of Jīngzhào, the Observer of Zhèxī,
reported that his grand general Wáng Guóqīng (王國清) had rebelled,
and was executed.
Originally,
Yìzhí, hearing of the disturbances in Biànzhōu, was afraid,
and wanted to distribute gold and silk to reward the soldiers.
Someone said,
"To reward them without a clear reason
might only increase suspicion."
So he stopped.
But externally, there were already those who knew about it,
which is why Guóqīng rebelled.
Yìzhí attacked and captured him,
and also killed over two hundred of his followers.
The "Kǎo Yì" (考異) says: The old biography of Yìzhí states:
"At that time, there was a drought in Jiāng-Huái (江、淮),
and the water level was low.
The Transfer and Transport Commissioner's accumulated money and silk
could not be transported by canal.
Guóqīng pointed to this as a reward,
inciting and instigating the provincial soldiers to plan a rebellion.
Before the event, someone reported it,
so Guóqīng was arrested and put in prison.
Thousands of his followers shouted loudly,
broke into the prison, seized Guóqīng, and brought him out.
They then intended to plunder extensively.
Yìzhí ascended a tower and said to his generals and officers: 'Whoever can execute the rebels,
for each one captured,
will be rewarded ten million [cash].'
The multitude rejoiced,
turned their weapons against the rebel faction,
captured Guóqīng and over three hundred others,
and all were beheaded."
Now we follow the Veritable Records.
39 Wáng Jì (王稷), the Prefect of Dézhōu,
inherited his father Wáng È's (王鍔) remaining wealth,
and his family was rich and prosperous.
Lǐ Jǐnglüè (李景略), the Jìedùshǐ of Hénghǎi, coveted his wealth.
Lǐ Jǐnglüè
should be Lǐ Quánlüè (李全略).
He secretly ordered his soldiers to kill Jì,
slaughter his family,
and take his daughter as a concubine,
reporting it as a military rebellion.
An elephant has tusks but is burned for its body;
this is due to wealth.
Wáng È barely escaped with his life, but calamity befell his son.
This is why a junzǐ knows the difficulty of holding onto wealth!
40 When the court was suppressing Lǐ Sù (李㝏),
it sent Wèi Wénkè (韋文恪), the Director of the Ministry of Gates, to comfort Wèibó.
Shǐ Xiànchéng (史憲誠) submitted a memorial requesting Lǐ Sù be granted the banner and staff of a Jìedùshǐ.
He also built a "horse-head" (馬頭) at Líyáng,
to create a posture for crossing the river.
Along the river bank, earth was piled and trees planted on both sides leading to the water's edge,
to facilitate troops and horses entering boats;
this was called a "horse-head."
His manner and rites were arrogant and disrespectful.
But when he heard of Lǐ Sù's death,
his manner and rites immediately became respectful,
saying:
"Xiànchéng,
a Hu (胡) barbarian,
is like a dog;
though it may be beaten,
it will never leave its master."
"Chuí" (捶),
read as bǐ ruǐ fān.
read as lì zhì fān.
41 In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
the Empress Dowager visited Huáqīng Gōng (華清宮).
On the day Xīnwèi,
the Emperor himself went via the covered walkway to Huáqīng Gōng,
and then hunted at Líshān (驪山),
returning to the palace that very day.
The Empress Dowager returned several days later.
42 On the day Bǐngzǐ,
the Prince of Jí, Xiāng (緗), died.
Xiāng
was a son of Shùnzōng.
43 On the day Gēngchén,
the Emperor played polo with eunuchs in the palace.
A eunuch fell from his horse,
which startled the Emperor,
who then contracted a wind-illness,
unable to walk.
From then on, people did not hear of the Emperor's daily activities.
The Chancellors repeatedly requested an audience,
but received no reply.
Péi Dù (裴度) submitted three memorials requesting the establishment of an heir apparent,
and also requested an audience.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Xīnmǎo,
the Emperor met his ministers at Zǐchén Diàn (紫宸殿),
seated on a large "rope bed" (繩牀).
Chéng Dàchāng (程大昌) in "Yǎn Fánlù" (演繁露) says: The "folding bed" (交牀) of today,
its design originally came from the barbarians,
and was first called a "Hu bed" (胡牀).
The Suí dynasty, due to a prophecy mentioning "Hu,"
changed its name to "folding bed."
Emperor Mùzōng (穆宗) of Táng met his ministers at Zǐchén Diàn on a large rope bed,
so it was again called a "rope bed."
I (the annotator) observe that "folding beds" and "rope beds"
are still found in people's homes today,
but they are two different things.
A "folding bed" has legs that cross like an "X" made of wood.
Horizontal pieces of wood are placed both in front and behind the legs,
flattening its base,
allowing it to sit steadily on the ground.
At the upper ends of the legs,
horizontal pieces of wood are also placed in front and behind, flat on top.
These horizontal pieces have holes through which ropes are threaded,
making it possible to sit on.
The crossing point of the legs is also made round,
penetrated by iron,
so it can be folded and carried,
or opened for sitting.
Because its legs cross,
it is called a "folding bed."
A "rope bed"
is made of planks.
When a person sits on it,
its width in front can accommodate the knees,
it has a backrest behind,
and armrests on the sides,
where one can rest their arms.
Its four legs rest on the ground.
Only over ten eunuchs attended by his side,
and people's minds were somewhat eased.
Lǐ Féngjí (李逢吉) stepped forward and said:
"Prince Jǐng (景王) is already grown;
I request he be established as heir apparent."
Péi Dù requested an immediate imperial edict,
to fulfill the expectations of all under heaven.
Soon,
officials from both secretariats also successively requested the establishment of an heir apparent.
On the day Guǐsì,
an edict was issued establishing Prince Jǐng, Zhàn (湛), as the Crown Prince.
The "Kǎo Yì" says: Liú Kē's (劉軻) "Niú Yáng Rìlì" (牛羊日曆) states:
"When Emperor Mùzōng's illness did not improve,
the Chancellors debated establishing Emperor Jìngzōng (敬宗) as the Crown Prince.
At that time, Niú Sēngrú (牛僧孺) alone harbored a different plan,
wishing to establish one of the other princes.
Sēngrú then openly declared in court: 'Liáng Shǒuqīan (梁守謙) and Wáng Shǒuchéng (王守澄) will be unfavorable to His Majesty.'
He also sent Yáng Yúqīng (楊虞卿) and Hàn Gōng (漢公) and their ilk to declare publicly: 'Wáng Shǒuchéng intends to plot a deposition and establishment.'
He also ordered his followers to put up posters on walls along streets and gates,
and to carve white characters on the ground beside roads or among the grass in the imperial gardens wherever Emperor Mùzōng had traveled,
hoping to instigate great chaos;
his malevolence was thus."
This comes from partisan remarks
and is not to be trusted.
44 In this year,
the Xuānmíng Lì (宣明曆) calendar was first put into use.
When Emperor Xiànzōng (憲宗) ascended the throne,
Xú Áng (徐昂) of the Bureau of Astronomy presented a new calendar, saying:
"Observations began in the second year of Yuánhé,
but there was no 'bùzhāng' (蔀章) calculation.
As for the predictions of 'fāliǎn qǐbì' (發斂啟閉),
the old methods were followed,
and measurements did not match."
When the Emperor ascended,
believing that with the succession of generations,
a calendar reform was necessary,
he issued an edict to the court astronomers to revise and compile the calendar,
naming it Xuānmíng.
Its calculations for qi (氣) and suò (朔), fāliǎn (發斂), and the positions of the sun and moon
all followed the old techniques of "Dàyǎn" (大衍),
while the gǔilòu (晷漏) and jiāohùi (交會)
were slightly increased or decreased.
Punctuation by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖), checked by Nìe Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
compiled by imperial command.
Hòu Xué Tiāntái (後學天台)
Chángqìng (長慶) 3rd Year
(Guǐmǎo, 823)
1 Spring,
first month,
on the day Guǐwèi,
money was bestowed upon the two army commanders and below.
Second month,
on the day Xīnmǎo,
cotton, silk, and silver vessels were bestowed upon the commanders and military commissioners, each according to their rank.
"Mián" (綿) [cotton]
should be
"jǐn" (錦) [brocade].
[Zhāng (章): The twelve-line edition correctly writes
"jǐn" (錦).]
2 Hùbù Shìláng Niú Sēngrú
had long been highly favored by the emperor.
Initially,
Hán Hóng’s son, Yòuxiāowèi Jiāngjūn Gōngwǔ, plotted for his father
to use wealth to connect with officials both inside and outside the court.
After Gōngwǔ died,
Hóng subsequently passed away.
His young grandson Shàozōng succeeded him.
A slave in charge of the treasury and a clerk brought a lawsuit to the Yùshǐ Fǔ (Censorate).
The emperor pitied them
and personally reviewed all of Hóng’s property registers.
Among all those in power, both inside and outside the court,
"those in power"
refers to officials, both inside and outside the court, who held actual authority.
Only in Zhū Jù’s small script was it written:
"On a certain date,
sent ten million cash to Hùbù Niú Shìláng,
but it was not accepted."
The emperor was greatly pleased,
and showed it to his attendants, saying:
"Indeed,
I have not erred in knowing people!"
In the third month,
on the day Rénxū,
Sēngrú was made Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
At this time, Sēngrú and Lǐ Déyù both had hopes of entering the premiership.
Déyù was sent out as Zhèxī Guānchásǐ,
and was not promoted for eight years.
By Emperor Wénzōng’s Dàhé third year,
through Péi Dù’s recommendation,
Lǐ Déyù was finally summoned from Zhèxī,
but was again obstructed by Lǐ Zōngmǐn,
and sent out to be the commander of Huá.
Sēngrú was brought in as prime minister.
From this, the enmity between Niú and Lǐ deepened even further.
Kǎoyì (Discussions on Variants) says: The old biography of Déyù says:
"Initially,
Lǐ Féngjí returned to court from Xiāngyáng.
He secretly bribed petty people
to fabricate accusations against Yú Fāng.
In the eighth month,
Yuán Zhěn and Péi Dù were both dismissed.
Féngjí replaced Péi Dù as prime minister.
Once he gained power,
he was eager to seek revenge.
At that time, Déyù and Sēngrú both had hopes of becoming prime minister.
Féngjí wanted to bring in Sēngrú,
fearing that Shēn and Déyù would thwart him within the court.
In the ninth month,
Déyù was sent out to Zhèxī,
and soon after, Sēngrú was brought in as Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
From this, their mutual enmity deepened even further."
Perhaps Déyù held suspicion and resentment towards Féngjí for this reason,
but it was not necessarily all due to Féngjí's intention!
3 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Jiǎwǔ,
Ānnán reported that the Láoluó of Lùzhōu were attacking and plundering prefectures and counties.
In Wǔdé first year, the prefectures of Ānhǎi and Yùshān in Níngyuè Commandery were established as Yùshān Zhōu.
In Zhēngguān first year,
the prefecture was abolished,
belonging to Qīnzhōu.
In Emperor Gāozōng’s Shàngyuán second year,
Lùzhōu was re-established,
extending three hundred *lǐ* east to the border of Liánzhōu.
4 On the day Bǐngshēn,
money was bestowed upon the Gōngfèngguān of Xuānhuīyuàn:
those in purple robes received one hundred and twenty *mín*,
down to the Chéngzhǐ, each received a different amount.
After the mid-Tang period,
the Xuānhuīyuàn was established,
with eunuchs in charge of it.
For grand court ceremonies and birthday celebrations for the emperor,
the Xuānhuīshǐ would announce the imperial response.
Xú Dù’s Què Sǎo Biān says:
"The Xuānhuīshǐ
was originally an official position for eunuchs in the Tang dynasty,
so their responsibilities were all minor matters.
In our current dynasty, scholars are used instead.
Their rank is second only to the two prime ministerial departments.
There are Southern and Northern Bureaus;
the Southern Bureau has even superior qualifications and prestige compared to the Northern Bureau.
However, their duties mostly follow the old Tang system.
Bestowing new fire to the imperial household,
and the registers of various departmental heads down to Chóngbān, Nèishì, Gōngfèng, various departmental artisans, and soldiers,
as well as promotions, temporary leave, and interrogations for those below the three *bān* ranks,
spring and autumn grand banquets and imperial birthday celebrations,
welcoming and receiving imperial favors for *jiédu* commanders,
displaying lanterns on the Lantern Festival,
seasonal sacrifices,
Khitan tributes,
inner court scholars attending the emperor,
overseeing their provisions,
tribute items from inside and outside the palace,
annual clothing and belts for court entertainers,
imperial outings to the suburbs, court audiences with the sacred image,
bestowing feasts,
national mourning days,
separate household registers and property division for those below departmental heads,
and leave for various departmental artisans, and so on."
Now observing what Mùzōng bestowed,
it is clear that the officials of the Xuānhuīyuàn were numerous.
5 Initially,
Zhèng Zhù of Yìchéng,
was short,
looked downwards,
yet was cunning, treacherous, flattering,
and skilled at discerning people's intentions.
Yìchéng Xiàn
belonged to Jiàngzhōu.
It was originally the territory of Hàn Jiàng Xiàn.
During the Suí dynasty, it was renamed Yìchéng Xiàn,
named after the ancient Yìchéng city in the county.
Chuǎi,
pronounced *chū wěi fān*.
He was extremely poor and itinerant.
He once sought to gain favor with a *yájiàng* in Xúzhōu through his medical skills.
The *yájiàng* was pleased with him
and recommended him to Jiédu Shǐ Lǐ Suò.
Suò found his medicines quite effective
and consequently favored him greatly,
appointing him as *Yátuī*.
*Yátuī*
was below the *Jiédù tuīguān*.
He arbitrarily wielded power and authority,
which troubled the military governor's staff.
Jiānjūn Wáng Shǒuchéng informed Suò of the public sentiment
and requested his removal.
Suò said:
"Although Zhù is like this,
he is a man of extraordinary talent.
General, please try to speak with him.
At that time, many palace eunuchs were promoted to various *wèi jiāngjūn* positions,
known as *nèi jiāngjūn*.
It is not too late to remove him."
So, Zhù was sent to pay respects to Shǒuchéng.
Shǒuchéng initially showed reluctance,
but reluctantly met him.
Not long after they sat down to talk,
Shǒuchéng was greatly pleased,
invited him to the central hall,
and chatted and laughed intimately,
regretting that they had not met sooner.
The next day,
he said to Suò:
"Zhéng shēng is indeed as you said."
From then on, he was also favored by Shǒuchéng,
and his influence and power grew.
Suò appointed him as *Xúnguān*,
seating him among the honored guests.
Once Zhù gained influence,
fearing that the *yájiàng* who recommended him might reveal his origins,
he secretly accused him of other crimes to Suò,
and Suò had him killed.
When Shǒuchéng entered the capital to serve as Zhī Jīmì,
he took Zhù with him to the west,
provided him with a residence,
and supported him.
He then recommended him to the emperor,
who also treated him generously.
Since the emperor fell ill
(The emperor fell ill in the eleventh month of last winter;
details are in the previous volume),
his influence tilted the balance of power inside and outside the court.
Zhù entered and exited his home day and night,

Chéng Dàchāng said: In the seventh year of Zhēnyuán of Dèzōng,

Soon after, it was further commanded that two regularly attending officials must be granted an audience daily
to inquire about government affairs;
this was called "rotational audience."
This means that besides "waiting for audience,"
there was also "rotational audience."
Those truly called "waiting for audience"
were the chief officials of various departments.
Those named "rotational audience"
were officials who were not yet chief officials but were among the regularly attending officials,
and were also able to be granted alternate audiences.
Those referred to as "secondary audience officials"
are "rotational audience officials,"
permitted to be junior to "waiting for audience" officials and await audience.
Thus, "secondary audience" cannot be precisely "waiting for audience."
When people today write,
whenever they mention "waiting for audience,"
they name it "secondary audience,"
which may not be accurate.
However, the terms became so common
that even Tang people themselves did not differentiate.
In the Kàichéng era,
an imperial edict stated: "Henceforth, on days when officials enter the palace,
'secondary audience officials' are not to follow the ranks out;
they should all stand below the pine tree on the east steps.

they are to collectively proceed to the incense table and each report their department's public affairs."
The Left and Right Historians were to withdraw together after the "secondary audience officials" finished reporting.
What is said here is that chief officials of various departments who were "waiting for audience"
were named "secondary audience officials."
If one examines the system,
it is indeed a mistake to equate "waiting for audience" with "secondary audience officials."
I have examined that after the mid-Tang period,
after the chancellors had their audience in Yányīng
and withdrew,
both "waiting for audience officials" and "rotational audience officials" were granted audience,
and could collectively be called "secondary audience officials."
The so-called "secondary audience officials"
refers to those who gained audience after the chancellors,
not after the "waiting for audience officials."
The Tang people were not mistaken initially;
it was Chéng Tàizhī who made the mistake.

they were always provided by the local commandery itself.
