and it does not say it was on a different day.
We now follow the *Jìngzōng Shílù*.
(All were exiled to Lingnán or border regions.)
On Yǐsì,
Wénzōng ascended the throne,
and his name was changed to Áng.
On Wùshēn,
his mother, Lady Xiāo, was honored as Empress Dowager,
and Empress Dowager Wáng was honored as Empress Dowager Bǎolì.
At this time,
Empress Dowager Guō resided in the Xīngqìng Palace,
Empress Dowager Wáng resided in the Yì'ān Hall,
and Empress Dowager Xiāo resided in the Dànèi.
The Emperor was filial and diligent by nature,
serving the three palaces equally.
From this point onward,
"the Emperor" refers to Wénzōng.
He first made offerings at the imperial ancestral temple and altars of heaven and earth,
then attended to the three palaces,
and only then proceeded to his imperial bedchamber.
Empress Dowager Xiāo was
from Mǐn.
On Gēngxū,
Hanlin Scholar Wéi Chǔhòu was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
As a prince, the Emperor deeply understood the evils of the two preceding reigns.
The two reigns refer to those of Mùzōng and Jìngzōng.
"Cháo" is pronounced zhí-yáo.
Same below.
He dedicated himself to good governance,
abandoning extravagance and embracing frugality.
An edict was issued to dismiss all palace women who did not have specific duties,
resulting in the dismissal of over three thousand people.
The hawks and hounds of the Wǔfāng were,
in accordance with the precedent of Yuánhé,
largely released, with only a small number kept for hunting.
The annual supplies for the palace
were all adjusted to conform to the precedent of Zhēnyuán.
The Department of Music, Hanlin Academy, and the General Directorate
reduced over twelve hundred positions,
The General Directorate
was the Yùan General Directorate.
All offices
were the inner imperial offices.
The clothes and provisions
were excessive favors granted by Jìngzōng.
All were returned to the control of the relevant officials.
Previously ordered embroidered and carved items
were all abolished.
During Jìngzōng's reign,
court audiences were held no more than once or twice a month.
The Emperor now restored the old system,
holding court on every odd-numbered day,
meeting with the Prime Ministers and all ministers to discuss government affairs,
often for a long time before concluding.
Although officials on duty were previously established,
they were never summoned for consultation.
Now, they were frequently invited for discussions.
Court was adjourned or dismissed on even-numbered days.
The court and the land rejoiced together,
believing that an era of peace was to be hoped for.
A ruler truly desirous of good governance is rarely seen.
If a ruler, in the early days of his reign,
can do one or two things that refresh the public's sight and hearing,
the expectations of the world become great.
However, there were ultimately none who could live up to the world's expectations;
Wèi Gāoguìxiānggōng, Jìn Huáidì, Táng Dézōng, and Wénzōng are examples.
Tàihé First Year
(Dīngwèi, 827)
1. Spring,
Second month,
On Yǐsì,
a general amnesty was granted,
and the reign title was changed.
2. Lǐ Tóngjié occupied Cāngjǐng,
and the court had not questioned it for a year.
In the third month of the previous year,
Lǐ Tóngjié took the post of Provisional Military Governor of Hénghǎi.
Third month,
on the first day of Rénxū,
he sent his personal secretary Cuī Cóngcháng to present a memorial, and he, along with his younger brothers Tóngzhì and Tóngxùn, personally appeared before the court,
requesting to obey the imperial decree.
3. Although the Emperor was open to listening and accepting advice, he could not be firm and decisive.
Matters discussed and decided with the Prime Ministers
were often reversed soon after.
Summer,
Fourth month,
on Bǐngchén,
Wéi Chǔhòu debated intensely at Yányīng,
and consequently requested to resign his position;
the Emperor repeatedly comforted him.
4. Wáng Pèi, the Jìedùshǐ of Zhōngwǔ, passed away.
On Gēngshēn,
Gāo Yǔ, the Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Zhōngwǔ.
Since the Dàlì era,
many Jìedùshǐ were appointed from the imperial army.
High-ranking generals of the imperial army,
to obtain these posts, would borrow money from wealthy families at exorbitant interest,
"bèi" means the interest is double the principal.
"Chēng" means the interest and principal are equal.
"Chēng" is pronounced chǐ-zhèng.
The amounts often exceeded hundreds of millions,
and only then could they obtain the position,
never through the executive officials.
Upon arriving at their garrisons,
they would heavily tax the people to repay their debts.
When Pèi died,
Péi Dù and Wéi Chǔhòu first memorialized to appoint Yǔ as his replacement.
The court and the land rejoiced, saying:
"From now on, there will be few 'debt-ridden commanders'!"
5. Fifth month,
on Bǐngzǐ,
Wū Chóngyìn, the Jìedùshǐ of Tiānpíng, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Hénghǎi,
and Lǐ Tóngjié, the former Deputy Jìedùshǐ of Hénghǎi, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Yǎnhǎi.
The court still worried that the Jìedùshǐ of Hénán and Hébèi might instigate Tóngjié to resist the decree,
so Shǐ Xiànchéng of Wèibó was granted the title Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
On Dīngchǒu,
Lǐ Zàiyì of Lúlóng, Kāng Zhìmù of Pínglú, and Wáng Tíngcòu of Chéngdé were granted inspecting official titles.
6. Wáng Bō, the Salt and Iron Commissioner, arrived at court from Huáinán,
earnestly seeking a high position.
The silver vessels he presented numbered in the thousands,
and the silk fabrics in the hundreds of thousands.
Sixth month,
on Guǐsì,
Bō was appointed Zuǒ Púyè and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
7. Autumn,
Seventh month,
on Guǐyǒu,
Emperor Ruìwǔ Zhāomǐn Xiàohuángdì was buried at Zhuānglíng;
Zhuānglíng is located five *lǐ* northwest of Sānyuán County, Jīngzhào.
8. Lǐ Tóngjié claimed to be detained by his officers and soldiers,
and did not accept the imperial decree.
On Yǐyǒu,
Wáng Zhìxīng, the Jìedùshǐ of Wǔníng, memorialized, requesting to lead his army of thirty thousand men,
with five months' provisions self-provided, to suppress Tóngjié,
which was granted.
Eighth month,
on Gēngzǐ,
Tóngjié's official titles and ranks were stripped,

and Wū Chóngyìn, Wáng Zhìxīng, Kāng Zhìmù, Shǐ Xiànchéng, Lǐ Zàiyì, along with Lǐ Tīng, the Jìedùshǐ of Yìchéng, and Zhāng Fán, the Jìedùshǐ of Yìwǔ, were each ordered to lead their respective armies to suppress him.
Tóngjié sent his sons and younger brothers
with treasures, precious objects, and female entertainers to bribe the various garrisons north of the Yellow River.
On Wùwǔ,
Lǐ Zàiyì apprehended Tóngjié's nephew
and presented the bribes along with him to the court.
Shǐ Xiànchéng (史憲誠) had marital ties with Lǐ Quánlüè (李全略).
When Tóng Jié (同捷) rebelled,
he secretly supplied him with grain.
Péi Dù (裴度) was unaware of his actions,
believing Xiànchéng (憲誠) had no disloyal intentions.
Xiànchéng (憲誠) sent a trusted clerk to the Secretariat to ask for instructions.
Wéi Chǔhòu (韋處厚) said to him:
"Duke Jìn (晉公) guaranteed your envoy's master with his life before His Majesty;
Péi Dù (裴度) was enfeoffed as Duke of Jìn (晉國公).
A Jìedùshǐ (節度使) is the master of a circuit,
hence his subordinate clerks referred to him as 'envoy's master.'
'Shǐ' (使)
is pronounced 'shū lì' (疏吏).
Just await his actions;
there are already court regulations!"
Xiànchéng (憲誠) was frightened
and dared not communicate with Tóng Jié (同捷) again.
Wáng Tíngcòu (王庭湊) sought an axe and banner for Tóng Jié (同捷) but failed to obtain them.
So he helped him rebel,
dispatching troops to the border to harass the Wèi (魏) army.
He also sent an envoy with lavish bribes to the Shatuo (沙陀) chieftain Zhūyé Zhíyí (朱邪執宜),
intending to ally with him,
but Zhíyí (執宜) refused to accept.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
Wū Chóngyìn (烏重胤), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Tiānpíng (天平) and Hénghǎi (橫海), attacked Tóng Jié (同捷)
and repeatedly defeated him.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Bǐngyín (丙寅),
Chóngyìn (重胤) died.
On the day Gēngchén (庚辰),
Lǐ Huán (李寰), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Bǎoyì (保義), was made Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hénghǎi (橫海).
In the third year of Mùzōng's (穆宗) Chángqìng (長慶) era (823 CE),
the two prefectures of Jìn (晉) and Cí (慈) were established as the Bǎoyì (保義) Army.
9 In the twelfth month,
on the day Gēngxū (庚戌),
Wáng Zhìxīng (王智興) was given the additional title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
1 In spring,
in the third month,
on the day Jǐmǎo (己卯),
Wáng Zhìxīng (王智興) attacked Dìzhōu (棣州)
and burned its three gates.
2 Since the end of the Yuánhé (元和) era,
the eunuchs had become increasingly rampant,
holding the establishment of the Son of Heaven in their grasp.
Mùzōng (穆宗) and His Majesty were both placed on the throne by eunuchs.
No one dared to speak.
His Majesty
personally presided over the policy examinations for candidates.
Liú Fén (劉蕡), a worthy, upright, and peaceful man from Chāngpíng (昌平),
submitted a policy essay,
enumerating its disasters.
Its summary read:
"What Your Majesty should worry about first
is that the palace will change, the altars of soil and grain will be endangered, the empire will be overthrown, and the land within the seas will be in chaos."
He also said:
"If Your Majesty wishes to stop the gradual usurpation and assassination,
then you should occupy the correct position and draw close to upright people,
keep far from the ignoble who wield knives and saws,
and befriend the straightforward and outspoken.
Let the chancellors be able to fully exercise their responsibilities,
and let the various officials maintain their posts.
How can five or six close and familiar individuals oversee all the great policies of the empire!
Disaster accumulates within the inner court,
and treachery arises from the palace chambers.
Your servant fears that Cáo Jié (曹節) and Hóu Lǎn (侯覽) will be reborn today."
Cáo Jié (曹節) and Hóu Lǎn (侯覽) are seen in the Annals of Emperor Huán (桓帝) of Han.
'Fù' (復)
is pronounced 'fú yòu' (扶又).
"Loyal and worthy men have no trusted appointments,
while palace attendants hold the power to depose and enthrone.
This caused the former sovereign to not end his reign properly,
and Your Majesty to not begin his reign properly."
This refers to the eunuchs assassinating Jìngzōng (敬宗) and enthroning His Majesty.
The Gǔliáng Zhuàn (穀梁傳) of the Spring and Autumn Annals says: In the first year of Duke Dìng (定),
the Spring King does not speak of the first month,
because Dìng (定) had no proper beginning.
Why did Dìng (定) have no proper beginning?
The end of Duke Zhāo (昭) was not a proper end;
the beginning of Dìng (定) was not a proper beginning.
Since Zhāo (昭) had no proper end,
Dìng (定) therefore had no proper beginning.
"The threads of power have been weakened,
and the vassal ministers are unruly.
Some may not understand the principles of a subject,
initiating rebellion under the guise of 'pacifying the sovereign';
failing to investigate the subtleties of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
they raise troops under the banner of 'expelling evil.'"
'Wēi' (微)
refers to the subtleties of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
These two sentences
imply Fén (蕡) feared that powerful vassals would initiate rebellion and raise troops
under the pretext of 'expelling evil ministers from the sovereign's side.'
"Punitive expeditions will certainly originate from the regional lords."
In the era of Zhāozōng (昭宗),
the armies of Qí (岐) and Biàn (汴) clashed,
using the extermination of eunuchs as a pretext,
ultimately fulfilling Liú Fén's (劉蕡) words.
"Why does Your Majesty not block the path of insidious evil,
dismiss the familiar and disrespectful ministers,
restrain the intention to invade, coerce, and threaten,
and restore the duty of maintaining the household?
Prohibit what should be prohibited,
and worry about what should be worried about!
If one cannot govern in the beginning,
one must govern later;
if one cannot rectify the beginning,
one must rectify the end;
then one can reverently uphold the ancient canons,
and successfully inherit the great foundation.
In ancient times, the downfall of Qín (秦) was due to its tyranny,
and the downfall of Hàn (漢) was due to its weakness.
Tyranny causes traitorous ministers to fear death and harm the sovereign."
This refers to Zhào Gāo (趙高).
Gāo (高) was also a eunuch.
This refers to imperial relatives by marriage and eunuchs.
Fén (蕡)'s intention specifically points to eunuchs.
"Not nipping the sprouts of danger.
I humbly submit that Your Majesty should deeply consider the sorrow of the fallen Hàn (漢)
to stop its gradual development."
Fén (蕡) probably meant that Jìngzōng (敬宗) died due to his cruelty,
and he also feared that His Majesty, being benevolent and weak, could not control the eunuchs.
"Then the distant path of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors can be pursued."
"Three, Five"
refers to the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.
"Your servant heard that when Emperor Yuán (元帝) of Hàn (漢) first ascended the throne,
he reformed over seventy matters."
Its summary can be found in chapter 28, in the first and second years of Emperor Yuán's (元帝) Chūyuán (初元) era of Han.
"His reputation was very good,
but subsequently, the government became daily more chaotic,
the dynasty's lifespan daily declined,
villains daily grew stronger,
and the common people daily suffered
because he was unable to select and appoint wise men,
losing control of the reins of power."
Citing Emperor Yuán (元帝) of Hàn (漢) as a warning
probably means that the Emperor's move from extravagance to frugality was similar to Emperor Yuán (元帝) of Hàn (漢),
and his indecisive leisure was also similar to Emperor Yuán (元帝) of Hàn (漢).
"If Your Majesty can truly restore state power to the chancellors,
and entrust military command to the generals,
then there will be nothing in your heart that is not understood,
and nothing in your conduct that is not trusted."
He also said:
"Laws should be uniform,
and offices should be properly named.
Currently, there are divisions between external officials and internal officials,
and separate bureaus for the Southern Administration and Northern Administration.
Officials who attend court assemblies in the Southern Court are
called 'external officials'
or 'Southern Administration.'
Eunuchs establish bureaus inside the Xuánwǔ (玄武) Gate,
and the two army commanders protect the various camps within the imperial park.
They are called 'internal officials'
or 'Northern Administration.'
Sometimes a crime is punished externally but a law is broken internally.
Laws issue from multiple sources,
leaving people without guidance.
This is truly because the military and agrarian sectors have different powers, and internal and external laws differ."
He also said:
"Today, the Ministry of War knows nothing of military registers,
merely attending court;
the Six Armies do not manage military affairs,
merely cultivating honorary ranks.
The Ministry of War
held the duties of the ancient Ministry of War.
The Six Armies,
including supreme generals, grand generals, generals, and commanding generals, all cultivated honorary ranks.
Military regulations are attached to the duties of internal ministers."
This refers to the commissioners for inspecting military affairs and various surveillance commissioners.
"They despise civil officials like mortal enemies;
once they step into the military gate,
they view farmers as mere grass.
Their strategy is insufficient to eliminate fierce rebels, yet their deceit is enough to manipulate authority and power.
Their courage is insufficient to guard the altars of soil and grain, yet their violence is enough to invade villages and hamlets.
They restrain vassal ministers,
encroach upon chancellors,
undermine royal decrees,
and disrupt court governance.
They flaunt the prestige of military men,
using it above to control the sovereign;
they assume the Emperor's mandate,
using it below to command heroes.
They harbor intentions of hiding treachery and observing opportunities,
without the righteousness of upholding integrity and dying for the cause.
How can this be the intent of the former kings who established civil and military order!"
He also said:
"Your servant is not unaware that words spoken invite calamity,
and plans executed lead to death.
But I grieve over the danger to the altars of soil and grain,
and pity the suffering of the living.
How can I bear to indulge the taboos of the time
and usurp a single favor from Your Majesty's mandate!"
The Rítuals of Zhōu (周禮) states: One mandate receives office.
Later generations considered the conferral of a primary-grade official as one mandate.
3 In the intercalary month,
on the *bǐngxū* day, the first day of the month,
Shǐ Xiànchéng reported that he had dispatched his son, Vice Ambassador Táng, and the Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ Qí Zhìshào, with twenty-five thousand troops to advance on Dézhōu to suppress Lǐ Tóngjié.
At the time, Shǐ Xiànchéng wanted to aid Lǐ Tóngjié,
but Táng tearfully remonstrated,
and moreover requested to send troops to suppress him;
Shǐ Xiànchéng could not refuse.
4 On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
twenty-two men including Péi Xiū, Lǐ Hé, Lǐ Gān, Dù Mù, Mǎ Zhí, Cuī Yú, Wáng Shì, and Cuī Shènyóu, who were of 'Virtuous and Upright' caliber,
passed the examination,
and were all appointed to official positions.
The examining officials, including Zuǒ Sànqí Chángshì Féng Sù, saw Liú Fén's policy proposals,
and were all full of admiration,
but fearing the eunuchs,
did not dare to select him.
When the imperial edict was issued,
public opinion was clamorous in proclaiming the injustice.
The remonstrance officials and censors wanted to make a memorial,
but the chief ministers suppressed them.
Lǐ Hé said:
"Liú Fén failed the examination,
while we passed;
how can we not be ashamed!"
He then submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Fén's policy proposals
have had no equal since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties.
Now, the responsible officials, because Fén's proposals directly criticized those around the emperor,
dared not bring them to His Majesty's attention,
fearing that the path for loyal and upright men would be blocked,
and the imperial order would thus be severed.
Moreover, my own proposals are far inferior to Fén's,
and I beg that the position granted to me be revoked to commend Fén's integrity."
There was no reply.
Consequently, Fén was unable to serve at court,
and ended up as a staff censor in a military governor's headquarters.
A *shǐfǔ* was
the headquarters of a Jiédùshǐ.
A *yùshǐ* was
an honorary official position held by a staff member,
also called a *xiàn guān*.
Péi Xiū was Dù Yòu's grandson;
Mǎ Zhí was
Mǎ Xūn's son;
Dù Yòu served through the three reigns of Dé, Shùn, and Xiàn,
reaching the position of grand counselor.
Mǎ Xūn's affairs are found in volume 230, first year of Dézōng's Zhēnyuán era.
The 'Differences in Examination' notes: The old transmission
has "Xūn" (勛)
written
as "Xūn" (曛),
which is an error.
Mǎ Xūn's affairs are found in Dézōng's Veritable Records.
Wáng Shì was Wáng Qǐ's grandson;
Cuī Shènyóu was
Cuī Róng's great-great-grandson.
Wáng Qǐ's affairs are found in volume 241, first year of Mùzōng's Chángqìng era.
Cuī Róng distinguished himself through his literary works during Wǔ Hòu's reign.
5 Summer,
the sixth month,
Jìn Wáng Pǔ passed away;
on the *xīnyǒu* day,
he was posthumously honored as
Dàohuái Tàizǐ.
6 Initially,
when Xiāo Tàihòu was young, she left her hometown and
had one younger brother;
when the Emperor ascended the throne,
he ordered the Fújiàn Guānchásǐ to search for him,
but his whereabouts were unknown.
There was a tea-transport laborer named Xiāo Hóng.
Whenever tea merchants traded tea,
they would submit a certain amount as one *gāng* (consignment) and pay tax to the government.
A merchant, Zhào Zhěn, introduced him to the wife of Lǚ Zhāng, a close relative of the Empress Dowager,
who also could not verify him,
and went with him to see the Empress Dowager.
The Emperor believed he had found the true maternal uncle,
and on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
appointed him Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ.
This laid the groundwork for Xiāo Hóng's fraud to be discovered, leading to his banishment and death.
Previously,
悉薦 (xījiàn) was pronounced in the *fanqie* method.
7 Fēngzhōu Cǐshǐ Wáng Shēngcháo rebelled;
on the *gēngchén* day,
Ānnán Dūhù Wǔlíng Hán Yuē attacked and beheaded him.
Old records state: Fēngzhōu is eleven thousand five hundred *lǐ* from the capital.
Sòng Bái said: Fēngzhōu
governs Jiāníng Xiàn,
which was the territory of Hàn Mílěng Xiàn.
Wǔlíng was
the territory of Hàn Lín Yuán Xiàn;
the Suí dynasty established Wǔlíng Xiàn,
and in the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Lángzhōu.
朝 (*cháo*),
pronounced as *zhí yáo* in *fanqie*.
8 Wáng Tíngcòu secretly assisted Lǐ Tóngjié with troops and salt provisions.
The Emperor wanted to punish him;
autumn,
the seventh month,
on the *jiǎchén* day,
an imperial edict ordered the Zhōngshū to assemble all officials to discuss the matter.
No one below the Prime Minister dared to object,
but Wèiwèi Qīng Yīn Yòu alone believed:
"Although Tíngcòu is allied with the rebels,
the matter is not yet fully exposed.
It would be better to tolerate him for now
and focus on suppressing Lǐ Tóngjié."
On the *jǐsì* day,
an edict was issued condemning Tíngcòu,
ordering neighboring circuits to strictly prepare their defenses,
and allowing him to reform himself.
9 In the ninth month, on the *dīnghài* day,
Wáng Zhìxīng reported the capture of Dìzhōu.
10 Lǐ Huán led his troops from Jìnzhōu to his garrison,
but he did not restrain his soldiers;
they were brutal wherever they passed.
Upon arrival, he held back his troops and did not advance,
merely sitting and demanding provisions.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Lǐ Huán was appointed Xiàsuí Jiédùshǐ.
11 On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
an imperial edict stripped Wáng Tíngcòu of his official titles and ranks,
and ordered all armies to advance and suppress him from four directions.
12 Wáng Zhìxīng was promoted to Shǒu Sītú,
and Fù Liángbì, the former Xiàsuí Jiédùshǐ, was appointed Hénghǎi Jiédùshǐ.
13 Yuè Wáng Gǔn passed away.
14 On the *gēngxū* day,
Róngguǎn reported that the Ānnán army was in turmoil,
and had expelled Dūhù Hán Yuē.
15 Winter,
the tenth month,
Yáng Wáng Xīn passed away.
Xīn was
Xiànzōng's son.
16 Wèibó defeated the Hénghǎi troops at Píngyuán,
and consequently captured it.
17 In the eleventh month,
on the *guǐwèi* day, the first day of the month,
Yìdìng Jiédùshǐ Liǔ Gōngjì reported attacking Lǐ Tóngjié's Jiāngù (Solid) Fortress,
and capturing it;
Lǐ Tóngjié had built a fortress to the west of Cāngzhōu
to resist the government forces,
naming it Jiāngù.
At this time, the various armies from Hénán and Héběi had been suppressing Lǐ Tóngjié for a long time without success.
Whenever there was a small victory,
they would exaggerate the number of enemy heads and captives to obtain rich rewards.
The imperial court spared no effort to provide for them,
exhausting the resources of Jiāng and Huái regions.
18 Fù Liángbì passed away upon reaching Shǎn.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Zuǒ Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn Lǐ Yòu was appointed Hénghǎi Jiédùshǐ.
19 On the *jiǎchén* day,
Zhāodé Sì within the Forbidden City caught fire.
A fire caused by nature is called a calamity (*zāi*),
a fire caused by humans is called a fire (*huǒ*).
Several hundred people died in the fire.
20 In the twelfth month,
on the *dīngsì* day,
Wáng Zhìxīng reported that Bīngmǎshǐ Lǐ Jūnmóu had led troops across the Jìhé River,
and conquered Wúdì.
Wúdì was
the northern border of the ancient Qí Guó,
the place where King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed Tàigōng and bestowed upon him the privilege of wearing special shoes;
in the Hàn dynasty, it was Yángxìn Xiàn;
there was Wúdìgōu (Wudi Canal) in its territory,
connecting to the sea;
in the Táng dynasty, it was Wúdì Xiàn,
belonging to Cāngzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is one hundred and seven *lǐ* southeast of the prefecture.
21 On the *rénshēn* day,
Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Wéi Chǔhòu passed away.
22 Lǐ Tóngjié's military situation became increasingly dire.
Wáng Tíngcòu was unable to rescue him,
so he sent someone to persuade the Wèibó general Qí Zhìshào
to kill Shǐ Xiànchéng and his son and seize Wèibó.
Qí Zhìshào then rebelled,
leading his two thousand troops back to threaten Wèizhōu.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
Jiànyì Dàfū Bó Qí was ordered to conciliate Wèibó,
and also to dispatch Yìchéng and Héyáng troops to suppress Qí Zhìshào.
23 On the *wùyín* day,
Hànlín Xuéshì Lù Suí was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
24 On the *xīnsì* day,
Shǐ Xiànchéng reported that Qí Zhìshào's troops were stationed at Yǒngjì.
In the seventh year of Dàizōng's Dàlì era,
Tián Chéngsì divided Línqīng from Wèizhōu and established Yǒngjì Xiàn,
which belonged to Bèizhōu.
An imperial edict ordered Yìchéng Jiédùshǐ Lǐ Tīng to lead the various campaigning armies from Cāngzhōu to suppress Qí Zhìshào.
Punctuated by Róng Zhàozǔ, reviewed by Niè Chóngqí.
Compiled by imperial command
by Sīmǎ Guāng.
Later
Táihé third year
1 In spring,
the first month,
Qí Zhìshào, with Chéngdé's allied forces, plundered Bèizhōu.
Bèizhōu
is two hundred and ten *lǐ* north of Wèizhōu.
2 Three thousand troops from Yìchéng's traveling camp were first stationed in Qízhōu,
and sent to Yǔchéng.
Zhī (之)
means "to go."
One source has
"tún" (屯, to be stationed).
Yǔchéng
was the land of Hàn Zhù'ā County.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo, it was renamed Yǔchéng
because there was an ancient city to the west of the county where Yǔ rested.
It belonged to Qízhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: it is one hundred and thirty *lǐ* northwest of the prefecture.
Lǐ Yòu, the Jiedushi of Hénghǎi, campaigned against and executed them.
3 Lǐ Tīng and Shǐ Táng combined forces to attack Qí Zhìshào
and defeated him;
Zhìshào led his five thousand men and fled to Zhènzhōu.
4 Lǐ Zàiyì reported an attack on Cāngzhōu Chánglú
and captured it.
Cāngzhōu
governed Qīngchí County.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Chánglú Town belonged to Qīngchí.
5 On the *jiǎchén* day,
Zhāoyì reported that Qí Zhìshào's remaining fifteen thousand men surrendered to his own command
and were settled in Luò
zhōu.
6 In the second month,
Lǐ Yòu, the Jiedushi of Hénghǎi, led the traveling camp troops of various circuits to attack Lǐ Tóngjié
and defeated him,
advancing to attack Dézhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Dézhōu
is two hundred and thirty *lǐ* northeast to Cāngzhōu.
7 Shí Xióng, Wǔníng's troop commander for capturing enemies,
was brave
and loved his soldiers;
Wáng Zhìxīng was cruel and tyrannical.
The army wanted to expel Zhìxīng and install Xióng.
Zhìxīng, aware of this,
took advantage of Xióng's merits
and requested his appointment as a prefect.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
Xióng was made the prefect of Bìzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Bìzhōu was originally Hàn Dàngqú County land.
During Hòuwèi Dàtǒng's reign, Nuòshuǐ County was established where the prefecture now is.
In Táng Wǔdé Year 8, Bìzhōu was established,
named after Bìshān Mountain one *lǐ* west of the county.
It is one thousand eight hundred and twenty-two *lǐ* southwest of the capital.
8 Shǐ Xiànchéng, hearing that Cāngjǐng was about to be pacified, was afraid.
His son, Táng, persuaded him to come to court.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
Xiànchéng sent Táng to present a memorial requesting to come to court,
and also requested that his jurisdiction be subject to orders.
9 After Shí Xióng left,
Wáng Zhìxīng of Wǔníng killed over a hundred people in the army who were friendly with Xióng.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the *wùwǔ* day,
Zhìxīng reported that Xióng was stirring up unrest in the army
and requested his execution.
The Emperor, knowing Xióng was innocent,
spared him from death
and exiled him permanently to Báizhōu.
This laid the groundwork for Wǔzōng to reuse Shí Xióng.
In Wǔdé Year 3,
Bó Bái County was established by dividing land from Hépǔ County.
In Year 4, Nánzhōu was established.
In Year 6, it was renamed Báizhōu.
It is six thousand seven hundred and fifteen *lǐ* from the capital.
Both the prefecture and county were named after Bóbái Jiāng River.
10On the *wùchén* day,
Lǐ Zàiyì reported an attack on Cāngzhōu
and breached its outer wall.
Luóchéng (羅城)
is the outer city wall.
Over three thousand officers and soldiers in the city fled to Zhènzhōu.
Lǐ Tóngjié sent a letter to Yòu requesting surrender.
Yòu also submitted the letter with his report.
Bǎi Qí, a Grand Master of Remonstrance, received an imperial edict to offer comfort and assurance.
The traveling camp liked to exaggerate its power and influence to control the various generals,
and the generals already disliked this;
when Lǐ Tóngjié requested to surrender to Yòu,
Yòu sent his general Wàn Hóng to temporarily guard Cāngzhōu;
Qí suspected Tóngjié's deception
and personally led several hundred cavalry to rush into Cāngzhōu,
executed Hóng for his actions,
and took Tóngjié and his family members to the capital.
On the *yǐhài* day,
they arrived at Jiānglíng.
Jiānglíng
was the land of Hàn Āndé County.
During the Suí dynasty, Āndé was divided,
and a county was established at the old city of Jiānglíng.
In the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Dézhōu.
Then Tóngjié was beheaded,
his head was presented,
and Cāngjǐng was completely pacified.
In the fifth month,
on the *gēngyín* day,
Lǐ Zàiyì was promoted to *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Shílù* writes
"*gēngyín*" (庚寅),
which is an error.
After three years,
it was barely subdued.
The Emperor started attacking Tóngjié in the first year of his reign,
and it took three years until this point.
Qí claimed it as his own achievement.
The generals detested him
and competed to submit memorials to criticize him.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Qí was demoted to *Sīhù* of Xúnzhōu.
Xúnzhōu
was ancient Lóngchuān land.
The Suí dynasty established Xúnzhōu.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Shílù*:
"In the fourth month,
Lǐ Yòu recovered Dézhōu.
Tóngjié requested to surrender to Yòu.
Yòu suspected his deception.
Bǎi Qí requested to enter Cāngzhōu with three hundred cavalry;
Yòu agreed.
Qí directly entered Cāng[zhōu],
arrested Tóngjié and his family members, and went to the capital."
The imperial edict also said:
"He presumptuously put on a grand display,
took advantage of the dangerous situation, acted recklessly,
commanded and suppressed,
and ignored reports.
He recklessly entered Cāngzhōu,
unilaterally executed a major general,
appointed rebel officers,
and secretly sent away the chief villain."
The old biography says:
"When Cāng and Dé were pacified,
the generals, jealous of Qí claiming credit,
competed to submit memorials criticizing him.
The Emperor, having no choice,
demoted him to *Sīhù* of Xúnzhōu."
The new biography says:
"Tóngjié requested surrender.
Yòu sent Wàn Hóng to temporarily guard Cāngzhōu,
but Tóngjié had not yet left.
Qí rode into Cāng[zhōu] with three hundred cavalry,
executed Hóng for his actions,
and went to the capital with Tóngjié.
After they had set out,
a spy reported that Wáng Tíngcòu intended to ambush Tóngjié with elite troops.
Qí then beheaded him and presented his head.
The generals were jealous of his achievement,
and submitted numerous memorials slandering him.
Wénzōng, having no choice,
demoted Qí to *Sīhù Cānjūn* of Xúnzhōu."
Thus, Qí did indeed act presumptuously to claim credit,
but it is also true that the generals were jealous of him and submitted criticisms,
and Wénzōng had no choice but to demote him.
This is also the reality.
As for being granted death, it was because Mǎ Guóliàng reported that he accepted Tóngjié's slaves and silk.
11On the *rényín* day,
Shǐ Táng, the Acting Deputy Envoy of Wèibó, requested to change his name to Xiàozhāng.
12In the sixth month,
on the *bǐngchén* day,
an imperial edict said:
"The traveling camps on all four sides of Zhènzhōu shall each return to their respective commands to rest,
and shall only focus on protecting their borders,
not interacting with each other;
only if Tíngcòu shows obedience
should his memorials be delivered,
all others shall not be accepted."
13On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Shǐ Xiànchéng was appointed concurrently as *Shìzhōng* and Jiedushi of Hézhōng;
Lǐ Tīng was concurrently appointed Jiedushi of Wèibó.
Lǐ Tīng was originally commander of Yìchéng,
and was concurrently made Jiedushi of Wèibó.
Shǐ Xiàozhāng was appointed Jiedushi.
14Previously,
Lǐ Yòu, hearing that Bǎi Qí had killed Wàn Hóng,
was greatly alarmed
and his illness worsened significantly.
The Emperor said:
"If Yòu dies,
it will be Qí who killed him!"
On the *guǐyǒu* day,
Qí was granted the right to commit suicide.
15Lǐ Chéng, the Jiedushi of Hédōng, reported receiving a letter from Wáng Tíngcòu,
requesting to return Jǐngzhōu;
The *Kǎoyì* states: According to this, Jǐngzhōu originally belonged to Hénghǎi.
It was probably due to Lǐ Tóngjié's rebellion
that Tíngcòu occupied it.
After Tóngjié was pacified,
Tíngcòu, in fear, returned it.
16 In the first month, the emperor dispatched a palace envoy to bestow a banner and staff upon Shǐ Xiànchéng,
on *Guǐyǒu*,
who arrived at Wèizhōu.
At this time, Lǐ Tīng had returned his army from Bèizhōu to Guǎntáo,
procrastinating and not advancing.
Guǎntáo
was forty-five *lǐ* north of Wèizhōu.
On *Jiǎxū*,
the army mutinied,
killed Xiànchéng,
and enthroned Língwǔ Hé Jìntāo, the Provisional Military Commissioner of the Imperial Guard, as acting Military Governor (*liúhòu*).
Lǐ Tīng advanced to Wèizhōu,
but Jìntāo resisted him
and prevented his entry.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Jìntāo sent out troops to attack Lǐ Tīng;
Tīng was unprepared,
suffered a great defeat,
and fled in disarray.
A textual variant states: The New Biography of Jìntāo says:
"Jìntāo issued an order saying: 'Since you have forced me,
you must obey my orders.'
The multitude responded, 'Yes, yes.'
'Those who killed the former envoy and the supervising commissioner,
write down their names.'
More than ninety people were executed,
and those who were coerced were released.
He wore plain mourning clothes and wept,
and all the generals and officials came to offer condolences.
An imperial edict appointed him acting Military Governor."
Based on Jìntāo's alliance with Wáng Tíngcòu to resist Lǐ Tīng,
and his surprise attack on Tīng,
utterly defeating him,
how could he have acted in such a way!
The new biography is probably based on Liǔ Gōngquán's Stele of Virtuous Governance, which says:
"The Duke said to his generals and soldiers: 'Since you have forced me to be your leader,
you must carefully listen and obey.'
He ordered the general in charge of all affairs to instruct them, saying: 'List the names of the violent faction who harmed the former envoy and the supervising commissioner,
and gather them in the courtyard;
do not let any escape the net.'
In the end, ninety-three people were captured.
With black and white clearly distinguished,
and good and evil without error,
they were publicly executed among the assembled multitude and discarded,
to everyone's delight.
The Duke then wore plain mourning clothes and wept,
and the generals and officials offered condolences in order."
This may involve exaggerated praise.
We now follow the old biography.
He hastened to Qiǎnkǒu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* says: Guǎntáo County in Wèizhōu has Qiǎnkǒu Town.
*Qù*
is pronounced *qī yù*.
His baggage and weapons were all abandoned.
Zhāoyì soldiers rescued him,
and Tīng barely escaped,
returning to Huátái.
Lǐ Tīng's original commandery was Huázhōu.
Héběi had been engaged in war for a long time,
and provisions and transport were insufficient,
causing the imperial court much weariness.
In the eighth month,
on *Rénzǐ*,
Jìntāo was made Military Governor of Wèibó,
and the three prefectures of Xiāng, Wèi, and Chán were returned to him.
17 Cāngzhōu, after the chaos of war,
had bones covering the ground,
empty cities and desolate wilderness,
with less than three or four tenths of its households surviving.
On *Guǐchǒu*,
Yīn Yòu, Grand Commandant of the Imperial Guards, was appointed Military Governor of Qí, Dé, Cāng, and Jǐng.
In this year,
Qízhōu was first subordinated to Hénghǎi.
He shared the hardships with his soldiers,
pacified the common people,
encouraged them to farm and cultivate mulberry,
and scattered refugees gradually resumed their livelihoods.
Previously,
the 30,000 soldiers of the local army all relied on the Department of Finance for their sustenance;
within one year of Yòu's arrival,
tax revenues could support half of them;
in the second year,
he requested that all grants from the Department of Finance be abolished;
after three years,
the population had multiplied,
and granaries were full.
Historians say that if a regional commandery gets the right person,
it can transform desolation into prosperity.
18 Wáng Tíngcòu, through neighboring commanderies, subtly expressed his intention to submit;
on *Rénshēn*,
Tíngcòu and his generals and soldiers were pardoned,
and their official ranks and titles restored.
19 Lǐ Déyù, the Observer of Zhèxī, was summoned to be Minister of War;
Péi Dù recommended him for chancellor.
At this time, Lǐ Zōngmǐn, Vice Minister of Personnel, had the backing of eunuchs,
and on *Jiǎxū*,
Zōngmǐn was made Grand Councillor (*tóng píngzhāngshì*).
20 The emperor was naturally frugal;
in the ninth month,
on *Xīnsì*,
he ordered that palace eunuchs and below should not wear gauze, thin silk, brocade, or fine silk;
in his leisure time after court,
he entertained himself only with books and history,
never paying attention to music, entertainment, or hunting.
The imperial son-in-law, Wéi Chǔrén, once wore a lined gauze headscarf,
and the emperor said to him:
"I admire your family's pure and simple background,
which is why I chose you for marriage."
Chǔrén married Princess Xīnfēng, daughter of Mùzōng.
"Let other noble relatives do as they please,
you do not need to."
21 On *Rénchén*,
Lǐ Déyù was made Military Governor of Yìchéng.
Lǐ Zōngmǐn, disliking his encroachment,
therefore sent him away.
22 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on *Bǐngchén*,
Lǐ Tīng was made Junior Mentor of the Crown Prince.
23 Lù Suí said to the emperor:
"The responsibility of a chancellor is heavy;
it is not appropriate to concurrently manage trivial financial and economic affairs,
as Yáng Guózhōng, Yuán Zài, and Huángfǔ Bó did;
these were all acts of treacherous officials
and should not be emulated."
The emperor agreed.
Thereupon, Péi Dù resigned from the Department of Finance;
the emperor granted it.
24 In the eleventh month,
on *Jiǎwǔ*,
the emperor offered sacrifices at the Altar of Heaven;
a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
All regions were forbidden from presenting exotic and ingenious items,
and fine, delicate fabrics were all prohibited,
and their looms destroyed.
25 On *Bǐngshēn*,
Dù Yuányǐng, Military Governor of Xīchuān, reported that Nánzhào had invaded.
Yuányǐng, as a former chancellor,
was elegantly self-important.
Dù Yuányǐng became chancellor to Mùzōng at the beginning of Chángqìng.
He focused solely on accumulating wealth,
reducing the clothing and rations of soldiers.
The soldiers guarding the southwestern border,
lacking sufficient clothing and food,
all entered the barbarian territory to plunder for their own needs,
and the barbarians, in turn, provided them with clothing and food;
thus, the barbarians knew all about the strengths, weaknesses, movements, and stillness within Shǔ.
Nánzhào, led by Cuōdiān, planned a large-scale invasion.
Cuōdiān assassinated and enthroned rulers, thereby monopolizing the government of Nánzhào.
*Cuō*
is pronounced *cái hé*.
Yuányǐng did not believe it;
when Cuōdiān's troops reached the border cities,
there was no defense whatsoever.
The barbarians used Shǔ soldiers as guides,
and successfully captured Xī and Róng prefectures in a surprise attack.
On *Jiǎchén*,
Yuányǐng dispatched troops to battle south of Qióngzhōu,
and the Shǔ army was utterly defeated;
the barbarians then captured Qióngzhōu.
26 Wáng Zhìxīng, Military Governor of Wǔníng, came to court.
27 An imperial edict ordered the dispatch of troops from Dōngchuān, Xīngyuán, and Jīngnán to rescue Xīchuān;
in the twelfth month,
on the first day, *Dīngwèi*,
troops from È-Yuè, Xiāng-Dèng, Chén-Xǔ, etc., were again dispatched to follow.
28 Wáng Zhìxīng was appointed Military Governor of Zhōngwǔ.
Zhìxīng moved from Xú to Chén.
29 On *Jǐyǒu*,
Guō Zhāo, Military Governor of Dōngchuān, was made Military Governor of Xīchuān,
concurrently acting as Military Governor of Dōngchuān.
Cuōdiān led his troops directly from Qióngzhōu to Chéngdū.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* says: From Qióngzhōu eastward to Chéngdū is 260 *lǐ*.
On *Gēngxū*
they captured its outer city walls.
Dù Yuányǐng led his multitude to hold the inner citadel to resist them,
attempting to flee several times.
On *Rénzǐ*,
On the *jǐwèi* [day, the 30th day],
Dǒng Zhòngzhì (董重質), Grand General of the Right Wing Army, was made Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of all the Shéncè (神策) Circuits and the Western Chuān (川) Campaign.
Troops from Tàiyuán (太原) and Fèngxiáng (鳳翔) were also dispatched to Western Chuān.
The Nánzhào (南詔) invaded Eastern Chuān,
and entered Zǐzhōu (梓州), Western Chuān.
Zhāo’s (釗) troops were few and weak, unable to fight.
The character “Zhāo” (釗)
should
have the character “Guō” (郭)
above it.
The Shu (蜀) text is correctly thus.
Cuódiān (嵯顛) wrote back saying:
“Dù Yuányǐng (杜元穎) harassed and disturbed us,
hence we raised troops to retaliate.”
He made peace with Zhāo and withdrew.
The Man (蠻) remained in the western suburbs of Chéngdū (成都) for ten days.
Initially, they comforted and appeased the people of Shǔ (蜀),
and the markets and shops were peaceful.
As they were about to leave,
they plundered tens of thousands of women, children, and artisans, as well as treasures, and departed.
The people of Shǔ were terrified,
many threw themselves into the river,
and their floating corpses choked the river as they drifted downstream.
Cuódiān personally led the rear of the army.
When they reached the Dàdù Shuǐ (大度水),
Cuódiān said to the people of Shǔ:
“South of here is our territory.
You may now weep to bid farewell to your homeland.”
Everyone wailed,
and those who jumped into the water to die numbered in the thousands.
From then on, the craftsmanship of Nánzhào was equal to that in Shǔ.
Cuódiān sent an envoy to present a memorial,
stating:
“The Man have always paid tribute and performed their duties.
How would we dare to violate the border?
It is simply that Dù Yuányǐng did not care for his soldiers,
and they resented and suffered under Yuányǐng.
They competed to guide us,
praying for our advance to punish the tyrannical commander.
As we did not succeed in punishing him,
we have no way to comfort the hearts of the Shǔ soldiers.
We wish Your Majesty to punish him.”
On the *dīngmǎo* [day],
Yuányǐng was again demoted to Sīmǎ (司馬) of Xúnzhōu (循州).
An imperial edict ordered Dǒng Zhòngzhì and the troops from all circuits to withdraw.
Guō Zhāo (郭釗) arrived in Chéngdū,
and established a pact with Nánzhào
not to invade each other.
An imperial edict sent a central envoy to bestow the imperial credentials upon Cuódiān.
In the 1st year [of Dàhé (大和)],
spring, 1st month,
on the *xīnsì* [day],
Niú Sēngrú (牛僧孺), Jìedùshǐ of Wǔchāng (武昌), entered the court.
On the *wùzǐ* [day],
his son Yǒng (永) was established as the Prince of Lǔ (魯).
Lǐ Zōngmǐn (李宗閔) recommended Niú Sēngrú.
On the *xīnmǎo* [day],
Sēngrú was made Bīngbù Shàngshū (兵部尚書) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
Thereupon, the two colluded to ostracize Lǐ Déyù’s (李德裕) faction.
*Pái* (排)
means to push aside.
*Bìn* (擯)
means to reject.
When Nánzhào invaded Chéngdū,
an imperial edict ordered Shānnán Xīdào (山南西道) to dispatch troops to relieve it,
as mentioned in the previous year.
The Jìedùshǐ of Shānnán Xīdào
governed Xīngyuán Fǔ (興元府).
Before they arrived,
the Man had withdrawn and returned.
The Xīngyuán troops had a fixed quota,
and an imperial edict ordered that all newly recruited soldiers be disbanded.
In the 2nd month,
on the *yǐmǎo* [day],
Jiàng (絳) summoned all the new troops,
informed them of the imperial decree, and dismissed them,
also granting them grain and wheat.
They all left discontentedly.
They went to bid farewell to the supervising censor.
The supervising censor Yáng Shūyuán (楊叔元) resented Jiàng for not deferring to him,
and provoked them by criticizing the meagerness of the gifts.
The crowd grew angry,
shouted loudly,
plundered the armory,
and rushed towards the commissioner’s headquarters.
Jiàng was feasting with his subordinates,
unprepared, and fled to the northern city wall.
Someone advised him to be lowered down and escape,
but Jiàng said:
“As a marshal, how can I flee!”
He waved to the investigating official Zhào Cúnyuē (趙存約) to leave.
Cúnyuē said:
“Cúnyuē has received your trust,
how can I simply escape!”
The general Wáng Jǐngyán (王景延) fought bravely against the rebels and died.
Jiàng, Cúnyuē, and the observation judge Xuē Qí (薛齊) were all harmed by the rebellious soldiers.
The rebels then slaughtered Jiàng’s family.
*Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The new biography says:
“Yáng Shūyuán disliked Jiàng.
He sent someone to persuade the soldiers, saying:
‘He will collect your recruitment fees,
and you will return to being commoners.’
All the soldiers were enraged,
then shouted and rushed in,
seizing weapons from the armory.
Jiàng was feasting,
unprepared,
and so he grasped his staff and ascended the parapet.
Someone suggested that he could escape by being lowered from the city wall,
but Jiàng did not agree,
and subsequently met his demise.”
The *Shílù* (實錄) says:
“Jiàng summoned all the soldiers,
informed them of the imperial decree, and dismissed them,
distributing grain and wheat from the granary as rewards to the multitude.
They all left discontentedly.
As they exited the camp gate,
some of the crowd requested to bid farewell to the supervising censor.
The supervising censor Yáng Shūyuán was greedy for wealth and favored by the emperor.
He had long resented Jiàng for not deferring to him,
and had been at odds with Jiàng for a long time.
At this point, he used the meager rewards to incite them.
The disbanded soldiers then rebelled.”
We follow this account.
On the *wùwǔ* [day],
Shūyuán reported that Jiàng had collected the recruitment fees from the new troops, leading to the rebellion.
On the *gēngshēn* [day],
Wēn Zào (溫造), Shàngshū Yòuchéng (尚書右丞), was made Jìedùshǐ of Shānnán Xīdào.
At this time,
officials from the three ministries jointly submitted memorials discussing the injustice of Lǐ Jiàng (李絳).
Jiànyì Dàfū (諫議大夫) Kǒng Mǐnháng (孔敏行) fully presented how Shūyuán had incited the rebellious soldiers,
and the emperor finally understood.

Now, those who neglect their duties are merely fined their salaries,
and the pressing concern is entrusted to inner eunuchs,
thus treating the ancestral temple as Your Majesty's private affair and rendering all officials mere empty positions."
The emperor approved of his words,
immediately recalled and stopped the Zhongshǐ 中使,
and ordered the appropriate authorities to repair it.
7. On the day Bǐngchén 丙辰,
Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ Lǐ Déyù 西川節度使李德裕 memorialized that he had dispatched envoys to Nánzhào 南詔 to reclaim the abducted common people,
and four thousand people were recovered and returned.
Kǎoyì 考異 says: Déyù's Déyù's Xīnán Bèibiānlù 西南備邊錄 says:
"Nánzhào 南詔 returned 5,364 captured men and women to us."
The Old Chronicles say:
"He also sent people into Nánzhào 南詔 to seek the artisans they had captured,
and over four thousand monks, Daoists, and skilled artisans
returned to Chéngdū 成都."
According to the Shílù 實錄 (Veritable Records), it says
"about four thousand people,"
which is followed here.
8. In autumn,
in the eighth month,
on the day Wùyín 戊寅,
Cuī Yǎn 崔郾 was appointed Ëyuè Guānchásǐ 鄂岳觀察使, having been Shǎn Guó Guānchásǐ 陝虢觀察使.
Ëyuè 鄂岳 was a region encompassed by mountains and bordered by rivers,
at the junction of Bǎiyuè 百越, Bāshǔ 巴蜀, Jīnghàn 荊漢;
the area had many bandits
who plundered passing boats,
and killed all, regardless of age, until none remained.
When Yǎn 郾 arrived,
he trained soldiers and disciplined the troops,
built méngchōng 蒙衝 (assault boats) to pursue and suppress them,
méngchōng 蒙衝
were warships.
Zhì 治 is
pronounced zhízhī (zhì).
He executed them all.
When Yǎn 郾 was in Shǎn 陝,
he governed with leniency and benevolence;
sometimes, for a month, no one would be flogged.
However, upon arriving in Ë 鄂,
he imposed severe punishments;
when asked the reason,
Yǎn 郾 said:
"The land of Shǎn 陝 is barren and its people are poor.
I hardly had time to comfort them, still fearing they would be alarmed.
Ë 鄂 is a perilous land with mixed populations.
Their barbarian customs are fierce, cunning, and prone to crime;
without using severe punishment,
order cannot be achieved.
It is vital in governance to know how to adapt to change;
this is what is meant."
9 Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ Lǐ Déyù reported:
"Among the Shu soldiers, those who are weak, sick, old, or infirm
have never been reviewed throughout their lives.
I ordered the establishment of a standard of five *chǐ* five *cùn* [in height],
and dismissed over 4,400 people.
*Jiǎn*
means to select.
*Qù*
is pronounced *qiāng lǚ fān*.
We have already recruited 1,500 northern soldiers,
who are now mixed with the local soldiers,
training each other,
and becoming more proficient day by day.
Furthermore,
the weapons made by Shu artisans
were merely decorative and unusable.
I now bring in artisans from other regions to craft them,
and none are not sturdy and sharp."
In the ninth month,
Xīdámóu, the deputy envoy of Wéizhōu of the Tǔbō, requested to surrender,
leading all his troops to Chéngdū.
Déyù sent Yú Zàngjiǎn, acting governor of Wéizhōu, to lead troops to occupy the city.
On *gēngshēn*
he fully reported the situation,
and furthermore said,
"If we send 3,000 *shēngqiāng* [unassimilated Qiang]
to burn the Thirteen Bridges
and strike at the heart of the Western *Róng*,
we can wash away our long-standing shame.
This is what Wéi Gāo regretted to his dying day he could not achieve!"
During the reign of Dèzōng,
Wéi Gāo repeatedly dispatched troops to attack Wéizhōu,
but could not take it.
The hundred officials were convened to deliberate,
and all requested to follow Déyù's plan.
Niú Sēngrú said:
"The territory of Tǔbō
spans ten thousand *lǐ* on each of its four sides.
Losing one Wéizhōu
will not diminish its power.
Lately, we have been cultivating good relations,
agreeing to withdraw garrison troops.
For the Central Kingdom to defend against the *Róng*,
upholding faith is paramount.
If they come to demand, 'Why did you break faith?'
and pasture horses in Wèirúchuān—
there is the Wèirúshǔi in Yuánzhōu's Xiāoguānxiàn,
and west of the water is Báicǎojūn—
*Wèi*
is pronounced *yūwù fān*.
With ten thousand cavalrymen traversing Huízhōng,
their anger expressed directly,
they could reach Xiányángqiáo in less than three days.
At that time, what use would a hundred Wéizhōu be, thousands of *lǐ* away to the southwest?
We would merely abandon trust,
incurring harm with no benefit.
This is something even a common man would not do,
let alone the Son of Heaven!"
The Emperor agreed,
and issued an edict to Déyù to return the city to the Tǔbō,
and to hand over Xīdámóu and all those who came with him.
The Tǔbō executed them all at the border,
with extreme cruelty.
Déyù's resentment towards Sēngrú deepened greatly because of this.
This lays the groundwork for Lǐ Déyù's subsequent argument regarding Wéizhōu during Emperor Wǔzōng's reign.
10 In winter,
the tenth month,
on *wùyín*,
Lǐ Déyù reported that Nánzhào had invaded Cuīzhōu,
capturing three counties.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on *rénzǐ*,
an edict was issued to release prisoners due to drought and floods.
The court officials requested to confer an honored title, calling him Emperor Tàihé Wǔwǔ Zhìdé;
Wéi Wēn, the Right *Bǔquē*, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Now that floods and drought are causing disaster,
I fear this is not the time to adorn with glorious titles."
The Emperor approved of this,
and declined to accept.
2 In the third month,
on *xīnchǒu*,
Wáng Zhìxīng, the Wǔníng Jiédùshǐ, was concurrently appointed Shìzhōng
and made Chóngwǔ Jiédùshǐ;
Lǐ Tīng, the Bīnníng Jiédùshǐ, was made Wǔníng Jiédùshǐ.
3 Huíhú Zhāolǐ Kèhán was killed by his subordinates,
and his nephew, Hútèlè, was enthroned.
4 When Lǐ Tīng previously governed Wǔníng,
there was a *cāngtóu* who became a *yájiàng*.
Consulting the old and new histories,
Lǐ Tīng had never previously governed Wǔníng.
I suspect this *cāngtóu* might have followed Tīng's elder brother, Yuàn Sù, who governed Wǔníng,
and thus became a *yájiàng*.
Tīng first sent a trusted aide to Xúzhōu to express solicitude to the generals and soldiers.
The *cāngtóu*, not wanting Tīng to return,
persuaded the soldiers
to kill the aide
and cannibalize him.
Tīng was afraid,
and firmly declined due to illness.
On *xīnyǒu*,
Gāo Yǔ, the former Chóngwǔ Jiédùshǐ, was made Wǔníng Jiédùshǐ.
5 In summer,
the fifth month,
on *jiǎchén*,
Lǐ Déyù reported the repair of Qiónglái Guān and the relocation of Cuīzhōu's administrative seat to Táidēngchéng.
Qiónglái Guān
is sometimes written Qióngxiá Guān,
which is incorrect.
Qiónglái Guān is in Yǎzhōu's Róngjīngxiàn,
the so-called Qiónglái Jiǔzhé Bǎn,
where Wáng Zūn scolded his driver.
Zhù Mù said: Qiónglái Guān is ninety *lǐ* north of Cuīzhōu.
Cuīzhōu was previously administered from Yuècuīxiàn.
Sòng Bái said: Yuècuī
was the Han-era Qióngdū region.
Táidēng
was the Han-era Máoniú region.
Lǐ Xīnchuán said: Qiónglái Guān
is near Róngjīng,
sixty *lǐ* from Lízhōu.
6 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Yuán Wáng Kuí passed away.
Kuí
was a son of Dàizōng.
7 In winter,
the tenth month,
on *jiǎzǐ*,
Lǔ Wáng Yǒng was established as Crown Prince.
Initially,
the Emperor considered Jìn Wáng Pǔ,
the eldest son of Jìngzōng,
who was cautious and earnest,
wishing to make him his heir.
He happened to die—
Jìn Wáng Pǔ died in the second year of Tàihé,
see the previous volume—
so the discussion of establishing an heir had been long delayed,
and it was only now that it was carried out.
8 In the eleventh month,
on *yǐmǎo*,
Duàn Wénchāng, the Jīngnán Jiédùshǐ, was made Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ.
Wáng Jiànyán, the Xīchuān Jiānjūn, entered the court to manage the Bureau of Military Affairs (*Shūmì*),
and repeatedly told the Emperor:
"Handing over Xīdámóu to appease the barbarians' hearts
cuts off all future surrenders,
which is not a good strategy."
The Emperor also regretted it,
particularly blaming Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Niú Sēngrú for the miscalculation.
Those allied with Lǐ Déyù then said
"Sēngrú has a grudge against Déyù and sabotaged his achievement."
The Emperor grew even more distant from him.
*Yóu*
means to consider it a fault or transgression.
*Shū*
means feelings are not close.
It happened that the Emperor was presiding over Yányīng,
and said to the chancellors:
"When will there be peace under Heaven?
Do you also have intentions regarding this?"
He reproached them for holding office without performing their duties,
and having no desire to assist in governing and promoting culture.
Sēngrú replied, "Peace has no fixed form.
Today, the four barbarians do not invade each other,
and the common people are not scattered.
Although this is not perfect governance—
*zhìlǐ*
is equivalent to *zhìzhì*
and *kāng*
means peace—
it is not within the reach of us ministers."
After withdrawing,
he said to his colleagues:
"The Emperor's expectations are such that
how can we long remain in this position?"
He then submitted repeated memorials requesting to resign.
In the twelfth month,
on *yǐchǒu*,
Sēngrú, as Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was made Huáinán Jiédùshǐ.
Your subject, Sīmǎ Guāng 司馬光, says: When the ruler is enlightened and the ministers are loyal,
superiors issue orders and inferiors obey,
talented and good people are in office,
sycophants and villains are dismissed and kept at a distance,
rites are observed and music is performed,
punishments are fair and government is just,
traitors and bandits disappear,
weapons of war are sheathed,
feudal lords submit,
the four barbarian tribes are brought to submission,
families have enough and people are prosperous –
this is the manifestation of Great Peace.
At this time,
eunuchs monopolized power,
coercing the emperor from within,
and he could not keep them at a distance;
provincial governors held military power,
acting arrogantly from without,
and he could not control them;
soldiers killed and drove out their commanders,
defying orders and establishing themselves,
and he could not interrogate them;
military campaigns were launched annually,
taxes and levies grew more urgent daily,
bones and flesh lay scattered across the fields,
and looms and spinning wheels in the villages were empty –
yet Niú Sēngrú 牛僧孺 called this Great Peace.
Is this not a fabrication!
At the time Wénzōng 文宗 sought to bring order,
Niú Sēngrú 牛僧孺 held the office of assisting the ruler.
When promoted, he sought comfort and favor to usurp his position;
when demoted, he deceived the emperor and misled the world to steal a reputation.
What greater crime is there than this!
According to the *Book of Documents*’s “Juǒng Mìng” 冏命,
“morning and evening assist the ruler,”
which did not exclusively refer to prime ministers.
Wēn Gōng 溫公 adopted the meaning of assisting and supporting,
and thus considered it the responsibility of the prime minister.
Moreover, the Duke criticized Niú Sēngrú 牛僧孺 for his conduct in advancement and retreat,
also implying those who later usurped positions and stole reputations like Sēngrú 僧孺.
Zhì 治,
is pronounced like the characters “zhí lì” 直吏.
9 Zhēn Wáng Chéng 珍王誠 died.
The *New Book* states:
“Chéng” 誠
is written
as “Chéng” 諴.
Chéng 諴 was
Dézōng’s 德宗 son.
10On the *Yǐhài* 乙亥 day,
Liú Cóngjiàn 劉從諫, Military Governor of Zhāoyì 昭義, entered court.
11On the *Dīngwèi* 丁未 day,
Lǐ Déyù 李德裕, former Military Governor of Xīchuān 西川, was appointed Minister of War.
Earlier,
Lǐ Zōngmǐn 李宗閔 and Déyù 德裕 had a quarrel,
the details of which can be found in Volume 241, Mùzōng’s 穆宗 Chángqìng 長慶 first year.
The emperor regarded Déyù 德裕 with great favor,
and he was soon to become prime minister.
Zōngmǐn 李宗閔 tried every means to thwart this but failed.
Dù Cóng 杜悰, Mayor of Jīngzhào 京兆, was a partisan of Zōngmǐn 李宗閔.
He once visited Zōngmǐn 李宗閔,
and seeing him look worried,
said:
“Is it not about the great military official?”
The Ministry of War manages military affairs,
and the Minister is its head.
Therefore, Cóng 杜悰 used a veiled reference to call him the great military official.
“Indeed.
How can you help me?”
Cóng 杜悰 said:
“I have a plan
that can resolve your long-standing grudge,
but I fear you cannot use it.”
Zōngmǐn 李宗閔 said:
“What is it?”
Cóng 杜悰 said:
“Déyù 李德裕 is learned but did not enter through the imperial examinations.
He often feels dissatisfied by this.
If he were made examiner of the imperial examinations,
he would surely be pleased.”
Zhī jǔ 知舉 means
Zhī gòng jǔ 知貢舉 (examiner of the imperial examinations).
He said:
Jiān 間
is pronounced as written.
“Think of a second option.”
Cóng 杜悰 said:
“Otherwise, appoint him as Grand Censor.”
Zōngmǐn 李宗閔 said:
“This would be acceptable.”
Cóng 杜悰 repeatedly discussed and agreed with him,
then went to visit Déyù 李德裕.
Déyù 李德裕 greeted him with a bow, saying:
“Why do you visit this quiet place?”
Cóng 杜悰 said:
“Jìng’ān Xiànggōng 靖安相公 sent me to convey his message.”
Lǐ Zōngmǐn 李宗閔 resided in Jìng’ān Fāng 靖安坊,
and was therefore referred to by this name;
similar to how Liú Chóngwàng 劉崇望 later resided in Guāngdé Fāng 光德坊,
and was called Guāngdé Liúgōng 光德劉公.
Déyù 李德裕 was surprised and delighted, tears streaming down,
and said:
“This is a great official position at the imperial gate.”
According to Táng 唐 regulations:
at grand court assemblies,
the Grand Censor led his subordinates in arranging the ranks of all officials.
At dawn, they arrayed themselves between the two towers.
Hence, it was considered a great official position at the imperial gate.
“Please convey my repeated gratitude.”
Zōngmǐn 李宗閔 then conspired with the Palace Aide Yáng Yúqīng 楊虞卿,
and the matter was consequently suspended.
Niú Sēngrú 牛僧孺 was heavily afflicted by the fear of loss,
while Lǐ Déyù 李德裕 had a keen desire for advancement.
This is what is called,
if Chǔ 楚 lost,
Qí 齊 did not necessarily gain either.
He was the younger brother of Yáng Rǔshì 楊汝士.
Yáng Rǔshì 楊汝士 is mentioned in Volume 241, Mùzōng’s 穆宗 Chángqìng 長慶 first year.
1 Spring,
First month,
on the *Jiǎwǔ* 甲午 day,
Liú Cóngjiàn 劉從諫, Military Governor of Zhāoyì 昭義, was promoted to Concurrent Prime Minister,
and sent back to his garrison.
Originally,
Cóngjiàn 劉從諫 considered himself loyal and righteous.
Upon entering court,
he wished to request another garrison.
Upon his arrival,
he saw that the court’s authority was divided,
and many high officials made solicitations.
He thus began to hold the court lightly.
The *Kǎoyì* 考異 states: The *Bǔ Guóshǐ* 補國史 states:
“During Wénzōng’s 文宗 reign,
Liú Cóngjiàn 劉從諫 had an audience at court,
and received abundant favors.
He considered himself unparalleled among the regional lords of Héshuò 河朔,
and somewhat boasted of his loyalty as a subject.
All civil and military officials flocked to his door.
Cóngjiàn 劉從諫 widely distributed gold and silks,
bribing various influential figures,
seeking to ascend to a prime ministerial seat.
Most people agreed,
but Prime Minister Lǐ Gùyán 李固言 alone said nothing.
Cóngjiàn 劉從諫 wanted to gain his favor,
but ‘jade cannot be stained.’
He wanted to flatter his intentions,
but ‘water cannot be pierced.’
His attendants dared not lead his sincere entreaties.
During a holiday,
he visited Gùyán’s 固言 private residence,
expressing his sincere and earnest feelings,
even repeatedly.
The Prime Minister sternly said to him: ‘Your late father, Púyè 僕射, with his achievements in Dōngpíng 東平,
governed Lù 潞 for over twenty years.
After his death,
you, Púyè 僕射, took charge of military affairs,
and thus received the imperial appointment.
The court, considering your late father’s merits,
did not cease rewarding and extending them,
allowing you to hold a frontier command,
a position as important as a minister of the Southern Palace.
How can this be considered grace exceeding your station,
and for what would you repay the nation with loyalty?
If you, Púyè 僕射, were to request a frontier garrison,
to greatly expand your strategies,
and recover territory and borders,
that would be a meritorious achievement.
Would the court not, considering the gravity of the prime ministerial office,
bestow rewards and titles for such accomplishments?
How can you so easily seek it with such petty impatience!
I used to believe that you, Púyè 僕射, were heroic and loyal,
foremost among frontier officials.
But now you seek to wear the prime ministerial seal,
carry the imperial staff,
and return gloriously to your old domain.
This is merely what ordinary stubborn frontier officials of Héshuò 河朔 do.
Where is your loyalty and integrity?
I am deeply disheartened.’
Cóngjiàn 劉從諫 was startled and silenced,
bowing twice and hurrying out.
However, Cóngjiàn 劉從諫 heavily bribed favored officials,
and within ten days, he was indeed granted the Concurrent Prime Minister title with his current office,
and promptly resigned to return to his garrison.
The prime ministers bid him farewell at the post station.
Prime Minister Lǐ 李 said to him: ‘You, Prime Minister, are young and flourishing.
Strive to repay the national grace,
and hopefully protect your family,
lest you bring calamity upon your descendants.’
Cóngjiàn 劉從諫 struck his head with his tablet,
shed tears, and departed.
Upon reaching his garrison,
he said to his subordinates and officers: ‘Yesterday, when I had an audience at the imperial court,
I observed all the court’s virtues.
Only Lǐ Gōng 李公 was upright and clear,
awe-inspiring and venerable,
truly a great minister of the state!’”
However, Gùyán 固言 was not a prime minister this year,
so this account is erroneous.
Now we follow the *Shílù* 實錄 (Veritable Records).
This serves as an explanation for Liú Cóngjiàn’s 劉從諫 stubbornness.
2 After Wáng Zhìxīng in Xúzhōu,
the soldiers were arrogant and unruly,
and Military Governor Gāo Yǔ could not control them;
the Emperor was concerned about this.
On *jiǎyín* [day],
Cuī Gǒng, the Military Governor of Lǐngnán, was appointed Military Governor of Wǔníng.
When Gǒng arrived at the commandery,
he governed with appropriate leniency and strictness,
and the people of Xúzhōu found peace.
Gǒng
was Guǎn’s younger brother.
For Cuī Guǎn,
see five years above.
3 In the second month,
on *guǐhài* [day],
Yáng Zhìchéng, the Military Governor of Lúlóng and acting Minister of Public Works, was promoted to acting Minister of Personnel.
Envoy Xú Dí
Xú Dí
was an envoy from Lúlóng.
Sòng Bái said: In the first month of Dàlì 12th year,
an imperial edict stipulated that all circuits should first establish a temporary commander for the capital,
and all were to be changed to chief envoys of their respective circuits.
“(He said:) ‘The military does not understand the court's system.
They only know that a Minister changing to Grand Councillor is a promotion,
but do not know that a Minister of Public Works changing to Minister of Personnel is a betterment.
If the imperial envoy goes there,
I fear he will not be allowed to leave.’ ”
Since the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
the Minister of Personnel was considered the Grand Minister,
and no other departmental minister dared to compare.
How could the envoys from the various Táng prefectures not know this?
That Xú Dí dared to go to the Grand Councillor and utter these words
was simply because inferiors had become so overbearing towards superiors that they had no scruples.
“The imperial envoy will not be allowed to leave” meant that he would certainly be detained.
The Grand Councillors did not take it seriously.
4 On *bǐngxū* [day],
Lǐ Déyù, the Minister of War, was made concurrently Grand Councillor.
When Déyù entered to express thanks,
the Emperor discussed factionalism with him,
and he replied:
“Currently, one-third of the court officials belong to factions.”

At that time, Yáng Yúqīng, a Supervising Secretary, along with his cousin Rǔ Shì, a drafter in the Central Secretariat, his younger brother Hàn Gōng, a Director in the Ministry of Revenue, Zhāng Yuánfū, a drafter in the Central Secretariat, and Xiāo Huàn, a Supervising Secretary, etc., were adept at forming connections.
They relied on powerful figures,
interfering with the administration above,
and obstructing the relevant departments below,
seeking official positions and examination degrees for scholars.
They always succeeded.
The Emperor heard of this and disliked it,
so when he spoke with Déyù, he brought up this matter first;
Déyù then took the opportunity to oppose those he disliked.
An old saying regarding the Niú-Lǐ affair
stated that Déyù used Yān fá Yān (Yan to attack Yan),
a saying with much truth in it.
Zhāng Zhòngfāng, a Left Palace Aide, once challenged Lǐ Jífǔ's posthumous name.
When Lǐ Jífǔ died,
the officials gave him the posthumous name Jìngxiàn.
Zhāng Zhòngfāng, a Director in the Ministry of Finance, argued that it was too generous.
Because of this, Xiànzōng demoted Zhòngfāng
and bestowed the posthumous name Zhōngyì.
Sòng Bái said: According to Táng regulations,
when an official of the third rank or higher, or a detached official of the second rank or higher, died,
subordinate clerks would record their conduct and report it to the Ministry of Merit and Promotion.
Their previous appointments would be checked and verified,
and then submitted to the Court of Imperial Sacrifices for a proposed posthumous name.
After that, it would be reported again to the Ministry of Merit and Promotion.
The officials of the Grand Council would then deliberate and decide,
and only then would it be reported to the Emperor.
If someone possessed profound virtue in reclusion,
and their reputation and achievements were clearly evident,
even without official rank,
a posthumous title of "Teacher" could also be requested for them.
Zhòngfāng claimed illness and did not come out.
In the third month,
on *rénchén* [day],
Zhòngfāng was appointed as Guest Service Official, Divided Office.
5 Yáng Zhìchéng was angered that he did not receive the post of Grand Councillor,
and detained Wèi Bǎoyì, the Imperial Edict Envoy, as well as Jiāo Fèngluán, the Spring Robe Envoy, and Yǐn Shìgōng, the envoy for sending the Xī and Qìdān.
After the middle period of Táng,
whenever a military governor received an additional title,
an imperial envoy was usually sent to convey the order,
who was called the Imperial Edict Envoy.
Jiāo Fèngluán for delivering spring robes,
and Yǐn Shìgōng for escorting the envoys of the two tribes,
had all arrived in Yōuzhōu at the same time,
and thus were all detained by him.
On *jiǎwǔ* [day],
he sent his adjutant Wáng Wényǐng to express gratitude and decline the office.
On *bǐngshēn* [day],
the official patent and an imperial rescript were again bestowed upon him.
Since the Táng dynasty,
whenever an official declined an office,
there was always an imperial rescript declining to disapprove the appointment.
6 Héwáng Qǐ passed away.
Qǐ
was the son of Shùnzōng.
7 On *gēngxū* [day],
Yáng Yúqīng was made Prefect of Chángzhōu,
and Zhāng Yuánfū was made Prefect of Rǔzhōu.
The Táng dynasty established Chángzhōu from the Suí dynasty's Pílíng Commandery;
it was 2,843 *lǐ* southeast of the capital.
The Suí dynasty established Yīzhōu in Xiāngchéng Commandery,
which was later renamed Rǔzhōu;
it was 982 *lǐ* east of the capital.
The Emperor again spoke of factionalism,
and Lǐ Zōngmǐn said:
“Your servant has long known about it,
which is why I have not given Yúqīng and his kind important offices.”

Mù (牧) probably refers to the *Jiédùshǐ* (節度使) of that time.
In the poem *Cǎishú* (采菽),
'dian the domains of the Son of Heaven' (殿天子之邦).
Máo Shì's (毛氏) commentary says: *diàn* (殿)
means 'to guard'.
Its pronunciation is *dīng liàn fān*.
Weapons and armor are dull and worn out;
this is due to the failure to drill and train.
This is the first failing.
A hundred men carry halberds,
living off government provisions,
but bear the name of a thousand men.
Great generals and lesser aides
pocket the surplus.
'Lesser aide'
refers to a *bìjiàng* (裨將).
*Cāo* (操)
is pronounced *qī dāo fān*.
They take pleasure in the army's prolonged idleness.
Thus, those actually bearing arms are always few,
