This is the failing of not demanding actual numbers for provisions.
This is the second failing.
When they win a minor victory, they exaggerate their achievements,
rushing to present reports to solicit great rewards.
Sometimes they receive two awards in a day,
or multiple enfeoffments in a month.
Before the triumphant return song is sung,
their official rank has already been elevated.
'Win a battle'
means to play a triumphal song upon returning.
'Official rank'
refers to recording their official grade.
*Huán* (還)
is pronounced *xuán*.
Their land and mansions are vast,
'land and mansions'
is like saying 'land and residences'.
Their descendants are appointed to office.
How could they be willing to seek out danger and face death,
to exert themselves for us!
This is the failing of excessive rewards.
This is the third failing.
If they lose many soldiers and overturn great cities,
they simply flee to the capital,
then get demoted to a prefecture and depart.
'Flee to the capital'
means escaping to the capital city.
'Demoted to a prefecture and depart'
means being demoted to *cìshǐ* (刺史).
*Sàng* (喪)
is pronounced *xī làng fān*.
Their demeanor is quite calm.
Before a year passes,
they are already standing on the altar steps again.
'Standing on the altar steps'
means being reinstated to the altar of a great general.
This is the fourth failing.
Great generals are not allowed to wield military authority exclusively.
Favored officials and imperial envoys come one after another to command them.
'Favored officials'
also refers to eunuchs who rely on imperial favor.
Just as the drums are about to sound,
one says it must be an 'eclipsing moon' formation,
another says it must be a 'fish scale' formation.
The whole army of ten thousand men
swirls and wanders in confusion and alarm.
'Swirls and wanders'
means 'to wander',
'to hesitate'.
*Huǎng* (愰)
is pronounced *hū guǎng fān*.
Then they (the enemy) capture our drums and banners.
This is the failing of not entrusting responsibility and requiring accountability.
This is the fifth failing.
If one truly wishes to prepare for war and clear away the filth now,
but then follows the previous wrongs,
it cannot be done."
He also wrote a discourse on maintaining the state,
thinking:
"Those who debate today all say: 'For the stubborn and recalcitrant,
we use good generals and strong soldiers as reins and bit,
and high positions and splendid titles to fill their stomachs.
They are kept peaceful and not defiant,
held externally and not unrestrained.
This is like raising and taming tigers and wolves without displeasing their hearts.'
Hùan (豢),
means 'to raise'.
Rǎo (擾),
means 'to tame',
'to comply'.
Fú (拂),
is read as fú (咈).
This is how the state was maintained during Dàlì and Zhēnyuán periods.
Why must we fight fiercely,
tormenting our people,
and only then be satisfied?"
I, your humble servant, say: Between the Dàlì and Zhēnyuán periods,
this very approach led to disaster.
At that time,
if someone held a few dozen cities
and a thousand or a hundred soldiers,
the imperial court would treat them exceptionally,
leniently applying laws to them.
Thereupon, they would look arrogant and speak boastfully,
establishing their own households,
breaking regulations and eroding laws,
vying for power and luxury.
The Son of Heaven would cultivate his prestige and not question them,
and the officials would maintain tranquility and not reprimand them.
Princes and marquises would be granted titles,
transcending established records to receive them.
Fán shǎng gōng zhě lù qí gōng ér jiā zhī fēng jué (凡賞功者錄其功而加之封爵) means recording their achievements and bestowing titles upon them.
Wú gōng ér yuè chāo shòu zhī yǐ jué (無功而超越授之以爵), means bestowing titles upon them without merit, transcending established rules.
This is called yuè lù (越錄).
Shòu (受),
is read as shòu (授).
They would be supported with armrests and staffs.
Yán bù cháo zhě cì zhī jī zhàng (言不朝者賜之几杖), means those who did not attend court were granted armrests and staffs,
to appease their hearts.
Imperial princes would marry into their families.
Xī (息),
means 'son'.
Yìn (胤),
means 'heir', 'successor'.
The sons of border generals in Héběi
mostly married princesses.
Nothing was left unprovided.
As a result, their territories expanded,
their armies grew stronger,
their usurpations and imitations became more egregious,
and their extravagant ambitions flourished.
Consequently, land and official positions,
were almost entirely partitioned,
but the greedy hearts of these rogues
had not yet reached their limit.
So they assumed excessive names and titles,
some becoming emperors or kings,
forming alliances and swearing oaths of independence,
calmly and fearlessly,
sending out soldiers to plunder in all directions to satisfy their ambitions.
Thus, Zhào, Wèi, Yān, and Qí rose up and proclaimed loudly,
and Liáng, Cài, Wú, and Shǔ followed suit and echoed them.
This refers to Zhū Tāo, Wáng Wǔjùn, Tián Yuè, and Lǐ Nà establishing themselves as kings.
Lǐ Xīliè, Lǐ Qí, and Liú Pì then caused chaos.
Hé (和),
is read as huò (戶臥翻).
Those who wished to emulate them
were found everywhere.
When the times encountered Xiàowǔ,
referring to Xiànzōng,
Xiāo (宵),
means 'donning clothes at night',
referring to putting on clothes before dawn.
Gàn (旰),
means 'eating late',
referring to eating at sunset.
Pondering at night and deliberating in the morning,
he was able to eliminate the powerful [threats] and bring the lesser ones back.
Otherwise,
the outskirts of Zhōu and Qín
would have nearly become hunting grounds for trespassers!
Jǐ wéi fàn liè zāi (幾為犯獵哉) means they would almost become grounds for illegal hunting.
The outskirts of Zhōu and Qín
refer to Hénán and Guānnèi.
If desires are not fulfilled, anger arises;
if anger arises, contention and chaos follow.
Therefore, there are teachings and corporal punishment in the family,
laws and penalties in the state,
and military expeditions throughout the realm.
This is how desires are curbed and contention is suppressed.
Between the Dàlì and Zhēnyuán periods,
they completely reversed this principle,
attempting to quell boundless contention with meager possessions.
Qū qū zhī yǒu (區區之有),
refers to the imperial court's titles and appointments.
Sāi (塞),
is read as sè (悉則翻).
They were almost unable to move or wield power.
Now, people do not realize this error,
but instead take it as a principle.
Jīng (經),
means 'constant principle'.
Alas!
The state-maintaining strategy of Dàlì and Zhēnyuán,
let us forever take heed of it!"
He also annotated Sūnzǐ,
writing a preface for it,
in which he believed:
"Military affairs
are a form of punishment;
a great punishment,
using weapons and armor.
They are also matters of governance.
For disciples of the Master (Kǒngzǐ),
these were truly the affairs of Zhòngyóu and Rǎnyǒu.
I do not know from which era or by whom it was divided into two paths, 'civil' and 'military',
operating separately.
This caused gentry scholars to not dare speak of military matters,
or even to be ashamed to speak of them.
If anyone did speak of them,
the world considered them coarse, violent, and strange,
not to be counted among respectable people.
Alas!
Losing the foundation,
this is the most severe loss!
The Lǐ Jì says: 'If the four borders are full of fortresses,
this is the disgrace of the qīng and dàfū.'
This records the words from Qū Lǐ.
Establishing a state
and destroying a state
has never happened without military means.
Those who command armies must be sagacious, wise, capable, knowledgeable, and widely learned scholars to achieve success,
deliberating in the imperial court.
Once the military situation is settled,
then it is entrusted to generals.
Hànzǔ said: 'Those who point out tracks are people.'
Zhǐ zōng (指蹤),
refers to pointing out animal tracks.
This differs slightly from the Hàn Shū in how the meaning is derived from the text.
This interpretation is correct.
Those who serve as prime ministers say:
'Military affairs are not my business;
I ought not to know about them.'
The jūnzi says: 'One should not occupy that position then!'"
Observing Wēn Gōng's adoption of Dù Mù's words,
one can see his usual elucidation of the duties of a prime minister.
17Formerly, Zhèng Zhù (鄭注), the Military Commissioner of Bīnnìng (邠寧),
relied on Wáng Shǒuchéng (王守澄).
His power and influence were overwhelming,
and the emperor deeply detested him.
In the ninth month,
on the day bǐngyín (丙寅),
Li Kǔan (李款), a Palace Censor, submitted a memorial impeaching Zhù from within the palace:
“He secretly communicates with imperial envoys
and openly connects with court officials,
travelling back and forth between two places.”
“Two places”
refers to his going back and forth between the Southern Secretariat (Nányá) and the Northern Bureau (Běisī).
The character 使 (shǐ)
is pronounced suò lì.
The character 朝 (cháo)
is pronounced zhí yáo.
“He lurks by day and acts by night,
usurping imperial authority.
People dare not speak,
but communicate with their eyes on the roads.
I request that he be handed over to the judicial authorities.”
Within ten days,
dozens of memorials were submitted.
Shǒuchéng hid Zhù in the Right Army (Yòujūn).
Wáng Shǒuchéng was then the Right Army Eunuch Commissioner (Yòujūn Zhōngwèi),
thus he could hide Zhù.
Li Hóngchǔ (李弘楚), a general of the Left Army (Zuǒjūn), said to Wéi Yuánsù (韋元素):
“Zhèng Zhù is unmatched in treachery and cunning.
If this fledgling (卵鷇) is not eliminated,
and is allowed to grow wings,
he will surely become a national calamity.
Now, because he has been impeached by the Censor, he is hidden in the army.
Hóngchǔ requests to use the Zhōngwèi’s intention,
falsely claiming to be ill,
and summon him to treat it.
When he arrives, the Zhōngwèi will invite him to sit,
and Hóngchǔ will attend at his side.
Upon a signal glance from the Zhōngwèi,
we will seize him and beat him to death.
The Zhōngwèi can then go before the emperor, kowtow and beg for forgiveness,
and fully explain his villainy.
Yáng and Wáng will surely assist the Zhōngwèi in speaking.”
Yáng and Wáng
refer to Yáng Chénghé (楊承和) and Wáng Jiànyán (王踐言).
At the end of the Yuánhé (元和) reign,
when Mùzōng (穆宗) was enthroned,
Wéi Yuánsù also had the merit of participating in the decisive planning.
Yuánsù considered it sound
and summoned him.
When Zhù arrived,
he was obsequious and groveling (蠖屈鼠伏),
and flattering words flowed like a spring.
Yuánsù unconsciously held his hand and conversed intimately,
listening attentively and forgetting his weariness.
Hóngchǔ watched and waited
again and again,
but Yuánsù paid him no heed,
lavishly gifted Zhù with gold and silk, and sent him away.
Hóngchǔ angrily said:
“The Zhōngwèi missed today’s opportunity to act decisively,
and will surely not escape future disaster!”
He then resigned his military post and left.
Soon after,
a carbuncle erupted on his back, and he died.
Wáng Yá (王涯)’s appointment as chancellor
was influenced by Zhù;
this must have been through Zhù to connect with Wáng Shǒuchéng.
Consequently, Li Kǔan’s memorial was suppressed.
Shǒuchéng spoke to the emperor about Zhù and had him released.
Soon, he was appointed Palace Censor (Shìyùshǐ)
and concurrently Administrator of the Right Shence Army (Yòushéncè Pànguān).
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Kāichéng Jìshì* says:
“In the fifth year,
Mèng Wénliàng (孟文亮), a general of the Jinwu Army (Jīnwǔ Jiāngjūn), was sent to garrison Bīnjiāo (邠郊).
Because of his marital relations with Zhù,
he memorialized to have him appointed Military Commissioner (Jūnsīmǎ).
Passing through Fèngtiān (奉天),
Wáng Cóngliàng (王從亮), the Defense Commissioner (Fángèshǐ) and Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Dàfū), disdained his character
and did not treat him with proper courtesy.
Zhù slandered Cóngliàng to Shǒuchéng,
who ultimately framed him,
had him beaten with a stick and banished.
Not long after,
Wénliàng died,
and Zhù was dismissed from his post and returned to the city.
Shǒuchéng secretly installed him as a military strategist.
At that time, Liú Cóngjiàn (劉從諫) of Zélù (澤潞) initially wanted to execute Zhù,
but fearing his power and influence,
instead appointed him Deputy Military Governor (Jiédù Fùshǐ).
As soon as he arrived in Lùzhōu (潞州),
within a span of ten days,
the emperor happened to recover from his illness.
In the eleventh month of the seventh year of Dàhé (大和),
he was urgently summoned to the capital.
It happened to be that time,
and the Sacred Body recovered.
The emperor was pleased with him.
From then on, his imperial favor gradually grew,
and all officials in the court, provinces, prefectures, counties, and military
followed his lead.
On the thirteenth day of the ninth month of the seventh year,
Palace Censor Li Kǔan impeached Zhù, saying: ‘He secretly communicates with imperial envoys
and openly connects with court officials,
travelling back and forth between two places,
seeking wealth through divination,
lurking by day and acting by night,
usurping imperial authority.
People dare not speak,
but communicate with their eyes on the roads.
His influence is growing stronger,
and he may become a source of disaster.
His crime is unforgivable,
and he should be publicly executed.
Zhèng Zhù should be handed over to the proper authorities.’
At that time, Wáng Yá held a prominent position in the court,
which was due to Zhù.
Moreover, fearing Shǒuchéng’s factional support,
the memorial was suppressed and not acted upon.
Zhù then secretly absconded to a military command.”
Li Déyù (李德裕)’s *Wénwǔ Liǎngcháo Xiàntì Jì* states:
“In the late spring of the eighth year,
the emperor sighed to the chancellors about the lack of skilled doctors in the realm,

who was proficient in dietetics and elixirs.
Some wished to place him in the Hanlin Academy of Arts and Techniques (Hànlín Jìshù Yuàn),
others wanted him to be the Administrator of the Left Shence Army (Zuǒshéncè Pànguān).
Zhù himself claimed that as an official, he did not desire such positions.
Shǒuchéng then used Cóngjiàn’s memorial to have him appointed Military Commissioner (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ).
When he went to take up his post,
Zōngmǐn (宗閔) again sent Yáng Jiǎn (楊儉), an administrator from Shānnán (山南), to Zélù (澤潞) to make an agreement with Cóngjiàn,
ordering him to recommend Zhù for re-entry to the capital.”
Now, we follow the *Shílù*.
18On the day jiǎyín (甲寅),

19When the ministers and above

Tóng and Huà
refer to Tóngzhōu (同州) and Huàzhōu (華州).

He then rewarded Jìléng with a Tōngtiān sash.
A Tōngtiān rhinoceros-horn sash.

20On the day gēngzǐ (庚子),
the emperor first suffered a stroke (風疾)
and could not speak.
Thereupon, Wáng Shǒuchéng recommended Zhèng Zhù, the Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì (Zhāoyì Xíngjūn Sīmǎ), as a skilled physician.
The emperor summoned Zhù to the capital.
After drinking his medicine,
it proved quite effective,
and thus he gained imperial favor.
The seed of the Gānlù (甘露) Incident was sown.

The Eighth Year of Tàihé (太和八年)
(jiǎyín (甲寅), 834 CE)

in autumn,
eighth month,
Xīnmǎo,
the Emperor wanted to appoint Zhòngyán as a Jiànguān,
and place him in the Hànlín.
Lǐ Déyù said:
"Your Majesty must be fully aware of Zhòngyán's past actions.
How can he be placed among the close attendants?"
Officials of the Two Provinces were all close attendants.
"However, should we not allow him to correct his mistakes?"
He replied:
"I have heard that only Yán Huí could not repeat his mistakes.
The mistakes of those sages and worthies
were merely due to insufficient thought,
or straying from the middle path.
As for Zhòngyán's evil,
it is ingrained in his fundamental nature,
how can he truly reform!"
The Emperor said:
"Lǐ Féngjí recommended him,
and I do not wish to go back on my word."
He replied:
"Féngjí, as a chancellor,
recommended a treacherous person to mislead the state;
he is also a criminal."
The Emperor said:
"In that case, appoint him to another office."
He replied:
"That is also unacceptable."
The Emperor looked at Wáng Yá,
and Yá replied:
"Acceptable."
Déyù waved his hand to stop him. The Emperor turned and saw it,
his expression showing great displeasure, and then dismissed the matter.
Initially,
when Yá heard that the Emperor wanted to employ Zhòngyán,
he drafted an indignant memorial of remonstrance;
however, seeing the Emperor's firm intention,
and fearing the power of Zhòngyán's faction,
he changed his stance.
Soon after, Zhòngyán was appointed Sì mén zhùjiào.
Sì mén zhùjiào
was a rank eight official, junior grade.
Déyù was about to leave the Zhōngshū,
and he said to Yá:
"I am pleased that the Gěishìzhōng has sealed the edicts!"
Yá immediately summoned Sù and Cì and said:
"Lǐ Gōng has just left a message,
instructing the two Gélǎo not to seal the edicts."
"Liúyǔ"
refers to the words left behind when he was about to depart.
Officials of the two provinces called each other Gélǎo.
The next day,
this was reported to Déyù.
Déyù exclaimed in surprise:
"Déyù did not wish for the edicts to be returned sealed.
It should have been communicated to my face.
Why send someone to relay the message?
Moreover, if the Yǒusī seals and rejects something,
how can it still take the prime minister's intentions into account?!"
The two left disheartened.
In the ninth month,
on the Xīnhài day,
Zhèng Zhù, the Deputy Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì, was summoned to the capital.
Last year, Zhèng Zhù went to assist the Zhāoyì army,
a matter detailed in the previous volume.
As Lǐ Zōngmǐn, the Jìedùshǐ of Shānnánxīdào, was displeased with Déyù,
Zōngmǐn was brought in to counter him.
On the Rénxū day,
an imperial edict summoned Zōngmǐn from Xīngyuán.
7. In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Xīnsì day,
the Yōuzhōu army mutinied,
driving out Jìedùshǐ Yáng Zhìchéng and Supervising Eunuch Lǐ Huáiwǔ,
and promoted Commander Shǐ Yuánzhōng to take charge of the provisional administration.
8. On the Gēngyín day,
Lǐ Zōngmǐn was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
Lǐ Déyù, who was Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was dismissed as Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and made Jìedùshǐ of Shānnánxīdào.
On this day,
Lǐ Zhòngyán was appointed Hànlín Shìjiǎng Xuéshì.
Gěishìzhōng Gāo Zhū, Zhèng Sù, Hán Cì, Jiànyì Dàfū Guō Chénggǔ, and Zhōngshū Shèrén Quán Qú, among others, opposed it,
but could not prevent it.
Chénggǔ
was the grandson of Xī.
Xī
was the son of Guō Zǐyí.
This refers to the son of Déyú.
Quán Déyú
served as chancellor at the beginning of Yuánhé era.
Qú's pronunciation.
"Quán" is pronounced like "qiú" and "yú" as "fān".
9. On the Yǐsì day,
the Gòngyuàn requested the reintroduction of poetry and rhapsody examinations for Jinshi candidates,
which was granted.
In the Táng Dynasty, the Shàngshū Shěng was located to the east of the main street north of the Zhūquè Gate,
occupying an entire ward, with the Six Ministries attached alongside it.
In a separate ward in front of the Shàngshū Shěng was the southern court of the Lǐbù,
which was the Gòngyuàn.
The abolition of poetry and rhapsody examinations was mentioned in the previous volume, last year.
It was restored
because Lǐ Déyù had been dismissed from his chancellorship.
10. Lǐ Déyù presented a memorial to the emperor,
requesting to remain in the capital.
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
Déyù was appointed Bīngbù Shàngshū.
11. Yáng Zhìchéng passed through Tàiyuán.
Lǐ Zàiyì personally assaulted him,
intending to kill him.
Yáng Zhìchéng pursued Zàiyì, a matter detailed in the previous volume, fifth year.
"Ōu"
is pronounced "wū kǒu fān."
Zàiyì killed Zhìchéng's wife, children, and accompanying officers and soldiers.
The court, considering Zàiyì's merits,
did not pursue the matter.
Lǐ Zàiyì had achieved merit in pacifying Cāngjǐng.
"Jiàng"
is pronounced "jí liàng fān."
Zhìchéng's mother was buried in Yōuzhōu,
and Zhìchéng excavated and took her wealth.
Zàiyì memorialized requesting Zhìchéng's heart to sacrifice to his mother,
but this was not permitted.
12. In the eleventh month,
Wáng Tíngcòu, the Jìedùshǐ of Chéngdé, died.
The army enthroned his son, Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ Yuánkuí, to oversee the provisional administration.
Yuánkuí changed his father's ways,
treating the court with extreme deference.
13. Shǐ Yuánzhōng presented the imperial robes and other illicit items made by Yáng Zhìchéng.
On the Dīngmǎo day,
Zhìchéng was exiled to Lǐngnán,
and killed on the way.
14. Lǐ Zōngmǐn stated that since Lǐ Déyù's imperial mandate had already been issued,
he should not act on his own convenience.
This was in response to Déyù's self-request to remain in the capital.
On the Yǐhài day,
Déyù was again appointed Jìedùshǐ of Zhènhǎi,
and no longer concurrently held the title of Píngzhāngshì.
At that time, Déyù and Zōngmǐn each had their own factions,
pushing against and supporting each other.
Those not of their faction were pushed aside,
while those of the same faction were supported.
"Jǐ"
is pronounced "zǐ xī fān,"
and also "zǐ xì fān."
"Yuán"
is pronounced "yú yuán fān,"
and also "yú juàn fān."
He often sighed, saying:
"It is easier to remove the rebels in Héběi
than to remove the factionalism at court!"
Your servant Guāng says: The incompatibility between gentlemen and petty men
is like ice and charcoal, which cannot coexist in the same vessel.
Therefore, when a gentleman gains position, he dismisses petty men;
when a petty man gains power, he obstructs gentlemen.
This is a natural principle.
However, when a gentleman promotes the worthy and demotes the unworthy,
his heart is public-spirited,
and his criticisms are factual.
When a petty man praises what he likes and condemns what he dislikes,
his heart is self-serving,
and his criticisms are slanderous.
Public-spirited and factual conduct is called uprightness,
while self-serving and slanderous conduct is called factionalism.
It is up to the ruler to distinguish between them.
Thus, when an enlightened ruler is in charge:
he assesses virtue to arrange positions,
and measures ability to grant offices;
these are the words of Xún Qīngzǐ.
"Duó"
is pronounced "tuó luò fān."
"Liáng"
has the sound of "liáng."
The guilty are punished;
treachery cannot confuse him,
and flattery cannot sway him.
If this is the case,
how can factionalism arise?
A benighted ruler, however, is not like this.
He cannot see clearly,
nor can he make firm decisions;
the righteous and the wicked advance together,
and praise and criticism arrive simultaneously;
choices are not made by himself,
and power and favor secretly shift to others.
It is then that slanderers achieve their ambitions and the discourse of factionalism arises.
Just as wood rots and insects are born,
and vinegar sours and gnats gather,
so when there is factionalism at court, the ruler should blame himself and not blame his ministers.
If Wénzōng truly worried about the factionalism of his ministers,
why did he not examine whether their praises and criticisms were factual
or slanderous,
whether those they promoted or demoted were worthy
or unworthy,
whether their hearts were public-spirited
or self-serving,
and whether the people were gentlemen
or petty men?
If they were factual,
worthy,
public-spirited,
and gentlemen,
not only should their words be used,
but they should also be promoted.
If they were slanderous,
unworthy,
self-serving,
and petty men,
not only should their words be discarded,
but they should also be punished.
If this were done,
even if one tried to drive them to form factions,
who would dare?
To neglect this
and instead resent the difficulty of managing ministers,
is like not sowing or weeding and then resenting the overgrown fields.
If factionalism within the court cannot be eliminated,
how much less the rebels of Héběi!
Wēn Gōng's present argument was made for Xī and Fēng.
15. On the Bǐngzǐ day,
Lǐ Zhòngyán requested to change his name to Xùn.
16. Yōuzhōu reported that the Mòzhōu army had mutinied,
and the whereabouts of the Prefect, Zhāng Yuánfàn, were unknown.
17. In the twelfth month,
on the Jǐmǎo day,
Zhèng Zhù, the Deputy Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì, was appointed Tàipú Qīng.
Guō Chénggǔ repeatedly submitted memorials arguing against this,
but the emperor did not listen.
Thereupon, Zhù deceitfully submitted a memorial firmly declining the appointment,
and the emperor sent an imperial envoy to bestow the patent of appointment upon him a second time,
but he refused to accept it.
The historian records Zhèng Zhù's treacherous acts in extreme detail.
18th day of the guǐwèi cycle (of the 60-day calendar),
Shǐ Yuánzhōng was appointed acting Military Governor (liúhòu) of Lúlóng.
A Different Account says: The Veritable Records state: In the eleventh month,
Zhènzhōu reported that Shǐ Yuánzhōng, acting Military Governor of Yōuzhōu, had been driven out by the three armies of Yíng and Mò,
and his whereabouts were unknown.
Later records do not mention Yuánzhōng returning to Yōuzhōu,
but here there is a new appointment for him,
presumably because of the military unrest in Mòzhōu,
Zhènzhōu reported based on a mistaken rumor.
19th. At first,
Sòng Shēnxī and Imperial Censor-in-Chief Yǔwén Dǐng received a secret imperial edict to execute Zhèng Zhù,
and ordered Wáng Fán, Prefect of Jīngzhào, to capture him.
Fán secretly showed a "tángtiē" (Hall Document) to Wáng Shǒuchéng;
the document was issued by the Department of State Affairs (Zhèngshì Táng),
hence it was called a tángtiē.
Fán
pronounced fú yuán fān.
Wáng Shǒuchéng deeply appreciated Fán.
Fán also had a good relationship with Lǐ Xùn,
so Xùn and Zhù jointly recommended him,
and he was summoned from his post as Circuit Intendant (guānchásǐ) of Zhèxī to be Assistant Minister of the Left (shàngshū zuǒchéng).
Wáng Fán's dangerous and impetuous nature was certainly enough to bring disaster upon himself,
and historical accounts of his involvement in the Gānlù Incident also have their origins here.
1st day. In spring,
the first month,
on the yǐmǎo day,
Wáng Yuánkuí was appointed Military Governor (jiédùsǐ) of Chéngdé.
2nd day. Cháo Gōngcòu passed away,
and was posthumously granted the title Prince of Qí.
Zhāngwáng Còu was demoted to Cháo Gōng;
this event is recorded in Volume 5, Year 5.
3rd day. Zhèng Zhù submitted a memorial saying there were disasters in the Qín region,
and that public works should be undertaken to ward them off.
On the xīnmǎo day,
1,500 soldiers from the Left and Right Shéncè armies were dispatched to dredge the Qǔjiāng and Kūnmíng Ponds.
The Yōng Lù states: The Táng Qǔjiāng was originally Qín Gāizhōu.
In the Hàn dynasty, it became the Lèyóu Yuàn (Garden),
with the highest elevation and wide views in all directions.
When the Suí dynasty built the capital,
Yǔwén Kǎi considered its location in the southeastern corner of the capital,
being high and inconvenient, so he left this area vacant, not making it into residential blocks,
but instead excavated it to form a pond as an auspicious charm.
Also, the Huáng Qú river water flowed from outside the city from the south,
so the Suí dynasty then encompassed it from outside the city,
entering the city to form the Fúróng Chí (Lotus Pond),
and also becoming the Fúróng Yuán (Lotus Garden).
During Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's time,
the pond's circumference was over six lǐ,
in Táng it was seven lǐ,
occupying thirty qǐng of land,
and had been further expanded.
Its location was south of the Lónghuá Sì in the Shēngdào Fāng, southeast of the city.
Kūnmíng Chí,
excavated by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
was southwest of Cháng'ān,
with a circumference of forty lǐ.
The Sānfǔ Gùshì states: The pond's circumference was 320 qǐng.
The Cháng'ān Zhì states: It is now farmland.
If it could be used as farmland,
then it was not a place with water.
So where did the Hàn dynasty draw its water from?
The Cháng'ān Zhì, citing the Shuǐ Jīng, says: The Jiāoshuǐ flows west to the Shí'è,
created when Emperor Wǔ dug the Kūnmíng Chí.
There is a Shítà Yàn (Stone Weir),
thirty-two lǐ southwest of the county seat.
Thus, the Kūnmíng Chí, which was over 300 qǐng in circumference,
used the water from this weir.
Kūnmíng's base was high,
so its downstream flow could still be dammed and channeled for use by the capital city.
Consequently, three separate branches were dug alongside the city,
benefiting both inside and outside the city.
This pond still exists.
The Kuòdì Zhì states: The Fēng and Hào rivers were both dammed and diverted into Kūnmíng Chí,
with no remaining branches.
The Kuòdì Zhì was compiled during Emperor Tàizōng's reign,
so in the early Táng, it was still dammed and utilized,
and even during Emperor Wénzōng's time, it was still dredged.
Therefore, the Tújīng (Illustrated Gazetteer) must have been compiled after Emperor Wénzōng,
hence it had dried up and become farmland.
4th day. In the third month,
Jìwáng Jiū passed away.
Jiū was
Emperor Shùnzōng's son.
5th day. On the bǐngchén day,
Shǐ Yuánzhōng was appointed Military Governor (jiédùsǐ) of Lúlóng.
6th day. At first,
when Lǐ Déyù was Circuit Intendant (guānchásǐ) of Zhèxī, Dù Zhòngyáng, the wet nurse of Zhāngwáng, was exiled to Jīnlíng due to her involvement in Sòng Shēnxī's affair.
An imperial edict commanded Déyù to settle her.
At that time, Déyù had already left Zhèxī.
Fù Mǔ (Wet Nurse) means a female teacher.
Chǔ pronounced chāng lǚ fān.
Lí pronounced lì zhì fān.
Déyù was summoned from Zhèxī, as seen in Volume 5, Year 3;
he was stationed in Shǔ, as seen in Year 4;
the Sòng Shēnxī affair is seen in Year 5.
The chronological discrepancies should be investigated.
Assistant Minister of the Left Wáng Fán and Vice Minister of Revenue (hùbù shìláng) Lǐ Hàn memorialized that Déyù had heavily bribed Zhòngyáng,
secretly plotting with Zhāngwáng,
to commit treason.
The Emperor was extremely angry,
and summoned the chancellors, Fán, Hàn, Zhèng Zhù, and others to confront them.
Fán and Hàn vehemently slandered him,
but Lù Suí said:
"Déyù would not do such a thing.
If what you say is true,
then I should also be punished!"
The accusers then became somewhat silent.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Déyù was appointed to the secondary post of Bīnkè (Imperial Guest) with no practical duties.
7th day. On the guǐsì day,
Zhèng Zhù was appointed Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud (tàipúqīng),
concurrently Imperial Censor-in-Chief (yùshǐ dàfū).
Zhù finally accepted it,
and then recommended Lǐ Kuǎn, a Clerk in the Bureau of Provisions (cāngbù yuánwàiláng), to replace him, saying:
"Though the crime against me is groundless in principle;
Lǐ Kuǎn's sincerity
is truly serving the ruler with utmost loyalty."
Kuǎn's memorial against Zhù is found in the previous volume, previous year.
A Different Account: The Gānlù Jì states:
"Contemporary opinion sometimes held that Kuǎn outwardly sought a reputation for integrity but secretly served Zhù."
However, Kuǎn's impeachment memorial against Zhù exposed all his hidden wicked acts.
How could someone act in such a way against another and still secretly collude with him!
This was merely the suspicion of ordinary people at the time when they saw Zhù recommend Kuǎn to replace himself.
We do not adopt this view.
Xiào bù huài yán means to laugh without losing one's dignity.
8th day. On the bǐngshēn day,
Lù Suí, Minister of the Chancellery (ménxià shìláng) and Chancellor (tóng píngzhāngshì),
was appointed Military Governor (jiédùsǐ) of Zhènhǎi.
He was hurried to his post and
not permitted a farewell audience;
this was due to his defending Lǐ Déyù.
A Different Account says: The Old Suí Biography states:
"Déyù was demoted to Administrator (zhǎngshǐ) of Yuánzhōu,
and Suí did not sign the memorial, which was the beginning of Zhèng Zhù's resentment,
leading to his posting to Zhèxī."
However, according to the Veritable Records,
Suí's posting occurred four days before Déyù's demotion.
We do not adopt this view.
9th day. Initially,
Jiǎ Sù of Hénán, Prefect of Jīngzhào,
was narrow-minded, impetuous, and rash.
He had a grudge against Lǐ Déyù,
but was friendly with Lǐ Zōngmǐn and Zhèng Zhù.
On the Shangsì Festival,
a banquet was given for all officials at Qǔjiāng.
In ancient times, the Shangsì was precisely the first sì day of the third month;
from the Wèi dynasty onwards, it was simply held on the third day of the third month,
no longer necessarily on a sì day.
During the Zhēnyuán era of Táng, three "Orderly Festivals" were established,
allowing officials to choose scenic locations for recreation,
and the third day of the third month was one of them.
The Yin (Prefect) usually dismounted outside the main gate
and bowed to the Imperial Censors.
Sù, relying on his noble status and influence,
rode straight in.
Yang Jiǎn and Sū Tè, Attendant Censors in the Palace (diànzhōng shìyùshǐ), argued with him.
Sù cursed, saying:
"You yellow-faced boys dare to do this!"
He was punished by having his salary docked.
Sù was ashamed of this and
requested to be assigned to an external post.
An imperial edict appointed him Circuit Intendant (guānchásǐ) of Zhèxī;
he had not yet departed,
when on the wùxū day,
Sù was appointed Minister of the Chancellery (zhōngshū shìláng) and Chancellor (tóng píngzhāngshì).
10th day. On the gēngzǐ day,
an imperial decree stated that when the Emperor first fell ill some time ago,
referring to the winter of Year 7,
Déyù never came;
furthermore, when he was in Xīshǔ, he was responsible for collecting 300,000 mín in overdue funds,
which distressed the common people.
Déyù was demoted to Administrator (zhǎngshǐ) of Yuánzhōu.
11 Initially,
Sòng Shēnxī was found guilty.
The details of the case are in Volume 5 of the preceding chapter.
Although the Emperor outwardly showed tolerance,
inwardly he could not bear it.
Lǐ Xùn and Zhèng Zhù, having gained favor,
surmised the Emperor's intentions.
Xùn then, while lecturing,
frequently hinted at the matter to the Emperor.
The Emperor, seeing his talent and eloquence,
believed Xùn could be trusted to conspire in important matters.
Moreover, since both Xùn and Zhù had advanced through Wáng Shǒuchéng,
the Emperor hoped the eunuchs would not suspect them,
and thus secretly told them everything.
Xùn and Zhù then took it upon themselves to eliminate the eunuchs.
A variant account states: The old tradition holds that when the Emperor presented the Yì Jīng commentary to his trusted ministers,
he had already conspired with Xùn to eliminate the eunuchs.
However, the Bǔ Guóshǐ says:
"Xǔ Kāngzuǒ presented sixty volumes of new commentaries on the Spring and Autumn Annals and the Chronicles of the Warring States.
The Emperor asked about the incident where the gatekeeper assassinated Yú Jì, the Ruler of Wú.
Kāngzuǒ claimed that the meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals was profound,
and that he had not yet thoroughly investigated it,
so he dared not easily explain it.
Later, the Emperor asked Lǐ Zhòngyán,
and Zhòngyán then thoroughly explained it to the Emperor.
The Emperor said: 'There are many treacherous ministers around me,
how can I not worry about a disaster like that of Yú Jì?'
Zhòngyán said: 'Your Majesty is mindful of what has not yet manifested;
your servant wishes to follow your sacred plan.'"
The Shílù records,
"This year, in the fourth month, on the day guǐhài,
Xǔ Kāngzuǒ presented thirty volumes of compiled Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn.
In the fifth month,
on the first day yǐsì,
thirty volumes of the Imperial Collection of Zuǒ Shì Chronicles of the Warring States were officially sent to the Imperial Archives."
If so, the Emperor's conspiracy with Xùn to eliminate the eunuchs must have been at this time.
However, when Emperor Wénzōng spoke with Xùn,
eunuchs must have surrounded them,
and it is feared that he would not have dared to speak openly and clearly,
as stated in the Bǔ Guóshǐ.
They deliberated day and night,
and whatever they proposed to the Emperor was followed without exception,
their influence becoming blazing and formidable.
Zhù mostly stayed in the inner palace,
and sometimes when he was off duty,
guests filled his gate,
and bribes piled up like mountains.
Outsiders only knew that Xùn and Zhù relied on the eunuchs to wield power and authority,
not knowing that they had a secret conspiracy with the Emperor.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Qiú Shìliáng, the Right Leader of the Imperial Guards and Duke of Xīngníng, had rendered meritorious service.
Xīngníng was the territory of Hàn's Lóngchuān County.
During the Jiāng Zuǒ period, Xīngníng County was established.
In the Táng Dynasty, it belonged to Xún Prefecture.
From then on, there was a rift.
Xùn and Zhù planned for the Emperor
to promote and elevate Shìliáng to divide Shǒuchéng's power.
In the fifth month,
on the day yǐchǒu,
Shìliáng was made the Left Commissioner of the Divine Strategy Army,
replacing Wéi Yuánsù,
with Shìliáng taking his place.
12 On the day wùchén,
Wáng Fán, the Left Executive Assistant,
was appointed Minister of Revenue,
in charge of public finance.
In the capital, a rumor spread that Zhèng Zhù was making elixirs of immortality for the Emperor,
which required the hearts and livers of young children.
The people were terrified, and the Emperor heard of it and disliked it.
Zhèng Zhù had long disliked Yáng Yúqīng, the Metropolitan Prefect of Jīngzhào,
and conspired with Lǐ Xùn to frame him,
claiming that this rumor originated from Yúqīng's family.
The Emperor was enraged.
In the sixth month,
Yúqīng was sent to the Imperial Censorate prison.
Zhù sought an official position in the two ministries (Chancellery and Secretariat),
but Lǐ Zōngmǐn, a Grand Councillor and Minister of the Secretariat, refused.
Zhù then slandered him to the Emperor.
Coincidentally, Zōngmǐn interceded for Yáng Yúqīng,
and the Emperor, enraged,
shouted at him to leave.
On the day rén yín,
he was demoted to Administrator of Míng Prefecture.
Míng Prefecture was the territory of Mào County in the Later Hàn Dynasty.
In the twenty-sixth year of Kāiyuán of the Táng Dynasty, Míng Prefecture was established,
located four thousand three hundred lì southeast of the capital.
Wéi Yuánsù, the Left Commissioner of the Divine Strategy Army, and the Privy Councilors Yáng Chénghé and Wáng Jiànyán,
wielded power in the court.
Their power struggle with Wáng Shǒuchéng was incompatible,
so Lǐ Xùn and Zhèng Zhù used this to send Chénghé to Xīchuān,
Yuánsù to Huáinán,
and Jiànyán to Hédōng,
all as military supervisors.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the first day jiǎchén,
Yáng Yúqīng was demoted to Administrator of Qián Prefecture.
Qián Prefecture was Gàn County in the Hàn Dynasty.
In the Jìn Dynasty, Nánkāng Commandery was established.
In the Suí Dynasty, it became Qián Prefecture,
located four thousand seventeen lì southeast of the capital.
On the day gēngxū,
the Zǐyún Tower was built at Qūjiāng.
The Zǐyún Tower was south of Qūjiāng;
after repeated periods of chaos and destruction,
it had fallen into disrepair,
and now it was rebuilt.
On the day xīnhài,
Lǐ Gùyán, the Imperial Censor-in-Chief,
was appointed Grand Councillor and Minister of the Chancellery.
Lǐ Xùn and Zhèng Zhù drew up a strategy for universal peace for the Emperor,
believing that they should first eliminate the eunuchs,
next recover Hé and Huáng,
and then clear Hébĕi.
They presented their strategies
as clearly as pointing to the palm of one's hand.
The Emperor believed it to be true,
and their favor and trust grew daily.
Initially,
Lǐ Zōngmǐn, as Minister of Personnel, became a Chancellor through the efforts of the Imperial Son-in-Law Shěn Jié, the female scholar Sòng Ruòxiàn, and the Privy Councilor Yáng Chénghé.
When he was demoted to Míng Prefecture,
Zhèng Zhù exposed his past actions.
On the day rénzǐ,
he was again demoted to Grand Administrator of Chǔ Prefecture.
In the fourteenth year of Dàlì of Emperor Dàizōng,
Guò Prefecture was changed to Chǔ Prefecture,
located four thousand two hundred seventy-eight lì southeast of the capital.
Shū Yuányú, a compiler and concurrent official in the Eastern Capital, was friendly with Lǐ Xùn.
When Xùn gained power,
Yuányú was summoned to be Assistant Director of the Right Bureau,
concurrently an Investigating Censor in charge of miscellaneous affairs.
He investigated Yáng Yúqīng's case.
The Táng system stipulated that there were six Investigating Censors;
the most senior among them was in charge of miscellaneous affairs,
and was called the "Investigating Censor in charge of miscellaneous affairs."
On the day guǐchǒu,
he was promoted to Deputy Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
Yuányú was Yuánbāo's elder brother.
Shū Yuánbāo is mentioned in Volume 5 of the preceding chapter.
Lǐ Hàn, the Minister of Personnel, was demoted to Administrator of Fén Prefecture.
Xiāo Huàn, the Minister of Justice, was demoted to Administrator of Suí Prefecture.
Fén Prefecture was the territory where Emperor Wéndì of Hàn enfeoffed the Prince of Dài,
making Zhongdu his capital.
It was one thousand two hundred six lì from the capital.
Suí Prefecture was originally the old fortress of Déyáng County in the Hàn Dynasty.
In the Eastern Jìn Dynasty, Suíníng Commandery was established.
In the Later Zhōu Dynasty, Suí Prefecture was established,
located two thousand three hundred twenty-nine lì from the capital.
At this time, Lǐ Xùn and Zhèng Zhù successively ousted three Chancellors.
The three Chancellors were Lǐ Déyù, Lù Suí, and Lǐ Zōngmǐn.
Thus, every slight favor or grievance from their entire lives was repaid.
18 Lǐ Xùn memorialized that there were too many monks and nuns,
causing waste and detriment to both public and private affairs.
On the day dīngsì,
an imperial edict ordered that in all locations, monks and nuns who failed to meet the standard in scripture recitation tests
should all be compelled to return to secular life.
The establishment of temples and the private ordination of individuals were forbidden.
Everyone at the time said that Zhèng Zhù would soon become Chancellor.
Lǐ Gān, an Investigating Censor, declared openly at court,
"When the white edict appointing him comes out,
I will surely destroy it in the court!"
On the day guǐhài,
Gān was demoted to Administrator of Fēng Prefecture.
A variant account states: The old tradition says:
"Zhèng Zhù entered the Hanlin Academy as Imperial Lecturer.
When Shū Yuányú became Chancellor,
Zhù also sought to enter the Secretariat.
Gān publicly declared at court, '...'
and was demoted to Fēng Prefecture."
However, at this time, Yuányú had not yet become Chancellor,
so the old tradition is mistaken.
As the Emperor did not want him to become Chancellor,
the matter was ultimately dropped.
20 On the day jiǎzǐ,
Lǐ Xùn, a Doctor of the National University,
was appointed Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs and Editor of Imperial Edicts,
retaining his former position as Scholar of the Imperial Academy.
21 Shěn, the Grand General of the Left Imperial Insignia, was demoted to Administrator of Shào Prefecture.
In the eighth month,
on the day bǐngzǐ,
Lǐ Zōngmǐn was again demoted to Household Register Clerk of Cháo Prefecture.
Sòng Ruòxiàn was granted death.
On the *dīngchǒu* day of the 22nd year,
Zhèng Zhù (鄭注), the Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud, was appointed Minister of Works,
and concurrently assigned as Hanlin Lecturer-Academician.
Zhù liked to wear a deer skin robe,
considering himself a recluse.
The Emperor treated him as a mentor and friend.
When Zhù first gained favor,
the Emperor once asked Lǐ Yù (李玉), a Hanlin Academician and Vice Minister of Revenue:
"Do you know of Zhèng Zhù?
Have you ever spoken with him?"
He replied:
"Not only do I know his name,
but I also deeply understand his character.
He is a treacherous person.
If Your Majesty favors him,
I fear it will be of no benefit to your sagely virtue.
As your humble servant, I am close to you;
how could I associate with such a person!"
On the *wùyín* day,
Lǐ Yù was demoted to Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (江州).
Later, he was again demoted to Secretary of the Households for Liǔzhōu (柳州).
Jiāngzhōu
is 2,948 *lǐ* southeast of the capital.
On the *bǐngshēn* day of the 23rd year,
an imperial edict stated that Yáng Chénghé (楊承和) had harbored Sòng Shēnxī (宋申錫),
and Wéi Yuánsù (韋元素) and Wáng Jiànyán (王踐言)
had colluded with Lǐ Zōngmǐn (李宗閔) and Lǐ Déyù (李德裕), both inside and outside the court,
receiving bribes from them.
Chénghé was to be placed in Huānzhōu (驩州),
Yuánsù in Xiàngzhōu (象州),
and Jiànyán in Ēnzhōu (恩州),
and were to be sent there in shackles by local authorities.
"Sent in shackles" means
to be put in a cangue and guarded during transport.
Xiàngzhōu is 4,989 *lǐ* from the capital,
and Ēnzhōu is 6,500 *lǐ* from the capital.
Yú Qīng (虞卿) was demoted to Secretary of the Households for Qiánzhōu (虔州),
Hàn Fénzhōu (漢汾州) to Marshal,
and Huàn Suízhōu (澣遂州) to Marshal.
Soon after, an envoy was dispatched to order Chénghé, Yuánsù, and Jiànyán to commit suicide.
Wéi Yuánsù's death was as Lǐ Hóngchǔ (李弘楚) had predicted.
His coffin was also opened, and his corpse flogged.
On the *jǐhài* day,
Luó Lìyán (羅立言), formerly Inspector of Lúzhōu (廬州), was appointed Vice Minister of Agriculture.
Lìyán was a corrupt official
who obtained the position by bribing Zhèng Zhù.
When Zhèng Zhù entered the Hanlin Academy,
Gāo Yuányù (高元裕), a Palace Secretary, drafted the imperial edict,
stating that Zhù served the Emperor and his relatives with medicine.
Zhù resented this;
he then reported that Yuányù had once gone outside the city to see off Lǐ Zōngmǐn.
On the *rénchén* day,
Yuányù was demoted to Inspector of Làngzhōu (閬州).
Làngzhōu,
ancient Bāzǐ (巴子) State,
was Làngzhōng (閬中) County during the Qín (秦) dynasty,
Lóngzhōu (隆州) during the Western Wèi (魏) dynasty,
and renamed Làngzhōu during the Xiāntiān (先天) era of the Táng (唐) dynasty to avoid a taboo.
It is 1,915 *lǐ* from the capital.
He was the sixth-generation descendant of Gāo Shìlián (高士廉).
Gāo Shìlián,
maternal uncle of Zhǎngsūn Wújí (長孫無忌),
served Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖) and Emperor Tàizōng (太宗).
At that time, court officials whom Zhù and Lǐ Xùn (李訓) disliked
were all designated as partisans of the two Lǐs (Lǐ Zōngmǐn and Lǐ Déyù)
and were demoted or banished daily, leaving few in their ranks.
The court was agitated,
and the Emperor was aware of it.
Xùn and Zhù, fearing they might be undermined,
on the *guǐmǎo* day, the first day of the ninth month,
persuaded the Emperor
to issue an edict:
"Regarding those who were relatives or protégés of Déyù and Zōngmǐn,
apart from those already demoted or dismissed before today,
no further inquiries shall be made."
Public sentiment somewhat stabilized.
Wáng Yá (王涯), the Salt and Iron Commissioner, proposed reforming the tea regulations in Jiānghuái (江淮) and Língnán (嶺南),
increasing the tax.
In the ninth year of Emperor Dézōng's (德宗) Zhēnyuán (貞元) era,
tea was first taxed.
In the prefectures and counties where tea was produced, and at major routes for merchants outside the tea mountains,
officials were entrusted to assess three grades of market value,
taxing one-tenth of each.
In the first year of the Chángqìng (長慶) era,
Wáng Bō (王播), the Salt and Iron Commissioner, proposed increasing the tea tax by fifty percent.
Now, the regulations were again changed, and the tax increased even more severely.
On the *gēngshēn* day, Lǐ Tīng (李聽), the Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng (鳳翔), was appointed Military Commissioner of Zhōngwǔ (忠武),
replacing Dù Cóng (杜悰).
When Emperor Xiànzōng (憲宗) died,
everyone said it was the work of the eunuch Chén Hóngzhì (陳弘志).
See Volume 241, fifteenth year of Yuánhé (元和).
Lǐ Xùn advised the Emperor to summon him.
Upon his arrival at Qīngní (青泥) Post Station,
on the *guǐhài* day,
he was beaten to death with a cudgel.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The old account says:
"After Lǐ Xùn held power,
he immediately planned to execute the palace eunuchs.
Chén Hóngqìng (陳弘慶) had been blamed for regicide since the end of the Yuánhé era,
so he sent people to beat him to death with a cudgel."
However, Lǐ Xùn was not yet a chancellor at this time.
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄).
Zhèng Zhù sought to be appointed Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng.
Lǐ Gùyán (李固言), a Palace Administration Secretary and concurrently Grand Councilor, disagreed.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Gùyán was appointed Military Commissioner of Shānnán Xīdào (山南西道).
The *Kǎoyì* states: Sòng Mǐnqíu's (宋敏求) *Xuānzōng Shílù* (宣宗實錄) says:
"Gùyán was irritable and impetuous,
lacking gravitas.
At that time, Xùn and Zhù were in power.
Although Gùyán was a chancellor, he actually disliked being associated with Zōngmǐn,
so he was sent out as the Military Commissioner of Xīngyuán (興元)."
However, Gùyán had fabricated the case against Yáng Yúqīng (楊虞卿),
which led to Zōngmǐn's dismissal as chancellor and Gùyán's replacement of him.
How could he be a partisan of Zōngmǐn!
We now follow the *Kāichéng Jìshì* (開成紀事).
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Kāichéng Jìshì* says:
"Zhù recommended Shū Yuányú (舒元輿) and Lǐ Xùn for promotion to the chancellorship.
Zhù himself went to the chancellor Lǐ Gùyán to request the Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng position.
Gùyán was firm and refused,
while only Wáng Yá and Jiǎ Sù (賈餗) supported him."
This event occurred on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month.
The *Jìshì* is mistaken.
We now follow the *Shílù*.
As his power and position grew,
he became quite wary of Zhù.
He plotted to combine forces inside and outside the court to eliminate the eunuchs,
and thus sent Zhù to Fèngxiáng.
His actual intention was that after eliminating the eunuchs,
he would also deal with Zhù.
Zhù wanted to recruit talented and reputable individuals from prominent families as his assistants.
He requested Wéi Wēn (韋溫), a Supernumerary Secretary of the Ministry of Rites,
to be his Deputy Commissioner.
(It refers to a Deputy Military Commissioner.)
Someone said:
"Refusing him will surely lead to trouble."
Wēn replied:
"When choosing between calamities, it is best to choose the lighter one.
Refusing him will only result in a distant demotion,
but accepting will bring unforeseen disaster."
In the end, he declined.

On the *wùchén* day, Wáng Shǒuchéng (王守澄), the Right Vice Commander of the Divine Stratagems Army, acting Right Army General-in-Chief, and Director of the Palace Attendants Bureau, was appointed Commissioner of Inspection of the Imperial Army for the Left and Right Divine Stratagems Armies,
and concurrently Commander of the Twelve Guards.
The Táng (唐) dynasty, following the Suí (隋) system,
established Sixteen Guards.
The Twelve Guards commanded the troops of various prefectures,
named the Left and Right Guards,
Left and Right Valiant Cavalry Guards,
Left and Right Martial Guards,
Left and Right Awe-Inspiring Guards,
Left and Right Commander Guards,
and Left and Right Patrol Guards.
By the Kaiyuan (開元) era,
the *Fǔbīng* (府兵) system gradually deteriorated.
So, 120,000 elite cavalry were recruited,
divided among the Twelve Guards,
10,000 men per Guard.
Afterward, repeated upheavals and disasters occurred,
and the armies of the Twelve Guards no longer resembled their former peaceful state.
By honoring Shǒuchéng with an empty title,
his power was effectively stripped.
On the *jǐsì* day, Shū Yuányú, the Imperial Censor-in-Chief and concurrently Vice Minister of Justice, was appointed Vice Minister of Justice,
and Lǐ Xùn, a Bureau Director of the Ministry of War, drafting Imperial Edicts, and concurrently Hanlin Lecturer-Academician, was appointed Vice Minister of Rites,
both concurrently Grand Councilors.
Xùn was also ordered to enter the Hanlin Academy every two or three days to lecture on the *Yì* (易).
As Imperial Censor-in-Chief, Yuányú
would impeach anyone whom Xùn and Zhù disliked;
through this, he became a chancellor.
Moreover, the Emperor, learning from Lǐ Zōngmǐn and Lǐ Déyù who had many partisans,
considered Jiǎ Sù and Yuányú to be humble and newly advanced officials.
Sù was orphaned young
and lived as a guest between Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮).
Yuányú was from a humble background
and did not socialize with scholars.
The Emperor hoped that they would not form factions.
Xùn,
rising from a banished person,
attained the position of chancellor within a year.
The Son of Heaven fully entrusted him.
Whether Xùn was in the Central Secretariat
or the Hanlin Academy,
all affairs of the realm were decided by him.
Wáng Yá and others would comply with his suggestions,
fearing they would fall short;
from the Vice Commanders, Privy Councilors, and generals of the Imperial Guards,
all trembled upon seeing Xùn,
bowing and kowtowing in greeting.
On the *rénshēn* day, Lǐ Xiàoběn (李孝本), a Bureau Director of the Ministry of Justice and concurrently Acting Imperial Censor, was provisionally appointed Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
Xiàoběn,
a descendant of the imperial clan,
gained advancement by relying on Xùn and Zhù.
30 Lǐ Tīng (李聽) relied on his long-standing achievements and old connections,
and did not show respect to Zhèng Zhù (鄭注).
Zhù replaced Tīng as the military governor of Fèngxiáng (鳳翔).
He first sent his牙將 (yájiàng) Dān Jùn (丹駿) to the army to comfort and reward them.
Dān (丹)
is the surname;
Jùn (駿)
is the given name.
The surname genealogy states: The Dān (丹) surname
is descended from Dān Zhū (丹朱).
The character 勞 (láo)
is pronounced as "lì dào fān" (力到翻).
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Yǐhài (乙亥),
Tīng was appointed Táizǐ Tàibǎo (太子太保) and Fēnsī (分司).
Dù Cóng (杜悰) was again appointed Zhōngwǔ Jiédùshǐ (忠武節度使).
Zhèng Zhù (鄭注) always prided himself on his strategies for governing the country.
When the emperor asked him for methods to enrich the people,
Zhù had no answer.
So he requested a tea monopoly.
Thereupon, Wáng Yá (王涯) was additionally appointed Quèchá Shǐ (榷茶使).
Yá knew it was not feasible but dared not disobey.
People greatly suffered from it.
31 Zhèng Zhù (鄭注) wanted to win the praise of monks and nuns,
and firmly requested to abolish the purge (shātài 沙汰).
This was granted.
In the seventh month of that year,
Lǐ Xùn (李訓) requested to purge monks and nuns.
32 Lǐ Xùn (李訓) and Zhèng Zhù (鄭注) secretly spoke to the emperor,
requesting to eliminate Wáng Shǒuchéng (王守澄).
On the day Xīnsì (辛巳),
a palace envoy, Lǐ Hǎogǔ (李好古), was dispatched to his residence to bestow poisoned wine,
and kill him.
He was posthumously granted Yángzhōu Dàdūdū (揚州大都督).
Xùn (訓) and Zhù (注) had originally advanced through Shǒuchéng (守澄).
Zhù's (注) affairs can be found in Volume 223, Mùzōng (穆宗) Chángqìng (長慶) 3rd year.
Xùn's (訓) affairs can be found in the 8th year of the previous emperor.
Everyone was pleased with Shǒuchéng's (守澄) acceptance of sycophancy, but detested Xùn (訓) and Zhù's (注) sinister cunning.
Thus, the rebellious faction of Yuánhé (元和) was almost entirely eliminated.
On the day Yǐyǒu (乙酉),
Zhèng Zhù (鄭注) departed for his post.
33 On the day Gēngzǐ (庚子),
Péi Dù (裴度), the Resident Administrator of the Eastern Capital, Sītú (司徒), and concurrently Shìzhōng (侍中), was additionally appointed Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令).
Other appointments remained as before.
Those Lǐ Xùn (李訓) promoted and supported
were mostly reckless and dangerous individuals.
However, he also occasionally enlisted respected figures from across the empire to appease the public,
such as Péi Dù (裴度), Línghú Chǔ (令狐楚), and Zhèng Tán (鄭覃), all of whom were venerable talents from successive reigns,
and had long been suppressed by those in power,
assigned to minor positions.
Xùn (訓) brought them all into high offices.
Because of this, even scholars and officials hoped that he could truly bring about great peace,
not just the Son of Heaven being deceived by him.
However, discerning individuals saw his extreme arrogance
and knew he would soon fail.
34 In the eleventh month,
on the day Bǐngwǔ (丙午),
Guō Xíngyú (郭行餘), the Dàlǐ Qīng (大理卿), was appointed Bīnnìng Jiédùshǐ (邠寧節度使).
On the day Guǐchǒu (癸丑),
Lǐ Zàiyì (李載義), the Hédōng Jiédùshǐ (河東節度使) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事), was concurrently appointed Shìzhōng (侍中).
On the day Dīngsì (丁巳),
Wáng Fán (王璠), the Hùbù Shàngshū (戶部尚書) and Pàn Dùzhī (判度支), was appointed Hédōng Jiédùshǐ (河東節度使).
On the day Wùwǔ (戊午),
Lǐ Shí (李石), the Jīngzhào Yǐn (京兆尹), was appointed Hùbù Shìláng (戶部侍郎) and Pàn Dùzhī (判度支);
Luó Lìyán (羅立言), the Jīngzhào Shàoyǐn (京兆少尹), was temporarily placed in charge of the prefecture's affairs.
Shí (石)
was the fifth-generation grandson of Shénfú (神符).
Xiāngyì Wáng Shénfú (襄邑王神符)
was the younger brother of Huái'ān Wáng Shéntōng (淮安王神通).
On the day Jǐwèi (己未),
Hán Yuē (韓約), the Tàifù Qīng (太府卿), was appointed Zuǒ Jīn Wúwèi Dà Jiàngjūn (左金吾衛大將軍).
Initially,
Zhèng Zhù (鄭注) and Lǐ Xùn (李訓) plotted that
when Zhù (注) arrived at his post,
he would select several hundred strong men,
all carrying white staves
and concealing axes,
to serve as his personal guards.
In this month,
on the day Wùchén (戊辰),
Wáng Shǒuchéng (王守澄) was buried by the Chǎnshuǐ (滻水).
The Yōng Lù (雍錄) states: The Chǎnshuǐ (滻水) originates from the western border of Lántián (藍田) County.
It flows slightly northward to the west of Báilù Yuán (白鹿原),
then proceeds towards the capital city.
Wáng Shǒuchéng (王守澄) was likely buried southwest of Báilù Yuán (白鹿原).
Zhù (注) then brought his personal guards with him.
He also memorialized that all internal eunuchs, from the zhōngwèi (中尉) downwards, should gather at the Chǎnshuǐ (滻水) to attend the funeral.
Zhù (注) would then close the gates,
order his personal guards to axe them,
leaving no survivors.
Once the plan was settled,
Xùn (訓) and his associates plotted:
"If this matter succeeds,
then Zhù (注) will exclusively claim the credit.
It would be better to have Xíngyú (行餘) and Fán (璠), under the pretext of going to their posts,
recruit many strong men as their personal troops,
and also use the officers and soldiers from the Jīn Wú (金吾) office,
to execute the eunuchs ahead of schedule,
and then eliminate Zhù (注) as well."
Xíngyú (行餘), Fán (璠), Lìyán (立言), Yuē (約), and Zhōngchéng (中丞) Lǐ Xiàoběn (李孝本)
were all individuals Xùn (訓) had long favored.
Therefore, he placed them in key positions,
and plotted with only these few people and Shū Yuányú (舒元輿).
No one else knew of it.
On the day Rénxū (壬戌),
the emperor presided in the Zǐchén Diàn (紫宸殿).
When the officials had taken their places,
Hán Yuē (韓約) did not report peace.
According to Táng (唐) regulations: Whenever there was court,
after the emperor ascended his throne,
the Jīn Wú Jiàngjūn (金吾將軍) would report:
"All is peaceful inside and outside the left and right wings."
"Last night, a sweet dew appeared on the pomegranate tree behind the left Jīn Wú (金吾) office.
Your subject reported it through the gate."
It means that the report was heard during the night,
and since the palace gates were already locked,
it was passed through the gate to be presented.
The prime minister also led the officials in congratulating the emperor.
Xùn (訓) and Yuányú (元輿) urged the emperor to personally go and observe it,
to accept the heavenly auspicious sign.
The emperor assented.
The officials withdrew,
and took their places in the Hányuán Diàn (含元殿).
Zǐchén (紫宸)
was the inner palace;
Hányuán (含元)
was the front palace.
The emperor wished to go and observe the sweet dew,
so the officials withdrew from Zǐchén (紫宸) and emerged,
lining up in the Hányuán Diàn (含元殿),
because the guards of the left and right Jīn Wú (金吾) were positioned in front of the Hányuán Diàn (含元殿) on the left and right.
The emperor rode in a soft palanquin out of the Zǐchén Mén (紫宸門).
A soft palanquin
was made by stacking cushions and mattresses,
with a wooden frame underneath,
carried by people.
He first ordered the prime ministers and officials of the two departments to go to the left guard post to inspect it,
and they returned after a long while.
Xùn (訓) reported:
"Your subject and the others have verified it,
and it is probably not genuine sweet dew.
It should not be hastily announced."
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: According to this, Xùn (訓) and Hán Yuē (韓約) jointly plotted,
falsely creating the sweet dew,
but Xùn (訓) himself said he feared it was not a true auspicious sign.
This was to make the eunuchs all go to the Jīn Wú (金吾) to re-examine it,
and then ambush and execute them.
Therefore, the imperial edict drafted by Línghú Chǔ (令狐楚) on the 22nd also stated,
"the chief villain still requested a re-examination."
Now we follow the official record.
The emperor said:
"How can this be so?!"
He looked to the left and right Zhongwèi (中尉) Qiú Shìliáng (仇士良) and Yú Zhìhóng (魚志弘) and ordered them to lead all the eunuchs to inspect it.
After the eunuchs had left,
Xùn (訓) immediately summoned Guō Xíngyú (郭行餘) and Wáng Fán (王璠) and said:
"Come and receive the imperial edict!"
Fán (璠) trembled and dared not step forward.
Only Xíngyú (行餘) prostrated himself below the hall.
At this time, several hundred troops under the command of these two men
were all holding weapons and standing outside the Dānfèng Mén (丹鳳門).
Xùn (訓) had already sent someone to summon them,
ordering them to enter and receive the edict.
Only the Eastern soldiers entered.
These were Hédōng (河東) soldiers.
"Eastern"
is missing
"Hé" (河)
above it.
【Zhāng (章): Kǒng (孔) edition correctly has
"Hé" (河)
character.
Qiú Shìliáng and others arrived at the left camp to inspect the sweet dew.
Hán Yuē's color changed and he sweated.
Shìliáng was surprised and said,
"General, why are you like this?"
Presently, the wind blew and the curtains rose,
revealing many armed men,
and the sound of weapons was heard.
Shìliáng and the others were startled and fled out.
The doorkeeper tried to close the gate,
but Shìliáng shouted at him,
and the bolt could not be fastened.

was the son of Huī;
Qián Huī is mentioned in Volume 241, first year of Chángqìng of Mùzōng.
(Jiǎnnéng was) the son of Lún;
Lú Lún, along with Jí Zhōngfú, Hán Hóng, Qián Qǐ, Sīkōng Shǔ, Miáo Fā, Cuī Tóng, Gěng Wěi, Xiàhóu Shěn, and Lǐ Duān, were all equally famous for their poetry,
known as the "Ten Talents of Dàlì."
(Jié was) Xiāo Fǔ's younger brother.
Xiāo Fǔ served Xiànzōng and Mùzōng,
reaching the position of chancellor.
History states that Qián Kěfù and others were all sons of prominent families
who lost their lives by associating with the wrong person.
On the dīngmǎo day,
an imperial edict stripped Zhù of his official titles and ranks,
and ordered neighboring circuits to hold their troops and observe the situation.
Chén Jūnyì, the Grand General of the Left Shéncè Army, was appointed Jiedù Envoy of Fèngxiáng.
On the night of the wùchén day,
Zhāng Zhòngqīng sent Lǐ Shūhé and others to present Zhù's head.
The Kǎoyì states: According to the Shílù,
Zhù's head was already delivered on the jiǎzǐ day.
However, the Kāichéng Jìshì records that the edict stripping him of his official titles was only issued on the twenty-sixth day,
stating that when Zhèng Zhù was first executed,
the capital was not yet aware.
Lǐ Qián's Yǐmǎo Jì also states that Zhāng Zhòngqīng lured and killed Zhù on the dīngmǎo day.
This is consistent with the Kāichéng Jìshì.
But the Kāichéng Jìshì's biography of Zhù says he played court on the twenty-sixth day,
which might be an error.
The Yǐmǎo Jì states that Zhù entered court on the gēngshēn day,
which was the nineteenth.
He reached Fúfēng,
heard of Xùn's defeat,
and then returned.
This seems closer to the truth.
The Shílù's date might be too early.
The Xīn Běnjì states that Zhāng Zhòngqīng killed Zhù on the wùchén day.
Therefore, the date is not recorded here due to uncertainty.
People's spirits somewhat stabilized,
and the various armies in the capital finally returned to their camps.
An imperial edict was issued stating that generals and soldiers who had rendered meritorious service in quelling the rebellion or had formed up their ranks
would receive varying official ranks, titles, and rewards.
The Right Shéncè Army captured Hán Yuē in Chóngyìfang.
On the jǐsì day,
he was executed.
Qiú Shìliáng and others were all promoted and transferred to varying degrees.
From then on, all affairs of the empire were decided by the Northern Directorate,
and the chancellors merely processed documents.
The eunuchs' power grew even stronger,
intimidating the Son of Heaven,
looking down upon the chancellors,
and bullying court officials as if they were grass.
Whenever matters were deliberated in the Yányīng Hall,
Shìliáng and others would invariably bring up Xùn and Zhù to refute the chancellors.
Refute (折),
pronounced zhé.
(The chancellors said): "Xùn and Zhù were indeed the leaders of the rebellion,
but we do not know through whom Xùn and Zhù first gained advancement?"
The eunuchs were somewhat humbled,
and the officials relied on this.
At that time, the Central Secretariat only had empty walls and broken houses,
lacking all necessities.
Jiāngxī and Húnán presented one hundred and twenty portions of clothing and provisions
to be used for the chancellors to recruit attendants.
On the xīnwèi day,
Lǐ Shí submitted a memorial, saying:
"If a chancellor is loyal and upright without evil,
he will be protected by divine spirits;
even if he encounters bandits,
they will not be able to harm him.
If he harbors treachery within,
even with heavy guards,
spirits will be able to punish him.
I wish to exhaust my sincere heart in repaying the country.
I shall simply follow the established practice, and having Jinwú soldiers escort me is sufficient;
I request that the clothing and provisions offered by the two circuits
both be stopped."
This was granted.
In the twelfth month,
on the *Rénshēn* day, which was the first day of the month,
Gù Shīyōng was exiled to Dānzhōu.
When he reached Shāngshān,
he was granted death.
36 The salt and iron commissioner, Línghú Chǔ, memorialized to abolish the tea monopoly.
It was approved.
When Wáng Yá was executed,
the tea monopoly was then abolished.
37 The Ministry of Finance memorialized to confiscate Zhèng Zhù’s family property,
obtaining over a million bolts of silk,
and other items in proportion.
On the *Gēngchén* day,
the Emperor asked the chancellors,
“Are the wards and markets peaceful yet?”
Lǐ Shí replied,
“They are gradually peaceful.
However, the cold has been exceptionally severe recently,
which is probably due to excessive executions.”
Zhèng Tán said,
“The close relatives of the criminals have all already died.
’Zhōuqīn’ (周親):
Kǒng Ānguó said: ‘Zhōu’ (周) means ‘to the utmost.’
At that time, the eunuchs deeply resented Lǐ Xùn and others,
and anyone related to them by *guāgē qīn* (瓜葛親),
where *guāgē* (瓜葛) implies attachment.
This means not closely related,
or perhaps through intermediate relations like maternal cousins, they attached themselves to express friendship,
like vines and gourds.
The executions and demotions were unceasing,
hence the two chancellors spoke of it.”
After Lǐ Xùn and Zhèng Zhù were executed,
the six circuit inspection commissioners were summoned.
Tián Quáncāo, still furious about Xùn and Zhù’s plot,
declared on the road,
“When I enter the city,
all those in scholarly attire,
regardless of status, must be put to death!”
On the *Kuǐwèi* day,
Quáncāo and others rode swiftly by post-horse into the Jīnguāng Mén.
Jīnguāng Mén
is the second gate from the north on the west side of Cháng’ān city.
Scholars and commoners screamed and ran in all directions,
dust rising everywhere.
Officials from the Two Departments and various ministries heard of it
and all scattered,
some even riding off without having time to fasten their belts and socks.
Zhèng Tán and Lǐ Shí were in the Central Secretariat,
watching the clerks and soldiers gradually flee.
Tán said to Shí,
“The rumors are quite unsettling;
we should leave and avoid it for now!”
Shí replied,
“A chancellor’s position is esteemed and his prestige great,
the people’s hearts depend on him,
he cannot act lightly!
The truth of the matter is not yet known;
if we sit firm and calm the situation,
it might stabilize.
If even the chancellors run,
then the inner and outer courts will be in chaos.
Furthermore, if disaster truly strikes,
fleeing will not save us!”
Tán agreed.
Shí sat and reviewed documents,
calm and composed.
Imperial envoys successively shouted,
“Close the gates of the various ministries in the Imperial City!”
The *Liùdiǎn* states: The Táng capital had three concentric walls: the outermost was called the Jīngchéng (京城),
the inner one was called the Huángchéng (皇城),
and the innermost was called the Gōngchéng (宮城),
also known as Zǐchéng (子城).
The Dàmínggōng Palace City had five gates on its south side;
the Wàngxiān Mén was to the left of the Dānfèng Mén.
”Shuài” (帥)
is read as “lǜ” (率).
“The bandits have arrived;
it’s not too late to close the gates.
Please observe the changes calmly;
it is not appropriate to show weakness!”
It only settled down after late afternoon.
On this day,
the street ruffians in the wards and markets all wore scarlet and black,
holding bows and knives, looking north.
Seeing the gates of the Imperial City closed,
they were about to plunder.
If not for Shí and Jūnshǎng calming the situation,
the capital would have been thrown into chaos again.
At that time, officials of the Two Departments who were on duty
all bid farewell to their families.
38 On the *Jiǎshēn* day,
an imperial edict ordered the cessation of repairs to the Qǔjiāng pavilions and halls.
They had been repaired at Zhèng Zhù’s suggestion,
and were halted after Zhù’s execution.
39 On the *Dīnghài* day,
an imperial edict stated:
“Regarding the relatives and partisans of the rebels,
except for those already executed or specifically named for arrest,
all others are to be left unquestioned.
Officials of various ministries,
though coerced and misled,
are all pardoned.
No one else is permitted to accuse or threaten them.
Those who have fled and are in hiding
shall not be pursued further.
Within three days, each is allowed to return to their original ministry.”
At that time, the imperial guards were unruly and tyrannical.
Zhāng Zhòngfāng, the Yǐn of Jīngzhào, dared not challenge them.
The chancellors deemed him incompetent
and sent him out as the Cìshǐ of Huázhōu,
replacing him with Xuē Yuánshǎng, the Síóng Qīng.
Yuánshǎng once visited Lǐ Shí’s residence
and heard Shí loudly arguing with someone in the main hall.
Yuánshǎng sent someone to observe,
who reported that a Shéncè Army general was presenting a grievance.
Yuánshǎng hurried in
and reproached Shí, saying,
“You, Chancellor, assist the Son of Heaven and maintain order throughout the realm.
Now, you cannot even control a single army general nearby,
allowing such disrespect.
How can you subdue the four barbarians!”
He immediately rushed out, mounted his horse,
ordered his attendants to seize the general,
and waited at Xiàmǎ Qiáo.
The *Géběn Dàmínggōng Tú* states: Xiàmǎ Qiáo is north of Jiànfú Mén.
The general had already taken off his clothes and was preparing for punishment.
His faction complained to Qiú Shìliáng.
Shìliáng sent a eunuch to summon Yuánshǎng, saying,
“The Zhōngwèi requests the presence of the Grand Yǐn.”
Yuánshǎng said,
“I have official business for the moment;
I will arrive shortly.”
He then flogged the general to death.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Kāichéng Jìshì* records Wáng Huì, the Bìmìshū Shàojiàn, as Yǐn of Jīngzhào.
However, Xuē Yuánshǎng had already become Yǐn of Jīngzhào,
so the *Jìshì* is incorrect.
“Báifú” (白服)
refers to the plain clothes worn when awaiting punishment.
“How dare this foolish scholar flog an imperial army general to death!”
Yuánshǎng said,
“The Zhōngwèi is a high minister,
and the Chancellor is also a high minister.
If a person under the Chancellor were disrespectful to the Zhōngwèi,
what would be done?
If a person under the Zhōngwèi is disrespectful to the Chancellor,
can he be excused!
The Zhōngwèi is integral to the state;
you should uphold the law for the state.
Yuánshǎng has already come in prisoner’s attire;
it is solely up to the Zhōngwèi whether I live or die!”
Shìliáng knew the general was already dead
and there was nothing he could do.
So, he called for wine and happily drank with Yuánshǎng before they parted.
Originally,
when Wǔ Yuánhé died,
an imperial edict ordered bows, arrows, and *mòdāo* from the imperial treasury to be given to the Jīnwǔ guard
to protect the chancellors.
This event is recorded in volume 239, Xīanzōng Yuánhé tenth year.
“Cóng” (從)
is pronounced with the *cái yòng* (才用) fanqie.
By this time,
all such measures were abolished.
Kāichéng First Year
(*Bǐngchén*, 836)
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the *Xīnchǒu* day, which was the first day of the month,
the Emperor went to Xuānzhèng Diàn,
pardoned the empire,
and changed the reign title.
Qiú Shìliáng requested to use the Shéncè guard to protect the palace gates.
Jìanyì Dàfū Féng Dìng argued against it,
saying that although the troops of the Sixteen Guards of the Southern Court were by this time nominally existing but actually defunct,
using the Northern Army to guard the Southern Court
would mean that the Outer Court would also be commanded by the Northern Bureau,
thus disrupting Tàizōng’s established order
and increasing the eunuchs’ power and influence.
Hence, Féng Dìng argued against it.
Dìng
was Sù’s younger brother.
Féng Sù
was Zhīzhìgào at the beginning of Mùzōng’s Chángqìng era.
2 In the second month,
on the *Guǐwèi* day,
the Emperor spoke with the chancellors,
lamenting that memorials from all directions were flowery but not elegant.
Lǐ Shí replied,
“Ancient people wrote prose based on events;
today’s people harm events with their prose.”
3 Zhāoyì Jiédùshǐ Liú Cóngjiàn
submitted a memorial requesting the punishment of Wáng Yá and others,
and further stated:
"Yá and his associates were scholars,
who enjoyed national honor and favor.
All wished to protect themselves and their families;
how could they possibly plot rebellion!
Xùn and his ilk genuinely intended to eliminate the two Eunuch Grand Secretaries,
conceiving this scheme to save their own lives,
which led to mutual slaughter.
To falsely accuse them of rebellion,
I fear, is truly unjust.
If indeed the prime ministers had other intentions,
they should have been handed over to the proper authorities
to be judged according to the penal code.
How could inner court officials be allowed to lead armed troops,
wantonly pillaging and looting,
extending their violence to gentry and commoners alike,
causing widespread killing and injury!
Blood flowed throughout the city gates.
(Emperor Wǔ of Hàn built the Jiànzhāng Palace,
which was said to have a thousand gates and ten thousand households.
Later generations thus referred to palace gates as 'a thousand gates'.)
They investigated minor branches,
causing fear and suspicion both inside and outside the court.
I wished to personally go to the imperial court
to present what was right and wrong,
but I feared I would also be implicated and executed,
and the matter would remain unresolved.
I shall diligently repair the frontiers,
and train the soldiers,
to be the heart and lungs of Your Majesty within,
and a bulwark for Your Majesty without.
If traitorous officials become uncontrollable,
I swear to clear the emperor's side with my death!"
On the day of Bǐngshēn,
Liú Cóngjiàn was promoted to Jiǎnjiào Sītú.
4 The Tiāndé Army reported that three thousand households of the Tǔyùhún
came to Fēngzhōu to surrender.
5 In the third month,
on the day of Rén'yín,
Lǐ Déyù, the Chángshǐ of Yuánzhōu, was appointed Cìshǐ of Chúzhōu.
(Yuánzhōu was the land of Yíchūn County during the Hàn dynasty.
The Suí dynasty established Yuánzhōu.
It is 3,580 *lǐ* southeast of the capital.
Chúzhōu is 2,564 *lǐ* away.)
6 Zuǒ Púyè Línghú Chǔ
gently memorialized:
"Wáng Yá and others have already suffered their punishment,
their families exterminated,
and their remains discarded.
I request that officials be ordered to collect and bury them,
in accordance with the benevolent spirit of spring."
The emperor was saddened for a long time,
and ordered the Jīngzhào
to collect and bury Yá and the eleven others west of the city,
each granted one
suit of burial clothes.
(The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Kāichéng Jìshì* says:
"Jīngzhào Yǐn Xuē Yuánshǎng buried Yá and seven others at Zhāngcūn, west of the city."
This account follows the New Biographies.
The bones were discarded in the Wèishǔi River.)
7 On the day of Dīngwèi,
Huángchéng Liúshǒu Guō Jiǎo
(According to old regulations: when the imperial carriage makes an inspection tour,
a *liúshǒu* is appointed for the capital.
The fact that the emperor is currently in the capital and a *huángchéng liúshǒu* is appointed
needs to be investigated.
From the memorial below,
it can be known that the appointment of a *huángchéng liúshǒu*
was the eunuchs' intention.)
memorialized:
"For all ceremonial guards with sharp blades,
I request that they all be transferred to the Jūnqì Shǐ."
(The Jūnqì Shǐ was the commander of the military armory,
one of the inner court officials.)
This was approved.
(Ceremonial swords were made of wood,
decorated with silver,
merely having the appearance of a sword.)
8 Liú Cóngjiàn again sent his tooth-general Jiāo Chǔcháng
to submit a memorial declining the official position,
declining the Jiǎnjiào Sītú.
("Fù" (復) is read fú yòu fān (扶又翻).)
"What your servant has presented
concerns the fundamental well-being of the nation.
If it can be heard, then Yá and his associates should be vindicated;
if it cannot be heard, then the awards should not be granted arbitrarily!
How can there be unredressed grievances of the dead,
while the living enjoy emoluments!"
He then openly exposed the crimes of Qiú Shìliáng and others.
On the day of Xīnyǒu,
the emperor summoned Chǔcháng,
comforted him, and sent him away.
At that time, Shìliáng and his ilk were behaving arbitrarily,
and court officials worried daily about their families being ruined.
When Cóngjiàn's memorial arrived,
Shìliáng and his associates were intimidated.
Because of this, Zhèng Tán and Lǐ Shí were roughly able to manage government affairs,
and the emperor, relying on them, also gradually became stronger.
9 Summer,
fourth month,
on the day of Yǐmǎo,
Lǐ Zōngmǐn, the Sīhù of Cháozhōu, was appointed Sīmǎ of Héngzhōu.
All those whom Lǐ Xùn had implicated as partisans of Lǐ Déyù and Zōngmǐn
were gradually reinstated.
10 Prince Zī Xié passed away.
(Xié was a son of Xiànzōng.)
11 On the day of Jiǎwǔ,
Lǐ Gùyán, the Jiédùshǐ of Shānnán Xīdào, was appointed Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Zuǒ Púyè Línghú Chǔ
replaced him.
12 On the day of Wùxū,
the emperor and the prime ministers
casually discussed the merits and flaws of poetry.
Zhèng Tán said:
"Among excellent poems,
none surpasses the Three Hundred Poems (the *Shījīng*),
all composed by the people to satirize or praise contemporary politics.
The kings collected them to observe customs;
it is not heard that kings composed poetry.
The poems of later literati
are flowery but insubstantial,
without benefit to affairs.
Both the Last Emperor Chén and Emperor Yáng of Suí were skilled in poetry,
yet they could not avoid national demise.
What can Your Majesty gain from it!"
(Historians say that Zhèng Tán was able to adhere to classical scholarship to assist his sovereign.)
The emperor greatly esteemed him.
13 On the day of Jǐyǒu,
the emperor held court in the Zǐchén Hall.
The prime ministers,
after presenting their reports, bowed in thanks.
Outside, a false rumor spread:
"The emperor wishes to let the prime ministers command the imperial guards,
and they have already received the imperial favor."
Because of this, suspicion and obstruction arose again,
both inside and outside the court.
People were anxious,
and for several days, officials and commoners dared not undress for sleep.
On the day of Yǐchǒu,
Lǐ Shí memorialized, requesting that Qiú Shìliáng and others be summoned
to personally dispel their doubts.
The emperor summoned Shìliáng and others to come forth,
and the emperor, Shí, and others jointly enlightened and appeased them,
so that they would no longer be suspicious or fearful.
Only then was the matter resolved.
14 In the intercalary month,
on the day of Yǐyǒu,
Lǐ Tīng, the Tàizǐ Tàibǎo and Fēnsī,
was appointed Hézhōng Jiédùshǐ.
The emperor once sighed and said:
"To entrust him with troops without doubt,
to place him in a leisurely post without resentment,
The two daughters of Lǐ Xiàoběn were inducted into the Right Army,
the Right Army
being the Right Shéncè Army.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Wèi Mó, Right Shíyí, submitted a memorial,
believing:
"Your Majesty does not indulge in sensuous pleasures
and has frequently released palace women to marry widowers.
