I have secretly heard that for several months,
the Jiàofāng has been selecting and testing hundreds [of women],
and the Zhuāngzhái is still acquiring properties;
within the Táng court, there are Jiàofāng Envoys and Zhuāngzhái Envoys,
all held by eunuchs.
They do not avoid imperial relatives,
greatly stirring up public criticism.
Your servant secretly regrets this.
In the past, when Hàn Guāngwǔ once glanced at a screen depicting eminent women,
Sòng Hóng still sternly spoke out,
and Guāngwǔ immediately removed it.
During Guāngwǔ's time,
Sòng Hóng was the Dàsīkōng.
Once, during a banquet,
a new screen on the imperial seat depicted eminent women,
and the emperor repeatedly looked at it.
Hóng, with a solemn expression, said:
'I have not seen anyone who loves virtue as much as they love beauty!'
The emperor immediately had it removed.
He smiled and said to Hóng:
'When one hears what is right, one obeys;
is this acceptable?'
Hóng replied:
'Your Majesty's advancement in virtue
fills your servant with immeasurable joy!'
Does Your Majesty wish to be inferior to Guāngwǔ?"
The emperor immediately released Lǐ Xiàoběn's daughter.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù records
"two daughters of Xiàoběn were taken into the palace,"
"Xiàoběn's second daughter was taken into the palace."
The reason for this discrepancy
is probably that both of Xiàoběn's daughters were registered in the Right Army [after his confiscation],
and the elder daughter was taken into the palace first,
which Mó did not know;
when the second daughter was also taken,
Mó then knew and submitted his memorial.
The emperor said:
"I selected and acquired women
to bestow upon the various princes.
I pitied Xiàoběn's daughter,
who was orphaned and exposed at a young age,
and therefore took her in to raise her in the palace.
Mó is able to speak fully even in ambiguous situations;
he can be said to love me
and not disgrace his ancestor!"
He commanded the Zhōngshū to draft an excellent decree to reward him.
Mó
was the fifth-generation descendant of Wèi Zhēng.
Wèi Zhēng served Tàizōng with integrity.
In the eighth month,
on the Jiǎchén day,
Xiāo Hóng, the Jìedùshǐ of Fūfāng, who had fraudulently claimed to be the empress dowager's younger brother (this matter began in volume 243, Dàhé 2nd year),
was exiled to Huānzhōu
and was granted death along the way.
Zhào Zhěn, Lǚ Zhāng, and others were all exiled to Lǐngnán.
Originally,
Lǐ Xùn knew of Hóng's fraud.
Hóng, fearing this,
invited Xùn's elder brother, Zhòngjīng, to his staff.
Before this,
for those who were appointed Jìedùshǐ from the Shéncè Army,
the army would provide funds for their travel expenses,
and upon reaching their post,
they would repay three times the amount.
Someone who had been appointed to Fūfāng from the Left Army—
the Left Army
being the Left Shéncè Army—
the army demanded repayment from Hóng.
Hóng, relying on Xùn's influence, refused to pay.
When the army then demanded repayment from the son of a deceased Jìedùshǐ,
Hóng instructed the son to block the prime ministers and plead his case himself,
but Xùn ruled against him.
Chóu Shìliáng consequently resented Hóng.
The empress dowager had a paternal half-brother in Mǐnzhōng,
who was frail and unable to reach the capital himself.
A man from Mǐn, Xiāo Běn, learned the proper names of the empress dowager's internal and external relatives from him
and, through Shìliáng, conveyed this information to the emperor,
also exposing Hóng's fraud.
Hóng was thus punished.
The emperor, believing Běn to be the true empress dowager's brother,
on the Wùshēn day,
promoted him to Right Zànshàn Dàfū.
In the ninth month,
on the Dīngchǒu day,
Lǐ Shí reported to the emperor that Sòng Shēnxī was loyal and upright,
but had been slandered by malicious individuals,
banished to a remote wilderness, and died there,
without yet having his name cleared.
The emperor bowed his head for a long time,
then tearfully said:
"I have long known this matter was a mistake,
but treacherous people forced me,
for the great plans of the state,
my brother almost could not be saved."
This refers to Zhāngwáng Còu.
[Jǐ,
pronounced jūyī fān.]
"I barely kept my head.
It was not only inner court officials;
there were also those in the outer court who assisted them.
This was all due to my lack of discernment.
If I had met Hàn Zhāodì,
there would surely have been no such injustice!"
This refers to Hàn Zhāodì knowing the fraud of Yān, Gài, and Shàngguān.
The emperor was deeply saddened and regretful,
showing a look of shame.
On the Gēngchén day,
an edict was issued to fully restore Shēnxī's official titles and ranks,
and his son, Shènwēi, was appointed Wèi of Chénggù.
Chénggù County belonged to Xīngyuán Fǔ.
Lǐ Shí employed Hán Yì, Yuanwailáng of the Department of Metallurgy, to handle financial documents.
[Àn,
same as àn,
meaning official documents.]
[Punctuation mark.]
Yì was imprisoned.
Shí said:
"I initially employed Yì because I thought he understood money and grain,
but I did not know his greed was so extreme!"
The emperor said:
"The prime minister should simply use people when they are known to be capable,
and punish them when they err.
If this is done, it is easy to find capable people.
The people you employ, you do not conceal their faults;
this can be called utterly impartial.
Former prime ministers were fond of covering up the faults of the people they employed,
not wanting them to be impeached.
This is a great flaw!"
In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the Dīngsì day,
Yì was demoted to Sīhù of Wúzhōu.
Wúzhōu
was named after Cāngwú Commandery,
and was 5,500 *lǐ* from the capital.
[Hǎo,
pronounced hūdào fān.]
[Hé,
pronounced hùgài fān,
also hùdé fān.]
After the Gānlù Incident,
the emperor was constantly unhappy.
The number of polo matches between the two armies was reduced by six or seven tenths.
Although banquets, music, and various performers crowded the court,
he never smiled.
In his private quarters, he would sometimes wander and gaze into the distance,
or sigh to himself.
On the Rénwǔ day,
the emperor said to the prime ministers in the Yányīng Hall:
"Whenever I discuss affairs of the world with you,
I cannot help but feel sorrow."
They replied:
"Governing cannot be achieved quickly."
[Wéi lǐ,
means the same as wéi zhì.]
"Whenever I read books,
I am ashamed to be an ordinary ruler."
Lǐ Shí said:
"Currently, among both inner and outer court officials,
there are still many petty people who cause suspicion and obstruction.
I wish Your Majesty would treat them with greater leniency.
For those who are public-minded, upright, and adhere to the law, such as Liú Hóngyì and Xuē Jìléng,
Your Majesty should also commend and reward them to encourage good deeds."
On the Jiǎshēn day,
the emperor again said to the prime ministers:
"When I discuss affairs of the world with you,
there are matters that cannot be implemented due to circumstances;
when I retire, I can only drink strong wine to seek oblivion!"
They replied:
"This is all the fault of your servants."
21 The relevant officials, deeming the accumulated abuses in the Zuǒzàng to have long existed,
requested an inspection.
They further stated that guāndiǎn whose crimes predated the amnesty,
should be pardoned.
The Shàng granted permission.
Subsequently, it was indeed discovered that some silk fabrics were falsely claimed to be stained and soiled.
An imperial edict was issued to pardon them.
Jǐshìzhōng Dí Jiānmó returned the imperial edict, saying:
“When guāndiǎn commit embezzlement,
it is logically unpardonable!”
The Shàng admonished him, saying:
“At the beginning, when the relevant officials requested the inspection,
I already granted permission.
Rather than lose trust,
I would rather lose a criminal.
Your Lordship’s ability to perform your duty,
I commend greatly!”
22 Twelfth month,
gēngxū day,
Lú Jūn, Cǐshǐ of Huàzhōu, was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Lǐngnán.
Lǐ Shí spoke to the Shàng, saying:
“Lú Jūn’s appointment to Lǐngnán,
was celebrated by all court officials.
They believed that Lǐngnán, a rich and fertile land,
in recent years, was obtained through heavy bribes to the Běisī;
now that the Běisī does not interfere with court power,
Your Majesty should also reward this.
It is hoped that both internal and external officials will uphold the law,
which is the foundation of good governance.”
The Shàng agreed.
When Jūn arrived at the zhèn,
he became famous for his integrity and benevolence.
23 jǐwèi day,
Shū Wáng Zòng passed away.
Zòng was
a son of Shùnzōng.
1 Spring,
Second month,
jǐwèi day,
the Shàng said to the zǎixiàng:
“When recommending people, do not ask about their closeness or distance.
I heard that Dòu Yìzhí served as xiàng;
Dòu Yìzhí served as xiàng during the Chángqìng and Bǎolì eras.
If relatives or old friends are truly talented,
to avoid suspicion and abandon them,
this is also not ultimate impartiality.”
2 Jūn Wáng Wěi passed away.
Wěi was
a son of Shùnzōng.
3 Third month,
a comet appeared in the Zhāng constellation,
over eight zhàng long.
Rénshēn day,
an edict ordered the removal of music and reduction of meals,
distributing one day’s meal allowance over ten days.
4 Summer,
Fourth month,
jiǎchén day,
the Shàng met with Zhōngshū Shèrén, Hànlín Xuéshì concurrently Shìshū Liǔ Gōngquán in the biàndiàn.
Liǔ Gōngquán was previously appointed Hànlín Shìshū Xuéshì;
now he was Hànlín Xuéshì concurrently Shìshū.
“This garment has already been washed three times!”
Everyone praised the Shàng’s virtue of frugality;
Gōngquán alone remained silent.
The Shàng asked him why.
He replied:
“Your Majesty, being the Son of Heaven,
possesses wealth within the four seas.
You should advance the worthy and dismiss the unworthy,
accept admonitions,
and make rewards and punishments clear;
only then can you achieve yōngxī.
Wearing washed garments,
is but a minor detail.”
The Shàng said:
“I know that a shèrén should not again serve as a jiànyì.
Dù Yòu’s Tōngdiǎn states: ‘A Zhōngshū Shèrén is
the highest post for a scholar,
a splendid choice of the court,
unsurpassed by other officials.’
I must ask Your Lordship to take on this role.”
yǐsì day,
Gōngquán was appointed Jiànyì Dàfū,
with other duties remaining as before.
5 wùxū day,
Hànlín Xuéshì, Gōngbù Shìláng Chén Yíxíng was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
6 Sixth month,
the Héyáng army mutinied.
Jiédùshǐ Lǐ Yǒng fled to Huáizhōu;
the soldiers burned the prefectural yamen,
killed Yǒng’s two sons,
and plundered extensively for several days before stopping.
Yǒng was
a Cháng'ān city resident,
registered with the imperial guards.
He obtained a fāngzhèn through bribes.
Wherever he went, he relied on his connections,
was greedy, cruel, and lawless.
His subordinates could not endure his rule,
and therefore rebelled.
dīngwèi day,
Yǒng was demoted to Zhǎngshǐ of Lǐzhōu.
Lǐzhōu is
one thousand eight hundred ninety-three lǐ southeast of Jīngshī.
Lǐ
sounds like lǐ.
Wùshēn
day, Zuǒ Jīnwú Jiāngjūn Lǐ Zhífāng was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Héyáng.
7 Autumn,
Seventh month,
guǐhài day,
Zhènwǔ reported that over three hundred Dǎngxiàng encampments plundered and fled.
8 Jǐshìzhōng Wéi Wēn, serving as Tàizǐ Shìdú,
arrived at the Dōnggōng in the morning,
but only gained an audience at noon.
Wēn admonished him, saying:
“The Tàizǐ should rise at cockcrow,
inquire about wellbeing and inspect meals.
Records state: When Wén Wáng was shǐzǐ,
he dressed at the first crow of the cock,
went to the outer gate of the sleeping quarters,
and asked the eunuch in attendance,
‘How is the well-being today?’
The eunuch replied:
‘Well.’
Wén Wáng was then pleased.
If there was any discomfort,
the eunuch would inform Wén Wáng.
Wén Wáng’s expression would be worried,
and he could not walk properly.
Not until it returned to normal,
would he also return to normal.
When food was presented, he would certainly check the temperature.
Shǐ Zhào said: ‘Cooked food is called yōng,
a prepared meal is called shàn.’
The word shàn means ‘goodness.’
The Tàizǐ could not heed his words,
setting the stage for the Tàizǐ’s unfortunate end.
Xīnwèi day,
Wéi Wēn was dismissed from his current post.
9 One hundred and fifty Tūjué encampments in Zhènwǔ rebelled,
plundering the garrison fields.
Wùyín day,
Jiédùshǐ Liú Miǎn defeated them.
10 Eighth month,
gēngxū day,
Lady Wáng, a Zhāoyí, was made Dé fūrén.
Lady Yáng, a Zhāoróng, was made Xián fūrén.
The Táng adopted the Suí system,
with one person each as Guì, Shū, Dé, and Xián,
designated as fūrén.
These were of the first rank (zhèng yīpǐn).
Zhízhōng was made Prince Xiāng,
Yán Yáng was made Prince,
and Chéngměi was made Prince Chén.
Guǐchǒu day,
Imperial son Zōngjiǎn was established as Jiǎng Wáng.
Jiǎng was
the name of an ancient state.
The Zuǒzhuàn lists: Fán, Jiǎng, Xíng, Máo, Zuò, Jì.
11 The Héyáng soldiers, having driven out Lǐ Yǒng,
incited each other daily,
desiring to create chaos.
Ninth month,
Lǐ Zhífāng sought out and captured over seventy leaders of the rebellion,
and executed them all.
The remaining factions were distributed to outer garrisons,
and then stability was restored.
12 Winter,
Tenth month,
the Shíjīng of the Guózǐjiàn were completed.
Liú Xù said: “At that time, the Shàng favored literature.
Zhèng Tán, as zǎichén, concurrently served as pàn Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
Following the example of Cài Yōng in the Hòu Hàn, who carved inscriptions on steles and placed them in the Tàixué,
he initiated the carving of the Jiǔjīng onto stone tablets.
All scholars corrected errors.
The Shàng also ordered Hànlín lèzì guān to standardize the calligraphy,
which again deviated from the teaching methods.
Therefore, for several decades after the Shíjīng were erected,
renowned scholars did not even glance at them,
considering them useless clutter.”
13 Fújiàn reported that a commoner from Jìnjiāng, Xiāo Hóng, claimed to be a relative of the Tàihòu.
Jìnjiāng was
formerly the land of Jìn’ān Xiàn in Jìn’ān Jùn.
Wú established Dōng’ān Xiàn,
Jìn changed its name to Jìn’ān,
Suí changed it to Nán’ān.
In the eighth year of Kāiyuán, Jìnjiāng Xiàn was separated from Nán’ān,
and it was subordinate to Quánzhōu.
14 Wùshēn day,
Ménxià Shìláng, Tóng Píngzhāngshì Lǐ Gùyán was re-appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and appointed concurrently Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ.
15 Jiǎyín day,
the Yùshǐtái reported that Xiāo Hóng’s claim was fraudulent;
an edict ordered him to be conveyed back to his hometown,
instructing that he be provided with food at each stop on his journey back.
It was hoped that his true identity would be revealed.
Punctuated by Zhōu Yīliáng, revised by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command.
Later scholars
Tiantái
The third year of Kāichéng (wùwǔ, 838).
1. Spring,
First month.
On the day jiǎzǐ,
Lǐ Shí entered court.
On the way, thieves shot at him,
causing a minor injury.
His attendants scattered,
and Lǐ Shí's horse, startled,
galloped back to his mansion.
Again, thieves ambushed and attacked him at the ward gate,
cutting off his horse's tail.
In the Táng dynasty, all southern wards had gates,
which were opened and closed at specific times.
斷 (duàn)
is pronounced duǎn.
The emperor was greatly alarmed when he heard of this,
and ordered the Shéncè Six Armies to dispatch soldiers for protection,
issuing urgent edicts to the central and local governments to apprehend the thieves.
However, nothing was found.
On the day yǐchǒu,
only nine officials attended court.
The capital was only secure after several days.
2. On the day dīngmǎo,
the deceased Qí Wáng Còu was posthumously honored as Huái Yì Tàizǐ.
This shows the emperor knew of Còu’s injustice.
The case of Còu being wrongly accused can be found in volume 244, Tàihé 5th year.
3. On the day wùshēn,
Yáng Sìfù, the Salt and Iron Transport Commissioner and Minister of Personnel,
and Lǐ yù, the Vice Minister of Personnel and acting Minister of Personnel, were both appointed Associate Administrators.
Kǎoyì says: The old tradition states:
"In the third year,
Yáng Sìfù assisted in governance,
and recommended Lǐ yù,
who was appointed Associate Administrator in his original capacity."
However, Lǐ yù and Yáng Sìfù were appointed together,
so we follow the Veritable Records.
判 (pàn)
refers to acting Minister of Personnel.
使 (shǐ)
refers to Salt and Iron Transport Commissioner.
Lǐ yù was the son of Yúlíng.
Yáng Yúlíng can be found in volume 237, Xiànzōng, Yuánhé 3rd year.
於 (yú)
is pronounced wū.
4. Lǐ Shí, the Secretariat Grandee and Associate Administrator,
after the Gānlù Incident,
when people's hearts were fearful and precarious,
and eunuchs were rampant and tyrannical,
disregarded his own safety for the country,
and thus roughly re-established order.
Qiú Shìliáng deeply detested him
and secretly sent thieves to kill him,
but they failed.
Lǐ Shí was afraid,
and repeatedly submitted memorials claiming illness to resign his position.
The emperor deeply understood his reasons but could do nothing.
On the day bǐngzǐ,
Lǐ Shí was appointed Associate Administrator
and concurrent Military Governor of Jīngnán.
5. Chén Yíxíng was straightforward by nature
and disliked Yáng Sìfù's character.
Whenever political matters were discussed,
they often denounced each other.
On the day rénchén,
Chén Yíxíng resigned due to a foot ailment,
but it was not permitted.
6. The emperor ordered Wèi Máo, the Imperial Diarist, to present his grandfather, Wénzhēn Gōng's, ceremonial tablet.
Wèi Zhēng's posthumous title was Wénzhēn.
"It is about the person, not the tablet."
The emperor said:
"It is also like the gāntáng tree."
This means that the people of Zhōu thought of Shào Gōng,
cherished his gāntáng tree and dared not cut it down;
now, thinking of Wèi Zhēng's integrity,
one should also cherish his old ceremonial tablet.
7. Yáng Sìfù wanted to bring Lǐ Zōngmǐn back into office,
fearing that Zhèng Tán would obstruct him.
So he first ordered a eunuch to hint to the emperor.
When the emperor held court,
he said to the grand councilors:
"Lǐ Zōngmǐn has been outside the capital for many years;
he should be given an official position."
Lǐ Zōngmǐn's demotion can be found in the previous volume, Tàihé 9th year.
"If Your Majesty pities Lǐ Zōngmǐn's distant exile,
he should only be moved a few hundred *lǐ* closer to the north;
he should not be reappointed.
If he is reappointed,
I request to resign my position first."
Chén Yíxíng said:
"Lǐ Zōngmǐn previously disrupted governance through factionalism.
Why does Your Majesty favor such a petty person?"
纖人 (xiānrén)
is equivalent to saying "villain" or "petty person."
"Matters should be handled with moderation;
one should not simply act out of love or hatred."
The emperor said:
"He can be given a prefecture."
Zhèng Tán said:
"Giving him a prefecture is too generous;
he should only be the Sīmǎ of Hóngzhōu."
Hóngzhōu
is 3090 *lǐ* southeast of the capital.
The emperor said:
"Giving him a prefecture causes no harm."
After Zhèng Tán and the others withdrew,
the emperor said to Zhōu Jìngfù, the Imperial Diarist, and Wèi Máo, the Imperial Diarist:
"Is it acceptable for the grand councilors to quarrel like this?"
According to Táng regulations: the Imperial Diarists and Imperial Recorders were in charge of recording the emperor's daily activities and decrees.
When the emperor held court in the main hall,
the Imperial Diarist stood on the left,
and the Imperial Recorder on the right.
When an order was given,
they would bow to the steps to listen.
After each court session,
when the emperor discussed political matters with the grand councilors,
the Imperial Diarists and Recorders also stood on either side.
If the court session was held in the Zǐchén Inner Cabinet,
they would stand on either side of the incense table, below the hall.
Since Zhèng Tán and the others had just left after their noisy argument,
the emperor then asked them.
"Indeed, it is unacceptable.
However, Zhèng Tán and the others were merely expressing their loyalty and indignation,
unaware of their own behavior."
On the day dīngyǒu,
Lǐ Zōngmǐn, the Sīmǎ of Héngzhōu, was appointed Prefect of Hángzhōu.
According to Táng regulations: Héngzhōu
was a middle-tier prefecture.
Hóngzhōu
was a top-tier prefecture,
a Metropolitan Prefecture.
Hángzhōu
was a top-tier prefecture.
The Sīmǎ of a middle-tier prefecture
was a rank 5b official.
The Sīmǎ of a Metropolitan Prefecture
was a rank 4b official.
The Prefect of a top-tier prefecture
was a rank 3b official.
Lǐ yù
therefore actively used his high position to oppose Zhèng Tán and Chén Yíxíng.
Whenever political matters were discussed,
right and wrong clashed sharply,
and the emperor could not make a decision.
History states that Wénzōng's discernment was insufficient to illuminate the truth.
8. Third month.
The Zāngkē barbarians raided Qīngxī Town in Fúzhōu.
The Zāngkē Man were 900 *lǐ* east of Fúzhōu,
and 2400 *lǐ* east of Chénzhōu.
涪 (fú)
is pronounced fú.
9 Initially,
at the end of the Tài-Hé reign,
Dù Cōng was the Jíe-Dù-Shǐ of Fèng-Xiáng.
An imperial edict was issued to purge monks and nuns.
This matter is discussed in the previous volume under the eighth year of Tài-Hé.
Near Fǎ-Mén-Sì,
a popular rumor spread that the Buddha's sarira manifested auspicious signs.
The Buddha's sarira was at Fǎ-Mén-Sì,
hence the rumor.
The Inspector-General wanted to report it,
but Cōng said:
"The colors of clouds and objects change;
how can they be constant?
If the Buddha truly loves monks and nuns,
he should manifest in the capital."
Not long after,
a white rabbit was captured.
The Inspector-General again wanted to report it,
saying:
"This is an auspicious omen from the West."
Cōng said:
"Wild beasts are untamed;
it is better to keep it for now."
It died within ten days.
The Inspector-General was displeased,
believing it to be an obstruction of sagely virtue,
and independently drew a picture and presented it.
When Zhèng Zhù replaced Cōng as governor of Fèng-Xiáng—
According to the previous volume of the Tōng-Jiàn,
in the eighth year of Tài-Hé,
in the ninth month,
on the Gēng-Shēn day,
Lǐ Tīng, the Jíe-Dù-Shǐ of Fèng-Xiáng, was made Jíe-Dù-Shǐ of Zhōng-Wǔ,
replacing Dù Cōng.
On the Dīng-Mǎo day,
Zhèng Zhù was made Jíe-Dù-Shǐ of Fèng-Xiáng.
Zhù falsely accused Tīng of greed and tyranny during his time in Fèng-Xiáng.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Yǐ-Hài day,
Tīng was made Tài-Zǐ Tài-Bǎo and assigned to subsidiary duties,
and Dù Cōng was again made Jíe-Dù-Shǐ of Zhōng-Wǔ.
If it is as written in the previous volume,
then Dù Cōng governed Zhōng-Wǔ,
not Fèng-Xiáng.
Zhù also presented a white pheasant.
That year,
in the eighth month,
sweet dew fell upon the cherry trees in front of the Zǐ-Chén-Diàn.
The emperor personally plucked and tasted it,
and all officials offered congratulations.
In the eleventh month of that year,
the incident of the Jīn-Wǔ sweet dew occurred.
Later, when Cōng was Gōng-Bù Shàng-Shū and Pàn-Dù-Zhī,
Hé-Zhōng reported the sighting of a Zōu-Yú.
Poetic annotations: Zōu-Yú is
a righteous beast,
white with black markings,
it does not eat living creatures,
and appears when there is utmost sincerity.
Sī-Mǎ Xiāng-Rú's Fēng-Shàn Shū says: "A host of beasts,
joyful in our sovereign's park,
white-bodied with black patterns,
their demeanor is pleasing."
Shī-Gǔ commented: "This refers to the Zōu-Yú."
The Shān-Hǎi-Jīng says: "The Zōu-Yú resembles a tiger,
five-colored,
its tail longer than its body."
The emperor said to Cōng:
"Lǐ Xùn and Zhèng Zhù both used auspicious omens to carry out their rebellion.
Thus I know that auspicious objects are not a blessing to the state.
When you were previously in Fèng-Xiáng,
you did not report the white rabbit,
you truly were prescient."
He replied:
"In antiquity, a diagram emerged from the Hé river,
and Fú-Xī used it to draw the Eight Trigrams;
a book emerged from the Luò river,
and Dà-Yǔ used it to categorize the Nine Divisions.
All were beneficial to humanity,
hence they are truly estimable.
As for auspicious omens of birds, beasts, plants, and trees,
when have they ever not existed?
Liú Cōng was rebellious and tyrannical,
yet yellow dragons appeared three times;
Shí Jì-Lóng was cruel and violent,
yet he obtained sixteen azure qilin and seven white deer,
which he used to pull a 'zhī-gài' carriage.
Shí Hǔ,
whose courtesy name was Jì-Lóng—
The Táng dynasty avoided imperial taboo names,
hence he is referred to by his courtesy name.
How can auspiciousness reside in virtue?
Xuán-Zōng once served as Lù-Zhōu Bié-Jià.
During the Zhōng-Zōng reign,
Xuán-Zōng was Lù-Zhōu Bié-Jià.
Lù-Zhōu reported nineteen auspicious omens,
and Xuán-Zōng said: 'When I was in Lù-Zhōu,
I only knew to diligently attend to my duties,
I knew nothing of these auspicious objects.'
I wish Your Majesty would focus solely on the prosperity and peace of the common people as the nation's blessing,
and disregard all others."
The emperor approved of this.
Another day,
he said to his prime ministers:
"When the times are harmonious and the year is bountiful,
this is the highest auspicious sign;
what true benefit are auspicious grains and spirit ganoderma?"
The prime ministers then said:
"The Chūn-Qiū records disasters and anomalies to warn rulers,
but does not record auspicious omens.
This is why!"
It is probably Zhèng Tán who said this.
In summer,
the fifth month,
on the Yǐ-Hài day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Regarding auspicious omens in all circuits,
none shall be reported,
nor shall dispatches be sent to the relevant authorities.
The Lày-Xiǎng ceremony at the Tài-Miào
(Táng system: Sacrifices were offered at the Tài-Miào in the four mid-season months and during the Lày ceremony.)
(The Táng Lày ceremony was held in the Yín month.)
(In the second year of Tiān-Bǎo of Xuán-Zōng, the Xuán-Yuán Huáng-Dì temple in Xī-Jīng was designated as the Tài-Qīng-Gōng.)
shall all be suspended."
The Liù-Diǎn states: "All major auspicious omens are to be reported immediately by memorial,
and all civil and military officials are to proceed to the palace gate to offer congratulations."
"Other omens are to be reported at year-end by memorial,
the relevant authorities inform the ancestral temple,
and all officials proceed to the palace gate to offer congratulations."
"Also, the Yí-Zhì-Lìng states: major auspicious omens are to be reported immediately by memorial;
medium and minor auspicious omens are to be reported to the relevant authorities,
and presented to the throne on New Year's Day."
Now all of these are suspended.
The Kǎo-Yì states: The Shí-Lù says:
"Initially,
the emperor said to his prime ministers: 'Is not a bountiful year and peaceful populace the highest auspicious sign?'
The prime ministers then mentioned that the Chūn-Qiū does not record auspicious omens.
The emperor deeply agreed,
and thus issued this edict."
The Bǔ-Guó-Shǐ considered it to be based on Dù Cōng's advice;
now both are included.
10 Initially,
Wáng Yàn-Píng, the Jíe-Dù-Shǐ of Líng-Wǔ, embezzled over seven thousand strings of cash.
The emperor, considering his father Zhì-Xīng's merits,
(Wáng Zhì-Xīng had the merit of suppressing Hèng-Hǎi.)
exiled him to Kāng-Zhōu.
Yàn-Píng secretly appealed to the three Jíe-Dù-Shǐ of Wèi, Zhèn, and Yōu.
(The Wèi marshal was Hé Jìn-Tāo;
the Zhèn marshal was Wáng Yuán-Kuí;
the Yōu marshal was Shǐ Yuán-Zhōng.)
The emperor had no choice,
and in the sixth month,
on the Rén-Yín day,
changed his posting to Sī-Hù of Yǒng-Zhōu.
11 In the eighth month,
on the Jǐ-Hài day,
Jiā-Wáng Yùn died.
Yùn was
the son of Dài-Zōng.
The mother of Crown Prince Yǒng (永), Wáng Dé (王德), was out of favor,
and died after being slandered by Yáng Xián (楊賢).
The Táng (唐) adopted the Suí (隋) system,
with one each of Guì (貴), Shú (淑), Dé (德), and Xián (賢),
who were called Fūren (夫人),
of the first rank.
During the Kāiyuán (開元) era,
Xuánzōng (玄宗) considered the four ranks to be like stars to the Empress.
Since there was already an Empress,
to have another four was
contrary to the established law.
So he established Huì (惠), Lì (麗), and Huá (華),
to replace the three Fūren (夫人).
Later, Guì (貴) was re-established,
restoring the system of four from the early Táng (唐).
With close access to petty people,
Xián (賢) slandered him day and night.
In the ninth month,
on the day Rénxū (壬戌),
the Emperor convened the Yányīng (延英) court,
summoning the prime ministers, officials from the two departments (Liǎngshěng 兩省), censors (Yùshǐ 御史), and secretaries (Lángguān 郎官).
He enumerated the Crown Prince's faults and misdeeds,
and discussed deposing him,
saying:
"Is he fit to be the Son of Heaven?"
The ministers all said:
"The Crown Prince is young,
and may still be able to change his ways.
The foundation of the state is of the utmost importance;
how can it be lightly disturbed?"
The Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞) Dí Jiānchē (狄兼謩) argued with particular earnestness,
even to the point of tears.
The Gěishìzhōng (給事中) Wéi Wēn (韋溫) said:
"Your Majesty has only one son.
If you do not teach him,
and he is brought to this state,
how can it be the Crown Prince's fault alone?"
On the day Guǐhài (癸亥),
six scholars from the Hànlín Academy (Hànlín Xuéshì 翰林學士) and sixteen military commissioners of the Shéncè Six Armies (Shéncè Liùjūn Jūnshǐ 神策六軍軍使) again submitted memorials arguing against it,
and the Emperor's resolve softened slightly.
That evening,
the Crown Prince was finally allowed to return to the Shǎoyáng Court (Shǎoyáng Yuàn 少陽院).
As for the Rú Jīngshǐ (如京使) Wáng Shàohuá (王少華) and others,
the Táng (唐) established the Rú Jīngshǐ (如京使),
filled by military officials,
an inner court position,
whose specific duties are unknown.
13 The Yìwǔ (義武) Jìedùshǐ (節度使) Zhāng Fán (張璠) had been in his post for fifteen years.
In the third year of Mùzōng's (穆宗) Chángqìng (長慶) era (823),
Fán (璠) replaced Chén Chǔ (陳楚) in governing Yìwǔ (義武).
When he fell ill,
he requested to return to court.
Before the court could make arrangements,
his illness worsened,
and he instructed his son Yuányì (元益) to bring the entire family back to court,
and not to follow the old customs of Héběi (河北).
When he died,
the army wished to enthrone Yuányì (元益).
The Guānchá Liúhòu (觀察留後) Lǐ Shìjì (李士季) disagreed,
so the multitude killed him,
and also killed more than ten other generals.
On the day Rénshēn (壬申),
Lǐ Zhòngqiān (李仲遷), the Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Yìzhōu (易州), was made Yìwǔ (義武) Jìedùshǐ (節度使).
Hé Qīngcháo (何清朝), the Mǎjūn Dūyúhòu (馬軍都虞候) of Yìwǔ (義武), defected and returned to court.
On the day Guǐyǒu (癸酉),
he was appointed Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Yízhōu (儀州).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Liáozhōu (遼州) was Lèpíngjùn (樂平郡).
In the third year of Táng (唐) Wǔdé (武德) (620), Liáozhōu (遼州) was established.
In the eighth year, it was changed to Jīzhōu (箕州).
In the second year of Xiāntiān (先天) (713),
due to Xuánzōng's (玄宗) taboo name,
it was changed to Yízhōu (儀州).
14 The court considered the Yìchāng (義昌) Jìedùshǐ (節度使) Lǐ Yànzuǒ (李彥佐) to have been in his post for a long time.
In the sixth year of Tàihé (太和) (832),
Lǐ Yànzuǒ (李彥佐) replaced Yīn Yòu (殷侑) in governing Yìchāng (義昌).
On the day Jiǎxū (甲戌),
Liú Yuē (劉約), the Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Dézhōu (德州), was made Jìedù Fùshǐ (節度副使),
with the intention of replacing him.
15 Since the Kāichéng (開成) era,
when Shéncè (神策) officers were promoted,
they often did not report it to the Emperor,
but directly sent a document to the Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令) to review and implement,
with promotions and changes occurring almost daily.
After the Gānlù Incident (Gānlù Zhī Biàn 甘露之變),
eunuchs' usurpation of power reached this extent.
On the day Guǐwèi (癸未),
an imperial edict was first issued that all promotions of Shéncè (神策) officers must first be reported to the Emperor,
the document then sent to the Zhōngshū (中書) for inspection
before implementation.
It was first reported to the Emperor,
the inner court then sent the document to the Zhōngshū (中書),
which then inspected their records of service and implemented it.
16 In winter,
the tenth month,
the Jìandūn (監軍) of Yìdìng (易定) reported that the army would not accept Lǐ Zhòngqiān (李仲遷),
and requested that Zhāng Yuányì (張元益) be made Liúhòu (留後).
17 Crown Prince Yǒng (永) remained unrepentant.
On the day Gēngzǐ (庚子),
he died suddenly.
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: According to the record, Wénzōng (文宗) later saw a pole-climber (yuánchóngzhě 緣橦者) and wept, saying:
"I, as the Son of Heaven,
cannot even preserve one son!"
Then he killed Liú Chǔcái (劉楚材) and others.
Thus, the Crown Prince did not die a natural death.
However, matters of the palace were secret,
and outsiders did not know the details,
so the official records only say:
"He remained unrepentant to the end,
and died suddenly on that day."
18 On the day Yǐsì (乙巳),
Guō Mǐn (郭旼), the Zuǒ Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn (左金吾大將軍), was made Bīnníng (邠寧) Jìedùshǐ (節度使).
19 The prime ministers debated sending troops to suppress Yìdìng (易定).
The Emperor said:
"Yìdìng (易定) has small territory and poor people,
and half of its military resources rely on the Ministry of Finance (Dùzhī 度支).
If we press them, they will stop at nothing.
If we take it slowly, changes will occur on their own.
We should just carefully guard the four borders and wait for them."
So Zhāng Yuányì (張元益) was appointed Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Dàizhōu (代州).
After a while,
the army indeed had dissenting opinions,
and submitted a memorial citing the inconvenience of Lǐ Zhòngqiān (李仲遷) as an excuse,
so the court dismissed Zhòngqiān (仲遷).
In the eleventh month,
an edict was issued to await Yuányì's (元益) departure from Dìngzhōu (定州).
All the Yìwǔ (義武) officers and soldiers who had initially plotted to enthrone Yuányì (元益)
were pardoned and not questioned.
20 Lǐ Yànzuǒ (李彥佐), the Yìchāng (義昌) Jìedùshǐ (節度使), was made Tiānpíng (天平) Jìedùshǐ (節度使),
and Liú Yuē (劉約) was made Yìchāng (義昌) Jìedùshǐ (節度使).
21 On the day Dīngmǎo (丁卯),
Zhāng Yuányì (張元益) departed from Dìngzhōu (定州).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Bǔ Guóshǐ (補國史) says:
"Zhāng Gōngfán (張公璠) of Yìdìng (易定) died,
and the three armies requested that Gōngfán's (公璠) son Yuányì (元益) succeed him in military command.
Gōngfán (公璠) was the grandson of Xiàozhōng (孝忠).
During Gōngfán's (公璠) last moments,
he admonished Yuányì (元益) to return to the capital.
The three armies again followed the example of the three circuits of Yōu (幽), Zhèn (鎮), and Wèi (魏),
self-appointed a commander,
and awaited an imperial decree.
The court's plan was undecided.
Prime Minister Wèi Gōng (衛公) wanted to attack and conquer them.
Zhēnmù Gōng (貞穆公) argued that it was not yet time to raise an army,
and that they should first perform the rites of condolence and bestowal,
summoning Yuányì (元益) to the capital.
If he refused the order and became unruly,
it would not be too late to punish him.
They presented their pros and cons before the Emperor,
but the court's decree was not issued.
Zhēnmù Gōng (貞穆公) had a secret memorial,
presenting the imperial edict to summon Yuányì (元益), which stated: 'Edict to Zhāng Yuányì (張元益): Your great ancestor Xiàozhōng (孝忠)'s
achievements are arrayed in tripods and vessels,
enduring eternally.
Your ancestor Màozhāo (茂昭)
upheld the inherited teachings,
and did not let the spirit of righteousness fall.'
Et cetera.
Wénzōng (文宗) read the intent of the edict,
and it deeply matched his sagacious plan.
When the edict reached Dìngzhōu (定州),
Yuányì (元益) bowed to the edict and wept bitterly,
burned his mourning clothes,
and requested to die before the multitude.
The officers and soldiers of the three armies kowtowed facing south,
danced and wept,
and helped Yuányì (元益) to his mourning hut,
requesting the Jìandūnshǐ (監軍使) and the staff to each act as Liúhòu (留後) according to the example of other circuits.
Gōngfán (公璠) then brought his entire family to the capital.
An edict appointed Chén Jūnshǎng (陳君賞), a Shéncè Jūnshǐ (神策軍使), as commander."
The so-called Zhēnmù Gōng (貞穆公)
was Lǐ Déyù (李德裕).
However, according to the official records, Fán (璠)
was an army officer from Dìngzhōu (定州), not Xiàozhōng's (孝忠) grandson.
Also, Lǐ Déyù (李德裕) was not prime minister in this year.
The Bǔ Guóshǐ (補國史) is likely based on hearsay,
and cannot be relied upon.
We now follow the official records.
On the 22nd day, Gēngwǔ [of the 8th month],
the Emperor questioned Hànlín Xuéshì Liǔ Gōngquán regarding outside opinions.
He replied,
"Guō Mǐn's appointment to Bīnníng
is widely regarded with suspicion."
The Emperor said,
"Mǐn
is the nephew of the Shàngfù.
Dézōng made Guō Zǐyí the Shàngfù.
The Empress Dowager
is the Grand Empress Dowager Guō.
Since a Golden Guard became a minor military commissioner,
what cause for criticism is there from outside?"
He replied,
"It is not that Mǐn should not be a Jiédùshǐ.
I heard that Your Majesty recently took two of Mǐn's daughters into the palace.
Is this true?"
The Emperor said,
"Yes,
they entered to serve the Grand Empress Dowager."
Gōngquán said,
"Those outside do not know this,
and all say that Mǐn offered his daughters to the inner palace,
and thus obtained a regional command."
The Emperor bowed his head for a long time and said,
"If that is the case, what should be done?"
He replied,
"Only by sending them back to their home from the Southern Palace [Nánnèi]
will the outside talk cease!"
On that day,
the Grand Empress Dowager sent a palace envoy to escort the two daughters back to Mǐn's home.
The Grand Empress Dowager resided in Xīngqìng Gōng;
Xīngqìng Gōng was called the Nánnèi.
使,
read as "shū lì fān".
還,
read as written.
On the 23rd day, the Emperor was fond of poetry.
He once wished to establish a poetry academy,
but Lǐ Déyù said,
"Today's poets are frivolous
and offer no benefit to governance."
So he stopped.
On the 24th day, Jiǎxū,
Càizhōu Cìshǐ Hán Wēi was appointed Yìwǔ Jiédùshǐ.
After Zhāng Yuányì had left Dìngzhōu,
Hán Wēi was then appointed.
On the 25th day, Hédōng Jiédùshǐ, Sītú, and Zhōngshū Lìng Péi Dù requested to return to the Eastern Capital due to illness.
Péi Dù built a residence in the Jíxián Lǐ of the Eastern Capital,
called Lǜyě Táng.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
an imperial edict ordered Dù to enter and oversee governmental affairs,
and sent a palace envoy to urge him to set out.
On the 26th day, Zhèng Tán repeatedly submitted memorials to resign his post.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
an imperial edict stated: "He is to enter the Zhōngshū [Provincial Secretariat] once every three to five days."
On the 27th day, in this year,
Tǔbō Yǐtài Zānpǔ died,
and his younger brother Dámó ascended the throne.
Yǐtài was often ill
and entrusted governance to his high ministers,
so he was barely able to maintain his position
and for a long time did not cause border troubles.
Dámó was dissolute and cruel;
his people did not support him,
and disasters followed one another,
causing Tǔbō to further decline.
Note: When Tǔbō declined,
and Huíhú declined,
then Táng also declined.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: "The death of Yǐtài and the ascension of Dámó
are not recorded in the *Shílù*,
nor are they found in the *Jiù Chuán* or *Xù Huìyào*.
Now we supplement this based on the *Guóshǐ*."
1 In spring,
in the intercalary first month,
on the day Jǐhài,
Péi Dù arrived at the capital.
Due to illness, he returned to his residence;
this was his Cháng'ān Pínglè Lǐ residence.
The Emperor offered condolences and bestowed gifts;
envoys were numerous.
In the third month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
he passed away,
and was posthumously granted the title Wénzhōng.
The Emperor was surprised that Dù had no farewell memorial,
so he questioned his family
and found a half-draft,
expressing concern that the heir apparent was not yet settled,
without mentioning private matters.
Dù's physical appearance did not surpass that of an ordinary person,
yet his prestige extended far to the four barbarian tribes.
When the four tribes saw Táng envoys,
they would always ask about Dù's age, whether he was being used or dismissed;
for more than twenty years, he was a person whose presence affected the nation's weight, like Guō Zǐyí.
2 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Wùchén,
the Emperor praised Dù Cōng, the son of Pàndùzhī Dù Cōng.
Yáng Sìfù and Lǐ Déyù then requested that Dù Cōng be appointed Hùbù Shàngshū.
Chén Yíxíng said,
"Imperial favor should come from above;
since ancient times, no state has ever been lost without power residing with the ministers."
Lǐ Déyù said,
"Your Majesty once told your servant,
'A ruler should choose prime ministers,
but should not doubt prime ministers.'"
In the fifth month,
on the day Dīnghài,
the Emperor discussed state affairs with the prime ministers.
Chén Yíxíng again said that it was inappropriate for authority and power to reside with subordinates.
Lǐ Déyù said,
"Yíxíng's intention is to suspect that there are those among the prime ministers who manipulate Your Majesty's authority.
Your servant has repeatedly sought to retire;
if I could obtain the title of Wángfù,
that would be my good fortune."
Wángfù was
a sinecure,
held by officials demoted from prime ministerial or executive posts.
"Your Majesty's governance in Kāichéng元年 and Kāichéng二年 was exceptionally good;
in Kāichéng三年 and Kāichéng四年, it gradually declined."
Yáng Sìfù said,
"In the first and second years, Zhèng Tán and Yíxíng were in power;
in the third and fourth years, your servant and Lǐ Déyù were together in power.
The fault lies entirely with your servant!"
He then kowtowed and said,
"Your servant dares not enter the Zhōngshū again!"
The Zhèngshìtáng was located in the Zhōngshū Shěng.
The Emperor sent an envoy to summon him back,
and comforted him,
saying,
"Zhèng Tán spoke improperly,
why are you so hasty!"
Tán rose and apologized, saying,
"Your servant is foolish and clumsy;
my intention was not directed at Sìfù;
that it came to this so abruptly
is because Sìfù does not tolerate your servant."
Sìfù said,
"Tán says that governance declines year by year,
not only should your servant be punished,
but it also impinges on the sacred virtue of the Emperor."
He then withdrew,
and submitted three memorials to resign his post.
The Emperor sent a palace envoy to call him out,
and on the day Guǐsì,
he finally attended court.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Zhèng Tán was dismissed as Yòupúshè,
and Chén Yíxíng was dismissed as Lìbù Shìláng.
Tán's nature was honest and frugal;
Yíxíng was also upright and unyielding,
hence Sìfù and others deeply resented them.
History says that petty men spare no effort
to oust virtuous gentlemen.
3 On the 28th day, the Emperor, considering that Yántiě Tuīguān and Jiǎnjiào Lǐbù Yuánwàiláng Yáo Xù was capable of investigating difficult cases,
ordered him to provisionally [quánzhī] serve as Zhífāng Yuánwàiláng.
Yòuchéng Wéi Wēn did not approve,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"Lángguān are pure selections of the imperial court;
it is not appropriate to reward capable officials with such posts."
The Emperor then appointed Xù as Jiǎnjiào Lǐbù Lángzhōng,
retaining his former post as Yántiě Tuīguān.
Yáo Xù was to provisionally serve as Zhífāng Yuánwàiláng,
but Wéi Wēn contested it;
when he was made Jiǎnjiào Lǐbù Lángzhōng,
Wēn no longer spoke,
likely because, according to Táng regulations, subordinates of regional commanders and various commissioners often held jiǎnjiào [acting/supervising] official titles,
whereas quánzhī [provisionally serving] was a substantive official post.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
the Emperor asked Prime Minister Yáng Sìfù about this matter.
He replied,
"Wēn's ambition is to clarify the ranks of officials.
If all capable officials are denied 'pure stream' positions,
then who will manage the affairs of the realm for Your Majesty!
I fear this resembles the custom of the declining Jìn Dynasty."
However, the Emperor always respected Wēn,
and ultimately did not override his principles.
4 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Guǐwèi,
Zhāng Yuányì was appointed Zuǒxiāowèi Jiāngjūn,
and his mother, Hóumòchén Shì, was granted the title Zhàoguó Tàifūrén,
and bestowed two hundred bolts of silk.
During the Yìdìng rebellion,
Hóumòchén Shì persuaded the generals and soldiers,
and also cautioned Yuányì to obey the imperial decree,
hence she was rewarded.
5 On the day Jiǎchén,
Tàicháng Qīng Cuī Dān was appointed Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
Dān
was the younger brother of Yǎn.
6 In the eighth month,
on the day Xīnhài,
Fūwáng Jǐng passed away.
Jǐng
was the son of Xiànzōng.
7 On the guǐyǒu day,
Liú Cóngjiàn, Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì, reported:
“Xiāo Běn falsely claims to be the Empress Dowager’s younger brother.
Everyone, high and low, says Xiāo Hóng is the real one.
Because Běn came from the Left Army,
Hóng was suppressed by the Táisī.
The matter of Xiāo Běn is seen in the first year of the previous volume.
The matter of Xiāo Hóng is seen in the second year.
Táisī
refers to the officials of the Yùshǐ Tái,
who were in charge of investigating Xiāo Hóng.
I request to report this to Your Majesty.
I beg that Hóng be summoned to the capital
to be interrogated face-to-face with Běn,
to determine who is genuine and who is fake.”
An imperial edict ordered the Sānsī to interrogate them.
8 In winter,
tenth month,
on the yǐmǎo day,
the Emperor asked Wèi Mó, Qǐjū Shèrén, for the records to examine them.
Jìzhù
is the same as Qǐjūzhù.
In the early Zhēngguān era,
the Gěishì Zhōng and Jiànyì Dàfū were concurrently in charge of the Qǐjūzhù,
or supervised the Qǐjū matters.
Whenever the court session ended, matters were discussed for recording.
One Qǐjū Láng would hold a brush and record in front,
followed by the official historians.
Later, Qǐjū Shèrén were again appointed,
to stand on either side, holding brushes,
entering the hall with the Prime Ministers.
If the court session was in the Zǐchén Nèi Gé,
they would flank the incense table,
standing below the hall,
directly at the second chīshǒu.
The ink was mixed and brushes moistened
right there in the hollows,
which at the time were called
“Chītóu.”
When Gāozōng presided over court, he did not decide matters;
when something was presented,
he would only decline to see it.
When Xǔ Jìngzōng and Lǐ Yìfǔ were Prime Ministers,
their proposals often involved matters they feared others would know.
They ordered the Qǐjū Láng and Shèrén to receive imperial decrees at court;
after court, they would all exit with the hundred officials,
not daring to hear about confidential state affairs.
During the Chángshòu era,
Prime Minister Yáo Shú proposed that after court,
one Prime Minister should record the main points of military and state affairs,
to form a Shízhèng Jì,
which would be sent to the History Bureau monthly.
However, it was often used to praise and commend,
not reflecting the true facts,
and was abandoned not long after.
The Qǐjū Láng, therefore, gradually edited and revised imperial edicts,
to supplement the deficiencies of the national history.
The Qǐjū Shèrén’s original duty was to record words,
only compiling imperial edicts,
and not involving other matters.
In the early Kāiyuán era,
an edict again ordered that historical officials who were not cungfèng
should all enter with the court session,
positioned after the Qǐjū Láng and Shèrén.
When Lǐ Línfǔ monopolized power,
this was again abolished.
In the ninth year of Tàihé,
an edict ordered the Qǐjū Láng and Shèrén,
on days they entered the inner chamber,
to prepare paper and brushes,
and stand below the chītóu,
restoring the practice of the Zhēngguān era.
He said:
“The records record both good and bad,
thereby serving as a warning to rulers.
Your Majesty need only strive to do good,
and need not view the history!”
The Emperor said:
“I have previously viewed them.”
He replied:
“That was the fault of the historical officials of those days.
If Your Majesty views the history personally,
then the historical officials will surely have something to conceal or avoid,
how can they gain trust from later generations!”
The Emperor then stopped.
9 Yáng requested that the Emperor’s younger brother, Ān Wáng Róng, be established as heir.
The Emperor consulted with the Prime Ministers,
and Lǐ Déyù opposed it.
On the bǐngyín day,
Kìngzōng’s youngest son, Chén Wáng Chéngměi, was established as Crown Prince.
This lays the groundwork for Yáng and Chéngměi being killed.
On the dīngmǎo day,
the Emperor visited the Huìníng Hall for music and entertainment.
There was a boy climbing a pole,
and a man ran back and forth below him like a madman.
The Emperor found this strange.
His attendants said:
“He is his father.”
The Emperor’s tears flowed, and he said with sadness:
“Though I am the Son of Heaven,
I cannot keep even one son alive!”
He summoned Lǐu Chǔcái and three others from the Jiaofang,
and Zhāng Shíshí and nine other palace women, and rebuked them, saying:
“It was all you who brought about the former Crown Prince,
and now a new Crown Prince has been established,
do you want to do it again?”
He had them arrested and handed over to officials.
On the jǐsì day,
they were all executed.
The Emperor was deeply saddened by this,
and his old illness worsened.
10 In the eleventh month,
the Sānsī concluded that neither Xiāo Běn nor Xiāo Hóng was the true Empress Dowager’s younger brother.
Běn was stripped of his official name and exiled to Àizhōu,
and Hóng was exiled to Dānzhōu.
Àizhōu
was the Jiǔzhēn Prefecture in the Hàn dynasty.
The Liáng dynasty established Àizhōu.
It is 8,800 lì from the capital.
He was ultimately unable to get there himself.
12 On the yǐhài day,
the Emperor's illness slightly improved.
He sat in the Sīzhèng Hall
and summoned Zhōu Chí, who was the attending scholar on duty.
He bestowed wine upon him
and then asked:
“To which former ruler can I be compared?”
He replied:
“Your Majesty is a ruler like Yáo and Shùn.”
The Emperor said:
“How dare I compare myself to Yáo and Shùn!
The reason I ask you
is whether I am like Zhōu Nǎn or Hàn Xiàn.”
Chí was startled and said:
“They were rulers of fallen states!
How can they be compared to Your Sacred Virtue!”
The Emperor said:
“Nǎn and Xiàn were controlled by powerful feudal lords.
Now I am controlled by my household slaves.
Judging by this,
I am probably worse off!”
Tears then fell and soaked his lapel.
Chí prostrated himself on the ground, weeping.
From then on, the Emperor no longer held court.
The Kǎo Yì states: Gāo Yànxiū’s Táng Quē Shǐ says:
“Wénzōng was often depressed after the Kāichéng era.
In the fifth year,
spring,
his wind-paralysis slightly improved.
He sat in the Sīzhèng Hall
and asked Zhōu Chí the above.
Afterward, his dragon-visage was suppressed,
and tears fell on his robes.
Rǔnán Gōng prostrated himself, sobbing,
bowed twice and withdrew.
From then on, he no longer held court,
until he passed away.”
According to the Shílù,
in the next year,
first month,
first day,
the Emperor was unwell
and did not receive court greetings.
On the fourth day,
the Emperor died.
It is feared this was not the fifth year, spring.
Now, following the Xīn Chuán,
it is placed here.
12 In this year,
the total number of households in the realm was 4,996,752.
13 Huíhú Prime Minister Ān Yǔnhé and Tèlè Cháigé plotted rebellion.
Zhāngxìn Kèhán killed them.
Prime Minister Juéluówù was outside with troops.
He bribed Shātuó Zhūyé Chìxīn with three hundred horses,
borrowing his troops to jointly attack the Kèhán.
The Kèhán’s army was defeated;
he committed suicide.
The people of the country established Yányè Tèlè as Kèhán.
It happened to be a year of plague and heavy snow,
and many sheep and horses died,
so the Huíhú then declined.
Chìxīn was
the son of Zhíyí.
On the day of Gēngchén,
Lǐ Déyù entered to express his gratitude,
and spoke to the Emperor, saying:
“The essential points for achieving good governance –
‘zhìlǐ’
is synonymous with ‘zhìzhì’ –
are that the righteous and the corrupt,
these two, are inherently incompatible.
The righteous point to the corrupt as corrupt,
and the corrupt also point to the righteous as corrupt.
It is very difficult for the ruler to distinguish between them.
Your servant believes that the righteous are like pine and cypress,
standing firm and independent;
the corrupt are like vines and creeping plants,
unable to rise on their own unless they attach to other things.
Thus, the righteous serve the ruler with a single mind,
while the corrupt compete to form factions.
The late Emperor was well aware of the harm caused by factions,
yet those he employed were ultimately all factional individuals.
This was precisely because his resolve was not firm,
allowing insidious individuals to exploit the opportune moment and infiltrate.
‘Jiān,’
read ‘gǔxiàn’ in Classical Chinese;
the ‘jiān’ below is likely the same.
Sometimes they would deceive and mislead,
and only then would the ruler's heart begin to doubt.
Consequently, he would inquire among minor officials to scrutinize the administrators.
For example, in the late years of Dézōng,
those he listened to and appointed were only people like Péi Yánlíng and his ilk.
The prime ministers merely signed imperial edicts,
which is why governmental affairs became increasingly chaotic.
If Your Majesty can truly carefully select virtuous talents to be prime ministers,
and immediately dismiss any who are treacherous or deceitful,
always ensure that all governmental affairs emanate from the Secretariat (Zhōngshū),
and wholeheartedly delegate authority,
remaining firm and unwavering,
then what worry will there be that the realm will not be well-governed!”
He also said:
“The late Emperor liked to maintain formality with his high officials,
tolerating small faults without speaking of them.
Accumulating day by day and month by month,
this led to disaster and ruin.
This was a major error.
I wish Your Majesty would take it as a warning!
If your servants are at fault,
Your Majesty should question them face-to-face.
If the matter is truly baseless,
they can clarify it;
if it is factual,
their arguments will naturally be exhausted.
Small faults can be forgiven to allow for repentance,
while major crimes should be met with punishment and condemnation.
If this is done,
there will be no suspicion or discord between ruler and subject.”
The Emperor praised and accepted this.
Previously,
when Lǐ Déyù was in Huáinán,
an imperial edict summoned the supervising general Yáng Qīnyì.
Everyone said he would certainly be made a privy councilor,
but Lǐ Déyù treated him with no special deference.
Yáng Qīnyì secretly resented this.
One day,
Lǐ Déyù alone invited Yáng Qīnyì,
set a banquet in the central hall,
and treated him with extreme warmth and respect.
He displayed several tables of rare treasures,
and after the banquet,
gave them all to him.
Yáng Qīnyì was overjoyed beyond expectation.
When he reached Biànzhōu,
an imperial edict ordered him to return to Huáinán.
Yáng Qīnyì returned everything that had been given to him.
Lǐ Déyù said:
“What is the worth of this!”
Meaning, how much could these items be worth?
Later, Yáng Qīnyì indeed became a privy councilor;
when Lǐ Déyù came to power,
Yáng Qīnyì played a considerable role.
Historians say that Lǐ Déyù also could not avoid relying on eunuchs to become prime minister.
7 Initially,
west of Yīwú,
and north of Yānqí,
there was a tribe called the Xiájiásī,
who were the ancient Jiānkūn,
or Jiégǔ in early Táng.
Later, they changed their name to Xiájiásī.
For Jiégǔ paying tribute,
see Volume 298, Tàizōng, Zhēnguān 22nd year.
The “Kǎoyì” states: Lǐ Déyù’s Huìchāng Yīpǐn Jí, in the “Anfǔ Huíhú Zhìzuò” section,
writes “Gēzhīsī,”
and also writes
“Gēyúsī.”
We now follow Lǐ Déyù’s Huìchāng Fápàn Jì, Dù Mù Jí, Xīn and Jiù biographies, and Shílù.
From then on, they were isolated and had no communication with China.
Their chieftain was named Ārè.
He established his headquarters at Qīngshān,
which was forty days’ camel journey from the Huíhú headquarters.
Qīngshān is west of the Jiànhé river.
The Tǔbō and Huíhú often bribed them with gifts,
and granted them official titles.
When the Huíhú declined,
Ārè began to call himself Kaghan.
The Huíhú sent their chancellor to lead troops to attack them,
and they warred for over twenty years,
being repeatedly defeated by the Xiájiásī,
who cursed the Huíhú, saying:
“Your destiny is exhausted,
we will surely seize your Golden Tent!”
The Golden Tent
was the tent where the Huíhú Kaghan resided.
When Juéluówù killed Zhāngxìn
and enthroned Gǎnsà –
the event is mentioned in the previous year –
the Xiájiásī utterly defeated them,
killing Gǎnsà and Juéluówù.
The “Kǎoyì” states: The old biography writes
“Jùlùwèihè.”
We now follow the new biography.
The various Huíhú tribes fled and scattered.
Their chancellor Sàzhí, and the TeLè Páng and fifteen other tribes, fled west to the Gélàlù.
One branch fled to the Tǔbō,
and another branch fled to Ānxī.
Kaghan’s brothers Wōmòsī and others,
along with his chancellors Chìxīn, Púgù, and TeLè Nàjiéchuài,
each led their people to the frontier fortress of Tiāndé,
trading grain and food with the various barbarians,
and at the same time seeking to become internal subjects.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day of Bǐngchén,
Wēn Déyí, the Military Commissioner of Tiāndé, reported:
“The routed Huíhú troops are encroaching upon Xīchéng.
Xīchéng
is the Xīshòuxiángchéng of Shuòfāng.
It is not seen afterwards.
‘Gèng’
means to stretch across.
There is fear and unrest.”
An imperial edict ordered Liú Miǎn, the Jìngwǔ Military Governor, to station troops at Yúngāguān to prepare for them.
The “Xīn Zhì” states: The Chányú Fǔ has Yúngāguān.
The Jìngwǔ Military Governor governed the Chányú Fǔ.
‘Jiā’
is read ‘gǔyá’ in Classical Chinese,
and also ‘jūgā.’
The “Kǎoyì” states: The new biography and Shílù write
“Yúngāguān.”
We now follow Yīpǐn Jí.
8 Hé Jìntāo, the Wèibó Military Governor, died.
The army appointed his son Hé Chóngshùn, the Dutou Military Commissioner, to manage affairs as Acting Military Governor.
9 Empress Dowager Xiāo moved to the Jìqìng Hall of Xīngqìng Palace,
and was styled Empress Dowager Jìqìng.
Empress Dowager Xiāo was the mother of Wénzōng.
10In the eleventh month,
on the day of Guǐyǒu, the first day of the month,
the Emperor visited Yúnyáng for a hunt.
11According to custom,
when a new emperor ascended the throne,
officials from both Secretariats (Liǎngshěng) jointly signed the documents.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Péi Yízhí, the Remonstrance Official (Jiànyì Dàfū), omitted his name,
and was consequently dismissed to become the Prefect of Hángzhōu.
The “Kǎoyì” states: The new biography says:
“When Wǔzōng ascended,
Péi Yízhí looked at the imperial documents and refused to sign.”
We now follow Wǔzōng Shílù.

12Qiú Shìliáng, Grand Master of Eminent Rank, General-in-chief of the Left Guard, and concurrent Director of the Imperial Eunuchs, requested to secure an蔭 (yìn) privilege for his son to become a Qiānniú officer based on his Grand Master rank.
The Táng system: The Qiānniú Bèishēn was in charge of carrying the imperial sword,
wearing embroidered flower ornaments,
green robes,
and holding an ivory tablet,
serving as palace guards and attendants.
Sòng Bái said: The Táng system: Qiānniú and Jìnmǎ appointments
were both hereditary (zǐyīn).
“The rank of Grand Master (Kāifǔ) indeed warrants an荫 (yìn) privilege for a son.”
The Táng system: All officials from the fifth rank and above could secure an荫 (yìn) privilege for a son.
Grand Master (Kāifǔ) was of the first rank,
and should have been entitled to an荫 (yìn) privilege for a son.
Qiú Shìliáng was ashamed and enraged.
Lǐ Déyù also considered Zhōngmǐn a member of Yáng Sìfù’s faction,
and disliked him,
dismissing him to become the Prefect of Wùzhōu.
Wùzhōu,
in the Spring and Autumn period, was the western border of Yuè;
in the Hàn dynasty, it was part of Wūshāng county, Kuàijī Commandery.
The Wú established Dōngyáng Commandery.
The Chén established Jìnzhōu.
When the Suí pacified Chén, it became Wúzhōu.
Because its location corresponded to the Wùnǚ constellation in astronomy,
it was renamed Wùzhōu.
It was four thousand seven hundred *lǐ* southeast of the capital.
‘Wù’
is read ‘wángyù’ in Classical Chinese.
13In the twelfth month,
on the day of Gēngshēn,
Hé Chóngshùn was appointed to manage the affairs of Wèibó as Acting Military Governor.
14The imperial prince Jùn was made a king.
Huìchāng Yuánnián
(Xīnyǒu, 841)
1 Spring,
first month,
Xīnsì,
the Emperor sacrificed at the Round Mound,
issued a general amnesty,
and changed the reign title.
2 Liú Miǎn reported that the Huíhú had retreated,
and an imperial edict ordered Miǎn to return to his post.
He returned to his post from Yúngāguān.
3 Second month,
thirteen Huíhú tribes near the royal encampment established Wūxītèlè as Wūjiè Kèhán,
and he protected Cuòzǐshān to the south.
The Xīnzhì states: Ten Lǐ north of Pìtíquán, one enters the desert,
passing Jīlùshān and Lùěrshān to reach Cuòjiǎshān.
According to Lǐ Déyù,
Cuòzǐshān is three hundred Lǐ east of Shìjiābó.
The Kǎyì states: According to Fápànjì,
Wūjiè was established in the second month,
which we follow here.
The Hòutáng Xiànzǔ Jìniánlù states: Prince Wūxītèlè,
brother of Hésà,
and uncle of Hútèlè,
was forced by the Xiájiásī,
and led his followers to submit.
Upon reaching Cuòzǐshān,
he established himself as Kèhán.
In the seventh month of the second year,
he was enfeoffed as Wūjiè Kèhán.
4 Third month,
Jiǎxū,
Chén Yíxíng, the Grand Master of Censors, was made Menxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
5 Originally,
Liú Hóngyì and Xuē Jìléng, Managers of the Bureau of Military Affairs, were favored by Wénzōng,
but Qiú Shìliáng disliked them.
The Emperor's enthronement
was not the intention of these two men and the chief ministers,
hence Yáng Sìfù was sent out as Húnán Guāncháshǐ,
and Lǐ Chǔ was sent out as Guìguǎn Guāncháshǐ.
Shìliáng repeatedly slandered Hóngyì and others to the Emperor,
advising the Emperor to eliminate them.
On Yǐwèi,
Hóngyì and Jìléng were granted death,
and palace envoys were dispatched to Tánzhōu and Guìzhōu to execute Sìfù and Chǔ.
The Húnán Guāncháshǐ administered Tánzhōu.
The Guìguǎn Guāncháshǐ administered Guìzhōu.
Tánzhōu,
anciently Chángshā Jùn,
is two thousand four hundred forty-five Lǐ south of the capital.
Qín took the Lùliáng territory and established Guìlín Jùn.
Wú established Shǐ'ān Jùn in Guìlín.
Liáng established Guìzhōu,
which is four thousand seven hundred sixty Lǐ by water and land from the capital.
"The Son of Heaven is young,
newly enthroned;
this matter should not be handled carelessly!"
On Bǐngshēn,
Déyù, along with Cuī Gǒng, Cuī Dān, and Chén Yíxíng, submitted memorials three times,
and also invited the Military Commissioners to the Central Secretariat,
making them report to the Emperor.
They believed:
"Dézōng suspected Liú Yàn of unsettling the Crown Prince and killed him,
which was considered an injustice by all within and outside the court.
The disloyal commanders of the two rivers used this as a pretext due to their fear;
Dézōng later regretted it,
and recorded his descendants.
Liú Yàn's death is mentioned in volume 226, Dézōng, Jiànzhōng Yuánnián.
Lǐ Zhèngjǐ and others requesting Yàn's punishment is in the second year.
In early Xīngyuán,
the Emperor realized his mistake
and allowed Yàn's remains to be buried.
In Zhēnyuán Fǔnián,
Yàn's son Zhíjīng was promoted to Tài Cháng Bóshì,
and Zōngjīng to Mìshūláng.
They were exiled to their deaths;
afterward, he regretted it
and wept for them.
Sòng Shēnxī's exile is in volume 244, Dàhé Wǔnián.
The regret is in the previous volume, Kāichéng Yuánnián.
For '為',
read 'yúwěi' (yúwèi).
Chǔ
begged for an even heavier demotion;
if they were truly intolerable,
they should still be interrogated first.
It would not be too late to execute them
after their crimes were clearly established.
Now, without consulting us ministers,
envoys were immediately dispatched to execute them.
Everyone is shocked.
We wish for the Yányīng Hall to be opened for an audience!"
By dusk,
the Yányīng Hall was opened,
and Déyù and others were summoned.
Lǐ Déyù and others, weeping, spoke frankly:
“Your Majesty should treat this matter with extreme caution,
lest you later regret it!”
The Emperor said:
“I will not regret it.”
He ordered them to sit three times,
but Lǐ Déyù and others said:
“We humbly request Your Majesty to spare these two men from death,
lest they die and the multitude deem it an injustice.
As we have not yet received a holy decree,
we dare not sit.”
After a long while,
the Emperor finally said:
“I will release them specifically for your sakes.”
Lǐ Déyù and others leaped down the steps and bowed in dance.
The Emperor summoned them to ascend and sit,
sighing:
“When I inherited the throne,
how could the Chéngxiàng be counted as such!
Lǐ Yu, Jì Líng, their ambition was for Chén Wáng,
Chén Wáng,
is Chén Měi.
Ān Wáng,
is Róng.
Ān Wáng, on the other hand, was exclusively attached to Yáng.
Yáng requested the enthronement of Ān Wáng,
hence that statement.
If Ān Wáng had realized his ambition back then,
how could I have this day?”
Lǐ Déyù and others said:
“This matter is obscure,
its truth or falsehood difficult to discern.”
The Emperor said:
“Yáng once had an illness;
Wénzōng allowed his younger brother Xuánsī to attend him for over a month,
through this, he was able to convey his intentions.
I carefully questioned the palace women;
the circumstances are perfectly clear,
it is not false.”
He then recalled the two envoys.
One envoy had already gone to Tán,
the other to Guì.
Lǐ Yu was the Cìshǐ of Zhāozhōu.
Zhāozhōu is four thousand four hundred thirty-six Lǐ from the capital.
The Kǎyì states: The Old Annals:
“On the seventeenth day of the eighth month of the fifth year of Kāichéng,
Wénzōng was buried at Zhānglíng.
Liú Hóngyì and Xuē Jìlíng, who knew the Pímì, led the imperial guards to protect the funeral carriage.
The two had always been praised and favored by Wénzōng,
and Chóu Shìliáng disliked them,
feeling uneasy.
Because of this, they wanted to turn their weapons to execute Shìliáng and Hóngzhì.
The Lúbùshǐ Wáng Qǐ and the Shānlíngshǐ Cuī Dān discovered their plot
and first informed the Lúbù troops.
On that day, Hóngyì and Jìlíng were executed,
and Yáng Sìfù was made Húnán Guānchásǐ,
Lǐ Yu was made Guìguǎn Guānchásǐ,
and the Zhōngchéng Péi Yízhí was made Hángzhōu Cìshǐ,
all because of Hóngyì and Jìlíng.”
Jiǎ Wěi’s Táng Nián Bǔlù states:
“In the eighth month of the fifth year,
it is said that in this month, the Pímìshǐ Liú Hóngyì and Xuē Jìlíng were executed.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he was particularly wary of eunuchs,
and Jìlíng and Hóngyì greatly feared him.
When Wénzōng was about to be buried at Zhānglíng,
they gathered imperial guards,
intending to discuss dethronement and enthronement.
Thanks to the Shānlíngshǐ Cuī Dān and the Lúbùshǐ Wáng Qǐ and others who resisted and succeeded,
Hóngyì and Jìlíng were captured and killed.”
The Old Biography of Wáng Qǐ:
“In the eighth month,
he was appointed Shānlíng Lúbùshǐ.
The Pímìshǐ Liú Hóngyì and Xuē Jìlíng, fearing execution,
intended to plot dethronement and enthronement with the Shānlíng soldiers.
Qǐ and the Shānlíngshǐ knew of their plot,
secretly reported it,
and they were all executed.”
The Old Biography of Sìfù:
“In the ninth month of the fifth year,
he was demoted to Húnán.
The next year,
Jìlíng and Hóngyì were executed.
The palace people said: ‘The two previously attached themselves to Sìfù and Lǐ Yu,
which was unfavorable to Your Majesty.’
Wǔzōng was impetuous by nature,
and immediately ordered imperial envoys to Húnán and Guìguǎn to kill Sìfù and Lǐ Yu.”
However, if Hóngyì and Jìlíng had already been executed in the eighth month of last year,
Sìfù and others should not have been demoted again in this month.
The Old Annals, Wáng Qǐ’s biography, and Sìfù’s biography contradict each other.
Now we follow the Shílù.
The Shílù also states:
“At that time, there were those who again tried to move the Emperor’s heart with that matter.
The Emperor became furious
and wanted to kill them.
Once the imperial envoys had departed,
even the Chéngxiàng did not know of it.
Dù Cōng, the Hùbù Shàngshū and Pàndùzhī, galloped to see Déyù”
and so on.
The Old Biography of Sìfù states:
“The Chéngxiàng Cuī Dān, Cuī Gǒng, and others urgently requested an audience in the Yányīng Hall,
speaking frankly”
and so on.
The Xiàntìjì states:
“On the twenty-fourth day of the third month of the first year of Huìchāng,
I was on leave at home.
Towards evening, I heard that one imperial envoy went east
and another went south,
to deal with the two former Chéngxiàng and Péi Yízhí.
I sent someone to ask Cōng, the Yántiě Chéngxiàng, Dù Shàngshū of the Dùzhī, and Lú Yǐn of Jīngzhào.
They all said they had heard envoys had departed
but did not know the reason.
I then drafted a memorial.
On the twenty-fifth day, I entered the Zhōngshū Shěng early.
Chéngxiàng Gǒng arrived shortly after,
Cuī Dān arrived next,
and Chén Xiàng arrived last,
by which time it was already the sìshí.
I asked the three Chéngxiàng to meet for a meal,
while I returned to the hall to write the memorial,
requesting an audience in the Yányīng Hall.
After submitting the memorial, there was no reply.
At noon, I again wrote and submitted a second memorial,
also requesting that the Pímìshǐ be summoned to the Zhōngshū Shěng to ask if this matter was true or not.
The Pímìshǐ replied: ‘I dared not speak earlier.
Since the Chéngxiàng knows,
it is just those two men: Sìfù and Lǐ Yu.’
Déyù said: ‘This matter is extremely serious.
Your Majesty did not inquire at all
before sending the envoys,
and there is no one who is not startled and fearful.
Please attach this to Déyù’s memorial.
If the holy decree suspects Déyù’s sentiment or motive,
please first severely demote me,
but this one matter must not be carried out again!
Déyù and others dared not leave the Zhōngshū Shěng until night,
requesting an early audience in the Yányīng Hall.’
By the shēnshí,
it was reported that the Yányīng Hall would be opened.
I invited the Chéngxiàng and officials of the two departments and said: ‘The Emperor is resolute by nature.
If any one person submits a memorial to make inquiries,
he will certainly not give up.
Déyù will try his utmost to plead and rescue them,
followed by kowtowing until his head bleeds.
If Déyù cannot save them,
then others certainly cannot.’
When summoned into the Yányīng Hall,
Déyù led the three Chéngxiàng to stand before the imperial couch to report on the matter,
weeping and sobbing, and so on.
After the Emperor released them,
he again ordered Déyù to summon the Chéngláng and officials of the two departments to make an announcement.”
Now we follow the Shílù,
also incorporating the Xiàntìjì.
Sòng Bái states: In the sixth year of Tiānfú,
he was appointed Xiūzhuàn Qǐjūzhù.
Jiǎ Wěi memorialized:
“I have observed that in the Imperial Archives, from Táng Gāozǔ to Dàizōng, there are already annals and biographies.
For Dézōng, the Shílù also exists.
From Wǔzōng to Jǐyīn Fèidì, a total of six reigns,
there is only one volume of Wǔzōng’s Shílù,
and the rest are missing.
I have now collected extant writings and legends from elders
and compiled sixty-five volumes,
titled Táng Nián Bǔyílù,
to prepare for future historical compilation by the Imperial Archives.”
An imperial edict praised it
and submitted it to the Imperial Archives.
6 Summer,
sixth month,
on the Yǐsì day,
an edict stated:
“From now on, when subjects discuss the crimes of others,
they should all request that the matter be handed over to the Yùshǐ Tái for investigation,
and must not ask for it to be kept within the court,
to prevent slander and wickedness.”
7 Hé Chóngshùn, the Liúhòu of Wèibó, was appointed Jiéduwěi.
8 The Emperor ordered the Daoist priests Zhào Guīzhēn (趙歸真) and others to establish a Jiǔtiān (九天) Daoist ritual platform in the Three Palaces,
and personally bestowed upon them talismans and registers.
Daoist talismans and registers originated with Zhāng Dàolíng (張道陵),
flourished under Kòu Qiānzhī (寇謙之),
and were revered and believed in by Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) of the Later Wèi (魏) and Emperor Wǔzōng (武宗) of Táng (唐).
"Shòu" (授),
should be
"Shòu" (受).
[He was] demoted to the rank of Shìcáo (士曹) in Hénánfǔ (河南府).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Shílù* (實錄) says:
"Daoist priests Zhào Guīzhēn (趙歸真) and eighty-one others established a Jiǔtiān (九天) Daoist ritual platform in the Three Palaces,
and the Emperor personally transmitted talismans and registers.
Wáng Zhé (王哲), the Right Shíyí (拾遺), submitted a memorial,
requesting that *jìnshì* (進士) and *míngjīng* (明經) graduates not be ordained as Daoist priests,
but this was not followed.
He then submitted another memorial admonishing against the pursuit of immortality,
in very direct and forceful terms,
and was demoted to Cānjūn (參軍) of the Shìcáo (士曹) in Hénánfǔ (河南府)."
The *Jiùjì* (舊紀) states:
"Líu Xuánjìng (劉玄靜), a Daoist priest from Héngshān (衡山), was appointed Xuánwéiguǎn Xuéshì (崇玄館學士),
and ordered to practice talismans and registers in the Forbidden Palace with Daoist priest Zhào Guīzhēn (趙歸真).
Líu Yànmó (劉彥謨), the Left Bǔquē (補闕), remonstrated vehemently,
and Yànmó (彥謨) was demoted to Hùcáo (戶曹) in Hénánfǔ (河南府)."
According to the *Shílù* (實錄),
in the ninth month of the previous year, Guīzhēn (歸真) had already been ordered to establish a Daoist ritual platform,
and personally received talismans and registers.
Zhé (哲)'s memorial stated,
"At the beginning of the imperial enterprise,
it is not appropriate to show excessive reverence and belief."
At this point, this matter occurred again,
similar to Líu Yànmó (劉彥謨)'s incident in the *Jiùjì* (舊紀).
Now we follow the *Shílù* (實錄).
9 In autumn,
in the eighth month,
Qiú Shìliáng (仇士良) was promoted to Guānjūnróngshǐ (觀軍容使).
10 Tiándé Jūnshǐ (天德軍使) Tián Móu (田牟) and Jūnjiān (監軍) Wéi Zhòngpíng (韋仲平) wished to attack the Huíhé (回鶻) to seek merit,
and memorialized, stating:
"The rebellious Huíhé (回鶻) general Wōmòsī (嗢沒斯) and others are encroaching upon
the frontier.
The Tǔyùhùn (吐谷渾), Shātuó (沙陀), and Dǎngxiàng (党項) have been their enemies for generations,
so we request to personally lead troops to expel them."
The Emperor ordered his court officials to discuss this,
and the deliberators all believed that Wōmòsī (嗢沒斯) had rebelled against his Khagan and come,
so they should not be accepted.
It would be appropriate, as Móu (牟) and others requested,
to attack them.
The Emperor asked the prime minister,
Lǐ Déyù (李德裕), who believed:
"Even a cornered bird flying into one's bosom
should be kept alive.
Moreover, the Huíhé (回鶻) have repeatedly rendered great service,
such as assisting in the recovery of the two capitals
and pacifying the An (安) and Shi (史) rebellions.
Their tribes are scattered,
poor and without a home,
relying on the Son of Heaven from afar,
without a single offense against the frontier.
How can we take advantage of their distress and attack them!
It would be appropriate to send envoys to pacify and comfort them,
and transport grain to give to them.
This is how Emperor Xuān (宣) of Hàn (漢) subdued Hūhánxié (呼韓邪)."
The matter of Hūhánxié (呼韓邪) is found in Volume 27 under Gānlù (甘露) third year of Emperor Xuān (宣) of Hàn (漢).
"This is what is called 'lending weapons to bandits and provisions to thieves',"
a saying of Lǐ Sī (李斯) of Qín (秦) in the *Shǐjì* (史記).
Déyù (德裕) said:
"Those Tǔyùhùn (吐谷渾) and others each have their own tribes.
When they see profit, they are keen and eager to advance;
when things are unfavorable, they scatter like startled birds and fish,
each fleeing to their nests.
How could they be willing to fight to the death for the state!
Today, the Tiándé (天德) city garrison has barely over a thousand soldiers;
if the battle is unfavorable,
the city will surely fall.
It would be better to pacify and reassure them with kindness and righteousness;
they will certainly not become a threat.
Even if they do invade the border,
we would still need to levy large armies from various circuits to suppress them.
How can we let Tiándé (天德) alone attack them!"
At that time, an imperial edict appointed Hónglúqīng (鴻臚卿) Zhāng Jiǎ (張賈) as the Xúnbīanshǐ (巡邊使),
to investigate the true situation of the Huíhé (回鶻),
but he had not yet returned.
The Emperor asked Déyù (德裕):
"Wōmòsī (嗢沒斯) and others are requesting to surrender;
can we trust them?"
He replied:
"Among the people in court, I dare not guarantee anyone,
let alone dare to guarantee the intentions of barbarians thousands of *lǐ* (里) away!
However, calling them rebellious generals
I fear is inappropriate.
If the Khagan were in his country,
and Wōmòsī (嗢沒斯) and others led their forces here,
then it would indeed be improper to accept them.
Now we hear that their country is defeated and in chaos, without a ruler,
and their generals and ministers have fled and scattered,
some fleeing to Tǔbō (吐蕃),
some to Gélúolù (葛邏祿).
Only this branch relies on the great state from afar.
Observing their memorial,
it is urgent and sincere.
How can they be called rebellious generals!
Moreover, Wōmòsī (嗢沒斯) and others arrived at Tiándé (天德) in the ninth month of last year,
and Wūjiè (烏介) was only established in the second month of this year,
so there is no master-servant relationship between them.
I wish that an edict be issued to Hédōng (河東) and Zhènwǔ (振武) to strengthen their defenses and guard their borders in preparation,
and only after they attack towns and cities,
then expel them with military force.
If they do some minor looting among the Tǔyùhùn (吐谷渾) and other tribes,
let them retaliate themselves;
we should not assist them with official troops.
First, let them fight to break their alliances.
This is in military strategy,
but those who practice it do not realize it.
*Chāo* (抄),
*chǔ jiāo* (楚交) pronunciation.
Always ensure that great trust is not lost,
and pacify them appropriately.
Even though they are barbarians,
they will surely know gratitude."
On the *Xīnyǒu* (辛酉) day,
an edict was issued to Tián Móu (田牟) to restrain his officers, soldiers, and various barbarians.
"Various barbarians" refers to the Tǔyùhùn (吐谷渾), Shātuó (沙陀), Dǎngxiàng (党項), and other tribes.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Jiùjì* (舊紀) says:
"In the eighth month,
Wūjiè (烏介) sent an envoy to announce the death of the former Khagan,
and that his people had acclaimed him Khagan.
Now he is bringing Princess Tàihé (太和) south to seek refuge with the great state.
At that time, Wūjiè (烏介) reached the frontier,
and Wōmòsī (嗢沒斯) and Chìxīn (赤心) were fighting and killing each other.
Chìxīn (赤心) led several thousand tents near the western city,
and Tián Móu (田牟) reported this.
Wūjiè (烏介) also ordered his minister Jiégānjiāsī (頡干迦斯) to memorialize requesting to borrow Tiándé (天德) city,
and further begged for grain, stores, oxen, and sheep.
An edict ordered Wáng Huì (王會) and Lǐ Shīyǎn (李師偃) to go and convey comfort,
ordering them to allow the princess to enter the court,
and relieve them with twenty thousand *shí* (石) of millet."
The *Jiùdéyùzhuàn* (舊德裕傳) says:
"At the end of Kāichéng (開成),
the Huíhé (回鶻) were defeated by the Xiájíagāsī (黠戛斯),
their tribes scattered,
and Wūjiè (烏介) brought Princess Tàihé (太和) south.
In the second month of Huìchāng (會昌) second year,
they established their headquarters on the frontier,
sent envoys to seek military aid and provisions,
to recover their original country,
temporarily borrowing Tiándé Jūn (天德軍).
Tián Móu (田牟) requested to attack them with the Shātuó (沙陀) and Tuìhún (退渾) tribes;
this was submitted to the hundred officials for deliberation,
and most deliberators agreed with Móu (牟)'s memorial.
Déyù (德裕) said so and so.
The Emperor deemed it correct,
and allowed to lend thirty thousand *shí* (石) of rice."
The *Fápànjì* (伐叛記) says:
"In the second month of Huìchāng (會昌) first year,
the Huíhé (回鶻) traveled far across the desert,
suffering extreme hunger,
and exchanged gold and treasures with the frontier tribes for provisions.
The border people coveted their wealth,
and developed intentions to plunder.
By the autumn of that year,
Chéngshǐ (城使) Tián Móu (田牟) and Jūnjiān (監軍) Wéi Zhòngpíng (韋仲平) submitted a memorial stating that the Tuìhún (退渾) and Dǎngxiàng (党項) had old grudges against the Huíhé (回鶻),
and wished to lead their own troops to expel them.
At that time, there were only one thousand officers and soldiers inside Tiándé (天德) city,
and half of them were administrative personnel.
The Emperor ordered the prime ministers to discuss,
and Déyù (德裕) verbally memorialized so and so.
On the twenty-fourth day of the eighth month,
