he requested that an edict be granted to Tián Móu (田牟) and Zhòngpíng (仲平),
stating that Hàn (漢) soldiers and Fān (蕃) and Hún (渾) were not allowed to attack the Huíhé (回鶻) first,
and the words are found in the memorials of the *Huìchāngjí* (會昌集)."
According to the *Jiùjì* (舊紀) and *Shílù* (實錄), both were compiled from various books,
and events often differ in sequence.
Now we follow the *Fápànjì* (伐叛記) and *Yīpǐnjí* (一品集).
On the *Wùchén* (戊辰) day of the new moon,
an edict ordered Hédōng (河東) and Zhènwǔ (振武) to strengthen their defenses in preparation.
Móu (牟) was the younger brother of Bù (布).
Tián Bù (田布) was the son of Hóngzhèng (弘正),
and died in the rebellion of Shǐ Xiànchéng (史憲誠).
11 On the *Guǐsì* (癸巳) day,
a rebellion broke out in Lúlóng Jūn (盧龍軍),
killing Jiédùshǐ (節度使) Shǐ Yuánzhōng (史元忠),
and acclaiming Chén
Xíngtài (行泰) to temporarily manage affairs.
12 Lǐ Déyù requested to send an envoy to comfort the Huíhú,
and to transport thirty thousand *hú* of grain to bestow upon them.
The Emperor was doubtful about this.
In the intercalary month,
on the *jǐhài* day,
he opened the Yányīng hall
and summoned the chancellors to discuss it.
Chén Yíxíng was at the waiting area.
From Emperor Dézōng's time onwards in the Táng dynasty,
when ministers requested an audience in the Yányīng,
they would generally request it at the Yányīng Gate.
The *Huìyào* states: In the fifteenth year of Yuánhé,
an imperial edict ordered the opening of a convenient gate within the western corridor of the Xīshàng Gémén,
to provide a route for chancellors to go from the palace gate to the Yányīng.
When Sòng Shēnxī incurred displeasure,
the chancellors were summoned to enter the Yányīng for an audience from the Zhōngshū.
Lǐ Déyù said:
"Currently, the conscripted troops have not yet assembled,
and Tiāndé is isolated and precarious.
If we do not use this grain to feed the starving barbarians [and thereby cause them to]
be quiet and peaceful,
should Tiāndé fall,
to whom will the blame fall!"
Lǐ Déyù's original plan was correct;
as for these words,
they were merely to silence Chén Yíxíng.
If one speaks of the larger strategy of warfare,
one would naturally not consider the gain or loss of a single city.
This flaw persisted from Táng to Sòng.
Alas,
how easily can one speak of it!
So, he did not dare to speak.
The Emperor then agreed to provide twenty thousand *hú* of grain to relieve them.
13 Niú Sēngrú, formerly the *Jiédùshǐ* of Shānnán Dōngdào and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*, was appointed Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Tàishī*).
Previously, the Hànshǔi river had overflowed,
destroying civilian homes in Xiāngzhōu.
Therefore, Lǐ Déyù considered this Sēngrú's fault and dismissed him.
To dismiss him meant
to assign him to an idle position.
History states that Lǐ Déyù dismissed Niú Sēngrú out of personal resentment.
14 The Lúlóng Army rebelled again,
killing Chén Xíngtài and
installing the *Yájiàng* Zhāng Jiàng.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The Old Annals say:
"In the tenth month,
Zhāng Jiàng, the commander of the Xióngwǔ Army of Yōuzhōu, sent the military official Wú Zhòngshū to court,
stating that Xíngtài was cruel and tyrannical,
and requesting to use the garrison troops to attack him.
This was permitted.
In that month,
Xíngtài was executed,
and Jiàng was then made acting commander of military affairs.
In the second year,
in the first month,
Jiàng was made acting governor,
and was also bestowed the name Zhòngwǔ."
To make two people into one is
a mistake.
Now, we follow the Old Biography of Zhòngwǔ, *Fápànjì*, and *Shílù*.
Initially,
Chén Xíngtài expelled Shǐ Yuánzhōng
and sent a supervising attendant
with a memorial from the army's chief general to request the *jiéyuè* (credentials of a *jiédùshǐ*).
Lǐ Déyù said:
"I am very familiar with the situation in Héshuò.
Recently, the court has always sent envoys to bestow edicts too quickly,
thus the army's sentiments have become entrenched.
If we leave them unaddressed for several months,
changes will surely arise on their own.
Now, I request to keep the supervising attendant,
and not send an envoy, to observe them."
Soon after, the army indeed killed Xíngtài
and installed Zhāng Jiàng,
again requesting the *jiéyuè*.
The court also did not inquire.
At that time, Zhāng Zhòngwǔ, the commander of the Xióngwǔ Army, raised troops to attack Jiàng.
The Xióngwǔ Army
was in Guǎnghànchuān, Jìzhōu.
He claimed that Jiàng was cruel and tyrannical
and requested to use his own army to attack him.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Zhòngshū arrived in the capital.
The Emperor ordered the chancellors to question him about the situation.
Zhòngshū said:
"Xíngtài and Jiàng are both outsiders,
so the people do not support them.
Zhòngwǔ is an old general of Yōuzhōu.
Zhòngwǔ
is the son of Zhāng Guāngcháo, an old general of Fányáng.
He is literate
and skilled in military affairs;
the people look up to him.
Previously, when Zhāng Jiàng first killed Xíngtài,
he summoned Zhòngwǔ,
intending to yield the governorship to him,
but one or two hundred people in the headquarters disagreed;
when Zhòngwǔ reached Chāngpíng,
Jiàng again sent him back.
Now, we estimate that as soon as Zhòngwǔ departs Xióngwǔ,
the army will have already driven out Jiàng."
Lǐ Déyù asked:
"How many soldiers are there in Xióngwǔ?"
He replied:
"Eight hundred regular soldiers,
and five hundred local militia outside."
Local people organized into soldiers
were called local militia.
"The troops are few,
how can they achieve success?"
He replied:
"It lies in gaining the support of the people.
If the people do not follow,
what good are thirty thousand troops?"
Déyù asked again:
"What if he fails?"
He replied:
"All the provisions of Yōuzhōu are in Guīzhōu and the seven northern garrisons.
Guīzhōu is 290 *lǐ* south of Yōuzhōu,
and 250 *lǐ* east of Tánzhōu.
Tánzhōu has the seven garrisons of Dàwáng, Běilái, Bǎoyào, Lùgù, Chìchéng, Yāolǔ, and Shízi.
Guī
is pronounced 'jū' (居).
Then, if he occupies the Jūyōng Pass—
the old Jūyōng Pass, also known as Jūndū Pass, is 35 *lǐ* northwest of Jūndūxíng in Chāngpíng County, Yōuzhōu;
according to current reckoning, Jūyōng Pass is 110 *lǐ* north of Yānjīng—
Yōuzhōu will be in distress itself!"
Based on Wú Zhòngshū's words,
Lǐ Déyù was firmly convinced of Zhāng Zhòngwǔ's strategy.
His order to put him in charge of Yān's affairs,
how could it have been in vain!
Déyù memorialized:
"Xíngtài and Jiàng both had chief generals submit memorials,
threatening the court
and demanding the *jiéyuè*,
so they could not be granted.
Now Zhòngwǔ has first
raised troops himself to quell the rebellion for the court;
granting it to him would seem justifiable."
Déyù was not yet able to guarantee Zhāng Zhòngwǔ,
and also feared contradicting his earlier discussion on the situation in Héshuò,
hence this.
Zhòngwǔ soon captured Yōuzhōu.
15 The Emperor hunted at Xiányáng.
16 In the eleventh month,
Lǐ Déyù memorialized:
"Now that the Huíhú have been defeated and dispersed,
the whereabouts of Princess Tàihé are unknown.
If we do not send an envoy to inquire,
then the barbarians will surely believe that the state surrendered a princess to the barbarian court,
not out of cherishing her.
This would both fail the princess
and wound the barbarians' feelings.
I request to send the *Tōngshì Shèrén* Miáo Zhěn with an imperial edict to Wòmòsī,
ordering him to transmit it to the princess.
This can also serve to ascertain Wòmòsī's intentions, whether compliant or rebellious."
This was followed.
17 The Emperor was quite fond of hunting and martial games.
Martial games refer to *qiújú* (football), horseback archery, *shǒubó* (hand-to-hand combat), etc.
'Hǎo' is pronounced 'hào'.
His rewards were very generous.
He once visited Empress Dowager Guō.
Empress Dowager Guō was Emperor Xiànzōng's empress,
thus the Emperor's grandmother.
She was then residing in Xīngqìng Palace for her retirement.
The Empress Dowager advised him to accept remonstrances.
The Emperor returned
and took all the remonstrance memorials to read them.
Many advised against hunting.
From then on, the Emperor's hunting excursions became fewer,
and there were no longer excessive rewards for the Wǔfāng.
18 On the *guǐhài* day,
Cuī Dān, *Zhōngshū Shìláng* and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*, was appointed *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*
and concurrently *Jiédùshǐ* of Xīchuān.
19 Early on,
the Qíjiāsi, having defeated the Huíhú,
obtained Princess Tàihé.
They claimed to be descendants of Lǐ Líng.
The Táng records state: "The Qíjiāsi people are all tall,
with red hair,
fair complexions,
and green eyes.
Those with black hair are considered inauspicious,
and those with black eyes are definitely said to be descendants of Lǐ Líng."
They sent ten Dágān to escort the princess back to Táng.
The Huíhú Wūjiè Kèhán led his troops to intercept the Dágān,
slaughtered them all,
held the princess captive,
crossed the desert to the south,
and encamped on the border of Tiāndé Commandery.
The border of Tiāndé Commandery
extended three hundred *lǐ* north to the desert entrance.
He declared that the Kèhán had been enthroned
and sought imperial investiture.
Wūjiè also sent his minister Jiégāngāsi and others to submit a memorial,
requesting the loan of a city, Zhènwǔ, to house the princess and the Kèhán.
The Kǎoyì states: "The Xīn Chuán says:
'The Dágān escorted the princess to return,
but Wūjiè, enraged,
attacked and killed the Dágān,
crossed the desert to the south,
and advanced to attack Tiāndé City.
Liú Miǎn stationed troops at Yúngā Guān to repel them.' "
However, Wūjiè was then relying on Táng for aid;
how could he dare to attack Tiāndé!
We now follow the old *jì*, *chuán*, and *shílù*.
On the *gēngchén* day,
an edict was issued dispatching Right Golden Seal Grand General Wáng Huì and others to inquire about the Huíhú,
and to provide twenty thousand *hú* of rice.
An imperial rescript was also bestowed upon Wūjiè Kèhán,
admonishing him
that "it is advisable to lead your multitude to gradually restore your old territory;
to drift and reside by the frontier is
certainly not a good plan."
It further stated:
"To request the loan of Zhènwǔ City,
there has been no such precedent in previous dynasties.
If you wish to move to another suitable place
and seek the support of a great nation's influence,
you must also reside south of the desert.
I shall permit the princess to enter court
to personally inquire about the matters.
If there is a need for assistance,
I will certainly not be stingy."
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Zhāng Zhòngwǔ was appointed Lúlóng Military Governor.
2 The court, considering the Huíhú encamped north of Tiāndé and Zhènwǔ,
appointed Assistant Minister of War Lǐ Shì as frontier inspector,
to assess the capabilities of the generals.
Shì
was the son of Yōng.
Lǐ Yōng is mentioned in volume 240, Yuánhé 12th year.
3 In the second month,
Huáinán Military Governor Lǐ Shēn entered court.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
Shēn was appointed Vice Director of the Central Secretariat, Chancellor, and Comptroller of Finance.
4 Hédōng Military Governor Fú Chè repaired the old garrison of Pájiù Fēng to guard against the Huíhú.
Pájiù Fēng overlooked the great desert to the north,
faced Yún and Shuò to the east,
and faced Zhènwǔ to the west.
Pá,
pronounced as *pú bā*.
He also repaired the two Xīcháng cities, East and Middle, to strengthen the strategic position of Tiāndé;
this was approved.
5 Right Remonstrance Official Liǔ Gōngquán had always been on good terms with Lǐ Déyù.
Cuī Gǒng proposed him for Academician of the Jíxián Academy and Administrator of the Academy Affairs.
In the 13th year of Xuánzōng's Kāiyuán era,
the Lìzhèng Shūyuàn was renamed Jíxián Diàn Shūyuàn.
Officials of the fifth rank and above served as Academicians,
those of the sixth rank and below as Associate Academicians.
One chancellor served as Academician in Charge of Academy Affairs,
one remonstrance official as Deputy in Charge of Academy Affairs.
Additionally, one Administrator of the Academy and
one Eunuch Overseer of the Academy were appointed.
In the 4th year of Yuánhé,
Academicians and Associate Academicians of the Jíxián Yùshūyuàn were all of the fifth rank,
following the Kāiyuán precedent,
with one senior Academician serving as Administrator of Academy Affairs.
Due to this matter, Gōngquán was demoted to Crown Prince's Household Administrator.
This is why Déyù could not escape the disaster of factionalism.
6 The Huíhú again memorialized, requesting provisions,
and also an investigation into what had been plundered by the Tǔyùhún and Dǎngxiàng,
and again requested the loan of Zhènwǔ City.
An edict was issued, dispatching the inner envoy Yáng Guān to bestow a letter upon the Kèhán,
admonishing him that the city could not be lent,
but other matters would be dealt with accordingly.
In the third month,
Lǐ Shì returned from his frontier inspection
and praised Zhènwǔ Military Governor Liú Miǎn as having authority and strategy,
capable of handling important affairs.
At that time, Hédōng Military Governor Fú Chè was seriously ill;
the term *jíshèn* means seriously ill.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
Miǎn was appointed to replace him.
Liabilities General of the Golden Seal Lǐ Zhōngshùn was appointed Zhènwǔ Military Governor.
Assistant Director of the Palace Buildings Miáo Zhěn was dispatched to bestow imperial investiture upon Wūjiè Kèhán,
instructed to proceed slowly,
station himself in Hédōng,
and await the Kèhán's position to stabilize
before proceeding further.
However, the Kèhán repeatedly encroached upon and harassed the frontier,
and Zhěn ultimately did not proceed.
7 The Huíhú’s Wàimòsī, because Chìxīn was cunning and hard to predict,
first informed Tián Móu, saying,
“Chìxīn plans to violate the frontier.”
Then he lured Chìxīn and Púgù and killed them.
Nàjié Chuài took Chìxīn’s seven thousand tents of followers and went east.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Fápànjì* says:
“Chìxīn, the prime minister, wanted to violate the frontier.
Wàimòsī first expressed his sincerity to Tián Móu,
then lured Chìxīn to jointly meet the Kèhán,
and had him executed beneath the Kèhán’s tent.
The soldiers Chìxīn commanded then scattered and went east,
seeking refuge in Yōuzhōu.”
The *Yīpǐnjí Yōuzhōu Jìshènggōng Bēi* says:
“Chìxīn, relying on his strength and acting with arrogance,
secretly plotted a great transgression;
he was deceived by Wàimòsī,
who lured him to jointly meet the Kèhán,
and had him executed beneath the tent.
His followers greatly dispersed,
pressing eastward toward Yúyáng.”
The *Jiùchuán* says:
“The Huíhú prime minister Chìxīn, along with the co-prime minister Púgù, and the Tèlè Nàjié Chuài, led their followers and did not submit to Wūjiè.
Chìxīn wanted to violate the frontier.
Wūjiè sent his subordinate Wàimòsī to first express sincerity to Tián Móu,
then lured Chìxīn to jointly meet Wūjiè,
and executed Chìxīn beneath the Kèhán’s tent,
along with Púgù.
Nàjié won the battle,
taking full possession of the seven thousand tents under Chìxīn,
looking east toward Zhènwǔ and Dàtóng,
occupying Shìwéi, Hēishā, and Yúlín,
and entering the northwest border of Yōuzhōu’s Xióngwǔ Army from the southeast.”
The *Xīnchuán* says:
“Wàimòsī, considering Chìxīn cunning and deceitful,
and difficult to control,
secretly agreed with Tián Móu
to lure Chìxīn and execute him beneath the tent.”
According to the *Yīpǐnjí Cì Kèhán Chìshū*, although it says,
“Last year Wàimòsī already reached the nearby border,
now that the Kèhán has been established,
he has again submitted.”
Yet, the meaning of the letter granted to the Kèhán also says:
“Since the beginning of the destruction of his native country, Wàimòsī
fled and arrived at the frontier first,
not following the Kèhán and Princess for two years.”
This indicates that Wàimòsī had his own followers;
although he nominally submitted to Wūjiè,
he never went in person.
How could he have executed Chìxīn and Púgù beneath the Kèhán’s tent?
Furthermore, if Chìxīn did not submit to Wūjiè,
how could he have agreed to follow Wàimòsī to jointly meet Wūjiè?
It is likely that Wàimòsī himself disliked Chìxīn’s cunning,
lured him to his own tent, and killed him.
We now follow the *Xīnchuán*.
Furthermore,
the *Fápànjì* mentions Wàimòsī killing Chìxīn
consecutively with Wūjiè’s arrival at Tiāndé,
and the *Jiùchuán* is also similar.
The *Xīnchuán* places it under the summoning of troops from various circuits to attack Wūjiè.
According to the *Yīpǐnjí*,
it states that Huíhú arrived at Héngshuǐ Zhà,
but it is unknown whether it was under Nàjié Tèlè
or sent by the Kèhán.
Probably
the character “Tèlè”
was missing the character
“lè”
after “Nàjié Te”,
so it should be Nàjié Chuài.
If so, the barbarians attacked Héngshuǐ after Chìxīn’s death,
hence it is placed here.
“Huíhú troops reached Héngshuǐ.”
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states: Fú Chè reported that Huíhú plundered Héngshuǐ,
an event that occurred in the first month before Lǐ Shì’s frontier inspection.
According to the *Yīpǐnjí*, this memorial says,
“It is appropriate to secretly issue an edict to Liú Miǎn and Zhōngshùn,”
so the memorial must have been after Lǐ Zhōngshùn garrisoned Zhènwǔ.
Probably Chè submitted the memorial while in Tàiyuán,
and Yuán Déyù made this memorial after Miǎn was appointed to Hédōng,
hence it is placed here.
“Now they have retreated and encamped east of Shìjiāpō.”
Lǐ Déyù memorialized:
“Shìjiāpō is three hundred *lǐ* west of the Kèhán’s tent.
Wūjiè moved his tent to secure Cuòzǐ Shān at that time.
They were sent by the Kèhán.
It is appropriate to temporarily state that these troops do not obey the Kèhán’s command
and are wantonly plundering the border.
Secretly instruct Liú Miǎn and Zhòngwǔ –
Zhòngwǔ
is Zhāng Zhòngwǔ –
if they can attack and drive them away,
the action will also have a justifiable reason.
By destroying this detachment,
the Kèhán will surely realize his fear.”
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the *gēngchén* day,
Tián Móu, the Tiāndé Commissioner of Defense, reported:
“The Huíhú’s incessant harassment
has prompted me to deploy three thousand troops to resist them without waiting for an imperial decree.”
On the *rénwǔ* day,
Lǐ Déyù memorialized:
“Tián Móu is utterly ignorant of military strategy.
Barbarians are skilled at field battles
but poor at assaulting cities.
Móu should simply hold fast and await the gathering of troops from various circuits.
Now he has deployed his entire army to battle;
if by chance he suffers a defeat,
the city will be empty.
How can it be defended?
I hope an imperial envoy will be urgently dispatched to stop him.
If engagement has already occurred,
then issue an edict for the Qiāng and Hún from Yúnzhōu, Shuòzhōu, and Tiāndé to each send troops to fiercely attack the Huíhú,
and all captured spoils
shall be taken by them.
The Huíhú have been displaced for two years,
their food supplies are exhausted,
and their morale is easily shaken.
It is advisable to order Tián Móu to entice surrenders,
provide them with food, and transfer them to Tàiyuán,
not to keep them in Tiāndé.
Although Wàimòsī’s true intentions are not yet known,
it is important to grant him official titles and rewards soon.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The preface to the *Yīpǐnjí Yìyù Guīzhōng Chuán* states:
“In the second year,
fourth month,
on the *jiǎshēn* day,
Wàimòsī, the Great Tèlè of the Huíhú, led the Tèlè and prime ministers of his country to submit.”
However, this memorial from the eighteenth day of the fourth month already mentioned Wàimòsī sending a message of submission.
It is probable that Wàimòsī had sent a message of submission to Tián Móu at the time he wanted to execute Chìxīn,
and only on the twentieth day did he lead his followers to Tiāndé.
Thus, the imperial decree appointing him as Grand General of the Left Guards says:
“Repeatedly offered sincere allegiance,
communicating it to the border general;
subsequently apprehended the rebellious barbarian,
showing no disloyalty to his sovereign or kin.
He restrained his starving and dying followers,
not allowing even the slightest transgression.
Observing his conduct,
his great integrity is very clear.”
It is likely that when the Huíhú fell into chaos and perished,
Wàimòsī originally came to submit to Táng with Chìxīn and others,
but the border officials were suspicious and obstructed them.
Therefore, Chìxīn and others became angry and wanted to violate the frontier.
However, Wàimòsī first informed the border officials,
lured Chìxīn’s followers to flee east,
and Wàimòsī then led his own followers to surrender to Táng.
This also served as a counter-espionage tactic.
Furthermore, in order to reward his loyalty and righteousness,
and to provide a justification for military action,
so that various distant and near tributary states would know that only the Kèhán was being held responsible for defying authority,
and there was no intention to completely exterminate the Huíhú.
Shí Xióng is skilled in battle and unrivalled;
I request that he be appointed Deputy Commissioner of Tuánliàn of Tiāndé,
to assist Tián Móu in military affairs.”
The Emperor approved all his suggestions.
Initially,
during the Tàihé reign,
the Dǎngxiàng of Héxī harassed the border.
Wénzōng summoned Shí Xióng from Báizhōu (Xióng was exiled to Báizhōu; see Volume 244, Tàihé 3rd year).
He repeatedly achieved military merits,
but due to Wáng Zhìxīng,
he was not greatly promoted.
By this time,
Déyù recommended and employed him.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
Wàimòsī led the Tèlè and prime ministers of his country, over two thousand two hundred people, to surrender.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Yīpǐnjí* states that the memorial from Wàimòsī and the Tèlè was submitted on the fourth day of the fifth month;
the *Shílù* places it on the *bǐngshēn* day of the fifth month.
This is likely based on the date the memorial arrived.
We now follow the preface to the *Guīzhōng Chuán*.
8 The Emperor trusted Lǐ Déyù,
but the Commissioner of the Army Logistics, Qiú Shìliáng, disliked him.
At that time, the Emperor was about to receive an honorific title
and issue a general amnesty from the Dānfèng Lóu.
Someone informed Shìliáng that
the prime minister and the Commissioner of Finance were discussing drafting an edict to reduce the clothing and food rations of the imperial guards, as well as fodder for horses.
Shìliáng publicly announced to the crowd,
“If this happens,
on that day,
the soldiers will surely cause an uproar in front of the tower!”
Déyù heard of this,
and on the *yǐyǒu* day,
requested an audience at Yányīng Diàn to defend himself.
The Emperor was angry
and immediately dispatched eunuchs to announce to both armies:
“There is absolutely no such thing in the amnesty edict.
Furthermore, all amnesty edicts originate from My will,
not from the prime minister.
How did you get this information?”
Shìliáng then became terrified and embarrassed, bowing in apology.
On the *dīnghài* day,
the officials offered the honorific title of Rénshèng Wénwǔ Zhìshén Dàxiào Huángdì to the Emperor;
a general amnesty was granted throughout the empire.
9 In the fifth month,
on the day Wùshēn,
Hónglú Qīng Zhāng Jiǎ was dispatched to pacify Wòmmòsī and others,
with Wòmmòsī appointed as Zuǒ Jīnwú Dà Jiāngjūn and Huáihuà Jùnwáng;
the other tribal chiefs were awarded ranks and honors accordingly.
Their troops were granted five thousand hù of rice
and three thousand pǐ of silk.
Nàjié Chuài led his forces from Zhènwǔ and Dàtóng,
eastwards via Shìwéi and Hēishā,
southwards towards Xióngwǔ Jūn,
and threatened Yōuzhōu.
Lúlóng Jiédùshǐ Zhāng Zhòngwǔ sent his younger brother Zhòngzhì with thirty thousand soldiers to intercept them.
They were soundly defeated,
with countless numbers beheaded and captured.
All seven thousand of their tents were taken,
and distributed among the various circuits.
Nàjié Chuài fled,
and Wūjiè Kèhán captured and killed him.
The Kǎyì states: The Fápàn Jì says:
"Zhòngwǔ recruited and accepted the surrender of the dispirited soldiers who defected from Chìxīn and the tribes under the Kèhán, totaling more than thirty thousand people,
distributing them among the various circuits.
Thus, the Huíhú people became few and weak."
Both the Xīn and Jiù Jì do not mention Zhòngwǔ defeating the Huíhú.
The Jiù Huíhé Zhuàn states:
"Zhòngwǔ utterly defeated Nàjié's forces,
capturing all seven thousand tents,
and killing and capturing a total of ninety thousand old and young.
Nàjié was hit by an arrow,
pierced through his camel's saddle, and secretly escaped.
Wūjiè captured and killed him."
The Yīpǐn Jí Yōuzhōu Jì Shènggōng Bēi says:
"The Duke received the surrender of thirty thousand people, two Tèlè, one Kèhán's sister, and four Dàdūdū Wài Zǎixiàng,
as well as countless other Píwáng and Qíjiàng, which cannot all be recorded."
None of these books specify the month and day when Zhòngwǔ defeated Nàjié Chuài,
so it is appended here.
At that time, although Wūjiè's forces had diminished,
they still numbered a hundred thousand,
stationed at Lǘmén Shān, north of Dàtóng Jūn.
Yáng Guān returned from Huíhú,
and the Kèhán submitted a memorial requesting food, cattle, and sheep.
The memorial was presented upon Yáng Guān's return.
The imperial decree replied:
"As for food, you are permitted to purchase three thousand dàn at Zhènwǔ, using the price of horses.
Since Sù and Dài, the Huíhú have traded horses with the Central Plains,
and their value has been repaid according to their worth.
As for agricultural produce,
the Central Plains forbids its people from slaughtering livestock;
sheep
are scarce in the Central Plains,
coming from the various northern barbarians,
and the state has never levied them.
Wòmmòsī, since his own country was first shattered,
first sought refuge at the border.
He has not followed the Kèhán for two years now.
We fear his suspicion and jealousy" (this refers to Wūjiè).
"The previous Kèhán, precisely because of his suspicion, cruelty, and lack of kin,
caused internal division and external rebellion.
The current Kèhán, having lost territory and being a distant guest,
should especially strive to rectify past mistakes.
If he were again to engage in fratricide,
then which trusted minister by the Kèhán's side would dare to feel secure?
Our duty is to love all equally,
and We have already accepted his surrender."
(This refers to accepting Wòmmòsī's surrender.)
"For the court to uphold faith and righteousness,
would this not be a win-win situation,
deeply aligning with good intentions!"
10 Wòmmòsī entered the court.
In the sixth month,
on the day Jiǎshēn,
Wòmmòsī's department was established as Guīyì Jūn,
and Wòmmòsī was appointed as Zuǒ Jīnwú Dà Jiāngjūn,
serving as Jūnshǐ.
11 Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Chén Yíxíng was dismissed and made Zuǒ Púshè.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Shàngshū Yòuchéng Lǐ Ràngyí was appointed as Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
12 Tián Mǎnchuān, a person from Lánzhōu, rebelled by occupying the prefectural city.
Liú Miǎn attacked and executed him.
13 Wòmmòsī requested to settle his family in Tàiyuán
and exert all his strength with his younger brothers to defend the border.
An imperial edict commanded Liú Miǎn to care for his family.
Wūjiè Kèhán again sent his prime minister to submit a memorial,
requesting to borrow troops to help restore his country,
and also to borrow Tiāndé Chéng.
The imperial edict did not grant permission.
Initially,
the Khaghan went back and forth between Tiāndé and Zhènwǔ,
plundering the Qiāng and Hún.
He also encamped north of Pátóu Fēng.
Sòng Bái said: Pátóu Fēng is in Shuòchuān.
Envoys returned from Mònán,
but the Khaghan did not obey the imperial edict.
Lǐ Déyù believed
that "Nàjiéchuài is encamped north of the mountains.
Wūjiè fears that Nàjiéchuài might conspire with the Xī and Qìdān to intercept him,
and thus dares not stray far from the frontier.
I hope an edict will be issued to Zhāng Zhòngwǔ, instructing the Xī and Qìdān to join the Huíhú in eliminating Nàjiéchuài,
so that the Khaghan can return north."
Even after Nàjiéchuài's death,
the Khaghan still did not leave.
Arguers then suggested that the Huíhú were waiting for the horse price.
An edict was issued to give them all the horse price,
but they still did not leave.
In the eighth month,
the Khaghan led his forces past Pátóu Fēng to the south,
suddenly entering Dàtóng Chuān,
driving and plundering tens of thousands of cattle and horses belonging to various barbarians in Hédōng,
fighting their way to the city gates of Yúnzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Yúnzhōu
is the site of ancient Píngchéng.
Three hundred *lǐ* north to the Great Wall is the barbarian territory.
Today, Dàtóng County, the seat of the Dàtóng Prefecture of the Great Yuán,
administers Yúnzhōng and Báidēng two counties;
there is also Yúnnèi Prefecture,
administering Róufú and Mánchuān two counties.
The Tǔyùhún and Dǎngxiàng all took their families and entered the mountains to avoid them.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
an edict was issued to dispatch troops from Chén, Xǔ, Xú, Rǔ, Xiāngyáng, and other places to garrison Tàiyuán, Zhènwǔ, and Tiāndé,
to drive out the Huíhú next spring.
The *Kǎyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
"In the sixth month,
the Huíhú invaded Yúnzhōu,
and Liú Miǎn led Tàiyuán troops to resist them."
It also says:
"Liú Miǎn went to relieve Yúnzhōu
but was defeated by the Huíhú."
In the seventh month, it further says:
"Wūjiè passed Tiāndé,
reached Pátóu Fēng,
suddenly entered Dàtóng Chuān,
drove tens of thousands of cattle and horses of the Tàiyuán tribes,
and fought his way to Yúnzhōu."
The *Xīnjì* states:
"In the first month,
the Huíhú invaded Héngshuǐ Zhà,
and pillaged Tiāndé and Zhènwǔ armies.
In the third month,
the Huíhú invaded Yún and Shuò.
In the sixth month,
Liú Miǎn battled the Huíhú at Yúnzhōu
and was defeated."
According to the memorial on Huíhú affairs in *Yīpǐn Jí*:
"Your servants heard from Yáng Guān that
because the Huíhú 'Red Heart' forces were mostly scattered north of the mountains,
fearing that they would join the Xī, Qìdān, and Shìwěi to intercept the Khaghan,
they did not dare to leave far.
Now, an imperial edict is granted to Zhòngwǔ,
ordering him to convey the imperial will.
Because the Huíhú once showed loyalty,
and also because they were shattered
and attached themselves to the state,
the court, by principle, must show compassion and protection.
Now, the Xī, Qìdān, and others should combine forces with them
to eliminate the scattered troops of the 'Red Heart,'
and send the Khaghan gradually out of the Hàn territory,
to avoid his lingering."
Although this memorial lacks a date,
it must have been after Yáng Guān returned from the Huíhú, after the 'Red Heart' died, and before Nàjiéchuài was defeated.
Also, a letter to the Khaghan says:
"Just recently, several envoys returned,
all saying that the Khaghan was only waiting for the horse price.
Yet, when it was to be handed over,
it was heard that his residence had moved repeatedly."
This means that the Khaghan demanded the horse price,
and the court then gave him all of it.
Furthermore, a memorial dated the nineteenth day of the seventh month says:
"It is hoped that a letter will be granted to the Khaghan: 'We have received Wōmòsī's memorial,
stating that when they were in their own country, each had their allotted horses,
and the silk for their horse price should have been released,
requesting it to be used as tribute.
As the Khaghan's native country is broken
and has long been on the frontier,
this has already been considered and appropriately handled with Wōmòsī.
The silk for the horse price allotted to Wōmòsī and those below him
shall be bestowed upon the Khaghan.'"
Therefore, the payment of their horse price must have been before the nineteenth day of the seventh month.
At that time,
the Huíhú must not yet have invaded Yúnzhōu,
defeated Liú Miǎn,
burst into Dàtóng Chuān,
or plundered Tàiyuán's cattle and horses.
Thus, the court was accommodating their requests,
wishing them to leave the frontier and go north sooner,
and had no intention of attacking and suppressing them yet.
Also, the *Shílù* states:
"In the eighth month,
on the *rénxū* day, the first day of the month,
Lǐ Déyù memorialized, requesting to send Shí Xióng to attack the camp, retrieve the princess,
and capture the Khaghan.
On the *wùchén* day,
he again memorialized that the plan to attack the camp should be temporarily halted.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
an edict was issued to dispatch troops from Chén, Xǔ, Xú, Rǔ, and Xiāngyáng to garrison Tàiyuán, Zhènwǔ, and Tiāndé for reinforcement."
According to *Yīpǐn Jí*,
Déyù's memorial discussing the attack on the Huíhú says:
"Your servant has repeatedly received imperial decrees,
stating that since the Huíhú are gradually approaching Pátóu Fēng,
they must be attacked soon.
Your servant has heard that barbarians do not understand siege warfare,
only know how to charge on horseback.
Your servant estimates that they will certainly not deploy scouts or set up ambushes,
nor will they attack camps.
If Shí Xióng is ordered to lead the Yìwǔ cavalry, along with the Tuìhún cavalry,
and elite infantry as flanks,
to launch a silent night attack,
success will surely be easy."
The memorial is undated.
The *Shílù*, citing a memorial from the seventh day, states that
the matter of Shí Xióng's camp attack discussed on the first day of this month
should be temporarily halted,
hence it is placed on the first day of the month.
At this time, it still said "gradually approaching Pátóu Fēng,"
which means they did not yet know that they had passed south of Pátóu Fēng.
Also, a memorial on Huíhú affairs dated the seventh day of the eighth month says:
"Since the Huíhú arrived north of Pátóu Fēng,
several tens of days have passed,
and reports have been silent,
with no further incursions.
Observing their situation,
it is no different from when they were on the border of Tiāndé and Zhènwǔ.
The matter of Shí Xióng's camp attack that your servants discussed on the first day of this month
should be temporarily halted,
and the situation should be further observed."
According to the intention of this memorial,
it indicates that they were completely unaware that the Khaghan had deeply encroached upon Yúnzhōu.
Also, a memorial requesting the dispatch of Chén-Xǔ and other troops dated the tenth day of the eighth month says:
"Your servants already reported yesterday at Yányīng,
requesting Tàiyuán, Zhènwǔ, and Tiāndé to increase military preparations,
and further requesting the conscription of troops from Chén, Xǔ, Xú, Rǔ, Xiāngyáng, and other places.
When the river ice freezes,
we deeply fear that the Khaghan will suddenly cross the river,
and also connect with the Tǔfān,
which would be a serious problem,
requiring strict precautions.
The summoned troops from various circuits must not be delayed;
they must reach their respective locations
before the ice freezes."
Therefore, the Huíhú's sudden entry into Dàtóng Chuān to invade Yúnzhōu must have been in early eighth month.
On the first and seventh days, it was still unknown,
and only on the ninth day was it reported,
thus troops were discussed to be dispatched for defense and expulsion.
The *Shílù* and *Xīnjì* are both erroneous.
Now we follow the *Jiùjì*.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
Wōmòsī and his brothers Ālìzhī, Xíwùchuài, and Wūluósī were all granted the surname Lǐ,
and named Sīzhōng, Sīzhēn, Sīyì, and Sīlǐ.
Wōmòsī was named Sīzhōng,
Ālìzhī was named Sīzhēn,
Xíwùchuài was named Sīyì,
and Wūluósī was named Sīlǐ.
The *Kǎyì* says: The *Jiùjì* states:
"In the sixth month,
Wōmòsī and others arrived at the capital.
An edict appointed Wōmòsī as Guīyì Jūnshǐ
and granted him the name Lǐ Sīzhōng.
The Huíhú chancellor Shòuyéwù was appointed Guīyì Jūnfùshǐ
and granted the name Lǐ Hóngshùn."
The *Jiù Huíhú Zhuàn* says:
"In the winter of the second year and spring of the third year,
three hundred thousand people from seven Huíhú tribes successively surrendered at Yōuzhōu.
An edict ordered them to be distributed among various circuits.
There were Wōmòsī, Shòuyéwù, and others from various tribes who surrendered at Zhènwǔ.
They were all granted the surname Lǐ
and named Sīzhōng, Sīzhēn, and Sīyì."
Now we follow the *Shílù*.
He was named Hóngshùn;
and Hóngshùn was appointed Guīyì Jūnfùshǐ.
The emperor sent Huíhú
Shíjièzhí back to his country, bestowing a letter upon the Khagan.
Kǎoyì says: The old records place this imperial edict under Liú Miǎn and Zhāng Zhòngwǔ as commanders-in-chief.
According to a report dated the eighteenth day of the eighth month from Yīpǐn jí:
"Over the past two days, your servants have privately heard outside opinions saying that
Shíjièzhí has been in the capital for a long time,
and is thoroughly familiar
with everything, whether big or small.
Yesterday, because he was taken into the Hónglú Temple,
fearing the court's handling of him,
he requested to be sent as an envoy,
his intention being to escape.
" It also says:
"Shíjièzhí previously had two sons who fled,
and they must have already entered Huíhú territory.
It is to be expected that he will not be wholehearted in his efforts on this trip!
We humbly request that Liú Miǎn be promptly summoned
to recall him wherever he is.
" Thus, the sending of Shíjièzhí with the letter to the Khagan must have occurred before this report.
It is unknown whether he was indeed recalled later.
"Since that country was destroyed by the Gějísī,
and they came to our borders seeking refuge,
our compassion and acceptance have been unstinting.
Now the Khagan still remains near the frontier,
and has not discussed returning to his homeland,
sometimes plundering Yún and Shuò prefectures,
or raiding Qiāng and Hún tribes.
Judging his true intentions from afar,
it seems he relies on the ties of marriage;
believing that by offering Princess Tàihé as a hostage, he can coerce Zhōngguó.
Chuǎi,
rhymes with chū wěi.
Hǎo,
rhymes with hū dào.
In reality, he harbors plans for raids and incursions.
Generals and ministers, both inside and outside the court, all requested his annihilation,
but my feelings are profoundly for self-restraint,
and I cannot bear to rejoice in misfortune.
The Khagan should quickly choose a good plan,
lest he invite future regret!"
The emperor also ordered Lǐ Déyù to reply on behalf of Liú Miǎn to the letter from the Huíhú chancellor, Jiégān Jiāsī,
stating:
"The Huíhú have come from afar to seek refuge;
they should emulate Hūhánxié, who sent a son to serve,
and personally came to court.
The affair of Hūhánxié can be found in the chronicle of Emperor Xuān of Hàn.
If you beg for mercy and pity,
then our relief and assistance
will be given without any qualms.
It means without any qualms in one's heart.
If you remain arrogant and obstinate,
demanding beyond expectation,
as if still in your own country,
and furthermore deeply penetrate our borders,
plundering incessantly,
how can it be appropriate to seek aid and maintain good relations!
Your letter also states that barbarians are easily aroused and difficult to pacify;
if angered,
they cannot be controlled again.
The Huíhú were destroyed by the Gějísī,
and the bodies of their entire nation's generals and ministers were abandoned in the wilderness,
and the tombs of successive Khagans
are separated by a vast distance.
The anger of the Huíhú
is not directed at them,
them
refers to the Gějísī.
but is unleashed in Zhōnghuá.
How can Heaven, Earth, and the spirits tolerate such behavior!
In the past, Zhìzhī did not serve the great Hàn,
and was ultimately annihilated.
This matter is recorded in the chronicles of Emperor Xuān and Emperor Yuán of Hàn.
This should not be forgotten!"
On Wùzǐ,
Lǐ Déyù and others submitted a report,
saying,
"If as per the previous imperial edict,
the three circuits of Hédōng and others strictly guard,
the three circuits
are Hédōng, Lúlóng, and Zhènwǔ.
taking advantage of the time when the Huíhú people are exhausted and their horses weak,
and the government troops are free from the hardship of severe cold,
then the Yōuzhōu troops should be ordered to halt their stationing in their own circuit to await orders.
If it is feared that once the river ice solidifies,
the Huíhú will again make incursions,
and they must be expelled early,
then a decision should be made within a few months,
while the weather is not yet cold.
By reinforcing the Hédōng troops with Hèshuò troops,
success will surely be achieved within two months.
Now we hear public opinions are diverse,
with differing views,
if the public sentiment is not uniformly consulted,
it will ultimately be swayed by empty words.
We hope that the high-ranking officials will be ordered to convene for a discussion!"
The emperor assented to the edict.
At that time, many deliberators believed it was advisable to wait until next spring.
In the ninth month,
Liú Miǎn was made concurrently the Commissioner for Pacifying Huíhú.
If expulsion was necessary,
he was to command the troops of the various marching armies.
Zhāng Zhòngwǔ was made the Eastern Commissioner for Pacifying Huíhú,
and was to command the marching armies in his own circuit, as well as the Xī, Qìdān, Shìwéi, and other tribes.
Lǐ Sīzhōng was made the General of the Héxī Dǎngxiàng and the Commissioner for Suppressing Huíhú on the Southwest Front.
This Héxī
refers to the west of the Northern River.
Miǎn was ordered to garrison at Yànmén Pass.
Yànmén Pass is in Yànmén County, Dàizhōu,
which is Jínglǐng Pass.
Previously,
the Xī and Qìdān were subject to the Huíhú,
each having an overseer envoy,
who annually supervised their tribute and taxes,
and also spied on Táng affairs.
Zhāng Zhòngwǔ sent his staff officer Shí Gōngxù to command the two tribes,
and they killed over eight hundred Huíhú overseer envoys and others.
Zhòngwǔ defeated Nàjié Chuài,
and captured the wives and children of the Shìwéi chieftains.
The Shìwéi offered gold, silk, sheep, and horses for their ransom,
but Zhòngwǔ refused,
saying:
"Only kill
the overseer envoys, then they will be returned!"
On Guǐmǎo,
Lǐ Déyù and others reported:
"Sūn Chóu, an official reporting from Hédōng, has just arrived,
saying that the Huíhú camp has moved forty *lǐ* closer to the south.
Liú Miǎn believes this must be because the Qìdān are not in agreement with them,
and they fear an ambush.
According to the current situation,
it is indeed suitable for expulsion.
Your servants asked Sūn Chóu,
if combining forces with Yōuzhōu to expel the Huíhú,
how many more troops would be needed.
Chóu said not many more troops were needed;
only the Dàtóng troops were few,
and an additional thousand men from Yìdìng would suffice.
" The emperor assented to all.
An imperial edict ordered Hédōng, Yōuzhōu, Zhènwǔ, and Tiāndé to each dispatch large armies,
to move their camps forward slightly,
to press the Huíhú.
The emperor heard the name of Báimán, the Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince,
and wished to make him a chancellor,
so he asked Lǐ Déyù.
Déyù had always disliked Báimán,
and therefore said Báimán was old and ill,
and unable to attend court.
His paternal cousin, Mǐnzhōng, the Vice Director of the Left Bureau,
whose literary skills were no less than Báimán's,
also possessed talent and discernment.
On Jiǎchén,
Mǐnzhōng was made a Hanlin Academician.
This was a prelude to Mǐnzhōng undermining Déyù.
Lǐ Sīzhōng requested to join forces with six thousand cavalry from Qìbì, Shātuó, and Tǔyùhún to attack the Huíhú.
On Yǐsì,
Hé Qīngcháo, the Prefect of Yínzhōu, and Qìbì Tōng, the Prefect of Wèizhōu, were ordered to divide command of the Hédōng barbarian troops and proceed to Zhènwǔ,
to be under Lǐ Sīzhōng's command.
Tōng
was the fifth-generation descendant of Hélì.
The Qìbì tribe and their encampments
attached themselves to Zhènwǔ during the Tàihé reign.
Qìbì Hélì
came to court during Emperor Tàizōng's reign,
and then remained to serve as an imperial guard.
Wèi,
rhymes with yū wù.
Qì,
rhymes with qī qǐ.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on Dīngmǎo,
Imperial Prince Xiàn was made Prince Yì,
and Qí was made Prince Yǎn.
When he reached Wèizhōu,
he encountered Guóxiàng Shàng Sīluó who was encamped on Bóhánshān.
Kǒngrè attacked him.
Sīluó abandoned his baggage and fled west to Sōngzhōu.
Wáng Yá said: "From Lóngzhōu's Qīngchuānzhèn, entering the Tǔbō territory directly reaches the city of the former Sōngzhōu,
which was where Tǔbō formerly established its military governorship."
Sīluó mobilized troops from Sūpí, Tǔyùhún, Yángtóng, and other tribes,
assembling eighty thousand,
to defend Tāoshuǐ.
He burned the bridge to resist the advance.
When Kǒngrè arrived,
he spoke to the Sūpí and others across the water, saying:
"The treacherous minister has disrupted the country,
and Heaven has sent me to execute him.
How can you assist a rebel!
I am now a prime minister,
and I can command all the troops in the country.
If you do not comply,
I will annihilate your tribes!"
The Sūpí and others were suspicious and did not fight.
Kǒngrè led his elite cavalry across the water,
and the Sūpí and others all surrendered.
Sīluó fled west.
He was pursued and captured,
and killed.
Kǒngrè absorbed all his forces,
totaling over one hundred thousand.
From Wèichuān
to Sōngzhōu,
everything in his path was devastated and destroyed,
with corpses piled high.
Punctuation by Zhōu Yīliáng, reviewed by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial decree.
Hòu Xué Tiāntái
Huìchāng third year
(Guǐhài, 843)
1 Spring,
first month.
The Huíhú Wūjiè Kèhán led his forces to invade and press upon Zhènwǔ.

Liú Miǎn sent Shí Xióng, the Cìshǐ of Línzhōu, and Wáng Féng, the Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ, to lead three tribes of the Shātuó Zhūxié Chìxīn, along with three thousand cavalry of the Qìbì and Tuòbá, to raid their encampment.
The Tuòbá
are the Dǎngxiàng tribe.
帥 is
read as shuài.
契,
Qīqìt fān.
The Kǎoyì states: The old "Biography of Huíhú" says "Shí Xióng, Cìshǐ of Fēngzhōu."
The "Jiànián Lù" of Hòutáng Xiànzǔ says "Shí Xióng, Cìshǐ of Shízhōu."
However, at this time Tián Móu was the Cìshǐ of Fēngzhōu.
We now follow the "Shílù."
Xióng reached Zhènwǔ,
climbed the city wall and observed the strength of the Huíhú forces,
seeing several dozen felt carts.
A felt cart
is a cart with a felt covering.
乘,
Shéngzhèng fān.
They resembled Han people.
He sent spies to inquire,
who reported:
"It is the princess's tent."
Xióng sent a spy to tell her, saying:
"Since the princess has come here,
it is her home;
she should seek a way to return!
I am now going to send troops to attack the Kèhán.
Please, Princess, covertly protect yourself with your attendants,
stop your carts, and do not move!"
Xióng then dug more than ten holes in the city wall,
led his troops out at night,
and directly attacked the Kèhán's main tent.
When they reached his tent,
the barbarians finally became aware.
The Kèhán was greatly alarmed,
not knowing what to do.
He abandoned his baggage and fled.
Xióng pursued and attacked him.
On the day of Gēngzǐ,
he utterly defeated the Huíhú at Shāhúshān.
Shāhúshān is Hēishān.
He fled with several hundred cavalry.
Xióng welcomed Tàihé Gōngzhǔ and returned.
The Kǎoyì states: The old "Biography of Shí Xióng" says:
"In the third year,
the Huíhú greatly plundered Yún and Shuò.
Liú Miǎn stationed the army of Tàiyuán in Yúnzhōu.
Miǎn said to Xióng: 'The state, for the sake of the princess,
does not wish to attack urgently.
We, who defend the frontier, only need to eliminate the threat,
and can act on our own authority.'
Xióng received the instruction
and personally selected elite cavalry,
obtaining the Shātuó tribe,
and also mixed barbarian troops from Qìbì and Tuòbá.
They departed from Mǎyì at night,
directly heading towards Wūjiè's main tent.
At that time, the barbarian tents were pressing upon Zhènwǔ.
After Xióng entered the city,
he ascended the battlements to observe their numbers,
and saw several dozen felt carts, and so on.
Thereupon, he welcomed the princess back to Tàiyuán."
The "Biography of Huíhú" states:
"Wūjiè set up camp eighty *lǐ* from Yōuzhōu.
That night,
Liú Miǎn of Hédōng led his troops and arrived suddenly.
Wūjiè fled in alarm,
camping northeast, relying on Hèjiě Shìwèi.
He did not have time to take Tàihé Gōngzhǔ with him as he fled.
Shí Xióng's troops encountered the princess's tent,
and thus welcomed her back to the country."
The "Jiànián Lù" of Hòutáng Xiànzǔ states:
"Miǎn reported to the Emperor to be the vanguard.
The Huíhú Kèhán set up his main tent at Shāhúshān.
The Emperor and Shí Xióng advanced silently at night,
surrounding his main tent.
Wūjiè Kèhán fled with light cavalry.
The Emperor visited Tàihé Gōngzhǔ at the main tent,
respectfully bringing her back to the country."
According to the "Yīpǐn Jí,"
a memorial dated the seventeenth day of the tenth month of Huìchāng second year states:
"I have learned that Liú Miǎn is quite skilled in frontier affairs,
but when it comes to making decisions at critical moments,
he cannot avoid hesitation.
I deeply fear that being overly cautious
will gradually cause him to miss opportunities.
I request that an imperial edict be bestowed upon Liú Miǎn, saying:
'Previously, because the Huíhú had not yet caused disturbances,
we focused on appeasement.
Now that they have killed frontier people
and driven off cattle and horses,
there have been repeated edicts ordering their swift expulsion.
You should assess what is opportune,
adapt to circumstances at critical moments,
and not be overly doubtful,
awaiting all instructions from the court.
Since you have been granted the title of envoy
and made responsible for coordinating all armies,
all matters on the frontier are entrusted to you.
Henceforth, should you need to move camps or advance troops,
you shall seize all opportunities yourself,
without necessarily awaiting further instructions!'"
The "Shílù" states: On Wùyín,
an edict to Liú Miǎn was issued, as mentioned before.
According to Déyù's memorial,
how could Miǎn dare not await imperial decrees,
but rather send Shí Xióng to raid the Kèhán's main tent,
especially since there was already an edict stating that no further reports were necessary?
The old "Biography of Déyù" states:
"Déyù said: 'North of Pátóu Fēng is the desert.
Open field battles there require cavalry.
If we oppose them with infantry,
it is logically difficult to guarantee victory.
What Wūjiè relies on now is the princess.
If a brave general leads cavalry
and captures the princess,
the barbarians will defeat themselves.'
The Emperor approved of this,
and immediately ordered Déyù to draft the dispositions."
The "Fápàn Jì" states:
"The Emperor asked about the plan for the raid.
Déyù reported: 'If we fight the Huíhú in an open field battle with infantry,
there will surely be no chance of victory.
The Huíhú always bring the princess with them as a hostage.
I have thought of a plan.
I estimate that the Huíhú will certainly not expect an attack on their camp.
Shí Xióng is courageous and unrivaled.
If he is ordered to select the sharpest soldiers from the Fān, Hún, and Hàn troops,
advance silently at night,
he will surely capture the princess,
and the Kèhán might also be captured.'
The Emperor agreed.
So, Shí Xióng was ordered to lead the Fān, Hún, and Hàn troops to advance at night.
The Huíhú indeed had no scouts or ambushes on the road,
and only became aware when they reached their tents.
They then captured the princess,
but the Kèhán fled with light cavalry."
According to this, Déyù later personally requested to be stationed to supervise the camp raid,
while Shí Xióng saw the princess's main tent from the city wall and welcomed her,
which was not due to Déyù's strategy.
We do not adopt this account.
Over twenty thousand of their tribesmen surrendered.
On the day of Bǐngwǔ,
Liú Miǎn's victory report arrived.
Lǐ Sīzhōng came to court.
As a surrendered Huíhú general,
he feared suspicion from frontier generals and requested to bring his brother Sīzhēn and others, as well as Ài Hóngshùn, all back to the imperial court.
On the day of Gēngxū,
Shí Xióng was made the Dūfángyùshǐ of Fēngzhōu.
Wūjiè Kèhán fled to seek refuge with the Hēichēzǐ tribe.
Hú Qiáo said: To the north of Xiágá is the Chányú Tūjué,
and further north are the Hēichēzǐ.
They are skilled at making wagons and tents.
Their people know filial piety and righteousness,
but their land is barren and produces nothing.
A detailed examination of the Old and New Histories shows that
the Hēichēzǐ are a branch of the Shìwéi.
According to the imperial edict granted to the Xiágás at that time,
the Hēichēzǐ were more than a thousand *lǐ* away from the Han border.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: The Old History's biography of the Huíhé says:
"Wūjiè fled in alarm some four hundred *lǐ* to the northeast,
camped with the Hèjiě Shìwéi,
married his sister to a Shìwéi,
and became dependent on them."
Now, we follow the *Fá Pàn Jì*, the *Shílù*, and the New History.
The Old History's biography of Zhāng Zhòngwǔ also says:
"After Wūjiè was defeated,
he relied on the Kāngjū to survive,
and moved all his remaining people to seek shelter with the Hēichēzǐ."
This is because Lǐ Déyù's *Jì Shèng Gōng Bēi* states:
"Wūjiè, along with the Dīnglìng, sought peace;
he relied on the Kāngjū to survive;
he moved all his remaining people,
and humbled himself before the Hēichē."
What they referred to as Kāngjū
was merely using the story of Zhìzhī;
this led to the error.
2 In the second month,
on the *Gēngshēn* day which was the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
3 An imperial edict ordered the disbanding of the Guīyì Army.
The establishment of the Guīyì Army is recorded in the previous volume, last year.
Generous provisions and rewards were given.
4 On the *Xīnwèi* day,
the Xiágás dispatched an envoy, Zhùwúhésuǒ, to present two famous horses.
The New History says: Zhùwú
is a barbarian surname.
Hé means 'fierce',
Sù means 'left',
referring to one who is valorous, fierce, and skilled at left-handed archery.
"Suǒ"
is written as
"Sù".
Sòng Bái said: Suǒ is in the rising tone.
On the *Jiǎxū* day,
he was granted an imperial audience,
and his rank was above that of the Bóhǎi envoys.
The Emperor wished to order Zhào Fān to seek Ānxī and Běitíng from the Xiágás.
Lǐ Déyù and others memorialized, saying:
"Ānxī is more than seven thousand *lǐ* from the capital,
and Běitíng is more than five thousand *lǐ*.
Even if we were to obtain them,
we would have to re-establish a Dūhù,
and station ten thousand Tang soldiers there.
We do not know where these troops would be mustered,
nor how provisions would be transported.
This would be exchanging real expense for an empty name,
which is not a wise plan."
The *Kǎo Yì* states: Déyù's biography says:
"In the second month of the third year,
Zhào Fān reported that the Xiágás were attacking the Ānxī and Běitíng Dūhùfǔ,
and that an army should be dispatched to provide support."
Déyù's memorial was consistent with this.
The *Xiàn Tì Jì* says:
"In the third year,
on the eleventh day of the second month,
at Yányīng,
Déyù memorialized: 'On the ninth day, an imperial proclamation was received,
ordering your humble servants to instruct Zhào Fān
to request Ānxī and Běitíng from the Xiágás.
I deeply fear this is not feasible.'"
The rest of his words are also consistent with this.
According to the *Shílù*:
"On the *Xīnwèi* day,
Zhùwúhésuǒ first arrived,
and Zhào Fān was ordered to entertain him.
On the *Bǐngzǐ* day,
the Zhōngshūménxià memorialized about the imperial proclamation received on the ninth day."
Its words are also consistent with the *Xiàn Tì Jì*.
It is unknown which book Sòng consulted to obtain these *Xīnwèi* and *Bǐngzǐ* dates.
For now, we will omit these dates
and append them below Zhùwúhésuǒ's imperial audience to signify uncertainty.
5 Cuī Gǒng, Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was dismissed and made Yòu Púshè.
6 The Xiágás requested imperial enfeoffment.
Lǐ Déyù memorialized that
it would be advisable to establish friendly relations with them,
and let them personally lead troops to seek out and kill the culprits who murdered the envoy.
The Xiágás had sent an envoy to escort Princess Tàihé,
but the envoy was killed by the Huíhé.
This event is recorded in the previous volume, last year.
The Emperor feared that if he conferred the title of Kèhán, they would not observe the etiquette of a vassal state,
and would follow the example of the Huíhé in demanding annual tributes and selling horses.
He was hesitant and undecided.
Déyù memorialized:
"The Xiágás have already proclaimed themselves Kèhán.
Now, we wish to leverage their strength,
so I fear we cannot be stingy with this title.
The Huíhé had the merit of pacifying Ān Lùshān and Shǐ Sīmíng,
hence they were given an annual tribute of twenty thousand bolts of silk,
and allowed to engage in market trade.
The Xiágás have never rendered service to the Central Kingdom;
how dare they suddenly demand bribes or tributes!
If we are concerned they will not act as vassals,
we should make an agreement with them,
stating that only if they act as vassals like the Huíhé
will the enfeoffment be carried out.
Furthermore, we should emphasize their common surname to show kinship,
and make them observe the rites of descendants."
The Emperor followed his advice.
7 On the *Gēngyín* day,
Princess Tàihé arrived in the capital,
and was re-enfeoffed as Āndìng Dàzhǎnggōngzhǔ.
Princess Tàihé had been married to the Huíhé in the first year of Chángqìng,
and now she was able to return.
"Āndìng"
is written as
"Dìng'ān" in the New History.
Zhǎng is pronounced as zhī zhàng fān.
The princess proceeded to Guāngshùn Gate,
removed her ceremonial attire,
took off her hairpins and earrings,
and apologized for the Huíhé's ingratitude and the impropriety of her marriage alliance.
Tang princesses who married into barbarian tribes were called
"Héfān Gōngzhǔ" (Princesses of Harmonious Marriages).
Now, Princess Tàihé, due to the Huíhé's border incursions,
personally apologized for the impropriety of her *héfān*.
Qù is pronounced as qiāng lǚ fān.
Afterward, she entered the palace.
Yáng'ān and six other
princesses did not come to console Princess Āndìng;
each was punished with a forfeiture of salary, goods, and bolts of silk.
Princess Yáng'ān was the daughter of Emperor Shùnzōng.
Sòng Bái said: Those who did not come were Princesses Yáng'ān, Xuānchéng, Zhēnníng, Yìníng, Línzhēn, Zhēnyuán, and Yìchāng – seven princesses.
8 Hé Chóngshùn, the Jiédùshǐ of Wèibó, was granted the personal name Hóngjìng.
9 In the third month,
Zhào Fān, Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud, was appointed Commissioner for the Pacification and Conciliation of the Xiájiāsī.
The Emperor ordered Lǐ Déyù to draft a letter to the Qaghan of Xiájiāsī,
instructing him with the words:
"In the twenty-first year of Zhēnguàn, the former lord of Xiájiāsī personally came to court.
'Twenty-first year'
should be
'twenty-second year'.
Up until Tiānbǎo,
tribute never ceased.
Recently, they were isolated by the Huíhú.
The Huíhú oppressed various barbarian tribes.
The Qaghan was able to take revenge and wipe out grievances,
a great achievement and courageous act,
unparalleled in recent history.
Now, the remnant Huíhú forces number less than a thousand men,
scattered in mountains and valleys.
Since the Qaghan has grievances with them,
they must be completely annihilated;
should any embers remain,
they will certainly cause future trouble.
Moreover, we have heard that the origin of the Qaghan's clan name
is the same as ours."
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: "The Son of Heaven bestows surnames (xìng) and clan names (shì);
feudal lords may only be granted clan names,
not surnames,
as they are subordinate to the Son of Heaven."
Hence, the "Zuo Zhuan" for the eighth year of Yǐn says: "Wú Hài died.
The Duke asked Zhòng Zhòng about clan names."
Zhòng Zhòng replied:
"The Son of Heaven establishes virtue,
and based on birth, bestows a surname,
grants land and designates a clan name.
Feudal lords use a given name (zì) as a posthumous title,
and thence it becomes a clan name.
If an official has hereditary merits,
then there is an official clan;
the same applies to fiefs."
According to this statement,
the Son of Heaven bestows a surname based on the birth of a feudal lord's ancestor.
Dù Yù's commentary says: "If Shùn was born in Guīruì,
his surname was bestowed as Guī;
when Shùn's descendants were enfeoffed in Chén,
their clan name was designated based on the land they were enfeoffed with.
Shùn's descendants had the surname Guī and the clan name Chén."
Therefore, Zhèng Bóyì's "Yì Yì" says: "The Yán Dì's surname was Jiāng,
bestowed by Tàihào.
The Huáng Dì's surname was Jī,
bestowed by the Yán Dì.
Thus, Yáo bestowed Bóyí with the surname Jiāng,
Yǔ with the surname Sì,
Qì with the surname Zǐ,
and Jì with the surname Jī,
recorded in historical texts."
As Zhèng says,
this means the Son of Heaven bestows surnames.
Feudal lords bestow clan names upon their ministers and high officials.
If of the same surname,
the Duke's son is called Gōngzǐ,
the Gōngzǐ's son is called Gōngsūn.
The Gōngsūn's son's kinship is already distant,
and cannot reach the Duke directly,
so the given name of the paternal grandfather (wángfù zì) is used as a clan name.
If the son of the principal wife,
then the zì of the five-character sequence Bó, Zhòng, etc., is used as a clan name,
such as Zhòngsūn and Jìsūn of Lǔ.
If a son of a concubine or secondary wife,
then a twenty-character zì is used as a clan name,
such as Zāng Shì and Zhǎn Shì.
If of a different surname,
then the official title of the father or ancestor, or the fiefdom enjoyed, is used as a clan name: those taking official titles as clan names
are Sīmǎ and Sīchéng;
those taking fiefdoms as clan names
are Hán, Zhào, Wèi.
Generally, those granted a clan name (shì zú) are
only granted it if they are ministers (qīng).
Those with great merit are granted a clan name (zú) while alive,
such as Shū Sūn Déchén.
Even if a Gōngzǐ (prince),
if he has great merit and virtue,
then the Gōngzǐ's zì is bestowed as a clan name,
such as Xiāng Zhòng Suí.
If without merit or virtue,
a clan name is granted only after death,
such as Wú Hài.
If a descendant becomes a minister,
his lord does not bestow a clan name;
he himself uses his paternal grandfather's zì as a clan name.
Clan names (shì) and lineages (zú),
when contrasted, are distinct;
when used loosely, they are interchangeable.
Hence, in the "Zuo Zhuan", under the question about clan names to Zhòng Zhòng, it says,
'The Duke ordered to use his zì as the Zhǎn Shì',
which is this.
Surnames (xìng) and clan names (shì) can also be used interchangeably when spoken loosely.
Therefore, the "Chūnqiū" mentions Jiāng Shì and Zǐ Shì,
where Jiāng and Zǐ are both surnames but referred to as clan names (shì)."
The Qaghan is a descendant of the Dūwèi.
"Prefect of Běipíng" refers to Lǐ Guǎng.
"Dūwèi" refers to Lǐ Líng.
The Dūwèi
refers to Lǐ Líng.
The difference in status is clear.
Now, we wish to officially invest the Qaghan
and specially add a splendid title.
However, since the Qaghan's intentions are not yet known,
we shall first send an envoy to convey our sentiments.
When Zhào Fān returns,
another envoy will be appointed to perform the full ceremony."
From the time the Huíhú arrived at the frontier and the Xiájiāsī submitted tribute,
whenever there were imperial edicts,
the Emperor often ordered Lǐ Déyù to draft them.
Lǐ Déyù requested that the Hanlin Academicians be entrusted with this task,
but the Emperor said:
"The Academicians cannot fully satisfy me;
you must do it yourself."
10 Liú Miǎn memorialized:
"Over three thousand Huíhú of the Guīyì Army and forty-three chieftains, in accordance with the edict, were to be distributed among various circuits.
However, they all cried out loudly,
occupied the Hūtuó River with their linked camps,
and refused to obey orders.
They have all been put to death.
The Huíhú who surrendered at Yōuzhōu, numbering over thirty thousand in total,
have all been dispersed among various circuits."
11 Lǐ Déyù re-examined the matter of Wéizhōu and Sī Dámóu.
The matter is found in Volume 244, Wénzōng, Tàihé 5th Year.
"Wéizhōu is situated on a high mountain peak,
with three sides facing a river,
strategically located at the intersection of the barbarians' flat plains and
the path for Chinese troops to enter.
Initially,
when Hé and Lǒng were both lost,
only this [Wéizhōu] remained.
The Tǔbō secretly married women to those guarding the gate of this prefecture.
Twenty years later,
two sons grew up,
secretly opened the camp gate,
led soldiers in at night,
and thus it was captured by them.
It was called 'City of No Worries'.
From then on, they could concentrate their forces on the western frontier
and no longer worry about the southern route.
'Concentrating forces on the western frontier'
refers to the Tǔbō concentrating forces to attack Qí, Lǒng, Bīn, Jīng, Líng, and Xià.
'No longer worry about the southern route'
refers to Xīchuān being south of the Tǔbō.
Speaking from Cháng'ān's perspective,
Xīchuān is also south of Jiànguān.
If the Tǔbō were to invade Shǔ,
the southern route would be through Wéi and Mào,
and the northern route through Suīzhōu.
[This worried] successive emperors until late in the day (gànshí).
During Zhēnyuán,
Wéi Gāo wished to administer Hé and Huáng,
and required this city as a starting point.
All troops exerted their utmost,
attacking fiercely for several years.
Although Lùn Mǎng Rè was captured and returned,
the city was too strong to be taken in the end.
See Volume 236, Dézōng, Zhēnyuán 17th and 18th Years.
卒 (zú),
pronunciation is 'zì xù fān'.
Your subject first arrived in Xīshǔ,
outwardly promoting the nation's prestige,
and inwardly securing the border defenses.
Wéizhōu, trusting your subject's command,
came to submit with empty walls.
Your subject then accepted their surrender,
and the Southern Barbarians were awe-struck.
The eight states in Xīshān
all wished to become internal dependencies.
As for the cities of Héshuǐ and Qījī, etc., belonging to Tǔbō,
and the Héjiāng Shǒuzhuō city in Yìzhōu,
Qījī city and this city were originally Tang territory,
lost to Tǔbō.
If they must be recovered,
it would reduce the number of garrison troops in eight places,
and we would effortlessly recover over a thousand *lǐ* of old territory.
Moreover, the year before Wéizhōu surrendered,
Tǔbō was still besieging Lǔzhōu.
Lǔzhōu
is one of the six Húzhōu of Héqu,
located on the western border of Yòuzhōu.
When your subject first accepted their surrender,
I swore by Heaven,
and personally promised to report to the throne
that each would receive rewards.
Those who did not agree with your subject at the time
immediately slandered your subject.
An imperial edict commanded your subject to seize and send Xīdámóu and others, ordering them to be executed by their own people.
How could your subject bear to abandon trust and seek temporary peace at the cost of over three hundred lives!
I submitted numerous memorials arguing the case,
begging for mercy and release.
The imperial reply was severe and urgent,
ultimately ordering their capture and return.
They were bound with three wooden restraints,
carried in bamboo litters,
and as they were about to set off,
they cried out in injustice, "Wuwu!"
The generals and officials facing your subject
all shed tears.
Those who escorted them were further mocked and ridiculed by the Fān commanders,
who said: "Since they have already surrendered to 'them'
(This means Tǔbō referred to China as 'them'),
(*Shuài*,
pronounced *suǒlèi*),
and yet these surrendered people are now executed within Han territory,
wantonly acting with cruelty
to solidify division!"
(This means that if the Róngmán had any inclination to turn towards the interior,
they would fear the brutal slaughter by Tǔbō
and would not dare to harbor rebellious thoughts again,
thus consolidating control through tyranny.)
"Following this with spears and lances
blocks the path of loyalty and sincerity
and gratifies the cruel and tyrannical.
Since ancient times,
such a thing has never happened.
Although the time has passed by one *jì*,
the opportunity belongs to a thousand years."
(Meaning a rare opportunity that comes once in a thousand years.)
(*Shǔ*,
pronounced *zhīyù*.)
"May each be granted posthumous honors!"
An imperial edict posthumously granted Xīdámóu the title of Right Wèi Jiāngjūn.
Your subject Guāng says: Commentators often doubt the taking or rejecting of Wéizhōu,
unable to decide the right or wrong of Niú and Lǐ.
Your subject believes that in the past, when Xún Wú besieged Gǔ,
some Gǔ people requested to betray the city.
Wú did not permit it,
saying:
"If someone betrays our city,
it is something I greatly despise.
If someone brings a city to me,
why should I like it?
I cannot desire a city and thus bring forth treachery."
He made the Gǔ people kill the traitors and repair their defenses.
(Seen in *Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Zhuàn*.)
Speaking of benefits,
Wéizhōu is small while trustworthiness is great.
Speaking of harms,
Wéizhōu is a slow matter while Guānzhōng is urgent.
So, for those planning for Tang,
what should come first?
Xīdámóu in Tang would be considered one who submitted to civilization;
in Tǔbō, he would inevitably be a rebellious subject.
Why pity him for his execution?
Moreover, what Dédéyù said was for benefit,
and what Sēngrú said was for righteousness.
Even a common man who pursues profit and forgets righteousness is ashamed of it,
how much more so the Son of Heaven!
For example, a neighbor has an ox
that escapes and enters one's house.
Some advise the elder brother to return it,
while others advise the younger brother to steal it.
Those who advise returning it say:
"Stealing it is unrighteous,
and it will lead to a lawsuit."
Those who advise stealing it say:
"He once stole our sheep,
why be constrained by righteousness!
An ox is a large animal;
selling it can enrich the family."
From this perspective,
the right and wrong of Niú and Lǐ
can be clearly seen.
At the beginning of Yuányòu,
four garrisons including Mǐzhī were abandoned and given to Xīxià,
which was largely the consensus of the national opinion at the time.
12th year of Xià,
4th month,
Xīnwèi day,
Lǐ Dédéyù requested to retire to a leisure position.
The Emperor said:
"You repeatedly resign your post,
which leaves me unsettled for days.
(*Bùdé suǒ*
means not at ease in one's place.)
How can you ask to leave!"
13th year,
Liú Cóngjiàn, Jíedùshǐ of Zhāoyì, repeatedly memorialized about Qiú Shìliáng's crimes.
(See volume 245, Wénzōng Tàihé 8th year.)
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Cóngjiàn had a horse nine *chǐ* tall,
which he presented,
but the Emperor did not accept it.
(*Zhōulǐ*: horses eight *chǐ* or more are called *lóng*,
seven *chǐ* or more are called *lái*,
six *chǐ* or more are called *mǎ*.)
A horse nine *chǐ* tall
was rare.
(*Gāo*,
pronounced *gǔbào*.)
Cóngjiàn angrily killed his horse.
From this, he and the imperial court became mutually suspicious and resentful.
He then recruited fugitives,
repaired and completed weapons,
and neighboring regions secretly prepared for him.
Cóngjiàn monopolized horse pasturage and merchant trade,
earning 50,000 *mín* in cash annually.
He also sold iron and boiled salt, earning tens of thousands of *mín*.
Major merchants all borrowed his *yázhí*,
(*yázhí*
refers to the official positions of generals and officers in front of the *yá*—headquarters),
and engaged in trading.
Merchants, relying on Cóngjiàn's influence,
often oppressed generals and officials wherever they went,
and all the circuits disliked them.
Cóngjiàn fell ill,
and said to his wife, Péi-shì:
"I served the imperial court with loyalty and integrity,
but the imperial court does not understand my will,
and all the circuits do not support me.
If I die,
and another takes charge of this army,
then my family will have no cooking fire!"
He then conspired with his staff members Zhāng Gǔ and Chén Yángtíng to imitate the practices of the various garrisons in Héběi.
He appointed his younger brother, Yòu Xiāowèi Jiāngjūn Cóngsù's son Zhěn, as Yánèi Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ,
his nephew Kuāngzhōu as Zhōngjūn Bīngmǎshǐ,
the clerk Wáng Xié as Yáyá Qīnshì
Bīngmǎshǐ,
and his slave Lǐ Shìguì as Shǐzhái Shíjiāng Bīngmǎshǐ.
Liú Shǒuyì, Liú Shǒuzhōng, Dǒng Kěwǔ, and Cuī Xuándù were to command the *yá* troops separately.
Gǔ was from Yùnzhōu;
Yángtíng
was from Hóngzhōu.
Cóngjiàn soon passed away,
but Zhěn secretly kept the death a secret.
Wáng Xié advised Zhěn:
"We should just follow the precedent of the Bǎolì era.
(In the first year of Jìngzōng's Bǎolì reign,
Liú Wù died,
and Cóngjiàn succeeded him; this event is seen in volume 243.)
The ceremonial banners and symbols will arrive on their own.
Just strictly obey the Jiānjūn,
generously bribe the imperial envoy,
do not send troops out of the four borders,
and secretly prepare within the city."
He made the *yáyá* Jiāng Yín submit a memorial requesting an imperial physician.
The Emperor sent the eunuch Jiě Cháozhèng to inquire about the illness with a physician.
Zhěn also pressured the Jiānjūn Cuī Shìkāng to report that Cóngjiàn was ill,
and requested that his son Zhěn be appointed as Liúhòu.
The Emperor sent the Gōngfèngguān Xuē Shìgàn to convey an imperial message, saying:
"I fear Cóngjiàn's illness is not yet stable,
so he should temporarily seek treatment in Dōngdū.
After he recovers somewhat,
he will be given a different appointment.
Furthermore, Zhěn should come to court,
and he will certainly be generously granted official titles."
(*Gōngfèngguān* was also a eunuch.)
The Emperor consulted the chief ministers about the affairs of Zé-Lù.
Most of the chief ministers believed:
"The embers of the Huí-Hú have not yet been extinguished,
and the borders still require vigilance.
To again campaign against Zé-Lù
would be beyond the nation's strength.
We request that Liú Zhěn be provisionally appointed to oversee military affairs."
The censors and other officials who memorialized likewise held this view.
Lǐ Dé-Yù alone said:
"The situation in Zé-Lù is different from that of the Three Commands of Hé-Shuò.
Hé-Shuò has been accustomed to rebellion for a long time,
and its people are difficult to transform.
For this reason, throughout successive reigns,
it has been disregarded.
Zé-Lù is located near the heartland,
and its army has always been known for its loyalty and righteousness.
It once routed Zhū Tāo
and captured Lú Cóng-Shǐ.
The routing of Zhū Tāo is mentioned in volume 231, Dè-Zōng, Zhēn-Yuán 1st year.
The capture of Lú Cóng-Shǐ is mentioned in volume 238, Xiàn-Zōng, Yuán-Hé 3rd year.
Lǐ Bào-Zhēn established this army,
mentioned in volume 223, Dài-Zōng, Yǒng-Tài 1st year.
He dispatched Lǐ Jiān to escort the coffin back to the Eastern Capital.
Mentioned in volume 235, Zhēn-Yuán 10th year.
Furthermore, the chief ministers lack foresight.
After Liú Wù's death,
they procrastinated and handed the command to Cóng-Jiàn.
Cóng-Jiàn was arrogant and difficult to control,
repeatedly submitting memorials to coerce the court.
The matter is recorded in the annals of Wén-Zōng.
Now they again propose to hand military authority to a mere boy.
If the court were again to acquiesce and grant it to him,
then which of the various commands throughout the four quarters would not think of emulating his actions?
The Emperor's prestige and authority would no longer be effective!"
The Emperor said:
"By what method do you propose to control him?
Can it truly be achieved?"
He replied:
"Zhěn relies on the Three Commands of Hé-Shuò.
If only Zhèn and Wèi do not side with him,
then Zhěn will be powerless.
If we dispatch high-ranking officials to persuade Wáng Yuán-Kuí and Hé Hóng-Jìng,
Wáng Yuán-Kuí is
the military commissioner of Zhèn;
Hé Hóng-Jìng is
the military commissioner of Wèi.
The successive emperors allowed them to pass down their positions,
which has become an established precedent,
unlike Zé-Lù.
Now, the court is preparing to deploy troops against Zé-Lù
and does not wish to send additional imperial guards to Shān-Dōng.
As for the three prefectures in Shān-Dōng that belong to Zhāo-Yì,
delegate the task of attacking them to the two commands;
The three prefectures in Shān-Dōng
refer to Xíng, Míng, and Cí.
After the rebels are pacified, bestow generous official titles and rewards.
If the two commands obey the orders
and do not obstruct the imperial army from the side,
then Zhěn will surely be captured!"
The Emperor was pleased and said:
"I agree with Dé-Yù;
there will be no regrets."
Thereupon, he resolved to campaign against Zhěn.
The "Kǎo-Yì" states: According to the old annals, biographies, and the "Shí-Lù" (Veritable Records) regarding Dé-Yù's words,
they all come from the "Fá-Pàn-Jì" (Record of Punishing Rebels).
The "Fá-Pàn-Jì" places this event at the time Liú Cóng-Jiàn first died in the fourth month.
By this point,
the Emperor and his chief ministers had already decided to punish and campaign,
and the collective deliberations of the officials and the chief ministers' second discussion
were merely formalities.
Dé-Yù's words should have been at the beginning of the matter;
the "Shí-Lù"'s placement here
is an error.
The Emperor ordered Dé-Yù to draft an imperial edict to Wáng Yuán-Kuí, the Military Commissioner of Chéng-Dé, and Hé Hóng-Jìng, the Military Commissioner of Wèi-Bó.
Its gist was:
"The command of Zé-Lù
is different from your situation.
Do not make plans for your descendants,
wishing to maintain a relationship like the 'auxiliary and the chariot wheel.'
An ancient saying goes: 'The auxiliary and the chariot wheel depend on each other.'
'Chariot'
is pronounced *chǐ zhē fān*.
Then blessings will naturally extend to your future generations."
On the day Dīng-Chǒu,
the Emperor held court,
praised the edict's concise and pointed language,
and said:
"It is correct to directly inform them thus!"
He also bestowed an edict upon Zhāng Zhòng-Wǔ,
stating that
"the embers of the Huí-Hú have not yet been extinguished,
and there are many anxieties on the frontier.
We exclusively entrust you with repelling the invaders."
This was because Kè-Jiè Kè-Hán was still in Hēi-Chē-Zǐ.
(Zhāng Zhòng-Wǔ) respectfully listened and obeyed.
Jiě Cháo-Zhèng arrived at Shàng-Dǎng.
The "Kǎo-Yì" states: The "Shí-Lù" says:
"At that time, twenty days had passed since Cóng-Jiàn's death."
According to Jiāng Yín and others,
he had not been seen by his envoy since the 6th day of the fourth month.
However, the court was suspended for Cóng-Jiàn on the day Xīn-Sì.
From the 6th to Xīn-Sì
was only eighteen days.
The "Shí-Lù" contradicts itself;
therefore, we do not adopt this.
"The prime minister is in a critical condition
and unable to receive the imperial edict."
Cháo-Zhèng wanted to force his way in,
but the cavalry commanders Liú Wǔ-Dé and Dǒng Kě-Wǔ stood at the curtain.
Cháo-Zhèng feared other complications
and quickly retreated.
Zhěn presented gifts worth several thousand *mín*
and again sent his牙将 Yá-Jiāng, Liáng Shū-Wén, to express gratitude.
Xuē Shì-Gàn entered the territory;
neither inquired about Cóng-Jiàn's illness,
straightway implying they already knew of his death.
The Chief Custodian Guō Yì and others then sent out a large army
to Lóng-Quán-Yì to await the imperial envoy,
requesting that the precedent of Hé-Shuò be applied.
They also spoke to the supervising censor.
Cuī Shì-Kāng was timid
and dared not disobey.
Thereupon, the generals and officials helped Zhěn to appear before the soldiers and populace,
and announced the mourning.
Shì-Gàn ultimately could not enter the Yá-Mén,
and Zhěn also did not accept the imperial edict.
Yì was
a native of Yǎn-Zhōu.
When Jiě Cháo-Zhèng returned to report,
the Emperor was enraged,
had him flogged,
and banished him to Gōng-Líng;
Jiāng Yín and Liáng Shū-Wén were imprisoned.
On Xīn-Sì,
the court first suspended for Cóng-Jiàn,
bestowing upon him the title of Grand Tutor,
and decreed that Liú Zhěn escort the coffin back to the Eastern Capital.
He also summoned Liú Cóng-Sù
and ordered him to write a letter to admonish Zhěn,
i.e., the father was to write a letter to admonish his son.
Cóng-Sù was then in court as a general of the Right Vanguard.
'Jiàn'
is pronounced *xián biàn fān*.
On Dīng-Hài,
Wáng Mào-Yuán, Military Commissioner of Zhōng-Wǔ, was appointed Military Commissioner of Hé-Yáng;
