Lǐ Shí was made Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince and a resident official in the eastern capital,
Cuī Yuánshì, the Military Commissioner of Hézhōng, was made Military Commissioner of Hédōng,
and Shí Xióng was made Military Commissioner of Hézhōng.
Yuánshì
was the younger brother of Yuánlüè.
Yuánlüè
was the father of Cuī Xuàn, who was currently a chancellor.
5 Jǐwèi,
Shí Xióng captured Sānzhài and Yībǎo, including Liángmǎ.
Originally,
the Tùhún Lǐ Wànjiāng returned to Lǐ Bàoyù in Lùzhōu,
grazing his horses at Jīnliángsì.
The land had good water and grass,
and the horses were as numerous as ducks and strong;
the world called them Jīnliáng breed.
Liángmǎzhài was probably established in that area.
6 Xīnyǒu,
Tàiyuán presented Yáng Biàn and fifty-four of his associates,
all of whom were executed at Gǒujílǐng.
According to Sòng Bái's *Xù Tōngdiǎn*,
Gǒujílǐng is in the east market of the capital city.
7 Rénshēn,
Lǐ Déyù said to the Emperor:
"Some things are indeed brought to success through stimulation: Your Majesty ordered Wáng Zǎi to advance to Cízhōu,
and Hé Hóngjìng dispatched troops;
a guest army was sent to punish Tàiyuán,
and the garrison soldiers captured Yáng Biàn first.
Now Wáng Zǎi has long delayed his advance,
I request to transfer Liú Miǎn to garrison Héyáng,
and further order him to lead two thousand elite soldiers from Yìchéng directly to Wànshàn,
placing them under Zǎi's very nose.
If Zǎi understands the court's intention,
he will surely not dare to linger.
If Zǎi advances,
Miǎn with his heavy troops in the south,
will also make their presence felt."
The Emperor said:
"Excellent!"
Wùyín,
Liú Miǎn, the Military Commissioner of Yìchéng, was made Military Commissioner of Héyáng.
8 Wáng Féng attacked Kāng Liángquán, a general of Zhāoyì,
and defeated him.
Liángquán abandoned Shíhuìguān
and retreated to garrison Gǔyāolǐng.
9 The Qíěrjísi sent generals Dìdéyīsī Nánzhū and others to offer tribute,
saying they wished to move to the Uighur royal encampment,
and asked for the date to dispatch troops and the meeting place.
The Emperor issued an edict,
instructing them
that "this autumn when the Khagan attacks the Uighurs and the Hēichēzi,
the four garrisons of Yōuzhōu, Tàiyuán, Zhènwǔ, and Tiāndé shall dispatch troops to important roads,
to intercept the fleeing remnants,
then you will be formally enfeoffed,
and all according to the precedent of the Uighurs."
10 The court, seeing the decline of the Uighurs
and internal strife in Tǔbō,
discussed restoring the four garrisons and eighteen prefectures of Hé and Huáng.
During the height of Kāiyuán,
Lǒngyòu and Héxī were merely divided into two garrisons.
After their fall,
Tǔbō divided them into four garrisons.
The eighteen prefectures were: Qín, Yuán, Hé, Wèi, Lán, Shàn, Jiē, Chéng, Táo, Mín, Lín, Kuò, Dié, Dàng, Gān, Liáng, Guā, and Shā.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states
that Yǐ Méng was made Border Inspector in the second month of next year, Rén Yín.
Rén Yín
was the twenty-fifth day.
According to *Yīpǐnjí*,
a memorial dated the twenty-second day of the second month of Huìchāng Year 4 states:
"Because Lǐ Huí and others reported that the Qíěrjísi envoy said
that this winter they definitely want to collect the remnants of the Uighur Khagan from the Hēichēzi,
they earnestly hope that the nation's troops will respond.
An imperial edict has already been given to the Qíěrjísi envoy upon his return,
permitting Yōuzhōu, Tàiyuán, Zhènwǔ, and Tiāndé to each dispatch troops to important roads for interception."
It also says:
"Furthermore, all the troops north of Dài shall be fully prepared."
It also says: The Yōuzhōu forces are numerous,
so there is no need to prepare them beforehand;
wait until early winter for a eunuch to be dispatched with a further imperial edict.
The Qíěrjísi envoy came in the second month of Year 4,
so what Déyù's memorial refers to as 'this winter,' 'defending in autumn,' and 'early winter'
all refer to events of Year 4.
It is impossible for Yǐ Méng to be made Border Inspector only in the second month of Year 5.
Méng's mission must have been in the spring or summer of this year.
The exact month and day are unknown,
so it is provisionally attached here.
It was also ordered that Tiāndé, Zhènwǔ, and Hédōng should train their soldiers and sharpen their weapons,
awaiting the Qíěrjísi attack on the Uighurs this autumn,
and to intercept those scattered troops coming south.
All these matters were entrusted to Méng and the Military Commissioner-cum-Inspector of Militias to deliberate and report.
Méng
was the grandson of Yàn.
Liú Yàn died by slander at the beginning of Jiànzhōng.
11 The Daoist Zhào Guīzhēn was made Professor of Daoist Affairs for the Right Street.
12 Jízàng Fēngzàn, a general of the Tǔbō Lùn Kǒngrè, disliked Kǒngrè's cruelty
and defected to Shàng Bìbì.
Kǒngrè dispatched troops to attack Bìbì in Shànzhōu.
Bìbì divided his troops into five routes to resist them.
Kǒngrè retreated to garrison Dōnggǔ.
*Jiǔyù Zhì* says: Fifteen *lǐ* southeast of Hézhōu is Dōnggǔbǎo,
established in Xīníng Year 7 of the Sòng dynasty.
His water source was cut off.
Kǒngrè, with more than a hundred horsemen, broke through the encirclement and fled to garrison Bóhánshān.
His remaining forces all surrendered to Bìbì.
13 Summer,
fourth month,
Wáng Zǎi advanced to attack Zézhōu.
14 The Emperor was fond of immortals,
and the Daoist Zhào Guīzhēn gained favor.
The remonstrating officials repeatedly spoke against this.
Bǐngzǐ,
Lǐ Déyù also remonstrated, saying:
"Guīzhēn
was a criminal during the reign of Jìngzōng.
See Volume 243, Bǎolì Year 2."
The Emperor said:
"When I have nothing to do in the palace, I discuss Dao with him to relieve my worries.
As for matters of governance,
I invariably ask you and other officials in attendance.
Not even a hundred Guīzhēn can mislead me."
Déyù said:
"Petty men, seeing where advantage lies,
rush towards it like moths to a flame.
I hear that for the past ten days,
Guīzhēn's gate
has been crowded with carriages and horses.
I beg Your Majesty to be deeply wary of this!"
15 Wùyín,
Wáng Qǐ, Left Grand Mentor, was appointed Concurrently Manager of Affairs,
and additionally Military Commissioner of Shānnán Xīdào.
Qǐ, being a civil official who had never held governing power,
was directly appointed to the rank of Minister-Commissioner,
an unprecedented occurrence.
He firmly declined.
After the mid-Táng period,
those who were Military Commissioners and Concurrently Manager of Affairs were called Minister-Commissioners.
*Bǐ*
(read *pí zhì fān*) means 'precedent'.
"There is no distinction between internal and external chancellors.
If I have any shortcomings,
you should send a flying memorial to inform me!"
16 Lǐ Déyù found that local government assistant officials were too numerous,
and memorialized to have Liǔ Zhòngyǐng, a Bureau Director of the Ministry of Personnel, reduce their number.
Sixth month,
Zhòngyǐng memorialized a reduction of one thousand two hundred and fourteen officials.
*Kǎoyì* says: *Xiàntì Jì* says:
"Two thousand and two officials were reduced."
The *New Biography* says:
"More than two thousand officials were dismissed."
The *Old Biography* of Liǔ Zhòngyǐng says:
"One thousand two hundred officials were reduced,"
which is followed here.
He was the son of Gōngchuò.
Liǔ Gōngchuò served under Xiàn and Mù,
held various regional governorships and mayoralties of the capital,
and had a reputation for achievements.
17 A eunuch exposed Qiú Shìliáng's past wickedness,
and several thousand weapons were found in his home.
An edict stripped him of his official rank and titles
and confiscated his family's property.
In the autumn of the 18th year,
in the seventh month,
on the *xīnmǎo* day,
the Emperor discussed with Lǐ Déyù about deploying Wáng Féng with troops to garrison Yìchéng.
The Emperor said:
“I hear that Féng is too strict in applying the law,
is that so?”
He replied:
“Your servant also once questioned him on this,
and Féng said: ‘With naked blades before us,
if the law is not strict,
who would be willing to advance!’”
The Emperor said:
“There is reason in his words,
you should summon him again and admonish him!”
Déyù then spoke of how Liú Zhěn should not be pardoned.
The Emperor said:
“Indeed.”
Déyù said:
“When Lǐ Huáiguāng had not yet been subdued,
locusts and drought plagued the capital,
rice cost a thousand cash per *dǒu*,
and the grand granary had no more than a few tens of days’ supply for the Son of Heaven and the six palaces.
Dézōng gathered all his officials,
and dispatched the palace eunuch Mǎ Qīnxù to inquire.
Lǐ Bì, the Left Sanqí Chángshì, took a paulownia leaf, crumpled and broke it,
and gave it to Qīnxù to present.
Dézōng summoned him and asked the reason,
and he replied: ‘The relationship between Your Majesty and Huáiguāng as sovereign and subject
is like this leaf, it cannot be mended!’
From this, Dézōng’s resolve was fixed.
After Huáiguāng was defeated,
he was then appointed prime minister,
and solely entrusted for several years.”
See the Record of Dézōng.
“He was also a truly extraordinary scholar!”
Lǐ Bì’s achievements as a prime minister
were notably praiseworthy.
Observing this, one can trust the accounts,
and those Tang people who slandered him were all mistaken.
The 19th year: The Emperor heard that singing girls in Yángzhōu were skilled at playing drinking games,
and ordered the Huáinán Supervising Military Commissioner to select seventeen of them and present them.
The Supervising Military Commissioner requested Dù Cōng, the Military Governor, to assist in the selection,
and also wished to choose beautiful women from good families,
train them, and then present them.
Cōng said:
“The Supervising Military Commissioner received the imperial decree personally,
I dare not interfere!”
The Supervising Military Commissioner pleaded repeatedly,
but he did not comply.
The Supervising Military Commissioner was enraged,
and fully reported the situation in a memorial.
The Emperor, upon reading the memorial, was silent.
His attendants requested that a joint decree be issued to the Military Governor to select together.
The Emperor said:
“To order a frontier region to select singing girls to enter the palace,
how could this be the act of a sagely Son of Heaven!
Dù Cōng did not yield to the Supervising Military Commissioner’s wishes,
displaying the conduct of a great minister,
truly the talent of a prime minister.
I am very ashamed!”
He immediately ordered the Supervising Military Commissioner not to select any more.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
Cōng was appointed *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The new table states
that Cōng became prime minister in the intercalary month, on the *rénxū* day.
Now, we follow the Veritable Records.
When Cōng made his intermediate obeisance,
which refers to entering to express thanks after receiving an appointment,
the Emperor said:
“You did not follow the Supervising Military Commissioner’s words,
I know you have a heart to bring about a sagely reign.
Now that I appoint you prime minister,
it is as if I have gained a Wèi Zhēng!”
Wǔzōng’s expectations for Dù Cōng were thus,
however, while Cōng was in the prime minister’s position,
his discussions and remonstrances
are not praised in history.
Punctuation by Zhōu Yīliáng, reviewed by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Compiled under imperial order by Sīmǎ Guāng.
Hòuxuétiāntái
Huìchāng fourth year
1. Intercalary month,
on the *rénxū* day,
Lǐ Shēn, Zhongshū Shìláng and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*, was appointed *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*
and concurrently Huáinán Military Governor.
2. Lǐ Déyù memorialized:
“Gāo Dí, an officer presenting reports from Zhènzhōu—
Regional governors dispatched their staff officers to present reports,
hence they were called 'officers presenting reports'—
believed that: ‘The rebels are fond of using a 'stealth troop' tactic,
secretly withdrawing troops from various places and concentrating them in one location.
The government forces often press them closely,
resulting in defeat;
after one or two months,
they again move troops stealthily to another place.
Government forces must understand this situation;
unless they are coming to attack cities or fortifications,
they should strictly avoid engaging them.
They will not linger for more than three days,
and must disperse back to their old garrisons.
If they repeatedly return empty-handed like this,
they will naturally lose morale.
Government forces should secretly dispatch spies to ascertain where troops are being withdrawn,
and strike them while they are undefended;
there will be no failure.’
Secondly,
‘Although the troops garrisoned in Zhèn and Wèi are numerous,
they ultimately cannot divide the rebel strength.
Why?
Their encampments do not move from their old positions,
and they penetrate deep once every three or two months,
burning and plundering before leaving.
The rebels merely hold fast to their city walls and fortifications,
and do not care about the common people outside the city.
It is advisable to order them to advance their camps to occupy critical points,
gradually pressing them.
If it remains as it is today,
the rebels will not consider it a threat at all.’
I hope an imperial edict will be issued to all generals,
making them aware of this!”
Gāo Wénduān, a trusted general of Liú Zhěn, surrendered,
stating that the rebels were short of food,
and ordered women to rub husks of grain and pound them for the army’s supply.
Déyù questioned Wénduān about strategies to defeat the rebels.
Wénduān believed:
“If the government forces directly attack Zézhōu now,
I fear many soldiers will be killed,
and the city will not be easy to take.
Zézhōu has about fifteen thousand troops,
and the rebels often divide more than half their forces,
lying in ambush in mountain valleys.
When they observe the government forces becoming exhausted from attacking the city,
they will gather from all sides to relieve it,
and the government forces will surely suffer defeat.
Now I request that the Chén–Xǔ army be ordered to cross the Gānhé river and establish a camp.
From the camp, a continuous double wall should be built,
encircling Zézhōu.
Daily, a large army should be deployed outside to repel relief forces.
When the rebels see the siege closing in,
they will surely come out for a great battle;
after their defeat,
the city can then be taken by capitalizing on the momentum.”
Déyù memorialized, requesting an imperial edict to show this to Wáng Zǎi.
Wénduān further said:
“Gùzhèn Zài’s four cliffs are extremely steep,
making it impossible to attack.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Cízhōu’s Wǔ’ān county has Gùzhèn Zhèn.
West of Wǔ’ān,
north to Liáozhōu, over three hundred *lǐ*.
Everyone drinks from the stream,
which is about a *lǐ* away
to the east of the stronghold.
It is advisable to order Wáng Féng to advance his troops and press upon it,
cutting off its water supply.
In no more than three days,
the rebels will surely abandon the stronghold and flee,
and the government forces can then pursue them.
Fifteen *lǐ* ahead is Qīnglóng Zài,
which also has four extremely steep cliffs,
and its water source is outside the stronghold,
so it can be taken by the same method.
Fifteen *lǐ* to its east is Qìnzhōu city.”
Qìnzhōu governed Qìnyuán County,
which was the territory of Hàn’s Shàngdǎng Gǔyuǎn County.
*Qìn*,
pronounced *qìn* (seventh tone).
Wénduān further said:
“Dūtóu Wáng Zhāo leads ten thousand troops guarding Míngzhōu.
Liú Zhěn has already exterminated Xuē Màoqīng’s clan,
and also executed Tán Cháoyì and his two brothers, the commanders of the Xíng–Míng relief forces.
Zhāo is naturally suspicious and fearful;
Zhěn sent an envoy to summon him,
but Zhāo refused to enter.
His soldiers are all clamoring,
so Zhāo will certainly not be used by Zhěn.
However, Zhāo and his soldiers’ families are all in Lùzhōu,
and the soldiers fear that if they surrender, they will be killed by the government forces,
so calling them will surely not make them come.
The only way is to convey a message to Zhāo,
to make him lead his troops into Lùzhōu to capture Zhěn.
If the mission is accomplished,
he should be promised appointment as a military governor of another circuit,
and also richly rewarded,
so that he might be willing to comply.”
Déyù memorialized, requesting an imperial edict for Hé Hóngjìng to secretly dispatch someone to convey this message.
Liú Zhěn was young and weak.
Yāyá Wáng Xié and Zháinèi Bīngmǎshǐ Lǐ Shìguì held sway,
specializing in amassing wealth.
The treasury was overflowing,
but the generals and soldiers who performed merits received no rewards.
Consequently, the people's hearts were alienated and resentful.
Liú Cóngjiàn’s wife, Madame Péi,
was a descendant of Péi Miǎn's collateral line.
Péi Miǎn had been a prime minister during the two reigns of Sùzōng and Dàizōng.
Her younger brother, Péi Wèn,
commanded troops in Shāndōng.
Liú Zhěn wanted to summon him to take charge of military and political affairs.
Shìguì feared that Wèn’s arrival would usurp his power
and expose his misdeeds.
So he said,
"The affairs in Shāndōng depend on the success of the fifth maternal uncle (Péi Wèn).
If we summon him,
we will lose the three prefectures."
So they stopped.
The three prefectures were
Xíng, Míng, and Cí.
Wáng Xié recommended Wáng Zhāo to be the Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ of Míng Prefecture.
Zhāo gained the support of the populace
but often disregarded the regulations of the Shǐfǔ (governor's headquarters).
His colleagues Gāo Yuánwǔ and Ān Yù reported that he had disloyal intentions.
Zhěn summoned him,
but Zhāo declined, saying,
"I have not yet accomplished any small merit since arriving in Míng Prefecture,
which truly fills me with shame and regret.
I beg to be allowed to stay for a few more months,
and then I will report to the governor's headquarters."
This was permitted.
Wáng Xié proposed taxing merchants,
and for each prefecture, a military commander (jūnjiàng) was dispatched to oversee it.
It was called "taxing merchants,"
but it was actually registering the assets of registered households.
Biānhù
means the same as biānmín (registered people).
Jiàng (commander),
pronounced as 'liàng'.
All assets were valued as bolts of silk,
and two-tenths were taken,
with the valuation often set high.
The people exhausted their disposable wealth and dried provisions to pay it.
Those who could not fulfill it
were all anxious and uneasy.
Fú cái (disposable wealth) refers to assets that are not fixed to land,
but are circulated and exchanged to generate profit.
Qiú (dried provisions),
pronounced as 'qǔ'.
Xiōng (anxious),
pronounced as 'xiōng'.
The military commander Liú Xī was particularly greedy and cruel.
Liú Cóngjiàn had dismissed him from service;
however, Xī heavily bribed Wáng Xié.
Xié, knowing that Xíng Prefecture had the most wealthy merchants,
appointed Xī to take charge there.
Péi Wèn's troops were called
"Yèfēi" (Night Flyers).
Many of them were sons of wealthy merchants.
When Xī arrived,
he detained all their fathers and elder brothers.
The soldiers complained to Wèn,
and Wèn pleaded on their behalf,
but Xī refused,
replying with insolent words.
Wèn was enraged.
He secretly plotted with his subordinates to kill Xī and return to the imperial court,
and he also informed the governor (cìshǐ) Cuī Gǔ.
Gǔ agreed.
On the day of Bǐngzǐ,
Gǔ and Wèn closed the city gates,
executed four prominent generals in the city,
and surrendered to Wáng Yuánkuí.
At that time, Gāo Yuánwǔ was at Dǎng Shān.
Hearing of this,
he also surrendered.
"Dǎng Shān"
should probably be written as
"Yáo Shān".
Earlier, the Shǐfǔ had given cloth to the soldiers of Míng Prefecture,
one bolt per person,
but soon a notice (tiē) arrived to deduct the winter allowance.
When the tax-collecting military commander arrived in Míng Prefecture,
Wáng Zhāo took advantage of the people's uneasiness
and said to the soldiers:
"The Liúhòu (acting military commissioner) is young;
the administration is not his own doing.
Now the granaries are full,
enough to last ten years.
How can we not distribute some
to comfort the toiling soldiers!
The Shǐfǔ's notice should not be used."
He then opened the warehouses,
giving each soldier one bolt of silk
and twelve shí (piculs) of grain.
The soldiers were greatly pleased.
Zhāo then closed the city and surrendered to Hé Hóngjìng.
Ān Yù was in Cí Prefecture.
Hearing that the two prefectures had surrendered,
he also surrendered to Hóngjìng.
Wèi Yuántán and other Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ of Yáo Shān surrendered to Wáng Yuánkuí,
but Yuánkuí, because they had not surrendered earlier,
executed them all.
In the eighth month,
on the day of Xīnmǎo,
Zhèn and Wèi reported that the three prefectures of Xíng, Míng, and Cí had surrendered.
The prime ministers entered to offer congratulations.
Lǐ Déyù said,
"The foundation of Zhāoyì is entirely in Shāndōng.
With the surrender of the three prefectures,
then Shàngdǎng will surely face changes within days."
The Emperor said,
"Guō Yì will certainly execute Liú Zhěn to redeem himself."
Déyù said,
"It is indeed as Your Sagely foresight predicted."
The Emperor said,
"What should be dealt with first now?"
Déyù requested that
Lú Hóngzhǐ be appointed Liúhòu of the three prefectures.
The Kǎoyì (examination of differences) states: Old records and biographies all write
"Hóngzhèng".
The Shílù (veritable records), Xīnjì (new annals), and biographies all write
"Hóngzhǐ",
which we follow here.
"Lest Zhèn and Wèi request to occupy the three prefectures,
making it difficult for the court to approve or disapprove."
The Emperor agreed.
An imperial edict ordered Lú Jūn, the Jìedùshǐ of Shānnán Dōngdào and concurrently of Zhāoyì, to proceed to Zhèn by post-horse.
The people of Lù (Lù Prefecture, i.e., Shàngdǎng) heard that the three prefectures had surrendered,
and were greatly alarmed.
Guō Yì and Wáng Xié plotted to kill Liú Zhěn to redeem themselves.
Zhěn's second cousin (zàicóngxiōng) Liú Kuāngzhōu, who was the Zhōngjūnshǐ and concurrently Yāyá (staff officer),
Zàicóngxiōng
means they shared the same great-grandfather.
Cóng (cousin),
pronounced as 'cóng'.
said to Zhěn,
"The Thirteenth Lord (Kuāngzhōu) is in the Yáyuan (staff office).
Liú Kuāngzhōu
is the thirteenth (in seniority).
Yáyuan
is where the Yāyá conducts affairs.
I fear that the Thirteenth Lord will be suspicious of me and that I will be punished,
and by this, Shāndōng will be lost.
If we can indeed get the Thirteenth Lord not to enter,
then the various generals will dare to speak openly,
and by gathering from the multitude,
we will surely find a good strategy."
Zhěn summoned Kuāngzhōu and explained this to him,
asking him to claim illness and not enter.
Kuāngzhōu angrily said,
"While I am in the Yáyuan,
the various generals dare not harbor any different plans.
If I leave the Yáyuan,
my family will surely be exterminated!"
Zhěn insisted, and Kuāngzhōu had no choice but to snap his fingers and depart.
Yí sent Dǒng Kěwǔ (who was close to Zhěn) to persuade Zhěn, saying:
"The rebellion in Shāndōng
was caused by your fifth maternal uncle.
Who in the city dares to guarantee their own safety?
What does the acting commander intend to do now?"
"Fifth maternal uncle"
refers to Péi Wèn.
Liú Zhěn was acting commander himself,
hence the address.
"There are still fifty thousand people in the city now,
we should just close the gates and hold fast."
Kěwǔ said:
"That is not a good plan.
It would be better for the acting commander to bind himself and return to court,
like Zhāng Yuání.
Yuání's story can be found in Volume 246, during Wénzōng's Kāichéng third year.
And let Guō Yí be the acting commander.
When you receive a military commission,
you can gradually escort your mother, wife, children, and all your wealth back to the Eastern Capital.
Wouldn't that be excellent?"
"Mother"
refers to Liú Cóngjiàn's wife, Madame Péi.
"How could Yí be willing to do that?"
Kěwǔ said:
"Kěwǔ has already sworn a solemn oath with him,
he will certainly not betray you."
Thereupon, he led Yí in.
After Zhěn and Yí had secretly agreed,
Zhěn reported it to his mother.
His mother said:
"Returning to court is indeed a good thing,
but I only regret it is too late.
I could not protect my own brother—
referring to Péi Wèn surrendering Xíngzhōu.
You must decide for yourself!"
Zhěn then came out of the gate in plain clothes,
and by his mother's command, appointed Yí as the Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ.
Wáng Xié had already ordered the generals to line up in the outer hall.
After Yí had bowed and thanked Zhěn,
'Yǐ'
means 'bì' (finished).
Zhěn was preparing his luggage in the inner hall.
Lǐ Shìguì heard of this,
and led several thousand soldiers from the rear courtyard to attack Yí.
Yí shouted at them, saying:
"Why don't you take your rewards yourselves,
instead of wanting to die with Lǐ Shìguì!"
The soldiers then retreated
and collectively killed Shìguì.
Yí replaced the generals and officials,
deployed the soldiers,
and everything was settled within one night.
The next day,
Dǒng Kěwǔ was sent to see Zhěn, saying:
"Please discuss public affairs."
Zhěn said:
"Why not speak of it!"
Kěwǔ said:
"I fear startling your mother."
Thereupon, he led Zhěn on foot out of the Ya Gate,
to the Northern Residence.
The Northern Residence
was the separate residence of the Zhāoyì Jìedùshǐ,
located north of the commander's residence,
hence called the Northern Residence.
During the height of the drinking,
he said:
"The matter today is to preserve the entire household of the Grand Preceptor.
Liú Wù was granted the title of Grand Preceptor.
Then the imperial court will surely show compassion."
Zhěn said:
"As you say,
that is my desire."
Kěwǔ then stepped forward and grasped his hand,
and Cuī Xuándù cut him down from behind.
Consequently, Zhěn's clan was arrested,
and from Kuāng Zhōu downwards, even infants in swaddling clothes were all killed.
'Qiǎng'
is pronounced 'jǔ liǎng'.
'Bǎo'
is pronounced 'bǎo'.
In the early Chángqìng era of Mùzōng,
Liú Wù first commanded Zhāoyì.
Three generations,
twenty-six years, and then it was destroyed.
They also killed twelve families closely befriended by Liú Cóngjiàn and his son: Zhāng Gǔ, Chén Yángtíng, Lǐ Zhòngjīng, Guō Tái, Wáng Yǔ, Hán Máozhāng, Máoshí, Wáng Wò, Jiǎ Xiáng, and others,
along with their sons, nephews, grandsons, and sons-in-law, leaving no one.
Zhòngjīng
was Xùn's elder brother;
Tái
was Xíngyú's son;
Yǔ
was Yá's cousin once removed;
Máozhāng and Máoshí
were Yuē's sons;
Wò
was Fán's son;
Xiáng
was Sù's son.
During the Gānlù Incident,
Zhòngjīng and others fled and returned to Cóngjiàn.
Cóngjiàn cared for them.
Lǐ Zhòngjīng and others barely escaped the disaster of Gānlù,
yet ultimately were slaughtered along with Liú Cóngjiàn's clan.
This was indeed Heaven gathering them to annihilate them.
Yí carried out executions daily,
until blood flowed like mud.
Then he put Zhěn's head in a box,
sent an envoy with a memorial and a letter,
and surrendered to Wáng Zǎi.
When the head passed through Zézhōu,
Liú Gōngzhí led his camp in loud wailing,
and also surrendered to Zǎi.
On the Yǐwèi day,
Zǎi reported the situation.
On the Bǐngshēn day,
the prime ministers entered to offer congratulations.
Lǐ Déyù memorialized:
"There is no need to re-establish acting commanders for Xíng, Míng, and Cí prefectures.
Just send Lú Hóngzhǐ to comfort the three prefectures and the two circuits of Chéngdé and Wèibó."
The emperor said:
"How should Guō Yí be dealt with?"
Déyù said:
"Liú Zhěn was merely a foolish boy.
Obstinately deploying troops and resisting orders,
it was all Yí who masterminded it for him.
And when his forces were isolated and strength exhausted,
he then betrayed Zhěn to seek reward.
If such a one is not executed,
how can evil be punished!
It is appropriate, while the imperial armies are still in the region,
to execute Yí and the others!"
The emperor said:
"My intention is also thus."
Thereupon, an edict was issued for Shí Xióng to lead seven thousand men into Lùzhōu,
to counter the rumors.
The rumors can be found in the previous volume, third year.
It was said that Yí and others could be pardoned,
but the emperor looked intently and did not respond.
Déyù said:
"This spring, Zé Lù is not yet pacified,
and Tàiyuán is troubled again.
If not for the emperor's firm resolution,
how could these two rebels be pacified!
Outside opinions suggest that if this were in a previous reign,
they would have been pardoned long ago."
The emperor said:
"You do not know that Wénzōng's heart and mind were not aligned with yours,
how can you comment on that!"
Lú Jūn was dismissed from Shānnán Dōngdào
and specially appointed as Zhāoyì Jìedùshǐ.
On the Wùxū day,
Liú Zhěn's head was sent to the capital.
An imperial edict stated:
"The five prefectures of Zhāoyì are granted a one-year exemption from taxes and levies.
The prefectures and counties through which the army passed will have their autumn taxes for this year remitted.
Since Liú Cóngjiàn, Zhāoyì has arbitrarily increased taxes and levies;
all of these are now to be exempted.
All registered local militia are to be disbanded and sent back to farming.
Generals and soldiers of all circuits who have performed meritorious service
shall be granted additional rewards according to their rank."
After Guō Yí had killed Liú Zhěn,
he daily awaited his military commission;
but when he heard no news for a long time,
he said:
"I must be transferred to another command."
Thereupon, he reviewed his horses and saddlery,
and prepared his travel gear.
When he heard that Shí Xióng was arriving,
he was terrified and lost color.
When Xióng arrived,
Yí and the others completed their visit and congratulations.
The imperial envoy Zhāng Zhòngqīng said:
"Guō Dūzhī's official appointment will arrive tomorrow;
Guō Yí was the Zhāoyì Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ,
hence the title.
Come to the evening assembly to receive it!"
'Zhū Gāobān'
refers to the various generals.
Generally, regional commands and prefectures and counties had both morning and evening assemblies,
where all generals, officers, and soldiers gathered.
The Hézhōng soldiers
were those commanded by Shí Xióng who had entered Lùzhōu.
'Huán'
is pronounced like 'huàn'.
When Yí and others arrived,
their names were called, and they were led in.
All the generals who were unruly and resisted the imperial army
were seized and sent to the capital.
Hé Hóngjìng was promoted to Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
On the Dīngwèi day,
an edict ordered the exhumation of Liú Cóngjiàn's corpse,
to be exposed in the Lùzhōu marketplace for three days.
Shí Xióng took his corpse, placed it on the polo field, and hacked it to pieces.
On the day of Wùshēn,
Lí Dédù was promoted to Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant) and Duke of Zhàoguó.
Lí Dédù firmly declined.
The Emperor said:
"My only regret is not having enough official rewards for you!
If you were truly undeserving,
I would certainly not give it to you."
Initially,
Lí Dédù had observed that
"Since Hán Quányì's time,
when Dézōng dispatched Hán Quányì to quell Wú Shǎochéng,
and he was defeated at the Yīnshǔi.
There were three main shortcomings: Firstly,
imperial edicts were sent to the front lines,
three or four times a day,
and the chief ministers were often not privy to them.
Secondly,
the army supervisors each commanded military affairs according to their own opinions,
preventing the generals from having sole discretion over advances and retreats.
Thirdly,
each army had eunuchs acting as supervisors,
who selected several hundred of the army's bravest and most skilled as their personal guard (yáyì).
Those who fought in formation
were all timid and weak soldiers;
in every battle,
the supervisor had his own signal flag –
a signal flag
was a separate banner,
which the army would watch to determine their advances and retreats.
(Jiān,
pronounced Gǔ Hán Fān.
Shǐ,
pronounced Shū Lì Fān.)
With their personal guards protecting them,
if they saw the army falter slightly,
they would immediately hoist their flag and be the first to flee,
causing the formation to collapse."
Lí Dédù then discussed this with the Privy Councilors Yáng Qīnyì and Liú Xíngshēn,
and they agreed to issue an edict preventing supervisors from interfering in military administration,
allowing each supervisor to take ten men for every thousand soldiers as a personal guard,
who would be rewarded according to regulations for their achievements.
Both Privy Councilors agreed,
and reported it to the Emperor for implementation.
From the defense against the Huíhú until the demobilization in Zélù,
this system was maintained.
Unless an imperial edict originated from the Zhōngshū (Chancellery),
no other edicts were issued from within (the palace).
With commands thus simplified,
generals could employ their strategies,
hence they achieved success wherever they went.
The historian recounts Lí Dédù's actions,
to show why the mid-Táng period failed,
and why Wǔzōng succeeded.
Since the start of the military campaigns,
when the three prefectures of Hébĕi sent envoys to the capital,
Lí Dédù always directly instructed them, saying:
"Although the military strength of Hèshuò is formidable,
it cannot stand on its own;
it must rely on the court's official titles and authority to maintain the morale of the army.
Go tell your master:
Instead of having your generals invite the envoys bearing imperial decrees of appeasement to demand official titles,
how about you exert yourselves with loyalty and righteousness,
achieve merits and accomplishments,
gain the trust of an enlightened ruler,
so that favors emanate from the court?
Would that not be more honorable!
Furthermore, to speak of what my own eyes and ears have witnessed:
Lí Zǎiyì in Yōuzhōu,
served the state with loyalty to pacify Cāngjǐng;
even when he was expelled by the army,
he did not fail to become a Jìdùshǐ,
later garrisoning Tàiyuán,
and rising to the position of chief minister.
Yáng Zhìchéng sent a general to intercept an imperial envoy's horse to demand an official position;
when he was expelled by the army,
the court ultimately did not pardon his crime.
(Both incidents are recorded in previous annals.)
Lí Dédù again reported his words to the Emperor,
and the Emperor said:
"Indeed, it should be explained to them clearly like this."
Consequently, the three prefectures dared not harbor dissenting ambitions.
3 In the ninth month,
an imperial edict assigned Zézhōu to the jurisdiction of the Héyáng Jìdù.
This implemented Lí Dédù's proposal from three years prior.
4 On the day of Dīngsì,
Lú Jūn entered Lùzhōu.
Lú Jūn was naturally magnanimous and loved his people.
Before Liú Zhěn was pacified,
Lú Jūn had already assumed the title of Zhāoyì Jìdù,
(the details are in the previous volume, third year).
When fighting the people of Lù,
he often praised Lú Jūn's virtues in front of the formations.
Upon arriving at his post,
and entering the Tiānjǐng Pass,
any Zhāoyì stragglers who returned to him
were all treated generously by Lú Jūn,
and popular sentiment was greatly appeased,
whereupon Zhāoyì became secure.
Liú Zhěn's generals Guō Yì, Wáng Xié, Liú Gōngzhí, Ān Quánqìng, Lí Déshù, Lí Zuǒyáo, Liú Wǔdé, Dǒng Kěwǔ, and others arrived in the capital,
and were all executed.
Your subject Guāng says: Dǒng Zhòngzhì in Huáixī,
(the incident is recorded in the Xìanzōng Annals).
Wú Yuánjì and Liú Zhěn,
were merely puppets in the hands of performers.
These two individuals initially incited others to rebellion,
and ultimately betrayed their master for profit;
their death was indeed insufficient for their crimes.
However, Xìanzōng used them previously,
and Wǔzōng executed them later;
your foolish subject believes both erred.
Why so?
Rewarding treachery
is not righteous;
killing those who surrender
is not trustworthy.
If righteousness and trustworthiness are lost,
how can one govern the state!
In the past, Hàn Guāngwǔ treated Wáng Láng and Liú Pénzǐ only to the extent of not killing them,
knowing that they would not surrender unless their strength was exhausted.
Were Fán Chóng, Xú Xuān, Wáng Yuán, Niú Hán, and their ilk
not people who aided rebellion?
Yet Guāngwǔ did not kill them;
(all these incidents are recorded in the Guāngwǔ Annals).
For they could not be executed again.
If, after being pardoned, they were to escape and rebel again,
then their death would certainly be beyond reproach!
As for people like Yì and the others,
pardoning them from death and exiling them to a distant land,
never to return in their lifetime,
would have been acceptable;
killing them
was wrong!
5 Wáng Yǔ and Jiǎ Xiáng and others had already been killed by Yì.
Lí Dédù again issued an edict stating that
"The rebel traitors Wáng Yá and Jiǎ Sù and their descendants have already been executed in Zhāoyì,
announced to the whole country,"
which discerning people criticized.
Wáng Yá and Jiǎ Sù
were not rebels.
Even if they were attached to the wrong people,
harming their families,
and causing misfortune to their state,
their crime would not amount to utter annihilation without any surviving offspring.
Lí Dédù clearly fabricated their guilt,
as if truly using Guō Yì to bring about divine punishment;
it is fitting that discerning people criticized this.
Furthermore, he ordered the surrendered generals of Zhāoyì, Lí Pī, Gāo Wénduān, Wáng Zhāo, and others, to list the Zhāoyì officers and soldiers who were complicit with Liú Zhěn,
and all were executed,
with many dying.
Lú Jūn suspected injustice and excessive killings,
and memorialized requesting leniency,
but was not heeded.
Among the cities subordinate to Zhāoyì, some had previously shown disrespect to Wáng Yuánkuí;
Wáng Yuánkuí searched for and found over twenty such people,
and executed them;
the remaining populace feared,
and again closed their city gates to defend themselves.
On the day of Wùchén,
Lí Dédù and others memorialized:
"Now that the rebel scourge is pacified,
and all have become the state's cities and towns,
how can Wáng Yuánkuí be allowed to exhaust his troops in attacking them!
We request that an imperial envoy be dispatched
to bestow an imperial edict upon the officers and soldiers within the city,
to pacify and reassure them,
and moreover, issue an edict for Wáng Yuánkuí to withdraw his troops to his garrison,
and also order Lú Jūn to send his own envoy to pacify them."
This was followed.
On the day of Yǐhài,
Lí Dédù and others requested the Emperor to accept an honorific title,
and further stated:
"Since ancient times, emperors,
upon achieving great accomplishments, must announce them to Heaven and Earth;
moreover,
Xuānyì Tàihòu is to be enshrined in the ancestral temple."
(Upon ascending the throne, the Emperor posthumously honored his mother, Lady Wéi, as Xuānyì Tàihòu.)
The Emperor was startled and said:
"The rituals for the altars and ancestral temples
indeed should be performed urgently,
but as for an honorific title,
I dare not accept it!"
After five memorials,
he finally consented.
6 Lí Dédù memorialized:
"According to the report from the Yōuzhōu official,
it is known through reconnaissance that there is disunity within the Huíhú,
the Khagan wishes to go to Ānxī,
but his tribesmen say that their relatives are all in Táng,
so it would be better to return to Táng;
moreover, they have already fallen out with the Shìwéi,
so it is estimated that they will surrender soon,
or perhaps destroy each other.
We request that a knowledgeable imperial envoy be sent
(meaning: to send a suitable and knowledgeable person as an envoy).
To inform them that Zhèn and Wèi have pacified Zhāoyì,
and only the Huíhú remain unvanquished,
and Zhòngwǔ still holds the title of Northern Pacification Commissioner,
so he should think early about achieving merits."
7. Lǐ Déyù resented the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù) and Resident Minister of the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū Liúshǒu), Niú Sēngrú, and the Prefect of Húzhōu (Húzhōu Cìshǐ), Lǐ Zōngmǐn.
He said to the Emperor:
"Liú Cóngjiàn occupied Shàngdǎng for ten years.
During the Tàihé period, he came to court.
Sēngrú and Zōngmǐn were in power,
but did not keep him.
They promoted him to chancellor and let him go.
This incident can be found in Volume 244, Wénzōng, Tàihé 7th year.
It took the strength of the entire realm to finally defeat him,
which is all the fault of these two men."
Déyù also sent people to Lùzhōu to search for correspondence between Sēngrú, Zōngmǐn, and Cóngjiàn.
Finding nothing,
he then ordered the Clerk (Kǒngmù Guān), Zhèng Qìng, to claim that Cóngjiàn burned all letters from Sēngrú and Zōngmǐn as soon as he received them.
An imperial edict ordered Qìng to be arrested and interrogated by the Censorate (Yùshǐ Tái).
The Grand Censor (Zhōngchéng), Lǐ Huí, and the Director of Miscellaneous Affairs (Zhīzá), Zhèng Yà, believed it to be true.
According to Táng regulations, there were six Supervising Censors (Shìyùshǐ) in the Censorate.
The one with the longest tenure served as the Director of Miscellaneous Affairs (Zhīzá Shì),
known as Zázhuān.
When the report of Zhěn's defeat arrived,
Sēngrú sighed deeply in regret.
This was to please Déyù and falsely accuse Sēngrú.
The Emperor was furious,
and appointed Sēngrú as Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shàobǎo) and Resident in the Eastern Capital (Fēnsī).
Zōngmǐn was appointed Prefect of Zhāngzhōu (Zhāngzhōu Cìshǐ).
On Wùzǐ day,
Sēngrú was demoted again to Prefect of Tīngzhōu (Tīngzhōu Cìshǐ),
and Zōngmǐn to Chief Administrator of Zhāngzhōu (Zhāngzhōu Zhǎngshǐ).
In the 1st year of Chuígǒng (685 CE),
Zhāngzhōu was established from the southwestern border of Fúzhōu,
named after the Zhāng River to its south.
According to old records: it is 7,300 lǐ southeast of the capital.
8. The Emperor went to Hù for a hunt.
9. In the eleventh month,
Niú Sēngrú was again demoted to Chief Administrator of Xúnzhōu (Xúnzhōu Zhǎngshǐ).
Zōng
mǐn was banished permanently to Fēngzhōu.
10. In the twelfth month,
Wáng Zǎi, Military Governor of Zhōngwǔ (Zhōngwǔ Jiédùshǐ), was appointed Military Governor of Hédōng (Hédōng Jiédùshǐ).
Shí Xióng, Military Governor of Hézhōng (Hézhōng Jiédùshǐ), was appointed Military Governor of Héyáng (Héyáng Jiédùshǐ).
The "Kǎoyì" says: The "Shílù" states:
"In the ninth month,
Lú Jūn reported that
on the 17th day,
Shí Xióng's army returned to Mèngzhōu."
However, Xióng was not yet Military Governor of Héyáng at that time,
so the "Shílù" is incorrect.
11. The Emperor went to Yúnyáng for a hunt.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on Jǐyǒu day, the new moon,
the assembled officials offered the honorific title Rénshèng Wénwǔ Zhāngtiān Chénggōng Shéndé Míngdào Dàxiào Huángdì.
The honorific title initially did not include
the character "Dào."
An imperial decree then ordered it to be added.
At this time, the Emperor deeply trusted the Daoist priest Zhào Guīzhēn and others.
He even personally received Daoist registers.
Therefore, a decree ordered the assembled officials to add
the character "Dào"
to the honorific title.
But they did not know that what they called "Dào"
was not what we call "Dào."
On Gēngxū day,
the Emperor visited the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào).
On Xīnhài day,
he offered sacrifices to Hào Tiān Shàngdì and
granted a general amnesty.
2. The Wàngxiān Tái was built in the southern suburbs.
3. On Gēngshēn day,
Empress Dowager Yì'ān, née Wáng, passed away.
In the 5th year of Tàihé,
the chancellors proposed
that the titles of Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihuáng Tàihòu) and Empress Dowager Bǎolì were not distinct.
Previous imperial edicts dared not explicitly state them,
referring to them all by their palaces.
Now, Empress Dowager Bǎolì resides in the Yì'ān Palace,
so it is appropriate to call her Empress Dowager Yì'ān.
An edict approved this.
4. Lú Hóngxuān, Supervisor of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān), was appointed Military Governor of Yìwǔ (Yìwǔ Jiédùshǐ).
Hóngxuān was naturally magnanimous and not easily offended.
His administration was simple and straightforward,
which suited his subordinates.
According to the laws of Héběi,
those who conversed in private in the army were beheaded.
When Hóngxuān arrived,
he abolished this law.
The various commanders in Héběi feared that their subordinates would conspire against them,
so they enforced strict laws against private conversations in the army,
to control them with rigidity.
Lú Hóngxuān, upon arriving in Zhōngshān,
abolished this law.
West of Fēihú,
the cost of transporting grain exceeded the price of the grain itself.
Hóngxuān sent officials to guard it.
Coincidentally, there was a spring drought.
Hóngxuān ordered the military and civilians to go and collect it as they wished.
All the grain entered the territory,
with an agreement to repay it when the autumn harvest ripened.
At that time, Chéngdé and Wèibó both suffered from famine,
but only the region of Yìdìng was unaffected.
5. Lǐ Shēn, Military Governor of Huáinán (Huáinán Jiédùshǐ), impeached Wú Xiāng, Magistrate of Jiāngdū, for embezzling "journey ration money."
The "Xīnshū Bǎiguān Zhì" states: The Director of Guests (Zhǔkè Lángzhōng)
manages foreign envoys.
Envoys returning from the southeast are given "journey rations for sea travel."
Envoys returning from the northwest are given "journey rations for desert crossing."
As for officials on long public journeys,
they must be provided with rations calculated by distance.
However, since rations are heavy and cannot be transported far,
their value is estimated in money.
Hence, there is "journey ration money."
The estimated value of his provisions was considered stolen goods,
a crime punishable by death.
Xiāng was
the nephew of Wú Wǔlíng. (Wú Wǔlíng is mentioned in Volume 239, Xiànzōng, Yuánhé 10th year.)
Many commentators said he was wronged,
and remonstrating officials requested a review.
An edict dispatched Supervising Censors (Jiānchá Yùshǐ) Cuī Yuánzǎo and Lǐ Chóu to review it.
They returned, saying:
"Xiāng did indeed embezzle journey ration money.
Yán Yuè was originally from Qúzhōu,
and had served as a staff officer in Qīngzhōu.
His wife was also from a gentry family,
which differed from the previous case."
Déyù considered that there was no room for modification (no "withholding or giving"),
and in the second month,
demoted Yuánzǎo to Judicial Administrator of Duānzhōu (Duānzhōu Sīhù),
and Chóu to Judicial Administrator of Tīngzhōu (Tīngzhōu Sīhù).
There was no further investigation,
nor was it handed over to the judicial authorities for detailed judgment.
Instead, following Shēn's report,
Xiāng was sentenced to death.
Remonstrance Grandees (Jiànyì Dàfū) Liǔ Zhòngyǐng and Jìng Huì both submitted memorials arguing against it,
but they were not accepted.
Chóu was from
Jìnjiāng.
Sòng Bái said: Quánzhōu governs Jìnjiāng County.
In the Jìn Dynasty, it was Jìn'ān County.
The Suí Dynasty abolished the commandery and made it a county.
He was Xīn's younger brother.
Jìng Xīn is mentioned in the previous volume, 3rd year.
6. Lǐ Déyù appointed Liǔ Zhòngyǐng as Mayor of Jīngzhào (Jīngzhào Yǐn).
Zhòngyǐng, who was always on good terms with Niú Sēngrú,
thanked Déyù, saying:
"I did not expect such favor and praise from the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi)!
To repay your great kindness,
how could I not follow the example of Lord Qízhāng's household?"
Déyù did not consider this an offense.
During the Suí Dynasty, Niú Hóng was enfeoffed as Lord Qízhāng (Qízhāng Gōng).
Niú Sēngrú was probably his descendant,
which is why people at the time also called him Lord Qízhāng.
Sòng Bái said: Qízhāng County belonged to Bāzhōu.
It was originally the land of Jiāmēng County in the Hàn Dynasty.
The Liáng Dynasty established Qízhāng County,
named after Mount Qízhāng, eight lǐ east of the county.
7. In summer,
the fourth month,
on Rén Yín day,
Lǐ Shì, Surveillance Commissioner of Shǎn and Guó (Shǎn Guó Guānchásǐ), was appointed envoy to confer a title upon the Qīrjí (黠戛斯) Khagan.
8. In the fifth month,
on Rén Xū day,
Empress Gōngxī was buried outside the Bǎichéng of Guānglíng.
Empress Dowager Yì'ān was posthumously titled Gōngxī.
As the Empress was not the consort of Mùzōng,
she was buried beside Guānglíng but not interred together.
9. Dù Cóng, Assistant Minister of the Left (Ménxià Shìláng) and Grand Chancellor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì), was dismissed and made Executive Assistant (Yòu Púshè).
Cuī Xuàn, Assistant Minister of the Right (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Chancellor, was dismissed and made Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū).
On Yǐchǒu day,
Lǐ Huí, Assistant Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shìláng), was appointed Assistant Minister of the Right and Grand Chancellor,
retaining his post as Director of Revenue (Pàn Hùbù).
10. The Ministry of Rites (Cíbù) reported a survey of 4,600 temples,
40,000 hermitages (lánruò),
and 260,500 monks and nuns across the empire.
The Ministry of Rites was in charge of monks and nuns,
so they were ordered to conduct the survey.
"Ruò" (若)
is pronounced "rén zhě fān."
The "Shìshì Yàolǎn" states: "Lánruò"
is the Sanskrit word "āraṇya,"
which in Táng means "absence of contention."
The "Sìfēnlǜ" says it is "a quiet, empty place."
The "Zhìdùjīng" says it is "a place of detachment."
The "Dàbēijīng" says it is "free from all anger."
11. An imperial edict conferred upon the Qīrjí Khagan the title Zōngyīng Wǔchéng Míng Kèhán.
12. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Bǐngwǔ day, the new moon,
there was a solar eclipse.
13 Shàng (武宗) abhorred the monks and nuns for wasting and damaging the empire,
desiring to eliminate them.
The Daoist priest Zhào Guīzhēn and others further encouraged him.
So, he first destroyed the zhāotí and lánruò in the mountains and wilds.
