there was a solar eclipse.
Emperor Xuānzōng Yuánshèng Zhìmíng Chéngwǔ Xiànwén Ruìzhì Zhāngrén Shéncōng Yìdào Dàxiào,
whose personal name was Yí,
changed his name to Chén upon his accession.
He was the 12th son of Xiànzōng.
According to the *Tōngjiàn*'s records of Tang emperors’ titles,
from Xuánzōng onwards,
the titles inscribed in the tomb epitaphs and imperial decrees are considered correct.
Xuānzōng’s posthumous title was Shèngwǔ Xiànwén Xiàohuángdì.
The title Yuánshèng Zhìmíng Chéngwǔ Xiànwén Ruìzhì Zhāngrén Shéncōng Yìdào Dàxiào
was a posthumous honorific bestowed in the 13th year of Xiántōng.
The first year of Dàzhōng
(Year *dìngmǎo*, 847)
In spring,
the first month,
on *jiǎyín*,
the Emperor offered sacrifices at the Round Mound,
granted a general amnesty,
and changed the era name.
In the second month,
Zhāng Zhòngwǔ,
Military Governor of Lúlóng, was granted the title of Concurrent Chancellor (*Tóng Píngzhāngshì*),
in recognition of his victory over the Huíhú.
Was Shí Xióng not also one who defeated the Huíhú?
On *guǐwèi*,
due to drought, the Emperor
reduced his meals, stopped musical performances,
released palace women,
set free his hawks and falcons,
ceased construction projects,
and ordered Lú Shāng, Assistant Minister of the Central Secretariat and Concurrent Chancellor, and Fēng Áo, Censor-in-chief, to review and resolve the cases of prisoners in the capital.
Mà Zhí, Minister of the Grand Court of Judicial Review, memorialized, stating:
“Lú Shāng and others are eager to grant leniency,
exempting all who deserve the death penalty from execution.
Those officials who committed embezzlement or intentional murder,
who are ordinarily not pardoned in general amnesties,
are now pardoned due to this review,
which will leave corrupt officials without deterrence or fear,
and cause the deceased to harbor unredressed grievances,
which I fear is not the way to dispel drought and bring about harmony.
In ancient times, when Zhōu suffered famine,
conquering Yīn led to a bountiful year.
The words of Níng Zhuāngzǐ in the *Zuǒzhuàn*
were spoken to initiate the punitive expedition against Xíng.
Punishing Xíng brought rain.
Therefore, executing criminals and villains
aligns with Heaven’s will,
and redressing grievances and resolving stagnation
fulfills the sage’s heart.
I request a further review and decision.”
An imperial edict ordered officials of the Fifth Rank and above from the Two Ministries to discuss it.
Officials of the Fifth Rank and above from the Two Ministries
refers to those from the Remonstrance Official and Secretariat Drafter upwards.
At first,
when Lǐ Déyù was in power,
he appointed Bái Mǐnzhōng as a Hanlin Academician.
(See Volume 246, second year of Huìchāng.)
When Déyù lost power,
Mǐnzhōng, seizing on the Emperor’s anger,
exerted all his efforts to oppose him,
instructing his partisan Lǐ Xián to accuse Déyù of crimes.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* records:
“Bái Mǐnzhōng and Línghú Táo,
during the Huìchāng era,
were not suspected by Déyù of being part of a faction and were placed in high office.
However, when Déyù lost power,
they clapped their hands and pointed fingers,
conspiring to oust him.
Cuī Xuàn also resented Déyù for being dismissed from the chancellorship at the end of Huìchāng.
In the early Dàzhōng era,
Mǐnzhōng again recommended Xuàn for a position in the Central Secretariat,
and then ordered his partisan Lǐ Xián to accuse Déyù of secret misdeeds during his time as Chancellor,
dismissing Déyù from his post as Left-behind Official and
appointing him as Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince with concurrent duties in the Eastern Capital.”
According to old biographies,
Táo entered as an Imperial Edict Compiler from the post of Prefect of Húzhōu
in the second year of Dàzhōng,
and Xuàn entered as Chancellor from the Military Governor of Hézhōng
in the third year.
This was not the case at this time. The *Shílù* is mistaken.
Now, according to the *Tōngjiàn*’s record of Línghú Táo as Imperial Edict Compiler,
it was between the sixth and seventh months of this year.
The title Prefect of Húzhōu had
the character
“former.”
(with concurrent duties in the Eastern Capital).
Zhāng Lù, Left Remonstrance Official, and others memorialized, saying:
“Your Majesty, due to the drought, is reviewing prisoners,
fearing there may be unredressed grievances.
However, the death penalties now pardoned
have no grievances to be redressed.
I fear that wicked and opportunistic individuals will constantly wish for floods and droughts to occur.
It is advisable to follow what Mà Zhí proposed.”
An imperial edict approved this,
and all were judged according to the law.
Zhí was appointed Assistant Minister of Justice
and Commissioner of Salt and Iron Monopolies.
Zhí was well-known for his literary talent and administrative skills at the time,
but Lǐ Déyù did not value him.
When Bái Mǐnzhōng took power,
all those whom Déyù had disdained
were promoted out of sequence.
Lú Shāng was appointed Military Governor of Wǔchāng.
Cuī Yuánshì, Minister of Justice and Acting Commissioner of Finance, was appointed Assistant Minister of the Chancellery;
Wéi Cóng, Hanlin Academician and Assistant Minister of Revenue, was appointed Assistant Minister of the Central Secretariat,
both concurrently holding the title of Chancellor.
5 The intercalary month,
an imperial edict stated:
"For the temples abolished in the fifth year of Huìchāng,
if there are monks who can repair them,
they are permitted to reside in them themselves,
and officials must not prohibit it."
At this time, the emperor and the prime minister were intent on reversing the policies of Huìchāng,
so the abuses of monks and nuns all returned to their former state.
Observing what is written in the Tōngjiàn,
the rights and wrongs of Huìchāng and Dàzhōng can be seen.
6 On the day Jǐyǒu,
Empress Dowager Jìqìng, of the Xiāo clan, passed away.
Empress Xiāo
was the mother of Wénzōng.
During Wǔzōng's reign, she moved to reside in the Jìqìng Diàn,
hence she was referred to by that name.
7 In the fifth month,
Zhāng Zhòngwǔ, the Jìedùshǐ of Yōuzhōu, greatly defeated the Xī tribes.
8 Lùn Kǒngrè of Tubó, taking advantage of Wǔzōng's mourning,
enticed the Dǎngxiàng and the remnants of the Huíhú to raid Héxī.
An imperial edict ordered Wáng Zǎi, the Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng, to lead the armies of Dàiběi to attack them.
The armies of Dàiběi
refers to the armies north of the Xínglǐng mountains.
They crossed the Yellow River from Línzhōu,
fought Kǒngrè at Yánzhōu,
defeated, and put him to flight.
9 In the sixth month,
Lǐ Yè, the Hónglú Qīng, was appointed as an envoy to confer the title of Yīngwǔ Chéngmíng Kèhán on the Xiájiāsī.
10 The Emperor said to Bái Mǐnzhōng:
"When I followed Xìanzōng's funeral procession in the past,
we encountered wind and rain on the road,
and all the officials and the imperial concubines scattered and fled.
Only the Shānlíngshǐ, who was tall and had a long beard,
clung to the imperial carriage and did not leave.
Who was he?"
He replied:
"Lìnghú Chǔ."
The Emperor said:
"Does he have a son?"
He replied:
"His eldest son, Xù, is currently the Cìshǐ of Suízhōu."
The Emperor said:
"Is he capable of being a prime minister?"
He replied:
"Xù suffered from rheumatism in his youth.
His second son, Táo,
formerly the Cìshǐ of Húzhōu,
possesses talent and ability."
The Emperor immediately promoted him to Kǎogōng Lángzhōng and Zhī Zhìgào.
When Táo entered to express his gratitude,
the Emperor asked him about the events of Yuánhé,
and Táo replied in great detail.
The Emperor was pleased,
and thus conceived the intention of giving him an important position.
This set the stage for Lìnghú Táo's rise to power.
11 In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the day Bǐngshēn,
Lǐ Huí, the Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì and concurrently Jìedùshǐ of Xīchuān.
12 The Empress Zhēnxìan was buried beside the Guānglíng mausoleum.
Empress Dowager Jìqìng Xiāo
was posthumously honored as Zhēnxìan.
13 The Emperor fostered harmony among his brothers,
building the Yōnghé Diàn within the Shíliù Zhái.
According to Huìyào,
in this year, an imperial edict stated
that the Qīnqīn Lóu was named Yōnghé Diàn,
and seven hundred rooms of separate buildings and corridors were constructed.
Sòng Bái said: The Yōnghé Diàn was in the Mùqīn Yuàn.
Banquets were held,
music was played,
and polo was enjoyed to the fullest.
When any of the princes fell ill,
the Emperor often personally visited their bedchambers to inquire after them,
with worry visible on his face.
14 The Tujue plundered grain shipments and travelling merchants.
Shǐ Xìanzhōng, the Jìedùshǐ of Zhènwǔ, attacked and defeated them.
The Kǎoyì states: It is observed that the Tujue had perished long ago,
but there might still have been remnants living north of Zhènwǔ.
I believe these Tujue remnants were those who had sought refuge within the frontier and submitted.
15 In the ninth month,
on the day Dīngmǎo,
Zhèng Guāng, the Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Pínglú.
Guāng,
a native of Rùnzhōu,
was the empress dowager's brother.
16 On the day Yǐyǒu,
Wú Rǔnà, formerly the Wèi of Yǒngníng,
pleaded that his brother Xiāng's crime did not warrant death,
saying, "Lǐ Shēn and Lǐ Déyù colluded,
deceived Wǔzōng,
and unjustly killed my brother.
I request that Cuī Yuánzǎo, Sīhù of Jiāngzhōu, and others be summoned to confront and clarify."
Wú Xiāng's death is mentioned in the previous volume, under Wǔzōng, fifth year of Huìchāng.
On the day Dīnghài,
an imperial edict ordered the Yùshǐ Tái to thoroughly investigate and report the truth.
"Thoroughly investigate"
means to exhaustively probe the facts.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Gēngxū,
the Yùshǐ Tái reported
that, based on the injustice of Wú Xiāng as listed by Cuī Yuánzǎo,
it was as Wú Rǔnà had stated.
On the day Wùwǔ,
Lǐ Déyù, the Tàizǐ Shàobǎo and Fēnsī, was demoted to Cháozhōu Sīmǎ.
17 The Lìbù reported
that 383 official positions were re-added to the prefectures and counties that had been reduced in the fourth year of Huìchāng.
1 In the first month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ,
the ministers presented the honorific title "Shèngjìng Wénsī Héwǔ Guāngxiào Huángdì";
a general amnesty was granted to the empire.
2 Initially,
when Lǐ Déyù was in power,
someone recommended Dīng Róulì as being upright and honest, suitable for an admonishing official,
but Déyù could not employ him.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Róulì became the Yòu Bǔquē;
when Déyù was demoted to Cháozhōu,
Róulì submitted a memorial pleading his innocence.
On the day Bǐngyín,
he was demoted to Nányáng Wèi for flattery and attachment.
History records that Dīng Róulì possessed a sense of right and wrong.
Nányáng County
was the land of Wǎn County, where Nányáng Commandery of the Hàn dynasty was governed.
During the Suí dynasty, it was renamed Nányáng County,
and in the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Dèngzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is 120 lǐ northeast of the prefecture.
3 Lǐ Huí, the Jìedùshǐ of Xīchuān, and Zhèng Yà, the Guìguǎn Guānchásǐ, were implicated for previously failing to uphold justice in Wú Xiāng's case.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
Huí was demoted to Húnán Guānchásǐ,
Yà was demoted to Xúnzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Lǐ Shēn's official appointments for three terms were posthumously revoked.
Lǐ Shēn had already died,
hence the posthumous revocation.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
he was demoted to Duānzhōu Cìshǐ.
4 Yèniǎn Kèhán of the Huíhú relied on Xī King Shíshèláng for sustenance;
but when Zhāng Zhòngwǔ greatly defeated the Xī forces,
as seen in the fifth month of the previous year,
their numbers dwindled daily.
By this time,
those remaining, from nobles downwards, numbered fewer than five hundred,
and they relied on the Shìwéi.
Envoys entered to offer congratulations for the New Year.
These were Huíhú envoys.
Zhāng Zhòngwǔ sent an envoy to retrieve Yèniǎn and others;
when Yèniǎn heard of this,
he fled westward at night with his wife Gěluò, son Tèlèsīdú, and nine other horsemen.
The remaining followers pursued them but could not catch them,
and they wept greatly together.
The Shìwéi divided the remaining Huíhú into seven parts.
Seven clans jointly divided them.
The Shìwéi had the Lǐngxībù, Shānběibù, Huángtóubù, Rúzhěbù, Póguōbù, Nèběibù, and Luòdānbù,
in total seven clans,
all residing northeast of Liǔchéng,
the closest being three thousand lǐ away, the farthest over six thousand lǐ.
The Xiájiāsī sent their prime minister Ābō to lead seventy thousand Hú soldiers to capture the Huíhú,
greatly defeating the Shìwéi,
and gathering all the remaining Huíhú to return north of the desert.
There were still a few tents
that stealthily hid in the mountains and forests,
raiding other Hú tribes;
another tribe, the Pánglè,
previously in Ānxī,
also declared themselves Kèhán,
residing in Gānzhōu,
controlling the various cities west of the desert.
Their clan was weak,
and they occasionally offered tribute.
5 In the second month,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
Lìnghú Táo, the Zhī Zhìgào, was appointed Hànlín Xuéshì.
The Emperor once had him read the Jīnjìng
written by Tàizōng.
The book Jīnjìng
was authored by Tàizōng.
"In times of great disorder, the unworthy are always employed;
in times of great governance, the loyal and virtuous are always employed."
The Emperor stopped him and said:
"Anyone seeking to achieve great peace
should take these words as paramount."
He also had the Zhēngguān Zhèngyào inscribed on a screen,
and would read it with a serious expression and clasped hands.
The Emperor wanted to know the names and numbers of all officials.
Lìnghú Táo said:
"Below the sixth rank,
officials are of low status and numerous,
all appointed by the Lìbù;
above the fifth rank,
they are appointed by imperial decree of the government,
each having a register
called the Jùyuán."
The Emperor ordered the prime minister to compile five volumes of the Jùyuán Yùlǎn,
which were presented to him,
and he always kept them on his desk.
6 [Lì] [Huángzǐ] [Zé] was appointed Prince of [Pú].
The emperor desired to build the Five Princes' Residence at [Dàmínggōng]
to house his younger imperial sons.
He summoned the diviner [Chái] [Yuèmíng] to survey the site.
[Yuèmíng] replied:
"For common households,
whose residences are not permanent,
there are cases of moving from a [yángzhái] (house for the living) to a [yīnzhái] (tomb),
or from a [yīnzhái] to a [yángzhái].
Regarding conflicts, misfortunes, and blessings,
masters have their theories.
The [yīnyáng] school speaks of 'Three Punishments':
[yín] punishes [sì],
[sì] punishes [shēn],
[shēn] punishes [yín];
[chǒu] punishes [xū],
[xū] punishes [wèi],
[wèi] punishes [chǒu];
[zǐ] punishes [mǎo],
[mǎo] punishes [zǐ];
[chén] punishes [chén],
[wǔ] punishes [wǔ],
[yóu] punishes [yóu],
[hài] punishes [hài].
As for 'Clash' ([kè]):
metal clashes with wood,
wood clashes with earth,
earth clashes with water,
water clashes with fire,
fire clashes with metal.
As [Rú] [Chún] said: The 'Law Palace' ([fǎgōng])
is the main hall of the ceremonial residence ([lùqǐn]).
[Yīnyáng] books do not originally speak of imperial families."
The emperor approved of his words
and bestowed upon him a bolt of silk before dismissing him.
7 Summer,
Fifth month,
on the [jǐwèi] day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
8 [Cuī] [Yuánsì], Menxià Shìláng and Tong Pingzhangshi, was dismissed and made Hùbù Shàngshū.
[Zhōu] [Chí], Bīngbù Shìláng, Pàndùzhī, and Hùbù, along with [Mǎ] [Zhí], Xíngbù Shìláng and Yántiě Zhuǎnyùnshǐ, were both appointed Tong Pingzhangshi.
"幷" ([bìng]),
should be written
"並" ([bìng]).
Previously,
when [Chí] was the [Yìchéng] Jiédùshǐ,
he appointed [Wéi] [Ào] as his Pànguān.
When [Chí] became prime minister,
he said to [Ào]:
"My strength is small, but my responsibility is great. How can you assist me?"
[Ào] replied:
"I wish for you, Chancellor, to have no power."
[Chí] was astonished,
not understanding what he meant.
[Ào] said:
"Official rewards and punishments
should be decided in conjunction with all under heaven,
not shifted by your personal likes, dislikes, joys, or angers.
When the world governs itself,
what power is there for you to wield?"
[Chí] deeply agreed with this.
[Ào]
was the son of [Guànzhī].
9 On the [jǐmǎo] day,
Empress Dowager [Guō] passed away at [Xìngqìnggōng].
Sixth month,
[Wáng] [Hào], a Jiǎntǎo Guān of the Lǐyuàn, was demoted to Jùróng Lìng.
The Táng dynasty’s Tàichángsì had one Xiūzhuàn and one Jiǎntǎo Guān in the Lǐyuàn.
[Sòng] [Bái] said: In the fourth month of the ninth year of [Zhēnyuán] (793 AD),
an imperial edict decreed that the Tàichángsì should appoint one Xiūzhuàn and one Jiǎntǎo Guān for the Lǐyuàn,
making them permanent positions.
Jùróng county
belonged to Shēngzhōu.
[Sòng] [Bái] said: Jùróng county
was originally a Hàn county,
named after the [Máoshān] mountain within its borders,
which was originally called [Jùqǔshān].
Previously,
when Emperor [Xiànzōng] passed away,
the current emperor suspected Empress Dowager [Guō] of being involved in his demise.
Moreover, [Zhèng] Tàihòu was originally a maidservant of Empress Dowager [Guō]
and harbored an old grudge.
Therefore, when the emperor ascended the throne,
his treatment of Empress Dowager [Guō] was particularly disrespectful.
Empress Dowager [Guō] was displeased.
One day,
she ascended the [Qínzhènglóu],
which was the [Qínzhèng Wùběn] building built by Emperor [Xuánzōng]
in [Xìngqìnggōng].
When the emperor heard of this,
he was greatly angered.
That very night,
she passed away.
Outsiders had somewhat divergent opinions about this.
The former *Jiédùshǐ* of Fèngxiáng, Shí Xióng, went to the government to report on his achievements at Hēishān and Wūlǐng.
Government
here refers to the Zhèngshìtáng.
The achievements at Hēishān and Wūlǐng are both mentioned in the previous volume, under Emperor Wǔzōng's Huìchāng third year.
*Kǎoyì* says: This comes from Fàn Chū's *Yúnxī Yǒuyì*.
It mistakenly identifies Wūlǐng as Tiānjǐng.
This is an error.
The powerful officials, knowing that Shí Xióng had been recommended by Lǐ Déyù,
said:
"The achievements of former days,
the imperial court rewarded them with the three garrisons of Pú, Mèng, and Qí.
That is sufficient."
Pú
refers to Hézhōng.
Mèng
refers to Héyáng.
Qí
refers to Fèngxiáng.
Shí Xióng died in vexation.
12. In the eleventh month,
on the *gēngwǔ* day,
Princess Wànshòu married the *Qǐjū Láng*, Zhèng Hào.
Zhèng Hào
was the grandson of Zhèng Yīn.
Zhèng Yīn served as Chancellor at the beginning of Yuánhé.
Zhèng Hào served as *Jiàoshū Láng* and *Yòushíyí Nèigòngfèng*,
and was known for his literary elegance.
The princess
was the emperor's beloved daughter,
so Zhèng Hào was chosen to marry her.
The responsible officials, following old regulations, requested the use of a silver-decorated carriage.
The emperor said:
"I wish to transform the empire through frugality.
This must begin with those closest to me."
He ordered that a bronze-decorated carriage be used, as for external imperial consorts.
According to Táng regulations, princesses rode an *yànzhái* carriage.
A first-rank external imperial consort
rode a white bronze *yàndú* carriage.
All were to follow the rules for commoners,
being admonished not to slight their husband's family,
nor to involve themselves in current affairs.
He further declared in an imperial decree:
"If you violate my admonitions,
there will surely be disaster like that of Tàipíng and Ānlè."
Zhèng Hào's younger brother, Yǐ,
once suffered from a serious illness.
The emperor sent an envoy to visit him.
Upon returning,
he asked,
"Where is the princess?"
The envoy replied:
"She is watching a play at Cí'ēnsì Temple."
The emperor was furious and
sighed:
"No wonder gentry families are unwilling to intermarry with my family;
there is truly a reason!"
He immediately ordered the princess to be summoned to the palace,
made her stand on the steps,
and did not look at her.
The princess, in fear,
wept and begged for forgiveness.
The emperor reproached her, saying:
"How can you, when your young brother-in-law is ill, not visit him,
but instead watch a play!"
Since the Jìn dynasty,
a sister-in-law referred to her husband's younger brother as *xiǎoláng*.
*Shěng*
is pronounced *xījǐng*.
Because of this, throughout the emperor's reign,
all imperial relatives were scrupulous in observing propriety and law,
like the gentry families of Shāndōng.
13. On the *rénwǔ* day,
Empress Yì'ān was buried beside Jǐnglíng.
This was against ritual.
Emperor Xiànzōng did not correct the beginning,
which led to Emperor Xuānzōng not correcting the end.
14. Wéi Cóng, *Zhōngshū Shìláng* and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*, was appointed *Tàizǐ Bīnkè* and *Fēnsī*.
15. In the twelfth month,
Cuī Gǒng, *Jiédùshǐ* of Fèngxiáng, reported a victory over the Tǔbō and
the recapture of Qīngshuǐ.
Qīngshuǐ was formerly under Qínzhōu.
Sòng Bái says: Qīngshuǐ
was an old Hàn county,
its territory being that originally granted to Qín Zhòng.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Qīngshuǐ County is ninety *lǐ* from Qínzhōu.
Sòng Bái says: During the Chángxīng era,
Qīngshuǐ County was moved to Shàngguī Township.
The Qīngshuǐ in the *Jiǔyù Zhì* is the one moved during Chángxīng.
It was temporarily under Fèngxiáng.
16. The emperor saw many descendants of the *gōngqīng* from Emperor Xiànzōng's reign
and promoted them.
When Dù Shèng, *Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng*, had his second audience,
the emperor asked about his family background.
He replied:
"My father, Huáng Cháng,
was the first to request Emperor Xiànzōng to supervise the state."
This event is found in volume 236, Yǒngzhēn first year.
*Cháo*
is pronounced *zhíyáo*.
Péi Nǐn, *Hànlín Xuéshì*, was the son of Dù Zhī.
When the emperor visited the Hànlín Academy,
he personally appointed him *Chéngzhǐ*.
17. Lùn Kǒngrè of Tǔbō dispatched his general Mǎngluó Jízàng with twenty thousand troops to raid the western border.
Shàng Bìbì dispatched his general Tuòbá Huáiguāng to attack him in Nángǔ.
They inflicted a great defeat,
and Jízàng surrendered.
1. In spring,
the first month,
the emperor discussed with his chancellors who was the best upright official during the Yuánhé era.
Zhōu Chí said:
"Your subject once governed in Jiāngxī,
and heard that *Guānchásǐ* Wéi Dān's virtues benefited the eight prefectures.
Forty years after his death,
the old and young sing and miss him
as if Wéi Dān were still alive."
On the *yǐhài* day,
an imperial edict commanded Dù Mù, *Shǐguǎn Xiūzhuàn*, to compose a monument to Wéi Dān's lasting affection to commemorate him,
and also promoted his son, Zhōu, *Héyáng Guānchá Pànguān*, to *Yùshǐ*.
2. In the second month,
Lùn Kǒngrè of Tǔbō garrisoned at Hézhōu,
and Shàng Bìbì garrisoned at Héyuánjūn.
Héyuánjūn is east of Shànzhōu.
Sòng Bái says: Héyuánjūn was established in Niè
[Huáng],
originally the watchtowers of Zhào Chōngguó.
Shàng Bìbì's generals wanted to attack Lùn Kǒngrè.
Shàng Bìbì said:
"No.
Our army, having won quickly, is complacent, while they are desperate and fighting to the death.
The battle will surely be unfavorable."
The generals did not listen.
Shàng Bìbì, knowing they would surely be defeated,
held the Héquiáo bridge to await them.
The generals were indeed defeated.
Shàng Bìbì gathered the remaining troops,
burned the bridge,
and returned to Shànzhōu.
Holding the Héquiáo bridge meant that
the retreating defeated soldiers had a way back.
Once the defeated troops had crossed,
burning the bridge to block the river
could cut off Lùn Kǒngrè's pursuit.
History says Shàng Bìbì was skilled in warfare.
3. The Tǔbō prefectures of Qín, Yuán, and Ānlè, and the seven passes including Shímén, came to surrender.
During Emperor Gāozōng's time,
the Tǔyùhún, pressured by the Tǔbō,
migrated to Shànzhōu.
Unsettled there, they again migrated to the border of Língzhōu.
In Xiánhēng third year,
Ānlèzhōu was established in the former Míngshā County of Língzhōu to settle them.
During the Ān-Shǐ Rebellion,
the Tǔbō took Ānlèzhōu,
and the Tǔyùhún again migrated to the borders of Shuòfāng and Hédōng.
Within Yuánzhōu's borders are seven passes: Shímén, Yìzàng, Zhìshèng, Shíxiá, Mùjìng, Mùxiá, and Liùpán.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
"Kāng Jìróng, *Jīngyuán Jiédùshǐ*, reported that Tǔbō chancellor Lùn Kǒngrè killed the *Dōngdào Jiédùshǐ*,
and presented a memorial surrendering the three prefectures and seven passes."
The *Xiànzǔ Jìniánlù* also says
"killed the *Dōngdào Jiédùshǐ*,
and presented a memorial."
However, *Bǔ Guóshǐ* describes Lùn Kǒngrè's affairs in great detail.
He only surrendered in the fifth month of the fifth year;
he had not surrendered at this time.
Nor does it mention him killing the *Dōngdào Jiédùshǐ*.
Furthermore, if Lùn Kǒngrè had surrendered with the three prefectures and seven passes,
the imperial court would surely have granted him official titles and rewards.
Why were only the border generals rewarded, and not Lùn Kǒngrè?
It is probably that the three prefectures and seven passes,
due to the chaos in the Tǔbō kingdom,
surrendered to Táng on their own initiative.
The imperial court dispatched various circuits to receive and settle them.
It was not Lùn Kǒngrè who led them to surrender.
The *Shílù* is mistaken.
An edict ordered Jīngyuán, Língwǔ, Fèngxiáng, Bīnníng, and Zhènwǔ all to send troops to receive them.
4. Wáng Zǎi, *Hédōng Jiédùshǐ*, came to court,
and bribed powerful favorites,
seeking to be appointed *Shǐxiàng* and *Xuānwǔ*.
Zhōu Chí, *Xíngbù Shàngshū* and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*, submitted a memorial criticizing this.
Wáng Zǎi then returned to his garrison.
Wéi Ràng, *Fùmǎ Dūwèi*, sought to be *Jīngzhàoyǐn*.
Zhōu Chí stated that *Jīngzhàoyǐn* could not be held by someone lacking talent and prestige.
Wéi Ràng's proposal was ultimately shelved.
Zhōu Chí also advised the emperor against opening up the border.
"Opening up the border"
refers to campaigning in Héxī.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Zhōu Chí was appointed *Dōngchuān Jiédùshǐ*.
Cuī Xuàn, *Yùshǐ Dàfū*, was appointed *Zhōngshū Shìláng* and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*.
Wèi Fú, *Bīngbù Shìláng* and *Pàn Hùbù*, was appointed *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*.
5. On the *guǐsì* day,
Lúlóng reported that *Jiédùshǐ* Zhāng Zhòngwǔ had died,
and the army had established his son, *Jiédù Yáyá* Zhí Fāng.
6 Hànlín Xuéshì Zhèng Hào (鄭顥) said to the Emperor:
“Zhōu Chí (周墀) entered the government as a minister for his outspokenness,
and was also dismissed as a minister for his outspokenness.”
The Emperor was deeply moved and enlightened.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Zhī (墀) came to express his gratitude [for a previous promotion];
he was promoted to *Jiǎnjiào Yòu Púyè* (檢校右僕射).
7 On the *wùxū* day,
Zhāng Zhífāng (張直方) was made Acting Military Governor of Lúlóng (盧龍).
8 In the fifth month,
the Xúzhōu (徐州) army mutinied,
driving away Military Governor Lǐ Kuò (李廓).
Kuò (廓)
was the son of Chéng (程).
Lǐ Chéng (李程) can be seen in volume 243, Chángqìng (長慶) fourth year.
Right Palace Remonstrance Zhèng Lǔ (鄭魯) memorialized on the situation,
and further said:
“I fear that with the new wheat not yet harvested,
the Xú (徐) army will certainly mutiny;
quickly appoint a good commander
to save this region.”
The Emperor did not heed him.
When Xúzhōu (徐州) indeed mutinied,
the Emperor remembered Lǔ’s (魯) words,
and promoted him to *Qǐjū Shèrén* (起居舍人).
The Military Governor of Yìchéng (義成), Lú Hóngzhǐ (盧弘止), was made Military Governor of Wǔníng (武寧).
The soldiers of Wǔníng (武寧) had always been arrogant,
especially the Silver Blade Battalion (*Yín Dāo Dū*),
who repeatedly drove away their commanders.
When Hóngzhǐ (弘止) arrived at the garrison,
the *Dū Yúhòu* (都虞候) Hú Qìngfāng (胡慶方) again plotted rebellion;
Hóngzhǐ (弘止) executed him,
pacified the rest,
and instructed them in loyalty and righteousness.
The military administration was thenceforth at peace.
9 In the sixth month,
on the *wùshēn* day,
Zhāng Zhífāng (張直方) was made Military Governor of Lúlóng (盧龍).
10 The Military Governor of Jìngyuán (涇原), Kāng Jìróng (康季榮), captured Yuánzhōu (原州).
Yuánzhōu (原州) was originally governed from Gāopíng (高平),
but after the Ān-Shǐ (安史) Rebellion, it was lost to the Tǔbō (吐蕃).
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the *dīngsì* day,
the Military Governor of Língwǔ (靈武), Zhū Shúmíng (朱叔明), captured Chánglèzhōu (長樂州).
“Chánglè” (長樂)
should be
“Ānlè” (安樂).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Ānlèzhōu (安樂州) was established in Língzhōu (靈州) Míngshā (鳴沙) County.
The character *lè* (樂)
is pronounced *luò*;
the same below.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
the Military Governor of Bīnníng (邠寧), Zhāng Jūnqù (張君緒), captured Xiāoguān (蕭關).
Xiāoguān (蕭關) County,
according to old records,
belonged to Yuánzhōu (原州).
On the *jiǎxū* day,
the Military Governor of Fèngxiáng (鳳翔), Lǐ Pín (李玭), captured Qínzhōu (秦州).
An imperial edict ordered the Bīnníng (邠寧) military to temporarily move its forces to Níngzhōu (寧州) to respond to Hexi.
In the eighth month,
on the *yǐyǒu* day,
Chánglèzhōu (長樂州) was renamed Wēizhōu (威州).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Língzhōu (靈武) Míngshā (鳴沙) County was originally part of Hàn (漢) Fùpíng (富平) County;
in the Later Zhōu (周), Huìzhōu (會州) was established,
and in the Suí (隋), Huánzhōu (環州) was established,
named after the circular bend of the Great River.
In the Shénlóng (神龍) era of the Táng (唐),
Mòchuò (默啜) raided,
moving the county to the abandoned Fēng’ān (豐安) city.
In the Xīantōng (咸通) third year, it was restored,
and Ānlèzhōu (安樂州) was established on the old county site.
In the Dàzhōng (大中) third year,
it was changed to Wēizhōu (威州).
Over a thousand elderly and young people from Hé-Lǒng (河隴) came to the imperial court.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The *Shílù* (實錄) states several thousand people.
We now follow the old tradition.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
the Emperor appeared at the Yánxǐmén (延喜門) gate tower to see them.
Yánxǐmén (延喜門) was at the northeast corner of the Imperial City.
The *Liùdiǎn* (六典) says: The eastern side of the Imperial City had two gates,
the northern one called Yánxǐ (延喜),
the southern one Jǐngfēng (景風).
Yánxǐmén (延喜門) was outside Chéngtiānmén (承天門) on the transverse street,
directly east to Tōnghuàmén (通化門).
They shed their Hu (胡) clothing
and donned Han (漢) caps and belts.
All observers shouted "Long live the Emperor!"
An imperial edict ordered:
“Recruit common people to reclaim and cultivate land in the three prefectures and seven passes.
For five years, they shall be exempt from rent and taxes.
From now on, criminals in the capital who are to be exiled shall all be assigned to the ten locations.
The ten locations
are the three prefectures and seven passes.
The government shall provide oxen and seeds and grain.
The four circuits
are Jìngyuán (涇原), Bīnníng (邠寧), Língwǔ (靈武), and Fèngxiáng (鳳翔).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: The historians commented: The name *yíngtián* (營田) (military agricultural colonies) originated because there were many vacant lands along the borders.
Frontier soldiers were stationed there,
and they were tasked with sowing and cultivating to supplement military provisions.
This was called *túntián* (屯田).
Later, when warfare arose in the central plains,
the number of households decreased,
and there were many idle fields in the countryside.
Those in charge of finances established such colonies following the border model,
naming them *yíngtián* (營田).
As this system continued for years,
it was no longer only for soldiers,
but strong peasant households were recruited,
and they were called *yíngtiánhù* (營田戶) (military agricultural households).
Furthermore, families whose officials had failed in their duties or committed crimes
had their lands and residences confiscated
and were also attached to this system.
From then on, all circuits had *yíngtiánwù* (營田務) (military agricultural bureaus).
The character *zhǒng* (種)
is pronounced zhāngyǒng (章勇) in reverse order (i.e., *zhòng*).
The *Dùzhī* (度支) (Bureau of Finance) was entrusted with its implementation.
In Shénlóng (神龍) first year, Wēnchí (溫池) County was established,
belonging to Língzhōu (靈州);
in this year, it belonged to Wēizhōu (威州).
The county has salt pans.
All were given double clothing and rations,
meaning clothing and rations were double that of other garrison soldiers.
Along the roads, fortresses and stockades were to be built.
Merchants traveling and trading and soldiers' children transmitting family letters
were not to be detained at passes and garrisons.
As for the prefectures and counties in the border areas of Shānnán (山南) and Jiànnán (劍南) that were lost to the Tǔbō (吐蕃),
they shall also be recovered according to strength.”
Since Guǎngdé (廣德),
the Western Qiāng (羌) had invaded the Shānnán (山南) interior,
and Jiē (階) and Chéng (成) prefectures were lost.
Wénzhōu (文州) was moved to Jiànnán (劍南),
and many prefectures in the Western Mountains were also lost to the Tǔbō (吐蕃).
According to records, Jiēzhōu (階州) was at that time Wǔzhōu (武州).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Jiēzhōu (階州) was the land of Hàn (漢) Wǔdū (武都);
the Later Wèi (魏) pacified Wǔdū (武都),
built a city on Xiānlíng (仙陵) Mountain,
and established Wǔdū (武都) garrison.
The Western Wèi (魏) first established Wǔzhōu (武州).
In the early Dàlì (大曆) era,
it was lost to the Tǔbō (吐蕃) along with Qínzhōu (秦州).
In Dàzhōng (大中) third year, it was recovered,
Wǔzhōu (武州) was re-established,
and in Jǐnglì (景曆) first year, it was changed to Jiēzhōu (階州).
11 In winter,
the tenth month,
the Bèibiān (備邊) Treasury was renamed Yánzī (延資) Treasury.
The Bèibiān (備邊) Treasury was first established in the Wǔzōng (武宗) Huìchāng (會昌) fifth year, as seen above.
12 The Military Governor of Xīchuān (西川), Dù Cōng (杜悰), memorialized on capturing Wéizhōu (維州).
13 In the intercalary eleventh month,
on the *dīngyǒu* day,
the chief ministers requested that the Emperor be given an honored title for recovering Hé-Huáng (河湟).
The Emperor said:
“Xiànzōng (憲宗) always had the ambition to recover Hé-Huáng (河湟).
See volume 238, Yuánhé (元和) fifth year.
This was when forces were being used in the two Hexi regions.
Now, it is merely the fulfillment of his predecessors' ambition.
Let us deliberate on adding an honored posthumous title to the temples of Shùnzōng (順宗) and Xiànzōng (憲宗) to commemorate their meritorious achievements.”
14 The Military Governor of Lúlóng (盧龍), Zhāng Zhífāng (張直方),
was cruel and violent,
and loved hunting.
The army was about to mutiny.
Zhífāng (直方), aware of this,
feigned going out to hunt,
and then fled with his entire family back to the capital.
The army promoted the *yájiàng* (牙將) Zhōu Chén (周綝) to be Acting Military Governor.
When Zhífāng (直方) arrived in the capital,
he was appointed *Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn* (金吾大將軍).
15 On the *jiǎxū* day,
Shùnzōng (順宗) was posthumously honored with the title Zhìdé Hóngdào Dàshèng Dà’ān Xiàohuángdì (至德弘道大聖大安孝皇帝);
Xiànzōng (憲宗) was posthumously honored with the title Zhāowén Zhāngwǔ Dàshèng Zhìshén Xiàohuángdì (昭文章武大聖至神孝皇帝).
The spirit tablets were also re-inscribed.
Since the Tiānbǎo (天寶) era,
when additional posthumous titles were bestowed upon various emperors,
the jade tablets in their mausoleums and their spirit tablets had never been re-inscribed.
16 On the *jǐwèi* day,
Lǐ Déyù (李德裕), *Sīhù* (司戶) of Yázhōu (崖州), died.
17 The Military Governor of Shānnán Xīdào (山南西道), Zhèng Yá (鄭涯), memorialized on capturing Fúzhōu (扶州).
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: Fúzhōu (扶州),
governed from Tóngchāng (同昌) County,
was occupied by the Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) through successive generations.
The Western Wèi (魏) expelled the Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾)
and established Dèngzhōu (鄧州) and Dèngníng (鄧寧) Commandery there,
named after the pacification of the Dèngzhì (鄧至) Qiāng (羌).
In the early Suí (隋),
Fúzhōu (扶州) and Tóngchāng (同昌) County were re-established;
it was one thousand six hundred and ninety *lǐ* southwest of Cháng'ān (長安).
After Guǎngdé (廣德), it was lost to the Tǔbō (吐蕃).
Zhou Yiliang (周一良) and Rong Zhaozu (容肇祖) punctuated, Nie Chongqi (聶崇岐) re-collated.
Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
compiled by imperial order
Hòuxué Tiāntái (後學天台)
In the 4th year of Dàzhōng
(Gēngwǔ, 850 CE)
Spring:
In the 1st month,
on the day Gēngchén,
an amnesty was granted to all under Heaven.
In the 2nd month,
Qínzhōu was put under the jurisdiction of Fèngxiáng.
Qínzhōu originally belonged to the Lǒngyòu Military Commissioner,
but at this time it had been newly recovered
and was assigned to Fèngxiáng.
Summer:
In the 4th month,
on the day Gēngxū,
Mǎ Zhí, Vice Minister of the Chancellery and concurrently Grand Chancellor, was appointed Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng.
When the emperor ascended the throne,
Mǎ Yuánzhì, Commissioner of the Left Army, had been instrumental.
When Emperor Wǔzōng was critically ill,
Mǎ Yuánzhì, as Commissioner of the Left Shéncè Imperial Guard,
established the emperor as Imperial Grand-uncle.
Zhí recounted their common ancestry with him.
The emperor bestowed a precious belt upon Yuánzhì,
who then gave it to Zhí.
Zhí wore it to court,
and the emperor saw and recognized it.
Zhí's expression changed,
and he dared not conceal the truth.
The next day,
he was dismissed from his chancellorship.
Dǒng Móu, Zhí's personal clerk, was arrested
and sent to the Imperial Censorate for interrogation.
The full extent of Zhí's collusion with Yuánzhì was discovered,
and he was further demoted to Prefect of Chángzhōu.
Chángzhōu was
the ancient city of Jìzǐ of Yánlíng.
Later it became Pílíng,
in the Jìn dynasty it was Jìnlíng,
and in the Táng dynasty it was Chángzhōu,
2843 *lǐ* southeast of the capital.
In the 6th month,
on the day Wùshēn,
Wèi Fú, Vice Minister of War and concurrently Grand Chancellor, passed away.
Cuī Guīcóng, Minister of Revenue and concurrently Administrator of Financial Affairs, was made Grand Chancellor.
Autumn:
In the 8th month,
Bái Mǐnzhōng was appointed Administrator of the Yánzīkù treasury.
Last year, the Bèibiānkù treasury was renamed Yánzīkù.
Zhōu Lún, Military Commissioner of Lúlóng, passed away.
The army formally petitioned to appoint Zhāng Yǔnshēn, Assistant Administrator and concurrently Commander of Infantry and Cavalry, as Acting Commissioner.
In the 9th month,
on the day Dīngyǒu,
this was granted.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: In the 7th month of the 4th year,
Zhōu Lún passed away,
and Zhāng Yǔnshēn became Acting Commissioner.
A note states: The old annals also do not record the year and month the court appointed Lún as Military Commissioner.
Here it only says,
"Zhōu Lún, Military Commissioner of Yōuzhōu, died,
and the soldiers appointed Zhāng Yǔnshēn as Acting Commissioner."
The *Shílù* states:
"In the 9th month,
the generals of Yōuzhōu formally petitioned for Assistant Administrator Zhāng Yǔnshēn to manage affairs as Acting Commissioner."
Zhāng Yǔnshēn's old biography states:
"In the 4th year of Dàzhōng,
Zhōu Lún, the frontier commander, fell ill,
and formally recommended Yǔnshēn as Acting Commissioner;
the court approved his memorial."
Now, this information is incorporated.
According to the *Tōngjiàn*, Zhōu Lún died in the 8th month.
The *Kǎo Yì* considers it to be the 7th month.
The Dǎngxiàng caused border troubles,
and troops from various circuits were dispatched to suppress them.
For years there was no success,
and the cost of garrisons and provisions was endless.
Kǒng Wēnyù, Right Remonstrance Official, submitted a strongly worded memorial,
which angered the emperor.
He was demoted to Administrative Assistant of Liǔzhōu.
Wēnyù was
the nephew of Kuí.
Kǒng Kuí is mentioned in Volume 240, under the 12th year of Yuánhé of Emperor Xiànzōng.
Lùn Kǒngrè of Tǔbō sent the monk Mǎngluó Línzhēn with troops to build a bridge south of Jīxiàngguān,
in order to attack Shàng Bìbì's army at Báitǔlǐng.
The *Shuǐjīngzhù* states: Sixty *lǐ* west of Zuǒnánjīn, there is Báitǔchéng,
and northwest of the city flows the Báitǔchuān River.
The area is west of Fènglín County in Táng Hézhōu.
Judging by this,
Jīxiàngguān is also within the borders of Hézhōu.
The campaign was unsuccessful,
so he again sent Mólí Pízǐ and Zhúlú Gǒnglì
with troops to occupy Máoniúxiá to resist them.
Gǒnglì requested,
"Let us hold our ground and defend the dangerous passes.
Do not engage in battle,
but use surprise troops to cut off their supply lines,
so they cannot advance to fight
nor retreat to return.
In no more than a month,
their forces will surely collapse."
Pízǐ did not follow this advice.
Gǒnglì said,
"I would rather be a useless person
than a general who loses a battle."
He feigned illness
and returned to Shànzhōu.
Pízǐ engaged in battle and was
defeated and killed.
Bìbì's provisions ran out,
so he left Tuòbá Huáiguāng to guard Shànzhōu,
and led over 3,000 tribesmen to seek water and pasture west of Gānzhōu.
Kǒngrè heard that Bìbì had abandoned Shànzhōu,
and personally led 5,000 light cavalry to pursue him.
Upon reaching Guāzhōu,
Sòng Bái states: Guāzhōu is
340 *lǐ* southeast to the border of Sùzhōu.
He then plundered the eight prefectures of Héxī, including Shàn and Kuò,
Sòng Bái states: Kuòzhōu is
180 *lǐ* north to Shànzhōu,
and 280 *lǐ* southeast to Fènglín County in Hézhōu.
He cut off the noses and feet of the weak and old
and women,
and impaled infants on spears for sport,
and burned their homes.
Over five thousand *lǐ* of land
was almost completely devastated.
Winter:
In the 10th month,
on the day Xīnwèi,
Línghú Táo, Academician-in-waiting and Vice Minister of War, was made Grand Chancellor.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: The old annals place this in the 11th month.
Now following the *Shílù* and the new and old annals.
In the 11th month,
on the day Rén Yín,
Liú Zhuàn, Academician, was appointed Imperial Commissioner for Recalling and Pacifying Dǎngxiàng in the Campaigns West of the Capital.
Zhāng Yǔnshēn, Acting Commissioner of Lúlóng, was appointed Military Commissioner.
In the 12th month,
Lǐ Yè, Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng, and Lǐ Shì, Military Commissioner of Hédōng, were both concurrently appointed Commissioners for Recalling and Pacifying Dǎngxiàng.
Kǒng Wēnyè, Vice Minister of Personnel, informed the Executive Council that he sought an external official post.
Bái Mǐnzhōng said to his colleagues,
"We must examine ourselves.
Vice Minister Kǒng is unwilling to remain at court."
Wēnyè was
the nephew of Kuí's younger brother.
Kǒng Wēnyè's conduct is not recorded in history,
but people at the time respected him likely due to his family's reputation.
Spring:
In the 1st
month,
on the day Rénxū,
Tiāndé Command reported that Zhāng Yìcháo, Acting Prefect of Shāzhōu, had sent an envoy to surrender.
Yìcháo was
a native of Shāzhōu.
At that time, Tǔbō was in great disorder,
and Yìcháo secretly gathered local heroes,
planning to break free and return to the Táng.
One day,
he led his armored forces, shouting at the city gate.
The Táng people all responded,
and the Tǔbō garrison commander fled in panic.
Yìcháo then took charge of the prefecture's affairs
and sent a memorial to surrender.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: The *Bǔ Guó Shǐ* writes
"Yìcháo".
Now following the *Shílù*, and the new and old annals and biographies.
Péi Xiū, Vice Minister of War, was appointed Commissioner of Salt and Iron Transportation.
Xiū was
the son of Sù.
Péi Sù is mentioned in Volume 235, under the 12th year of Zhēnyuán of Emperor Dézōng.
Annually, the rice transported from the Jiāng and Huái rivers did not exceed 400,000 *hú*.
Officials and soldiers embezzled, stole, and sank the shipments,
so that less than three or four tenths of the boats reached Wèicāng.
This greatly fell short of Liú Yàn's methods.
Xiū thoroughly investigated these abuses
and established ten regulations for grain transport,
resulting in 1,200,000 *hú* of rice reaching Wèicāng annually.
The emperor became aware that the Dǎngxiàng's rebellion was due to the frontier commanders profiting from their sheep and horses,
repeatedly cheating and seizing them,
or arbitrarily executing people.
The Dǎngxiàng could not endure their resentment
and thus rebelled.
Therefore, he appointed Lǐ Fú, Right Counsel-Remonstrant, as Military Commissioner of Xiàsuí.
From then on, erudite officials were successively chosen to replace the greedy and cruel frontier commanders,
and before their departure, they were personally cautioned and encouraged.
The Dǎngxiàng thus became pacified.
Fú was
the younger brother of Shí.
4 The Emperor thought that the Dǎngxiàng (Tanguts) of Nánshān and Píngxià had long remained unsubdued.
Those Dǎngxiàng residing in Qìngzhōu
were called the Dōngshānbù (Eastern Mountain Department);
those residing in Xiàzhōu
were called the Píngxiàbù (Píngxià Department);
and those who had fled and settled in Nánshān
were the Nánshān Dǎngxiàng (Southern Mountain Dǎngxiàng).
Zhào Xún's *Jùmǐ tújīng* states: "The Dǎngxiàng tribes north of Yínzhōu and Xiàzhōu,
who live in river valleys and marshes,
are called the Píngxià Dǎngxiàng;
those south of Ānzhōu and Yánzhōu,
who live in mountains and valleys,
are called the Nánshān Dǎngxiàng."
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Tángnián Bǔlù* states:
"South of Sōngzhōu there is a snow-covered mountain,
hence it is called Nánshān.
Píngxià
is a river's name."
I (the compiler) note that the *Tángnián Bǔlù*
is merely the work of superficial scholars.
Now, I do not wish to discuss geography further;
let us provisionally discuss this according to the principles of the *Tōngjiàn*.
A *Kǎoyì* (Critical Examination)
examines the similarities and differences in various books to determine what is correct,
explains their meanings,
and entrusts this to future scholars.
Since there are no similarities or differences to examine regarding the saying about Nánshān,
to cite it now
is probably not the original intention of the *Kǎoyì*.
Cuī Xuàn suggested
that a high minister should be dispatched to pacify them.
In the third month,
Bái Mǐnzhōng was appointed Sīkōng (Minister of Works) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (Concurrently Administrator of Affairs),
and additionally served as Zhāotǎo Dǎngxiàng Xíngyíng Dūtǒng (Supreme Commander of the Expeditionary Army for Subduing the Dǎngxiàng) and Zhìzhìděngshǐ (Commissioner for Control and Other Matters).
The *Zhíyuán* states: The position of Zhìzhìshǐ began with this.
Mǐnzhōng requested to follow Péi Dù's precedent,
to select court officials as his generals and aides,
and this was granted.
Péi Dù's precedent is found in Volume 240, under Emperor Xiànzōng, Yuánhé 12th year.
In the fourth month,
Sūn Jǐngshāng, Left Jiàn Yì Dàfū (Grand Master Remonstrant of the Left), was appointed Zuǒ Shùzǐ (Left Attendant to the Crown Prince),
and additionally served as Bīnnìng Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (Military Administrator for the Bīnnìng Army);
Jiǎng Shēn, Zhī Zhìgào (Drafting Secretary), was appointed Yòu Shùzǐ (Right Attendant to the Crown Prince),
and additionally served as Jiédù Fùshǐ (Deputy Military Commissioner).
Shēn
was Jì's younger brother.
Jiǎng Jì is found in Volume 244, under Emperor Wénzōng, Tàihé 5th year.
Initially,
the Emperor ordered Bái Mǐnzhōng to select a good son-in-law for Princess Wànshòu.
Mǐnzhōng recommended Zhèng Hào.
At that time, Hào had already married a Lady Lú,
and when he reached Zhèngzhōu,
an official dispatch recalled him.
Princess Wànshòu marrying Zhèng Hào is found in the previous year's volume.
Zhèngzhōu was 1,105 *lǐ* from the capital.
Because of this, Hào repeatedly slandered Mǐnzhōng to the Emperor.
When Mǐnzhōng was about to depart for his post,
he said to the Emperor:
"Zhèng Hào was unhappy about marrying the Princess,
and resents me to the core.
When I was in the government, he could do nothing to me;
now that I am outside,
Hào will surely harm me.
My death is only a matter of days!"
The Emperor said:
"I have known this for a long time.
Why do you speak of it so late!"
He ordered his attendants to retrieve a small *chéng* wood box from the imperial quarters and gave it to Mǐnzhōng, saying:
"These are all letters from Master Zhèng slandering you.
If I had believed them,
how could I have entrusted you with such responsibilities until today!"
Mǐnzhōng returned,
placed the *chéng* wood box before a Buddha,
burned incense, and revered it.
Mǐnzhōng's army was stationed in Níngzhōu.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
Shǐ Yuán, the envoy of Dìngyuǎn City, defeated over nine thousand Dǎngxiàng tents in Sānjiāogǔ.
Sānjiāogǔ is within Xiàzhōu territory.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"The Píngxià Dǎngxiàng
have already settled peacefully.
Píngxià
is a place name,
within Xiàzhōu territory.
When Lǐ Jìqiān rebelled during the Sòng dynasty,
he moved half of the officials and people of Suízhōu to Píngxià to establish a stronghold,
which was a strategic location between Yínzhōu and Xiàzhōu.
It is heard that those who emerged from the mountains, compelled by hunger and cold,
still engaged in plunder,
but Píngxià would not tolerate them,
leaving them nowhere to go.
It is appropriate to instruct Lǐ Fúcún to persuade them
and grant them unused land within the borders of Yínzhōu and Xiàzhōu.
If they can reform and assimilate,
they shall be treated like infants;
all their past wrongdoings
will be overlooked,
and if there are any grievances,
they may submit petitions to the local garrisons to plead their case.
However, if they again trespass on the border,
or retreat back into the mountains,
refusing to obey orders,
they shall be put to death without mercy.
Officers and soldiers with merits shall be recognized and rewarded;
those who are wounded or killed shall receive generous solace.
The common people of the four circuits of Língzhōu, Xiàzhōu, Bīnzhōu, and Fūzhōu
shall be exempted from taxes and corvée for three years,
and neighboring circuits shall have their rents and taxes reduced as appropriate.
Previously, the greed and depravity of border generals
led to their resentment and rebellion.
From now on, upright and benevolent individuals must be chosen to govern them.
If they again cause invasion and rebellion,
the border generals shall be punished first,
and then the bandits shall be suppressed."
5 Lùn KǒngRè of Tǔbō (Tibet) was cruel and tyrannical,
and many of his subordinates rebelled.
Tuòbá Huáiguāng sent people to entice and persuade them.
Some of his followers dispersed and lived in
tribes,
while others surrendered to Huáiguāng.
KǒngRè found himself isolated,
so he publicly declared to his followers:
"I shall now go to the Tang court
and borrow 500,000 soldiers to punish those who do not submit.
Then I will make Wèizhōu the capital of my kingdom,
and ask the Tang to enfeoff me as Zānpǔ.
Who would dare not obey!"
In the fifth month,
KǒngRè came to court.
The Emperor dispatched Lǐ Jǐngràng, the Left Chéng (Assistant Minister), to the Lǐbīnyuàn (Reception Bureau) to inquire about his wishes.
KǒngRè's demeanor was arrogant and haughty,
and his words were absurd.
He requested to be appointed Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner) of Héwèi.
The Emperor did not allow it.
He was summoned to an audience in the Three Halls,
treated like an ordinary foreign guest,
given gifts, and sent back.
KǒngRè departed discontentedly,
and returned to Luòménchuān.
He gathered his old followers.
KǒngRè was originally the Luòmén Tǎojīshǐ (Commander for Suppressing Rebels of Luòmén) of Tǔbō.
At that time, there was a prolonged rain,
and food was scarce.
His followers gradually dispersed,
until only about three hundred people remained.
They fled to Kuòzhōu.
6 In the sixth month,
Imperial Prince Rùn was made Prince È.
7 Jìnshì (Palace Graduate) Sūn Qiáo submitted a memorial, stating:
"The common people, men farming and women weaving,
cannot even clothe and feed themselves adequately,
while all the monks sit idly in lavish houses,
wearing fine clothes and eating exquisite food.
It is estimated that ten households cannot support one monk.
Emperor Wǔzōng was indignant at this situation.
'Fèn qí rán'
means indignant at its being so.
It implies making monks grow their hair and return to being commoners.
Since Your Majesty's ascension,
you have restored abandoned temples,
and the sound of axes throughout the land has not ceased until today;
the number of ordained monks has almost returned to its former state.
Even if Your Majesty cannot eliminate accumulated abuses like Emperor Wǔzōng,
how can you revive what has already been abolished!
Recently, Your Majesty wished to repair the East Gate of the capital,
and the remonstrating officials submitted a memorial,
and the work was immediately halted.
Are the temples now being restored
as urgent as the East Gate?
Are the efforts expended
as strenuous as those for the East Gate?
I humbly request that an enlightened edict be issued soon,
that monks not yet restored should not be restored,
and temples not yet repaired should not be repaired,
so that the common people may still find some respite."
In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Zhōngshūménxià (Department of the Central Secretariat) reported:
"Your Majesty reveres Buddhism,
and everyone below strives to follow suit.
We fear that financial and material resources may be insufficient,
and this might lead to trouble and disturbance for the people.
We hope that local officials will be instructed to exercise appropriate restraint.
Regarding the monks to be ordained, it is also requested that those with virtuous conduct be selected;
if rude and unrefined individuals are permitted,
it would not be a sign of respect for the Dharma.
As for village Buddhist shrines,
it is requested that their repairs be postponed until the end of military campaigns."
At this time, military campaigns were being waged to recover Hézhōu and Huángzhōu.
8 In the eighth month,
Bái Mǐnzhōng reported that the Nánshān Dǎngxiàng also requested to surrender.
At this time, military campaigns had lasted for years,
and the national treasury was quite depleted.
An edict was issued, pardoning the Nánshān Dǎngxiàng,
and allowing them to settle down peacefully.
After a long time,
Cóng was transferred from Sīxūn Yuánwàiláng to be Mùzhōu Cìshǐ.
Mùzhōu
was called Xīndū Jùn by Wú,
and was named Mùzhōu by Suí,
taking its meaning from the prosperity of the people and harmony, both internal and external.
It was three thousand six hundred fifty-nine *lǐ* southeast of the capital.
The Emperor bestowed purple upon him.
When Cóng had made his obeisance,
he advanced and said,
after expressing thanks,
he advanced and spoke.
"The scarlet robe I wear
was borrowed from a *cìshǐ*."
The Emperor immediately said,
"I will grant you a scarlet robe now."
The Emperor greatly valued robes and insignia.
The officials in charge always kept several sets of scarlet and purple robes on hand when accompanying him,
to be ready for rewards.
Sometimes not one of them was used for half a year.
Therefore, at that time, scarlet and purple were considered an honor.
The Emperor greatly respected the Hànlín Xuéshì.
As for promotions,
he would always check the years and months,
believing that official titles and ranks should not be privately granted to close ministers.
4 In autumn,
the ninth month,
on the day *bǐngxū*,
Gāo Shàoyì, Right Sànqí Chángshì, was appointed Shǎnmín Guóguān Chásǐ.
An imperial envoy passed through Xiáshí.
Xiáshí
was Xiáo Xiàn during Suí.
In the fourteenth year of Zhēngguān, its administrative seat was moved to Xiáshí Wù,
and its name changed to Xiáshí,
subordinate to Shǎnzhōu.
Shǎn is
pronounced *shān rǎn*.
The envoy whipped a postman until he bled;
Shàoyì sealed the postman's biscuit and presented it [to the Emperor].
When the imperial envoy returned,
the Emperor rebuked him, saying,
"How could such food be easily obtained in the deep mountains!"
He was banished to Gōnglíng.
5 Imperial Prince Qià was enfeoffed as Huái Wáng,
Ruì as Zhāo Wáng,
and Wén as Kāng Wáng.
6 The Emperor hunted north of the park.
This was hunting north outside the park city.
He asked about the county [of a man he met],
who replied,
"I am a person from Jīngyáng."
"Who is the magistrate?"
He replied,
"Lǐ Xíngyán."
"How is his governance?"
He replied,
"He is stubborn by nature.
There were several bandits,
and the military demanded them.
The military refers to the various armies of the Northern Bureau.
The Tang people called the various circuit *jiédù* and *guānchá* as *shǐjiā*,
the various prefectures as *zhōujiā*,
and the various counties as *xiànjiā*.
Sǒu,
pronounced *shān kè fān*.
He killed them all."
When the Emperor returned,
he affixed his name to a pillar in his sleeping palace.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Xíngyán was appointed Hǎizhōu Cìshǐ.
When he came to express his thanks,
the Emperor bestowed gold and purple upon him.
He asked,
"Do you know why you are wearing purple?"
He replied,
"I do not know."
The Emperor ordered the post on the palace pillar to be brought and shown to him.
7 Regarding the Gānlù Incident,
the Emperor saw in the 245th scroll that it occurred in the eighth year of Dàhé during Wénzōng's reign.
He issued an edict to exonerate Wáng Yá, Jiǎ Sù, and others who were innocent,
declaring them all innocent of their wrongful charges.
The Emperor summoned Hànlín Xuéshì Wèi Ào,
on the pretext of discussing poetry,
and, dismissing his attendants,
spoke to him, saying,
"Recently, what do people outside say about the power of the inner attendants?"
He replied,
"Your Majesty's authority and decisiveness
are not comparable to previous reigns."
The Emperor closed his eyes and shook his head, saying,
"Not at all,
not at all!
I still fear them.
End of sentence.
He replied,
"If we discuss this with the outer court,
I fear there might be a recurrence of the Tàihé incident.
It would be better to select talented and insightful individuals among them and consult with them."
The Emperor said,
"That is the last resort.
From those who wear yellow and green to those who wear scarlet,
they are all grateful,
but once they wear purple, they conspire as one!"
Since Shàngyuán of Táng,
officials of the third rank and above wore purple;
fourth rank wore deep scarlet;
fifth rank wore light scarlet;
sixth rank wore deep green;
seventh rank wore light green;
eighth rank wore green;
ninth rank wore deep blue;
officials outside the regular ranks and commoners wore yellow.
Tàizōng's regulations stipulated that
the Nèishì Shěng should not have third-rank officials;
the Nèishì was the chief official,
of the fourth rank,
whose duty was merely to guard the palace gates
and receive yellow robes and rations.
By Xuánzōng's time,
eunuchs could reach the rank of third-rank general,
have *qǐjǐ* displayed at their gates,
and were allowed to wear purple.
Yī,
pronounced *yú jì fān*.
Táo feared that the innocent would be implicated indiscriminately,
so he secretly memorialized, saying,
"Simply do not spare those who are guilty,
and do not fill vacancies when they occur.
Naturally, they will gradually diminish
until they are gone."
The eunuchs secretly saw his memorial,
and from this, their enmity with the court officials intensified,
and the Northern and Southern Bureaus became like fire and water.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day *jiǎshēn*,
Chéngdé Jūn reported that *Jiédùshǐ* Wáng Yuánkuí had died.
The army enthroned his son, *Jiédù Fùshǐ* Shàodǐng.
On the day *guǐmǎo*,
Shàodǐng was made Chéngdé Liúhòu.
2 In the second month,
Lǐ Jūnshì, Lǐquán Lìng, was appointed Huáizhōu Cìshǐ.
Initially,
the Emperor was hunting on the Wèi River.
About ten elders
gathered at a Buddhist temple.
The Emperor asked them,
and they replied,
"We are people of Lǐquán.
The county magistrate, Lǐ Jūnshì, has governed exceptionally well.
His term is full, and he is due to leave office.
We are going to the prefecture to beg for him to stay,
so we are praying to Buddha here,
hoping our wish will be granted."
When the position of Huáizhōu Cìshǐ became vacant,
the Emperor personally wrote the appointment of Jūnshì.
The chief ministers could not fathom it.
When Jūnshì came to express his thanks,
the Emperor used this to encourage him,
encouraging him with the words he had heard from the elders.
3 In the third month,
an edict ordered Bīnníng *Jiédùshǐ* Bì Xián to return to Bīnzhōu.
Previously,
because Hé and Huáng had recently submitted,
and the Dǎngxiàng were not yet pacified,
the Bīnníng army was moved to Níngzhōu.
This event is recorded in the third year of the previous scroll.
Xiān,
pronounced *xī jiàn fān*.
Both Nánshān and Píngxià
were peaceful.
The military provisions for Wēi, Yán, and Wǔ three prefectures were sufficient.
In the fifth year,
Wǔzhōu was established at Xiāoguān in Yuánzhōu.
Lǐsuǒ,
means administrative seat.
The Bīnníng army was originally based in Bīnzhōu,
one hundred twenty-five *lǐ* north to Níngzhōu.
4 In summer,
the intercalary fourth month,
an edict was issued stating,
"The distribution of corvée labor in prefectures and counties is unequal.
From now on, each county shall compile a *chākēbù* based on the wealth of the people and the lightness or heaviness of the labor,
send it to the *cìshǐ* for inspection and endorsement,
and then lock it in the magistrate's hall.
Whenever there is corvée labor, the magistrate shall be entrusted to determine
the assignment according to the *bù*."
The modern *chākēbù* began with this.
5 In the fifth month,
on the day *bǐngyín*,
Wáng Shàodǐng was appointed Chéngdé *Jiédùshǐ*.
6 The Emperor was observant and had a strong memory.
He could recognize the names of all the servants and cleaners in the palace,
and, knowing their talents and dispositions,
he would summon and employ them
without making any mistakes.
He memorized
the names of all the officials and jailers involved in legal cases throughout the empire
after a single glance.
When the Ministry of Finance submitted a memorial regarding stained silk,
they mistakenly wrote "清" (clear) instead of "漬" (stained).
Sūn Yǐnzhōng, the Secretariat Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, thinking the Emperor would not notice,
simply completed it.
In the late Táng dynasty,
Secretariat Directors of the Bureau of Military Affairs were filled by court clerks.
During the Five Dynasties, they were filled by generals of various guards.
In the Sòng dynasty, they were filled by scholars,
thus becoming a pure selection.
When a memorial from the Ministry of Finance was sent out from the inner court to the Central Secretariat,
the Central Secretariat would proclaim its endorsement and resubmit it.
After it was returned and presented to the Emperor,
this was called "fùrù" (resubmitting).
Those who arbitrarily altered memorials and reports were punished and demoted.
The Emperor secretly ordered Hànlín Academician Wéi Ào to compile a book detailing the geography, local products, and various advantages and disadvantages of the prefectures.
He wrote it himself and presented it,
without even his sons and brothers knowing.
It was called the Chǔfèn Yǔ (Words of Disposal).
Another day,
Xuē Hóngzōng, the Prefect of Dèngzhōu, came to express his gratitude.
Dèngzhōu
was nine hundred and thirty *lǐ* southeast of the capital.
He said to Wéi Ào,
"The Emperor's handling of our prefecture's affairs is astonishing."
Wéi Ào inquired,
and found that everything was from the Chǔfèn Yǔ.
While Wéi Ào was in the Hànlín Academy,
the Emperor would sometimes send an imperial envoy to convey an edict or draft a decree.
If there was anything objectionable,
Wéi Ào would say,
"This matter requires an imperial rescript
before I dare to implement it."
He would delay until dawn
and then present a memorial discussing it.
The Emperor usually followed his advice.
7 In autumn,
seventh month,
the Zhèdōng army mutinied,
expelling Surveillance Commissioner Lǐ Nà.
Lǐ Nà
was the nephew of Lǐ Xùn.
Lǐ Xùn is mentioned in volume 239, Táng Xiànzōng, Yuánhé 10th year.
He treated the generals and soldiers disrespectfully,
which caused the rebellion.
8 Huáinán suffered a famine,
and many people became refugees.
The Military Governor, Dù Cōng, was engrossed in feasting and entertainment,
and state affairs were neglected.
When the Emperor heard of this,
on *Jiǎwǔ*,
he appointed Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Cuī Xuàn as Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and concurrently as Military Governor of Huáinán.
On *Dīngyǒu*,
Dù Cōng was made Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince and a *fēnsī* official.
9 In the ninth month,
on *Yǐhài*,
Lǐ Nà was demoted to Prefect of Lǎngzhōu,
and Supervisor Wáng Zōngjǐng was given forty strokes of the cane
and exiled to Gōnglíng.
An edict was also issued stating,
"From now on, if a military official fails in discipline,
the supervisor will also be punished."
Shěn Xún, the Minister of Rites, was appointed Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèdōng.
Shěn Xún
was the son of Shěn Chuánshī.
Shěn Chuánshī
was the son of Shěn Jìjì.
10 In winter,
eleventh month,
Liǔ Zhòngyǐng, the Minister of Personnel, was appointed Minister of War
and concurrently Commissioner of Salt and Iron Monopolies.
There was a commoner physician, Liú Jí.
A commoner physician had no office in the Imperial Medical Bureau
and was not summoned to the Hànlín Academy,
but sold his medical skills among the populace.
Therefore, he was called a commoner physician.
The Emperor issued an edict to the Salt and Iron Commission to appoint him as a field official.
All copper, iron, and salt fields had officials overseeing them.
Liǔ Zhòngyǐng memorialized, "If a physician's skill is refined,
he should be appointed a medical official.
If he is entrusted with duties concerning copper and salt,
how can his performance be evaluated?
Moreover, a field official is of low rank,
not suitable for the Emperor's personal decree.
Your subject dares not obey the edict."
The Emperor immediately wrote in reply,
"Liú Jí should be granted a hundred bolts of silk
and sent away."
Another day,
he saw Liǔ Zhòngyǐng
and commended him, saying,
"Your discussion on Liú Jí's matter was excellent."
The Emperor once suffered from inability to eat.
He summoned the physician Liáng Xīn to diagnose his pulse.
After treating him for several days,
he recovered well.
Liáng Xīn then requested an official position for himself.
The Emperor did not permit it,
but simply ordered the Salt and Iron Commissioner to give him three thousand *qián*
monthly.
11 Kāng Jìróng, the Grand General of the Right Wēiguards, had previously been the Military Governor of Jīngyuán.
He embezzled two million *mín* of public money.
When the matter was discovered,
Kāng Jìróng requested to repay it with his family assets.
The Emperor considered Kāng Jìróng's merits in opening up the Hé and Huáng regions.
Kāng Jìróng's merits are mentioned in the previous volume, 3rd year.
The Supervising Secretary sealed and returned the imperial edict.

This was called "túguī" (crossing out and returning).
In the twelfth month,
on *Gēngchén*,
Kāng Jìróng was demoted to Chief Clerk of Kuízhōu.
Kuízhōu
was two thousand two hundred and forty-three *lǐ* south of the capital.

insistently sought a sinecure.
On *Jiǎwǔ*,
Zhèng Zhīdé was appointed Crown Prince's Guest and a *fēnsī* official.
Crown Prince's Guest
and a *fēnsī* official in the Eastern Capital.
1 In spring,
first month,
on *Dīngsì*,
Zhèng Lǎng, the Grand Censor, was appointed Minister of Public Works and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.

Péi Xiū requested that a Crown Prince be established early.
The Emperor said,
"If a Crown Prince is established,

Who would say that Táng Xuānzōng was discerning?
I do not believe it.

on *Bǐngxū*,
Péi Xiū resigned due to illness;
it was not permitted.

on *Xīnhài*,
an edict stated:

Meritorious service to the state
refers to suppressing Ān Lùshān and Shǐ Sīmíng.

There are no alarms on the northern border.

Yǐpánglì
is Mánglè,
