4 The Emperor, knowing that the Jīngzhào (京兆) region had long been misgoverned,
in summer,
the fifth month,
on the Dīngmǎo (丁卯) day,
appointed Wéi Ào (韋澳), a Hànlín Xuéshì (翰林學士) and Gōngbù Shìláng (工部侍郎), as Jīngzhào Yǐn (京兆尹).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The *Zhēnlíng Yíshì* (貞陵遺事) and *Dōngguān Zòujì* (東觀奏記) both state:
“The Emperor, seeing that Cuī Hǎn (崔罕) and Cuī Yǐng (崔郢) had both failed in their official duties,
personally appointed Ào (澳) as Jīngzhào Yǐn (京兆尹).”
According to the *Dàzhōng Zhìjí* (大中制集),
Ào (澳) replaced Hǎn (罕),
and Yǐng (郢) replaced Ào (澳).
Therefore, the statement that Hǎn (罕) and Yǐng (郢) both failed in their official duties
is incorrect.
Now, we follow the *Shílù* (實錄), *Xīnjì* (新紀), *Jiùjì* (舊紀), and *Xīnchuán* (新傳).
Once he took office,
the powerful and noble restrained themselves.
A steward of Zhèng Guāng's (鄭光) estate was oppressive and unruly,
and for years had failed to deliver the accumulated rent and taxes.
Ào (澳) arrested and shackled him.
The Emperor questioned Ào (澳) at Yán Yīng (延英).
Ào (澳) fully reported the situation.
The Emperor said:
“How do you intend to deal with him?”
Ào (澳) replied:
“I intend to apply the law.”
The Emperor said:
“Zhèng Guāng (鄭光) is very fond of him.
What about that?”
He replied:
“Your Majesty personally appointed me from the inner court to be Jīngzhào (京兆),
and the Hànlín Xuéshì Yuàn (翰林學士院) is in the inner court.
If Zhèng Guāng's (鄭光) estate steward, who has been a parasite for years,
is allowed to escape severe punishment,
it would mean Your Majesty’s law only applies to the poor.
I would not dare to accept such an edict.”
The Emperor said:
“That is truly so.
He meant that Wéi Ào's (韋澳) submission was indeed reasonable.
This statement was indeed influenced by the affection for the Empress Dowager’s relatives.
read *tā jì* (他計).
Could his death be pardoned?”
He replied:
“I dare not disobey the edict.
I wish that you would allow me to hold him for a while,
and release him only after the taxes have been fully collected.”
The Emperor said:
“That is clearly acceptable.
He meant Wéi Ào’s (韋澳) words
were clearly practicable.
I am deeply ashamed.”
Ào (澳) returned to the government office,
meaning the Jīngzhào Fǔ (京兆府).
He oversaw the collection of several hundred *hú* (斛) of grain,
and only then returned the steward to Guāng (光).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The *Dōngguān Zòujì* (東觀奏記) states:
“The Empress Dowager spoke to the Emperor on his behalf.
The Emperor questioned Ào (澳) at Yán Yīng (延英).
Ào (澳) fully reported the entire matter.
The Emperor said:
‘If the rent is paid today,
should he be released?’
Ào (澳) replied:
‘It is still within the deadline.
Tomorrow, it will not be permissible.’
The Emperor went in to report to the Empress Dowager, saying:
‘Wéi Ào (韋澳) cannot be defied.
Let us send money to pay it instead.’
Within moments, the rent was paid.”
Now we follow Liǔ Pín’s (柳玭) *Xù Zhēnlíng Yíshì* (續貞陵遺事).
5 In the sixth month,
on the Wùyín (戊寅) day,
Péi Xiū (裴休), Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事), was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事)
and made Xuānwǔ Jiédùshǐ (宣武節度使).
6 Wéi Jǐn (韋厪), Sīnóng Qīng (司農卿), desired the Xìazhōu Jiédùshǐ (夏州節度使) position.
A diviner, knowing this,
came to Jǐn’s (厪) gate and said:
“I am skilled at propitiating the stars;
no official position I seek goes unfulfilled.”
Jǐn (厪) believed him.
At night,
he set up the sacrificial offerings in the courtyard.
The diviner said:
“Please write your official rank once yourself.”
After receiving it,
he shouted to the sky:
“Wéi Jǐn (韋厪) has a rebellious intention,
ordering me to sacrifice to Heaven.”
Jǐn's (厪) entire household bowed and wept, saying:
“We beg you, mountain man, to spare the lives of a hundred mouths!”
They gave him all the household’s valuables and treasures.
The patrolmen, surprised by the diviner’s bright clothes,
arrested him as a thief.
The diviner, in distress,
said:
“Wéi Jǐn (韋厪) ordered me to sacrifice to Heaven.
I wanted to report him, but he begged me with his family’s wealth.”
The matter reached the Emperor.
In autumn,
the ninth month,
the Emperor summoned Jǐn (厪) and personally interrogated him.
Fully understanding his innocence,
he said to the Chancellor:
“Wéi Jǐn (韋厪) is a prominent family from the south of the capital.
In the south of the capital,
the Wéi (韋) and Dù (杜) families resided,
thus called Wéiqū (韋曲) and Dùqū (杜曲).
The saying goes:
‘Wéi (韋) and Dù (杜) of the city’s south,
are a foot and five inches from Heaven.’
Do not let the prison guards humiliate him.”
He immediately handed the diviner over to Jīngzhào (京兆),
who was flogged to death,
and demoted Jǐn (厪) to Yǒngzhōu Sīmǎ (永州司馬).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The *Dōngguān Zòujì* (東觀奏記) and *Shílù* (實錄) state:
Sīnóng Qīng (司農卿) Wéi Jǐn (韋厪) was demoted to Yǒngzhōu Sīmǎ (永州司馬);
because Jǐn (厪) secretly ordered the diviner to perform black magic at night,
the Yùshǐ Tái (御史臺) impeached and reported him.
Fàn Xù’s (范攄) *Yúnxī Yǒuyì* (雲谿友議) says: Tàipú Qīng (太僕卿) Wéi Jǐn (韋厪) desired the Xìazhōu Jiédùshǐ (夏州節度使) position, etc.,
and was demoted to Pānzhōu Sīmǎ (潘州司馬).
Now, the official title follows the *Dōngguān Zòujì* (東觀奏记) and *Shílù* (實錄),
while the account of the event is taken from *Yúnxī Yǒuyì* (雲谿友議).
7 Zhèng Hào (鄭顥), Hùbù Shìláng (戶部侍郎), Pàn Hùbù (判戶部), and Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉) —
from the mid-Táng (唐) dynasty onwards,
the empire's finances and taxes all belonged to the Hùbù (戶部).
Du Zhī (度支) and Yán Tiě (鹽鐵) were often managed by other officials.
A Hùbù Shìláng (戶部侍郎) who also served as Pàn Hùbù (判戶部) thus gained knowledge of the Hùbù (戶部) department's income and expenditure of money, goods, grain, and silk.
A Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉) was one who married a princess.
His father, Zhīdé (祗德),
wrote to him, saying:
“I hear you have already been appointed Pàn Hùbù (判戶部);
this is the year of my certain death.
I also hear you desire to become Chancellor;
that will be the day of my certain death!”
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: Liú Chóngyuǎn’s (劉崇遠) *Jīnhuázǐ Zábiān* (金華子雜編):
“Once Hào (顥) was Pàn Hùbù (判戶部),
he pursued high official positions very eagerly.
At that time, my late father was still stationed in Shāndōng (山東).
Upon hearing this,
he sent a letter to Hào (顥)”
and so on.
According to the *Shílù* (實錄),
in the twelfth month of the ninth year,
Hào’s (顥) father, Zhīdé (祗德), was a Bīnkè (賓客) and Fēnsī (分司).
The *Jīnhuázǐ* (金華子) stating he was stationed in Shāndōng (山東)
is incorrect.
He repeatedly submitted memorials to resign from arduous duties.
The duties of the Hùbù (戶部) were numerous and complex.
In the tenth month,
on the Yǐyǒu (乙酉) day,
Hào (顥) was appointed Mìshū Jiān (祕書監).
8 The Emperor sent an envoy to Ānxī (安西) to pacify the Huíhú (回鶻) envoys.
Upon reaching Língwǔ (靈武),
it happened that the Huíhú Khagan had sent envoys to offer tribute.
In the eleventh month,
on the Xīnhài (辛亥) day,
he was formally invested as Wòlù Dēnglǐ Luórì Mò Mìshī Hégūlù Pígā Huáijiàn Kèhán (嗢祿登里羅日沒密施合俱錄毗伽懷建可汗),
with Wèi Wèi Shàogīng (衞尉少卿) Wáng Duānzhāng (王端章) serving as the envoy.
9 Lǐ Jǐngrang (李景讓), Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書), submitted a memorial saying:
“Mùzōng (穆宗) was Your Majesty’s elder brother,
and Jìngzōng (敬宗), Wénzōng (文宗), and Wǔzōng (武宗) were sons of your elder brother.
It is permissible for Your Majesty to bow to your elder brother,
but is it permissible to bow to your nephews?
This prevents Your Majesty from personally serving the Seven Temples.
It is fitting to move the spirit tablets of the four rulers out of the Tàimiào (太廟).
The four rulers
refer to the spirit tablets of Mùzōng (穆宗), Jìngzōng (敬宗), Wénzōng (文宗), and Wǔzōng (武宗).
An edict commanded all officials to deliberate on the matter,
but it was not resolved and thus halted.
People at the time regarded Jǐngrang (景讓) lightly because of this.
They looked down on him for pandering to the Emperor’s desires.
10 An imperial decree
stated: “Set up ordination platforms in the Línggǎn (靈感) and Huìshàn (會善) monasteries.
Monks
and nuns who need to fill vacancies are to be selected by elder monks.
They will be issued official certificates
to go to the two platforms to receive ordination.
From the two capitals, ten eminent monks (Dàdé, 大德) shall be chosen to oversee the matter.
A monk who is capable of upholding precepts and practicing asceticism is called a Dàdé (大德).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: According to Táng (唐) regulations, monasteries have Gāngwéi (綱維) and Dàdé (大德);
the Dàdé (大德) is in charge of teaching.
Those who are qualified will be issued a certificate
and sent back to their home prefectures.
Without an official certificate from the ordination platform,
no one is allowed to be privately accommodated.
Furthermore, old monks and nuns should be selected first.
If there are no qualified old monks and nuns,
then outsiders may be selected.”
2 At first,
Líu Zhuàn, Minister of Revenue and Fiscal Commissioner,
was a Hanlin Academician,
and the Emperor deeply valued him.
At the time, he was the Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng,
and the Emperor issued an imperial edict summoning him to court.
Zhuàn reported his departure from Hédōng,
and only then did outsiders become aware of it.
On the day Wùwǔ,
Zhuàn was made Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
The 'Kǎo Yì' states: The 'Dōngguān Zòujì' says:
"In the eleventh year,
the Emperor issued an imperial edict recalling him.
Upon his arrival,
he was appointed Minister of Revenue and Fiscal Commissioner.
On the seventeenth day of the twelfth month,
during an audience,
the Emperor handed Zhuàn the imperial calendar,
instructing him to choose an auspicious day in the latter half of the month.
Zhuàn did not comprehend the Emperor's intention,
so the Emperor said: 'Just choose a day for an official appointment.'
Zhuàn knelt and reported: 'The twenty-fifth day is very good.'
The Emperor smiled and said: 'On that day, I shall appoint you as Prime Minister.'
This was kept secret,
and no one in the world knew.
Gāo Shí was an aide in Fèngxiáng,
and Shí was an old subordinate of Zhuàn.
On the twenty-fourth day,
he bade farewell to Zhuàn at his private residence in Xuānpínglǐ.
Shí said: 'I estimate that in a few days,
you will surely meet the expectations of all.'
Zhuàn smiled and said: 'It will be tomorrow that I meet everyone's expectations,
why wait a few days!'
Shí dared not speak.
The next morning,
he was indeed appointed,
and only then was this matter leaked to Shí."
The 'Shílù' and 'Zhuàn Zhuàn' state:
"On the seventeenth day of the first month of the following year,
during an audience,
the Emperor handed Zhuàn the calendar,
instructing him to choose an auspicious day.
Zhuàn knelt and reported: the twenty-fifth day."
We follow this now.
He was the fifth-generation descendant of Rén Guǐ.
Líu Rén'guǐ served Gāozōng and Empress Wǔ,
entering and exiting as both general and prime minister.
Zhuàn and Cuī Shènyóu discussed state affairs before the Emperor.
Shènyóu said:
"We should only differentiate between ranks and classes,
to repay even a small part of your grace."
Zhuàn said:
"In the past, Wáng Yífǔ (Wáng Yǎn, styled Yífǔ, of the Jìn dynasty)
advocated superficiality,
leading to the desolation of the central plains.
Now, in this glorious era,
we should adhere to names and demand substance,
making each official live up to their position;
if we hastily prioritize ranks and classes,
I do not know when the day of good governance will come!"
Shènyóu had no reply.
3 Xuānyuán Jí arrived in Cháng'ān.
The Emperor summoned him into the forbidden palace
and asked:
"Can longevity be learned?"
He replied:
"If a ruler suppresses desires and promotes virtue,
then they will naturally receive great
and lasting blessings.
Why seek longevity elsewhere!"
He stayed for several months,
then firmly requested to return to the mountains,
and so he was allowed to leave.
Xuānyuán Jí's request to return
was a lesson from the events at the end of the Huìchāng reign.
4 In the second month,
on the first day, Jiǎzǐ,
the court nobles were excused from paying respects at Guānglíng and from offering incense on memorial days,
and all palace women were moved to the imperial mausoleums.
This was due to assigning the crime of Chén Hóngzhì's regicide to Mùzōng.
In the early Táng dynasty,
emperors had the rite of visiting the mausoleums.
If the Son of Heaven did not personally visit,
then the Grand Master of Ceremonies would perform the rites at the mausoleums.
In the fifth year of Xiǎnqìng under Gāozōng,
an edict decreed that for the annual spring and autumn inspections,
the Three Ducal Ministers should perform the rites at the mausoleums,
with the Junior Minister of Ceremonies as their deputy.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies was to provide the imperial equipage,
and this was recorded in the statutes.
Initially,
the Zhēnguān rites stipulated annual inspections of the mausoleums in the middle months of spring and autumn.
By the time of Empress Wǔ,
envoys were sent to the mausoleums to pay respects on the middle months of the four seasons, on birthdays, and on memorial days.
In the fourth year of Zhēnyuán,
Bāo Jí, Libationer of the Directorate of Education, stated:
"In the second and eighth months of each year,
the court nobles pay respects at the imperial mausoleums.
Those in charge of the mausoleum administration
escort them to the mausoleums,
but the rites are cursory
and fail to fully express reverence."
Thereupon, the Grand Master of Ceremonies drafted a ceremony based on the old rites,
which the court nobles and various officials performed in sequence,
paying their respects and returning.
Offering incense on memorial days
refers to the rite of paying respects at the mausoleums.
There was also the rite of offering incense at Buddhist monasteries on memorial days.
Sòng Bái said: According to the Táng system, when offering incense on national memorial days,
it was initially only performed at monasteries and Daoist temples in the capital city.
In the fifth year of Zhēnyuán,
in the eighth month,
an edict commanded that all superior prefectures throughout the empire should perform the rite of offering incense according to the prescribed form on national memorial days.
Whenever emperors passed away,
palace women who had no children were all sent to the imperial mausoleums to serve day and night,
providing washing and combing,
arranging bedding,
serving the dead as if they were alive.
5 On the day Wùchén,
Cuī Shènyóu, Minister of the Central Secretariat and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Dōngchuān.
The 'Kǎo Yì' states: The 'Táng Quē Shǐ' says:
"One day, Prime Minister Grand Preceptor Cuī Gōng was consulted in the private palace.
The Emperor wanted to ascend the tower to issue a general amnesty.
The Grand Preceptor reported thus and so.
A few days later,
he was dismissed from managing state affairs."
The 'Jiù Zhuàn' says:
"Initially,
Shènyóu and Xiāo Yè were both in the Hanlin Academy,
but their relations were not harmonious.
When Shènyóu became prime minister,
he dismissed Yè as an academician.
Soon after, Yè became Fiscal Commissioner,
and Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
enjoying great imperial favor.
Yè brought Zhuàn in to manage state affairs together,
and then sent Shènyóu out to Dōngchuān."
The 'Dōngguān Zòujì' says:
"After Líu Zhuàn became prime minister,
he discussed state affairs with Shènyóu before the Emperor.
Shènyóu said: 'We should only differentiate between ranks and classes.'
Zhuàn said thus and so.
Shènyóu could not reply.
Consequently, his imperial favor gradually waned,
and he was soon dismissed as prime minister to become Jìedùshǐ of Dōngchuān,
losing his Tóng Píngzhāngshì title."
We follow 'Táng Quē Shǐ' now.
The Emperor wished to ascend the tower to issue a general amnesty.
In the early Táng,
emperors resided in the Western Palace,
and usually issued amnesties from the Chéngtiānmén Tower.
From Gāozōng onwards,
emperors resided in the Eastern Palace,
and usually issued amnesties from the Dānfèngmén Tower.
Ascending the tower incurs vast expenses and must be done for a worthy reason;
moreover, amnesties should not be too frequent."
According to the Táng system, whenever the Emperor ascended the tower to issue an amnesty,
the six armies and twelve guards all received rewards,
hence it is said that "it incurs vast expenses."
Líu Wēnsǒu said: By custom,
unless there was a major pardon, the Emperor would not ascend the tower,
and both military and commoners would receive grants.
(The character "數" here means "frequent".)
He said:
"How can I acquire a worthy reason!"
Shènyóu said:
"Your Majesty has not yet established an heir apparent,
and the four seas are looking forward to it.
If this rite is performed,
even the suburban sacrifices would be appropriate,
let alone ascending the tower!"
At that time, the Emperor was taking elixirs from Daoist practitioners,
and already felt agitated and thirsty,
but outsiders did not know.
His suspicions and jealousy were deep,
and upon hearing this,
he bowed his head and said nothing more.
Historians say that Xuānzōng did not establish the national foundation early enough,
allowing Wáng Zōngshí to establish the eldest son and usurp the merit of setting the succession.
(The character "復" here means "again" or "moreover".)
Shènyóu was dismissed as prime minister.
6 Bóhǎi Wáng Yízhèn died.
On the day Guǐwèi,
his younger brother Qiánhuǎng was made King of Bóhǎi.
7 Summer,
fourth month.
Líu Yì, Commander of the Right Street and Imperial Son-in-Law Commandant, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Bīnníng.
The Commanders of the Left and Right Streets, along with the Generals of the Left and Right Jīnwǔ,
were in charge of separately inspecting the six streets and patrolling. (This refers to the Emperor's sister.)
8 On the day of Gēngzǐ,
Wáng Lìnghuán (王令寰), a commander in Lǐngnán (嶺南), rebelled,
imprisoning Jíedùshǐ (節度使) Yáng Fā (楊發).
Fā
was from Sūzhōu (蘇州).
9 On the day of Wùshēn,
Xiàhóu Zī (夏侯孜), Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng, 兵部侍郎) and Commissioner of Salt and Iron Monopolies (Yántiě Zhuǎnyùnshǐ, 鹽鐵轉運使), was made a Grand Chancellor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì, 同平章事).
10 In the fifth month,
on the day of Bǐngyín,
Liú Zhuàn (劉瑑), Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū, 工部尚書) and Grand Chancellor, passed away.
Even when critically ill, Zhuàn
still wrote memorials discussing affairs,
and the Emperor deeply regretted his loss.
11 Lǐ Suì (李燧), Right General-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards (Yòu Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn, 右金吾大將軍), was appointed Jíedùshǐ of Lǐngnán.
An imperial envoy had already been dispatched to bestow upon him the credentials,
but Jǐshìzhōng (給事中) Xiāo Fǎng (蕭倣) returned the imperial edict sealed.
The Emperor was then listening to music
and did not have time to summon another imperial envoy,
so he sent an entertainer to chase after him.
The credentials returned just as they reached Suì’s gate.
The “Kǎoyì” (考異) states: This comes from the Dōngguān Zòujì (東觀奏記),
but it is not known when Suì (璲) was appointed to Lǐngnán.
According to the “Shílù” (實錄),
in the ninth year of Dàzhōng (大中),
Wéi Shǔ (韋曙) was appointed Jíedùshǐ of Lǐngnán.
He died in the first month of this year,
and Yáng Fā (楊發) replaced him.
In the third month,
Xiāo Fǎng spoke of Liǔ Guī (柳珪).
In the fourth month,
Suì (璲) was transferred from Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng Qīng, 司農卿) to Right General-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards.
In the fifth month,
news of the Lǐngnán rebellion was heard.
It was likely then that Suì was appointed to Lǐngnán;
and Fǎng returned the edict
because he considered Suì not to be a talent for quelling unrest.
It is placed here now.
He was the paternal cousin of Fú (俛).
Xiāo Fú (蕭俛)
served as chancellor at the beginning of Mùzōng’s (穆宗) Chángqìng (長慶) reign.
On the day of Xīnsì,
Lǐ Chéngxūn (李承勛), Jíedùshǐ of Jīngyuán (涇原), was appointed Jíedùshǐ of Lǐngnán.
Troops from neighboring circuits were dispatched to suppress the rebels,
and they pacified the region.
12 On this day,
the Húnán (湖南) army mutinied.
Commander Shí Zàishùn (石載順) and others expelled the Commissioner (Guānchásǐ, 觀察使) Hán Cōng (韓悰)
and killed Commander-in-Chief of the Guards (Dūyāyá, 都押牙) Wáng Guìzhí (王桂直).
Cōng had treated his officers and soldiers disrespectfully,
which led to this misfortune.
13 In the sixth month,
on the day of Bǐngshēn,
the Jiāngxī (江西) army mutinied.
Commander Máo Hè (毛鶴) expelled the Commissioner Zhèng Xiàn (鄭憲).
14 Initially,
Lǐ Zhuō (李涿), Protector-General of Ānnán (安南 Dūhù).
The “Kǎoyì” states: In the “Shílù,”
it is sometimes written as
"Zhuó" (琢)
and sometimes as
"Zhuō" (涿).
Fán Chuò’s (樊綽) “Mán Shū” (蠻書) also writes
"Zhuō."
Both the “Shílù” and the “Xīnshū” (新書) contain biographies of Lǐ Zhuó (李琢), who was the son of Tīng (聽).
In the third year of Dàzhōng,
he was appointed Jíedùshǐ of Yìchāng (義昌) from Governor (Cìshǐ, 刺史) of Míngzhōu (洺州).
In the ninth year,
ninth month,
he was appointed Jíedùshǐ of Pínglú (平盧) from General of the Imperial Guards (Jīnwú Jiāngjūn, 金吾將軍),
but it does not say he ever served as Protector-General of Ānnán.
Given that the position of Protector-General (Dūhù) was low-ranking,
and since Zhuó (琢) was already Jíedùshǐ of Yìchāng,
he should not have been Protector-General.
It is suspected that the one who served as Protector-General was a different Lǐ Zhuō (李涿),
not the son of Tīng.
forcibly purchased horses and cattle from the Mán (蠻) people,
giving only one *dǒu* (斗) of salt for one head;
he also killed the Mán chief Dù Cúnchéng (杜存誠).
All the Mán people harbored resentment and anger,

The “Kǎoyì” states: The “Jiù Jì” (舊紀) says:

In Fēngzhōu (峯州) there was Línxī Yuán (林西原).
Fēngzhōu was northwest of Ānnán,

In the south, there were hot, malarial vapors (yánzhàng, 炎瘴),

the vapors lessened.
The Mán took advantage of this time to raid,

Their chief was Lǐ Yóudú (李由獨),

The Administrator (Zhīzhōu, 知州) of Fēngzhōu spoke to Zhuō (涿),

The Jíedùshǐ of Tuòdōng (拓東) of Nánzhào lured him with a letter,
marrying his son to the Jíedùshǐ’s niece
and appointing him as an escort officer (Yāyá, 押牙) in Tuòdōng.
Yóudú then led his people to submit to Nánzhào.
From then on, Ānnán began to suffer from Mán incursions;
in this month,
the Mán raided Ānnán.
The “Kǎoyì” states: The “Shílù” does not mention the year and month of Zhuō’s appointment to Ānnán.
The “Mán Shū” says:
"In the eighth year of Dàzhōng,
the Protector-General of Ānnán, Tǎn (⿰⺘亶), disbanded the winter garrisons in Línxī Yuán.
The cave chiefs (Dòngzhǔ, 洞主) Lǐ Yóudú and seven other chieftain leaders (wǎnshǒulǐng, 綰首領) were enticed by the Mán,
re-established kinship ties,
and through daily visits and monthly interactions,
gradually suffered encroachment."
It also says:
"The Táohuā Mán (桃花蠻), originally under Yóudú’s jurisdiction,
also served as border garrisons.
Since the eighth year of Dàzhōng,
the Zhīzhōu of Fēngzhōu presented a memorial to Lǐ Zhuō (李涿),
requesting to disband the six thousand winter defense soldiers
and not to establish defenses along the borders of Wèi (味), Zhēn (真), and Dēng (登) prefectures.
Yóudú and his brothers were unable to resist,
and the Mán Jíedùshǐ of Zhàdōng (柘東) sent letters,
marrying his niece to Yóudú’s youngest son,
and appointing him as an escort officer in Zhàdōng.
From then on, all seven Wǎn caves were taken over by the Mán."
The “Jiù Jì” states:
"In the eleventh month of the fourth year of Xiántōng (咸通),
Liú Tuì (劉蛻) and others stated: Línghú Táo (令狐綯) accepted bribes from Lǐ Zhuō (李涿) for his appointment to Ānnán,
which led to the Mán incursions."
The “Shílù” states:
"In the sixth month of the second year of Xiántōng,
an imperial edict said: 'It is heard that during Lǐ Zhuó’s (李琢) time in Ānnán,
he killed Dù Cúnchéng,
and his greed and cruelty were quite excessive,
causing resentment among the valleys and caves.'"
According to this,
it is clear
that Mán incursions were originally caused by Lǐ Zhuó’s (李涿) greed, cruelty, and lack of strategy.
However, from the eighth to the eleventh year of Dàzhōng,
neither the “Jiù Jì” nor the “Shílù” mention the Mán as a border threat.
This is probably because there were only minor raids and thefts along the border at the time,
and they did not dare to attack prefectures and counties;
it was only when they attacked Ānnán at this point
that the “Jiù Jì” and “Shílù” began to record it.
It is also not known if this raid on Ānnán was the same as what Zhèng Yán (鄭言) referred to in his "Píng Yǎnlù" (平剡錄) as having reached Jǐntián Bù (錦田步).

"Whenever a provincial government (fānfǔ, 藩府) changes hands,

using the surplus as a measure of their performance,
and the court accordingly commends and rewards them.
I humbly submit that the financial resources of a provincial government
have a fixed origin.
Unless there are excessive levies,
or the dismissal of officers and soldiers,
or the reduction of their provisions and rations,
how can there be any surplus?!
The recent unrest in several southern circuits
is all due to this reason.
Once a change occurs,
all the accumulated wealth is plundered;
moreover, dispatching troops to suppress the rebellion
incurs a hundredfold expense.
In that case, what benefit does the court ultimately gain?!
I beg that from now on, provincial chief officials (chánglì, 長吏)
shall not increase levies,
nor reduce rations and stipends,
but only restrict banquets and entertainment
and economize on extravagant expenses.
Only those who can then achieve a surplus
should be rewarded."
The Emperor praised and accepted this.

Táo's heavy robes were soaked with sweat.

8 Hé Hóngjìng [何弘敬], the Jiédùshǐ [節度使] of Wèibó [魏博], was additionally appointed Jiān Zhōngshūlìng [兼中書令].
*Kǎoyì* [考異] says: *Dōngguān Zòujì* [東觀奏記]:

*Dōngguān Zòujì* [東觀奏記] is incorrect.
9 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Xīnmǎo [辛卯],

10 In the eleventh month,
on the day Wùwǔ [戊午],
Xiāo Yè [蕭鄴], Mènxià Shìláng [門下侍郎] and Tóng Píngzhāngshì [同平章事], was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì [同平章事]

11th of the twelfth month,
on the day Jiǎshēn,
Dù Shěnguán (杜審權), Hanlin Academician Serving as Chief (Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ) and Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng), was appointed as Co-equal to the Grand Councilor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì).
Shěnguán

Dù Yuányǐng,

Sūn Miǎn (孫愐) said: "Qiú (裘)
was originally Chóu (仇).

'Qiú' (裘)."

In the first year of Shénlóng (神龍),
Xiàngshān County (象山縣) was established by dividing Nínghǎi (寧海) and Mào (鄮).

In the second year of Guǎngdé (廣德),

Shuài (帥),

We follow this.
The gates of Míngzhōu city were closed during the day.

Yǎn

Zhèdōng was in turmoil.
The Regional Commander (Guānchásǐ) Zhèng Zhīdé (鄭祗德) dispatched the Deputy Commander of Punitive Expeditions (Tǎojī Fùshǐ) Liú Qíng (劉勍)
and Deputy General (Fùjiàng) Fàn Jūzhí (范居植) with three hundred soldiers,

13th. The Grand Chancellor (Sīkōng), Minister of the Left (Ménxià Shìláng), and Co-equal to the Grand Councilor, Línghú Táo (令狐綯), had been in power for many years.
He was jealous of those who surpassed him,
causing concern both within and outside the court.
His son, Línghú Hào (令狐滈), frequently abused his power and accepted bribes.
After Emperor Xuānzōng (宣宗) passed away,
officials eagerly attacked his shortcomings.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
Táo, as Co-equal to the Grand Councilor,
was appointed Military Commissioner of Hézhong (Hézhōng Jiédùshǐ).

Bái Mǐnzhōng (白敏中), formerly Military Commissioner of Jīngnán (Jīngnán Jiédùshǐ) and Co-equal to the Grand Councilor, was appointed Grand Councilor (Sītú) and concurrently Minister of the Left (Ménxià Shìláng) and Co-equal to the Grand Councilor.
14th. Originally,
Wéi Gāo (韋皋) in Xīchuān
opened the Qīngxī Road (青溪道) to communicate with the Mán (蠻) barbarians.
The Qīngxī Road was the Qīngxī Pass (Qīngxī Guān) road.
He also selected Mán children and gathered them in Chéngdū (成都),
teaching them writing and arithmetic,
intending to comfort, please, and control them.
Once their studies were complete, they would leave,
and other children would replace them.
This continued for fifty years.
Nearly a thousand Mán children studied in Chéngdū,
and the military administration grew tired of providing for them.
Furthermore,
when Mán envoys came to pay tribute,
they benefited from the gifts and favors,
and the number of retainers accompanying them gradually increased.
When Dù Cóng (杜悰) was Military Commissioner of Xīchuān,
he submitted a memorial requesting a reduction in their number.
An imperial edict approved it.
Fēngyòu (豐祐) of Nánzhào (南詔) was angered.
His envoy for the winter festival left a memorial at Cuīzhōu (巂州) and returned.
He also demanded the return of the Mán students.
His official communication was insolent.
From then on, tribute was not paid on time,
and the border was frequently disturbed.
Coincidentally, Emperor Xuānzōng passed away,
and a palace envoy was sent to announce the mourning.
At that time, Fēngyòu of Nánzhào had just died,
and his son Qíulóng (酋龍) ascended the throne.
He angrily said:
"My country also has a bereavement,
but the imperial court does not send condolences.
Furthermore, the imperial edict was bestowed upon the late king."
So he housed the envoy in an outer guest house,
treating him very shabbily.
When the envoy returned,
he reported the situation in full.
The Emperor noted that Qíulóng did not send an envoy to announce the mourning,
and also that his name was close to Emperor Xuánzōng's (玄宗) taboo name (Huì).
The character Lóng (龍) was close to Emperor Xuánzōng's taboo name.
Qíulóng then declared himself emperor,
establishing the state of Dàlǐ (大禮).
To this day, the state of Yúnnán (雲南) is called Dàlǐ.
He dispatched troops and captured Bōzhōu (播州).
This laid the groundwork for Nánzhào's attacks on Shǔ (蜀) and Jiāozhǐ (交趾).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: "Neither the *Jiù Jì* (舊紀) nor the *Shílù* records the capture of Bōzhōu in this year.
Only the *Xīn Jì* (新紀) has it.
The *Shílù* states:
'In the third month of the sixth year of Xiántōng (咸通),
Lú Pān (盧潘) reported: in the thirteenth year of Dàzhōng (大中),
the Southern Mán captured Bōzhōu.' "
The *Bǔ Guó Shǐ* (補國史) says:
"From the beginning of Dàzhōng, the number of tribute envoys and hostage princes from Yúnnán in Xīchuān gradually increased.
The Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) memorialized a request for reform and reduction,
and an imperial edict permitted it.
The edict was recorded and sent to Yúnnán,
and Yúnnán's reply was insolent."
The *Xīn Nánzhào Zhuàn* (新南詔傳) says: "Tribute arrived annually,
and many followers accompanied it.
Dù Cóng (杜悰), upon entering the court from Xīchuān,
memorialized that there should not be too many Mán retainers admitted.
Fēngyòu (豐祐) was angered,
and immediately insolently demanded the hostage princes,
referring to the Mán children studying in Chéngdū."
However, Dù Cóng entered the court in the tenth month of the second year of Xiántōng,
and Fēngyòu had already died in the thirteenth year of Dàzhōng.
Therefore, the proposal to reduce Mán retainers
could not have occurred after Cóng's entry to court.
The *Xīn Zhuàn* is mistaken.

First Year of Xiántōng (咸通)

In the eleventh month of this year,
the reign title was changed to Xiántōng.
1st. Spring,
first month,

Tóngbǎi Guān is located on Tiāntái Mountain (天台山) in Tángxīng County (唐興縣), Táizhōu.
During the Sòng (宋) dynasty, Tángxīng County was renamed Tiāntái County.
Tóngbǎi Guān was bestowed the plaque Chóngdào Guān (崇道觀).
Guān (觀),

On the day Yǐchǒu,

Yuèzhōu was greatly alarmed.
At that time, the Two Zhè (二浙) regions had long been peaceful.
People were unaccustomed to warfare.
Weapons and armor were rusty and dull,
and existing troops numbered less than three hundred.
Zhèng Zhīdé further recruited new soldiers to augment them.
However, military officials accepted bribes,

Zhīdé dispatched his son, the Junior General (Zǐjiàng) Shěn Jūnchóng (沈君縱), Deputy General (Fùjiàng) Zhāng Gōngshǔ (張公署), and Wanghǎi Town General (Wànghǎi Zhèn Jiàng) Lǐ Guī (李珪).
Zǐjiàng,
a junior general.
Wanghǎi Town is in Míngzhōu territory.
Today's Dìnghǎi County (定海縣) is that place.
In the fourteenth year of Yuánhé (元和),
Xuē Róng (薛戎), Regional Commander of Zhèdōng, memorialized that Wanghǎi Town was over seventy *lǐ* from Míngzhōu,
overlooking the vast sea,

Jiàng (將),

One stream comes from the east of Xīnchāng County (新昌縣),

When they were halfway across,

All three generals died,

gathered from all sides like clouds.
Their numbers reached thirty thousand,

Among the minor chieftains, Liú Wǎng (劉暀) was chosen for his strategy,

then even generous provisions are taken for granted and not seen as benevolence by the officers and soldiers.
*Duò*,

(He ordered them) to fight the rebels;

At night, they sat awaiting dawn,

Even a Confucian scholar,
Wáng Shì,

The *tàizǐ bīnkè*
was an idle official.

on the *xīnhài* day, the first day of the month,

The Emperor asked him about his strategy for suppressing the rebels.

"Your servant, in regretting the expense for the state, would not say that.
If there are many troops, the rebels will be defeated quickly,

If there are too few troops to defeat the rebels,

Then, the bandits in Jiāng and Huái will rise up like bees to respond.
The state's expenditures all rely on Jiāng and Huái.
If communication is cut off,
then from the Nine Ancestral Temples above,
down to the Ten Armies below,
After Sùzōng,

the Shénwǔ Army was abolished.
The following year,

but the name "Ten Armies" remained.
How can their expenses be calculated!"
The Emperor looked at the eunuch and said:

Qiú Fǔ divided his forces to plunder Qú and Wùzhōu.
Wùzhōu's *yāyá* Fáng Zhì and *sǎnjiàng* Lóu Céng

*Sǎn*,

The rebels could not enter.

The people of Míngzhōu consulted each other, saying:
"If the rebels enter the city,

prepared weapons,

During the Wú period, the western boundary of Zhāng'ān was set up as Shǐpíng Xiàn.

Wherever they went, they captured the young and strong,

When the generals returned to Yuè,

The generals then requested, saying:
"We grew up in the army,

This year we had the privilege of following your Excellency to defeat the bandits,

Wáng Shì said:
"This is easy to understand.
The bandits gathered grain to tempt the hungry;
if we provide them with food,
then they will not become bandits.
Furthermore, the various counties had no defending soldiers;

the grain in the granaries would have merely served to provision them."
They asked again:
"Why did you not set up beacons and signal fires?"
Wáng Shì said:
"Beacons and signal fires are for summoning relief troops,

they would only startle the soldiers and common people,
causing them to collapse into chaos on their own."
They asked again:
"Why did you use timid soldiers as scout cavalry and give them few weapons?"
Wáng Shì said:
"If brave soldiers wield sharp weapons,
when they encounter the enemy, they will fight without assessing their strength;
if they die in battle,

Everyone said:
"This is beyond our comprehension!"
From the Zhìdé reign period onwards,

Now, Wáng Shì's suppression of Qiú Fǔ

This is probably because after the middle period of the Táng dynasty,
families kept private histories.
Wáng Shì
was a scholar's son;
after his success,
those who recorded the events could not help but exaggerate.
The *Tōngjiàn* followed their texts and arranged them,
without realizing their redundancy.
Róngzhāi Suíbǐ says: The *Tōngjiàn* used *Píng Shàn Lù* to record the events of suppressing Qiú Fǔ,
which likely also noted this.
The *Kǎoyì* in thirty volumes,
where discussions and corrections of Táng events account for more than half,
is also due to the multitude of Táng private histories.

Déyù's demotion is found in volume 248, Xuānzōng's Dàzhōng first year.
Kǎoyì says: Péi Dàn's Lǐ Tàiwèi Nánxíng Lù [Record of Grand Commandant Lǐ's Southern Journey]
contains a memorial by Right Shíyí and Nèigōngfèng Liú Yè, dated the 26th day of the ninth month of Xiántōng second year,
which broadly states:
"My son Yè,
who was demoted to Lìshān Wèi,
last year received His Majesty's decree of renewal,
extending the grace of release,
and was transferred to Chēnxiàn Wèi.
He has now died at the place of his demotion."
It also says:
"His blood relatives are already gone,
his family property is entirely depleted."
It also says:
"His dry bones have not yet returned to their tomb,
and his one son has also perished in the Jiāng and Xiāng rivers."
It also says:
"Regarding Lǐ Déyù,
I request a special posthumous grant of an official position."
The edict stated "granted as memorialized."
The annotation in Shílù [Veritable Records] cites Dōngguān Zòujì [Records of Memorials from the Eastern Bureau] as saying:
"Prime Minister Línghú Táo dreamt that Déyù said: 'I have already departed this enlightened era.
I hope that Your Excellency will have pity on me
and allow me to be buried in my homeland.'
Táo related this in detail to Déyù's son, Hào.
Hào said: 'Lǐ Wèigōng incurred public wrath,
and Prime Minister Cuī Xuàn and Prime Minister Wèi Mó are both his enemies.
As they currently hold power,
they will certainly raise objections before the Emperor.
It is not yet possible to speak of this.'
A few days later,
when the Emperor was about to sit in Yányīng [Hall],
Táo again dreamt that Déyù said: 'My bones are scattered on the sea,
and I yearn to return to my homeland.
As I have an old acquaintance with Your Excellency,
I hope you will pity me and grant this.'
Upon waking,
he again said to Hào: 'Just now, the spirit of Wèigōng still appeared formidable.
If I do not speak,
I will certainly incur misfortune.
Tomorrow, when I enter the Zhongshū [Provincial Secretariate],
I will speak of this to my colleagues.'
Thereupon, he memorialized before the Emperor,
who granted permission for his son, Yè, the Lìshān Wèi of Méngzhōu, to escort the coffin back for burial."
Furthermore,
at that time, Liǔ Zhòngyǐng was defending Dōngshǔ,
and held a memorial service in Jīngnán,
commissioning his subordinate Lǐ Shāngyǐn to write an essay stating:
"Respectfully receiving the new imperial favor,
he returns to his former abode."
It also states:
"His body remains in Shǔjùn,
his path separated from Yīchuān."
Yet Yè's memorial states:
"His solitary bones have not yet returned to their tomb."
Yè [the son] was only transferred to Chēnxiàn Wèi at the beginning of Yìzōng's reign,
which is not clear.
Perhaps it was a forgery by later generations,
and not Yè's original memorial.
The Shílù annotation also says:
"Bái Mǐnzhōng, while Zhōngshū Lìng,
wrote a letter to Right Shùzǐ Duàn Quánwěi, stating: 'The late Wèigōng, Tàiwèi,
disaster arose like the owl,
resentment accumulated like the river fish.
His close associates scattered like rain in the western garden,
his sons and nephews drifted like tumbleweeds in the southern lands.
Having once received a glance of favor,
he successively held the three highest offices,
maintaining his life until his natural end,
a memorial request has been added to bestow an honorary title.'
Quánwěi had once been Déyù's subordinate in Xīchuān,
which is why Mǐnzhōng mentioned it in his letter."
According to this, it seems to have been initiated by Mǐnzhōng,
but several sources attribute the posthumous restoration of office
mostly to Yè's memorial.
Déyù had always been kind to Mǐnzhōng.
Mǐnzhōng, having previously served as prime minister,
not only exiled him far away,
but now also usurped his credit.
How despicable!
According to Liú Yè's memorial, it states:
"Last year, I received His Majesty's decree of renewal,
extending the grace of release."
This indicates that this memorial was submitted in Xiántōng first year,
not the second year.
It is traditionally said:
"Yè served as Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ.
Due to Lǐ Déyù's death in exile at Zhūyá,
during the Dàzhōng reign,
Línghú Táo held power,
and although there were many amnesties and pardons,
Déyù did not receive imperial favor.
When Yìzōng ascended the throne,
Táo was in a border region.
During a general amnesty for the suburban sacrifice to Heaven,
Yè presented a memorial on this matter."
In Lǐ Tàiwèi Nánxíng Lù,
Yè was not yet Hànlín Xuéshì at this time.
After submitting this memorial,
the Emperor's rescript stated:
"Immediately instruct the palace eunuchs to summon him to the Hànlín Academy to serve as a scholar,
the rest as memorialized."
Jīnhuá Zǐ Zábīan says:
"Xuānzōng once privately traveled past the Yánzī Kù [Treasury],
and seeing the continuous grand buildings and mountains of money and silk,
asked his attendants: 'Who built this treasury?'
The attendants replied: 'During Prime Minister Lǐ Déyù's administration,
he used the annual surplus from throughout the empire for readiness.
Since then,
when there were emergencies on the border,
there was no shortage of provisions,
for which this is truly relied upon.'
The Emperor said: 'Where is he now?'
He replied: 'He was demoted to Yázhōu for his involvement in the Wú Xiāng case.'
The Emperor said: 'If he had such merit for the country,
how could a minor offense warrant such a severe condemnation!'
Because of this, Minister Liú Yè was able to submit a memorial requesting his posthumous rehabilitation.
The Emperor, upon reading the memorial,
then granted his posthumous promotion and permission for reburial."
However, Xuānzōng had always disliked Déyù.
Thus, upon his accession, he immediately banished him.
How could he not know he was in Yázhōu and say,
"how could it warrant such a severe condemnation!"
Furthermore, Liú Yè's rehabilitation request was during Yìzōng's time.
This account is extremely shallow and crude,
and is not accepted here.
15 On the jǐhài day,
Xiàhóu Zī, Menxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was made Tóng Píngzhāngshì
and appointed Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ.
Bì Xián, Hùbù Shàngshū and Pàndùzhī, was made Lǐbù Shàngshū and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
16 Ānnán Dūhù Lǐ Hù recaptured Bōzhōu.
Bōzhōu belonged to Qiánzhōng Dào;
in Dàzhōng thirteenth year,
it was captured by Yúnnán.
This was not part of Ānnán's jurisdiction.
Lǐ Hù crossed the border to recover it,
wishing to take credit for it,
but he did not know that the barbarian troops had taken advantage of the emptiness to capture Ānnán.
Hù,
pronounced "hù."
Fù,
pronounced "fú yòu fān."
17 In the eleventh month,
on the dīngchǒu day,
the Emperor performed sacrifices at the Huánqiú [Altar of Heaven];
there was an amnesty,
and the reign title was changed.
On the 18th day of the twelfth month,
on the day Wùshēn,
the indigenous people of Ānnán, allied with Nánzhào forces, totaling over 30,000 men, took advantage of the weakness to attack Jiāozhǐ
and captured it.
The 'Kǎoyì' states: The 'Xīn Nánzhào Zhuàn' says:
"During the Dàzhōng era,
Lǐ Zhuó served as the Commissioner for Frontier Affairs of Ānnán.
He was harsh, corrupt, and selfish,
exchanging a peck of salt for an ox.
The Yi people could not endure it,
and allied with the Nánzhào general Duàn Qiúqiān to capture the Ānnán Protectorate,
calling themselves the 'Báiyī Mòwàng Jūn' (White-clad Daredevils).
Yìzōng severed their tributary relations,
whereupon they captured Bōzhōu.
Lǐ Hù, the Protector of Ānnán, was garrisoned in Wǔzhōu.
In the first year of Xiántōng (860 CE),
he was attacked by the barbarians,
abandoned the prefecture, and fled.
The Son of Heaven rebuked Hù
and replaced him with Wáng Kuān."
However, during Xuānzōng's reign,
Nánzhào never captured Ānnán.
According to the 'Xīn Zhuàn',
it seems that Ānnán was already captured during the Dàzhōng era,
and then Wǔzhōu was captured again in the first year of Xiántōng.
Moreover, Lǐ Hù lost Ānnán,
and only then fled to Wǔzhōu,
he was not in Wǔzhōu when he abandoned it.
The 'Xīn Zhuàn' is mistaken;
we now follow the 'Shílù'.
The 'Xīn Zhì' states that among the territories governed by Yōngguǎn,
there were also Xiǎnzhōu, Wǔzhōu, and Shěnzhōu,
all of which were later abolished.
According to this,
Wǔzhōu should be within Yízhōu's borders.
On the 1st day of
the first month of spring,
an imperial edict ordered troops from Yōngguǎn and neighboring circuits to relieve Ānnán
and attack the Southern Barbarians.
On the 2nd day of
the second month, Bái Mǐnzhōng, Grand Councilor, was made concurrent Grand Councilor and appointed Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng;
Dù Cōng, Left Executive of the Secretariat and Administrator of Finance, was made concurrent Palace Assistant Secretary and Grand Councilor.
One day,
the two Commissioners of Military Affairs visited the Secretariat.
Yáng Gōngqìng, the Commissioner of the Xuanhui Bureau, arrived shortly after.
He alone bowed to Cōng to receive an imperial edict.
To "receive an imperial edict"
means to receive an imperial decree.
He withdrew to the west wing.
The three Grand Councilors were Bì Xián, Dù Shěnquán, and Jiǎng Shēn.
The document he produced
was a memorial submitted
when Xuānzōng was critically ill,
requesting that Prince Yùn act as regent.
He also said:
"Those Grand Councilors who were unnamed at the time
should be punished for rebellion."
Cōng reread it repeatedly
for a long time,
then said:
"Our Sacred Lord has ascended the throne,
and all regions rejoice in his support.
This document today
is not something a minister should pry into."
He resealed it and handed it back to Gōngqìng,
saying:
"If His Majesty wishes to punish the Grand Councilors,
he should present the imperial decree face-to-face in the Yányīng hall
and clearly carry out the execution or condemnation."
Gōngqìng left.
Cōng then sat with the two Commissioners of Military Affairs,
and said to them:
"Internal and external ministers
are as one body,
and the Grand Councilors and Commissioners of Military Affairs jointly participate in national governance.
Now His Majesty has newly ascended the throne
and is not yet familiar with the myriad affairs of state.
He relies on the assistance of both internal and external officials.
It is imperative to prioritize benevolence and love,
and put punishment and execution last.
How can one abruptly approve of killing Grand Councilors?
If His Majesty makes this a habit,
then the Palace Military Commissioners and Commissioners of Military Affairs will gain great power in the forbidden palace."
At that time, the two Palace Military Commissioners and two Commissioners of Military Affairs were called the 'Four Nobles'.
"If they speak of killing Grand Councilors,
then His Majesty's hand will become 'slippery' [i.e., accustomed to bloodshed],
and the Palace Military Commissioners and Commissioners of Military Affairs will also be implicated in disaster.
How can one not worry about this?
The 'Six Dynasties' refers to Xiànzōng, Mùzōng, Jìngzōng, Wénzōng, Wǔzōng, and Xuānzōng.
One should not let the court administer law based on likes and dislikes."
The two Commissioners of Military Affairs looked at each other silently,
and then slowly said:
"We should fully convey your words to His Majesty.
Without your profound virtue,
no one else would achieve this."
They left, ashamed and fearful.
The three Grand Councilors came to see Cōng again,
subtly inquiring about the imperial intention,
but Cōng said nothing.
The three Grand Councilors were terrified,
begging for the preservation of their families.
Cōng said:
"Do not worry about anything else."
Afterward, there was silence,
and no further imperial decrees.
When the Yányīng hall opened,
the Emperor's expression was very pleased.
It is likely that this account is based on Dù Cōng's family records,
and its tone and emphasis may exaggerate the truth.
Hóng Mài's 'Suíbǐ' states: According to the day Yìzōng ascended the throne,
there were four Grand Councilors:
Línghú Táo,
Xiāo Yè,
Xiàhóu Zī,
and Jiǎng Shēn.
By this time, only Shēn remained;
the other three had been dismissed.
Xián and Shěnquán were appointed by Yìzōng himself,
so this incident did not occur.
This is likely a fabrication of unofficial histories.
Wēn Gōng entrusted the Tang affairs to Fàn Zǔyǔ,
and his careful selection can be considered thorough,
yet it is still like this.
Truly, how difficult it is to compile history!
The 'Kǎoyì' states: The 'Xīn Zhuàn' says:
"When Xuānzōng was critically ill,
the Commissioner of Military Affairs, Wáng Guīzhǎng and others, falsified an imperial edict to enthrone Prince Yùn.
When Yìzōng ascended the throne,
he wished to punish the high ministers,
but Cōng intervened."
However, the one who enthroned Prince Yùn was Wáng Zōngshí.
The 'Xīn Zhuàn' says Guīzhǎng,
which is an error.
We now follow the 'Bǔ Guóshǐ'.
At this time, the scholar-officials deeply resented the eunuchs.
If an incident involved even a slight connection,
the public would collectively reject the person.
Yè Jīng, a *jìnshì* from Jiànzhōu, once attended a banquet of the Xuānwǔ Army
and recognized the face of the supervising eunuch.
After he passed the imperial examination,
he was traveling in Cháng'ān with his contemporaries
and encountered the eunuch on the road.
They exchanged bows from horseback.
Because of this, public criticism became clamorous,
and he remained disgraced and failed for the rest of his life.
Their dislike was such.
The Calamity of Partisan Proscriptions in the Eastern Hàn was probably similar.
Yet, the integrity of figures like Lǐ and Dù was so awe-inspiring
that even a thousand years later,
those who read of their deeds still feel a solemn reverence in their hearts.
The late Tang poets could not even approach a ten-thousandth of their stature,
yet they also caused the calamity of the 'Pure Stream' [i.e., honest officials].
Alas!
Shěn (沈),
pronounced 'chí-lín fān'.
On the 3rd day,
Fú Wáng Wǎn passed away.
Wǎn was a son of Shùnzōng.
4 In summer,
in the sixth month,
on the Guǐchǒu day,
Wáng Kuān, the Defender of Yánzhōu, was appointed as the Commissioner of Ānnán.
At that time, Lǐ Hù, having gathered local troops from Wǔzhōu,
attacked the Jīnmán,
and recaptured Ānnán.
The imperial court, blaming him for the loss of the territory,
demoted him to Sīhù of Dānzhōu.
When Lǐ Hù first arrived in Ānnán,
he killed Dù Shǒuchéng, a chieftain of the Mán.
Thereupon, Dù Shǒuchéng’s clan members incited the Dàojīnmán to capture Jiāozhǐ.
The imperial court, considering the Dù clan to be powerful,
sought to appease them,
hoping to make use of their strength.
Therefore, it posthumously granted Dù Shǒuchéng’s father, Dù Cúnchéng, the title of Jīnwú Jiāngjūn.
It further brought up the crime of Lǐ Hù killing Dù Shǒuchéng,
and exiled him permanently to Yázhōu.
Liú Xù says: In the fourth year of Wǔdé of the Táng dynasty,
the Suí dynasty's Zhūyá Jùn was established as Yázhōu.
South from Xúwén Xiàn in Léizhōu,
a four hundred and thirty li journey by boat,
crossing the great sea,
reaches Yázhōu.
Sòng Bái says: In the sixth year of Kāibǎo of the Sòng dynasty,
the land of the old Yázhōu was assigned to Qióngzhōu,
and Zhènzhōu was then renamed Yázhōu.
The Kǎoyì says: The Shílù states:
“Furthermore, an imperial edict was bestowed upon Wáng Kuān, saying,
‘It is heard that during Lǐ Zhuó’s time in Ānnán,
he killed Dù Cúnchéng,
and Lǐ Hù further dealt with his son, Dù Shǒuchéng,
causing the Dàojīnmán to be incited,
leading to the fall of the city.
When you arrive at the garrison,
you are to request all previous imperial edicts from Lǐ Hù
and examine them one by one.’
Initially,
when Lǐ Zhuó was at the garrison,
Dù Cúnchéng, a Mán chieftain who was the Inspector of Àizhōu and concurrently the Commander of the Local Troops, secretly incited the Xī Dòng Yí and Láo to act as their guides.
Lǐ Zhuó, perceiving his disloyalty,
put him to death.
When Lǐ Hù arrived at the garrison,
the Mán attacked Ānnán.
Lǐ Hù fled to Wǔzhōu,
summoned local troops to recapture the city.
However, Dù Cúnchéng’s household troops were very numerous,
and the imperial court sought to appease them,
so Dù Cúnchéng was posthumously granted the title of Jīnwú Jiāngjūn.
Lǐ Hù was demoted to Dānzhōu for his failure to defend.”
The Bǔguóshǐ states:
“The Mán attacked Ānnán.
Lǐ Hù fled to Wǔzhōu,
summoned local troops to recapture it,
achieving considerable merit.
He killed the chieftain Dù Cúnchéng,
for resisting and wavering, not exerting full effort against the enemy,
and also for the crime of the Dòng Yí Láo acting as guides.
After Lǐ Hù was demoted to Dānzhōu,
because Dù Cúnchéng’s Xī Dòng were strong and fierce,
and his household troops were numerous,
with his sons and brothers successively commanding the armies,
all demonstrating loyalty and bravery,
the military government greatly relied on them.
The imperial court also sought to appease them,
so it again invoked the law,
permanently exiled Lǐ Hù to Yázhōu,
and posthumously granted Dù Cúnchéng the title of Jīnwú Jiāngjūn,
to entice them to exert their full strength.
Former Inspector of Yánzhōu, Wáng Zhòu, was appointed as Dūhù.”
Upon examination, Dù Shǒuchéng, the son of Dù Cúnchéng killed by Lǐ Hù,
had already been expelled by Wáng Shì.
Lǐ Hù killed him within ten days of his arrival,
not because of resistance and lack of effort.
Wáng Kuān replaced Lǐ Hù,
not Wáng Zhòu.
The Bǔguóshǐ is mistaken.
Now, only the matter of Lǐ Hù recapturing Ānnán is taken,
all other parts follow the Píngyǎn Lù and Shílù.
Upon examination, if the Táng court considered the killing of Dù Shǒuchéng as Lǐ Hù’s crime,
then Dù Shǒuchéng should have been granted an official title,
not his father.
This is why I raised doubts earlier.
5 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
the Nánzhào
attacked Yōngzhōu
and captured it.
Previously,
Guǎng, Guì, and Róng three circuits jointly dispatched three thousand soldiers to garrison Yōngzhōu,
replaced every three years.
The Commissioner Duàn Wénchǔ requested to recruit local troops from the provisions and rations of the three circuits to replace them,
and the imperial court granted permission.
Only about five hundred men were recruited.
Duàn Wénchǔ entered the court as Jīnwú Jiāngjūn.
The Commissioner Lǐ Méng, profiting from the vacant quotas of provisions and rations,
dismissed all garrison soldiers from the three circuits,
only retaining the recruited troops to guard the Zuǒ and Yòu Jiāng.
This was seven or eight tenths less than the original number,
so the Mán people seized the opportunity to invade the empty territory.
At that time, Lǐ Méng had already died.
The Commissioner Lǐ Hóngyuán had only been at the garrison for ten days,
having no troops to resist them.
The city fell.
Lǐ Hóngyuán and the Supervising Eunuch escaped to Luánzhōu.
Sòng Bái says: Yōngzhōu
was the ancient city of Nányuè.
In the Jìn dynasty, Jìnxīng Jùn was established.
In the Suí dynasty, the commandery was abolished and became Xuānhuà Xiàn.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé of the Táng dynasty,
Nánjìnzhōu was established here.
In the sixth year of Zhēngguān,
it was renamed Yōngzhōu.
It was five thousand six hundred li from Cháng'ān.
Luánzhōu
was the territory of Qín Guìlín Jùn.
In the Táng dynasty, Chúnzhōu was established,
later renamed Luánzhōu.
It was five thousand three hundred li from the capital,
and three hundred li west of Yōngzhōu.
The Mán departed,
and then they returned.
Lǐ Hóngyuán was demoted to Sīhù of Jiànzhōu for this.
Duàn Wénchǔ was then Diànzhōng Jiān,
and was again appointed Commissioner of Yōngguǎn.
Upon his arrival at the garrison,
scarcely one-tenth of the city's inhabitants remained.
Duàn Wénchǔ
was the grandson of Duàn Xiùshí.
Duàn Xiùshí died in the rebellion of Zhū Cǐ.
6 Dù Cóng memorialized:
“The Nánzhào have submitted for seventy years.
During the Zhēnyuán period,
the Nánzhào submitted again.
The Jīnmán were all submissive.
‘Shuàifú’ means to lead one another to submit.
They should not be lightly estranged.
Furthermore, an envoy should be sent to offer condolences and sacrifices,
and inform the Qīngpíng Guān and others that the new king's name violates the imperial taboo,
hence the failure to issue an investiture edict.
This matter first appeared in the previous volume in the thirteenth year of Dàzhōng.
Then an envoy should be sent to issue the investiture edict,
so as to preserve the overall situation.”
The Emperor accepted this.
Mèng Mù, Langzhong of the Zuǒ Sī, was appointed as the Envoy for Condolences and Sacrifices.
Before he departed,
it happened that the Nánzhào attacked Kuìzhōu
and assaulted Qiónglái Guān,
so Mèng Mù did not proceed.
The Kǎoyì says: The Shílù places this in the twelfth month of this year.
According to the Bǔguóshǐ:
“Dù Bīngōng re-entered the government as a chief minister,
suggesting sending an envoy for condolences and sacrifices,
ordering them to change the name.
As soon as the envoy was appointed,
the city of Yuèkuì had already been breached,
and Qiónglái Guān was being attacked.
The envoy delayed for several months without departing.”
Therefore, the appointment of Mèng Mù as envoy must have been before the attack on Kuìzhōu.
The Shílù recording it in the twelfth month is mistaken.
Upon examination, the Nánzhào had already proclaimed themselves emperor
and captured Ānnán;
how could this be glossed over?
Dù Cóng merely wished to appease them,
thus feigning ignorance of their illegitimate imperial title and attributing the capture of Ānnán to the local Mán.
7 In winter,
in the tenth month,
Zhèng Yá, the Yùshǐ Dàfū, was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Shānnán Dōngdào.
In the eleventh month,
he was given the additional title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the Gēngyín day, which was the first day of the month,
the Jīn subject offered the honorable title of Ruìmíng Shèng Xiàodé Huángdì to the emperor.
A general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
2 Jiǎng Shēn, Zhongshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
was made Tóng Píngzhāngshì
and appointed Jiédùshǐ of Hézhōng.
3 In the second month,
Prince Dì, Zhuì, passed away.
7 The Língnán region was formerly divided into five guǎn (administrative circuits):
Guǎng, Guì, Yōng, Róng, and Ānnán.
All were subordinate to the Língnán Jiédùshǐ.
Cài Jīng memorialized to request that Língnán be divided into two jiédù circuits;
this was granted.
In the fifth month,
an imperial edict designated Guǎngzhōu as the Eastern Circuit [jiédù],
and Yōngzhōu as the Western Circuit [jiédù].
Furthermore, Gōng and Xiàng prefectures from Guì Guǎn,
and Téng and Yán prefectures from Róng Guǎn were transferred to Yōng Guǎn.
Soon after, Wéi Zhòu, the Língnán Jiédùshǐ, was appointed Eastern Circuit Jiédùshǐ,
and Cài Jīng was appointed Western Circuit Jiédùshǐ.
Cài Xí was in Ānnán with troops from various circuits.
Cài Jīng was jealous of him,
fearing he would achieve merit,
and memorialized, stating:
"The Southern Man have retreated far away,
and the border regions are without danger.
Martial men, seeking merit,
wrongfully occupy garrison troops,
uselessly expending provisions and transport.
This is because the desolate remote areas are far away,
making verification difficult,
thus allowing them to commit their deceitful acts.
I request to dismiss the garrison troops,
and have each return to its original circuit."
The imperial court granted this.
Xí repeatedly memorialized that the Mán barbarians had been watching for an opportunity for a long time,
and preparations could not be dispensed with,
begging to retain five thousand garrison troops;
this was not heeded.
Xí, knowing that the Mán bandits would certainly arrive,
and that Jiāozhǐ was lacking both soldiers and food,
utterly exhausted in both strategy and strength,
wrote a memorial detailing ten certain deaths and submitted it to the Zhōngshū;
at the time, the grand councilors believed Cài Jīng's words,
and ultimately did not consider it.
The grand councilors eagerly sought to save on the costs of provisions and transport,
thus Cài Jīng's words were easily accepted,
and Xí's plea was not granted.
Shěng,
pronounced Xǐ Jǐng.
8 In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Xúzhōu army mutinied
and drove away Jiédùshǐ Wēn Zhāng.
The Kǎo Yì says: The old account states:
"Zhāng,
at the end of Xiántōng, was the Xúsì Jiédùshǐ.
The Xúzhōu牙卒 (elite guards) were called the Yíndāo Jūn (Silver Sabre Army),
and were quite arrogant and tyrannical.
When Zhāng arrived,
he executed over five hundred of the most vicious among them,
and thereafter the army feared the law."
However, the one who executed the Yíndāo Jūn was
Wáng Shì.
The old account is erroneous.
Initially,
after Wáng Zhìxīng obtained Xúzhōu,
he recruited two thousand brave and fierce men,
calling them the Yíndāo, Diāoqí, Ménqiāng, Jiámǎ, and other seven armies.
He always kept over three hundred men for his personal guard,
sitting with drawn blades under the awnings in the side corridors,
with a change every month.
Thereafter, many jiédùshǐ were literati officials,
and their soldiers gradually became arrogant.
If things were slightly not to their liking,
one man would shout loudly,
and all his followers would echo him,
and the jiédùshǐ would often flee through the back door.
The previous jiédùshǐ, Tián Móu, even sat and drank with them,
clasping their arms and patting their backs,
or even holding a clapper and singing for them.
The cost of rewards and provisions
amounted to tens of thousands daily.
In wind, rain, cold, or heat,
he would further comfort and entertain them,
yet they would still often clamor
and incessantly demand things.
After Móu died,
Zhāng succeeded him.
The arrogant soldiers had long heard of Zhāng's strict nature
and feared him.
Zhāng openly soothed and comforted them,
but the arrogant soldiers remained suspicious and distrustful.
All the wine and food he bestowed upon them never passed their lips.
One day,
they finally gathered in a clamor and drove him away.
The imperial court, knowing Zhāng was innocent,
on the day of Yǐhài,
appointed Zhāng as Bīnníng Jiédùshǐ,
and Wáng Shì, the Zhèdōng Guānchásǐ, as Wǔníng Jiédùshǐ.
9 Xiàhóu Zī, the former Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was appointed Zuǒ Púshè and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
10The Zhōngwǔ and Yìchéng armies, which had followed Wáng Shì in suppressing Qiú Fǔ, were still in Zhèdōng.
An edict ordered Shì to lead them to Xúzhōu.
When the arrogant soldiers heard this,
they were greatly frightened.
In the eighth month,
Shì arrived at Dàpéng Guǎn.
Dàpéng Guǎn was outside Xúzhōu city.
Dàpéng
is what Péngzǔ referred to when he said,
"Shang had Dàpéng dominating the feudal lords."
Another account says: Péngzǔ's surname was Jiān,
given name Kēng.
He served Emperor Yáo,
lived through Yú and Xià until the Shāng dynasty,
and was eight hundred years old.
He was enfeoffed in Péngchéng,
hence the people of Péngchéng named the馆 after him.
Shì, after three days in office,
feasted the generals and soldiers of the two garrisons,
then sent them back to their garrisons.
He donned armor and wielded weapons,
ordered the arrogant soldiers to be surrounded,
and had them all killed.
Shào Zé, the commander of the Yíndāo Dū, and several thousand others all died.
The Kǎo Yì says: The old account states:
"When Shì arrived at the garrison,
he executed all seven armies, including the Yíndāo,
and the Xú Fāng region was pacified."
The Jīnhuázǐ Zábiān says:
"Wēn Zhāng lost control in Xúzhōu.
Shì was transferred from Héyáng to govern it.
Shì brought the entire Héyáng army to his new post.
When the generals and soldiers of Xúzhōu heard of Shì's arrival near the border,
they first sent three hundred vanguard troops to meet him.
Shì, in casual attire, sat on a folding chair and received their salutations.
After it was finished,
he then questioned them about their crime of driving away their commander,
and ordered them all beheaded in front of his tent,
leaving not a single person.
Soon after, others arrived in succession,
unaware of the fate of those who had died earlier.
Upon arrival, they were also beheaded,
and none escaped.
This continued for several days,
until several thousand men of the Yíndāo Dū were nearly wiped out.
These wolf-like men,
who normally believed they could devour others,
at this juncture, with Shì wearing a padded jacket and a sleeveless jacket,
sitting precariously with his slippers,
all the instigators went to their deaths with bowed hands,
not one daring to resist.
Afterwards, their relatives were amazed
and could not understand it themselves."
However, if several thousand people were killed at once,
how could anyone not know?
Furthermore, Shì was appointed Wǔníng from Zhèdōng,
not Héyáng.
We now follow the Shílù (Veritable Records).
On the day of Jiǎzǐ,
an imperial edict stated that Xúzhōu was formerly subordinate to Zīqīng Dào.
After Lǐ Wèi submitted himself,
the Xúhǎi Shǐ (Xúhǎi Commissioner) position was first established.
(See volume 227, Dézōng, Jiànzhōng 3rd year.)
Háo and Sì prefectures were specifically attached.
(See volume 233, Zhēnyuán 4th year.)
Since the suppression of rebels and bandits,
the Wǔníng circuit has become a hotbed of unrest.
Now, it is changed to Xúzhōu Tuánliànshǐ (Xúzhōu Militia Commissioner),
subordinate to the Yǎnhǎi Jiédù.
Háo Prefecture is restored to Huáinán Dào,
and a Sùsì Dū Tuánliàn Guānchásǐ (Sùsì Capital Militia and Observation Commissioner) is established in Sùzhōu.
(In Yuánhé 4th year of Xianzong,
Fúlí and Qí from Xúzhōu,
and Hóng from Sìzhōu were detached
to establish Sùzhōu,
whose seat of government was Yǒngqiáo,
on the Biànshuǐ river at the southern border of Xúzhōu,
at a confluence of boat and cart routes.
Sòng Bái said: Sùzhōu
was named after the ancient Sù kingdom.)
One thousand men shall guard Xúzhōu,
and the rest shall be distributed among Yǎn and Sù.
Furthermore, Wáng Shì is appointed Wǔníng Jiédùshǐ,
concurrently Xú, Sì, Háo, and Sù Zhìzhìshǐ (Commissioners of Arrangement).
Shì is entrusted with Yang Xuánzhì, the supervisor of the army, to allocate the generals and soldiers to various circuits.
After completion, he shall lead the Zhōngwǔ and Yìchéng armies to Biànhuá,
then send each back to its original circuit,
and personally proceed to the capital.
For the generals and soldiers of the Yíndāo and other armies who fled and hid,
they are permitted to surrender within one month,
and all will be pardoned.
11 Cài Jīng, the Jiédùshǐ of Lǐngnán Xīdào, governed with severity and cruelty.
He established the torture of roasting and branding,
causing resentment throughout the entire region.
Consequently, he was expelled by the soldiers of Yǒngzhōu.
Lǐngnán was divided into two military commands,
with the Xīdào governing Yǒngzhōu.
Téngzhōu,
located in the territory of Měnglíng County during the Hàn dynasty,
was established as Téngzhōu by the Táng dynasty.
It was five thousand six hundred *lǐ* from the capital.
He recruited local militia and adjacent native troops to attack Yǒngzhōu.
The crowd, being a motley assembly,
constantly disintegrated and fled.
They went to depend on Guìzhōu,
but the people of Guìzhōu resented their division
and did not admit them.
This was because they had detached the *Guìguǎn Xúnshǔ* and made it subordinate to the Xīdào Jiédù.
An imperial edict demoted him to Sīhù of Yázhōu,
but he refused to take up the post.
He returned,
and upon reaching Línglíng,
an imperial edict ordered him to commit suicide.
Zhèng Yú, the Guìguǎn Guānchásǐ, was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Lǐngnán Xīdào.
12 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the *bǐngshēn* day,
Imperial Prince Yì was made King Wèi,
Tíng was made King Liáng,
and Jí was made King Shǔ.
13 In the eleventh month,
Sùnzōng’s son Jī was made King Qí,
and Xiànzōng’s son Fèn was made King Róng.
14 The Nánzhāo, led by fifty thousand *Mán*, invaded Ānnán.
Dūhù Cài Xí sent an urgent appeal.
An imperial edict ordered two thousand troops from the Jīngnán and Húnán circuits,
and three thousand "righteous conscription youths" from Guìguǎn,
to proceed to Yǒngzhōu.
"Righteous conscription youths"
refers to those who enlisted in the army voluntarily.
15 Wéi Zhòu, the Jiédùshǐ of Lǐngnán Dōngdào, reported:
"The *Mán* invaders will certainly head for Yǒngzhōu.
If we do not protect it first,
and hastily march a long distance,
I fear the *Mán* will take advantage of the emptiness behind us to cut off the supply route."
Thereupon, an imperial edict ordered Cài Xí to station troops at Hǎimén.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
"An edict ordered Xí to temporarily stay at Hǎimén."
This meant to abandon Jiāozhǐ
and retreat to station troops at Hǎimén.
However, Xí was still in Jiāozhǐ at the time of his death.
It is likely that by the time the imperial edict arrived,
Xí was already besieged
and could not communicate.
In the twelfth month,
Xí again requested more troops.
An imperial edict ordered a thousand archers from Shānnán Dōngdào to go to his aid.
At that time, the Nánzhāo had already besieged Jiāozhǐ,
and Xí was holding out in the city,
so no relief troops could reach him.
16 Prince Yì, Chǎn, passed away.
17 In this year,
the Wōmò first sent tribute.
The Wōmò
was the name for the slaves of the Tǔbō.
Whenever the Tǔbō dispatched troops,
their wealthy households often sent their slaves to accompany them,
frequently with a dozen or more from a single family.
Thus, the Tǔbō forces were numerous.
When Lùn Kǒngrè rebelled,
many slaves were without masters,
so they banded together to form tribes,
scattered between Gān, Sù, Guā, Shā, Hé, Wèi, Mín, Kuò, Dié, and Dàng.
The weak among the Tǔbō, in turn, attached themselves to them.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the *gēngwǔ* day,
the Emperor offered sacrifices at the Yuánqiū;
there was a general amnesty throughout the realm.
2 On this day,
the Nánzhāo captured Jiāozhǐ.
Cài Xí's左右 (attendants) were all gone.
He fought on foot with all his might,
taking ten arrows in his body.
He wanted to head for the supervisor's boat,
but the boat had already left the shore.
He subsequently drowned in the sea.
His staff officer, Fán Chuò, carried his seal and swam across the river.
From one hundred *lǐ* southwest of Bóbái County in Báizhōu, descending the Běixù Shān,
exiting into Mǎmén Jiāng,
crossing the sea,
one reaches the border of Ānnán.
The river where Fán Chuò carried the seal and crossed
is this very river.
He ran to the water's edge east of the city.
Yuán Wéidé, the Yúhòu of Jīngnán, and others said to the crowd:
"We have no boats,
to enter the water is to die.
It is better to return to the city and fight the *Mán*.
For one man to exchange his life for two *Mán*
is also advantageous."
So they returned to the city
and entered the Dōngluómén.
The Dōngluómén
was the east gate of Ānnán's Luóchéng.
Wéidé and the others unleashed their troops and killed over two thousand *Mán*.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
"In the second month,

Cài Xí, the Ānnán Jīnglüèsǐ and concurrently Jiǎnjiào Gōngbù Shàngshū, reported: 'The *Mán* bandits Yáng Sījiàn and Mǎ Guānggāo, the Fúyé County Magistrate of Luófúzhōu, led their host of five or six thousand men,
and encamped at the southwest corner of the city.'
Wéi Zhòu, the Jiédùshǐ of Lǐngnán Dōngdào, reported: 'The *Mán* bandits, on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month,
approached the city of Ānnán.
The Jīnglüèsǐ and concurrently Jiǎnjiào Gōngbù Shàngshū Cài Xí led out troops to fight them,
with casualties on both sides.
On the third day of the first month,
the bandit forces besieged the city,
attacking with great urgency.
Xí used siege crossbows from atop the city to shoot at them.
By the seventh day,
the city fell.
Xí died from a crossbow bolt to his right shoulder.
His family and over seventy retainers all perished at the hands of the bandits.
The administrator Fán Chuò carried the seal and crossed the river.
The troops from Jīngnán, Jiāngxī, È’yuè, and Xiāngzhōu suddenly arrived at the water's edge east of the city,
but having no boats, they turned back.
They then collectively entered the Dōngluómén,
killing barely one or two thousand *Mán*.
By night,
the bandit relief troops arrived,
and then massacred the city.' "
However, these two reports seem to have been compiled by later generations from *Mán Shū*,
and they contain many discrepancies.
For example, Yáng Sījiàn,
appears in two places in *Mán Shū*,
both written as
"Yáng Sījìn."
This was likely a mistake in cursive script for
"Jiàn."
Indeed.
Although they were barbarians,
how could they be named
"Sījiàn"?
The *Zhāng Jǐnlǐ Qíjiù Zhuàn* records Gāo Pián's dispatch to Yúnnán,
also mentioning Yáng Sījìn,
the Jiédùshǐ of Shànlán.
The *Xīn Shū* also inherited this mistake, rendering it as
"Jiàn."
Furthermore, what *Mán Shū* refers to as Sījìn and Guānggāo leading
were merely five or six thousand Táohuā *Mán*,
not the entire host of *Mán*.
The *Bǔ Guóshǐ* states that fifty thousand *Mán* attacked Ānnán,
not just five or six thousand men.
Moreover, on the twenty-first day of the twelfth month,
the Nuǒxíng Mán, Máng Mán, and Táohuā people were already outside the city.
How could they only begin to approach Ānnán on the twenty-seventh day?
*Mán Shū*'s statement that they approached the city on the twenty-seventh day
merely records the day the Hémán and Xúnchuán Mán were seen;
and the statement about the second and third days of the first month
merely records the day when *Jūzǐ* were shot with siege crossbows,
not the day they began to besiege the city.
Furthermore, at the moment of the city's fall and frantic escape,
unless Fán Chuò himself was there,
how could he know the details?
The number of people killed by the four circuits' troops entering the city
was only known through the monk Wúhàn's account.
Wéi Zhòu was in Guǎngzhōu;
how could his report be exactly like Fán Chuò's account?
Its falsity is clear.
The *Xīn Zhuàn* says:
"That night,
the *Mán* then massacred the city,"
which also follows the *Shílù* and is mistaken.
The *Mán* general Yáng Sījìn first came out of the zǐchéng to rescue them.
The zǐchéng
was a small inner city.
The Nánzhāo twice captured Jiāozhǐ,
killing and capturing nearly one hundred fifty thousand people.
They left two thousand troops,
and made Sījìn occupy Jiāozhǐ city.
The *Xīdòng Yíluó*, regardless of distance, all surrendered to him.
An imperial edict recalled all troops from various circuits who had gone to Ānnán,
and had them stationed to protect Lǐngnán
Xīdào.
3 The Emperor indulged in unrestrained feasts.
Zuǒ Shíyí Liú Tuì submitted a memorial, saying:
"Currently, Xīliáng is building a city,
and the decision on whether to grant or reclaim it has not yet been made;
Xīliáng
is Jǐliángzhōu,
as this was the time when advancement in construction was being contemplated.
All military forces are on the roads.
For the past month or so,
it has not been a time of peace.
If Your Majesty does not express concern and sympathy to show those near and far,
then how can you expect them to exert their utmost effort unto death!
It would not be too late
to curtail entertainment and wait
for the distant people to be settled and at peace."
It means that waiting for the distant people to be settled and at peace,
and then indulging in entertainment,
would still not be too late.
4 In the second month,
on the *jiǎwǔ* day of the new moon,
the Emperor visited and paid respects at the Sixteen Mausoleums.
The Sixteen Mausoleums
refer to Xiànlíng, Zhāolíng, Qiánlíng, Dìnglíng, Qiáolíng, Tàilíng, Jiànlíng, Yuánlíng, Chónglíng, Fēnglíng, Jǐnglíng, Guānglíng, Zhuānglíng, Zhānglíng, Duānlíng, and Zhēnlíng.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Paying respects at sixteen mausoleums
cannot be accomplished in one day,
and the old histories do not record the date of return to the palace.
*Táng Nián Bǔ Lù* says: In the second month,
on the *gēngzǐ* day.
To pay respects at sixteen mausoleums in one day
is even harder to believe.
5 The Tiānxíong Army was established in Qínzhōu.
Dàizōng indulged Tián Chéngsì
by bestowing the title "Tiānxíong Army" upon Wèibó,
but later, due to their rebelliousness and arrogance,
he abolished it.
Now, the Tiānxíong Army was re-established in Qínzhōu.
Towards the end of the Táng dynasty,
Wèibó regained the title of Tiānxíong Army,
and Qínzhōu was no longer called Tiānxíong.
The former Left Jīn Wú General Wáng Yànshí was appointed Tiānxíong Jíedùshǐ.
Yànshí
was the son of Zǎi.
Zǎi's father, Zhìxīng, adopted him as a son,
as seen in Volume 247, Huìchāng Fourth Year.
6 In the third month,
Guīyì Jíedùshǐ Zhāng Yìcháo reported that he personally led seven thousand Fān and Hàn soldiers to recapture Líangzhōu.
7 The Southern Barbarians raided Zuǒ and Yòu Jiāng,
gradually encroaching upon Yōngzhōu.
Zhèng Yú was afraid,
stating that as a Confucian minister, he lacked military strategy,
and requested that a military official be appointed.
The imperial court summoned Yìwǔ Jíedùshǐ Kāng Chéngxùn to the capital,
intending to have him replace Yú,
and further issued an edict to select several military officers and several hundred soldiers to accompany him.
These were selected from the Yìwǔ Army.
*Jiào*
is pronounced *hù jiào*.
8 Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Bì Xián, observing that many of his colleagues engaged in illegal private dealings,
claimed illness and resigned his position;
in summer,
the fourth month,
he was dismissed and made Bīngbù Shàngshū.
9 On the *gēngxū* day,
a band of thieves entered Xúzhōu and
killed government officials;
Cǎoshǐ Cáo Qìng suppressed them.
10 Kāng Chéngxùn arrived in the capital
and was appointed Língnán Xīdào Jíedùshǐ,
and ten thousand soldiers from the four circuits of Jīng, Xiāng, Hóng, and È were dispatched to accompany him.
11 In the fifth month,
on the *wùchén* day,
Hàng Xúeshì Chéngzhǐ and Bīngbù Shìláng Yáng Shōu were appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Shōu
was the younger brother of Fā.
Xuānzōng, in order to open the Hé and Huáng,
added honorific titles to the revered names of Shùn and Xiàn Zōng.
The relevant officials deliberated on remaking the ancestral tablets
and inscribing new posthumous titles;
Fā believed that making new tablets
had no precedent in ancient texts
and firmly opposed it.
Those knowledgeable in ritual praised him,
and he became well-known because of this.
Thus, he was able to become a Chancellor.
12 On the *yǐhài* day,
Róngguǎn was abolished
and subordinated to Língnán Xīdào,
and Gōng and Xiàng two prefectures were again subordinated to Guìguǎn.
Last year, Gōng and Xiàng were subordinated to Língnán Xīdào.
13 On the *wùzǐ* day,
Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Dù Shěnquán was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
serving concurrently as Zhènhǎi Jíedùshǐ.
14 In the sixth month,
the Ānnán Dūhùfǔ was abolished,
and the provisional Jiāozhōu was established at Hǎimén Zhèn;
Right Jiānmén Jiāngjūn Sòng Róng was appointed provisional Jiāozhōu Cǎoshǐ,
and Kāng Chéngxùn concurrently took charge of Ānnán and the various military encampments.
15 In the intercalary month,
Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Dù Cōng was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
serving concurrently as Fèngxiáng Jíedùshǐ;
Bīngbù Shìláng and Pàn Dùzhī Hénán Cáo Què was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
16 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the *xīnmǎo* day of the new moon,
there was a solar eclipse.
17 The Annan Protectorate was re-established at Háng Jiāozhōu.
Kǎoyì says: The Shílù recorded Jùnzhōu as Jiāozhōu.
Bǔguóshǐ also agrees.
It also says,
Xiàhóu Zhēnjiàogōng requested to appoint Gāo Pián as Jùnzhōu Jìntǎoshǐ.
According to Dìlǐzhì,
there is no Jùnzhōu.
Bǔguóshǐ also says: Hǎimén,
is now Yànzhōu.
Dìlǐzhì states that
Yànzhōu belongs to Lúzhōu Dūdūfǔ,
and Lǐngnán also does not have it.
Ten thousand soldiers from Shāndōng were dispatched to garrison it.
At that time, soldiers from various circuits who came to aid Ānnán were camped in Lǐngnán.
Jùduàn.
These four characters are superfluous.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Xiāng and Lí have the same source,
dividing into two rivers.
To the south is the Líshuǐ,
and to the north is the Xiāngchuān.
Between the Xiāng and Lí,
the land is over a hundred paces wide,
called Shǐ'ānqiáo.
When the Hàn attacked Nányuè,
they set out from Línglíng,
went down the Líshuǐ,
which is this route.
The Xiāngshuǐ originates from Yángshuòshān in Shǐ'ānxian, Línglíng.
From the southwest of Línglíng,
it is called Língqú.
Xīnshū says: Guìzhōu has the Líshuǐ,
which flows out from Hǎiyángshān.
It is commonly said that Qín ordered Shǐ Lù to attack Yuè,
and he dug it to create a canal.
Mǎ Yuán attacked Zhēng Cè,
and again maintained it to facilitate transport of provisions.
Later, it was destroyed by river floods,
and the canal became shallow.
Lǐ Bó of the Táng dynasty later dredged it.
Fàn Chéngdà's Guìhǎi Yúhéng Zhì says: The Xiāng and Lí rivers
both originate from Hǎiyáng in Língchuān.
After flowing for a hundred *lǐ*,
they divide, one going north and the other south.
The one going north is called Xiāng,
with dense shoals and rapid rapids.
After another two thousand *lǐ*, it reaches Chángshā,
