where the water gradually slows down.
The one going south is called Lí,
with three hundred and sixty named shoals.
After another twelve hundred *lǐ*, it reaches Pānyú and enters the sea.
It also says: The Língqú is in Xīng'ānxian, Guìzhōu.
When Qín Shǐhuáng was garrisoning the mountains,
Shǐ Lù dug this for transportation, which is its historical trace.
The Xiāngshuǐ originates from Hǎiyángshān south of Yúnquán.
From here it flows down the Róngjiāng and Zāngkē.
Originally, it flowed south to Xīng'ān, Guǎngxī.
The water flows through it,
and the terrain is the highest.
The two rivers are far apart and do not connect.
Lù first created this canal,
diverting a branch of the Xiāng's flow to inject into the Róng,
so that the northern water could merge southward,
and northern boats could cross the mountains.
The method of constructing the canal
involved building a stone weir shaped like a plowshare in the sandy rapids of the Xiāng river,
sharpening its front,
and thus splitting the Xiāng's flow into two,
redirecting it.
For sixty *lǐ*, the water flows through the canal,
entering the Róngjiāng,
and together they flow south.
The canal circles the Xīng'ān border,
its depth is only a few feet,
and its width is over a *zhàng*.
Within the sixty *lǐ*,
thirty-six lock gates were installed.
The locals simply call them *dòuzhōu*.
After entering one *dòu*, the gate is closed again.
The *dòu* waits for the water to accumulate before gradually proceeding.
Thus, it can ascend along the cliffs
and descend like water pouring from a height.
Even boats carrying a thousand *hú*
can travel back and forth.
In terms of water management ingenuity,
none compares to the Língqú.
Líng,
pronounced *líng*.
Lí,
pronounced *lí*.
(Character with water radical and phonetic component zhǐ)
The various armies lacked provisions.
Chén Pánshí from Rùnzhōu submitted a memorial,
requesting the construction of large boats capable of carrying a thousand *hú*
to transport rice from Fújiàn by sea.
It would reach Guǎngzhōu in less than a month.
This was followed,
and the army's provisions were sufficient.
However, the officials, under the pretext of "peaceful hiring,"
seized merchants' boats,
abandoned their goods on the shore,
and if the boats were lost at sea due to storms,
the officials imprisoned the *gānglì* (gang-officers) and boatmen,
forcing them to compensate for the rice.
People suffered greatly from this.
18 In the eighth month,
Wéi Zhòu, the Jìdùshǐ of Lǐngnán Dōngdào, reported in a memorial,
"The barbarians will certainly advance towards Yōngzhōu.
I request that troops be divided to garrison Róng and Téng Prefectures."
Róng and Téng Prefectures are two hundred and seventy *lǐ* apart.
19 Prince Kuí, Jī Zī, passed away.
Zī
was the emperor's younger brother.
20 An imperial edict appointed Wú Déyìng and others, the Géménshǐ, as Guǎnyìshǐ.
The Censorate memorialized: According to established practice,
Censors inspected post stations.
In the middle of the Táng dynasty, the Géménshǐ position was established,
filled by eunuchs,
responsible for serving at court assemblies,
and introducing princes, chancellors, officials, and foreign envoys for audiences and departures.
In the early Táng, this was the duty of the Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén.
During Xuánzōng's Kāiyuán era,
supervising censors were concurrently appointed to inspect post stations.
By the twenty-fifth year,
supervising censors were appointed to oversee the post stations of the two capitals.
In Dàlì fourteen,
one censor in each of the two capitals was put in charge of post stations,
called Guǎnyìshǐ.
Sòng Bái said: In the early Yuánhé era,
when Liú Pì was being campaigned against,
postal transport was very busy.
Xiànzōng appointed eunuchs as Guǎnyìshǐ.
Xuē Cúnchéng, a supervising censor, and other remonstrance officials
successively memorialized against it,
and it was abolished.
It was replaced.
The emperor stated that the imperial edict had already been issued
and could not be changed.
Liú Tuì, a Zuǒshíyí, memorialized:
"In the past, the Viscount of Chǔ established Chén as a county.
Upon a single word from Shēnshú, he re-enfeoffed it.
Zuǒzhuàn: The Viscount of Chǔ, due to Xiàshì's disorder in Chén,
therefore attacked Chén.
He then entered Chén,
killed Xià Zhēngshū,
and consequently made Chén a county.
Shēnshú did not offer congratulations at the time.
When the Viscount of Chǔ asked why,
he replied:
'Xià Zhēngshū murdered his lord;
his crime was great.
To punish and execute him was your lord's righteousness.
Now, by making Chén a county,
you are coveting its wealth.
Is this not unacceptable?'
The king said:
'Excellent!'
and then re-enfeoffed Chén.
I heard that when Zhāng Xuánsù remonstrated,
it was abolished that very day.
(See volume 193, Zhēngguān four.)
To accept remonstrance like flowing water,
how can there be something already issued that cannot be changed!
Moreover, the edict originates from Your Majesty,
and can be changed by Your Majesty.
Why should it be impossible!"
The emperor did not listen.
21 The Qíjiāsī sent their minister Hégē Yīnánzhī to present a memorial requesting classics and books and to send envoys annually with horses to request the calendar.
They also wished to attack the Huíhú
and have all territories from Ānxī restored to the Táng.
This was not permitted.
22 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the *jiǎxū* day,
Línghú Hào, the Cháng'ān Wèi and Jíxián Jiàolǐ, was appointed Zuǒshíyí.
On the *yǐhài* day,
Liú Tuì, the Zuǒshíyí, memorialized:
"Hào's family has no rule for juniors and children,
and though a commoner, he wields the power of a chancellor."
Qǐjūláng Zhāng Yún said:
"Hào's father, Táo, appointed Lǐ Zhuó to Ānnán.
(See the previous volume, Xuānzōng, Dàzhōng twelve.)
This was due to Hào taking bribes,
entrapping his father in wrongdoing."
In the eleventh month,
on the *dīngyǒu* day,
Yún again memorialized:
"When Hào's father, Táo, was in power,
people called him the 'White-clothed Chancellor'."
Hào also submitted a memorial to resign,
and was then reassigned as Zhànshìfǔ Sīzhí.
The Táng dynasty's Tàizǐ Zhànshìfǔ had two Sīzhí,
ranked principal seventh grade upper,
responsible for impeaching palace officials and commanding the guards' troops.
23 On the *xīnsì* day,
the Sùsì Guāncházhǐ was abolished,
and Xúzhōu was re-established as a Guāncháfǔ,
with Háo and Sì subordinated to it.
In the eighth month of the previous year,
the Xúzhōu military command was abolished.
On the 24th day of the twelfth month,
Nánzhào attacked Xīchuān.
On the 25th, Shěn Xún, the Jiédùshǐ of Zhāoyì, had a servant named Guī Qín,
who had an affair with Xún's maidservant.
Xún wanted to kill him,
but did not succeed.
On the Yǐyǒu day,
Guī Qín incited his yájiàng to rebellion,
attacked the residence,
and killed Xún.
On the 1st day of spring,
the first month,
Lǐ Bīn, the Jīngzhàoyǐn, was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Zhāoyì,
and Guī Qín's heart and liver were taken to sacrifice to Shěn Xún.
On the 2nd day, Línghú Táo, the Jiédùshǐ of Huáinán, pleaded on behalf of his son Hào, who had been wronged.
Zhāng Yún was demoted to Xīngyuán Shàoyǐn,
Liú Tuì to Huáyīn Lìng.
An imperial edict stated:
"Although the loyalty of the frank and outspoken is commendable,
the responsibility for oversight cannot be escaped."
On the 3rd day, the Bǐngwǔ day,
Xīchuān reported
that Nánzhào had attacked Cuīzhōu.
The Cìshǐ, Yù Shìzhēn, defeated them,
capturing over a thousand men.
Considering that Yù Shìzhēn would lose the defense due to greed and treachery the following year,
this victory report must have been exaggerated.
Yán Qìngfù, a Dàjiàng of Zhōngwǔ, requested to build two new cities, Xīn'ān and Èróng,
which was granted.
These two cities
were built within the borders of Cuīzhōu.
On the 4th day, Zhāng Yīn, the Jīnglüèshǐ of Róngguǎn, was additionally put in charge of Jiāozhōu affairs.
The garrison troops at Hǎiménzhèn were increased to twenty-five thousand,
and Yīn was ordered to advance and capture Ānnán.
In the second month,
on the Jǐsì day,
Lǐ Fú, the Xíngbù Shàngshū and Yántiě Zhuǎnyùnshǐ, was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì and concurrently Jiédùshǐ of Xīchuān.
On the 6th day, the Jiǎshēn day,
Xiāo Yè, the former Jiédùshǐ of Xīchuān, was demoted to Shānnán Xīdào Guāncháshǐ.
In the third month,
on the Dīngyǒu day,
a comet appeared in Lóu,
three chǐ long.
On the Jǐhài day,
the Sītiānjiān reported:
"According to the star catalog,
this is called Hányù,
a propitious star."
The emperor was greatly pleased.
The Táng Sītiānjiān,
a third-rank official,
was in charge of observing celestial phenomena and checking the calendar.
Historians say that in the late Táng, the Sītiān officials were confused about celestial phenomena,
mistaking omens for auspicious signs.
"Please proclaim this to all within and outside the capital,
and record it in historical documents."
This was granted.
On the 8th day, Kāng Chéngxùn arrived at Yōngzhōu,
where the barbarian invaders became more rampant.
An imperial edict ordered troops from eight circuits—Xǔ, Huá, Qīng, Biàn, Yǎn, Yùn, Xuān, and Rùn—to be dispatched and placed under his command.
Chéngxùn did not set up scouts.
Nánzhào, leading nearly sixty thousand Mán barbarians, attacked Yōngzhōu.
When they were about to cross the border,
Chéngxùn then dispatched ten thousand troops from six circuits to resist them,
using Liáo as guides,
deceiving them.
When the enemy arrived,
no preparations were made,
and eight thousand troops from five circuits were all annihilated.
Only the Tiānpíng Army, which arrived a day later,
escaped.
The Tiānpíng Army
was from Yùn.
They were terrified and did not know what to do.
Lǐ Xíngsù, the Jiédù Fùshǐ, led his men to build moats and fences.
As soon as they were completed,
the barbarian army had already formed a siege.
After four days,
they prepared siege engines.
The generals requested to divide their forces at night to attack the barbarian camp,
but Chéngxùn refused.
A junior officer from Tiānpíng strongly argued repeatedly,
and then permission was granted.
The junior officer led three hundred brave soldiers.
At night,
they lowered themselves out,
scattered to burn the barbarian camps,
and beheaded over five hundred.
The barbarians were greatly alarmed.
A day later,
they lifted the siege and departed.
Chéngxùn then sent several thousand troops from various armies to pursue them.
The number of captives killed was less than three hundred,
all of whom were Xi Liáo who had been coerced.
Chéngxùn swiftly reported a victory,
claiming a great defeat of the barbarian bandits,
and all within and outside the capital offered congratulations.
In the summer,
the fourth month,
Xiāo Zhì, the Bīngbù Shìláng and Pàn Hùbù, was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Zhì
was the grandson of Fù.
Xiāo Fù was a prime minister during Dézōng's reign.
On the 10th day, Kāng Chéngxùn was granted the title Jiǎnxiào Yòupúyè,
as a reward for his achievement in defeating the barbarians.
All other meritorious officials who received awards
were Chéngxùn's relatives and close associates.
The officers who burned the camp were not promoted a single rank,
which caused resentment and anger in the army,
and the news spread through the roads.
In the fifth month,
an imperial edict stated:
"Xúzhōu's local customs are robust,
and its elite soldiers are strong.
Recently, due to the disbandment of the Jié,
many have absconded.
It is appropriate to order the Xúsì Tuánliànshǐ to select and recruit three thousand soldiers to go to Yōngzhōu for defense and garrison duty.
Once the situation outside the ridges is settled,
they shall be replaced and returned."
In the autumn,
the seventh month,
Xīchuān reported that the Guǐzhǔ of Liǎnglín intercepted and
defeated the Nánzhào barbarians.
Shǐ Zhào commented: The Liǎnglín tribe
is the kingdom of Dōngmán,
seventy lǐ from the Wùdèng kingdom.
Although its territory is small, all tribes respect it as their leader,
calling it the Dàguǐzhǔ.
The character 敗 (bài) here is pronounced 'bǔ mài'.
Bǎo Sài Chéngshǐ Dù Shǒulián, who did not follow Nánzhào,
led his troops to Lízhōu and surrendered.
On the 13th day, Wèi Zhòu, the Jiédùshǐ of Língnán Dōngdào, fully understood Kāng Chéngxùn's actions,
and wrote to the prime minister.
Chéngxùn also became suspicious and fearful,
and repeatedly submitted memorials pleading illness.
Therefore, Chéngxùn was appointed Yòu Wǔwèi Dàjiàngjūn and Fēnsī.
Kǎoyì says:
Supplement to the Guóshǐ.
"Wèi Zhòu, the Jiédùshǐ of Língnán Dōngdào, also managed military provisions.
He secretly ordered his officers and clerks in Yōngzhōu
to report everything,
regardless of its magnitude,
so he knew everything.
He further investigated and found that many of the reported victories were false,
and reported what he had heard to the prime minister.
Chéngxùn was already suspicious and fearful,
and used illness as an excuse to avoid responsibility.
He was appointed Yòu Wǔwèi Dàjiàngjūn and Fēnsī Dōngdū."
The biography of Chéngxùn in the Xīzōng Shílù states:
"When Nánmán captured Jiāozhǐ,
Chéngxùn was made Jiédùshǐ of Língnán Xīdào.
After more than a year,
he pacified it,
and was granted the title Jiǎnxiào Yòupúyè.
He disagreed with neighboring commanders,
and was dismissed as Yòu Wǔwèi Dàjiàngjūn."
This is what his family's biography states.
We now follow the Bǔ Guóshǐ, Yìzōng Shílù, and Xīn Zhuàn.
Furthermore, the four prefectures of Róngguǎn were separately established as a Jīnglüèshǐ.
The Xīnshū Fāngzhèn Biǎo states that
in the first year of Xiántōng (860),
Róngguǎn was abolished,
and its prefectures were subordinate to Yōngguǎn.
At this time, Nánzhào knew that Yōngzhōu was empty and exhausted,
and no longer invaded.
Zhāng Yīn for a long time dared not advance to take Ānnán.
Xiàhóu Zī recommended General of the驍wèi, Gāo Pián, to replace him.
The 'Kǎo Yì' states: Supplement to the National History:
“Zhāng Yīn was a fierce general,
but lacked foresight.
For a year, he dared not advance.
Chancellor Xiàhóu Zhēnjiàogōng alone submitted a secret memorial,
requesting the use of General of the驍wèi, Gāo Pián.
There was an imperial edict
appointing him as Commander for the campaign in Jùnzhōu with his original title,
and soon after, he was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Ānnán.
All the troops led by Zhāng Yīn were to be placed under Lord Gāo's command.”
Considering that in the first month of this year,
an imperial edict commanded Zhāng Yīn to advance and recover Ānnán,
if it were "a year later,"
then Xiàhóu Zī would have already been dismissed as Chancellor.
We now follow the 'Shílù' and attach it here.
The 'Shílù' states
that Gāo Pián's official title was Yòulǐngjūn Shàngjiāngjūn,
which is too high.
We now follow the Supplement to the National History.
The 'Jiù Jì' states:
“In the fourth month of the fifth year,
the Southern Man invaded Yōngguǎn.
Gāo Pián, the Jīnglüèshǐ of Qínzhōu, was ordered to lead five thousand imperial guards
to gather with the armies of various circuits to resist them.”
This is not adopted now.
All the troops led by Zhāng Yīn were handed over to him.
Gāo Pián
was the grandson of Gāo Chóngwén.
During Xiànzōng's reign,
Gāo Chóngwén had the merit of pacifying Shǔ.
Gāo Pián read widely
and enjoyed discussing ancient and modern affairs.
Many palace eunuchs in the two armies praised him.
"Two armies"
refers to the Zuǒ and Yòu Shéncè armies.
"Yù" (譽)
has the pronunciation 'yú'.
When the Dǎngxiàng rebelled,
he led ten thousand imperial troops to garrison Chángwǔ,
achieving repeated successes.
He was promoted to Fángyùshǐ of Qínzhōu,
and again achieved success.
Therefore, he was entrusted with Ānnán.
14 In winter,
the eleventh month,
Xiàhóu Zī, Menxià Shìláng and Tóngpíngzhāngshì, was appointed Tóngpíngzhāngshì
and Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng.
15 On Rén'yín,
Lù Yán, Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ and Bīngbù Shìláng, was appointed Tóngpíngzhāngshì;
he was thirty-six years old at the time.
This establishes the basis for Lù Yán's subsequent misfortune due to his high position.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on Dīngsì,
Empress Yì'ān was first given a co-sacrificial place in the temple of Xiànzōng.
At this time, Wáng Hào again served as Jiǎntàoguān of the Ritual Bureau,
reiterating his previous proposal,
and the imperial court eventually followed it.
Wáng Hào's proposal can be found in Volume 248, Xuānzōng Dàzhōng 2nd Year.
2 Those from various circuits who presented private eunuchs:
During the Tang dynasty, various circuits annually presented eunuch boys,
known as "private eunuchs" (sībái).
Therefore, many eunuchs were from Mǐn (Fujian).
Dù Xuānyóu, Observer of Fújiàn, would send officials to offer sacrifices at his ancestors' tombs every Hánshí Festival.
The eunuchs were grateful to him, and
on Gēngshēn,
Dù Xuānyóu was appointed Observer of Xuānshè.
People at the time called him
"Imperial Envoy's Tomb Household."
3 In the third month,
Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóngpíngzhāngshì Xiāo Zhì died.
4 In summer,
the fourth month,
Gāo Qú, former Jìedùshǐ of Dōngchuān, was appointed Bīngbù Shìláng and Tóngpíngzhāngshì.
Gāo Qú
was the son of Gāo Yuánxù.
5 Yáng Shōu suggested:
"The Man invaders have not been pacified for years.
Six or seven out of ten soldiers from Hébù, garrisoned in Lǐngnán, die from malaria and mist.
I request that grain be accumulated in Jiāngxī,
and thirty thousand strong crossbowmen be recruited
to assist Lǐngnán,
as the route is nearer and more convenient.
Furthermore, a Jìe should be established to enhance his authority."
This was approved.
In the fifth month,
on Xīnchǒu,
the Zhènnán Army was established in Hóngzhōu.
6 Yù Shìzhēn, Prefect of Cuízhōu, was greedy and cunning.
He plundered the two Lín Mán tribes to exchange for gold.
Nánzhào again invaded Cuízhōu.
The two Lín Mán tribes opened their gates and admitted them.
Nánzhào slaughtered all the garrison soldiers,
and Yù Shìzhēn surrendered to them.
7 On Rén'yín,
Yán Zhuàn, Observer of Guìguǎn, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Zhènnán.
Yán Zhuàn
was a collateral grandson of Yán Zhèn.
8 In the sixth month,
Gāo Qú died.
9 Xú Shāng, Yùshǐ Dàfū, was appointed Bīngbù Shìláng and Tóngpíngzhāngshì.
10 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Imperial Prince Kǎn was enfeoffed as Yǐngwáng,
and Imperial Prince Yǎn as Pǔwáng.
11 Gāo Pián trained his troops at Hǎimén,
but had not yet advanced.
The supervising eunuch Lǐ Wéizhōu disliked Gāo Pián
and wished to remove him.
He repeatedly urged Gāo Pián to advance.
Gāo Pián crossed with five thousand men first,
agreeing with Lǐ Wéizhōu to send troops as reinforcement.
After Gāo Pián departed,
Lǐ Wéizhōu kept the remaining troops,
not sending a single soldier to follow him.
In the ninth month,
Gāo Pián arrived at Nándìng.
In the fourth year of Gāozǔ's Wǔdé reign,
Nándìng County was established by dividing Sòngpíng County, which was under Jiāozhǐ's jurisdiction.
At that time, it belonged to the Ānnán Protectorate.
The Ānnán Protectorate
was Jiāozhǐ.
Sòng Bái said: Nándìng County
was the territory of Xījuǎn County in Hàn Rì'nán Commandery.
They were harvesting fields
when Gāo Pián launched a surprise attack,
greatly defeating them.
The 'Kǎo Yì' states: Both the 'Jiù Jì' and 'Shílù' say that in the fifth month, Gāo Pián reported a major defeat of the Línyì Man in Yōngguǎn.
However, Línyì is in Hǎinán,
and after Zhìdé, it was called Huánwáng,
having been cut off from China for a long time.
Liú Xù merely saw "Southern Man" and called them Línyì,
which is an error.
The New History of Nánzhào also states that Gāo Pián crossed the river with five thousand picked soldiers
and defeated Línyì troops in Yōngzhōu,
which also follows this error.
The 'Jiù Jì' also states:
"In the autumn of this year,
Gāo Pián advanced from Hǎimén,
defeated the Man army,
and recovered the Ānnán Protectorate."
This is probably because Gāo Pián set out from Hǎimén this autumn,
thus it was said that Ānnán was recovered.
The recovery of Ānnán actually occurred in the next year.
The Supplement to the National History states:
"In the fifth year,
ninth month,
Lord Gāo fought bravely,
defeating the Fēngzhōu Man in Nándìng County."
However, Zhāng Yīn was in charge of Jiāozhōu in the first month of the fifth year,
and received an imperial edict to recover Ānnán.
The Supplement to the National History states that he did not advance for a year,
and so Gāo Pián replaced him.
How then could Gāo Pián have already defeated the Fēngzhōu Man in the ninth month of that very year?
The Supplement to the National History also states:
"After Gāo Pián defeated the Fēngzhōu Man,
for nearly four months,
no report arrived.
The imperial court replaced him with Wáng Yànquán.
In the sixth month,
Lord Gāo advanced and recovered Ānnán."
It also does not say which year's sixth month.
Probably Gāo Pián defeated the Fēngzhōu Man in the ninth month of the sixth year.
And defeated Ānnán in the sixth month of the seventh year.
The 'Shílù' also states:
"In the ninth month,
Gāo Pián reported defeating the Man encampments in Lóngzhōu,
and burning their provisions, etc.
An imperial edict commanded Gāo Pián to defend the current border,
as a recent amnesty document had already granted clemency.
Awaiting their repentance,
it was not yet necessary to pursue them deeper."
However, the amnesty occurred in the eleventh month of the following year.
This edict must have been issued after Gāo Pián had pacified Ānnán;
the 'Shílù' is mistaken.
The New History also states that Gāo Pián attacked the Nánzhào garrison at Lóngzhōu,
and the Man chieftain burned his wealth and livestock and fled to Lóngzhōu,
which is Lóngbiān County under Ānnán's jurisdiction.
12 In winter,
the twelfth month,
on Rénzǐ,
Grand Empress Dowager Zhèng died.
The 'Kǎo Yì' states: The old chronicles say she died at the end of Dàzhōng,
which is an error.
We now follow the 'Shílù'.
1 Spring,
second month,
Guīyì Jiédùshǐ Zhāng Yìcháo reported that the Huíhú Gù Jùn of Běitíng had captured Xīzhōu, Běitíng, Lúntái, Qīngzhèn, and other cities.
Běitíng
was originally Tíngzhōu, established in the Zhēnguān reign.
In Cháng'ān second year,
the Běitíng Dūhùfǔ was established.
Seven hundred *lǐ* to the west was Qīnghǎi Zhèn.
Further west was Yánchéng,
and three hundred twenty *lǐ* west of that was Lúntái Xiàn.
"Huíhú Gù Jùn"
is rendered as "Púgù Jùn"
in both the *New History* and the main text of the *Kǎoyì*.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Shílù* says:
"Yìcháo reported that Jùn had recovered Xīhé, and that the various tribes, Hu and Hàn, had all submitted.
He also submitted a memorial congratulating the recovery of Xīzhōu and other cities."
The *New Tubó Biography* says:
"In the seventh year,
Jùn attacked and took Xīzhōu,
and received all the tribes."
According to the Dàzhōng fifth year,
Yìcháo presented the maps and registers of eleven prefectures,
and Xīzhōu was already among them.
The current statement that Xīzhōu was only now recovered
likely means that although its maps and registers were obtained at the time,
the territory was still occupied by Tubó.
Regarding Lùn Kǒngré lived in Kuòzhōu,
gathering various surrounding tribes,
intending to create border troubles,
but they did not follow.
Wherever he went, he made enemies,
and had no place to stay.
His enemies reported him to Tuòbá Huáiguāng in Shànzhōu.
Huáiguāng led his troops to attack and defeat him.
Sòng Bái said: Shànzhōu is one hundred eighty *lǐ* south of Kuòzhōu.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* says:
"Yìcháo also reported that Shànzhōu Chéngshǐ Zhāng Jìyóng escorted the captured Lùn Kǒngré, sent by Tuòbá Huáiguāng's subordinates,
along with his personal equipment and armor,
and all were presented as tribute."
The *New Tubó Biography* says:
"Shànzhōu Chéngshǐ Zhāng Jìyóng fought with Shàng Kǒngré,
defeated him,
and collected his weapons and armor to offer them."
We now follow the *Bǔguóshǐ* and *Shílù*.
2 Third month,
Wùyín,
Liú Tóng, Jiédùshǐ of Hédōng, was made Jiédùshǐ of Xīchuān.
Initially,
Nánzhào besieged Xīzhōu.
The Dōngmán Làngjī tribe exerted full effort to assist them,
and consequently massacred its city.
This refers to the capture of Xīzhōu last year.
Dǎo Zhōngwǔ's garrison troops attacked Làngjī
and annihilated them.
Nánzhào consequently resented the Táng.
Nánzhào dispatched Qīngpíngguān Dǒng Chéng and others to Chéngdū.
Jiédùshǐ Lǐ Fú received them with ceremonial guards.
According to custom,
Nánzhào envoys would prostrate themselves in the courtyard when meeting a Jiédùshǐ.
Chéng and others said:
"The Biāoxìn has responded to Heaven and conformed to man."
Nánzhào, since Xúnmèngcòu,
has called its ruler Biāoxìn,
which means "lord" in their夷語 (Yi language).
They thus usurped the title,
claiming to have responded to Heaven and conformed to man.
The messages went back and forth,
from dawn until noon without resolution.
The generals and soldiers were all indignant.
Fú then ordered them to be seized and beaten,
and then chained and imprisoned.
When Liú Tóng arrived at the post,
he released them,
and memorialized to send them back to their country.
An imperial edict summoned Chéng and others to the capital,
where they were received in a separate palace hall,
richly rewarded,
consoled, and sent away.
3 Chéngdé Jiédùshǐ Wáng Shàoyì
had been in command for ten years.
In Dàzhōng eleventh year,
Shàoyì succeeded to the post.
The army and people found him convenient.
When he fell ill,
he summoned his elder brother Shàodǐng's son, Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ Jǐngchóng, and told him:
"My elder brother, because of your youth,
entrusted the military administration to me.
You are now grown,
and I return the military administration to you.
Strive to uphold it:
be loyal to the court above,
and harmonious with neighboring *fān* below.
Do not let fall the enterprise of my elder brother;
this will be your achievement."
Having finished speaking,
he died.
History states that Wáng Shàoyì, when nearing death,
remained clear-minded.
4 Intercalary month,
Tubó raided Bīnnìng.
Jiédùshǐ Xuē Hóngzōng repelled them.
5 Summer,
fourth month,
the former Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ Lǐ Fú was demoted to Qíwáng Fù.
This was for beating and imprisoning the Nánzhào envoys.
Qíwáng Jī was
Sùnzōng's son.
6 Fifth month,
Empress Xiàomíng was buried beside the Jǐnglíng,
with her spirit tablet placed in a separate ancestral temple.
Empress Xiàomíng was
Xuānzōng's mother, Empress Dowager Zhèng.
Empress Yì'ān Guō,
who was Xiànzōng's primary empress,
was enshrined with him in the Tàimiào.
Empress Zhèng,
being a secondary consort,
was enshrined in a separate ancestral temple;
this was according to ritual.
7 Sixth month,
Wèibó Jiédùshǐ Hé Hóngjìng died.
The army established his son, Zuǒ Sīmǎ Quánhào, as Liúhòu.
8 Wáng Jǐngchóng was made Chéngdé Liúhòu.
9 Nánzhào Qiúlóng dispatched Shànchǎn Jiédùshǐ Yáng Jí
to assist Ānnán Jiédùshǐ Duàn Qiúqiān in defending Jiāozhǐ.
Shànchǎn Fǔ was
a secondary capital of Nánzhào,
located northwest of Jiāozhǐ.
Zhào Nuòméi was made Fúxié Dūtǒng.
According to the *Shílù*,
Fúxié Xiàn belonged to Luófú Zhōu,
likely established by Nánzhào.
Gāo Pián was able to augment his army,
attack Nánzhào,
and repeatedly defeat them.
Victory reports reached Hǎimén,
but Lǐ Wéizhōu concealed them all,
so for several months there was no news.
The Emperor was puzzled by this
and questioned Wéizhōu.
Wéizhōu reported that Pián was stationed in Fēngzhōu,
toying with the enemy and not advancing.
The Emperor was enraged
and sent Yòu Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn Wáng Yànquán to replace Pián as commander in Ānnán.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Bǔguóshǐ* refers to both Pián and Yànquán as Ānnán Jiédùshǐ.
However, at that time, Ānnán only had Dūhù, Jīnglüè, and Zhāotǎo Shǐ;
there was no Jiédùshǐ.
The old biography of Wáng Zhìxìng
lists nine sons,
but Yànquán's name is not among them.
The *Shílù* also states that Yànquán was appointed to replace Pián as Jiédù, but without a date;
this is likely a lacuna.
He wished to severely demote him.
Yànquán
was a cousin of Zhìxìng.
Wáng Zhìxìng served under four reigns: Dé, Shùn, Xiàn, and Mù.
Later, as Wǔníng Shuài,
he was especially greedy and arrogant.
Pián severely defeated the Nánzhào Man in Jiāozhǐ,
killing and capturing many,
and then besieged Jiāozhǐ City.
10 Autumn,
seventh month,
Hé Quánhào was made Wèibó Liúhòu.
11 Winter,
tenth month,
Jiǎshēn,
Yáng Shōu, Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was demoted to Xuānshè Guānchásǐ.
Shōu was extravagant and ostentatious by nature.
His gatekeepers, servants, and slaves often relied on him to commit malpractices for profit.
Yáng Xuánjià's brothers received bribes from regional commanders
and frequently made requests to him,
but Shōu could not fully comply.
Xuánjià became angry,
taking this as a betrayal,
and therefore had him dismissed.
12 Tuòbá Huáiguāng entered Kuòzhōu with five hundred cavalry,
captured Lùn Kǒngré alive,
first amputated his feet,
enumerated his crimes, and then beheaded him,
sending his head to the capital.
His followers fled east to Qínzhōu.
Shàng Yánxīn intercepted and attacked them,
defeated them,
and memorialized to have them all relocated to Lǐngnán.
Tubó subsequently declined and disappeared.
The fate of Qǐlíhú's lord and ministers is unknown.
The matter of Qǐlíhú first appears in volume 246, Wǔzōng Huìchāng second year.
Gāo Pián (高駢) besieged Jiāozhǐ (交趾) for over ten days.
The barbarians were extremely distressed and exhausted,
and the city was about to fall,
when he received a dispatch from Wáng Yànquán (王晏權).
Wáng Yànquán had already set out with Lǐ Wéizhōu (李維周) and a large army from Hǎimén (海門).
Pián (駢) immediately handed over military command to Wéi Zhòngzǎi (韋仲宰)
and returned north with over a hundred men from his retinue.
Earlier,
Zhòngzǎi (仲宰) had sent a junior envoy, Wáng Huìzàn (王惠贊),
and Pián (駢) had sent a junior officer, Zēng Gǔn (曾袞), to report the victory at Jiāozhǐ (交趾).
When they reached the sea,
they saw banners and flags approaching from the east.
They asked the patrol boats—
"Patrol boats"
refers to scout boats.
The two men deliberated, saying:
"Wéizhōu (維周) will surely seize our report and detain us."
So they hid among the islands.
After Wéizhōu (維周) had passed,
they immediately hastened to the capital.
When the emperor received the memorial,
he was greatly pleased
and immediately promoted Pián (駢) to Examining Administrator of the Ministry of Public Works (jiǎnjiào gōngbù shàngshū 檢校工部尚書)
and reinstated him as military commissioner (zhèn 鎮) of Ānnán (安南).
Pián (駢) reached Hǎimén (海門) and returned.
Wáng Yànquán (王晏權) was dull and timid;
his every action was subject to Lǐ Wéizhōu's (李維周) command.
Wéizhōu (維周) was fierce and greedy,
so the various generals would not serve him.
Consequently, the heavy siege was lifted,
and more than half of the barbarians fled.
When Pián (駢) arrived,
he again spurred on his officers and soldiers to attack the city,
and subsequently captured it.
He killed Duàn Qiúqiān (段酋遷) and Zhū Dàogǔ (朱道古), a local barbarian who had guided Nánzhào (南詔) forces,
beheading over thirty thousand people.
A textual variant states: "According to the old record: In the tenth month,
Pián (駢) reported that the barbarian invaders had been completely pacified."
The Veritable Records (Shílù 實錄) states:
"In the ninth month,
Pián (駢) reported the killing of the barbarian chieftain Guīshǒuqiān (皈首遷) and Zhū Dàogǔ (朱道古), and over three thousand beheadings."
Below the entry for the `bǐngshēn` (丙申) day of the tenth month,
it also says
"Pián (駢) reported the recovery of Ānnán (安南)
and the dispersal of the barbarian invaders."
It also says
"Yáng Jìsī (楊緝思), Duàn Qiúqiān (段酋遷), and Zhū Dàogǔ (朱道古) were defeated,
and over thirty thousand were killed."
The New Records (Xīnjì 新紀) states:
"In the tenth month,
Gāo Pián (高駢) captured Ānnán (安南)."
It is hereby noted that Guīshǒuqiān (皈首遷)
is a miswriting of Duàn Qiúqiān's (段酋遷) name.
The capture of the city and the defeat of Jìsī (緝思) and others in the Revised National History (Bǔ Guóshǐ 補國史) are the same event.
The Veritable Records (Shílù 實錄) divides it into two months,
but it is unclear what basis it uses.
The New Nánzhào (南詔) Biography says:
"In the seventh year,
sixth month,
Pián (駢) reached Jiāozhōu (交州),
fought several victorious battles,
and his soldiers fought with fierce enthusiasm.
He beheaded their general Zhāng Quán (張詮),
and Lǐ Zhālóng (李溠龍) led ten thousand men to surrender.
He captured the three forts of Bōfēng (波風).
Jìsī (緝思) came out to fight but was defeated
and fled back to the city.
The soldiers pursued him,
leaped over the ramparts, and entered,
beheading Qiúqiān (酋遷), Nìxiē (昵些), and Nuòmèi (諾眉).
Over thirty thousand heads were presented,
and Ānnán (安南) was pacified."
This is because Pián (駢) arrived in Ānnán (安南) in the sixth month,
and the account concludes with that.
Ānnán (安南) was not actually pacified in the sixth month.
We now follow the New and Old Records.
Pián (駢) also crushed two barbarian caves (dòng 洞) allied with Nánzhào (南詔),
executed their chieftains,
and seventeen thousand local barbarians submitted.
14 In the eleventh month,
on the `rénzǐ` (壬子) day,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the empire.
An imperial edict commanded the armies in Ānnán (安南), Yōngzhōu (邕州), and Xīchuān (西川) to each defend their borders
and no longer launch offensives against Nánzhào (南詔).
Liú Tóng (劉潼) was entrusted with explaining that
if they could restore their former good relations,
all past offenses would be forgiven.
15 The Jìnghǎi (靜海) Army was established in Ānnán (安南),
with Gāo Pián (高駢) appointed as Jiedushi (jiédùshǐ 節度使).
From this point until the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
Ānnán (安南) became a Jìnghǎi (靜海) military governorship (jiézhèn 節鎮).
The troubles for Ānnán (安南) had lasted nearly ten years,
and only now were they pacified.
Pián (駢) built the Ānnán (安南) city wall,
which was three thousand paces in circumference,
and constructed over four hundred thousand houses.
16 In the twelfth month,
the Qìrgíz (Xiájiásī 黠戛斯) sent General Yǐzhī Liánjǐ (乙支連幾) to present tribute,
memorializing a request to send saddled horses to welcome the envoy for the imperial investiture and for the calendar for the year of the Boar (Hài nián 亥年).
That year was `bǐngxū` (丙戌);
`hài` (亥)
was the following year.
17 Wáng Jǐngchóng (王景崇), the Acting Military Commissioner (liúhòu 留後) of Chéngdé (成德), was appointed Jiedushi (jiédùshǐ 節度使).
18 The emperor enjoyed music, banquets, and excursions.
The number of court musicians (yuègōng 樂工) serving in the palace often approached five hundred.
There were no fewer than ten banquets (yànshè 宴設) each month.
"Banquet" (yànshè 宴設)
refers to banquets held in the palace.
During the Sòng (宋) dynasty, court eunuchs referred to this as `páidāng` (排當).
It meant that the food and drinks included delicacies from both land and sea.
He never grew tired of them,
and the gifts often amounted to a thousand strings of cash.
Whether at Qūjiāng (曲江), Kūnmíng (昆明), Bàchǎn (灞滻), Nángōng (南宮), Běiyuàn (北苑)—
Nángōng (南宮)
was Xīngqìnggōng (興慶宮).
Běiyuàn (北苑) was the Forbidden Park (Jìnyuàn 禁苑),
north of the imperial city.
At Zhāoyìng (昭應) was Huáqīnggōng (華清宮).
At Xiányáng (咸陽) was Wàngxiánlóu (望賢樓).
They did not wait for arrangements to be made;
the relevant offices always prepared music, food and drink, and tents and canopies.
The imperial princes (zhūwáng 諸王) stood by their horses, ready to accompany the retinue.
Each time the emperor went on an excursion,
the accompanying officials from both inside and outside the court numbered over a hundred thousand,
and the expenses were incalculable.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Hé Quánhào (何全皞), the Acting Military Commissioner (liúhòu 留後) of Wèibó (魏博), was appointed Jiedushi (jiédùshǐ 節度使).
2 In the second month,
Zhāng Yìcháo (張義潮), Jiedushi (jiédùshǐ 節度使) of Guīyì (歸義), came to court.
In the fifth year of Xuānzōng's (宣宗) Dàzhōng (大中) reign (851 CE),
Zhāng Yìcháo (張義潮) surrendered Shāzhōu (沙州)
and was soon granted the Guīyì (歸義) military governorship (jié 節).
Now he came to court.
His kinsman Wéi Shēn (惟深) was ordered to guard Guīyì (歸義).
3 From Ānnán (安南) to Yōng (邕) and Guǎng (廣),
the sea route had many submerged rocks that caused ships to capsize.
Gāo Pián (高駢), Jiedushi (jiédùshǐ 節度使) of Jìnghǎi (靜海), recruited workers to clear them,
making maritime transport unobstructed.
4 The six barbarian clans near Xīchuān (西川)—
The six barbarian clans are: one, Méngmán (蒙蠻);
two, Yímán (夷蠻);
three, Émán (訛蠻);
four, Lángmán (狼蠻);
five, Wùdèngmán (勿鄧蠻);
six, Báimán (白蠻).
`Jìn` (近)
is a transcription of `jīn` (靳).
When there were no invaders, they claimed loyalty;
when there were invaders, they always served as the vanguard.
Only the Bīlóng (卑籠) tribe was fully devoted to Táng (唐),
and was an enemy of the barbarians.
The imperial court bestowed upon them the surname Lǐ (李)
and appointed their chief as Prefect (cìshǐ 刺史).
Liú Tóng (劉潼), the Jiedushi (jiédùshǐ 節度使), sent a general with troops to assist them
in attacking the six barbarian clans,
burning their settlements
and beheading over five thousand people.
5 The court musician (yuègōng 樂工) Lǐ Kějǐ (李可及) was skilled at composing new melodies.
In the third month,
the emperor appointed Kějǐ (可及) as General of the Left Wēi Guard (zuǒwēiwèi jiāngjūn 左威衞將軍).
Cáo Què (曹確) remonstrated, saying:
"Tàizōng (太宗) established over six hundred civil and military official positions,
saying to Fáng Xuánlíng (房玄齡): 'I reserve these for the worthy scholars of the realm;
merchants, artisans, and other commoners
should not hold them.'
In the Dàhé (大和) era (827-835 CE),
Wénzōng (文宗) wished to appoint the court musician (yuègōng 樂工) Wèichí Zhāng (尉遲璋) as an Officer (shuài 率) in a princely establishment (wángfǔ 王府).
Dòu Xúnzhí (竇洵直), a Rectifier of Omissions (shíyí 拾遺), remonstrated,
and he was instead made Prefect of Guāngzhōu (光州).
I beg Your Majesty to follow the precedents of these two reigns
and appoint Kějǐ (可及) to a different office."
The emperor did not comply.
6 In summer,
the fourth month,
the emperor fell ill,
and his favored eunuchs (chǒngchén 寵臣) rarely saw him.
7 In the fifth month,
on the `bǐngchén` (丙辰) day,
a general review of prisoners throughout the empire was ordered.
Except for those who were major criminals and could not be pardoned,
all others had their sentences reduced by one degree.
8 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the `rényín` (壬寅) day,
Qí Wáng (蘄王) Jī (緝) died.
Jī (緝)
was a son of Shùnzōng (順宗).
9 The people of Huáizhōu (懷州) complained of drought.
Liú Rénguī (劉仁規), the Prefect (cìshǐ 刺史), posted a notice forbidding them to do so.
The people were enraged
and rebelled together,
driving out Rénguī (仁規).
Rénguī (仁規) fled and hid in a village house.
The people entered the prefectural residence,
plundered his family's wealth,
climbed the tower, and beat drums.
After a long while, order was restored.
10th jiǎzǐ,

Yú Cóng, who was a Military Affairs Vice Minister (Bīngbù Shìláng), Commissioner for Salt and Iron Transport (Yántiě Zhuǎnyùnshǐ) for all circuits, and a Grand Commandant驸马都尉 (Fùmǎ Dūwèi), was made Administrator with the Same Authority as the Grand Councillor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì).
11th, Yáng Shōu, the Surveillance Commissioner (Guānchásǐ) of Xuān-Shè, passed by Huáyùe Temple.
Huáyùe Temple was located in Huáyīn County, Huázhōu.
Huá
is pronounced hù huà fān.
He ordered a shaman to pray;
the county magistrate (xiànlìng) falsely accused Shōu of a crime.
Wéi Bǎohéng, a Right Remonstrance Official (Yòu Shíyí), further stated that
Shōu, while previously a Grand Councillor (xiàng),
appointed Yán Zhuàn as Jiangxī Circuit Military Governor (Jiāngxī Jiédùshǐ),
receiving a million cash,
and also established a shipbuilding office (zàochuánwù),
and people complained of his embezzlement.
In the 8th month,
on the gengyín day,
Shōu was demoted to Administrator (Sīmǎ) of Duānzhōu.
The "Examination of Discrepancies" (Kǎoyì) says: The old tradition (jiùchuán) states:
"Wéi Bǎohéng became a Grand Councillor,
and then revealed Shōu's hidden misdeeds,
saying that he had previously appointed Yán Zhuàn as Jiangxī Circuit Military Governor,
receiving a bribe of a million [cash].
The next year,
he was demoted to Administrator of Duānzhōu."
According to this, Bǎohéng had not yet become a Grand Councillor at that time,
so the old tradition is mistaken.
Now, we follow the Veritable Records (Shílù).
12th, in the 9th month,
the Emperor's illness recovered.
13th, in winter,
the 12th month,
Xìn Wáng [AS-98D4] passed away.
14th, Wéi Zhòu, the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Lǐngnán Dōngdào, was made Administrator with the Same Authority as the Grand Councillor.
Punctuated by Róng Zhàozǔ, collated by Niè Chóngqí.
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by Imperial Edict.
After School Heaven Terrace
Xiántōng 9th year
(wùzǐ, 868)
1st, in summer,
the 6th month,
Lǐ Shīwàng, the Junior Administrator (Shǎoyǐn) of Fèngxiáng, submitted a memorial, saying:
"Xīzhōu controls and blocks Nánzhào,
serving as its vital thoroughfare.
Chéngdū is far away,
making it difficult to control.
I request the establishment of the Dìngbiān Army,
stationing heavy troops in Xīzhōu,
and making Qióngzhōu the seat of administration."
Lǐsuǒ means the same as zhìsuǒ.
Shàng
is pronounced shí zhǎng fān.
Xī
is pronounced suǐ.
Qióng
is pronounced qú róng fān.
Shīwàng was appointed Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Xīzhōu,
concurrently Military Governor of the Dìngbiān Army,
Surveillance Commissioner of Méi, Shǔ, Qióng, Yǎ, Jiā, Lí and other prefectures,
and overall commander of all the various barbarians (Zhū Mán) and commander of all circuit expeditionary forces and administrative commissioners.
Shīwàng, desiring to monopolize regional power,
therefore proposed this plan;
in reality, Qióng is only 160 lǐ from Chéngdū,
and Xī is a thousand lǐ from Qióng.
His deception was of this magnitude.
This set the stage for Lǐ Shīwàng to bring about an invasion through the Dìngbiān Army.
2nd, initially,
Nánzhào had captured Ānnán,
as seen in the 4th year of the previous fascicle.
800 men were separated to garrison Guìzhōu,
initially agreeing to rotate every three years.
Cuī Yànzēng, the Surveillance Commissioner of Xú-Sì,
was a nephew of Shènyóu.
Cuī Shènyóu first appeared in the Dàzhōng 11th year of Xuānzōng's reign in the previous fascicle.
Cóng
is pronounced cái yòng fān;
the same applies to cóngsūn below.
The court considered the Xú troops arrogant,
and ordered him to pacify them.
The Palace Guard Commandant (Dū Yāyá) Yǐn Kān and the Drill Instructor (Jiàoliànshǐ) Dù Zhāng
— in the 5th month of Dàzhōng 6th year,
an imperial edict stated: in all military administrations throughout the empire that have soldiers and horses,
those who understand military strategy and are skilled in archery and horsemanship should be selected to serve as Drill Instructors,
and they should constantly conduct drills
during the annual training season.
The army resented them.
Those garrisoned in Guìzhōu had already served for six years,
and repeatedly requested to be relieved and return.
Kān reported to Yànzēng
that due to the emptiness of the military treasury,
the expenses for dispatching troops would be considerable,
and requested that the garrison soldiers be kept for another year;
Yànzēng agreed.
When the garrison soldiers heard this,
they became enraged.
Xǔ Jí, the Chief of the Palace Guard (Dū Yúhòu),
and the army officers Zhào Kělì, Yáo Zhōu, and Zhāng Xíngshí, were all former bandits from Xúzhōu,
whom the prefecture and county could not suppress.
They were recruited and released [from punishment]
and appointed to guard positions.
Coincidentally, Lǐ Cóng, the Surveillance Commissioner of Guìguǎn, was transferred to Húnán.
The new commissioner had not yet arrived.
In autumn,
the 7th month,
Jí and others revolted,
killing the chief commander Wáng Zhòngfǔ,
and elevating Páng Xún, the Commissioner for Grain Provisions (Liángliào Pànguān), as their leader.
According to Táng regulations,
whenever an army was on campaign,
a Commissioner for Grain Provisions with the Army was appointed;
if the army was small, a Deputy Commissioner for Grain Provisions was appointed.
Xún
is pronounced xǔ yún fān.
They plundered wherever they went,
and seized weapons from the Guìzhōu arsenal, returning north to Xúzhōu.
Huán
is pronounced xuán,
and also as written.
Piāo
is pronounced pǐ miào fān.
When the court heard of this,
in the 8th month,
they dispatched Gāo Pǐn Zhāng Jìngsī to pardon their crimes.
The "New Book of Official Titles" (Xīnshū Bǎiguān Zhì) states: The Inner Palace Bureau (Nèishì Shěng) had 1,696 high-ranking officials (gāo pǐn).
The garrison soldiers then ceased their plundering.
3rd, Gāo Pián, former Military Governor of Jìnghǎi, was made Grand General of the Right Martial Guard (Yòu Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn).
Pián requested that his nephew Xún replace him in guarding Jiāozhǐ,
and this was granted.
4th, in the 9th month,
on the wùxū day,
Lú Dān, the Military Governor of Shānnán Dōngdào, was made Military Governor of Xīchuān;
due to the existence of the Dìngbiān Army,
he did not hold the titles of Commander-in-Chief of the Various Barbarians and Pacification Commissioner (Tǒng Yā Zhū Mán Ānfǔ děng Shǐ).
Since the Dìngbiān Army was established by partitioning Xīchuān,
all the various barbarians (Zhū Mán) were within the patrol area of the Dìngbiān Army.
5th, Páng Xún and others reached Húnán.
The Húnán Surveillance Commissioner's (Húnán Guānchásǐ) seat was in Tánzhōu.
They were ordered to surrender all their armor and weapons.
Cuī Xuàn, the Military Governor of Shānnán Dōngdào, heavily guarded key strongpoints,
so the Xú soldiers dared not enter the territory,
and instead sailed down the river eastward.
Xǔ Jí and others conspired among themselves, saying:
"Our crimes are greater than those of Yíndāo [Silver Knife].
Yíndāo is seen in the 3rd year of the previous fascicle.
We fear that if we are attacked and robbed along the way,
or disperse and cause trouble,
we will surely be pickled and minced if we reach Xúzhōu!"
So each of them used their private wealth to make armor, weapons, and banners.
Passing through Zhèxī,
they entered Huáinán.
Línghú Táo, the Military Governor of Huáinán, sent envoys to comfort and encourage them,

They all broke the heads off hoes and sharpened them,
holding them as they responded to the call for enlistment.
Neighboring circuits, upon hearing that Xún had occupied Xúzhōu,
each dispatched troops to secure strategic points.
However, the government forces were still few,
while the rebel numbers grew daily,
and the government forces repeatedly suffered defeats.
The rebels then captured nearly ten counties, including Yútái.
To the east of Sòngzhōu was Mòshān.
The people fled and hid on it.
Xún dispatched his general Zhāng Xuánrěn to besiege it.
There was a drought at the time,
and the mountain springs dried up,
causing tens of thousands of people to die of thirst.
Someone advised Xún, saying:
“The Liúhòu merely wishes to obtain the Jiéyuè.
He should act with deference and propriety in serving the Son of Heaven,
externally restrain his soldiers,
and internally pacify the common people;
then perhaps he can achieve his goal.”
Although Xún did not implement this advice,
he still performed incense offerings on national mourning days.
From the mid-Táng dynasty onwards,
on every national mourning day,
the emperor ordered all prefectures across the realm to set up vegetarian feasts and burn incense in temples and monasteries.
In the early Kāichéng period,
Lǐbù Shìláng Cuī Lí, considering this practice without canonical basis,
submitted a memorial requesting its abolition.
Soon after, it was restored.
Bì Zhòngxún’s Mùfǔ Yàxián Lù states: National mourning day incense offerings
originated in the Later Wèi dynasty.
Táng Huìyào states: In Tiānbǎo seventh year,
an imperial edict instructed the monks, nuns, and Daoists of Huá, Tóng, and other prefectures
to perform rituals and dispense vegetarian meals at Lóngxīng Sì on national mourning days.
By Zhēnyuán fifth year,
Chǔzhōu memorialized, saying,
“Our prefecture is not among those required to perform incense offerings.
We request to perform incense offerings like Qú, Wù, and other prefectures.”
An imperial decree said
“Granted.”
The note also appeared earlier.
Whenever a commander of a Fāngzhèn hosted a grand banquet for his officers and soldiers,
he would don court robes,
and the commander and his subordinates would face west towards the imperial palace to express gratitude,
stating that all blessings came from the emperor’s grace.
On Guǐmǎo,
Xún heard that the imperial envoy had entered the border,
and believed that he would certainly be bestowed with the banner and insignia (Jiéyuè).
Everyone congratulated him.
The next day,
the imperial envoy arrived,
but only reproached Cuī Yánzēng and the supervising general Zhāng Dàojǐn,
and demoted their officials.
Xún was greatly disappointed,
and thereupon imprisoned the imperial envoy,
not allowing him to return.
An imperial edict appointed Kāng Chéngxùn, the Right Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn, as Yìchéng Jiédùshǐ and Xúzhōu Xíngyíng Dōuzhāotǎoshǐ;
Wáng Yànquán, the Shénwǔ Dàjiāngjūn, as Xúzhōu Běimiàn Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ;
and Dài Kěshī, the Yǔlín Jiāngjūn, as Xúzhōu Nánmiàn Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ.
Kǎoyì states: The Old Annals:
“In the tenth year, first month,
Wáng Yànquán, the Shénwǔ Dàjiāngjūn, was appointed Wǔníng Jiédùshǐ.
Yànquán was
Zhìxìng’s cousin.
Kāng Chéngxùn, the Right Shéncè Dàjiāngjūn, was appointed Xú-Sì Xíngyíng Dōuzhāotǎoshǐ.
In total, eighteen generals
were in charge of the forces from various circuits, numbering seventy-three thousand and fifteen men.
On the first day of the first month,
the army advanced to attack Xúzhōu.”
It also says:
“Chéngxùn’s main army attacked Sùzhōu.
The rebel general Liáng Pī came out to battle,
and was repeatedly defeated.
Thereupon, Chéngxùn was granted the title of Yìchéng Jiédùshǐ.”
Shílù states:
“In the ninth year, twelfth month,
Kāng Chéngxùn, the Right Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn, was appointed Yìchéng Jū Jiédùshǐ and Xú-Sì Xíngyíng Bīngmǎ Dōuzhāotǎoshǐ.
Chéngxùn did not proceed to his post.
Chén Fáng, the Jiédù Fùshǐ, was appointed to take charge of the Liúhòu affairs.
Wáng Yànquán was appointed Xú, Sì, Háo, Sù, and other prefectures’ Guānchásǐ and Xúzhōu Běimiàn Xíngyíng Zhāotǎo, etc., and
Yǔlín Jiāngjūn Dài Kěshī was appointed Xúzhōu Nánmiàn Xíngyíng Zhāotǎo, etc.”
Péngmén Jìluàn and Xīn Jì state that
the appointments of Chéngxùn and others as Zhāotǎoshǐ were all in the eleventh month.
Tángnián Bǔlù states:
“On the Gēngshēn day of the eleventh month,
Kāng Chéngxùn, the Tàiyuán Jiédùshǐ, was appointed Dōutǒng
to suppress Xúzhōu.”
However, Gēngshēn was the first day of the twelfth month,
and Chéngxùn’s previous official position was also not Tàiyuán Jiédùshǐ.
The Bǔlù is incorrect.
Now we follow Péngmén Jìluàn and Xīn Jì.
Chéngxùn submitted a memorial requesting the three Shatuo [Shātuó] tribes under Zhūyé Chìxīn.
The Shātuó, Sàgé, and Ānqìng were divided into three tribes.
An imperial edict granted this request.
Páng Xùn (龐勛), seeing that Lǐ Yuán (李圓) had besieged Sīzhōu (泗州) for a long time without success,
sent his general Wú Jiǒng (吳迥) to replace him.
On the day bǐngwǔ,
the attack on Sīzhōu (泗州) resumed,
continuing day and night without cease.
At this time, the imperial envoy Guō Hòuběn (郭厚本)
*Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The old chronicles and *Shílù* (實錄) record
"Xī Hòuběn" (郗厚本);
now following *Péngmén Jìluàn* (彭門紀亂) and old biographies.
had reached Hóngzé (洪澤),
*Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) says: There is Hóngzé Zhèn (洪澤鎮) in Huái Yīn Xiàn (淮陰縣) of Chǔzhōu (楚州).
but dared not advance.
Xīn Dǎng (辛讜) requested to go seek aid,
and Dù Tāo (杜慆) permitted him.
On the night of dīngwèi,
Dǎng (讜) took a small boat and secretly crossed the Huái (淮) River.
Arriving at Hóngzé (洪澤),
he spoke to Hòuběn (厚本),
but Hòuběn (厚本) would not listen.
By dawn,
Dǎng (讜) returned.
On the day jǐyǒu,
the rebels attacked the city with greater urgency,
intending to burn the water gate.
The city was almost unable to defend itself.
Dǎng (讜) again requested to go seek aid.
Tāo (慆) said:
"Last time you went and merely returned;
what good will it do to go now?"
Dǎng (讜) replied:
"If I obtain troops on this trip, I will return alive;
if not, I will die."
Tāo (慆) tearfully bade him farewell.
Dǎng (讜) again took a small boat, carrying a door panel as a shield, broke through the encirclement and left.
He saw Hòuběn (厚本),
and explained the advantages and disadvantages to him.
Hòuběn (厚本) was about to agree,
when Yuán Gōngbiàn (袁公弁), the commander of Huáinán (淮南), said:
"The rebel forces are like this;
we may not even be able to protect ourselves,
how can we spare time to save others!"
Dǎng (讜) drew his sword, glared at Gōngbiàn (公弁) and said:
"The rebels are attacking the city from a hundred directions;
its fall is imminent.
You received an imperial edict to provide relief but you hesitate and do not advance.
Not only do you fail the nation's grace from above!
If Sīzhōu (泗州) cannot be held,
then Huáinán (淮南) will become a battlefield for the bandits.
How can you alone survive?
I shall kill you before I stop
He stood up,
intending to strike him.
Hòuběn (厚本) stood up,
embraced him and restrained him.
Gōngbiàn (公弁) barely escaped.
Dǎng (讜) then looked back towards Sīzhōu (泗州),
and wept bitterly all day.
The soldiers and officers all shed tears for him.
Hòuběn (厚本) then promised to give him five hundred men,
and then asked his officers and soldiers.
All the officers and soldiers wished to go.
Dǎng (讜) prostrated himself
and kowtowed to thank the officers and soldiers.
He then led them to the southern bank of the Huái (淮) River.
Seeing the rebels attacking the city,
an army official said:
"The rebel forces already seem to have entered the city;
it would be better to turn back."
He feared the rebels and dared not advance the troops,
saying it would be convenient to return the army and leave.
Dǎng (讜) seized his topknot.
Lǎn (攬) means
to grasp or hold.
The soldiers and officers collectively saved him,
saying:
"The assistant commissioner is one of us,
he must not be killed."
Dǎng (讜) said:
"To speak wildly on the battlefield and mislead the masses
cannot possibly be forgiven!"
The crowd begged but could not prevail,
so they tried to wrest him away.
Dǎng (讜) had always been very strong,
and the crowd could not take him.
Dǎng (讜) said:
"Let the officers and soldiers simply board the boats,
and I will release this man."
The crowd rushed to board the boats,
and then Dǎng (讜) released him.
If any soldier looked back,
Dǎng (讜) would strike him with his sword.
He drove them to the north bank of the Huái (淮),
marshaled his troops and attacked the rebels.
Tāo (慆) deployed troops on the city wall to respond to him,
and the rebels were defeated and fled.
They beat drums and shouted, pursuing them
until dusk before returning.
Páng Xūn 遣 his general Liú
Jí to lead several thousand elite soldiers to assist Wú Jiǒng in attacking Sìzhōu.
Liú Xíngjí, from Háozhōu, sent his general Wáng Hónglì to lead troops to join them.
On the day Wùwǔ,
Dù Shěnquán, Jìedùshǐ of Zhènhǎi,
governed Zhènhǎi Commandery in Rùnzhōu.
On the day Jǐwèi,
Xíngyuē led his troops to Sìzhōu.
The rebels ambushed them in Huáinán,
surrounding them.
As there were few soldiers in the city,
they could not provide rescue.
Xíngyuē and his soldiers all perished.
Previously,
Línghú Táo had sent Lǐ Xiāng with several thousand soldiers to relieve Sìzhōu.
They joined forces with Guō Hòuběn and Yuán Gōngbiàn, encamping at Dūliáng Chéng.
Dūliáng Chéng
was located on Dūliáng Shān, north of Xūyí Xiàn in Sìzhōu.
Xiàng Ānshì said: "Dūliáng Xiàn has a small mountain.
The water on the mountain is extremely clear and shallow.
All kinds of orchids grow on this mountain,
with green leaves and purple stems.
Locals call orchids 'Dūliáng,'
hence the county was named after it."
After the rebels defeated Zhái Xíngyuē,
they capitalized on their victory to besiege them.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ,
Lǐ Xiāng and others led their troops out to battle,
suffering a great defeat.
The rebels then captured Dūliáng Chéng
and seized Xiāng and Guō Hòuběn, sending them to Xúzhōu.
The Kǎoyì says: The old annals record:
"In the tenth month,
the rebels' attack on Sìzhōu became urgent.
Línghú Táo feared losing the Huáikǒu,
so he ordered general Lǐ Xiāng to go to its aid.
The entire army was annihilated.
Xiāng and the Dūjiān Guō Hòuběn were both captured by the rebels
and sent to Xúzhōu."
The Biography of Línghú Táo says:
"When the rebels heard that Xiāng was coming to reinforce,
they sent someone to deliver a letter to Táo,
with humble and compliant language,
saying: 'The imperial court has repeatedly issued edicts of amnesty and pardon,
but only two or three individuals are resisting.
We plan to remove them day and night,
and then we will surrender ourselves and await orders.
We hope that you, Excellency, will guarantee us.'
Táo immediately reported this to the emperor,
requesting that Xūn be granted insignia and authority.
He also cautioned Lǐ Xiāng to only guard the Huáikǒu,
as the rebels had already offered surrender,
and not to create conflict.
Because of this, Xiāng's army disarmed and rested peacefully,
removing their vigilance and preparations.
Day after day, they faced the rebel army,
laughing and chatting.
One day,
the rebel army seized an opportunity and cavalry and infantry directly entered Xiāng's camp.
Five thousand Huái soldiers were all captured alive
and sent to Xúzhōu,
where they were steamed and eaten by the rebels.
Xiāng and the Jūnjūn Guō Hòuběn had their hands and feet severed by Páng Xūn
to be displayed to Kāng Chéngxùn's army.
At that time, Dù Shěnquán of Zhèxī dispatched a thousand troops,
and Lǐ Xiāng arranged to rendezvous with them.
The general Zhái Xíngyuē was renowned for his bravery.
Before the Zhè army arrived, Xiāng's army was defeated.
The rebels then divided their forces,
setting up Huáinán banners,
mimicking a battle.
Xíngyuē's army saw this and
rushed towards it.
A thousand men were all captured by the rebels
and sent to Xúzhōu.
After Táo lost the army,
the imperial court appointed Mǎ Jǔ to replace Táo as Jìedùshǐ of Huáinán."
The Biography of Xīn Dǎng says:
"Xiāng led five thousand to reinforce,
but the rebels feigned surrender and
defeated them at Huáikǒu.
Xiāng and Guō Hòuběn were both captured by the rebels."
The Péngmén Jìluàn says:
"Because Sìzhōu held firm,
Xūn sent Liú Jí to conspire to attack and seize it.
At that time, the three circuits of Huáinán, Xuān, and Rùn sent troops to garrison the old city of Dūliáng Shān,
which was separated from Sìzhōu only by the Huái River.
The rebel multitude then secretly crossed the Huái River at night,
and by dawn, they were pressing on the city.
The Háozhōu rebel commander Liú Xíngjí also sent Wáng Hónglì to invade and plunder Huáinán.
Thereupon, they gathered their forces and urgently attacked,
and the government troops abandoned the city to engage in battle.
On the thirtieth day of the eleventh month,
the rebels then utterly defeated the government troops,
killing two thousand people
and taking seven or eight hundred alive as captives.
They also captured their generals Lǐ Xiāng and others,
all of whom were sent to Xúzhōu.
The rebels then occupied the Huáikǒu,
cutting off the courier route."
It also says:
"After the rebels defeated Dài Kěshī,
Línghú Táo was afraid,
so he sent an envoy to entice and persuade them,
promising to petition for insignia on their behalf."
The Xù Huángwáng Bǎoyùnlù says:
"On the twenty-ninth day of the eleventh month,
Dù Shěnquán, Jìedùshǐ of Zhèxī, dispatched Dūtóu Zhái Xíngyuē with two thousand soldiers to come to the rescue.
On the thirtieth day,
as Xíngyuē was leading his troops about to enter Sìzhōu,
he was again rushed upon by the rebels.
Xíngyuē occupied a hill,
but was soon surrounded.
The soldiers in the city could not go out to rescue him.
The rebels then opened their encirclement.
Xíngyuē, not knowing it was a trap,
then tried to escape,
but ran into an ambush laid at the foot of the hill.
In a short while, he was killed,
not a single horse remained.
The rebels then surrounded Huáikǒu Zhèn.
The Huáinán Dūyāyá Lǐ Xiāng and Zhènjiàng Yuán Gōngbiàn, leading three thousand cavalry and infantry, were surrounded.
From the thirtieth day of the eleventh month to the fifth day of the twelfth month,
Lǐ Xiāng donned his armor and led his army out.
They were ambushed and hunted down, all killed.
Those who returned to the garrison
hoisted surrender flags.
Over ten thousand soldiers, old and young, within the garrison
were plundered and driven to Háozhōu.
Guō Hòuběn was killed at this time."
We now follow the Xù Bǎoyùnlù.

This refers to the route for tribute and couriers from the southeast to the capital being cut off.
Kāng Chéngxùn’s army was stationed at Xīnxīng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Nínglíng County in Sòngzhōu has Xīnxīng Town.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Línhàn County in Sùzhōu has Liǔzǐ Town,
which is now ninety lǐ north of Sùzhōu.
Fàn Chéngdà’s Běishǐ Lù says: From Línhàn County, travel forty-five lǐ north
to Liǔzǐ Town.
Zhāng Shùnmín’s Chēnháng Lù says: Liǔzǐ Town is south of Yǒngchéng County.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Yǒngchéng belongs to Bózhōu,
and is one hundred fifteen lǐ northeast of the prefecture.
At that time, only ten thousand soldiers had gathered from various circuits.
Chéngxùn, deeming his forces unequal to the enemy,
retreated to Sòngzhōu.
Páng Xūn thought the government army was not to be feared,
so he dispatched his generals Dīng Cóngshí and others, each leading several thousand men, to raid Shū and Lú to the south,
and invade Yí and Hǎi to the north.
They captured Shùyáng, Xiàcài, Wūjiāng, and Cháo County.
Shùyáng,
was Lǐnqīu County in the Hàn dynasty;
later the Northern Wèi changed its name to Shùyáng;
in the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Hǎizhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is one hundred eighty lǐ southwest of the prefecture.
Xiàcài,
was an ancient county in the Hàn dynasty;
in the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Yǐngzhōu.
Wūjiāng,
was Wūjiāng Pavilion in Dōngchéng County during the Hàn dynasty;
the Suí dynasty established Wūjiāng County;
in the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Hézhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is thirty-five lǐ northeast of the prefecture.
Cháo,
was Jūcháo County in the Hàn dynasty;
in the Suí dynasty, it became Xiāng’ān County;
in the seventh year of Wǔdé,
Xiāng’ān was renamed Cháo County,
and belonged to Lúzhōu.
Shù,
pronounced shí yù.
They killed the Prefect Gāo Xīwàng.
They also raided Hézhōu.
Chúzhōu is one hundred fifty lǐ south of Hézhōu.
He invited the bandits to ascend the tower and drink with him,
ordered his soldiers to all remove their armor,
designated two men he favored as his sons,
begging for their lives to be spared,
leaving the rest to the bandits' discretion.
The bandits then extensively plundered the city,
killing over eight hundred soldiers.
The Kǎoyì states: The Péngmén Jìluàn records:
"Several hundred bandit rebels from the mountains of Guāng and Cài
attacked and captured Chúzhōu,
killed Prefect Gāo Xīwàng,
and submitted to Páng Xūn."
The Jiù Jì records:
"In the eleventh month,
after Wú Jiǒng had captured Lǐ Xiāng,
he ordered his junior generals Zhāng Xíngjiǎn and Wú Yuē to attack Chúzhōu,
captured Prefect Gāo Xīwàng,

Xíngjiǎn then advanced to attack Hézhōu.
Prefect Cuī Yōng ascended the city tower
and spoke to Wú Yuē as mentioned,
whereupon the city's residents were plundered,
