Xūn also ordered Líu Zhì to attack Háozhōu,
which he captured,
imprisoning Prefect Lú Wànghúi in the Húichē Guǎn.
Wànghúi died of depression and indignation."
The Shílù records:
"In the intercalary month,
the bandits captured Hézhōu and Háozhōu."
In the second month of the following year, it further states:
"Xūn dispatched Zhāng Xíngjiǎn to attack Chúzhōu,
entered the city,
and harmed Prefect Gāo Xīwàng."
The Xīn Jì records:
"In the twelfth month,
the bandits captured Chú and Hé."
Now, the capture of Háozhōu follows the Péngmén Jìluàn,
and the capture of Chú and Hé is placed after the capture of Lǐ Xiāng.
The relief troops for Sìzhōu were cut off,
and provisions were almost exhausted;
people ate thin gruel.
In the intercalary month,
on the Jǐhài day,
Xīn Dǎng spoke to Dù Tāo,
requesting to go out and seek aid from Húai and Zhè.
That night,
he led ten brave volunteers,
carrying long-handled axes—
Kē means axe handle—
and stealthily went to chop down the bandit's water stockade and break out.
The next morning,
the bandits realized it,
and blocked their front with five boats,
pursuing them along the banks with five thousand men.
The bandit boats were heavy and slow,
while Dǎng’s boat was light and swift.
They fought vigorously for over thirty lǐ
and managed to escape.
On the Gǔimǎo day,
they reached Yángzhōu and met Línghú Táo;
on the Jiǎchén day,
they reached Rùnzhōu and met Dù Shěnguán.
Yángzhōu is over fifty lǐ south of Rùnzhōu.
It was rumored that it had already fallen.
After Dǎng arrived,
Shěnguán dispatched Commander Zhào Yì with two thousand armored soldiers
to transport five thousand hú of rice and five hundred hú of salt, together with Húainán, to relieve Sìzhōu.
Dài Kěshī led an army of thirty thousand across the Huái River.
They fought their way forward,
and the rebels abandoned all their defenses south of the Huái River.
Kěshī wanted to first capture the mouth of the Huái River,
and then rescue Sìzhōu.
On the *rénshēn* day,
they besieged Dūliáng chéng.
There were few rebels in the city.
They bowed from atop the city walls, saying:
"We are just about to discuss with the commander our surrender."
Kěshī withdrew five *lǐ* for them.
The rebels fled that night.
The next morning,
only an empty city remained.
Kěshī, relying on his victory, made no preparations.
That day, there was a heavy fog.
The rebel
general Wáng Hónglì led tens of thousands of troops in a rapid, direct advance and arrived suddenly.
"Jíjìng" (疾徑)
is similar to "jiéjìng" (捷徑) (shortcut).
It means not following the main road,
but taking a direct path,
to gain speed and convenience.
The government forces did not have time to form ranks,
and were greatly defeated.
Commanders and soldiers either perished by weapons or drowned in the Huái River.
Only a few hundred people escaped.
Tens of thousands of weapons, supplies, provisions, carts, and horses were lost.
The rebels displayed the heads of Kěshī, the supervising envoy, and the generals and officers in Péngchéng.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Xù Bǎoyùn lù* says:
"On the eighteenth day of the first month,
Dài Kěshī was defeated and lost.
The rebels then became even more rampant."
The *Péngmén Jìluàn* says:
"Kěshī led thirty thousand troops, intending to first capture the mouth of the Huái River,
and then rescue Sìzhōu.
On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month,
at daybreak,
they besieged the rebels at the foot of Dūliáng Shān.
The rebels were about to surrender,
but Kěshī, relying on his strong army,
made no preparations.
A rebel general named Wáng Hónglì
led tens of thousands of men,
took a shortcut to rescue them,
and charged forward.
The government army was routed and scattered,
and consequently defeated.
Kěshī, along with the supervising envoy and all generals and officers, perished in the battle.
Thereupon, Páng Xūn thought that he had no strong enemies before him."
The *Jiùjì* says:
"In the twelfth month,
Kěshī fought continuously with the rebels.
The rebel factions were repeatedly defeated,
abandoning all their defenses south of the Huái River.
In the first month of the tenth year,
Kěshī was appointed as the Pacification Commissioner for the Cáozhōu Provisional Command.
At that time, rebel generals Liú Xíngjí and Wú Jiǒng were attacking and besieging Sìzhōu.
Kěshī, emboldened by his victory, went to their rescue,
stationing his troops at Shíliáng Yì.
The rebels retreated.
Kěshī pursued them,
capturing Xíngjí alive.
The rebels held Dūliáng chéng.
They bowed from atop the city walls, saying: 'We are about to discuss with the commander our surrender.'
Kěshī, knowing their predicament,
withdrew his troops five *lǐ*.
There was water on the west side of the city,
and the main army was on the other three sides.
The rebels then fled by wading through the water during the night.
Early the next morning,
when the city gates were opened,
there were only a few sick old women.
Before the imperial army could properly array themselves in the camp,
the next day,
at dawn,
in a heavy fog,
a large rebel army arrived.
Kěshī, who was very drunk,
rode out alone
and was killed by Guō Zhēn from Hóngxiàn.
The entire army was annihilated.
Rebel general Wú Jiǒng advanced and again besieged Sìzhōu."
It also says:
"Páng Xūn memorialized: 'The three thousand soldiers from Lǐngnán who were previously deployed by the road need winter and spring clothing.
We now wish to dispatch someone to send them to Yōngguǎn.'
Liú Yǔnzhāng, the Observer of Èyuè, submitted a letter stating: 'Páng Xūn has gathered a multitude of one hundred thousand.
If we now send people to reach the Lǐngbiǎo region,
and the garrisoned soldiers join forces with Xūn,
then the disaster will not be small.'
Soon an imperial edict ordered Páng Xūn to cease and desist,
and also commanded the disciplinary officials of the various Jiāng and Huái circuits to apprehend him."
The *Shílù* places Kěshī's defeat under the intercalary month,
but also mentions the thirteenth day of the twelfth month.
The *Xīnjì* states the *rénshēn* day of the twelfth month,
which also uses the date from the *Jìluàn*.
According to the *Jìluàn*, there is a "Làyuè" (臘月)
above it,
and it also says,
"thirteenth day of the twelfth month,"
with no intercalary month below it.
It is suspected that it means the thirteenth day of the intercalary month.
However, according to the *Xù Bǎoyùn lù*,
on the eleventh day of the intercalary month,
Xīn Dǎng left Sìzhōu,
and on the fourteenth day,
arrived in Yángzhōu to request troops and provisions.
If Kěshī was in Dūliáng at that time,
then Dǎng would certainly not have abandoned Kěshī to go to Yáng and Rùn.
If Dǎng's departure occurred after Kěshī's defeat,
then Línghú Táo would have been too busy saving himself,
how could he have had time to save Sìzhōu!
If Kěshī's defeat occurred in the first month,
then the *Xīnjì* states that Mǎ Jǔ had already been dismissed as the Southern Pacification Commissioner in the twelfth month.
In essence,
it must have been after Xīn Dǎng went to Yáng and Rùn,
which is why it is placed here.
Páng Xūn considered himself invincible in the world.
He issued proclamations,
distributing them to all camps and villages.
Consequently, the people and gentry of Huáinán were terrified,
often fleeing to the Jiāngzuǒ region.
Línghú Táo, fearing his encroachment,
sent an envoy to Xūn to persuade and instruct him,
promising to petition for him to receive an imperial banner and axe (as a military governor).
Xūn then ceased hostilities and awaited the imperial command.
Because of this, Huáinán was able to gradually gather its scattered soldiers
and repair its defenses.
At that time, the road to Biàn had been cut off.
All traffic between Jiāng and Huái went through Shòuzhōu.
Ascending the Huái from Shòuzhōu led directly into the Yǐng and Biàn roads.
Taking advantage of his victory, he besieged Shòuzhōu,
plundering tributes from various circuits and merchants' goods,
thus cutting off that road again.
Xūn became even more arrogant,
spending his days in feasting and revelry.
Zhōu Chóng admonished him, saying:
"From ancient times, many have become arrogant, complacent, extravagant, and indulgent,
gaining and then losing,
achieving and then failing.
How much more so for those who do so before gaining or achieving anything!"
A large number of troops from various circuits gathered at Sòngzhōu.
Xúzhōu began to be fearful.
The number of volunteers decreased,
while requests for reinforcements from various camps came one after another.
Xūn then sent his followers to scatter into the villages
and conscript people into the army.
Seeing that his army already numbered tens of thousands
and provisions were exhausted,
he then collected wealth from rich households and merchants,
taking seven or eight tenths of it,
leading to hundreds of families being exterminated for concealing wealth.
Moreover, those who had joined Xūn in raising an army in Guìzhōu were particularly arrogant and violent.
They seized people's property
and abducted women.
Xūn could not control them.
Consequently, the people within the region all grew weary and suffered from this,
Wáng Yànquán (王晏權) commanded troops but was repeatedly repulsed.
The imperial court ordered Cáo Xiáng (曹翔), military governor (節度使) of Tàiníng (泰寧), to replace Yànquán as the Commander of the Northern Front (北面招討使) for Xúzhōu (徐州).
Yǎn hǎi (兗海),
was styled the Tàiníng Army (泰寧軍).
The *Kǎoyì Zhèngwén* (考異正文) states: Cáo Xiáng and Mǎ Jǔ (馬舉) were the Commanders of the Southern and Northern Fronts for Xúzhōu.
The note says: *Péngmén Jìluàn* (彭門紀亂) writes
"Mǎ Shìjǔ" (馬士舉),
we now follow the *Xīnjì* (新紀).
The *Jìluàn* (紀亂) says:
"Wáng Yànquán was repeatedly attacked by the rebels,
and although he did not suffer a decisive defeat or heavy casualties,
he frequently retreated.
The imperial court again appointed Cáo Xiáng, governor (牧) of Lǒngzhōu (隴州), to lead the military governorship of Yǎnhǎi (兗海),
serving as the Grand Commander of the Northern Front (北面都統招討等使).
Furthermore, Hégōng (何公), marshal of Wèibó (魏博), dispatched Xuē Yóu (薛尤) to lead 30,000 troops to attack the rebels from both sides;
Cáo Xiáng's army was stationed at Téng (滕) and Pèi (沛),
and the Wèibó (魏博) army was at Fēng (豐) and Xiāo (蕭),
their total forces numbering sixty to seventy thousand men."
It also says that the rebels attacked Hǎizhōu (海州) and Shòuzhōu (壽州),
and were defeated in both instances.
It also says that Xīn Dǎng (辛讜) relieved Sìzhōu (泗州),
although this is placed under the first month,
it is a retrospective account of earlier events.
The *Shílù* (實錄) states:
"In the second month,
Mǎ Jǔ was appointed military governor of Huáinán (淮南),
serving as the Commander of the Southern Front (南面招討使).
Initially,
Kāng Chéngxùn (康承訓) led his generals to advance and attack Xúzhōu on the first day of the first month,
but failed,
and the rebels besieged Shòuzhōu.
Wáng Yànquán was repeatedly attacked by the rebels,
retreating and not daring to engage in battle,
so Cáo Xiáng was appointed military governor of Yǎnhǎi (兗海) and other prefectures,
serving as Commander of the Northern Front.
Wèibó (魏博) dispatched Xuē Yóu (薛尤) to lead 3,000 troops
to attack the rebels from both sides.
The rebel forces attacked Hǎizhōu (海州),
and the garrison troops engaged them,
inflicting a great defeat.
Kāng Chéngxùn led his forces and encamped west of Liǔzi (柳子)."
All these are based on this and are erroneous.
The *Xīnjì* (新紀),
states that Xiáng and Jǔ were appointed Commanders of the Southern and Northern Fronts
in the twelfth month, and there was no intercalary month.
Now, because Xiáng cooperated with Wèibó (魏博) in attacking Xúzhōu, and this is mentioned,
it is placed at the end of the year.
According to the *Kǎoyì* (考異),
and the matter of Mǎ Jǔ relieving the siege of Sìzhōu (泗州) the following year,
then in the main text of the *Tōngjiàn* (通鑑),
after "Cáo Xiáng (曹翔) became the Commander of the Northern Front for Xúzhōu,"
there should be
"Mǎ Jǔ (馬舉) was appointed military governor of Huáinán (淮南), serving as the Commander of the Southern Front,"
fourteen characters.
These fourteen characters
were omitted in transmission.
Comment: Hé Quánhào (何全皞) was the military governor of Wèibó (魏博).
Wèibó (魏博) was originally called the Tiānxíong Army (天雄軍) and never moved to another garrison,
so I suspect the historian added
the character
"qián" (前)
(former).
Or it is said: at that time Qínzhōu (秦州) was called the Tiānxíong Army (天雄軍),
and the Wèibó (魏博) army's title was abolished,
so the character
"qián" (前)
was added.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: *Péngmén Jìluàn* (彭門紀亂) says:
"Yóu commanded 30,000 men,
and together with Cáo Xiáng's army,
they totaled sixty to seventy thousand men."
The *Shílù* (實錄) states:
"Wèibó (魏博) submitted a memorial requesting to dispatch 3,000 troops to assist in attacking Xú (徐) and Sì (泗)."
The *Jiùjì* (舊紀) states:
"Hé Hóngjìng (何弘敬) of Wèibó (魏博) memorialized: 'The commander of this circuit has inspected 13,000 soldiers to proceed to the field camp.'"
Although the names are mistaken,
we take the number of people.
Yóu's army was stationed at Fēng (豐) and Xiāo (蕭).
All four counties belonged to Xúzhōu (徐州).
Téng (滕),
the state of Lord Téng (滕子) during the Spring and Autumn period;
during the Suí (隋) dynasty, Téng County was established.
Sòng Bái (宋白) says: Because there is Téng City forty *lǐ* southwest of the county.
Fēng (豐),
an ancient county of the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) says: Téng (滕) is one hundred ninety-five *lǐ* north of the prefecture.
Pèi (沛) is one hundred forty *lǐ* northwest.
Fēng (豐) is one hundred forty *lǐ* northwest.
Xiāo (蕭) is fifty *lǐ* west.
Xiāo County is also named after the ancient state of Xiāo (蕭國).
6 That year,
Jiānghuái (江淮) suffered drought and
locusts.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Kāng Chéngxùn (康承訓) led the armies of various circuits, over 70,000 men, and encamped west of Liǔzi (柳子).
From Xīnxīng (新興) to Lùtáng (鹿塘), a distance of thirty *lǐ*,
their palisades were connected.
Xúzhōu (徐州) soldiers were distributed to guard the four borders,
leaving less than a few thousand men in the city,
which finally made Páng Xūn (龐勛) afraid.
Many civilians dug holes in the ground and hid in them.
Xūn sent men to search and dig them out for his army,
but could only get twenty to thirty people a day.
Páng Xūn's (龐勛) general Mèng Jìngwén (孟敬文) guarded Fēng County,
cunning and fierce, with many soldiers,
and planned to betray Xūn,
creating his own omens.
When Xūn heard of this,
and coincidentally Wèibó (魏博) was attacking Fēng (豐),
Xūn sent a trusted general to lead 3,000 men to help Jìngwén defend Fēng (豐);
Jìngwén made an agreement with him to jointly attack the Wèibó (魏博) army,
and praised his bravery.
After "sānqiān" (三千)
there should be
the character
"rén" (人).
The character 'jiāng' (將)
for 'jiāngjiàng' (將將) is pronounced 'bìng' (並) and 'jíliàng' (即亮).
'Yù' (譽)
is pronounced 'yú' (余).
When the new army engaged the Wèibó (魏博) army,
the new army
refers to the army recently attached to Páng Xūn.
The new army was completely annihilated.
Xūn then sent an envoy to deceive him, saying:
"Wáng Hónglì (王弘立) has already captured Huáinán (淮南),
and the acting governor (留後) wishes to go and garrison it himself;
he has summoned all generals,
wishing to select one who can defend Xúzhōu (徐州)."
Jìngwén was pleased
and immediately galloped to Péngchéng (彭城).
Before he reached the city by several *lǐ*,
Xūn's (勛) ambush captured him,
and on the *Xīnyǒu* (辛酉) day,
he was killed.
2 On the *Dīngmǎo* (丁卯) day,
Princess Tóngchāng (同昌公主) married Wéi Bǎohéng (韋保衡), a Right Reminder (右拾遺),
and Bǎohéng was made a Palace Censor (起居郎) and Imperial Son-in-Law (駙馬都尉).
Tóngchāng (同昌)
was a commandery name in the Suí (隋) dynasty,
and in the Táng (唐) dynasty it was Chángfēn (常芬) County in Diézhōu (疊州).
She was the daughter of Guō Shú (郭淑),
and the emperor particularly loved her,
emptying the palace of treasures and curiosities for her dowry.
She was granted a residence in Guǎnghuà (廣化) ward,
with windows and doors decorated with various jewels.
Well railings, medicine mortars, troughs, and chests
were also made of gold and silver.
Baskets and hampers were woven from gold threads.
She was given five million *mín* of cash,
and other items were commensurate.
3 The Xú (徐) rebels attacked Hǎizhōu (海州).
The Xú rebels
refers to the troops sent by Páng Xūn.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) says: Xúzhōu (徐州) is four hundred eighty *lǐ* east of Hǎizhōu (海州).
They cut the bridge pillars along the rebels' route but did not sever them.
*Shū* (殊)
means 'to sever'.
They cut the bridge pillars but did not let them break completely,
waiting for the rebels to cross, step on them, and fall in.
'Duàn' (斷)
is pronounced 'duǎn';
the 'suǒduàn' (鎖斷) and 'fǔduàn' (斧斷) below are the same.
When the rebels crossed,
the bridge collapsed.
They scattered in panic and confusion,
and the ambushing troops attacked,
annihilating them all.
Those attacking Shòuzhōu (壽州) were again defeated by the Southern Route Army,
with several thousand killed or captured.
The Southern Route Army
refers to the troops from Huái (淮) and Zhè (浙).
'Fù' (復)
is pronounced 'fúyòu'.
Xīn Dǎng, with the army from Zhéxī, arrived at Chǔzhōu.
The imperial envoy, Zhāng Cúnchéng, aided them with boats.
The Xú rebels deployed troops by water and land,
locking off the Huái River.
The Zhéxī army feared their strength
and dared not advance.
Dǎng said:
"I request to be the vanguard.
If we win, follow me;
if we lose, you may flee."
Still, they wouldn't move.
So Dǎng recruited several tens of dare-to-die warriors from the army,
formally appointed them to official positions,
and first led three rice boats and one salt boat straight ahead against the current with the wind.
The rebels attacked them from both sides.
Arrows struck the boat planks like heavy rain.
Those attacking from both sides
were the rebel soldiers on both banks.
[The character] 艘 (sōu) [means] a boat.
[The pronunciation is] sū zāo fān [a transcription method].
[The character] 著 (zhù) [means] strike.
[The pronunciation is] zhí lüè fān [a transcription method].
Dǎng led the masses in a desperate fight,
cut through their lock with an axe,
and thus managed to pass through.
The people on the city walls shouted so loudly that it shook the earth.
Dù Tāo and his generals and subordinates all wept as they welcomed him.
On the day *Yǐyǒu*,
from the city walls, they saw a fleet of boats with sails unfurled approaching from the east.
They recognized its flag as that of the Zhéxī army.
About ten *lǐ* from the city,
the rebels arrayed fire boats to block them.
The sails stopped, unable to advance.
Tāo ordered Dǎng to lead dare-to-die warriors out to meet them,
charged through the rebel formation on warships,
and saw Zhāng Cúnchéng leading nine rice boats.
[Cúnchéng] said:
"The generals and soldiers hesitated on the way,
and Cúnchéng repeatedly wished to commit suicide.
Fearing the enemy, I dared not advance,
so I advanced and retreated.
Now they won't advance again."
Dǎng loudly declared:
"The rebels are not many;
they are very easy to deal with!"
This was to boost the morale of the troops and make them advance.
[The character] 易 (yì) [means] easy.
[The pronunciation is] yǐ shǐ fān [a transcription method].
When the rebels saw their fierce and sharp momentum,
they avoided them,
and thus [the army] was able to enter the city.
In the second month,
Yáng Shōu, the Sīmǎ of Duānzhōu, was banished to Huānzhōu for life
and soon after was granted death.
More than ten of his subordinates, partisans, and friends were exiled to Lǐngbiǎo for life.
In the beginning,
Péi Tǎn, the Shàngshū Yòuchéng, had his son marry Shōu's daughter.
The dowry and gifts were extremely lavish,
with utensils and ornaments embellished with rhinoceros horn and jade.
Tǎn saw them
and angrily said:
"You will ruin my family!"
He immediately ordered them to be destroyed.
Afterwards, Shōu was indeed ruined by bribery.
Kāng Chéngxùn sent Zhūyé Chìxīn to lead three thousand Shatuo cavalry as the vanguard.
They broke formations and repelled the enemy.
The armies of the Ten Circuits admired their bravery and prowess.
The Ten Circuits
refer to Yìchéng, Wèibó, Fūyán, Yìwǔ, Fèngxiáng, Hénghǎi, Tàiníng, Xuānwǔ, Zhōngwǔ, and Tiānpíng.
Sùzhōu's Línhuàn County
was named after the Huàn River.
[According to] the North-South border map: the Huàn River originates in Bózhōu,
flows south into the Huái,
and directly reaches Wǔhékǒu.
Chìxīn led five hundred cavalry, wielded his mace, and charged through the encirclement,
rescuing Chéngxùn.
The rebel forces scattered and fled.
They then combined their forces and attacked,
defeating them.
Chéngxùn fought many battles with the rebels,
and the rebel army was repeatedly defeated.
Wáng Hónglì boasted about his victory at Huáikǒu,
referring to his defeat of Dài Kěshī.
Páng Xūn approved of this.
On the day *Jǐhài*,
Hónglì led his troops across the Suī River.
At night,
they attacked Lùtángzhài.
At dawn,
they besieged it.
Hónglì and his generals observed from a vantage point,
believing that success was imminent.
The Shatuo cavalry broke through the encirclement from left and right,
moving in and out like lightning.
The rebels scattered and shifted position.
The Shatuo cavalry unleashed their horses and trampled them.
All the armies within the fortress rushed out and fought fiercely,
and the rebels were greatly defeated.
The government forces pressed them to the Suī River,
and countless drowned.
From Lùtáng to Xiāngchéng—
this Xiāngchéng is not the Xiāngchéng of Rǔzhōu,
but another Xiāngchéng between Xú and Sù.
Over twenty thousand heads were cut off.
Hónglì escaped alone on horseback.
The captured common people he had driven before him all scattered into the mountains and valleys,
no longer returning to the camp.
Supplies, provisions, and equipment were abandoned, piled up like mountains.
At that time, there was an imperial edict
that whenever the armies defeated the rebels and
captured farmers,
they should all be released.
From then on, whenever the rebels encountered government forces,
the people they had captured would first collapse and flee on their own.
Páng Xūn and Xǔ Jí, considering Hónglì's arrogance and sloth led to defeat,
wanted to execute him.
Zhōu Chóng spoke on his behalf to Xūn, saying:
"Hónglì achieved two victories that have not yet been rewarded.
The two victories
refer to taking Háozhōu
and defeating Dài Kěshī.
To disregard his achievements and record his faults
would be to avenge the enemy.
All the generals would be afraid.
It would be better to pardon him
and hold him accountable for future achievements."
So Xūn released him.
Hónglì gathered only a few hundred scattered soldiers
and requested to capture Sìzhōu to compensate for his failure.
Xūn increased his troops and dispatched him.
In the third month,
on the day *Xīnwèi*,
Wéi Bǎohéng, the Qǐjūláng, was appointed Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū
and concurrently Hànlín Xuéshì.
Yǐng Wáng Kǎn was transferred and made Wēi Wáng.
Kǎn
was an imperial prince.
After Kāng Chéngxùn defeated Wáng Hónglì,
he advanced and pressed against Liǔzi,
fighting dozens of battles with Yáo Zhōu within a month.
On the day *Dīnghài*,
Zhōu led his troops across the water,
meaning across the Huàn River.
Zhōu retreated and fled.
The government forces pursued him,
and then besieged Liǔzi.
There was a great wind,
and fires were set on all four sides.
The rebels abandoned their stronghold and fled.
The Shatuo cavalry intercepted them with elite horsemen,
slaughtering almost all of them
from Liǔzi to Fāngchéng.
Fāngchéng,
in the *New Book*, is written as
"Fāngtíng."
They cut off the head of their general, Liú Fēng.
Zhōu, with several tens of his subordinates, fled to Sùzhōu.
Liáng Pī, the defending general of Sùzhōu, had a long-standing grudge against him.
He opened the city gates to let them in,
then seized and executed them.
Páng Xūn 聞 zhī dà jù,
yǔ Xǔ Jí yì zì jiāng chū zhàn.
Zhōu Chóng qì yán yú Xūn yuē:
"Liǔzǐ dì yào bīng jīng,
Yáo Zhōu yǒnggǎn yǒu móu,
jīn yī dàn fùmò,
wēi rú lěi luǎn,
bù ruò suì jiàn dà hào,
xī bīng sì chū,
juélì sǐ zhàn."
Yòu quàn shā Cuī Yànzēng yǐ jué rénwàng.
Shùshì Cáo Jūncháng yì yán:
"Xúzhōu shānchuān bù róng liǎng shuài,
jīn guānchásǐ shàng zài,
gù liúhòu wèi xīng."
Zéi dǎng jiē yǐ wéi rán.
Xià,
sì yuè,
rénchén,
Xūn shā Yànzēng jí jiānjūn Zhāng Dàojǐn, Xuānwèishǐ Qiú Dàfū,
liáozuǒ Jiāo Lù, Wēn Tínghào,
bìng qí qīnshǔ, bīnkè, púqiè jiē sǐ;
duàn Huáinán jiānjūn Guō Hòuběn, dōuyáyá Lǐ Xiāng shǒuzú,
yǐ shì Kāng Chéngxùn jūn.
Xūn nǎi jí zhòng yángyán yuē:
"Xūn shǐ wàng guóēn,
dàyán yǐ bōgào yuē yángyán.
Wàng guóēn,
wèi wàng jīngjié yě.
Jīnrì zhī shì,
qián zhì yǐ guāi.
Zì cǐ,
Xūn yǔ zhū jūn zhēn fǎn zhě yě,
dāng sǎo jìngnèi zhī bīng,
lùlì tóngxīn,
zhuǎnbài wéi gōng ěr."
Zhòng jiē chēng shàn.
Yúshì mìng chéng zhōng nánzǐ xī jí qiúchǎng,
réng fēn qiǎn zhū jiàng bǐwū dà suǒ,
gǎn nì yī nánzǐ zhě zú qí jiā.
Xuǎn dīngzhuàng,
dé sān wàn rén,
gēng zào qízhì,
gěi yǐ jīngbīng.
Xǔ Jí děng gòng tuī Xūn wèi Tiāncè Jiāngjūn, Dàhuì Míngwáng.
Xūn cí Wángjué.
Xiān shì,
Xīn Dǎng fù zì Sìzhōu yǐn xiāoyǒng sìbǎi rén yíng liáng yú Yáng, Rùn,
zéi jiá'àn gōng zhī,
zhuǎnzàn bǎilǐ,
nǎi dé chū.
Zhì Guǎnglíng,
zhǐ yú gōngguǎn,
bù gǎn guījiā,
zhōu zài yánmǐ èr wàn shí,
qián wàn sānqiān mín,
yǐwèi,
huán zhì Dǒushān.
Dǒushān,
zài jīn Xūyí xiàn,
yì yuē Dǒushān,
lín huái liú;
Dǒushān zhī dōng,
zé gǔ Xūyí.
Jù zhī yú Xūyí,
mì bù zhànjiàn bǎiyīwǔshí sōu yǐ sè Huái liú,
yòu zòng huǒchuán nì zhī.
Dǎng mìng yǐ chángchā tuō guò,
zì mǎo zhàn jí wèi,
zhòngguǎ bù dí,
guānjūn bù lì.
Zéi fù mù yú zhànjiàn,
páng chū sìwǔ chǐ wéi zhànpéng,
Dǎng mìng yǒngshì chéng xiǎozhōu rù qí xià,
shǐrèn suǒ bù néng jí,
yǐ qiāng jié huǒniú fén zhī,
zhànjiàn jì rán,
rán,
wèi huǒrán yě.
Guānjūn nǎi dé guò rù chéng.
Kǎoyì yuē: Xù Bǎoyùn Lù yuē:
"Èr yuè qī rì,
Xīn Dǎng jiǎndiǎn xiāoyǒng,
lǐng kōng chuán shí'èr zhī bān liáng,
èrshí rì,
què dào Chǔzhōu,
sì yuè liù rì,
lí Chǔ,
bā rì,
zhì Dǒushān xià,
shì rì èrgēng hòu,
rù Sìzhōu."
Àn zhēngyuè èrshíqī rì,
Dǎng yíng mǐ chuán jiǔ zhī rù Sìzhōu,
èr yuè liù rì,
wèi yìng shí jǐn fù chū.
Yòu èrshí rì què dào Chǔzhōu,
bù yìng zhù sìshíwǔ rì rán hòu lí bǐ.
Yòu shàng yǒu èr yuè shí rì shòu Dǎng yùshǐ,
bù yìng xià yún èr yuè qī rì Dǎng chū bān liáng.
Yí shì
"sān yuè"
zì yě.
Páng Xūn yǐ fù Jǔzhí wèi Dàsīmǎ,
yǔ Xǔ Jí děng liúshǒu Xúzhōu.
Huò yuē:
"Jiāngjūn fāng yào bīngwēi,
bù kěyǐ fùzǐ zhī qīn,
shī shàngxià zhī jié."
Nǎi lìng Jǔzhí qū bài yú tíng,
Xūn jù àn ér shòu zhī.
Shí Wèibó lǚ wéi Fēngxiàn,
Páng Xūn yù xiān jí zhī,
bǐngshēn,
yǐn bīng fā Xúzhōu.
9 Wùxū,
yǐ qián Huáinán Jiédùshǐ, Tóng Píngzhāngshì Línghú Táo wèi Tàibǎo, fēnsī.
Yǐ Táo zài Huáinán sàng shī,
mìng Mǎ Jǔ dài zhī.
10 Páng Xūn yè zhì Fēngxiàn,
qián rù chéng,
Wèibó jūn jiē bù zhī zhī.
Wèibó fēn wéi wǔ zài,
qí jìn chéng zhě tún shù qiān rén,
Xūn zòng bīng wéi zhī,
zhū zài jiù zhī,
Xūn fú bīng yàolù,
shā guānjūn èr qiān rén,
yú jiē fǎn zǒu.
Zéi gōng zài bù kè,
zhì yè,
jiěwéi qù.
Guānjūn wèi qí zhòng,
qiě wén Xūn zì lái,
zhū zài jiē xiāo kuì.
Cáo Xiáng fāng wéi Téngxiàn,
wén Wèibó bài,
yǐn bīng tuì bǎo Yǎnzhōu.
Cáo Xiáng,
Tàiníng shuài,
běn zhì Yǎnzhōu,
gù tuì bǎo zhī.
Yùn qí zīliáng,
chuánxí Xúzhōu,
shèng zì kuādà,
wèi guānjūn wèi guózéi yún.
Mǎ Jǔ jiāng jīngbīng sān wàn jiù Sìzhōu,
yǐsì,
fēnjūn sāndào dù Huái,
zhì zhōng liú,
dà zào,
shēng wén shù lǐ.
Zéi dà jīng,
bù cè zhòngguǎ,
liǎn bīng tún chéngxī zài.
Jǔ jiù wéi zhī,
zòng huǒ fén zhà,
zéi zhòng dà bài,
zhǎn shǒu shù qiān jí;
Wáng Hónglì sǐ,
Wú Jiǒng tuì bǎo Xúchéng,
Sìzhōu zhī wéi shǐ jiě.
Sìzhōu bèi wéi fán qī yuè,
Sìzhōu zì qùnián jiǔ yuè mò shòu wéi.
Miànmù jiē shēng chuāng.
In this month,
Piàoxìn Qiúlóng of Nánzhào led his entire nation to invade,
bringing tens of thousands of troops to attack Dǒngchōng Wūbù,
and defeated them.
Dǒngchōng Wūbù
were barbarians attached to the frontier of Xīchuān.
The barbarians advanced to invade Guīzhōu.
Ān Zàiróng, the Dìngbiān Commander, defended Qīngxī Pass.
The barbarians attacked it.
Zàiróng retreated to camp north of the Dàdù River,
and they shot arrows at each other across the water
for nine days and eight nights.
The barbarians secretly divided their army, opening a
path,
crossed Xuěpō,
and suddenly arrived at Mùyuánchuān.
Xuěpō
is the slope of Xuělǐng.
Mùyuánchuān is located on the border of Luómù County, Jiāzhōu.
In the second year of Líndé,
the raw barbarians were pacified,
and Luómù County and Mùzhōu were established;
later Mùzhōu was abolished,
and Luómù was assigned to Jiāzhōu;
in the Sòng dynasty, Luómù was again abolished and made a town,
belonging to Éméi County.
Now, Jiāzhōu has Mùchuān Town in Qiánwéi County.
The entire army was annihilated.
In the twelfth month,
on the day of Dīngyǒu,
the barbarians, dressed in the clothing of Yǎn-Hǎi,
feigned defeat,
and arrived at the riverbank, calling for boats.
After they had crossed,
the multitude realized it,
and then Qiánwéi fell.
They unleashed their troops to burn and plunder the territories of Líng and Róng Prefectures.
Qiánwéi
was a Hàn commandery name.
The Later Zhōu established Wǔyáng County.
In the early years of Kāihuáng of the Suí,
its name was changed to Qiánwéi,
named after the mountains.
Under the Táng, it belonged to Jiāzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: it is one hundred twenty *lǐ* southeast of the prefecture.
Qián,
read as jū yán.
The barbarian army gathered in large numbers at Língyún Temple,
opposite Jiāzhōu.
Jiāzhōu
was the territory of Nán'ān County, Qiánwéi Commandery, Hàn.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng opened up the outer frontier
and established Qīngzhōu,
taking Qīngyī as its name.
The Western Wèi changed Qīngzhōu to Méizhōu,
taking Éméi Mountain as its name.
The Later Zhōu again called it Qīngzhōu,
and then changed it to Jiāzhōu,
taking Jiā Commandery of Hàn as its name.
The Suí again changed it to Méizhōu.
The Táng again called it Jiāzhōu,
and separately established Méizhōu in the territory of Hàn Wǔyáng County.
Língyún Temple is on the southern mountain of Jiāzhōu.
During the Kāiyuán era,
the monk Hǎitōng, at the confluence of the Dújiāng, Mòshuǐ, and Méngshuǐ rivers,
on the bank of the fierce currents and raging waves,
carved a great Maitreya statue into the mountain.
It was over three hundred sixty *chǐ* high,
and a seven-story pavilion was built to cover it.
Mín and Dìngbiān Supervising Army Zhāng Yǔnqióng arrayed troops to resist them.
The barbarians secretly dispatched surprise troops to cross from Dōngjīn,
attacking the imperial army from both sides,
killing Yán Qìngshī, the General of Zhōngwǔ Commandery.
The rest of the troops scattered,
and Mín and Yǔnqióng escaped.
On the day of Rénzǐ,
Jiāzhōu fell.
Qìngshī
was the younger brother of Qìngfù.
Dòu Pāng personally led troops to resist the barbarians at the Dàdù River.
Piàoxìn deceptively sent several Qīngpíng Officials to Pāng to negotiate peace.
Before Pāng finished speaking with them,
the barbarians rushed to cross on boats and rafts.
The Zhōngwǔ and Xúsù armies formed ranks to resist them.
Xúsù
was formerly the Wǔníng Army.
Because this army frequently rebelled,
the military commissioner position was abolished.
Chén,
read as zhèn (formation).
He tried to hang himself in his tent.
Miáo Quánxù, a general from Xúzhōu, stopped him,
saying:
"Why has the Commander-in-Chief come to this!"
Quánxù, with Ān Zàiróng and the Zhōngwǔ generals, arrayed troops and went out to battle.
Pāng then fled alone on horseback under the cover of night.
The three generals conspired, saying:
"Now our numbers are no match for theirs.
If we fight again tomorrow morning,
all of us will perish.
It is better to attack them at night,
to cause them to be startled and confused,
and then withdraw."
Thereupon, they entered the barbarian camp at night,
firing bows and crossbows indiscriminately.
The barbarians were greatly alarmed,
and the three generals then led their entire army away.
The barbarians advanced and captured Lí and Yǎ.
The people fled and hid in the mountains and valleys.
The defeated armies burned and plundered everywhere.
Pāng fled to Dǎojiāng.
Dǎojiāng
was originally Dū'ān County established by Liú Shǔ.
The Later Zhōu changed it to Wènshān.
The Táng changed it to Dǎojiāng,
belonging to Péngzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: it is ninety *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
When the barbarians arrived,
the city was already empty,
and they passed through without obstruction.
Kǎoyì states: Zhāng Yún's Xiántōng Jiěwéilù says:
"In the tenth year,
tenth month,
the Southern Barbarians attacked Dǒngchōng Wū Tribe,
destroying their lair.
Chōngwū protected his people in the northern palisade.
Soon after, the barbarians suddenly arrived at Mùyuánchuān,
and then pressed upon Jiāzhōu.
From Qīngxī Pass in the south, they invaded Lí and Yǎ."
Zhāng Jǐnlǐ's Qíjiù Zhuàn says:
"In the eleventh year,
on the day of Gēngyín,
the Jìedùshǐ Lú Púshè Dān.
In winter,
tens of thousands of Yúnnán barbarians invaded the frontier,
broke through Qīngxī Pass,
attacked the Dàdù River,
then advanced and captured Chénlí,
assaulted Qiónglái,
directly reaching Yǎ and Qióng."
According to Jiěwéilù and the New and Old Annals, all state that the barbarian invasion occurred in the winter of the tenth year;
to exclusively place it in the winter of the eleventh year
is an error.
The Xīn Zhuàn says:
"In the tenth year,
they invaded,
using troops to hold Qīngxī Pass,
secretly leading a multitude to cut trees and open a path,
directly through Xuěpō.
In midsummer,
two thousand soldiers froze to death,
emerging at Mùyuán
and spying on Jiāzhōu."
According to the text, the barbarians arrived at Mùyuánchuān in the eleventh month,
which is not midsummer;
the Xīn Zhuàn is in error.
The Shílù also states:
"Piàoxìn left Shànchǎn on the third day of the tenth month,
each person carrying only one *dǒu* of roasted rice with them.
An edict was then issued to Gāo Pián to take advantage of the lack of military preparedness in their country
and attack Shànchǎn,
to relieve the conflict."
According to the text, Pián was then the Jìedùshǐ of Yùnzhōu,
not in Ānnán;
it is likely the Shílù is in error.
An edict was issued for Zuǒ Shénwǔ General Yán Qìngfù to lead troops to reinforce.

Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng
by imperial decree
Hòu Xué Tiāntái
Xiántōng Eleventh Year
(Gēngyín, 870)
1 Spring,
First Month,
on the first day of Jiǎyín,
your humble subjects offered the honorific title of Ruìwén Yīngwǔ Míngdé Zhìrén Dàshèng Guǎngxiào Huángdì;
a general amnesty was granted to the empire.
2 The people of Xīchuān, hearing that barbarian invaders were about to arrive,
vied to flee into Chéngdū.
At that time, Chéngdū had only the Zǐchéng,
and no moat.
The land occupied by each person
was no more than one mat’s width.
When it rained, they wore sieves and basins on their heads to shelter themselves.
Water was also scarce,
so they took muddy water from Móhē Chí,
clarified it, and drank it.
The Chéngdū Jì states: Móhē Chí was within Zhāng Yí’s Zǐchéng.
When Suí’s Shǔwáng Xiù took earth to build and expand the Zǐchéng,
it became a pond.
A Hu monk saw it and said:
“Móhē Gōngpíluó.”
This is because the Hu monk meant
“Móhē”
as ‘great’,
and “Gōngpíluó”
as ‘dragon’,
meaning that this pond was vast and had a dragon.
Hence, it was named Móhē Chí.
Some say Xiāo Móhē dug it,
which is incorrect.
The pond is now twelve lǐ southeast of Chéngdū Xiàn.
The generals and soldiers were not accustomed to military preparations.
Jiédùshǐ Lú Dān summoned Péngzhōu Cìshǐ Wú Xínglǔ to act as Cānmóu,
and together with the former Lúzhōu Cìshǐ Yáng Qìngfù,
(A textual note says: The Xīnchuán states,
“Lúzhōu Cìshǐ Yáng Qìng.”
The Jǐnlǐ Qíjiù Chuán states,
“Jiāzhōu,”
which is an error.
Now we follow the Jiěwéilù.)
selected commanders,
assigned duties,
erected battle platforms,
prepared catapults and rolling logs,
manufactured equipment,
and tightened patrols.
Previously,
many generals and soldiers in Xīchuān held empty titles,
and received no stipends.
At this time,
a notice was posted to recruit brave and capable men,
who were appointed to actual positions,
and given generous provisions and rewards.
Those who answered the call gathered like clouds.
Qìngfù then admonished them, saying:
“You are all sons and brothers of the army,
young, talented, and brave.
In times of peace, you have no means to advance yourselves.
Now that barbarian invaders are rampant,
this is your opportunity to attain wealth and honor!
How can you not strive?”
They all cheered and leaped with joy.
Thereupon, weapons were arrayed in the courtyard,
and they were made to test their individual skills,
competing two by two to determine who was superior.
Their bravery and timidity were observed, and they were promoted or demoted accordingly.
Three thousand elite soldiers were selected,
known as
“Tújiàng”.
Xínglǔ was
a native of Péngzhōu.
On the day of Wùwǔ,
the barbarians reached Méizhōu.
Dān sent the Assistant Jiédùshǐ Wáng Yǎn and others to deliver a letter to their influential minister Dù Yuánzhōng,
and negotiate peace with him.
The barbarians replied:
“Our movements
are solely dependent on His Majesty’s pleasure.”
3 Lù Yán and Wéi Bǎohéng submitted a memorial, stating:
“When Kāng Chéngxùn attacked Páng Xùn,
he dallied and did not advance,
nor could he eliminate all of the remaining rebels.
Moreover, he was greedy for spoils,
and did not report his achievements in a timely manner.”
On the day of Xīnyǒu,
he was demoted to Shǔwáng Fù and Fēnsī.
Shǔwáng Jí was
the Emperor’s son.
(A textual note says: The Xīnchuán states:
“Chancellors Lù Yán and Wéi Bǎohéng impeached Chéngxùn for dawdling in attacking the rebels,
being greedy for spoils,
and not reporting his achievements in a timely manner,
leading to his demotion to Shǔwáng Fù and Fēnsī Dōngdū.”
However, at this time, Bǎohéng was not yet a chancellor.
It was probably due to his relationship as the husband of an imperial princess
that the Emperor adopted his suggestion,
thus allowing him to oust Chéngxùn.)
4 The Nánzhào army advanced to Xīnjīn.
Xīnjīn was
the territory of Hàn’s Wǔyáng Xiàn.
Later Zhōu changed it to Xīnjīn.
Under Táng, it belonged to Shǔzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is seventy lǐ southeast of the prefecture.
Lú Dān sent the Assistant Jiédùshǐ Tán Fèngsì to deliver a letter to Dù Yuánzhōng,
asking his reason for coming.
The barbarians detained him and did not send him back.
Dān sent an envoy to report the emergency to the court,
and also requested that an envoy be sent to negotiate peace,
to relieve the immediate crisis.
The court ordered Zhī Sìfāngguǎn Shì and Tàipú Qīng Zhī Xiáng to be the Xuānyù Tōnghé Shǐ.
The Yàn Gōng Lèiyào states: According to old regulations,
among the Tōngshì Shèrén,
one senior member would oversee all affairs of the guest house,
called the Guǎnzhǔ.
All tributes and memorials from all directions were received by him and presented.
After the middle period of Táng,
other officials began to be appointed to take charge of the Sìfāngguǎn Shì.
This also caused a delay,
and the defenses of Chéngdū were consequently somewhat completed.
On the day of Jiǎzǐ,
the barbarians marched rapidly north,
and captured Shuāngliú.
Shuāngliú was
the territory of Hàn’s Guǎngdū Xiàn.
During Suí, Shuāngliú Xiàn was established.
Under Táng, it belonged to Chéngdū Fǔ.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is forty lǐ south of the prefecture.
On the day of Gēngwǔ,
Dān sent Assistant Jiédùshǐ Liǔ Pán to see them.
Dù Yuánzhōng handed Pán a letter,
saying:
“This is the protocol for the Biao xìn to meet with the military command after peace is established.”
The protocol treated him as a king,
and the language was extremely arrogant.
They also sent people carrying a colorful canopy to the south of the city,
saying they wanted to set it up in the Shǔwáng Tīng to house the Biao xìn.
When Suí’s Shǔwáng Xiù garrisoned Shǔ,
he built the Tīngshì,
which was extremely grand.
(The term Tīng
is translated in other texts.)
On the day of Guǐyǒu,
Dìngbiān Jūn was abolished,
and the seven prefectures were returned to Xīchuān.
The seven prefectures were
Qióng, Méi, Shǔ, Yǎ, Jiā, Lí, and Cuì.
On this day,
the barbarian army arrived beneath the walls of Chéngdū.
The day before,
Lú Dān had sent the Vanguard Patrol Envoy Wáng Zhòu to Hànzhōu to inquire about the relief forces,
and to urge them on.
At that time, six thousand men from Xīngyuán and four thousand from Fèngxiáng had already reached Hànzhōu.
Dòu Pāng, with four thousand men from Zhōngwǔ, Yìchéng, and Xúsù, rushed from Dǎojiāng to Hànzhōu,
joining the relief forces to save himself.
On the day of Dīngchǒu,
Wáng Zhòu, with over three thousand men from Xīngyuán, Zī, and Jiǎn, encamped at Píqiáo.
(Píqiáo is
in the southern border of Hànzhōu.)
They fought unfavorably and
retreated to defend Hànzhōu.
At that time, Chéngdū daily awaited the arrival of relief forces,
but Dòu Pāng, considering his loss of territory,
(meaning the loss of Dìngbiān Jūn,)
whenever relief forces arrived from the north,
would persuade them, saying:
“The barbarian host outnumbers the government army by tens of times.
The government army has come a long way and is exhausted,
it is not easy to rush forward now.”
All the generals believed him,
and all were hesitant and did not advance.
Chéngdū’s commander Lǐ Zìxiào secretly colluded with the barbarians,
wanting to burn the granary east of the city as an inside signal.
He was arrested and killed in the city.
A few days later,
the barbarians indeed attacked the city,
but after a long time,
receiving no response from within the city, they stopped.
In the second month,
on the *Guǐwèi* day,
the *Mán* tribes, using scaling ladders and battering rams, attacked Chéngdū from all four sides.
Those on the city walls used hooks and ropes to pull the attackers closer.
"Ladders" (梯)
refers to cloud ladders (*yúntī*);
"rams" (衝)
refers to battering rams (*chōngchē*).
"Huán" (繯),
pronounced *yúshàn*,
means to twist ropes into a ring-hook,
applied to their ends.
All the attackers died.
Lú Dān ordered Yáng Qìngfù and the acting Left Army Commander Lǐ Xiāng to each lead elite troops to sally forth and fight.
They killed and wounded over 2,000 *Mán* tribesmen.
As night fell,
they burned over 3,000 of the enemy's siege implements and returned.
The people of Shǔ were generally timid,
but their elite troops had recently been praised and promoted by Qìngfù,
and also motivated by generous rewards,
their courage doubled.
Those who could not sally forth
were all frustrated and eager to fight.
A few days later,
the bandits took civilian fences,
piled them up wet and bent them,
making them into "shelters" (*péng*).
They placed men underneath,
lifted them to reach the city and undermine it.
Arrows and stones could not penetrate them,
and fire could not burn them.
"Rán" (然),
is the same as "rán" (燃),
meaning to burn.
The attackers again died.
On the *Yǐyǒu* day,
Zhī Xiáng sent an envoy to the *Mán* tribes to negotiate peace.
On the *Dīnghài* day,
the *Mán* tribes withdrew their troops and requested peace.
On the *Wùzǐ* day,
an envoy was sent to welcome Zhī Xiáng.
At this time, Yán Qìngfù was about to arrive with reinforcements.
Xiáng said to the *Mán* envoy:
"I received an imperial edict to proceed to Dìngbiān to negotiate peace.
Now, Yúnnán is besieging Chéngdū,
which is contrary to the imperial edict of that day.
Furthermore, the court's reason for making peace
was to prevent them from attacking Chéngdū.
Now, arrows and stones are exchanged day and night,
how can this be called peace!"
The *Mán* tribes, seeing that the peace envoy did not arrive,
on the *Gēngyín* day,
advanced again to attack the city.
On the *Xīnmǎo* day,
troops from the city sallied forth to attack them,
and they retreated.
Previously,
Wéi Gāo had summoned the Nánzhāo to defeat the Tǔbō.
Afterwards, the *Mán* tribes complained that they had no armor or crossbows.
Gāo ordered craftsmen to teach them,
and after several years,
all the armor and crossbows among the *Mán* tribes became excellent and sharp.
Also,
the three tribes of Dōngmán, Jūnàshí, Wùdèng, and Mèngchōng assisted Gāo in defeating the Tǔbō and performed meritorious service.
This event is recorded in Volume 233, Dēzōng's Xīngyuán Fifth Year.
The Dōngmán deeply resented the Táng,
and allied themselves with Nánzhāo.
Whenever they followed Nánzhāo in raiding,
they exerted themselves fully,
and if they captured Táng people,
they would torture and kill them.
The court demoted Dòu Pāng to Sīhù of Kāngzhōu,
and appointed Yán Qìngfù as the Jíedùshǐ of Dōngchuān.
All the armies reinforcing Shǔ
were placed under Qìngfù's command.
On the *Guǐsì* day,
Qìngfù arrived at Xīndū.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Xīndū County is 45 *lǐ* north of Chéngdū Prefecture.
On the *Jiǎwǔ* day,
Qìngfù encountered [the *Mán*],
and Qìngfù thoroughly defeated the *Mán* army,
killing over 2,000 people.
Several thousand Shǔ civilians eagerly grabbed scythes and white staves to assist the government troops,
their shouts shaking the fields.
On the *Yǐwèi* day,
tens of thousands of *Mán* infantry and cavalry arrived again.
At this time, the Right Wǔwèi Supreme General Sòng Wēi arrived with 2,000 men from Zhōngwǔ.
He immediately joined the various armies in battle.
The *Mán* army was utterly defeated,
over 5,000 people died,
and they retreated to secure Xīngsù Shān.
Wēi advanced his army to Tuójiāng Yì.
Tuójiāng Yì
is in Xīnfán County, Chéngdū Prefecture.
In the *Yǔ Gòng*,
Mín Shān guides the river,
splitting into the Tuó.
Tuó (沱)
is pronounced *tuóhé*.
The *Mán* tribes sent their minister Yáng Dìngbǎo to Zhī Xiáng to request peace.
Xiáng said:
"You should first lift the siege and withdraw your troops."
Dìngbǎo returned,
but the *Mán* siege of the city remained as before.
Those inside the city did not know that reinforcements had arrived,
but merely saw them repeatedly requesting peace,
and thus knew that the reinforcements must be victorious.
On the *Wùxū* day,
the *Mán* tribes again requested peace;
their envoys went back and forth ten times.
Those in the city also responded ambiguously.
The *Mán* tribes, knowing that reinforcements were nearby,
attacked the city even more urgently.
The *Piàoxìn* (King of Nánzhāo) and his subordinates personally stood amidst the arrows and stones.
On the *Gēngzǐ* day,
the government army reached the city walls and fought with the *Mán* tribes,
seizing their Shēngqiān Qiáo.
Shēngqiān Qiáo
is also known as Shēngxiān Qiáo.
It was built by Lǐ Bīng in the Qín dynasty,
and was formerly called Qīxīng Qiáo.
The *Mán* tribes themselves burned their siege equipment and fled.
By dawn,
the government army realized this.
At first,
the court had ordered Yán Qìngfù to rescue Chéngdū,
and commanded Sòng Wēi to garrison Mián and Hàn as a reserve force.
Mián and Hàn
are names of two prefectures.
Sòng Wēi performed the most meritorious deeds in defeating the *Mán* army,
and Qìngfù resented him for it.
Wēi fed his soldiers, intending to pursue the *Mán* army.
The warriors in the city also wished to combine forces with the northern army and advance together.
Qìngfù issued an official document to Wēi,
taking away his troops,
and ordering him to return to Hànzhōu.
The *Mán* tribes reached Shuāngliú,
blocked by the newly dug river.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Xīnjīn County in Shǔzhōu has Xīnchuān Town.
They were in utter disarray and lost their composure.
"Lost their composure" (失度)
means they lost their usual behavior.
After a bridge was built,
they were able to cross,
and they broke the bridge as they left.
Weapons, armor, and clothing were abandoned on the road,
which greatly angered the people of Shǔ.
Yán Shībēn, the Cìshǐ of Lízhōu, gathered several thousand scattered soldiers and secured Qióngzhōu.
The *Mán* tribes besieged it,
but after two days,
failing to conquer it,
they also abandoned it and left.
Yán Qìngfù then taught the people of Shǔ to build "yōngmén" cities.
Outside the city gates,
separate walls were built to shield the city gates,
called *yōngmén*.
What people today call "bāguàqiáng" are these.
He planted "deer antlers" (*lùjiǎo*),
and divided the camps into "pù".
"Deer antlers" were made by cutting wood
and planting them outside the city,
to obstruct attacks.
What people today call "páichā" are these.
Separate barracks were set up,
called "yíng",
to house soldiers.
Small huts were erected on the city walls,
for the garrison soldiers to dwell in and keep watch,
called "pù".
"Pù" (鋪)
is pronounced *pǔgù*.
From then on, Chéngdū was never again attacked.
Previously,
the staff officers (*yájiàng*) of Xīchuān had ranks but no official titles.
After repelling the Nánzhāo,
four people were granted the official title of Jiānchá Yùshǐ for their merits.
This is what is meant by "official title".
Each person had to pay 300 *mín* in "tánglì qián".
The poor suffered from this.
Meritorious individuals were granted official titles but were still required to pay money;
the historians said that the Táng's governing system was greatly corrupted.
5. In the third month,
Cáo Què, the Left Púshè and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was appointed as Jíedùshǐ of Zhènhǎi while retaining the title Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
6. In summer,
fourth month,
on the *Bǐngwǔ* day,
Wéi Bǎohéng, the Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ and Bīngbù Shìláng, was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
7. The remaining remnants of the Xú rebels still gathered in villages to commit banditry,
scattered between Yǎnzhoū, Yùnzhōu, Qīngzhōu, and Qízhōu.
An edict ordered Xiàhóu Tóng, the Guāncháshǐ of Xúzhōu, to recruit and pacify them.
8. In the fifth month, on the *Dīngchǒu* day, Wú Xínglǔ, the Cìshǐ of Qióngzhōu, was appointed Liúhòu of Xīchuān.
7. On the day of Bǐngzǐ,
Yú Cóng (于琮), the Jiedushi (節度使) of Shānnán Dōngdào (山南東道), was demoted to be Grand Tutor (傅) to Prince Pǔ (普王) and Fēnsī (分司).
Prince Pǔ Yǎn (普王儼)
was the imperial son.
Later he ascended the throne
and was known as Xīzōng (僖宗).
On the day of Xīnsì,
Lǐ Dāng (李當), Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞), Wáng Fěng (王渢), Lìbù Shìláng (吏部侍郎),
Lǐ Dū (李都), Zuǒ Sànqí Chángshì (左散騎常侍), Zhāng Xī (張裼), Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ Bīngbù Shìláng (翰林學士承旨兵部侍郎),
Fēng Yànqīng (封彥卿), former Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人), and Yáng Shú (楊塾), Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū (左諫議大夫), were demoted.
On the day of Guǐwèi,

Yán Qí (嚴祁), Gōngbù Shàngshū (工部尚書), Lǐ Kuàng (李貺), Jìshìzhōng (給事中), Zhāng Duó (張鐸), Jìshìzhōng, Lǐ Jìngzhòng (李敬仲), Zuǒ Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn (左金吾大將軍), Xiāo Gòu (蕭遘), Qǐjū Shèrén (起居舍人), Lǐ Dú (李瀆), Zhèng Yàntè (鄭彥特), and Lǐ Zǎo (李藻) were demoted.
All were banished to the south of Hú (湖) and Lǐng (嶺).
They were punished because they were very close to Yú Cóng.
Lǐ Kuàng
was the son of Lǐ Hàn (李漢).
Xiāo Gòu
was the son of Xiāo Zhì (蕭寘).
Lǐ Hàn is mentioned in volume 245, Wénzōng (文宗) Dàhé (大和) 9th year.
Xiāo Zhì is mentioned in volume 250, 5th year.
On the day of Jiǎshēn,
Yú Jǐng (于琄), former Pínglú Jiedushi, was demoted to Chief Clerk (長史) of Prince Liáng's (涼王) Residence and Fēnsī.
Yú Huái (于⿰王褱), former Húnán Guānchásǐ (湖南觀察使), was demoted to Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Yuánzhōu (袁州).
Yú Huái and Yú Jǐng
were both elder brothers of Yú Cóng.
Soon after, Yú Cóng was further demoted to Cǐshǐ of Sháozhōu (韶州).
During the Suí (隋) dynasty, Sháozhōu was established in Qǔjiāng (曲江) County,
named after Sháoshí (韶石), eighty lǐ to the north of the county.
It was 4,932 lǐ from the capital.
Yú Cóng's wife was Princess Guǎngdé (廣德公主),
the emperor's younger sister.
Guǎngdé County
belonged to Xuānzhōu (宣州).
When she traveled, her palanquin faced his;
when seated, she held Yú Cóng's belt.
Yú Cóng was thus spared.
At that time, many princesses were arrogant and unrestrained,
but Princess Guǎngdé always followed the laws and regulations.
She treated Yú's clan, both senior and junior, with perfect禮 (lǐ).
She was praised both within and outside the court.
8. In the 6th month,
Zhāng Gōngsù (張公素), the Liúhòu (留後) of Lúlóng (盧龍), was appointed Jiedushi.
9. Wéi Bǎohéng (韋保衡) wanted to appoint his faction member Péi Tiáo (裴條) as a Lángguān (郎官),
but he feared the upright and strict Lǐ Zhāng (李璋), Zuǒchéng,
lest he would not "pass" the appointment.
The Shàngshū Zuǒchéng and Yòuchéng (右丞)
collectively oversaw the six ministries and twenty-four bureaus.
For Lángguān,
if an unsuitable person was appointed or granted,
the Zuǒchéng and Yòuchéng could impeach them
and prevent them from assuming office in the ministry.
"Shàng" (上) here means "pass".
Lǐ Zhāng said:
"Court appointments and transfers
should not be questioned."
In autumn,
the 7th month,
on the day of Yǐwèi,
Lǐ Zhāng was appointed Guānchásǐ of Xuānshè (宣歙).
10. In the 8th month,
Zhāng Yìcháo (張義潮), the Guīyì (歸義) Jiedushi, died.
Cáo Yìjīn (曹義金), the Chángshǐ of Shāzhōu (沙州), temporarily commanded the military headquarters.
An imperial edict appointed Cáo Yìjīn as Guīyì Jiedushi.
After this, the Central Plains experienced much unrest,
and imperial orders could not reach far.
The Huíhú (回鶻) conquered Gānzhōu (甘州),
and most of the other prefectures under Guīyì were seized by the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡).
From the late Táng (唐) dynasty until the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
the lands of Hé (河) and Huáng (湟) became entirely occupied by barbarians,
and China could not recover them.
"Cháo" (朝) here is pronounced "Zhíyáo".
11. In winter,
the 12th month,
Xuānzōng (宣宗) was posthumously honored with the posthumous title Yuánshèng Zhìmíng Chéngwǔ Xiànwén Ruìzhì Zhāngrén Shéncōng Yìdào Dàxiào Huángdì (元聖至明成武獻文睿智章仁神聰懿道大孝皇帝).
12. Lǐ Guóchāng (李國昌), the Zhènwǔ (振武) Jiedushi, relied on his achievements and acted arrogantly,
often executing local officials without authorization.
The court could not control him,
so Lǐ Guóchāng was transferred to be the Dàtóng (大同) Military Defense Commissioner (防禦使).
Lǐ Guóchāng claimed illness and did not go.
Historians say that the Shātuó (沙陀) were already unruly,
and did not need to wait for Duàn Wénchǔ (段文楚) to be killed before committing evil.
1. In spring,
the 3rd month,
on the day of Guǐsì,
the emperor sent an imperial envoy to Fǎmén Sì (法門寺) to welcome the Buddha's relics.
Many ministers remonstrated,
some even saying that Xīanzōng (憲宗) died soon after welcoming the Buddha's relics.
This event is found in the chronicle of Xīanzōng, Yuánhé (元和) 14th year.
Death
is something people greatly taboo,
let alone mentioning it before the ruler!
To speak of it to this extent
was difficult for people.
The emperor said, "If I can see it alive,
I will have no regrets even if I die!"
Many pagodas, precious canopies, incense chariots, banners, flowers, and standards were made to welcome them,
all adorned with gold, jade, brocade, embroidery, pearls, and kingfisher feathers.
Between the capital city and the temple, a distance of three hundred lǐ,
the roads were filled with carriages and horses,
day and night without interruption.
In summer,
the 4th month,
on the day of Rén'yín,
the Buddha's relics arrived in the capital.
They were escorted by imperial guards, military weapons, and public and private music,
the sound shaking the heavens and lighting the earth,
stretching for dozens of lǐ.
The splendor of the procession
surpassed that of suburban sacrifices;
the time of Yuánhé was far inferior.
Wealthy households lined the streets with decorated towers and "unrestricted assemblies,"
competing in extravagance.
The emperor ascended the Ānfú Mén (安福門),
descended from the tower and bowed in prostration.
"Bowing in prostration"
is a Hú (胡) style of bowing.
"Mó" (膜) is pronounced "Mòhū".
Gold and silk were bestowed upon monks and elderly residents of the capital who had witnessed the Yuánhé events.
The Buddha's relics were welcomed into the imperial palace.
After three days,
they were placed in Ānguó Chónghuà Sì (安國崇化寺).
From the prime ministers downwards, everyone competed to donate gold and silk,
an uncountable amount.
Following this, a decree of grace was issued,
and prisoners throughout the realm were released.
2. In the 5th month,
on the day of Dīnghài,
Lù Yán (路巖), the Xīchuān (西川) Jiedushi, was additionally appointed Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令).
The "Kǎo Yì" (考異) states: The "Jǐnlǐ Qíjiù Zhuàn" (錦里耆舊傳) says:
"In the 8th month of the 12th year,
Lù Gōng (路公), using the strategies of Biān Xián (邊咸) and Guō Chóu (郭籌),
memorialized to establish the Dìngbiān Jūn (定邊軍) Jiedushi in Qióngzhōu (邛州).
He then ordered the blocking of the Dàdù Hé (大渡河),
repaired the southern road of Qiónglái (邛崍) Pass,
and selected young men from the Dántīng (檀丁) clan to teach them how to use 'chopping and stabbing knives,'
appointing them as officers of the righteous army
to manage and train soldiers."
The "Xīn Zhuàn" (新傳) says:
"When Lù Yán arrived in Xīchuān,
following the barbarian raids on the border,
Lù Yán exerted himself to comfort and pacify them.
He established the Dìngbiān Jūn in Qióngzhōu,
blocked the Dàdù River,
repaired the old passes,
and taught young men from the Dántīng clan to fight and stab,
enrolling them in the garrisons.
As a result, the eight nations of Xīshān (西山) came to court.
For his efforts,
he was promoted to additionally hold the title of Zhōngshū Lìng."
However, the establishment of the Dìngbiān Jūn was by Lǐ Shīwàng (李師望).
Both the "Qíjiù Zhuàn" and "Xīn Zhuàn" are mistaken.
3. Nánzhào (南詔) attacked Xīchuān,
and then attacked Qiánnán (黔南).
Qín Kuāngmóu (秦匡謀), the Qiánzhōng Jīnglüèsǐ (黔中經略使), had too few troops and could not resist.
He abandoned the city and fled to Jīngnán (荊南).
Dù Cóng (杜悰), the Jīngnán Jiedushi, imprisoned him and reported it to the court.
In the 6th month,
on the day of Yǐwèi,
an imperial edict ordered Qín Kuāngmóu's execution,
the confiscation of his family's property,
and that officials search for and report any relatives who should be implicated.
Qín Kuāngmóu
was from Fèngxiáng (鳳翔).
4. Wáng Duó (王鐸), Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事), was made Tóng Píngzhāngshì
and concurrently Xuānwǔ (宣武) Jiedushi.
At that time, Wéi Bǎohéng wielded power, relying on imperial favor.
As Liú Zhān (劉瞻) and Yú Cóng had previously held prime ministerial positions
and did not treat him with respect,
he slandered and expelled them.
Wáng Duó
was the examiner (主文) when Wéi Bǎohéng passed the imperial examination.
In Táng rites, the chief examiner of the Ministry of Rites was called "Zhǔwén".
Lǐ Zhāng and Wáng Duó were jinshi (進士) in the same year as Wéi Bǎohéng,
and both had always held a low opinion of Wéi Bǎohéng's character.
Wéi Bǎohéng subsequently dismissed them all.
The "Kǎo Yì" states: The "Jiù Zhuàn" (舊傳) says:
"Wéi Bǎohéng, seeing Yáng Shōu (楊收) and Lù Yán in the Zhōngshū,
did not treat them with courtesy
and fabricated charges to expel them."
However, when Yáng Shōu was punished,
Wéi Bǎohéng was not yet a prime minister.
It is likely that although Wéi Bǎohéng was only an imperial academician (學士),
Yìzōng (懿宗) favored and trusted him,
hence he was able to slander Yáng Shōu.
It also says:
"After the princess died,
the imperial favor and courtesies gradually diminished."
However, the dismissals of Lù Yán, Yú Cóng, Wáng Duó, and Xiāo Gòu
all occurred after the princess's death.
This translation follows the "Shílù" (實錄).
5 In the autumn,
seventh month,
on the day Wùyín,
the emperor's illness became critical.
Liú Xíngshēn, Left Army Commander, and Hán Wényuē, Right Army Commander, enthroned the youngest son, Prince Pǔ, Yǎn.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Fàn Zhì’s *Wǔdài Tōnglù* states:
“Lǐ Zhèn of Liang said to Hán Yífàn, the Commander of Shǎnzōu: ‘When Emperor Yì first passed away,
Commander Hán killed the elder son and enthroned the younger for his own gain,
thereby throwing the realm into chaos.
Does Your Excellency now wish to do the same!’
Yífàn
was Wényuē’s grandson.”
According to this, Emperor Yìzōng had eight sons.
Emperor Xīzōng was the fifth.
The old and new histories do not record the seniority of the other sons,
nor do they state their ultimate fate,
nor which prince was indeed killed.
On the day Gēngchén,
an edict was issued:
“Yǎn is established as Crown Prince.”
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Xù Bǎoyùn Lù* states:
“On that day,
the prime minister Xiāo Yè and others went directly to the emperor's bedchamber to inquire about his illness.
The emperor faintly uttered the words ‘Zhèn’
and then stopped.
All the officials could not help but cry out, losing their voices,
and those within and without the court all wept.”
According to this, at that time, Prime Minister Wéi Bǎohéng was in the highest position;
Xiāo Yè was not a prime minister.
Therefore, this account is not adopted.
On the day Xīnsì,
the emperor passed away in the Hánníng Hall.
He was forty-one years old.
Emperor Xīzōng ascended the throne.
In the eighth month,
on the day Dīngwèi,
his mother, Consort Wáng Guì, was posthumously honored as Empress Dowager.
Liú Xíngshēn and Hán Wényuē were both enfeoffed as dukes of states.
6 Great floods occurred in Guāndōng and Hénán.
7 In the ninth month,
the relevant authorities presented the posthumous title Huì’ān for the late Empress Dowager.
“Late Empress Dowager”
refers to the emperor’s mother, Wáng Guì.
The character “shàng” (上)
is pronounced “zhǎng” (掌) at this time.
8 Wéi Bǎohéng, the Sītú, Ménxià Shìláng, and Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
was accused of secret affairs by his enemies.
Bǎohéng was demoted to Assassin of Hèzhōu.
The musician Lǐ Kějí was exiled to Língnán.
Kějí was favored by Emperor Yìzōng.
Once, when he was arranging a marriage for his son,
Emperor Yìzōng bestowed upon him two silver pots of wine.
Upon opening them, there was no wine, but they were filled with solid objects.
Xīmén Jìxuán, the Right Army Commander, repeatedly spoke about this,
but Emperor Yìzōng did not listen.
Kějí once received a large quantity of gifts,
which he transported in official carts.
Jìxuán said to him:
“One day, when your family is ruined,
these things will again be carried back in official carts.
This is not receiving gifts;
it is merely tiring out the oxen!”
When he was exiled to Língnán,
his property was confiscated,
and it was indeed as Jìxuán had said.
Historians say that when a common man is overly favored, misfortune will follow.
9 Lù Yán, the Jìedùshǐ of Xīchuān, was concurrently appointed Shìzhōng.
Wáng Jǐngchóng, the Jìedùshǐ of Chéngdé, was promoted to Zhōngshūlìng.
Hán Jūnxíong, the Jìedùshǐ of Wèibó, Zhāng Gōngsù, the Jìedùshǐ of Lúlóng, and Gāo Pián, the Jìedùshǐ of Tiānpíng, were all appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Jūnxíong was also granted the name Yǔnzhōng.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Old traditions write it as
“Yǔnzhōng” (允忠).
The *Shílù* and new traditions all write it as
“Yǔnzhōng” (允中).
We follow the latter.
10 In winter,
tenth month,
on the day Yǐwèi,
Xiāo Fǎng, the Zuǒ Púyè, was appointed Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
11 Wéi Bǎohéng was again demoted to Magistrate of Chéngmài, Yázhōu.
Chéngmài
was a county during the Suí dynasty;
in the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Qióngzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: It is fifty-five *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
His younger brother, Bǎoyì, a Hànlín Xuéshì and Bīngbù Shìláng, was also demoted to Sīhù of Bīnzhōu.
His close associate, Liú Chéngyōng, a Hànlín Xuéshì and Hùbù Shìláng, was demoted to Sīmǎ of Fúzhōu.
Chéngyōng
was the son of Yǔxī.
See Liú Yǔxī in volume 236, Shùnzōng, Yǒngzhēn first year.
12 On the day Guǐmǎo,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the realm.
13 Lù Yán, the Jìedùshǐ of Xīchuān, enjoyed music, women, and banquets,
delegating military and governmental affairs to his close attendants Biān Xián and Guō Chóu.
They would always act first and report later.
Those above and below feared them.
Once, during a grand review,
the two discussed matters,
secretly writing on paper, showing it to each other, and then burning it.
The army believed they had other designs,
and were startled and uneasy.
The imperial court heard of this.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Wùchén,
Yán was transferred to be Jìedùshǐ of Jīngnán.
Xián and Chóu secretly knew the reason,
and thus fled.
14 Xiāo Yè, the Yòu Púyè, was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì
and concurrently Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng.
15 In the twelfth month,
on the day Jǐhài,
an imperial edict ordered the Buddhist relics to be sent back to Fǎmén Temple.
16 Lù Yán was again demoted to Assassin of Xīnzhōu.
The first year of Qiánfú
(Jiǎwǔ, 874)
The reign title was changed in the eleventh month of this year.
1 In spring,
first month,
on the day Dīnghài,
Lú Xī, a Hànlín Xuéshì, memorialized,
stating:
“Your Majesty has just ascended the great throne;
it is fitting that you deeply consider the common people.
The state having its people
is like plants having their roots.
If they are nurtured and irrigated in autumn and winter,
then they will flourish in spring and summer.
I have secretly observed that Guāndōng suffered drought last year.
From Guó to the sea,
meaning from Guózhōu eastward to the sea.
Autumn harvests were almost nonexistent,
and winter vegetables were very scarce.
The poor ground *péngshí* as flour
and stored槐 leaves as relish.
Some became even more frail and emaciated,
and could hardly gather
anything.
In years of poor harvest,
they would scatter to neighboring regions.
‘Zhī’ (之)
means ‘to go’.
With nowhere to turn,
they would remain in their hometowns,
waiting to die in ditches.
As for remitting outstanding taxes,
there is truly nothing left to collect.
However, the prefectures and counties, due to having imperial tribute and Tri-Bureau funds,
the Hùbù, Zhuǎnyùn, and Yántiě constituted the Tri-Bureau.
often inflict beatings.
Even if they dismantle their houses and fell trees,
hire out their wives and sell their children,
it can only cover the expenses of the officials’ food and drink.
‘Suǒyóu’ (所由)
refers to the officers and clerks who urge and collect taxes.
Moreover, beyond taxes,
there are other levies.
If the court does not offer comfort and support,
the common people will truly have no means of livelihood.
I beg that an imperial edict be issued to the prefectures and counties,
ordering that all outstanding and remnant taxes
be entirely suspended from collection,
to await the silkworm and wheat seasons.
Furthermore, let the local public granaries be opened,
and relief be promptly distributed.
Emperor Tàizōng established public granaries (*yìcāng*) and Ever-Normal Granaries (*chángpíngcāng*) to prepare for famine.
After Emperor Gāozōng,
public granaries were gradually borrowed from to cover other expenses,
and by the Shénlóng era, they were almost exhausted.
Emperor Xuánzōng re-established them upon his ascension,
but they were again abolished during the An–Shi Rebellion.
By the ninth year of Dàhé under Emperor Wénzōng,
the remaining funds from across the realm were used to establish principal capital for the Ever-Normal and public granaries,
which was annually increased to purchase grain for relief.
With vegetable leaves and tree sprouts,
followed by mulberries,
there will gradually be something edible.
However, in these next few months,
the situation is especially urgent,
and implementation cannot be delayed.”
The emperor assented to his words,
but the relevant authorities ultimately failed to implement it,
leaving it merely an empty document.
2 Lù Yán (路巖) travelled to Jiānglíng (江陵),
where an imperial edict stripped him of his official titles and ranks,
and he was exiled to Dānzhōu (儋州) for life.
Lù Yán (路巖) had a handsome appearance.
After being imprisoned in Jiānglíng (江陵) for two nights,
his hair and beard turned completely white.
Soon after, he was granted permission to commit suicide,
and his family's property was confiscated.
When Lù Yán (路巖) was prime minister,
he had secretly memorialized,
"When officials of the third rank and above are sentenced to death,
envoys should be ordered to excise three inches of their Adam's apple and present it."
The Adam's apple
is the part where the throat connects above and below.
By this time,
he himself suffered this misfortune,
and the place where he died was the same couch on which Yáng Shōu (楊收) had been granted death.
The historians say that Heaven's retribution is never mistaken.
Yáng Shōu's (楊收) death sentence is recorded in the previous volume, Xiántōng (咸通) 10th year.
All were executed.
Initially,
when Lù Yán (路巖) assisted Cuī Xuàn (崔鉉) in Huáinán (淮南),
he served as an Assistant (支使).
According to the Táng (唐) system,
a Jìedùshǐ (節度使) had a Zhǎngshūjì (掌書記) on his staff;
an Guāncháshǐ (觀察使) had a Zhīshǐ (支使),
who was in charge of memorials, letters, and documents,
also a duty of a secretary.
Cuī Xuàn (崔鉉) said:
"Lù Shí (路十) will eventually hold that office."
Lù Yán (路巖) was
the tenth in his family.
"That office" refers to
being a prime minister.
He did not leave Cháng'ān (長安)
and became prime minister in ten years.
When he moved from Censor (監察) to the Hànlín (翰林) Academy,
Cuī Xuàn (崔鉉) was still in Huáinán (淮南).
Hearing of this,
he said:
"Lù Shí (路十) has now entered the Hànlín (翰lín) Academy,
how can he grow old!"
Everything happened as Cuī Xuàn (崔鉉) had predicted.
3 Yú Cóng (于琮), the Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent (太子少傅), was appointed Co-Administrator of Affairs with the Grand Secretariat (同平章事).
He was also appointed Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Shānnán Dōngdào (山南東道).

on the Jiǎwǔ (甲午) day,

Jiǎnlíng (簡陵) is forty-five li northwest of Fùpíng (富平) County, Jīngzhào (京兆).
5 Zhào Yǐn (趙隱), Minister of the Censorate (中書侍郎) and Co-Administrator of Affairs with the Grand Secretariat (同平章事), was appointed Co-Administrator of Affairs with the Grand Secretariat (同平章事)
and Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Zhènhǎi (鎮海);
Péi Tǎn (裴坦), Governor (刺史) of Huázhōu (華州), was appointed Minister of the Censorate (中書侍郎) and Co-Administrator of Affairs with the Grand Secretariat (同平章事).
6 Liú Zhān (劉瞻), Governor (刺史) of Guózhōu (虢州), was appointed Minister of Punishments (刑部尚書).
When Liú Zhān (劉瞻) was demoted,
he was demoted in the 12th year of Yìzōng (懿宗)'s Xiántōng (咸通) reign.
None were not pained and sorrowful.
When he returned,
people from both markets in Cháng'ān (長安) pooled money to hire performers to welcome him.
Cháng'ān (長安) city was divided into East and West markets.
He changed his arrival date

The "Kǎoyì" (考異) states: The "Yùquán Zǐ Jiànwénlù" (玉泉子見聞錄) says:
"Initially,
when Liú Zhān (劉瞻) was banished south,
regardless of whether people were virtuous or not,
everyone expressed pain and sorrow for him.
When he was almost in the capital,
the prominent figures of the East and West markets jointly pooled money and silks,
recruited many performers,
and planned to meet him outside the city.
Liú Zhān (劉瞻) learned of this,
changed his arrival date, and took a different route.
When Liú Zhān (劉瞻) became prime minister,
he had no other particular talent;
it was merely because Lù Yán (路巖) incurred public hatred at the time,
and Liú Zhān (劉瞻) was impeached by him,
so people's hearts turned towards him.
In reality, he was not worthy of much discussion."
According to records, Liú Zhān (劉瞻) was renowned for his integrity and prudence.
When Yìzōng (懿宗) was in a fit of rage,
Liú Zhān (劉瞻) alone was able to disregard his own safety
and save hundreds of people from death.
For Yùquán Zǐ (玉泉子) to consider him unworthy of discussion,
is that not a slander!
7 In summer,
the fifth month,
on the Yǐwèi (乙未) day,
Péi Tǎn (裴坦) passed away.
Liú Zhān (劉瞻) was appointed Minister of the Censorate (中書侍郎) and Co-Administrator of Affairs with the Grand Secretariat (同平章事).
Initially,
when Liú Zhān (劉瞻) was banished south,
Liú Yè (劉鄴) sided with Wéi (韋) and Lù (路),
and jointly slandered him.
Wéi (韋) and Lù (路) refer to Wéi Bǎohéng (韋保衡) and Lù Yán (路巖).
Liú Yè (劉鄴) was inwardly fearful.
In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the Dīngsì (丁巳) day, the first day of the month,
Liú Yè (劉鄴) invited Liú Zhān (劉瞻)
and hosted a banquet at the Salt and Iron Bureau.
Liú Yè (劉鄴) was appointed prime minister as Salt and Iron Transport Commissioner,

On the Xīnwèi (辛未) day,

8 Cuī Yànzhāo (崔彥昭), Assistant Minister of War (兵部侍郎) and acting Commissioner of Finance (判度支), was appointed Minister of the Censorate (中書侍郎) and Co-Administrator of Affairs with the Grand Secretariat (同平章事).
Cuī Yànzhāo (崔彥昭)
was the nephew of Cuī Yuán (崔𣰤).
Cuī Yuán (崔𣰤) was prime minister during the reigns of Xiànzōng (憲宗) and Mùzōng (穆宗).
Cóng (從) is pronounced Cái Yòng (才用).
He was also the grand-nephew of Wáng Zhèngyǎ (王正雅).
Wáng Zhèngyǎ (王正雅) is mentioned in volume 244, Dàhé (大和) 5th year of Wénzōng (文宗).
Wáng Níng (王凝) was Cuī Yànzhāo's (崔彥昭) maternal cousin.
The sisters of one's mother are called maternal cousins.
Wáng Níng (王凝) had passed the imperial examination earlier.
He once saw Cuī Yànzhāo (崔彥昭) in casual clothes
and jokingly said to him:
"You'd be better off taking the Míngjīng (明經) examination."
Cuī Yànzhāo (崔彥昭) was enraged,
and thus a deep enmity formed.
In the Táng (唐) dynasty, the Jìnshì (進士) examination was highly regarded, while the Míngjīng (明經) was less so,
hence at that time there was a saying:
"Burn incense to honor Jìnshì (進士) graduates,
set up screens to test Míngjīng (明經) graduates."
The enmity between Cuī Yànzhāo (崔彥昭) and Wáng Níng (王凝)
stemmed from this.
Cuī Yànzhāo's (崔彥昭) mother said to her maidservant:
"Make more socks and shoes for me,
for Wáng (王) Assistant Minister and his son will surely be banished,
and I will go with my sister."
Cuī Yànzhāo (崔彥昭) bowed and wept,
apologizing and saying:
"I certainly would not dare."
Wáng Níng (王凝) was thus spared.
The "Kǎoyì" (考異) states: This comes from "Zhōngcháo Gùshì" (中朝故事),
which says:
"Cuī Yànzhāo (崔彥昭) replaced Wáng Níng (王凝) as Commissioner of Salt and Iron,
and became prime minister after half a year."
According to the Veritable Records (實錄),
Cuī Yànzhāo (崔彥昭) did not replace Wáng Níng (王凝) as Commissioner of Salt and Iron.
The rest of the account is adopted.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Liú Yè (劉鄴), Minister of the Left (門下侍郎) and Co-Administrator of Affairs with the Grand Secretariat (同平章事), was appointed Co-Administrator of Affairs with the Grand Secretariat (同平章事)
and Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Huáinán (淮南).
Zhèng Tián (鄭畋), Assistant Minister of Personnel (吏部侍郎), was appointed Assistant Minister of War (兵部侍郎).
Lú Xí (盧攜), Academician-in-waiting (學士承旨) of the Hànlín (翰lín) Academy and Assistant Minister of Revenue (戶部侍郎), retained his official post
and was also appointed Co-Administrator of Affairs with the Grand Secretariat (同平章事).
The "Kǎoyì" (考異) states: The old biography of Zhèng Tián (鄭畋) says:
"In the 4th year of Qiánfú (乾符),
he was promoted to Assistant Minister of Personnel (吏部侍郎);
soon after, an imperial edict was issued,
appointing him Co-Administrator of Affairs with the Grand Secretariat (同平章事) in his original post."
Now, following the Veritable Records,
he became prime minister in this year.
9 In the eleventh month,
on the Gēngyín (庚寅) day,
the sun reached its southernmost point.
Winter Solstice,
the sun reaches its southernmost point.
Summer Solstice,
the sun reaches its northernmost point.
The reign title was changed.
The reign title was changed to Qiánfú (乾符).
Shàng (上),
pronounced Shí Zhǎng (時掌).
10 Hán Yǔnzhōng (韓允中), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Wèibó (魏博), passed away.
The army established his son, Jiǎn (簡), Deputy Jìedùshǐ (節度副使), as acting military governor (留後).
16 Sòng Wēi (宋威) attacked Wáng Xiānzhī (王仙芝) below the city of Yízhōu (沂州),
and thoroughly defeated him.
A textual variant note states: The Veritable Records (實錄) for
the twelfth month of last year, says:
"Sòng Wēi (宋威) advanced from Qīngzhōu (青州) with Assistant Commissioner Cáo Quánzhǐng (曹全晸) to attack Wáng Xiānzhī (王仙芝),
and Xiānzhī (仙芝) was defeated and fled."
According to this, if Xiānzhī (仙芝) was defeated and fled in the twelfth month of last year,
how could he have remained quiescent for half a year in between?
It must be because Wēi (威) was appointed Commissioner of Pacification and it was reported successively.
In reality, Xiānzhī's (仙芝) defeat occurred in this month,
not in the twelfth month.
Wēi (威) reported that Xiānzhī (仙芝) was dead,
and so the troops from various circuits were dispatched,
and he himself returned to Qīngzhōu (青州);
all the officials came to offer congratulations.
Three days later,
the prefectures and counties reported that Xiānzhī (仙芝) was still alive,
and continued to attack and plunder as before.
At this time, the troops had just been rested,
but an imperial edict ordered their re-mobilization,
and the soldiers were all resentful and thought of rebellion.
In the eighth month,
Xiānzhī (仙芝) captured Yángzhái (陽翟) and Jiāchéng (郟城).
An imperial edict ordered Cuī Ānqián (崔安潛), Military Governor of Zhōngwǔ (忠武), to dispatch troops to attack him.
Ānqián (安潛)
was the younger brother of Shènshēn (慎由).
Cuī Shènyóu (崔慎由)
served as Chancellor under Xuānzōng (宣宗).
Cáo Xiáng (曹翔), Military Governor of Yì (義), led five thousand infantry and cavalry, along with Yìchéng (義成) troops, to guard the Eastern Capital palace.
Zēng Yuányù (曾元裕), Left Sanjǐ Chángshì (左散騎常侍), was made Assistant Commissioner of Pacification
to guard the Eastern Capital.
Another edict ordered Lǐ Fú (李福), Military Governor of Shānnán Dōngdào (山南東道), to select two thousand infantry and cavalry to guard the strategic routes of Rǔ (汝) and Dèng (鄧).
Xiānzhī (仙芝) advanced to threaten Rǔzhōu (汝州).

An edict ordered Lǐ Kǎn (李侃), Military Governor of Bīnníng (邠寧), and Línghú Táo (令狐綯), Military Governor of Fèngxiáng (鳳翔), to select one thousand infantry and five hundred cavalry to guard Shǎnzhōu (陝州) and Tóngguān (潼關).
17 Wáng Jǐngchóng (王景崇), Military Governor of Chéngdé (成德), was additionally appointed Concurrent Grand Imperial Chancellor (中書令).
18 In the ninth month,
on the day Yǐhài (乙亥), the first day of the month,

19 On the day Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
Wáng Xiānzhī (王仙芝) captured Rǔzhōu (汝州)
and seized the Prefect, Wáng Liáo (王鐐).
Liáo (鐐)
was a paternal cousin of Duó (鐸).
The Eastern Capital was greatly alarmed.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志), Rǔzhōu (汝州) was 160 *lǐ* (里) north of the Eastern Capital.
On the day Yǐyǒu (乙酉),
an imperial edict pardoned Wáng Xiānzhī (王仙芝) and Shàng Jūncháng (尚君長) of their crimes,
