to persuade them to surrender.
Xiānzhī (仙芝) captured Yángwǔ (陽武)
and attacked Zhèngzhōu (鄭州).
Léi Yīnfú (雷殷符), Adjutant to the Overseeing Commissioner of Zhāoyì (昭義), was stationed at Zhōngmóu (中牟).
Zhōngmóu (中牟)
was an ancient county in the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
In the Suí (隋) dynasty, it was called Jiāchéng (郟城).
In the first year of Dàyè (大業) (605 AD),
it was renamed Pǔtián (圃田).
In the third year of Wǔdé (武德) (620 AD) of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
it was renamed Zhōngmóu (中牟)
and belonged to Zhèngzhōu (鄭州).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: It is 70 *lǐ* (里) west of Biànzhōu (汴州).
He defeated and drove them away.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Xiānzhī (仙芝) attacked Táng (唐) and Dèng (鄧) to the south.
20 Gāo Pián (高駢), Military Governor of Xīchuān (西川), constructed the outer city wall (羅城) of Chéngdū (成都).
He instructed the monk Jǐngxiān (景仙) to survey and plan it.
It measured twenty-five *lǐ* (里) in circumference.
He summoned all the county magistrates to organize laborers and allocate duties.
Chéngdū Fǔ (成都府) administered ten counties: Chéngdū (成都), Huáyáng (華陽), Xīndū (新都), Xīpǔ (犀浦), Xīnfán (新繁), Shuāngliú (雙流), Guǎngdū (廣都), Pí (郫), Wēnjiāng (溫江), and Língchí (靈池).
Pǐ (庀),
pronounced *pǐbì*,
means to prepare.
Fù (賦),
pronounced *bù*,
means to distribute; to distribute and assign them to service.
The soil of Shǔ (蜀) was loose and poor,
so it was paved with bricks.
Within ten *lǐ* (里) around the city, earth was taken,
and all hills and mounds were leveled,
without leaving any depressions to harm cultivation.
Laborers were replaced after no more than ten days,
and the multitude rejoiced at this fairness.
The work was accomplished without needing beating or flogging.
Construction began on the day Guǐchǒu (癸丑) in the eighth month
and was completed on the day Wùzǐ (戊子) in the eleventh month.
When the work began,
Pián (駢) feared that Nánzhào (南詔) might announce an invasion.
Although they might not decide to come,
the laborers would surely be alarmed and disturbed.
So he reported that he had sent Jǐngxiān (景仙) to Nánzhào (南詔) under the pretext of traveling,
to persuade and instruct the *Piàoxìn* (驃信) to submit to China,
and furthermore promised to give him a princess in marriage.
The Xīnshū (新書) states
"the Buddhist monk Jǐngxiān (景仙)",
which makes
the meaning of the text clear.
Shuì (說),
pronounced *shuruì*.
Qī (妻),
pronounced *qīxì*.
For a long time, no decision was made.
Pián (駢) also loudly declared his intention to inspect the frontier,
with beacon fires communicating day and night,
reaching the Dàdù Hé (大渡河),
but in reality, he did not go,
causing the barbarians to be anxious and fearful.
Thus, until the city was completed,
there were no alerts of "wind and dust" (enemy movements) from the frontier guards.
Previously,
when generals and officials from Xīchuān (西川) entered Nánzhào (南詔),
the *Piàoxìn* (驃信) would always remain seated to receive their bows.
Pián (駢), knowing that their custom favored Buddhism,
therefore sent Jǐngxiān (景仙).
The *Piàoxìn* (驃信) indeed led his ministers to welcome and bow to him,
and believed and followed his words.
21 Wáng Xiānzhī (王仙芝) attacked the two prefectures of Yǐng (郢) and Fù (復),
and captured them.
22 Wáng Yǐng (王郢) requested to surrender through Lǔ Shí (魯寔), Prefect of Wēnzhōu (溫州).
Shí (寔) repeatedly submitted memorials on his behalf,
Yǐng (郢), however, delayed with his troops
and did not arrive for half a year,
insisting on being appointed Commander of Wànghǎizhèn (望海鎮).
The court did not permit it,
appointing Yǐng (郢) as Right Commander of the Imperial Guards (右率府率).
The Táng (唐) had ten Commanders of the Imperial Guards,
and the Right Commander of the Imperial Guards was one of them.
The wealth he had previously plundered
was all ordered to be given to him.
23 In the twelfth month,
Wáng Xiānzhī (王仙zhi) attacked Shēn (申), Guāng (光), Lú (廬), Shòu (壽), Shū (舒), and Tōng (通) prefectures.
According to the Tángshū Dìlǐzhì (唐書地理志),
Tōngzhōu (通州) belonged to Shānnán Dōngdào (山南東道),
which is the Dázhōu (達州) of the Sòng (宋) dynasty.
Zhōu Shìzōng (周世宗) established Tōngzhōu (通州) from the Jìnghǎijūn (靜海軍) of Nán Táng (南唐),
which is the Tōngzhōu (通州) of Huáinán Dōng (淮南東) today.
Its territory in the Táng (唐) dynasty was the eastern part of Hǎilíng (海陵) county in Yángzhōu (揚州).
There was no Tōngzhōu (通州) in the Huáinán Dào (淮南道) during the Táng (唐) dynasty,
so this must be a mistake.
Referring to the following text,
"Tōng" (通)
should be
An edict ordered Xuē Néng (薛能), Military Governor of Gǎnhuà (感化), to select several thousand elite soldiers to assist.
Zhèng Tián (鄭畋), because his advice was not followed,
feigned illness and requested to resign,
but was not permitted.
So he submitted a memorial, saying:
"Since the report of victory from Yízhōu (沂州)—
meaning Sòng Wēi (宋威) reported defeating Wáng Xiānzhī (王仙芝) below the city of Yízhōu (沂州).
Shàng (上),
pronounced *shíchǎng*—
(the rebels) have plundered and captured five or six prefectures,
creating devastation over thousands of *lǐ* (里).
Sòng Wēi (宋威) is old and sick.
Since his false report,
he has been particularly distrusted by the various circuits.
False report
refers to reporting that Xiānzhī (仙芝) was dead.
He has no intention of advancing to suppress (the rebels).
Zēng Yuányù (曾元裕), with his troops in Qí (蘄) and Huáng (黃),
is only waiting to retreat at the slightest sign of trouble.
If the rebels capture Yángzhōu (揚州),
then Jiangnán (江南) will no longer belong to the state.
Cuī Ānqián (崔安潛) has extraordinary prestige,
Zhāng Zìmiǎn (張自勉) is a valiant and excellent general,
and the Imperial Park Commissioner Lǐ Zhuàn (李瑑),
grandson of Prince Xīpíng (西平王) Shèng (晟),
is stern and courageous.
I request that Ānqián (安潛) be made Commander-in-Chief of the Campaigning Army,
Zhuàn (瑑) be made Commissioner of Pacification to replace Wēi (威),
and Zìmiǎn (自勉) be made Assistant Commissioner to replace Yuányù (元裕)."
A textual variant note states: Although the Veritable Records (實錄) records Tián's (畋) memorial in this month,
it does not state whether it was implemented or not.
The Xīnjì (新紀) then states here
"Ānqián (安潛) was made Commander-in-Chief of the Campaigning Army for the various circuits,
Lǐ Zhuàn (李瑑) was made Commissioner of Pacification against the Grass Bandits,

However, in the next year,
Wēi (威) and Yuányù (元裕) remained as Commissioner and Assistant as before.
The Xīnjì (新紀) is mistaken.
24 Soldiers from Qīng (青) and Cāng (滄) prefectures, garrisoned in Ānnán (安南) –
Qīngzhōu (青州) belonged to Pínglú Jūn (平盧軍);
Cāngzhōu (滄州) belonged to Yìchāng Jūn (義昌軍) –
upon reaching Guìzhōu (桂州),
expelled the Surveillance Commissioner Lǐ Zàn (李瓚).
Zàn (瓚)
was the son of Zōngmǐn (宗閔).
Lǐ Zōngmǐn (李宗閔)
served as Chancellor during the Dàhé (大和) era.
Guìguǎn Supervisor of the Army, Lǐ Wéizhōu, was arrogant and tyrannical.
Zàn humbly deferred to him,
gradually losing the ability to control him.
Guìguǎn had eight hundred soldiers.
The Defense Commissioner only had a hundred men;
the rest all belonged to the Supervisor of the Army.
He also participated in the plot to oust the commander,
forcibly taking the seals of the two commissioners.
The "seals of the two commissioners"
refers to the seals of the Observation Commissioner and the Defense Commissioner.
"Shuài" (帥)
is pronounced "suǒ lèi fān".
"Shǐ" (使)
is pronounced "shū lì fān";
the same applies below.
He forcibly
seized the money for the envoy from Zhaozhōu.
According to the Táng system,
the taxes of the various prefectures were divided into three parts: first, "shànggōng,"
to be transported to the capital;
second, "sòngshǐ,"
to be transported to the local circuit;
and third, "liúzhōu,"
kept to cover the expenses of the local prefecture.
Yǔmó was
Chè's son.
Zhāng Chè is mentioned in volume 242, Mùzōng's Chángqìng first year.
25 The Deputy Pacification Commissioner and Army Supervisor, Yáng Fùguāng, reported that Shàng Jūncháng's younger brother, Ràng, was occupying Cháyáshān,
and the government army had retreated to defend Dèngzhōu.
Fùguāng was
Xuánjià's adopted son.
Yáng Xuánjià is mentioned in volume 250, Yìzōng's Xiántōng fourth year.
26 Wáng Xiānzhī attacked Qízhōu.
The Qízhōu Prefect, Péi Wò,
was a *jìnshì* whom Wáng Duó had promoted when he was in charge of examinations.
Wáng Liáo was among the rebels,
and Xiānzhī had him write a letter to persuade Wò.
Wò made a pact with Xiānzhī,
to withdraw his troops and not fight,
promising to petition for an official post for him.
Liáo also persuaded Xiānzhī to agree to the terms.
Wò then opened the city gates and allowed Xiānzhī, Huáng Cháo, and some thirty others to enter the city.
He hosted a banquet,
displayed a large amount of goods and bribes to present to them,
and submitted a memorial detailing the situation.
Many of the prime ministers said:
"The late emperor did not pardon Páng Xūn,
and he was eventually executed within a year.
This matter is mentioned in the previous volume, Xiántōng ninth and tenth years.
"Zú" (卒)
is pronounced "zǐ xù fān".
This is not comparable to Páng Xūn;
pardoning crimes and granting official posts will
only encourage further villainy."
Wáng Duó strongly insisted,
and it was permitted.
Xiānzhī was then appointed Assistant Officer of the Left Divine Strategy Army and concurrently Censor,
and an imperial envoy was dispatched to Qízhōu to present him with the official appointment document.
Xiānzhī was very pleased to receive it,
and Liáo and Wò
both congratulated him.
Before they had withdrawn,
Huáng Cháo, angered that he had not received an official post,
furiously said:
"At first, we all swore a great oath
to rampage throughout the land.
Now he alone takes an official post in the Left Army,
leaving these five thousand odd men with nowhere to go!"
The *Kǎoyì* says: When Xiānzhī and Cháo first rose up,
it was said that their numbers reached tens of thousands within a few months.
The fact that there were only five thousand here
indicates that they were a motley crowd,
gathering and dispersing unpredictably.
He injured Xiānzhī's head,
and his followers clamored endlessly.
Xiānzhī, fearing the anger of his followers,
consequently refused the appointment.
He extensively plundered Qízhōu;
half of the city's inhabitants
were driven out and half killed,
and their dwellings were burned.
Wò fled to Èzhōu,
and the imperial envoy fled to Xiāngzhōu.
The "imperial envoy"
refers to the imperial envoy who delivered the official appointment document.
The rebels then divided their forces: three thousand odd men followed Xiānzhī and Shàng Jūncháng,
and two thousand odd men followed Cháo,
each departing on separate routes.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Wáng Kūn's *Jīngtīng Lù* says:
"In the fourth year of Qiánfú (877),
the *dīngyǒu* year,
in midsummer,
a comet appeared in the sky.
The bandits Huáng Cháo and Shàng Jūncháng ran riot,
that is, in the *wùxū* year, the fifth year.
The mad bandit Wáng Xiānzhī rose from Yùn and Fēng,
and invaded Rǔ and Zhèng.
Then the great bandit Huáng Cháo, Shàng Jūncháng, and other bandit leaders,
barely over a thousand men,
attacked and captured Rǔzhōu,"
and so on.
It also says:
"Huáng Cháo headed towards Mǐn and Guǎng and departed,
Xiānzhī pointed south towards Yùnzhōu,
Shàng Jūncháng lingered between Chén and Cài.
Fulfilling an ominous wish,
over three thousand bandits belonged to Xiānzhī and Jūncháng,
and over two thousand men were under Huáng Cháo's command."
The following year,
in the second month,
Xiānzhī captured Èzhōu,
and Cháo captured Yùnzhōu,
which means Cháo did not head towards Mǐn and Guǎng,
nor did Xiānzhī head towards Yùn.
Wáng Kūn's book
contains many discrepancies in dates and events;
only those that are credible are selected.
Róng Zhàozǔ punctuated, Niè Chóngqí re-collated.
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by imperial order.
Posterior
Scholar
Qiánfú Fourth Year
(*dīngyǒu*, 877)
1 Spring,
first month,
Wáng Yǐng lured Lǔ Shí into a boat,
and captured him.
Wáng Yǐng then, through Lǔ Shí, requested surrender.
This event is mentioned in the previous volume, last year.
When the court heard of it,
Sòng Hào, the Grand General of the Right Dragon Martial Army, was appointed Pacification Commissioner for the various circuits of Jiāngnán.
In addition to the previously levied troops from various circuits,
troops were further dispatched from the three circuits of Zhōngwǔ, Xuānwǔ, and Gǎnhuà.
Chénxǔ was
the Zhōngwǔ Army;
Biàn Sòng was
the Xuānwǔ Army;
Xúzhōu was
the Gǎnhuà Army.
Old and new combined, there were over fifteen thousand men,
all under Hào's command.
In the second month,
Yǐng attacked and captured Wànghǎizhèn,
plundered Míngzhōu,
and then attacked Táizhōu,
capturing it.
Prefect Wáng Bǎo retreated to defend Tángxīng.
Tángxīng is
today's Tiāntái County,
located 110 *lǐ* west of Táizhōu.
2 Wáng Xiānzhī captured Èzhōu.
3 Huáng Cháo captured Yùnzhōu,
and killed the Military Commissioner Xuē Chóng.
4 Since Qú Lóng Sīlì ascended the throne of Nánzhǎo,
he had been a border menace for nearly twenty years.
Qú Lóng ascended the throne in Xuānzōng's Dàzhōng thirteenth year.
"Qú" (酋)
is pronounced "cí yóu fān".
And his kingdom was also exhausted.
Qú Lóng died,
and was posthumously honored as Emperor Jǐngzhuāng.
His son Fǎ ascended,
changed the era names to Zhēnmíng, Chéngzhì, and Dàtóng,
and the kingdom's name was Hètuò,
also called Dàfēngrén.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Xú Yúnqián's *Nánzhǎo Lù* says:
"Nánzhǎo's alternative name was Hètuò,
and later they also called themselves Dàfēngrén,"
thus adopting *fēng* as the state name.
Fǎ loved hunting and heavy drinking,
entrusting
state affairs to his ministers.
In the intercalary month,
Xīn Dǎng, the Military Commissioner of Lǐngnán Xīdào, reported that Nánzhǎo had dispatched Tuóxī Duàn Cuōbǎo and others to request peace.
Among Nánzhǎo officials, there was the Tuóxī,
equivalent to China's Assistant Official.
"Cuō" (瑳)
is pronounced "qī hé fān",
also "qī kě fān".
"The troops from various circuits garrisoned at Yōngzhōu for many years,
the cost of provisions
has exhausted China.
I request that their peace request be granted,
so that the weary and sick can rest their shoulders."
An imperial edict granted it.
Dǎng dispatched General Dù Hóng and others to carry letters and silks,
sending Cuōbǎo back to Nánzhǎo.
Only a few troops from Jīngnán and Xuānshè remained to garrison Yōngzhōu;
seven-tenths of the remaining troops from other circuits were reduced.
5 Wáng Yǐng (王郢) rampaged through Zhèxī (浙西).
Zhènhǎi (鎮海) Jìedùshǐ (節度使) Péi Qú (裴璩) set up strict defenses,
and did not engage him in battle.
Secretly, he recruited his partisan Zhū Shí (朱實) to surrender,
disbanding six or seven thousand of his followers,
and seizing over two hundred thousand units of weapons and equipment,
along with a corresponding amount of boats, grain, and silk.
An imperial edict appointed Shí (實) as Jīnwǔ Jiāngjūn (金吾將軍).
Thereupon, Yǐng's (郢) party scattered;
Yǐng (郢) gathered his remaining followers
and went east to Míngzhōu (明州).
Yǒngqiáo (甬橋) Zhèn'è Shǐ (鎮遏使) Liú Jùróng (劉巨容) shot and killed him with tube-arrows.
Liú Jùróng (劉巨容), as the Sùzhōu (宿州) Yǒngqiáo (甬橋) Zhèn'è Shǐ (鎮遏使), led troops to suppress Wáng Yǐng (王郢).
Tube-arrows (筒箭):
only a little over a foot long,
they were placed inside a bamboo tube,
notched onto the bowstring,
and the bamboo tube was tied to the wrist.
When the bow was drawn and released,
the tube would spring backward,
propelling the arrow to shoot at the enemy,
piercing straight through.
See Biànwù (辯誤) for details.
In Qiánfú (乾符) second year,
Wáng Yǐng (王郢) rebelled,
and by this time, he was pacified.
Shè (射),
is also read "yì".
Qú (璩)
was the great-great-grandson of Xǔ (諝).
Péi Xǔ (裴諝) is mentioned in volume 206, Dàlì (大曆) fourteenth year of Dàizōng (代宗).
Cóng (從),
is read "cáiyòng".
6 In the third month,
Huáng Cháo (黃巢) captured Yízhōu (沂州).
7 In summer,
fourth month,
on the day Rénshēn (壬申), the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
8 The bandit leader Liǔ Yànzhāng (柳彥璋) plundered Jiāngxī (江西).
9 There was a military rebellion in Shǎnzhōu (陝州),
driving out the Guāncháshǐ (觀察使) Cuī Jié (崔碣);
Jié (碣) was demoted to Huáizhōu Sīmǎ (懷州司馬).
10 Huáng Cháo (黃巢) and Shàng Ràng (尚讓) joined forces and secured Cháyá Shān (查牙山).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Old Records state:
"In the fourth year, third month,
Cháo (巢) captured Yùnzhōu (鄆州).
In the seventh month,
he entered Cháyá Shān (查牙山)
and joined Wáng Xiānzhī (王仙芝).
In the fifth year, second month,
Jūncháng (君長) and Xiānzhī (仙芝) both died.
Shàng Ràng (尚讓), because his brother was killed,
extensively plundered Huáinán (淮南)."
The Old Biography states:
"In the fifth year, eighth month,
Wáng Duó (王鐸) beheaded Wáng Xiānzhī (王仙芝).
Before this,
Shàng Jūncháng's (尚君長) younger brother Ràng (讓), because his brother was killed while serving as an envoy,
led his followers into Cháyá Shān (查牙山).
Huáng Cháo (黃巢) and Huáng Kuí (黃揆), eight brothers in all, led several thousand bandits to depend on Ràng (讓)."
According to the Shílù (實錄),
in Qiánfú (乾符) second year,
Xiānzhī (仙芝) captured Cáo (曹) and Pú (濮),
and Cháo (巢) had already raised troops to support him.
In the third year, twelfth month,
Zhāotǎo Fù Dūdūjiān (招討副都監) Yáng Fùguāng (楊復光) reported:
"The bandit Shàng Ràng (尚讓) occupies Cháyá Shān (查牙山),
and the government troops have retreated to Dèngzhōu (鄧州)."
In the fourth year, fourth month,
Huáng Cháo (黃巢) led his followers to secure Cháyá Shān (查牙山).
In the winter of that year,
Jūncháng (君長) then died.
The Jīngtīng Lù (驚聽錄) states:
"Cháo (巢) and Xiānzhī (仙芝) both entered Qízhōu (蘄州),
and Cháo (巢) was angered that Xiānzhī (仙芝) alone received an official position,
striking Xiānzhī (仙芝) and injuring his face,
thus they divided their forces."
At that time, Jūncháng (君長) was also present,
so it was not after Xiānzhī (仙芝) died
that Cháo (巢) then depended on Ràng (讓).
Furthermore, according to the Old Records,
after Xiānzhī (仙 zhī) died,
Wáng Duó (王鐸) first became the Dūtǒng (都統) to suppress the bandits.
But the Old Biography says
"Wáng Duó (王鐸) beheaded Xiānzhī (仙芝)",
and also previously said
"killed Zhāng Lín (張璘),
then captured Guǎngzhōu (廣州)",
and previously said
"captured Huázhōu (華州),
then attacked Tóngguān (潼關)",
the narration is disjointed and illogical.
We now follow the Shílù (實錄).
11 In the fifth month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ (甲子),
Gěishì Zhōng (給事中) Yáng Sǔn (楊損) was appointed Shǎnjí Guāncháshǐ (陝虢觀察使).
Upon arriving at his post, Sǔn (損)
executed the instigators of the rebellion.
Sǔn (損)
was the son of Sìfù (嗣復).
Yáng Sìfù (楊嗣復) served Wénzōng (文宗).
12 Initially,
Guìguǎn (桂管) Guāncháshǐ (觀察使) Lǐ Zàn (李瓚) misgoverned.
His Zhīshǐ (支使) Xuē Jiānshí (薛堅石) repeatedly tried to rectify him,
but Zàn (瓚) would not comply.
When Zàn (瓚) was driven out,
Lǐ Zàn (李瓚) being driven out is recorded in the previous year of the preceding volume.
Bèi (被),
is read "píyì".
Jiānshí (堅石) sent dispatches to neighboring circuits,
prohibiting and blocking the rebellious troops,
thus pacifying the region.
An imperial edict promoted Jiānshí (堅石) to Guózǐ Bóshì (國子博士).
13 In the sixth month,
Liǔ Yànzhāng (柳彥璋) attacked and captured Jiāngzhōu (江州),
seizing Cǐshǐ (刺史) Táo Xiáng (陶祥)
and forcing Xiáng (祥) to submit a memorial.
Yànzhāng (彥璋) also attached his own surrender document.
An imperial edict appointed Yànzhāng (彥璋) as Yòu Jiānmén Jiāngjūn (右監門將軍)
and ordered him to disband his followers and report to the capital;
Liú Bǐngrén (劉秉仁), a Zuǒwǔwèi Jiāngjūn (左武衞將軍), was appointed Jiāngzhōu Cǐshǐ (江州刺史).
Yànzhāng (彥璋) did not comply.
With over a hundred warships, he fortified the Pénjiāng (湓江) as a water stronghold.
The Pénjiāng (湓江) is outside Jiāngzhōu (江州) city,
connecting to the Dàjiāng (大江),
hence it is called Pénjiāng (湓江).
Pén (湓),
is read "púbēn".
14 Zhōngwǔ (忠武) Dūjiāng (都將) Lǐ Kěfēng (李可封), returning from frontier duty,
arrived at Bīnzhōu (邠州).
He coerced the commander,
demanded outstanding arrears of grain and salt,
and stayed for four days,
causing alarm throughout the entire region.
In autumn,
seventh month,
upon returning to Xǔzhōu (許州),
Jìedùshǐ (節度使) Cuī Ānqián (崔安潛) investigated and executed all of them.
15 On the day Gēngshēn (庚申),
Wáng Xiānzhī (王仙芝) and Huáng Cháo (黃巢) attacked Sòngzhōu (宋州).
The troops from the three circuits engaged in battle,
but were unsuccessful.
The three circuits' troops were
Pínglú (平盧), Xuānwǔ (宣武), and Zhōngwǔ (忠武).
On the day Jiǎyín (甲寅),
Zuǒwēiwèi Shàngjiāngjūn (左威衞上將軍) Zhāng Zìmiǎn (張自勉) led seven thousand Zhōngwǔ (忠武) troops to relieve Sòngzhōu (宋州).
They killed over two thousand bandits,
and the bandits lifted the siege and fled.
Wáng Duó (王鐸) and Lú Xié (盧攜) wanted Zhāng Zìmiǎn (張自勉) to place his troops under the command of Sòng Wēi (宋威) Jìedù (節度).
Zhèng Tián (鄭畋) believed that Wēi (威) and Zìmiǎn (自勉) already harbored suspicions and resentment,
and if Zìmiǎn (自勉) were under Wēi's (威) command,
he would surely be killed,
so Tián (畋) refused to endorse the memorial.
In the eighth month,
on the day Xīnwèi (辛未),
Duó (鐸) and Xié (攜) complained to the Emperor,
asking to be dismissed;
on the day Gēngchén (庚辰),
Tián (畋) requested to return to Chǎnchuān (滻川) to recuperate from illness.
Chǎnchuān (滻川) is east of Cháng'ān (長安).
Chǎn (滻),
pronounced "chǎn".
The historian notes that Xīzōng (僖宗) was unable to stabilize national policies.
16 Wáng Xiānzhī (王仙芝) captured Ānzhōu (安州).
17 There was a military rebellion in Yánzhōu (鹽州),
driving out Cǐshǐ (刺史) Wáng Chéngyán (王承顏).
An imperial edict ordered Gāopǐn (高品) Niú Cóngguī (牛從珪) to go and appease them;
Chéngyán (承顏) was demoted to Xiàngzhōu Sīhù (象州司戶).
Chéngyán (承顏) and Cuī Jié (崔碣) had always had good reputations for governance,
but were driven out by arrogant soldiers due to their strictness.
The court demoted them along with those who caused chaos through greed and tyranny,
which people at the time regretted.
The historian notes that in the late Táng (唐) dynasty, rewards and punishments were inappropriate,
and also states that the ruler was dimwitted and governance was chaotic,
so capable officials not only could not display their talents,
but also could not escape punishment.
The army requested that their general Wáng Zōngchéng (王宗誠) be made Cǐshǐ (刺史).
An imperial edict ordered Zōngchéng (宗誠) to report to the capital,
and all the officers and soldiers were pardoned,
and moreover, granted generous allowances.
18 On the day Yǐmǎo (乙卯),
Wáng Xiānzhī (王仙 zhī) captured Suízhōu (隨州),
seizing Cǐshǐ (刺史) Cuī Xiūzhēng (崔休徵).
Shānnán Dōngdào (山南東道) Jìedùshǐ (節度使) Lǐ Fú (李福) sent his son to lead troops to relieve Suízhōu (隨州),
but he died in battle.
Fú (福) memorialized requesting reinforcements,
and Zuǒwǔwèi Dàjiāngjūn (左武衞大將軍) Lǐ Chāngyán (李昌言) was sent with five hundred Fèngxiáng (鳳翔) cavalry to assist.
Xiānzhī (仙 zhī) then moved on to plunder Fù (復) and Yǐng (郢).
Zhōngwǔ (忠武) Dàjiāng (大將) Zhāng Guàn (張貫) and four thousand others, along with Xuānwǔ (宣武) troops, reinforced Xiāngzhōu (襄州),
but fled back through the mountainous paths between Shēn (申) and Cài (蔡);
an imperial edict ordered Zhōngwǔ (忠武) Jìedùshǐ (節度使) Cuī Ānqián (崔安潛) and Xuānwǔ (宣武) Jìedùshǐ (節度使) Mù Rényù (穆仁裕) to send people to bring them back.
"To bring them back" means to instruct and discipline the officers and soldiers, making them return to provide aid.
In the winter of the 19th year [of Qiánfú (872 CE)],
in the tenth month,
Lǐ Kǎn, the Jìedùshǐ of Bīnnìng, memorialized that he had dispatched troops to punish Wáng Zōngchéng,
who was beheaded,
and the rest of his partisans were pacified.
They were followers of Wáng Chéngyán, whom they had driven away.
Zhèng Tián, Wáng Duó, and Lú Xi debated the use of military force before the Emperor.
Tián did not prevail,
withdrew,
and then submitted another memorial,
stating:
"Since Wáng Xiānzhī's initial disturbances,
according to Kǒng Ānguó's commentary on the Shàngshū: chù (俶)
means 'beginning'.
rǎo (擾)
means 'disorder'.
The character chù (俶) is pronounced chǐ liù fān.
Troops have been continuously mobilized,
exhausting provisions and supplies.
This means that all the resources of this circuit were used to supply provisions and supplies for the soldiers on campaign.
Many prefectures have been plunged into misery,
yet they dared not violate his territory.
Furthermore, he entrusted the troops of this circuit to Zhāng Zìmiǎn
to relieve the siege of Sòngzhōu,
allowing the grain transport from Jiāng and Huái to flow freely,
preventing it from falling into enemy hands.
Now, by imperial favor, all seven thousand troops under Zìmiǎn are ordered to be commanded by Zhāng Guàn,
and subordinated to Sòng Wēi.
End of sentence.
Wēi, in turn, submitted a memorial making false accusations.
To suffer humiliation after achieving merit,
I secretly lament this.
Ān Qián led his forces discreetly,
achieving victories more than once.
Suddenly, all his strong troops are given to others,
and a good general returns empty-handed.
If a powerful enemy were to suddenly arrive,
how would we be able to resist them!
I request that four thousand of the Zhōngwǔ troops be given to Wēi,
and the remaining three thousand be commanded by Zìmiǎn
to guard his territory.
This would neither infringe upon Sòng Wēi's merit
nor cause Ān Qián shame."
At the time, Lú Xi disagreed,
and the Emperor could not decide.
Tián again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Sòng Wēi has deceived the court
and suffered numerous crushing defeats.
It is also heard that Wáng Xiānzhī submitted seven pleas for surrender,
but Wēi did not report them.
The court and common people are indignant,
believing that military law should be strictly enforced.
Given such circumstances,
he should not again be entrusted with military authority.
I wish to discuss this with the Interior Ministers."
The Interior Ministers
refers to the two Chief Eunuchs and the two Grand Secretaries of the Privy Council.
The request was not followed.
A mutiny occurred in the Hézhōng army,
driving out Jìedùshǐ Liú Móu,
and allowing the troops to burn and plunder.
Dòu Jǐng, the Jīngzhàoyǐn, was appointed as the Hézhōng Xuānwèi Zhìzhìshǐ.
Huáng Cháo pillaged Qí and Huáng.
Qí and Huáng are one hundred sixty-five *lǐ* apart.
Four thousand heads were taken.
Cháo then fled.
In the eleventh month,
on the day *jǐyǒu*,
Dòu Jǐng was appointed as the Hézhōng Jìedùshǐ.
Yáng Fùguāng, the Deputy Commander of the Expeditionary Forces, sent someone to persuade Wáng Xiānzhī,
and Xiānzhī sent Shàng Jūncháng and others to surrender to Fùguāng.
Sòng Wēi sent troops to intercept Jūncháng and the others on the way.
In the twelfth month,
Wēi memorialized that he had fought Jūncháng and the others southwest of Yǐngzhōu,
captured them alive, and presented them;
Fùguāng memorialized that Jūncháng and the others had actually surrendered and
were not captured by Wēi.
An imperial edict ordered Shìyùshǐ Guī Rénshào and others to investigate.
The Xìngpǔ says: In the Zuǒzhuàn,
the Hú
state, a feudal state (zǐguó),
had the surname Guī.
It was destroyed by Chǔ,
and some descendants took the state name as their clan name,
while others took the surname as their clan name.
Jūncháng and the others were executed at Gǒujílǐng.
Huáng Cháo captured Kuāngchéng,
and then captured Púzhōu.
Kuāngchéng County
belonged to Huázhōu, originally Hán Chángyuán County.
Sòng Bái says: During the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty, Kuāngchéng County was established at Fùgūchéng,
named after the old Kuāngchéng south of the county,
which was the place Confucius feared.
Pú (濮)
is pronounced bómù fān.
Liú Bǐngrén, the Cǐshǐ of Jiāngzhōu, traveled to his post by post-horse,
and entered Liǔ Yànzhāng's naval camp in a single boat.
The bandits, caught off guard,
immediately greeted him with obeisance.
Bǐngrén beheaded Yànzhāng
and dispersed his followers.
Liǔ Yànzhāng was a bandit for nine months before his defeat.
Wáng Xiānzhī raided Jīngnán.
Yáng Zhīwēn, the Jìedùshǐ,
was Zhīzhì's elder brother.
Yáng Zhīzhì is mentioned in the previous volume, Yìzōng, Xiántōng 11th year.
He was unskilled in military matters,
and when someone reported the bandits' approach,
Zhīwēn dismissed it as false
and made no preparations.
At that time, the Hànshuǐ was shallow and narrow,
and the bandits crossed at Jiǎqiàn.
The Jiǔyùzhì states: Yǐngzhōu, Chángshòu County, has Jiǎqiàn Town.
Qiàn (塹)
is pronounced qīyàn fān.
In the spring of the 1st year [of Qiánfú (874 CE)],
in the first month,
on the day *dīngyǒu* (the first day of the month),
there was heavy snow.
Zhīwēn was receiving felicitations,
for on New Year's Day and the Winter Solstice,
all prefectures and garrisons would receive felicitations from their generals and officials,
and even counties and towns did the same.
They then captured the outer wall (Luóchéng).
His generals and aides worked together to defend the inner city (Zǐchéng),
but by evening,
Zhīwēn still had not appeared.
The generals and aides requested Zhīwēn to go out and reassure the soldiers,
but Zhīwēn walked in a gauze cap and black fur robe.
The generals and aides requested Zhīwēn to wear armor to guard against stray arrows.
Zhīwēn, seeing the soldiers fighting back,
still composed poetry for his staff,
and sent an envoy to request urgent help from Lǐ Fú, the Jìedùshǐ of Shānnándōngdào.
Fú personally led all his troops to rescue them.
At that time, there were five hundred Shatuo troops in Xiāngyáng,
and Fú went with them.
Upon reaching Jīngmén,
they encountered the bandits.
During the Jìn dynasty, a portion of Biān County
was separated to establish Chánglín County.
In the 21st year of Dédzōng's Zhēnyuán (805 CE), Jīngmén County was again separated from Chánglín and established,
belonging to Jiānglíng Prefecture.
The Jiǔyùzhì states: It is about one hundred sixty *lǐ* north of the prefecture.
They defeated them.
Upon hearing this, Xiānzhī
burned and plundered Jiānglíng and departed.
Jiānglíng City originally had thirty thousand households,
but by this time, three or four tenths of the inhabitants had died.
On the day *rényín*,
Zēng Yuányù, the Deputy Commander of the Expeditionary Forces, severely defeated Wáng Xiānzhī east of Shēnzhōu.
Ten thousand were killed,
and ten thousand others who surrendered were dispersed.
An imperial edict, citing Sòng Wēi's prolonged illness,
dismissed him as Commander of the Expeditionary Forces and
ordered him to return to Qīngzhōu;
Sòng Wēi was originally the commander of Pínglú,
and upon dismissal as Commander of the Expeditionary Forces, he returned to his garrison.
Zhāng Zìmiǎn, the Cǐshǐ of Yǐngzhōu, became the Deputy Commander.
On the day *gēngxū*,
Gāo Pián, the Jìedùshǐ of Xīchuān, was appointed as the Jìedùshǐ of Jīngnán and concurrently the Salt and Iron Transport Commissioner.
In the fifth month,
on the *bǐngshēn* day which was the first day of the month,
Zhèng Tián and Lú Xié discussed the matter of the Man barbarians.
Xié wished to make peace and establish kinship with them,
but Tián strongly argued that it was unacceptable.
Xié grew angry,
flung his sleeve, and stood up.
His sleeve caught on an inkstone, which fell to the ground
and broke.
The Emperor heard of this
and said,
"When ministers insult each other like this,
how can they serve as a model for the Four Seas!"
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
both Tián and Xié were dismissed and made Palace Guest of the Crown Prince, assigned to separate duties.
*Kǎoyì* (Investigation of Discrepancies) states: The Old Annals say:
"In the fifth month of the sixth year,
the rebels besieged Guǎngzhōu,
and wrote letters to Lǐ Tiáo and Cuī Qiú,
requesting the *jiéyuè* of Tiānpíng."
Tián and Xié debated fiercely in the Central Secretariat,
using disrespectful language,
and both were dismissed,
assigned to separate duties."
Tián's biography says:
"In the fifth year,
Huáng Cháo crossed the Jiāng and Huái rivers eastward.
His army numbered a million,
and he repeatedly captured prefectures and cities in his path.
In the sixth year,
he captured Ānnán Fǔ
and occupied it.
He then sent a letter to Cuī Qiú, the Observer of Zhèdōng, requesting the *jiéyuè* of Yùnzhōu.
Qiú said, 'The rebel's power is difficult to contain;
it would be advisable to grant it to him
to eliminate the trouble of him looking north.'
The Son of Heaven ordered all officials to discuss it.
Initially,
when Huáng Cháo first rose,
Chancellor Lú Xié, knowing that Gāo Pián, the Observer of Zhèxī, had military accomplishments,
recommended him to be the Military Commissioner of Huáinán,
ordering him to block the rebel's advance.
Soon after, Pián was made Commander of the Allied Armies of All Circuits.
When Cuī Qiú's memorial arrived,
the court officials discussed it,
with some requesting to grant him a *jié* to alleviate the crisis.
Tián adopted the general opinion,
wishing to bind him with the military command of Nánhǎi.
Xié, having initially employed Gāo Pián,
wished for him to achieve merit and secure a victory,
saying: 'Gāo Pián's military strategy is unparalleled,
and the troops of Huái are very sharp.
Now that the armies of various circuits are gathering,
these petty, insignificant bandits
are not worth exterminating.
Why should we abandon the effort and show timidity,
and thus disband all the armies?'
Tián said: 'The rebellion of Cháo was
originally caused by famine years,
and people united for gain,
thus becoming numerous.
South of the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
half the land has been ravaged.
The state has long not used troops;
everyone has forgotten how to fight.
Local *jié* generals merely close their gates and defend themselves,
still unable to resist.
It is better to forgive their faults and be tolerant,
temporarily bestowing imperial favor.
They originally united for gain due to famine years;
once they encounter a year of plenty,
who would not yearn for their homeland?
Once their multitude disperses,
Cháo will be like meat on a chopping block.
If at this juncture we do not attack with strategy,
relying entirely on military force,
I fear the troubles of the empire will be unending!'
The Empress Dowager agreed.
However, the Left Palatial Aide Yú Cóng said: 'Nánhǎi has the profit of maritime trade,
annually contributing pearls and jewels.
If it falls into the hands of the demon rebels,
the national treasury will gradually become depleted and exhausted.'
The Emperor also hoped for Pián's success,
and thus followed Xié's proposal.
When discussing the imperial edict in the Central Secretariat,
Tián said: 'The demon rebels number a million,
running rampant across the land.
Lord Gāo delays and plays with the rebels,
having no intention of eliminating them,
and now we are to protect them as well.
They have achieved their goal.
The safety of the imperial destiny
rests on the decisions of us three or four people.
If you rely on Huáinán to wage war,
I know not where to dismount my carriage!'
Xié grew angry,
flung his sleeve and stood up,
soiled his sleeve on the inkstone,
and then threw it.
Xīzōng heard of it,
and angrily said: 'When ministers insult each other,
how can they serve as a model for the Four Seas!'
Both men were dismissed from government. "
Xié's biography says:
"In the fifth year,
Huáng Cháo captured Jīngnán, the outer walls of Jiāngxī, and the prefectures of Ráo, Jí, Qián, Xìn, etc.
From Zhèdōng, he captured Fújiàn,
then reached Lǐngnán,
captured Guǎngzhōu,
killed the Military Commissioner Lǐ Tiáo,
and then submitted a memorial requesting a *jiéyuè*.
Initially,
when Wáng Xiānzhī rose in Hénán,
Xié recommended Sòng Wēi, Qí Kèràng, Zēng Gǔn, and others who possessed military strategy,
and appointed them as Commissioners for Pacification.
However, when Sòng Wēi killed Shàng Jūncháng,
it caused the rebels to spread everywhere.
The court then appointed Chancellor Wáng Duó as the Commander-in-Chief,
which deeply displeased Xié.
Cuī Qiú, the Marshal of Zhè and others, submitted memorials requesting to grant Huáng Cháo the *jiéyuè* of Guǎngzhōu.
The Emperor ordered the chancellors to discuss it.
Xié, seeing Wáng Duó as the commander-in-chief,
wished to infuriate Huáng Cháo,
and firmly insisted that the rebels should not be granted military control (*jiézhì*),
but only be given the title of a mere *shuàifǔ shuài*;
he argued with his colleague Zhèng Tián,
threw an inkstone to the ground,
and thus both were dismissed."
*Shílù* (Veritable Records) states:
"In the fifth month of the fifth year,
on the *bǐngshēn* day, which was the first day of the month,
on this day,
Chancellors Zhèng Tián and Lú Xié discussed the matter of the Southern Man barbarians.
Xié proposed sending a princess to establish peace,
but Tián strongly argued that it was unacceptable,
and debated right and wrong.
Xié grew angry,
flung his sleeve and stood up,
his sleeve was stained with ink from the inkstone,
and he then threw and shattered it.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
Tián and Xié were both made Palace Guest of the Crown Prince, assigned to separate duties."
A note says:
"Old histories and miscellaneous writings all say that 'Tián and Xié discussed the *jiézhì* of Huáng Cháo,
and were dismissed due to angry contention.'
However, Zhèng Yánchāng's biography of Tián states 'discussed the Man barbarian matter,'
which cannot be corroborated.
Yet, what was recorded at that time is probably not erroneous."
Again, Tián's biography says:
"At that time, Huáng Cháo attacked and captured Jiāng and Zhè,
and submitted a memorial requesting a *jiéyuè*.
Tián and his colleague Lú Xié deliberated on attacking and suppressing him, and selecting and appointing generals and commanders,
and there were many disagreements.
Also, the Southern Zhào Man barbarians requested to send a princess for peace,
but Tián strongly argued that it was unacceptable,
and thus debated it,
whereupon he and Xié were both dismissed from chancellorship."
Again, Xié's biography says:
"Xié's personal character was very crude,
and his speech was also improper.
He and Zhèng Tián were both maternal grandsons of Lǐ Áo.
When they served together in government,
their discussions did not align.
Initially,
when Wáng Xiānzhī rose in Hénán,
Xié recommended Sòng Wēi, Qí Kèràng, Zēng Gǔn, and others who possessed military strategy,
and appointed them as Commissioners for Pacification.
All their efforts to suppress the rebels were fruitless,
leading to the rebels spreading everywhere.
He also supported Gāo Pián's request,
wishing to make peace with the Nánzhào Man barbarians by sending a princess.
Zhèng Tián opposed it,
deeming it unacceptable.
They argued fiercely before the Emperor,
and thus both were dismissed."
The Old Annals state:
"In the fifth month of the sixth year,
the rebels besieged Guǎngzhōu,
and furthermore wrote to Lǐ Tiáo, the Military Commissioner of Guǎngnán, and Cuī Qiú, the Observer of Zhèdōng,
seeking their recommendation,
and requesting the *jiéyuè* of Tiānpíng.
Qiú and Tiáo submitted memorials discussing this.
Chancellors Zhèng Tián and Lú Xié debated in the Central Secretariat,
using disrespectful language,
and both were dismissed as Palace Guest of the Crown Prince, assigned to separate duties in the Eastern Capital."
According to both old and new biographies, and the Old Annals, Tián and Xié were dismissed as chancellors in the sixth year.
The Veritable Records, New Annals, and the tables place it in the fifth month of this year.
The Veritable Records and New Book contradict each other.
However, Sòng Shì's writings mention it multiple times,
knowing that the two were dismissed in the fifth month,
there must be some basis,
so we follow it now.
Cuī Hàng, the Vice Minister of Personnel, was made Vice Minister of Revenue, and also given the title of Grand Councillor.
9 The Emperor above was troubled by the banditry,
Wáng Duó said:
"I am the chief of the prime ministers,
but in court, I am insufficient to share His Majesty's worries.
I request to personally lead the various generals in suppressing them."
Thus, Duó was appointed Shǒu Sītú (守司徒) concurrently Shìzhōng (侍中),
and made Jīngnán Jiédùshǐ (荊南節度使) and Nánmiàn Xíngyíng Zhāotǎo Dūtǒng (南面行營招討都統).
Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Old Records state:
"In the second month of the fifth year,
Duó personally requested to lead the army to suppress the rebels.
The Son of Heaven, considering Sòng Wēi's (宋威) misguided strategy in killing Shàng Jūncháng (尚君長),
appointed Duó as Jiǎnjiào Sītú (檢校司徒) concurrently Shìzhōng (侍中), Ménxià Shíláng (門下侍郎), Jiānglíng Yǐn (江陵尹), Jīngnán Jiédùshǐ (荊南節度使),
and Zhū Dào Bīngmǎ Dūtǒng (諸道兵馬都統)."
The Old Biography states:
"In the fourth year,
the rebels captured Jiānglíng (江陵),
Yáng Zhīwēn (楊知溫) failed to defend it,
and Sòng Wēi's (宋威) strategy to defeat the rebels was flawed.
The court deliberated on a commander-in-chief,
and Lú Xié (盧攜) stated that Gāo Pián (高駢) had accumulated many military achievements,
and should be entrusted with military power;
but public opinion did not agree.
Duó memorialized to the court: 'I wish to personally lead the various armies to sweep away the bandits.'
The court agreed.
In the fifth year,
Duó was appointed Shǒu Sītú (守司徒), Ménxià Shíláng (門下侍郎), Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事),
concurrently Jiānglíng Yǐn (江陵尹), Jīngnán Jiédùshǐ (荊南節度使),
and Zhū Dào Xíngyíng Bīngmǎ Dūtǒng (諸道行營兵馬都統)."
Now, it follows the Shílù (實錄) and Xīnjì (新紀), and Biǎo (表).
10 In the fifth month,
on the Xīnmǎo (辛卯) day,
an imperial edict granted silver to the Hédōng (河東) soldiers.
The soldiers of Yájiàng (牙將) Hè Gōngyǎ's (賀公雅) division mutinied,
burning and looting three cities.
The New Book, Geography Treatise: From the time Gāo Zǔ (高祖) raised an army in Jìnyáng (晉陽),
and since Tiānshòu (天授),
it was considered the Northern Capital,
and the Jìnyáng (晉陽) Palace, as in the Suí (隋) dynasty, was not abolished.
The palace was in the northwest of the capital,
its walls were two thousand five hundred and twenty paces in circumference,
and forty-eight feet high.
The capital city had the Fén (汾) River on the left and the Jìn (晉) River on the right,
with Qiánqiū (潛丘) in the middle,
four thousand three hundred and twenty-one paces long,
three thousand one hundred and twenty paces wide,
and fifteen thousand one hundred and fifty-three paces in circumference,
its height was forty feet.
East of the Fén (汾) was the Eastern City,
built by Chángshǐ (長史) Lǐ Jì (李勣) in the eleventh year of Zhēngguān (貞觀).
Between the two cities was the Middle City,
built during Empress Wǔ's (武后) time,
to connect with the Eastern City.
South of the palace was Dàmíng (大明) City,
which was the old palace city.
Jiédùshǐ (節度使) Lǐ Kǎn (李侃) and the Jiānjūn (監軍) personally went out to appease them,
executing Jìng (敬) at the Yámén (牙門) for them,
and then peace was restored.
11 Tàiníng Jiédùshǐ (泰寧節度使) Lǐ Xì (李係)
was Shèng's (晟) great-grandson.
He had eloquence but no courage or strategy.
Wáng Duó (王鐸), considering his family's history of good generals,
recommended him as Xíngyíng Fù Dūtǒng (行營副都統) concurrently Húnán Guānchásǐ (湖南觀察使).
Appointing officials based on family background without evaluating their talent
is a common problem in ancient and modern times.
This lays the groundwork for Duó and Xì's failure to defend and their destruction of the populace.
To block the path north of the ridge,
and resist Huáng Cháo (黃巢).
12 Hédōng Dūyúhòu (河東都虞候) secretly arrested Hè Gōngyǎ's (賀公雅) soldiers every night,
exterminating their clans.
On the Dīngsì (丁巳) day,
nearly a hundred remaining rebels called themselves
"Bàoyuān Jiāng (報冤將)" (Revenge Generals),
extensively looting three cities,
burning the homes of Mǎbù Dūyúhòu (馬步都虞候) Zhāng Kǎi (張鍇) and Fǔchéng Dūyúhòu (府城都虞候) Guō Bó (郭昢).
Jiédùshǐ (節度使) Lǐ Kǎn (李侃) issued an order,
stating that due to the unrest in the military command,
and to cater to the army's sentiment,
Kǎi and Bó were arrested,
executed at the Yámén (牙門),
and their families were banished;
Hè Gōngyǎ (賀公雅) was made Mǎbù Dūyúhòu (馬步都虞候).
Kǎi and Bó, before their execution,
cried and said to the crowd:
"Those we killed were all secretly reported by the Arresting Thieves Bureau.
Dying unjustly today,
is there no brave warrior to save us!"
Thereupon, the soldiers again raised a great clamor,
seizing Kǎi and Bó and returning them to the Dūyúhòu Sī (都虞候司).
Soon an order was issued,
restoring them to their former positions,
and recalling their families;
more than thirty families, including Yuán Yìzōng (元義宗) of the Arresting Thieves Bureau, were arrested
and exterminated.
On the Jǐwèi (己未) day,
Mǎbù Dūjiàoliànshǐ (馬步都教練使) Zhū Méi (朱玫) and others were appointed Sānchéng Zhǎncuòshǐ (三城斬斫使) (Execution Commissioners of the Three Cities),
leading soldiers to divide and capture the Bàoyuān Jiāng (報冤將),
executing them all,
and the military city finally settled.
13 Huáng Cháo (黃巢) wrote to Zhèdōng Guānchásǐ (浙東觀察使) Cuī Qiú (崔璆) and Língnán Dōngdào Jiédùshǐ (嶺南東道節度使) Lǐ Tiáo (李迢),
requesting the Tiānpíng Jiédùshǐ (天平節度使) post.
The two memorialized on his behalf;
the court did not permit it.
Cháo again submitted a memorial requesting the Guǎngzhōu Jiédùshǐ (廣州節度使) post.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Xù Bǎoyùn Lù (續寶運錄) states:
"Huáng Cháo (黃巢) first requested Guǎngfǔ (廣府) concurrently Shǐxiàng (使相),

In early summer, Huáng Cháo's (黃巢) troops were stationed in Guǎngnán (廣南).
He repeatedly waited for an imperial edict, but none came down,
so he unleashed attacks and looting.
In the sixth month of summer, Huáng Cháo (黃巢) submitted a memorial,
calling himself 'Yìjūn Bǎiwàn Dūtǒng concurrently Sháo (韶) and Guǎng (廣) and other Prefectures' Guānchá Chǔzhì (觀察處置) and other Commissioners.'
It concluded with 'Memorial of the fifteenth day of the sixth month.'
In autumn,

the Inner Eunuch Qiú Gōngdù (仇公度) was sent bearing an imperial handwritten edict and six official notices for Guǎngnán (廣南), Yōngfǔ (邕府), Ānnán (安南), Āndōng (安東) and other circuits' Jiédùshǐ (節度使), Zhǐhuī Guānchásǐ (指揮觀察使), Kāiguógōng (開國公), and five hundred households of enfeoffment,

The memorial concluded: 'Submitted on the first day of the tenth month of Guǎngmíng (廣明) first year.'
Gōngdù (公度) and others arrived in the capital on the twenty-ninth day of the tenth month of that year."
If what the Bǎoyùn Lù (寶運錄) says is true,
then on the first day of the tenth month of Guǎngmíng (廣明) first year,
Cháo was still in Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
However, in that month, Cháo had already entered Cháng'ān (長安).
Now, it follows the Old Records.
Zuǒ Púyè (左僕射) Yú Cóng (于琮) believed:
"Guǎngzhōu (廣州) is a gathering place for maritime trade and precious goods;
how can it be given to the rebels!"
So it was also not permitted,
and instead, an alternative official post was discussed.
In the sixth month,
the prime ministers requested to appoint Cháo Fǔ
Shuài (率) (Commander of the Palace Guards).
This was followed.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Old Records state:
"In the fifth month,
the rebels besieged Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
and also wrote to Guǎngnán Jiédùshǐ (廣南節度使) Lǐ Tiáo (李迢) and Zhèdōng Guānchásǐ (浙東觀察使) Cuī Qiú (崔璆) to seek recommendation,

Cháo's (巢) forces suffered a great epidemic from spring to summer,
with three or four tenths dying.
He wanted to occupy Língbiǎo (嶺表) and make it his permanent lair,

Yòu Púyè (右僕射) Yú Cóng (于琮) deliberated as stated above.

14 Lǐ Kǎn (李侃), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hédōng (河東), pleaded illness because of repeated disturbances in the military administration,

eighth month,
on the Jiǎzǐ (甲子) day,
Kǎn (侃) departed from Jìnyáng (晉陽).
Soon after, Lǐ Wèi (李蔚), the Liúshǒu (留守) of Dōngdū (東都), was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事)
and made Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hédōng (河東).
15 Gāo Pián (高駢), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Zhènhǎi (鎮海), memorialized:
"I request that Láng Yòufù (郎幼復), the acting Cìshǐ (刺史) of Shūzhōu (舒州), be appointed Liúhòu (留後)
to guard Zhéxī (浙西).
I will dispatch Zhāng Lín (張璘), the Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ (都知兵馬使), with five thousand troops to guard the strategic passes in Chénzhōu (郴州).
Wáng Chóngrèn (王重任), the Bīngmǎ Liúhòu (兵馬留後), will lead eight thousand troops to intercept in Xúnzhōu (循州) and Cháozhōu (潮州).
I will lead ten thousand troops from Dàyǔlǐng (大庾嶺) directly to Guǎngzhōu (廣州) to attack Huáng Cháo (黃巢).
If Cháo (巢) hears of my arrival,
he will surely flee.
I beg Your Majesty to order Wáng Duó (王鐸) to guard the strategic passes with thirty thousand troops from his command in Wúzhōu (梧州), Guìzhōu (桂州), Zhāozhōu (昭州), and Yǒngzhōu (永州)."
The emperor disallowed it.
16 In the ninth month,
Huáng Cháo (黃巢) obtained the commission documents of a Shuàifǔ Shuài (率府率),
was greatly enraged,
cursed the government officials,
and urgently attacked Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
On that very day, he captured it,
seized Jìedùshǐ (節度使) Lǐ Tiáo (李迢),
and then plundered the prefectures and counties of Lǐngnán (嶺南).
Cháo (巢) ordered Tiáo (迢) to draft a memorial expressing his intentions.
Tiáo (迢) said:
"I have successively received national grace,
and my relatives fill the court.
My arm may be severed,
but a memorial cannot be drafted."
Cháo (巢) killed him.
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Jīngtīng Lù (驚聽錄) says:
"Lǐ Tiáo (李迢) was held captive by the rebels,
then the coastal areas were burned,
Guìzhōu (桂州) was also captured,
and next Húnán (湖南) was attacked.
They encamped at Héngzhōu (衡州),
where they learned that Wáng Xiānzhī (王仙芝) had already died in battle in Shāndōng (山東),
and Shàng Jūncháng (尚君長) had been captured and sent to Xiánjīng (咸京).
Thereupon, Lǐ Tiáo (李迢) was summoned,
and out of rage, he was tripped and harmed."
The Xīnjì (新紀) says:
"In the eleventh month,
on the Xīnyǒu (辛酉) day,
Huáng Cháo (黃巢) captured Jiānglíng (江陵)
and killed Lǐ Tiáo (李迢)."
The Xīnchuán (新傳) says:
"In the tenth month,
Cháo (巢) occupied Jīngnán (荊南) and coerced Lǐ Tiáo (李迢) to draft a memorial to report to the Son of Heaven;
Tiáo (迢) refused,
Cháo (巢) was enraged
and killed him."
The Běimèng Suǒyán (北夢瑣言) says:
"Huáng Cháo (黃巢) entered Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
captured Lǐ Biāo (李佋),
and took him with the army to Jīngzhōu (荊州),
ordering Biāo (佋) to draft a memorial expressing his intentions.
Biāo (佋) said:
'My kin fill the court,
and I have for generations received national grace.
My arm may be severed,
but I will ultimately not draft the memorial.'
He was killed at Jiāngjīn (江津)."
Today, the Shílù (實錄) is followed.
17 In winter,
tenth month,
Gāo Pián (高駢), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Zhènhǎi (鎮海), was made Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Huáinán (淮南),
and also appointed Salt and Iron Transport Commissioner.
Zhōu Bǎo (周寶), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Jīngyuán (涇原), was made Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Zhènhǎi (鎮海),
which laid the groundwork for the future conflict between Pián (駢) and Bǎo (寶).
Bǎo (寶) was from Píngzhōu (平州).
18 While Huáng Cháo (黃巢) was in Lǐngnán (嶺南),
three or four tenths of his soldiers died from malaria and epidemics.
His followers advised him to return north to achieve great things.
Cháo (巢) agreed.
From Guìzhōu (桂州), he constructed dozens of large rafts
and, taking advantage of the torrential waters,
descended the Xiāngjiāng (湘江),
passing through Héngzhōu (衡州) and Yǒngzhōu (永州).
On the Guǐwèi (癸未) day,
he arrived beneath the city walls of Tánzhōu (潭州).
Lǐ Xì (李係) fortified the city and dared not sally forth to battle.
Cháo (巢) urgently attacked,
and within a day,
captured it.
Xì (係) fled to Lángzhōu (朗州).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) says: From Tánzhōu (潭州) to Lángzhōu (朗州) is over three hundred eighty lǐ.
Floating corpses blocked the river as they drifted downstream.
Shàng Ràng (尚讓), capitalizing on the victory, advanced to besiege Jiānglíng (江陵),
with a host numbering five hundred thousand.
At that time, troops from various circuits had not yet gathered,
and the Jiānglíng (江陵) garrison numbered less than ten thousand.
Wáng Duó (王鐸) left his general Liú Hànróng (劉漢宏) to defend Jiānglíng (江陵)
and himself led his troops towards Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) says: From Jiānglíng (江陵) to Xiāngyáng (襄陽) is four hundred forty lǐ.
Shuài (帥)
is read as lǜ.
Qù (趣)
is pronounced qī yù.
After Duó (鐸) left,
Hànróng (漢宏) heavily plundered Jiānglíng (江陵).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Jiùjì (舊紀) says:
"In the second month of Guǎngmíng (廣明) first year,
Cháo (巢) captured Tánzhōu (潭zhou),
Wáng Duó (王鐸) abandoned Jiānglíng (江陵)
and fled to Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
and Hànróng (漢宏) heavily plundered."
The Shílù (實錄) says:
"In the intercalary month,
Húnán (湖南) reported: Huáng Cháo's (黃巢) rebel forces descended from Héngzhōu (衡州) and Yǒngzhōu (永州),
and on the twenty-seventh day of the tenth month, captured Tánzhōu (潭州)."
The Xīncháo Chuán (新巢傳) says:
"In the early Guǎngmíng (廣明) era,
the rebels from Lǐngnán (嶺南) attacked the various commanderies of Húnán (湖南),
attacked Tánzhōu (潭zhou)
and captured it."
The Jiùcháo Chuán (舊巢傳) says:
"Cháo (巢) wished to occupy the lands of Nánhǎi (南海)
and await an imperial decree there.
In that year,
from spring to summer,
his forces suffered a great epidemic,
with thirteen or fourteen tenths dying.
The multitude urged him to return north to secure greater advantages,
and Cháo (巢) had no choice.
In the first year of Guǎngmíng (廣明), he crossed the Five Ridges to the north,
invading Hú, Xiāng, Jiāng, and Zhè."
According to this, the Jiùjì (舊紀) and Jiùchuán (舊傳) both state that Wáng Duó (王鐸) was defeated in the first year of Guǎngmíng (廣明).
Today, the month and day follow the Shílù (實錄),
and the events follow the old history.
Furthermore, according to the Jiùjì (舊紀) and Jiùchuán (舊傳),
Liú Hànróng (劉漢宏) was originally a general under Wáng Duó (王鐸).
When Duó (鐸) left, Hànróng (漢宏) remained in Jiānglíng (江陵) and heavily plundered,
thus becoming a bandit.
The Shílù (實錄) uses this,
but adds the words
"earlier"
beneath Duó (鐸) fleeing to Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
If Duó (鐸) was in Jiānglíng (江陵),
and Hànróng (漢róng) was at that time a minor bandit,
how could he enter his city and heavily plunder?
Even if Hànróng (漢róng) had previously raided and plundered Jiānglíng (江陵),
it would be completely unrelated to Huáng Cháo's (黃巢) affairs.
Why then say
"more than half a month later,
the rebel forces then occupied the city"?
The Wúyuè Bèishǐ (吳越備史) says:
"Hànróng (漢宏) was originally a minor official in Yǎnzhōu (兗州),
who led the troops of his prefecture to resist the Huáng Cháo (黃巢) rebels,
then killed his general,
plundered supplies and rebelled.
Later,崔 Kǎi (崔鍇), the former Cìshǐ (刺史) of Háozhōu (濠州), was ordered to persuade him to surrender."
According to this,
Hànróng (漢宏) was originally a minor bandit.
The Xīnchuán (新傳) uses this,
but says that Duó (鐸) persuaded him to surrender.
Perhaps Hànróng (漢宏) was originally a minor bandit,
and in the interim surrendered to Duó (鐸) and became a subordinate general.
When Duó (鐸) left Jiānglíng (江陵),
Hànróng (漢宏) again heavily plundered and became a bandit,
and later surrendered to Cuī Kǎi (崔鍇),
thus becoming a Tang subject.
The gentry and common people fled and hid in the valleys.
There was heavy snow,
and frozen corpses filled the fields.
More than ten days later,
the rebels arrived.
Hànróng (漢宏) was from Yǎnzhōu (兗州).
He led his troops north to become a minor bandit.
19 In the intercalary month,
on the Dīnghài (丁亥) day, the first day of the month,
Lǐ Wèi (李蔚), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hédōng (河東), fell ill.
Lǐ Shào (李卲), the Gōngjūn Fùshǐ (供軍副使), was temporarily appointed Guānchá Liúhòu (觀察留後),
and Lǐ Fènggāo (李奉皋), the Jiānjūn (監軍), was temporarily appointed Bīngmǎ Liúhòu (兵馬留後).
On the Jǐchǒu (己丑) day,
Wèi (蔚) died.
Zhāng Kǎi (張鍇) and Guō Fú (郭昢), the Dū Yúhòu (都虞候), submitted a petition to remove Shào (卲).
Zhuàng (狀) means a memorial.
Kǎi (鍇) and Fú (昢) then submitted a memorial to dismiss Lǐ Shào (李卲) and promote Dīng Qiú (丁球).
Chù (絀) is pronounced chǒu lǜ.
7. On the *bǐngshēn* day
Zhèng Tián was appointed acting co-regent (*tóng píngzhāngshì*).
8. Gāo Pián, Military Commissioner (*jiédùshǐ*) of Huáinán, was appointed Overall Commander of the Eastern Front (*dōngmiàn dūtǒng*).
Zhèng Cóngzhuǎng, Military Commissioner of Hédōng, was additionally appointed Minister Attendant (*shìzhōng*)
and retained his position as Commander of the Imperial Camp for Pacification and Investigation (*xíngyíng zhāotǎoshǐ*).
Chén Jǐngsī, supervising general of Dáiběi,
in the *Kǎoyì* (Textual Variations) states: The *Shílù* (Veritable Records) writes
"Jǐngsī" (景斯),
but I follow Xuē Jūzhèng’s *Wǔdàishǐ* (History of the Five Dynasties).
When he arrived at Jiàngzhōu,
he was about to cross the Hé river.
Qú Zhēn, Prefect (*cìshǐ*) of Jiàngzhōu,
who was also a Shātuó,
said to Jǐngsī:
"The rebel forces are currently strong,
it is not advisable to advance lightly.
It would be better to return to Dáiběi and recruit soldiers."
So he and Jǐngsī both returned to Yànmén.
9. Yáng Fùguāng, Palace Eunuch Director (*shūmìshǐ*), was appointed Supervisor of the Imperial Camp for the Southwestern Front (*jīngxīnánmiàn xíngyíng dūjiān*).
10. Huáng Cháo appointed Zhū Wēn as Overall Commander of the Imperial Camp for the Southeastern Front (*dōngnánmiàn xíngyíng dōuyúhòu*),
leading troops to attack Dèngzhōu.
In the third month,
on the *xīnhài* day,
Dèngzhōu fell.
Prefect Zhào Jiè was captured.
The rebels then garrisoned Dèngzhōu to block Jīng and Xiāng.
*Jiǔyùzhì* (Records of the Nine Regions): Dèngzhōu is 180 *lǐ* south of Xiāngzhōu;
Xiāngzhōu is 457 *lǐ* south of Jīngzhōu.
11. On the *rénzǐ* day,
Chén Jìngxuān was appointed acting co-regent (*tóng píngzhāngshì*).
On the *jiǎyín* day,
Jìngxuān memorialized to dispatch Lǐ Chuí, commander of the Left Yellow Head Army (*zuǒ huángtóujūnshǐ*), to lead troops to attack Huáng Cháo.
The Xīchuān Yellow Head Army
was established by Cuī Ānqián.
This matter first appeared in the previous volume, Qiánfú Year 6.
Chuí (鋋),
pronounced *shí yán fān*.
12. On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Zhèng Tián was appointed Overall Commander of the Imperial Camps for the Four Fronts of the Capital (*jīngchéng sìmiàn zhūjūn xíngyíng dūtǒng*).
An imperial edict was bestowed upon Tián:
"All barbarian and Han generals and soldiers who distinguish themselves by meritorious service in facing difficulties
shall be appointed officials by imperial rescript."
Tián memorialized to appoint Chéng Zōngchǔ, Military Commissioner of Jīngyuán, as Deputy Overall Commander (*fùdūtǒng*),
and Táng Hóngfū, former Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng, as Army Adjutant (*xíngjūn sīmǎ*).
Huáng Cháo dispatched his generals Shàng Ràng and Wáng Bō, leading a force of 50,000, to raid Fèngxiáng.
"Wáng Bō" (王播),
the *Xīnshū* (New Tang History) writes
"Wáng Fán" (王璠).
Tián himself led several thousand soldiers,
displaying many banners and flags,
sparsely arrayed on a high ridge.
The rebels, taking Tián for a mere scholar,
scorned him and advanced with drums beating,
without proper formation.
Tián's ambush was sprung,
and the rebels were thoroughly defeated at Lóngwěi Pí.
Both the Old and New Tang Histories write
"Lóngwěi Pō" (龍尾坡),
only the Old Annals write
Qíshān County, Fèngxiáng Prefecture,
in early Táng, was administered from Zhāngbǎo.
In Wǔdé Year 7, its administration was moved to Lóngwěi City,
which was northeast of the old city of Píngyáng.
Corpses lay for dozens of *lǐ*.
13. Someone wrote a poem on the gate of the Secretariat (*shàngshūshěng*) to mock the rebels.
Shàng Ràng was enraged,
and all officials in the Secretariat and gate guards
had their eyes gouged out and were hung upside down.
He extensively searched the city for anyone who could compose poetry,
and killed them all.
Those who were literate were given menial tasks.
In total, more than three thousand people were killed.
14. Qú Zhēn and Lǐ Yǒujīn arrived at Dàizhōu
and recruited soldiers for more than ten days,
obtaining 30,000 men.
All were miscellaneous barbarians from the north
and were encamped west of Guō.
This refers to west of Guō County, Dàizhōu.
Guō (崞),
pronounced *guō*.
Zhēn and Yǒujīn could not control them.
Yǒujīn then persuaded Chén Jǐngsī, saying:
"Although we now have tens of thousands of troops,
if there is no general of prestige and trustworthiness to command them,
there will ultimately be no success.
My brother, Sītú and his son,
surpass others in courage and strategy,
and are revered by the masses.
If the General-in-Chief (*piàojì*) sincerely memorializes the Son of Heaven to pardon their crimes
and summon them as commanders,
(Lǐ Guóchāng was appointed Inspecting Sītú for his merit in pacifying Páng Xūn.)
The General-in-Chief (*piàojì*)
was the highest rank for military officers in the Táng system.
Since Gāo Lìshì,
many eunuchs held the rank of General-in-Chief (*piàojì*),
hence Jǐngsī is referred to by this title.
The mad rebels are not worth pacifying!"
Jǐngsī thought this was correct
and sent an envoy to the temporary court to report it.
An edict was issued as requested.
Yǒujīn took 500 cavalry, carrying the imperial edict, to Dádá to welcome him.
(Lǐ Kèyòng had entered Dádá;
see previous volume, Guǎngmíng Year 1.)
The *Kǎoyì* (Textual Variations) states: The *Shílù* (Veritable Records):
"Chén Jǐngsī carried the imperial edict into Dádá to summon Lǐ Kèyòng.
The army was encamped in Yùzhōu.
Kèyòng then extensively plundered the military garrisons north of Yànmén."
Xuē Jūzhèng’s *Wǔdàishǐ* (History of the Five Dynasties):
"Before this,
Jǐngsī and Lǐ Yǒujīn mobilized 5,000 cavalry from the Shātuó tribes to proceed south to the capital.
Yǒujīn was the cousin of the Martial Emperor.
In the second month of Zhōnghé Year 1,
Yǒujīn's army arrived at Jiàngzhōu,
about to cross the river.
Prefect Qú Zhēn said to Jǐngsī: 'The Cháo rebels are currently strong;
it would be better to return to Dáiběi first
and then gradually consider the advantages and disadvantages.'
In the fourth month,
Yǒujīn's army returned to Yànmén.
Qú Zhēn arrived at Dàizhōu.
Within half a month,
he recruited 30,000 soldiers
and encamped them west of Guō County.
These troops were all from the five northern tribes,
unfamiliar with military regulations.
Qú Zhēn and Lǐ Yǒujīn could not control them.
Yǒujīn said to Jǐngsī the aforementioned,
and Jǐngsī agreed.
He promptly memorialized the temporary court.
The Son of Heaven then appointed the Martial Emperor as Military Commissioner of Yànmén,
and further ordered him to suppress the rebels with his own army.
Lǐ Yǒujīn dispatched 500 cavalry with the imperial edict to summon the Martial Emperor from Dádá.
The Martial Emperor immediately led 10,000 men from the Dádá tribes towards Yànmén."
According to this, Jǐngsī requested a pardon for Guóchāng and his son,
but only Kèyòng arrived.
This is probably because Guóchāng was already old,
and only Kèyòng was sent.
In this year,
Kèyòng only attacked and plundered Tàiyuán,
and also captured Xīn and Dài prefectures.
In the twelfth month of the following year,
he was initially appointed Military Commissioner of Yànmén, following his previous role as Acting Military Commissioner (*liúhòu*) of Xīn and Dài.
It is probable that at this point, only his crimes were pardoned,
and he was reinstated as Defense Commissioner (*fángyùshǐ*) of Dàtóng.
After capturing Xīn and Dài,
he proclaimed himself Acting Military Commissioner (*liúhòu*).
The imperial court summoned him again,
and only then was he appointed Military Commissioner of Yànmén.
The *Xuē Shǐ* (History by Xue) is mistaken.
The *Xīnbǐao* (New Table) states:
"In Zhōnghé Year 2,
Xīn and Dài Prefectures of Hédōng were made subordinate to the Military Commissioner of Yànmén.
The Dàtóng Military Commission was changed to the Yànmén Military Commission,
with its seat in Dàizhōu."
This is the proof.
15. The officials who followed the imperial carriage
gradually gathered in Chéngdū.
Nearly 200 officials from the Northern and Southern Bureaus attended court.
Tributes from various circuits and the Four Barbarians were ceaseless.
The treasuries of Shǔzhōng were full,
no different from the capital.
Rewards were abundant,
and soldiers were joyful.
16. Huáng Cháo captured Wáng Huī
and forced him into office.
Huī feigned muteness
and refused.
More than a month later,
he escaped to Hézhōng
and secretly sent a silk memorial via a hidden path to the temporary court.
Jiān (間),
pronounced *gǔ xiàn fān*.
17. Zhūgě Shuǎng, former Military Commissioner of Xiàsuí,
again presented a memorial from Héyáng, submitting himself.
Last year, when Huáng Cháo entered the pass, Zhūgě Shuǎng surrendered to him.
18 Yòuzhōu Cìshǐ Tuòbá Sīgōng
in the sixteenth year of Kāiyuán,
established Yòuzhōu with the remaining people of the Six Hú Prefectures.
In the first year of Qiányuán,
he administered the Jīnglüè Army,
later moving its seat to Chángzé County.
Chángzé
was the land of Sānfēng County, Shuòfāng Commandery, in the Hàn dynasty.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: Ōuyáng Xiū's *Wǔdài Shǐ* writes
"Tuòbá Sījìng,"
suggesting that the *Xuē Shǐ* avoided a national taboo.
However, the *Jiù Tángshū* and *Shílù* both write
"Sīgōng."
The *Shílù* states:
"In the ninth month of the second year of Tiānfù,
Lǐ Sījìng, the Jiedushi of the Wǔdìng Army, surrendered his city to Wáng Jiàn.
Sījìng's original surname was Tuòbá;
he was the younger brother of Sīgōng, the Jiedushi of Fūxià, and Sīxiào, the Jiedushi of Bǎodà.
Sīxiào retired,
appointing Sījìng as acting Jiedushi of Bǎodà,
who then ascended to full Jiedushi,
and later moved to the Wǔdìng Army."
The *Xīn Tángshū Dangxiàng Zhuàn* says:
"Sīgōng was the Jiedushi of Dìngnán;
after his death,
his brother Sījiàn succeeded him as Jiedushi.
Sīxiào was the Jiedushi of Bǎodà;
being old,
he recommended his brother Sījìng as acting Jiedushi of Bǎodà,
who soon became full Jiedushi."
Therefore, Sīgōng and Sījìng were two different people.
Sījìng later joined Lǐ Màozhēn,
and perhaps was granted the imperial surname,
thus changing his surname to Lǐ.
Xiū conflated them into one person,
which is a mistake.
The *Xīn Shū* states: The Dǎngxiàng formed tribes based on their surnames,
and the Tuòbá clan was the strongest.
They formed an alliance to suppress the rebels.
Qí Kèjiǎn, the commander of Fèngtīan Garrison, sent an envoy to Zhèng Tián to offer his services.
On the day *Jiǎzǐ*,
Tián issued a proclamation to all the princely commanders under heaven,
calling for them to unite their forces to suppress the rebels.
At that time, the Son of Heaven was in Shǔ,
and imperial decrees could not get through.
The world believed the imperial court could not recover,
but upon receiving Tián's proclamation,
they vied to dispatch troops in response.
The rebels, afraid,
dared not again spy on the area west of the capital.
19 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the first day *Wùyín*,
Wáng Duó was given the additional title of Shìzhōng.
20 Tuòbá Sīgōng was temporarily appointed acting Jiedushi of Xiàsuí.
This laid the foundation for the Tuòbá clan's rise to power and their eventual control over Xīxià.
21 Huáng Cháo appointed his general Wáng Méi as Jiedushi of Bīnnìng.
Zhū Méi, the commander of Tōngsài Garrison in Bīnzhōu, raised an army to execute him,
yielding the position of Jiedushi to another general, Lǐ Chónggǔ,
and personally led troops to attack Cháo.
At this time,
Táng Hóngfū was encamped north of the Wèi River,
Wáng Chóngróng was encamped at Shāyuàn,
Wáng Chǔcún was encamped at Wèiqiáo,
Tuòbá Sīgōng was encamped at Wǔgōng,
and Zhèng Tián was encamped at Zhōuzhì.
Hóngfū, emboldened by the victory at Lóngwěi,
advanced close to Cháng'ān.
On the day *Rénwǔ*,
Huáng Cháo led his troops eastward.
Chéng Zōngchǔ was the first to enter through Yánqiū Gate;
there was a gate in the imperial garden city of Cháng'ān,
its western exit was called Yánqiū Gate.
Chǔcún led five thousand elite soldiers into the city at night.
The townspeople rejoiced,
cheering and rushing out to welcome the government troops,
some pelting the rebels with瓦礫 (tiles and rubble),
others collecting arrows to supply the government troops.
Zōngchǔ and others, fearing that the various generals would share their merit,
did not report to Fèngxiáng or Fūxià.
They plundered gold, silk, and concubines.
Chǔcún ordered his soldiers to tie white cloth as a distinguishing mark;
some young men in the market districts stole this mark to rob people.
The rebels camped in the open on Bàngshàng,
'camping in the open' means spending the night without shelter.
And as the various armies did not follow up,
they led their troops back to attack them,
entering through various gates,
fighting a great battle in the midst of Cháng'ān.
Zōngchǔ and Hóngfū died.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: The *Jiù Jì*, *Zhuàn*, and *Xīn Zhuàn* all state that Hóngfū was defeated in the second month of the second year.
The *Jīng Tīng Lù*, *Táng Nián Bǔ Lù*, *Xīn Jì*, and *Shílù* all place it in the fourth month of this year.
The *Xīn Jì* is particularly detailed about the date,
and we follow it now.
This was a devastating defeat,
with eight or nine out of ten dying.
Chǔcún gathered the remaining troops and returned to his camp.
On the day *Dīnghài*,
Cháo re-entered Cháng'ān.
Angered by the people's assistance to the government troops,
he unleashed his soldiers to slaughter them,
so that blood flowed like rivers,
which was called 'washing the city'.
Thereupon, all the government armies retreated,
and the rebel's power grew even stronger.
Wáng Pǔ, the Tongzhou Cìshǐ appointed by the rebels, Qiáo Qiān, the Huazhou Cìshǐ, and Sòng Yán, the Shangzhou Cìshǐ, hearing that Cháo had abandoned Cháng'ān,
all led their troops to flee to Dèngzhōu.
Zhū Wēn executed Pǔ and Qiān,
released Yán,
and sent him back to Shāngzhōu.
22 On the day *Gēngyín*,
Tuòbá Sīgōng and Lǐ Xiàochāng fought the rebels at Tǔ
qiáo,
but were unsuccessful.
23 An imperial edict appointed Wáng Chóngróng, acting Jiedushi of Hézhōng, as full Jiedushi.
24 The rebel masses bestowed upon Huáng Cháo the honorific title of Chéngtiān Yìngyùn Qǐshèng Ruìwén Xuānwǔ Huángdì.
25 A pair of pheasants gathered in the mansion of Guǎnglín Prefecture.
Soothsayers interpreted this as an omen that wild birds gathering indicated
that the city would soon be empty.
Gāo Pián was displeased by this,
and so issued a proclamation to the four directions,
claiming he would personally lead an expedition to suppress Huáng Cháo,
dispatching all 80,000 troops from within his jurisdiction
and 2,000 ships,
with splendid flags, armor, and weapons.
In the fifth month,
on the day *Yǐ*
wèi,
he moved his camp to Dōngtáng.
Dōngtáng
is east of the current Yángzhōu city,
meaning the embankment from Wāntóu to Yílíng today.
*Sōu*
is pronounced Sū Zāo fān.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: The *Yāoluàn Zhì* says:
"From the twelfth day of the fifth month, he moved to Dōngtáng,
until the sixth day of the ninth month, when he returned to his residence,
over ninety days,
to ward off the omen of the pheasant's crow."
However, from the twelfth day of the fifth month to the sixth day of the ninth month is
one hundred and sixty-three days,
not over ninety days.
We now follow the *Jiù Zhuàn*.
Pián used strong winds and waves as an excuse,
or claimed the timing was unfavorable,
and ultimately did not set out.
26 Lǐ Kèyòng sent a dispatch to Hédōng,
stating that he had received an imperial edict to lead 50,000 troops to suppress Huáng Cháo,
ordering them to prepare provisions and relays (*dùn dì*).
'Dùn' refers to setting up food and drink along the road for the army,
'dì' refers to setting up postal stations.
Kèyòng encamped east of the Fén River.
Cóngzhòng rewarded and comforted him,
supplying his provisions and fodder,
but he did not set out for several days.
Kèyòng personally came to the city wall and shouted loudly,
asking to meet Cóngzhòng.
Cóngzhòng ascended the wall and saluted him.
On the day *Guǐhài*,
he again requested to dispatch troops and for rewards and provisions.
Cóngzhòng presented him with a thousand strings of cash and a thousand *hú* of rice.
On the day *Jiǎzǐ*,
Kèyòng unleashed his Shātuó troops to plunder the residents,
causing great alarm in the city.
Cóngzhòng sought help from Qìbí Zhāng, the Jiedushi of Zhènwǔ.
Zhāng led his Tujue and Tuyuhun troops to relieve him,
destroying two Shātuó camps.
Kèyòng pursued and fought to the south of Jìnyáng city.
Zhāng led his troops into the city,
and the Shātuó plundered Yángqǔ and Yúcì before returning.
27 When Huáng Cháo
captured Cháng'ān, Zhōngwǔ Military Governor Zhōu Jí surrendered to him.
Last year, in the eleventh month, Zhōu Jí was appointed Zhōngwǔ Military Governor.
In the twelfth month, Huáng Cháo captured Cháng'ān.
[Emperor Xīzōng] urgently summoned Surveillance Commissioner Yáng Fùguāng.
Previously, Yáng Fùguāng had been made Zhōngwǔ Surveillance Commissioner,
stationed in Dèngzhōu,
to block the bandits' right flank.
After Huáng Cháo had taken Cháng'ān,
he dispatched Zhū Wēn to garrison Dèngzhōu.
Yáng Fùguāng then went to Xǔzhōu to join Zhōu Jí.
Thus, he was summoned for a night banquet.
"Lord Zhōu is a servant of the bandit,
which will be disadvantageous to the Internal Attendant.
You should not go."
In the Táng dynasty, the Head of the Bureau of Internal Attendants was the Internal Attendant Director;
the Internal Attendant was the Deputy.
Therefore, the attendants referred to Yáng Fùguāng by this title.
"Things have come to this;
it would be unrighteous to seek to save myself."
He then went to him.
As the wine flowed freely,
Zhōu Jí spoke of the imperial court.
Yáng Fùguāng wept,
and after a long while,
said:
"What moves a man is grace and righteousness!
You rose from a commoner to a ducal lord.
How can you abandon an eighteen-generation Son of Heaven and serve a bandit?!"
From Gāozǔ to Xīzōng, there were eighteen generations.
"I alone cannot resist the bandit.
Therefore, I feign submission but plot against him in my heart.
Today I summoned you
precisely for this reason."
Thereupon, they poured wine as an oath.
Shǐ Zhào says: To drip wine.
Yáng Fùguāng dispatched his adopted son Shǒu Liàng to kill the bandit envoy at the post station.
At that time, Qín Zōngquán occupied Càizhōu
and did not obey Zhōu Jí's command.
Yáng Fùguāng led three thousand Zhōngwǔ troops to Càizhōu
and persuaded Qín Zōngquán to jointly raise troops to attack Huáng Cháo.
Qín Zōngquán dispatched his general Wáng Shú with three thousand troops to follow Yáng Fùguāng to attack Dèngzhōu,
but he lingered and did not advance.
Yáng Fùguāng executed him
and absorbed his army,
dividing eight thousand Zhōngwǔ men into eight divisions.
He dispatched the staff generals Lù Yànhóng, Jìn Huī, Wáng Jiàn, Hán Jiàn, Zhāng Zào, Lǐ Shītài, Páng Cóng, and one other to command them.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Liú Shù's *Shíguó Jìnián* states that below "eight divisions,"
there are only seven names, including Wáng Jiàn.
This is because other books do not record them.
Wáng Jiàn starts here.
[Wáng Jiàn was from] Wǔyáng;
Hán Jiàn
was from Chángshè;
Yànhóng, Huī, Zào, and Shītài
were all from Xǔzhōu.
Yáng Fùguāng led the eight divisions to fight Zhū Wēn,
defeated him,
and then captured Dèngzhōu.
He pursued the fleeing enemy to Lánqiáo and then returned.
Lánqiáo
is south of Lántián Pass.
The pronunciation of "還"
is "xuán,"
and also as written.
28 Zhāoyì Military Governor Gāo Xún joined Wáng Chóngróng in attacking Huázhōu
and captured it.
29 In the sixth month,
on the day *wùxū*,
Zhèng Tián was appointed Minister of Works concurrently Palace Gate Affairs Attendant-in-Waiting and Chancellor,
retaining his position as Commander-in-Chief.
30 Lǐ Kèyòng encountered heavy rain
and led his troops north, returning.
He seized Xīnzhōu and Dàizhōu
and remained in Dàizhōu.
The *Kǎoyì* says: *Tángmò Jiànwénlù* states:
"On the thirtieth day of the sixth month,
the Shātuó army turned back
and retook Xīnzhōu and Dàizhōu."
*Tàizǔ Jìniánlù* states:
"Encountering heavy rain,
on the twenty-third day of the sixth month,
the army returned to Yànmén."
Xuē Jūzhèng's *Wǔdài Shǐ* agrees with *Jìniánlù*.
Note that Xīnzhōu and Dàizhōu originally belonged to Hédōng,
and were only transferred to Yànmén in the second year of Zhōnghé.
We now follow *Jiànwénlù* and *Shílù*.
31 Bīnníng Military Deputy Commander Zhū Méi stationed troops at Xīngpíng.
Xīngpíng County
is eighty-five *lǐ* west of Cháng'ān.
Yú Jìng says: Zhōu Zhàngqiū is
today's Xīngpíng.
He besieged Xīngpíng.
Zhū Méi retreated to Fèngtiān and Lóngwěi Pí.
32 Xīchuān Yellow Head Army Commander Lǐ Chéng led ten thousand men,
and Gǒng Xián led five thousand men.
Gǒng
is a surname.
Gǒng Jiǎngōng was a minister in Zhōu,
and Gǒng Shuò was a grandee in Jìn.
They formed two camps
and fought Huáng Cháo,
winning repeatedly.
Chén Jìngxuān dispatched Shenjī Camp Commander Gāo Rénhòu with two thousand men to reinforce them.
The Shenjī Camp
was also established by Cuī Ānqián;
the details are in the previous volume, Qiánfú sixth year.
33 In autumn,
seventh month,
on the day *dīngsì*,
the reign era was changed,
and a general amnesty was declared.
The reign era was changed to Zhōnghé.
34 On the day *gēngshēn*,
Wéi Zhāodù, Hanlin Academician Bearer of Edicts and Vice Minister of War, was made Chancellor.
35 Lùn Ān returned from Bǎijǐng Dǎn.
Zhèng Cóngdǎng, without even removing his boots,
executed him
and exterminated his clan.
*Xuē*
is the same as *xuē* (boot).
The *Kǎoyì* says: *Tángmò Jiànwénlù* states:
"On the thirtieth day of the sixth month,
the Shātuó retook Xīnzhōu and Dàizhōu.
The Provincial Administrator dispatched Training Commissioner Lùn Ān, Army Commander Wáng Chán, Gāo Biàn, and the Uighur and Tubò armies to set up camp at Bǎijǐng to defend.
In that month,
Lùn Ān and others struck camp
and returned to the prefecture."
Note that "in that month"
means the thirtieth day.
Within a single day,
it is impossible for so many things to happen;
it must be incorrect.
It also says:
"By the fourteenth day of the seventh month,
the Chancellor arranged a meal for the generals and others.
At the table, he seized Lùn Ān,
who had not removed his boots,
had him dealt with in the polo ground,
and exterminated his family.
He also dispatched Patrol Commander Wēn Hànchén with troops to set up camp at Bǎijǐng as before.
In that month,
Minister Qìbì led his troops back to Zhènwǔ."
We now follow this.
Qìbì Zhāng led troops back to Zhènwǔ.
36 Initially,
when the imperial carriage arrived in Chéngdū,
the Shǔ army was awarded three *mín* of cash per person.
Tián Lìngzī, as the Commander and Administrator of the Imperial Travelling Palace,
whenever gold and silk were contributed from the four quarters,
he would distribute them to the armies accompanying the emperor without a single day's pause,
but the Shǔ army received nothing.
The Shǔ army expressed quite a few complaints.
On the day *bǐngyín*,
Lìngzī hosted a banquet for the local and guest *dōutóu*s.
The local army refers to the Shǔ army.
The Shǔ army.
The guest army refers to the armies accompanying the emperor.
The armies accompanying the emperor.
In the middle period of the Táng dynasty,
the supreme commander of all armies was called a *dōutóu*.
By later times,
a unit of an army was called a *dū*,
and its commander was called a *dōutóu*.
He then bestowed gifts,
and all the *dōutóu*s bowed and accepted.
However, Guō Qí, the Yellow-Head Army Commander of Xīchuān, alone refused to accept,
stood up, and said:
"The generals receive abundant stipends and provisions every month,
more than enough,
and constantly think about how difficult it is to repay such kindness;
how could they dare to be insatiable!
Considering that the Shǔ army guards the palace alongside the other armies,
yet the rewards and bounties are vastly different,
there is considerable dissatisfaction,
and I fear that a change might occur one day.
I wish that the *jūnrong* would reduce the gifts to the generals and share them equally with the Shǔ army,
so that locals and guests are treated alike;
then everyone, high and low, would be fortunate!"
Lìngzī remained silent for a while,
then said:
*Jiān*
(pronounced as written).
"What merits have you ever had?"
Qí replied:
"I grew up in Shāndōng,
serving in expeditions and garrisons on the frontiers.
I fought seventeen battles against the Dǎngxiàng and
over ten battles against the Qìdān,
my body is covered in sword wounds;
I also participated in the expedition against the Tǔyùhún,
where my ribs were injured and my intestines protruded,
but I sewed them up with a thread and returned to battle."
Lìngzī then personally poured wine from a separate flask to give to Qí.
Qí knew it was poisoned,
but having no choice,
he bowed twice and drank it;
upon returning,
he killed a maidservant,
sucked her blood to neutralize the poison,
and vomited several *shēng* of black liquid.
He then led his unit in a rebellion.
On the day *dīngmǎo*,
