they plundered and burned the markets.
Lìngzī escorted the Son of Heaven to the eastern city,
closed the gates, ascended the tower,
and ordered all armies to attack them.
Qí led his troops back to their camp.
Chén Jìngxuān ordered his *dōuyáyá*, Ān Jīnshān, to lead troops to attack them.
Qí broke through the encirclement at night and escaped,
fleeing to Guǎngdū.
The Suí dynasty renamed Guǎngdū County to Shuāngliú County.
In the second year of Lóngshuò of the Táng dynasty, Guǎngdū County was again separated from Shuāngliú and established,
subordinate to Chéngdū Prefecture.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: it is forty-five *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
Only one *tīnglì* followed him to rest by the river bank.
Qí said to the *tīnglì*:
"Duke Chén knows I am not guilty;
however, the military administration is alarmed and disturbed,
and cannot be left unsettled.
You have served me faithfully from beginning to end,
and now I have a way to repay you.
You take my seal and sword and go to Duke Chén, saying: 'Guō Qí fled across the river,
I struck him with my sword,
and he fell into the water,
his corpse drifting downstream;
I obtained his seal and sword to present.'
Duke Chén will certainly believe your words
and display the seal and sword in the market to reassure the populace.
You will receive a generous reward,
and my family will also be safe and sound.
From here, I will go to Guǎnglíng
to return to Duke Gāo."
He meant he wanted to flee to Yángzhōu to join Gāo Pián.
"You can secretly tell my family this."
He then took off his seal and sword, handed them to him, and escaped.
The *tīnglì* presented them to Jìngxuān,
who indeed spared Qí's family.
The emperor daily and nightly associated exclusively with the eunuchs,
discussing affairs of the realm,
and treated external officials with extreme aloofness.
On the day *gēngwǔ*,
the Left Reminder Mèng Zhāotú submitted a memorial,
stating:
"In times of peace and order,
all, near and far, should be of one mind;
in times of great difficulty,
the court and the provinces should especially be united.
Last winter, when the imperial carriage travelled west,
it did not inform the Southern Bureau,
which led to the slaughter of the chancellors, *púyè*, and others below,
referring to Dòulú Zhuàn, Cuī Hàng, Yú Cóng, and the like.
Furthermore, those court officials who have arrived now
have all braved death and hardships,
faithfully serving their sovereign from afar.
It is right that from now on we should share prosperity and adversity equally.
I humbly observed that the Yellow-Head Army rebelled the night before last,
and Your Majesty alone, with Lìngzī, Jìngxuān, and other inner officials, closed the city gates and ascended the tower,
neither summoning Wáng Duó and others nor bringing court officials into the city;
the next day,
Your Majesty did not meet with the chancellors,
nor did you express comfort to the court officials.
'The next day' means 'tomorrow.'
Tomorrow.
To this day, we do not know if Your Sacred Self is well,
let alone those who are distant!
If Your Majesty's humble subjects do not care for their sovereign,
their crime is certainly punishable by death;
but if Your Majesty does not care for your humble subjects,
where is the righteousness in that!
The realm
is the realm of Gāozǔ and Tàizōng,
not the realm of the Northern Bureau;
the Son of Heaven
is the Son of Heaven of the Four Seas and Nine Provinces,
not the Son of Heaven of the Northern Bureau.
The Northern Bureau may not be entirely trustworthy,
and the Southern Bureau may not be entirely useless.
How can the Son of Heaven and the chancellors be utterly unrelated,
and all court officials be like strangers?
If this continues,
I fear that the time of recovery
will still burden Your Sacred Thoughts,
and those who hold positions without merit
will enjoy peace and comfort.
I have been favored with honor and glory,
and my duty is to offer benefit.
Although it is pointless to admonish what is done,
what is yet to come can be pursued."
Both phrases are from the *Lúnyǔ*.
Lìngzī concealed it and did not present it.
On the day *xīnwèi*,
he forged an imperial edict to demote Zhāotú to Supervisor of Household Registers for Jiāzhōu,
and sent men to drown him in the Màyí Ford.
Màyí Mountain
is seven *lǐ* east of Méishān in Méizhōu.
The mountain is shaped like the chin of a toad (*má*),
hence its name.
The mountain overlooks a river ford,
and today there is a shrine for Reminder Mèng.
*Má*
(pronounced *mójiā fān*).
When an emperor kills an admonishing minister,
his country is bound to perish.
For a eunuch to presumptuously kill an admonishing minister,
has never happened since ancient times.
This is not only harmful to your country,
but also truly ill-fated for your own person.
Therefore, before the Táng dynasty fell, Lìngzī himself perished first.
*Sāi*
(pronounced *xīzé fān*).
37 Lǐ Xiàochāng, the Military Commissioner of Fūyán, and Tuòbá Sīgōng, the Acting Military Commissioner of Xiàzhōu, were stationed at Dōngwèiqiáo.
Huáng Cháo sent Zhū Wēn to resist them.
Wáng Chǔcún, the Military Commissioner of Yìwǔ, was appointed Commander of the Expeditionary Forces for the Southeast,
and Zhū Méi, the Deputy Military Commissioner of Bīnnìng, was appointed Military Commissioner.
38 August.
On the night of *jǐchǒu*,
stars intersected like weaving threads,
some as large as cups or bowls,
and only stopped on the day *dīngyǒu*.
39 Regarding the military governor of Wǔníng, Zhī Xiáng,
according to the table of border regions in the New Book of Tang,
in the eleventh year of Xiántōng of Yìzōng's reign,
the military governorship of Xúzhōu was re-established,
and given the title Gǎnhuà Army.
From this point until Tiānfù,
the old designation of Wǔníng was never restored.
The text below uses Shí Pǔ, the acting military governor of Gǎnhuà, being appointed military governor as proof that
Wǔníng is a mistake,
and it should be
"Gǎnhuà".
Both men were promoted and sponsored by Zhī Xiáng.
When Pǔ arrived in the Eastern Capital,
he falsely claimed it was Zhī Xiáng's order
to recall the army to join with Fán's forces.
They massacred Héyīn,
plundered Zhèngzhōu, and moved eastward.
When they reached Péngchéng,
Zhī Xiáng welcomed and comforted them,
rewarding them very generously.
Pǔ sent his trusted confidants to persuade Zhī Xiáng, saying:
"The multitude is pressing me;
please surrender your seal and bestow it upon me."
Zhī Xiáng could not control them,
and went to reside in Dàpéngguǎn.
Pǔ took charge of the affairs himself.
Fán said to Pǔ:
"Secretary Zhī has shown kindness to the people of Xúzhōu;
if he is not killed,
it will surely lead to future regrets."
Pǔ disagreed
and sent Zhī Xiáng back to the court.
Fán ambushed him with soldiers at Qīlǐtíng.
The pavilion was seven *lǐ* from Péngchéng,
hence its name.
An imperial edict appointed Pǔ as acting military governor of Wǔníng.
Pǔ submitted a memorial recommending Fán as the prefect of Sùzhōu.
Fán was greedy and tyrannical upon taking office.
Pǔ replaced him with his general Zhāng Yǒu and
had him killed.
40 Yáng Fùguāng memorialized to elevate Càizhōu to the Fèngguó Army,
with Qín Zōngquán as the defensive commissioner.
Wáng Xù, a butcher from Shòuzhōu, and his brother-in-law Liú Xíngquán gathered a force of five hundred men,
seized their native prefecture,
and after more than a month,
further captured Guāngzhōu.
Wáng Xù proclaimed himself general
and had a force of over ten thousand men;
Qín Zōngquán memorialized to appoint him as the prefect of Guāngzhōu.
Wáng Cháo, an assistant magistrate of Gùshǐ County,
traditionally, a county assistant was a county丞 (magistrate's aide).
According to Tang regulations,

below the county 丞, 簿 (registrar), and 尉 (commander) were司功佐 (aide for merits), 司倉佐 (aide for granaries), 司戶佐 (aide for households), 司兵佐 (aide for military affairs), 司法佐 (aide for justice), and 司士佐 (aide for scholars),
all of whom were county assistants.
Lù Zhèn's Jiǔguó Zhì says: Wáng Cháo was a county clerk in his youth.
Perhaps the character
was omitted in transmission?
Wáng Xù appointed Wáng Cháo as his military chief,
putting him in charge of provisions and reviewing soldiers,
trusting him greatly.
This marks the beginning of the Wáng Cháo brothers,
setting the stage for Wáng Cháo's overthrow of Wáng Xù.
41 Gāo Xún fought with Huáng Cháo's general Lǐ Xiáng at Shíqiáo.
Shíqiáo
is the place where the Jin general Wáng Zhèn'è defeated the Qin army.
Gāo Xún fled to Hézhōng.
Lǐ Xiáng took advantage of the victory to recapture Huázhōu.
In May of that year,
Gāo Xún captured Huázhōu.
42 Tuòbá Sīgōng, acting military governor of Xiàsuí, was appointed military governor.
43 Zōngzhèng Shǎoqīng, Prince Sī Cáo Wáng Guīnián, returned from Nánzhào.
The Biao-Xin presented a memorial of submission,
requesting to fully comply with the imperial decree.
Guīnián's mission to Nánzhào
is mentioned in Volume 237, Guangming First Year, Sixth Month.
Shàng (on, up),
here to be read as “zhǎng” (to be in charge of).
44 Lǐ
Xiàochāng and Tuòbá Sīgōng fought with Shàng Ràng and Zhū Wēn at Dōngwèiqiáo.
They were defeated
and withdrew.
Historians say that all the regional governors who were loyal to the emperor
withdrew due to the exhaustion of their armies.
45 Initially,
Gāo Pián and Zhōu Bǎo, the military governor of Zhènhǎi, both came from the Shéncè Army,
and Pián treated Bǎo as an older brother.
However, when Pián later gained wealth and merit first,
he gradually came to slight Bǎo;
eventually, their territories bordered each other,
and they frequently quarreled over minor matters,
thus creating a rift.
Huáinán and Zhènhǎi Army were neighboring territories,
with only one river as their boundary.
数 (number),
here pronounced as “suò” (to contend, dispute).
Bǎo prepared his fleet to wait for him,
wondering why he delayed so long;
he consulted his strategists,
and some said:
"Lord Gāo is taking advantage of the court's many troubles
and has ambitions to annex Jiāngdōng.
He claims to be coming to our aid,
but in reality, he might be planning against us!
We should be prepared."
Bǎo did not believe it
and sent someone to spy on Pián,
who showed no intention of moving north.
At that time, Pián sent someone to arrange a meeting with Bǎo at Guāzhōu to discuss military affairs.
Bǎo then believed what his advisors had said
and feigned illness, refusing to go,
and moreover told the envoy:
"I am not Lǐ Kāng.
Does Lord Gāo again wish to make military achievements for his family to deceive the court?"
Gāo Chóngwén executed Lǐ Kāng,
the event is recorded in Volume 237, Yuánhé First Year of Xiànzōng.
Pián again sent an envoy to rebuke Bǎo,
saying, "How dare you slight a high official?"
Bǎo insulted him, saying:
"We are both military governors on opposite sides of the river.
If you are a high official,
am I merely a street guard?"
From then on, they became bitter enemies.
Pián stayed at Dōngtáng for over a hundred days.
Imperial edicts repeatedly urged him to advance,
but Pián submitted a memorial,
claiming that Bǎo and Liú Hànghóng, the observer of Zhèdōng, would become future troubles.
On the day Xīnhài,
he again dismissed his troops and returned to his residence.
In reality, he had no heart to confront the difficulties,
but only wanted to ward off the ominous omen of pheasants gathering.
46 Gāo Pián summoned Dǒng Chāng, the commander of Shíjìng Town, to Guǎnglíng,
wanting to fight Huáng Cháo with him.
Qián Liú, Dǒng Chāng's general, persuaded Chāng, saying:
"I observe that Lord Gāo has no intention of suppressing the rebels.
It would be better to use the excuse of defending our hometown and leave him."
Chāng followed his advice,
and Pián allowed Chāng to return.
At that time, Lù Shěnzhōng, the prefect of Hángzhōu, was about to take up his post.
When he reached Jiāxīng,
Jiāxīng
was originally Yóuquán County in the Han Dynasty,
renamed by Wú,
and belonged to Sūzhōu in the Tang Dynasty,
located 140 *lǐ* southwest of the prefecture.
Shěnzhōng was afraid and returned.
Chāng proclaimed himself the commander of Hángzhōu's military escort and acting prefect,
and sent his officers to request recognition from Zhōu Bǎo.
Bǎo could not control him
and memorialized to appoint him as the prefect of Hángzhōu.
47 Dù Xióng, a bandit from Línhǎi, captured Táizhōu.
48 On the day Xīnyǒu,
the imperial prince Zhèn was established as the King of Jiàn.
49. Cháo Yì’s (昭義) ten generals, Chéng Lín (成麟), killed Gāo Xún (高潯).
Chéng Lín (成麟) killed Gāo Xún (高潯) after the latter was defeated and retreated at Shíqiáo (石橋).
Tiānjǐng Guān (天井關) garrison commander Mèng Fānglì (孟方立) raised troops and attacked Lín (麟),
killing him.
The “Kǎo Yì” (考異) states: The “Shílù” (實錄) says:
“Zélù (澤潞)牙將 Liú Guǎng (劉廣) occupied Lùzhōu (潞州) and rebelled.
Tiānjǐng Guān (天井關) garrison commander Mèng Fānglì (孟方立) led his garrison troops to attack Guǎng (廣),
killing him,
and declared himself Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu 留後).
He then moved the military title to Xíngzhōu (邢州).
Earlier,
when Gāo Xún (高潯) was reinforcing the capital,
Guǎng (廣) led his army to Yángpíng (陽平)
and planned a rebellion,
but did not proceed.
He returned to occupy Lùzhōu (潞州),
declared himself Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu 留後),
and enforced laws with severe cruelty.
The three armies feared him.
Fānglì (方立) seized the opportunity to attack and kill him.”
It also says:
“Gāo Xún (高潯), the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ 節度使) of Cháo Yì (昭義), was demoted to Administrator (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Duānzhōu (端州).”
The “Zhōnghé Sān Nián Shílù” (中和三年實錄) also says:
“Initially,
Mèng Fānglì (孟方立) killed Gāo Xún (高潯) and established himself.”
Xuē Jūzhèng’s (薛居正) “Wǔdài Shǐ Fānglì Zhuàn” (五代史方立傳) says:
“In Zhōnghé (中和) second year (882 CE),
he was the garrison commander of Zézhōu’s (澤州) Tiānjǐng Guān (天井關).
At that time, Huáng Cháo (黃巢) was invading Guān Fǔ (關輔),
and the changes in commanders of prefectures and commanderies were like a game.
Prior to this,
Shěn Xún (沈詢) and Gāo Shí (高湜) had successively served as Military Governors (Jiédù 節度) of Cháo Yì (昭義),
but were negligent in military administration.
When Guī Qín (歸秦) and Liú Guǎng (劉廣) rebelled,
Fānglì (方立) saw the opportunity during the change of Lù (潞) commanders,
took advantage of their unpreparedness,
led his garrison troops directly into Lùzhōu (潞州),
and declared himself Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu 留後).”
The “Xīn Jì” (新紀) says:
“In the eighth month,
Gāo Xún (高潯), the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ 節度使) of Cháo Yì Jūn (昭義軍), battled Huáng Cháo (黃巢) at Shíqiáo (石橋)
and was defeated.
His ten generals, Chéng Lín (成麟), killed Xún (潯)
and entered Lùzhōu (潞zhou).
In the ninth month,
on the Jǐsì (己巳) day,
Mèng Fānglì (孟方立), a garrison commander of Cháo Yì Jūn (昭義軍), killed Chéng Lín (成麟)
and declared himself Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu 留後).”
The “Fānglì Zhuàn” (方立傳) only renders Chéng Lín (成麟) as Chéng Lín (成鄰),
the rest is as in the “Xīn Jì” (新紀).
According to the “Qiánfú Èr Nián Shílù” (乾符二年實錄):
“In the tenth month,
the Cháo Yì Jūn (昭義軍) mutinied,
expelled Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ 節度使) Gāo Shí (高湜),
and demoted Shí (湜) to Sīhù (司戶) of Xiàngzhōu (象州).”
Liǔ Bīn’s (柳玭) biography states
“demoted to Gāoyào (高要)尉.”
In the eleventh month of the third year,
an imperial edict to Hán Jiǎn (韓簡) of Wèibó (魏博) stated:
“Liú Guǎng (劉廣) expelled Commander Nán (⿰⺘亶權)”
and so on.
This means Guǎng (廣) expelled Shí (湜),
and Nán (⿰⺘亶) occupied Lùzhōu (潞州).
Xuē Shǐ’s (薛史) “Mèng Fānglì Zhuàn” (孟方立傳) also says Shěn Xún (沈詢) and Gāo Shí (高湜) were negligent in military administration,
leading to the rebellions of Guī Qín (歸秦) and Liú Guǎng (劉廣).
This means Guǎng’s (廣) rebellion was earlier.
The “Jiù Jì” (舊紀) says:
“In the ninth month,
Gāo Xún’s (高潯)牙將 Liú Guǎng (劉廣) returned to Lùzhōu (潞州).
In this month,
Xún’s (潯) Tiānjǐng Guān (天井關) garrison commander Mèng Fānglì (孟方立) attacked Guǎng (廣),
killed him,
and declared himself Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu 留後).
Xún (潯) was demoted to Administrator (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Duānzhōu (端州).”
This is likely an error in the “Jiù Jì” (舊紀),
which the “Shílù” (實錄) followed.
Xuē Shǐ’s (薛史) “Fānglì Zhuàn” (方立傳) says:
“Seeing the change of Lù (潞) commanders,
he led troops into Lùzhōu (潞州).”
It does not state which commander changed.
If he did not expel a commander,
how could he occupy the prefecture?
The event lacks a cause,
which is very negligent.
The “Jiù Jì” (舊紀) might have mistakenly attributed Gāo Shí’s (高湜) incident to Gāo Xún (高潯).
The “Shílù” (實錄) here says Guǎng (廣) was killed,
and the next year it says Xún (潯) was killed,
contradicting itself.
The “Xīn Jì” (新紀) and the biography (傳) both say Chéng Lín (成麟) killed Xún (潯),
and Fānglì (方立) killed Lín (麟) with quite detailed dates and facts,
so there must be a source.
We follow this now.
He was a native of the prefecture.
50. Zhōngwǔ (忠武) Supervising Army (Jiānjūn 監軍) Yáng Fùguāng (楊復光) garrisoned Wǔgōng (武功).
51. Yǒngjiā (永嘉) bandit Zhū Bāo (朱褒) captured Wēnzhōu (溫州).
Sòng Bái (宋白) says: Wēnzhōu (溫州), Yǒngjiā Jùn (永嘉郡),
was the eastern border of Huìjī Jùn (會稽郡) in the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
In the fourth year of Yǒnghé (永和) in the Later Hàn (後漢), Yǒngníng Xiàn (永寧縣) was established.
Emperor Míng (明帝) of Jìn (晉) established Yǒngníng Jùn (永寧郡),
soon after it belonged to Yǒngjiā Jùn (永嘉郡).
After Suí (隋) pacified Chén (陳),
the commandery was abolished.
In the sixth year of Wǔdé (武德) of Táng (唐), Jiādōng Zhōu (嘉東州) was established.
In the first year of Zhēnguān (貞觀), the prefecture was abolished,
and the county belonged to Kuòzhōu (栝州).
In the second year of Shàngyuán (上元), Wēnzhōu (溫州) was established by dividing Yǒngjiā (永嘉) and Āngù (安固) counties from Kuòzhōu (栝州),
named after Wēnjiào Lǐng (溫嶠嶺).
52. Fèngxiáng (鳳翔) Marching Army Sīmǎ (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ 行軍司馬) Lǐ Chāngyán (李昌言) led his army to garrison Xīngpíng (興平).
At this time, Fèngxiáng’s (鳳翔) granaries and treasuries were depleted,
rewards and provisions were meager,
and food supplies were insufficient.
Chāngyán (昌言) knew there were few troops in the prefectural city,
and thus incited his troops.
In winter,
the tenth month,
he led his army back to attack the prefectural city.
Zhèng Tián (鄭畋) ascended the city wall and spoke to his soldiers.
His troops all dismounted and bowed, saying: “Our Duke (Xiànggōng 相公) indeed has not let us down.”
Tián (畋) said:
“If the marching army can restrain its soldiers and cherish the people,
and destroy the bandits for the country,
then it can also be considered acting in accordance with loyalty.”
Expelling a commander is an act of rebellion, while suppressing bandits to obtain a military standard (Jīngjié 旌節) is an act of loyalty.
For Wèi (為), read Yúwěi (于偽).
On that day, he went west to Xíngzài (行在).
53. Tiānpíng (天平) Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ 節度使) and Southern Pacification Commissioner (Nánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ 南面招討使) Cáo Quánzhěng (曹全晸) died in battle against the bandits.
The army established his elder brother’s son Cúnshí (存實) as Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu 留後).
54. In the eleventh month,
on the Yǐsì (乙巳) day,
Mèng Kǎi (孟楷) and Zhū Wēn (朱溫) attacked the Fū (鄜) and Xià (夏) armies at Fùpíng (富平).
The two armies were defeated
and fled back to their respective circuits.
The two armies were
those of Lǐ Xiàochāng (李孝昌) and Tuòbá Sīgōng (拓跋思恭).
55. Zhèng Tián (鄭畋) arrived at Fèngzhōu (鳳州).
From Fèngxiáng (鳳翔) west to Fèngzhōu (鳳州) is three hundred ninety-five *lǐ*.
An edict appointed Tián (畋) as Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shǎofù 太子少傅) with divided duties.
Lǐ Chāngyán (李昌言) was appointed Fèngxiáng (鳳翔) Military Governor (Jiédù Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ 節度行營招討使).
56. Péi Chè (裴澈), the Minister of the Left (Ménxià Shìláng 門下侍郎) and Grand Councilor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì 同平章事), was appointed Observer-Commissioner (Guānchásǐ 觀察使) of Èyuè (鄂岳).
57. Zhōu Bǎo (周寶), the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ 節度使) of Zhènhǎi (鎮海), was granted the title of Grand Councilor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì 同平章事).
58. Suìchāng (遂昌) bandit Lú Yuē (盧約) captured Chǔzhōu (處州).
In the second year of Chìwū (赤烏) of Sūn Quán (孫權) of Wú (吳),
Píngchāng Xiàn (平昌縣) was established by dividing Tàimò (太末).
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) of Jìn (晉) renamed it Suìchāng (遂昌).
In the eighth year of Wǔdé (武德) of Táng (唐), it was merged into Sōngyáng (松陽).
In the first year of Jǐngyún (景雲), Suìchāng Xiàn (遂昌縣) was re-established
and belonged to Chǔzhōu (處州).
The “Jiǔ Yù Zhì” (九域志) says: It is two hundred forty *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
Note that Wēn (溫) and Chǔ (處) two prefectures were originally the territory of one commandery, Yǒngjiā (永嘉), in the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
In the Suí (隋) dynasty, it was Kuòzhōu (栝州) and Yǒngjiā Jùn (永嘉郡).
In Wǔdé (武德) of Táng (唐), Kuòzhōu (栝州) was established,
and Dōngjiā Zhōu (東嘉州) was also divided off,
initially dividing into two prefectures.
Dōngjiā Zhōu (東嘉州) later became Wēnzhōu (溫州);
Kuòzhōu (栝州) was renamed Chǔzhōu (處州),
to avoid the name of Emperor Dézōng (德宗).
59. In the twelfth month,
Jiāngxī (江西) general Mǐn Xù (閔勗), garrisoning Húnán (湖南),
returned.
Passing through Tánzhōu (潭州),
he expelled Observer-Commissioner (Guānchásǐ 觀察使) Lǐ Yù (李裕)
and declared himself Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu 留後).
The “Kǎo Yì” (考異) states: The “Shílù” (實錄) and “Xīn Zhuàn” (新傳) write “Mǐn Xū” (閔頊).
We now follow Chéng Kuāngmào’s (程匡袤) “Táng Bǔ Jì” (唐補紀).
60. Huà (感化) Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu 留後) Shí Pǔ (時溥) was appointed Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ 節度使).
61. Xiàzhōu (夏州) was granted the title Dìngnán Jūn (定難軍).
62. Initially,
Gāo Pián (高駢) was garrisoning Jīngnán (荊南).
In the fifth year of Qiánfú (乾符), Pián (駢) was garrisoning Jīngnán (荊南).
He commanded the Man (蠻) army,
which followed Pián (駢) to Huáinán (淮南).
They fled back,
gathered a thousand men,
attacked Lángzhōu (朗州),
and killed Administrator (Cìshǐ 刺史) Cuī Zhù (崔翥).
An edict appointed Mǎn (滿) as Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu 留後) of Lángzhōu (朗州).
In the middle of the year,
he led three or four attacks, invading Jīngnán (荊南),
entering its outer city walls,
burning and plundering before leaving.
This caused great suffering to the people of Jīng (荊).
Zhōú Yuè (周岳) of Zōuxī (陬溪) once hunted with Mǎn (滿)
and fought over meat,
intending to kill Mǎn (滿),
but failed.
Zōuxī (陬溪)
should be within Wǔlíng (武陵) Prefecture.
Zōu (陬)
is pronounced like "cè jiū" (側鳩) inverted.
He also gathered a crowd and attacked Héngzhōu (衡州),
driving away the Cìshǐ (刺史) Xú Hào (徐顥).
An imperial edict appointed Yuè (岳) as Cìshǐ (刺史) of Héngzhōu (衡州).
The Mán (蠻) leader Xiàng Huái (向⿰王褱) from Shímén (石門)
also assembled several thousand Yí (夷) and Liáo (獠) people to capture Lǐzhōu (澧州),
killing the Cìshǐ (刺史) Lǚ Zìmù (呂自牧),
and proclaiming himself Cìshǐ (刺史).
The State of Wú (吳) divided Língyáng (零陽) County to establish Tiānmén (天門) Commandery.
The Suí (隋) dynasty abolished it and made it Shímén (石門) County.
During the Táng (唐) dynasty, it belonged to Lǐzhōu (澧州).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: it is ninety-two lǐ (里) west of the prefecture.
Wáng Duó (王鐸), believing Gāo Pián (高駢) as the Commander-in-Chief of All Circuits had no intention of suppressing the rebels,
took it upon himself, as prime minister,
to express his indignation and request to go forth,
sincerely weeping,
even repeatedly;
the emperor assented.
Kěnkǔan (懇款)
means sincere.
Xiāng (相)
is pronounced like "xī liàng" (息亮) inverted.
In the 1st month of spring,
on the Xīnhài (辛亥) day,
Wáng Duó (王鐸) was appointed concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令)
and made Commander-in-Chief of All Circuits' Expeditionary Forces.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Old Annals state:
"In the 7th month of the 1st year of Zhōnghé (中和),
Duó (鐸) was made Commander-in-Chief.
In the 12th month,
he led an army of thirty thousand to the imperial domain
and encamped at Zhōuzhì (盩厔)."
Duó's (鐸) biography in the Old History is also placed in the 1st year.
The Táng Nián Bǔlù (唐年補錄) states:
"In the 11th month of the 1st year,
on the Yǐsì (乙巳) day,
an edict appointed Duó (鐸) as Commander-in-Chief.
In the 12th month,
on the Yǐhài (乙亥) day,
Duó (鐸) encamped at Zhōuzhì (盩厔)."
The Xù Bǎoyùn Lù (續寶運錄) states:
"In the 8th month of the 1st year,
Duó (鐸) was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Empire."
The Táng Bǔjì (唐補紀) states:
"In the 4th month of the 1st year of Zhōnghé (中和),
Gāo Pián (高駢) led his army and stationed at Dōngtáng (東塘).
From the 5th month, he departed from the prefectural seat
and returned in the 9th month.
The court immediately appointed Duó (鐸) as Commander-in-Chief of all circuits' troops
to recover Cháng'ān (長安),
and Duó (鐸) became the Commander-in-Chief."
The dates in various books differ thus.
The New Annals state:
"In the 1st month of the 2nd year,
on the Xīnhài (辛亥) day,
Wáng Duó (王鐸) was made Commander-in-Chief of All Circuits' Expeditionary Forces,
and Gāo Pián (高駢) was dismissed as Commander-in-Chief."
According to the Imperial Records' edict responding to Gāo Pián (高駢) in the 4th month,
the dismissal of the Commander-in-Chief should be in this year.
We now follow the Imperial Records.
The New Annals and the Old and New Biographies of Pián (駢) state:
"Emperor Xīzōng (僖宗), knowing Pián (駢) had no intention of going to the rescue,
then appointed Duó (鐸) as Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Capital's Four Sides and All Circuits' Expeditionary Troops,
with Wéi Zhàodù (韋昭度) as Commissioner for Salt and Iron Transport in the Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮) regions.
Pián (駢), having lost military authority
and also his profitable power,
threw up his sleeves and loudly denounced,
repeatedly submitting memorials debating the matter,
with disrespectful language."
However, Pián's (駢) dismissal as Commander-in-Chief,
while retaining his previous role as Commissioner for Salt and Iron Transport of All Circuits,
only occurred in the 5th month.
The Běimèng Suǒyán (北夢瑣言) states:
"When Wáng Duó (王鐸) first defended Jīngnán (荊南),
Huáng Cháo (黃巢) invaded,
and he fled at the mere sight of them.
Later,
when leading troops at Tóngguān (潼關),
Huáng Cháo (黃巢) sent a message saying:
'Prime Minister is a scholar,
and not my match;
do not soil my blades,
lest you bring about your own defeat.'
Later, he arrived at the travelling court in Chéngdū (成都)
and was appointed Commander-in-Chief of All Circuits.
This is why Gāo Pián (高駢) presented a memorial,
referring to him as a general of a defeated army."
However, Duó (鐸) was demoted after losing a battle in Jīngnán (荊南),
and never led troops at Tóngguān (潼關).
Pí Guāngyè's (皮光業) Jiànwén Lù (見聞錄) states his appointment as Commander-in-Chief was in the 2nd month of this year,
which is also an error.
Moreover, the Old Annals, biographies, and New Biography
state Duó (鐸) was only Commander-in-Chief of All Expeditionary Forces.
The New Annals write Commander-in-Chief.
The Imperial Records, both at the time of initial appointment and dismissal, refer to him as Commander-in-Chief,
but often say Commander-in-Chief of All Expeditionary Forces in between.
Furthermore, Xīmén Sīgōng (西門思恭) was Supervisor of All Expeditionary Forces.
At the time, many generals were Commanders-in-Chief.
It is suspected that Duó (鐸) being Commander-in-Chief of All Expeditionary Forces is correct.
When the troops were dismissed, he returned to the government.
Gāo Pián (高駢) retained only the office of Commissioner for Salt and Iron Transport,
his positions as Commander-in-Chief and other commissioners were abolished.
Wáng Duó (王鐸) was allowed to appoint his own generals and aides.
Tài Zǐ Shǎo Shī (太子少師) Cuī Ānqián (崔安潛) was appointed Deputy Commander-in-Chief.
On the Xīnwèi (辛未) day,
Zhōu Jí (周岌) and Wáng Chóngróng (王重榮) were appointed Right and Left Sīmǎ (司馬) of the Commander-in-Chief of All Expeditionary Forces.
Zhūgě Shuǎng (諸葛爽) and Xuānwǔ (宣武) Jiédùshǐ (節度使) Kāng Shí (康實) were appointed Right and Left Vanguard Commanders.
Shí Pǔ (時溥) was appointed Commissioner for Urging and Dispatching Logistics, Tribute Grain, and Defense.
Logistics from the Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮) regions
all passed through Xúzhōu (徐州) territory,
hence Pǔ (溥) was given this post.
Wáng Chǔcún (王處存), Lǐ Xiàochāng (李孝昌), and Tuòbá Sīgōng (拓跋思恭) were appointed Commanders-in-Chief for the Northeast and West of the Imperial Capital.
Yáng Fùguāng (楊復光) was appointed Supervising Commissioner for the Southern Expeditionary Forces.
Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人) Zhèng Chāngtú (鄭昌圖) was appointed Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬) of Yìchéng (義成) Jiédù (節度).
Gěishìzhōng (給事中) Zhèng Jùn (鄭畯) was appointed Pànguān (判官).
Zhí Hóngwénguǎn (直弘文館) Wáng Tuán (王摶) was appointed Tuīguān (推官).
Sīxūn Yuánwàiláng (司勳員外郎) Péi Zhì (裴贄) was appointed Zhǎngshūjì (掌書記).
Chāngtú (昌圖)
was a paternal cousin of Cóngdǎng (從讜).
Jùn (畯)
was Tián's (畋) younger brother.
Tuán (摶)
was the great-grandson of Yú (璵).
Wáng Yú (王璵) served Emperors Xuánzōng (玄宗) and Sùzōng (肅宗) through sacrificial prayers,
as mentioned in previous annals.
He was Tǎn's (坦) son.
Péi Tǎn (裴坦) is mentioned in Volume 251, 10th year of Yìzōng (懿宗) Xiántōng (咸通) era.
Chóngyíng (重盈)
was Chóngróng's (重榮) elder brother.
Huáng Cháo (黃巢) appointed Zhū Wēn (朱溫) as Cìshǐ (刺史) of Tóngzhōu (同州),
ordering Wēn (溫) to take it himself.
In the 2nd month,
Mǐ Chéng (米誠), Cìshǐ (刺史) of Tóngzhōu (同州), fled to Hézhōng (河中),
and Wēn (溫) then occupied it.
This laid the groundwork for Zhū Wēn (朱溫) to return Tóngzhōu (同州) to the state.
On the Jǐmǎo (己卯) day,
Tài Zǐ Shǎo Fù (太子少傅) and Fēnsī (分司) Zhèng Tián (鄭畋) was appointed Sīkōng (司空) concurrent Ménxià Shìláng (門下侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
He was summoned to the travelling court,
and all military affairs were to be consulted with him.
Wáng Duó (王鐸) was appointed Pàn Hùbùshì (判戶部事).
Zhū Wēn (朱溫) attacked Hézhōng (河中),
and Wáng Chóngróng (王重榮) defeated him.
Lǐ Chāngyán (李昌言) was appointed Commander-in-Chief for the West of the Imperial Capital.
Zhū Méi (朱玫) was appointed Commander-in-Chief for Hénán (河南).
Zhū Méi (朱玫) was then stationed in Bīnníng (邠寧);
how could he leave the pass to command the various prefectures east of Hénán (河南)?
This Hénán (河南)
refers to the southern bank of the great Yellow River from Lóngmén (龍門) eastward to Pújīn (蒲津).
Hú Gōngsù (胡公素), Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of Jīngyuán (涇原), died.
The army sought orders from Commander-in-Chief Wáng Duó (王鐸),
who, acting on imperial authority, appointed General Zhāng Jūn (張鈞) as Liúhòu (留後).
Lǐ Kèyòng (李克yòng) attacked Wèizhōu (蔚州).
In the 3rd month,
Zhènwǔ (振武) Jiédùshǐ (節度使) Qìbì Zhāng (契苾璋) reported a joint campaign with Tiāndé (天德) and Dàtóng (大同) to suppress Kèyòng (克用).
An imperial edict instructed Zhèng Cóngdǎng (鄭從讜) to correspond and cooperate.
8 Chén Jìngxuān frequently dispatched people to various counties and towns to spy on affairs.
These were called "searchers" (xúnshìrén),
and wherever they went, they demanded many things.
Two such men passed through Zīyáng Town.
At that time, a town was established in Zīyáng County, Zī Zhōu.
Later, the Northern Wèi divided Zīzhōng to establish Zīyáng County,
because its territory was on the south (yáng) side of the Zī River.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Zīyáng is 120 lǐ northwest of Zī Zhōu.
The town commander, Xiè Hóngràng, invited them,
but they did not come.
Suspecting he was guilty,
that night,
he fled and joined the bandits.
The next morning,
the two men left,
and Hóngràng was actually innocent.
The bandit catcher, Yáng Qiān, enticed Hóngràng to surrender, then arrested him and sent him to the commissioner,
claiming to have captured him in battle
in order to gain merit.
Jìngxuān did not investigate him;
instead, he had Hóngràng flogged twenty times on the back,
nailed him to the west wall for fourteen days,
poured boiling oil on him,
and then applied glue and hemp to his wounds.
The cruelty was extreme,
and those who saw it felt he was wronged.
There was also Qiōng Zhōu staff officer Qiān Néng,
who, due to public business, missed a deadline.
To avoid flogging,
he fled and became a bandit.
Yáng Qiān again enticed him.
As Néng was about to surrender,
he heard of Hóngràng's injustice,
cursed Yáng Qiān loudly,
and in his indignation, turned to banditry.
He plundered good citizens,
and those who did not comply had their entire families killed.
Within a month,
his followers numbered ten thousand.
He organized them into military units
and assigned ranks and positions.
Ranks and positions (zhíjí)
referred to the various levels of military officers, from yáyá and kǒumùguān downwards,
with each having distinct duties and grades.
He attacked and captured cities and towns,
leaving devastation in his wake wherever he went.
Previously,
there were few bandits in Shǔ,
but from then on, they arose in profusion,
and the prefectures and counties could not control them.
Jìngxuān dispatched staff general Yáng Xíngqiān with three thousand men,
and Hú Hónglüè and Mò Kuāngshí with two thousand men each to suppress them.

9 Qí Kèjiǎn was appointed General of the Right Shéncè Army, concurrently holding the posts of Generals of the Left and Right Shéncè Armies, Commander of the Eight Inner and Outer Garrisons, and Jìedùshǐ of Bóyě and Fèngtīan.
10 The Fūfáng Army was granted the designation Bǎodà.
11 Summer,
fourth month,
jiǎwǔ day:
Chén Jìngxuān was additionally granted the concurrent title of Shìzhōng.
12 Hèlián Duó and Lǐ Kějǔ fought against Lǐ Kèyòng,
and were unsuccessful.
13 Previously,
Gāo Pián was fond of immortals.
There was a Daoist alchemist Lǚ Yòngzhī who, having fled due to involvement with a sorcerous faction, took refuge with Pián.
Pián treated him generously
and appointed him to a military post.
Yòngzhī was
the son of a tea merchant from Póyáng.
Póyáng was
an ancient county during the Hàn dynasty;
during the Táng, it was part of Ráo Zhōu,
and the ancient county seat was located east of the present-day county.
He was skilled in understanding human nature.
During his leisure time from alchemy (lúdǐng),
lúdǐng
refers to the process of refining minerals
and transforming cinnabar into gold and silver, etc.
Therefore, Pián thought him even more extraordinary
and gradually placed more trust in him.
Pián's old generals, Liáng Zuǎn, Chén Gǒng, Féng Shòu, Dǒng Jǐn, Yú Gōngchǔ, and Yáo Guīlǐ, had always been highly favored by Pián.
Yòngzhī wanted to monopolize power,
so he gradually removed them through stratagem.
Pián then took away Zuǎn's troops,
exterminated Gǒng's family,
and Shòu, Jǐn, Gōngchǔ, and Guīlǐ were all alienated.
When Yòngzhī learned that those above and below harbored resentment and
feared a clandestine uprising,
he requested the establishment of Surveillance Envoys.
Pián immediately appointed Yòngzhī to lead them,
recruiting over a hundred cunning and treacherous individuals,
who roamed through the lanes and alleys.
They were called
"Cházǐ" (Inspectors),
and nothing, not even a commoner scolding his wife or cursing his son,
escaped their knowledge.
Whenever Yòngzhī desired to seize people's goods and wealth
or abduct their women,
he would fabricate charges of rebellion,
flog and torture them into confession,
kill the person, and take their possessions.
Hundreds of families were thus ruined and destroyed.
People exchanged glances on the roads,
and even though generals, officials, soldiers, and commoners lived in their homes,
they all stood on one foot and held their breath (i.e., were extremely fearful).
Yòngzhī also wished to use military might to control the various generals,
so he requested to select and recruit twenty thousand brave and valiant soldiers from the various armies,
named the Left and Right Mòxié Guards.
Pián immediately appointed Zhāng Shǒuyī and Yòngzhī as the commanders of the Left and Right Mòxié Armies,
assigning officers and officials like a military governor's headquarters.
Their weapons were sharp and efficient,
and their uniforms were luxurious and clean.
Whenever they went out or came in,
their escort numbered nearly a thousand people.
Yòngzhī had over a hundred concubines,
and his self-indulgence was extravagant.
When his expenses were insufficient,
he would detain the tribute convoys of the Three Departments for his own household.
The Three Departments' tribute convoys
referred to those dispatched by the Hùbù, Dùzhī, and Yántiě bureaus for transport to the imperial court.
Yòngzhī still feared that someone might expose his wicked schemes,
so he said to Pián:
"Immortals are not difficult to summon;
it's just a pity that scholars cannot sever worldly ties,
which is why they are unwilling to descend!"
Pián then dismissed all his guests,
cutting off all social interactions.
Guests,
generals, and officials were all denied audience;
if someone absolutely had to see him,
they were first ordered to bathe, fast, and purify themselves,
and only then could they be seen.
As soon as their obeisance was complete,
they were led out again.
Because of this, Yòngzhī was able to wield power and authority exclusively,
without any scruples,
and within the territory, Pián's existence was no longer recognized.
This laid the groundwork for Bì Shīduó to attack Yòngzhī and kill Pián.
Fù,
read as Fú Yòu Fān.
In the 14th year, Wáng Duó led the armies from Liǎngchuān and Xīngyuán to encamp at Línggǎn Sì.
Jīngyuán forces were stationed west of the capital,
Yìdìng and Hézhōng forces north of the Wèi River,
Bīnnìng and Fèngxiáng forces at Xīngpíng,
Bǎodà and Dìngnán forces at Wèiqiáo,
and Zhōngwǔ forces at Wǔgōng.
Imperial armies gathered from all four directions.
Huáng Cháo's power was already constricted;
his orders did not extend beyond Tóng and Huá prefectures.
At this time, Huáng Cháo's general Zhū Wēn occupied Tóng Zhōu,
and Lǐ Xiáng occupied Huá Zhōu,
hence his authority was limited to these two prefectures.
Huá,
read as Hù Huà Fān.
Agricultural activities were entirely abandoned,
and in Cháng'ān city, a dòu of rice cost thirty guàn.
The rebels sold
people to the imperial army for food,
and the imperial army sometimes seized people from mountain strongholds and sold them.
A person cost several hundred guàn,
with the price determined by their stoutness or leanness.
Punctuation by Róng Zhàozǔ, reviewed by Niè Chóngqí
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by imperial decree
Hòu Xué Tiāntái
The second year of Zhōnghé
(Rén Yín, 882)
The fifth month,
Mǐn Xù, the Inspector of Húnán, was provisionally appointed Jìedùshǐ of Zhènnán.
In the sixth year of Xiántōng,
the Zhènnán Army was established in Hóng Zhōu.
Mǐn Xù was at this time occupying Tán Zhōu,
and the Jìedùshǐ title for Hóng Zhōu was bestowed upon him,
intending to make him fight and destroy Zhōng Chuán.
The court feared that other provincial inspectors would emulate this,
so they disallowed it.
Previously,
Wáng Xiānzhī had plundered Jiāngxī.
Zhōng Chuán, a man from Gāo'ān, gathered aboriginal tribesmen
and built strongholds in the mountains.
Gāo'ān was originally Jiànchéng County of Yùzhāng in the Hàn dynasty.
In the fifth year of Wǔdé of the Táng dynasty,
it was renamed Gāo'ān,
belonging to Hóng Zhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì states: it is one hundred twenty lǐ south of the prefecture.
Xiānzhī captured Fǔ Zhōu but could not hold it.
Chuán entered and occupied it.
An imperial edict immediately appointed him as its Prefect.
By this time,
he had also expelled Gāo Màoqīng, the Inspector of Jiāngxī,
and occupied Hóng Zhōu.
Fǔ Zhōu is two hundred forty lǐ northwest of Hóng Zhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Fǔ Zhōu was Línchuān Commandery,
territory of Nánchāng County in the Hàn dynasty.
Wú established Línchuān Commandery;
when Suí pacified Chén,
the commandery was abolished and made a prefecture.
At that time, General Administrator Yáng Wǔtōng was sent on a mission to pacify the area,
and thus it was named Fǔ.
The matter is recorded in the previous volume, previous year.
(The court) ordered Xù to take charge of it;
the Zhènnán Army had been abolished,
and was now re-established.
Xù was ordered to consequently suppress Chuán.
Xù understood the court's intention to pit the two bandits against each other to their mutual destruction,
and declined to go.
2. Jiā Huáinán Jiédùshǐ Gāo Pián (加淮南節度使高駢) was concurrently appointed Shìzhōng (侍中).
His position as Yántiě Zhuǎnyùnshǐ (鹽鐵轉運使) was abolished.
Since Pián (駢) had already lost military authority,
and now was deprived of control over profits,
he rolled up his sleeves and loudly denounced [the situation].
In the spring of this year, his post as Dūtǒng (都統) was abolished,
and he had already lost military authority;
now, with the abolition of his Yántiě Zhuǎnyùn (鹽鐵轉運) position,
he also lost control over profits.
Gòu (詬) is pronounced gǔ hòu fān (古候翻),
also xǔ hòu fān (許候翻).
His words were disrespectful,
the gist of which was:
"It is Your Majesty who does not use this humble subject,
certainly not this humble subject who has betrayed Your Majesty."
He also said:
"The treacherous ministers have not yet awoken,
Your Majesty is still deluded,
unmindful of the burning of the ancestral temples,
unpained by the destruction of the imperial tombs."
He also said:
"Wáng Duó (王鐸) is a general who ruined his army,"
referring to the defeat at Jiānglíng (江陵) in the sixth year of Qiánfú (乾符).
Fèn (僨) is pronounced fāng wèn fān (方問翻).
"Cuī Ānqián (崔安潛) repeatedly achieved victories against the rebels,"
he had nothing to point out and expose,
so he spoke of his greed and corruption in Shǔ (蜀).
In the sixth year of Xiántōng (咸通) of Yìzōng (懿宗),
Ānqián (安潛) governed Shǔ (蜀).
He also said:
"Among those currently employed,
from high-ranking commanders
down to auxiliary generals,
in my estimation,
all can be captured sitting down."
He also said:
"Do not let a hundred generations have a minister harboring resentment,
or a thousand ages retain the shame of 'scraping the mat'."
"Scraping the mat"
refers to the affair of the King of Huáinán (淮南) in the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
found in the Hànjì (漢紀).
"The Liú (劉) family is revived,"
meaning that with the bandits rampant in Shāndōng (山東),
there will be someone like Liú Jì (劉季) rising again among them.
"How can it be only in the past!"
He also referred to the affair of Qín Zǐyīng (秦子嬰) to allude to the emperor.
"Now, virtuous talents are in the wilderness,
and wicked people fill the court,
leading Your Majesty to become a ruler of a fallen state.
What plan will these fellows devise!"
Gù Yún (顧雲) generally arranged Gāo Pián's (高駢) vehement denunciation into a memorial.
The gist of it was:
"Controlling profits means holding the 'pottery basins' in hand,"
meaning he monopolized the salt profits of Jiānghuái (江淮).
The two phrases "pottery basins"
are found in the Hàn Wǔdì Jì (漢武帝紀).
"Directly reaching the various garrisons north and west of the capital, and the Shéncè (神策) army,
all were under his command,
showing the extent of his controlling power;
and he was honorably made Sītú (司徒),
and gloriously became Tàiwèi (太尉)."
According to the Xīnshū Gāo Pián Zhuàn (新書高駢傳): Pián (駢) commanded Xīchuān (西川);
afterwards,
he was promoted to Jiǎnjiào Sītú (檢校司徒);
after the two capitals fell,
the Son of Heaven still hoped Pián (駢) would achieve merit,
and promoted him to Jiǎnjiào Tàiwèi (檢校太尉).
"How could he be of use?"
He also said:
"I have for a long time entrusted you with military authority,
but you could not suppress the prime culprit.
Since he escaped the net at Tiāncháng (天長) and crossed the Huái (淮) River,"
the event is found in Volume 253, Guǎngmíng (廣明) first year.
"He suddenly ravaged the capital region,
for three years from beginning to end.
The army of Guǎnglíng (廣陵) did not leave its assigned territory,
loyal ministers accumulated hopes,
brave warriors stirred up ridicule,
so I promoted senior ministers
and executed major bandits."
He also said:
"The intention of relying on you from the past,
suddenly has no way to be voiced as a complaint.
Gazing fixedly towards the southeast,
only increases sorrow and grief!"
He also said:
"Xiè Xuán (謝玄) defeated Fú Jiān (苻堅) at Féishuǐ (淝水),"
found in the Jìn Xiàowǔdì Jì (晉孝武帝紀).
Found in the Xiànzōng Jì (憲宗紀).
He also said:
"The ancestral temples burned,
the imperial tombs were desecrated,
the tortoise and jade destroyed in their caskets—
whose fault is this!"
Using the words of Confucius in the Lúnyǔ (論語).
Precious tortoises and precious jades
are all stored in caskets;
if they are destroyed while in their caskets,
the guardians cannot deny their fault.
"'Treacherous ministers have not yet awoken'
—who would acknowledge such words?
'Your Majesty is still deluded'
—I dare not accept such a statement!"
He also said:
"You could not even bind Huáng Cháo (黃巢) at Tiāncháng (天長),
how can you capture all the generals while sitting down!"
He also said:
"You say the Liú (劉) family is revived,
but you don't know who its leader is.
Comparing me to Liú Xuán (劉玄) and Zǐyīng (子嬰),
how greatly you slander me!"
He also said:
"Moreover, the heavenly mandate has not yet fallen,
the imperial order is still intact,
the three spirits are not obscured,
all systems are still in place.
The etiquette between ruler and minister,
and the distinctions between superior and inferior,
ought to be observed,
and not allowed to collapse.
Although I am but a youth,
how can I be lightly insulted!"
When harsh words arrive,
one must retort,
comparing right and wrong,
and clarifying one's own rectitude.
This is the behavior of squabbling commoners in alleys.
In ancient times, official proclamations
from Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏) onwards usually enumerated their crimes;
how could it come to this!
The Tōngjiàn (通鑑) recorded this as a warning for future generations.
From this point, tribute payments completely ceased.
3. Cáo Cúnshí (曹存實), the acting governor of Tiānpíng (天平), was appointed Jiédùshǐ (節度使).
In the first year [of Guǎngmíng (廣明)],
Cáo Quánzhěng (曹全晸) died fighting the rebels,
so, acceding to the army's request,
his nephew was appointed commander.
4. Huáng Cháo (黃巢) attacked Xīngpíng (興平),
and the Xīngpíng (興平) armies retreated to Fèntiān (奉天).
At this time, the armies of Fèngxiáng (鳳翔) and Bīnnìng (邠寧) were stationed at Xīngpíng (興平).
5. Jiā Héyáng Jiédùshǐ Zhūgě Shuǎng (加河陽節度使諸葛爽) was concurrently appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
6. In the sixth month,
Zhāng Jūn (張鈞), the acting governor of Jīngyuán (涇原), was appointed Jiédùshǐ (節度使).
In the second month of this year,
Wáng Duó (王鐸), acting on imperial authority,
appointed Zhāng Jūn (張鈞) as acting governor of Jīngyuán (涇原);
the event is found in the previous volume.
7. Duàn Yànmó (段彥謨), the Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of Jīngnán (荊南), and the Supervising Eunuch Zhū Jìngméi (朱敬玫) were at odds.
Jìngméi (敬玫) separately selected three thousand brave warriors,
called the Zhōngyǒng Jūn (忠勇軍),
and personally led them.
Yànmó (彥謨) plotted to kill Jìngméi (敬玫);
on the day Jǐhài (己亥),
Jìngméi (敬玫) first led his troops to attack Yànmó (彥謨),
and killed him.
Duàn Yànmó's (段彥謨) holding of Jīngnán (荊南) began in Volume 253, Guǎngmíng (廣明) first year.
Shuài (帥)
is read as lǜ (率).
8. The Shǔ (蜀) people Luó Húnqíng (羅渾擎), Jù Húsēng (句胡僧), and Luó Fūzǐ (羅夫子) each gathered several thousand followers to respond to Qiān Néng (阡能).
Yáng Xíngqiān (楊行遷) and others fought them,
but were repeatedly unsuccessful,
and requested more troops.
The provincial capital's troops were exhausted,
so Chén Jìngxuan (陳敬瑄) searched all the soldiers from the warehouses and gates to provide to them.
In this month,
a major battle took place at Gānqī (乾谿).
According to the following text,
at this time the various bandits had reached Shuāngliú (雙流),
and were arrayed against the government troops.
Gānqī (乾谿) must be within the borders of Shuāngliú (雙流).
Qián (乾)
has the sound of gān (干).
Xíngqiān (行遷) and others, fearing punishment for lack of achievement,
seized many villagers as captives and sent them to the provincial capital,
dozens or hundreds daily.
Jìngxuan (敬瑄) did not question them,
and had them all beheaded.
Among them were also old and weak people and women;
observers sometimes asked them,
and they all said:
"We were just farming and spinning hemp,
when government troops suddenly entered the village,
tied us up and brought us here.
We truly don't know what crime we committed!"
9 In autumn,
seventh month,
on the day Jǐsì,
Zhōng Chuán was appointed Observer of Jiāngxī,
in accordance with Gāo Pián's request.
After Chuán had departed Fúzhōu,
Wēi Quánfěng, a native of Nánchéng, reoccupied it.
Nánchéng
was an ancient county in the Hàn dynasty,
and belonged to Fúzhōu in the Táng dynasty.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states
it was two hundred and twenty *lǐ* west of Fúzhōu.
10 Shàng Ràng attacked Yíjūn fort.
In the seventh year of Tàipíng Zhēnjūn of the Later Wèi,
Yíjūn County was established in Yíjūn Chuān.
Later, Yíjūn Commandery was established.
The Suí abolished the commandery and made it Yíjūn County.
The Táng incorporated Yíjūn County into Huáyuan County of Jīngzhào.
At this time, the armies serving the emperor had set up a fort at the former Yíjūn County.
Two or three tenths of the rebels froze to death.
11 Hán Qiú, a man from Shǔ, gathered several thousand followers to support Qiānnéng.
The Kǎoyì states: Zhāng Qíjiù's biography says:
"In the sixth month of the third year,
Hán Qiú rebelled,
and the rebel leader Qiānnéng from Qióngzhōu gradually encroached upon Shǔzhōu territory."
We now follow the biography of Gōu Yánqìng and the *Shílù*.
12 Zhōu Bǎo, the Military Governor of Zhènhǎi, reported that Gāo Pián had, on his own authority, appointed the rebel leader Sūn Duān as Observer of Xuānshè.
An imperial edict ordered Bǎo and Péi Qiányú, the Observer of Xuānshè, to raise troops to resist him.
13 Nánzhào submitted a memorial requesting the princess to be sent early.
When Guīnián, the Heir to Prince Cáo, was an envoy to Nánzhào,
the emperor appointed a宗室 (zōngshì) woman as Grand Princess Ānhuà
and promised the marriage.
The Kǎoyì states: Zhāng Qíjiù's biography says:
"On the third day of the ninth month of the first year of Zhōnghé,
Yúnnán's *Biāoxìn* sent *bùxiè* Yáng Qígōng and others bearing a state letter to make peace
and welcome the princess.
The Grand Tutor, borrowing the protocol for a deputy envoy, went out to the suburbs to welcome them.
When the *bùxiè* first met,
he bowed to the deputy envoy and said, 'Please do not prostrate.'
When the Grand Tutor heard this,
he was extremely angry.
The court informed them that they would await further discussion and the finalization of the carriage and attire regulations.
Subsequently, there was an imperial decree,
and they ultimately returned empty-handed."
We now follow the Yúnnán Shìzhuàng and the *Shílù*.
14 Dōngfāng Kuí, the Acting Military Governor of Bǎodà, was appointed Military Governor
and concurrently Commissioner for Pacification and Annihilation of the Eastern Sector of the Capital's Marching Army.
According to the records, Lǐ Xiàochāng led his Fúshī army to serve the emperor.
Last year, he was attacked by Huáng Cháo
and fled back to his own circuit.
Dōngfāng Kuí likely replaced Lǐ Xiàochāng.
15 In the intercalary month,
Hán Jiǎn, the Military Governor of Wèibó, was additionally granted the concurrent title of Shìzhōng.
16 In the eighth month,
Zhèng Shàoyè, Minister of the Board of War and Administrator of Finance, was appointed Grand Councilor with the concurrent title of Military Governor of Jīngnán.
17 Liú Hàn-hóng, the Observer of Zhèdōng, dispatched his younger brother Hàn-yòu and Xīn Yuē, the Commander of Cavalry and Infantry, leading twenty thousand troops to encamp at Xīlíng,
planning to annex Zhèxī.
Dǒng Chāng, the Prefect of Hángzhōu, sent Qián Liú, the General-in-Chief of Military Affairs, to resist them.
On the day Rénzǐ,
Liú crossed the river at night under fog,
raided their camp,
and utterly routed them.
Almost all of them were killed.
Hàn-yòu and Xīn Yuē both fled.
From this point, Háng and Yuè engaged in warfare,
and Liú Hàn-hóng was captured by Qián Liú.
The character Liú
is read as *lìqiú fān*.
18 Hán Jiǎn, the Military Governor of Wèibó, also harbored ambitions of annexation.
He personally led thirty thousand troops to attack Héyáng,
and defeated Zhūgě Shuǎng at Xiūwǔ.
Shuǎng abandoned the city and fled.
Jiǎn left troops to garrison it, then plundered Xíng and Míng before returning.
19 Lǐ Guóchāng led his clan from Dádá to relocate to Dàizhōu.
Since Lǐ Kèyòng had already occupied Dàizhōu,
his father led his clan back from Dádá.
The character Shuài
is read as *shuài*.
20 Zhū Wēn, appointed Defense Commissioner of Tóngzhōu by Huáng Cháo, repeatedly requested additional troops to defend Hézhōng.
Mèng Kǎi, who was in charge of military affairs of the right army, suppressed him
and did not report it.
Wēn saw Huáng Cháo's military power shrinking daily,
and knew he was on the verge of ruin.
His close generals, Hú Zhēn and Xiè Tóng, advised Wēn to return to the imperial court.
In the ninth month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
Wēn killed his army supervisor Yán Shí
and surrendered the entire prefecture to Wáng Chóngróng.
Wēn treated Chóngróng as an uncle.
Wēn's mother, Lady Wáng,
shared the same surname as Chóngróng,
hence he treated Chóngróng as an uncle.
The character Jiān
is read as *gǔxián fān*.
The character Jiàng
is read as *hùjiāng fān*.
The character Chóng
is read as *zhílóng fān*.
He had Tóng present a memorial to the temporary imperial residence.
Zhū Wēn returned to the Táng through Wáng Chóngróng,
but Chóngróng's descendants were exterminated by Zhū Wēn,
and the Táng dynasty's reign was also extinguished by Wēn.
The character Huá
is read as *hùhuà fān*;
the same below.
He was a man from Fúzhōu.
Lǐ Xiáng, seeing that Chóngróng treated Wēn generously,
also wished to surrender to him,
but was reported by the army supervisor.
Huáng Cháo killed him.
Xiáng occupied Huázhōu, as mentioned in the previous volume for the preceding year.
21 There was a mutiny in Guìzhōu army.
They drove out the Military Governor, Zhāng Cóngxùn,
and appointed Cuī Zhuó, the former Military Commissioner of Róngguǎn, as Military Governor of Língnán Xīdào.
22 Wáng Jìngwǔ, a major general of Pínglú, expelled the Military Governor Ān Shīrú
and made himself Acting Military Governor.
23 Initially,
the court appointed Tāng Dǐng, a surrendered general of Páng Xùn, as Prefect of Lánzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Lánzhōu
was the territory of Fényáng County in the Hàn dynasty.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
there were no commanderies or counties in this area.
Cáo Gōng then established Xīnxīng Commandery here.
At the end of the Later Wèi dynasty, Lánzhōu was established here,
named after Mount Kělán within its borders.
The character Jiàng
is read as *hùjiāng fān*.
The character Jiāng
is read as *jíliàng fān*.
The character Lán
is read as *lúhán fān*.
The court suspected him,
and transferred Dǐng to be Prefect of Huáizhōu.
Zhèng Cóngdàng dispatched an envoy bearing a letter of appointment to bestow it upon him.
In winter,
tenth month,
on the first day of Gēngzǐ,
Dǐng killed the envoy,
occupied the city and rebelled,
allying himself with the Shātuó.
On the day Rén Yín,
Cóngdàng dispatched Zhāng Yánqiú, the Commander of Cavalry and Infantry, to lead troops to suppress him.
24 The rebel leaders Hán Xiùshēng and Qū Xíngcóng raised an army,
blocking the Xiájiāng road.
On the day Guǐchǒu,
Chén Jìngxuan dispatched his staff officer Zhuāng Mèngdié to lead two thousand men to suppress them.
The Kǎoyì states: Zhāng Qíjiù's biography says:
"In the third year,
ninth month,
Hán Xiùshēng, a rebel from the canyon road.
Tenth month,
Qū Xíngcóng, a rebel from the canyon road, rebelled.
Grand Tutor Chén dispatched staff officer Zhuāng Èrmèng to lead two thousand men,
and on the twentieth day of the tenth month,
they set off for the canyon road."
Gōu Yánqìng's biography states, under the rebellion of Hán Qiú in the seventh month of the second year of Zhōnghé,
it also says:
"Hán Xiùshēng and Qū Xíngcóng from the canyon road rebelled.
The Lord of Chuān selected and mustered three thousand soldiers,
and dispatched staff officer Zhuāng Mèngdié to lead them.
On the day Guǐchǒu of the tenth month,
they set off for the canyon road
to suppress Hán Xiùshēng."
This is probably referring to the suppression in the tenth month.
The *Shílù* adopted Gōu's biography,
but mistakenly stated under the seventh month:
"Hán Xiùshēng and Qū Xíngcóng caused chaos.
Jìngxuan dispatched Major General Zhuāng Mèngdié with three thousand troops to suppress them."
The Xīn Chuán says:
"Hán Xiùshēng, the Prefect of Fúzhōu, and others rebelled in the canyons."
We now follow Gōu's biography.
31 Lǐ Xiáng (李詳) was formerly a common soldier who, with others, pursued Huáng Sīyè (黃思鄴).
The `Kǎoyì (考異)` states: The `Shílù (實錄)` says:
"Lǐ Xiáng (李詳) led the 'Yáyì (牙隊)' soldiers to slay the pseudo-Inspector, Huáng Sīyè (黃思鄴).
They promoted Wáng Yù (王遇), the Garrison Commissioner of Huáyīn (華陰), as their leader,
and surrendered to Hézhōng (河中).
Wáng Duó (王鐸), acting under imperial authority, appointed Yù (遇) as Inspector."
However, Huáng Yè (黃鄴) and Huáng Cháo (黃巢) both died in Hǔlánggǔ (虎狼谷),
so the `Shílù (實錄)` is mistaken.
We now follow the new `Huáng Cháo Zhuàn (黃巢傳)`.
(Yù (遇)) surrendered Huázhōu (華州) to Wáng Chóngróng (王重榮).
Wáng Duó (王鐸), acting under imperial authority, appointed Yù (遇) as Inspector.
32 Qiānnēng's (阡能) faction became increasingly rampant,
gradually infiltrating the territory of Shǔzhōu (蜀州).
The phrase "qīnyín (侵淫)"
is used as a metaphor for the gradual erosion and spread of an ulcer or boil.
(The governor) appointed the staff officer Gāo Rénhòu (高仁厚) as the Commissioner for Overall Pacification and Command,
and sent him with five hundred soldiers to replace (the current commander).
The day before his departure,
a vendor selling `mài mǐ (⿺麥丏)`
entered and exited the camp several times from dawn until noon.
The guards suspected him,
seized and interrogated him,
and indeed, he was a spy for Qiānnēng (阡能).
Rénhòu (仁厚) ordered his bonds released,
and kindly questioned him.
He replied:
"I am a villager.
Qiānnēng (阡能) imprisoned my parents, wife, and children,
saying,
'If you return after scouting,
and bring back accurate information, your family will be spared;
otherwise,
all will die.'
I did not wish to do this."
Rénhòu (仁厚) said:
"I truly know your situation,
how could I bear to kill you!
I will now release you to return
and save your parents, wife, and children.
Just tell Qiānnēng (阡能): 'High Minister Gāo (高尚書) will set out tomorrow,
bringing only five hundred men;
there are not many soldiers.'
However, since I am saving your entire family,
you must secretly tell the people in the stronghold for me: 'The Commander (僕射) pities all of you good people,
who are controlled by the rebels,
and for whom there is no alternative.
The High Minister (尚書) wishes to save and cleanse you all.
When the High Minister arrives,
you should all abandon your weapons, come forward, and surrender.
The High Minister will have people write the character
"Guīshùn (歸順)"
on your backs,
and send you back to your former occupations.
The only ones to be executed
are Qiānnēng (阡能), Luó Húnqíng (羅渾擎), Gōu Húsēng (句胡僧), Luó Fūzǐ (羅夫子), and Hán Qiú (韓求) — these five men.
He will certainly not harm the common people indiscriminately.'"
The spy replied:
"These are all the sincere desires of the common people.
If the High Minister (尚書) knows all this and pardons them,
who would not dance for joy and obey his command!
One mouth will spread it to a hundred,
a hundred to a thousand;
like rivers surging and seas boiling,
it cannot be stopped.
By the time the High Minister arrives,
the common people will surely all rush to him like infants seeing their kind mother.
Qiānnēng (阡能) will be isolated,
and will be captured immediately!"
The next day,
Rénhòu (仁厚) led his troops and set out.
When they reached Shuāngliú (雙流),
Bái Wénxiàn (白文現), the Commissioner of Interception, came out to welcome them.
Rénhòu (仁厚) looked around at the trenches and palisades,
and angrily said:
"Qiānnēng's (阡能) laborers,
whose followers are all just farming people,
yet an entire prefectural army, for over a year, could not capture them!
Now I see the trenches and palisades are repeatedly and tightly constructed like this;
no wonder they could sleep soundly and eat their fill,
nurturing the bandits and seeking credit!"
He ordered Wénxiàn (文現) to be brought out and executed.
The Supervising Censor (監軍) vehemently pleaded for his life,
and after a long time,
he was finally spared.
Rénhòu (仁厚) ordered all the trenches and palisades leveled,
leaving only five hundred soldiers to guard them.
All the remaining soldiers he took with him.
He also summoned troops from various strongholds,
and they gathered one after another.
When Qiānnēng (阡能) heard that Rénhòu (仁厚) was approaching,
he sent Luó Húnqíng (羅渾擎) to establish five strongholds west of Shuāngliú (雙流),
and ambushed a thousand soldiers in the Yěqiáo Jìng (野橋箐) to intercept the government army.
Shǔ (蜀) people refer to a dense bamboo grove as a `jìng (箐)`.
Lǐ Xīnchuán (李心傳) said: `Jìng (箐)`
refers to a forest grove,
pronounced with a `zī yíng` (咨盈) initial.
Moreover, Xuē Néng (薛能), who was skilled in regulated verse,
wrote two lines in his `Biānchéng Zuò (邊城作)`:
"The scattered Man (蠻) households are distant,
the bird's nest in the `jìng (箐)` is solitary."
He self-noted: "Shǔ (蜀) people refer to tax-paying households as `páihù (排戶)`,
and to forests as `cóngjìng (叢箐)`."
Shǐ Zhào (史炤) said: `Jìng (箐)`,
pronounced `cāng diàn qiè` (倉甸切),
probably takes the falling tone,
which is also permissible.
(Rénhòu (仁厚)) led his troops to besiege it,
ordering no killing.
He sent people in plain clothes into the enemy ranks to announce
what he had said to the spy yesterday.
The bandits were greatly pleased,
shouting and clamoring,
scrambling to abandon their armor and weapons to surrender,
bowing as if mountains were collapsing.
Rénhòu (仁厚) graciously appeased them all,
writing on their backs
the character
"Guīshùn (歸順)"
on their backs.
The remaining people in the stronghold scrambled out to surrender.
Húnqíng (渾擎) fled in panic,
leaping over the palisade.
His followers seized him and brought him to Rénhòu (仁厚).
Rénhòu (仁厚) said:
"This is a fool,
not worth speaking to."
He was shackled and sent to the prefectural office.
Rénhòu (仁hou) ordered all five strongholds and their armor and weapons burned,
keeping only the banners.
A total of four thousand people surrendered.
The next morning,
Rénhòu (仁厚) said to the surrendered:
"Initially, I wanted to send you back immediately,
but the common people in the strongholds ahead do not yet know my intentions.
They might have worries or doubts.
I will use you to go ahead for me,
passing by Chuānkǒu (穿口) and Xīnjīn (新津) Stronghold,
showing them the character on your backs and announcing it.
Chuānkǒu (穿口)
is the newly dug mouth of Xīnjīn (新津).
The character `wéi` (為)
is pronounced `yú wěi` (于偽) reverse initial.
Then you may return."
The `Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志)` states that
in Ānrén (安仁) County of Qióngzhōu (邛州) there is Yángòng (延貢) Stronghold.
Ānrén (安仁) was the territory of Línqióng (臨邛) County in the Qín (秦) dynasty.
In the second year of Wǔdé (武德),
Ānrén (安仁) County was established.
The `Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志)`: The county is thirty-eight `lǐ` (里) northeast of Qióngzhōu (邛州).
Every fifty people formed a squad,
waving banners and shouting loudly:
"Luó Húnqíng (羅渾擎) has already been captured alive
and sent to the Commander's (使府) office.
The main army is approaching.
All of you in the strongholds,
quickly come out and surrender like us,
and you will immediately become good citizens;
there will be no trouble!"
When they reached Chuānkǒu (穿口),
where Gōu Húsēng (句胡僧) had set up eleven strongholds,
the people in the strongholds scrambled out to surrender.
Húsēng (胡僧) was greatly alarmed,
drew his sword to stop them,
but the crowd threw bricks and stones at him,
collectively seizing him and presenting him to Rénhòu (仁厚).
His five thousand and more followers all surrendered.
The next morning,
(Rénhòu (仁厚)) burned the strongholds,
making the surrendered carry banners and lead the way.
Just as they went from Shuāngliú (雙流) to Xīnjīn (新津),
Hán Qiú (韓求) had set up thirteen strongholds, and all welcomed surrender.
Qiú (求) himself threw himself into a deep trench,
but his followers hooked him out.
He was already dead;
they cut off his head and presented it.
The officers and soldiers wanted to burn the strongholds,
but Rénhòu (仁厚) stopped them, saying:
"The surrendered people have not yet eaten."
He ordered them to first transport out the provisions,
and then burn them.
The newly surrendered eagerly cooked their meals,
and ate with those who had surrendered earlier and brought the message,
talking, laughing, singing, and playing musical instruments.
"Gē (歌)"
refers to singing aloud.
"Chuī (吹)" refers to playing instruments like the `shēng` (笙) and `dí` (笛).
The next day,
Rén-hòu (仁厚) allowed the surrenderers from Shuāng-liú (雙流) and Chuān-kǒu (穿口) to return home first.
He then had the surrenderers from Xīn-jīn (新津) carry flags and lead the way,
saying:
"Once you enter the territory of Qióng-zhōu (邛州),
you may disperse and return home."
Luó-fū-zǐ (羅夫子) had established nine strongholds in Yán-gòng (延貢).
His followers, the previous night, seeing the firelight from Xīn-jīn (新津),
had already been unable to sleep.
When the Xīn-jīn (新津) people arrived,
Luó-fū-zǐ (羅夫子) escaped, abandoned his strongholds, and fled to Qiān-néng (阡能).
His followers all surrendered.
The next day,
Luó-fū-zǐ (羅夫子) reached Qiān-néng’s (阡能) stronghold.
He plotted with him to gather all their forces for a decisive battle.
Before the plan was finalized,
as dusk approached,
surrenderers from Yán-gòng (延貢) arrived.
Qiān-néng (阡能) and Luó-fū-zǐ (羅夫子) rode around inspecting the strongholds,
intending to deploy troops,
but the followers all refused to respond.
Rén-hòu (仁厚) led his troops to press on them overnight.
The next morning,
the various strongholds, knowing that the main army was close,
shouted and clamored, rushing out to
seize Qiān-néng (阡能).
Qiān-néng (阡能), in his distress, jumped into a well,
but was captured by the crowd
and did not die.
They also captured Luó-fū-zǐ (羅夫子),
who then committed suicide by cutting his own throat.
The crowd carried Luó-fū-zǐ’s (羅夫子) head,
bound Qiān-néng (阡能),
and drove them forward to meet the government army.
Upon seeing Rén-hòu (仁厚),
they surrounded his horse, shouting, crying, and bowing, saying:
"The common people have suffered injustice for a long time,
with nowhere to lodge a complaint.
Since the spy returned,
it was precisely the peddler (yù-mái-zhě 鬻⿺麥丏者) released by Rén-hòu (仁厚).
Every moment felt like a year.
Now, meeting the Shàng-shū (尚書),
is like emerging from the nine springs to see the daylight,
like dying and then being reborn."
Their clamor could not be stopped.
*Huān* (讙)
is synonymous with *xuān* (諠).
Rén-hòu (仁厚) dispatched his generals to receive their surrender.
Rén-hòu (仁厚) campaigned for a total of six days,
and all five bandits were pacified.
According to the *Jiǔ-yù-zhì* (九域志),
Shuāng-liú (雙流) county is forty *lǐ* (里) south of Chéng-dū (成都).
From there south,
to Xīn-chuān-kǒu (新穿口),
then south to Xīn-jīn (新津),
then south to Yán-gòng (延貢),
then south to Qiān-néng-zhài (阡能寨).
Estimating the distances between them,
each is no more than forty or fifty *lǐ* (里).
Gāo Rén-hòu (高仁厚) knew that the people of Shǔ (蜀) did not willingly follow rebellion,
but were coerced by the power of the five bandits.
He used their mindset to guide them,
hence all those coerced immediately surrendered,
and the army advanced without delay, pacifying the five bandits.
*Kǎo-yì* (考異) states: Zhāng Qí-jiù's (張耆舊) biography says:
"In the winter of the third year of Zhōng-hé (中和) (883 CE),
Qiān-néng (千能) became increasingly powerful,
and the government army was constantly defeated in battle.
Chén Jìng-xuān (陳敬瑄) then sent Rén-hòu (仁厚) to suppress him.
On the fifth day of the eleventh month,
Rén-hòu (仁厚) set out.
On the sixth day,
he captured Luó Hún-qíng (羅渾擎).
On the seventh day,
he captured Gōu Hú-sēng (句胡僧)
and obtained Hán Qiú’s (韓求) head.
On the ninth day,
he captured Qiān-néng (千能)
and obtained Luó-fū-zǐ’s (羅夫子) head.
On the twenty-second day of the eleventh month, he returned,
entering through the north gate of the city.
Three days later, a grand banquet was held.
Five days later, his merits were discussed.
Gāo Gōng (高公) was promoted from *Jiǎn-xiào Bīng-bù Shàng-shū* (檢校兵部尚書) to *Jiǎn-xiào Zuǒ Pú-shè* (檢校左僕射)
and appointed *Méi-zhōu Cì-shǐ* (眉州刺史)."
Although Zhāng’s (張) writing is colloquial and shallow,
and contains some contradictions,
it narrates events in great detail.
If not for this book,
Rén-hòu's (仁厚) achievements would have been completely lost.
Gōu Yán-qìng’s (句延慶) biography says:
"In the second year of Zhōng-hé (中和) (882 CE),
Rén-hòu (仁厚) beheaded the five bandits
and returned triumphantly to the prefecture.
In the winter, on the *wù-yín* (戊寅) day of the twelfth month,
the Emperor ascended the Dà-xuán-lóu (大玄樓),
and Gāo Rén-hòu (高仁厚) and his generals and officers paid their respects at the Qīng-yuǎn-qiáo (清遠橋).
Three days later,
a grand banquet was held,
and Gāo Rén-hòu (高仁厚) was appointed *Méi-zhōu Cì-shǐ* (眉州刺史)."
Yán-qìng (延慶) does not state what book he used to know that Qiān-néng's (千能) defeat was in the winter of the second year.
However, if Rén-hòu (仁厚) captured Hán Xiù-shēng (韓秀昇) before the tenth month of the third year,
then his capture of Qiān-néng (千能) must have been even earlier.
In the twelfth month,
the first day (*shuò* 朔) was *jǐ-hài* (己亥);
there was no *wù-yín* (戊寅) day.
The date must be mistaken.
The *Shí-lù* (實錄) (Veritable Records) states:
"In the tenth month of the second year,
the rebel Qiān-néng (阡能) defeated the government army in Shǔ-zhōu (蜀州).
Chén Jìng-xuān (陳敬瑄) sent Gāo Rén-hòu (高仁厚) to suppress him."
The *Shí-lù* (實錄) mentions Gōu's (句) biography describing the campaign against Qiān-néng (阡能),
which follows the entry about the tenth month, *guǐ-chǒu* (癸丑) day, when troops were dispatched via the Xiá (峽) route to suppress Hán Xiù-shēng (韓秀昇),
and it was appended there.
The tenth month is also a mistake.
The *Shí-lù* (實錄) further states:
"In the twelfth month,
Rén-hòu (仁厚) presented Qiān-néng's (阡能) head.
The Emperor ascended the Dà-xuán-lóu (大玄樓) to express comfort to the returning generals and soldiers.
Rén-hòu (仁厚) was appointed *Jiǎn-xiào Gōng-bù Shàng-shū* (檢校工部尚書) and *Méi-zhōu Fáng-yù-shǐ* (眉州防禦使)."
This entry also follows Gōu's (句) biography, omitting the specific date.
Moreover, in the tenth month of this year, *wù-chén* (戊辰) day,
the prefectures of Méi (眉), Hàn (漢), Péng (彭), Mián (綿), etc., were all promoted to *Fáng-yù-shǐ* (防禦使) (Defense Commissioners),
which is why *Cì-shǐ* (刺史) (Prefect) was changed to *Fáng-yù* (防禦).
Since the exact month and year of Gāo Rén-hòu’s (高仁厚) capture of Qiān-néng (阡能) are unknown,
it is recorded here based on the *Shí-lù* (實錄).
He was then provisionally appointed *Zhèn-è-shǐ* (鎮遏使) (Suppressing and Stopping Commissioner)
to settle the households.
Thereupon, Chén Jìng-xuān (陳敬瑄) displayed the heads of Hán Qiú (韓求) and Luó-fū-zǐ (羅夫子) in the marketplace
and impaled Qiān-néng (阡能) and Luó Hún-qíng (羅渾擎) at
the west side of the city.
After seven days, they were [AS-FE47] removed.
Qiān-néng’s (阡能) registrar, Zhāng Róng (張榮),
originally a *jìn-shì* (進士) from Ān-rén (安仁),
had repeatedly failed the examinations.
He then joined Qiān-néng (阡能),
becoming his chief strategist
and writing his manifestos.
After Qiān-néng's (阡能) defeat,
he sought mercy from Rén-hòu (仁厚) with a poem.
Rén-hòu (仁厚) sent him to the prefecture,
where he was impaled in the horse market.
Apart from these, not a single person was executed.
In the twelfth month,
Rén-hòu (仁厚) was appointed *Méi-zhōu Fáng-yù-shǐ* (眉州防禦使).
Chén Jìng-xuān (陳敬瑄) posted a proclamation in Qióng-zhōu (邛州),
stating that all close relatives of Qiān-néng (阡能) and others would not be investigated.
Not long after,
the *Cì-shǐ* (刺史) of Qióng-zhōu (邛州) reported that Qiān-néng’s (阡能) uncle, Xíng-quán (行全), and his entire family of thirty-five people had been arrested and imprisoned,
requesting permission to apply the law.
"Apply the law" meant that relatives of rebels were to be implicated and executed.
Someone replied:
"The Duke (Gōng 公) has already issued a proclamation
ordering no investigation,
yet the *Cì-shǐ* (刺史) has again arrested them.
There must be a reason for this.
If we kill them now,
not only will it cause the Duke to lose great trust,
but I fear that Qiān-néng's (阡能) party will rise up again in confusion!"
Jìng-xuān (敬瑄) followed this advice,
dispatching his *yā-yá* (押牙) Niú Yūn (牛暈).
He gathered the people at the prefecture gate,
broke the fetters, and released them.
He then inquired into the reason,
and it turned out that Xíng-quán (行全) indeed possessed fertile land,
which the *Cì-shǐ* (刺史) wanted to buy.
Xíng-quán (行全) refused to sell it,
so the *Cì-shǐ* (刺史) resented him.
Jìng-xuān (敬瑄) summoned the *Cì-shǐ* (刺史),
intending to prosecute him,
but the *Cì-shǐ* (刺士) died of grief.
Another day,
Xíng-quán (行全), hearing that his family was spared due to Xī (溪),
secretly sent Xī (溪) a hundred *liǎng* (兩) of *shí-bó-jīn* (蝕箔金) (etched foil gold) as a reward.
The *Bó-wén-lù* (博聞錄) states: "There are *shí-bó-jīn* (蝕箔金), *fǎ-jīn* (法金), and fractional gold pieces. The fractional gold pieces are beaten into thin sheets.

One *liǎng* (兩) of yellow alum, one *liǎng* (兩) of chicken manure alum, half a *liǎng* (兩) of copper sulfate, one *fēn* (分) of saltpeter, one *liǎng* (兩) of *xìn-tǔ* (信土), and one *liǎng* (兩) of red earth are ground and mixed.
This is then mixed with saline water and brushed onto the gold sheets, which are then heated until dry.
This process of brushing and heating is repeated.
After three such repetitions,
a layer of cow dung ash is applied.
It is then placed in a crucible over a strong fire and calcined for one day. Afterwards, it is removed
and washed clean with warm water.
What remains is gold;
what is etched away is silver.
" "This is Grand Preceptor Rén-míng (仁明),
Chén Jìng-xuān (陳敬瑄) was *Jiǎn-xiào Tài-shī* (檢校太師),
hence he is referred to as such.
Are you sending a reward with malicious intent?"
He returned the gold
and expelled Xíng-quán (行全).
The historians say that Táng Xī (唐溪) possessed the demeanor of an ancient gentleman.
33 Zhèng Cóng-dǎng (鄭從讜), Military Commissioner of Hé-dōng (河東), reported the capture of Lán-zhōu (嵐州),
arrested Tāng Húi (湯㣥),
and beheaded him.
Tāng Húi (湯㣥) had surrendered the city to the Shā-tuó (沙陀).
34 Lǐ Kè-yòng (李克用), Provisional Military Commissioner of Xīn (忻) and Dài (代) prefectures, was appointed Military Commissioner of Yàn-mén (鴈門).
35 Initially,
the imperial court appointed Zhèng Shàoyè [鄭紹業] as Jīngnán [荊南] Jiedùshǐ [節度使].
At that time, Duàn Yànmó [段彥謨] was in control of Jīngnán [荊南].
Shàoyè [紹業] was wary of him,
and it was more than half a year
before he arrived at his post.
When the Emperor went to Shǔ [蜀],
he recalled Shàoyè [紹業]
and made Yànmó [彥謨] the Jiedùshǐ [節度使].
Yànmó [彥謨] was killed by Zhū Jìngméi [朱敬玫].
In the third month of that year,
Zhū Jìngméi [朱敬玫] killed Duàn Yànmó [段彥謨].
Shàoyè [紹業] feared Jìngméi [敬玫],
delayed his advance,
and the army was without a commander for a long time.
By this time,
Jìngméi [敬玫] had appointed the Yāyá [押牙] Chén Rú [陳儒] to oversee the prefecture.
Rú [儒]
was from Jiānglíng [江陵].
36 Jiā [加] Fèntiān [奉天] Jiedùshǐ [節度使] Qí Kèjiǎn [齊克儉] and Hézhōng [河中] Jiedùshǐ [節度使] Wáng Chóngróng [王重榮] were both given the title Tóng Píngzhāngshì [同平章事].
37 Lǐ Kèyòng [李克用] led an army of forty thousand to Hézhōng [河中].
The *Kǎoyì* [考異] says: The *Shílù* [實錄] places this in the first month of the following year.
We follow the *Xīn* [新], *Tàizǔ Jìniánlù* [太祖紀年錄], and Xuē Jūzhèng’s [薛居正] *Wǔdài Shǐ* [五代史].
*Cháng* [嘗],
means *shì* [試] (to test).
Kèyòng’s [克用] younger brother Kèrang [克讓] was killed by a monk at Nánshān Temple [南山寺].
His servant Hún Jìntōng [渾進通] went over to Huáng Cháo [黃巢].
Since Gāo Xún’s [高潯] defeat,
(Xún’s [潯] defeat
is discussed in the previous volume, previous year).
no one dared to advance.
When Kèyòng’s [克用] army arrived,
the rebels feared them,
saying:
"The Yājūn [鵶軍] has arrived!
We must avoid their sharp edge."
Kèyòng’s [克用] soldiers all wore black,
hence they were called the Yājūn [鵶軍].
Cháo [巢] then captured more than ten monks from Nánshān Temple [南山寺],
and sent an envoy with an imperial edict and heavy bribes,
using Hún Jìntōng [渾進通] to approach Kèyòng [克用] to seek peace.
Kèyòng [克用] killed the monks,
wept for Kèrang [克讓],
accepted the bribes and distributed them among his generals,
burned the imperial edict,
and sent the envoy back.
The *Kǎoyì* [考異] says: The *Tàizǔ Jìniánlù* [太祖紀年錄] states:
"Initially,
Kèrang [克讓] was defeated in battle at Tóngguān [潼關].
He fled from the rebels to Nánshān [南山],
hiding in a Buddhist temple.
At night,
he was killed by a mountain monk.
His steward, Hún Jìntōng [渾進通], escaped by charging through weapons [冒刃]
and went over to Huáng Cháo [黃巢].
The rebels had always feared Tàizǔ [太祖].
Hearing of his arrival,
they intended to seek good relations,
so they captured more than ten monks who had harmed Kèrang [克讓]
and killed them.
Cháo [巢] ordered his general Mǐ Zhòngwēi [米重威] to bring heavy bribes and a false edict,
using Hún Jìntōng [渾進通] to meet Tàizǔ [太祖].
He then summoned his generals,
took their bribes,
and publicly burned their false edict."
Xuē Shǐ [薛史] *Kèrang Zhuàn* [克讓傳] says:
"During the Qiánfú [乾符] period,
he was granted the title of Jīnwú Jiāngjūn [金吾將軍] for his achievements
and remained as a palace guard.
Originally,
when Yìzǔ [懿祖] returned to court,
Xiànzōng [憲宗] granted him a residence in Qīnrén Fāng [親仁坊].
When Wǔhuáng [武皇] rose up in Yúnzhōng [雲中] and killed Duàn Wénchǔ [段文楚],
the emperor ordered the inspector Wáng Chǔcún [王處存] to surround Qīnrén Fāng [親仁坊] by night
and capture Kèrang [克讓].
At dawn,
the armies clashed.
Kèrang [克讓] and more than ten horsemen drew their bows and spurred their horses,
breaking through the encirclement.
Several thousand government troops pursued them.
By the time they reached Wèiqiáo [渭橋],
hundreds had died.
Kèrang [克讓] seized a boat at Xiàyáng [夏陽] and crossed the river,
returning to Yànmén [鴈門]."
We note that Kèrang [克讓] (this Kèrang [克讓] should probably be Kèyòng [克用])
was still in Yúnzhōu [雲州] at that time.
Saying Yànmén [鴈門]
is an error.
The *Hòutáng Yìzǔ Jìniánlù* [後唐懿祖紀年錄] says:
"His elder brothers Kègōng [克恭] and Kèjiǎn [克儉] were both executed."
We note that at this time, Guóchāng [國昌] was still requesting to attack Kèyòng [克用],
so the imperial court would certainly not have executed his sons.
It was probably after Guóchāng [國昌] and Zhènwǔ [振武] refused to be replaced
that Kègōng [克恭] and Kèjiǎn [克儉] were executed.
Xuē Shǐ [薛史] also says:
"The following year,
Wǔhuáng [武皇] was cleared of wrongdoing,
and Kèrang [克讓] re-entered the palace guard.
When Huáng Cháo [黃巢] attacked the capital,
Xīzōng [僖宗] fled to Shǔ [蜀].
Kèrang [克讓] was guarding Tóngguān [潼關] at that time
and was defeated by the rebels."
We note that Guóchāng [國昌] refused to be replaced in the fifth year of Qiánfú [乾符]
and the imperial court sent troops to attack him.
In the sixth year,
Kèyòng [克用] was never cleared of wrongdoing.
How could Kèrang [克讓] have entered the palace guard?
In the first year of Guǎngmíng [廣明],
Guóchāng [國昌] and his son's army were defeated
and they fled to the Dádá [達靼].
In the winter of that year,
Huáng Cháo [黃巢] captured Cháng'ān [長安].
How could Kèrang [克讓] have been guarding Tóngguān [潼關], been defeated in battle, and died in a Buddhist temple?
Perhaps when he was surrounded and captured by the imperial court,
he fled to a Buddhist temple in Nánshān [南山]
and was killed by a monk.
That is unknown.
Since the matter is now difficult to clarify,
we merely state that he was killed by a temple monk.
In the third year of Wǔdé [武德],
Héyáng [郃陽] was divided to establish Héxī Xiàn [河西縣].
In the third year of Qiányuán [乾元],
Héxī [河西] was renamed Xiàyáng [夏陽],
belonging to Hézhōng Fǔ [河中府],
and later belonging to Tóngzhōu [同州].
Xià [夏],
pronunciation: *hù yǎ fān*.
38 Mèng Fānglì, after killing Chéng Lín,
see Volume One, First Year.
The people of Lù requested Supervisor Wú Quánxù to act as Liúhòu.
In this year,
Wáng Duó issued a private decree appointing Mèng Fānglì to manage affairs in Xíngzhōu.
Fānglì refused to accept,
and imprisoned Quánxù;
he wrote a letter to Duó,
