refusing Duó's command yet writing to Duó,
hoping to achieve his private desires.
Duó then appointed Zhèng Chāngtú to manage affairs of the Zhāoyì Army.
Subsequently, the court appointed Wáng Huī, Right Minister of the Department of State Affairs and Commissioner of Rent and Taxes, as Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and concurrently Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì.
Huī, seeing that the imperial carriage had been moved,
and the central plains were in turmoil,
and Fānglì exclusively occupied the three prefectures of Xíng, Míng, and Cí in Shāndōng,
he estimated that the court lacked the power to control him.
Xíng, Míng, and Cí,
were considered Shāndōng relative to Lùzhōu.
Duó (estimate),
pronunciation 'tuó luò fān'.
He requested that the appointment be temporarily entrusted to Chāngtú.
An imperial edict appointed Huī as the Liúshǒu of Dàmíng Palace, and Commissioner for Pacifying, Administering, and Repairing Imperial Mausoleums in the metropolitan area.
Dàmíng Palace was also known as Dōngnèi.
At that time, Huáng Cháo still occupied the capital,
Dàmíng Palace had been seized by the rebels,
and many imperial mausoleums had been opened and damaged.
This position was given to Huī,
awaiting recovery.
He departed in less than three months,
and Fānglì then moved the Zhāoyì Army to Xíngzhōu,
proclaimed himself Liúhòu,
and memorialized his general Lǐ Yīnruì as the Cìshǐ of Lùzhōu.
This laid the groundwork for Lùzhōu's rebellion against Mèng Fānglì.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
"In the first month of the fourth year of Zhōnghé,
Zhèng Chāngtú, Acting Sīmǎ of Yìchéng Army, was appointed Zhōngshū Shèrén.
In the third month,
the Xíngzhōu army mutinied,
killing their commander Chéng Lín,
and Zhèng Chāngtú, Zhōngshū Shèrén, was given interim authority as Zhāoyì Liúhòu."
However, Chéng Lín had already been killed by Mèng Fānglì,
and moreover, he was not in Xíngzhōu;
Xíngzhōu was governed by Fānglì.
Furthermore, by then Lùzhōu was already occupied by Lǐ Kèxiū,
so how could Chāngtú go there to be Liúhòu?
Also, in the fifth month of that year,
Wáng Huī, Right Minister of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and concurrently Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì.
Huī submitted a memorial earnestly explaining the inconvenience,
and was then reinstated to his original position as Liúshǒu of Dàmíng Palace.
The old biography of Wáng Huī says:
"Initially,
the Lùzhōu army mutinied,
killing Chéng Lín,
and Zhèng Chāngtú, Minister of War, was given interim authority to manage affairs of the Zhāoyì Army.
At that time, Mèng Fānglì had carved out three prefectures in Shāndōng,
forming a separate commandery.
Shàngdǎng's only dependent prefecture was Zézhōu,
and many among the military personnel favored Fānglì,
whom Chāngtú could not control.
The prime ministers memorialized to request that an important minister be appointed to govern it,
so Huī was granted probationary Left Minister of the Department of State Affairs, Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and Inspector of Zé, Lù, Xíng, Míng, Cí.
At that time, the imperial carriage had not yet returned,
and brigands gathered east of the passes.
Lǐ Kèyòng of Hédōng was contending with Mèng Fānglì for Zé and Lù.
Believing that the court's military strength would surely be insufficient,
Huī submitted a memorial stating: 'Zhèng Chāngtú has been in charge for several months,
and has already established deep roots;
Mèng Fānglì exclusively occupies three prefectures,
leading to accumulated grievances.
If we recruit from outside, the people of Lù will bear resentment;
if we appease those within, the generals of Xíng will grow more suspicious.
Disaster is raging after the burning,
what plan can be made for what is already lost?
We must observe victory and defeat,
then decide safety and danger.
I humbly implore Your Sacred Benevolence to broadly seek counsel from the court,
choose who can be entrusted,
and let reason prevail for the long term.'
The Son of Heaven then appointed Chāngtú to govern it,
and Huī as Commissioner for Rent, Taxes, and Military Supplies for all circuits."
The new biography of Mèng Fānglì says:
"Fānglì attacked Chéng Lín,
beheaded him,
then divided Xíng, Míng, and Cí into a commandery,
made Xíng the prefectural seat,
and named it Zhāoyì Army.
The people of Lù requested Supervisor Wú Quánxù to act as the Army's Liúhòu.
At that time, Wáng Duó commanded the imperial armies of all circuits,
and seeing that Lù was unsettled,
he issued a private decree appointing Fānglì to manage affairs in Xíngzhōu.
Fānglì refused,
imprisoned Quánxù,
and wrote a letter to Duó,
requesting a Confucian scholar to govern Lù.
Duó sent his advisor, Zhōngshū Shèrén Zhèng Chāngtú, to oversee affairs of Zhāoyì,
intending for him to become Jìedùshǐ.
Emperor Xīzōng himself appointed the old prime minister Wáng Huī as Jìedùshǐ.
At that time, the Son of Heaven was in Xīhé,
Guānzhōng was in chaos,
Fānglì had seized territory, and Lǐ Kèyòng was eyeing Lùzhōu.
Huī estimated that the court could not control them,
so he firmly yielded to Chāngtú.
Chāngtú governed for less than three months,
then departed.
Fānglì then memorialized Lǐ Yīnruì as Cìshǐ,
and moved his headquarters to Lónggāng.
Coincidentally, Kèyòng became Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng.
Qí Shěnhuì, an officer of the Zhāoyì Army, requested an army
to restore the Zhāoyì Army.
Kèyòng killed Yīnruì,
then annexed Lùzhōu,
and memorialized Kèxiū as Liúhòu."
According to this, Wáng Duó was dismissed as commander-in-chief in the first month of the third year,
so Chāngtú's appointment as Zhāoyì Liúhòu must have been in the second year.
Chāngtú departed Lù in less than three months.
Since Huī yielded Lù to Chāngtú,
then Huī's appointment as Zhāoyì must not have been in the fifth month of the fourth year.
The dates in the *Shílù* are all incorrect.
If Fānglì had already proclaimed himself Zhāoyì Liúhòu and moved the army's designation to Xíngzhōu,
then he would not have merely occupied three prefectures.
If he wanted to establish a separate commandery,
he should have established a different army name, and certainly would not have called it Zhāoyì alongside Lùzhōu.
If Lù was merely a dependent prefecture,
he should have appointed the Cìshǐ himself,
not written to Wáng Duó again requesting a Confucian scholar;
even if he requested one,
Duó should have appointed Chāngtú as Cìshǐ of Lùzhōu,
not said "managing affairs of the Zhāoyì Army,"
and could not have made Zézhōu a dependent prefecture.
It is probably that after Fānglì killed Chéng Lín,
because Xíngzhōu was his hometown,
he wished to move the commandery there.
Therefore, he went to Xíngzhōu himself,
but the people of Lù did not follow,
so they requested Quánxù as Liúhòu.
Fānglì, seeing that popular sentiment was not settled,
did not dare to establish himself.
Thus, he imprisoned Quánxù,
outwardly showing compliance,
and used the pretext that an ordinary person could not be a commander to request from Wáng Duó
a Confucian scholar.
His intention was that a Confucian scholar would be easy to control,
wishing to outwardly honor him as commander while personally monopolizing the administration of the army,
gradually plotting to replace him.
Subsequently, Chāngtú arrived in Lù,
intending to exercise the commander's authority,
but the three prefectures of Shāndōng were already controlled by Fānglì,
who did not obey the commander's orders.
Only Zézhōu in the south
could still be commanded.
Therefore, Wáng Huī's memorial stated:
"Chāngtú has been in charge for several months,
and has already established deep roots."
This means he had been in Zé and Lù for a long time,
and the people had gradually become attached to him,
something Huī could not match.
It also said:
"Fānglì exclusively occupies three prefectures,
leading to accumulated grievances."
This means Chāngtú wanted to exercise the commander's authority,
but Fānglì did not fulfill his duty as a subordinate general,
and they eyed each other,
thus accumulating grievances.
It also said:
"If we recruit from outside, the people of Lù will bear resentment;
if we appease those within, the generals of Xíng will grow more suspicious."
This means that since Xíng and Lù had already formed a rift,
if Huī went there and showed favor to Xíng, the people of Lù would resent him for favoring the rebel;
if he showed favor to Lù, the generals of Xíng would suspect him of plotting against them.
It also said:
"We must observe victory and defeat,
then decide safety and danger."
This means that only if Chāngtú could defeat Fānglì
would Zhāoyì then be secure.
Chāngtú ultimately did not feel secure in Lù,
so he entrusted the military command to Fānglì and departed.
Fānglì then proclaimed himself Liúhòu,
moved the army's designation to Xíngzhōu,
made Lù a dependent prefecture,
and memorialized Yīnruì as Cìshǐ.
Therefore, the new biography places the relocation of the headquarters to Lónggāng after Yīnruì became Cìshǐ,
which is the evidence for this.
Thereupon, the people of Lù resented this and summoned the Shātuó.
At the time Huī was appointed Jìedù,
Kèyòng still dared not contend for Zé and Lù.
Wú Quánxù
was probably the supervisor when Fānglì first entered the Lù prefectural office.
Therefore, Wáng Duó appointed him Liúhòu.
After Fānglì imprisoned him,
he was probably expelled.
Qí Shěnhuì was probably the supervisor during Zhèng Chāngtú's time.
The *Tàizǔ Jìniánlù* states:
"Fānglì captured Shěnhuì,
and proclaimed himself Liúhòu."
Xuē Jūzhèng's *Wǔdài Shǐ Fānglì Zhuàn* states:
Its text contains
"Slaying Qiānnéng is like cutting grass;
eliminating Xiùshēng is like burning a nest."
Therefore, Xiùshēng's defeat
must have been before this date.
Zhāng Chuán records the defeat of Xiùshēng in the fourth year, fourth month.
In the fourth year, tenth month, tenth day,
it is also recorded that the Tiěquàn was bestowed upon the Chuānzhǔ Tàishī,
and it says:
"In the third year of Zhōnghé, the *guǐmǎo* year,
tenth month, *jiǎzǐ* first day,
fifth day *wùchén*."
The text is the same as in the Bǔlù and Shílù,
such was their senility.
Jù Chuán took Zhāng's account and changed the year;
Shílù used Jù's year but changed the day.
The rise and fall of Qiānnéng, Hán Xiùshēng, and others,
their exact timing is unknown.
Now we follow the Shílù.
17 Lǐ Kèyòng, along with Zhōngwǔ General Páng Cóng, Hézhōng General Bái Zhìqiān, and others, led their troops forward,
and fought the Huáng Cháo army at Wèinán.
They fought three battles in one day,
all victorious.
The Yìchéng, Yìwǔ, and other armies followed,
and the rebel multitude fled in disarray.
On *jiǎchén*,
Kèyòng and others entered the capital through Guāngtài Gate.
Huáng Cháo fought with all his might but could not win,
so he set fire to the palaces and fled.
The Kǎoyì says: The Old Records state:
"In the fourth month,
on *gēngzǐ*,
the Shātuó and other armies advanced towards Cháng'ān.
The rebels resisted them at Wèiqiáo,
were greatly defeated, and returned.
Lǐ Kèyòng pursued them in triumph.
On *jǐmǎo*,
Huáng Cháo gathered his remaining forces
and fled through Lántián Pass.
On *gēngchén*,
the capital city was recovered,
and Yáng Fùguāng announced the victory."
Examining this, the first day of this month was *dīngyǒu*,
so there was no *jǐmǎo* or *gēngchén*.
Jìng Xiáng's Liáng Tàizǔ Biānyílù says:
"In the fourth month, on *yǐsì*,
Cháo burned down almost all the palaces, government offices, temples, and residences,
and, gathering his remaining partisans, fled beyond Lántián.
The next day,
the Emperor and all the armies recovered Cháng'ān."
The Shílù says:
"On *jiǎchén*,
Lǐ Kèyòng, along with Zhōngjié General Páng Cóng, Hézhōng General Bái Zhìqiān, Héngyě General Mǎn Cún, and Cháoyì General Kāng Shīzhēn, thrice defeated the rebels at Wèiqiáo,
and utterly routed them.
The Yìchéng, Yìwǔ, and other armies advanced in pursuit.
On *yǐsì*,
rebel Cháo burned the palaces of Cháng'ān,
gathered his remaining forces, and fled east through Guāngtài Gate,
escaping via Lántián Pass.
All the armies then advanced and recovered the capital."
The Xīnjì says:
"In the third month, on *rénshēn*,
Lǐ Kèyòng fought Huáng Cháo at Língkǒu
and defeated him.
In the fourth month, on *jiǎchén*,
he again defeated him at Wèiqiáo.
On *bǐngwǔ*,
the capital was recovered."
The Old Biographies say:
"On the eighth day of the fourth month,
Kèyòng, joining with Zhōngwǔ Cavalry General Páng Cóng, encountered the rebels at Wèinán.
They fought a decisive battle and achieved three victories,
utterly defeating the rebel army.
On the night of the tenth,
rebel Cháo's forces scattered and fled.
The next morning,
Kèyòng entered through Guāngtài Gate
and recovered the capital.
Rebel Cháo exited Lántián, by Qīpán Road, and fled east towards Guāndōng."
The New Biographies say:
"Kèyòng dispatched his subordinate General Yáng Shǒuzōng to lead Hézhōng General Bái Zhìqiān, Zhōngwǔ General Páng Cóng, and others, who advanced first to attack the rebels at Wèiqiáo.
They fought three battles and were thrice victorious.
Thereupon, all the *jiédù* troops were emboldened,
none daring to hold back.
They entered through Guāngtài Gate.
The rebels collapsed,
and were pursued north to Wàngchūn,
entering the Shēngyáng Diàntà.
Cháo fled by night,
his forces still numbering 150,000.
Their clamor suggested they were heading towards Xúzhōu,
exiting Lántián,
and entering Shāngshān."
Chéng Kuāngróu's Tángbǔjì says:
"Yáng Fùguāng led the twenty thousand odd soldiers of the Shídào Xíngyíng Jiédùshǐ Wáng Chóngróng, Lǐ Kèyòng, and others, and attacked from Guāngtài Gate,
pursuing them to below Shēngyáng Hall,
killing over ten thousand rebels.
The Huáng Cháo army was defeated,
fleeing from the battlefield,
and exiting through Lántián Pass."
The Hòutáng Tàizǔ Jìniánlù says:
"On *yǐsì*,
Cháo was defeated, burned the palaces, and fled east.
Tàizǔ advanced and recovered the capital."
The Tángnián Bǔlù says:
"On the eighth day,
Kèyòng and others fought at Wèinán,
defeating the rebel army three times.
On the ninth day,
Cháo fled."
Examining Yáng Fùguāng's official report, it says:
"On the eighth day of this month,
Yáng Shǒuzōng and others, accompanying Kèyòng, first entered the capital from Guāngtài Gate."
It also says:
"The rebels still formed a strong formation,
coming to resist the government army.
From *mǎo* to *shēn*,
they were utterly defeated and immediately fled,
retreating south into Shāngshān."
Therefore, the government army entered the city on the eighth day,
and the rebels, losing the battle, fled.
This is the most reliable account,
and we follow it now.
The Battle of Wèinán
must have been before the eighth day;
all other accounts are mistaken.
The government army looted and plundered,
no different from the rebels.
Few houses and people in Cháng'ān remained.
Cháo entered Shāngshān from Lántián.
Huáng Cháo had previously dispatched troops to guard the Lántián road,
thus he was able to escape by this route.
The government troops were busy seizing plunder,
not urgently pursuing,
so the rebels escaped.
Yáng Fùguāng dispatched an envoy to announce the victory.
The Kǎoyì says: Zhāng Qí Jìujiùchuán says:
"In the third year of Zhōnghé,
the northern route reported that Huáng Cháo was defeated and fled on the tenth day of the first month,
and Cháng'ān city was recovered.
In the third month,
the northern route's expeditionary force recovered the city,
and the generals and soldiers all returned."
Jù Yánqìng Jìujiùchuán says:
"In the fourth year,
the northern route reported that Huáng Cháo was defeated and fled on the tenth day of the first month,
and Cháng'ān was recovered.
In the third month,
the northern route's expeditionary force defeated Huáng Cháo's generals and soldiers, and they all returned."
Yánqìng moved all the events of the fourth year to the third year,
and the events of the third year to the fourth year,
without moving the month and day.
His errors are even worse than.
Now it merely says the victory was announced,
without specifying the month and day.
An imperial edict ordered 20,000 soldiers from the Zhōngwǔ and other armies to remain,
entrusting Dàmínggōng Liúshǒu Wáng Huī and Jīngjī Zhìzhìshǐ Tián Cóngyì with their deployment
to guard Cháng'ān.
In the fifth month,
Zhū Méi, Lǐ Kèyòng, and Dōngfāng Kuí were promoted to Tóngpíngzhāngshì.
Shǎnzōu was elevated to a *jiédù*,
with Wáng Chóngyíng appointed as *jiédùshǐ*.
Yánzhōu was also established as the Bǎosài Army,
with Bǎodà Xíngjūn Sīmǎ and Yánzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Xiàogōng appointed as *jiédùshǐ*.
These were rewards for defeating Huáng Cháo and recovering the capital city.
Among all the generals,
he was the youngest,
yet he defeated Huáng Cháo
and recovered Cháng'ān,
his merit being foremost,
and his military power the strongest;
all the generals feared him.
Kèyòng had one eye slightly impaired,
and people at the time called him
"Dúyǎnlóng" (One-Eyed Dragon).
An imperial edict stated that because Cuī Qiú's family was noble and his person prominent,
yet he served as Huáng Cháo's prime minister for three full years
without fleeing or hiding,
he was to be executed wherever found.
18 Huáng Cháo sent his brave general Mèng Kǎi to lead ten thousand men as the vanguard
to attack Càizhōu.
*Jiédùshǐ* Qín Zōngquán met him in battle but was defeated.
The rebels advanced to attack his city,
and Zōngquán then declared allegiance to Cháo
and joined forces with him.
Initially,
when Huáng Cháo was in Cháng'ān,
Zhào Chōu, the Cìshǐ of Chénzhōu and of Wǎnqiū, said to his generals and subordinates:
Wǎnqiū
was Xiàngxiàn of the Latter Wèi dynasty.
The Suí dynasty renamed it Wǎnqiū,
and under the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Chénzhōu.
Xiàngchéngxiàn, under its jurisdiction,
was the place where Mòlíngxiàn was temporarily established by the Eastern Wèi dynasty.
The Suí dynasty renamed it Xiàngchéng.
Chōu,
rhymes with chāng-niú.
"If Huáng Cháo does not die in Cháng'ān,
he will certainly head east,
and Chénzhōu will be his target.
Moreover, Huáng Cháo has always been an enemy of Zhōngwǔ.
Since Huáng Cháo first rose up,
he has repeatedly fought with Sòng Wēi, Zhāng Zìmiǎn, and others,
and these were all Zhōngwǔ's troops.
Therefore, he repaired the city walls and moats,
refurbished weapons and armor,
and accumulated fodder and grain.
Within sixty *lǐ*,
any common people who had provisions
were all moved into the city.
He extensively recruited brave warriors
and had his younger brother Chǎng Xǔ and son Lù Lín lead them in divisions.
After Mèng Kǎi had taken Cáizhōu,
he moved his troops to attack Chénzhōu
and encamped at Xiàngchéng.
Zhào Chōu first showed weakness,
then, seizing the moment when they were unprepared,
he attacked them,
killing and capturing almost all of them,
taking Mèng Kǎi alive
and beheading him.
When Huáng Cháo heard of Mèng Kǎi's death,
he was shocked and terrified.
He gathered all his forces and camped by the Yīnshuǐ River.
In the sixth month,
he joined forces with Qín Zōngquán and besieged Chénzhōu,
digging five layers of moats
and attacking it from a hundred directions.
The people of Chénzhōu were greatly alarmed,
but Zhào Chōu addressed them, saying:
"Zhōngwǔ has always been known for its righteousness and bravery,
and Chénzhōu is reputed to have strong soldiers.
Moreover, my family has long enjoyed the emoluments of Chénzhōu,
and I swear to live or die with this prefecture.
Men should seek life in the midst of death.
Furthermore, to die for the country,
is it not better than to live as a servant of bandits!
Anyone who voices a different opinion shall be executed!"
He repeatedly led his elite troops to open the gates and sally forth to attack the rebels,
defeating them.
Huáng Cháo grew more enraged,
set up camp north of the prefecture,
built palaces and offices for a hundred officials,
and prepared for a prolonged siege.
At that time, there were no accumulated provisions among the people.
The rebels plundered people for food,
throwing them alive into mortars and mills,
and consuming them bones and all.
The place where food was supplied was called
"Chōngmó Zài" (Pounding and Grinding Camp).
Chōngmó Zài
refers to the place where mortars and mills were set up.
*Duì* (mortars) for pounding,
*wăi* (mills) for grinding.
*Mó*,
rhymes with mò-wò.
From Hénán, Xǔ, Rǔ, Táng, Dèng, Méng, Zhèng, Biàn, Cáo, Pú, Xú, Yǎn, and dozens of other prefectures,
all were subjected to its poison.
This Hénán
refers to Luòzhōu Hénán Fǔ.
*Bèi*,
rhymes with pí-yì.
19 Initially,
Liú Qiān, a man from Shàngcài, was a junior officer in Lǐngnán.
The Jiédùshǐ Wéi Zhòu admired his talent.
During the Xiántōng era,
Wéi Zhòu was commander of Lǐngnán.
Liú Qiān attacked bandits
and frequently achieved success.
In the *xīn chǒu* year,
Liú Qiān was appointed Cìshǐ of Fēngzhōu.
Liú Qiān's rise began here.
20 Yáng Shīlì, Jiédùshǐ of Dōngchuān, was promoted to Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
21 Zhū Quánzhōng, Jiédùshǐ of Xuānwǔ, led his several hundred troops to his post.
In autumn,
seventh month,
on the *dīng mǎo* day,
he arrived in Biànzhōu.
At that time, Biànzhōu and Sòngzhōu were suffering from famine,
and both public and private resources were exhausted.
Inside,
the arrogant army was difficult to control;
outside, they were attacked by powerful enemies,
with battles every day.
The hearts of the people were anxious and fearful,
yet Zhū Quánzhōng's courage grew stronger.
An imperial edict, stating that Huáng Cháo had not yet been pacified,
appointed Zhū Quánzhōng as Dū Zhāotǎoshǐ of the Northeast Front.
This laid the groundwork for Zhū Quánzhōng's eventual annexation of various garrisons with Xuānwǔ's troops and the usurpation of the Táng dynasty.
22 The Nánzhào sent Bùxiè Yáng Qígōng to welcome the princess.
An imperial edict instructed Chén Jìngxuàn to write a letter,
declining by saying:
"The imperial carriage is on a tour,
and the ceremonial articles are not yet prepared.
We will await its return to the capital,
and then she will be sent."
Yáng Qígōng did not comply
and proceeded directly to Chéngdū.
23 Lǐ Kèyòng (李克yòng) led his troops back to Yànmén (雁門) from Cháng'ān (長安).
Soon there was an imperial edict
appointing Kèyòng (克yòng) as the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hédōng (河東),
and summoning Zhèng Cóngdǎng (鄭從讜) to the temporary imperial residence.
Kèyòng (克yòng) then passed through Yúcì (榆次) on the eastern route
to visit his father in Yànmén (雁門).
Kèyòng (克yòng) soon posted a proclamation in Hédōng (河東),
comforting the army and people, saying:
"Do not cling to old grievances;
each should settle in their homes and occupations."
As the people of Hédōng (河東) had previously fought against Kèyòng (克yòng) numerous times,
he feared they would not feel secure,
hence this proclamation.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Old Annals state:
"In the fifth month,
Lǐ Kèyòng (李克yòng) was appointed Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hédōng (河東).
In the seventh month,
an edict summoned Zhèng Cóngdǎng (鄭從讜) to the temporary imperial residence."
The New Annals state:
"In the fifth month,
Cóngdǎng (從讜) became Sīkōng (司空) with the concurrent title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事)."
Jiǎ Wěi's (賈緯) Tángnián Bǔlù (唐年補錄) states:
"In the fifth month,
an imperial decree: 'Lǐ (李), whose taboo name is Kě (可), is Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事),
and concurrently the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hédōng (河東).'"
(A note says:
"According to Xuē Shǐ (薛史), in the sixth year of Jìn Tiānfú (晉天福),
in the second month,
Jiǎ Wěi (賈緯) presented the Tángnián Bǔlù (唐年補錄) to the throne."
It also says:
"Jiǎ Wěi (賈緯), a native of Huòlù (獲鹿), Zhēndìng (真定),
found the imperial annals of the Táng (唐) emperors from Wǔzōng (武宗) onwards to be incomplete and unrecorded.
He therefore collected recent hearsay and various unofficial histories, arranged them by year and month,
and compiled them into the Tángnián Bǔlù (唐年補錄),
in sixty-five volumes.
He served the Táng (唐), Jìn (晉), Hàn (漢), and Zhōu (周) dynasties,
hence he did not dare to refer to Kèyòng (克yòng) by his given name.")
The Old Biography of Cóngdǎng (從讜) states:
"In the third year,
Kèyòng (克yòng) was appointed Jìedù (節度) of Hédōng (河東),
replacing Cóngdǎng (從讜).
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month,
Cóngdǎng (從讜) left Tàiyuán (太原).
The journey was plagued by bandits,
and he stopped in Jiàngzhōu (絳州)
for several months.
In winter,
an imperial envoy was sent to summon him to the temporary imperial residence,
and he resumed his role in governance."
Tángmò Jiànwénlù (唐末見聞錄) says:
"In the fifth month,
an imperial decree appointed Minister Lǐ (李) as Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Yànmén (雁門).
On the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month,
Privy Councillor Lǐ (李), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Yànmén (雁門), passed through the road east of the prefecture.
Within the sixth month,
an appointment order arrived,
stating that the Grand Councillor was to be replaced and proceed to the capital, and Grand Councillor Lǐ (李), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Yànmén (雁門), was appointed Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hédōng (河東).
On the fifteenth day,
the Grand Councillor departed through the Xīmíng (西明) Gate.
Within that month,
the new envoy, Grand Councillor Lǐ (李), issued a proclamation
to pacify the soldiers and common people in the city,
saying: 'Do not harbor old grievances,
each should secure their home.'"
It also says:
"King Jìn (晉), whose taboo name is Kèyòng (克yòng),
on the first day of the fifth month of Zhōnghé (中和) three years,
was appointed Píngzhāngshì (平章事) from Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Yànmén (雁門),
and concurrently Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hédōng (河東)."
Upon examining the appointment of Kèyòng (克yòng) to Hédōng (河東) and Cóngdǎng's (從讜) resumption of governance,
the dates vary among the different texts.
The Old Annals record Kèyòng's (克yòng) appointment in the fifth month and Cóngdǎng's (從讜) arrival at the temporary imperial residence in the seventh month,
without mentioning his appointment as prime minister.
The New Annals state he was already prime minister in the fifth month,
which is even more erroneous.
The Old Biography of Cóngdǎng (從讜) states he left Tàiyuán (太原) on the fifteenth day of the fifth month,
which also contradicts the Annals.
The imperial decree in the fifth month of Tángnián Bǔlù (唐年補錄)
only commends Kèyòng (克yòng), Zhū Méi (朱玫), and Dōngfāng Kuí (東方逵) three people;
the wording of the decree is crude,
raising doubts about its authenticity.
The Tángmò Jiànwénlù (唐末見聞錄) initially states his appointment to Hédōng (河東) was in the sixth month,
then later says it was on the first day of the fifth month.
According to the Shílù (實錄), Hòutáng Tàizǔ Jìniánlù (後唐太祖紀年錄), and Xuē Jūzhèng's (薛居正) Wǔdài Shǐ (五代史), all place it in the seventh month;
we now follow this.
Cóngdǎng (從讜) became the Liúshǒu (留守) of Dōngdū (東都) in the ninth month of this year,
and only re-entered the prime ministership in the second month of Guāngqǐ (光啟) two years.
24 Yáng Fùguāng (楊復光), General-in-Chief of the Left Xiāowèi (驍衞), died in Hézhōng (河中).
Fùguāng (復光) was magnanimous and fond of loyalty and righteousness,
skilled at comforting his soldiers,
and the army mourned for him for several days.
The eight commanders, Lù Yànhóng (鹿晏弘) and others, each dispersed with their troops.
Tián Lìngzī (田令孜) had always feared and resented him,
and hearing of his death,
was greatly pleased.
He then dismissed Fùgōng (復恭), Fùguāng's (復光) elder brother and the Púmìshǐ (樞密使), appointing him Fēilóngshǐ (飛龍使).
Lìngzī (令孜) wielded sole power,
and no one could oppose him,
except Fùgōng (復恭) who often argued with him over right and wrong.
Therefore, Lìngzī (令孜) detested him,
and Fùgōng (復恭) then claimed illness and returned to Lántián (藍田).

25 Wáng Róng (王鎔), acting Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Chéngdé (成德), Lè Xíngdá (樂行達), acting Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Wèibó (魏博), and Zhū Xuān (朱瑄), acting Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Tiānpíng (天平), were appointed Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of their respective circuits.
26 Zhèng Tián (鄭畋), Sītú (司徒), Ménxià Shìláng (門下侍郎), and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事),
though enduring exile,
still strictly adhered to the regulations.
Tián Lìngzī (田令孜) sought a Lángguān (郎官) position for his Aide, Wú Yuán (吳圓).
Wú Yuán (吳圓) was a subordinate official of Tián Lìngzī (田令zī).
'為' is pronounced yú (于) wěi (偽) [for wèi (為)].
Chén Jìngxuàn (陳敬瑄) wished to be placed above the prime ministers.
Tián (畋), based on historical precedents, argued that although the rank of 'Shǐxiàng' (使相) was high,
they were all subordinate to the true prime ministers,
and he strongly contested this.
In the late Táng (唐),
any Jìedùshǐ (節度使) holding the concurrent title of Píngzhāngshì (平章事) and Inspector of the three departments, or holding the titles of Sāngōng (三公) or Sānshī (三師),
were all called 'Shǐxiàng' (使相).
"The military harbors suspicions and jealousy;
Tián (畋) must not be allowed to accompany the emperor beyond this point."
In the first year,
Chāngyán (昌言) advocated for Tián's (畋) expulsion to seize Fèngxiáng (鳳翔),
so the two instigated someone to memorialize the throne,
leading to Tián's (畋) dismissal as prime minister.
From then on,
the court's promotion and demotion of prime ministers
were largely controlled by the regional governors.
'從' is pronounced cái (才) yòng (用) [for cóng (從)].
He was then dismissed and made Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (太子太保),
and his son, Bīngbù Shìláng (兵部侍郎) Níngjī (凝績), was made Pēngzhōu (彭州) Cìshǐ (刺史),
so he could care for his father.
Sòng Bái (宋白) says: In the third year of Táng Chuígǒng (唐垂拱),
Pēngzhōu (彭州) was established from Jiǔlóng (九隴) County, Yìzhōu (益州),
named after the ancient Tiānpéng (天彭) Pass.
'養' is pronounced yáng (羊) shàng (尚) [for yǎng (養)].
27 In the eighth month,
on the jiǎchén (甲辰) day,
Lǐ Kèyòng (李克yòng) arrived in Jìnyáng (晉陽).
From this point, Lǐ Kèyòng (李克yòng) regarded Jìnyáng (晉陽) as the base for contending for天下.
He garrisoned Dáizhōu (代州).
28 Húnán (湖南) was elevated to Qīnhuà (欽化) Army,
and the Guāncháshǐ (觀察使) Mǐn Xù (閔勗) was appointed Jìedùshǐ (節度使).
29 In the ninth month,
Chén Jìngxuàn (陳敬瑄) was given the concurrent title of Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令)
and promoted to the title of Yǐngchuān (潁川) County King.
30 Shí Pǔ (時溥), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Gǎnhuà (感化), established a camp at the Yīnxuǐ (𣷽水) River;
to block Huáng Cháo's (黃巢) troops
and to provide support for Chénzhōu (陳州).
31 Chén Rú (陳儒), acting Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Jīngnán (荊南), was appointed Jìedùshǐ (節度使).
Méng Fānglì, Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì,
considering that Lùzhōu was strategically rugged and its people fierce,
frequently usurping their commanders,
wished to gradually weaken them.
Thus, he moved the administrative seat to Xíngzhōu.
This event was mentioned in the previous year.
"Shuài" (帥)
is pronounced "suǒ lèi" (所類).
The people of Lù were displeased.
The Supervising Eunuch Qí Shěnhuì, capitalizing on the people's unrest,
secretly sent Ān Jūshòu, the commander of Wǔxiāng Town, with a wax pill to request aid from Lǐ Kèyòng,
asking to restore the military headquarters to Lùzhōu.
Wǔxiāng and Héyáng’s巡屬 Liáozhōu shared a border,
hence its commander was sent to request aid.
After this, the Fāngzhèn often established town commanders in various counties,
and the county magistrates could no longer perform their duties.
Sòng Bái said: Wǔxiāng County was originally the territory of Niè County in the Hàn dynasty.
In the Jìn dynasty, Wǔxiāng Commandery was first established,
and the county belonged to it.
In the tenth month,
Kèyòng dispatched his general Hè Gōngyǎ and others to go there,
but they were defeated by Fānglì.
He then dispatched Lǐ Kèxiū to attack them.
On the Xīnhài day,
Lùzhōu was captured.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Shílù* says:
"Kèyòng memorialized to appoint Lǐ Kèxiū as Jìedùshǐ,
thus dividing the five prefectures of the Zhāoyì Army into two commanderies."
Xuē Jūzhèng’s *Wǔdài Shǐ*, in the biography of Méng Fānglì, states:
"The people of Lù secretly requested aid from Wǔhuáng.
In the tenth month of Zhōnghé 3rd year,
Wǔhuáng sent Lǐ Kèxiū with troops to go there.
Fānglì resisted and fought,
utterly defeating them.
From this, he successively recovered the two commanderies of Zé and Lù,
and then appointed Kèxiū as Jìedùshǐ."
According to Xuē's *Shǐ*, in the biography of Zhāng Quányì:
"Zhūgě Shuǎng memorialized to appoint Quányì as Zézhōu Cìshǐ.
After Shuǎng died,
Lǐ Hǎnzhī occupied Zézhōu."
It seems Kèxiū only obtained Lùzhōu,
while Zé was taken by Héyáng.
After this, Kèyòng sent troops out every year to contest Shāndōng.
Half of the people in the three prefectures were captured or slain,
and the fields were barren.
Xíng, Míng, and Cí, the three prefectures of Zhāoyì, were in Shāndōng.
The imperial clan daughter was enfeoffed as Princess Ānhuà Zhǎnggōngzhǔ.
Qìngzhōu, Ānhuà Commandery.
Liú Hànhóng, with over a hundred thousand troops, advanced from Xīlíng
to attack Dǒng Chāng.
On the Wùwǔ day,
Qián Liú crossed the river to meet them in battle,
utterly defeating them.
Hànhóng changed his clothes, carried a fish-cutting knife, and fled.
He made the enemy think he was a cook,
and they did not suspect he was Hànhóng.
On the Jǐwèi day,
Hànhóng reassembled his remaining forty thousand troops and fought again.
Liú again defeated them,
beheading his brother Hànróng and general Xīn Yuē.
In the eleventh month,
on the Jiǎzǐ day (the first day of the month),

Xuē Jūzhèng’s *Wǔdài Shǐ* only says "spring of the 4th year."

On the day Dīngchǒu,
at the second drum of the night,
"Second drum of the night" (夜二鼓)
means the second watch of the night (夜二更).
The watchman beats the drum once for each watch;
for the second watch, he beats the drum twice.
Therefore, the second watch is called the "second drum" (二鼓),
also known as "yǐyè" (乙夜).
Yáng Màoyán could not resist,
so he led his troops, abandoned his camp, and fled.
Several nearby camps, seeing the deputy envoy flee,
also fled.
The Dōngchuān people consolidated their forces and attacked the central army from the south.
Gāo Rènhòu, hearing this,
opened his camp gates wide,
set up torches to illuminate the area,
and personally led his soldiers to form two wings, lying in ambush on either side of the road.
When the bandits arrived,
seeing the gates open,
they dared not enter.
They turned back.
Gāo Rènhòu sprung his ambush, attacking them.
The Dōngchuān troops fled in great panic.
They were pursued to the city walls,
forced into the moats,
and a great number were slain and captured before [Gāo Rènhòu] returned.
Gāo Rènhòu considered that among those who had abandoned their camps and fled,
many would have to be executed the next morning.
So he secretly summoned the registrar, Zhāng Sháo,
and instructed him, saying:
"You must quickly send dozens of foot scouts on separate routes to pursue those who fled.
"Foot scouts" (步探子)
are those sent on foot to scout out the enemy,
hence their name.
"Tàn" (探)
pronounced as "tā gàn" (他紺翻).
"Everyone is unaware,
Gāo Rènhòu, with the merit of pacifying Qiānnēng and others,
has been promoted to Jiǎnjiào Púshè.
Tomorrow morning at the assembly,
do not worry."
All generals of the marching army
would report to the main general's camp for assembly every morning.
The multitude believed him,
and by the fourth drum,
all had returned to their camps.
Only Yáng Màoyán had fled to Zhāng Bǎ,
and was overtaken there.
"Jiǔyù Zhì" states: "In Qī Xiàn of Zǐzhōu, there is Zhāng Pá Zhèn."
"Bǎ" (把)
should be written as
[Gāo Rènhòu] rejoiced, saying:
"All have returned!"
The next morning,
the generals assembled,
thinking that Gāo Rènhòu was truly unaware.
After sitting for a long while,
Gāo Rènhòu said to Yáng Màoyán:
"Last night, I heard that the deputy envoy, personally leading his men,
fled to Zhāng Bǎ.
Is this true?"
[Yáng Màoyán] replied:
"Last night, I heard that the bandits were attacking the central army,
and my attendants said that the Púshè had already left.
So I galloped my horse to follow.
After ascertaining it was false,
I returned to the camp."
Gāo Rènhòu said:
"Both I and the deputy envoy received orders from the Son of Heaven
to lead troops to suppress the bandits.
If I were to flee first,
the deputy envoy should shout at me to dismount,
enforce military law,
take over command of the army,
and then report to the throne.
Now, the deputy envoy has fled first,
and moreover, has been deceitful.
What should be done according to principle?"
Yáng Màoyán bowed and said:
"I deserve death."
Gāo Rènhòu said:
"Indeed!"
He ordered his attendants to escort him down,
and executed him.
All the generals trembled.
Gāo Rènhòu then summoned the dozens of captives from the previous night,
released their bonds, and let them return.
He released the captives,
instructing them to return and report these events.
[The enemy] said:
"Their military law is so strict and orderly;
from now on, our troops cannot sally forth again!"
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" states: "The Jìn people attacked Zhèng,
conducted a hunt there, and returned.
This was the strategy of Zhōngháng Huánzǐ.
He said:
'Show them discipline,
and make them deliberate before coming.'
Thereupon, Zhèng became afraid.
Afterward, they ultimately requested peace from Jìn.
That strict and orderly military discipline
makes enemies fear,
has indeed been true since ancient times."
pronounced as "fú yòu" (扶又翻).
14On the day Gēngchén,
Shí Pǔ sent his general, Lǐ Shīyuè, with an army of ten thousand men to pursue Huáng Cháo.
15On the day Guǐwèi,
Gāo Rènhòu deployed his troops below the city of Lùtóu Guān.
Zhèng Jūnxióng and others brought out all their troops to fight.
Gāo Rènhòu set an ambush behind his formation,
feigning defeat and retreat.
Zhèng Jūnxióng and others pursued them.
The ambush was sprung,
and Zhèng Jūnxióng and others were greatly defeated.
That evening,
they fled back to Zǐzhōu.
Chén Jìngxúan dispatched three thousand troops to reinforce Gāo Rènhòu's army,
advancing to besiege Zǐzhōu.

Later Scholar Heaven Terrace
Fourth year of Zhōnghé [era]
(Jiǎchén year, 884)
1 In the sixth month,
on the day Rénchén,
Gāo Rénhòu, Acting Military Governor of Dōngchuān, reported that Zhèng Jūnxióng had beheaded Yáng Shīlì and surrendered.
Rénhòu had besieged Zǐzhōu for a long time without success,
so he wrote a letter and shot it into the city,
addressing its generals and soldiers:
"Rénhòu cannot bear to see both jade and stone burned together in the city.
For your sake, I will slow down the attack for ten days,
allowing you to achieve success on your own.
If Yáng Shīlì's head is not sent out within ten days,
I will divide my existing forces into five shifts,
with each shift attacking day and night.
This will be very easy for us,
but you will certainly be exhausted.
If it does not fall within five days,
we will advance from all four sides,
and its capture will be certain.
You gentlemen, consider this!"
A few days later,
Jūnxióng shouted to the crowd,
"The Son of Heaven executes only the chief villain;
others are not involved!"
The crowd cheered "Long live!",
made a great commotion,
and stormed into the prefectural office.
Yáng Shīlì committed suicide,
and Jūnxióng carried his head out to surrender.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Zhāng Qíjiù's biography states:
"In the fourth year,
on the first day of the seventh month,
Military Commissioner Gāo sent a swift dispatch into the city, saying so-and-so,
and Shīlì committed suicide.
On the third day of the seventh month,
Generals Zhāng and Zhèng brought Shīlì's head and surrendered.
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
Military Commissioner Gāo ascended Dōngchuān."
Jù Yánqìng's biography says: "In the third year,
fifth month,
Duke Gāo advanced to the foot of Dōngchuān city.
He shot a flying dispatch into the city,
and Shīlì slit his own throat.
On the day Xīnyǒu of the seventh month,
Shīlì's head arrived in Chéngdū."
The *Shílù* states:
"On the day Bǐngshēn of the sixth month,
Gāo Rénhòu reported that Zhèng Jūnxióng, the commander of Dōngchuān, had captured and beheaded Yáng Shīlì,
and sent his head to the traveling court.
On that day,
an imperial edict appointed Rénhòu as Military Governor of Dōngchuān."
The *Xùbǎoyùnlù* states:
"In the second month,
Yáng Shīlì, Observer of Zǐzhōu, rebelled.
An imperial decree ordered the Shu generals Gāo Rénhòu and others to suppress him.
On the third day of the sixth month,
Zǐzhōu was recovered, and Yáng Shīlì's head was received before the imperial carriage."
The *Xīnjì* states:
"On the day Xīnyǒu of the seventh month,
Yáng Shīlì was executed."
Today, we follow the *Xùbǎoyùnlù* for the date,
and the *Shílù* for the event.
Chén Jìngxúan nailed his son to the north of the city.
Jìngxúan's three sons went out to watch,
and the nailed man shouted,
"This fate will soon reach you too!
You, my younger brothers, must strive to achieve it in the future!"
The three sons rode their horses back.
Gāo Rénhòu was appointed Military Governor of Dōngchuān.
2 On the day Jiǎchén,
Lǐ Shīyuè, a general of Wǔníng, and Shàng Ràng pursued Huáng Cháo to Xiáqiū,
and defeated him.
Sòng Bái said: The *Chūnqiū* mentions Zhūzǐ Yì coming and being imprisoned in Fùxiá.
Dù Yù's annotation says: It was a Lǔ city.
To the northwest of Píngyáng County, Nánpíngyáng Commandery, there is Xiáqiū city.
In Han times, it was Xiáqiū County.
敗 (bài, defeat),
read as "bài" (补迈翻).
Huáng Cháo fled to Lánghǔgǔ.
Lánghǔgǔ
is in the southeastern part of Tài Shān, within the Láiwú area.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
Huáng Cháo's nephew, Lín Yán, beheaded Huáng Cháo's brothers, wife, and children,
intending to present them to Shí Pǔ;
but he encountered the Shātuó Bóyě army,
who seized them,
and also beheaded Yán, presenting his head to Pǔ.
Huáng Cháo had raised an army as a bandit in the third year of Qiánfú.
He was destroyed after ten years.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Xùbǎoyùnlù* states:
"Shàng Ràng surrendered at Xúzhōu.
Huáng Cháo fled to Jié Shān,
where he was hard pressed by various armies,
so he spoke to his nephew Zhū Yánzhī, saying so-and-so.
His nephew repeatedly could not bear to strike,
so Huáng Cháo slit his own throat and gave it to his nephew.
As his nephew was bringing it,
it was seized by the Shātuó Bóyě on the way,
and both the nephew's head and Huáng Cháo's head were sent to the Supreme Commander's camp at the same time."
The *Jiùjì* states:
"In the seventh month,
on the day Guǐyǒu,
the rebel general Lín Yán surrendered, having beheaded Huáng Cháo, Huáng Kuí, and Huáng Bǐng."
The *Jiùzhuàn* states:
"Huáng Cháo entered Tài Shān.
Shí Pǔ, the military governor of Xúzhōu, sent general Zhāng Yǒu with Shàng Ràng's forces to capture him.
Upon reaching Lánghǔgǔ,
Huáng Cháo's general Lín Yán beheaded Huáng Cháo and his two younger brothers, Yè and Kuí, and seven others, along with his wife and children, and sent them in boxes to Xúzhōu."
The *Xīnjì* states:
"On the day Rénwǔ of the seventh month,
Huáng Cháo was executed."
The *Xīnzhuàn* states:
"Huáng Cháo, with his plans thwarted,
said to Lín Yán: 'If you take my head and present it to the Son of Heaven,
you can attain wealth and honor; do not let others profit from it.'
Yán,
who was Huáng Cháo's nephew,
could not bear to do it.
Huáng Cháo then slit his own throat,
but did not finish himself off.
Yán then beheaded him,
placed the head in a box, and was about to go to Shí Pǔ,
but the Bóyě army from Tàiyuán killed Yán and presented both his and Huáng Cháo's heads."
Today, we follow the *Xīnzhuàn*.
3 Qín Zōngquán, Military Governor of Càizhōu, unleashed his troops in all directions,
encroaching upon and devouring neighboring circuits.
Zhū Xuān, Military Governor of Tiānpíng, had a force of thirty thousand men.
His younger cousin, Jǐn,
was the bravest in the army.
Zhū Quánzhōng, Military Governor of Xuānwǔ, was attacked by Zōngquán,
and was in a very difficult situation.
He sought help from Xuān.
Xuān sent Jǐn to lead troops to his aid,
and they defeated Zōngquán at Héxiāng.
Quánzhōng was grateful for this
and swore brotherhood with Xuān.
Zhū Quánzhōng was a treacherous and petty man.
When his military strength was weak,
he swore brotherhood with Zhū Xuān.
Once his military strength grew,
he would turn hostile and become an enemy,
surely seeking to exterminate and slaughter to satisfy his ambition before stopping.
How could such a person share glory and achievement?
4 Autumn,
seventh month,
on the day Rénwǔ,
Shí Pǔ sent an envoy to present the heads of Huáng Cháo, his family members, and his concubines.
The emperor ascended the Dàxuánlóu to receive them.
The Dàxuánlóu was the main south gate tower of the Luó Chéng in Chéngdū.
When Gāo Pián built the Luó Chéng in Chéngdū,
after its completion,
he divined by the *Zhōu Yì*,
obtaining Dà Xù.
Pián said:
"Xù means 'to nourish.'
Aided by strength, firmness, and sincerity,
its brilliance will be renewed daily.
What greater auspiciousness could there be!
The character's lower part should be removed, and the upper part retained."
Hence, he named it Dàxuán Chéng.
"You are all children of meritorious nobles,
who have received national grace for generations.
Why did you follow the rebels?"
The leader among them replied:
"The mad rebel was fierce and rebellious.
The state, with a million troops,
lost the imperial ancestral temple
and was forced to move to Bā and Shǔ.
Now Your Majesty blames a single woman for being unable to resist the rebels.
Where do you place the dukes, ministers, generals, and commanders?"
The emperor asked no further questions,
and they were all executed in the marketplace.
People vied to give them wine;
the others were all sorrowful, terrified, and drunken,
but the leader alone neither drank nor wept,
and even as she faced execution,
her demeanor was stern.
The *Kǎoyì* states: Zhāng Qíjiù's biography states:
"In the third year of Zhōnghé,
on the twentieth day of the fifth month,
the northern army advanced with Huáng Cháo's head, wife, and son."
Today, we do not take its year and month, but rather its event.
5 Zhū Quánzhōng attacked Qín Zōngquán,
and defeated Zōngquán at Yīnshuǐ.
In the 13th year, Lù Yànhóng 引兵東出 Xiāngzhōu.
Qín Zōngquán dispatched his generals Qín Gào and Zhào Déyīn to lead troops to join him.
Together they attacked Xiāngzhōu,
and captured it.
Liú Jùróng, Jìedùshǐ of Shānnán Dōngdào, fled to Chéngdū.
Liú Jùróng was unwilling to pursue and annihilate Huáng Cháo,
wishing to foster the rebels for his own benefit.
He regarded Xiāngyáng as his túqiú (place of retirement),
but his territory was seized by Zhào Déyīn,
and he himself died at the hands of Tián Lìngzī.
To toy with rebels and invite trouble for the sovereign,
what benefit did it ultimately bring!
The Kǎoyì says: According to the Shílù:
"In the fourth month of the first year of Guāngqǐ,
the Càizéi attacked and captured Xiāngzhōu,
and Liú Jùróng died there."
The Xīnchuán says:
"Yànhóng led his subordinates east out of Xiāng and Dèng.
Zōngquán sent Zhào Déyīn to join Yànhóng's army to attack Xiāngzhōu.
Jùróng could not defend it,
and fled to Chéngdū.
In the first year of Lóngjì,
Tián Lìngzī killed him."
Examining this, Yànhóng had already occupied Xǔzhōu in the eleventh month of the fourth year of Zhōnghé.
Furthermore,
the reason Jùróng fled to Chéngdū
was because the Son of Heaven was in Shǔ.
Now we follow the Xīnchuán.
(He was) from Càizhōu.
Yànhóng led his troops to plunder Xiāng, Dèng, Jūn, Fáng, Lú, and Shòu,
and then returned to Xǔzhōu.
Lù Yànhóng, from Xǔzhōu, joined Yáng Fùguāng in serving the emperor.
See volume 254, first year of Zhōnghé.
Sòng Bái said: Jūnzhōu
was the land of Wǔdāng County in the Hàn dynasty.
In the seventh year of Yǒngmíng during the Qí dynasty,
Qíxīng Commandery was established in what is now Yúnxiāng County.
The Western Wèi established Xīngzhōu,
which was soon renamed Fēngzhōu.
In the first year of Wǔchéng during the Zhōu dynasty,
it was moved from what is now Yúnxiāng city to Yáncén city.
This is where the commandery seat is today.
The Suí dynasty renamed it Jūnzhōu,
named after the Jūn River.
(He) abandoned the garrison and fled.
Yànhóng then occupied Xǔzhōu.
The Kǎoyì says: According to the Shílù:
"Lù Yànhóng captured Xǔzhōu,
killed Jìedùshǐ Zhōu Jí,
and occupied his garrison."
It also says:
"Initially,
Yànhóng occupied Xīngyuán.
His generals Wáng Jiàn and others led their troops to return to the acting court.
Thereupon, an imperial edict ordered the Forbidden Army to attack him.
Yànhóng was afraid,
abandoned the city, and returned to his hometown.
Zhōu Jí, hearing of his arrival,
fled.
Yànhóng declared himself Liúhòu,
and the imperial court consequently appointed him with the imperial staff."
It first says "killed,"
then later says "fled,"
which contradicts itself.
Now we follow the latter account.
The imperial court could not punish him,
and so made him Jìedùshǐ of Zhōngwǔ.
In the 14th year, in the twelfth month,
on the day Jǐchǒu,
Chén Jìngxúann submitted a memorial declining the titles of Sānchuān Dūzhīhuī, Zhāotǎo, Zhìzhì, and Ānfǔ and other envoys.
This was granted.
Last year, because Yáng Shīlì raised an army,
Jìngxúann concurrently held the titles of Sānchuān Dūzhīhuī and others.
Since Shīlì was already dead,
he therefore declined them.
In the 15th year, initially,
Huáng Cháo had plundered Fújiàn.
See volume 253, fifth year of Qiánfú.
He was known as Jiǔlóngjūn.
Zhèng Yì, Fújiàn Guānchásǐ, memorialized to make him Tuánliàn Fùshǐ.
Lǐ Lián, Cìshǐ of Quánzhōu and Zuǒxiāng Dūyúhòu, committed a crime
and fled into the mountain caves.
Yán defeated him.
Yì, fearing Yán's pressure,
memorialized to have Yán replace him.
On the day Rén Yín,
Yán was appointed Fújiàn Guānchásǐ.
Yán governed with both authority and benevolence,
and the Mǐn people were at peace.
The 16th year. Wáng Duó, Jìedùshǐ of Yìchāng and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng,
was lavish in his upkeep.
When he passed through Wèizhōu,
his concubines formed a retinue,
and his attire and equipage were resplendent,
like the manner of peaceful times.
From Xùn, son of Lè Yànzhēn, Jìedùshǐ of Wèibó,
ambushed him with several hundred soldiers at Gāojībó south of Zhāng.
They surrounded and killed him,
and more than three hundred of his retainers and followers also died.
They plundered his possessions, carriages, and concubines and returned.
The history says that Wáng Duó, with the manners of peaceful times, acted in an era of chaos,
leading to his own death and the ruin of his family.
He incited theft and debauchery,
bringing it upon himself.
From (從),
read cái yòng fān.
Huán (還),
read cóng xuān fān,
also as written.
The imperial court could not investigate.
The 17th year. The Bīnníng Army was granted the designation Jìngnán.
In the 18th year, that same year,
Chén Shèng, Yúháng Zhènshǐ, expelled Liǔ Chāo, Mùzhōu Cìshǐ.
Wáng Jìngrǎo, Rǔyīn Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ of Yǐngzhōu, expelled his Cìshǐ.
Rǔyīn
was a Hàn county,
and in the Táng dynasty it was under Yǐngzhōu.
Rǎo (蕘),
read rú zhāo fān.
The imperial court then appointed him Cìshǐ.
The 19th year. Sūn Xǐ, a rebel leader from Jūnzhōu, gathered several thousand people,
planning to attack the prefectural city.
Lǚ Yè, the Cìshǐ, did not know what to do.
Fēng Xíngxí of Wǔdāng, a Dūjiāng, ambushed troops south of the river.
Wǔdāng
was a Hàn county,
and in the Táng dynasty it was under Jūnzhōu.
The area south of the river (江南)
is south of the Hàn River.
Shuài (帥),
read suǒ lèi fān.
Jiàng (將),
read jí liàng fān.
(He) said:
"The people of the prefecture, if they get a good magistrate,
none will fail to give their allegiance.
However, the soldiers you brought with you are too many,
and the people of the prefecture fear plundering,
still harboring doubts.
It would be better to station your army north of the river,
and you alone, with your trusted light cavalry, advance.
Xíngxí requests to go ahead,
to inform and persuade the people of the prefecture,
and none will fail to submit."
Xǐ thought this was correct
and followed him.
Once they crossed the river,
the army officers came to greet them.
The ambush was sprung,
and Xíngxí personally struck Xǐ,
beheading him.
All those who followed Xǐ died,
and the army north of the river, seeing this, all fled.
The Jìedùshǐ of Shānnán Dōngdào reported his achievement.
An imperial edict appointed Xíngxí as Jūnzhōu Cìshǐ.
To the west of the prefecture was Chángshān,
which was on the route from Xiāng and Dèng to Shǔ.
Many bandits occupied it,
plundering tributes and taxes.
Xíngxí campaigned against and executed them,
and the Shǔ road was thus opened.
The 20th year. Lǐ Chāngyán, Jìedùshǐ of Fèngxiáng, was ill.
He memorialized to have his younger cousin, Chāngfú, act as Liúhòu.
After Chāngyán died,
an imperial edict appointed Chāngfú as Fèngxiáng Jìedùshǐ.
The Kǎoyì says: No books record the year and month of Chāngyán's death.
Only the biography of Lǐ Chāngfú in the Shílù says:
"Lǐ Chāngyán was ill
and requested Chāngfú to temporarily act as Liúhòu.
After Chāngyán died,
an imperial edict appointed him Jìedùshǐ."
According to the Shílù,
in the fifth month of the third year of Zhōnghé,
Chāngyán was promoted to Jiǎnjiào Sītú.
In the second month of the first year of Guāngqǐ,
Chāngfú first appears.
Therefore, Chāngyán's death is appended to the end of the fourth year of Zhōnghé.
At 21:00, although Huáng Cháo had been suppressed,
Qín Zōngquán again became rampant.
He ordered his generals to deploy troops,
plundering neighboring circuits.
Chén Yàn invaded Huáinán,
Qín Xián invaded Jiāngnán,
Qín Gào captured Xiāng, Táng, and Dèng prefectures,
Sūn Rú captured Dōngdū, Mèng, Shǎn, and Guó prefectures,
Zhāng Zhì captured Rǔ and Zhèng prefectures,
Lú Táng attacked Biàn and Sòng prefectures.
From Sūn Rú downwards,
these events all occurred after this year.
The histories generally refer to them.
Scarcely anyone survived.
His brutality was even worse than Huáng Cháo's;
his army never transported provisions;
they carried salted corpses in carts to follow them.
Salt was used to fill the corpses of dead people,
to provide food for the army.
*Cóng* (從),
read as *fān* (翻).
To the west, it reached Guānfǔ;
to the east, it extended to Qīng and Qí prefectures;
to the south, it spread out from Jiāng and Huái prefectures.
Among the surviving prefectures and garrisons, only a single city was barely held.
Looking as far as the eye could see for a thousand *lǐ*,
there were no more signs of habitation.
The emperor was about to return to Cháng'ān,
fearing Qín Zōngquán would cause trouble.
The first year of Guāngqǐ
(Yǐsì, 885)
The *yuánhào* was changed in the third month of this year.
1 Spring,
first month,
on the *wùwǔ* day,
an edict was issued to offer pacification and amnesty to him.
2 On the *jǐmǎo* day,
the imperial carriage departed from Chéngdū.
Chén Jìngxuān escorted it to Hànzhōu and then returned.
3 The Loyal and Brave Army recruited by Zhū Jìngméi, the Supervising Eunuch of Jīngnán, was violent and overbearing.
Chén Rú was troubled by this.
When Zhèng Shàoyè was garrisoned in Jīngnán,
in the first year of Guǎngmíng,
Zhū Jìngméi recruited the Loyal and Brave Army;
Zhèng Shàoyè was garrisoned in Jīngnán
in the same year.
Both events are seen in the previous scroll.
*Héng* (橫),
read as *hù mèng fān*.
When the army returned,
Chén Rú informed Péi Cóng,
asking him to eliminate them.
Chéng Jūncóng, a general of the Loyal and Brave Army, heard of this,
led his troops, and fled to Lángzhōu,
fleeing to Léi Mǎn.
*Shuài* (帥),
read as *lǜ*.
More than a hundred people were killed.
From then on, Péi Cóng again took sole control of military administration.
Léi Mǎn repeatedly attacked and plundered Jīngnán.
Chén Rú offered heavy bribes to repel him.
The Huáinán generals Zhāng Huái and Hán Shīdé rebelled against Gāo Pián,
seizing Fù and Yuè prefectures,
and styling themselves governors.
Chén Rú requested Zhāng Huái to act as Provisional Commissioner of Military Affairs and
Hán Shīdé to act as Provisional Deputy Military Commissioner,
leading troops to attack Léi Mǎn.
Hán Shīdé led his troops up the gorges, plundered extensively,
and returned to Yuèzhōu;
Zhāng Huái returned his troops, pursued Chén Rú, and replaced him.
Chén Rú was about to flee to the traveling court,
but Zhāng Huái intercepted and brought him back,
imprisoning him.
In the second year of Zhōnghé,
Chén Rú replaced Zhèng Shàoyè,
and was defeated by this time.
Zhāng Huái
was a native of Wèi
Prefecture.
He was greedy and cruel,
and the former Jīngnán generals were almost completely eradicated.
Before this,
Zhū Jìngméi had repeatedly killed high-ranking generals and wealthy merchants to enrich himself.
The imperial court sent the imperial envoy Yáng Xuánhuì to replace him.
Zhū Jìngméi remained in Jīngnán.
He once dried his clothes,
and Zhāng Huái saw them and desired them.
He sent soldiers to attack him at night,
killed Zhū Jìngméi,
and took all his wealth.
Zhāng Huái disliked the fierce and valiant Staff Officer Guō Yǔ
and wanted to kill him.
Guō Yǔ gathered a thousand men, fled,
and on the *gēngshēn* day,
attacked Guīzhōu,
seized it,
and styled himself governor.
Guō Yǔ was Chéng Ruì from Qīngzhōu.
He had committed murder and fled,
changing his name.
Guō Yǔ was originally a bandit
who surrendered to Chén Rú
and was made a general.
*Gēng* (更),
read as *gōng héng fān*.
According to Xuē Shǐ (History of the Liáng Dynasty),
Chéng Ruì was chivalrous in his youth.
He killed a person while drunk,
was captured by his enemies,
then shaved his head and became a monk,
adopting the surname Guō.
4 Lú Guāngchóu, a bandit chief from Nánkāng, captured Qiánzhōu,
styled himself governor,
and made Tán Quánbò, a fellow townsman, his chief strategist.
Nánkāng was the land of Nányě County in Hàn.
Wú divided Nányě and established Nán'ān County.
Jìn changed it to Nánkāng.
In Táng, it belonged to Qiánzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì (Record of the Nine Regions)
states it was eighty *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
*Kǎo Yì* (Critical Review of Discrepancies) states: Ouyáng Xiū's *Wǔdài Shǐ* (History of the Five Dynasties) says:
"Lú Guāngchóu and Tán Quánbò were both Nánkāng natives.
Lú Guāngchóu had an imposing appearance,
but no other particular talents.
Tán Quánbò, however, was brave and had strategic insight.
Yet Tán Quánbò always admired Lú Guāngchóu as a person.
At the end of the Táng dynasty, when numerous bandits arose,
Tán Quánbò gathered a following
and established Lú Guāngchóu as their leader.
At this time, Wáng Cháo attacked and captured Língnán.
Tán Quánbò attacked Wáng Cháo
and took Qián and Sháo prefectures from him."
*Shíguó Jìnián* (Chronology of the Ten Kingdoms) says:
"Tán Quánbò promoted Lú Guāngchóu to be his chief strategist.
They were victorious wherever they went.
In the early Guāngqǐ era,
they occupied Qiánzhōu,
and Lú Guāngchóu styled himself governor.
In the middle of the Tiānfù era,
they captured Sháozhōu,
and Lú Guāngchóu made his son Yánchāng defend it."
According to the *Xīn Jì* (New Record),
in the first month of the first year of Guāngqǐ,
Lú Guāngchóu captured Qiánzhōu.
In the second year of Tiānfù,
he captured Sháozhōu.
Ouyáng Xiū's assertion that Qián and Sháo prefectures were taken simultaneously
is an error.
We now follow the *Xīn Jì*.
5 Qín Zōngquán demanded taxes and levies from Wáng Xù, the governor of Guāngzhōu.
Wáng Xù could not provide them;
Qín Zōngquán was enraged and
dispatched troops to attack him.
Wáng Xù was fearful,
assembled all five thousand soldiers from Guāng and Shòu prefectures,
drove the officials and common people across the river,
made Liú Xíngquán his vanguard,
and plundered Jiāng, Hóng, and Qián prefectures.
In this month,
he captured Dīng and Zhāng prefectures,
but could not hold any of them.
Wáng Xù's army entered Fújiàn from here,
serving as capital for the Wáng Cháo brothers' independent rule.
6 Qín Zōngquán raided Yǐng and Bó prefectures.
Zhū Quánzhōng defeated him at Jiāoyí.
Jiāoyí was within the borders of Chéngfù County, Bózhōu.
According to Xuē Shǐ, Liáng Jì (Annals of the Liáng Dynasty),
in the first year of Lóngdé,
Jiāoyí County of Bózhōu was renamed Yífù.
Thus, Jiāoyí was already a county at that time.
*Bàile* (敗),
read as *bǔ mài fān*.
"Yífù" (夷父)
should be
"Chéngfù" (城父).
7 Second month,
on the *bǐngshēn* day,
the imperial carriage arrived at Fèngxiáng.
Third month,
on the *dīngmǎo* day,
it arrived at the capital.
Thorns filled the city,
and foxes and rabbits roamed freely.
The emperor was sorrowful and unhappy.
On the *jǐsì* day,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the *yuánhào* was changed.
The *yuánhào* was changed to Guāngqǐ.
This applied only to the several dozen prefectures of Héxī, Shānnán, Jiànnán, and Língnán.
8. Qín Zōngquán 秦宗權 proclaimed himself emperor,
and established a bureaucracy.
Kǎo Yì 考異 says: The old biography of Zōngquán 宗權
merely states that after the bandit Cháo 巢 was executed,
he usurped the imperial title.
The Shílù 實錄 says:
"In the tenth month of the following year,
Xiāngwáng 襄王 ascended the throne,
but Zōngquán 宗權 had already proclaimed himself emperor.
[The court] did not approve."
Neither the Xīn Jì 新紀 nor the Jiù Jì 舊紀 mention this,
so it is unknown in what month or year Zōngquán 宗權 proclaimed himself emperor.
Now, because of Shí Pú 時溥's appointment as Dūtǒng 都統, it is recorded here.
9. Lúlóng Jǐedùshǐ 盧龍節度使 Lǐ Kějǔ 李可舉 and Chéngdé Jǐedùshǐ 成德節度使 Wáng Róng 王鎔 resented Lǐ Kèyòng's 李克用 strength,
while Yìwǔ Jǐedùshǐ 義武節度使 Wáng Chǔcún 王處存 was close to Kèyòng 克用,
even marrying his niece Yè 鄴 to Kèyòng's 克用 daughter.
Moreover,
among the various garrisons north of the Yellow River,
only Yìwǔ 義武 still belonged to the imperial court.
Kějǔ 可舉 and others feared that they might spy on Shāndōng 山東.
This Shāndōng 山東
refers to the area east of Héngshān 恆山.
"Sì 伺" is pronounced xiàng lǐ.
They then conspired together, saying:
"Yì 易 and Dìng 定
are the remnants of Yān 燕 and Zhào 趙."
The land of Yìzhōu 易州
was originally the southern border of Yān 燕,
and Zhōngshān 中山 originally belonged to the state of Zhào 趙,
hence it is said "remnants of Yān 燕 and Zhào 趙."
They also persuaded Yúnzhōng Jǐedùshǐ 雲中節度使 Hèlián Duó 赫連鐸 to attack Kèyòng 克用 from the rear.
Kějǔ 可舉 dispatched his general Lǐ Quánzhōng 李全忠 with 60,000 soldiers to attack Yìzhōu 易州,
and Róng 鎔 dispatched his general with troops to attack Wújí 無極.
Wújí 無極
was an ancient county in the Hàn 漢 dynasty,
named after Wújí Shān 無極山.
In the Táng 唐 dynasty, it belonged to Dìngzhōu 定州.
The Jiǔyù Zhì 九域志 says: It is ninety lì 里 south of the prefectural city.
Kèyòng 克用 dispatched his general Kāng Jūnlì 康君立 and others with troops to relieve them.
10. In the intercalary month,
Qín Zōngquán 秦宗權 dispatched his brother Zōngyán 宗言 to raid Jīngnán 荊南.
11. Initially,
Tián Lìngzī 田令孜 in Shǔ 蜀 recruited fifty-four divisions of new troops,
each division having a thousand men,
and assigned them to the two Shéncè 神策 armies,
forming ten armies to command them.
Moreover, there were over ten thousand officials in the Nányá 南牙 and Běisī 北司 combined.
At this time, the various fānzhèn 藩鎮 each monopolized taxes and tributes;
Hénán 河南, Hébĕi 河北, Jiāng 江, and Huái 淮 no longer submitted supplies to the court.
The Sānsī 三司 and Zhuǎnyùn 轉運 had no sources for transfer and dispatch.
The Dùzhī 度支 only collected taxes and tributes from Jīngjī 京畿, Tóng 潼, Huá 華, Fèngxiáng 鳳翔, and a few other prefectures.
This was insufficient,
so rewards and gratuities were not given on time,
and the soldiers had complaints.
Lìngzī 令孜 was troubled by this
and did not know what to do.
Previously,
the salt from the two ponds in Ānyì 安邑 and Xièxiàn 解縣 both belonged to the Yántiě 鹽鐵 (Salt and Iron Commission),
and officials were appointed to monopolize them.
Sòng Bái 宋白 says: The salt affairs of the two ponds
originally belonged to the Dùzhī 度支,
and their officials were the various Circuit Inspectors.
In the sixteenth year of Zhēnyuán 貞元 (799),
Shǐ Móu 史牟, as the Lángzhōng 郎中 of the Jīnbù 金部 (Bureau of Finance), oversaw the pond affairs,
and then memorialized to establish the Quèyán Shǐ 榷鹽使 (Salt Monopoly Commissioner).
"Xiè 解" is pronounced hù mǎi.
"Què 榷" is pronounced qì yuè.
Wáng Chóngróng 王重榮, the Hèzhōng Jǐedùshǐ 河中節度使, monopolized them.
When the emperor fled to Shǔ 蜀,
all internal and external officials lost their posts.
Wáng Chóngróng 王重榮 secretly occupied Hèzhōng 河中
and gained exclusive control of the profits from the salt ponds.
Lìngzī 令孜 memorialized to restore the old system, affiliating them with the Yántiě 鹽鐵.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Lìngzī 令孜 personally assumed the concurrent post of Commissioner of the Salt Monopoly for the Two Ponds.
The Táng Huìyào 唐會要 says: In the fifteenth year of Yuánhé 元和 (820),
the Hébĕi Shuìyán Shǐ 河北稅鹽使 (Hebei Salt Tax Commissioner) was changed to Quèyán Shǐ 榷鹽使.
Later, Hébĕi 河北 was lost again,
and the Quèyán Shǐ 榷鹽使
was limited to the two ponds in Ānyì 安邑 and Xièxiàn 解縣.
Chóngróng 重榮 repeatedly submitted memorials to protest,
and an imperial envoy was sent to admonish him,
but Chóngróng 重榮 refused.
At that time, Lìngzī 令孜 often dispatched his trusted confidants to spy on the fānzhèn 藩鎮,
and anyone who did not support him,
he immediately plotted against.
Lìngzī's 令孜 adopted son Kuāngyòu 匡祐 was sent to Hèzhōng 河中.
Chóngróng 重榮 treated him very well,
but Kuāngyòu 匡祐 was extremely arrogant,
causing the entire army to be indignant.
Chóngróng 重榮 then enumerated Lìngzī's 令孜 crimes and misdeeds,
blaming him for his lack of propriety.
The supervising envoy explained on his behalf,
and Kuāngyòu 匡祐 barely escaped.
Kuāngyòu 匡祐 returned
and reported this to Lìngzī 令孜,
advising him to plot against Chóngróng 重榮.
In the fifth month,
Lìngzī 令孜 transferred Chóngróng 重榮 to be Táiníng Jǐedùshǐ 泰寧節度使,
appointed Táiníng Jǐedùshǐ 泰寧節度使 Qí Kèràng 齊克讓 as Yìwǔ Jǐedùshǐ 義武節度使,
and Yìwǔ Jǐedùshǐ 義武節度使 Wáng Chǔcún 王處存 as Hèzhōng Jǐedùshǐ 河中節度使,
while also issuing an edict ordering Lǐ Kèyòng 李克用 to assist Chǔcún 處存 in taking up his post with Hédōng 河東 troops.
This laid the groundwork for Lǐ Kèyòng 李克用 and Wáng Chóngróng 王重榮 to join forces and attack the imperial court.
12. The Lúlóng 盧龍 troops attacked Yìzhōu 易州.
Their subordinate general Liú Rén'gōng 劉仁恭 dug a tunnel into the city
and captured it.
Rén'gōng 仁恭 was from Shēnzhōu 深州.
Lǐ Kèyòng 李克用 personally led troops to relieve Wújí 無極
and defeated the Chéngdé 成德 troops.
The Chéngdé 成德 troops retreated to defend Xīnchéng 新城.
Kèyòng 克用 advanced again and attacked them,
routing them,
and taking Xīnchéng 新城.
The Chéngdé 成德 troops fled,
and were pursued to Jiǔmén 九門,
where over ten thousand heads were cut off.
After the Lúlóng 盧龍 troops took Yìzhōu 易州,
they became arrogant and complacent.
Wáng Chǔcún 王處存 secretly dispatched three thousand soldiers at night, disguised in sheepskins, to approach the city.
The Lúlóng 盧龍 troops thought they were sheep
and rushed out to plunder them.
Chǔcún 處存 attacked vigorously,
routing them,
and recaptured Yìzhōu 易州.
Lǐ Quánzhōng 李全忠 fled.
13. Wáng Chóngyíng 王重盈, the Shǎnjiǎo Jǐedùshǐ 陝虢節度使, was given the concurrent title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì 同平章事.
14. After Lǐ Quánzhōng 李全忠 lost his army,
fearing punishment,
he gathered his remaining troops and attacked Yōuzhōu 幽州.
In the sixth month,
Lǐ Kějǔ 李可舉, in dire straits,
committed self-immolation with his entire family by climbing a tower.
In the second year of Qiánfú 乾符 (875),
Lǐ Màoxūn 李茂勳 obtained Yōuzhōu 幽州.
It was extinguished in the second generation,
after eleven years.
15. Lǐ Hǎnzhī 李罕之, the Dōngdū Liúshǒu 東都留守 (Defender of the Eastern Capital), and Qín Zōngquán's 秦宗權 general Sūn Rú 孫儒 had been in a standoff for several months.
Hǎnzhī's 罕之 troops were few and their food supply was exhausted,
so he abandoned the city
and retreated west to Mǐnchí 澠池.
Zōngquán's 秦宗權 forces then captured the Eastern Capital.
The Jiǔyù Zhì 九域志 says: Mǐnchí Xiàn 澠池縣 is one hundred and fifty-six lì 里 west of the capital city.
"Mǐn 澠" is pronounced mí yǎn.
Sūn Rú 孫儒 captured the Eastern Capital,
but it is said "Zōngquán's 秦宗權 forces" because Rú 儒 was Zōngquán's 秦宗權 general.
16. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Lǐ Quánzhōng 李全忠 was appointed Lúlóng Liúhòu 盧龍留後 (Acting Military Governor of Lúlóng).
Cháo drew his troops and was about to return to Guāngzhōu,
having instructed his subordinates
not to harm even an autumn hair in the places they passed through.
When they reached Shāxiàn,
in the 6th year of Yǒnghuī,
Shāxiàn was established and settled separately,
subordinate to Dīngzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is 124 lǐ west of Nánjiànzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Shāxiàn
is an ancient vestige of Nánpíng.
In Jìn, it was Yánpíng Xiàn;
in the 4th year of Tàiyuán,
it was changed to Shāshù;
in the early Wǔdé period of Táng,
it was established as Shāxiàn.
The elders and gentry, offering cattle and wine, blocked the road
and asked Cháo to remain as a prefectural commander.
Cháo then led his troops to besiege Quánzhōu.
24In the 9th month,
on the day Wùshēn,
Chén Jìngxuan was appointed Commander-in-Chief and Commissioner for the various prefectures of Sānchuān and Xiá Neì.
Táng divided Sānchuān, each as a separate commandery,
and the various prefectures within Xiá Neì belonged to Guī and Xiá,
subordinate to the Jīngnán Military Commissioner.
Now Chén Jìngxuan commanded and managed them all,
with Tián Lìngzī supporting him.
25The Cài army besieged Jīngnán.
The Cài army
was Qín Zōngyán’s army, sent by Qín Zōngquán.
In the 1st month of this year,
Zhāng Huái imprisoned Chén Rú.
Huái
killed Kuāng and Rú.
26In winter,
in the 10th month,
on the day Guǐchǒu,
Qín Zōngquán defeated Zhū Quánzhōng at Bājiǎo.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: There is Bājiǎo Zhèn in Jùnyí Xiàn of Biànzhōu.
敗 (bài),
pronounced bù mài.
27Wáng Chóngróng sought aid from Lǐ Kèyòng.
The Kǎoyì states: The Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù says:
“Zhū Méi and Lǐ Chāngfú often formed alliances to enter the court and audience with the Son of Heaven,
pointing out advantages and disadvantages,
devising strategies and plans,
not assisting Tàizǔ,
but rather harboring and protecting the rebel Wēn.
Tàizǔ’s anger grew even more intense.
At that time, Tián Lìngzī disliked Tàizǔ’s close ties with Hézhōng,
and reported: ‘Wáng Chóngróng has drawn Táiyuán northwards;
his intentions are clear and he should not be kept in a nearby key position.
Wáng Chǔcún of Dìngzhōu is loyal and devoted;
I request that he be appointed commander of Pú,
and Chóngróng be moved to Dìngzhōu.’
The Son of Heaven followed this.
Chóngróng was indignant and displeased,
and reported to Tàizǔ: ‘The sovereign has only just returned to righteousness;
ministers are being cast aside.
At this moment, I am innocently expelled.
Your Excellency should discern their true intentions.
Where shall I go today!’
It happened that Tàizǔ was angry at Zhū Méi and his ilk,
and immediately replied: ‘I shall advance with you, beating drums, out of Sǐshuǐ Guān,
and after executing the rebels,
these scoundrels will be removed
like a swift wind scattering goose feathers.’
Chóngróng said: ‘My territory borders Bīn and Qí.
If Your Excellency marches east of the pass,
the two villains will surely lay siege to my city.
It is better to first eliminate one villain
and remove him from the sovereign’s side.’ ”
Ouyáng Xiū’s Wǔdài Shǐ says:
“Chóngróng sent someone to deceive Kèyòng, saying: ‘The Son of Heaven has decreed to Chóngróng
that when Kèyòng arrives,
he is to be executed jointly with Chǔcún.’
Then he forged an imperial edict and showed it to Kèyòng, saying: ‘This is Zhū Quánzhōng’s plot.’
Kèyòng believed it.”
Based on this, the court at that time was wary of Chóngróng,
and Kèyòng also knew this,
so it is unlikely this incident occurred.
We now follow the Jìnián Lù.
Zhū Quánzhōng attacked Kèyòng at Shàngyuányì,
and the court could not punish him,
which Kèyòng resented.
He gathered various Hu tribes
and discussed attacking Biànzhōu.
Chóngróng replied:
“Wait until I first eliminate Quánzhōng,
then I will sweep away these scoundrels like autumn leaves!”
Kèyòng said:
“If I wait for Your Excellency to return from east of the pass,
I will have already become a captive.
It is better to first eliminate the evil at the sovereign’s side,
then it will be easy to capture Quánzhōng later.”
At that time, Zhū Méi and Lǐ Chāngfú were also secretly allied with Zhū Quánzhōng.
Kèyòng then submitted a memorial, saying:
“Méi and Chāngfú are in collusion with Quánzhōng,
intending to jointly destroy your servant.
Your servant cannot but save himself.
I have already gathered 150,000 Fān and Hàn troops,
and I am resolved to cross the Hé next year
and attack the two commanderies from north of the Wèi River;
I will not approach the capital,
ensuring no alarm or disturbance.
After executing the two commanderies,
I will turn my army to destroy Quánzhōng to avenge this humiliation.”
The Emperor sent an envoy to explain and release him.
釋 (shì),
means to resolve.
Zhū Méi 欲朝廷討克用，
數遣人潛入京城，
燒積聚，
或刺殺近侍，
聲云克用所為，
於是京師震恐，
日有訛言。
Tián Lìngzī sent Méi and Chāngfú with their own armies, as well as the Shéncè, Fū, Yán, Líng, Xià, and other armies, each of
to garrison Shāyuàn
to attack Wáng Chóngróng.
The Kǎoyì says: The Xīn Tián Lìngzī Zhuàn states:
"Lìngzī personally led an expedition to attack Chóngróng,
commanding Méi and other troops, 30,000 strong, to encamp at Shāyuàn."
We now follow the Shílù.
A distress call was sent to Lǐ Kèyòng,
and Kèyòng led his troops to respond.
In the 11th month,
Chóngróng sent troops to attack Tóngzhōu.
The prefect, Guō Zhāng, sallied forth to battle
and was defeated and killed.
Chóngróng and Méi's forces were locked in a standoff for over a month.
When Kèyòng's army arrived,
he and Chóngróng encamped together at Shāyuàn,
and submitted a memorial requesting the execution of Lìngzī, Méi, and Chāngfú;
an imperial edict sought to reconcile them,
but Kèyòng did not listen.
In the 12th month,
on the day Guǐyǒu,
they engaged in battle.
Méi and Chāngfú were greatly defeated.
The Kǎoyì says: The Xīn Zhuàn states:
"Kèyòng submitted a memorial requesting the execution of Lìngzī and Méi.
The emperor sought reconciliation,
but Kèyòng did not comply;
a great battle was fought at Shāyuàn,
and the imperial army was defeated.
Méi fled back to Bīnzhōu,
and both he and Chāngfú were ashamed to be used by Lìngzī,
so they returned and allied with Chóngróng.
The Shéncè army collapsed,
and Kèyòng pressed towards the capital.
Lìngzī, having exhausted his options,
then kidnapped the emperor and fled at night through the Kāiyuǎnmén.
Since the rebels broke into Cháng'ān,
they burned the palaces and dwellings, seven or eight tenths of them.
Later, Jīngzhào Wáng Huī repaired and restored them to a roughly complete state.
At this point,
Lìngzī proclaimed: 'Wáng Chóngróng has rebelled.'
He ordered the burning of the palace city.
Only the Zhāoyáng and Pénglái palaces barely survived."
Commentary: Lìngzī escorted the emperor to a nearby vassal state to avoid the chaos,
his intention was also to return once the troops had withdrawn.
Why would he burn the palace city?
This is likely not true.
The Shílù states:
"In the 6th month,
Lìngzī sent the Bīn and Qí armies to attack Chóngróng.
In the 9th month,
the Bīn and Qí armies began to garrison Shāyuàn.
Chóngróng sought aid from Kèyòng.
In the 11th month,
Kèyòng and Chóngróng confronted the enemy at Shāyuàn.
They submitted a memorial requesting the execution of Lìngzī and Zhū Méi.
In the 12th month, on the day Guǐyǒu,
they engaged in battle,
and Zhū Méi was defeated and fled."
The Tàizǔ Jìniánlù states:
"In the 11th month,
Chóngróng sent envoys to request troops,
and also stated that the two prefectures intended to attack him.
Tàizǔ wanted to attack Zhū Wēn first,

The dates vary among the different texts like this.

In short,
