and incites chaos and trouble.
Yesterday, I received your esteemed command to welcome the imperial carriage
(this means Gòu (遘) summoned Méi (玫) to welcome the imperial carriage),
but it turned out like threatening the monarch.
Our hearts for serving the country are extreme,
and our strength to fight the bandits is exhausted.
How can we bow our heads and lower our ears
to be controlled by the hands of eunuchs!
There are still many descendants of the Lǐ (李) clan.
Why doesn't Your Excellency reconsider your plans for the benefit of the state?"
Gòu (遘) replied:
"The emperor has been on the throne for more than ten years,
and has committed no major faults or evils.
It is precisely because Lìngzī (令孜) holds power close at hand
that the emperor cannot rest easy.
The emperor often speaks of it,
weeping incessantly.
Recently, the emperor initially had no intention of leaving.
Lìngzī (令孜) arrayed troops in front of the tent,
coercing him to depart
without allowing him to wait until dawn.
The fault lies entirely with Lìngzī (令孜),
and who does not know this!
You have devoted yourself to the imperial house.
You should just lead your troops back to your garrison,
present a memorial, and welcome the imperial carriage.
Dethroning and establishing a new emperor is a grave matter,
difficult even for Yī (伊) and Huò (霍).
I, Gòu (遘), dare not accept such an order!"
Méi (玫) exited,
and declared:
"I will establish a king from the Lǐ (李) clan.
Anyone who dares to voice a different opinion shall be executed!"
In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the rénzǐ day,
Zhū Méi forced the officials at Fèngxiáng to enthrone Xiāngwáng Yūn and appoint him as acting supervisor of military and state affairs.
He authorized him to confer titles and make appointments,
and then dispatched high-ranking officials to Shu to welcome the Emperor.
He made the officials swear an oath at Shíbí Yì.
Méi ordered Xiāo Gòu to draft the enthronement document,
but Gòu declined, citing a decline in his literary skills.
So, Méi had Zhèng Chāngtú, the Minister of War and Administrator of the Ministry of Revenue, draft it.
On the yǐmǎo day,
Yūn accepted the enthronement document.
Méi concurrently appointed himself as the Commander of the Left and Right Shéncè Ten Armies.
The "Kǎoyì" (Examination of Differences) states: The "Shílù" (Veritable Records) says:
"Méi appointed himself as Grand Chancellor."
However, there was no such official position in the Táng dynasty.
Furthermore, in the fifth month,
Méi added the title of Shìzhōng (Chamberlain) for himself.
It is likely that those who wrote novels in the late Táng period
referred to Píngzhāngshì (Chancellor) or Shìzhōng as Grand Chancellor,
and the "Shílù" mistakenly followed their phrasing.
When things reached this point,
Xiāo Gòu had nowhere to hide between heaven and earth.
The character "帥" (shuài)
should be read as "shuài" (to lead).
Each established a vice-commissioner,
and all matters of the Three Departments were entrusted to them.
The officials in Hézhōng, led by Cuī Ānqián and others, submitted a memorial to Xiāngwáng
to congratulate him on his enthronement.
When the Emperor departed from Cháng'ān,
the officials did not follow him;
those who fled to Hézhōng
were referred to as the Hézhōng officials.
8 Tián Lìngzī, knowing that he was intolerable to the world,
recommended Yáng Fùgōng, the Commissioner of Military Affairs, as the Commander of the Left Shéncè Army and Inspector of the Imperial Army.
Lìngzī himself was appointed as the Supervisor of Western Chuān.
The "Kǎoyì" states: Both the "Jiù Jì" (Old Annals) and "Shílù" say
"In the second month,
Lìngzī was made Supervisor of Xīchuān."
The "Jiù Chuán" (Old Biographies) says:
"Lìngzī, fearful,
had Yáng Fùgōng replace him,
followed the Emperor to Liángzhōu,
and sought to be the Supervisor of Xīchuān."
The "Xīn Chuán" (New Biographies) says:
"Lìngzī remained and did not leave,
and when the Emperor fell ill,
he then went to Chéngdū
and submitted a memorial to resign his office and seek medical treatment."
This likely adopted Zhāng's account.
According to Wáng Jiàn's "Jìshì" (Record of Events):
"In the fourth month,
on the gēngshēn day,
he reached Bāozhōng.
Lìngzī, his crimes and transgressions being numerous,
and fearing disaster,
then appointed himself Supervisor of Xīchuān
to avoid direct criticism,
and again planned to make a stronghold with Jìngxuān."
We follow this account now.
This provides the basis for Jìngxuān and Lìngzī's joint command.
Wáng Jiàn was appointed Governor of Lìzhōu,
Jìn Huī as Governor of Jízhōu,
Zhāng Zào as Governor of Wànzhōu,
and Lǐ Shītài as Governor of Zhōngzhōu.
Wáng Jiàn and others returned to Tián Lìngzī.
See the previous volume, Zhōnghé, fourth year, eleventh month.
9 In the fifth month,
Zhū Méi appointed Xiāo Gòu, the Minister of the Secretariat and Grand Chancellor, as太子Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince).
Méi himself added the titles of Shìzhōng (Chamberlain) and Commissioner of Salt and Iron and Transport for all circuits.
He added Péi Chè as Administrator of Finances,
and Zhèng Chāngtú as Administrator of the Ministry of Revenue.
He appointed Gāo Pián, the Military Governor of Huáinán, to concurrently serve as Grand Chancellor
and Commissioner of Salt and Iron and Transport for Jiāng and Huái, and Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Army for all circuits.
Lǚ Yòngzhī, the Right Commander of the Huáinán Army and Prefect of Hézhōu, was appointed Military Governor of Lǐngnán Dōngdào.
He made extensive grants of titles to please the regional commanders.
He dispatched Xiàhóu Tán, the Assistant Minister of Personnel, to proclaim his decrees in Héběi,
and Yáng Zhì, the Assistant Minister of Revenue, to proclaim them to the various regional commanders in Jiāng and Huái.
Six or seven tenths of them accepted his mandate,
and Gāo Pián even presented a memorial urging his advancement.
Historians say that when Xīzōng fled to Shānnán again,
the world had already given up hope,
and his return was merely fortunate.
Lǚ Yòngzhī established his headquarters and set up his administration,
acting in every way as Pián's equal.
He forced all of Pián's trusted aides and competent officers
to join him,
and in all his actions,
he no longer consulted Pián.
Pián grew suspicious of him,
secretly wishing to reclaim his authority,
but Yòngzhī's roots were already deep,
and there was nothing he could do.
Yòngzhī, aware of this,
was greatly alarmed.
He consulted his partisans, the former Finance Commissioner Zhèng and the former Prefect of Lúzhōu Dǒng Jǐn,
and said:
"This is indeed too late."
Meaning that Pián had not realized it sooner.
He said:
"Cáo Mèngdé said: '
I would rather betray others than let others betray me.' "
In the late Hàn dynasty,
Cáo Cāo, fleeing the troubles caused by Dǒng Zhuó,
traveled incognito eastward.
He passed by his old friend Lǚ Bóshē,
who brought out his five sons to perform host and guest courtesies.
Cāo heard the sound of dishes
and thought they were plotting against him.
He drew his sword and killed all eight people before leaving.
Afterward, he said sadly:
"I would rather betray others than let others betray me."
Mèngdé
was Cáo Cāo's courtesy name.
Zhèng likely advised Yòngzhī to plot against Pián.
He and Jǐn together wrote a sealed letter and gave it to Yòngzhī.
Its contents were secret;
no one knew what they were.
The plots of Zhèng and Jǐn
will be seen in the next volume, Guāngqǐ third year.
Xiāo Gòu pleaded illness and returned to Yǒnglè.
According to the "Xīn Shū" (New Book),
Gòu's younger brother, Qú, was the Magistrate of Yǒnglè,
and Gòu went to stay with him.
Yǒnglè County
belonged to Hézhōng Prefecture and was established in the early Wǔdé reign.
Sòng Bái said: Yǒnglè County was originally the territory of Hànběi County in the Hàn dynasty.
In the second year of Wǔchéng of Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu,
it was renamed Yǒnglè.
In the second year of Bǎodìng, it was abolished,
and its territory was assigned to Ruìchéng.
In the second year of Wǔdé of Táng,
it was re-established by dividing Ruìchéng.
The character "樂" (lè)
is pronounced "luò".
Initially,
Lǐ Chāngfú, the Military Governor of Fèngxiáng, conspired with Zhū Méi to enthrone Xiāngwáng.
However, Méi later made himself Chancellor and monopolized power.
Chāngfú was enraged,
refused to accept his official position,
and instead communicated with Xīngyuán.
An imperial edict conferred on Chāngfú the title of 検校司徒Jiǎnxiào Sītú (Acting Minister of Works).
Zhū Méi dispatched his general Wáng Xíngyú to lead 50,000 troops from Bīnnìng and Héxī to pursue the imperial entourage.
Since the reign of Dàizōng,
Héxī had been lost to the Tǔbō.
Xuānzōng recovered Hé and Huáng,
and Zhāng Yìcháo retook Liángzhōu,
and Héxī again became subservient to Táng.
The Emperor abandoned Sànguān and fled,
and Xíngyú advanced to garrison Fèngzhōu.
At this time,
most of the tributes and taxes from the various circuits
went to Cháng'ān,
not to Xīngyuán.
The character "之" (zhī)
means "to go".
The Emperor wept,
not knowing what to do.
Dù Ràngnéng said to the Emperor:
"Yáng Fùguāng and Wáng Chóngróng jointly defeated Huáng Cháo
and recovered the capital city,
and they are on good terms.
This matter is seen in the previous volume, Zhōnghé third year.
If a high-ranking official is sent to persuade him with great righteousness,
and also convey Fùgōng's intentions,
he should reasonably reconsider and return to the state."
The Emperor agreed,
and sent Liú Chóngwàng, the Right Grand Master Remonstrant, as an envoy to Hézhōng,
carrying an imperial edict to persuade Chóngróng.
Chóngróng immediately obeyed,
dispatched an envoy to present 100,000 bolts of silk,
and requested to attack Zhū Méi to redeem himself.
On the wùxū day,
Xiāngwáng Yūn sent an envoy to Jìnyáng to bestow an imperial edict upon Lǐ Kèyòng,
stating:
"Halfway along the journey,
the six armies rebelled and caused disorder,
and His Majesty suddenly passed away.
I was nominated by the regional commanders,
and have now accepted the enthronement."
Zhū Méi also sent a letter to Kèyòng.
Kèyòng, hearing that the plot originated from Méi,
was greatly enraged.
His general, Gài Yù, advised Kèyòng:
"The imperial carriage has been moved,
and the world blames me.
If we do not punish Méi
and depose Lǐ Yūn,
there will be no way to cleanse ourselves."
Kèyòng agreed,
burned the imperial edict,
imprisoned the envoy,
and issued a proclamation to neighboring circuits,
stating:
"Méi dares to deceive the feudal regions,
openly declaring His Majesty's sudden demise.
Our circuit has already dispatched 30,000 Fān and Hàn troops to advance and suppress the ruthless rebel.
We should collectively achieve a great功功gōng (merit)."
Yù
was from Wèizhōu.
10 Qín Xián (秦賢) assailed Sòng Biàn (宋汴).
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) defeated him south of Wèishì (尉氏).
On the day *Guǐsì*,
he dispatched the Capital Commander Guō Yán (郭言) with 30,000 infantry and cavalry to attack Càizhōu (蔡州).
11 In the sixth month,
Yang Shǒuliàng (楊守亮), the Grand Commander of the Imperial Escort, was made Military Commissioner of Jīnshāng (金商) and Commissioner for the Management of the Jīngjī (京畿) region.
The Imperial Escort Command
was also one of the fifty-four commands of the Shéncè (神策) Army.
Yang Shǒuliàng, Wáng Chóngróng (王重榮), and Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) jointly attacked Zhū Méi (朱玫).
Shǒuliàng's (守亮) original surname was Zī (訾),
and his given name was Liàng (亮).
He was from Cáozhōu (曹州).
Both he and his younger brother Xìn (信) were adopted sons of Yáng Fùguāng (楊復光).
They were renamed Shǒuliàng (守亮) and Shǒuxìn (守信).
Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) sent an envoy with a memorial stating:
"I am about to dispatch troops to cross the Yellow River,
eliminate the rebellious faction,
and welcome the imperial carriage.
I request an imperial edict for all circuits to cooperate with me."
Previously,
all the people of Shānnán (山南) said that Kèyòng (克用) had allied with Zhū Méi (朱玫),
causing widespread fear among the populace.
When the memorial arrived,
the emperor showed it to his attendant officials
and also informed the various garrisons in Shānnán (山南),
which thereupon brought calm.
However, Kèyòng's (克用) memorial still mentioned Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠).
The emperor had Yáng Fùgōng (楊復恭) send a letter to him saying:
"Wait until the affairs of Sānfǔ (三輔) are settled."
The Han dynasty referred to Jīngzhào (京兆), Fēngyì (馮翊), and Fúfēng (扶風) as Sānfǔ (三輔).
In the Tang dynasty, this referred to the Jīngjī (京畿) region.
12 Zhōu Yuè (周岳), the Prefect of Héngzhōu (衡州), sent troops to attack Tánzhōu (潭州).
Mǐn Xù (閔勗), the Military Commissioner of Qīnhuà (欽化), invited Huáixī (淮西) general Huáng Hào (黃皓) into the city to defend it together.
The Huáixī (淮西) general
was a general of Qín Zōngquán (秦宗權).
In the first year of Zhōnghé (中和),
Mǐn Xù (閔勗) occupied Tánzhōu (潭州),
but was defeated at this time.
Hào (皓) was captured
and killed.
13 Zhōu Bǎo (周寶), the Military Commissioner of Zhènhǎi (鎮海), dispatched his staff general Dīng Cóngshí (丁從實) to raid Chángzhōu (常州).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *New Ji* (新紀) says:
"Dīng Cóngshí (丁從實), a general of Wǔníng (武寧) Army, captured Chángzhōu (常州)."
We now follow Pí Shì Jiànwénlù (皮氏見聞錄).
Yù (郁) fled to Hǎilíng (海陵).
In the first month of this year,
Zhāng Yù (張郁) captured Chángzhōu (常州).
Bà (霸)
was a general of Gāo Pián (高駢).
He garrisoned Hǎilíng (海 líng),
which had 50,000 households
and 30,000 soldiers.
14 In autumn,
seventh month,
Qín Zōngquán (秦宗權) captured Xǔzhōu (許州)
and killed Military Commissioner Lù Yànhóng (鹿晏弘).
In the fourth year of Zhōnghé (中和),
Yànhóng (晏弘) had occupied Xǔzhōu (許州),
but was defeated and perished at this time.
15 Wáng Xíngyú (王行瑜) attacked Xīngzhōu (興州).
Yáng Shèng (楊晟), the Military Commissioner of Gǎnyì (感義), abandoned his post and fled.
He occupied Wénzhōu (文州).
An edict ordered Lǐ Chán (李鋋), the Grand Commander of Baoluan, and Lǐ Màozhēn (李茂貞) and Chén Pèi (陳佩), the Grand Commanders of the Imperial Escort, to garrison Dàtángfēng (大唐峯) to resist him.
Màozhēn (茂貞)
was from Bóyě (博野).
His original surname was Sòng (宋),
and his given name was Wéntōng (文通).
He was granted a new surname and given name for his achievements.
Lǐ Màozhēn (李茂貞) began here.
16 The Qīnhuà (欽化) Army was renamed Wǔ'ān (武安).
The promotion of the Húnán (湖南) Observer to Qīnhuà (欽化) Army is seen in the previous scroll, Zhōnghé (中和) 3rd year.
Gēng (更),
pronounced as gōng héng fān.
17 In the eighth month,
Lǐ Quánzhōng (李全忠), the Military Commissioner of Lúlóng (盧龍), died.
His son Kuāngwēi (匡威) was appointed acting commissioner.
18 Wáng Cháo (王潮) captured Quánzhōu (泉州)
and killed Liáo Yànruò (廖彥若).
In the eighth month of the previous year, Wáng Cháo (王潮) had besieged Quánzhōu (泉州),
and captured it at this time.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *New Ji* (新紀) says:
"In the eighth month,
Wáng Cháo (王潮) captured Quánzhōu (泉州),
and Prefect Liú Yànruò (劉彥若) died there."
According to all other books, it is
"Liáo Yànruò" (廖彥若).
The *New Ji* (新紀) has
"Liú" (劉),
which is probably a mistake.
(Wáng Cháo) dared not infringe upon Fúzhōu (福州) territory.
He sent an envoy to surrender to Yán (巖).
Yán (巖) memorialized for Cháo (潮) to be made Prefect of Quánzhōu (泉州).
Cháo (潮) was profound and brave, with wisdom and strategy.
Once he obtained Quánzhōu (泉州),
he rallied the dispersed,
equalized taxes, and built up his army.
The officials and people were pleased and submitted.
He confined Wáng Xù (王緒) in a separate residence.
Xù (緒), ashamed,
committed suicide.
19 In the ninth month,
Zhāng Xíngshí (張行實), a general of Zhū Méi (朱玫), attacked Dàtángfēng (大唐峯).
Lǐ Chán (李鋋) and others attacked and repulsed him.
Mǎn Cún (滿存), a general of Jīnwǔ (金吾), fought with the Bīn (邠) army,
defeated them,
recaptured Xīngzhōu (興州),
and advanced to garrison Wànrènzhài (萬仞寨).
20 Lǐ Kèxiū (李克脩) attacked Mèng Fānglì (孟方立).
On the day *Jiǎwǔ*,
he captured his general Lǚ Zhēn (呂臻) at Jiāogāng (焦岡),
and captured Gùzhèn (故鎮), Wǔ'ān (武安), Línmíng (臨洺), Hándān (邯鄲), and Shāhé (沙河).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) states: Wǔ'ān (武安) County in Míngzhōu (洺州) has Gùzhèn (固鎮) Town.
21 In Cháng'ān (長安), the hundred officials, including the Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince Péi Qú (裴璩), urged Xiang Wáng Yūn (襄王熅) to ascend the throne.
In winter,
tenth month,
Yūn (熅) ascended the imperial throne
and changed the era name to Jiànzhēn (建貞). He remotely honored the emperor as Tàishàng Yuánhuáng Shèngdì (太上元皇聖帝).
22 Dǒng Chāng (董昌) said to Qián Liú (錢鏐):
"If you can take Yuèzhōu (越州),
I will give you Hángzhōu (杭州)."
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Shílù* (實錄) says:
"On the day *Xīnwèi*,
Dǒng Chāng (董昌), the Prefect of Hángzhōu (杭州), was made Observer of Zhèdōng (浙東)."
According to this, in the eleventh month of this year,
Liú (鏐) first captured Yuèzhōu (越州).
In the twelfth month, Hán Hóng (漢宏) was captured,
and Chāng (昌) first styled himself as Acting Administrator of the Zhèdōng (浙東) Military Command.
The *Shílù* (實錄) is mistaken.
"If not,
it will eventually become a future problem."
So, he led troops from Zhūjì (諸暨) towards Píngshuǐ (平水).
He cut mountains and opened a road for 500 *lǐ*,
emerging at Cáoyánuó Dài (曹娥埭).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) states: Huìjī (會稽) County in Yuèzhōu (越州) has Píngshuǐ (平水) Town and Cáoyánuó (曹娥) Town.
Píngshuǐ (平水) is now more than forty *lǐ* southeast of Yuèzhōu (越州).
From here, south across the mountains,
emerging at Xiǎojiāng (小江),
then along the Shànxī (剡溪) twenty *lǐ* east,
to Cáoyánuó Dài (曹娥埭).
Dài (埭),
pronounced tú nài fān.
Liú (鏐) fought with the Zhèdōng (浙東) army,
repeatedly defeated them,
and advanced to garrison Fēngshān (豐山).
23 Zhāng Xióng (張雄) and Féng Hóngduó (馮弘鐸), staff generals of Gǎnhuà (感化), offended Shí Pǔ (時溥), the Military Commissioner.
Xúzhōu (徐州) was originally called Wǔníng Jūn (武寧軍).
After the abolition of the military commission during Xiántōng (咸通),
it was soon restored to a military commission
and renamed Gǎnhuà Jūn (感化軍).
Some mention Wǔníng (武寧) in between,
which is a mistake.
Later, after Shí Pǔ (時溥) died,
Zhū Liáng (朱梁) first restored Xúzhōu (徐州) as Wǔníng Jūn (武寧軍).
(Zhāng Xióng and Féng Hóngduó) fled across the river,
raided Sūzhōu (蘇州),
and occupied it.
Xióng (雄) styled himself Prefect,
gradually amassed troops to 50,000,
with over a thousand warships,
and called himself Tiānchéng Jūn (天成軍).
24 Zhūgě Shuǎng (諸葛爽), the Military Commissioner of Héyáng (河陽), died.
His senior generals Liú Jīng (劉經) and Zhāng Quányì (張全義) installed Shuǎng's (爽) son Zhòngfāng (仲方) as acting commissioner.
Quányì (全義)
was from Línpú (臨濮).
In the fourth year of Wǔdé (武德),
Línpú (臨濮) County was established by dividing Léizé (雷澤) County,
belonging to Púzhōu (濮州).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) states: It is sixty *lǐ* south of the prefecture.
Pú (濮),
pronounced bó mù fān.
25 Lǐ Kèxiū (李克脩) attacked Xíngzhōu (邢州),
but failed and returned.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Tàizǔ Jìniánlù* (太祖紀年錄) says:
"The people of Xíng (邢) came out to fight
and were again defeated.
Mèng Fānglì (孟方立) sought help from Wáng Róng (王鎔) of Zhènzhōu (鎮州),
who dispatched 30,000 troops to reinforce him.
Our army then retreated."
The *Old Róng Zhuàn* (舊鎔傳) says:
"At that time, the Son of Heaven was in exile,
and the nine regions were in turmoil.
Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) of Hédōng (河東) eyed Shāndōng (山東) like a tiger,
planning to annex it.
Róng (鎔) cultivated relations with heavy bribes
to maintain good terms.
When the Jìn (晉) army attacked Mèng Fānglì (孟方立) at Xíngzhōu (邢州),
Róng (鎔) often supplied them with fodder and provisions."
According to this,
Róng (鎔) assisted Kèyòng (克用) in attacking Xíngzhōu (邢州).
It is unclear which is correct.
We adopt neither here.
On the 26th day of the eleventh month,
on the day of bǐngxū,
Qián Liú conquered Yuèzhōu,
and Liú Hàn-hóng fled to Táizhōu.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù says
Hàn-hóng was killed before Dǒng Chāng eliminated Zhèdōng.
According to Fàn Jǐng's Wúyuè Bèishǐ,
Hàn-hóng's defeat and flight until his death in the twelfth month are all dated.
We follow this now.
On the 27th, Ān Shī-rú, the Jìedùshǐ of Yìchéng, delegated governance to the liǎngxiāng Dūyúhóu Xiàhóu Yàn and Dù Biāo.
The two became arrogant and tyrannical,
and the army resented them.
The xiǎoxiào Zhāng Xiāo secretly went out,
gathered two thousand men, and attacked the prefectural city.
Shī-rú had Yàn and Biāo beheaded to placate them,
and the army gradually quieted down.

Yīn Yíng-sūn, a Tàicháng Bóshì, deliberated,

"My cause is accomplished!"

Their generals Zhāng Zhì were camped in the northern suburbs,
and Qín Xián was camped at Bǎnqiáo.
"Northern suburbs"
refers to the plains north of Biànzhōu city,
which is Chìgāng.
According to old histories, Bǎnqiáo was west of Biànzhōu city.
They had thirty-six camps,
stretching over twenty *lǐ*.
Quánzhōng said to his generals:
"They are conserving their strength and resting their troops,
about to attack us.
They don't know that Zhū Zhēn has arrived.
They think our forces are few,
and that we are timidly defending ourselves.
We should attack them by surprise
and strike first."
So, he personally led his troops to attack Qín Xián's camp.
The soldiers eagerly vied for the vanguard.
Xián was unprepared,
and Quánzhōng successively captured four camps,
beheading over ten thousand.
The Cài people were greatly alarmed,
considering it divine.
Quánzhōng also sent his staff general Guō Yán from Xīnyě to recruit soldiers in Héyáng, Shǎn, and Guó.
He returned with over ten thousand men.
Bì Shīduó's troops suddenly arrived outside Guǎnglín city.
The city was thrown into alarm and disorder.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
Lǚ Yòngzhī led his elite troops,
enticing them with lavish rewards, and sallied forth to fight fiercely.
Shīduó's troops retreated slightly.
Only then was Yòngzhī able to break bridges and block gates for defense.
On this day,
Gāo Pián ascended the Yánhé Pavilion.
Hearing the clamor,
his attendants informed him of Shīduó's rebellion.
Gāo Pián was startled
and urgently summoned Yòngzhī to question him.
Yòngzhī calmly replied:
"Shīduó's troops wish to return,
but were blocked by the gate guards.
I have already dealt with the situation appropriately;
they are expected to disperse soon.
Should they not,
it will merely require one warrior of Xuánnǚ.
Please do not worry, my Duke!"
Gāo Pián said:
"Recently, I have noticed much of your absurdity.
You must do well;
do not make me like Zhōu Shìzhōng!"
"Zhōu Shìzhōng"
refers to Zhōu Bǎo,
whose story is in the previous volume, same year.
Gāo Pián felt dismayed and disheartened.
After a while,
Yòngzhī retreated, feeling ashamed and uneasy.
Shī Duó (師鐸) retreated and camped at Shānguāng Sì (山光寺).
Shānguāng Sì (山光寺)
is north of Guǎnglíng (廣陵) city.
He showed great remorse.
On Guǐchǒu (癸丑) day,

Shī Duó (師鐸) was then pleased.

On Jiǎyín (甲寅) day,

Wěiqū (委曲) means Pián's (駢) handwritten note.
Shī Duó (師鐸) had initially hoped for Pián's (駢) old generals to visit and inquire,

Pī (披) means to open or divide.
To break a dam to release water.

Kān (戡) had not yet spoken,

From this, Gāo (高) and Lǚ (呂) finally parted ways.
That night,

On Wùwǔ (戊午) day,

Yòngzhī (用之) ordered his generals to search the city for able-bodied men.
Regardless of whether they were court officials or scholars,

from dawn till dusk,
without rest.
Fearing they might communicate with the external invaders,
he frequently changed their positions.
When their families brought them food,
no one knew their whereabouts.
Because of this, the people in the city also regretted that Shī Duó (師鐸) had entered the city late.
Pián (駢) sent his general Shí È (石鍔)

Shī Duó (師鐸) immediately sent his son back,

Pián (駢), fearing that Yòngzhī (用之) would slaughter their family,

The Commissioner's Residence is where the officials of the Military Commissioner's office conduct affairs.
On Xīnyǒu (辛酉) day,

On Guǐhài (癸亥) day,

On Jiǎzǐ (甲子) day,
the defenders at the southwestern corner of Luóchéng (羅城) burned the battle grates to respond to Shī Duó (師鐸).
Zhàngé (戰格) are made of arranged wood;

Yòngzhī (用之) led his thousand men to fight fiercely north of Sānqiáo (三橋).
Shī Duó (師鐸) was on the verge of defeat,

Pián (駢) summoned Liáng Zuǎn (梁纘) to guard the inner city with over a hundred Zhāoyì (昭義) troops.

Shī Duó (師鐸) let his troops plunder extensively.

Zhèng Hànzhāng (鄭漢章) and others were all promoted accordingly.
Shēn Jí (申及), Left Moxie (莫邪) Grand Marshal,
originally a brave general from Xúzhōu (徐州).

see Zhonghe (中和) 2nd year in volume 254.
He said to Pián (駢),

Jícǐ (及此) means at this time.
Before Shī Duó (師鐸) realizes it,

Then, dispatch troops from all the garrisons,

King Líng (靈王) of Chǔ (楚) once said,

It happened that Zhāng Xióng (張雄) arrived at Dōngtáng (東塘).

Shī Duó (師鐸) moved into the Commissioner's Residence,

Bì Shīduó thought this was completely wrong.

his followers were ashamed of his initial aggressive actions,
and concealed his wrongdoings.
After he took over Lángzhōu,
many accounts mention his official appointments and transfers,
especially avoiding mention of his attack on Xīchuān and Chén Jìngxúān at the end of Guāngqǐ.
Some place it in the Wéndé era, after Wéi Zhaōdù was appointed to govern Shǔ but Chén Jìngxúān refused to hand over power.
Others say that the imperial court stripped Chén Jìngxúān of his official titles,
and Wáng Jiàn then joined Wéi Zhaōdù in a punitive expedition,
all portraying it as an army acting under imperial orders to defend the emperor.
Therefore, Lǐ Hào’s Shǔ Shū, Máo Wénxī’s Jìshì, Zhāng Jǐnlǐ’s Qíjiù Zhuàn, Yáng Kān’s Píngshǔ Dézhèng Bēi, Wú Róng’s Shēngcí Táng Bēi, Féng Juān’s Dàtīng Bì Jì, and Shōufù Qióngzhōu Bì Jì,
all compiled and recorded at that time,
contradict each other.
Wú Róng says: In the *zuò’è* year (Jǐyǒu),
Chancellor Wéi was ordered to attack Shǔ.
He also says: In the year after the Holy Emperor ascended the throne,
an edict appointed Grand Chancellor Wéi to govern Shǔ,
and troops were raised under the Chancellor to suppress the disloyal.
Soon after, he was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Yǒngpíng and Commander-in-Chief.”
Now, according to the Jiù Xīzōng Jì:
“In Guāngqǐ 3rd year (887), 12th month,
Gù Yànlǎng of Dōngchuān and Wáng Jiàn, Prefect of Bìzhōu, united their forces of 50,000 to attack Chéngdū.
Chén Jìngxúān reported the difficulty to the court,
and an edict was issued to the imperial envoy to convey instructions.”
The Táng Nián Bǔlù says:
“In Guāngqǐ 3rd year (887), 12th month,
due to the confrontation between Chén Jìngxúān of Xīchuān and Gù Yànlǎng of Dōngchuān,
an edict ordered Lǐ Màozhēn to write to them and mediate a resolution.”
This is largely consistent with what is recorded in the Táng Zhuāngzōng Gōngchén Lièzhuàn, Táng Lièzǔ Shílù, Wǔdài Shǐ Wáng Jiàn Zhuàn, Zhuāngzōng Shílù, and Fàn Zhì’s Wǔdài Tōnglù Wáng Yǎn Zhuàn.
Wéi Zhaōdù was first appointed Jìedùshǐ of Xīchuān in Wéndé 1st year (888), 6th month,
and arrived in Chéngdū in the 10th month.
Chén Jìngxúān refused to hand over power.
Wéi Zhaōdù memorialized that Chén Jìngxúān was rebelling,
and on the *dīnghài* day of the 12th month,
Wéi Zhaōdù was appointed Commander of the Punitive Expedition,
and Wáng Jiàn Jìedùshǐ of Yǒngpíng.
According to the calendar,
the 1st day of the 12th month of that year was *jiǎzǐ*,
so *dīnghài*
was the 24th day.
In the 1st month of Lóngjì 1st year, *dīngyǒu* (889),
the imperial decree finally reached Chéngdū.
Wú Róng based his account on the month and year Wéi Zhaōdù received his appointment as Commander of the Punitive Expedition,
hence he said that Shǔ was attacked in the *zuò’è* year (Jǐyǒu),
which was the year after Zhaōzōng ascended the throne.
Grand Duke Wéi was appointed to govern Shǔ in the previous year.
Perhaps Wú Róng mistakenly thought “attacking Shǔ” was “governing Shǔ.”
The Jiù Jì says:
“In Wéndé 1st year (888), 6th month,
Wéi Zhaōdù was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Xīchuān and Pacification and Control Commissioner of the Two Chuān.”
The Xīn Shū Zhaōzōng Běnjì says:
“In Wéndé 1st year (888), 10th month,
Chén Jìngxúān rebelled.
On the *dīnghài* day of the 12th month,
Wéi Zhaōdù was appointed Commander of the Punitive Expedition.”
All these are correct.
However, the Jiù Jì mistakenly says that in Lóngjì 1st year (889), 1st month,
Wéi Zhaōdù was appointed Guardian of Dōngdū.
In the 5th month,
Wáng Jiàn captured Chéngdū
and declared himself Acting Jìedùshǐ.
The Xīn Shū Chén Jìngxúān Zhuàn entirely uses Zhāng Qíjiù’s biography.
