44 In the twelfth month,
the *Kǎoyì* says: According to the *Chánglì*,
the intercalary eleventh month began on a *gēngzǐ* day,
and the twelfth month began on a *jǐsì* day.
The *Xīn* and *Jiù Jì* have no record of intercalary months,
so they are not seen.
The *Xīn Jì*'s twelfth month *guǐsì* is in this month,
which also takes the eleventh month as intercalary.
The *Yāoluàn Zhì* has a "latter eleventh month."
The *Shíguó Jìnián* also has an intercalary eleventh month.
Only Xuē Jūzhèng's *Wǔdài Shǐ* and the *Liáng Jì* have an intercalary month after the twelfth month.
The *Shílù* says,
the intercalary twelfth month began on a *gēngzǐ* day.
This is not adopted now.
On a *guǐsì* day,
Zhào Déyīn (appointed as Provisional Military Commissioner of Shānnán Dōngdào by Qín Zōngquán) captured Jīngnán.
The Jiedushi,
Zhāng Huái,
left his general Wáng Jiànzhào to defend the city and departed.
In the first year of Guāngqǐ (885),
Zhāng Huái had occupied Jīngnán,
and was defeated at this time.
The *Xīn Shū* says: When the city fell,
Huái died,
unrecognized by anyone,
and was thrown into a well along with others.
Chén Fán, Prefect of Fùzhōu, followed Huái to Jiānglíng,
secretly cut off his head and placed it in a bag,
then fled to the capital to present it,
and was appointed Governor of Ānzhōu.
This differs from the above.
45 Chén Rú, Governor of Ráozhōu, captured Qúzhōu.
According to Lù Zhèn's *Jiǔguó Zhì*: Chén Rú
was a bandit from Tóng'ān.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì*: Ráozhōu is seven hundred twenty-nine *lǐ* southeast of Qúzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Qúzhōu,
in the Spring and Autumn period, was the western frontier of Yuè,
and in the Jìn dynasty, it was within the territory of Dōngyáng.
The *Yúdì Zhì* says: In the third year of Chūpíng (192) during Emperor Xiàn's reign of the Hàn,
Xīn'ān county was established by partitioning Tàimò;
in the first year of Tàikāng (280) of the Jìn,
because Hóngnóng also had a Xīn'ān,
its name was changed to Xìn'ān;
in the fourth year of Wǔdé (621) of the Táng,
Qúzhōu was established by partitioning the western border of Wùzhōu in Xìn'ān county.
There had previously been a great flood
which divided a mountain into three channels,
hence it was called Sānqú,
and the prefecture was named after it.
46 Fēng Jìngzhāng, a bandit chief from Shàngcài, captured Qízhōu.
47 On an *yǐwèi* day,
Zhōu Bǎo died in Hángzhōu.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Wúyuè Bèishǐ*:
"Bǎo died of illness."
The *Shílù*:
"Qián Liú welcomed him to the prefecture,
where he died of a sudden illness at Zhāngtíngduó."
The *Xīn Jì*:
"In the tenth month, on a *dīngmǎo* day,
Qián Liú killed Zhōu Bǎo."
The *Shíguó Jìnián*:
"In this month, on an *yǐwèi* day,
Bǎo died.
Some say: Qián Liú killed him."
The *Xīn Zhuàn* says:
"Qián Liú welcomed Bǎo to Zhāngtíng;
not long after,
he killed him."
We follow the *Wúyuè Bèishǐ* now.
48 Qián Liú appointed Dù Léng as Commissioner for Deployment in Chángzhōu.
He ordered Ruǎn Jié and others to advance and attack Rùnzhōu.
On a *bǐngshēn* day,
they captured it;
Liú Hào fled,
and Xuē Lǎng was captured and brought back.
In the third year of Guāngqǐ (887),
Liú Hào had expelled Zhōu Bǎo and supported Xuē Lǎng,
and was defeated at this time.
Moreover,
from this time onwards,
the armies of Yáng Xíngmì and Sūn Rú contended alternately for Chángzhōu and Rùnzhōu,
and the people of these two prefectures died in the warfare and famine,
with only one or two out of ten surviving.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Wúyuè Bèishǐ*:
"Next year,
in the first month, on a *bǐngyín* day,
Rùnzhōu was captured, and Xuē Lǎng was executed."
However, Lǎng was executed in Hángzhōu,
so it could not have been on the same day.
We follow the *Shíguó Jìnián* now.
The first year of Wéndé
(888, *wùshēn*)
The era name was changed in the second month of this year.
1 Spring,
first month,
on a *jiǎyín* day,
Sūn Rú killed Qín Yàn, Bì Shīduó, and Zhèng Hànzhāng.
When Yàn and others returned
to Zōng Héng,
their followers still numbered over two thousand;
afterwards, they were gradually seized by Rú.
Their subordinate general Táng Hóng, knowing that disaster was inevitable,
and fearing collective death,
falsely accused Yàn and others of secretly summoning the Biàn army.
Rú killed Yàn and others,
and appointed Hóng as Commander of the Cavalry.
2 Zhāng Shǒuyī and Lǚ Yòngzhī both returned to Yáng Xíngmì.
He again compounded immortal elixirs for the generals,
and also wished to meddle in the affairs of the military administration.
Yáng Xíngmì became angry and killed him.
Zhāng Shǒuyī's death was fitting;
he was greedy for profit and usurped power,
a habit he could not change.
3 Shí Fán, a general from Cài, leading over ten thousand men, raided Chén and Bó,
the two prefectures of Chén and Bó.
On a *guǐhài* day,
Quánzhōng was appointed Grand Commander of the Army for the Four Fronts of Càizhōu,
replacing Shí Pǔ.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Xīn Jì*:
"In the first month, on a *guǐhài* day,
Quánzhōng was appointed Grand Commander of Càizhōu."
The *Biānyílù* says:
"In the second month, on a *guǐwèi* day,
the Emperor reported that Shí Pǔ had obstructed our concurrent governorship
and presented the details of the matter.
On a *bǐngxū* day,
the Emperor issued an imperial decree dated the twenty-fifth day of the first month of the Táng emperor,
appointing [Quánzhōng] Grand Commander of the Army for the Four Fronts of Càizhōu."
Thus, *bǐngxū* was the day Quánzhōng received the edict.
The *Shílù* and Xuē Jūzhèng's *Wǔdài Shǐ* both say the second month, *bǐngxū*,
and were therefore mistaken.
The *Jiù Jì*:
"In the fifth month, on a *dīngyǒu* day,
an edict appointed Quánzhōng as Grand Commander of Càizhōu."
The month and day are especially mistaken.
We follow the *Biānyílù* and *Xīn Jì* now.
4 Zhāng Tíngfàn arrived in Guǎnglǐng,
and Yáng Xíngmì treated him with great courtesy.
When he heard that Lǐ Fán was coming to be Provisional Military Commissioner,
he was angry and showed signs of refusal.
Tíngfàn secretly sent someone to inform Quánzhōng
that he should personally lead a large army to the commandery.
Quánzhōng followed this advice;
upon reaching Sòngzhōu,
Tíngfàn fled from Guǎnglǐng and arrived,
saying:
"Xíngmì cannot be subdued yet."
On a *jiǎzǐ* day,
Lǐ Fán arrived,
saying that the Xú army was blocking the road.
The Xú army
refers to Shí Pǔ's army.
5 On a *bǐngyín* day,
Qián Liú executed Xuē Lǎng.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Xīn Jì*:
"On a *bǐngyín* day,
Xuē Lǎng was executed.
Qián Liú captured Rùnzhōu."
The *Shíguó Jìnián*:
"On a *dīngsì* day,
Lǎng was executed."
We follow the *Wúyuè Bèishǐ* now.
Xuē Lǎng expelled Zhōu Bǎo,
as seen in the previous year in the preceding volume.
6 In the second month,
Zhū Quánzhōng memorialized, requesting to appoint Yáng Xíngmì as Provisional Military Commissioner of Huáinán.
7 On an *yǐhài* day,
the Emperor was unwell.
On a *rénwǔ* day,
he departed Fèngxiáng.
On a *jǐchǒu* day,
he arrived in Cháng'ān.
On a *gēngyín* day,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed.
Wéi Zhāodù was concurrently appointed Minister of the Central Secretariat.
8 The Military Governor of Wèibó, Lè Yànzhēn,
was arrogant and unlawful.
He conscripted the people from six prefectures
(The six prefectures
were Wèi, Bó, Bèi, Xiàng, Chán, and Wèi.)
to build a square wall of eighty *lǐ*
around Wèizhōu.
(This was the outer wall of Wèizhōu.)
His son, Cóngxùn,
was particularly cruel and dangerous.
After he killed Wáng Duó,
(This event is recorded in the previous volume, under the fourth year of Zhōnghé.)
Cóngxùn gathered more than five hundred fugitives to be his personal guards,
calling them "Sub-generals" (Zǐjiàng).
The牙兵 *Yábīng* (elite guards) suspected him,
and there was widespread unrest.
(The Wèibó *Yábīng* originated with Tián Chéngsì,
and they were accustomed to deposing and appointing their commanders.
Now Lè Cóngxùn had established personal guards,
and the *Yábīng* suspected that they were being targeted,
hence their unrest.)
The character 將
is pronounced *jiàng*.
They changed their clothes and escaped,
stopping in a nearby county.
Yànzhēn then appointed Cóngxùn as the Prefect of Xiàngzhōu.
Cóngxùn sent people to Wèi to transport armor, weapons, gold, and silk,
which crisscrossed the roads.
The *Yábīng* grew even more suspicious.
Yànzhēn, in fear,
requested to abdicate his position
and become a monk at Lóngxīng Temple.
(Lè Yànzhēn obtained Wèibó in the third year of Zhōnghé
and was overthrown at this time.)
The *Kǎoyì* (Critical Discernments) states: The old account says:
"Yànzhēn, in fear and peril, died."
The *Shílù* (Veritable Records) states:
"Yànzhēn, in fear,
sought to abdicate his position
and retired to Lóngxīng Temple.
The army forced him to become a monk."
The *Jiù Jì* (Old Annals) states:
"The Wèibó army rioted
and drove out Yànzhēn."
If he had died,
it would not have said "drove out."
We now follow the *Shílù*.
Cóngxùn led thirty thousand troops to the city walls.
Wén Huī did not come out to fight,
so the multitude killed him again,
and nominated the *yájiàng* (elite guard officer) Luó Hóngxìn of Guìxiāng to oversee the affairs of the Acting Military Governor.
Previously,
someone had said,
"I saw an old man with a white beard
who said Hóngxìn would become the local ruler."
After Wén Huī died,
the crowd gathered and shouted,
"Who wishes to be the Military Governor?"
Hóngxìn came out and replied,
"The white-bearded old man has already appointed me."
The crowd looked around and said,
"He can,"
and thus established him.
Hóngxìn led his troops out
and fought Cóngxùn,
defeating him.
The *Dì Jì* (Imperial Records) of the *Jiù Shū* (Old Book) states that in this year, the Wèibó army rioted
and drove out their commander, Lè Yànzhēn.
Yànzhēn's son, the Prefect of Xiàngzhōu, Cóngxùn, led his troops to attack Wèizhōu.
The *Yájūn* (elite army) appointed their junior officer Luó Zōngbiàn as Acting Military Governor
and sent out troops to resist him.
This likely combines the names of Zhào Wén Huī and Luó Hóngxìn into one person.
The character 敗
is pronounced *bài*.
Nèihuáng
was a Hàn dynasty county,
which at this time belonged to Wèizhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (Record of the Nine Domains) states: The county is one hundred twenty-four *lǐ* southwest of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái says: Wèi considered the north of the Yellow River as "inner"
and the south as "outer."
Since Chénliú had Wàihuáng,
this was Nèihuáng.
Therefore, the county seat was nineteen *lǐ* northwest of the present-day county.
Previously,
Zhū Quánzhōng was about to attack Càizhōu,
and sent his *yáyá* (elite guard officer) Léi Yè with ten thousand *liǎng* of silver to request grain from Wèi.
After the *Yábīng* drove out Yànzhēn,
they killed Yè at the guesthouse.
After Cóngxùn was defeated,
he sought aid from Quánzhōng.
9 Initially,
Lǐ Hǎnzhī, the Military Governor of Héyáng, and
Zhāng Quányì swore an oath by cutting their arms,
and they were very close.
Hǎnzhī was brave but lacked strategy,
and his nature was also greedy and violent.
He made light of Quányì,
and hearing of his diligence, thrift, and hard work in farming,
laughed and said,
"This is just a rustic fellow!"
Quányì heard this but was not offended.
Hǎnzhī repeatedly requested grain and silk,
and Quányì always gave it to him.
However, Hǎnzhī's demands were insatiable,
and Hénán could not supply them.
If anything fell short of his desires,
he would immediately chain Hénán's chief officials and beat them in Héyáng.
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Hénán is eighty-five *lǐ* northeast of Héyáng.)
Quányì would say,
"How can we not give
what Grand Commandant Lǐ
requests!"
He made every effort to serve him,
appearing to fear him,
which made Hǎnzhī even more arrogant.
Hǎnzhī's subordinate forces did not farm,
relying solely on plundering for resources.
They consumed people as food.
At this time, he mobilized all his troops to attack Jiàngzhōu.
Wáng Yǒuyù, the Prefect of Jiàngzhōu, surrendered to him.
He then advanced to attack Jìnzhōu.
Wáng Chóngyíng, the Military Governor of Hùguó, secretly allied with Quányì to plan against him.
Quányì secretly dispatched his garrison troops.
(Zhāng Quányì was the Administrator of Hénán.
Each of the eighteen counties had a garrison commander leading garrison troops,
which were militia.)
Taking advantage of the emptiness, he launched a surprise attack on Héyáng.
At dawn,
he entered the three cities.
(Héyáng had the Southern City, Northern City, and Zhōngtǎn City.)
Quányì captured all of Hǎnzhī's family
and then concurrently held the position of Military Governor of Héyáng.
Hǎnzhī fled to Zézhōu.
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Héyáng is ninety *lǐ* north of Zézhōu.)
10In the third month,
on the *wùxū* day (the first day of the month),
there was a solar eclipse,
which was total.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Jiù Jì* states:
"Emperor Xīzōng's officials presented him with the honorary title Shèngwén Ruìdé Guāngwǔ Hóngxiào Huángdì.
In the third month,
on the *wùxū* day (the first day of the month),
he received the imperial decree in the main palace."
The *Zhāozōng Jì* states:
"In the first year of Dàshùn,
in the first month,
on the *wùzǐ* day (the first day of the month),
officials presented him with the honorary title Shèngwén Ruìdé Guāngwǔ Hóngxiào Huángdì."
How could two emperors have exactly the same honorary title?
We now follow the *Xīn Jì* (New Annals),
which attributes this honorary title solely to Emperor Zhāozōng.
11On the *jǐhài* day,
the Emperor's illness recurred.
On the *rényín* day,
his condition became critical.
His imperial younger brother, Jíwáng Bǎo,
was older and virtuous,
and all the ministers had hopes for him.
Yáng Fùgōng, the Commissioner of Ten Armies, requested that his younger brother, Shòuwáng Jié, be enthroned.
On this day,
an imperial edict was issued,
establishing Jié as the Imperial Younger Brother and Heir Apparent (Huáng Tàidì),
and making him supervisor of state affairs.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Táng Nián Bǔlù* (Supplemental Records of Tang History) states:
"After Emperor Xīzōng's illness recurred in the imperial pavilion,
he suddenly collapsed and died.
Yáng Fùgōng and others secretly concealed the death
and, at that time, among the princes residing in the sixteen residences who were accompanying the emperor,
they then nominated the Emperor [Zhāozōng] in the grand residence to supervise the state.
Above the Emperor [Zhāozōng] were Shèngwáng and Yíwáng,
both sons of Emperor Yìzōng.
The Emperor [Zhāozōng] was the third among the six princes."
The *Jiù Jì* states:
"All the ministers considered Jíwáng the most virtuous,
and also superior to Shòuwáng,
and intended to enthrone him.
Only Yáng Fùgōng requested that Shòuwáng supervise the state."
According to research, Zhāozōng
was the seventh son of Yìzōng.
Jíwáng Bǎo
was the sixth.
The *Xīn* (New) and *Jiù* (Old) Biographies record eight sons of Yìzōng,
but no Shèngwáng or Yíwáng.
We now follow the *Jiù Jì*.
The Emperor had eight brothers.
Tíng had died early.
Six kings were present,
residing in the six princely residences.
The Chancellor and others went to see him.
On the *guǐmǎo* day,
the Emperor died in Língfú Hall.
He was twenty-seven years old.
The Imperial Younger Brother and Heir Apparent Jié changed his name to Mǐn,
and Wéi Zhāodù was made Acting Prime Minister.
When Zhāo Zōng ascended the throne,
his physical appearance was bright and refined,
with a heroic spirit.
He enjoyed literature,
and seeing Xi Zōng's authority diminished
and the court daily losing prestige,
he had the ambition to restore former glories.
He treated high-ranking ministers with respect,
and dreamed of recruiting wise and heroic figures.
At the beginning of his reign,
everyone, both inside and outside the court, rejoiced.
People were tired of chaos and longed for order.
Following Xi Zōng's reign,
and witnessing Zhāo Zōng's initial policies,
they believed he was capable of great achievements.
12 Zhū Quánzhōng gathered provisions in Sòngzhōu,
intending to attack Qín Zōngquán.
It happened that Lè Cóngxùn came to report an emergency,
so he moved his army to station at Huázhōu.
He sent Dudaya Lǐ Tángbīn and others with thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Càizhōu,
and sent Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ Zhū Zhēn and others to divide their forces to rescue Lè Cóngxùn.
Kǎoyì says: Xuē Jūzhèng's Wǔdài Shǐ, in Zhēn's biography, states:
"Zhēn's army was at Nèihuáng,
and defeated Lè Cóngxùn's more than ten thousand men."
However, Zhēn went to rescue Cóngxùn, and it says he defeated Cóngxùn,
which is an error.
Gě Cóngzhōu's biography states:
"He followed Tàizǔ across the river,
captured the garrisons of Líyáng, Lǐgù, and Línhé,
and upon reaching Nèihuáng,
defeated the Wèi army of over ten thousand men."
According to both Xuē Shǐ's imperial annals and biographies,
all say Tàizǔ sent Zhū Zhēn and others to rescue Cóngxùn,
only Cóngzhōu's biography says he followed Tàizǔ,
which is probably an error.
They captured the three garrisons of Líyáng, Línhé, and Lǐgù.
Yuánfēng Jiǔyù Zhì states that
Chánzhōu has Línhé County,
sixty lì west of the prefecture.
Wèizhōu's Wèi County has Lǐgù Township.
Xuē Shǐ's Jìn Jì: West of Yè there is a stockade called Lǐgù,
where the Qīngqí river flows alongside.
They defeated the Wèi army of over ten thousand men,
capturing their general Zhōu Rú and ten others.
13 Lǐ Kèyòng appointed his general Kāng Jūnlì as the Southern Front Commander,
supervising five generals: Lǐ Cúnxiào, Xuē Ātán, Shǐ Yǎn, Ān Jīnjùn, and Ān Xiūxiū, with seven thousand cavalry,
to assist Lǐ Hǎnzī in attacking Héyáng.
Zhāng Quányì defended the city within its walls,
and with food running out in the city,
he sought aid from Zhū Quánzhōng,
offering his wife and children as hostages.
14 Wáng Jiàn attacked Péngzhōu,
and Chén Jìngxuàn came to its rescue,
so Wáng Jiàn withdrew.
Wáng Jiàn plundered Xīchuān extensively,
and all twelve prefectures suffered from his incursions.
Xīchuān governed twelve prefectures: Yì, Péng, Shǔ, Hàn, Jiā, Méi, Qióng, Jiǎn, Zī, Yǎ, Lí, and Mào.
Bèi,
pronounced Pí Yì.
15 Summer,
fourth month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
the Emperor's mother, Lady Wáng, was posthumously honored as Empress Gōngxiàn.
16 On the day Rénwǔ,
Sūn Rú raided Yángzhōu,
and captured it.
Kǎoyì says: The Shílù states Rú captured Yángzhōu in the fifth month,
perhaps referring to the date the report arrived.
Now, according to the Old Annals, it was the first day of the fourth month, Rénwǔ,
the New Annals say Wùchén,
and the Yāoluàn Zhì says the first day of the fourth month, Guǐwèi,
and Jiǎshēn,
Rú captured Yángzhōu.
Wú Lù Shíguó Jìnián has no specific day,
only stating the fourth month.
We now follow the Old Annals and Jìnián.
Rú proclaimed himself Military Governor of Huáinán.
Hángmì was about to flee to Hǎilíng,
but Yuán Xí advised him to return to Lúzhōu
to plan a new offensive,
which Hángmì followed.
17 Zhū Quánzhōng sent his generals Dīng Huì, Gě Cóngzhōu, and Niú Cúnjié with tens of thousands of troops to rescue Héyáng.
Lǐ Cúnxiào ordered Lǐ Hǎnzī to attack the city with infantry,
while he himself led the cavalry to counter-attack at Wēn,
Wēn County,
belonging to Mèngzhōu.
Mèngzhōu's administrative seat was Héyáng.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Wēn is seventy lì east of Héyáng.
Shuài,
pronounced Shuaì.
Ān Xiūxiū, fearing punishment,
fled to Càizhōu.
The Biàn people divided their forces to cut off the Tàiháng Pass,
and Kāng Jūnlì and others, fearing this,
led their troops back.
Quánzhōng memorialized to appoint Dīng Huì as Acting Military Governor of Héyáng,
and re-appointed Zhāng Quányì as Mayor of Hénán.
Huì,
was from Shòuchūn;
Cúnjié,
was from Bóyáng.
Quányì was grateful to Quánzhōng for getting him out of trouble,
and from then on wholeheartedly attached himself to him.
Zhū Quánzhōng thus gained control of Luò and Mèng.
Quányì was responsible for supplying their provisions and weapons without shortage.
Lǐ Hǎnzī was Prefect of Zézhōu,
and concurrently held the title of Military Governor of Héyáng.
Hǎnzī left his son Qí to serve Kèyòng,
while he himself returned to Zézhōu,
specializing in banditry and plunder.
For several hundred lì between Huái, Mèng, Jìn, and Jiàng,
there were no prefects in the prefectures,
no magistrates in the counties,
no wheat or grain in the fields,
and no smoke from cooking fires in the towns,
for almost ten years.
Between Hézhōng and Jiàngzhōu, there was Moyún Mountain,
extremely high,
where people gathered for protection,
and bandits could not approach.
Hǎnzī attacked and captured it,
and people at the time called him
"Lǐ Moyún".
18 Lè Cóngxùn moved his army to Huánshuǐ.
Luó Hóngxìn sent his general Chéng Gōngxìn to attack Cóngxùn,
beheading him,
and both he and his father Yànzhēn were publicly displayed with their heads at the camp gate.
On the day Guǐsì,
he sent an envoy with generous gifts to reward Quánzhōng's army,
requesting to establish good relations.
Quánzhōng then recalled his army.
An imperial edict appointed Luó Hóngxìn as acting Military Governor of Wèibó.
19 Guīzhōu Prefect Guō Yǔ attacked Jīngnán,
expelling Wáng Jiànzhào,
who had occupied Jīngnán the previous year.
An imperial edict appointed Yǔ as Acting Military Governor of Jīngnán.
After the military devastation in Jīngnán,
there were only seventeen households remaining.
Yǔ exerted himself in governance,
pacifying and gathering the devastated populace,
promoting commerce and agriculture.
In his later years, the population almost reached ten thousand households.
In the third year of Zhāo Zōng's Tiānfù era,
Chéng Ruì was defeated and killed by Huáinán general Lǐ Shénfú.
The "later years" mentioned
probably refer to this period.
Zhì,
pronounced Zhí Lì.
No one made supporting the people their priority,
except Huázhōu Prefect Hán Jiàn, who pacified and gathered the displaced,
and encouraged farming and sericulture.
Within a few years,
the people became wealthy and the army well-supplied.
People at the time called them "North Hán and South Guō".
Qín Zōngquán's subordinate general Cháng Hòu occupied Kuízhōu.
Yǔ, with his general Rǔyáng Xǔ Cún, attacked and captured it.
After a long time,
the imperial court appointed Yǔ as Military Governor of Jīngnán,
and Jiànzhào as Military Governor of Wǔtài.
Qiánzhōu's Wǔtài Army.
Yǔ's memorial regarding his name and deeds can be found in the previous volume, Guāngqǐ First Year.
20 Lǐ Kèyòng was given the additional title of concurrent Shìzhōng.
21 Fifth month,
on the day Jǐhài,
Zhū Quánzhōng was given the additional title of concurrent Shìzhōng.
22 Zhào Déyīn, having lost Jīngnán,
Jīngnán had been taken by Chéng Ruì at that time.
On the day Rén'yín,
offered Shānnán Dōngdào to surrender.
In the fourth year of Zhōnghé,
Qín Zōngquán had sent Zhào Déyīn to occupy Xiāngyáng,
and now he surrendered.
Jiàng,
pronounced Hù Jiāng.
Quánzhōng memorialized to request Déyīn as his deputy.
An imperial edict designated Shānnán Dōngdào as Zhōngyì Army,
with Déyīn as its Military Governor,
also serving as Deputy Commander of the Càizhōu Four-Front Campaign Army.
23 Zhū Quánzhōng, having secured Luò and Mèng,
had no worries from the west.
He then dispatched a large army to attack Qín Zōngquán,
inflicting a major defeat on Zōngquán south of Càizhōu.
The Old Book's Imperial Annals state: The Càizhōu Campaign Army reported a major defeat of the bandits at Lóngpí,
and then advanced to press on the bandit's city.
Zōngquán was garrisoned in Zhōngzhōu,
Zhōngzhōu
being the inner city of Càizhōu.
24 Fèngxiáng Military Governor Lǐ Màozhēn was given the additional title of concurrent Jiǎnjiào Shìzhōng.
25 Chén Jìngxuan (陳敬瑄) was then attacking Wáng Jiàn (王建),
and the tribute was cut off.
It was said that Chén Jìngxuan had previously regularly paid tribute,
but was then distressed by warfare,
which led to its cessation.
Wáng Jiàn therefore took this as Chén Jìngxuan's crime and questioned him.
Finding nothing to plunder on his retreat,
he wished to cease hostilities.
Zhōu Xiáng (周庠) and Qímú Jiàn (綦毋諫) thought this was not advisable.
Zhōu Xiáng said:
"Qióngzhōu (邛州)'s city walls and moats are strong and complete,
with provisions for several years.
It can be occupied and made a base."
Wáng Jiàn said:
"I have been in the army for a long time.
I observe that those who wage war, if they do not rely on the Son of Heaven's prestige,
the hearts of the multitude easily scatter.
It is better to elaborate on Chén Jìngxuan's crimes,
memorialize the imperial court,
and request a high minister to be appointed commander and assist him,
then success may be achieved."
So he had Zhōu Xiáng draft a memorial,
requesting to campaign against Chén Jìngxuan to atone for his sins,
and also sought Qióngzhōu.
Gù Yànlǎng (顧彥朗) also memorialized requesting a pardon for Wáng Jiàn's crimes,
and to move Chén Jìngxuan to another garrison to pacify the two Chuān (川) prefectures.
Wáng Jiàn raised troops within the Eastern Chuān (東川) circuit to attack Western Chuān (西川),
and the prolonged conflict unsettled
both Chuān prefectures.
Initially,
during the chaos of Huáng Cháo (黃巢),
the Emperor was the Prince of Shòu (壽王),
and followed Emperor Xīzōng (僖宗) to Shǔ (蜀).
The details are in volume 254, the first year of Guǎngmíng (廣明) of Emperor Xīzōng.
Many princes traveled on foot to the mountains and valleys.
The Prince of Shòu was exhausted
and could not go on,
lying on a large stone.
Tián Lìngzī (田令孜) arrived from behind,
urged him to move,
and the Prince said:
"My feet hurt.
I hope the Commander-in-chief can give me a horse."
Tián Lìngzī said:
"This is a deep mountain,
where can one get a horse!"
He whipped the Prince to make him go forward.
The Prince looked back and said nothing,
harboring resentment in his heart.
When he ascended the throne,
he sent someone to supervise the Western Chuān army,
but Tián Lìngzī did not obey the imperial decree.
Tián Lìngzī relied on Chén Jìngxuan
and refused to leave Western Chuān.
He wanted to control him with authority.
Coincidentally, he received memorials from Gù Yànlǎng and Wáng Jiàn,
knowing that Tián Lìngzī's reliance was Chén Jìngxuan.
In the sixth month,
Wéi Zhāodù (韋昭度) was appointed concurrently as Grand Councilor (中書令),
acting as Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Western Chuān,
and concurrently as Pacification Commissioner and Commissioner of Affairs (招撫制置等使) of the two Chuān prefectures,
and Chén Jìngxuan was summoned to be Grand General of the Dragon Martial Army (龍武統軍).
Wáng Jiàn's army was at Xīndū (新都).
At that time, the local strongmen of Miánzhú (綿竹), Hé Yìyáng (何義陽), and Ānrén (安仁), Fèi Shīqín (費師懃), etc.,
in the third year of Wǔdé (武德),
Ānrén County was established by dividing Línqióng (臨邛) and Yīzhèng (依政),
subordinate to Qióngzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: it is thirty-eight *lǐ* northeast of the prefecture.
Fèi,
father *fèi* (*fú*) fan.
Qín,
*jù jīn* fan.
Their forces numbered sometimes ten thousand,
sometimes a thousand.
Wáng Jiàn sent Wáng Zōngyáo (王宗瑤) to persuade them,
and they all led their forces to join Wáng Jiàn.
After providing them with provisions,
Wáng Jiàn's army revived.
26 The Yòuguó Army (佑國軍) was established at Hénán Fǔ (河南府),
with Zhāng Quányì (張全義) as Jìedùshǐ.
27 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Lǐ Hǎnzhī (李罕之) led Hédōng (河東) troops to raid Héyáng (河陽).
Dīng Huì (丁會) attacked and repelled them.
28 Fèngzhōu (鳳州) was elevated to a Jìedù Fǔ (節度府),
and Xīng (興) and Lìzhōu (利州) were detached and put under its jurisdiction,
with Mǎn Cún (滿存), the Fèngzhōu Defense Commissioner (防禦使), as Jìedùshǐ and Grand Councilor (同平章事).
In the second year of Zhōnghé (中和) of Emperor Xīzōng,
the Gǎnyì Army (感義軍) was established from Xīng and Fèng prefectures,
with Yáng Shèng (楊晟) as Jìedùshǐ,
to guard Sànguān (散關),
but the army headquarters had not yet been established.
After Yáng Shèng was defeated and fled,
no new commander was appointed.
Now the army headquarters was established at Fèngzhōu,
and Mǎn Cún was appointed Jìedùshǐ.
29 Luó Hóngxìn (羅弘信), acting Commissioner of Wèibó (魏博), was appointed Jìedùshǐ.
30 In the eighth month,
on the day *wù chén*,
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) captured the southern city of Càizhōu (蔡州).
31 Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) feared the threat of Sūn Rú (孫儒)
and wanted to launch a light attack on Hóngzhōu (洪州).
Yuán Xí (袁襲) said:
"Zhōng Chuán (鍾傳) has long been established in Jiāngxī (江西).
In the second year of Zhōnghé,
Zhōng Chuán occupied Hóngzhōu.
It is not easy to scheme against him.
Zhào Huáng (趙鍠) has newly acquired Xuānzhōu (宣州).
Last year, Zhào Huáng acquired Xuānzhōu.
Huáng,
*hù zhōu guāng* fan.
The hearts of the multitude are not attached to him.
Your Excellency should humble your words and offer generous gifts
to persuade Sūn Duān (孫端) of Hézhōu (和州) and Zhāng Xióng (張雄) of Shàngyuán (上元)
to cross the Jiāng (江) from Cǎishí (採石) and invade his territory.
He will surely come to meet them in battle.
Your Excellency can cross the Jiāng from Tóngguān (銅官) and join them."
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: there is Tóngguānzhǔ (銅官渚) in Tónglíng (銅陵) County, 140 *lǐ* northeast of present-day Chízhōu (池州).
Yáng Xíngmì followed his advice,
sent Cài Chóu (蔡儔) to guard Lúzhōu (廬州),
and led his generals to cross from Sǎntán (糝潭).
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: there is Sǎntánzhen (糝潭鎮) in Wúwéi (無為) County of Wúwéi Army.
Presently, the river flows east from Sǎntánkǒu (糝潭口) past Níxìkǒu (泥汊口),
then further east past Zhàjiāngkǒu (柵江口).
Shuài,
read as *lǜ*;
the same below.
Sǎn,
*sāng gǎn* fan.
Sūn Duān and Zhāng Xióng were defeated by Zhào Huáng.
Zhào Huáng's generals Sū Táng (蘇塘) and Qī Lǎng (漆朗) led an army of twenty thousand and encamped at Géshān (曷山).
There is Géshān southwest of Dāngtú (當塗) County in Xuānzhōu,
and to its east is Dōngliángshān (東梁山).
"Your Excellency should lead your troops swiftly to Géshān,
fortify your defenses,
and if they seek battle in vain,
they will think we are afraid and timid.
Taking advantage of their laxity,
they can be defeated."
Yáng Xíngmì followed this.
Sū Táng and the others were greatly defeated,
and Xuānzhōu was then besieged.
Zhào Gānzhī (趙乾之), Zhào Huáng's elder brother, led troops from Chízhōu to relieve Xuānzhōu.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé,
Chízhōu was established from Qiūpǔ (秋浦) and Nánlíng (南陵) counties of Xuānzhōu.
In the first year of Zhēnguān (貞觀),
the prefecture was abolished.
In the first year of Yǒngtài (永泰),
Chízhōu was re-established from Qiūpǔ and Qīngyáng (青陽) of Xuānzhōu, and Zhìdé (至德) of Ráozhōu (饒州).
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Chízhōu is 325 *lǐ* east of Xuānzhōu.
He defeated them.
Jiǔhuáshān (九華山),
in Qīngyáng County of Chízhōu,
was formerly named Jiǔzǐshān (九子山).
Lǐ Bái (李白) renamed it Jiǔhuá because its peaks resembled lotus flowers.
Yáng Xíngmì appointed Yǎ (雅) as Chízhōu Commissioner of Affairs.
32 In the ninth month,
Zhū Quánzhōng, due to insufficient provisions
and the belief that Qín Zōngquán (秦宗權)'s devastated forces were not a cause for concern,
withdrew his troops.
On the day *bǐng shēn*,
he dispatched Zhū Zhēn (朱珍) with five thousand troops to escort Liú Zàn (劉瓚), the Prefect of Chǔzhōu (楚州), to his post.
Zhū Quánzhōng considered himself concurrently in charge of Huáinán (淮南),
and Chǔzhōu was within his circuit,
so he appointed the Prefect himself.
33 Qián Liú (錢鏐) sent his cousin Qián Qiú (錢鏶) to lead troops to attack Xú Yuē (徐約) at Sūzhōu (蘇州).
34 In winter,
the tenth month,
Xú (徐) troops intercepted Zhū Zhēn and Liú Zàn, preventing them from advancing.
Xú troops were
Shí Pú (時溥)'s troops.
They captured Pèi (沛) and Téng (滕) counties,
slaughtering and capturing tens of thousands.
35 Mèng Fānglì (孟方立) sent his general Xī Zhōngxìn (奚忠信) with thirty thousand troops to raid Liáozhōu (遼州).
Liáozhōu was originally the land of Shàng'ài (上艾) and Zhān (沾) counties in the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
The Jìn (晉) dynasty established Lèpíng (樂平) Commandery.
In the third year of Wǔdé,
Liáozhōu was established.
In the eighth year,
it was renamed Jīzhōu (箕州).
In the first year of Xiāntiān (先天),
to avoid Emperor Xuánzōng (玄宗)'s personal name,
it was renamed Yízhōu (儀州).
In the third year of Zhōnghé,
it was restored to Liáozhōu.
He greatly defeated them,
capturing Xī Zhōngxìn and sending him to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
36 On the day *xīn mǎo*,
Emperor Huìshèng Gōngdìng Xiào (惠聖恭定孝皇帝) was buried at Jìnglíng (靖陵).
Jìnglíng
is ten *lǐ* northeast of Fèngtiān (奉天) County in Jīngzhào (京兆).
37 Chén Jìngxuan and Tián Lìngzī, hearing that Wéi Zhāodù was approaching,
prepared their troops and fortified the city to resist him.
38 In the eleventh month,
Shí Pú (時溥) personally led seventy thousand infantry and cavalry and garrisoned them at Wúkāng Zhèn (吳康鎮).
Xuē Jūzhèng’s (薛居正) *Wǔdài Shǐ* (五代史) states that
Zhū Zhēn (朱珍) attacked Fēng (豐)
and captured it.
Shí Pú (時溥) then led his entire army to engage in battle south of Fēng (豐) at Wúkāng Lǐ (吳康里).
He was soundly defeated.
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) again dispatched a separate general to attack Sùzhōu (宿州),
and its prefect Zhāng Yǒu (張友) surrendered to him.
39 On the day *bǐngshēn*,
Qín Zōngquán's (秦宗權) separate general attacked and captured Xǔzhōu (許州),
seized Wáng Yùn (王蘊), the acting military governor (Liúhòu) of Zhōngwǔ (忠武),
and retook Xǔzhōu (許州).
Last year, Zōngquán (宗權) was defeated by Quánzhōng (全忠),
abandoning Xǔzhōu (許州).
Wáng Yùn (王蘊) was probably appointed by Quánzhōng (全忠).
40 In the twelfth month,
Cài (蔡) general Shēn Cóng (申叢) seized Zōngquán (宗權),
broke his legs and imprisoned him,
then surrendered to Quánzhōng (全忠).
Quánzhōng (全忠) appointed Cóng (叢) as the acting military governor (Liúhòu) of Càizhōu (蔡州).
41 Initially,
Yáng Shèng (楊晟), the military governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Gǎnyì (感義), having already lost Xīng (興) and Fèng (鳳) (see
*Shàng Juǎn* (上卷), Guāngqǐ (光啟) second year),
Wáng Jiàn (王建) attacked Xīchuān (西川).
Tián Lìngzī (田令孜), considering Shèng (晟) an old general of his,
falsely appointed him military governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Wēiróng Jūn (威戎軍)
and had him defend Péngzhōu (彭州).
Yáng Shèng (楊晟) was formerly the commander (Zhǐhuīshǐ) of Shéncè (神策).
Chén Jìngxuān’s (陳敬瑄) prefect of Méizhōu (眉州), Shān Xíngzhāng (山行章), led an army of fifty thousand and fortified Xīnfán (新繁) to relieve him.
Xīnfán (新繁) was
the Hàn (漢) Fán Xiàn (繁縣).
The Latter Lord of Shǔ (蜀) added
the character "Xīn" (新)
to it.
In the Táng (唐) dynasty, it belonged to Chéngdū Fǔ (成都府).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) says: it is twenty-five *lǐ* (里) northwest of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái (宋白) says: Xīnfán (新繁) was originally the Hàn (漢) Fán Xiàn (繁縣).
In the tenth year of Yánxī (延熙) of the Latter Lord of Shǔ (蜀),
the Hú (胡) people of Liángzhōu (涼州) led their followers to surrender and settled
in Fán Xiàn (繁縣).
The households were moved here,
and the common people called it Xīnfán (新繁).
The county name was changed according to popular custom.
42 On the day *dīnghài*,
Wéi Zhāodù (韋昭度) was appointed Campaign Recruiter and Commander (Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ),
Yáng Shǒuliàng (楊守亮), the military governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Shānnán Xīdào (山南西道), was made his deputy,
and Gù Yànlǎng (顧彥朗), the military governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Dōngchuān (東川), was made Army Chief Clerk (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ).
Qióng (邛), Shǔ (蜀), Lí (黎), and Yǎ (雅) were separated to establish Yǒngpíng Jūn (永平軍),
with Wáng Jiàn (王建) appointed as its military governor (Jiédùshǐ),
with its seat in Qióngzhōu (邛州),
also serving as Commander-in-Chief (Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ) of all armies in the campaign.
On the day *wùzǐ*,
Chén Jìngxuān (陳敬xuān)'s official titles and ranks were stripped.
43 Yáng Shǒuhòu (楊守厚), the military governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Shānnán Xīdào (山南西道),
captured Kuízhōu (夔州).
According to the *Xīn Shū* (新書),
Yáng Shǒuliàng (楊守亮) was leading Shānnán Xīdào (山南西道) at this time,
and Shǒuhòu (守厚) was the prefect of Miánzhōu (綿州).
Was it not Yáng Shǒuliàng (楊守亮) who sent Shǒuhòu (守厚) to capture Kuízhōu (夔州)?
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ (王崇武), collated by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖) and Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
by imperial decree.
Later Generation Tīantái (天台) Disciple
Lóngjì (龍紀) First Year
(Jǐyǒu (己酉), 889 CE)
1 Spring,
first month,
on the day *guǐsì* at dawn,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the reign era was changed.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Táng Nián Bǔlù* (唐年補錄) says:
"In the first month,
on the day *guǐsì*,
the second year of Wéndé (文德) was changed to the first year of Lóngjì (龍紀).
All officials presented the emperor with the honorary title 'Shèngwén Ruìdé Guāngwǔ Hóngxiào Huángdì' (聖文睿德光武弘孝皇帝)."
The *Xīn* (新) and *Jiù Jì* (舊紀) and the *Shílù* (實錄) state that the honorary title was conferred in the first month of the following year,
so the *Bǔlù* (補錄) is mistaken.
The *Jiù Jì* (舊紀) also says:

"Wéi Zhāodù (韋昭度), military governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Jiànnán Xīchuān (劍南西川) and commissioner for pacification and organization of the two Chuān (Chuān Zhāofǔ Zhìzhìshǐ), was appointed Acting Director (Liúshǒu) of Dōngdū (東都)."
However, Zhāodù (昭度) only became Acting Director (Liúshǒu) in the second year of Dàshùn (大順),
so the *Jiù Jì* (舊紀) is mistaken.
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄) in all cases.
2 Liú Chóngwàng (劉崇望), Academician of the Hànlín Academy (Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ) and Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng), was appointed concurrently to the Grand Council (Tóng Píngzhāngshì).
3 Biàn (汴) general Páng Shīgǔ (龐師古) captured Sùqiān (宿遷)
and garrisoned his troops at Lǚliáng (呂梁).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) says: Xúzhōu (徐州) Péngchéng Xiàn (彭城縣) has a Lǚliáng Hóng Zhèn (呂梁洪鎮).
He was utterly defeated
and returned to defend Péngchéng (彭城).
4 On the day *rénzǐ*,
Cài (蔡) general Guō Fán (郭璠) killed Shēn Cóng (申叢)
and sent Qín Zōngquán (秦宗權) to Biàn (汴),
informing Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) that
"Cóng (叢) was plotting to re-establish Zōngquán (宗權)."
Quánzhōng (全忠) appointed Fán (璠) as the acting military governor (Liúhòu) of Huáixī (淮西).
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) also annexed Huáixī (淮西) to connect Xiāng (襄) and Dèng (鄧),
making his power even greater.
5 On the day *wùshēn*,
Wáng Jiàn (王建) severely defeated Shān Xíngzhāng (山行章) at Xīnfán (新繁),
killing and capturing nearly ten thousand people.
Xíngzhāng (行章) barely escaped with his life.
Yáng Shèng (楊晟) was afraid
and moved his garrison to Sānjiāo (三交).
Xíngzhāng (行章) garrisoned at Méngyáng (濛陽),
and they remained in a standoff with Jiàn (建).
In the second year of Yífèng (儀鳳),
Méngyáng Xiàn (濛陽縣) was established by dividing the three counties of Jiǔlǒng (九隴), Luò (雒), and Shífāng (什邡),
and it belonged to Péngzhōu (彭州).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) says: It is thirty-one *lǐ* (里) east of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái (宋白) says: The county is north of Méng Jiāng (濛江),
hence it is called Méngyáng (濛陽).
6 In the second month,
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) sent Qín Zōngquán (秦宗權) to the capital,
where he was beheaded at Dúliǔ (獨柳).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Jiù Jì* (舊紀) says:
"In the second month, on the day *jǐchǒu*,
Lǐ Fán (李璠), the Army Chief Clerk (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ) of Biànzhōu (汴州), supervised the escort of Qín Zōngquán (秦宗權) and his wife Zhào (趙) to be presented,
and he was beheaded at Dúliǔ (獨柳)."
The *Shílù* (實錄) says:
"In the third month,
Quánzhōng (全忠) presented Zōngquán (宗權),
who was beheaded at Dúliǔ (獨柳)."
The *Xīn Jì* (新紀) says:
"In the second month, on the day *wùchén*,
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) captured Zōngquán (宗權) and presented him.
On the day *jǐchǒu*,
Zōngquán (宗權) was executed."
However, Zōngquán (宗權) left Biàn (汴) in the first month,
so he should not have arrived at Cháng'ān (長安) only in the third month.
If he was presented as a captive on *wùchén*,
he should not have been executed only on *jǐchǒu*.
Therefore, it simply says "in the second month."
In the cage cart, Zōngquán (宗權) craned his neck and said to Kuí (揆):
"Does the Minister (Shàngshū) perceive Zōngquán (宗權) as a rebel?
I merely failed to demonstrate my loyalty."
All who watched laughed.
Kuí (揆) was
a distant grandson of Tì (逖).
Sūn Tì (孫逖) served as Vice Minister of Personnel (Xíngbù Shìláng),
and Kuí (揆) was his fifth-generation collateral grandson.
7 In the third month,
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) was additionally appointed concurrently Minister of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng)
and advanced to the noble rank of Prince of Dōngpíng Commandery (Dōngpíng Jùnwáng).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Jiù Jì* (舊紀) places this in the fourth month,
enfeoffed as Prince of Dōngpíng (Dōngpíng Jùnwáng).
Xuē Jūzhèng’s (薛居正) *Wǔdài Shǐ* (五代史) places it in the third month,
also saying he was enfeoffed as Prince of Dōngpíng (Dōngpíng).
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄), which only adds the title Minister of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng).
According to the *Kǎoyì* (考異),
then the
six characters "advanced to the noble rank of Prince of Dōngpíng Commandery" (進爵東平郡王)
should be removed.
However, according to the imperial annals in the *Jiù Shū* (舊書),
in the first year of Guāngqǐ (光啟),
Quánzhōng (全忠) was enfeoffed as Prince of Pèijùn (沛郡王).
Although he had not yet been advanced to the rank of Prince of Dōngpíng (Dōngpíng) at this time,
he was certainly already enfeoffed as a prince.
His military power grew even stronger.
Zhào Déyīn (趙德諲), military governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Fèngguó (奉國), was additionally appointed Minister of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng).
In the second year of Zhōnghé (中和) of Xīzōng (僖宗),
Càizhōu (蔡州) was designated Fèngguó Jūn (奉國軍),
and Qín Zōngquán (秦宗權) was appointed its military governor (Jiédùshǐ).
In the first year of Wéndé (文德),
Xiāngzhōu (襄州) was designated Zhōngyì Jūn (忠義軍),
and Zhào Déyīn (趙德諲) was appointed its military governor (Jiédùshǐ).
Since Zōngquán (宗權) had perished,
the Fèngguó (奉國) governorship had never been bestowed upon anyone.
Zhào Déyīn (趙德yīn) also never concurrently held the Fèngguó (奉國) governorship.
Therefore, "Fèngguó" (奉國)
should be changed to
"Zhōngyì" (忠義).
He was appointed military governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Zhōngwǔ (忠武),
with Chénzhōu (陳州) as its administrative seat.
Zhōngwǔ (忠武) was originally governed from Xǔzhōu (許州).
Zhào Chōu (趙犨), a native of Chén (陳),
had also rendered meritorious service in defending Chén (陳),
and so the administrative seat was moved to Chén (陳).
*Chōu* (犨) is pronounced like *chāng* (*chāng*) and *niú* (*niú*).
He entirely entrusted all matters of the military government to his younger brother Chǎng (昶),
and submitted a memorial requesting to retire.
An imperial edict appointed Chǎng (昶) to replace him as military governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Zhōngwǔ (忠武).
Not long after, Chōu (犨) died.
8 On the day of Bǐngshēn,
Qián Qiú
captured Sūzhōu.
In the winter of the previous year,
Qián Qiú attacked Sūzhōu;
details are found in the previous volume.
In Guāngqǐ 3rd year,
Xú Yuē occupied Sūzhōu,
but now he fled and died.
9 In summer,
in the 4th month,
the Shǎnguó army was bestowed the designation Bǎoyì.
10 In the 5th month,
on the day of Jiǎchén,
Ruǎn Jié, the Commissioner of Rùnzhōu, died.
Qián Liú appointed Jìngjiāng Army Commander Chéng Jí to replace him.
11 Lǐ Kèyòng greatly mobilized his troops,
sending Lǐ Hǎnzī and Lǐ Cúnxiào to attack Mèng Fānglì.
In the 6th month,
they captured Cí and Míng prefectures.
Fānglì dispatched his chief generals Mǎ Gài and Yuán Fèngtāo with tens of thousands of soldiers to resist them.
They fought at Liúlí Pō,
where Fānglì’s army was greatly defeated,
and both generals were captured.
Kèyòng, taking advantage of the victory, advanced to attack Xíngzhōu.
Fānglì was by nature suspicious and jealous,
and many of his generals resented him.
By this time, none of them served Fānglì.
Fānglì, ashamed and fearful,
drank poison and died.
In Zhōnghé 2nd year,
Mèng Fānglì occupied Xíngzhōu.
He had always won the hearts of his soldiers,
and the populace supported him as Provisional Governor.
The Differences in Records states: The Veritable Records say:
“Kèyòng stationed his brother Kèxiū to guard Lù,
and sent Ān Jīnjùn, the Prefect of Zézhōu, to attack Fānglì.
Fānglì then rallied the various garrisons for rescue,
and his general Xī Zhōngxìn attacked Liáozhōu.
Kèyòng again sent Lǐ Hǎnzī and others to attack urgently.
Fānglì’s general Mǎ Gài came out to battle,
and was captured by Hǎnzī.
Gài said: ‘If you wish to take Xíngzhōu,
you should first capture Cízhōu.’
Then, combining their forces, they besieged Cízhōu.
Fānglì and Xī Zhōngxìn led a large army to battle;
their army was defeated,
and Cízhōu fell.
Fānglì returned to Xíngzhōu alone on horseback,
and Zhōngxìn died there.
Fānglì was ashamed of this,
and thus planned his own death.
The three armies established his brother Qiān,
and sought aid from Biànzhōu.
Zhū Quánzhōng sent Wáng Qiányù to assist him.
Wáng Róng of Zhènzhōu sent a letter to Kèyòng to make peace and retreated.”
The Táng Nián Bǔ Lù states:
“Fānglì’s strategist Shí Yuánzuǒ was captured by Ān Jīnjùn.
Jīnjùn questioned him,
and Yuánzuǒ requested to attack Cízhōu and
defeat Xī Zhōngxìn.
Jīnjùn then killed him.
Fānglì, indeed, led his troops with Zhōngxìn into Cí.
Jīnjùn battled them,
and greatly defeated them.
Zhōngxìn died,
and Fānglì entered Xíngzhōu alone on horseback.
Ashamed to face the elders,
he committed suicide.”
Xuē Jūzhèng’s Wǔdài Shǐ, Fānglì’s biography, states:
“In the 6th month,
Lǐ Cúnxiào took Míng and Cí prefectures.
Fānglì sent Mǎ Gài and Yuán Fèngtāo, leading all their forces, to meet the enemy at Liúlí Pō.
Cúnxiào struck them,
annihilating them completely,
and capturing Mǎ Gài and Fèngtāo alive.
Initially,
Fānglì was by nature harsh and impatient,
and his benevolence did not reach his subordinates.
During the siege, which lasted for several tens of days,
he personally patrolled the city at night to comfort and encourage,
but those guarding the parapets were all arrogant.
Fānglì knew it was hopeless,
and so drank poison and died.
His cousin, Qiān, the Prefect of Míngzhōu,
had always won the hearts of the soldiers,
and the populace then supported him as Provisional Governor,
seeking aid from Biàn.
At that time, Liáng Zǔ was attacking Shí Pú,
so no relief forces were sent.”
According to records, Lǐ Hǎnzī captured Cízhōu,
and only then captured Mǎ Gài.
The Veritable Records state that
“Gài advised Hǎnzī to capture Cízhōu,”
which is likely a mistake, confusing Shí Yuánzuǒ with Gài.
Furthermore,
then advanced to attack Míngzhōu,
so to say that
“he and Fānglì led a large army to battle”
is also a mistake.
The Old Annals state:
“In the 6th month,
Mèng Fānglì, Jìedùshǐ of Xíng and Míng, died.
The three armies supported his brother Qiān, the Prefect of Míngzhōu, as Provisional Governor,
and Lǐ Kèyòng dispatched troops to attack him.”
The New Annals state:
“In the 6th month,
Lǐ Kèyòng invaded Xíngzhōu.
Mèng Fānglì, Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì Army, died.
His brother Qiān declared himself Provisional Governor.”
According to the Táng Nián Bǔ Lù, Wáng Róng’s memorial reported on the situation of the chief generals of Xíng and Míng,
stating that
“Mèng Fānglì suddenly departed from the illustrious era,
and the three armies and common people together installed his close brother, Qiān, the Prefect of Míngzhōu, to provisionally handle military affairs as Provisional Governor.”
And the New and Old Annals, the Veritable Records, and Xuē Shǐ’s Fānglì biography all state that his brother Qiān was established.
Only Tàizǔ Jì Nián Lù and Xuē Shǐ’s Wǔ Huáng Jì state that his nephew Qiān was established,
which is likely an error.
We now follow the consensus of other books.
Quánzhōng requested passage through Wèibó,
but Luó Hóngxìn did not permit it.
Quánzhōng then sent his chief general Wáng Qiányù with several hundred elite armored soldiers,
taking a secret route into Xíngzhōu to defend it together.
12 Yáng Xíngmì besieged Xuānzhōu.
Food in the city was exhausted;
people resorted to cannibalism.
The Commander Zhōu Jìnsī occupied the city and drove out Zhào Huáng.
Huáng was about to flee to Guǎnglíng,
but Tián Yún pursued and captured him.
Soon after,
the people in the city seized Jìnsī and surrendered.
Xíngmì entered Xuānzhōu.
The generals vied to seize gold and silk,
but Xú Wēn alone took control of the rice granaries
and made congee to feed the starving.
Wēn was
a native of Qúshān.
Huáng’s general Zhōu Běn from Sùsōng,
whose bravery surpassed all in the army,
was captured by Xíngmì but released,
and made a subordinate general.
Sùsōng was
the land of Hàn Wǎnxìan.
During the Liáng dynasty, Gāotáng Commandery was established.
The Suí dynasty abolished the commandery
and established Sùsōng County.
During the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Shūzhōu.
The Jiǔ Yù Zhì states: It is 140 li southwest of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Sùsōng County,
during the Yuánshǐ era of the Hàn dynasty, was Sōngzī County,
belonging to Lújiāng Commandery.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, seeing that Jīngzhōu had Sōngzī County,
changed it to Sùsōng.
Guān,
pronounced like ‘guàn’.
All others scattered,
only Lǐ Déchéng followed Huáng and did not leave.
Xíngmì gave him a daughter from his clan in marriage.
Déchéng was
a native of Xīhuá.
Xíngmì submitted a memorial to the court,
and an imperial edict appointed Xíngmì as the Surveillance Commissioner of Xuān and Shè.
Zhū Quánzhōng and Zhào Huáng had an old friendship,
so he sent an envoy to request his release.
Xíngmì consulted Yuán Xí.
Xí said:
“It is better to behead him and send his head.”
Xíngmì followed his advice.
Soon after,
Xí died.
Xíngmì wept for him, saying:
“Does Heaven not wish to accomplish my great deeds?
Why must it break my arms and legs?
I prefer clemency, but Xí always urged me to kill.
Perhaps this is why he did not live long!”
Sūn Rú sent troops to attack Lúzhōu.
Cài Chóu surrendered the prefecture to him.
13 Zhū Zhēn拔蕭縣,
seized and held it.
He faced off against Shí Pǔ,
and Zhū Quánzhōng wanted to go there himself to oversee the situation.
Zhēn ordered all armies to repair their horses' girth straps.
Lǐ Tángbīn's subordinate general, Yán Jiāo, alone was lazy and remiss.
The army clerk reproached him.
Tángbīn was enraged,
and went to Zhēn to complain about it.
Zhēn was also enraged,
considering Tángbīn rude,
and drew his sword and killed him.
Zhēn and Tángbīn had been at odds for a long time,
and Zhēn, in a fit of anger, killed him,
without any further consideration.
(It was said that Tángbīn was plotting rebellion.)
The Huáinán Left Sīmǎ, Jìng Xiáng,
feared that Quánzhōng, in his anger,
might make an inappropriate decision in haste.
Therefore, he kept the messenger,
and waited until night,
before calmly reporting it.
Quánzhōng was indeed greatly surprised.
Xiáng then devised a plan for him:
falsely arrest Tángbīn's wife and children and imprison them,
and send cavalry to comfort and appease the troops.
Quánzhōng followed this advice,
and the army then became stable.
In autumn,
seventh month,
Quánzhōng went to Xiāoxiàn.
Before he arrived,
Zhēn came out to greet him.
Quánzhōng ordered his warriors to seize him,
accused him of arbitrary killing, and executed him.
Jìng Xiáng plotted for Quánzhōng to take Zhū Zhēn,
still using his previous stratagem.
Quánzhōng was angry,
and threw a bed at him,
so he withdrew.
If Quánzhōng had not killed Zhū Zhēn,
would Zhēn have been willing to serve Quánzhōng?
Huò Cún and others pleaded for him,
but Quánzhōng did not consider it.
為
is pronounced "yú wěi fān".
On the dìngwèi day,
(Quánzhōng) arrived at Xiāoxiàn,
and appointed Páng Shīgǔ to replace Zhēn as Supreme Commander.
In the eighth month,
on the bǐngzǐ day,
Quánzhōng advanced to attack Shí Pǔ's fortifications.
It happened to rain heavily,
so he withdrew his troops.
14 In winter,
tenth month,
the Pínglú Jìedùshǐ, Wáng Jìngwǔ, died.
His son, Shīfàn,
was sixteen years old.
The army promoted him to acting Jìedùshǐ.
The Dìzhōu Cìshǐ, Zhāng Chán, did not comply.
An imperial edict appointed the Crown Prince's Junior Tutor, Cuī Ānqián, concurrently as Shìzhōng,
to serve as Pínglú Jìedùshǐ.
Chán welcomed Ānqián to the prefecture
and jointly attacked Shīfàn with him.
This laid the groundwork for Wáng Shīfàn to kill Zhāng Chán.
15 The Gěishìzhōng, Dù Rúxiū, was appointed Sūzhōu Cìshǐ.
Qián Liú was displeased,
and appointed Shěn Càn, who was managing affairs in the prefecture, as Commander for Arrangement and Control.
Shěn Càn controlled the military power,
and Dù Rúxiū merely held an honorary position.
16 Yáng Xíngmì dispatched the Commander of Horse and Foot, Tián Yūn, and others to attack Chángzhōu.
At that time, Qián Liú's general, Dù Léng, was defending Chángzhōu.
17 In the eleventh month,
the Emperor changed his name to Yè.
18 The Emperor was about to offer sacrifices at the Yuánqiū.
According to old customs,
the Palace Envoys and Chief Commissioners of Military Affairs all wore plain robes and attended;
in the time of Xīzōng,
they already wore robes with a border and a tablet;
by this time,
the relevant authorities were again ordered to make ceremonial robes.
Ceremonial robes
refer to the ceremonial cap, sword, and girdle ornaments.
The Emperor issued a handwritten note instructing them, saying:
"What you all have discussed is most appropriate.
There are occasions to act expediently;
do not let a minor flaw hinder a great ceremony."
Thereupon, eunuchs began to wear swords and girdle ornaments when attending the sacrifices.
The Examination of Differences states: According to the records, although Tián Lìngzī and Yáng Fùgōng wielded power that shook the throne,
their official positions did not exceed that of General of the Left/Right Wǔwèi,
so the other eunuchs must have held lower ranks.
However, various texts do not show what grade of ceremonial robes the eunuchs at that time desired to wear.
On the jǐyǒu day,
sacrifices were offered at the Yuánqiū,
and a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
When the Emperor was in his princely residence,
he had always detested eunuchs.
When he ascended the throne,
Yáng Fùgōng relied on his support and performed meritorious service.
(The support is mentioned in the previous volume, previous year.)
The Emperor was displeased.
He consulted the prime ministers on many political matters.
Kǒng Wěi and Zhāng Jùn advised the Emperor to suppress the power of eunuchs, following the precedent of the Dàzhōng reign.
Fùgōng often rode in a sedan chair to the Tàijí Hall.
The Tàijí Hall
was the front hall of the Western Palace.
When the Emperor was discussing rebels in the four directions with the prime ministers,
Kǒng Wěi said:
"If there are those around Your Majesty who are about to rebel,
what about the four directions?"
The Emperor looked startled and asked him.
Wěi pointed to Fùgōng and said:
"Fùgōng is Your Majesty's household slave,
yet he rides in a sedan chair into the front hall,
raises many strong men as adopted sons,
and has them control the imperial guards
or serve as regional governors.
If this is not rebellion, what is it?"
Yáng Fùgōng appointed his adopted son Yáng Shǒulì as Tiānwēi Army Commander,
Shǒuxìn as Yùshān Army Commander,
Shǒuzhēn as Lóngjiàn Jìedùshǐ,
Shǒuzhōng as Wǔdìng Jìedùshǐ,
Shǒuhòu as Miánzhōu Cìshǐ.
Many other adopted sons served as prefectural governors,
known as "Outside Residence Gentlemen."
He also had six hundred adopted sons
supervising the armies of various circuits.
(Fùgōng replied:) "My strong adopted sons
wish to win the hearts of the soldiers
and protect the nation.
How could they be rebelling?"
The Emperor said:
"If you wish to protect the nation,
why do they not bear the surname Lǐ instead of Yáng?"
Fùgōng had no reply.
Fùgōng's adopted son, Yáng Shǒulì, Commander of the Tiānwēi Army,
originally named Hú Hónglì,
was the bravest in the six armies,
and everyone feared him.
The Emperor wanted to punish Fùgōng,
but feared Shǒulì would cause trouble.
He said to Fùgōng:
"I want your 'Hú son' to be by my side."
Fùgōng presented Shǒulì to the Emperor.
The Emperor bestowed upon him the name Lǐ Shùnjié,
and made him responsible for the keys of the six armies.
The Northern Army's six armies
were all stationed in separate encampments within the imperial gardens,
and each encampment had its own gate,
opened and closed morning and evening.
He was promoted to Tiānwǔ Commander
and given the title of Zhènhǎi Jìedùshǐ,
and soon thereafter granted the title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
The Tiānwǔ was also one of the fifty-four commands of the Shéncè Army.
期
is read as 'jī'.
A court official requested permission for him to attend a meeting with all civil and military officials.
Kǒng Wěi ruled that they should not assemble.
(His judgment was that) the court official's request
should not lead to the assembly of all officials.
Shùnjié was displeased.
Another day,
he subtly mentioned it.
Wěi said:
"Prime ministers are the teachers and elders of all officials,
hence they have audience meetings.
Your Excellency's position is merely that of a commander.
To hold an audience with all officials in the Political Affairs Hall,
does that sit well with your conscience?"
Shùnjié dared not speak further.
Zhū Quánzhōng requested to lead the Salt and Iron Commission.
Kǒng Wěi alone firmly opposed it,
saying to the presenting official:
"If Duke Zhū needs this position,
it cannot be achieved without raising an army!"
Quánzhōng then desisted.
Historians say that Kǒng Wěi, as prime minister of Táng,
wished to revive the administrative system,
but unfortunately was constrained by the times
and could not realize his ambitions.
19 Tián Yūn attacked Chángzhōu,
and dug a tunnel into the city.
In the middle of the night,
banners, armor, and weapons emerged from the sleeping quarters of the Commander of Arrangement and Control, Dù Léng.
He was then captured,
and thirty thousand troops were stationed in Chángzhōu.
20 Zhū Quánzhōng dispatched Páng Shīgǔ with troops from Yǐngshàng to advance towards Huáinán,
to attack Sūn Rú.
The Sòng dynasty had temporarily established Luófán County within the Rǔyīn Prefecture.
Later, the Northern Wèi made the county the administrative seat of Xiàcài Commandery.
Later, the Northern Qí abolished the commandery.
The Suí changed it to Yǐngshàng County.
In Táng, it belonged to Yǐngzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is one hundred and seventeen lǐ east of the prefecture.
趨
is pronounced 'qī yù fān'.
21st day of the 12th month,
on the *Jiǎzǐ* day,
Wáng Jiàn defeated Shān Xíngzhāng and Xīchuān cavalry commander Sòng Xíngnéng at Guǎngdū;
Xíngnéng fled back to Chéngdū,
Xíngzhāng retreated to defend Méizhōu.
On the *Rénshēn* day,
Xíngzhāng requested to surrender to Jiàn.
22nd day, on the *Wùyín* day,
Sūn Rú led his troops from Guǎnglíng across the Jiāng (Yangtze River),
on the *Rénwǔ* day,
he drove out Tián Yūn,
took Chángzhōu,
and appointed Liú Jiànfēng to guard it.
Rú returned to Guǎnglíng,
Jiànfēng then drove out Chéng Jí,
and took Rùnzhōu.
Chéng Jí had been guarding Rùnzhōu for Qián Liú.
23When Liú Jùróng, the former Jìedùshǐ of Shānnán Dōngdào, was in Xiāngyáng,
there was a certain Shēntú Shēng who taught him how to make gold by burning medicines.
When Tián Lìngzī’s younger brother passed through Xiāngyáng,
Jùróng showed him the gold.
Later, Lìngzī resided in Chéngdū.
In the fourth year of Zhōnghé,
Jùróng fled from Xiāngyáng to Chéngdū.
He did not share the secret with Lìngzī,
who resented him.
In that year,
Lìngzī killed Jùróng
and exterminated his clan.
First year of Dàshùn
(*Gēngxū*, 890)
1 Spring,
first month,
on the *Wùzǐ* day, the first day of the month,
his ministers presented the honorary title "Shèngwén Ruìdé Guāngwǔ Hóngxiào Huángdì";
the era name was changed.
2 Lǐ Kèyòng urgently attacked Xíngzhōu.
Mèng Qiān, with his provisions exhausted and strength spent,
captured Wáng Qiányù and the Biàn soldiers and surrendered.
In the second year of Zhōnghé under Xīzōng,
Mèng Fānglì had occupied the three prefectures of Xíng, Cí, and Míng;
it was at this point that his domain perished.
The *Kǎoyì* says: *Tángmò Jiànwénlù*:
"In the first year of Lóngjì,
the great army besieged and broke the city of Xíngzhōu.
Mèng Qiān came to surrender,
and Lǐ Cúnxiào was appointed Xíngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the eleventh month,
on the fourth day,
Mèng Qiān was appointed Assistant Training Commissioner."
*Tàizǔ Jìniánlù* and Xuē Jūzhèng’s *Wǔdài Shǐ Tàizǔ Jì*
both state
"In the first year of Dàshùn,
Lǐ Cúnxiào urgently attacked Xíngzhōu.
The Xíng commander Mèng Qiān surrendered the three prefectures of Xíng, Míng, and Cí to us,
capturing Zhū Wēn’s general Wáng Qiányù and three hundred others and presenting them,"
but without a specific month.
*Tàizǔ Jìniánlù* also states:
"Tàizǔ moved Mèng Qiān to Tàiyuán,
and appointed the great general Ān Jīnjùn as Xíngmíng Tuánliànshǐ."
Xuē's *Shǐ Mèng Qiān Zhuàn* states:
"In the first year of Dàshùn,
in the second month,
Qiān captured Wáng Qiányù and others and begged for surrender.
Emperor Wǔ ordered Ān Jīnjùn to replace him."
We now follow the *Shílù*.
Xuē's *Shǐ Qiányù Zhuàn* states:
"At that time, Tàizǔ’s great army was campaigning against Yǎn and Yùn,
and had not yet come to their rescue.
The people of Xíng were distressed and disloyal,
so Qiān bound Qiányù and sent him to Tàiyuán,
where he was soon killed."
It is to be noted that at this time Quánzhōng was attacking Shí Pǔ,
not yet campaigning against Yǎn and Yùn.
The *Qiányù Zhuàn* is mistaken.
3 On the *Rényín* day,
Wáng Jiàn attacked Qióngzhōu.
Chén Jìngxuan dispatched his general Píngchéng Yáng Rú with three thousand soldiers to assist Cìshǐ Máo Xiāng in defending it.
Xiāng went out to battle
and was repeatedly defeated.
Yáng Rú ascended the city wall
and, seeing the strength of Jiàn’s forces,
sighed:
"The Tang dynasty’s mandate is exhausted.
Grand Duke Wáng governs his troops strictly but without cruelty;
perhaps he can protect the people!"
Thereupon, he led his division to surrender.
Jiàn adopted him as a son
and changed his name to Wáng Zōngrú.
On the *Yǐsì* day,
Jiàn left Yǒngpíng Jìedù Pàn guān Zhāng Lín as Qióngnán Zhāo'ān Shǐ,
and led his troops back to Chéngdū.
He attacked Chén Jìngxuan again.
He was from Xǔzhōu.
Chén Jìngxuan divided his troops and set up camps in the counties of Xīpǔ, Pí, Dǎojiāng, etc.
In the second year of Chuígǒng,
Xīpǔ county was established by separating it from Chéngdū county.
Pí
was an ancient Han county;
in Tang it was all subordinate to Chéngdū Fǔ.
*Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Pí county is forty-five *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
Regardless of the number of family members,
one adult male was conscripted per household.
They gathered bamboo and wood,
transported bricks and stones,
and at night ascended the city walls
to beat clappers and patrol,
without rest.
Wéi Zhàodù camped at Tángqiáo,
Wáng Jiàn camped outside Dōngchāngmén;
Jiàn was very deferential to Zhàodù.
On the *Xīnhài* day,
Jiǎnzhōu general Dù Yǒuqīan captured Cìshǐ Yuán Qiánsōng and surrendered to Jiàn.
Jiàn appointed Yǒuqīan as acting Zhīzhōushì.
4 The Biàn general Páng Shīgǔ and others, with a force reportedly of one hundred thousand,
crossed the Huái River,
claiming to be coming to the aid of Yáng Xíngmì.
They captured Tiāncháng,
and on the *Rénzǐ* day,
they took Gāoyóu.
"Xià" means "surrender."
5 Second month,
on the *Jǐwèi* day,
Zīzhōu general Hóu Yuánchuò captured Cìshǐ Yáng Kān and surrendered to Wáng Jiàn.
Jiàn appointed Yuánchuò as acting Zhīzhōushì.
6 On the *Yǐchǒu* day,
Zhū Quánzhōng was promoted to Shǒu Zhōngshūlìng.
7 Páng Shīgǔ led his troops deep into Huáinán.
On the *Jǐsì* day,
he fought Sūn Rú at Língtíng.
*Jiǔyù Zhì*: There is Língtíng town in Xīnghuà county, Tàizhōu.
8 Yáng Xíngmì dispatched his general Mǎ Jìngyán with five thousand soldiers
to exploit the weakness and seize Rùnzhōu.
Lǐ Yǒu led twenty thousand soldiers and garrisoned Qīngchéng,
preparing to attack Chángzhōu.
Ān Rényì, Liú Wēi, and Tián Yūn defeated Liú Jiànfēng at Wǔjìn.
Last year,
Sūn Rú had sent Liú Jiànfēng to occupy Cháng and Rùn.
During the Jìn dynasty, Wǔjìn county was established by separating it from Qú'ā county.
During the Liáng dynasty, it was renamed Lánlíng.
During the Suí dynasty, it was abolished.
In the second year of Chuígǒng during the Tang dynasty,
Wǔjìn county was again established by separating it from Jìnlíng,
and it was subordinate to Chángzhōu.
*Jiǔyù Zhì* states
that the county has Qīngchéng town.
Yǒu was
from Héféi;
Wēi was
from Shèn county.
9 Lǐ Kèyòng led his troops to attack Hèlián Duó, the Fángyùshǐ of Yúnzhōu,
and captured its eastern city.
Duó sought aid from Lúlong Jìedùshǐ Lǐ Kuāngwēi.
Kuāngwēi led thirty thousand soldiers to his assistance.
On the *Bǐngzǐ* day,
Xíngmíng Tuánliànshǐ Ān Jīnjùn died from an arrow wound,
and Hédōng Wànshèngjūn commander Shēn Xìn rebelled and surrendered to Duó.
When the Yōuzhōu army arrived,
Kèyòng withdrew.
10Shí Pǔ sought aid from Hédōng.
Lǐ Kèyòng dispatched his general Shí Jūnhé with five hundred cavalry to his assistance.
11Lǐ Kèyòng inspected Lùzhōu.
Because the provisions were not generous,
he was angry with Zhāoyì Jìedùshǐ Lǐ Kèxiū,
cursed him, and flogged him.
Kèxiū was ashamed and indignant, which developed into an illness.
In the third month,
he died.
The *Kǎoyì* states: *Tàizǔ Jìniánlù*:
"Tàizǔ sent Lǐ Hǎnzhi and Lǐ Cúnxiào to attack Xíngzhōu.
In the tenth month,
he ordered the army to return to base,
passing through Shàngdǎng.
Kèxiū was naturally stingy.
Tàizǔ’s attendants demanded bribes from Kèxiū.
Within ten days,
several hundred thousand [cash] were spent.
Still, it was deemed that the entertainment and provisions were not ample,
and taking issue with this,
Kèxiū was flogged, and Tàizǔ returned to Tàiyuán.
Soon after, Kèxiū fell ill from shame and indignation."
Xuē's *Shǐ Kèxiū Zhuàn* states:
"In the first year of Lóngjì,
Emperor Wǔ launched a major expedition to attack Xíng and Míng.
When the army returned,
he took the opportunity to confer titles at Shàngdǎng."
It is to be noted that *Tàizǔ Jì* only states that Hǎnzhi and Cúnxiào attacked Xíngzhōu,
not that he went in person.
Perhaps Hǎnzhi and Cúnxiào besieged Xíngzhōu,
while Kèyòng merely garrisoned a large army on the border to provide support.
He returned earlier in the tenth month,
while Hǎnzhi and Cúnxiào continued to besiege Xíngzhōu.
Thus, Mèng Qiān surrendered in the first month.
This laid the groundwork for Lùzhōu’s rebellion against Kèyòng.
12The Xuānxì army was bestowed the title Níngguó,
and Yáng Xíngmì was appointed Jìedùshǐ.
13th year of Xià,
4th month,
Zhāng Jūn, a general from Sùzhōu, expelled and assassinated Inspector Zhāng Shàoguāng,
and defected to Shí Pǔ.
Last year, Zhū Quánzhōng had taken Sùzhōu.
Pǔ led troops to raid Dàngshān.
Quánzhōng dispatched Imperial Guard Deputy Commander Zhū Yǒuyù to attack him,
killing over three thousand men
and capturing Shí Jūnhé.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Xī Xiàng’s *Liáng Tàizǔ Shílù*
first states "4th month, bǐngchén,"
then states "yǐmǎo, Pǔ led troops."
According to the *Chánglì*,
yǐmǎo
was the last day of the 4th month.
The *Shílù* is incorrect.
He was Quánzhōng’s son.
14th year, yǐchǒu,
Chén Jìngxún dispatched Rèn Cónghǎi, Inspector of Shǔzhōu, to lead twenty thousand troops to rescue Qióngzhōu.
They were defeated.
Rèn Cónghǎi wished to surrender Shǔzhōu to Wáng Jiàn.
Jìngxún killed him,
and appointed Xú Gōngshì as the new Inspector of Shǔzhōu.
bǐngyín,
Zhū Shí, Inspector of Jiāzhōu, surrendered the prefecture to Jiàn.
bǐngzǐ,
Wén Wǔjiān, a local strongman from Bódào, seized Xiè Chéng'ēn, Inspector of Róngzhōu, and surrendered to Jiàn.
Bódào
was formerly the state of Bóhóu.
During the Hàn dynasty, a county was established,
serving as the seat of Jiànwéi Commandery.
During the Liáng dynasty, Róngzhōu was established there.
Bó is
read as "pú běi fān."
15th year, Hèlián Duó and Lǐ Kuāngwēi submitted memorials requesting to attack Lǐ Kèyòng.
Taking advantage of his misfortune.
"Kèyòng will eventually become a national menace.
Now, taking advantage of his defeat,
your servant requests to lead the three armies of Biàn, Huá, and Mèng."
The three circuits of Biàn, Huá, and Mèng
all belonged to Quánzhōng at that time.
Shuài
is read as "lǜ."
The three circuits of Hébĕi
refer to Lǐ Kuāngwēi of Lúlóng, Wáng Róng of Chéngdé, and Luó Hóngxìn of Wèibó.
Initially,
Zhāng Jùn advanced through the patronage of Yáng Fùgōng,
as recorded in volume 254, Guāngmíng 1st year of Xīzōng.
Later, he attached himself to Tián Lìngzī and slighted Fùgōng.
When Fùgōng regained influence,
he deeply resented Zhāng Jùn.
During the chaos of Xiāngwáng Yūn,
Tián Lìngzī went to rely on Chén Jìngxún.
After this,
Fùgōng regained influence
and was especially trusted and relied upon.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The old biography states:
"During the second flight to Shānnán,
Fùgōng replaced Lìngzī as Grand Eunuch,
and Zhāng Jùn was dismissed from his post as Administrator of Political Affairs.
When Zhāozōng was still a prince,
he deeply detested eunuchs.
Fùgōng had rendered great service in supporting his enthronement,
and relied on this favor to wield power.
The Emperor was displeased.
At that time, many who sought favor said that Zhāng Jùn possessed strategy
and could devise grand plans.
He was reappointed as prime minister
and given the charge of State Finance Commissioner."
According to the old annals, *Shílù*, new annals, and tables,
Zhāng Jùn was appointed Executive of Political Affairs in the 9th month of Guāngqǐ 3rd year,
and was not dismissed until his military defeat and demotion in Dàshùn 2nd year.
There was no dismissal in between.
The old biography is incorrect.
We now follow the new biography.
He often compared himself to Xiè Ān and Péi Dù.
When Kèyòng campaigned against Huáng Cháo and was stationed in Hézhōng,
as recorded in volume 255, Zhōnghé 23rd year of Xīzōng,
Wáng Duó was the Commander-in-Chief,
and Zhāng Jùn was the Staff Officer.
Upon hearing of Zhāng Jùn's appointment as prime minister,
he privately said to the imperial envoy:
"Master Zhāng is fond of empty talk but lacks practical use;
he is a man who will bring ruin.
If the Emperor employs him based on his reputation,
he will surely bring chaos to the world in the future."
Zhāng Jùn heard this and bore a grudge.
The Emperor leisurely discussed with Zhāng Jùn the order and disorder of ancient and modern times.
Zhāng Jùn said:
"Your Majesty is so wise and discerning,
yet the inner court is controlled by powerful officials,
meaning the inner court is controlled by eunuchs,
and the outer court is controlled by regional commanders."
The Emperor asked what was most urgent at present.
He replied:
"There is nothing better than strengthening the army to subdue the realm."
Thereupon, the Emperor widely recruited soldiers in the capital,
reaching a total of one hundred thousand men.
When Quánzhōng and others requested to attack Kèyòng,
the Emperor ordered officials of the Three Departments and Censorate of fourth rank and above to deliberate on it.

(Lǐ Cúnxiào) captured Kuí and the eunuch Hán Guīfàn, who was carrying the granted credentials, and over five hundred of his personal guards.
He pursued the remaining troops at Diāohuánglǐng
and annihilated them.
Cúnxiào shackled Kuí and Guīfàn
with white silk
and paraded them below the Lùzhōu city wall, saying:
"The imperial court has appointed Chancellor Sūn as the Lù commander,

Hán Guīfàn bore the Emperor's command,
so he was called an envoy.
Shuài,
pronounced suǒ lèi.
Shǐ,
pronounced shū lì.
He ordered the Chancellor to take charge."
He then presented them to Kèyòng.
Kèyòng imprisoned them,
and later tried to persuade Kuí,
wishing to make him Deputy Military Commissioner of Hédōng.
Kuí said:
"I am a high minister of the Son of Heaven.
To die in battle is my lot;
how can I serve a military commander of a frontier region!"
A military governor's office was situated in a frontier region;
Sūn Kuí disparaged it,
calling him a "regional commander."
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu.
(Kèyòng) then ordered him to be sawn with a saw,
but the saw could not cut through.
Kuí cursed, saying:
"You dead dog slave!
When sawing a person, you should use planks to clamp him.
How can you not know this!"
So they clamped him with planks,
and he cursed incessantly

23 On the Bǐng Yín day,
Sūn Rú attacked Rùnzhōu.

It happened that Yáng Xíngmì's general Lǐ Yǒu captured Sūzhōu,

establishing a 'Requisition and Supervision Bureau.'
He coerced them with shackles and scourges

found life unbearable.
27 Lǐ Hǎnzhi sent an urgent appeal to Lǐ Kèyòng.
He was besieged by Biàn troops.
The 28th day of the ninth month,
Rén Yín,
Zhū Quánzhōng's army was stationed at Héyáng.
When the Biàn army first besieged Zézhōu,
they called out to Lǐ Hǎnzhī, saying:
"Xiànggōng always relies on Hédōng
and lightly disregards 'Dāngdào.'
'Dāngdào'
refers to 'Běndào,'
which the Biàn army called themselves.
Gé Púshè has entered Lùfǔ,
Zhāng Xiànggōng
refers to Zhāng Jùn;
Gé Púshè
refers to Gé Cóngzhōu.
The Shātuó have no hole to hide in,
so by what road can Xiànggōng seek survival?"
When Lǐ Cúnxiào arrived,
he selected five hundred elite cavalry
and rode around the Biàn camp, shouting:
"I am
the Shātuó who seeks a hole,
desiring your flesh to satiate my soldiers;
let the fat ones come out to fight!"
Biàn general Dèng Jìyún,
also a valiant general,
led his troops out to battle,
and Cúnxiào captured him alive.
That evening,
Lǐ Dǎng and Lǐ Chóngyìn gathered their forces and fled.
Cúnxiào and Hǎnzhī pursued and attacked them,
reaching Mǎláo Shān,
where they greatly defeated them,
killing and capturing tens of thousands,
and pursued them to Huáizhōu before returning.
Cúnxiào then led his troops to attack Lùzhōu again.
Gé Cóngzhōu and Zhū Chóngjié abandoned Lùzhōu and returned.
Wù Shēn,
Quánzhōng publicly rebuked his generals for their failure and defeat,
executed Lǐ Dǎng and Lǐ Chóngyìn, and returned.
The 'Kǎoyì' states: 'Táng Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù' records:
"In the sixth month,
Lǐ Chóngjié and Gé Cóngzhōu occupied Lùzhōu.
Lǐ Chóngyìn, Dèng Jìyún, and Zhāng Quányì led seventy thousand soldiers to attack Zézhōu.
Lǐ Cúnxiào led three thousand cavalry to provide aid.
Initially,
the Biàn army attacked the city gate,
shouting to Lǐ Hǎnzhī, '...'
Lǐ Cúnxiào was enraged by their words,
led five hundred iron cavalry to pursue and attack,
entered Jìyún's camp gate,
and captured alive more than ten of their generals.
That night,
Biàn general Lǐ Dǎng withdrew his army and fled.
Cúnxiào and Hǎnzhī pursued and attacked them to Mǎláo Shān,
beheaded ten thousand,
pursued and ambushed them,
reaching Huáizhōu before returning.

Gé Cóngzhōu led his forces to abandon the city and flee."
'Tángmò Jiànwén Lù' records:
"In the intercalary ninth month,
the Zhaóyì army's front report stated that Zhaóyì soldiers had pulled down and eliminated fugitives,
recovered the cities,
captured fifty remaining partisans,
bound them with kerchiefs and sent them up.
By the twentieth day,
the Commander of the Traveling Camp, Lǐ Cúnxiào, had turned his forces and returned to headquarters."
Xuē Jūzhèng's 'Wǔdài Shǐ Liáng Tàizǔ Jì' records:
"In the ninth month,
Rén Yín,
the Emperor arrived at Héyáng,
and dispatched Lǐ Dǎng to lead troops towards Zé Lù.
When they reached Mǎláo Chuān,
they were defeated by the Jìn forces.
The Emperor then dispatched Zhū Yǒuyù and Zhāng Quányì to lead elite troops to the north of Zézhōu for reinforcement.
Soon after, Chóngjié and Cóngzhōu abandoned Lù and returned.
Wù Shēn,
the Emperor publicly rebuked the generals for the crime of losing the army,
executed Lǐ Chóngyìn as a public warning,
and then withdrew the army."
The 'Shílù' records:
"In the ninth month,
Jiǎ Shēn Shuò,
Kāng Jūnlì urgently attacked Lùzhōu.
Zhū Quánzhōng was stationed at Héyáng,
and dispatched Lǐ Dǎng to lead troops towards Zé Lù.
When they reached Mǎláo Shān Chuān,
they engaged in a great battle with the Bìng army,
but were unsuccessful.
Dèng Jìyún was captured.
He again dispatched Zhū Yǒuyù and Zhāng Quányì to the north of Zézhōu for reinforcement.
Gé Cóngzhōu and Zhū Chóngjié led their forces to abandon Lùzhōu and return."
Based on this, if Lǐ Cúnxiào had already defeated Lǐ Dǎng in the sixth month
and pursued him to Huáizhōu,
and Huáizhōu is only one day's journey from Héyáng,
how could he have only arrived at Héyáng in the ninth month?
Dǎng's defeat must have been one or two days before the Wù Shēn day of the ninth month.
This is probably because the 'Jìnián Lù' concludes by mentioning Cóngzhōu's occupation of Lùzhōu.
The ninth month:
Jiǎ Shēn Shuò,
the nineteenth day Rén Yín,
the twenty-fifth day Wù Shēn.
If Quánzhōng arrived at Héyáng and then dispatched Dǎng and others to rush to Zé Lù,
and after their defeat,
Cóngzhōu and others abandoned Lù and returned,
how could all these events have occurred within seven days?
This is impossible!
Probably Xuē Shǐ, due to Dǎng's defeat,
traces back to earlier events.
If Cóngzhōu had already abandoned Lùzhōu on the second day of the ninth month,
how could those attacking Zézhōu after the nineteenth day
still say "Gé Sīkōng has entered Lùfǔ"?
Probably the 'Shílù' followed the 'Jìnián Lù' and made an error.
Now, Quánzhōng's comings and goings, months and days, follow Xuē Shǐ,
while the events are drawn from various books.
Lǐ Kèyòng appointed Kāng Jūnlì as the Acting Military Governor of Zhaóyì,
and Lǐ Cúnxiào as the Prefect of Fénzhōu.
Cúnxiào believed his achievement in capturing Sūn Kuí was great
and that he should govern Zhaóyì,
but Jūnlì obtained it,
making him furious and refuse to eat for several days.
He indulged in executions,
and thus began to harbor thoughts of rebellion against Kèyòng.
Lǐ Kuāngwēi attacked Wèizhōu,

Hèlián Duó led tens of thousands of Túbō and Xiájjiásī troops to attack the Zhēlǔ Army,

Kèyòng dispatched his general Lǐ Cúnxìn to attack them,
but he was not victorious.
He then ordered Lǐ Sìyuán to be Cúnxìn's deputy,
and they then defeated them.
Kèyòng followed with a large army,

The 'Kǎoyì' states: 'Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù' records:
"That month,
Yōu Commander Lǐ Kuāngwēi allied with Hèlián Duó,

battled at Lè'ān Zhèn,

This probably refers to the date when the memorial arrived.
'Tángmò Jiànwén Lù' records:

Mentioning the nineteenth day again after the twenty-ninth day

Now, it is simply placed in this month,
without specifying the day.
The 'Xīn Zhì' states: Hédōng Dào has Wǔzhōu,
which administers Wéndé Xiàn,
but the year of its establishment is missing.
Tens of thousands were captured and killed.

The others were ashamed and stopped.
Yáng Xíngmì appointed his general Zhāng Xíngzhōu as the Military Commissioner of Chángzhōu.

Now, following 'Wúyuè Bèi Shǐ',

Láo,
(pronounced Lǔ Hào).

33 The government army exited Yīndì Pass,

Lǐ Kèyòng dispatched Xuē Zhìqín and Lǐ Chéngsì to lead three thousand cavalry to encamp at Hóngdòng.
Hóngdòng,
was Hán Yáng Xiàn during the Hàn dynasty.
In the first year of Yìníng,
it was renamed Hóngdòng,
taking its name from Hóngdòng Lǐng north of the county,
and belonged to Jìnzhōu.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: it is 55 lǐ north of the prefecture,
and another 295 lǐ north to Fénzhōu.
In the first year of Yìníng,
Zhàochéng Xiàn was established by dividing Huòyì,
because during the Spring and Autumn period, Duke Xiàn of Jìn destroyed Gěng and bestowed it upon Zhào Sù,
thus it was called Zhàochéng,
and belonged to Jìnzhōu.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: it is 85 lǐ north of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: The Shǐjì states: King Mù of Zhōu enfeoffed Zàofù in Zhàochéng.
The commentary notes: it is in Yǒng'ān Xiàn, Hédōng.
I (the author) observe that Sòng Bái already considered Zhàochéng to be the place where Zàofù was enfeoffed,
and then here he again quotes the Shǐjì commentary.
How is one to reconcile this!
Cúnxiào learned of this,
and set up an ambush to await them.
The Jian's troops suffered disadvantages,
and the forces of Jìngnán and Fèngxiáng fled without fighting.
The Hédōng troops pursued the defeated enemy in victory,
reaching the west gate of Jìnzhōu;
Zhāng Jùn sallied forth to battle,
and was again defeated.
Nearly three thousand government troops died.
The armies of Jìngnán, Fèngxiáng, Bǎodà, and Dìngnán had already crossed the river to return west.
Zhāng Jùn alone had the imperial guards and Xuānwǔ army, totaling ten thousand men,

According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Jìnzhōu is 125 lǐ south of Jiàngzhōu.

Cúnxiào advanced to attack Jìnzhōu.

he consulted with his subordinates, saying:
"Zhāng Jùn is a prime minister;
capturing him is of no benefit.
The Son of Heaven's imperial guards should not be harmed."
So he retreated fifty lǐ and encamped.
Although Lǐ Cúnxiào was fierce,
he still dared not attack and seize a prime minister,

The Shuǐjīng Zhù: The Táoshuǐ river originates from Qīngxiāng Shān in Wénxǐ Xiàn, Hédōng.

exiting at
what is called Hánkǒu.

it merges with the Sùshuǐ,
which is the mouth of Hánshān.
