"After Zhū Quánzhōng attacked and captured Xúzhōu,

Xuē Shǐ's Biography of Lǐ Chéngsì:
"Initially,
when the main army entered Yīndì,
Xuē Zhìqín and Chéngsì led three thousand cavalry to resist them,

Chéngsì led an army to take it.

which was captured in thirteen days."
Note that the Biography of Lǐ Cúnxìn contains no mention of attacking Jìn and Jiàng.
It seems that in the Jiù Jì,
Lǐ Cúnxiào had already rebelled against Tàiyuán in the tenth month,
so all accounts of this battle refer to Lǐ Cúnxìn.
The Shílù followed this and was mistaken.
According to the Wǔdài Jì, biographies, and Tàizǔ Jìniánlù,
it should have been Lǐ Cúnxiào.
Furthermore, Xízhōu was subordinate to the Hézhōng Jìdù.
What is said about "entering Yīndì Pass and encroaching upon Fénxí"
means "beside the Fén River,"
where low-lying wet land is called *xí*.
Also, the Jìniánlù and Shílù mistakenly identify Zhāng Xínggōng as the Prefect of Jìnzhōu.
This is also an error.
We now follow Xuē Shǐ.
If the Prefect of Jìnzhōu had already fled,
how could Jùn and Jiàn have secured the city?
The Shílù is mistaken.
We now follow the Biography of Lǐ Cúnxiào.
The Táng Bǔ Jì's statement that Cuī Yìn was the Commissioner of Hézhōng Jìdù
is even more egregious an error.
Other various books are referenced as needed.
"My father and son for three generations,
received favor from four courts.
We defeated Páng Xùn,
eliminated Huáng Cháo,
deposed the Prince of Xiāng,
preserved Yìdìng,
captured Yí and Guóchāng, Kèyòng, three generations throughout the four reigns of Wǔ, Xuān, Yì, and Xī.
The defeat of Páng Xùn is seen in Volume 251, Yìzōng's Xiántōng 10th year.
The elimination of Huáng Cháo is seen in Volume 255, Xīzōng's Zhōnghé 3rd and 4th years.
The deposition of the Prince of Xiāng is seen in Volume 256, Guāngqǐ 2nd year.
The preservation of Yìdìng is seen in Guāngqǐ 1st year.
The wearing of the white jade seal
was not necessarily without my strength!
If the attack on Yúnzhōu is considered my crime,
then Tuòbá Sīgōng's taking of Fūyán,
Tuòbá Sīgōng took Fūyán
and gave it to his younger brother, Sīxiào.
And Zhū Quánzhōng's attack on Shí Pǔ at Xú,
and his attack on Zhū Xuān at Yùn,
these events are all mentioned above.
Rewarding them and punishing me,
how could I be without an argument!
Moreover, when the court was in imminent danger,
it praised me as Hán, Péng, Yī, and Lǚ;
but after it was secure,
it reviled me as Róng, Jié, Hú, and Yí.
Today, do not those who wield troops and achieve merit in the world
fear Your Majesty's future revilement!
Furthermore, if I truly have committed grave crimes,
the six armies should conquer me.
There are already established laws and punishments.
Why must they wait for me to be weak before seizing me!
Now that Zhāng Jùn has deployed his army,
it is indeed difficult for me to remain inactive.
I have already gathered fifty thousand Barbarian and Han troops,
intending to go directly to Pú and Tóng
and fight with Jùn.
If I do not win,
I am willing to accept being stripped of my titles.
Otherwise,
I will approach the palace gate with light cavalry,
頓首丹陛，
訴姦回於陛下之扆坐，
納制敕於先帝之廟庭，
然後自拘司敗，
恭俟鈇質。 」
司敗，
即司寇之官。
濬已敗，
朝廷震恐。
濬與韓建踰王屋至河陽，
撤民屋為栰以濟河，
河南王屋縣有王屋山。
王屋，
漢河東垣縣地，
後魏置長平縣，
後周置王屋郡，
隋廢郡為縣。
九域志：縣在孟州西北一百三十里。
考異曰：實錄明年二月云：
「時張濬、韓建兵敗後，
為克用騎將李存信所追，
至是，
方自含山踰王屋，
出河清，
達于河陽。
河溢無舟檝，
建壞民廬舍為木罌數百渡河，
人多覆溺。 」
似太晚。
今因濬、建走，
終言之。
是役也，
朝廷倚朱全忠及河朔三鎮；
及濬至晉州，
全忠方連兵徐、鄆，
雖遣將攻澤州而身不至。
行營乃求兵糧於鎮、魏，
鎮、魏倚河東為扞蔽，
皆不出兵；
惟華、邠、鳳翔、鄄、夏之兵會之。
兵未交而孫揆被擒，
幽、雲俱敗，
幽，
李匡威；
雲，
赫連鐸。
故濬軍望風自潰。
34十二月，
孫儒拔蘇州，
殺李友。
考異曰： 莊宗列傳：
「楊行密，
壽州壽春人。
初據本州，
秦宗權遣孫儒及行密同攻陷揚州，
儒專據之。
龍紀元年，
儒出軍攻宣州，
行密襲據揚州，
稱留後，
北通時溥，
儒引軍攻之。
大順元年，
行密禦備力竭，
率衆夜遁，
出據宣州。 」
此說最為差誤。
國朝開寶中，
薛居正脩五代史，
江南未平，
不見本國舊史，
據昭遠所記及唐年補錄作行密傳，
但知行密非壽春人，
改為廬州；
又知行密非受宗權命與孫儒同陷揚州，
餘皆無次敍。
今按吳錄、太祖紀及高遠唐烈祖實錄行密傳云：
「光啟三年，
十月，
秦彥、畢師鐸出走，
行密入揚州。
十一月，
孫儒圍揚州。
文德元年，
四月，
儒陷揚州，
行密奔廬州。
八月，
自廬州帥兵攻宣州。
龍紀元年，
六月，
陷宣州，
殺趙鍠。
大順二年，
七月，
孫儒再渡江攻宣州。
景福元年，
六月，
執斬儒，
復歸揚州。 」
且龍紀元年孫儒方強，
行密新得宣州，
安能襲據揚州踰年哉！
近脩唐書行密傳，
全用吳錄事迹，
乃云
「儒進攻行密，
行密復入揚州，
北通時溥，
扞儒。
朱全忠遣龐師古助行密，
敗於高郵，
行密懼，
退還宣州。 」
蓋承莊宗列傳、五代史之誤而不考正也。
焚潤州廬舍，
夜遁。
儒使沈粲守蘇州，
又遣其將歸傳道守潤州。
楊行密遣安仁義破錢鏐之兵而取常、蘇、潤，
孫儒又從而奪之，
民之死於兵者，
不知其幾矣。
35辛丑 ，
汴將丁會、葛從周擊魏，
渡河，
取黎陽、臨河，
黎陽，
漢古縣，
唐屬衞州。
九域志：在州東北一百二十里，
隋分黎陽縣置臨河縣，
唐屬相州。
衞，
漢朝歌縣；
紂所都朝歌城，
在今縣西；
隋大業二年，
改曰衞縣，
唐屬衞州。
九域志：衞州汲縣有淇門鎮。
36是歲，
置昇州於上元縣，
以張雄為刺史。
至德二載，
以潤州江寧縣置昇州，
上元二年廢，
今復置。
考異曰：新地理志：
「光啟三年，
以上元等四縣置昇州。 」
張雄傳：
「大順初，
以上元為昇州，
授雄刺史。 」
吳錄馮弘鐸傳：
「大順元年，
復以上元為昇州，
命弘鐸為刺史。 」
按是時雄尚存。
今從雄傳。
正月，
羅弘信軍于內黃。
丙辰 ，
朱全忠擊之，
五戰皆捷，
至永定橋，
斬首萬餘級。
弘信懼，
遣使厚幣請和。
全忠命止焚掠，
歸其俘，
還軍河上。
魏博自是服於汴。
2 庚申 ，
制以太保、門下侍郎、同平章事孔緯為荊南節度使，
中書侍郎、同平章事張濬為鄂岳觀察使。
二人罷相，
以晉、絳喪師也。
御史中丞徐彥若為戶部侍郎、同平章事。
昭緯，
慎由從子；
崔慎由相宣宗。
從，
才用翻。
商之子也。
徐商見二百四十九卷宣宗大中十二年。
Yáng Fùgōng sent men to kidnap Kǒng Wěi at Chánglèpō.
Chánglèpō is Chánglèbǎn.
All his belongings were lost,
and Wěi barely escaped.
Lǐ Kèyòng again sent an envoy to present a memorial, saying:
“Zhāng Jùn, for the sake of Your Majesty’s eternal dominion,
sought his own temporary glory,
and knowing the deep enmity between your servant and Zhū Wēn,
secretly allied with him.
Your servant now has no official rank,
and is known as a criminal;
I dare not return to Your Majesty’s domain.
I wish to temporarily reside in Hézhōng.
For all my movements and actions,
I await your command.”
I (the author) secretly believe that Kèyòng’s memorial
was secretly instructed by Yáng Fùgōng.
Zhāng Jùn was made Cìshǐ of Liánzhōu.
An imperial edict was bestowed upon Kèyòng,
restoring all his official ranks and titles,
and ordering him to return to Jìnyáng.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The old annals state:
“The Grand Army was stationed at Jìnzhōu.
Kèyòng sent the imperial envoy Hán Guīfàn back to court,
and through him presented a memorial to appeal his grievances,
saying, ‘The treacherous minister Zhāng Jùn relies on Quánzhōng
to alienate meritorious officials.’
The court wished to appease his resentment
and submitted the matter to the ministers for deliberation on its feasibility.
The discussions of the Left Púshè Wéi Zhāodù and others”
and so on.
This was in the twelfth month.
However, in this year, Zhāodù was campaigning against Chén Jìngxuan,
so the old annals are mistaken.
We now follow the *Shílù*.
3 Sūn Rú led all the troops from Huái and Cài across the Jiāng River.
On Guǐyǒu,
he advanced south from Rùnzhōu, fighting as he went.
Tián Yūn and Ān Rényì were repeatedly defeated and retreated,
and all of Yáng Xíngmì’s garrisons fled at the mere sight of the enemy.
Rú’s general Lǐ Cónglì suddenly arrived at Dōngxī in Xuānzhōu.
Dōngxī
is in Xuānchéng,
now called Wǎnxī.
The hearts of the multitude were filled with dread.
That night,
he sent his general from Héféi, Tái Méng, with five hundred men to station on the west bank of the stream.
Xīxī
is the west bank of Wǎnxī.
He went back and forth several times,
leading Cónglì to believe that a large army was following,
so he hastily retreated.
Rú’s vanguard reached Lìshuǐ.
Lìshuǐ
was the Hàn county of Lìyáng;
during the Suí dynasty, Lìshuǐ county was separated from it.
At that time, it belonged to Shēngzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: It is eighty-five *lǐ* east of the prefecture.
Shénfúyáng retreated to feign weakness,
and Rú’s army did not prepare defenses.
Shénfú led elite troops to attack them by night,
capturing and beheading a thousand men.
4 In the second month,
Lǐ Kèyòng was given the additional title of Shǒu Zhōngshūlìng,
and Lǐ Hǎnzhi’s official ranks and titles were restored.
Zhāng Jùn was demoted again to Sīhù of Xiùzhōu.
5 Wéi Zhāodù, leading over ten myriad troops from various circuits, campaigned against Chén Jìngxuan.
For three years he could not conquer him.
In the first year of Wéndé, Zhāodù was sent to suppress Xīchuān,
and by this time, three years had passed.
The court deliberated on ceasing military action.
In the third month,
on Yǐhài,
an edict was issued restoring Jìngxuan’s official ranks and titles.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The new annals say:
“In the second month,
on Yǐsì,
Chén Jìngxuan was pardoned.
On Jǐwèi,
an edict ordered Wáng Jiàn to cease military action,
but he did not obey.”
The *Shíguó Jìnián* also says:
“In the second month,
on Yǐsì,
Jìngxuan’s official ranks and titles were restored.”
However, the *xīnsì* was the first day of the second month,
and there was no Jǐwèi,
so the new annals are mistaken.
We now follow the *Shílù*.
Gu Gu Yànlǎng was ordered to return to Zǐzhōu,
and Wáng Jiàn to Qióngzhōu.
6 Wáng Shīfàn sent the Dūzhīhuīshǐ Lú Hóng to attack Zhāng Chán, the Cìshǐ of Dìzhōu.
Hóng turned his troops back to attack Shīfàn.
Shīfàn sent someone to greet him with a heavy bribe,
saying:
“Shīfàn is childish
and incapable of such a heavy responsibility.
I wish to abdicate,
and it would be an act of benevolence for you, my lord, to spare my life.”
Hóng, believing Shīfàn to be young,
trusted him
and made no preparations.
Shīfàn secretly told the junior officer Ānqiū Liú Xún:
Ānqiū
was a Hàn county,
anciently the state of Gēnmóu;
in the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Mìzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: It is one hundred and twenty *lǐ* northwest of the prefecture.
*Jiào*,
read *hù jiào* (*hù jiāo*).
*Xún*,
read *xú xīn* (*xú xīn*).
“If you can kill Hóng,
I will make you a great general.”
When Hóng entered the city,
Shīfàn concealed armored soldiers and hosted a banquet for him.
Xún killed Hóng and several of his associates at the table.
Shīfàn comforted and exhorted his soldiers,
rewarding them generously and making solemn vows.
He personally led the attack on Dìzhōu,
captured Zhāng Chán,
and beheaded him.
Cuī Ānqián fled back to the capital.
Shīfàn made Xún the Mǎbù Fù Dūzhīhuīshǐ.
An imperial edict appointed Shīfàn as Pínglú Jiédùshǐ.
Shīfàn was harmonious, prudent, and fond of learning.
Whenever the magistrate of his home county arrived at his post,
Shīfàn would always prepare ceremonial guards and go to pay his respects.
The magistrate dared not accept this,
so Shīfàn ordered his *kèjiàng* to hold him,
and made the magistrate sit in the main hall.
*Kèjiàng*
are those who preside over introductions and announce guests,
a position of ceremonial authority under the bell in the Hàn and Jìn dynasties.
*Jiàng*,
read *jí liàng* (*jí liàng*).
*Lìng*,
read *lì dīng* (*lì dīng*).
*Tīng*,
read as *tīng* (*tīng*).
He would then say,
“I am commoner Wáng Shīfàn,”
and bow to him in the courtyard.
Some of his subordinates remonstrated,
but Shīfàn said:
“I respect my hometown,
thus teaching my descendants not to forget their origins!”
The *Shī* says: For the mulberry and the catalpa tree,
one must show respect.
The commentary states: One must not fail to respect
what one’s father has planted.
7 Zhāng Jùn reached Lántián,
then fled to Huázhōu to rely on Hán Jiàn,
and secretly sought help from Zhū Quánzhōng with Kǒng Wěi.
Quánzhōng presented a memorial appealing for Wěi and Jùn,
and the court had no choice but
to allow them both to go as they pleased.
Wěi returned from Shāngzhōu
and also resided in Huázhōu.
8 Ān Zhījiàn, the Jiédùshǐ of Xíngmìng, secretly communicated with Zhū Quánzhōng.
After Ān Jīnjùn died,
Lǐ Kèyòng appointed Ān Zhījiàn to replace him as governor of Xíng and Mìng.
Zhījiàn, fearful,
fled to Qīngzhōu.
The court appointed Zhījiàn as Shénwǔ Tǒngjūn.
Zhījiàn, leading three thousand of his subordinates, was about to proceed to the capital.
Passing through Yùnzhōu,
Zhū Xuān, who was currently on good terms with Kèyòng,
ambushed him by the river
and beheaded him.
The *Xuē Shǐ* says: Ān Zhījiàn fled to Qīngzhōu,
and was returning to court by ascending the river from Dìzhōu.
Zhū Xuān ambushed and beheaded him by the river.
*Shuài*,
read as *lǜ* (*lǜ*).
9 Summer,
fourth month.
A comet was seen among the Sāntái.
The Sāntái are the six stars below Dǒukuí, paired two by two.
*Jiàn*,
read *xián biàn* (*xián biàn*).
It was over ten *zhàng* long.
On Jiǎshēn,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
10 In the city of Chéngdū, there was a shortage of food,
and abandoned children filled the streets.
Fathers and sons could not support each other,
to the extent that they abandoned their children.
Patrols found them,
and reported it to Wéi Zhāodù.
Zhāodù said:
"The entire city is severely hungry;
how can we bear not to save them!"
He released them without questioning.
Some also reported to Chén Jìngxüan.
Jìngxüan said:
"I regret having no means to save the starving.
Since they can do this,
do not forbid it!"
Consequently, the number of hawkers gradually increased,
but what they sold amounted to no more than a *dǒu* or a *shēng*.
They cut bamboo tubes,
one and a half inches in diameter,
five fen deep,
measured rice with them and sold it.
Each tube cost over a hundred cash,
and the starved littered the ground.
The strong among the military and commoners preyed upon the weak,
and even officers executing them could not stop it.
So, more cruel laws were enacted,
such as severing at the waist,
or diagonal splitting.
The dead followed one after another, yet the acts did not cease.
People's eyes and ears grew accustomed to it,
and they no longer feared.
Officials and commoners became increasingly desperate daily,
many planning to surrender.
Jìngxüan captured all their clansmen and parties and killed them,
with extreme cruelty.
Xú Gēng of Chéngdū, the Internal and External Commander and Governor of Méizhōu,
was kind and lenient by nature,
and saved thousands of lives.
Tián Lìngzī said:
"You hold the power of life and death, yet you punish not a single person.
Do you harbor ulterior motives?"
Gēng was afraid,
and that night,
he took captives and prisoners and executed them in the marketplace.
Wáng Jiàn saw the decree to cease hostilities
and said:
"A great achievement is on the verge of completion;
why abandon it!"
He consulted with Zhōu Xiáng.
Xiáng advised Jiàn to ask Grand Councilor Wéi to return to court,
and attack Chéngdū alone,
conquer and possess it.
Jiàn submitted a memorial requesting:
"Chén Jìngxüan and Tián Lìngzī's crimes are unforgivable."
"Qǐng" (request),
should probably be
"Chēng" (state).
*Kǎo Yì* (Textual Variations) states: *Shíguó Jìnián* (Annals of the Ten Kingdoms): The court deliberated that Jiàn did not obey the imperial decree,
and could not be controlled,
so he was further appointed Military Commissioner for Pacification and Control of the Xīchuān Expeditionary Army.
This appointment was likely made after Zhāodù's return to court.
Zhāodù could do nothing about it,
and thus was unable to return east.
Jiàn persuaded Zhāodù, saying:
"Now the regional governors east of the passes are devouring each other.
This is a serious internal illness.
Your Excellency should return to the imperial court early
and strategize with the Son of Heaven.
Jìngxüan is merely
a trivial scabies [AS-FE5D] [AS-FBEE] flea;
he should be dealt with over time.
Task me,
and I can handle it!"
Zhāodù hesitated, undecided.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
Jiàn secretly ordered Dōngchuān general Táng Yǒutōng and others to seize Luò Bǎo, Zhāodù's close aide, at the entrance of the Provisional Government Office,
and cannibalize him.
Wéi Zhāodù attacked Chéngdū
and established a provisional government office to manage affairs.
*Luǎn*,
pronounced *lìyǎn* fan (Qieyun pronunciation).
Zhāodù was greatly frightened,
and immediately feigned illness,
handing his seal and credentials to Jiàn,
and issuing a dispatch for Jiàn to act as acting Commissioner for the Three Agencies.
The Three Agencies
are the Military Governor, the Pacification Commissioner, and the Control Commissioner.
He returned east that same day.
Jiàn escorted him to Xīndū,
knelt and offered a drink before his horse,
weeping and bowing as they parted.
*Guìshāng*
means kneeling and offering a cup.
Jiànmén:
Zhūgé Liàng established the pass.
In the second year of Táng Shènglì (699),
Pu'ān, Yǒngguī, and Yīnpíng were separated
to establish Jiànmén County,
subordinate to Jiànzhōu.
*Jiǔyù Zhì* (Record of the Nine Regions): It is fifty-five *lǐ* northeast of the prefecture.
The Eastern Army was not reinstated.
When Zhāodù arrived at the capital,
he was appointed Retainer of Dōngdū.
*Kǎo Yì* states: *Jiùjì* (Old Annals):
"In the first year of Lóngjì (889),
in the first month,
Zhāodù became Retainer of Dōngdū."
*Shílù* (Veritable Records):
"In the second year of Dàshùn (891),
in the third month,
on the *yǐhài* day,
Chén Jìngxüan's official titles and ranks were reinstated.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Zhāodù was appointed Retainer of Dōngdū."
According to this, if Zhāodù had already been appointed Retainer,
not holding the Xīchuān Military Governor and Pacification Commissioner posts,
then he should have disbanded his troops and returned east,
and should not have remained there.
Even if he were forced to stay,
how could the various armies possibly obey him,
and why would Wáng Jiàn need to persuade him, saying:
"Your Excellency should return to the imperial court early
and strategize with the Son of Heaven!"
Old traditions say:
"Jiàn coerced and persuaded Zhāodù
to submit a memorial requesting to return to the capital.
Jiàn held Jiànmén with heavy forces,
and urgently attacked Chéngdū.
When Zhāodù returned,
he was made acting *Sīkōng* and concurrently Retainer of Dōngdū."
The new traditions also say the same.
It is probably that in the third month of this year,
after Jìngxüan's official titles were reinstated,
Zhāodù was merely summoned back to court.
Wáng Jiàn refused to cease hostilities,
and Zhāodù, being constrained by him,
also jointly memorialized,
believing that Jìngxüan was unforgivable.
Subsequently, being coerced by Jiàn,
he handed over his troops and returned east.
The imperial court blamed him for losing his position,
hence he was demoted to Retainer,
as stated in the new and old traditions.
We follow this now.
Furthermore, when Zhāodù first besieged Chéngdū,
Yáng Shǒuliàng was Deputy Pacification Commissioner,
Gù Yànlǎng was Army Commander,
and Wáng Jiàn was Commander-in-Chief,
all at the foot of Chéngdū city.
When Zhāodù returned east,
only Jiàn was there,
and Zhāodù handed his troops to him.
The other two are not seen.
According to the imperial decree of the *yǐhài* day in the third month,
it only states that Yànlǎng and others were ordered to return to their respective garrisons,
which means Shǒuliàng had already returned earlier.
Yànlǎng must have also returned upon receiving this decree,
leaving only Zhāodù and Jiàn there.
However, Jiàn ordered Dōngchuān general Táng Yǒutōng to cannibalize Luò Bǎo,
which means Yànlǎng returned in person but left his troops to jointly attack Chéngdū.
Jiàn urgently attacked Chéngdū,
with beacon fires and trenches extending fifty *lǐ* around the city.
There was a dog butcher, Wáng Yāo,
who requested to feign punishment and defect into the city to persuade its inhabitants,
causing disunity among them.
Jiàn sent him.
Yāo entered and met Chén Jìngxüan and Tián Lìngzī,
telling them
that "Jiàn's troops are exhausted and out of food,
and are about to flee."
When he went out, he sold tea in the market,
secretly praising Jiàn's bravery and might to officials and commoners,
and the strength of his military force.
Consequently, Jìngxüan and others became lax in their defense,
while the populace grew fearful and anxious.
Jiàn also sent his general Zhèng Wò of Jīngzhào to feign surrender to scout the city.
Jìngxüan appointed him as a general,
and made him guard the city walls.
Afterwards, he feigned another defection and returned.
Jiàn thus knew the full extent of the city's strengths and weaknesses,
and appointed Wò as Commander-in-Chief of the Direct Guards,
changing his name to Wáng Zōngwò.
11 Zhōu Yuè, Military Governor of Wǔ'ān, was appointed Military Governor of Lǐngnánxīdào.
*Fāngzhèn Biǎo* (Table of Regional Garrisons): In the third year of Zhōnghé (883),
the Húnán Observer was promoted to Military Governor of Qīnhuà Command.
In the first year of Guāngqǐ (885),
it was renamed Wǔ'ān Army.
12 Lǐ Kèyòng launched a major attack on Hèlián Duó,
defeating his troops on the river,
on the North River.
*Bài* (defeat),
pronounced *bǔmài* fan (Qieyun pronunciation).
13 Yáng Xíngmì dispatched his generals Liú Wēi and Zhū Yánshòu with an army of thirty thousand to attack Sūn Rú at Huángchí.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Xuānzhōu’s Dāngtú County has Huángchí Town.
Yánshòu
was from Shūchéng.
Sūn Rú’s army was at Huángchí.
In the fifth month,
there was a great flood,
and all the camps were submerged.
He then returned to Yángzhōu,
ordering his general Kāng Wàng to hold Hézhōu,
and Ān Jǐngsī to hold Chúzhōu.
Hé and Chú
are one hundred and fifty *lǐ* apart.
14 On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
the imperial son Yòu was made King Dé.
15 Yáng Xíngmì dispatched his general Lǐ Shénfú to attack Hé and Chú.
Kāng Wàng surrendered,
and Ān Jǐngsī fled.
16 In the autumn,
seventh month,
Lǐ Kèyòng urgently attacked Yúnzhōu.
Hèlián Duó ran out of provisions
and fled to the Tǔyùhún tribe.
Hèlián Duó
was originally a chieftain of the Tǔyùhún.
In the Kāichéng period,
his father, leading three thousand households of his people, voluntarily submitted.
He had defended Yúnzhōu for fifteen years,
until its fall at this time.
The Kǎoyì states: The Old Annals and the Veritable Records both say,
"Kèyòng led his troops out through Jǐngxíng,
garrisoned at Chángshān,
and extensively plundered Shēn and Zhào.
Lúlong's Lǐ Kuāngwēi personally led over ten thousand infantry and cavalry to reinforce Wáng Róng."
According to the Annals of Emperor Tàizǔ of Táng,
at this time Kèyòng was attacking Hèlián Duó.
After pacifying Yúnzhōu,
he then attacked Wáng Róng.
The Veritable Records likely followed the error of old accounts.
Furthermore, the Annals state:
"In the seventh month,
Tàizǔ advanced his army
to Liǔchéng,
where Hèlián Duó's strength failed and provisions ran out,
so he fled into Tǔyùhún,"
and so on.
The Veritable Records state:
"Kèyòng dispatched a general to urgently attack Yúnzhōu."
This is because it previously stated that Kèyòng personally attacked Wáng Róng.
According to the Annals,
the attack on Wáng Róng was later.
The Veritable Records are mistaken.
Kèyòng memorialized to appoint his grand general Shí Shànyǒu as the Defense Commissioner of Dàtóng.
17 Zhū Quánzhōng sent an envoy to Yáng Xíngmì to arrange a joint attack on Sūn Rú.
Rú, relying on his strong army,
wished to first destroy Xíngmì,
then confront Quánzhōng.
He sent dispatches to the various regional governors,
enumerating the crimes of Xíngmì and Quánzhōng,
and further said:
"After pacifying Xuān and Biàn,
I shall lead my army to the court
to eliminate the evil at the ruler's side."
Thereupon, he completely burned the dwellings in Yángzhōu,
drove all the able-bodied men and women across the river,
and killed the old and weak for food.
Xíngmì’s generals Zhāng Xùn and Lǐ Déchéng secretly entered Yángzhōu,
extinguished the remaining fires,
and obtained several hundred thousand *hú* of grain to relieve the starving populace.
The people of Yángzhōu hated Sūn Rú and were grateful to Yáng Xíngmì.
Had Sūn Rú not died at Xuānzhōu,
the people of Yángzhōu would certainly have submitted to Yáng Xíngmì.
Xùn, on Xíngmì’s orders, provided food to him.
This is why Jiàn was grateful to Xíngmì.
This sets the stage for Zhāng Jiàn's surrender to Xíngmì.
18 Xíngmìng Jiedushi Lǐ Cúnxiào persuaded Lǐ Kèyòng to attack Zhènzhōu.
Kèyòng agreed.
In the eighth month,
Kèyòng journeyed south through Zélù,
then crossed into the territory of Huáimèng.
19 Zhū Quánzhōng dispatched his general Dīng Huì to attack Sùzhōu,
capturing its outer city.
In the first year,
summer,
fourth month,
Sùzhōu general Zhāng Jūn had submitted to Shí Pǔ.
20 On the *yǐwèi* day,
Sūn Rú moved out from Sūzhōu to garrison at Guǎngdé.
Shěn Yuē said: Guǎngdé County,
probably established by Wú.
Liú Xù said: Guǎngdé County,
was Gùzhàng of Hàn.
During Sòng, Guǎngdé of Xuānzhōu
and Gùzhàng of Wúxīng
were separated to establish Suī'ān County.
In the second year of Zhìdé of Táng,
it was changed to Guǎngdé,
named after the old city of Guǎngdé within the county's borders,
and belonged to Xuānzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: it is one hundred and twenty *lǐ* east of the prefecture.
Rú besieged his encampment.
Xíngmì's general Lǐ Jiǎn of Shàngcài, leading over a hundred men, fought fiercely,
broke through the encampment,
and rescued Xíngmì.
21 Wáng Jiàn's attack on Chén Jìngxúan became increasingly urgent.
Jìngxúan was defeated every time he sallied out to fight.
Most of the prefectures and counties within his jurisdiction were captured by Jiàn.
Yīróng Jiedushi Yáng Shèng provided him with food at times.
Jiàn garrisoned troops at Xīndū,
cutting off the route to Péngzhōu.
Tián Lìngzī made Péngzhōu into Wēiróng Commandery.
He encouraged the officers and soldiers,
but none responded.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
Tián Lìngzī ascended the city wall and addressed Jiàn, saying:
"This old man was once very kind to you,
why do you distress me so?"
Jiàn replied:
"How dare I forget the kindness of a father and son!
This refers to Lìngzī adopting Jiàn as a foster son.
I have no choice but to do this.
If Grand Preceptor changes his mind,
what more could I ask for!"
Grand Preceptor
refers to Chén Jìngxúan.
The character *fù*
is pronounced *fú yòu*.
Lìngzī personally carried the seal and tally of Xīchuān to Jiàn’s camp and handed them to him.
The Old Book states: In the first year of Lóngjì,
on the *rénchén* day, the first day of the fifth month,
Wáng Jiàn, the Prefect of Hànzhōu, captured Chéngdū,
moved Chén Jìngxúan to Yǎzhōu,
and Jiàn proclaimed himself Provisional Military Commissioner,
and again used Tián Lìngzī as Supervisor of the Army.
The accounts of events differ,
and there is also a two-year discrepancy in the dating.
Jiàn wept and thanked him,
asking to resume their father-son relationship as before.
Earlier,
Jiàn often enticed his officers and soldiers, saying:
"Chéngdū city is as prosperous as embroidered flowers.
Once we seize it, gold, silk, and women will be yours for the taking.
We'll take turns as Jiedushi every other day!"
On the *rén'yín* day,
Jìngxúan opened the gates to welcome Jiàn.
In the first year of Guǎngmíng of Xīzōng,
Chén Jìngxúan had been garrisoned in Xīchuān,
and now his rule ended.
He sent people to enter the city first.
He then addressed his officers and soldiers, saying:
"You and I have fought a hundred battles over three years,
and now we have finally taken the city.
You will not lack wealth and honor.
Be careful not to burn or plunder the markets.
I have already entrusted Zhāng Qíng to protect them.
If he fortunately apprehends someone and reports it to me,
I may still pardon them;
but if he first executes them and then reports,
I will not be able to save them!"
Soon after, some soldiers violated the order.
Qíng apprehended over a hundred people,
all of whom he struck in the chest and killed.
Their bodies were piled in the market,
and no one dared to offend.
Therefore, people at the time called Qíng
"Zhāng the Chest-Striker."
On the *guǐmǎo* day,
Jiàn entered the city
and proclaimed himself Provisional Commissioner of Xīchuān.
A junior officer Hán Wǔ repeatedly mounted his horse in the Prefect's office hall.
The staff officer stopped him.
The Prefect's office hall
is the Jiedushi's office hall.
The staff officer
is an official
who manages affairs of the Jiedushi's headquarters.
The character *shù*
is pronounced *suǒ jiǎo*.
The character *shàng*
is pronounced *chí zhǎng*.
"[The] Sītú promised me that we would take turns as Jiedushi every other day;
why should I dismount?"
Jiàn secretly sent men to assassinate him.
Initially,
when Chén Jìngxúān resisted the imperial decree,
Tián Lìngzī, desiring to usurp his military and political power,
said to Jìngxúān:
"Third Elder Brother is highly respected.
Jìngxúān is the third [son].
朝,
read as 'zhāo' (遙翻).
It would be better to entrust everything to me.
I will daily record events and submit them for your review.
You, Elder Brother, can simply live in lofty ease."
Jìngxúān, having always lacked intelligence,
gladly agreed.
From then on, all military affairs were no longer decided by him,
leading to his downfall.
Wáng Jiàn appointed Jìngxúān's son, Táo, as the Cìshǐ of Yǎzhōu,
and made him accompany Táo to his post.
The following year,
he was dismissed and returned,
taking up residence in Xīnjīn,
where he was supported by the taxes and levies of one county.
On the day of Guǐchǒu,
Wáng Jiàn dispatched soldiers to forage for food in various zhōus,
and changed Wén Wǔjiān's name to Wáng Zōngruǎn,
and Xiè Cóngběn's to Wáng Zōngběn.
He changed their names
and adopted them as foster sons.
更,
read as 'gēng' (工衡翻).
Wáng Jiàn treated them with respect and utilized their talents.
Historians say this is how Wáng Jiàn was able to possess Shǔ.
22 Yáng Fùgōng, the Liùjūn Shí'èrwèi Guānjūnróngshǐ and Zuǒshéncèjūn Zhōngwèi, commanded the palace guard troops,
and held exclusive control over court politics.
All his adopted sons became Jiédùshǐ and Cìshǐ,
and he also raised six hundred eunuch sons,
all of whom became Jūnjūn.
His adopted sons Yáng Shǒuzhēn, the Lóngjiàn Jiédùshǐ, and Yáng Shǒuzhōng, the Wǔdìng Jiédùshǐ, failed to deliver tribute and taxes,
and submitted memorials slandering and belittling the imperial court.
The Lóngjiàn Jiédù
governed the four zhōus of Lóng, Jiàn, Lì, and Láng.
The Wǔdìng Jiédù
governed the four zhōus of Yáng, Guǒ, Jiē, and Fú.
The emperor's maternal uncle, Wáng Huái, sought to be a Jiédùshǐ.
The emperor consulted Fùgōng,
who deemed it impossible.
Wáng Huái was enraged
and insulted him.
Wáng Huái frequented the imperial palace
and was quite influential.
Fùgōng disliked him,
and memorialized to have him appointed as the Qiánnán Jiédùshǐ.
At this time, the Qiánzhōng Jiédù was renamed Yǒngtài Army,
and south of Qiánzhōng were the Jīmí Mánzhōu.
It is unknown where the Qiánnán Jiédù was established.
Could it be that Yáng Fùgōng intended to kill Wáng Huái
and specially created this command to bestow upon him?
惡,
read as 'wù' (烏路翻).
黔,
read as 'qián' (渠今翻).
Yìchāng county in Lìzhōu has Jíbǎijīn.
Yìchāng station has ancient cypresses,
which locals call 'Jíbǎi',
thus naming the ford.
According to Yáng Fùgōng's biography,
Wáng Huái traveled via Xīngyuán to Jíbǎijīn.
His clan members and retainers all died,
reported as a boat accident.
The emperor knew Fùgōng's deed
and deeply resented him.
Lǐ Shùnjié, having gained favor and power,
contended with Fùgōng for authority,
and reported all of Fùgōng's secret affairs to the emperor.
The emperor then appointed Fùgōng as the Fèngxiáng Jūnjūn;
Fùgōng was resentful
and refused to go,
claiming illness
and requesting retirement.
In the ninth month,
on the day of Yǐmǎo,
Fùgōng was made Shàngjiāngjūn and retired,
bestowed with a small table and staff.
When the envoy returning with the imperial decree arrived,
Fùgōng secretly sent his confidant Zhāng Wǎn to assassinate him.
23 Wáng Chóngyíng, the Hùguó Jiédùshǐ, was additionally appointed Zhōngshūlìng.
24 Gù Yànlǎng, the Dōngchuān Jiédùshǐ, passed away.
The army collectively nominated his younger brother, Gù Yànhuī, to act as Liúhòu.
25 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day of Rénwǔ,
Zhāng Jūn, the Cìshǐ of Sùzhōu, surrendered to Dīng Huì.
26 On the day of Guǐwèi,
Wáng Jiàn, the Yǒngpíng Jiédùshǐ, was appointed Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ;
on the day of Jiǎshēn,
the Yǒngpíng Army was abolished.
Last year, the Yǒngpíng Jiézhèn was established in Qióngzhōu and conferred upon Wáng Jiàn.
Once Wáng Jiàn obtained Xīchuān,
he was granted the Xīchuān Jiédù and the Yǒngpíng Army was abolished;
this was Wáng Jiàn's intention.
He focused on governance,
accepted frank advice,
was generous and enjoyed scholars,
employed people according to their talents,
and was humble and frugal;
however, he was suspicious and fond of killing,
and many meritorious and famous generals
were often executed on various pretexts.
27 Yáng Fùgōng's residence was near Yùshānyíng.
According to old histories,
Yáng Fùgōng's residence was in Zhāohuàlǐ.
近,
read as 'jìn' (其靳翻).
He frequently went to visit it.
Someone accused Fùgōng of conspiring with Yáng Shǒuxìn to rebel.
On the day of Yǐyǒu,
the emperor ascended Ānxǐlóu,
deployed troops for self-defense,
and ordered Lǐ Shùnjié, the Tiānwēidū Jiāng, and Lǐ Shǒujié, the Shéncèjūnshǐ, to lead troops to attack his residence.
Zhāng Wǎn led his household retainers to resist,
household retainers
were people privately kept and raised by Yáng Fùgōng.
帥,
read as 'shuài'.
Shùnjié and others could not overcome them.
On the day of Bǐngxū,
the palace guards secured Hánguāngmén.
Hánguāngmén
was the first gate from the west on the southern side of the Imperial City.
Wishing to plunder the two markets,
they encountered Liú Chóngwàng,
who stopped his horse and admonished them, saying:
"The Son of Heaven is personally supervising the battle east of the street.
You are all guards of the palace,
and should kill the rebels in front of the tower to gain merit,
do not covet small gains,
and bring upon yourselves a bad name!"
The multitude all replied:
"Yes."
Thereupon, they followed Chóngwàng eastward.
Yáng Shǒuxìn's forces, seeing the troops approach,
then dispersed and fled.
Yáng Shǒuxìn and Fùgōng took their clan and exited through Tōnghuàmén,
hurrying to Xīngyuán.
Tōnghuàmén
was the first gate from the north on the eastern side of Cháng'ān city.
趣,
read as 'qū' (七喻翻).
Zhāng Wǎn was captured
and beheaded.
The Yǒng'āndū
was also one of the fifty-four dūs of the Shéncè Army.
Yáng Shǒuliàng, Yáng Shǒuzhōng, Yáng Shǒuzhēn, and Yáng Shǒuhòu, the Cìshǐ of Miánzhōu, jointly raised troops to resist the imperial court,
using the pretext of punishing Lǐ Shùnjié.
Shǒuhòu
was also an adopted son of Fùgōng.
28 Lǐ Kèyòng attacked Wáng Róng,
severely defeating the Zhèn troops at Lóngwěigāng,
slaying and capturing tens of thousands.
He then captured Línchéng,
and attacked Yuánshì and Bǎixiāng.
Xuē Jūzhèng said: Lóngwěigāng is northwest of Línchéng.
Línchéng was originally Fángzǐ,
renamed in the first year of Tiānbǎo,
and along with Yuánshì and Bǎixiāng, all belonged to Zhàozhōu.
Jiǔyùzhì: Línchéng is 130 lǐ southwest of Zhàozhōu.
Kǎoyì said: Táng Tàizǔ Jìniánlù states:
"Attacked Yuánshì,
beheaded a thousand heads,
advanced and captured Báoshuǐ,
then attacked Bǎixiāng."
However, Báoshuǐ belonged to Yìzhōu.
Kèyòng was attacking Zhènzhōu to rescue Yì and Dìng,
he certainly would not take that territory,
which is likely a mistake.
Lǐ Kèyòng plundered extensively and returned,
encamping in Xíngzhōu.
29 In the eleventh month,
Guō Zhū, the Dūjiāng of Cáozhōu, killed Guō Cí, the Cìshǐ,
and surrendered to Zhū Quánzhōng.
Cáozhōu
was under the jurisdiction of Zhū Xuān, the Tiānpíng Jiédùshǐ.
30 Zhū Jǐn, the Tàiníng Jiédùshǐ, led over ten thousand men to attack Shānzhōu.
In the late Táng dynasty,
Shānfù and Dàngshān of Sòngzhōu,
Chéngwǔ of Cáozhōu,
and Yútái of Yǎnzhōu
were used to establish Shānzhōu.
Jiǔyùzhì: Yǎnzhōu is 280 lǐ southwest of Shānzhōu.
Shānzhōu at that time belonged to Zhū Quánzhōng.
單,
read as 'shàn' (音善).
31 On the day of Yǐchǒu,
Liú Zhījùn, the Jiāng of Shí Pǔ, led two thousand men and surrendered to Zhū Quánzhōng.
Zhījùn,
was a fierce general of Xú.
Shí Pǔ's army was weakened thereafter.
Zhū Quánzhōng appointed Zhījùn as Zuǒyòukāidào Zhǐhuīshǐ.
32 In the beginning,
Lǐ Cúnxiào, the Resident Commissioner of Xíng, Míng, and Cí Prefectures,
and Lǐ Cúnxìn were both adopted sons of Lǐ Kèyòng,
but they were not on good terms.
Cúnxìn was favored by Kèyòng.
Cúnxiào, being in Xíng Prefecture,
wished to achieve great merits to surpass him,
and thus proposed capturing Zhèn and Jì;
see the previous volume, Dàshùn 2nd year.
This was not immediately approved.
When Wáng Róng besieged Yáoshān,
Cúnxiào went to relieve it,
but failed.
Kèyòng appointed Cúnxìn as the Commander-in-Chief of the Fān and Hàn Cavalry and Infantry,
to attack them together with Cúnxiào.
The two harbored suspicions against each other,
delaying their advance.
Kèyòng then dispatched Lǐ Sìxūn and others to defeat them.
This event is seen in the first month of that year in the previous account.
They slandered Cúnxiào, saying he had no intention of attacking the rebels,
and suspected him of having a private agreement with them.
When Cúnxiào heard this,
he thought that despite his merits for Kèyòng,
his trust and consideration did not match that given to Cúnxìn.
Gù
means 'on the contrary'.
and fearing disaster,
he secretly allied with Wáng Róng and Zhū Quánzhōng,
submitting a memorial to the imperial court, offering the three prefectures in submission.
Variant Readings: According to the *Shílù*:
"In the 10th month of Dàshùn 1st year,
Lǐ Cúnxiào, the Taìyuán general and Prefect of Xíng Prefecture, took the marching army from Jìn Prefecture and occupied Xíng Prefecture."
According to the *Jiùjì*:
"In the 11th month,
on the *Guǐchǒu* day,
Lǐ Cúnxiào, the Taìyuán general and Prefect of Xíng Prefecture, relying on his merit of capturing Sūn Kuí,
was to be made the Commander of Zhāoyì,
but resented Kèyòng for appointing Kāng Jūnlì.
Cúnxiào led the marching army from Jìn Prefecture back to Xíng Prefecture,
occupied the city,
submitted a memorial declaring allegiance,
and also sent letters to Zhāng Jùn and Wáng Róng requesting aid."
According to the *Tángmò Jiànwénlù*:
"On the 24th day of the 10th month,
Lǐ Cúnxiào led troops to attack Jìn Prefecture,
then fled back to Xíng Prefecture,
and rebelled.
He wrote to Chancellor Zhāng Jùn, saying: 'I have governed the three prefectures
for almost two years now.'
He also said: 'I often thought that during the time Ān Zhījiàn was here,
I would submit to the imperial court.
If my neighbors did not protect me,
my family would suddenly suffer immense hardship.
Because of this hesitation,
I dared not make it clear,
leading to the abrupt break in friendly relations with my neighbors last year.
This was not my wish,
but was due to Lǐ Mǒu's commands.'
He also said: 'Since the wars of this spring,
I truly wished to cease hostilities.
Since the 15th day of the 9th month,
Lǐ Mǒu's men
urged me to advance south to Zhào Prefecture.
Lǐ Mǒu was coerced
to enter via the Tǔmén Road,
directly reaching Zhèn Prefecture.
On the 14th day of this month,
the Zhāoyì army, people, and all others requested me to temporarily act as the Resident Commissioner of the infantry and cavalry,
and submit to the imperial court.'
The Great King heard that Cúnxiào had rebelled,
and was greatly enraged.
He issued an order
to first dispatch a major general to advance,
swiftly reach Xíng Prefecture,
and await further commands.
They were not to engage in combat arbitrarily,
but only to besiege small strongholds,
specifically awaiting the main army."
According to the *Táng Tàizǔ Jìniánlù*, Xuē Jūzhèng's *Wǔdài Shǐ Jì*, *Zhuàn*, *Shílù*, and *Xīnjì*,
all state that in the 10th month of Jǐngfú 1st year,
Cúnxiào rebelled against Taìyuán
and submitted to the imperial court;
while the *Jiùjì* and *Tángmò Jiànwénlù* place it in the 10th month of Dàshùn 1st year.
The *Jiùjì* might be speaking of later events in connection.
Examining this, in the 3rd month of the 2nd year,
Ān Zhījiàn had just rebelled against Taìyuán,
yet this text already mentions Zhījiàn.
It also says:
"I have governed the three prefectures
for almost two years now."
Cúnxiào only became the Military Governor of Xíng, Míng, and Cí in Dàshùn 2nd year.
By Jǐngfú 1st year,
it would indeed be two years.
Therefore, the *Shílù*'s statement that the Prefect of Xíng Prefecture occupied Xíng Prefecture
is also due to an error in the *Jiùjì*.
The letter from Cúnxiào recorded in the *Jiànwénlù*
was likely sent to Wáng Róng,
mistakenly stating it was to Zhāng Jùn.
The imperial edict appointed Cúnxiào as the Military Governor of Xíng, Míng, and Cí,
but did not permit him to gather troops.
33 In the 11th month,
Zhāng Suì, the Prefect of Hóu Prefecture under Shí Pǔ, and Zhāng Jiàn, the Prefect of Sì Prefecture, submitted their prefectures to Zhū Quánzhōng.
34 On the *Yǐwèi* day,
Zhū Quánzhōng dispatched his son, Yǒu Yù, leading an army of 100,000 to attack Pú Prefecture,
capturing it and
seizing its Prefect, Shào Lún.
Pú Prefecture
was under the jurisdiction of Zhū Xuān.
Pú
is pronounced 'bómù'.
35 Sūn Rú's general Wáng Tán captured Wù Prefecture,
and its Prefect Jiǎng Huái fled to Yuè Prefecture.
In Zhōnghé 4th year,
Jiǎng Huái occupied Wù Prefecture.
36 Cài Chóu, the Prefect of Lú Prefecture, unearthed the ancestral tomb of Yáng Xíngmì.
In Guāngqǐ 3rd year,
Yáng Xíngmì left Cài Chóu to guard Lú Prefecture;
the next year,
Chóu submitted the prefecture to Sūn Rú;
after Rú's defeat,
Chóu then took up arms to resist Xíngmì.
He sent an envoy to Zhū Quánzhōng with his seal to request aid.
Quánzhōng, disliking his perfidy,
accepted his seal
but did not provide aid,
and instead sent a dispatch to Xíngmì;
Xíngmì thanked him.
Xíngmì dispatched the Commander-in-Chief of the Marching Army, Lǐ Shénfú, to lead troops to attack Chóu.
37 The Xuānmíng Calendar was gradually becoming inaccurate.
When Mùzōng ascended the throne,
he believed that after generations of succession,
the calendar system must be revised.
He thus ordered officials in charge of astronomy to revise and compile calendrical methods,
named Xuānmíng.
In the 12th month,
it was submitted.
It was named Jǐngfú Chóngxuán Calendar.
Biān Gāng, along with Hú Xiùlín, the Assistant Supervisor of the Imperial Observatory, and Wáng Chí, the Military Administrator of Jūn Prefecture, revised and compiled the new calendar,
but the methods were entirely from Gāng.
Gāng was skilled in calculation,
capable of rapidly and repeatedly performing multiplication and division.
From this, the methods of simplicity, directness, and interpolation arose,
while the traditional methods of grand design and meticulous sequencing were abandoned.
Although the calculation methods were convenient and easy,
they were all obscure regarding their fundamental principles.
Shàng
is pronounced 'shí zhǎng'.
38 On the *Rénwǔ* day,
Wáng Jiàn dispatched his general Huá Hóng to attack Yáng Shǒuliàng in Láng Prefecture,
defeating him.
Jiàn sent his Military Governor's Commissioner Zhèng Xù from Yánlíng as an envoy to Zhū Quánzhōng;
Yánlíng
was the land of Qǔ'ē County during the Hàn dynasty.
In the Jìn dynasty, Yánlíng Commandery was established separately.
In the Suí dynasty, its administrative seat was moved to Dāntú.
In Wǔdé 3rd year,
it was moved to the old commandery seat
and belonged to Rùn Prefecture.
Today's Yánlíng Town in Dānyáng County is that very place.
Xù emphasized its dangerous terrain.
Quánzhōng did not believe him.
Xù said:
"If I do not report it,
I fear it will mislead your military strategy."
Quánzhōng laughed heartily.
39 In this year,
Zhōng Wénjì, the Prefect of Míng Prefecture, died,
and his general Huáng Shèng proclaimed himself Prefect.
Lù Zhèn's *Jiǔguó Zhì*: Huáng Shèng,
a native of Yín County, Míng Prefecture,
served as a general for years.
When Prefect Zhōng Wénjì died,
he then occupied the commandery.
1 In spring,
1st month,
Shí Pǔ dispatched troops to attack Sù Prefecture,
and its Prefect Guō Yán died in battle.
In Dàshùn 2nd year,
Zhū Quánzhōng captured Sù Prefecture;
this event is seen in the previous volume.
2. Gù Yànhuī (顧彥暉), the acting Military Governor of Dōngchuān (東川), already had a grudge against Wáng Jiàn (王建).
In Dàshùn (大順) 2nd year (891 CE),
Yáng Shǒuliàng (楊守亮) attacked Dōngchuān (東川).
Wáng Jiàn (王建) sent troops to rescue it,
intending to seize it in the process,
but he did not succeed.
From this, he became estranged from Gù Yànhuī (顧彥暉).
This matter is also mentioned in the previous volume.
[He] submitted a memorial requesting a renewed grant of a *jié* (節) to Yànhuī (彥暉).
In Dàshùn (大順) 2nd year (891 CE),
the imperial court sent a eunuch to grant the *jié* (節) to Gù Yànhuī (顧彥暉),
but Yáng Shǒuhòu (楊守厚) intercepted and seized it.
Therefore, a renewed grant was requested.
This was to reaffirm the previous decree.
Zǐzhōu (梓州) had not been attacked, yet he sent troops to rescue it.
Why?
It was not to rescue it,
but to send troops to assist Gù Yànhuī (顧彥暉) to engage the army of Xīchuān (西川).
Jiàn (建) sent troops and defeated the Dōngchuān (東川) and Fèngxiáng (鳳翔) armies at Lìzhōu (利州).
Yànhuī (彥暉) sought peace,
requesting to break off relations with Mào Zhēn (茂貞).
This was then granted.
3. Lǐ Màozhēn (李茂貞), the Military Governor of Fèngxiáng (鳳翔), personally requested to be stationed at Xīngyuán (興元).
An imperial edict appointed Màozhēn (茂貞) as Military Governor of Shānnán Xīdào (山南西道) and concurrently Wǔdìng (武定).
Xú Yànruò (徐彥若), Minister of the Secretariat and concurrently Grand Councilor, was made Grand Councilor
and concurrently Military Governor of Fèngxiáng (鳳翔).
*Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The Old Annals place this in the *guǐwèi* (癸未) day of the 7th month.
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄) and New Annals.
Màozhēn (茂貞) wanted to hold Fèngxiáng (鳳翔) concurrently
and did not obey the edict.
4. In the 2nd month,
on the *jiǎxū* (甲戌) day,
Wáng Jiàn (王建), Military Governor of Xīchuān (西川), was given the concurrent title of Grand Councilor.
5. Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) led his army to besiege Xíngzhōu (邢州).
Wáng Róng (王鎔) sent his tooth-general Wáng Zànghǎi (王藏海) with a letter to relieve the situation.
Kèyòng (克用) was enraged,
executed Zànghǎi (藏海),
and advanced his troops to attack Róng (鎔),
defeating the Zhèn (鎮) troops at Píngshān (平山).
Píngshān (平山) was Hàn (漢) Púwú (蒲吾) county,
in the Suí (隋) it was Fángshān (房山) county.
In Zhìdé (至德) 1st year (756 CE),
it was changed to Píngshān (平山) county,
belonging to Zhènzhōu (鎮州).
*Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) says: It is sixty-five *lǐ* (里) west of the prefecture.
On the *xīnsì* (辛巳) day,
[they] attacked Tiāncháng (天長) garrison,
but could not take it in ten days.
Róng (鎔) led out an army of thirty thousand to relieve it.
Kèyòng (克用) met them in battle at the foot of Chìrì Lǐng (叱日嶺),
decisively defeating them,
beheading over ten thousand men.
The remaining troops scattered and fled.
The Hédōng (河東) army had no food,
so they dried the corpses and ate them.
6. Shí Pǔ (時溥) sought aid from Zhū Jǐn (朱瑾).
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) sent his general Huò Cún (霍存) with three thousand cavalry to garrison Cáozhōu (曹州) to prepare for this.
Jǐn (瑾) led twenty thousand troops to rescue Xúzhōu (徐州).
Cún (存) led his troops to meet them,
and together with Zhū Yǒuyù (朱友裕), they jointly attacked the Xú (徐) and Yǎn (兗) forces at the foot of Shífó Shān (石佛山),
decisively defeating them.
Shífó Shān (石佛山) is near Péngchéng (彭城).
Xuē (薛) History says: Shífó Shān (石佛山) is south of Péngmén (彭門).
*Shùzhēng Jì* (述征記) says: South of Péngchéng (彭城) is Shífó Shān (石佛山),
its summit is two *zhàng* (丈) two *chǐ* (尺) square.
On the *xīnmǎo* (辛卯) day,
the Xú (徐) army reappeared,
and Cún (存) died in battle.
Huò Cún (霍存) relied on his victory and did not anticipate the Xú (徐) army reappearing,
and thus was defeated and died in battle.
*Fù* (復) is pronounced *fú yòu fān* (扶又翻).
7. Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) advanced and took Jǐngxíng (井陘).
Lǐ Cúnxiào (李存孝) led troops to rescue Wáng Róng (王鎔),
and then entered Zhènzhōu (鎮州),
conferring with Róng (鎔).
Róng (鎔) again sought aid from Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠).
Quánzhōng (全忠) was currently battling Shí Pǔ (時溥),
and could not provide assistance,
but merely sent Kèyòng (克用) a letter,
saying,
"There are one hundred thousand elite troops at Yè (鄴),
but they are being held back and have not advanced."
Kèyòng (克用) replied,
"If you indeed have troops stationed at Yè (鄴),
I eagerly await your arrival.
If you truly wish to decide victory or defeat,
I wish to contend at the tail of Chángshān (常山)."
On the *jiǎwǔ* (甲午) day,
Lǐ Kuāngwēi (李匡威) led troops to rescue Róng (鎔),
defeating the Hédōng (河東) army at Yuánshì (元氏).
Kèyòng (克用) withdrew to Xíngzhōu (邢州).
Róng (鎔) rewarded Kuāngwēi (匡威) at Gǎochéng (藳城),
presenting him with two hundred thousand in gold and silk in return.
8. Zhū Yǒuyù (朱友裕) besieged Péngchéng (彭城).
Shí Pǔ (時溥) repeatedly led out troops,
but Yǒuyù (友裕) kept his ramparts closed and did not fight.
In the 11th month of last year,
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) sent Yǒuyù (友裕) to attack Péngchéng (彭城).
This describes the prolonged standoff.
*Shù* (數) is pronounced *suǒ jiǎo fān* (所角翻).
Yǒuyù (友裕) did not pursue;
this refers to the battle at the foot of Shífó Shān (石佛山).
Quánzhōng (全忠) was enraged
and sent an urgent letter to the commander Páng Shīgǔ (龐師古),
ordering him to take over the command
and also investigate the matter.
The letter was mistakenly delivered to Yǒuyù (友裕).
Yǒuyù (友裕) was greatly terrified
and fled into the mountains with two thousand cavalry.
According to Xuē (薛) History, the biography of Yuánzhēn (元貞) Empress Zhāng (張) states
"twenty cavalry."
The biography of Zhū Yǒuyù (朱友裕) states
"several cavalry."
Two thousand cavalry is too many;
twenty cavalry should be correct.
He hid at the residence of his paternal uncle, Quányù (全昱).
Zhū Quánzhōng's (朱全忠) brothers originally lived in Dàngshān (碭山).
Quányù (全昱) was Quánzhōng's (全忠) eldest brother.
*Dàng* (碭) is pronounced *táng* (唐).
[He] sent Yǒuyù (友裕) to go alone to Biànzhōu (汴州) to see Quánzhōng (全忠).
[Yǒuyù (友裕)] wept and bowed prostrate in the courtyard.
Quánzhōng (全忠) ordered his attendants to seize and subdue him,
intending to execute him.
To seize means to grasp his topknot;
to subdue means to press down his neck.
*Zú* (捽) is pronounced *zuó mò fān* (昨沒翻).
[Yǒuyù (友裕)] wept and said,
"You abandoned your troops
and submitted yourself for punishment.
Your lack of any other intention is clear."
Quánzhōng (全忠) understood and spared him,
making him acting prefect of Xǔzhōu (許州).
Yǒugōng (友恭) was Lǐ Yànwēi (李彥威) from Shòuchūn (壽春).
As a child, he was a servant in Quánzhōng's (全忠) household.
*Kǎoyì* (考異) states: Xuē Jūzhèng's (薛居正) *Wǔdài Shǐ* (五代史), biography of Gāo Jìxīng (高季興), identifies Yǒugōng (友恭) as Lǐ Qīláng (李七郎), a merchant from Biàn (汴).
*Shíguó Jìnián* (十國紀年) identifies him as a merchant from Shòuchūn (壽春).
The biography of Yǒugōng (友恭) says:
"Yànwēi (彥威) served Tàizǔ (太祖) from childhood."
We follow this.
Lady Zhāng (張),
from Dàngshān (碭山),
was resourceful and strategic.
Quánzhōng (全忠) respected and feared her.
Even in military and government affairs,
he would sometimes consult with her.
If he was about to lead troops out,
and halfway there,
the Lady thought it inadvisable,
she would send a messenger to summon him back,
and Quánzhōng (全忠) would immediately turn back.
Páng Shīgǔ (龐師古) attacked Fóshān Zài (佛山寨)
and captured it.
Fóshān Zài (佛山寨) is Shífóshān Zài (石佛山寨).
9. When Lǐ Kuāngwēi (李匡威) went to rescue Wáng Róng (王鎔),
he was about to depart Yōuzhōu (幽州).
His family gathered to bid farewell.
All his family gathered at the envoy's residence to see him off.
Kuāngwēi (匡威) became drunk and molested them.
In the 2nd month,
Kuāngwēi (匡威) returned from Zhènzhōu (鎮州).
When he reached Bóyě (博野),
Kuāngchóu (匡籌) occupied the military headquarters and declared himself acting Military Governor,
using a tally to recall the campaigning troops.
Kuāngwēi's (匡威) forces scattered and returned,
and he remained in Shēnzhōu (深州) with his close associates.
Shēnzhōu (深州) is one hundred fifty *lǐ* (里) southeast of Bóyě (博野).
He sent the judicial officer Lǐ Bǎozhēn (李抱真)
to submit a memorial,
requesting to return to the capital.
The capital had repeatedly undergone great chaos,
and upon hearing of Kuāngwēi's (匡威) arrival,
the markets were greatly terrified,
saying,
"The Golden-headed King is coming to usurp the state!"
Some gentry and commoners hid in mountains and valleys.
Wáng Róng (王鎔) was grateful to him for losing territory because of him.
[He] was grateful for him rescuing himself which led to losing Yōuzhōu (幽州).
[He] built a residence for him
On the 10th day, Liǔ Pín (柳玭), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Yúzhōu (渝州), was made Cìshǐ of Lúzhōu (瀘州).
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志), Yúzhōu is 760 lǐ (里) west of Lúzhōu.
Pín (玭)
is pronounced like "bù tián" (部田).
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The Xīn Chuán (新傳) says:
"Pín was demoted to Cìshǐ of Lúzhōu for an offense
and died there."
The Běimèng Suǒyán (北夢瑣言) also states that he was banished and appointed to Lúzhōu.
In both the Xīn Shū (新書) and Jiù Shū (舊書),
the year and month of Pín's demotion are not mentioned.
Now we follow the Shílù (實錄).
In this month, Pín moved from Yúzhōu to become Cìshǐ of Lúzhōu,
which must have been after his initial demotion from Yúzhōu and then his transfer to Lúzhōu;
the Xīn Chuán and Běimèng Suǒyán are mistaken.
The world considered filial piety, fraternity, ritual, and law to be upheld by the literati and officials.
It is said that since Yuánhé (元和), the family has been renowned.
The Emperor wished to make him a chancellor,
but the eunuchs disliked him,
so he was banished to an outer post for a long time.
Pín once admonished his children and younger brothers, saying:
"Indeed, high family status
is something to fear, not to rely upon.
When establishing oneself and conducting oneself,
if one makes even a single mistake,
the offense will be more severe than for others,
and one will have no way to face one's ancestors underground after death.
This is why it is to be feared.
High family status easily fosters arrogance,
and a prosperous clan is envied by others;
noble conduct and true talent
are not readily believed by people,
but a slight flaw
is pointed out by everyone: this is why it cannot be relied upon.
Therefore, sons of wealthy families
should apply themselves even more diligently to study,
and exert themselves even more in conduct,
merely to be comparable to others!"
If the children and nephews of the Liǔ (柳) clan could always uphold Pín's admonitions,
each striving for self-cultivation,
they would still be a renowned family today.
Wáng Jiàn (王建) repeatedly requested the killing of Chén Jìngxuān (陳敬瑄) and Tián Lìngzī (田令孜),
but the imperial court refused.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the Yǐhài (乙亥) day,
Jiàn sent someone to accuse Jìngxuān of plotting rebellion,
and killed him in Xīnjīn (新津).
Chén Jìngxuān resided in Xīnjīn;
see the previous volume, Dàshùn (大順) second year.
He was imprisoned and died.
Jiàn had Fēng Juān (馮涓), the Jiédù Pànguān (節度判官), draft a memorial, which said:
"Opening a box and releasing a tiger,
Kǒng Xuānfù (孔宣父) did not blame others;
slaying a snake on the road,
Sūn Shū'áo (孫叔敖) certainly did not do it for personal gain.
The Lúnyǔ (論語) states that Confucius rebuked Rǎn Yǒu (冉有) and Jì Lù (季路), saying:
'When a tiger or rhinoceros escapes from its cage,
whose fault is it?'
Chǔ's Sūn Shū'áo, when he was a child,
went out to play and returned,
sorrowful and refusing to eat.
His mother asked him why,
and he tearfully replied:
'Today I saw a two-headed snake,
and I fear I have not many days left to live.'
His mother said:
'Where is the snake now?'
He said:
'I heard that those who see a two-headed snake will die,
and I feared others would see it again,
so I have already buried it.'
His mother said:
'Do not worry,
you will not die.
I have heard
that Heaven rewards those with hidden virtues with blessings.'
When people heard of it,
they all understood his benevolence.
One should act preemptively, lest the opportunity be lost within the trap."
Juān (涓) was Sù's (宿) grandson.
Fēng Sù's (馮宿) affairs can be found in volume 245, Kāichéng (開成) first year.
Juān (涓)
is pronounced like "guī yuān" (圭淵).
The Biàn (汴) army attacked Xúzhōu (徐州),
but failed to overcome it for months.
They had been attacking Xúzhōu since the eleventh month of last year,
and by now it was the fifth month.
"The timing of the army's advance was not good,
hence no success."
Quánzhōng (全忠) thought this was true.
Jìng Xiáng (敬翔) said:
"Now we have been attacking the city for months,
at great cost,
and the people of Xú (徐) are already exhausted;
it will fall any day now.
If the officers and soldiers hear this,
they will slacken in their attack."
Quánzhōng then burned the letter.
On the Guǐwèi (癸未) day,
Quánzhōng personally led his forces to Xúzhōu;
on the Wùzǐ (戊子) day,
Páng Shīgǔ (龐師古) captured Péngchéng (彭城),
and Shí Pǔ (時溥) and his entire clan ascended the Yànzǐ Lóu (燕子樓) and immolated themselves.
During Xīzōng's (僖宗) Zhōnghé (中和) first year,
Shí Pǔ occupied Xúzhōu,
and now he perished.
When Zhāng Jiànfēng (張建封) was garrisoned in Xú (徐),
he had a beloved concubine named Pànpàn (盻盻).
After Jiànfēng's death,
in Zhāng's old residence, there was a small building
called Yànzǐ (燕子).
Pànpàn, mourning her old love, did not marry,
and lived in this building for over ten years,
lonely and melancholy.
(From Bái Lètiān Jí (白樂天集)).
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù says:
"In the fifth month,
Biànzhōu reported the capture of Xúzhōu."
The Jiù Jì (舊紀) says:
"In the fourth month,
Biàn generals Wáng Chóngshī (王重師) and Niú Cúnjié (牛存節) seized Xúzhōu."
The Jiù Chuán (舊傳) says:
"Pǔ sought aid from Zhū Jǐn (朱瑾) of Yǎnzhōu (兗州),
who dispatched troops to save him,
but they encountered heavy snow,
ran out of provisions, and returned.
Biàn generals Wáng Chóngshī and Niú Cúnjié entered by ladder at night,
and Pǔ, with his wife and children, ascended the tower and immolated themselves, dying.
This was in Jǐngfú (景福) second year."
The Xīn Jì (新紀) says:
"In the fourth month,
on the Wùzǐ day,
Zhū Quánzhōng captured Xúzhōu,
and Shí Pǔ died."
Xuē Jūzhèng's (薛居正) Wǔdài Shǐ Liáng Jì (五代史梁紀) says:
"On the Dīnghài (丁亥) day,
Shīgǔ took Péngmén (彭門)
and presented Pǔ's head."
The Táng Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù (唐太祖紀年錄) says:
"In the fourth month,
Lǐ Hǎnhào (李罕之) of Zézhōu (澤州) reported: 'Defectors from Huáimèng (懷孟) report that Biàn general Páng Shīgǔ captured Xúzhōu on the eighth day of this month,
and Xú commander Shí Pǔ and his entire clan perished.'"
After Wēn (溫) took Xú (徐),
he fraudulently requested the imperial court to appoint a commander;
Zhaozōng (昭宗) then appointed Sūn Chǔ (孫儲), the Bīngbù Shàngshū (兵部尚書), as Xú commander,
but then Wēn dismissed him with other pretexts
and had his own general garrison it.
The eighth day of the fourth month
was probably an error in the news transmitted from Hédōng (河東).
Now we follow the Biānyí Lù (編遺錄) and Xīn Jì.
On the Jǐchǒu (己丑) day,
Quánzhōng entered Péngchéng (彭城),
appointed Zhāng Tíngfàn (張廷範), the Cìshǐ of Sòngzhōu (宋州), as Acting Gǎnhuà Liúhòu (感化留後),
and memorialized to request the imperial court to appoint a civilian as Jiédùshǐ (節度使).
13 Lǐ Kuāngwēi was in Zhènzhōu.
He completed the city walls and moats for Wáng Róng,
repaired the armor and weapons,
and treated him like a son.
Kuāngwēi, believing Róng to be young
and fond of the local customs of Zhēndìng,
secretly plotted to seize control.
Lǐ Bàozhēn, returning from the capital,
devised a strategy for him,
secretly winning over his generals and soldiers with favors.
The Wáng family had been in Zhèn for a long time,
and the people of Zhèn loved them,
not favoring Kuāngwēi.
On Kuāngwēi's忌日 (death anniversary),
Róng went to his residence to mourn.
The day one's parents die
is observed by a son as the 忌日.
The residence
was Lǐ Kuāngwēi's temporary lodging.
Ambushers seized him.
Róng quickly embraced Kuāngwēi and said:
"Róng is besieged by the Jìn people
and almost perished!"
"Jìn people"
refers to Lǐ Kèyòng's army from Hédōng.
pronounced jūyī fān.
"If you wish to obtain the four prefectures,
this is indeed Róng's desire."
Zhèn, Jì, Shēn, Zhào are the four prefectures.
"If I yield my position to you,
then the generals and soldiers will not resist you."
Kuāngwēi believed this to be true,
and rode side-by-side with Róng.
"駢馬" (piánmǎ),
means "side-by-side on horses."
Just then, there was a great wind, thunder, and rain,
and the roof tiles all shook.
Kuāngwēi entered the east side gate.
This was the east side gate of Zhènzhōu's Yáchéng (governor's headquarters).
As soon as he entered the gate, he was blocked by the Zhèn troops,
cutting off his reinforcements.
They punched and beat Kuāngwēi's armored guards,
seized Róng onto a horse,
and carried him up onto a roof.
Once the Zhèn people had Róng,
they attacked Kuāngwēi,
killed him,
and exterminated his clan and party.
The "Kǎoyì" (critical review) states: The "Shílù" (veritable records) says
Kuāngwēi was killed in the fifth month,
fearing the memorial arrived late.
The "Jiù Jì" (Old Annals) states:
"In the sixth month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
Lǐ Kuāngwēi of Yōuzhōu plotted to harm Wáng Róng.
The three armies of Héngzhōu attacked Kuāngwēi
and killed him."
The "Jiù Chuán" (Old Biographies) and "Táng Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù" (Chronicle of Emperor Tàizǔ of Táng) all say the fifth month.
The "Xīn Jì" (New Annals) says
the fourth month, on the day Dīnghài.
According to Kuāngchóu's memorial, it was the nineteenth day of the fourth month.
The first day of that month was Jǐsì.
The nineteenth day
was Dīnghài.
We follow this now.
His body was gaunt and thin.
When he was seized by Jūn Hé,
his neck was sore and his head was tilted for several days.
Lǐ Kuāngchóu memorialized that Róng had killed his elder brother,
requesting to raise troops to avenge the wrong;
the imperial edict did not permit it.
14 The Yōuzhōu general Liú Rēngōng led troops to garrison Wèizhōu.
They overstayed their replacement date,
and the soldiers longed to return home.
When Lǐ Kuāngchóu was established,
the garrison soldiers appointed Rēngōng as their commander,
and returned to attack Yōuzhōu.
Upon reaching Jūyōng Pass,
they were defeated by the garrison troops.
The "fǔbīng" (garrison troops)
were the army of the Yōuzhōu Jiédùshǐ.
"敗" (bài),
pronounced bùmài fān.
Lǐ Kèyòng treated him generously.
This laid the groundwork for Lǐ Kèyòng to seize Yōuzhōu.
15 Lǐ Shénfú besieged Lúzhōu;
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
Yáng Xíngmì personally led troops to Lúzhōu.
Tián Yún led his army from Xuānzhōu to join him.
Initially,
Zhāng Hào, a man from Càizhōu known for his bravery, served Qín Zōngquán.
Later he followed Sūn Rú.
After Rú's defeat,
he returned to Xíngmì.
Xíngmì treated him generously
and made him a general to garrison Lúzhōu.
Cài Chóu rebelled,
and Hào switched to serving him again.
When the siege became critical,
Hào climbed over the city wall and surrendered.
Xíngmì assigned him to Yuán Zhěn, the commander of the Yínqiāng Dū.
Zhěn, seeing Hào's perfidy,
reported to Xíngmì
and requested to kill him.
Xíngmì, fearing Zhěn would not tolerate him,
placed him in his personal army.
This laid the groundwork for Zhāng Hào to kill Yáng Wò.
He was a man from Chénzhōu.
16 Wáng Yànfù and Wáng Shěnzhī attacked Fúzhōu,
but it had not fallen for a long time.
In the second month of the previous year,
Wáng Cháo sent Yànfù and others to attack Fúzhōu.
In the third year of Zhōnghé of Emperor Xīzōng,
the Zhèdōng Guānchá (Observer of Eastern Zhè) was promoted to Yìshèng Jiédù;
in the third year of Guāngqǐ,
it was changed to Wēishèng Jiédù.
Five thousand troops from Wēn, Tái, and Wù Prefectures were dispatched to relieve it.
Yànfù and Shěnzhī, seeing the city was strong
and relief troops were about to arrive,
and with many casualties among their soldiers,
reported to Wáng Cháo,
wishing to withdraw the troops and plan for a future attempt.
Cháo did not permit it.
They requested Cháo to personally come to the encampment.
Cháo replied:
"If troops are exhausted, add more troops.
If generals are exhausted, add more generals.
If both troops and generals are exhausted,
I will come myself."
Yànfù and Shěnzhī were fearful,
and personally braved arrows and stones to launch an urgent assault.
In the fifth month,
the food in the city was exhausted.
Huī knew he could not hold out.
At night,
he handed over his seal to the supervising censor,
abandoned the city, and fled.
The relief troops also returned.
On the day Gēngzǐ,
Yànfù and others entered the city.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
Huī fled to Yánhǎi Dū,
where he was killed by his generals and soldiers.
In the second year of Wéndé,
Fàn Huī occupied Fúzhōu.
He proclaimed himself Liúhòu (acting military governor),
wore plain clothes to bury Chén Yán,
married his daughter to Chén Yán's son Yánhuì,
and generously supported his family.
Tīng and Jiàn Prefectures surrendered.
Over twenty groups of bandits in the Linghai region either surrendered or dispersed.
It means the bandits either surrendered or dispersed.
From this point, the Wáng family completely occupied the Seven Mǐn region.
"降" (jiàng),
pronounced hùjiāng fān.
17 In the intercalary month,
Qián Liú, the Wǔshèng Fángyùshǐ (Defense Commissioner of Wǔshèng), was made Sūháng Guāncháshǐ (Observer of Sū and Háng).
Qián Liú had united Háng and Sū,
hence this appointment.
Lǐ Chán, the Yàodé Dūtóu, was made Zhènhǎi Jūn Jiédùshǐ;
Sūn Wéishèng, the Xuānwēi Dūtóu, was made Jīngnán Jiédùshǐ.
Yàodé and Xuānwēi
were also among the fifty-two divisions of the Shéncè Army.
"黔" (qián),
pronounced qújīn fān.
"鋋" (chán),
pronounced chán.
Chén Pèi, the Pěngrì Dūtóu, was made Língnán Dōngdào Jiédùshǐ,
all with the concurrent title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
At that time, Lǐ Màozhēn was unruly.
The emperor, finding military officials difficult to control,
wished to replace them with imperial princes.
Therefore, Chéng and the other four were all granted favors,
relieved of their military authority,
and ordered to proceed to their garrisons.
Later, the four individuals were not heard to have reached their garrisons,
likely because each had their own territories to hold,
and the four were unable to proceed.
The "Kǎoyì" states: The "Jiù Jì" (Old Annals) says:
"In the third month, on the day Gēngzǐ,
Chén Pèi was made Língnán Dōngdào Jiédùshǐ,
Cáo Chéng was made Qiánzhōng Jiédùshǐ,
Lǐ Chán was made Zhènhǎi Jiédùshǐ,
and Sūn Wéishèng was made Jīngnán Jiédùshǐ.
At that time, the court deliberated that Màozhēn was arrogant and defied imperial orders,
and military officials were difficult to control,
so the power of the five generals was removed."
We now follow the "Shílù,"
which only mentions four generals.
18 Lǐ Kuāngchóu dispatched troops to attack Wáng Róng's Lèshòu and Wǔqiáng,
to avenge the disgrace of Kuāngwēi's death.
In the autumn of the 19th year [of Tiānfù 天復 (901 CE)],
in the seventh month,
Wáng Róng 王鎔 dispatched troops to relieve Xíngzhōu 邢州;
Lǐ Kèyòng 李克用 defeated them at Píngshān 平山.
On the day of Rénshēn 壬申,
he advanced to attack Zhènzhōu 鎮州.
Wáng Róng, in fear,
requested to contribute 200,000 units of provisions and soldiers to assist in attacking Xíngzhōu.
Lǐ Kèyòng agreed.
Lǐ Kèyòng organized his troops at Luánchéng 欒城,
and combining them with Wáng Róng's 30,000 soldiers, advanced to garrison Rènxuàn 任縣.
Rèn 任 [county]
was an ancient county in the Hàn 漢 dynasty,
but was later abolished.
The Rèn 任 of the Táng 唐 dynasty
was in the territory of Nánliánxiàn 南䜌縣 of the Hàn 漢 dynasty.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé 武德 (621 CE),
Rènxuàn 任縣 was established,
with its seat in Yuànxiāngchéng 苑鄉城,
southeast of Xíngzhōu.
Zhì 治,
pronounced like Zhí 直.
Liúlí Pī 琉璃陂 [“Glazed Bank”],
is within the borders of Lónggāngxiàn 龍岡縣, Xíngzhōu.
On the day of Dīnghài 丁亥,
Yáng Xíngmì 楊行密 captured Lúzhōu 廬州
and beheaded Cài Chóu 蔡儔.
His attendants requested to dig up Cài Chóu's parents' graves.
Yáng Xíngmì said:
"Cài Chóu incurred guilt by doing this;
why should I imitate him!"
Cài Chóu had dug up Yáng Xíngmì's grandfather's grave,
as mentioned in the previous year.
Lǐ Màozhuāng 李茂莊, Jìedùshǐ 節度使 of Tiānxíong 天雄, was
At this time, Qínzhōu 秦州 was called Tiānxíong Jūn 天雄軍.
Qián Liú 錢鏐 mobilized 200,000 civilian laborers and the soldiers of the Thirteen Dū 都 [commands] to build the outer wall of Hángzhōu 杭州,
which had a circumference of 70 *lǐ* 里.
Qián Liú started with the Eight Dū 都 soldiers;
later, his forces grew daily,
and he established Thirteen Dū 都.
The present outer wall of Hángzhōu
was built by Qián Liú.
Zhāng Xióng 張雄, Cìshǐ 刺史 of Shēngzhōu 昇州, died.
The *Kǎoyì* 考異 states: "According to the *Xīn Jì* 新紀, it was Gēngzǐ 庚子 of the eighth month,
likely the day the memorial arrived.
We now follow the *Shíguó Jìnián* 十國紀年."
Lǐ Màozhēn 李茂貞, presuming on his achievements, became arrogant and overbearing.
He submitted memorials to the throne and sent letters to Dù Ràngnéng 杜讓能,
using insolent language.
The emperor was enraged
and wished to subjugate him.
Lǐ Màozhēn again submitted a memorial,
which roughly stated:
"Your Majesty, though noble as the Lord of Ten Thousand Chariots,
could not protect the person of your maternal uncle;
the maternal uncle
refers to Wáng Huái 王頵,
whose affair is mentioned in the previous volume, Dàshùn 大順 second year.
Nor could you execute the mere underling Fùgōng 復恭."
It also said:
"Now the court merely observes strength and weakness,
without considering right and wrong."
It further said:
"Law is applied to the weak and infirm,
while favors are granted to the strong and vigorous."
Lǐ Màozhēn's memorial was indeed arrogant in its wording,
but the political reality of the time was indeed like this.
The saying "when dealing with things, if there is a *zīzhū* 錙銖 of weight,
it is treated with appropriate weight;
if there is a *zīzhū* of lightness,
it is treated with appropriate lightness" [refers to this].
Liú Jùn's 劉峻 *Guǎng Juéjiāolùn* 廣絕交論 states: "The steelyard is used to weigh lightness and heaviness;
the floss is used to ascertain the breath."
The commentary says: "This means operating a steelyard to weigh the lightness and heaviness of power,
and holding floss to measure the coarseness or fineness of breath."
"Military sentiment is easily swayed,
and war horses are difficult to restrain.
I only worry that the people of the royal domain
will suffer calamity because of this.
In ancient times, the kings
had a thousand *lǐ* square as their royal domain,
considering it their capital area.
Where will this lead from here!"
The emperor became even more enraged
and decided to subjugate Lǐ Màozhēn,
ordering Dù Ràngnéng to take sole charge of the matter.
Dù Ràngnéng remonstrated, saying:
"Your Majesty has just ascended the great throne,
and the nation's path is not yet peaceful.
Lǐ Màozhēn is close to the national gate;
according to the *Jiǔyù Zhì* 九域志, Fèngxiáng 鳳翔 is only 280 *lǐ* east of Cháng'ān 長安.
If by any chance we do not succeed,
regret will be futile."
The emperor said:
"The royal house grows weaker day by day,
and decrees do not pass beyond the national gate.
This is a time for men of ambition to be indignant and grieved.
'If the medicine does not cause dizziness and extreme discomfort,
the illness will not be cured.'
This is a quote from the *Shū* 書 (Book of Documents), *Yuè Mìng* 說命.
The commentary says: 'Just like taking medicine,
it must cause extreme dizziness and discomfort,
only then will the illness be removed.'
Míng 瞑,
pronounced like Mòbiàn 莫遍.
Xuàn 眩,
pronounced like Xuánbiàn 玄遍.
Míngxuàn 瞑眩 [means]
extreme discomfort.
To pass the days quietly
and idly watch decline
— [this is not acceptable].
You just arrange the military provisions for me,
and I will entrust the use of troops to the various princes.
I will not blame you for success or failure!"
Dù Ràngnéng said:
"If Your Majesty is determined to proceed,
then all ministers, both within and outside the court, should unite their efforts to achieve your holy will;
it should not be solely entrusted to me."
The emperor said:
"You hold the position of prime minister;
Dù Ràngnéng was then the prime minister.
You should not avoid this matter!"
Dù Ràngnéng wept and said:
"How dare I avoid the matter!
Moreover, what Your Majesty wishes to do
is the aspiration of Xiànzōng 憲宗;
but the time is not yet right,
and circumstances do not permit it.
I only fear that one day I will merely suffer the execution of Cháo Cuò 晁錯,
without being able to avert the calamity of the Seven States.
The affair of Cháo Cuò is found in the annals of Hàn Jǐngdì 漢景帝.
I will follow you unto death!"
Dù Ràngnéng already knew he was bound to die.
He planned and arranged affairs
for over a month without returning
to his private residence.
Diào 調,
pronounced like Túdiào 徒弔.
As his eyes and ears,
if Dù Ràngnéng uttered a word in court in the morning,
the two garrisons would surely know it by evening.
Lǐ Màozhēn instructed his partisans to gather several hundred to a thousand market people.
They surrounded Xīmén Jūnsuì 西門君遂, the Guānjūnrōngshǐ 觀軍容使, and appealed to him from horseback, saying:
"The Qí Commander
The Qí Commander
refers to Lǐ Màozhēn.
Fèngxiáng 鳳翔 was originally Qízhōu 岐州.
Shuài 帥,
pronounced like Suǒlèi 所類.
is without fault, yet he makes the common people suffer greatly."
Xīmén Jūnsuì said:
"This is a matter for the prime minister;
it is beyond my scope."
The market people then waylaid Cuī Zhāowěi 崔昭緯 and Zhèng Yánchāng 鄭延昌, appealing to them from their sedan chairs.
According to old regulations: when court officials entered court,
they all rode horses.
When the Sòng 宋 dynasty was displaced during the Jiànyán 建炎 era,
because the streets of Yángzhōu 揚州 were slippery,
court officials were first allowed to ride sedan chairs.
Observing this,
it seems that some prime ministers at the end of the Táng dynasty also rode sedan chairs.
"This matter has been solely entrusted to Dù Tàiwèi 杜太尉 by the sovereign;
we are not privy to it."
The market people then, in chaos, threw tiles and stones.
The two prime ministers dismounted their sedan chairs and fled to hide in commoners' homes,
barely escaping,
losing their official seals and court robes.
The emperor ordered the capture and execution of those who led the protest.
His resolve to use military force grew stronger.
Some people in the capital fled and hid in mountains and valleys,
which severe punishment could not prevent.
In the eighth month,
Sìzhōu 嗣周, the Prince of Tán (Tán Wáng 郯王), was appointed Jīngxī Zhāotǎoshǐ 京西招討使.
The *Kǎoyì* states: "According to records, Sùnzōng's 順宗 son was enfeoffed as Prince of Tán.
Sìzhōu must be his descendant.
After the Huìchāng 會昌 era,
to avoid the taboo name of Wǔzōng 武宗,
the character
'Tán' 郯
was changed to
'Tán' 覃."
However, Wǔzōng's taboo name was Chán 瀍,
later changed to Yán 炎.
If the *Kǎoyì* is correct,
then it was to avoid
the character 'Tán' 郯
because its radical was from
the character 'Yán' 炎.
On the 25th day, *bǐngchén* (丙辰),
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) sent Tián Yūn (田頵) to lead 20,000 Xuānzhōu (宣州) troops to attack Shèzhōu (歙州).
Pèi Shū (裴樞), the *cìshǐ* (刺史) of Shèzhōu, defended the city,
but it did not fall for a long time.
At that time, many generals who served as *cìshǐ* were greedy and tyrannical,
but Táo Yǎ (陶雅), the *tuánliàn shǐ* (團練使) of Chízhōu (池州), was generous and won the people's hearts.
The people of Shè (歙) said:
"If Táo Yǎ becomes our *cìshǐ*,
we will obey his command."
Xíngmì immediately appointed Yǎ as the *cìshǐ* of Shèzhōu,
and the people of Shè accepted him.
Yǎ treated Shū with full courtesy,
and sent him back to the court.
Shū
was the great-grandson of Pèi Zūnqìng (裴遵慶).
Pèi Zūnqìng is mentioned in volume 222 under the second year of Shàngyuán (上元) of Sùzōng (肅宗).
On the 26th day, Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) ordered Páng Shīgǔ (龐師古) to move his troops to attack Yǎnzhōu (兗州),
and fought Zhū Jǐn (朱瑾),
defeating him repeatedly.
In the ninth month,
on the day *dīngmǎo* (丁卯),
Qián Liú (錢鏐) was appointed *Zhènhǎi Jiédùshǐ* (鎮海節度使).
The title of *Wǔshèng Fángyùshǐ* (武勝防禦使) of Hángzhōu (杭州) was elevated to *Zhènhǎi Jiédùshǐ*.
The Táng (唐) court originally established the Zhènhǎi (鎮海) army in Rùnzhōu (潤州).
Now this title was bestowed upon Qián Liú in Hángzhōu.
In the first year of Guānghuà (光化),
Liú requested to move the army to Hángzhōu.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: In the fifth month of this year,
Lǐ Zhēn (李鋋) was appointed *Zhènhǎi Jiédùshǐ*,
and ordered to proceed to his post.
The reason for re-appointing Liú now is that,
at that time Ān Rényì (安仁義) had already occupied Rùnzhōu.
Furthermore, Sūn Wéishèng (孫惟晟) was appointed to Jīngnán (荊南),
but Chéng Ruì (成汭) had already occupied Jīngnán.
How could these two proceed to their posts?
It was merely to strip them of their military authority;
in reality, they did not reach their posts but returned.
The *Shílù* (實錄) states that
the Zhènhǎi (鎮海) army's designation was moved to Hángzhōu.
According to the *Wúyuè Bèishǐ* (吳越備史),
this year Liú was first appointed *Zhènhǎi Jiédùshǐ*,
still concurrently holding the position of *Rùnzhōu Cìshǐ*.
It was not until the first year of Guānghuà
that the Zhènhǎi army was moved to Hángzhōu.
The *Shílù* is mistaken.
On the 28th day, Lǐ Cúnxiào (李存孝) attacked Lǐ Cúnxìn's (李存信) camp at night,
and captured Sūn Kǎolǎo (孫考老), the *Fèngchéng Jūnshǐ* (奉誠軍使).
Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) personally led troops to attack Xíngzhōu (邢州),
digging trenches and building ramparts to encircle it.
Cúnxiào frequently launched sudden attacks on the trenches and ramparts,
but could not complete them.
Yuán Fèngtāo (袁奉韜), a staff officer from Hédōng (河東), secretly sent someone to tell Cúnxiào:
"His Royal Highness will return to Jìnyáng (晉陽) as soon as the trenches are completed.
The only one the *Shàngshū* (尚書) fears is His Royal Highness.
Lǐ Kèyòng was at that time enfeoffed as the Prince of Lǒngxī Commandery.
Cúnxiào was likely also a *Jiǎnjiào Shàngshū* (檢校尚書).
If Your Royal Highness returns,
how can a short distance of trenches
hinder the *Shàngshū*'s sharp vanguard?"
Cúnxiào thought this was true,
and held his troops, not attacking.
Ten days later,
the trenches and ramparts were completed,
making it impossible for anything to cross,
and Cúnxiào was thus trapped.
Dèng Jìyún (鄧季筠), a general from Biàn (汴), who was attacking Xíngzhōu with Kèyòng,
fled back with light cavalry.
Dèng Jìyún was captured,
as mentioned in the previous volume under the first year of Dàshùn (大順).
He was ordered to lead the imperial guards.
On the 29th day, *yǐhài* (乙亥),
Tán Wáng Sīzhōu (覃王嗣周) led 30,000 imperial guards to escort Xú Yànruò (徐彥若), the *Fèngxiáng Jiédùshǐ*, to his post,
encamping at Xīngpíng (興平).
Lǐ Màozhēn (李茂貞) and Wáng Xíngyú (王行瑜) combined their forces, nearly 60,000 men,
and encamped at Zhōuzhì (盩厔) to resist them.
The imperial guards were all newly recruited young men from the marketplace,
while Màozhēn and Xíngyú's troops were battle-hardened border soldiers.
On the day *rénwǔ* (壬午),
Màozhēn and others advanced and pressed Xīngpíng.
The imperial guards all fled at the mere sight of them.
Màozhēn and others, capitalizing on their victory, advanced to attack Sānqiáo (三橋).
The capital was greatly shaken,
and the gentry and common people scattered.
The market people again gathered at the palace gates to request the execution of those who first proposed the use of military force.
Cuī Zhāowěi (崔昭緯) harbored malice against Dù Ràngnéng (杜讓能), the *Tàiwèi* (太尉) and *Ménxià Shìláng Tóng Píngzhāngshì* (門下侍郎、同平章事),
and secretly sent a letter to Màozhēn, saying:
"The use of military force is not the emperor's intention;
it all originates from Grand Commandant Dù."
On the day *jiǎshēn* (甲申),
Màozhēn arrayed his forces at Língāo Yì (臨皋驛).
Língāo Yì
was west of Cháng'ān (長安) city.
He requested Dù's execution.
Ràngnéng said to the emperor:
"I have already said this before.
Please use me as the solution."
This meant attributing the blame to Ràngnéng to resolve the military conflict.
He said:
"I bid you farewell!"
On that day,
Ràngnéng was demoted to *Wúzhōu Cìshǐ* (梧州刺史).
Wúzhōu was 5,500 *lǐ* (里) from the capital.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Emperor Wǔ (武) of Hàn (漢) established Cāngwú (蒼梧) Commandery,
administering Guǎngxìn (廣信) County;
the Suí (隋) dynasty established Cāngwú Commandery,
administering Cāngwú County;
the Táng dynasty made it Wúzhōu.
"Discarding the good counsel of your officials,
and creating deep rifts with your vassals,
during the consultation,
the evidence remained firm."
Furthermore, Xīmén Jūnsuì (西門君遂), the *Guānjūnshǐ* (觀軍使), was exiled to Dānzhōu (儋州);
Lǐ Zhōutóng (李周潼), the *Nèi Shūmìshǐ* (內樞密使), to Yázhōu (崖州);
and Duàn Xǔ (段詡) to Huānzhōu (驩州).
On the day *yǐyǒu* (乙酉),
the emperor ascended the Ānfú Mén (安福門),
and executed Jūnsuì, Zhōutóng, and Xǔ.
Ràngnéng was further demoted to *Léizhōu Sīhù* (雷州司戶).
An envoy was sent to Màozhēn, saying:
"The three men who misled Us into raising troops
are these three;
it is not Ràngnéng's fault."
The eunuchs Luò Quánguàn (駱全瓘) and Liú Jǐngxuān (劉景宣) were appointed Left and Right Commanders of the Imperial Guards.
On the day *rénchén* (壬辰),
Wéi Zhāodù (韋昭度), the *Dōngdū Liúshǒu* (東都留守), was appointed *Sītú* (司徒) and *Ménxià Shìláng Tóng Píngzhāngshì*;
Cuī Yìn (崔胤), the *Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng* (御史中丞), was appointed *Hùbù Shìláng Tóng Píngzhāngshì*.
Yìn
