was the son of Shènyóu (慎由).
Cuī Shènyóu (崔慎由) served Emperors Wén (文), Wǔ (武), and Xuān (宣),
and was a prime minister during the Dàzhōng (大中) period.
He was deeply allied with Cuī Zhāowěi,
and thus obtained the position of prime minister.
His uncle Ānqián (安潛) said to his close associates:
"Our father and elder brother toiled to establish our family,
only to have it ruined by this 'black lad'!"
"Black lad"
was Yìn's nickname.
Lǐ Mào-zhēn (李茂-貞) held his troops and did not withdraw.
He requested that Dù Ràng-néng (杜讓-能) be executed before he would return to his garrison.
Cuī Zhāo-wěi (崔昭-緯) again sided with him to incriminate Dù Ràng-néng (杜讓-能).
In winter,
in the tenth month,
Ràng-néng (讓-能) and his younger brother, Hùbù Shìláng (戶部侍郎) Hóng-huī (弘-徽), were granted death by suicide.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The *Xù Bǎoyùn Lù* (續寶運錄) says:
"In the second year of Dàshùn (大順)
Prime Ministers Dù Ràng-néng (杜讓-能) and Kǒng Wěi (孔-緯) observed that the imperial capital frequently suffered from disorder and chaos,
and the court administration was in disarray.
At this time, following the wishes of the various circuits,
the imperial guard troops numbered fifty-four *dū* (都),
filling every barracks.
Additionally, the neighboring regional commanders,
desiring to conduct punitive expeditions,
would directly command their own armies.
As for Lǐ Mào-zhēn (李茂-貞) of Qíyáng (岐-陽),
the previous emperor had enfeoffed him as Tàizǐ (太-子).
His original surname was Sòng (宋),
a governor of Yángzhōu (洋-州).
His ancestor had gained merit by suppressing Liú Cóng-jiàn (劉從-諫) of Zhāo-yì (昭-義),
and his descendants continuously received titles and rewards.
After King Shòu (壽) ascended the throne,
he dispatched Lǐbù Shìláng (禮部侍郎) Xuē Tíng-guī (薛廷-珪) with a sealed letter and full ceremonial rites,
to enfeoff him as Qí Wáng (岐-王).
Mào-zhēn (茂-貞) had, during the Zhōnghé (中和) era [881-885],
submitted to Tián Lìng-zī (田令-孜), the commissioner of military affairs, becoming his adopted son,
named Tián Yàn-bīn (田彥-賓).
This was presumably to curry favor with his power.
Zhū Wēn (朱-溫) of Biànzhōu (汴-州) was enfeoffed as Dōngpíng Wáng (東平王) by the previous emperor.
Up to the present emperor,
Xuē Tíng-guī (薛廷-珪) was again dispatched as the master of ceremonies,
and Yán Wáng (延-王) as the envoy for conferment,
to enfeoff him as Liáng Wáng (梁-王).
Furthermore, as Qí Wáng (岐-王) and the Northern Bureau [eunuchs]
were on very friendly terms,
the prime ministers were very much at odds.
They repeatedly submitted memorials saying: 'Your minister is now stationed in Xiányáng (咸-陽),
and dares not enter the Zhongshu to question their crimes.
Dù Ràng-néng (杜讓-néng) and others should be subjected to the ultimate penalty.'
When the memorial was presented,
the emperor was displeased.
He then issued an edict commanding Prime Ministers Kǒng (孔) and Dù (杜) to go to Xiányáng (咸-陽) to apologize.
When the two prime ministers arrived in Xiányáng (咸-陽) and met Qí Wáng (岐-王),
they trembled and could not speak.
Qí Wáng (岐-王) was furious,
and ordered them to return to the Zhongshu Province to reflect on their mistakes.
No sooner had they arrived at Zhongshu
than the emperor again dispatched them,
ordering them to plead for Qí Wáng's (岐-王) forgiveness.
This back and forth occurred three times.
Qí Wáng (岐-王) then memorialized again, saying: 'When the two prime ministers met your minister,
they did not utter a single word.
Such neglect of duty disgraces the sacred reign.
I request that the court regulations be applied,
and other worthy and virtuous individuals be selected.'
The emperor was displeased.
An imperial edict was issued to dismiss them from managing political affairs.
As a last resort, Kǒng Wěi (孔-緯) was made Jīngnán Jiédù (荊-南節度),
and Dù Ràng-néng (杜讓-néng) was made Hézhōng Jiédù (河-中節度).
Three days later,
they were demoted to Lǐngbiǎo (嶺-表).
Thirty *lǐ* (里) outside the capital gate,
both were granted death by suicide.
At that time, Qí Wáng (岐-王) led five thousand elite soldiers and resided in Xiányáng (咸-陽).
After the two prime ministers were demoted,
he withdrew."
These are all erroneous accounts.
We now follow the *Shílù* (實錄).
It states,
"Ràng-néng (讓-néng) promoted the crooked and put aside the upright,"
using Confucius's words from the *Lúnyǔ* (論-語),
meaning to promote the crooked
and set aside and not employ the upright.
In an era of decline and chaos,
how could there be public right and wrong?
*Cuò* (錯),
pronounced *qiān gù fān* (千故翻).
"They trafficked in justice and sold offices,
accumulating wealth exceeding tens of millions."
From then on, all court actions and decisions were submitted to Bīn (邠) and Qí (岐).
The Southern and Northern Bureaus (Nán Běi Sī) (南-北司) often attached themselves to these two garrisons to seek favors.
There were Cuī Chán (崔-鋋) and Wáng Chāo (王-超),
who served as *Pànguān* (判-官) for the two garrisons.
Whenever the Son of Heaven approved or disapproved of something,
those who were displeased
would immediately appeal to Chán (鋋) or Chāo (超).
These two would then instruct Mào-zhēn (茂-貞) and Xíng-yú (行-瑜) to submit memorials to argue against it.
If the court hesitated even slightly,
their language would already be disrespectful.
An imperial edict was issued to reinstate Mào-zhēn (茂-貞) as Fèngxiáng Jiédùshǐ (鳳-翔節度使) and concurrently Shānnán Xīdào Jiédùshǐ (山-南西道節度使) and Shǒu Zhōngshū Lìng (守中書令).
Thereupon, Mào-zhēn (茂-貞) gained complete control over Fèngxiáng (鳳-翔), Xīngyuán (興-元), Yáng (洋), Lǒng (隴), Qín (秦), and fifteen other prefectures.
Fèngxiáng (鳳-翔) was originally one garrison,
Xīngyuán (興-元) and Shānnán Xīdào (山-南西道) another,
Yángzhōu Wǔdìngjūn (洋-州武定軍) another,
and Qínlǒng Tiānxíongjūn (秦-隴天雄軍) another.
Historians say Lǐ Mào-zhēn (李茂-貞) simultaneously controlled four garrisons.
On the 30th (Wùxū 戊-戌),
Wáng Cháo (王-潮), the Prefect of Quánzhōu (泉-州), was appointed Fújiàn Guānchásǐ (福-建觀察使).
On the 31st, Ní Zhāng (倪-章), the Prefect of Shūzhōu (舒-州), abandoned the city and fled.
Ní Zhāng (倪-章) and Cài Chóu (蔡-儔) had allied their forces.
Chóu (儔) had already been defeated,
hence Zhāng (章) fled.
On the 32nd, Wáng Xíng-yú (王-行瑜), the Bīnníng Jiédùshǐ (邠-寧節度使), Shǒu Shìzhōng (守侍中), and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令), requested to be appointed Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令).
Wéi Zhāo-dù (韋昭-度) secretly memorialized:
"Tàizōng (太-宗), by holding the position of Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) and managing state affairs,
eventually ascended to the throne.
Since then, it has not been granted to a subject.
Only Guō Zǐ-yí (郭子-儀), due to his great achievements, was appointed Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令),
yet he avoided and yielded it his whole life.
How can Xíng-yú (行-瑜) lightly discuss it!"
In the eleventh month,
Xíng-yú (行-瑜) was appointed Tàishī (太-師),
granted the title Shàngfù (尚-父),
and also given an iron certificate.
On the 33rd, in the twelfth month,
Zhū Quán-zhōng (朱全-忠) requested to move the Salt and Iron Bureau to Biànzhōu (汴-州) to facilitate military supply.
Cuī Zhāo-wěi (崔昭-緯) believed that Quán-zhōng (全-忠), having recently defeated Xú (徐) and Yùn (鄆),
had doubled his military strength.
If he were to also control the Salt and Iron Bureau,
he would become uncontrollable.
So, an imperial edict was issued to explain and admonish him.
On the 34th, Biàn (汴) general Gě Cóng-zhōu (葛從-周) attacked Zhū Wēi (朱-威), the Prefect of Qízhōu (齊-州).
Zhū Xuān (朱-瑄) and Zhū Jǐn (朱-瑾) led their troops to rescue him.
According to the *Fāngzhèn Biǎo* (方鎮表),
Qízhōu (齊-州) at that time belonged to the Pínglú Jiédù (平-盧節度).
Judging from the incident of Zhū Qióng (朱-瓊) surrendering to Biàn (汴) in the third year of Qiánníng (乾-寧)
Qízhōu (齊-州) had already been annexed by Yǎn (兗) and Yùn (鄆).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The *Biān Yílù* (編遺錄) records the tenth month, *Yǐwèi* (乙-未).
We now follow Xuē Jū-zhèng's (薛居-正) *Wǔdài Shǐ* (五-代史), *Liáng Jì* (梁-紀).
On the 35th, initially,
Zhōu Yuè (周-岳), the Wǔ'ān Jiédùshǐ (武-安節度使), killed Mǐn Xù (閔-勗),
and occupied Tánzhōu (潭-州).
See volume 256, second year of Xīzōng (僖-宗) Guāngqǐ (光-啟)
When the generals came to mourn,
Dèng Chù-nà (鄧處-訥) said:
"I and you gentlemen all received great kindness from *Púyè* (僕-射).
Mǐn Xù (閔-勗) was *Jiǎnjiào Shàngshū Yòupúyè* (檢校尚書右僕射) and Qīnhuà Jiédùshǐ (欽-化節度使).
He appointed Chù-nà (處-訥) as Prefect of Shàozhōu (邵-州),
hence the mention of receiving kindness.
Lù Zhèn's (路-振) *Jiǔ Guó Zhì* (九國志) states:
Dèng Chù-nà (鄧處-訥), from the Qiánfú (乾-符) era [874-879] of the Tang,
followed Mǐn Xù (閔-勗) in conquering barbarians in Ānnán (安-南).
Xù (勗) became the commander of Tán (潭),
and appointed Chù-nà (處-訥) as *Bīngmǎ Liúhòu* (兵馬留後) of Shàozhōu (邵-州).
*Chù* (處),
pronounced *chāng lǚ fān* (昌呂翻).
I wish, with you gentlemen, to exert the full strength of one prefecture
to avenge *Púyè* (僕-射).
Is this acceptable?"
They all replied:
"Excellent!"
Thereupon, he trained his troops and sharpened his weapons.
Eight years later,
he allied with Léi Mǎn (雷-滿), the Prefect of Lángzhōu (朗-州).
Léi Mǎn (雷-滿) and Zhōu Yuè (周-岳) had a grudge over a piece of meat.
They conquered the city,
beheaded Yuè (岳),
and Chù-nà (處-訥) declared himself *Liúhòu* (留-後).
No sooner had Dèng Chù-nà (鄧處-訥) obtained Tánzhōu (潭-州)
than Liú Jiàn-fēng (劉建-鋒) and Mǎ Yīn (馬-殷) were already planning their move.
First year of Qiánníng (乾-寧)
(*Jiǎyín* 甲-寅, 894)
In spring,
the first month,
on the day *Yǐchǒu* (乙-丑), the first day of the month,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed.
Lǐ Mào-zhēn (李茂-貞) came to court,
displayed a large military escort for his protection, and returned to his garrison after several days.
Lǐ Kuāng-chóu (李匡-籌) was appointed Lúlóng Jiédùshǐ (盧-龍節度使).
In the second month, Zhū Quán-zhōng (朱全-忠) personally led an attack on Zhū Xuān's (朱-瑄) army at Yúshān (魚-山).
Yúshān (魚-山) is located between Xūchāng (須-昌) and Dōng'ē (東-阿) counties in Yùnzhōu (鄆-州).
The armies of Yǎn (兗) and Yùn (鄆) suffered a great defeat,
with over ten thousand dead.
5 Zhèng Qǐng, who was Right Attendant Censor (Yòusànqí Chángshì), was appointed Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shìláng) and Grand Councilor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì).
Qǐng was fond of humor
and often composed 'riddle-ending' poems (xiēhòu shī),
satirizing current affairs.
'Riddle-ending' meant
stating the context for the poem, but leaving the riddle's answer unsaid.
He personally noted on the official roster,
"Appointed to be a prime minister."
The official roster (bānbù)
listed the names of those at court.
A hall official went to inform him.
Qǐng laughed and said,
"Gentlemen, you've made a great mistake!
Even if there were no other people in the world,
it would not yet be Zhèng Qǐng!"
The official said,
"This is a special imperial decree."
Qǐng said,
"If that is truly the case,
what can be done about people laughing?"
Soon after, congratulatory guests arrived.
Qǐng scratched his head and said,
"Riddle-ending Zhèng Wǔ becomes prime minister!"
Zhèng Qǐng was the fifth in his generation,
and because he composed xiēhòu poems,
his style was then called 'Riddle-ending Zhèng Wǔ style' (xiēhòu Zhèng Wǔ tǐ).
He repeatedly declined but was not permitted to refuse,
so he assumed his duties.
6 Dèng Chùnà, the Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Shàozhōu, was appointed Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Wǔ'ān.
7 Zhāng Jūn, the Military Governor of Zhāngyì, died.
He submitted a memorial requesting his elder brother, Zhāng Pán, be appointed Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu).
At that time, Jīngzhōu was under the Zhāngyì Military Governorship.
Pán's
courtesy name was Yuánfān.
8 In the third month,
Wú Tǎo, the Inspector of Huángzhōu, surrendered the entire prefecture to Yáng Xíngmì.
Huángzhōu was then subordinate to È'yuè,
and È'yuè
was the Wǔchāng Army (Wǔchāngjūn).
According to the New History of the Five Dynasties, Dù Hóng's Biography,
Wú Tǎo
was a commoner from Yǒngxīng County (Yǒngxīngxiàn), Èzhōu,
who rose as a leader of local militia
and occupied Huángzhōu.
9 Food in Xíngzhōu city was exhausted.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
Lǐ Cúnxiào ascended the city wall and said to Lǐ Kèyòng,
"Your son, by your royal grace, has attained wealth and honor.
If not for being troubled by slanderous villains,
how could I abandon our father-son relationship and follow enemies?
I wish to see Your Majesty once;
I will have no regrets even in death!"
Kèyòng sent Lady Liú to see him.
Lady Liú led Cúnxiào out to meet Kèyòng.
Cúnxiào prostrated himself, bowing his head to the ground, and begged forgiveness, saying,
"Your son, though he performed minor services,
Lǐ Cúnxìn pressured me,
leading to this misguided situation!"
Kèyòng shouted at him,
"You sent letters to Zhū Quánzhōng and Wáng Róng,
slandering me in a thousand ways.
Did Cúnxìn teach you that too?"
He was imprisoned,
taken back to Jìnyáng,
and torn apart by chariots at the gateway (yámén).
The "Kǎoyì" (Examination of Differences) states: The "Tàizǔ Jìniánlù" (Chronicle of Emperor Tàizǔ's Reign) records:
"Earlier, the Biàn generals Dèng Yún and Ānkāng Bā, the military officer Liú ǔzi, and the court official Hán Guīfàn, who was captured in Lùzhōu, were all implicated with Cúnxiào
and executed on the same day.
The cavalry general Xuē Ātán, in fear,
committed suicide."
According to the Old History,
Kèyòng captured Guīfàn,
but soon sent him back.
Guīfàn then attached a memorial appealing his innocence,
and there is no mention of him returning to Jìnyáng.
Xuē Jūzhèng's "Wǔdài Shǐ" (History of the Five Dynasties), in Dèng Jìyún's Biography, states
that he later escaped from Xíngzhōu back to Biàn.
The "Jìniánlù" is mistaken.
Cúnxiào's Biography states:
"When Martial Emperor (Wǔhuáng) exited Jǐngxíng [Pass],
intending to press on Zhēndìng,
Cúnxiào personally met Wáng Róng
and divulged military secrets.
Martial Emperor was furious
and only executed the previously captured Biàn general Ānkāng Bā."
No one in Kèyòng's army could match him.
He always led cavalry as the vanguard,
invincible wherever he went.
Donning heavy armor,
with a bow at his waist and a spear at his thigh,
he alone wielded an iron mace, breaking through enemy formations,
causing tens of thousands to recoil.
He always had two horses with him;
when one horse tired slightly,
meaning the horse was somewhat fatigued and lacked strength,
he would switch, moving like a blur.
Kèyòng valued his talent,
expecting that at his execution, the generals would surely plead for him,
and thus he would release him.
However, the generals were jealous of his ability,
and not a single person spoke up.
After his death,
Kèyòng ceased to attend to affairs for ten days.
He secretly resented the generals,
but did not condemn Lǐ Cúnxìn at all.
There was also Xuē Ātán,
whose bravery was comparable to Cúnxiào's.
The generals were jealous of him,
and he often felt frustrated.
He secretly communicated with Cúnxiào.
When Cúnxiào was executed,
fearing exposure,
he committed suicide.
From then on, Kèyòng's military strength gradually weakened,
while Zhū Quánzhōng alone prospered.
History states that Kèyòng, by clipping his own wings,
thus failed to compete successfully with Biàn.
10 Zhū Quánzhōng sent the military general Zhāng Cónghuì to soothe and appease Shòuzhōu.
Cónghuì insulted the Inspector Jiāng Yànwēn and drank with other generals at night.
Yànwēn suspected they were plotting against him.
The next day,
he executed all the generals present at the banquet,
then wrote a letter apologizing to Quánzhōng and committed suicide.
The army acclaimed his son, Jiāng Cóngxù, to manage military and prefectural affairs.
Quánzhōng had Cónghuì cut in half at the waist.
11 In the fifth month,
Qián Liú, the Military Governor of Zhènhǎi, was promoted to Grand Councilor.
12 Liú Jiànfēng and Mǎ Yīn led their troops to Lǐlíng.
The character '澧' (Lǐ)
should be
Lǐlíng was located within the borders of Hàn's Línxiāng County (Línxiāngxiàn).
In the Later Hàn, it was divided to form Lǐlíng County (Lǐlíngxiàn),
but it was abolished during the Suí dynasty.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé,
Lǐlíng County was established by dividing Chángshā
and belonged to Tánzhōu.
The "Jiǔyù Zhì" (Records of the Nine Regions) states: It is one hundred and sixty lǐ east of the prefecture.
Mǎ Yīn arrived at the pass first.
He sent an envoy to Jiǎng Xūn,
and Xūn and others rewarded the troops with oxen and wine.
Mǎ Yīn's envoy persuaded Xūn, saying,
"Liú Xiáng possesses both wisdom and bravery.
Looking at the later account, Yáo Yànzhāng said to Mǎ Yīn,
'You and Liú Lóngxiáng are of one body,'
this must have omitted the character
'龍' (lóng).
'Shuō' (說)
is pronounced 'Shì Ruì' (式芮).
Yì (翼) and Zhěn (軫) were divisions of Chǔ's Jīngzhōu.
Chángshā entered the sixteenth degree of Zhěn.
His elite forces are invincible.
For you to resist him with a few thousand local troops (xiāngbīng)
will be difficult.
According to the New History,
Jiǎng Xūn and Dèng Jìchóng were both local strongmen (tǔháo) of Shàozhōu.
The soldiers they led were all local people,
hence they were called local troops.
It would be good for you to gain wealth and honor
and return to your hometown, wouldn't it?"
Xūn and the others agreed
and told their subordinates,
"The eastern army has promised to let us return."
Liú Jiànfēng and other troops came from the east,
so Jiǎng Xūn and others called them the 'eastern army' (dōngbīng).
They abandoned their banners, armor, and weapons and fled.
Jiànfēng ordered his vanguard to wear their armor,
display their banners,
and rush to Tánzhōu.
The people of Tánzhōu thought the Shàozhōu troops had returned
and made no preparations.
Jiànfēng entered the prefectural office directly.
Dèng Chùnà was still feasting,
and he was captured and executed.
On the day Wùchén,
Jiànfēng entered Tánzhōu
and declared himself Acting Military Governor.
13 Wáng Jiàn (王建) attacked Péngzhōu (彭州).
People in the city resorted to cannibalism.
Zhào Zhāng (趙章), commander of the inner and outer forces of Péngzhōu (彭州), surrendered.
Wáng Xiānchéng (王先成) requested the construction of a Lóngwěi Dào (龍尾道).
It was attached to the Nǚqiáng (女牆).
A sloping ramp was built from outside the city,
winding upwards,
attached to the short wall on top of the city.
The front of this path was high and the back was low,
with the back sinking into the ground,
resembling a dragon's drooping tail.
Hence it was called Lóngwěi Dào (龍尾道).
屬 (shǔ),
to be read as yù (欲).
Nǚqiáng (女牆)
is the short wall on top of a city,
what is called Pí (陴).
On the day of Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
the Xīchuān (西川) troops scaled the city wall.
Yáng Shèng (楊晟) still led his forces in a fierce battle,
but the Knife Troop Commander Wáng Màoquán (王茂權) slew him.
In the first year of Wéndé (文德),
Yáng Shèng (楊晟) acquired Péngzhōu (彭州).
Wáng Jiàn (王建) attacked Péngzhōu (彭州),
and only captured it after more than two periods,
he was also exhausted.
Jiàn (建) wished to make Shī Jiàn (師建) a general.
Shī Jiàn (師建) wept and declined, saying:
"Shī Jiàn (師建) swore to live and die with Sītú Yáng (司徒楊).
I cannot bear to face the sun and moon again.
Only a quick death would be a kindness."
He was urged repeatedly,
but he would not comply,
so he was killed,
but given a respectful burial and sacrifice.
Zhào Zhāng's (趙章) name was changed to Wáng Zōngmiǎn (王宗勉),
Wáng Màoquán's (王茂權) name was changed to Zōngxùn (宗訓),
and Wáng Zhāo's (王釗) name was changed to Zōngjǐn (宗謹),
Lǐ Wǎn's (李綰) name was changed to Wáng Zōngwǎn (王宗綰).
14 On the day of Xīnmǎo (辛卯),
Zhèng Yánchāng (鄭延昌), Minister of the Secretariat and concurrently Grand Chancellor, was dismissed and made Right Executive Assistant.
15 Zhū Xuān (朱瑄) and Zhū Jǐn (朱瑾) sought help from Hédōng (河東).
Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) dispatched cavalry generals Ān Fúshùn (安福順) and his younger brothers Fúqìng (福慶) and Fúqiān (福遷) to lead five hundred elite cavalry troops, borrowing a path through Wèi (魏),
to cross the river and assist them.
16 Dù Hóng (杜洪), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Wǔchāng (武昌), attacked Huángzhōu (黃州),
because Wú (吳) had rebelled and allied itself with Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密).
17 In the sixth month,
on the day of Jiǎwǔ (甲午),
Zhāng Tíngfàn (張廷範), Prefect of Sòngzhōu (宋州), was made Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Wǔníng (武寧),
in accordance with Zhū Quánzhōng's (朱全忠) request.
Xúzhōu (徐州) had previously been renamed Gǎnhuà Jūn (感化軍).
After it came under Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠),
it was restored to Wǔníng Jūn (武寧軍).
18 Fēng Jìngzhāng (馮敬章), Prefect of Qízhōu (蘄州), ambushed the Huáinán (淮南) army.
Zhū Yánshòu (朱延壽) attacked Qízhōu (蘄州),
but failed to capture it.
Qízhōu (蘄州)
was subordinate to Wǔchāng (武昌) in its jurisdiction.
19 On the day of Wùwǔ (戊午),
Lǐ Xī (李谿), Academician-in-waiting, Minister of Rites, was made concurrently Grand Chancellor.
As the imperial edict was being proclaimed,
Liú Chónglǔ (劉崇魯), Director of the Waterways Bureau and Compiler of Edicts, stepped forward, seized the proclamation, and wept loudly.
強 (qiáng) 奪 (duó) 取 (qǔ) 之 (zhī) 為 (wéi) 掠 (lüè).
When asked the reason,
he replied:
"Xī (谿) is corrupt and evil,
clinging to Yáng Fùgōng (楊復恭) and Xīmén Jūnsuì (西門君遂),
thus he managed to be in the Hanlin Academy.
He has no capacity for grand statesmanship,
and I fear he will endanger the nation."
Xī (谿) was ultimately dismissed and made Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince.
Xī (谿)
was the grandson of Yōng (鄘).
Lǐ Yōng (李鄘) is mentioned in the biography of Xiànzōng (憲宗).
Cuī Zhāowěi (崔昭緯) feared that Xī (谿) would become chancellor
and diminish his own power,
so he had Chónglǔ (崇魯) obstruct him.
Xī (谿) submitted ten memorials to defend himself,
vilely slandering:
"Chónglǔ's (崇魯) father, Fú (符), accepted bribes and perverted the law.
When the matter was discovered, he committed suicide.
His younger brother, Chóngwàng (崇望), had deep connections with Yáng Fùgōng (楊復恭).
Chónglǔ (崇魯) bowed before Tián Lìngzī (田令孜) in the court
and drafted a memorial urging the enthronement of Zhū Méi (朱玫).
Yet he claims that I colluded with inner court officials!
How is this different from embracing stolen goods and crying 'thief!'?
Moreover, according to custom,
coarse silk turbans and mournful sashes
are not allowed into the forbidden palace.
Gěnjīn (絁巾)
means silk turban.
Cǎn (慘) means light-colored.
Shī (絁),
read as zhī (支) in 式 (shì) 支 (zhī) fanqie.
Chónglǔ (崇魯) should have submitted a memorial to argue his points,
how could he weep loudly in the main hall?
Under 豈 (qǐ)
there should be
宜 (yí)
or
當 (dāng)
for the meaning of the sentence to be clear.
He has no manners befitting a subject,
I request that his crime be punished."
An imperial edict suspended Chónglǔ (崇lǔ) from his current post.
Xī (谿) continued to submit memorials incessantly,
requesting that Chónglǔ (崇lǔ) be executed or exiled.
His memorials contained thousands of words,
with no insult left unsaid.
20 Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) heavily defeated the Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾),
killed Hèlián Duó (赫連鐸), and
captured Bái Yìchéng (白義誠).
The "Kǎo Yì" (考異) says: The old records state:
"In the sixth month, on the day of Rénchén (壬辰),
Kèyòng (克用) attacked and captured Yúnzhōu (雲州),
seized Hèlián Duó (赫連鐸),
and put Xuē Zhìqín (薛志勤) in charge of Yúnzhōng (雲中)."
According to the "Táng Tàizǔ Jìniánlù" (唐太祖紀年錄), "Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn" (莊宗列傳), and Xuē Jūzhèng's (薛居正) "Wǔdài Shǐ Wǔhuáng Jì" (五代史武皇紀), all state that
in the second year of Dàshùn (大順),
Wǔhuáng (武皇) captured Yúnzhōu (雲州),
and Duó (鐸) fled to Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾).
This is an error.
The new record states:
"In the sixth month,
Hèlián Duó (赫連鐸) fought Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) in Yúnzhōu (雲州)
and died there."
The "Tàizǔ Jìniánlù" (太祖紀年錄) says:
"In the tenth month,
when attacking Lǐ Kuāngchóu (李匡籌),
the army reached Xīnchéng (新城),
and many border soldiers wished to join.
Hèlián Duó (赫連鐸) and Bái Yìchéng (白義誠) had suffered numerous defeats,
and by this time were in dire straits with nowhere to go.
They tied themselves up and crawled on their knees
to the military gate.
Tàizǔ (太祖) lightly enumerated their crimes,
ordered them to be whipped, and then released them."
Xuē Shǐ (薛史) "Wǔhuáng Jì" (武皇紀) and "Tǔyùhún Zhuàn" (吐谷渾傳) also state
"Duó (鐸) and others surrendered,
and were ordered to be whipped and then released."
"Xuē Zhìqín Zhuàn" (薛志qín 傳) says:
"Wáng Huī (王暉) occupied Yúnzhōu (雲州) and rebelled.
He was pacified,
and Zhìqín (志qín) was made Dàtóng (大同) Defense Commissioner."
This differs from the old records.
The "Táng Mò Jiànwénlù" (唐末見聞錄) says:
"In the sixth month,
Yúnzhōu (雲州) was recovered,
Hèlián Duó (赫連鐸) was dealt with,
Bái Yìchéng (白義誠) was captured alive,
and the army advanced to the Yōuzhōu (幽州) border before returning to the capital after inspection."
The new record is based on this.
We now follow it.
21 In autumn,
seventh month,
Lǐ Màozhēn (李茂貞) dispatched troops to attack Làngzhōu (閬州),
capturing it.
Yáng Fùgōng (楊復恭), Yáng Shǒuliàng (楊守亮), and Yáng Shǒuxìn (楊守信) led their clan members to break through the siege and flee.
Yáng Fùgōng (楊復恭) and others fled to Làngzhōu (閬州),
as seen in Jǐngfú (景福) first year.
帥 (shuài),
read as lǜ (率).
22 Zhèng Qíng (鄭綮), Minister of Rites and concurrently Grand Chancellor, feeling that he did not meet public expectations,
repeatedly submitted memorials to resign his post.
An imperial edict granted him retirement as Junior Guardian to the Crown Prince.
Xú Yànruò (徐彥若), Grand Censor, was made Minister of the Secretariat, concurrently Minister of Personnel, and Grand Chancellor.
23 Yáng Shǒuhòu (楊守厚), Prefect of Miánzhōu (綿州), died.
His general Cháng Zàiróng (常再榮) surrendered the city to Wáng Jiàn (王建).
24 Yáng Fùgōng (楊復恭), Shǒuliàng (守亮), and Shǒuxìn (守信) were about to flee from Shāngshān (商山) to Hédōng (河東).
When they reached Qiányuán (乾元),
in the first year of Wànsuì Tōngtiān (萬歲通天), Ānyè Xiàn (安業縣) was established by dividing Fēngyáng (豐陽) in Shāngzhōu (商州).
In the first year of Qiányuán (乾元),
it was renamed Qiányuán Xiàn (乾元縣)
and belonged to Shāngzhōu (商州).
They were captured.
In the eighth month,
Hán Jiàn (韓建) presented them below the palace gate,
where they were executed at Dúliǔ (獨柳).
Fùgōng (復恭) and his sons were wiped out by this time.
The reason for his retirement
was stated as:
"Chéngtiānmén (承天門) was the old property of the Suí (隋) dynasty.
Chéngtiānmén (承天門) was the south gate of the Tàijí (太極) Palace in Cháng'ān (長安),
built by Yǔwén Kǎi (宇文愷) at the command of Emperor Wéndì (文帝) of Suí (隋).
It was originally named Zhāoyángmén (昭陽門).
The Táng (唐) dynasty renamed it Chéngtiānmén (承天門),
hence Fùgōng (復恭) said so.
Do not present offerings."
Shǒuliàng (守亮)
was Fùguāng's (復光) adopted son,
so he was called his nephew.
The emperor had originally enfeoffed Shòu Wáng (壽王).
To depose the old statesman who established the succession,
there is such an ungrateful disciple-emperor!
Kāng Jūnlì, Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì, went to Jìnyáng to pay respects to Lǐ Kèyòng.
On the *jǐwèi* day,
Kèyòng gathered his generals for a drinking and gambling session.
In the heat of the wine,
Kèyòng spoke of Lǐ Cúnxiào,
weeping uncontrollably.
Kāng Jūnlì had always been close to Lǐ Cúnxìn,
and a single remark displeased Kèyòng.
Kèyòng drew his sword and slashed him,
imprisoning him in the Mǎbù Division.
At the end of the Táng dynasty, all garrisons established prisons in the Mǎbù Division,
which are now called the Bīngmǎ Division.
忤 (wǔ),
pronounced *wúgù*.
On the *gēngshēn* day, the first day of the month,
he was released,
but Kāng Jūnlì had already died.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Xuē Jūzhèng's *Wǔdàishǐ* states:
"After Lǐ Cúnxiào died,
Emperor Wǔ deeply regretted it,
and was angry that none of his generals could alleviate his sorrow;
Kāng Jūnlì displeased him with a single word,
and Emperor Wǔ bestowed poisoned wine upon him, causing his death."
The *Tángmò Jiànwénlù* says:
"On the thirtieth day of the eighth month,
the Xiànggōng drank late into the night at his residence on the left street,
drew his sword and wounded Kāng Jūnlì, Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì,
and sent him to the Mǎbù Division for detention.
By the first day of the ninth month,
he was released,
and soon after, he passed away."
The *Xuē Shǐ*'s account of being "bestowed poisoned wine"
is probably a euphemism for the event.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
Imperial Prince Yǔ was enfeoffed as Dì Wáng,
Xì as Qián Wáng,
Yīn as Yí Wáng,
and Yī as Suí Wáng.
Liú Rén'gōng repeatedly presented strategies to Lǐ Kèyòng through Gài Yù,
wishing to obtain ten thousand soldiers to seize Yōuzhōu.
Kèyòng was then attacking Xíngzhōu,
and he dispatched several thousand soldiers,
intending to install Rén'gōng in Yōuzhōu,
but he did not succeed.
This refers to events before the eleventh month of this year.
He frequently encroached upon the territory of Hédōng.
Kèyòng was enraged,
and in the eleventh month,
he launched a major expedition to attack Lǐ Kuāngchóu,
capturing Wǔzhōu,
and advancing to besiege Xīnzhōu.
Xīnzhōu
administered four counties: Yǒngxīng, Fánshān, Huái'ān, and Lóngmén.
The histories do not record its initial establishment,
but its territory was to the northwest of Guīzhōu.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Táng Tàizǔ Jìniánlù* states:
"In the eleventh month,
on the *rénchén* day,
the grand army captured Jiécòu,
and advanced to take Yángmén and Jiǔzi.
On the *wùxū* day,
Wǔzhōu was taken.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
Xīnzhōu was attacked,
and a camp was set up in its northwest corner."
According to the *jǐwèi* day being the first day of the eleventh month,
there are no *rénchén*, *wùxū*, or *jiǎyín* days.
The *Jìniánlù* is mistaken.
We now follow the *Shílù*.
Zhāng Pàn, the acting Liúhòu of Jīngyuán, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Zhāngyì.
Zhū Quánzhōng sent an envoy to Sìzhōu,
who was rude
and disrespectful to the Cìshǐ Zhāng Jiàn.
Jiàn surrendered the entire prefecture to Yáng Xíngmì.
Sìzhōu,
originally under the jurisdiction of Xúzhōu,
thenceforth became possessed by Yáng Xíngmì.
Quánzhōng seized the returning envoy
and took all his tea.
This marked the beginning of hostilities between Yáng Xíngmì and Zhū Quánzhōng.
This laid the groundwork for Quánzhōng's attack on Xíngmì.
In the twelfth month,
Lǐ Kuāngchóu dispatched a grand general leading tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry to relieve Xīnzhōu.
Lǐ Kèyòng selected elite troops to meet them in battle at Duànzhuāng,
where he thoroughly defeated them.
Duànzhuāng
is southeast of Xīnzhōu.
He captured three hundred officers,
paraded them
and executed them outside the city walls.
That evening,
Xīnzhōu surrendered.
On the *xīnhài* day,
he advanced to attack Guīzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Guīzhōu is two hundred eighty *lǐ* southeast of Yōuzhōu,
and two hundred forty *lǐ* southwest of Wèizhōu.
媯 (Guī),
pronounced *jūwéi*.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
Kuāngchóu again sent troops out of Jūyōng Pass.
Kèyòng sent elite cavalry to confront them from the front to wear them out,
and dispatched infantry general Lǐ Cúnshěn to attack them from another path, ambushing them from behind.
The Yōuzhōu army was utterly defeated,
with tens of thousands killed or captured.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
Lǐ Kuāngchóu fled with his family to Cāngzhōu.
Lú Yànwēi, Jìedùshǐ of Yìchāng, coveted his baggage train and concubines,
and sent troops to attack him at Jǐngchéng,
killing him
and capturing all his followers.
Lǐ Cúnshěn's original surname was Fú,
and he was from Wǎnqiū.
Kèyòng adopted him as a son.
The *Xuē Shǐ* says:
Fú Cúnshěn initially followed Lǐ Hǎnzhī;
when Hǎnzhī was pressed by Zhūgě Shuǎng,
he retreated to Huáizhōu for protection,
and his subordinates dispersed.
Cúnshěn then joined Lǐ Kèyòng.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
Kèyòng advanced his army to Yōuzhōu,
and its grand general requested surrender.
Kuāngchóu had always been dull and cowardly.
When he first took control of the military government,
his elder brother Kuāngwēi heard of it
and said to his generals:
"My brother lost, my younger brother gained,
it remains within our family,
what regret is there?
But I lament Kuāngchóu's lack of talent,
unable to preserve it.
If he can hold it for two years,
it will be fortunate."
In the second year of Jǐngfú,
Kuāngchóu gained Yōuzhōu,
and it was indeed barely two years until this point.
Wáng Xíngyuē, Jìedùshǐ of Kuāngguó, was given the additional title of Jiǎnwèi Shìzhōng.
Wú Tǎo feared the pressure from Dù Hóng.
Dù Hóng's attack on Wú Tǎo is mentioned in the fifth month above.
Xíngmì appointed Qū Zhāng, the commander of the vanguard, as acting governor of Huángzhōu.
This set the stage for Qū Zhāng being attacked and captured by the Biàn army.
In this year,
twenty thousand barbarians from Huángliándòng besieged Tíngzhōu.
Huángliándòng
is south of Nínghuà County in Tíngzhōu,
and the current Tánfēi Qì is that location.
The barbarians withdrew,
and Chéngxūn pursued them,
attacking and defeating them at Jiāngshuǐkǒu.
The Mǐn region was largely pacified.
Wáng Cháo dispatched officials to tour the prefectures and counties,
encouraging agriculture and sericulture,
stabilizing taxes,
maintaining good relations with neighboring circuits,
and protecting the borders to allow the people to rest.
The Mǐn people were at peace.
Liú Qiān, Cìshǐ of Fēngzhōu, died.
His son, Liú Yǐn, observed mourning on the Hè Jiāng.
The Hè River originates from Shílóng in Fùchuān County, Hèzhōu,
and
combines
with the Guìlǐng River
to form the Hè Jiāng.
Over a hundred local inhabitants plotted a rebellion,
but Yǐn executed them all in one night.
Liú Chóngguī, Jìedùshǐ of Língnán, summoned and appointed him as Yòudū Yāyá and Hèshuǐ Zhènshǐ;
not long after,
he was recommended to be Cìshǐ of Fēngzhōu.
This was the beginning of Liú Yǐn's career.
In the second month,
on the *xīnmǎo* day,
Chāng, wearing a *yǎn* gown and a *miǎn* cap, ascended the gate tower of the inner city
and immediately assumed the imperial throne.
He displayed all the auspicious objects in the courtyard to show the multitude.
Previously,
at the end of the Xiántōng period,
a rumor circulated between Wú and Yuè that there was a large bird in the mountains,
with four eyes and three feet,
whose call was
"Luópíng Tiāncè."
Those who saw it would suffer misfortune.
The common folk widely painted its image and sacrificed to it.
When Chāng usurped the title,
he said,
"This is my *yuèzhuó*."
He then proclaimed himself Emperor of the Great Yuè Luópíng State,
changed the reign title to Shùntiān.
Kǎoyì says: Wúyuè Bèishǐ says,
"On the *guǐmǎo* day,
Chāng usurped the title of emperor,
established the reign title Shùntiān,
and the state name Luópíng."
The reign title is sometimes said to be Tiāncè,
or Dàshèng,
but these are all incorrect.
Luó Yǐn's "Wúyuè Xíngyíng Lùbù" says:
"Luópíng is
the name of the founding state;
Shùntiān is
the beginning of the reign."
It also says:
"The general's gates are called Tiāncè Towers,
and the assembly hall is the Xuānshì chamber.
It is clearly announced what it is called,
saying, 'He provisionally assumes the throne of the Luópíng State.'
Chāng's seal inscription says, 'Seal of Governing the State by Shùntiān.'"
*Shíguó Jìnián* also says,
"The reign title is Shùntiān."
*Kuàijī Lù* says Tiāncè,
which is probably a mistake.
We now follow *Bèishǐ*.
He ordered his subordinates to refer to him as
"Shengren."

He appointed Lǐ Miáo, the former Prefect of Hángzhōu; Jiǎng Huái, the former Prefect of Wùzhōu; Dù Yǐng, the Deputy Salt and Iron Commissioner of the Two Zhè districts; and Lǐ Yú, the former Administrator of Field Cultivation, as chancellors.
He also appointed Wú Yáo and others as Academicians of the Hanlin Academy, and Lǐ Chàngzhī and others as Grand Generals.
Chāng sent a letter to Qián Liú,
informing him of his provisional assumption of the throne of the Luópíng State,
and appointed Liú as the Overall Commander of the Two Zhè districts.
Liú sent a letter to Chāng saying:
"Instead of closing the gates to act as Son of Heaven,
leading your nine clans and the common people into misery,
would it not be better to open the gates and act as a Jìedùshǐ,
enjoying wealth and honor throughout your life?
If you repent now,
it is still not too late!"
Chāng did not listen.
Liú then led an army of thirty thousand to the city of Yuèzhōu.
Upon reaching the Yíng'ēn Gate—
Yíng'ēn Gate,
the western gate of Yuèzhōu city.
—he bowed twice and said:
"Your Majesty holds positions both as general and chancellor.
Why abandon security for danger?
Liú has brought his army here
to await Your Majesty's repentance, that is all.
Even if Your Majesty does not cherish yourself,
what sin have the local gentry and common people committed
to be exterminated along with Your Majesty's clan?"
Chāng was afraid.
He sent two million in silver to reward the army,
and arrested Wú Yáo, the chief instigator, and several shamans and sent them to Liú,
also requesting to await the Son of Heaven's punishment.
Liú withdrew his troops and returned,
reporting the situation.
Reported to the court.
Wáng Chóngyíng's son, the Báoyì Jìedùshǐ Gǒng,
Wáng Chóngyíng had previously garrisoned Shǎn and Guó;
Wáng Chóngróng was killed by his subordinates,
Chóngyíng replaced him in Hézhōng,
and his son Gǒng succeeded him in garrisoning Shǎn and Guó.
Shǎn and Guó were called the Báoyì Army.
Gǒng,
pronounced *jūyǒng*.
and the Prefect of [unclear character] Zhōu, Yáo, raised an army to attack Wáng Kē,
and submitted a memorial stating that Kē was not a son of the Wáng clan.
He also wrote a letter to Zhū Quánzhōng,
saying,
"Kē was originally a servant of my family;
he should not be heir."
Kē submitted a memorial to state his case
and also sought aid from Lǐ Kèyòng.
The emperor sent a eunuch envoy to mediate.
The emperor esteemed Lǐ Xī's literary accomplishments.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
he reappointed Xī as Minister of Revenue and Grand Chancellor.
Last year, Lǐ Xī was appointed chancellor,
but Liú Chónglǔ thwarted it and it was stopped;
this event is in the previous volume.
Zhū
Quánzhōng's army was stationed at Shànfù.
Shànfù County,
at that time part of Shàn Prefecture.
Shàn,
pronounced *shàn*.
Fù,
pronounced *fǔ*.
Zhū Yǒugōng was then besieging Zhū Jǐn in Yǎnzhōu.
Lǐ Kèyòng memorialized to appoint Liú Réngōng as acting military governor of Lúlóng,
and left troops to garrison it.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
he returned to Jìnyáng.
Gāo Sījì and his brothers, from Guīzhōu,
were militarily capable
and respected by the Yān people.
Kèyòng appointed them all as commanders,
sharing command of the Yōuzhōu army.
Their subordinate soldiers
were all local strongmen from north of the mountains.
Guī, Tán, and other prefectures were all north of the mountains in Yōuzhōu,
also called Shanhou.
After a long time,
the Hédōng troops garrisoned in Yōuzhōu became tyrannical.
Sījì's brothers restrained them by law,
executing many.
Kèyòng was angry
and reproached Réngōng.
Réngōng pleaded that it was the work of the Gāo brothers,
so Kèyòng killed them both.
Réngōng wanted to win the hearts of the Yān people,
so he again brought their sons and placed them under his command,
treating them generously.
This laid the groundwork for Réngōng's rebellion against Kèyòng.
Fù,
pronounced *fúyòu*;
the same below.
Cuī Zhāowěi was deeply allied with Lǐ Màozhēn and Wáng Xíngyú.
Whenever he discovered faults of the emperor
or secrets of the imperial court,
he would inform them all.
Cuī Zhēn, the Deputy Military Commissioner of Bīnnìng,
was a clansman of Zhāowěi.
When Lǐ Xī re-entered the chancellorship,
Zhāowěi sent Zhēn to tell Xíngyú:
"Previously, the appointment of the Minister of the Department of State Affairs was already issued,
but Wéi Zhāodù thwarted it.
This event is in the previous volume, Jǐngfú second year.
They conspired to mislead the sagely ear,
and I fear there will again be an incident like that of Grand Preceptor Dù."
Dù Ràngnéng,
this event is also in the previous volume, Jǐngfú second year.
Zhāodù lacks the qualities of a chancellor;
he should be dismissed to an honorary position.
Sàn,
pronounced *xīdàn*.
"Regarding military matters,
We shall consult with the regional governors;
as for appointing chancellors,
that should come from Our own judgment."
Xíngyú and others continued to argue.
In the third month,
Xī was again dismissed to be Junior Mentor of the Crown Prince.
Wáng Gǒng and Wáng Yáo requested the court to appoint a commander for Hézhōng.
An imperial edict appointed Cuī Yìn, Secretary of the Chancellery and Grand Chancellor, as Grand Chancellor
and concurrently Military Commissioner of Hùguó;
and Wáng Tuán, Minister of Revenue and Director of the Ministry of Revenue, as Secretary of the Chancellery and Grand Chancellor.
Wáng Kē
was the son-in-law of Lǐ Kèyòng.
Kèyòng memorialized that Chóngróng had rendered meritorious service to the state,
referring to defeating Huáng Cháo and deposing King Xiāng, in which Wáng Chóngróng had both rendered meritorious service.
Wáng Gǒng formed strong ties with the three military governors Wáng Xíngyú, Lǐ Màozhēn, and Hán Jiàn,
and repeatedly submitted memorials asserting that Kē was not a son of the Wáng clan,
requesting that Kē be made Prefect of Shǎnzhōu and Gǒng be made Prefect of Hézhōng.
The emperor informed them that he had already agreed to Kèyòng's memorial
and would not permit it.
Yǔn,
means to follow.
This set the stage for the three military governors to raise troops and enter the capital city,
and for Kèyòng to execute Wáng Yáo and suppress the three military governors.
Shǎn,
pronounced *shǐrǎn*.
Wáng Róng was promoted to concurrently hold the title of Palace Attendant.
15 Yáng Xíngmì floated along the Huái River to Sīzhōu.
The Defender, Tái Méng, elaborately prepared tents and provisions.
[The surname] Tái (臺) in Xìngyuàn [says]: The Tái surname [originated from]
the descendants of Tái Dài.
In the Later Hàn dynasty, there was the recluse Tái Tóng.
In the Jìn dynasty, there was the術士 Tái Yàn.
In Former Zhào, there was the Grandee Remonstrant Tái Yàngāo.
Gōng (供) [meaning]
jù yòng fān.
After [Yáng Xíngmì] departed,
Méng found a patched and mended garment in his sleeping quarters,
and promptly sent an envoy to return it.
"Zhàn" (綻)
should be
zhàng xiàn fān.
Nì (䘺)
also means to patch.
Shǐ (使) [meaning]
shū lì fān.
"[I was] poor and humble in my youth,
and dare not forget my origins."
Méng was very ashamed.
Yáng Xíngmì attacked Háo Zhōu,
captured it,
and seized the Prefect Zhāng Suì.
Suì had sided with Zhū Quánzhōng, as seen in volume one, Jǐngfú first year.
Yáng Xíngmì's soldiers plundered and seized a son of the Lǐ clan from Xúzhōu,
who was eight years old.
Yáng Xíngmì adopted him as his son.
The Nán Táng Shìjiā says: Lǐ Bìn,
a native of Xúzhōu,
was the son of Lǐ Róng.
Róng met with chaos and his end is unknown.
Bìn was orphaned young,
and drifted between Háo and Sī.
Yáng Xíngmì obtained him when he attacked Háo Zhōu,
and adopted him as his son.
Yáng Xíngmì said to his general Xú Wēn:
"This child's physique, temperament, and understanding
are quite extraordinary.
I believe that [Wò] will certainly not be able to tolerate him;
I now bestow him upon you as a son."
Wēn named him Zhīgào.
Zhīgào served Wēn
with diligence and filial piety exceeding his own sons.
He once offended Wēn,
and Wēn flogged and expelled him;
upon his return,
Zhīgào greeted and bowed at the gate.
Wēn asked:
"Why are you still here?"
Zhīgào wept and replied:
"Where can a child go, abandoning his parents!
When a father is angry and sends [his child] back to the mother,
it is the normal course of human affairs."
Wēn consequently loved him even more,
and made him manage household affairs;
no one in the family disagreed.
When he grew up,
he loved books and was skilled in archery,
with a heroic and grand demeanor.
Yáng Xíngmì often said to Wēn:
"Zhīgào is a brilliant talent,
none of the generals' sons can compare to him."
The story of Xú Zhīgào begins here;
later, he reverted to the surname Lǐ
and his name was Bìn.
On the day of Dīnghài,
Yáng Xíngmì besieged Shòuzhōu.
16 The emperor, due to the prevalence of bandits in the capital region,
to the extent that some scaled walls to enter the palace or encroached upon imperial tombs,
wished to order the imperial princes to lead troops to patrol and keep order,
and also to send them to various regions to comfort the regional governors.
The officials in charge of the Southern and Northern Bureaus feared that this would be disadvantageous to themselves,
and submitted numerous memorials to remonstrate.
The emperor had no choice but,
in summer,
in the fourth month,
to issue an edict to dismiss all of them.
17 The imperial court, considering Dǒng Chāng's diligence in tribute payments,
and that his current actions
resembled a mental illness,
decreed to pardon his crime
and allow him to return to his hometown.
18 Lù Xīshēng, Minister of the Board of Revenue and concurrently Chancellor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì), was dismissed and made Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent.
19 Yáng Xíngmì besieged Shòuzhōu
but could not take it, and was about to return;
on the day of Gēngyín,
his general Zhū Yánshòu requested to try attacking again.
He captured it in one drum roll,
because Yáng Xíngmì was about to return and [the defenders] were lax in their defense,
so it was captured in one drum roll.
Gāo Yànwēn offered Shòuzhōu to Zhū Quánzhōng,
who appointed Jiāng Cóngxù as its Prefect.
Yáng Xíngmì captured him
and thus gained control of Háo and Shòu prefectures.
Not long after,
several tens of thousands of Biàn troops attacked Shòuzhōu.
The prefecture had few soldiers,
and officials and commoners were terrified.
Yánshòu decreed
that each banner in the army consist of twenty-five cavalrymen.
He ordered Lǐ Hòu, commander of the Black Cloud Troop, to lead ten banners to attack the Biàn troops,
but they were unsuccessful.
Yánshòu was about to execute him,
but Hòu claimed that their numbers were unequally matched,
and requested more troops to go again,
vowing to die if unsuccessful.
Chái Zàiyòng of Rǔyáng, who was a Chief Adjutant (Dū Yāyá), also pleaded for him.
Lù Zhèn's Jiǔ Guó Zhì says: Chái Zàiyòng was originally named Cún,
and served Sūn Rú,
forming a sworn brotherhood with a junior officer.
Someone accused the junior officer of rebellion,
and Rú executed him.
Cún was seized and brought forth,
interrogated as to why he rebelled,
but did not reply.
When asked again,
he replied:
"I formed a sworn brotherhood with him;
if he rebelled, then I rebelled.
Since you have punished him,
what more is there to ask!"
Rú found him extraordinary and said:
"If you truly did not rebel,
I will reuse you."
Consequently, he changed his name.
Wéi (為) [meaning]
yú wěi fān.
Hòu fought desperately,
and Zàiyòng assisted him.
Yánshòu led his entire army to press the attack,
and the Biàn troops were defeated and fled.
Hòu was from Cáizhōu.
Lǐ Hòu was
a remnant soldier of Sūn Rú.
Yáng Xíngmì also sent troops to raid Liánshuǐ
and captured it.
Historians say that Yáng Xíngmì's territory gradually expanded.
Liánshuǐ County in Sīzhōu.
Dù Yòu said: Hàn Dynasty's Qiúyóu County.
Sòng Bái said: According to Qiúyóu City,
it is now Sùyù County.
During the Wèi Dynasty, it was called Hǎi'ān County.
During the Jìn Dynasty, it was part of Sùyù's territory.
The Sòng Dynasty established Dōnghǎi Commandery.
Later Wèi changed it to Hǎi'ān Commandery.
The Suí Dynasty abolished the commandery
and established Liánshuǐ County.
20 Qián Liú memorialized that Dǒng Chāng's usurpation
was unforgivable,
and requested to use his own provincial troops to suppress him.
Qián Liú originally harbored the ambition of absorbing Dǒng Chāng.
Taking advantage of Dǒng Chāng's assumption of a reign title,
he acted under the guise of loyalty to the Great Court and requested to suppress him.
21 Wéi Zhāodù, Grand Tutor, Minister of the Department of the Gate Affairs, and concurrently Chancellor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì), retired as Grand Protector.
22 On the day of Wùxū,
Liú Jiànfēng was appointed Military Governor of Wǔ'ān.
Jiànfēng appointed Mǎ Yīn as Grand Commander of All Cavalry and Infantry, Internal and External.
This sets the stage for Mǎ Yīn to replace Jiànfēng.
23 Yáng Xíngmì sent an envoy to Qián Liú,
stating that Dǒng Chāng had already reformed
and should be pardoned.
Yáng Xíngmì wanted to preserve Dǒng Chāng to check Qián Liú later,
preventing him from competing with himself.
The envoy urged [Dǒng Chāng] to pay homage to the court.
24 Hédōng sent its generals Shǐ Yǎn and Lǐ Chéngsì with ten thousand cavalry to swiftly enter Yùn.
Lǐ Kèyòng sent Shǐ Yǎn and others again to relieve Yǎn and Yùn,
but they would not be able to return.
Deploying a large army for distant campaigns
has been avoided since ancient times.
25 In the fifth month,
an edict was issued to strip Dǒng Chāng of his official titles and ranks,
and entrusted Qián Liú with suppressing him.
26 Initially,
Wáng Xíngyú (王行瑜) sought the post of Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) but did not obtain it.
This is seen in the Emperor's scroll, second year of Jǐngfú (景福).
Within the Jīnèi (畿內) there were eight garrison armies,
subordinate to the Zuǒ (左) and Yòu (右) Armies.
These were the Zuǒ (左) and Yòu Shéncè (神策) Armies.
Hán Jiàn (韓建) sought one;
Héyáng (郃陽),
a Hàn (漢) county,
belonged to Tóngzhōu (同州) in the Táng (唐) dynasty.
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: the county is one hundred and twenty *lǐ* east of the prefecture.
Hé (郃)
has the sound *hé*.
*Jìn* (近),
pronounced like *qí jìn* (其靳);
same below.
Wáng Xíngyú (王行瑜) sought one.
Liángyuán (良原) County,
belonged to Jīngzhōu (涇州).
"These are the Son of Heaven's Imperial Guards,
how can they be granted!"
Wáng Kē (王珂) and Wáng Gǒng (王珙) contended for Hézhōng (河中).
Xíngyú (行瑜), Jiàn (建), and Lǐ Màozhēn (李茂貞) all pleaded for Gǒng (珙),
but could not succeed,
and were ashamed of it.
Gǒng (珙) sent someone to speak to the three commanders, saying:
"Kē (珂) refuses to be replaced and has formed a marriage alliance with Hédōng (河東),
which will certainly be disadvantageous to all of you,
I ask that we attack him."
Xíngyú (行瑜) ordered his younger brother, Wáng Xíngyuē (王行約), the Jiédu Shǐ (節度使) of Kuāngguó (匡國), to attack Hézhōng (河中).
At that time, Tóngzhōu (同州) was made into the Kuāngguó (匡國) Army.
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: Tóngzhōu (同州) is seventy-five *lǐ* east of Hézhōng (河中).
Xíngyú (行瑜) then, with Màozhēn (茂貞) and Jiàn (建), each leading several thousand elite troops, entered the capital.
On the *Jiǎzǐ* (甲子) day,
they arrived at the capital city.
The residents of the wards and markets all fled and hid.
The Emperor went to Ānfú Mén (安福門) to await them.
The three commanders grandly displayed their armed forces,
prostrated themselves and bowed at the gate.
The Emperor approached the veranda,
and personally questioned them, saying:
The end of the eaves is called *xuān* (軒).
pronounced like *qù jí* (去吉).
"You gentlemen did not present a memorial and await a reply,
but instead presumptuously brought troops into the capital city.
What do you intend to do?
If you cannot serve Ourself,
We ask today to cede the path to the worthy!"
Xíngyú (行瑜) and Màozhēn (茂貞) sweated and could not speak.
Only Hán Jiàn (韓建) roughly explained the reason for their coming to the capital.
The Emperor held a banquet with the three commanders.
The three commanders reported, saying:
"The Nán (南) and Běi (北) Offices have formed factions with each other,
disrupting and disordering the court administration.
Wéi Zhāodù (韋昭度) made a poor decision in attacking Xīchuān (西川).
The matter of attacking Xīchuān (西川) is found in volumes 257 and 258.
This did not accord with the public's will.
We request that he be executed."
The Emperor did not grant it yet.
On that day,
Xíngyú (行瑜) and others killed Zhāodù (昭度) and Xī (谿) at Dūyíng Yì (都亭驛).
Dūtíng Yì (都亭驛)
was on the west street outside Zhūquè Mén (朱雀門),
the second *fāng* (坊) coming north from Hánguāng Mén (含光門).
They also said:
"Wáng Kē (王珂) and Wáng Gǒng (王珙) have not differentiated between the legitimate and illegitimate heirs.
We request to remove Wáng Gǒng (王珙) from Hézhōng (河中),
transfer Wáng Xíngyuē (王行約) to Shǎn (陝),
and Wáng Kē (王珂) to Tóngzhōu (同州)."
The Emperor granted all of these requests.
Originally,
the three commanders plotted to depose the Emperor
and enthrone Prince Jí (吉) Bǎo (保).
By this time,
they heard that Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) had already raised an army in Hédōng (河東).
Xíngyú (行瑜) and Màozhēn (茂貞) each left two thousand soldiers to garrison the capital,
and with Jiàn (建), all took leave to return to their garrisons.
The Hùbù Shàngshū (戶部尚書) Yáng Kān (楊堪) was demoted to Yǎzhōu Cìshǐ (雅州刺史).
Kān (堪)
was the son of Yúqīng (虞卿).
Yáng Yúqīng (楊虞卿) is seen in the annals of Wénzōng (文宗).
27 Initially,
Cuī Yìn (崔胤) was appointed Jiédu Shǐ (節度使) of Hézhōng (河中).
Xuē Zhìqín (薛志勤), an envoy from Hédōng (河東), publicly declared:
"Although Cui (崔) is of weighty virtue, to replace Wáng Kē (王珂) with him is not as generous to our duke as Liú (劉) of Guāngdé (光德) would be."
Liú Gōng (劉公) of Guāngdé (光德) was
the Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿) Liú Chóngwàng (劉崇望).
Guāngdé (光德)
was a *lǐ* (里) (ward) name,
within Cháng'ān (長安) city.
In the late Táng (唐),
prominent ministers
were often referred to by the ward in which they resided.
Guāngdé Fāng (光德坊)
was the sixth *fāng* (坊) coming north along the third street west of Zhūquè Jiē (朱雀街),
where the Jīngzhào Fǔ (京兆府) was located.
Hearing Zhìqín's (志勤) words,
Chóngwàng (崇望) was demoted to Zhāozhōu Sīmǎ (昭州司馬).
Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用), hearing that the troops of the three garrisons had violated the palace,
immediately dispatched thirteen envoys to mobilize the Northern Army.
The Northern Army
consisted of the barbarian troops from Dàiběi (代北).
28 In the sixth month,
on the *Gēngyín* (庚寅) day,
Qián Liú (錢鏐) was appointed Zhèdōng Zhāotǎo Shǐ (浙東招討使);
Liú (鏐) again dispatched troops to attack Dǒng Chāng (董昌).
29 On the *Xīnmǎo* (辛卯) day,
Kǒng Wěi (孔緯), former Jūnzhōu Cìshǐ (均州刺史), and Zhāng Jùn (張濬), Sīhù (司戶) of Xiùzhōu (繡州), were both appointed Tàizǐ Bīnkè (太子賓客).
On the *Rénchén* (壬辰) day,
Wěi (緯) was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書),
and his rank and title were restored;
on the *Guǐsì* (癸巳) day,
he was appointed Sīkōng (司空),
concurrently Ménxià Shìláng (門下侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì (同平章事).
Zhāng Jùn (張濬) was appointed Bīngbù Shàngshū (兵部尚書) and Zhū Dào Zūyōng Shǐ (諸道租庸使).
Kǒng Wěi (孔緯) and Zhāng Jùn (張濬)'s demotion is seen in volume 258, first year of Dàshùn (大順).
Now the Emperor wished to reuse them.
Jùn (濬) resided in Chángshuǐ (長水).
The Emperor, seeing that Cuī Zhāowěi (崔昭緯) and others maintained external relations with the regional governors,
forming factions and conspiring against each other,
desired to find upright and unyielding officials,
and therefore rapidly promoted Wěi (緯) and Jùn (濬).
Wěi (緯), being ill,
was carried by litter to the capital.
Upon seeing the Emperor,
he tearfully and firmly declined;
the Emperor did not permit it.
30 Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) raised a large army of Fān (蕃) and Hàn (漢) soldiers and marched south.
He submitted a memorial stating that Wáng Xíngyú (王行瑜), Lǐ Màozhēn (李茂貞), and Hán Jiàn (韓建) had brought troops to violate the palace,
and had harmed ministers,
requesting to attack them.
Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) was actually allied with Wáng Kē (王珂),
and publicly denounced the crimes of the three commanders in his memorial to request an attack.
Xíngyú (行瑜) and the others were greatly afraid.
Kèyòng's (克用) army arrived at Jiàngzhōu (絳州).
The Cìshǐ (刺史) Wáng Yáo (王瑤) closed the city gates and resisted them;
Kèyòng (克用) advanced and attacked.
After ten days,
he captured it,
beheaded Yáo (瑤) at the army gate,
and killed over a thousand who had resisted in the city.
In autumn,
seventh month,
on the *Bǐngchén* (丙辰) day (new moon),
Kèyòng (克用) arrived at Hézhōng (河中).
Wáng Kē (王珂) welcomed him on the road.
The Kuāngguó Jiédu Shǐ (匡國節度使) Wáng Xíngyuē (王行約) was defeated at Cháoyì (朝邑).
On the *Wùwǔ* (戊午) day,
Xíngyuē (行約) abandoned Tóngzhōu (同州) and fled.
On the *Jǐwèi* (己未) day,
he arrived at the capital.
Xíngyuē's (行約) younger brother, Wáng Xíngshí (王行實), was then the Zuǒjūn Zhǐhuīshǐ (左軍指揮使).
The Shéncè (神策) Zuǒjūn (左軍) is not this.
The west of Zhūquè Jiē (朱雀街) was called the Xīshì (西市).
The Shatuo (沙陀) general was about to arrive.
He requested that the Emperor's carriage proceed to Bīnzhōu (邠州).
On the *Gēngshēn* (庚申) day,
the Shūmì Shǐ (樞密使) Luò Quánguàn (駱全瓘) memorialized, requesting that the Emperor's carriage proceed to Fèngxiáng (鳳翔).
The Emperor said:
"We received Kèyòng's (克用) memorial,
and he is still stationed in Hézhōng (河中).
Even if the Shatuo (沙陀) reach here,
We Ourselves have means to withstand them.
You gentlemen should simply each soothe your own armies,
and not let them waver."
The Left and Right Army Commander Lǐ Jìpéng
was Lǐ Màozhēn's adopted son.
Chéng Dàchāng's Yōng Lù says: The Northern Army's Left and Right Armies
were both within the imperial park.
The Left Three Armies were east of the inner East Park,
which was east of the Dàmínggōng Park.
The Right Three Armies were west of Jiǔxiān Mén.
Jiǔxiān was at the northwest corner of the inner East Park.
The Left Three Armies were
the Zuǒ Shéncè, Zuǒ Lóngwǔ, and Zuǒ Yǔlín Armies.
The Right Three Armies were
the Yòu Shéncè, Yòu Lóngwǔ, and Yòu Yǔlín Armies.
I note that what Yōng Lù refers to as the Left and Right Six Armies
were the palace guards after Dài Zōng and Dé Zōng.
When Xī Zōng fled to Shǔ in Guǎngmíng era,
these Six Armies disintegrated.
Tián Lìngzī recruited 52 new divisions in Chéngdū,
assigning them to the Left and Right Shéncè Armies.
From then on,
all those referred to as the Left and Right Armies
were these forces,
encamped inside and outside the capital,
and no longer exclusively in the imperial park.
If Wáng Xíngshí and Lǐ Jìpéng were the Left and Right Army Commanders at this time,
I suspect they were the forces left by the two commanders of Bīn and Qí to guard the palace, having divided themselves into Left and Right.
Lǐ Jìpéng plotted with Luò Quán’guàn to seize the emperor and take him to Fèngxiáng.
The Eunuch Commissioner Liú Jǐngxuān and Wáng Xíngshí learned of this
and wanted to seize the emperor and take him to Bīnzhōu.
Kǒng Wěi directly reprimanded Jǐngxuān,
believing it was not permissible to lightly abandon the palace.
Towards evening,
Jìpéng repeatedly requested the imperial carriage to depart.
Thereupon, Wáng Xíngyuē led the Left Army to attack the Right Army,
their shouts and drums shaking the ground.
The emperor heard the commotion
and ascended Chéngtiān Lóu,
intending to issue an edict to stop them.
The Běng Rì Division Commander Lǐ Jūn led his own troops
to guard below the tower.
Lǐ Jìpéng attacked Jūn with Fèngxiáng soldiers.
Wáng Xíngyuē attacked the Right Army because
Lǐ Jìpéng intended to first seize the imperial carriage and take it to Qí.
Lǐ Jìpéng should have fought with Xíngyuē,
but instead attacked Lǐ Jūn,
because Jūn was guarding the emperor,
preventing his seizure and forced removal.
The emperor clung to the building's rafters;
his attendants helped him up and down the stairs.
Jìpéng then set fire to the palace gate,
smoke and flames obscuring the sky.
At this time, there were six divisions of Yánzhōu soldiers garrisoned in the capital,
who were always feared by the two armies.
The emperor urgently summoned them to enter and provide protection.
Once they arrived,
the two armies retreated,
returning to Bīnzhōu and Fèngxiáng respectively.
The city fell into great chaos,
with mutual looting.
The emperor, along with the princes and close attendants, fled to Lǐ Jūn's camp.
The Hùbì Division Commander Lǐ Jūshí led his troops to arrive subsequently.
The Hùbì Division was also one of the fifty-four Shéncè divisions,
or some say it was the Hùbì Dū.
帥 (shuài)
is read as 率 (shuài).
Someone reported that Wáng Xíngyú and Lǐ Màozhēn intended to personally come and welcome the imperial carriage.
The emperor feared being coerced by them.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
with soldiers from Jūn's and Jūshí's divisions guarding him,
he exited through Qǐxià Mén.
Qǐxià Mén was

Tōngzhōu Prefect Lǐ Yànzhāo led his two thousand troops and surrendered to Jiàn.
Tōngzhōu
is modern-day Dázhōu.
Lǐ Yànzhāo was also a Féngxiáng general.
Lǐ Kèyòng sent his chief secretary, Lǐ Xíjí, to the capital to express gratitude.
In the first year of Jǐngfèng,
the Military Governor's headquarters established the post of chief secretary.
After Kaiyuán,
all military commissions established this post.
They were responsible for documents related to imperial audiences, diplomatic visits, recommendations for sacrifices, and prayers,
as well as edicts and matters of promotion and demotion.
"For years,
Guānfǔ has been unrestful.
Guān refers to the passes of Pú, Tóng, Lǒng, Shǔ, and Lántián.

Guānnèi is the land of the Han Three Fǔ.
Therefore, seize Féngxiáng,
for one effort, everlasting peace.
The time must not be lost.
Your servant's army is stationed north of the Wèi River,
awaiting only orders to advance."
The Emperor consulted with his high-ranking officials.
Some said:
"If MàoZhēn is again destroyed, then the Shātuó will become too powerful,

The Emperor then bestowed an edict upon Kèyòng,
praising his loyalty.
Kuǎn means sincerity.
"The disloyalty
of Xíngyú was the most severe.
Since Our relocation,

Kèyòng obeyed the edict and stopped.
Afterwards, he privately told the imperial envoy:

However, if MàoZhēn is not removed,

Later, when Lǐ MàoZhēn again attacked the capital,

Some of his staff said:
"Now that we are so close to the imperial court,
how can we not enter to meet the Son of Heaven!"
Kèyòng hesitated, unable to decide.
Gài Yù said to Kèyòng:
"Previously, Wáng Xíngyú and his ilk let their troops run riot and behave outrageously,
causing the imperial carriage to wander
and the common people to scatter.
Today, the Son of Heaven has not yet settled,
and people's hearts are still uneasy.
If Your Highness leads your troops across the Wèi River,
I fear it will again alarm the capital.
Gài Yù meant that Lǐ Kèyòng could not dismiss his army and enter the court.
If he entered with his army,
it would be a repeat of the actions of the three marshals of Bīn, Qí, and Huá.
The priority is to serve the Emperor,
not to have an audience.
Please consider this carefully!"
Kèyòng laughed and said:
"Even Gài Yù does not want me to enter the court,
let alone the people of the world!"
He then submitted a memorial stating:
"Your servant commands a large army,
and does not dare to directly enter for an audience,
also fearing that the tribal soldiers will disturb the residents north of the Wèi River."
On the Xīnhài day,
he led his troops eastward, returning home.
When the memorial reached the capital,
everyone, high and low, finally felt at ease.
An edict granted the Hédōng soldiers 300,000 strings of cash.
After Kèyòng left,
Lǐ MàoZhēn became arrogant and tyrannical as before.
Many prefectures and counties in Hexi were occupied by MàoZhēn.
Hexi refers to the prefectures of Liáng, Guā, Shā, and Sù.
When Zhū Quánzhōng left Yǎnzhōu,
Zhū Qióng died, and Quánzhōng returned.
Zhū Jǐn sealed the city and did not sally forth again.
When Cóngzhōu's general returned,
he spread a rumor,
"The relief forces from Tiānpíng and Hédōng have arrived.

In the middle of the night,
he secretly returned to his old camp.
Jǐn, thinking Cóngzhōu's elite troops had all departed,

Cóngzhōu burst out and fought fiercely,

From this point on, Shǐ Yǎn and Lǐ Chéngsì subsequently joined Zhū Jǐn and entered Huáinán.
Jiā Shèng, the Defense Commissioner of Ānzhōu,

fearing disaster,

(Bǐngchén, 896)

spring month,
first month,

*Sàng* [lost],

Quánzhōng was planning to attack Yǎn and Yùn,

Whenever Hóngxìn sent gifts,

“shòu” [receive].
