Páng Shīgǔ ordered his generals to dismantle timber to build a bridge.
On the night of Yǐwèi,
Shīgǔ led his central army across first.
Zhū Xuān abandoned his ramparts and fled by night.
Gě Cóngzhōu captured Xuān and his wife and son and presented them."
However, after the great drought during Wáng Mǎng's time, the Jǐshuǐ
could no longer cross the Yellow River and flow south.
From then on, there was no Jǐshuǐ south of the Yellow River.
The Biān Yílù states:
"In the fifth month,
cavalry were dispatched to the front at Yùnzhōu to recall Cóngzhōu,
who was to proceed directly to Huánshuǐ to lead the army,
replacing Hóu Yán.
Shīgǔ was left to attack Yùn."
The Liáng Tàizǔ Shílù states:
"In the first month of the fourth year,
the army at Huánshuǐ was again mobilized for a major expedition against Yùn.
On the fifteenth day, Xīnmǎo,
they encamped outside the river to the southwest.
Páng Shīgǔ ordered his generals to dismantle timber to build a bridge, planning to cross during the night.
On the day Guǐsì,
the vanguard, with a hundred trusted men, secretly breached the river mouth.
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
the pontoon bridge was assembled by the water.
On the night of Yǐwèi,
Shīgǔ's central army crossed first,
and the sound shook within the ramparts.
When Zhū Xuān heard of this,
he abandoned his ramparts and fled."
The Biān Yílù states:
"In the first month of the fourth year, on the day Jǐmǎo,
Zhū Xuān's troops were few and his provisions exhausted,
so he dared not sally forth to battle.
However, with deep moats and high ramparts,
it was difficult to cross.
Cóngzhōu and Shīgǔ then took small boats from within the Qīnghé,
gathered wild kudzu vines and reeds,
and twisted them into huge cables.
They then built a pontoon bridge south of its walls.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
the work was completed.
Our army crossed the bridge,
and Zhū Xuān fled."
None of these mention the Jǐshuǐ.
Shīgǔ had already defeated the Yùn army at Mǎjiá in the third month of the previous year,
pursuing them to the west gate,
and established a camp at the former Luò Tíngzi.
That he crossed first on the night of Yǐwèi
was probably over the Qīnghé water below Yùnchéng,
presumably diverted by Zhū Xuān to surround the city for a solid defense.
Therefore, Shīgǔ and others built a pontoon bridge to ferry the army across.
Since the river could be breached,
it is clear it was not a natural waterway.
The Old Annals record:
"On the day Guǐwèi,
Páng Shīgǔ captured Yùnzhōu.
Zhū Xuān and his wife, Róngshì, broke through the encirclement and fled.
When Xuān reached Zhōngdū,
he was killed by villagers.
Róngshì was captured by the army."
The New Annals record:
"On the day Bǐngshēn,
Quánzhōng captured Yùnzhōu."
The Shílù records:
"In the second month,
on the first day, Bǐngwǔ,
Yùnzhōu was captured.
Xuān reached Zhōngdū,
where he was killed by rogue soldiers.
His wife Róng became a nun upon arriving in Biàn."
According to Xuē Shǐ,
they encamped by the Jǐshuǐ on Xīnmǎo,
which means Yùn had not yet fallen on Guǐwèi.
The New Annals state Yùn fell on Bǐngshēn,
and the Shílù states the second month,
which is probably an approximate date of the report's arrival.
We now follow the Biān Yílù and the New Annals.
3 On the day Jǐhài,
Sūn Wò was dismissed from his posts as *Jiédùshǐ* of the Fèngxiáng Four-Front Field Army, etc.
Lǐ Màozhēn was pardoned,
hence the disbandment of the Fèngxiáng Four-Front Field Army.
According to the Fāngzhèn Biǎo,
in the first year of Guānghuà (898),
Yánzhōu's Bǎosài *Jiédù* was changed to Níngsài *Jiédù*.
4 Qián Liú sent his *Xíngjūn Sīmǎ*, Dù Léng, to relieve Wùzhōu.
Ān Rényì moved his troops to attack Mùzhōu,
but failed and returned.
Ān Rényì's attack on Wùzhōu is mentioned in the previous volume, last year.
*Huán*,
pronounced *xuān* in a variant,
or as is.
5 Zhū Quánzhōng entered Yùnzhōu
and appointed Páng Shīgǔ as the acting military governor (*liúhòu*) of Tiānpíng.
The Kǎoyì states: The Old Annals, Liáng Tàizǔ Shílù, and Xuē Jūzhèng's Wǔdài Shǐ, in the biography of Shīgǔ, all say that Shīgǔ was the *liúhòu* of Yùnzhōu.
The Biān Yílù and Xuē Shǐ's Liáng Jì both state
"Yǒuyù".
According to the Biān Yílù,
"In the third month,
on the day Bǐngzǐ,
Yǒuyù was made *liúhòu* of Yùnzhōu,
and Shīgǔ was made *liúhòu* of Xúzhōu."
Presumably, Shīgǔ was initially appointed to guard Yùnzhōu,
then Yǒuyù replaced him,
and Shīgǔ was transferred to Xúzhōu.
Zhū Jǐn left his grand general Kāng Huáizhēn to guard Yǎnzhōu
and, with the Hedōng generals Shǐ Yǎn and Lǐ Chéngsì, plundered the borders of Xúzhōu to supply military provisions.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: One hundred and ten *lǐ* south of Yǎnzhōu
is the border of Xúzhōu.
Gě Cóngzhōu was dispatched to lead troops to attack Yǎnzhōu.
When Huáizhēn heard that Yùnzhōu had already fallen
and Biàn troops had arrived suddenly,
he surrendered.
In the second month,
on the day Wùshēn,
Cóngzhōu entered Yǎnzhōu
and captured Jǐn's wife and children.
Zhū Jǐn returned,
with nowhere to go.
He led his followers toward Yízhōu,
but the prefect Yǐn Chǔbīn did not receive him.
He fled to Hǎizhōu for safety,
but was pressed by Biàn troops.
With Shǐ Yǎn and Lǐ Chéngsì, he led the common people of the prefecture across the Huái River
and fled to Yáng Xíngmì.
In the second year of Guāngqǐ (886),
Zhū Jǐn took Yǎnzhōu,
and now he was defeated.
The table shows Jǐn as nominal *Jiédùshǐ* of Wǔníng.
*Lǐng*
means to nominally hold a position from afar (*yáolǐng*).
Quánzhōng took Jǐn's wife
and led his army back.
Lady Zhāng met him at Fēngqiū.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Fēngqiū county
is sixty *lǐ* north of Biànzhōu.
The Lady requested to see her.
Jǐn's wife bowed,
and the Lady returned her bow,
weeping as she said:
"Yǎn and Yùn are of the same surname as *Sīkōng* (Quánzhōng),
and vowed to be brothers.
Due to a minor grievance and resentment,
you raised an army to attack each other,
causing my sister-in-law to suffer such humiliation here.
If Biànzhōu were to fall one day,
would I not be like my sister-in-law today!"
Quánzhōng then sent Jǐn's wife to a Buddhist temple to become a nun
and executed Zhū Xuān at Biànqiáo.
Thereupon, Yùn, Qí, Cáo, Dì, Yǎn, Yí, Mì, Xú, Sù, Chén, Xǔ, Zhèng, Huá, Pú all came under Quánzhōng's control.
Yùn, Qí, Cáo, Dì
belonged to the Tiānpíng Army;
Yǎn, Yí, Mì
belonged to the Tàiníng Army;
Xú, Sù
belonged to the Gǎnhuà Army;
Chén, Xǔ
belonged to the Zhōngwǔ Army;
Zhèng, Huá, Pú
belonged to the Xuānyì Army.
These are the territories of these five military commands.
They also submitted to Quánzhōng.
Lǐ Cúnxìn, who was in Wèizhōu,
heard that Yǎn and Yùn had both fallen,
and led his troops back.
Huáinán had long been skilled in naval warfare
but unfamiliar with cavalry archery.
After obtaining the Hedōng, Yǎn, and Yùn troops,
its military prestige greatly increased.
Shǐ Yǎn and Lǐ Chéngsì were both fierce generals from Hedōng,
and Lǐ Kèyòng greatly valued them.
He sent envoys through secret paths to Yáng Xíngmì to request their return;
Xíngmì agreed
and also sent envoys to Kèyòng to mend relations.
6 On the day of Wùwǔ,
Wáng Jiàn dispatched Huá Hóng, the Cìshǐ of Qióngzhōu, and Wáng Zōngyòu, the Cìshǐ of Péngzhōu, to lead an army of fifty thousand to attack Dōngchuān.
He appointed Wáng Zōngjǐn, the Cìshǐ of Róngzhōu, as the Xiānfēngshǐ of the Xīmiàn Xíngyíng of Fèngxiáng.
They defeated Lǐ Jìhuī and others, generals of Fèngxiáng, at Xuánwǔ.
Xuánwǔ
was the Dī Dào County during the Hàn dynasty.
The Jìn dynasty changed its name to Xuánwǔ.
In the early Táng dynasty, it belonged to Yìzhōu.
At this time, it belonged to Zǐzhōu.
The Sòng dynasty changed its name to Zhōngjiāng.
It was ninety *lǐ* west of Zǐzhōu.
The character 敗 (bài)
is pronounced "bù mài" (as a fanqie).
Míng Chóngběn
was the adopted son of Mào Zhēn.
7 On the day of Jǐwèi,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
8 The Emperor offered a sacrifice at the temporary ancestral temple.
At that time, the Emperor was residing in Huàzhōu.
The Tàicháng Lǐyuàn requested the provisional establishment of a temporary ancestral temple to facilitate the offering of sacrifices.
9 On the day of Gēngshēn,
Wáng Jiàn appointed Wáng Zōngkǎn, the Juéyúndū Zhī Bīngmǎshǐ, as the Yìngyuánkāixiá Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ,
leading eight thousand troops towards Yúzhōu.
He appointed Wáng Zōngruǎn, the Juéshèngdū Zhī Bīngmǎshǐ, as the Kāijiāng Fángsòng Jìnfèngshǐ,
leading seven thousand troops towards Lúzhōu.
On the day of Xīnyǒu,
Wáng Zōngkǎn captured Yúzhōu
and compelled Cìshǐ Móu Chónghòu to surrender.
On the day of Guǐyǒu,
Wáng Zōngruǎn captured Lúzhōu
and beheaded Cìshǐ Mǎ Jìngrú,
thus opening the gorge route for the first time.
Yúzhōu and Lúzhōu
were both jurisdictions of Dōngchuān.
Wáng Jiàn's ambition was to expand his territory,
using the opening of the gorge route for tribute as a pretext.
The character 趨 (qū)
is pronounced "qī yù" (as a fanqie).
Lǐ Jìzhāo, a general from Fèngxiáng, came to the rescue of Zǐzhōu.
He left a subordinate general to guard Jiànmén.
Wáng Zōngbō, a general from Xīchuān, attacked and captured him.
10On the day of Yǐhài,
Sūn Wò, Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was dismissed from his current official positions.
Zhū Pǔ, Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was dismissed to become Mìshūjiān.
After Pǔ assumed power,
none of his proposals were effective.
Zhū Pǔ boasted that peace could be achieved in a little over a month (see the previous year in the earlier volume).
Mǎ Dàoyīn, Tàizǐ Zhànshì, gained favor with the Emperor through astronomy,
and Xǔ Yánshì, Jiāngzuòjiān, through medicine.
Hán Jiàn falsely accused the two of crimes and had them killed.
He further claimed that Wò and Pǔ had colluded with the two,
hence their dismissal from premiership.
Mǎ Dàoyīn and Xǔ Yánshì were close to the Emperor.
It is certain that the two prime ministers used them to present matters to the Emperor.
This must have happened.
11An edict appointed Yáng Xíngmì as the Jiāngnán Zhūdào Xíngyíng Dūtǒng,
to lead an expedition against Dù Hóng, the Jiédùshǐ of Wǔchāng.
According to Hóng's biography in the *Xīn Shū*,
Hóng had allied himself with Zhū Quánzhōng
and cut off the tribute route from the southeast.
It was for this reason that Yáng Xíngmì was ordered to attack him.
12Zhāng Jí captured Shàozhōu
and apprehended Jiǎng Xūn.
The attack by the Tán soldiers on Jiǎng Xūn began in the first month of the third year (see the earlier volume).
The character 佶 (jí)
is pronounced "jù yǐ" (as a fanqie).
13In the third month,
on the day of Bǐngzǐ,
Zhū Quánzhōng memorialized to appoint Gě Cóngzhōu, the Cìshǐ of Cáozhōu, as Tàiníng Liúhòu;
Zhū Yǒuyù as Tiānpíng Liúhòu;
and Páng Shīgǔ as Wǔníng Liúhòu.
Zhū Quánzhōng memorialized to bestow these three prefectures upon the three generals to build up his faction.
At this time, Huàndé was probably renamed Wǔníng again.
14Wáng Gǒng, the Bǎoyì Jiédùshǐ, attacked Wáng Kē, the Hùguó Jiédùshǐ.
Kē sought assistance from Lǐ Kèyòng,
while Gǒng sought assistance from Zhū Quánzhōng.
Zhāng Cúnjìng and Yáng Shīhòu, generals of Xuānwǔ, defeated the Hézhōng army south of Yīshì.
Lǐ Sìzhāo, a general of Hédōng, defeated the Shǎn army at Yīshì,
and again at Zhāngdiàn,
thus lifting the siege of Hézhōng.
Shīhòu
was from Jīngōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states:
There is Jīngōu Town in Wànshòu County, Yǐngzhōu.
Wànshòu
was Bǎichǐ Town of Rǔyīn County during the Táng dynasty.
The Sòng dynasty established it as a county in the sixth year of Kāibǎo.
He was the adopted son of Lǐ Kèróu, Lǐ Kèyòng's younger brother.
15The Gǎnyì Army was renamed Zhāowǔ,
with its seat of government in Lìzhōu.
Sū Wénjiàn, formerly the Jìngnàn Jiédùshǐ, was appointed as its Jiédùshǐ.
16Summer,
fourth month.
Lǐ Jìtáng, the Tóngzhōu Fángyùshǐ, was appointed Kuāngguó Jiédùshǐ.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Shílù* records:
"Tóngzhōu was granted the title of Kuāngguó Army,
and Lǐ Jìtáng, the Fángyùshǐ, was appointed Kuāngguó Jiédùshǐ."
According to the *Xīn Fāngzhèn Biǎo*,
in the second year of Qiánníng,
Tóngzhōu was granted the title of Kuāngguó Army.
Wáng Xíngyuē had previously served as Kuāngguó Jiédùshǐ.
It seems that after Xíngyuē's death,
Jìtáng was only a Fángyùshǐ,
and now the old name was restored.
He was Mào Zhēn's adopted son.
17Lǐ Xún, Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū, was appointed Liǎngchuān Xuānyùshǐ,
to mediate and reconcile Wáng Jiàn and Gù Yánhuī.
18On the day of Xīnhài,
Qián Liú dispatched Gù Quánwǔ and others to lead three thousand troops from the sea route to relieve Jiāxīng.
On the day of Jǐwèi,
they arrived at the city,
attacked the Huáinán army,
and utterly routed them.
The siege of Jiāxīng by Huáinán began in the second year (see the earlier volume).
19Dù Hóng, being attacked by Yáng Xíngmì,
sought aid from Zhū Quánzhōng.
Zhū Quánzhōng dispatched his general Niè Jīn to raid Sìzhōu,
and Zhū Yǒugōng to attack Huángzhōu.
Yáng Xíngmì dispatched Mǎ Xún and others, the Yòu Hēiyúndū Zhǐhuīshǐ, to relieve Huángzhōu.
Qú Zhāng, the Cìshǐ of Huángzhōu, hearing of Yǒugōng's arrival,
abandoned the city
and led his troops south to secure Wǔchāng Zhài.
Wǔchāng
was an ancient county during the Hàn dynasty.
During the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Èzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: It is one hundred eighty *lǐ* northeast of the prefecture,
and is now established as Shòuchāng Jūn.
20On the day of Guǐhài,
Gù Quánwǔ and other generals from Liǎngzhè defeated eighteen Huáinán encampments
and captured three thousand Huáinán officers and soldiers, including Wèi Yuē.
Tián Yūn, a Huáinán general, was stationed at Yìtíng Dài.
The Liǎngzhè army pursued him, emboldened by their victory.
On the day of Jiǎxū,
Yūn fled back from Húzhōu.
He retreated his army from Jiāxīng,
took the route through Húzhōu,
and returned to Xuānzhōu.
Over a thousand of Yūn's troops died.
21Hán Jiàn harbored ill will towards Zhāng Yī, Xíngbù Shàngshū, and several others.
He falsely accused them in memorials
and had them demoted.
22In the fifth month,
Cuī Hóng, the Fèngguó Jiédùshǐ, was given the additional title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
23On the day of Xīnsì,
Zhū Yǒugōng constructed a pontoon bridge at Fán Gǎng.
Three *lǐ* west of Wǔchāng, there is Fán Shān.
Below the mountain is Fán Xī,
which flows into the river,
called Fánkǒu.
Zhū Yǒugōng probably spanned the river with a pontoon bridge,
reaching Fánkǒu,
to attack Wǔchāng.
On the day of Rénwǔ,
he captured it,
seized Qú Zhāng,
and then took Huángzhōu.
The *Kǎoyì* states: Xuē Jūzhèng's *Wǔdài Shǐ* (Biographies of Liáng) records:
"On Dīngchǒu of the fifth month,
Zhū Yǒugōng sent an envoy to report
that he had thoroughly defeated the Huáinán bandits at Wǔchāng
and recaptured Huángzhōu and Èzhōu."
The *Xīn Jì* records:
"On Rénwǔ,
Zhū Quánzhōng captured Huángzhōu,
and Cìshǐ Qú Zhāng died there."
Zhū Yǒugōng's biography mentions Zhái Zhāng.
The *Shíguó Jìnián* writes Qú Zhāng.
The *Wú Lù* states: "captured Cìshǐ Qú Zhāng,"
which should be reliable.
24On the day of Bǐngxū,
Wáng Jiàn appointed Zhāng Lín, the Jiédù Fùshǐ, to guard Chéngdū.
Zhāng Lín
was Wáng Jiàn's trusted confidant.
When Jiàn attacked Chén Jìngxuān,
he also made him guard Qióngzhōu.
Huá Hóng's name was changed to Wáng Zōngdí.
Huá Hóng had earned merits in numerous battles.
Wáng Jiàn therefore adopted him as a son to harness his strength and utility.
However, the intention to kill Hóng was probably already nascent at this time.
The character 華 (Huá)
is pronounced "hù huà" (as a fanqie).
25In the sixth month,
on the day of Jǐyǒu,
Qián Liú went to Yuèzhōu to receive the Jiédùyuè of Zhèndōng.
26 Lǐ Mào-zhēn (李茂貞) memorialized:
"Wáng Jiàn (王建) attacked Dōng-chuān (東川),
waged war for years,
and did not heed imperial edicts."
How could Wáng Jiàn have only attacked Dōng-chuān!
Many of the prefectures under Lǐ Mào-zhēn's (李茂貞) jurisdiction in Shān-nán (山南)
had also been seized by Jiàn (建);
unable to control him,
[Lǐ Mào-zhēn] wished to use the emperor's decree to confront him.
On the Jiǎ-yín (甲寅) day,
Jiàn (建) was demoted to Southern Prefectural Governor (Nán-zhōu Cì-shǐ 南州刺史).
The New Gazetteer states: In Wǔ-dé (武德) 3rd year,
Qíán-nán (黔南) barbarians were opened up,
and Nán-zhōu (南州) was established.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Nán-zhōu (南州),
in the Warring States period, was part of Bā (巴) state's territory;
during the Qín (秦), it was Bā (巴) Commandery's land;
in the Hàn (漢), it was Jiāng-zhōu (江州) territory.
In Táng (唐) Wǔ-dé (武德) 3rd year,
the eastern boundary of Yú-zhōu (渝州) was demarcated,
and Nán-zhōu (南州) was established.
On the Yǐ-mǎo (乙卯) day,
Mào-zhēn (茂貞) was made Military Governor (Jié-dù-shǐ 節度使) of Xī-chuān (西川).
Qín (覃) Prince Sì-zhōu (嗣周) was made Military Governor (Jié-dù-shǐ 節度使) of Fèng-xiáng (鳳翔).
27 On the Guǐ-hài (癸亥) day,
Wáng Jiàn (王建) captured the southern stockade of Zǐ-zhōu (梓州),
and seized its general Lǐ Jì-níng (李繼寧).
On the Bǐng-yín (丙寅) day,
the Imperial Envoy (Xuān-yù Shǐ 宣諭使) Lǐ Xún (李洵) arrived at Zǐ-zhōu (梓州).
In the 4th month,
Lǐ Xún (李洵) received his commission and set out as envoy,
arriving only in the 6th month.
On the Jǐ-sì (己巳) day,
he met Jiàn (建) at Zhāng-pá (張杷) stockade.
Jiàn (建) pointed to the flag-bearer and said:
"The feelings of the warriors
cannot be suppressed."
28 Qín (覃) Prince went to take up his post,
but Lǐ Mào-zhēn (李茂貞) refused to be relieved.
Given Lǐ Mào-zhēn's (李茂貞) cunning and ferocity,
how could he have been willing to surrender Fèng-xiáng (鳳翔) to another,
and risk danger to contend for Shǔ (蜀)!
29 The Níng-yuǎn (寧遠) Army was established in Róng-zhōu (容州),
with Lǐ Kè-yòng's (李克用) grand general Gài Yù (蓋寓) as its Military Governor (Jié-dù-shǐ 節度使).
When Lǐ Kè-yòng (李克用) pacified Wáng Xíng-yú (王行瑜),
Gài Yù (蓋寓) was given the title of Surveillance Commissioner (Guān-chá-shǐ 觀察使) of Róng-guǎn (容管) for his merits.
Now he was promoted to Military Governor (Jié-dù-shǐ 節度使).
30 In autumn,
7th month,
Chéng Ruì (成汭), Military Governor (Jié-dù-shǐ 節度使) of Jīng-nán (荊南), was additionally appointed Sī-zhōng (侍中).
31 Hán Jiàn (韓建) sent a letter to Lǐ Mào-zhēn (李茂貞);
Mào-zhēn (茂貞) lifted the siege of Fèng-tiān (奉天),
and Qín (覃) Prince returned to Huá-zhōu (華州).
32 Lǐ Jì-huī (李繼徽), Military Governor (Jié-dù-shǐ 節度使) of Tiān-xióng (天雄), was made Military Governor (Jié-dù-shǐ 節度使) of Jìng-nán (靜難).
Lǐ Jì-huī (李繼徽) moved from Qín-zhōu (秦州) to Bīn-zhōu (邠州);
Bīn-níng (邠寧) also fell into Lǐ Mào-zhēn's (李茂貞) possession.
Nán (難) is pronounced dàn (旦).
33 On the Gēng-xū (庚戌) day,
Qián Liú (錢鏐) returned to Háng-zhōu (杭州),
returning to Háng (杭) from Yuè (越).
On the Yǐ-wèi (乙未) day,
Sōng-jiāng (松江) was captured;
Sōng-jiāng (松江) is 40 *lǐ* (里) south of Sū-zhōu (蘇州),
where Huái-nán (淮南) had established a stockade to defend it.
On the Wù-xū (戊戌) day,
Wú-xī (無錫) was captured;
Wú-xī (無錫) was a Hàn (漢) county,
and during the Táng (唐) it belonged to Cháng-zhōu (常州).
The Jiǔ-yù Zhì (九域志) states it is 91 *lǐ* (里) east of the prefecture.
On the Xīn-chǒu (辛丑) day,
Cháng-shú (常熟) and Huá-tíng (華亭) were captured.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Cháng-shú (常熟) County,
from the Later Hàn (後漢) to Wú (吳), was the Captain of Salt Officials (Sī-yán Dū-wèi 司鹽都尉);
in the Jìn (晉), Nán-shā (南沙) County was established;
in the Liáng (梁), Cháng-shú (常熟) County was established.
It is 130 *lǐ* (里) east of the present Kūn-shān (崑山) County;
the old city of Cháng-shú (常熟) is there.
The Jiǔ-yù Zhì (九域志) states it is 75 *lǐ* (里) north of Sū-zhōu (蘇州).
In Tiān-bǎo (天寶) 10th year,
Huá-tíng (華亭) County was established by dividing Jiā-xīng (嘉興),
belonging to Sū-zhōu (蘇州), southwest of the prefecture;
it now belongs to Xiù-zhōu (秀州).
34 Originally,
Lǐ Kè-yòng (李克用) seized Yōu-zhōu (幽州) (see volume 259, Qián-níng (乾寧) 1st year).
He left garrison troops and ten trusted generals to manage its crucial affairs,
and after military provisions, all taxes and levies were sent to Jìn-yáng (晉陽).
When the Emperor went to Huá-zhōu (華州),
Kè-yòng (克用) summoned troops from Rén-gōng (仁恭),
and also sent letters to Wáng Róng (王鎔), Military Governor (Jié-dù-shǐ 節度使) of Chéng-dé (成德), and Wáng Gào (王郜), Military Governor (Jié-dù-shǐ 節度使) of Yì-wǔ (義武),
desiring to join them in pacifying Guān-zhōng (關中)
and escorting the Son of Heaven back to Cháng-ān (長安).
Rén-gōng (仁恭) declined, citing the Khitan invasion,
stating that troops were needed for defense,
and requested to obey the command after the barbarians retreated.
Kè-yòng (克用) repeatedly urged him,
and envoys followed one after another,
but for several months,
no troops were dispatched.
Kè-yòng (克用) sent a letter reproaching him,
whereupon Rén-gōng (仁恭) threw the letter to the ground,
cursed insolently,
imprisoned Kè-yòng's (克用) envoy,
and intended to kill the Hé-dōng (河東) garrison general.
The garrison general fled and escaped harm.
Kè-yòng (克用) left troops to garrison Yōu-zhōu (幽州) (see the previous volume, Qián-níng (乾寧) 2nd year).
In the 8th month,
he personally led an attack on Rén-gōng (仁恭).
Those who planned for Kè-yòng (克用) would have first mobilized the troops of Hé-dōng (河東) to serve the emperor.
After the situation was settled,
then they would have moved forces to Yān (燕) to punish [Rén-gōng (仁恭)].
Where could Liú Rén-gōng (劉仁恭) have escaped his death then!
[Kè-yòng (克用)] did not think of this,
but hastily raised an army out of anger,
and his defeat was thus understandable.
35 The Emperor wished to go to Fèng-tiān (奉天) personally to attack Lǐ Mào-zhēn (李茂貞),
and ordered the chancellors to discuss it.
The chancellors strongly remonstrated,
and so [the plan] was abandoned.
The discussants generally believed that Zhāo-zōng (昭宗) was angry and did not consider the difficulties,
but it was also lamentable.
36 Yán Wáng Jǐepī (戒丕) returned from Jìnyáng (晉陽).
Jǐepī (戒丕) had gone to Jìnyáng (晉陽) to see the emperor, as recorded in the previous year's entry.
"Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
you have had hostile relations with the close輔 (fǔ, 'aides').
The close辅 (fǔ) are
Bīn (邠), Qí (岐), Tóng (同), and Huá (華).
Vicious elements rejoice in misfortune,
causing unrest to the imperial carriage.
Recently, your servant proposed disbanding the military power,
truly fearing unforeseen changes.
Now I hear that Yán Wáng (延王) and Tán Wáng (覃王) still harbor sinister plots.
I wish Your Majesty would make a decisive judgment without hesitation,
to control the situation before it turns chaotic."
The *Zhōu Shū* (周書) says: "Control the governance before it becomes chaotic."
Jiàn (建) submitted this memorial, citing it.
This was Lǐ Jùchuān's (李巨川) statement.
Hán Jiàn (韓建) had long wanted to kill the princes,
but he feared Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用),
and thus dared not act.
Once Yán Wáng (延王) returned,
knowing that Kèyòng's (克用) troops could not reach them,
he decided to press for their execution.
"How could it come to this!"
For several days, there was no reply.
So Jiàn (建), with Zhī Shūmì (知樞密) Liú Jìshù (劉季述), forged an imperial decree and dispatched troops to surround the Sixteen Residences.
The princes disheveled their hair,
some climbing walls,
others scaling roofs,
shouting:
"Your Majesty, save your sons!"
Jiàn (建) herded the eleven princes—Tōng (通), Yí (沂), Mù (睦), Jì (濟), Sháo (韶), Péng (彭), Hán (韓), Chén (陳), Tán (覃), Yán (延), and Dān (丹)—to Shídī Gǔ (石隄谷),
and slaughtered them all.
Shídī Gǔ (石隄谷)
is west of Huázhōu (華州).
Ōuyáng Xiū's (歐陽修) *Jígǔ Lù* (集古錄) states: "The shrine of the princes at Yáo Kēng (殽阬),
now called the Wǔbù Shén Miào (五部神廟),
has statues of Shídī Xīshù Gǔ Wǔlóu Xiānshēng (石隄西戍樹谷五樓先生) and Dōngtái Yùshǐ Wáng Jiǎn Jiāngjūn (東臺御史王剪將軍).
The meaning is unclear.
Its stele says:
'Shídī Shù Gǔ (石隄樹谷),
south to Shāng (商) and Luò (雒).'
It also says:
'In previous generations, it was prosperous,
and officials and common people flourished,
with Yùshǐ Dàfū (御史大夫), generals, and governors.
Thus, a shrine was erected to commemorate their achievements.'
From this, we know that the title Wǔbù (五部)
existed since the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
If so,
then Shídī (石隄)
is the deity of Shídī Gǔ (石隄谷),
one of the Wǔbù Shén (五部神).
Hán Jiàn (韓建) of Táng (唐) killed the princes at Shídī Gǔ (石隄谷),
which is probably this valley."
The Yáo Kēng Shén Cí (殽阬神祠)
is in Zhèngxiàn (鄭縣) of Huázhōu (華州).
*Kǎo Yì* (考異) says: "The Old Annals record:
'On this day,
the eleven princes from Tōng (通) and Tán (覃) downwards, along with their attendants, were all herded by Jiàn's (建) soldiers
to Shídī Gǔ (石隄谷),
and without regard for age,
they were all killed.'"
The Táng (唐) Supplementary Annals record:
"The princes of the Six Residences,
according to previous discussions,
requested to establish a Diànhòu Dū (殿後都, 'rear guard unit').
Hán Jiàn (韓建) resented this and was angry,
submitting a memorial to dispute it,
and he and the princes exchanged criticisms.
The emperor then tied up Hán Wáng (韓王) Kèliáng (克良) and ten others below him and sent them to Hán Jiàn's (韓建) residence.
Jiàn (建) surrounded them with thorn bushes in the main hall,
and for a night did not grant them an audience.
A military official remonstrated,
and so the princes were requested to return to the palace,
and the Diànhòu Dū (殿後都) was disbanded."
The New Annals record:
"In the eighth month,

Hán Jiàn (韓建) killed Tōng Wáng (通王) Zī (滋), Yí Wáng (沂王) Yān (湮), Sháo Wáng (韶王), Péng Wáng (彭王), Sì Hán Wáng (嗣韓王), Sì Chén Wáng (嗣陳王), Sì Tán Wáng (嗣覃王) Sì Zhōu (嗣周), Sì Yán Wáng (嗣延王) Jǐepī (戒丕), and Sì Dān Wáng (嗣丹王) Yǔn (允)."

According to Hán Jiàn's (韓建) memorial in the Old Annals, there were eight people: Mù Wáng (睦王), Jì Wáng (濟王), Sháo Wáng (韶王), Tōng Wáng (通王), Péng Wáng (彭王), Hán Wáng (韓王), Yí Wáng (儀王), and Chén Wáng (陳王).
The New Genealogical Records of the Imperial Clan state that
the emperor initially sent Sì Yán Wáng (嗣延王) Jǐepī (戒丕)
and Sì Dān Wáng (嗣丹王) Yǔn (允) to see Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用),
and there was also Tán Wáng (覃王) Sì Zhōu (嗣周),
making a total of eleven.
The New Annals and biographies
render "Yí" (儀)
as "Yí" (沂).
According to records, Zhāozōng's (昭宗) son Yīn (禋) was enfeoffed as Yí Wáng (沂王),
so another member of the imperial clan should not have been enfeoffed with the same title.
The Yí Wáng (儀王) in the Old Annals
is probably more reliable.
37 Sūn Wò (孫偓), Minister of Rites, was demoted to Sīmǎ (司馬) of Nánzhōu (南州).
Zhū Pò (朱朴), Palace Secretary, was first demoted to Sīmǎ (司馬) of Kuízhōu (夔州), then again demoted to Sīhù (司戶) of Chēnzhōu (郴州).
*Kǎo Yì* (考異) says: "The *Shílù* (實錄) records:
'Pò (朴) was demoted to Sīhù (司戶) of Chēnzhōu (郴州).'"
Xuē Tíngguī's (薛廷珪) written decree for Fènggé (鳳閣) states that Pò (朴) was removed from Bìshū Jiān (祕書監) and appointed Shǔ Wáng Fù (蜀王傅), dividing duties in the eastern capital, saying:
"He harbored designs without regard for imperial regulations,
and sought audiences without authorization from the prime minister's office."
It further says:
"He still hoped for consultations,
coming to disrupt the clear governance."
Another decree demoted him to Sīmǎ (司馬) of Qúzhōu (渠州), saying:
"Remonstrating officials presented memorials,
and the Censorate spoke strongly,
pointing out his rebellious plots
and his resentful and jealous schemes to promote corruption."
This differs somewhat.
We follow the *Shílù* (實錄) here.
Hé Yíng (何迎) was rapidly promoted to Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū (右諫議大夫),
but at this time was also demoted to Sīmǎ (司馬) of Húzhōu (湖州).
Hé Yíng (何迎) had recommended Zhū Pò (朱朴) to the emperor, as recorded in the previous year's entry.
38 Zhōng Chuán (鍾傳) wished to attack Zhōu Bèi (周琲), Governor of Jízhōu (吉州), who was from Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Bèi (琲) led his followers to flee to Guǎnglíng (廣陵).
Bèi (琲) is pronounced [AS-FE4A] [AS-FBED] in one transcription,
and also Pú Mèi (蒲昧).
Shuài (帥)
is read as Shuài (率).
39 Wáng Jiàn (王建) fought Gù Yànhuī (顧彥暉) in over fifty battles.
In the ninth month, on the day *Guǐ Yǒu* (癸酉), the first day of the month,
he besieged Zǐzhōu (梓州).
Zhōu Déquán (周德權), Governor of Shǔzhōu (蜀州), said to Jiàn (建):
"Your Excellency has contended with Yànhuī (彥暉) for Dōngchuān (東川) for three years.
The soldiers are exhausted by arrows and stones,
and the common people are burdened by transport.
The bandits in Dōngchuān (東川) occupy many prefectures and counties.
Yànhuī (彥暉) is weak and without strategy.
Desiring a temporary peace,
he entices them with great benefits,
relying on their aid,
and thus holds firm and does not surrender.
If we now send people to convey fortune and misfortune to these bandit leaders,
rewarding those who come with official positions
and threatening those who do not submit with military force,
then that which he relies on
will instead be used by us."
Jiàn (建) followed this advice,
and Yànhuī's (彥暉) position became increasingly isolated.
Déquán (德權) was from Xǔzhōu (許州).
40 On the day *Dīng Chǒu* (丁丑),
Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) arrived at Ānsài Jūn (安塞軍).
Ānsài Jūn (安塞軍) is east of Wèizhōu (蔚州)
and west of Guīzhōu (媯州).
The New Gazetteer states: "Southwest of Dīnglíng Chuān (丁零川) in Yōuzhōu (幽州) is Ānsài Jūn (安塞軍)."
On *Xīn Sì* (辛巳),
he attacked it.
Dān Kějí (單可及), a general from Yōuzhōu (幽州), led cavalry there.
Kèyòng (克用) was drinking wine,
and the vanguard reported:
"The enemy is here!"
Kèyòng (克用), drunk, said:
"Where is Rén'gōng (仁恭)?"
The reply was:
"Only Kějí (可及) and his like are seen."
Kèyòng (克用) glared and said:
"What are Kějí (可及) and his like as enemies!"
He immediately ordered an attack.
On that day, there was a heavy fog,
making it impossible to distinguish people.
Yáng Shīkǎn (楊師侃), a Yōuzhōu (幽州) general, ambushed troops at Mùguā Jiàn (木瓜澗).
According to the New Book,
Mùguā Jiàn (木瓜澗) is also within Wèizhōu (蔚州) territory.
More than half were lost.
Historians say that Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) underestimated the enemy
and also did not have the right weather conditions,
hence his defeat.
The Yōuzhōu (幽zhou) troops withdrew.
Historians say that Kèyòng (克用) survived his defeat by Heaven's will.
He reproached his generals Lǐ Cúnxìn (李存信) and others, saying:
"I neglected matters due to drunkenness,
but why did you not strongly remonstrate!"
The rebellion of Xíngzhōu (邢州),
the rout at Shēnxian (莘縣),
and the defeat at Mùguā Jiàn (木瓜澗)
were all Lǐ Cúnxìn's (李存信) fault.
Yet Kèyòng (克用) continued to trust and employ him,
which can be called a failure in administering justice.
41 Lǐ Yànhuī (李彥徽), Governor of Húzhōu (湖州), wished to attach the prefecture to Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密).
Last year, Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) had recommended Yànhuī (彥徽) to govern Húzhōu (湖州), hence his desire to attach to him.
Yànhuī (彥徽) fled to Guǎnglíng (廣陵),
and Shěn Yōu (沈攸), the commander-in-chief, returned the prefecture to Qián Liú (錢鏐).
From this point, Qián Liú (錢鏐) acquired Húzhōu (湖州).
42 Zhāng Lián (張璉), Jiedushi of Zhāngyì (彰義), was appointed Commander of the Northwest Expeditionary Forces of Fèngxiáng (鳳翔),
to attack Lǐ Màozhēn (李茂貞).
43. Then, Wáng Jiàn was again appointed as Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Xīchuān and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
Wáng Gǎo, Jìedùshǐ of Yìwǔ, was promoted to Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Lǐ Màozhēn, the new Jìedùshǐ of Xīchuān, was stripped of his official titles and ranks,
and his name was reverted to Sòng Wéntōng.
Initially, at Lǐ Màozhēn’s request, Wáng Jiàn was attacked;
but later, because Màozhēn defied orders,
Wáng Jiàn was pardoned and Màozhēn was attacked instead.
The imperial court's decrees,
issued in the morning, were changed by evening.
Which of the regional lords would then respect and trust them?
The imperial prestige was not upheld;
this was self-inflicted.
Lǐ Màozhēn being granted his original name is seen in volume 256, Guāngqǐ (光啟) second year.
44. After Zhū Quánzhōng acquired Yǎn and Yùn,
his army and weapons became even stronger.
He then launched a major attack on Yáng Xíngmì,
sending Páng Shīgǔ with seventy thousand troops from Xú, Sù, Sòng, and Huá to encamp at Qīngkǒu.
Qīngkǒu
is the present-day Qīnghékǒu.
Gě Cóngzhōu encamped at Ānfēng with troops from Yǎn, Yùn, Cáo, and Pú,
intending to march towards Shòuzhōu.
Ānfēng
was one of the six counties of the Hàn dynasty;
its old city was south of the county.
The Later Hàn established Ānfēng County.
By the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Shòuzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: Ānfēng County
is over sixty *lǐ* southeast of the prefecture.
The Shòuzhōu of the Táng dynasty
was administered from Shòuchūn County,
which was the Shòuyáng (壽陽) area during the Six Dynasties.
Towards the end of the Five Dynasties,
Zhōu Shìzōng conquered Shòuzhōu
and moved its administration to Xiàcài.
Therefore, the Sòng dynasty’s Ānfēng was southeast of Shòuzhōu.
Huáinán was shaken with fear.
45. Lǐ Jìtáng, Jìedùshǐ of Kuāngguó, heard that the court was attacking Lǐ Màozhēn and became afraid.
Hán Jiàn further instigated him,
and Jìtáng fled to Fèngxiáng.
In winter,
tenth month,
Jiàn was appointed Jìedùshǐ of both the Zhènguó and Kuāngguó armies.
Hán Jiàn now held both Tóng and Huá.
46. On the day *Rénzǐ*,
Hóu Shào, Prefect of Suìzhōu, led a force of twenty thousand.
On the day *Yǐmǎo*,
Wáng Rénwēi, Prefect of Hézhōu, led a force of one thousand.
On the day *Wùwǔ*,
Lǐ Jìpǔ from Fèngxiáng brought two thousand relief troops.
All surrendered to Wáng Jiàn.
Jiàn's assault on Zǐzhōu became more urgent.
On the day *Gēngshēn*,
Gù Yánhuī gathered his clan and adopted sons for a communal drink.
He sent Wáng Zōngbì to surrender to Jiàn.
(Wáng Zōngbì being captured by the Dōngchuān (東川) army is mentioned in the previous volume, second year.)
He ordered his adopted son Yáo to kill him and those drinking with him,
then Yáo committed suicide.
In the third year of Xīzōng's Guāngqǐ reign,
Gù Yánlǎng obtained Dōngchuān,
which passed to his younger brother Yánhuī,
and was now destroyed.
In the second year of Qiánníng (乾寧),
Wáng Jiàn began attacking Dōngchuān,
and it took three years to conquer it.
Jiàn ordered Wáng Zōngwǎn to lead a detachment to raid Chāng, Pǔ, and other prefectures,
and appointed Wáng Zōngdí as Acting Prefect of Dōngchuān.
47. Liú Réngōng submitted a memorial stating:
"Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) causelessly raised an army to attack me.
My forces utterly defeated his party at Mùguājiàn (木瓜澗).
I request to personally lead the army to attack Kèyòng."
An imperial edict denied this.
He also sent a letter to Zhū Quánzhōng.
Quánzhōng memorialized to promote Réngōng to Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and the court assented.
Réngōng then sent an envoy to thank Kèyòng,
expressing his uneasiness about leaving or staying.
Kèyòng's reply briefly stated:
"Now you wield authority, command troops,
govern the people, and legislate;
when you promote scholars, you expect them to repay your kindness, and when you select generals, you hope they will reciprocate your favors.
If you yourself do not adhere to this,
how can others be trusted?
Kèyòng meant that just as Réngōng betrayed him,
others would also betray Réngōng.
The character '將' (jiāng),
is pronounced *liàng* (亮).
Suspicion and jealousy arise from within the private chambers.
One holds a *Gānjiàng* (干將) sword but dares not bestow it upon others;
one holds a covenant tablet, but what words can one inscribe as an oath?"
48. On the day *Jiǎzǐ*,
Imperial Prince Mì was established as Jǐngwáng (景王),
Zuò as Huīwáng (輝王),
and Qí as Qíwáng (祁王).
49. Zhāng Lián, Jìedùshǐ of Zhāngyì, was promoted to Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
50. Yáng Xíngmì and Zhū Jǐn led thirty thousand troops to resist the Biàn army at Chǔzhōu.
Another general, Zhāng Xùn, brought troops from Liánshuǐ to join them.
(In the second year of Qiánníng,
Yáng Xíngmì first captured Liánshuǐ and ordered Zhāng Xùn to guard it.)
Páng Shīgǔ encamped at Qīngkǒu.
Someone said:
"The encampment ground is low-lying
and cannot be occupied for long."
He did not listen.
Shīgǔ, relying on his numerous troops, underestimated the enemy
and often played *yìqí* (弈棊).
Zhū Jǐn blocked the upper reaches of the Huái River,
intending to flood the camp.
Someone reported this to Shīgǔ,
but Shīgǔ considered it misleading the troops
and had him executed.
In the eleventh month,
on the day *Guǐyǒu*,
Jǐn and the Huáinán general Hóu Zàn
led five thousand cavalry in a covert crossing of the Huái,
using Biàn (汴) banners.
They approached his central army from the north.
Zhāng Xùn broke through the stockade and entered.
The soldiers were thrown into disarray and resisted the attack.
The Huái River waters rose greatly,
and the Biàn army was terrified and chaotic.
Xíngmì led his main army across the Huái
and attacked them from both sides with Jǐn and others.
The Biàn army was utterly defeated.
Shīgǔ and over ten thousand heads of officers and soldiers were beheaded,
and the remaining troops scattered.
Gě Cóngzhōu was encamped northwest of Shòuzhōu.
Zhū Yánshòu, Tuanlian envoy of Shòuzhōu,
attacked and defeated him.
He retreated and garrisoned at Háozhōu,
but upon hearing of Shīgǔ's defeat,
he fled back.
Xíngmì, Jǐn, and Yánshòu pursued them, capitalizing on their victory,
and caught up at the Pèishuǐ.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註) states: The Pèishuǐ originates southwest of Lújiāng (廬江) Qiánxiàn (潛縣),
northeast of Huòshān (霍山),
then flows northeast past the east of Liùxiàn (六縣),
then northwest past the west of the old city of Ānfēng County,
and north into the Huái River.
The Lèipiān (類篇) states: Pèi (淠),
pronounced *bìzhìqiè*,
a river name,
in Yìyáng.
According to current records, the Pèi River is ten *lǐ* west of Láiyuǎn (來遠) Town.
Láiyuǎn Town is the same as Dōngzhèngyáng (東正陽),
two hundred *lǐ* east of Shòuzhōu.
The Huáinán army attacked them,
killing and drowning almost all of them.
Cóngzhōu escaped.
Niú Cúnjié, Commander of the Rear Troops, dismounted and fought on foot,
allowing the various armies to cross the Huái.
They went without food for four days,
and encountered heavy snow.
Biàn soldiers froze and starved to death along the road;
fewer than a thousand returned.
Quánzhōng, upon hearing of the defeat,
also fled back.
Xíngmì sent a letter to Quánzhōng saying:
"Páng Shīgǔ and Gě Cóngzhōu are not worthy opponents.
You should come to the Huái River yourself for a decisive battle."
Xíngmì held a grand assembly of his generals
and said to his acting military commissioner, Lǐ Chéngsì:
"Initially, I wanted to head for Shòuzhōu first,
but you said it was better to go to Qīngkǒu first.
If Shīgǔ were defeated,
Cóngzhōu would flee on his own.
Now it has turned out exactly as you predicted."
He rewarded him with ten thousand *mín* of cash,
rewarding his accurate prior calculation.
Xíngmì treated Chéngsì and Shǐ Yǎn very generously,
bestowing upon them the best residences and concubines.
Therefore, the two men served Xíngmì with all their might,
repeatedly achieving merit,
and eventually died in Huáinán.
Xíngmì thereby secured control over the area between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
and Quánzhōng could not contend with him.
51. On the day *Wùyín*,
Lady Hé, a consort, was established as empress.
The empress was from Dōngchuān,
and gave birth to Dèwáng (德王) and Huīwáng.
52. Wáng Cháo, Jìedùshǐ of Wēiwǔ, had a younger brother, Shěnzhī,
who was Deputy Surveillance Commissioner.
He made a mistake,
and Cháo still flogged him,
but Shěnzhī showed no resentment.
When Cháo became critically ill,
he passed over his sons Yánxīng, Yánhóng, Yánfēng, and Yánxiū,
and ordered Shěnzhī to take charge of military affairs.
In the twelfth month,
on the day *Dīngwèi*,
Cháo died.
Shěnzhī offered to yield to his elder brother, Shěn Guī, Prefect of Quánzhōu.
Shěn Guī, recognizing Shěnzhī’s merits,
declined the offer.
Shěnzhī then styled himself Acting Prefect of Fújiàn
and memorialized to the imperial court.
On the day *rénxū*,
Wáng Jiàn returned from Zǐzhōu.
On the day *wùchén*,
he arrived at Chéngdū.
That year,
Shùnhuà, the *Piaoxin* of Nánzhāo, sent a letter box to the emperor and a *dūshuǎng* decree in a wooden clip to the Central Secretariat,
using the reign title Zhōngxīng.
The imperial court wanted to respond with an imperial edict.
Wáng Jiàn submitted a memorial, saying:
"Nánzhāo is a minor barbarian tribe,
not worthy of an imperial edict.
With your servant in the southwest,
they will surely not dare to violate the frontier."
This was adopted.
Between Lízhōu and Yǎzhōu, there were "shallow barbarians" named Liú Wáng, Hǎo Wáng, and Yáng Wáng,
each with their own tribe.
The long valleys in the great mountains southwest of Lízhōu and Yǎzhōu
were all inhabited by barbarians,
their locations being deep and remote.
However, the three kings' tribes resided close to the Hàn border,
hence they were called "shallow barbarians."
They were sent to scout Nánzhāo,
and they also accepted bribes from Nánzhāo to spy on the situation in Chéngdū.
Whenever a *jiédùshǐ* arrived in office,
the three kings would lead their chieftains to the prefecture.
The *jiédùshǐ* would attribute this to his own prestige and virtue,
reporting it to the imperial court.
However, the three kings secretly colluded with the grand generals.
If a *jiédùshǐ* displeased a grand general,
the grand general would incite the various barbarians to cause disturbances.
Previously, most *jiédùshǐ* were civil officials
who did not wish to stir up trouble,
so the grand generals often used this to demand appeasement,
and Nánzhāo also relied on them to repeatedly cause border troubles.
When Wáng Jiàn garrisoned Xīchuān,
he cut off their old allowances
and executed the *dōu yáyá* Shān Xíngzhāng to punish them.
Shān Xíngzhāng was
an old general of Chén and Tián.
Wáng Jiàn executed him because of his collusion with the shallow barbarians,
both to demonstrate his might to the various barbarians
and to completely remove old problems.
No watchtowers were set up, and no soldiers were garrisoned.
This refers to the area south of Qióngláiguān.
Later, he dispatched Wáng Zōngbò to attack Nánzhāo,
and the three kings leaked military intelligence.
They were summoned and executed.
The historian says that the art of pacifying the borders
lies solely in thoroughly understanding the true nature of the barbarian tribes near the frontier and thwarting their treachery,
then foreign barbarians will not dare to insult or move.
Zhāng Dàogǔ, the Right *Shíyí*, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The state faces five dangers and two disorders.
In ancient times, Emperor Wén of Hàn, soon after ascending the throne,
became thoroughly familiar with state affairs.
Now Your Majesty has been on the throne for ten years."
(Emperor Wén of Dé ascended the throne in the first year of Dé,
making it ten years by this point;
if counted by changing the reign title the year after ascending,
it would be nine years.)
"Emperor Tàizōng internally pacified the Central Plains
and externally opened up the four barbarian regions,
and countries beyond the seas
all submitted as vassals.
Now, the former dynasty's territory has shrunk almost completely.
Although your servant is humble,
I secretly grieve that Your Majesty's court and state have first been manipulated by treacherous officials
and will ultimately be possessed by rebel officials!"
The fall of Hàn and Táng
truly resembled Zhāng Dàogǔ's words.
Dàogǔ was demoted to *Sìhù* of Shīzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Shīzhōu
was the land of Wūxiàn in Hàn.
Emperor Dà of Wú divided Wūxiàn to establish Shāqúxiàn.
In the third year of Jiàndé of the Later Zhōu, Shīzhōu was established here.
Táng followed this.
Old records state: Shīzhōu is
2709 *lǐ* south of the capital.
This was proclaimed to the remonstrating officials.
Zhaozōng, in the midst of hardship and danger,
still punished those who spoke out,
so his downfall was fitting.
He was a native of Qīngzhōu.
This is the only instance of Zhāng Dàogǔ appearing in the *Tōngjiàn*;
his place of origin is noted,
probably out of lament.
The first year of Guānghuà
(In the eighth month of this year, he returned to the capital,
then the reign title was changed.)
1. Spring,
first month.
Zuǒzhè, Jiāngxī, Wǔchāng, and Zīqīng each sent envoys to the imperial court
to request Zhū Quánzhōng be made *dū tǒng*
to suppress Yáng Xíngmì.
Qián Liú of Zuǒzhè,
Zhōng Chuán of Jiāngxī,
Dù Hóng of Wǔchāng,
and Wáng Shīfàn of Zīqīng
all feared Yáng Xíngmì's strength
and thus aligned with Zhū Quánzhōng.
2. Wáng Shīfàn, *Jiédùshǐ* of Pínglú, was granted the additional title of *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*.
Zīqīng was the Pínglú Army.
3. Liú Chóngwàng, *Shàngshū* of the Ministry of War, was made *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*
and concurrently *Jiédùshǐ* of Dōngchuān.
Fény Hángxí, *Fángyùshǐ* of Zhāoxìn, was made *Jiédùshǐ* of Zhāoxìn.
(According to the "Table of Frontier Prefectures," the *Fángyùshǐ* of Zhāoxìn was established in the first year of Guānghuà,
with its seat in Jīnzhōu,
which differs from this account.)
4. An imperial edict was issued acknowledging faults and ceasing military action,
restoring Lǐ Màozhēn's name, office, and rank.
All troops from various circuits sent to attack Fèngxiáng were disbanded.
This was Hán Jiàn's intention.
5. On the day *rénchén*,
Wáng Kē, *Jiédùshǐ* of Hézhōng, personally went to Jìnyáng to welcome him.
Lǐ Kèyòng sent his general Lǐ Sìzhāo to guard Hézhōng.
6. Lǐ Màozhēn and Hán Jiàn both sent letters to Lǐ Kèyòng,
stating that the imperial carriage had been away from the capital for years,
requesting reconciliation and joint support for the imperial house,
and also requesting craftsmen to help repair the palaces.
Kèyòng agreed.
7. Originally,
when Wáng Jiàn attacked Dōngchuān,
Gù Yànhuī sought aid from Lǐ Màozhēn.
Màozhēn ordered his generals to lead troops to rescue him;
this event is mentioned above.
(They falsely claimed to have changed their ways
and would jointly support the Son of Heaven with Hán Jiàn.
When they heard that Zhū Quánzhōng was constructing palaces in Luòyáng
and repeatedly memorialized to welcome the imperial carriage,
Màozhēn and Hán Jiàn became fearful.
They requested to repair the palaces and return the emperor to Cháng'ān.
An edict appointed Hán Jiàn as the commissioner for repairing the palaces.)
(The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
"Jiàn, seeing the temporary palace was humble and low
and lacked a place for viewing,
memorialized to offer his villa south of the city.
Jiàn initially repaired the southern estate,
built towers and observatories,
and dug ponds,
intending to make it a southern inner court
and perform acts of deposition and establishment.
His uncle Fēng, seeing his arrogance,
said to Jiàn:
'You are merely a commoner from Chén and Xǔ.
Taking advantage of the times of chaos and danger,
you have reached the position of a regional commander.
You cannot be grateful for the kindness of your sovereign and father,
but instead wish to carry out deposition and establishment with the hundred *lǐ* of land in Tóngzhōu and Huázhou.
Your family's destruction is imminent.
I would rather take my own life first
to avoid being implicated by you.'
From this, Jiàn slightly mitigated his ambition.
When Lǐ Màozhēn memorialized requesting assistance in building palaces and gardens,
and also heard that Zhū Quánzhōng was renovating Luòyáng
and repeatedly memorializing to welcome the imperial carriage,
Jiàn became fearful.
Therefore, he urgently undertook the repair of Cháng'ān,
led the various circuits to assist in the work,
and personally supervised the progress.")
(My opinion: If Jiàn wished to depose and establish,
why would he first build a southern inner court?
This is not accepted here.)
Jiàn ordered the *dūjiāng* Cài Jìngsī to supervise the work.
After its completion,
in the second month,
Jiàn personally went to inspect it.
8. Qián Liú requested to move the Zhènhǎi Army to Hángzhōu.
This was granted.
The Zhènhǎi Army was originally based in Rùnzhōu;
now the army designation was moved to Hángzhōu.
9. Lǐ Màozhēn was reinstated as *Jiédùshǐ* of Fèngxiáng.
10. Third month.
On the day *jǐchǒu*,
Wáng Shěnzhi was appointed Acting *Liúhòu* of Wēiwǔ.
11 Zhū Quánzhōng dispatched Vice-envoy Wànnián Wéi Zhèn to report on affairs,
requesting to concurrently govern Tiānpíng Circuit.
The imperial court did not grant this at first,
but Wéi Zhèn forcefully argued for it.
After Mùzōng and Jìngzōng,
imperial authority had already weakened,
yet the officers sent by the fānzhèn to report to the court dared not argue forcefully before the court.
Zhū Quánzhōng was appointed Military Governor of the Xuānwǔ, Xuānyì, and Tiānpíng Circuits.
Zhū Quánzhōng appointed Wéi Zhèn as Acting Military Governor of Tiānpíng,
and former Tái Zhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Zhèn as Vice Military Governor of Tiānpíng.
According to Ōuyáng Xiū's history, in Lǐ Zhèn's biography,
Lǐ Zhèn was a Jīnwú Wèi Jiāngjūn,
and was appointed Tái Zhōu Cìshǐ.
Bandits rose in Zhèdōng,
so he did not proceed to his post.
Instead, he returned west, passing through Biàn,
and presented a strategy to Zhū Quánzhōng.
Zhū Quánzhōng retained him,
and he was subsequently employed by Zhū Quánzhōng.
He was Lǐ Bǎozhēn's great-grandson.
Between Dàizōng and Dézōng's reigns,
Lǐ Bǎozhēn governed Zhāoyì Circuit
and achieved great merit.
12 Huáinán general Zhōu Běn rescued Sū Zhōu,
but he was defeated by Liǎngzhè general Gù Quánwǔ.
Huáinán general Qín Péi, with three thousand soldiers, captured Kūnshān and garrisoned it.
Kūnshān
was formerly the land of Hàn Lóu Xiàn.
The Liáng dynasty divided Lóu Xiàn to establish Xìnyì Xiàn,
and then divided Xìnyì to establish Kūnshān Xiàn,
named after Kūnshān Mountain within its borders.
In the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Sū Zhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states
it was seventy *lǐ* east of the prefecture.
13 Mǎ Yīn, the Cìshǐ of Tán Zhōu and Administrator of the Húnán Military Headquarters, was appointed Acting Military Governor of Wǔ'ān Circuit.
At that time, within Húnán's seven prefectures,
the bandit chief Yáng Shīyuǎn occupied Héng Zhōu,
Táng Shìmín occupied Yǒng Zhōu,
Cài Jié occupied Dào Zhōu,
Chén Yànqiān occupied Chén Zhōu,
Lǔ Jǐngrén occupied Lián Zhōu,
and the Lù Zhèn Jiǔguó Zhì states: Táng Mín and Cài Jié both gathered local people to occupy their prefectures.
Chén Yànqiān, a Guìyáng native,
killed Cìshǐ Huáng Yuè
and occupied Chén Zhōu.
Lǔ Jǐngrén originally followed Huáng Cháo,
but was left in Lián Zhōu due to illness
and subsequently occupied it.
Shuài,
pronounced like suǒ lèi fān.
Chén,
pronounced like chǒu lín fān.
This laid the groundwork for Mǎ Yīn to conquer all these prefectures.
14 Lú Yànwēi, Military Governor of Yìchāng Circuit,
was cruel and tyrannical,
and also disrespectful to neighboring circuits.
He quarreled with Liú Rén'gōng, Military Governor of Lúlóng Circuit, over salt profits.
Liú Rén'gōng dispatched his son Liú Shǒuwén to lead troops to attack Cāng Zhōu.
Lú Yànwēi abandoned the city
and fled with his family to Wèi Zhōu.
Luó Hóngxìn did not admit him,
so he fled to Biàn Zhōu.
In the first year of Guāngqǐ (885),
Lú Yànwēi obtained Cāng and Jǐng,
and now perished.
Liú Shǒuwén was appointed Acting Military Governor of Yìchāng.
Liú Rén'gōng's military power became increasingly formidable,
having combined the forces of Yōu and Cāng circuits,
hence his power grew.
He harbored ambitions to annex Héshuò
and requested the imperial insignia for Liú Shǒuwén,
but the court had not yet approved.
When an imperial envoy arrived in Fányáng,
Liú Rén'gōng told him:
"I will obtain the insignia myself,
I merely desire the genuine article from Cháng'ān;
why repeatedly refuse my petitions!
Tell them that for me!"
His defiance and arrogance were thus.
15 Zhū Quánzhōng and Liú Rén'gōng established good relations
and together, the Wèibó army attacked Lǐ Kèyòng.
Summer,
Fourth month,
on the *dīngwèi* day,
Zhū Quánzhōng arrived beneath Jùlù city,
defeated over ten thousand Hédōng soldiers,
and pursued the fleeing enemy to Qīngshān Pass.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Xíng Zhōu Lónggāng Xiàn,
Suí Wéndì established Qīngshān Xiàn in the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng (596),
Suí Yángdì abolished it and merged it into Lónggāng at the beginning of Dàyè (605).
Bèi,
pronounced like bǔ mài fān.
16 Wáng Kē, Military Governor of Hùguó Circuit, was given the concurrent title of Shìzhōng.
17 On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Zhū Quánzhōng dispatched Gě Cóngzhōu to divide his troops and attack Míng Zhōu.
On the *wùchén* day,
he captured it
and beheaded Cìshǐ Xíng Shànyì.
18 Fifth month,
on the *jǐsì* day, the first day of the month,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
19 Gě Cóngzhōu attacked Xíng Zhōu,
and Cìshǐ Mǎ Shīshù abandoned the city and fled.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
Cí Zhōu Cìshǐ Yuán Fèngchén committed suicide.
Zhū Quánzhōng appointed Gě Cóngzhōu as Acting Military Governor of Zhāoyì,
to defend the three prefectures of Xíng, Míng, and Cí, and then returned.
From then on, Bìng and Biàn annually contended for the three prefectures of Xíng, Míng, and Cí.
20 Lǐ Jìmì, Military Governor of Wǔdìng Circuit, was appointed Military Governor of Shānnán Xīdào Circuit.
Lǐ Jìmì moved from Yáng Zhōu to Xīngyuán.
21 The imperial court heard that Wáng Jiàn had already appointed Wáng Zōngdí as Acting Military Governor of Dōngchuān,
so it recalled Liú Chóngwàng
to be Bīngbù Shàngshū,
and still appointed Wáng Zōngdí as Acting Military Governor.
22 Húnán general Yáo Yànzhāng spoke to Mǎ Yīn,
requesting to take the five prefectures of Héng, Yǒng, Dào, Lián, and Chén,
and also recommended Lǐ Qióng as a general.
Mǎ Yīn appointed Lǐ Qióng and Qín Yànhuī as Youyì Envoys for the seven prefectures north of the ridge,
with Zhāng Túyīng and Lǐ Táng as their deputies.
The five prefectures, together with Tán and Shào, make seven.
They beheaded Yáng Shīyuǎn,
led their troops towards Yǒng Zhōu,
besieged it for over a month,
and Táng Shìmín fled and died.
Mǎ Yīn appointed Lǐ Táng as Yǒng Zhōu Cìshǐ.
23 Sixth month,
Zhào Xǔ, Cìshǐ of Háo Zhōu, was appointed Military Governor of Zhōngwǔ Circuit.
Zhào Xǔ
was the younger brother of Zhào Chóu.
24 Autumn,
Seventh month,
Léi Mǎn, Military Governor of Wǔzhēn Circuit, was given the concurrent title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
The Fāngzhèn Biǎo states: In the first year of Guānghuà (898),
Wǔzhēn Circuit was established,
administering Lǐ, Lǎng, and Xù three prefectures,
with its seat in Lǐ Zhōu.
25 Zhào Kuāngníng, Military Governor of Zhōngyì Circuit, heard of Zhū Quánzhōng's defeat at Qīngkǒu.
Zhōngyì Army was Shānnán Dōngdào.
The defeat at Qīngkǒu was in November of the previous year.
Zhū Quánzhōng dispatched Wèishì Shú Cóng, Cìshǐ of Sù Zhōu, to lead troops to attack him.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
they captured Táng Zhōu,
seized Zhào Kuānglín, Cìshǐ of Suí Zhōu,
and defeated Xiāng Zhōu troops at Dèngchéng.
26 Eighth month,
on the *gēngxū* day,
Huá Zhōu was renamed Xīngdé Fǔ.
This was because the imperial carriage had been stationed there.
27 On the *wùwǔ* day,
Biàn general Kāng Huáizhēn attacked Dèng Zhōu,
captured it,
and seized Cìshǐ Guó Xiāng.
Zhào Kuāngníng, in fear,
sent an envoy to submit to Zhū Quánzhōng,
and Zhū Quánzhōng accepted.
This laid the groundwork for Zhū Quánzhōng to attack Zhào Kuāngníng again.
28 On the *jǐwèi* day,
the imperial carriage departed Huá Zhōu.
On the *rénxū* day,
it arrived in Cháng'ān.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm,
and the reign era was changed.
The reign era was changed to Guānghuà.
The Emperor desired the fānzhèn to live together in harmony,
and appointed Zhāng Yǒufú, Tutor to the Heir Apparent, as Pacification Commissioner for Hédōng and Biàn Zhōu.
He bestowed an imperial edict upon Lǐ Kèyòng and Zhū Quánzhōng,
and also ordered the chancellors to write to them,
to make them reconcile.
Lǐ Kèyòng wished to obey the edict,
but was ashamed to humble himself first,
so he sent a letter to Wáng Róng,
asking him to communicate with Zhū Quánzhōng.
Zhū Quánzhōng did not comply.
Zhū Quánzhōng's military power was strong at the time,
hence he did not comply.
29 Ninth month,
on the *yǐhài* day,
Hán Jiàn was promoted to Protector Grand Tutor and Prefect of Xīngdé.
Earlier,
the Emperor had been stationed in Huá Zhōu,
and consequently Huá Zhōu was made Xīngdé Fǔ.
Luó Hóngxìn was made Protector Shìzhōng.
30 On the *jǐchǒu* day,
Wáng Zōngdí, Acting Military Governor of Dōngchuān, spoke to Wáng Jiàn,
saying that Dōngchuān's territory was five thousand *lǐ* in extent,
and the exchange of official documents often took several months.
He requested that the five prefectures of Suí, Hé, Lú, Yú, and Chāng be separated to form another circuit.
Wáng Jiàn reported this to the court.
31 Gù Quánwǔ (顧全wǔ) attacked Sūzhōu (蘇州);
the city and the relief troops all ran out of food.
On the jiǎshēn (甲申) day,
Tái Méng (臺濛), the Sūzhōu (蘇州) Cìshǐ (刺史) appointed by Huáinán (淮南), abandoned the city and fled.
A city of gold and a moat of boiling water
cannot be held without grain.
Though Tái Méng (臺濛) was a good general from Huáinán (淮南),
what could he do?
Quánwǔ (全武) conquered Sūzhōu (蘇州).
In the third year of Qiánníng (乾寧) [896 CE],
Huáinán (淮南) captured Sūzhōu (蘇州).
Now, it truly is as Gù Quánwǔ (顧全武) said, and it has been restored.
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: Wúxī (無錫) County, Chángzhōu (常州), has Wàngtíng (望亭) Town,
which is forty-five lǐ (里) north of Sūzhōu (蘇州),
and another forty-five lǐ (里) to Wúxī (無錫).
Bài (敗),
read bǔ mài (補邁).
Quánwǔ (全武) led over ten thousand men to attack it;
Péi (裴) frequently sallied out to fight,
making the sick don armor and wield spears,
and the strong draw bows and crossbows.
Quánwǔ (全武) was repeatedly forced to retreat by them.
Seeing the power and range of their bows and crossbows,
he therefore retreated.
Gòu (彀),
read jū hòu (居候).
Wèi (為),
read yú wěi (于偽).
Quánwǔ (全武) had once been a monk.
Péi (裴) sent a sealed letter to surrender.
Quánwǔ (全武) was pleased,
and summoned his generals to open the letter.
It was a scroll of Buddhist scriptures.
Quánwǔ (全武) was greatly ashamed,
and said:
"Péi (裴) doesn't fear death,
how can he have time to play tricks on me!"
He reinforced his troops and attacked the city,
diverting water to flood it.
The city wall broke,
food ran out,
and Péi (裴) then surrendered. [43)Qián Liú (錢鏐) prepared a feast for a thousand people to await him.
Then he came out.
"Nǎi (乃)"
should be
【Zhāng (章): The Yǐ (乙) eleven-line edition correctly writes
Looking at the preceding text of the Tōngjiàn (通鑑),
Qín Péi (秦裴) took Kūnshān (崑山) with three thousand men and defended it.
When he surrendered,
his emaciated soldiers numbered less than a hundred.
This means that almost all of his soldiers died in battle and defense,
and those who survived were barely one-thirtieth.
"So weak,
how dare he stubbornly resist for long!"
Lǚ (旅),
means multitude.
Relying on a multitude to resist and defend
is called lǚjù (旅拒).
"Péi (裴) will not betray Lord Yáng (楊公);
now his strength is exhausted and he surrenders,
it is not a surrender from the heart."
Liú (鏐) praised his words.
Gù Quánwǔ (顧全武) also advised Liú (鏐) to pardon him.
Liú (鏐) agreed.
People at the time called Quánwǔ (全武) a zhǎngzhě (長者) [a venerable elder].
Gù Quánwǔ (顧全武) was very discerning and broad-minded,
which is why he was able to assist Qián Liú (錢鏐) in holding one region.
Zhǎng (長),
read zhī liǎng (知兩).
32 Luó Hóngxìn (羅弘信), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Wèibó (魏博), passed away.
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: Xuē Jūzhèng's (薛居正) Wǔdài Shǐ (五代史), the biography of Hóngxìn (弘信) in the Liáng Jì (梁紀), and the Tàizǔ Jìniánlù (太祖紀年錄) all state that Hóngxìn (弘信) died in the eighth month.
According to records, in the eighth month Zhāozōng (昭宗) returned to the capital,
and Hóngxìn (弘信) still received additional official titles.
The Jiù Jì (舊紀) and biography state he died in the ninth month;
we follow this now.
The Shílù (實錄) says tenth month,
which approximates when the memorial arrived.
33 Zhū Yǒugōng (朱友恭), a Biàn (汴) general, led troops back from Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮),
passing through Ānzhōu (安州).
Zhū Yǒugōng (朱友恭) conquered Huángzhōu (黃州)
and returned via Ānzhōu (安州).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: Huángzhōu (黃州) is three hundred lǐ (里) west of Ānzhōu (安州).
He planned to seize the Biàn (汴) army.
In winter,
tenth month,
on the jǐhài (己亥) day,
Yǒugōng (友恭) attacked and killed him.
34 Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) dispatched his generals Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭) and Zhōu Déwēi (周德威) with twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to exit Qīngshān (青山),
intending to recover the three prefectures east of the mountains.
The three prefectures east of the mountains were Xíng (邢), Míng (洺), and Cí (磁);
in the fifth month of that year,
Gě Cóngzhōu (葛從周) captured them.
On the rén yín (壬寅) day,
they advanced to attack Xíngzhōu (邢州);
Gě Cóngzhōu (葛從周) sallied out to fight,
and utterly defeated them.
Sìzhāo (嗣昭) and others led their troops to retreat into Qīngshān (青山).
Cóngzhōu (從周) pursued them,
intending to cut off their retreat route.
The infantry disintegrated on its own,
and Sìzhāo (嗣昭) could not control them.
At this time, Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源), the commander of the Héngchōng (橫衝) division, arrived with his troops.
The Xuē Shǐ Míngzōng Jì (薛史明宗紀) states: Luó Hóngxìn (羅弘信) attacked and defeated Lǐ Cúnxìn (李存信) at Xīnxiàn (莘縣).
The Emperor [Míngzōng (明宗)] fought desperately to cover the rear of the army and returned.
Emperor Wǔ (武皇) praised his achievement,
and immediately named the five hundred cavalry under his command the Héngchōng Dū (橫衝都).
"If we also leave,
the situation will be unsustainable.
I will try to attack them for you."
Sìzhāo (嗣昭) said:
"Excellent!
I will follow behind you."
Sìyuán (嗣源) then dismounted, sharpened his arrows,
positioned his formation on high ground,
and directed left and right.
The people of Xíng (邢) could not fathom him.
Sìyuán (嗣源) charged directly forward and fought fiercely.
Sìzhāo (嗣昭) followed him,
and Cóngzhōu (從周) then retreated.
Déwēi (德威) was a person from Mǎyì (馬邑).
Mǎyì (馬邑) was an old county name from Qín (秦) and Hàn (漢) times,
long abandoned.
In the fifth year of Kāiyuán (開元) [717 CE],
Shànyáng (善陽) County of Shuòzhōu (朔州) was divided
to establish Mǎyì (馬邑) County at the old Dàtóng (大同) military city,
subordinate to Shuòzhōu (朔州).
35 On the guǐmǎo (癸卯) day,
Wáng Shěnzhī (王審知), Liúhòu (留後) of Wēiwǔ (威武), was appointed Jìedùshǐ (節度使).
36 Luó Shàowēi (羅紹威) was made Zhī Wèibó Liúhòu (知魏博留後).
37 On the dīngsì (丁巳) day,
Wáng Zōngdí (王宗滌), Liúhòu (留後) of Dōngchuān (東川), was appointed Jìedùshǐ (節度使).
38 Zhāng Quányì (張全義), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Yòuguó (佑國), was additionally appointed attendant counselor (兼侍中).
39 Wáng Gǒng (王珙) led Biàn (汴) troops to raid Hézhōng (河中).
Wáng Kē (王珂) sent an urgent message to Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用).
Kèyòng (克用) dispatched Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭) to rescue them,
defeating the Biàn (汴) troops at Húbì (胡壁).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: Rónghé (榮河) County, Hézhōng (河中) Prefecture, has Húbì (胡壁) Town.
Rónghé (榮河) was Táng (唐) Bǎodǐng (寶鼎) County,
renamed during the Xiángfú (祥符) reign of Sòng (宋).
Bài (敗),
read bǔ mài (補邁).
Wáng Zhù (王柷), former Cìshǐ (刺史) of Chángzhōu (常州),
was firm and upright in character,
and enjoyed public esteem.
He was summoned by imperial decree,
and people at the time thought he would soon become prime minister.
Passing through Shǎn (陝),
Wáng Zhù (王柷) was on his way to be summoned
and passed through Shǎnzhōu (陝州).
Shǎn (陝),
read shī rǎn (失冉).
Gǒng (珙) requested to perform the rites of a nephew to him.
Zhù (柷) firmly refused.
Gǒng (珙) was angry.
Gǒng (珙), sharing the same surname as Zhù (柷),
and Zhù (柷) being older,
and about to become prime minister,
requested to perform the rites of a nephew
to forge a familial bond with him.
But Zhù (柷) refused.
Gǒng (珙) believed that Zhù (柷) slighted his humble family background and was cutting ties,
thus he was angry.
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: Zhù (柷) became a Gěishìzhōng (給事中) and was killed.
The Jiù Jì (舊紀) and Shílù (實錄) both lack a date.
Now, due to Gǒng's (珙) attack on Hézhōng (河中), this event is attached here.
Gǒng (珙) plundered his belongings
and reported it as a boat capsize.
The imperial court dared not investigate.
The historian states that the authority of the Táng (唐) court was ineffective,
and the regional governors were violent and tyrannical.
Wáng Zhù (王柷) suffered their cruel killing,
yet no one dared to question it.
Jié (詰),
read qù jí (去吉).
40 In the intercalary month,
Qián Liú (錢鏐) appointed his general Cáo Guī (曹圭) as the Sūzhōu Zhìzhìshǐ (蘇州制置使),
and sent Wáng Qiú (王球) to attack Wùzhōu (婺州).
41 In the eleventh month,
on the jiǎyín (甲寅) day,
Imperial Prince Zhēn (禎) was enfeoffed as Yǎwáng (雅王),
and Xiáng (祥) as Qióngwáng (瓊王).
42 Luó Shàowēi (羅紹威), Liúhòu (留後) of Wèibó (魏博), was appointed Jìedùshǐ (節度使).
43 Chén Jí (陳岌), Cìshǐ (刺史) of Qúzhōu (衢州), requested to surrender to Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密).
Qián Liú (錢鏐) ordered Gù Quánwǔ (顧全武) to attack him.
Zhū Quánzhōng considered that Cuī Hóng, the Jìedùshǐ of Fèngguó, was communicating with Yáng Xíngmì.
Huaíxī
and Huaínán were neighboring circuits.
Hóng, fearing this,
requested to send his brother, Commander-in-chief Xián, as a hostage,
and also said:
"The officers and soldiers are stubborn and unruly
and do not accept discipline.
Please allow me to send two thousand men to your command to participate in campaigns."
Quánzhōng agreed to this.
This set the stage for Zhū Quánzhōng sending Cuī Xián to recruit soldiers, and for the Cai generals to kill Xián, abduct Hóng, and flee to Huaínán.
Cúnjìng
was from Cáozhōu.
45 In the twelfth month,
Xuē Zhìqín, the Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì, passed away.
When Lǐ Kèyòng pacified Wáng Xíngyú,
see the previous volume, Qiánníng Second Year.
Kèyòng said:
"Xíngyú relied on his achievements to coerce the sovereign,
which is why I, with you, attacked and executed him.
On the day we defeated the rebels yesterday,
I first memorialized urging Sū Wénjiàn to proceed to his post.
See the same source.
Qù
is read as cù.
If I were to change my mind two or three times again,
the opinions of the court and the populace
would surely clamor that we are acting like Xíngyú.
Our feelings, yours and mine, are like one body,
so there is nothing I would withhold.
After I return to my post,
I will again discuss and reward your achievements for you."
Hǎnzhī was displeased and withdrew,
privately saying to Gài Yù:
"Since Hǎnzhī lost Héyáng,
he has relied on the great protection [of the Prince].
Many years have passed.
Lately, I have grown old
and weary of military life.
If His Majesty and the Grand Tutor would show pity,
The King
refers to Lǐ Kèyòng,
the Grand Tutor
refers to Gài Yù.
and allow me a few years to rest my troops and recuperate from illness,
and then return to my hometown to live out my old age,
that would be fortunate."
Yù spoke for him,
but Kèyòng did not respond.
Whenever a circuit governor's post became vacant,
Hǎnzhī was not considered,
and Hǎnzhī was deeply dejected.
Yù feared he might have other intentions,
and urgently spoke for him.
Kèyòng said:
"It's not that I begrudge Hǎnzhī a single post;
but Hǎnzhī
is a hawk:
when hungry, he is useful;
when full, he flies away!"
He spoke this, recalling Cáo Cāo's way of controlling Lǚ Bù.
Bèi
is pronounced pū mèi.
When Zhìqín passed away,
there was no commander for ten days.
Hǎnzhī led Zézhōu troops into Lùzhōu by night,
occupying it.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Zézhōu is 165 lǐ north of Lùzhōu.
Shuài
is pronounced suǒ lèi.
He said:
"Xuē Tiěshān is dead.
Xuē Zhìqín rose with Kèyòng from Dàiběi,
originally named Tiěshān.
Fearing that unruly elements might cause trouble,
Hǎnzhī has taken the liberty to suppress and pacify,
awaiting the Prince's decision."
Cáizhǐ means to decide whether it is permissible or not.
Kèyòng sent someone to reprimand him.
Hǎnzhī then sent his son
to pledge allegiance to Zhū Quánzhōng,
seizing Héběi generals Mǎ Gài and others, and Qìnzhōu Cìshǐ Fù Yáo, and sending them to Biànzhōu.
Kèyòng sent Lǐ Sìzhāo with troops to attack him.
From this point,
Lǐ Kèyòng could no longer contend with Zhū Quánzhōng for Xíng, Míng, and Cí, but only for Zé and Lù.
He gathered Hǎnzhī's family and sent them to Jìnyáng.
He first took Zézhōu,
catching Lǐ Hǎnzhī unprepared,
and also captured his family.
History records that Lǐ Sìzhāo was skilled in military strategy.
46 Yáng Xíngmì sent Chéng Jí
back to Liǎngzhè in exchange for Wèi Yuē and others.
Huaínán captured Chéng Jí; see the previous volume, Qiánníng Third Year.
Liǎngzhè captured Wèi Yuē; see last year, fourth month.
Yáng and Qián contended for Sūzhōu.
Tái Méng, Zhōu Běn, and Qín Péi were all famous Huaínán generals,
but they were trapped by the Zhè people,
and ultimately could not hold the city.
Yáng Xíngmì knew that Qián Liú was not to be underestimated,
so he returned Chéng Jí in exchange for Wèi Yuē,
intending to resolve the conflict.
Qián Liú also knew he was not as strong as Yáng Xíngmì,
so he quickly agreed.
47 Zēng Gǔn, the Cìshǐ of Sháozhōu, raised an army and attacked Guǎngzhōu.
Wáng Huái, a general from the prefecture, led warships to assist him;
Liú Yǐn, the Xíngjūn Sīmǎ of Qīnghǎi, defeated them in one battle.
Liú Tóng, a general from Sháozhōu, again occupied Zhēnbīn and Hánzhēn.
Yǐn attacked and killed him.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the Dīngwèi day,
Cuī Yìn, the Zhōngshū Shìláng兼Lìbù Shàngshū,
was dismissed from his current posts;
Lù Yǐ, the Bīngbù Shàngshū, was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Cuī Yìn and Lù Yǐ were appointed and dismissed in alternation.
2 Zhū Quánzhōng memorialized to appoint Lǐ Hǎnzhī as the Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì,
and also memorialized to appoint Dīng Huì, acting Liúhòu of Héyáng, Wáng Jìngrǎo, Liúhòu of Wǔníng,
and Zhāng Kē, Liúhòu of Zhāngyì, all as Jìedùshǐ.
Héyáng and Wǔníng were both affiliated with Zhū Quánzhōng;
only Zhāng Kē was in Jìngzhōu,
and requesting a jǐeyuè for him
was also a way to secure his allegiance.
3 Yáng Xíngmì and Zhū Jǐn led tens of thousands of troops to attack Xúzhōu,
encamping at Lǚliáng.
Zhū Quánzhōng sent cavalry general Zhāng Guīhòu to rescue them.
4 Liú Rén'gōng dispatched one hundred thousand troops from twelve prefectures, including Yōu and Cāng.
The twelve prefectures: Yōu, Zhuó, Yíng, Mò, Píng, Yíng, Jì, Guī, Tán, Cāng, Jǐng, and Dé.
Yōuzhōu's jurisdiction also included Wèi, Xīn, and Wǔ three prefectures,
which Liú Rén'gōng kept to guard against Héběi,
not dispatching their troops.
He attacked Bèizhōu,
captured it,
and slaughtered all ten thousand households in the city,
throwing their corpses into the Qīngshuǐ.
Qīngshuǐ
is the water of Qīnghé.
Rén'gōng advanced to attack Wèizhōu,
encamping north of the city;
Luó Shàowēi, the Jìedùshǐ of Wèibó, sought aid from Zhū Quánzhōng.
5 Zhū Quánzhōng sent Cuī Xián back to Càizhōu.
Cuī Hóng had sent his brother Xián as a hostage,
see last year.
In the second month,
Cuī Jǐngsī and other Cai generals killed Xián,
abducted Cuī Hóng,
and led all the soldiers and people across the Huaí River to flee to Yáng Xíngmì.
The soldiers and people gradually deserted and returned.
Settling in one's native land and being reluctant to move
is a common human sentiment.
Quánzhōng ordered Zhū Yǒuyù, the Cìshǐ of Xǔzhōu, to guard Càizhōu.
6 Zhū Quánzhōng personally led troops to relieve Xúzhōu.
Yáng Xíngmì heard of this
and withdrew his troops;
the Biàn people pursued and caught up with them at Xiàpī.
Xiàpī
was an ancient county,
under Xúzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
Jiǔyù Zhì,
180 lǐ east of Xúzhōu.
Quánzhōng reached Huīzhōu,
In this year,
Zhū Quánzhōng memorialized to establish Huīzhōu using Dàngshān, Yúchéng, and Dānfù from Sòngzhōu,
and Chéngwǔ from Cáozhōu.
This was the domain of Dānzhōu.
and then returned.
7 In the third month,
Zhū Quánzhōng dispatched his generals Lǐ Sī'ān and Zhāng Cúnjìng with troops to relieve Wèibó,
and they encamped at Nèihuáng.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Nèihuáng County is 214 *lǐ* southwest of Wèizhōu.
On the *Guǐmǎo* day,
Quánzhōng stationed his central army at Huázhōu.
Liú Rén'gōng said to his son, Shǒuwén:
"Your courage is ten times that of Sī'ān.
You should first capture these rat-like fellows,
and then seize Shàowēi!"
So, he sent Shǒuwén and his brother-in-law Shàn Kějí with 50,000 elite troops to attack Sī'ān at Nèihuáng.
On the *Dīngwèi* day,
Sī'ān ordered his general Yuán Xiàngxiān to lay an ambush to the right of Qīngshuǐ.
The Qíshuǐ River flows east past Nèihuáng,
where it is called Báigōu Shuǐ,
also known as Qīnghé Shuǐ.
Fányáng,
an ancient county of the Hàn dynasty,
was merged and abolished into Nèihuáng during the Táng dynasty.
Dù Yòu said: The ancient city of Hàn's Fányáng County is northwest of Nèihuáng County.
Shǒuwén pursued them,
and upon reaching north of Nèihuáng,
Sī'ān rallied his troops and returned to battle.
The ambush was sprung,
attacking them from both sides.
The Yōuzhōu army was greatly defeated,
Kějí was beheaded,
and three thousand men were killed or captured.
Shǒuwén barely escaped with his life.
Kějí
was a valiant general of Yōuzhōu,
known as
"Shàn Wúdí" (Shàn the Invincible).
The Yàn army lost morale after losing him.
Lǐ Kèyòng underestimated Shàn Kějí and suffered the defeat at Mùguājiàn;
Liú Rén'gōng underestimated Lǐ Sī'ān, and Shàn Kějí lost his head.
Therefore, those who employ troops are warned against underestimating the enemy.
喪 (*sàng*),
pronunciation *xī làng fān*.
He was from Chénliú.
At this time, Gé Cóngzhōu, leading eight hundred elite cavalry from Xíngzhōu, had already entered Wèizhōu.
On the *Wùshēn* day,
Rén'gōng attacked the Shàngshuǐ Pass and Guǎntáo Gate.
Guǎntáo Gate
was the north gate of Wèizhōu city.
Exiting this gate
led to Guǎntáo County,
hence the name of the gate.
He said to the gatekeepers:
"There is a great enemy ahead,
so do not look back."
He ordered the gate's leaves to be shut.
Cóngzhōu and his men fought desperately,
and Rén'gōng was again greatly defeated,
capturing his generals Xuē Tūjué and Wáng Kuàiláng.
The next day,
the forces of Biàn and Wèi, emboldened by their victory, combined their armies and attacked Rén'gōng,
destroying eight of his camps.
Rén'gōng and his son burned their camps and fled.
The people of Biàn and Wèi pursued them relentlessly,
reaching Línqīng,
where they drove his forces into the Yǒngjì Canal,
causing countless deaths by drowning.
The Zhèn people also dispatched troops to intercept them in the eastern territory.
The Zhèn people
refers to Wáng Róng's troops.
Shēn and Jì
are the eastern territories of Zhào.
Corpses piled up against each other.
From then on, Rén'gōng never recovered,
and Quánzhōng became even more overbearing.
The military might of Yōu and Bīng were both thwarted,
hence Quánzhōng became even more overbearing.
橫 (*héng*),
pronunciation *hù mèng fān*.
He was a Hú person from Héxī.
According to Xuē Shǐ: Hè Délún's
ancestors were tribal people from Héxī.
His father, Huáiqìng,
was attached to the Huázhōu army
as a minor officer,
so Délún was a Huáya general in his youth.
When Liú Rén'gōng attacked Wèizhōu,
Luó Shàowēi sent an envoy to cultivate good relations with Hédōng
and also to request aid.
On the *Rénwǔ* day,
Lǐ Kèyòng dispatched Lǐ Sìzhāo to lead troops to relieve them.
It happened that Rén'gōng had already been defeated by the Biàn troops,
so Shàowēi again broke off relations with Hédōng.
Since Lǐ Cúnxìn's defeat at Xīnxiàn,
Wèi had cut ties with Bīng,
but now through seeking aid, they re-established contact.
The Bīng troops had not yet arrived,
and the Biàn people had achieved success,
so they again severed ties with Bīng.
8 Gé Cóngzhōu, capitalizing on the momentum of defeating Yōuzhōu,
attacked Hédōng from Tǔmén,
capturing Chéngtiānjūn.
His separate general Shì Shūcóng entered from Mǎlǐng.
Mǎlǐng
is eighty *lǐ* southeast of Tàiyuán Prefecture's Tàigǔ County.
The Jìn divided Hàn's Zhān County to establish Lèpíng County,
which belonged to Liáozhōu during the Táng dynasty.
Yúcì,
an ancient county,
belonged to Tàiyuán Prefecture during the Táng dynasty.
Shūcóng had a valiant general named Chén Zhāng,
known as
"Chén Yèchā" (Chen the Yaksha),
who served as the vanguard.
Folk tales speak of ghost emissaries in the underworld called Yakshas.
People at the time likened Chén Zhāng's fierceness and terror to that of a Yaksha,
hence the appellation.
"Hédōng's reliance is Zhōu Yángwǔ (Zhōu Déwēi's childhood name was Yángwǔ).
I seek a prefecture as a reward."
Kèyòng heard this
and used it to warn Déwēi.
Déwēi said:
"He's just talking big."
They battled at Dòngwō.
Dòngwō River originates from the northern mountains of Zhān County,
flows east and then bends south,
passing east of the ancient city of Shòuyáng County,
and west of the south of Yúcì County.
This is according to the commentary on the *Shuǐjīng*.
Wèi Shōu's *Dìxíng Zhì* states: Dòngwō River has five sources,
one from Mùguālǐng,
one from Zhānlǐng,
one from Dàliánshān,
and one from below Yuánguò Shrine.
The five streams merge,
hence it was called Tóngguò,
which later changed to Dòngwō.
It is noted that when Gāo Huán established his grand chancellor's residence in Jìnyáng,
Wèi Shōu had already entered service in the hegemon's administration.
When Qí succeeded Wèi,
Jìnyáng was made a secondary capital.
Wèi Shōu often traveled with his lord to and from Jìnyáng Palace,
so he ought to have known the place names accurately.
Déwēi said to his subordinates:
"When you see Chén Yèchā, run."
Chén Zhāng indeed pursued them.
Déwēi wielded his iron mace, struck him, and knocked him off his horse,
capturing him alive and presenting him.
Thereupon, he attacked Shūcóng,
greatly defeating him and
beheading three thousand enemy soldiers.
Shūcóng abandoned his camp and fled.
Déwēi pursued him,
exiting through Shíhuì Pass,
and again beheaded over a thousand.
Cóngzhōu also withdrew.
9 On the *Dīngsì* day,
Zhū Quánzhōng dispatched Dīng Huì, the Jìedùshǐ of Héyáng, to attack Zézhōu,
and he captured it.
In the twelfth month of the previous year,
Hédōng troops had taken Zézhōu.

"On the *Dīngsì* day,

"On the *Dīngsì* day,

is an error.

"In the third month,
Zhōu Déwēi defeated Shì Shūcóng at Dòngwō Post.

garrisoning Lùzhōu.

Gé Cóngzhōu again entered Lùzhōu to replace Dīng Huì,

Both the *Liáng Shílù* and *Xuē Shǐ Liáng Jì* state that Cóngzhōu was sent into Lùzhōu in the sixth month;
