10 The Prefect of Wùzhōu, Wáng Tán, was besieged by the two Zhè circuits.
In the intercalary month of the previous year,
the two Zhè circuits' forces attacked Wùzhōu.
It is noted that Xuānxiè Observation
had previously been elevated to Níngguó Army,
with Tián Yún as its Jìedùshǐ.
pronunciation *shū shè fān*.
In the fourth month,
Yún dispatched Kāng Rú and others, who were campaigning army commanders, to relieve it.
11 In the fifth month,
on the *Jiǎwǔ* day,
Wǔxìn Army was established at Suízhōu,
with five prefectures including Suí and Hé subordinated to it.
This was Wáng Jiàn's aspiration.
12 Lǐ Kèyòng sent Lǐ Jūnqìng, the Commander of Fān and Hàn Cavalry and Infantry, to lead troops to attack Lǐ Hǎnzī.
On the Jǐhài day,
they besieged Lùzhōu.
Zhū Quánzhōng moved his garrison to Héyáng.
On the Xīnchǒu day,
he sent his general Zhāng Cúnjìng to relieve them.
On the Rén'yín day,
he again sent Dīng Huì to lead troops to follow.
They severely defeated the Hédōng troops,
and Jūnqìng lifted the siege and departed.
Kèyòng executed Jūnqìng and his subordinate generals Yī Shěn and Lǐ Hóngxí.
He appointed Lǐ Sìzhāo as the Commander of Fān and Hàn Cavalry and Infantry,
to replace him in attacking Lùzhōu.
13 On the Gēngxū day,
Kāng Rú and others defeated the Liǎngzhè troops at Lóngqiū.
Lóngqiū
was originally Tàimò County in the Hàn dynasty.
In the eighth year of Zhēngguān, its name was changed to Lóngqiū,
which is today's Lóngyóu County.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: it belongs to Qúzhōu,
seventy-five lǐ east of the prefecture.
Bèi (敗)
is pronounced Bùmài.
Wáng Qiú was the main general
who, while attacking Wùzhōu, was captured at Lóngqiū,
probably because the Zhè troops fought against the Xuān troops.
In the first year of Jǐngfú,
Wáng Tán captured Wùzhōu,
but lost it by this time.
14 In the sixth month,
on the Yǐchǒu day,
Lǐ Hǎnzī's illness became critical.
On the Dīngmǎo day,
Quánzhōng memorialized to appoint Hǎnzī as the Military Commissioner of Héyáng,
and Dīng Huì as the Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì.
Not long after,
he again appointed his general Zhāng Guībà to guard Xíngzhōu,
and sent Gé Cóngzhōu to replace Huì in guarding Lùzhōu.
The Kǎoyì says: The Yí Lù records:
"In the sixth month,
on the Yǐchǒu day,
Lǐ Hǎnzī's illness became severe,
and he requested to return to Héyáng.
On the Dīngmǎo day,
the Emperor ordered the main army to withdraw,
and appointed Dīng Huì to temporarily manage and pacify
Shàngdǎng.
The Emperor then returned east."
It does not mention sending Cóngzhōu into Lù.
Xuē Jūzhèng's Wǔdài Shǐ, Liáng Jì records:
"In the sixth month,
the Emperor memorialized to appoint Dīng Huì as the Military Commissioner of Lùzhōu,
because Lǐ Hǎnzī's illness was critical.
He also sent Gé Cóngzhōu via the Gùzhèn road into Lùzhōu,
to reinforce Dīng Huì."
The Liáng Shílù and Hòutáng Jì both say "replaced Huì."
From this point until Lùzhōu was broken and
Hè Délún fled,
Huì's name is no longer seen.
Perhaps after Lǐ Hǎnzī died,
Huì was recalled to guard Héyáng,
and Cóngzhōu replaced him,
but this is uncertain.
Now, because Huì was stationed in Lù,
we conclude the narration.
15 Wáng Zōngjí, a great general of Xīchuān, was appointed Military Commissioner of Wǔxìn.
This was at Wáng Jiàn's request.
His original surname was Gān,
and he was from Hóngzhōu.
16 On the Dīngchǒu day,
Lǐ Hǎnzī died in Huáizhōu.
Lǐ Hǎnzī traveled from Lùzhōu to Héyáng,
and died upon reaching Huáizhōu.
17 Wáng Gǒng, the Military Commissioner of Bǎoyì,
was of a suspicious and cruel nature.
Even his wife, children, and close associates
could never feel secure.
At this time, his army mutinied,
and he was killed by his subordinates.
In the early Zhōnghé reign of Xīzōng,
Wáng Chóngyíng was stationed in Shǎn.
The position was passed to his son Gǒng,
and it ended at this time.
18 In autumn,
seventh month,
Chén Hànbīn, Zhū Quánzhōng's garrison commander at Hǎizhōu, requested to surrender to Yáng Xíngmì.
Zhāng Xùn, the Inspector of Huáihǎi, considering that Hànbīn's intentions were still unclear,
led two thousand troops with Wáng Wǎn of Lújiāng, the Defense Commissioner of Liánshuǐ, directly to Hǎizhōu,
and thus occupied the city.
Yáng Xíngmì thereby gained control of Hǎizhōu.
Qù (趣)
is pronounced Qīyù.
19 Chéng Ruì, the Military Commissioner of Jīngnán, was additionally appointed Grand Chancellor.
20 Mǎ Yīn sent his general Lǐ Táng to attack Dàozhōu.
Cài Jié gathered many barbarians,
ambushed them in a defile to attack,
and severely defeated Táng's troops.
Táng said:
"The barbarians rely only on mountains and forests.
If we fight on flat ground,
how can they defeat me!"
So he ordered to burn the forests with the wind,
the fire illuminated heaven and earth,
the barbarians fled in alarm,
and he then captured Dàozhōu,
seized Jié,
and beheaded him.
21 Zhū Quánzhōng recalled Gé Cóngzhōu from Lùzhōu,
and made Hè Délún guard it.
In the eighth month,
on the Bǐngyín day,
Lǐ Sìzhāo led his troops to the foot of the Lùzhōu city walls,
and divided his forces to attack Zézhōu.
On the Jǐsì day,
Liú Qì, a Biàn general, abandoned Zézhōu and fled.
The Hédōng troops advanced and captured Tiānjǐng Pass.
Lǐ Xiàozhāng was appointed Prefect of Zézhōu.
"Lǐ Xiàozhāng"
should be
"Lǐ Cúnzhāng."
Lǐ Sìzhāo daily encircled the city with cavalry,
captured those gathering fodder and grazing,
and harvested all the grain within thirty lǐ of the city.
On the Yǐyǒu day,
Délún and others abandoned the city and fled by night,
heading towards Húguān.
Hè Délún's troops could not go out of the city to gather fodder and graze,
the grain outside the city was also empty,
and both provisions and reinforcements were cut off,
so their flight was inevitable.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Húguān County is twenty-five lǐ east of Lùzhōu.
Qù (趣)
is pronounced Qīyù.
Lǐ Cúnshěn
is Fú Cúnshěn.
Many were killed and captured.
Gé Cóngzhōu arrived with reinforcements,
but hearing that Délún and others had already been defeated,
he returned.
22 In the ninth month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
Lǐ Màozhēn, the Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng, was appointed Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng and Zhāngyì.
In the spring, first month of this year,
Zhū Quánzhōng memorialized to appoint Zhāng Kē as the Military Commissioner of Zhāngyì.
The Zhāng clan had been stationed in Jīngzhōu,
with three commanders in total.
Now Lǐ Màozhēn was appointed to concurrently hold the position.
23 Lǐ Kèyòng memorialized to appoint Mèng Qiān, the Prefect of Fénzhōu, as Acting Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì.
This sets the stage for Mèng Qiān's rebellion against Lǐ Kèyòng at Lùzhōu.
24 Wáng Shīfàn, the Military Commissioner of Zīqīng, faced internal rebellion in Yí and Mì.
At this time,
Zhū Quánzhōng completely held the entire Henan region,
and Wáng Shīfàn was also subservient to him.
If Yí and Mì rebelled internally,
to whom would they turn?
Also, he did not seek aid from Quánzhōng but from Yáng Xíngmì.
This matter needs investigation.
In winter,
tenth month,
Xíngmì sent Tái Méng, the Prefect of Hǎizhōu, and Wáng Wǎn, the Vice Commissioner, to lead troops to assist him.
They captured Mìzhōu,
and returned it to Shīfàn.
When preparing to attack Yízhōu,
he first sent scouts,
who reported:
"All the flags in the city are lowered and drums silenced."
Wǎn said:
"This must mean they are prepared,
and relief troops are near, so we cannot attack."
The generals said:
"Mì has already fallen,
what can Yí do!"
Wǎn could not stop them,
so he ambushed troops in the forest to await them.
The generals attacked Yízhōu but could not capture it.
Relief troops arrived,
and they retreated.
Whose troops were these relief troops?
Wǎn launched his ambush and defeated them.
25 In the eleventh month,
Zhū Jiǎn, a commander from Shǎnzhōu, killed Lǐ Fán,
proclaimed himself Acting Military Commissioner,
and submitted to Zhū Quánzhōng,
requesting to change his name to Yǒuqiān,
to be counted among his nephews and nieces.
Zhū Quánzhōng thus additionally held Shǎn and Guó.
Gēng (更)
is pronounced Gōnghéng.
26 Zhào Kuāngníng, the Military Commissioner of Zhōngyì, was additionally appointed Grand Chancellor.
27 Mǎ Yīn sent his general Lǐ Qióng to attack Chénzhōu,
captured Chén Yànqiān,
and beheaded him.
He advanced to attack Liánzhōu.
Lǔ Jǐngrén committed suicide,
and all of Húnán was pacified.
Mǎ Yīn thus gained complete control of the Húnán region.
On the 28th day of the twelfth month,
Luó Shàowēi, Jìedùshǐ of Wèibó, was given the concurrent title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ, collated by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by Imperial Edict
Hòu Xué Tiān Tái
Guānghuà third year
(Gēngshēn, 900 CE)
1. In the spring,
first month,
Kāng Rú, a general from Xuānzhōu, attacked Mùzhōu;
this general from Xuānzhōu
was dispatched by Tián Yùn.
2. In the second month,
on the day Gēngshēn,
Wáng Jiàn, Jìedùshǐ of Xīchuān, was concurrently appointed Zhōngshūlìng.
3. On the day Rénshēn,
Wáng Shěnzhī, Jìedùshǐ of Wēiwǔ, was given the concurrent title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
4. On the day Rénwǔ,
Cuī Yìn, Shàngshū of the Ministry of Personnel, was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and also Jìedùshǐ of Qīnghǎi.
5. Lǐ Kèyòng mobilized a large number of soldiers and civilians to repair the city walls and moats of Jìnyáng,
fearing an attack by Zhū Quánzhōng.
治,
pronounced zhì.
"The King's prestige resounds throughout Huá and Yí;
it would be appropriate to deploy troops to secure the four borders,
not to busy oneself with repairing city walls and moats,
which diminishes prestige and encourages banditry."
Kèyòng thanked him
and rewarded him with gold and silk.
6. In the summer,
fourth month,
Lǐ Chéngqìng, Jìedùshǐ of Dìngnán Military Command, was given the concurrent title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
7. Zhū Quánzhōng sent Gé Cóngzhōu to lead 100,000 troops from the four garrisons of Yǎn, Yùn, Huá, and Wèi to attack Liú Rén'gōng.
In the fifth month,
on the day Gēngyín,
Dézhōu was captured,
and the governor Fù Gōnghé was beheaded;
on the day Jǐhài,
Liú Shǒuwén was besieged in Cāngzhōu.
Rén'gōng again sent envoys with humble words and generous gifts to seek aid from Hédōng,
and Lǐ Kèyòng dispatched Zhōu Déwēi with 5,000 cavalry to go out through Huángzé,
attacking Xíng and Míng to relieve him.
Huángzé Pass
is in Huángzélǐng of Liáoshān County, Liáozhōu.
8. The army in Yōngzhōu mutinied,
driving out Jìedùshǐ Lǐ Huì;
in the third year of Xiántōng of Yìzōng,
the Jinglüèshǐ of Yōngguǎn was promoted to Jìedùshǐ of Lǐngnán Xīdào.
鐬,
pronounced huì.
9. In the sixth month,
on the day Guǐhài,
Wáng Zōngdí, Jìedùshǐ of Dōngchuān, was given the concurrent title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
10. Wáng Tuán, Sīkōng, Ménxià Shìláng, and Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
was intelligent and magnanimous,
and was acclaimed as a good prime minister at the time.
Speaking of that time,
he was called a good prime minister,
meaning he was better than others.
Cuī Yìn daily plotted with the emperor to remove the eunuchs,
and the eunuchs became aware of this.
From this, the Southern and Northern Bureaus grew to hate each other more,
each aligning with a military governor for support to contend for power.
Tuán feared that this would lead to chaos,
and gently spoke to the emperor, saying:
"A ruler should strive to understand the general situation
and avoid any partiality.
Who doesn't know the弊 (abuses) of the eunuchs' authority?
However, their power cannot be eliminated suddenly;
it is advisable to wait until the many difficulties gradually subside
and then deal with them appropriately.
I hope Your Majesty does not lightly reveal your words to hasten treacherous changes."
When Yìn heard this,
he slandered Tuán to the emperor, saying:
"Wáng Tuán is treacherous and wicked,
and has already become an external accomplice for Dàobì and his ilk."
The emperor became suspicious of him.
When Yìn was dismissed from his prime ministerial post,
Yìn was dismissed from his prime ministerial post last year,
as seen in the previous volume.
he hated him even more.
When he was sent to govern Guǎngzhōu,
he sent a letter to Zhū Quánzhōng,
fully relating Tuán's words.
In the second month of that year,
Yìn was sent out to Guǎngzhōu.
Tuán's words were those he had gently spoken to the emperor.
遺,
pronounced wèi.
Quánzhōng reported:
"Yìn should not leave the post of chief minister;
Tuán and the imperial envoys are in collusion,
jointly endangering the state."
He repeatedly submitted memorials.
Although the emperor understood the situation,
pressured by Quánzhōng,
he had no choice.
Yìn was recalled as soon as he reached Húnán.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
Yìn was appointed Sīkōng, Ménxià Shìláng, and Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
while Tuán was dismissed to be Gōngbù Shìláng.
Dàobì was made Supervisor of Jīngnán Army,
and Wùxiū Supervisor of Qīngzhōu Army.
On the day Wùchén,
Tuán was demoted to Cìshǐ of Xīzhōu;
on the day Jǐsì,
he was again demoted to Sīhù of Yázhōu;
Dàobì was exiled to Huānzhōu,
and Wùxiū to Àizhōu;
on that same day,
they were all granted the order to commit suicide.
Tuán died at Lántián Post Station,
and Dàobì and Wùxiū died at Bàqiáo Post Station.
Lántián Post Station is in Lántián County.
Bàqiáo Post Station is south of Cháng'ān city,
near Bàqiáo.
The power shook the entire realm,
and the eunuchs all looked askance,
unable to suppress their indignation.
This laid the groundwork for the rebellion of Liú Jìshù and Hán Quánhuì.
勝,
pronounced shèng.
11. Liú Rén'gōng's general led 50,000 Yōuzhōu troops to relieve Cāngzhōu,
encamping at Gānníng Military Command.
Gānníng Military Command
is 100 li west of Cāngzhōu;
it was established during the Gānníng era.
Sòng Bái said: Gānníng Military Command
was originally the site of the ancient Lútái Military Command,
later Fēngqiáo Town,
on the bank of the Yù River,
bordering Cāng and Yōu Prefectures.
In the sixth year of Xiǎndé of Zhōu,
after recovering Guānnán,
it was first established as Gānníng Military Command.
The Jiǔyù Zhì says: The military command was first established in the seventh year of Tàipíng Xīngguó.
He personally led elite troops to engage in battle at Lǎo'yādī,
Lǎo'yādī
is southeast of Gānníng Military Command.
beheading 30,000,
and Rén'gōng fled to hold Wǎqiáo.
Wǎqiáo
is south of Guīyì County, Zhuózhōu,
30 li from Mòzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Wǎqiáo is also called Wǎzijìqiáo,
south of Zhuózhōu,
east of Yìzhōu.
When Zhōu Xiǎndé recovered the three passes,
considering its strategic position controlling Yōu and Jì,
it was established as Xióngzhōu.
In the seventh month,
Lǐ Kèyòng again sent the Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ Lǐ Sìzhāo to lead 50,000 troops to attack Xíng and Míng to relieve Rén'gōng,
defeating the Biàn army at Nèiqiū.
Wáng Róng sent envoys to mediate peace between Yōu and Biàn.
As there had been continuous rain for a long time,
Zhū Quánzhōng recalled Cóngzhōu.
Cāngzhōu was low and wet,
with rainwater,
making it difficult to station troops,
and he also wanted to relieve Xíng and Míng,
hence the recall.
12. On the day Gēngxū,
Mèng Qiān, Resident Administrator of Zhāoyì, was made Jìedùshǐ.
13. On the day Jiǎyín,
Wáng Jiàn, Jìedùshǐ of Xīchuān, was concurrently appointed Dū Zhǐhuī Zhìzhì and other posts for the two circuits of Dōngchuān and Xìnwǔ Army.
At that time, Wǔxìn Army was established in Suìzhōu.
"Xìnwǔ"
should be
"Wǔxìn."
Wáng Jiàn concurrently commanded and managed the two circuits,
thus he could control Zōngdí and Zōngjí. This was likely the court's hint to appoint him to this.
14 In the eighth month,
Lǐ Sìzhāo again defeated the Biàn army at Shāmén Hé.
"Shāmén Hé"
is probably a mistake for
"Shā Hé,"
which is Shāhé County in Xíngzhōu.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Biān Yílù* records:
"On the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month,
Lǐ Jìntōng led barbarian bandits out of Bìngzhōu to attack Míngzhōu.
On the *yǐchǒu* day of the eighth month,
a large army was dispatched to assist them.
The Emperor himself soon after led the Imperial Guard in continuous northern campaigns.
The next day,
they reached Huátái.
A report rushed from the front line said that
Míngzhōu had already fallen,
and the Prefect Zhū Shàozōng, having climbed over the battlements,
fell and injured his foot,
and was captured by the bandits."
The *Táng Tàizǔ Jìniánlù* records:
"In the eighth month,
Lǐ Sìzhāo again encountered the Biàn army at Shāmén Hé
and defeated them in battle.
They advanced to attack Míngzhōu,
and the Prefect Zhū Shàozōng fled with his family by night.
Our forces pursued and overtook them,
capturing him."
The *Tángmò Jiànwénlù* records:
"On the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month,
Sìzhāo advanced his army down to Shāndōng.
On a certain day, Shāndōng reported a victory,
having recovered Míngzhōu
and captured Zhū Wēn's nephew, the Prefect."
The *Jiùjì* records:
"In the eighth month,
on the *gēngchén* day,
Sìzhāo attacked Míngzhōu
and took it."
Xuē Shǐ's *Liángjì* records:
"In the eighth month,
Hédōng sent Lǐ Jìntōng to raid and seize Míngzhōu."
The *Xīnjì* also places it on the *gēngchén* day,
which is the twenty-fifth.
The *Shílù* places it in the ninth month,
probably referring to when the memorial reached the court.
We now follow the *Biān Yílù*.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
Zhū Quánzhōng led his troops to relieve it.
Before he arrived,
Sìzhāo captured Míngzhōu
and took the Prefect Zhū Shàozōng prisoner.
Quánzhōng ordered Gě Cóngzhōu to lead troops to attack Sìzhāo.
15 The Xuānzhōu general Kāng Rú, having exhausted his provisions,
fled back from Qīngxī.
Kāng Rú had attacked Mùzhōu in the first month of this year.
Qīngxī was
in the territory of Hánxī County.
Later, Xīn'ān County was separated and established.
During the Suí dynasty, it was renamed Zhìshān.
In the first year of Wénmíng,
it was restored to Xīn'ān.
In the twentieth year of Kāiyuán,
it was renamed Huánchún.
In the first year of Yǒngzhēn,
to avoid the personal name of Xiànzōng,
it was renamed Qīngxī,
belonging to Mùzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: The county is one hundred sixty-six *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
16 In the ninth month,
Gě Cóngzhōu crossed the Zhāngshuǐ from Yèxiàn
and encamped at Huánglóng Zhèn.
Zhū Quánzhōng personally led thirty thousand men of the central army across the Míngshuǐ and set up camp.
Lǐ Sìzhāo abandoned the city and fled;
he abandoned Míngzhōu city and fled.
They ambushed and attacked him,
utterly defeating him.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Táng Tàizǔ Jìniánlù* records:
"Gě Cóngzhōu attacked Míngzhōu,
and Sìzhāo abandoned the city and returned.
In this campaign,
Wáng Héláng and Yáng Shīyuè fell into enemy hands,
and Míngzhōu was again taken by Biàn."
The *Tángmò Jiànwénlù* records:
"On the second day of the ninth month,
Sìzhāo's soldiers suffered a defeat and retreated,
and Wáng Héláng was captured by Biànzhōu."
The *Biān Yílù* and Xuē Jūzhèng's *Wǔdài Shǐ* *Liángjì* record:
"In the eighth month,
the Emperor sent Gě Cóngzhōu to garrison Huánglóng Zhèn,
and personally led the central army across the Míng to encamp.
The Jìn people were afraid and fled by night,
and Míngzhōu was pacified again."
The *Tángjì* records:
"In the ninth month,
the Biàn commander personally led thirty thousand troops to besiege Míngzhōu,
and Sìzhāo abandoned the city and returned.
Gě Cóngzhōu lay in ambush at Qīngshān Kǒu,
and Sìzhāo's army suffered a disadvantage."
The *Shílù* records:
"In the ninth month,
Sìzhāo abandoned Míngzhōu
and was defeated at Qīngshān Kǒu."
We now follow the *Tángmò Jiànwénlù*, *Tángjì*, and *Shílù*.
According to the *Tángjì* recorded in the *Kǎoyì*,
it is probably the *Hòutángjì*.
17 Cuī Yìn resented Xú Yànruò, who as Grand Preceptor, Menxià Shìláng, and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, ranked above him.
Yànruò also sought to resign.
Xú Yànruò could be said to have understood the intention of Yáo Zēng to attack him and remove him.
Only Xūē Wáng Zhīróu was in Guǎngzhōu.
Zhīróu's garrisoning of Guǎngzhōu is seen in volume 260, Qiánníng first year.
On the *yǐsì* day,
Yànruò was made Tóng Píngzhāngshì
and appointed Jìnghǎi Jiédùshǐ.
Previously,
Chéng Ruì, the Jìngnán Jiédù, considered Lǐ and Lǎng originally to be under his jurisdiction,
but they were occupied by Léi Mǎn.
In the second year of Sùzōng's Zhìdé era,
the Jìngnán Jiédù was established,
administering the ten prefectures of Jīng, Lǐ, Lǎng, Yǐng, Fù, Kuí, Xiá, Zhōng, Wàn, and Guī.
Later, its administration expanded, and its divisions were not uniform.
Since Léi Mǎn occupied Lǐ and Lǎng,
the Wǔzhēn Jūn Jiédù was also separately established.
The imperial court did not permit it,
and Ruì harbored considerable resentment.
Xuē Shǐ says: Ruì memorialized to request their annexation,
but Yànruò, as prime minister,
firmly opposed it,
which caused Ruì to resent him.
Ruì hosted a banquet
and casually brought up the matter.
Yànruò said:
"Your Excellency holds a high position in the regions,
comparing yourself to Huán and Wén,
Chéng Ruì was promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng,
hence he was called Linggōng.
Do you then resent the imperial court?!"
Ruì was greatly ashamed.
18 On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Cuī Yuǎn, Menxià Shìláng兼Lìbù Shàngshū, and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was dismissed from his current posts.
Péi Zhì, the Xíngbù Shàngshū, was made Menxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Zhì
was Tǎn's younger brother.
Péi Tǎn is mentioned in volume 251, Yìzōng Xiántōng tenth year.
19 Guìguǎn was promoted to Jìngjiāng Jūn,
and Liú Shìzhèng, the commander, was made Jiédùshǐ.
Zhū Quánzhōng, believing Wáng Róng was secretly communicating with Lǐ Kèyòng,
moved his troops to attack him.

this is the opportunity for a hegemon.
Now, my lord, you are to be the Huán and Wén of Táng,
upon whom the fate of security and danger rests.
Lǐ Zhèn flattered Zhū Quánzhōng by comparing him to Qí Huán Gōng and Jìn Wén Gōng.
Shǔ,
sounds like zhú.
If they dare to imprison and depose the Son of Heaven,
and you cannot punish them,
how will you ever command the other feudal lords again?
Moreover, once the young emperor's position is secured,
all power in the realm will fall into the hands of the eunuchs.
This would be handing over the hilt of the great sword to others."
Zhū Quánzhōng had a great realization.
He immediately imprisoned Xīdù and Fèngběn,
and dispatched Zhèn to the capital to gather intelligence.
Xùn,
sounds like huǐng,
also xuānzhèng.
He also sent his trusted clerk Jiǎng Xuánhuī to the capital
to conspire with Cuī Yìn.
He also summoned Chéng Yán to come to Dàliáng.
The Kǎo Yì states: Xuē Jūzhèng's Wǔdài Shǐ, biography of Lǐ Zhèn:
"In the eleventh month,
Tàizǔ sent Zhèn to make a report to Cháng'ān.
The hostel official Chéng Yán reported to Zhèn, saying: 'Middle Commander Liú has ordered his nephew Xīzhēn to come discuss a great matter.'
Upon arrival,
Yán first informed him: 'The sovereign is strict and urgent,
and the internal officials are worried and fearful.
The Left Middle Commander intends to carry out a deposition,
and I dare to inform you of this.'
Zhèn looked at Xīzhēn and said: 'A hundred-year-old slave serving a three-year-old master,
disturbing the state is unrighteous,
deposing a monarch is inauspicious.
I dare not hear of such things.
Moreover, the Prince of Liáng, with an army of a million, is assisting the Son of Heaven.
Please consider this carefully!'
Xīzhēn was greatly disheartened and left.
Zhèn returned,
and Liú Jìshù indeed stirred up rebellion.
Chéng Yán led the hostel officials from various circuits to drag the emperor down from the hall to enthrone the young emperor.
When Zhèn reached Shǎn,
Shǎn had already celebrated.
Guard Commander Hán Yífàn spoke of the matter,
and Zhèn said: 'When the Benevolent Emperor first ascended to the heavens,
Middle Commander Hán killed the elder and enthroned the younger to benefit his own power,
thus bringing chaos to the realm.
Now, general, do you wish to do so again!'
Yífàn
was the grandson of Wényuē.
From then on, he dared not speak."
The Biān Yílù states:
"Although the sovereign heard of the matter,
he did not know the details,
but merely harbored indignation.
On the dìngwèi day,
the sovereign departed from the Dìngzhōu army front.
In the twelfth month,
on the wùchén day,
he reached Dàliáng,
wishing to secretly plan a restoration.
He then sent Lǐ Zhèn to investigate the matter.
Upon Zhèn's return,
he further elaborated on what was appropriate.
Soon after, he sent Jiǎng Xuánhuī to secretly plan the great cause with Cuī Yìn."
Xuē Shǐ Liáng Jì states:
"Jìshù imprisoned Zhāozōng,
and enthroned Prince Dé Yù as emperor.
He then sent his adopted son Xīdù to come and say
that he wished to surrender the Táng imperial regalia to the emperor.
At that time, the emperor was still in Héshuò.
Hearing this,
he hurriedly returned to Biàn.
The grand plan had not yet been decided.
Just then, Lǐ Zhèn returned from his mission to Cháng'ān,
and thereupon spoke to the emperor as stated above.
The emperor realized the situation,
and thereupon requested Zhèn to go on another mission to Cháng'ān
to secretly plan the restoration with the current chief minister."
I note that if Lǐ Zhèn had already expressed dissent before Jìshù's deposition and enthronement,
how could he then dare to re-enter Cháng'ān to plot the restoration with Cuī Yìn?
Therefore, I follow the Biān Yílù.
(Note: During the Zhēnmíng era,
the court historians Lǐ Qí, Zhāng Gǔn, Xī Yīnxiàng, and Féng Xíjiā compiled the Tàizǔ Shílù.
It contained many omissions and deficiencies.
Jìng Xiáng separately compiled thirty volumes to supplement its shortcomings,
titled Dàliáng Biān Yílù.)
Furthermore, the Táng Tàizǔ Jìniánlù and the old biography of Zhāng Jùn
both state that Zhāng Jùn advised the various commanders to restore the emperor.
However, the Liáng Shílù and Lǐ Zhèn's biography both state that Zhāng Jùn advised Quánzhōng to align with the palace eunuchs,
which contradicts the Jìniánlù and the old biography.
It is likely that the Liáng Shílù is mistaken,
and Zhèn's biography relies on the Shílù.
The Táng Bǔ Jì states:
"Since the regent took office,
almost fifty days passed.
No memorials arrived,
and the court and populace were alarmed and fearful.
Droughts were frequent,
and rainbows appeared with their backs to the sun.
Cuī Yìn, seeing these inauspicious signs,
then plotted an internal change.
He secretly sent letters and proclamations beyond the passes,
spreading rumors and words in the streets.
Zhū Quánzhōng sealed Cuī Yìn's proclamation and personal letter, etc., and sent them to Jìshù, saying:
'He has already turned traitor.
You should plan otherwise soon.'
Not long after,
Jìshù showed this letter to Cuī Yìn, saying: 'Recently we were united in assisting the imperial house,
but now you are stirring up strife among the frontier regions.
I am uncertain why you, Excellency, have come to this!'
Yìn merely said, 'There is no such thing.
I have been framed.
Forged names on waxed tablets have existed since ancient times.
If the Guard Commander becomes strangely enraged,
then I beg you to spare my family.'
Jìshù then spoke with him
and swore to protect him from beginning to end.
That very night, Yìn wrote a letter of thanks to Quánzhōng, saying:
'Yesterday, with sincere loyalty, I consulted your esteemed ears,
but instead received a sealed letter shown to Left Army Commander Liú Gōng.
That person already knows my intention.
Today, I swore an oath with Yìn
not to harm each other.
However, I entrust myself to you, my lord, as my main protector,
for I can then be truly safeguarded.
I also send two maidservants and two fine horses.'
Quánzhōng read the letter and cursed loudly, saying:
'Liú Jìshù, I have served the king alongside him for twelve or thirteen years,
with the relationship of brothers.
I specifically told someone to report to him,
but he could not plan for himself,
and instead showed it to Prime Minister Cuī,
implying I am two-faced and three-sided.
This is truly intolerable!
If I do not kill this man,
I will not be named Zhū!'
He then threw the letter to the ground,
imprisoned the messenger,
and sent a swift runner directly to Prime Minister Cuī.
From then on, he conspired with Dàliáng on the great matter."
I note that Cuī Yìn had always relied internally on Zhāozōng
and externally on Quánzhōng,
opposing the eunuchs.
Now that Zhāozōng was deposed,
the reason Yìn was not yet killed
was because of his close relationship with Quánzhōng.
How could Quánzhōng have shown his letter to Jìshù?
Jìshù hated Yìn to the core.
If he had received this letter,
he would have immediately killed Yìn.
How could he have shown it to Yìn and sworn an oath with him?
This is highly illogical,
and all because Chéng Kuāngróu sided with the eunuchs
and was resentful of Yìn's turmoil.
Yáng Xíngmì was additionally granted the concurrent title of Shìzhōng.
His brother Xún claimed the title of Prefect himself.
29 The crown prince had been on the throne for several weeks,
but many memorials from the [Fānzhèn]藩鎮 did not reach [the court].
Wáng Zhòngxiān's王仲先 nature was harsh and scrutinizing.
He had long known that the Left and Right Armies had many accumulated abuses,
and when he became the [Zhōngwèi]中尉,
he meticulously audited the army's money and grain.
Those found to have embezzled or committed malpractices
were severely beaten,
and the debts they owed were urgently collected;
the officers and soldiers were quite uneasy.
Sūn Dézhāo孫德昭, a [Xióngyì Jūnshǐ]雄毅軍使 from Yánzhōu鹽州, was a [Zuǒ Shéncè Zhǐhuīshǐ]左神策指揮使.
Ever since Liú Jìshù劉季述's deposition and enthronement,
he had constantly felt indignant and resentful.
Cuī Yìn崔胤 heard of this
and sent his [Pànguān]判官, Shí Jiǎn石戩, to associate with him.
The [Pànguān]判官
was the [Dùzhī Yán Tǐe Pànguān]度支鹽鐵判官.
[Jiǎn]戩,
read as 'qiǎn' (淺).
Jiǎn戩, knowing his sincerity,
secretly conveyed Yìn's胤 intention to him, saying:
"Since the Former Emperor was confined,
from high officials in the court and abroad down to the common soldiers,
who does not gnash their teeth in anger!
Now the rebels are only Jìshù季述 and Zhòngxiān仲先;
if you can truly execute these two,
and welcome the Former Emperor back to the throne,
then your wealth and honor will be unsurpassed for a time,
and your loyalty and righteousness will flow through a thousand generations;
if you hesitate and cannot decide,
then the glory will fall into the hands of others!"
Dézhāo德昭 bowed and replied:
"Dézhāo德昭 is but a small officer;
how dare I presume to take charge of [such] a great national affair!
If the Chancellor has a command,
I would not begrudge death."
Jiǎn戩 reported this to Yìn胤.
Yìn胤 tore a strip from his sash,
wrote a letter by hand, and gave it to him.
Dézhāo德昭 then allied with Dǒng Yànbì董彥弼 and Zhōu Chénghuǐ周承誨, commanders of the Qīngyuǎn Dū清遠都 of the Right Army.
Qīngyuǎn Dū清遠都
was also one of the fifty-four [Dū]都 of the [Shéncè]神策 Army.
[Fù]復,
read as 'fú yòu' (扶又).
The 1st year of Tiānfù天復
(Xīnyǒu辛酉, 901)
In this year, April
was when the reign title was changed.
1 Spring,
in the 1st month,
on the day [Yǐyǒu]乙酉, the first day of the month,
Wáng Zhòngxiān王仲先 entered the court.
When he reached Ānfú Mén安福門,
Sūn Dézhāo孫德昭 captured and beheaded him.
He galloped to Shàoyáng Yuàn少陽院,
knocked on the door, and shouted:
"The rebel has been executed!
Please, Your Majesty, come out and reward the soldiers."
Empress Hé何 did not believe it,
and said:
"If that is truly so,
bring his head!"
Dézhāo德昭 presented his head,
and the Emperor then, with the Empress, broke down the door and came out.
[Fēi]扉,
means a door leaf.
According to the Xīnshū Yíwèi Zhì新書儀衞志: The main gate of the Tàijí Gōng太極宮 is called Chéngtiān Mén承天門.
Chéngtiān Mén承天門 is divided into the East and West Corridor Gates.
One enters Chánglè Mén長樂門 from the East Corridor,
and Yǒng'ān Mén永安門 from the West Corridor.
For all court assemblies,
there are gate-guarding teams inside each gate.
[Lè]樂,
pronounced 'luò'.
Zhōu Chénghuǐ周承誨 captured Liú Jìshù劉季述 and Wáng Yànfàn王彥範, who arrived shortly after.
Before they could be interrogated, they were already beaten to death by a chaotic mob.
Xuē Qíwò薛齊偓 threw himself into a well and died,
but was pulled out and beheaded.
The families of these four individuals were exterminated,
and over twenty of their associates were also executed.
The eunuchs brought the Crown Prince, who was hiding in the Left Army,
and presented the Imperial Seal of the State.
The Emperor said:
"Yù裕 is young and weak; he was enthroned by these wicked villains,
which is not his fault."
He ordered him to return to the Eastern Palace,
demoted him to Prince Dé德,
and restored his name to Yù裕.
When Yù裕 was enthroned by the eunuchs,
his name was changed to Zhěn縝;
now his old name is restored.
On the day [Bǐngxū]丙戌,
Sūn Dézhāo孫德昭 was appointed [Tóng Píngzhāng Shì]同平章事,
and concurrently [Jìnghǎi Jiédùshǐ]靜海節度使.
The [Jìnghǎi Jūn]靜海軍
was in Ānnán安南;
Sūn Dézhāo孫德昭 held this title remotely.
On the day [Dīnghài]丁亥,
Cuī Yìn崔胤 was promoted to [Sītú]司徒;
Yìn胤 firmly declined.
The Emperor's favor and treatment towards Yìn胤 grew even more profound.
On the day [Jǐchǒu]己丑,
Zhū Quánzhōng朱全忠, hearing that Liú Jìshù劉季述 and others had been executed,
broke Chéng Yán's程巖 feet
and sent him in shackles to the capital.
Liú Xīdù劉希度, Lǐ Fèngběn李奉本, and others were all beheaded in the marketplace.
From this, he respected Lǐ Zhèn李振 even more.
Lǐ Zhèn李振 had requested the execution of Liú Jìshù劉季述 and others when he met the Emperor.
On the day [Gēngyín]庚寅,
Zhōu Chénghuǐ周承誨 was appointed [Lǐngnán Xīdào Jiédùshǐ]嶺南西道節度使,
and granted the name Lǐ Jìhuǐ李繼誨.
Dǒng Yànbì董彥弼 was appointed [Níngyuǎn Jiédù]寧遠節度,
and granted the surname Lǐ李,
both with the title [Tóng Píngzhāng Shì]同平章事;
they, along with Lǐ Jìzhāo李繼昭, remained for guard duty,
and after ten days were allowed to return home,
which was the system of taking ten-day leave.
People at the time called them
"the Three Chancellor Envoys."
Not long after,
Zhōu Chénghuǐ周承誨 and Dǒng Yànbì董彥弼 again colluded with the eunuchs,
but Sūn Dézhāo孫德昭 alone refused to do so.
On the day [Guǐsì]癸巳,
Zhū Quánzhōng朱全忠 was advanced to the title of Prince of Dōngpíng東平.
The [Kǎo Yì]考異 states: The old annals say:
"In the 2nd month,
Quánzhōng全忠 was made [Shǒu Zhōngshū Lìng]守中書令
and promoted to Prince of Liáng梁."
Xuē Jūzhèng's薛居正 Five Dynasties History, Annals of Liáng梁, says:
"In the 1st month,
on the day [Guǐsì]癸巳,
the Emperor was promoted to Prince of Liáng梁,
in recompense for his meritorious service in restoring order."
The [Shílù]實錄 says:
"On the day [Guǐsì]癸巳,
Zhū Quánzhōng朱全忠, Prince of Pèijùn沛郡, was granted the title of [Dìngmóu Xuānlì Gōngchén]定謀宣力功臣,
and promoted to Prince of Dōngpíng東平."
The New Annals say:
"In the 2nd month,
on the day [Xīnwèi]辛未,
Quánzhōng全忠 was enfeoffed as Prince of Liáng梁."
According to the [Biānyílù]編遺錄,
in the 2nd month of this year, on the day [Xīnwèi]辛未, a memorial was submitted declining the title of Prince of Liáng梁.
The edict of the 2nd month of the 3rd year says:
"The Rabbit Garden, a famous state,
Suīyáng睢陽, a profound territory,
gloriously receives the imperial decree
and greatly opens up a fiefdom;
he may hold the titles of [Tàiwèi]太尉 and [Zhōngshū Lìng]中書令,
and be promoted to Prince of Liáng梁."
Perhaps he had already been enfeoffed as Prince of Liáng梁 this year,
but Quánzhōng全忠 declined it and did not accept,
so he was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Dōngpíng東平,
and only in the 3rd year was he promoted to Prince of Liáng梁.
However, the edict of the 3rd year already refers to his former official title as Prince of Liáng梁,
which is probably an error.
Now, we follow the [Shílù]實錄.
2 On the day [Bǐngwǔ]丙午,
an imperial decree stated:
"In recent years, when Chancellors reported to the Emperor in the [Yányīng]延英 hall,
the [Shūmìshǐ]樞密使 stood beside them,
engaging in fervent disputes;
after leaving,
they would claim that the Emperor's will had not been fully agreed upon,
and would make changes again,
thereby undermining authority and disturbing governance.
From now on, all shall follow the old system of Dàzhōng大中;
only after the Chancellors have finished their reports may the [Shūmìshǐ]樞密使 ascend the hall to receive official matters."
In the Dàzhōng大中 era, it was customary that whenever Chancellors had an audience in the [Yányīng]延英 hall,
the two [Zhōngwèi]中尉 would descend first,
the [Shūmìshǐ]樞密shǐ would await the imperial command west of the hall,
and only after the Chancellors had finished their reports
would the [Shūmìshǐ]樞密shǐ receive matters before the imperial desk.
All were partisans of Liú Jìshù劉季述.
3 Lǐ Màozhēn李茂貞, [Jiédùshǐ]節度使 of Fèngxiáng鳳翔 and Zhāngyì彰義, came to court;
Màozhēn茂貞 was additionally appointed [Shǒu Shàngshū Lìng]守尚書令.
Since Emperor Tàizōng太宗 of Táng唐 ascended the throne as [Shàngshū Lìng]尚書令,
this title was no longer conferred upon others.
Guō Zǐyí郭子儀 had rendered great service,
but even when offered, he dared not accept it;
Wáng Xíngyú王行瑜, relying on his power and strength,
sought it but ultimately did not obtain it.
This shows that both ruler and ministers, high and low,
still knew to uphold the laws of previous dynasties.
Now, conferring it upon Lǐ Màozhēn李茂貞,
the laws of Táng唐 are utterly disregarded,
reaching an extreme point in this matter.
He was advanced to the title of Prince of Qí岐.
After Liú Jìshù and Wáng Zhòngxiān had died,
Cuī Yìn and Lù Yǐ memorialized, saying:
"The rise of calamity and chaos
is all due to the eunuchs commanding the military.
We beg Your Majesty to let Yìn lead the Left Army
and Yǐ lead the Right Army;
then the regional governors will not dare to invade and oppress,
and the royal house will be honored."
The Emperor hesitated for two days and did not decide.
Lǐ Màozhēn heard of this
and angrily said:
"Cuī Yìn has not yet seized military power,
but he already wants to eliminate the regional governors!"
The Emperor summoned Lǐ Jìzhāo, Lǐ Jìhuì, and Lǐ Yànbì to deliberate on it,
and they all said:
"Your servants' families have been in the army for generations;
we have never heard of literati serving as army commanders.
If they are subordinate to the Southern Bureau,
there will certainly be many changes,
it is not as convenient as returning control to the Northern Bureau."
The Emperor then said to Yìn and Yǐ:
"The generals and soldiers do not wish to be subordinate to civil officials;
you gentlemen should not insist on this."
Thereupon, he appointed Privy Councilors Hán Quánhuì and the Fengxiáng Supervising Commissioner Zhāng Yànhóng as the Left and Right Zhongwèi.
Hán Quánhuì
was also the former Fengxiáng Supervising Commissioner.
This laid the groundwork for Hán Quánhuì to abduct the Emperor to Fengxiáng.
Zūnměi said:
"Even one army is impossible to control,
how much less two armies!"
According to the Xīnshū Huànzhě Zhuàn,
Yán Zūnměi had previously served as the Left Shéncè Guānjūn Róngshǐ,
hence he spoke thus.
Chǔ,
read as chāng lǚ.
Yuán Yìjiǎn and Zhōu Jìngrōng were appointed Privy Councilors.
Lǐ Màozhēn resigned and returned to his garrison.
Cuī Yìn, believing that the eunuchs commanding the military
would eventually become a threat close at hand,
wanted to control them with external forces.
He hinted to Lǐ Màozhēn to leave three thousand soldiers in the capital
to serve as imperial guards,
with Lǐ Jìyún, Lǐ Màozhēn's adopted son, commanding them.
Hàn Wò, the Left Jiànyì Dàfū from Wànnián, thought this was unacceptable.
Yìn said:
"The soldiers themselves are unwilling to leave;
it is not that I am keeping them."
Wò said:
"Why were they summoned in the first place?"
Yìn had no reply.
The Xīnshū Hàn Wò Zhuàn states
that Yìn summoned Lǐ Màozhēn to court
and made him leave his kinsman Jìyún to guard the palace.
Therefore, he directly asked this, and Yìn had no reply.
Wò,
read as yú jiǎo.
"If these soldiers are kept, both the family and the state will be in danger;
if they are not kept, both the family and the state will be at peace."
Yìn did not listen.
Lǐ Jìyún eventually abducted the Emperor with the eunuchs to Fengxiáng.
The Kǎoyì states: The Táng Bǔjì says:
"On the eighth day of that month,
Lǐ Màozhēn came to court,
left two thousand men to guard the right street, and then returned.
Cuī Yìn reported to Zhū Quánzhōng,
requesting three thousand men to be stationed beside his residence in the Southern Ward.
When Fengxiáng abducted the Emperor westward,
Zhū Quánzhōng secretly loaded weapons onto carts,
claiming they were tribute silk,
and the men pushing the carts were all government soldiers,
who entered Cuī Yìn's residence.
People were alarmed
unlike before.
Cuī Yìn repeatedly sent people to summon Zhū Quánzhōng, but he did not arrive."
The Xīn Zhuàn says:
"Hán Quánhuì and others, knowing that Cuī Yìn would not rest until he had eliminated them,
therefore prompted Lǐ Màozhēn to leave four thousand selected soldiers as imperial guards,
with Lǐ Jìhuī in command;
Yìn also prompted Zhū Quánzhōng to send two thousand soldiers to reside in the Southern Bureau,
with Lóu Jìngsī leading them."
This is probably taken from the Táng Bǔjì.
According to Hán Wò's Jīnluan Mìjì,
Wò told Zhāozōng:
"When it was time to keep the soldiers,
I argued with Cuī Yìn five or six times.
Yìn said: 'I really did not keep the soldiers;
it is the soldiers who refused to leave.'
I said: 'Why were they summoned in the first place?'
Yìn also said: 'I am pleased that the Qí soldiers only left three thousand men.'"
Based on this,
it was Yìn who summoned Lǐ Màozhēn to court,
and still kept his soldiers.
Moreover, the Jiùjì, Liáng Shílù, Biān Yílù, Xuē Jūzhèng's Wǔdài Shǐ Liángjì, and other works
do not mention that Zhū Quánzhōng ever sent soldiers to guard the capital.
If what the Táng Bǔjì says is true,
that Qí and Biàn each sent several thousand soldiers to garrison the capital,
then when Zhāozōng wished to go west,
the soldiers from the two regions would surely have first fought below the palace gate,
or else the Biàn soldiers would have all been killed by the eunuchs,
or else they would have fled first.
Now there is no such event;
this is probably what Chéng Kuāngróu heard from hearsay,
and he also sided with the eunuchs,
deeply hating Cuī Yìn,
so it is not entirely credible.
However, the reason Yìn wanted to keep Lǐ Màozhēn's soldiers as his aid
was probably because Lǐ Màozhēn regarded the execution of Liú Jìshù as his own accomplishment,
and would certainly be of the same mind as him in enmity.
But the eunuchs enticed him with profit,
and he then allied with the eunuchs.
Now we follow the Jīnluan Jì.
4 After Zhū Quánzhōng had subdued Héběi,
he wanted to first capture Hézhōng to control Hédōng.
On the day Jǐhài,
he summoned his generals and said:
"Wáng Kē is an incompetent fellow,
relying on Tàiyuán to become arrogant and wasteful.
I will now cut the waist of the long serpent;
you gentlemen, bind him with a single rope for me!"
This means that the two garrisons of Hédōng and Hézhōng were allied to connect with Cháng'ān,
and now if Hézhōng were taken,
it would be like cutting Lǐ Kèyòng's waist.
Duàn,
read as dīng guǎn.
Wèi,
read as yú wěi.
On the day Gēngzǐ,
he dispatched Zhāng Cúnjìng to lead thirty thousand soldiers from Sìshuǐ across the river and emerge via the Hánshān Road to attack it.
Hánshān
is east of Jiàngzhōu.
When Zhāng Jùn was defeated,
he exited Hánkǒu to Héyáng,
crossed the river and returned west;
this is that road.
On the day Wùshēn,
Cúnjìng arrived at Jiàngzhōu.
Jìn and Jiàng did not expect his arrival
and had no defenses whatsoever.
On the day Gēngxū,
Táo Jiànzhāo, the Prefect of Jiàngzhōu, surrendered to him;
on the day Rénzǐ,
Zhāng Hànyú, the Prefect of Jìnzhōu, surrendered to him.
Zhū Quánzhōng sent his generals Hóu Yán to guard Jìnzhōu
and Hé Yīn to guard Jiàngzhōu,
stationing twenty thousand soldiers to block the path for Hédōng's reinforcements.
The court feared that Zhū Quánzhōng would enter Guānxi,
and urgently issued an imperial edict to reconcile;
Zhū Quánzhōng did not comply.
Kē sent secret envoys to report urgently to Lǐ Kèyòng.
The roads were successively blocked,
as Kèyòng's Bian troops had already occupied Jìn and Jiàng,
preventing his own troops from advancing.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: from Tàiyuán southwest two hundred and sixty lǐ to Fénzhōu;
from Fénzhōu south three hundred and fifty lǐ to Jìnzhōu;
from Jìnzhōu south one hundred and twenty-five lǐ to Jiàngzhōu;
from Jiàngzhōu southwest sixty-five lǐ to Hézhōng Fǔ.
Relief troops would choose convenient routes and move through gaps,
certainly not entirely following the postal roads.
However, Bian troops had already garrisoned Jìn and Jiàng to block the vital passes,
even if the Bìng troops could advance via shortcuts,
the Bian troops would block the dangerous passes ahead
and guard the crucial points behind,
preventing them from relieving Hézhōng by advancing,
or returning to Tàiyuán by retreating.
"Your son will be a captive any day now;
how can you, venerable sir, bear not to save him!"
Kèyòng replied:
"Now the enemy troops block Jìn and Jiàng;
our numbers are unequal.
If we advance, both you and I will perish.
It would be better to join Wáng Láng and your entire clan in returning to the court."
Since the Jìn dynasty,
fathers-in-law have all called their sons-in-law "láng";
this is still the case today.
[Lǐ Màoqīng] said:
"The Son of Heaven has newly returned to his rightful place.
He has issued edicts to the vassal towns not to attack each other,
but to jointly assist the imperial house.
Now Zhū Gōng disregards the edicts,
being the first to raise troops and attack;
his intentions are clear.
If Hézhōng falls,
then Tóng, Huá, Bīn, and Qí will all be unable to protect themselves.
Tóng and Huá refer to Hán Jiàn;
Bīn refers to Lǐ Màozhēn's adopted son Jìhuī;
Qí is the area governed by Màozhēn.
This situation is inevitable.
You, venerable sir, should immediately lead the troops from the various towns in Guānzhōng,
firmly defend Tóngguān,
and go to rescue Hézhōng.
I know myself to be unwarlike,
and wish to be granted a small town to your west;
please take possession of this land.
The safety of Guānzhōng
and the longevity of the state's mandate
depend on this action of yours.
I beg you to consider it carefully!"
Màozhēn had always lacked foresight and
did not reply.
If Lǐ Màozhēn had been able to save Hézhōng at this time to connect with Hédōng,
then later Fèngxiáng would certainly not have suffered the distress of being besieged.
5 In the second month,
on the jiǎyín day, the first day of the month,
the Hédōng general Lǐ Sìzhāo attacked Zézhōu
and captured it.
On the yǐmǎo day,
Zhāng Cúnjìng led his troops from Jìnzhōu;
on the jǐwèi day,
they arrived at Hézhōng
and immediately besieged it.
Wáng Kē, in dire straits,
intended to flee to the capital,
but popular sentiment was divided,
and it so happened that the pontoon bridge was damaged,
and ice floes blocked the river,
making boat travel very difficult.
"Pontoon bridge" refers to the pontoon bridge at Pújīn.
The seat of Hézhōng Fǔ was Hédōng Xiàn,
and a pontoon bridge was built to connect to Héxī Xiàn,
providing the route west into Cháng'ān.
"Sè" (塞) is pronounced like "sì" (悉).
He personally exhorted the city defenders,
but they all failed to respond.
The guard general Liú Xùn said:
"Now the people are agitated.
If we go out at night to cross the river,
there will certainly be a chaotic scramble for boats.
If one person causes trouble,
the situation will be unpredictable.
It is better to temporarily offer submission to Cúnjìng
and gradually plan our alignment."
Kē followed his advice.
On the rénxū day,
Kē planted a white banner on a corner of the city wall,
and sent an envoy with his official seal to request surrender to Cúnjìng.
Cúnjìng asked him to open the city gates.
Kē said:
"I have a generational relationship with Zhū Gōng.
Kē's father, Zhòngróng, was treated as an uncle by Zhū Quánzhōng.
"Fēn" (分) is pronounced like "fúwèn".
I will wait for Zhū Gōng to arrive,
and I will personally surrender the city to him."
Cúnjìng agreed,
and also sent a runner to inform Quánzhōng.
On the yǐchǒu day,
Quánzhōng arrived in Luòyáng
and was delighted to hear this.
Whenever an army commander
brings a powerful force to confront a weaker one,
he will surely say:
"With such a force,
who can withstand it?
With this to attack a city,
what city cannot be conquered?"
This is to intimidate the enemy with a display of strength.
However, there have been many instances where the weaker side, with firm resolve and unity of purpose, has defended,
causing large forces to be trapped below strong cities.
Therefore, those skilled in warfare do not rely on large numbers as a certainty,
and consider attacking cities the least desirable option.
Wáng Kē's willingness to surrender
was why Zhū Quánzhōng was delighted.
On the wùchén day,
he arrived at Yúxiāng,
which, according to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
Yúxiāng
is sixty lǐ east of Hézhōng Fǔ.
He expressed his deepest sorrow;
and all the people of Hézhōng were pleased.
Kē wanted to come out with his hands bound and leading a sheep,
but Quánzhōng quickly sent someone to stop him, saying:
"How can I forget the kindness of Grand Preceptor, my maternal uncle!
Quánzhōng returned to the state through Zhòngróng,
hence he spoke thus.
How could I face my maternal uncle in the underworld on another day!"
Then Kē came out to meet him with ordinary courtesy.
They clasped hands and sighed,
riding side-by-side into the city.
Quánzhōng appointed Zhāng Cúnjìng as the Acting Governor of Hùguó Army,
and Wáng Kē and his entire clan were moved to Dàliáng.
In the first year of Guǎngmíng of Xīzōng,
Wáng Zhòngróng occupied Hézhōng,
which was then passed to his brother Zhòngyíng and then to his son Kē,
lasting twenty-two years before its demise.
Zhū Quánzhōng thus gained control of Hézhōng, Jìn, and Jiàng.
He sent someone to kill Kē in Huázhōu.
Quánzhōng, hearing that Lady Zhāng's illness was critical,
hastily returned east from Hézhōng.
Lady Zhāng was
Quánzhōng's wife.
Lǐ Kèyòng dispatched an envoy with lavish gifts to request a renewal of friendly relations with Quánzhōng;
Quánzhōng, though he sent an envoy in reply,
was angered by the arrogant tone of Lǐ Kèyòng's letter,
and resolved to attack him.
Kǎoyì says: In the Tángmò Jiànwén Lù it states:
"In the sixth month of Qiánníng fourth year (897),
a military commander was sent as an envoy to Biànzhōu,
his letter said thus and so,
and the reply from Biànzhōu said thus and so."
According to Quánzhōng's letter,
it contained
"the year before last, your esteemed son was captured at Huánshuǐ;
last year, your various generals were again seized at Qīngshān,"
and also stated
"Zhèn and Dìng have submitted,
Pú and Jìn have sought peace,"
which clearly indicates it was not Qiánníng fourth year (897).
Tángnián Bǔlù states:
"In the fifth month, day Rénwǔ, of Tiānfù first year (901),
an imperial edict appointed Zhū Quánzhōng concurrently as the commander of Hézhōng,
and also ordered him to establish peace with Tàiyuán.
Initially,
the imperial court, fearing that Quánzhōng's annexation of Héshuò
and his capture of Pújīn
would inevitably lead to an outbreak of war and mutual invasion,
issued an edict to Tàiyuán and Yímén,
ordering them to strive for peaceful relations.
At that time, Tàiyuán also recognized Quánzhōng's growing strength
and first sent a letter to invite peace."
Quánzhōng's letter's wording is the same as in the Jiànwén Lù.
Quánzhōng, in his reply to Tàiyuán,
also submitted a memorial saying:
"Your servant and Tàiyuán had, in previous years, first forged a joyful alliance,
and any subsequent occasional suspicion
was merely due to each contending for status."
It also said:
"However, judging from the intent of the incoming letter,
the hostility has not yet ceased."
And it further stated:
"Your servant, having scrutinized the intent of this communication,
feels even more indignation,
and dares not proceed to establish peace,
for fear of failing the imperial trust;
I have already dispatched my various armies to launch an expedition."
Xù Bǎoyùn Lù records Quánzhōng's memorial as saying:
"Your servant had already withdrawn troops from the Héfǔ region,
and proceeded to Tàiyuán for an expedition;
I have repeatedly reported the full details,
which have been duly analyzed and submitted to the throne.
On the twenty-third day of this month,
your servant led my personal guard to Dōngdū,
where Lǐ Kèyòng's special envoy, Zhāng Tè, arrived with a letter for your servant,
along with camels, horses, bows, arrows, silver vessels, and bolts of silk, etc.,
to seek peace with your servant.
As for Zhāng Tè,
your servant has already given him a reply and sent him back.
In the same month, the soldiers withdrawn from Héfǔ
were immediately ordered to garrison temporarily at Héyáng;
currently, arrangements are being made to recover Lùzhōu,
and then the forces will proceed in succession to Tàiyuán for an expedition.
The letter from Lǐ Kèyòng to your servant
is respectfully enclosed with this memorial.
Submitted in the second month of Tiānfù fourth year (904)."
On the second day of the third month of that year,
the memorial reached the Emperor,
and Emperor Zhāozōng's imperial edict of the eighth day of the third month said thus and so.
The mention of Tiānfù fourth year (904)
is a significant error.
Biān Yílù states:
"In the second month of Tiānfù first year (901),
Lǐ Kèyòng dispatched military commander Zhāng Tè with an official document and generous gifts to appease the resentment,
and (Quánzhōng) also sent a military commander with a letter in reply."
It also says:
"On day Xīnsì,
the Emperor desired to lead the army north,
and immediately march against the northern barbarians.
Recently, Lǐ Kèyòng, with flattering words and lavish gifts,
requested to establish friendly relations,
and the matter was fully reported to the throne."
The wording is the same as in the Bǔlù.
Táng Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù states:
"In the sixth month of Tiānfù first year (901),
Tàizǔ, seeing that the Liáng bandits were currently strong
and difficult to defeat in battle,
feigned submission to delay their plans,
and thus dispatched Staff Officer Zhāng Tè with gifts of money, horses, and a letter to explain his intentions,
requesting to restore old friendships.
The letter elaborately described the might of the five northern tribes' soldiers and horses,
all of whom were his foreign allies.
Zhū Wēn was displeased upon seeing it,
and ordered Jìng Xiáng to compose a reply,
whose wording was crude and awkward,
which people ridiculed."
Xuē Jūzhèng's Wǔdài Shǐ, Biàng Jì, states:
"In the second month of Tiānfù first year (901),
Lǐ Kèyòng sent his staff officer Zhāng Tè to propose an alliance,
and the Emperor also dispatched an envoy in reply."
Lǐ Xíjí Zhuàn states:
"During the Tiānfù period,
Emperor Wǔ discussed restoring friendly relations with Liáng,
and ordered Xíjí to draft a letter to present to Liángzǔ."
The letter's wording is the same as in the Jiànwén Lù,
but the dates are inconsistent.
According to Quánzhōng's reply to Tàiyuán, which states
"the envoy arrived on the twenty-second of this month,"
and his memorial further states
"first, troops were withdrawn from Héfǔ to proceed to Tàiyuán,"
and also states
"arrived in Dōngdū on the twenty-third,"
then Kèyòng's letter reaching Quánzhōng
must have been in late second month of Tiānfù first year (901).
We now follow the Biān Yílù and Liáng Jì.
6. Wáng Pǔ, a Scholar of the Hànlín Academy and Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Revenue, was appointed Assistant Minister of the Chancellery and concurrently Grand Councilor.
Péi Shū, Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Personnel, was appointed Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Revenue and concurrently Grand Councilor.
Pǔ
was the grand-nephew of Zhèngyǎ;
Wáng Zhèngyǎ is mentioned in volume 244, Emperor Wénzōng's Dàhé fifth year (831).
"Cóng" (grand-nephew)
is pronounced "cái yòng" (cái yǒng).
Therefore, Yǐn quotes it.
7. The late Prince Mù Yǐ was posthumously honored with the title Gōng'āi Tàizǐ.
Yǐ was killed by eunuchs, as mentioned last year.
8. Liú Réngōng, Military Governor of Yōuzhōu, and Luó Shàowēi, Military Governor of Wèibó, were both granted the concurrent title of Shìzhōng.
9. In the third month,
on the day Guǐwèi, the first day of the month,
Zhū Quánzhōng arrived in Dàliáng.
He returned to Dàliáng from Hézhōng.
On day Guǐmǎo,
he dispatched Shì Shūcóng and others to lead an army of fifty thousand to attack Lǐ Kèyòng.
They entered via Tàiháng,
while Zhāng Wéngōng, a commander from Wèibó, entered via Xīnkǒu in Cízhōu.
When Emperor Wǔzōng attacked Liú Zhěn,
he opened a new road from Liáozhōu,
reaching Wǔ'ān County in Cízhōu,
hence it was called Xīnkǒu.
Zhāng Guīhòu, the Prefect of Míngzhōu, entered via Mǎlǐng,
and Wáng Chǔzhí, Military Governor of Yìwǔ, entered via Fēihú.
Shěn Kuò said: The peak of the Northern Sacred Mountain, Chángshān,
is called Dàmào Shān.
Since the Shí Jìn ceded Yān and Yún to the Khitan,
Dàmào Shān was made the dividing ridge boundary.
The Fēihú Road
is west of Dàmào Shān.
It goes north from Yínyě Zhài, passes Dǎomǎ Guān,
crosses the northern border,
then re-enters between Shíménzǐ and Lìngshuǐ Pù, passing through Píngxíng and Méihuí two fortresses,
to reach Dàizhōu.
Today, there are many ancient steles of the Táng dynasty in the Dàmào Temple.
In a pavilion in front of the main hall, there is an inscription by Lǐ Kèyòng which says:
"Lǐ Kèyòng, Military Governor of Tàiyuán and Hédōng, personally led five hundred thousand infantry and cavalry,
to punish Yōulíng,
and returned via Fēihú Road,
then returned to Yànmén."
Shūcóng entered Tiānjǐng Guān
and advanced to Ángchē.
Ángchē
is Ángchē Guān,
located at Ángchē Lǐng in Zézhōu.
On day Xīnhài,
Cài Xùn, the Prefect of Qìnzhōu,
surrendered the city.
Gài Zhāng, a commander from Hédōng,
went to Hóu Yán to surrender,
and was immediately appointed acting Prefect of Qìnzhōu.
"Gài"
is pronounced "gǔ hé" (gǔ hé),
and is a surname.
On day Rénzǐ,
Shūcóng captured Zézhōu,
and Lǐ
Cúnzhāng abandoned the city and fled.
Shūcóng advanced to attack Lùzhōu,
and Mèng Qiān, Military Governor of Zhāoyì, surrendered to him.
Lǐ Shěnjiàn and Wáng Zhōu, garrison commanders from Hédōng, leading ten thousand infantry and two thousand cavalry, went to Shūcóng and surrendered;
Shūcóng pressed on towards Jìnyáng.
In summer,
fourth month,
on day Yǐmǎo,
Shūcóng passed through Shíhuì Guān
and encamped at Dòngwō Yì.
Dòngwō Yì
is situated by the Dòngwō River.
On day Dīngsì,
Zhāng È, Prefect of Liáozhōu, surrendered.
A separate force led by Bái Fèngguó, reinforced by Chéngdé troops, entered via Jǐngxíng.
On day Jǐwèi,
they captured Chéngtiān Jūn,
and signaled with beacon fires to Shūcóng.
10. On day Jiǎxū,
the Emperor visited the Imperial Ancestral Temple;
on day Dīngchǒu,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the empire,
and the reign title was changed.
Wáng Yá and seventeen other families were exonerated.
Wáng Yá and others were executed as mentioned in volume 245, Emperor Wénzōng's Dàhé ninth year (835).
Cuī Yìn intended to execute the eunuchs,
hence he first exonerated Wáng Yá and others.
In the eleventh month,
Yáng Fùgōng 楊復恭 served as the Grand Director,
borrowing the profits from the salt gabelle's year-long麴 (qu) wine sales to support the two armies.
From then on, he was unwilling to return them.
By this time,
Cuī Yìn 崔胤 drafted an amnesty,
including the text of the amnesty and various conditions.
It permitted brewers to make their own麴 (qu) wine,
but they had to pay a monthly tax on wine sales.
The麴 (qu) wine previously made by the two armies
was to be sold at a reduced price,
and no more could be sold after the seventh month.
The Military Governor of Dōngchuān 東川, Wáng Zōngdí 王宗滌, requested a replacement due to illness.
Wáng Jiàn 王建 memorialized to appoint the Commander of Cavalry and Infantry, Wáng Zōngyù 王宗裕, as acting military governor.
Shì Shúcóng 氏叔琮 and others led their troops to the foot of Jìnyáng 晉陽 city,
repeatedly challenging,
causing great fear within the city.
Lǐ Kèyòng 李克用 ascended the city wall to prepare defenses,
having no time to eat or drink.
At that time, heavy rain fell for several tens of days,
and much of the city wall collapsed,
which was immediately repaired.
Héddōng 河東 generals Lǐ Sìzhāo 李嗣昭 and Lǐ Sìyuán 李嗣源 dug a secret gate,
and at night,
sallied forth to attack the Biàn 汴 encampment,
repeatedly achieving kills and captures.
Lǐ Cúnjìn 李存進 defeated the Biàn 汴 army at Dòngwō 洞渦.
At that time, the Biàn 汴 army was numerous,
but fodder and provisions were insufficient.
With prolonged rain,
the soldiers suffered from malaria and dysentery,
so Zhū Quánzhōng 朱全忠 recalled his troops.
In the fifth month,
Shì Shúcóng 氏叔琮 and others returned via Shíhuìguān 石會關.
The *Kǎoyì 考異* states, citing the *Biān Yílù 編遺錄*:
"In the fourth month,
on the day *rénxū* 壬戌,
Lǐ Kèyòng 李克用 sent Zhāng Tè 張特 with a letter requesting an alliance of goodwill,
and then commanded all armies to hold their positions.
A special envoy was sent to Tàiyuán 太原,
promising reconciliation.
Moreover, the soil in Bīngzhōu 並州 was cold,
and the seasons were very late.
As there were many warhorses,
wild grass was insufficient for fodder,
so Shì Shúcóng 氏叔琮 was immediately ordered to turn back his troops."
The *Hòutáng Tàizǔ Jì 後唐太祖紀* states:
"In the fifth month,
Shì Shúcóng 氏叔琮 and the rebel armies from all four sides retreated."
Xuē Shǐliáng Jì 薛史梁紀 states that
the return of the army was in the fourth month.
The *Hòutáng Jì 後唐紀* states that
the Biàn 汴 army retreated in the fifth month.
Probably Zhū Quánzhōng 朱全忠 ordered the army to return in the fourth month,
but Shì Shúcóng 氏叔琮 and others left Jìnyáng 晉陽 in the fifth month,
hence the discrepancies in the national histories.
Héddōng 河東 generals Zhōu Déwēi 周德威 and Lǐ Sìzhāo 李嗣昭 pursued them with five thousand elite cavalry,
killing and capturing many.
Earlier,
Fénzhōu 汾州 Prefect Lǐ Táng 李瑭 had surrendered his prefecture to the Biàn 汴 army.
Kèyòng 克用 sent his general Lǐ Cúnshěn 李存審 to attack it,
and took it in three days,
capturing Táng 瑭
and beheading him.
When Shì Shúcóng 氏叔琮 passed through Shàngdǎng 上黨,
Mèng Qiān 孟遷 led his clan to move south with him.
Zhū Quánzhōng 朱全忠 sent Dīng Huì 丁會 to replace and guard Lùzhōu 潞州.
This laid the groundwork for Dīng Huì 丁會's eventual defection to Lǐ Kèyòng 李克用.
Zhū Quánzhōng 朱全zhong memorialized requesting the removal of the Military Governor of Hézhōng 河中,
and secretly prompted the officials and common people to request him as commander.
On the day *guǐmǎo* 癸卯,
Quánzhōng 全忠 was appointed Military Governor of the Four Circuits: Xuānwǔ 宣武, Xuānyì 宣義, Tiānpíng 天平, and Hùguó 護國.
At this time,
from Pú 蒲 and Shǎn 陝 eastward,
to the sea,
south to the Huái 淮 River,
and north to the Hé 河 River,
all the circuits were under Zhū Quánzhōng 朱全忠's control.
If Quánzhōng 全忠 had expanded his territory by integrating neighboring circuits,
he should have concurrently governed Yòuguó 佑國, Héyáng 河陽, and Shǎnguó 陝虢,
not bypassed these three circuits to govern Hézhōng 河中.
The reason Quánzhōng 全忠 governed Hézhōng 河中 was
to control the imperial court above,
and to control Lǐ Kèyòng 李克用 below.
On the day *jǐyǒu* 己酉,
Qián Liú 錢鏐, Military Governor of Zhènhǎi 鎮海 and Zhèndōng 鎮東, was granted the additional title of Grand Imperial Counselor.
When Cuī Yìn 崔胤 abolished the two armies' sale of麴 (qu) wine,
the prohibition was also extended to nearby circuits.
Lǐ Màozhēn 李茂貞, regretting the loss of profit,
memorialized to request an audience at court to discuss the matter.
Lǐ Màozhēn 李茂貞 was in Fèngxiáng 鳳翔,
a nearby circuit, hence his contention over the profit from麴 (qu) wine sales.
When Màozhēn 茂貞 arrived in the capital,
Quán Huì 全誨 formed a deep alliance with him.
Cuī Yìn 崔胤 then became fearful,
secretly favoring Zhū Quánzhōng 朱全忠 even more,
and became an enemy of Màozhēn 茂貞.
Zhāng Quányì 張全義, Military Governor of Yòuguó 佑國, was concurrently appointed Minister of the Secretariat.
In the sixth month,
on the day *guǐhài* 癸亥,
Zhū Quánzhōng 朱全忠 proceeded to Hézhōng 河中.
The *Kǎoyì 考異* states: Xuē Jūzhèng's 薛居正 *Wǔdài Shǐ Liáng Jì 五代史梁紀* says:
"On the day *gēngshēn* 庚申,
the Emperor departed from Dàliáng 大梁."
We now follow the *Biān Yílù 編遺錄*.
When the Emperor returned to the legitimate path,
Secretariat Drafter Línghú Huàn 令狐渙 and Palace Remonstrant Hán Wò 韓偓 were both involved in his plans.
Therefore, they were promoted to Academicians of the Hànlín 翰林 Academy,
frequently summoned for discussions,
and consulted on confidential matters.
Huàn 渙 was
the son of Táo 綯.
At this time, the Emperor entrusted all military and state affairs to Cuī Yìn 崔胤.
Whenever he submitted a memorial,
the Emperor conversed with him at ease,
sometimes until candles were lit.
The eunuchs feared him and eyed him with suspicion,
all consulting Yìn 胤 before acting.
Yìn 胤's ambition was to eliminate all of them.
Hán Wò 韓偓 repeatedly advised, saying:
"Matters should not be pushed too far.
It is not acceptable to have none of these people at all;
I fear their faction might be driven to extremes,
causing further trouble."
Yìn 胤 did not listen.
On the day *dīngmǎo* 丁卯,
the Emperor summoned Wò 偓 alone
and asked,
"Among the imperial envoys, those who commit evil are as numerous as a forest.
How should they be dealt with?"
He replied,
"In the rebellion in the Eastern Palace,
which imperial envoy was not equally evil!
The time to deal with them should have been on New Year's Day
(meaning when Liú Jìshù 劉季述 and others were executed).
The Emperor said,
"At that time,
why did you not speak of this to Cuī Yìn 崔胤?"
He replied,
"I saw Your Majesty's edict stating,
'Apart from Liú Jìshù 劉季述 and the other four families,
no one else will be questioned.'
For a ruler, the most important thing
is trustworthiness.
Since this edict was issued,
it should be firmly upheld.
If even one more person is executed,
everyone will fear death.
Subsequently, quite a few have already been dismissed,
which is why they are so apprehensive and unsettled.
Your Majesty would do better to select a few of the most wicked ones,
clearly declare their crimes,
and execute them according to the law.
Then, conciliate the rest, saying: 'I feared you might think I harbored intentions [against you],
but from now on, you may have no doubts.'
Then select the loyal and honest among them to be their leaders.
If their followers do good, reward them;
if they commit crimes, punish them.
All will then feel secure.

he will surely become a future calamity.”
Quánzhōng heard that Jiàn had submitted a memorial advising the Son of Heaven to proceed to Fèngxiáng,
so he led his troops to press against Jiàn’s city.
Jiàn met him, riding alone.
Quánzhōng rebuked him,
and Jiàn replied:
“I, Jiàn, am illiterate.
All memorials, proclamations, and manifestos
were written by Lǐ Jùchuān.”
Quánzhōng, considering that Jùchuān had often devised strategies for Jiàn,
had him beheaded at the army gate.
The execution of Lǐ Jùchuān was too late.
常為 (cháng wéi)
is pronounced “yú wěi.”
“You have made a promise to someone.
You may now return home in splendor.”
The people of Hàn said:
“To be rich and honored yet not return to one’s hometown
is like traveling in brocade at night.”
Hán Jiàn
was from Chángshè, Xǔ Prefecture.
衣 (yī)
is pronounced “yú jì.”
On the Dīngsì day,
Jiàn was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Zhōngwǔ Circuit,
administering Chén Prefecture.
The Táng dynasty established the Zhōngwǔ Army in Xǔ Prefecture.
When Huáng Cháo moved east from Cháng'ān,
Zhào Chōu,
a native of Chén,
had rendered meritorious service in defending Chén Prefecture.
The imperial court conferred the Zhōngwǔ Jìedùshǐ on him,
and he petitioned to move the seat of the Zhōngwǔ Army to Chén Prefecture.
It should be noted that at this time the Son of Heaven had already gone west.
Hán Jiàn’s transfer from Huá to Chén
was all arranged by Zhū Quánzhōng,
and not formally appointed by memorial.
To immediately make him Zhōngwǔ Jìedùshǐ,
from whom did he receive the order?
(Quánzhōng) feared that Hán Jiàn might escape midway and return to Qí;
he also feared that having been in Huá for a long time,
his generals and soldiers might rob him.
The Kǎoyì (Investigation of Discrepancies) states: The Biān Yílù (Compiled Remnants) records:
“The Emperor led his troops to press against Huá Prefecture.
Hán Jiàn rode a light horse out of the city wall and surrendered.
The Emperor dined and drank with Jiàn at the Xīxī Pavilion,
then returned to the Chìshuǐ camp.
After ten days,
Jiàn was invited to serve as Zhōngwǔ Jìedùshǐ.”
The Liáng Tàizǔ Shílù (Veritable Records of Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng) states:
“On the Yǐmǎo day,
the main army reached Huá Prefecture.
Jiàn came to surrender.
On the Jiǎchén day,
Jiàn was appointed Acting Prefect of Huá Prefecture,
with Gōng Lín, a Staff Administrator of Xuānwǔ, assisting him.”
The Táng Tàizǔ Jìniánlù (Chronological Records of Emperor Tàizǔ of Táng) states:
“On the Bǐngchén day,
the Biàn army attacked Huá Prefecture.
After nine days,
Jiàn surrendered the city.”
The Táng Bǔjì (Supplemental Records of Táng) states:
“Wáng Xíngyuē, the Prefect of Tóng Prefecture, closed the city gates and ascended the ramparts.
Quánzhōng hacked open the city gates
and massacred the inhabitants,
leaving no one alive.
Hán Jiàn of Huá Prefecture heard of this
and went thirty Lǐ out of the city to meet him.
At the meeting point, he merely said: ‘Your Lordship’s ancestral home is Xǔ Prefecture.
You should now return home in splendor.’
Then men were dispatched to escort him east of the pass.”
Old traditions say:
“Jiàn sent Lǐ Jùchuān to Hézhōng to make an offer of surrender.
Jìng Xiáng, disliking his literary skill,
advised Quánzhōng to kill him.”
Xuē Jūzhèng’s Wǔdài Shǐ Liáng Zǔ Jì (History of the Five Dynasties, Annals of Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng) states:
“On the Bǐngchén day,
the Emperor memorialized to appoint Jiàn Acting Military Commissioner of Zhōngwǔ,
urging him to take up his post.”
The Shílù states:
“On the Yǐmǎo day,
Quánzhōng took Huá Prefecture.
On the Bǐngchén day,
he reached Wǔgōng,
and transferred Jiàn to be Zhōngwǔ Jìedùshǐ.”
It should be noted that there was no Jiǎchén day in this month.
The character Bǐngchén is likely a mistake.
If Quánzhōng took Huá Prefecture on Yǐmǎo,
how could he have reached Wǔgōng so quickly on Bǐngchén!
The Táng Bǔjì also states:
“Zhāozōng, unaware that Cuī Yìn was falsely issuing imperial decrees,
heard that Zhū Quánzhōng had conquered and taken two prefectures.
On the third day of the eleventh month, at the haì hour (9-11 PM),
he fled westward.”
It should be noted that Xíngyuē was the Jìedùshǐ when Kèyòng took Tóng Prefecture.
Chéng Kuāngróu’s absurdities are often of this kind.
Now, we follow the Liáng Tàizǔ Shílù for the date of taking Huá Prefecture,
and the Zhāozōng Shílù for the death of Lǐ Jùchuān.
Zhào Xǔ, the Zhōngwǔ Jìedùshǐ, was transferred to be Kuāngguó Jìedùshǐ.
Zhào Xǔ’s transfer to Tóng Prefecture
was also not an imperial decree from the Son of Heaven.
In the third and fourth years of Qiánníng (896, 897),
the imperial carriage was in Huá Prefecture.
Hán Jiàn heavily taxed them.
In two years,
he collected nine million strings of cash.
By this time,
Quánzhōng took all of it.
History states that those who amass wealth from ancient times
mostly accumulate it for others.
At this time, the capital had no Son of Heaven,
and the temporary imperial residence had no Chancellor.
Cuī Yìn had Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince Lú Wò and over two hundred others submit a petition requesting Zhū Quánzhōng to go west to welcome the imperial carriage.
He also sent Wáng Pǔ to Chìshuǐ to meet Quánzhōng and discuss matters.
The Kǎoyì states: The Biān Yílù records:
“At that time, Cháng'ān had no sovereign,
the imperial court had no directives.
The Emperor was in Qí, without assisting ministers.
Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
no chaos and disorder has been like today’s.
Yìn requested Wáng Pǔ to travel from Xījīng to Chìshuǐ
to ask the Emperor to advance his army to welcome the imperial carriage.
On the Wùwǔ day,
he departed from Chìshuǐ.”
Xuē Jūzhèng’s Wǔdài Shǐ Liáng Jì (History of the Five Dynasties, Annals of Liáng) states:
“On the Jǐwèi day,
(he) departed from Chìshuǐ.”
It should be noted that the Táng Tàizǔ Jìniánlù states:

Cuī Yìn, leading the hundred officials, lined up to welcome him.”
The Biān Yílù states:
“Yìn requested Wáng Pǔ to come from Xījīng to the Chìshuǐ army camp for discussion.”
The Shílù says
“Yìn temporarily resided in Huá Prefecture,”
and also says
“Yìn summoned Pǔ to Chìshuǐ.”
Both are mistakes.
The old Jì also states:
“Yìn ordered Pǔ to go to Chìshuǐ
to urge Quánzhōng to welcome the imperial carriage.”
We follow this.
The date of departure from Chìshuǐ follows the Biān Yílù.
“If I advance, I fear the slander of coercing the sovereign;
if I retreat, I harbor the shame of failing the nation;
yet I dare not but exert myself.”
On the Wùwǔ day,
Quánzhōng departed from Chìshuǐ.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
Lú Guāngqǐ, Minister of War, was appointed acting Chief Administrator of the Chancellery.
At that time, there was no Chancellor,
so he was temporarily appointed to administer.
句 (gōu)
is pronounced “gǔ hòu.”
當 (dāng)
is pronounced “dīng làng.”
On the Rénxū day,
(they) arrived at Fèngxiáng.
When Zhū Quánzhōng arrived in Cháng'ān,
the Chancellor, leading the hundred officials, lined up to welcome him at Chánglè Pō;
the next day, upon his departure,
they again lined up to bid farewell at Língāo Post Station.
Lining up to welcome and lining up to bid farewell
were not actions appropriate for a vassal.
Cuī Yìn’s subservience to Zhū Quánzhōng to this extent
was a plan to save himself from death,
not a plan for the Táng dynasty.
After the eunuchs were executed,
Yìn also died at Quánzhōng’s hands.
It was fitting.
帥 (shuài)

Because he was able to protect Cuī Yìn and the hundred officials.

Jì Zhāo then offered all of his eight thousand soldiers.
Sūn Dézhāo feared Zhū Wēn’s domineering suspicion.
Quán Zhōng sent his judicial officers Lǐ Zé and Péi Zhù to present a memorial to the emperor,
stating:
"I received a secret edict and a letter from Cuī Yǐn,

Hán Quán Hùi and others issued a forged imperial edict in reply, saying:

Mào Zhēn dispatched his general Fú Dào Zhāo to garrison Wǔ Gōng to resist Quán Zhōng.
According to the *Jiǔ Yù Zhì*: Wǔ Gōng County

33 On *Dīng Mǎo*,

The title "participate in confidential affairs"
had not been formally granted by the Táng court for a long time;
Lú Guāng Qǐ temporarily exercised the authority of an official of the Central Secretariat (Zhōng Shū) to perform it.
34 On *Wù Chén*,
Zhū Quán Zhōng arrived at Fèng Xiáng

The *Kǎo Yì* states: The *Shí Lù* says:

However, Quán Zhōng left Cháng'ān on *Guǐ Hài*,
arriving at Qí on *Yǐ Chǒu* and *Bǐng Yín*,

We now follow the *Biān Yí Lù* and *Xīn Jì*.
"The Son of Heaven fled from disaster,

If the Prince of Qí was not involved in the conspiracy,
why bother with explanations!"
The Emperor repeatedly issued edicts for Quán Zhōng to return to his garrison,
but Quán Zhōng merely submitted a memorial to respectfully decline.
The repeated edicts for Quán Zhōng to return to his garrison
were issued by Hán Quán Hùi and Lǐ Mào Zhēn, who held the Emperor captive to command him.
Quán Zhōng submitted a memorial to respectfully decline,
as if he dared not defy the imperial command,
but his true intention was elsewhere.
On *Xīn Wèi*,
he moved his troops north towards Bīn Zhōu.
This was Quán Zhōng's true intention.
Mào Zhēn's adopted son Jì Hūi garrisoned Bīn;
Bīn and Qí
were like the interdependence of chariot and axle,
if Bīn was taken first, Qí would be isolated.
According to the *Jiǔ Yù Zhì*: Fèng Xiáng is two hundred and twenty-two *lǐ* northeast of Bīn Zhōu.

a white edict: 'Lú Guāng Qǐ may be appointed Remonstrance Official (Jiàn Yì Dà Fū) and participate in confidential affairs (cān zhī jī wù).'

These were all the intentions of the eunuchs;

On *Yǐ Hài*,

When Quán Zhōng entered the pass westward,

The Hàn dynasty's Píng Yáng County

When the Táng Fǔ Bīng system was still in place, there was a Píng Yáng Prefecture.

on *Wù Yín*,

On *Wù Xū*,

38 Zhōng Chuán, Military Governor of Jiāng Xī, led troops to besiege the Prefect of Fǔ Zhōu, Wēi Quán Fěng.
A heavenly fire burned his city,
and the soldiers and people were startled and alarmed.
"讙" (*huān*),
same as "諠" (*xuān*).
Chuán said:
"To take advantage of someone's danger
is not benevolent."
So he prayed:
"Let Quán Fěng's crime

The fire soon stopped.
When Quán Fěng heard of this,
he apologized for his transgressions and submitted to Chuán's command,
giving his daughter in marriage to Chuán's son, Kuāng Shí.
It is recounted that when [Jiàn] Chuán 傳 was young, he once hunted

He fought with it.
The tiger clawed his shoulder,
but Chuán 傳 also held the tiger's waist and wouldn't let go.
Others around jointly killed the tiger,
and thus he escaped.
When he became noble later,
he regretted it,
and often warned his sons, saying:
"A scholar in life values wisdom and strategy.

The *Shī* 詩 says: "Bare-chested and wrestling a tiger."

means to fight it bare-handed.

1. Spring,
first month,
on the *guǐchǒu* 癸丑 day,

Mènghóuyuán 孟侯原 to the west,
and Báilùyuán 白鹿原 to the north,
making it the "Three Plains" (Sānyuán 三原).
In the seventh year of Tàipíng Zhēnjūn 太平真君 of the Later Wèi 後魏 Dynasty,
the *Hùjūn* 護軍 was abolished,
and a county was established.
(This was) to divide Zhū Quánzhōng's 朱全忠 troop strength.

2. On the *dīngmǎo* 丁卯 day,

3. On the *bǐngzǐ* 丙子 day,

At that time, Màozhēn 茂貞 did not come out to fight.
Quánzhōng 全忠 heard there were Hédōng 河東 troops,

on the *wùyín* 戊寅 *shuò* 朔 day,

at this time, it had not yet been changed.
The historical records mix them up.
On the *yǐwèi* 乙未 day,
the Biàn 汴 army of 100,000 camped south of Pú 蒲.
Pú 蒲 was an ancient Hàn 漢 county,
