Gōngbù Shìláng, Píngzhāngshì Wéi Yífàn suffered his mother's death.
Before "Píngzhāngshì"
there
should be
the character "Tóng".
He discussed with Hán Wò,
and Wò said:
"If you seek long-term benefit,
then it is best not to take up the post for now;
if it is the Emperor's direct intention,
then there is certainly no objection.
However, the Biàn army will soon besiege the city,
and the isolated city is hard to defend,
and your family is in the east,
how can you not worry?"
Yífàn then feigned illness.
*Yíwén* means to claim illness.
16Zhènhǎi, Zhèndōng Jiédùshǐ, Péngchéng Wáng Qián Liú was promoted in peerage to Yuè Wáng.
From a Prince of a Commandery to a Prince of a State.
17In the sixth month,
on the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Zhōngshū Shèrén Sū Jiǎn was appointed Gōngbù Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
At that time, Wéi Yífàn was in mourning.
Those in mourning slept on straw and used an earth clod for a pillow,
hence "cǎotǔ".
Since the Emperor did not use Yífàn,
Màozhēn and the eunuchs, fearing that the Emperor would appoint people himself,
jointly recommended Jiǎn,
so he was appointed.
18On the *dīngchǒu* day,
Zhū Quánzhōng's army was stationed in Guóxiàn.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* says: Guóxiàn
is thirty-five *lǐ* south of Fèngxiáng Fǔ.
Sòng Bái says: Guóxiàn.
The *Lǐjì Zhù* refers to
"Guó"
as
"Guō,"
and the Guóshū Chéng one hundred *lǐ* south of Wǔdū is it.
Furthermore, the *Dìlǐ Zhì* says: Guó
was annexed into Yōng by the Hàn dynasty.
The present Guóxiàn
was established as Wǔdū Jùn by the Later Wèi dynasty;
in the thirteenth year of Dàtǒng of the Later Zhōu dynasty,
Luòyì Xiàn city of Tóngzhōu was moved to the west of Wǔdū city,
and Luòyì Xiàn was established;
in the third year of Dàyè of the Suí dynasty,
Luòyì was renamed Guóxiàn.
19 Fēng Hóngduó (馮弘鐸), Military Governor of Wǔníng (武寧), resided between Xuānzhōu (宣州) and Yángzhōu (揚州).
Xuānzhōu (宣州)
was held by Tián Yùn (田頵);
Yángzhōu (揚州)
by Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密).
Fēng Hóngduó (馮弘鐸) held Shēngzhōu (昇州), situated between these two garrisons.
However, relying on the strength of his tower ships,
he did not defer to either power.
Tián Yùn (田頵), Military Governor of Níngguó (寧國), wished to seize him.
He hired Fēng Hóngduó’s (馮弘鐸) workers to build warships.
The workers said:
"Lord Fēng (馮公) sought durable timber from afar,
hence his ships last long.
Such wood is unavailable here."
Tián Yùn (田頵) said:
"Just build them."
The character '第 (dì)'
means 'just' or 'only'.
Fēng Huī (馮暉) and Yán Jiàn (顏建), Fēng Hóngduó's (馮弘鐸) generals, persuaded Hóngduó (弘鐸) to attack Tián Yùn (田頵) first.
Hóngduó (弘鐸) agreed,
leading his troops southwards,
claiming to attack Hóngzhōu (洪州).
Zhōng Chuán (鍾傳) held Hóngzhōu (洪州).
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) sent someone to stop him;
he did not comply.
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) was then the Supreme Commander of all circuits south of the Yangtze (南面諸道都統),
thus he wanted to control Fēng Hóngduó’s (馮弘鐸) military movements.
On the xīn-sì day
Tián Yùn (田頵) led his fleet and counterattacked at Gěshān (葛山),
decisively defeating him.
The New History (新書) renders it
"Héshān (曷山),"
which should be followed.
Zhāng Shùnmín's (張舜民) Chēn Xíng Lù (郴行錄) states: "Hèshān Jī (褐山磯) is slightly west of Dàxìnkǒu (大信口),
forty-odd *lǐ* south of Wúhú (蕪湖) county."
The character '帥 (shuài)'
is pronounced 'shuài'.
20 On the jiǎ-shēn day,
Lǐ Màozhēn (李茂貞) launched a massive army,
personally leading it,
and fought Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) north of Guóxiàn (虢縣).
He was severely defeated and returned,
with over ten thousand dead.
On the bǐng-xū day,
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) sent his general Kǒng Qíng (孔勍) out of Sǎnguān (散關)
to attack Fèngzhōu (鳳州),
capturing it.
On the dīng-hài day,
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱ánzhōng) advanced his army to the foot of Fèngxiáng (鳳翔) city.
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠), in court attire, faced the city and wept,
saying:
"Your servant merely wishes to escort the imperial carriage back to the palace."
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) used a righteous pretext to carry out his deception.
The character '朝 (cháo)'
is pronounced 'zhí yáo'.
Then, five stockades were built to encircle it.
21 Fēng Hóngduó (馮弘鐸) gathered his remaining troops and moved along the river, intending to enter the sea.
In the first year of Guāngqǐ (光啟) of Xīzōng (僖宗),
Zhāng Xióng (張雄) occupied Shàngyuán (上元);
after Zhāng Xióng (張雄) died,
Fēng Hóngduó (馮弘鐸) succeeded him.
By this time, Fēng Hóngduó (馮弘duó) perished;
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) thus acquired Shēngzhōu (昇州).
He sent an envoy to reward the army,
and also to persuade Fēng Hóngduó (馮弘duó) saying:
"Your followers are still numerous.
Why abandon yourselves beyond the vast sea?
Although my administration is small,
it is sufficient to accommodate your followers,
allowing each officer and official to find their place.
What do you say?"
Fēng Hóngduó's (馮弘duó) attendants all wept and obeyed.
With the army's morale broken,
could Fēng Hóngduó (馮弘duó) possibly avoid submitting to Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密)?
How could he achieve that!
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) personally boarded a light boat to welcome him,
with only a dozen attendants,
in plain clothes,
unarmed.
He boarded Fēng Hóngduó's (馮弘duó) boat,
comforted and consoled him,
and the entire army was moved and pleased.
He appointed Fēng Hóngduó (馮弘duó) as Deputy Military Governor of Huáinán (淮南),
and provided him with generous lodgings and provisions.
Previously,
Fēng Hóngduó (馮弘duó) had sent his staff officer Dāntú (丹徒) Shàng Gōngnǎi (尚公迺) to Yáng Xíngmì (楊行mì) to request Rùnzhōu (潤州).
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行mì) refused.
Shàng Gōngnǎi (尚公迺) boldly declared:
"If you do not grant it,
I only fear you cannot rival our tower ships!"
By this time,
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行mì) said to Shàng Gōngnǎi (尚公迺):
"Do you still remember asking for Rùnzhōu (潤州)?"
Shàng Gōngnǎi (尚公迺) apologized, saying:
"Generals and officers each serve their own lord."
The character '為 (wéi)'
is pronounced 'yú wěi'.
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行mì) laughed and said:
"If you serve this old Yang (楊叟) as you served Lord Feng (馮公),
you will have no worries!"
During the rebellions of Tián Yùn (田頵) and Zhū Yánshòu (朱延壽),
Shàng Gōngnǎi (尚公迺) devoted all his loyalty and strength to Yáng Xíngmì (楊行mì), laying the groundwork.
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行mì) appointed Lǐ Shénfú (李神福) as Administrator of Shēngzhōu (昇州).
Yáng Xíngmì (楊 Xíngmì) used Lǐ Shénfú (李神fú) to govern Shēngzhōu (昇州)
to control Xuānzhōu (宣州) and Rùnzhōu (潤州) from the side.
22 Yáng Xíngmì (楊行mì) dispatched troops to suppress Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠),
appointing Deputy Military Governor Lǐ Chéngsì (李承嗣) to temporarily oversee the affairs of the Huáinán (淮南) military government.
The military officials intended to transport provisions with large warships.
The Commander of All Soldiers and Horses (都知兵馬使), Xú Wēn (徐溫), said:
"The transport route has been unused for a long time;
reeds and rushes block it.
Huáng Cháo (黃巢) rebelled,
Gāo Pián (高駢) was disloyal,
and the supplies from Jiang (江) and Huai (淮) no longer reached the capital,
hence the route has been unused for a long time."
The character '塞 (sè)'
is pronounced 'xī zé'.
"It should be easier to pass."
When the army reached Sùzhōu (宿州),
there was prolonged rain,
and the heavy loads could not advance.
The soldiers showed signs of hunger,
but the small boats arrived first.
Yáng Xíngmì (楊 Xíngmì) thereupon admired Xú Wēn (徐溫),
and began to discuss military matters with him.
This laid the groundwork for Xú Wēn (徐溫) to usurp the Yáng (楊) family's three generations of dynastic rule and establish his adopted son.
The campaign failed,
and they eventually returned due to insufficient provisions.
23 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Kǒng Qíng (孔勍) captured Chéngzhōu (成州) and Lǒngzhōu (隴州);
the soldiers offered no resistance.
Upon reaching Qínzhōu (秦州),
the people of the prefecture defended the city,
so he returned via Gùguān (故關).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: "Fèngzhōu (鳳州) is two hundred seventy *lǐ* west of Chéngzhōu (成州),
and two hundred fifty *lǐ* north of Lǒngzhōu (隴州);
also, from Lǒngzhōu (隴zhōu) west to Qínzhōu (秦zhōu) is also two hundred fifty *lǐ*."
Kǒng Qíng (孔勍) went west from Fèngzhōu (鳳州) to take Chéngzhōu (成zhōu),
then north from Chéngzhōu (成zhōu) to take Lǒngzhōu (隴zhōu),
and then west from Lǒngzhōu (隴zhōu) to Qínzhōu (秦zhōu).
All three prefectures belonged to Lǐ Màozhēn (李茂zhēn) at that time.
Furthermore,
fifty *lǐ* east of Qīngshuǐ (清水) county in Qínzhōu (秦zhōu) is Dàzhèn Guān (大震關).
In the sixth year of Dàzhōng (大中),
Xuē Kuí (薛逵), Defense Commissioner of Lǒngzhōu (隴zhōu), moved and built Ānrǒng Guān (安戎關) on Lǒngshān (隴山).
From then on, Dàzhèn Guān (大震關) was called Gùguān (故關).
Today, west of Lǒngzhōu (隴zhōu) is Gùguānshān (故關山),
and southwest of that is Qīngshuǐ (清水) county.
In the sixth year of Dàzhōng (大zhōng),
Xuē Kuí (薛逵), Defense Commissioner of Lǒngzhōu (隴zhōu), submitted a memorial:
"We respectfully observe that the western border of the Yuán (源) region
is critically located at Gùguān (故關).
Although there are defenses,
there is no complete system of control.
It is situated remotely atop steep mountains,
merely pursuing height and depth.
Now, moving to a vital strategic point,
it is truly capable of control and defense.
We humbly request it be renamed Ānrǒng Guān (安戎關)."
24 When Wéi Yífàn
was Chancellor, he received many bribes
and promised official positions.
Later, he was dismissed due to his mother's mourning period,
and was daily assailed by creditors.
*Zào* (譟)
means "clamorous."
His debts were particularly heavy,
hence he was eager for reinstatement,
daily sending people to the two Chief Eunuchs, the Grand Councillors, and Lǐ Màozhēn to request it.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
Emperor Zhaozong ordered Hán Wò to draft the edict for Yífàn's reinstatement.
Wò said:
"My arm can be broken,
but this edict cannot be drafted!"
He immediately submitted a memorial arguing that Yífàn had suffered a bereavement only a few months prior,
and to hastily order his reinstatement
was truly shocking to public opinion
and detrimental to the national honor.
Two court eunuchs from the Hanlin Academy angrily said:
"Academician, do not treat death as a game!"
At that time, Hán Quánhuì and others had dispatched two court eunuchs to supervise the Hanlin Academy,
to prevent the Emperor from secretly discussing state affairs with them,
and also to manage the transmission of edicts and submission of memorials.
As Wò refused to draft the edict,
they were angry.
He undressed and went to sleep;
the two eunuchs had no choice but to report this.
The Emperor immediately ordered the drafting to be stopped.
This means the drafting of the edict was stopped.
In the eighth month,
on the *yǐhài* day, the first day of the month,
the court attendance was settled,
but there was no "white edict" to proclaim.
"Court attendance settled"
means that the hundred officials had taken their positions.
The Academician had not drafted the edict,
so there was no "white edict" to proclaim.
Those who heard were greatly shocked.
Màozhēn entered and saw the Emperor, saying:
"Your Majesty has appointed a Chancellor, but the Academician refuses to draft the edict.
How is this different from rebellion!"
The Emperor said:
"You gentlemen recommended Yífàn,
and I did not object;
the Academician refuses to draft the edict,
and I also will not object.
Moreover, what he presented
is clear in reason and fact,
how can I not follow it!"
Màozhēn left displeased,
and upon reaching the Secretariat,
he saw Sū Jiǎn and said:
"Treacherous factions
are exactly as before."
He wrung his wrist for a long time.
Yífàn continued his efforts tirelessly.
Màozhēn told people:
"I truly do not understand the decorum of scholars,
and was misled by Yífàn.
He should be placed in Bīnzhōu."
This meant he would send Yífàn away.
25 Lǐ Màoxūn, Military Governor of Bǎodà, led his troops to garrison Sānyuán
to assist Lǐ Màozhēn.
Zhū Quánzhōng dispatched his generals Kāng Huáizhēn
and Kǒng Qíng to attack them.
Màoxūn fled.
Màoxūn was
Màozhēn's cousin.
26 Originally,
after Sūn Rú died (for details, see Volume 259, Jǐngfú First Year),
Qián Liú admired his ferocity and bravery,
and made him his central army commander,
calling them the Wǔyǒng Division.
Dù Léng, the Army Administrator, advised:
"Wolves are wild at heart;
later, they will surely become a grave danger.
I request that they be replaced with local people."
Liú did not heed him.
"Local people"
refers to people from Zhèxī.
Liú went to Yǐjǐn Commandery.
Qián Liú was
from Lín'ān.
After he became noble,
he changed his residence's encampment to Yǐjǐn Camp,
and then elevated it to Yǐjǐn City.
Whenever he visited Yǐjǐn City,
he hosted banquets for old folks,
and all the mountains and forests were covered with brocade.
He was managing the irrigation channels of Yǐjǐn Commandery.
*Shuài* (帥)
is read as *lǜ*.
*Zhì* (治)
is pronounced *zhí zhī* (直之).
*Xù* (洫)
is pronounced *ní bī* (泥逼).
Xu Wǎn requested Liú to stop the labor,
but he refused.
On the *jiǎ*
*xū* day,
Liú presided over a banquet for his generals.
Wǎn planned to assassinate Liú at the banquet,
but did not succeed,
feigning illness and leaving early.
Liú found this strange.
On the *dīnghài* day,
he ordered Wǎn to lead his contingent back to Hángzhōu first.
When Wǎn reached the outer city,
he unleashed his troops to burn and plunder.
Xǔ Zàisī, Commander of the Left Wǔyǒng Division, joined him with his welcoming troops.
"Welcoming troops" means
Xǔ Zàisī, knowing Qián Liú was returning,
led troops to welcome him.
Liú's son Chuán'yīng
and Mǎ Chuò, Commander of the Three Cities, and others closed the gates and resisted him.
Pān Cháng, a staff general, attacked Wǎn.
Wǎn retreated to Longxing Temple.
Liú returned.
When he reached Lóngquán,
Lóngquán is Lóngjǐng,
located on Fēnghuáng Ridge, southwest of Hángzhōu city,
fifteen *lǐ* from the city.
He galloped to the north of the city.
He ordered Chéng Jí to erect Liú's banners and drums and engage Wǎn.
Liú, in plain clothes, took a small boat and arrived at the northeast corner of the inner city wall at night,
entering by climbing over the wall.
Since Emperor Gaozong established his temporary residence in Hángzhōu,
the inner city wall of Hángzhōu served as the imperial city.
The northeast corner
is now outside Héníng Gate.
Liú personally executed him,
and only then did those in the city know of Liú's arrival.
Dù Jiànhuī, Commander of Wǔ'ān, entered to reinforce from Xīnchéng.
*Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Xīnchéng County
is one hundred and thirty *lǐ* southwest of Hángzhōu.
Jiànhuī burned everything.
Jiànhuī
was Léng's son.
Gāo Yàn, Prefect of Húzhōu, heard of the trouble
and dispatched his son Wèi to lead troops for reinforcement.
They reached Língyǐn Mountain.
*Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Húzhōu is one hundred and fifty-five *lǐ* south of Hángzhōu.
Língyǐn Mountain
is twelve *lǐ* west of Hángzhōu city,
where Língyǐn Temple is located.
*Nàn* (難)
is pronounced *nǎi dàn*.
Earlier,
Liú had built the outer wall of Hángzhōu (for details, see Volume 259, Jǐngfú Second Year).
"A tower every ten paces should make it secure."
Luó Yǐn of Yúyáo, the Secretariat Director, said:
"The towers would be better if they faced inwards."
At this time, people found Yǐn's words to be prophetic.
"Towers"
refers to the watchtowers on the city wall.
Towers facing outwards
are for defense against enemies.
Now Xú Wǎn occupied the outer wall of Hángzhōu,
and Qián Liú attacked from outside,
thus people regarded Luó Yǐn's words about towers facing inwards as prophetic.
27 On the *gēngxū* day,
Lǐ Màozhēn launched a night attack on Fèngtiān,
capturing Biàn generals Ní Zhāng and Shào Táng and returning.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
Màozhēn launched a large force
and fought Zhū Quánzhōng,
but did not win.
They returned at dusk,
and the Biàn troops pursued them,
almost entering the West Gate.
28 On the *jǐhài* day,
Wéi Yífàn, former Vice Minister of Revenue and Grand Councilor, was reinstated again,
and Yáo Jì was ordered to draft the edict.
Yífàn did not decline,
and immediately submitted a memorial of thanks.
The next day,
he resumed his duties.
29 Xīchuān troops requested passage through Xīngyuán,
stating they sought passage to aid the emperor.
On the day of Xīnchǒu,
Xīchuān's vanguard general, Wáng Zōngbō, attacked it,
but failed,
and retreated to defend the mountain stronghold.
His trusted aide, Liǔ Xiūyè, said to Zōngbō:
"You committed your entire clan to another;
if you do not fight to the death for him,
how will you protect yourself?"
Liǔ Xiūyè
was Wáng Zōngbō's original Kǒngmùguān.
Wáng Zōngbō
was formerly Xǔ Cún;
his defection to Wáng Jiàn is recorded in volume 260, Qiánníng second year.
為,
pronounced Yú wěi.
"I will fight a decisive battle with you all
to achieve glory;
if not,
we will die here!"
Thereupon, he broke through the four strongholds of Jīnniú, Hēishuǐ, Xīxiàn, and Bāochéng.
In Wǔdé third year,
Jīnniú County was established from Miángǔ in Lìzhōu;
in Bǎolì first year,
it was merged into Xīxiàn of Xīngyuán Fǔ.
Today, 60 *lǐ* east of Sānquán County, there is Jīnniú Yì.
Yúdì Guǎngjì states: On Dàjiànshān there is Xiǎoshímén,
a passage through the mountain,
over six *zhàng* long.
In ancient times, Qín wanted to invade Shǔ but did not know the way,
so they made five stone oxen,
placed gold under their tails,
claiming they could excrete gold,
intending to present them to Shǔ.
The King of Shǔ, being strong but poor,
ordered the five Dīng to open a road to lead them in.
Qín then sent Zhāng Yí and Sīmǎ Cuò to lead troops to attack Shǔ,
conquering it.
This was called Shíniú Dào;
the place where the oxen were placed
was called Shíniú Yì.
Bāochéng was
Hàn Bāozhōng County,
the ancient Bāoguó.
Suí renamed it Bāochéng,
and Táng placed it under Xīngyuán Fǔ.
Jiǔyù Zhì states: The county is 45 *lǐ* west of the prefecture;
there is also Bāochéng Zhèn.
An arrow pierced his left eye,
reaching his right eye,
but the arrowhead did not come out.
Wáng Jiàn licked his wound himself;
the pus broke and the arrowhead came out.
Wáng Jiàn's act resembled Wú Qǐ sucking a carbuncle, or Tàizōng sucking blood.
校,
pronounced Hù jiào.
舐,
pronounced Zhí shì.
創,
pronounced Chū liáng.
Jì Mì was defeated in battle,
and fled back to Hànzhōng.
The Xīchuān army, capitalizing on their victory, arrived at the city walls.
Wáng Zōngdí led his troops to be the first to ascend,
and thus captured it.
Jì Mì requested surrender
and was relocated to Chéngdū;
in Guānghuà second year,
Lǐ Jì Mì gained Xīngyuán,
but was defeated at this time.
Wáng Jiàn thus took control of the entire Shānnán Xīdào.
降,
pronounced Hù jiāng.
With five thousand cavalry,
Zōngdí entered and garrisoned Hànzhōng.
Wáng Jiàn said:
"Jì Mì ravaged the Sānfǔ,"
Lǐ Jì Mì followed Lǐ Màozhēn,
and Màozhēn encroached upon and hunted in the Jīdiàn.
Jì Mì was presumably complicit in these crimes,
which is why Wáng Jiàn said this.
Unwilling to kill him,
he restored his original surname and given name as Wáng Wànhóng,
but did not summon him for audiences.
The generals disdained him,
and Wànhóng spent his days drinking,
while actors also mocked him;
overwhelmed by sorrow and indignation,
Wànhóng, in a drunken state, threw himself into a pond and died.
An imperial edict appointed Wáng Zōngdí as the Jiédùshǐ of Shānnán Xīdào.
Zōngdí possessed courage and strategy,
and gained the hearts of the people,
which made Wáng Jiàn wary of him.
Jiàn built a mansion gate,
painted in vermilion,
which the people of Shǔ called
"Huàhónglóu."
Jiàn believed that Zōngdí's name corresponded to this.
Zōngdí's original surname was Huá, and his given name was Hóng.
The change of name is recorded in volume 261, Qiánníng fourth year.
He then concocted rumors against him.
Jiàn summoned Zōngdí to Chéngdū
and questioned him harshly.
Zōngdí said:
"The three Shǔ are nearly pacified.
Dōngchuān, Xīchuān, and Hànchuān constituted the three Shǔ.
詰,
pronounced Qù jí.
It is now permissible to kill a meritorious minister."
Jiàn ordered Táng Dàoxí, the Commander of the Imperial Cavalry, to ply him with wine at night
and then strangle him.
Chéngdū markets ceased operations for this,
and camps wept continuously,
as if mourning a close relative.
Jiàn appointed Commander Wáng Zōnghè as acting Liúhòu of Xīngyuán.
Dàoxí,
a native of Lángzhōu,
initially served Jiàn as a child dancer,
and later gradually became involved in strategic planning.
This laid the groundwork for Wáng Jiàn's heir, Yuányīng, to kill Táng Dàoxí.
30 In the ninth month,
on the day of Yǐsì,
Zhū Quánzhōng, due to prolonged rain
and illness among his soldiers,
summoned his generals to discuss withdrawing troops.
Gāo Jìchāng, Commander of the Imperial Guard in Hézhōng, and Liú Zhījùn, Commander of the Left Vanguard, said:
"Heroes throughout the realm
have been watching this move for a year;
Zhū Quánzhōng has been leading troops since last winter,
nearly a year until now.
從,
pronounced Cái yòng.
How can we abandon it and leave?"
Quánzhōng was troubled by Lǐ Màozhēn's strong defense and refusal to sally forth.
Jìchāng requested to use a ruse to lure him out.
He recruited someone who could enter the city as a spy.
The cavalryman Mǎ Jǐng volunteered,
saying:
"This mission is certain death;
I ask Your Majesty to provide for my wife and children."
錄 means
to provide for and care for them.
Jǐng did not accept.
At this time, Quánzhōng had sent Zhū Yǒulún to dispatch troops from Dàliáng,
who were expected to arrive the next day,
so troops would have to be sent to meet them.
Jǐng requested to be given a swift horse and be allowed to leave with the miscellaneous cavalry at that time.
Quánzhōng agreed,
and ordered all armies to fodder their horses and feed their soldiers well.
At dawn on Dīngwèi,
they lowered their banners and concealed themselves,
so the camp was silent as if uninhabited.
Jǐng and all the cavalry exited,
suddenly spurred their horses west,
feigning desertion,
entered the city, and reported to Màozhēn:
"Quánzhōng's army has fled,
leaving only nearly ten thousand wounded and sick soldiers to guard the camp.
They will also leave tonight;
please attack quickly!"
Thereupon, Màozhēn opened the gates,
and sent his entire army to attack Quánzhōng's camp;
Quánzhōng sounded his drums in the central army,
all hundred camps emerged,
unleashing their troops to attack.
He also sent several hundred cavalry to occupy the city gates,
blocking their retreat.
They trampled and crushed them,
killing and wounding almost all.
Màozhēn was disheartened by this,
and began to discuss peace with Quánzhōng,
escorting the imperial carriage back to the capital,
no longer using imperial edicts to order Quánzhōng back to his post.
Quánzhōng memorialized Gāo Jìchāng as Sòngzhōu Tuánliànshǐ.
This was a reward for his strategy.
He was from Xiáshí and was originally Zhū Yǒugōng's servant.
Ōu Shǐ states: Gāo Jìchāng and Dǒng Zhāng were both household slaves of Lǐ Ràng, a wealthy man in Biàn,
whom the world called Lǐ Qīláng.
Zhū Quánzhōng adopted him as a son,
and changed his name to Zhū Yǒugōng.
Shíguó Jìnián believes that Yǒugōng was originally Lǐ Yánwēi, a merchant from Shòuzhōu;
the Tōngjiàn follows this.
Now, according to Ōu Shǐ, based on Xuē Shǐ,
Shíguó Jìnián is consistent with Wáng Jǔ's Tiānxià Dàdìng Lù.
31 On the day of Wùshēn,
Lǐ Sījìng, the Jiédùshǐ of Wǔdìng,
surrendered Yángzhōu to Wáng Jiàn.
Wáng Jiàn thus also acquired the territory of Yángzhōu.
32 On the day of Xīnhài,
Lǐ Màozhēn sent all his cavalry to neighboring prefectures for fodder.
On the day of Rénzǐ,
Zhū Quánzhōng dug a centipede trench to surround Fèngxiáng,
and set up dog posts and bell frames to sever internal and external communication.
33 On the day of Guǐhài,
Màozhēn was appointed Jiédùshǐ of the four garrisons of Fèngxiáng, Jìngnán, Wǔdìng, and Zhāowǔ.
Wǔdìng and Zhāowǔ had already been captured by Wáng Jiàn at this time.
34 Someone advised Qián Liú to cross the river east and secure Yuèzhōu,
to avoid the calamity from Xú and Xǔ.
Xú and Xǔ
refer to Xú Wǎn and Xǔ Zàisī.
難 (nàn, calamity)
is pronounced with initial n and final an in Dàn;
the same below.
“If the matter does not succeed,
we shall die here together;
how can we cross east again!”
Liú feared that Xú Wǎn and others would seize Yuèzhōu,
so he dispatched the grand general Gù Quánwǔ with troops to garrison it.
Quánwǔ said:
“Yuèzhōu is not worth going to;
it is better to go to Guǎnglíng.”
之 (zhī)
also means “to go.”
Guǎnglíng was governed by Yáng Xíngmì.
“Why?”
He replied:
“I hear Wǎn and others are plotting to summon Tián Yūn;
when Tián Yūn arrives,
Huáinán will assist them,
and they will be unbeatable.”
Jiànhuī said:
“During Sūn Rú’s calamity,
the King once showed kindness to Duke Yáng;
if we go and inform him now,
he ought to repay us.”
Liú ordered Quánwǔ to urgently appeal to Yáng Xíngmì.
Quánwǔ said:
“Going empty-handed will be useless;
please let me take a prince as a hostage.”
Liú ordered his son Chuánliáo
to be Quánwǔ’s servant,
and to accompany him to Guǎnglíng,
and also to seek a marriage alliance with Xíngmì.
Passing through Rùnzhōu,
the commander Ān Rénwú admired Chuánliáo’s clarity and beauty,
and intended to exchange ten servants for him;
Quánwǔ bribed the gatekeeper at midnight and escaped.
Ān Rénwú was known as a famous general of Huáinán,
holding the responsibility of a sole city,
yet the prohibitions on entry and exit through his gate were not strict;
he was not a good defender.
Wǎn and others indeed summoned Tián Yūn.
Yūn led troops to join them,
first sending his trusted subordinate Hé Ráo to say to Liú:
“I request Your Majesty to move east to Yuèzhōu,
vacating the governmental offices to await you;
do not kill the soldiers!”
Liú replied:
“Rebellions in the army,
what place is without them!
You, as a military governor,
are assisting rebels in their treason.
If you want to fight, then fight quickly;
why such boastful talk!”
Yūn built a fortress, cutting off the path for passage.
Liú was troubled by this,
and offered a reward of a prefecture to anyone who could seize that land.
Chén Zhāng, the Director of Qúzhōu, led three hundred soldiers out of the city in a fierce attack,
and thus seized the land.
Liú immediately appointed him Prefect of Qúzhōu.
Observing this,
it seems that at that time, the Directors of the various prefectures were subordinate to the Prefects.
Gù Quánwǔ arrived in Guǎnglíng
and persuaded Yáng Xíngmì, saying:
“If Tián Yūn achieves his ambition,
he will surely become a threat to Your Majesty.
If Your Majesty recalls Yūn,
King Qián requests to offer his son Chuánliáo as hostage,
and also seeks a marriage alliance.”
Xíngmì agreed,
and married his daughter to Chuánliáo.
35 In winter,
tenth month,
Lǐ Yǎn arrived in Yángzhōu.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: The *Shíguó Jìnián Zhù* and the *Shǔ Shū*’s biography of Zhāng Gé say:
“His younger brother Xiū
served the Táng as a Censor,
and was dispatched as an envoy to Yángzhōu.
Hearing of the calamity at Chángshuǐ,
he changed his name to Lǐ Yǎn.”
The *Jiǔguó Zhì* says:
“Lǐ Yǎn was originally the youngest son of the Left Grandee Secretary Zhāng Jùn,
named Bō.
He began his career as a Collator,
then was promoted to Right Remonstrance Official.
When Jùn was killed by Zhū Quánzhōng,
Bō fled from Chángshuǐ to Fèngxiáng.
Zhaozōng bestowed his surname and given name upon him.
He came as an envoy,
wishing to recruit troops for revenge.”
Xíngmì’s letter to Zhū Quánzhōng states:
“We selected Zhāng Shù from the Remonstrance Bureau,
and sent him to carry our mandate to your humble domain,
bestowing upon him the rank of Registrar,
and granting him a place in our household register.”
The biographies of Zhaozōng and Jùn in both the *New and Old Táng Shū* all state:
“In the third year of Tiānfù,
twelfth month,
Quánzhōng killed Jùn at Chángshuǐ.”
If so, when Yǎn came as an envoy,
Jùn was still alive.
The character “Shù”
might be confused with
the character “Xiū,”
or perhaps his name was also Bō?
The *Shílù* states:
In this month,
Yǎn was first appointed as Commissioner of Jiānghuái,
and Xíngmì was made King of Wú and Commander of the Eastern Campaign.
This is an error.
According to Xíngmì’s letter,
Yǎn had already been granted the surname Lǐ when his father was alive,
and was sent to admonish Xíngmì to suppress Quánzhōng.
In the spring of the following year,
after Quánzhōng had captured Fèngxiáng,
Yǎn then remained in Huáinán,
not daring to return to court.
Whenever there was an enfeoffment or appointment,
he would inform Yǎn,
present the imperial edict before Xuánzōng’s image in Zǐjí Palace,
prostrate himself twice, and then issue it.
Xuánzōng decreed that all prefectures and counties under heaven
should establish Zǐjí Palaces to honor Xuányuán Emperor.
下 (xià, to issue)
is pronounced with initial h and final uài in Hù Jià.
36 Wáng Jiàn attacked and captured Xīngzhōu,
appointing his military commissioner Wáng Zōnghào as Prefect of Xīngzhōu.
Wáng Jiàn also annexed Xīngzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Xīngzhōu
was Jǔ County of Hàn’s Wǔdū.
The Shǔ established the Wǔxīng Supervisorship,
later the Later Wèi made it Wǔxīng Garrison,
and later changed it to Dōngyìzhōu.
The Suí changed the prefecture to Shùnzhèng Commandery.
The Táng established Xīngzhōu in Wǔdé,
naming the prefecture after Wǔxīng.
37 On the night of Wùyín,
Lǐ Màozhēn’s adopted son Yànxún led three regiments of infantry to defect to the Biàn army;
on Jǐmǎo,
Lǐ Yàntāo followed.
On Gēngchén,
Zhū Quánzhōng sent his staff member Sīmǎ Yè to present a memorial to the city.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: The *Shílù*:
“On Gēngchén,
Sīmǎ Fēng presented a memorial.
On Rénwǔ,
he met with Quánzhōng’s envoy Sīmǎ Fēng.”
Xuē Jūzhèng’s *Wǔdài Shǐ* biography of Sīmǎ Yè:
“When the great army was beneath Qí,
he was sent to present a memorial to Zhaozōng,
re-entering and then departing.”
The *Shílù* writing
“Fēng”
is an error.
On Jiǎshēn,
he again sent an envoy to offer bear fat;
Lù Diàn’s *Píyǎ* states: Bear fat is also called bear white.
Bears
live in mountains,
hibernate in winter.
There is white fat in their hearts like jade,
which tastes very delicious,
commonly called bear white.
All offerings were first shown to Lǐ Màozhēn,
who was made to open and inspect them,
but Màozhēn did not dare to open them either.
On Bǐngxū,
he again sent an envoy to request to negotiate a peace alliance with Màozhēn,
and that people going out of the city to gather firewood would not be plundered.
On Dīnghài,
Quánzhōng submitted a memorial requesting to repair the palaces and welcome the imperial carriage.
On Jǐchǒu,
the Director of the Directorate of Education Xuē Chāngzuò and the Inner Envoy Wáng Yánjì were sent to carry an imperial edict to Quánzhōng.
Inner Envoy
is the same as Middle Envoy.
Often, Liang officials avoided Zhū Quánzhōng’s personal name
by changing 中 (zhōng, middle) to 內 (nèi, inner).
績 (jì)
is pronounced with initial h and final uài in Hù Wài,
and also with initial h and final uì in Hù Duì.
On *Guǐsì*,
Lǐ Mào-zhēn again sent out troops to attack the Biàn army's stockade west of the city,
but was defeated and returned.
Zhū Quán-zhōng dressed the surrendered soldiers in crimson robes
and had them call out to the people inside the city.
Many Fèng-xiáng soldiers climbed down ropes at night
or left under the pretext of gathering firewood and did not return.
Thereafter, when Lǐ Mào-zhēn occasionally sent out troops to attack the Biàn army,
most were unwilling to fight
and scattered back.
Lǐ Mào-zhēn suspected that the Emperor had a secret agreement with Zhū Quán-zhōng.
On *Rén-yín*,
he further increased guards outside the northern wall of the imperial compound.
In the eleventh month,
on *Guǐ-mǎo* (the first day of the month),
Lǐ Mào-xūn, the Jìe-dù-shǐ of Bǎo-dà, led his more than ten thousand troops to rescue Fèng-xiáng,
encamping on the slope north of the city,
and lit beacons to signal to those inside the city.
On *Jiǎ-chén*,
the Emperor sent Zhào-guó Fū-rén to check and found both envoys of the Xúe-shì-yuàn absent.
He urgently summoned Hán Wò and Yáo Jì,
and secretly met them outside the Tǔ-mén gate,
holding hands and weeping.
Yáo Jì urged the Emperor to return quickly,
fearing they might be seen by others;
the Emperor promptly left.
Zhū Quán-zhōng sent his generals Kǒng Qíng and Lǐ Huī to lead troops to surprise attack Fū and Fāng prefectures, exploiting their weakness.
On *Rén-zǐ*,
they captured Fāng Prefecture.
On *Jiǎ-yín*,
there was a heavy snow.
The Biàn army advanced through it at night.
At the fifth watch,
they reached the city walls of Fū Prefecture.
(*Jiǔ-yù Zhì*: Fāng Prefecture is 110 *lǐ* north of Fū Prefecture.)
The Biàn army entered the city.
There were still eight thousand soldiers in the city,
who fought until noon.
The Fū people finally lost.
"Gré-dòu" (格鬬) means
close combat with short weapons,
two opponents facing each other,
competing with strength.
*Kǎo-yì* says: *Biān Yí-lù* records:
"In the twelfth month, on *Guǐ-yǒu*,
Kǒng Qíng and Lǐ Huī were sent to lead troops to attack Fū Prefecture,
to divert Lǐ Zhōu-yí's army.
On *Jǐ-hài*,
our army attacked and breached the walls of Fū,
capturing Lǐ Zhōu-yí's relatives.
Lǐ Huī was then appointed acting military commander of Fū Prefecture.
Within a few days, Lǐ Zhōu-yí sent his staff advisor to open communications and express goodwill.
Only then did the Emperor agree to withdraw the troops."
*Liáng Tài-zǔ Shí-lù* records:
"In the eleventh month, on *Guǐ-mǎo*,
Lǐ Zhōu-yí, the commander of Fū, led more than ten thousand provincial troops to encamp below the Lǎo-tán Temple.
The Emperor ordered Kǒng Qíng and Lǐ Huī to swiftly capture it by exploiting its weakness.
On *Rén-zǐ*,
Kǒng Qíng and others captured Zhōng-bù Commandery.
On *Jiǎ-yín*,
there was heavy rain and snow.
The main army advanced through it at night.
At the fifth watch,
they reached his camp
and captured it."
Comment: From *Guǐ-mǎo* to *Jǐ-hài* is nearly sixty days.
How could Fū and Biàn have completely avoided fighting during their standoff?
We now follow the *Táng* and *Liáng Shí-lù* (Tang and Liang Veritable Records).
Lǐ Jì-qióng.
Kǒng Qíng comforted and provided for the families of Lǐ Mào-xūn and his officers and soldiers,
keeping them in their homes without disturbance,
and appointed Lǐ Huī as acting military administrator.
When Lǐ Mào-xūn heard this,
he withdrew his troops and fled.
Prioritizing battle over defense,
this was why Lǐ Mào-xūn was defeated;
generously treating their families to win them over,
this was why Lǐ Mào-xūn turned his heart towards Zhū Quán-zhōng.
The Biàn army sounded drums and horns every night,
making the ground within the city seem to tremble.
The attackers cursed the people on the city walls, saying,
"You brigands who kidnapped the Son of Heaven!"
The defenders on the city walls cursed the people below, saying,
"You brigands who seized the Son of Heaven!"
That winter,
there was heavy snow.
Food ran out in the city.
Countless people died from freezing and starvation;
some were already being eaten by others before they had died.
Human flesh was sold in the market,
costing one hundred cash per *jīn*,
while dog meat cost five hundred.
Lǐ Mào-zhēn's provisions also ran out,
and he served dog and pig meat for imperial meals.
The Emperor sold his imperial robes and the clothes of the young princes in the market to meet expenses,
and sliced pickled persimmons to feed the imperial horses.
On *Bǐng-zǐ*,
Wéi Yí-fàn, the Hù-bù Shì-láng and Tóng Píng-zhāng-shì, passed away.
On *Guǐ-hài*,
Zhū Quán-zhōng sent people to cut the grass outside the city to distress those inside.
On *Jiǎ-zǐ*,
Lǐ Mào-zhēn increased guards at the palace gates,
which were the gates of the temporary palace.
They mutually blamed and resented each other.
Sū Jiǎn repeatedly worked to promote Hán Wò to prime minister,
speaking to Lǐ Mào-zhēn, the Eunuch Commanders, and the Privy Councilors,
and also sent a trusted clerk to inform Hán Wò.
Hán Wò angrily said:
"You and Lord Wéi were recalled from exile,
and within a month reached the position of prime minister,
yet ultimately could do nothing;
now, with disaster imminent,
do you wish to stain me with this?"
Tián Yún urgently attacked Háng-zhōu,
and had also prepared boats to cross the river from Xī-líng;
Qián Liú sent his generals Shèng Zào and Zhū Yù to resist and defeat him.
In the twelfth month,
Lǐ Mào-xūn sent an envoy to surrender to Zhū Quán-zhōng,
and changed his name to Lǐ Zhōu-yí.
At this point, all the prefectures and garrisons in Shān-nán under Lǐ Mào-zhēn had fallen to Wáng Jiàn,
and all the prefectures and garrisons in Guān-zhōng had fallen to Zhū Quán-zhōng,
leaving him to guard an isolated city.
He then secretly plotted to eliminate the eunuchs to redeem himself,
sending a letter to Zhū Quán-zhōng which said:
"The source of the troubles and chaos
is entirely due to Quán-huì (referring to the eunuchs);
I welcomed the Emperor here
to guard against other bandits.
Since you are determined to restore the imperial state,
I ask you to escort the Emperor back to the palace.
I, with my worn armor and depleted troops,
will join you in exerting my strength."
"Worn armor and depleted troops"
uses the words of Zhāng Yí from the Warring States period.
"Diāo" (彫) means half-damaged.
"I raised troops and came here
precisely because the imperial carriage had been moved.
If you can cooperate,
that is certainly my wish."
Yáng Xíng-mì sent someone to summon Tián Yún, saying:
"If you do not return,
I will send someone to replace you as military governor of Xuān-zhōu."
Gu Gōng-wǔ's suggestion was put into action.
On *Gēng-chén*,
Tián Yún was about to return.
He demanded 200,000 *mín* of army provisions from Qián Liú,
and also asked for Qián Liú's son as a hostage,
intending to marry his daughter to him.
Qián Liú said to his sons:
"Wèi" (謂)
means to speak to.
(Sentence break.)
"Who can be Tián's son-in-law?"
No one replied.
Qián Liú wanted to send his youngest son, Chuán-qiú,
but Chuán-qiú refused.
Qián Liú was angry
and was about to kill him.
His second son, Chuán-guàn, requested to go.
Lady Wú wept, saying:
"How can you put our son in a tiger's mouth!"
Chuán-guàn said:
"To alleviate the nation's difficulties."
"Shū" (紓)
means to alleviate.
"Nán" (難) is pronounced *nǎi-dàn-fān*.
He bowed twice and left.
Qián Liú wept as he saw him off.
At this time,
Qián Liú's intention for succession
was already set on Chuán-guàn.
The enemy's intentions were unpredictable,
so he dared not open the city gates and go out directly,
thus he climbed down by rope.
Qián Liú seized Chuán-qiú's seal of the Inner Palace Guard.
This was because he refused to go as a hostage.
Zhāng Hóng (張洪), the Commander of the Guest Army in Yuèzhōu (越州), suspected himself of being a confederate of Xú Wǎn (徐綰).
The Guest Army
was likely composed of Sūn Rú's (孫儒) disbanded soldiers.
Chén Zhāng (陳璋), the Cìshǐ (刺史), took them in.
Dīng Zhāng (丁章), a general from Wēnzhōu (溫州), drove out Cìshǐ Zhū Áo (朱敖);
Áo fled to Fúzhōu (福州).
In the first year of Zhōnghé (中和) of Emperor Xīzōng (僖宗),
Zhū Bāo (朱褒) captured Wēnzhōu,
but now he was defeated.
Wáng Shěnzhi (王審知) was at that time occupying Fúzhōu.
Tián Yún (田頵) sent an envoy to recruit him.
The route passed through Qúzhōu (衢州);
Chén Zhāng allowed him to come and go,
and Qián Liú (錢鏐) consequently resented Zhāng.
This set the stage for Qián Liú to scheme against Chén Zhāng.
According to records, Tián Yún was garrisoned in Xuānzhōu (宣州) at this time.
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: Xuānzhōu is south to Shèzhōu (歙州),
from Shèzhōu south to Mùzhōu (睦州),
from Mùzhōu south to Wùzhōu (婺州),
from Wùzhōu south to Chǔzhōu (處州),
from Chǔzhōu east to Wēnzhōu.
This route is direct.
The reason for taking the route from Wēnzhōu via Qúzhōu
is probably that Mùzhōu was under the jurisdiction of Liǎngzhè Xún (兩浙巡),
and its governor did not communicate with Tián Yún,
so Yún's envoy dared not take that route.
From Qúzhōu to Wùzhōu,
from Wùzhōu to Chǔzhōu,
from Chǔzhōu to Wēnzhōu,
there is no other way.
At that time, Lú Yuē (盧約) occupied Chǔzhōu,
which was also under the jurisdiction of Liǎngzhè Xún.
The reason Qián Liú resented Zhāng but not Yuē was
that Lú Yuē was merely kept under loose control,
while Chén Zhāng was originally one of his subordinates.
46 On the day of Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
the Emperor summoned Lǐ Màozhēn (李茂貞), Sū Jiǎn (蘇檢), Lǐ Jìhuì (李繼誨), Lǐ Yànbì (李彥弼), Lǐ Jìjí (李繼岌), Lǐ Jìyuǎn (李繼遠), and Lǐ Jìzhōng (李繼忠) for a meal
to discuss peace with Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠).
The Emperor said:
"Among the princes of the Sixteen Mansions and below,
several people die each day from cold and starvation.
The princes within the palace and princesses and imperial consorts—
The princes of the Sixteen Mansions
were the Emperor's brothers and collateral relatives.
The princes within the palace and princesses
were the Emperor's sons and daughters.
One day we ate *tāngbǐng* (湯餅)."
*Tāngbǐng*
means grinding wheat into flour,
making cakes from the flour,
and throwing them into boiling water to cook them.
It is what Huáng Tíngjiān (黃庭堅) referred to as
"deeply pouring water to boil cakes."
This is it.
Chéng Dàchāng (程大昌) in his *Xù Yǎnfánlù* (續演繁露) says: *Shìmíng* (釋名) states: *Bǐng* (餅) means *bìng* (併, to combine);
it is combining dough by kneading it.
*Zhēngbǐng* (蒸餅, steamed cakes) are a type of *tāngbǐng*,
each named according to its form.
"What do you, sirs, think?"
None replied.
The Emperor said:
"We must make peace quickly!"
More than ten soldiers from Fèngxiáng (鳳翔) intercepted Hán Quánhuì (韓全誨) at the Left Yíntái Gate (左銀臺門).
The Dàmíng Palace (大明宮) city walls in Cháng'ān (長安) had Left and Right Yíntái Gates,
and the Fèngxiáng temporary palace also had such gates,
indicating it was as if they were in the Cháng'ān palace.
"The entire realm is in misery,
the entire city is starving to death,
all because of a few of you military commanders!"
Quánhuì kowtowed and complained to Màozhēn,
who said:
"What do mere soldiers know!"
He ordered two cups of wine to be poured,
they drank facing each other, and then dispersed.
He also complained to the Emperor,
who also appeased him.
Lǐ Jìzhāo (李繼昭) said to Quánhuì:
"In the past, Military Commander Yáng (楊軍容) destroyed the clan of Yáng Shǒuliàng (楊守亮) —
See Volume 259, first year of Jǐngfú (景福), first year of Gānníng (乾寧).
He cursed him insultingly

47 In this year,
Lú Guāngchóu (盧光稠), Cìshǐ of Qiánzhōu (虔州), attacked Língnán (嶺南)
and captured Sháozhōu (韶州).
Although Sháo and Qián Prefectures are more than six hundred *lǐ* (里) apart,
they are only separated by the Dàyǔ (大庾) Ridge, and are actually adjacent.
*Kǎoyì* (考異) states: According to the *Xīnjì* (新紀), Guāngchóu died this year,
and his staff officer Lǐ Tú (李圖) declared himself Acting Prefect.
However, *Shíguó Jìnián* (十國紀年) and Ōuyáng Xiū's (歐陽修) biography of Guāngchóu in the *Wǔdài Shǐ* (五代史) state he died in the fifth year of Kāipíng (開平).
The *Xīnjì* is mistaken.
(He) then besieged Cháozhōu (潮州).
Liú Yǐn (劉隱) of Qīnghǎi (清海)
dispatched troops to attack and drive him away,
and pressed on to attack Sháozhōu, taking advantage of the victory.
Yǐn's younger brother Zhì (陟) thought that Yánchāng (延昌) had aid from Qiánzhōu,
and it should not be taken hastily;
Yǐn disagreed
and consequently besieged Sháozhōu.
At that time, the river flooded,
and supplies could not be sustained.
Transporting grain from Guǎngzhōu (廣州) to supply the Sháozhōu field army
required going upstream;
when the river flooded, the water was swift and rapid,
making it impossible to go upstream,
thus supplies could not be sustained.
His general Tán Quánbò (譚全播) ambushed ten thousand elite soldiers in the valleys,
and sent his weak troops to challenge.
He greatly defeated Yǐn south of the city,
and Yǐn fled back.
Quánbò attributed all the merits to his generals,
and Guāngchóu esteemed him even more.
48 Dèng Jìnsī (鄧進思), Cìshǐ of Yuèzhōu (岳州), died,
and his younger brother Jìnzhōng (進忠) declared himself Cìshǐ.

His reputation was known at the time and his governance had actual results, meaning his name matched his reality.

(They were) resisted by Cuī Yìn

Quán Zhōng (全忠) left Jiédù Pàn Guān (節度判官) Péi Dí (裴迪) to guard Dàliáng (大梁).
Shī Fàn (師範) sent a runner with a letter to Dàliáng (大梁).
Dí (迪) questioned him about affairs in the east,
and the runner's expression changed.

Dí (迪) dismissed others and questioned him,

Dí (迪) did not have time to inform Quán Zhōng (全忠),

This set the stage for Zhū Yǒuníng (朱友寧)'s death in battle and Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠)'s later extermination of Wáng Shīfàn (王師範).
On *Wùshēn* (戊申),

*Shuài* (帥)

The *Yùshí Shǐ (御食使)*,

The Privy Council was divided into Eastern and Western Bureaus;

Lǐ Jìyún (李繼筠), Lǐ Jìhuì (李繼誨), Lǐ Yànbì (李彥弼), and the *Nèi Zhū Sī Shǐ (內諸司使)* Wéi Chǔtíng (韋處廷) and sixteen others were also executed.

According to the *Jīnluan Jì (金鑾記)*, *Táng Nián Bǔlù (唐年補錄)*, *Táng Shílù (唐實錄)*, and *Hòu Táng Jìnián Lù (後唐紀年錄)*, the names of the eunuchs executed on the sixth day

If Jìyún (繼筠) and the others are counted as well,

"Those who previously coerced and detained the imperial carriage,

now he was presumably the *Sì Zhèn Guānchá Pàn Guān (四鎮觀察判官)*.
Although Quánhuì (全誨) and the others had been executed,

Màozhēn (茂貞) suspected that Cuī Yìn (崔胤) was instructing Quán Zhōng (全忠) to insist on taking Fèngxiáng (鳳翔).

and three vermilion imperial rescripts were granted.
Xuē Shǐ (薛史) records Duàn Huái (段徊)'s memorial during Emperor Zhuāngzōng (莊宗)'s reign:
"According to Táng (唐) regulations,
if in times of annual disaster or famine,
the national resources were insufficient,
and the Emperor wished to seek essential economic measures,
then vermilion imperial rescripts would be issued from within to consult various officials."
All his former official titles and ranks were restored,
but Yìn (胤) ultimately claimed illness and did not come.
Màozhēn (茂貞) was afraid,
and personally wrote a letter to Yìn (胤),
using very humble language.
Quán Zhōng (全忠) also wrote a letter summoning Yìn (胤),
even joking with him, saying:
"I have not yet seen the Emperor,
so I need you to come and distinguish right from wrong."
Yìn (胤) then came.
The reason Cuī Yìn (崔胤) initially dared not come
was that he was waiting for Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠)'s command.
However, the Emperor's repeated summons failed to bring him,
yet a single letter from Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) caused him to arrive immediately.
A subject serving his ruler
must know the priorities and relative importance.
On *Jiǎyín* (甲寅),
Fèngxiáng (鳳翔) finally opened its city gates.
On *Bǐngchén* (丙辰),
Quán Zhōng (全忠) inspected the various camps,

The Emperor sent the Lady of Zhàoguó (趙國夫人) and the Lady of Fēngyì (馮翊夫人) to Quánzhōng (全忠)'s camp to question him about this.
The two ladies had different ranks within the imperial consorts, one being of a *guó (國)* level and the other of a *jùn (郡)* level.
"Question" here
means questioning why, after reconciliation, he again sent troops to attack.
Lǐ Màozhēn (李茂貞) requested that his son Kǎn (侃) marry Princess Píngyuán (平原公主),

Princess Píngyuán (平原公主)
was the daughter of Empress Hé (何后).
The Empress was hesitant,
but the Emperor said:

How could he know that the imperial couple would completely entrust their lives to Quánzhōng (全忠),
and there would be no one left to rescue them!"
The Empress then agreed.
On *Rénxū* (壬戌),
Princess Píngyuán (平原公主) married Sòng Kǎn (宋侃);
to avoid marriage between people of the same surname,
Kǎn (侃)'s original surname was restored.
In ancient times, even marrying a teacher's daughter was considered improper.

By this time, seventy-two eunuchs had been executed in Fèngxiáng (鳳翔).
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) also secretly ordered the Jīngzhào (京兆) region to search for retired officials who had not accompanied the imperial retinue
and executed ninety of them.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
the imperial carriage departed Fèngxiáng,
and visited Quánzhōng’s camp.
Quánzhōng, in plain clothes, awaited punishment;
the Emperor ordered the Commissioner of the Guest Bureau to proclaim an edict pardoning him.
At that time, the Commissioner of the Guest Bureau
was in charge of the affairs of the Palace Gate,
hence he was ordered to proclaim the edict of pardon.
It merely reported that all was well.
According to Táng regulations, at the main court, there were three guards—the Imperial, Meritorious, and Valiant—standing guard.
The Generals of the Left and Right Jīnwú would send one person each to report peace.
The removal of the three guards
was probably because they feared Quánzhōng would be afraid to enter due to the strictness of the imperial guard.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Wáng Yǔchēng’s *Wǔdài Shǐ Quē Wén* states:
“Zhāozōng feigned that his shoelace had come undone,
and called to Liángzǔ, saying: ‘Quánzhōng, tie my shoe.’
Liángzǔ, having no choice,
knelt and tied it,
sweating profusely.
At that time, the Son of Heaven still had imperial guards accompanying him,
and Zhāozōng intended for his attendants to seize Liángzǔ and kill him,
but none dared to make a move.
From then on, Liángzǔ often failed to appear when summoned;
thereafter, all of Zhāozōng’s imperial guards were removed,
and all were replaced with men from Biàn.”
According to our assessment, at that time Quánzhōng commanded a hundred thousand troops,
and Zhāozōng had just escaped from Mào Zhēn’s clutches,
placing himself under Quánzhōng’s protection;
how could he dare to plot such a thing!
Perhaps someone wanted to emulate Hàn Gāozǔ’s humiliation of Qíng Bù,
but it is also feared that Zhāozōng would not have been able to carry it out.
Therefore, this account is not adopted.
*Qù*,
pronounced *qiānglǚ* (*qianglu*).
The Táng system of official attire
included court robes (*cháofú*) and official robes (*gōngfú*).
Court robes
were full dress;
official robes
were simpler attire.
He bowed his head and shed tears;
the Emperor ordered Hán Wò to help him up.
The Emperor also wept,
saying:
“The imperial ancestral temple and the altars of grain and soil
rely on you to be secure again;
I and my clan
rely on you for a new lease on life.”
He personally untied his jade belt and bestowed it upon him.
After a brief rest,
they set off.
Quánzhōng, riding alone, led the way for more than ten *lǐ*,
and the Emperor bade him farewell;
this was all Zhū Quánzhōng feigning respect.
He himself remained to command the rear guard,
burning and dismantling the various camps.
Yǒulún
was the son of Cún.
Cún
was Quánzhōng’s second elder brother.
That evening,
the imperial carriage rested at Qíshān;
on the *dīngmǎo* day,
they reached Xīngpíng,
where Cuī Yìn first led the hundred officials to welcome and pay respects.
Yìn was reinstated as Minister of Works (*Sīkōng*), Vice Director of the Department of the Palace Gate (*Ménxià Shìláng*), and Grand Councillor (*Tóng Píngzhāngshì*),
and continued to oversee the Three Offices as before;
when the imperial carriage arrived at Fèngxiáng,
Cuī Yìn’s official rank had been demoted,
but now it was restored.
On the *jǐsì* day,
they entered Cháng’ān.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
Quánzhōng and Cuī Yìn met together.
Yìn memorialized:
“In the early days of the dynasty, during times of peace,
eunuchs did not command troops or participate in government.
Since the Tiānbǎo era,
eunuch power has gradually grown.
At the end of the Zhēnyuán era,
the Yǔlín Guards were divided into the Left and Right Shéncè Armies for convenience of imperial escort,
and eunuchs were first appointed to command them,
with two thousand men as the established number.
The Shéncè Army entering the palace to guard the inner court
began with Dàizōng’s Yú Cháoēn.
Dèzōng first divided them into Left and Right at the end of Zhēnyuán.
*Cóng*,
pronounced *cáiyòng* (*caiyong*).
They seized the authority of the various bureaus,
connived with each other,
and collectively acted unlawfully;
on a grand scale, they incited regional governors,
endangering the state;
on a smaller scale, they sold offices and manipulated justice,
corrupting court governance.
The decline and chaos of the royal house
stem from this.
If their root is not cut,
the disaster will never cease.
I request that all Commissioners of the various bureaus be dismissed,
their affairs be fully returned to the ministries and courts,
and all regional military supervisors be recalled to the capital.”
The Emperor assented.
On that day,
Quánzhōng used his troops to drive several hundred eunuchs, including Dìwǔ Kěfàn, to the Bureau of Palace Attendants (*Nèishì Shěng*),
and killed them all.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Jiù Jì* states:
“On the *xīnwèi* day,
Dìwǔ Kěfàn and seven hundred other palace officials
were all granted death at the Bureau of Palace Attendants.”
The *Jīn Luán Jì* states:
“On the twenty-eighth day,
Dìwǔ Kěfàn and four hundred and fifty others were dealt with.”
The *Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù* states:
“More than a hundred eunuchs from the various internal bureaus and over two hundred accompanying the emperor to Fèngxiáng,
were all beheaded at the Bureau of Palace Attendants.”
The *Jiù Chuán* is consistent with the *Jìnián Lù*.
The *Xīn Chuán* states:
“Yìn and Quánzhōng discussed executing Dìwǔ Kěfàn and over eight hundred others at the Bureau of Palace Attendants.”
The *Liáng Tàizǔ Shílù* states:
“On the day following the *jǐsì* day,
Dìwǔ Kěfàn and over five hundred other eunuchs were executed at the Bureau of Palace Attendants,
and orders were issued to search and deal with their kind throughout the capital region and various provinces to eliminate them completely.”
The *Táng Nián Bǔ Lù* says:
“Seven hundred and ten eunuchs were executed.”
According to our assessment, the *Jiù Jì* and *Biān Yílù* both state
“On the *xīnwèi* day of the first month,
Kěfàn and others were executed.”
However, the *Liáng Shílù*, *Táng Bǔ Jì*, *Xù Bǎoyùn Lù*, *Jīn Luán Jì*, *Táng Nián Bǔ Lù*, Xuē Jūzhèng’s *Wǔdài Shǐ Liáng Jì*, and *Xīn Táng Jì*,
either state the day after *jǐsì*, or the twenty-eighth day;
we follow this latter.
Though Quánzhōng and Yìn memorialized to dismiss the Commissioners of the various bureaus
and recall military supervisors to the capital,
in reality, they were executed on that very day,
and it was not until the *guǐyǒu* day of the second month that an edict was issued granting them death.
Therefore, Zhāozōng mourned and offered sacrifices to them.
This was carried out both inside and outside the palace.
Those who were on missions abroad
were ordered to be arrested and executed wherever they were found,
leaving only thirty young and weak eunuchs in yellow robes for sweeping and cleaning.
Eunuchs of lower official rank wore yellow.
*Sǎ*,
pronounced *suǒmài* (*suomai*),

*Sǎo*,

Your servant Guāng says:
The eunuchs’ exercise of power,

This was because they frequently entered and exited the palace,

Among them, there were also some with cunning intelligence

and when sent on errands, there was the effect of fulfilling expectations.
Unless the ruler was of supreme wisdom,
discerning the true nature of things

When the Dōnghàn declined,

The reason for this was none other than that
the Hàn did not hold military power,
whereas the Táng did hold military power.
Tàizōng, learning from the abuses of previous generations,

Mínghuáng first demolished the old regulations,

Sòng Qí said: Tàizōng decreed that the Directorate for Palace Affairs should not have officials of the third rank.
The director was to be an attendant,

Their duties were merely guarding the gates, sweeping the courts, and overseeing provisions.
During Wǔhòu's time,

By Zhōngzōng's reign,

However, those wearing scarlet and purple were still few.
Xuánzōng enjoyed a long period of peace,

His ambitions grew great and his extravagance excessive.
He did not value or economize on rewards, titles, and ranks.
During the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras,

Those who received imperial favor were immediately appointed third-rank generals,

長 (zhǎng),

朝 (cháo),

In Xiànzōng's later years,

During Bǎolì's reign, the emperor fraternized with petty individuals.
Liú Kèmíng and Sū Zuǒmíng became traitors.
Subsequently, the princes of Jiàng and the emperors Wén, Wǔ, Xuān, Yì, Xī, and Zhāo, six in all,

Wáng Shǒuchéng, Qiú Shìliáng, Tián Lìngzī, Yáng Fùgōng, Liú Jìshù, and Hán Quánhuì were their leaders.
They even referred to themselves

Their roots were deep and their hold firm,

The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states: Duke Jìn was gravely ill

Earl Qín sent Yī Huǎn for him,

The duke dreamed his illness transformed into two young boys who said:
"He is a good physician.
Fearing he will harm us,

One of them said:
"If we reside above the *huāng* [diaphragm]

what can he do to us!"
When the physician arrived,

"The illness cannot be cured.
It is above the *huāng*
and below the *gāo*.
To attack it is impossible,
to reach it is insufficient.
Medicine cannot reach it,

肓 (huāng),

The bandits defiled the palace,

the following year,
he abdicated in favor of Liáng."
This is a transmission error by Guāngxiàn.
Zhāozōng also had no Empress Wáng.
The Prince Pú mentioned in the Jīnluan Jì
was probably Prince Dé, whose title was changed.
On the day Gēngchén,
Quánzhōng was granted the additional title of Grand Guardian,
appointed Deputy Marshal,
and elevated to the rank of Prince of Liáng.
Yìn was appointed Minister of Education and concurrently Grand Counselor.
Yìn, relying on Quánzhōng’s power,
exercised his authority arbitrarily;
the Emperor’s every move and action were reported to him.
Among the court officials who had accompanied the Emperor to Fèngxiáng,
more than thirty were demoted or banished.
Rewards and punishments depended on his likes and dislikes;
those he liked were rewarded,
those he disliked were punished.
Everyone was extremely cautious and afraid.
Jìng Xiáng was appointed Grand Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury,
and Zhū Yǒuníng was made Military Governor of Níngyuǎn.
The Níngyuǎn Army,
located in Róngzhōu,
was at this time occupied by Páng Jùzhāo.
Military Governors with official titles since the Five Dynasties
were of this type.
He was appointed Military Governor of Tiānxíong,
and soldiers were dispatched to escort him to Qínzhōu.
Zhī means
to go.
The Qí soldiers blocked the road,
so he could not arrive.
Huán means
xuān (a phonetic transcription, pronounced like xuān),
or as written.
6 Initially,
when Hán Wò, Hanlin Academician-in-waiting, passed the jinshi examination,
Zhào Chóng, Censor-in-chief, presided over the examination.
When the Emperor returned from Fèngxiáng,
he wanted to appoint Wò as chief minister.
Wò recommended Chóng and Wáng Zàn, Assistant Minister of War, to take his place.
The Emperor intended to follow this, but Cuī Yìn detested the division of his power,
and made Zhū Quánzhōng intervene.
Quánzhōng met the Emperor and said:
"Zhào Chóng is a frivolous leader,
Wáng Zàn is without talent or usefulness.
How can Hán Wò presumptuously recommend them as chief ministers!"
Seeing Quánzhōng’s extreme anger,
the Emperor had no choice.
On the day Guǐwèi,
Wò was demoted to Sīmǎ of Púzhōu.
The Emperor secretly shed tears and bid farewell to Wò.
Wò said:
"This person is no longer what he used to be –
referring to Zhū Quánzhōng.
I cannot bear to witness the disgrace of usurpation and regicide!"
Alas!
How late Hán Wò realized this!
Yet, how could Emperor Zhāozōng have felt after hearing Wò’s words!
He could only resort to heavy drinking.
7 On the day Jǐchǒu,
the Emperor ordered Zhū Quánzhōng to write to Lǐ Màozhēn,
demanding the return of Princess Píngyuán.
Màozhēn dared not disobey
and immediately sent her back.
Princess Píngyuán was married to Màozhēn’s son, Sòng Kǎn,
as mentioned in the previous volume last year.
8 On the day Rénchén,
Zhū Yǒuyù was appointed Military Governor of Zhènguó.
The Kǎoyì says: The Shílù states:
"On the day Rénchén,
Xīngdé Fǔ was restored as Huázhōu,
and given the name Gǎnhuà Army,
with Yǒuyù as its Military Governor."
According to the Biān Yílù,
in the third year of Tiānyòu,
an edict on the day Yǐchǒu of the intercalary twelfth month stated,
"The title of Zhènguó
and the name of Xīngdé
should both be abolished."
Xuē Jūzhèng’s Wǔdài Shǐ Dìlǐzhì states:
"Huázhōu was the Gǎnhuà Army
during the Liáng."
The Liáng Gōngchén Zhuàn states:
"In the third year of Tiānfù,
Yǒuyù temporarily oversaw the Zhènguó Army as its acting commander."
We now follow the Shílù.
9 On the day Yǐwèi,
Quánzhōng memorialized to keep ten thousand infantry and cavalry in the former two armies.
At this time, the two Shéncè armies had already disbanded,
but their encampments and offices still existed.
He also appointed Zhāng Tíngfàn, a general from Biàn, as Palace Gardens Commissioner,
Wáng Yīn as Imperial City Commissioner,
and Jiǎng Xuánhuī as Street Commissioner.
Thus, Quánzhōng’s partisans were extensively deployed throughout the imperial guards and the capital environs.
The Táng Northern Gate imperial guard troops
were all stationed in the palace gardens;
the various offices and government agencies and the Southern Court imperial guards
were all quartered within the imperial city;
the private residences of officials and the residents of wards and markets
were all quartered on either side of Zhūquè Street.
Now, Quánzhōng had appointed his trusted confidants to all these positions,
so the power over the capital environs was entirely his.
Driving away a viper only to get a tiger,
this describes Zhāozōng’s situation.
Quán Zhōng heard that Yǒu Níng had died,
and personally led an army of two hundred thousand, marching day and night to confront them.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day Rénzǐ,
they reached Línqú.
Línqú,
a Hàn dynasty county,
belonged to Qīngzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is forty lǐ southeast of the prefecture.
Wáng Shīfàn came out to battle,
and the Biàn army thoroughly defeated him.
Wáng Màozhāng closed his encampment, feigning fear,
and when the Biàn army slightly relaxed,
he destroyed the palisade and sallied forth.
He rode swiftly into battle,
and when the battle was fierce, he retired and sat down,
summoning his generals to drink wine.
Soon after, he rejoined the battle.
Quán Zhōng climbed to a height and saw this.
He asked a surrendered soldier,
learned it was Màozhāng,
and sighed,
"If only I could have this man as my general,
pacifying the world would be no challenge!"
Zhū Quánzhōng saw Wáng Màozhāng's calm composure in the face of the enemy,
and therefore desired to acquire him.
However, Màozhāng later submitted to Liáng,
attacked Huáinán, and attacked Zhèn,
but in both cases was defeated and did not recover.
People are indeed not easy to know.
The Biàn army then retreated.
Màozhāng estimated that his forces were unequal to the enemy,
and that night,
he led his army back.
Quán Zhōng dispatched Yáng Shīhòu, the Cāozhōu Prefect, to pursue him,
catching up at Fǔtáng.
Fǔtáng,
a Hàn dynasty Ānqíu County,
in the second year of Qiányuán,
had its seat moved to the old Chāng'ān city,
and was consequently renamed Fǔtáng,
belonging to Mìzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì: It is one hundred and twenty lǐ northwest of the prefecture.
The Xuē Shǐ Dìlǐ Zhì states: Fǔtáng County of Mìzhōu,
in the second year of Kāipíng of Liáng,
was renamed Ānqíu.
In the first year of Tóngguāng of Táng,
it reverted to its old name.
In the seventh year of Tiānfú of Jìn,
it was renamed Jiāoxī,
to avoid a temple taboo.
In Sòng, it was again called Ānqíu.
Qián Yù fought to the death,
and Shīhòu captured and killed him.
Lǐ Qián Yù sacrificed his life to save Wáng Màozhāng's army;
his bravery was extraordinary.
Yáng Shīhòu gained Zhū Quánzhōng's recognition from then on.
He was a native of Yǐngzhōu.
Zhāng Xùn heard that Màozhāng had left,
and said to his generals,
"The Biàn people are coming,
how shall we resist them?"
The generals requested to burn the city, plunder it, and return.
Xùn said,
"No."
He sealed the armories and treasuries,
planted banners on the city walls,
sent the weak and frail to the front,
and personally led the elite troops as a rearguard as they departed.
Quán Zhōng dispatched Wáng Tán, the Zuǒ Tàbái Commander, to attack Mìzhōu.
In all military movements,
the vanguard has a Tàbái detachment,
for scouting ambushes and observing the enemy's distance and strength.
Wáng Tán saw the banners,
but only dared to enter the city several days later.
Suspecting an ambush,
he advanced slowly and cautiously.
Thus, he did not pursue further.
Xùn returned with his entire army intact.
History states that the reason Yáng Xíngmì was able to preserve Jiānghuái
was that all his generals at that time were able to fully exert their wisdom and strength.
On the 27th, a Dīngmǎo day,
Wáng Zōnghè, the Acting Military Governor of Shānnánxī Circuit, was appointed Jìedùshǐ.
This was at Wáng Jiàn's request.
On the 28th, Chén Xún, the Mùzhōu Prefect, rebelled against Qián Liú,
raising an army to attack Lánxī.
In the fifth year of Xiánhēng, Lánxī County was established from the western border of Jīnhuá in Wùzhōu,
named after the stream.
The Jiǔyù Zhì: It is fifty-five lǐ northwest of the prefecture.
Dù Jiànhuī, the Wǔ'ān Chief Commander, was related by marriage to Xún,
and Liú suspected him,
but Jiànhuī remained silent.
At that time, a close attendant of Xún defected,
and a letter from Jiànhuī to Xún was found,
which contained only words of warning and counsel.
Liú was then pleased.
Jiànhuī's older cousin, Jiànsī, slandered Jiànhuī, saying he secretly stockpiled weapons
and plotted rebellion.
Liú sent someone to search,
and while Jiànhuī was eating,
the messenger went directly into his bedchamber.
Jiànhuī paid no attention,
and because of this, Liú regarded him with even greater trust and respect.
In the eighth month,
on the first day, a Wùchén day,
Zhū Quánzhōng left Yáng Shīhòu, the Qízhōu Prefect, to attack Qīngzhōu,
and personally returned to Dàliáng.
Zhū Quánzhōng, provoked by the death of Zhū Yǒuníng,
launched an angry attack on Qīngzhōu.
He certainly desired to conquer and raze it in one fell swoop.
Yet, he left it and returned to Biàn,
knowing that Qīngzhōu's city walls were strong and Wáng Shīfàn's forces were still powerful,
not easily taken overnight.
Therefore, he had Yáng Shīhòu besiege it.
On the 30th, a Gēngchén day,
Wáng Jiàn, the Xīchuān Jìedùshǐ and King of Xīpíng, was given the additional title of Sītú
and promoted to King of Shǔ.
He was promoted from a Prince of a Commandery to a King of a State.
Wáng Zōngběn, the former Yúzhōu Prefect,
(Wáng Zōngběn had previously been appointed Yúzhōu Prefect by Wáng Jiàn,
and had been dismissed from office and returned to Chéngdū,
hence the "former.")
requested to send troops to take Jīngnán.
Jiàn agreed,
appointing Zōngběn as Kāidào Chief Commander,
to lead troops down the Gorges.
The Gorges
refer to the Three Gorges.
Previously,
Tián Yūn, the Níngguó Jìedùshǐ, had defeated Féng Hóngduó,
(The event is detailed in the second year of the previous volume.)
and consequently sought to have Chí and Shè prefectures placed under his jurisdiction.
The Táng dynasty had established the Xuān, Shè, and Chí Observer.
These two prefectures originally belonged to Xuānzhōu's jurisdiction,
so Tián Yūn sought them due to his merits.
Granting them would make Tián Yūn even stronger,
so it was not permitted.
All sought bribes from Yūn,
because he had obtained much treasure by defeating Féng Hóngduó.
"The officials know I am about to be imprisoned!"
When he returned,
he pointed to the southern gate of Guǎnglín and said,
"I cannot enter here again!"
Yūn's army was strong and his wealth abundant,
and he was fond of attacking and conquering.
After Xíngmì pacified Huáinán,
he wished to protect the borders and bring peace to the people,
constantly restraining Yūn,
but Yūn did not comply.
When Qián Liú was pardoned,
(The event is detailed in the second year of the previous volume.)
he secretly harbored rebellious intentions.
Lǐ Shénfú said to Xíngmì,
"Yūn will certainly rebel;
we should deal with him early."
Xíngmì said,
"Yūn has rendered great services.
(Tián Yūn joined Yáng Xíngmì in Lúzhōu,
and his defeats of Zhào Huáng, Sūn Rú, and Féng Hóngduó
were all great achievements.)
If we kill him now,
all the generals will feel insecure!"
Yūn had a good general named Kāng Rú,
whose counsel often disagreed with Yūn's.
Xíngmì, knowing this,
promoted Rú to Lúzhōu Prefect.
(Promoting Rú
was a way to sow discord with Yūn.)
His clan was exterminated.
Rú said,
"When I die,
Lord Tián's downfall will be imminent!"
Yūn then raised troops together with Ān Rényì, the Rùnzhōu Tuánliàn Commissioner.
(The Kǎoyì states: "The Shíguó Jìnián:
'Zhū Quánzhōng, hearing of Tián Yūn and others' rebellion,
falsely issued an imperial decree stripping Wáng's official titles,
appointing Yūn, Dù Hóng, Zhōng Chuán, and Qián Liú as Four-Front Pacification Commissioners,
and distributing the decree along the border.
Wáng knew it was a deceitful fabrication.'
However, the New and Old Jì, Shílù, and Liáng Tàizǔ Jì
all have no mention of stripping Xíngmì's official titles or appointing Dù Hóng and others as Pacification Commissioners.
Therefore, this is not accepted.)
Dōngtáng
refers to Yángzhōu's Dōngtáng,
where Huáinán's warships were gathered.
The opposite bank was the border of Rùnzhōu,
hence Rényì was able to burn them.
(Jiàn,
pronounced 'hù àn fān'.)
Tián Yūn dispatched two envoys disguised as merchants.
They went to Shòuzhōu to plot with Zhū Yánshòu, the Jìedùshǐ of Fèngguó.
The imperial court had appointed Zhū Yánshòu as Jìedùshǐ of Fèngguó;
see the second year of the previous volume.
An envoy
(shū lì fān)
said,
"These are not merchants."
One of them was killed,
and their letter was seized
and reported to Yáng Xíngmì.
Shàng Gōng then returned to Yáng Xíngmì;
see the second year of the previous volume.
Shénfú, fearing that Dù Hóng would intercept them,
publicly declared that he had been ordered to attack Jīngnán,
and gathered his troops and prepared boats.
By evening,
he proceeded downstream along the river,
only then informing his officers and men that they were to attack Tián Yūn.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Ān Rényì attacked Chángzhōu.
(Jiǔyù Zhì: From Rùnzhōu southeast to Chángzhōu is 171 lǐ.)
He cursed Rényì vehemently.
Rényì said,
"He dares to insult me;
he must be prepared."
So he withdrew.
On the day Rénchén,
Yáng Xíngmì appointed Wáng Màozhāng as the Commander of the Rùnzhōu Field Army
to attack Rényì,
but did not succeed.
He dispatched Xú Wēn to lead troops to reinforce him.
Xú Wēn changed their clothes and banners
to be like Wáng Màozhāng's troops.
Rényì, not knowing that reinforcements had arrived,
again went out to battle.
Xú Wēn fought fiercely
and defeated him.
Lǐ Cúnshěn, when rescuing Hézhōng,
and capturing Biàn cavalry,
also used this tactic.
Yáng Xíngmì's wife
was Zhū Yánshòu's sister.
Yáng Xíngmì treated Zhū Yánshòu with familiarity and contempt,
which Zhū Yánshòu resented and was angry about,
secretly colluding with Tián Yūn.
(The "Lǚ'áo" states: When virtue is abundant, one does not treat others with familiarity and contempt.
If you treat a gentleman with familiarity and contempt,
you will not be able to fully utilize his heart;
if you treat a small person with familiarity and contempt,
you will not be able to fully utilize his strength.
Yáng Xíngmì treated Zhū Yánshòu with familiarity and contempt,
almost leading to the downfall of his state and loss of his family.
It was only after being in peril that he succeeded.
How can one not be warned?)
He allied with Zhū Yánshòu;
he also sent an envoy to Dàliáng to inform Zhū Quánzhōng.
Zhū Quánzhōng was greatly pleased
and dispatched troops to garrison Sùzhōu in response.
(Zhū Quánzhōng was pleased that Yáng Xíngmì had a exploitable weakness,
but he could not deploy a large army to attack his rear,
because internally, Zīqīng was not yet subdued,
and to the west there was Fèngxiáng, and to the north there was Tàiyuán.
He feared they might seize the opportunity to destabilize the imperial court.)
He was from Chízhōu.
Yáng Shīhòu garrisoned Línqú,
publicly announcing that he was going to Mìzhōu,
leaving his baggage train at Línqú.
(Jiǔyù Zhì: Línqú County is 40 lǐ southeast of Qīngzhōu,
and another 260 lǐ to Mìzhōu.)
Qú (音劬).
Zhòng (直用 fān).
On the day Guǐmǎo,
Wáng Shīfàn led his troops to attack Línqú.
Yáng Shīhòu's ambushing troops fought fiercely
and utterly defeated them,
killing over ten thousand men
and capturing Wáng Shīfàn's brother, Wáng Shīkè.
The next day,
5,000 Láizhōu soldiers came to rescue Qīngzhōu.
Yáng Shīhòu intercepted and attacked them,
killing and capturing almost all of them.
He then moved his encampment to the base of their city walls.
(Kǎoyì states: According to the "Liáng Tàizǔ Shílù":
"In the ninth month,
on the day Guǐmǎo,
Yáng Shīhòu exhorted his troops to fight decisively,
and the Qīng forces were utterly defeated,
fleeing north,
with 10,000 killed.
Shīfàn's brother, Shīkè, was captured.
The next day,
Láizhōu Commandery dispatched 5,000 provincial troops and local militia to reinforce the Qīng ramparts.
Our army intercepted and annihilated them,
with hardly one or two surviving.
Immediately, the camp was moved to press against their city walls."
The "Táng Shílù" is generally similar to this.
Biānyílù states:
"In winter,
tenth month,
on the day Dīngmǎo,
Yáng Shīhòu successively reported victories at Línqú,
north and on all four sides of Qīngzhōu,
repeatedly killing and defeating enemy factions,
capturing and beheading many.
By the eleventh month,
Wáng Shīkè, the Prefect of Láizhōu, led 6,000 men, intending to enter Qīngqiū directly
to assist in its defense;
Yáng Shīhòu ambushed and intercepted them,
killing almost all of them."
Further down, there is also
"On the day Dīnghài,
it was the emperor's birthday.
News was received of Zhū Yǒulún's death."
The birthday was the 21st day of the tenth month,
and Zhū Yǒulún's death also occurred in the middle of the tenth month.
Further down, there is another mention of the eleventh month.
It is suspected that the "eleventh month" above
might be
"eleventh day"
or
"seventh day."
It also states:
"On the first day,
Shīfàn requested surrender."
It is suspected that the character
"twenty"
was omitted.
The 21st day
is the day Wùwǔ.
Now following the "Liáng Shílù.")
Zhū Yánshòu's plot was somewhat leaked.
(Zhū Yánshòu's collusion with Tián Yūn
had been going on for a long time and was now somewhat exposed.)
When facing Zhū Yánshòu's envoys, he often acted confused and disoriented,
sometimes bumping into a pillar and falling to the ground.
(Seeing A as B,
seeing a dog as a cat,
this is seeing things in a confused manner.
A pillar is something easily seen,
yet bumping into it,
all this was feigning blindness to deceive people.)
He said, "I am unfortunately blind.
All my sons are young.
The affairs of the military headquarters should all be entrusted to my third maternal uncle."
His wife repeatedly sent letters to Zhū Yánshòu;
(The wife was Zhū Yánshòu's sister.
Zhū Yánshòu was her third brother.)
secretly ordering Xú Wēn to prepare for it.
When Zhū Yánshòu arrived at Guǎnglín,
Yáng Xíngmì welcomed him to the sleeping quarters,
seized and killed him.
(According to the text, Shàng Gōng had seized Tián Yūn's two envoys.
Tián Yūn later sent Dù Xúnhè to Shòuzhōu,
so Zhū Yánshòu must have known that the previous two envoys had been apprehended.
Yáng Xíngmì summoned him,
yet he had no self-doubt
and went to his death.
Was it that his intelligence was lacking?
Or was it that Heaven deprived him of his judgment?)
Xú Wēn issued an order to his troops,
and they all obeyed.
(Xú Wēn had followed Yáng Xíngmì since Lúzhōu,
and with Liú Wēi, Táo Yǎ, and others, they were called the thirty-six heroes.
He must have had a way to win the hearts of Zhū Yánshòu's soldiers,
which is why they all obeyed his orders.)
Zhū Yánshòu's wife was dismissed from her position.
Earlier,
when Zhū Yánshòu was responding to the summons,
his wife, Lady Wáng, said to him,
"The outcome of your journey is unknown.
I wish you would send an envoy daily to reassure me!"
One day,
no envoy arrived.
Lady Wáng said,
"The matter is clear!"
She organized her servants,
armed them, and closed the gates.
When cavalry arrived to arrest them,
she gathered her family,
piled up treasures,
and lit a hundred torches to burn down the mansion,
saying,
"I vow not to let my pure body be disgraced by the enemy."
She then threw herself into the fire and died.
(The historian states that Zhū Yánshòu's wife had wisdom and could uphold her integrity.)
Zhū Yánshòu's enforcement of laws was strict.
He liked to use a small force to attack a large one.
He once sent 200 men to fight the Biàn army.
There was one man who was supposed to remain behind
but requested to go.
Zhū Yánshòu, considering it a violation of orders,
immediately executed him.
35 Tián Yūn (田頵) attacked Shēngzhōu (昇州).
He captured Lǐ Shénfú's (李神福) wife and children,
and treated them well.
In the second year of Tiānfù (天復),
Tián Yūn (田頵) conquered Shēngzhōu (昇州).
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) had appointed Lǐ Shénfú (李神福) as the Inspector of Shēngzhōu (昇州).
At that time, Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) had dispatched Shénfú (神福) to attack È (鄂),
so Yūn (頵) took advantage of the vulnerability to attack.
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) says: Xuānzhōu (宣州) is three hundred and sixty *lǐ* (里) north of Shēngzhōu (昇州).
Yūn (頵) sent an envoy to him, saying:
"If you recognize the opportune moment,
I will divide the territory with you and we shall rule as kings.
Otherwise,
none of your family will be spared!"
Shénfú (神福) said:
"I served the King of Wú (吳王) as a common soldier.
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) was enfeoffed as the King of Wú (吳王).
Hence, he is called the King of Wú.
It is against my principles to trade my wife and children for my aspirations.
Yūn (頵) has an elderly mother.
To disregard her and revolt,
not even understanding the Three Cardinal Guides,
some suspect Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) kept Tián Yūn's (田頵) mother in Guǎnglíng (廣陵).
A detailed examination of the whole affair shows
that Tián Yūn's (田頵) mother Yīn (殷) followed Yūn (頵) when he was in Xuānzhōu (宣州).
Lǐ Shénfú (李神福) was probably saying that since Yūn (頵) had a mother,
he should not act recklessly,
for if he raised an army and was defeated,
then disaster would surely befall his mother.
The Three Cardinal Guides are
that the ruler is the guide for the ministers,
the father is the guide for the son,
and the husband is the guide for the wife.
He beheaded the envoy and advanced,
and all his soldiers were inspired.
Yūn (頵) dispatched his generals Wáng Tán (王壇) and Wāng Jiàn (汪建) to lead a naval force to meet them in battle.
In the second year of Guānghuà (光化),
Tián Yūn's (田頵) general Kāng Rú (康儒) captured Wùzhōu (婺州),
and Wáng Tán (王壇) returned it.
On the *dīngwèi* (丁未) day,
Shénfú (神福) reached Jíyáng Jī (吉陽磯),
where he encountered Tán (壇) and Jiàn (建).
Tán (壇) and Jiàn (建) seized his son Chéngdǐng (承鼎) and displayed him.
Shénfú (神福) ordered his attendants to shoot him.
Shénfú (神福) said to his generals:
"They are numerous, we are few;
we must win by stratagem."
At dusk,
they engaged in battle.
Shénfú (神福) feigned defeat,
leading his boats upstream;
moving against the current is called *sù* (泝).
pronounced *sūgù fān* (蘇故翻).
*Shàng* (上),
pronounced *shízhǎng fān* (時掌翻).
Shénfú (神福) then returned
and attacked them downstream.
Tán (壇) and Jiàn's (建) turreted ships arrayed many torches.
Shénfú (神福) ordered his army:
"Strike wherever you see torches."
They struck where Tán (壇) and Jiàn (建) were located.
When ships display torches,
they cannot illuminate themselves,
but the enemy, looking at them,
