1 In spring,
the first month,

Quánzhōng secretly memorialized that Sītú (司徒) and Shìzhōng (侍中), Pàn Liùjūn Shí'èrwèi Shì (判六軍十二衞事), Chōng Yán-Tiě Zhuǎnyùnshǐ (充鹽鐵轉運使), Pàn Dùzhī (判度支) Cuī Yìn, was monopolizing power and bringing chaos to the state,
sowing discord between the ruler and his ministers.
He also requested the execution of Cuī Yìn's partisans: Xíngbù Shàngshū (刑部尚書) and Jīngzhàoyǐn (京兆尹), Liùjūn Zhūwèi Fùshǐ (六軍諸衞副使) Zhèng Yuán-guī, Wēiyuǎn Jūnshǐ (威遠軍使) Chén Bān, and others.
He requested that they all be put to death.
On the day Yǐsì,
an imperial edict demoted Cuī Yìn to Tàizǐ Shàofù (太子少傅) and assigned him to a detached post (fēnsī),
Zhèng Yuán-guī was banished to Xúnzhōu Sīhù (循州司戶),
and Chén Bān to Còuzhōu Sīhù (湊州司戶).
At that time, there was no Còuzhōu;
"Còu" (湊)
should be
"Zhēn" (溱).
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
an edict was issued detailing the crimes of Cuī Yìn and his associates.
Péi Shū was appointed Pàn Zuǒ Sānjūn Shì (判左三軍事) and Chōng Yán-Tiě Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
Dúgū Sǔn was appointed Pàn Yòu Sānjūn Shì (判右三軍事) and concurrently Pàn Dùzhī.
The soldiers recruited by Cuī Yìn were all disbanded and sent away.
Bīngbù Shàngshū (兵部尚書) Cuī Yuǎn was made Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎),
and Hànlín Xuéshì (翰林學士), Zuǒ Shíyí (左拾遺) Liǔ Càn was made Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū (右諫議大夫),
both appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
The *Kǎo Yì* (考異) states: The Old Biography records:
"The day before Cuī Yìn was condemned,
Liǔ Càn was summoned to the inner palace to draft imperial edicts.
On the day Cuī Yìn died,
as evening approached,
Liǔ Càn emerged from the inner palace,
his vanguard shouting 'Xiànggōng (相公) is coming!'
People had not yet seen the imperial edicts,
so they could not fathom the reason."
The New Biography states:
"When Cuī Yìn died,
Zhāozōng secretly promised Liǔ Càn the position of chancellor (xiàng),
but outsiders knew nothing of it.
At dusk,
he emerged from the Forbidden Palace,
and the cry of 'Zǎixiàng (宰相)' was raised,
greatly startling the people."
However, Cuī Yìn had not yet died,
and Liǔ Càn had already been appointed Píngzhāngshì.
The Old and New Biographies' claim that this happened after Cuī Yìn's death
is an error.
He was Càn's grand-nephew.
Since the Yuánhé (元和) era,
the Liǔ (柳) family had been known for its integrity, uprightness, refinement, and elegance,
with each generation inheriting its virtues.
But with Liǔ Càn, its family reputation collapsed,
fulfilling the saying,
"A family of nine generations of high officials is destroyed in a single act."
Liǔ Bīn's family instructions (jiāxùn) proved to be empty words.
The character "Cóng" (從)
is pronounced in the *cái yòng* (才用) fanqiè.
On the day Wùshēn,
Zhū Quánzhōng secretly ordered the Sùwèi Dūzhǐhuīshǐ (宿衞都指揮使) Zhū Yǒuliàng to besiege Cuī Yìn's residence with troops,
killing Cuī Yìn, Zhèng Yuán-guī, Chén Bān, and several of Cuī Yìn's close associates.
Cuī Yìn had committed the crime of misleading the state,
but he did not have a heart to betray the state.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: The Old Biography records:
"When Quánzhōng attacked Fèngxiáng,
Cuī Yìn was residing in Huázhōu,
where he drew up a plan for Quánzhōng to become king."
It also states:
"When the Son of Heaven returned to the palace,
Quánzhōng returned east.
Cuī Yìn, with power in his hands,
feared Quánzhōng's eagerness to usurp the throne.
He then plotted with Zhèng Yuán-guī to recruit soldiers and weapons,
using the pretext of resisting Lǐ Màozhēn.
Quánzhōng knew his intention
and agreed to it,
ordering several hundred Bìanzhōu (汴州) soldiers to enter the pass and enlist.
When Yǒulún died,
Quánzhōng became enraged.
He dispatched his son, Sùwèi Jūnshǐ (宿衞軍使) Yǒuliàng, to execute Cuī Yìn,
and the enlisted soldiers suddenly appeared."
The *Táng Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù* (唐太祖紀年錄) states:
"As his power grew,
he realized Zhū Wēn harbored ambitions of usurpation.
Fearing that disaster might strike one day, bringing ruin to the state along with him,
he devised a plan for his own safety.
While outwardly cordial with Zhū Wēn,
his private sentiments gradually diverged.
He secretly plotted with Yuán-guī,
doubling the number of recruited soldiers
and repairing armor,
working tirelessly day and night.
Zhū Wēn observed this
and secretly ordered several thousand of his brave and strong subordinates
to pretend to be stragglers
and enlist in the capital.
Cuī Yìn drilled them daily in archery and crossbows,
but the Liáng (梁) soldiers feigned timidity and weakness,
sometimes holding their bows backwards and their arrows incorrectly,
as if incompetent.
Cuī Yìn did not recognize their deception.
Shortly after, Zhū Yǒulún fell from his horse during a polo game and died.
Wēn grew even more displeased.
He also heard that Cuī Yìn intended to take the Son of Heaven and flee to Jīngxiāng.
Wēn then declared,
'Cuī Yìn is about to throw the world into chaos,
overthrowing the imperial court.
He should be promptly executed,
lest the matter escalate.'
The Son of Heaven was about to dismiss Cuī Yìn from his governmental duties
and demote him to Tàizǐ Bīnkè (太子賓客),
and Zhèng Yuán-guī to Xúnzhōu Sīhù.
Before the order could be carried out,
Wēn's son, Yǒuliàng, led troops to attack Cuī Yìn.
At dawn,
he captured him.
He then attacked Zhèng Yuán-guī at the capital prefecture
and captured him.
Both Cuī and Zhèng were beheaded and their heads presented at Qíxià."
The *Shílù* (實錄) states:
"Cuī Yìn, from a lineage of chancellors for generations,
nevertheless harbored the ambition to destroy the Táng (唐) dynasty."
However, Cuī Yìn was secretly cunning, treacherous, impatient, and rash,
and his crimes were certainly many.
Yet, he originally summoned Quánzhōng
to use his military power to eliminate the eunuchs.
Once the eunuchs were executed,
Quánzhōng's military power grew stronger,
and he then harbored ambitions of usurpation.
Cuī Yìn, in turn, tried to use cunning and deceit to deal with Quánzhōng,
so Quánzhōng, realizing his intent, killed him.
If one were to say that the Táng imperial house fell due to Cuī Yìn, that would be acceptable.
However, the Old Biography states
"Cuī Yìn drew up a plan for Quánzhōng to become king,"
and the *Shílù* states
"Cuī Yìn harbored the ambition to destroy the Táng dynasty."
This is probably not necessarily true.
Cuī Yìn was already a prime minister (shàngxiàng) in the Táng court.
To destroy Táng and establish Liáng (梁),
what benefit would that bring him?
Even if Cuī Yìn truly had this ambition,
he would only worry that Quánzhōng's usurpation would not be swift enough.
Why would he then plot to resist him?
This is what is called "all evil attributed to one person."
The *Jìnián Lù* (紀年錄) describes the relationship between Zhū and Cuī,
which comes closer to the truth,
so we follow it now.
However, the *Jìnián Lù*'s statement that their heads were presented at Qíxià
is an error.
Furthermore,
when Quánzhōng left Cháng'ān,
he left behind ten thousand infantry and cavalry.
Why would he lack soldiers,
and why would he need to order Bìanzhōu soldiers to enlist again?
If these soldiers were needed to suddenly appear and capture Cuī Yìn during training,
Cuī Yìn had already been demoted and was living at home;
a single man could control him.
Why use such a scheme?
It is probable that Quánzhōng, seeing that Cuī Yìn had recruited many soldiers,
feared he might plot against him.
Therefore, he had Bìanzhōu soldiers enlist
to observe their movements and thwart their plans,
not to use these soldiers to execute Cuī Yìn.
People initially did not know this,
but when Cuī Yìn was executed, they all suddenly appeared,
and only then did people realize they were Bìanzhōu soldiers.
2 Originally,
the Emperor was in Huázhōu.
In the third and fourth years of Qiánníng,
the Emperor was in Huázhōu.
These events are detailed in Volume 260 and Volume 261.
The one who initiated this plot
was Cuī Yìn.
Quánzhōng often ordered Dōngdū Liúshǒu (東都留守) and Yòuguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ (佑國軍節度使) Zhāng Quányì to repair the palaces and residences.
When Quánzhōng conquered Bīnzhōu,
he held the wives and children of Jìngnán Jūn Jiédùshǐ (靜難軍節度使) Yáng Chóngběn as hostages in Hézhōng.
This event is detailed in Volume 262, Tiānfù (天復) First Year.
The character "Zhì" (質)
has the sound *zhì*.
The character "Nán" (難)
is pronounced in the *nǎi dàn* (乃旦) fanqiè.
Quánzhōng had a private affair with her,
and later returned her.
Yáng Chóngběn was enraged
and sent a message to Lǐ Màozhēn, saying:
"The Táng dynasty is about to perish,
how can my father bear to sit by and watch?"
Lǐ Màozhēn had adopted Yáng Chóngběn as his son
and changed his name to Lǐ Jìhuī,
which is why he addressed him as "father."
His name was changed back to Lǐ Jìhuī.
Yáng Chóngběn reverted to his original name.
See Volume 262, Tiānfù First Year.
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
Quánzhōng led troops to station at Hézhōng.
On the *dīngsì* day,
the Emperor ascended the Yánxǐ Lóu.
Zhū Quánzhōng sent his general Yájiàng Kòu Yànqīng to present a memorial,
stating that the Bīn and Qí armies were pressing on the Jīdiàn,
and requesting the Emperor to move the capital to Luòyáng.
When he descended the樓 *lóu*,
Péi Shū had already received a letter from Quánzhōng,
urging all officials to travel east.
Péi Shū was the Prime Minister,
and also recommended by Zhū Quánzhōng;
thus he was ordered to urge all officials.
Viewed in this light,
can it be said that he was not an adherent of Quánzhōng?
On the *wùmǎo* day,
the scholars and common people were driven away,
wailing filled the roads,
and they cursed, saying:
"The treacherous minister Cuī Yìn summoned Zhū Wēn to overturn the ancestral altars and land,
causing us to wander and suffer to this extent!"
They attributed the blame to the fact that in the first year of Tiānfù, Yìn summoned Zhū Quánzhōng to execute the eunuchs,
and the disaster had now reached this point.
Yìn could not but bear the responsibility.
This continued for over a month.
On the *rénxū* day,
the imperial carriage departed Cháng'ān.
Quánzhōng appointed his general Zhāng Tíngfàn as the Yùyíng Shǐ.
At that time, as the Son of Heaven moved east,
the escorting soldiers became the Yùyíng,
and an *shǐ* was appointed to oversee all their affairs.
The office of Yùyíng Shǐ began here.
Its timber was taken,
floated down the Wèi River and along the Hé River.
Cháng'ān from then on became ruins.
Quánzhōng levied tens of thousands of able-bodied men and artisans from the various prefectures north and south of the Hé River.
At that time, the various prefectures north and south of the Hé River were all attached to Zhū Quánzhōng.
The able-bodied men and artisans levied would certainly not include those from the four prefectures of Zhèn, Dìng, Yōu, and Cāng.
Those prefectures in Jiāng, Zhè, Hú, and Lǐng that were attached to Quánzhōng
all contributed goods and wealth to assist him.
In Jiāng, there was Dù Hóng of È'yuè,
and Zhōng Chuán of Hóngzhōu.
In Zhè, there was Qián Liú.
In Hú, there was Mǎ Yīn of Tánzhōu,
and Léi Yànwēi of Lǐzhōu.
In Lǐng, there was Liú Yǐn of Guǎngzhōu.
All of these were attached to Quánzhōng.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
the imperial carriage arrived at Huázhōu.
The people lined the streets shouting "Long live!"
The Emperor wept and said to them:
"Do not shout 'Long live!'
I will no longer be your lord!"
He was lodged in the Xīngdé Gōng and
said to his attendants:
"The common saying goes: 'Sparrows freeze to death on Hégān Mountain,
why not fly away to a place of joy?'
I am now adrift,
not knowing where I will finally land!"
Thereupon, tears flowed down, drenching his lapels,
and those around him could not bear to look up.
In the second month,
on the *yǐhài* day,
the imperial carriage arrived at Shǎn.
As the palaces in Dōngdū were not yet completed,
it stopped in Shǎn.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Quánzhōng came from Hézhōng to pay respects.
The Emperor invited Quánzhōng into his private chambers to see Empress Hé.
The Empress wept and said:
"From now on, our family's couple entrusts ourselves to Quánzhōng!"
Imperial Prince Zhēn was enfeoffed as Duānwáng,
Qí as Fēngwáng,
Fú as Héwáng,
Xǐ as Dēngwáng,
and Yòu as Jiāwáng.
Jiàn appointed Wáng Zōnghù, the Cìshǐ of Qióngzhōu, as Běilù Xíngyíng Zhǐhuīshǐ,
to lead troops to meet the Fèngxiáng army and welcome the imperial carriage.
Upon reaching Xīngpíng,
they encountered the Biàn army
and could not advance, so they returned.
Jiàn began to appoint officials using his own inked decrees,
saying:
"We will memorialize to the court after the imperial carriage returns to Cháng'ān."
Yáng Xíngmì appointed officials by expediency,
still claiming it was based on Lǐ Yǎn's mission.
As for Wáng Jiàn, he simply did it himself.
on the *dīngwèi* day,
Zhū Quánzhōng was concurrently appointed to oversee the affairs of the Zǒuyòu Shéncè and the Six Armies and various guards.
After Cuī Yìn was executed,
Zhū Quánzhōng then exclusively controlled the imperial guards.
In reality, he distributed his private loyalists around the Emperor,
merely using the pretext of overseeing their affairs.
On the *guǐchǒu* day,
Quánzhōng hosted a banquet in his private residence.
Zhū Quánzhōng was busy campaigning,
and had only just obtained Shǎnzhōu.
How could he have the leisure to build a private residence?
In reality, the place where he settled upon arriving in Shǎnzhōu was simply considered his private residence.
The Heavenly King hunted at Héyáng.
Jìn Wéngōng met with the feudal lords there.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"To summon a sovereign as a minister
is not to be instructed."
How could someone host a banquet in a private residence and invite the sovereign to attend?
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Quánzhōng bade farewell to the Emperor,
proceeding first to Luòyáng to supervise the repair of the palaces.
The Emperor hosted a banquet for him and his ministers.
After it concluded,
the Emperor alone kept Quánzhōng and Hán Jiàn, the Jiédùshǐ of Zhōngwǔ, to drink.
The Empress came out,
personally holding a jade goblet to offer wine to Quánzhōng.
Jìnguófūrén could be seen whispering to the Emperor.
Jiàn tapped Quánzhōng's foot.
Quánzhōng thought he was plotting against him,
so he did not drink,
feigned drunkenness, and left.
Quánzhōng memorialized to designate Cháng'ān as Yòuguó Jūn.
In the third year of Guāngqǐ,
the Yòuguó Jūn Jiédù was established in Luòyáng.
Now that the capital was moving to Luòyáng,
the Yòuguó Jūn was therefore moved to Cháng'ān.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: "According to the Hénán Fǔ, it was already Yòuguó Jūn.
Now Jīngzhào Fǔ bears the same name.
This is probably because since the imperial carriage was already in Hénán,
there was no need for a military title there,
so its name was moved to Jīngzhào.
In the second year of Tiānyòu,
Zhèng Cóng was still the Xījīng Liúshǒu Pàn Guān.
Thus, even if a military title was established,
the capital name still remained."
Liú Zhījùn, the Cìshǐ of Zhèngzhōu, was appointed as the Kuāngguó Jiédùshǐ.
On the *dīngsì* day,
the Emperor again sent a secret envoy with a silk imperial edict to urgently appeal to Wáng Jiàn, Yáng Xíngmì, Lǐ Kèyòng, and others,
ordering them to rally the various fānzhèn to plan for restoration,
saying:
"When I arrive in Luòyáng,
I will be imprisoned by them,
and all imperial edicts will come from their hands.
My intentions will no longer be able to be conveyed!"
Qián Chuánliáo was a hostage of Yáng Xíngmì,
as seen in the previous volume, second year of Tiānfù.
Lǐ Shénfú, the Xíngjūn Sīmǎ of Huáinán, was appointed as È'yuè Zhāotǎoshǐ,
and again led troops to attack Dù Hóng.
Tián Yún had already been pacified,
so Lǐ Shénfú was again sent to attack Dù Hóng.
They requested to abandon È'yuè and restore their former good relations.
Xíngmì replied:
"We will cease military action and restore good relations
only after the Son of Heaven returns to Cháng'ān."
Yáng Xíngmì's ambition was to expand his territory,
while Zhū Quánzhōng's ambition was to usurp the Táng.
Quánzhōng was unable to rescue Dù Hóng,
hence this statement.
Xíngmì's reply
used the pretext of a heavenly punitive expedition to refute their proposal;
his true ambition was not this.
(The character
好,
read *hāo* from *dào fān*.)
7 Summer,
4th month,
day Xīnsì.
Zhū Quánzhōng reported that the palaces in Luòyáng were complete,
and requested the Imperial carriage to depart early,
with memorials following one after another.
The Emperor repeatedly sent palace women to convey that the Empress had recently given birth,
and was not yet fit for travel,
requesting to wait until the 10th month to travel east.
Zhū Quánzhōng suspected the Emperor was hesitating, waiting for a change of circumstances,
suspecting the Emperor was lingering to await the loyal armies from various circuits.
He said to his aide Kòu Yànqīng:
"You must go quickly to Shǎn,
and immediately urge the Emperor to depart!"
For a subject to summon his sovereign —
what kind of words are these!
Huá Dū had no loyalty to his lord before he committed evil;
gentlemen only realized this when he attacked the Kǒng clan.
But as for Zhū Quánzhōng's intentions,
manifest in his expression,
and revealed in his words,
did he have a lord,
or did he not have a lord?
Furthermore, according to records, during the Xī Hàn dynasty, sycophantic officials referred to the Son of Heaven as
"Xiànguān."
Since the Dōng Hàn dynasty, he has been called
"Guójiā."
During the Táng dynasty, within the palace, the Son of Heaven was commonly referred to as
"Zhái Jiā."
Occasionally, he was informally called
"Guānjiā."
Some say: the meaning is probably derived from the Five Emperors (Wǔdì) who "governed" (guān) the realm,
and the Three Kings (Sānwáng) who "familialized" (jiā) the realm.
On day Dīngyǒu,
the Imperial carriage departed Shǎn;
on day Rényín,
Zhū Quánzhōng met the Emperor at Xīn'ān.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Xīn'ān County is seventy *lǐ* west of Luòyáng.
The Directorate of Astronomy (Sītiānjiàn) reported:
"The astral phenomena show changes,
expected this autumn,
unfavorable for eastward travel."
This was a portent of the assassination and rebellion in the Empress's palace (Jiāodiàn).
How clearly did Heaven manifest its signs to warn!
Was it not evident?
Thereupon,

Zhū Quánzhōng ordered Imperial Physician Xǔ Zhāoyuǎn to accuse Director of Imperial Physicians (Yīguān Shǐ) Yán Yòuzhī, Directorate of Astronomy (Sītiānjiàn) Wáng Chí, Director of Inner Palace (Nèi Dūzhī) Wéi Zhōu, Lady of the State of Jìn (Jìnguó Fūrén) Kězheng, and others of plotting against the Marshal,
and had them all arrested and killed.
In the late Táng dynasty, the office of Yīguān Shǐ was established to oversee imperial physicians.
The Nèi Dūzhī,
in the prosperous Táng, was an official of the Palace Eunuch Bureau (Nèishì Shěng).
By the Sòng dynasty,
following the Táng system,
there were Left and Right Banner Chief Directors (Zuǒ Yòu Bān Dū Dūzhī), Left and Right Banner Directors (Zuǒ Yòu Bān Dūzhī), and Vice Directors (Fù Dūzhī) of the Nèishì Shěng.
Yán Yòuzhī and Wáng Chí died
because they spoke of astral phenomena;
Wéi Zhōu and Kězheng died
because they whispered in the Emperor's ear.
The Marshal (Yuánshuài) was
Zhū Quánzhōng.
On day Guǐmǎo,
the Emperor rested at Gǔshuǐ.
Gǔshuǐ
is west of Luò Chéng.
The character "qì"
is pronounced "qù lì fān."
The Six Armies (Liùjūn) were all scattered and perished.
The remaining polo players (jīqiú gòngfèng) and inner garden boys (nèiyuán xiǎo'ér), totaling over two hundred people,
followed the Emperor eastward.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Hòutáng Jìnián Lù* states five hundred people;
the *Shílù* (Veritable Records) follows this.
We now follow the Old Annals and Xuē Shǐ.
Zhū Quánzhōng set up a feast for them in a tent,
and had them all strangled to death.
He had previously selected over two hundred people of similar age and stature,
dressed them in their clothes,
and replaced them as imperial guards.
The Emperor was initially unaware,
realizing it only after several days.
From then on, all those around the Emperor in charge of various duties and commands
were Zhū Quánzhōng's men.
On day Jiǎchén,
the Imperial carriage departed Gǔshuǐ,
entered the palace,
and proceeded to the main hall (Zhèngdiàn) to receive court felicitations.
At that time, the Zhēnguān Diàn was considered the main hall,
and the Chóngxūn Diàn the inner hall.
The character "cháo"
is pronounced "zhí yáo fān."
On day Yǐsì,
the Emperor proceeded to Guāngzhèng Mén.
After the relocation to Luòyáng,
the names of the palace gates were changed,
and Chánglè Mén was renamed Guāngzhèng Mén.
The reign era was changed.
It was changed to Tiānyòu.
An imperial edict was issued to attack Lǐ Màozhēn and Yáng Chóngběn.
On day Wùshēn,
an imperial edict decreed that among the various inner palace offices, only nine directorates, such as the Bureau of Military Affairs (Xuānhuī), were to be retained.

At that time, only the two directorates of Xuānhuī, Xiǎomǎ Fāng (Small Stables Office), Fēngdé Kù (Fengde Treasury), Yùchú (Imperial Kitchen), Kèshěng (Guest Office), Gémén (Palace Gate Bureau), Fēilóng (Flying Dragon Office), and Zhuāngzhái (Estates Office) were retained.
All others were abolished.
Furthermore, no inner palace ladies (nèi fūrén) were to be appointed as directors.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Biān Yílù* says:
"On day Wùshēn,
when the imperial carriage first arrived in Luò Dū,
expenses were vast;
moreover, national resources were not abundant,
and all matters were being started from scratch.
Therefore, idle offices and bureaus were curtailed,
and from now on, apart from retaining the nine directorates such as Xuānhuī,
all others were abolished,
and inner palace ladies (nèi zhōng fūrén) were no longer to be appointed as directors."
This was because after the eunuchs were initially executed,
the directors of all inner palace offices were led by inner palace ladies (nèi fūrén),
and only at this point were outsiders used.
However, the *Shílù* (Veritable Records) changed "chōng shǐ" (appointed as director) to "xuān shì" (performing duties),
which is an error.
According to the text, after the eunuchs were executed,
inner palace ladies (nèi fūrén) conveyed imperial edicts and served as directors of various inner palace offices.
Since they indeed conveyed imperial edicts,
then the *Shílù*'s "xuān shì" (performing duties)
was not necessarily an error.
However, it was not until Tiānyòu 3rd year
that palace women were stopped from conveying imperial edicts,
hence the *Shílù* is considered erroneous here.
Wáng Yīn was appointed Director of the Xuānhuī Northern Directorate (Xuānhuī Běiyuàn Shǐ) concurrently Imperial City Commissioner (Huángchéng Shǐ).
Zhāng Tíngfàn was appointed Jīnwú Jiāngjūn (General of the Imperial Guards) concurrently Street Commissioner (Jiē Shǐ).
Wéi Zhèn was appointed Prefect of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn) concurrently Vice Commissioner of the Six Armies and Various Guards (Liùjūn Zhūwèi Fùshǐ).
Furthermore, Zhū Yǒugōng, acting Military Governor of Wǔníng (Wǔníng Liúhòu), was summoned to be Left Supreme General of the Dragon Martial Army (Zuǒ Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn).
Shì Shúcóng, Military Governor of Bǎodà (Bǎodà Jiédùshǐ), was appointed Right Supreme General of the Dragon Martial Army (Yòu Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn).
They were in charge of the imperial guard;
all were Zhū Quánzhōng's trusted confidants.
On day Guǐchǒu,
Zhāng Quányì was appointed Military Governor of Tiānpíng (Tiānpíng Jiédùshǐ).
On day Yǐmǎo,
Zhū Quánzhōng was appointed Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of the four circuits of Hùguó, Xuānwǔ, Xuānyì, and Zhōngwǔ.
Zhū Quánzhōng was previously Military Governor of the four circuits of Xuānwǔ, Tiānpíng, Xuānyì, and Hùguó;
because Zhāng Quányì had for many years managed the repairs of Luòyáng,
and now Luòyáng had become the capital
and was not to be a military governorship,
Tiānpíng was therefore conferred upon Zhāng Quányì,
while Zhū Quánzhōng himself concurrently held Zhōngwǔ as one of his four circuits.
8 Qián Liú, Prince of Yuè (Yuè Wáng) and Military Governor of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng, sought to be enfeoffed as King of Wúyuè (Wúyuè Wáng);
the imperial court refused.
Zhū Quánzhōng spoke on his behalf to the authorities,
and he was then re-enfeoffed as King of Wú (Wú Wáng).
In the 1st year of Tiānfù,
Qián Liú was enfeoffed as Prince of Yuè.
The character "wèi"
is pronounced "yú wěi fān."
The character "gēng"
is pronounced "gōng héng fān."
9 Wèibó was renamed Tiānxióng Jūn.
Dàizōng had renamed Wèibó as Tiānxióng Jūn to honor Tián Chéngsì;
during Dézōng's time,
Tián Yuè rebelled,
but later submitted again,
and was appointed Military Governor of Wèibó.
Now the old designation of Tiānxióng Jūn was restored.
On day Guǐhài,
Luó Shàowēi, Military Governor of Tiānxióng (Tiānxióng Jiédùshǐ) and Prince of Chángshā Commandery (Chángshā Jùnwáng), was advanced in rank to Prince of Yè (Yè Wáng).
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ, reviewed by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Compiled by imperial order by Sīmǎ Guāng.
Hòuxuétiāntái.
Tiānyòu 1st year
(Jiǎzǐ, 904)
1. 5th month,
day Bǐngyín.
Zhāng Hànyú, Military Governor of Héyáng (Héyáng Jiédùshǐ), was granted the concurrent title of Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
2. The Emperor feasted Zhū Quánzhōng and all the officials at Chóngxūn Diàn.
At that time, the front hall of the Luòyáng palace was the Zhēnguān Diàn,
and the inner court was the Chóngxūn Diàn.
The Emperor again invited Zhū Quánzhōng to a feast in the inner hall;
Zhū Quánzhōng was suspicious
and did not enter.
The Emperor said:
"If Zhū Quánzhōng does not wish to come,
then let Jìng Xiáng come."
Zhū Quánzhōng pushed Jìng Xiáng away,
saying:
"Xiáng is also drunk."
Zhū Quánzhōng suspected the Emperor wanted to harm him,
and since Jìng Xiáng was his confidant,
he therefore did not allow him to enter either.
The character "zhāi" (擿)
is pronounced "tā dí fān."
On day Xīnwèi,
Zhū Quánzhōng returned east;
on day Yǐhài,
he arrived at Dàliáng.
3. Zhōngyì Jiédùshǐ Zhào Kuāngníng dispatched a naval force upstream into the Three Gorges to attack Wáng Jiàn's Kuízhōu.
Zhào Kuāngníng used Xiāngyáng's forces to spy on Kuímén.
Kuízhōu is in the upper reaches of the Three Gorges.
To attack it by ascending the river,
hence it is called "shàng xiá" (going upstream through the gorges).
Shàng,
pronounced "shí zhǎng".
Wànzhōu Cìshǐ Zhāng Wǔ made an iron cable to block the middle of the river,
and erected palisades at both ends,
calling it
"Suǒxiá" (Locked Gorges).
4. In the sixth month,
Lǐ Màozhēn, Wáng Jiàn, and Lǐ Jìhuī sent dispatches, combining their forces to attack Zhū Quánzhōng;
Quánzhōng appointed Zhènkuó Jiédùshǐ Zhū Yǒuyù as Xíngyíng Dūtǒng,
to lead infantry and cavalry to strike
them.
At this time,
the Shu forces did not advance,
and Zhū Quánzhōng's military strength could not reach them.
He ordered Zhū Yǒuyù to attack Qí and Bīn only.
He led his troops to garrison in Tóngzhōu.
Liú Xún was in Fūzhōu,
close to Lǐ Màozhēn and Jìhuī,
with no supporting forces connected.
Therefore, he was ordered to abandon Fūzhōu and return to garrison in Tóngzhōu,
joining forces with Zhū Yǒuyù.
Fū,
pronounced "fū".
On the day Guǐchǒu,
Quánzhōng led his troops from Dàliáng westward to attack Màozhēn and others;
In autumn,
seventh month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ,
he passed through Dōngdū and had an audience;
on the day Rénshēn,
he arrived at Hézhōng.
5. The generals of Xīchuān advised Wáng Jiàn to take advantage of Lǐ Màozhēn's decline
to attack and seize Fèngxiáng.
Jiàn consulted with Jiédù Pànguān Féng Juān,
who said:
"Weapons are instruments of ill omen,
they harm the people and deplete resources,
and should not be exhausted.
It means not to exhaust military strength.
Pushing military strength to its limit,
being fond of war and never resting,
this is exhausting military strength.
If the situation becomes one where two cannot coexist,
Liang
(Zhū Quánzhōng)
and Jin
(Lǐ Kèyòng)
raise armies against Shu,
even if Zhūgě Liàng were reborn,
he would not be able to resist them.
Fèngxiáng is
a screen for Shu.
It would be better to make peace with them,
form a marital alliance.
When there is no trouble, focus on farming and training soldiers,
securing the borders.
When there is trouble, observe their opportune moments,
and act when an opening appears.
This way, complete safety can be achieved."
Jiàn said:
"Excellent!
Although Màozhēn is of mediocre talent,
he has a reputation for being fierce and strong,
and is feared far and wide.
He is insufficient to contend with Quánzhōng,
but more than sufficient to defend himself.
To use him as our screen
offers great benefits."
Thereupon, he cultivated good relations with Màozhēn.
Wáng Jiàn had already annexed the prefectures south of the mountains,
guarding them by blocking the passes.
Outside the passes, he relied on Lǐ Màozhēn as a screen,
hence he cultivated good relations with him.
Hǎo,
pronounced "hū dào".
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Màozhēn dispatched Pànguān Zhào Huáng to Xīchuān
to seek a marriage alliance for his nephew, Tiānxióng Jiédùshǐ Jìxūn;
Jiàn gave his daughter to him in marriage.
Màozhēn repeatedly requested goods and weapons from Jiàn,
and Jiàn gave them all.
To abandon military resources to strengthen an enemy,
how could this be Wáng Jiàn's original intention!
Relying on him for protection,
he did not find his requests excessive.
Shù,
pronounced "suǒ jiǎo".
Wáng Jiàn imposed heavy taxes,
and no one dared to speak about it.
Féng Juān took advantage of Jiàn's birthday to present a eulogy,
first praising his accomplishments and virtues,
then speaking of the people's suffering.
Jiàn, feeling ashamed, apologized, saying:
"With loyal advice like yours,
what worry is there for accomplishments!"
He bestowed gold and silk upon him.
From then on, taxes were slightly reduced.
Historians say that Féng Juān offered advice through a eulogy,
hence his remonstrance was easily accepted.
Liǎn,
pronounced "lì shàn".
6. Initially,
when Zhū Quánzhōng escorted the imperial carriage back from Fèngxiáng,
(see volume 263, Tiānfù 3rd year).
Huán,
pronounced "cóng xuān", also as is.
And since his age was already mature,
(Quánzhōng) disliked him,
privately telling Cuī Yìn:
"Prince Dé once coveted the imperial throne,
(referring to his being established by Liú Jìshù).
The event is found in volume 262, Guānghuà 3rd year and Tiānfù 1st year.
Why do you not speak of it!"
Yìn reported it to the Emperor.
The Emperor asked Quánzhōng,
Quánzhōng said:
"Between Your Majesty and your son,
how dare I, your minister, secretly comment?
This Cuī Yìn is selling me out."
Historians remark on Zhū Quánzhōng's cunning.
(The Emperor) daily feared unforeseen misfortune,
and spent the entire day drinking heavily with the Empress,
sometimes weeping opposite each other.
Quánzhōng ordered Púmìshǐ Jiǎng Xuánhuī to spy on the Emperor,
knowing all his movements and actions.
The Emperor casually said to Xuánhuī:
"Prince Dé is my beloved son.
Why is Quánzhōng so determined to kill him?"
Thereupon, tears flowed,
and he bit his middle finger until blood flowed.
Xuánhuī reported everything to Quánzhōng.
Historians comment on Zhāo Zōng's indiscretion leading to disaster.
Cóng,
pronounced "qiān róng".
Niè,
pronounced "wǔ jié".
Yǔ,
pronounced "niú jù".
At that time, Lǐ Màozhēn, Yáng Chóngběn, Lǐ Kèyòng, Liú Rén'gōng, Wáng Jiàn, Yáng Xíngmì, and Zhào Kuāngníng exchanged dispatches,
all using "restoring the dynasty" as their pretext.
Quánzhōng was leading his troops westward to attack (Qí and Bīn).
Fearing a sudden change internally,
he wished to establish a young ruler
to facilitate the plan of abdication.
So he dispatched Pànguān Lǐ Zhèn to Luòyáng
to plan this with Xuánhuī, Zuǒ Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn Zhū Yǒugōng, and Yòu Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn Shì Shúcóng.
In the eighth month,
on the day Rén Yín,
the Emperor was in Jiāodiàn.
Jiāodiàn is
the Empress's palace.
Shǐ Zhào said: Jiāodiàn is also referred to as Jiāofáng.
(The assassins) said there was an urgent report from the front.
"Jūnqián" (the front) refers to
the campaign headquarters of the western expedition.
Lady Péi Zhēnyī opened the door and saw soldiers,
saying:
"Why are there soldiers for an urgent report?"
Shǐ Tài killed her.
Xuánhuī asked:
"Where is His Supreme Majesty?"
Zhāoyí Lǐ Jiànróng stood by the window and cried out:
"Rather kill us,
do not harm His Majesty!"
The Emperor, who was drunk,
hastily rose,
and in a single robe, ran around a pillar.
Shǐ Tài pursued and assassinated him.
He was thirty-eight years old.
(Shǐ) Tài also killed (Lǐ Jiànróng).
He also wanted to kill Empress Hé,
but the Empress pleaded for mercy from Xuánhuī,
and was then released.
Empress Hé begged Jiǎng Xuánhuī for her life, but ultimately died because of Xuánhuī.
How could bending her principles to prolong her life for a few years
be compared to sacrificing herself for Zhāo Zōng without losing her integrity!
On the day Guǐmǎo,
Jiǎng Xuánhuī fabricated an imperial edict, claiming that Lǐ Jiànróng and Péi Zhēnyī had committed regicide,
and that Huīwáng Zuò should be established as Crown Prince,
renamed Hū,
to oversee state affairs.
He also fabricated an order from the Empress
for the Crown Prince to ascend the throne before the coffin.
Those in the palace were terrified
and dared not cry aloud.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
Zhāoxuān Dì ascended the throne,
at the age of thirteen.
7. Lǐ Kèyòng again appointed Zhāng Chéngyè as Supervisor of the Army.
(Lǐ Kèyòng hid Zhāng Chéngyè, see previous volume, Tiānfù 3rd year).
Jiān,
pronounced "gǔ xián".
8 Huáinán general Lǐ Shénfú (李神福) attacked Èzhōu (鄂州) but did not take it.
In the 3rd year of Tiānfù (天復)
Lǐ Shénfú (李神fú) began to attack Èzhōu (鄂州).
In the 1st year of Tiānyòu (天祐)
Both events are seen in the previous scroll.
Returning to Guǎnglíng (廣陵),
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) appointed Liú Cún (劉存) of Bìyáng (泌陽), the governor of Shūzhōu (舒州) (military commissioner of the militia), to replace him as Commander of Pacification;
Bìyáng (泌陽)
was the land of Húyáng (湖陽) county in the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
The Later Wèi (後魏) established Shímǎ (石馬) county,
which was later corrupted to Shàngmǎ (上馬).
It was abolished in the 1st year of Zhēnguàn (貞觀)
In the 16th year of Kāiyuán (開元)
In the 1st year of Tiānbǎo (天寶)
belonging to Tángzhōu (唐州).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Bìyáng (泌陽) county was originally the land of Wǔyīn (舞陰) county in the Hàn (漢) dynasty, etc.
Same as above.
The Táng (唐) changed it to Bìyáng (泌陽),
because the land was on the sunny side (south) of the Bì (泌) River.
Tángzhōu (唐州) was governed there.
Bì (泌),
sounds like "bīng mèi fān".
Tái Méng (臺濛), the Surveillance Commissioner of Xuānzhōu (宣州), died.
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) appointed his son Wò (渥), the Commander of the Inner Teeth Troops, as the Surveillance Commissioner of Xuānzhōu (宣州).
Xú Wēn (徐溫), the Commander-in-Chief of the Right Teeth, said to Wò (渥):
"The King is gravely ill, and the legitimate heir is sent out to a vassal state.
This must be the plot of a treacherous minister.
When you are summoned another day,
if it is not my (Wēn's) envoy or the King's official letter,
be sure not to come quickly!"
The orders issued by feudal lords within their territories
were called official letters (lìngshū 令書),
to distinguish them from the imperial edicts, proclamations, and decrees issued by the Son of Heaven.
Jí (亟),
sounds like "jì lì fān".
This set the stage for Xú Wēn (徐溫) to summon Wò (渥).
9 In the 9th month,
on the day Jǐsì (己巳),
the Empress was honored as Empress Dowager.
10 Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) led his troops north to garrison Yǒngshòu (永壽),
then south to Luògǔ (駱谷).
Stationing troops at Yǒngshòu (永壽)
was to bring about the Bīn (邠) troops;
from there south to Luògǔ (駱谷)
was to bring about the Qí (岐) troops.
On the day Xīnwèi (辛未),
he returned east.
11 In winter,
in the 10th month,
on the day Xīnmǎo (辛卯), the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
12 When Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) heard that Zhū Yǒugōng (朱友恭) and others had assassinated Zhāo Zōng (昭宗),
he feigned surprise,
cried loudly
and threw himself to the ground,
saying:
"These wretches have betrayed me,
causing me to bear a wicked name for ten thousand generations!"
On the day Guǐsì (癸巳),
he arrived at the Eastern Capital,
returning east from the army front to the Eastern Capital.
He again saw the Emperor and declared that it was not his intention,
requesting to punish the traitors.
The Emperor was Zhāo Xuān Dì (昭宣帝).
The traitors were the regicides.
There were soldiers guarding the Emperor who plundered rice in the market.
On the day Jiǎwǔ (甲午),
Quánzhōng (全忠) reported that Zhū Yǒugōng (朱友恭) and Shì Shūcóng (氏叔琮) did not restrain their soldiers,
who harassed and disturbed the markets.
He used this as a crime for the two men,
still not daring to openly charge them with regicide.
He restored Lǐ Yànwēi's (李彥威) name.
Lǐ Yànwēi (李彥威) was from Shòuzhōu (壽州),
a guest in Biànzhōu (汴州),
who amassed wealth and was chivalrous.
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) loved him and treated him as a son.
A textual variant is found in scroll 259, 2nd year of Jǐngfú (景福).
Soon after, all were granted self-execution.
Yànwēi (彥威) cried out loudly at his execution:
"Selling me to stop the calumny of the world,
what about the ghosts and spirits!
With actions like this,
how can one hope for a successor!"
On the day Bǐngshēn (丙申),
Zhāng Quányì (張全義), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Tiānpíng (天平), came to court.
On the day Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
Quánzhōng (全忠) was again appointed Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Xuānwǔ (宣武), Hùguó (護國), Xuānyì (宣義), and Tiānpíng (天平);
Quányì (全義) was appointed Hénán Yǐn (河南尹) concurrently Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Zhōngwǔ (忠武) and acting supervisor of the Six Armies and Various Guards.
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) concurrently held Zhōngwǔ (忠武),
and Zhāng Quányì (張全義) led Tiānpíng (天平),
as seen in the previous scroll for the previous year.
After Zhū Yǒugōng (朱友恭) and Shì Shūcóng (氏叔琮) were executed,
Quányì (全義) was put in charge of the imperial guards.
On the day Yǐsì (乙巳)
Quánzhōng (全忠) resigned and departed for his garrison.
On the day Gēngxū (庚戌),
he arrived at Dàliáng (大梁).
13 Zhū Yǒuyù (朱友裕), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Zhènguó (鎮國), died in Líyuán (棃園).
He died in the temporary camp at Líyuán (棃園).
14 Guāngzhōu (光州) rebelled against Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密)
and surrendered to Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠).
Xíngmì (行密) sent troops to besiege it.
Both Guāngzhōu (光州) and Èzhōu (鄂州) sent urgent appeals to Quánzhōng (全忠).
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) sent his general Liú Cún (劉存) to attack Dù Hóng (杜洪) in Èzhōu (鄂州).
On the day Wùchén (戊辰),
Quánzhōng (全忠) personally led 50,000 troops from Yǐngzhōu (潁州) to cross the Huái (淮) River.
From Yǐngshàng (潁上) county in Yǐngzhōu (潁州) he took Zhèngyáng (正陽) to cross the Huái (淮) River.
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states that Huòqiū (霍丘) county is 127 li east of Shòuzhōu (壽州).
According to Yuánfēng (元豐), Shòuzhōu (壽州) was governed from Xiàcài (下蔡).
The Huáinán (淮南) troops lifted the siege of Guāngzhōu (光州) and returned to Guǎnglíng (廣陵).
They held their troops and did not engage in battle.
Quánzhōng (全忠) dispatched his generals to heavily plunder Huáinán (淮南) to starve them out.
15 Qián Liú (錢鏐) secretly sent Yè Ràng (葉讓), the Commander of the Luóchéng (羅城) Garrison in Qúzhōu (衢州), to kill the Prefect Chén Zhāng (陳璋).
The plot was leaked.
Qián Liú (錢鏐) resented Chén Zhāng (陳璋) as seen in scroll 262, 2nd year of Tiānfù (天復).
Zhāng (璋) beheaded Ràng (讓) and rebelled,
surrendering to Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密).
16 In the beginning,
Mǎ Yīn's (馬殷) younger brother, Cóng (賨),
was brave and resolute by nature.
He served Sūn Rú (孫儒)
as the Commander of the Bǎishèng (百勝) (Hundred Victories) Army;
naming the army for its hundred battles and hundred victories.
He served Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密)
and repeatedly achieved merit,
rising to Commander of the Hēiyún (黑雲) (Black Cloud) Army.
Xíngmì (行密) once casually asked about his brothers,
and then realized he was Yīn's (殷) younger brother.
He was greatly surprised and said:
"I always wondered at your grand and imposing demeanor,
indeed you are no ordinary man.
I should send you home."
Cóng (賨) wept and declined, saying:
"Cóng (賨) is a remnant soldier from Huáixī (淮西).
Mǎ Cóng (馬賨) rose with Qín Zōngquán (秦宗權) and Sūn Rú (孫儒) in Huáixī (淮西),
hence this statement.
Húnán (湖南) is close by,
and I often heard news of my brother.
Cóng (賨) has served Your Majesty for a long time,
and does not wish to return."
Xíngmì (行密) insisted on sending him.
That year,
Cóng (賨) returned to Chángshā (長沙).
Xíngmì (行密) personally saw him off in the suburbs.
When Cóng (賨) arrived in Chángshā (長沙),
Yīn (殷) memorialized to appoint Cóng (賨) as Vice-Jìedùshǐ (節度使).
Another day,
Yīn (殷) discussed paying tribute to the Son of Heaven.
Cóng (賨) said:
"King Yáng (楊) has vast territory and strong forces.
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) was enfeoffed as King of Wú (吳),
hence he is referred to as such.
It would be better to establish good relations with him,
so that he can be a great help in urgent times,
and a small benefit for trade and travel."
Yīn (殷) became angry and said:
"King Yáng (楊) does not serve the Son of Heaven.
If the imperial court were to launch a punitive expedition one day,
the blame would fall upon me.
You propose this argument,
do not bring disaster upon me!"
The historian states that Mǎ Yīn (馬殷) feared Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠).
17 In the beginning,
Xú Yànruò (徐彥若), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Qīnghǎi (清海), left a memorial recommending Vice-Jìedùshǐ (節度使) Liú Yǐn (劉隱) to temporarily act as Military Governor.
This event is seen in scroll 262, 1st year of Tiānfù (天復).
Yuǎn (遠) traveled far to Jiānglíng (江陵),
heard that there were many bandits in Língnán (嶺南),
and also feared that Yǐn (隱) would not accept the replacement,
so he dared not proceed.
The imperial court recalled Yuǎn (遠).
Yǐn (隱) sent an envoy with a heavy bribe to win over Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠),
who then memorialized to appoint Yǐn (隱) as Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Qīnghǎi (清海).
The historian states that Liú Yǐn (劉隱) relied on Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠).
2nd year of Tiānyòu (天祐)
(Yǐchǒu 乙丑, 905)
1 In spring,
in the 1st month,
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) sent his generals to advance and press upon Shòuzhōu (壽州).
At this time, Shòuzhōu (壽州) was governed from Shòuchūn (壽春).
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) sent his generals from Huòqiū (霍丘) to advance and press upon it.
2 Rùnzhōu's Tuánliànshǐ, Ān Rénshì, was brave and decisive, and won the hearts of his soldiers.
Therefore, Huáinán general Wáng Màozhāng attacked him,
but failed to overcome him for over a year.
Wáng Màozhāng's attack on Rùnzhōu
was first mentioned in the previous volume in the 8th month of Tiānfù 3rd year.
"I will not forget your achievements.
Ān Rénshì joined Yáng Xíngmì,
defeated Zhào Huáng and Sūn Rú,
and pacified Xuān and Rùn;
all were meritorious.
You should be appointed as Deputy Commander of the Expeditionary Army,
but you will not command troops."
Rénshì refused to comply.
Màozhāng dug a tunnel into the city,
and thus conquered it.
Rénshì led his whole family up a tower,
and the crowd dared not approach.
Ān Rénshì was known as the best archer among the Huáinán generals,
and the crowd feared him,
so they dared not approach.
Only Lǐ Déchéng was different.
At this point, Rénshì summoned Déchéng to ascend the tower,
and said to him:
"You are courteous,
I now consider this your merit."
He also presented his favorite concubine to him.
Déchéng led them down,
and then had Rénshì and his son executed in Guǎnglíng market.
Tián Yún, Zhū Yánshòu, and Ān Rénshì
were the most prominent among the Huáinán generals.
The alliance of these three rebels
was not enough to trouble Yáng Xíngmì.
Within a year,
they were successively captured and annihilated.
Xíngmì was indeed a formidable talent.
3 The forces of Liǎngzhè besieged Chén Xún in Mùzhōu.
Chén Xún's rebellion against Qián Liú was first mentioned in the previous volume in Tiānfù 3rd year.
During the night, the army was startled,
and many soldiers climbed over the ramparts and fled.
His attendants and the deputy general Hán Qiú rushed to report it,
but Yǎ calmly lay still and did not respond.
After a short while, things settled down on their own,
and all the fugitives returned.
History states that in the art of leading troops,
only stillness is sufficient to control movement.
Being defeated by Yǎ,
Yì and Qiú were captured and brought back.
4 On the day Gēngwǔ,
Zhū Quánzhōng ordered Lǐ Zhèn to take charge of Qīngzhōu affairs,
replacing Wáng Shīfàn.
Zhū Quánzhōng alleviated his worries about the west,
and then ordered Lǐ Zhèn to replace Wáng Shīfàn.
5 Quánzhōng besieged Shòuzhōu,
but the people of the city remained behind their walls and did not sally forth.
Quánzhōng then withdrew from Huòqiū.
Zhū Quánzhōng sent his generals to press the city of Shòuzhōu,
while he remained encamped at Huòqiū as a rear force.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
he arrived at Dàliáng.
Huòqiū to Dàliáng is over nine hundred *lǐ*.
6 When Lǐ Zhèn arrived in Qīngzhōu,
Wáng Shīfàn moved his whole family west.
Upon reaching Púyáng,
he wore plain clothes and rode a donkey forward.
Upon reaching Púyáng, he had already entered Zhū Quánzhōng's jurisdiction,
hence he wore a prisoner's garb and rode a donkey to request punishment.
Pú,
pronounced *bómù fān*.
Quánzhōng treated him as a guest.
He formally appointed Lǐ Zhèn as the Liúhòu of Qīngzhōu.
7 On the day Wùxū,
Zhū Quányù, who was Ānnán Jiédùshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was made Tàishī,
and retired from office.
Quányù
was Quánzhōng's elder brother,
stupid and incapable.
He had previously held the position of Ānnán,
but Quánzhōng personally requested his removal.
8 On this day was the *Shè* (Earth God) sacrifice.
Since ancient times,
the *Shè* sacrifice has been held on a *wù* day.
*Wù*
signifies earth.
After the beginning of spring, after five *wù* days, it is the *Shè* day.
Yǎ Wáng Zhēn
and Qióng Wáng Xiáng
set up a banquet at Jiǔqǔchí.
Jiǔqǔchí was in the Luòyuàn.
They were all strangled to death
and their bodies thrown into the pond.
9 Zhū Quánzhōng sent his general Cáo Yánzuò with troops to jointly defend Èzhōu with Dù Hóng.
On the day Gēngzǐ,
Huáinán general Liú Cún attacked and captured it.
In the 1st month of Tiānfù 2nd year,
the Huáinán army attacked Èzhōu,
and conquered it after more than two cycles.
All were executed.
In Guāngqǐ 2nd year of Xīzōng,
Dù Hóng occupied Èzhōu,
and it fell at this time.
10On the day Jǐyǒu,
Emperor Shèngmù Jǐngwén Xiào was buried at Hélíng.
Hélíng is on Àoláishān in Gōushì Xiàn, Hénán,
and in this year its name was changed to Tàipíngshān.
11In the 3rd month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
Wáng Shīfàn was appointed Héyáng Jiédùshǐ.
12On the day Wùyín,
Dúgū Sǔn, who was Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was made Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and appointed Jìnghǎi Jiédùshǐ;
this was merely to relieve Dúgū Sǔn of political duties.
The Jìnghǎi army was based in Jiāozhōu,
outside the Línghǎi region.
How could Sǔn possibly reach there!
On the day Jiǎshēn,
Péi Shū, who was Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was made Zuǒ Púyè,
and Cuī Yuǎn was made Yòu Púyè,
both being relieved of political duties.
Previously,
Liǔ Càn passed the imperial examination,
and within four years became Chancellor.
He was cunning and frivolous by nature.
At that time, the Emperor's close attendants were all trusted confidants of Zhū Quánzhōng,
and Càn went out of his way to serve them.
His colleagues Péi Shū, Cuī Yuǎn, and Dúgū Sǔn were all respected figures in the imperial court,
and they looked down on him.
Càn resented this.
Hér Wáng Fù Zhāng Tíngfàn—
Hér Wáng Fú was also a son of Zhāozōng.
—was favored by Quánzhōng,
and he memorialized to have Tíngfàn appointed Tàicháng Qīng.
Shū said:
"Tíngfàn is a meritorious minister.
He is fortunate to have a regional command."
This means, "He is fortunate to have a regional command where he can be placed."
The Tàicháng Qīng manages rites and music,
hence it is called "Music Minister."
This means that the positions for meritorious individuals should be commensurate with their status,
and not rely on the Music Minister position for honor.
Zhū Quánzhōng was then Grand Marshal of all circuits,
hence he is referred to as such.
Quánzhōng heard this,
and said to his aides:
"I always thought Péi Shísì's character and discernment were truly pure,
and that he would not join the frivolous faction."
Péi Shū
was the fourteenth son.
"His true nature is now revealed."
This means that he still adhered to pure discussion.
Therefore, all three were dismissed.
Yáng Shè, Lìbù Shìláng, was made Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Shè was
the grandson of Shōu.
Yáng Shōu is mentioned in Yìzōng's annals;
he became chancellor,
but was demoted and died for a crime.
When he heard he was to become chancellor,
he wept with his family,
saying to his son Níngshì:
"This is an misfortune for our family,
and will surely harm you."
13Liú Yǐn, Qīnghǎi Jiédùshǐ, was given the additional title Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
14On the day Rénchén,
Héyáng Dū Yāyá Gài Yù died.
He left a letter advising Lǐ Kèyòng to reduce building projects,
lighten taxes,
and seek out talented individuals.
History states that Gài Yù did not forget to show loyalty to Lǐ Kèyòng even in his last moments.
Gài,
pronounced *gǔ hè fān*,
is a surname.
Shěng,
pronounced *suǒ jǐng fān*.
15Summer,
4th month,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
a comet appeared in the northwest.
16Huáinán general Táo Yǎ assembled troops from Qú and Mù to attack Wùzhōu.
In Guānghuà 3rd year,
Tián Yún took Wùzhōu.
Afterwards, Yún was attacked by Yáng Xíngmì,
and Qián Liú took Wùzhōu,
sending Shěn Xià to guard it.
175th month,
the Ministry of Rites reported that
the Emperor should perform the Southern Suburb Sacrifice upon his ascension;
an imperial edict commanded it to be held on the day Jiǎwǔ of the 10th month.
This set the stage for Zhū Quánzhōng to kill Liǔ Càn and Jiǎng Xuánhuī.
On the 18th day, *yǐchǒu* (乙丑),
a comet stretched across the sky.
Comets are for the removal of the old and the establishment of the new,
a sign of a change of surname (dynasty).
Xuē Jūzhèng’s (薛居正) *Wǔdài Shǐ* (五代史) states: In the first month of that year, on the *jiǎchén* (甲辰) day,
a comet appeared in Běihé (北河),
passing through Wénchāng (文昌),
and was more than three *zhàng* (丈) long.
In the fifth month, on the *yǐchǒu* (乙丑) day,
it reappeared in Xuānyuán (軒轅) and Dàjiǎo (大角),
extending to Tiānshì Yuán (天市垣),
its light shining fiercely.
Liǔ Càn (柳璨), relying on Zhū Quánzhōng’s (朱全忠) power,
abused his authority to grant favors and inflict punishments.
At that time, there was a celestial anomaly,
and the prognosticators said:
"Both ruler and minister will suffer calamity;
it is fitting to execute people to avert it."
Càn then submitted a memorial to Quánzhōng, listing those he had long disliked, saying:
"These individuals gather followers and engage in wrongful discussions,
harboring resentment and private criticism.
They should be used to avert this calamity."
Lǐ Zhèn (李振) also spoke to Zhū Quánzhōng, saying:
"The court is in disarray
precisely because these superficial and frivolous officials disturb the order and discipline;
and if the Prince wishes to accomplish a great undertaking"
(meaning usurpation),
"it would be better to eliminate all of them."
Quánzhōng agreed.
On the *guǐyǒu* (癸酉) day,
Dúgū Sǔn (獨孤損) was demoted to Inspector (刺史) of Dìzhōu (棣州), [32) Péi Shū (裴樞) to Inspector of Dēngzhōu (登州),
and Cuī Yuǎn (崔遠) to Inspector of Láizhōu (萊州).
On the *yǐhài* (乙亥) day,
Lù Yǐ (陸扆), Minister of Personnel (吏部尚書), was demoted to Judicial Administrator (司戶) of Púzhōu (濮州),
and Wáng Pǔ (王溥), Minister of Works (工部尚書), to Judicial Administrator of Zīzhōu (淄州).
On the *gēngchén* (庚辰) day,
Zhào Chóng (趙崇), retired Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince (太子太保致仕), was demoted to Judicial Administrator of Cáozhōu (曹州),
and Wáng Zàn (王贊), Vice Minister of War (兵部侍郎), to Judicial Administrator of Wéizhōu (濰州).
All others, whether from noble families
or advanced through the imperial examinations,
who served in the Three Departments or the Censorate,
and maintained a reputation for integrity,
or whose fame was somewhat notable,
were all labeled as frivolous,
and demoted and exiled without a single day passing without such an event.
The gentry was completely emptied.
On the *xīnsì* (辛巳) day,
Péi Shū was again demoted to Judicial Administrator of Lóngzhōu (瀧州).
Liú Xù (劉昫) states: Lóngzhōu administered Lóngshuǐ (瀧水) County,
which was originally the land of Duānxī (端溪) County in the Han dynasty.
The Jin dynasty divided Duānxī to establish Lóngxiāng (龍鄉) County.
The Sui dynasty changed Lóngxiāng to Píngyuán (平原) County,
and then again to Lóngshuǐ.
When the Tang dynasty pacified Xiāo Xiǎn (蕭銑),
it established Lóngzhōu.
Lóng (瀧)
is pronounced *lǘ jiāng* (閭江) according to the fanqie method.
Cuī Yuǎn was demoted to Judicial Administrator of Báizhōu (白州).
On the 19th day, *jiǎshēn* (甲申),
Zhào Kuāngníng (趙匡凝), Jiedushi (節度使) of Zhōngyì (忠義), sent an envoy to establish good relations with Wáng Jiàn (王建).
Zhào Kuāngníng allied with Huáinán (淮南) in the east
and communicated with Bashǔ (巴蜀) in the west,
intending to establish neighborly relations to resist Zhū Quánzhōng,
which inadvertently provoked Zhū Quánzhōng's army.
Hǎo (好)
is pronounced *hū dào* (呼到) according to the fanqie method.
In the sixth month,
on the *wùzǐ* (戊子) day (the first day of the month),
an imperial decree ordered Péi Shū, Dúgū Sǔn, Cuī Yuǎn, Lù Yǐ, Wáng Pǔ, Zhào Chóng, Wáng Zàn, and others to commit suicide in their respective places of exile.
At that time, Quánzhōng gathered Péi Shū and others, along with more than thirty other demoted court officials, at Báimǎyì (白馬驛).
Báimǎyì was in Báimǎ (白馬) County, Huázhōu (滑州).
He threw their bodies into the river.
Originally,
Lǐ Zhèn had repeatedly attempted the imperial examinations
but never passed.
Therefore, he deeply resented the gentry,
and said to Quánzhōng:
"These fellows always call themselves 'clear stream' (清流).
It would be fitting to throw them into the Yellow River to make them a 'turbid stream' (濁流)!"
Quánzhōng laughed and agreed.
Whenever Zhèn traveled from Biàn (汴) to Luò (洛),
there would invariably be exiles from the court.
People at the time called him an "owl" (鴟梟).
He would dismissively gesture and command all court officials,
waving his chin to direct
and using his breath to order,
meaning he relied on Zhū Quánzhōng's power and unrestrained his arrogance.
Quánzhōng once sat with his staff and guests under a large willow tree.
Quánzhōng alone said:
"This willow would be suitable for making chariot hubs."
No one responded.
Several guests rose and replied:
"It would be suitable for making chariot hubs."
Quánzhōng became furious and shouted in a stern voice:
"You literati are good at flattering people and playing along with them!
All of you are of this sort!
Chariot hubs must be made of *jiáyú* (夾榆).
*Shuōwén* (說文) says: *Yú* (榆) is
white *fén* (枌).
What is called *jiáyú*
is today's *tiányú* (田榆),
which grows in field ridges.
Its bark resembles that of the locust tree (槐),
its wood grain is firm, dense, and red.
When sawn into implements,
it is strong and durable.
A chariot hub is where all the spokes meet,
so its wood should be firm and dense.
Lǚ Fǔ (呂俛) said: *Jīyú* (櫅榆) is suitable for making chariot hubs.
*Ěryǎ* (爾雅) states that
it is also a white jujube.
*Jī* (櫅)
is pronounced *xiāng jī* (相稽) according to the fanqie method."
He looked around and said:
"What are you waiting for?"
Dozens of attendants
seized and
beat to death all those
who had said,
"It would be suitable for making chariot hubs."
On the *jǐchǒu* (己丑) day, [124) Péi Zhì (裴贄), retired Minister of Works (司空致仕), was demoted to Judicial Administrator of Qīngzhōu (青州),
and soon after was ordered to commit suicide.
The remaining targets of Liǔ Càn’s anger
were still more than a dozen,
but Zhāng Wénwèi (張文蔚) strongly intervened to resolve the matter,
and so he stopped.
At that time, many literati avoided the chaos
and did not attend court.
On the *rénchén* (壬辰) day,
an imperial decree ordered that they be supervised and dispatched by their local prefectures and counties,
and that none should delay.
Lǐ Yángǔ (李延古), former Junior Officer of Merit (司勳員外郎),
and grandson of Déyù (德裕),
left office and resided at Píngquán (平泉) Manor.
Lǐ Déyù had Píngquán Manor,
located within the jurisdiction of Hénán Fǔ (河南府).
Déyù’s *Píngquán Jì* (平泉記) states: "My late father envisioned
and concentrated his gaze on Yīchuān (伊川).
From that, I developed the aspiration to retire to Hélùo (河洛).
At Lóngmén (龍門), I acquired the former residence of Mr. Qiáo (喬處士),
cleared the thorns,
and drove away foxes and badgers to establish it."
Kāng Pián (康駢) states: Píngquán Manor is thirty *lǐ* (里) from Luòchéng (洛城).
He was demoted to Administrator (主簿) of the Court of the Imperial Insignia (衞尉寺).
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the *guǐhài* (癸亥) day,
Liǔ Xùn (柳遜), retired Guest of the Crown Prince (太子賓客致仕), was demoted to Military Administrator (司馬) of Cáozhōu.
On the 21st day, *gēngwǔ* (庚午) night,
Lǐ Gōngquán (李公佺), a general of the Tiānxíong (天雄) army, conspired to rebel with the palace guard.
Luó Shàowēi (羅紹威) became aware of it.
Gōngquán burned the prefecture offices,
plundered,
and fled to Cāngzhōu (滄州).
Luó Shàowēi then executed Zhāng Běn (張本), a general of the palace guard.
Quán (佺)
is pronounced *qiě yuán* (且緣) according to the fanqie method.
Piāo (剽)
is pronounced *pǐ miào* (匹妙) according to the fanqie method.
At that time, Liú Shǒuwén (劉守文) occupied Cāngzhōu.
In the eighth month,
Wáng Jiàn dispatched Wáng Zōnghè (王宗賀) and others, former Jiedushi of Shānnán Xīdào (山南西道), to lead troops to attack Fény Hángxí (馮行襲), Jiedushi of Zhāoxìn (昭信), in Jīnzhōu (金州).
Fény Hángxí was allied with Zhū Quánzhōng.
23 Zhū Quánzhōng, believing that Zhào Kuāngníng was in communication with Yáng Xíngmì in the east,
and had intermarried with Wáng Jiàn in the west,
on the Yǐwèi day,
dispatched Yáng Shīhòu, the Jìedùshǐ of Wǔníng, to lead troops to attack him.
On the Jǐhài day,
Quánzhōng followed with a large army.
*Kǎo Yì* says: Both the *Liáng Tàizǔ Shílù* and Xuē Jūzhèng's *Wǔdài Shǐ* (Liáng Chronicles) state:
"In the seventh month, on the Gēngwǔ day,
Yáng Shīhòu was dispatched to lead the vanguard to attack Zhào Níng at Xiāngzhōu.
On the Xīnwèi day,
the Emperor marched south."
The *Táng Shílù* says:
"In the seventh month,
Quánzhōng reported that Kuāngníng was secretly communicating and befriending Xīchuān and Huáinán,
and had also sent his younger brother to exclusively govern Jīngnán.
He requested that his official titles and ranks be stripped,
and that his commander Yáng Shīhòu had already been sent to suppress him.
The next day,
Quánzhōng personally led his army forward."
The *Biān Yílù* says:
"In the eighth month, on the Rénchén day,
Wǔníng's Yáng Shīhòu was first drawn out;
he arrived on that day,
and then the attack on Xiāngzhōu commander Zhào Kuāngníng was discussed.
On the Yǐwèi day,
a large number of carts and soldiers were dispatched,
entrusting Yáng Shīhòu with the overall military command.
On the Jǐhài day,
the Emperor led his personal retinue of infantry and cavalry to follow the main army,
spending the night at Wèishì."
We follow this account now.
*Xuē Shǐ* says:
"Tàizǔ intended to usurp the throne,
and as Kuāngníng and his brothers each held a Fānzhèn,
he sent an envoy to first convey his intentions.
Níng, weeping before the envoy,
replied, 'Having received profound grace from the state,
how dare I harbor other ambitions with the changing times!'
When the envoy returned to report,
Tàizǔ was greatly enraged.
In the autumn of the seventh month of Tiānyòu ěrnián (905 CE),
Yáng Shīhòu was dispatched to lead troops to attack him.
On the Xīnwèi day,
Quánzhōng marched south,
presenting a memorial detailing Kuāngníng's crimes,
and requesting the stripping of his official titles and ranks."
We note that Quánzhōng had coerced Emperor Zhāozōng to relocate to Luòyáng.
Kuāngníng, along with Xíngmì and others, had issued a manifesto to various regions to jointly attack him.
How could Quánzhōng possibly consult him about usurping the throne?
We do not adopt this account.
24 Lú Yuē, the Cìshǐ of Chǔzhōu, sent his younger brother Jí to capture Wēnzhōu,
and Zhāng Huì fled to Fúzhōu.
In Tiānfù sānnián (903 CE),
Zhāng Huì had occupied Wēnzhōu;
he was defeated now.
Wáng Shěnzhī was then occupying Fúzhōu.
From Wēnzhōu, going south through Píngyáng Xiàn and crossing the Hǎipǔ leads directly to the Fúzhōu border.
*Jiǔyù Zhì* says,
Wēnzhōu is three hundred and twenty *lǐ* southeast to the Fúzhōu border,
and from the border to Fúzhōu is five hundred and twenty *lǐ*.
25 Qián Liú dispatched Fāng Yǒngzhēn to relieve Wùzhōu.
The Huáinán army had been attacking Wùzhōu since the first month.
26 Originally,
Sīkōng Tú, a Yuánwàiláng of the Lǐbù and Zhìzhìgào, abandoned his official post and resided in Wángguāngǔ in Yúxiāng,
Wángguāngǔ being in the Zhōngtiáo Shān range of Yúxiāng Xiàn.
He would not rise (to office).
Liǔ Càn summoned him with an imperial edict;
Tú, fearful,
went to Luòyáng for an audience,
feigning senility and wildness,
dropping his tablet and losing his composure.
Càn then issued another edict,
which briefly stated:
"Having cultivated a high status to defy the era,
akin to moving mountains to seek fame."
It also said:
"Neither Bó Yí nor Liǔxià Huì,
difficult to reside in a just court.
May be sent back to his mountain."
Tú was a native of Línhuái.
27 Yáng Shīhòu captured seven prefectures: Táng, Dèng, Fù, Yǐng, Suí, Jūn, and Fáng.
All seven prefectures belonged to the Zhōngyì Army's jurisdiction.
In the ninth month,
on the Xīnyǒu day,
Shīhòu was ordered to construct a pontoon bridge at Yīngǔkǒu;
Xiāngzhōu's Gǔchéng Xiàn has Yīnchéng Zhèn.
According to old histories,
Yīngǔkǒu is sixty *lǐ* west of Xiāngzhōu.
On the Guǐhài
day, he led his troops across the Hàn River.
The pontoon bridge was completed, and they crossed.
On the Jiǎzǐ
day, Zhào Kuāngníng led twenty thousand troops and arrayed them on the banks of the Hàn River.
Shīhòu engaged them in battle,
thoroughly defeating them,
and then advanced directly to the city walls.
That evening,
Kuāngníng set fire to the administrative city,
and led his clan and subordinate officers along the Hàn River to Guǎnglíng.
In Xīzōng's Zhōnghé sìnián (884 CE),
Zhào Déyīn occupied Xiāngzhōu,
which was passed down to his son Kuāngníng,
and was lost now.
Yáng Xíngmì was then occupying Guǎnglíng;
Kuāngníng traveled along the Hàn River into the Yangtze River,
flowing eastward to take refuge there.
The character Shuài
is read as Shuài;
likewise below.
On the Yǐchǒu
day, Shīhòu entered Xiāngyáng;
on the Bǐngyín day,
Quánzhōng arrived shortly after.
When Kuāngníng reached Guǎnglíng,
Yáng Xíngmì jokingly said to him:
"When you were in your post,
you annually sent gold and silk to Quánzhōng;
now that you are defeated,
you come to me?"
Kuāngníng replied:
"Princes serve the Son of Heaven;
to annually submit tribute and taxes is their duty,
not to submit to a rebel!
My returning to you today
is precisely because I did not follow the rebel."
Xíngmì treated him generously.
28 On the Bǐngyín day,
the Emperor's younger brother Tí was enfeoffed as Yǐng Wáng,
and Yòu as Cài Wáng.
29 On the Dīngmǎo day,
Zhào Kuāngmíng, the Jìedùshǐ of Jīngnán, led twenty thousand troops,
