Many court officials secretly harbored resentment and anger,
but Lǐbù Shàngshū (禮部尚書) Sū Xún (蘇循) alone openly declared:
“The achievements of Liáng Wáng (梁王) are outstanding and great,
and the mandate of heaven has shifted.
The court should quickly yield and abdicate.”
No court official dared to disobey.
On Xīnsì (辛巳) day,
Quánzhōng (全忠) was appointed Xiàngguó (相國),
overseeing all state affairs.

Twenty-one circuits, including Xuānwǔ (宣武), Xuānyì (宣義), Tiānpíng (天平), Hùguó (護國), Tiānxíong (天雄), Wǔshùn (武順), Yòuguó (佑國), Héyáng (河陽), Yìwǔ (義武), Zhāoyì (昭義), Bǎoyì (保義), Róngzhāo (戎昭), Wǔdìng (武定), Tàiníng (泰寧), Pínglú (平盧), Zhōngwǔ (忠武), Kuāngguó (匡國), Zhènguó (鎮國), Wǔníng (武寧), Zhōngyì (忠義), and Jīngnán (荊南), were designated as Wèiguó (魏國).
Xuānwǔ (宣武) controlled Biàn (汴), Sòng (宋), Bó (亳), Dān (單).
Xuānyì (宣義) controlled Rǔ (汝), Zhèng (鄭), Huá (滑).
Tiānpíng (天平) controlled Yùn (鄆), Cáo (曹), Pú (濮), Jì (濟).
Hùguó (護國) controlled Hézhōng (河中), Jìn (晉), Jiàng (絳), Cí (慈), Xí (隰).
Tiānxíong (天雄) controlled Wèi (魏), Bó (博), Bèi (貝), Wèi (衞), Chán (澶), Xiāng (相).
Wǔshùn (武順) controlled Zhèn (鎮), Jì (冀), Shēn (深), Zhào (趙).
Yòuguó (佑國) controlled Jīngzhào (京兆), Shāng (商), Huá (華).
Héyáng (河陽) controlled Mèng (孟), Huái (懷).
Yìwǔ (義武) controlled Dìng (定), Qí (祁), Yì (易).
Zhāoyì Jūn (昭義軍) controlled Lù (潞), Zé (澤).
Bǎoyì (保義) controlled Xíng (邢), Míng (洺), Cí (磁).
Róngzhāo (戎昭) controlled Jīn (金), Jūn (均), Fáng (房).
Wǔdìng (武定) controlled Yáng (洋).
Tàiníng (泰寧) controlled Yǎn (兗), Yí (沂), Mì (密).
Pínglú (平盧) controlled Qīng (青), Zī (淄), Qí (齊), Dì (棣), Dēng (登), Lái (萊).
Zhōngwǔ (忠武) controlled Chén (陳), Xǔ (許).
Kuāngguó (匡國) controlled Tóng (同).
Zhènguó (鎮國) controlled Shǎn (陝), Guó (虢).
Wǔníng (武寧) controlled Xú (徐), Sù (宿).
Zhōngyì (忠義) controlled Xiāng (襄), Dèng (鄧), Suí (隨), Yǐng (郢), Táng (唐), Fù (復), Ān (安).
Jīngnán (荊南) controlled Jīng (荊), Guī (歸), Xiá (峽).
He was still to be granted the nine bestowments.
Quánzhōng (全忠) was enraged by the delay
and declined to accept.
In the twelfth month,
on Wùzǐ (戊子) day,
the Shūmìshǐ (樞密使) Jiǎng Xuánhuī (蔣玄暉) was ordered to carry an imperial handwritten edict to Quánzhōng (全忠) to convey the intention.
On Guǐsì (癸巳) day,
Xuánhuī (玄暉) returned from Dàliáng (大梁),
stating that Quánzhōng (全忠)’s anger had not subsided.
On Jiǎwǔ (甲午) day,
Liǔ Càn (柳璨) submitted a memorial, saying:
“The people’s hopes lie with Liáng Wáng (梁王);
it is time for Your Majesty to release this heavy burden.”
On the same day, Càn (璨) was dispatched to Dàliáng (大梁) to express the intention of abdication,
but Quánzhōng (全忠) refused.
Earlier,
Càn (璨) had harmed too many court officials; this was known as the Bái Mǎ Zhī Huò (白馬之禍).
Càn (璨), Jiǎng Xuánhuī (蔣玄暉), and Zhāng Tíngfàn (張廷範) frequently held banquets together,
forming a deep bond,
and plotted the abdication on behalf of Quánzhōng (全忠).
Hé Tàihòu (何太后) tearfully sent palace maids Ā Qián (阿虔) and Ā Qiū (阿秋) to convey her message to Xuánhuī (玄暉),
asking that after the abdication,
her mother and son be spared.
Wáng Yīn (王殷) and Zhào Yīnhéng (趙殷衡) slandered Xuánhuī (玄暉),
claiming
that “he held a night banquet with Liǔ Càn (柳璨) and Zhāng Tíngfàn (張廷範) at Jīshàn Táng (積善堂),
and swore an oath with the Empress Dowager by burning incense,
vowing to restore the Táng (唐) dynasty.”
Hé Tàihòu (何太后) was residing in Jīshàn Gōng (積善宮) at that time.
On Yǐwèi (乙未) day,
Xuánhuī (玄暉) and the Fēngdé Kùshǐ (豐德庫使) Yīng Xù (應頊) and Yùchúshǐ (御廚使) Zhū Jiànwǔ (朱建武) were arrested and imprisoned in Hénán (河南) prison;
Hénán Fǔ (河南府) prison.
Zhào Yīnhéng (趙殷衡) provisionally acted as the judge of Xuānhuī Yuàn (宣徽院) affairs.
Quánzhōng (全忠) submitted three memorials declining the titles of Wèi Wáng (魏王) and the nine bestowments;
On Dīngyǒu (丁酉) day,
an edict permitted him to do so.
Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) was furious,
intending to kill Jiǎng Xuánhuī (蔣玄暉) and others before proceeding with the matters of Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉).
The memorials declining the offers were written by Jìng Xiáng (敬翔)’s instruction;
the edict permitting the decline was issued because Wáng Yīn (王殷) and others understood Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠)’s unspoken intentions.
However, Quánzhōng (全忠) had already renovated the Dàliáng (大梁) administrative residence to resemble a palace.
Historians recorded his true intentions to show the world and future generations.
Jiǎng Xuánhuī (蔣玄暉) was beheaded,
and Yīng Xù (應頊) and Zhū Jiànwǔ (朱建武) were beaten to death.
On Gēngzǐ (庚子) day,
the offices of Shūmìshǐ (樞密使) and Xuānhuī Nányuànshǐ (宣徽南院使) were abolished,
leaving only one Xuānhuī Shǐ (宣徽使),
with Wáng Yīn (王殷) appointed to it,
and Zhào Yīnhéng (趙殷衡) as deputy.
On Xīnchǒu (辛丑) day,
an imperial edict abolished the practice of palace women conveying imperial decrees.
In Tiānfù (天復) third year, eunuchs were executed,
and inner court ladies were used to convey imperial decrees.
The “Kǎoyì” (考異) is found earlier.
The “Kāiyuán Lǐshū” (開元禮疏) states: When Jìn Kāngxiàn Chǔ Hòu (晉康獻褚后) attended court but did not sit,
palace women conveyed her commands to the officials.
The Zhōu (周) and Suí (隋) dynasties followed this practice, and the state continued it without change.
The “Táng Liùdiǎn” (唐六典) states: The Pángpín Sīzàn (宮嬪司贊) were in charge of assisting in court assemblies,
and in all court sessions,
they led guests to stand in the palace courtyard.
Up to Tiānyòu (天祐) third year, an imperial edict stated:
“Palace women’s duties
are originally for internal affairs.
Henceforth, on days when the Yányīng (延英) court sits,
only junior eunuchs (小黃門) are to attend and lead,
and palace women are not permitted to go in and out.”
This is precisely the imperial edict of this year.
Hénán (河南) was ordered to display the bodies at the city gate
and gather a crowd to burn them.
Hénán (河南) refers to Hénán Fǔ (河南府).
Jiē (揭) is pronounced “qí yē,”
meaning to raise.
After Xuánhuī (玄暉) died,
Wáng Yīn (王殷) and Zhào Yīnhéng (趙殷衡) again falsely accused Xuánhuī (玄暉) of having a private affair with Hé Tàihòu (何太后),
with Ā Qiū (阿秋) and Ā Qián (阿虔) acting as intermediaries.
On Jǐyǒu (己酉) day,
Quánzhōng (全忠) secretly ordered Yīn (殷) and Yīnhéng (殷衡) to murder the Empress Dowager at Jīshàn Gōng (積善宮),
and issued an edict to posthumously demote the Empress Dowager to a commoner.
A son deposing his mother is a recurrence of the affair of Jìn Jùnyáng (晉峻陽).
On Gēngxū (庚戌) day,
due to the mourning of the Empress Dowager,
court was suspended for three days.
Having demoted the mother to a commoner,
yet suspending court for three days.
Demoting her to a commoner extinguished natural affection,
and suspending court for three days was neither the proper mourning ritual for a mother
nor sufficient to alleviate the wound to natural affection.
The officials and subjects of Táng (唐) were no longer true officials and subjects of Táng (唐).
Cháo (朝) is pronounced “zhí yáo.”
On Xīnhài (辛亥) day,
an edict stated that due to internal chaos in the palace,
the ritual of paying respects at the suburban altars and ancestral temples on the first Xīn (辛) day of the first month of the coming year was abolished.
Táng (唐) no longer performed the suburban sacrifice.
On Guǐchǒu (癸丑) day,
Shǒusīkōng (守司空) concurrently Ménxià Shìláng (門下侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事) Liǔ Càn (柳璨) was demoted to the Prefect of Dēngzhōu (登州).
Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿) Zhāng Tíngfàn (張廷範) was demoted to Sīhù (司戶) of Láizhōu (萊州).
On Jiǎyín (甲寅) day,
Càn (璨) was beheaded outside the Shàngdōng Mén (上東門),
and Tíngfàn (廷範) was torn apart by chariots in the marketplace.
From the abolition of the suburban sacrifices onward,
all these were Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠)’s long-held intentions.
“The traitor Liǔ Càn (柳璨),
his death is fitting!”
46 Xīchuān general Wáng Zōnglǎng could not hold Jīnzhōu,
so he burned its cities and towns
and fled to Chéngdū.
Wáng Zōnglǎng had only defended Jīnzhōu for three months.
A memorial was submitted requesting,
"Jīnzhōu is desolate and ruined;
we beg to move the administration to Jūnzhōu,"
which was granted.
Xíng Xí was further made acting commander of Wǔ'ān Jūn.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù says it was changed to Wǔníng Jūn,
while the Xīnbǎo says it was changed to Wǔdìng Jūn.
However, Wǔníng is the army name for Xúzhōu,
and Wǔdìng is the army name for Yángzhōu;
they should not have the same name.
The notes in Xùbǎoyùnlù say:
"In the autumn of Tiānfù 7,
the commander of the Biàn army, known as Féng Qīngmiàn,
changed his surname to Zhū,
was granted Zhū Quánzhōng's seal and ribbon,
and became the Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu (
should be
Yángzhōu's Cìshǐ, Yáng Shǒuzuǒ, had surrendered to Fèngxiáng in Jǐngfú 1,
and was later eliminated by Zhū Quánzhōng.
In the autumn of this year,
the second commander of Shǔ, Wáng Zōngwǎn, recaptured Jīnzhōu.
Dūyāyá Quán Guì led his troops to surrender,
was granted the surname Wáng,
given the name Zōnglǎng,
and appointed Cìshǐ of Jīnzhōu."
The Biānyílù further states, in Tiānyòu 3, second month:
"Xíng Xí had already established his banner in Jūnzhōu,
and therefore appointed Hán Gōng to oversee affairs in Jīnzhōu,
and requested the imperial court to abolish the Fángyùshǐ position,
and not establish the Róngzhāo Jūn."
Comparing these various books,
it seems that the current position is that Xíng Xí simultaneously commanded Yángzhōu,
and it was not a change of Róngzhāo to Wǔdìng Jūn.
Both the Shílù and Xīnbǎo are mistaken,
and the Xùbǎoyùnlù for Tiānfù 7 is also mistaken.
According to the Kǎoyì,
then
"Wǔ'ān Jūn"
should be
"Wǔdìng Jūn,"
and this is also confirmed by consulting the Old and New Histories.
47 Chén Xún could not defend Mùzhōu,
and fled to Guǎnglíng,
being pressed by the troops of Liǎngzhè.
In Zhōnghé 4 of Xīzōng,
Chén Shèng occupied Mùzhōu,
and it was lost under Xún.
48 When Yáng Wò departed Xuānzhōu,
he wanted to take his tents and personal guards with him,
but the Guānchásǐ, Wáng Màozhāng, refused.
Wò was enraged.
After he inherited the position,
he dispatched Mǎbù Dūzhīhuīshǐ Lǐ Jiǎn and others to lead troops to attack him.
How long had Yáng Wò held his position
before he incurred enmity with a provincial general?
Such was his narrow-mindedness;
he was certainly unfit to rule a state and its people.
49 Húnán troops raided Huáinán,
and Huáinán Yánèi Zhīhuīshǐ Yáng Biāo repelled them.
1 Spring,
first month,
Rénxū.
Língwǔ Jiédùshǐ Hán Xùn memorialized that more than 7,000 Tǔfān cavalry were encamped in Zōnggāo Gǔ,
preparing to attack Wòmò and take Liángzhōu.
Zhào Xún's Jùmǐtújīng states: From Língwǔ, passing through the Hèlán Shān road,
west to Liángzhōu is nine hundred lǐ.
2 Lǐ Jiǎn's army suddenly arrived at Xuānzhōu.
Wáng Màozhāng assessed that he could not defend it,
and led his troops to flee to Liǎngzhè.
His personal guard, Shàngcài Diāo Yànnéng, declined, citing his aged mother,
and did not go with them.
He ascended the city wall and addressed the populace, saying:
"The King's Mansion ordered me to pacify you all.
Yáng Wò and his son both govern Guǎnglíng with a princely title,
hence the Huáinán military government is called the King's Mansion."
The populace was thus calmed.
Táo Yǎ, fearing that Màozhāng would cut off his retreat,
led his troops back to Xīzhōu,
and Qián Liú recaptured Mùzhōu.
From this point, Mùzhōu belonged to the Qián clan,
and the Yáng clan could not contend for it.
Xī,
pronounced 'shū shè fān'.
Changed name to Jǐngrén.
3 Yǐchǒu.
Qu Chéngyù, Jiànghǎi Jiédùshǐ, was additionally appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Qu Chéngyù took control of Ānnán amidst the chaos.
4 Initially,
Tián Chéngsì, while garrisoning Wèibó,
selected and recruited five thousand brave and skilled soldiers from six prefectures to form the Yájūn.
This event is recorded in Volume 222, Dàizōng Guǎngdé 1.
They served as his trusted inner circle;
from then on, fathers and sons succeeded each other,
relatives and factions became entrenched,
and with the passage of years, they grew more arrogant and unruly.
If anything was slightly unsatisfactory,
they would exterminate the old commander's family and replace him.
Since Shǐ Xiànchéng, all were established by their hand.
Mùzōng Chángqìng 2 established Shǐ Xiànchéng,
Wénzōng Dàhé 3 established Hé Jìntāo,
Yìzōng Xiántōng 11 established Hán Yǔnzhōng,
Xīzōng Zhōnghé 3 established Yuè Yànzhēn,
Wéndé 1 established Zhào Wénwò,
and soon after, Luó Hóngxìn was established.
Their power could not be restrained.
When Zhū Quánzhōng besieged Fèngxiáng,
(The siege of Fèngxiáng is mentioned in Zāozōng Tiānfù 1, 2, and 3.)
he wanted to borrow their troops to execute them.
Quánzhōng, with matters being urgent,
did not have time to grant his request,
but secretly agreed.
When Lǐ Gōngquán revolted,
(Lǐ Gōngquán's revolt in the seventh month of last year is mentioned above.)
he again sent his Yájiàng Zāng Yánfàn to urge Quánzhōng.
Quánzhōng then mobilized one hundred thousand troops from various Hénán garrisons,
and dispatched his general Lǐ Sī'ān to lead them,
to rendezvous with Wèi and Zhèn troops and encamp at Shēnzhōu Yuèchéng;
(Wèi and Zhèn refer to the Wèibó and Zhènjì garrisons.)
"Yuèchéng"
is probably
"Yuèshòu."
to suppress them for harboring Lǐ Gōngquán.
It happened that Quánzhōng's daughter, who was married to Shàowēi's son Tíngguī, died.
Quánzhōng sent his Kèjiàng Mǎ Sìxūn to conceal armored soldiers in *tuó* bags,
(A bottomed bag is called *náng*, a bottomless one is called *tuó*.)
(Tuó, pronounced 'tà gè fān'.)
and Lǐ Zhí Bīng
(Lǐ Zhí Bīng refers to brave and skilled soldiers specially selected to serve as constant personal guards, not rotated.)
on carrying poles,
(Dàn, pronounced 'dū làn fān'.)
falsely claiming they were for the funeral.
Quánzhōng himself followed with a large army,
claiming to be going to the mobile camp.
The Yájūn were not suspicious at all.
Gēngwǔ.
Shàowēi secretly sent men into the arsenal to cut the bowstrings and armor ties.
That night,
Shàowēi led his several hundred retainers and guests,
and together with Sìxūn attacked the Yájūn.
The Yájūn wanted to fight, but their bows and armor were all unusable,
so they were slaughtered throughout the camp.
All eight thousand families,
including infants and children, were wiped out.
At dawn,
Quánzhōng led his troops into the city.
5 Xīnwèi.
Páng Jùzhāo, acting Liúhòu of Níngyuǎn, and Yè Guǎnglüè, Liúhòu of Língnán Xīdào, were both appointed Jiédùshǐ.
Both men were able to hold their respective territories,
and were therefore commissioned.
6 Gēngchén.
Qián Liú went to Mùzhōu.
The Jiǔyùzhì states that Hángzhōu is three hundred and fifteen lǐ southwest of Mùzhōu.
7 Xīchuān general Wáng Zōngruǎn attacked Guīzhōu,
and captured its general Hán Cóngshí.
Guīzhōu belonged to Jīngnán.
8 Chén Zhāng, hearing that Táo Yǎ had returned to Xī,
retreated from Wùzhōu to defend Qúzhōu.
The Liǎngzhè generals Fāng Yǒngzhēn and others took Wùzhōu,
and advanced to attack Qúzhōu.
In the ninth month of last year,
Huáinán troops took Wùzhōu.
Chén Zhāng had originally allied Qúzhōu with Huáinán,
and now retreated from Wùzhōu to defend it.
9 Yáng Wò dispatched Xiānfēng Zhīhuīshǐ Chén Zhīxīn to attack Húnán.
Third month,
Yǐchǒu.
Zhīxīn captured Yuèzhōu,
expelling Cìshǐ Xǔ Déxūn.
In Tiānfù 3 of Zāozōng,
Húnán general Xǔ Déxūn took Yuèzhōu,
and now abandoned it.
This laid the groundwork for Chén Zhīxīn's forces to be annihilated.
10 Wùyín.
Zhū Quánzhōng was appointed Sānsī Dūzhìzhìshǐ of Yántiě, Dùzhī, and Hùbù.
The term Sānsī originated here.
Quánzhōng declined the appointment.
11 Summer,
fourth month,
Guǐwèi, first day of the month.
There was a solar eclipse.
12 After Luó Shàowēi had executed the Yájūn,
all the armies in Wèi were terrified.
Although Shàowēi repeatedly appeased them,
their suspicion and resentment grew even stronger.
Zhū Quánzhōng camped east of Wèizhōu city for several tens of days,
intending to tour the northern campaign.
At this time, Shǐ Rénfù, a Yájiàng of Tiānxíong, rebelled,
gathering tens of thousands of people and occupying Gāotáng.
Gāotáng
was an ancient county during the Hàn dynasty,
and during the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Bózhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states
it was 110 lǐ northeast of the prefecture.
Many counties within Tiānxíong's jurisdiction responded to him.
Quánzhōng moved his army into the city,
and sent envoys to recall the campaigning troops to attack Gāotáng.
When they reached Lìtíng,
Lìtíng County belonged to Bèizhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states
it was 90 lǐ east of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: The territory of Lìtíng County,
from the Later Wèi to the Gāo Qí,
belonged to Shū County.
In the 16th year of Kāihuáng of the Suí dynasty, Lìtíng County was established south of the Yǒngjì Canal,
remotely named after the Hàn dynasty's Lìchéng County.
According to the Hàn Dìlǐ Zhì,
Lìchéng belonged to Xìndū Jùn
and was within the borders of Tiáo County.
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Lìtíng.
In the 1st year of Wànsuì Dēngfēng of the Táng dynasty, it was moved and established by the Pánhé River,
70 lǐ west of ancient Lìchéng.
They aligned with Rénfù.
Lǐ Zhōuyí, Left Sīmǎ of the Marshal's Residence, and Fú Dàozhāo, Right Sīmǎ, attacked them.
Nearly half were killed.
They advanced to attack Gāotáng
and conquered it.
All soldiers and civilians in the city, young and old, were killed.
Shǐ Rénfù was captured
and sawn to death.
Previously,
Rénfù had sought aid from Hédōng and Cāngzhōu.
Lǐ Kèyòng sent his general Lǐ Sìzhāo with 3,000 cavalry to attack Xíngzhōu to relieve him.
At that time, Xíngzhōu had only 200 soldiers.
Niú Cúnjié, the Tuánliànshǐ, defended it.
Sìzhāo attacked for seven days but could not conquer it.
Quánzhōng sent Zhāng Jūn, the Right Zhǎngzhí Dūjiāng, with several thousand cavalry to assist Cúnjié in defending the city.
Jūn ambushed Sìzhāo at Mǎlǐng,
attacked him,
and defeated him.
Sìzhāo fled.
Liú Shǒuwén, the Jìedùshǐ of Yìchāng, sent 10,000 soldiers to attack Bèizhōu,
and then attacked Jìzhōu,
capturing Tiáo County,
and advancing to attack Fùchéng.
Tiáo and Fùchéng
were both ancient counties of the Hàn dynasty,
and during the Táng dynasty, they belonged to Jìzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states:
Tiáo County was 150 lǐ northeast of the prefecture;
Fùchéng was 160 lǐ east of the prefecture.
Tiáo
is pronounced tiáo.
Zōngchéng County belonged to Wèizhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states
it was 170 lǐ northwest of the prefecture.
The Cāngzhōu troops departed.
The Cāngzhōu troops were those sent by Liú Shǒuwén.
On the day of Bǐngwǔ,
Zhòngbà abandoned the city and fled.
Hú Guī, a Biàn general, pursued and beheaded him.
13 Zhōng Chuán, the Jìedùshǐ of Zhènnán, appointed his adopted son Yáng Yánguī as the Cǐshǐ of Jiāngzhōu.
When Chuán died,
the army established his son Kuāngshí as Liúhòu.
Yánguī resented not being established
and sent envoys to surrender to Huáinán.
The Kǎoyì states: According to the Shílù:
"Initially,
Zhōng Chuán adopted a monk from Shànglán Yuàn as his son,
named Yánguī,
and appointed him Cǐshǐ of Jiāngzhōu.
When Chuán died,
he then summoned the Huái army to capture his city."
This follows the Shíguó Jìnián and Wú Shǐ.
14 In the fifth month,
on the day of Dīngsì,
Zhū Quánzhōng went to Míngzhōu,
then toured the northern border,
inspecting military preparations.
He returned
and entered Wèi.
15 On the day of Bǐngzǐ,
the Róngzhāo Army was abolished,
and Jūn and Fáng were merged and subordinated to the Zhōngyì Army;
both were subordinate to Shānnán Dōngdào.
Féng Xíngxí was transferred from Jūnzhōu to Tóngzhōu.
16 Yáng Wò appointed Qín Péi, the Cǐshǐ of Shēngzhōu, as the Dūzhāotǎoshǐ of the Southwest Campaign,
leading troops to attack Zhōng Kuāngshí in Jiāngxī.
This was initiated by Zhōng Yánguī.
17 In the sixth month,
on the day of Jiǎshēn,
the Zhōngyì Army was again designated Shānnán Dōngdào.
In the first year of Wéndé of Xīzōng, Shānnán Dōngdào was designated the Zhōngyì Army.
18 Zhū Quánzhōng considered Cháng'ān to be adjacent to Bīn and Qí,
and frequently subjected to warfare.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Cháng'ān was 275 lǐ northwest to Bīnzhōu and
309 lǐ west to Fèngxiáng.
Shù
is read suǒjiǎo fān.
Hán Jiàn was originally allied with Lǐ Màozhēn.
Zhū Quánzhōng feared he would revert to that,
hence he moved him.
19 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Zhū Quánzhōng captured Xiāngzhōu.
At this time, the rebellious Wèi troops were scattered, occupying Bèi, Bó, Chán, Xiāng, and Wèizhōu.
Quánzhōng dispatched his generals to attack and suppress them.
By this time, he had completely pacified them,
and led his army back south.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù places this in the sixth month.
This now follows the Biānyí Lù and Táng Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù.
The Biānyí Lù states:
"On the day of Guǐwèi in the seventh month,
the emperor raised troops and departed from the Wèi capital."
According to the Chánglì,
the first day of this month was Rénzǐ,
so there was no Guǐwèi.
The Biānyí Lù is mistaken.
Quánzhōng remained in Wèi for half a year,
from entering Wèi in the first month until this time, half a year.
He killed nearly 700,000 cattle, sheep, and pigs.
Provisions were commensurate.
The bribes and gifts amounted to nearly a million more.
By the time he left,
the accumulated stores were completely empty.
Although Shàowēi was rid of his coercion,
the Wèi army became weak thereafter.
Shàowēi regretted it,
saying to others:
"Even if you combine the iron of six prefectures and forty-three counties,
you cannot make this file (cuò)! "
Wèizhōu administered fourteen counties: Guìxiāng, Yuánchéng, Wèi, Guǎntáo, Guānshì, Shēn, Cháochéng, Chānglè, Línhé, Huánshuǐ, Chéng'ān, Nèihuáng, Zōngchéng, and Yǒngjì.
Bózhōu administered six counties: Liáochéng, Bópíng, Wǔshuǐ, Qīngpíng, Tángyì, and Gāotáng.
Xiāngzhōu administered six counties: Ānyáng, Yè, Tāngyīn, Límlǜ, Yáochéng, and Línzhāng.
Wèizhōu administered five counties: Jí, Wèi, Gòngchéng, Xīnxiāng, and Líyáng.
Bèizhōu administered eight counties: Qīnghé, Qīngyáng, Wǔchéng, Jīngchéng, Línqīng, Zhāngnán, Lìtíng, and Xiàjīn.
Chánzhōu administered four counties: Dùnqiū, Qīngfēng, Guānchéng, and Línhuáng.
Cuò
means a file (lǜ),
made by casting;
it also explains cuò as a mistake.
Luó, referring to the mistake of killing the Yá soldiers, used the metaphor of casting a file.
On the day of Rénshēn,
Quánzhōng arrived at Dàliáng.
The Kǎoyì states: The Biānyí Lù says Rénchén,
which is also mistaken.
20 Qín Péi reached Hóngzhōu
and camped at Liáozhōu.
The generals requested to block the water and establish a stockade,
but Péi did not comply.
Zhōng Kuāngshí indeed sent his general Liú Chǔ to occupy it.
The generals blamed Péi,
but Péi said:
"Kuāngshí has only one brave general, Chǔ.
If he leads his troops to defend the city, it cannot be captured quickly.
I deliberately used this strategic point to lure him."
Not long after,
Péi broke the stockade,
captured Chǔ,
and then besieged Hóngzhōu.
Táng Bǎo, the Cǐshǐ of Ráozhōu, surrendered.
21 In the eighth month,
on the day of Yǐyǒu,
Lǐ Màozhēn sent his son Kǎn as a hostage to Xīchuān;
Wáng Jiàn appointed Kǎn as the Zhī of Péngzhōu.
22 Zhū Quánzhōng considered Yōu and Cāng to be mutually supportive and a threat to Wèi.
Yōu refers to
Liú Rén'gōng;
Cāng refers to
Liú Shǒuwén;
father and son supported each other.
On the day of Jiǎchén,
he led his army and departed from Dàliáng.
23 The Zhèzhè forces besieged Qúzhōu.
These were Fāng Yǒngzhēn's troops.
Yáng Wò sent Zhōu Běn, Grand Marshal of the Left Flank of Horse and Foot Troops, to lead soldiers to meet Zhāng.
When Běn reached Qúzhōu,
the Zhè people lifted the siege,
arrayed their forces beneath the city,
Zhāng led his multitude and submitted to Běn,
and the Zhèzhè forces took Qúzhōu.
Huáinán had been contesting with the Zhè people over the three prefectures of Wù, Mù, and Qú.
By this point, all had returned to the Qián clan.
Chén,
read as zhèn.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
"The Zhè people are near us but do not move;
they belittle us.
Please attack them!"
Lǚ Shīzào, emboldened by the victory at Qīngshān,
was overbearing towards the Zhè people.
Jìn,
its pronunciation is jìn.
"I received orders to welcome Envoy Chén.
He is here now.
Why should we fight again?
They must be prepared for us."
Thereupon, he led his troops back.
Běn formed the rearguard.
The Zhè people pursued them.
Běn set up an ambush midway,
and greatly defeated them.
24 In the ninth month,
on the first day, Xīnhài,
Zhū Quánzhōng crossed the river from Báimǎ.
On Dīngmǎo,
he arrived at Cāngzhōu,
and encamped at Chánglú.
Dù Yòu said: Cāngzhōu had Chánglú County.
In the Hàn dynasty, it was Cānlú.
Hù
The Sòng dynasty abolished the county and made it Chánglú Township,
subordinate to Qīngchí County.
The Cāng people did not come out.
Luó Shàowēi provided supplies and transport.
From Wèi to Chánglú, a distance of five hundred lǐ,
the road was never without traffic.
He also built a Marshal's headquarters in Wèi.
Wherever they passed, courier stations provided wine, food, tents, and utensils.
The tens of thousands of people, high and low,
lacked nothing.
Luó Shàowēi generously served Zhū Quánzhōng,
not only to repay kindness,
but also fearing that he would take advantage of the opportunity to attack Guó and seize Yú.
25 Qín Péi captured Hóngzhōu,
and returned with Zhōng Kuāngshí and five thousand captives.
In the second year of Zhōnghé of Emperor Xīzōng,
Zhōng Chuán occupied Hóngzhōu,
and it fell with Kuāngshí.
Péi was appointed Commissioner for the Pacification of Hóngzhōu.
The Yáng clan of Huáinán thus gained possession of the territory of Jiāngxī.
26 Yáng Chóngběn, Jìngnàn Jìedùshǐ, attacked Xiàzhōu with troops from Fèngxiáng, Bǎosài, Zhāngyì, and Bǎoyì.
"Bǎoyì"
should be
"Bǎodà",
for the Bǎoyì Army governed Xíng, Míng, and Cí,
which were in Shāndōng;
while the Bǎodà Army governed Fū and Fáng,
and these garrisons, along with Bīn and Qí, were all in Guānxī.
Nàn,
pronounced nài.
Xià,
pronounced xià.
Over three thousand heads were taken,
and Liú Yànhuī, the Prefect of Fángzhōu, was captured.
Fángzhōu
was under the jurisdiction of the Bǎodà Army.
This confirms that the earlier text's
"Bǎoyì"
was clearly an error.
27 Liú Réngōng came to the rescue of Cāngzhōu,
but was repeatedly defeated in battle.
He then issued an order throughout his territory:
"All men aged fifteen and above,
and under seventy, shall prepare their own weapons and provisions and proceed to the field camp.
After the army has departed,
if even one person remains in a village,
they shall be executed without pardon!"
Someone advised,
"Now that all the old and weak are gone,
and women cannot transport supplies,
if this order is strictly enforced,
there will be many unjustly executed."
He then commanded that all those capable of bearing arms should go,
tattooing their faces with the characters
"Dìngbàdū".
Scholars were tattooed on their wrists or arms
with the characters
"Yīxīn Shìzhǔ".
Consequently, throughout the territory,
all scholars and commoners,
except for infants, were tattooed.
He obtained 100,000 soldiers
and encamped at Wǎqiáo.
At that time, the Biàn army built ramparts and besieged Cāngzhōu,
so that not even birds or rats could pass through.
Réngōng, fearing their strength,
dared not fight.
Food ran out in the city.
They ate dirt molded into balls,
or plundered and devoured each other.
Zhū Quánzhōng sent someone to persuade Liú Shǒuwén, saying:
"The relief forces are not capable of reaching you;
why not surrender early?"
Shǒuwén ascended the city wall and responded:
"To me, Yōuzhōu
is like a father and son.
King Liáng is conquering the world with great righteousness.
If a son betrays his father and comes to you,
how will you use him?"
Quánzhōng was ashamed by his straightforward words
and slowed his attack.
28 In winter,
the tenth month,
on Bǐngxū,
Wáng Jiàn first established a Traveling Chancellery in Shǔ.
The examination of discrepancies states: The Xù Bǎoyùn Lù says that this official notice was issued on the sixth day of the tenth month of the sixth year of Tiānfù.
This means it was in the tenth month of this year.
He wept aloud,
declaring:
"Since the Imperial Carriage moved eastward,
meaning Emperor Zhāozōng moved to Luò.
I request temporary establishment of a Traveling Chancellery,
following the precedents of Lǐ Shèng and Zhèng Tián,
to bestow official titles by imperial decree."
According to records, when Lǐ Shèng campaigned against Zhū Cǐ,
he was stationed at Dōngwèiqiáo.
He only requested to temporarily appoint his aides Zhào Guāngxiǎn, Táng Liángchén, and Zhāng Yù as prefects of the three prefectures of Yáng, Lì, and Jiàn,
to secure the vital routes to Shǔ and Hàn,
but the emperor did not have time to agree.
Later, he temporarily appointed Zhāng Yù as Junior Prefect of Jīngzhào to manage fodder and grain within the capital region,
and memorialized to grant important offices to Mèng Shè and Duàn Wēiyǒng, surrendered generals of Lǐ Huáiguāng.
He never bestowed titles by imperial decree.
Zhèng Tián's acting on his own authority is found in volume 254, first year of Guǎngmíng of Emperor Xīzōng.
29 Liú Réngōng sought aid from Hédōng,
with over a hundred envoys sent successively.
Lǐ Kèyòng resented Réngōng's perfidy.
Liú Réngōng rebelled against Lǐ Kèyòng with Yōuzhōu,
and also allied with Zhū Quánzhōng to attack him.
This was what Kèyòng deeply resented.
His son Cúnxù advised him, saying:
"The current situation in the world is that
seven or eight tenths of it have submitted to Zhū Wēn.
Even powerful states like Wèibó, Zhèn, and Dìng have attached themselves to him.
North of the river,
only I and Yōu and Cāng can cause trouble for Wēn.
Now Yōu and Cāng are hard-pressed by Wēn.
If I do not join forces with them to resist him,
it will not be to my advantage.
One who aspires to rule the world should not dwell on petty grievances.
Moreover, he once troubled me, and now I am saving him from his plight.
By winning him over with virtue,
one achieves both fame and substance in a single stroke.
This is the time for my resurgence;
it must not be missed."
History says that Lǐ Cúnxù's wisdom and insight could supplement what his father lacked.
He consulted with his generals and aides about summoning Yōuzhōu troops to attack Lùzhōu,
saying:
"For them, it can relieve the siege;
for me, it can expand my territory."
Thereupon, he promised peace to Réngōng
and summoned his troops.
Réngōng sent Lǐ Pǔ, Commissioner of Mobilization,
to lead 30,000 troops to Jìnyáng.
Kèyòng sent his generals Zhōu Déwēi and Lǐ Sìzhāo to lead troops and jointly attack Lùzhōu.
30 Xiàzhōu sent an urgent appeal to Zhū Quánzhōng.
On Wùxū,
Quánzhōng sent Liú Zhījùn and his general Kāng Huáiwīng to relieve it.
Yáng Chóngběn led 50,000 troops from six garrisons
and encamped at Měiyuán.
According to the preceding text,
Yáng Chóngběn led troops from only five garrisons.
It must be that the troops of Qín and Lǒng were combined to make six garrisons.
Chóngběn was greatly defeated
and returned to Bīnzhōu.
31 Léi Yánwēi, Wǔzhēn Jìedùshǐ,
repeatedly raided Jīngnán.
Acting Military Governor Hè Quán closed the city and defended himself.
In September of last year,
the Biàn general Hè Quán defended Jīngnán.
Gāo Jìchāng, Prefect of Yǐngzhōu, was appointed to replace him.
Gāo Jìchāng thereupon took possession of Jīngnán.
Ní Kěfú thereupon submitted to Gāo Jìchāng.
The Láng troops
were Léi Yánwēi's troops.
32 In the eleventh month,
Liú Zhījùn and Kāng Huáizhēn
(Judging from this,
the preceding text mistakenly wrote
"Huáiyīng." )
surrendered;
Liú Zhījùn was granted the title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and Kāng Huáizhēn was made Bǎoyì Jiédùshǐ.
(Perhaps Kāng Huáizhēn was immediately appointed to Fūzhì.
"Bǎoyì"
should be
"Bǎodà";
this is evidenced by the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn's entry for the following year, which mentions Bǎopíng Jiédùshǐ Kāng Huáizhēn,
or perhaps it was indeed Bǎoyì from that point on.)
The Western Army
refers to the Bīn and Qí armies.
33 Gāo Yàn, the Cìshǐ of Húzhōu, died,
and his son, Lǐ, succeeded him.
34 In the twelfth month,
on the Yǐyǒu day,
Qián Liú memorialized to recommend Xíngjūn Sīmǎ Wáng Jǐngrén;
an imperial edict appointed Wáng Jǐngrén as the acting Níngguó Jiédùshǐ.
(Wáng Jǐngrén is Wáng Màozhāng,
who abandoned Xuānzhōu and returned to Qián Liú in the first month of this year.
The Kǎoyì states: Xuē Jūzhèng's Wǔdài Shǐ says:
"Liú appointed him as a Xíngjūn Sīmǎ for both prefectures,
and fully reported the situation.
Tàizǔ then reappointed him as the acting Xuānzhōu Jiédùshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì."
Ōuyáng Xiū's Wǔdài Shǐ says:
"Liú memorialized for Jǐngrén to be the acting Xuānzhōu Jiédùshǐ."
We follow this account now.)
35 Zhū Quánzhōng divided tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry,
and dispatched Xíngjūn Sīmǎ Lǐ Zhōuyí to lead them
from Héyáng to relieve Lùzhōu.
36 In the intercalary month,
on the Yǐchǒu day,
Zhènguó Jūn Xīngdé Fǔ was abolished and restored to Huázhōu,
subordinate to the Kuāngguó Jiédù,
and Jīn and Shāng prefectures were ceded to Yòuguó Jūn.
(The unification of Tóng and Huá into one circuit
and the cession of Jīn and Shāng to Yòuguó
were all intended to bolster their resources to defend against Bīn and Qí.)
37 Initially,
when the grim news of Zhāozōng's death reached Lùzhōu,
Dīng Huì, the Zhāoyì Jiédùshǐ, led his officers and soldiers in mourning, weeping for a long time.
When Lǐ Sìzhāo attacked Lùzhōu,
Huì surrendered his entire army to Hédōng.
(The Kǎoyì states: Táng Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù says:
"On the Dīngyǒu day,
Dīng Huì opened the gates and surrendered.
In the intercalary twelfth month,
Tàizǔ made Lǐ Sìzhāo the commander of Lùzhōu."
Xuē Jūzhèng's Wǔdài Shǐ, the Liáng Jì, places it in the intercalary month,
while the Hòutáng Jì places it in the twelfth month.
We now follow the New and Old Táng Jì, Xuē Shǐ Liáng Jì, and the Biānyílù.)
When Huì met Kèyòng,
he cried and said:
"I, Huì, did not fail to hold out due to lack of strength.
The King of Liáng has brutalized the Táng court,
and though I have received his grace of promotion and elevation,
I truly cannot bear what he has done,
and so I have come to surrender my life."
(One who lacks a sense of right and wrong is not human.
Dīng Huì, then, possessed a sense of right and wrong!)
He was placed above all the generals.
On the Jǐsì day,
Zhū Quánzhōng ordered his armies to prepare siege equipment,
intending to attack Cāngzhōu.
On the Rénshēn day,
he heard that Lùzhōu had fallen;
on the Jiǎxū day,
he withdrew his troops.
Before this,
fodder and grain from north and south of the Hé [River] had been requisitioned,
transported by water and land to the front lines,
piling up in the various camps.
When Quánzhōng was about to return,
he ordered all of it to be burned,
the smoke and flames extending for several lǐ,
and that which was in boats was to be scuttled and sunk.
Liú Shǒuwén sent a letter to Quánzhōng, saying:
"Your Highness, for the sake of the people,
pardoned my transgressions,
lifted the siege, and departed—
this is Your Highness's benevolence.
The tens of thousands of mouths in the city
have not eaten for several months.
Rather than burning it into smoke
or sinking it into mud,
I humbly beg for the remainder to save them."
Quánzhōng therefore left several granaries for him.
(Liú Shǒuwén's words were humble and his situation pitiable,
so even Quánzhōng's cruelty was moved by it.)
Yí (遺)
is pronounced as Jì Fān.
Qǐ (乞)
has the sound of qì.
Wèi (為)
is pronounced as Yú Wěi Fān.
The Hédōng army advanced to attack Zézhōu,
but failed and retreated.
38 Péng Gān, the Cìshǐ of Jízhōu, sent an envoy to request surrender to Húnán.
(With Zhōng Shì already destroyed,
Péng Gān therefore requested surrender to the Mǎ Shì.)
Gān (玕)
has the sound of gān.
Lù Zhèn's Jiǔguó Zhì writes
Zhōng Chuán appointed him as Cìshǐ of Jízhōu.
Punctuation by Dèng Guǎngmíng, re-collated by Niè Chóngqí
